# Volume Front Matter

## Series Title Page

The Complete Course of the Fathers, or Universal Library—complete, uniform, convenient, economical—of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the very extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which everything that each Father has written on any topic may be surveyed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately possible for the reader to discover which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture. The most accurate edition, and readily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent similarity throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In this series appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. The Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition costs 1,200 francs; the Greek-Latin edition, 1,300 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# The Complete Works of John Scotus

## [Column I]

# Prologue

## I. Purpose of the Edition

### § 1

If you ask, kindly reader, what principal reason urged me to collect and polish the theological books of John Scotus, I shall briefly explain to you the rationale of my undertaking. For approximately thirteen years ago, when I happened upon John’s books, being almost wholly inexperienced and unskilled in theological and philosophical literature, I confess that I was considerably impressed by the impressive and almost singular subtlety of argument displayed by this ninth-century writer. Yet I was also offended by the rashness of certain men among us who exalt and proclaim his philosophical and theological theories, since everyone knows that his principal work, entitled *On the Division of Nature*, was condemned to the flames by Pope Honorius III and, nearly two hundred years ago, when it was printed in England, was entered in the Index of Forbidden Books.

Even then I had resolved to investigate more carefully both what John Scotus had accomplished through his writings and in what places he had gone astray, and at some time to weigh both sides fairly and set the result forth for the honor and benefit of the holy Church. Not long afterward, during a scholarly journey that I undertook through Germany, Switzerland, Italy, and Belgium, I was given the opportunity, among the other critical studies to which I was devoting myself, to investigate which of John Scotus’s books survived hidden in libraries and to bring to light whatever I discovered, in order to form a fuller judgment of him.

Although I examined very many libraries for this purpose, I nevertheless succeeded in finding not very many manuscript copies of his books. From these manuscripts I transcribed fragments of no little importance, which we now publish for the first time. Finally, with greater benefit, I recently visited the Royal Library of Paris. When I found there several manuscripts of John Scotus’s books, I thought that these too ought to be put to use. Accordingly, I carefully examined the books *On Predestination* and *On the Division of Nature* against their testimony. I also examined, not without benefit, the Laon manuscript that had generously been sent to me in Paris.

As for the fact that we have included in this *Patrology* a complete edition of Scotus’s surviving works, without omitting the book of doubtful authenticity on principles, which he entitled *On the Division of Nature*, I do not think anyone will readily find it surprising who has considered that learned men rightly judge John Scotus, with his exceedingly sharp and profound arguments—arguments for which he also rather often drew material from Plato and Aristotle—to be, in a certain broader sense, a precursor of what is called Scholastic Theology, and, through his translation of the works of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, his expositions of those works, and his other frequently allegorical theories, a precursor, as it were, of what is called mystical theology.

The theologians of the Middle Ages made especially extensive use of John Scotus’s translation of the works circulated under the name of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite. Since they themselves did not know Greek, they read in John Scotus’s Latin translation the books whose author they all revered as Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, an apostolic Father, and they illustrated that translation with their own commentaries.

[Column II]

Therefore, since John Scotus is altogether the sort of writer whose works ought scarcely to be absent from a complete course of ecclesiastical writers, we judged that preparing a complete edition of his works was both appropriate and not wholly foreign to the purpose of this collection. If anything occurs in these works that may reasonably offend you, we have not failed, in the *Notices to the Reader* prefixed to the edition, to point out the principal errors wherever necessary, nor have we failed here and there to correct in accompanying notes what is argued falsely or less accurately. Moreover, in the treatise *On the Life and Teachings of John Scotus* prefixed to this edition of his works, his errors are sharply criticized.

If anyone should nevertheless think that we have neglected something in pointing out John Scotus’s errors, both the difficulty of the matter and the limitations of the time that could be granted to us for preparing the edition will excuse us.

### § 2

So much, then, concerning the purpose of this edition. Two matters remain for us: first, to enumerate the manuscripts we used; and second, to explain what we have been able to ascertain about John Scotus’s life. In doing so, however, I did not hesitate to make use of the treatise on the life and teachings of John Scotus published several years ago by an anonymous author, which we have decided to place before the works. Since it is well composed in its more important chapters, it will remain only to clarify certain points on which we must disagree with its author.

# II. Manuscripts

### § 3

First, with regard to the manuscripts, in editing the previously unpublished and almost unknown *Expositions on the Celestial Hierarchy of Saint Dionysius*, we used three. One of them, Vatican manuscript 652, elegantly written at the beginning of the eleventh century, consists of fifty-eight leaves of smaller folio format. It contains only those expositions of John Scotus.

On the first leaf, a hand apparently of the fourteenth century added: “This little book is from …”; the word following *from* can scarcely be read, and everything else has been completely obliterated. Likewise, apparently a hand from the end of the thirteenth century wrote in the lower part of the leaf: “we are [sic!] of all theologians this,” words which, although someone tried to wash them out, can still be clearly distinguished.

Four or five glosses of three or four words are found in the margin. Since I could scarcely make them out, I disregarded them. The person who copied the book scarcely ever grasped its meaning; consequently, the punctuation is utterly false. Indeed, two words are quite often contracted into one, while others are divided. Errors are more frequent at the ends of lines. The Greek words that occur are badly written.

Since Carolus Greith, now provost and official of the church of Saint Gall in Switzerland, had transcribed the expositions from this manuscript, he generously gave me access to his copy, which I later also carefully collated at Rome anew against the manuscript.

### § 4

The second is manuscript Latin 380 of the Royal Bavarian Library at Munich, formerly the Electoral Library of the most serene dukes of both Bavaria, as is shown by their insignia affixed to the inside of the cover. It is a parchment manuscript of the thirteenth century, quarto, written in fairly neat minuscule letters with ordinary abbreviations. It is mutilated at the beginning and now consists of ninety-six leaves.

The titles and chapter numbers are illuminated. The initials, executed in red with blue pigment, are elegantly worked, and are often furnished with strokes extending almost to the end of the leaf. Here and there, by various hands, the writing has been altered in the actual line of the text by scraping or correcting, and quite a few additions have been written above or in the margin.

It contains the following:

### 1. Folio 1, column 1, to folio 4, column 2

A fragment of the translation of the *Celestial Hierarchy*. It begins:

“of superabundant [Column III] light, of pre-perfect perfection; for nothing is perfect, or universally without need of perfection, except what is truly perfect and pre-perfect in itself.”

Chapter XI begins:

“Now that these matters have been determined, it is worthy of attention for what reason we have been accustomed to call all the angelic substances together celestial powers,” and so forth.

It ends with the words:

“But we have passed over those possessing the same power as the aforesaid, and, taking account of the proportion of the discourse, we venerate in silence what is hidden above us.”

“Here ends the book of blessed Dionysius, bishop of Athens, one of the Areopagites, on the Celestial Hierarchy.”

### 2. Folio 5, column 1, to folio 19, column 1

The ecclesiastical hierarchy translation of John Saracen. It begins with an illuminated title:

“Here begins the book on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.”

Chapter I: “The prologue of John Saracen to Master John of Saraberiis concerning the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.”

It begins:

“After the translation of the angelic hierarchy, I postponed the translation of the ecclesiastical hierarchy,” and so forth.

The prologue is followed by the translation, which ends as follows:

“Therefore, my friend, grant me yourself the more perfect illumination, and show my eyes the more fitting and more uniform beauties that you are able to see; for I am confident that I shall kindle in you the sparks of the divine fire that I mentioned above.”

“Here ends the book of Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Athens, addressed to Timothy, bishop of Ephesus, on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.”

### 3. Folio 19, column 2, to folio 24, column 1

A treatise by an anonymous author, written in much smaller letters and with many abbreviations. It begins with an illuminated title:

“Here begins a certain good treatise, which is not among the books of Dionysius.”

It continues to the seventh leaf, at the words “be mindful,” and so forth. [A later hand wrote *hospitii*—“of hospitality”—in black ink above the word *memor*.]

It begins with the words:

“Every cognition is either initial or derived from some pre-existing cognition. Every initial cognition, however, is either particular or universal. If it is particular, it will be sense, experience, or memory; if universal, it will be understanding,” and so forth.

It ends as follows:

“For there are angels who have received this as their office: that miracles should be performed through their ministry and powers be manifested among human beings through their mediation. These constitute the order called the Powers. They are said to be present at the altar when the bread is changed into the body of Christ. Those will belong to their company to whom it has been given spiritually, as a spiritual gift, to perform miracles.

“Opposed to this order is that fellowship of demons through whose ministry illusions are produced to deceive human beings. Those who devote themselves to magical tricks and divinations will belong to their company or assembly. The first article of the description properly indicates the aforesaid in saying ‘not encountering laws.’ The angels just mentioned do not encounter laws, since they exist for the sake of the law, nor do they perform many miracles.

“There are also other angels who have received this as their office.”

In the margin is written: “Something is missing.”

The remainder of folio 24, column 1, is covered with matters of no importance, written very badly by a later hand in pale ink. Folio 24, column 2, contains sayings of Augustine, written better by another later hand in fairly black ink.

### 4. Folio 25, column 1, to folio 42, column 1

John Saracen’s book *On the Divine Names*. It begins with an illuminated title:

“Here begins the first book on the Divine Names.”

Chapter I: “The prologue of John Saracen to Odo, reverend abbot of Saint Dionysius, on the books of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite on the Divine Names.”

It begins:

“Remembering your hospitality and my promise, I waited a long time for a letter from your eminence. Since you could not send one for many reasons, I fulfilled my promise,” and so forth.

It ends with the words:

“and we have handed down and shall hand down, insofar as we are capable of speaking and those to whom it is said to hear are capable of hearing, doing no injury to the tradition—unless perhaps we are weak in understanding or explaining these matters. [Column IV] Let them nevertheless be held and spoken in the manner pleasing to God; and thus, according to us, this is the end of the divine names that can be understood. With God as our guide, we shall pass on to symbolic theology.”

In the margin, illuminated words have been added:

“Here ends Dionysius the Areopagite’s book on the Divine Names.”

### 5. Folio 42, column 1, to folio 43, column 2

His book *On Mystical Theology*. It begins with an illuminated title written in the margin:

“Here begins the prologue of the same John Saracen to the same Odo, abbot of Saint Dionysius, on the book of Mystical Theology.”

It begins:

“Before mystical theology, symbolic theology should be translated. For,” and so forth.

It ends with the words:

“Since the perfect and united cause of all things is also above every affirmation, and its excess is above every negation, simply removed from all things and beyond the whole.”

“Here ends the book of the great Areopagite, Dionysius, on Mystical Theology.”

### 6. Folio 43, column 2, to folio 48, column 2

A translation of the letters. It begins with a title written in the margin:

“Here begin the letters.”

“The first letter, to the monk Gaius,” beginning:

“Darkness is concealed by light, and still more by much light; ignorance is concealed by cognitions, and still more by many cognitions. This is said excessively, but not according to privation,” and so forth.

The final letter ends with the words:

“But I am entirely worthy of belief concerning what was previously known to you, learning from God and saying that you will be released from the prison that is on Patmos, return to the land of Asia, make imitations there, and hand them on to those who will come after you.”

“Here it ends.”

### 7. Folio 49, column 1, to folio 95, column 2

The expositions of John Scotus. They begin with an illuminated title:

“Here begin the expositions of John Scotus on the hierarchies of Saint Dionysius.”

They begin with the words:

“The first book of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite,” and end with:

“and only in the mind.”

These expositions are written somewhat more neatly than the other parts of the manuscript. The titles are illuminated, and the words of the translation in the first chapter are marked by an illuminated line; in the other chapters they are marked by a line drawn in black ink. The same applies to the individual words of the translation whenever they are repeated.

The Greek words that occur are written with the greatest corruption. A different hand, apparently of the fourteenth century, which I have marked B*, often altered the text by scraping or correcting it in the actual line, or by writing above it; quite a few marginal additions were also made. A third hand, approximately contemporary with the first, which we have marked B**, occasionally wrote certain words in the margin in somewhat paler ink. A later hand rarely wrote in the margin; we have marked it “later hand.” If the first hand itself appeared to have made the correction, we have indicated this as “corrected by B.”

It should further be noted that on folios 71, column 2; 72, column 2; 73, column 2; 74, column 2; 75, column 2; 77, column 2; 78, column 2; 83, column 2; 84, column 2; 85, column 2; 87, column 2; 89, column 2; 90, column 2; 91, column 2; and 95, column 2, some matters of no importance have been written at the extreme top of the parchment.

Moreover, on certain leaves a later hand of the fifteenth or sixteenth century wrote many things in the margin with a white stylus. These have, however, been so obliterated that they can no longer be read.

The remaining portion of folio 95, column 2, and folio 96 is covered with matters extremely difficult to read and of no importance.

It remains to mention that, in the fragment of the translation found on folios 1, column 1, to 4, column 2, fragments of John Scotus’s expositions on the Celestial Hierarchy have been written in the margin, in very small letters, by either the same hand or another approximately contemporary hand.

Although most of these are found below in the expositions that we have published, we nevertheless thought that they should be presented here individually, in order, with the chapters to which they belong noted, and in the sequence in which they occur in the manuscript. I have added the numbers of the columns in which they occur below.

## Chapter XI

**Scotus.** How the understanding is joined to essence, reason to power, and the inner sense to operation, and how the two trinities of human beings and angels are nevertheless one, is sufficiently explained in the book *On Nature* [*peri phiseon*]. See below, column 230.

## Chapter XIII

*Apology*, which means defense or satisfaction. Below, column 235.

Understand this of snow and ice, which are dissolved before warmth appears in them, or of substances [Column V] that cannot be heated in any way, namely, substances that are extremely cold. Therefore all cold things are called, as it were, dead, while hot things are called living, because through warmth all matter is formed and reformed corporeally. Below, column 237.

Fire performs two things: warmth and illumination. Its power of warming goes everywhere, but its illuminating power is checked in dense matter; for its illumination does not extend to everything. He calls the operation in fire that produces warmth “primitive.” Below, column 238.

This is to be understood as meaning that, for God himself and for intellectual and rational creatures, to be, to shine, and to see are the same thing. Their being is their light and vision. Below, column 240.

Because of false gods, such as the gods of the nations, or saints who are gods by grace, not by nature. Below, column 240.

The meaning is this: the cause of all things establishes that whatever essence is placed above another essence should convey, through itself, the divine lights that follow it, or carry them inward, or bear them above. The word *ἐποχετεύεσθαι* [“to be conveyed or channeled”] can be transferred to all these meanings. Below, column 240.

**Scotus.** This is beautifully said, because every celestial essence becomes and is called a participation of its properties, or because they subsist insofar as they participate. Below, column 242.

This is mystically signified by the pivots of the temple, or by the unchangeable foundation in the secret singularity. Below, column 244.

**Scotus.** The face of the one seated upon the throne—that is, the superessential height of God—is veiled by wings, because the angels look upon it reverently and tremblingly. The feet of the one seated are his deepest traces throughout the universal creation. The celestial essences cover them with two wings, fearing to investigate how the Lord, although he is above all things, is diffused through all things; how he is superessential and the essence of all things; and how he is everywhere, without whom nothing can exist.

They continually fly with two wings because of the eternal imitation of the divine operation. Behold, in the six wings, the perfection of intelligible movements is explained. But the fact that there are two wings signifies either the love, contemplation, and action of the maker and of the things made, or the twofold division of divine knowledge into affirmation and negation. One clothes him by affirming of him everything that exists; the other strips him by removing these things; and both are true. Below, columns 245–246.

“Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts.” In this threefold hymn, one essence in three persons or substances is praised. Below, column 246.

This brightness is understood as none other than the eternal Word, which perfects all the saints in their intellects, in the innermost recesses of the Father and in their primordial causes, before the ray issuing from the inaccessible light of divinity comes forth to those nearest to it. Below, column 246.

Three orders; hence he calls him a leader, because what one does is understood to be done by all. Below, column 248.

## Chapter XIV

They are defined thus: the understanding and knowledge of the Celestial Hierarchy are implanted in them; for their substance and number are intelligence and substance. Below, column 257.

## Chapter XV

A later hand added several interpretations to this chapter in letters extremely difficult to read, including some by John Saracen and the following by Scotus:

**John Scotus.** “Separate” [*discretus*]: for it is thickened by no other element, but remains separate in its purity. Below, column 256.

“Rebounding” [*resiliens*]: struck by every body, whether by clouds, rocks, or iron; for every collision creates fire.

[Note: [Column V] A later hand added “separate” and what follows up to the word “creates.”]

Below, column 256.

As if to say: images signify that the same dispositions exist in the first, middle, and last things. Below, column 258.

An eagle sees more sharply than a human being; a dog smells more powerfully. Below, column 258.

“And according to rational understanding, by continuity.” For the power of rational knowledge is continuous; it will cease to subsist before it can lack rational knowledge even for a moment. Below, column 259.

Just as the sense of smell distinguishes contrary exhalations from those that are congenial. Below, column 259.

“Productive” refers to the hands, “operative” to the arms, and “active” to the shoulders, in which, as in a kind of hinge of action, movement first revolves and then extends through the arms into the hands.

In the rational soul, in the mind, its first movement is like certain shoulders of its own. Then, descending through the progression of numbers, as if through certain arms, it receives the name “operation” in the craftsman’s estimation; while it is extended into the effect of the moved body, it is not improperly called productive.

Thus, as I believe, in the celestial minds, while by a first movement, as it were, they contemplate above themselves the primordial causes in the Beginning of all things, which is God, their movement is action; while they conform in themselves what they see above themselves, it is operation; but when they make and bring about what must be made in nature according to the analogy of what they contemplate above themselves and conform in themselves, their movement may properly be called productive or effective. Below, column 261.

Similarly, in the translation of the letters of Pseudo-Dionysius found on folios 43, column 2, to 48, column 2, the same hand added a considerable number of glosses in the margin, in the same tiny letters. After carefully examining them, I found that they were taken from the scholia of Saint Maximus.

### § 5

Third, in editing John Scotus’s *Expositions on the Celestial Hierarchy of Saint Dionysius*, I used manuscript no. 1 of the Bruges Library, a parchment manuscript in large folio format, from the fifteenth century (the printed source repeats “XV,” so the second date is uncertain). It contains John Scotus’s translation of the works of Pseudo-Dionysius, arranged in such a way that, for each chapter, the expositions of Saint Maximus, Hugh of Saint Victor, John Saracen, and others are appended, including the expositions of our John Scotus on the Celestial Hierarchy.

John Scotus’s expositions are not complete, however. They end on folio 171, column 2, with these words:

“For example, the first Hierarchy grants divine illuminations to the second, the second to the third, and the third to the fourth, which exists among human beings” (see below, column 239), so that the ending is lacking.

Collections of this kind of expositions on the books of Pseudo-Dionysius, [Column VI] translated into Latin by John Scotus, frequently occur from the fourteenth century onward. I examined two very similar copies at Rome, in Vatican manuscripts 177, parchment, folio, fourteenth century, 208 leaves, and 176, parchment, folio, fourteenth century, 295 leaves. In these manuscripts also, those expositions of John Scotus that we now publish for the first time are found scattered among the expositions of other writers and appended to the individual chapters of the translation.

Since, because of lack of time, I was unable to examine these Vatican manuscripts thoroughly, I often corrected passages of the expositions that had been corrupted or altered according to the testimony of the Bruges manuscript. But so that you may understand the arrangement of these collections, I wish to transcribe on this occasion the compiler’s preface, recovered from the Bruges and Vatican manuscripts.

## A Brief and Very Necessary Explanation of the Arrangement of the Whole Work That Follows, and of Its Usefulness to Readers

Your timely and untimely, pious, and provident insistence, beloved, compels me to apply whatever diligence I can to a new and unusual work full of vigils and care; and you place upon the shoulders of your friend, especially weak shoulders, an unbearable burden.

But because love makes every difficulty light and almost nothing, with Christ as guide and forerunner I shall willingly undertake what you urge, although I do not fail to recognize that in this work I shall not escape the tongues of detractors who gnaw at others.

I am not greatly moved, however, by the utterly empty barking of the envious against the truth, knowing most certainly that this work, if by the Lord’s gift it is brought to completion, will be of no small benefit—not only to you but also to all who inspect it carefully and faithfully—in many matters, especially for an easier knowledge of visible and transitory things, of those things that are false and deceptive and never stable anywhere, for contempt of happiness, and for a more certain understanding of spiritual things and a sober desire for that true, stable, and eternal blessedness.

Your discernment knows that, just as no evil can be avoided unless it is known, so no good can be desired if it is unknown. Augustine says: “In no way is what is completely unknown loved.”

Once knowledge of these things has been acquired, with grace assisting, what is commanded in the psalm is easily fulfilled: “Turn away from evil and do good.” You know that these two commands comprise the two parts of justice.

I therefore desire to arrange the first part—the angelic Hierarchy of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite—with its expositions in the following manner. After the chapters prescribed in sequence, which the commentators preface at the beginnings of their treatises for the clarification of the entire work, have been set out, and after the explanation of the text has been reached, I shall insert, adding absolutely nothing of my own and omitting nothing from the commentators’ expositions, first the chapter containing the text of the Hierarchy. Immediately afterward I shall place beneath it the gloss corresponding to that chapter, translated from Greek into Latin.

Then the exposition of the prescribed chapter according to the great Hugh of Saint Victor will be added; next, that of John Scotus; and finally, the explanation of the same chapter by John Saracen.

The order of this arrangement will therefore be such that, after the prescribed chapter of the text, the expositions of the venerable Doctors will follow, each headed by the name of its expositor. By this abbreviation, the understanding of the heavenly mysteries contained in the text of the Hierarchy will be made readily accessible to the reader, insofar as human weakness permits, and the burdensome necessity of turning through many books will be removed.

It should be noted, however, that the glosses translated from Greek into Latin by Anastasius, librarian of the apostolic see, were published partly by blessed Maximus the Confessor and partly by Saint John, bishop of Scythopolis. Nevertheless, I have decided to place them all under the name of Maximus in this work, lest the reader’s intention be in any way confused because of the identity of the names—namely, John of Scythopolis, John Scotus, and John Saracen.

Nor can our heading thereby rightly be accused of falsehood. For since one and the same spirit speaks in all heralds of the truth, as the Lord says, “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you,” it is certain that, because of the fellowship of the same Spirit, in the kingdom of Catholic truth each thing belongs to all and all things belong to each.

Therefore, because of the same Spirit speaking in them, John does not begrudge judging as his own what Maximus said, nor does Maximus consider alien to himself what John said.

It must also be carefully considered that wherever a double text occurs, the interlinear text belongs especially to the explanation of John Scotus and John Saracen, as will become abundantly clear in the sequence of the book.

For the labor of this present work I desire no other recompense than this: that through the prayers and merits of this supreme theologian, second only to the blessed Apostles, and of the blessed men concerning whom he deserved to know and write so much, I may obtain assistance in the present life and fellowship with the angels in the future.

Therefore, I pray, let there be present to me, obtained through your prayers, the illuminating glory of my dark mind—that is, of me—so that, going before, cooperating with, and following upon it, this work, so sweet, so useful, and so delightful, suitable to the minds of those devoted to sacred theology, may receive an auspicious beginning, an ordered progress, and an appropriate and fitting conclusion. Amen.

Such, then, concerning the manuscripts from which we have now published for the first time John Scotus’s *Expositions on the Celestial Hierarchy*.

### § 6

I recovered the prologue of John Scotus’s *Expositions on the Books of Pseudo-Dionysius on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* from three manuscripts: Leipzig University Library manuscript 188, parchment, folio, thirteenth century; Vatican manuscript 177, parchment, folio, fourteenth century; and manuscript Sorbonn. 1355 of the Royal Library of Paris, parchment, quarto, thirteenth century.

The Leipzig manuscript, which contains John Scotus’s complete translation of the works of Pseudo-Dionysius, presents [Column VII] this prologue prefixed to the book on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy. In the Vatican manuscript, which contains added expositions by various authors, including John Scotus, on the book of the Celestial Hierarchy, the same prologue has been prefixed to the book on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, though mutilated at the beginning. The Paris manuscript likewise has the prologue prefixed to the same book of Pseudo-Dionysius.

Accordingly, on the testimony of these three manuscripts, this prologue now appears for the first time.

It remains to mention that in the Darmstadt manuscript, formerly Cologne manuscript 30, parchment, twelfth century, and also in the Munich manuscript of Othlo, from the eleventh century—both of which will be described below in § 13—the words of the prologue beginning “The doctrine of the preceding chapters” and continuing to “having explained again the mystery of the synaxis,” followed by “Its theory” (see below, columns 268 and 1071), are displayed at the beginning of the book on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.

### § 7

I have found nowhere any trace of John Scotus’s expositions on the book *On the Divine Names*. I did, however, discover his expositions or glosses on Pseudo-Dionysius’s *Mystical Theology* in the Vienna manuscript of ecclesiastical history, no. CXXXVI, parchment, fourteenth century, quarto, fifty-one leaves.

The expositions occupy folios 33–39 and are so badly written that I had to spend a great deal of time and labor transcribing and preparing them. Nevertheless, my work was not wasted, since I succeeded in restoring the text almost everywhere.

The manuscript contains the following:

Folios 1–4: Indulgences and relics of the churches of the city of Rome; folios 4–19: a treatise of the master Samuel the Israelite, by which the coming is proved; folios 20–22: letters of Pope Clement VI sent to the Romans concerning the Jubilee year; folios 22–24: a letter sent by Lucifer to the Pope and the ecclesiastical princes; folios 24–26: a petition addressed to Clement VI on behalf of Lord Emperor Ludwig, dated 18 September 1343; folios 26–27: a copy of a letter of the King of England sent to the Supreme Pontiff, dated September of the fourth year of the French reign and the seventeenth of the English reign (it is extant in Raynaldus); folios 27–29: a copy of the summons of a Tribune elected by the Roman people, who summoned Lord Ludwig, who calls himself emperor, and Lord Charles, King of Bohemia, and all the princes and archbishop-electors of the Roman king; folios 29–33: the Sibyl’s Prologue; folios 33–39: the expositions of John Scotus, edited by us; folios 39–51: a book containing many horrifying events in the near future: “Come with me in tribulation against and opposed to the approaching Antichrist,” etc.

Moreover, inserted on folios 28–29 is a not inconsiderable Examination of the Manichaeans of the Middle Ages, which, taking this opportunity, we communicate here for the benefit of readers. It is as follows:

### In the examination of someone

First, he is to be ordered to swear that, without any deceit, deception, or ambiguity of meaning, and according to his understanding and hearing, he will answer everything that is asked. After the oath has been taken, if he is literate, he is to be questioned about the Athanasian Creed, “Whoever wishes,” verse by verse and article by article.

[Note: [Col. VII] The Codex reads “of Anastasius.”]

Afterward, whether he is literate or not, he is to be questioned about the following articles, with repeated and explicit reminders concerning the manner and faithfulness of his oath:

Do you believe in God the almighty Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit, and that in this Trinity there is one God, the one Creator of heaven and earth, of bodies and souls, of visible and invisible things, and of all creatures?

Do you believe that human souls are not those demons and evil spirits that fell from heaven?

Do you believe that no demon will ever be saved, nor any of those human beings who die in the sins that we Catholics call mortal?

Do you believe that those souls whom Christ redeemed he took with himself from the underworld into heaven; and that the souls of the Apostles and of the other saints reign with Christ in heaven; and that they can procure patronage for us who live on earth?

Do you believe that the prayers and alms that we make for the faithful departed benefit them?

[Note: [Col. VII] The Codex reads *quae* (“which”) instead of *quas* (“which,” feminine accusative plural).]

Do you believe that the dead will rise?

And that the Law of Moses was given by God and not by the devil?

Do you believe that the person who baptizes truly makes little children Christians; that baptism administered to little children in water is not to be repeated or altered in some other manner as though that were better; and that a child below the age of reason can be baptized fully and perfectly, in the faith of the parents and of the Church?

Do you believe that sin is forgiven through repentance?

Do you believe that sin is not forgiven without contrition of heart, confession of the mouth, and satisfaction in deed?

[Note: [Col. VII] The Codex omits non, “not”; I have supplied it by conjecture.]

Do you believe that bread can be changed into the true body of Christ?

[Col. VIII] Do you believe that confession is not sufficient to God alone, nor to a layman, but only to a priest?

Do you believe that those who remain joined together without separation can be saved?

Do you believe that confirmation is +++ more than elsewhere, and that those who have not vowed abstinence can eat meat without sin?

[The wording is materially uncertain; the scope of the critical marks is preserved as printed.]

Do you wish to be obedient to the Pope and to our other prelates denounced to you by us?

Do you also believe that no one can be saved without the Catholic faith?

Do you believe that indulgences reasonably granted by prelates can be beneficial?

Do you believe that the mortal sin of a priest who has not yet been cut off (?) cannot impede any sacrament celebrated by him?

Do you believe that certain lies are not mortal sins, and that an oath is not sinful in three cases?

Do you believe that secular judges do not sin when they justly condemn people to death?

Do you believe that every human being, even a preacher, must work with his hands?

Do you believe that a person can be damned through free choice and saved with cooperating grace, so that no necessity of salvation or damnation is innate in him?

Do you believe that after the day of judgment there will be no consolation for the damned?

Do you believe that a person can be saved while possessing property?

Do you believe that second or third marriages are not condemnable?

Do you believe that the Old Testament has been fulfilled through the New, and that both are good?

Do you believe that it is spiritually beneficial, and beneficial even for a little child, to attend the divine offices—especially the solemn celebrations of Mass—and to offer offerings there, for eternal reward?

Do you believe that fasts, pilgrimages to the thresholds of the saints, and nocturnal vigils undertaken at the prompting of prayers are of great value for the remission of sins and for the recompense of eternal life?

Do you believe that there are purgatorial punishments?

Do you believe that the Son of God is coequal with the Father; that he was truly incarnate in humanity at Bethlehem from Mary, ever-virgin; that he, the Son of God, God and man, was circumcised, baptized by John, tempted by the devil, truly suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried; that he descended into the underworld; that on the third day he rose from the dead; that he appeared to his disciples; and that, while they watched, he ascended into heaven and departed, the Holy Spirit having been sent from heaven to them; that the Apostles preached this Catholic faith throughout the whole world, approved it by arguments and authorities, and by the signs that followed; and that this very Catholic faith, which they had thus preached, was first preached and confirmed by blessed Peter at Antioch and afterward at Rome, and that his successors in the apostolate have held it down to the present and confess it today? Do you yourself also confess and firmly hold this, as though you were about to depart from it?

After this, he takes a second oath that he wishes to obey the Pope and the prelates named to him.

A third oath is that he will never knowingly have familiarity with those who say or believe the contrary; that he will never fail to betray and accuse them wherever they may be or wherever he may find them; that he will name them explicitly; and that he will never listen to them preach that all heretics are to be converted this year.

### § 8

I now come to the homiletic and exegetical books of John Scotus. Of these, only his homily on the prologue of the Holy Gospel according to John survives. It was first published from the codex of the Alençon library by M. Félix Ravaisson in the book entitled *Reports on the Libraries of the Departments of the West*. Paris, 1841, octavo, pp. 334 ff. It was published again in the book entitled *Scotus Erigena and Scholastic Philosophy*, by M. Saint-René Taillandier. Strasbourg and Paris, 1843, octavo, pp. 299 ff. We have reproduced the text of the first editor, emending it here and there. But the editor did not say what sort of codex it was.

### § 9

As for the exegetical books of John Scotus on Sacred Scripture, only fragments of a commentary on the Holy Gospel according to John survive. M. Félix Ravaisson first published them from manuscript codex Laudunensis 81 in the book entitled *General Catalogue of the Manuscripts of the Public Libraries of the Departments, Published under the Auspices of the Minister of Public Instruction*. Volume One. Paris, National Printing Office, 1849, quarto, pp. 503 ff. There, on p. 47, he says of these fragments:

> “The manuscripts of the library of Laon offer a fairly large number of unpublished monuments, or at least monuments that I believe to be such. In the Appendix at the end of the volume, several pieces will be found brought together which seemed to me, for various reasons, worthy of publication. The first is a considerable fragment of a commentary on the Gospel of Saint John, which I believe I may attribute to the celebrated founder of medieval philosophy and mystical theology, John Scotus Erigena. This piece bears neither a title nor the author’s name in the manuscript; but it seems impossible to me not to recognize John Scotus’s work in it.

> “First, the handwriting of the manuscript belongs to the ninth century, the period in which this person lived; then the work itself is conceived and executed throughout in his manner, which is very easy to recognize. The doctrine is precisely that whose development is presented in the great dialogue *On the Division of Nature*, and which is borrowed almost entirely from the writings of the so-called Saint Dionysius the Areopagite and his commentator Saint Maximus. The authors cited by preference in our Commentary are Saint Dionysius, Saint Maximus, and Saint Gregory of Nazianzus—that is, the favorite authors of John Scotus, and those whom he was almost the first to make known in the West.

> “Here one displays that knowledge of the Greek language which was one of the principal grounds for the admiration of his contemporaries toward the learned Irishman, and which he parades in all his works. Like him, the writer affects the use of Latinized Greek words; finally, the diction has that wholly distinctive poetic turn which characterizes the writings of Scotus Erigena. It is exactly the style of his Homily on the Gospel of Saint John, which I have published elsewhere and which, moreover, is entirely distinct from the present commentary.

> “Unfortunately, we have here only a fragment of this work, comprising the commentary on most of the first five chapters of Saint John and the beginning of the sixth. It is greatly to be regretted that we do not at least possess the commentary on the rest of this last chapter. There one would doubtless have found a complete exposition of Scotus Erigena’s doctrine concerning the Eucharist—a doctrine of which, until now, judgment has generally been formed only from that of Berengar of Tours, who professed to follow it but who, it seems, departed from it quite substantially.

> “The following two passages from the fragment we publish provide some new illumination concerning the theory proper to our author:

> “ ‘Spiritually we sacrifice him [the Savior], and intellectually we eat him with the mind, not with the tooth. The spiritual man . . . denies that Christ is flesh, since he understands that it has already been changed into spirit . . . His [Christ’s] flesh has been exalted and changed into a rational soul.’

> “From the first of these two passages it seems to follow that John Scotus denied the real presence of the body of Jesus Christ, whereas Berengar claimed to admit it and to reject only transubstantiation. In the second, one perceives the reason on which he based his opinion: namely, that the flesh of Jesus Christ had been changed into spirit and that, consequently, Jesus Christ no longer had a body and was pure spirit. Indeed, in *On the Division of Nature*, although Scotus Erigena acknowledges a body for Jesus Christ, he maintains that this body is wholly spirit, free from all conditions either of time or of space; and he adds that all bodies will be such in the glorified state of the future life. He had borrowed this theory of spiritual bodies from the Fathers of the Greek Church, such as Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, and from Saint Ambrose, who generally agrees with them.”

What John Scotus’s doctrine concerning the Holy Eucharist was will be examined below. M. Félix Ravaisson described the codex as follows, at the place cited, p. 85:

> “It comes from Notre-Dame of Laon. This commentary is incomplete. The manuscript begins with ‘He came to his own,’ that is, ‘he was incarnate in human nature,’ and ends, in the course of the explanation of the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves, with the words: ‘agreeing with two senses.’ It is not the commentary of Bede or of Alcuin; in all likelihood it is that of John Scotus Erigena. One notices in it frequent citations of Greek words and sometimes Latinized Greek words—for example, *chasmate*, from Greek *χάσματι*. Now it is known that Scotus Erigena liked to display his knowledge of the Greek language in this way. One also finds in it the clearly recognizable doctrine of the author of *On the Division of Nature*.”

So much for that. I myself carefully examined the codex recently sent to me in Paris with generosity by the French government. First of all, although the codex contains no mention of the author, there can be no doubt to a knowledgeable reader that it is John Scotus’s commentary.

The codex has no folio numbers and consists of forty-eight folios. It is mutilated at the beginning. On the first sixteen folios there is a first fragment, written in the characters of the tenth or eleventh century, most beautifully in black ink; each page normally has twenty-three lines. The twenty-six folios that follow contain a second fragment. Of these, the first eight and the first page of the ninth are written in the same hand, in ink much paler than that of the first fragment; the remaining folios are in the same black ink as the first fragment. There are twenty-four lines on a page. Finally, a third fragment consists of five folios, written by another hand in a similar but more cramped and careless script. I counted twenty-nine lines on a page. Four times the scribe added in the lower or upper margin entire sentences that he had omitted. On the second page of the fifth folio the fragment ends in such a way that it occupies only ten lines of that page.

We have therefore reprinted these three fragments published by M. F. Ravaisson. Since the codex had reached my hands only late, I arranged for various readings and entire sentences neglected or omitted by him to be added at the end of the edition. I also discovered a fourth fragment, which had completely escaped his notice. After leaving a space of three lines, the same hand as that of the first and second fragments added this fragment in ink that was paler but equally neat. There can scarcely be any doubt that it is a fragment of the same commentary. I therefore thought that this little piece, too, should be added at the end of the edition. The final page of the codex is occupied by an Easter table.

Since matters therefore stand thus, I suspect that the writer of the codex, having begun carefully to copy the commentary, soon grew weary of the task undertaken and entrusted its continuation to another. When the latter reached the passages concerning the Holy Supper (John 6:11), he abandoned the work altogether, lest he himself appear to defend the absurdities that John Scotus is said to have taught concerning the Holy Eucharist; he added only the fourth fragment, concerning the sacrifice of the Mass, for his own use. Later, several membranes whose doctrinal content was likewise offensive were cut away. To prevent further losses, a more recent binding was then provided.

You may clearly observe that the first fragment ends precisely where the false doctrine of original sin begins, and the second at John 4:28. I should also mention that at the end of Fragment III (below, col. 347), the word *cerebrum* is clearly legible in the scribe’s hand, substituted for an erased word. That is sufficient concerning this commentary.

### § 10

We must now pass to the systematic books of John Scotus. Of these, the one entitled *On Predestination* has been collated against the testimony of the Paris codex of Saint-Germain 1314, formerly 634. It is a parchment codex of the tenth century, quarto, neatly written, consisting of 204 folios. It is preserved in the Royal Library at Paris. John Scotus’s book occupies folios 96,1–150,2. The chapter titles are found in the codex; only the title of the first chapter is missing. A later hand added the chapter numbers in paler ink.

Mauguin alone published the book from the Corbie Codex of the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in the collection entitled *Works and Fragments of Ancient Authors Who Wrote in the Ninth Century on Predestination and Grace*. Paris, 1650, quarto, vol. I, pp. 109 ff. It seems quite probable that this is the same codex that Mauguin used. Since he performed his task with extreme negligence, we have thoroughly polished and restored the text according to the codex.

### [Col. XI] § 11

In preparing the text of the books *On the Division of Nature*, we made highly fruitful use of the extensive apparatus of emendations and variant readings transcribed from the Paris codex, which appears at the end of Gale’s edition. It is impossible to say how much labor the preparation of this intricate and thorny book cost us. The punctuation had to be properly established, many corrupt passages emended, and the meaning of the words elucidated.

In all these matters, Thomas Gale, who first published the book under the title *The Five Long-Desired Books of John Scotus Erigena on the Division of Nature, Together with an Appendix from the Greek and Latin Ambigua of Saint Maximus*, Oxford, 1681, did almost nothing. The other editor, who recently sent it to press again, C. B. Schlüter, under the title *The Five Books of John Scotus Erigena on the Division of Nature: A Revised and Corrected Edition*, Münster in Westphalia, 1838, octavo, not only revised and corrected nothing, but actually increased the typographical errors and completely neglected the entire apparatus of emendations and variant readings added to the first edition. Although this ought to be a reproach to any other author, it must be excused in the distinguished Schlüter, who was himself deprived of his eyesight and could prepare the edition only through the assistance of others who were less skilled.

After I had thus devoted no small amount of work and care to reviewing the text, I happened to find four notable codices in Paris. New labors, new toil! Time pressed, the book’s publisher urged me on, the printers were waiting, and the difficulties of the thorny and corrupt work impeded me. Nevertheless, I hope that nothing of greater importance escaped my diligence. I collated all these codices.

The first is codex Saint-Germain 309, formerly 548, large folio, parchment, of the eleventh century, beautifully written in black ink. It consists of 447 pages, the last of which has only fourteen lines. It ends with the words:

> “What envy of the good angels concerning the salvation of the human race and its return to its Father is understood—that substance of his, that is, the grace of the image, which, serving the devil in the inn of this mortal life, he dissipated.”

See Book V, chapter 38, below, col. 1015.

On the front of the first page, on one side, a sixteenth-century hand wrote “Saint Peter of Corbie”; on the other, at the edge of the parchment, a thirteenth- or fourteenth-century hand wrote in minuscule letters:

> “This book belongs to the convent of Corbie; but the monks have a memorandum concerning this book *peri phision*, though not the whole of what the memorandum says: let it either be burned or returned to the monks of blessed Vincent at Laon. For it would be better, I believe, that it be burned because of the condemned heresies contained in it.”

A seventeenth-century hand, apparently, added on one side “John Scotus Erigena” and on the other “Saint-Germain-des-Prés.”

The codex begins with a decorated title:

> “Here begins the first book *περὶ φύσεων* [On Natures] of the Master. ‘Often, as I pondered…’ ”

Glosses are found here and there in the margins. Quite often the subject matter has been written in decorated letters in the margin. This seems to be the same Paris codex of Saint-Germain that was used by Peter Alixius and others, from whom Thomas Gale obtained the variant readings transcribed from the Saint-Germain codex. If I judge correctly, the person who collated the codex performed his task rather negligently.

I should add that on an attached paper folio a more recent hand, which I suspect to be that of Peter Alixius, wrote:

> “Here are contained all the books of John Scotus Erigena *περὶ φύσεων*, except for twenty-two pages, which are found in another book.”

I do not know what other book he means, unless it is manuscript codex Saint-Germain 830, formerly 549, which will be described shortly.

The second is codex Latin Royal Library of Paris 1764, large folio, parchment, of the twelfth century, written in two columns. It has no folio numbers. It contains various works of Saint Ambrose, Alcuin, Jerome, and Gregory. The final forty-five folios contain Book I and part of Book II of *On the Division of Nature*. It ends with the words:

> “He generated a filiated substance and a proceeding substance.”

See below, Book II, chapter 23. It is full of errors. I suspect that this is the very mutilated Thuanus codex concerning which Thomas Gale observes, at the words “and proceeding substance”: “Here the codex that formerly belonged to Thuani is defective.” For it seems to have passed from the Colbert collection into the Royal Library.

At the end of the fragment of *On the Division of Nature*, the same hand added, in worn letters exceedingly difficult to read, the following poem:

> O sacred one . . . under one saving effort,  
>   
> For whom the work shines red with gems mixed with incense,  
>   
> I do not know who, having seen the fists, could say what they mean.  
>   
> For him Christ becomes love, virtue, glory, radiance  
>   
> Of the body, bone, and hands, with all the limbs together,  
>   
> The filth of the prison, and the frenzy and frenzy of wild beasts,  
>   
> And distinguishing thin threads with beautiful lightning.  
>   
> The flower-bearing ears accord in song with the Muses,  
>   
> So learned in weaving with golden sapphire,  
>   
> Whoever has joined the face to this clean linen cloth,  
>   
> They do not feel blows, bonds, hunger, rods, torments, chains,  
>   
> Nor the evils, nor the serpent’s venom itself.

[Note: [Col. XII] The Codex reads *fulcor*, “radiance,” instead of *fulgor*.]

[Note: [Col. XII] The Codex reads *rabemque*, “frenzy,” instead of *rabiemque*.]

[Note: [Col. XII] The Codex reads *Que quis*, “whoever,” instead of *Quisquis*.]

[Note: [Col. XII] The Codex reads *Non mulu serpentes*; the reading is corrupt.]

I do not rashly conjecture that this is a poem of John Scotus. But I confess that I do not clearly understand what the corrupted verses are intended to mean.

The third is codex Saint-Germain 280, formerly 166, large folio, parchment, of the twelfth century. It consists of 235 folios. Two fragments of the books *On the Division of Nature* occur on folios 192–235. One begins with the words:

> “Rational, mortal, visible: plainly, an angel is neither a rational animal, nor mortal, nor visible,” etc.

See below, Book I, chapter 4. It ends on folio 222,2 with the words:

> “Do you see, therefore, how true reason makes a category…”

See below, Book I, chapter 74.

The other begins on folio 223,1 with the words:

> “Thus far concerning divisions and concerning unions,” etc.

See below, Book II, chapter 13. It ends on folio 235,2 with the words:

> “Not only do I concede this, but I also understand that the most excellent motion of the soul around the unknown God, beyond every creature, is most truly called and subsists as intellect. But how, or in what manner, intellect, while remaining within the boundaries of human nature…”

See below, Book II, chapter 23.

This codex therefore agrees almost everywhere with the first Saint-Germain codex, 309.

Finally, the fourth is codex Saint-Germain 830, formerly 549, parchment, folio, of the eleventh century, most beautifully written. It consists of 207 folios, containing Books IV and V of *On the Division of Nature*. Folio 207,1 has only five lines. The subject matter is very frequently written in the margin.

On the attached paper folio are the words:

> “Books Four and Five of John Scotus Erigena’s *περὶ φύσεων*,”

written in the same hand that I suspected above to be that of Peter Alixius.

On the front of the first parchment folio, a fourteenth-century hand wrote:

> “On superessential nature.”

A recent seventeenth-century hand apparently added:

> “Saint Peter of Corbie.”

So much, then, concerning the codices that we used in polishing these books. I was unable to examine codex 1976 of the city library of Avranches. M. F. Ravaisson described it in his book *Reports to the Minister*, etc., p. 197, as follows:

> “No. 1976, folio; thirteenth century. This volume contains the final part of John Scotus’s *Periphision* [*περὶ φύσεων*, On Natures], namely Books III and a half. Another volume contains the first part of the same work, namely Book I and a half of Book II. For this same John wrote five books *On the Division of Nature*, exceedingly obscure and requiring careful reading.”

### § 12

Since these two systematic works survive complete, only a small fragment remains of the third, *On the Egress and Regress of the Soul to God*. But this book was formerly found complete in the Electoral Library at Trier, as testified by the learned G. of Northausen, who around the year 1594 was collecting in Germany manuscript codices with which the Vatican Library might be enriched.

In manuscript codex Vallicellianus C. 28, entitled *Index of Volumes That in the Time of Cardinal Baronius Were Preserved in Various Libraries at Rome and Elsewhere*, p. 192, he recorded the following:

> “The parchment manuscript codices that I remember seeing among the heap of books of the Metropolitan Church of Trier are these.”

A catalogue follows, in which, under no. 15, the following is found:

> “The work of John Scotus the Benedictine, who was one of the four first founders of the University of Paris, *On the Egress and Regress of the Soul to God*, written in a Platonic style. Although it has been sprinkled with some error concerning the Holy Trinity, as Alexander of Hales and the scholastic doctors after him note, it can nevertheless be preserved for the use of theologians, when they wish to examine Scotus’s error at its very source for a fuller understanding of the Scholastics.”

I searched for the codex at Trier in vain. Mabillon saw a codex of this book at Clairvaux near Audamaropolis, which he described in *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Section IV, Part II, p. LXVI. Nor does this codex appear to survive.

Since Carolus Greith published a small fragment of that book, recovered from codex Collection 596, parchment, quarto, of the Christian Library, in *Vatican Spicilegium*, Frauenfeld, 1838, pp. 80 ff., we now present it here, newly collated according to that codex. It survives on the ninth folio of this codex, of exceptionally beautiful whiteness, written in a tenth-century hand.

### § 13

Now we must speak of John Scotus’s translations. For he translated into Latin quite a number of works of the ancient Greeks. Among these, the translation of the works of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite easily acquired the greatest fame. When the Emperor Michael Balbus gave their Greek exemplar as a gift to Louis the Pious in the year 827, John Scotus, at the command of Charles the Bald, undertook a translation made word for word, but obscure and exceedingly difficult to understand.

Since a better and clearer translation was lacking, John Scotus’s translation was read for many centuries and illuminated by the commentaries of the most eminent theologians of the Middle Ages. Hence one still frequently finds it in manuscript libraries.

Among the codices I examined, the first place is held by codex Emmeram. B. XLIV, folio, today designated codex Regensburg Saint Emmeram 137 of the Royal Library of Munich, parchment, folio, from the end of the tenth century, consisting of 113 folios. The titles and initials of the chapters are illuminated. At the beginning of each book, beautiful golden initials shine. It contains only the translation of the works of Pseudo-Dionysius.

The codex was written most neatly by the very illustrious Othlo, a monk of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg. His verses at the end read:

> Here I am, little Othlo, commonly called by that name,  
>   
> Though corrupted by every kind of evil deed,  
>   
> Yet sufficiently ready to write this work for you,  
>   
> Holy Dionysius, most renowned martyr of Christ.  
>   
> Therefore, I ask, remember me in your sacred prayers;  
>   
> And you who read, I ask you to seek pardon for me.

Through the kindness of our government, we were permitted carefully to examine the codex sent to us at Bonn.

[Col. XIV] The second place is held by codex 971 of the Vienna Library, formerly Salzburg 157, eleventh century, quarto, consisting of 152 folios. On the inner part of the cover are written these words:

> “This book belongs to Saint Radbert and the canons of Salzburg; whoever removes it, let him be anathema.”

This codex contains nothing except that complete translation. The individual books begin with painted initials, and the chapters with decorated initials. The codex is written very neatly, but toward the end—that is, in the *Mystical Theology* and in the letters of Saint Dionysius—it is full of errors.

The third is the Vienna codex 754, formerly theological codex CCXVII, parchment, folio, from the beginning of the twelfth century, consisting of 100 folios. As a fourteenth-century hand on folio 45,2 testifies, it formerly belonged to the Augustinian canons regular in the New City. Denis described this codex, which is of no negligible authority, in *Manuscript Codices of the Palatine Library at Vienna*, Latin volume I, pp. 677 ff. We shall therefore refrain from saying more about it here.

Two codices are added, the Darmstadt and the Munich codices. The former, as is stated on the front of the first folio, once belonged to the greater church at Cologne and was later granted to the Friars Minor. It is a parchment folio codex of the twelfth century. It consists of 103 folios, containing the complete translation. Hartzheim described the codex in his *Historical-Critical Catalogue of the Manuscript Codices of the Library of the Metropolitan Church of Cologne*, Cologne, 1752, quarto, p. 20, under no. 30. Continuous scholia of Saint Maximus, rendered into Latin, have been written in the margin.

The letters of Saint Dionysius end on folio 101,1, where one reads:

> “The ten letters of Dionysius the Areopagite, made archbishop of Athens, are complete.”

There follow part of Polycrates’ letter to Pope Victor (*Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History* V.24), and the story of the young robber whom John the Evangelist recalled from his crime and restored to the Church (*Clement of Alexandria, Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?*, chapter 42; *Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History* III.23). The remaining part of the parchment is occupied by matters of no importance.

The other Munich codex, Latin Fürstenfeld 9, folio, from the fifteenth century, is partly paper and partly parchment, arranged so that four paper folios alternate with two parchment folios. It consists of 359 folios. The complete translation is written most neatly on folios 1–109; the rest of the codex is occupied by the commentary of Lord Albert, Bishop of Regensburg, on the books of Pseudo-Dionysius.

It remains to mention the two Vatican codices, 177 and 176, which we described above in § 5. They likewise contain the complete translation, arranged as we noted, so that commentaries by various authors are appended to the individual chapters.

Accordingly, on the authority of these seven codices, we reviewed John Scotus’s Preface and the verses prefixed to the translation, as well as the very poor summary found at the end of the translation. But in reviewing the text of the translation itself we used only three codices: the Munich codex of Othlo, the Darmstadt codex, and the Fürstenfeld codex. Nor did I record all their variant readings; I thought that only the more important variants should be added.

Moreover, we inspected the codex of this translation, Leipzig 188, parchment, folio, of the thirteenth century, which we cited above in § 6; the Florentine codex Plut. LXXXIX, Sup. 15, parchment, large folio, of the eleventh or beginning of the twelfth century, consisting of 253 folios, where the translation occurs on folios 1–104; the Ghent and Paris codices; and numerous other codices of lesser value, which it would seem both tedious and irrelevant to enumerate here.

I prefixed to the translation the letter of Anastasius the librarian, which is likewise prefixed to the translation in the Florentine codex mentioned above and in the two Vatican codices 176 and 177, as well as in certain others that we examined. We reviewed the text of this letter against the authority of Usserius’s edition in the *Collection of Irish Letters*, the Strasbourg edition of the works of Saint Dionysius from 1503, and those codices. But we regret that, through a lapse of memory, we attributed to the single Florentine codex the variant readings taken from three codices. We must therefore frankly acknowledge here this error, which it is no longer possible to correct.

It should also be noted that the translation, together with commentaries by various authors, was published at Strasbourg in 1503 under the title:

> *The Works of Dionysius, in the Old and New Translation, Including the Most Recent Translation by Marsilio Ficino, with Commentaries by Hugh, Albert, Thomas, the Orator of Ambrose, the Bishop of Lincoln, and the Bishop of Vercelli.*

A new enlarged edition appeared at Cologne under the title:

> *All the Extant Works of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, Martyr, Bishop of Athens, and Apostle of the Gauls, Rendered in Five Translations and Clarified by the Commentaries of the Reverend Dionysius of Rikel, Carthusian, Now Edited Again with the Greatest Care and Diligently Freed from the Innumerable Errors with Which They Had Previously Abounded.*

Cologne, in the year of Christ’s birth 1556, January, folio. We used this second edition in preparing the translation.

Taking this opportunity, we may add a few remarks concerning the monk Othlo, whose distinguished codex we have just praised, on the authority of the Munich codices. He was a monk of the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg. He lived at the end of the tenth and the beginning of the eleventh century. Pez published his works from the autographs in *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. III, part II, pp. 142 ff. The autographs still exist in the Royal Library of Munich, codices Emmeram E. CXIII, quarto, and b. 10, octavo.

In one of them, folio 112, Othlo lists the books that he copied in his own hand:

> “I also wrote three books of the Gospels, and two with epistles and gospels, which are called lectionaries, together with their offices; likewise two volumes of Saint Augustine, containing eight books in one and five in the other; the Conferences of the Fathers; and the Hierarchy.”

From the same autograph, Mabillon published Othlo’s book in *Ancient Analecta*, Paris edition, 1723, pp. 108 ff., under the false title:

> *A Little Book by an Anonymous Monk of Regensburg Concerning His Temptations, Varied Fortune, and Writings.*

The book is entitled in the codex:

> “Here begins the book concerning the temptation of a certain monk.”

Mabillon’s text is filled with errors and truncated at the end, so that a new edition reviewed against the autograph would be highly desirable.

In the other autograph, codex CXIII, folios 1–16, there is Othlo’s little manual book *On the Admonition of Clerics*, which appeared without the author’s name in the works of Bede, Cologne, 1688, vol. II, pp. 200 ff., under the title:

> “A Little Book on Substances.”

Oudin, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, cols. 1687 and 1706, and Fabricius, in his bibliography under Bede, conjectured that it was the work of a Benedictine monk no earlier than the eleventh or twelfth century.

The little book is followed on folios 16–18 by a poem of Othlo, entitled:

> “A Metrical Sermon Specifically Addressed to Clerics,”

which Pez neglected. Since it recalls the clergy to repentance in the year 1000, when they were expecting the end of the world, we have arranged to insert those verses here for the benefit of readers. They are as follows:

# Othlo’s Metrical Sermon Addressed Especially to Clerics

O dear brothers, teachers and masters  
of the holy Church, under the condition of the clergy,  
I beg you, listen to the words I now wish to speak.  
Since the time is near when the world will be destroyed,

[5] you who love the promise of everlasting life,  
strong athletes, keep your mind’s hope above.  
Do not possess anything in this world through loving it.  
For there remains for you the fruit of a better homeland,  
if only you sincerely strive to deserve it rightly.

[10] To seek that homeland, despise the present life,  
except for those uses by which you hasten there  
and by which your bodies are sustained in the meantime.  
Let it not deceive you if abundance of wealth increases;  
if there are riches, do not perish through them.

[15] For when God grants these things, through them he tests everyone,  
to see who chooses to remain faithful in his gifts.  
The advantages of the world are not otherwise brought under anyone’s control,  
[Col. XVI] although very many now desire to be powerful,  
intent, plainly, more on the banquets of the age,

[20] than on supplying the needs of the souls entrusted to them.

But you, brothers, fleeing what belongs to the world,  
steadfastly seek the riches of your souls.  
For what is great honor worth, if the burden of honor is so great?  
What benefit is there, in the end, if you take possession of the whole world,  
[25] only to suffer endless torment after its downfall?

Therefore we must be attentive and afraid,  
lest the unlearned people perish through our crimes.  
For we, taught through the doctrines of the sacred law  
so that we might give the rest examples of good living,  
[30] and, if the matter demanded it, whenever occasion arose,

might endure death even for the companions of our faith,  
stumble at the very first encounters with impiety,  
as though we were nothing against the enemy’s forces [the printed *nil nisi contra* is syntactically uncertain].  
And what seems still more grievous and pitiable,  
[35] we not only flee the duty to which we are commanded,

but also, tearing apart what has been entrusted to us like wolves,  
we ravage some things and wickedly abandon others.  
For those to whom, as fathers, we ought to provide food,  
if any force of circumstance or the season of the year should demand it,  
[40] we come to them like cruel robbers

and carry away those things—a miserable thing to say—  
which another’s piety has given in Christ’s name.  
When sinners, fearing the evil deeds they have committed,  
flee to us to obtain pardon,  
[45] we are found either more terrifying than the matter and the need require,

or more merciful than is permitted;  
or, disdaining to decide anything about these matters,  
we leave them, with merely due caution, to those whom we know to be accomplices of criminals.

[50] Because we are bound up in concern for the world  
and perform the office of a duke or a viceroy,  
we cannot properly weigh the care of the people entrusted to us;  
and it would be unworthy for us, so distinguished and so powerful,  
to provide ourselves to a degenerate crowd.

[55] There are many others for whom this labor is suitable,  
to teach the common people and to preside over them well by their example.  
We, the nobles of the world, are evidently born for leisure,  
so that we may pursue only the amusements of dogs and birds  
and enjoy whatever pleases us as these delights.

[60] For the wealth of this life seeks out those elders  
who devote themselves to the games mentioned above,  
nor is extravagance considered wrong when worldly custom demands it.  
These things, if not in words, are nevertheless affirmed in practice,  
as the daily custom of the clergy itself proves.

[65] There is also another vice that must be mentioned alongside the others:  
the crime of one who is thought to possess something  
remains for us a reason to abuse that person’s goods.  
Then, once the possessions have been seized, no one corrects the wretched man,  
so that, having in some measure made amends here

for what he has committed, [70] he might escape the flames  
of everlasting punishment.  
But who could be so learned as to pass through one by one  
the matters in which we are convicted of being the authors of crimes—  
we who know divine affairs more than others?

Provided that our celebrated honor is maintained throughout the world,  
[75] and we are made radiant by various pageants,  
nothing remains unharmed by us, however it is accomplished—  
whether by wicked asking or, what is worse, by seizure.  
Whoever cannot carry out the harm will at least plan it in his mind:

thus the flight of teachers becomes the cause of death for those who follow,  
[80] and there is no more grievous plague than when the shepherd is the enemy of the flock.  
For while the clergy abuses the world with excessive boldness,  
what else can the unlearned then contemplate  
except to think that all things are likewise permitted to everyone?

We rightly weep, then, who harbor such hearts.  
[85] Indeed, days will come, if we are not cleansed of these things,  
although excessive laughter now occupies us,  
while eternal pain surrounds those destined for torment.  
What more good do we do than the Jews or the Pharisees,

whom we read were whitewashed on the outside but foul in heart,  
[90] while we wish to fulfill the ordinances only with the tongue?  
As my spirit tells me, alas, we are worse than they.  
Finally, if they had known anything beyond the legal precepts,  
perhaps they would have pursued this great wickedness less.

But we, seeing in books not only their crime  
[Col. XVII] [95] but also the deeds of many others,  
some things composed for the vengeance of the wicked,  
others spoken in hope of the reward of the righteous,  
can know past events as though they were present,  
yet we do not fear to persist in similar vices.

[100] We curse them because they devoted themselves to such perversities,  
not considering that the same error holds us,  
who honor God’s commandments only with our lips.  
For they too worshiped God with their mouth, as we do,  
as God himself testifies through the words of the prophet Isaiah,

[105] which Christ later also spoke to the Jews:  
“This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me.”  
Often indeed we speak of holy religion,  
and proclaim heavenly things in magnificent words,  
placing heavy burdens on the shoulders of others,

[110] which we ourselves do not wish to touch even with a finger,  
as though the Lord had no concern for such matters  
and his customary anger did not rebuke us when we sin.  
Choose, therefore, a place where you may gather together,  
you who are permitted and who have also been granted the power,

[115] under pastoral care, to convert the world,  
so that, when the time of pardon arrives, we may renew our conduct;  
and just as love of piety first began to grow cold through us,  
so now, through us, let it grow warm again.  
For I judge that the various troubles this world now produces

[120] arise altogether from our sins,  
since we retain no care for those subject to us  
but cast them down to the lowest depths by our wicked examples.  
Thus the whole world is corrupted on every side;  
thus it also happens that we are considered worthless,

[125] when the clerical office follows the work of laymen,  
and laymen likewise are appointed to the clerical order.  
Yet it is clear that the two sins are far from equal.  
In the end, those sin more who, knowing more, set the example:  
“From everyone to whom much has been given, much will also be required.”

## § 14

Thomas Gale published in mutilated form, in the Appendix to the books *On the Division of Nature*, pp. 1–45, John Scotus’s version of Saint Maximus’s *Ambigua*, which he had received from the distinguished Mabillon [cf. *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, saec. IV, pt. II, p. LXVI]. I have encountered no manuscripts of this version. I suspect that in the manuscript of the Paris library of the Arsenal, from which M. F.
