Ravaisson published three poems concerning Saint Maximus—*Rapports*, etc., pp. 356 ff.—the complete version may also be found. I regret that recently, when I was in Paris, access to the manuscripts of that library was not available. Accordingly, using my best efforts, and also employing the corrections of Thomas Gale appended at the end of his edition, we have presented the text, corrected here and there to the best of our ability.

## § 15

As was customary in those times among learned men who lived at the royal court—Alcuin alone need be recalled here—to compose poems on feast days or on other occasions and sing the praises of the king or queen, of Christ, and of the saints, so our Scot also composed *Verses*, which are found in the Vatican manuscripts of the Christina Library, nos. 1587 and 1709. Since the Most Eminent Cardinal Angelo Mai was the first to publish those poems in *Classical Authors Published from Vatican Manuscripts*, vol. V, pp. 426 ff., they now appear again, revised and corrected by me in accordance with those same manuscripts.

Manuscript 1587 is a parchment codex of the tenth or eleventh century, in octavo, consisting of sixty-six folios. The poems are read on fols. 57,1–64,2. In the other manuscript, no. 1709, a parchment codex of the eleventh century in octavo, the poems occur on fols. 16,2–18,1. From the former I wish to offer another poem by an anonymous author, found on fol. 4. It is as follows:

### Verses collected after the model of common syllables [reading uncertain]

A darkened mind swells with the darkness of death;  
a humble man ascends heaven from the mournful earth.  
Thus there is now hope of climbing to the blessed kingdoms of heaven.  
May his love endure; in whose heart, through him,  
may there be for you, O young man, the ardor of holy wisdom [the syntax is corrupt as printed].  
*Soph a nota tuae et mens nota sophiae*: “Soph[a], the mark of yours, and the mind, the mark of wisdom” [corrupt as printed].

This is honor, this the soul’s virtue, this the illustrious order.

[Col. XVIII] Store up treasure in heaven; empty the sacks of treasures.  
Christ’s court holds Christ in its breast—and is itself a court.

### On the girl Galla

You never give, Galla, though you always promise to the one who asks.  
If you always deceive, Galla, I now ask you: refuse.

### On a man afflicted with scabs

A shameful, useless beast; shameful is a field without grass [the supplied *capus* is uncertain, perhaps *campus*, “field”],  
a shrub without foliage, and a head without hair.

### To a drunkard

Tell me, tell me, drunkard: are you alive, or are you oppressed by death?  
Look, you lie pale; look, you rest without a mind.  
You sense neither good nor evil, neither hard nor soft.  
You differ from the fate of one buried dead only in this:  
a faint breath pricks the wretched limbs from beneath.

### On wine

Great are you, Bacchus, and great is your power everywhere;  
you have always carried off the palm against those who fight you.

M. F. Ravaisson extracted John Scotus’s verses on Saint Maximus from a manuscript of the Arsenal. We now reproduce them as published in his book entitled *Rapports*, etc., pp. 356–358. The editor did not indicate what sort of manuscript it is.

Thomas Gale testifies in the preface to the books *On the Division of Nature* that verses by John Scotus exist in a Benedictine manuscript at Cambridge. There can be no doubt that he understood these to be the same verses which the late Dr. Oehler copied about ten years ago from Cambridge, Corpus Christi College manuscript no. 223, of the ninth century. Although I repeatedly asked the brother who inherited the manuscript to grant me a copy for the use of this edition, I did not obtain one; indeed, I received no reply. Nor did the Cambridge scholars comply with my request that the poem be copied for my use. I was therefore able to publish only the end of the poem, which Dr. Oehler had shared with a friend. On his own testimony, the poem consists of 101 verses and is dogmatic-ascetic in subject.

Verses on Saint Dionysius are found at the beginning and end of the version of his works. Likewise, four verses occur at the beginning of the book *On Predestination*. Cousin extracted two verses from a manuscript of the Royal Library, *Fragments philosophiques*, vol. III, appendix, p. 326. We have added them below. Other verses that seemed attributable to John Scotus we have entered above, in § 11.

There are also John Scotus’s rough and dreadful Greek verses, published from a Saint-Germain manuscript in uncial letters together with Latin glosses, in the Preface to C. Labbe’s *Glossaries*. Although they are so corrupt that, as Angelo Mai himself testifies in the cited passage, p. 451, they seem scarcely capable of being restored, nevertheless we believe that we have labored over their correction and repair not without result. They are therefore published here again in a corrected form. I searched in vain for the Saint-Germain manuscript in the Paris Royal Library.

By chance a Greek poem came into my hands, written in Latin letters of the ninth century and accompanied by Latin glosses. When, about five years ago, the distinguished Dr. M. C. B. Bock had copied it from a manuscript of the Burgundian Library at Brussels and sent it to our Lersch—alas, taken from us by a premature death—I recognized as soon as I inspected it that it contained John Scotus’s verses. When I was recently in Brussels, I could not inspect the manuscript, which had been sent to France. It is manuscript no. 10078–10084, a parchment folio codex of the twelfth century. It contains Fulgentius’s *Virgiliana* and glosses on obscure expressions. I suspect that these verses, composed in honor of Saint Dionysius, are numbered among those glosses.

## § 16

The distinguished D. Pitra recently promised that in volume II of the *Spicilegium Solesmense* he would publish John Scotus’s commentaries on Martianus Capella. I regret that they have not yet appeared. Most recently, when I was in Paris, I believe that I discovered these commentaries in the manuscript of Saint-Germain 1110, formerly 589, a parchment codex. I did not, however, have enough leisure to copy them. Therefore, when I asked D. Pitra, through a letter delivered by the purchaser of this book, to grant me [Col. XIX] a copy of his manuscript for comparison and use in this edition, I received no reply from him either.

Nevertheless, I shall not omit briefly to describe that Saint-Germain manuscript, so that he may use it for his own purposes. It is a parchment folio codex, written in two columns by a thirteenth-century hand and mutilated at the end. It consists of 125 folios, on which various works are found.

On fols. 31,1–38,2 there is book I of *On the Division of Nature*, extending to chapter 32, at whose end a fragment concludes with the words: “For every nature, whether of essences or of accidents, is immutable.” I overlooked this when examining the three manuscripts praised above in § 11.

On fols. 47,1–115,2 there are *Annotations on Martianus*, which I suspect to be by John Scotus. They begin:

“We have learned that the author of this fable, Martianus, was by origin a Carthaginian and also a Roman citizen; hence, in the Latin manner, he was called *tetronomos*, that is, ‘named with four names’: Martianus, Mineus, Felix, and Capella. Martianus was his proper name; Mineus was from his complexion, as they say, because he was red; Felix—we do not know whether he lived happily or not; Capella, however, because a certain *satyra* [‘satire’ or ‘female satyr’; the reading is uncertain], whether his nurse or his admonitress, may have been so called, as is plainly evident from his writings when he named [her], etc.”

On fol. 67,2 one reads: “Here begins the exposition of the second book of the marriage of Philology and Mercury”; on fol. 89,2: “The section on rhetoric ends”; on fol. 90,2: “Here begin these few remarks on Martianus’s geometry”; on fol. 97,2: “The section on geometry ends; the section on arithmetic begins”; and on fol. 107,2: “These few remarks on Martianus’s music.”

The commentaries end on fol. 115,2 with these words:

“*Decertum*, that is, *decertatum*, ‘contested.’ *Urbs Elisae*, that is, Carthage. *Jugariorum*, that is, Martianus was from the province of Jugaria. *Marcidam*, that is, ‘ancient.’ *Veternum*, ‘ancient.’ Here also ends the Gloss on Music. Thanks be to God.”

The words that follow to the end of the codex were written by another hand.

# III. OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF JOHN SCOTUS

## § 17

So much for the manuscripts we used in preparing this edition. It remains for us to say something about the life and writings of John Scotus, on certain points concerning which we must disagree with the author of the essay printed below.

First of all, in explaining the name *Erigena*, all who have hitherto written about John Scotus have been considerably mistaken. Nor is this surprising, since the word *Erigena* is nothing but a corruption of the genuine name *Ierugena*, a corruption that, in my opinion, arose only in the fifteenth century. This is readily proved by the authority of the manuscripts.

For in all the surviving writings of John Scotus, only the name “John Scotus” is prefixed in the manuscripts. Thus, in the manuscripts of the *Expositions of the Celestial Hierarchy*, one reads: “Here begin the expositions of John Scotus”; in the manuscript of the *Exposition of Mystical Theology*: “Here begins the prologue of John Scotus,” and so forth. The verses of the Vatican manuscript are entitled “of John ΣΚΟΘΘΙ”; the verses of the Cambridge manuscript bear the name “John Scotus” at their head; and the homily is entitled “Homily of John Scotus.”

Only in the version of the works of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite is there another surname in place of *Scotus*—not indeed *Erigena*, but *Ierugena*. For in the oldest manuscripts that we have examined, the Munich manuscript of Othlo and two Viennese manuscripts, one reads:

“Here begin the books of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, which John Ierugena translated from Greek into Latin.”

Likewise, the Fürstenfeld manuscript at Munich and both Vatican manuscripts have *Ierugena*. Only the Florentine and Darmstadt manuscripts have *Eriugena*.

Since this is so, the question now arises: what does the surname *Ierugena* mean? I do not know whether it is difficult to discover. It is composed of Ἱεροῦ, namely of νῆσος, “island,” and *gena*, so that it means “born from the island of the saints.” Everyone knows that [Col. XX] Ireland was anciently called by this name.

*Ierou* is derived from ἱερός, “holy,” and the name *Ierugena* is formed from the genitive ἱεροῦ according to Latin usage, just as *Grajugena* is formed. By this name our own Scot honors Saint Maximus in the following verse:

> Whoever loves to praise the form of beautiful Wisdom,  
> let him read you constantly, Maximus the Greek-born.

Here, then, is the simplest and unquestionably true explanation of that name. Later writers, who understood the version less well, changed it into *Eriugena*, apparently in order to allude to the name Erin. Subsequently, when the letter *u* was often written more like the letter *y*, learned men read *Erygena* and *Erigena* for *Ierugena*; Trithemius seems to have been almost the first to do so.

Thus the very ingenious conjectures of learned men, who supposed that John Scotus came from the land of Ergene, the village of Eriuven, or the city of Aire, and the detailed discussions of this name found below in the essay, collapse as groundless. Nor should it be omitted here that contemporary writers never call John by any other surname than *Scotus* or *Scotigena*, and that in the manuscripts John Scotus and John Ierugena are never read together as a single name. Rather, as we have noted, one finds either “John Scotus” or “John Ierugena.” In only one of the Vatican manuscripts of the poems and in the title of the version of Saint Maximus’s *Ambigua* is he called “John the Most Wise,” or simply “John.”

The objections recently made by an anonymous writer in the encyclopedia entitled *Kirchenlexicon oder Encyclopaedie der Catholischen Theologie*, by H. S. Wetzer and B. Welte, under “Joannes Scotus Erigena,” do not seem to stand in the way. He argued that my opinion is no less doubtful than those of others and does not exceed the limits of conjecture. On the contrary, our opinion rests on the authority of the manuscripts, in which John is explicitly called *Ierugena*. As for the sense of the surname, I believe that I have reached it not by conjecture but by the true origin of the word.

The words of Prudentius rebuking Scotus now fit perfectly:

> Ireland sent you alone, the sharpest-minded of all men,  
> to Gaul, so that Ireland might obtain through your learning  
> what no one without you could know.

Nor can it now be an objection that William of Malmesbury testifies that he read John Scotus called *Heruligena* in a manuscript of the version. For *Eruligena* is nothing other than *Erinigena*, that is, “born from the island Erin,” which is almost a Latin translation of the word *Ierugena*. The manuscript spellings *Eruligena* and *Erinigena* scarcely differ, since *uli* and *ini* correspond closely in them.

## § 18

There is another question that has exercised the ingenuity of learned men no less: the book of John Scotus that is said to have been written on the Holy Eucharist. None of the contemporary writers mentions a separate book on the Eucharist by John Scotus. Hincmarus merely touches upon the error that the sacrament of the altar is not the true body and true blood of the Lord, but only a memorial of his true body and blood, and he attributes it clearly enough to John Scotigena.

Likewise, Adrevald, a monk of Fleury in the ninth century, entitled the book he composed on the body and blood of the Lord *Against the Stupidities of John Scotus*. Gerbert—or whoever that anonymous author of the Cellotian work was—who wrote in the tenth century about the Paschasian controversy, lists nearly all the others who at that time published books on the body and blood of the Lord, but omits our John Scotus.

Only Berengar of Tours eventually brought to public notice a book of John Scotus on the Eucharist, from which, he said, Berengar himself had derived his very serious error. Later, under the name of John Scotus, the book was condemned in many synods, torn apart, and consigned to the fire. What, then? Did the synods condemn in John Scotus something that was not really his?

[Col. XXI] The matter, however, seems to stand as follows. In Berengar’s *Book on the Holy Supper*, which appeared under the title *The Later Book of Berengar of Tours on the Holy Supper against Lanfranc*, first published from the Wolfenbüttel manuscript by A. F. and F. Th. Vischer, Berlin, 1834, p. 37, these words are found:

> “As for John, I myself heard you telling certain people why he was torn apart: because in a certain passage of his writing he had stated that the things consecrated on the altar are a figure, sign, and pledge of the body and blood of the Lord.”

All this fits the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, which has very often been published under the name of Ratramnus. For toward its end the same words repeatedly occur. Moreover, Ascelin’s words, drawn from that book of John Scotus—“These things are enacted in appearance, not in reality”—are found word for word in Ratramnus’s book.

Certainly it could have happened that two writers between whom there was a great similarity of intellect, especially in those times, happened by chance to use the same words and even the same complete sentence. But that this should actually have happened in the words under discussion is so far from probable that we may dispense with further demonstration. Nor do those words correspond so completely to the truth that they contain nothing capable of being turned into a reproach against their author.

Thus it scarcely seems doubtful that Berengar used Ratramnus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, and that it was Ratramnus’s book that was condemned, torn apart, and burned in the synods. The manuscripts I have examined testify that it belonged to Ratramnus: formerly the manuscript of Lobbes, now belonging to Monsieur Vergauwen of Ghent, a tenth-century manuscript described by Mabillon in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. VI, preface, nos. 83, 129, and 130; Heidelberg 8. XX, an eleventh-century manuscript formerly belonging to the abbey of Salem, cited by Mabillon in the *Itinerary*, *Analecta*, Paris, 1733, fol. 14, 17; and two manuscripts at Göttweig, nos. 58 and 312. All of these, without exception, entitle the book as Ratramnus’s. The Lobbes manuscript, indeed, has the following words:

> **HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF RATRAMNUS ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD.**

“But how did it happen,” you will ask, “that during the Berengarian controversy no one appeared who referred the book to its true author, Ratramnus? How did it happen that the synods did not discover its true author?”

I answer these questions with others that are no less appropriate. If Berengar was using a book by John Scotus, how did it happen that neither he nor his school ever appealed to the closely similar book of Ratramnus, which greatly favored his error? How did it happen that throughout the entire controversy no mention whatever was made of Ratramnus’s books?

The synods judged the book, not its author. Ratramnus’s book also employs such an intricate and singular style of expression that learned men could easily have allowed it to be attributed to John Scotus. Yet among the ancients no one ever cites two separate books on the Holy Eucharist, one by John Scotus and one by Ratramnus, as the work of the same writer.

Now, if there is good reason to doubt that John Scotus wrote a separate book on the Holy Eucharist, where did he disseminate his errors and absurdities concerning the most holy sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood?

He disseminated them in his commentary on the Holy Gospel according to John, which ends in chapter 6, verse 11, just when he had begun to speak about the Holy Eucharist. In my opinion, he also disseminated them in the *Expositions of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, in which he had to discuss the sacrament of the Holy Eucharist more extensively. For when, in the first chapter of the *Expositions of the Celestial Hierarchy* that we have published, he attacked the Paschasians, there can scarcely be any doubt that afterward, when he came to Dionysius’s doctrine of the Holy Eucharist, he set out his own opinion at great length.

[Col. XXII] I therefore suspect that those expositions too were cut up and destroyed, and for this reason are now missing from the manuscripts.

Hincmarus, then, briefly censures in these writings the errors of John Scotus concerning the body and blood of the Lord; and Adrevald the monk refuted the absurdities contained in these writings. Later, when Berengar of Tours came upon Ratramnus’s book, he persuaded both himself and others that it was by John Scotus. Although this book does not openly state the Berengarian errors, its uncertain and ambiguous definitions are such that it may rightly be called a kind of matrix both of the Berengarian and of the Calvinist heresy concerning the body and blood of the Lord.

Nor are the two passages from the commentary on the Holy Gospel according to John cited by M. F. Ravaisson—see § 9—of such a kind as to shed new light on John Scotus’s doctrine of the Holy Eucharist. For Scotus’s words—“we sacrifice him [the Savior or mystical Lamb] spiritually, and intellectually we eat him in the mind, not with the tooth”—although they may not seem to express the whole truth, do not in fact cross the limits of truth.

Indeed, Scotus professes that Christ is sacrificed: but how is he sacrificed if he is not really present? He is sacrificed spiritually and really; he is eaten intellectually and really, by the mind and by the mouth, not by the tooth. This passage is therefore very similar to one found below, in column 140, in the *Expositions on the Celestial Hierarchy*.

Nearly the same may be said of the other passage:

> “The spiritual man . . . no longer merely denies that Christ is flesh, understanding that flesh has already been turned into spirit; he also removes from him the status of a rational soul. For just as his flesh was exalted and changed into a rational soul, so his rational soul was both subjected to and changed into intellect.”

Whatever opinion one may hold about these statements, it does not follow from them that Christ is now deprived of a body or no longer possesses a complete human nature. Rather, John Scotus seems chiefly to be trying, as an opponent of Paschasius, to distinguish carefully between the natural body and the glorified body.

Do not be surprised that we have entirely disregarded in this edition the fragment on the Holy Eucharist published by M. F. Ravaisson from the Avranches manuscript, *Rapports*, etc., pp. 372 ff., and reprinted by Tallandier in *Scot Érigène*, etc., p. 325. Ravaisson writes of it:

> “It may perhaps be a fragment of Berengar of Tours, perhaps of Scotus Erigena, whose *On the Body of the Lord* is lost.”

But the distinguished scholar’s hope was disappointed. It is a fragment of Ratramnus’s book, repeatedly printed a hundred times, and is found almost word for word in its middle. This seems to have entirely escaped the distinguished editors.

## § 19

Third, it remains to examine a matter no less difficult to resolve: what relationship existed between John Scotus and the Byzantines of his time. It is beyond doubt that in his book *On the Division of Nature* John Scotus generally supports the Greek doctrine concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit more than the Latin doctrine. Nor does he fail everywhere to praise the wisdom of the Greeks. He always displays in his writings his familiarity with Greek literature and, as though all wisdom had to be sought from the Greeks, proclaims their praise everywhere in the most exalted terms.

Since John Scotus therefore possessed great authority with Charles the Bald, what if Photius and the Byzantines, who at that time were preparing a schism, tried to draw into their party a courtier who was most devoted to the Greeks and very powerful? Although nothing certain is established about this matter, it is nevertheless sufficiently clear that John Scotus stood on Photius’s side, if not in actual action, at least in the inclination of his mind.

This is shown most plainly by the verses of a most objectionable tendency [Col. XXIII] that he appended to the version of the works of Saint Dionysius. They are as follows:

> Once you were built for noble patrons;  
> now, alas, ill subjected to slaves, Rome, you fall.  
> Your kings have deserted you for so long,  
> and your name and honor have passed to the Greeks.  
> Flourishing Constantinople is called the new Rome;  
> in morals and walls, ancient Rome, you are collapsing.  
> Empire has passed away, but pride has remained with you;  
> the worship of avarice overwhelms you too greatly.  
> The common people, drawn from the farthest regions of the world,  
> the slaves of slaves, are now your masters.  
> Among you no noble or upright ruler remains;  
> and your freeborn people cultivate the Pelasgian fields.  
> You have cut down living saints with a cruel wound;  
> now you are accustomed to sell their dead limbs.  
> If the merit of Peter and Paul did not sustain you,  
> you would already for a long time have been wretched Rome.

These verses, published without the author’s name in the works of Bede, Basel edition of 1563, part I, p. 538, and Cologne edition, vol. I, p. 449, are genuinely by John Scotus. This is established by the old manuscripts mentioned above: the Munich manuscript of Othlo, two Viennese manuscripts, and the Fürstenfeld manuscript. In all of them the poem is appended to the end of the version.

Nor should it disturb you that you read that “the common people, drawn from the farthest regions of the world, the slaves of slaves, rule in Rome.” These words almost certainly refer to the Saracens, who at that time repeatedly threatened Rome with sword and fire. See Muratori, *Annals of Italy*, vol. V.

But if John Scotus was indeed the man who, as now seems scarcely open to doubt, favored at the royal court in Paris the Greeks who resisted the Holy Apostolic See, what wonder is it that Pope Nicholas I reproached the king because the books of Saint Dionysius, translated into Latin by John Scotus, had been released to the public without apostolic approval? He demanded that this John—who, as common report said, was certainly not wise in some matters—be brought to Rome, or at least removed from the Paris school, of which he was once said to have been head, lest he be found to mix the grains of tares and darnel with the wheat of sacred eloquence and offer poison to those seeking bread.

What Nicholas accomplished by these letters is not recorded.

Nor should we omit here that the stories told by some about John Scotus’s long journeys through Greece and the East cannot be proved by any sound evidence. Labbe, indeed, correctly observes in the Preface to the *Glossaries* that John Scotus and the other little teachers of Greek letters of his age were not so versed in that language that one should suppose them to have migrated from Carolingian Gaul to Athens. This is sufficiently demonstrated both by John Scotus’s crude Greek poems and by his translations, in which he shows himself in Greek to be nothing more than a slave to words.

Nevertheless, among his contemporaries he was considered highly skilled in Greek letters. I would not doubt that he is the John meant in the following passage from the *Psilotrum* for externally drying harmful humors and removing hairs that are displeasing, in manuscript 2940, quarto, an eleventh-century manuscript of the municipal library of Avranches:

> “Moreover, not only does it destroy hairs, as was said above, but it also restrains the onset of harmful humors. The bishop Pardulus often used it, as did the grammarian Fregus, who used to say: ‘Whoever uses this three times in March need not fear the trouble of fevers during the year.’ The Greek sages too, as I heard from John, make especially frequent use of this medicine. Nor perhaps did he ever need to take another potion for drying the humors.”

M. F. Ravaisson, *Rapports*, etc., p. 132.

## § 20

Nothing is known about John Scotus’s parents and relatives except that he had a brother named Aldelmus. This is indicated by Saint-Germain manuscript 1108, formerly 442, fol. 42,1, where, at the head of a parchment covered by a calendar table, a hand probably of the ninth century wrote in the margin [Col. XXIV]:

> “Aldelmus, brother of John Scotus, made this page  
> . . . hold the letter in the year of the Lord  
> 896; in the following year, the darkness  
> of twelve letters, from M. F. Z.,  
> and so forth  
> begins  
> the leap . . .  
> where the thirteenth  
> line  
> receives  
> . . .”

The manuscript is cited by Cousin, *Unpublished Works of Abelard*, appendix, p. 622.

## § 21

Recently Dr. J. B. Weiss, in his book *History of Alfred the Great*, Schaffhausen, 1852, advanced the opinion that John Scotus came from Gaul to England at the invitation of King Alfred and died at Malmesbury in 891. His argument rests on two chronicles: the Peterborough Chronicle of England and the Thuan Chronicle of France.

The former was edited by Joseph Sparke in *Various English Historians, Now First Published from Manuscripts*, 1723, and by Giles, London, 1845. Under the year 891 it contains the following:

> “The Normans killed the bishop of Worms. John Scotus, a monk of Malmesbury, died, stabbed, as is said, with the styluses of boys whose teacher he was.”

The chronicle of the Thuan Library—Du Chesne, *Historians*, vol. III, p. 359; Bouquet, *Historians*, vol. VII, p. 253—offers this:

> “At the request of Alfred, John Scotus returned from France, where he had been with Charles the Bald.”

But the authority of these chronicles must be examined. Who would not suspect that at this point the Thuan Chronicle relies on William of Malmesbury? That the passage in the Peterborough Chronicle flowed from the same source is already indicated plainly enough by the story about the boys’ styluses, with the words “as is said” added.

Finally, I do not understand on what grounds he can claim that the passage of Asser concerning John the Old Saxon is spurious. For even if we grant that Asser’s passage, which begins “from a certain time,” is not genuine, faith should not on that account be denied to his account of John the Old Saxon, the first abbot of Athelney, which immediately precedes it.

John, invited to England by King Alfred together with Grimbald, can scarcely be doubted to be this same Old Saxon, the abbot of Athelney. Perhaps careful investigations in England will succeed in uncovering new evidence by which this question concerning John Scotus’s return to England may be brought to a definitive resolution.

## § 22. The order in which John Scotus’s surviving books were written and published can scarcely be determined. It is certain only that the *Expositions of the Celestial Hierarchy* were composed after the books *On the Division of Nature*, to which they refer. That the books *On the Division of Nature* were dedicated to Wulfadus may be inferred from their conclusion, as established by our collation of the manuscript of Saint-Germain. Wulfadus, treasurer of the church of Reims, took part in the Council of Quierzy held against Gottschalk in 849. Ordained by Ebbo, he was deprived of his rank at the Council of Soissons in 853. Later summoned by Charles the Bald, he instructed the king’s son Carloman at the royal court. There he seems to have entered into friendship with John Scotus. In 865 Pope Nicholas I restored to their former ranks the clerics ordained by Ebbo. Shortly afterward Wulfadus, through the favor of Charles the Bald, obtained the archbishopric of Bourges. He died in 876. On this subject see Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. III, and *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 477. The time at which John Scotus’s *Book on Predestination* was composed is readily inferred. Likewise, the poem printed below as number I refers to the war between Charles the Bald and Louis, king of Germany. When the other writings of John Scotus were composed is not known.

If the ancient catalogues of John Scotus’s writings are to be trusted, many of his works are missing, either lost or lying hidden in libraries. From these catalogues, therefore, I wish to record here those works that are not listed among the testimonies of Thomas Gale printed below.

Vincent of Beauvais (+1264), in the *Historical Mirror*, book XXV, chapter 42, under the heading “On the empire of Charles the Bald and the writings of John Scotus,” reports the following:

> At this time John Scotus flourished, a man of penetrating intellect and honeyed eloquence. Long before, when the din of wars was resounding everywhere, he had crossed over to France to Charles the Bald. At Charles’s request he translated the *Hierarchy of Dionysius the Areopagite* from Greek into Latin, word for word. He also composed a book which he entitled, in Greek, *peri physeōs merismou*, that is, *On the Division of Nature*, a work highly useful for resolving questions, provided that one pardons him in certain matters in which he departed from the path of the Latins while fixing his eyes intently upon the Greeks. In succeeding years he was attracted to England by Alfred’s generosity and came there; at the monastery of Malmesbury he was, as the story goes, pierced with writing-styles by the boys whom he taught, and was regarded as a martyr. His epitaph was as follows:
>
> John, the holy sophist, lies enclosed in this tomb,
>
> Who, while still alive, was enriched with wondrous doctrine.
>
> At last, by martyrdom, he deserved to ascend
>
> To Christ’s kingdom, where all the saints reign forever.
>
> These verses are rough and lack the polish of a modern age.
>
> He adds: This John Scotus the philosopher, as Lanfranc says, was unsound in the faith. Hence his book on the Eucharist was read and condemned at the Synod of Vercelli, held under Pope Leo IX, in the same year in which Lanfranc purged himself of Berengar’s error. This same John also wrote a commentary on the *Hierarchy of Dionysius.

I was unable to consult the forty-sixth book of Helinand’s chronicle, whom Vincent cites as his authority. Helinand’s chronicle was published by Bertrand Tissier in the *Library of Ancient Writers of the Cistercian Order*. Antoninus of Florence (+1459), in his chronicle, section IX, chapter 2, title XVI, § 3, reproduces Vincent word for word.

Trithemius (+1516), explicitly distinguishing between two John Scotuses, one of whom he says was Bede’s disciple, was, in my opinion, misled by the passage of Vincent of Beauvais who, in the same work, book XXIV, confused everything when he wrote:

> Four monks, disciples of Bede—namely Rabanus and Alcuin, Claudius and John Scotus—were the founders of this school at Paris.

However one understands these words, they do not accord with the truth. Trithemius therefore reports the following in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, Frankfurt edition, 1601, p. 252:

> John Scotus, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, formerly a pupil and disciple of Bede the monk and most renowned teacher, and a colleague of Albinus, came with him from Britain into Gaul and was held in high esteem by the Emperor Charles the Great. Since he was learned in every kind of writing, he published, in distinguished language, distinguished little works, of which the following are reported: three books on the Gospel of Matthew; one book on human duties; one book on the division of Nature. He also composed many other works that have not come to my notice. He flourished in the time of the Emperor Charles the Great, in the year of Our Lord 800.

Then, on p. 254 of the same work, he adds:

> John, called Erigena, a monk learned in the divine Scriptures and most highly educated in the disciplines of secular learning, fully instructed in Greek and Latin eloquence, subtle in intellect and composed in speech, at the command of Charles, son of Louis and brother of the Emperor Lothair, translated into Latin the *Hierarchy* and the books of Dionysius, four books. He wrote four books upon them, and certain other works. He flourished under the Emperor Lothair, in the year of Our Lord 850.

Likewise, in his *Book on Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book II, chapter 27, under the heading “On John Scotus,” he relates:

> John Scotus, a monk, in England a pupil of the venerable priest Bede, companion and colleague of the aforementioned Lord Alcuin, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and magnificently instructed in secular literature, wrote works of no contemptible value for reading, of which few have come to my notice: four books on the Gospel of Matthew; one book on human duties; and many others. He flourished in the year of Our Lord 780, under Charles.

In the same work, book III, chapter 212, he appended the following notice:

> On Saint John Scotus the martyr: John Scotus, a monk of Malmesbury in England, a learned man of religious conduct, whom we also mentioned in the second volume, was held in high esteem by the Emperor Charles the Bald. At last he was crowned with martyrdom and passed from death to life. For he was pierced with the writing-styles of the boys whom he taught, at the instigation, I do not know of whom; after his death he became famous for many miracles. I read in a certain writing that he was bishop of Mecklenburg under the archbishop of Bremen. His feast is celebrated on 10 November. He flourished in the year of Our Lord 880, under Charles the Bald, and lived for many years after him. Others maintain that he flourished under Henry IV, in the year of Our Lord 1060. But the former opinion seems to me more consistent with the chronicles and therefore more probable—unless perhaps there were two men, killed at different times by the same kind of martyrdom.

John Bale (+around 1560), who likewise distinguishes two John Scotuses, reports the following in his book entitled *Summary of the Writers of Greater Britain*, 1548, fol. 57:

> John of Mailros, Scot by surname and by nation, colleague of Alcuin and formerly, together with him, a disciple of the venerable Bede, was also a frequent hearer while he was teaching the liberal arts at Cambridge. Since he was extraordinarily skilled in both languages, Latin and Greek—as nearly all historians report with unanimous testimony—he crossed the Ocean with the English merchants, taking with him Claudius Clement, a man of equal learning, and reached Paris. There, when he had appeared publicly in the marketplace among the others, and had brought from his homeland nothing except the liberal disciplines, he loudly proclaimed, together with his companion, that he professed wisdom and had it for sale.
>
> When King Charles, surnamed the Great, heard this, he provided what was necessary and immediately retained them, so that they might generously educate the young noblemen of the Franks who flocked to them from every direction. The frequent gathering of those who came there caused Paris at once to possess a very celebrated school. At Alcuin’s urging Charles decreed that henceforth there should be a general study of the liberal arts there, that Claudius should preside over it, and that John should go to Pavia, so that he might establish the beginnings of a school there as well.
>
> At the request of his students, John composed, in elegant language, highly distinguished works, especially these: three books on the Gospel of Matthew; one book on human duties; one book on divine offices; one book on the division of Nature; one book on the Germans according to Irenicus; one book of commentaries on the Scriptures; one book of learned homilies. I have no doubt that he composed many more than these. His book *On the Division of Nature* is useful for resolving questions, but, according to Antoninus, it greatly displeased the Papists because in many matters he agrees with the Greeks against their unsound doctrines.
>
> In the year of our redemption 792, Charles placed him in charge of the monastery of Saint Augustine at Ticinum, or Pavia; some believe that he eventually died there as an old man, while Solvathius was ruling the Scots. It is sufficiently clear from these statements that Alcuin and John were among the most learned of the English.
>
> Then, on fol. 64, he relates the following about our John Scotus:
>
> John Patricius, otherwise Erigena, British by nation, that is, a Welshman of England, born in Menevia, the city of the Demetians, or at Saint David’s, of a patrician father, is called a philosopher by most writers, but by others—incorrectly—a Scot. When the Danes were harassing the English with raids and wars, and everything there was filled with upheaval, he undertook a long pilgrimage all the way to Athens and spent many years laboring over Greek, Chaldaic, and Arabic writings. For he visited every place and school of the philosophers, even the oracle of the sun itself, which Aesculapius had built for himself. There he humbly served a certain exceedingly abstemious man, so that under his guidance he might investigate all the secrets of philosophy.
>
> At last, having discovered what he had sought through such very long labor, he returned to Italy and Gaul. There, because of his astonishing learning, he was welcomed by Charles the Bald and, after him, by Louis the Stammerer. In the year of Our Lord 858 he translated into Latin the books of Dionysius the Areopagite on the celestial Hierarchy, which had then been sent from Constantinople.
>
> Some time afterward he went to Britain and became a monk in the monastery at Menevia, which is said to stand at the shrine of David, in the farthest borders of Wales. But he could not remain hidden there for long. Summoned from there by Alfred, king of the English, he was appointed tutor both to Alfred himself and to his children. At Alfred’s urging, besides the other monuments of his learning, he translated from Greek into three languages—Chaldaic, Arabic, and Latin—the *Moral Works of Aristotle*, or *On the Secrets of Secrets*, concerning the proper governance of princes, a most exquisite work. With this outstanding man, or with this kind of star of genius, Alfred adorned his academy at Oxford, then newly begun. John was the first publicly to teach the liberal arts there.
>
> This John, exceedingly sharp in intellectual subtlety, wrote several works in which he discussed certain matters of our religion with the greatest precision, especially: one book *On the Immaculate Mysteries*; one book *On Faith against the Barbarians*; one book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*; one book *For the Education of the Sons of Noblemen*; one book of translations of Dionysius; nine books of Aristotle’s *Moral Works* [I have not left the passage or title].
>
> Four books of commentaries on the *Hierarchy*; one book on *Mystical Theology*; one book of paraphrastic volumes; one book of letters to various persons; one book on the doctrines of the philosophers; and still other works.
>
> In his book on the Eucharist he confessed his faith from the Scriptures, thinking and teaching precisely what he had learned from the Bible and Augustine, and what he knew the priest Bertram had taught in Gaul. That book was later condemned at the Synod of Vercelli by Leo IX, Roman pontiff, because it opposed their profit.
>
> At last, in the monastery of Malmesbury, to which he had withdrawn for recreation, he was killed while reading by certain pupils with daggers, in the year of Christ 884, perhaps not without the instigation of the monks, although afterward they numbered him among the martyrs of the Church. Nearly all historians are deceived who declare that this man and the preceding John Scotus of Mailros were one and the same, blinded by the closeness of the times and by the similarity of their names and learning. The watchful Argus, or the clear-sighted reader, will see that it is not sufficiently consistent that he should have heard Bede and lived to this age, unless at least one hundred and seventy years are granted to him.

After the apostate Bale, hear Leslie, bishop of Ross (+1593), distinguished for steadfastness and sincerity of faith. In his book entitled *On the Origin, Customs, and Deeds of the Scots*, book X, Rome 1578, p. 188, he wrote the following about John Scotus:

> John Scotus, a man most learned in divine matters, brought great distinction to our nation. After spending many years at Athens in Greek studies, he was summoned from there into Gaul by Louis, Emperor of the Romans. Besides the other monuments of his learning, at the command of Louis Augustus himself he rendered the *Hierarchy of Saint Dionysius* into Latin. The work survives, illuminated by the commentaries of Hugh of Saint Victor, the theologian.
>
> Shortly afterward he was sent by Charles III as ambassador to England, to Alfred, king of the English, in order to congratulate that excellent prince on having, after his victory over the Danes, made peace with the Scots and the Franks. Because of his exceptional learning, Alfred made him his guest and appointed him tutor to the royal children.
>
> Later, while teaching divine and human letters to a large audience in the monastery of Malmesbury, certain utterly corrupt young men, whose insolence and depravity of conduct he had rebuked too sharply, killed him by stabbing him with daggers. By the authority of the supreme pontiff, the king piously arranged that he should be numbered among the martyrs of Christ and that an imposing monument should be erected to him in the same monastery.

## § 23

These testimonies, whatever their worth, seemed to us worth adding. The errors scattered through John Scotus’s surviving books rest either upon the writings of Pseudo-Dionysius or were drawn from similar Neoplatonic books, of which the Parisian libraries seem to have supplied him with some abundance. Occasionally he also cites the false opinions of Origen. Among the Greek Fathers he adduces Saints Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory of Nazianzus, and Saint Basil; among the Latins, Augustine and Ambrose, in defense of his own positions. Nor were there lacking contemporary theologians who, imbued with the sound teaching of the holy Fathers, vigorously and learnedly attacked the philosophical method that he repeatedly proclaimed for resolving theological questions—a method wholly opposed to the character of theological learning in his age. It is established from the controversy over predestination that Prudentius of Troyes and Florus of Lyons belonged to this number.

For the rest, John Scotus himself reveals that he was a man of lofty intellect, rare acumen, extensive learning, and remarkable fluency in speech. Among ancient authors he praises Cicero, Virgil, Horace, Pliny, Boethius, and others. It is regrettable that he made so little use, for the benefit of the Church, of the gifts of mind in which he excelled.

Oudin discusses John Scotus more fully in his *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Erigena,” and in the *Literary History of France*, vols. IV and V. The following separate works on John Scotus should be mentioned: Peder Hjort, *John Scotus Erigena, or On the Origin of a Christian Philosophy and Its Sacred Calling*, Copenhagen 1823; Franz Anton Staudenmaier, *John Scotus Erigena and the Learning of His Age*, Part I, Frankfurt am Main 1834; M. Saint-René Taillandier, *Scot Erigène and Scholastic Philosophy*, Strasbourg and Paris 1843; Nic. Möller, *John Scotus Erigena and His Errors*, Mainz 1844; *A Dissertation on John Scotus Erigena*, Bonn 1845. We have arranged for this latest dissertation, written in Latin, to be placed before this edition.

## § 24

It remains for me to state that the manuscripts I used are indicated at the beginning of each individual book. The abbreviations I have employed are customary. In those books that I edited first, I followed the scribal hand scrupulously; in the variant readings I even retained the dots placed above or below the letters, which are signs of erasure. In this matter I wished to be more scrupulous than negligent. I corrected the first sixteen sheets at Paris; I was able to read through the remainder, which had been sent to Bonn, only once. If typographical errors should occur here and there in this work, so full of labor and hardship, I ask that you excuse them kindly.

“Through the foreign city and through the chaos” [Greek: *Dia tēs poleōs tēs allotrias kai tou chaous*].

The reading *fulica*, which, in book III, chapter 42 of *On the Division of Nature*, below, column 748, I conjectured too hastily, I now retract: the manuscript reading, with a single letter changed, *loligo*, should be retained. On this fish see Pliny.

Finally, the passage “Whether it passes through daily tides or ebbs, whether *malinas* or *ledones*” in book V, chapter 3 of *On the Division of Nature*, below, column 874, where I suspected corruption, is sound—whether one writes *ledones* on the authority of the Paris manuscripts, or, with Gale’s first edition, *lidunas*. For the words *malina* and *ledo*, or *liduna* or *leduna*, signify “the lunar increases and decreases of the Ocean”; such is the testimony of Du Cange in his *Glossary* and of Scaliger in his notes to Varro’s *On the Latin Language*, book IV, Bipont edition, vol. II, p. 52. See also Forcellini’s lexicon, under *liduna*, and Fabri’s *Thesaurus*.

Lastly, although the letters of Pope Hadrian II, being unrelated to our purpose, have been appended at the end, I did not wish to oppose the request of the purchaser who asked for them.

And these, kind reader, are the things I had to say. If anything among them seems plausible to you,

> Give your hand; or, if it is false, gird yourself against it.

Bonn, 21 September 1852.

[Col. 0001]

# A DISSERTATION ON JOHN SCOTUS ERIGENA, BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

[Note: Published at Bonn by Adolph Marcus, 1835.]

# ON THE LIFE AND TEACHING OF JOHN SCOTUS ERIGENA. PART ONE

## CHAPTER I. Where and when John Scotus Erigena was born

[Col. 0001A]

Since it seemed necessary to discuss first the homeland of John Scotus Erigena, the authorities on these matters usually provide little certainty about it, since they diverge in different directions. Some say that he was born in Ireland; others assert that England was his homeland; and there are even those who scarcely hesitate to think of that land which we now call Scotland. In the midst of such great variety of opinion, we shall try to set forth what, in our judgment, appears to bear the greatest appearance of truth: following the very oldest writers and assisted, moreover, to a considerable degree by the conjecture of Thomas Gale of Oxford.

[Note: John Scotus Erigena’s five long-desired books *On the Division of Nature*. An appendix from the *Ambigua* of Saint Maximus, in Greek and Latin, is added. Oxford, from the Sheldonian Theatre, 1681. Testimonies of the ancients concerning John Scotus Erigena are found on p. 5 and following.]

[Col. 0001B]

It was formerly customary for people to have a surname derived from their homeland, and the same practice was followed in our subject’s case. For his familiar name, John Scotus Erigena—or Eriugena—undoubtedly contains two additions intended to indicate his homeland. We shall first examine the former. That he was called Scotus because he was a Scot, that is, a member of the Scottish people, is certain, since contemporary authors, and the most authoritative among them, repeatedly testify that he was Scottish by nation.

Indeed, Pope Nicholas I, in a letter concerning our subject to Charles the Bald, writes: “John, a Scot by birth.”

[Note: See Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History of the Ninth and Tenth Centuries*, dissertation XIV, § 4 at the end. Gale, in the work cited, *Testimonies*, pp. 6 and 8.]

Pardulus, bishop of Laon, who likewise mentions our subject, says: “We compelled that Scot who is in the king’s palace—Charles the Bald’s—John by name, to write.”

[Note: See Gale, in the work cited, *Testimonies*, p. 5. This same passage of Pardulus, from a letter written by him to the church of Lyons, appears in the *Book of the Church of Lyons on Three Letters*, chapter 39. See *Maxima Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, Lyons edition, vol. XV, p. 688A.]

Precisely the same is asserted by those who call him “Scotigena.” They are Hincmar, archbishop of Reims,

[Note: See Hincmar, *On the Predestination of God and Free Will*, chapter 31.]

and Anastasius the librarian.

[Note: See the fragment of a letter written by Anastasius to Charles the Bald in Gale, in the work cited, *Testimonies*, p. 8.]

[Col. 0002A]

Since, then, our John was Scottish by nation, and since everyone agrees on this point at least concerning his homeland, we think it must be admitted without hesitation that it was in those islands which we call by the name of Great Britain. It follows naturally that John was born in some part of Great Britain in which Scottish people had their dwelling at that time. Those regions were chiefly Ireland, Scotland, and Wales.

The matter of Ireland and Scotland is too well known to require explanation.

[Note: See Thomas Moore, *History of Ireland*, vol. I, chapters 6 and 7; Isidore, *Origins* XIV, 123; Bede the Venerable, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* I, 1; Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 206; *New Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, by M. L. Ellies du Pin, vol. VII, p. 77, note a.]

A few words, however, should perhaps be said about Wales. Although in that land people distinct from the Scottish nation established a separate and definite settlement, we nevertheless think, on the basis of the strongest arguments, that Scots also settled there with them and lived there at the time when our subject was born.

[Col. 0002B]

First, it is self-evident that this western coast of England, called Wales, because it lay close to the Scots—a people so restless and warlike, who had inhabited Ireland even before the birth of Christ—had already, for many centuries before our John, frequently been visited by Scots, whether through warfare or migration. Nor do we search fruitlessly for evidence of this among the historians of Ireland.

[Note: See Thomas Moore, in the work cited.]

Was it not inevitable, when such opportunities arose, that Scottish people should remain here and there throughout Wales and establish homes for themselves? Furthermore, there is no doubt that in the course of time the people of the Picts, having departed from Scotland, settled within the borders of Wales and became the ancestors of those very Welsh who still exist.

[Note: See Thomas Moore, in the work cited.]

Since it is established from the historical books that the Scots were extremely closely connected with the Picts and joined themselves to them as faithful companions in their migrations and wars,

[Note: See Thomas Moore, in the work cited—at this point see Bede the Venerable, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* I, 1—pp. 174 ff., 180, 273.]

there can certainly be no doubt that Scots also inhabited Wales together with the Picts and, while retaining their own name as Scots, lived among the Picts.

[Col. 0003A]

Nor is the chronology inconsistent with our reasoning. These events took place around the year 600 after the birth of Christ,

[Note: See Thomas Moore, in the work cited.]

and our John, so far as we have discovered, was born around the year 800 after the birth of Christ, without the inhabitants of Wales having changed during that period.

It remains to cite the authority of Thomas Gale, who, seeking to prove the same point as we do, explicitly says that “the Scots at some time occupied the borders of the Welsh,”

[Note: See Thomas Gale, in the work cited, p. 10.]

as is stated in the book of the church of Llandaff and in Gerald of Wales.

From what has been set out, it is apparent that those who maintain that Ireland, Scotland, or even England was our subject’s homeland may all be judging correctly, although he was Scottish by nation. We must now examine each position separately.

Those who wish our John to have been born in Ireland use several arguments.

[Note: See *Literary History of France*, by the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, vol. V, p. 416; Du Pin, *New Library*, in the work cited, namely vol. VII, p. 77; Thomas Moore, in the work cited, vol. I, chapter 13; German translation, vol. I, p. 354, and elsewhere.]

We shall present their substance in order and examine it carefully at the same time.

The first argument is that John was Scottish by birth, while Ireland at that time was the proper dwelling-place of the Scots. This argument collapses as soon as one considers that Scots also lived in Scotland and Wales at that time.

Next they cite Saint Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, who lived at the same time as John and, speaking of him, says: “Ireland sent you, alone of all, the sharpest-witted man, to Gaul.”

[Note: See Thomas Gale, in the work cited, *Testimonies*, p. 5; he takes this passage from Saint Prudentius’s book *Against the Scot on Predestination*, chapter 14. See *Maxima Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, Lyons edition, vol. XV, p. 534E. Here Saint Prudentius contrasts “the Irish learning of Erigena” with “his own Celtic eloquence,” although, as he himself says of himself, he was

> Born in the West, brought forth and raised among the Celts.

See *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 240, and Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. III, p. 6.]

But not even from this does anything follow except that John came from Ireland to Gaul; it in no way proves that he was also born in Ireland. Perhaps, however, you will think that we have interpreted Saint Prudentius’s words too literally. We do not refuse to grant more than that. John may perhaps have devoted himself to letters for a long time in Ireland and, having thus been educated by the Irish, gone to Gaul. We shall show below that this appears in fact to have happened.

[Note: In chapter II.]

This concession of ours will fully satisfy the words of Saint Prudentius. Certainly a certain Mark was repeatedly called an Irishman although he had been educated in Ireland and was British by nation, as Eric of Auxerre writes about him at the end of book I of *The Miracles of Saint Germanus*.

[Note: See Thomas Gale, in the work cited, *Testimonies*, p. 6. Eric’s book appears in P. Labbe’s *Manuscript Library*, vol. I.]

A third argument remains, to which the authorities usually attribute considerable weight.

[Col. 0004A]

Thomas Moore indeed thinks it possesses such force that it can almost overcome the weight of any opposing argument. C. B. Schlueter also says:

[Note: See J. Scotus Erigena, *The Five Books on the Division of Nature*, revised and corrected edition, Münster in Westphalia, 1838, p. 3.]

> Thomas Moore relies, in confirming his position, upon “the most certain arguments.”

They argue as follows:

> Ireland was the homeland of our John because there could have been no other reason for his bearing the surname Erigena than that he was born in Erin, that is, Ireland.

We have therefore reached the second surname of our John, which, as we already noted above, is supposed to indicate his homeland.

We concede that this surname appears to have been bestowed upon John from his homeland, since all learned men, from ancient times onward, have agreed entirely on this point. We deny that it appears to have been derived from Erin as his homeland; indeed, since the first two arguments did not show that John was born in Ireland, we think that this argument rather shows that he was not born in Ireland.

[Note: *Erigena* is merely a corrupted form of the name *Jerugena*, meaning “originating from the island of the saints,” namely Ireland. Therefore the more extensive discussion of the surname *Erigena* at this point appears wholly groundless and should be rejected. See our Prooemium. —Editor’s note.]

First, one may rightly wonder why he should have been called by the semi-barbarous term *Erigena* rather than by the purely Latin *Hibernigena*. Furthermore, as the highly learned Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, already observed, from *Erin* there should have been formed not *Erigena* but *Erinigena*. Some do say that John was also called *Eringena*, but their conclusion lacks all authority, since, so far as we have discovered, no one before Trithemius spoke of *Eringena*. It is also sufficiently clear from Thomas Gale that in the earliest times John was called nothing other than *Erigena* or even *Eriugena*.

[Col. 0004C]

[Note: See Thomas Gale, in the work cited, *Testimonies*, p. 9.]

For Thomas Gale writes in the work cited:

> All manuscript codices, as though with one voice and consistently, display either *Erigena* or *Eriugena*.

[Note: I can scarcely believe that *Erigena* is read in the ancient codices. What the manuscripts we ourselves examined contain may be read in our Prooemium. —Editor’s note.]

And:

> In ancient books he is more often called *Eriugena* than *Erigena*. Certainly, in a manuscript of extreme antiquity now preserved in the library of Trinity College, Cambridge, which Archbishop James Ussher and I also used, he is written *Eriugena*, not *Erigena*. So too Suffridus Petri found it in his copies; so Dionysius Petavius found it in his; and so Philip Labbe.

[Note: In the “most ancient” books, that John is called *Erigina* was neither taught by Thomas Gale nor does it seem at all probable. In the most ancient codices he is called *Jerugena*; in others, from the eleventh or twelfth century, *Eriugena*. I have nowhere found the name *Erigena* in the codices. —Editor’s note.]

Finally, everyone agrees that in our subject’s time many men from Ireland came to Gaul, flourishing greatly in the reputation of their learning; yet you will find no one who was called *Erigena*. All were called either Scots, Irish, or Scots-Irish.

[Col. 0005A]

Eric of Auxerre writes to Charles the Bald:

[Note: See Thomas Moore, in the work cited, I, 13.]

> Why should I mention Ireland, which, disregarding the danger of the sea, migrates with almost its entire troop of philosophers to our shores?

The same matter may be investigated in James Ussher, archbishop of Armagh, in the preface to his collection of Irish letters. For this highly learned man lists many Irishmen who became known for their learning during the times of Charlemagne, Charles the Bald, and Alfred the Great. Yet no one has been found who was surnamed *Erigena* because of his Irish homeland.

We therefore regard it as absolutely certain that John was not surnamed *Erigena* in order to indicate that he was “born from Erin.”

[Note: Above we said “born in Erin”; a more precise grammatical form requires “born from Erin.” Compare *anguigena*, “born of a snake”; *alienigena*, “born of a foreign land”; *Latonigena*, “born of Latona”; and so forth.]

Rather, the surname *Erigena* came to him from elsewhere.

[Col. 0005B]

When learned men understood this, they began to inquire whether some traces could be discovered from which the name *Erigena* might appear to have been derived.

Everyone has now concluded—and we approve the conclusion—that the name *Erigena*, no less than the name *Scotus*, relates to the explanation of our subject’s origin. Thus, since the name *Scotus* indicates his nation and consequently his homeland, the name *Erigena* indicates the region itself, or the town itself, in which he first saw the light of this world.

Following this reasoning, G. Mackenzie attempted by conjecture to establish that Scotland was John’s homeland.

[Note: See G. Mackenzie, *Lives and Characters of Scottish Writers*, Edinburgh, 1708, folio, vol. I, p. 49.]

For in Scotland there is a town called Ayr, which may perhaps have produced John, since the name *Erigena* could easily have been derived from the name of that town.

[Col. 0005C]

This, then, is everything that learned men have brought forward in order to claim John for Scotland as his homeland. But until something more certain or more probable is found, we do not think that anyone can readily rest satisfied with it.

Since we see that nothing has been brought forward either from Ireland or from Scotland, Thomas Gale brought evidence from Wales. His opinion is approximately this: the name *Erigena* is not a compound, but is simply derived from the name of his birthplace. He discusses that birthplace as follows:

[Note: See Thomas Gale, in the work cited, *Testimonies*, p. 10.]

> Ergene is a considerable part of Herefordshire, bordering Wales; indeed, at this time it was one of the kingdoms of Wales, tributary to Alfred. In this district I find a place called Eriuven,

[Col. 0006A]

> a word that differs little from *Eriugen*

[Note: It should be noted here that, as we showed above, our subject is called *Eriugena* as well as *Erigena* in the most ancient books. This matter is certainly of the greatest importance.

[Note: That John is called *Erigina* in the “most ancient” books was neither taught by Thomas Gale nor does it seem at all probable. In the most ancient codices he is called *Jerugena*; in others, from the eleventh or twelfth century, *Eriugena*. I have nowhere found the name *Erigena* in the codices. —Editor’s note.]]

[Note: That John is called *Erigina* in the “most ancient” books was neither taught by Thomas Gale nor does it seem at all probable. In the most ancient codices he is called *Jerugena*; in others, from the eleventh or twelfth century, *Eriugena*. I have nowhere found the name *Erigena* in the codices. —Editor’s note.]

> —and, in contracted form, *Ergene*. Today the entire land is called by the Welsh themselves *Erynug*, or *Ereinuc*. Anyone who observes how many changes usually occur when other barbarous words are twisted into conformity with the Latin norm will not begrudge me these slight variations in this word. Indeed, the book of the church of Llandaff in volume III of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, and Gerald of Wales in his *Description of Wales*, will provide fuller information about this little region. The latter notes that it was part of the diocese of Menevia.

[Note: It may therefore be that some truth lies behind the belief of Bulaeus (*Universal History of Paris*, vol. I, p. 609) and Wood (*History and Antiquities of Oxford*, p. 15), who, on the authority of Bale and Pits, think that the town called Saint Menevia, or the Shrine of David, was John’s birthplace. We shall show below, in chapter V, that little confidence can be placed in these authorities when they report on John Scotus Erigena.]

> This same little province is also mentioned in the *Domesday Book*, where I read as follows: “These were the customs of the Welsh in the time of Edward the Confessor in Archenefeld, that is, Ergene.”

We therefore believe that no one will fail to approve this conjecture concerning the homeland of Scotus [Col. 0006B]. At any rate, it appeals to us so strongly that, since we seem unable to extract anything else that comes closer to probability, we think we should rest content with it at this point. [Note: [Col. 0005D] Please refer back to what we have just noted concerning the name *Jerugena*, or *Erigena*, and also to what is discussed above in our Prooemium concerning this chapter. **EDITORIAL NOTE.**] We do so all the more willingly because we see that the very learned Dr. C. F. Hock likewise holds this opinion, whose judgment ought to carry great weight with us. [Note: [Col. 0006D] Cf. his short work on J. Scotus Erigena, found in the *Bonn Journal*, fascicle XVI, pp. 33–57.]

It remains for us now to consider the time at which John was born. Although the ancient authors have written nothing explicit even on this subject, there are nevertheless indications from which at least something may be inferred. For his period of conspicuous distinction in learning can be established with some degree of certainty.

[Col. 0006C] We possess several verses composed by him [Note: [Col. 0006D] Cf. *Acts of the Saints of the Order of St Benedict*, Part II, p. 512.], which, since they mention John VIII, the Supreme Pontiff [Note: [Col. 0006D] It may be questioned whether the Pope John VIII praised in these verses is actually meant; nor are there arguments by which one could establish this. **EDITORIAL NOTE.**], cannot have been written before the end of the year 872 after the birth of Christ. Yet, apart from the fact that he seems to have died approximately in the year 875, as may be inferred with some degree of probability from the letter written by Anastasius the Librarian to Charles the Bald concerning our John [Note: [Col. 0006D] Cf. Nat. Alex., *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. VI, dissertation on J. Scotus Erigena, § 1, VI.], there is no demonstrable evidence whatever— as we shall show below (chapter V)—that he lived beyond approximately the year 875.

Furthermore, it is sufficiently well established that by approximately the year 850 our John had become known throughout Gaul for such distinction in learning [Col. 0007A] that, during the controversy among eminent men concerning predestination, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, and Pardulus, bishop of Laon, induced him to set forth his own judgment on the matter in writing [Note: [Col. 0007D] Cf. above, col. 1, note c.]. Scotus’s book on predestination appeared in the year 851 [Note: [Col. 0007C] Cf. Nat. Alex., *Ecclesiastical History*, ninth–tenth centuries, dissertation V, § VI, no. VII; *Literary History of France*, vol. V, middle of p. 422, end of p. 248, middle of p. 229.]. To this must be added the fact that Scotus, as we shall show in chapter III, had certainly already translated the books of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite from Greek into Latin at the command of Charles the Bald before 850. But if anyone carefully weighs this matter itself, he will, we think, readily concede that John had probably already been in Gaul for several years before 850.

This conclusion is strengthened extraordinarily by the fact that St Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, had, as we seem able to affirm beyond doubt, already entered into close friendship with our John before 847, while residing at the court of Charles the Bald himself. In his book entitled *On Predestination against J. Scotus* (Erigena)—a book provoked by the very work of John Scotus on predestination that we have mentioned—St Prudentius addresses him as a man bound to him by an already long-standing intimacy. At the very beginning of the book [Note: [Col. 0007D] Cf. *Maxima Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, vol. XV, p. 468D.] he says:

> “John, I received your blasphemies, after reading through that book of your perversity, all the more painfully because I embraced you with greater intimacy and loved you with a particular affection,”

and at the end of the same book [Note: [Col. 0007D] Cf. the same work, p. 592B] he writes:

> “Having written these things in the name of God, according to the capacity of my weakness and also for the sake of your correction, Brother John, I gladly make a brief note of each point.”

Now St Prudentius, brought as a small child from his native Spain into Gaul and educated there, lived for several years at the court of Charles the Bald before he was entrusted—or was to be entrusted—with the diocese of Troyes, devoting himself exclusively to literary studies [Note: [Col. 0007D] Erigena too was there. See above, col. 1, note c.]. We find that by the year 847 he had already assumed the diocese of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0007D] Cf. *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 240 ff., and the authors cited there.]. Since this is so, everyone will readily agree with Thomas Moore, who follows Lanigan in these matters, when he thinks that Erigena came to the Franks around the year 845 [Note: [Col. 0007D] Cf. his *History of Ireland*, vol. I, chapter 13. German translation, vol. I, p. 354.].

If, then, what has so far been argued concerning Scotus’s age is, as we shall readily believe, not far from the truth, his year of birth can be determined with somewhat greater certainty by consulting William of Malmesbury. He is, so far as we have discovered, the earliest author who deliberately treated Erigena’s history and whom later chroniclers, as usually happens, followed almost word for word on this matter. In two passages, which Thomas Gale transcribed in full from his “unpublished” works [Note: [Col. 0008D] Cf. Thomas Gale, the same work, testimonia, pp. 5, 7.], he clearly states that Erigena, already a mature man and equipped with every kind of learning, went to Gaul to Charles the Bald, who, because he perceived in him an extraordinary knowledge of letters, received him most graciously into his court. Nor do we have any reason to distrust William in this matter, as we shall have occasion to do in other matters below.

Since he uses nearly the same words in both places, we shall quote only the one that is especially clear [Note: [Col. 0008D] Cf. Gale, the same work, p. 7]:

> “He [Erigena], leaving his homeland, came to Francia to Charles the Bald, by whom he was received with great favor and counted among his household; and he conversed with him on serious matters as well as in jest … because the king was captivated by his extraordinary learning.”

If, then, we finally wish to determine the year we are seeking more precisely, the following points must be observed: [Col. 0008B] first, it can be shown rather that Erigena, although he was still alive toward the end of 872, died before 875 than that he lived beyond that year; second, around the year 845 he was already of mature age and equipped with every kind of learning. Once you take into account the circumstances of those times, when it was not easy for anyone before his thirtieth year to acquire such renown for learning, you will readily conclude with us that Erigena appears to have been born approximately between the years 800 and 815 after the birth of Christ.

However the matter may stand, we certainly do not fear that anyone will oppose us with Staudenmaier and Schlueter, who followed him [Note: [Col. 0008D] Cf. the book cited above, col. 4, note g, p. III.], and who maintain that Erigena was born around the year 828 [Col. 0008C], relying on the following arguments [Note: [Col. 0008D] Cf. Staudenmaier, *John Scotus Erigena and the Learning of His Age*, Part I, Frankfurt am Main, 1834, p. 126 ff.; at the bottom of p. 126, however, as is clear from what follows, “858” is mistakenly printed for “853”]:

> “Around the year 853 Erigena was already distinguished by a sufficiently great reputation”—

as we have seen, this had already happened to him several years before that date—

> “his writings breathe the youthful ardor of his mind”—

such arguments are in themselves ordinarily very weak; moreover, if we believe Hock [Note: [Col. 0008D] Cf. the book cited above, col. 6, note g.], we find the opposite in every respect—

> “and therefore it may confidently be concluded that Erigena was then, at the time in question, twenty-five years old.”

## Chapter II. John Scotus’s learning and literary culture, and from whom he acquired them

When we review only what has already been discussed concerning Scotus in the preceding chapter, it will be easy and appropriate to state that, considering the conditions of his age, he was distinguished by no ordinary learning, and indeed that among his contemporaries scarcely anyone could be found comparable to him in this respect. Scotus’s learning must now be pursued somewhat more carefully. We wish, however, to make one general observation at the outset: whatever praise is bestowed upon him here is not intended to be bestowed without taking the circumstances of his age into account.

First, we find in him a sufficiently extensive knowledge of Latin literature. He praises Boethius, Pliny, Virgil, Cicero, and others, most of whom he himself read [Note: [Col. 0009C] Cf. *On the Division of Nature* I.56; III.11; IV.7; III.34–36; I.16; I.33; II.17; III.33; I.43, 45, 8, 10, 7, 59, etc.; *On Predestination* XVIII.]. He wrote a great deal in Latin, and his prose as well as his poetry is clear, full, and almost elegant. This led people to honor him with the surname “Chrysostom” [Note: [Col. 0009C] Cf. Staudenmaier, p. 206; Gale, *Testimonia*, p. 13.].

Moreover—and this is certainly remarkable—he had acquired a knowledge of the Greek language, and not a mediocre one. It is true that he seems to have read scarcely any of the classical writers of Greece [Col. 0009B]; yet among the Church Fathers, as they are called, he knew the Greeks far better than the Latins. At least, he very frequently cites the former as witnesses and pursues them with abundant praise [Note: [Col. 0009C] He cites Plato often, although he does not seem to have examined his works himself; cf. *On the Division of Nature* III.36. If he saw any of them with his own eyes, it was Aristotle; cf. Roger Bacon apud Wood, *History of the University of Oxford* I, p. 15. See also *On the Division of Nature* II.29; III.21, 26, 27, 30, 32, 33, 34; IV.16; IV.1; II.28; IV.3; V.23; I.10, etc., etc.]. He inserted much Greek into his writings, especially those composed in a poetic genre; entire Greek verses are found in his poems [Note: [Col. 0009D] Cf. Schlueter’s edition, pp. 597, 601, 602, 603, 604, 609. (Angelo Mai, *Classical Authors*, vol. V, pp. 431, 438, 440, 441, 442, 450; below, poem II, vv. VI, VII, VIII. **EDITORIAL NOTE.**)] [Note: [Col. 0009D] Indeed, he composed entire Greek poems—uncultivated and harsh, certainly, and not testifying that he had migrated to Athens during the age of Charles the Bald—which are printed below by us. **EDITORIAL NOTE.**]. At the request of King Charles the Bald, he also translated several books of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite and the Scholia of a certain Maximus, themselves said to be spurious, from Greek into Latin [Note: [Col. 0009D] Cf. below, chapter III.].

As for those who have suspected that Erigena knew Hebrew or Syriac [Note: [Col. 0009D] Cf. *John Scotus Erigena, or On the Origin of a Christian Philosophy and Its Sacred Vocation*, by Dr Peter Hiort, Copenhagen, 1823, p. 44 ff.; Hegel, *Lectures on the History of Philosophy*, vol. III (*Complete Works*, vol. XV), pp. 160–161. [Col. 0010C] Hegel’s errors concerning Scotus are almost as numerous as his statements.], they were certainly deceived by their supposition. For it is sufficiently clear that, except for a very few matters—and those concerning Hebrew and Syriac rather than genuinely Hebrew or Syriac—he did not possess such knowledge.

In one place only [Note: [Col. 0010C] Cf. *On the Division of Nature* II.19–20.] he produces some Syriac, but in such a way that he himself indicates that he owes it to St Basil. He mentions Hebrew matters more often, but not with greater learning, since he had certainly not examined them with his own eyes. We may be referred [Note: [Col. 0010C] Cf. Hiort, the same work.] to a passage in book II, chapter 20, of *On the Division of Nature*, where we read:

> “Now the earth was invisible and unformed”—

so the Septuagint translators rendered it—

> “or, according to the Hebrew truth, ‘Now the earth was empty and void.’”

With equal justification we could be referred to several other passages [Col. 0010A]. But it is clearer than daylight how little weight these passages possess by themselves [Note: [Col. 0010C] Cf. Staudenmaier, p. 206 ff., note 5. Moreover, the very expression “Hebrew truth” undoubtedly refers to St Jerome’s version, for this was the name given to it.]. Nor are there lacking other passages in which Erigena embraces obvious errors of the Septuagint translators and of the Vulgate, without thinking at all about the “Hebrew truth” [Note: [Col. 0010D] For example, *On the Division of Nature* II.29, where he gives a thoroughly erroneous translation of Psalm 110 (Vulgate 109), verse 3.].

In book V, chapter 38, of *On the Division of Nature*, he writes:

> “Jehoshaphat is composed of Ἰαώ (*Iao*) and Καφάτ (*Kaphat*). And Ἰαώ has many interpretations: for it is interpreted as ‘visible,’ or ‘Lord,’ or ‘glory,’ or ‘existing,’ or ‘was,’ or ‘is,’ and ‘will be’; while Καφάτ is translated as ‘judgment.’”

He certainly would not have written this if he had not taken his Hebrew material from some Greek source, but had himself examined a Hebrew manuscript of the sacred Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0010D] At the very least, we think he would not have written the Hebrew name *Jehoshaphat* as *Josaphat*, following the Greeks, who lack the letter *h*, and consequently the usage of the Vulgate; nor would he have divided the name into Ἰαώ—which is not Hebrew—and Καφάτ, but into *Jeho* [*Yahweh*] and *schaphat*.]. To this may be added the fact that in *On the Division of Nature* V.2, middle, where he proposes an interpretation of the name “Cherubim,” he praises Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite and Epiphanius as the authorities for that interpretation [Col. 0010B], citing Epiphanius’s book *On Hebrew Names*.

Do not suppose, however, that by this discussion we intend to detract anything from Scotus’s praise. We did not wish to have counted among his virtues qualities that he did not possess; and it will soon become clear how this very discussion bears upon the resolution of another question concerning Scotus.
