Whatever was taught in the schools during Scotus’s time, apart from sacred Scripture, was for the most part confined within the limits of the liberal arts. Nor was there anyone among his contemporaries who extended the boundaries of those arts beyond the compendia that were then commonly in circulation. John therefore deserves praise for appearing to have become so familiar with these books [Col. 0010C] that he virtually lived in them. Certainly, although he does not name all those books in every passage, he declares everywhere in his writings that the subjects they contain were thoroughly familiar to him. It would be tedious, and we do not think it necessary, to cite individual passages as evidence of this [Note: [Col. 0010D] Anyone wishing to examine the individual passages may consult *On the Division of Nature* I.16, 22, 29, 32, 33, 39, 46, 53; III.38; V.4; especially III.34–36; and *On Predestination*, chapter XVIII.].

For above we already heard William of Malmesbury relate that Charles the Bald, “captivated by the extraordinary learning” possessed by Scotus, indulged him greatly in all matters. [Col. 0011A] One point, however, should be noted here. We have found that when our Scotus discusses mathematical subjects, he is astonishingly far removed from mathematical precision. This is true on other occasions as well, but especially in *On the Division of Nature* III.34–36, where he explains at length what he considers most probable concerning the measurement of the earth, the moon, and so forth [Note: [Col. 0011D] For this reason we also believe that Schlueter was mistaken when he says (p. III) that “King Charles the Bald called Scotus to Paris and appointed him master of mathematics ….” It must also be admitted that we have found no witness at all on whose authority Schlueter can plausibly be thought to have made this statement.].

We have therefore reached the point at which we must demonstrate what knowledge of philosophy and theology John possessed.

We are certain and fully assured that he was sufficiently familiar with all the subjects that theologians studied in that age. How devoted he was to the Greek Fathers of the Church has already been explained above, and there is no need to repeat it; nor did he neglect the Latin Fathers, although he cites their testimony less frequently [Col. 0011B]. He appears to have valued Augustine more highly and to have read him more carefully than any of the Greeks [Note: [Col. 0011D] Cf. *On the Division of Nature* I.43; IV.14, where he calls him “the most learned and most divine theologian” and “so great and so eminent a man,” adorning him with further praises and demonstrating the greatest diligence in reading him; also I.45; II.15, 20, 23, 28, 29; III.8, 16, etc., etc.].

And with what devotion did he study sacred Scripture? With what concentration of all his powers did he endeavor to explain it most carefully? We see innumerable proofs of this diligence even in the books of *On the Division of Nature* alone. Finally, there could be no other reason why, on two occasions when learned men disagreed over theological matters, he himself was compelled by the most serious men to write, as we shall soon examine in a separate discussion [Note: [Col. 0011D] Chapter IV.].

The fact that he is said to have allowed his excessively acute philosophical intellect too much authority within the limits of theology, although true, does not invalidate our judgment.

As for philosophy, all competent judges of the matter do not hesitate to award Scotus the palm above all his contemporaries. Let the celebrated J. Brucker come forward, who wrote as follows in his *Critical History of Philosophy* [Note: [Col. 0011D] Cf. vol. III, Leipzig edition, 1741, p. 614 ff.]:

> “No one in this century—the ninth—stood out more prominently for philosophical distinction than J. Scotus.”

And again:

> “He received the name of ‘wise man’ because of his extraordinarily unique knowledge of philosophy. In Scotus’s small body dwelt a great intellect—extraordinarily acute and excellent, so that no one in philosophy surpassed him in that age.”

Other men whose judgment ought likewise to carry the greatest weight with us entirely agree with these statements of Brucker, to which we could add many others equally honorable to Scotus [Col. 0011D] [Col. 0012A] [Note: [Col. 0011D] Cf. Dr Hock, the same work, p. 33 ff.; Tennemann, *History of Philosophy*, vol. VIII, part I, p. 65 ff.; the learned Benedictines of the Congregation of St Maur in *Literary History*, vol. V, p. 417, etc., etc.]. We have deliberately called as witnesses here only those who thoroughly detest Erigena’s philosophy itself.

On this point we may once again transcribe Brucker’s words, especially since they simultaneously and most clearly declare what this philosophy was—something that will be useful to us in the final part of this chapter. Brucker says [Note: [Col. 0012D] Cf. the same work, p. 621. The reason why we have preferred to use Brucker’s words rather than our own in explaining Erigena’s philosophy is, we think, obvious. Nor are we greatly troubled by the fact that one or another person wishing to hunt for verbal quibbles could easily find something to criticize in Brucker’s wording.] that Scotus’s entire philosophy comes down to this:

> “That all things whatsoever are contained in God not only radically and virtually, but also essentially; and therefore that all things have proceeded and flowed from God from eternity, have been distinguished into various classes of lower and higher, worse and better beings, and are finally destined to return to their own source and origin—that is, to God.”

Brucker also rightly writes the following about the same philosophy of Erigena [Col. 0012B] [Note: [Col. 0012D] Cf. the same work, p. 620.]:

> “Although, in its external dialectical method and its order of treatment, it resembles Aristotle, whom Scotus, being thoroughly acquainted with the Greek language, appears to have read, it nevertheless expresses in its entirety the system of the later Alexandrian Platonists, and makes it clear that he [Scotus] drew his entire metaphysics from Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite and philosophized according to the principles of those philosophers.”

Enough has now been said about Scotus’s learning. We come to the question for whose sake we inserted that entire discussion here: from what sources Scotus acquired his learning.

Although, at the time when in our judgment Erigena was born—at the beginning of the ninth century—the study of letters lay almost entirely dormant throughout Scotland and England, he could nevertheless very easily have laid the first foundations of his learning and education in either place, whether his homeland was Scotland or, as seems to us most certain, England. Asser, that very learned man whose most faithful services Alfred the Great employed in reviving literary studies, was educated and instructed in that very region [Note: [Col. 0012D] In the part, as tradition relates (cf. above, chapter I), of the diocese of Menevia; and Asser devoted himself to learning at Menevia itself. Cf. Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book XXXVIII, no. 71.], in which we have said Erigena appears to have been born. Nor is it disputed that this took place not long afterward.

But when we consider how extensive and how precise Erigena’s knowledge of subjects was, we are inevitably directed to Ireland, which in those times was both a flourishing center—almost the seat—of the best arts [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cf. Thomas Moore, *History of Ireland*, vol. I, chapter 13, German translation, vol. I, pp. 341–354.] and was visited by an almost innumerable multitude of foreigners who devoted themselves to literary studies [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cf. Thomas Moore, the same work, pp. 351, 331.].

We may therefore infer—admittedly as a conjecture, but a very certain one—that our Scotus owed to Ireland at least the substance of that more refined learning in which he excelled. There he could find teachers of Latin and Greek [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cf. Thomas Moore, the same work, p. 350, and Usher, whom he cites, in *Irish Letters*.]; there he could learn the liberal arts, theology, and, specifically, dialectical philosophy [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cf. Thomas Moore, the same work, p. 352.].

This conjecture is shown to be entirely true by the passage of St Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, which we cited above. In it this learned man, both Scotus’s contemporary and his former friend turned adversary, says to him [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cf. St Prudentius, *Against J. Scotus on Predestination*, chapter 14, *Maxima Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, Lyons edition, vol. XV, p. 534E]:

> “Ireland sent you, alone of all men, most acute, to Gaul, so that Gaul might gain through your learning what none but you could know; but far be it that Celtic eloquence should admit your obscurities.”

What could be clearer than this? In almost explicit words he confirms that Erigena was educated in Ireland and thus proceeded to Gaul.

We have just said that Scotus could have learned “dialectical philosophy” in Ireland, without mentioning philosophy itself, although, as we saw in the first part of this chapter, he was also sufficiently well versed in that. We did so because only that dialectic, in which the external form of Erigenian philosophy is visible, could have come to him from Ireland. His philosophy itself, as is made clear by Brucker’s words quoted above [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cf. chapter II, col. 12, note g.], came from elsewhere.

We shall present a striking testimony to this from Erigena himself, found in his preface to the *Scholia of St Maximus on Gregory the Theologian* [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cf. Thomas Gale, *Appendix*, p. II.]. In that passage he accurately describes in a few words the character of his entire philosophy, introducing the description as follows:

> “Perhaps I would not have entered into such dense darkness—[the darkness of] St Maximus—unless I had seen the blessed Maximus mentioned above, in the course of his work, introduce the most obscure statements of St Dionysius the Areopagite, whose symbolic and theological meanings I recently translated for you [Note: [Col. 0013D] That is, for Charles the Bald. Cf. below, chapter III.] at your command as well, and clarify them in a marvelous manner. This was to such an extent that I could not doubt that divine mercy, which illuminates the hidden things of darkness, had in its ineffable providence arranged that what in the aforementioned blessed Dionysius’s books seemed most obscure to us, or scarcely accessible and beyond the reach of our understanding, should be disclosed by the most learned Maximus through his clearest explanations. For example, to mention one of many cases, how the cause of all things …”

[Col. 0014A] From this it may now be judged sufficiently clearly from what sources Erigena’s philosophy arose, and that he first became acquainted with those books of Pseudo-Dionysius in Gaul.

At this point we must not pass over the fact that many authors habitually mention, sometimes with excessive confidence and sometimes more cautiously, the long journeys by which Erigena is said to have traversed both Greece and the East for the sake of study before he went to Gaul. We believe that these reports deserve no credence whatever. They are so far from resting on any sufficiently firm authority or other sound basis that arguments by which they can be entirely refuted may readily be brought forward.

Bale and Pitsaeus, then, who composed a “literary history of the Britons,” were, so far as we know [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cf. Brucker, the same work, p. 615; Thomas Gale, the same work, testimonia, p. 9.], the first to write about these travels [Col. 0014B]. But from Brucker and Thomas Gale [Note: [Col. 0014D] Cf. the cited passages.] we already understand that they attempted in vain to defend and affirm them.

They attach great importance to certain words which, as we read, Roger Bacon preserved as “the words of Erigena himself” in the work of Anthony Wood [Note: [Col. 0014D] Cf. *History and Antiquities of the University of Oxford*, 1674 folio, book I, p. 15.], provided that Roger Bacon did not err concerning their author [Note: [Col. 0014D] Cf. Hiort, pp. 38, 39; Staudenmaier, pp. 145–147.]. But, if we see the matter correctly, we must admit that even those words cannot necessarily be attributed to Bacon.

The passage is written as follows:

> “Roger, namely Bacon … praises him [Scotus] as a most trustworthy interpreter of languages … and further thinks that he should be credited with the fact that we possess certain genuine and authentic Aristotelian books. ‘I left no place,’ that John says, ‘nor temple in which philosophers were accustomed to compose and deposit their secret works, that I did not visit; nor did I fail to seek out any person whom I believed to possess any knowledge of philosophical writings.’”

These words, then, if they are not even Bacon’s, are still more uncertainly Erigena’s. Let them be regarded as both Bacon’s and Erigena’s. What follows from that? Do they speak of the journey we mentioned above? They will collapse once we set against them, as we are about to do, arguments that are weightier and more certain [Note: [Col. 0014D] It also appears that the distinguished Dr Hock was influenced by the words attributed to Erigena here. For, conceding this point, he writes as follows concerning the journeys (the same work, p. 35): “After great travels, which he had devoted to the search for philosophical works and to associating with the wise men of his age, he came to the court of Charles the Bald.” That is: “Having undertaken great journeys in search of philosophical works and in order to meet the wisest men of his age, he came to the court of Charles the Bald.” **EDITORIAL NOTE.**].

Finally, there are those who think that Scotus’s journey should not be called into question for the reason that we find in him knowledge of so many things which he could have learned nowhere except in the East. But we believe that we have already answered this in this very chapter. Scotus did not know Hebrew or Syriac; he could have learned Greek literature in Ireland; and we have also demonstrated from what source his philosophy flowed.

Nor does the observation made by learned men [Note: [Col. 0015D] Cf. Hock, the same work, p. 33, note 2; Ritter, *History of Philosophy*, Hamburg, vol. IV, p. 361, note 4.] that Erigena’s philosophy closely resembles that of the Indians—called the Sāṃkhya and Yoga philosophies—carry any weight. It would not be new or unheard-of if Scotus and the authors of those Indian philosophies had each independently produced their own offspring and descendants; and we know that the very philosophers whom Erigena chose as his guides and teachers plundered the treasuries of Indian philosophers to a considerable extent.

Now that we have shown how little probability there is in the reports circulated about our John’s travels, we shall briefly explain the principal reason why we consider them wholly baseless. First, we possess a fragment of a letter that Anastasius the Librarian, Scotus’s contemporary and great admirer, sent about him to Charles the Bald. In it he very clearly demonstrates that he had never heard anything about any distant journey of his. He writes [Note: [Col. 0015D] Cf. Thomas Gale, *Testimonia*, p. 8.]:

> “It is also remarkable how that barbarian man—I mean John—who, situated at the ends of the earth, could be thought as distant from human society as he was from the speech of another language, was able to grasp such things intellectually and translate them into another language.” [Note: [Col. 0015D] The reference is to the books of Pseudo-Dionysius, which Erigena translated from Greek into Latin. This gives us still less reason to doubt those who deny that he had been in Greece.]

Furthermore, St Prudentius, whom we have also heard was Scotus’s contemporary and became his adversary after having been his friend, would certainly have mentioned the East or Greece when he spoke of Ireland as Erigena’s teacher [Note: [Col. 0015D] Cf. above, col. 13, note e.], if he had known anything about those regions.

In addition, no passage whatever can be produced from Erigena’s writings in which he speaks of foreign philosophers with whom he had the opportunity to converse in person, or mentions any journey undertaken for purposes of study. He always cites authors whose books he could have examined in Ireland or Gaul.

Finally, we simply cannot understand what learning could have been acquired in Greece at that time. Even there we do not find philosophy flourishing brilliantly: Athens had fallen silent [Note: [Col. 0015D] Cf. Brucker, the same work, p. 615.].

That is enough on so trivial a matter. Let us proceed to the rest.

## Chapter III. What position Scotus held with Charles the Bald

Although Charles the Bald left much to be desired in himself that belongs to a good king, he nevertheless did not neglect the best arts for that reason [Col. 0015D]. Eric of Auxerre, who was his contemporary, adorns him with the highest praises on this subject. There is no reason to distrust those praises, although they occur in a letter written to Charles the Bald himself, since we possess considerable evidence by which they can be confirmed [Note: [Col. 0015D] Cf. Staudenmaier, the same work, pp. 151–159, who has gathered a very large body of testimonies from every source. [Col. 0016D] In describing this passage of Eric, however, we have several times departed from Staudenmaier, preferring to follow Bolland (*July*, vol. VII, pp. 221F–222A).].

Eric writes:

> “Above all, you prepare eternal remembrance for yourself by representing not merely adequately, but surpassing with incomparable ardor, the devotion of your most famous grandfather Charles toward the immortal disciplines; for what he drew forth from smoldering ashes, you advance everywhere through manifold encouragement, both through benefactions and through authority … You have made it your particular concern that, wherever in the world masters might flourish in the arts whose chief pursuit philosophy professes, your Highness might bring them from every quarter for public instruction, draw them by kindness, and invite them by generosity … What need is there to mention Ireland, which, disregarding the danger of the sea, migrates almost in its entirety, together with its whole company of philosophers, to our shores? Every one of them who is more learned willingly imposes exile upon himself, so that he may serve the most wise Solomon according to his desire …”

Among these men distinguished by their learning, some summoned and others coming voluntarily to Charles, as we see from Eric, the reputation of John Scotus certainly stood out among all the rest in later generations.

But on what grounds most modern writers say that he was summoned by Charles the Bald, we certainly do not understand. William of Malmesbury—the first, as may be inferred from Thomas Gale [Note: [Col. 0016D] Cf. Thomas Gale, the same work, testimonia, p. 5.], to have written on this matter, and the author whom Simeon of Durham, Matthew of Westminster, and others copied almost word for word—says in three places [Note: [Col. 0016D] In book V of *On the Bishops*, unpublished (Gale, *Testimonia*, p. 5); in a letter to a certain Peter (from the Thuane manuscript in Thomas Gale, the same work, p. 7); and in *The Deeds of the Kings of the English* II.4.] in nearly identical words:

> “Scotus, leaving his homeland, crossed over to Francia to Charles the Bald, by whom he was received with great favor and counted among his household …”

Moreover, in *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, he adds that, amid the clash of wars resounding everywhere, Scotus went to Gaul.

We explained in the first chapter when he seems to have withdrawn to Charles: around the year 845.

Having secured for himself a true Maecenas in this man, he is said to have made such use of Charles’s accessibility that he did not greatly trouble himself about Horace, to whom Augustus is reported to have written that he should “take for himself some measure of authority with him, as though he had been his intimate companion.” William of Malmesbury indeed says [Note: Cf. Gale, cited work, pp. 5–6]:

> “Scotus,” he says, “would discuss with him (Charles) matters both serious and amusing, and was his inseparable companion both at table and in the bedchamber. He possessed much wit and refined charm, examples of which still survive today [Note: Cf. Gale, cited work, Appendix, p. 88.], such as the following. He had taken his seat at table opposite the king, on the other side of the board. As the cups were passed around … Charles, with a rather cheerful expression, after some further incidents, saw John do something that offended French courtesy; so he reproved him wittily and said: ‘What is the difference between a *Sottus* [fool] and a *Scottus* [Scot]?’ The latter returned the familiar insult upon its author and replied: ‘Only the table!’ … The king was not angered; captivated by his extraordinary learning, he was unwilling to rise up against the Master even in words. That is what he habitually called him.
>
> “Again, when a servant had brought the king, who was dining, a dish containing two very large fish together with one small one, he gave it to the Master to divide among two clerics seated beside him. They were men of gigantic stature; he himself was extremely small in body. Then, always finding some honorable way of provoking the merriment of the diners, he kept the two larger fish for himself and distributed the smaller one between the two clerics. When the king reproved him for the unfair division, he said: ‘No, I have done well and fairly, for here is one small man’—speaking of himself—‘and two large fish,’ touching the fish; ‘and likewise, turning to them, here are two enormous, great clerics and one tiny one,’ again touching the fish.”

Thus, as we see, our John, bound to Charles by the closest intimacy, lived in the royal palace itself and amid the highest prominence of public life. Bishop Pardulus of Laon likewise bears witness to this; writing about the year 853, he said of him: “That Scot who is in the palace of King Charles, named John” [Note: Cf. Chapter I, column 9, note c.]. From this one may infer that, from the time when he came to Charles, he continued for many years to live in the royal palace. We do not know, however, whether this may be inferred with still greater certainty from those poems of Scotus that Schlueter appended to his edition of the books *On the Division of Nature*. They were certainly composed at different times and repeatedly show with the utmost clarity that he regarded himself as one who was supported by Charles [Note: Cf. Poems XI, 4; VI, 35–41; II, 69–72; I, 77–81; I, 46–77 …]. This seems also to be confirmed in the highest degree by the fact that Scotus himself says in the preface to his book *On Predestination* that, through Charles’s kindness and generosity, he had been granted the opportunity to devote to literary studies the time that others had to spend in the conduct of affairs. How long he may be thought to have remained there we shall see shortly [Note: Chapter V.], when we discuss his final fate.

Nor, as is clear from Malmesbury, do they call John the Master of Charles alone; he is also said to have presided for many years over that famous “Palatine School” [Note: Cf. Staudenmaier, cited work, p. 159, note 5, and p. 166, note 1.]. We have numerous authorities for this claim. We shall cite one whom the others followed, and whom they had good reason to follow if his testimony truly belongs to him. There is a passage in a letter written by Nicholas I, Supreme Pontiff, to Charles the Bald, in which, as many maintain, the following should be read:

> “For this reason we earnestly beg and command Your Devotion that you have the aforesaid John brought before our Apostolate, or at least that you not permit him to remain in Paris, in the School” (that is, the school), “whose head” (that is, its director) “he is reported to have been formerly …” [Note: These are the words of Nicholas I as found in Bulaeus, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. I, p. 184. He says that he took them from an ancient copy, citing “Gabriel Naudé’s *Collection from the Oxford Library*.” Yet someone has been found to accuse Bulaeus of fraud, on the ground that he himself inserted the words concerning “the Parisian School and its director Erigena.” But the fact that others who possessed only certain extracts from Nicholas’s letter did not read those words in them does not disprove Bulaeus’s good faith; nor does the fact that they read certain things that were absent from Bulaeus’s copy. For, as Staudenmaier rightly observes, Bulaeus may perhaps have possessed only extracts.]

Concerning the date on which this letter was written, Bulaeus gives: “Given in the third year of our Apostolate,” which is the year 860; others say that it was given approximately five years later. If this passage of the letter is genuinely his—and we do not doubt that it is—then our Scot, around the years just mentioned, had long since not merely participated in the literary studies of Paris but had presided over them. How long afterward he remained in that honor and position we simply do not know. Nor have we found anything written anywhere that reveals whether he was sent to Rome at Nicholas’s command. Staudenmaier (pp. 166–167) asserts that he was not sent; nor is there reason to accuse him of excessive rashness. For it is well established how dear Erigena was to his king, and that this same king had also on other occasions paid little attention to the commands of supreme pontiffs.

It remains to say a few words about certain more serious tasks that, as we learn, Charles additionally entrusted to John. There were altogether two: first, that he translate into Latin several books of Pseudo-Dionysius and the *Scholia* of a certain Maximus on Gregory the Theologian (which are likewise believed to be spurious); second, that, when a dispute over the Holy Eucharist had arisen through Paschasius Radbertus, he himself explain the matter in writing [Note: It is by no means established that Charles the Bald commissioned John to disclose his own view of the Holy Eucharist in the Paschasian controversy. What our author did in that conflict has been explained in the Preface. Editorial observation.]. The second matter will be treated in detail in the following chapter, where we shall discuss the theological controversies in which Erigena became involved; here it need only be mentioned and may otherwise be passed over. Concerning the first, what we have to say is as follows.

Michael Balbus had sent Louis the Pious several writings of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite as a gift—not, as some have thought [Note: Cf. *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 425; Hiort, cited work, p. 43; and Baronius, *Annals*, under the year 824, etc.], in the year 824, but in the year 827; nor had they been translated into Latin, as learned men likewise supposed [Note: Cf. Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXIV, no. 59; *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 425, etc.], but were in Greek. That this chronology is correct was demonstrated by the distinguished Pagi in his *Critique of Baronius’s Annals* [Note: Cf. Pagi, *Critique of Baronius’s Annals*, under the year 827, no. XIV.]. The abbot Hilduin, who himself had received them for safekeeping, removes every doubt from our minds that the books were written in Greek; he wrote of them as follows [Note: Cf. Hilduin’s letter to Louis the Pious, prefixed to the *Areopagitica* (Cologne edition). Hilduin’s passage is found in Staudenmaier, p. 163, and in Pagi at the cited place.]:

> “For we received as a great gift those authentic books, written in the Greek language …”

At that time the Gauls held these trifles in the highest esteem. They believed that they were the work of that Dionysius who had first been bishop of Athens and who was thought to have spread the divine teaching of Jesus Christ in Gaul [Note: Cf. Scotus’s poems X, XI, and XII, in Schlueter’s edition, pp. 607–609.]. Since scarcely anyone could then be found throughout Gaul who possessed not merely an ordinary but some knowledge of the Greek language, Louis therefore seems immediately to have arranged for something like a translation of these books, and to have done so through Hilduin, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis, to whom he had entrusted them for safekeeping [Note: Cf. Staudenmaier, p. 163 ff.]. Whatever the nature of this translation may have been, it is scarcely mentioned anywhere; therefore, if it existed, it could certainly not have been held in high regard [Note: Cf. Staudenmaier, pp. 163–164.].

Accordingly, Charles the Bald, who was devoted above all to learning, especially sacred learning, when he found in Erigena a man unusually skilled in the Greek language, did not think that he ought to let slip the opportunity, granted him by fortune, of finally obtaining a proper interpretation of those books. Therefore, at his command, Erigena applied himself to translating the books of Pseudo-Dionysius into Latin [Note: Cf. Erigena’s preface to his translation of the *Scholia* of Saint Maximus, in Thomas Gale’s edition of *On the Division of Nature*, Appendix, pp. II–III.]. Which books of that author he rendered into Latin Erigena himself recounts in a dedicatory letter written to Charles, which he prefixed to his Latin version of the *Areopagite* [Note: This letter was published both by James Ussher in *A Collection of Irish Letters*, Paris, 1665, 4to, p. 40 ff., and in the *Areopagitica*—that is, a collection of several ancient translations of the Areopagite—which appeared in print at Cologne in 1530 and 1536, folio.]: the books *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, *On the Divine Names*, *On Mystical Theology*, and, in addition, ten letters.

When this work had been completed, Erigena, again at the same king’s command, undertook the second task, translating the *Scholia* of Saint Maximus from Greek into Latin [Note: Cf. Erigena, at the place cited above, column 13, note g.]. Thus, when our Scot had been given access to these books—which, as we have already indicated above [Note: Compare the note cited above.], he too believed to be the works of the holy men Dionysius and Maximus—his intellect was so attracted by both the excellence of the wisdom they contained and the authority of those who had composed them that, as we explained in the following chapter, he devoted himself entirely to them and derived from their sacred philosophy the whole basis of his own.

The authors provide no clear information about the time during which he was occupied with these tasks. We believe, however, that this occurred not long after his arrival in Gaul, even before the year 850. Certainly, in his book *On Predestination*, which he composed around the year 850, he had already put forward much more and very different material [Note: To say nothing of other matters, he had already set forth in *On Predestination* the doctrine concerning sin and the punishment of sin that he owed to the Areopagite. Cf. below, Chapter IV, column 27, note c. Nevertheless, what we observed in the preceding chapter from a passage in Erigena’s preface to the *Scholia* of Saint Maximus (cf. above, column 13, note g) makes it in no way likely that he knew the books of the Areopagite before he came to Charles the Bald.] than one would suppose he could have learned solely from Irish philosophers or theologians. Moreover, since Charles, who beyond doubt ardently desired to read the Areopagite, had received Erigena as his guest, we do not think that he long remained forgetful of his Greek manuscript. Finally, as far as we know, nowhere except in that dedicatory letter prefixed to his translation of the Areopagite did Erigena indicate in any way that he had come to Gaul from elsewhere. In that place, however, he wrote:

> “This cake, filled with the sacred nectar of the Greeks, I, John the stranger, **σπένδω**—‘offer as a libation’—to my Charles” [Note: Cf. Schlueter, p. 608.].

But whatever conclusion one may reach on this matter [Note: Schlueter seems to have established that Erigena was not induced to undertake this task until after the year 855. After mentioning the Council of Valence, held in that very year (cf. Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book 34, no. 95; Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, centuries IX and X, dissertation V, § XI), he continues as follows in his edition (p. IV): “After this Charles the Bald urged Erigena to translate Dionysius” [sic]. Yet we have been unable in any way to discover where he learned even this.], Dionysius’s work was completed before the year 860 or 865. The following letter of Nicholas I, Supreme Pontiff, concerning the matter is found in Bulaeus (cf. column 25, note f):

> “Nicholas, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, glorious king of the Franks … But recently we grieved, as it was reported to our Apostolate, that a certain man named John, a Scot by nationality, had recently translated the work of Dionysius the Areopagite into Latin, although, according to the custom of the Church, it ought to have been sent to us and approved by our judgment. Especially since this same John is said long ago to have been a man of great learning, but is widely reported not to have sound judgment in certain matters … Given in the third year of our Apostolate.”

This is the year 860; but others maintain that the letter was written approximately in the year 865 [Note: Cf. Staudenmaier, cited work, p. 166, note 1.].

It is uncertain whether Nicholas I’s complaint that those books had not yet been sent to him means that they were sent afterward. We know nothing about the matter [Note: Cf. Staudenmaier, p. 166 ff.].

Several years later Anastasius the Librarian wrote to Charles the Bald as follows concerning Erigena’s translation of the Areopagite [Note: Ussher, *Irish Letters*, p. 45 ff.]:

> “It is also astonishing how that barbarian man … was able to grasp such things intellectually and transfer them into another language … But this was accomplished by that craftsman, the Spirit, who made him at once ardent and eloquent; for unless he had burned with the fire of charity through the grace of that Spirit, he would certainly never have received the gift of speaking in tongues … Since he was humble in spirit, he did not presume to abandon the exact force of the wording … Hence it came about that he entangled so great a man—Dionysius the Areopagite—in the difficulties of a certain labyrinth, and placed him, in a manner, more invisible in deeper caves; and the man whom he had undertaken to interpret he rendered still in need of interpretation.”

William of Malmesbury judges Erigena’s translation in precisely the same way, as do those who follow him, Simeon of Durham and Matthew of Westminster. Malmesbury says:

> “He translated word for word” [Note: Cf. Thomas Gale, cited work, testimony, p. 6.]. “As a result, the Latin text is scarcely intelligible, being constructed more according to Greek flexibility than according to the arrangement of our own language”—that is, Latin.

They believe that it was precisely because Erigena’s translation was so obscure that it was later consigned to oblivion, and that only a very few copies survived into something approaching our own time [Note: Cf. *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 426.] [Note: This is mistaken: numerous manuscript copies of that translation are still found in libraries today; as far as I know, it was printed only two or three times in the sixteenth century. Cf. the Preface. Editorial observation.]. It appeared in print at Cologne together with several other ancient translations of Pseudo-Dionysius [Note: Cf. above, column 19, note g.].

The other work of Erigena mentioned above—a translation of the *Scholia* on Gregory the Theologian—was published by Thomas Gale of Oxford together with the books *On the Division of Nature* [Note: Cf. John Scotus Erigena, *Five Books on the Division of Nature*. Appended is an Appendix from the *Ambigua* of Saint Maximus, in Greek and Latin. Oxford, from the Sheldonian Theatre, 1681.]. He says that he had obtained it through the efforts of John Mabillon [Note: Cf. Thomas Gale, cited work, testimony, p. 12.].

## CHAPTER IV. Erigena’s participation in the theological controversies in which he was involved

As we have already shown, there were altogether two theological battles fought in Gaul during Scotus’s time, which we shall now mention. One arose concerning predestination through Gottschalk, a monk of Orbais; the other was raised concerning the Holy Eucharist by Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of the Gallic monastery of Corbie.

In accordance with the plan of our work, however, we shall not explain those quarrels in their entirety, but only those parts that belonged to Scotus and that seem necessary for shedding light on Scotus’s own position in these matters.

Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, therefore condemned Gottschalk as convicted of the predestinarian heresy, together with the first synod held at Quierzy in the year 849 [Note: He was indeed a monk of Orbais, but not a Gaul by nationality; he was a Saxon. His father was Count Berno, of the noblest Saxon lineage. They report that Gottschalk, while still a small boy, was “offered to God” by his parents in the monastery of Fulda. Walafrid Strabo, whom he had as his closest friend, devoted himself to literary studies there together with him. Cf. Walafrid, poem in the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon edition, vol. XV, p. 231 C–G. When he grew older, weary of the monastic life, he asked Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, to permit him, since he had been brought into it unwillingly, to leave it with his consent. Otgar did not fail him in this request. But Hrabanus, abbot of Fulda (in 829), approached Emperor Louis by letter and demonstrated to him that children were bound forever by their parents’ vow. As a result, Gottschalk was forced to remain. Nevertheless, he did not wish to stay any longer in the monastery of Fulda under Hrabanus, and withdrew to the Gauls, where he concealed himself in the monastery of Orbais. Cf. Mabillon, *Annals*, book XXX, no. 30; the Magdeburg Centuries, century IX, chapters 9 and 10, Basel edition, columns 404, 543, 546.] [Note: Cf. Mansi, *New and Most Extensive Collection of the Councils*, vol. XIV, columns 919 C–922 E.]. The Second Council of Mainz, under Hrabanus, had already condemned him the preceding year; Hrabanus had been made archbishop of Mainz at that very time [Note: Cf. Mansi, cited work, columns 913 D–918 E.]. For before that council Gottschalk, who on journeys through Italy and Germany had first spoken of a twofold predestination, had been accused of this error; and that same synod had sent him, after condemning him, to Hincmar, metropolitan of the monks of Orbais [Note: Since the monastery of Orbais properly belonged to the diocese of Soissons, and only together with that diocese came under the jurisdiction of the metropolitan of Reims, Gottschalk ought to have been sent not to the archbishop of Reims but to the bishop of Soissons. Hincmar himself, however, declares in the letter sent to Nicholas I, preserved by Flodoard (cf. Flodoard, *Ecclesiastical History of Reims*, book III, chapters 12–14), why Gottschalk was judged chiefly by him rather than by the bishop of Soissons: “because Rothad, whose parish he belonged to, did not know how to resist him.” Rothad was also deprived of his bishopric (cf. *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 500).].

What judgment the Council of Mainz pronounced against Gottschalk is shown by Hrabanus’s letter, written to Hincmar after the council had concluded its deliberations on this very matter. In that letter he says [Note: Cf. Mansi, cited work, column 914 E ff.]:

> “Gottschalk came to us at Mainz introducing new superstitions and a harmful doctrine concerning God’s predestination, and leading the people into error. He said that God’s predestination exists in evil just as it exists in good, and that there are in this world certain people who, because of God’s predestination—which compels them to go to death—cannot correct themselves from error and sin, as though God had made them from the beginning incapable of correction and destined to go to destruction subject to punishment.”

The Council of Quierzy, to which Hincmarus had brought Gottschalk, whom he had had sent to him for a fresh judgment, fully ratified this decision; moreover, it inflicted the most severe punishment on that unfortunate monk because of the obstinacy he had displayed. Hincmarus recounts the matter in his book *On Predestination* [Note: Cf. Mansi, cited work, column 919 E ff.; the Church of Lyon, *Book on Three Letters*, chapter 24, in the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon edition, vol. XV, pp. 679 C–D.]:

> “Gottschalk was found, both in the city of Mainz and here, to be a heretic and incorrigible. Stripped of priestly honor … and, because of his irrevocable obstinacy … beaten with rods like a wicked man … he was confined in a prison, lest he harm others, since he had been unwilling to benefit himself.”

The pitiful punishment inflicted on Gottschalk moved people, as such things commonly do, both to pity and to indignation. And if anyone was less concerned by the matter, there arose eminent theologians who feared that Hincmarus had acted unjustly in judging Gottschalk’s doctrines to be infected with the predestinarian error.

Indeed, whatever Gottschalk’s doctrine may otherwise have been, no one could possibly infer from the words with which he explained it to the Council of Mainz, insofar as those words still survive, what both Hincmarus and Hrabanus attributed to him and condemned in him together with their synods. Hincmarus himself reports these words; and what is certainly of the greatest importance here, he reports them in his own book *On Predestination* [Note: Cf. chapter V; chapter XXI; chapter XXIV; chapter XXVII.]. He says that Gottschalk brought forward two writings at the Council of Mainz, one of which was “a confession of faith concerning predestination,” while the other was “a booklet addressed to Hrabanus” [Note: We have not wished to transcribe Gottschalk’s own words, since some allowance had to be made for brevity. They are also found in Natalis Alexander. Cf. Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, centuries IX and X, dissertation V, § III.]. He gives the former in full and quotes fragments from the latter.

These words of Gottschalk, however, do not contain the predestinarian heresy. They do not maintain that from all eternity God predestined one portion of humanity to live well and rightly, and another to act badly and wickedly; the former, consequently, to the blessedness of eternal life, and the latter to the everlasting misery of the life to come—so that nothing at all would be left to human free will. On the contrary, they state clearly enough that God predestined the impious to “eternal death,” and did not will that they be “saved forever,” but did so “on account of their evil merits,” because he “had foreknown that they would become exceedingly wicked.” Thus it seems that only the expressions used by Gottschalk could have caused offense. Yet similar expressions are also found in Saint Augustine [Note: Cf. *The City of God* XV, 1: “There is one society of human beings which is predestined to reign eternally with God, and another to undergo eternal punishment with the devil.” Ibid. XXII, 24, at the end, Tauchnitz edition, Leipzig, 1825, vol. II, p. 412: “What, then, will God give to those whom he predestined to life, since he also gave these things to those whom he predestined to death?” Such expressions are found throughout other writings of Saint Augustine as well.], and we believe that Gottschalk took his own expressions from those books. For he himself says in that writing addressed to Hrabanus [Note: Cf. above, in this column, notes a and b. John Scotus, *On Predestination against Gottschalk*, chapter XI, § 2: “Gottschalk,” he says, “is accustomed especially to refer the grounds of his abominable doctrine to Augustine.”]:

> “What ought to be held concerning free will … especially against the Pelagians … is known to have been taught more fully by Blessed Augustine. Therefore I would have preferred you, Hrabanus, to rely upon the assertions of that same teacher rather than upon the erroneous opinions of Gennadius of Massilia …”

This very matter aroused the efforts of the foremost theologians. They thought that Hincmarus, in condemning Gottschalk’s doctrine of predestination, had attacked Saint Augustine. They therefore fiercely opposed Hincmarus and his friend Pardulus, bishop of Laon, who had given him the most faithful assistance in Gottschalk’s case. Among Hincmarus’s and Pardulus’s adversaries, Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, and Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, were especially prominent [Note: Cf. *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 354; Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, centuries IX and X, dissertation V, § VI; *Maxima Bibliotheca of the Ancient Fathers*, Lyon edition, vol. XV; Gilbert Mauguin, *The Works and Many Fragments of Ancient Authors Who Wrote on Predestination and Grace in the Ninth Century*, Paris, 1650, 2 vols., 4to. In these libraries of the Fathers and in Mauguin, the individual writings of the authors we have mentioned, insofar as they survive, can readily be found; therefore we have refrained from giving more precise references.]. In their writings all of them defended the predestination of evil people as well, using nearly the same expressions as Gottschalk, since those expressions were also Saint Augustine’s. They cannot in any way be blamed on this account, since they did not wish those expressions to bear the meaning that Hincmarus and his associates attributed to them.

Hincmarus, however, was reduced almost to desperation by these writers, contrary to what he had hoped. For he understood well enough that, since the most celebrated theologians taught a predestination both of the wicked and of the good—or a twofold predestination, which he himself had condemned in Gottschalk—he would have to contend for his reputation, standing, and every distinction. He therefore thought that writers had to be opposed with writers. Thus, on Hincmarus’s side, among others, and especially our Scotus, who in published books attacked that twofold predestination [Note: We have spoken only of the twofold predestination, not of the other two questions—first, human free will; second, whether Christ died for all human beings or only for those predestined to life—which were also vigorously debated—because the former was the chief issue and, as it were, the parent of all the rest, while Scotus did not concern himself with those remaining questions.] were enlisted [Note: Cf. the Church of Lyon, *Book on Three Letters*, chapter 39, in the *Maxima Bibliotheca of the Ancient Fathers*, Lyon edition, vol. XV, p. 687 H ff.].

Scotus therefore composed his book *On Predestination against Gottschalk* and published it in the year 851 [Note: Cf. above, Chapter I, column 7, note b.]. This work of Scotus appeared in print only once; it is found in Mauguin’s book, which we shall cite below (note e).

*On Predestination* comprises nineteen chapters, preceded by a preface and followed by an epilogue; it is not a particularly large volume. As the preface states, it was sent to Hincmarus of Reims and Pardulus of Laon; Scotus writes that he had acted as the advocate of their cause.

His sole task, therefore, was to defeat with suitable arguments the twofold predestination defended by Hincmarus’s and Pardulus’s adversaries, or, failing that, to show that Gottschalk was genuinely akin to the predestinarian heresy. We shall examine somewhat more carefully how diligently he conducted himself in these matters. The other points concerning Scotus’s book, now in our hands, that seem worthy of mention will be explained afterward.

There is no doubt that Gottschalk embraced “that diabolical dogma.” For we read [Note: Cf. chapter I, § 4; chapter IV, § 1 ff., and passim.]:

> “According to Gottschalk’s doctrine, there are two predestinations in God, one of the good and another of the wicked. By the compulsion of the former, one portion of humanity is made to live rightly and reach eternal blessedness; by the inescapable necessity of the latter, another portion of mortals is made both to live wickedly and to fall into eternal misery.”

With the utmost indignation, the bitterest abuse is heaped upon Gottschalk [Note: Cf. the Preface; chapter I, §§ 2 and 4; chapter II, § 1; chapter III, §§ 4–5; chapter XI, § 2; epilogue, § 3.]. Although Scotus’s chief concern ought to have been to prove that unfortunate man guilty of so great an error rather than merely accuse him, he nevertheless did not even attempt to produce the slightest argument by which he could satisfy the role of his patrons in this matter. Nowhere does he demonstrate that Gottschalk is held by the guilt of the predestinarian heresy; everywhere he repeatedly asserts it.

Nor was the expectation of his own side less disappointed in the other task that, as we noted, Scotus ought to have completed. For although he fought most vigorously against the terrors of the two predestinations, he attacked only what he ought not to have concerned himself with, and scarcely cared about what he ought properly to have attacked; he assaulted the latter, as they say, only with a leaden sword. What Hincmarus and his associates had condemned in Gottschalk he attacked justly; what ought properly to have been attacked was what the adversaries of Hincmarus’s party had, so to speak, defended in Gottschalk. These matters differ from one another as widely as heaven from earth, as we explained above.

He everywhere undertook to attack the former [Note: Cf. chapter I, § 2; chapter II, §§ 1 and 6; chapter XI, § 1; chapter IV, § 3. To these must also be added nearly all the arguments by whose force (chapters II–VIII) he attempts to overthrow his twofold predestination, insofar as they are intended to prove that God can neither obstruct human free will nor compel anyone to depart from the precepts of morality.]. We may grant that he made some attack upon the latter, because among the arguments by which he tried to overthrow the former there are some that one might say were also directed against the latter [Note: Cf. chapters IX–XIX, the substance of which we shall shortly present.].

Yet concerning whether the former was defeated or not defeated, we do not find even a word from any of those against whom Scotus had to wage this battle; they themselves had also utterly rejected it. But how far they considered the latter unconquered we shall show below [Note: At the end of the first section of this chapter.]. We therefore believe that it is already sufficiently clear what sort of advocate Scotus proved to be: he was more harmful than useful to the cause of his own side.

The greatest commotion, and the greatest astonishment and indignation among people at that time, were aroused by the fact that Scotus’s book did indeed breathe the deepest piety toward God, yet was filled to overflowing with a vast multitude of errors, absurdities, and astonishing propositions of a kind that people of that age would never even have heard mentioned. We shall now explain this as far as possible and discuss the substance of the entire book.

Its substance consists roughly in the following claim: there are not two predestinations in God [Note: Namely, those that Scotus attributes to Gottschalk and that impose upon human beings either a necessity of “living” or a necessity of “perishing.”], but only one, and that one is the predestination of good people.

There are very many and highly diverse arguments for this position. We shall explain as carefully as the nature of this volume permits those that seem most worthy of mention. They are arranged in such a way that nothing contributes more to revealing Scotus’s true intellectual character.

**I.** “The divine will and divine predestination are both free from every necessity that might either impel or impede them: the former because it is the supreme cause of all things; the latter because, like the divine will, it is God” [Note: Cf. II, §§ 1, 2, and 6; III, § 1. Scotus says that those things which are “substantial,” not “accidental,” to God are God. Cf. II, § 2.].

What follows from this? We do not see what he means, unless perhaps one supposes either that the divine will is the same as the human will, or that, because the former is free, the latter must also be free. Scotus leaves us uncertain, except that elsewhere [Note: Cf. VIII, §§ 1–4.] he writes:

> “The divine creative will ought to have created its human will like itself, that is, free.”

**II.** “Whatever is predicated of God—such as essence, wisdom, and power—is one.” “But nothing is said of him more truly and honorably than predestination.” “Therefore predestination too is one” [Note: Cf. II, 3–6; III, 1, 4, 5.].

**III.** “Non-being is contrary to essence; perishing to life; sin to justice; misery to blessedness. Therefore their causes—the two predestinations—must also be contrary to one another. The divine nature, however, which is one and simple, cannot contain them joined together within itself” [Note: Cf. III, 2.].

**IV.** “Good and upright people are compelled to virtue by no necessity; they are aided, however, by divine grace, with which they cooperate through their human freedom” [Note: Cf. IV, 3–8; III, 7.].

**V.** “Evil and wicked people are driven by no compulsion to sin or to perish, although the sacred authors, in a certain abusive manner of speaking, commonly say that they are predestined to death, destruction, or punishment. Every sin, and every punishment of sin, arises from the human will itself, when it makes evil use of free choice” [Note: Cf. V, §§ 1–5; VI, §§ 1–3.].

Concerning the freedom of the will, Scotus teaches the following:

> “A person who can live only rightly and not wickedly is not completely free; for free choice is the choice either of good or of evil” [Note: Cf. V, §§ 8–9.].

From this point onward—beginning with chapter IX—“a full abundance will flow for you from a generous horn,” rich in errors and absurdities. Since this occurred much less frequently in the earlier part, we have generally passed over there whatever belonged to that category.

And in this part (chaps. IX–XIX) Scotus leads his argument by certain long and gloomy detours. We have thought that the whole matter, gathered into a single body, could be reduced to the following points. [Col. 0027B]

Whatever is thought to be sin, whatever is called the punishment of sins—absolutely nothing exists. “For no one, unless he is devoid of understanding, fails to see that everything called sin, and its consequences—death and misery—are nothing other than corruptions of integral and blessed life, so that each of these is opposed to one of those: sin to integrity, death to life, misery to blessedness. The former exist; the latter do not exist at all. The former are understood within the boundaries of natural forms; the latter are known unknowingly in the defect and privation of those forms. The former have matter, form, and appearance; the latter lack matter, form, and appearance.” [Note: [Col. 0027C] Compare X, 4, 5, 3; XV, 1, 3, 5–6; and elsewhere. In this passage, moreover, we wish to set forth once and for all and in general Scotus’s view of sin, punishment, and whatever belongs to the same category, which he follows in *On Predestination*. [Col. 0027D]]

From this it must be understood what Scotus’s expressions mean, such as “sin is nothing” and “the punishments of sin are nothing.”

Now sin itself and the punishments of sins must be described more precisely.

Sin is not a nature [Note: [Col. 0027D] That is, a “thing that truly exists,” “that has some substantial being.” Compare X, 5.] (“for it would follow that, since God created nature, sin is from God” [Note: [Col. 0027D] Compare XV, 4.]), but belongs to free will. It is “the perverse movement of a free will that misuses its own freedom, when someone turns away from divine and truly abiding things and turns toward mutable and uncertain things.” “Sin, then, and its consequences abandon the highest principle of all things and strive to return downward into nothingness the good things whose corruptions they are. By contrast, those things opposed to sin and its consequences—integrity, life, and blessedness—tend upward and seek that one principle of all things. For what does the wickedness of all the impious and of the devil desire except to withdraw from him who is supreme being so far that their nature, if divine law permitted it, would return to nothingness? Hence wickedness is so called because it strives to be *nequicquam*, that is, nothing.” [Note: [Col. 0027D] Compare VI, XVI, 4–6; X, 1, 4; XVIII, 7, and elsewhere. At this point Scotus’s opinion concerning original sin should not, it seems, be passed over. In *On Predestination* it is expressed approximately in these words: “All human beings sinned in the first human being. Although God created in him the general nature of the human race, that nature could not sin, since God had made it. Therefore it is necessary that God substituted in the first human being the individual will of all human beings as well; and thus it was not the universality of the nature of all, but the individual will of each person, that sinned in him.” Compare XVI, § 3. [Col. 0028C]]

Since this is so, the punishment of sins is now readily explained. It is nothing other than “the torments of the will that sins, by which it is afflicted while it is not permitted to possess the things that it wrongly or unworthily desires.” [Col. 0028B] “For while the wickedness of the impious desires nothing other than to withdraw from him who is supreme being so far that their nature may return to nothingness, difficulty arising from the eternal laws resists it, preventing it from falling as far as it would wish. From that difficulty it suffers; in suffering it is tormented, punished, and tortured.” [Note: [Col. 0028D] Compare XVI, 4; XVIII, 7. Careful attention must be paid to what is properly afflicted by punishment. Just as, therefore (compare the preceding notes d and e), it is not nature that sins but perverse will, so it is not nature that is punished but that same perverse will. A passage from chapter XVI, § 1, could very appropriately be transferred here: “What, then? If no nature has been punished, will it therefore be miserable? I do not see how. For what reason will any nature be miserable unless it has been punished? Therefore, if no nature can be punished, no nature will be miserable. But every nature is either God or made by him. It is utterly mad to suppose that the creative nature is capable of misery; nor do I find that the creative nature, by which natures were created, should punish those natures by justice. No nature, then, will be punished; and what is not punished will not be miserable.” Compare XVI, 2, 6. [Col. 0028D]]

Having explained these matters, we think it is already evident whom the reasoning concerning punishments requires us to regard as their author. We have therefore thought it appropriate to bring together here what is taught concerning him.

The perverse will, which we have shown properly both to sin and to be punished, receives those torments of its own—from which it suffers because of its insatiable desire, as though “seeking in vain to break through the bars set against life”—from no other source than this very perversity and desire of its own. “For there are no other instruments for torturing impiety than impiety itself; each person’s punishment will be made from his own sin; his pride is sufficient to torture the devil.” “From the same source as sin comes death; from the same source as death comes misery, which is punishment or torment.” [Note: [Col. 0028D] Compare XVI, 6; XV, 8, and many other passages.]

From what has been said about sin and its punishment, we think it is clear that Scotus, if he wishes to remain consistent, must deny that it occurs by God’s will and command—not sin, which he has already expressly denied elsewhere [Col. 0029A], but the punishment of sin. Nor are we mistaken. For he continually forbids anyone to think that any of these things are brought about by God. Since nothing exists, it does not “come from God, from whom only those things come which are said truly to exist”; and whatever arises from the perverse will of human beings cannot in any way be referred to God as its author. [Note: [Col. 0029D] Compare III, 3; X, 1–5, and frequently elsewhere.] God merely permits these things, so that they “may occur through the spontaneous and free movement of a rational creature misusing its natural goods”; they are merely “abandoned by God, so that those who are to be punished may be punished by their own perversity.” [Note: [Col. 0029D] Compare X, 1–5; XVII, 2.]

Once it has been granted that neither sin nor its punishment exists or derives its origin from God, it is now easily demonstrated that these things are not even foreknown by that supreme divinity, much less predestined for anyone. [Col. 0029B] The matter is settled by definition. “For divine predestination is the preparation and disposition, before the ages, of all the things that God was going to do.” [Note: [Col. 0029D] Compare II, 2; XI, 6–7; XII, 1 ff.] “In God, however, foreknowledge has as much force as predestination, precisely because they are one.” Foreknowledge would indeed exceed the bounds of predestination if it were thought to extend also to those things that God did not make, such as sins. But whatever God did not make does not exist; therefore it is not foreknown by him. Moreover, “predestination and foreknowledge are both of one and the same divine nature, in which there is no more or less of one thing than another. Where there is simplicity of nature, there is no diversity, because in it all things are one.” [Note: [Col. 0029D] Compare XV, 3–4; 5–6; XVIII, conclusion of the preface.]

It is therefore perfectly clear that neither sins nor their punishments are foreknown or predestined by God. [Col. 0029C] [Note: [Col. 0029D] Compare XV, 1; XVI, 6; XVII, 1, and elsewhere.]

But if, nevertheless, “God is said both to have made these things and to have foreknown or predestined them,” God arranged this in order to exercise our understanding—both in his Scriptures and in their interpreters—so that, on hearing such modes of expression, our attention might awaken to understand what mystical meaning lies hidden in them, rather than what the plain surface of the words displays. [Note: [Col. 0029D] Compare XVI, 6; compare XVII, 2; X, 1 ff.]

What he calls the mystical meaning here is explained in many passages. He writes, therefore, that very many things must be understood “contrarily”: “in secular literature the Fates are called *Parcae* because they spare no one, and light because it does not shine”; “in the divine Scriptures Judas the betrayer is found called a friend by Jesus, although he was an enemy; called chosen, although he was not chosen; and many similar examples.” [Note: [Col. 0029D] Compare X, 1 ff.; XV, 6–7, 2; XIII, 1 ff.] [Col. 0029D] “Accordingly,” he says, “I do not see why the holy fathers should have hesitated confidently to express, in a beautiful mode of speech, that people were predestined to punishment or destruction”—meaning, in place of “not predestined”—“whenever they chose to set this down in the sequence of their books. [Col. 0030A] If the Lord was not ashamed to call his betrayer chosen”—meaning, in place of “not chosen”—“why should Saint Augustine have been ashamed to call that same betrayer predestined”—meaning, in place of “not predestined”? [Note: [Col. 0029D] Compare XIII, 2; IX, 5, where, however, he explains this matter quite differently: he says that foreknowledge and predestination are predicated of God not properly but contrarily because temporal succession does not apply to him; X, 1 ff.; XII, 2; XV, 2, and elsewhere.]

“Therefore, whenever impious people are said to be predestined, and whatever things are said concerning them, it must be interpreted according to that most beautiful and salutary mode of contrariety.”

With good people, however, and with their virtue and rewards, the matter is different. These things truly exist, have been made by God, and are given by God’s infinite benevolence and grace. Their predestination, therefore, may truly and properly be so called; and when it is taught by Holy Scripture and the holy fathers, it is not to be understood contrariwise. [Note: [Col. 0030D] XI–XIV. It is certainly remarkable that Scotus, although he everywhere declared the predestination of wicked people to be necessary as the cause of their acting wickedly, nevertheless did not consider the predestination of good people as a necessary cause of living well.]

Before proceeding to the remaining matters, it seems appropriate to append to our discussion what Scotus appended to his own: namely, his opinion concerning the eternal fire in hell. It is as follows: “It can scarcely be believed that this is anything other than the very element that is the fourth element of the world. Nor is it incongruous to believe that the bodies of the saints will be changed into an ethereal quality, which cannot be consumed by another; but that the bodies of the impious will pass into an airy quality, so that they may suffer from the fire above. Hence, after his fall, the devil was thrust down from the ethereal region, and an airy body was joined to him against his will, in which he might pay the penalties of his pride.” [Note: [Col. 0030D] Here, we think, everyone will recall Origen.] “And if it seems incredible to anyone that bodies can burn forever and yet not perish, let him look at the salamander living in fire; let him look at asbestos stone.” [Note: [Col. 0030D] Compare XIX, 1–4. Above he said that conscience alone is punished.]

[Col. 0030C] We now come to the method of argument and demonstration that Scotus adopted in this book. This may perhaps have become sufficiently clear from what we have related concerning the subject of the whole book. We have seen, then, that he proceeded by a route very different from that of the other theologians of his age—and one appropriate to himself. They relied almost exclusively on the testimonies and authorities of Holy Scripture and the holy fathers; he used, as he writes, the “rules of the disputational art.” They submitted themselves to the authorities of Holy Scripture and the holy fathers with a devout and simple mind; he subjected those authorities to the harsh and arrogant domination of his intellect. We certainly remember how, with contemptuous artifices, he made whatever he saw working against him appear to work for him. By this art, what opponent could he not overthrow! [Col. 0030D] It is true that he too adduces passages from Holy Scripture and Saint Augustine as arguments for his own position; but he does so in such a way that, to use his own words, those passages had previously been approved by his own position. [Note: [Col. 0030D] Scotus committed precisely the same error in his books *On the Division of Nature*. Compare Hock, in *Bonner Zeitschrift*, fasc. XVI, [Col. 0031D] p. 50. Compare also *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 420 ff.]

Nor can we refrain from bringing forward, as they say, a classic passage from Scotus’s books *On the Division of Nature* concerning this matter. It concerns the authority of Holy Scripture and the holy fathers. He writes [Note: [Col. 0031D] Compare *On Nature*, I, 71.]: “Authority proceeded from true reason, never reason from authority. Every authority, however, that is not approved by true reason appears weak. True reason, moreover, does not need to be strengthened by the support of any authority.”

And, by heaven, when we have seriously criticized Scotus’s undertakings, we must not silently pass over the things by which they may be excused. At the command of Charles the Bald (compare above, chapter III), he had translated the books of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite and Maximus, which he believed in fact and reality to have been written by the men to whom they were customarily attributed. Thus, to a very considerable extent, it was because of the supreme authority of those holy men that he came to love so intensely whatever he found in their books that he thought nothing truer, nothing more divine than their teaching, and considered it impossible to doubt that whatever he had learned either in Holy Scripture or from the holy fathers could be reduced to the philosophy of those men. Yet Scotus was one who regarded as sacred whatever he had persuaded himself was true, and freely confessed it in its proper place. For he says in the first book *On Nature* [Note: [Col. 0031D] Chapter 69.]: “I am not so terrified by authority, nor do I fear the assault of minds less capable, that I should be ashamed to proclaim openly whatever true reason clearly gathers and defines without uncertainty—especially since such matters ought to be discussed only among the wise, for whom nothing is sweeter to hear than what is established by true reason, nothing more delightful to investigate when it is sought, and nothing more beautiful to contemplate when it is found!” To this must be added that Scotus’s piety toward God must be called truly extraordinary, so that Anastasius the Librarian praises him as “holy in every respect.”

Finally, we shall surely be doing something worthwhile if we report, in condensed form, the arguments by which Erigena attempts to justify the use of his “dialectical art.” He says [Note: [Col. 0032D] Compare *On Predestination*, I, 1 ff.]: “Since every method of pious and perfect teaching, by which the rationale of all things is most clearly discovered, is established in philosophy, certain matters concerning its divisions must be discussed. For, as Saint Augustine says, it is believed that ‘philosophy is not one thing and religion another, since those whose teaching we do not approve do not share the sacraments with us either.’” [Col. 0031D] What else is it to discuss philosophy than to set forth the rules of true religion, by which God, the supreme cause of all things, is both humbly worshiped and rationally investigated? It follows from this that true philosophy is true religion, and conversely that true religion is true philosophy. Although this is divided in many ways, it is nevertheless recognized as having four principal parts, arranged in pairs, which are necessary for solving every question and which we may call in Latin the divisive, definitive, demonstrative, and resolutive parts. [Col. 0032A] We shall show examples of them in the course of this work. For no educated person doubts that by these, as by a useful and honorable fourfold crossroads of human reasoning, one reaches the very discipline of disputation, which is truth. We are necessarily commanded to use the rules of this discipline when we are compelled to respond against a certain Gottschalk.”

What kind of philosophy does he here assert to be identical with true religion? Is it the philosophy commonly called by that name in those times, which scarcely, or not even scarcely, went beyond the limits of dialectic? Scotus’s own words, unless perhaps they must be interpreted “contrarily,” certainly signify a philosophy whose one or primary function in this matter is to provide and supply the instruments and devices by which philosophers construct their royal edifices. But whence comes such great confusion in all things? Some refer its cause to Erigenian pantheism. [Note: [Col. 0032D] Compare I, v. Görres, *Christian Mysticism*, vol. I, p. 243.] Schlueter, by contrast, asserts [Note: [Col. 0032D] Compare I. Sc. Erig., p. XVI.] that “this proposition—that true philosophy is identical with true religion—is no more suspect in the mouth of our author than the teaching of nearly all the holy fathers, namely, that Christ’s revelation is the highest wisdom and contains all philosophy.” But Schlueter openly declares that he had not even looked at Erigena’s book to determine that proposition. How, then, could he have strayed so far from its true meaning? Erigena’s philosophy [Col. 0032C] certainly includes dialectic, but we would not say that dialectic is contained in “Christ’s revelation,” nor would any of the holy fathers have said so.

For our more precise understanding of that passage of Erigena, it seems to us especially helpful to consider what he writes in his books *On the Division of Nature* [Note: [Col. 0032D] Compare IV, 4.]: “That art which is called dialectic (*διαλεκτική*) was not produced by human contrivances, but was established in the nature of things by the author of all arts, discovered by the wise, and employed for the benefit of skillful investigation of things.”

Yet we should not, we think, neglect this possibility either: perhaps Scotus made true philosophy identical with true religion for the sole purpose of indicating that they do not in any way resist or oppose one another. Thus, since neither disparages the other, but one can live in the greatest harmony with the other, either may also be summoned to the aid of the other whenever this seems necessary or useful.

Enough has now been said about our Erigena’s book *On Predestination*; let us proceed to the remaining matters.

After Scotus’s book had been published, Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, detected in it matters that “in some way departed from his own understanding.” He sent them, arranged in nineteen chapters—the same number that we have said the book contains—to Saint Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, so that “whatever he found in them departing from the truth, he might provide fitting and ample answers from the books of the Gospels and the authorities of Catholic teachers for each chapter that deviated from them.” [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare Saint Prudentius, *Against Scotus on Predestination*, preface, *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon, vol. XV, p. 467 F.] Nor did Prudentius disregard Wenilo’s request. First, however, he wished to acquaint himself with Scotus’s book itself. When he had done so, he vigorously attacked it in a separate work. [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare the preceding note.]

In this undertaking he found an ally in the Church of Lyon. [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare *The Church of Lyon’s Book Against Scotus’s Erroneous Definitions*, *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. I, p. 611 ff. The author of this book is uncertain. Some say that its author was Florus, a deacon of the Church of Lyon; others attribute it to Saint Remigius, archbishop of Lyon, or to Ebbo, bishop of Grenoble. Compare Ludovic Cellot, S.J., *History of Gottschalk*, p. 140 ff.] For the writings of that “empty-talking and chattering man”—“utterly vain, full of lies and error, contrary to the faith and truth of God”—had also “come” to that Church. To learned men they were objects of ridicule, but by the unlearned, who “held that man in admiration as though he were learned,” they could be read only at the greatest risk either to the readers themselves or to the detriment of the Christian religion. [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare *The Church of Lyon’s Book*, preface, vol. I, p. 611 H.]

Each of Scotus’s two opponents proceeded in much the same way. Following his tracks as closely as possible, almost sentence by sentence, as soon as they detected anything that seemed to depart from the truth, they marked it with the greatest severity. If he had opposed the rules of the dialecticians, they attacked him with dialectical rules; if he had shown insufficient agreement with the authority of the sacred Scriptures or of the ecclesiastical fathers, they attacked him with the testimony of those very authorities. They also frequently attempted to refute by opposing testimonies and authorities what Scotus had established by reasoning. There are even passages where, carried away by anger at his errors, they do not hesitate to tear him apart with insults.

Saint Prudentius, indeed, where Scotus argues [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare Saint Prudentius, book I, p. 519 H ff.] that “God may be said to foreknow in place of not knowing, and likewise to predestine in place of not predestining,” attacks him in these words: “O intellect infected with poisons! O understanding incomparably darkened by the shadows of errors! For never before you did any heretic admit this wicked interpretation. At least none of the Catholics conceived in his mind that ‘to know’ could mean ‘not to know,’ and ‘to predestine’ could mean ‘not to predestine,’ or either understood or urged that they should be understood in this way.” Saint Prudentius’s book contains countless statements of this kind.

The Church of Lyon, moreover, did not cease fighting against Scotus even afterward. For Saint Remigius, archbishop of Lyon, presiding over the Council of Valence, held in the year 855 by fourteen bishops, brought it about that Scotus’s teaching should also be condemned by that synod. Thus, among the other statements against Scotus in the canons of that synod, there are the following: [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare the Council of Valence in Mansi, vol. XV, col. 1 ff.] “We utterly reject the foolish little questions and almost childish fables, and the porridge of the Scots, which bring nausea to the purity of the faith, lest Christian minds be corrupted by them and fall away from the simplicity and chastity of the faith that is in Christ Jesus.” [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare book I, canon VI, col. 6 D ff.]

And this: “These nineteen chapters of Scotus, concluded most foolishly in syllogisms—in which the devil’s invention rather than any argument of faith is detected—we utterly expel from the pious hearing of the faithful, and, so that such things and similar ones may be avoided, we forbid them in every respect by the authority of the Holy Spirit. We also judge that the introducers of novelties should be corrected, lest they be struck more severely.” [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare book I, canon IV, col. 5 D.]

The Council of Langres (859) fully approved this judgment of the Council of Valence. For in its fourth canon it says: “The nineteen chapters, concluded most foolishly and falsely in syllogisms by a certain Scotus, in which not an argument of faith but rather an invention of faithlessness is manifest—constructed by no philosophical art whatsoever, as some arrogantly boast, but most unskillfully concluded by empty deception and fraud—we utterly expel from the pious hearing of the faithful.” [Note: [Col. 0033D] Compare Mansi, vol. XV, col. 538 A–B.]

It is also reported that Nicholas I, supreme pontiff, confirmed the canons of these councils by the authority of the Apostolic See. [Note: [Col. 0034D] Mabillon, in *Annals*, book XXXV, no. 58, leaves the matter uncertain. Schlueter (book I, p. IV) writes: “Nicholas I confirmed the canon of the Council of Valence,” adding: “‘The poison’ of Erigena’s doctrines was censured, but Erigena himself was not condemned.”]

As far as we know, Scotus did not even react to these proceedings. Staudenmaier turns this very fact to his praise. [Col. 0034C] Compare Staudenmaier, pp. 196–197.]

We now come to that other controversy among theologians of which we said Scotus was a participant.
