Paschasius Radbertus [Note: [Col. 0034D] He was born in the region of Soissons, apparently in the humblest circumstances. From childhood he followed monasteries and monastic affairs, and eventually entered the monastery at Corbie, where he became first a monk and later its abbot. He lived through the first half of the ninth century and, by the standards of his age, was highly accomplished in learning and doctrine. Compare *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 287 ff., and the authors cited there.] (in the year 844) sent Charles the Bald, who had requested it, his work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, although it had been composed long before and had then been revised in many places. [Note: [Col. 0034D] Compare Martène and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio of Ancient Writings and Monuments*, vol. IX, col. 374 A ff., where Paschasius’s work itself, together with the prefaces to Charles, is printed.]

Although his whole purpose is to defend and confirm the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation—though he could not yet use that term—by arguments drawn both from Holy Scripture and from the works of the holy fathers, nevertheless certain statements occurred in this book that seemed to some to be new and previously unheard-of, and that might cause offense in some places. Examples of this kind [Note: [Col. 0035C] Compare Dr. L. I. Ritter, *Handbook of Church History*, second edition, vol. II, pp. 186–194.] are the following:

“[The Holy Eucharist] is plainly no other flesh than that which was born of Mary, suffered on the cross, and rose from the tomb.” [Note: [Col. 0035C] Compare Paschasius, chapter I, in Martène and Durand, vol. IX, col. 383 A ff.]

“Truly the flesh of Christ, which was crucified and buried; truly the sacrament of that flesh, which through the priest, upon the altar, in the word of Christ, is divinely consecrated by the Holy Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0035C] Compare Paschasius, chapter IV, in Martène and Durand, vol. IX, col. 391 D ff.]

Accordingly, Charles the Bald—perhaps himself not entirely pleased by those statements—commissioned Ratramnus of Corbie [Note: [Col. 0035C] Compare Ratramnus, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, preface to Charles the Bald. This book was published in a French translation by Jacques Boileau. Paris, 1712, 12mo; the Latin appeared at Cologne in 1532 and often thereafter, though not as Ratramnus’s book but as Bertram’s. Mabillon teaches, however, that these two names designate one and the same man. *Acta Benedictina*, fourth century, part II, preface, no. 81.] and John Scotus [Note: [Col. 0035D] Compare Berengarius of Tours, letter to Richard the abbot, in Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 785 B ff.] to set forth in writing what the true teaching of Holy Scripture and the holy fathers concerning the body and blood of the Lord was; he urged them to do so by his will and authority. Ratramnus’s book survives; Scotus’s has been consumed by the hostility of time.

Nevertheless, the disagreements that arose among learned men concerning these books and their authors must not be omitted here. There were those who thought that only one work on the Holy Eucharist—the work we have said was Ratramnus’s—had been written at Charles’s command, and who attributed it not to Ratramnus but to Scotus. They have long since been so thoroughly answered that today no one can be found who refers that book to Scotus rather than to Ratramnus as its author. [Note: [Col. 0035D] Compare Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, fourth century, part II, preface, nos. 81–89; Jacques Boileau, preface to Ratramnus, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*; *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 337 ff.; Dr. L. I. Ritter, *Handbook of Church History*, second edition, vol. II, p. 192 ff.; Dr. L. J. J. Döllinger, *Textbook of Church History*, vol. I, p. 409.]

When this dispute had ended, another suspicion concerning that book of Scotus arose. We think that this question can best and most easily be settled if we first explain somewhat more precisely the principal arguments by which it is established that Scotus wrote about the Holy Eucharist. Witnesses to this fact include both Scotus’s contemporaries and Berengarius of Tours and the learned men who lived with him.

Among the former are Adrevaldus, a monk of Fleury, a man highly praised for his learning [Note: [Col. 0035D] Compare *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 515 ff.], and Hincmar, archbishop of Reims. Adrevaldus composed “a little work on the body and blood of the Lord against the absurdities of John Scotus,” a notable fragment of which Luc d’Achery published in the *Spicilegium of Ancient Writers*. [Note: [Col. 0035D] Compare *Spicilegium*, first edition, Paris, beginning in 1655, quarto, vol. XII, p. 30 ff.; and second edition, Paris, beginning in 1723, folio, vol. I, p. 150 ff. The work of Adrevaldus is also discussed, among others, in *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 519. [Col. 0036C]] This fragment does nothing except demonstrate and confirm, by numerous passages from Saint Jerome, Saint Augustine, and Pope Saint Gregory, the true presence of Jesus Christ in the Holy Eucharist.

Hincmar’s testimony is less explicit, but it is not altogether to be disregarded. For, sharply noting certain errors into which Saint Prudentius and John Scotus had fallen, he says in his book *On Predestination* [Note: [Col. 0036C] Chapter 31.]: “There are also other things which they say contrary to the truth of the Catholic faith: namely … that the sacrament of the altar is not the true body and true blood of the Lord, but only a memorial of his true body and blood.” Since this statement cannot in any way apply to Saint Prudentius, it must apply to John Scotus. And if it applies to Scotus, it seems to have been drawn by learned men from one of his books, because we still read in his books nearly all the other errors that Hincmar criticizes in the same passage. [Note: [Col. 0036C] Compare Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, fourth century, part II, preface, no. 132.]

If these considerations leave any scruple in our minds, Berengarius of Tours and almost all the learned men who lived with him will remove it entirely. To summarize the matter briefly: apart from Berengarius himself, who praises John Scotus’s book on the Holy Eucharist in almost countless passages, says that it was written at the command of King Charles against Paschasius [Col. 0036C], and maintains that he alone approves its teachings [Note: [Col. 0036C] Compare Berengarius’s letter to Richard, in Mansi, vol. XIX, col. 735 A ff.; his letter to Lanfranc, in Mansi, col. 768 A–B; and his letter to Ascelin, in Mansi, cols. 735 C–776 D. The same matter is also very frequently found in Berengarius’s book that G. E. Lessing was the first to recover from the Wolfenbüttel library. [Col. 0036D]], not only individual learned men who dealt with him privately or publicly in gatherings of theologians [Note: [Col. 0036D] Compare Lanfranc, *Commentary Against Berengarius*, in Mansi, col. 759 D and elsewhere; Durand, abbot of Troarn, in Mansi, col. 782 D–E; Ascelin’s letter to Berengarius, in Mansi, col. 777 A–C; and the anonymous author—who writes that he attended the councils held against Berengarius—in the *Short Work on Berengarius’s Multiple Condemnation*, in Mansi, col. 757 E.], but also almost all the synods with which Berengarius had dealings, and which were attended in large part by distinguished bishops and learned men [Note: [Col. 0036D] On the Council of Vercelli (1050), compare Mansi, vol. XIX, cols. 757 E ff., 773 E, and 778 E; on the Roman Council (1059), the same volume, cols. 902 A–B and 759 A; on the Council of Paris (1050), compare Durand of Troarn in Mansi, col. 782 E; on the Council of Tours (1054), compare William of Malmesbury in Thomas Gale, *Testimonies*, book I, p. 8.], knew, read, and condemned John Scotus’s book on the Holy Eucharist. No one is reported to have arisen among so great a multitude of eminent men, who had been almost continuously occupied for so many years with Berengarius’s case, whose opinion concerning the author of that book was different. It is therefore certainly unsurprising that from those times onward all historians and critics have held it established that Scotus composed, at the command of King Charles, a book on the Holy Eucharist against Paschasius, and that Berengarius later used that book.

In our own age, however, someone has said that the Berengarian book was not Scotus’s but Ratramnus’s [Note: [Col. 0037D] This seems to us highly probable as well, and we discuss it more fully in the *Proem*. We cannot refrain from disagreeing with the author of the commentary concerning what he has put forward on this chapter. Compare the *Proem*. Editorial note.]—that it had been falsely attributed to John Scotus. Thus it would not even be certain whether Scotus ever published any work on the Holy Eucharist. [Col. 0037B] [Note: [Col. 0037C] Compare F. W. Laufs, “On the Writing of John Scotus on the Eucharist, Which Was Considered Lost,” in the volume entitled *Theological Studies and Criticisms*, by Dr. Ullmann and Dr. Umbreit, I, 4, p. 755 ff.]

But although that scholar was acute and subtle in argument, he nevertheless did not, as far as we can see, succeed in dislodging us from such an ancient possession. To make this clear, we shall briefly present and examine the substance of the matter. [Note: [Col. 0037C] Although this matter deserves more careful investigation, many causes prevent us from undertaking it now. [Col. 0037D]]

First, he affirmed that whatever Berengarius and his contemporaries had said about their Scotus could also be said about Ratramnus’s book, and he wished it to be concluded from this that the two books were not two but one and the same. This has some force, but it is by no means the whole case. He would certainly have the right to draw that conclusion if Scotus’s book had been described to us in greater detail and if the descriptions fitted Ratramnus’s work altogether, so that similar features could not easily be found in two books by two different authors. But only very few things are reported about Scotus’s book, and from them it is easier to infer that it was different from Ratramnus’s book than that it was one and the same with it.

Indeed, some things have been written about Scotus [Note: [Col. 0037D] Cf. Laufs, loc. cit., pp. 763, 765. What is read on p. 763—“of Charlemagne, his predecessor” …—stands as follows in Dacherius: “of Charlemagne, his predecessor …” In Mansi (Conciliorum collectio, vol. XIX, col. 736 A) it is written: “of Charlemagne, his predecessor.” But if in that letter of Berengarius to Richard one may read: “let him know” (Henry I, king of the French), “that what John Scot writes, he wrote at the prompting and request of Charlemagne, his predecessor …,” with what justification can one infer from this passage that the book to which Berengarius refers was written and sent to “the emperor Charlemagne” in the same manner as Ratramnus’s work? Furthermore, we believe that these very words prefixed to Ratramnus’s book are not Ratramnus’s own; for in the oldest manuscript codex, which Mabillon saw (Acta Benedictina, century IV, vol. II, preface, no. 83), it was written as follows: “Here begins Ratramnus’s book on the body and blood of the Lord. You commanded, glorious Prince …” Finally, there is nothing in it to show that Scotus is said to have written at Charles’s command in the same way as Ratramnus, since in the affair of Gottschalk both Ratramnus and Lupus of Ferrières composed their books at Charles’s command, whereas Scotus composed his “with Charles’s approval.”], which can be transferred to Ratramnus in almost the same way; but these facts need not greatly disturb us, because in those times authors writing about the same subject often used nearly the same arguments, almost the same expressions, and a similar style of composition [Note: [Col. 0038D] Cf. Mabillon, Acta Benedictina, century IV, part II, preface, no. 88.]. Nor, on the other hand, are there lacking things known to us from Scotus which do not seem readily attributable to Ratramnus [Note: [Col. 0038D] Cf. Laufs, loc. cit., pp. 764, 765, 766 n. a, 768.]. It is said that these passages, when slightly adapted, can be made to fit Ratramnus; but, if they have already been taken from their proper setting, the question also arises whether, with a little further adaptation, they might fit a completely different author.

We see that great weight is attributed to Ascelinus [Note: [Col. 0038D] Cf. Laufs, pp. 757–760.], who wrote about Scotus in a letter to Berengarius as follows: he said, in explaining that Gregorian prayer [Note: [Col. 0038D] “May your sacraments, O Lord, accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now perform in outward form we may receive in the reality of the things themselves.”]: “among other things contrary to our faith: ‘These things are performed in outward form, not in reality.’” The following passage of Ratramnus is believed to have been indicated by Ascelinus’s words:

“‘May your sacraments, O Lord, we ask, accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now perform in outward form we may receive in the reality of the things themselves.’ It says [that is, that prayer] that these things are performed in outward form, not in reality—that is, by representation, not by the manifestation of the thing itself. Form and reality differ from one another. Therefore the body and blood that are performed in the Church differ from that body and blood which is known to have been glorified by resurrection in Christ’s body. This is a pledge and an outward form; the other is the reality itself. For this is performed until one reaches the other.” Once the other has been reached, this will be removed.

What in this passage is contrary to our faith? Lanfranc himself, Berengarius’s fiercest opponent, spoke in a similar way [Note: [Col. 0038D] Cf. Mabillon, Acta Benedictina, century IV, part II, preface, no. 88.]. When Ratramnus says in this passage, in his own words, “These things are performed in outward form, not in reality,” he explains the words of the Church according to the Church’s meaning. If Ascelinus could reproach any author for this, his head must have been incurably insane and required three Anticyras. We think that everyone must see that a very different passage of that Erigenian work which Ascelinus had before his eyes, reconstructed from Ascelinus’s own words, must be established as the passage in question.

We have discussed this passage of Ascelinus at greater length because it was thought to contain a great deal that opposed our position, although, as we have seen, it contains much more that supports it.

The following points, among those by which we are attacked, next seem worthy of mention. “That anonymous author of Cellot’s account [Note: [Col. 0039D] Cf. P. Cellot, Historia Gothescalci praedestinationis, Paris, 1655, folio. In the appendix, pp. 539–548.] knew, in writing about the Paschasian controversy, both the writings of others and Ratramnus’s book, but none of Scotus [Note: [Col. 0039D] Cf. Laufs, loc. cit., p. 779.].” But that Anonymous did not cite several books relevant to the matter—for example, that of Haimo, bishop of Halberstadt [Note: [Col. 0039D] Cf. Histoire littéraire de la France, vol. V, p. 124.]. Nor, by Hercules, can anything more be inferred from the fact that “Sigebert of Gembloux and others who discussed ecclesiastical writers did not praise Scotus’s book on the Holy Eucharist”: for we have found none of those authors who reviewed Scotus’s books with sufficient accuracy. Apart from his translation of the Areopagite, which he mentions in chapter 94, Sigebert mentions absolutely nothing.

It remains for us briefly and concisely to present whatever further points may seem defensible. First, then, Ratramnus’s book does not contain the opinion concerning the Holy Eucharist that Berengarius embraced. Berengarius denied that the substance of the bread and wine remained [Note: [Col. 0039D] Cf. Ritter, Handbuch der Kirchengeschichte, second edition, vol. II, p. 211.]; Ratramnus, although he sometimes uses obscure and ambiguous language, nevertheless did not on this matter depart from the sense of the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0039D] Cf. Mabillon, Acta Benedictina, century IV, part II, preface, no. 91 ff.; Histoire littéraire de la France, vol. V, p. 335 ff. For this reason the Magdeburg Centuriators also readily concede this much: that Ratramnus contains the seeds of transubstantiation!].

Moreover, during those times when the Berengarian struggle was raging and John Scotus’s book was repeatedly read and condemned, Ratramnus was known as the author and composer of the work which we know to have been written by him. That anonymous author of Cellot’s account—whether, with Mabillon, we identify him as Heriger, abbot of Lobbes [Note: [Col. 0039D] Cf. Mabillon, Acta Benedictina, century IV, part II, preface, § III.], who died in 1007, or, as Pez attempts to show [Note: [Col. 0039D] Thesaurus anecdotorum, vol. I, introductory dissertation, p. LXIX.], Gerbert, who later occupied the papal see—must certainly be regarded as having testified, not long before the Berengarian disturbances, that Ratramnus was the author of his book. To this may be added the fact that Mabillon saw two manuscript codices of Ratramnus, easily older than Berengarius and marked with Ratramnus’s name; one of them was entered as Ratramnus’s book in a catalogue of books drawn up in 1049 [Note: [Col. 0040D] Cf. Mabillon, loc. cit., preface, no. 83; Du Pin, Nouvelle bibliothèque, vol. VII, p. 68; Histoire littéraire de la France, vol. V, p. 339.].

[Col. 0039D] With these points thus set forth, we seem to have vindicated Scotus’s work on the Holy Eucharist with a sufficiently substantial weight of argument.

[Col. 0040A] At this point we cannot sufficiently wonder what happened to the two men, Staudenmaier and Schlueter, who, scarcely [Note: [Col. 0040D] Cf. Staudenmaier, J. Scotus Erigena, pp. 202–203.]—indeed, scarcely at all [Note: [Col. 0040D] Cf. Schlueter, J. Scotus Erigena, On the Five Books of The Division of Nature, p. V.]—doubting that Scotus was falsely regarded in Berengarius’s time as the author of that book, nevertheless assert with complete confidence that he both wrote, along with Ratramnus, against Paschasius and, as Schlueter says in interpreting Staudenmaier, “with Ratramnus chiefly elucidated the spiritual significance of the doctrine.” For once the testimonies of the Berengarian period are removed, no evidence of this remains [Note: [Col. 0040D] Cf. Laufs, loc. cit., pp. 768–779.]. As for Adrevald of Fleury and Hincmar of Rheims, whom we heard above, if they alluded to some book of Scotus, we believe that they did not target the one used by Berengarius. This will soon become clear.

[Col. 0040B] The fate of this Erigenian book was certainly bitter. Berengarius, praising it as an authority for his doctrine, inflicted mortal wounds upon it. It was read and condemned at Paris, in a council held under King Henry [in 1050] [Note: [Col. 0040D] Cf. Mansi, vol. XIX, col. 782 E.]; it was read and condemned “under anathema” in the synods assembled at Vercelli and Rome [in 1050] under Leo IX, Supreme Pontiff [Note: [Col. 0040D] Cf. Mansi, loc. cit., col. 757 E ff., col. 773 E, col. 778 E, col. 760 D ff.]. Later, an even harsher decision was made against it. For Pope Nicholas II, together with the Roman council [in 1059], compelled Berengarius by his authority to throw it—he himself throwing it, while all those present looked on—into a fire lit for that purpose [Note: [Col. 0040D] Cf. Mansi, loc. cit., cols. 902 A–B, 759 A.].

Finally, since Scotus’s own book has long since ceased to be seen, what opinion he proposed concerning the body and blood of the Lord must be inferred from Berengarius’s views, since Berengarius was accustomed continually to boast that Scotus was the source of his doctrine [Note: [Col. 0040D] Cf. Ritter, loc. cit., vol. II, p. 189, and above, col. 36, note k.]. This opinion is especially set forth in that writing of Berengarius against Lanfranc which G. E. Lessing, until then unknown to more recent scholars, brought out from the hiding places of the Wolfenbüttel library; it is now sufficiently exposed in the open and known to the public [Note: [Col. 0040D] Cf. Ritter, loc. cit., vol. II, p. 211 ff.]. Therefore, if we wished to explain it here, we would seem merely to be repeating what has already been done.

Here, however, a certain difficulty arises. From what we said about Adrevald and Hincmar’s accusations against Scotus, it appears that he utterly denied the true and real presence—as it is called—of Jesus Christ in the Holy Eucharist. But since Berengarius himself did not dare to teach this, and since we do not find that Scotus was blamed for it by Berengarius’s opponents, in our opinion it was not found in that book of Scotus which Berengarius possessed. Yet this does not seem surprising in Scotus [Col. 0041A], for he often set opposing things against one another in conflict [Note: [Col. 0041C] Cf. Scotus’s The Division of Nature.].

Nor is there no reason to say that he followed Adrevald and Hincmar to some extent. Among Scotus’s poems, which Schlueter says he published from palimpsests of Angelo Mai, there is one [Note: [Col. 0041D] Poem 3, On Easter (Angelo Mai, Classici auctores, vol. V, p. 432; Schlueter, p. 597).] that unmistakably indicates this error. After describing the Passover of the Israelites crossing the Red Sea, it continues:

“These were once the images [ἰνδάλματα] of Christ who was to come,  
in whom shine forth the things long hidden.

He alone, victorious, after the world’s ruler had been overthrown,  
after three days leaped forth from Erebus.

And first, treading upon death, he passed into the heights,  
for he alone was free by divine power from Tartarus.

Pouring out the pure libations of his own blood,  
he dedicates a new Passover, the world having been saved.

The Lord himself freely sacrifices himself as priest;  
it was the sacrifice which alone pleased the Father.

The sacrifice that cleansed the whole world from guilt,  
the world which the first man had been able to destroy.

From one came death; by one it was driven out;  
by a good death, the evil death is conquered and perishes.

Christ, the first fruits, opened the barriers of the tomb,  
restoring what had been lost to our nature.

Now the sacred symbols of these things are celebrated,  
while they are presented to the eyes, though already known to the minds;

while the devout mind tastes in its heart the body of Christ,  
the stream of the sacred blood, and the world’s ransom;

while we recall the Lord’s Supper through the years,  
while the choir itself sings many hymns in harmony.

At the eternal banquets, which mystical signs represent,  
deign, O Christ, to feed your Charles.”

The passage concerning the Holy Eucharist which Hoefler [Note: [Col. 0041D] Die deutschen Päpste, section II, p. 80.] brought forth from a certain commentary on the celestial hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite also belongs here; this commentary is said to have been written by our Scotus [Note: [Col. 0041D] Cf. below, chapter VI, at the end, On the doubtful writings of Erigena, no. III.]. The passage itself is as follows:

“It follows: ‘and the assumption of the divine Eucharist into the one principality’ [Note: [Col. 0041D] “Participation” should apparently be read. Cf. below, note g.]. Observe how beautifully and explicitly he asserts that this visible Eucharist, which the priests of the Church prepare daily upon the altar, is a typological likeness of the spiritual participation [Note: [Col. 0041D] Cf. note e.] of Jesus, whom we taste faithfully by the intellect alone—that is, whom we understand and receive into the inner depths of our nature—for our salvation, spiritual growth, and ineffable deification. Therefore, he says, the human mind, ascending from sensible things toward the likeness and equality of the heavenly powers, ought to judge that the visible divine Eucharist, formed within the Church, is above all a type of participation [Note: [Col. 0041D] From these passages it seems clear on what grounds we judged above, in note e, that “participation” should be read instead of “principality.”] in him, by which we now participate in Jesus through faith, and in which we shall participate in the future through vision [Note: [Col. 0041D] “We shall be united.”], and shall be united with him through love [Note: [Col. 0041D] “We shall be united.”]. What, then, will they reply to this most splendid trumpet of the great theologian Dionysius, who insist on asserting that the visible Eucharist signifies nothing other than itself? While that most resounding trumpet cries out that those visible sacraments are not to be worshiped or embraced as the reality, because they are signs of the reality; nor were they instituted for their own sake, since the goal of understanding does not lie in them, but on account of the incomprehensible power of the reality, which is Christ, in the unity of his human and divine substance, beyond everything sensed by bodily sensation, above everything perceived by the power of the intellect—the invisible God in both his natures.”

[Note: [Col. 0041D] The passage is corrupt and partly mutilated. A complete version, corrected against three manuscripts, appears in the Expositions of John Scotus, now published by us for the first time, below, col. 140. See what we have observed there concerning this passage. EDITORIAL NOTE.]

## CHAPTER V

On certain other matters relevant to illuminating Scotus’s life, and especially on his final fate.

[Col. 0042B]

After Scotus came to Charles the Bald, as we have shown to be exceedingly probable, around the year 845, Charles kept him for many years thereafter not only as a companion and friend, but also—something we have likewise reported at greater length—prompted him by his own wish to undertake many important tasks. How long Scotus remained in that position and honor is uncertain, although we seem sufficiently assured that the time when he departed from it was scarcely before the year 863. For, leaving aside other less certain evidence [Note: [Col. 0041D] For example, the letter which we related in chapter III that Pope Nicholas I wrote to Charles the Bald concerning our John [Col. 0042C]. For in that letter, as it is found in Bulaeus, Erigena is said to have long ago been “head of the Parisian school”—that is, of what was called the palace school. From this one may infer that, at the time when Nicholas I composed that letter, Scotus was still residing in the king’s “palace.” As we said, everyone agrees that the letter was written either in 860 or five years later.], there exists a poem by Scotus to Charles [Note: [Col. 0042D] Poem 1, Angelo Mai, loc. cit., p. 426 ff.; Schlueter, pp. 593–595.] in which the clearest traces are found that, when he wrote it, he was still staying in Charles’s palace. Since he boasts, as was customary, of the victory which Charles had shortly before won over the Northmen, it must have been written in 862 [Note: [Col. 0042D] Cf. Mabillon, Annales, book XXXV, nos. 93–94 and the end of no. 107.].

But even if he did not live in the palace, he nevertheless lived in Charles’s kingdom until at least the year 873. This is attested by those verses already mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0042D] Cf. chapter I, col. 6, note h.]. For in them Hincmar of Rheims, a certain Liuddo, a Greek who seems to have been with Hincmar [Note: [Col. 0042D] Cf. Mabillon, Annales, book XXXV, no. 58; book XXXVIII, no. 72.], and Pope John VIII, who is known to have been placed in that dignity at the end of the year 872, are commemorated with great honor [Note: [Col. 0043] It does not in fact follow from these verses that Liuddo was Greek. He is mentioned in Flodoard, History of Rheims III.12–13. EDITORIAL NOTE.].

[Col. 0043A] We believe that he composed those verses at the end of his life. For nothing else is found that he wrote afterward [Note: [Col. 0043D] Cf. Mabillon, Annales, book XXXVIII, no. 72.], and scarcely three years later Anastasius, the Roman librarian, mentioned him in a letter sent to Charles the Bald in such a way that one would think he was already dead. After complaining that he had been so obscure in translating the Areopagite, he added the following [Note: [Col. 0043D] Cf. Natalis Alexander, dissertation XIV in the ecclesiastical history of the ninth and tenth centuries, § I, no. VI.]: “I believe that he did not do this for any other reason than that, being humble in spirit, he did not presume to abandon the proper meaning of the word.” According to Natalis Alexander, who says that it was read thus in a manuscript of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus at Bourges, this letter was written “on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction,” which is the year 875.

[Col. 0043B] No more certain evidence of this matter has reached our time. Nor is it found in any historical testimony which we can trust without danger of error that establishes where Erigena ended his life, except that Mabillon says: “He seems to have remained in France.”

There are indeed some who contend that Scotus lived longer and was even summoned to England by Alfred the Great around the year 880, that he attained the dignity of abbot there, and that, when he was killed by a violent death, he was even counted among the “holy martyrs.” This account, after having stood unshaken for nearly two hundred years, was vigorously attacked in our own time by the most diligent historians, led and encouraged by Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0044C] Cf. Acta Benedictina, century IV, vol. II, p. 506 ff.]. In our own age, however, someone has appeared who attempted to restore the desperate case to its former standing [Note: [Col. 0044D] We mean Staudenmaier; cf. his book entitled John Scotus Erigena, etc., etc., p. 110 ff. Schlueter agrees with him in his edition of The Books of The Division of Nature, p. V ff.]. How unsuccessfully he did so, although he found a supporter, can, we think, be shown briefly.

However great a heap of testimonies those who defend the story amass [Note: [Col. 0045C] Staudenmaier’s work contains more than any of the authors we have seen; accordingly, we refer to his book those who wish to investigate the matter.], they trace the earliest evidence back to writers who lived two hundred or more years after Scotus—namely, Abbot Ingulf and William of Malmesbury. Those who wrote later generally take refuge in the authority of these men. Those whom they place among the rest of the crowd as the moon among lesser fires agree almost word for word with Malmesbury, except that where he cautiously expresses doubt, they generally assert the matter confidently. There is no doubt whatever, as Natalis Alexander already saw, that Malmesbury was copied word for word by them [Note: [Col. 0045C] Cf. Natalis Alexander, dissertation in the ecclesiastical history of the ninth and tenth centuries, § III. Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, admits in his chronicle under the year 1225 that a new history of the English was his guide; yet he relates the story of Scotus under the year 878 in almost the same words as William of Malmesbury (The Deeds of the Kings of England II.4). Staudenmaier did not cite Alberic. But those whom he did cite themselves clearly declare that William of Malmesbury supplied them with his words. For they too reproduce almost word for word what William of Malmesbury relates (cf. Gale, loc. cit., testimonies, pp. 6 and 8), as we have already said. We judge that he is the author of these words from the fact that where he writes “as I have understood,” they have “as is understood”; and where he says “he [Scotus] wrote a very useful book,” one of them says: “he wrote a book which he says is useful.” “He wrote” is said of Scotus. But “he says,” since it cannot refer to Scotus—for Scotus nowhere says such things about his own book—must refer to the person from whom this writer learned of the book’s usefulness; everyone will identify that person as William of Malmesbury.].

Thus the matter comes down to Ingulf and Malmesbury as the final line of defense. Although they have transmitted the story in explicit terms, they are not authors whom people ordinarily regard as especially trustworthy; and, as we have already observed, they are the first after Scotus’s time—being separated from it by two hundred or more years—to speak of Scotus’s journey to England. We must therefore carefully consider how much credence they deserve in this matter, or rather, whether perhaps, because of the differing character of the arguments, all credibility should be denied them on this point. We have, in fact, weighty arguments differing from their testimony.

First, Asser of Menevia, abbot of Bangor and bishop of Sherborne, whom Alfred had summoned to him because of his outstanding literary learning and whose most faithful service he employed in properly cultivating the study of the liberal arts, makes very careful mention in the Life of Alfred that he wrote of the learned men who came to Alfred and of whom he himself was practically a colleague. Yet he says nothing at all about our Scotus, although he would certainly have mentioned him, as a man distinguished by the highest praise of learning, if Scotus had ever come to Alfred [Note: [Col. 0046C] Cf. Histoire littéraire de la France, vol. V, p. 419.].

This one fact is enough to refute several Malmesburys and Ingulfs. Furthermore, Malmesbury writes as though Scotus, immediately after the arrival in Gaul of the letter which Nicholas I sent concerning him to Charles the Bald [Note: [Col. 0046C] Cf. above, chapter III, col. 17, notes e and f.], left Gaul and went to Alfred, “enticed by his generosity,” although it is universally acknowledged that before the year 880 Alfred, distracted by numerous wars, had not even thought of enticing learned men to him; and, finally, that the letter had already been written either in 860 or five years later [Note: [Col. 0046C] Cf. Staudenmaier, p. 166.].

Ingulf then made his Scotus abbot of the monastery at Athelney, whereas Malmesbury took his own Scotus to the monastery at Malmesbury [Note: [Col. 0046D] Cf. Staudenmaier, p. 136; Rerum Anglicarum scriptores post Bedam praecipui, Frankfurt, 1601, folio, p. 870. See above, note d.]. Ingulf, moreover, plainly shows where this error arose. For he writes [Note: [Col. 0046D] Cf. above, note a.]: “Alfred, attracting from Old Saxony John, surnamed Scotus, a philosopher of exceptionally keen intellect, appointed him head of his monastery at Athelney.”

But Asser, in the Life of Alfred [Note: [Col. 0046D] Cf. Mabillon, “Historical Eulogy of John, Abbot of Athelney,” Acta Benedictina, century IV, part II, pp. 507 ff.], reports that Alfred summoned from Gaul “a certain John, a priest and monk, an Old Saxon [Note: [Col. 0046D] That is, a Saxon originating from Germany, as Mabillon demonstrated by many examples, loc. cit., pp. 508–509. The distinguished scholar further thought that this Old Saxon had lived among the Gauls in the monastery of Corbie, where at that time several Saxons from Germany were being educated.] by birth, a very learned man, whom he later appointed abbot of the monastery at Athelney.”

Ingulf, who knew these facts and who also seems to have heard of John Scotus, that clever philosopher, as a man very well known among the Gauls in approximately Alfred’s time, had to treat the two men whom he encountered as one and the same, and added the name of the latter to the name of the former as though it were a surname.

Since Staudenmaier chiefly follows Malmesbury, let us say a few things about Malmesbury separately. In this account, then, he repeatedly fell into serious error concerning our Scotus.

We have already given one example, and there are others. For he says [Note: [Col. 0046D] Cf. Gale, loc. cit., testimonies, pp. 6–8.] that Florus [Note: [Col. 0046D] That is, St. Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, whose name was “Florus Prudentius Galindo”—or Florus, a deacon of Lyons, to whom some attribute a book of the Church of Lyons against Scotus.] wrote against Scotus’s book The Division of Nature, although Florus wrote against the book On Predestination, and other works of the same kind.

Nor should we overlook the fact that in his book On the Deeds of the Kings of England [Note: [Col. 0046D] Cf. Natalis Alexander, work cited, § III.] he relates the matter as doubtful, using expressions such as “it is believed,” “as is reported,” and “which I would not state with any uncertainty.” Yet elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0047D] In Gale, loc. cit., pp. 6–8.] he has no doubts at all. As for what he adds in those very passages—“as I understood from the writings of King Alfred, John settled at lofty Malmesbury”—this scarcely moves us, since matters otherwise stand as we have explained them. Perhaps he understood from the king’s writings that “John had settled at Malmesbury,” but added on his own, in almost the same manner as Ingulf, that “this John was John Scotus Erigena.”

Errors of this kind very often beset writers of the sort to which William belongs. The whole matter also admits of an easier explanation if we take that John to have been, like our Scotus, a member of the Scottish people. We know that in that age a very large number of learned men of Scottish origin, especially men who came from Ireland, lived in England and Gaul [Note: [Col. 0047D] Cf. above, chapters I–III.]. To this may be added a still more significant fact, expressly attested by the annals of Hyde [Note: [Col. 0047D] Cf. Gale, loc. cit., testimonies, p. 5.]: among those who under King Alfred instructed the youth at Oxford in the liberal arts, there was, besides John the Old Saxon [Note: [Col. 0047D] John the Old Saxon is the man whom the annals of Hyde call “the colleague of St. Grimbald.” It is established that Alfred summoned both men from the Continent.] mentioned above, also John, a monk of the Church of Menevia.

Could it therefore have happened that Alfred sent this same man, after he had held that office for some time, to the monastery at Malmesbury, just as he appointed John the Old Saxon abbot of Athelney? Could it have happened that this very man, since he is called a monk of the Church of Menevia, was either a Scot or was called one? Certainly, we remember that we showed above—chapter II, col. 12, note h, and chapter I—that men of Scottish origin undoubtedly lived in that very region of Menevia, and that our Scotus himself appears to have been born there [cf. chapter II, col. 12, note h].

## CHAPTER VI

On those writings of Erigena which we have not yet reviewed.

After the translations of Pseudo-Dionysius and St. Maximus, and after the books On Predestination and On the Holy Eucharist, which have already been mentioned, we have decided to discuss at length those works which are likewise genuinely Erigenian: several poems, the treatise On the Vision of God, and the five books On the Division of Nature [Note: [Col. 0047D] Some people also speak of letters. But apart from those that serve as prefaces to the translations of the Areopagite and Maximus, none exist and none are mentioned.]. As for the works additionally attributed to Scotus by some writers without any probable justification, since we cannot judge their case without the aid of the books themselves, we think that from this point onward they should simply be enumerated.

Therefore, the poems of Scotus that have become known to us number fourteen [Col. 0048A]: one is found in the preface to the book on predestination; two were appended to the preface of the translation of Pseudo-Dionysius; Cangius published one in the preface to Labbe’s glossary; Schlueterus, as he says, brought forth ten new ones from the codices of Angelo Mai [Note: [Col. 0047D] Cf. his edition of the *Book on the Division of Nature*, vol. I, p. 593 ff.] [Note: [Col. 0047D] Schlueterus was not the first to bring those poems forth from the codices of the Vatican Library, but repeated in print the edition published by Angelo Mai, *Classici Auctores*, vol. V, pp. 426 ff. Cf. the Preface. EDITOR’S NOTE.]. The shortest has four verses, the longest as many as eighty. They were almost all sent to Charles the Bald. Their subjects are for the most part drawn from the writings of philosophers and theologians: “Christ crucified,” “the cross,” “Easter,” and similar themes are sung. They contain many errors, nearly the same as those found in the books *On the Division of Nature* and *On Predestination*. They show their author to have been much more learned than distinguished by poetic ability. They contain altogether very many passages so dull and at the same time so contrived that they cannot fail to offend a diligent reader. Nevertheless, considering the circumstances of those times, they are unquestionably worthy of the highest praise. Walafridus Strabo, at any rate, could not wrest from Our Author the palm either of facility or of elegance.

Mabillonius discovered the little book *On the Vision of God* in a manuscript codex at Clairmarais, near Saint-Omer. After him, so far as we know, no one who saw the book has existed, although several have searched for it most diligently [Note: [Col. 0047D] Cf. *Acta Benedictina*, section IV, part II, p. LXVI; Thomas Gale, cited work, p. 12; Hiort, cited work, p. 46.].

Mabillonius reports that its beginning was as follows: “Treatise of John Scotus on the Vision of God. All bodily senses arise from the conjunction of soul and body [Note: [Col. 0048D] He also writes in Book II of *On the Division of Nature*, chapter 23: ‘External sense is a certain conjunction of soul and body.’].” If he is not mistaken, he says that the subject of the little book dealt with the same matter as Letter XXX of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, to Gottschalk, monk of Orbais. This letter of Lupus [Note: [Col. 0048D] Cf. *Maxima Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, etc., Lyons, vol. XV, p. 15 E ff.] explains a passage found in Saint Augustine’s *Books on the City of God*, XXII, 29: “concerning the character of the vision by which the saints will see God in the age to come.”

Several manuscript codices of the five books *On the Division of Nature*, or *περὶ φύσεως μερισμοῦ* [*On the Division of Nature*], which are likewise called *On Natures*, or *περὶ φύσεως* [*On Nature*], have been discovered [Note: [Col. 0048D] Cf. Thomas Gale, testimony, p. 12; Mabillonius, *Acta Benedictina*, section IV, part II, p. LXVI; *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 423.]. Mabillonius says that two of them were written in Scotus’s own time; nevertheless, none bore the author’s name. William of Malmesbury and Hugh of Saint Victor were the first [Note: [Col. 0048D] Cf. Thomas Gale, testimony, pp. 12, 6–7; Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, *Chronicle* under the year 1225, ed. Leibniz, vol. I, pp. 514–515.]—so far as we can establish with certainty—to attribute his books to our Scotus. Nevertheless, even at the beginning of the thirteenth century there were some who thought them to be the work of Amalric of Bena [Note: [Col. 0048D] Cf. Thomas Gale, testimony, p. 12.]. The abbot Trithemius and Bale even referred these books to John Scotus, whom they call of Melrose, a contemporary of the Venerable Bede [Note: [Col. 0048D] Cf. Thomas Gale, cited work, p. 12.]. But in truth, if anyone compares the books *On Natures* with Erigena’s [Col. 0049A] [Note: [Col. 0049D] [Col. 0049A] This note appears at the foot of columns 49 and 50, but the callout symbol (*) has not been printed in the text.] Cf. what we noted in the Preface concerning this edition. It is regrettable that Schlueterus, himself deprived [Col. 0050D] of the light of his eyes, could prepare the edition only through others less knowledgeable in these matters. EDITOR’S NOTE.] book *On Predestination*, even while engaged in some other activity, no doubt whatsoever will remain for him. This is why agreement on this matter has long since been reached among learned men, as though with one voice.

As for what Thomas Gale writes in the preface to his edition (p. 4)—that trustworthy witnesses affirm that Florus [Note: [Col. 0049D] Cf. above, Chapter V, column 46, note l.] corrupted these books in order to refute them—this is altogether an empty suspicion. Those witnesses are, we believe, Matthias of Westminster (under the year 883), and perhaps anyone who swore by his statement. But whoever they are, since that Florus—whom the Westminster chronicler claims to be “unknown”—attacked not the books *On Natures* but the book *On Predestination*, they were grievously mistaken. Moreover, to anyone who reads the books themselves carefully there appears such coherence among the parts, and such a connection among the arguments, that the most learned Hockius, relying on this argument alone, rightly rejected Thomas Gale’s suspicion as groundless [Note: [Col. 0049D] Cf. *Bonn Ephemerides*, fascicle XVI, p. 37.].

The books *On the Division of Nature* have been printed altogether twice: they first appeared at Oxford in 1681 through Thomas Gale, of Oxford; then in 1838 at Münster in Westphalia through C. B. Schlueterus, of Münster. The later edition is far inferior to the earlier because of the multitude of errors, of which not even an index was appended [Note: [Col. 0049D] And here we cannot complain too seriously! In Gale there is an enormous multitude of errors: in many places complete words and complete verses are missing. Schlueterus removed only very few of these, and new errors are not lacking. Gale, however, had collected his errors with the greatest diligence; he had inserted in his index excellent “variant readings,” as they are called, from a Parisian manuscript codex. This index of Gale extends over ten pages of the largest format. Schlueterus, however, scarcely attended to Gale’s index anywhere, nor did he wish to attend to it. His own printer indeed asserted that Schlueterus was accustomed to say: “That work is not worth doing.” Therefore one should scarcely value his edition at all, and should call it rather “corrupted” [Col. 0050D] than, as he himself does (p. I), “corrected.”].

The external form of argumentation that Scotus uses in these books is dialogue: he portrays a master conversing with a disciple, and conducts the whole discussion properly through their alternating speeches. Like the master, the disciple at one moment asks questions and at another is questioned; and, if one excepts the deeper and speculative knowledge of philosophy and theology, as we call it, scarcely any school could be called more learned.

Since the subject and character of the whole work must properly be discussed in the second part of our writing, we think it sufficient here to adopt once more as our own the words of Bruckerus that we quoted above. Bruckerus says, then [Note: [Col. 0050D] Cf. *Critical History of Philosophy*, vol. III (Leipzig edition, 1741), p. 621. We would also ask you to consult what was said above about these very expressions of Bruckerus, Chapter II, column 11, note d.], that Scotus’s entire philosophy comes down to this:

> All things whatsoever that exist are contained in God not only radically and virtually, but also essentially; and therefore all things have proceeded and flowed forth from God from eternity, and, having been distinguished into various classes of lower and higher, worse and better beings, will at last return to their source and origin—that is, God.

Everyone sees how accurately this philosophy reproduces that turbid—if I may use the word—Alexandrian chaos of the later Platonists, as they are called; and this has been demonstrated by us at greater length in Chapter II. We therefore think it already clear in itself why some philosophers have detested this Erigenian philosophy as intensely as possible, while others, on the contrary, have embraced it with the greatest eagerness. The number of those who praised it, although exceedingly small in the memory of our fathers, has in our own age increased enormously—and not, indeed, beyond the judgment of those who are wise! Anyone who wishes to become acquainted with a portion of them should consult Schlueter’s preface [Col. 0050B], p. VII ff. Yet, in that senate—“as though inspired by a higher spirit”—we see at least one person (pp. XII–XIII) whom a censorious brow might very easily disturb from that position. If we wished to enumerate those who have condemned it, the day would certainly fail us [Note: [Col. 0050D] Cf. above, Chapter II, column 11, note e, where we cited some of them.]. Therefore, in this place we shall recount only what was done against the books *On Natures* by those who have sat at the helm of the holy Church.

Thus it was at the beginning of the thirteenth century that Amalric of Bena, David of Dinant (or Dinanto), and the rest of their faction were violently troubling the Church throughout Gaul. So far as has been handed down in memory, they owed their teaching almost entirely to John Scotus’s book *On the Division of Nature*. Gerson, a most learned man and chancellor of the University of Paris, says that Amalric taught the following [Col. 0050C] [Note: [Col. 0050D] Cf. *The Complete Works of John Gerson*, ed. Ellies du Pin, Antwerp, vol. IV, column 821 ff. See also Tennemann, *History of Philosophy*, vol. VIII, part I, p. 316 ff.]:

> All things are God: God and all things. Creator and creature are the same. God is called the end of all things because all things will return into him, so that in him they may rest immutably; and they will remain one individual and unchangeable thing. Just as Abraham and Isaac are of one and the same nature, so all things are one, and all things are God; for God is the essence of all creatures, etc.

David of Dinant, Amalric’s disciple, is reported to have taught the same things in almost the same words [Note: [Col. 0050D] Cf. Thomas Aquinas, *Commentary on the Four Books of the Sentences*, Book II, distinction XVII, question I, article I; and Albertus, *Summa of Theology*, part I, tract IV, question XX. See Tennemann, cited work.]. Nothing is more similar to Erigenian doctrine than their position. We shall explain this below. Nor was this matter hidden in that age. Historians explicitly relate that Amalric compiled the work of our Scotus [Note: [Col. 0050D] Cf. Gerson and Tennemann, cited above (note f).]. They also report that those to whom the matter belonged not only condemned Scotus’s book [Col. 0051A], but ordered it to be burned publicly and solemnly [Note: [Col. 0051D] Cf. Gerson and Tennemann, cited work; Thomas Gale, testimony, p. 12; *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 423.].

Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, who is regarded as exceedingly trustworthy [Note: [Col. 0051D] The distinguished G. G. Leibniz proves this at greater length in the preface to the second volume of the edition of Alberic that he prepared.], records the following under the year 1225:

> The letters of the supreme pontiff, Honorius III: “. . . this year, concerning the solemn condemnation of a certain book of John Scotus. Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops and bishops, etc.  
> 
>  The enemy does not cease to sow tares over the good seed, etc. Recently, as our venerable brother the bishop of Paris has informed us, a certain book entitled *Periphyseon* has been discovered, teeming with so many worms of heretical depravity that it was justly rejected by our venerable brother the archbishop of Sens and his suffragans, assembled in a provincial council, by the judgment of God.  
> 
>  Since, therefore, as we have learned, the book is held in certain monasteries and other places, and several members of religious communities and learned men . . . occupy themselves most diligently with reading the said book . . . we, striving in accordance with the duty of pastoral care to prevent the corruption that such a book might introduce, strictly command and order you all and each of you, in virtue of the Holy Spirit, diligently to search for this little book; and wherever it happens to be found, whether whole or in part, to send it to us without delay, if this can safely be done, so that it may be solemnly burned. Otherwise, you yourselves are to burn it publicly, expressly enjoining upon your subjects that whoever among them has or may have copies of the said book, in whole or in part, must not delay surrendering them to us; and that all who, after this command or proclamation has come to their knowledge, knowingly presume to retain the book, whole or in part, for more than fifteen days, shall incur the sentence of excommunication and shall not escape the stigma of heretical depravity. Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February,” etc.

After these things had been decreed by Honorius III against the books *On Natures*, with the ultimate penalty, one might think that for the next four hundred and fifty years they were almost entirely consigned to oblivion, until the work of Thomas Gale, of Oxford, was printed. Nor did those who, in the meantime, compiled the Index of Prohibited Books by order of the holy Council of Trent take any concern for Scotus’s books *On Natures*. But as soon as it was reported [Col. 0052A] that books long ago condemned had again been published in their entirety, they were entered at Rome into the Index of Prohibited Books, where they have retained their place down to the present day [Note: [Col. 0051D] Cf. the Mechlin edition of the *Index of Prohibited Books*, 1838, p. 122.].

Nevertheless, Schlueterus is in no way to be blamed because, although he professes himself a Catholic, he republished those books in disregard of the authority of the supreme pontiffs. For when he had recently been warned of this very matter, he informed the person who warned him, through a young man who was his close friend, that he had never heard, nor could he believe, that any work of John Scotus Erigena had been placed in the Index of Prohibited Books; perhaps, deceived by the similarity of the names, that person had transferred to John Scotus Erigena what he had found concerning John Duns Scotus.

[Col. 0052B] We now come simply to report those works that one person or another has attributed to Erigena without sufficient reason. They are generally the following [Note: [Col. 0052D] Cf. *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 427 ff.; Thomas Gale, testimony, pp. 11 and 13. We have chiefly followed that history, which, although later, appears to have discussed this matter more accurately than Thomas Gale.]:

I. “Extracts from Macrobius on the Differences and Correspondences of the Greek and Latin Verb.”

II. “Homily on the Beginning of the Gospel according to John.”

These two are generally thought probably to be Erigenian.

III. “Commentary on Dionysius the Areopagite.”

Perhaps no one has seen this work—although those whom we cited above [note d] as our authorities persuaded themselves that they had. In our own age, however, Dr. Greith, parish priest of Saint Gall, discovered in the Vatican Library [Note: [Col. 0052D] Cf. Hoefler, *The German Popes*, part II, p. 80 ff.] “Expositions by John Scotus on the Celestial Hierarchy of the Pseudo-Areopagite.” It has not yet been printed, except that Hoefler brought out from it a passage [Col. 0052C] on the Holy Eucharist, which we too have transcribed above (at the end of Chapter IV) [Note: [Col. 0051] We have now published for the first time the surviving fragments of the commentary, recovered from the codices. EDITOR’S NOTE.]. The style of this passage is sufficiently Erigenian.

IV. Latin translations both of the *Moral Works of Aristotle* and of the *Various Stories of Marvels*. It is easier to deny that the former belong to Scotus than to grant that they do; concerning the latter, there is no hesitation in denying it.

V. “Commentary on the Gospel according to Matthew,” “Treatise on Human Duties,” etc., etc.

Whenever these books are said to have been written by a John or by some Scotus, they are immediately attributed to our John by learned men who are accustomed to have great confidence in their conjectures. In fact, they are shown to be owed almost entirely to other authors who happened to share with our author one name or the other, John or Scotus.

## SECOND PART

[Col. 0051]

### § 1

[Col. 0051D]

Under the name of Nature (*natura*, or *φύσις*) is comprehended whatever “can either be perceived by the mind or surpasses the mind’s apprehension.”

### § 2

[Col. 0053A]

I. “The first and highest division of Nature is into those things which are and those things which are not.” (I, 1.)

There are, however, five “modes” in which something may be said either “to be” or “not to be.”

### § 3

“The first seems to be that by which reason teaches that everything which falls under bodily sense or under the apprehension of intelligence may reasonably be said to be; whereas those things which, by the excellence of their nature, evade every sense, understanding, and reason may rightly appear not to be.” Thus, in this mode, certain accidents of each essence are said to be, while the essences themselves are said not to be; for essences are recognized not by “what they are” but only by “that they are.” (I, 2–3.)

### § 4

[Col. 0053B]

“The second mode is considered in the orders of created natures. Each order may be said both to be and not to be. For the affirmation of the lower is the negation of the higher; the negation of the lower is the affirmation of the higher,” etc. (I, 4.)

### § 5

“In the third mode, those things which are known to have been generated from their causes in formed matter, in times and places, we say by a certain customary usage to be; whereas those things which are still contained in the very recesses of Nature and do not yet appear in formed matter . . . we say, by the same customary usage, not to be.” (I, 5.)

### § 6

[Col. 0053C]

“The fourth mode, according to the philosophers, not implausibly says that only those things truly are which are comprehended by the intellect alone; whereas those things that vary, are gathered together, and are dissolved through the spaces of places and the movements of times are truly said not to be.” (I, 6.)

### § 7

“The fifth mode is discerned by reason in human nature alone. Since this nature, by sinning, abandoned the dignity of the divine image in which it properly subsisted, it deservedly lost its own being and is therefore said not to be; but when, restored by the grace of God, it is brought back to the original state of its substance, it begins to live [Note: [Col. 0053D] Everything that belongs to humankind will eventually be reduced substantially into the divine substance—and, together with humankind, the remaining ‘nature of visible things’ as well. We shall explain this more fully below.].” (I, 7.)

### § 8

[Col. 0053D]

“We see, therefore, that we must take care not to suppose that those things which Scotus comprehends under the name of Nature, and declares can in several ways be said either to be or not to be, in any way include things that truly and properly ought to be called nothing, things that truly and properly are found nowhere. Thus the case is entirely different when Scotus denies that sins and the punishments of sins are [Note: [Col. 0053D] Cf. above, chapter 27, section IV, column, note c ff.]; for sins and punishments are truly nothing to him, since they are understood only as privations of things that are [Note: [Col. 0053D] Cf. *On the Division of Nature*, I, 3.].”

### § 9

II. But there is another and much more important division of Nature.

“This division appears to receive four species: the first is that which creates and is not created; the second, that which is created and creates; the third, that which is created and does not create; the fourth, that which neither creates nor is created. Two of these four are opposed to each other: the third is opposed to the first, and the fourth to the second. But the fourth is placed among impossibilities, its distinguishing characteristic being that it cannot exist.

“‘The fourth species troubles me greatly,’ says the disciple; ‘for I would dare to have no hesitation at all about the other three, since the first is understood in the cause of all things that are and are not; the second in the primordial causes; and the third in those things that are known in generation and in times and places [Note: [Col. 0053D] That fourth species of Nature is placed “among impossibilities” in such a way that it is not a fourth entity subsisting in itself and distinct from the other three. We shall show below that our fourth species of Nature is one and the same as the first species, namely God himself. For since God brought forth from himself whatever is contained within the compass of created things, he is called the uncreated and creating Nature; but since at some time he will comprehend all those things restored into himself, bringing nothing further forth from himself, he is called the uncreated and non-creating Nature. Cf. II, 2; III, 23.]. But it is necessary to discuss each of them with greater subtlety.’” (I, 1; II, 1.)

### § 10

A. “The first species of Nature, then, appeared to be that which creates and is not created.”

This “is rightly predicated of God alone: for he alone, creating all things, is understood to exist without a beginning, because he alone is the principal cause of all things that have been made from him and through him; and therefore he is also the end of all things that are from him, for all things desire him. He is the beginning, because all things that participate in essence are from him; he is the end, because all things move toward him, seeking the rest of their movement and the stability of their perfection.” (I, 12.)

### § 11

“From the essence of the things that are, from the wondrous order of things, and from the stable movement of all things, theologians rightly understood Nature the creator to be, to know, and to live. Accordingly, investigators of truth handed down that the Father is understood through essence, the Son through wisdom, and the Holy Spirit through life. Thus they taught that the Trinity exists in unity.

“They called unity the one cause of all things [Col. 0054D]. But, contemplating this unity in its wondrous multiplicity, they understood three substances [Note: [Col. 0054D] In Book II, 29, he writes: ‘One essence in three substances, and three substances in one essence—or, according to the usage of the Roman language: one substance in three persons, and three persons in one substance.’ Cf. II, 23, 34.]: the unbegotten, the begotten, and the proceeding. They called the relation of the unbegotten to the begotten the Father; the relation of the begotten to the unbegotten they called the Son; and the relation of the proceeding to the unbegotten and the begotten they called the Holy Spirit. Thus Abraham is the name of a substance—or person—and Isaac is the name of a substance; the relation of the former to the latter is called father, and the relation of the latter to the former is called son.” (I, 14.)

### § 12

Concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, Scotus favors the opinion of the Greeks much more than that of the Latins. He says, then, that just as the one divine essence is said to exist in three substances, and so forth, so—since the divine essence is the cause of all things—it may also be said that one cause exists in three causes. But since nowhere in the nature of things does one cause arise from two causes, he does not see how the Holy Spirit could proceed from the Father and the Son, two causes [one cause [Note: [Col. 0055D] Scotus himself seems to have noticed how invalid this line of reasoning is; to those who criticize it he responds that, guided solely by the nature of things, one arrives at knowledge of the divine Being and the holy Trinity! Cf. II, 31, at the end. Scotus further maintains, in his doctrine of the Holy Trinity, that no one should suppose “that the Son was born from the essence of the Father, or that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the essence of the Father, since the Son was born from the person of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the person of the Father: for one may say that the Son was born from the Father and that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, and yet the substance, not the person, is not peculiar to the Father.” (34.)]. If you say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son because he proceeds from the Father through the Son, this scarcely amounts to anything, since the Son himself also has the Father as his cause (II, 19; II, 30–35). Nevertheless, he does not dare to refuse belief that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. For he thinks that the holy Latin fathers, if anyone were to question them about this matter, would “reasonably” “respond” in this way, and that it might perhaps be defended by the authority of sacred Scripture. (II, 33.)

### § 13

“Whether the ten categories can truly and properly be predicated of the divine Being is difficult to say. In this question, however, apophatic (*ἀποφατική*) and cataphatic (*καταφατική*) theology are useful: the former denies, the latter affirms, that the divine substance is this or that among the things that exist, such as essence, goodness, the sun, a star, water, a lion, a bear,” and so forth. These statements appear to contradict one another, but since they concern the divine substance, they are altogether in agreement. For cataphatic theology does not say that the divine substance is that thing properly, but that it may be called so metaphorically; apophatic theology, however, maintains that the divine substance is neither truly that thing nor properly called by that name.

Erigena rejoices with immortal delight in these theologies, which he received so beautifully from Saint Dionysius the Areopagite. (I, 14, 16, 78, etc.; Preface to Maximus’s *Ambigua* [Gale, appendix, p. IV].) At length he argues that there is no one among Aristotle’s ten categories that can truly and properly be predicated of God [Col. 0055D]; whenever cataphatic theology affirms any one of them of him, it is immediately denied by apophatic theology. (I, 17–80.)

### § 14

“God has nothing opposed to him [Note: [Col. 0056D] Cf. below, §§ 18–20.]. Since nothingness is opposed to essence, and evil to goodness, etc., God is not essence, goodness, etc., but more than essence—superessential—and more than goodness—supergood—and so forth. Everything that is predicated of God with the particles *super-* or ‘more than’ contains those two theologies: in its utterance it has the form of cataphatic theology, but in its meaning the force of apophatic theology.” (I, 16.)

### § 15

It is therefore clear from what we have set out above that God is almost entirely inaccessible to the vision of the human mind. Yet he knows himself. One must indeed say altogether that “God does not know what he is,” that “God does not know himself as something,” and statements of the same kind; but this is the true power of the faculty of knowing that exists in God. For God truly is not a “what,” nor is he “in something”; that is, he is not some definite thing, nor is he contained and circumscribed in any of those things that exist and are included among created things. (II, 28–29.)

But if you ask how God should be thought to know the things he knows, the answer will be: “He contemplates neither sensible things through sense, nor intelligible things through intellect, nor sensible things through intellect, nor intelligible things through sense, but all things in their eternal reasons.” (Preface to the translation of the *Ambigua* of Saint Maximus, in Gale’s appendix, p. IV; *On the Division of Nature*, II, 20, 28; V, 17.)

Those “eternal reasons” are the so-called “ideas,” the “principal exemplars” of all things that God was going to make. These belong only to substantial things, and they too are substantial things. (Cf. below, §§ 23–30.) Hence Scotus rightly maintains also this: “Divine knowledge is the cause [Col. 0056C] of all things that are”; “whatever God is not the cause of, he does not know”; “the knowledge of things that are”—that is, in God—“is truly those things that are.” (II, 20, 28; V, 27; III, 4. Then cf. also his *On Predestination*, above, Chapter IV.)

### § 16

Since no category is properly predicated of God, the ninth category, *πράττειν* [to act], does not apply to him either. Yet God is said to have created. But creating and being must be regarded as one and the same in God.

“God did not exist before he made all things. His making is coeternal with God and coessential to him. God and his making—that is, his action—are one simple and indivisible thing; for God, who is innumerable, does not admit number into himself. When, therefore, we hear that God makes all things, we ought to understand nothing other than that God is in all things, that is, that the essence of all things subsists. For he alone truly is through himself, and whatever is truly said to be in the things that are is he alone. None of the things that are truly exists through itself; but whatever is truly understood in him receives true being through participation in that one who alone exists through himself.” (I, 74.)

### § 17

[Col. 0057A]

This very passage of Scotus provides us with a convenient transition to another discussion of his creating Nature.

Nothing, then, appears clearer at this point! One might say that a dreadful monster of pantheism is visible to the eyes! It is written in explicit words that the creating Nature, which we have said is called God, is in all the things that he made in such a way that it itself is the sole and true essence of those things. And we find Erigena speaking in precisely the same way very often. Thus, in Book I of *On the Division of Nature*, chapter 73, he says:

> “God is thought to come to be universally in his creatures, since in them he is understood not only to be present, without whom they cannot exist, but also to be their essence.”

And in the same book, chapter 3:

> “For God is the essence of all things, and he alone truly is.”

Nor should it go unnoticed that in this last passage the very thing Scotus calls essence is also called by him substance, and is described with sufficient precision that we are compelled to acknowledge it as substance in the true and proper sense.

In Book II of *On the Division of Nature*, chapter 2, he says:

> “What if you join the creature to the Creator in such a way that you understand nothing else in it besides him who alone truly is? For nothing outside him is said to be truly essential, since all things that are from him are, insofar as they are, nothing other than participation in him who alone subsists from himself and through himself. Will you deny that Creator and creature are one? Not easily; for it seems ridiculous to resist this.”

### § 18

[Col. 0057C]

This too must be referred to what Our Author asserts above (§ 14): that nothing at all is opposed to God. Hence, since “nothingness” is opposed to “essence,” God is not essence but more than essence, or superessential. For if nothing is opposed to God, we think it must certainly be granted that there is nothing besides God—that is, that God is whatever is.

Setting this matter aside, let us follow the consequence that Scotus himself proposed: since “nothingness” is opposed to “essence,” God is not essence but more than essence, or superessential. This superessentiality is therefore predicated of the divine Being [Note: [Col. 0057D] In other passages the divine Being is also called superessential for other reasons—for example, because it occupies, as it were, a more exalted place of essence above all things, because it is “the source of all essences,” and for reasons of the same kind. But these are not relevant here. Below (§ 22) we shall make clear that those explanations do not conflict with the one we are presenting here.] because it is somehow constituted above that “essence” to which “nothingness” is opposed [Col. 0057D] (above, § 8), in such a way that it is itself, as it were, a third thing, by which those things that are opposed to one another are simultaneously comprehended and, so to speak, made “concordant” and bound together in “harmonious peace.”

For Scotus has the following:

> Catholic faith and true reason confess that God is infinite, and more than infinite—for he is the infinity of all infinities—and simple, and more than simple—for he is the simplicity of all simple things. And they believe or understand that nothing exists together with him, since he is the circumference of all things that are and are not, of all things that can be and cannot be, and of things that appear to be contrary or opposed to him—not to mention things similar and dissimilar. For he is the similarity of similar things, the dissimilarity of dissimilar things, the opposition of opposites, and the contrariety of contraries. He gathers and composes all these things in a single concord, through a beautiful and ineffable harmony [Note: [Col. 0057D] We therefore think that Schlueterus’s statement about Scotus is entirely justified (p. XIII): “The learned Hegelian—as we may use this word—with his dialectical monism recalls Erigena in very many ways.”].

(I, 74.)

To this same explanation of the divine superessentiality established by Erigena belongs also what he says repeatedly (I, 3, 73): “The being of all things is the super-being of divinity.”

[Col. 0058B]

Because of the importance of the matter, let us add this passage as well:

> Yet no one who believes devoutly and understands the truth fails immediately to exclaim that the supernatural and superessential creative cause of the whole universe is above every life, wisdom, and power, and above all things that are spoken, understood, and perceived by every sense, while it is the causal principle of all these things, the essential middle filling them, and the consummating end—and the circumference enclosing all things that are and are not.

(III, 1.)

### § 19

This superessential God, then, is situated, as it were, above all things that are, all things that are thought, and all things that escape the mind’s vision, in such a way that he embraces all of them with his essence as a kind of body of the universe, fills them with his essence, and brings them into being through his essence.

Thus, when Scotus denies that Aristotle’s category of essence can properly be predicated of his divine Being—since nothingness is opposed to it, whereas God has nothing opposed to him [Note: [Col. 0058D] He also denies that it can be predicated of God because God is not “a certain and defined substance” that is found here or there “among the number of created substances.” Cf. above, § 15; II, 28–29.]—he is very far from removing from God the essence of the universe. Rather, he explicitly leaves that essence to him and indeed plainly and explicitly attributes it to him.

### § 20
But those who have paid attention will object to us that Erigena, having distinguished from the beginning four species of Nature, said that God, or Nature not created but creating, was also a species of Nature, and thus opposed it diametrically, as they say, to the third species of Nature, Nature created but not creating. Let Erigena himself satisfy them. Concerning Nature not created but creating, that first species or form of Nature, he says:

“If it is proper to call the first cause of all things a species or form, it surpasses every form and species, since it is the formless principle of all forms and species . . . We call the formless principle God for this reason: so that no one may suppose that he is counted among the number of forms, since he is the cause of all forms. For everything formed desires him [Note: That is, as it seems to us, ‘everything formed (just as it proceeded from him, so also) participates in his essence,’ and is substantially united with him. Cf. I, 12–13. 74; III, 1. 3–4.], since he is infinite in himself, and more than infinite; for he is the infinity of all infinities.” (II, 1.)

§ 21.

Thus, as we judge, it is evident that, according to Scotus’s opinion, no substance whatsoever is found in this universe except the substance of the divine Nature that creates, nor, as he himself says (II, 2), can anything “outside it truly be called essential”! If anyone should still doubt this matter, we hope that he will be firmly convinced when we discuss the remaining forms of Nature.

§ 22.

Nevertheless, the nature of our undertaking seems to require that we now try, insofar as possible at present, to explain and dispel what we see has deceived more than a few people in this Erigenian matter [Note: Cf. Schlueter, p. XVIII ff.]. There are altogether several passages in the books *On the Division of Nature* in which Erigena, perhaps accommodating himself to ordinary human understanding, wrote as though he regarded God as separate from this universe [Note: Cf. Schlueter, loc. cit.]. For, among other things, we read the following:

“God himself, in himself, beyond every creature, is comprehended by no intellect.” (I, 3. 7, etc.) We read likewise (II, 1, etc.):

“By a metaphor, a creature may be called by the name of God, because it has been made by God [Note: Schlueter (p. XIX) ought to have taken these passages into consideration; certainly he would have produced them in Scotus’s defense, since they would have been much more impressive as arguments.].”

We do not wish to enumerate one by one the points by which these statements can readily be refuted. We say only this: it follows spontaneously from Erigena’s own philosophy that he could have taught both these things and those which we heard him teaching above (§§ 16–21).

Now, this philosophy is substantially as follows, as will be demonstrated at greater length below. God the Father—Nature not created but creating—created from eternity in his only-begotten Son; that is, he substantially emitted from his own substance Nature created and creating, the “primordial causes” of all things whatsoever contained within the body of the universe, that is, the “ideas” and “principal exemplars” [Col. 0060A]. Then the same God the Father, through the Holy Spirit, “divided and multiplied” these primordial causes into their effects, namely, Nature created but not creating, this entire universe of things. He did so in such a way that the causes were not cast down from their proper seat, which they had occupied from all eternity in God himself, and so that, through their substantial participation alone, that which is truly and properly said to exist in this universe—namely, the essence and substance of all things—would be precisely what it is.

Finally, Nature created but not creating, which had been substantially unfolded through created and creating Nature from uncreated and creating Nature, will retrace the same path and be substantially rolled back into uncreated and creating Nature [Note: “For,” says Scotus (book III, chapter 4), “the whole river flows principally from its source, and through its channel the water that first rises in the spring is continually and without interruption poured forth: so divine goodness, essence, life, wisdom, and everything that is in the source of all things” (that is, in God [cf.
