IV, 1]) “first flows into the primordial causes and makes them exist; then, through the primordial causes, it flows into their effects in an ineffable manner, through the orders of the universe appropriate to them, always flowing through the higher things” [Col. 0060D] “toward the lower, and again, through the most secret pores of Nature, by a most hidden passage, returning to its source.” Although, however, in this way God becomes all things in all things, he does not cease to be above all things.” (III, 20.)].

Scotus therefore holds that there is absolutely no substance in anything except the divine substance, and that God is, as it were, separated and set apart from the things he created [Col. 0060B].

Since this is so, we certainly do not see how it can be that someone who treats the matter with somewhat greater attention, as soon as Erigena, perhaps accommodating himself to the common manner of speaking, has spoken as though he professed God to be distinct from created things, should immediately seem to encounter an objection in his own thought, and should judge that Scotus—accused of pantheism since ancient times—not merely ought to be acquitted, but should even be crowned and exalted with every kind of honor, “since he has not overstepped the straightedge of truth.” Indeed, by heaven, if Schlueter had tried to understand Scotus’s philosophy in the manner we have now explained, he would not have attempted so fruitlessly to excuse and defend him. But we shall also have to meet him on this point at greater length below. Enough has now been said about Nature not created but creating.

§ 23.

B. “The second species of Nature is that which creates and is created.”

“This species is to be understood only in the primordial causes of things, as is generally thought. The primordial causes themselves are usually called by the Greeks *πρωτότυπα* (*prōtótypa*), that is, primordial exemplars; or *προορίσματα* (*proorísmata*), that is, predestinations; likewise *θεῖα θελήματα* (*theîa thelḗmata*), that is, divine wills; or even *ἰδέαι* (*idéai*), that is, species or forms, in which the immutable reasons of all things to be made were established before they existed [Note: Since, in this discussion of the primordial causes, Erigena is presenting the Platonic doctrine of ideas, we thought it especially worthwhile at this point to explain briefly what a Platonic idea properly was. Let us use Brucker’s words. He says in *Hist. crit. phil.*, vol. III, p. 905: ‘For Plato, an idea is not that which arises from the contemplation of individual objects—the notion of universality and the concept of some general thing—but ideas are the essential exemplars of all individual things, possessing *αὐτουσία* (*autousía*), in accordance with whose nature and character individual things have been formed, and which grant these things a true, certain, and stable essence. These ideas arise from the divine mind and are rooted in it, but possess their own proper substance.’].”

“And they are not improperly so called, since the Father—that is, the principle of all things—in his Word, namely his only-begotten Son, preformed the reasons of all things that he willed to be made, before the things came to be.” (II, 2. 36.)

§ 24.

“The primordial causes, therefore, since they are causes not of some things but of all visible and invisible things, must necessarily be without number. Although they do not have a fixed order, so that any one of them could be first in number, Saint Dionysius nevertheless seems rightly to have established these ten as first: goodness in itself, essence in itself, life in itself, reason in itself, intelligence in itself, wisdom in itself, virtue in itself, blessedness in itself, truth in itself [Col. 0061B], and eternity in itself [Note: They are called “per se” because they ‘are participations of the one cause of all things, and no creature has been interposed between them and the one cause of all.’ (II, 36; III, 1.)].

“Among the primordial causes, which divine sages call the principles of all things, are therefore all the virtues and reasons [Note: Hiortius translates these words as *alle thätigen, lebendigen Begriffe* (‘all active, living concepts’).] which the Father once and simultaneously made in the Son, and according to which the order of all things is woven from the highest to the lowest—that is, from the intellectual creature, which after God is nearest to God, down to the lowest order of all things, which contains bodies.” (III, 14, 1; II, 36.)

§ 25.

“The primordial causes of visible things possess exceptional subtlety, an ineffable simplicity of nature, and an obscurity that has not been revealed by any light of color or distinction of forms; but the primordial causes of intellectual essence possess incomprehensible height and an infinite diffusion of themselves through all things, which is perceived by no sense and comprehended by no intellect. Because of the excellence of their ineffable purity, they have deserved to be called darkness. They are known from their effects—that is, from their processions into sensible and intelligible genera and forms—because it is known that they exist, but it is not understood what they are.” (II, 17. 20.)

§ 26.

“If anyone wishes to know whether those principal exemplars understand themselves before they flow forth into the things of which they are causes, the answer must briefly be that God made them in his wisdom [Note: That is, in his only-begotten Son. Cf. above, § 12; *On the Division of Nature* II, 22.], so that they would know not only themselves but also the things of which they are the principles. For it must not be believed that anything foolish and ignorant of itself was created in divine wisdom.” (II, 18, 20; V, 24.)

§ 27.

“Those primordial causes, moreover, existed from all eternity. They were indeed made, but in such a way that neither did their eternity precede their making, nor did their making precede their eternity. For when the Son was born from the Father—that is, when this was accomplished from all eternity—the substantial predestinations (that is, the primordial causes) were made in the Word of God. We believe, therefore, that the primordial causes are coeternal with the Father and the Son.” (III, 16; II, 20–21.)

Although Scotus explicitly said in these passages that the primordial causes are “coeternal” with the Father and the Son, elsewhere he maintains that they are not altogether “coeternal” with them.

“For,” he says, “we call the primordial causes coeternal with God because they subsist always in God without any temporal beginning; but we do not call them coeternal with him because they begin to exist not from themselves but from their creator, whereas the creator himself in no way begins to exist.”

There is an even more remarkable argument attached to this explanation of the matter [Col. 0062B]:

“If in the very cause of all causes, in the Holy Trinity, some procession is understood—for the deity that begets and sends precedes the deity that is begotten and proceeds, although the deity is one and inseparable—it is neither surprising nor incredible that the cause of all causes should precede those of which it is the cause.” (*On the Division of Nature* II, 21; III, 5 ff.)

“Although it cannot be grasped how the primordial causes can be both made and eternal, the matter is nevertheless illustrated by the example of numbers, which are simultaneously eternal and made: eternal in the monad, made in the multiplication of the monad.” (III, 11 ff.)

§ 28.

Those living principal exemplars of all the virtues and reasons through which the universe of the natures of things is constituted, which we have called primordial causes (§§ 23–24), are therefore not only coeternal with God (§ 27), but have also been joined to God from all eternity and consequently have existed in God himself. For they were created, founded, or made by God the Father, the supreme principle of all things, in his only-begotten Son, so that they have always “subsisted in him.” (§§ 23–24; §§ 26–27.)

How, however, the primordial causes were founded in the only-begotten Word of God “surpasses every intellect and is known only to the Word in which they were founded.” (III, 16–17.) Nevertheless, Erigena writes elsewhere:

“For just as a river flows principally from its source, and the water that rises in the source is poured forth through its channel, so divine goodness, essence, life, wisdom, and everything that is in the source of all things (that is, in God [cf. IV, 1]) flows into the primordial causes and makes them exist.” (III, 4.)

§ 29.

These very words clearly declare also that the primordial causes are substantial exemplars of things, which flowed substantially from the divine substance and possess the same essence as God himself. Scotus consistently teaches this. Among many other passages, we read the following:

“Holy Scripture says: ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth’; that is, God the Father founded the universe of the whole visible and invisible creation in God the Son. And what could the Father found in his beginning, in his Word, in his only-begotten Son, that the Son himself [Note: Something that would not be ‘consubstantial with the Son himself.’ Cf. III, 17; II, 20 ff.; III, 8–9; especially V, 24 ff.] would not be? Otherwise he would not have founded it in him. Or how could he allow a word to come into being in himself [Note: That is, the complex of the primordial causes or Nature created and creating. Cf. § 30.] that was not consubstantial with him? For light does not admit darkness into itself, nor does truth receive fiction into itself.” (III, 17.)

Then we find this passage (III, 1):

“In all the primordial causes, this rule is uniformly observed: that they are, in themselves, principal participations of the one cause of all, which is God” (cf. II, 36).

What this “participation” properly means is explained by Erigena at greater length (III, 3). We find the substance of his explanation stated as follows:

“From this it is most easily understood that participation is nothing other than the derivation of a second essence from a higher essence.”

Thus the primordial causes are participations of the one cause of all things, which is God, in such a way that “their essence is derived from his essence,” that is, “as water has flowed forth from a spring.” (Cf. III, 3–5.)

§ 30.

Nor should Schlueter’s opinion be passed over here [Note: Cf. p. XVIII ff.], namely, that J. Goerres was completely mistaken [Note: Cf. *Christliche Mystik*, vol. I, pp. 243–244.] when he wrote that the Nature created and creating posited by Erigena was the only-begotten Son of God. Both men were led into error, Schlueter more seriously than Goerres. For Scotus’s position is this.

From all eternity God the Father begot his only-begotten Son for himself (cf. above, § 11). Then the Father, likewise from all eternity, created in this Son—that is, substantially emitted from his own substance—the primordial causes and principal exemplars of the whole universe of things. These are entirely of the same substance as the Son, and their complex constitutes Nature created and creating (§§ 23–29).

Thus Nature created and creating—the universal principal exemplar, as it were, of the whole universe to be founded—not only is contained in the only-begotten Son of God but is also of the same substance as he. Scotus could therefore, in a certain sense, rightly teach as doctrines of his philosophy what Goerres says.

Accordingly, he maintained (III, 9) that “the Word itself (that is, the Son of God) and the principal reason of the entire multiplicity of the created universe (that is, Nature created and creating) are one and the same thing.” He went even further. For he asserts most confidently (III, 20–21) that the “Son of God” was “created, not begotten, and made part of the number of creatures.”

Yet, since what we have explained above is taught elsewhere with sufficient consistency, and since no one can fail to see that in these passages (III, 9, and especially III, 20–21) Scotus was carried away by his desire to prove something else, we do not think that his statements—that the Son “is one and the same thing with Nature created and creating” and that “the Son of God is created”—should be entirely excised root and branch.

§ 31.

C. We now come to “the third species of Nature, which is created and does not create.”

“This species is understood in those things that are known through generation, times, and places; that is, in the ultimate effects of the primordial causes.” (I, 1; IV, 1.)

§ 32.

The primordial causes of all things, therefore, which are contained within Nature created but not creating—the principal exemplars which God had founded from all eternity in his Son—always subsisted in that same only-begotten Son of God. (§§ 23–30; III, 8–9.)

“But while they are understood to have been established in the beginning of all things, in the only-begotten Word of God, they are one and simple, and are defined or separated by no known order. They undergo this condition in their effects. For when they proceed or flow into their effects, multiplied to infinity, they receive a pluralization of themselves that is numerous and ordered.

“The matter becomes clearer to those who contemplate a circle and the lines drawn from the center to it. For all the lines are one in the center and are in no way separated; but when they extend outward from the center, the spaces by which they are separated begin to increase, until they reach the outer circumference, where their intervals are measured at their greatest width.” (III, 1 ff.)

§ 33.

“Then the one cause of all things, God, just as he founded the primordial causes in his Son, so through the Holy Spirit divides and multiplies them into their effects. Holy Scripture says: ‘And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.’ The easiest understanding of this appears if, as they say a certain Syrian translated it, one reads: ‘And the Spirit of God brooded over the waters.’

“For the Holy Spirit brooded over the waters of the primordial causes, so that they might flow into those things of which they are the causes; that is, he nourished them by the warmth of divine love. For this is why eggs are brooded over by birds: so that the inward and invisible power of the seeds hidden in them may burst forth, through the measured progression of places and times, into visible and bodily forms of beauty.” (II, 36, 19–22.)

§ 34.

“This division and multiplication of the one cause of all things, which is God, into all things that exist takes place in such a way that it descends first through the general essence of all things, then through the most general genera, next through the more general genera, then through the more particular species, down to the most particular species, by means of differences and properties.” (III, 3–4; II, 2; preface to Maximus’s *Ambigua*, Gallic edition, appendix, p. III.)

§ 35.

“From this it follows that whatever has been constituted by the one principle of all things through natural descents down to the extremity of the whole of Nature, which contains bodies, participates in that one principle of all things, that one source of all things. For participation is nothing other than derivation from a higher essence, and a distribution from that which first possesses being to a second thing, so that it may exist.” (III, 3.)

“The primordial causes, between which and the cause of all things no creature has been interposed, immediately participate in that one cause of all things; they themselves are participated in by the remaining orders of things, insofar as they are the causes of those orders. For whatever things are good are participations of goodness in itself; whatever things possess essence are participations of essence in itself; whatever things live are participations of life in itself.” It is not contrary to the truth to understand the other principles in the same way, and so forth (cf. § 24). (III, 3–4; II, 36; III, 1.)

§ 36.

“Just as the primordial causes exist and subsist solely through participation in the one cause of all things from which they flowed, so all the orders of things after them, which flowed from them, exist and subsist solely through participation in them.” (II, 36; III, 1. 8–9, 3–4. 20.)

In these passages, one would say that it is expressly taught that the substances themselves of all the things by which this universe is constituted descended from the seat of the primordial causes—which is in the Son of God—into this universe, while retaining that seat at the same time. This is taught even more explicitly in other passages (cf. III, 4. 25; below, § 38).

But in the fifth book (chapter 14 ff.) we read:

“Just as the primordial causes themselves do not abandon wisdom (that is, the Word of God), so substances themselves do not abandon the causes but always subsist in them; and just as the causes do not know how to exist outside substance, so substances cannot flow outside the causes.

“It remains, therefore, that this world was fashioned and compacted from the qualities of substances. By qualities I mean, as the wise customarily call them, all things that happen to substances, because they are mutable and revolve around their substances.

“Yet we do not therefore suppose that the aforesaid qualities of substances entirely abandon their own substances, around which they revolve, and enter into the matter of the sensible world; rather, in a wondrous and ineffable manner known only to its maker, they always remain both around their own substances, to which they are inseparably attached, and complete and compose this world in a certain intelligible manner through their combinations.”

And again, in the fifth book (chapter 25):

“All things that vary according to places and times and are subject to bodily senses are to be understood not as the substantial and truly existing things themselves, but as certain transitory images and representations of those truly existing things. An example of this reasoning is the voice and its image, which is called *ἠχώ* (*ēchō*, ‘echo’), or bodies and their shadows: all of these are proved to be not things themselves but false images of things.”

But since Erigena speaks in this manner only in a few passages, we have thought that we ought chiefly to follow that opinion which he seems everywhere else to express. It will nevertheless be enough to show that we have not neglected this other view. (Cf. below, § 64.)

§ 37.

Once these matters have been set forth, it is, as we judge, clearer than daylight what our Scotus taught in the books *On the Division of Nature* both about the origin and about the substance of Nature created but not creating, by which name he calls this universe of things. For, if anyone ever expressed what is called an emanative system, it was he.

Since in our own age there have been some who, perhaps believing that this was not Scotus’s true position, scarcely or not at all doubted that Scotus’s reasoning was entirely sound and intact and in no way to be accused of what is called pantheism [Note: Cf. Schlueter’s preface, p. VI ff.], we shall add to this discussion one or two further passages from the books *On the Division of Nature*, from which, if possible, the character of this Erigenian doctrine may be recognized even more clearly. We shall then see that this very doctrine is the true position of the books *On the Division of Nature*.

§ 38.

I. “What am I to say about those who think that the world was made from that nothing which signifies the negation of all essence, or the privation or absence of essence? I do not know. For I do not see why they do not consider” what ought especially to be considered. (III, 22.)

We have closed Scotus’s words in our own words for this reason: we could not transcribe what he added to them. For, by whirling himself around as though through an exceedingly dense forest of nonsense, he harasses and torments those whom he challenged with the words we have just quoted in full.

He explains in many passages (III, 19–23) the one and only opinion he follows concerning that nothing—namely, whether it is some definite matter from which God composed the world. The substance of his explanation is this:

“By the name nothing we signify the ineffable, incomprehensible, and inaccessible brilliance of divine goodness (or Nature), unknown to every intellect, human or angelic—for it is superessential and supernatural—which, when thought of in itself, neither is, nor was, nor will be” (cf. above, §§ 1–8);

“for it is understood in none of the things that exist, since it surpasses all things. But when, through a certain ineffable condescension, it is contemplated by the eyes of the mind in the things that are, it alone is found to be in all things, and it is, was, and will be.”

He says likewise (III, 17):

“The matter of which it is written that God made the world is from him and in him, and he is in it, insofar as it is understood to exist. For God does not need another matter, which he himself is not, in which to make himself; otherwise he would seem powerless and imperfect in himself.”

II. “God is the creating cause of all existing and non-existing things, created by no one, one principle, one origin, and the one universal source of all things, flowing from no one, while all things flow from him.” (IV, 1.)

III. “God himself is the maker of all things and is made in all things; and while he is sought above all things, he is found in no essence, for he does not yet possess being. But while he is understood in all things, nothing subsists in them except he alone; and it is not that this is this and that is not this, but he is all things.

“Therefore, descending first from the superessentiality of his nature, in which he is said not to be, he is created by himself in the primordial causes and becomes the principle of all essence, all life, all intelligence, and of all things contemplated in the primordial causes by gnostic theory.

“Then, descending from the primordial causes, which occupy a certain middle position between God and creation—that is, between that ineffable superessentiality beyond every intellect and manifest Nature in its substantial form—he becomes apparent to pure minds in the effects of those causes and is openly disclosed in his theophanies.

“Then he proceeds through the manifold forms of the effects down to the lowest order of the whole of Nature, which contains bodies. Thus, advancing in an orderly way into all things, he makes all things and becomes all things in all things; and while he becomes all things, he does not cease to be above all things.

“He makes all things from nothing: that is, from his superessentiality he produces essences, from his supervitality lives, from his superintellectuality intellects, and from the negation of all things that are and are not the affirmations of all things that are and are not.” (III, 20.)

Cf. also III, 4. 17. 23, where the same matter is expressed in almost the same words.

IV. After Scotus has explained what has just been set forth (§ 38, III; *On the Division of Nature* III, 20) in his own complete words, he continues in this manner:

“These matters are exceedingly difficult and remote from those who think about bodily and visible things through the senses; but to those who spiritually ascend to the knowledge of truth, they become most truly clear. For who, unwilling to behold the clear light of wisdom, on hearing such things would not immediately burst out:

“‘Are they insane who say these things? For how can the invisible, incorporeal, incorruptible God descend from himself and create himself in all things, so that he may be all things in all things, and proceed down to the utmost ugliness and most vile corruptions of this visible world, into forms and species, so that he may himself also be in them, if he is all things in all things?’

“Is the one who says that there can be no ugliness at all in the whole universe of creation ignorant? For what occurs in part God does not permit to occur in the whole; and the ugliness of the universe is not ugly, nor does wickedness harm it, nor does error err.”

In the same way elsewhere also (cf. III, 17), the opinion both of sound reason and of Christian doctrine—namely, that the substance of this universe is entirely different from the divine substance—is expressly and deliberately refuted and is almost made a subject of ridicule.

V. Finally, we shall add one passage that also shows how harshly and insolently Scotus mistreated, distorted, and corrupted the meaning of Holy Scripture in order to bend it to his own opinion. This is plainly a matter that cannot fail to arouse in sound minds both the deepest pity and indignation.

After many statements—perhaps nothing more delirious has ever been said—some of which we have already reported above (§§ 29, 33), and after many ravings about the very beginning of Genesis, the following is taught:

“‘Let there be light!’ That is: ‘Let the primordial causes proceed from the incomprehensible secrets of their nature into comprehensible forms and species.’

“‘And light was made.’ That is: ‘At God’s will and command, the obscurity of the primordial causes proceeded into manifest forms and species.’

“‘And God divided the light from the darkness.’ That is: ‘He separated knowledge of the effects from the obscurity of their principal causes. For the division of light from darkness is the separation of things appearing through forms and species from their principles, in which they surpass every intellect.’

“For this reason he first said: ‘And God saw the light, that it was good.’ That is: ‘It pleased God that the original causes, founded before every creature and beyond every intellect, should be manifested to intellects, whether human or angelic, suffused with a certain light of intelligence.’

“‘And he called the light day, and the darkness he called night.’ That is: ‘He granted contemplative minds to call the manifestation of visible and invisible things through forms and species day, but to call their incomprehensible height in their principles night.’

“‘And evening was made and morning was made, one day.’ For although a division and difference is understood between the obscurity of the causes and the clarity of the effects, it is nevertheless one and the same day—that is, one and the same understanding of them. For one creature is not understood to have been made in the causes and another to have been founded in the effects of the causes; rather, it is one and the same creature, in the eternal reasons, as though in certain darknesses of the most secret wisdom, remote from every intellect, and, in the processions of reason into effects, yielding to intellects, as though manifested in a certain day of perfect knowledge [Note: In a similar manner, and sometimes even worse, when explaining the entire ‘work of the six days’ (III, 24–40; IV, 3 ff.), the things that Holy Scripture narrates with the greatest clarity are twisted by being bound to the doctrines of Erigenian philosophy.].” (III, 25.)

§ 39.

It does not seem out of place, if we now complete our discussion of Erigenian pantheism with the arguments that Schlueter has brought against us, so that those who will read these pages may more easily understand the matter.

§ 40.

We therefore seem at last to have the right to assert that Erigena taught in reality and in fact what we said above (§ 22) contained his entire philosophy: that the primordial causes of all things whatsoever contained in this body of the universe flowed and emanated substantially from the divine substance, and that these primordial causes, the principal exemplars, then flowed and emanated into their effects, this very universe of things.

They did so in such a way that they were not cast down from their own seat, which they had occupied from all eternity in God himself and in his heavenly splendor, and so that, through their substantial participation alone, that which is properly said to exist in this universe is precisely the substance of all things.

§ 41.

Scotus could therefore—and indeed, if this was his true opinion, ought to have done so—both posit, together with those who follow pantheism, only one substance in all things, namely a divine substance, and at the same time, according to the common manner of speaking of people who think rightly, acknowledge a God whose seat and dwelling, so to speak, is above the whole nature of things, who created that entire nature of things and, so to speak, transcends it in his essence.

This would be so provided only that he did not explicitly maintain that the divine substance is entirely different from the substance of those things said to have been created by God.

§ 42.

But far from maintaining the proposition we have placed last, anywhere in the books *On the Division of Nature*, he does almost the opposite throughout those books: sometimes while discussing other matters [Note: To say nothing of other passages, it is very frequently written that ‘the world is from God’ and similar statements. Cf. above, § 10; *On the Division of Nature* II, 19–20, and almost the entire work.], and sometimes deliberately teaching what we have just stated in brief; moreover, in several passages (above, § 38, I and IV) he vigorously defends it against those who think otherwise.

Those things, moreover, which we observed could and ought to be taught by Erigena—“that God’s seat, as it were, and dwelling place is above the whole of nature”; “that God is the cause of the whole of nature”; “that this entire universe of things is surpassed by the excellence of the divine essence”—these, then, and similar statements we find in many places in the books *On the Division of Nature*. For we read there [Col. 0069D] repeatedly (I, 3, 7, and elsewhere): “God Himself, in Himself, is comprehended by no intellect, being beyond every creature”; likewise (IV, 1): “God is the creative cause of all existing and non-existing things”; and this (I, 17):

“The significations of the Categories, which are properly discerned in created things, may not absurdly be predicated of the cause of all things, though not properly but metaphorically. For if any Category were properly predicated of God, it would necessarily follow that God was a genus. But God is neither a genus, nor a species, nor an accident”; [Col. 0070A] and again (II, 1):

“God is not the genus of creation, nor is creation the species of God, just as creation is not the genus of God, nor is God the species of creation. God is not the whole of creation, nor is creation a part of God; nor is creation the whole of God, nor God a part of creation. God is metaphorically called both genus and whole, species and part; for everything that is in Him and from Him may reasonably be predicated of Him, though by a certain intelligible contemplation of the universe. I call the universe God and creation”; finally, also this (III, 1):

“The creative cause of the whole created universe is supernatural and superessential, and is above all life, wisdom, and virtue, and above all things that are spoken, understood, or perceived by any sense, while it is the principle, causal source, and essential middle filling all these things, and the consummating end—[Col. 0070B] and the circumference enclosing all things that are and that are not.”

§ 43.

These things, then, and similar statements are necessarily found in the books *On the Division of Nature*. Yet it is certainly astonishing that, although these statements seem merely to report the common usage of human speech, Scotus is nevertheless found to have written these very things in far fewer places than one might expect.

Who, moreover, does not see that these passages do not in any way weaken—let us not say overthrow—the Eriugenian pantheism which we explained above? On the contrary, they belong among those passages [Col. 0070C] that teach pantheism plainly and explicitly.

Since this is so, we are convinced that nothing at all can be extracted from the books *On the Division of Nature* that declares that they themselves can be freed from the pantheism expressed by what is called the emanative system.

§ 44.

Nevertheless, Schlueter (pp. XIV ff.) believes that he has discovered elements that entirely absolve the teaching of those books from pantheism. In that passage he argues against Goerres, to whom he attributes the following opinion:

“By developing the ideas and notions of the Areopagite, Scotus incurred, through a certain necessity, the ancient danger of pantheism, which lay hidden in the writings of the Areopagite . . . . He taught that created creating Nature is the *Logos*, that is, the middle placed between uncreated creating Nature (God) and created non-creating Nature (creation). Thus the triune God was mingled by Scotus with creation . . . . Erigena taught that creating Nature is created because the superessential and superqualitative God, as He proceeds through the theophanies from ‘namelessness’ (*aonomasia*) to ‘all-naming’ (*pantonomasia*), becomes, through this procession—insofar as He unfolds Himself through ideas . . .—in some manner all things in all things.”

[Note: [Col. 0069D] On Goerres’s view, Schlueter ought to have written this: “Erigena taught that created creating Nature is the *Logos* [Col. 0070D] because Erigena taught that God proceeds through the theophanies from ‘namelessness’ (*aonomasia*) to ‘all-naming’ (*pantonomasia*), and that it may also be said that God creates Himself through this procession.”]

Some further statements from Goerres concerning the return of all things into God are added to these [Col. 0071A]. Since they are of no importance here, we have considered that they should be omitted.

Schlueter then summarizes Goerres’s entire accusation in these words (p. XVI):

“(Erigena) professes pantheism when he affirms that the *Logos*, God the Son, emanating from the Father, is the Father’s creature.”

§ 45.

Goerres, thus distorted and mutilated, is now easily defeated. But if anyone wishes to know by what principal arguments he was attacked, they are approximately these:

I. “Although,” says Schlueter (p. XVIII), “in some passages created creating Nature seems to be confused with the Logos, or not sufficiently distinguished from Him, yet in many passages the world created in the Logos and made through the Logos is distinctly distinguished from the Logos, eternally begotten, although it is joined with the Logos when it is opposed to created non-creating Nature, and is then called both created and creating Nature. Moreover, in the expositions which Scotus gives concerning the Holy Trinity, he distinguishes the individual Persons according to the dogma, and thus says that the Logos is eternally begotten, neither proceeding nor created.”

The passages in which this distinction between the Logos and created creating Nature, and between the Logos and created non-creating Nature, seems to shine forth most clearly—apart from those passages in which the begotten God is distinguished from the generating and proceeding God no less than from creation—are cited from among many [Col. 0071C] as follows:

Book II, 21:

“Every creature begins to exist, because it was when it was not; it was in causes, but was not in effects. It is therefore not altogether truly co-eternal with eternity.”

Then there are passages in Books III, 16–18, and II, 22, in which, as we too observed above (§§ 28, 30), “the whole universe of creation is said to have been made and founded in the only-begotten Son of God.”

II. Schlueter then continues approximately as follows (p. XIX):

“But if in other passages (III, 20 ff.) Erigena maintains that God is created in all things, or that God is in Himself and becomes in creatures, he merely follows, as many others have done, that reading of St. John the Evangelist, I, 3–4: ‘Whatever has been made, in Him was life. And the life was . . . . . .’ [Col. 0071D] Surely, however, it would be unjust to accuse Erigena of pantheism on account of these words! Does not even a painter who is painting a picture of the king answer, when asked what he is doing, ‘The king is being made’?”

After forcing several passages from St. Augustine and A. Günther into a context entirely foreign to them, Schlueter has the following (p. XX):

“Come, then, let us also be indulgent toward Erigena when he says: ‘God is in Himself; He becomes in creatures,’ since, on account of Paul’s statement, ‘who is through all things and in all things,’ he has nowhere neglected the other statement of the same Apostle, ‘who is above all things.’”

To prove this point, Schlueter cites *On the Division of Nature* IV, 5, near the end, where we read:

“God is both above all things and in all things, for He Himself is the essence of all things, who alone truly is.”

III. Having warned (p. XX) that no one should in any way suppose that the Eriugenian quaternary of Nature is identical with the dogmatic Holy Trinity, Schlueter (p. XXII) entirely absolves Scotus from blame on the grounds that, “if he had followed pantheism, he could not have taught what he did teach:

a) that God is supernatural and superessential and above all things perceived by any sense, while He is the causal principle of all these things, the essential middle filling them, the consummating end—and the enclosing circumference—and that neither the Aristotelian category of substance nor the other nine categories [Col. 0072B]”—all of which, as Scotus says (I, 17), are properly discerned in created things—“can apply to God.”

b) “That the human will is free to choose either good or evil, and that the human race, having transgressed in Adam and thereby become subject to death, was saved in Christ and through Christ and restored to eternal life.”

c) “That the pride of Lucifer, who wished by his own power to be God, was a detestable crime.”

d) “That God causes many things to occur outside the common order of nature, in order to show that He alone is Lord.”

To these a fifth point is added:

“That Scotus, if he had followed pantheism, could not everywhere have retained and correctly explained the classically dogmatic conception of the Holy Trinity.”

[Note: [Col. 0071D] Here we have not quoted Schlueter’s exact words, but have written approximately what he himself presented in his own words from Erigena’s argument. We have omitted the passage from *On the Division of Nature* II, 1 [Col. 0072D], since we already gave it above in § 42.]

We thus have all the arguments by whose weight Schlueter seemed to himself to have sufficiently and more than sufficiently restrained not only Goerres, but, together with Goerres (cf. p. XIV), everyone who had ever accused Scotus of pantheism.

§ 46.

We have described these arguments so carefully not because we wish to attribute much weight to them—which, once Erigena’s entire system has been explained more precisely by us, is certainly unnecessary—but lest anyone accuse us of arrogance for asserting that arguments to which any weight could be given are scarcely worthy of it.

I. How greatly, then, has Goerres’s accusation (§ 44) been distorted and mutilated! He had made sufficiently clear what kind of pantheism Erigena would have fallen into when he said that, “by developing the ideas of the Areopagite, he incurred the danger of pantheism.” Although this point is of the greatest importance in deciding the matter, as we have demonstrated at considerable length (§§ 22, 40–43), Schlueter ignored it.

Nor did he suffer this injustice—or whatever other name one may give it—with impunity. For we think that this was the reason why he believed that Erigena’s doctrine, thoroughly infected with pantheism, could be absolved from the guilt of pantheism. For those very things which we showed (§§ 40–43) could and ought to be taught and adopted by Eriugenian pantheism together with the common usage of people who judge correctly—things that certainly ought to have offended no one in Erigena’s doctrine—misled Schlueter, as he openly declared in his defense. We do not know whether this would have happened if he had attended more carefully, as justice required, to Goerres’s warning.

II. But what are we to make of this statement (cf. § 44): “(Erigena) professes pantheism when he affirms that the *Logos*, the Son of God, emanating from the Father, is the Father’s creature”? We scarcely understand what it is meant to convey.

Did we teach pantheism by teaching that the Son [Col. 0073B] of God was not begotten but created? Yet Schlueter, as we believe is evident from his reply to this point (cf. § 45), ought to have written:

“(Erigena) professes pantheism because he does not distinguish either created creating Nature or created non-creating Nature from the only-begotten Son of God, consubstantial with God the Father.”

[Note: [Col. 0073D] Goerres, to whom this statement is attributed, did not say this.]

Schlueter denies that Scotus failed to distinguish these things. But we demonstrated long ago that, with respect to substance—the one matter on which everything here is evidently based—both created creating Nature and created non-creating Nature are confused in the books *On the Division of Nature* with the only-begotten Son of God, consubstantial with His Father (§§ 29–38). Schlueter, we think, failed to notice that what he properly needed to demonstrate was that there could be a diversity of substances.

III. If, moreover, we read in him (cf. § 45, II) that, whenever Erigena says, “God is in Himself and becomes in creatures,” or, “God is created in all things,” he should be indulged in this matter—as though these were the only expressions on account of which an accusation of pantheism could be brought against Erigena—we certainly do not see what happened here to Schlueter, who nevertheless ought to have read Erigena through when he undertook to publish him!

IV. Nor did he have any greater success in the things he amassed, as they say, “by way of excess” (cf. § 45, III). For even if one or another of these statements—which we scarcely believe—could be found to conflict with Eriugenian pantheism, why did Schlueter not consider whether Erigena, when teaching it, might perhaps have been insufficiently consistent with himself? For there are places where he contradicts himself [Col. 0073D], and not merely in the most insignificant matters.

[Note: [Col. 0074D] Cf. Hock in *Ephemerides Bonnenses* XVI, pp. 42–43.]

The fact that he inserted certain elements of Christian doctrine into his book is so far from removing the book’s depravity that those elements themselves became infected with the book’s entire depravity, with the greatest harm to them. We have already seen this with many of them, and we shall see it with still more.

Moreover, in this matter Schlueter does not seem even to have dreamed of how carefully those who in our own age teach pantheism retain at least the names of the same doctrines of the Christian religion.

V. Schlueter says (p. VI):

“Many have misunderstood Erigena in many ways. It is not easy to defend each of his statements if it is torn from the context of the discourse. But we venture to affirm that, if one considers him as a whole, he nowhere transgressed the exact bounds of truth.”

These words seem to indicate that Schlueter wished not to bring forward isolated statements of Erigena occurring here and there, by which Erigena might be attacked, but to penetrate into the innermost recesses of Eriugenian philosophy, so that in those places one might perceive what the system itself is doing. If we speak frankly, this method would greatly please us.

But this meaning cannot be present in those words, because it would follow that Schlueter had forbidden the very method of attack which he himself employed in defending Erigena.

For it is clearer than daylight from what his little book has so far supplied us that he did not penetrate into the hidden recesses of that philosophy, nor, apparently, did he wish to penetrate into them. Therefore, what we said about his entire defense seems to us to have been said with justice. What should he have regarded as more important in defending Scotus than to carry out most carefully precisely the task that he entirely neglected?

Finally, we must also say that we are completely ignorant of what sort of pantheism he imagined and conceived in his mind. For he writes (p. XIV):

“Some people, among whom Thomas Moore and Dr. C. F. Hock seem to be numbered, entangled in the prejudices of more recent systems that are less favorable to the true freedom of Christian speculation, are indeed very careful lest God be confused pantheistically with creation in the manner of the pagans; but they are not at all afraid of the abyss that once again gapes between the two, an abyss which, according to St. Paul (Ephesians II, 13 ff. and Colossians I, 19), our Savior closed in such a way that He ‘made both one.’”

§ 47.

After explaining in the books *On Nature* what has been taught concerning created non-creating Nature—this whole universe of things—the course of the sun and moon, the distances they have, the way in which all bodies are composed of the four elements, the nature of man and of his senses, and other matters of the same kind, which chiefly because they have little bearing on those matters that ought properly to concern us throughout this work, we have rightly considered that they should be omitted.

There are, however, other matters in these books that are of far greater importance for our purpose. Since, on account of the connection of the arguments, they can easily be added to the discussion of created non-creating Nature itself, we have decided to transfer them here. We refer especially to major parts of Christian doctrine, which we shall find miserably polluted by the filth of Eriugenian philosophy.

§ 48.

We said (§ 33) that it happened through the operation of God Himself that the primordial causes flowed forth into their effects, and that consequently all things contained in this universe were cast down from their very high dignity into a much lower condition (II, 11).

This, however, does not conflict with divine goodness, because, “as true reason teaches, it may be said that this world would not have burst forth into various sensible forms if God had not foreseen the fall and destruction of the first man, who abandoned the unity of his nature. After his fall, man, warned by such punishment of his miserable destruction, was able to recognize himself as having fallen from the highest things to the lowest, from eternal things to temporal, and from spiritual things to bodily things, so that he might seek to return to the former state of his dignity by repentance and by fulfilling the divine laws which he had transgressed.” (II, 12.)

§ 49.

These very words of Scotus also show what, to use the language of theologians, the transgression of the first man is for him. The “fall and destruction of the first man” is so called because he “abandoned the unity of the divine nature”—in which, together with the primordial causes of the remaining things, he possessed the proper seat of his dignity and essence [I, 7; IV, 10; II, 6 ff.]—and was thus cast down “from the highest things to the lowest, from eternal things to temporal things”!

Scotus teaches this consistently, as it sufficiently accords with his philosophy. (Cf. § 50 ff.)

§ 50.

“The first man, by transgressing, abandoned that dignity with which he had been adorned in the primordial causes. Hence he fell from an angelic mode of essence and multiplication to one that was bestial. For this reason he was also divided into male and female, whereas previously, in his eternal causes, he had no division of the sexes, but was simply man. Again, after the universal resurrection of all bodies, which is said to occur at the end of the world, this division of the sexes will no longer exist.

Such a union of male and female was first accomplished in our Savior when He rose; for in Him, as the Apostle says, there is neither male nor female.” (II, 6 ff.; IV, 9, 12, 15.)

§ 51.

“Man first fell within himself when he was tempted by the devil. If he had remained in the condition in which God had originally created him, he would not have fallen upon the devil. He therefore first descended, driven on by the movement of a perverse will, and plunged himself into temporal things; but in falling he was wounded and stripped by the devil.” (IV, 15; cf. IV, 23.)

§ 52.

“By the merit of sin, bodies were given to the first human beings. Before sin, man had been so spiritual that he needed no use of bodily senses, but enjoyed only the activity of the intellect.” (IV, 16, 19.)

§ 53.

But what monsters of absurdity are these! Was this entire universe created by God, or thrust down into a worse condition, so that there might be given to man—whom God had foreseen would soon go there of his own accord—a place for repentance and correction?

Is this what they call the transgression of the first man: that he descended from the seat of the primordial causes—that is, from God Himself and His only-begotten Son—to this earth, inhabited by brute animals?

Not merely after sin, but solely because of sin, were two human beings made by the division of one man! Did the devil receive human beings within the range of his missile! Were the bodies that we bear given to the human race!

What is this, if not a mockery and travesty, so to speak, of Christian doctrine and Sacred Scripture?

But—and this is certainly of the greatest importance to us—how entirely this matter arose, and necessarily had to arise, from the philosophy and character of this book alone! For otherwise Scotus neither despised nor rejected Christian doctrine or Sacred Scripture in any way; he did only this: he adapted them to the principles of his philosophy. We have already observed above (§ 38, I, V) by what art he accomplished this, and we shall immediately demonstrate it with several clear pieces of evidence.

§ 54.

[Col. 0076C]

“We say that God’s plantation, the paradise in Eden, was nothing other than human nature itself, insofar as it had been made from the beginning in the image of God—that is, in its principal dignity. In it the tree of life, namely the Word of the Father, produced every kind of life; in its midst the fountain of all good things, namely the same divine Wisdom, flowed; its four rivers, flowing from one fountain, are the four principal virtues of the soul, proceeding from one Wisdom, from which every virtue and good action spring forth.”

“One man is said to have been created in paradise—that is, in that condition of blessedness—in whom both man and woman are understood [according to the Fathers?]. The man is the mind, *nous* (νοῦς), presiding over the whole of human nature; the woman is bodily sense, *aisthēsis* (αἴσθησις), to which the mind, consenting incautiously, is destroyed.

The serpent who was in that paradise is illicit pleasure, through which the things that delight the carnal sense are damnably desired. After man had fallen into a stupor and gone to sleep, God made a woman from his rib—that is, when man had turned the attention of his mind, with which he ought always and inflexibly to have contemplated his Creator, toward the pleasures of material things and had yielded himself to the desire for carnal intercourse, he entirely cut himself off from the power of eternal and blessed contemplation and, emptied of every virtue, fell into the pleasure of sensible things and withdrew completely from the spiritual senses.

When man had thus fallen from the dignity of his nature, he also acquired his division into husband and woman, and his propagation in the likeness of cattle.”

“Although many of these things are narrated by Sacred Scripture as having taken place before man’s fall, this does not conflict with our opinion. For we are not unaware that it is a very common figure of Sacred Scripture, called by the Greeks ‘the later before’ (*hysteron proteron*, ὕστερον πρότερον) or ‘anticipation’ (*prolēpsis*, πρόληψις), and by the Latins ‘inverted order’ (*praeposterum*) or ‘anticipation.’” (IV, 16–23.)

§ 55.

By such an artifice, then, Scotus has almost entirely corrupted whatever of Sacred Scripture and whatever of Christian doctrine has entered into his philosophy. In this matter he was thoroughly consistent with himself. We seem to have done a particularly worthwhile thing if, in order to prove this even more clearly, we give a brief account of what is taught concerning the redemption of human beings ruined by Adam’s guilt, concerning sin, and concerning the punishment of sin.

§ 56.

“All things that proceed from the cause of all things”—that is, either God or the only-begotten Son of God [cf. §§ 28–30]—“and from the primordial causes established in it, would become worthless, indeed would perish completely, if they could not and did not return to their source.” (V, 36.)

“Therefore God, the Word of God, in whom all things were made causally and subsist, descended according to His divinity into the effects of the causes that subsist in Him, namely into this sensible world.”

“That He assumed human nature alone”—that is, descended into human nature alone—“happened for this reason: that in man every visible and invisible creature is contained”—for man consists of soul and body [cf. *On the Division of Nature* II, 3 ff.].

“The Word of God descended for no other reason than to save, according to His humanity, the effects of the causes which, according to His divinity, He possesses eternally and unchangeably, and to recall them into their causes, so that the effects might be saved in those causes by an ineffable union, just as the common cause itself”—the Word of God—“was saved.

“For if the Wisdom of God did not descend into the effects of the causes that live eternally in it, the order of the causes would perish. For when the effects of the causes perish, no cause would remain, just as, when the causes perish, no effects would remain; for these things arise and perish together according to the relation of correlatives, or together and forever remain.”

“Thus the whole world has already been restored specially in the incarnate and humanized Word of God”—that is, thus far only in the humanity, as it is called, of the divine Word. “But at the end of the world it will be restored generally and universally in the same Word. For what He accomplished specially in Himself, He will accomplish generally in all things.

“I do not mean merely in all human beings, but in every sensible creature. For the Word of God Himself, when He assumed human nature, omitted no created substance which He did not assume. And therefore, if He saved and restored the human nature which He assumed, He certainly restored every creature, visible and invisible.” (V, 25; cf. V, 27, 36 [p. 289, Oxford edition]; III, 20; IV, 5 [p. 170, Oxford edition]; IV, 4; II, 9.)

This, if anything is, must certainly be called a specimen of Eriugenian ingenuity. How miserably he polluted and disgraced this part of Christian doctrine in those dank marshes of his primordial causes and the effects flowing from them!

[Col. 0078B] Nor could Scotus, if he wished to remain sufficiently consistent with himself, say in the words of the Church: “Who for us human beings and for our salvation descended from heaven!” Rather, in accordance with the principles of his philosophy, he would have to say: “Who for Himself and for this entire universe, for His own salvation and for the salvation of this entire universe, descended from heaven!”

§ 57.

Since we are finally going to explain the Eriugenian work’s doctrine concerning sin and the punishment of sin, anyone who knows the doctrine of the work *On Predestination* (cf. above, Chapter IV) will also have much of this already familiar.

A. I. Whatever is called evil is not found substantially in the nature of things. For it has no proper and definite substance, but is nothing other than a certain movement. That movement, however, belongs not to nature—for in that case it would be referred to God Himself, who made nature—but to the free will.

“Evil, considered in itself, is altogether nothing other than the irrational and perverse movement of free will.”

“For the will,” as it is written elsewhere, “free to choose the good, made itself enslaved to the pursuit of evil.” (IV, 16 [Oxford edition, pp. 205–206]; V, 26, 36 [Oxford edition, pp. 282, 285, 288]; IV, 14, 22, 23.)

II. Nevertheless, since free will too has been given by God, we may rightly call that perverse movement, if only for this reason, not properly “evil” but merely “illicit.” (V, 36 [Oxford edition, pp. 282, 285, 288].)

III. But in certain other passages Our Author seems to have perceived the true nature of the matter much more sharply. At least, he asserts with sufficient confidence, among other things, the following:

“That perverse movement is seen to be outside nature and derived from bestial intemperance”;

“evil finds no other seat in the nature of things except where falsehood possesses it, that is, in bodily sense”;

“since evil does not arise from a natural cause”—that is, from nature made by God—“it seems more correct to call ‘lustful desire’ its cause than evil will; for this desire is precluded by natural goods.”

(IV, 16 [Oxford edition, pp. 206, 205]; IV, 22 [Oxford edition, p. 215]; V, 36 [Oxford edition, pp. 286–287].)

IV. Since evil is neither a certain substance nor a “natural accident,” Scotus also maintains this: the divine Mind knows no evil and no wickedness.

For divine knowledge is the cause of existing things [Note: [Col. 0079D] Cf. above, § 15]; therefore whatever it knows must necessarily come to be in the nature of things. But what is not found in the nature of things cannot be found in divine knowledge.

God, then, does not know any transgressors of the divine law. He knows their substances, and everything that He made in them and that subsists in Him; but what happens to them through their perverse movements, contrary to the nature established by Him, He entirely ignores. (V, 27 [the same place, p. 259].)

Scotus frequently teaches this very point in almost the same words (cf. II, 28; *On Predestination*, above, Chapter IV, col. 27, note c ff.). We have already indicated above (§ 15) how it arose in the hidden recesses of Eriugenian philosophy.

Our Scotus was therefore, we think, insufficiently consistent with himself in affirming in certain passages that those things which are believed to have been made in human beings by God, but which according to Erigena’s philosophy must be said to have happened to them because of the first man’s sin, were made in them by the supreme divine power for this reason: because He had foreseen that the first man would sin. (IV, 14 [Oxford edition, p. 195], 23 [ibid., p. 216]; cf. II, 12.)

Nor, by heaven, are we unaware how our Author habitually strove with all his might, as the saying goes, to prevent his own philosophy from appearing opposed to Christian doctrine. In this matter, we think, it could very easily have happened that he trimmed one of the two too much for the benefit of the other.

[Col. 0079C] But if God is really thought to be ignorant of all sins, should He not also be thought not even to care about them? From this it follows not only that the one who has sinned is not punished by God—a doctrine which Scotus himself explicitly taught both in the book *On Predestination* (cf. above, Chapter IV) and in the books *On the Division of Nature* (cf. below, § 59, B. IV)—but also, and much more seriously, that if we are about to transgress, or have transgressed, moral precepts in any matter, we cannot even be led to think of that supreme love with which God embraces us, and thus be drawn away from our errors by the consideration which ought certainly to provide the keenest stimulus to upright people.

Nor can a person who has sinned repent in a sound-minded way because he has shown himself unworthy of God’s fatherly love. But after setting out what Scotus thinks concerning the punishments of sinners, we shall say more about this matter.

V. Just as Scotus taught in the book *On Predestination* that “this perverse movement, which he calls sin, strives, when divine and truly abiding things have been abandoned, to reach nothingness itself,” so too we read in the books *On the Division of Nature*:

“Wickedness is the intellectual soul’s forgetfulness of natural goods”—that is, of things that truly are—“and the failure of the operation of the virtues implanted for the end in nature, together with the irrational movement of the natural powers, through deceptive judgment, toward something other than the end.

“By ‘end’ I mean the cause of things that are”—that is, God, as ‘the source of all true essence’ [IV, 1; III, 4]—“which all things naturally desire,” since “there is no creature that wishes or desires to be nothing, nor that shrinks from the possibility of not being.”

[Note: [Col. 0079D] Here we must attend to what has been said concerning the primordial causes and their effects. The primordial causes contain the true substance of all things; the effects, if anyone considers them in themselves, are said to be nothing. Hence those that strive to depart still farther, as it were, from the primordial causes and to pursue their path with an even more intense spirit hasten toward “non-being”; whereas those that hasten to return to the primordial causes, having abandoned them, are truly hurrying toward “being.”]

(V, 26 [Oxford edition, p. 256]; V, 3.)

But enough of this for now. It has been explained sufficiently at length what Scotus properly understands by wickedness, and likewise by virtue, insofar as it is opposed to wickedness. Let us proceed to the remaining matters.

B. I. “Wickedness will reach its consummation and will remain in no nature. Accordingly, our nature will not always be held by wickedness; but when all evil”—that is, that perverse movement which tends toward “non-being”—“has come to an end, it will return to the good.”

“For just as the shadow of the earth, when the sun’s rays contract it, finally vanishes altogether, so wickedness, which occupies our nature like a certain shadow of our sins, will be contracted and utterly abolished by the abundance of eternal goodness, when the irrational movements of the human soul are converted into rational affections of truth.”

“When the irrational movement has been circumscribed and entirely ended by the breadth of goodness, human nature will be moved rationally according to the natural virtues implanted in it, raised upright toward the heights and always desiring its cause.” (V, 26 [Oxford edition, pp. 259–260]; V, 28 [ibid., p. 264].)

Apart from asserting by these words that all wickedness will one day cease—that is, that whatever is moved perversely will eventually arrive at God after being moved rightly—Scotus also teaches by the very fact that he affirms that everything indulging in perverse movement will return to its proper end, with the possible exception of “demons,” as is found in another passage (V, 31), that human beings too, even against their will and certainly without willing it, will be driven from the path of perversity and compelled to their true end.

But once this is granted, what room is left for freedom in the exercise of what we call virtue? Yet Erigena, although he excels in the artifices which he employs in these matters, does not seem to have been driven entirely into a corner. How he may perhaps have extricated himself, although he cannot thereby escape his gravest errors, we shall see after a brief interval. (Cf. § 57, B. III, b.)

II. When all wickedness and impiety have come to an end, who will remain wicked or impious? For it is through wickedness and impiety alone that people are wicked and impious.

But if all things are to return to God, whom they abandoned by sinning, will it not follow that no punishment of the impious, no eternal death of misery, will remain? From this, however, the greatest difficulties arise.

Where, then, will the eternal punishment be into which the impious are to go? Where will be that heat of the flames of eternal fire into which the severity of the most just Judge will send the wicked, saying: “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire”? (V, 27.)

Scotus resolves this matter by answering two principal questions: “What will the punishments be?” and “Who will be punished?”

III. a) What will the punishments be?

“We do not believe that there are different forms of punishments in any place or at any time. They will exist only in the perverse movements of evil wills and corrupted consciences, and in the complete overthrow of perverse power—that is, in the total extinction of every capacity for sinning, doing harm, and acting impiously.

“Where is Judas the betrayer tormented?”

“Nowhere, except in his polluted conscience!”

“What punishment does he suffer?”

“Late and useless repentance, by which he is always consumed.”

“Each person who lives impiously will be tormented by the very appetite for vices with which he burned in the flesh, as by a kind of inextinguishable flame.” (V, 29.)

The punishments of evildoers, therefore, exist only in their perverse will and in the conscience of the evildoers themselves. Scotus maintained this carefully both in his book on predestination and in the books *On the Division of Nature*. Hence many have asserted that Scotus entirely rejected the eternal punishments of impious people. But Scotus denied nothing other than what all rightly thinking people deny: that these punishments have some definite place, or one filled with actual fire. (Cf. V, 37.)

[Note: Scotus openly professes eternal punishments in his *Expositions of the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter VIII, § 2, where he says: “For the ineffable mercy of divine goodness does not permit the nature that it made like itself to suffer deformity eternally. It does, however, permit it to be corrected for a time, so that, instructed by its most just hardships, it may return more eagerly and fervently to its own dignity. Reason certainly does not allow the image of God to be detained in eternal disgrace. Otherwise misery would be coeternal with blessedness, evil with goodness, and the kingdom of the devil with the kingdom of God. We do not say this as though no punishment were eternal, since each person will be blessed or condemned eternally by his own conscience; we say only that no nature is punished in any way.” Compare also what we have observed elsewhere in this passage. — Editorial note.]

Now, concerning the very nature and character of punishments, much more precise statements are found in certain other passages. Two positions seem to be proposed, although they can very easily be reconciled with one another.

In several places we find statements of this kind:

“The impious will weep while suffering empty images of sensible things.”

“For the impious there will always be fantasies and various false appearances of mortal things, corresponding to the various movements of their evil thoughts.” (V, 31.)

Elsewhere, however, we read:

“This is the whole punishment of which people speak as belonging to free and perverse will: its lustful impulse will be restrained, so that it cannot seize what it unlawfully desires; that is, it will be prevented from its unlawful movements, so that it cannot reach the end of its desire.” (V, 36 [Oxford edition, p. 282].)

We therefore think that these two positions should be joined as follows: we should retain in its proper sense the position stated later, and refer the other to it. For this latter position occurs repeatedly in the books *On the Division of Nature* (cf. V, 29), and is taught in the book *On Predestination*; moreover, it agrees far better with Scotus’s view of sin than does the former position. Whoever withdraws from what truly exists and strives toward what does not exist commits sin. What pain, then, could you inflict on such a person that would actually be more beneficial to him than rightly and simply restraining him from this most perverse movement?

Nor should the earlier position be neglected, for Scotus can defend the later one only with its assistance. We shall explain the matter briefly. I have shown that the impious will be subjected to eternal punishments. Once the later position has been established, it follows of itself that there will eternally be people who hasten toward things said not to exist and are held back from this perverse movement as if by a violent hand. But, as we shall see below, Erigena denies that these things will remain forever; after “the consummation of this age,” as he says, they will no longer exist. What follows? As soon as those things have vanished, surely no impious person will be found who can hasten toward them or be restrained from them. Will the punishments therefore cease? The earlier position removes this difficulty.

Moreover, Scotus has written in one place as though only ignorance and lack of knowledge of divine things will torment the impious (V, 31 [Oxford edition, p. 270]). This is certainly what is read in almost all the relevant passages, and the position also accords in some way with Hegelian reasoning [Note: Cf. Baltzer, *Contributions toward a Mediation of a Correct Judgment concerning Catholicism and Protestantism*, fascicle I, pp. 9–11.]: the rewards of good people are said to consist in this, that “true contemplations will be theirs,” and that “they will rejoice in the true contemplation of God, while the impious are tormented by fantasies of mortal things.” (V, 31 [ibid., p. 270]; V, 39.) In the first book, chapter 8, we also read:

“We think that the blessedness of the saints is nothing other than the pure and immediate contemplation of the divine essence itself.”

Those who have sworn allegiance to Hegel’s words are known to have fallen into these opinions for a very different reason from that of our author.

Having therefore shown what the future punishments will be, we must proceed to the second question.

### b. Who are to be punished?

[Col. 0082D]

This question may perhaps seem pointless. If there are people to be punished, surely the impious are the ones to be punished. But in Scotus this is a matter of considerable importance. For he writes:

“The impious people themselves—that is, the nature and substance of impious people, since it has proceeded from God himself—cannot possibly be punished.” (V, 30–31, 35; *On Predestination*, above, chapter IV.)

“Nor is this [nature] deserving of punishments, since it neither sins nor can sin.” (Cf. § 57, A, I.)

Nevertheless:

“Those torments, which are called punishments, cannot exist without a natural subject that they torment.” (V, 30 and following.)

For this “knotty difficulty to be rightly resolved, we must establish that something is punished which is not substance but merely inheres in substance, while the substance itself remains entirely free from every punishment.”

Now, this perverse will inheres in human substance. Just as it sins by its own power, so it is punished by itself alone; and just as it does not at all contaminate the natural good—the human nature in which it inheres—with its sins, so it does not in any way torment, through the torments by which it is punished, the natural subject whose accident it is and in which it is contained. Thus the irrational movements of evil wills are punished in those who participate in a good, rational, and impassible nature.” (V, 30–31 [Oxford edition, pp. 267–270].)

“Thus human nature will remain and always remain no less in evil people than in good people—safe, whole, undefiled, and free from every contrary passion. Nevertheless, it is capable of contrary qualities, namely, good and evil wills, virtue and disgrace”; and, finally, in this way “it is also capable of contrary passions.” (Ibid., pp. 270–271.)

### IV.

Once these matters have been discussed, it is easy to understand why Scotus was justified in writing the following:

“God punishes sins, or, to speak more accurately, permits them to be punished.”

“The evil will of transgressors is the efficient cause of every sin and of every punishment of sin.” (Ibid., pp. 269–270.)

In the book *On Predestination* (cf. above, chapter IV), where the very connection of the arguments demanded a much more vigorous investigation of the true author of punishments, he strove with all his strength to maintain that God establishes no punishments. More than that, his own philosophy compelled him to teach this. According to its principles, God knows nothing except what is “substance” or a natural accident of substances, and therefore “is entirely ignorant” of “everything that is called evil,” since evil is not found among these things. (Cf. § 57, A, IV.)

Consequently, even if God himself establishes for impious people the punishments by which they are punished, he does so unwittingly, and certainly not willingly. Thus God does not punish sins; at most, he “permits them to be punished.”

[Note: Although Schlueter undertook to defend Scotus’s position “concerning evil and the punishments of sins” (pp. XIII and following), and therefore deliberately examined it, he seems not to have discovered even one of the errors that we have identified! — Editorial note.]

## § 58

This entire doctrine of our author concerning sins and the punishments of sins, as we believe we have sufficiently demonstrated, is filled with a very great multitude of extremely serious errors. To review them individually all over again would, we think, produce nothing but weariness. The consequences that can be drawn from these trifles, however, and that may bring the greatest harm to the practical conduct of life, must be placed in clearer light.

Everything rests especially on this one claim: that God is said neither to care about nor to know in any way either those who sin or the things that are sinned. Only the conscience of evildoers afflicts the person who indulges in sin, and only the conscience of evildoers can deter anyone from sinning. Does this not almost completely overturn, scatter, and remove from human view everything established for restraining the desires of crime?

Neither fear of an angry punishing God, nor dread of grieving a loving God, will move people to become more steadfast or more upright, so that they do not gratify and extinguish their burning desire to sin by sinning, if they follow Scotus’s doctrine. Yet how few will grant so much to their conscience that they choose it alone as their guide and never abandon it, even when the force of pleasure attracts them?

And if this doctrine were applied to ordinary life, once all the “barriers”—to use Virgil’s words—“and lofty mountains” imposed upon raging desires for sin had been removed, it would utterly confuse and destroy everything.

## § 59

We have finally arrived at that fourth species of Nature which neither is created nor creates. The matters belonging here, however, are not so much pernicious above all the rest as they are ridiculous. Since we have dealt at greater length with those matters that were properly harmful, we shall be briefer here, where you might perhaps call the doctrines merely old wives’ tales.

## § 60

### D.

“The fourth species of Nature, which neither is created nor creates, is plainly God himself. For the divine nature is believed not to be created because it is the primordial cause of all things, beyond which there is nothing from which it could be created. But when, after the return of the entire created universe into its primordial causes, which are contained in the divine nature itself, no further nature will be produced from it or multiplied into sensible or intelligible species, it is not without reason that it is both believed and understood to create nothing.” (IV, 26–27.)

## § 61

[Col. 0084D]

“There are very strong arguments from sensible things demonstrating that this future return will take place. The heavenly sphere bearing the stars returns to the same position in the space of twenty-four hours; the sun reaches the same point of the equinoctial diameter, after four years have elapsed, at the same moment of time. What shall we say of creatures of the air and earth, shoots, and plants? Do they not similarly observe their seasons, in which they burst forth into offspring, flowers, leaves, and fruits?

“And it must be stated simply that no corporeal creature is enlivened by a vital movement without returning to the beginning of its movement. The same must also be understood of the whole world. For its end is its beginning, which it desires; and when it has found it, it will cease—not so that its substance will perish, but so that it will return to its causes.

“Similarly, the conceptions of rational souls, as is demonstrated by the example of the liberal arts, return to their beginnings, in which they establish the end of their movement; for in all these things the beginning and the end are the same. In all human beings there is one and the same desire: to exist, to exist well, and to exist perpetually. And if every natural movement does not cease until it reaches its end, what can hold back human nature so that it does not reach what it seeks? Therefore, it is also clear concerning human nature that it will return to God.”

## § 62

[Col. 0085B]

“Everything that has proceeded from God will return by the same path by which that procession took place. Just as that procession occurred by everything flowing down from higher things to lower things (cf. § 34), so in the return the lower things will always be converted into the higher. For true reason does not permit higher things either to be contained by lower things, or drawn down by them, or consumed by them. Lower things, however, are naturally drawn and absorbed by higher things—not so that they cease to exist, but so that in the higher things they may be preserved more fully, subsist, and become one.” (V, 8, 20; II, 5 and following.)

## § 63

“Thus lower things are absorbed by higher things, not so that they cease to exist, but so that they may be preserved and subsist more fully in the higher things. Evidence of this is found in the nature of things. Air does not lose its substance when it is wholly converted into sunlight, so completely that nothing appears except light, even though light is one thing and air another. A metal, melted in fire, appears to be converted into fire while the substance of the metal remains intact. In the same way, I think that corporeal substance will pass into soul—not so that what exists will perish, but so that it may remain safe in a better essence.” (V, 8, 20, 39, and passim.)

## § 64

This point is impressed upon us again and again: “lower things are always absorbed by higher things in such a way that the substance of the lower things remains safe.” (V, 20, 39.)

From this you may also conclude that things which are absorbed were imparted a true and proper substance from the primordial causes; and this substance itself, when things return to their causes, is said to remain safe and uncorrupted.

But especially in the fifth book, where the return of all things is discussed, the other position that we have already explained above (cf. § 36) is set out more fully. The following is therefore taught:
