Since it was not the substances of things themselves that flowed forth from the causes in order to fashion this world, but rather this world was constructed and composed from the “qualities” of the substances that remained in the causes, “the return is not a return of substances, which remain immutably and indissolubly in themselves, but of qualities, quantities, and other accidents, which are mutable and transitory in themselves and subject to places and times, generation and corruption.” (V, 13–16.)

## § 65

Whatever else concerning the return of all things may seem worth remembering, if we consider the matter generally and as a whole, Scotus himself sets out in condensed form in the following words:

“We have thought it appropriate to append certain theories concerning the return of effects into their causes—that is, into the principles in which they subsist. Three modes of this return again presented themselves.

“The first is considered generally in the transformation of the entire sensible creation contained within the compass of this world—that is, of all bodies, whether they are subject to bodily senses or escape them because of their excessive subtlety. Thus there is no body within the fabric of corporeal nature—whether it is enlivened only by a vital movement, secretly or openly vegetating, or possessing an irrational soul and bodily sense—that does not return to its hidden causes. For it will not be reduced to nothing, since it has been established substantially by the cause of all things.

“The second mode of this speculation has its place in the general return of the whole of human nature, saved in Christ, to the original state of its condition, to a kind of paradise, and to the dignity of the divine image, through the merit of the one whose blood was shed in common for the salvation of all humanity. Thus no human being will be deprived of the natural goods in which he was created, whether he lived well or badly in this life. In this way the ineffable and incomprehensible diffusion of divine goodness and generosity will appear in all human nature, since nothing that proceeds from the supreme Good is punished.

“The third mode of the theory of return concerns those who will not merely ascend into the sublimity of the nature established in them, but will also, through the abundance of divine grace that will be given through Christ and in Christ to his elect, pass superessentially beyond all the laws and limits of nature into God himself, and will be one in him and with him.

“Their return is distinguished as if by certain seven stages. The first will be the transformation of the earthly body into vital movement; the second, of vital movement into sense; the third, of sense into reason; and then of reason into mind, in which the end of the whole rational creation is established.

“After this union, as it were, of the five parts of our nature—body, vital movement, sense, reason, and intellect—so that they are not five but one, with the lower parts perfected by the higher, not so that they cease to exist but so that they become one, three further stages of ascent will follow.

“The first is the passage of the mind into knowledge of all things that exist after God; the second, of knowledge into wisdom, that is, intimate contemplation of truth insofar as this is granted to a creature; the third, which is also the highest, is the supernatural sinking of the most purified minds into God himself, like the darkness of an incomprehensible and inaccessible light, in which the causes of all things”—that is, of the elect or “deified”—“are hidden.

“And then night will be illuminated like day: the most secret mysteries will be opened in some ineffable manner to the blessed and illuminated intellects. Then the most perfect solidity of the octonary number, as if of a supernatural cube, will be completed. In its type the sixth Psalm is titled, ‘A Psalm of David concerning the octave.’

“The Lord’s resurrection also took place on the eighth day for no other reason than that the blessed life which is to come after the sevenfold revolution of this life through the seven days, after the consummation of the world, might be mystically signified—when human nature, as we have said, will return to its beginning through an eightfold ascent. Five of these stages are within the limits of nature, and three are supernatural and superessential within God himself. Then the fivefold number of the creature will be joined to the threefold number of the Creator, so that nothing will appear except God alone, just as in the purest air nothing appears except light alone.” (V, 39. Cf. V, 8, 16, 20–21, 22, 25 [Oxford edition, p. 254; a passage from book IV, 14, should be transferred to this place (ibid., p. 194)], 36 [ibid., pp. 289–290], 37 [ibid., pp. 293–294], 38 [ibid., pp. 301, 308–309].)

Having explained in this way what the subject matter of the books *On the Division of Nature* is, and having looked, in accordance with the wording of the proposed question, at the method of discussion and demonstration that our Scotus pursued in them, there seems scarcely anything more to say. We believe that we have already set out in the explanation of the subject matter of these books as much as is necessary.

The method is not unlike the one we observed in the book *On Predestination*. Many things are assumed as though they were true in themselves; many are confirmed by authorities, especially Pseudo-Dionysius and Pseudo-Maximus; and from these, through subsequent reasoning, certain new conclusions are produced—sometimes with considerable subtlety, but at other times rather ineptly.

Since this has resulted in a philosophy and theology that are for the most part a tasteless fabrication, continually shaped by mistaken opinion, it was inevitable that Erigena himself should at some point realize how greatly they conflicted not only with things believed true by the common agreement of all, but also with what Christian doctrine taught. As soon as he noticed this, he considered nothing more urgent than to adapt whatever contradicted his principles to the doctrines of his own system.

In this matter he excels with remarkable skill. He has handled and tortured a great many passages of Holy Scripture and many doctrines of Christianity so miserably, and polluted them with such a disgraceful appearance, that we scarcely think anyone could endure looking upon them. But enough of this. Since we have explained the matters themselves at length, only a very few words on these points will suffice.

Anyone who examines this second part of our work with sufficient care will certainly concede that, in response to the wording of the proposed question—“Whether, and to what extent, J. Scotus Erigena’s book *On the Division of Nature* agrees both with right reason and with Christian doctrine”—the answer must be that the book, if one considers its entire subject matter, its entire system, and its entire character, agrees in no respect either with right reason or with Christian doctrine. It was therefore rightly condemned by Honorius III, Supreme Pontiff, as “teeming with the worms of heretical depravity.”

For, apart from the fact that it teaches the most explicit pantheism both incidentally and deliberately—that is, the pantheism associated with what is called the emanative system—it also committed the further offense of miserably corrupting several of the most serious doctrines of Christianity according to the decrees of this pantheism, and mutilating them to such an extent that the greatest harms to practical life cannot fail to result from them.

[Col. 0087]

# THOMAS GALE’S PREFACE TO THE EDITION

*Titled: The Five Long-Desired Books of John Scotus Erigena, On the Division of Nature. With an Appendix from the Ambiguities of Saint Maximus, in Greek and Latin.* Oxford, from the Sheldonian Theatre, 1681.

[Col. 0087D] (Page III.)

To settle the controversies that had arisen in past centuries concerning John Erigena and his writings, learned men thought it most advisable to publish the very books over which the disputes had arisen. Only then, as though the documents had been brought forward, would everyone have a freer and easier opportunity to judge.

At the request of Hincmar and Pardulus, who were then highly celebrated in Gaul for their learning and holiness, Erigena wrote a book against Gottschalk on predestination. Ecclesiastical men of those times expressed very different judgments about that book. Those who seem to think that they judge the matter somewhat more acutely say that Scotus’s opponents did not attack him but struck at Hincmar through his flank.

The work began to circulate among a few people; indeed, for some time only nineteen chapters were in circulation, excerpted by his enemies. In obscure matters we generally imagine more than is true. Many therefore began to suspect that Erigena was being treated maliciously; they complained that he had been crushed by fabricated accusations and false hostility. These complaints seemed unlikely to end before the complete work appeared. At last, however, those who would more readily have condemned it to darkness brought it out.

The same John Erigena composed a work on the Eucharist at the command of Charles the Bald. Immediately, this writing too became the subject of controversy. Two hundred years later Scotus’s book was burned on ill-omened logs. You ask why? Vincent of Beauvais replies in the *Doctrinal Mirror*: because Berengar had admired Scotus too much.

When intellects are punished, authority grows. Once the book had been destroyed, disagreements about it increased more and more; for almost nine centuries the saw was drawn through suspicions and obscure and doubtful conjectures. At last the book emerged, as some maintain, under the name of Ratramnus. What happened afterward?

> Then the winds subsided, and all at once  
> the blast came to rest.

For the little book was found to be neither so sacred nor so horrible, provided that a malicious interpreter was absent. Thus anger that is not the greatest sometimes inflicts the greatest injuries.

[Col. 0089B] (Page IV.)

For a long time learned men searched everywhere for the books *On the Division of Natures*—Greek *peri physeōn merismou*—which the same John was said to have composed. Certainly the writers of English history had praised that work with exceptional distinction and had proclaimed it very useful for solving certain perplexing questions.

Whom would this not make salivate? Who would not be inflamed with the desire to see the John who, like Elijah among the Jews or Agapius among the Greeks, so successfully untied the knots of *δυσεπηβόλων ἀποριῶν*, “difficult-to-apprehend perplexities”?

Hence someone, as though sighing, said: “If that book of Scotus has come back to life!” Another, speaking of a book he had never seen, said: “Everything is sad and harsh.” Behold, then, good people: here before you is the book you seek.

> He comes, having left the hiding-place of the dead  
> and the gates of darkness.

But whether, resurrected from the tomb, it also bears the scars of Florus Prudentius Galindus—as Hector bore the wounds inflicted by Achilles—I do not yet know with sufficient certainty. Reliable witnesses certainly assert that Florus corrupted these books so that he could refute them more easily.

I know only this: I have knowingly and deliberately altered nothing. All the absurdities, Scotian mush, fogginess, errors, and slips of every kind that I found, I have left intact—not to disgrace the man, but to testify to my own fidelity.

In the meantime, I shall not interpose my authority concerning this work; it ought plainly to have none. I wish the judgment of the readers to remain free and unimpeded.

When Erigena wrote these things, the Latins did not feel particularly friendly toward the Greeks. Photius occupied the see of Constantinople. Nicholas I had written encyclicals to the Gauls to refute the errors of the Greeks. The hostility of outsiders harmed our John, and he was therefore thought to be foisting bad wares upon people because he was continually making much of his Greeks.

But if he uses the opinions of the Fathers as they themselves set them out in their writings; if fraud, trickery, every paralogism, and every dishonest concealment are absent from this man—let those who condemn in him what they either approve or overlook in those Fathers decide the matter.

[Note: That the false doctrines of our Scotus are rightly condemned or rejected is sufficiently clear from the arguments discussed in the preceding essay. — Editorial note.]

Moreover, the subject he treats seems to offer him some protection, since it is slippery and subtle. The Greeks call it *peri Archōn*, “On Principles”; and who, whether Greek or Latin, has not suffered some human failing in cultivating it?

Grant that a sensitive reader may find very much to criticize in this writer. Certainly, however, he will not find lacking either a humble mind toward the Fathers of the Church or a pious mind toward God. He could therefore have been mistaken; he did not wish to be a heretic.

But I had no intention of writing either Erigena’s life or his defense, and I shall not make his quarrels my own. I have never wished to contend, and I have no leisure for it now. Whoever wishes to know more about John Erigena should read the testimonies about him that I have gathered below, most of which have hitherto been produced by no one.

[Col. 0089]

# SOME TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING JOHN SCOTUS ERIGENA

[Col. 0089D] (Page V.)

Prudentius of Troyes, in his book against John Scotus:

“You alone of all, most acute, were sent forth from Ireland to Gaul.”  
—Ironic.

Pardulus, bishop of Laon, concerning John Scotus:

“But because these matters strongly disagreed with one another, we compelled that Scot who is at the royal palace of Charles the Bald, named John, to write.”

From the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*:

“Humbald of Cambrai, thoroughly instructed in the studies of the liberal arts, became the follower of John Scotus, who at that time was spreading the rays of wisdom throughout Gaul. Remaining attached to his teaching for a long time, he learned both divine and human things …”

[Col. 0090D] An anonymous chronicle preserved by Chesne, volume III:

“At the request of Aelfred, John Scotus returned from Francia, where he had been with Charles the Bald.”

Roger of Wendover, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 883:

“In the year 883 Master John Scotus, a man of penetrating intellect, came to England.”

From the *Life of Abbot Grimbald*, apparently written by Gotcelin:

“King Aelfred, on the advice of Ealdred, archbishop of Canterbury, sent envoys to the monastery of Saint Bertin to summon Grimbald. Among them the priest John and Asser, men of the greatest learning and liveliest intellect, were pre-eminent.”

[Col. 0091A] The Hyde Annals:

“In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 886, in the second year after Saint Grimbald’s arrival in England, the University of Oxford was begun. In sacred theology Saint Neot and Grimbald were lecturers; in grammar and rhetoric, the monk Asser; in dialectic, music, and arithmetic, John, a monk of the church of Menevia; and in geometry and astronomy, John, a monk and colleague of Saint Grimbald.”

William of Malmesbury, in the unpublished fifth book *On the Bishops*:

“In the time of this Aelfred, John Scotus came to England, a man of penetrating intellect and great eloquence. Long before, after leaving his homeland, he had crossed into Francia to Charles the Bald, who received him with great distinction and counted him among his household. He conducted serious business and jokes with him alike, and was his inseparable companion both at table and in the bedchamber. He possessed much wit and refined humor, examples of which still survive, including the following.

“He had taken his seat at the table opposite the king, on the other side of the board. As the cups proceeded and the dishes were consumed, Charles, with a rather cheerful expression, noticed John doing something which offended French courtesy. After some other remarks, he reproved him courteously and said: ‘What is the difference between a fool and a Scot?’

“He returned the customary insult to its author and replied: ‘Only the table.’ The king had asked about the difference in character; John had answered about the distance between their places. The king was not angered, for he was captivated by John’s miraculous learning and did not wish to rise against his teacher even in words; this was the familiar way he addressed him.

“Again, when a servant had offered the king a dish containing two very large fish together with one smaller fish, the king gave it to the teacher to divide among two clerics seated beside him. The fish were enormous, while John himself was exceedingly small in body. Then, always finding some honorable way to provoke the merriment of the diners, he kept the two larger fish for himself and distributed the smaller one between the two clerics.

“When the king accused him of unfair division, he replied: ‘On the contrary, I have acted well and fairly. Here is one small man,’ he said of himself, ‘and two large fish,’ touching the fish. Then, turning to the clerics, he said: ‘Here are two large and immense clerics, and one small fish,’ again touching the fish.

“At Charles’s request he translated the *Hierarchy* of Dionysius the Areopagite from Greek into Latin, word for word. As a result, the Latin text is scarcely intelligible, since its construction follows Greek flexibility more than the arrangement of our own language.

“He also composed a book entitled *peri physeōn merismou*—that is, *On the Division of Nature*—which is very useful for solving certain perplexing questions, provided that he is forgiven in those matters where he departed from the path of the Latins while directing his eyes sharply toward the Greeks. For this reason he was also thought to be a heretic, and a certain Florus wrote against him. In the book *peri physeōn* there are indeed very many passages which, unless carefully examined, may appear contrary to the faith of Catholics.

“Pope Nicholas is known to have shared this opinion. In a letter to Charles he says:

“‘It has been reported to our apostolate that a certain man named John, a Scot by birth, has recently translated into Latin the work of Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, which he wrote in Greek concerning the divine names and the heavenly orders. According to custom, this work ought to have been sent to us and approved by our judgment, especially since, although this John is said to possess great learning, it is frequently reported that he did not think soundly in certain matters.’

“Because of this disgrace, I believe, he became tired of Francia and went to King Aelfred. Attracted by the king’s generosity, and eminent in his learning, as I have learned from the king’s writings, he settled at Malmesbury, where after some years he died a harsh and bitter death, pierced by the styluses of the boys whom he taught. Thus, while powerful wickedness and a feeble hand repeatedly failed and repeatedly attacked, he met an agonizing death.

“For some time he lay in honorable burial in the church of Saint Laurence, which had witnessed the unspeakable murder. But when divine favor had granted him an illumination of fire over many nights, the monks were warned and transferred him to the larger church. Placing him on the left side of the altar, they proclaimed his martyrdom in these verses:

> In this tomb lies the holy sophist John,  
> who, while still alive, was enriched with wondrous doctrine.  
> At last, through martyrdom, he deserved to ascend  
> into Christ’s kingdom, where all the saints reign forever.”

(Page VII.) The same William, in the same book:

“Warinus of Lira, a monk, was appointed in place of Turald. When he first came to the abbey of Malmesbury, paying little regard to the deeds of his predecessors, he was carried along by a certain arrogance and disgust toward the bodies of the saints.

“Finally, the bones of Saint Meildulf, of venerable memory, and of the others who had formerly been abbots there and later bishops in various places, and who, out of reverence for their patron Aldhelm, had ordered that they be buried in that place, were removed. Ancient reverence had honorably arranged them in two stone basins on either side of the altar, with wooden partitions placed between the bones of each.

“All these remains, I say, he gathered together like a heap of rubble, and, as though they were the remains of worthless slaves, banished them from the doors of the church. And, so that nothing might be lacking from his shamelessness, he also removed Saint John Scotus, whom the monks venerated almost as highly as Saint Aldhelm. He ordered all of them to be carelessly concealed in a remote corner of the basilica of Saint Michael and shut in with stones. O the times, O the customs! Who could pursue such audacity with reproach worthy of it?” And so forth.

The same, from the Thuane Manuscript:

“To his Peter, his William, a participant in divine philosophy.”

> “You practice the custom of brotherly affection, most loving brother, in deeming me worthy of so difficult a consultation. For it is an assumption of charity that you judge me not unequal to so great a task. You command me to set down in writing whence John Scotus originated, where he died, and whom common opinion agrees to have been the author of the book called *περὶ φύσεων* (*On Natures*); and, since an unfavorable rumor has been spread about that book, to clarify in a brief treatise what in it seems especially opposed to the Catholic faith. The first request, I think, I shall fulfill well enough if I answer promptly, since the truth of such matters is not hidden from me. But the second—to summon before judgment a man deservedly renowned throughout the Latin world for his learning, and long since dead both to life and to envy—is more than my strength dares undertake. I also willingly shrink from lying in wait for the labors of great men, because, as someone has said, ‘He acts dishonorably who displays ingenuity in another man’s book.’ Therefore I almost resisted such imperious commands, unless I had long ago resolved to defer to you in all things, as to a most grateful parent—even in matters that would burden my brow and imperil my reputation. [Col. 0092C]

> “John, therefore, surnamed Scotus, refutes the opinion that he was a native of that people by calling himself *Heruligena* in the title of the *Hierarchy*. There was once a very powerful people of the Heruli in Pannonia, which history records as having been almost destroyed by the Lombards. He, having left his homeland, came to France to Charles the Bald. Received by him with great favor, he was counted among his intimates and, as I have said elsewhere, exchanged with him both serious conversation and jokes; he was his constant companion at table and in the bedchamber. There was never any disagreement between them, because the king was captivated by the marvel of his learning and, though sometimes quick to anger against his teacher, was unwilling to rise up against him even in words. [Col. 0092D]

> “At the king’s request he translated Dionysius’s *Hierarchy* from Greek into Latin, word for word. Consequently the Latin is scarcely intelligible, since it is constructed more according to the fluidity of Greek than according to the arrangement of our language. He also composed a book which he entitled *περὶ φύσεων μερισμοῦ*, that is, *On the Division of Nature*, a work highly useful for resolving certain intricate questions, provided that one forgives him in those matters where he departed from the path of the Latins while fixing his eyes too intently upon the Greeks. [Col. 0093A]

> “He was a man of extensive and curious reading, acute but, as I have said, inelegant in his skill as a translator. Speaking in the words of Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church, I believe that he acted thus for no other reason than that, being humble in spirit, he did not presume to abandon the proper meaning of a word, lest he should in any way depart from the truth of the sense. He was learned to the point of provoking envy, a footman of the Greeks, and sprinkled through his books many things that Latin ears could not accept. Knowing how offensive these would be to his readers, he concealed them either under the persona of his interlocutor or beneath the cloak of the Greeks. For this reason he was thought a heretic, and a certain Florus wrote against him. [Col. 0093B]

> “For in the book *περὶ φύσεων* there are very many passages which, in the judgment of many, seem to depart from the Catholic faith. Pope Nicholas is known to have held this opinion. In his letter to Charles he says:

> “‘It has been reported to our Apostolate that a certain John of yours, by race a Scot, has recently translated into Latin the work of the blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, which he composed in Greek concerning the divine names and the celestial orders. It ought, according to custom, to have been sent to us and submitted to our judgment for approval, especially since, although this John is proclaimed to possess great learning, it has long been commonly reported that he was unsound in judgment on certain matters. Therefore let your diligence make good what has hitherto been omitted, and send us the aforesaid work without any hesitation.’ [Col. 0093C]

> “Because of this disgrace, I believe, he grew weary of France and came to England to King Alfred. Drawn by the king’s generosity and patronage, he held an eminent position at Malmesbury, as I have learned from his writings. There, after some years, he was stabbed with writing-styles by the boys whom he taught and gave up his soul amid a grievous and bitter torment. While great wickedness and weak hands repeatedly failed and repeatedly attacked him, he suffered a bitter death. [Col. 0093D]

> “For some time he lay in that church which had witnessed the dishonorable murder. But when divine favor granted him an appearance of fiery light on many nights, the monks, warned by it, transferred him to the larger church. They placed him on the left side of the altar and proclaimed him a martyr in these verses:

> “Buried in this tomb is the holy sophist John,  
> Who, while alive, had already been enriched by wondrous doctrine;  
> At last, by martyrdom, he deserved to ascend to heaven,  
> Where all the saints reign forever through the ages.

> “Anastasius likewise praises him, while he was still alive, for his eminent holiness, in these words addressed to Charles:

> “‘It is also wondrous how that barbarian man—I mean John—who, situated at the ends of the earth, could be thought as far removed from men in his manner of life as he was distant from another language in speech, was able to grasp such things in understanding and transfer them into another language. I mean John Scotigena, a man, as far as I have learned, holy in every respect. But this was accomplished by that artificer Spirit who made him at once ardent and speaking. For unless he had burned with the fire of charity through the grace of that Spirit, he would certainly never have received the gift of speaking in languages. For master Charity taught him what he accomplished for the instruction and edification of many.’ [Col. 0094A]

> “Thus various writings alternate between praise of him and disgrace, although for a long time the praises have outweighed the blame. Such was the power of the craftsman’s eloquence that all Gaul submitted its hand to his teaching. But if anyone longs for greater boldness, let him consider that the council assembled at Tours in the time of Pope Nicholas delivered a harsher judgment—not against him, but against his writings. These, then, are approximately the matters that give rise to controversy … [lacuna].”

## John Pyke, in his book *On the Anglo-Saxon Kings*

[Pag. IX]

> “Alfred summoned Saint Grimbald and others with him through envoys; attracting into his kingdom men from Mercia and from the farthest ends of the earth whom he knew to excel in learning, he increased their honors.” [Col. 0094A]

## John Rossus, in his book *On the Kings*

> “King Alfred united to himself Saint Grimbald, a Flemish monk from the monastery of Saint Bertin, together with his associates John and Asser, and John the Welshman from the monastery of Saint David.” [Col. 0094B]

## John of Tritheim, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

> “John, called Erigena, a monk learned in the divine Scriptures and most highly educated in secular learning, fully instructed in Greek and Latin eloquence, subtle in intellect and composed in speech,” and so forth.

## John Leland, in Book II of *On British Writers*

> “Alfred held in esteem and intimacy Plegmund, Werefrid, Asser of Menevia, Grimbald, John the monk originally from transmarine Saxony, and John Scotus, who translated the *Hierarchy* of Dionysius.” [Col. 0094C]

These are the testimonies that seemed to me most certainly to identify this John Scotus. What Bale wrote about his father Patrick, his journey to Athens, and his extraordinary proficiency in the Eastern languages, however, wins no credence from me. Since the surname Erigena, which is attributed to our John, has not yet, in my view, been sufficiently understood, I shall set forth my conjectures about it. [Col. 0094D]

What William of Malmesbury says in the letter cited above—that Scotus called himself *Heruligena* in the title of the *Hierarchy*—I would not readily accept as true. For all the manuscript codices contradict him with something like a single voice and consistently display either *Erigena* or *Eriugena*. William had read in Asser and Ingulf that a certain John Ealdsaxon was with Alfred; and so, because the Heruli had once been a people in ancient Saxony, he judged this John to have originated from the Heruli.

If anyone nevertheless believes that these words did not fall accidentally from the Malmesbury writer, let him reasonably argue on his behalf that ancient writers report the Heruli to have once settled among the Irish. On this matter one may consult Lazius, *On the Migrations of Peoples*, and Beatus Rhenanus, whom he summons to his side. [Col. 0095A]

I am no more persuaded by the opinion of those who make John an Irishman from the word *Erigena*. In ancient books he is more often called *Eriugena* than *Erigena*. Certainly, in a manuscript of extreme antiquity—now preserved in the Library of Trinity College, Cambridge—which Archbishop Ussher used, and which I too have used, the name is written *Eriugena*, not *Erigena*. Suffridus Petri likewise has it so; Dionysius Petavius found it so in his copies; and so did Philip Labbe.

Moreover, the word *Erin*, “Irish,” produces not *Erigena* but *Erinigenam*; and in this form P. Marca correctly rendered the word in a letter about this John addressed to Luc d’Achery. Nor should anyone be moved by the fact that this John is so often called Irish. It happened because he had spent a long time studying among that people, which at that time was a workshop of liberal learning. [Col. 0095B]

Rossus, in his book *On the Kings*, cites the following from an ancient writer concerning Ireland:

> “When English studies had been suspended [by Gregory I from the time of Augustine], learning flourished in Scotland and Ireland. Ireland, however, was then the storehouse and nurse of all knowledge. Saint Cedda studied there, previously a disciple of Saint Aidan, bishop of Lindisfarne, and afterward bishop of York, and finally of Lindsey and all Mercia. His fellow student in Ireland was Egbert … [lacuna] … and many men distinguished in character and learning from England.” [Col. 0095C]

I said that he was called Irish because he had devoted himself there to learning. The same happened in the case of a certain Mark, who was commonly called Irish although he was British by nationality and had been educated in Ireland, as Eric of Auxerre writes about him at the end of Book I of *On the Miracles of Saint Germanus*. The same happened in the case of Saint Patrick, Pelagius, and many others.

To summarize my conjecture briefly, I think that this John was called Erigena from his place of birth, as it appears. Ergene is a not insignificant part of Herefordshire, bordering Wales. Indeed, at this time it was one of the kingdoms of Wales subject to Alfred. In this district I find a place called Eriuven, a word that differs little from *Eriugen* and, in contracted form, *Ergene*. The whole region is now called by the Welsh themselves *Erynug* or *Ereinuc*.

Anyone who observes how many changes are usually made in twisting other barbarous words into a Latin form will readily grant me these slight alterations in this word. The *Book of the Church of Llandaff*, in Volume III of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, and Gerald of Wales, in his description of Wales, chapter 3, will give fuller information about this small region. Gerald notes that it was part of the diocese of Menevia, where Asser was archbishop. That Asser was related to the Asser who heard John Erigena teaching. [Col. 0095D]

This little province is also mentioned in the *Domesday Book*, where I read:

> “These were the customs of the Welsh in the time of King Edward in Archenfield, that is, Ergene.”

Both Gerald and the *Book of Llandaff* further note that the Scots at one time occupied the borders of Wales; hence the surname Scotus may also have been attached to our John. [Col. 0096A]

But to return: this too seems to be confirmed by the fact that John Erigena is expressly called Welsh by writers. Thus he is called by the compiler of the Hida annals, and by Rossus in his book *On the Kings*. Indeed, he himself not obscurely indicates that he was Welsh in a poem addressed to Charles the Bald:

> “I, John the stranger, devote myself to my Charles …”

For the words “Welshman” and “stranger” are equivalent.

The writer of Grimbald’s life reports that John was sent with Asser as an envoy to Flanders to invite Grimbald, in Alfred’s name. It is not improbable that Master John undertook this embassy with his pupil. Through Fulco—then, in the year 882, archbishop of Reims and recently abbot of Bertin—John had heard of the reputation of Grimbald of Bertin. When John returned to England in 883, he recommended Grimbald to Alfred. From this followed the embassy in or around the year 884, for Grimbald arrived here in 885.

These things have been said so that no one may suppose that Erigena was at this time lingering in Gaul. [Note: What has been argued thus far concerning the surname Erigena and John Scotus’s return to England seems either wholly false or incapable of proof by any sound arguments. See our Preface. Editor’s observation.] [Col. 0095D; Col. 0096D]

But more on this matter shortly.

Finally, those who insist that this John was Irish both by race and by family may be asked why he alone among so many of his countrymen was surnamed Erigena. The Saxon Annals bear witness, as does Eric of Auxerre, along with others cited by the most learned James Ussher, archbishop of Armagh, in the Preface to his *Irish Letters*, that very many Irishmen—or Irish Scots—became known to the learned world during the times of Charlemagne, Charles the Bald, and Alfred, and afterward. Yet no one among them is known to have received the name Erigena as a national designation. All are called either Irish, Scots, or Irish Scots. [Pag. XI; Col. 0096B]

I now turn to a review of the writings of Scotus Erigena. I shall first list those works of his about which no uncertainty is found among the ancients. That John published:

1. One book *On the Eucharist*.
2. Four translations of Dionysius the Areopagite, namely: *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, *On the Divine Names*, and *On Mystical Theology*.
3. One book *On Predestination*, against Gottschalk.
4. Translations of Saint Maximus’s *Ambigua* concerning Saint Dionysius and Gregory the Theologian.
5. A treatise *On the Vision of God*.
6. Five books *On the Division of Nature*.
7. Letters.
8. Verses. [Col. 0096C]

The following are also attributed to him:

9. Commentaries on Martianus Capella.
10. Excerpts from Macrobius.
11. One book *On the Discipline of Scholars*.
12. A certain disputation with Theodore the Studite.
13. A translation of Aristotle’s *Moral Works*.
14. A translation of Aristotle’s book *On the Government of Princes*.
15. Commentaries on Aristotle’s *Categories*.
16. *Philosophical Doctrines*.
17. Homilies.
18. *On the Faith against the Barbarians*.
19. Paraphrastic volumes, or commentaries, on Dionysius the Areopagite. [Col. 0096D]

### 1. *On the Eucharist*

Some think that this first work has perished; others believe that it still exists under the name of Bertram, or Ratramnus. Among others, this matter may be investigated in Petrus de Marca, in Luc d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, Volume II, and in the learned Jean Mabillon’s Preface to Part II of Volume IV of the *Acts of the Benedictines*. [Col. 0097A]

### 2. Translations of Dionysius

The translations of Dionysius exist in manuscript codices, some of which I have seen and which, as far as conjecture allows, belong to the century in which John Scotus lived. On these, see Anastasius the Librarian and Philip Labbe in his edition of Anastasius the Librarian. They have also been printed.

Some observe that, because of this translation, John first came under suspicion of having unsound views concerning the faith. [Col. 0097B]

### 3. *On Predestination*

The third work, *On Predestination*, was printed at Paris in the year of our salvation 1650. You may find it among the ninth-century writers collected by the royal councillor Gilbert Mauguin, together with various judgments and censures of the ancients concerning that book.

### 4. The translation of Maximus’s *Ambigua*

Saint Maximus wrote an exposition of several difficult passages occurring in the works of Saint Dionysius and Gregory of Nazianzus. John Erigena translated these *Ambigua* into Latin. I do not know whether he translated Maximus’s entire work, since I have not yet obtained the complete Greek text of Saint Maximus.

What you read here at the end was obtained partly through the kindness of the distinguished Emeric Bigot, who examined for my use a copy made from the Royal Library of France, and partly from my own manuscript, which contains many of Maximus’s writings. [Pag. XII; Col. 0097C]

To return to Scotus: the translation which I publish here was shared with me by the distinguished John Mabillon, renowned for his learning and kindness, whom I mentioned above. Apart from the features readily observable in the books *On the Division of Nature*, this translation sufficiently demonstrates that Erigena was, in Greek, plainly a beginner.

### 5. *On the Vision of God*

The same distinguished J. Mabillon discovered a book *On the Vision of God* in a manuscript at Clairmarais, near Saint-Omer, bearing this title and beginning:

> **Treatise of John Scotus on the Vision of God.**  
> All bodily senses arise from the conjunction of soul and body.

I tried to have this book of Scotus sent to me, but so far success has not answered my efforts. [Col. 0097D]

### 6. *On the Division of Nature*

I am now publishing for the first time the five books *On the Division of Nature*. My own, otherwise poorly supplied, library furnished them to me. Our codex seems to have been written six hundred years ago.

Since I did not consider it sufficiently safe to rely upon a single copy, especially for a work exposed to controversy, I first carefully examined the passages which Scotus cited from the ancient Fathers. As a result, our codex gained several corrections. Then, when I learned that another copy of this work was preserved in the monastery of Saint-Germain at Paris—perhaps the only second copy besides mine, since the Codex Thuaneus was very mutilated—I obtained, through the kindness of friends, among whom the first was the distinguished Petrus Alix, variant readings from that Paris manuscript. These made good in many places omissions caused either by the haste of our scribes or by defects in the codex itself. [Col. 0098A]

If anyone afterward notices in this edition discrepancies from the manuscript copy, let him know that they arose unintentionally and by chance—not through design, not through deliberate fraud, but through the human weakness that does not see everything.

Abbot Trithemius attributes these five books to John Scotus, whom they call of Mailros. Bale follows him, and errs along with one who is erring. For, to say nothing of the historians—who all unanimously attribute this work to Scotus Erigena—it is sufficiently clear from the translation of the *Ambigua* that one and the same person was the author of both works.

These books had doubtless circulated for a long time without the author’s name. Our copy lacked it; the Paris codex lacked it as well. Indeed, the author’s name was so completely unknown that the work was condemned at Paris before it was established whose offspring it was. [Col. 0098B]

Martin the Pole writes about it as follows, as I read it in two manuscripts belonging to the Reverend Father in Christ, William, archbishop of Canterbury:

> “This book [*περὶ φύσεων*, *On Natures*] is listed among the other books condemned at Paris, and is called the book of Amalric.”

The last words do not appear in the printed books of Martin the Pole. William of Malmesbury was the first to restore the work to its author. Erigena, as it is reasonable to suppose, had acknowledged the matter among his own people, which he had concealed from outsiders.

### 7. Letters

No one, as far as I know, has seen any letters of Scotus except those which he prefixed to his books. Nevertheless, there can be no doubt that he wrote others. At the end of this volume I have appended an unpublished letter which Erigena wrote to Charles the Bald concerning his translation of Saint Maximus. [Col. 0098C]

### 8. Verses

I would gladly have omitted the verses if Bale had not thought them worthy of mention. Some occur at the end of the letter prefixed to the book *On Predestination*; others stand before the *Areopagitic Works* translated by Scotus. Some are also found in Labbe’s *Glossary*, which Cangius published. Finally, several poems by Scotus to Charles are found in a Benedictine manuscript at Cambridge, although these may perhaps be the same as those which the Reverend Ussher published long ago.

The following works are also attributed to Scotus Erigena. Whether rightly or wrongly, I do not decide. [Col. 0098D]

### 9. Commentaries on Martianus Capella

Certain commentaries on Capella, written by a fairly ancient hand, are preserved in the library of the distinguished Sir John Cotton, baronet. But they are anonymous, and for several reasons I think they should rather be attributed to Dunchad, bishop of Ireland. A work of Dunchad is held in the library of our King Charles.

### 10. Excerpts from Macrobius

Concerning the excerpts from Macrobius, the distinguished James Ussher, archbishop of Armagh, writes:

> “Those excerpts too are thought to be by our John which circulate among the writings of Macrobius, concerning the differences and affinities of the Greek and Latin word, and so forth. The distinguished P. Pithoeus likewise held this opinion.”

So he writes in his *Irish Letters*. [Col. 0099A]

### 11. *On the Discipline of Scholars*

Buleus thinks that this John wrote the work in his *History of the University of Paris*. I hold a different view. For although our Scotus was a barbarian and situated at the ends of the earth, as Anastasius the Librarian describes him, he was certainly not barbarized—*ἐβαρβαρώθη*—to the same degree as the author of that little book. Nor would the men of his age ever have given him the name of Chrysostom if they had thought him the maker of such a work.

### 12. Disputation with Theodore the Studite

The disputation with Theodore the Studite does not seem to belong to this John, since Theodore was somewhat older than could allow him to reach the time of our Scotus. Moreover, the disputation seems to have concerned the veneration of images, which was being debated in the time of Alcuin and John Scotus of Mailros.

This disputation therefore seems to belong to the latter rather than to Erigena. I am told that it is preserved in the famous Royal Library of France. [Col. 0099B]

### 13. Aristotle’s *Moral Works*

I do not know whether he translated Aristotle’s *Moral Works*. I suspect that this labor belongs to another Scotus.

### 14. Aristotle’s *On the Government of Princes*

The translation of the Aristotelian book, as it is thought, *On the Government of Princes*, is not the work of this Scotus, whatever the overconfident Bale may have written. I possess several copies of that book and have seen others. In all of them the translator is called John Patricius of Hispania.

Many think this work identical with the preceding one; I do not agree with them.

### 15. Commentaries on Aristotle’s *Categories*

The commentaries on Aristotle’s *Categories* are this John’s work—his *πόνημα*, or composition—if I correctly understand Hugh and Peter of Saint-Victor. I know, however, that in a certain catalogue of the Bodleian Library the same work bears the name of another Scotus. I pronounce no judgment concerning books I have not seen. [Col. 0099C]

### 16–18. Other works

The *Philosophical Doctrines*, the *Homilies*, and *On the Faith against the Barbarians* are all entirely unknown to me. If Bale had seen them, he would certainly also have supplied their beginnings.

### 19. Paraphrastic volumes on Dionysius

Concerning the paraphrastic volumes, or commentaries, on Dionysius, I possess nothing beyond a slight suspicion. I suspect that they may be the *παραθέσεις*—“annotations” or “scholia”—of John of Scythopolis, which Anastasius the Librarian translated; or perhaps the paraphrase of some abbot of Vercelli.

Furthermore, anyone who wishes to know what judgment the ancients held concerning the writings of John Erigena should read the writers on the history of Gottschalk, Vossius, Ussher, Mauguin, Cellot, as well as Petrus de Marca, Jean Mabillon, and P. Alix. [Col. 0099D]

William of Malmesbury taught us by what kind of death John perished; but he does not state with certainty when he ceased to be among the living. It is established from Roger of Wendover that Scotus returned to England in the year of salvation 883—or, according to others, in 884. The great Baronius wrote that he died in that same year, 883. But in support of his opinion he cites only our native historians as witnesses, and they do not say this; for they speak of his death in that year by a kind of anticipation. [Col. 0100A]

“After several years” from 883, says William of Malmesbury, “he gave up his soul after being stabbed with writing-styles.” In the second year after Grimbald’s arrival—he came to England in 884 or 885—Scotus taught at Oxford, if we are to believe the Hida Annals, which either first or alone make this assertion. I have no reliable information about the rest of his life.

He died an undeserved death. Grateful posterity wished to make him immortal and therefore long celebrated his birthday on the fourth day before the Ides of November. Arnold Wion mentions him honorably in *The Lignum Vitae* and notes that in the Roman Martyrology printed in 1580 he retained his full place and honor, although later editions of the Martyrology removed him entirely.

John seems to me to have been born under such a destiny that he would always undergo the alternating judgments of men about him. Anastasius the Librarian proclaims him holy in every respect; others report him as a liar, a fool, a madman, or a heretic. The boys of Malmesbury kill him; the monks construct his tomb. Some abbots honor him almost as highly as their own Aldhelm; Warinus regards him nearly as refuse. Some insert him into their calendars; others strike him out. Thus his fame and name have long been afflicted by something like a recurrent fever. [Col. 0100B]

On the place of his burial alone all agree. The *Catalogue of the Saints Buried in England*, now preserved in the Benedictine College at Cambridge, writes of him in Saxon letters:

> “Saint Maildun, Saint Aldhelm, and John the Wise rest in Malmesbury.”

The Cottonian Codex, from Gotzelin of Bertin, says the same. Nor does the Malmesbury Librarian, as we have seen, depart from this account; neither does an ancient annotation once read in the Merton Library at Oxford:

> “Saint Aldhelm and John the Wise rest in the place called Malmesbury.”

A statue was also erected in honor of this John in the church of Malmesbury Abbey, with this inscription:

> “John Scotus, who translated Dionysius from Greek into Latin.” [Col. 0100C]

So Leland writes in his *Itinerary*.

This is what I had to say about John Erigena at present. [Col. 0100D]

---

## C. B. Schlueter’s Preface to the Edition Entitled

*The Five Books of John Scotus Erigena on the Division of Nature*

[Col. 0101]

Revised and corrected edition. Added are thirteen hymns of the author to Charles the Bald, taken from the palimpsests of Angelo Mai. Münster in Westphalia, printed and published at the expense of the Asthendorff Bookshop, 1838.

[Col. 0101A] (p. III.) John Scotus Eriugena [Note: [Col. 0101C] Cf. the excellent work written by Prof. Dr. Staudenmaier, *John Scotus Eriugena and the Science of His Age*, vol. I, Frankfurt am Main, 1834. What that most learned man discussed there on pp. 102–213, we have set out here briefly, differing from his opinion only in matters of lesser importance.] was by nationality an Irishman [Note: [Col. 0101C] Thomas Moore confirms this with the most certain arguments in his book *History of Ireland*, vol. I, chapter 13. Staudenmaier thinks that Eriuven, a place in Britain, was Eriugena’s homeland; others, interpreting the surname Scotus incorrectly, have believed that he was born in the land now called Scotland.], born perhaps around the year 828. In his native country, at that time the most celebrated in the cultivation of learning, he became highly educated in the study of the liberal arts, Greek learning as well, and philosophy [Note: [Col. 0102C] Indeed, he is said to have learned Hebrew and perhaps even Syriac; cf. *John Scotus Eriugena: A Contribution to the History of Christian Philosophy, with Particular Regard to the Accounts of Hiort and Staudenmaier*, edited by Dr. C. Hock, *Ephemerides Bonnenses*, fascicle 16, 1835.]. Once these studies had been completed, perhaps already then initiated by priestly ordination—although some think that he remained a layman, while others speak of distant journeys on which he visited Greece and even the East—he went, like many of his countrymen at that time, to Gaul.

There King Charles the Bald, energetic and industrious in promoting learning, summoned him to Paris and appointed him master of mathematics and dialectic [Note: [Col. 0101C] It is not recorded that John Scotus was a master of mathematics and dialectic. Cf. the above-cited essay *On John Scotus*, chapter II, column 11, note a. —Editor’s annotation.], and head of the palace school, which was then highly renowned. The king was greatly pleased by his cheerfulness and by his witty and ingenious sayings; consequently, Eriugena soon became Charles’s closest friend, indeed often his table companion and housemate. Without doubt, he also had considerable influence in encouraging, even outside Paris and throughout the Frankish kingdom, the study of letters and the liberal arts.

But soon afterward he became entangled in various troublesome difficulties. For when the Saxon monk Gottschalk had proposed at that time that there was a twofold predestination, one of the blessed and the other of the reprobate, he was on this account subjected to the harshest punishment by Hincmar, archbishop of Reims. Moved by this, several distinguished theologians—Prudentius, Florus the Deacon, Lupus, Amolo, Saint Remigius, and others—undertook to defend Gottschalk; and at length they brought Hincmar to the point of summoning other experts in dogmatic matters to defend him as well.

Among these Eriugena, taking up the archbishop’s cause, wrote, around the year 852, his still-extant book *On Predestination* against Gottschalk [Col. 0102A], thereby acquiring many opponents. Finally, Pope Nicholas I approved what Saint Remigius had taught and confirmed the canons of the Council of Valence that concerned this controversy [Note: [Col. 0101C] Nor is this based upon the testimony of the ancients. Cf. the cited essay, chapter IV. —Editor’s annotation.]. Although Eriugena’s doctrines were also criticized there as “poison,” Eriugena himself was not condemned. Nevertheless, several writers of later ages pleaded his cause and maintained that his writings had been corrupted.

After this, King Charles the Bald urged Eriugena to translate once more into Latin the works of (Pseudo-)Dionysius the Areopagite, written in Greek, which Michael Balbus, emperor of the Eastern Roman Empire, had presented in the year 827 to Charles’s predecessor, Louis the Pious. Eriugena fulfilled the king’s wish [Col. 0102B], but was criticized by Pope Nicholas I because he, although “great in learning,” already enjoyed, in the judgment of many, a dubious reputation with regard to orthodoxy, and had published without the approval of the Supreme Pontiff a book so liable to be falsely interpreted. (859.)

Some relate that the pope ordered Eriugena, because of this matter, to be sent from Paris and brought to Rome; others say that the book was then sent to him as well for his approval [Note: [Col. 0101D] Pope Nicholas I himself requests that Charles the Bald have John, who is frequently said by common report not to think soundly in certain matters, brought before him at Rome, or at least not allow him to remain in study at Paris, lest he be found to mix the tares and darnel of error with the grains of sacred eloquence and offer poison to those seeking bread. Cf. the letters of Pope Nicholas I prefixed by us to John Scotus’s translation of the works of Pseudo-Dionysius, as well as what is discussed on this matter in the cited essay. —Editor’s annotation.]. We do not know why the pope’s will was not obeyed, nor do we see that the pope himself afterward insisted that his order be carried out.

Nevertheless, although the pope had criticized Eriugena, his contemporary Anastasius, the Roman librarian, praised our author no less for that same translation than for “his holy life.” He praised him in such a way that he confessed that the excellence of intellect and virtue displayed by Eriugena could derive only from the extraordinary efficacy of a particular divine grace infused through the Holy Spirit. This is evidence of what opinion was held of him at Rome and even in the papal court, although he had once been covered with an ambiguous reputation. Anastasius thought that the only point deserving criticism in the translation was Eriugena’s excessive effort to render the original word for word, although he attributed that effort to Eriugena’s “humility.”

Finally, around the year 870, the doctrine of Paschasius Radbertus concerning the Eucharist—which posited Christ’s presence as almost excessively corporeal and thus virtually Capernaitic—had stirred up a new controversy in the Church. Eriugena also became involved in this controversy and, chiefly together with Ratramnus, elucidated the spiritual significance of the doctrine. We do not know what precisely he taught concerning the Eucharist, since the book attributed by some to Eriugena may already have perished before the eleventh century [Col. 0103B] [Note: [Col. 0103D] It seems to us most probable that John Scotus never wrote a separate book on the Eucharist, as we have shown in the preface. —Editor’s annotation.]. For there is no doubt that either this same book, or another book on the Eucharist whose authority Berengar employed, which was condemned at the council held at Paris under King Henry I and burned at the Council of Vercelli in 1050, was written neither by Eriugena nor by a certain Bertram, but by Ratramnus [Note: [Col. 0103D] Cf. Döllinger, *Textbook of Church History*, Regensburg and Landshut, 1836, vol. I, p. 409.].

Eriugena’s greatest and most serious work, however, is the dialogue *On the Division of Nature*, consisting of five books. We do not know when it was written; but it acquired far less authority than it deserved. It is the first theological work in the West that is as learned as it is ingenious and that, possessing an entirely philosophical character, sets forth doctrines upon which scholastic logic and the mystical theology of the Middle Ages may be regarded as largely founded [Col. 0103C]. But when, in the thirteenth century, certain Albigensian heretics continually had several passages of this work on their lips and boasted of Eriugena’s authority, Pope Honorius III ordered that copies of the book be sought out everywhere and burned.

Besides these principal works written by Eriugena, we considered only thirteen hymns worthy of mention—those found by Angelo Mai in a palimpsest manuscript and appended at the end of our edition. We have not wished to mention the rest here, since some were destroyed by the hostility of time [Note: [Col. 0103D] Cf. Hock, cited work.].

Perhaps both the disagreements that had gradually arisen between Eriugena and several ecclesiastical leaders in Gaul and that old summons from Pope Nicholas I induced Eriugena to do what is now nearly beyond doubt—probably around the year 883 or somewhat later—to go to England when summoned by Alfred the Great [Col. 0103D]. There, at Oxford, he taught mathematics and dialectic for some time at the university of letters. Finally, having become abbot of the monastery at Malmesbury, he died after being murdered by the styluses of his mutinous pupils [Col. 0104A] (p. VI) [Note: [Col. 0103D] Our John is a different man from John, abbot of Ethelingay, who was killed by hired assassins.].

Tradition relates that after his death a wondrous light was seen above his tomb and continued to shine until a more honorable tomb had been prepared for him in the larger church of Malmesbury, near the altar [Note: [Col. 0103D] We stated in the preface that what is related about John Scotus’s return to England [Col. 0104D] and about his death is not established fact. Cf. the cited essay, chapter V. —Editor’s annotation.]. For this reason, no less than on account of the integrity of his life, he was commemorated among the holy martyrs in the martyrologies of the Franks and the English until the year 1583, when the liturgical books of the Romans were introduced.

He lived a holy life, and his life itself was never censured; only his doctrine was occasionally criticized, although, as we have seen, the reports that earlier accusations had been brought against his orthodoxy are uncertain and ambiguous. He was small in stature; but in cultivation of mind he was distinguished, with a keen and lofty intellect, knowledge as broad as it was profound, and a dialectic worthy of Plato and Proclus. Finally, through a certain divine inspiration of mind by which he perceived, investigated, and contemplated to the very end all that was exalted and noble, he surpassed very many of his contemporaries, even among the most learned.

Many people misunderstood Eriugena, and in many different ways; this was almost inevitable, since he strove to express every truth as sharply as he could, and, indulging his genius, embraced opposites so fully that, discussing the same matter in different places from different and contrary perspectives, he almost exceeded the proper measure in both directions. For this reason, it is not easy to defend each of his statements if it is torn from the context of his discourse. Yet we dare to affirm that, if one considers him as a whole, he nowhere departed by a hair’s breadth from the truth—something that would have been wholly incompatible with the singular holiness of his life.

Indeed, the familiar saying advanced by the most celebrated poet of our time—“The history of the world is the judgment of the world” [Note: “Die Weltgeschichte ist das Weltgericht.” Schiller. Cf. Th. Gale’s preface to the books *On the Division*, final page.]—although sometimes found to be true, nevertheless very often misleads. The same happened in Eriugena’s case: almost all who criticized or praised him were utterly unequal to grasping his depth and acuity, and therefore judged him unjustly. Only very few understood correctly the lofty mind with which he was endowed.

Certainly, even the praise of those who, declaring our philosopher a precursor of Spinoza, exalted as highly as they could “his pantheism and his sense abhorrent to the Catholic Church” [Note: Cf. Tennemann, *History of Philosophy*, vol. VIII, section I, pp. 53 and 72.]—that praise Eriugena himself would entirely and justly reject.

Let us now hear some less unfair judgments pronounced by more recent writers, so that we may to some extent see what place Eriugena occupies in the choir of learned doctors of all ages [Col. 0105A]. After the well-known Thomas Gale, who admired Eriugena’s acumen and has so far been the only person to publish the books *On the Division* [Note: *The Five Books of John Scotus Eriugena on the Division of Nature, Long Desired*. Oxford, 1681. Cf. ibid., p. 8, for the testimonies in Gale’s preface.], the first who must be named is Dr. Peter Hjort, a Dane of outstanding talent and learning, who formerly taught philosophy and German literature at Sorø and now does so at Copenhagen.

By a little book published in 1823 [Note: *John Scotus Eriugena, or On the Origin of a Christian Philosophy and Its Sacred Calling*. By Dr. Peder Hjort, professor of German literature at Sorø. Copenhagen, 1823.], he rendered the greatest service to Eriugena by bringing his character and excellence once more into the light and public recognition. Hjort’s work, apart from its preface, is divided into three parts.

In the first, the author discusses with great learning the origin of Western literature and the periods of Theodoric the Ostrogoth, Charlemagne, Charles the Bald, and Alfred the Great, insofar as they concerned the advancement of literature, and he narrates the life of Eriugena [Col. 0105B]. The whole of the second part is devoted to explaining Eriugena’s philosophical system; although briefly and in outline, it nevertheless gives, if considered as a whole, a clear and accurate sketch of it. In the third part, Christian philosophy is explained as it was developed in the Middle Ages by the scholastic doctors and in subsequent centuries by more recent philosophers down to our own age, and the holy task it has received is set forth.

The author, a friend of Hamann and Baader, followed in part Hegel’s dialectical method in treating the history of philosophy. Yet it is sufficiently clear from the passage in which he deals most beautifully with this matter that he knew and understood truly how highly Eriugena valued the authority of Sacred Scripture and the Fathers. Cf. p. 47 ff. If one listens to Hjort, Eriugena’s doctrines are nothing other than a philosophical exposition of the Christian faith, discovered by “one who philosophizes rightly, piously, and catholically.”

(P. VIII.) But the distinguished Antonius Staudenmaier, now professor of Catholic theology at the University of Freiburg, achieved far more. In the book mentioned above [Col. 0106A], gathering an exceedingly rich body of material for the history of Eriugena, he wrote with the greatest diligence about the periods in which Eriugena himself flourished and those immediately preceding them, so that it became clear from where his doctrine and learning had arisen. The same learned man no less accurately describes the influence Eriugena exerted upon the scholastic disciplines of the Middle Ages, both mystical and logical, directing his principal effort toward demonstrating the soundness, integrity, and orthodoxy of our author’s mind.

Since it would be too lengthy for the purpose of this preface to quote even in part all the passages of the greatest importance from the aforesaid book—which should be regarded as a preliminary study toward a fuller and more complete representation of Scotus’s system than has yet been attempted—it will suffice to recommend the entire work most earnestly to all who are pursuing this subject with greater diligence.

Albert Kreutzhage, academic judge at the venerable University of Göttingen, a writer who has served philosophy admirably through both talent and purity of purpose, also embraces everything elegantly and concisely. In the book cited in the margin [Note: [Col. 0106C] *Communications on the Influence of Philosophy upon the Development of the Inner Life*. Münster, at Theissing, 1831, pp. 216 ff.], he extols each of the virtues of our Philosopher with worthy praise, as though inspired by some higher spirit.

We mean Eriugena’s native and inventive character; his acumen; his depth; his truly Christian philosophy; the beauty and loftiness of his language; his learning; the purity of his sentiments; and the divinity proper to Spiritualism—by which, indeed, he may be compared with the most celebrated of all poets, Dante, a man no less great than that poet, though for a long time unjustly undervalued and neglected through an injury done to him [Col. 0106C]. Finally, he praises Eriugena’s system, which, although touching upon pantheism, nevertheless does not cross the boundaries of creationism and in no way dissolves the distinction between Creator and creature.

Indeed, since it is scarcely possible to express fully in Latin the elegance of his words, let us insert them here [Note: [Col. 0105D] Here is the Latin version of that letter, by which we believe we have captured the author’s meaning:

“Today, dearest friend, I have finished the volume of Scotus Eriugena *On the Division of Nature*, and I praise and celebrate the chance that placed that splendid and rare work in my hands. In reading through the discussion concerning the primordial causes, one must recognize again and again that this work contains, in abundance, the primordial causes of innumerable philosophical ideas, each of which afterward became the soul and, as it were, the center of entire philosophical systems. Indeed, if certain modern philosophers wished to be candid, I think they would openly confess that their principal idea was supplied to them by Eriugena and that the various paths they themselves entered were opened to them by the aid of Eriugena’s deepest and sharpest genius.

“The foundation of modern investigations concerning self-conscious mind and the threefold nature of that mind, together with the higher insights that have flowed from it into the understanding of the nature of God and the explanation of certain very weighty doctrines of the Christian religion—in short, the chief discovery of modern philosophy—was proposed long ago by Eriugena in these words:

“‘For the mind both generates knowledge of itself, and from itself proceed its love of itself and its knowledge of itself, by which both the mind itself and its knowledge of itself are joined together.’

“Eriugena’s mode of expression is no less admirable. Everywhere inspired, it displays the rare union of the highest depth with the sharpest intellect, so that as you read you seem almost to be carried away into a temple or sacred grove filled with wondrous images and echoing with divine voices that disclose the innermost secrets of life. In general, the study of spiritual philosophy produces this effect: first, the material life, together with the principle hidden within it—the obscure principle of negation and abstract cognition, which is no less obscuring than it is obscure—is increasingly weakened; then the desire kindled by that principle, which drives us to spend our life amid the things of the lower realm, is increasingly subdued. Thus the deadly weapons and confused tumult of these lower powers can no longer penetrate into that higher region where everything is bathed in the light of divine nature and truth.

“‘Its whole appearance becomes a ray,

“‘reflected at the summit of the Primum Mobile,

“‘which from there receives life and power.

“‘And as a hillside in water, at its base,

“‘seems to see itself adorned,

“‘with all its greenery and abundance of little flowers,

“‘so, standing above the surrounding light,

“‘I saw mirrored in more than a thousand thresholds

“‘whatever of us has returned upward.

“‘And if the lowest tier gathers within itself

“‘so great a light, how wide must be

“‘the extent of this rose in its outermost petals?’”

(Dante, *Paradiso*, canto XXX, verses 106 ff.)

“Günther would designate Eriugena’s system, according to his usual practice, by the name ‘pantheism of dependence.’ Nor can it be denied that it often grazes the side, as it were, of pantheism. In general, all spiritual systems tend in that direction; indeed, they can easily pass into pantheism if the first parts of the self-conscious mind are assigned primacy, if the laws of thought are then accepted as creative powers of the world, and if their creative force is referred only to their relations with one another. The result is that spirit becomes all in all.

“Eriugena, however, does not cross those boundaries that separate pantheism from the doctrine of creation. For even where he approaches those boundaries most closely—as in the deification of the saints—he accurately distinguishes the creature from the Creator according to essence. This is clearly shown by the example drawn from light, which fills the air and seems to transform it entirely into its own nature, yet does not abolish the distinction.

“Certainly, Eriugena’s primordial causes, upon whose unfolding and reversion the world depends in such a way that particulars remain in universals, recall Hegel to mind. But Eriugena does not mean a return that abolishes essence, and therefore not identity, but rather the immanence of the creature in the Creator. These causes, first exerting their power, generate Eriugena’s categories. Whereas Kant’s categories, being subjective, overthrow and destroy the world, Eriugena’s categories, being objective and real, establish and construct it. For they explain the conditions under which intelligibles, substances, become sensible; and since the categories are at once substances and sensible things, they also demonstrate the identity of these two with one another.

“Now, equipped with an accurate knowledge of the natural sciences, mathematics, and astronomy as they existed both in his own ninth century and in earlier times, and thoroughly imbued with the books of the Greek philosophers and the writings of the Fathers, Eriugena vigorously labors to extract, by the philosophical path of careful inquiry, the solid kernel of truth contained in the Christian religion. By this path he reaches the most weighty conclusions and, in a rare example—matched among later scholastic philosophers, if one considers acumen, only by Thomas Aquinas—clearly demonstrates that the true relation between philosophy and the Christian religion is by no means one of hostile conflict. Rather, only together can they attain their goal, which consists in the knowledge of truth: namely, that through knowledge truth may become wholly alive within us and that we may be in it.

“But if philosophy and the Christian religion are separated and torn apart, philosophy climbs only the barren peaks of the rocks, and the higher it rises, the more it loses solid truth. Nothing remains for it except to reason in the empty air about its own shadow. Again, in the Christian religion dogmas then stiffen until they appear almost like material and external forms, and the dull and timid eyes of those who have bared their feet in the sacred place but covered their eyes with a veil can no longer behold the inner and living life within them. Thus the revelation that dogmas provide concerning the most serious questions of our nature is no longer understood, nor is the fullness of the truth with which they abound recognized.

“But truth can vivify and liberate only when we know both it and ourselves through it—what we were, what we are, what we must recover, what the purpose of our life is, and what relation exists between us, God, and the world.” —Editor’s annotation.]

“Today, my dear friend, I have finished the little folio volume of Scotus Eriugena, *On the Division of Nature*, and I praise the chance that placed this splendid and rare work in my hands. In the discussion of the primordial causes in the second book (p. IX), one must repeatedly acknowledge that this work contains in abundance the primordial causes of countless philosophical ideas, which since then have had to serve individually as the life-principle and center of entire philosophical systems. Indeed, it seems that if some modern philosophers were candid, they would have to confess that Eriugena supplied them with their principal thoughts, and that from the abundance of his acumen and depth they derived the impulses of their systems in very divergent directions . . . .

“The basis of modern investigations into self-consciousness and its trinity, the deeper insights gained from this into the essence of the Godhead, the meaning of certain important doctrines of Christianity, creation, and cognition—in short, one of the most important discoveries of modern philosophy—was already expressed by Eriugena in these words: ‘For the mind generates knowledge of itself, and from itself proceed love of itself and knowledge of itself, by which both it and its knowledge of itself are joined together.’

“The rare union in Eriugena of the highest acumen and depth also expresses itself in his remarkable style, which everywhere breathes inspiration, so that while reading one is continually maintained in a state as though one were in a temple or sacred grove filled with wondrous images and voices of spirits prophesying the innermost secrets of life. In general, the study of spiritualistic philosophy has the remarkable consequence that material life, together with the dark and darkening principle hidden within it of negating and abstract behavior (p. X), is increasingly weakened, while the striving kindled by that principle to fill existence with objects from the lower realm is increasingly subdued. Thus its destructive and deadly arrows and the broken sounds of its baneful power of destruction cannot penetrate into that region where everything is transfigured in the light of divine essence and truth.

“‘She appears wholly as a ray, and this ray

“‘flows back, reflected upon the arch of the highest heaven,

“‘giving it life and creative power.

“‘And as a hill bends its image toward a stream at its foot,

“‘as though it saw itself, beautifully adorned

“‘with green and the enamel of flowers, in that mirror,

“‘so everything that has returned upward from us

“‘seemed to mirror itself in the light,

“‘raised all around upon a thousand steps.

“‘And if the lowest of the ranks gathers within itself

“‘so much light, how broad must be

“‘the outer leaves of this rose when fully unfolded!’”

“Dante is indeed a divine seer, and A. W. Schlegel has himself risen to the level of that poet in this fragment of his translation . . . .

“Günther would classify Eriugena’s system as ‘pantheism of dependence,’ and it probably cannot be denied that it often passes close by pantheism. All purely spiritualistic systems approach this boundary; indeed, they can pass into pantheism if the standpoint of self-consciousness is declared to be the highest, and the laws of thought are then transferred to the world as creative agents, while their creative activity consists solely in their relations with one another, through which spirit becomes all in all.

“Eriugena nevertheless maintains the boundary between pantheism and creation. Even where he comes closest to this boundary—for example, in the deification of the saints—he sharply distinguishes Creator and creature according to essence, as the striking example used there makes clear: the light fills the air and seems to transform it entirely into itself, but nevertheless allows the distinction to remain.

“Eriugena’s primordial causes, in their world-establishing unfolding and return—with the particular remaining within the universal—do indeed recall Hegel. But by this Eriugena does not designate a return that abolishes and absorbs, and therefore not an identity, but the immanence of the creature in the Creator. Their immediate unfolding, the categories of Eriugena, which in their objective reality represent and construct the world—whereas Kant’s subjective categories destroy it—appear as the designation of the conditions under which the noumena, the substances, translate themselves into appearance. And because the categories are identical with substance and its appearance, the identity of these two with each other is also emphasized.

“Equipped with an exact knowledge of the state of the physical sciences, mathematics, and astronomy in his age, the ninth century, and in earlier times, thoroughly familiar with the ancient literature of Greek philosophy and the achievements of the Fathers (p. XI), Eriugena seeks to know philosophically and with strict scientific rigor the pure content of truth in Christianity. He obtains the most extraordinary results and shows, in a manner surpassed among later scholastic philosophers, with regard to acumen, by none but Thomas Aquinas, that the true relation of philosophy to Christianity is not hostile, but that both can attain their goal only in close union: to know the truth, so that through knowledge truth may become penetratingly alive within us and we may be in it.

“If, on the other hand, philosophy and Christianity are separated and held apart, philosophy climbs only barren rocky peaks, where, the higher it rises, the more it loses concrete truth, and in the emptied air can only speculate about its own shadow. In Christianity, however, dogma then stiffens as though materialized into an external form, and the dull and timid eyes of those who, while in the sacred place, remove their shoes from their feet but draw a veil over their eyes, can no longer see its rich inner life, hear the revelation it contains concerning the highest questions of our existence, or recognize the fullness of truth within it.

“Yet truth can enliven and liberate us only by enabling us to know it and, through it, ourselves: what we were, what we are, what we are to regain, what the task of our existence is, and in what relations we stand to the world and to God.”

As we continue to present the judgments pronounced by certain recent and learned writers concerning Eriugena, the next to meet us is Philippe Gerbet, a philosopher among the French who is distinguished in our time for piety and learning. Although he is less favorable to Scotus’s orthodoxy, he nevertheless compares Eriugena’s intuition with a dawn that suddenly arose over the cradle of philosophy. He calls Eriugena’s doctrine—a doctrine received from the Areopagite, who joined the remnants of Eastern systems with Christian dogma, and which Eriugena mixed with his own notions and ideas—a system whose sublimity and gigantic breadth rival the boldest endeavors of Indian philosophy [Note: [Col. 0109] Cf. *Introduction to the Philosophy of History*, by Abbé Philippe Gerbet, Paris, 1832, third lecture, pp. 101 ff.].
