After Gerbet has reviewed Eriugena’s doctrines concerning fourfold nature; concerning the analysis and synthesis of the primary divine unity, or creation; likewise concerning the names of God, who is without any name; and finally concerning the return of all things, gradually rising into God, and eternal apocatastasis; and after he has clearly and accurately sketched the outlines of the system, although it seems to him to savor of pantheism, he finally observes that Eriugena was raised to such a great and lofty perception of the world not so much by logical art as by a certain sublime and immense intuition. Logic there appears subject to metaphysics, not as its mistress, but almost as its servant.

Nevertheless, in the books *On the Division* he found scattered traces and fragments of a certain logical system, which broadly corresponds in some way to the other system, namely the system of nature. Using an almost mechanical mode of expression, he asserts that two series of ideas—the philosophical and the theological—run, as though split apart, side by side throughout the entire work. In the philosophical series, he says, the author does not escape pantheism; in the theological, however, he alters and bends it in an effort to adapt it to dogma.

If the public affairs of the tenth century had been less turbulent and less hostile to minds being raised toward higher studies, Gerbet thinks that a school might have arisen which, avoiding Eriugena’s errors, would have approached the intuitive knowledge and reason of the Eastern thinkers.

With Gerbet it will be appropriate to compare three of the most distinguished philosophers in Germany: Friedrich von Schlegel, Franz von Baader, and Anton Günther. The first of these does not doubt that medieval philosophy would have achieved a happier success if, besides St. Bernard, Anselm, and others, it had followed above all Erigena, whom he calls a Christian philosopher equally clear and simple, removed from every false zeal for investigating things, and making use of his own better judgment.[Note: *Philosophie der Geschichte*, vol. II, p. 159. Cf. Hugo v. St. Victor, by Dr. Liebener, p. 7; and *On the Mystical Theology of John Charlier of Gerson*, by Dr. Hundshagen, *Illgen’s Journal for Historical Theology*, vol. IV, no. 1, pp. 82 ff.] The other, Fr. von Baader, a most distinguished man, as early as 1824, both in the book he entitled *Fermenta cognitionis* and elsewhere, directed his readers’ minds toward the speculative ideas of Erigena’s works. Frequently citing him wherever he himself agrees with him, he does not indeed deny that Erigena here and there touched upon pantheism;[Col. 0111C] but he censures only the notion of Evil proposed by him, by which he fell into a neological abstraction and was therefore rightly disapproved by the Catholic Church.[Note: *Fermenta cognitionis*, fascicle VI, p. XXVI. Cf. also his *Speculative Dogmatics*, fascicle IV, lecture 9, “On the Blessing and Curse of the Creature”; and “On the Concept of the Good—or Positively Become—and of the Not-Good—or Negatively Become—Finite Spirit.”]

Dr. A. Günther, however, when he discusses the effects of Protestantism,[Note: Cf. *Vorschule zur spekulativen Theologie*, part II, *Incarnation Theory*, Preface, p. XII.] praises the ancient freedom of Catholics in speculative matters. Comparing it with the present timidity of the Church’s prelates, which entered together with Protestantism, he could, along with St. Augustine, bring forward the example of Erigena all the more aptly, since everything said to have been done against him by the Church during the first centuries after Erigena is so uncertain.

No less learned a writer on the history of philosophy, Rixner,[Note: *Handbook of the History of Philosophy*, vol. II, pp. 10–16. Cf. Appendix, pp. 3–10.] assesses Erigena, according to his merit, as a great and singular philosopher, distinguished by dialectical and mystical art and knowledge,[Col. 0111D] and at the end of the second volume of his history of philosophy added a fuller epitome of the works *On the Division of Nature* and *On Predestination*. [Col. 0112A] Yet we were greatly surprised that we found the learned Hegel, who so variously recalls the memory of Erigena in his own dialectical—if we may use the word—monism, to have known Erigena’s works only by hearsay or from disconnected excerpts. For it could not otherwise have happened that he treated him so cursorily and with such profound superficiality, as we really find him doing in his history of philosophy.[Note: *Lectures on the History of Philosophy*, vol. III, pp. 159–161.] Nevertheless, Hegel acknowledges that true philosophy began with Erigena; he calls him a follower of the Neoplatonists and of Dionysius the Areopagite. He says that his philosophy is profound and correct, but—not a claim one can scarcely imagine Hegel making—that it is unsupported by exegesis and the authority of the Fathers, indeed that it almost amounts to syncretism!

Among those more recent writers who not only, like Hegel, almost ignored Erigena or neglected him with disdain, but also, following the injustice of earlier times, thought they were acting piously while once again confirming and sharpening the deep-rooted prejudice against him,[Note: The ancients who judged the false opinions of J. Scotus with the greatest severity do not seem to have been led by prejudice; for he taught many things that do not accord with the truth. **Editor’s observation.**] we see some who, partly motivated by an understandable fear that Christian dogma and the opinion about our author traditionally handed down from antiquity might be harmed, set aside right and equity in judging Erigena’s merits. Others join them whose intellect, since they desire to treat Christianity in a purely historical manner, despises every speculative investigation and deeper explanation of dogma that has ever emerged. Finally, others, entangled in the prejudices of recent systems that are less favorable to the true freedom of Christian speculation[Col. 0112C] and confine it within excessively narrow limits, are extremely careful lest God be confused pantheistically with the creature in the manner of the pagans, but have no fear whatever of the abyss[Note: Cf. Hoffmann’s *Vestibule to the Speculative Doctrine of Franz Baader*, p. 67; “On the Relation of Theism to Christianity.”] that again gapes between the two—an abyss which, according to St. Paul (Ephesians 2:13 ff. and Colossians 1:19), our Savior closed in such a way that he “made both one.” Among such men seem to be numbered the writers of the literary history of the Franks, the Maurists, Thomas Moore, and Dr. C. F. Hock—men deserving no small esteem both for their character and for their intellectual acumen and learning. Yet we shall not quarrel with them, because the matter in question, on account of the singular method they follow in investigating[Col. 0112D] and judging matters, could scarcely be settled here.

Now let us enter into combat with another opponent—not of Erigena himself, perhaps, but of his doctrine—who, thoroughly acquainted with mythology as well as history, and no less instructed in the depths of Christian speculation, perceiving it clearly and embracing it with love, was accustomed finally to judge it wholly without bias or anger and from direct examination; yet now, strangely, he is seen in the hostile ranks. We mean J. Görres, a professor teaching in Munich, a man distinguished for learning and intellectual acumen. We deliberately postponed his opinion of Erigena until the end of our citations, in order to oppose to his judgments concerning Erigena’s orthodoxy—since almost all the criticisms of the others come back to these—several arguments drawn especially from Erigena himself, and, with the reverence that is due, to provide both him and all who are able to judge this matter[Col. 0113B] with an occasion to reread Erigena’s writings. For although we are prepared to accept arguments-supported responses from all those who, even after reading Erigena’s entire work, maintain that his views are discordant with the Christian faith, we are nevertheless led by a good and firm hope that in this way a more favorable outcome than has hitherto been achieved will be prepared for the judgment to be passed upon Erigena.

J. Görres does indeed praise Erigena,[Note: Cf. *Christian Mysticism*, vol. I, p. 243.] who was the first to explain Genesis scientifically and who carried this explanation, with great intellectual acumen, astonishingly through every detail. He likewise approves his depth and boldness in attempting to advance beyond the boundaries of the Areopagitic system, by joining Plato’s dialectic with Aristotle’s logic.[Col. 0113C] But, he says, as Erigena unfolded the ideas and notions of Dionysius the Areopagite, he once again, by a kind of necessity, encountered the ancient danger of pantheism—a danger that had remained hidden in the writings of the Areopagite only because of their more universal and less explicit exposition, and that, since it could scarcely have been avoided at that time, emerged in our author with a certain integrity and innocence of mind.

This confusion of the creature with God already appears, he says, at the beginning of the book on the Eucharist—that is, on Predestination—where Erigena argues that true religion and true philosophy are one and the same thing. Görres then adduces Erigena’s familiar fourfold division of nature, in which J. Görres asserts that created and creating nature is the *Logos*, placed as the middle term between uncreated and creating nature (God) and created and non-creating nature (the creature).[Col. 0113D] Thus, he says, the triune God mingled with the creature, and Erigena was consequently compelled to declare the Son of the Father to be a creature. Because of this error, Erigena could not advance far beyond the system and boundary of the Areopagite. For he did not introduce the Trinity into the speculation on mystical matters, as the Areopagite had neglected to do. Rather, following the Areopagite’s footsteps and his book *On the Divine Names*, he treated, just as the Areopagite did, only the one essence of God, by almost the same method of contemplation, though more scholastically, being content so long as he asserted the divine unity.

Görres says that Erigena teaches creating nature to be created for this reason: because God, who is superessential and superqualitative, while proceeding, as it were, from *aonomasia* to *pantonomasia* through theophanies, becomes through this procession, insofar as he explains himself through ideas—whether these are called divine volitions (*θεῖα θελήματα*), predestinations (*προορίσματα*), or archetypes (*πρωτότυπα*)—in some manner all things in all things. Finally, he remarks that Erigena treats acutely and ingeniously the sevenfold return of created and non-creating nature to God, the passage of lower things into higher things, and the return of all things into God, who alone ultimately remains; but that here too he did not escape the error of pantheism.

If we now briefly examine what has just been said concerning the value to be assigned to Erigena’s judgments, insofar as they concern dogma and science, everything that Görres considers blameworthy and objectionable in him comes down to these three points:

1. Erigena attributed too much to human reason and, mixing the things of reason with divine utterances, did not sufficiently distinguish revelation[Pag. XVI] from philosophy. He declared that true philosophy is true religion, and that true religion is true philosophy. Tennemann also asserts this, but counts it among Erigena’s merits.[Note: *History of Philosophy*, vol. VIII, part I, p. 72; cf. p. 53.]

2. He professes pantheism:

   a. When he asserts that the *Logos*, God the Son proceeding from the Father, is a creature of the Father.

   b. When he teaches that all creatures, in the universal restoration of all things, are absorbed by God—that is, by the one substance.[Col. 0114C]

3. He did not advance beyond the boundaries of the Areopagitic system and its superessential divine unity, which surpasses all things, and he omitted to introduce the dogmatic notion of the Holy Trinity into mystical and speculative theology.

To these three points which Görres notes in criticism of Erigena, a fourth must be added, which many have brought against him:

4. He did not recognize the nature and gravity of moral Evil; indeed, he taught that in the universal restoration of all things the infernal punishments would come to an end.

### On the first point

We answer that the proposition, “True philosophy is true religion, and, conversely, true religion is true philosophy,” can be understood in two different senses. In the mouth of our author it is no more suspicious than the teaching of nearly all the holy Fathers: namely, that Christ’s revelation is the highest wisdom and contains all philosophy. From this it follows, conversely, that true philosophy is also the same as true religion and does not imply a truth different from or separate from it.

That Erigena did not despise either Sacred Scripture or the testimonies of the Fathers is proved by so many passages in the books *On the Division* that it would be ridiculous to establish this more fully by citing them individually. Let us offer only two passages. One testifies to the humility that our author always maintained in investigating divine matters, however great his freedom and boldness when he examined those same matters through reason illuminated by divine grace; the other shows that although he trusted himself, with the aid of reason, to understand Scripture, penetrate, extract, and explain its hidden meaning, he nevertheless believed that he was never permitted to raise himself higher or speak about divine matters beyond the light of the Holy Scriptures and without their assistance.

In the second book *On the Division* he says: “For what good is that speed which the pure contemplation of truth eludes, or what harm is there in that very slowness to which the desired face presents itself?”—and in the same place, p. 130 (II, 23).

(Pag. XVII.) The other passage is in book I, p. 69 (I, 66).[Col. 0115B]

“For indeed, concerning God, nothing should be said or thought by those who live chastely and piously and diligently seek the truth except what is found in Holy Scripture; nor should anything other than his own significations be used by those who either believe or argue about God. For who would dare claim to have discovered anything about the ineffable nature by himself, beyond what that nature itself has uttered concerning itself in its holy instruments—I mean its theological instruments?”

Cf. also book II, p. 105 (II, 15), and book IV, pp. 393–394 (IV, 17).

A completely more careful reading of Erigena will undoubtedly convince every reader of sound and just judgment that Erigena never even dreamed of that autonomous and, so to speak, solipsistic reason posited by more recent philosophers. Indeed, unless the ray of truth from the divine Word and the testimonies of the holy Fathers, aided at the same time by the ray of an inner light, touched him,[Note: Cf. Ackermann, *The Christian Element in Plato*, p. 213.] he knew no use of reason and no activity of the mind deprived of grace that would not necessarily lack power, resources, substance, and a successful outcome. Nowhere, not even in passing, did he utter a proposition savoring of that rationalism.

That definition of philosophy in Erigena nevertheless became suspect because it seemed capable of signifying the insane idea that this or that merely philosophical system, constructed by human art according to one’s pleasure, is true and the one religion, rather than that the true religion, received by faith, understood, and manifested in works, is true philosophy.[Note: Cf. book II: “For there is no other salvation of faithful souls than to believe what is truly proclaimed concerning the one principle of all things and to understand what is truly believed.” And book I: “Looking only so far as the ray of the divine utterances extends.”]

For the rest, Erigena clearly distinguishes the boundaries of theology from those of philosophy, considering both their objects and the powers and faculties of the mind by which they are prepared and conceived. To theology he assigns the contemplation of the Holy Trinity, the primordial causes, and eternal things; to philosophy, the perception and investigation of things made and appearing through places and times. He calls the former wisdom, administered chiefly through the intellect—that is, the mind—and the latter knowledge, administered chiefly through reason, or the soul.[Col. 0116A] He calls the former theology and the latter, in the narrower sense, philosophy, or physics, although he declares that Scripture and the grace of the divine Word are altogether necessary for the fruitful success of both. Cf. book III, p. 187 (III, 3).

(Pag. XVIII.) ### On the second point, a

Although in the books *On the Division* there are some passages in which the archetypal world eternally established in God the Logos—the notion now commonly called the idea of creation—seems to be confused with, or insufficiently distinguished from, the second person of the Holy Trinity, many other passages are found that definitively and precisely distinguish from the eternally begotten Word the world created in that same Word and made, as he himself says, through that Word, and perfected by the Holy Spirit,[Col. 0116B] as an eternally established nature—that is, a created nature—even though, when joined with the divine Logos and opposed to created and non-creating nature, which we usually call the real world, or the universe, the same nature is called both created and creating.

Moreover, in his various expositions of the Holy Trinity, Erigena distinguishes the individual persons, or *hypostases* (*ὑποστάσεις*), with the utmost strictness and in accordance with dogma; consequently, he also says that the *Logos* is eternally begotten, neither eternally proceeding nor eternally created.

Apart from those passages in which the begotten God is distinguished from the generating and proceeding God no less than from the creature, let us cite many of the passages in which that distinction between the Logos and created and creating nature, and still more clearly between the Logos and created and non-creating nature—that is, the creature properly so called—seems to us to shine forth most clearly:[Note: Cf. book II: “Every creature begins to be, because it was when it was not; it was in its causes, but it was not in its effects. Therefore it is not altogether coeternal with eternity in the true sense.”]

Book III, p. 228 ff. (III, 16):

“Let us therefore believe and, insofar as is granted, behold with the mind’s eye that all visible and invisible things, and whatever the whole universe of creation contains, were at once eternal and made in the only-begotten Word of God; and that neither eternity preceded their making nor their making preceded eternity. For their eternity was made, and their eternal establishment lies in the dispensation of the Word.”

Book III, p. 232 (III, 17):

“The unshaken authority of divine Scripture therefore compels us to believe that the universe of the whole creation was established in the Word of God, but that the reason for that establishment surpasses every intellect and is known only to the Word in whom it was established.”[Col. 0116D]

Book III, p. 239 (III, 18):

“For Holy Scripture says: ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth’; that is, God the Father established the universality of the whole visible and invisible creation in God the Son. And what could the Father establish in his beginning, in his Word, in his only-begotten Son, that the Son himself was not? Otherwise he would not have established it in him.” (Pag. XIX)[Col. 0117A]

[Note: Cf. book II, p. 122 (II, 22), “For what purpose” etc., and p. 124 (II, 22), “Therefore all things” etc.]

If, in other passages of the cited book III, p. 245 ff. (III, 18), Erigena, agreeing with the sense there recalled, follows the words of St. Basil, who says (*Homily 8 on Genesis*), “The divine Word is the nature of the things that have been made,” and asserts, “God is created in all things,” or “God is in himself, and comes to be in creatures,” then, like J. Tauler, S. Suso, and many other Fathers after him, he is merely following the ancient and very widespread reading of St. John the Theologian—that is, the Evangelist—chapter 1, verses 3–4: “Whatever was made, in him was life, and the life was the light of men.”

Similarly, Suso, p. 164:

“All creatures, in respect of their outflowing that remains within, are eternally in the One, in a God-living, God-knowing, God-essential beingness, as the Gospel says at the beginning: ‘What was made, in him eternally was life.’”[Note: *The Life and Writings of Heinrich Suso, Called Amandus*, by Melchior Diepenbrock, 2nd ed., Regensburg, 1837.]

[Note: This may be rendered in Latin as follows: “All creatures, since they have flowed forth and yet remain within, are eternal in the One, living in God, knowing God, as though deified, as it is read in the Gospel: ‘What was made, in him was life.’” **Editor’s observation.**]

It would surely be unjust to accuse either Suso or Erigena of pantheism on account of such words and similar expressions! Does not a painter who paints the image of a king in colors reply, when asked what he is doing, “The king is coming to be”? So too St. Augustine:

“Let God grow, then—he who is always perfect—grow in you. For the more you understand God, and the more you grasp him, the more God seems to grow in you. Yet he himself does not grow, but is always perfect. Yesterday you understood little; today you understand more; tomorrow you will understand much more. The light of God itself grows in you, so that God seems to grow, although he always remains perfect. It is as though someone’s eyes were healed from their former blindness and he began to see a little light, then saw more the next day and still more on the third day: the light seems to grow for him, yet the light is perfect, whether he sees or does not see. So too is the inner man: he progresses in God, and God seems to grow in him; yet he himself diminishes, so that he may fall away from his own glory and rise into the glory of God.”[Col. 0117C]

[Note: Cf. Gügler, *The Sacred Art of the Hebrews*, vol. I, p. 36. Also *On the Division*, book IV, p. 332 (IV, 7), “Hence St. Augustine” etc., where St. Augustine teaches in wondrous words precisely what Erigena teaches. Also p. 341 (IV, 9), “Therefore concerning the intellect” etc.; book V, p. 475 (V, 24), “For what is wisdom” etc.]

A. Günther likewise writes in his book *Thomas a Scrupulis*, p. 223:

“And what else could this love be than that love by which God also loves himself in the creature, because in it he finds his eternal thought again, encountering in it, as it were, a moment of his own life?”[Note: This may be rendered in Latin as follows: “And what other love can this be than that by which God loves himself, and in creatures, in which he finds his eternal idea, encounters, as it were, a moment of his own life?” **Editor’s observation.**]

Let us therefore also be indulgent toward Erigena when he says: “God is in himself; he comes to be in creatures,” since, because of Paul’s statement, “who is through all things and in all things,” he never neglected the Apostle’s other statement, “who is above all things.”[Note: Cf. book IV, p. 320 (IV, 5), “I wonder why” etc.]

Finally, beware of supposing that Erigena’s so-called quaternary division of nature, as a formal division, is in any way identical with the holy Trinity of dogma, which he teaches and confirms in explicit words. Erigena’s own explanation of the fourth and the first nature—that is, of uncreated and non-creating nature, and of uncreated and creating nature—says that both are one and the same nature,[Note: Cf. book III, p. 248 (III, 23), “But what is theological” etc.] named thus according to the different perspectives of the procession and return of things.[Col. 0118B] This sufficiently demonstrates that the division is to be understood, in part, as merely subjective and formal. Once Erigena’s doctrine of the Trinity has been explained, this will appear even more clearly.

### On the second point, b

In a similar way, we do not deny that certain other passages in the work *On the Division*, where the universal restoration of things at Christ’s second coming and the Last Judgment are discussed, may seem to savor of pantheism to someone who pays insufficient attention and considers the sequence of thoughts and force of the words too carelessly. Nevertheless, many more passages affirm the contrary, and almost the whole of the fifth book of the work will altogether convince any prudent reader that the doctrine of the absorption by God of all things at the consummation of the age—a doctrine according to which the creature would perish rather than be glorified and more fully saved—was entirely foreign to Erigena’s mind.[Col. 0118C]

For he expressly establishes not only several degrees of the righteous in eternal blessedness,[Note: Cf. book I, p. 8 (I, 8): “For each person, as we have said, will possess within himself knowledge of the only-begotten Word of God, insofar as grace will be granted to him. For as great as the number of the elect, so great will be the number of dwelling places; as great as the multiplication of holy souls, so great will be the possession of divine theophanies.” And book V, p. 586 (V, 38): “When there will be not only a general sabbath in all divine works, but also a special Sabbath of Sabbaths in the holy angels and holy human beings; and the house of God will be filled, in which each person will be established according to the order fitting to him: some lower, some higher, some in the sublimity of nature, others above every natural power, near God himself.” Also pp. 513 (V, 31), 474 (V, 24), and 550 (V, 36).]

who, foreseen and predestined in Jesus according to their merits, will thereafter see God without end, but he also teaches and describes that a fixed number of the elect, by singular grace, will attain deification above every natural power. Indeed, he expressly rejects and abhors that disastrous error according to which all created things perish in God and are confused with God, who alone remains.

If you wish to consider the many beautiful analogies Erigena uses to explain and clarify in some manner this deification (*θέωσις*) of the future age, you will immediately have no doubt about the matter. These analogies include, for example, iron glowing in fire, which, having become wholly fire, nevertheless does not cease to be iron; air illuminated, which, having become wholly solar light, nevertheless remains air; and stars, which disappear when the sun rises and yet do not cease to exist. Such comparisons can be found among nearly all reputable speculative theologians of the early centuries and the Middle Ages; they clearly signify not a confusion of God with the creature, but rather the penetration, indwelling, and mutual presence of both.[Note: Cf. book III, p. 243 (III, 20), “Then through” etc.]

Yet according to St. Paul, the human being who adheres to God becomes one spirit with God. Nor did any of the ancient theologians turn to reproach those who enthusiastically professed that God became man for this purpose: that humanity might be restored to the power by which it could become God, or be deified: “For we are his offspring”; cf. 1 Corinthians 6:17.

For the present, it will suffice to cite the passages in which our author expressly rejects a pantheistic union of God with the creature, by which the creature would be absorbed and perish:

Book III, p. 243 (III, 20). Cf. also the beginning of book V:

“Therefore the transformation of human nature into God is not to be understood as the destruction of substance, but as the marvelous and ineffable return to the original state which it had lost through transgression.”

Again:

“For true reason does not permit higher things either to be contained by lower things, drawn down by them, or consumed by them. Lower things, however, are naturally drawn and absorbed by higher things—not so that they cease to exist, but so that in them they may be more fully saved and subsist, and be one.”

And, as he also notes in book V:

“Not, as we have often said, through a confusion or destruction of essences or substances.”

Finally, also p. 559 (V, 37).

Gregory of Nyssa, in the same place:

“Entirely, at the time of the resurrection, according to the blessed transformation that will take place in the Holy Spirit, through the grace of the incarnate God, the flesh will be absorbed by the soul in the spirit, and the soul by God.”[Note: Cf. note f.]

(Pag. XXII.) Finally, if Erigena followed pantheism, he could not teach what he does teach:

[Col. 0119D] 1. That God is the superessential cause of all things,[Note: Cf. book III: “Yet no one among those who piously believe and understand the truth fails immediately and without hesitation to exclaim that the creative cause of the whole universe is supernatural and superessential, above all life, wisdom, and power, and above everything that is said, understood, and perceived by any sense, since it is the causal principle of all these things, their essential middle that fills them, and their consummating end, stabilizing and bringing every movement to rest, and, as their encompassing boundary, circumscribing all things that are and are not.””] and that neither the category of essence, or *οὐσία*, nor any of the other nine categories can apply to God.[Note: See books I and II: “For God is not a genus of the creature” etc.]

[Col. 0120A] 2. That the human will is free to choose either good or evil, and that the human race, having transgressed in Adam and become subject to death, was saved in Christ and through Christ and restored to eternal life.[Note: Cf. book V, p. 521 (V, 34), “For it seems” etc.; and p. 516 (V, 31), “Although” etc. … “the fourth” etc.; and book IV, p. 370 (IV, 14), “For he foreknows many things of which he is not the cause” etc.; and book V, pp. 535, 540, 542 (V, 36).]

3. That Lucifer’s pride—he desired to be God by his own power—was a detestable crime. Cf. book V.

4. That God causes many things to occur outside the ordinary order of nature, thereby showing that he alone is Lord and that there is no other—and consequently that miracles can occur. “It must not,” he says, “be investigated by any conjectures of the mind why natural things, once established from invisible causes in the power of seeds, should proceed into sensible forms not all at once but at intervals of time and place, as though they could not happen otherwise if the divine will, which is bound by no law, judged that they should happen otherwise. For many things often occur contrary to the customary course of nature, so that it may be shown to us that divine providence can administer all things not in one way only, but in many ways and in an infinite manner.” Cf. book III, p. 229 (III, 16).

5. He could not have maintained and correctly explained in every passage the classically dogmatic notion of the Holy Trinity. But, in order to expound this matter more fully, we now undertake at the same time to refute the third objection noted above.

### On the third point

Erigena certainly introduced the Holy Trinity into speculative theology and explained it, according to the Athanasian Creed and the notion received by the universal Church,[Col. 0120C] through sixfold analogy. For the most part he presents and interprets these likenesses in the words of the dogma itself, in the same way that St. Bonaventure, St. Bernard (Pag. XXIII), and, even before them and Erigena, St. Augustine employed the analogy drawn from the memory, intellect, and will of the human soul—which is one and simple in itself, and so forth—for the same purpose.

Erigena indeed offers:

1. An analogy drawn from the common nature of all created things, whether they are rational or irrational. For all agree in this, that in them the following are one: Essence, Power, and Operation (*οὐσία, δύναμις, ἐνέργεια*). The first, without the intervention of time, begets the second, as it were; the third proceeds from the first through the second and manifests the whole.[Note: Cf. book I, “Therefore God” etc.; and in the same place, “But without essence”; book II, p. 126 (II, 23), “Nothing to me” etc.]

2. The second analogy, which is also found among some Fathers before Erigena, is: Being, willing, knowing. Erigena reduces these to the preceding analogy;[Col. 0121A] for he shows that willing pertains to the Power, while knowing pertains to the Operation of rational creation.[Note: Cf. book V, p. 509 (V, 31), “Not otherwise” etc., where passages from Augustine and Dionysius are cited.]

3. The third analogy is taken from irrational creation, namely from solar light: the Sun, the Sun’s Ray, and the Splendor proceeding from both.

4. The fourth concerns rational creation alone and is manifested in the human soul and its movements or faculties: Intellect or Mind, Reason, and Inner Sense (*νοῦς, λόγος, διάνοια*).[Note: Cf. book II, p. 127 (II, 23), and in the same place: “… for the likeness of the Father in the mind, of the Son in reason, and of the Holy Spirit in sense shines forth most clearly.”]

5. The fifth likewise shines forth from the image of the divine mind: Mind, Knowledge, Discipline.

6. Likewise: Mind, Knowledge of itself, Love of itself in the human soul. When this soul turns toward the light that illuminates all things, it becomes the most perfect image of the Holy Trinity.[Note: Cf. book II, p. 161 (II, 31), where Augustine is also cited. Also book II, p. 113 (II, 19), and the second book as a whole.]

## IV. On the Theory of Evil, Which Is Certainly Not Altogether Sufficient

Only a few observations need to be made here concerning the theory of evil followed by Erigena [Col. 0121B]. Since our author, distinguished alike for piety and cheerfulness, is almost like Adam before his transgression, seeing God in everything and everything in God, and striving continually to know him, his speculation is chiefly occupied with describing good things—namely, the gifts and divine endowments through which God glorifies himself in the work of creation, redemption, and the future consummation, and blesses the creature—with [Pag. XXIV] the sublime joy of intellectual admiration and love [Note: [Col. 0121D] Cf. Book V, p. 538 (V, 36): “O quantum,” etc.]. For this reason nothing was more alien to him than that gloomy Dualism and obscure severity of the Manichaeans.

Yet who will deny that, in depicting the universe of things, whiteness and blackness can, without any diminution of truth [Col. 0121C], be composed and mixed in various and differing ways, and that one may prevail over the other according as, in the philosopher, fear and law, or love—which is the fulfilment of the law and the perfection of wisdom—occupies the more prominent place; according as the pain of sin and sorrow for the crime committed by a human being, or the joy of redemption and the blessed consciousness of the glorious and adorable work accomplished by God made man, outweighs the other in his mind?

But the question is whether Erigena, following Saint Augustine, was mistaken concerning the origin of evil when he placed it neither in God nor in any principal cause of evil existing from eternity, nor in the creature as God’s work, nor consequently in the will of man or angel insofar as it was divinely given [Col. 0122A], but solely in the unlawful movement of that will and its abuse [Note: [Col. 0121D] Cf. Book IV: “And because no evil is found substantially in the nature of things, nor proceeds from any definite and natural cause—for, considered in itself, it is altogether nothing except an irrational, perverse, and imperfect movement of rational nature—it finds no other seat in the whole creation except where falsity possesses it; the proper possession of falsity, however, is bodily sense.” And further in the same place: “Whose womanly sense, to which the mind (Adam’s νοῦς) unwisely consenting, is lost,” etc.; and Book V, p. 544 [Col. 0122C] (V, 36). Cf. also Ackermann, *Christliches im [Col. 0122D] Plato* [“The Christian Element in Plato”], p. 187.]. Did he therefore deny the abomination and shamefulness of evil, and neglect and despise the holy laws and institutions of God enacted and ordered against it?

Yet if one gathers his statements on this subject briefly and in summary, one finds that his view agrees almost entirely with the teaching of Dionysius the Areopagite and Saint Augustine. In this sphere, then, into which man fell by transgression—having been driven, as Augustine says, from good things not to evils, but to lesser goods mixed with good and evil—Erigena believed that the very vices which, although not willed by God, nevertheless deform human nature by his permission, should in some manner be turned to the praise not of man, but of the Creator [Col. 0122B] [Note: [Col. 0122D] Cf. Book V, p. 533 (V, 35): “And this is evil,” etc.; and in the same place, p. 522 (V, 35): “For one thing,” etc.].

For he maintains that no vice exists which is not the shadow of some virtue—for example, “anger of correction, lust of repose,” etc.—or in [Pag. XXV] comparison with which the virtue opposed to it, whose defect and privation it is, does not acquire greater praise and become more highly exalted [Note: [Col. 0122D] Cf. Book V, p. 521 (V, 35): “For it seems,” etc.; and p. 552 (V, 36), and elsewhere.]. Thus he also does not deny that the beautiful phantasy of evil, colored under the appearance of good, is created by God and therefore good [Note: [Col. 0122D] Cf. Book V, p. 540 (V, 36): “For most clearly,” etc.]; but he does deny that the falsehood and evil concealed beneath that appearance, and covered by it as by an abyss, are good.

Furthermore, he affirms that at the consummation of the age, when all things will return into God and God will be all in all, all wickedness will perish [Note: [Col. 0122D] Cf. Book V, p. 516 (V, 31): “For one thing,” etc.]. Nor, he says, does the universe sin against God—that is, this whole world, considered under the aspect of eternity and through its causes [Col. 0122C] [Note: [Col. 0122D] Cf. Book V, p. 538 (V, 36), and Ackermann, p. 320; nevertheless cf. also pp. 231 and 302.]—but it is exceedingly good before God [Note: [Col. 0122D] Cf. Book V, p. 521 (V, 35): “For it seems,” etc., and ibid. p. 522 (V, 35): “For one thing,” etc.], even after the transgression of man redeemed by the grace of Christ.

All these statements, rightly understood, contain a sound and honorable meaning. Indeed, in Dionysius the Areopagite and Saint Augustine one can find many passages of the kind that might, with equal or even greater justice, give rise to suspicion. For example, the former insists that “evil is altogether nothing” [Note: [Col. 0122D] Cf. *Die angebl. Schriften des Areopagiten Dionys, von Engelhardt* [“The Alleged Writings of Dionysius the Areopagite, by Engelhardt”], vol. I, p. 97; and *Christliches in der Plat. Philosophie* [“The Christian Element in Platonic Philosophy”] by Ackermann, pp. 51, 183, and 187.], in order to signify its absolute impotence and vanity; the latter calls the devil himself, who “from the beginning was a murderer and both spoke and committed falsehood,” good insofar as he exists, or participates in being. Again, when he compares evil contending with good in the history of the world to the rhetorical antitheses by which speech is made more vigorous; when he observes that through the wicked a greater victory is prepared for those who pursue truth and virtue [Note: [Col. 0123D] Cf. Book V, p. 521 (V, 35): “For it seems,” etc., together with the remarkable words of Augustine himself quoted there, and p. 523 (V, 31): “For what,” etc.]; and finally, when, with Leibniz, he treats a large part of what is called evil as nothing other than something less good and less perfect, lacking only a greater degree of reality.

Erigena scarcely says anything different when he maintains that God punishes no nature, nor anything in any creature that he himself has made, but only that causeless nothing which God did not make, although he foresaw it; indeed, that this very evil punishes itself according to the eternal laws implanted by God in rational creation, through the irrational and unnatural movement of a [Pag. XXVI] perverse will, since it is continually frustrated and yet does not cease from willing evil [Note: [Col. 0123D] Cf. Book V, p. 513 (V, 31): “But for the impious,” etc., and p. 531 (V, 31): “For we have considered,” etc.].

Erigena treats at considerable length both pride, which he calls the head of all wickedness and especially detests in Lucifer, and the false and lustful movement of the will and the desire for carnal intercourse that existed in Adam, and the serpent-like concupiscence which entices and deceives Eve—that is, sense (αἴσθησις)—and then through her Adam—that is, intellect (νοῦς) [Note: [Col. 0123D] Cf. column 129, note e, and elsewhere.]. He calls pride and lust the greatest folly, and in no way approves the words with which the first parents attempted to excuse themselves before the judge after transgressing the divine command.

From original sin he derives not only profound ignorance of divine things, evil desire of the mind, death, and the other evils, but also the material body of man, which he thinks is signified by the coats of skins that God made for the first parents [Col. 0123C]. He even derives from it the sexual distinction and division of male and female, together with the propagation of the human race in its present animal and humanly unworthy form. This, he says, will cease in the future age, when, at the universal return of things, all matter will burn like hay in the flame and this entire world will be destroyed.

Finally, concerning the punishments of the damned: although expressions such as “eternal punishments, eternal penalties, eternal condemnation, unquenchable flame, the irrevocable judgment of God” are frequently found in Erigena [Note: [Col. 0124D] Cf. Book V, p. 505; ibid. pp. 510, 552, 553, and 558 (V, 30, 36, 37).], and others of the same kind, nevertheless in many other passages he appears to advance the contrary opinion, which abolishes the eternity of punishments.

For he says that no one is deprived by God of natural or innate goods [Note: [Col. 0124D] Cf. Book V, p. 510; ibid. pp. 533 and 534 (V, 31, 36)], and that the damned, at the time of the resurrection and universal restoration, when all wickedness has perished, will not deform the renewed world by any shadow or discordant harmony. Rather, through a certain theophany—although one very different from the beatific vision of the righteous—they will see God, who will then appear as all in all [Col. 0124A]. They will not, however, eternally participate in the glory, grace of deification, or blessedness of the elect righteous.

Moreover, in other passages he affirms that after death they are punished by the empty phantasies of things for which, even in this life [Pag. XXVII], they were restlessly and insatiably driven by longing, and by a Tantalus-like desire [Note: [Col. 0124D] Cf. Book V, pp. 503, 512, 513, 516, and 517 (V, 29, 31, 32).].

Finally, it should be observed that in the ninth century the Christian doctrine concerning the punishments of the damned had not yet been defined and established by the Church with the same precision as it was later, in the thirteenth century, through the Fourth Lateran Council. This is perfectly clear from Erigena’s own words [Note: [Col. 0124D] Cf. Book V, p. 490; ibid. p. 508 (V, 27, 31).]. Indeed, in addition to Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory Nazianzen, Basil, and even Ambrose and Jerome frequently taught the universal restoration (apokatastasis) of things, establishing along with it the end of eternal punishments [Col. 0124B].

After we have recalled these matters concerning Erigena’s life, character, and writings, and have likewise brought forward the testimonies concerning him delivered by the most distinguished men of former times and, still more, of the present age, while also reviewing the most serious accusations repeatedly made against his doctrines, we now present to the benevolent reader this exceedingly rare work, which we have taken pains to cleanse, insofar as we were able, of the typographical errors of the first and hitherto only published copy [Note: [Col. 0123D] Thomas Gale in fact used three manuscripts in preparing the first edition: the mutilated manuscript of Thuane, his own complete manuscript, and a Parisian manuscript, as he himself testifies in the testimonies reproduced above. EDITOR’S NOTE.], chiefly in order to provide an occasion for a new and more careful investigation into the merits of this distinguished man, who for so long has been burdened by an evil reputation.

Compare, therefore, benevolent reader, Erigena’s system of the division of Nature with Spinoza’s ethics [Col. 0124C] and with the other pantheistic systems of the moderns. You will notice, as we believe, that so many great and excellent minds could be led astray by what was merely the appearance of a certain true and genuine divine wisdom. This certainly would not have happened if Erigena’s and the others’ systems—marked by far greater profundity, abundance, and intellectual penetration, and at the same time more consonant with Christian dogma—had not, through the hostility of the times, remained hidden from so many of their contemporaries. Otherwise Erigena would surely have surpassed and overshadowed them by the splendor of his intellect.

We nevertheless hope that the philosophy of our age, especially that which is most speculative and possesses dialectical power, may be led by Erigena’s doctrines to a happier conclusion. For this philosophy, after abandoning every sensible form and every true and sincere imagination, nature, history, and positive dogma, and devoting itself solely to the universal notion of abstract and autonomous (αὐτόνομος) reason, desires to do and devise everything, to accept nothing and understand nothing by faith, to abolish everything and establish nothing, and is already on the point of falling into absolute nihilism [Col. 0124D]. Erigena favors the universal notion and dialectical art, yet he does not altogether abandon or deny history, the dogma of faith, or visible form, nor does he [Pag. XXVIII] despise them [Col. 0125A].

We do not, however, deny that Hegel’s speculation, especially when compared with critical philosophy and subjective idealism, has deserved well of Christian philosophy and theology, and that it has in some measure certainly opened a way toward the easier understanding of Erigena’s writings.

Finally, all who devote appropriate attention to the reading of our author will gladly recall those ages when it was more readily available, and almost natural, for human beings both to believe in faith and to investigate by reason the connections and causes of things, and to reconcile one with the other. For although that age was harsh and violent in the extreme, its people nevertheless often knew how to unite a certain divine sublimity with the deepest humility, poverty of mind with the richest abundance of eternal truths, and life and great works with lofty and profound thought [Col. 0125B].

For this reason they were able to express in life as well as in writing, more readily, the union of philosophy and poetry with religion demanded by the true and eternal idea—a union which some moderns have begun once more to long for as though in a kind of prophetic dream [Col. 0126A]. Let the image of this great intellect therefore be placed beside the portraits of Dante, Bonaventure, J. Boehme, and a few others who, for a time unjustly oppressed by the hostility of the ages, obscured by neglect, and almost unknown, now at last enjoy the favor and respect befitting them among the most eminent Christian philosophers and poets.

And you, all who still sigh for the divine and eternal and pursue and love that wisdom which by its light illuminates all who are truly wise, whether small or great: may this monument of Erigena be for you a source of profound and peace-giving delight, instruction, and strong confirmation in holy faith and piety [Col. 0126B]. Come and taste how gracious the Lord is!

Münster in Westphalia, 4 January 1838.

C. B. SCHLUETER,  
Private lecturer in philosophy at the Royal Prussian Academy at Münster in Westphalia.

[Col. 0125]

# JOHN SCOTUS’S EXPOSITIONS ON THE CELESTIAL HIERARCHY OF SAINT DIONYSIUS

Vatican Codex 652, eleventh century | A |

Münster Codex, Latin manuscript 380, twelfth century | B |

A second hand in the same codex | B* |

A third hand in the same codex | B** |

Bruges Codex no. 1, fourteenth or fifteenth century | C |

# THE EXPOSITIONS OF JOHN SCOTUS ON THE HIERARCHIES OF SAINT DIONYSIUS BEGIN

[Note: [Col. 0125] A has “dyonisii,” and so everywhere. B* has “dionisii,” and so everywhere.]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0125C]

The first book of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite [Note: [Col. 0125] A, B, and C read “ariopagitae.”], entitled *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, is composed in a sequence of fifteen chapters. The title of the first is:

“Because every divine illumination, proceeding variously according to goodness into the things foreseen”—that is, because every illumination of divine goodness, which proceeds in manifold ways to bring about the things foreseen, remains simple in itself [Note: [Col. 0127] So A and B.]. While it is universally diffused into the things that exist [Note: [Col. 0127] B: “universally into the things that exist.”], so that they may exist—for there is no other subsistence of all sensible and intelligible things than the illumination and diffusion of divine goodness—it does not cease to be simple and inexhaustible in itself.

For it is an unfailing fountain, flowing forth into all things that exist with infinite multiplicity. It not only flows and proceeds into all things so that they may subsist, but also joins together all things that subsist from it, in it, and through it into one ineffable harmony [Note: [Col. 0127] A and B read “armonia,” and so everywhere], so that in the universe there is multiplicity [Col. 0127B] through infinite multiplication, while in it all things are one through incomprehensible union.

This is what he means when he says: “It remains simple, and not only this, but unifies the illuminated”—that is, those brought into being through its illumination and procession. The entire title of the first chapter is therefore:

“Because every divine illumination, proceeding variously according to goodness into the things foreseen, remains simple, and not only this, but unifies the illuminated.”

### § 1

The chapter itself begins with a saying of the apostle James: “Every good gift”—or, to translate the words more literally and exactly, “Every best giving and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.”

This apostolic saying distinguishes divine giving from divine donation by a remarkable difference. It assigns the best giving to the constitution of universal creation, and perfect donation to the generosity of divine grace, because everything that exists participates in divine goodness in two ways: the first is seen in the constitution of nature, the second in the distribution of grace. Nothing in universal creation lacks these two things. Everything that exists subsists and participates in divine grace according to the analogy appropriate to it.

It should be noted that the statement does not simply say: “Every best giving and every perfect gift.” For, primordially, in all things that exist, a natural gift already constituted precedes; afterward the increase of perfect donation is distributed to it [Note: [Col. 0127] B reads “the gift given.”] [Note: [Col. 0127] B reads “subsistently”; B* corrected this to “to the constituted gift.”].

And so that you may recognize the clearest distinction between giving and donation, observe what he says: “Every best giving”—that is, every constitution of a creature is very good, just as it is written: “And God saw, and behold, everything was very good.” But because no constitution is perfect unless it turns toward the Creator, he adds: “and every perfect gift.”

Thus the best constitution of nature comes first, and the turning toward the Creator is added to it for perfection. Do not be surprised, then, that we have said that no constituted creature can become perfect unless it turns toward the Creator. For true reason teaches that all things which exist must look toward their cause, from which, through which, and in which they subsist, in order to be perfected.

Intellectual and rational things turn immediately and directly toward the one principle of the universe; things lacking intellect and reason turn toward it through a certain intervening mediation of rational and intelligible things. Every best giving and every perfect donation, therefore, is from above—that is, it descends from above. From whom, if not from the ineffable fountain of all good things, the Father of lights?

Whatever, whether through bodily sense serving as an intermediary or through pure intellect investigating, is clearly perceived and known in the universe, in the constitutions of nature and the perfections of grace, proceeds from nowhere else than the Father of lights.

The Father of lights is the heavenly Father, the first and innermost light. From him is born the true light, his Word, through whom all things were made [Note: [Col. 0127] B omits “and”], and in whom all things were constituted: his only-begotten Son. From him—I mean the Father—there proceeds a light coessential with himself and with his Word: the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, in whom and through whom the gifts of grace are distributed to all things.

This, then, is the triune light and the triune goodness: three substances in one essence, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; one God, one goodness, one light diffused into all things that exist, so that they may subsist essentially; shining in all things that exist, so that all may be turned toward the love and contemplation of its beauty [Note: [Col. 0127] A and B read “pulcritudinis,” and so everywhere]; surpassing all things that exist, so that all may enjoy the fullness of their perfection; and making all things one in itself. From the Father of lights, therefore, all lights descend.

But perhaps someone will say: How are all things that exist lights? Although the entire universe of things was founded by the Father through the Son and the Holy Spirit—for the Father wills, the Son makes, and the Holy Spirit cooperates—it should properly and specially be said of the intellectual and rational lights that they were created by the Father of lights through the begotten light and through the proceeding light. The rest, however, should be believed to be illuminated rather than to be lights.

But we can easily answer this by sound reasoning. First, it must be said that, if the Father of lights is light in himself—for he would not be the Father of lights if light did not subsist in him—then he made all things in his wisdom, which itself is also light [Note: [Col. 0127] B omits “is”], since it is coessential with the Father of lights. Is it not therefore necessary to think that all things which the Father, who is light, created in his wisdom, the light coessential with him, should be believed and understood as created lights [Note: [Col. 0127] B omits “as”]?

The Father, moreover, is the Father of his wisdom. Therefore he must himself be the Father of all that he made in his wisdom—namely, their Father. The Lord himself also clearly confirms this when he says: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth.”

There is another argument as well, which clearly teaches that the entire visible and invisible creation is light created by the Father of lights. If the supreme goodness, which is God, made everything that he willed for this reason: because he is himself invisible and inaccessible light, surpassing every sense and intellect, and wished through the things made by him to descend, as through certain little lights, into the knowledge of intellectual and rational creation—as the Apostle also teaches when he says, “His invisible things are perceived by the creature of the world through the things that have been made”—what wonder is it if everything that introduces inaccessible light in some way into pure intellects so that it may become accessible, illuminating minds and recalling them to the knowledge of their Creator, is understood as light without any obstacle to reason?

Let us take an example from the innermost orders of nature. This stone or this piece of wood is a light for me; and if you ask how, reason urges me to answer you as follows. When I consider this stone or that one, many things occur to me which illuminate my mind. I observe that it subsists as something good and beautiful according to its proper analogy; that it is separated from the other genera and species of things by difference of genus and species; that it is contained within its own number, by which it becomes one thing [Note: [Col. 0129] B reads “by which it is”]; that it does not exceed its own order; and that it seeks its proper place according to the quality of its weight.

As I observe these and similar features in this stone, they become lights for me—that is, they illuminate me. I begin to consider whence such properties belong to it, and I perceive that these properties are not naturally present in it through the participation of any creature, visible or invisible. Then, guided by reason, I am led above all things into the cause of all, from which are distributed to all things their place and order, number and form, genus, goodness and beauty [Note: [Col. 0129] B omits “from which ... beauty”], essence, and all the other gifts and endowments.

Similarly, every creature, from the highest to the lowest—from the intellectual being down to the body—is an illuminating light to those who refer it and themselves to the praise of the Creator, diligently seek him, burn to find him in all things that exist, and strive to praise him above all things. Considered according to its own principles and made clear by the mind’s lucid gaze, it is plainly luminous [Col. 0129D].

Hence the structure of this whole world becomes a great light, composed as it were of many parts and many lamps, so that the pure forms of intelligible things may be revealed and contemplated by the mind’s vision, while divine grace and the power of reason cooperate in the hearts of faithful and wise people.

[Col. 0130A] The theologian therefore beautifully calls God the Father of lights, because from him are all things in which and through which he manifests himself to all, unifies them, and makes them conformable to the light of his wisdom.

Blessed Dionysius, bishop of Athens, wishing to write about the celestial hierarchy—that is, the heavenly episcopate of the supermundane powers, in which, after the primordial causes, the Father of lights chiefly and principally multiplies his best gifts and perfect donations to infinity, recalls them into unity in himself—began with the following theory, which he subsequently explains:

“But also every procession of the manifestation of the lights, moved by the Father, coming to us most excellently and abundantly, again fills us as a unifying power and turns us toward the unity and deifying simplicity of the gathering Father” [Note: [Col. 0129] “of the Father” is omitted by A and B; B* added it in the margin].

Since blessed James seemed to have spoken only of the procession and multiplication of divine lights through the gifts of nature and the gifts of grace, while remaining silent concerning their union and restoration to their source, Dionysius rightly adds this statement.

It is as though he were saying: Not only are the divine gifts and endowments—which, after the angelic substances, are especially bestowed upon human minds still weighed down by mortal flesh—from above and descending from the Father of lights; the entire procession of divine illumination, which through an ineffable paternal movement comes to us most abundantly and in manifold ways, also fittingly fills us with its grace, since it is a power that unifies and restores us, and turns us toward the Father himself. He gathers to himself what proceeds from him, unifies in himself what is diverse, deifies what is conformed to him, and makes simple what has been multiplied as though into infinite multiplicity [Col. 0130C] [Note: [Col. 0129] A and C read “simplifies.”].

It is not improperly asked, however, why the Greeks call him πατροκίνητος—that is, “moved by the Father” or “father-moved.” How the immutable is moved, by what it is moved, and toward what and for what purpose it is moved, is profitably investigated by the wise.

He moves himself, then, not locally or temporally, but superessentially; he is moved above places and times by himself. No cause precedes which might move him, since he himself is the first and only cause of all movements. He is movement and rest, stable movement and mobile rest.

By what argument, I ask, do you prove that the immovable Father is moved? I argue from the name. If you ask what that name is, listen. In both languages, Greek and Latin, he is called “Father.” In Greek the word is composed as πατήρ, that is, πάντα τηρῶν [Note: [Col. 0129] B* adds in the margin: “patir, that is, pantateron”], meaning “preserving all things.” Does it not seem right that he who preserves and saves all things which he made in his only-begotten Son should move in order to guard all things?

Hear also this: he is called Father and God—that is, Θεός [Note: [Col. 0129] B* adds in the margin: “theos”]—“running,” a name derived from the verb θέω [Note: [Col. 0129] So C and B*; B* has *theo* in place of θέω; A and B read: “the name θέω [B: deo] from the verb”], which means “I run” [Col. 0130D]. For he runs through all things, filling and giving substance to all things [Note: [Col. 0131] C reads “ran.”].

And what is the nature of his movement? His Word is his movement; his speech is his movement. Of him the Psalmist says: “His word runs swiftly”; and the Word itself says of itself: “The word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.”

Hear also another movement of the Father, coessential with him and with his Son: the proceeding movement called the Spirit of truth, whom the Father sends in the name of his Son.

The supreme Trinity, therefore, is a threefold immovable movement: the Father moves by begetting his Son, in whom and through whom he made all things; the Son moves by doing what the Father wills; the Spirit moves by cooperating with the Son and with the Father’s will.

Dionysius discusses at length the movement of supreme goodness in preserving, making, and perfecting all things. But it should be noted that in this sentence [Note: [Col. 0131] A and C read *perioda*], as in many others and almost everywhere, we have translated simple verbs in place of [Note: [Col. 0131] “pro” is omitted by A, B, and C; added conjecturally.] the compound verbs found in the Greek [Note: [Col. 0131] C reads “opposed verbs”], to make the most difficult ideas easier to enter. Thus, for φωτοφανείας [Note: [Col. 0131] A, B, and C read φωτοφανιας; B* adds in the margin: “instead of ahotofanias”], that is, “the manifestation of lights,” we have used only “illumination”; and for ἀγαθοδότως [Note: [Col. 0131] B* adds in the margin: “that is, agadothos”], which is adverbially “excellently,” we have used “abundantly” or “well and generously” [Note: [Col. 0131] A reads “obtime”].

The expression “fills us,” which we used, was translated from the ambiguous Greek word ἀναπλᾷν [Note: [Col. 0131] So A and B], but it can also be translated as “folds us together,” giving the following sense:

“As the procession of divine illumination abundantly multiplies us into infinity, so it again folds us together, unifies us, and restores us to the simple unity of the Father who gathers and deifies us.”

I say this because the intention of almost the whole of blessed Dionysius throughout these books concerns the infinite multiplication of the self-subsisting supreme Good into all things, which of themselves would neither exist nor subsist as good unless they existed and were good through participation in its essence and goodness; and it concerns the return and restoration of that manifold multiplicity to the supreme Good itself, in which infinite multiplicity reaches its end and becomes one.

He confirms this with apostolic testimony, saying: “For from him are all things and unto him,” as the divine word says. It is as though he were saying:

“For this reason divine power gathers and folds us together toward the unity and deifying simplicity of the gathering Father, as the holy apostolic statement testifies” [Note: [Col. 0131] So C; A and B omit “simplicity.”].

[Col. 0131D]

### § 2

He continues:

“Therefore, invoking Jesus, the paternal light which is true light [Note: [Col. 0131] “from light” is absent from the Greek text and from Scotus’s translation], which illuminates every human being coming into the world, through whom we have gained access to the principal light, the Father, we shall contemplate, as far as possible, the illuminations handed down by the Father in the most sacred utterances.”

He now begins to discuss the celestial hierarchies—that is, the heavenly episcopates.

The order of the words is as follows: “Shall we not, therefore, contemplate, as far as possible, the illuminations handed down by the Father in the most sacred utterances, invoking Jesus?”

The meaning is this:

Since all things come from the Father himself and return to him, shall we not—who invoke Jesus, who is the paternal light, namely light from light and true light from true light, illuminating every human being coming into the world—contemplate in him and through him, restored [Note: [Col. 0131] A and C read “is restored”] through him, the illuminations handed down by the Father in the most sacred utterances, as far as possible?

Through Jesus, that is, we have gained access to the principal light, which is the Father. For that inaccessible light of the Father was incomprehensible to us before the light begotten by him, which is Christ, was incarnate and became man. Once he was made human and assumed our nature, we gained access to the invisible Father. For while we understand Christ’s humanity, we certainly come to know, insofar as it is granted us to know, the hidden divinity both of Christ and of the Father and of the Spirit of both [Note: [Col. 0131] B reads “the added divinity,” whereas A and C read “the hidden divinity”]. Hence Christ himself says: “Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father.” That is: whoever understands me as true God and man understands my Father in me, because I am in the Father and the Father is in me, and I and the Father are one.

Shall we, then, contemplate the illuminations handed down by the Father in the most holy utterances—that is, the divine visions which the Father handed down to us in the sacred Scriptures—so far as is possible for us, who are still enclosed in the flesh?

Or, as the Greek reads more explicitly, ἀνανεύσωμεν [Note: [Col. 0131] B* adds in the margin: “ananeusomen”], that is, shall we raise the inclination of the inner eyes of the heart [Col. 0132C] [Note: [Col. 0131] Conjecture; A has *interiorisin*; B has *interiorisi n*; B* appears to have added the dots; C reads, “that is, it is strange, the inner”]?

[Note: [Col. 0131] B reads “we shall be raised”; C reads “we shall draw out.”]

This, however, he says because, through the prophetic visions—which the Greeks call θεοφανίαι (*theophaníai*), that is, divine apparitions [Note: [Col. 0131] B* writes *theophanias* in the margin]—the arrangements and dispositions of the heavenly powers, which he calls hierarchies, have been introduced into human minds chiefly through formations resembling or differing from certain sensible things. And this is what he added: “We shall contemplate, as far as we are able, the hierarchies of the heavenly minds, manifested to us by them symbolically [Note: [Col. 0131] AB *simbolice*; likewise B almost everywhere, though A sometimes has this form.] and anagogically”—that is, through the illuminations of the divine utterances, handed down by God to prophetic minds, we shall contemplate the dispositions of the heavenly intellects, not through those illuminations in themselves, but through symbols, that is, through signs resembling sensible things—sometimes pure, sometimes unlike and confused—and through anagogy [Col. 0132D], that is, through the mind’s ascent into divine mysteries [Note: [Col. 0131] B *misteria*, throughout], as far as permission is granted us, as they have been manifested.

And since the Father of lights, from whom all things proceed and to whom all things return, is the beginning and source of the entire illumination of invisible substances—whether first in the visions of theologians [Col. 0133A], or afterward in the minds of spiritual men, to whom it has been granted to know the divine secrets [Note: [Col. 0133] AB *archana*, likewise almost everywhere]—for this reason he added: “And receiving with immaterial [Note: [Col. 0133] B reads *materia*, with *libus* supplied above by B*] and unshaking eyes of the mind the principal and superprincipal glory of the divine Father, which manifests to us, in figured symbols, the most blessed hierarchies of the angels, we are restored again through it into its own simple ray” [Note: [Col. 0133] B omits “with immaterial … into its own simple ray,” from “*immaterialibus*” through “*simplum suum*.”] [Note: [Col. 0133] A has *restituuntur*, “they are restored.”]

Observe how, in each of these periods, he teaches both the procession of divine illumination from God the Father to us and, again, our restoration through that very procession and multiplication of glory into the simple ray of the light that proceeds from him [Note: [Col. 0133] AC *periodas*]. The arrangement of the words in this period is as follows: “We are restored again”—namely, through that manifold giving—“into its own ray,” when we receive, with immaterial and unshaking eyes of the mind, but at the same time with spiritual and feeble vision of contemplation [Note: [Col. 0133] A has *similiter*, “similarly”], “the principal and superprincipal”—that is, more-than-principal—“glory of the divine Father,” namely, the illumination given by the divine Father, which manifests to us, in figured symbols—that is, through significant forms—the most blessed hierarchies of the angels.

It is as though he had said plainly: When, by intellectual vision and the gaze of a wavering mind, we apprehend the principal and more-than-principal glory proceeding from the divine [Note: [Col. 0133] So ABC; perhaps it should read: “the glory proceeding from the divine Father.”], through which the most blessed hierarchies of the angels are manifested to us by means of certain symbols, we are restored again through it into its own simple ray.

And it should be noted that here too, as above, we have translated simple words by compound expressions. For what is expressed by θεαρχικοῦ πατρός (*thearchikou patros*)—“of the divine Father”—and by φωτοδοσία (*photodosía*), we have rendered as “glory” [Note: [Col. 0133] B* has written in the margin *photodosian* for “and for what is expressed by *photodosian*.”]. For θεαρχικός (*thearchikós*) cannot be translated literally except by a circumlocution [Note: [Col. 0133] AB *perifrasin*; likewise *f* for *ph* almost everywhere]. The Father is called θεαρχικός (*thearchikós*) because he is the beginning of the whole Godhead: of the Son through generation [Note: [Col. 0133] So C; AB simply give *deitas*, “Godhead,” for “of the Son through generation,” which makes no sense], and of the Holy Spirit through procession.

Φωτοδοσία (*photodosía*), moreover, means “the giving of lights,” which refers especially to the Father, who is the giver of all lights. Therefore, although what can be translated by circumlocution could be expressed as “the principal and more-than-principal giving of lights from the Father, who is the beginning within the Godhead,” it seemed easier to us to set down—though longer in verbal form—“the principal and superprincipal glory of the divine Father” [Col. 0133D] [Note: [Col. 0133] So BC; AB has “of the glory”], following the principle by which we often find that the Greeks themselves use simple words for compound ones [Col. 0134A]. For they very frequently put θεῖον πατέρα (*theion patéra*)—“divine Father”—for θεαρχικῷ πατρί (*thearchikō patri*)—“thearchic Father” [Note: [Col. 0133] C* has written in the margin: “that is, *thionpatera*”—“divine Father”]—and λαμπρίαν (*lamprían*)—“splendor” or “glory”—for φωτοδοσία (*photodosía*) [Note: [Col. 0133] So AB; B* has written in the margin: “that is, *photodosia lamptyron*”; C gives: “and for *photodosia*, *lamptyron*”]. [Note: [Col. 0133] So BC; AB has the singular *ponit*, “puts.”]

But what is that simple ray of the Father’s glory, into whose presence we are restored by that glory itself, once it has been understood with immaterial and unwavering eyes of the mind? This question is rightly asked. And, as I inquire, nothing more probable presents itself for belief and understanding than the Word of God the Father [Note: [Col. 0133] A recent hand has written in the margin of B: “which is the Word of God the Father, into the whole …”], which, like a ray from the inaccessible and invisible sun—that is, from the Father—is diffused throughout the whole of sensible and intelligible creation, and especially and principally into angelic and human intellects. It fills all things, perfects what is imperfect, penetrates what is shut up, illuminates mysteries, forms visions [Col. 0134B] in the interior senses of theologians, opens the intellects of those who wish to seek and understand those visions, and manifests itself, according to the capacity of each, to all who behold it in themselves.

Anyone can most readily establish this from the continuation of the present chapter. For it follows: “For neither is it ever separated from its own singular unity”—that is, the glory of the Father of lights itself, once purely and firmly understood by us, restores us into its own ray of simplicity [Note: [Col. 0133] So C; A and B have “of the glory” (B* appears to have added a point)]—“because that ray is abandoned neither in any place nor at any time by its own singular unity,” that is, by its simplicity.

For what is simpler than the Word of God, when it is contemplated in itself within its own Father, above all things, insofar as it allows itself to be contemplated? And what is more manifold than that same Word, when it is extended over all things that have been made in it and through it [Col. 0134C], and is distributed in many ways to intellects capable of understanding?

And do not suppose that the glory of the Father is one thing and the ray of the Father another. The glory of the Father—the ray of the Father—is his own Son, who glorified the Father to the world, who is uniform above all things [Note: [Col. 0133] B omits “who glorified the Father … is uniform”], and the form of all things [Note: [Col. 0133] C has “of human beings” instead of “of all things,”], yet is multiform in all things, and is the manifoldness of all things, especially in angelic and human minds.

And he makes this clear when he says: “For the anagogical and unifying harmonization of the things that have been foreseen, it is multiplied and proceeds most excellently and beautifully; yet it remains within itself, fixed uniformly in unchangeable likeness, and proportionally extends into itself those who look into it, insofar as is lawful, and unifies them according to the simplicity of its own unity” [Note: [Col. 0133] B has “of the things that are foreseen.”] [Note: [Col. 0133] B has “extends into itself.”]

That is: Although the divine ray does not abandon its own simplicity and singular unity, it is nevertheless beautifully multiplied and proceeds into the things that have been foreseen [Note: [Col. 0135] So ABC], for their anagogical and unifying harmonization—that union, namely, which leads upward [Note: [Col. 0135] B: “which is upward and leads”] and unifies all things.

For all things would neither subsist nor return to their beginning, which is above—that is, to the Father of all—if that ray, ineffable as it is, were not diffused into all things, so that all things might subsist, become one in it, and be joined to their own beginning [Note: [Col. 0135] B* corrects *efficerent*, “might make,” to *efficerentur*, “might be made.”]—as though someone were to ask: “In what way, and why, is the simple multiplied?”

And while it is beautifully multiplied and proceeds into all things, it remains within itself; it moves without changing, fixed in its own uniformity; and those who look into it, insofar as is lawful—that is, insofar as it is permitted and granted to them—it extends into itself according to their own proportion [Col. 0135B]. That is, it raises them up to itself and unifies them in the likeness of its own simple unity.

But because that ray is in itself incomprehensible, invisible, and inaccessible to every creature—for it surpasses all the senses and every intellect—it could not appear to all the things in which it is multiplied except through certain veils connatural to us, through which it willed in some manner to manifest itself to us while we still remain in this flesh.

It follows: “For it is not otherwise possible for the divine ray to shine upon us except when it is anagogically veiled by the variety of sacred veils, and prepared naturally and appropriately for the things that belong to us through paternal providence” [Note: [Col. 0135] B has *hiis*, “these,” as everywhere].

It is as though he had said: Paternal providence, and the ineffable concern of divine love for our salvation and restoration [Note: [Col. 0135] So AC; B has “redemption”] to the things that we abandoned by sin, has veiled the ray, invisible in itself, with various sacred veils according to the principles of anagogy. From things that are connatural and appropriate to us, it has prepared a certain mode of apparition, so that he might be comprehensible to us who cannot otherwise be comprehended [Note: [Col. 0135] The manuscripts read *studio invisibili*, “with invisible concern” (corrected here contextually to *studium invisibile*, “invisible concern”).]

Concerning these veils, this book, which is about the celestial hierarchy, and the following book, which is entitled *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, as well as the third book, *On the Divine Names*, treat abundantly. But if you ask, we shall offer a brief foretaste from among the many examples, for the clarification of the present period.

In this book, therefore, the veils with which the divine ray is veiled and which are prepared for our sake through paternal providence are the prophetic visions [Note: [Col. 0135] B* has written in the margin: “Concerning prophetic vision and the manner of revelation, and why revelation takes place in this way.”].
