Through the agency of the angelic powers, these visions have been formed in the memory of theologians in the likeness of sensible things naturally suited to our weakness, which still submits to bodily senses [Col. 0135D] [Note: [Col. 0135] A and B have *subcumbenti*; B* corrects this to *succumbenti*], for our instruction and for our restoration from our childish state [Col. 0136A]—the state in which we cling to sensible things—through intelligible stages of maturity, by which the rational soul grows through action and knowledge, until we attain the perfect man, that is, the fullest contemplation of Christ, who is the end of our perfection, and in him and with him the most perfect union.

Thus [Note: [Col. 0135] So ABC; B* corrects to *Utique*, “certainly,” and adds in the margin: “Concerning the different modes of apparitions”] the supreme and holy Trinity itself, and especially the Son himself, and all the heavenly powers, appeared to the prophets in certain divine likenesses: in human form, in the form of a lion, a calf, an eagle, and a horse [Note: [Col. 0135] B has *equina*, “equine,” with the spelling *equuina*], and they are formed in symbols similarly figured as being of different colors, fiery, misty, amber-like, riverine, wheel-shaped, swiftly moving, and in other such forms [Note: [Col. 0135] B** has added in the margin: “which are.”]

In the following book, however [Note: [Col. 0135] B has added in the margin: “This is discussed in the following book, which is about the ecclesiastical hierarchy”], the same ray of God—the Word—and the heavenly powers are taught to be conformed for our sake through the visible and bodily sacraments of the Old and New Testaments [Col. 0136B].

For example, in the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0135] So AC; B has “dwelling place”] there was the ark [Note: [Col. 0135] AB have *archa*, likewise throughout] of the covenant, signifying for our sake the Word of God incarnate; and there were two Cherubim [Note: [Col. 0135] B has *Cherubin*, likewise throughout] flying around the ark on either side [Note: [Col. 0135] So BC; A has “fluttering”], in the likeness [Note: [Col. 0135] So AC; B has “in the likeness of”] of the superheavenly substances, which eternally and intelligibly fly around the Lord Jesus Christ.

Likewise, again, in the temple the same ark and the Cherubim were present in the same type, together with the other legal symbols. In the New [Testament] [Note: [Col. 0135] B has “in the ninth”] as well [Note: [Col. 0135] So ABC; supply “Testament”], there are the sacraments of baptism, the altar, the chalice, wine, bread, priests, and the mystical chrism, along with the other things that are placed as figures of Christ. To discuss these now would be both lengthy and superfluous, since they are treated at great length in the second book.

In the book that is about the divine names [Note: [Col. 0135] B* has added in the margin: “This is discussed in the third book, which is about the divine names,”] the *peripetasmata* [Note: [Col. 0135] AB have *perypetasmata*; B* writes above: “that is, rays”; C has *per ypetasmata*], that is, the veils or coverings of the ray, are the principal causes—for example, goodness, essence, life, wisdom, truth, power, and similar attributes [Col. 0136C].

And, to put it briefly, all the forms of visible and invisible creation, and all allegories, whether in deeds or in words, throughout the whole sacred Scripture of both Testaments, are veils of the paternal ray; and the ray itself, according to its flesh, is the greatest veil of itself according to its divinity, and is connatural to us.

Additional textual apparatus: [Col. 0133] AC read *multiplicationem*; B also reads *multiplicationem*, apparently with a point added by B*. B omits *hujus* (“of this”), while C reads *ejus* (“of it”); A reads *recepimus* (“we received”). B* writes *thearchicoy patris* in the margin for θεαρχικοῦ πατρός, and *thearchicos* for θεαρχικός at its occurrences; it also writes “and for what is *photodosian*” and adds *est visum* (“it seemed”) after *nobis visum*. B reads *conspectum* (“sight/presence”) for *conspectu*. [Col. 0133] B* supplies the marginal heading “On the simplicity and multiplicity of God.” In A, a recent hand has written a word above *claritas* that may be read as either *radius* (“ray”) or *Pater* (“Father”); B* writes “Father” and adds in the margin, “It compares the Father to brightness, the Son to the ray.” [Col. 0133C] The commentator’s discussion of the simple and compound Greek expressions begins here. [Col. 0134D–0135A] The discussion of the ray’s unchanged simplicity continues across this page division. [Col. 0135] AC omit *ac* (“and”) in “various and sacred veils.” B* also supplies the marginal heading, “What is treated in this book,” before the account of prophetic visions; the following marginal heading, already translated above, concerns prophetic vision, the mode of revelation, and why revelation occurs thus. B reads *sursum est, ducit* (“is above, leads”) for *sursum ducit* (“leads upward”).

Source preparation: Supplied local source; translated as part of this section.

§ 3. [Col. 0135] Therefore, judging our most holy hierarchy, the *τελετάρχις* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “that is, *theletarchis*, that is, most perfect.”]—the institution of sacred things—to be worthy of imitation of the supermundane celestial hierarchies, it handed down the said immaterial hierarchies in material figures and formal [Note: A: “formable.”] arrangements, making them diverse.

The order of the words is [Note: B* writes above: “is”]: “Therefore the *τελετάρχις* institution of sacred things,” that is, the *teletarchic* [Note: Corrected by B*; AB: “teletarchial.”] priesthood [Col. 0136D], “handed down, judging our most holy hierarchy worthy of the supermundane imitation of the celestial hierarchies, and making the said immaterial hierarchies diverse through material figures and formal [Note: Thus BC; A: “formable.”] arrangements.” [Col. 0137A]

And the meaning is as follows: Since the Father’s providence multiplies its simple ray through veils that are connatural to us, so that it might recall us—scattered on account of original sin—to the pristine simplicity of our nature, in which we were made according to the image [Note: A: “image”; A has this spelling almost everywhere, B very often.] of the divine unity, for that reason it also handed down and established our most holy hierarchy—that is, the most holy ecclesiastical episcopate. This was done by the very *τελετάρχις* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “theletarchis”] institution of sacred things, which in Greek is called *τελετάρχις ἱεροθεσία*, that is, the *τελετάρχη* [Note: Thus AB, ending the adjective in *-is, -e* according to Latin usage; among the Greeks such an adjective ends in *-is, -i*. B* adds in the margin: “theletarchis ierotesa, that is, theletarche.”] priesthood. For it indicated that our hierarchy—I mean our hierarchy—was worthy of the supermundane likeness of the celestial episcopates, so that the Church, which is still in the pilgrimage of this life, scattered through places and [Note: B** writes below: “through times.”] times, variously [Note: Printed *variatim*; B was erased/corrected from *variatir*; C reads *udriatum* (an obscure or corrupt form).] through diverse mysteries, manifold in teachings and composed in symbols of the celestial virtues, might ascend toward the unity and equality of those virtues, in which there is no diversity [Col. 0137B].

And it made the aforesaid hierarchies—that is, the celestial essences—although [Note: AC: *dum* (“although/while”); B: *cum* (“although/when”).] immaterial by nature and above all places, times, material figures, forms, and arrangements, diverse through material figures, forms, and arrangements, after the likeness of our hierarchy, which is still on earth; that is, it multiplied them in diverse visions, symbols, and allegories, and conformed them to our weakness. For their simplicity and unintelligible unity could not of themselves shine upon us [Note: B* corrected to “was not possible”; C: “impossible.”] (B* writes *va* above the word).

But [Note: Corrected *autem* (“but”); ABC read *aut* (“or”).] *τελετάρχις ἱεροθεσία*, that is, the *τελετάρχη* [Note: Again, the adjective ends in *-e* rather than *-i*. B* adds in the margin: “theletarchis aut ierotesie, that is, theletharce.”] priesthood, is the supreme and holy Trinity, the hierarchy of all hierarchies, from which all hierarchies in heaven and on earth have been made, ordered, and handed down [Col. 0137C].

Why, then, is the supreme Trinity called by that name, *τελετάρχις* [Note: C: “which is called *theletarchis*.” B* adds in the margin: “theletarchis, called the father.”] (*τελετή* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “telete.”] among the Greeks means a purifying sacrifice for all sins, through which a human being is made God), and by this means the holy Trinity called one God? Because it is the cause and principle of our entire purification and deification, it is rightly and reasonably called *τελετάρχις* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “teletarchis.”], that is, *τελετωάρχη* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “theletarche.”], namely, the principle of purifications and their consummation. For among the Greeks *ἀρχή* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “arche.”] signifies both “beginning” and “end.” The cause of our restoration according to nature is itself the cause of our sanctification and perfection according to grace [Col. 0138A].

By a similar reasoning, the same supreme Trinity is appropriately called *ἱεροθεσία*, as though it were *ἱερῶν θεσία*, that is, “the institution of sacred things” [Note: The words “Trinity *ἱεροθεσία* … institution of sacred things” are omitted in B; B* writes “con” above *convenienter* and adds in the margin: “Trinity *ἱεροθεσία*, that is, *ierotesia*, as though *ἱερῶν θεσία*, that is, *ierontesia*.”]. For it is itself the first and immovable foundation of all the sacred mysteries through which our rational nature is instructed in teaching, purified in action, illuminated by knowledge, and perfected by the power of deification [Note: B* adds in the margin: “Note: he numbers the operations as ordered in relation to one another, namely, to instruct, purify, illuminate, perfect; elsewhere only three are given, with instruction omitted.”].

And [Note: C and corrected B: *ac* (“and”); A: *aut* (“or”).] if someone were to ask [Note: *interrogarit*; C: *interrogaverit*; B* corrects to *interrogaret*.] why the celestial substances, which no perceptible form or figure circumscribes and no composition of parts joins together, are varied and multiplied through diverse forms, figures, and arrangements—whether inwardly in prophetic visions or outwardly through bodily senses—he added these words: “so that proportionately [Note: BC and A both transmit *proportionabiliter*.] we may ascend from the most sacred formations to the simple and unfigured heights and likenesses.” [Col. 0138B]

That is: For this reason the celestial hierarchies are varied in our likeness through most sacred formations, so that through those holy images we may ascend into the simple likeness of the celestial virtues, which is without every kind of imagination, and thus [Note: Printed *et hoc etiam*; B reads *et etiam*; C *et hec etiam*.] become like them in all things and in every respect. The reasoning added below [Note: *ratio subnexa*, “the reasoning joined below.”] also suggests this. For he says:

“Since it is impossible for our mind to ascend to the immaterial imitation [Note: B repeats the conjunction: *et imitationem et contemplationem*.] [Col. 0138C] and contemplation of the celestial hierarchies unless it uses a material guidance appropriate to itself.”

As though he were saying: Our mind, surrounded and deceived on every side by the thick darkness of diverse beloved errors [Note: Thus AB*; BC: “delinquencies” (*delictorum*); B* corrected this to *dilectorum* and entered the same correction in the margin.], false thoughts, and material imaginings [Note: B: “phantasms”; B generally writes *f* for *ph*, as does A very often], cannot be exalted—through theological grace—to the immaterial imitation, that is, the natural likeness, of the citizens of heaven, nor to the contemplation of the highest cause of all, unless it first makes use of an introduction through material things in order to reach this goal.

Finally, he consequently adds what this material guidance itself is [Note: A has *quid sit*; B omits it and B** supplies *quae sit* in the margin; C reads *quae sit*. A writes *manus ductio* as two words.], by which the human mind may be lifted to the height of angelic nature and grace, toward uniform equality [Note: Conjectural correction; A: “uniform inequality”; B: “uniform into equality”; B* corrected to “uniformly”; C: “uniform equality”], saying:

“Considering visible forms to be images of invisible beauty”—that is, while it considers and firmly judges that the visible forms which it contemplates either in the nature of things or [Note: B has *se* in place of *seu* (“or”).] in the sacred mysteries of divine Scripture were neither made for their own sake nor to be desired or proclaimed for their own sake, but are images of invisible beauty [Col. 0139A]—through them divine providence recalls human minds to the very pure and invisible beauty of its truth, which everything that loves, whether knowingly or unknowingly, loves and toward which everything that loves tends.

The same is to be understood of the other matters that follow. [Note: B* adds: “is”; C: “is to be understood.”] And concerning “sensible sweetnesses as figures of invisible distribution,” the words “considering” are supplied from above.

By “sensible sweetnesses” he means bodily odors, which the sense of smell receives as a figure of invisible distribution: just as [Note: *quemadmodum* is omitted in B.] through the outward sense of the nostrils we distinguish pleasant or unpleasant qualities of odors, so through the inward sense we may distinguish the intelligible distribution of virtues through each species by the power of discernment, and separate them with the most careful gaze of reason from opposing vices or from those attempting to imitate them through false imagination [Col. 0139B] [Note: Thus AC; B: “to alter them.”].

Hence it is that the most holy sacrament of chrism, as well as the fumigation of incense [Note: B* adds in the margin: “Concerning the sacrament of chrism and the fumigation of incense.”], is prepared by the priests of the Church as a figure of the inward sweetness of virtue and the distribution of virtues [Note: Thus ABC.].

And “material lights” are an image of immaterial brilliance; here again the words “considering” are supplied from above. In this place, instead of *φωτοδοσίας* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “photodosias.”], that is, “the giving of lights” [Note: Thus CB*; AB: “of giving.”], we have placed *luculentiae* [“of brilliance”] [Note: Thus C; AB: “brilliantly.”]. Material lights [Note: AB spells this *matherialia*, as does A often and B rarely]—whether those naturally ordered in the spaces of heaven or those produced on earth by human art—are images of intelligible lights, above all of that true light itself which illuminates every human being coming into the world, and which always and unquenchably burns in angelic and [Note: “In” is omitted in AC.] human intellects [Col. 0139C].

He continues: “And, according to the intellect, accessible sacred disciplines of contemplative fullness.” Here too “considering” is supplied [Note: Thus AC; B: “considering,” with punctuation apparently added by B*]; “to be images” is likewise supplied [Note: Thus AC; “to be images” is omitted in B].

He asserts that the seven disciplines which philosophers call the liberal arts are signs of the fullness of intelligible contemplation [Note: Thus C and corrected in B with illuminated letters; AB: “of contemplation”], through which God and creation are known most purely. He calls those sacred disciplines *διεξοδικάς* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “dyexodicas.”], that is, “accessible,” because they are accessible and clear to those who understand them, or because they are certain paths by which we enter into knowledge of things.

The disciplines may likewise be understood, according to a more familiar interpretation [Note: C reads *notiore* (“more familiar”); B has the near-corrupt *nocicie*; A *noticione*.] of *διεξοδικάς* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “diexodicas.”], as “flowing through” [Note: Thus C, with a marginal correction in B*; AB: “among.”]. For just as many waters flow together from different springs and run down into the bed of a single river, so natural and liberal disciplines are united in one and the same signification of inward contemplation [Col. 0139D] [Note: Thus C; AB: “signification”], which the highest fountain of all wisdom, who is Christ [Col. 0140A], communicates everywhere through diverse theological speculations.

And perhaps this is what is said through the Psalmist concerning the blessed man: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside the courses of waters,” that is, like Christ, into whose typological signification all the natural arts converge, within whose boundaries the whole of divine Scripture is contained. For there is no sacred Scripture that lacks the rules of the liberal disciplines.

“And the united and ordered dispositions of the orders of the arrangements that are here.” This means: all the orders of arrangements which the human mind considers in the sensible things of this present life, whether arising from nature or from the rational invention [Note: Thus AC; B: “rational invention.”] and activity of wise human beings, are to be regarded as images of that united and ordered state of spiritual disposition [Col. 0140B] through which the human soul adheres immutably to the divine virtues.

He continues: “And the taking up of the participation [Note: Corrected by B*; AB: “of the principation.”] of Jesus [Note: B* corrects to *Jesu*; AB read *in unum*, a graphically similar but different phrase.] in the most divine Eucharist.” Observe [Note: Printed *Intuere*; C reads *inthure*.] how beautifully and explicitly he asserts that this visible Eucharist, which the priests of the Church prepare daily [Note: AB spells this *cottidie*, as everywhere; C: *cothidie*] on the altar from the sensible matter of bread and wine, and which, once prepared and sanctified, they receive bodily, is a typological likeness [Note: C reads *typi quam*, a divided/corrupt form corresponding to printed *typicam*.] of spiritual participation [Note: Thus CB*; AB: “of principation.”] in Jesus, whom [Note: *quem* is omitted in C.] we faithfully taste through the intellect alone—that is, whom we understand and take into the inward [Note: B* corrects *inque* to *in quem*.] bowels of our nature—for our salvation, spiritual growth, and ineffable deification.

Therefore, he says, the human mind, ascending from sensible things toward the likeness and equality of the celestial virtues [Col. 0140C], ought to regard the visible divine Eucharist, formed [Note: Printed *conformatam*; C reads neuter *conformatum*.] in the Church, as supremely a type of that participation by which we now participate in Jesus through faith, and in the future shall participate in him through vision, and shall be united to him through love.

What, then, do those who wish to assert that the visible Eucharist signifies nothing other than itself answer to this splendid trumpet of the great theologian Dionysius, when that trumpet clearly cries out that those visible sacraments are not to be worshiped as such, nor embraced as the truth, because they are significant of the truth, nor were they invented for their own sake, since the end of understanding [Note: C reverses the order to *finis intelligentiae*.] is not in them, but because of the power of the incomprehensible [Note: B: *incomprehensibilis incomprehensibilem*; in Migne, *-em* is printed above the *-is* of *incomprehensibilis* to represent the manuscript reading.] truth, through which [Note: Printed *qua*; C reads *quae*.] Christ exists [Col. 0140D] in the unity of his human and divine substance [Col. 0141A] [Note: C: “of his divine and human substance”], beyond everything perceived by bodily sense, above everything apprehended by the power of the intellect, the invisible God in both his natures?

[Note: What John Scotus discusses here concerning the Holy Eucharist does not appear in fact to depart from Christian truth. For he attacks those who wish to assert that the visible Eucharist signifies nothing other than itself. All theologians of the Church teach with one accord that the species in the Holy Eucharist contain something typological and figurative. Nor does Scotus himself fail openly to show that he acknowledges in the Holy Eucharist more than a “memory,” more than a mere symbol, since he teaches that it is taken into the inward bowels of our nature for our salvation … and ineffable deification. Therefore, although he is attacking the Paschasians in this passage, scarcely anything in his words seems to be present that ought to be turned into a reproach against him.]

And whatever else has been handed down to the celestial essences in a supermundane manner, but to us symbolically. In a brief statement, blessed Dionysius teaches that not only human minds still held fast in the flesh know the truth through sensible symbols, but also angelic intellects, freed from every carnal weight, know it through invisible significations, which theology calls theophanies. For the truth is not comprehensible in itself to any creature, whether rational or intelligible [Note: C: “incomprehensible”]; it is exalted above every sense and intellect [Note: C: “and above every sense”], remote from every visible and invisible creature.

Therefore, he says, it appears to the celestial essences in a supermundane manner—that is, above all sensible forms of this world [Col. 0141B]—but to us through sensible symbols. For even the angels do not know through themselves [Note: C and A retain *per se*; AB omit *per* (“through”).] what God is, or what truth is [Note: Thus AC; B omits “is”]; this has been removed from every creature. They know only that they exist, that truth exists superessentially, and that all things proceed from it.

For the sake, therefore, of this, our [Note: *nostram* is omitted by AB and supplied from the Greek text and John Scotus’s version.], *θέωσιν* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “theosin, that is, deification.”]—the con-rational [Note: B* adds in the margin: “of our nature.”] deification of our nature—the merciful principle of perfection, revealing the celestial hierarchies to us and making our hierarchy [Note: *ierarchiam nostram* is omitted by AB and supplied from the Greek text and John Scotus’s version.] their fellow-minister according to the capacity of our natural power through the likeness of its deiform sanctification, portrayed the supercelestial intellects in sensible images [Note: Corrected *sensibilibus*; AB read *sensibus*, “senses.”] in the sacred compositions of scriptural utterances, so that [Note: Printed *quatenus*; AB spell *quatinus*.] it might lead us back through [Note: A and B read *et per*, “and through.”] sensible things to intellectual things, and from sacredly figured symbols to the simple heights of the celestial hierarchies [Col. 0141C].

### Recapitulation

*Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις* [Note: AB: *ἀνακεφαλείωσις*; B, in illuminated letters in the margin: “Anacephaleosis, that is, recapitulation”; C: “Aacephaleosis, that is, recapitulation.”] is the recapitulation of the whole chapter, requiring only a very brief explanation, since it has been set forth in the preceding material. We may therefore understand it briefly as follows:

For the sake of this con-rational deification of our nature, coequal with angelic nature—that is, our deification—the merciful and most clement principle of perfection (for some translate *φιλανθρωπίαν* [Note: B adds in the margin: “philantropian.”] as “mercy,” some as “humanity,” that is, love of humanity [Col. 0142A], and some as “clemency”; *φιλάνθρωπος* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “philantropos.”] means “merciful,” “humane,” or “clement,” and God is such; and he himself is *τελεταρχία* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “teletarchia.”], that is, the beginning of perfect purification)—manifests the celestial hierarchies to us and perfects our hierarchy, their companion [Note: Conjectural reading, instead of “and our companion.” A has “that lot”; B “and … lot”; B* adds in the margin “according to,” so that the reading should be “and according to the lot.” C: “according to the lot.”] according to the possibility of our natural power, through the likeness of his sanctification [Note: AC read *sive* (“or”); B reads *sine* (“without”).], deiform in relation to angelic substances, by which he sanctifies us.

And through sensible forms he described the divine intellects in the typological configurations of divine utterances, so that he might lead us through things subject to the senses into things contemplated by intellect alone [Note: Thus CB*; AB: “which they consider”], and through individually figured symbols [Note: B reads “single symbols,” with punctuation added and *symbols* written above by B*; AC read *singula* (“individual”).] raise us into the simple loftiness of the celestial virtues.

The holy Trinity itself, therefore, is our *θέωσις* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “theosis is.”], that is, deification. [Col. 0142B] [Note: B* adds in the margin: “How we are deified.”] For it deifies our nature by leading it through sensible symbols into the height of angelic nature [Note: Thus C; A and B: “evangelical nature”], and deifies it in those who pass beyond all things into God himself [Note: Thus AC; B: “those which.”].

It is itself our *τελεταρχία*, that is, the beginning of our most perfect purification and sanctification; it is the first and supreme hierarchy. For there is no order in heaven or on earth—that is, in that commonwealth which is constituted under the worship of the one true God from rational and intelligible, that is, human and angelic, nature—whose rationale does not precede in it and proceed from it [Note: Thus BC; A: “from him”], from the highest down to the lowest, or which is not recalled into it from the lowest up to the highest.

It manifests the virtues to us in figures and forms suited to our weakness, so that through them, as through certain steps [Col. 0142C] which it constructed in the divine utterances [Note: Thus AC; B: “in the divine”; B* writes “divine” in the margin after the prefix *pro-*], we may ascend—from the deeds of the patriarchs [Note: A: “patriarchs”], I mean, and the evangelical parables, and all the virtues which the Lord accomplished in the flesh, and the visible sacraments of the New Law, which were both begun and sanctified by the Lord himself, frequently practiced, celebrated, and enlarged by the holy apostles—through the steps of action and knowledge, with divine grace leading, assisting, and cooperating with us, until we arrive together with the angels [Col. 0143A] at the simplest and purest contemplation of immutable truth.

But perhaps we have expounded the first chapter at greater length than the matter requires. Nevertheless, the diligent reader, if I am not mistaken, will discover how much it discloses in what follows.

The treatise on the first chapter ends [Note: “Chapter” is omitted in B; B* adds in the margin: “title.”]. Here begins the discussion of the second.

## CHAPTER II

The *ἐπίγραμμα* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “ep ygrama, that is, superscription.”] of the second chapter is:

“That divine and celestial things are beautifully manifested even through dissimilar symbols.”

“Divine,” he says, and “celestial”—that is, the celestial virtues, [which] [Note: *quas* is omitted by ABC and supplied conjecturally.] theologians divide into three hierarchies, as will be explained in the course of the present work—are beautifully manifested and signified to us through symbols, although those symbols are dissimilar to them [Note: B: “to these”]. [Col. 0143B]

For there is no sensible form that entirely attains the likeness of intelligible things. They differ from one another by a great distance [Note: B* adds in the margin: “Here he notes the distinction of the three kinds of vision.”], and those things are wholly dissimilar which appear outwardly through bodily sense, or inwardly in a fantastic manner [Note: B* adds in the margin: “Note that he calls ecstasy a fantastic vision.”], as do the visions of those dreaming, or of those suffering in the spirit a mental ecstasy, which the Greeks call *ἔκστασιν* [Note: AB: *ἐξτασιν*; B* adds in the margin: “that is, ecstasy”; C: *extasym*], and those things which are understood in themselves through the pure and inward gaze of the mind, with no phantasy or sensible form interposed [Note: B* adds in the margin: “He notes the third kind of vision.”].

But because our mind, as was said in the preceding chapter, cannot immediately ascend to the inward contemplation of intelligible things, without any intervening interval, divine providence has fittingly interposed dissimilar symbols—similar to us, who are still held fast by bodily senses [Col. 0143C], but dissimilar to pure intellects—to whose contemplation our intellect is led through them.

§ 1. It is necessary, therefore, as I judge, first to explain what we consider the speculation—or, that is, the definition—of every hierarchy to be. This is what the order of things requires, I think: before we come to the explanation of the dissimilar symbols through which the mind is introduced to the pure vision of the celestial powers, we must first clarify what kind of speculation, that is, what kind of definition, we judge the whole hierarchy, or universal hierarchy, to possess.

[Note: [Col. 0143] So C; AB: “of the explanations.”]

[Note: [Col. 0143] Conjecture; ABC: “human.”]

For there is a general hierarchy, which must be defined in general, since it is subdivided into many hierarchies that are, as it were, its species and that receive their special definitions from those who praise them. And what each species of the general hierarchy contributed to its divine praisers—that is, what kind and what degree of beauty it bestowed upon those who, through it and in it, continually offer divine praises [Col. 0143D] in action and knowledge—must also be explained.

[Note: [Col. 0143] “Contributed” is omitted in AB and added in the margin by B**.]

[Note: [Col. 0143] C: “what the species of the general divine hierarchy contributed to its praisers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0143] So the text; AB likewise; C: “that is.”]

[Note: [Col. 0143] So C; A: “are frequented”; B: “are frequented” (B* appears to have added a punctuation mark).]

Next, it is necessary to praise the celestial hierarchies according to their manifestation in the sacred writings—with “it is necessary” understood from the preceding words. That is, as though he were saying: After considering the general hierarchy, its forms and species, and the usefulness of each of them to its divine praisers—that is, to those who sing divine praises with inward and outward praise—it is consequently necessary to praise, glorify, and proclaim the celestial hierarchies according to their symbols in the divine writings, through which, although they are dissimilar, they are manifested to us.

[Note: [Col. 0143] So C; AB omits “in”; B* adds it above the line.]

And it is likewise necessary to say by what divine formations the sacred descriptions of the writings represent the celestial orders.

[Note: [Col. 0143] A: “arrangements”; C: “descriptions.”]

“When,” he says, “the matters mentioned above have been considered in their proper and natural order, it is necessary to say what divine formations the sacred descriptions of the holy writings form and shape”—that is, what holy assimilation of forms they fashion to signify the celestial orders—“whether they are simple and distinguished from one another by natural differences, such as the likeness of a human being, a lion, or an eagle, or whether one mixed and composite image is formed from various images of natural things, such as a wheel within a wheel and the four mixed animals joined to one another in each of their members.”

[Note: [Col. 0143] B: “descriptions of the holy writings”; AC: “the sacred description.”]

[Note: [Col. 0143] A: “is formed.”]

He continues: “And to what truth must one ascend through the forms,” or, more explicitly, “through fictitious forms into that which is not fictitious.” It follows, he says, that we must say to what kind of pure and sincere truth of intelligible things, entirely free from fiction, we ought to ascend with the clear vision of the mind. And in what manner must we ascend so high?

He continues: “So that we too may not, in the same way as many others, uncleanly suppose the celestial and godlike minds to be certain many-footed beings, possessing many faces, formed according to the bovine character of cattle or the bestial appearance of lions, and fashioned according to the hooked-beak appearance of eagles or according to the threefold movement of the wings of flying creatures.”

[Note: [Col. 0143] B: “many,” with an erased correction.]

That reason, he says, admonishes us to fly beyond all prophetic visions and formations by the vision of the mind, so that we too, like many who think carnally about spiritual realities and, believing through their unclean thoughts that nothing exists beyond what they perceive with bodily sense, may not suppose—having become like them—that the minds of the celestial and godlike angelic powers naturally possess many feet, although they are entirely without the structure of bodily limbs; that some possess many forms mixed together, although they are free from every visible form, whether distinct or confused; that some have the figure of irrational cattle, some the image of fierce lions, some the form of eagles, whose natural characteristic is the curvature of the beak; and that some possess six flying wings, distributed in three ways: one pair covering the animal’s face, another pair covering its feet, and the third pair always flying with wings extended upward.

[Note: [Col. 0143] B: “nothing,” written *nichil*; this spelling occurs throughout.]

[Note: [Col. 0143] So C; AB: “thoughts”; B*: corrected from *cogitationes* to *cogitationibus*.]

[Note: [Col. 0143] AB: “formed”; B*: “forms.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] So C and corrected B*; AB: “flying.”]

For these are the dissimilar symbols fashioned in the prophetic visions by angelic activity in the spirit of the prophets, for our instruction and introduction to the purest knowledge of the celestial essences in themselves, with every fantastic fabrication removed.

[Note: [Col. 0145] B* adds in the margin: “What is formed in the spirits of the prophets as likenesses is formed through the ministry of angels.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] So C and corrected B*; A: “fantastic”; B: “phantasy.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B*: “Intellectual vision is always necessary for understanding prophecy made in the spirit.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] Corrected B*; AB: “knowledge”; C: “thoughts.”]

If anyone should think about these prophetic fictions carelessly, so as to place the end of his knowledge in them—

[Note: [Col. 0145] B has “the end of his mind” instead of “in them.”]

—and not ascend beyond them into contemplation of the intelligible realities of which they are images, his mind is not only left unpurified and untrained, but is also most disgracefully polluted and most foolishly oppressed. It is unnecessary to insert the passages of the prophets in which such visions are read, since they present themselves more clearly than daylight to everyone versed in Holy Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 0145] BC: “Holy.”]

He continues: “And let us imagine certain fiery wheels above heaven, and material thrones necessary for the Divinity to recline upon, and certain multicolored horses, and armed commanders of commanders, and whatever else has been handed down to us from the writings in sacred and figurative variety through the manifold forms of manifestative symbols.”

[Note: [Col. 0145] B: *quasdas*; C: *quidem*.]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B*: corrected *imaginemus*; C: *ymaginemur*.]

[Note: [Col. 0145] So C and radically corrected B*; AB: “commanders.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B* adds below: “of this kind.”]

In all the clauses of this period, which is a four-membered structure, the meaning is disclosed by what precedes in this way: “And so that we may not imagine fiery wheels above heaven”—that is, in the supercelestial essences, where there is no sensible fire—“and so that we may not imagine material thrones there,” that is, seats made of bodily matter, necessary for the Divinity to recline upon, or, more explicitly, suitable or adapted to that purpose; “and so that we may not imagine in spiritual natures armed commanders of commanders”—that is, armed leaders of the commanders of the armies.

[Note: [Col. 0145] The reading is emended; A: *periodicoli*; B: *periodicol’*; C: *peridicolis*.]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B*: corrected *imaginemur*; C: *ymaginemur*.]

[Note: [Col. 0145] A: *vero*.]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B*C: “as above.”]

For ἀρχιστρατηγός (*archistratēgos*) means, as it were, ἀρχῶν τοῦ στρατοῦ ἡγεμών (*archōn tou stratou hēgemōn*), “leader of the commanders of the army.”

[Note: [Col. 0145] AB C: “archistrategos.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B* adds in the margin: “that is, from *archon*, *stratou*, and *hēgemōn*.”]

By this name the commanders of the celestial army’s commanders are signified. They are therefore not merely commanders of the celestial army but also commanders of those commanders.

So that such empty and presumptuous imagining may not creep into our minds, we must ascend above all visible things to the truth of intelligible realities through dissimilar symbols, lest the symbols be taken as though they themselves were the intelligible realities of which they are symbols; and we must separate what is fictitious from what is true.

He continues: “For theology has used fabricated sacred formations with great artistry for intellects that are not formed by images, relieving our mind, as has been said, providing for it by a mode of return proper and connatural to it, and conforming the anagogical sacred Scriptures to that mode of return.”

He means that theology—namely, that power naturally present in human minds by which they seek, investigate, contemplate, and love divine principles—has used fabricated, that is, fictitious, holy imaginings to signify divine intellects that lack every written and sensible figure and form. By such an art of fictitious images it relieves our mind—or, more explicitly, it takes care of our mind—providing for it by a mode of return proper and connatural to it, namely, one skillfully formed through images of sensible things. These are connatural to us while we still remain in the flesh because of our sins, and by means of them it conformed the sacred Scriptures to anagogical interpretation—that is, to a mode of interpretation leading the mind upward.

[Note: [Col. 0145] B: “our sins.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B: *ante*; C and corrected B*: the reading lacks *ante*.]

It is as though he were saying openly: Just as poetic art, through fictitious tales and allegorical likenesses, composes moral or physical teaching for the training of human minds—for this is proper to heroic poets, who praise figuratively the deeds and character of brave men—so theology, like a kind of poetry, shapes Holy Scripture [Col. 0146C] through fictitious imaginings for the care and restoration of our mind, leading it away from outward bodily senses, as though from a kind of imperfect childhood, into the perfect knowledge of intelligible realities, as into a certain maturity of the inner human being.

[Note: [Col. 0145] AC: *componunt*; B: *componunt*, with punctuation apparently added by B*.]

[Note: [Col. 0145] Corrected; AB: “a certain.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] So C and radically corrected B*; AB: “of inner beings.”]

For the human mind was not made for the sake of divine Scripture, which it would in no way have needed if it had not sinned; rather, Holy Scripture was composed for the sake of the human mind, woven together in various symbols and teachings, so that through its introduction our rational nature—which, by transgressing, fell away from the contemplation of truth—might be led back again to the height of its former pure contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0145] B*: “Divine Scripture would not have been necessary for humanity if it had not sinned.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B: *contexa*; B*: corrected to *contexta*; C: *connexa*.]

[Col. 0146D] § 2. He continues: “But if anyone thinks that the sacred compositions should indeed be accepted as representations of simple substances, which are in themselves unknown and incontemplable to us, yet judges the sacred descriptions of the holy intellects in the writings to be inappropriate…”

After criticizing those who carnally and disgracefully interpret the divine symbols and divine imaginings with which Holy Scripture was composed for our sake—those who believe that the symbols and imaginings are neither imaginings nor symbols but that the supercelestial powers themselves appeared in the prophetic spirits in their own natural forms, made by the Creator of all, so that no mystical or allegorical meaning should be sought in these appearances, but only a kind of bare and simple history of naturally produced things—the perceptive teacher turns and argues against those who do not deny but plainly believe that the sacred composite formations of divine Scripture should be accepted and understood as representations of simple substances that are in themselves unknown and incontemplable to us, while judging it inappropriate that such descriptions of the holy intellects should occur in the sacred writings.

For they say: The theologians—that is, the divine prophets—ought not to have committed to sacred writings descriptions so dishonorable, confused, and so very far removed from the truth of the holy intellects. Properly speaking, a description is an imagining of forms most like the things of which it is a description; but such things ought not to appear in the spirits of the prophets.

[Note: [Col. 0147] So ABC; “they say” is to be supplied.]

They are led to the point of believing that through the descriptions of divine Scripture one should understand not holy intellects but certain rational movements of the human mind if the descriptions are honorable, and irrational movements if they are shameful and confused, since they attempt to interpret everything from our own movements.

[Note: [Col. 0147] Corrected B*; ABC: “customs.”]

“If, then,” he says, “it seems to anyone that, although it combines many things into one, the sacred compositions should not be accepted for their own sake but on account of certain simple things unknown and invisible to us, and that they are altogether unsuitable for holy intellects,” he continues: “And, to put it this way, the whole theater of angelic names is harsh.”

[Note: [Col. 0147] So AB; C: “combining many things into one.”]

That is: If it seems to the same person that one should speak in this way about the sacred compositions—“All this theater of angelic names is harsh and inappropriate for holy intellects, and should be judged more theatrical and monstrous fiction than something signifying the supercelestial essences”—then “angelic names” means that it is titled with the names of angelic images.

He says that the theologians, when descending to bodily form in order to represent universally incorporeal beings, ought to have formed and manifested them through proper and, as far as possible, kindred representations drawn from things among us that are most precious, immaterial, and also transcendent.

And if the person who judges the imaginings of Holy Scripture inappropriate for the holy angelic intellects thinks that the theologians—perfect beings, that is—when descending from the height of divine contemplation to bodily form, namely to something resembling bodies, wishing to signify through certain likenesses of sensible things what surpasses sense, ought to have formed the universally incorporeal beings—that is, the wholly incorporeal powers—through proper and, as far as those theologians could manage, kindred, that is, connatural, representations.

[Note: [Col. 0147] B writes above the line: “reform.”]

The prefix *re-* is superfluous here, and “reformed” has been used in place of “formed.” First, they form them in their own spirits, in which the visible forms of the angelic powers are, as it were, originally shaped through the administration of the divine will; afterward they manifest them in divine writings in order to instruct and purify our mind.

[Note: [Col. 0147] So C; A: “administration”; B: “administration” (B* appears to have added punctuation).]

The theologians ought not to have made likenesses of the incorporeal beings from the lowly forms of material things—for example, from the forms of human beings, lions, and other animals, which are composed from this earthly, humble, and fragile matter. From these, I say, they ought not to have formed the likenesses of incorporeal beings.

[Note: [Col. 0147] B* adds in the margin: “On prophecy.”]

For he attributes to the prophets themselves the visions that the angels describe in their spirits. But they should have been formed from things that we regard as most precious and, as it were, immaterial: namely, from an ethereal, fiery, and celestial nature, which is so close and near to the supercelestial substances that it is not improperly called spirit, since it is not incongruously similar to incorporeal spirits.

“How and also according to transcendent essences,” as it may be translated more explicitly—that is, “how, and in the manner in which, images of transcendent essences ought to be made.”

[Note: [Col. 0147] “And transcendent” is omitted by B and added in the margin by B*.]

Therefore he continues: “And not surrounding the heavenly and godlike simplicities with the earthly and lowest multiformities.” It is as though he were saying: The theologians ought not to assimilate earthly things to heavenly things, the basest and most remote things of the whole creation to godlike things, or composite multiformities to simple things.

[Note: [Col. 0147] B: “creatures”; then “of creation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0147] In Migne, *ae* is printed above the *as* of *creaturas* to represent the manuscript reading.]

They ought to have signified heavenly things through heavenly things, godlike things through the highest natures of this world, and the simplicities of simple things through simple elements. This would also have been more elevating for us. It would be as though he were saying: If the theologians had done this—if they had imagined sublime intellects from the sublime natures of this world—our mind would certainly have been raised more sublimely into the knowledge of intelligible realities.

[Note: [Col. 0147] “Future” is omitted by B.]

“And it would not lead supermundane manifestations into inappropriate dissimilarities,” or, more explicitly, “into obscure dissimilarities.” That is: Not only would it have been possible for our mind to ascend more sublimely; it would also not have led the imaginings of supermundane powers into incongruous and dark dissimilarities.

[Note: [Col. 0147] The reading is corrected in B*; A and B: “would lead into inappropriate [things]”; C: “into suitable [things].”]

He continues: “Nor would this wrongfully injure the divine powers.” What I have said—that the theologians ought to describe them in this way—would not unjustly injure the divine powers. For what greater injury is there than to mark the celestial with earthly images, the divine with mortal ones, and the simple intellects with composite images?

[Note: [Col. 0149] Emended; ABC: “marks.”]

“And likewise it would not deceive our mind by inserting itself into unclean compositions.” It is as though he were saying: In the same way, this would not deceive our mind, which is ready to insert itself into unclean compositions. He calls these compositions unclean either because they are made from the likeness of earthly animals, or because they are compounded from various forms of different animals, or certainly because they are imagined from unclean beasts forbidden by the law and prohibited as food, such as lions and horses.

[Note: [Col. 0149] B: *subduceret*, “would withdraw”; the text has *non seduceret*, “would not deceive.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149] A omits *in*.]

[Note: [Col. 0149] C: *in mundas*, “into clean things”; the context requires “unclean.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149] So AC; B: “from in”; in Migne, “in” is printed above “from” to represent the manuscript reading.]

And perhaps people will even suppose that the supercelestial regions are filled with certain leonine and equine multitudes, with the bellowing discourse of praises, with the flying command of angels, with other animals, and with baser materials, as though the dwellings of the supercelestial powers had been laid open to what is incongruous with celestial inhabitants and to what is base and subject to suffering, namely, what is vile, mortal, and perishable, through describing in every respect deformed—or, more explicitly, wholly dissimilar—likenesses of the manifestative writings.

[Note: [Col. 0149] B*: corrected *replere*, “to fill,” to *repleri*, “to be filled”; C: *deiformes*, “godlike.”]

That is, perhaps also—and this is the more serious error—those who think only of earthly things and are completely ignorant of heavenly things will suppose that the theologians fill the supercelestial regions not with images but with real lions and a real multitude of horses, with the *hymnologia* (*ὑμνολογία*), literally “the discourse of hymns,” that is, a discourse of praises or a laudatory discourse, as though there were oxen in the supercelestial regions capable of praising God by their natural lowing—and as though there were there angelic principalities naturally bounded by the forms of flying creatures, together with other animals of diverse kinds.

[Note: [Col. 0149] B*: “that is, hymnology.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149] AB: “hymnology.”]

They might even suppose that base materials, which grow from the earth, inhabit the supercelestial regions—something utterly abhorrent for a human being to imagine—as though the dwelling places of the supercelestial powers had been laid open to what is incongruous with celestial inhabitants and to what is base and subject to suffering, namely, what is vile, mortal, and perishable.

[Note: [Col. 0149] AB: “abhorrent,” as throughout.]

[Note: [Col. 0149] So C; A: “unknowable”; B: “unknowable” (B* appears to have added punctuation).]

[Note: [Col. 0149] So C and radically corrected B*; AB: “exposed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149] B: “are.”]

This would happen through describing, that is, while the theologians describe, utterly deformed—or, more explicitly, utterly dissimilar—likenesses in the manifestative writings, that is, in the divine writings, in which not the supercelestial intellects themselves in their own being but their likenesses are clearly and openly manifested.

[Note: [Col. 0149] B*: corrected *difformes*, “dissimilar”; C: *deiformes*, “godlike.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149] B*: radically corrected; AB: “of the manifestator”; C: “manifestative.”]

And so, lest such things deceive carnal minds, the theologians ought not to have represented the celestial powers in their visions through such vile images of vile things.

Thus far the speech has been presented in the person of one criticizing the theologians in their divine descriptions. Now the teacher refutes him, saying:

“But the search for truth, as I believe, shows that the most sacred wisdom of the writings has provided for both matters very carefully in its formations of the celestial minds, so that it neither, as someone might perhaps say, injured the divine powers nor fixed us passibly in the lowliness of the images.”

[Note: [Col. 0149] “In the formations of the celestial minds” is omitted; supplied from the verse.]

It is as though he were saying: It is not as you falsely prophesy, whoever you are.

[Note: [Col. 0149] ABC: “prophetic.”]

You criticize the visions, but, as I believe—and I am not mistaken—the search for and discovery of truth most clearly shows that the most sacred wisdom of the divine writings, when describing the forms of the celestial powers, carefully provided for these two things: that it would not, as someone might perhaps say—as I say, and as does everyone who understands correctly—offer an insult to the divine powers, nor hold our mind passibly in the visible and humble descriptions of the divine images.

[Note: [Col. 0149] B omits “wisdom”; C has “the wisdom of the virtues of the divine writings,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0149] “So that it would not” is omitted in AB; B* adds it in the margin; C has “so that it would not,” omitting “so.”]

Indeed, to the extent that images of the divine powers are mystically fashioned as vile from vile things, humble from humble and earthly animals, to that extent the powers themselves are praised and exalted. For there is no greater praise than that which is derived from the comparison of opposites. Or, certainly, the divine administration through the angels contemplated in prophetic visions not material and earthly forms but their celestial and spiritual principles.

[Note: [Col. 0149] A: *eaque*, “and that”; the text reads *ea*, “that.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149] B has a corrupt reading, apparently “contemplation …”; the text is corrected to “contemplated.”]

For we often see wise people praising greater virtue in the more insignificant species of animals, fruits, and plants than in the more beautiful ones. What is more insignificant than a mustard seed, or what is more precious than its virtue, since it is compared both with the Catholic faith and with Christ himself, as the Gospel parable teaches?

[Note: [Col. 0149] “Christ” is omitted by B.]

[Note: [Col. 0149] B: “evangelist”; in Migne, *c* is printed above the *s* of *evangelista* to represent the manuscript reading.]

The reasons why for our instruction formless intellects, which lack every figure, are imagined through forms and figures are then added in sequence:

“For,” he says, “as for the reason why the forms of the formless and the figures of those lacking figures were beautifully provided, no one would say that our analogy is the sole cause, since it is unable to extend itself immediately into invisible contemplations and desires proper and connatural modes of return, which place before us possible formations of supernatural and formless speculations.”

[Note: [Col. 0149] B*: corrected *dixerit*, “would say,” from *dicit*, “says.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149] Emended; A and B: “a certain person”; B* appears to have added punctuation.]

[Note: [Col. 0149] “Forms and figures” is omitted by B.]

It is as though he were saying: No one who understands correctly would say that the forms and figures provided for the formless intellects, which lack figures, have one single cause—namely, our still weak and mortal proportion, which for that reason cannot ascend to the contemplation of the invisible divine minds without some intermediate medium. It always desires the sensible-image guides that are proper and connatural to it. Since these are accessible to us for knowledge, they place before us, that is, first show us, formations—images, certainly—of the formless, that is, of those lacking form, and of the supernatural speculations of the divine minds, weighed down by thoughts.

[Note: [Col. 0151] BC: “thoughts”; B*: corrected to “cognitions.”]

[Note: [Col. 0151] Conjecture; ABC: “weighed down.”]

[Note: [Col. 0151] B*: corrected *speculationem*, “speculation,” for the transmitted reading.]

He rightly calls the divine minds “speculations,” because they can be understood only through the highest gnostic power of contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0151] B: “gnostic,” with punctuation apparently added by B*.]

This, then, is not the only cause of the prophetic imaginings. For another cause, no less important, and perhaps even more important, is brought forward, which he connects next when he says:

“But because it is also most fitting to the mystical writings to conceal through incomprehensible divine riddles the sacred truth and to make the hidden truth of supermundane intellects inaccessible to many.”

[Note: [Col. 0151] B* adds in the margin: “Why Holy Scripture speaks figuratively and parabolically; this same thing is said by this gloss of John Scotus and John the Saracen.”]

There is, he says, another cause of the sacred descriptions in the divine Scriptures, one most fitting and most appropriate to the mysteries of the divine writings. It is this: to conceal the sacred and secret truth of the supermundane spirits and to make it inaccessible to many through incomprehensible and divine riddles—that is, through very difficult and inaccessible divine obscurities—to those who are unworthy of pure knowledge of the celestial powers.

[Note: [Col. 0151] So C; AB: “description.”]

[Note: [Col. 0151] B: “most fitting”; B* adds above the line: “and most appropriate.”]

There is therefore a most honorable reason for the obscurity of the incomprehensible formations of divine Scripture: to make the secret truth of the angelic minds hidden and inaccessible to many polluted minds. And why is this so? Hear what follows:

“For not everyone is holy, nor is knowledge granted to everyone, as the writings say.”

He would be speaking openly as follows: The mystical writings were therefore right to conceal the truth of the supermundane intellects through riddles and to place it hidden and inaccessible, because not every human mind is pure and sanctified or worthy of the contemplation of truth; for it is corrupted by many sins and deceptive thoughts. Nor is the highest knowledge granted to everyone, as the divine Scriptures testify.

[Note: [Col. 0151] B: “the Scriptures testify”; C: “as the divine Scriptures prohibit.”]

[Note: [Col. 0151] “Mind” is omitted by AB; C has it, and B* adds it in the margin.]

And this is not attributed to the generosity of divine goodness but to the slowness and ill will of the polluted mind, as it is written: “Wisdom does not enter into a malicious soul.”

[Note: [Col. 0151] B: “spoken”; C: “ill will.”]

The truth of the divine intellects is therefore open and accessible only to pure and sanctified minds, even when it is presented through the enigmatic description of mystical images in the visions of the prophets. And perhaps this is what the divine Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then we shall see face to face.”

[Note: [Col. 0151] C: “in an enigma”; B* adds above the line: “in an enigma.”]

After he has refuted and driven back those who, deceived by their unclean thought, believe that the celestial powers are circumscribed by the sensible forms of earthly animals and that nothing else signifying anything appeared in the spirits of the theologians except the powers themselves in their own being, as well as those who not only do not deny but readily accept the meaningful images of invisible things incomprehensible to us when described in the spirits of the prophets, yet approve the view that these images are inappropriate for angelic intellects, he turns his speech and again argues against the person who thinks that the causes of the descriptions of the divine images are deformed.

[Note: [Col. 0151] A: “deformed causes, deformed”; B: “deformed causes, godlike—deformed”; in Migne, an *i* is printed above the first *e* and above the *o* of the second *deformed* to indicate the manuscript reading.]

He says:

“But if anyone should judge the causes of the descriptions of the images to be deformed, saying that it is dishonorable for shameful formations to be attributed to godlike and most holy dispositions, it is sufficient to say to him…”

[Note: [Col. 0151] B* radically corrected; AB: “depositions.”]

“If anyone,” he says, “should judge the causes of the descriptions of the images to be deformed, whatever irrational or rational movements of the mind they may be, and should say that the godlike and most holy orders of angels are dishonored if such shameful formations of mystical visions are attributed to them, it is enough to answer his pernicious opinion: There are two modes of sacred manifestation. One is, as it were, consequential, on account of the similar images of the sacred figures that arise; the other is formed from dissimilar constructions of forms into what is altogether incongruous and indecorous.”

[Note: [Col. 0151] B* adds above the line: “there is.”]

[Note: [Col. 0151] Taken from the text of the translation; AB: “which thus,” with B* adding “is.”]

There are, he says, two modes by which the sacred manifestations of the holy angels are made through images in divine Scripture. One is formed through certain complete, appropriate imaginings of spiritual substances and intelligible powers, by which the rational soul is adorned, as in the Prophet: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne,” and in the Apocalypse: “A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet.” These images are taken from human ideas and from likenesses of the soul’s spiritual ornaments.

The other mode is formed through representations of fierce and proud beasts, such as a lion and a horse; of shameful creatures, such as a bear and a worm; or, in what is thought to be most distant of all, of deranged human beings, such as David at the gate of Gath; of drunken men, such as Noah and Lot; or of furious beings, as is very often read: “The Lord was angry,” and “His fury burned,” and through the configurations of other things like these.

[Note: [Col. 0153] So C and corrected B*; AB: “of the proud.”]

[Note: [Col. 0153] So C; AB omits “as”; B* adds it above the line.]

To this is also added a confusion of forms, when in one and the same image human, calf-like, and eagle-like species are monstrously mixed together, which is clearly altogether contrary to complete and natural forms. The examples of the first mode he then adds, saying:

[Additional apparatus notes]

[Note: [Col. 0143] B**: *que*, corrected; ABC: *que*.]

[Note: [Col. 0143] B: *consequentibus*, corrected at the root to *consequenterque*; AC: *consequentibusque*.]

[Note: [Col. 0143] So CB*; AB: *varietatem*, “variety,” for *veritatem*, “truth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0143] AB: *velud* for *velut*.]

[Note: [Col. 0143] AB: *ammonet*, a spelling used throughout, for *admonet*.]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B: *mens*, “mind,” in place of *in eis*, “in them.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B: *cogitationis suae finem*, “the end of his thought,” for *finem cognitionis suae*, “the end of his knowledge.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] BC: *opportunos*, “suitable,” for *opportunos*; the gloss also gives *coaptatos*, “adapted.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] AB and the Greek text and version: *ἀτεχνῶς*, “without art / entirely,” for *artificialiter*, “artfully.”]

[Note: [Col. 0145] B adds in the margin: “What theology is.”]
