§ 3. Thus the blessedness of the superessential θεαρχία [thearchy] is to be worshiped. The mystical traditions of the revelatory utterances sometimes praise it as reason, intellect, and essence, thereby declaring its divine rationality and wisdom, its truly existing subsistence, and the true cause of the subsistence of those things which exist; they also represent it as a kind of light and call it life. He says: The blessedness of the θεαρχία [thearchy], that is, of the supreme Deity, which surpasses all essences, is to be worshiped and adored. In the mystical traditions of the divine utterances, which manifest intelligible powers through certain figures, it is often praised under the figure of reason, intellect, and essence, since it surpasses every reason and wisdom—“intellect” being the term he uses here.

Every intellect that understands the truth is wisdom. It is called “essence” and is represented as a kind of subsisting light, more than existence and substance, because it is the true and unchangeable cause of the subsistence of those things which exist. It is called “essence,” represented as a kind of light, and called, as it were, “life,” since it is beyond every light and every life, the inexhaustible fountain of all light and life. These, then, are its principal and marvelous supermaterial forms, and those of the supercelestial powers that surround it.

He next adds: “Existing as more glorious than such marvelous reformations, and proved in some way to surpass material formations, while failing, even so, of a thearchic [divine] likeness to the truth.” He says: Such are the marvelous forms, so great and so exalted, which are more glorious and are proved, in whatever way, to surpass and excel all material formations and images—that is, they are praised. Nevertheless, even if they are so excellent and supermaterial, they fall short of the divine likeness; that is, they do not attain to its divine likeness when the truth is considered.

This is what follows: “For it is beyond every essence and life, no light characterizing it”—that is, depicting or forming it—“and every likeness of it in reason and intellect is incomparably left behind.” That is: every reason and intellect is alienated from its likeness. For there is no reason or intellect that can attain its likeness, since it is incomparable. Every visible and invisible creature is abandoned and made insignificant when compared with the supreme and supernatural nature, which is beyond all things.

[Col. 0154B] The second mode of formation follows. It appears wholly inconsequent and unbecoming—that is, unsuitable to the divine powers and deformed. At times, however, it is praised in a supermundane manner through dissimilar manifestations from the utterances themselves, which call it invisible, infinite, and incomprehensible, and through those things by which is signified not what it is, but what it is not.

He says: The second mode of the divine manifestations by which the superessential Divinity is praised in the divine Scriptures as being above the whole world is twofold. For it is either imagined through dissimilar and unsuitable forms, very far removed from it—as we said above—or it is indicated through those things by which not what it is but what it is not is signified, when it is called invisible, infinite, and incomprehensible.

When divine Scripture calls the supreme Deity and goodness invisible, infinite, and incomprehensible, it does not signify what it is. For invisibility, infinity, and incomprehensibility are not its essence; rather, Scripture shows what it is not. It is not visible, finite, or comprehensible.

And since there are two modes of divine signification, it is signified either affirmatively—for example, when it is predicated of it that it is essence, goodness, life, wisdom, truth, and by other names of similar powers, which seem most fitting to the divine height and subsistence—or negatively, when it is called invisible, infinite, incomprehensible, inaccessible, and unsearchable, along with the other things pronounced of it by way of negation.

Therefore he adds: “For this, I think, is more powerful in it.” He says: I consider the negative mode more powerful and more fitting in the signification of the supreme Deity, when we worship and adore it. For the ineffable truth and divine existence is indicated more forcefully and more nearly by negation than by affirmation.

This is what follows: “For, as the hidden and sacerdotal tradition has introduced, we truly say that it is not, in some respect, one of the things that are; but we are ignorant of its superessential and invisible and ineffable infinitude.” It is as though he said: Therefore the negative mode is preferred to the affirmative in divine signification, because we truly say that the Deity, which rises above all things, is not any one of the things that are, while we do not know what its superessentiality, invisibility, ineffability, and infinitude are. We do not truly say that it is one of the things that are when we affirm it to be something belonging to them.

For it is no essence and no goodness, since it is superessential, more than goodness, and exalted above everything that is spoken and understood. Therefore he adds: “If, then, removals in divine matters are true, but affirmations are incompact, manifestation through dissimilar formations is more suited to the obscurity of mysteries.”

He says: If removals—that is, negations, which the Greeks call ἀποφάσεις [apophaseis, negations]—are true in divine signification, but affirmations, which they call καταφάσεις [kataphaseis, affirmations], are not compact and fitting in those same divine significations, then God is truly denied to be one of the things that are, whereas he is not truly predicated as being one of them, since he is superessentially removed from all things and above all things.

Manifestation through dissimilar formations is certainly much more suited to the obscurity of mysteries—that is, of ineffable things—than manifestation through similar formations. It is as though he said: If negation is true in divine matters, but affirmation is not true and is metaphorical—for God is truly called invisible, but is not truly and properly called visible; likewise, he is truly called infinite and incomprehensible, whereas finite and comprehensible are not said of him properly but in a certain mode of speech—what is surprising if forms that are far unlike natural and simple forms, mixed, confused, and deformed, are more effective for signifying divine and ineffable things than the absolute, simple, and wholly unconfused images of natural forms?

To put it more clearly: I understand God more when I hear it predicated of him, “He is not essence; he is not goodness,” because he is superessential and more than good, than when I hear, “He is essence; he is goodness.” The latter exalts God above all things; the former numbers him among all things.

By the same reasoning, when in the holy visions of the holy prophets I read of a beautiful, complete, and wholly natural human figure as signifying him who in himself subsists beyond every form and figure, without form or figure, I can more easily be deceived into thinking that God himself, the uncircumscribed one, is circumscribed by a human figure, and that the invisible and ineffable one can be seen and that something can be said about him. But when in those same visions I find the image of a winged and flying human being, signifying the celestial powers or the Divinity itself as penetrating all things with swift flight, I am not easily deceived, because I have neither seen nor read nor heard of a winged and flying human being in the nature of visible things. It is monstrous and wholly alien to human nature.

Even poetic fictions, in the utterly false story of Daedalus’s flight, did not dare to imagine that feathers and wings naturally grew from his body; for that would be incredible and deformed. Consequently, I am more readily led to deny that the divine powers and God himself are circumscribed and deformed by such an image, since everything contrary to nature is shameful and deformed, than to suppose that such figures naturally exist in the heavens.

Immediately, without any delay, I perceive that those images in holy Scripture signify natural things—things that are indeed simple and devoid of every sensible and circumscribed form—but not the actual natures that are intimated through these significations for the purification of our earthly thoughts.

Therefore, just as negation is preferred to affirmation in signification, so unsuitable and deformed appearances are preferred to beautiful and fitting images and manifestations of divine things, whether these surpass bodily senses—as do the angelic powers—or every intellect—as does the Divinity itself—ineffably.

What we have said about the figure of the flying human being is also to be understood of the winged lion and calf, of the eagle configured with a human face, and of the other confused figures, as well as of those that are excessive within the same genus, such as those animals having six wings. For just as all these deny natural forms, so they most clearly imply that the celestial powers are devoid of all such appearances.

It follows: “And now, therefore, the sacred descriptions do not fill the celestial ornaments of the utterances with ugly things—as the final translation explicitly renders it—when they manifest them through dissimilar constructions of forms, and through these show the excellences of the supermundane powers as superior to all material things together.”

He briefly concludes what he has said above, refuting those who think carnally about divine things and suppose that they are circumscribed by sensible forms, whether complete and not exceeding the mode of nature, or confused, or excessive, as was said above. He likewise refutes those who accept that the images are significant but consider them unworthy of the dignity of the angelic and transcendent nature, and also those who maintain that the causes of spiritual images are ugly and irrational.

This is what he says: “And now, therefore”—that is, after the divine truth has been considered and divine wisdom consulted—“the sacred descriptions do not fill the celestial ornaments of the holy utterances”—that is, the holy images—with material things, as foolish people suppose, when they manifest them through forms unlike themselves; through these dissimilar forms they show the heights of the supermundane powers as superior to all material species together.

Having finished this controversy, he turns his discourse to the praise of dissimilar similitudes and says: “For since the more dissimilar, or, as it is more significantly translated, obscure, similitudes lead our mind back more effectively, I do not think that any wise person will contradict this.”

He says: I do not think that any of those who possess wisdom will contradict me when I say that dissimilar or obscure similitudes lead our mind back more than similar and clear ones into the true contemplation of the celestial powers.

He also urges this by the following reasoning: “For in the more precious sacred formations it is easy to be deceived, when people suppose that the celestial essences are golden in form, and that there are certain men radiant as lightning, clothed in beautiful garments, shining brightly, with a white and fiery yet harmless brilliance, and when theology has figured the celestial intellects in whatever other similar imagined forms.”

He says: In precious—that is, beautiful and nature-like—holy images, those can very easily be deceived who imagine that the celestial substances have golden forms and that certain luminous men exist there, clothed in beautiful garments, shining harmlessly with a white and fiery radiance. Those who imagine that other similar forms, resembling configurations of human bodies, inhabit the heavens are unable rightly to conceive or purely to know the intelligible subsistences of spiritual and invisible powers. And, what is more pitiable, among the multitude of human beings scarcely the very smallest number of the wise is found who cannot be deceived by such an error and who refuse to approve false things in place of true ones.

It follows: “So that those who understand nothing higher than visible goods might not suffer this, the holy restorative wisdom of the theologians also wonderfully descended to dissimilar forms.”

He says: So that the simple and imprudent souls of the faithful might not suffer this—that is, so that, deceived by their false imaginings, they might not suppose that the uncircumscribed spirits of the celestial powers were circumscribed by golden forms and beautiful shapes of the human body, its limbs, and weapons, clothed in the most precious garments, and, taking opportunities even from prophetic visions, might not deceive themselves and fashion in their thoughts abominable idols far removed from divine understanding—the most wise theology, taking account of human folly, also descended to dissimilar images of deformed forms, which neither the nature of visible things accepts nor the sublimity of invisible things permits to be fitting to itself.

It is as though holy theology openly cried out: Just as such deformed and dishonorable images, which natural simplicity rejects and beauty ridicules, are refuted by the ineffable sincerity and incomprehensible uniformity of the celestial intellects, even though they appeared in their most obscure figures, so—and no otherwise—those most beautiful images that are thought to accord with human dignity are universally removed from the pure and uncircumscribed subsistence of those same intellects.

The most truthful contemplation of truth proclaims that all these sacred figures in divine Scripture are significant, not substantial, and does not allow our material element, remaining in ugly images, to come to rest in them.

He says: Theology does not allow our material element—that is, our mind, which is most readily inclined toward material things—to insert itself into material realities, to rest by remaining in ugly images, and to set the goal of its thought in them. Rather, it reaches obscure and unsuitable similitudes.

The Greek has προσύλον ἡμῶν, that is, “our material element”—namely, everything in our soul that is most readily inclined toward the likeness of our material body and irrationally bends toward love of visible things.

But theology cleanses the upward-moving part of the soul and, through the ugliness of the compositions, suggests—more literally, pricks or goads—the mind: neither justice nor truth approves that the supercelestial and divine spectacles are in truth like ugly things, nor do material things approve such a likeness.

He says: This is what provident theology does: cleansing the soul upward—that is, the higher part of the rational soul, which the wise call the mind or intellect—from every contagion of false phantasms [variant: thoughts]. In place of what we translated “upward toward the soul,” the Greek has ἀνωφερὲς τῆς ψυχῆς, that is, “that which is borne upward in the soul.”

For the mind, which is the highest part of our nature, is always borne upward toward spiritual things by natural desire. Hence the Apostle says: “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.” Therefore this part of us is purified through the administration of divine theology, so that, once purified, it may become fit and prepared for the contemplation of the celestial powers and of the cause of all things.

“And suggesting”—or, as it is more literally translated, “pricking” or “goading”—the mind: theology does this through the ugliness of the compositions, that is, through the deformed mixtures of images. It suggests to the mind that, as it seems to the foolish, the divine and supercelestial spectacles are, in truth, like ugly images.

That they are neither just nor true—that is, neither justice nor truth approves this—nor do the material things themselves become similar to the supercelestial essences of the uncircumscribed spirits; rather, by their very forms they reject such a likeness. For all material things naturally desire to be transferred into spiritual things, whereas spiritual things do not wish to incline toward the lowly and most worthless extremity of material things, since this is impossible.

It is possible for lower things to ascend to higher things, but for higher things to descend to lower things by natural transformation is impossible.

And if someone should say, “It therefore appears that blessed Dionysius is saying, by the foregoing arguments, that the angelic powers entirely lack bodies,” a brief response must be given.

He denies them earthly and material bodies—mortal, corruptible bodies distinguished by the composition of limbs, circumscribed by sensible forms and local spaces, changeable through time—as well as images of all these, whether inwardly in the phantasies of memory or outwardly in the impression of the senses. He utterly denies that the divine minds possess such bodies.

But he does not deny that they possess spiritual bodies, simple and not confined by the outlines of any sensible forms, but rather affirms that they possess bodies most like and most suitable to the divine minds themselves. In these bodies—namely, their celestial and exceedingly subtle bodies—they have often appeared visibly to human eyes, as to Abraham and Tobias, transforming the invisible and uncircumscribed qualities of their spiritual bodies into whatever visible forms they wished to use in manifesting themselves to human beings.

Thus far concerning the theology provident for the purification of our soul, through its descent to the most humble, confused, and dishonorable configurations of material things [variant: reformations], by which the divine minds are signified.

Now he begins to discuss why divine theology did not without reason take the likenesses of invisible things from every visible creature. Therefore it follows: “But it is also necessary to understand this: nothing that exists is universally deprived of participation in the good, since, as the truth of the utterances says, ‘all things are very good.’”

He says: We must understand that no creature is wholly deprived, according to its proper proportion, of participation in the supreme good. For Scripture says: “And God saw, and behold, all things were very good.”

And if this is so, what is surprising if, in material things, an opportunity for the contemplation of intelligible things is taken, so that, since all things participate in the supreme good, the human soul may ascend from the likeness of lower goods to the knowledge of higher things? And this is what follows:

## § 4

It is therefore possible to understand from all things the good contemplations and to fashion from materials the aforementioned dissimilar likenesses for invisible and intellectual realities, with intellectual realities possessing in one way what has been distributed among sensible things in another. If, he says, all things participate in the supreme Good, then we must certainly understand from all things—that is, contemplate in all material things—the good contemplations of immaterial realities, and from sensible materials form the aforementioned dissimilar likenesses, so that through them the invisible and intellectual powers may be understood, since the power of intellectual realities and the nature of sensible things are perceived not in the same way but in [Col. 0160C] different ways.

He consequently adds:

> For indeed, fury exists in irrational beings as a result of an affective movement, and their furious movement is filled with all irrationality; but in intellectual beings the irascible element must be understood in another way.

“Fury,” he says, “and anger are inherent in beasts without reason through an affective but nevertheless natural movement, or, as it is written in Greek, ἐξ ἐμπαθοῦς ὁρμῆς (*ex emphathous hormēs*), ‘from affective impulse’ or ‘passion’; and their irrational movement is full of anger and fury,” as in lions and the other savage wild animals, whose furious rage can scarcely be subdued. Yet such movements are not censured in them, since they are natural and without them the proper nature of those beasts could not be complete: [Col. 0160D] a gentle lion is not a lion. But when such an impulse of fury and anger is predicated of God, or of intellectual or rational wisdom, though still of a creature, [Col. 0161A] it must be understood in another sense from that in which it is perceived in beasts.

He therefore continues:

> Declaring, as I think, their manly rationality and their implacable repose in divine and immutable foundations.

Accordingly, when fury and anger are read of intellectual natures, they signify not a savage impulse but, by a certain likeness, a manly, strong rationality and an implacable—that is, irreprehensible—repose in divine and ever-abiding essences. Thus, by a most beautiful metaphor, fury in a beast, namely an irrational movement, is understood as rational vigor and strength in an intellectual nature; and the anger of a beast signifies the irreprehensible repose of the divine mind in divine establishments, which remain always and unchangeably.

Irrational fury, then, is an image of rational [Col. 0161B] strength; anger and savage impulse are a symbol of the perpetual, implacable and irreprehensible repose of intellectual minds in divine severity and in the immutable love of justice, without any flattery.

Do you see how the lower goods, which proceed from participation in the supreme Good, are images of the first goods and of those nearest to the supreme Good?

And do not be surprised that the blessed master called ἀμείλικτον ἕξιν (*ameilikton hexin*), that is, “implacable repose,” in divine and immutable foundations. For implacable repose is a severe and inflexible possession, unchanging in its love of heavenly virtues.

Nor does this conflict with what the Lord says:

> “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.”

For those who are meek toward evil—that is, from every kind of wickedness [Col. 0161C] free—must become implacable toward the good: toward the severe and diligent guardianship of good virtues. Moved by a praiseworthy zeal for them, they must never cease fighting against every vice, always watchful lest any vice prevail, while resting in the peace of the virtues they guard.

Hence the Apostle says :

> “Be angry and do not sin.”

And elsewhere, concerning spiritual fury and praiseworthy pride , he commands:

> “Set your minds on the things above, not on the things on earth.”

In the same way, he continues, we say that desire in irrational beings is an unreflective and material passibility, engendered without restraint in mutable things from natural movement or habit, together with a continuous irrational appetite for bodily pleasure, compelling every animal [Col. 0161D] toward what is desirable according to sense.

He seeks a brief [Col. 0162A] explanation. For he says:

> In the same way—that is, just as we spoke of fury—we must also speak of what we have said concerning the irrational desire of irrational animals.

For irrational desire is nothing other than an unreflective—that is, without rational deliberation—and material, innate passibility, which arises from natural movement or frequent habit, without any self-restraint, in an impatient love of mutable things , and it is the constant activity of irrational bodily lust, which compels every animal to rush headlong toward what is desirable according to sense.

But when we surround intellectual realities with dissimilar likenesses and shape desire in conformity with them, we must understand it as divine love of immateriality beyond reason and intellect, [Col. 0162B] and as an inflexible and unneedy desire for superessentially chaste and impassible contemplation, and for truly eternal and invisible communion with that pure and most exalted radiance and invisible beauty [the supplied *formicam*, literally “ant,” is uncertain here]. And it receives power in what is sufficient, unchangeable and incapable of being afflicted by anyone, through an unconfused and immutable love of divine beauty and a universal return to that which is truly to be desired.

“While,” he says, “we place dissimilar likenesses drawn from the nature of material and irrational things around intellectual realities like certain garments, and fashion desire in conformity with them, we must understand through desire not an irrational movement but divine love.”

What is divine love? [Col. 0162C] It is a praiseworthy desire for immateriality, which surpasses every reason and intellect. We must likewise understand that desire as the figure of an inflexible and self-sufficient—that is, not arising from lack of temporal things—superessential, chaste, and passionless desire for contemplation, and of eternal and truly invisible union with that pure and most lofty brightness and invisible beauty from which every form and beauty has been made.

And this spiritual desire receives power—or, to express it more significantly, purity, according to the ambiguous Greek term τὸ ἀκρατές (*to akratēs*) in what is sufficient, that is, strong, energetic, vigorous, and unchangeable; namely, in what is sufficient, energetic, and vigorous, [Col. 0162D] and also unchangeable, and in what cannot be afflicted by [Col. 0163A] anyone [the printed *a nullo affligi potest* says “can be afflicted by no one”; B* adds an explicit negative, as recorded below].

By all these names, I think, he signifies the divine power, which grants to those who desire it a sufficient, energetic, vigorous, and unchangeable power; and this power, or purity, cannot be afflicted or conquered by any opposing virtue.

All this is given because of the undisturbed, clear, and immutable love of divine beauty, and because of the universal return to that which is truly to be desired, namely the supreme Good, which everything capable of love desires.

## § 4 continued

After he has treated the very dissimilar likenesses which holy theology introduces from the natural movements of irrational beasts in order to signify the virtues of rational intellectual minds, [Col. 0163B] he most appropriately adds what irrationality itself in irrational beings and insensibility in things without sensation can be defined as in the things to which they naturally belong, and what they signify when applied to divine intellects:

> But irrationality itself and insensibility, in irrational animals or inanimate materials, we properly call a deficiency of reason and sense; but in animate, immaterial, and intellectual essences we religiously and fittingly confess it to signify their supereminence, as beings beyond the world, over our transitory and bodily reason and material sense, which has been alienated from incorporeal minds.

“Irrationality,” he says, “in irrational animals is a deficiency of reason; insensibility in materials lacking a sentient soul is a deficiency of sense—[Col. 0163C] and this is what it properly means.”

But when irrationality and insensibility are predicated of immaterial and intellectual essences, we piously and fittingly confess that insensibility signifies what is supereminent in immaterial beings, and irrationality what is supereminent in intellectual beings: namely, the power of their contemplation, which surpasses all our sense and our reason, while our transitory and bodily reason—that is, reason still weighed down by mortal flesh—and our material sense are very far removed from incorporeal minds.

The Apostle uses this form of expression when he says:

> “The foolishness of God is wiser than human beings,”

praising the superiority of divine wisdom under the figure of foolishness.

Therefore, when I read or hear that intellectual essences [Col. 0163D] appeared or were signified under the forms of irrational animals, or in the likeness of material things lacking soul and sense, I must understand not a deficiency [Col. 0164A] of reason and sense but their supereminence, by which they surpass our reason and our sense.

For we do not yet comprehend by reason and sense the height of the nature of the supercelestial beings, until we reach equality with them.

It is therefore possible to fashion forms that are not discordant with heavenly realities, even from the lowly parts of matter, since matter itself, possessing subsistence from the truly good, has throughout its material arrangement certain echoes of intellectual beauty.

Through these echoes it is possible to be led back to the immaterial primordial forms, by accepting, as has been said, dissimilar likenesses and defining them according to the properties of intellectual and sensible things—not in the same way, but compactly and beautifully.

It should be noted that, because of the abundance [Col. 0164B] of Greek expression, prepositions are often inserted without increasing the meaning. The three most common are “again/up,” “and,” and “toward”: ἀνά, καί, πρός; likewise κατά, which is rendered in different ways. We did not wish to omit these prepositions, for the sake of careful interpretation, especially since the attentive reader will observe where they are necessary and where they are superfluous.

Thus, he says—that is, it is necessary—to form forms that are not discordant but suitable for signifying heavenly essences, even from the lowly parts of earthly and mortal matter. This is not without reason, since matter itself possesses substance from the supreme Good, which alone truly exists, throughout all its material orders, and has certain echoes—that is, reverberations—of intellectual beauty.

[Col. 0164C] By “echoes,” I mean reverberations, which in Greek are called ἀπηχήματα (*apēchēmata*) , images of intelligible things. Just as the image of a voice reverberates from a rock or some hollow place, or as the image of a body is reflected in a mirror , so images of the intellectual beauty of heavenly powers answer back from every earthly and most lowly material thing.

It is therefore possible for our mind to be led through these echoes to the immaterial primordial forms, which the Greeks call ἀρχετυπίας (*archetypias*, “archetypes”) , of which they are reverberating images—yet in such a way that the likenesses themselves are understood dissimilarly in the material things from which they reverberate and in the immaterial realities to which they correspond.

For fury is defined one way in a lion and another way in an angel. And the same likenesses must not be [Col. 0164D] considered in the same manner, but according to the differences of material things and the heights of immaterial realities.

The property of each is defined compactly and beautifully in [Col. 0165A] intellectual virtues and sensible materials.

For example, irrationality is a deficiency of reason in animals without reason; but in heavenly essences it is the supereminence of reason, or supra-rationality, by which they surpass all our reason and sense.
