## § 5

We shall find the mystical theologians not only wonderfully fashioning these things in conformity with the descriptions of the heavenly orders, but also sometimes with the divine manifestations themselves.

“These things,” he says, “which we have mentioned concerning the formation of heavenly realities from portions of matter, we find the divine theologians fashioning in a wonderful way not only for the description of heavenly beings, but also sometimes applying them to the manifestations of the divine itself—that is, to manifestations of the supreme and holy Deity—[Col. 0165B] so that by the same dissimilar, that is, widely divergent, likenesses both the heavenly essences and their supreme and universal cause of all that exists may be signified.”

For this reason he adds three modes of divine representation:

> Sometimes they praise the Deity itself through precious lights: as the sun of justice, as the morning star rising holily in the soul, and as light shining without veil and intellectually.

These are the most precious and exalted parts of this world.

At other times they use things from the middle regions—that is, from the regions of the world: a fire shining harmlessly, and water giving the fullness of life; and, to speak symbolically, water entering into the womb and overflowing in immeasurably surging rivers.

Observe [Col. 0165C] how beautifully and briefly he explains each point.

This visible sun is an image of the invisible sun of justice; and the morning star signifies the holy illumination of faith that soon rises in the soul of the faithful.

The first illumination of a rational soul returning to its Creator is the gift of faith, which is both bestowed and signified through the sacraments of baptism. Therefore the faith of the supreme and consubstantial Trinity, which first rises and appears in the soul of the faithful, is not inappropriately indicated by holy theologians under the symbol of the light-bearing star.

That mystical star is followed by a bright dawn: namely, the splendor of action and knowledge in the strongest hope of future blessedness. Then the sun appears, surely the clearest manifestation of the supreme and holy Theophany, and the most ardent power of divine love shines forth [Col. 0165D] in those who both contemplate and love the truth itself, kindled by the ineffable heat of grace and attracted by its beauty.

This is what he means by:

> “As light shining without veil and intellectually.”

When the most radiant star of faith begins to rise in the morning—that is, [Col. 0166A] at the beginnings of the human soul’s conversion to its God—then immediately afterward the most beautiful splendor of practice, that is, of the exercise of the virtues, begins to shine, and the golden-red radiance of natural philosophy, namely knowledge of all things that exist after God, begins to glow.

All this is accomplished only in the hope of future glory. Beyond all these things, after the great inner light of the human being—that is, after the extraordinary radiance of divine theology, which alone contemplates divine things, surpassing every intellect, through the knowing power of most ardent love—what follows but the unveiled light of truth itself? This is light free from every veil of sensible figures, shining of itself in divine minds through the height of intellectual contemplation.

And consider these three representations [Col. 0166B] of divine wisdom, introduced from the most exalted parts of the material world: the sun, the morning star, and the ethereal light, which shines everywhere and always, is overshadowed by no darkness, and is hindered by no obstacle of earthly bodies or of any mass that confines it. Rather, it is spread everywhere, free and most pure.

From the middle regions of the world—that is, from the elements of air and water—the Theologian took two likenesses, namely fire and water.

Physicists assert that in the upper regions of the air, which adjoin the ethereal spaces, there are harmless flames. They are harmless because they find no material substance there in which they might burn, since the most subtle spirit circulates in the height of the air.

[Col. 0166C] This fire, I think, represents the one who says of himself:

> “I am a consuming fire.”

For the supreme and holy Trinity, the one God, turns and consumes human souls in which he dwells, not to harm them but so that he alone may appear in them; not to consume their substance but to perfect their blessedness.

Water signifies the fullness of inward wisdom. When it first enters secretly and invisibly into the hidden recesses of the rational soul, as into a certain womb, it flows by an ineffable course into open rivers of virtues and overflows into immeasurable streams of divine doctrines.

Hence the Lord says:

> “Whoever believes in me,” as Scripture says, “rivers of living water will flow from his womb.”

The text continues:

> Sometimes, however, they take things from the lowest regions: [Col. 0166D] fragrant ointment and the cornerstone. They also surround him with a bestial form, fitting him with the appearance of a lion and a panther, clothing him in the likeness of a leopard and a raging bear.

After the representations from the middle regions of the world, the paradigms of the lowest regions [Col. 0167A] are introduced in due order.

The lowest regions of the world are those constituted by the structure of the earthly mass. Although they occupy the lowest and seemingly most worthless place in the nature of visible things, they are not lowest in the power of their signification of divine realities. Rather, they are lofty and incomprehensible, and especially significant of the twofold nature of the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

Christ, then, is the fragrant ointment. In his likeness, under the figure of the Church, theology says:

> “While the king was at his table, the nard in her gave forth its fragrance.”

Recall the mystical woman who shortly before the Passion poured the alabaster jar upon the Lord’s head, and the house was filled with its fragrance. This means that the whole world has been filled with the most fragrant doctrine of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, [Col. 0167B] and of the other mighty works he performed for us.

The Catholic Church compounds this mystical ointment in the consecration of the chrism.

Christ is the cornerstone, whom the faithless Jews reject, but who has become a cornerstone for us. In him the Church, gathered from Jews and Gentiles, is joined together. In him rational and intellectual nature—namely, angelic and human nature—has been made one.

For he is our peace, who has made both one. In him divinity and humanity, the Word and flesh, have become one substance in two natures.

And who is capable of adequately explaining the angularity of Christ? Apart from what we have said about the union of circumcision and foreskin, and likewise of heavenly and earthly things—that is, [Col. 0167C] of intellectual and rational creation—in one divine and supreme city, and apart from the union of divinity and humanity in him, the holy Fathers transmit a fivefold mode of his angularity.

For in himself he united both sexes—male and female—into the simplicity of the divine image according to which the human being was made.

> “In Christ,” says the Apostle, “there is neither male nor female.”

In him, through the grace of his Resurrection, the inhabited world and paradise become one paradise.

In him, in a general sense, earth and heaven become one heaven through the likeness of human and angelic life.

In him, bodily and spiritual creation become one spiritual creation through the union of substance, as lower things everywhere pass over into [Col. 0167D] higher things.

In him, every creature is joined to the Creator in reality itself through vision.

Do you see the fivefold angularity of Christ? We have discussed each of these points more extensively [Col. 0168A] in the books περὶ φύσεων (*peri physeōn*), that is, *On Natures*.

He is the lion from the tribe of Judah, who conquers the world and its prince. In the form of a lion the strength of Christ is expressed, as well as the irrational fury by which he utterly despises and destroys the wicked powers that oppose us and everything opposed to the virtues.

He is also mystically a panther. For the panther is called *panther* as though it were “most bestial”; it is the fiercest of all beasts.

This figure is understood in Christ in two ways. It may be taken by contraries, so that through the excessive fierceness of this beast the ineffable mercy and gentleness of divine goodness may be signified—the mercy and gentleness by which he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

Or, by a metaphor drawn from the fiercest beast, it represents the zeal of divine goodness, [Col. 0168B] by which he devours and consumes all the bestial and irrational movements of our nature.

The leopard and the raging bear are introduced under the same figure.

The rational, and more than rational, love of divine goodness continually desires to destroy the irrational and more than irrational movements of our nature, and to consume the nature itself within itself—freed and rescued from every bestial impulse—by the ineffable bites of divine nourishment.

The text continues:

> “I shall add what seemed to be the most lowly of all and to signify even more, since the divine sages have also handed down that it fashions itself in the form of a worm.”

“I shall add,” he says, “to the representations already mentioned that symbol which seemed to be more lowly than all and to signify more—or, as it is more explicitly [Col. 0168C] translated, to be more obscure or dissimilar.”

For the divine sages, that is, the theologians, handed down that Wisdom itself formed itself in the shape of a worm, perhaps in the passage where it speaks through the prophet:

> “I am a worm and not a human being.”

This is understood of Christ, who was not born from male seed. Rather, just as a worm arises from the simple substance of earth, so he assumed flesh from the womb of the perpetual and undefiled Virgin.

Nothing in the nature of material things is lower than a worm, which is conceived from simple mud ; yet through it the incarnation of God the Word is represented, an incarnation that surpasses every sense and intellect.

> “Who will declare his generation?”

It may also be understood in this way: “I am a worm and not a human being,” that is, “I am a worm, and not a human worm.”

[Col. 0168D] As though he were saying:

“I, who am more than human, penetrate the secrets of all nature, as a worm penetrates the bowels of the earth—something no other participant in human nature [Col. 0169A] can do.”

This interpretation agrees with what is written in another psalm:

> “And my substance is in the lower parts of the earth,”

that is, “My substance, which is Wisdom in itself, subsists in the lower parts of the earth,” namely, in the innermost recesses of created nature.

To exist belongs to all things; to exist above all things belongs to the Divinity.

The worm, then, which penetrates the hidden depths of the whole creation, is the Wisdom of the Father. Although he is human, he surpasses all humanity.

Hear the Apostle speaking of himself:

> “Paul, an apostle, not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.”

Is he not that mystical worm in whose image, after five hundred years have passed, a worm is born from the ashes of the Arabian bird—I mean the phoenix—consumed by the flame of its own breast, [Col. 0169B] and is restored to its former verdure?

Christ, indeed, was consumed by the heat of the Passion that he had willingly undertaken, and he descended into hell as a wondrous worm.

But immediately after three days he returned, and his apostles, who had seen him burning upon the cross, beheld him rising in a spiritual body and, flying on the wings of the virtues, ascending to his Father, and were astonished.

### Textual notes

The lemmata and their English meanings identify the passages; entries follow source order.

- inveniemus — we shall find. [Note: [Col. 0165] Thus the Greek text and translation. AB read *invenimus*, “we find/have found.”]
- dispositionum — of the orders. [Note: [Col. 0165] A reads singular accusative *dispositionem*, “order/arrangement,” instead of genitive plural *dispositionum*.]
- ut solem — as the sun. [Note: [Col. 0165] Thus C. AB read *et*, “and,” instead of *ut*, “as.”]
- ut stellam — as the star. [Note: [Col. 0165] B reads *et*, “and.”]
- et ut lumen — and as light. [Note: [Col. 0165] B omits *ut*, “as.”]
- Haec — these, the precious and exalted parts. [Note: [Col. 0165] The supplied note reads *Sit ABC* (literally “let it be ABC”), apparently *Sic ABC*, “thus ABC”; the printed form is retained here.]
- symbolice dicendum — to speak symbolically. [Note: [Col. 0165] B* appears to correct *dicendum*, “to be said,” to *dicendo*, “in/by saying.”]
- in ventrem — into the womb/belly. [Note: [Col. 0165] Thus C and B*’s correction. AB read *invenire*, “to find.”]
- Siquidem — for indeed. [Note: [Col. 0165] ABC write it as two words, *Si quidem*, “if indeed.”]
- stella matutina — the morning star. [Note: [Col. 0165] Thus C. A reads *Stellam matutinam*, and B *stellam matutinam*, accusative instead of nominative; B* appears to have added punctuation.]
- hoc est — that is. [Note: [Col. 0165] AB omit *est*, “is.”]
- in matutinis … animae — in the morning … of the soul. [Note: [Col. 0165] B omits this whole span, including the explanation of the beginning of the human soul’s conversion.]
- superantia — surpassing, qualifying divine things. [Note: [Col. 0165] This is a conjecture. A reads *superant a gnostica*, “they surpass, from a gnostic [power]”; B *superant agnostica*, “they surpass agnostic [things/power]”; C *superat gnostica virtute flagrantissime*, “it surpasses by gnostic power most ardently,” etc. The constructions are difficult and retained rather than silently normalized.]
- per se ipsum — through itself. [Note: [Col. 0165] B omits *se*, “itself.”]
- altitudine — through the height. [Note: [Col. 0165] B* corrects to nominative *altitudo*, “height,” instead of ablative *altitudine*.]
- refulgens — shining forth. [Note: [Col. 0165] B omits *refulgens*.]
- ubique — everywhere, of ethereal light. [Note: [Col. 0165] B reads *ubi*, “where”; B* writes *ubique*, “everywhere,” above.]
- nullaque tenebrarum caligine — and by no darkness of shadows. [Note: [Col. 0165] AB read *nulloque t. calig.*, retaining the abbreviated following words and masculine/neuter *nulloque* instead of feminine *nullaque*, “and by no.”]
- nullo — by no, qualifying obstacle. [Note: [Col. 0165] B reads *nulloque*, “and by no.”]
- suscepit — took, of the Theologian’s two likenesses. [Note: [Col. 0165] B reads *accepit*, “received/took.”]
- qui — which, referring to the air. [Note: [Col. 0165] A reads *qua*, a feminine/ablative form, instead of masculine nominative *qui*.]
- Innocuae — harmless, of the upper flames. [Note: [Col. 0165] B* adds in the margin: “The argument here is that fire in the upper region neither consumes nor burns, but only shines, because it finds no bodily matter there on which to act by burning.”]
- reperiunt — they find. [Note: [Col. 0165] B spells it *repperiunt*.]
- veluti — as, of the outflow into rivers. [Note: [Col. 0165] A reads *velut*, “as/as though.”]
- pantheris — of a panther. [Note: [Col. 0165] B* adds in the margin *vel pantherae*, “or *pantherae*,” an alternative genitive form meaning “of a panther.”]
- speciem — appearance. [Note: [Col. 0165] B*’s correction by erasure. A reads *specimen*, “example/likeness,” instead of *speciem*, “appearance.”]
- pardalin eam — [clothing] it as a leopard. [Note: [Col. 0165] AB join the words as *pardalineam*, “leopard-like,” an adjective instead of noun and pronoun.]
- constituuntur — are constituted. [Note: [Col. 0167] A has *con*; a later hand adds *constituuntur*, “are constituted,” in that manuscript’s margin.]
- constitutione — by the constitution/structure. [Note: [Col. 0167] Thus C. A and B read accusative *constitutionem*, “constitution/structure,” instead of ablative *constitutione*.]
- obtinent — occupy. [Note: [Col. 0167] B spells it *optinent*, as frequently elsewhere.]
- utriusque — of each/both, qualifying nature. [Note: [Col. 0167] B and B* have *utrius*; B* writes *-que* above, completing *utriusque*, “of each/both.”]
- Unguentum — ointment. [Note: [Col. 0167] Thus C and B*’s correction. A spells it *ungentum*; B *ingentum*. These are the actual manuscript forms of the ointment word.]
- alabastrum — alabaster vessel. [Note: [Col. 0167] B spells it *alabaustrum*.]
- Lapis angularis — cornerstone. [Note: [Col. 0167] B* adds in the margin: “Why Christ is called the cornerstone.”]
- duabus — two, qualifying natures. [Note: [Col. 0167] B*’s correction. AB read masculine/neuter *duobus* instead of feminine *duabus*, both meaning “two.”]
- effecta — made/become, of one substance. [Note: [Col. 0167] B* writes *est*, “is/has,” above to complete the verb.]
- angulositatem — angularity, the first question concerning Christ. [Note: [Col. 0167] Thus AB. C reads *anguloritatem*, a variant formation for “angularity.”]
- praeter — apart from/besides. [Note: [Col. 0167] A reads *propter*, “because of.”]
- ait — says, in the Apostle’s statement about the sexes. [Note: [Col. 0167] B omits *ait*.]
- neque — nor, before female. [Note: [Col. 0167] B reads *nec*, likewise “nor.”]
- in re — in reality. [Note: [Col. 0167] B joins the words as *inre*.]
- angularem — angular, in the fivefold mode. [Note: [Col. 0167] Conjectural. A reads *angulorem*, a malformed variant apparently intended as “angular”; BC read *angulorum*, “of angles.”]
- περὶ φύσεων — On Natures. [Note: [Col. 0167] B* adds in the margin: “namely, concerning natures.”]
- contemnit — despises. [Note: [Col. 0167] B spells it *contempnit*, here and throughout.]
- pantheri — panther, in the mystical identification. [Note: [Col. 0167] Thus ABC; the supplied form is *pantheri*.]
- vult — wills, that all should be saved. [Note: [Col. 0167] ABC omit *vult*; B* adds it in the margin.]
- aut — or, introducing the second interpretation. [Note: [Col. 0167] Thus C. A reads *ac*, “and”; B omits it; B* adds *aut*, “or,” in the margin.]
- quo — by which, of divine zeal. [Note: [Col. 0167] Thus C and B*’s correction by erasure. AB read *quod*, “which/that,” instead of ablative *quo*.]
- devorat — devours. [Note: [Col. 0167] A reads *devoverat*, “he had vowed/devoted,” not “devoured.”]
- imaginatur — is represented. [Note: [Col. 0167] B reads *imaginatus est*, “was/has been represented,” rather than the present tense.]
- omnium — of all, in the quoted introduction to the worm. [Note: [Col. 0167] Omitted; the editor supplied *omnium* from the translation and Greek text.]
- omnium — of all, in the exposition of the worm. [Note: [Col. 0167] B* corrects to dative/ablative *omnibus*, “to/than all,” instead of genitive *omnium*.]
- vilius — more lowly. [Note: [Col. 0167] AB omit *vilius*; C has it, and B* adds it in the margin.]
- vel ut — or, as, introducing the more explicit translation. [Note: [Col. 0167] Thus C. A and B read *velud*, a spelling of “as/as though.”]
- vel — or, between more obscure and dissimilar. [Note: [Col. 0167] B reads *quam*, “than.”]
- per prophetam — through the prophet. [Note: [Col. 0167] Thus C. AB omit *per*, “through.” B* first corrects by erasure to nominative *propheta*, “prophet,” then restores accusative *prophetam*, adding *per* in the margin.]
- Nihil — nothing, in the comparison of the worm’s lowliness. [Note: [Col. 0167] B* adds in the margin *Not. morum (?) ad humilitatem*—“Note on conduct (?) toward humility.” The source itself questions *morum*.]
- limo — mud. [Note: [Col. 0167] A reads *umo*, an uncertain form in place of *limo*, “mud.”]
- ego — I, in the second explanation of the worm. [Note: [Col. 0167] B* adds in the margin: “I am a worm and not a human being.”]
- vermis — worm, after non homo. [Note: [Col. 0167] B reads *vermis*, “worm,” with punctuation added by B*.]
- penetro — I penetrate. [Note: [Col. 0167] Thus C and B*’s correction. AB spell it *penitro*; no different meaning is implied by the spelling.]
- substantia mea — my substance, in the exposition. [Note: [Col. 0169] B omits *mea*, “my.”]
- sapientia — wisdom. [Note: [Col. 0169] B corrects to accusative *sapientiam*, “wisdom,” instead of nominative *sapientia*.]
- sinibus — recesses/bosom, of created nature. [Note: [Col. 0169] Thus C. AB read *finibus*, “boundaries/limits.”]
- dum est homo — while he is human. [Note: [Col. 0169] B omits *est*, “is”; B* writes it above.]
- quingentesimo — five-hundredth, qualifying year. [Note: [Col. 0169] B spells it *quingentissimo*.]
- phoenicis — of the phoenix. [Note: [Col. 0169] ABC spell it *fenicis*, retaining the genitive sense.]

It follows: Thus all theologians and prophets, formed by the hidden inspiration [Note: [Col. 0169] B: “obscure inspiration.”] of the Holy Spirit, distinguish the Holy of holies from the holy and undefiled things, and honor a holy representation unlike them [Note: [Col. 0169] A: “and.”], so that divine things may neither be handled by the impure nor the devoted contemplators of wondrous images remain as though these were true forms. And they honor divine things by true negations and, down to the lowest [realms], by various likenesses of compacted resonances.

“In this way,” he says [Note: [Col. 0169] *inquit* omitted in B, added in the margin by B*.], all the theologians of representations—whom he now calls *theosophers*, that is, “those wise in divine things”—and all the prophets, formed by the hidden inspiration of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0169] *occulta* omitted in B.], distinguish the Holy of holies from the holy and undefiled things [Note: [Col. 0169] C thus; B *sanctis contaminatis*, “holy contaminated things”; B* corrected above to *sanctis et incontaminatis*, “holy and undefiled things.”].

It is as though he said plainly: By the symbols of dissimilar representations—which are rightly called undefiled, because they have been inscribed by the divine Spirit in the minds of theologians and prophets—the Holy of holies, that is, intellectual essences and Divinity itself, are distinguished from the holy and undefiled things through the theologians’ ineffable administration of supreme wisdom. Thus those holy and immaculate symbols are reverently venerated by those who understand what they signify, while the Holy of holies, whose images they are [Note: [Col. 0169] *sunt* omitted in B, added in the margin by B*.], is separated from them by intellectual discernment.

The divine symbols, therefore, are holy [Note: [Col. 0169] B: “are holy things”;], but the realities whose symbols they are are the Holy of holies [Note: [Col. 0169] B: “are holy things”;], that is, the holy intellects of holy things. “And they honor a holy representation unlike them”: that is, the representation of those divine realities, although it is far unlike the intellects signified through it, is honored by the holy theologians and prophets [Note: [Col. 0169] B: “and.”]. For while they purely understand the realities signified, they honor those realities first, since they are divine and supramundane. Consequently, they also rightly venerate their representations [Note: [Col. 0169] B has *significationes*, “significations,” instead of *figurationes*, “representations”], whether these have been transferred from the higher, middle, or lowest parts of material creation; and, by intellectual distinction and discernment, they separate the realities themselves from their representations. They do not accept representations in place of true intellects, nor true intellects in place of representations; rather, with all confusion removed, they assign to each its own definitions and cognitions.

And as though someone were asking why dissimilar holy symbols of holy intellects are both represented and honored by theologians [Note: [Col. 0169] B: “dissimilar symbols”;]—for it would seem more reasonable [Note: [Col. 0169] B* adds above the line: *interpositio*, “insertion.”] that similar symbols should be conformed to holy intellects than dissimilar ones—the reason for the dissimilar representations is given. And [Note: [Col. 0169] B* written above the line: *Ad*, “and.”], he says, this that you ask has been discovered so that divine things may not be “easy to handle,” that is, so that divine intellects may not become accessible and exposed to the impure: namely, to polluted human beings contaminated by the filth of sins, impiety, or perhaps pride. Such people are not permitted even to see the perceptible mysteries of divine things, much less to handle them. For when they behold the divine mysteries, they despise them as childish matters and playthings signifying no spiritual understanding [Note: [Col. 0169] B: “intellectual understanding.”].

It should be noted that where we translated “easy to handle,” the Greek has εὐχείρωτα, which we may render “easy.” The sense, then, is this: For this reason the wise in divine things shape the mysteries of divine realities in forms unlike those realities themselves—obscure, mixed [Note: [Col. 0169] The words “which we may render … mixed” are omitted in B and added in the margin by B*.], and taken from material things—so that the divine mysteries may not become easy for impure souls, unworthy of the knowledge of truth, to understand. This is one reason for the dissimilarity of the holy images.

The other is the reason he adds next, saying: “Nor may the devoted contemplators of wondrous *agalmata* remain as though they were true forms” [Note: [Col. 0169] B* has a marginal note explaining what *agalma* means.]. For this purpose also the representations were made obscure and dissimilar: namely, so that those who diligently contemplate wondrous *agalmata*, that is, divine representations [Col. 0170D], may not place the end of their contemplation in the forms themselves, supposing them to be real and not representational, and refusing to raise the power of their inward contemplation beyond them.

Such an error has seized, and still seizes, many—indeed almost everyone [Note: [Col. 0169] B: “everyone”—who suppose that perceptible mysteries signify nothing higher than themselves [Col. 0171A]. By this very fact they approve false things as true, deceive themselves, and mislead the simpler-minded, remaining in the representations and neglecting to fix the mind’s gaze upon their true mystical meaning.

The Apostle says of such people: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” For the letter kills everyone who thinks that nothing exists beyond what he perceives, since he neither can nor wishes to reach the spirit, that is, the meaning of the letter itself. Here it should be noted that the blessed Apostle does not mean only that letter [Note: [Col. 0171] *dicit*, “says,” omitted by ABC and supplied conjecturally] which is the image of speech, but generally all mystical figures, whether described in words, deeds, or representations of perceptible things throughout the whole sequence of divine Scripture. Through these, the mysteries of spiritual and supramundane realities are signified for the exercise of the human mind and its elevation from earthly things to heavenly ones [Note: [Col. 0171] B* marginal note: “He signified.”].

Now *agalma*, whose singular nominative is declined in the plural as *agalmata*, is understood in several ways even by the Greeks themselves [Note: [Col. 0171] B* marginal note: “The word *agalma* has several meanings.”]. They call every expressed image that produces joy in those who look upon it an *agalma* [Note: [Col. 0171] B: “impressed image.”]. They also call an idol [Note: [Col. 0171] AB: *ydolum*] or image [Note: [Col. 0171] A: *symulachrum*] an *agalma*, especially when it is extremely similar to the one whose image and likeness it is [Note: [Col. 0171] B* adds in the margin: “or whose image it is”; *est* omitted in B.]. Indeed, *agalma* is said as though from ἄγαν ἅλμα [Note: [Col. 0171] B* marginal note: “that is, *aganamia*”], that is, “a very lofty thing.”

Thus the holy theologians also honor divine mysteries by true negations, that is, through negations that are truly predicated of divine things. As was said above, in statements about divine things the negations are true [Note: [Col. 0171] B: “and true”; A: “these negations”;], whereas affirmations are metaphorical and, as it were, acquired externally [Col. 0171C], or altogether unconnected—that is, not proper. They honor divine things not only through true negations but also through various likenesses, or, as it is translated, through alien likenesses of compacted resonances, that is, consonant representations, down to the lowest [levels], namely, the forms and appearances of material and bodily things. For just as, as was established above [Note: [Col. 0171] *est* omitted in B, added above the line by B*.], divine things can be more honored—that is, more expressly signified—through true negations than through transferred affirmations, so those same divine things are conveyed to human minds more fully and significantly through the alien likenesses and representations of the lowest material things than through the beautiful forms of heavenly and rational realities.

For just as one who says of God, “He is invisible; he is incomprehensible [Note: [Col. 0171] *incomprehensibilis est* omitted in B]; he is not substance; he is not essence; he is none of the things that exist”—for he surpasses everything that is said and understood—speaks of him properly, so one who says of him, “He is essence, he is substance, he is goodness, he is truth,” and other similar things, speaks not properly but metaphorically [Note: [Col. 0171] *de eo* omitted in B.]. And accordingly, just as the one who denies that he is any particular thing honors him more than the one who affirms that he is some particular thing [Note: [Col. 0171] *eum* omitted in ABC and added in the margin by B*], so the one who surrounds him with the form of a beast signifies and honors him more than the one who represents him in human form, adorned with gold and gems and clothed in precious garments, or enclosed within the most splendid heavenly bodies [Note: [Col. 0171] B has *consignificat*, “signifies together with,” instead of *significat*. *qui* omitted in B.].

For the latter thinks that he subsists in this way; but the former is not deceived when he presents [Note: [Col. 0171] Conjecture; ABC have *tractat*, “handles.”] bestial, ugly, or confused forms concerning him. Led by natural insight and true reason, he confidently denies altogether that he is thus [Note: [Col. 0171] B: “thus confidently”; B* corrected above to “confidently denies that he is thus.”].

It follows: “Therefore it is not inconsequential if they also fashion the heavenly essences according to the stated causes through inconvenient, dissimilar likenesses.”

“Not irrationally,” he says, “and not inconsistently [Note: [Col. 0171] B: “consequently”; B* corrected above to *inconsequenter*, “inconsistently”], according to the causes stated above, the holy theologians form the heavenly essences through inconvenient—or, more significantly translated, obscure and dissimilar—likenesses.”

Thus far he has discussed the exposition of the holy representations of supramundane intellects. What follows is an apology explaining why he entered upon this inquiry [Note: [Col. 0171] *venerit* omitted in AB and added in the margin by B*; C has “why he came into this acquisition.”]. He therefore begins his defense in this way:

“For perhaps we would not have entered into the inquiry, nor into anagogical interpretation, through diligent investigation of divine things, out of necessity, equally not” [Note: [Col. 0171] B* marginal correction: “not equally.”].

“Perhaps not,” he says; for the causal conjunction *enim*, “for,” is superfluous [Note: [Col. 0171] A: *vaccat*, “is superfluous.”]. “We would not have entered into this inquiry concerning the mystical representations of Holy Scripture out of necessity, that is, from poverty of understanding; for the mystical meaning of the holy representations was not hidden from us. Nor would we have entered into anagogy—that is, into the sense that leads upward—through diligent investigation of the divine symbols, unless their deformity had forced us [Note: [Col. 0171] C and B* corrected above; AB have “did not force us”] to the manifestational reformation of the angels. This deformity does not allow our mind to remain in the dissimilar constructions of the forms; rather, it makes the mind struggle to deny material passions to spiritual substances and become accustomed to being purely extended through visible things into the supramundane heights.”

It is as though he said: We would not descend into the diligent investigation of this inquiry concerning divine symbols unless the deformity—or, as it were, ugliness—of the forms through which the angelic powers are manifested in the divine Scriptures compelled and forced us, as though unwilling [Note: [Col. 0171] *nos* omitted in AB, added above the line by B*.]. This deformity does not permit our mind to remain in the dissimilar forms of the divine intellects [Col. 0173A]. By this he means condescension toward those who receive the divine symbols carnally. But it permits our mind to struggle against the false fantasies of those who think vainly [Note: [Col. 0173] C thus; A has the fragment *vana cogitati...*, later corrected to *vanas cogitantium*; B has *vanas cogitantium*], to deny that material passions belong carnally to spiritual substances [Note: [Col. 0173] C and B* corrected; AB have “and that material things are passive”], and, becoming accustomed—that is, learning—it permits our mind to extend itself purely, namely, to be carried undefiled through visible mysteries into the supramundane heights of the divine intellects.

He concludes this briefly by saying: “These things have indeed been said by us because of the material and inconvenient descriptions of the angelic images in the divine utterances.”

After the apology there follows a brief division of the work to come. For he says: “Next, however, it is necessary to distinguish what we judge the hierarchy itself to be and what benefit the hierarchy itself brings to those who have received a place in the hierarchy” [Note: [Col. 0173] A: “what”; B: “to distinguish later”; conjecture: AB have “the hierarchy itself.”].

That is: henceforth we must distinguish, defining with clear boundaries, what we understand the general hierarchy, that is, the priesthood, itself to be, and what benefit each particular hierarchy brings to those who participate in the general hierarchy [Note: [Col. 0173] *videlicet* omitted in B]. The entire purpose of this work is to discuss the general priesthood and its forms.

Then follows the prayer: “Let Christ be the guide of the discourse, if I may say so, my Christ, the inspiration of the manifestation of the whole hierarchy” [Note: [Col. 0173] B*: “it is permitted.”]. “The guide,” he says, “of my discourse, if I may say so, is my Christ, from whom the whole priestly configuration begins and receives inspiration” [Note: [Col. 0173] B*: *ierarchiae* corrected from AB’s *ierarchiae*].

At the end of the entire chapter he addresses Timothy [Note: [Col. 0173] AB: *Thimotheum*], bishop of Ephesus—or certainly all who might read this discourse—saying:

“But you, O child, according to the holy legislation of our priestly tradition, listen yourself in a holy and seemly manner, having become divinely instructed in the wondrous things that have been said, in God and in doctrine; and, veiling the holy things within the secret place of your soul, guard them from the impure multitude as things without form. For it is not lawful [Note: [Col. 0173] B*: “it is lawful,” corrected above to “it is not lawful.”], as the utterances say, to cast before swine the undisturbed, light-bearing, and beneficent ornament of invisible pearls” [Note: [Col. 0173] *beneficumque* corrected in B; A has *benefictumque*, B *beneficiumque*.].

By these words he exhorts all ministers of the divine mysteries, as the priestly proclamation teaches, to listen in a holy and honorable manner to the divine utterances, perfected in God and in divine doctrine; to enclose the holy mysteries within the secret places of the soul; and to guard them from the impure multitude of those who think carnally and are utterly ignorant of spiritual things [Note: [Col. 0173] C and B* corrected; AB have “and of the spiritual thing”], a multitude unworthy [Col. 0174A] not only of the visible mysteries but also of their understanding [Note: [Col. 0173] B: “which is impure and unworthy”; *etiam* omitted in B and added above the line by B*.].

These things are uniform, for they signify one thing, in which all things are one. Divine Scripture forbids casting the invisible pearls of the divine intellects before swine—that is, before proud and impure human beings—and [forbids casting] their ornament—by “pearls” I mean their distinct, luminous, and beneficent adornment [Note: [Col. 0173] B* adds “and luminous.”]—that is, an adornment beneficent and deifying to those who love and understand it.

# CHAPTER III

Its preface is: “What the hierarchy is, and what benefit comes through the hierarchy” [Note: [Col. 0173D] The words “Its preface … benefit” are supplied conjecturally and in accordance with the faithfulness of J. Scotus’s version. After finishing Chapter II, A proceeds, leaving a space of nearly six lines, directly with the words of the following chapter. B, however, gives the false title in illuminated letters: “Chapter Eight” (B* adds in the margin: “Chapter III”), and likewise continues with the words of the following chapter.].

## § 1

“The hierarchy, according to me, is a divine order and knowledge and action, assimilated, insofar as possible, to the divine form, ascending proportionally into the likeness of God according to the divinely imparted illuminations.”

The chapter begins with a definition of the hierarchy. “According to me,” he says—that is, insofar as I understand it—the hierarchy is a divine order, knowledge, and action. He therefore concludes the definition of the hierarchy in three parts. For in every divine priesthood it is necessary to consider these three things: by what order and rank someone is established, perfects, and is perfected; how he is illuminated and illuminates in knowledge—that is, in the understanding and discipline of divine things—and to what extent he advances, is purified, and purifies in the performance of the commandments.

Accordingly, the perfected disposition of the soul is accomplished in order, knowledge of spiritual realities in knowledge, and observance of the divine commandments in action. In this threefold triangle the fullness of the universal Church is formed, whether in heaven or on earth. Hence the confession of the highest Good, from which these three proceed, is threefold. Hence also the conversion of the rational creature to its God is threefold: it is reformed through faith, hope, and charity, and returns to its natural dignity and grace.

It should also be noted that the theologian has used a change in the definition of the hierarchy. The definition itself seems to proceed directly as follows: “The hierarchy is action, knowledge, and divine order” [Note: [Col. 0173] C thus; *est* omitted in AB and added above the line by B*.]. For in the ascents of the virtues, action in carrying out the divine commandments comes first. Through it the inward eye of the soul—or of the rational [Note: [Col. 0173] The words *sive rationalis* omitted in B and added in the margin by B*; above *rationalis* B writes “of the human being”] or intellectual [Note: [Col. 0173] B* writes above the line “of the angel”] creature—is purified, so that it may endure the innermost rays of the highest Good, diffused throughout all things, free and released from every vain fantasy and every darkness of the vices.

Then follows the vision of knowledge, which naturally desires to contemplate everything that exists after God and to refer to the praise of the Creator everything that it can examine with the powers of understanding. From there each person ascends into his own order—by “order” I mean the most perfect disposition of divine contemplation—subject according to the grace granted to him; that is, into God himself, to whom he will be like and in whom he will stand immutably.

This is what follows: “Assimilated to the divine form insofar as possible,” that is, the hierarchy itself and all who participate in it are made like the divine form, namely, the form of all that God is, insofar as a creature can participate in the likeness of the Creator; and it ascends into that likeness proportionally and fittingly, according to the illuminations divinely imparted to it [Col. 0175B], whether through the dignity of reason and intellect by nature [Note: [Col. 0175] A: “through the dignity”;], or through grace, which raises those who participate in it above natural illuminations into God himself.

After the definition of the hierarchy, there follows praise of the supreme Good, whose likeness every hierarchy desires:

“Divine beauty, as simple, as best, and as consummative (*τελεταρχικά*) [Note: [Col. 0175] B* marginal note: *theletarchica*, that is, consummative], is pure from every dissimilarity in general, distributive according to the worth of each person’s proper light [Note: [Col. 0175] The words “distributive … proper light” are omitted in AB and added in the margin by B*.], and perfective in the most divine sacrifice according to the compact and immutable formation of those perfected toward itself.”

“It is pure,” he says, “and wholly clean and free from every dissimilarity” [Note: [Col. 0175] B*: “from every [dissimilarity].”] is divine beauty—and not without reason, since it is simple, best, and the source of perfections and illuminations. For divine beauty itself is simple and best [Note: [Col. 0175] B* adds *est*, “is.”], and every purified life naturally desires to cleave to it and become like it. It deserved to be called *τελεταρχική* [Note: [Col. 0175] B* marginal note: *theletarchica*] by the holy theologians for no other reason than that it is *τελετὴ ἀρχῆς* [Note: [Col. 0175] ABC have *τελετὴ ἀρχίς*; B* adds *theletarchis* in the margin], that is, the principal sacrifice and the purifying sacrifice of the rational and intellectual creature.

It purifies the heavenly minds from ignorance of the highest Good and from that proud and irrational movement by which the apostate spirits have been cast down [Note: [Col. 0175] C thus; AB have *principati*, “made princes”; B* corrected to *projecti*, “cast down”] into eternal torment. It purifies human minds from every misty darkness that obstructs the eye of the mind—which philosophers call reason—from seeing the truth and delighting in its beauty. It purifies from every guilt deserving death and, finally, purifies from death itself eternally.

For the humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ is not the beginning of purification, although it was itself sacrificed as the holy and unique offering for the purification of the whole world, as it is written: “The blood of Christ, his Son”—that is, the Son of the Father—“cleanses us from every sin.” Rather, his divinity, together with that of the Father and the Holy Spirit, the one God, is the beginning of all purification, illumination, and perfection. This does not mean that that sacrifice, namely divinity, was sacrificed to anything superior to itself, since nothing is above it; rather, by that manner of speaking in which the cause is signified through the deed [Note: [Col. 0175] C and B* corrected; AB have *perfectum*, “perfected”], it is called a sacrifice. And since it is itself the cause and beginning of purification [Note: [Col. 0175] B: “is the purification”], it is not improperly called purification and sacrifice, since it is more than a sacrifice.

Hence Dionysius himself says in *Mystical Theology*, in the negations: “Nor is it a sacrifice,” wishing to declare of it that it is more than a sacrifice and the source of sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0175] B reverses the order: “wishing to declare that it is more than a sacrifice.”].

Why, then, did he add: “But distributive…”? [Note: [Col. 0175] B* marginal note: “From this point the exposition is lacking until almost the first third of Chapter VII. A later hand, apparently of the fifteenth century, added: ‘From this point, where after the beginning of Chapter III it says “distributive according to the worth of the proper light,” etc., the exposition is lacking until the seventh paragraph of Chapter VII, where after the beginning it says: “But the Cherubim themselves, their cognition and vision of God,” etc.’”]

[The divine itself …] [Col. 0176B] [lacuna: the manuscript’s long dotted gap marks a missing portion of the exposition. The accompanying editorial note states that the middle of the sentence has been cut away, and that neither the textual space nor any sign in the manuscripts indicates exactly that anything is missing here. In the manuscripts, immediately after “the divine itself,” the same line continues with “receptive of the giving of lights,” as though these were words of the same sentence, although in reality they already belong to Chapter VII. Thus a considerable part of the exposition is missing from this point almost to the middle of Chapter VII.]

# CHAPTER VII

[lacuna] “receptive of the giving of lights,” or, as it is translated more plainly, “receptive of the most exalted illumination,” that is, capable of receiving it.

For they possess the gnostic virtue, that is, the disposition of knowledge; they possess a God-seeing [Note: [Col. 0175] B* corrected to “a bare,” or “naked,” reading] contemplation that considers God; and the capacity for the most exalted illumination. They possess theoretical (*tereticam*) knowledge, that is, contemplative knowledge of the pre-operative virtue of divine beauty. They possess the fullness of wise tradition, namely, doctrine, which makes the souls capable of it wise [Note: [Col. 0175] A: “made wise.”]. They possess abundant communication toward the secondary orders, that is, toward the orders that follow them, of wisdom given by diffusion—or, as it is translated more plainly, “of wisdom granted by diffusion.”

The sense is this: They communicate to the orders that follow them the wisdom granted to them, by diffusion—that is, for the diffusion or in the diffusion of the wisdom first bestowed upon them—and through them it is diffused to the orders that follow [Note: [Col. 0175] B* corrected; AB have “scattered.”]. For first the highest Wisdom, which is God, is diffused immediately into them; then through them that diffusion flows down into lower beings like a river leaping downward [Col. 0176D].

After explaining the names of the Seraphim and Cherubim [Note: [Col. 0177] B has *seraphin et cherubin*, as very often] he next proceeds to explain the meaning of the word “Thrones” [Note: [Col. 0177] B* corrected; AB have “the meanings.”]:

“The very highest and compacted seats, diligently exalted above every disgrace of subjection, bearing upward supramundanely to the summit, and from every extremity ineffably placed on high in the most exalted region, and immutably and steadily established with all their powers around the truly exalted [One], receptive of the divine advent in complete impassibility and immateriality, God-bearing, and servantlike, open to divine receptions.”

In this sentence it is clear that certain very high and elevated seats are diligently raised above every lowering through degradation or trampling, bearing upward supramundanely; inflexibly placed on high from every extremity; immovably and firmly founded with universal virtues around the truly highest [One]; receptive of the divine advent in complete impassibility and immateriality; God-bearing; and, in the manner of servants, a seat open for divine receptions.

“The very highest and compacted or elevated seats,” he says—for the same expression is understood from what precedes. The Greek word is ambiguous: ἐπηρμένων may derive either from the verb ἐπάρω [Note: [Col. 0177] AB appear to read ἐπάρμω], meaning “I compact” or “I join together,” or from ἐπαίρω [Note: [Col. 0177] AB have ἐπάρω], meaning “I lift up” [Note: [Col. 0177] Caution: the manuscripts read *sustollo*, “I lift up.” Perhaps *sublevo*, “I raise up,” should be read; the two words differ scarcely at all in writing. *Sublevo* is expected because above the manuscripts twice had *sublevatarum*, “elevated,” not *sublatarum*, “lifted up.”]—and it is uncertain from which it is derived. He carefully explains this.

What does he explain? Clearly, that those seats are exalted, or raised above every disgrace, namely, the lowliness of subjection; or, more expressively translated, that they are raised above every lowering by trampling or walking upon them.

The sense is this: The name “Thrones” teaches that the highest divine seats are diligently exalted above every disgrace of subjection beneath the feet of many [Note: [Col. 0177] C and B* corrected *infirmitatis*, “weakness,” from *infimitatis*, “lowliness”], and above every low place that is worn down and diminished by the soles of those who trample and walk upon it—that is, humbled and placed beneath them. Therefore, just as things lofty and elevated are raised to the greatest height above the common level, which is trampled and walked upon everywhere as though disgracefully, so the order of the Thrones and of those like them—on which Divinity, reigning and judging all things, sits—is exalted above all and removed from the common lowliness, that is, from every material and lowly creature. The name “Thrones” teaches this most clearly.

It also teaches their virtue, which carries them above the world into the highest Good and ineffably raises them from every extremity of bodily creation—which appears, in comparison with intelligible realities, low and vile—to the most exalted [place], namely, God, who is most exalted and by participation in whom the Thrones themselves are exalted.

It teaches that they are “placed” or “founded,” that is, their placement and foundation, immutably, steadily, and firmly established with all their virtues around the truly exalted [One], namely, the highest Good, which, just as it is truly good, is also truly exalted.

It also teaches that they are “receptive,” that is, receptive of the divine advent from above, without passion or materiality, but in complete impassible immateriality. For they surpass all passible matter.

It also teaches that they are “God-bearing,” that is, that their virtue bears God. For they carry and convey God in the manner of servants—that is, obediently they praise him for carrying and conveying all things. For he is not carried but carries; he is not conveyed but conveys; nor does he sit in anything who causes everything to sit—that is, to rest—in him [Note: [Col. 0177] C and B* corrected; AB have *quae*, “which”].

It teaches that they are “open,” or, as it is translated more plainly, “offered,” that is, a seat for divine receptions. For they are the most exalted seats [Note: [Col. 0177] A: *subgesti*], lofty seats prepared and open for divine receptions—that is, for the reception of divine intellects—and spread open and suited for the divine session [Note: [Col. 0177] *et* omitted in B, apparently erased by B*].

## § 2

This, then, is the explanation of the names themselves, insofar as they concern us. “This,” he says, “is, as it seems to us and as it is understood by us, the exposition of the names of the three orders of the first hierarchy. But we must say what hierarchy we consider theirs.” That is, we must state what hierarchy—or what kind of hierarchy—we judge theirs to be [Note: [Col. 0177] C and corrected B*: *arbitramus*; AB *arbitramus*.].

I think it has already been sufficiently said that the contemplation of their entire hierarchy depends inflexibly upon a God-imitating, Godlike form [Note: [Col. 0177] According to the translation of Scotus and the Greek text; AB *imitati*, B* corrected to *imitate*.], and that every hierarchical activity is divided into sacred participation [Col. 0178C] and the transmission of pure purification, divine light, and perfecting knowledge.

“Every”—that is, the contemplation, or plainly the definition, of the universal hierarchy—“depends inflexibly upon a God-imitating, Godlike form” [Note: [Col. 0177] So C; AB *imitati*, B* *imitate*.], that is, upon what hangs down from above [Note: [Col. 0177] B* corrected; B *pendit*; C *quae suppendit*.] and derives its origin from the likeness [Note: [Col. 0177] A *similitudinem*.] of the divine beauty. For earlier, in the third chapter, he defined the universal hierarchy by saying: “Hierarchy is likeness and unity with God, insofar as possible.” I think it has now been sufficiently said that it is inflexible—that is, immutable.

I also think it has been sufficiently said that every hierarchical activity, or, as it is more plainly translated, every hierarchical operation, is divided into sacred participation in the principal hierarchy of all, which is the Divinity, and the transmission, from higher beings to lower, of pure purification, with no dissimilarity mixed into it; likewise into participation in and transmission of divine light; and into participation in and transmission of perfecting knowledge [Col. 0179A] [Note: [Col. 0179] B omits “and into perfecting knowledge … transmission.”]. For in the aforementioned third chapter [Note: [Col. 0179] B *capitulo tertio*.] he previously declared this threefold mode of the whole hierarchy: purification, illumination, and perfection. First it purifies those who participate in it; then it illuminates them with the knowledge of divine intellects; finally it perfects them in the immutable disposition of that knowledge.

Now let us proceed worthily to speak of the most exalted intellects and of how the hierarchy according to them is manifested by the sacred utterances. It is as though he were saying: Since the definition and division of the whole hierarchy have already been sufficiently stated by us above, let us now proceed worthily to speak of the highest divine intellects, namely, the principal orders of the first hierarchy; that is, let us inquire how the hierarchy that exists according to them—the hierarchy constituted in them—is manifested in the sacred utterances [Col. 0179B].

The first essences, which have been placed after their substantializing thearchy [Note: [Col. 0179] B* adds *sunt* above the line; AB omit *sunt*, which is present in the translation.] and arranged, as it were, in its vestibules, surpassing every created power, invisible and visible, must be judged to possess a proper and wholly uniform hierarchy.

The order of the words is this: It must be estimated—or plainly judged [Note: [Col. 0179] B* adds above the line: “that is, judged.”]—that a proper and wholly uniform hierarchy, equal in its orders, has been established in the first heavenly essences, which have been placed after their substantializing thearchy, namely, the Divinity, and arranged, as it were, in its vestibules—that is, in the orders nearest to it—surpassing every created power, invisible and visible.

For the first heavenly essences, placed and ordered in the first hierarchy [Note: [Col. 0179] B omits *hierarchia*; B* adds it in the margin.], surpass all created powers.

They must therefore be judged pure—not as though they had been freed from unclean stains and defilements, nor as though they had been received into material imaginings [Note: [Col. 0179] B* writes above the line: “as we are.”], but as pure from every subjection, higher than the other heavenly essences, and placed above every exalted temple, in accordance with the most excellent chastity, above all Godlike powers.

He now begins to treat more fully of the qualities of the first hierarchy [Note: [Col. 0179] B* corrects *qualitatem* to *qualitates*.]. “Pure,” he says—that is, cleansed from every dissimilarity—the first essences, namely, those of the heavenly hierarchies, must be considered, or, as it is more clearly translated, must be said to be pure, not as though they had been freed from unclean stains and defilements [Note: [Col. 0179] B* adds in the margin: “not pure as …,” and so forth.].

It is as though he were saying plainly: They are not liberated in the way that we mortal human beings are liberated from the unclean stains of sins and from the defilements of all our uncleanness, when divine grace performs and cooperates in our purification [Col. 0179D]. Nor are they received in the way that we are received when divine grace recalls us from material imaginings—that is, from the false and empty representations of material things by which the carnal soul, living wholly according to the flesh, is oppressed by desire for temporal things [Col. 0180A] [Note: [Col. 0179] A *cupidinem*; B *cupidinem*, with punctuation added by B*.] and led astray through the labyrinths of various errors, and, worst of all, is drawn away from the love and knowledge of truth. For they have never been stained by the filth of sins, never been oppressed or corrupted by material imaginings, and never been driven away from contemplation of the highest good [Note: [Col. 0179] B has *sunt repulsae*, “have been driven away.”].

Rather, they are pure and higher than the other heavenly essences, cleansed from every subjection—or, as it may be translated more explicitly, from every diminution—that is, from the contemptible inferiority and extremity of all material, mortal, local, and temporal things in comparison with the immaterial and immortal heavenly essences, which are without every local and temporal movement [Col. 0180B].

And this is what follows: “Placed above every exalted temple,” or, as it is translated more simply, “above every exalted sacred thing” [Note: [Col. 0179] Conjecture, in place of *sacro templo* in ABC]: for the Greeks call every sacred thing *ἱερός* (*hieros*), and especially a temple, “they are placed above all the most Godlike powers.”

“Above every exalted temple”—that is, above every perfect [Note: [Col. 0179] A *profecto*, “certainly.”], pure [Note: [Col. 0179] Conjecture, in place of ABC *modo*.], and undefiled spirit in which God both dwells and is worshiped, they are placed.

The text continues: “And received by their own movement in themselves, and by that same movement according to the inflexible order of those who love God” [Note: [Col. 0179] B* corrected in the margin to *ineffabiliter*, “ineffably.”].

From the preceding passage the verb must be supplied: it must be estimated or said [Note: [Col. 0179] B* corrected *dicendum*, “to be said.”] that the first essences have been received inflexibly [Note: [Col. 0179] B* corrected to *ineffabiliter*, “ineffably.”]. For they cannot be bent; they are turned about as though in a circular or spherical motion, by their own movement in themselves—that is, by a movement originating from themselves, since they move of themselves—and by that same movement. Their movement is uniform, since the expressions “stable movement” and “mobile stability” are most truly predicated of it.

And this is what follows: “According to the immutable movement of the God-loving order.” Every God-loving order turns around God with an immutable movement [Note: [Col. 0179] C and corrected B*: *inconversibili*; AB *inconversabili*.]—that is, with a movement that is in no way variable, but always uniform.

But what he says, “by their own movement in themselves,” requires careful investigation. If all things are moved by God, as true reason teaches, how are the heavenly essences, and especially the primordial ones, said to move around God by their own movement in themselves? For if someone should say that every creature, from the highest to the lowest, possesses its own movement—namely, a natural movement—one might ask him: What, then, is so great about placing it among the praises of the heavenly and most excellent Throne, if the same thing contributes no less to the praise of a worm, since every creature naturally possesses its own movement?

Perhaps, however, it is not unreasonable to answer this question as follows: Whatever is not moved by a creature superior to it, but receives the beginning of its movement immediately from the sole cause of all things, is rightly said to be moved by no one, since the cause of its movement is superessential and surpasses everything that is and everything that is not.

The other orders of the created universe, although they establish the beginning of their movement in the one cause of all things, are nevertheless moved and governed not immediately by him, but gradually through higher beings, with the lower always moved and governed through the higher.

Thus the most excellent orders of the heavenly essences are beautifully called and are *αὐτοκινητοί* (*autokinētoi*), that is, moved by themselves, because they move themselves through themselves and are moved from themselves. They are moved by no one superior to them except God himself, who is not properly the principle of the movement of any one thing, because he is the universal principle of all. But what is universal to all is proper to none.

For this reason not only the primordial causes of all things but also the most excellent heavenly orders are called *αὐτοκινητοί* [Col. 0181B].

The human soul, too, is not unreasonably called by philosophers *αὐτοκινητός* (*autokinētos*), that is, moved by itself [Note: [Col. 0181] So also the corrected reading in B*; AB *motam*, “moved,” feminine accusative.], because no creature is nearer to God. If it did not sin, it would be governed by no order superior to itself, since no order superior to it would arise—just as there will be none when it is recalled to the dignity of its original nature [Note: [Col. 0181] B perhaps *quum*, “when.”].

“And wholly ignorant of insult toward those subject to them.” This means that, although they have been established after God at the summit of the universal creation, they nevertheless do not know how to insult, or, as it is more plainly translated, to despise, those subject to them. And not only this: they also admonish and recall the orders subject to them to the love and knowledge of the common Creator [Note: [Col. 0181] B *admouent*, “urge.”].

He adds correspondingly: “But having the purest station of their own Godlike particularity, not liable to fall and immutable.”

That is: they not only do not know contempt toward those subject to them, but also possess the purest station of their own Godlike particularity, not liable to fall and immutable. For their purest station is plainly a foundation that does not fall, and rightly so, because it is immutable; it does not know how to be moved.

And what is that station? What is that foundation? It is plainly their own Godlike particularity, which every creature desires, whether knowingly or unknowingly; it is wholly free from chance and mutability and inflicts neither neglect nor contempt upon any creature it has made.

Thus the excellent essences, being altogether like and near to the very Form, following and imitating it in every respect, are moved in the immutable state and beauty of their nature, following the exemplar of the divine Principality [Note: [Col. 0181] B has *principalis principatus*; in Migne, *tus* is printed above *lis* in *principalis* to represent the manuscript reading.] [Note: [Col. 0181] C has *exempli*; AB *exempla*; B* corrects it to *exemplo*.], which they follow without any dissimilarity, by ineffable piety and love toward those subject to them, allowing none of them to perish or to be despised in any way [Note: [Col. 0181] C and A have *erga subjectos sibi subjectos*; B has the same, apparently with punctuation added by B*.].

“And again contemplative of sensible symbols and of intellectual speculation.”

From what precedes, it must also be supplied that they are to be judged contemplative of sensible symbols or of intellectual speculation, with “symbols” likewise understood. This sentence can be understood in two ways. The sense may be: They are contemplative of the sensible symbols or of the intellectual things—that is, of hidden understanding. For they contemplate the meaning of sensible symbols just as they contemplate that of intellectual ones.

The sensible symbols whose meaning the heavenly powers contemplate are the sacraments of the Old Law—for example, the tabernacle and everything that the Lord commanded to be done in it; then the visions of the prophets in various forms and figures; and finally the ecclesiastical mysteries of the New Testament. The holy angels clearly perceive the inner light of all these [Note: [Col. 0181] B *dare*; B* corrected to *clare*, “clearly.”].

What the intellectual symbols are does not readily occur to us, unless perhaps we say that the theophanies themselves, in which the form of truth—by itself invisible to every intellect—is present, are intellectual symbols for them in a manner still unknown to us: symbols lacking the likeness of material things. Thus, in the theophanies—that is, the divine appearances—which they contemplate with the intellectual eye, they perceive the innermost divine meanings, just as we are commanded, insofar as it is granted to us to understand, to recognize certain hidden divine mysteries through sensible symbols [Note: [Col. 0181] B *mysteria occulta*, “hidden mysteries.”].

It may also be understood in this way: The excellent essences must be judged contemplative of sensible symbols, or contemplative of intellectual speculation—that is, of the knowledge of intellectual things of whatever kind. We are not compelled to supply “symbols” in both places, but only in the first: “contemplative of intellectual things,” so that each person may supply what seems more plausible, whether things, mysteries, powers, or similar matters [Col. 0182C].

But how the heavenly essences, being wholly incorporeal, contemplate sensible symbols requires no small investigation, unless perhaps we say that they assume the condition of spiritual bodies, so that they know sensible things through the senses. Or certainly we must believe that they can perceive not only intellectual but also sensible things without any assistance from bodily senses, just as Elisha [Note: [Col. 0181] AB *helisaeus*.] saw Naaman the Syrian washing himself in the Jordan with the spiritual eye.

Nor are they to be judged as having been brought back to God by the variety of the sacred-scriptural theory, but as filled with all the knowledge of immaterial, higher light [Note: [Col. 0183] B* corrects the reading toward *immateriali scientia*, “immaterial knowledge.”], and as filled, insofar as permitted, with contemplation of the formative and principal beauty, and of the superessential and thrice-shining contemplation [Note: [Col. 0183] B* corrects the syntax to *refertas*, “filled.”].

He does not mean that they should be judged contemplative of sensible symbols and of intellectual things—that is, of lofty understanding—as though they had been brought back to God from the variety of sacred-scriptural contemplation [Note: [Col. 0183] B* adds in the margin: “nor as …”]. For our mind, having abandoned the divine intellects through transgression, is brought back to them again through the variety and manifoldness of contemplation of sacred Scripture; but the principal essences of the first hierarchy are not brought back to God in this way. Rather, they are filled and satisfied with all the knowledge of immaterial and higher—that is, more divine—light, and, insofar as is permitted to a creature [Col. 0183B], with contemplation of the formative and principal beauty, and of the superessential and thrice-shining contemplation [Note: [Col. 0183] A omits the second *et*; B* corrects the text, and B seems to have had it.]. They are full of the supermundane knowledge of the light that surpasses every light, and of the causal beauty that gives form to all things, and thus of superessential contemplation [Note: [Col. 0183] B* adds “of light” in the margin.].

The hierarchy of the heavenly essences that surpass the others is therefore said to be full of superessential and thrice-shining contemplation—or “thrice-appearing,” or, as it is translated more simply, “triple-light”—because it immediately beholds, before the other lower essences, the superessential cause of the whole universe.

It is also rightly called triple-light because it shines three times: for it most clearly radiates in the three substances of one and the same essence for those who seek it devoutly and understand truly. It shines in the Father, from whom all things are; it shines in the Word, through whom all things are; and it shines in the gift [Note: [Col. 0183] B corrected; AB *domo*, “house,” evidently an error.] through which all things are blessed.

It should also be noted that where we translated “of beauty,” the Greek has *κάλλους* (*kallous*) [Note: [Col. 0183] Emended; AB *καλλου*, C *καλλοι*.], which may be translated both as “of form” and as “of beauty.” The sense does not differ, for divine goodness is formative and also beautifying of all things [Note: [Col. 0183] A reads *et formica*, evidently an error for *et formifica*.].

“Likewise made worthy through the communication of Jesus,” or, as it is translated more simply, “likewise worthy through communion with Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0183] AB *velut*; B *velud*; C *vel ut*.]. From what precedes, “made worthy” must be supplied: they must be judged worthy [Note: [Col. 0183] C and corrected B*; AB *digna*.] of communion—that is, of participation in Jesus. He says “likewise” so that we may understand either that, just as they were made worthy of the aforementioned powers, so also they were made worthy of communion with Jesus, or that the three orders of the first hierarchy were likewise—that is, equally—made worthy of communion with Jesus.

“They do not represent the Godlike likeness in sacredly made images, in formative figures, but, truly approaching him, in the first participation in the knowledge of his Godmaking lights.”

“They do not,” he says, “in sacredly made images”—that is, not in symbols divinely fashioned as ours are [Note: [Col. 0183] B *diviniter*, “divinely.”]—“formatively,” that is, in some definite form, represent, or more explicitly, reproduce, the Godlike likeness in themselves. For they are not still like children being formed in symbols and holy representations of the divine likeness by which we are now deified in faith [Note: [Col. 0183] A *deificamus*, “we deify.”] and will be deified in appearance [Note: [Col. 0183] B* adds “and in appearance” above the line.]. Rather, truly—that is, without any representation—they approach Jesus himself and possess the first participation in the knowledge of his Godmaking lights, that is, of his illuminations which deify them [Note: [Col. 0183] B* corrects ABC *deificum* to *deificorum*.]. No image, sacrament, or formed representation stands between them and Jesus Christ, to whom they are near.

“And because what is like God has been granted to them in the most subordinate way”—the preceding verb must again be repeated: “it must be judged” [Note: [Col. 0183] B* supplies *est aestimandum* above the line; AB *et*, “and.”]—“because what is like God has been granted to them.” That is, the likeness of God has been granted to them in the most subordinate way, namely, in the closest subordination [Note: [Col. 0183] C and corrected B*; AB *proximo*.]. For although all things are subject to God, the most subject—that is, the nearest subject—to him is the threefold order of the first hierarchy.

“And, insofar as possible, they participate in his preparatory-working power, in his deifying and human-loving powers.”

Since, he says, the divine likeness has been granted to them as to the nearest subject, these orders therefore also participate, insofar as is granted to them, in the preparatory-working power that works beforehand in them, in his deifying and human-loving—that is, merciful or humanity-loving—powers, since these powers cooperate in and administer our salvation and deification [Note: [Col. 0183] AB omit *cum*; B* adds it in the margin; C has *ut*.].

“And likewise perfected—not as illuminated by the analytical knowledge arising from the sacred variety, but as filled with the first and transcendent deification, according to the highest possible knowledge among angels of divine works.”

They must likewise be judged perfected—that is, perfected equally with the preceding benefits—not as though they had been illuminated, as we are, by the sacred variety of symbols in analytical knowledge or discipline [Note: [Col. 0183] A and B: *in analyticam scientiam vel disciplinam*, “into analytical knowledge or discipline”; B* adds punctuation.]. For *ἐπιστήμην* (*epistēmēn*) signifies both: it is translated both as “knowledge” and as “discipline.”

Our mind, illuminated through that discipline which the Greeks call *ἀναλυτική* (*analytikē*), is brought back through the sacred variety of symbols into the height of heavenly deification. For dialectical discipline has two parts, one called *διαιρετική* (*diairetikē*), the other *ἀναλυτική* (*analytikē*). *διαιρετικὴ* possesses the force of division: it divides the unity of the highest genera from the top downward until it reaches indivisible species and establishes the limit of division in them. *Ἀναλυτική*, on the other hand, beginning from the indivisible things and proceeding upward through the same stages by which the other descended, turns back and gathers the divisions of the opposite part and restores them to the unity of the highest genera. For this reason it is called “reductive” or “returning” [Note: [Col. 0185] B *recitiva*; B* corrected to *reditiva*, “returning.”].

Accordingly, the rational soul, paying the penalty for its transgression, was divided and split into the manifold and multiform desires of temporal things, as if by a certain diaeretic power [Note: [Col. 0185] Conjecture; AB *quedam diaretica vi*; B* corrects *diaretica* to *dialetica*.]—or, according to C, “was imparted by a certain dioretic power” [Note: [Col. 0185] C *quadam dioretica impertita*.]—until it set the limit of its division in the love of bodily things [Note: [Col. 0185] B* corrects *posuerit*, “may have set,” to *posuit*, “set.”], beyond which it could not go.

But afterward, anticipated, saved, assisted, and recalled by the grace of its Creator, it is gathered back into itself through certain analytical steps, and then restored, through the power of deification, to the unity of its Creator, which it had torn apart by sinning.

It is not so with the heavenly essences, especially the eminent ones, which had never broken the unity of their Creator [Note: [Col. 0185] B *diruperant*; B* corrected to *diruperunt*, “had broken.”]. They must not be judged to be brought back by *ἀναλυτική* [Note: [Col. 0185] ABC *ἀναλυτικα*.], that is, by reductive or returning knowledge [Note: [Col. 0185] C; AB *recidiva*, “restorative.”]. Rather, as beings filled with the first and transcendent deification, according to the most eminent knowledge of divine works, insofar as it is granted to angels, we must honor them, because they are immediately illuminated and perfected by the divine power itself.

And this is what follows:

“For they are not sanctified through other holy essences, but by the thearchy itself” [Note: [Col. 0185] From the Greek text and the translation; AB has *hierarchia*, “hierarchy.”], “they are immediately extended toward it, surpassing every transcendent power and order; they are placed in wholly most chaste strength; they are led, insofar as is permitted, into contemplation of immateriality and invisible beauty; as the first essences around God, they are initiated into the knowable principles of divine works [Note: [Col. 0185] A, B, and C read *fieri*, “to be made”; B* adds *trans-* above the line and corrects an erased reading to *feri*, perhaps *dici*, “to be said.”]; and they have been most exaltedly sanctified by the prince of perfection.”

This sentence requires no explanation, although in some places the interpretation is uncertain. Where we translated “toward the wholly most chaste strength,” it may also be translated “toward the wholly most chaste inflexibility.” For the Greek has *ἀρρεπές* (*arre­pes*) [Note: [Col. 0185] AB *ἀρρεπης ἀπρεπης*; C *panarepes*; the Greek text reads *παναρρεπές*.], which signifies both strength and inflexibility [Note: [Col. 0185] B omits *est*, “is.”]. The sense nevertheless does not differ, since true strength cannot be bent by anyone.

Likewise, where we have “invisible beauty,” one may put “intelligible beauty,” with the same meaning. For invisible beauty is nothing other than intelligible beauty, since *εὐπρέπεια* (*euprepeia*) can be translated both as “beauty” and as “comeliness” [Note: [Col. 0185] AB *εὐπρεπια*; C *euprepia*.].

Where we have “insofar as permitted,” one may say “insofar as it is allowed,” “insofar as the law permits,” or “insofar as is just.” For the one Greek word *θεμιτόν* (*themiton*) is translated in all these ways, since whatever is *fas* is permitted, lawful, and just.

Likewise, where we have, “as the first essences around God, they are initiated into the knowable principles of divine works,” instead of “initiated” one may translate “perfected,” “taught,” “instructed,” or “imbued.” All these interpretations derive from the one Greek verb *μυοῦμαι* (*myoumai*), whose third-person plural is *μυοῦνται* (*myountai*) [Note: [Col. 0185] AB *μυονται*; C *myan*.], and it can be translated by all the interpretations just mentioned, which suit this passage. For when *μυοῦνται* is translated as “they close their eyes,” I do not see how that meaning fits the present sentence [Note: [Col. 0185] AB *μύονταν*; C *myonte*.].

Where we have “they have been sanctified,” we may also put “sacrificed” and “offered,” while retaining the same meaning [Note: [Col. 0185] C and corrected B*; AB *posuimus*, “we have placed.”].

The “prince of perfection” is what is called in Greek *τελεταρχὶα* (*teletarchia*), namely, the Divinity itself, which most exaltedly—that is, at the summit of the universe—sanctifies, sacrifices, and offers the orders of the first hierarchy to itself.

## § 3

Thus the theologians plainly declare that the subordinate orders of the celestial essences are orderly instructed by those established above them in deifying knowledge; but that the highest of all are illuminated by the very Principle of Divinity, insofar as is permitted by divine law. [Note: In A, *a* is omitted; B* adds it in the margin.]

The theologians, he says, declare this most openly—namely, the prophets in their visions: that within the dispositions, or plainly ordered ranks, of the celestial essences, the subordinate orders are instructed by those established above them, that is, by the higher orders, according to an ordered law, in deifying sciences—that is, in the manifold disciplines of divine intelligences, which deify them. But the higher than all the others—namely, the three orders of the first hierarchy, which surpass the other celestial essences in dignity—are illuminated by Divinity itself, insofar as divine law permits, in ineffable doctrines.
