For Divinity itself teaches the orders nearest to it; they, in turn, instruct those below them; and thus, step by step, divine teaching descends through the higher orders to the lower, down to the last ornament. [Col. 0186C]

For they introduce certain of these essences as having been sacredly instructed by those preceding them: that the Lord is the Lord of the celestial powers and the King of glory, received into the heavens in human form.

He proves what he has said by an example. “For,” he says, “the theologians introduce in their visions certain essences instructed by those above them.” And in what have they been instructed? Plainly in this: that the Lord of the celestial powers and the King of glory, in the very humanity which he had received from us and for our sake, was taken up into the heavens. That is, the humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the Lord of powers and the King of glory, was exalted after the resurrection into his own divinity, which they call “the heavens”; and that, while the properties of both natures—namely, the divine and the human—remain unchangeably through the unity of substance, just as the Word became flesh, so flesh became the Word: wholly God in all his natures.

And do not be surprised that Christ’s divinity is called “the heavens” in the plural. For if he himself is the manifold and infinite Wisdom of the Father, although he is one and indivisible; and if Christ’s divinity itself is the Father’s one and singular house, yet in it are many dwelling places, what prevents the same reality from being believed and understood as both “heaven” and “the heavens”? “Heaven,” on account of the excellence of its supersubstantiality; “the heavens,” on account of the manifold infinity of its wisdom, for “there is no number of his wisdom.” [Col. 0187A]

Certain celestial powers, however, continually learn from those above them how Jesus is the Lord of the celestial powers and the King of glory, and how his humanity has been assumed into divinity—not so that they may understand the manner of his assumption, for it surpasses every intellect, but so that they may recognize that the assumption itself has taken place supernaturally and ineffably.

Others, however, seeking him with Jesus Christ himself [Note: C omits *Christum*; it is present in the translation and in the Greek text], and learning from him, on our behalf, the knowledge of his divine activity, reveal him teaching them and lavishly manifesting to them his human kindness. [Col. 0187B]

“The theologians,” he says, “also introduce certain”—that is, the most excellent—“celestial essences as always being immediately with Jesus himself, seeking and learning from him the knowledge of his divine activity on our behalf,” that is, of his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. And they introduce Jesus himself as teaching them immediately and manifesting these things to them, lavishly bestowing—that is, bestowing on them before he bestows on the others, or, as it may also be translated, lavishly displaying—his human, that is, his merciful kindness toward the salvation of the human race. [Note: B reads *eis* for *eis*; the difference is orthographic.]

“For I discuss justice,” he says, “and the judgment of Salvation.” [Col. 0187C]

The statement of Holy Scripture confirms that the Lord Jesus always teaches the celestial essences nearest to him. “I,” he says—namely, Jesus—“discuss the justice and judgment of the Savior,” indeed of myself, who am the salvation, peace, and redemption of celestial and terrestrial beings. For what greater justice is there than that the Creator should recall from their errors the creature whom he had made in his own image and restore it to likeness with himself? And what greater judgment than that he should punish in the creature what he did not make, and liberate what he did make?

Hence the Psalmist says: “I shall sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord”—mercy, namely, in liberating nature; judgment, in punishing sin.

But I wonder that even the first celestial essences—and indeed all of them together—so surpass the others in thearchic illuminations that they reverently seek questions indirectly. [Col. 0187D] [Note: A and B read “so that reverently.”]

The order of the words is: “I wonder because the first of the celestial essences reverently seek answers indirectly, and all of them together so greatly surpass the thearchic illuminations.” The meaning is this:

“I wonder,” he says, “when the holy theologians introduce the first celestial essences as being taught immediately by him, because he, although he surpasses all the others together in divine illuminations to the extent we have stated, nevertheless makes them seek answers indirectly—that is, as though a higher nature intervened—in a reverent manner, that is, timidly. The Greek term is *eulabōs* (εὐλαβῶς), ‘reverently’ or ‘cautiously.’ For *eulabeia* (εὐλάβεια) is timidness or modesty joined with love.

For they do not ask him directly, ‘Why are your garments red?’—or, as is found in the better exemplars, ‘Why are your scarlet garments?’ Rather, they deliberate among themselves before asking, or, more simply translated, they hesitate or waver among themselves before speaking. [Note: C and B* corrected the reading; A and B have *cunctanter*, ‘hesitantly.’ B reads *esitant*; B* adds *hesitant* above the line.]

This may also be understood as follows: ‘For they do not ask him on that account’—that is, they do not ask Jesus himself on that account. For he said ‘indirectly,’ that is, as though indirectly, though not altogether indirectly; indeed, no creature is higher than they and could intervene between them and Jesus, as has been firmly established by the arguments stated above. [Col. 0188B]

Why, then, do they ask as though indirectly, rather than altogether immediately or altogether indirectly? He gives the reason: “Among themselves they deliberate whether to ask”—or, as it is translated more clearly, “whether to speak.” They deliberate, being terrified by the loftiness of the mysteries, whether they should ask or not. And this very deliberation is called by the theologians a kind of intermediary.

Therefore it is neither an intermediary nor a non-intermediary.

It seems to me, however, that the theologians understood this deliberation of the exalted essences from nowhere other than the very vision which describes two Cherubim [Note: B has *cherubin*, as throughout] looking at one another and, as it were, taking counsel—a meaning which this teacher also seems to have intended in what follows.

“Showing that they learn and desire deifying knowledge”—that is, by this deliberation they show that they learn and seek from Jesus the deifying knowledge which deifies them. [Note: B* alters the wording to “deifying knowledge”; C reads “showing indeed that they learn and deifying knowledge.”]

But they do not leap ahead of the illumination implanted in them through the divine procession. That is, they do not seek divine knowledge in such a way as to anticipate the illumination implanted in them through the divine procession. [Note: B omits the words from “the implanted illumination” through “procession.”]

For they seek nothing unless, through the prior procession of the divine light, they first know whether they should seek, what they should seek, and how they ought to seek it. This is what he says: “Not leaping ahead of the implanted illumination of the divine procession.” [Col. 0188D]

Is it not, then, the first hierarchy of the celestial intelligences—sanctified by the very *telētarchia* (τελεταρχία), the Principle of Perfection, which is extended immediately into it—purified, illuminated, and perfected by the most holy purification, filling it proportionately with the abundant light of an already-perfect consummation?

The order of the words is:

“Is not, then, the first hierarchy of the celestial intelligences purified, illuminated, and perfected by the very *telētarchia*—that is, by Divinity itself, which is the principle and source of the priestly offering” [Note: B* adds “and principle” above the line], “sanctified—or, as it may be translated more suitably, though less customarily, ‘made high-priestly’—in the manner in which the most holy purification is extended immediately into it; filling it proportionately with abundant light, with infinite light, with very great light, or with most pure light? For all these expressions are translated from the one Greek word *apletou* (ἀπλέτου). ‘Of an already-perfect consummation’ may also be translated ‘of the already-perfecting or consummative *telētarchia*.’ Plainly, it fills it—that is, the hierarchy; for the *telētarchia* fills the first hierarchy with its infinite light.”

It is pure from every diminution, full of the first light, and perfect through participation in the knowledge and science given first. [Col. 0189B] [Note: B* corrected *voluminis* to *luminis*; C omits *vero*.]

“Pure,” he says, “from every diminution”—that is, entirely free from every subjection. For it is subject to no creature in order or dignity. It is full of the first light, namely, the divine light, and perfect; participating in the knowledge and science given first—that is, participating in the knowledge and science given by the First, or, as it may be more suitably translated, participating in the knowledge and science given first.

“And, comprehending this also”—I may perhaps say this not improperly—“because the assumption of divine knowledge is purification, illumination, and perfection.”

As though someone had asked what that purification, illumination, and perfection are, he answers: “Comprehending”—that is, summarily gathering it together—“and I may not improperly have said that the assumption of divine knowledge is purification, illumination, and perfection.” For one and the same divine knowledge, once assumed, both purifies, illuminates, and perfects those who receive it.

Where we have placed “not improperly,” the Greek has *ouk apeikotōs* (οὐκ ἀπεικότως), which is suitably and properly translated “not unfittingly” or “not unbecomingly.” [Col. 0189C]

And again, as though someone were asking: “What does the assumption of divine knowledge purify? What does it illuminate? What does it perfect? And in what way?” he immediately explains:

“It purifies from ignorance, as it were, by the orderly implanted knowledge of more perfect doctrines; it illuminates by divine cognition itself, through which it purifies the one who did not previously contemplate and makes that one manifest through a higher illumination; and it perfects again by that same light, according to the stable possession of the most lucid knowledge of doctrines.”

“It purifies,” he says, “as it were”—that is, for example, from ignorance—“by the orderly implanted knowledge of more perfect doctrines,” namely, by the knowledge of more perfect doctrines implanted in the first order of the celestial essences, which is the subject of discussion. For the doctrines of the first hierarchy have been implanted in it more perfectly than in the others, and its knowledge is more perfect. [Col. 0189D–0190A]

For it continually learns from Divinity itself the divine mysteries which are hidden from it.

“It illuminates by divine cognition itself”—that is, by the same divine knowledge through which it also purifies the one who did not previously contemplate, namely, the first hierarchy, which does not contemplate unless it has first been purified. “Which manifests”—that is, which divine cognition itself reveals—the hierarchy through the higher illumination granted to it than to the others. And “perfecting” again, as though at a third stage, by the same light of knowledge—that is, in the knowledge of the most lucid doctrines, which exists as a stable possession.

Thus the assumption of divine knowledge first purifies the first hierarchy through the implanted knowledge of more perfect doctrine. Then it illuminates it—though before it is purified it does not contemplate—through the disclosure of a higher illumination of divine mysteries. Third, by the same illumination, it perfects it in an unchangeable possession of the clearest doctrines.

For it is one thing to purify from ignorance, another to illuminate through instruction, and another to perfect the mind in the unshaken possession of knowledge of the most purely understood divine realities. [Note: B* adds *est* above the line.]

## § 4

This, then, insofar as concerns our knowledge, is the first disposition of the celestial essences: standing immediately in God’s circuit and around God, and simply and unceasingly circling his eternal knowledge, according to the most excellent arrangement that is perpetually mobile insofar as this is granted to angels.

“This,” he says, “insofar as it is granted to our knowledge”—that is, to human knowledge—to recognize, “is the first disposition of the celestial essences,” that is, the first order, “in God’s circuit and around God.” Generally speaking, like the other essences, it is in God’s circuit; specifically, however, it is around God. It stands immediately, with no creature intervening.

For the twelve tribes of Israel also encamped on every side around the tabernacle of the testimony, though at a greater distance; but immediately and most closely around the tabernacle were the high priests and Levites.

It stands—for it itself stands—and simply, that is, universally, and unceasingly circles—or, if you wish to translate it so, incomprehensibly encompasses—his eternal knowledge.

Thus it stands, and while it stands, it universally and unceasingly, or incomprehensibly, circles or encompasses God’s eternal knowledge. It stands because it remains uniformly in the same state; it encompasses and circles universally [Col. 0190D] because there is nothing in the divine mysteries which it does not investigate: “For the spirit searches even the depths of God.” And it does so unceasingly because it is always in motion; incomprehensibly, because neither by itself [Note: C reads *nec a se*; A has *necesse*, B *ncce*] nor by those below it is it understood how or in what manner it encompasses or circles God’s eternal knowledge.

It encompasses eternal knowledge, not so as to circumscribe it externally, but so as to survey it internally. What creature could encompass the eternal knowledge of its Creator, which contains and compresses all things within itself?

According to the most excellent arrangement that is perpetually mobile insofar as this is granted to angels. For its arrangement—that is, its state—is always mobile, and its motion is arranged, uniformly stable.

What wonder is this, when even the stable motion of this sensible sphere exists because it moves uniformly, and its mobile state exists because it is always in motion? [Note: B omits the words “and its mobile state, because it is always in motion.”]

Seeing many and blessed contemplations purely, illuminated by simple and immediate splendors, and filled with divine nourishment.

“Many,” he says, “and blessed theories the first hierarchy sees purely.” The divine Wisdom itself, which it clearly beholds, is manifold and blessed. But because this manifold Wisdom is simple and indivisible, it first pours its simple splendors into the first hierarchy, by which it is illuminated and, as though filled with divine nourishment—or, more plainly translated, filled with divine joy—it is satisfied.

It has been made worthy of a manifold first effusion, but alone of the intimate and unifying unity of divine nourishment; and worthy of much communion with God and cooperation with him through the likeness, insofar as possible, of good dispositions and actions.

The construction of the words is as follows: “It has been made worthy of the manifold first effusion of Wisdom before the other hierarchies, but alone”—that is, uniquely—“of the intimate,” plainly nearest, “and unifying unity of divine nourishment.” For not every unity is unifying, but only the divine unity. “And it has been made worthy of much communion with God and cooperation with him.”

For it communicates with him first of all—that is, it participates in him—and cooperates with him in the administration of the whole creation established below it. How does it communicate and cooperate? In likeness, namely, in likeness to that communion and cooperation, through good dispositions and actions insofar as this can occur.

Thus, in the likeness of good dispositions—that is, virtues, for virtue is a rational or intellectual disposition of the mind—and in the likeness of good actions, it communicates with God and cooperates with him.

And, knowing many divine things in a superordinate manner, it has been made a participant, insofar as is permitted, in divine knowledge and cognition.

It has been made so insofar as is permitted—that is, insofar as it is lawful, permissible, and just [Note: B reads *et*; the correction adds *est*. C has “in participation, insofar as is permitted, that is, lawful and unjust,” apparently corrupt].—in participation in divine knowledge and cognition, knowing, as it does, many things supereminently, with “divine intelligences” understood.

Next follows:

“Therefore theology also handed down its praises to those who are on earth, in which the eminence of its most exalted illumination is wonderfully manifested.”

He calls “its praises” the praises by which theology glorifies God, and says that it handed them down to human beings. [Note: B omits “in which it is wonderfully manifested … handed down.”]

For some of them—that is, some participants in it, namely, the first hierarchy—are handed down by the theologians as speaking sensibly, that is, in a perceptible manner, like the sound of many waters: “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place.” [Note: The words “in which the eminence … is wonderfully manifested” were omitted above; B adds them in the margin but indicates that they should not be inserted here.]

Others proclaim that very praiseworthy and most devout theology: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory.” [Note: A and B read this way; in the Greek, *Theos* (“God”) is absent.]

Where we have placed “most devout,” the word may also be translated “most honorable” or “very worthy of worship.” [Note: C and B* correct the reading; A and B have “worshipping.”]

But when he says that they speak sensibly, it is not readily clear whether they hymn the aforesaid praises with bodily senses and a sensible voice, as though through certain spiritual bodies naturally joined to them—bodies in which divine history also teaches that they appeared to human eyes—or whether this is because they appeared in prophetic visions as though sensible, the praises being uttered in the likeness of sensible voices.

Nevertheless, however they may exist, this theologian testifies that these praises are produced by the exalted essences of the first hierarchy.

For he says:

“Now we have already disclosed, insofar as possible, these most exalted hymnologies of the celestial minds in the works concerning divine praises; and enough has been said about them there, insofar as concerns us. From them, for admonition, it is sufficient at the present time to say only this.”

From this statement we can understand that he himself wrote the work concerning divine praises, since in the book *On the Divine Names* he introduced certain passages from the love-hymns of Saint Hierotheus, in which nothing is discussed concerning the praises mentioned above.

Where we have placed “admonition,” the Greek has *hypomnēsis* (ὑπόμνησις), that is, “admonition” or “remembrance.” [Col. 0192C]

“It is sufficient,” he says, “to say these few things from the divine praises at the present time, for admonition or remembrance.”

Because the first disposition was illuminated, insofar as is permitted, in theological knowledge by the thearchic goodness—that is, because the first hierarchy was illuminated in theological knowledge by divine goodness itself.

And do not be surprised at the construction “illuminated in theological knowledge.” For it is correct; we say, for example, “I am illuminated by you in an art,” or “I am taught by you in a discipline.” [Note: B corrects *illumino* by adding “or, I am instructed”; C reads “I illuminate you in an art.”]

From this goodness, as a deiform hierarchy, it subsequently handed the same thing on to others. That is: from the same divine goodness—or, more plainly translated, from that same divine goodness—“as a deiform” hierarchy. For just as divine goodness gives form to all things, so the first hierarchy itself is deiform toward the other hierarchies that follow it; that is, it gives them form as God does.

“And it subsequently handed the same thing on to others”—that is, it distributed to the others, namely to those that follow it, the same divine goodness by which it is first illuminated. [Col. 0192D]

Introducing this briefly, that is, introducing this point briefly, the hierarchy itself says:

“It is lawful for the most devout, more than praiseworthy, and most praiseworthy thearchy to be known and praised as blessed by intellects that receive God, for they are, as the sayings declare, deiform divine places of thearchic rest.”

This is what the first hierarchy briefly introduces, namely, that it is lawful, and according to law and justice, for the most devout—or most honorable, or very worthy of worship—and supremely praiseworthy and most praiseworthy Divinity to be known as blessed and praised by intellects that receive God.

For these intellects, which receive God, are deiform divine places of divine rest, as the sacred sayings testify. God rests in them.

*Theodochos* is derived as though from Greek *theou dochē* (θεοῦ δοχή), that is, “receiver of God.” By this name every pure mind, whether human or angelic, may be called. For God rests in both kinds of beings.

And because it is a monad and unity, it is three substantially.

The first hierarchy of heaven also introduces this to the hierarchies that follow it: that the thearchy, that is, Divinity, is a monad—that is, a unity—and is three substantially. For Divinity is unity in essence and Trinity in substances.

Although among us *monas* and *henas* have the same translation—*monas* means “unity,” and likewise *henas* means “unity”—there seems to be the following difference between them: *monas* properly denotes unity itself, from which all numbers proceed; for it is the principle and cause of all plurality. *Henas*, however, denotes the unity of substances, whether in the superessential essence—which is God—or in genera, or in forms, and generally in all things that participate in one and the same essence.

Divine goodness, then, is a *monas*, because it is the principle and cause of all things that exist; but it is a *henas*, because it is unity in three substances, and three substances in the unity of essence.

“Extending its goodness in providence over all things that exist, from the supercelestial essences down to the furthest reaches of the earth.” [Col. 0193D]

This too the first hierarchy introduces in praise of Divinity: that from the highest celestial essences down to the furthest reaches of the earth it directs its goodness, namely its providence, toward all things that exist.

And no one should suppose that I translated *extendens* (“extending”) through ignorance in place of the Greek feminine participle *dieisa* (διεῖσα), which derives from the verb *dieimi* (διείμι), “I reach” or “I penetrate.” [Note: The manuscripts have *praevenio*, “I anticipate”; the emendation gives *pervenio*, “I reach.”] I did so for ease of understanding. [Note: B reverses the word order to “I did this for ease of understanding.”]

But if someone wishes to follow the proper meaning of the translation, instead of “extending” he may say “causing to reach” or “causing to penetrate,” so that the meaning is:

“From the supercelestial essences down to the furthest reaches of the earth, it causes its goodness—that is, its providence—to penetrate all things that exist.”

“As the superprincipial principle and cause of every essence, encompassing and binding together all things superessentially in an immeasurable holding.”

“Not improperly,” he says, “does its providence extend over all things, or penetrate all things. For it is the superessential principle of every essence, and it encompasses and binds together all things in an immeasurable manner.”

Here likewise, for the sake of easier understanding, I translated “binding together” for the Greek participle *peridedragmenē* (περιδεδραγμένη), which properly means “grasping with the palm or fist.”

The seventh chapter ends. The eighth begins.

# CHAPTER VIII

Its preface is:

“Concerning the Dominions, Virtues, and Powers, and concerning their middle hierarchy.”

[Note: In A, in illuminated letters: “The seventh chapter ends. The eighth begins; its preface is concerning the Dominions, Virtues, and Powers, and concerning their middle hierarchy.” In B, in illuminated letters: “The ninth chapter, concerning the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels, and concerning their final hierarchy.” B* adds at the bottom of the parchment: “Chapter VIII, concerning the Dominions, Virtues, and Powers, and concerning their middle hierarchy.”]

[Additional textual apparatus: At Col. 0185, A reads *supposi* for *suppositi* (“subordinate”); B* corrects *si* to *sic* (“thus”). At Col. 0187, B reads *est dominus* (“is Lord”); B has *illius* (“of that one”) for *ipsius* (“of himself”); A and B read *eas Jesum*, while the version and Greek text read *ipsum Jesum* (“Jesus himself”); B* corrects *in medietatem* / B’s *immedietatem* to *in medietate* (“indirectly”); B reads *eis* (“to them”); B reads *praelargienter* (“lavishly”); A has *quidem* (“indeed”); A has *et* (“and”); B* corrects *tua* (“your”) in both questions concerning the red and scarlet garments; the corrected reading is *apud seipsas* (“among themselves [fem.]”), against A and B’s masculine *seipsos*; C and the original correction of B* read *cunctantur* (“they hesitate”), against A and B’s *cunctanter* (“hesitantly”); B has *esitant*, with B* adding *hesitant* (“they hesitate”); B* adds *est* after “firmly established”; the conjectural *interrogarent* (“whether they should ask”) replaces A and B’s *deliberabant* (“they deliberated”); C and corrected B* read *ipsa deliberatio* (“this deliberation”), against A and B’s *ipse*; A has *velut* for *veluti* (“as it were”); B has *nec* (“nor”); B’s form is *cherubin*, throughout; B* corrects *deificam scientiam* (“deifying knowledge”), while C has the defective reading “showing indeed that they learn and deifying knowledge”; B omits *se* (“them”); B corrects *a* (“from”); B has an additional *per* (“through”); B reads *dicitur* (“is said”); B* corrects *Nonne* (“Is it not?”); A has *ierarchi* for *ierarchia* (“hierarchy”); the words “which is extended immediately into it” are omitted by A and B and supplied from the version and Greek text.

At Col. 0189, B* adds “and principle” after “chief of sacrifices”; A, B, and C read *quod* (“which”) where B* punctuates it and adds *et* (“and”); A reads *ea* (“it”) for *eam* (“into it”); B has *siquidem* (“indeed”) for *quidem*; A and B have *voluminis* (“of a volume”) for corrected *vero luminis* (“of the true light”), while C omits *vero*; C reads *absoluta* (“free”), while A and B have *absolutam*; A and B omit *et* (“and”) after “comprehending”; B has *sapientiae* (“of wisdom”) for *scientiae* (“of knowledge”); B* adds “from ignorance”; A reads *Perfectionis* (“of perfection”) for *perfectiores* (“more perfect”); B* adds *est scientia* (“is knowledge”); C and corrected B* read *prius* (“before”), against A and B’s *proprius* (“properly”); B has *vero* (“indeed”) for *eam* (“it”); B* adds *est* (“is”) after *aliud* (“one thing”).

At Col. 0190–0191, A reads *est et, inquit* (“is and, he says”), with *et* deleted in B; B has *scilicet* (“namely”); B’s corrupt reading is *essentiarium cognicio dispositio*; A and B read *circumitu* for *circuitu* (“circuit”); B omits *plane* (“plainly”); B first wrote *circumiens* and then corrected it to *circuiens*; B* punctuates *circumit* (“it circles”); B corrects *circuit* (“it circles”); B has *quoniam* (“because”); B reads *illa* (“that one”) for *ipsa* (“itself”); A has *eum* (“him”) for *eam* (“it”); B omits the second *se* (“itself”); A and B have *spere* for *sphaerae* (“sphere”); A and B read *simplos* for *simplices* (“simple”); B* corrects *atque* (“and”); B reads *et* (“and”) where the corrected text has *est* (“is”), and C preserves the corrupt continuation “in participation, insofar as is permitted, that is, lawful and unjust …”; A has *intra* (“within/on earth”) for *in terra* (“on earth”); B omits *dicere* (“to speak”), B* corrects it to *dicendo* (“speaking”), and B reads *hoc est a* (“that is, from”) for *a* (“from”); A and B write *ymnizant* for *hymnizant* (“they hymn”); B has *dicere eos* (“them to speak”); B has *corpora spiritualia* (“spiritual bodies”) for *spiritualia corpora*.

At Col. 0191–0193, B* corrects *ammonitionem* to *admonitionem* (“reminder”); B’s corrupt reading is *quia ipsam theologicam*; C and corrected B* read *dispositio* (“disposition”), against A and B’s *depositio* (“depositing”); B* supplies the alternative *erudior* (“I am instructed”) to correct *illumino* (“I illuminate”); A and B omit *ipsam* (“the very”); C and corrected B* have *benedictam* (“blessed”), against A and B’s *benedicta*; B* corrects *theotochis* to *theodochis* (“God-receiving”); B* adds *est* (“is”) after *quantum possibile* (“insofar as possible”); A and B omit *et* (“and”) in “monad and unity”; B reads *introducit* for *subintroducit* (“introduces incidentally”); B* adds *est* after *monas*; A and B write *enahs* for *enas*; A and B have *sive in superessentiali* (“whether in the superessential”), while C has the corrupt *su superessentiali*; B omits *est* (“is”); corrected B reads *novissima* (“furthest things”), against A’s *novissimum* and B’s *novissimam*; the emendation *pervenio* (“I reach”) replaces A, B, and C’s *praevenio* (“I anticipate”); B reverses the order to “I did this for ease of understanding.”]

§ 1. We must now pass to the exposition of the middle [Note: [Col. 0193] B* has added *est in* above the line.] of the celestial intellects, examining those Dominations with supramundane eyes, insofar as this is possible, and truly the objects of contemplation of the divine Powers and Virtues. After the explanation, he says, of the first and most exalted hierarchy, we must now pass to the middle hierarchy, which is also the second, examining—or, as it is more properly translated, contemplating—those Dominations [Note: [Col. 0193] A reads *donationes*.] with intellectual eyes according to our capacity; and similarly, in the case of the true [Note: [Col. 0193] Thus C, with B* correcting; AB read *vere potentie*.] objects of contemplation of the divine Powers and Virtues, “we must pass” is to be understood. For each designation of the essences above us signifies their proper virtues [Note: [Col. 0193] Thus in AB; the translation reads: “the designation of God signifies their imitative, deiform properties,” which agrees word for word with the Greek text.].

Therefore, I judge that the manifestative designation of the holy Dominations declares a certain complete ascent, free from every disgrace of abasement. We can also interpret it in this way: a certain non-servile ascent, free from every degradation of subjection. He likewise applied this expression in his praises of the Thrones. For to walk on foot is disgraceful and an indication of abasement and subjection—that is, servitude. From this the ascent of the celestial Dominations is free and complete: that is, their height is directed upward. Nothing earthly, nothing base, nothing servile diminishes their height.

Their height in no way resembles [Note: [Col. 0195] Corrected; AB read *dissimilitudinem*.] the dissimilarities of tyrants—that is, it does not stain or color itself [Note: [Col. 0195] Thus C; A has *set ingit*, B *fringit*; the original hand corrected it to *fingit*.] with them—or become one of those tyrannical dissimilarities. For tyrannical domination is unlike true Domination [Note: [Col. 0195] A reads *similis*.]. The heavenly Dominations, however, rule neither tyrannically nor arrogantly, but moderately and humbly, in love of God and of those subject to them.

“I judge that the universally inclined, freely [Note: [Col. 0195] B reads *liberatiliter* (apparently punctuated by B*); B* added *et liberaliter* above the line.] severe domination, set above every petty [Note: [Col. 0195] B has *minuti*; B* added *-ve* above the line.] servitude” is to be understood as meaning: “the universally inclined, moderate, humble, and freely severe—or, as it may be translated, irreproachable [Note: [Col. 0195] B has *irrepreshensibilem*; punctuation was added and *s* written above the line by B*, so that *irrepressibilem* may be read.]—domination set above every diminishing servitude.”

“Not needing subjection of any kind and removed from every dissimilarity, continually desiring kyriarchy [Note: [Col. 0195] Corrected by B*; A has *kyiarchiae*, B *kyrarchiae*.].” I judge this [Note: [Col. 0195] Thus BC; B* corrects *declinare*; A reads *declinare*.] to declare that it needs no subjection [Note: [Col. 0195] A reads *subvectionis*.] except to God alone [Note: [Col. 0195] B first had *solo*, then *soli*; the latter was written above the second *o* by B*. [Col. 0196D] In Migne, *i* is printed above the second *o* of *solo* to represent the manuscript reading.] [Note: [Col. 0195] A reads *ex*.] and to the hierarchy preceding it [Note: [Col. 0195] Thus C, with B* correcting; AB have *praecidenti*.]; and that it is removed from every dissimilarity that would make it deformed and unlike its Creator [Note: [Col. 0195] The manuscript reads *ortatori creatori*; in Migne, *cre* is printed above *ort* in *ortatori* to represent the manuscript reading. B* added punctuation and apparently wrote *cre* above the line.] [Note: [Col. 0195] Corrected by B*; ABC read *inficiat*.] and that it continually desires kyriarchy [Note: [Col. 0195] Thus AC; B has *kyriarchiam*.]—that is, the Divinity itself, which is called *kyriarchia* [Note: [Col. 0195] Thus C, with B* correcting; AB have *kyrarchia*.], since it is the ruler and source of all domination.

And it conforms, as far as possible, both itself and what comes after it in a deiform manner to the likeness of that naturally subsisting power itself. We have interpreted this sentence in an expanded form because the Greek has κυρία [Note: [Col. 0195] AB have κυῤῥια.], whose proper meaning cannot be expressed by a single word, but rather as follows: “a naturally subsisting power.” The sense is: “It continually desires likeness to the *kyrian* [Note: [Col. 0195] B has *kyriam*.] itself,” that is, to the power which subsists naturally and in itself; and this is nothing other than the Divinity subsisting in and through itself, which, insofar as possible, conforms both that domination itself and what comes after it in the lower orders.

It seems possible [Note: [Col. 0195] B reads *sic breviter posse*.] to translate the passage briefly in this way: “And conforming itself and what comes after it, insofar as possible, to the likeness of that same proper likeness [Note: [Col. 0195] B has *propriam ejusdem*.] of itself [Note: [Col. 0195] B* added *est* above the line.]”—so that the sense is: “And I judge that it declares the domination to be desirous of conforming and shaping itself, insofar as possible, to the proper likeness of that same thing, clearly the kyriarchy, and of conforming and shaping what comes after it in a deiform manner.”

“And turned toward no vain-seeming things, but toward that which properly is, the universal.” In all the clauses of this sentence [Note: [Col. 0195] Thus C; A has *colus*, B *coliis*.], that is, members [Col. 0196A], “I judge that it declares” is to be understood.

By “that which properly is, the universal,” he means the highest good, which properly is and is the universal good. For all good things are not good in themselves, but are good by participation in the universal good, which is truly [Note: [Col. 0195] Thus C, with B* correcting; AB read *quid vero*.] good. Therefore he says: “toward no vain-seeming things,” that is, toward none of those things [Note: [Col. 0195] A omits *eorum*; B added it in the margin.] which, considered in themselves, appear vain. He uses *videntium* for *visorum*, that is, “things which are seen,” in the very customary [Note: [Col. 0195] Corrected by B*; ABC read *usitatissimo*.] manner of the Greeks; and because it is derived from the verb δόκομαι [Note: [Col. 0195] B* added in the margin: *dochomaym*.], “I see” and “I seem” [Note: [Col. 0195] B* corrected *et* to *vel*.], since the word is common, the sense is: “but [Note: [Col. 0195] B* corrects *et*.] I judge that it declares her to be turned not toward any of those things which appear vain, because they do not subsist in themselves, but toward that which properly is and is universal.”

It should be observed that the Greeks sometimes call God by the neuter form ὄν, “that which is,” and sometimes by the masculine form ὦν, “he who is.”

“And made, insofar as possible, ever in participation in the kyriarchic [Note: [Col. 0195] From the translation and Greek text; A reads *chiriarchie*, B *kiriarchie*, C *kyriarchie*.] deiformity.” This final statement is entirely clear. For what he says—that it was made a participant in the deiformity of the kyriarchy [Note: [Col. 0195] AB have *kyriarchie*.]—is common to all the celestial essences. For all their virtue is in participation in the Deity [Note: [Col. 0195] Thus C; AB have *sunt*.], which is the ruler of the Dominations [Note: [Col. 0195] Thus C, with B* correcting; AB have *qui*.].

As for the holy Virtues themselves [Note: [Col. 0195] B* added in the margin: “Concerning the Virtues.”], I judge that their designation declares a certain strong and unchanging manliness in all their deiform operations, not weakened by any feebleness in receiving the divine illuminations implanted in them, powerfully led back in imitation of God [Note: [Col. 0195] A has *imitatione*.], not abandoning through its own weakness the deiform movement, but firmly bearing toward the superessential and power-making virtue [Note: [Col. 0195] Corrected by B*; AB have *pontificam*.], and made, insofar as permitted, an image like that virtue [Note: [Col. 0195] From the translation and Greek text; AB have *facta*.], and powerfully turned toward that virtue as its source, while proceeding in a deiform manner toward the second as the giver of virtue.

The designation “Virtues,” he says, declares their strong and unchanging manliness—or vigor or excellence—in all deiform operations. This manliness is not weakened by any feebleness in receiving the divine illuminations implanted in them; it is powerfully led back, that is, led upward, in imitation of God. It does not abandon through its weakness—which never weakens—the deiform movement [Note: [Col. 0195] Thus C, with B* correcting; AB have *reliquit*.], but firmly bears itself, that is, firmly tends toward the superessential, plainly divine, virtue, which [Note: [Col. 0195] B* placed dots beneath *quae* and wrote *per* above it.] makes itself powerful [Note: [Col. 0195] B omits *facit*.] and which [Note: [Col. 0195] B reads *quae se*.] has become the image of that superessential virtue, being like the virtue itself. It is powerfully turned toward that virtue, rightly the source of all virtues, since it is both their ruler and their beginning; and it also gives virtue to the second and proceeds in a deiform manner, that is, after the pattern of the divine procession.

It should be noted that where we have rendered [Note: [Col. 0197] Corrected by B*: for *quod ubi posuimus*, A and B read *ubi posuimus quod*; C reads *quod non posuimus*.] “like the virtue” and “the giver of virtue,” the Greek has compound words, which we cannot translate as compounds unless, perhaps, though unusually, we say δυναμοειδῆ [Note: [Col. 0197] In the manuscripts δυναμοειδῆ is written in such a way that it can very easily be misread as δυναμίαν; therefore B* added in the margin: “that is, *dynamosian*.”], “virtue-formed.” As for δυναμοδότως [Note: [Col. 0197] B* added in the margin: “that is, *dinamodotos*.”], although it appears to be an adverb, it can be translated only by nouns if the result is not to be excessively unusual. For this reason we said: “like the virtue” and “the giver of virtue.”

As for the holy Powers themselves [Note: [Col. 0197] B* added in the margin: “Concerning the Powers.”], that is, the designation itself of the holy Powers [Note: [Col. 0197] A reads *ips. nom. sanct. potest. nominationem aestimo*; B reads *ips. n. s. p. nominationem aestimo*.], I judge that it declares an arrangement equal in power to the divine Dominations and Virtues [Note: [Col. 0197] Thus ABC.], well adorned and unconfused in its reception of divine things, and an ordered [Note: [Col. 0197] B* adds: “that is, arrangement.”] disposition of supramundane and intellectual authority. This disposition is not tyrannically directed toward inferior things in its authoritative operations [Note: [Col. 0197] B reads *sunt inferiora*.], but is powerfully led back into the divine things after those that are well ordered, and, after itself, deiformly leads back what follows it. It is made like the power-making [Note: [Col. 0197] Corrected by B*; AB read *pontificam*.] *exousiarchy* [Note: [Col. 0197] B* wrote above the line: “alternatively, causal power.”], insofar as permitted, and reveals it to the angels, insofar as possible, through an authoritative virtue in the orders well adorned by it.

The designation of the holy Powers, he says, declares an equal-in-power [Note: [Col. 0197] Thus AB; C has *aequipotentem*.] or equally ordered [Note: [Col. 0197] Thus ABC.] arrangement alongside the divine Dominations and Virtues, well ordered and unconfused. It is not tyrannically—that is, it is not impelled by an abusive exercise of power toward what is subject to it, in a fabricated [Note: [Col. 0197] Thus C; AB have *inficta*.] likeness of authoritative virtues—but is powerfully—or, as it is more properly translated, most powerfully—led back into the divine things after those that are well ordered; that is, after the beautifully ordered virtues of the first hierarchy that precede it. It deiformly leads back what is ordered after it, that is, beneath it [Note: [Col. 0197] Thus C and the original hand corrected by B*; AB have *idem*.], plainly leading it upward. It has been made, insofar as permitted, like the power-making *exousiarchy*, that is, the Divinity, which is called ἐξουσιοποιός [Note: [Col. 0197] A has *ego ουσιοποιε*; B has *ego ουσιοποιος*.] because it makes powers, and ἐξουσιαρχία [Note: [Col. 0197] A and B have *ego ουσιαρχια*; B* corrected it to ἑκουσ-.] because it is the ruler and source of powers. It reveals that *exousiarchy* [Note: [Col. 0197] AB have *ego ουσιαρχιαν*; B* corrected it to *εκουσ-*.] to the angels, insofar as possible, through an authoritative virtue in the well-ordered ranks established through it—namely, through its own arrangement, by which the lower ranks are ordered.

Possessing these deiform properties, the middle arrangement of the celestial spirits is purified, illuminated, and perfected, as has been said, by the divine illuminations implanted in it a second time through the first hierarchical arrangement [Note: [Col. 0197] Corrected by B*; AB have *hierarchy*.], and, through that middle arrangement [Note: [Col. 0197] B* adds in the margin: “that,” i.e. the first hierarchy.], conveyed to the third hierarchy in a second manifestation [Col. 0198A].

He says: The middle adornment of the celestial spirits possesses these proper and deiform virtues; therefore it is purified, illuminated, and perfected, as was said in the preceding chapter concerning the first hierarchy. It is purified, illuminated, and perfected from no other source than the divine illuminations implanted in it a second time. “Second” is an adverb [Note: [Col. 0197] A writes *Ad verbum*.], for the former—the first hierarchical arrangement—participates in the divine illuminations first, whereas this one participates in them second through the former [Note: [Col. 0197] Corrected by B*; ABC read *ierarchiam*.]. And through that middle arrangement they are again conveyed into the third hierarchy in a second manifestation, as through a second manifestation [Note: [Col. 0197] B has *sanctam*; B* wrote *secundam* above the line.] of the divine illuminations themselves—or, as it is more properly translated, they are distributed.

## § 2

Accordingly, by another expression, we shall make the coming of a statement through one angel into the hearing of another angel a symbol [Note: B* in the margin adds: “symbol, that is, an example or demonstration.”] from afar of a perfection that is more than perfect and, through its procession, hidden in the succession [Note: B: “succession.”] of things. He says: “We shall make these conversations of the heavenly citizens—by which we see a statement coming through one angel into another angel, in whom it is heard—a sign from afar of a perfection that is more than perfect, that is, of a perfection greater than perfect, and hidden through its procession in succession.” It is as though he were saying plainly:

“We human beings, who investigate divine meanings not by experience but by inference, shall make an argument and a most evident sign of how that which is more than perfect and hidden through an obscure procession descends gradually and in ordered succession from afar—that is, from the very height of the divine sublimity, which is removed by the greatest distance from all things that exist—into the successive order of the heavenly powers.” And this is that argument and sign: a statement certainly comes through one angel from the highest Divinity into another angel, in whom the spoken word is turned into hearing [Note: B: “the word is turned.”]—not because bodily senses exist in them, but because prophetic vision has been formed in this way.

If, therefore, what the highest Good commands descends from the first hierarchy into one hierarchy and then another, as though into one angel and then another, in whom that statement is heard, this is unmistakably a sign of the divine procession through ordered degrees from the highest to the lowest—that is, from the most excellent heavenly essences down to human beings, who are also called angels when they announce to those below them the divine plan that they receive through the higher angels.

He says this so that we may understand the wondrous disposition of things, through which divine Providence orders the fullness of the created universe by an ineffable procession. For the wise concerning our sacred offerings [Note: B* adds in the margin: “that is, sacrifices or sacraments.”] say that plenitudes of divine things, shining by themselves, are more perfect than those that exist through the participation of others in contemplation [Note: B* adds in the margin: “that is, contemplative.”].

He confirms what he stated beforehand by the testimony of the high priests. “The wise,” he says, “who perfectly understand our sacred and mystical sacrifices and offerings [Note: B: “offerings and sacrifices.”], say that the plenitudes of divine intellects shining immediately by themselves—that is, divine intellects which, by themselves and immediately, shine with complete fullness—are more perfect than contemplative participations [Note: B: “perfections, participations.”], namely, contemplative intellects [Note: B* and AB correct this to “contemplative,” plural], which participate in divine contemplation through other powers.”

We can gather this briefly: divine intellects that immediately participate in divine contemplation by themselves are more perfect than the others, which receive that same contemplation through the mediation of higher beings [Note: B omits “which”; B* adds it in the margin]. [Note: B omits “contemplation”; “receive” is written in B as “conceive.” In Migne, *sus* is printed above *con* in *concipiunt* to represent the manuscript reading.]

Observe that where we have placed “the wise,” the Greek has δεινοί (*deinoi*), for which one may say “reverend,” “skilled,” or “wise.” This is how I understand it. In the same way, I judge the immediate participation of the angelic orders—those stretched out first toward God—to be more perfect through the mediation of the perfect.

“As,” he says, “those who shine by themselves are more perfect than those who receive light through others, so I judge the angelic orders that are immediately and first extended toward participation in God to be more perfect than the perfect” [Note: B* adds in the margin: “that is, than those who are perfect”], namely, than those who have been perfected with some mediation interposed.

Where we have placed “more perfect,” the Greek has ἐναργεστέραν [Note: AB have ἐνεγγεστερον], which we can render “more perfect,” “more powerful,” or certainly “more efficacious.”

For this reason, in our sacerdotal tradition the first intellects are called the perfecting, light-giving, and purifying powers of those below, since through them the lower beings are led back to the superessential Principle of all things by themselves [Note: B* adds in the margin: “by themselves, that is, through them”], and are made participants, insofar as is lawful for them, in the purifications, illuminations, and perfections of the Theletarch [Note: B* adds in the margin: “of the Theletarch,” that is, of the one who directs the accomplishment].

For this is the divinely promulgated [Note: B has “diffused,” corrected to “promulgated.”] law of the divine *taxiarchy* [Note: A has *taxiarchica*, B *taxiarchica*]: through the first, the second participate in divine illuminations.

In this one very plain [Note: ABC have *per plana*, “through plain [words].”] and most lucid statement he briefly discloses and summarizes the order and dignity of the heavenly essences. “Therefore,” he says, “our human sacerdotal doctrine calls the first three orders of the first heavenly hierarchy the perfecting, light-giving, and purifying powers, because through them the lower orders are led back to the Principle of all things, which is superessential—namely, to God—and are made participants, insofar as is permitted, in the purifications, illuminations, and perfections of the Theletarch, that is, of the divine one who directs accomplishment.”

“Divinity” [Note: C has “divinity”; AB have “divinely.”], as has often already been said [Note: B* adds above: “has been said”], is called *teletarch* or *teletarchy*, because it is the beginning and ruler of sacrifices. And this law was handed down from the divine *taxiarchy*—that is [Note: AB omit “is”; C has it, and B* adds it above]—from the very Godhead, which is therefore called *taxiarchy* because it is the beginning and ruler of the whole ordering, as though from τάξεων ἀρχή [Note: B* adds in the margin: “taxeon archē”], “the beginning of orders”: namely, that the second contemplations should participate in divine illuminations through the first.

You will also find this expressed many times by the theologians [Note: B* adds above: “by the theologians”]. It is as though he were saying: “You will find this law inculcated not only by the sacerdotal tradition but also very frequently by the prophets themselves.”

For when the divine and paternal humanity [Note: B* writes above: “that is, piety”], instructing Israel in a change of life for its sacred salvation and handing it over to nations that were avenging and harsh, for correction, through every kind of providential leading toward what is better, both released it from captivity and mercifully restored it to its former well-being [Note: B* corrects “conversabiliter” to “conversibiliter”], one of the theologians, Zachariah, saw—as I judge—one of the first angels, one of those who are concerned with God. The designation “angel” is common to all of them [Note: B* corrects “common” to “common to all”; B* adds in the margin: “The matter of Israel’s captivity and restoration is common to all the angels, as it is stated in the prophecy”], learning from God himself consoling words about this, as has been said.

The order of the words is: “For one of the theologians, plainly of the prophets, named Zachariah, sees one of the first angels, namely one of the principal Powers that are concerned with God, as I judge. For this name, ‘angel,’ as I said, is common to all the heavenly powers because of their angelic—that is, announcing—designation. He sees him learning from God himself: for that one of the first angels learned immediately from God himself consoling words about this, plainly about Israel’s return. This occurred, as has been said, in prophetic vision, when the divine and paternal humanity—that is, clemency—released the captivity and indulgently restored Israel to its former well-being, instructing Israel in a change of life—that is, so that it might be converted—for its sacred salvation. For he did not wish to hand it over to its enemies through the harshness of vengeance, but wished to correct and save it through the gentleness of mercy. And while handing it over to avenging—or, as it is more suitably rendered here, restraining—and harsh or severe nations for correction [Note: B has “for reproof”], this was through every kind of leading of those under providence [Note: B* adds in the margin: “or ‘every kind,’ that is, plainly, the general leading of all”]—that is, through the manifold guidance toward what is better of those who are governed and corrected by divine Providence [Note: A omits “and corrected”].”

Where we said “well-being,” the Greek has εὐπάθειαν (*eupatheian*) [Note: B* adds in the margin: “that is, eupathia”], which Cicero wished to translate as *constantia*, “steadfastness.” The Greeks themselves call εὐπάθεια *εὐεργεσία* (*euerge­sia*) [Note: The reading is conjectural; AB have ἐνέργεια, B* adds in the margin: “that is, *euergesía*, beneficence,” and C has *eitergesia*], that is, “beneficence.”

According to the Stoics there are three *eupatheiai* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “*eupathiai*; likewise, according to the Stoics, there are three *eupatheiai*, that is, good passions”]: wishing, joy, and caution. They are established only in the mind of the wise person. By “wishing” I mean love of the good; by “joy,” rejoicing over the discovery of truth; and by “caution,” careful consideration of things [Note: A recent hand of the fifteenth century wrote in the upper part of the parchment: “Love is a unitive power transforming the lover into the beloved.”].

We, however, say that *eupatheiai* [Note: B* adds in the margin: “eupathiai”] are joy [Note: B* adds in the margin: “joy, love, hatred, and sadness, when they are in the mind of the wise, are virtues”], love, hatred, and sadness, when they are virtues in the mind of the wise, as in: “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven”; likewise: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father”; and elsewhere: “You know, Lord, that I love you”; “I have hated the wicked” [Note: B has “hated” spelled with an additional *h*]; “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.”

But when they are considered in the mind of the foolish, they are rightly called κακοπάθειαι (*kakopatheiai*) [Note: AB have κακοπαθιαι, C has *kacopathie*], that is, “evil passions” [Note: C has this reading, and B* corrects AB’s “lead” to “are rightly called”]. If, however, joy can be understood in the soul of a foolish person—for joy is gladness that is never followed by sadness, and this cannot happen to the foolish.

Then he sees another of the subordinate angels coming to meet the first, as though to receive illumination and participation [*metalepsis*] [Note: The reading is emended; AB have *metalempsin*, B* corrects to *metalempsim*].

Zachariah himself saw another of the lesser angels come to meet the first, in order to receive illumination—namely, the divine revelation that had first been spoken by God himself to the highest angel. And *metalepsis* [Note: The reading is emended; A has *metalempsin*, B *metalempsim*, C *metallempsim*], that is, perception—namely, participation. For *metalepsis* [Note: A has *metalempsis*, B *metalenpsis*, C *metallempsis*] properly means participation [Note: B has “but” instead of “for”].

Then, having been instructed by him in the divine plan as by a high priest, he sees him turned to teach the theologian.

“Then,” he says, “he sees the angel who has been instructed in the divine plan by that first angel, as by a high priest, and sees the theologian himself plainly turned to teach this to Israel, which he learned from the first angel through the second.”

It can also be translated: “and to teach the theologian who is turning” [Note: Conjecture; AB have “to say”; C omits “to teach the theologian”], so that the sense is: “And he sees the angel—the prophet himself—turning in order to learn this.”

“For Jerusalem will be inhabited fruitfully” [Note: B* adds in the margin: “that is, abundantly”] “by a multitude of people.”

He took this interpretation from the Septuagint. Jerome [Note: A has *Ieronymus*, B *Ieronimus*] translated it: “For Jerusalem will be inhabited without a wall by a multitude of people.” Yet the meaning is the same in both. For the one who said “fruitfully” understood it as the abundant multiplication of the people returning from captivity [Note: B has “purification”]; while the one who translated “without a wall” wished to signify the same meaning, as though he were saying: “There will be such a multitude of people that it cannot be enclosed by a wall.”

The other theologian, Ezekiel [Note: AB have *iezechiel*, as throughout], he says, likewise testifies that this was most sacredly promulgated to the Cherubim by the most glorious Divinity established above them.

He confirms by the testimony of the other theologian what he stated beforehand: namely, that divine plans received immediately by the first angels are formed through the lower angels in the spirits of the theologians [Note: B has “formed”; B* corrects it to “are formed”]. He says:

“The other theologian, Ezekiel, says that this which follows was most sacredly—that is, divinely—promulgated by the Cherubim [Note: B* adds in the margin: “cherubim”], established by that most glorious Divinity which is superessential; that is, it was handed down [Col. 0202B] immediately to the Cherubim themselves [Note: B* corrects AB’s “of him” to “themselves”; B* adds in the margin: ‘transferring Him’].”

For Israel, as has been said, is a disciplinary beneficence leading through chastisements toward what is better: divine justice condemns the guilty and has justified the innocent [Note: B has “condemns,” spelled *condempnat* throughout].

“Leading Israel”—that is, while it was leading Israel, as it is said in divine Scripture—“disciplinary humanity,” that is, divine clemency, which through leading disciplines those whom it wishes to free and brings them toward what is better.

This is taught to the first one after the Cherubim, girded about the loins with sapphire, who was clothed according to the hierarchical symbol in a *podera* garment.

But the divine *taxiarchy* commands the other angels who held axes to be taught by the one before them [Note: B* corrects “the former” to “the one before”] about this divine judgment.

“This,” he says, “that is, the judgment by which the guilty are condemned and the innocent justified, is taught to the first angel—that is, to one of the heavenly order that follows the Cherubim, for example, one of the Dominions, Powers, or Authorities. For the Cherubim were first instructed immediately by the Divinity itself about this judgment; and the Cherubim themselves first teach the one after them [Note: C has this reading; AB have “to teach”], who was girded about the loins with sapphire and was also clothed in a *podera* according to the symbol [Note: B* adds in the margin: “the hierarchical one, that is, the hierarchical figure, because the hierarchy uses visible figures to designate invisible things”], according to the vesture of the high priest in Israel.

“For the high priests were girded with loincloths—that is, breeches or girding garments—adorned with sapphire and other precious stones. They were also clothed in a *podera*, namely, a tunic reaching to the feet. It is called *podera* because it hung down as far as πóδες (*podes*) [Note: AB have *podas*], that is, as far as the feet [Note: A omits ‘as far as’]. Thus, in such a high-priestly vesture, the first angel after the Cherubim appeared to the prophet.”

The divine *taxiarchy*, that is, the highest Good that orders all things, commands through the Cherubim that the other angels who held axes be taught by the angel before them [Note: B* corrects “the former” to “the one before”] this divine judgment, so that they might learn the divine justice concerning the distinction between the guilty and the innocent.

“To the one order,” he says, “the Cherubim—or, simply, to the Cherubim themselves—for Cherubim and Seraphim are Hebrew names common to both numbers [Note: C and B* correct AB’s “nuri” to “numbers”]. For *Cherub* and *Cherubim* are both used in the singular by *syntaxis*, that is, by the construction of numbers. The same is true of *Serub* [Note: B has *serup*, B* corrects it to *serap*, C has *cherub*] and *Seraphim*: both are masculine names and can have either singular or plural number.”

Thus the divine *taxiarchy* said to those Cherubim that the one immediately after them [Note: B has *pose*, B* corrects it to *per se*] should pass through the middle of the city.

This can be understood simply as referring to the one who is first after the Cherubim; but it was the Cherubim themselves who said that he should pass through the middle of Jerusalem [Note: A has “the middle”]. By “the middle” he means that which is divided between the guilty and the innocent [Note: A has “divided” in the feminine form]. And he says that he should give a sign—namely, the sign of Christ’s cross—on the foreheads of the innocent.

For the sign T [Note: C omits the letter T] was placed on their foreheads. Who among the faithful does not know that the letter Tau bears the likeness of a cross? Therefore only those are delivered who faithfully believe in the Lord’s cross. “For we reckon,” Paul says, “that a human being is justified by faith.”

But the others held axes, and they were commanded to spare no one. It is beautifully said that one of the innocent marks them [Note: B* adds in the margin: “the foreheads of the innocent”], and with no other sign than the cross. For there is one Christ who, by the power of his Passion, delivers those who believe in him.

But the others carried axes—that is, cutting tools—which signify building more than destruction. They represent the severity of divine justice, which, through the angels—plainly, through the preachers of the Church—separates virtues from vices and nature from guilt, cuts away what is superfluous [Note: B* corrects “cuts” to “cuts off”], and shapes what is natural; from these elements they construct a house suitable for the divine possession.

But they are forbidden to approach those who are free solely through faith in the divine Passion when they first undergo the sacrament of baptism [Note: B* corrects AB’s “free” to “freed”; C has “free persons”]. For they have already been cut down [Note: B* corrects this to “they have already been cut down”]; every superfluity has been cut away from them by the gift of faith [Note: C and B* correct A’s “of faith”].

For whoever, after receiving the grace of baptism, has not sinned will not need correction for offenses. For he is once and at the same time cleansed from every original and personal sin.

But he does need to be cleansed from ignorance of the divine sacraments. For one who is ignorant of divine meanings cannot enter the way of truth, nor contemplate its light, without which no one will be deified.

Indeed [Note: B adds in the margin: “It is not enough to draw out the weapon if he wishes to heal the wound”], it is not enough for someone to withdraw an arrow from a wound unless there is someone to apply medicine for the healing of the wound [Note: A, B, and C have “is present”].

For the grace of baptism grants only this: that past offenses do not harm us and that we are born into divine sonship [Note: B* adds in the margin: “What the grace of baptism bestows”]. It does not, however, grant that future sins will not be committed. This is entrusted by divine grace, through repentance, to free choice [Note: B* adds in the margin: “What is required for avoiding sin after baptism: repentance through grace, providence through free choice”]—to divine grace through repentance, and to free choice through foresight.

For a person can take care not to sin rashly, but not without grace [Note: B* adds in the margin: “A person can avoid sin, but not without grace”]. Grace can forgive sins, but not without the human being’s good will. For God does not wish to draw unwilling people, but willing ones, lest he appear to reduce the gift of free choice to servitude [Note: B* adds in the margin: “On justification: grace and the use of free choice, or good will, are required”].

Thus the first one after the Cherubim marks the foreheads of the innocent. They were guilty, but through the sign they have been made guiltless.

Why, then, is Christ crucified called the first after the Cherubim? Hear the Psalmist: “You have made him a little lower than the angels.” Do you wish to know how he was made lower? Hear Paul: “He emptied himself,” he says, “taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness [Note: B has “likeness” in the ablative form] of human beings, obedient to the Father even unto death”; hear the sign marked on the foreheads: “even the death of the cross.”

He alone marks them, for he alone delivers them. His angels strike with axes [Note: B* adds in the margin: “That good angels are executors of punishments to be inflicted”]; through his ministers he builds himself a house from human nature cut into shape, brought from its formlessness into the form of him in whose image it was made.

But the fact that they are commanded to strike with axes [Note: B* corrects “with an axe” to “with axes”], sparing no one with their eyes, signifies the severity of divine Scripture [Note: B has “teaching”] in the discernment and correction [Note: B has “reproof”] of offenses, of which he is judge.

For it belongs to good teachers to discern justly [Note: B* adds above: “justly”], not to flatter. Therefore God does not destroy the nature he made, but separates from it that which corrupts it.

For the ineffable compassion of divine goodness does not permit the nature that he made like himself to suffer deformity eternally. He permits it to be corrected for a time, so that, instructed by its most just afflictions [Note: B has “troubles”], it may return more eagerly and ardently to its own dignity.

Reason does not permit the image of God to be held in eternal disgrace. Otherwise misery would be coeternal with blessedness, evil with goodness, and the kingdom of the devil with the kingdom of God.

We do not say this as though no punishment were eternal [Note: AB have *pena*, as throughout], since each person will either be blessed or condemned eternally by his own conscience, but only that no nature will be punished in anything [Col. 0205D].

[Note: “J. Scotus taught almost the same things repeatedly concerning nature not being punished, and concerning eternal punishment as nothing other than the eternal consciousness of sins, and also in *On Predestination*, chapter XVI. Prudentius rightly responds to this: ‘That God punishes sinners, all the pages of the divine utterances testify. … You hear of God punishing, and of a human being punished, and not only of a human being, but also of the earth punished as his penalty, and yet you deny that nature is punished by nature? … Either the Creator himself, by his almighty command, punishes rational natures that rebel against and disobey him, or by a judgment that is sometimes manifest, sometimes hidden, but never unjust, he commands or permits created natures to be punished by created natures.’ And concerning eternal punishments he says: ‘Do you wish, following Origen—or, according to you, solely—understand punishments as nothing other than consciousness of sins, or merely the absence of blessedness? … But orthodox interpreters, on the authority of Holy Scripture, hold that there is not only another punishment but also a twofold punishment of Gehenna,’ and so forth.”]

Let us return to the subject. Beautifully, therefore, the harmonious visions of the two prophets—I mean Zachariah and Ezekiel—confirm that God immediately teaches the highest essences that are around him, and that afterward the orders are taught in due order: the first through the first of the second, the second through the second of the third, the third through the third of the fourth—that is, the orders of the theologians [Note: AC have “this is”; B omits “is”].

For Zachariah says that he saw one of the first angels learning from God himself [Note: B* corrects AB’s “descending” to “learning”; C has “descending from him”]. Another angel of the lower orders came to meet him, learning the divine counsels through the first, as though in the second degree. Then that second angel, as though a high priest, instructed the theologian—I mean Zachariah—if one wishes to understand in this way what the teacher says: “Then he sees the theologian, instructed by the angel who came to meet him as by a high priest, turned; and he sees him teach this, because Jerusalem will be inhabited fruitfully.”

But if someone wishes to understand it as follows—“then he sees the instructed angel coming to meet him, taught by the first, who learned from God, as by a high priest”—it will follow that not the angel who came to meet him, but the first angel who learned from God, is to be understood as the high priest. Then the meaning will be: “And he saw the theologian turned and saying this,” that is, he saw the second angel, instructed by the first, teaching the theologian who had been turned [Note: B has “holy”] that Jerusalem would be inhabited fruitfully.

Ezekiel, however, says first that the Cherubim were taught by that most glorious Divinity itself; then, through them, the first one after them is taught—the one who was seen in priestly clothing; and through him the angels are taught, as though in the third degree.

Thus the order is: the Cherubim are instructed by God himself; from the Cherubim the first one—whoever he may be—from the orders of the second hierarchy is taught; and he in turn teaches the other angels of the third hierarchy, through whom the mind of the theologians is finally illuminated.

In Zachariah’s vision, however, it seems doubtful whether that other angel who came to meet one of the first angels, through whom the theologian was instructed, belonged to the orders of the second or the third hierarchy.

For no one should find it strange that he is called a high priest, since all the minds of the three heavenly hierarchies can be called high priests. For they are pontiffs, although their pontificates are not equal; some indeed precede others.

Unless perhaps someone should say that he was one of the orders of the second hierarchy, through which the third is taught as through a kind of mediation [Note: C has “the third”; AB have “of the third”]. And if this is so, we shall be compelled to understand either that another angel lower than that mediator stood between him and the theologian, if human beings are taught through the third hierarchy, or certainly that not only the holy theologians [Note: Conjecture; ABC have “holy theologians”] can be taught through the angels of the third hierarchy, but also through those of the middle and even of the first hierarchy, and even immediately by the Divinity itself. This must not be denied.

Dionysius himself seems to assert the same thing in his book *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, where he says that human minds, according to each person’s own proportion, are implanted in the three heavenly hierarchies.

For who would deny that the Apostle, caught up into the third heaven, was plainly in the third hierarchy, where, in the middle of it, he heard ineffable words from God himself?

What, perhaps, would someone say about the angel who said to Daniel, “The word has gone forth”? Or about the first angel himself receiving fire from the midst of the Cherubim? Or about that angel’s fuller manifestation of the angelic order, since he also puts fire into the hands of one clothed in a holy robe? Or about the one who calls the most divine Gabriel and says to him, “Make him understand the vision”? Or about whatever other things have been said by the sacred theologians concerning the deiform adornment of the heavenly hierarchies [Note: Conjecture: A has *therarchiarum*, B *thearchiarum*, B* corrects to *therarchiarum*; perhaps *cherarchiarum* was read for *ierarchiarum*, from which the error may have entered], to which the ordering of our hierarchy has been assimilated insofar as possible, and which will possess angelic beauty [Note: A has “likeness”] insofar as it has been formed in images [Note: B* adds above: “has”], fashioned through it and brought back together with the superessential source of the whole hierarchy.

Which angel spoke to Daniel is made clear by sacred history [Note: AB have *istoria*, as throughout; C has *hystoria*]. Daniel himself says:

“While I was still speaking in prayer, behold, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, flew swiftly and touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice. And he taught me and spoke with me and said: ‘Daniel, now I have gone forth to teach you and to make you understand. At the beginning of your prayers the word went forth; but I have come to declare it to you, because you are a man of desires. Therefore pay attention to the word and understand the vision: seventy weeks’”—and the whole passage that follows concerning the return of the people from captivity and the coming of Christ.

This is what blessed Dionysius briefly introduces when he says: “What perhaps would someone say about the angel who says to Daniel, ‘The word has gone forth’?” In Greek this is expressed as ἐζῆλθεν ὁ λόγος (*ezēlthen ho logos*) [Note: AB have the corrupt form ξηλθενογοσι; C says that the Greek is given as “what Jerome has”], for which Jerome wrote: “The word has gone forth”—either from the mouth of King Darius, so that Jerusalem might be rebuilt [Note: C has “might be rebuilt”; A and B have “is rebuilt,” corrected by B*], or certainly from God himself through the angel into the mind of the prophet [Note: B* adds in the margin: “Supply here and in the following questions: unless someone inferior has been instructed by a superior and receives teaching”].

But what follows—“or about the first angel himself receiving fire from the midst of the Cherubim”—is taken from Ezekiel, who says:

“And I looked, and behold, upon the firmament that was above the head of the Cherubim, something like a sapphire stone, like the appearance of a likeness, appeared alone above it. And he said to the man clothed in linen, and he said: ‘Enter into the midst of the wheels that are between the Cherubim, and pour out over the city.’”

This is what follows: “or about that angel’s fuller manifestation,” that is, the symbol of the same Ezekiel, which is clearer for displaying the angelic order, since the Cherubim also put fire into the hands of the one clothed in a holy robe.

Although this does not seem to be written in exactly that way in the vision mentioned above—for there it is written only:

“And he said to the man who was clothed in linen, and he said: ‘Enter into the midst of the wheels that are beneath the Cherubim and fill your hand with coals’” [Note: AC have “which are”; B omits “are” and B* adds it in the margin]—

it can nevertheless be understood either that it was written this way in the edition of the Seventy Interpreters, from which blessed Dionysius introduced all these things, or that he himself understood it in this way: “Fill your hand with coals,” with the unstated meaning being “with the coals that the Cherubim themselves will hand over to you” [Note: B* corrects AB’s “they themselves” to “themselves”; C has “them”].

And again, what follows—“or about the one who calls the most divine Gabriel and says to him, ‘Make him understand the vision’”—is taken from the Book of Daniel [Note: B* adds above “is”; C omits “is”], where it says:

“And it happened,” Daniel says, “when I, Daniel, saw the vision and sought understanding, behold, there stood before me something like the appearance of a man. And I heard the voice of a man, and he cried out and said: ‘Gabriel, make him understand this vision.’”

All these things, therefore, were written and seen in the prophets and introduced by this blessed teacher for the very reason that we might understand that the minds of the heavenly beings have ordered ranks: some are taught and illuminated immediately by God himself, while they in turn teach and illuminate, step by step, those below them, who are taught and illuminated by those above.

And this is what he says: “and whatever other things [Note: A has *quencunque*] from …” [The supplied text ends mid-sentence.]
were spoken by the sacred theologians [Col. 0208A] concerning the godlike adornment of the heavenly hierarchies [Note: [Col. 0207] C reads *archearchiarum*; A, *archearchiarum*; B, *archearchicarum*], an adornment to which our own hierarchy has been made similar, insofar as this is possible for human beings [Note: [Col. 0207] B* adds this in the margin], in its own orders. For it imitates the beauty of the angels, insofar as it can, through sensible figures and symbols. For the Lord Jesus Christ himself teaches them by the presence of his contemplation; he still instructs us through symbols, until we come into unity. And this is what he says: “the beauty of the angels” [Note: [Col. 0207] B. added in the margin: “Concerning the vision in the homeland”], insofar as it will be possessed in images.

For now it possesses a likeness of the heavenly beings in divine symbols; then it will possess their beauty in the primordial exemplars, insofar as this can come to be, in images. By “images,” I think, he means the theophanies, in which both the angels themselves and human beings, glorified into an equal blessedness with them, will see God himself, since he both is and will be invisible in himself to every intellect [Note: [Col. 0207] B* added in the margin: “Take care, since it is said in John 3, ‘we shall see him as he is’; but this can be said with regard to the capacity of the whole”]. For his superessentiality surpasses every intellect.

Therefore our hierarchy will possess the beauty of the angels insofar as it can be possessed in theophanic images or likenesses, formed by that adornment—namely, the adornment of the heavenly powers. For the ecclesiastical hierarchy is both ordered and formed through the heavenly powers, and is led back to the superessential One of every hierarchy, namely, to the very cause of all things.
