# CHAPTER IX. Whose Title Is: Concerning Princes, Archangels, and Angels, and Their Final Hierarchy

[Note: [Col. 0207D] The ninth chapter, concerning Principalities, Archangels, and Angels, and their last hierarchy; B, in illuminated letters: “The tenth chapter, whose title is: Repetition of the Angelic Synaxis”; but on the lower part of the parchment [Col. 0208D] B* wrote: “IX. Concerning Princes and Principalities, and Archangels and Angels, and their final hierarchy.”]

[Col. 0208C]

## § 1

The remaining ornamentation for our contemplation, which brings the angelic hierarchies to completion, is arranged by the godlike Principalities, Archangels, and Angels [Note: [Col. 0207] A: “in contemplation”]. [Note: [Col. 0207] B*: corrected in the main text from “disposed” to “disposed” (plural).]

What remains, he says, is our contemplation of that ornamentation itself, which encloses and terminates all the angelic hierarchies and is constructed from Principalities, Archangels, and Angels. First, I think it necessary to state, as far as possible for me, the manifestations of the holy designations. Just as, in his explanations of the first and middle hierarchies [Note: [Col. 0207] The words “Just as … hierarchy” are omitted by B.], he first explained the interpretations of the names [Note: [Col. 0207] “Interpretations” is omitted by B and supplied in the margin by B*.], and then the proper and common powers and administrations of each order, so now, in his explanation of the third hierarchy, he first undertakes to explain the interpretations—which he calls the manifestations [Col. 0208D]—of the designations.

He consequently adds:

“For the designation of the heavenly Principalities manifests in a godlike manner their principal leading forth, together with sacred order and the most fitting principal virtues; and it manifests that these are universally turned toward the principal principle, and that the others are led hierarchically, and, as far as possible, reformed toward that same princely principle; and it manifests its superessential taxis, the adornment of the principal virtues.” [Note: [Col. 0209] “Turned toward” is omitted by AB and supplied in the margin by B*.]

He declares, he says, that the very designation of the heavenly Principalities manifests their principal leading forth—that is, that they are the princes and leaders of all nations throughout the habitable world. And this is done in a godlike manner, namely, in the likeness of the one true God, who alone is the supreme prince and leader of all.

“With sacred order and the most fitting principal virtues” means: with holy and divine ordering, and with virtues most appropriate to the dignity of a principality. They not only rule the nations and are their leaders through their virtues, but they also universally turn these virtues of theirs [Note: [Col. 0209] In place of “these their,” B has “their these.”] toward the super-principal principle—plainly, God, who is the principle of all principles, the principal principle [Note: [Col. 0209] “God … principle” is omitted by B.], and more than a principal principle.

For this is common to all heavenly minds: first, to turn toward their cause, so that they may be formed by it; and afterward, toward those beneath them, so that they may accomplish in them what they receive as something to be done from the one cause of all. This is what he means by “to turn them universally toward the super-principal principle.” One should understand: the designation of the heavenly Principalities declares that their virtues are wholly turned toward God, who is the super-principal principle.

“And to be led hierarchically, and, as far as possible, reformed toward that same princely principle.” This means that the designation itself declares not only that the proper virtues of the Principalities are turned toward the principle of all, but also that the virtues beneath them—whether human or angelic—over which they exercise principality and authority are led through them in priestly order. They are reformed, according to their capacity, toward that same princely principle, plainly the supreme good, which perfects every principality through its own virtue.

It is as though he said: the heavenly Principalities lead and reform not only their own virtues toward that principle which brings every principle to completion, but also the others over which they exercise principality.

“And to manifest its superessential taxis, the adornment of the principal virtues” [Note: [Col. 0209] So AC; B has “to manifest”; B* adds “manifest” above “and.”] means that the designation of the Principalities manifests the adornment of the principal virtues and the superessential taxis of that principle—namely, of the super-principal principle [Note: [Col. 0209] “Namely” is omitted by B]. The adornment of the heavenly Principalities most clearly declares to us the superessential taxis of the supreme good, which is God.

God is the prince and principle of the entire heavenly army. It should be noted that the order of soldiers is properly called τάξις (*taxis*) in Greek. Therefore God himself is called ταξίαρχος (*taxiarchos*) and ταξιαρχία (*taxiarchia*), because ἀρχός and ἀρχή—that is, “prince” and “principle”—subsist universally as the heavenly army’s prince and principle.

## § 2

The designation itself of the holy Archangels [Note: [Col. 0209] B* adds in the margin: “Concerning the Archangels.”] [Note: [Col. 0209] B* adds in the margin: “designation.”] is equal in power to that of the heavenly Principalities. For, as I have said, their hierarchy and disposition—of the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels [Note: [Col. 0209] B has “of the archangels”—are one.

The designation, he says, of the holy Archangels is of the same power as that of the heavenly Principalities. The names “Principalities” and “Archangels” have equal significance. For there is one hierarchy and one disposition of them—namely, of the Archangels and Principalities [Col. 0210B], and of the Angels, as was stated above [Note: [Col. 0209] B* adds “is” in the margin].

Where we have translated “equal in power,” the Greek has ὁμοταγής (*homotagēs*) [Note: [Col. 0209] B’s later hand adds *omotages* in the margin], for which we may say “equal in power,” “colleague” [Note: [Col. 0209] So C and B*’s correction; AB has *colliga*], or “equally honored.”

Nevertheless, since there is no hierarchy that does not contain first, middle, and last powers, the holy order of the Archangels is received as the communicative middle of the hierarchical extremes [Note: [Col. 0209] B has “of the hierarchy”; the order is supplied in the margin by B*].

This is what he means: although the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels are one hierarchy and one disposition, they are nevertheless distinguished by no small difference. The order of the Archangels occupies the proportion of a middle between the two extremes—that is, between the order of the Principalities and the angelic order [Note: [Col. 0209] B has “occupies”; this is its usual form]. For there is no hierarchy, whether human or angelic, that does not possess first, middle, and last powers.

The order of the Archangels is therefore intermediate between the Principalities, as the higher order, and the Angels, as the lower. This proportion of the middle is nothing other than a hierarchy—that is, priestly communication. For the distinct orders communicate in one thing: all together desire the supreme good and all together participate in it, although not equally.

This is what follows: “For it communicates with the most sacred Principalities [Note: [Col. 0209] B reads: “the order of the Archangels communicates with …,” and so forth] and with the holy Angels.”

He next explains what this communicative middle is like:

“With the former, because it is principally turned toward the superessential principle and is reformed toward it as far as possible; and it unites the Angels according to their well-adorned, well-ordered, and invisible governances [Note: [Col. 0209] B omits “their well-adorned and well-ordered”; B* corrected AB’s *dicatus* to “governances”].”

With those former orders, he says—that is, with the Principalities—the order of the Archangels communicates because it is principally turned toward the superessential principle, namely God, just as the Principalities themselves are, and is reformed toward it as far as possible. It also unites the Angels according to their well-adorned, well-ordered, and invisible presidencies. The Principalities themselves do this as well.

For they unite the Angels for participation in the superessential principle. Just as their adornment, order, and intelligible principality communicate God, so they unite the Angels to themselves [Note: [Col. 0211] So C; AB has *vivificant*, “make alive”], and through the Archangels as middle beings they cause the Angels to communicate in God and strive to raise them into their fellowship.

“With the latter,” he continues, “because the order is also prophetic toward them, receiving the divine illuminations hierarchically through the first powers, announcing them in a godlike manner to the Angels, and manifesting them through the Angels to us, according to the sacred analogy of each of those who are divinely illuminated.”

With these latter—that is, with the Angels—the order of the Archangels communicates because it is prophetic toward them, that is, because it has a prophetic order. The Archangels are prophets of the Angels: they receive the divine illuminations hierarchically—that is, in priestly order—through the first powers, namely the Principalities that precede them, and manifest those illuminations to us through the Angels, according to the holy analogy of each human being illuminated by God.

The Archangels therefore possess a communicative fellowship with the Angels in two ways. First, they announce to the Angels the illuminations of divine wisdom that they themselves receive through the virtues preceding them. Second, through the Angels they manifest to us the illuminations transmitted to them.

Here it is understood that, just as the Archangels are mediators between the Principalities and the Angels, so the Angels are mediators between the Archangels and human beings.

At this point a question arises that should not be disregarded:

If these three orders of the third hierarchy—the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels—are *homotageis*, that is, equal in power [Note: [Col. 0211] B has “equally powerful”], or colleagues [Note: [Col. 0211] So C; AB has *colligae*], or equally honored [Note: [Col. 0211] So C and B*’s correction; AB has “or humbly”], how are the Archangels mediators between the Principalities, which are superior to them, and the Angels, whom theological teaching has handed down as the last of all the heavenly powers?

The same question arises not only concerning the third hierarchy, but also concerning the second, which is the middle hierarchy, and concerning the first. For how are the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones colleagues and equal in power, if the Cherubim occupy the middle position between the first powers, the Seraphim, and the last powers, the Thrones? The same must be considered concerning the Virtues, Powers, and Dominations.

In this question, nothing more suitable occurs to me to say than that all are equally powerful in their desire for the fellowship of the superessential cause of all, but that in participation in it they possess multiple degrees of ascent and descent. Each order of heavenly minds is capable of divine illuminations according to its own analogy. None of them is deprived of these illuminations, since they are poured out upon all in common.

For air, water, and earthly bodies are not equally capable of the sun’s rays, yet those rays are poured equally over all, and, rebounding from all, shine back from them. So it is with all intellectual and rational minds. There is none of them—whether pure or contaminated—that is without the divine ray [Note: [Col. 0211] So C and B*’s correction; A has “expressed it”].

They do not, however, become equally capable of it; nor is this caused by any weakness in the ray, but by the capacity of the souls. Why all angelic and human minds are not equally capable of the divine ray, blessed Dionysius himself explained elsewhere.

For if God had created the whole universe equally, without any distinction or particularity among the various orders, and without the ascent and descent of different degrees, perhaps no order would arise in the commonwealth of natures. If no order arose, there would be no harmony. And if there were no harmony, no beauty would follow [Note: [Col. 0211] “Beauty” is omitted by B and supplied in the margin by B*].

For in things wholly alike there is neither harmony nor beauty. Harmony is the unification of dissimilar and unequal things [Note: [Col. 0211] B adds “is” in the margin]. But that the universe of created nature should lack the beauty of harmony would be judged utterly unfitting for the Creator of all.

Furthermore, if no one who philosophizes correctly doubts that the whole creation has been established in the most beautiful harmony, it follows that none of the wise may hesitate concerning its order. The subject now is not apostate angels and contaminated human beings, who, by reason of their wickedness, repel the ray of divine illumination from themselves [Note: [Col. 0211] B has “the ray from themselves”], but the natural order of universal nature [Note: [Col. 0211] C has “created nature”].

The text continues [Note: [Col. 0211] B* adds in the margin: “Concerning the Angels”]:

“For the Angels themselves, as we said above, comprehensively complete all the dispositions of the heavenly minds, insofar as they must be completed, possessing the angelic character among the heavenly essences” [Note: [Col. 0211] “Angelic” is omitted by AB and supplied in the margin by B*].

Therefore, he says, the Archangels announce the higher illuminations to us through the Angels because the Angels, as was stated above, fill out and complete all the dispositions—that is, the adornments—of the heavenly minds. They do this insofar as they must be completed, namely according to the manner in which the disposition of the heavenly minds [Note: [Col. 0211] B has “of the heavenly minds”] must be completed and determined [Note: [Col. 0211] “Is” is omitted by ABC and supplied above by B*].

He adds the explanation of this:

“Possessing the angelic character among the heavenly essences.”

It is as though he said: they do this because, among the heavenly essences, they possess a certain character by which they are specially called Angels. This character is known only to the gnostic power [Note: [Col. 0211] So C and B*’s correction; AB has “power”], and through it the properties of the individual orders of heavenly minds are distinguished [Note: [Col. 0211] So AC; B has “are distinguished,” with punctuation added by B*] and distributed.

The text continues [Note: [Col. 0211] B adds “And they are”]:

“And among us they are more appropriately called Angels than the former orders, insofar as their hierarchy is more significantly concerned with us and is more fully circumscribed.”

He now gives the reason why all the heavenly essences are generally called angels by theologians, while the last order, which is closest to human beings, is specially called angelic [Note: [Col. 0213A] B reverses the word order: “is called angelic”].

“Among us,” he says, “the Angels are more appropriately named than the preceding powers, because they approach us more closely than the higher orders and announce and disclose more divine mysteries to us.”

“Insofar as their hierarchy is more significantly concerned with us and is more fully circumscribed” means that they are more appropriately named Angels among us than the preceding powers to the extent that their hierarchy is concerned with what is more significant—that is, what is announced to us through them more clearly and expressly.

Observe that “more significantly” or, as it is translated expressly, “more manifestly,” are not comparative adverbs but comparatives of neuter nouns.

“And is more fully circumscribed,” that is, their adornment is more fully circumscribed for us [Note: [Col. 0213] B has “their adornment for us”], for understanding. Everything that is easily understood appears, in a certain way, circumscribed by the intellect [Note: [Col. 0213] “By the intellect” is omitted by B]. The higher powers are far removed from us, who are still enclosed within the boundaries of our earthly dwelling [Note: [Col. 0213] So C and B*’s correction; AB has “are enclosed”], so that we cannot ascend, by the free flight of the mind, to understand heavenly things with pure contemplation.

The text continues:

“For the most excellent disposition, as has been said, drawing near in an orderly manner to the hidden one itself, as it is nearest to it in the first place, must be considered to sanctify the second, secretly forming it.”

The order of the words is: “For the most excellent disposition must indeed be considered, as drawing near in an orderly manner to the hidden one itself in the first place, secretly forming and sanctifying the second” [Note: [Col. 0213] A has “the second” in the masculine form].

The meaning is this: the last order, which is closest to us, is therefore more appropriately called angelic by us because the most excellent disposition of the heavenly essences—namely, the first hierarchy, as being nearest to the hidden one itself, plainly God, who is called hidden because he surpasses every intellect—must be regarded and understood without hesitation as sanctifying, that is, ordering, or, as it is properly translated, offering as a sacrifice, the second hierarchy. It forms the second hierarchy secretly—that is, hiddenly and invisibly—and remains most remote not only from human intellects but even from angels.

For just as it is ineffable, incomprehensible, and hidden from all the hierarchies how the first hierarchy is ordered and sanctified, or sacrificed, by God himself, so it is remote and unknown how the second hierarchy is ordered by the first, and the third by the middle hierarchy, from that same cause of all [Note: [Col. 0213] So C; AB has “by that same one”]. If these things are unknown and incomprehensible even to the heavenly essences, what wonder is it if they cannot be comprehended by us?

“But the second,” which is completed by the holy Dominations, Virtues, and Powers, “rules over the hierarchy consisting of Principalities, Archangels, and Angels” [Note: [Col. 0213] B* corrected “of that which is” to “of it”; above, B* adds “from the Principalities”].

It is clear what he means: “The second hierarchy must be considered to rule over the third hierarchy.” For just as the first sanctifies and leads the second, so the second sanctifies and leads the third [Note: [Col. 0213] So C and B*’s correction; AB has “says”]. Its principality is plainly the latter’s guide.

The first hierarchy must be considered to rule over the third more manifestly than the first hierarchy rules over the middle, but more secretly—that is, more loftily and more secretly—than the third hierarchy, namely the one established after it, rules.

This may be expressed as follows: the middle hierarchy is more manifest than the first but more hidden than the third, because things that approach the cause of all are more hidden and incomprehensible than those ordered farther away from it.

The first hierarchy, immediately after God, is therefore the most hidden because it occupies the region nearest to the altogether unknowable cause. The third, which occupies the extremity of the heavenly essences, is the most manifest, insofar as heavenly powers can be manifested. The middle hierarchy, because it occupies neither the nearest nor the outermost position, is manifest in comparison with the interior hierarchy but is shown by the theologians to be hidden in comparison with the exterior one.

“The manifestative disposition of the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels is to command human hierarchies successively.”

From what precedes, one must understand: the manifestative disposition—that is, the adornment of the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels, namely the third hierarchy—must command human hierarchies in succession according to the divine ordering [Note: [Col. 0213] B* adds in the margin: “that is, successively, after it has been commanded by the higher orders”].

The manifestative disposition is called the third hierarchy because it manifests the divine counsels to human hierarchies. Just as the first rules the middle and the middle rules the third, so the third rules human hierarchies.

If you ask why he calls human hierarchies plural, you will find in the book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* three human hierarchies corresponding to the three heavenly hierarchies. It would be tedious to discuss them here.

Where we have translated “successively,” the Greek has δι’ ἀλλήλων, which may be translated “in turn” or “through one another.” The sense is: the Principalities rule and command the human orders through the Archangels, and the Archangels through the Angels [Note: [Col. 0213] So C and corrected in the margin by B*; AB has “through the angels”].

One may also say, not incongruously, as I think, that the third heavenly hierarchy rules human beings in turn, since divine history also teaches that angels obey holy human beings, and this is read in their deeds.

For it is written in the Apocalypse that the Angel said to John, when John wished to worship him: “I am your fellow servant.”

Thus there is, in due order, a leading back and conversion to God, communication and unity; and there is also a procession most fittingly implanted by God in all the hierarchies [Note: [Col. 0215] A has “hierarchical”], proceeding communicatively and with the most sacred adornment.

Therefore, he says, the order of the hierarchies descends step by step from the higher orders in this manner [Note: [Col. 0215] “In this manner” is omitted by B], from the higher to the lower [Note: [Col. 0215] So AC; B has “from the higher descends,” with a point added by B*], so that again, through the same order, the lower orders may be led back and converted through the higher to God, and to the one principle of all, and may communicate together and be one in him [Note: [Col. 0215] A marginal comment reads: “likewise, all are one in one,” and so forth].

Nevertheless, the procession of all these things comes from nowhere else than God. From him it is most fittingly and commonly implanted in all hierarchical orders, though not without difference, and from him the procession itself comes with the most sacred adornment.

For just as all things are converted toward him through return, so all things are brought forth from him through procession.

Hence theology distributes our hierarchy among the Angels, naming Michael the prince of the Jewish people and the others friends of the nations.

“For the Most High established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the Angels of God.”

Since, he says, procession descends from the one cause of all, both of angelic and human hierarchies, and return ascends again to that same cause, theology therefore distributes our hierarchy among the Angels—that is, it hands down our hierarchy as distributed among the Angels.

It names Michael the prince of the Jewish people. From this one indication we learn that the other nations of the entire world have their own angelic princes, whom it calls “friends of the nations.” For they teach the peoples over whom they preside to turn to the worship of the one true God [Note: [Col. 0215] “They teach … to turn” is omitted by A].

Michael is interpreted as “Who is like God?” or “strong peace,” that is, “the peace of God,” or “a man of virtue.”

As for the statement, “The Most High established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the Angels of God,” it should not, in my opinion, be understood as though there were as many nations and languages as there are Angels of God. Rather, there are as many boundaries of the nations as there is a number of angels who have been specially appointed as their princes [Note: [Col. 0215] “Alone into divine illuminations” is omitted by AB and supplied in the margin by B*].

## § 3

But if someone asks how the people of the Hebrews alone were led back into divine illuminations, while the other nations were held in the darkness of ignorance and unbelief before the incarnation of the Word of God, even though all likewise had angelic guides, as the Hebrews did, the answer must be that the right knowledge of the Angels concerning the other nations must not be blamed for their error concerning nonexistent gods [Note: [Col. 0215] B* corrected “of the other nations”].

He says that no one should blame the right knowledge—that is, the right judgments—of the holy Angels because of the error of the other nations concerning nonexistent things, namely false gods that do not exist. For those false gods are shown to be demons, their deceptions, and the irrational contrivances of those most wretched rational souls.

He aptly calls the commands and principalities of the Angels “right knowledge.” For they do not rule the nations entrusted to them in any other way than through knowledge and wisdom. Intellectual creatures are capable of knowledge and wisdom, as it is written: “You made the heavens in understanding” [Note: [Col. 0215] B* corrected “you made” to “he made”].

“But they themselves,” he continues, “having fallen away through their own deviations from the straight return that is toward the divine, through self-love and pride, and, by divine permission suitably fitted to them, through the worship of their own opinions” [Note: [Col. 0215] B has “through the worship of opinions divinely and suitably fashioned for them”].

The order of the words is: “But it is necessary to blame those very peoples of the nations, who have fallen away—fallen backward—through their own deviations, that is, through the irrational movements of their own will, from that straight return, namely from the straight path of true religion itself, which is directed toward the divine and leads to the worship of the true God” [Note: [Col. 0215] So C and B*’s correction; AB has “the living one”], “and this happened to them through self-love.”

They loved themselves rather than their God; puffed up with pride, they served the creature more than the Creator, and they were led astray by the worship of their own opinions. That this should happen to them in a manner corresponding to them, according to divine providence—that is, in accordance with the divine plan—was permitted [Note: [Col. 0215] B* adds below: “was permitted”].

For God gave them over to a reprobate mind, so that they might do what is not fitting.

The Hebrew people themselves are also reported to have suffered this. That is, the Hebrew people are said to have departed from the straight path by which the one God is worshiped, just as the other nations did, and to have worshiped idols; therefore they suffered divine vengeance.

“For you rejected the knowledge of God,” he says, “and went after your own heart” [Note: [Col. 0215] In place of “the knowledge of God, he says,” B has “he says, the knowledge of God”].

For we do not possess a coerced life, nor are the divine lights of provident illumination blinded by the independent power of those provided for. Rather, the dissimilarity of intellectual visions, in relation to the superabundant gift of light from the Father’s goodness [Note: [Col. 0215] B reverses the order: “the Father’s goodness”], either makes it wholly unshared and undistributed for their reformation, or makes their participation different—small or great, dark or clear—in the one, simple, ever-unchanging, and superabundant radiance of the fountain [Note: [Col. 0215] B* corrected AB’s “ever”].

In this statement he strongly commends the free choice of rational creatures and the superabundant and infinite outpouring of illuminations from the Father’s goodness upon human minds in common.

He says: “We human beings possess not a coerced but a free life.” It is as though he said:

The Creator and disposer of all nations did not appoint angelic princes over them so that they might convert them against their will and without the desire of free choice to his worship. If this were done, the glory of the divine image would be reduced to servitude and become worthless. Rather, he foreordained his Angels over peoples that did not know him so that, through a hidden and intelligible admonition, the intellectual being might lead the rational being back, by spontaneous movement, to knowledge of its Creator.

For we do not possess a coerced life.

Since the divine lights of provident illumination—that is, of divine providence, which illuminates every human being coming into this world—are so infinite and so common that they cannot, through any independent power of free choice in those for whom provision is to be made, be blinded—that is, obscured and alienated—from the common knowledge of all intellectual and rational beings [Note: [Col. 0217] “And” is omitted by B; B has “be prevented”], therefore he says:

“Nor are the divine lights of provident illumination blinded by the independent power of those provided for.”

For whether intellectual or rational creatures remain within their natural movements [Note: [Col. 0217] B* corrected AB’s “among” to “within”] and do not break through them, or whether they wish to transgress the limits of nature through contrary movements—just as they exceed the divine laws—they cannot be deprived wholly and generally of the divine illuminations.

But the dissimilarity of intellectual visions, or faces—ὄψις (*opsis*) can signify both “vision” and “face” [Note: [Col. 0217] B writes *oys*]—makes the gift of light from the superabundant, that is, more than abundant, goodness of the Father [Note: [Col. 0217] B reverses the phrase to “the Father’s goodness”] either wholly unshared and undistributed for the reformation of those visions, or makes their participation different.

There are some who do not wish to share in the ray of divine illumination present to them, or to have it distributed to them. They voluntarily close the eyes of their intellect so as not to receive the divine light, abusing the gift of free choice, and rejecting what is distributed to them for their reformation. For “their foolish heart was darkened” [Note: [Col. 0217] B has “for it was darkened”].

Or the same dissimilarity of intellectual faces makes their participations different—small or great, obscure or clear [Note: [Col. 0217] B* adds above: “or clear”]. Some participate in the divine light less, others more; some more obscurely, others more clearly.

This is the ray of the fountain, one, simple, immutable, always existing in the same manner, and superextended [Note: [Col. 0217] The main text of AB has “superextended” in the plural; B* corrected it]. It is the ray of the Word of God, plainly, born from the fountain of the Father’s goodness and poured universally over all intellectual eyes, whether anyone receives it or not.

For this visible sun also diffuses the ray of its light equally upon all [Note: [Col. 0217] A has “diffuses” in an erroneous form], yet it is not equally shared by all upon whom it is diffused [Note: [Col. 0217] “By all upon whom it is diffused” is omitted in the manuscripts and supplied here by conjectural emendation]. It penetrates glass, is reflected by flint [Note: [Col. 0217] Emended reading; AB has the corrupt “if it may strike through”], passes through pure air, and rebounds from a watery cloud.

§ 3. Then, since certain alien gods did not rule the other nations as well—nations from which we too have turned our gaze toward that great and abundant sea of the divine light, prepared and opened for all for their reception [Note: [Col. 0217] A reads *intradictionem* instead of *in traditionem*]—for Scripture testifies that the Most High established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God, and that Michael is the prince of the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0217] B reads “Greeks,” C “Hebrews.”], this is subsequently understood to mean that certain alien gods did not rule the other nations either—nations from which we too have turned our gaze, that is, in which we have believed—toward that open, great, and abundant sea prepared for all for their reception [Note: [Col. 0217] A reads *intradictionem*].

For the sea of infinite goodness is ready to give itself to all who are able to share in it; it is denied to no one, because it envies no one. For there is no acceptance of persons with God, and it desires to be shared by all. By “alien gods,” however, he means demons, whom the alien nations worshiped apart from the Hebrews, ignorant that the children of God had been appointed to rule them [Col. 0218B].

There is one principle of all things, and the ruling angels, according to each nation, led back to it those who followed them [Note: [Col. 0217] B* corrected *principante* to *principantes*; A and B read *gentes*; the reading “angels” is corrected from the Greek and the text, where A and B have “peoples.”]. For there is one principle of all things, to which the ruling angels brought back, among the individual nations, those who followed them—namely, obeyed them.

Next follows praise of Melchisedech, king and priest of the Hebrews. Melchisedech is to be understood as the supreme priest, the dearest friend of God among existing beings—not non-existent beings, but the truly existing Most High God [Note: [Col. 0217] B* corrected *existentibus* to *existentium*.].

This praise may be expressed in clearer words, so that the sense is: Melchisedech is to be understood to be supreme priest, not of those things which exist, but of the truly existing Most High God, and God’s dearest friend among those things which exist [Note: [Col. 0217] A and C read *non eorum existere*; B has the words in the reverse order; B omits *quae sunt*.]. It may also be interpreted in this way: Melchisedech is to be understood as the supreme priest, the dearest friend of existing things—not of things that do not exist, but of the Most High God himself, who truly exists [Col. 0218C].

The sense, however, is nearly the same; it is as though he were saying: Melchisedech is to be understood as being, as it were [Note: [Col. 0217] Conjecture; A reads *quem*, “whom”; C *qui est*, “who is.”], the supreme priest and dearest friend of those who exist with God; yet he is not the priest of things that do not exist, but of the Most High God himself, who truly exists [Note: [Col. 0217] B omits “The sense, however, is nearly the same … Most High God.”]. For in this straightforward way the theosophers themselves called Melchisedech not merely God’s friend but also his priest.

Or did the wise men openly signify by this that he not only converted them to the God who truly is, but also, as supreme priest, led others to the true and only Divinity by the return which is directed to it [Note: [Col. 0217] B* corrects *esse* in A and B to *ea quae est*; B* corrects their *reductionem* to *reductione*.]?

Or perhaps, he says, the divine wise men called Melchisedech not merely God’s friend but also God’s priest, so that they might signify clearly and evidently to the wise that he not only turned the Hebrews, plainly, toward God, but that, as supreme priest, he also led people from other nations out by that return which leads to the true and only Divinity, namely, by faith, action [Col. 0219A], and contemplation [Note: [Col. 0219] In place of *actu et*, A reads *actue*, and C *et actione et*.].

Beautifully, then, after the angels who rule the individual nations, Melchisedech is introduced—namely, the king and priest of the Most High God, who converted many not only from the Hebrew people but also from other peoples to the worship of the true God. Although this is not written in sacred history, we must in no way doubt that the truth of these events existed [Note: [Col. 0219] B* corrected *veritate* to *veritatem*.], persuaded to believe this doubtful matter by two very weighty arguments.

First, blessed Dionysius would not have stated such things without hesitation if he had not learned them from apostolic authority, handed down by those whom he had seen and heard. Second [Note: [Col. 0219] B reads “second”; C “second, because.”], the Old Testament records no patriarch who bore as great a figure of Christ as Melchisedech himself [Note: [Col. 0219] C reads *sit*; A has *et eius*, and B *ut eius*, with B* adding *quod*.].

Although Christ is Hebrew by the origin of his flesh, he nevertheless brought forth the elect not only from the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0219] C reads *ab*; B omits it, while B* adds it above the line], but also from all nations; for them he both constructed his one Church as a house belonging to himself and joined it to himself as a bride beloved by him in spiritual marriage [Note: [Col. 0219] C and B* read “in spiritual marriage”; A and B have “spiritually under the yoke.”]. This mystery was foreshadowed under the symbol of Melchisedech.

Beautifully, as I have said, after the angels who are princes of the nations [Note: [Col. 0219] ABC read “princes”; B* corrected the form to the singular “prince.”] he is introduced, so that by this we may understand that not only angels but also holy human beings rule individual languages and nations according to the worship of the divine dispensation and the laws of wisdom.

After this mystical commemoration of Melchisedech, he turns his attention to the examples by which angels are shown to rule the nations, saying:

§ 4. “And we shall also admonish your supreme-priestly understanding of this: that, while an angel was ruling Pharaoh among the Egyptians, and while an angel appointed for the purpose presided over the prince of the Babylonians, the provident and governing power of the providence and dominion of all things was distributed according to visions [Note: [Col. 0219] B reads “gifts”; B* corrected this to “dominions.”], and ministers of the true God were appointed leaders over those nations.”

“We shall admonish,” he says, “O Timothy [Note: [Col. 0219] Emendation; A and B read *Thimothe*, C *Otymothee*], your supreme-priestly understanding, so that you may know without hesitation this: that the provident and governing power—that is, the providence and power—of the providence and dominion of all things, namely, of the Word of God, who is the providence and dominion of all things, was distributed according to visions, that is, according to what was revealed in prophetic visions [Note: [Col. 0219] B reads “related”; B* corrected it to “revealed.”], and that ministers of God were appointed leaders over those nations.”

This is proved by the angel ruling Pharaoh—when an angel ruled Pharaoh among the Egyptians, as Joseph saw—and by the appointed ruler, when the proper angel presided over the prince of the Babylonians, as Daniel saw [Note: [Col. 0219] B* corrected *propriis* to *proprio*; C reads “and by the proper ruler, while the angel …”].

By these clearest examples it is made unquestionably evident that angels of God preside over all nations and that they revealed visions to the prophets.

The order and character of the prophetic vision are then appended: “The manifestation of the angelic formation of the vision, revealed by the angels immediately to the holy men Daniel and Joseph from God through the angels.” This is a hyperbaton [Note: [Col. 0219] B* corrected the form; A and B have *Yperbatonem*, C *Yprobaton*.], whose order is: “The manifestation, revealed by the angels, of the formations of the vision [Note: [Col. 0219] C and B* read *formationum*; A and B have *formationem*], that is, of the angelic formations [Note: [Col. 0219] B reads “angelic,” rather than “of angels,”], immediately from God through the angels to the holy men Daniel and Joseph.”

The sense is this [Note: [Col. 0219] B reverses the words to “the sense is”]: all these things were brought to human knowledge through prophetic visions, when the manifestation—that is, the exposition—of the vision’s formations, namely, the imaginings and representations by which the prophetic spirits were formed, was revealed by the angels of angels, that is, by the higher angels to the lower angels [Col. 0220B]. Then this revealed manifestation itself was immediately handed down by the angels, from God, to the holy prophets [Note: [Col. 0219] B has “the manifestation is.”].

Thus, first the angels rule the archangels, for example, and consequently the archangels, through the angels, reveal the formations of prophecy to holy men; and all of this comes from God.

He then adds this in sequence: “There is one principle and providence of all things.” It is as though he were saying: no generations whatsoever are ruled by anyone—whether those that have already believed or those that are still held in the darkness of ignorance—except by the one providence of the one principle of all things [Note: [Col. 0219] A reads “of one”]. For divine goodness provides equally and commonly for all nations [Note: [Col. 0219] A omits “divine”].

He teaches this in connected sequence [Note: [Col. 0219] C reads *connexim*; A and B have *quo nexim*, corrected in B* to *quo connexim*]: “And it must in no way be thought that the Divinity fully guided the Jews, while angels ruled the other nations in a special or equally honorable manner, or in opposition, or that certain other gods ruled the other nations.”

It is as though he were saying openly: the Divinity must in no way be understood to have ruled the Jews fully—or, as it is translated more explicitly, consummatively, that is, beyond the other nations—by itself, without any angelic power intervening [Note: [Col. 0219] B omits “by itself”; B* adds it above the line], while angels ruled the other nations in a special manner, that is, individually [Note: [Col. 0219] B* adds in the margin: “that is, individually”], or with equal honor [Note: [Col. 0219] C reads “or equally”; A and B read “or neither”], namely, nations that are equally honorable—for example, Romans, Greeks, and others of the same kind and equally powerful—or in opposition, that is, as adversaries of other nations, whether to one another or to the Jews—or that certain other gods, plainly demons, ruled them.

I judge that this was said against the pride of the Jews, who assert that God himself rules them directly, not through any of his angels [Note: [Col. 0221] The reading is *suorum*, “of his own,” rather than the transmitted form], and therefore boast [Note: [Col. 0221] B omits “therefore they”] that they are more honorable than the other nations, as though Israel, the chosen people, enjoyed the special rule of the one God.

He continues: “But that utterance must also be understood according to the sacred understanding itself [Note: [Col. 0221] B* adds “is”].”

“Not according,” he says, “to the false and arrogant Jewish opinion by which they boast that they are, as it were, God’s own inheritance [Note: [Col. 0221] A and C read *iactant*, “they boast,” rather than *iactitant*, “they keep boasting”], but according to the divine providence itself, that utterance must be received”—that is, divine Scripture must be examined according to that sacred understanding which teaches that the commonwealth of universal creation is governed by a common providence and salvation [Note: [Col. 0221] C and B* read “salvation”; A and B have “for salvation.”].

Therefore it is added: “Not as though God, sharing our leadership with other gods or angels, assigned Israel to the rule and leadership of a nation while being content [Note: [Col. 0221] B reads *contempto*, “despising”; B* corrected it to *contento*, “being content”] with the other nations, but as though that one exalted providence of all things together distributed all human beings beneficially through the restorative guiding hands of their own angels, while Israel alone, for the most part, was turned beyond all others toward the illumination and knowledge of the true Lord.”

“Not as though,” he says, “God shared our leadership with other gods or angels”—that is, divided among other gods or angels the rule of us, namely, the other nations from which we are called to the worship of the one true God [Note: [Col. 0221] B* adds “and rule”—“the rule and leadership”]—as though he were content with Israel alone for the rule and leadership of a nation, so that he would be prince and leader of a nation, and of no nation except the Jewish one. Rather, it was as though one providence of all things together distributed all human beings beneficially, as the cause of the salvation of all, through restorative guiding hands—plainly, through the assistance of their own angels—while Israel alone, almost beyond all the nations, was turned toward the light and knowledge of the true Lord.

Hence theology, signifying that Israel had possessed God himself for the service of the true God, says: “The Lord’s portion was made.” Hence—that is, for this reason—because Israel alone, for the most part, was converted to knowledge, theology, signifying that Israel had possessed the Lord himself for his service, says: “The Lord’s portion was made.” It may also be interpreted as: “He was made”—with Israel understood—“the Lord’s portion” [Note: [Col. 0221] C omits *se*; A and B omit *quidem*.].

To show that he also assigned him individually among the other nations to one of the holy angels, so that through him he might know the one principle of all things, Michael said that he had led the Jewish people.

“He said this,” he says, “to show that the Lord himself assigned rule over the other nations individually to one of the holy angels” [Note: [Col. 0221] B* adds in the margin: “that is, individually; or, to speak more explicitly, one to one, or each one to each one, or individual ones to individual ones”], so that through him—namely, through the angel—he might lead the nation over which he presides to knowledge of the one principle of all things, which is the Lord himself. Therefore he said that Michael had led the Jewish people: through one leader explicitly named for one nation, he might indicate to us the other leaders of the other nations [Note: [Col. 0221] A and B have *insinueret*; C and B* read *insinuaret*], and overthrow the false opinion of the Jews, who suppose that no ruler except God himself rules them immediately.

He continues: “Teaching us openly that there is one providence, placed superessentially above all invisible and visible powers together” [Note: [Col. 0221] A reads “one”; A and B have “there is one providence of all things,” with B omitting the repeated phrase “of all things.”].

It is as though he were saying: for this reason theology assigns to each of the individual generations its own angel, assigning one to each, so that it may teach us openly that there is one providence, placed above every essence, which is established over all invisible and visible powers together [Note: [Col. 0221] A reads “one.”].

All the angels who rule the individual nations, following him as their own principle, extend every power toward him by essential will.

From what precedes the following must be supplied: the same theology teaches us that all the ruling angels of the individual nations extend—that is, raise up—every power toward him, following him, namely, obeying him, by essential will [Note: [Col. 0221] B reads “superessential will”], with the full freedom of the will [Note: [Col. 0221] C and B* read “plainly,” rather than B’s “full”], which exists essentially in human minds; that is, they extend every power of souls that freely follow them [Note: [Col. 0221] B* adds in the margin “or individual [powers]”] toward God himself as their own principle. This is fitting, because the Lord is the proper and only principle of rational creation.

The order of the words, therefore, is: theology teaches that all the powers follow the angels who rule the individual nations and extend themselves by essential will toward him as their own principle.

In this one sentence a wholly sound and very lofty doctrine is handed down to us.

First, that the holy angels are our rulers, and that they rule us for no other reason than to recall us from our errors and ignorances to knowledge of the one principle and cause of all things, which alone is our salvation, purification, illumination, perfection, supreme blessedness, and deification [Note: [Col. 0221] B* corrected *ut* to *et*; C omits *et*].

And no one of us is brought back unwillingly, lest the natural glory of the divine image—which was given to us above all in the freedom of the will—be disfigured [Note: [Col. 0221] A and C read *decoloretur*; B has *decoleretur*]. Rather, within the inward power of each of us there are given choice, freedom, and the possibility of returning to him in whose image we were made, and of being deified and blessed in him [Note: [Col. 0221] A and B have *deificiendi*; C and B* read *deificandi*], while he, through his angels, recalls us [Note: [Col. 0223] B* adds “and assists us”; C reads “calls us and assists us”], assisting us—he who loves the whole human race together.

## CHAPTER X

### Its title: The Repetition and Anagogy of the Angelic Order

[Note: [Col. 0223D] In A, in illuminated letters: “Chapter Ten,” whose title is “The Repetition and Anagogy,” with “of the order” supplied. In B, in illuminated letters: “Chapter Eleven,” entitled “Why All the Heavenly Essences Are Commonly Called Powers.” B* corrected “Eleven” in ink to “Ten,” punctuated the words “Why … are called,” and added in the margin: “The repetition and anagogy of the good angelic order.”]

In this chapter the exposition of the three heavenly hierarchies is briefly repeated, together with the gathering and distinction of their order [Note: [Col. 0223] B omits the sentence “In this chapter … distinction.”].

§ 1. Thus the most honorable disposition of the minds concerning God, sanctified by the teletarchic illumination [Note: [Col. 0223] A and B read *teletarchia*; B* corrected this to *teletharchica*]—that is, by the illumination of the one who perfects and consecrates—ascends immediately into it and is purified, illuminated, and perfected by the more hidden and more manifest illumination of the Divinity [Note: [Col. 0223] A reads “in the middle” instead of “immediately”].

“Connected,” that is, joined to one another and inseparably united, is the most honorable disposition itself—the sublime adornment, plainly, of the minds that are immediately concerning God: namely, the three orders of the first hierarchy [Note: [Col. 0223] A reads “in the middle” instead of “immediately.”]. This disposition exists through the teletarchic illumination, that is, through the Divinity itself, which is called teletarchic because it is the prince of perfections and sanctifications. It is sanctified—or, to translate more explicitly, although less customarily [Note: [Col. 0223] The word “translated” is omitted in ABC and added in the margin by B*]—“pontificated,” that is, raised and exalted into the pontifical order. For it is the first priesthood of the heavenly essences, established by God himself. By ascending immediately into it—plainly, into the teletarchic illumination—the other hierarchies that follow it are purified, illuminated, and perfected through the more hidden and more manifest illumination of the Divinity.

It is purified from every ignorance, illuminated by every wisdom, and perfected by every deification [Note: [Col. 0223] A and C read “deification”; B has “edification.”].

In what respect, then, is one and the same first hierarchy more hidden and more manifest? This is added: it is more hidden as being more invisible, more simplified [Note: [Col. 0223] B* corrected “more made simple” to “more simplified”], and more unified; but it is more manifest as having been given first, shining first, being more universal, and having the form more fully poured into it, as is fitting.

It is more hidden than the others because it is more invisible—or, as it may be translated more explicitly, more intellectual—because it is more intellectual than the others, owing to its immediate proximity to him who surpasses every intellect. It has also been made more simple and more unified. Thus, it is more hidden than the others in three ways: because it is more invisible and intellectual, because it is more simple, and because it has been constituted more unified.

For every creature, insofar as it is intellectual, simple, and unified, is proportionately more obscure than other creatures and more difficult to know, because it is closer to the wholly invisible and incomprehensible cause of all things [Col. 0224A].

It is more manifest as having been given first, that is: it is more manifest [Note: [Col. 0223] B* adds “is”] because it was given and constituted before all things—not in time, but in the dignity and sublimity of its nature; because it shines first, before all things, after the inaccessible light that created it; because it is more universal than the others, that is, more free from every variety and dissimilarity; and because the form of all things has been poured into it more fully, insofar as it can be comprehended—namely, the only-begotten Word of God, according to whom and through whom all things are formed [Note: [Col. 0223] C and B* read *ad*, “according to,” rather than A and B’s *at*.].

It is more manifest than all the other hierarchies in four ways. First, because it was created before all the others in the loftiness of nature; second, because it shines primordially after God, both upon those that follow it and upon itself [Note: [Col. 0223] B omits “and upon itself”]; third, because its orders are more universal, that is, more similar to one another; fourth, because more of the form of all things is diffused into it than into the others and is manifested in it more explicitly [Note: [Col. 0223] B omits the phrase “the form of all things is diffused.”].

The first heavenly hierarchy is therefore more obscure than the others because it is more manifest—that is, brighter—and it is brighter because it is more obscure. For its brightness surpasses the splendor of the other heavenly minds and brings darkness upon them, just as the sun becomes darkness to those who gaze at it. For it is wiser than all and more incomprehensible.

From it, in turn, proportionally, the second [Note: [Col. 0223] B omits “the second”], from the second the third, and from the third our own hierarchy are hierarchically led back according to the law of the well-ordering taxisarchy [Note: [Col. 0223] A and B read *ornantibus*; B* corrected this to *ornantis*], in divine harmony and proportion, toward the super-principal beginning and consummation of every good order [Col. 0224C] [Note: [Col. 0223] B* corrected *ierarchiae* to *ierarchice*; A has *ducitur* rather than *reducitur*.].

What he says is clear. The hierarchy nearest to God himself is led back into God himself, that is, it is said to be raised upward. From the first, the second is led back according to the proper proportion; from the second, the third; and from the third, our human hierarchy is led back according to the laws of the well-ordering taxisarchy—namely, of the Divinity—in divine unification and proportion.

And to what are they all led back? Upward, plainly, to the super-principal beginning and super-consummative consummation of every good order: plainly, to God himself, who is the beginning of all beginnings and more than a beginning, and the consummation of all consummations, that is, the end and more than the end. They are led back hierarchically—that is, each hierarchy is raised according to its own laws into the divine harmony and proportion [Col. 0224D].

§ 2. All are revealers, and angels of those who precede them. The first are revealers of the most honorable God who moves; the others proportionally are revealers of those who are moved by God.

All the heavenly powers are revealers and angels of those who precede them. Thus the orders of the first hierarchy, which are the most excellent of all, are revealers and angels of God, who moves all things, while the others proportionally are angels of those who are moved by God [Note: [Col. 0225] B* corrected *et angeli* to *angelis*; ABC read *angelis*.]. For just as the first hierarchy announces God himself, so the middle hierarchy announces the first to the third, and the third announces the middle to the fourth, which is ours [Note: [Col. 0225] A and B omit the longer sentence; B* adds it in the margin, and C reads: “They announce God himself; the second announces the first to the middle, and the third the middle to the fourth, which is ours.”].

To put it briefly: the lower orders, ascending step by step, are angels of the higher orders, and all are together angels of God.

For the superessential harmony of all things has foreseen and distributed to each rational and intellectual being as much in sacred adornment and ordered guidance as each order of the hierarchies itself has been placed in sacred and fitting order [Note: [Col. 0225] B* corrected *positos* to *positus*.].

“The superessential harmony,” he says—namely, the supreme cause of all things—“has foreseen distributing sacred adornment and ordered leading to each rational and intellectual creature to the extent that each individual order of the hierarchies is holy and beautifully arranged,” that is, to the extent required by the order of the hierarchies; to that extent is it distributed to it from the superessential unity of all things [Note: [Col. 0225] B reads “distribution” rather than “ordered leading.”].

We also see every hierarchy divided into first, middle, and last powers.

This too was stated in the preceding chapters: every hierarchy consists of three orders, two of which occupy the positions of the extremes, while the third occupies the middle position, as the order of the archangels stands between the principalities and the angels.

But the disposition itself, taken individually, has also been distinguished according to the divine harmonies. It is as though he were saying: we see not only individual hierarchies divided into first, middle, and last powers [Note: [Col. 0225] A reads “individual”], but we must also say that the superessential harmony has specially distinguished the general disposition of all the heavenly hierarchies, within the divine harmonies themselves—namely, within the unifications—according to the individual hierarchies [Note: [Col. 0225] A and B read “of the hierarchies”] into first, middle, and last powers [Note: [Col. 0225] A reads “decreed” rather than “distinguished.”].

Thus the hierarchy of powers, authorities, and dominions possesses the harmony of a proportional middle between the three orders of the first hierarchy and the three of the third hierarchy [Note: [Col. 0225] B omits “three.”]. For just as the middle hierarchy is preceded by the first, so the third is preceded by the middle; and conversely, just as the third is preceded by the middle, so the middle is preceded by the first. This precedence and succession are understood in terms of differences in participation in the divine illuminations.

Some receive them highly, others more highly, and others most highly [Note: [Col. 0225] B* adds “others most highly”]; or perhaps [Note: [Col. 0225] B omits “or”], not only are the individual hierarchies, but the general hierarchy itself, divided into first, middle, and last powers.

Yet it must be stated carefully that the disposition, taken individually—that is, the individual orders of the individual hierarchies [Note: [Col. 0225] A and B read “of the hierarchies”]—has been specially distinguished by the superessential harmony within the divine harmonies themselves [Note: [Col. 0225] C reads “within the first [harmonies]”] into first, middle [Note: [Col. 0225] C and B* add “and middle”], and last powers [Note: [Col. 0225] B omits “and last”; C and B* include it].

To put it more clearly: not only are individual hierarchies distinguished into three orders, but each individual order is also distinguished into first, middle, and last powers.

For example, the first hierarchy is distinguished into the Seraphim, as first powers; the Cherubim, as middle powers; and the Thrones, as last powers.

Again, the order of the Seraphim possesses its own first, middle, and last distinctions. The same is to be understood concerning the other orders of the individual hierarchies.

This is made clear by the words that follow. Therefore the theologians say that the most divine Seraphim themselves cry out, one to another [Note: [Col. 0225] B reads “and they themselves”], thereby, as I judge [Note: [Col. 0225] B and A read “as a testimony” rather than “as I judge”; B* corrected the reading], declaring that the first themselves hand down theological knowledge to the second.

“Therefore,” he says, “the theologians say that one Seraph cries out to another [Note: [Col. 0225] B omits “to another”; B* adds it in the margin; C reads “one Seraph cries out to another Seraph”], so that by this they might declare that those Seraphim who possess the first powers hand down theological knowledge—that is, contemplation of divine principles [Note: [Col. 0225] A and B read “contemplations”; C and B* read “contemplation”]—to the second Seraphim, who possess the second powers.”

The same reasoning is to be observed in the Cherubim and Thrones and in the orders of the remaining hierarchies.

Thus one Seraph precedes another Seraph, one Cherub another Cherub, one Throne another Throne, one Power another Power, one Authority another Authority, one Dominion another Dominion, one Principality another Principality, one Archangel another Archangel, and one Angel another Angel. Among human orders, one bishop precedes another bishop, one priest another priest [Note: [Col. 0225] A and B have the plural “of priests”; C and B* read the singular], one deacon another deacon, and so forth, so that under the same designations of the names the first, middle, and last powers are understood [Note: [Col. 0225] A and B have the singular “is understood”; C and B* read the plural].
