### § 3

I might perhaps add this also, not inappropriately: that each individual being, whether celestial or human, has within itself special, primary, intermediate, and final orders and powers, proportionately manifest through the proper upward-leading movements of each of the hierarchical illuminations mentioned, [Col. 0226D] through which each becomes a participant—so far as it is both right and possible—in the more-than-perfect perfection of the most fully luminous light of the super-unknowable purification.

[Col. 0227A] “I could,” he says, “add this also to what has been said, something that does not seem incongruous, although it may appear obscure.” And what is it? That not only the general hierarchy, and the orders of the particular hierarchies, and the individual orders themselves, but also every celestial and human soul has within itself special primary, intermediate, and final powers, proportionately manifested—that is, illuminated—through the proper upward-leading movements of each order mentioned. Through these proper upward-leading movements, each of the things previously mentioned becomes a participant in the more-than-perfect perfection of the most fully luminous light of the super-unknowable purification of the Divinity, [Col. 0227B] precisely as it is right and possible for it to be—that is, as participation in God permits it to be.

[Note: [Col. 0225] Conjecture; AB read *sit* (“may be”).]

God is the super-unknowable purification, the most fully luminous light, and the more-than-perfect—that is, more than perfect—perfection. For nothing is perfect in itself if it stands in need of universal perfection, except what is truly most perfect and more than perfect.

Therefore, he says, every human and celestial soul becomes a participant in divine purification, illumination, and perfection, since by itself it can neither be perfected, illuminated, nor purified. Nothing that exists is perfect in itself while it needs the perfection of all things universally—that is, participation in the one cause of all—except what is truly most perfect and more than perfect: [Col. 0227C] namely, the truly highest Good, which is perfect and more than perfect in itself, and the end and beginning of all perfections.

[Note: [Col. 0227] B reads *humanus animus et caelestis* (“the human soul and the celestial [soul]”).]

[Note: [Col. 0227] B omits *universalis* (“universal”).]

[Note: [Col. 0227] C reads *se* (“itself”); AB omit it, while B* added it in the margin.]

[Note: [Col. 0227] B reads *est et perfectissimum* (“is and most perfect”).]

[Note: [Col. 0227] B reads *et* (“and”) instead of *atque* (“and also”).]

If, then, one asks what the primary, intermediate, and final powers of each celestial and human soul are, the answer must be as follows.

We observe that the human soul possesses these three kinds of power. Its primary powers are intellectual: they are concerned, in a supernatural manner alone, with the cause of all things, which is God. Its intermediate powers are rational: they exercise their force in knowing the nature of all created things. Its final powers are those that direct their operations toward the soul’s natural impulses.

Nor, I think, would any rightly philosophizing person easily doubt that celestial souls also possess these powers, since celestial souls turn intellectually toward God, rationally toward the natures of things, [Col. 0227D] and, endowed with inward perception, toward their own natural impulses.

[Note: [Col. 0227] B reads *participare* (“to participate”).]

[Col. 0228A] The primary powers, whether in a celestial or a human soul, are called theological by the theosophists; the intermediate powers are physical; and the final powers are moral. The primary are appropriately so called because they perform the functions of their powers in relation to God; the intermediate, because they do so in relation to created nature; and the final, because they do so in relation to morals, which follow nature.

For a certain middle term of nature has been given between God and morals. Just as God, who is supernatural, precedes nature, so nature precedes morals. And just as moral powers follow natural powers, so natural powers follow divine powers.


#### Restored apparatus to § 3

- At *quod* (“that/what”), ABC have the printed reading; B* corrects it to *quid* (“what?”).
- At *in se ipso* (“within itself”), C and corrected B* have the singular form; AB read *ipsos* (“themselves,” masculine accusative plural).
- B omits *esse* (“to be”) in “as participation in God permits it to be.”
- At *sensu praediti* (“endowed with inward perception”), the printed wording is conjectural. A reads *sensus praedicti* (“the aforesaid sense”), B *sensu* (“with sense”), and C *sensu praedicti* (“with the aforesaid sense”).

### CHAPTER XI

Its title is: “Why all celestial essences are commonly called celestial powers—that is, why all celestial souls are called by the single name ‘powers,’ just as they are called by the common name ‘angels.’”

[Note: [Col. 0227D] A has this title. B has, in illuminated lettering: “Chapter twelve, whose title is: Why, according to human beings, the hierarchies are called angels.” B* first wrote *vocibus* (“by names”) for *vocantur* (“are called”), then substituted the following: “All celestial essences are commonly called celestial powers.”]

#### § 1

[Col. 0228B] Once these matters have been defined, it is worthwhile to understand why we customarily call all angelic essences alike celestial powers. For it must not be said that this is because, among the angels, the disposition of the powers is the last of all.

[Note: [Col. 0227] B reads *ratio reddenda est* (“the explanation must be given”).]

He does not give the same explanation for the common designation “powers” as for the designation “angels,” when the question is why all the essences are called angels. We cannot say that celestial souls are commonly called powers because the disposition of the holy powers is the last among the divine orders.

That explanation was given concerning the designation “angelic,” when it was asked why all celestial essences were generally called angels: namely, because the angelic order occupies the lowest place among all the celestial orders. The dispositions of the essences placed above them participate in [Col. 0228C] the holy and beautiful illumination of the last essences; the last essences, however, in no way participate in that of the first.

[Note: [Col. 0227] B reads *sanctam et decoram illuminationem* (“the holy and beautiful illumination”).]

[Note: [Col. 0227] B reads *ultima* (“the last”).]

[Note: [Col. 0227] C and B* read *proponit* (“he proposes”); AB have *proposita morditur*, evidently corrupt.]

He begins to accumulate the question proposed in this way: “The last essences participate in the holy and beautiful”—or, more explicitly, “they participate in the holy, fitting illumination”—of the essences placed above them.

[Note: [Col. 0227] B reads *sanctam et decoram* (“holy and beautiful”).]

[Note: [Col. 0227] AB read *veluti* (“as if”); C has *vel ut* (“or as”).]

[Note: [Col. 0227] B reads *decentem illuminationem* (“a fitting illumination”).]

This may be stated more clearly as follows: the dispositions placed above them—that is, the orders of the celestial essences—participate in the holy and beautiful illumination of the last powers, or, as it is more fittingly translated, in an illumination appropriate to the holy ones. The final essences, however, do not participate in the illumination appropriate to the holiness of the first illuminations.

There is no power in the last essences that does not subsist in the first; but [Col. 0228D] there are things in the first that do not subsist in the last.

He then proposes the following: “And for what reason are all the celestial powers called divine intellects, whereas the Seraphim, Thrones, and Dominations are not at all called divine intellects? For [Col. 0229A] the lowest essences are participated in by the most exalted essences with respect to universal properties.”

[Note: [Col. 0229] B* added in the margin *ab excelsis* (“from the exalted”).]

Therefore, he says, I propose this question: why are all the divine intellects called powers, but not the Seraphim, Thrones, or Dominations? For the lowest essences are participated in by the highest essences with respect to universal properties. It is therefore not surprising if the highest essences were designated by the names of the lowest, since there is no property in the lowest that the first do not share.

What is surprising, however, is why all the divine intellects are called by the name “powers,” when the powers are counted among the exalted substances.

[Note: [Col. 0229] A has *sunt* (“are”).]

For it is the first order of the middle hierarchy. Hence he adds: “For the Angels themselves, and before the Angels the Archangels, and the Principalities and Powers, which theology itself has ordered after the Powers, are [Col. 0229B] often commonly and likewise called by us celestial powers, just as are the other holy essences.”

[Note: [Col. 0229] C and B*’s corrected reading have *se virtutum* (“of the powers themselves”); AB read *servitutum* (“of services”), evidently corrupt.]

And for this reason it is not without justification that one asks why the lower and last orders are designated by the name of powers that are far above them.

#### § 2

We say, however, that when we commonly use the name “celestial powers” for all of them, we are not introducing any confusion of the properties of each disposition.

[Note: [Col. 0229] The phrase *appellatione significantur—virtutum* is omitted in B; B* added in the margin: “We say, however, that when we commonly use the designation ‘powers.’”]

He resolves the question he proposed. We say, he declares—that is, we answer—that we do not introduce any confusion of the properties of each order when we commonly use the designation “celestial powers” for all the divine souls.

It is as though he said: When we call all the divine souls by the name “powers,” we do not take away its own property from the order of the Powers, nor should we be judged to attribute that property indiscriminately to other essences, whether higher or lower. For [Col. 0229C] we are not signifying the property of the order of the Powers itself, but another power that is generally present in all the divine souls.

And this is what follows:

“But since, according to the supermundane account of their own nature, all the divine intellects are divided into three—essence, power, and operation—when, [Col. 0229D] without discrimination, we call all of them together, or some of them, celestial essences or celestial powers, we must be understood to signify, by circumlocution (*περιφραστικῶς*, *periphrastikōs*), those of whom we are speaking, by reference to the essence or power that exists in each of them.”

[Note: [Col. 0229] B’s later hand added in the margin *peryfrasticos*, “circumlocutorily.”]

[Note: [Col. 0229] B* added *est* (“it is”).]

The order of the words is: “It must be understood that we signify, by circumlocution, those of whom we are speaking when we call all of them together, or some of them, without discrimination, celestial essences or celestial powers, by reference to the essence or power that exists in each of them. For all the divine intellects are divided, according to their own supermundane nature, into three: essence, power, and operation.”

[Note: [Col. 0229] C reads *secundum*; AB omit it, while B* added it in the margin.]

[Col. 0230A] “We do not,” he says, “introduce confusion into the properties of the divine intellects by calling them by the name ‘powers.’ Rather, we must be understood to signify them by circumlocution (*περιφραστικῶς*, *periphrastikōs*), that is, by an indirect expression. We mean the divine souls of whom we are speaking, by reference to the general essence and general power—and, by implication, the general operation—that exists in each of them, when we call all the divine souls together, or some of them individually, without discrimination, that is, with a common and undifferentiated designation, celestial essences, celestial powers, or celestial operations.

“We do this for good reason. Their division is threefold: into essence, power, and operation. [Col. 0230B] Perhaps these are the three matters treated in the preceding chapter, where the primary, intermediate, and final powers of each celestial and human soul were discussed, so that we understand the primary powers as belonging to essence, the intermediate to power, and the final to operation.”

[Note: [Col. 0229] B reads *priori* (“preceding”) instead of *superiori* (“above”).]

“But how the intellect of essence, the reason of power, and the inward sense of operation are joined together, so that there are not two trinities, one of human beings and one of angels, but one, we have sufficiently discussed, I think, in the books *περὶ φύσεων* (*peri physeōn*, “On Natures”).”

[Note: [Col. 0229] B* added above the line *ut arbitror* (“as I think”); C likewise has *ut arbitror*.]

Nor should it be thought that we attach the superordinate property of the holy Powers—whose distinction from the other divine intellects we have already properly established—[Col. 0230C] to the lesser essences as well, as though in a reversal of the unconfused order of the angelic ranks.

From what precedes, the meaning is this: Nor, he says, should it be thought that we attach the superordinate property of the holy Powers, which we have properly distinguished from the other divine intellects, to the lesser essences as well, as though in a reversal and disturbance of the unconfused order—that is, the unconfused divine order.

It is as though he said: Let no one think that we add the property of the holy Powers to the lesser essences, or disturb the immutable and unconfused order. Rather, we teach that the general power—which is common both to all and to each individually—bestows the name “power” upon all and upon each.

[Note: [Col. 0229] AB read *et jam* (“and now”).]

[Note: [Col. 0229] A has *in confusione* (“in confusion”); B has *inconfusione* (“in an unconfused [order]”).]

[Note: [Col. 0229] A and B have *degeneralem*; C reads *sed de generali virtute, quae* (“but from the general power, which…”).]

[Note: [Col. 0229] C omits *et* (“and”); A has *in* instead of *et*.]

[Note: [Col. 0229] B* and a later hand in C corrected *impertiri* to *impartiri* (“to impart”).]

For, according to the explanation that we have often rightly given, the dispositions established above possess abundantly even the sacred properties of the lesser orders; but the last orders do not possess the superordinate universals of the higher orders, except in a particular way, through the illuminations that first appear in the higher orders and are distributed proportionately to the last.

[Note: [Col. 0229] A and B have *superfirmitate* (“superiority” or “established elevation”); the reading in the text is conjectural.]

[Col. 0230D] This repeats the distinction between the first and last celestial essences explained above. We have often, he says, given an account of the fact that the divinely superordinated souls do not abundantly possess the holy properties of the lower orders, since [Col. 0231A] the illuminations that first appear universally in the first orders are distributed to the last orders in particular, through the first orders and proportionately to them.

[Textual/exegetical note: Here the printed commentary says that the higher orders do *not* abundantly possess the holy properties of the lower orders; later it says that the first orders do possess those properties abundantly. Both statements are retained, since the supplied text is internally inconsistent at this point.]

This may be summarized briefly: the higher orders possess abundantly both their own properties and those of the lower orders. The divine illuminations that first appear in them, however, are not distributed abundantly—that is, universally—to the last orders as they are to the first; rather, they are distributed to the last through the first and in particular ways, according to the proportion appropriate to them.

[Note: [Col. 0229] B reads *ultimo* (“the last”).]

[Note: [Col. 0229] B has *eadem* (“the same”); C reads *eodem* (“in the same [way]”).]


#### Restored apparatus to Chapter XI

- In “because the disposition,” the printed *quia* (“because”) is replaced by *quoniam* (“since”) in AC.
- After “the disposition … is,” AB omit *est* (“is”); B* supplies it above the line, while C reads *sit* (“may be”).
- For *denominarentur* (“were designated”), B has the orthographic form *denominarrentur*.
- At “not of the order itself,” the text has *ipsius* (“of it”); B* corrects this to *ipsis* (“to/for them”).
- For *ordinis virtutum proprietatem* (“the property of the order of Powers”), B reverses the final words to *proprietatem virtutum* (“property of Powers”).
- In the first circumlocutory construction, after *aestimandum* (“it must be thought”), B* supplies *est* (“it is”).
- In the following phrase *Ordo dictionum* (“the order of the words”), B* again supplies *est* (“is”).
- B omits *ageretur* (“was being discussed”) in the reference to the primary, intermediate, and final powers.
- At “the inward sense is joined to operation,” ABC read *adunatur* (“is joined”), while B* corrects it to *adunetur* (“may be joined”).
- Where the text attaches the property of the holy Powers “also” to lesser essences, B* reads *etiam* (“also”); AB have *et jam* (“and now”).
- At “in particular,” the text reads *particulariter in*; the alternate reading is *particulariter autem in* (“but in particular”).

### CHAPTER XII

Its title is: “Why, according to human beings, the hierarchies are called angels—that is, why the chief priests of the earthly Church are still called angels.”

[Note: [Col. 0231] A omits *titulus* (“title”); it was added by conjecture.]

[Note: [Col. 0231D] A has this title. B, in illuminated lettering, has: “Chapter thirteen” (B* corrected *duodecimum*, “twelfth,” in ink), “whose title is: Why the prophet Isaiah is said to have been purified by a Seraph.” B* erased the words “by a Seraph ... Isaiah” and added in the margin: “Why the hierarchs of human beings are called angels.”]

#### § 1

This question also arises for those who carefully contemplate the intelligible utterances. [Col. 0231B] If the participants in the higher universals are not the last, for what reason is the chief priest, according to us, called “the angel of the Lord Almighty” by the utterances of Scripture?

[Note: [Col. 0231] B omits *nos* (“according to us”); B* added it in the margin.]

[Note: [Col. 0231] Emended; AB have the plural *nominantur* (“are called”).]

The question, he says, is also posed by those who carefully attend to the intelligible utterances. If, as he stated, the last orders do not participate in the universals of the higher orders, why is the chief priest called “the angel of the Lord Almighty” by Holy Scripture, when the angelic orders do not participate in the universal?

[Note: [Col. 0231] B has *possunt*; B* corrected it to *posuit*; C has *possit*.]

#### § 2

There is, I think, an explanation that is not contrary to what was defined earlier.

The order of the words is: “There is, I think, an explanation that is not contrary to the explanations previously defined.”

We say that the last orders are left behind by the universal and superordinate power of the higher orders.

[Note: [Col. 0231] B has *in universali* (“in the universal”).]

[Note: [Col. 0231] B reads *malorum* (“of evils”) instead of *majorum* (“of the higher”).]

[Note: [Col. 0231] Emended; AB read *relinquitur* (“is left behind,” singular).]

We say, he declares, that [Col. 0231C] the last orders are left behind—that is, surpassed—by the universal and superordinate power of the higher or, more properly translated, more honorable orders.

For the last orders participate in a middle and proportionate power.

[Note: [Col. 0231] C and the corrected reading in B* have *mediam ... proportionabilem ... virtutem* (“a middle, proportionate power”).]

He called it “middle” instead of particular, in accordance with a single and connective fellowship. For there is one fellowship belonging to all, although within it there are universals and particulars.

An example is this: the order of the holy Cherubim participates in higher wisdom and knowledge. The dispositions of the essences beneath them also participate in wisdom and knowledge, but in a particular and subordinate way in relation to the Cherubim.

Do not be troubled by the Greek construction, in which the verb μετέχω, meaning “I participate,” takes both a genitive and an ablative: μετέχω σου means “I participate in you” and “I participate in what belongs to you.”

[Note: [Col. 0231] C has *participio* (“I participate”); A and B have *participio* with a correction in B*.]

[Note: [Col. 0231] C has *participio tui et te* (“I participate in what belongs to you and in you”); A and B have corrupt readings, *participio potui et ate*.]

Such, he says, is the meaning: I say that the order of the holy Cherubim participates in higher wisdom and knowledge. [Col. 0231D] He used *altiorem* (“higher”) instead of *altius* (“more highly”).

[Col. 0232A] The dispositions of the lower essences beneath them—that is, beneath the Cherubim, or extending themselves beneath them—also participate in that same wisdom and knowledge, but with a particular and subordinate participation in relation to them, that is, in comparison with the Cherubim.

[Note: [Col. 0231] B omits *participatione* (“participation”).]

That he used the middle order of the first hierarchy as an example was done, I think, either for the sake of brevity or because the middle always implies the extremes.

[Col. 0232B] It is common to all the godlike intellectual beings to participate in wisdom and knowledge at all. But to participate attentively and first, or second, or below, is by no means common to all; rather, it is determined for each according to its proper proportion.

The point he makes is clear. It is common to all the divine intellects to participate in wisdom and knowledge. But to participate more attentively—that is, more perceptively and more fully—or first, or second, or lower, is not common to all. The first hierarchy participates first; the second participates second, that is, somewhat lower; the third lower still; and the fourth, namely the human hierarchy, lower again than the third, according to what was previously defined for each hierarchy by its proper proportion.

[Note: [Col. 0231] C and B* read *secundum* (“according to”); AB have *sicut* (“just as”).]

[Note: [Col. 0231] B has *diffinitum* (“defined”).]

[Note: [Col. 0231] A omits *prius* (“previously”).]

Nor, perhaps, would anyone in error define this differently concerning all the divine minds. It is as though he said: No one would mistakenly define the same matter concerning all the divine minds—that some participate first, others second, and others lower in knowledge and wisdom.

For each of the divine minds does not participate equally. [Col. 0232C] The first participate first through their own powers, the intermediate participate second, and the last lower down participate in knowledge and wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0231] B omits *quaeque* (“each”).]

[Note: [Col. 0231] A has *divini mentis*; C has *mentis divinae* (“of the divine mind”).]

[Note: [Col. 0231] C and B* have *primae* (“the first”).]

[Note: [Col. 0231] B’s corrected reading is *virtutes* (“powers”).]

[Note: [Col. 0231] B’s corrected reading is *mediae* (“the intermediate”).]

[Note: [Col. 0231] B’s corrected reading is *ultimae* (“the last”).]

For just as the first orders abundantly possess the holy and beautiful properties of the lower orders, so the last orders possess the properties of the first, though not in the same way, but at a lower level.

This has been said concerning their common participation: just as the first orders possess the properties of the orders beneath them, so the last possess the properties of the orders above them, though not in the same way, but at a lower level.

[Note: [Col. 0231] B has *propriorum* (“of those nearer”), evidently corrupt; AC read *priorum* (“of the earlier orders”).]

For the first possess the properties of the last universally, whereas the last possess the properties of the first particularly. There is no power in the last angel that is not in the highest; but there are many powers in the highest that are not in the last.

[Col. 0232D] Nothing, then, is disorderly, I think, if theology also calls the chief priest among us an angel: he participates according to his own power in the prophetic property of the angels and extends himself toward their manifest likeness, so far as is possible for human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0231] Conjecture; AB have *in profetica* (“in prophetic”).]

[Col. 0233A] If, he says, all divine souls, whether celestial or human, have been established as participants in wisdom and knowledge in common, although not equally, it is not disorderly if the chief priest among us is called an angel according to his own power, by which he participates in the prophetic property of the angels and extends himself toward their manifest likeness, so far as this is possible for a human being.

For just as the angels of the chief priests are prophets to human beings, so the chief priests are prophets of the ecclesiastical orders beneath them.

[Note: [Col. 0233] B* added in the margin *angeli* (“angels”) instead of *homini* (“to a human being”).]

[Note: [Col. 0233] A has *angelorum* (“of the angels”); B has *angelorum* with a correction in B*; C has *summi angeli* (“the chief angels”), apparently with the sense “the angels of the chief priests.”]

And just as angels manifest the divine mysteries to the chief priests—that is, announce them—so, [Col. 0233B] by the same analogy, the chief priests do not cease to announce those same mysteries to those beneath them.

#### § 3

You will also find that theology calls both the celestial and supernal essences gods, as well as among us those who are God’s beloved and wondrous men.

It is no wonder, he says, if theology has called the chief priest an angel of God, since you will find that the same theology calls the celestial essences gods, and human beings gods because they are friends of God. If human beings, then, are called gods, what is surprising if chief priests are called angels?

And indeed, because of the divine obscurity, which is at once beyond essence, removed from all things, and placed above all things, nothing similar to it can properly and altogether be named from it.

[Note: [Col. 0233] A has *supernos* (“supernal”); B has *supernos* instead of *supernas*.]

[Note: [Col. 0233] Conjecture; AB have *est*, which does not fit the context.]

[Note: [Col. 0233] B omits *omnino* (“altogether”).]

[Note: [Col. 0233] B has *eo* (“by it”) instead of *ea* (“by it,” referring to the feminine *bonitas* or *obscuritas*).]

[Col. 0233C] For the divine goodness is so hidden, invisible, beyond essence, and removed from all things that nothing is like it which can properly be named from it, so that God cannot properly be called “God,” “goodness,” or “truth.”

Nevertheless, every intellectual and rational power that is universally turned toward its unity in whatever manner, and that extends itself unceasingly toward the divine illuminations as far as possible, has, according to its power—if it is right to say so—become worthy of divine imitation and divine univocation.

[Note: [Col. 0233] B* corrected *unitationem* to *unitatem* (“unity”).]

[Note: [Col. 0233] B* added above the line *et qualiscunque* (“and of whatever kind”).]

[Note: [Col. 0233] B* added *est* (“is possible”).]

[Note: [Col. 0233] B* corrected *juxta* (“according to”) to *justum est* (“if it is right”).]

[Note: [Col. 0233] B reads *invocatione* (“invocation”) instead of *univocatione* (“univocation”).]

[Col. 0233D] Although, he says, the divine invisibility surpasses all things, so that no creature can properly be named from it, nevertheless every intellectual and rational power, of whatever kind, that is universally turned toward its unity and extends itself without ceasing toward its illuminations, as far as is possible for a creature, has, according to its own power—if it is permissible to say so—become worthy of divine imitation and divine univocation, that is, of divine likeness and a divine name.

[Col. 0234A] For the abundance of the ineffable divine goodness both grants its likeness and bestows its name upon all intellectual and rational souls that are universally turned toward it and extended toward it without interruption.

[Note: [Col. 0233] B* corrected *quaeque* to *quaecunque* (“whatever”).]

[Note: [Col. 0233] B* corrected *unitationem* to *unitatem* (“unity”).]

[Note: [Col. 0233] B* added *et* (“and”) before *qualiscunque* (“of whatever kind”).]

[Note: [Col. 0233] C and B corrected *extenti sunt* to *extentis* (“extended”).]

- At “in which, nevertheless,” B reads *in quantum* (“insofar as”) rather than *in qua* (“in which”).

### CHAPTER XIII

Its title is: “Why the prophet Isaiah is said to have been purified by a Seraph.”

[Note: [Col. 0233] A has *Esaias*, and does so throughout; B has *Isaias*, and does so almost throughout. B omits the title; B* added in ink: “Chapter XIII, whose title is: Why the prophet Isaiah is said to have been purified by a Seraph.”]

#### § 1

Come, let us also examine this according to our capacity: why the theologians say that a Seraph was sent.

“Come,” he says, “let us consider, according to the power of our understanding, the objection which may be raised against our argument. If, as we have said, the human hierarchy is ordered through the last order of the celestial powers, which is properly called angelic, why does a Seraph—one, that is, from the number of the first hierarchy—purify the prophet? [Col. 0234B] [Col. 0234B] For that belongs to the angels. Let us inquire, according to the capacity of our understanding, for what reason the theologians have said this.”

There would indeed be no question if we had not determined that neither can the Seraphim be called lower powers, nor is our hierarchy administered except through the lowest angels.

[Note: [Col. 0233] B’s corrected reading has *posset*; C has *ipse*.]

What follows is consequent upon this: “For someone might explain that it was not one of the subordinate angels, but a certain one among the highest essences in their ranks, who purifies the priest.” It can also be interpreted thus: “For anyone might reply that it is not one of the subject angels, but the Seraph himself—that is, one who is among the most honorable essential ranks—who purifies the prophet.”

[Note: [Col. 0233] B* corrected *maximis* to *de maximis* (“among the greatest”).]

[Col. 0234C] Yet both interpretations have one meaning; for ἀπορήσειε may be translated either “might explain” or “might reply,” and προφήτης likewise means both “priest” and “prophet.”

[Note: [Col. 0233] AB have ἀπορρηση; C has *apophysi*. AB have ὑποφητης; C has *prophytis*. C and corrected B have *responderet* (“might reply”); AB have *responderit*.]

#### § 2

Some therefore say that, in accordance with the definition already given of the fellowship of all intellects, the utterance does not name one of the first minds placed around God as having come for the prophet’s purification, but rather a certain one of the angels who preside over us, performing the purification of the prophet and called equivocally “Seraph” because of the fiery and heavenly removal of the sins mentioned and the raising up of the purified man into divine obedience.

He says that some wish to explain the question thus. In accordance with the definition of the fellowship of all celestial intellects previously given by them—not by us—they say that all celestial intellects are in such fellowship that all and each are commonly called by the names of all and each. Therefore, they say, [Col. 0234D] the theologians do not say that one of the Seraphim, but [Col. 0235A] one of the angels who preside over us, sacrifices—that is, purifies—the prophet; and that the divine utterance calls this angel “Seraph” because of the fervent, fiery, and heavenly removal of sins—that is, the purification—of the prophet. For he said that he had sinned in his words and had dwelt in the midst of a sinful people; and therefore he is purified, in order that he may be raised up into divine obedience, namely for preaching sins to the people.

[Note: [Col. 0235] B* corrected *nomina vocari* to *nomine vocari* (“to be called by the name”); C has *eloquium nominare Seraphim*. C and corrected B* have *resuscitetur* (“may be raised up”); AB have *resuscitatur*. B* corrected *praedicandum* to *praedicationem* (“for preaching”). C has *populo* (“to the people”); AB have *populum*, while B* corrected it to *populis*.]

For this reason, they say, the angel was made equivocal with “Seraph,” in order to signify thereby that all celestial powers possess the force of spiritual fire. For *Seraphim* is interpreted either “kindling” or “warming”; and every power through which God purifies us from our offenses and [Col. 0235B] illuminates our mind with the rays of his wisdom coming upon it warms and kindles a human being.

[Note: [Col. 0235] C has *calefacit* (“warms”); AB have *calefacta* (“warmed”).]

They further say that the utterance said simply “one of the Seraphim,” not one of the powers placed around God, but one of the purifying powers that preside over us.

[Note: [Col. 0235] The word *simpliciter* is omitted, but supplied from the version and Greek text. B* corrected *collocaturum* to *collocatarum*.]

They maintain their interpretation for this reason: Scripture did not say that one of the powers around God purified the prophet, but simply called a certain fiery Seraph, one of those presiding over us, which was sent to cleanse the prophet’s lips.

[Note: [Col. 0235] B has *et* for *ea*.]

#### Restored apparatus to Chapter XIII

- At “Come … let us examine,” A reads *quoniam* (“since”) where the text has *quod* (“that/why”).
- In the statement that the Seraphim cannot be named lower powers, B has *nec* (“and not”) for *neque* (“nor”).
- B omits *nisi* (“except”) from “nor is our hierarchy administered except through the lowest angels”; B* supplies it in the margin.
- A reads the feminine plural *quae* (“which”) for *qui* (“who”) in “one who is among the most honorable ranks.”
- At the beginning of the explanation “For this reason,” C and corrected B* read *Ea* (“by this [reason]”), while AB have *et* (“and”).
- At “the rays of his wisdom coming upon [the mind],” B spells *supervenientibus* as *superuenientibus*; the sense is unchanged.
- For “they say [Scripture] said,” A reverses the order to *aiunt dixisse*; the printed text has *dixisse aiunt*. The meaning is unchanged.

### § 3

The other, however, offered me a not altogether incongruous apology—that is, a defense—concerning the present matter, that is, concerning the present question. But he left unspoken who that “other” or “another” might be. *Apologia* may also be interpreted as “defense” and “satisfaction.” [Col. 0235]

For he says that the great angel who at that time was forming the vision, in order to teach the theologian divine things, placed that proper purifying sacrifice in God and, after God, in the pre-operating hierarchy. He says, then, that the great angel who formed the vision in the prophetic spirit and sacrificed the purification of his lips taught him divine commandments. For the theologian—that is, Isaiah himself—did not assign his own act of purification to himself, but to God, who is the beginning of all purifications; and he assigned it also to that first hierarchy, through which God pre-operates, and through the other succeeding celestial and human hierarchies, in which he accomplishes the purifying power.

Therefore, what God commanded to be done through the angel Seraphim—that is, to purify the prophet—he attributes not to the angel himself who performed it, but to God; and he says that Seraphim itself purified the prophet. [Col. 0235–0236A]

Blessed Dionysius follows and approves this interpretation as his own. For he adds:

“And is this account therefore true?” [The manuscripts have “not what?”] He says that the one who said this—that is, the one who put forward this interpretation—said:

“How does the divine power, coming into all things, fill”—understand, “fill all things”—“and immeasurably reach through all things, while again remaining invisible to all, not only as being superessentially removed from all, but also as secretly permitting its providential operations to enter into all things? Yet it also shines above all intellectual beings proportionately, and, imparting its own illumination to the most precious essences, through them, as through the first recipients, distributes its own illumination well and fittingly to subordinate beings, according to the contemplative measure of each disposition.”

He praises and teaches that the divine power comes into all things, fills all things, and penetrates all things through the infinite diffusion of itself, while remaining invisible to all because it is superessential and removed from all. Secretly it permits its providential actions to enter into all things—or, as it is translated more precisely, it causes them to reach all things—and, while remaining removed from all, it shines above all intellectual creatures in an ineffable manner, according to the proportion of each, that is, according to each creature’s capacity. It imparts its own illumination to the most precious beings, that is, to those established beneath it, and through them distributes that illumination well and fittingly to subordinate beings, according to the measured contemplation of each order.

Where we have translated *superlucet* as “shines above,” the Greek has ἐπιφαίνεται (*epiphainetai*), which may be translated “shines above,” “appears above,” or “shines upon.” Likewise, where we have translated *ingerens* as “imparting,” the Greek has ἐγχειρίζουσα [AB: εγχερυζουσα; C: *egchirisusa*], for which we may say “imparting,” “offering,” or “entrusting.” [Col. 0235]

To make this clearer, and to use proper examples—even though they fall short of God, who is removed from all things—let me present examples that are nevertheless more evident to us. The order and meaning are as follows:

“To speak more clearly: I shall persuade you concerning that distribution of the divine power among all things, both by proper examples and by examples that fall short—that is, that are not altogether like God, who is removed from all examples—by offering such paradigms.”

The distribution of the solar rays into the primal matter, being well apportioned, fills the more luminous matter of all things and, through it, more clearly reveals its own splendors.

The solar ray, he says, which extends through the spaces of this visible world, is well distributed into the primal matter—that is, into the ether and the upper air nearest to it—and, diffused through them, fills the matter more luminous than the other parts of the world, namely, the air and the ether, as we have said. Because of their extreme subtlety, with no corporeal density obstructing them, the solar ray penetrates these two parts of the world with ineffable speed and brightness, fills them, and, through that more luminous matter and within it, reveals its own splendors more clearly than elsewhere. [Col. 0236A–0237A]

When it approaches denser matter, however, it distributes a darker manifestation of itself, because of the resistance offered by the matters that are to be illuminated to the distributive condition of illumination. The same ray, when it reaches denser matter—specifically, the lower part of this air, which is made thicker and denser than the upper parts of the world by watery and earthy exhalations—and also reaches the nature of the waters, distributes the manifestation of itself more obscurely. This does not happen because the matter to be illuminated is slow in receiving the distributive condition of illumination. For these matters are not capable of receiving the higher light to such an extent as to attain the perfect condition of illumination. [Col. 0237]

A little later the text continues: “and from this it is compressed almost into complete non-distribution.” It is as though he were saying:

“Not long afterward, beneath the denser matters—that is, beneath the thickest earthly bodies, which are solid and do not provide access for light—the ray itself is compressed, so that it distributes almost none of its light”; that is, it is impeded. [Col. 0237B–C]

Again, the heat of fire distributes itself more fully among things that are more receptive, and among things that suitably resemble it and are well adapted to it. But toward essences opposed to its formative operations it reveals no trace, hidden from view, of its primitive operation [B: “from what is hidden, or hidden”; C: “from what is hidden”].

The first paradigm, drawn from the solar ray, is adopted to illustrate the visible world as it fills and illuminates it according to the quality and capacity of matter. The second is drawn from the quality of fire, namely, heat: it first and foremost warms what is capable of receiving it and resembles it, but it does not in any way reform essences opposed to its formative operations, that is, the coldest essences. Therefore all cold things are said to be called lifeless and deformed, while warm things are called living and beautiful, since every corporeal matter is formed and reformed through heat by the universal life that governs all bodies.

For this reason he said: “But toward essences opposed to its formative operations”—that is, toward essences rendered unsuitable for formation by their excessive coldness—the heat itself reveals no trace, hidden from view, of its primitive operation [B: “from what is hidden, or hidden”; C: “from what is hidden”].

He says beautifully: “the hidden trace of the primitive operation.” For the first operation of fire is to heat, and this is said to act secretly in all bodies. Heat is invisible. Why, then, is the action of heating placed before the action of illuminating, since both belong to fire? The answer is readily apparent when we clearly see that heat penetrates bodies more deeply than light. Dense bodies exclude light, but they cannot exclude heat. [Col. 0237–0238B]

If someone should say that light penetrates ice, whereas heat does not, let him observe that ice is dissolved not by the force of light but by that of heat. If heat did not enter it, it would not dissolve it.

The passage may also be translated in this way:

“But toward essences formed contrary to it, no hidden trace of the first operation appears.”

The meaning would be:

“In essences formed contrary to the nature of heat”—the manuscripts read “color”—“it impresses no, or at least no obscure, trace of the primitive operation, that is, of heating.”

For snow and ice cease to exist before they receive any trace of heat [AB: “ceasing to be”; C: “cease to exist”]. What should we say about the salamander, sleeping in fire and often even extinguishing the fire by the coldness of its body?

And this is an additional argument—that is, an argument stronger and clearer than the one just mentioned—because the first operation is admitted by things that are not akin to it [AB: “known”] through things that are suitable to them.

That is, heat is first permitted to reach bodies that are not akin to it—that is, not naturally related to heat—through suitable bodies that possess a natural affinity with it, that is, with heat itself [AB: “with it”]. The same meaning may also be expressed as follows:

“Because through things familiar to it and belonging to heat, the first operation is brought to things not naturally akin to it.”

He teaches this clearly by the examples that follow:

“For instance, making things fiery through fiery things that are easily moved”—that is, making warm the things that are easily moved by fiery qualities into heat—“and through these proportionately warming either water or something else that does not easily become fiery” [AB: “igniting”].

For example, the heat of the sun first penetrates and warms the air, which is akin to it, through an easy operation. Then, through the warmed air, it warms cold water or something else that cannot easily be warmed, in accordance with their natural compatibility. [Col. 0238C–0239A]

What follows is clear:

“According to this order, then”—that is, according to the likeness of light and heat—“the supernatural hierarchy of every visible and invisible good order, namely, the divine power, which is the beginning and ruler of the whole order, manifests the brightness of a fitting illumination—that is, of a proportional illumination—which first appears, bursting forth from its hidden sources, in which it is inaccessible in itself, into the nature of things. It manifests this brightness in the most abundant effusions, that is, in the most abundant outpourings, to the highest essences, which are plainly the nearest; and through them the essences that come afterward participate in the divine ray.” [The manuscripts read “the order of the arrangement”; one has “the essences that can.”]

These highest essences are the first to know God, to desire the divine power in a transcendent manner, and to become pre-operating powers. As far as possible, they have been made worthy of a virtue and action like God’s. They extend the essences after themselves toward a similar virtue—that is, insofar as the virtue of each essence is capable of receiving the divine ray—in a godlike manner, generously transmitting to them the brightness that comes upon them. Those essences in turn—that is, those established after the highest essences—transmit the brightness that comes upon them to the essences subject to them. Each transmits it first to the one that follows it. [Col. 0239]

For example, the first hierarchy gives divine illuminations to the middle hierarchy, the middle to the third, and the third to the fourth, which is among human beings.

A third paradigm follows:

“Does water itself not also reach all things proportionately?”

It is as though he were saying:

“Does water itself, just like the solar ray and the heat of fire, not reach all material things proportionately?”

We have translated this passage in this way for ease of understanding. It may nevertheless be translated more explicitly—although more obscurely—in the same sense:

“Does water, then, not also reach all things proportionately?” [The manuscripts omit “in”; one adds “is distributed.”]

As though he were saying:

“Is water not therefore distributed among all matters, reaching them proportionately”—that is, reaching them in due relation and in a manner similar to the solar ray and to heat?

For water secretly enters trees and herbs from the ground through their roots; thereafter, step by step, it passes into trunks and *thyrsi* (shoots) [AB: *tirsos*], branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.

Thus it is simultaneously the beginning of illumination for all illuminated things [“of illuminating things”]. [Col. 0239B–D]

After the paradigm we return to the subject at hand—that is, to the explanation of divine power and illumination.

“There is,” he says, “a common and universal beginning of illumination for all things illuminated or to be illuminated”—for either translation is possible for the Greek word φωτοζομένοις (*phōtizomenois*). “And what is that beginning?”

God is the beginning by nature, truly and properly, as the essence of light and as the cause of being and seeing.

For God alone is God by nature, and God alone is truly and properly God. The others who are called gods are either false gods, such as the gods of the nations and the demons, or, if they are true gods, they are gods not by nature but by grace. To them the prophet says:

“I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’”

“As the essence of light and the cause of being itself”—the word “as” is used here as a causal conjunction [the manuscripts read “for which”]. It is as though he were saying:

“God, who alone is God by nature, is recognized as the beginning of illumination for illuminated things because he is the essence of light.”

In him every light and everything illuminated subsists, because his essence is light and he is the cause of being itself. Whatever exists receives its being from no other source than from him who is superessential, and he is the cause of its seeing. [Col. 0239–0240B]

He has used infinitives in place of nouns [the manuscripts read “infinitive”]. Here it is beautifully made clear that, for God himself and for every rational and intellectual creature, being is not one thing, being light another, and seeing—that is, understanding through cognitive power—another. For them, being, shining, and seeing are the same thing. Their being is their light and their vision.

This “godlike and God-like” condition remains, which is properly translated as:

“establishing this in a godlike manner and in a manner like God”—namely, the one who is the cause of all things.

And what is that?

“For each essence placed above the one after it to convey the divine lights into that one through itself.”

That is, the one who is the cause of all things establishes that every essence placed above another essence carries—or conveys—through itself the divine lights into the essence that follows it [the manuscripts omit “into it”]. For ἐποχετεύεσθαι (*epocheteusthai*) may be translated “to carry across,” “to carry above,” or “to convey into.” [Col. 0239–0240C]

Therefore all the essences of the remaining orders marvel at the most excellent disposition of the celestial minds, which is, after God, the principle that follows him, as well as the principle of all sacred and divine knowledge and of divine imitation—as though through those essences divine illumination were distributed to all things and to us.

The order and meaning are as follows:

“Therefore they marvel”—or “judge,” for ἡγοῦνται (*hēgountai*) may be translated both “they marvel” and “they judge.” “They marvel” suits the meaning better here, because the statement concerns praise—“all the essences together marvel at the dispositions of all the remaining celestial essences.”

What do they marvel at? The most excellent disposition of the celestial minds, insofar as it follows after God.

And what do they marvel at—or praise—in it? That it is the principle, after God, of all sacred and divine knowledge and of divine imitation, since through those essences—namely, the essences of that most excellent disposition—divine illumination is distributed to all the other celestial essences and to us human beings, who share in human essence. For divine illumination is distributed through them, and they have been established as the one immediate principle after the one and first principle of all things, namely, God.

For this reason they refer every sacred and God-like operation to God as its cause.

The angels are to be understood here. Then they refer it to the first—that is, to the first godlike intellects—as the first agents and teachers of divine things, namely, of the lights. It is as though he were saying:

“Since the most excellent celestial disposition is immediately after God, the lower powers therefore refer all their sacred and God-like operation to themselves. But first they refer it to God, and consequently to the first intellects, which are the first agents and teachers of divine things”—understand, either of the power of the lights, or of the mysteries, or of the secrets, or of other similar things. [Col. 0240D–0241B]

What follows is a recapitulation of the interpretation of the names of the first hierarchy.

“Does not the first disposition of the holy angels therefore possess, more than all the others together, a fiery property?” [One manuscript places “a fiery property” after “possess.”]

It is as though he were saying:

“Although all the celestial powers possess a fiery property”—that is, a purifying operation—“does not the first hierarchy nevertheless possess it more than the others, since its first order is called Seraphim, that is, ‘those who burn’ or ‘those who warm’?”

“And does it not also possess the poured-out transmission of divine wisdom and the mystical knowledge of the most exalted divine illuminations?” More than all the others, the first disposition possesses this, since its second order is called Cherubim, that is, “a multitude of knowledge” or “an outpouring of wisdom.”

“And does it possess a seated property, bearing God and signifying divine reception?” Likewise, more than all the others, the first hierarchy possesses the property of the divine throne, which bears God and signifies divine reception, since its third order is called Thrones, that is, “seats.”

All the celestial powers therefore possess fiery power, an outpouring of wisdom, the mystery of knowledge, and the reception of the divine seat; but the first hierarchy possesses these more than all the others. [Col. 0241C–D]

The dispositions of the essences subject to them do participate, though in a lower degree, in the fiery, wise, and knowing receptive power of God [the manuscripts read “in wisdom and knowledge”; one has “the receptive power”].

He says:

“The disposed essences of the middle hierarchy, which are subject to the first, participate below in the fiery virtue of Seraphim, in the wise and knowing virtue of Cherubim, and in the receptive virtue of the Thrones.”

“And looking toward the first, and through them”—the first—“being fittingly made pre-operating through divine imitation, they are led back, as far as possible, into deiformity.”

That is:

“The second essences turn toward the first essences of the middle hierarchy and, through those first essences, which have rightly and fittingly been made pre-operating in the likeness of God, are led back into the possible form of deiformity”; that is, they are led upward [the manuscripts read “they are said”]. For *re* is very often used for *rursum*, “upward” or “back upward.”

Concerning the final celestial hierarchy and the human hierarchy, he leaves the meaning to be understood. For just as the second participates in the virtues of the first, so the third participates in the virtues of the second, and the fourth in those of the third. Thus the fiery, wise, knowing, and God-receptive virtue descends:

1. first from God into the first hierarchy;
2. second, through the first, into the second;
3. third, through the second, into the third;
4. fourth, through the third, into the fourth hierarchy.

It descends step by step, though not equally.

Again, the fourth is led back through the third, the third through the second, the second through the first, and the first through God himself into the virtues mentioned above [the manuscripts read “the second”; one manuscript corrects this].

Therefore they assign the holy properties that have been mentioned—participation in which comes about through the first essences existing after them—to those very essences, as hierarchies after God [the manuscripts read “that one”].

He says:

“Therefore they assign the holy properties mentioned above. For the proper operations of the angelic order, which is the last, are the purifications of the prophets and the other operations accomplished in human nature through the generosity of divine goodness. Participation in these properties comes about through the first essences existing after them” [the manuscripts read “of those existing after them”].

“They assign” means “they refer” [A: “is referred”] them to those very hierarchies, as existing after God—that is, because they are after God.

We may briefly gather the meaning as follows:

“The angelic order does not refer its own sacred operations to itself, but to those hierarchies that are after God, because it received them from those hierarchies.”

He says beautifully, “in which participation comes about through those existing after them,” because every celestial essence both becomes and is called a participant in its own properties.

The passage may nevertheless be interpreted more easily in this way:

“Therefore they assign the holy properties mentioned above, in participation in which the essences existing after them through the first essences come to be.”

For in Greek the expression is ὧν μετουσία (*hōn metousia*), “the participation of which,” and it may also be understood as “in participation in which.” For μετουσία (*metousia*) may be taken as a nominative case, while the dative is used in place of the ablative [A and B: “is placed”]. [Col. 0241–0242C]

## Ordered Textual Apparatus

“Corrected B*” below means the correction entered by the correcting hand of manuscript B; “radically corrected” means that the reading was corrected after erasure. Case, number, spelling, and word-order variants retain their source forms because English cannot always distinguish them.

### Column 0235: the purifying angel and divine illumination

- **“Not altogether incongruously” — *inconsequenter*.** A reads *in consequentem*, “toward the consequent/result.”
- **“A certain defense” — *quandam*.** Corrected B* has the feminine *quandam*; A and uncorrected B have masculine *quendam*, “a certain [man].”
- **“That other or another” — *alium seu alterum*.** A and C support these forms; B has only *alium*, “another.” The editor expects *Sed ille alius seu alter*, “But that other or another [person].”
- **“He taught him” — *eum docuit*.** Corrected B* has this reading; A and uncorrected B have *et docere*, “and to teach”; C has *et docuit*, “and he taught.”
- **“His own [act]” — *propriam*.** A and B add *purgat propriam*, literally “he purifies his own [act/person],” a grammatically difficult expansion.
- **“Not to himself” — *non sibi ipsi*.** C has the printed phrase; A and B have only *ipse*, “he himself.”
- **“Assigned” — *deputavit*.** Corrected B* has *deputavit*; A and uncorrected B have *deputatione*, “by assignment”; C reads *Isaias purgatur propriam*, a corrupt sequence, approximately “Isaiah is purified [his] own.”
- **“Through the angel” — *angelum*.** Corrected B* has accusative *angelum*; A, B, and C have dative or ablative *angelo*, “to/by the angel.”
- **“He attributes” — *attribuit*.** A and B omit the verb; B* adds it in the margin; C has passive *attribuitur*, “is attributed.”
- **“The Seraph itself” — *ipsum*.** Corrected B* has accusative *ipsum*; A, B, and C have dative *ipsi*, “to the Seraph itself.”
- **“And is this account?” — *Et numquid*.** Corrected B* has *numquid*, the interrogative “surely not?/whether”; A, B, and C have the divided *non quid*, “not what.”
- **“The one who said” — *qui*.** B was corrected after erasure to *qui*, “who”; A and uncorrected B have *quid*, “what.”
- **“How” — *Quomodo*.** B* corrects this to *quoniam*, “because.”
- **“Through all things” — *per omnia*.** A reads *in omnia*, “into all things.”
- **“Reaches” — *pervenit*.** B has *provenit*, “comes forth”; B* corrects it to *pervenit*, “reaches.”
- **“As” — *quasi*.** Corrected B* has *quasi*; A and uncorrected B have *quas*, “which [feminine plural].”
- **“To all intellectual beings” — *omnibus*.** Corrected B* has *omnibus*, “all”; A and uncorrected B have *communibus*, “common [beings/things].”
- **“Proportionately” — *proportionaliter*.** A and B omit it; it was supplied from the Latin version and Greek text.
- **“Itself” — *se*.** Corrected B* has the reflexive *se*, “itself”; A and uncorrected B have *sed*, “but.”
- **“Filling all things” — *implentem*.** A has ablative *implente*, “while [it] fills.”
- **“By its diffusion” — *diffusione*.** Corrected B* has ablative *diffusione*; A and uncorrected B have nominative *diffusio*, “diffusion”; C has accusative *diffusionem*.
- **“Or, as it is translated” — *ut*.** C omits *ut*, “as.”
- **“In a certain ineffable manner” — *ineffabili quodam modo*.** C and corrected B* have the printed phrase; A reads *ineffabiliter quomodo*, “ineffably how”; B has *ineffabili quomodo*, “by an ineffable how.”
- **“Its own illumination” — *propriam*.** The editor conjectures *propriam*, “its own”; A and B have *proprietatem*, “property”; C supports *propriam*.
- **“Its” — *suam*.** B has *suam* with punctuation adjusted by B*.
- **“Those established beneath it” — *constitutis*.** C has ablative plural *constitutis*; A and B have accusative plural *constitutas*.
- **Greek lemma for “shines above.”** The Greek is *ἐπιφαίνεται*, which may mean “shines above,” “appears above,” or “shines upon.”
- **Greek lemma for “imparting.”** The Greek is *ἐγχειρίζουσα*, “imparting,” “offering,” or “entrusting”; A and B read *εγχερυζουσα*, while C transliterates *egchirisusa*.
- **“Which distribution” — *quam*.** B* adds in the margin the clarification *quam scilicet distributionem*, “which, namely, distribution.”
- **“Through” — *per*.** A omits *per*; B has *pro*, “for,” corrected by B* to *per*, “through.”
- **“By proper examples” — *propria*.** Corrected B* has neuter plural *propria*, “proper [examples]”; A and B have adverb *proprie*, “properly.”
- **“Even though” — *etsi*.** A and B divide it as *et si*, “and if.”
- **“Falling short of God” — *deficientia Deo*.** A and B read *deficienti a Deo*, “to one falling short from God”; B* corrects this to *deficientia a Deo*, “things falling short from God.”
- **“The order and meaning together.”** A has *Ordo simul et sensus*; B has *Ordo sensus simul*, corrected by B* to *Ordo et sensus simul*; C reads *Ordo verborum similis et sensus*, “the order of the words is similar, and the meaning.”
- **“Not altogether” — *non omnino*.** C and corrected B* have the printed order; A has *omni non* and B *omnimon*, both corrupt forms.

### Column 0237: solar rays, fire, and heat

- **“Through it” — *per eam*.** Corrected B* has accusative *eam*; A and uncorrected B have ablative *ea*, “through/by it.”
- **“Well distributed” — *distributus*.** Corrected B* has *distributus*; A and B read *distributor*, “distributor”; C reads *distribuimus*, “we distribute.”
- **“Penetrates” — *penetrat*.** C and corrected B* have *penetrat*; A and B have the spelling *penitrat*.
- **“In it” — *in ea*.** Corrected B* has *in ea*; A, B, and C have *eam*, “it” as a direct object.
- **“Distributive manifestation” — *distributivam*.** Supplied from the Latin version and Greek text; A and B have the noun *distributionem*, “distribution.”
- **“Exhalations” — *exhalationibus*.** A and B read *exallationibus* (B* adjusts the pointing); C reads *exalationibus*. These are spelling forms for exhalations.
- **“Of the world” — *mundi*.** B omits *mundi*.
- **“And of the waters” — *et aquarum*.** This is conjectural. A and B have *ea quarum*, “those things of which”; B* corrects to *eis quarum*, “to/by those of which”; C has *eas quarum*, “those [feminine objects] of which.”
- **“To such an extent and [to] the perfect condition” — *et*.** A and C read *ut*, “that/so that”; B has *ut* with altered punctuation.
- **“A little later from this” — *ex*.** B reads *et*, “and,” for *ex*, “from.”
- **“Is compressed” — *coartatur*.** A reads *coortatur*; B has *coarctatur*, the standard spelling “is compressed,” with punctuation adjusted by B*.
- **“Not long afterward” — *non longe*.** C omits *non*; A and B have *non longo*, using the ablative adjective rather than adverb *longe*.
- **Second “is compressed” — *coartatur*.** A retains *coartatur*; B reads *coarctatur*, “is compressed,” with punctuation adjusted by B*.
- **“But toward” — *ad vero*.** Corrected B* has *ad*, “toward”; A and B have *at*, “but.”
- **“Opposed to its own formative operations” — *suis contrarias*.** B* supplies *suis contrarias*, “opposed to its own,” in the margin.
- **“Essences” — *essentias*.** B reads *absentias essentias*, “absences, essences,” with punctuation adjusted by B*. Migne prints *es* above *ab* in *absentias* to represent this manuscript reading.
- **“Hidden” — *absconso*.** For *absconso*, B* writes the correction or alternative *absconsum*, “hidden.”
- **“The visible world” — *mundum*.** B has the recurring spelling *mondum*, corrected by B* to *mundum*; C reads *mundam illuminante*, “illuminating [the feminine object].”
- **“First and foremost” — *primitusque*.** C has the printed form; A and B have corrupt *porimitusque*, with B* altering the punctuation.
- **“Are said” — *dicuntur*.** B has singular *dicitur*, “is said,” corrected by B* to plural *dicuntur*.
- **“From what is hidden” — *ex occultato*.** B has *ex occultato vel absconsum*, “from what is hidden, or hidden”; B* adds the alternative *vel absconsum* above the line; C has *ex occulto*, “from the hidden [thing].” Migne prints the alternative above *ex occultato*.
- **Second “hidden” — *absconso*.** B* corrects it to accusative *absconsum*.
- **“Which acts secretly” — *quae*.** B* corrects the relative to accusative *quam*.
- **“Is placed before” — *praeponitur*.** A reads *proponitur*, “is proposed/set forth.”
- **“Readily” — *facile*.** C and corrected B* have adverb *facile*; A and B have adjective *facili*, “easy.”
- **“Contrarily formed” — *contrarie*.** Corrected B* has adverb *contrarie*; A and B have *contraria*, “contrary [things]”; C has *contrarias*, feminine plural accusative.

- **“To receive” — *accipere*.** B* adds *sit accipere*, “that it may be to receive,” above the line.
- **“Not akin” — *non sunt cognata*.** Corrected B* has *cognata*, “akin”; A and B have *cognita*, “known.” The same *cognata/cognita* variation recurs in the explanation immediately afterward.
- **“Is admitted” — *admittitur*.** B corrects this verb; the uncorrected reading is not preserved separately in the supplied note.
- **“To the heat itself” — *ipsi*.** C and radically corrected B* have dative *ipsi*; A and uncorrected B have feminine nominative *ipsa*, “itself.”
- **“Either water” — *aut aquam*.** C and corrected B* have *aut aquam*; A and B read *autem qua*, “but by which.”

- **“Becoming fiery” — *ignescentium*.** C and corrected B* have *ignescentium*; A and B have the spelling *igniscentium*.
- **“The air akin to it” — *aerem sibi cognatum*.** A and B reverse the order to *sibi aerem*, “to itself the air.”

### Column 0239: the third paradigm and God as light

- **“According to this rationale of order” — *ordinationis rationem*.** B reverses the nouns: *rationem ordinationis*, “the rationale of order.”
- **“Of every good” — *omnis boni*.** C and radically corrected B* have genitive *boni*, “of good”; A and B have dative or ablative plural *bonis*, “to/by good things.”
- **“Those which come afterward” — *quae post sunt*.** C and radically corrected B* have *post sunt*, “are afterward”; A and B have *possunt*, “can.”
- **“The divine ray” — *divinum*.** Corrected B* has accusative *divinum*; A and B have ablative *divino*, “by the divine [ray].”
- **“These” — *Eae*.** B* adds the alternative *Hae*, another spelling of “these,” in the margin.
- **“Desiring transcendently” — *supereminenter*.** A has plural participle *supereminentes*, “surpassing”; B* radically corrects to singular accusative *supereminentem*, “the surpassing [power].”
- **“Pre-operating” — *praeoperatrices*.** B shortens this to *operatrices*, “operating agents.”
- **“As far as possible.”** B* supplies *est*, “is,” above the line after *possibile*.
- **“To God” — *Deo*.** The printed text is corrected to dative *Deo*; A and B have accusative *Deum*, “God” as direct object.
- **“With like virtue” — *virtute*.** A and B have accusative *virtutem*, “virtue” as direct object; B* adjusts the punctuation.
- **“And action” — *actione*.** A and B have accusative *actionem*; B* adjusts the punctuation.
- **“They have been made worthy” — *dignae effectae sunt*.** Corrected B* has the plural; A reads singular *effecta es*, “you have been made.”
- **“After themselves” — *post se*.** Corrected B* has *se*, “themselves”; A and B have *te*, “you.”
- **“Those established after” — *post*.** B omits *post*; B* supplies it in the margin.
- **“More explicitly” — *plus expresse*.** This is conjectural; A and B have *expressius*, “more explicitly”; B* corrects to *expressiusque*, “and more explicitly.”
- **“Although” — *quamvis*.** This is conjectural; A and B read *quam vos*, “than you.”
- **“Into all” — *in omnes*.** A and B omit *in*; B* supplies it above the line and adds *distribuitur*, “is distributed,” in the margin.
- **First “reaching proportionately” — *perveniens*.** The editor conjectures singular *perveniens*; A and B have plural *pervenientes*.
- **Second “reaching” — *perveniens*.** The editor conjectures *perveniens*; A reads *provenientes*, “coming forth,” and B *pervenientes*, “reaching.”
- **Third “reaching” — *perveniens*.** The editor conjectures nominative *perveniens*; A and B have dative *pervenienti*, “to the one reaching,” while B* corrects toward plural *pervenientes*.
- **“Shoots” — *thyrsos*.** A and B have the spelling *tirsos*.
- **“For all illuminated things” — *illuminatis*.** Corrected B* has *illuminatis*, “illuminated”; A and B have *illuminantis*, “of the illuminating one.”
- **“We return” — *revertimur*.** B* radically corrects this to singular *revertitur*, “it returns.”
- **Greek lemma for “illuminated or to be illuminated.”** The recovered Greek is *φωτοζομένοις*; the commentator explicitly permits both English senses.
- **“As the essence of light” — *ut*.** The Latin version and Greek text support *ut*, “as”; A and B read *et*, “and.”
- **“Causes” — *causales*.** B has *casualis*, “casual/accidental”; B* corrects to *causalis*, “causal.”
- **“They are gods” — *dii sunt*.** B reverses the words to *sunt dii*.
- **Causal “as” — *ut*.** B* corrects *ut* to *et*, “and.”
- **“Is used as [a causal conjunction]” — *pro*.** Corrected B* has *pro*; A and B have *pro qui apponitur*, the ungrammatical “for which is placed.”
- **“Every light and everything illuminated” — *omne lumen omneque*.** A and B have accusatives *omnem … omnemque*; B* adjusts the pointing.
- **“Everything that exists” — *Omne*.** B has accusative *omnem*, with punctuation adjusted by B*.
- **“Who is superessential” — *est*.** B omits *est*; B* supplies it above the line.
- **“Infinitives” — *Infinitiva*.** The editor emends to neuter plural *Infinitiva*; A and B have *infinita*, “infinite things.”
- **Second “causal” — *causalis*.** B again has *casualis*, “casual/accidental.”
- **“Through itself” — *per se*.** B omits *se*; B* supplies it in the margin.
- **“Into that one” — *in illam*.** A and B omit *in*; B* supplies it above the line.
- **Greek lemma for conveying upward.** The recovered Greek is *Ἐποχετεύεσθαι*, which may mean “to convey across,” “to convey above,” or “to convey into”; A and B read *ἐποχετευσθαι*.
- **“The dispositions [of all the remaining essences]” — *dispositionem*.** B* adds plural genitive *dispositionum*, “of the dispositions,” in the margin.
