- **Greek lemma for “they marvel/judge.”** The recovered Greek is *ἡγοῦνται*; it can mean “they judge” and is here taken as “they marvel.” B omits the following *et*, “and.”

### Column 0241: the celestial hierarchy

- **“The dispositions of all the remaining celestial essences.”** A and B transmit *dispositiones* in this syntactically difficult position.
- **“Consequent” — *consequens*.** B adds *consequens*, “following/consequent,” above the line.
- **“They marvel” — *mirantur*.** B originally has singular *miratur*, “it marvels,” corrected in the margin to plural *mirantur*.
- **“By divine illumination” — *divina*.** A reads accusative *divinam*, “divine [illumination]” as direct object.
- **“Have been established” — *substitutae sint*.** Corrected B* has the subjunctive phrase; A and B have indicative *sunt*, “are.”
- **“To the first [intellects]” — *in primos*.** B* supplies *in*, “to/into,” above the line.
- **“Does not?” — *Non*.** B corrects the printed *Non* to *Nonne*, explicitly marking a question expecting assent.
- **“Possesses a fiery property.”** B places *igneam proprietatem*, “fiery property,” together after *habet*, rather than separating adjective and noun.
- **“All celestial powers.”** B reverses the order to *caelestes virtutes omnes*.
- **Second “fiery property.”** The manuscripts omit *igneam*, “fiery”; the editor supplies it conjecturally.
- **“They possess” — *habent*.** A and B omit *habent*; B* supplies it in the margin.
- **“Fiery, wise, and knowing.”** The editor emends to *ignea sapienti et scienti*; A and B have corrupt *sapiencie sciencie*, while B* corrects toward *et sapientem scientemque*, “and wise and knowing.”
- **“God-receptive power” — *Dei susceptoria virtute*.** B* corrects to accusative *susceptoriam virtutem*, “receptive power.”
- **“Looking toward the first” — *aspicientes*.** Supplied from the Latin version and Greek text; A and B have *sapientes*, “wise.”
- **“Through them, by imitation” — *ut imitatione*.** B* corrects *ut*, “as,” to *in*, “in.”
- **“Divine imitation” — *divina*.** B was radically corrected to ablative *divina*; A and uncorrected B have accusative *divinam*.
- **“They are led upward” — *reductae/ducuntur*.** For the explanatory *ducuntur*, “are led,” A and B read *dicuntur*, “are said”; this is the context in which *re-* is glossed by *rursum*, “upward/back upward.”
- **“God-receptive” — *susceptoria*.** The editor conjectures “receptive”; A and B have *subsistentoria*, “subsistent/supporting.”
- **“Step by step” — *gradatim*.** A reads *quidem*, “indeed.”
- **“The fourth” — *quarta*.** Corrected B* has *quarta*; A and B have genitive *tertiae*, “of the third.”
- **“The second” — *secunda*.** B was radically corrected to nominative *secunda*; A and uncorrected B have accusative *secundam*.
- **“To those very [hierarchies]” — *illis*.** B was radically corrected to plural *illis*; A and uncorrected B have singular genitive *illius*, “of that one.”
- **“The purifications.”** B* supplies *est* before *purgationes*, producing the grammatically difficult “is the purifications.”
- **“In human nature” — *natura*.** Corrected B* has ablative *natura*; A and B have genitive or dative *naturae*, “of/to nature.”
- **“Existing” — *subsistentes*.** Corrected B* has plural *subsistentes*; A and B have singular genitive *subsistentis*, “of the one existing.”
- **“They refer” — *referunt*.** A reads passive singular *refertur*, “is referred.”
- **“After them” — *eas*.** The editor emends to feminine plural *eas*, “them”; A has masculine singular *eum*, “him,” and B neuter plural *ea*, “those things.”
- **Greek syntax of participation.** The recovered phrase *ὧν μετουσία* means “the participation of which,” but it may be construed as “in participation in which”; *μετουσία* can be nominative, while a dative may stand for an ablative.
- **“Is put” — *ponitur*.** Corrected B* supports the corrected verb; A and B have *positus*, “placed,” masculine singular.

[Col. 0242D] § 4. He says this, therefore—or, as it is more precisely interpreted: “The one who said this said, therefore”—that is, the one who expressed this meaning concerning the prophet’s purification by the Seraphim said that the vision had been received by the theologian from that divine power, through one of the holy and blessed angels who work upon us; and that, before the angel’s own illuminating guidance by which he led the theologian into that holy contemplation of the vision, he had placed—or, that is, referred—the vision to that Seraphim himself, by whom and through whom he was seen to purify the prophet.

“And he sees the most exalted essences sitting,” that is, the supremely exalted essences, insofar as this can be expressed through symbols—that is, insofar as what is ineffable can be expressed through symbols—placed after God and around God, upon the supreme summit, namely the superessential goodness, itself placed in the midst of the super-established powers. He briefly recalls the prophet’s vision, which is written as follows in the Hebrew text. For we do not have the Septuagint before us, which Dionysius follows:

> “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, lofty and raised up, and the things that were beneath him filled the temple. Seraphim stood above it; six wings belonged to one, six wings to the other. With two they covered his face, with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew. And one cried out to the other and said: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.’ And the lintels of the doorposts were shaken by the voice of the one crying out, and the house was filled with the smoke of incense. And he said: ‘Woe is me, for I have been silent, because I am a man of polluted lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people possessing polluted lips; yet with my eyes I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts.’ And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs; and he touched my mouth and said: ‘Behold, I have touched this to your lips, and your iniquity shall be taken away.’”

The theologian himself therefore learned through the visions that, according to every superessential transcendence, the divine is incomparably placed above every visible and invisible power.

“Isaiah,” he says, “learned through his visions that God alone is superessential, transcendent, and incomparably placed above every visible and invisible power.” It can also be interpreted: “The divine has been incomparably placed above every visible and invisible power.” By “the divine” he meant God himself, in accordance with the very common usage of the Greeks. For they say Θεός and θεῖον—that is, “God” and “the divine.”

Now “and indeed,” or “and certainly,” is understood from what precedes: he learned that the divine, understood universally, is transcendent above all that is most remote—or, “most exalted”—and is not like the first essences of existing things. For what essence can be like the superessential essence?

Moreover, he learned that the divine itself is the principle of all things and their substantializing cause, and that it is the hidden, singular, and immutable foundation of existing things; from it, plainly, both being and well-being belong even to the powers most firmly established.

What the prophet therefore sees—namely, the Lord sitting above the most exalted essences—signifies his superessentiality, remote from all things, and that universally he is the most remote of all things most exalted and most remote from every intellect, and that even the first essences are not like him. For he is left beyond every likeness, although, in order that something may be said about him, likenesses drawn from creation are applied to him.

But that he is the principle and substantializing cause of all things, and the hidden, immutable, and singular foundation, is mystically represented by the doorposts of the temple, around which all moving things revolve while they themselves remain immutable.

Next, the prophet was taught that the same most holy Seraphim are deiform powers. Through their sacred name—“Seraphim,” which means “burning”—he was taught, as far as possible, to introduce the ascensions of the fiery power into the form of the divine. We shall speak a little later, insofar as possible, about what is fiery.

The prophet was taught the ascensions of the Seraphim—that is, their elevations—into the deiform fiery power. Through understanding the name, he was instructed concerning their ascensions into the deiform fiery power. For a fiery power is like God insofar as his likeness is impressed upon sensible creatures. Hence he himself also says: “I am a consuming fire.”

The sacred formation expressed by the outspread wings signifies, in the first, middle, and final intellects, an unbounded and supremely high extension into the divine. That is, through the sacred formation expressed by the outspread wings: the prophet saw the outspread wings of the Seraphim and was taught an unbounded—that is, swift-flying—and supremely high extension, namely contemplation directed toward God, in the first, middle, and final intellects. For each heavenly essence, as was discussed above, possesses first, middle, and final powers.

The outspread wings therefore symbolize the height of understanding. But the intellectual theologian, seeing their manifold and multiform character, and seeing one vision distinguished by wings beneath the feet, another beneath the faces, and another in the middle wings, was led back from the vision itself by this threefold distinction of the wings—that is, he was led upward into knowledge of the things seen—through the manifold and many-sided power of the highest intellects manifested to him. This means that the manifold power of the highest intellects was manifested to the prophet in their many ways and in their many visions.

What the threefold division of the wings intimates he adds in due sequence, saying:

“And by their sacred fear”—the fear which they possess beyond the world, in their proud, audacious, and impossible investigation of higher and more serious things.

From what precedes the following is understood: the prophet was also taught by the Seraphim’s sacred fear—that is, by their pious and chaste fear—which they possess above this sensible world, in their proud, audacious, and impossible investigation of higher things, or divine mysteries. This is indicated by their covering their faces with two wings; and in their proud, audacious, and impossible investigation of more serious, deeper, or plainly divine mysteries, which is signified by their covering their feet with two wings.

Where we have rendered “proud,” the Greek has αὐθάδη, which may be expressed as “proud,” “ready,” “voluntary,” “self-willed,” or “asserting itself.”

And he was taught the unceasing and swift-flying movement of actions that imitate God, measured according to their proportion.

Here again “he was taught” is understood. The sense is this: through the two wings with which they were always flying, the prophet understood the unceasing and ever upward-moving motion, measured according to the proportion of actions that always imitate God.

The face of the Lord who sits upon the throne—that is, upon the most exalted heavenly essences—is his superessential height, by which he is known to be above all things and removed from all things. The Seraphim and the other heavenly powers tremble to behold this height, lest they should rashly investigate something about it with a proud, audacious, and impossible gaze. For “his judgments are inscrutable, and his ways unsearchable at every time.”

The terrified Seraphim therefore cover with two of their wings the face of that divine height. They fear to look upon it.

The feet of the one sitting upon the throne are his deepest vestiges throughout the universal creation that he established. The heavenly powers cover these with two wings, fearing to investigate how the Lord, although he is above all things, is diffused through all things and is everywhere, without whom nothing can exist, since he himself is the essence and substance of existing things, being superessential and supersubstantial.

With two wings, nevertheless, they continually fly about in the measured movement of their eternal action, because they always desire to look toward him and reverently seek him, lest in contemplating him they fall into any errors by which they might seem unworthy to be admitted to the vision of his ineffable and incomprehensible brightness.

There are many interpretations of the division of their six wings into these three pairs. The fact that they are six unmistakably signifies the perfection of the angelic nature and of its intelligible movements.

The two wings, however, either indicate the twofold character of the love by which they love their God and all things that have been made, because they have been made by him; or they indicate their action and contemplation; or the twofold division of theology, one part of which is affirmative and the other negative. One clothes God, by predicating of him everything that exists; the other strips him, by denying that he is any of the things that exist or can be spoken of. Both, nevertheless, are true and accomplish the same thing, although they appear to be contradictory.

He was also instructed in that divine and most precious ὑμνωδία—that is, “hymnody” or “praise with song”—when the angel shaped the vision according to the theologian’s own power and handed on its proper sacred knowledge.

By ὑμνωδία he means: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.” In this hymn the supreme goodness is praised in three substances. For there is one essence in three substances.

Ὑμνωδία is a compound word formed from ὑμνῶ and ᾠδή—that is, from “praise” and “song.” Ὑμνωδία is therefore praise accompanied by song.

The theologian was instructed in this praise when the angel formed the vision and, according to the theologian’s power, handed on the mystery of the praise.

The angel therefore taught him this also, namely, concerning what follows: that purification is, for those who are purified in whatever way, as far as possible, participation in the divine and unknowable brightness.

Purification, then, is the participation of all who are spiritually purified, however they are purified, in the unknowable divine brightness—that is, in the divine understanding which surpasses every intellect, insofar as it is possible for a rational and intellectual creature to participate in it.

This brightness, proceeding from the hidden causes of the Divinity itself, perfects all holy intellects through superessential concealment. In this concealment it becomes more manifest to the highest powers around it, somehow manifests itself more fully, and distributes itself.

But from where does it manifest itself and make itself more manifest? It does so when it bursts forth from its own hidden places, from all the unknown hidden causes of the Divinity itself. In this concealment of the Divinity, the brightness itself invisibly perfects all holy intellects.

This statement beautifully allows us to understand that he called no other brightness “the brightness” than the Word of God, namely the Son, who perfects all holy intellects in the most secret recesses of his Father, in their primordial causes. He proceeds, as it were, from the inaccessible light of the Divinity like a most brilliant ray, before making himself more manifest to the powers nearest to him, and before revealing how he exists—that is, how his manifestation can take place—and manifesting and distributing himself more fully to the others.

This is itself purification, illumination, and perfection—namely, participation in him.

It can also be interpreted as follows: “This brightness, proceeding from the hidden causes of the Divinity itself, whose superessential concealment perfects all holy intellects.” There is no difference in meaning.

Then, from the secondary, final, or our own intellectual powers, insofar as each of them has come into being according to the divine form, he leads his manifest illumination toward the laudable unknowability of his own concealment.

After the divine brightness, he says, bursts forth from its hidden places and first reveals itself more manifestly to the most exalted orders of the first hierarchy, which are nearest to it, it consequently leads its manifest illumination—or, more clearly translated, gathers it—toward the secondary or final orders, that is, toward the orders of the second or third heavenly hierarchy, or toward our intellectual powers, namely those of the human hierarchy, insofar as each power or hierarchy has been constituted by that divine brightness according to the divine form, that is, according to divine likeness.

For what purpose does it gather it? It gathers it toward the laudable unknowability of its own concealment, so that they may praise its most secret mysteries, unknown to all.

The divine brightness shines generally through each order, but how and in what sequence? “Through the secondary by means of the primary,” he says; and, if it is necessary to put it briefly, it is led from the hidden—that is, from its secret place—into the manifest through the primary powers. He leaves the rest to be understood: through the primary powers it is led to the secondary, through the secondary to the tertiary, and through the tertiary to the fourth, into manifestation.

The theologian learned this from the angel who led him into the light. It is as though he were saying: he learned it from the angel who introduced him into the light of the understanding of the vision.

This is what he means: purification and all divine operations, shining forth through the primary essences, are distributed among all the remaining orders according to the proportion of each one’s participation in the deifying realities.

No explanation is required.

For this reason he subsequently referred the fiery property of purification to the Seraphim themselves, after God. Since, he says, every divine operation is distributed to the remaining orders through the primary powers, the angel himself, who performed the prophet’s purification in the manner of fire, referred the prophet’s purification to the Seraphim themselves after God, because the angel was seen to purify the prophet from God through the Seraphim.

There is therefore nothing disorderly in saying that the Seraphim purifies the theologian. For God purifies all in this way, since he is the cause of all purification.

He next introduces an example. “More particularly”—the word “to be said” is understood—“we shall now use an example,” that is, we shall use an example close to the cause under discussion.

Just as among us the high priest, or the priest who purifies or illuminates through his ministers, is himself said to purify and illuminate, the orders purified through him referring their own sacred operations through themselves back to him—that is, while the purified orders, through the high priest himself, refer their own sacred operations through themselves back to him, as though he himself had done what they do—so the angel who perfects the theologian’s purification refers his own purifying knowledge and power, and the purification itself, to God as its cause, and then to the Seraphim as the first agent and high priest.

A comparison follows: “As someone perhaps might say, instructing one who had been purified with angelic reverence.” That is, the angel speaks to the prophet as though someone worthy of angelic reverence were instructing a purified person how and in what order he had been purified.

“Because in you, O man purified by me, whom I have purified, the beginning of the purification to be perfected is the exalted—or, as it is more precisely translated, the most remote—one: both the essence and the creator and the cause, who brings the first essences into being and, by his placement around himself, contains and preserves them unturning and free from falling, and moves himself into the first participations of his own providential operations.”

By teaching me this, he says, he declares the mission of the Seraphim itself. This example, as though spoken to the purified prophet concerning the cause and order of his purification, was taught to me by the one who instructed me concerning the prophet’s purification; he says that it reveals the mission of the Seraphim.

It is as though he were saying: “I, Dionysius, did not introduce this comparison; rather, the one who taught me what the Seraphim’s mission signified introduced it.”

And immediately he returns, as it were, to the words of the angel speaking to the prophet:

“The high priest himself, and after God the leader of the excellent essences, through whom I was taught to purify in a deiform manner.”

He calls the order and adornment of the Seraphim one high priest and leader after God—not, in my opinion, for any other reason than that such unity exists among the heavenly spirits that what one performs is understood to be performed unanimously by all.

It is therefore the Seraphim’s order and adornment itself—namely, the high priest—that purifies you through me, O Isaiah. Through him, the one who is the cause and maker of all purification brought forth from concealment its own providential actions, already directed toward us who are angels—that is, toward all intelligible and rational powers.

Here ends the resolution of the question:

“He indeed taught me this”—that is, the one who taught me what I have said concerning this question taught me this.

But who that person was, we do not know. We argue, however, either that it was the apostle Paul, whose disciple he was, or that it was Hierotheus, whom he extols with great praise in the book *On the Divine Names*. Whoever it was who instructed so great a man, we shall not doubt that he was wise.

The text continues:

“But to you, O Timothy, I hand on what I learned from him.”

“May I grant you, however, with your intellectual and discriminating knowledge, either to resolve one of the two proposed explanations of the causes under discussion from all doubt, and to honor it before the other as consequent, rational, and equally true.”

For, he says, we have said that the present question can be resolved in two ways. Either the angel who purified the prophet was called “Seraphim” because that name is common to all the heavenly powers. For a fiery purifying force exists in all of them in common, although not equally, and the very interpretation of the name “Seraphim” makes this clear.

Thus, some attempt to resolve the present question.

But what seems more probable to me is what I have argued: that the proper designation and proper powers of the highest intellects in no way belong to the final angels or to those presiding over us.

Therefore the angel who purified the prophet was called “Seraphim” by theology because he did not refer to himself the proper operation by which he purified the prophet, whose lips he touched with the mystical coal, but referred it to God himself, who is the cause and principle of all purification, and to the Seraphim itself, as though to a high priest, through whom he was seen to cleanse the prophet’s lips.

I grant you, with your intellectual and discriminating knowledge, either to free the other of the two previously mentioned solutions from all doubt, to establish it beyond question, and to honor that solution—which your intellectual knowledge has both freed and established—before the other; and either wholly to reject the one or to regard it as of little importance in comparison with the other, as having what is consequent, rational, and equally—that is, rightly—true.

Or, if neither of those explanations is sufficient for you, I grant you permission to find something closer to the truth either by yourself or from another whose understanding surpasses both my intention and yours. May it be disclosed, with God’s gift, either to you or to another from whom you wish to learn. It is understood that it is first received by the angels—that is, from God himself, who is the light, cause, and effect of all contemplation—and by the friends of the angels, namely the highest human beings, through whom the angels disclose to those below them the mysteries that they receive from God.

I grant that these things may be revealed to us through his contemplation, namely God’s more beloved contemplation—that is, through contemplation of the present question, which is more beloved to them than other matters.

## CHAPTER XIV

Its title is: “What the angelic number signifies.”

[Note: [Col. 0249D] In illuminated letters: “Chapter fourteen, whose title is …”; B omits the title; B* adds in large black letters: “Title of chapter XIV: What the transmitted angelic number signifies,” and in illuminated letters adds: “that is, given or defined by the Scriptures.”]

§ This too is worthy, as I think, of intellectual knowledge, because the tradition of the divine words says that there are “thousands of thousands” and “ten thousand times ten thousand,” revolving and multiplying the highest numbers known to us within themselves.

It is worthy, he says, of intellectual knowledge—that is, of knowledge of intellectual realities—to understand what divine Scripture teaches concerning the angelic numbers. For the tradition itself revolves the greatest limits of numbers known to us within itself and multiplies them within itself.

The tradition does not comprehend or define in these numbers the limits of the angels’ infinite multitude. Rather, recognizing the weakness of our reason, still confined within a mortal dwelling, it shows that our reason cannot ascend beyond the cubes of the number ten, and beyond the quantity produced by multiplying those cubes by themselves—that is, “thousands of thousands”—and then multiplying again the same ten in the thousands, because they arise from it, producing by multiplication the quantity “ten thousand times ten thousand.” For our reason can neither perceive nor name the infinity of the higher numbers.

Such is the power of numbers that their multiplication is considered infinite. Through these numbers, comprehensible and nameable by human reasoning, he wished to signify the infinite multitude of the heavenly beings.

It is a very frequent usage of divine Scripture to indicate the infinite through finite numbers.

This is written in the prophet Daniel, where he says:

> “I watched until thrones were set in place.”
>
> And:
>
> “The Ancient of Days sat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool. His throne was a flame of fire; its wheels were burning fire. A stream of fire, swift and rushing, came forth from before him. Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him.”

Thus the blessed Jerome translated it. Saint Dionysius, however, followed the ancient translation.

Through these numbers the tradition openly signifies the innumerable orders of the heavenly essences. For there are many hosts of the blessed army of supermundane intellects, surpassing the weak and restricted measure of material numbers known to us.

He does not say this because the numbers themselves, being cubic and existing only in reason, were material, but because we, who are still material and mortal, both think and name them within ourselves.

They are therefore called material numbers—or, at any rate, are called numbers material to us—because they are scarcely ever, or perhaps never, handled in the mind without images of material things.

And the blessed hosts of heavenly intellects are defined only by the gnostic wisdom—that is, by wisdom itself—which both made and ordered them. Divine wisdom is called gnostic, that is, cognitive, because it alone understands and comprehends all things that have been made through it or in it.

According to this wisdom they possess supermundane and heavenly understanding and knowledge, which has been bestowed upon them in the greatest abundance. For they are defined according to the measure in which heavenly understanding and knowledge is implanted in them.

Their substance and their number are understanding and knowledge. Hence it is said through the Psalmist:

> “You made the heavens in understanding,”

that is, “You made them understandings.”

By divine health—that is, by divine integrity—there are many forms of sapiential knowledge, which make them wise. And whose is that abundant sapiential knowledge? It belongs to no one except the existing principle and substantializing cause, and to the consummation of the containing power, from which heavenly understanding and knowledge has been bestowed in the greatest abundance upon the supermundane intellects.

[Col. 0251C]

§ 1. Let us proceed with what remains [Note: B* adds above: “Proceed, then”], allowing our intellectual eye, if it seems appropriate, to rest from its angelic exertion [Note: B omits “exertion”; B* adds it in the margin] amid the sublime contemplations, and descending again toward the divisible and multipartite breadth [Note: B reads “multipartite”] of the multiform variety of angelic specifications, entering into them as into consequent things, with theoretical power turned back analytically into the simplicity of the heavenly minds. He commands himself—or Timothy, to whom he wrote this—saying: “Let us proceed with what remains,” that is, “let us undertake what remains of the present work.” “Allowing to rest” [Note: B* corrects this; AB read “you will allow to rest”], or, as it is more precisely translated, “causing our intellectual eye to rest, if it seems appropriate to you, O Timothy,” from its angelic exertion [Note: “Exertion” omitted in B and added in the margin by B*], plainly from the angelic contemplation that has hitherto exercised its gaze upon the sublime contemplations of the heavenly essences; now, however, wishing to rest, or as it were to rest [Note: B* corrects this to “as it were”], upon the divisible and multipartite breadth [Note: B reads “multipartite”]—that is, the manifold surface of visible things—of the multiform variety of angelic formations. [Note: B* corrects AB’s “surface” to “superficies”; B* corrects AB’s feminine “multiform” to the form agreeing with “variety.”]

Those matters that we have already discussed can be contemplated by the wise solely with the mind’s eye, above everything that can be divided and multiplied [Note: A reads “everything” in the accusative feminine; the conjecture and AB read “which”], above every likeness and image of visible things. But the matters toward which we wish to turn the intellectual eye display the breadth—that is, the surface and appearance—of angelic forms. This surface is divisible and divided in many ways; yet in these forms the mind’s gaze seems to rest, as upon things familiar and known to it, and to labor less intensely than it does in the heavenly essences, in bodily matters [Col. 0252B].

This we do by descending again—that is, after contemplating sublime realities, by descending again into those angelic and mystical formations as into consequent things: although they do not correspond to, and are far unlike, the height and uniformity of the divine intellects, we nevertheless turn back analytically, by a theoretical power, into the simplicity of the heavenly minds. [Note: B* corrects AB’s “turned back” form to the singular “turned back”; AB read “reflected.”] For ἀναλυτική (“analytical”) is the discipline that resolves the interpretation of visible images [Note: B* corrects AB’s “interpretations”] into the uniformity of invisible intellects, which are without any form. Just as, symbolically, by means of images of visible things—whether distinct and appropriate or confused and inappropriate—he clothes the divine intellects, so analytically he strips those same intellects of every bodily likeness and configuration.

But let this first be known to you: how the resolutions of the sacredly formed images sometimes signify the same arrangements of the heavenly essences as sanctifying, and again as sanctified; how they signify the last orders as sanctifying and the first as sanctified; and how these same arrangements possess, as has been said, first, middle, and last powers, without any disorder being introduced according to the manner of such explanations [Note: B* corrects “explanations”; AB read “reasons”]. Above all else, he says, let this be known to you beforehand, so that you may understand how the resolutions—that is, the interpretations, or, as the Greek is more precisely rendered, the purifications, distinctions, or indications—of the sacred images by which the heavenly intellects are represented signify those same orders, which he calls the arrangements [Col. 0252D] of the heavenly essences, as sanctifying—that is, ordering—their inferiors, and again as sanctified [Note: Conjecture; AB read “sanctifying”; B* corrects to “sanctified”], that is, ordered by their superiors; so that one and the same order is both sanctifying those below it and sanctified by the order above it. They also signify how those same resolutions [Note: Conjecture; AB read “solutions”] represent the last orders of the heavenly essences as sanctifying, while the first orders, which belong to the first hierarchy, are represented as sanctified.

For example, one of the last orders sanctified the prophet Isaiah; yet there is no doubt that the Seraphim, to whom the prophet’s purification is assigned, are themselves sanctified by the very beginning and cause of all sanctifications, namely God. That the middle orders are both sanctified by those preceding them and sanctify those following them is declared by theological reasoning. The same arrangements, moreover, are signified as possessing first, middle, and last powers. This can be understood in two ways. Either it is said universally of the three heavenly hierarchies, so that the first possess first powers, the middle middle powers, and the last last powers [Note: B corrects “are possessed”; AB read “are possessed”]; or it is said of the individual orders of each hierarchy and of the individual intellects within those orders, in which a threefold power is understood, which is again distinguished in three ways. [Note: B reads “three-partite”; AB read “threefold.”]

For every divine order and mind possesses essence, power, and operation. It also possesses the power to be sanctified—by its superiors, as its first power; it possesses the power of its own sanctification, by which it is holy, as its second power; and it possesses the power to sanctify those following it, as its third. [Note: B corrects AB’s “sanctifying” to “to be sanctified.”] For to be sanctified is one thing, to possess sanctification another, and to sanctify another.

No disorderly principle is introduced—that is, no principle of confusion [Col. 0253C] or ambiguity—according to the manner of these explanations, plainly the resolutions and interpretations of the divine images. For if we were to say that certain beings are sanctified by those before them, and then that the earlier ones sanctify those same beings, and again that the sanctifiers of the last are sanctified by those very sanctified beings, a truly great disorder and confusion would be introduced [Note: “Truly” is omitted in B and added in the margin by B*]. It would be as though he were saying: If we used such expressions in explaining the sacred figures, the matter under discussion would be explained disorderly and confusedly—or rather, would be thrown into confusion—because of the excessive confusion and disordered construction of the terms [Note: Conjecture; AB read “examples”; B* corrects to “explanations”].

For what benefit is there if someone says that certain beings are sanctified by those before them, but does not at all distinguish which beings those earlier ones are? And if he says that the earlier beings sanctify those same beings, but remains completely silent about whom he means? And again, if he says that the sanctifiers of the last are sanctified, without showing which arrangements sanctify the last and by which sanctified beings those last ones are themselves sanctified?

But if we say that the same beings both sanctify and are sanctified [Note: B corrects “we said”], but never say that they sanctify those same beings or are sanctified by those same beings, and instead say that each is indeed sanctified by those before it, but sanctifies the last, perhaps someone could reasonably say that the sacredly formed figures in Scripture can beautifully and truthfully be surrounded by first, last, and middle powers [Col. 0254A].

If, he says, we say that the same heavenly arrangements both sanctify and are sanctified, but never—or, as it is more precisely translated, “not yet”—say that they are sanctifiers of the same beings or sanctified by the same beings, because this generates ambiguity [Note: Conjecture; A reads “generated fibolia,” B “fibolia generated,” and B* corrects to “ambiguity is generated”]; but say that each is sanctified by those before it—for no one can be sanctified except by one preceding it—and sanctifies the last, since the order of things requires every order sanctified by those before it to sanctify the last: if we speak in this way, then perhaps anyone may reasonably say that the sacredly made forms in Scripture can beautifully and truthfully be surrounded by first, last, and middle powers [Col. 0254B]. That is, he can maintain that the same forms sometimes correspond to first powers, sometimes to last powers, and sometimes to middle powers [Note: B reads “sometimes middle, sometimes last”].

For one and the same form can often represent, according to the appropriate passage of Scripture, the first, last, and middle power of each divine mind [Note: B reverses the order to “divine mind”]. Of these three powers there is a manifold interpretation, one of which—and the most approved—is the following:

“Thus, it will rightly associate with all the heavenly essences their being extended upward in reciprocal conversion [Note: B* corrects AB’s “conversable” to “reciprocal”], firmly coiled around themselves as guardians of their proper powers, provident toward those that come after them by a sociable procession, and participating in power, although they are set above some universally, as has often been said, and above others particularly and in subjection.”

The order and meaning of the words [Note: B* adds “is”] are as follows: “And it will unite” [Note: A reads “unite” without the prefix], the one who says that he can surround the same forms with first, last, and middle powers [Note: B reads “middle and last powers,” reversing the final order], “with all the heavenly essences, and not falsely unite them.” What will unite them with these? Clearly, being turned upward in reciprocal conversion [Note: B* corrects AB’s “conversable”]. For all the heavenly essences are commonly both converted and extended toward God. Their conversion from God is indeed their beautiful and true formation. This is their first power.

“And it will unite them with all the heavenly essences as firmly coiled around themselves, being guardians of their proper powers.” That is, while they are guardians of their own powers. For all beings guard their powers, lest they perish altogether, be diminished in any way, or be bent aside; and they coil themselves around them, lest they find a place for bending downward, and so that they may always remain in the same unchangeable state. This is their middle power.

“And it will unite them with all the heavenly essences as provident toward what is coming,” or as possessing the second power. For either translation can be derived from the Greek word δεύτερα (“second”) [Note: AB read δευρα]. “By sociable procession”—that is, through a sociable procession by which they join to themselves, in common love of the truth, the essences that follow them [Note: B omits “them”], namely those below them and proceeding after them. This is perhaps their last power.

“It will unite them with all the heavenly essences as being in participation of divine power” [Note: A omits “divine”]. For being in participation of divine power is a general property of them all, although some participate in it eminently and universally, and others particularly and submissively.

Through this common participation of all the heavenly essences in divine power—which all desire, though not equally—it comes about that all forms, images, figures, or whatever other name they may be called, are common in what they signify. For they signify their threefold power: conversion toward God, guardianship of their proper powers, and sociable providence toward those who follow them.

§ 2. We must begin with an argument and inquire, in the first resolution—that is, explanation [Note: “That is, explanation” is omitted in B]—of the prophetic representations, why theology is found honoring above almost all other things the fiery sacred description; that is, for what reason theology honors a fiery sacred configuration above other images.

You will therefore find theology not only forming fiery wheels [Note: The phrase “that is, you will find theology forming” is marked in B*; B omits the surrounding wording], but also fiery living creatures, men flashing like fire, and placing around those heavenly essences heaps of fiery coals [Note: Corrected in B*; AB read “with many heaps”]. You will also find theology speaking of rivers blazing with fire, with immeasurable sound—or, as it is more precisely translated, with immeasurable flow. It also says that the Thrones are fiery, and that the most exalted Seraphim, burning in heaven, signify this by their name [Note: “Signify” is supplied from the translation and Greek text]. That is: theology says that the most excellent Seraphim signify by their name that they themselves are burning. For Seraphim means “those who set on fire” or “burning ones.”

It can also be understood in this way: “and to signify,” that is, “and it signified.” The infinitive is used for the imperfect tense, a usage common both in Greek and in Latin. Thus theology signified by the name Seraphim that they are burning. And it assigns to them—the Seraphim, plainly—the property and operation of fire, and altogether, above and below—that is, among the higher and lower heavenly essences—it selectively honors the fiery construction of the forms [Note: B adds in the margin “heavenly,” perhaps referring back to “forms”].

I therefore judge that “fiery” signifies the most godlike character of the heavenly minds [Note: B* corrects AB’s “most godlike”]. I consider, he says, that the fiery configuration of the heavenly essences signifies nothing other than the divine form present in them, which in the sacred Scriptures is usually signified especially by fire. He adds next:

“For the holy theologians often describe the superessential and formless essence [Note: B* corrects AB’s “formless”] in fire, as though it possessed, if one may say so, many images of the divine property, just as images can belong to invisible things [Note: B* corrects “insofar as” to “just as”].” For no visible creature exists in which so many images of the divine are expressed [Note: B reads “imprinted”] as in fire.

The praise of sensible fire follows:

“For sensible fire is—this is how it should be said—”

The order of the words [Note: B* adds “is”] is: “Sensible fire is in all things, comes clearly through all things, and is removed from all things [Note: B* adds “from all things”]; it is at once luminous and, as it were, hidden; unknown in itself, when matter is not present with it—that is, when it does not possess matter in which it manifests its proper action” [Note: B* corrects “matter”]. It is unknown; for the proper action of fire is to burn and shine in some matter. Without some matter, it exists [Note: “Exists” is omitted in AB and supplied above the line by B*].

It is immeasurable, incomprehensible, and invisible in itself; at once powerful over all things—that is, powerful in all things—and able to bring whatever exists in them into its proper action, that is, to carry out its own action, so that they may be heated and illuminated. For just as things altogether without heat are like dead things, so, in the absence of light, they are deformed.

It is mobile; for nothing is more mobile than fire, since through it all bodies are moved, and without it nothing moves [Note: B* corrects “move” to “are moved”].

It gives itself to everything that in any way approaches it; that is, it pours itself into everything naturally akin to it.

It is the renewing guardian of nature; for through it all sensible things are renewed, and it is the guardian of the whole sensible nature, which dies in its absence.

It illuminates things veiled by its splendors; that is, it illuminates what is veiled by its splendors [Note: B* corrects AB’s feminine form to the neuter].

It is incomprehensibly bright; that is, while it shines, it is not comprehended.

It is distinct; for it is thickened by no other element, but remains distinct in its purity [Note: B reads “for no other element is distinct” in a reversed order].

It rebounds; for it rebounds from every body against which it is struck, from clouds [Note: B* corrects AB’s “cloudy place”], from stones, from iron, and from other bodies. Every collision creates fire.

It carries upward; for fire, once kindled, raises its flame upward, seeking spaces far removed from the earth.

It is sharp in its movement; for it penetrates all things sharply [Note: Conjecture; B reads “secretly”], with ineffable speed.

It is lofty; philosophers say that the empyrean heaven—that is, the fiery heaven—surrounds this sensible world [Col. 0257A] [Note: B reads “this fiery world”].

It does not receive the insult of diminution; for it is diminished nowhere, since it is wholly present everywhere in visible creatures, although it does not appear everywhere and equally [Note: A reads “and with equality”; B reads “equality,” with a mark by B*].

This can also be interpreted, not implausibly [Note: B reads “not incongruently”], as: “not accepting subjection to encroachment.” For it is subject to no bodily creature, because it is preeminent in all things [Note: B and AB read “subeminent”; B* corrects this to “preeminent”].

It is always in motion; for it does not stand still, but moves incessantly through all things, moving all things.

It is moved through itself; for it is moved by no bodily element.

It moves another element—“element” being understood—for it first moves the air through itself [Note: A omits “through”], then water through the air, and through water the earth and all earthly bodies.

It comprehends without being comprehended; for it devours and consumes within itself all dissoluble bodies, but is consumed by none. Water does not extinguish fire itself, but its operation [Note: “It itself” is printed in AB].

It does not need another; it needs no element, while it nourishes and sustains all things.

It is truly hidden; for its fiery nature is invisible [Note: B reads “the nature of fire is invisible”], but it manifests itself in its operations. It is felt by heat and seen by light.

It grows from itself; for it gives increase to all bodies and grows from no other element, but grows through itself, although it is said to be nourished by the exhalations of waters—not in order to grow from them, but in order to consume them within itself.

And, in the materials it receives, it manifests its magnitude [Note: A and B read “its magnitude and…”]; plainly, in burning materials it declares the magnitude of its heat.

It is active and powerful; for it acts powerfully upon the creatures below it, suffering from none of them.

It is invisibly present to all things at once; for it is present to all things in which it is thought to be absent. It is thought not to be present in ice and snow; yet if it were not present in them, they would not melt, nor would they participate in its heat [Note: “If not” is added in the margin by B*; AB read “color” rather than “heat”].

It is thought not to exist when neglected; that is, when it is neglected as something to be nourished by combustible matter, it is thought not to exist, and to be as it were dead.

But when suddenly illuminated by friction, as though by a certain natural and proper vengeance—that is, when it has been struck and aroused from its hidden rest—it suddenly shines, as though unwillingly, and, as though by a certain vengeance [Note: B* corrects AB’s accusative], naturally and properly attacks the matter it seizes. For it is natural and proper to it to shine immediately when struck, without any delay.

And again it is incomprehensibly impalpable; for it neither allows itself to be grasped nor touched [Note: B reads “nor”].

It is not diminished in all its richest self-givings; for it gives itself most richly to all things equally and is diminished in nothing, although it does not exercise its operations equally in all things. Indeed, it illuminates or heats some more and others less [Note: AB read “heats” incorrectly as “colors”].

Perhaps someone will find many beautiful properties of fire as images of divine operation, insofar as these can be imagined in sensible things. Perhaps, he says, whoever diligently investigates the powers of fire will find many properties of fire in which he will clearly discover images of divine operation, insofar as divine operation can be represented in sensible images.

God is in all things, since he is the essence of all things; he comes through all things, because he disposes all things; and he is removed from all things, because he is superessential and above all things. He shines in the creature he made, because he would be hidden and unknown in himself if he did not establish the universal creature as a kind of matter [Note: B reads “material substance”] in which he might appear [Note: B reads “appears”] and in which he might manifest his operations.

And who is ignorant of this, unless he is exceedingly foolish or exceedingly faithless: that God is immeasurable and invisible in himself? To summarize briefly everything that is proclaimed in praise of fire: these things can beautifully be proclaimed metaphorically of God [Note: B* corrects AB’s infinitive “to proclaim”].

Knowing this, therefore, the Theosophists form the heavenly essences from fire, signifying their godlike character and their possible imitation of God [Note: B* adds “possible”]. For if in a corporeal creature—in fire, I mean—there are many beautiful indications of divine operation, godlikeness, and imitation of God [Note: B* corrects AB’s corrupted reading], what must we think of spiritual and divine minds? There is no doubt that images of divine operations exist in them in greater and incomparable measure.

[Col. 0258C] § 5. He next treats of the human form. They also describe them as human-shaped; that is, the Theosophists describe the heavenly essences not only as fire-shaped but also as human-shaped, because of the intellectual and upward-looking powers of contemplation, since the human being is an intellectual creature made in the image of God, and because, when he moves himself naturally and rationally [Note: B reverses the order to “rationally and naturally”], he turns toward his God with contemplative powers directed upward; and because of the upright and luminous figure—that is, because of the upright and bright form of the body; and because the human being is naturally sovereign and royal, since human nature was created for command and governance of the whole sensible world [Note: B* corrects AB’s “creator”]; and because, according to sense, the human being is indeed the least powerful in comparison with the powers of the other irrational animals [Note: “Animals” is omitted in the manuscripts and supplied from the translation and Greek text], but according to the greatness of intellect he is the most powerful of all. That is, the power of bodily sense is minimal in comparison with the other animals. An eagle sees more sharply than a human being; a dog distinguishes smells more powerfully.

And the text continues: “but according to the greatness of intellect, the most powerful in virtue.” For just as he alone possesses less acuteness of sensation than many animals, so alone among all living creatures he possesses the power of understanding [Note: B* adds “above all creatures”].

And “according to rational intelligence, in continuity.” For the power of rational knowledge is continuous; he would cease to subsist before he could be without rational knowledge even for the smallest moment [Note: A and B read “salvation”; B* corrects to “in one”].

And “according to the nature of the soul, free and most powerful.” For among animals, no one except the human being has naturally been given free choice and the power of election. Here it is understood that the free choice of the will is to be counted among the gifts of nature, not among the gifts of grace [Note: A reads “gifts” as “given things”].

It is also possible, as I think, to find heavenly powers in each part of our bodily multipartite structure. He says that it is possible to find the heavenly powers—that is, images of the heavenly powers—in each of the members by which, as I judge, the manifold and divisible harmony of our body is constituted.

They say that the powers of sight signify the clearest gaze toward the divine lights; that is, when the Theosophists say that the clearest gaze of our eyes upon the divine lights, established by God in heaven, signifies the contemplative powers of the heavenly essences [Note: B omits “of the heavenly essences”]. Again, they say that the tender, fluid, unobstructed, sharply mobile, pure, and level direction of our eyes signifies, without suffering, the reception of divine illuminations—namely, the reception by which the heavenly powers receive divine illuminations [Note: B* corrects AB’s “powers” to “illuminations”].

For the pupil of the eyes is tender and fluid [Note: B* adds “and is fluid”], and, when healthy, is not obscured by dimness [Note: B* corrects AB’s “does not reflect dimness”].

After the eyes he places the sense of smell. As for the discriminating powers of smell [Note: Corrected; AB read “smell”], he means that they signify what is receptive, insofar as possible, of the distribution of the sweet-smelling reality above the intellect, and what distinguishes by knowledge what is not of this kind, and altogether rejects it.

The Theosophists, he says, say that the senses of smell, by which we distinguish exhalations [Note: AB read “exhalations” with a different spelling], signify in the heavenly essences that which receives above its intellect the distribution of what is sweet-smelling—namely, the gifts of divine graces—and that which distinguishes by knowledge those things that are not of this kind [Note: B* corrects AB’s “which” to “not”], that is, those that are not such; and that it altogether flees from them. For divine virtue distinguishes superessential things from their opposites, just as the sense of smell distinguishes sweet-smelling exhalations from those that are not sweet-smelling.

They say that the powers of the ears signify that which is receptive of, participates in, and possesses knowledge of divine inspiration—plainly, whatever that may be in the heavenly essences which participates in divine inspiration and possesses knowledge, that is, cognition [Note: B* corrects AB’s relative pronoun].

He uses “inspiration” in place of “vocal utterance,” in the manner in which the cause is put for the effect. The cause of the voice, however, is the ethereal spirit.

They say that the powers of taste signify the fullness of invisible, divine, nourishing foods and the receptivity of nourishing advances; that is, they say that the powers of taste signify the fullness of invisible and divine foods by which the heavenly essences are refreshed, and also signify that which receives them in themselves [Note: A reads “fullnesses”]. “Nourishing advances” means nourishing increases.

They say that the powers of touch signify the diagnostic faculty of what is suitable or harmful in knowledge. The powers, he says, that belong to the sense of touch signify the diagnostic faculty—that is, the discriminating faculty in knowledge—by which the heavenly essences distinguish what is suitable for them from what is harmful to them [Note: B reads “distinguishes”].

The first human being did not wish to enjoy this intelligible sense. He refused to follow the obedience suitable for him and to flee from the pride harmful to him, just as he refused to taste the food of eternal blessedness, whose fullness, if he had received it, would have nourished and advanced him through eternal increases of divine desire. Likewise, he refused with his intellectual ear to receive the voice commanding him to obey the commandments. He refused through intelligible smell to distinguish the sweet-smelling exhalations of eternal life from the foul exhalations of eternal death [Note: AB read “foul” with a different spelling]. He refused to contemplate the appearance of the most beautiful truth. He refused to raise himself upward toward him who deifies those who love him and cleave to him. Instead, bent down toward the pleasure and desire of carnal things, he fell, deprived of every spiritual sense.

Next he says that the eyelids and eyebrows signify the guardianship of the understanding of divine visions; this is to be understood as “they say that they signify.”

They say that youth and mature age represent that which continually renews the vital power—that is, that which always renews the vital power. But if you ask what “that” is, and what is meant whenever “that” is said in this discussion [Note: AB read “whenever” with a different spelling], I can answer in one way: “that” is the ineffable and manifold gift of divine distribution bestowed upon all the divine essences.

They say that the teeth represent the divisive power of the implanted nourishing perfection [Note: Corrected; A reads “nourished,” and B* radically corrects to “nourishing”]. The human teeth, he says, are said to represent the divisive—that is, discriminating—power that feeds the nourishing perfection implanted in the heavenly essences [Col. 0260D].

For every intellectual essence divides and multiplies, through provident power, the uniform intelligence given to it by a more divine—that is, superior—essence, so that it may guide the lower essence according to analogy. Therefore they say that discrimination is represented by the teeth [Note: B* corrects AB’s “by discrimination”], because it nourishes the intellectual perfection implanted in the heavenly essences. Each intellectual essence breaks up and multiplies, as though with the teeth of discrimination, the uniform intelligence given to it by a more divine or superior essence, through provident power and according to the guiding analogy of the lower essence.

He says “guiding” in place of “educating.” For divine mysteries, unless they are first communicated by teachers through intellectual teeth, cannot benefit disciples [Note: A reads “disciplines”], nor provide vital growth. A mustard seed, unless it has been crushed, does not know how to exercise its power.

They say that the shoulders, arms, and again the hands signify the productive [Note: B* corrects AB’s feminine form], operative, and active powers. For strength consists in these three members of the human body.

“Productive” refers to the hands, since they produce; “operative” to the arms, in which the whole force of operation exists; and “active” to the shoulders, in which, as upon a kind of hinge, the movement of action first turns, and then extends through the arms into the hands.

In a rational soul, the first movement of the soul is in the mind, as though in certain shoulders of its own. This movement is called action. Then, descending through progressive sequences [Note: B* corrects “progressive numbers” to “progressions of numbers”] as through certain arms, it receives the name of operation when it is extended into the effect of the moved body. It is not improperly called productive or effectual [Note: A omits “effectual”].

Thus, as I think, it is also in the heavenly minds. When, as though in a first movement, they look above themselves toward the primordial causes in the Principle of all things, which is God, their action is present [Note: B* adds “is”] when they conform within themselves what they see above themselves; it is operation when they do and accomplish what must be done in the nature of things according to the analogy of what they contemplate above themselves and conform within themselves; and their movement is not improperly called productive or effectual.

The heart, however, is a symbol of the deiform life that deiformly sows its own proper vital power into those things that have been foreknown. They say that the heart is a symbol—plainly, a sign—of the deiform life that exists [Note: [Col. 0261] *in* is omitted in AB and written above by B*.] in intellectual and rational creatures, which deiformly sows its own vital power into those things that divine providence foreknew before they came to be. Here it must be noted that all the powers imagined through the individual members of the human body can be referred not only to the celestial essences but also to the cause of all things, from which all powers proceed. From that cause, too, as from an innermost heart, the vital motion is distributed and sown into the whole of visible and invisible creation as though into a single body. Observe also that he says the heart is a symbol of the deiform life that sows vital power, and understand that this distinguished teacher teaches that the seat of the vital motion of our entire body is located not in the brain but in the heart.

The chest, again, signifies what is hard and protective, as proceeding from the underlying heart’s life-giving distribution [Note: [Col. 0261] B: “the distribution of the life-giving [power].”]. They say that the chest indicates the unconquerable guardianship of the life-giving distribution, which takes its origin from the heart situated beneath it. For the heart, since it is bodily situated beneath the chest [Note: [Col. 0261] Conjecture; AB have *sit*; B* writes above it *cum sit*, “since it is.”], is naturally placed, as it were, beneath the safe defense and firm protection of its own vital motion [Note: [Col. 0261] B* corrects *vitali*, the reading of AB.], by which it gives life through motion to the whole body. Where we have placed “hard,” the Greek has ἀδάμαστον [*adámaston*], which signifies both “hard” and “unsubdued” [Note: [Col. 0261] AB have *αδιμαστον* or *αμμαστον*.].

The back, moreover, signifies the continuity of all the fruit-bearing powers [Note: [Col. 0261] B* correction; AB: “of all.”]. The back of a human being signifies the continuity of the fruit-bearing powers. For just as the bones of the spine adhere to one another, and through their marrow the vital motion is diffused throughout the whole body—especially that motion which belongs to touch—so spiritual powers are joined to one another inseparably, so that wherever one is, there all are. For all proceed from one, namely charity, and each depends upon the others in a chain [Note: [Col. 0261] B* corrects *dependunt*, the reading of AB.], and they bring fruitfulness to angels and human beings. Where we have placed “fruit-bearing,” the Greek has ζωογόνων [*zōogónōn*], which properly signifies “fruitfulness.”

The feet, then—you should understand, they signify what is mobile, swift, and running in the motion of the one who is always proceeding toward divine things [Note: [Col. 0261] *in* is omitted in AB and written above by B*.]; that is, the mobile, swift, and running motion of the celestial essences toward the divine mysteries. For this reason the theology of the holy intellects also represented their feet as winged. “Winged” signifies an anagogical—that is, upward-leading—swiftness [Note: [Col. 0261] A: *sursumducente*.], and the active movement of the celestial journey upward [Note: [Col. 0261] B: *versus sursum*.]; that is, the celestial activity of the journey of the powers, which leads upward into the contemplation of truth and, by “bearing upward,” removes it from every lowliness. In other words, the winged feet of the holy intellects signify that they are removed from all the lowliness of bodily creation by “bearing upward,” that is, by intellectual contemplation, through which they are borne upward, flying toward the cause of things. The lightness of the wings itself signifies that there is nothing earthly in them, but that they ascend wholly, purely, and without weight into the heights.

It has been explained above [Note: [Col. 0261] *est* is omitted in AB and supplied above by B*.] that the lightness of the wings signifies that there is nothing earthly in the celestial essences, but that they ascend wholly pure and freed from every weight into the heights—plainly, toward God. It must be noted that this blessed teacher, like the other learned writers of the same language, very commonly conveys all genders and all numbers of all words and other significant parts of speech through singular neuter nouns, and often also through infinitives.

“Naked” and “barefoot,” “released” and “freed,” “immeasurable” and “pure,” signify, with respect to the addition of those things that are external [Note: [Col. 0261] B* writes *ab eorum* below the text.], something assimilated, as far as possible, to divine simplicity. It is as though he were saying: What else does it signify that the mystical images of the celestial essences were seen in the likeness of a naked man standing or walking without shoes, except that the divine minds are released—that is, free and unbound [Note: [Col. 0263] B* corrects *absolutis*, the reading of AB.]—and rationally enjoy God through their own will? And that they are immeasurable? For their nature is infinite and unbounded, except by their sole creator [Note: [Col. 0263] B* corrects *soli conditori*.], who defines and circumscribes all things. And that they are pure? That is, uncontaminated [Note: [Col. 0263] B* corrects *contaminati*, the reading of AB.] by the addition of external things, namely sensible and bodily realities, from which the celestial powers are altogether removed. And that they are similar to divine simplicity, insofar as creatures are capable of imitating it [Note: [Col. 0263] B adds above: “is.”]?

But since the simple and greatly manifold Wisdom again clothes the naked and gives them certain vessels to carry, let us—φέρε [*phére*] [Note: [Col. 0263] AB have *fere*; B* adds in the margin: “and come, then.”]—also unfold, insofar as possible, the sacred garments and instruments of the celestial minds. “Come,” he says—that is, let us proceed—for among the Greeks φέρε and ἄγε [*phére* and *áge*] are exhortatory adverbs [Note: [Col. 0263] AB: “*fere* and *age*.”]. Let us unfold, that is, explain, insofar as possible, what the sacred garments and sacred instruments of the celestial minds symbolize. For Wisdom—not only that Wisdom which is simple and greatly manifold—mystically shapes the celestial minds like naked human beings, but also clothes again those whom it describes as naked, and gives them certain vessels to carry, suited to their operations; these are called instruments. For an instrument, generally speaking, is every implement suited not only to musical but also to other operations [Note: [Col. 0263] Conjecture; instead of *et*, A and B have *de*, with punctuation adjusted by B*.].

I judge, then, that the bright and fiery garment signifies what is deiform according to the image of fire, and luminous because of the serenity in heaven [Note: [Col. 0263] B: “serenities in heaven.”]. He says that the bright and fiery garment of the sacred images signifies the deiformity of the divine minds, which is accustomed to appear in the image of fire, and their luminosity, which, like the most splendid ether disturbed by no breath, leads a tranquil life in heaven. Here one must understand “light” and “altogether invisible” either as intellectually illuminating or as intellectually illuminated. For in heaven the light is invisible and inaccessible; and one must understand “light in heaven” either as intellectually illuminating, as God is, or as intellectually illuminated, as are the divine intellects illuminated by God, who alone is the illuminating light and is illuminated by no one.

I judge, moreover, that the priestly garment signifies what leads to divine and mystical contemplations and the vow of the whole of life [Note: [Col. 0263] B has *aestima. aestimo.*; in Migne, an *o* is printed above the final letter of *aestima* to represent the manuscript reading.]. For it belongs to priests to lead those over whom they preside [Note: [Col. 0263] B has *possunt*, “they are able,” for *praesunt*.] into divine and mystical contemplations by the example of their conduct and the diligence of their teaching, and to devote their entire life—and the lives of their followers—to God.

I judge also that the belts signify the guardianship of the fruit-bearing powers themselves [Note: [Col. 0263] B* corrects *fecundare*, the reading of AB; *ipsarum custoditivum* is omitted and supplied from the translation and Greek text.], which make the soul fruitful in action and knowledge; the pagans chiefly attribute this guardianship to temperance and steadfastness. For steadfastness is the guardian of the virtues and, as it were, a belt girding their habit; this is what he adds next: “and gathering their habit into itself, turning it together into unity, and revolving circularly around itself with the natural likeness of a motion free from falling.” This means: The belt signifies the habit that gathers these virtues into one, and the habit itself, through the uniting of the virtues, turns back upon itself, just as a belt coils back upon itself [Note: [Col. 0263] A: “unravels.”] and revolves circularly around itself with an easy, natural movement free from falling.

For such is the difference between virtues and vices: vices are unlike one another and discordant with the reality itself, whereas the virtues are most similar to one another, like a smooth wheel rolled back upon itself, so that nearly all appear to be one and all are one [Note: [Col. 0263] A: “one appears.”], while nevertheless their natural differences are inherent in their harmony.

I judge also that the rods signify what is royal and ducal and defines everything rightly. Since a rod is the sign of kings or dukes, there is no doubt that everything rightly defined and measured imitates, in some way, the measure of a rod. Therefore in Greek it is written not simply ῥάβδους [*rhábdous*], “rods,” but εὐράβδους [*eúrhabdous*] [Note: [Col. 0263] Instead of *sed εὐράβδους*, B has *sede υραβδυς*.], that is, not merely rods but straight rods; for not every rod is straight.

The arrows and axes, moreover, signify the separating and discerning sharpness of the powers, which is effective and active. The arrows and axes, which he previously called the instruments of the celestial minds, signify, I judge, their discriminating power, by which, as with an axe, they separate unlike things from like: rational motions from irrational, the humble from the proud, those willing to correct themselves from those unwilling [Note: [Col. 0263] B* correction; A has “the repentant,” B “the powerful.”], those marked with T—that is, tau [Note: [Col. 0263] Correction; AB have *Ταῦ*, “tau.”]—from the unmarked, the faithful plainly from the unfaithful, and those who believe in the cross of Christ from those who do not believe. They signify the sharpness of the discerning powers, as an axe is sharp; their efficacy, as an arrow is swift; and their activity, as being full of action. For the divine power, discerning all things, penetrates what it discerns and acts without delay of time. Its willing is its action, whether it acts through itself or through its angels.

I judge that the geometric and tectonic—that is, fabricating—vessels signify the founding, building, and perfecting power; that is, the power by which the divine minds have been measured, founded, and placed immutably, without any collapse into apostasy. And how have they been built [Note: [Col. 0263] B* correction; AB: “having been built”]? Upon that foundation—namely, God the Word, our Lord Jesus Christ—upon whom, like an unshaken rock, the universal Church of rational and intelligible beings is built.

And how have they been perfected? In love and in the contemplation of truth. How, moreover, do they lead the lower essences back to that same foundation, into the same building and perfection [Note: [Col. 0265] B* corrects *addit*, the reading of AB; B* corrects *edem*, the reading of AB.]? He adds this afterward: “and whatever other things belong to the one who leads back and converts the secondary things of providence”—that is, whatever other symbols are introduced from the harmony of human bodies to signify divine providence, which leads back and converts the secondary intellectual and rational minds through the primary ones into participation in the one cause of all things [Note: [Col. 0265] A: “into participation.”].

At times those symbols that have been enacted—that is, performed—by the holy angels as instruments are also symbols of divine judgments directed toward us [Note: [Col. 0265] B: “are performed.”]. Some of them declare correcting discipline or punishing justice; others, deliverance from distress [Note: [Col. 0265] So AB; B* adds in the margin: “from distress.”], or the end of discipline, or the resumption of former steadfastness, or the addition of other gifts, small or great, sensible or invisible. And perhaps a discerning mind would not hesitate to join visible things beautifully to invisible things.

The vessels, he says, which divine Scripture teaches the angels to carry are sometimes symbols of the divine judgments by which we are judged. Some of them declare correcting discipline or punishing justice [Col. 0266A]; these two belong to the divine judgment, which is divided either toward correction through mercy or toward severity [Note: [Col. 0265] Conjecture; AB have *se veritatem*, “the truth.”] in punishment through justice. One is represented by the rod, as the Psalmist says: “the rod of correction, the rod of your kingdom”; the other by the axe [Note: [Col. 0265] B’s correction of the root; AB have *securum*]: “Already,” says the Forerunner [Note: [Col. 0265] B: “the precursor”], “the axe has been laid at the root of the tree; every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” [Note: [Col. 0265] “Of the tree” is omitted in A.].

Others signify deliverance from distress, or deliverance from ambushes. For in Greek one finds περιστάσεων ἐλευθερίαν [*peristáseōn eleutherían*] [Note: [Col. 0265] AB have *περιστασεως*.], in place of which we may say “deliverance from distress” or “deliverance from ambushes”; this too is represented by the rod. For we are chastised and stirred up by disciplines of mercy so that we may be freed from the distresses of our sins and from diabolical ambushes.

Or they signify the end of discipline: the end of all divine discipline is the habit of virtue and the building that is beautifully signified by the tectonic instruments.

Or they signify the resumption of former steadfastness [Note: [Col. 0265] Correction; A: “from the resumption.”]. In Greek there is εὐπαθείας [*eupatheías*]. Cicero interprets εὐπαθείαν [*eupátheian*] as “steadfastness,” as we have already said, following Saint Augustine: εὐπαθείαι [*eupátheiai*] are, that is, according to the Stoics, three forms of steadfastness: will, joy, and caution, and they exist only in the mind.

Here ends [Note: [Col. 0265] “Here ends” is omitted in A.].

[Col. 0265]

# JOHN SCOTUS’S EXPOSITIONS ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL HIERARCHY OF SAINT DIONYSIUS

Manuscript codex of the University Library of Leipzig, 188, parchment, thirteenth century. | A. |

Manuscript codex Vat. 177, parchment, fourteenth century. | B. |

Manuscript codex Sorbonn. 1355, Royal Library of Paris, parchment, thirteenth century. | C. |

[Col. 0265D] **HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE SECOND BOOK**

The second book, whose title is *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* [Note: [Col. 0265] A: *hierarchya*.], proclaims the unity of human nature, redeemed by the blood of our Savior, ordered, insofar as possible for those who are still mortal, according to the likeness of the celestial priesthood. Its high priest is the one who adapted it to himself through his grace [Note: [Col. 0265] So C; in codex A, *suam* is written above by a glossator.]. He is also the beginning, middle, and end of the entire hierarchy, both celestial and terrestrial, to whom all things are referred.

Our hierarchy, then, is divided in the likeness of the celestial hierarchy, namely into three hierarchies. Of these, the first in temporal order but the last in dignity is the legal priesthood [Note: [Col. 0265] C: *sit*, “may be.”]. It was distributed by the lawgiver Moses through very diverse [Note: [Col. 0265] C: *variis*; A: *vanis*.] and obscure symbols to a people still carnal and serving the letter rather than the spirit. Its greatest emblem was that tabernacle figuratively displayed on the Arabian mountain.

The second, which is also the middle one, is the priesthood that now exists—I mean the Church of the New Testament—established under grace, arranged partly through the visible symbols of the sacraments and perfected partly through the contemplation of truth. It is the end of the former first hierarchy and the beginning of the future hierarchy, which is the third. The third has now been begun in part, in the first fruits of contemplation, but will be perfected after the glory of the future resurrection [Col. 0267A], when, after the veils of the visible sacraments have been removed, we shall contemplate truth itself in manifest clarity [Note: [Col. 0267] So C; A: “the truth.”].

Therefore the present ecclesiastical hierarchy, as we have said, is midway between the former legal hierarchy and the future celestial one, since it not only performs and visibly considers the symbols of eternal realities, as did the former legal hierarchy, but also does not cease to investigate and discover their spiritual meaning, as will the future celestial hierarchy.

**Epigram** [Note: [Col. 0267] C: *Epygramma*; A: *epigrammata*.] concerning blessed Dionysius on this work, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*.

“You resolved the symbols of divine and wondrous sacred things through a uniform principle

into the singularity of the one light’s single radiance.”

[Col. 0267B] Thus begins the second book of Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Athens, addressed to Timothy the bishop, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* [Note: [Col. 0267] “Ecclesiastical” is omitted in A.].

The great Areopagite Dionysius wrote the second book to blessed Timothy, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*—that is, on the ecclesiastical sacred principate—dividing it most elegantly into the chapters that follow. He first sets forth the mystical sacrament, and then appends to each chapter the theory of the corresponding mystical sacrament.
