In these he shows that everything performed in the ecclesiastical sacraments and in the most sacred consecrations of the mysteries [Note: [Col. 0267] B: “in the sacraments, the consecrations of the mysteries, was performed.”] is carried out from heaven by the angelic ministry, according to the appropriateness of each order, together with the ministers of the altar, and especially by the hierarch [Note: [Col. 0267] B: *hierarchia*.], that is, the priest, who is rightly made one of the angels [Note: [Col. 0267] So C; B: “who is one of the angels”; A: “who is one angels.”].

In the ministry of the holy sacrifice of the Lord’s Passion, the most holy principality of the celestial army, together with its companions, always stands present in its proper order and office of praise [Col. 0268A]. He makes this especially clear in the consecration of the most sacred chrism, which is a uniform and single-order symbol of the most holy Eucharist. In this initiation of the chrism [Note: [Col. 0267] B: “unification.”], he plainly manifests that the order of the Seraphim surrounds the benevolent Jesus, who, being holy above all, sanctifies himself for us and fills us, perfected in him, with every sanctification, born from God [Note: [Col. 0267] So C; *ex* is omitted in AB.]. He also shows that the Seraphim intellectually praise the same Lord Jesus Christ with that many-praised hymn which the prophet describes himself as having heard the Seraphim cry, while the other angelic choirs likewise obey and sing “Alleluia” sensibly.

These are contained in the whole work *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, in seven chapters.

[Col. 0268B]

I. What the tradition of the ecclesiastical hierarchy is, and what its contemplation is.  
II. On the rites to be perfected in baptism.  
III. On the rites to be perfected in the synaxis.  
IV. On the rites to be perfected in the myron, and on what is offered in it.  
V. On priestly confirmations.  
VI. On the orders of those who are to be perfected.  
VII. On the rites to be perfected for those who are falling asleep [Note: [Col. 0267] The material numbered I–VII here appears above in A, after the epigram.].

He completes the teaching of the foregoing chapters in a twofold manner. First he explains how the mystery of the chapter is perfected [Note: [Col. 0267] A: “ministry.”]; then he gives a certain theory of the tradition—for example, first an exposition of the mystery of illumination, then its second theory; then an exposition of the mystery of the synaxis, followed by its theory; and so in the case of the rest.

The remaining material is missing.

[Col. 0267]

# JOHN SCOTUS’S EXPOSITIONS OR GLOSSES ON THE MYSTICAL THEOLOGY OF SAINT DIONYSIUS

From manuscript codex 136 of the Ecclesiastical History Library of the Imperial Library of Vienna, parchment, fourteenth century, very badly written. (G)*

**HERE BEGINS JOHN SCOTUS’S PROLOGUE TO THE MYSTICAL THEOLOGY OF BLESSED DIONYSIUS, BISHOP. PROLOGUE**

[Col. 0267D]

In the prologue to the book *On the Divine Names*, it is said, I believe, that the book *On Symbolic Theology* and the other books of Saint Dionysius are found less often for two reasons [Col. 0268D]. One is that the heretics, because these books openly acted against them, destroyed them as far as they could. The other is that the Catholics, bound by the injunction of the aforementioned Dionysius [Col. 0269A], were unwilling to reveal his writings to the ignorant multitude, but only to the learned and worthy, since the works surpassed the capacity of many. The learned have become scarce, chiefly, as I think, through the fault of those who confer the governance of churches upon anyone at all and have not shown consideration for learned men to whom they might entrust them [Note: [Col. 0269] Conjecture; the codex has “and did not look upon learned men.”].

Perhaps Jerome, the most distinguished writer [Note: [Col. 0269] Codex: *Jeronimus*.], did not number the excellent Areopagite [Note: [Col. 0269] Codex: *ariophagitam*.] among ecclesiastical writers because he did not think that his books, as eminent works, should be made available to common knowledge. For in his book *On Illustrious Men* he makes no mention of this teacher or of his books, although he records there others from the time of the apostles to his own day, praising them and mentioning which books they had written [Note: [Col. 0269] Conjecture; codex abbreviation: *celeb’*.].

**HERE BEGINS THE BOOK ON MYSTICAL THEOLOGY** [Note: [Col. 0269] Codex: *s.*]. **TEXT WITH GLOSSES** [Note: [Col. 0269] Codex: *catalogia*.].

[Col. 0269B]

“Supersubstantial Trinity,” and so forth.

The title of this book is *On Mystical Theology*, that is, “closed” or “hidden,” because everything said in it remains, as it were, entirely closed and hidden as inexplicable. The subject matter of this book is God himself, considered simply in himself as the cause of nature [Note: [Col. 0269] Conjecture; codex: “considered naturally.”], with reference to creatures [Note: [Col. 0269] Codex: “with a habit.”]. Its purpose is to commend the true wisdom of Christians and reject the wisdom of philosophers. Its usefulness is to lead persons to the inaccessible summit [Note: [Col. 0269] Correction; codex: *in via*, “on the way.”], that is, to unite them to God through a superintellectual knowledge and affection directed toward him, or, to say both in one word [Note: [Col. 0269] Conjecture; correction: “they say.”], through deification.

Its form, or method of treatment, is as follows. First, he invokes God, so that through him he may be directed to God. Second, he instructs Timothy how true wisdom is to be sought; there: “But you, O friend Timothy.” Third, he forbids the treasure of that wisdom to be shown to the unworthy, indicating the error by which they are prevented from finding true wisdom; there: “See, however, that no one.” Fourth, he shows, according to various reasons and ways, that every creature is affirmed and denied without contradiction; there: “It is necessary in it.” Fifth, he marvels that there are some to whom the grace of reaching God through superintellectual knowledge is given; there: “And not simply.” He does all this in the first chapter.

# CHAPTER I

## § 1. How the divine light is seen through the divine night, and the night itself is found through the setting of the lights

[Note: [Col. 0269] Conjecture; codex: “of the lamp.”]

There what is bright is darkened, what is great is contracted, what is human is deified, and what is unknown becomes still more unknown.

The divine light is the love of divine knowledge; the divine night is the incomprehensibility of that knowledge. When it is seen, God is known. But this incomprehensibility is found through the setting of the lights and through the surpassing of all the senses and mental powers [Note: [Col. 0269] Codex: “mental.”]. Once this has been attained, knowledge itself is darkened, because it is increased into the excess of a greater knowledge, and the breadth of the spoken or mental word is narrowed [Note: [Col. 0269] So the codex.] into the simplicity of the eternal Word.

There also takes place deification, that is, the transformation from human things into divine things. And what is unknown through the investigation of reason and intellectual activity becomes still more unknown through the excess of union, yet in such a way that this ignorance is the highest state within a greater knowledge.

## TEXT

“Supersubstantial Trinity, superdivine and supergood, beholding the divine wisdom of Christians, direct us to the superunknown and supersplendent summit of the mystical utterances, where the simple, absolute, and immutable mysteries of theology are covered according to the supersplendent darkness of the hiddenly spoken silence [Note: [Col. 0269] Correction; codex: *daca*, “teaching.”], which makes the superbright shine forth in the most obscure darkness and, in what is altogether intangible and invisible, fills us superabundantly with superbeautiful splendors, while we have no mental eyes. These things, then, have been requested by me in prayer” [Note: [Col. 0269] Correction; codex: *fuit*, “was.”].

## GLOSS

O threefold unity and one Trinity—that is, of the divine persons—surpassing every being with respect to the person of the Father, surpassing every wisdom and knowledge with respect to the person of the Son, and surpassing every existing goodness with respect to the person of the Holy Spirit: you who, by looking upon it, approve the wisdom of the faithful, and by approving it, look upon it—the wisdom through which God is known, which is, namely, Mary’s better portion [Note: [Col. 0269] Codex: *s.*, an abbreviation.].

By the direct ray proceeding from you to us, guide us, raising us to you, so that we may reach you through contemplation. You are the summit of the sacred Scriptures, superunknown to us but supersplendent in yourself. In you, namely, in that highest and most exalted summit, the meanings of sacred Scripture are profoundly closed and hidden, and, as in the simplest citadel, contracted and freed from the veils of words. Hence, just as they are simple, so also they are immutable and intelligible in only one way.

In that summit these meanings are also covered according to a light that possesses an excess of light, and therefore receives the name “darkness.” Its hidden splendor is the eternal Word, which the Father speaks inaudibly from eternity. In that supreme invisibility this Word makes God, who is most bright, shine from above; and, in this state of the Word, neither reason touches it by investigating nor understanding [Note: [Col. 0269] Conjecture; codex: *intelligii*.] considers it by contemplation. The Word pours itself over the celestial minds with rays eternally simple and effectively manifold—minds that are wholly eye to themselves, or that do not use material senses.

And I ask for these things from God, namely by way of creation, because they are understood only if they are obtained from God through creation. But now, why is the summit of divine secrets called superunknown, supersplendent, and supreme?

It is called “superunknown” because reason fails to reach it through investigation. It is called “supersplendent” because understanding fails to reach it through the superabundant outpouring of light [Note: [Col. 0271] Conjecture; codex: “fails and superflows.”]. It is called “supreme” because intelligence [Note: [Col. 0271] Conjecture; codex: *intelligii*.] fails to reach it through the surpassing union of affection.

There the meanings of sacred Scripture are simple because they are understood as they appear; they are absolute because they are held by no veils of utterances; and they are immutable because they are not reduced to this or that interpretation. They are covered because they are concealed by an exceedingly bright light.

This light is called by blessed Dionysius “the supersplendent darkness of the hiddenly spoken silence” [Note: [Col. 0271] Codex: *dyosiisio*.]. This is incomprehensibility, which is called “darkness” because of the excess of light; “spoken” because of the eternal Word that the Father speaks from eternity; “hiddenly supersplendent” because of the intimate, or inward, state of the superabundant outpouring of light [Note: [Col. 0271] So the codex]; and “of silence” because such generation of the Word is not perceived by intellectual hearing. Since it is not perceptible to intellectual hearing, it is therefore not narratable by the word of the mouth. Hence the saying: “Who will declare his generation?” As though it said: No one.

In that most obscure state, through the excess of light, God, who is by nature most bright, becomes supersplendent to the mind through the abundance of his rays. There reason touches nothing, because nothing there is investigable; there understanding sees nothing, because nothing there is contemplable. Yet human and angelic deified intelligences are filled superabundantly with the beautiful lights of divine radiance, seeing through themselves and through the things that proceed from themselves.

## TEXT

“But you, O friend Timothy, with respect to the mystical visions, leave behind, through strenuous effort, both the senses and intellectual activities [Note: [Col. 0271] Correction; codex: *oppositiones*, “oppositions”; Greek: ἐνέργειας, “activities”], and all sensible and intelligible things, and all existing things [Note: [Col. 0271] So the codex; the Greek text has καὶ πάντα οὐκ ὄντα καὶ ὄντα, ‘and all things that are not and that are,’ while the translation has ‘and every non-being and being.’]; and, insofar as possible, rise unknowingly to the union of the one who is above every substance and knowledge. For, through an excess beyond yourself and all things, holding on to nothing and freed from all things, you are purely borne upward toward the super-substantial ray, taking away all things and freed from all things” [Note: [Col. 0271] Correction; codex: “freed, bearing upward.”].

## GLOSS

The meaning is as follows. You, Timothy, who through true love have become another self for me, so that you may understand the secret contemplations about which I desire to instruct you, with the divine ray cooperating in this: with a strong effort of mind, leave behind the use of bodily senses together with sensible exercises, intellectual activities, the souls and angelic substances, and everything that they have declared to exist in the eternal Word, and everything that is contemplable in that Word. All these things must be passed beyond.

And, as your capacity requires, rise in a manner knowingly known where the eye does not see [Note: [Col. 0271] Conjecture; codex: *scienter uestir*; correction: *uidut*, “sees”], through the principal affection, toward union with God, who is ineffably placed above every substance and incomprehensibly placed above every knowledge, both human and angelic.

For when you have transcended yourself and all other things in purity, so that the love of them cannot hold you or impede you in any other way, you will be lifted up, purified from the final phantasies of the soul [Note: [Col. 0271] Codex: *fantasiis*.], by setting aside both spiritual and divine activities, toward the superbright light of the most hidden Deity. This Deity is called “darkness” because what is not seen is seen above, or what is not comprehended by us is understood above our understanding.

## TEXT

### § 2

“See, however, that none of the unlearned hear these things. By ‘these’ I mean those who have been formed in existing things, thinking that nothing exists super-substantially above existing things, but supposing that they know, according to the knowledge that exists among them, the one who makes darkness his hiding place. But if the mysteries of divine teachings are above these people, what should one say about those who are still more unlearned, whoever they may be, who fashion the cause placed above all things from the lowest existing things and say that it possesses nothing above the impious and multiform forms composed by them?”

## GLOSS

[The supplied source ends here, at the beginning of the gloss.]

Such is the meaning. Beware lest any unbeliever or inexperienced person hear these secrets. By such I mean those who rely upon natural arguments out of love for existing things [Note: [Col. 0271] The codex reads “upon the love of existing things and rely.”], firmly supposing that nothing exists above being—that is, above what is metaphorically called “substantive” [Note: [Col. 0271] The codex reads “metaphorically”—], which contains both created and uncreated things, according to their opinion. You derive this also from the saying in Exodus: “I am who I am.” But this was said as it presents itself to us in the first understanding, as a kind of reminder, so that he who was wholly “I am,” that is, being, might reckon himself to be with us. And those who think that through investigation of created things—which is general [Note: [Col. 0271] The codex reads “general or connatural.”] in them—they can attain to his knowledge or divine comprehension, which surpasses, beyond their petition, every cognition of the hidden sciences of such great philosophers [Note: [Col. 0273] Conjecture; the codex reads “of the philosophers.”], should consider how much more it surpasses the ignorance of those who figure God, who is the cause placed above all things, in the lowest materials of existing things [Note: [Col. 0273] Conjecture; the codex reading is corrupt.], which are inferior to living beings, and who moreover do not think that God possesses in himself anything more sublime than the manifold figures and forms which they impiously compose.

TEXT.

For one must posit and affirm in him all the affirmations concerning existing things, as the cause of all things, and again one must more properly deny all of them of him, as the one who exists above all things in a super-existing manner; nor should one suppose that negations are opposed to affirmations, but rather that he himself is above privations and above every negation and affirmation.

[Col. 0273B] § 3. Thus, then, the divine Bartholomew speaks, and [he speaks of] much theology and little theology, and of a broad and great Gospel, and again of a concise one—as it seems to me, understanding that saying supernaturally—for the cause of all things is expressed both in many discourses and likewise in brief utterances, and is rational, just as it is neither endowed with reason nor with intellect. For this reason it is placed above all things in a super-substantial manner, and appears not merely without a veil [Note: [Col. 0273] Correction; the codex reads “not only without a veil.”] but truly to those who pass beyond the unclean and the clean [Note: [Col. 0273] Correction; the codex reads “who pass through filth and purity.”], and go beyond the entire ascent of all the extremities of the saints, and abandon all divine lights, sounds, and heavenly discourses, and enter into the darkness where, as the sayings declare, the one who is above all things truly is.

GLOSS.

[Col. 0273C]

The meaning is this: Although those men understood these things, nevertheless, according to sound understanding, every form, figure, substance, and absolutely every creature must be attributed to him—not as to a subject, but as to the cause of all things—and must rather be removed from him more properly and truly, as from that to which nothing existing can adhere, insofar as he is God. And although existing things are attributed to God or removed from him, one must not believe that there is any contradiction between such affirmation and negation [Note: [Col. 0273] The codex reads “any.”]. Rather, one must understand that the cause of all things is superior to every negation [Note: [Col. 0273] Correction; the codex reads “to every transaction.”] and affirmation [Note: [Col. 0273] The codex reads “affirmation.”]. Therefore no affirmation or negation can be made concerning him.

In accordance with this consideration, the God-conformed Bartholomew writes that theology is expansive in words and contracted in meanings, and that the Gospel is broad in parables and great in histories, but again narrow and small in mysteries. By this I mean that blessed Bartholomew, filled with divine wisdom, possessed a supermundane understanding: namely, that God himself, who is the cause of all good things, is designated by many discourses [Col. 0274A] and likewise by very few, because he is grasped neither by reason nor by intellect, and therefore is not expressed in a word [Note: [Col. 0273] The codex reads “and that word.”], because he is placed above all things in a super-substantial manner.

But he is disclosed without a veil only to those who pass beyond all sensible and intelligible objects or spectacles, in which the exercise of intellectual contemplation is expended [Note: [Col. 0273] Correction; the codex reads “the exercise of intellectual contemplations.”], and who abandon altogether the illuminations belonging to the intellect, ambiguous inspirations, and eternal revelations, and enter through union into the super-intellectual incomprehensibility of God. There, according to the testimony of Scripture, God is in his proper form above unity and oneness, and above being and entity. For it is said in Exodus [Col. 0274B] that Moses ascended into the darkness in which God was.

TEXT.

For divine Moses is not simply commanded first to purify himself, and again to separate himself from those who are not such, and after every purification he hears the trumpets of many voices and sees many lights emitting flashes, pure and exceedingly radiant rays. Afterwards he is separated from the many and, with the chosen priests, reaches the summit of the divine ascents; although by this he is not yet with God, but contemplates—not God himself, for he is invisible—but the place where he is.

GLOSS.

The meaning is as follows. What we said above concerning the transcendence of the divine lights, sounds, and discourses, and concerning the vision of the darkness, is figuratively displayed in Moses himself. He is commanded not only to be purified in himself, so that he may contemplate God more deeply than others, but also to separate himself from the impure or unlike. After every purification of the senses from sensible things, and of the intellect from phantasms, he hears—or mentally perceives—inspirations of many intelligences, and contemplates many most luminous spectacles, flowing forth from above in abundant fullness, emitting rays with radiance, simple in substance and manifold in understanding.

At last, separated from the popular multitude—that is, from manifold material opinion [Note: [Col. 0273] Correction; the codex reads “material.”]—together with the principal affections, he ascends to behold God. Yet he does not see his substance, since it is invisible, but the place where God is [Col. 0274D]—whether that place is the serene heaven, the summit of a sapphire stone, a burning fire, or the peaks [Note: [Col. 0273] Correction; the codex reads “of the summit.”] of a mountain.

TEXT.

I think, however, that this signifies that the most divine objects seen and understood are certain underlying principles of realities, which transcend all the underlying things; through them the presence of him who is above every thought is manifested, coming upon the intelligible summits of his most holy places [Col. 0275A]. Then he is released both from the things seen and from those who see, and enters into the darkness of ignorance, which is truly mystical, in which he closes all cognitions [Note: [Col. 0275] Conjecture; the word in the codex is so corrupt that it cannot be read.], and in which all that exists of him who is above all things becomes wholly intangible and invisible. Being unknown to everything, to himself no less than to anything else, and altogether in the absence of every cognition according to what is better united [Note: [Col. 0275] For “according to” the codex reads “but.”], he knows super-mentally through the fact that he knows nothing.

GLOSS.

The meaning is this. It has been said that God is not seen, but the place where he is—that is, in certain creatures which are called the most divine underlying realities of visions and understandings, or the most divine places, because we contemplate nothing more divine with the mind. I think these designate the highest and eternal archetypes, principles, or exemplars of all creatures subject to God. Through them God becomes present and cognitively manifests himself to us, infusing into us and revealing the more principal and higher intelligences of those principles, which are intelligible to us in some fashion through a mirror [Note: [Col. 0275] The codex reads “spectacle.” The passage is extremely corrupt in the codex.].

Afterwards Moses is separated from those who had seen the place of God with him—that is, from all intelligible opinions—and is withdrawn from every intellectual understanding and mental vision. He enters into the darkness of ignorance because he is united to the divine incomprehensibility, whose summit is not penetrated by the intellect. This darkness is truly mystical, that is, closed, because it is truly the closure of every cognition; it encloses within itself the most secret things [Col. 0275C] and conceals all comprehensive cognitions, as in the first cause of all things.

Through this darkness every soul is united to God: that is, it is established above all things in a state of supreme excellence, which reason cannot touch through investigation, nor intellect contemplate through vision. Through this state the soul is separated from all other things and from itself, insofar as concerns the presence of its own intellectual cognition; and through the union of love—which effects converted cognition—it is intellectually united to God, to the unknown God [Note: [Col. 0275] Conjecture; the codex reads “unknown” in the feminine form.], by a cognition far better than intellectual cognition. In abandoning intellectual cognition, or the intellect, it knows the mind of the Lord—that is, through intellectual wisdom, which is above the gift of intellect. For the former recognizes God because of union, whereas the latter recognizes him through the principles of the Word.

The First Chapter ends.

CHAPTER II. How one ought to be united and offer hymns to the cause of all things and to the one who is above all things.

TEXT.

§ 1. We pray to become in this super-luminous darkness, and through not seeing and not knowing to see and know [Col. 0276A] him who is above every vision and cognition. In him, not seeing and not knowing is to praise the super-substantial one in a super-substantial manner, through the removal of all existing things, as those making an image according to nature remove the obstacles that hinder its pure, hidden vision, and by removal alone make manifest the beauty hidden in itself.

EXPOSITION OF THE TITLE.

“How one ought to be united.” The state of union cannot be attained in any other way except through the most fervent desire of mental prayer and through the power of a super-mental affection, which the eye of intellectual cognition cannot reach. Hence such cognition is said to come about through ignorance.

The proper hymn, or manner of praising God, is through negation or removal, as may be seen in the figure of a line, from which the beauty of the figure becomes more visible precisely through this.

The manner of this praise is also operative [Note: [Col. 0275] The codex reads “a small manner.”] in ascending from lower things to higher ones [Note: [Col. 0275] So the codex; perhaps read “and in this work.”].

TEXT.

“In this super-luminous darkness,” and so forth.

GLOSS.

The meaning is this. With the whole affection of our mind we desire to be in the super-luminous darkness—that is, in a super-intellectual state [Note: [Col. 0275] Conjecture; the codex reads “intellectual”; “super” has been added conjecturally.]—because it is more luminous [Note: [Col. 0275] Correction; the codex reads “and.”] than the intellectual state, so that through an excess of mind, by which the intellect does not see [Note: [Col. 0275] “Which” is omitted in the codex; supplied by conjecture.] or in any way know, we may be able to know and see God super-intellectually, namely through the removal of intellectual cognition, since God himself cannot in any way be reached by intellectual vision.

We also pray [Note: [Col. 0275] Conjecture; the codex reads “we are deprived.”] to be able to praise the super-substantial one in a super-substantial manner—that is, God, who surpasses every substance and every being—through the removal of all existing things. This is like what one sees in craftsmen who make an image from some lifeless material: by sculpting and cutting they remove the coarser outer parts of the material, which conceal and cover the pure image that naturally and potentially [Note: [Col. 0275] Correction; the codex reads “potentially” in an incorrect form.] lies within; and through the removal alone of such obstructions, without any addition, the beauty of the image’s own form, which had previously lain hidden, is revealed.

TEXT.

Yet I think that negations ought to be praised in a manner contrary to affirmations. For there, beginning from the first things, we descended through the middle things to the last; here, however, beginning from the last things [and ascending] [Note: [Col. 0275] “Descending through the middle things to the last” is omitted in the codex and supplied by conjecture.] to the more principal things, we again remove all things through the middle things to the extremes, so that we may openly know that ignorance, which is veiled from all knowable things amid all existing things, and may see that super-substantial darkness, hidden from every light among existing things [Note: [Col. 0275] Conjecture; the codex reads “going out.”].

GLOSS.

[Col. 0277A]

In the books previously mentioned, God was praised by affirmation; in this one, however, he must be praised through negations and the removal of all things, in a manner contrary to those [Note: [Col. 0277] The codex reads “which.”] affirmations [Note: [Col. 0277] Conjecture; the codex reads an abbreviated and unclear form.]. There we began with affirmation or the position of the principal things and descended through the middle things to the last. Here, however, beginning with the removal of the last things, we ascend step by step through the middle things to the removal of the principal things; and again, turning back toward the extremes, we remove everything from him together. We do this so that, without the veil of mystical signification, we may know the divine incomprehensibility, which surpasses every being and is truly hidden from every science in all creatures.

CHAPTER III. What the cataphatic, that is, affirmative, theologies are; and what the apophatic [Note: [Col. 0277] The codex has “cataphatically, apophatically” throughout.] or negative theologies are.

[Col. 0277B]

TEXT. [Note: [Col. 0277] The codex reads “Text po.”]

In the theological *hypotyposes* [Note: [Col. 0277] The codex reads a form corresponding to Greek ὑποτυπώσεσι.] we chiefly praised the proper affirmations of affirmative theology [Note: [Col. 0277] Correction; the codex reads “properly.”]: how the divine and good nature is called one; how it is three; what the paternity and filiation spoken of according to it signify; what the theology of the Spirit wishes to show; how, from the immaterial and simple Good, the lights that remain in the heart sprang forth; and how, by remaining in him, in themselves, and in one another, they continued co-eternally with their emanation, without going forth.

We also praised how Jesus, who is super-substantial, became substantial through the powers of human nature, and whatever else is expressed by the sayings and praised in the theological *hypotyposes* [Col. 0277C] [Note: [Col. 0277] Correction; the codex reads “they praise.”].

In the book On the Divine Names, we discussed how he is named good, how existing, how life [Note: [Col. 0277] Correction; the codex reads “arisen.”], how wisdom, how power, and whatever other intelligible names of God there are [Note: [Col. 0277] So the codex.].

In the symbolic theology, we discussed the transpositions of sensible terms to divine things: what the divine forms, parts, and instruments are; the divine places; what the ornaments, rages, griefs, and madnesses are [Note: [Col. 0277] Conjecture; the codex reads a corrupt form; the Greek text has μῆνιδες, while the version has “madnesses”]; the drunkennesses and excesses; the oaths and curses; the dreams and watchfulnesses; and whatever other holy, composite symbolic formations of God’s formation there are [Note: [Col. 0277] Correction; the codex reads “formation.”].

TITLE OF THIS CHAPTER.

The meaning is this. What are the cataphatic theologies [Note: [Col. 0277] The codex reads “cathephatic.”]? Blessed Dionysius treated cataphatic, that is, affirmative, theology in three books: in the book of the *hypotyposes*, in which he treated the distinctions of the persons; in the second, On the Divine Names; in the third, concerning the imposition of names used to designate divine things [Note: [Col. 0277] The codex has a highly corrupt form.]. In the fourth book—that is, the Mystical Theology—he treats apophatic, that is, negative, theology specifically. This removes from God all things, the lower, the middle, and the higher, so that through natural removal it may finally find God himself as the singular one.

TEXT.

“Therefore, in the theological [hypotyposes],” and so forth, as above.

GLOSS.

The meaning is this. In the treatise on the divine characters, that is, on the personal distinctions, we chiefly used affirmations or positions in divine praises. There we showed that the divine nature is one in essence and three in persons, and how paternity and filiation are to be understood, and what the property signifies which Holy Scripture attributes to the Holy Spirit, namely procession, according to the saying: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.”

We also treated how the fullness of invisible things, which remain fixed [Note: [Col. 0277] So the codex.] in the heart of the Father, springs forth from the immaterial and simple Good [Col. 0278B], that is, from the person of the Father. From him proceeds the person of the Son through generation, and the person of the Holy Spirit through procession. Each of them received the same fullness from the Father; hence the Son and the Holy Spirit remain in the Father, in themselves, and all three in one another. This fullness of lights remains in the Son and in the Holy Spirit co-eternal with the Father, from whom each of them has his origin, although the Father nevertheless remains wholly [Note: [Col. 0277] Correction; the codex reads “whole” in the feminine form.] in himself.

In that same book we also discussed how Jesus, who is super-substantial according to his divinity, became human according to true humanity, and many other matters, in accordance with the explicit testimonies of Scripture.

In the book On the Divine Names, we discussed how God is called good [Col. 0278C], how existing, how life [Note: [Col. 0277] Correction; the codex reads “arisen.”], how wisdom, and the other intelligible names of God.

In the symbolic theology, we discussed the transpositions of sensible names for the anagogical designation [Note: [Col. 0277] The codex reads “for designating anagogically.”] of invisible divine things. We showed how one should understand the attribution to God of forms, as in “who, being in the form of God”; figures, as in Hosea, “Like a lioness”; or parts, as in Ezekiel, “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his holy place”; or ornaments, as in “Clothed with weight”; or rages, as in “O Lord, not in your fury”; or griefs, as in “My soul is sorrowful”; or madnesses, as in Hosea, “Know that Israel is foolish, profane, and mad.” Nor did we treat only these things, but also other composite formations attributed to God in the book On the Symbolic Theology.

TEXT.

And I think that you have seen how the last things contain more discourses than the first. For the theological *hypotyposes* and the exposition of the divine names ought to consist of fewer discourses than the symbolic theology, since, the higher we look, the more the discourses are confused by the visions of intelligible things [Col. 0279A]. Thus now, when we enter into the darkness that is above the mind [Note: [Col. 0279] Correction; the codex reads “mountain.”], we shall find not brevity of discourse but perfect irrationality and imprudence [Note: [Col. 0279] Correction; the codex reads “prudence.”]. There, descending from higher things to the extremes, discourse expanded according to the measure of its descent into a proportionate multitude; but here, ascending from lower things to the supreme, it is contracted according to the measure of its ascent, and after every ascent it will be wholly without voice and wholly united [Note: [Col. 0279] The codex reads “is united.”] to the ineffable.

You may ask why, having first set forth the divine positions in their entirety [Note: [Col. 0279] Correction; the codex reads “being able.”], we begin the divine removal from the last things. Since we posit what is above every position, we ought to posit the affirmation that is more closely akin and subordinate to it; but when removing what is above every removal [Note: [Col. 0279] Correction; the codex reads “oblation.”], we ought to remove what is more distant from it. Or is life and goodness not more so than air and stone? And are “not drunkenness” and “not madness” not more so than what is neither said nor understood?

GLOSS.

The meaning is this. I think that you, Timothy, have perceived with the eyes of your mind that our later treatises abound more in words than the earlier ones. For it was necessary that the book on the divine characters, or personal distinctions, and the book on the divine names should be less prolix in words [Note: [Col. 0279] For “are” the codex reads “and.”] than the treatises of symbolic theology. The reason is that the higher and farther removed from the senses—or from imagination—the subject under discussion is, the less one must use sensible words, and the more the intellectual eye must be exercised.

Therefore, in this present book, where mention is made of the divine darkness, that is, of the incomprehensibility that surpasses every mind, angelic as well as human, or that is above the verbal and vocal understanding of the Word [Note: [Col. 0279] Conjecture; the codex reads “above the intellectual understanding of the Word.” Perhaps simply “understanding” is preferable.], we find not merely brevity of words but a perfect and incomparable excess of reason in investigation and of prudence in speaking worthily.

In the books mentioned above, the treatise descended from higher things to lower ones; in proportion to the greater or lesser prolixity, and the more we treated lower things nearer to the senses, the more it abounded in a proportional wealth of words. In the same sense . . . . . [Note: [Col. 0279] One word is missing.] the treatise now ascends from lower things to higher ones and is contracted, that is, compressed, according to the measure of its ascent.

When the excess of mind has been reached, all discourse, both of mouth and of mind, fails. For the true discourse of the mind does not speak the ineffable God, and nothing remains to the mind except to be wholly and entirely co-united to the ineffable [Note: [Col. 0279] Correction; the codex reads “with totality.”]. For when there is nothing intermediate between God and the mind, after every removal has been made from God, nothing remains except super-mental union with him.

Perhaps you ask what the reason is that we begin positions with the more worthy things, but removals with the lower things. The reason is this: when we wish to designate God, who is above every position, through position, it is fitting that we principally attribute to him those things that are more worthy and more closely related to him. But when we wish to designate him through removal, it is likewise fitting to remove from him that which appears to be farther from him.

For example, life and goodness are attributed to him more suitably and more closely than air or stone. Likewise, drunkenness or madness is removed from him more clearly than what is said or understood.

CHAPTER IV. That the cause of all sensible things is, through excellence, none of the sensible things.

[Col. 0280B]

EXPOSITION OF THE TITLE.

God, who is the most causal cause of all things, is rightly said to be none of the sensible things, whether active or passive. Therefore blessed Dionysius, wishing to show the excellence of this cause, removes from it the things that are farther removed, such as “not substance,” then “not being,” “not living,” as a stone, and “not rational,” as an animal. Here three lower levels of creatures are named, which he removes: namely, those that exist and live but do not sense; those that live but neither reason nor understand; and finally he removes everything [Col. 0280C] that can be subject to body or to the senses.

TEXT.

We therefore say that the cause of all things, existing above all things [Note: [Col. 0279] “Above” is omitted in the codex and supplied by conjecture], is neither without substance, nor without life, nor without reason, nor without mind; that it is not a body, nor a figure, nor a form; that it has neither quality nor quantity nor weight; that it is not in a place; that it is not seen; that it has no sensible touch; that it is not sensed and is not sensible; that it has no disorder; that it is not disturbed by disorders arising from material passions; that it is not powerless or subject to sensible accidents; that it does not lack light; that it has no variation, corruption, division, privation, passion, flux, or anything else belonging to sensible things, nor does it possess or constitute any of them.

GLOSS.

The meaning is this. We assert that God, who created all things, is neither something materially substantiated, nor living, nor using reason, nor exalted by mind [Note: [Col. 0279] The passage appears corrupt.]. He says that all these are removed both from one another and from God, because non-being is farther removed from God than are those things that exist and live but neither reason nor understand [Note: [Col. 0279] The codex reads “exist and live but do not reason, understand.”].

Next we remove from him everything corporeal and all the accidents of body or of a corporeal thing: figure, form, quality, quantity, weight, locality, and the properties of the senses, both active and passive. Likewise we remove from him the disorder arising from carnal desires, and the completion of carnal desire disturbed or rendered turbid by material passions [Note: [Col. 0281] The codex reads “passions.”].

We also remove from him impotence or weakness subject to sensible accidents. We remove from him the need for light, variation, generation, corruption, and division, since he is not composed of diverse things. Likewise we take away from him material passibility and temporal flux, since he neither is any of these things nor contains them in himself, nor is he any sensible thing.

CHAPTER V [Note: [Col. 0281D] Chapter V is omitted in the codex.] That the cause of all intelligible things is, through excellence, none of the intelligible things [Note: [Col. 0281] The codex reads “causal.”].

[Col. 0281B]

EXPOSITION OF THE TITLE.

Just as sensible things are removed from the most causative cause, since it is itself neither sensible nor intelligible, and since that sensible or intelligible thing which can be attributed to that cause belongs to a lower dignity, so this distance between creature and Creator unquestionably effects, without an intermediary, the excellence of the cause. Just as the cause is ineffable in itself, so it is incomparable with anything caused by it. Therefore, when no adequate comparison can be made with it, the cause falls under removal in relation to the senses [Note: [Col. 0281] The codex reads a corrupt form, “remoco.”].

TEXT.

[Col. 0281C]

Again, ascending, we say that it is neither soul nor mind; that it has neither imagination nor opinion, reason nor intellect; that it is neither reason nor intellect; that it is neither spoken nor understood; that it is neither number nor order, magnitude nor smallness, equality nor similarity, dissimilarity nor likeness; that it neither stands nor moves; that it neither practices silence nor possesses virtue; that it is neither virtue nor light; that it neither lives nor is life; that it is neither substance nor age nor time; that its touch is not intelligible; that it is neither knowledge nor truth, kingdom nor wisdom; that it is neither one nor unity, deity nor goodness; that it is not spirit as we see it; that it is neither sonship nor fatherhood; that it is not any other thing known by us or by any other of existing things; that it is not any existing thing, nor anything belonging to essences; that existing things do not know it according to what it is in itself, nor does it know existing things according to what they are as existing things; that there is no rational account of it, nor name, nor cognition; that it is neither darkness nor light, error nor truth; that there is neither a universal position nor a universal removal of it [Note: [Col. 0281] Correction; the codex reads “of it” in the wrong form]. Rather, when we make positions and removals of things other than it, we neither posit nor remove it.

For we neither posit nor remove it, since the cause of all things is perfecting, uniting, and unitary above every removal, and since, above every removal, it is the excess of the one absolutely freed from all things and above the whole.

GLOSS.

The meaning is this. Beginning the negations again with the higher divine things, we say that God, who is the cause of all things, is not soul, because he does not give life to a body; nor is he mind, because he does not stand above soul as its higher part; nor does he possess imagination by imagining divine or spiritual things; nor opinions, by inclining in different ways toward diverse judgments; nor reason, by distinguishing among uncertainties; nor intellect, by persisting in visible things alone [Note: [Col. 0281] The codex reads “and only.”]; nor is he reason, which distinguishes between good and evil; nor is he intellect, which persists in created visible things [Col. 0282B]; nor is he spoken, because he is ineffable; nor understood, because he is comprehensible by no one.

To proceed through the middle things toward the extremes, we again say that he is not number, because he cannot be proportioned into equal or unequal parts; nor magnitude, because he cannot be increased; nor smallness, because he cannot be diminished; nor equality, because he cannot be proportioned; nor similarity, because he cannot be compared with anything; nor dissimilarity, because he cannot differ from anything; nor does he stand, because he is not an immobile thing; nor does he move, because he is not changeable; nor does he practice silence, because he cannot be censured by mental or vocal speech.

To return through certain middle things toward the highest, and to bring the negations to an end in the highest created things, we say that he does not possess truth, as though he were made firm by another [Note: [Col. 0281] Conjecture; the codex reads “made firm.”], nor is he truth, as though he borrowed it from another; nor does he live, as though he were made sentient by another; nor is he life adapted to govern and accommodate a body; nor is he substance, materially substantiated; nor is he age, since he is not a span variable according to mode; nor is he time, since he is not a variable and changeable span.

Nor is he touch, since according to essence he is not touchable in any way; nor is he knowledge, since he is not knowable; nor is he truth, since he is not an intellect equal to something [Note: [Col. 0281] This appears to be the correct reading; the codex is corrupt.]; nor is he kingdom, since he is not subject to domination; nor is he wisdom, since he is not something that can be supported; nor is he one, since he cannot be increased into many; nor is he unity, since he is not materially indivisible; nor is he deity intelligible by us; nor is he goodness, since he is not an infusible quality; nor is he spirit intelligible by us; nor is he sonship, a subsistence materially produced from another [Col. 0282D] [Note: [Col. 0281] The codex reads “of the subsistent.”].

Nor is he anything fully known by us or by any existing being, whether human or angelic; nor is he intellectually anything among non-existing things or materially anything among existing things. Existing things do not know him according to what he is, nor does he know them according to what they exist as in themselves, but according to what they are in the Word.

Likewise, there is no rational investigation of him, no imposition of a name, and no refutation of cognition [Col. 0283A]. He is not darkness deprived of light, nor intelligible light, nor error by which the mind is deceived, nor truth by which the mind is illuminated through its own effort [Note: [Col. 0283] So the codex.] [Note: [Col. 0283] Conjecture; the codex reads a corrupt form.]. And altogether there is no position or removal of him.

Nevertheless, whatever else we posit concerning him or remove from him, we never position or remove him himself, since he is the perfect cause of all things above every position, and above every removal he is the excess of all things, absolutely freed from all and above all.

The exceedingly useful and very obscure work ends.

[Col. 0283]

HOMILY OF JOHN SCOTUS ON THE PROLOGUE OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN (CHAPTER 1:1–14).

First published from a manuscript of the library of Alençon by M. Félix Ravaisson, *Rapports sur les bibliothèques des départements de l’Ouest*, Paris, 1841, p. 334 ff.; reprinted afterward by M. Saint-René Taillandier, *Scot Érigène et la philosophie scholastique*, Strasbourg, 1843, p. 299 ff.

[Col. 0283B] Homily of John Scotus, translator of the Hierarchy of Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0283D] The codex reads “Hierarchy of Dionysius.”].

The spiritual voice of the eagle strikes the hearing of the Church. Let the outward sense receive the passing sound; let the inward mind penetrate the abiding meaning. The voice of the lofty-seeing bird—not one soaring above bodily air, ether, or the circuit of the entire sensible world, but one transcending every theory, beyond all things that are and that are not, on the swift-flying wings of intimate theology, with the eyes of a most clear and sublime contemplation. By “things that are” I mean those which do not altogether elude either human or angelic perception, since they exist after God and do not exceed the number of things created by the one cause of all; but “things that are not” are those which certainly surpass every power of intelligence. Thus blessed John the theologian soars above not only what can be understood and spoken, but also rises into those things which surpass all understanding and signification; and, carried beyond everything by an ineffable flight of mind, he is exalted into the mysteries of the one principle of all. Purely discerning the incomprehensible unity beyond essence of that principle and of the Word—that is, of the Father and the Son—as well as their distinct supersubstantiality, he begins his Gospel, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.”

O blessed John, you are not undeservedly called John. The name John is Hebrew; its interpretation in Greek is ᾧ ἐχαρίσατο [to whom he has shown favor], but in Latin, “to whom it has been given.”

[Note: [Col. 0283D] The passage must be restored in this way. The manuscript reads *oiexapicato*, which is ᾧ EXAPICATO; this seems entirely to have escaped the distinguished editors. Saint Jerome likewise interprets it: “John, in whom there is grace,” or “the grace of the Lord.” For it is derived from [illegible] and [illegible], so that it properly signifies “to whom Jehovah has shown favor.”]

For to which of the theologians was granted what was granted to you: to penetrate the hidden mysteries of the highest Good and to disclose to human minds and senses those things that were revealed and made clear to you? Tell me, I ask, to whom has so great and such a grace been granted? Perhaps someone will say: to the highest summit of the apostles—I mean Peter—who, when the Lord asked whom he supposed him to be, replied: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Yet, I think, one may say without rashness that Peter spoke such words more as a type of faith and action than of knowledge and contemplation, for Peter is set forth as the type of action and faith, whereas John imitates the type of contemplation and knowledge. One, indeed, reclined upon the Lord’s breast, which is the sacrament of contemplation; the other often wavered, as a symbol of hesitant action. For the practice of the divine commandments, before it arrives at a settled disposition, sometimes distinguishes the pure forms of the virtues, but sometimes its judgment is deceived, overshadowed by the clouds of carnal thoughts. The sharpness of intimate contemplation, however, once it has perceived the face of truth, is never thrown back, is never deceived, and is never hidden by any darkness.

Both, nevertheless, run to the tomb. The tomb of Christ is divine Scripture, in which the mysteries of his divinity and humanity are enclosed, as though fortified by a certain dense stone. But John runs ahead of Peter more swiftly. For the power of contemplation, once wholly purified, penetrates the inner secrets of divine works more sharply and swiftly than action that is still being purified. Nevertheless Peter enters the tomb first, and then John; and, just as both run, both enter. Peter signifies the symbol of faith; John, understanding. Therefore, since it is written, “Unless you believe, you will not understand,” faith necessarily goes before into the tomb of sacred Scripture; then understanding follows and enters, for faith prepares the way for it. Peter, then, recognized Christ already made God and man in time and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He flew very high. But higher flew the one who understood that the same Christ, God from God, had been begotten before all times, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.” Let no one suppose that we prefer John to Peter. Who could do this? Who could be higher among the apostles than he who is and is called their summit? We do not prefer John to Peter, but compare contemplation with action: contemplation already perfectly purified in the mind, and action still ascending in virtue toward an unchangeable disposition through the virtue that has already arrived [Note: [Col. 0285] Correction, R.; *pervenientem*]. For we are not now considering the dignity of the apostolic persons, but investigating the most beautiful distinction among the divine mysteries.

Peter, then—that is, the practice of the virtues—beholds the Son of God, wondrously and ineffably bounded by flesh, through the virtue of faith and action. John, however—that is, the highest contemplation of truth—marvels at the Word of God, in himself absolute and infinite, in his own principle, that is, in his Father. Peter, introduced by divine revelation, looks upon eternal and temporal things made one in Christ; John introduces into the knowledge of faithful souls only those things of Christ that are eternal.

The spiritual πετηνόν [“winged creature”; correction, manuscript *petatum*], swift-flying and God-seeing, by which I mean John the theologian, surpasses every visible and invisible creature, crosses beyond every intellect, and, deified, enters into the God who deifies. O blessed Paul, you were caught up, as you yourself affirm, into the third heaven; but you were not caught up beyond every heaven. You were caught up into paradise; but you were not caught up above every paradise. John transcends every created heaven and every created paradise—that is, every human and angelic nature. In the third heaven, O vessel of election and teacher of the nations, you heard ineffable words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak. John, observer of intimate truth, heard beyond every heaven, in the paradise of paradises—that is, in the cause of all things—the one Word through which all things were made; and he was pleased to speak that Word and preach it to human beings insofar as it can be preached to them, and he cries out confidently: “In the beginning was the Word.”

John, therefore, was not a man, but more than a man, when he surpassed both himself and all things that are and, borne aloft by the ineffable power of wisdom and the purest sharpness of mind, entered into those secrets in which the one essence in three substances and the three substances in one essence exist above all things. For he could not otherwise ascend into God unless he first became God. Just as the ray of our eyes cannot perceive the forms and colors of sensible things until it mingles with the sun’s rays and becomes one with them and in them, so the mind of the saints cannot receive the pure knowledge of spiritual things that surpass all intellect unless it is first made worthy to possess a participation in incomprehensible truth. Thus the holy theologian, transformed into God and made a participant in truth, declares that the Word of God subsists in God the Principle—that is, that God the Son subsists in God the Father. “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word.”

Behold the heavens opened—that is, the mystery of the highest and holy Trinity and Unity revealed to the world. Observe the divine angel ascending above the Son of Man, announcing to us that he himself was the Word in the beginning before all things; and then descending upon that same Son of Man and crying out: “And the Word was made flesh.” He descends, proclaiming that God the Word was supernaturally made man from a virgin among all things; he ascends, declaring that the same Word was superessentially begotten from the Father before and beyond all things.

“In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word.” It must be noted that in this passage the blessed Evangelist indicates not time but substance through the word *erat* (“was”). For its form, that is, *sum* (“I am”), from which it is irregularly inflected, contains a twofold meaning. Sometimes it signifies the subsistence of whatever thing is predicated of it, without any temporal change, and for this reason it is called a substantive verb; sometimes it expresses temporal changes according to the analogy of other verbs. Thus what he says—“In the beginning was the Word”—is as though he were plainly saying: “The Son subsists in the Father.” For who, being of sound judgment, would say that the Son ever subsisted temporally in the Father? There alone eternity is contemplated where alone unchangeable truth is understood.

And lest anyone suppose that the Word subsists in the beginning in such a way that no distinction of substances is understood to be present, he immediately adds: “And the Word was with God”—that is, the Son subsists with the Father in unity of essence and substantial distinction. Again, lest a poisonous thought should creep in anywhere, namely, that the Word is only in the Father and is with God, but that the Word itself does not subsist as God substantially and coessentially with the Father—for this error invaded the impious Arians—he straightaway adds: “And God was the Word.”

Seeing also that there would be those who might say that the Evangelist had not written of one and the same Word, “In the beginning was the Word” and “God was the Word,” but had intended one Word by “in the beginning” and another by “God was the Word,” he destroys the heretical opinion by adding in sequence:

“This was in the beginning with God,” as though he were saying: “This Word, which is God, was with God himself, and it was not something else that was in the beginning.” But the Greek exemplars make the meaning clearer. In them *οὗτος* is written, that is, “this one,” and it can refer to both—to the Word and to God—for these two nouns, Θεός and λόγος, are masculine in Greek. Thus it can be understood as follows: “And God was the Word; this one was in the beginning with God,” as if he had said with light brighter than daylight: “This God the Word was with God; it is he of whom I said: ‘In the beginning was the Word.’”

“All things were made through him.” Through God the Word himself, or through the Word who is God, all things were made. And what is “all things were made through him” except this: when he was born from the Father before all things, all things were made with him and through him? For his generation from the Father is itself the establishment of all causes, and the operation and effect of all things that proceed from causes into genera and species. Through the generation of God from God the Principle, all things were made.

Hear the divine and ineffable paradox, the secret that cannot be opened, the invisible, profound, incomprehensible mystery: through the one who was not made but begotten, all things were made, but were not begotten. The Principle from which all things are is the Father; the Principle through which all things are is the Son. When the Father speaks his Word—that is, when the Father begets his Wisdom—all things come to be.

The Prophet says: “You made all things in wisdom”; and elsewhere, introducing the person of the Father: “My heart has poured forth.” And what did his heart pour forth? He himself explains: “I speak a good word”—I speak a good Word; I beget a good Son. The heart of the Father is his own substance, from which the Son’s own substance was begotten. The Father precedes the Word not by nature but by causation. Hear the Son himself saying: “The Father is greater than I.” His substance is the cause of my substance. The Father, I say, precedes the Word causally; the Son precedes all things made through him naturally. The substance of the Son is coeternal with the Father. The substance of those things made through him began to exist in him before the ages of the world—not in time, but with time. For time itself was made among the other things that were made; it was not generated, but created together with them.

And what is the consequence of the word spoken by the mouth of the Most High? The Father did not speak in vain, fruitlessly, or without great effect; for human beings also produce something in the ears of their hearers when they speak to one another. We must therefore believe and understand three things: the Father speaking, the Word pronounced, and the things brought about through the Word. The Father speaks; the Word is begotten; all things are brought about. Hear the Prophet when he says, “He spoke, and they were made”—that is, he begot his Word, through whom all things were made.

And lest you should perhaps suppose that some of the things that are were made through the Word of God, while others were made or existed outside him through themselves, so that not all things that are and that are not might be referred to one principle, he adds the conclusion of the whole theology: “And without him nothing was made”—that is, nothing was made outside him, because he encompasses all things, comprehending them within himself; and nothing is understood to be coeternal, consubstantial, or coessential with him except his Father and his Spirit proceeding from the Father through him.

This is easier to understand in Greek. Where the Latins place *sine ipso* (“without him”), the Greeks have χωρὶς αὐτοῦ, that is, “outside him.” Likewise the Lord himself says to his disciples: “Outside me you can do nothing.” “You who could not be made through yourselves outside me,” he says, “what can you do outside me?” For there too the Greeks write not ἄνευ but χωρίς—that is, not “without,” but “outside.” I said that this is easier because, when someone hears “without him,” he may suppose “without his counsel or assistance,” and thus may not attribute everything, or all things, to him. But when he hears “outside,” nothing at all is left that was not made in him and through him.

“What was made in him was life.” After the blessed Evangelist had revealed, beyond every remotest mode of reasoning and understanding, the divine mysteries—namely, God the Word in God the speaker—leaving to contemplators of sacred Scripture the understanding of the Holy Spirit in both—for just as one who speaks necessarily breathes forth a spirit in the word he speaks, so God the Father simultaneously and at once begets his Son and produces his Spirit through the one begotten—and after he had established that all things were made through God the Son and that nothing subsists outside him, he directed the sequence of his theology, as though from another beginning, saying: “What was made in him was life.”

He had already said, “All things were made through him”; and, as though someone had asked him about the things made through God the Word—“How and in what way were the things made through him in him?”—he replied: “What was made in him was life.”

This sentence can be pronounced in two ways. One may distinguish it as: “What was made,” and then add, “in him was life”; or one may read it as: “What was made in him,” and then add, “was life.” Thus, in the two pronunciations, we contemplate two meanings.

For the theory expressed by the words “what was made”—that which is separated by places and times, distinguished by genera, forms, and numbers, either joined together or separated into sensible and intelligible substances—is not the same as the theory declaring that “what was made in him was nothing other than life,” so that the meaning is: all things made through him are life in him and are one. They were—that is, they subsist causally in him before they exist effectively in themselves.

For the things made through him are under him in one way, and the things that he himself is are in him in another way. Therefore all things made through the Word live unchangeably in him and are life. In him they were not and will not be in temporal intervals or local distinctions; rather, above all times and places, they are one in him and universally subsist: visible and invisible, corporeal and incorporeal, rational and irrational. In short, heaven and earth, the abyss, and whatever is in them live in him, are life, and subsist eternally. Even those things that seem to us to lack every vital movement live in the Word.

But if you ask how or by what manner all things made through the Word subsist in him vitally, uniformly, and causally, take examples from the nature of creatures; learn the Creator from the things made in him and through him. “His invisible things,” as the Apostle says, “are understood and perceived through the things that have been made.”

Observe how the causes of all things encompassed by the spherical form of this sensible world subsist together and uniformly in that sun which is called the world’s greatest luminary. From it proceed the forms of all bodies, the beauty of differing colors, and all the other things that can be predicated of sensible nature. Consider the manifold and infinite power of seeds: how the multitude of herbs, fruits, and animals is contained in individual seeds; how from them arises the beautiful and innumerable multiplicity of forms. Look with inward eyes at how the manifold rules in the art of the craftsman are one and live in the mind of the one arranging them; how an infinite number of lines subsists as one in a single point. Observe examples of this kind from nature. From these, as though borne beyond all things on the wings of physical theory, aided and illumined by divine grace, you will be able to look with the mind’s eye into the secrets of the Word and, insofar as is granted to human arguments seeking their God, to see how all things made through the Word live in him and are life.

For in him, as the divine mouth says, “we live and move and are”; and, as the great Dionysius the Areopagite says, the being of all things is the superessential divinity.

“And the life was the light of human beings.” The Son of God, whom, O blessed theologian, you previously called the Word, you now call life and light. You have not changed the names without reason, so that you might disclose to us their differing meanings. You called the Son of God the Word because through him the Father spoke all things, when he himself spoke and they were made; but you call him light and life because that same Son is the light and life of all things made through him.

And what does he illuminate? Nothing other than himself and his Father. He is therefore light: he illuminates himself, declares himself to the world, and manifests himself to those who do not know him. The light of divine knowledge withdrew from the world when humanity abandoned God. Thus eternal light declares itself to the world in two ways: through Scripture and through creation. Divine utterances must be learned, and their meaning must be conceived in your mind; in them you will know the Word. By bodily sense, perceive the forms and beauties of sensible things, and in them you will understand God the Word. In all these things truth will declare nothing else to you except the one who made all things, outside whom you will contemplate nothing, because he is all things. For in all things that are, whatever there is, he is. Just as there is no substantial good, so there is no essence or substance apart from him.

“And the life was the light of human beings.” Why did he add “of human beings”? As though the light belonged particularly and properly to human beings, although he is the light of angels, the light of the whole created universe, and the light of all visible and invisible existence? Or perhaps the Word who gives life to all things is called particularly and properly the light of human beings because in humanity he manifested himself to human beings, to angels, and to every creature capable of sharing in divine knowledge.

For he appeared neither through an angel to angels nor through an angel to human beings, but through a human being to both human beings and angels—not in an apparition, but in the true humanity which he wholly assumed into unity of substance. He bestowed knowledge of himself upon all who know him. The light of human beings, therefore, is our Lord Jesus Christ, who in human nature manifested himself to every rational and intellectual creature and revealed the hidden mysteries of his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father.

“And the light shines in the darkness.” Hear the Apostle: “You were,” he says, “once darkness, but now light in the Lord.” Hear Isaiah: “Light has dawned upon those sitting in the region of the shadow of death.”

“The light shines in the darkness.” By the merit of original sin, the whole human race was in darkness—not the darkness of the outward eyes, through which the forms and colors of sensible things are perceived, but that of the inward eyes, through which the forms and beauties of intelligible things are discerned; not in the darkness of this murky air, but in the darkness of ignorance of the truth; not in the absence of the light that reveals the corporeal world, but in the absence of the light that illumines the incorporeal world.

After the light arose from the virgin, the light shines in the darkness—that is, in the hearts of those who know it. Since the whole human race is divided, as it were, into two parts—those whose hearts are illumined by knowledge of the truth, and those who still remain in the darkest darkness of impiety and unbelief—the Evangelist adds: “And the darkness did not comprehend him.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: The light shines in the darkness of faithful souls and shines more and more, beginning from faith and advancing toward vision; but the unbelief and ignorance of impious hearts did not comprehend the light of the Word of God shining in the flesh. “For their foolish heart,” as the Apostle says, “was darkened,” and, while claiming to be wise, they became fools.

But this is the moral meaning. The physical theory of these words is as follows.

Even if human nature had not sinned, it could not shine by its own powers. It is not naturally light, but participates in light. It is capable of wisdom, but is not wisdom itself; through participation in wisdom it can become wise. Just as this air does not shine through itself, but is called darkness while nevertheless being capable of solar light, so our nature, considered in itself, is a certain dark substance, capable of and participating in the light of wisdom.

And just as the aforesaid air, when it participates in the sun’s ray, is not said to shine by itself, but the sun’s splendor is said to appear in it, so that it neither loses its natural obscurity nor fails to receive the light that comes upon it, so the rational part of our nature, when it possesses the presence of God the Word, knows intelligible things and its God not by itself but through the divine light implanted in it.

Hear the Word himself: “It is not you,” he says, “who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” By this single saying he wished to teach us to understand the same thing in other matters and always to hear, sounding ineffably in the ear of our heart: “It is not you who shine, but the Spirit of your Father who shines in you”—that is, he manifests to you that I shine in you, because I am the intelligible light of the world, that is, of rational and intellectual nature.

“It is not you who understand me, but I myself understand myself in you through my Spirit,” because you are not substantial light, but participation in light that subsists through itself. The light therefore shines in the darkness because the Word of God, the life and light of human beings, does not cease to shine in our nature, which, when investigated and considered in itself, is found to be a certain formless darkness. He did not wish to abandon it, although it had fallen into sin, nor did he ever abandon it: forming it by containing it through nature, and reforming it by deifying it through grace.

And because he himself, the light, is incomprehensible to every creature, “the darkness did not comprehend him.” For God surpasses every sense and intellect, and he alone possesses immortality. His light is called darkness by way of excellence, since no creature comprehends what or of what kind he is.

“There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.” Behold the eagle descending in gentle flight from the loftiest summit of the mountain of theology into the deepest valley of history, releasing the wings of the highest contemplation from the heaven of the spiritual world. Divine Scripture is a certain intelligible world, constituted by four parts as though by four elements.

Its earth, situated as if in the middle and lowest region like a center, is history. Around it, an abyss is poured out in the likeness of waters: moral understanding, which the Greeks commonly call *Ethics*. Around these two lower parts of the aforesaid world—I mean history and ethics—there revolves the air of natural science. By natural science I mean what the Greeks call *Physics*.

Outside and beyond all these there is the ethereal and fiery radiance of the empyrean heaven, that is, the sublime contemplation of divine nature, which the Greeks call *Theology*. Beyond it no intellect goes.

Thus the great theologian—I mean John—touching the highest peaks of theology at the beginning of his Gospel and penetrating the secrets of the heavens of spiritual heavens, rises beyond all history, ethics, and physics to those things that took place shortly before the incarnation of the Word. Then, in order to narrate history, he bends his flight down, as it were, toward a certain intelligible earth and says: “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.”

[Col. 0291D] He consequently introduces John into his own theology. Abyss calls to abyss in the voice of the divine mysteries. The Evangelist narrates the history of the forerunner; the one to whom it was granted to know the Word in the beginning commemorates the one to whom it was granted to go before the incarnate Word.

“There was a man,” he says. He did not simply say, “sent from God,” but “there was a man,” so that he might distinguish the man who participates in humanity alone and who goes before from the man united and joined with divinity and humanity who came after him; so that he might separate the passing voice from the Word who always and unchangeably remains; so that he might indicate the morning star appearing at the rising of the kingdom of heaven and declare the sun of righteousness coming upon the world.

He distinguishes the witness from the one to whom he bears witness, the one sent from the one who sends, the lamp shining in the darkness from the brightest light filling the world and destroying the darkness of death and sins throughout the human race.

The forerunner of the Lord, therefore, was a man, not God; but the Lord whose forerunner he was, was both man and God. The forerunner was a man destined to pass into God through grace; the one whom he preceded was God by nature, destined to accept humanity through humility and through the will to bring about our salvation and redemption.

He was a man sent. By whom? By God the Word, whom he preceded. His mission was his forerunning; crying out, he sends the voice ahead. “The voice of one crying in the wilderness”: the messenger prepares the advent of the Lord. His name was John—to whom it was granted to become the forerunner of the King of kings, the manifestor of the incarnate Word, the baptizer into spiritual sonship, and the witness to eternal light through his voice and martyrdom.

“He came for a testimony, to bear witness to the light”—to Christ, that is. Hear his testimony: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” And again: “He who comes after me has been made before me.” This is read more clearly in Greek as ἔμπροσθέν μου, that is, “before me,” “in front of me,” or “before my sight.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: He who, in the order of time, was born in the flesh after my birth, I saw prophetically before my sight, while I was still in the womb of my barren mother; I saw him conceived before me and made man in the womb of the virgin.

[Col. 0292C] “He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light.” Supply from what precedes and understand it thus: He was not the light, but was sent to bear witness to the light. The forerunner of the light was not the light.

Why, then, is he called a burning lamp and a morning star? He was a burning lamp, but he burned not kindled by his own fire, and he did not shine by his own light. He was a morning star, but he did not receive his own light from himself. The grace of the one whom he preceded burned and shone in him. He was not the light, but a participant in the light; what shone in him and after him did not belong to him. For, as we said above, no rational or intellectual creature is substantially light in itself; rather, it is light through participation in the one true substantial light, which shines everywhere in all things that shine intelligibly.

Therefore it is added: “But it was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into the world.” He calls the Son of God, subsisting through himself and begotten by God the Father, who subsists through himself, before all ages, the true light. He calls the same Son, made man from human beings for the sake of human beings, the true light.

He is the true light who says of himself: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not remain in darkness, but will have the light of eternal life.”

“It was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into the world.” What does “coming into the world” mean? Who is every human being coming into the world? From where does he come into the world? And into which world does he come?
