If you understand this of those who come from the hidden recesses of nature into this world through generation, in places and times, what kind of illumination is there in those born into this life in order to die, growing in order to decay, composed in order to be dissolved, falling from the rest of silent nature into the unrest of tumultuous misery?

Tell me, I ask, what kind of spiritual and true light was there for those born into a transitory and false life? Is this world a suitable dwelling for those alienated from the true light? Is it not rightly called the region of the shadow of death, the valley of tears, the depth of ignorance, and an earthly dwelling that weighs down the human mind and blunts its inner eyes against contemplating the true light?

We must not therefore understand the words “which enlightens every human being coming into the world” of those who proceed from the hidden causes of seeds into bodily forms. We must understand them of those who come spiritually through the generation of grace given in baptism into the invisible world; those who despise birth according to corruptible flesh and choose birth according to the spirit; who trample upon the world that is below and ascend into the world that is above; who abandon the shadows of ignorance and death and desire the light of wisdom and life; who cease to be sons of human beings and begin to become sons of God; who set aside and destroy within themselves the world of vices; who establish before the eyes of their minds the world of virtues and long with all their strength to ascend into it.

The true light therefore enlightens those who come into the world of virtues, not those who rush into the world of vices.

“He was in the world.” In this passage he calls “world” not only the visible creation in general, but also, more particularly, the substance of rational nature that exists in humanity. In all these things, then, and, to put it simply, in the created universe, the Word was the true light. He subsists and always was, because he never ceases to subsist in all things.

For just as the one who speaks, while speaking, causes his voice to cease to exist, so that it ceases and vanishes, if the heavenly Father ceased to speak his Word, the effect of the Word—that is, the created universe—would not subsist. The subsistence and continuance of the created universe is therefore the speech of God the Father: that is, the eternal and unchangeable generation of his Word.

This sentence may also reasonably be understood as referring solely to this sensible world: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him.” Lest anyone who shared in the Manichaean heresy should suppose that the world subject to bodily senses was created by the devil rather than by the Creator of all visible and invisible things, the theologian adds: “He was in the world”—that is, he was in this world, the one who contains all things—and “the world was made through him.” For the Creator of the universe does not dwell in works that belong to another, but in his own works, which he made.

We must observe that the blessed Evangelist used the word “world” in general. Nevertheless, we must understand three worlds.

The first is the world filled absolutely with the invisible and spiritual substances of the virtues. Whoever comes into it possesses full participation in the true light.

The second is opposed to the first, since it consists absolutely of invisible and corporeal natures. Although it occupies the lowest proportion of the universe, the Word was nevertheless in it, and it was made through the Word. It is the first step for those who wish to ascend to the knowledge of truth through the senses, for the forms of visible things draw the reasoning mind toward knowledge of invisible things.

The third world possesses the nature of a middle term. It unites within itself the higher world of spiritual things and the lower world of corporeal things; it makes one from the two and is understood in humanity alone, in which all creation is joined together.

For humanity consists of body and soul. Gathering the body from this world and the soul from the other world, it makes one ornament. The body possesses every corporeal nature, while the soul possesses every incorporeal nature. When these are joined together in one composition, they produce the whole worldly ornament of humanity. Therefore human beings are called “the whole”: for every creature is fused together in them as in a certain workshop.

Hence the Lord himself, when commanding his disciples to preach, instructed them: “Preach the Gospel to every creature.”

This world, then—that is, humanity—did not know its Creator. Held captive by the bonds of carnal thoughts, it neither wished to know its God through the symbols of the written law nor through the paradigms of visible creation.

“And the world did not know him.” Humanity did not know God the Word, either before his human manifestation, when he was divinity alone and unclothed, or after his human manifestation, when he was clothed in incarnation alone. It was ignorant of the invisible one and denied the visible one. It did not wish to seek the one who sought it; it did not wish to hear the one who called it; it did not wish to worship the one who deified it; it did not wish to receive the one who received it.

He came into his own, namely into those things which were made through him and which therefore are not undeservedly his own. And his own did [not] receive him. [Note: [Col. 0293D] “not” is not omitted by the manuscript; it is supplied by conjecture.] His own are all human beings whom he willed to redeem and did redeem.

But as many as received him, he gave them the power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name. The rational humanity of the world is now not divided, but rather the will; [Col. 0294D] those who receive the incarnate Word are separated from those who reject it. The faithful believe in the advent of the Word and willingly receive the Lord who is their own. The impious deny and obstinately refuse him: the Jews through envy, the pagans through ignorance. To those who receive him he gave the power to become sons of God; to those who do not receive him he still grants time to receive him. For the possibility of believing in the Son of God, and the possibility of becoming a son of God, is taken away from no one; for this depends upon human free choice and the cooperation of grace. To whom did he give the power to become sons of God? To those who receive him, namely [Col. 0295A] to those who believe in his name. Many receive Christ. The Arians receive him, but do not believe in his name: they do not believe that the only-begotten Son of God is consubstantial with the Father. They deny that he is ὁμοούσιος, that is, coessential with the Father; they affirm that he is ἑτεροούσιος, that is, of an essence other than the Father’s. Thus it does not profit them to receive Christ while they strive to deny his truth. But to those who receive Christ as true God and true man, and believe this most firmly, the possibility of becoming sons of God has been given.

Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. In ancient Greek copies it is written only: “Who were born not of bloods, but of God.” “Not of bloods,” he says, that is, not through bodily [Col. 0295B] procreations, are those who attain the adoption of sons of God through the merit of faith; but they are born of God the Father through the Holy Spirit into co-inheritance with Christ—that is, into co-sonship with the only-begotten Son of God. “Nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man.” A twofold sex is introduced, from which the multitude of those born in the flesh is propagated carnally: by the term “flesh” the Evangelist signifies the female condition, and by “man” the male.

And lest perhaps you should say, “It seems impossible for mortals to become immortal, for corruptible beings to lack corruption, for mere human beings to be sons of God, for temporal beings to possess eternity,” take from those things which are greater an argument by which you may give credence to the matter of which you doubt: “And the Word became flesh.” If, therefore, [Col. 0295C] what is greater unquestionably came first, why does it seem incredible that what is less can follow? If the Son of God became man—which none of those who receive him doubts—what wonder is it if a human being who believes in the Son of God is to become a son of God? For this purpose the Word descended into flesh, so that flesh—that is, a human being believing through the flesh in the Word—might ascend into him, and so that through the natural, only-begotten Son many might become adoptive sons. The Word became flesh not for his own sake but for our sake, since only through the flesh of the Word could we be transformed into sons of God. He descended alone and ascended with many; he makes gods out of human beings, he who made a human being out of God. “And he dwelt in us,” that is, he took possession of our nature, in order to make us participants in his nature. And [Col. 0295D] we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.

Where did you see, O blessed theologian, the glory of the incarnate Word, the glory of the Son of God made human? When did you see it? With what eyes did you behold it? With bodily eyes, I suppose, on the mountain at the time of the Transfiguration. For then you were present as the third witness of the divine glorification. You were present, as I think, in Jerusalem and heard the voice of the Father glorifying the Son, saying: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again.” You heard the crowds of children crying: “Hosanna to the Son of David.” What shall I say of the glory of the resurrection? You saw him rising from the dead when he entered, though the doors were shut, to you and your other fellow disciples. You saw his glory [Col. 0296A] as he ascended to the Father, when he was taken up into heaven by angels. And beyond all these things, with the loftiest contemplation of your mind, you beheld that Word, I say, in his beginning with his Father, where you saw his glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.

Full of grace and truth. There is a twofold understanding of this clause. It may be understood of the humanity and divinity of the incarnate Word, so that the fullness of grace is referred to his humanity, and the fullness of truth to his divinity. For our Lord Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word, received the fullness of grace according to his humanity, because he is the head of the Church and the firstborn of every creature—that is, of all humanity universally—which has been healed and restored in him and through him. I say “in him,” because he himself is the greatest and principal example of grace by which, with no preceding merits, a human being becomes God, and this was manifested first in him. I say “through him,” because from his fullness we have all received the grace of deification, through the grace of faith by which we believe in him and of action by which we keep his commandments.

The fullness of Christ’s grace may also be understood of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit, who distributes and effects the gifts of grace, is customarily called “grace.” The sevenfold operation of that Spirit filled Christ’s humanity and rested in him, as the prophet says: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear [Col. 0296C] of the Lord shall fill him.”

If, therefore, you wish to understand the words “full of grace” as said of Christ in himself, understand them of the fullness of his deification and sanctification according to his humanity. By deification I mean that by which man and God were united into the unity of one substance; by sanctification, that by which he was not only conceived of the Holy Spirit but also filled with the fullness of his gifts; and, as on the summit of the Church’s mystical lampstand, the lamps of graces shone in him and from him.

But if you prefer to understand the fullness of grace and truth of the incarnate Word as the New Testament, the same Evangelist seems shortly afterward to have held this view. For he says: “The Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” You will not speak incongruously if you say [Col. 0296D] that the fullness of the New Testament’s grace was bestowed through Christ and that the truth of the legal symbols was fulfilled in him. Thus the Apostle says: “In whom dwells bodily the fullness of divinity,” calling the mystical meanings of the Law’s shadows the fullness of divinity; Christ, by coming in the flesh, both taught and revealed that these dwell bodily—that is, truly—in himself, because he is the fountain and fullness of graces, the truth of the legal symbols, and the end of prophetic visions. To him be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0297]

JOHN SCOTUS’S COMMENTARY ON THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN.

From MS 81 of the Library of Laon, parchment, ninth century, quarto; first published by M. Félix Ravaisson in the book entitled *Catalogue général des manuscrits des bibliothèques publiques des départements*, vol. I, Paris, 1849, quarto, pp. 505 ff.

FRAGMENT I. CHAPTER I, 11–29

[Col. 0297A]

[lacuna]

He came to what was his own—that is, he was incarnate in the human nature which was made through him, and therefore is rightly his own. And his own did not receive him. This was said of the faithless Jews and of all the impious, who were unwilling to receive the Word of God—that is, they neither wished to believe in him nor to understand him. And lest anyone should suppose that all human beings failed to receive him—for from the beginning of the world there was never a time in which there were no recipients of the divine Word—he therefore added:

But as many as received him—that is, whoever believed in him—he gave them the power to become sons of God. He did not say, “He gave them the power to be saved,” or “He gave them the power to return to the former state and dignity of human nature,” but, in an ineffable gift impossible for any nature by itself, he gave them through the sublimity of his grace the power to become sons of God. To those who believe in his name—that is, to those who believe that they will receive knowledge of him [Note: [Col. 0297C] MS: *ei*, “to him”] and understanding through faith in this life, and by direct vision in the next.

Who were born not of bloods—that is, not of human seed—nor of the will of the flesh—that is, not of the female sex; for “flesh” often signifies the female sex—nor of the will of man—that is, not of male seed. This may also be understood as follows: “not of the will of the flesh,” so that what follows, “nor of the will of man,” serves as its exposition. For there are those who attribute the irrational impulse by which human beings are conceived in the flesh to the flesh alone, as though it had nothing to do with the soul, although flesh without a soul has no power in such matters. Therefore he adds, “nor of the will of man,” that is, “nor of the will of the whole human being.” Wise men often use the word “man” to designate a human being. But they were born of God—namely, through the grace of baptism, in which those who believe in Christ begin to be born from God.

But lest anyone should think it impossible for a mortal, carnal, fragile, corruptible human being to be raised to such glory as to become a son of God, the Evangelist, as though drawing breath and answering the hidden thoughts of unbelievers, set forth the strongest argument:

And the Word became flesh. As if he had said: “Do not be astonished that flesh—that is, mortal humanity—can pass over by grace into the sonship of God, since it is the greater miracle that the Word became flesh. For if what is higher descended to what is lower, why should it be surprising if what is lower ascends, through the agency of the grace of what is higher, into that which is higher—especially since the Word became flesh for this very purpose, so that humanity might become a son of God?” The Word descended into humanity so that through him humanity might ascend into God. For just as we say, “The Word became flesh,” so we may say, “Flesh also became the Word.”

“And the Word became flesh”: this evangelical statement recurs in the manner of proverbial sayings. “And he dwelt among us”—that is, he lived among us human beings. The Word dwelt among us; that is, he assumed our nature. “And we saw his glory”—namely, we whom he chose from the world saw his glory in the most manifest miracles, in the transfiguration on the mountain, and in the splendor of the resurrection; and not another glory, but “the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.” “Full of grace”: the implied sense is, “we saw him full of grace according to his humanity, and full of truth according to his divinity.”

John bears witness concerning him—namely, concerning the Word—and cries out; or, as it is read in Greek, “and he cried out, saying.” “This was he of whom I said,” or, as it is found in Greek, “of whom I was saying,” which is much more significant. For if he had used the perfect past tense, *dixi* (“I said”), he would have indicated that his preaching concerning Christ had already been completed. But the imperfect past, *dicebam* (“I was saying”), signifies both the beginning of John’s preaching of Christ and his continuing perseverance in that preaching.

“This was he”: “this” is a demonstrative pronoun referring to a present person. Thus it is understood that Christ was present in the place where John openly pointed him out in this manner. This is not surprising. The Lord himself, while still almost unknown to everyone, before he was baptized and began to preach, often used to come to John. Therefore John says, “This was he of whom I said.”

In this passage, as frequently in what precedes, the verb *erat* (“was”) does not express temporal meaning but substance, so that we understand “this was he” as though he had said plainly: “This is he; this one exists—the one of whom I was speaking to you.” To whom was he speaking? Clearly, to his own disciples, to whom he preached Christ when absent and pointed him out when present.

This becomes clear in what follows, where he says to his disciples: “Behold the Lamb of God, who is to come after me,” or, as it is written in other manuscripts, “who comes after me.” For the Greek word written there, ἐρχόμενος, is both a participle of past time and of future time.

“He was made before me.” As if he had said plainly: “Although he came into the world after me in the order of time, in his conception and birth, he was made before me—that is, he was placed before me in the order of dignity. For I am a pure and simple human being, whereas he is more than human, composed of humanity and divinity. He is Lord, I am servant; he is king, I am the forerunner.” Therefore it follows: “Because he was before me,” not only in the eternity of his divinity, but also in the dignity of his humanity.

But if someone examines the Greek wording attentively, he will understand what is said in another way: “He who is to come after me”—that is, “he who would come after me,” or “who came into the world after me”—“was made before me”; that is, “he appeared before me.” And just as I prophesied and knew him with spiritual eyes while I was still in the womb, so now I behold him made present before me—that is, coming—through bodily eyes. For the Greek expression ἔμπροσθέν μου is properly interpreted as “before me,” that is, “before my eyes.”

And what do I perceive in him, whether with spiritual or bodily eyes? Nothing other than that “he was before me,” or, more significantly in Greek, “because he was first of me.” He was therefore made present before me so that I might know that he was first—that is, that he preceded me in all things. For he precedes me in the fullness of grace. Whatever grace I possess, I receive from nowhere other than from the fullness of his grace. Therefore he added next:

And from his fullness we have all received. What fullness does he mean? None other than that of which he said above: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” For in Christ dwells the fullness of grace according to his humanity and the fullness of truth according to his divinity. Hence the Apostle says: “In him the fullness of divinity dwells bodily”—that is, truly.

But how does the fullness of grace according to humanity dwell in Christ [Note: [Col. 0299] The manuscript reads *possidet*, “possesses,” instead of *habitat*, “dwells”]? In no other way than that he is the first and greatest example of divine grace, in that Christ the human being, without any preceding merits, was assumed into unity of substance—or, as I shall say more commonly, of person. The fullness of truth is naturally in him, because he is the truth, as he himself testifies: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

Therefore, from his fullness according to both humanity and divinity we have all received. By “we all” he means those who received him from the people of Israel and those from the nations of the whole world who believed in him. We received grace, by which we believe in him, and truth, by which we understand him.

And this is what follows: “Grace for grace.” The implied sense is: “From his fullness we have received grace for grace”—namely, the grace of contemplation of truth in exchange for the grace of faith in confessing his incarnation; that is, the grace of direct vision in exchange for the grace of faith, and the grace of deification in the future in exchange for the grace of action and knowledge in the present.

And lest anyone who boasted in the Law should think that he had received grace and truth from the Law, he immediately added:

For the Law was given through Moses. As if he had said: “For this reason I say that we have all received grace and truth from the fullness of Christ, and not from the Law: because the Law was given only through Moses, and, when received according to the letter, bestows no grace upon those who receive it, since it is nothing other than a certain shadow and symbol of the New Testament.”

Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. This may also be understood as follows: when the Law is considered in Moses—that is, in the bare letter—it is merely Law; but when it is considered in Christ, it is grace and truth. For the spirit of the Law is grace and truth in Christ Jesus. Thus, considered in Moses, the Law is not grace and truth; but in Christ it is grace and truth.

Blessed Augustine distinguishes the Old Testament from the New in this way. He says: “The Law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the Law might be fulfilled.”

Thus he sets forth three things: Law, grace, and truth, signifying three hierarchies. The first is that of the Old Testament, handed down in the most obscure enigmas; the second, which we also call the middle one, is that of the New Testament, in which there is an abundance of grace and the clearest disclosure of the things that were mystically spoken and done in the Law; the third—I mean the heavenly hierarchy—already begins in this life and will be perfected in the life to come, when the contemplation of pure truth will be granted to those who are deified without any obscurity.

Thus the first hierarchy is signified by the name “Law,” the second by “grace,” and the third by “truth.” Whoever desires to know more fully about these three hierarchies should read Saint Dionysius the Areopagite [Note: [Col. 0299] The manuscript reads *Ariopagitam*.].

No one has ever seen God. To add to the fullness of Christ’s praise, what he says is added: “No one has ever seen God.” And humanity would, as it were, be deprived on this account of every human blessedness because of the divine invisibility—for the contemplation of God is true blessedness—if divine goodness had not come to its aid through the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God. In the flesh—that is, in the whole human being whom he assumed—he not only revealed himself, but also manifested to human beings the Father, previously altogether unknown, as he himself says: “I have manifested your name to the human beings whom you have given me.”

And again, when Philip asks and says, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us,” the reply is given: “Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father also.” And again: “No one has seen the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him.”

This must be understood not only of human beings but also of angels. For the angels likewise could not know their God, who surpasses every intellect, in his own nature, because he is invisible and unknowable. But through the incarnate Word they understood their Lord, namely, the Son of God, and in him and through him the whole Trinity, remote from all things.

Thus the incarnation of the Word of God benefited every rational and intellectual creature: the rational creature, by liberation from death, from diabolical servitude, and from ignorance of the truth; the intellectual creature, by enabling it to know its cause, which it had previously been unable to know. Hence the Apostle says: “In him all things that are in heaven and on earth have been restored.”

But it is not without reason that the question is asked why [Note: [Col. 0301D] MS: *cur cum*], in both the Old and the New Testament, it is frequently read that God appeared to human beings, either visibly to bodily eyes or invisibly in prophetic visions, while the Gospel says: “No one has ever seen God.” If it were said only of the Father that no one had seen him, the question would be very easily resolved: the persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit could often be understood to have appeared visibly, while the Father alone remained beyond all vision.

But since this is understood not of one person, but of the Trinity alone, which is one God, and since “No one has ever seen God” is understood of the essence and substance of the one Trinity, because it surpasses every intellect of rational and intellectual creatures, it is necessary to investigate what appeared when God is said to have appeared either visibly or invisibly.

Blessed Augustine unhesitatingly makes clear that the Son appeared in the Old Testament, but not in that substance in which he is equal to the Father; rather, he appeared in some created substance, whether visible or invisible. Likewise, when the Spirit is read to have appeared—for example, in the form of a dove—it must be thought that he appeared not in himself, in that substance in which he is coessential with the Father and the Son, but in an assumed created substance. Understand the same concerning the Father.

The visions of the prophets, in which the prophets are said to have seen God, were also produced through some assumed spiritual creature. Dionysius unequivocally asserts that the divine substance itself never appeared to them in itself, lest it be thought capable in any way of being seen or comprehended, since it is invisible and incomprehensible.

It is also asked whether this is said only of human beings who still live in this life, and not of the heavenly powers, which always remain in divine contemplation. To this it must be answered that no participant in human or angelic nature can contemplate God himself in his own nature.

For what is written in the Latin manuscript, “No one has seen God,” is written in Greek as “No one has seen God”: οὐδείς is interpreted as both *nemo* (“no one”) and *nullus* (“none”).

What, then, do holy human souls and the holy intellects of angels see when they see God, if they do not see God himself, whom they are said to see? Let us give a few examples from many. Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Again: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” John says in his epistle: “We know that we are sons of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know, however, that when he appears, we shall see him as he is.” Paul likewise says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face,” and other statements of the same kind.

What, I ask, do human beings and angels see, or what will they see, when both Saint Ambrose and Dionysius the Areopagite insist most plainly and without hesitation that God—I mean the supreme Trinity—has never appeared, does not appear, and will never appear to anyone in himself?

He will therefore appear in his theophanies—that is, in his divine manifestations—in which God will appear according to the height of each person’s purity and virtue. Theophanies are all visible and invisible creatures, through which and in which God has often appeared, appears, and will appear.

Likewise, the virtues of most thoroughly purified souls and intellects are theophanies; in them God manifests himself to those who seek and love him. In these, as in certain clouds, the saints are caught up to meet Christ, as the Apostle says: “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ,” calling “clouds” the most radiant heights of divine contemplation, in which they will always be with Christ.

Hence Dionysius says: “And if anyone says that he has seen him—namely, God—he has not seen him, but something made by him. For he is altogether invisible, known better through unknowing, and whose ignorance is true wisdom.”

The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father—or, as it is written in Greek, “who is in the bosom of the Father,” or “in the bosoms of the Father.” In some Greek manuscripts “the bosom of the Father” is expressed in the singular, and in others in the plural, as though the Father had many bosoms.

He has made him known. Thus the only-begotten Son made God known—that is, manifested him in himself—not insofar as his divinity, which is altogether invisible, but insofar as his humanity, which he assumed in order to manifest himself, his Father, and also his Holy Spirit to human beings and angels. For although the human soul is invisible in itself, through its bodily movements it manifests not what it is but that it exists.

And what does he mean by “who is in the bosom of the Father,” or “in the bosoms of the Father”? Is the bosom of the Father one thing and the only-begotten Son of the Father another? No: the only-begotten Son himself is the bosom of the Father. The Son is called the bosom of the Father because he made the Father known to the world.

The only-begotten Son is also the bosom of the Father because he is always in the secrets of the Father’s nature, as he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

Just as the only-begotten Son is the house of the Father, as he himself says, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places”—as if he had said, “In me, in whom the Father dwells as in his own house, there are many dwelling places; for in it each person will possess a dwelling corresponding to his merits and to his grace”—so also the Son is the bosom of the Father. For in him the Father receives and gathers those whom he wishes to receive and gather.

“He has made him known”: by the teaching and manifestation [Note: [Col. 0303D] MS: *doctrinam et manifestationem*, “the teaching and manifestation”] of his incarnation he demonstrated, demonstrates, and will demonstrate the invisible God, as he says in the very statement quoted a little earlier: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”

And this is John’s testimony. As if he had said: All that we have said, from the words “John bears witness” up to “he has made him known,” is the testimony of John the forerunner concerning the one whose forerunner he is.

Then, as though beginning the narrative from another starting point, he says: “When the Jews sent from Jerusalem,” and so forth. The order of the words is: “He confessed, and did not deny, when the Jews sent from Jerusalem priests and Levites,” and so forth.

But what did he not deny, and what did he confess?

Because I am not the Christ. The Jews thought that John the Baptist was the Christ, because it had been foretold by the prophets that he would come into the world. They also thought that he was Elijah the Tishbite, on account of his extraordinary abstinence, chastity, solitary life, extremely severe denunciation of sins, and very dreadful proclamation of future vengeance.

In addition, they thought that he—John, I mean—was one of the prophets risen again, because they saw that the great grace of prophecy had flourished exceedingly in him. “I am not,” he says, “the Christ, because I am the forerunner of Christ and the voice of one crying in the wilderness.”

Are you Elijah? And he said: I am not. This denial is understood in two ways. “I am not Elijah,” he said, “but I have come in the spirit and power of Elijah.” Or: “I am not Elijah; for he was merely a prophet, whereas I am not merely a prophet but also a forerunner.”

This does not mean that all the prophets are not forerunners of Christ, but that none of the prophets was born together with Christ in the same year and became his forerunner after so brief an interval.

Are you the prophet? He answered: No. This too is understood in two ways: either because he is more than a prophet, as Christ proclaims concerning him, and therefore denies that he is a prophet; or because he answered their opinion. For they thought that John was one of the prophets of a past age who had risen from the dead.

He therefore says: “I am not one of those prophets whom you suppose me to have been, risen again from their number and now preaching to you in person.”

They therefore said to him: Who are you? If you are not the Christ, or Elijah, or one of the prophets, tell us who you are, so that we may not return to those who sent us without an answer or any knowledge about you, unable to give them any reply.

What do you say about yourself? For we have heard that you preached about Christ, but you make no clear assertion about yourself. What, then, do you say about yourself?

I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness. “If you ask,” he says, “what I declare about myself, know that I am a voice.” He did not say, “I am a human being,” or “I am John, son of Zechariah,” but he said, “I am a voice.”

For he did not consider human substance in himself, nor human generation, since the forerunner of the Word was exalted beyond all these things. He abandoned everything contained within the world, ascended on high, and became the voice of the Word, so that he confessed no substance in himself except that which he received beyond every creature through the abundance of grace—namely, to be the voice of the Word.

This name was not imposed on him by himself, but long before by the prophet Isaiah—or rather, by the Holy Spirit through Isaiah. Thus: “I am a voice,” not “my voice,” but “the voice of one crying”; for “voice” is said relationally.

John is therefore the voice of the Word—that is, of the Word preaching through flesh. And where does the Word, whose voice John is, cry out?

In the wilderness. Many wish this wilderness to be understood as Judea and the whole of Israel. For Judea had been reduced to a wilderness, emptied of all divine worship and polluted by the filth of idolatry. It followed only the legal letter, emptied of every spiritual sense and defiled by various superstitions. And she who was previously called “confession”—for Judea is interpreted as “confession” [Note: Jerome: “Juda” means “praise” or “confession.” For it is derived from the verb HIPH., that is, “to confess.”]—had been turned altogether into a denial of the truth.

In this wilderness, therefore, both the voice of the Word and the Word himself first preached. But it is rightly asked why the forerunner of the Word is signified by the name “voice.”

A voice is an interpreter of the mind. Everything that the mind first thinks and orders invisibly within itself brings forth sensibly, through the voice, into the senses of those who hear. The mind—that is, the intellect of all things—is therefore the Son of God. For, as Saint Augustine says, he is the intellect of all things, indeed, all things.

His forerunner is fittingly called by the name “voice,” because he was first manifested to the world through him, saying, “Behold the Lamb of God,” and so forth.

In a higher contemplation, however, the wilderness is understood as the ineffable height of the divine nature, removed from all things. It is deserted by every creature because it surpasses every intellect, while it deserts no intellect. This is signified with complete clarity by the Greek word ἔρημος. For ἐρημία means “removal” and “loftiness,” which altogether suits the divine nature.

In that wilderness of divine exaltation, therefore, the Word cries out—the Word through whom all things were made. Hear Moses saying in Genesis: “God said: Let there be light”; God said: “Let there be a firmament.” Likewise, in all the works of the six days, “God said” comes first.

By the name “God” we understand the Father, while “he said” signifies the Word of God. The Word of God therefore cries out in the most remote solitude of divine goodness. His cry is the creation of all natures. For he calls those things that exist as though they did not exist, because through him God the Father cried out—that is, created—all that he willed to be made.

He cried out invisibly, before the world was made, that the world should be made. Coming into the world, he cried out visibly that the world should be saved. First he cried out eternally through his divinity alone, before the incarnation; afterward he cried out through his flesh.

And what does that voice of his—that is, his forerunner—cry out? Listen: “Make straight the way of the Lord.”

What is “Make straight the way of the Lord”? Is it not what follows, “Make his paths straight”? Make straight, therefore, the way of the Lord—that is, preach and believe rightly in the Lord, who is the way, as he himself says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”

This may also be understood as: “Make straight the way of the Lord”—that is, believe rightly in the Lord. For the Lord enters human hearts by no other way than faith, which is the Lord’s way.

As the prophet Isaiah said. Since the Evangelist saw Isaiah’s statement concerning the Lord’s forerunner written at greatest length in the Gospel according to Luke, he wished to omit it here, lest he appear to repeat the same statement unnecessarily.

At this point, it is not inappropriate, I think, to insert a few observations about the mystical names of the forerunner.

He is called “Voice” because, just as the voice precedes the conception of the mind, so John preceded the Word of God.

He is called Πρόδρομος, that is, “forerunner,” because John preceded the Lord not only in conception and birth, but also in the mystery of baptism and in the preaching of repentance.

He is called Φόσφορος, that is, “light-bearer,” because he first brought the light of the world to the world’s knowledge and bore it in himself.

John is called the morning star, which the Greeks call ἄστρον πρωϊνὸν, because, just as that star which astrologers call Lucifer precedes the rising of the sun, so the Lord’s forerunner appeared first to the world, followed by the Sun of righteousness.

Similarly, he is called by the Greeks ἀκριδομελιτροφὸς because of his abstinence from the ordinary foods of human beings. For ἀκρὶς means “locust,” μέλι means “honey,” and τροφὴ means “food” [Note: [Col. 0305] The manuscript reads θρόφος.]. Thus ἀκριδομελιτροφὸς means “one who eats locusts and wild honey.”

And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees [Note: [Col. 0305] The manuscript reads *Fariseis*.]. It is asked why Pharisees were sent to John. The answer is as follows: the Pharisees in particular desired to hear John because they had heard his general preaching to the people concerning the resurrection of all from the dead, especially where he said, “Brood of vipers, who will free you from the wrath that is to come”—namely, at the judgment after the resurrection.

For they themselves firmly believed and preached the resurrection of the dead. Accordingly, they are said to have agreed with Christ in many matters and also to have frequently assisted the Apostle Paul.

What then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet? It is asked why the Pharisees attributed the authority to baptize to Elijah or to some prophet. For they had heard in the prophets that Christ would come into the world and baptize. Knowing, therefore, that the Jordan had borne the figure of baptism, and that Elijah and Elisha had crossed it with dry feet, they did not doubt that the figure of baptism had preceded them in Elijah and Elisha, or that those very men had risen again and baptized. Accordingly, they did not ask, “Are you one of the prophets?” but only, “Are you the Prophet?”—namely, the one who prefigured baptism. He answered them:

“I baptize in water”; as though he were saying: “I merely dip in water for the cleansing of bodies, prefiguring the sanctification of body and soul in the one who truly baptizes. But there stands among you”—that is, he appears present to you—“the one whom you do not know, because you do not believe in him and do not recognize who he is.

“He is the one who is to come after me.” This is the one who, in divine discussion and proclamation, was determined before the world existed to come into the world after me, so that he might follow me as his forerunner. [Note: The manuscript reads “diffinitus.”] “Who was made before me”—that is, who was made present before the eyes of my mind and body. For I see him and recognize him in your midst, but you do not know him.

There is another interpretation of these words, as Maximus holds. John bears the figure of repentance, because he preached repentance; Christ, however, bears the figure of righteousness—not only because he judges the world, but also because he himself is eternal righteousness. Repentance cannot be undertaken except after the transgression of righteousness. Human nature, therefore, which transgressed the divine laws in paradise, under the person of John preaches and practices repentance; and it clearly proclaims that the substantial righteousness of the Word of God, which precedes it through divinity and is to come after it through the dispensation of the flesh, would restore human nature—I mean, human nature living according to the divine laws that it had rejected through pride—to the former state of eternal righteousness.

“Of whom I am not worthy,” and so forth. The footwear of the Word is his flesh, which he assumed from the Virgin and which is suggested figuratively by the image of footwear. For just as footwear is made from the hides of dead animals, so Christ’s flesh became mortal for us, so that through his death our death might be utterly destroyed. Christ’s flesh did not become mortal because of any sin of its own, as our flesh did; rather, after sin, through condescension to our nature, it was subject to suffering. He did not refuse to undergo death for us, but he did not take upon himself the cause of death—namely, sin. Therefore death could not hold him, because he was not its debtor. Death could not hold captive the one whom it had not found guilty.

From the first man, therefore, before sin, he received being without sin; from that same man, after sin, he received the capacity to die. Through these two things he restored our entire nature in himself. For he utterly abolished our death in himself and restored eternal life. By being free from sin, he manifested our nature in himself as it was before it sinned.

If, then, the footwear of the Word is the flesh of the Word, it is not inappropriate to understand the strap of his footwear as the subtlety and inscrutable complexity of the mysteries of the incarnation. The Forerunner judges himself unworthy to unravel the profundity of this mystery.

It should nevertheless be noted that he did not say, “I shall not undo the strap of his footwear,” but said, “I am not worthy to undo the strap of his footwear.” For he undoes the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation when he reveals Christ most openly to the world and discloses many things about his divinity and humanity. Yet he considers himself unworthy to perform this task.

Christ’s visible creation and Holy Scripture may also be signified by his footwear, for in them he fixes his footprints, as it were his feet. The garment of the Word is visible creation, which openly proclaims him and manifests his beauty to us. His garment is also Scripture, which contains his mysteries. The Forerunner considers himself unworthy to undo the strap of both of these—that is, to unravel the subtlety of creation and of the written word.

The Word has two feet, one of which is the natural reason of visible creation, and the other the spiritual understanding of divine Scripture. One is covered by the sensible forms of the sensible world, the other by the surface of the divine letters—that is, of the Scriptures.

The interpreters of divine law indicate the incarnation of the Word of God in two ways. One teaches that he was incarnate from the Virgin, by which incarnation he joined human nature to himself in unity of substance. The other asserts that the Word himself was, as it were, incarnate—that is, thickened or embodied—in the letters and in the forms and arrangements of visible things. The strap of this twofold footwear is the diligent inquiry into truth in all these matters and the exceedingly intricate investigation of it; the Forerunner judges himself unworthy to undo it.

These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing. “These things,” he says—that is, the things so far spoken by the Forerunner about the divinity and humanity of the Word of God, about the preaching of the Forerunner himself, and about his response to the Pharisees—“took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan,” that is, on the far side of the Jordan.

Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience.”

[Note: Jerome: “Bethany, his house of affliction, or house of obedience.” Bethany is derived from a verb meaning “to answer,” “to obey,” or “to be brought low.”]

There are two Bethanies. One is beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing; the other is on this side of the Jordan, not far from Jerusalem, where the Lord raised Lazarus. These matters, however, are full of mysteries.

Bethany beyond the Jordan mystically prefigures human nature, which became a house of obedience before it sinned. For it was created for this purpose: to obey the divine commandments given to it within the bounds of paradise—that is, within the natural goods proper to it—so that it would not withdraw from contemplation and love of its Creator, in whose image it was created, but would always cling to him.

Beyond the Jordan, Bethany—the human nature that had been exhausted by poverty in divine goods and by the dryness of the infusion of wisdom—remained beyond the streams of divine grace that were poured into it after the incarnation of the Word.

But Bethany in Judea, on this side of the Jordan and near Jerusalem, signifies that same nature, liberated through the incarnation of the Word of God and carried, through the streams of divine grace that are first distributed through the sacraments of baptism, as if into Judea—that is, into the true confession of faith, action, and knowledge—and into a house of obedience, that is, into the unity of the Church obedient to the divine laws. It was placed near Jerusalem.

Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.”

[Note: Saint Jerome: “Jerusalem, vision of peace.” J. Scotus interprets the word below as “temple of peace.” The word is derived from …]

This signifies the heavenly city, to which human nature has not yet altogether attained. We believe that this will happen after the universal resurrection of all, when human nature will be brought into the complete and fullest contemplation of God. Yet it is not far from the heavenly homeland while it still remains in the flesh, in the house of obedience. For in part it knows the truth, illuminated by the grace of its Redeemer; in part it prophesies, signifying through invisible symbols and mystical teachings those things that it does not understand in their purity.

Accordingly, in this one sentence of the evangelist, three hierarchies—that is, three priesthoods—are mystically indicated.

The first priesthood, which existed under the Law, is established as Bethany beyond the outpourings of grace and truth through Christ in the New Testament. This priesthood, I say, was far from Jerusalem—that is, from the vision of peace—because of its obscure mysteries, exceedingly difficult to understand, and because of the dense darkness of its commandments, which were very far removed from the light of truth.

The second priesthood is in the New Testament. It begins with the preaching of the Forerunner and will end at the end of the world, as Scripture says: “The Law and the prophets were until John, and from that time the kingdom of heaven.” This priesthood shines partly with the clearest knowledge of truth and is partly obscured in symbols.

The principal symbols of the New Testament are three τελεταί, that is, three mystical sacrifices: one is baptism, the second is the σύναξις—that is, communion in the body and blood of the Lord—and the third is the mystery of chrism.

[Note: The manuscript has “synaxios.”]

The third priesthood will be celebrated in the future life, in which there will be no symbols and no obscurity of figures, but the whole of truth will appear with the greatest clarity. Therefore the priesthood of the New Testament occupies a kind of middle position between the past of the Law and the future of blessed life.

For in some respects it contemplates truth as future, while in others it celebrates it in its ministries as past.

Bethany beyond the Jordan, therefore, prefigures the priesthood of the Law; Bethany on this side of the Jordan, not far from Jerusalem, prefigures the priesthood of grace; and Jerusalem prefigures the future life of the blessed.

In the priesthood of the Law, therefore, human nature itself was instructed and corrected, as if beyond the Jordan, under the law of nature and under the written law. After its transgression, it had obscured the image of God in itself through ignorance of the truth and had contaminated it through desire for temporal things.

In the priesthood of the New Testament, the same nature was illuminated under Christ, educated under the law of grace, and made, as it were, close and ready for the future priesthood. It was illuminated through faith, educated through hope, and brought near to the divine vision through love, insofar as it is still permitted, while placed in the flesh, to penetrate the heights of divine understanding.

But if you seek the difference among these three laws—the natural law, the written law, and the law of grace—understand it briefly.

The law of nature is the law that commands all human beings to love one another equally, so that, just as one and the same nature is common to all, there may also be a common love of all by all.

The written law is the law that prohibits the violation of the law of nature, distinguishes between virtues and vices, and bears the figure of the law of grace. I say that the written law itself is an aid to the law of nature, so that, since the law of nature was unable by itself alone to correct human nature, the force of the written law might restrain what ought to be prohibited and teach what ought to be fulfilled.

For the law of nature had been almost entirely abolished in human beings, to such an extent that it neither recognized its Creator nor was able to maintain any distinction between virtues and vices.

The law of grace is the law that teaches not only that human beings should love one another and that virtues and vices should be distinguished, but also, beyond these things—which is possible only through divine grace, to die for human beings not only when they are good but also when they are evil, if necessary. Christ fulfilled this law in himself when he suffered not only for all human beings but also for all the ungodly.

“Where John was baptizing.” John baptized beyond the Jordan, rightly, because the true baptism—which liberates the whole of human nature not only from original sin but also from personal sins in those who undergo it—did not yet exist. He baptized only in water, as if under a certain figure of the perfect baptism that was to follow in Christ.

He therefore baptized beyond the Jordan, that is, beyond the streams of divine gifts that had not yet begun, in Christ, to descend into human nature.

John was beyond the Jordan because John bore the figure of the law of nature and also of the written law. The law of nature was prefigured in John. For those who live piously and chastely under the law of nature, removed from every contamination of carnal conduct, ought to live, like John, as if in a certain solitude of divine virtues.

John also signifies the written law, because he is its end: “The Law and the prophets were until John.” But because he became not only a prophet but also a manifestor of Christ, he signifies not merely the Law but also the Gospel and grace. Therefore it follows: “And from that time the kingdom of heaven”—as if he had said: “In John, as at a certain boundary, the Law ends, and the manifestation of grace, which he calls the kingdom of heaven, begins from him.”

On the next day—or, as it is expressed more significantly in Greek, on another day—John sees Jesus coming toward him. “Another,” he says, that is, with another kind of knowledge. The first knowledge occurred when he manifested him to the crowds gathered there, saying, “This was the one of whom I said to you.” Now, as a second recognition, “on another day,” or “on the next day,” John sees Jesus coming toward him.

With a twofold perception—namely, of mind and body—John the Forerunner recognizes his Lord, whom he preceded, coming toward him, not only by the steps of his body but also by the approaches of his inward contemplation.

“Jesus came to John.” Jesus therefore came to John—that is, he deigned to be recognized by John according to his divinity and his humanity.

And he said: “Behold, the Lamb of God; behold, the one who takes away the sin of the world.”

He openly proclaims him to the people when he says, “Behold, the Lamb of God.” John calls the Word of God a lamb. For he was the one whom the mystical lamb in the Law prefigured. Nor is it surprising if the shadow is proclaimed concerning the truth. The legal lamb was a shadow; Jesus Christ was the truth, and, as it were, the body of the shadow.

He is also called a lamb for a reasonable purpose. A lamb supplies three things to those who possess it: milk, wool, and food from its flesh. Our Lord grants believers the clothing of virtues; he nourishes them with milk—that is, with the simple teaching of truth—and leads them to the perfect food of his divine contemplation.

Christ is called the Lamb of God because he was sacrificed for the whole world. Therefore it follows: “Behold, the one who takes away the sin of the world.”

“He takes away,” he says—not from one place to another, or from one time to another, but he takes it away altogether, so that it may no longer exist—and through the destruction of his most holy flesh he entirely destroys the whole sin of the world.

The sin of the world is called original sin, which is common to the whole world—that is, to human nature. Its guilt is now remitted by the grace of baptism, but it will itself be utterly destroyed at the end of the world, in the resurrection of all.

Original sin, then, is that sin by which the whole of human nature, created together and at once in the image of God—and in which all human beings, from the beginning of the world to its end, are one and were created together according to body and soul—transgressed the divine laws in paradise through disobedience, refusing to keep God’s commandment.

For it was not only that first Adam, who came into this visible world before the others from the generality of human nature, who sinned; all sinned before they came into the world. For when the Apostle says, “As in Adam all die, so in Christ all are made alive,” we do not understand this of that one and first man alone, but we understand the name Adam to signify human nature generally.

That individual Adam would not have been born into this corruptible world through generation if the transgression of human nature had not preceded it. The division of nature into two sexes—namely, male and female—and the generation, through corruption, of human succession and multiplication from them is the universal punishment of sin, by which the entire human race together transgressed God’s commandment in paradise.

[Note: J. Scotus teaches, most disastrously, that the first human being before the transgression was a simple human being, and only after sin was human nature divided into male and female. He explains more fully in his works On the Division of Nature the error that the multiplication of the human race arose from this division of the sexes and occurs through generation by corruption. This doctrine is reviewed in the discussion of J. Scotus placed above, Part II, § 50 and following.]

This general sin is therefore called original sin, and not without reason, since it is the sin of the common origin of all. On account of its guilt, which brings death and corruption, we are all debtors, except the Redeemer. For our Redeemer alone was left without sin in that mass of the whole human race, as a remedy for the wound, so that through him alone the wound of the entire nature might always be healed and, accordingly, everything that had been wounded might be restored to its former state of salvation.

Thus this original sin, together with the individual sins committed after generation into this world, is released by the abundance of baptismal grace through our Savior, so that they may no longer exist. And this is what the evangelist says: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.”

This is the one and singular mystical Lamb, in whose figure the Israelite people sacrificed individual lambs in each household at the time of Passover. We too, who believe in him after the completion of his incarnation, passion, and resurrection, and who understand his mysteries insofar as this is granted to us, spiritually sacrifice him and eat him intellectually with the mind, not with the teeth.

[Note: Here are traces of the absurdities that, according to Adrevald, J. Scotus taught about the most holy Eucharist. By contrast, Berengarius was compelled at Rome to subscribe to the formula: “That the bread and wine placed upon the altar, after consecration, are not only the sacrament but also the true body and blood of our Lord; and that they are handled and broken by the priests’ hands and ground by the teeth of the faithful, not merely sacramentally but also in truth.” These statements concern the species, for there is no division of the substance. Moreover, J. Scotus had taught above, in his expositions of the Celestial Hierarchy, that the most holy Eucharist is taken into the inward recesses of our nature, for our ineffable deification.]

Thus each believer in Christ, according to his own virtue and according to the disposition and quality of the virtue subject to him, is both crucified and crucifies Christ for himself, being crucified together with Christ.

One person is crucified to sin alone, when he becomes quiet, as if overwhelmed by a certain death, with respect to all its operations in the flesh and through his flesh; and he mortifies sin—that is, he nails it down with the nails of the fear of the Lord—by restraining all its impulses so that they cannot operate in his flesh.

Another is crucified to passions—that is, to the soul’s weak activities, by which it is first corrupted in itself before it operates through the body. For the activity of the soul is one thing, while the operation of the body is another. This person is crucified to the passions when he is healed through the powers of the restored soul.

Another is crucified to the fantasies of the passions—that is, to images of sensible things formed in the bodily senses, which the wise call passions—when his senses are closed to these fantasies, so that through them he is not shamefully drawn toward desire for any temporal thing.

Another is crucified to thoughts and the conceptions of the mind that he had drawn through the bodily senses from sensible things, so that he does not remain in them any longer, withdrawn from divine contemplation.

Another dies not only to the fantasies of the senses but altogether to all the senses themselves, so that he may not be led astray through them by any error.

Another lays aside all natural familiarity and disposition that he had acquired through the bodily senses toward sensible things, as if crucified to all those senses themselves.

Another extinguishes in himself every sensible movement, as if on a certain cross, so that he has no natural activity at all within himself.

Each of these crucifies Christ with himself. For each of the faithful will possess such faith in Christ, through the increase of understandings, as is the disposition he has in his mind through the growth of virtues. Whenever he dies to the modes of his former and lower life and is raised to higher degrees, then the opinions he has held about Christ—simple though they may be—will die in him and with him, and through faith and understanding he will be advanced to more sublime theophanies of Christ.

Thus Christ dies daily in his faithful and is crucified by them, when they destroy their carnal thoughts about him, or even their spiritual thoughts, though still imperfect, continually ascending higher until they arrive at true knowledge of him. For the infinite is formed infinitely even in the most purified minds.

Another rests perfectly from intellectual activity itself, as if completely dead; for he surpasses not only the natural activities of the soul but also its intellectual operations.

Another is crucified to active philosophy. Active philosophy is concerned with the unifications and distinctions of natural virtues. Active philosophy also considers, insofar as it can, the principles of the incarnate Word. The spiritual person, surpassing all these things—that is, the whole of moral philosophy, concerning the virtues of the soul and the flesh of Christ—transcends to natural contemplation in the Spirit, as if from a certain flesh of the Word to his soul.

Another dies to natural contemplation. Natural contemplation is the speculative power of the rational soul that Christ assumed. The spiritual person dies to it when he not only ceases to affirm that Christ is flesh, understanding that Christ’s flesh has already been transformed into spirit, but also dismisses the notion that Christ is a rational soul.

For just as his flesh was exalted and changed into a rational soul, so his rational soul was raised and transformed into intellect. Accordingly, whoever ascends perfectly to him must be carried, as if from a certain soul of Christ to his intellect, into the uniform and simple induction of contemplative knowledge into the mysteries.

Another, through negation, dies to that same simple theological knowledge, which revolves chiefly around the intellect of Christ, and mystically ascends, as if from a certain intellect of Christ to his divinity, into the very perfect and secret infinity of God, dying to all things that exist after God.

Thus the Lamb of God is slain in the hearts of the faithful, and by being slain is made alive; thus the sin of the world is taken away from all human nature. [Note: Thus the manuscript; perhaps read “from human nature” (humanae naturae).]

A question not to be dismissed now whispers to us. It is rightly asked how the Lamb of God—that is, the Savior of the world—takes away the original sin of the whole of human nature: whether it has already been taken away in reality and purged from the whole nature, or whether it is still removed only in hope and will be taken away in reality after the common resurrection of human nature.

For if human nature has already been freed in reality from original sin, why do those who are baptized daily in Christ receive, through the abundance of grace, remission of original sin and of their personal sins, which flow from original sin as from a certain spring?

Why also can those who are born in the flesh not be born without carnal concupiscence, which is nothing other than the punishment of original sin?

[Note: Everyone understands that the things J. Scotus argues concerning original sin and related matters through the end of this fragment do not sufficiently agree with Christian truth. His exceedingly false doctrine concerning these topics is discussed more fully in the commentary printed above, Part II, § 57 and following.]

For if the cause—I mean original sin—has been completely eradicated, why does its effect, or rather its punishment, still remain? Those who are born from that carnal concupiscence are cleansed from this punishment by the grace of baptism, beginning through the Spirit to be reborn in Christ, so that not only those who are begotten in the flesh through the concupiscence of the flesh require the remission of their parents’ sin, by which they are conceived, but also the remission of the common crime—namely, original sin—by which all human beings had universally sinned in the first man.

To this, therefore, it must be answered that the abolition and complete destruction of original sin has not yet occurred in reality, either universally in all or individually in each human being. This is reserved for the final victory at the end of the world, when, as the Apostle says, “the last enemy, death, will be destroyed.”

When death is universally destroyed—death, which is called “the last enemy” in the masculine gender, because in Greek θάνατος, that is, “death,” is masculine—its cause, original sin, must necessarily be utterly removed from human nature. The abolition of the cause will precede the abolition of the effect; that is, the destruction of original sin in all and in each will precede the destruction of death, likewise in the whole and in the part. Then what was spoken through the prophet will also be fulfilled: “I shall be your death, O death, and your bite, O hell.”

Human nature, therefore, has been liberated in hope; in the future it will be liberated in reality.

What, then, is given through the grace of divine generation—that is, through baptism—if original sin is not utterly uprooted?

To this it must be answered: through baptism only the guilt of original sin is released, while original sin itself still remains. For it is one thing to remove an arrow from a wound and another to heal the wound afterward.

This, then, is the whole of what the grace of baptism confers upon us. It frees us from the guilt of sin and raises us into the grace of divine sonship, so that, once the guilt has been dismissed, the wounds of our sins may begin to be healed. For as long as the guilt remains in the wound like a certain iron, no wound can be healed; once it has been removed, room is given to spiritual medicine.

[lacuna]

## Fragment II, Chapter III, 1–IV, 28

There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.

“Pharisee” is interpreted as “divided”; “Pharisees,” as “the divided.”

[Note: Saint Jerome: “Pherezites, separating, or scattered, or fruitful.” The name is derived from a root meaning “to separate,” that is, “to divide.”]

Their sect was divided from the other Jews, that is, from the scribes and Sadducees. For the Pharisees alone believed in the resurrection of the dead, while the others disputed it.

Nicodemus is interpreted as “victory of the people,” or “the victorious people,” bearing the figure of all those from the Jewish people who believed in Christ. Everyone who believes in Christ conquers the world.

“A ruler of the Jews”—that is, one of the rulers of the Jews—learned in the legal letter, a teacher of Israel.

He came to Jesus at night. According to Augustine, Nicodemus is presented as a figure of the catechumens. Catechumens—that is, those instructed in the faith but not yet baptized and not yet imbued with the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord—come to Christ possessing faith alone. Still ignorant of the power of baptism, which they have not yet received, they approach as if in a certain night of ignorance concerning the sacraments.

According to Gregory the Theologian, however, Nicodemus is understood as a kind of nocturnal disciple, representing those who believe in Christ most perfectly, so that nothing concerning the integrity of the Catholic faith is hidden from them, but who lack the light of perfected works. Fearing the assault and envy of the unbelieving Jews, as it were, because of their carnal thoughts and actions, they enjoy converse with Christ through faith alone, without confidence in good works.

Therefore the evangelist says: “He came to him at night.”

And he said to him: “Rabbi, we know that you have come as a teacher from God; for no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.”

From these words, with which Nicodemus appears to address Christ, it may be understood that Nicodemus himself was one of those who had believed shortly before, on the day of Passover, concerning whom it was said: “When he was in Jerusalem at Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name, seeing the signs that he performed.” For this is what his statement refers to: “No one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.”

Jesus answered and said to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone has been born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

It is asked why Jesus answered Nicodemus concerning the second birth, which is according to the spirit, when Nicodemus appears to have asked nothing about it. The answer is that the Lord saw that he had believed, as had the others who saw his signs, and had supposed that faith alone would be sufficient for them, without the power and sacraments of spiritual generation. He therefore immediately began to teach him about the birth that is according to the spirit.

It was as if he had said openly to him: “It is not enough for you merely to have believed in me unless you receive the sacraments of baptism and understand the power of spiritual generation.”

It should be noted that the Greek manuscripts read ἄνωθεν where the Latin manuscripts have denuo, “again,” so that the meaning is: unless someone has been born ἄνωθεν—that is, “from above”—with “from above” understood in place of “again.” This is easier to understand and more suitable to the two births, namely, the earthly and the heavenly.

For the Apostle says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly.”

There are indeed two births, as Augustine says: one from earth and the other from heaven, that is, from above; one from parents according to the flesh, the other from Christ and the Church according to the spirit; one in the likeness of beasts, through sin, into death, the other in the likeness of heavenly virtues, through grace, into life; one contrary to nature through transgression, the other according to nature through the remedy of sins.

Gregory the Theologian, however, asserts four births, which our Lord Jesus Christ also deigned to undergo for the salvation of human nature.

The first is that birth in which the whole human race was born together from nothing, concerning which it is written: “And God made man in his image and likeness.”

The second followed the transgression of man and arose from both sexes, in the likeness of the other animals. Concerning it the same Scripture says: “He made them male and female.” Through this birth the whole human race is multiplied without limit by earthly succession.

The third is according to the spirit, concerning which the Lord now says: “Unless someone has been born again.” In this birth human nature begins to return to its former seat, from which it fell.

The fourth will occur in the resurrection of all, when our entire nature, slain by death, will be born together into eternal life.

The first, therefore, is natural; the second exists because of sin; the third through the grace of the Redeemer; and the fourth according to nature and grace together. For the power of resurrection exists naturally in human nature, since eternal death is altogether contrary to it. What nature contributes to resurrection and what grace contributes is a matter for another discussion.

“He cannot see the kingdom of God.” The kingdom of God has several meanings.

The kingdom of God is the Church of the faithful, concerning which it is written: “The kingdom of God is within you.”

The kingdom of God is the whole of bodily and spiritual creation.

The kingdom of God is the heavenly virtues and the souls of the righteous.

The kingdom of God is the Son of God, who “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly.”

The kingdom of God is the vision of truth.

What he therefore says—“he cannot see the kingdom of God”—may properly be understood as: “He cannot know me, who am the kingdom of the Father.” For I am not merely the king of all things, but also that kingdom and all things. Thus the vision of truth is rightly both called and understood as the kingdom of God.

Nicodemus says to him: “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”

[Note: Corrected; the manuscript reads “be born.”]

He understood carnally, since he had as yet been born only according to the flesh, and therefore answered carnally, because he had not been born from the sacrament of baptism and the Spirit.

Nevertheless, he spoke truly, because no one can be born twice according to the flesh, just as no one can be born twice according to the spirit. For just as a human being is born once in the flesh from flesh, so a human being is born once from the spirit in the spirit. For once received, no one can repeat the sacrament of baptism.

Jesus answered: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone has been born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Here it is understood that seeing the kingdom of God is not one thing and entering the kingdom of God another, but the same thing. For whoever sees the kingdom of God enters it, and whoever enters it sees it. To see is to enter, and to enter is to see—that is, to know the truth. “Unless someone has been born of water and the Spirit,” that is, from the visible sacrament and invisible understanding. It is as though he had said plainly: Unless someone has visibly received the baptismal symbol [Col. 0316C] and has received the Spirit—that is, the understanding of that symbol—he cannot enter the kingdom of God.

It can also be understood in this way: “from water,” that is, from the visible sacrament, and from the Holy Spirit. The question is why the Lord ordained that the visible sacrament of baptism be performed in water, when it might seem that spiritual teaching alone, through faith, would suffice for the birth of a person from the Spirit. But this too must be said: since a human being is constituted from a visible body and an invisible soul, a visible sacrament was necessary for the purification of the visible body, just as invisible teaching concerning faith is necessary for the sanctification of the invisible soul. Although the visible sacrament of baptism seems to confer nothing yet upon the body in this life, nevertheless in the future resurrection [Col. 0316D] it will make what is mortal immortal, what is corruptible incorruptible, and so forth—all that will pertain to the glory of the future resurrection. Yet even in the present life the power of the sacrament sanctifies the bodies of believers, since they become the temple of God, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit?”

But if anyone desires to know fully the power of baptism, let him read Saint Dionysius the Areopagite in his book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*.

It follows: “What has been born from the flesh is flesh, and what has been born from the Spirit is spirit.” He repeats the two births [Col. 0317A], namely, from the flesh and from the Spirit. What has been born from the flesh—that is, from the first human being through the succession of the flesh—is flesh, that is, carnal. It should be noted that in this passage the word “flesh” signifies not flesh alone but the whole carnal person. Indeed, the soul is often called “flesh” in the sense of “carnal”; hence the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh.”

It should also be understood that, just as the whole carnal person, soul and body, is called flesh, so the whole spiritual person, soul and body, is spirit, because human beings who are born in Christ through the Holy Spirit become one with that Spirit in body and soul. [Col. 0317B] Here it is made clear that the sacrament of baptism prefigures the future transformation of flesh into spirit.

“Do not be amazed that I said to you: You must be born again.” It is as though he had said: Let it not seem amazing or unbelievable to you that a human being should be born again from the Spirit.

“The Spirit breathes where it wills.” Wherever the Holy Spirit wills to accomplish the power of his sanctification, there he breathes; there he completes sanctification. From this it is understood that faith, by which we believe in Christ, and the sacrament through which we are reborn, are gifts of the Holy Spirit, who breathes where he wills—that is, works in those in whom he wills to work, distributing to each his own gifts as he wills.

“And you hear his voice.” Concerning the voice of the Holy Spirit, it is enough to set down the words of Saint Augustine. For he says:

> “No one sees the spirit; how do we hear the voice of the spirit? The psalm sounds: it is the voice of the spirit. The Gospel sounds [Col. 0317C]: it is the voice of the spirit. The divine sermon sounds: it is the voice of the spirit. You hear his voice, and you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. If you too are born from the spirit, you will be like him. Whoever has not yet been born from the spirit does not know, concerning you, where you come from or where you are going. For this is what he says next: ‘So is everyone who has been born from the spirit.’”

Thus far the words of Augustine.

The voice of the Spirit, therefore, is the voice of Christ, which Nicodemus heard. But because he had not yet been born from the Spirit and did not understand where the Spirit comes from or where it goes, although he had heard his voice, it is said to him: “But you do not know where it comes from or where it goes,” because you have not yet been born from the Spirit.
