Therefore, although you hear my voice while I speak about my Spirit, you do not know where that Spirit comes from—that is, on what occasion he wills [Col. 0317D] a human being to be born from himself in the Spirit—or to what perfection he leads the human being who is born from him. For whoever is born from him becomes one with him. Just as that Spirit is holy by nature, so he makes the spirit born from him holy by grace.

“So is everyone who has been born from the spirit.” It is not as with you, Nicodemus, who have not yet been born from the Spirit and do not know where the Spirit comes from or where it goes, although you hear his voice. Everyone who is born from the Spirit and hears his voice—that is, understands it—also understands why he breathes in those in whom he wills to breathe and to what end he leads them.

Nevertheless, it seems to me that [Col. 0318A] what the Lord says, “So is everyone who has been born from the spirit,” is more easily understood if it is spoken interrogatively, so that the sense is: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes, because you have not yet been born from the Spirit. Is everyone like this?” It is as though he had said: Do you suppose that everyone born from the Spirit is such that he hears the voice of the Spirit but does not know where it comes from or where it goes? Do not think so. For if you are born from the Spirit, you will not only hear his voice but also know where he comes from and where he goes.

He comes from the Father through the Son, as it is written elsewhere: “Whom the Father will send in my name, so that those who believe in Christ may be born from him.” He returns to the Father through that same Son, leading those who are born from him into divine sonship.

Nicodemus answered and said to him: “How can these things happen?” He is still hesitating, having read the letter of the Law but being wholly ignorant of its spirit. The Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” For the Law, when read but not understood, kills; when read and understood, it gives life.

Accordingly, what the Lord preached about birth from the Spirit seemed impossible to Nicodemus. The Jewish pride that [Col. 0318B], through ignorance of the Spirit of divine teaching, denies that anything higher lies beyond the letter of the Law—in which divine mysteries are fragrant—is refuted. Thus Nicodemus is reproved by the Lord. The evangelist says:

Jesus answered and said to him: “You are the teacher of Israel, and you do not know these things?” Here it should be noted that the Lord did not say, “You are the teacher of Israel,” as an insult, but in order to crush the pride that knew nothing beyond the letter and carnal birth.

[Col. 0318C] “Amen, amen, I say to you, we speak what we know, and we testify to what we have seen, and you do not accept our testimony.” It is as though he had said plainly: Do you suppose, proud Jew, ignorant of the power of the divine utterances, that we speak what we do not know or testify to what we have not seen? It is not so. We speak what we know. Wisdom knows what it speaks and has seen what it testifies to; for it is itself Wisdom, which neither deceives nor is deceived. It is itself the vision that saw all things before they came to be. And this vision is the substance of the things that were seen; its testimony is true, because it is itself the truth. Everything that proceeds from the truth must be true.

Moreover, the Lord himself is the Father’s utterance, the Father’s discourse, and his Word. Concerning that discourse the Prophet says: “His word runs swiftly,” and he himself says of himself: “The word that I have spoken to you is not mine, but belongs to the Father who sent me.”

Consider, therefore, the force of the words, “we speak what we know,” since he is knowledge and utterance; and “we testify to what we have seen,” since he is vision and true testimony. By saying “our” in the plural, he suggests the mystery of the Holy Trinity.

[Col. 0318D] “And you do not accept our testimony,” because you do not believe in us, nor are you able to understand what we teach; for you have not yet been born from the Spirit.

“If I told you earthly things”—or, as it is read in Greek, “If I was telling you earthly things”—“and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?”

Nicodemus had asked, “How can these things happen?”, supposing birth from the Spirit to be impossible. But he hears from the Lord: “If I was telling you earthly things.” [Col. 0319A] The question arises why, when he seems to have said nothing earthly in the preceding discourse—for he spoke entirely of spiritual matters, teaching spiritual birth from the Spirit—he nevertheless said: “If I was telling you earthly things.”

The answer is that this reply does not refer to the preceding words but to what he had said earlier, on the day of Passover, when the Jews were asking for a sign: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He therefore says: If, a little earlier, I was speaking to you about the destruction of my earthly body, and you did not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things—that is, spiritual birth from the Holy Spirit, which is heavenly and divine?

If, then, you did not believe in the destruction of my earthly body in the Passion and its resurrection on the third day, why do you ask me to disclose to you the mysteries of spiritual birth, which, since you have not been reborn from the Spirit, you are altogether unable to believe? Nevertheless, I will tell you heavenly things, although you may not be able to understand them.

“And no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.” The word “ascended” is ambiguous as to its tense, whether it is past or present. In Greek, however, it is not ambiguous: it is in the past tense.

In this sentence the question is what the descent of the Son of Man is, and what his ascent is; what the heaven is into which he ascended, from which he descended, and in which he always remains while ascending and descending. But so that we do not delay by recounting the opinions of many on this subject, it is enough to state what seems more probable.

In divine Scripture [Col. 0319C] the heavenly Father, who is the beginning of all things, is frequently designated by the name “heaven.” The Gospel often says that the Lord rose into heaven, that is, into the Father. We must not believe that he raised his eyes to this bodily, bounded, mortal, starry heaven. He was therefore raising his eyes to the Father, so that those who looked upon him might believe without doubt that he had always been in the Father, toward whom he was directing his gaze.

Thus what he says, “No one has ascended into heaven [Col. 0319B] except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven,” is beautifully expressed in other words: No one has ascended to the Father except the one who descended from the Father, the Son of Man, who is in the Father.

He himself explained elsewhere what his descent and ascent are, saying: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; and again I am leaving the world and going to the Father.” His coming forth from the Father is therefore his becoming human; his return to the Father is the deification [Col. 0319D] of the human being he assumed and his elevation into the height of divinity.

He alone descended, because he alone was incarnate. But if he alone ascended, what hope is there for those for whom he descended? It is great and inexplicable, because all whom he saved ascend in him—now through faith in hope, but at the end through sight in reality—as John says in his Epistle: “We know that we are children of God; it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is.”

He alone therefore descended and he alone ascended, because he, together with all his members, is one God, the only Son of God. For in him all believers in him are one. Thus the one Christ, body together with its members, ascends to the Father.

[Col. 0320A] “And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

The truth itself explains its figure; it declares its shadow to be its own body. Sacred history relates that God’s people were afflicted by serpents in the wilderness and that their frequent bites caused great slaughter. But at the Lord’s command Moses made a bronze serpent, which he hung upon a tall tree, and ordered the people that whoever had been bitten by the dragons should look at the bronze serpent, and should be healed and freed from the serpentine wound.

All this is a shadow of what was to come—that is, a figure of Christ dying for the salvation of all those whom the serpents of their sins destroy with their poisonous bites. Moses himself is therefore Christ; the bronze serpent [Col. 0320B] is the death of Christ; the wood on which the serpent was hung is the cross of Christ, on which he underwent death for the salvation of all who believe in him.

The death of Christ is also fittingly figured by the serpent through the form by which the cause is put for the effect. For the serpent was the cause of Christ’s death. Thus the serpent figuratively displayed its effect, namely death, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.

There is a great difference between the letter and the Spirit, between figure and truth, between shadow and body. The letter is the event that sacred history narrates; the Spirit is the death of Christ that the Gospel proclaims. The serpent is figured as hung upon the wood; to those who looked upon it, it granted temporal life. The death of Christ grants eternal life to those who believe in him.

[Col. 0320C] But what does this have to do with the second birth from the Spirit? The question is not without reason, and it is easily answered. No one ascends in Christ to the Father except one who is born from the Spirit, so that he may be conformed to the image of the Son of God—that is, so that Christ may be formed in him and he may be one with Christ. Similarly, no one is saved through the death of Christ except one who is born from the Spirit; and no one is born from the Spirit through baptism except into the death of Christ, as the Apostle says: “We have been buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead to the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life.”

“For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.” He discloses the cause of human salvation, namely, the heavenly Father, from whom all salvation and restoration of human nature come through his only-begotten Son in his Spirit.

The Father’s love is therefore the cause [Col. 0320D] of human salvation: he loved the world so greatly that he gave his only-begotten Son—that is, handed him over to death—so that everyone who looks upon his death may not perish but have eternal life.

But the question is: Which world did God love? We must not believe that the Father loved this world, that is, the universe consisting of heaven and earth. For this world was made not for its own sake but for the sake of the higher world.

The Father therefore loved the higher world that he created in his own image and likeness, namely, human nature, so that he handed over his Son for it.

[Col. 0321A] It should be noted, however, that the world loved by the Father—that is, the human being—is not called “world” because it consists of the four elements, which is considered to be true only according to the body in the earthly human being still present; rather, the human being is called *kosmos* (κόσμος), because he is adorned according to the image and likeness of God, which is understood either exclusively or principally in the soul.

For in Greek, *kosmos* (κόσμος) properly means “adornment” or “ornament,” not “world.” And what creature is so adorned as the one created in the image of the Creator?

God therefore loved the world for this purpose, and gave the Son for it, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have life—not temporal life, but eternal life.

“God did not send his Son into the world”—that is, into human nature—“to judge”—that is, to condemn—“the world,” namely, the human being, on account of its sin, “but so that the world,” that is, human nature, “might be saved through him.”

[Col. 0321B] “Whoever believes is not judged, but whoever does not believe has already been judged.” Whoever believes in the Son of God is not judged, because all the sins for which he would be judged are forgiven him. Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe; consequently, he retains the sins for which he is judged, since he neither believes nor wishes his sins to be forgiven.

Here it should be noted that each person judges or does not judge himself. He does not judge himself who considers that his transgressions have been forgiven him and does not remain in the state for which he would be judged. But whoever does not believe judges himself, because he retains within himself what deserves judgment.

“He has already been judged.” He says “already,” still in the present tense. For although the judgment by which he judges himself worthy of condemnation is still hidden in this life, it will be revealed in the future.

[Col. 0321C] Why has he already been judged? Because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. Judgment—that is, eternal condemnation—is therefore nothing other than not believing in the Son of God, just as blessedness and life are nothing other than believing in and knowing the Son of God, as he himself says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true and only God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.”

It follows:

“This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world.” If the light had not come into the world, there would be no judgment concerning the world, as the Lord says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.”

The light, therefore—that is, the incarnation, teaching, Passion, and resurrection of the Word of God—judges the world. Whoever wishes to approach the light, that is, the Son of God, in order to believe in him and know him, is not judged. But whoever neither believes in him nor understands him will remain in his darkness, in which he will be condemned—that is, judged—because he does not wish to approach the light.

[Col. 0321D] “And human beings loved the darkness more than the light.” He appropriately says “human beings,” that is, carnal, impious, unbelieving people, not spiritual people. For spiritual people rise beyond humanity and transcend their nature through the grace of the one who enlightens them.

But why did human beings love darkness more than light? [Col. 0322A] He adds the reason in due order, saying: “For their works were evil.”

What are those evil works? Nothing other than impiety, unbelief, and hatred of the eternal light: the refusal to look upon it and the desire to remain in the darkness of sins.

“For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be exposed.” Thus the impious flee the light of truth, lest their impiety be made manifest, since all evil works are contained in it. For just as piety lacks no good work, so impiety lacks no evil work.

“But whoever practices the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God.” Who is the one who practices the truth—that is, who performs the good works commanded by the truth—except the one who believes in Christ? And who comes to the light, that is, to Christ and his teaching, so that his good works may be revealed because they have been done in God, except the one who believes in Christ and keeps his commandments?

[Col. 0322B] After this Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea, and so forth. It should not be supposed that immediately after the discussion with Nicodemus, which took place in Jerusalem, Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea. Rather, after some interval of time, they returned from Galilee to Judea.

In the moral sense, the land of Judea is the heart of believers. For Judea is interpreted to mean “confession” [Note: [Col. 0321D] On this interpretation of the word *Judea*, see above, col. 303.]. Confession, however, is twofold: there is confession of sins, and there is confession of divine praises.

Therefore, into whatever heart that twofold confession has entered—confession of sins and confession of divine praises—Jesus and his disciples come, that is, his teaching and illumination. There he remains and cleanses [Col. 0322C] that heart from all offenses. This is what follows:

“And there he stayed with them and baptized.” According to the literal sense, Jesus stayed with his disciples or with the Jews who believed in Judea. For it is ambiguous when he says “he stayed with them,” whether he means with his disciples, with the Jews who believed in him, or—as is more probable—with both.

“And he baptized.” Here the question arises: If Christ himself baptized, how does the evangelist say later: “Although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did”?

The answer is that Christ himself first baptized his disciples; afterward the disciples baptized those who believed in Christ. Although some think that he baptized no one personally, but is said to have baptized because he commanded his disciples to baptize.

It follows:

[Col. 0322D] “Now John was baptizing at Aenon (Αἰνών) [Note: [Col. 0321] The codex has *Aennon.], near Salim, because there was much water there.”

John was still baptizing in the Jordan while Christ had begun to baptize in Judea, both his disciples and, through them, others. [Col. 0322D] The Forerunner ought not to interrupt the mystery of his own forerunning before the one whose forerunner he was had begun to reveal the truth. The shadow still remained, because the light had not yet been wholly disclosed.

“At Aenon,” that is, “in the waters” [Note: [Col. 0321D] J. Scotus correctly interprets it as “in the waters.” For it is derived from *a fountain, a well*. Saint Jerome: “Aenon, the eye, or their fountain.”]; for *enon* [Note: [Col. 0321] Thus the codex has *enos* instead of *Aennon.] means “water” in Hebrew. Therefore he immediately adds, as though [Col. 0323A] explaining the meaning of the name [Note: [Col. 0323] This note appears at the foot of column 323, but the callout number (1) has not been printed in the text. Codex: “not.”]: “because there was much water there.”

Concerning Salim, however, they give various accounts. Some wish it to be understood as Jerusalem, which is not far distant from the Jordan. For, they say, it was first simply called Salim, then Jebus-Salem because it was possessed by the Jebusites, and afterward Jerusalem—that is, “temple of peace”—because of the celebrated and most glorious fame, spread to the ends of the world, of the most noble temple built by Solomon [Note: [Col. 0323D] Saint Jerome: “Jerusalem, vision of peace; it will fear perfectly.” The derivation of the word from *and*, that is, “house of peace,” is preferable to the other derivation from *and*, that is, “possession of peace.”].

Others, whose opinion, as I judge, deserves greater credence, say that Salem was a town situated beyond the Jordan, at the place where the Jordan enters the Asphalt Lake—that is, the bitumen lake—and that Melchizedek once reigned in that town, traces of which still remain. John baptized near it because there was much water there.

[Col. 0323B] “For John had not yet been sent into prison.” For after he was sent into prison, he immediately ceased baptizing, when Christ’s baptism began.

The question is what John’s baptism profited those who were baptized by him. In no way should we believe that it granted them remission not only of original sin but also of their personal sins [Note: [Col. 0323] The codex reads: “did not confer.”].

What, then, did it confer? Something great indeed. For just as instruction in the faith benefits catechumens who have not yet been baptized [Note: [Col. 0323] Codex: “baptism.”], so John’s baptism benefited those baptized in it before they underwent Christ’s baptism. For John preached repentance, foretold Christ’s baptism, and drew people toward knowledge of the truth that appeared to the world.

Do not the ministers of the Church do something similar every day? First they instruct those who come to the faith; then they rebuke their sins; then they promise remission of all sins in baptism; and thus they draw them toward knowledge and love of the truth.

To this is added [Col. 0323C], as an increase of the praise and usefulness that John’s baptism accomplished, that the Forerunner ought in all things to fulfill the effect of his forerunning. Just as he preceded Christ in birth and preaching, so also he preceded him in a likeness of baptism.

For just as dawn precedes the rising of the sun, so John’s sacraments preceded Christ’s works. And just as dawn in a certain way drives away the shadows, so the teaching and mystery of the Forerunner began to drive away the darkness of ignorance from the whole world.

Therefore, lest Christ’s true baptism suddenly appear to the world, a figurative baptism went before it, so that the truth might shine forth more deeply and clearly if the figure first smiled upon those sitting in darkness.

[Col. 0323D] The question is also asked why Christ was baptized by his servant. The answer is that Christ graciously consented to be baptized by his servant in order both to honor the office of his Forerunner and to make known to all the Jews and to the whole world that it was genuine.

But if this alone was the reason why the Lord was baptized by his servant, why was Christ not baptized by John alone? The humility of the Lord would have sufficed for the praise and testimony of the servant’s baptism.

The answer is that, if Christ alone [Col. 0324A] had been baptized by John, John’s baptism might seem to confer more upon those baptized than Christ’s baptism did. For a single baptism by which the Lord was baptized could more readily be regarded as superior to the baptism by which many were baptized by the Lord himself and by his disciples. To prevent this belief, many were baptized by John.

If it is asked whether Christ himself benefited in any way from being baptized by his Forerunner, some answer, not absurdly, that Christ effected a certain sanctification of John. That baptism, however, conferred nothing upon Christ.

Nevertheless, we know that Greek authors confidently assert that the sanctification of Christ’s humanity was increased through the sacrament of John’s baptism. They argue this especially from the descent of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove upon him when he had been baptized.

Nor is this surprising [Col. 0324B], since the evangelist says: “Jesus was advancing in wisdom and age and grace with God and human beings.” Why should it be surprising if Christ received a certain increase of his humanity through the sacrament of the baptism of his Forerunner—for example, through the merit of his humility, by which he did not disdain to undergo the baptism of his servant?

He received grace so that, through the power of his baptism, all who believe in him might receive remission of all sins, both original and personal.

Augustine also adds another reason why the Lord was baptized by his servant: lest catechumens, living chastely and piously after receiving the faith, should become proud, thinking that the mystery of baptism could add nothing to them since they were living according to the faith in which they had been instructed.

But lest they err in this [Col. 0324C] and labor in vain, the Lord wished to give them an example through his own baptism, so that none of them would dare to become puffed up when they saw that their Lord had undergone the baptism of his servant. For if the Lord did not disdain the baptism of his servant, by what reasoning would they refuse to undergo the baptism of their Lord?

[Col. 0324D] Thus a dispute arose between John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification. John’s disciples, seeing that many of the Jews had believed in Christ and had been baptized by his disciples, were moved by envy and questioned those Jews about purification—that is, about baptism.

They were astonished that others could baptize apart from John and his disciples, supposing John to be greater than Christ because they had seen Christ himself baptized by John in the Jordan not long before.

And they came to John, wishing to accuse Christ and his disciples, as though they were presuming to baptize in insult to him, and said to him:

[Col. 0325A] “Rabbi, the one who was with you beyond the Jordan, who at the time when he was baptized beyond the Jordan seemed to be your disciple, to whom you bore witness by saying, ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sin of the world’—look, he is baptizing now in Judea. We are greatly astonished, and everyone is coming to him. We therefore wish to ask you what you think of this presumption.”

John answered and said: “A human being cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0325] The codex reads: “receive anything.”].

In some Greek codices it reads: “unless it has been given to him from above, from heaven.”

The servant answered humbly those who were accusing his Lord. “A human being,” he said, “cannot receive anything.” It is as though he had said: Do you suppose me to be greater than the one whose servant and Forerunner I am? You are mistaken because you do not believe in him, and because you do not know what he is or where he came from; you suppose me to be what I am not.

But so that you may know who he is and what I am, hear my answer: “A human being cannot receive anything.” I am a human being, not God; but he is both God and human being. He is the one concerning whom I bore witness, saying: “From his fullness we have all received.”

I am therefore a human being [Col. 0325B]; I have received nothing from myself, since I do not possess anything that I could receive from myself. Whatever I have received, I have received from him. If I have received the grace of being a Forerunner, I received it from him.

You suppose that I am beyond human nature. Because you have heard that I was born through a miracle of divine power—not only from parents of advanced age, but, as it were, beyond the ordinary course of human nature—you therefore suppose that I am more than human. It is not so. I am merely human.

If you knew what I am, you would not exalt me beyond what I am; and if you knew who he is, you would in no way compare me with him. I am human; he is God. Whatever I have received, I received from him.

The most wise Forerunner of Christ distinguishes [Col. 0325C] in himself nature and grace. He attributes to himself what belongs to being human—that is, mortal, sinful, and earthly, made from the first earthly human being—and all the other things that he observed in himself and in other human beings as belonging to the weakness of human nature, to sin, and to the punishment of sin. He separates from himself the grace that he had received, not from merits but from the abundance of the fullness of the one whose Forerunner he was.

Two things are considered in a human being: the thing given and the gift. The thing given refers to nature; the gift refers to grace. Although neither of these exists except from God, as the Apostle says, “O human being, what do you have that you did not receive?”, Scripture nevertheless customarily attributes the thing given by nature to the human being himself, while attributing the gift to no one but God.

For God gave nature [Col. 0325D] for this purpose: that he might adorn it through grace. This is what John says: “A human being,” that is, human nature, “cannot receive anything of grace unless it has been given to him from heaven.”

Here John uses “the thing given” for “the gift,” a usage very frequently found in divine Scripture. “The thing given” can be understood as “the gift,” and “the gift” as “the thing given.” For the things given by nature and the gifts of grace are so joined that they seem to become inseparable. No rational nature exists that is entirely without the gift of grace.

“Unless it has been given from heaven.” From which heaven? From the Father, namely. Hear the Apostle James saying: “Every good thing given and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.”

These words agree entirely with what John says [Col. 0326A]: “A human being cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven,” that is, from the Father, who is the beginning of all good things; and if from the Father, then certainly first through the Son, from whose fullness we have all received.

“You yourselves bear witness to me.” Only this in your words agrees with me: you not only do not believe in the one who sent me, but you also regard his baptism as invalid, and yet you bear witness to me.

What I said was: “I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.” You heard these words from me when I was speaking about him beyond the Jordan. You certainly heard them when you said: “The one who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness.” If you heard them, why do you accuse me [Col. 0326B] of the one concerning whom I bore such witness, as though he had baptized many in insult to me?

I said: “I am not the Christ, but a simple human being.” I am not the one anointed by the Father with the fullness of the Spirit; he is the anointed one, and from his fullness I have received.

“But I have been sent before him”: I was sent into the world first, being born before him. He was God with God the Father before all ages; I am a human being sent in the flesh at the end of the age, before he was born in the flesh.

“Whoever has the bride is the bridegroom.” The Forerunner, seeing the thoughts of his disciples, who were making such statements about Christ and his baptism, and hearing their teacher’s reply concerning himself and his own baptism—when he said, “A human being cannot receive anything”—humbling himself and truthfully declaring concerning himself that he was an earthly human being, while they wanted to ask: “If you are merely a human being, and do not possess greater power and grace from yourself than what you received from him who is now baptizing in Judaea, and you say that you were sent before him, tell us, please: What are you beyond a human being, or how great [Note: [Col. 0325] Corrected; the manuscript reads *quanties*.] are you, and what grace did you receive from heaven?”—replied: “Whoever has the bride is the bridegroom.”

He who came on account of the Church came in order to have a bride, whom he is now beginning to call from the Jewish people, baptizing many Jews. He himself is the bridegroom. But I, as you suppose, am neither the bridegroom nor do I have a bride; rather, I count myself among the number of the bride. But so that you may know what I am, and what sort of grace I have from that bridegroom who has the bride, listen: “But the friend of the bridegroom.” I am not the bridegroom, but I have the bridegroom’s great grace: I am his friend. “He who stands and hears him rejoices with joy.”

I am the bridegroom’s friend, and I stand in his grace; I remain in his friendship; I do not fall. He protects me so that I may not fall; he grants me that I may not abandon his grace, but may always stand and hear him—hear his teaching, not merely outwardly with the ear of the body, but also inwardly with the ear of the heart, and inwardly more than outwardly. His voice is his testimony, by which he declares himself to be the Son of God and the bridegroom of the Church; and because I hear his word, I rejoice on account of the bridegroom’s voice.

Therefore John declares concerning himself what he says: “But the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy, [Col. 0327A] rejoicing on account of the bridegroom’s voice,” so that his disciples might openly understand what he himself was, and what Christ was—Christ in whom they still did not believe and whose baptism they had not received.

“This joy of mine, therefore, has been fulfilled.” It is as though he said: “My joy has been fulfilled in this: that I have become the bridegroom’s friend, that I stand in his grace, and that I hear the bridegroom’s voice, as he now calls the bride from the Jews in Judaea, and begins through himself both to preach and to baptize”—something you do not now perceive, because you do not believe in him.

And so that you may not wonder that he baptizes, that everyone comes to him in order to believe and be baptized, and that he has more disciples than I do:

“He must increase, but I must decrease.” He must increase in your minds—you who still regard him merely as a human being and as possessing no power—but he must increase so that you may recognize him not only as a true human being, but also as true God, equal to his Father. He must therefore increase in your thoughts, but I must decrease.

You think that I [Note: [Col. 0327] *me* is omitted in the manuscript; added by conjectural emendation.] am greater than I am, while he is less than he is. Your opinion of me within you will diminish; your opinion of him within you will increase. If you recognized this, you could have been strengthened by visible signs. I shall be beheaded; he will be exalted upon the cross, so that through this you may recognize that he must increase above all things in the minds of those who perfectly believe in him, while I must decrease, so that no one may think of me as anything beyond what I am and what I received from him.

The same thing is signified by the fact that he was born to increase as the light began, while the darkness diminished; whereas I was born to diminish as the light began, while the darkness began to increase.

It can also be understood in another way. John bears the figure of the Law, while Christ bears his own figure, that is, the figure of truth. When truth therefore appeared in the world, the Law began to decrease—that is, carnal works. Recognizing this, the Forerunner and prophet, and more than a prophet, said: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Because he is the truth, he will increase in the world—that is, he will be most clearly known by those who believe and will believe in him. But the Law, whose figure I bear, will decrease as truth increases.

“He who comes from above is above all.” Again the servant returns to a comparison between himself and his Lord. He who comes from above—that is, he who comes from the Father into the world to save the world—is above all. He surpasses not only me, his servant and Forerunner, but also all human beings; and not only human beings, but also all the heavenly powers, and everything that is and that is not.

This is not according to his divinity, but according to his humanity. For he is a human being and more than a human being. His divinity surpasses nothing, because it is all things.

“He who is of the earth is earthly and speaks of the earth.” He says this concerning himself, as though he were saying: “I, who am of the earth—that is, born of earthly parents, born from him to whom it was said, ‘You are earth and you will go into earth,’ that is, from that earthly human being from whom all earthly people have drawn sin and the punishment of sin, namely death—I am from him. And therefore I am earth, because I was born from earth, nor do I consider myself to be anything else.

“If I possess anything above this, I receive it from his fullness, before whom I was sent. And I speak of the earth—that is, I speak of the fragility of my nature, recognizing that it is nothing if it did not receive from above.”

And so that you may not wonder that John spoke of himself as though of a third person, this was not without reason, since he displays in himself the person of every earthly human being.

“He who comes from heaven is above all.” The words are the same, except that earlier he said, “He comes from above,” whereas now he says, “He comes from heaven.” What is the point of this repetition, and what does it mean? Perhaps “he comes from above” means one thing, and “he comes from heaven” another.

Christ comes from above; Christ comes from heaven; therefore he is above all and above everything. The following distinction can therefore be understood between “he comes from above” and “he comes from heaven”: by saying “he comes from above,” we may understand the height of human nature before the first human being’s transgression—a height from which we do not doubt that Christ came as a human being.

For if he came from humanity after sin, perhaps he would not be free from sin. But since he was free from sin, he should rightly be believed to have assumed humanity as it existed before sin. For our Lord Jesus Christ, the creator and savior of human nature, received from the first human being what existed before sin and, as it were, from a second human being what existed after sin.

What did he receive from humanity before sin? Freedom from sin, because human nature, before it sinned, was entirely free from sin. What did he receive from humanity after sin? To die for sin, without any guilt of sin.

When he therefore first said, “He who comes from above,” this is rightly understood as referring to him who came from the exalted human nature made in the image of God, before it sinned. For no one came from there except him alone. As many as came into the world came from the sinful human being; he alone, without sin, proceeded from humanity before sin.

But when he subsequently said, “He who comes from heaven is above all,” there we understand the Father to be signified by the name “heaven,” from whom Christ was sent into the world, just as he himself says: “I came out from the Father and came into the world.”

The only-begotten Son of God must therefore be believed to be above all things in two ways: first, because he is exalted above all humanity, since he came from humanity before it sinned; second, because, according to the height of his divinity, in which he is equal to the Father, he surpasses every creature.

“And what he has seen and heard, this he testifies.” What is it that the Son of God has seen? Nothing other than that he knew himself to be in the Father and to possess the Father’s equality.

“And he has heard.” What has he heard? He heard from the Father: “Today I have begotten you.” He therefore saw himself, according to his divinity, in his Father, and heard from his Father that the Father had begotten him equal to himself.

“This he testifies.” What does he testify? That he is the Son of God. And where does he testify this? Return to the preceding passage, where he himself says concerning himself: “For God did not send his Son into the world [Col. 0329A] to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.”

This, therefore, is what the Son of God saw, and concerning himself he bears witness.

“And no one receives his testimony.” If no one receives his testimony, why did he come, and what benefit did he bring to the world?

John the Forerunner, full of the divine grace of prophecy, foresaw those who would believe in Christ and receive his testimony, and those who would not believe in him and reject his testimony. Among those who do not believe and will not believe—prepared by themselves for destruction—no one has received the testimony of the Son of God. But among those who believe and will believe, there is no one who does not receive his testimony [Col. 0329B] and, consequently, no one who is not saved.

Therefore it follows:

“Whoever receives his testimony has certified that God is true.” That is, he has established this firmly in his heart and, as though with an unchangeable seal, enclosed it within perfect faith: that God is true.

This is understood more easily if the Greek wording is read: “Because God is true,” so that the meaning is: Whoever receives the testimony of the Son of God concerning himself—that he is the Son of God and that his Father sent him for the salvation of the world—firmly believes that God is true, since he testified concerning himself that he is true God and the Son of the true God.

“For he whom God sent speaks the words of God.” He says this only concerning the Son of God, who, because he was sent by God the Father, speaks the words of God.

Were not the prophets also sent by him? Were not the apostles also sent by him [Col. 0329C] and did they speak the words of God? What, then, does it mean that this is said of Christ alone: “He whom God sent speaks the words of God”?

For he seems to have said: “He whom God sent speaks the words of the God who sent him”—which the prophets did, and likewise the apostles. What great thing, then, is given to Christ that was not given to others?

Attend to the words: “He whom God sent”—namely, the Father—“speaks the words of God.” Since the one who was sent is also God, he therefore speaks the words of God. The meaning is: “He whom God sent is certainly God; consequently, his words are the words of God.” Therefore the words of the Son, who bears witness concerning himself that he is God, are the words of God.

The words of the prophets and apostles are the words of God because they spoke the words of God. For the Holy Spirit spoke in them. Nevertheless, those words are not attributed to them [Col. 0329D] as their words, but are the words of the true God.

Christ’s words are attributed to himself and are rightly called the words of God, because he is God by nature, wholly God, wholly wisdom, and in him is the fullness of God’s gifts.

Therefore it follows: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure.” It is as though he had said: “God gives his Spirit by measure to individual human beings,” as the Apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge,” and the rest of the distribution of spiritual gifts.

By these words it is shown that the Holy Spirit is given by measure to the members of the Church. The Apostle consequently says: “But one and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each his own gifts as he wills.” But to Christ, who is the head of the Church, God does not give the Spirit by measure. Rather, just as he wholly begot his Son from his whole self, so, when his Son became incarnate, he gave him his whole Spirit—not by participation, not by subdivisions, but generally and universally.

“The Father loves the Son and has given everything into his hand.” He explains why God gives the Spirit by measure to other human beings, but gives the Spirit to his Son not by measure but in its entirety.

Why? For no other reason than that the Father loves the Son. Therefore he gave him his whole Spirit and gave everything into his hand.

What does “everything” mean? Perhaps everything that was made in him? “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”; and the Psalm says, “You made all things in wisdom.” The Father therefore gave into his hand all those things that were made in the Son.

He gave everything into his hand in a higher sense—that is, everything that the Father possesses substantially, he gave to the Son, begetting him from himself equal to himself in all things.

“Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life.” Why? Because the Son himself is eternal life, as he himself says: “I am the truth and the life.” Rightly, therefore, whoever believes in the Son has eternal life.

It is as though he had said: Whoever believes in the Son has the Son himself, and consequently has eternal life, because the Son himself is eternal life.

“But whoever does not believe in the Son will not see eternal life.” In the same manner of expression: Whoever does not believe the Son will not see the Son, who is life.

“But the wrath of God remains upon him.” He does not say, “The wrath of God will come upon him,” but says, “It remains upon him.”

What is that wrath of God? Nothing other than that curse by which God cursed the sin of the first human being, who transgressed his commandment, saying: “Cursed is the earth in your works.” The effect of that wrath is death, corruption, and complete ignorance of the truth—all of which remain upon him.

Concerning that wrath the Apostle says: “You were once children of wrath, as were the others.” The wrath of God can be understood as original sin, since that original sin provoked God’s wrath against human nature. This original sin remains in those who do not wish to believe in him who died for them.

“Therefore, when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John”—although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did—Christ baptized and did not baptize.

He baptized, that is, he purified in the Spirit those whom not he himself, but his disciples, immersed in water in the body.

“He left Judaea and went again into Galilee.” After the Lord, who knows all hearts, learned that the Pharisees had heard that more disciples had come to him than to John, and that he had baptized more than John, he left Judaea.

The Pharisees, moved by envy against Christ and his disciples, saw John’s baptism becoming somewhat less esteemed, since John’s disciples had been drawn chiefly from the Pharisees, just as Christ’s disciples at that time also were. They saw, moreover, Christ’s baptism and the number of his disciples increasing. They also recognized that through Christ’s teaching the Law and the ceremonies of the Old Testament were being nullified—something they had not been able to recognize in John’s teaching.

Disturbed by such zeal, they were considering persecuting Christ, his disciples, and all who believed in him. On this occasion Jesus left Judaea—that is, the unbelieving Pharisees who were planning to persecute him.

He did this not as though timid or powerless. He could have remained unharmed in Judaea despite the persecution of the carnal and ungodly Pharisees. But he did so in order to leave an example for those who would believe in him, giving them by his example the power to flee from those who persecute them and to withdraw from them for a time, so that they might not be captured by them before the time pleasing and appointed by God. Consequently, he would have remained longer in Judaea if he had known that those whom he left would believe.

According to the laws of contemplation, Jesus left Judaea after he had received the beginning of the Church from the Jewish people, in those who believed in him. He left the carnal and faithless Jews, who followed the letter of the Law and were unwilling to approach the spirit of the letter, which is Christ.

The Lord therefore stayed in Judaea in order to save those whom he wished; he left Judaea, abandoning those whom, because of their pride, he rightly neglected to save. He abandoned the letter of the Law, which brings no one to perfection—for the Law brought no one to perfection—and from them he went again [to Galilee] [Note: [Col. 0331D] *Abiit* is omitted in the manuscript; added by conjectural emendation] into Galilee, that is, into the spiritual understanding of the letter itself, which is symbolically represented by Galilee.

Nor is it without significance that he says: “He went again into Galilee.” For he came from Galilee into Judaea, as it is written earlier: “After this Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judaea.”

Galilee bears the figure of heavenly life and divine goodness. From there the Lord, when he was born in the flesh, came into Judaea—that is, into the mysteries of the Law itself, which was first given to the Jews, as the Apostle says: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law.”

But because he did not wish to remain under the Law, nor did he leave those who would believe in him under the Law, lest they should be under the Law but rather under the Spirit, this is what the Apostle says: “That he might redeem those who were under the Law”—that is, recall them from the slavery of the carnal Law into the freedom of the Spirit. This is what it means: “He went into Galilee.”

“It was necessary for him to pass through Samaria.” Samaria is situated between Judaea and Galilee. That is, between the letter of the Law, which is signified by Judaea, and the eternal divine laws revolving around God, whose figure Galilee bears, the natural law is placed in the middle.

Since Christ first took the foundations of his Church from the letter of the Law, it was necessary for him to pass through the nations established under the law of nature, so that from them likewise he might call, by faith, chosen stones into the structure he had begun.

Samaria was possessed by foreigners—that is, by those who had used or abused both the legal letter, which was imposed upon Israel according to the flesh alone, and the natural law—so that, together with the universal Church, collected and built from both Jews and Gentiles, the builder himself might return into Galilee, the eternal blessedness.

That Galilee signifies eternal life can be inferred not only from its interpretation, but also from the divine deeds performed there. Galilee is interpreted as “a transmigration accomplished” or “a revolution” [Note: [Col. 0331D] Saint Jerome: “Galilee, something that revolves, or an accomplished transmigration, or a wheel.” J. Scotus correctly derives the word from *volvere*, “to roll”; the interpretation “transmigration” refers to *Gilgal*, Joshua 5:9.].

A transmigration has taken place in human nature through its Savior: first from the carnal Law into the natural laws, and again from these, beyond nature, into the eternal laws.

In Galilee also, according to the faith of the historical events, Christ was transfigured. Through this is signified the transformation of human nature into the former glory that it abandoned by sinning.

In Galilee he ascended a mountain on which he delivered to his disciples the teaching of the eightfold number, through which believers in Christ will pass into the blessedness of the future age, which is indicated by the number eight.

“But Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the estate that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.” As we said earlier, Samaria is a type of the Gentile people established under the natural law. The city of Samaria called Sychar represents the gathering of the faithful among that people who receive the faith of Christ.

For Sychar is interpreted as “conclusion” or “branch” [Note: [Col. 0331D] Saint Jerome likewise: “Sychar, conclusion or branch.”].

The people of the Gentiles had been enclosed. Scripture enclosed everything under sin. It is the branch cut from the wild olive and grafted into the olive tree whose branches were broken off.

It should be noted that Sychar is corruptly written for Sychem. Sychem is interpreted as “of the numbers” [Note: [Col. 0332D] Saint Jerome: “Corruptly written for Sichem, which is translated as ‘shoulders,’ so that Sychar came to be read; usage established this.” J. Scotus seems to have read *numeri*, “of the numbers,” instead of *humeri*, “of the shoulders”; but the interpretation “of the numbers” is not sufficiently accurate, for *Sichem* is derived from [the source text breaks off after *a*].]. The inquiry remains concerning those chosen from the Gentiles who are numbered.

And because natural reason arises from no other source than the cause of all good things, namely God, it is beautifully called the fountain of Jacob—that is, infinite reason proceeding from the Father’s height.

The fountain of Jacob also not unfittingly signifies this lowest part of the universe: everything visible confined within the boundaries of this sensible world.

To summarize briefly: the fountain of Jacob is a symbol either of sensible nature or of intelligible reason.

“Jesus, therefore, tired from the journey, sat thus upon the fountain.” Jesus’ weariness is his incarnation. For he assumed our nature, wearied by the labors and troubles of this world on account of original sin.

His journey is the descent of his divinity to assume the likeness of our nature. Without labor he created us through his divinity; with labor he created us through his humanity.

Remaining eternally in himself and in his Father, unchangeably, he moved himself, as it were, by a journey of temporal dispensation through the flesh.

“He sat upon the fountain.” Christ’s sitting signifies the possession of his unchanging divinity in our nature.

Our nature, however, is twofold: it consists of a visible body and an invisible soul. The twofold interpretation of the fountain indicates these two. For it was stated above that the rational soul and visible creature were figured by the fountain.

Since Christ’s humanity surpasses not only every visible creature but also every intellectual creature—for he is called a human being and more than a human being—he is appropriately said to have sat upon the fountain, although he was wearied from the journey.

The weakness of his humanity is stronger than every creature by right, because it was assumed into God.

“It was about the sixth hour.” The sixth hour prefigures the sixth age of the world.

The first age is counted from the expulsion of the first human being from paradise to the altar that Noah built after leaving the ark following the flood.

The second extends from that point to the altar on which Abraham was commanded by God to sacrifice Isaac.

The third extends from there to the altar of King David on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

The fourth extends from there to the altar of Zerubbabel in the rebuilt Temple.

The fifth extends from there to John’s baptism—or, as many reasonably think, to the true altar, namely Christ’s cross, which all the aforementioned altars prefigured.

From that point the sixth age extends to the end of the world; it is now in progress.

The seventh age is completed in the other life, in souls released from the body. This age begins with the martyrdom of Abel and will end at the end of the world with the resurrection of all.

After it, the eighth age will begin to appear, bounded by no end.

The perfect brightness of heavenly grace, which shone fully upon the world through Christ made human, may also be understood as typologically signified in the sixth hour. For the number six is a perfect number.

“A woman came from Samaria to draw water.” As we said earlier, Samaria suggests the figure of the Gentiles. The woman who came out from Samaria is the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Having accepted the faith of truth, she desires to draw from its fountain, that is, from Christ.

Again, the woman who came out from the city indicates human nature, which naturally desires the fountain of reason, so that it may satisfy its thirst—that is, its implanted desire for true knowledge. Before the incarnation of the Creator, who is the fountain of life, it was unable to fulfill this desire.

Nevertheless, it laboriously drank from the natural fountain of reason implanted within it, investigating the nature of things by physical movement, and the Creator and cause of that nature.

“Jesus said to her: Give me to drink.” His disciples had gone into the city to buy food.

Jesus, sitting upon the fountain, asks from the primitive Church, which he had chosen from the Gentiles, the drink of faith by which one believes in him. He asks from nature the drink of reason, by which its Creator and Redeemer is investigated.

The disciples who went into the city to buy food are the apostles sent into the world to purchase spiritual foods—that is, faith, action, and knowledge, by which the spiritual teachers of the Church are nourished.

First they ask faith from those to whom they preach; then actions appropriate to that faith; and finally knowledge of the truth, for whose sake both faith and action and knowledge are preached and brought to completion.

“The Samaritan woman therefore said to him: How is it that you, although you are a Jew, ask me for a drink, even though I am a Samaritan woman? For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.”

That Samaritan woman, who bore the type of the Church or of nature, marvels at the Lord, whom she did not yet know, but whom she knew only to have been a Jew. She wonders why he asked her for a drink, since she was a Samaritan woman.

“For,” she says, “Jews do not associate with Samaritans.”

Here, according to the literal sense, the question arises: What does the woman mean when she says, “Jews do not associate with Samaritans,” since the Samaritans lived under the Law of Moses and all its commands and symbols, and lived together with the Jews? Consequently, if they lived under one Law, one would also suppose that they shared food.

In what respect, then, did they not associate?

The answer is that Jews and Samaritans, although dwelling under one Law, worshiped one God, namely the Father, but disputed about the place of worship. The Jews thought that God should be worshiped nowhere except in the Temple that was in Jerusalem. The Samaritans, however, thought that God should be worshiped on the mountain of Samaria, where Jacob had lived.

In this respect, then, they did not associate: they differed concerning the place of worship.

For if the Jewish Law prohibited Jews from associating with Samaritans, perhaps Christ would not have asked the woman for the symbolic drink, nor would he have allowed his disciples to buy food from them. It must certainly be believed that he asked not for a bodily drink of water but for a spiritual drink of faith.

“Jesus answered and said to her: If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me to drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you water.”

It is as though he had said: “If you, woman, knew me and believed perfectly in me, and if you knew the gift of God—that is, the Holy Spirit—you would have asked me for a drink, and on account of your faith I would have given you living water, namely the Holy Spirit.”

“The woman said to him: Lord, you do not have a vessel for drawing, and the well is deep. How then do you have living water?”

The woman, still carnal and not yet believing, did not understand the words of the one speaking with her. For she thought that the Lord had spoken about sensible water, whereas he was treating of intelligible water.

As we said earlier, the deep well signifies either the depth of human nature or the lowliness of sensible and bodily creation, which is called “deep” because nothing in the universe of created things is lower than bodily nature.

The vessel for drawing signifies the study of wisdom by which the water of reason is brought forth from the innermost recesses of nature, while investigation treats of human substance or sensible creation in physical terms.

Saint Augustine argues that the deep well signifies the delight [Note: [Col. 0333D] The manuscript reads *delectationem*.] of bodily things, from which and in which delight itself rises like flowing water; the vessel for drawing signifies the desire of the carnal soul, which always longs to be satisfied by the delight [Note: [Col. 0335] The manuscript reads *delectionem*.] of temporal and bodily things.

It follows:

“Are you perhaps greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well, and drank from it himself, and his sons and his cattle?”

The Samaritan woman was a foreigner, yet she calls Jacob her father. Not without reason, since she had lived under the Law of Moses and possessed the estate that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.

When she says, “Are you perhaps greater than our father Jacob?” she seems to mean: “Are you of greater power than our father Jacob, who dug this well and had a vessel for drawing, by which he supplied water to himself, his sons, and his cattle?

“But you have neither a vessel for drawing nor any instrument for drawing water, and you promise to give me a drink,” while she still did not understand the words of the one speaking with her.

“Jesus answered and said to her: Everyone who drinks from this water, which you wish to draw, woman, and which you suppose I am asking you to give me, will thirst again”—that is, he temporarily extinguishes a temporal thirst.

“But whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will never thirst.” It is as though he were saying: “To whoever believes in me I give the gift of the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father through me; he will never thirst.”

For he will say with the Psalmist: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.”

“But the water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.” Spiritual water—that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit—springs up into eternal life.

Bodily water flows downward; spiritual water springs upward and carries with it those who drink it into eternal glory and blessedness.

“The woman said to him: Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst or come here to draw.”

Nature begins to know its Creator. For a desire for blessedness and true knowledge exists in rational creation; this was prefigured by the Samaritan woman.

The Church begins to understand more deeply the faith that it first began simply to draw, as it begins to enter into theological reasoning.

“Jesus said to her: Go, call your husband, and come here.” It is as though he had said: “You ask me for water springing up into eternal life, namely the Holy Spirit, by whose gift I give eternal life. You cannot drink such water unless you call your husband.

“Go, then, if you wish to drink; call your husband, and come here with him.” That is: “Believe in me, so that both you and your husband may drink in the Holy Spirit.”

In this passage the contemplation proceeds from the genus to the species. It was said above that the Samaritan woman is a symbol both of the universal Church gathered from the Gentiles and of universal human nature.

Now, however, the same woman presents the figure of each individual person established within the unity of the Church, and of each individual soul participating in human nature.

The woman, therefore, is the rational soul, whose husband is understood to be the mind, which is called by many names. For sometimes it is called intellect, sometimes mind, sometimes animus, and often also spirit.

Concerning this husband the Apostle says: “The husband is the head of the woman, Christ is the head of the man, and God is the head of Christ.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “The head of the rational soul is its husband, its intellect; the head of that intellect is Christ.”

This is the natural order of human creation: the soul is subjected under the rule of the mind, while the mind is subjected under Christ. Thus the whole human being is joined through Christ to God the Father.

The two sexes as well—the masculine and the feminine, which are externally observed in the body alone—display the inner dispositions of mind and soul [Note: [Col. 0335] The manuscript reads *praetendunt*.].

The rational soul has a threefold division: into the mind, reason, and the inner sense.

The mind is always turned toward God, and therefore is rightly called the husband and ruler of the other parts of the soul, since no other creature stands between it and its Creator.

Reason is concerned with the causes and knowledge of created things. Whatever the mind perceives through contemplation above, it hands over to reason; reason in turn entrusts it to memory.

The third part of the soul is the inner sense, which is subjected to reason as to a higher part and, through reason, is consequently subjected to the mind.

Under that inner sense, in the natural order, the outer sense is placed. Through it the whole soul animates and governs the fivefold bodily sense and gives life to the entire body.

Since the rational soul can receive nothing from heavenly gifts except through its husband—that is, through the mind, which holds the primacy over the whole nature—the woman, namely the soul, is rightly commanded [Note: [Col. 0335] The manuscript reads *invetur*.] to call her husband, her intellect, with whom and through whom she can drink spiritual gifts. Without him she cannot in any way share in heavenly grace [Note: [Col. 0335] *Potest* is omitted in the manuscript; added by conjectural emendation.].

Therefore he says: “Call your husband and come here.” Without your husband, do not presume to come to me at all. In the absence of the intellect, no one knows how to ascend to the heights of theology or participate in spiritual gifts.

“The woman answered and said to him: I have no husband.” Jesus said to her: “You have spoken well, because you have no husband.”

“You have spoken well,” he says. “I commend what you have said, because you have truly spoken” [Note: [Col. 0335] So the manuscript; perhaps *quia*, “because,” is intended.].

For I know that you do not have a husband—not because you said that you do not have one, but through myself, to whom it belongs to know all things.

For you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband; this you have truly said.

Regarding the five husbands of the mystical woman—that is, of the rational soul living carnally—the interpretations of commentators vary. Some understand them as the five books of the Mosaic Law. Their interpretation is not convincing, however, since the Mosaic Law was given only to the Jews, whereas this woman signifies the whole human soul in general.

Augustine understands the five bodily senses as the five husbands, under which it is beyond doubt that every soul [Note: [Col. 0337D] The manuscript reads: “each soul.”] lives before reaching the mature age at which it can use reason. Sight is active in infants, as are hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Beyond these, the carnal and still infantile soul can participate in nothing. When, however, it reaches adulthood, it is joined, as it were, to a sixth husband, namely reason.

Yet the carnal and foolish soul often neglects rational movement and submits, as though to a natural husband, to error, by which and through which it is deceived. Having abandoned the natural order, it desires what is contrary to its nature. Therefore it is said of him: “And the one whom you now have is not your husband.” You have abandoned your husband and refused to obey him; you have followed an adulterer, and thus become an adulteress.

But if you wish to drink from the water that I shall give you, go, call your husband, to whom you must become subject and with whom you must be joined in spiritual marriage. Abandon the adulterer, lest you be an adulteress; abandon the error by which you have been led astray. You have left your husband and violated the natural beauty of your chastity. Thus far Augustine.

Maximus asserts that the five husbands signify the five laws given to the human soul. The first was given to humanity in paradise before the sin, concerning the forbidden and prohibited tree. The second was given after humanity’s transgression and expulsion from paradise, concerning the multiplication of the human race. The third was given to Noah before the flood, concerning the construction of the ark. The fourth was given after the flood, concerning the divisions of the nations. The fifth was given to Abraham, concerning circumcision and the sacrifice of his son.

Under these five laws, as though under five husbands, the human soul was subject from the beginning of the world until the Law of Moses. But the law of the letter, which was given through Moses, was not given to liberate or justify the soul, but to accuse it and to weigh it down with the burden of the sacraments, which had brought it no salvation unless it fled for refuge to the grace of the New Testament. For the Law was given so that grace might be sought, while grace was given so that the Law might be fulfilled.

Since, therefore, the law of the letter contributed nothing to human nature for salvation—for the Law brought no one to perfection, but served only to increase transgressions, as the Apostle says: “The strength of sin is the law,” and again: “The Law entered in so that sin might abound”—the Lord appropriately says to the Samaritan woman: “And the one whom you now have is not your husband.” Abandon the letter; it is not your husband. Go to your husband, to the spirit of the letter. Call the law of grace, which is your husband; from him you will conceive spiritual offspring of virtues, and with him I shall give you the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which you will be able to believe in me.

Having therefore rejected the sixth husband, namely the carnal law, the rational soul is commanded to call its husband—that is, the New Testament, the law of grace, under which alone it could be saved.

The woman said to him: “Lord, I see that you are a prophet.”

When the woman learned from what the Lord had told her about the number of her husbands and about her adultery with a foreign husband that he was indeed a prophet, she immediately posed a question, as though saying: “Since I see you and know without doubt that you are a prophet, resolve for me the question over which Jews and Samaritans contend—namely, the place where God is to be worshiped, on account of which the Jews do not agree with us, that is, dissent from us.”

“Our fathers worshiped on this mountain.” That is, Jacob, his sons, and all the Samaritans who lived under the Mosaic Law. “And you say, Jews, that Jerusalem is the place where one ought to worship.”

In this, then, we disagree; in this we do not share a common position. We worship God on this mountain of Samaria, where Jacob worshiped; you worship in the Jerusalem temple. Since, therefore, I see that you are a prophet, I do not doubt that you know everything. Therefore settle this dispute between you and us: where ought we to worship God, here or in Jerusalem?

Jesus said to her: “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know.”

By these words he suppresses the boasting of the Samaritan woman and of all the Samaritans. The Samaritans believed that they were no less religious than the Jews. He therefore speaks in the person of the Jews—not of the impious, who did not receive him, but of the patriarchs and prophets and of those who had believed in him shortly before in Judea.

Therefore he says: “You worship the Father whom you do not know, but we worship the same Father whom we know.” For no one can worship the Father unless he has first worshiped the Son. Whoever believes in the Son knows the Son and therefore also knows the Father. For he says: “Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father also.”

You, then, woman, together with your entire people, do not know the Father whom you worship, because you have not yet believed in his Son, through whom one comes to knowledge of the Father. And this is what follows: “For salvation is from the Jews.” It is as though he were saying openly: “Therefore we know what we worship,” joining himself to the Jews who believe, “because salvation is from the Jews.” For Christ, who is the salvation of the whole world, is from the Jews—not only by the origin of his flesh, but also by the propagation of faith. From them arose faith and the primitive Church.

“But the hour is coming, and now is.”

By “the hour” he means his presence in the flesh. “You,” he says, “woman, are asking me about the place of worship. Therefore I tell you: the hour is coming; I am present, and I am now here in the flesh.”

“When the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.”

Before I came, no one could worship the Father in spirit and truth except the patriarchs and prophets, to whom my presence in the flesh was revealed through the Spirit before I came into the world.

Therefore, woman, true worshipers will worship neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but inwardly, in the innermost temple of their heart and understanding. The soul will first be purified through faith, illuminated through knowledge, and perfected through deification. On the mountain of theology they will worship in the Spirit—those who have been illuminated by the Holy Spirit.

For the Father seeks such worshipers: those who worship him in their spirit and in the truth of their knowledge. He concluded what he had foretold by saying:

“God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”

It is as though he were saying: “If God were corporeal, or were a body, perhaps he would seek bodily places in which to be worshiped. But since he is spirit, he seeks those who worship him in their spirit and understanding through true knowledge.”

[Note: The manuscript reads “qui a spiritu”; corrected in the text.]

The woman said to him: “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ.”

Because the Lord had foretold, “The hour is coming, and now is,” the woman thought that he was speaking of the Messiah—that is, of the Christ who was to come—whom she did not yet recognize as present, as though he were speaking of someone else. For she had heard from the prophets that Christ would come.

Therefore she says: “I know that the Messiah is coming.” She says “has come,” not “will come,” either to compare her words with the words of the prophet with whom she was speaking, or because, in some manner enlightened by the Spirit, she understood Christ as coming in the present; or because it is customary in speech to say of someone who is on the way, “He has come,” even though he has not yet arrived.

Messiah is a Hebrew name, which in Greek is interpreted as Christ—that is, “anointed.”

“When he comes, he will announce everything to us.”

She still did not perfectly understand that Christ was present, but, instructed by the prophets, she believed in the coming of Christ and in his future teaching. “He will announce everything to us”—namely, everything that pertains to the worship of himself and of his Father.

Jesus said to her: “I am he, the one speaking with you.”

First the Lord opened the woman’s understanding so that she might believe; then he revealed himself to her. She had indeed believed the prophets who had foretold the coming of Christ, and therefore she was worthy to speak with the one whom she believed would come, although she did not yet know him as present.

By the merit of this faith she came to the knowledge of Christ who was speaking about himself and saying: “I am that Christ himself. You know me as the one who was to come; now know me as the one who is present.”

And immediately his disciples came, and they were amazed that he was speaking with a woman.

Why were they amazed, since Christ had very often spoken with women? They were not therefore amazed that their Lord was speaking with a woman, but were amazed only that he was speaking with a Samaritan—that is, with a foreign woman—because they did not understand the mystery of the Church that was to come from the nations.

Yet no one said: “What are you seeking?” or “Why are you speaking with her?” The disciples did not dare question their Lord, fearing that he would rebuke them if they questioned him imprudently, since they were not yet able to understand the mystery of the future Church.

Therefore the woman left her water jar.

After the Church, or human nature, recognized the presence of the divine substance in the flesh, she left her water jar. She abandoned her carnal use; she abandoned the water and the pursuit of carnal knowledge.

[lacuna]

FRAGMENT III, CHAPTER 6:5–14

[lacuna] He could not see the crowd coming to him if he did not raise his eyes—he who had seen everything before the world was made and had never needed the instruments of bodily eyes in order to see.

Therefore he raises his eyes, teaching us to raise the eyes of our hearts, and showing that the whole world is converging from every direction toward the faith of Christ.

By Christ’s example we are also admonished to raise the eyes of our hearts, so that, if perhaps, with him teaching us and illuminating us inwardly, we are permitted to ascend to the height of action and knowledge, and also of theology, the crowd of carnal thoughts that follow us may not disturb us or cast us down from the height of contemplation. Rather, we should strive to nourish them with spiritual food, satisfying them insofar as they are able to receive it.

He says to Philip.

Philip, whose name is interpreted as “mouth of the lamp” [Note: A truly remarkable interpretation; the name Philip seems to have been derived from “mouth” and λαμπάς (“lamp”).], represents the preachers of the faith. While they are established with Christ on the height of contemplation, the Lord daily speaks to them about nourishing the crowd of carnal thoughts:

“Where shall we buy bread so that these people may eat?”

He said this to test him—that is, to inquire into his faith concerning the future miracle. God is not a tempter of evils. He tests the elect for the sake of proving them, not for the sake of overthrowing them. There are indeed two kinds of testing: one proves the faith of the righteous, while the other exposes the faithlessness of the impious.

For he himself knew what he was going to do.

The Lord, he says, tests Philip for the sake of proving him, not for the sake of learning what ought to be done. For he knew, before the world was made, all the miracles that he would perform in the world. When it says, “For he himself knew,” this does not mean that he knew at some earlier point in time, but that before all times he knew what he was going to do.

Philip answered him: “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive a little.”

Philip was still nourished with the milk of teaching and was not yet able to receive the solid food of true faith and knowledge. He answered according to the measure of his virtue, considering it impossible that so great a multitude could be fed with so few loaves.

For the sake of instruction, therefore, the Lord plays with Philip, testing the simplicity of his faith, so that through this he might learn to ascend higher and believe that no difficulty exists for God.

Thus the order of those who preach the Gospel, typologically represented—as we have said—by Philip, answers the Lord who tests them, that is, who proves and thereby also praises their faith:

“Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough.”

The number one hundred is perfect, for ten times ten produces it. When this number is doubled, it makes two hundred. Appropriately, it represents the perfection of good action and rational knowledge, which are not sufficient for feeding—that is, for instructing in faith—unless the height of theology is added to them.

The practice of virtues purifies the souls of the faithful alone, while knowledge illuminates them concerning created things. Yet that purification and illumination are not sufficient unless the state of perfect contemplation is added, which alone leads souls to the complete fullness of spiritual nourishment.
