One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, said to him: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two small fish; but what are these among so many?”

Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, answered with the same simplicity as Philip. Yet within that simplicity a manifold theory is contained.

This boy, who according to the historical account is understood either as one of the disciples or as a certain boy from the crowd that followed them, mystically signifies the lawgiver, namely Moses. He is not inappropriately called a kind of boy, since the Law itself, which was given through him, led no one to the mature age of perfect righteousness.

The lawgiver is called one boy because he prefigured by his deeds and foretold by his words the future unity of the Church. He said this—that is, in the Old Testament, which began to grow weak as the New Testament became clear, though it has not yet entirely passed away.

“He has five barley loaves.”

The five barley loaves are the five books of the Mosaic Law. They are appropriately called barley loaves because carnal people were nourished by them. Barley is properly food for beasts of burden, not for human beings.

The carnal people, still living under the letter and not abandoning the ancient condition of the first man, of whom it is written, “When man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them,” were counted among the number of brute animals. Consequently, they fed only on the letter, as on a kind of barley loaf mixed with chaff, and not on the spiritual marrow of the letter itself.

For the inner husks of chaff naturally cling to barley grains so closely that they can scarcely be separated from their marrow. They signify the difficulty of understanding the mysteries and commandments of the Law.

The number five in the five barley loaves can also appropriately be understood to indicate the five bodily senses. For the more a believer delights in those things received through the fivefold bodily sense, the more he will be counted among the brute animals that feed on barley.

But when, abandoning these senses—as I call them—through an increase of action and knowledge, he feeds on spiritual nourishment, he is no longer reckoned among brutes but among rational animals.

Since, therefore, no one is permitted to ascend to the height of virtues and contemplations unless he is first nourished by the signs of sensible things, the Lord appropriately distributes barley loaves to the crowd of faithful who follow him. If they preserve the faith they have received, he will lead them, once they have first been satisfied by these loaves [Note: [Col. 0341D] The manuscript reads: “having been satisfied.”], to the spiritual and higher nourishment of rational creation. Before they transcend bodily senses and everything received through them, they cannot be nourished by that higher food.

Thus, when he says, “But what are these among so many?” the meaning is as though he were saying: “What are the letter of the Law, or bodily senses and corporeal things? What benefit do they provide for so great a multitude of believers who will believe in you and seek spiritual nourishment—things that surpass every letter and every bodily sense?”

“For eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him.”

Jesus then said: “Make the people recline.”

Now there was much grass in the place.

The great quantity of grass signifies the letter of the Law, which was manifold in its symbols. The great quantity of grass also appropriately signifies the carnal thoughts that are introduced into the soul through bodily senses and that quickly flow out of it again.

It is also fitting that the disciples are commanded to make the people recline, since teachers of truth cannot raise those whom they have nourished to the height of contemplation unless they first begin to instruct them, as though in the lowest places, in the simplicity of the letter and of visible creation.

The first step toward ascending the height of virtues is the letter of Holy Scripture and the appearance of visible things. After reading the letter or examining creation, they ascend by the steps of right reason into the spirit of the letter and into the rational principle of creation.

The men therefore reclined, numbering about five thousand.

By the same method of interpretation by which the five loaves signify the five books of Moses, insofar as the letter is concerned, or the five bodily senses, the five thousand signify, with sound reasoning, the multitude of those who lived under the letter of the Law or who are still subject to carnal senses.

The number one thousand is perfect and cubic. Ten times ten times ten produces the sum of one thousand. When this is multiplied by the number five, it indicates the fullness of those living carnally. Once they have been instructed by sacred history and by the visible surface of things, they are about to pass over to the height of spiritual realities.

Jesus then took the loaves, and after giving thanks he distributed them to those who were reclining; likewise, he distributed as much of the fish as they wanted.

The Lord took the loaves because he himself gave the Law through Moses, so that the Law is properly called the Law of the one who gave it, not of the one through whom it was given as through a minister.

“And after giving thanks, he distributed them to those who were reclining.” To whom did he give thanks except the Father, who so loved the world that he gave his Son, through whom he would nourish the world with visible sacraments and sensible creatures, so that through these he might lead it to knowledge of himself and nourish it?

The two fish signify the two Testaments insofar as they pertain to sensible symbols. Fish are sensible symbols in water, within a people still carnal, though beginning to live perfectly.

When these symbols begin to be understood in a higher manner, they are rightly distributed to those who desire them, as much as they wish. To distribute is to distinguish visible symbols from the invisible meanings they contain and to divide them according to each person’s capacity.

Some wish the two fish to signify the two offices in the Law, namely the king and the priest; others, the prophets and the Psalms.

When they had been filled, he said to his disciples: “Gather up the fragments that remain, so that nothing may perish.”

The simple crowd of the faithful is filled and satisfied with the letter alone, with visible creation, and with visible symbols. The spiritual meanings of the letter, creation, and symbols are like certain remaining fragments that carnal people cannot yet take in. The teachers of the Church are commanded to gather them, so that nothing of those meanings may perish without being understood, but so that from them the rational desire of spiritual souls may be satisfied in divine contemplation.

The fragments, then, are the barley loaves: the subtle and difficult meanings of Holy Scripture and of sensible sacraments, which the teachers of the Church gather together so that nothing of them may perish—that is, so that nothing may remain undistributed to those capable of intelligible meanings.

So they gathered them and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves that remained after those who had eaten were satisfied.

The number twelve in the baskets typologically represents the capacity of the wise who gather spiritual meanings. The number twelve is exceedingly perfect. Considered in many ways—in the practice of virtues, in knowledge of things, and in theology, which concerns divine matters alone—it signifies the understanding of divine people.

First, the perfection of twelve is considered in that it is twice six. The number six indicates the perfection of good works in this life. When this is doubled, it grows, as it were, into the quantity of the number twelve, into eternal contemplation, which is the fruit of all good action.

Again, the number twelve contains within itself the harmonies of all music. It contains the diatessaron in the four compared with the three [Note: This refers to the harmonies of the Greeks]; it contains the diapente in the three and the two; and it contains the diapason between itself and six. Within the number eight there is also a complete diapason. It contains the tone between nine and eight. All these numbers are contained within the bounds of twelve.

Thus the harmony of all visible and invisible things joined together is represented by this number. This harmony is known and comprehensible, insofar as it is granted to human beings, only to those who understand divine things.

The number twelve is also divided into ten and two. Therefore it signifies both the law of the letter, which is based on ten, and the commandment of charity, which is doubled within itself and upon which the Law and the prophets depend.

Therefore those who fulfill the Law through the commandment of charity are themselves the baskets in which the spiritual fragments of divine meanings are both gathered and preserved, so that none of them may perish.

The same number is divided into seven and five. These numbers are attributed to the music of the human voice and indicate the marvelous harmony of all things returning to one end.

For five multiplied by itself produces twenty-five. Seven, however, is divided into two members, the greater of which is four and the lesser three. If, therefore, you multiply seven by its lower member, you will produce twenty-one. If you then add the greater member to that number, it will likewise become twenty-five. Thus five and seven are said to be multiplied toward one end.

The spiritual baskets, therefore, are those who arrive at the one end of eternal contemplation through the power of action and knowledge.

When the people saw the sign that Jesus had performed, they said: “This truly is the prophet who is to come into the world.”

Here again the imperfect crowd is reproved, because they said, on account of the visible sign and not on account of the intelligible power of the sign: “This truly is the prophet who is to come into the world.”

In this miracle, the quantity of five barley loaves raises, not without reason, the question why the fragments of only the five loaves, and not of the two fish, are gathered, from which twelve baskets are filled, when the Gospel says that five thousand people were satisfied by the five loaves and two fish.

The depth of this mystery seems obscure to me, so that it can scarcely be investigated. Augustine, in his exposition of John, says nothing about it but passes over it entirely.

Although it may seem sufficient to many that in Mark one reads: “They took up twelve baskets full of fragments, and from the fish,” so that one may understand: “They also took fragments from the fish,” whether other fragments or the same ones. But if they were other fragments, there were not twelve baskets but twenty-four; if they were the same, it would have been enough to say: “They took up twelve baskets of fragments.”

It seems that there is a mystery in the fact that, as though after the fragments of the bread had been gathered, he says, “and from the fish,” without qualification or addition.

Matthew and Luke, however, mention the fragments without distinction, leaving it uncertain whether they were only fragments of bread, as in John, or of bread and fish together.

Let us therefore try to investigate this as far as the light granted to our minds permits, without prejudging the interpretations of others.

We have already said that the five bodily senses, or the five books of Moses, are signified by the number five of the loaves, while the two fish signify the symbols of both Testaments.

The first question, then, is what difference exists among the mysteries of the two Laws—namely, the letter and grace—and among the symbols.

Mysteries properly are those things that are handed down according to the allegory both of deed and of word—that is, things that were both performed according to historical events and spoken because they are narrated.

For example, the Mosaic tabernacle was constructed according to an actual event, and it was spoken of and narrated in the text of Holy Scripture. Likewise, the sacraments of the legal sacrifices were performed according to history and were spoken of according to the narrative. Circumcision was likewise performed in the flesh and narrated in the letter.

In the New Testament as well, the mysteries of baptism, of the Lord’s body and blood, and of the holy chrism are celebrated according to actual events and handed down and described in writing.

This form of the sacraments—the allegory of deed and word—is reasonably called by the holy Fathers “mystery.”

There is another form that properly receives the name “symbol.” It is called an allegory of word, but not of deed, because it consists solely in words of spiritual teaching and not in sensible deeds.

Mysteries, therefore, are those things that in both Testaments were performed according to history and narrated according to the letter. Symbols, however, are things that were not performed but are spoken by teaching alone, as though they had been performed.

For example, in the Old Law it is written: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.” According to Augustine’s testimony, this is never read as having occurred historically. Nevertheless it was said and written and is handed down as though it had been done, although the truth of the divine history does not narrate that it happened.

Likewise, in the Psalms: “The mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep.” In these passages of Holy Scripture, and in many similar ones, an allegory of word alone—not of deed and word—is understood.

In the New Testament many things are narrated that, according to the truth of history, did not happen but were merely spoken as though they had happened. Such examples are found especially in the allegory of the Lord’s parables—for example, the parable of the rich man and poor Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom, and of the chasm placed between them, the flame, the tongue, and the finger. No authority hands down any of these as having occurred according to actual events; they were altogether spoken figuratively.

This form is recognized in nearly all the parables and is properly called symbolic, although it is the practice of Holy Scripture to use “symbols” for “mysteries” and “mysteries” for “symbols,” by a certain proximity and similarity.

Let us therefore posit a certain analogy by which we may persuade ourselves of what we wish to assert.

The people of carnal believers existed both in the Old Law and in the New. There is now someone who thinks that nothing exists beyond the letter and bodily senses [Note: [Col. 0345] “not” is omitted in the manuscript], because he cannot ascend higher than the letter of Scripture and the things received through the senses.

Likewise, perfect and wise people are narrated as having existed in the Old Law in action and knowledge of spiritual meanings, and in the New Testament as well. They ascend with Christ, like disciples, into the height of contemplation, as though onto a certain mountain, leaving behind the carnal who recline under the letter and the senses in the grass of temporal things.

“For all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass.”

Let us therefore imagine in our minds a certain multitude of simple believers residing on the sides of the mountain, or on the plain—that is, below the height of divine meanings.

For from the text of the Gospel it may be understood that the Lord fed the crowd not on the summit of the mountain but on a certain plain where there had been much grass. It says: “He went up into the mountain by himself,” so that, according to the historical events, we understand that the Lord first went up into the mountain alone with his disciples, then descended again to the lower places, and, after performing the miracle, returned alone once more to the mountain.

Five loaves and two fish are set before this multitude hungry for the faith of Christ—that is, the sacraments, which were both performed and written, and the symbols, which were spoken alone and not performed.

Christ takes the five loaves and two fish and gives thanks to the Father, who wished to nourish his faithful with symbols and sacraments. He hands them over to his disciples, his teachers, his ministers; they distribute them to the crowd.

The barley loaves are broken by the disciples when they divide the mysteries of both Laws into historical events and their spiritual meanings. Carnal people are nourished by the simple history; spiritual people gather the divine meanings of that history as though they were fragments.

The fragments that carnal people eat and by which they are satisfied are the historical events. The fragments that spiritual people eat are the divine meanings of those events.

For example, let the book of Genesis be read at the point where the passage of carnal Israel through the Red Sea is narrated. The still-simple Christian, reclining as though in the grass of temporal and carnal things, is nourished by the history alone. Whatever happened there was known through the five bodily senses.

For the Israelites were seen to cross the sea on dry feet, while the Egyptians were seen to have been killed. This was also heard by neighboring peoples. The sea water was tasted, smelled, and touched. The still-simple mind of the believer considers and reflects upon all these things within itself and is satisfied by them, as though by certain fragments of divine history.

It cannot grasp the meaning of the letter itself. Therefore those who understand spiritual things gather it, so that it may not perish but may benefit those capable of understanding.

Behold the five barley loaves: the mysteries of historical events, divided into letter and spirit, and, insofar as they are letter, corresponding to the five bodily senses.

[Note: One line is missing.]

[lacuna]

“Abraham,” he says, “had two sons, one indeed by a slave woman and the other by a free woman.”

Behold the first fragments of history, sufficient for the simple. He then adds the spiritual fragments, saying: “Now these things are the two covenants.”

Let the two fish be set before the same multitude—that is, the spiritual teaching of allegorical speech alone, not of events performed according to history.

This is contained, as it were, in the number two, because it is perceived through only two senses, namely sight and hearing; it cannot be perceived through the remaining senses. It is read with the eyes and heard with the ears, but is removed from smell, taste, and touch.

For example, using the same examples, let what is written in Exodus be read: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.” This symbol is read by the eyes and heard by the ears, but it cannot be broken, because it is not understood according to the truth of historical events; it was spoken only allegorically.

And because it is not divided, it is entrusted whole to the memory of carnal believers, so that they may believe that a spiritual meaning is present in these words, even though they do not understand it. Those who know spiritual things spiritually gather it all.

In symbols, therefore—that is, in expressions of spiritual teaching handed down through the allegory of word alone and not of deed—no fragments are gathered, because they are not divided into history and meaning. Only the meaning is considered in them; there is no deed.

Likewise, in the New Testament, to take an example from there as well, the mystery of the body and blood of our Lord is both celebrated sensibly according to historical events and [uncertain: “cerebrum” (?) is investigated according to spiritual understanding; the reading appears corrupt].

What is perceived externally and sensed by carnal people, who are subject to the fivefold bodily sense, is a barley loaf, because they cannot ascend to the height of spiritual understanding. It is, as it were, a fragment by which their carnal thought is satisfied.

The spiritual fragment belongs to those who are able to understand the height of the divine meanings of this mystery itself. Therefore it is gathered by them, so that it may not perish.

For a mystery formed from letter and spirit partly perishes and partly remains eternally. What is seen perishes, because it is sensible and temporal; what is not seen remains, because it is spiritual and eternal.

Let an example of a symbol be given: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.”

This is spoken alone; no historical event is recognized in it. Therefore it is received in its entirety in a simple manner by carnal people and in its entirety uniformly by spiritual people. No fragments can be made there, because there is nothing there to be understood according to history; everything pertains to theology, which surpasses every sense and understanding.

It is read by the eyes of those who read and perceived by the ears of those who hear. Thus, like two fish, the one and same theology of the Evangelist is received through the two senses appropriate to it.

[lacuna]

The rest is missing.

[Col. 0347]

JOHN SCOTUS’S BOOK ON PREDESTINATION

Reviewed against the manuscript of Saint-Germain 1314 (formerly 634), a tenth-century parchment quarto manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris.

Mauguin’s first edition … | M. |

NOTICE TO THE READER

[Col. 0347] John Scotus could scarcely have undertaken a more dangerous task than that of resolving, through his dialectical and philosophical arguments, the difficult and exceedingly obscure theological question “Concerning Predestination.”

Since he was able to make little progress in this matter, what wonder is it that he turned nearly all the weapons of his opponents against himself? Among these opponents, Prudentius of Troyes and Florus the deacon, in the name of the Church of Lyon, attacked Scotus’s book with the greatest vehemence as soon as it first appeared, and refuted it with the utmost erudition.

The reader should consult their writings, which have been printed in volumes 115 and 119 of this *Patrologia*.

Scotus is chiefly concerned to show that neither a double predestination nor a twofold predestination is sufficiently consistent with reason, but that there is only one predestination, belonging to the simplest divine unity. He endeavors to prove this by various arguments drawn from reason, from Holy Scripture, from Augustine, and from elsewhere. Yet the arguments he advances, and his doctrines, do not agree sufficiently with the truth without very often openly contradicting sound reason and the teaching of the Church. For he teaches:

“Foreknowledge and predestination are one and the same; predestination cannot exist relatively in God; nature is not punished by nature; nature, because it is from God, neither sins nor is punished; nor did the generality of nature sin in the first man—for if that nature had sinned, since it is one, it would certainly have perished altogether; it is only the individual will of each person that sins, while only the voluntary movement of desire is punished; the whole nature of the soul is will; every evil is sin and its punishment, and these are nothing; every defect or privation or sin of a perverse will, and its end—death and the misery of eternal punishments—are altogether nothing, and therefore are neither foreknown nor predestined; sins and their punishments are nothing; nor is that eternal fire a punishment, nor was it prepared or predestined for it [Col. 0349]; without doubt both the blessed and the wretched will dwell in it; this eternal fire is itself the fourth element of the world, where the bodies of the saints are changed into an ethereal quality, while the bodies of the wicked are to pass into an aerial quality; and in it the wondrous joy of natures within themselves is perfected, but the unspeakable torment of evil wills; and thus the bodies of all the ungodly, angels and human beings alike, will suffer the punishments of eternal fire, in such a way that the integrity of their substance will in no way perish, their beauty will in no way diminish, and their natural soundness will remain; thereafter all the goods of nature will shine forth in wondrous order for the adornment of the universe, except for the blessedness of which they will be deprived, while they suffer eternal distress. God is not the author or maker of punishments. Punishments are evils and therefore, since evil does not come from God, they are not from God. God does not punish what he made, nor does he take away from the things he made their natural goods. God always dwells in the nature that he created. Eternal fire was made to burn the devil and his angels, not to torment human beings. After the devil had been cast down from the ether, where, in an ethereal body, he could not feel punishments, an aerial body was added to him, in which he might feel the fire.”

When J. Scotus had openly put forward these and similar propositions, derived from the decrees of his philosophy and opposed to the teaching of the holy Church and of the sacred Scriptures, what wonder is it that he harmed rather than benefited those who had urged him to compose this book? Nor is it sufficiently clear why Archbishop Hincmar, easily the wisest of his contemporaries, summoned John Scotus to defend his position in such a work. Prudentius, however, attacked Scotus with weapons against which he could scarcely resist: the authorities of the holy Fathers. He amassed innumerable passages from them and assailed Scotus the courtier with the utmost severity. We too have not omitted to add, in their proper places, several passages from Prudentius’s *Recapitulation*, which he appended to the end of his work, in order to remedy each of Scotus’s errors by means of notes. To make known the weapons which our author turned against himself in this writing, we wish to set down several complete passages from the books of Prudentius and Florus, as well as the judgments of two synods.

Prudentius therefore begins the preface of his book, addressed to Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, as follows:

“Inflamed, as is fitting and necessary, by zeal for the Catholic faith and by the affection of true charity, most blessed father, you sent me a certain booklet containing nineteen chapters selected from the book of a certain Scotus which, as you say, diverge in some fashion from our understanding. You asked and admonished me to draw forth, from the books of the Gospels and of the Catholic doctors, abundant answers appropriate to each chapter that I might find deviating from the truth.

“Having carefully gone through these chapters and examined them attentively, I found in them the poisons of Pelagian faithlessness, and on several occasions the madness of Origen and the frenzy of the heretics called Collyridians—errors which, deservedly, were refuted by the most powerful defenders and champions of the Catholic faith and condemned, with the censure of the strictest justice, long before our times. I confess that I trembled and was terrified to see so many errors, once lulled to rest together with their authors, sprouting again in our own times; to see smoldering vapors once extinguished bursting forth anew, and, through their harmfulness, darkening the eyes of many.

“When I prepared myself, as you had ordered, to undertake their refutation, I was frightened by the difficulty of the labor and deliberated whether it should be wholly abandoned. But, weighing the authority of your admonition, I judged it better, with the fruit of obedience, even if less fully, to stumble to some extent than, through the foolish timidity of reverence for a father, to oppose you. Thus encouraged by the merits of your request and by the most earnest purity of the prayers of the one who was writing, I resolved, with diligent curiosity, to search through that same book, if some means might perhaps be found by which, from its sequence, I could more easily observe the tortuous contortions of so many errors.

“When by the grace of God—without which I am nothing and can do nothing—I had attained what I desired, I discovered, as far as I could by divine inspiration, that John, namely Scotus, was in every respect a follower of Pelagius, Caelestius, and their most ardent adherent and defender Julian. He barked against the Fathers of the orthodox faith and against the Catholic Fathers with such impudence that one might think that a single spirit had taught Julian and John, and that the same spirit had been in them, rather than that a different spirit had vomited through their tongues so many and such great nauseating blasphemies.

“For they equally attack the gratuitous grace of God, similarly deny the justice of God, and, with indistinguishable chatter, dissuade men from believing in original sin—which we contract at birth and from which we are released only by heavenly grace through the mystery of baptism. In a vanity closely resembling dialectical sophistry, they rave foolishly. They also distort the most correct understanding of the holy Scriptures and the most sound sense of the Catholic Fathers with such a neat convolutedness, as though nothing had ever been done against their errors.

“Since the Fathers, and especially the blessed Augustine, have answered them most fittingly and most abundantly, I did not think that pious readers would judge me presumptuous if, obedient with willing devotion to your admonitions, I offered, as a poor share, whatever I could in the treasuries of my Lord’s tabernacle, leaving to better and more learned men whatever they might be better able and more willing to offer. For, as Saint Jerome says, one person’s wealth cannot be disgraced by another’s poverty.

“Trusting, therefore, in his grace—which goes before us so that we may will what is good, and which we follow so that we may not will in vain—I carefully sought, by turning over the Fathers’ pages, consonant in every respect, to extract faithfully what antidote each of them had prepared against these same poisons, prefacing each doctor’s name and likewise identifying the book. I also inserted in many places the words of that same John, as he arranged them, placing his name before them together with the sign that is called theta [θ], which some used to mark propositions deserving condemnation.

“For if I have not inserted his words everywhere, since their excessive verbosity brings weariness to readers [Col. 0351], I have honestly opposed their meanings, insofar as my small capacity allowed.”

Then, in the first chapter against John Scotus, he attacks him in these words:

“Having gone through the book of your perversity, which you poured forth under the name of a certain Gottschalk against all Catholics, I received your blasphemies and impudence—by which you insolently assail the gratuitous grace of God and his inflexible justice—with all the greater distress because I embraced you more familiarly and loved you more particularly. For you have advanced so far into madness that you twist the most serious authority of the holy Scriptures by your depraved interpretations and teach that the meanings of the Catholic Fathers are to be inverted into perverse meanings.

“You fabricate for us, to be sure, a certain quadrivium for understanding the Scriptures. Yet our Fathers—all the Catholic interpreters—who, shining with divine and human wisdom, left many things imbued from heaven and explained them with great learning and clarity, while opening up numerous rules of interpretation and modes of expression, are proved to have completely disregarded this quadrivium, since they make no mention of it. Instead they proposed to us much better, holier, and more learned ways, supported by whose assistance we may both avoid the filth of your tricks and draw and pour forth the purity of the simplest faith from the clearest and sweetest springs, in the name and with the help of God’s assisting, indeed prevenient, grace.”

Nor does he rebuke him mildly a little later in the same chapter:

“Although we do not ignore that, at the Lord’s command, golden and silver vessels, and the varied beauty of garments and gems borrowed from the Egyptians, were offered to his tabernacle and ought to be offered with devotion, nevertheless, whenever the greatest necessity compelled action against those who, puffed up by such things, gloried in their vanities and counted the simplicity of our faith as foolishness, our Fathers were not forbidden to employ them as circumstances required; rather, they used them faithfully and prudently.

“But you, writing in opposition concerning the faith against the faithful, who rely on no sophisms, turn more shamelessly to sophistical ravings. Why? It is plainly evident that, eager for self-display and wishing to appear no longer a philosopher but a lover of ornament, you chose to thrust upon us things which you believed none of us could either understand, detect, or certainly refute. While you strive to please human beings—if indeed there are any who care for such things, which may eternal truth avert—you neither took care nor feared to displease him concerning whom the prophet solemnly foretells in such matters: ‘God has scattered the bones of those who please men; they have been confounded, because God has despised them.’

“Nor did you fear, with Achan, to bring a golden bar from the anathema of Jericho into the Lord’s camp, contrary to the prohibition, and now, together with him, to incur deservedly the sentence of divine punishment, unless you quickly repent and recover humbly.

“For all who have diligently searched the prophetic or apostolic writings, understood them vividly, and explained them faithfully—opening obscure things, adorning what is plain, unraveling the most tangled knots, and revealing allegories—devoted themselves above all to using that mode of speech by which even the simpler could grasp, without serious difficulty, what they heard or read.

“This practice was observed carefully by all; but it shines forth especially in the works of the blessed and most learned father Augustine, bishop of venerable memory, which he composed concerning Christian doctrine. In them, with the most learned humility and the humblest learning, he both established and taught that the inventions of portents such as yours and those like you must especially be avoided and shunned. The same is true of those works which he wished to be designated by the title *Questions or Expressions of the Heptateuch*, written with marvelous elucidation.

“Likewise, the blessed Jerome, incomparably learned in the literature of so many languages and books, repeatedly emphasizes in all his explanations, both prophetic and apostolic, that it was his greatest concern that the sayings of the holy Scriptures should be understood in their own right rather than made to serve the controversies of rhetoricians. He had been instructed, as it were, by the blow of the dreadful Judge: because of his excessive reading of Cicero, he was brought before him, severely beaten, and finally released through the prayers of those standing around him. He had sworn that he would never again meditate upon or read Cicero’s books. In his letter to the Galatians, he therefore expressed his contempt for this kind of disputation, saying, etc.”

In the third chapter the following passage occurs, from which it is gathered that John Scotus had not been invested with any rank of ecclesiastical dignity:

“Who would listen to you, a barbarian, invested with none of the ranks of ecclesiastical dignity and never to be invested by Catholics, barking against Gregory, the bishop of the city of Rome and of the apostolic see?”

In the fourteenth chapter Prudentius writes with the sharpest irony:

“‘Ireland,’ he says, ‘sent you alone, the keenest-witted of all, across to Gaul, so that by your learning it might obtain what no one without you could know. But far be it from us that Celtic eloquence, with such great floods of rivers overflowing, should admit your cloudiness, although the excellence of Christian humility by no means prevents one or the other from being supplied in turn through the service of charity; indeed, wherever it finds advantage, it judges that what is right should be offered alternately.’”

Finally, Prudentius’s book ends with these words:

“This is our faith, because this is the true, prophetic, apostolic, orthodox, and Catholic faith. I too could have pronounced an anathema against you, but I have waited for, preferred, and desired your correction rather than your destruction. Therefore I do not yet hurl against you the severity of anathema, because I exhort, admonish, and ask with all the affections of my heart that, in view of heavenly grace, you recover your senses, at last awaken from so deadly a lethargy, and seek out what Christian purity thinks; that you willingly inquire into it, grasp it humbly, accept it gently, follow it meekly, hold it devotedly, and carry it out faithfully in every respect.

“Abandon the quadrivium of vanity [Col. 0353], by following which you have become an exile from the way of truth. How much better and healthier it would be for you, relying upon the one true and eternal way, to ride upon the chariot of that humble way than, puffed up by the pride of your quadrivium, to choose to be carried off in different directions.

“The chariot of this way is the four Gospels, flowing from one fountain of paradise, by which the way of salvation is opened for us. The chariot of this way is the four virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—by which every excellence of character is adorned. The chariot of this way is the four kinds of divine utterance: historical, ethical, allegorical, and anagogical; by these, with grace illuminating us, we are led to every understanding of the sacred writings.

“If you had humbly and faithfully striven to follow these, you would never have fallen into such precipices of errors and abominations, indeed of blasphemies. But while you clung with such obstinacy to your convoluted quadrivium, you were unwilling to escape the saying of the book of Ecclesiasticus: ‘He who speaks sophistically is hateful; he will be deprived of everything. For grace has not been given to him by the Lord. For he has been deprived of all wisdom’ [Note: Ecclus. XXXVII, 23.]. And this: ‘In much speaking you will not escape sin’ [Note: Proverbs X, 19.].

“If you desire to be freed from these things, prostrate yourself as a suppliant before the most exalted humility of the crucified one, so that with the Apostle you may be able to say: ‘I judged myself to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified’ [Note: I Cor. II, 2.]. And again: ‘But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ [Note: Gal. VI, 14.].

“Having written these things in the name and with the help of God, according to the capacity and strength of my smallness, more devotedly than learnedly, also for the sake of your correction, brother John, I wish to annotate each item as briefly and concisely as possible, chapter by chapter, so that the attention of the reader and hearer may more firmly commend what has been read or heard to memory.”

Thus far from Prudentius’s book.

Florus of Lyons, who composed his book in the name of the Church of Lyons, vigorously attacks John Scotus with very similar weapons. He begins as follows:

“There have come to us—that is, to the Church of Lyons—the writings of a certain vain-speaking and chattering man who, disputing about divine foreknowledge and predestination with human and, as he himself boasts, philosophical arguments, has dared, without offering any rationale and without presenting the authority of Scripture or of the holy Fathers, to define, as though they were to be held and followed, things which by the faithful and by readers trained in sacred doctrine are judged, with God’s help, to be most easily rejected because they are utterly vain, contrary to the faith and truth of God, and full of falsehood and error; indeed, they are held up even to contempt and ridicule.

“But because, as we have heard, this same man is regarded by many as a kind of scholar and learned person, and by chattering or writing such things leads some into hesitation and makes others followers of his errors, as though he were saying something great, while he most perniciously occupies all his hearers and admirers with empty verbosity and windy loquacity, so that they submit humbly neither to the divine Scriptures nor to the authority of the Fathers but instead follow his fantastic ravings, we judged it altogether necessary, in the spirit of charity and in accordance with the duty of our place and order, to answer his insolence, with the Lord as our author.

“Thus all who wish faithfully to read these things with fear of God and concern for their salvation may truly recognize how necessary it is, especially in these most dangerous and final times, to cling firmly to the immovable truth of holy Scripture, to obey humbly the thoroughly founded authority of the holy orthodox Fathers, to close and block their ears to undisciplined and utterly vain verbosity, and to fear with their whole attention that saying of the Lord which we already almost see being fulfilled, in which he says: ‘Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes he will find faith on earth?’ [Note: Luke XVIII, 8.]

“And what the Apostle, in whom the same Lord was speaking, solemnly declares: ‘For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn to fables’ [Note: II Tim. IV, 4, 5.].

“Therefore, elsewhere also, speaking in the person of his beloved and chosen disciple, he most diligently warns every faithful person, and especially the pastoral order, saying: ‘O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and oppositions of the knowledge falsely so called’—*ψευδωνόμου γνώσεως*, that is, ‘of knowledge bearing a false name’—‘which some promising, have fallen away from the faith’ [Note: I Timoth. VI, 20.].

“Accordingly, having set out the words which he arranged in nineteen chapters of his little work, we undertake to answer, insofar as the Lord grants, not according to our own judgment but according to the holy Scriptures and the most blessed Catholic Fathers.”

Finally, it was a most grievous misfortune for John Scotus that two Gallican synods—the Synod of Valence in 855 and the Synod of Langres in 859—proscribed his book and its chapters, which contained more the invention of the devil than any argument of faith. One of them, moreover, sharply rebuked what were almost old-wives’ tales and the “Scottish porridge” that brought no small nausea to the purity of the faith.

For the fourth canon of the Synod of Valence reads:

“Those four chapters which were received by the council of our brethren with insufficient foresight, on account of their uselessness, or even their harmfulness and error contrary to the truth; and also the other nineteen, most ineptly concluded in syllogisms, although they are boastfully claimed to rely on no secular literature, in which the invention of the devil rather than any argument of faith is detected—we utterly reject from the pious hearing of the faithful. And, so that such things and similar things may be avoided, we prohibit them in every respect by the authority of the Holy Spirit; we also judge that the introducers of novelties must be chastised, lest they be struck more severely.”

[Col. 0355] The same synod’s sixth canon reads:

“But the inept little questions, and almost old-wives’ tales, and the Scottish porridge that brings nausea to the purity of the faith, which in these most dangerous and grave times, adding to the burden of our labors, have miserably and tearfully grown even to the division of charity—we utterly reject, lest Christian minds be corrupted by them and fall away from the simplicity and purity of the faith that is in Christ Jesus. And, so that fraternal charity may chastise its hearing by avoiding such things, we admonish in the love of the Lord Christ.

“Let the brotherhood remember that it is being oppressed by the gravest evils of the world, and that it is being cruelly suffocated by the abundant harvest of the wicked and by the chaff of frivolous people. Let it burn to overcome these things and labor to correct them; let it not burden the gathering of those who grieve and groan piously with superfluities, but rather embrace with a firm and true faith what the holy Fathers have sufficiently set forth concerning these and similar matters.”

The Synod of Langres, in 859, uses these words in its fourth canon:

“Furthermore, the nineteen chapters concluded by a certain Scot in the most inept and mendacious syllogisms, in which not an argument of faith but rather an invention of faithlessness is manifest, constructed by no art of philosophy whatsoever, as some arrogantly boast, but confused through empty deception and the most unskilled fraud—we utterly reject from the pious hearing of the faithful,” and so forth, as in canon 4 of the Synod of Valence.

Since these things are so, what wonder is it that the work of John Scotus, except for one Parisian manuscript, has vanished from all the libraries of manuscript books, so far as is known? The Benedictine authors of the work entitled *Literary History of France*, volume V, p. 420, passed the following judgment on John Scotus’s book:

“Reasoning is the path he proposes to himself. But besides the fact that reason is insufficient to decide questions of faith, the course of his reasoning shows that he did not even know how to reason correctly. No further evidence is needed than the absurdities and frequent contradictions into which he fell.”

Moreover, consult the discussion of this book of J. Scotus in the study printed above.

# THE BOOK OF JOHN SCOTUS ON DIVINE PREDESTINATION

## PREFACE

[Note: The preface of John Scotus is omitted from the manuscript; a later hand, probably of the fifteenth century, has written above it: “John Scotus, or Erigena.”]

To the illustrious lords, deservedly outstanding in defending the Christian faith, and endowed from above by the Father of lights with the divine gift of episcopal grace, Hincmar and Pardulus, John, your devoted servant, sends greetings in the Lord.

I cannot say how great and what kind of thanks I owe you for this: the abundant sublimity of your affection has not disdained to choose me as a collaborator, as though I were of some worth in defending the salvation of us all, which is the Catholic confession [Note: The manuscript has *chatholica*, as almost everywhere.]. In speech and understanding I am far unequal to your powers, but in faith and devotion I am fitted to affirm the truth with confidence.

For your endeavor is partly raised upward in contemplation to behold the truth, and partly [Note: Thus the manuscript; M. reads *parum—parum* (“a little—a little”).] restrained downward in action to govern the Church; whereas we, by contrast, are tossed about like a little ship amid the billowing, sail-bearing sea of the authority of our lord and master, the most glorious Charles, and are sometimes occupied with being brought to rest in the harbor of his serenity. We are scarcely ever allowed, for a very brief interval of time, to look upon the footsteps of wisdom [Col. 0356A].

Yet the measure of our capacity, whatever it may be, will bear witness to your most prudent and sound teaching. For just as the greatest and brightest lights of the world do not despise the nightly labors of the stars, but use their rays to perfect their own splendor and drive away the darkness of all shadows [Note: The manuscript has *utimur* (“we use”), whereas the edition has *utuntur* (“they use”).], so you, most devout Fathers, although the nobility of your eloquence is sufficient to guard against, refute, and destroy all the tricks of novel heresies, have nevertheless not disdained to strengthen, by the support of our reasoning, your most perfect definition of the faith of predestination [Note: The manuscript has *diffinitionem*, as everywhere.]. In this way both the beautiful virtue of your piety may be revealed to all, and the humility of our obedience [Note: The manuscript has *oboedientiae*, as everywhere.] may shine forth as not unworthy of esteem.

In this little work of ours, which at your command we have taken care to write as a testimony to your orthodox confession, hold fast what you discern to be true and attribute it to the Catholic Church; reject what is false and forgive us, who are human beings; believe what is doubtful until authority commands that it be rejected, or declares it true, or teaches that it must always be believed.

As for the inelegance of the connection of the words, I do not readily believe that it will disturb the constancy of your minds, so that weariness at hearing should seize your ears before love reaches those things which we have labored to persuade. If these things are true, the truth in them ought to be loved without regard to the words. “For it is,” as Augustine says, “a mark of excellent minds to love the truth in words, not the words. For what good is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish to open? Or what harm is there in a wooden one if it can, when we seek nothing except that what is closed should be opened?”

Therefore receive gladly the little gifts of our intellect, considering whatever usefulness they may have more than seeking elegance of expression, which is either scarcely present or not present at all.

Furthermore, we humbly implore your clemency that, whenever you find us saying that the equality of divine foreknowledge and predestination is meant with respect to the unity of the divine substance, in which they are one, you should know that this is what we intend. Likewise, when we said that things which do not exist can neither be known nor foreknown by God, do not think that we said this in the depravity with which certain people try to take away God’s foreknowledge. Rather, we said it for the reason by which we are taught that things which do not exist are not known, and that the knowledge of God is his substance, while his substance exists not in nothing but in something.

[Note: John Scotus himself appears to think that what he taught in this book concerning the equality of divine foreknowledge and predestination, as well as concerning divine ignorance of things that do not exist—among which he counts sin, death, punishments, and evil—departs altogether from the common understanding. Therefore he gives this preliminary warning, lest the minds of Catholics be excessively offended. In fact, however, that his teaching in these chapters departs far from the truth is readily apparent from the book itself.]

May the peace of Christ abound in your hearts.

Under Caesar, beneath Charles, the glory of the Franks flourishes,

On shore and sea, among fish and salt waters;

The sect of the devil’s dogma is condemned, and

By the care of shepherds the lovely faith shines forth.

## CHAPTER I. The Fourfold Quadrivium of Rules of the Whole of Philosophy Solves Every Question

[Note: The manuscript has *quadruvio*, as everywhere.]

[Note: The title is absent from the manuscript; I have supplied it from Prudentius.]

[Note: Concerning this, Prudentius says: “Neither that quadrivium nor any of the forms of worldly wisdom is sufficient to solve every question without the grace of God and faith, which works through love, together with earnest devotion and knowledge of the holy Scriptures.”]

### I

Since the method of every pious and perfect teaching, by which the rationale of all things is sought with the greatest diligence and found with the greatest clarity, is established in that discipline which the Greeks customarily call philosophy, we have judged it necessary to discuss briefly some of its divisions or parts.

“For thus,” says Saint Augustine, “it is believed and taught—which is the chief point of human salvation—that philosophy, that is, the pursuit of wisdom, is not one thing and religion another, since those whose teaching we do not approve do not share the sacraments with us” [Note: Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 5.].

What else is it to treat of philosophy than to set forth the rules of the true religion by which God, the supreme and principal cause of all things, is both humbly worshiped and rationally investigated? It follows from this that true philosophy is true religion, and conversely that true religion is true philosophy.

Although it is divided in many ways and by diverse methods, it is nevertheless recognized as having four principal parts, arranged in pairs, necessary for solving every question. The Greeks chose to name them *διαιρετική* (*diairetike*, divisive), *ὁριστική* (*horistike*, definitive), *ἀποδεικτική* (*apodeiktike*, demonstrative), and *ἀναλυτική* (*analytike*, analytical or resolutive). In Latin we may call them divisive, definitive, demonstrative, and resolutive.

The first of these separates one thing by dividing it into many; the second gathers one thing from many by defining it; the third opens up hidden things by demonstrating them through manifest things; and the fourth resolves composites by separating them into simple elements.

### II

We shall also show examples of these methods in the course of this work, insofar as the light itself—which illuminates the heart of those who seek it—opens for us an entrance into the matters we are attempting to enter. For no learned person doubts that, by means of this useful and honorable quadrivium of human reasoning, one reaches the very discipline of disputation, which is truth.

We are compelled to use the rules of this discipline while answering a certain *saphrophile*—a “lover of rottenness”—named Gottschalk, both the inventor and defender of his heresy, and his supporters—if indeed he has any, and may there be none. We are compelled to do so at the command of the most vigilant pastors of the Catholic Church, in whose fold he attempts to make such poison crawl, and especially with the approval of the most orthodox prince, our lord the venerable Charles. His greatest concern is to think rightly and piously about God, to refute the perverse doctrines of heretics by true arguments and by the authority of the holy Fathers, and finally to uproot them completely.

### III

Therefore, lest we appear to have entered into conflict with the defenders of falsehood unarmed, we shall not incongruously make use of the rules of the art of disputation.

Since both true and false propositions are made persuasive through the art of rhetoric, who would dare to say that truth, when defending itself against falsehood, ought to stand unarmed—so that those who attempt to persuade others of false things know how to make their hearer favorable, attentive, or teachable by means of a prologue [Note: The manuscript has *benivolum* and *proymio*.], while the defenders of truth do not; so that the former relate falsehoods briefly, clearly, and plausibly, whereas the latter present the truth in such a way that hearing it is wearisome, understanding it is impossible, and finally believing it is undesirable; so that the former attack the truth with deceptive arguments and assert falsehood, while the latter are unable either to defend the truth or to refute falsehood; so that the former, moving and driving the minds of their hearers into error by their speech, terrify, sadden, cheer [Note: The manuscript has *exilarent*.], and ardently exhort them, while the latter, defending the truth, drowse in sluggish coldness?

Who would be so foolish as to think this wise?

But since it has been said most truthfully, “There must be many heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you” [Note: I Cor. XI, 9.], let us also make use of this benefit of divine providence.

For heretics arise from those people who, even if they were in the Church, would nevertheless err. When they are outside, they are of great benefit—not by teaching the truth, which they do not know, but by stirring up carnal Catholics to seek the truth and spiritual Catholics to disclose it.

There are innumerable men approved by God in the holy Church; but approved men do not become manifest among us so long as we prefer, delighting in the darkness of our ignorance, to sleep rather than behold the light of truth [Note: The manuscript has *malumus* (“we prefer”), whereas the edition has *malunt* (“they prefer”).].

Therefore many are awakened from sleep by heretics, so that they may see and rejoice in the day of God. Let us therefore make use of heretics—not to approve their errors, but so that, defending Catholic discipline against their snares, we may be more watchful and more cautious, even if we are unable to restore them to salvation.

IV. Since, then, the ancient enemy always envies human blessedness, he does not cease to prepare snares [Note: [Col. 0359] So the codex; M. reads “and snares.”] for our salvation. Our salvation, however, begins from faith. Therefore he strives to destroy faith, seeking vessels suited to himself, into whose ears he may pour those poisons which his crafty malice stirs within, and outwardly into the ears of those unable to ward off the assault of his cunning. But because all his devices, by which until now he has tried to tear apart the unity of the Catholic faith, have been utterly exploded [Note: [Col. 0359] *sunt* (“have been”) is omitted by the codex.] through the working of divine grace by those who walked blessed and undefiled in the way of God’s law and searched his testimonies [Col. 0359C], lest any weapon of his wickedness escape notice, he now [Note: [Col. 0359] So the codex; M. reads “not.”] attempts by a new contrivance to loosen the wall of fortified faith; for through his minister, namely G[otescalc] [Note: [Col. 0359] The codex has “G.”, as everywhere], he asserts that there are two predestinations in God, by which he endeavors to take away both the most equitable merits of justice and the most merciful gifts of grace.

Since the human race is divided into the good and the wicked—for every human being is either good or wicked—and since, as the Truth says, the end of the wicked is eternal punishment, but that of the good is eternal life [Col. 0359D] [Note: [Col. 0359D] Romans 6:21], who are the wicked if not the impious, and who are the good if not the just? According to his own assertion, the inevitable and effective cause of all the just has been established in one predestination, and that of the impious similarly in another. One, he says, belongs to the just, the other to the impious; so much so that no one can arrive at the merit of justice or at its end—namely, eternal life—except by the immutable necessity of the one, while no one can be compelled to fall into the merit of impiety or into its end—namely, eternal punishment—except by the necessity of fate of the other [Note: [Col. 0359] The editor emends; the codex reads *fari*.]

This most foolish and cruel madness is first refuted by divine authority and then annulled by the rules of true reason. What, then? Is it not said through the prophet: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” [Col. 0359D] [Note: [Col. 0359D] Psalm 24:10]? This is explained more clearly elsewhere: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” [Col. 0360D] [Note: [Col. 0360D] Psalm 100:1]. In these words both the generosity of God’s gifts and the equity of his justice are commended with the greatest clarity.

## CHAPTER II. By an argument from necessity it is concluded that there cannot be two predestinations.

[Col. 0360B]

### I

Where, then, G[otescalc], are the necessities of your two predestinations? I say “your,” not “divine.” For your perversity fabricated them, and therefore they neither exist nor can exist. How can that be which strives to take away what exists? Wherever there is necessity, there is no will. Yet there is will in God. Therefore there is no necessity in him.

God made everything that he made by his own will, and by no necessity. What, indeed, could compel God to make anything? But if some cause compelled him to act, that cause would rightly be considered greater and better than he; and consequently it, not he, would be worshiped as the highest cause and God of all. But if the will of God is both piously believed and rightly understood to be the one and principal cause of the whole universe, then necessity is falsely imagined either in the will itself or before it.

Come now! If everything that is in God is God, and the will of God is in God, then the will of God is God. For in him being and willing are not different; rather, what being is, willing also is. Therefore, if God’s will is free—for it is impious to believe otherwise—and free will is wholly without necessity, then no necessity possesses God’s will.

Whatever [Note: [Col. 0359] So the codex; M. reads *quidquid*.] is rightly understood concerning the divine will must necessarily be understood similarly concerning his predestination. But all necessity has been expelled from the divine will. Therefore it has been expelled from his predestination.

### II

Or perhaps you say, heretic, that his will belongs to God’s substance, but not his predestination, so that for God being and willing are one thing, while being and predestining are another? But we can easily refute this by an argument drawn from definition. “Divine predestination,” says Augustine, “is the preparation and ordering, before the ages, of all things that God is going to do” [Note: [Col. 0360D] Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 17].

If, then, it is believed and understood that before the ages nothing existed except God alone, and no sane person doubts that God’s predestination existed before every creature, it follows that God’s predestination is God himself and belongs to his nature.

But perhaps you say that what is said of God before the world is not always said according to substance. For some things are predicated substantially, while others are predicated relatively. “Father,” “Son,” and “Lord” are not said according to substance but according to relation. Similarly, his predestination is expressed relatively to the things that have been predestined.

Hear Scripture speaking of Christ: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0361D] Colossians 2:3]. Tell me, please, what do you try to understand in these words? Do you perhaps judge that Christ’s knowledge and wisdom are accidents, and not his substance according to his divinity [Col. 0361B]? This is believed most absurdly and urged most falsely [Note: [Col. 0361D] Prudentius rightly observes that wisdom, truth, and will are predicated essentially of God, whereas predestination and foreknowledge are predicated relatively, and that therefore a distinction exists.]

For that supreme intellect, in which all things are—and indeed which is all things—although it is called by the rational nature, created to seek it, through names bearing different meanings, is nevertheless one and the same in itself, since it is the simple and manifold cause of all natures. Therefore what being is for God, being wise is also; what being wise is for him, that is also knowing; and what knowing is, that is also predestining.

Although every predestination is called foreknowledge, but not every foreknowledge predestination [Note: [Col. 0361D] Compare Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10], we do not mean this in the same way that we customarily say, in genera and their forms—for example, among the virtues with which the rational soul is adorned—that every prudence is a virtue, but not every virtue is prudence. Rather, we rightly say that what is virtue is prudence, and what is prudence is virtue. For in this way we do not signify the general virtue and its form, but express only the unity of the nature of virtue and prudence.

Therefore it is rightly said that all predestination is foreknowledge, but not all foreknowledge is predestination, so that we understand that what it is to foreknow is to predestine, and what it is to predestine is to foreknow [Note: [Col. 0361D] John Scotus likewise asserts in chapter 15, section 4, and elsewhere that foreknowledge and predestination are one and the same. [Col. 0362D] In reality they differ greatly from one another, since many things are foreknown that are not predestined, whereas nothing is predestined unless it is foreknown. Compare Prudentius.]

For they belong to one and the same substance, namely, the divine nature. Yet, when we hear “God’s foreknowledge,” we are not compelled to understand everything that we understand when we hear “his predestination,” just as, when we hear “virtue,” we are not necessarily compelled to seek everything that we seek when we hear “prudence.”

This argument, which is taken from effects to their cause, is not inappropriate if it is unfolded somewhat more fully.

### III

If, then, the virtues of the soul—which truly are nothing other than effects of that one supreme cause of all things, namely, the divine will—are understood in such a way that, although they are many, they nevertheless exist together inseparably because they are of the same nature—for where one cause is inferred, the same nature is established [Note: [Col. 0361] The codex reads *nanque*, as always.]—for in that in which one true virtue is found, all virtues are reasonably proved to exist; if, nevertheless, they allow themselves to be signified by various names, divided into its genera and forms down to individual species, and then multiplied into numbers—for as many virtues are said to exist as there are those [Note: [Col. 0361] So the codex; M. reads “in whom”] to whom they are given—what is astonishing about the ineffable cause of all things?

Although it lacks genera, forms, individuals, and numbers, nevertheless every genus, every form, every whole, and every number comes from it, since it is itself the first essence of the universe. Everything that exists derives from it the fact that it exists; it is the supreme form of all things. For what does everything that desires desire except it, the beginning of all things, whether knowingly or unknowingly? From it comes every whole, since it is wholly everywhere in itself. From it comes every number, because in itself it is multiplicity without end, number without number.

Since the divine substance, essence, nature, or whatever it may be called, is in itself one, individual, and inseparable—for unity is simple and immutable—it is nevertheless named through various meanings of words according to the dispositions of the human mind, by which it strives to return to the knowledge of its Creator. For a human being, having misused the freedom of his will, cannot arrive at him whom he abandoned without effort except through the effort of labor and the gift of cooperating grace [Note: [Col. 0362D] You should know clearly that no one can even conceive an eagerness for labor without at least the inspiration of God’s prevenient grace.]

### IV

Therefore human reason, understanding its God in various ways under the guidance of truth, calls him by different signs of appellation according to the modes of its understanding. Let us give, by way of example, a few instances out of many.

When the gaze of reason reaches the eternal intellect in which all things are—that is, God himself—in order to behold in him that the divine intellect possesses the fullest and most perfect knowledge of its own eternal and immutable substance, a knowledge surpassing every understanding of a creature, that divine knowledge by which God understands himself is properly called wisdom.

But when that same reason is joined to the eternal intellect, so that it sees in it the incomprehensible knowledge of all the natures created by it, it immediately calls this knowledge “science.” It is again called, as it were properly, science when it is perceived not only in all the good things which God, from himself and in his whole creation, determined before they existed should be made, but also in all the evils that arise through the perverse movement of a rational creature misusing its free will—namely, abandoning its Creator and falling into a lustful desire for the lowest things, although these too were created by him.

### V

This divine and, in a certain sense, general foreknowledge of all the good things of God and the evils of the perverse creature therefore deserved to be called foreknowledge, as has been said. Accordingly, God is said to foreknow the good and the wicked—if wicked things can be foreknown; the manner of this expression will be shown below.

The same knowledge is expressly called predestination for the sake of distinction [Note: [Col. 0363] The codex reads *et* (“and”); M. omits it.] and designation when it is seen only in divine works. Divine operation is recognized not only in the creation of all creatures, but also in those whom God prepared for eternal life through the purpose of his grace; and in that most hidden operation by which, from the evil movements of the reprobate—whom he justly abandons—he provides for the exercise of justice in those whom he has called by his predestination.

It is also recognized in the very qualities of the elements [Note: [Col. 0363] The codex reads *elimentorum*]. Although these qualities appear good by their own nature, since they come from the highest good, they are nevertheless experienced as punishments by those for whom the just Judge has prepared eternal torments according to the desert of his justice [Col. 0363C]. For this reason they are called evil, although they are naturally good.

By the connected reasoning of this argument [Note: [Col. 0363] The codex reads *conexione*], it is concluded that predestination is in God according to substance, though it cannot be understood as being relative [Note: [Col. 0363D] Prudentius rightly observes that predestination in God is always said relatively: “Being,” he says, “is referred to nothing else, whereas predestining can never be said except with reference to something.”]

### VI

Therefore, if by the name “wisdom,” by the name “knowledge,” and by the other names—such as virtue, power, justice, truth, eternity, operation, and the like—we signify, not inappropriately [Note: [Col. 0363] So the codex; M. reads “inappropriately.”], the one immutable essence of God and his indivisible simplicity [Note: [Col. 0363] So the codex; M. reads “the highest.”], it necessarily follows that the nature of that same inseparable essence is also most suitably indicated by the word “predestination.”

Furthermore, if it is impious to teach that there are two essences in God, or two wisdoms, knowledges, virtues, or any of the other things [Note: [Col. 0363] So the codex; M. omits “all.”] predicated of God, and to multiply or triple them or heap them up under any manifold form [Note: [Col. 0363] So the codex; M. omits “all”], whoever is convicted of asserting two predestinations in God is bound by the guilt of impiety.

There is one divine predestination, just as there is one divine operation, one divine wisdom, one divine substance, and one divine will. Tell me, then, G[otescalc], where can the two predestinations you assert be found? True reason does not allow them to exist in God, especially because of the force of necessity which you assert to be present in them.

Scripture cries out: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” [Note: [Col. 0363D] Psalm 111:2], and elsewhere: “Whatever the Lord willed, he made” [Note: [Col. 0363D] Psalm 113:3]. It did not say, “according to all his necessities,” but “according to all his wills,” which are without every necessity.

Although everything that God willed must necessarily exist, no necessity nevertheless either drives his will to do anything or holds it back from doing anything. Who, indeed, resists his will? We say that whatever God willed to be must exist in the sense that we ought to understand that everything God willed to be must exist in no other way than he willed it to exist. What he willed to exist does exist, and it exists because he willed it to be.

Thus, to those who see correctly, nothing other than the divine will itself presents itself as the necessity of the divine will. Just as the things that come to be come to be by God’s will, so by his will they come to be in no other way than as that will itself desired.

For if the necessity of all natures is the will of God, the will of God will be the necessity of the natures. But the will of God is the necessity of the natures that it itself created [Note: [Col. 0363] Corrected reading; the codex and M. read “which.”]. Therefore the necessity of the creatures that God created [Note: [Col. 0363] Corrected reading; the codex and M. read “which.”] will be the will of God. It follows that God’s will itself is necessity, and necessity itself is God’s will [Note: [Col. 0363] So the codex; M. reads “to be”].

Whatever we understand concerning the divine will, we must also understand entirely concerning God’s predestination.

## CHAPTER III. On the fact that reason does not allow two predestinations to exist.

[Col. 0364C]

### I

Let us now briefly repeat everything that the preceding reasoning has gathered together.

First, true reason has taught that the divine will is the highest, principal, and only cause of all that the Father made through his Truth, and that this will is wholly without any necessity that might either drive it or hinder it; rather, it is its own necessity. It is therefore wholly will.

Next, just as “will” is most correctly predicated of God according to substance, so “predestination” is most soundly predicated of him. This can be proved by the argument of wisdom, knowledge, truth [Note: [Col. 0363] So the codex; M. reads “knowledge and truth”], and the other things which no believer doubts are predicated substantially of God [Col. 0364D].

Therefore, if every necessity is removed from the divine will, it will certainly be removed from divine predestination [Note: [Col. 0363] So the codex; M. reads “is removed”]. For in God, willing is not one thing and predestining another, since he willed everything he made by predestining it, and predestined it by willing it [Note: [Col. 0364D] He argues falsely. Although no one predestines anything except by willing it, willing and predestining are nevertheless different. Prudentius observes that willing is said with reference to oneself alone, whereas predestination is referred to other things, and therefore the two are not identical.]

The rational soul also desires to signify its God through many expressions, yet these expressions indicate one and the same thing—namely, the ineffable essence of the Creator himself—even though some of the names are said relatively.

The movement of the human mind, by which it seeks to return to its beginning, strives to ascend step by step. Therefore, according to the modes of its ascent [Note: [Col. 0365] So the codex; M. reads *assentionis*], it finds signs of speech by which, obeying charity, it instructs the senses of those ascending with it or wishing to ascend, concerning what it understands within.

The following conclusion is then formed: if everything predicated of God is one, and nothing is said of God more truly or more honorably than “predestination,” then predestination is one. Error separates it, and blasphemy denies it, and in its place he has invented two predestinations from himself, neither of which can stand.

They therefore rightly do not exist at all, because they are neither true nor false. They are not true, because whatever contradicts truth does not come from truth. Everything that comes from truth must be true; therefore everything that contradicts truth must necessarily not be true.

But your two predestinations, G[otescalc], contradict truth; therefore they are not true.

They are not false either. For everything false seeks to be, under some likeness, what it is not. An example of this in the nature of things is the image of a voice, which the Greeks call ἠχώ (*ēchō*, “echo”), and the shadows of bodies; in art, the figures of paintings [Note: [Col. 0365] So the codex; M. reads “figure”], and other things of this kind.

For likeness, though not every likeness, appears to be the cause of falsity. Accordingly, whatever lacks any likeness to truth is not false. Your predestinations, G[otescalc], are shown to possess no likeness to truth; therefore they are not false.

But what are they? I do not find out, for they are nothing. And who can find nothing?

They are therefore found to be fabulous. For that is fabulous which is neither true nor probable, such as the flight of Daedalus, which never occurred and could never have occurred.

### II

There is also another argument, called the argument from effects to their cause, by which it is concluded that there are not two predestinations of God. The major premise of this argument is: it is necessary that the causes of all things which are contrary to one another should themselves become contrary to one another. Reason forbids one and the same cause to produce diverse things that are contrary to one another.

What, then, is contrary to essence if not non-being? To life, if not death? To justice, if not sin? To blessedness, if not misery?

Since it is evident that all these are contrary to one another, it follows that their causes must also become contrary to one another. For they cannot arise either from one cause or from two causes of the same kind.

Therefore, if the heretic asserts that there are two predestinations in God, of which one, as he says, not only produces life—what it means to be—but also compels it by its own violence, and then produces justice, which blessedness follows; while the other, being contrary in every respect to the former, not only produces sin—what it means not to be—but also compels it, and then produces the death that misery necessarily follows, then the predestinations themselves contradict one another.

But if the divine nature, the highest cause of all things that exist, is rightly believed to be manifold while remaining simple and one, then it is consequently necessary to believe that it admits no controversy within itself.

It therefore remains that there are not two predestinations in God which both produce and compel things that are discordant with one another. Neither of them can exist. For how can one believe that in God’s nature there is a cause compelling something by necessity, when he made everything he made through the goodness of his will and through the will of his goodness? His goodness is his will, and his will is his goodness.

### III

That predestination, therefore, does not exist which by its unavoidable necessity would compel life, justice, and blessedness; nor does that one exist which would compel the opposites of these good things—namely, death, sin, and misery.

This reasoning is concluded by an enthymeme [Note: [Col. 0365] The codex reads *entimematis*], an argument that is always drawn from contraries. Its proposition [Note: [Col. 0365] So the codex; M. reads “exposition”] is as follows:
