God cannot both be the supreme essence and not be the cause only of those things that come from him. But God is the supreme essence. Therefore he is the cause only of those things that come from him.

Sin, death, and misery do not come from God. Therefore God is not their cause.

The same syllogism can also be connected in this way [Note: [Col. 0365] The codex reads *conectitur*, as everywhere]:

God cannot both be the cause of things that exist and be the cause of things that are nothing. But God is the cause of things that exist. Therefore he is not the cause of things that do not exist.

Sin, and its effect—death, to which misery adheres—do not exist. Therefore neither God nor his predestination, which is what he himself is, can be their cause.

### IV

But since, heretic, in your first encounter—during which you incautiously began falsely to assert two predestinations, arrogantly labored insolently to defend them, fled when convicted by scant authority [Note: [Col. 0365] The editor emends; the codex reads *nodica*], and, struck down by the clearest truth, fell silent—you have, by falling silent, devised later things worse than the earlier, so that the reproach of the impious may be fulfilled in you, which is written: “The last error will be worse than the first” [Note: [Col. 0365D] Matthew 27:64].

Although you are not ashamed to deny that you proclaimed two predestinations—a claim which many nevertheless convict you of having made [Col. 0366D]—you are likewise not ashamed to assert again that there is one, but twofold. For in the delirious writings of your confessions, or rather of your betrayals of faith, wishing to defend the origin of your error, you cite the statement of Isidore:

“Predestination is twofold, whether of the elect to rest or of the reprobate to death” [Note: [Col. 0365D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chapter 6],

which you explain in this way:

“For,” he says, “there are not two, because they do not exist as two, but they are twofold—that is, divided into two parts” [Note: [Col. 0366D] Compare Gotescalc’s *Greater Confession*.]

Why, then, most shameless [Note: [Col. 0367] So the codex; M. reads “most imprudent”], weakened, enervated, and abandoned by every aid of truth, do you renew disputes by which you attempt secretly to withdraw yourself from that first shamelessness of yours [Note: [Col. 0367] So the codex; M. omits “your”], as though it were more tolerable and less resistant to truth to proclaim God’s predestination twofold—that is, divided into two—than to call it two?

You strive to prove this doubling or division by the example of charity.

“For,” you say, “what is called twofold predestination, divided between the elect and the reprobate, while being one though twofold, is like what is called twofold charity or love, although there are not two charities but one, though it is also twofold because it is directed toward God and neighbor” [Note: [Col. 0367D] Gotescalc, *Confession* I].

### V

O how truly it has been said of you: “From the locust the caterpillar will emerge” [Note: [Col. 0367] The codex reads *brucus*].

From your blasphemy against predestination [Col. 0367B] has emerged your blasphemy against charity, so that the later sin is the punishment of the earlier sin.

You therefore appear to hold the same belief about charity that you profess about predestination: you assert that both are twofold [Note: [Col. 0367] The codex reads *utranque*, as everywhere].

You concede, unless you are insane, that God is charity, as Scripture bears witness when it says: “God is charity” [Note: [Col. 0368D] John 4:16]. You did not dare deny that predestination is God, since you openly professed this in your confessions. For you wrote that God’s predestination is coeternal with him; would that in the other things you said about predestination you had consulted the truth as you did concerning its coeternity with God [Note: [Col. 0367] So the codex; M. omits “with God”].

There is therefore agreement between us concerning charity and predestination in this respect: charity is God, predestination is God, and God is one—one divine, eternal, immutable essence [Col. 0367C].

Therefore, if charity and predestination are predicated essentially of God, and if the divine essence, as no Catholic doubts, is unity, then charity is the highest and true unity; and predestination too is unity [Note: [Col. 0367] The editor conjectures; the codex reads *praedestinati o unitas sunt*, M. *p. u. sit*.].

Since it is one and alone immutable, it must be without number, because all numbers come from it. And since it lacks mutability, it cannot be multiplied. The first multiplicity is twofoldness; therefore the divine substance, which is unity, is not twofold.

It is beyond doubt that predestination is predicated essentially of God. The essence is unity. Therefore predestination is unity. Unity is not twofold. Therefore predestination is not twofold. Consequently it is not twin (*gemina*) either.

For how can there be a doubling where there is neither number nor plurality? Divine unity lacks numerical plurality. Therefore it lacks twofoldness.

The same reasoning applies to division into two parts [Note: [Col. 0367] So the codex; M. reads *bipertione*]. If predestination is most rightly predicated of the unity of the divine substance, and every true unity is without parts, then predestination is not divided into two parts [Note: [Col. 0367] The codex almost everywhere reads *bipertita*, rarely *bipartita*], because it is not composed of parts.

For just as the divine nature is not capable of genera, forms, differences, or numbers, since it is the cause of all these, so, being the author of every whole, it lacks the joining together of all the parts by which a whole is constituted [Col. 0368A].

With what shamelessness, then, do you not hesitate to declare predestination, which is God, and charity to be divided into two, adding the explanation “that is, twofold”?

Therefore, just as no believer dares to call God twofold, divided into two, or double, because that is impious, so it is sacrilegious to make predestination and charity twofold, double, or divided into two. Whatever is believed concerning God must necessarily also be believed concerning his predestination and charity.

### VI

O eternal charity, how great is the blindness with which those are struck who proclaim you twofold, when they find your heralds declaring you to be twofold, unable to distinguish by intellectual vision the difference between you and your command!

Your command, most powerful mistress, is said to be twofold because it is directed first toward you yourself, who are God, and then toward the neighbor, since you too are loved in him.

Nothing is loved in all things except love—which you are, simple, indivisible, and immutable substance—and nothing loves perfectly except you, the indissoluble bond by which all things are held together.

You therefore love, and you are loved; for this reason your command is called twofold. In part you command that you be loved in yourself, with no created nature interposed; in part you command that you be loved in the neighbor, with a created nature interposed [Note: [Col. 0367] So the codex; M. reads “likewise in itself”].

Are we, because of this, to believe you, indivisible unity, to be twofold? Will our love be multiplied according to the number of things we love [Col. 0368C]?

Do we not love everything that we love with the same love, even though one and the same love is not distributed equally to all—for it is bestowed more upon some and less upon others—while nevertheless remaining in itself without increase or diminution of its condition?

We are not commanded to love God with one love and the neighbor with another. Nor are we commanded, with one part of a single love, to cling to the Creator and, with another part, to cling to the creature. Rather, with one and the same love in its entirety we must embrace both God and neighbor.

The commandment of charity, therefore, is twofold, not charity itself. It is twofold because there is such a distinction in the commandment that God is to be loved for his own sake, whereas the neighbor is not to be loved for his own sake but for God’s sake.

Charity therefore loves God—that is, itself—in all things, and there is no doubling in it; consequently, there is no duplication.

### VII

It has therefore been established by the argument from charity what we ought to understand concerning the doubling of predestination. Predestination likewise is neither twofold, nor divided into two, nor double in itself, although some difference appears in its effects according to the principles of mercy and justice [Col. 0369A].

By one and the same predestination, God—just and merciful, powerful in all things—chose from the mass of the human race, originally corrupted in all except Christ, certain people to whom he was going to give what they would not possess from themselves, namely, his gifts by which they would live. Others he left [Note: [Col. 0369] The codex reads *reliquid*]; they would find in themselves their sins, by which they would perish.

To the former he gave the source from which blessedness would arise; to the latter he did not give it, but permitted the source from which their misery would suffer punishment [Note: [Col. 0369] The codex reads *pasura*].

For the former, it was not they but he himself who prepared life; for the latter, it was not he but they themselves who prepared death. His merciful goodness was the cause of reigning for the former; their own pride was both the cause and the effect of being tormented for the latter.

The other examples that you heap up in order to entangle predestination in a most absurd manner are more indications of your madness than of your error.

Tell me, please, by what reasoning did you take an argument from the bipartite work of God to persuade us of a twofold entanglement of predestination and charity, when God’s work is numerically multiple because it was created, whereas predestination and charity lack both plurality and number?

Because the divine work—that is, the universe of creatures—is divided, for example, into two principal kinds, spiritual and bodily, are we therefore compelled to double the predestination by which God arranged his future works?

But if we are compelled to do so, we will necessarily also be compelled to believe it fourfold, since Augustine says in his little works: “The divine works by which he created and governs the ages are distinguished according to a fourfold principle” [Col. 0369C].

The common virtue by which every wise soul is formed would likewise be multiplied fourfold, since the disposition of the soul is expressed through it in four virtues [Note: [Col. 0369] The codex reads “four”].

As though unity, although it is without all species and parts, did not nevertheless give rise to every species and all parts from itself! Or as though many impressions could not be made in wax from the impression of a single ring [Note: [Col. 0369] So the codex; M. reads “ring’s”]!

What was it that you said about the world divided into four parts? O leaden dagger! Do you perhaps think that predestination consists of two parts in the way that the world is composed of four elements [Note: [Col. 0369] The codex reads *conponitur*, as everywhere], although the world is one?

In the same way, what nonsense do you utter about a twofold tree? Do you perhaps think that the simplicity of predestination should be compared with the branches of trees?

Among those barrels which you order to be prepared for you, you are already wrapped up and suffocating. For rightly you ought to burn in oil and pitch, since you did not fear to teach wrongly both the light of charity and the mystery of predestination [Note: [Col. 0369] Concerning the four barrels, compare Gotescalc’s *Longer Confession*].

## CHAPTER IV. On the one, true, and only predestination of God.

I. It remains, therefore, to discuss the one, true, and only unchangeable [Col. 0370A] [Note: [Col. 0369] The codex reads *incommotabili*, as almost everywhere.] eternal predestination of the divine and all-powerful will, which is never and nowhere deceived. But first we must speak about the distinctive character of that heresy which tears it apart.

This heresy, then—Gotescalcian, if it may be called by that name—has been placed midway between two other mutually opposed heresies: plainly, between the one called Pelagian and the one that opposes it. One diminishes the gift of divine grace; the other condemns freedom of the will.

The Pelagian sect praises the freedom of the rational nature’s will to such an extent that it is sufficient, without the gift of grace, for perfecting human righteousness. Its opposing sect, however, affirms the gift of gratuitous grace, so that, with it alone working in a person and every effort of free will disregarded, every believer attains the summit of righteousness. Thus, as has been said, the one despises the gift of grace, the other the gift of freedom of will: equal in impiety, though differing as sects.

The sect now under discussion, however, is joined in the middle between both of these aforementioned extremes, which oppose each other, in such a way that it partly agrees with them and partly contradicts them, while claiming for itself what it insists that they do not possess [Note: [Col. 0369] The codex reads *uendicet*.]. For when it tries to establish as necessary and unavoidable causes, within the divine predestinations—as it itself imagines—all the virtues by which one reaches blessedness and all the vices by which one is plunged into misery, what else does it seem to advocate except the destruction of God’s gifts—that is, free choice of the will and the assistance of grace—by which, assuredly, the fullness of human righteousness is both begun and perfected? [Col. 0370C]

II. This new sect agrees with the Pelagian sect [Note: [Col. 0369] The codex reads *pelaginae*.] in asserting that the gift of gratuitous grace benefits a person nothing toward producing righteousness, but that only the necessity of predestination does so. It disagrees with it, however, in that it has entirely emptied the powers of free will and, most shamelessly [Note: [Col. 0369] The codex reads *inpudentissime*, as throughout.], by assigning all these matters to the necessity of predestination, denies that free will has power either to do good or to commit evil [Note: [Col. 0369] The codex reads *committere*.].

Yet in striving to remove the inclination of free will, it seems to agree with those who oppose the Pelagian sect; then again it conflicts with them when it maintains that the gifts of divine grace profit a person nothing. For those things are not gifts which occur not by will but by necessity, since it is known to all wise and foolish people that everything given is both offered by the will of the giver and received by the will of the recipient. [Col. 0370D]

The distinctive feature of this heresy, by which it is shown that the two sects between which it has been placed in the middle are without it, is the following. The Pelagian sect judges that the powers of free will, without the assistance of divine grace, are sufficient for accomplishing righteousness; its opponent judges that the gift of grace alone, without the effort of free will, is sufficient. But neither of them presumed to say that the necessity of predestination turns human beings either toward living well and justly or toward living badly and impiously. Therefore the empty necessity of predestination remains the distinctive property of this third heresy.

III. But all these poisonous darts of diabolical impiety are very easily repelled by the impregnable defenses of faith. Let us therefore use that form of reasoning which is called ἀποδεικτική—“demonstrative”—first against those who either deny or doubt that the grace of God exists and prevails for the salvation of the world. Our purpose is not to defeat the Pelagians, or their opponents on the other side—though equal in malice—for this has been sufficiently accomplished by the holy Fathers; rather, it is because the refutation of those two heresies is the overthrow of the heresy now under discussion. For there is no doubt that it flows from them. [Col. 0371B]

Those, therefore, who cannot see the grace of God should look at the salvation of the world. For these two propositions cannot simultaneously hold: that the world is saved and that the grace of God does not exist. If the world were not liberated by the grace of God, how would its salvation follow? Yet the salvation of the world and the grace of God can exist together. If, then, there is salvation for the world, the grace of God will necessarily exist.

We hold most firmly that salvation has come to the world. Let us therefore hold with the greatest certainty that the grace of God has shone forth. Let them hear the Apostle saying: “For the grace of God has appeared” [Note: [Col. 0371D] Titus 2:11.].

Next, those who either entirely deny or doubt the free choice of the human will must be answered in the same way. If you cannot believe that there is free will, you do not believe that the judgment of the world will take place. But if you cannot deny that the world will be judged, you will be compelled to confess free will. For these two things cannot both occur: that the world will be judged and that free will does not exist. By what justice, indeed, will there be a judgment if there is no free will?

Yet these two things can occur together: free will exists, and judgment will take place. If, therefore, there will be a judgment of the world, free choice of the will will necessarily exist. To deny that there will be a just judgment concerning the world is impious. Therefore it is impious not to believe that free will was given to human beings by God.

It has thus been established that human beings possess free will; that the gift of grace exists, insofar as it has been granted; that salvation has come to the world; and that judgment will take place. We must therefore walk along the royal road and turn aside neither to the right nor to the left. That is: free will must not be defended in such a way that good works are attributed to it without the grace of God; nor must grace be defended in such a way that, as though secure because of it, people love evil works. [Col. 0371D]

IV. We must now answer this third heresy, which the perverse thought of Gotescalc, inspired by the devil, added to the others. It plainly flows, with astonishing diabolical subtlety, from the two heresies mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0371] The codex omits *ex*; M. adds it.], since it appears partly to deny them and partly to confess them [Note: [Col. 0371] The codex reads *con fe sina*.]. For, as has been said, one of those heresies contends for free will, the other for grace; but this one [Note: [Col. 0371] M. corrects the codex’s *hic* to *haec*.] endeavors to destroy both free will and the gift of grace simultaneously, and consequently both the salvation of the world and its judgment.

It must therefore be resisted in the following way. Whoever cannot see—or rather, whoever does not wish to confess—that there is no unavoidable or coercive necessity in divine predestination, one that either compels God to do something in his creature or itself constitutes a necessary cause violently forcing rational life either to cling piously to its God by living rightly or to abandon its God by living impiously, should look at free choice of the will and the gifts of grace.

For these things cannot coexist: that free will and the gift of grace should exist together while the necessity of predestination also exists. How can both a necessary, coercive cause and a voluntary, effecting cause operate in one thing? [Note: [Col. 0371] The codex reads *possiunt*; M. reads *possint*.] Freedom of grace or of the will has no place where there is the unchangeable captivity of nature.

Yet these things can occur together: free will can exist with the gift of grace, while the necessity of predestination does not exist. For freedom plainly removes captivity. If, therefore, wherever freedom of will exists together with the gift of grace, the necessity of predestination cannot exist, it follows conversely that wherever the necessity of predestination exists, there can be neither free will nor the gift of grace.

We rightly believe, and perceive with the greatest clarity, that both free will and the gift of grace can exist in a human being. Let us therefore understand with the greatest firmness that the necessity of predestination cannot exist in a human being. Freedom of one’s own will has been given generally to every human being, but it is prepared, assisted, preserved, brought to completion, and crowned by the gift of grace only in the predestined. No one, in general, is driven or held captive by divine predestination; rather, each person is hindered by original and personal sin, according to the hidden but just judgment of God. [Col. 0372C]

V. Therefore, returning to true predestination [Note: [Col. 0371] Thus the codex; M. reads *redeam* (“let me return”).], with its guidance we firmly believe and see most clearly that it is one and only, substantial. God is true, and true is God’s predestination, which, before anything came to be—before the things made by it, through it, and in it came to be—foresaw that they were to be made according to measure, number, and weight, and ordered their making.

For it is the voluntary cause of all creatures and the causative will. Among them he formed the rational creature [Note: [Col. 0371] So the codex; M. reads *edidit*.] to understand him, so that it might be able to enjoy its highest good—that is, contemplation of its Creator—while granting it his gift, namely, freedom of its own will. By using that gift well—that is, by obeying the command of its Creator piously and humbly—it would always live justly and blessedly.

But if it used that same gift badly—namely, if it abandoned its Creator, who is the highest good, and clung through a perverse will to corruptible goods—deserved misery would follow as punishment. For the most shameful poverty of the will most justly follows one who deserts the most abundant and most beautiful blessedness [Note: [Col. 0373] The codex reads *aegestas*.].

The very art, therefore, by which all things were made, the supreme and unchangeable wisdom of God [Note: [Col. 0373] The codex reads *incommotabilisque*.], ordered by predestining that the rational creature should be made in such a way that it imposed no necessity upon it—one that would compel it by unavoidable violence to serve its God even unwillingly, or force it to abandon him even if it wished to cling to him. In the first case there would appear to be captivity of created reason; in the second, injustice on the part of the Creator.

In this way, with the most just and benevolent arrangement, it provided for the beauty of the whole universe’s nature, which it created in its own image and likeness: that it should serve God by will, not by necessity, according to the most upright governance of divine wisdom. Rational life could not have been made otherwise than voluntary, since it was created by that will which is the cause of all things, in the image and likeness of itself.

Or how could the divine will—the supreme reason of the universe, which is bound by no necessity because it possesses its own utterly free power—make the rational creature an image like itself, if it did not create its substance as a free and rational will?

VI. This is proved by the clearest argument, which is drawn from the sin of the first human being. Although, by sinning, he lost the blessed life, he did not lose his substance, which consists in being, willing, and knowing. For he exists, wills, and knows; he wills that he exist and know, and he knows that he exists and wills.

What, then, did the first human being have before sin that he lost after sin? He did not yet possess the blessed life, which would have been granted to him if he had kept the commandment. If we say that he lost free will, then he lost his nature. But if reason teaches that no nature can perish [Note: [Col. 0373D] Prudentius draws attention to this point: rational creatures cannot perish entirely, whereas irrational creatures can.], we are precluded from saying that he lost free will, which is undoubtedly substantial.

God did not create in humanity a captive will, but a free one; and that freedom remained after sin. For there is no sinful soul that does not will blessedness and will misery. What more, then, did he have before sin?

Before he committed sin, he wished to sin, but he did not wish to become miserable. Who, indeed, would dare say that he did not wish to become blessed, when even now, within the nature corrupted through him, the desire for blessedness remains?

Or did he perhaps lose by sinning the vigor and power of free will by which alone he could keep the commandment, if he wished? Accordingly, the vigor and power of free will were not in the first human being from his substance, but from the grace of the Creator. He lost that great gift by using free choice of the will badly. For he did not wish to do what he could do—that is, to keep the commandment—which, after sinning, he cannot do even if he wishes, unless grace assists him.

VII. Hence Augustine says in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*:

“If there were no other proofs, this prayer of the Lord alone would suffice for the case of grace that we defend, because it left us nothing in which we might glory as though it were our own. For, in showing that we must ask from God, it showed that our not departing from God is given only by God. Whoever is not led into temptation [Note: [Col. 0373] The codex reads *infert*.] does not depart from God. This does not at all lie within the powers of free will as they now exist. It had existed in human beings before the fall.

“Yet how powerful that freedom of the will was in the excellence of that first condition became evident in the angels, who, when the devil and his companions fell from the truth, stood firm and merited attaining the perpetual security of not falling—a state in which we are completely certain they now exist.

“After the human fall, God willed that it should belong solely to his grace that human beings approach him; and he likewise willed that it should belong solely to his grace that human beings not depart from him. He placed this grace in the one in whom we obtained our lot, predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things” [Note: [Col. 0373D] Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 7.].

How, then, should we understand what Saint Augustine says in the book *Enchiridion* [Note: [Col. 0373] The codex reads *enceiridon*.]】【：】【“】【: “By using free will badly, the human being both lost himself and free will itself” [Note: [Col. 0374D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 30.]—unless we should perhaps believe that he wished to teach the following: we should not take these words to mean that the first Adam lost his substance, which he could not have lost, but that he changed it into an inferior state, which he could do.

Human nature had been better then, when it possessed both willing and being able—one belonging to substance, the other to grace—than it is now, when it possesses willing alone without being able: that is, nature deserted by its gift.

VIII. Hence the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” [Note: [Col. 0374D] John 15:5.]. He did not say, “You can will nothing.” And the Apostle says: “For to will is present with me, but to accomplish is not” [Note: [Col. 0374D] Romans 7:18.].

Likewise, when the same Apostle says: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy” [Note: [Col. 0374D] Romans 9:16.], this is understood only insofar as there is one who wills and runs. For these two things are naturally implanted in the human being: he wills, and hence he is one who wills; and he desires blessedness, and hence he is one who runs.

Yet it is not of the one who wills or the one who runs to begin, perform, or complete good works; this is the gift of the merciful God. For just as a person placed in the densest darkness, though possessing the faculty of sight, sees nothing because he can see nothing before light comes from outside—though he senses it even while his eyes are closed, and, once they are opened, sees both it and everything around him in it—so the human will, as long as it is covered by the shadow of original and personal sin, is obstructed by that darkness [Note: [Col. 0373] The codex reads *tetigitur*.].

But when the light of divine mercy has shone upon it, it not only destroys the night of all sins and their guilt, but also opens, by healing, the sight of the weakened will and, by purifying it through good works, makes it capable of contemplating that light. But it is now time to return to the subject at hand.

## CHAPTER V. That no one is compelled by God’s foreknowledge or predestination to do either good or evil

I. Since these things are so, the order of matters whose execution is demanded by the usefulness of the present case requires, as a consequence, that—because God is not the author of any evils, and therefore predestination cannot be their effective cause either—we should draw arguments from God’s most certain foreknowledge, arguments established, as I think, by clear rules of reason.

We shall first show that just as God’s foreknowledge does not compel the sins it foreknows to occur, so his predestination does not bring about the sins it never predestines. For if foreknowledge did not make all the things that it foreknew occur, how could predestination bring about all the things that it did not predestine?

By his foreknowledge God foresaw the future evil deeds of human beings, but he is not their maker. By his predestination he is believed not to have predestined the future evil deeds of human beings; how, then, is he thought to make them happen?

What of it? Is it not madness to say that something which God foreknows and does not make occurs by his predestination, when he does not predestine it? If, therefore, both authority teaches and reason shows that God foreknew all sins but did not make them—for how can he be the maker of sins who is both their destroyer and their avenger?—and if he predestined no sin, with what shameless foolishness, or rather wickedness, is he thought by his predestination to compel the existence of things he did not predestine, when by his foreknowledge he does not compel them to occur but permits them?

II. If authority is sought that declares God to be foreknowing all evils that are not from him, but not their efficient cause, the words of our father Augustine in the third book *On Free Will* are sufficient:

“Unless I am mistaken, you would not immediately compel to sin one whom you foreknew would sin, nor would your foreknowledge itself compel him to sin, although without doubt he would sin. For otherwise you would not foreknow that this would happen.

“Thus, just as these two things are not opposed to each other—that you should know by your foreknowledge what another will do by his own will—so God, while compelling no one to sin, nevertheless foresees those who will sin by their own will.

“Why, then, should the just God not punish what, in his foreknowledge, he does not compel to happen? For just as you do not compel by your memory the things that have already happened, so God does not compel by his foreknowledge the things that are to be done in the future [Note: [Col. 0375] The codex omits *sunt*; M. adds it.].

“And just as you remember certain things that you have done, yet did not do everything that you remember, so God foreknows everything of which he is himself the author, yet he is not the author of everything that he foreknows. Of those things of which he is not the evil author, he is the just avenger.

“From this, then, understand already with what justice God punishes sins: because he does not make the things he knows will occur. For if, because he foreknows that they will sin, he ought not to repay sinners with punishment, then neither ought he to repay those who do what is right with rewards, because he likewise foreknows that they will do what is right.

“Rather, let us confess that it belongs to his foreknowledge that nothing future escapes him, and that it belongs to his justice that sin, because it is committed by the will, should not go unpunished in his judgment, just as foreknowledge does not compel it to occur” [Note: [Col. 0375D] Augustine, *On Free Will* III, 4.].

Since these things are so, it is as far from the truth to suppose that the sins of a creature should be attributed to the Creator, even though the things he foreknew would occur must occur, that, when you say that you cannot find how whatever must occur in his creature should not be attributed to him, I, by contrast, cannot find any way—and I affirm that no way can be found, indeed that there is no way—by which whatever must occur in his creature through the will of sinners should be attributed to him.

I therefore altogether cannot find, and affirm that it cannot be found and does not exist, any way in which our sins can be attributed to our Creator God, since even in these very sins I find him worthy of praise—not only because he punishes them, but also because they occur when people depart from his truth [Note: [Col. 0375] M. corrects the codex’s *recedit* to *receditur*.].

III. Accordingly, we must most firmly confess that these two things cannot occur together: that God’s foreknowledge of the sins he permits in his creature, by which he foreknew them, should not be their cause, while his predestination, by which he did not predestine them, should be their cause [Note: [Col. 0375] M. corrects the codex’s *causa* to *causam*.].

Whatever is established concerning sin, whether in general or in particular, must necessarily also be understood concerning its punishment. The punishment of sin is death. Whatever, therefore, is said concerning sin must necessarily be said concerning death. I am not speaking of every kind of death, but only of that which follows sin.

For we say, “We die to sin,” that is, “We die on account of the merit of sin.” Likewise, we say, “We die to sin” when, freed from sin, we live to righteousness.

If, then, the cause of every sin is established neither in God’s foreknowledge nor in his predestination [Note: [Col. 0375] So the codex; M. has *sic est futura* in place of *sit constituta*.], it is most certain that the cause of all death that follows sin is likewise not present in God’s predestination, just as it is not present in his foreknowledge.

Although holy authors customarily speak, in a kind of abusive expression, of people predestined to death, destruction, or punishment, we shall discuss this later, as the Lord reveals it.

IV. For the present, we must consider whether, just as God compels no one to sin either by his foreknowledge or by his predestination, so he compels no one to live piously [Note: [Col. 0377D] “In reality God compels no one to sin, but invites—indeed compels—many to live well by various forms of correction, as he himself says: ‘I will make you walk in my commandments,’ and again: ‘Compel them to enter.’ PRUD.].

Here we must observe that no will possesses true freedom if some cause has compelled it. Therefore, if some cause precedes the human will and forcibly drags it, unwilling, to think or do either good or evil, it follows that it is not truly free, but is not a will at all [Note: [Col. 0378D] “Please carefully observe that the will is in reality preceded by various causes of the healing and merciful God, but, toward evil, by none except the merits of its own perversity, which demand them.” Cf. PRUD.].

For where there is a cause that compels, there is no nature that wills. Yet human nature is not only will but also free will; and its freedom is not false but true, although after sin that freedom has been so corrupted that it is hindered by its punishment from either wishing to live rightly or, if it wishes, from being able to do so. From this misery, as the Apostle says, it is liberated by “the grace of God through Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0378D] Romans 7:25.], while natural freedom still remains—that is, the desire for blessedness, which has been naturally implanted in it. [Col. 0377B]

V. We must not, therefore, concede in any way that any compulsive cause, whether good or evil, precedes the will of a human being or of any other rational nature, lest it take away from that will the merit of its freedom—whether good, if it has lived well with the cooperation of divine grace, or evil, if it has lived badly through its own irrational and perverse movement.

Accordingly, no cause constrains a human being to live either well or badly. God is not the necessary cause of all good things in the way that fire is the cause of burning, the sun of heating or illuminating, or the coercive cause in the way that the senses are the cause of sleeping and thirst the cause of drinking. Rather, he is a voluntary cause, as wisdom is the cause of the wise person, sight of the one who sees, and reason of the one who reasons, and so forth.

Conversely, although the cause of all evils is the perverse movement of a rational substance that misuses the free choice of its will, that cause is not necessary, as sin is the cause of death and death of misery; nor is it coercive, as suffering is the cause of pain and pain of sorrow. It is voluntary, as lust is the cause of greed and greed of fraud.

VI. At this point we must answer those who, unwilling—indeed, scorning—to correct their sins, but complaining [Note: [Col. 0377] Conjecture; the codex reads *querentur*.] about divine action, commonly say shamelessly: “Why did God give human beings free will, by which alone they are convicted of sin? Would it not have been better if he had made them so that they could not sin?”

They also try to conclude this by a most false paralogism, proposing: “If free will is a gift of God; and every gift is good; and every good thing does no harm; therefore free will does no harm” [Note: [Col. 0377] So the codex; M. reads *et liberum*.].

But how can free will not do harm, when we sin through it? Or how does it appear to be God’s gift if it is an occasion of sinning? God ought not to have given any occasion of death. God ought to have made human beings incapable of sinning, since he could have made them so. For it is better not to exist than to exist in misery.

This perverse opinion is easily refuted by considered reasoning. They should be asked: “You who do not fear attributing the responsibility for your sins to the Creator of all things, why are you afraid to sin? Is it because you do not wish to die? Is God unjust—God forbid—when he punishes sins of which he gave the opportunity?”

Free will, therefore, is not the cause of sins, since it is God’s gift.

VII. They should also be asked: “Why are you afraid to die? Is it because you wish to live?” Death is especially to be feared for this reason: that it takes away life, whether of the body, the soul, or both.

If you wish to live, say whether you wish to live blessedly or miserably. No one wishes for a miserable life, since there is no one who does not desire a blessed life. Yet blessed life does not exist if it is acquired by a compelled will or possessed without freedom.

Or: if God had not given human beings free will, by which they might desire blessedness and cleanse themselves through good works, through which he might justly reward them with it, how would he justly crown with the glory of blessed life one who could not serve him by his own will?

VIII. But if you say, “Why did God not give human beings such free will, when he could have done so, that they would wish to live only piously and justly and could not wish otherwise, while they would neither wish nor be able to live impiously and unjustly?” the immediate answer is:

If God had created in human beings a will that could not move itself in every direction, whether rightly or perversely, it would not be wholly free, but free in part and not free in part: free to live justly, but not free to live unjustly.

If, therefore, there were necessity in any part of it, there would not be perfect freedom. Or how could one and the same will simultaneously be called free and not free? These are contradictory statements, because they cannot occur together. If it is true that it is free, it is false that it is not free; but if it is true that it is not free, it is false that it is free.

Thus free will would in no way stand if it limped in any respect.

If you say, “What harm would it do a human being if free will limped in some respect—that is, if he could not use it badly—provided only that, by using it well, he reached eternal life? For it is better to live blessedly than to possess complete freedom of the will,” your blindness is astonishing, or rather pitiable.

Do you not know what justice is? Certainly you do not. For if you knew with complete certainty, you would certainly remain silent.

Hear, then, what justice is. It is defined in this way: justice is giving to each person what is his own.

If no one can take away God’s justice, then stop barking against it [Note: [Col. 0377] So the codex; M. reads *desinite*.]. For how does God, the just judge, give the crown of life to a human being except to one who serves him piously? And who serves God piously except one who keeps his commandments?

And who keeps God’s commandments except the one who abhors doing what he forbids and desires, and strives, to do what he commands, with the assistance of his grace, without which he can do no good?

But what does he forbid except sinning, and what does he command except not sinning? Yet it would be pointless to forbid a human being to commit sin if he did not possess the free power to commit it. For what cannot occur is not forbidden. Or for what reason would he be commanded not to sin if he could in no way sin?

God ought to command what a human being could do. But I do not see how God could have wished to command what a human being could not do.

For, if—as you maintain—God created such free will in human beings that they could not sin by it but could only refrain from sinning, how did he forbid one thing, namely sinning, since, even if it were not forbidden, it would not exist, because what could not exist under the constraint of natural law could not exist? How, then, did he command [Note: [Col. 0379] The codex reads *iusit*.] the other thing, namely not sinning, since, even if it were not commanded to occur, it would necessarily have occurred?

For if a person could not sin because of a force imposed by nature, how could he sin?

IX. These arguments therefore establish that God both gave the first human being such a will and created it in him so freely that through it he could sin and could not sin, just as he could die and could not die.

Accordingly, the first commandment was placed midway between sinning and not sinning. It forbade one thing that could be done by the freedom of nature; it commanded another that both nature and grace permitted to be done. Thus, if he wished to obey it, he would justly [Note: [Col. 0379] Thus the codex; M. reads *et iuste* (“and justly”).] receive blessed life; but if he despised it, he would justly suffer the death he deserved and, consequently, misery.

Since these things are so, no Christian should doubt that God, the Creator of the universe, gave human beings free will—that is, the choice of either good or evil—and that he ought to have given it in no other way than as wholly free. Through this he would demonstrate what nature could accomplish in human beings without grace, what grace could accomplish in nature, what belongs to the merit of righteousness, what to the merit of sin, and finally what belongs to the gift of his ineffable generosity.

Thus, whoever diminishes free choice of the will—whether by reducing it, entirely removing it, or blaspheming it [Note: [Col. 0379] The codex reads *blasfemando*.]—is, beyond doubt, shown by both divine and human authority to be an enemy of the whole Christian discipline.

Hence Augustine says in the book *On True Religion*:

“This defect, which is called sin, if it seized an unwilling person like a fever, the punishment that follows the sinner and is called condemnation would rightly appear unjust. But sin is so entirely a voluntary evil that it is in no way sin if it is not voluntary. This is so evident that neither the small number of the learned nor the multitude of the unlearned disagrees about it.

“Therefore either we must deny that sin is committed, or we must confess that it is committed by the will. But no one rightly denies that the soul has sinned who admits both that it is corrected through repentance [Note: [Col. 0379] Thus the codex; M. reads *corrigi eam* (“that it be corrected”).] and that forgiveness is granted to the repentant, while the one who perseveres in sins is condemned by God’s just law [Note: [Col. 0379] So the codex; M. has *infra Dei legem* and in the margin *al. iusta Dei lege*.].

“Finally, if we do evil not by the will, no one at all should be rebuked or admonished; and once these things are removed, the Christian law and the discipline of every religion must necessarily be abolished.

“Sin is therefore committed by the will; and since there is no doubt that sin is committed, I see no reason to doubt that souls possess free choice of the will. For God judged that his servants would be better if they served him freely; and this could in no way happen if they served not by their will but by necessity” [Note: [Col. 0379D] Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 14.].

## CHAPTER VI. That every sin arises from no source other than the free choice of one’s own will

I. We must therefore hold with the greatest firmness that no sin—that is, no evil deed—and no punishment of sin arises from any source other than a human being’s own will, which misuses free choice [Note: [Col. 0379D] Observe that sin indeed arises from the human being’s own will, but its punishment is inflicted by God as just judge. Cf. Prud.].

For true reason finds no other way in which this can occur. To demonstrate this, we must use an argument drawn from comparison [Note: [Col. 0379] So the codex; M. reads *a rei comparatione*.].

If the human will is according to nature—a point about which it would be supremely foolish to doubt—then there is no doubt that it is not the highest of all wills. The chief reason is that it is mutable. For if it were the highest of all, how could it be mutable? It is therefore not supreme.

But since we see that it participates in supreme reason, we cannot doubt that it is itself a rational substance.

Furthermore, if rational nature rightly precedes irrational nature, it follows that mutable rational nature is inferior to unchangeable rational nature [Note: [Col. 0379] The codex reads *incommotabili*, as almost everywhere.], but superior to irrational and mutable nature.

We must therefore in no way believe that the supreme divine will of all things either persuaded the rational will it created to sin or compelled it to sin.

But how could an irrational will, such as that of animals, overcome a will better than itself, especially since, being without reason, it cannot itself sin? How could it persuade or compel to sin a will stronger than itself, one that uses reason?

There remains a will equal to it. If such a will exists, it is either free from vice or corrupted. But if it is free from vice, how could it persuade or compel vice to arise in its equal will? For no will free from vice produces vice in another will.

If, however, it is corrupted, it was not equal to the human will before sin. Every will free from corruption is better than one that is not.

It follows that every occasion of evil deed, and every punishment of it, lies in the human being’s own will.

## II

Hence Augustine, in the first book *On Free Choice*: “Therefore it follows that, since nothing equal or superior to a mind ruling and in possession of virtue makes it the slave of desire, on account of justice, while nothing inferior can do this on account of weakness—as the matters established between us teach—no other thing makes the mind the companion of desire than its own will and free choice; and it is just that it should pay the penalties for so great a sin. For what? Is that penalty itself to be considered small, namely, that desire rules over it, and, stripped of the wealth of virtue, drags it, poor and needy, through various places: now approving false things as true, now even defending them, now disapproving what it had previously approved, and nevertheless rushing into other falsehoods; now suspending its assent, and often fearing evident arguments; now despairing of the entire discovery of truth and clinging utterly to the darkness of folly; now striving toward the light of understanding and then again falling back through weariness, while in the meantime that kingdom of desires rages tyrannically and disturbs the whole human mind and life with various and contrary storms? Here with fear, there with desire; here with anxiety, there with empty and false joy; here with the anguish of a lost thing that was loved, there with the ardor of attaining what was not possessed; here with the pains of an injury received, there with the torches of vengeance—avarice can constrict it in every direction, luxury dissipate it, ambition add to it, pride inflate it, envy torment it, sloth bury it, obstinacy provoke it, submission afflict it, and countless other things that frequent and exercise the kingdom of that desire. [Note: [Col. 0381] The codex reads *nihil hominus* (“nevertheless”); M. reads *coarctare* (“constrict”); the codex reads *desipare* (“dissipate”); for *adjicere* (“add”), M. has *adurere* (“burn”) and records the marginal alternative *addicere* (“enslave”); the corrected codex reads *frequentantur* (“are frequented/exercised”).]

“Can we finally regard as no penalty at all what, as you see, all who do not cling to wisdom must necessarily suffer?” [Note: [Col. 0381] The word *non* (“not”) is omitted by the codex; M. reads *non adhaerent* (“do not adhere”), with *inhaerent* (“cling”) added in the margin.] [Note: [Col. 0381D] Augustine, *On Free Choice* I, 11.]

It is therefore established that what each person chooses to pursue and embrace lies in the will, and that the mind is brought down from the citadel of mastery and the right order by nothing except the will. It is also clear that, when someone uses a thing badly, it is not the thing that should be blamed, but the person who uses it badly.

## III

For this reason, we may now observe and consider whether doing wrong is anything other than pursuing, while neglecting eternal things—which the mind enjoys through itself and perceives through itself, and which, once loved, it cannot lose—those temporal things that are sensed through the body, the basest part of the human being, and that can never be certain, as though they were great and wondrous things.

For it seems to me that all wrongdoing—that is, sins—are contained in this one kind of act: whenever someone turns away from divine and truly abiding things and turns toward mutable and uncertain things. Although these things have been rightly placed in their own order and fulfill a certain beauty of their own, it is nevertheless the mark of a perverse and disordered mind to submit to those things by following which it ought rather, by divine order and right, to have mastery and which it ought to lead at its command.

# CHAPTER VII  
## That free choice of the will is to be counted among the goods that God bestows on human beings, although they use it badly. What is the cause of sin, and what is sin?

### I

Free choice, then, is not evil when someone uses it badly; rather, it must be counted among the goods bestowed on the human being by divine generosity, especially since it was given chiefly so that it might be used well. For human will is especially reproved in this respect: it preferred to use perversely the gift that had been given to it for right use.

But it is reasonably asked why it was able to use it badly. The answer is: because that is not a great good which no one can use badly. There are great goods bestowed by God on human beings, intermediate goods, and lesser goods. No one, indeed, uses the great goods badly. For who can use prudence, temperance, courage, or justice badly? But with intermediate and lesser goods, according to the choice of the user, one may live either rightly [Note: [Col. 0381] Thus the codex; M. has “use.”] or perversely.

For example, someone skilled in the discipline of disputation called dialectic—a discipline which, without anyone doubting it, is granted to human beings by God—can, if he wishes, use it well, since it was most certainly given for this purpose: it teaches those who are ignorant, distinguishes truth from falsehood, divides what is confused, gathers what is separate, and seeks truth in all things. Conversely, he can live disastrously [Note: [Col. 0381] Thus the codex; M. has “use.”], using it for a purpose for which it was not given: approving falsehoods as truths, leading others into error, confusing the minds of the simple with false arguments, and, by confusing them, darkening them so that their inner eye, which is the mind, cannot reach knowledge of truth itself in its purity.

Therefore, just as no one would deceive or be deceived by that discipline if it were counted among the great goods, so, if free choice were placed among the great goods, no one using it badly would fall at first, and no one would subsequently be punished for using it badly.

Who, however, does not see that human beings very frequently use badly the lesser goods entrusted to them by God—such things as bodily forms and their beauties—by which the vast multitude of human beings mortally gratifies various desires, although they would use those same things piously, justly, and rightly for the merit of their blessedness if they referred them to the praise of the Creator?

### II

But so that we may establish these points more clearly, the eloquent words of the holy Father Augustine should be presented. For he says in the second book *On Free Choice*:

“It has been established between us that the nature of the body is on a lower level than the nature of the mind, and therefore that the mind is a greater good than the body. If, then, among bodily goods we find some things that a human being can use wrongly, and yet for that reason we do not say that they ought not to have been given, since we acknowledge them to be goods, what wonder is it if there are also in the mind certain goods that we can use wrongly? But whatever things are goods could not have been given except by him from whom all goods come.

“You see how much good is lacking from a body that has no hands, and yet someone who works with his hands at savage or disgraceful deeds uses them badly. If you saw someone without feet, you would admit that a great deal of good was lacking from the integrity of his body; and yet you would not deny that someone who used his feet to harm another or dishonor himself used his feet badly.

“With our eyes we see this light and distinguish the forms of bodies, and this is among the most beautiful features of our body. Hence these members have been placed at a certain summit of dignity, and the use of the eyes contributes to preserving health and to many other conveniences of life. Yet many people do many disgraceful things with their eyes and compel them to serve desire. And you see how much good is lacking from the face when the eyes are absent. But when they are present, who gave them except God, the giver of all goods?

“Therefore, just as you approve these things in the body and, without looking at those who use them badly, praise him who gave these good things, so you ought to acknowledge free will—without which no one can live rightly—as both a good and divinely given, and confess that those who use this good badly should be condemned rather than that he who gave it should be said not to have ought to give it.” [Note: [Col. 0383D] Augustine, *On Free Choice* II, 18.]

### III

“Therefore, the virtues by which one lives rightly are great goods; the forms of any bodily things, without which one can live rightly, are lesser goods; but the powers of the mind [Note: [Col. 0383] Thus the codex; elsewhere, “of the soul.”], without which one cannot live rightly, are intermediate goods.

“No one uses the virtues badly; but with the other goods—that is, the intermediate and lesser ones—anyone can use them not only well but also badly. And no one uses virtue badly because the work of virtue is the good use of those things which we can also use badly. But no one uses something badly by using it well.

“Thus the abundance and greatness of God’s goodness has provided not only great goods but also intermediate and lesser goods. His goodness is more deserving of praise in the great goods than in the intermediate, and more in the intermediate than in the lesser goods; but it is more deserving of praise in all of them together than it would be if he had not bestowed them all.” [Note: [Col. 0383D] Augustine, the same work II, 19.]

### IV

“Therefore, the will, adhering to the common and immutable good, rules the first and great goods of the human being, although it is itself a certain intermediate good. But the will turned away from the immutable and common good and turned toward its own good, or toward an external or an inferior good, sins.

“It turns toward its own good when it wishes to be its own master; toward an external good when it strives to know what belongs to others or whatever does not pertain to itself; toward an inferior good when it loves bodily pleasure.

“Thus the human being, having become proud, curious, and lustful, is excluded from another life which, in comparison with the higher life, is death. Yet this life is governed by the administration of divine providence, which orders everything in fitting places [Note: [Col. 0383] “Administration,” with double *m* in the codex.] and distributes to each person according to his merits.

“Thus it comes about that neither are those goods in any way evil which sinners desire, nor is free will itself evil, though we have discovered that it must be counted among certain intermediate goods. Rather, evil is its turning away from the immutable good and its turning toward mutable goods. Since this turning away and turning toward are not compelled but voluntary, a deserved and just penalty of misery follows them.” [Note: [Col. 0384D] Augustine, the same work, at the end.]

### V

“But perhaps you will ask: since the will is moved when it turns away from the immutable good toward a mutable good, from where does this movement arise, which is certainly evil, although free will, because without it no one can live rightly, must be counted among goods?

“For if this movement—that is, the will’s turning away from the Lord God—is unquestionably sin, can we call God the author of sin? This movement, then, will not be from God. From where, therefore, will it be?

“If I answer you, when you ask this, that I do not know, perhaps you will be more sorrowful [Note: [Col. 0383] The codex has “perhaps,” as above.]? Yet I shall have answered truly. For what is nothing cannot be known.

“Only hold fast to unshaken piety, so that no good may occur to you, whether in sensation, understanding, or thought of any kind, which is not from God. Thus no nature occurs which is not from God. Whenever you see measure, number, and order in anything, do not hesitate to attribute it to God the artisan.

“But if you remove these things completely from anything, absolutely nothing will remain. For even if some beginning of a form remains in which you find neither measure, nor number, nor order—for wherever these are present, the form is perfect—you must remove that beginning of form which seems to lie beneath the artisan like matter for completion.

“For if the perfection of form is good, the beginning of form is already some good. Thus, once every good has been completely removed, absolutely nothing will remain [Note: [Col. 0383] Thus the codex; M. has: “not indeed something, but absolutely nothing will remain.”]. But every good is from God; therefore no nature exists that is not from God.

“Consider, then, where that movement of turning away belongs, which we admit to be sin, since it is a defective movement; and do not doubt that it does not belong to God, since every defect is from nothing. Yet because this defect is voluntary, it lies within our possibility [Note: [Col. 0383] Elsewhere, “power.”].

“For if you fear it, you must not will it; but if you do not will it, it will not occur. What, therefore, is safer than to be in that life where what you do not will cannot happen to you?

“But since a human being cannot rise voluntarily in the same way that he fell voluntarily, let us hold fast in firm faith to the hand of God stretched down to us from above—that is, to our Lord Jesus Christ; let us await him with certain hope and desire him with burning love.” [Note: [Col. 0385D] Augustine, the same work II, 20, at the beginning.]

# CHAPTER VIII  
## On the difference between human nature and its free choice

### I

Now we must knock at divine mercy, asking that it deign to open for us the difficulty of the question before us. For what distinguishes the free will of the human being, which arises from nature, from his free choice, which is clearly a gift of the Creator, is far removed and placed in the hidden recess of profound understanding.

Since Saint Augustine repeatedly impresses this upon us, we believe most clearly that the substantial trinity of the inner human being is contained in these three: essence, will, and knowledge. [Note: [Col. 0386D] Augustine, *Confessions* XIII, 11.]

For if supreme Wisdom, which wished to create human nature like itself, is one and three in itself, it rightly made the human being in this way: essence, will, and knowledge, which are three and yet one. For to be in rational life is not one thing and to will another, nor is to will one thing and to know another. Rather, its being is a knowing will; its will is a knowing essence; and its knowledge is a willing essence.

### II

These three, then, are one and one nature. Moreover, the whole nature of the soul is will. But we must consider whether that will, just as it is naturally will, is also naturally free, or whether it has from nature only that it is will, while it has from the gift of the Creator that it is free.

For although every good is either God himself or whatever is from him, we do not say that all goods which are from him are made by him in the same way. Of all the goods that God created, some arise from his goodness, others from his generosity.

Those which arise from his goodness are made substantially, together with all the accidents that naturally adhere to them, such as qualities, quantities, relations, positions, states, places, times, acting, and being acted upon. In this tenfold number, every created substance and all its natural accidents can be included.

Nor should it disturb us if certain things are called accidents [Note: [Col. 0385] The codex has “things that approach.”] that do not arise from nature. For they are not truly accidents, but absences or defects—that is, corruptions—of natural accidents. [Note: [Col. 0385] Thus the codex.]

Those things that come through the Creator’s generosity are properly called his gifts. This must be believed, since in every act of giving three things must necessarily be understood: the one who gives, what is given, and the one to whom it is given.

### III

Accordingly, God, the maker of all things, first created the substances of the universe that was to be made by him through his goodness; then he arranged to give gifts to each according to its degrees, through his generosity.

Among these substances, he established the nature of the human being in rational will [Note: [Col. 0385] Thus the codex; M. has “rational.”]. For the human being is not will simply because he is will, but because he is rational will. Remove rational will, and there will be no human being.

This does not mean, however, that if you remove the human being there is no rational will, for rational will is known to exist not only in the human being but also in the angel and in God himself.

It must therefore necessarily be considered what this human will has from nature and what it has from gift. Since it is clearer than daylight that it has naturally the fact that it is a substantial will, it remains to ask from where it has its freedom.

For it is not simply called will, but free will. If, therefore, it has from its own establishment [Note: [Col. 0385] Thus the codex; M. adds in the margin, perhaps “institution”; but without reason, since the reading “establishment” should be retained here and shortly afterward.] only that it is will, and not that it is free, it follows—if it is free, which it would be absurd to deny—that freedom was given to it by the gift of its Creator.

The difference between nature and free choice will therefore be such as this: human will received from its own establishment not only that it should exist, but also that it should be free.

### IV

The proposed question has still not been unlocked. For by the arguments presented above it has been established that the all-powerful divine will, which is constrained and impeded by no law, ought to create a will like itself, governed by the eternal laws of its Creator, constrained by no force from doing what it wished or compelled to do what it did not wish.

Whatever it preferred to do, whether good or evil, would not exceed the supremely wise discipline of its Creator, which would receive all the movements of free will, whether upright or perverse, within fitting orders.

The creator of the universe must not be believed to have made rational will servile. Or perhaps reason is not substantially present in the human being? Who would dare say this, since the true definition of the human being is: “The human being is a rational substance capable of wisdom”?

What wonder, then, if freedom belongs by nature to human will, when it is no wonder that reason is made through it? Or how could a servile will have been made by nature, when that future freedom is promised to it as the reward of obedience, since there will be no desire to sin?

God in no way destroys what he created in nature. Rather, he converts certain natural goods that he created into something better—not in order to remove from them what he made, but to add to them what he wished to add.

### V

Let the human body before sin serve as an example. It was first animal and afterward destined to become spiritual by merit of obedience, without any intervening death.

Why was it first animal? Was it because what had to be added to it on account of observance of the commandment was still lacking—that is, the spiritual state—and therefore it was animal because something was lacking from the perfection of nature, but was destined to be spiritual because nothing would be lacking from it?

From this it can be understood that the first human will was created naturally free. Yet something would have been added to it if it had wished to keep God’s commandment: just as the animal body could die because it was not yet perfect, so free will, still animal in merit because it was mortal, could sin because it was not yet perfect.

This perfection of freedom would certainly have been completed after the commandment had been kept, when the will to sin would have been entirely removed. Such will belong to that future freedom which our Lord Jesus Christ will give to those who love him.

But to strengthen this reasoning, let us use the argument that proceeds from the lesser to the greater. If we naturally have free sense in the eyes of our body, so that we use their light to see honorable or disgraceful things, what wonder is it if God established in the human being a will that would use its natural freedom honorably if it did not sin, or disgracefully if it did sin?

If, then, something is carried out naturally in our body, why should it not also be carried out in our soul, especially [Note: [Col. 0387] *Cum* is omitted in the codex and added conjecturally.] since wherever rationality is present, freedom must necessarily be present? Human will is substantially rational. Therefore it is substantially free.

### VI

Since this is so, we must consider more carefully what free choice is. It was unquestionably granted by God to human nature [Note: [Col. 0387] The codex has the misspelling “granted.”].

We habitually express both the substance of the human being and the gift in the same words, so that it is uncertain what they imply as nature and what as gift. For what else do we understand when we hear “free choice of the will” except the movement of free will? These words all express the nature of human will.

For will is free, rational, and mutable. Or, if it is mutable—which must certainly be admitted, since only God is rightly believed to be immutable—one may ask from where it is mutable.

The truest answer is: from the same source from which it is free. It is free by nature; therefore it is mutable by nature.

### VII

Next it is asked: from where is it moved? The answer is: by itself, because it is free.

Can it be moved by something else? It can, because there is a greater and better will by which it can be moved. What will is that? None other than the supreme and divine will, which created it and moves it.

Can it be moved by an equal or an inferior? [Note: [Col. 0387] Thus the codex; M. has “or by an inferior.”] It cannot. For if everything that moves is greater than what is moved, greater things necessarily do not allow themselves to be moved by lesser things. By similar reasoning, equals cannot move equals; otherwise they would not be equals, as movers and moved. Thus equals are moved by a cause stronger than themselves. [Note: [Col. 0387] M. has “by a stronger cause.”]

It plainly follows that human will is moved either by itself or by the one who created it.

When it is moved by itself, can it be moved both rightly and perversely? It can do either, as it wishes, because it possesses free movement. What if it is moved by the one who created it? Who would dare doubt that a right movement arises from that source?

Therefore, since the question concerns human will before sin, we must grant that by its own movement it could turn toward its God in willing, so as not to sin, and could turn away from him, in order to sin; but that it could be moved by the superior cause only so that it would not wish to sin.

If, then, as the investigation of the preceding reasoning teaches, the natural movement of the human substance—by which it would first turn toward knowing and loving its God and then toward itself—is understood to be effected by a twofold cause, one superior, which is common to all natures, and the other inferior, which is established in the human substance itself, what prevents us from referring all the upright movements of our mind to our Creator?

He moves himself without time or place; he moves our created spirit through time without place; and he moves our bodies through time and place.

He also inserted into our nature a cause by which we could move ourselves freely, rationally, and voluntarily toward attaining those things that we ought to pursue. This movement is rightly called the free choice of our will, because it is subject to our power.

For according to our right judgment we could direct it along a straight course; we could also restrain it. From where, then, would we have such a movement and such power except from God, who bestowed this distinctive gift upon us—something that would be both no small good of our nature and a praiseworthy gift of the Creator?

To him we ought to give ineffable thanks, not only because through the abundance of his goodness he created the nature of our mind rational, free, voluntary, and mobile, but also because through the gift of his generosity he granted us the ability to move ourselves by our own inclination, rationally, freely, and voluntarily.

This movement has been granted to no animal except the human being. If we are commanded to praise God for the beauty of the natures he created without rational freedom of will, how much more should we praise him for our substance, to which he gave such a gift that by its own movement it could adhere to its Creator and could restrain that movement, if it wished, so as not to depart from him?

Indeed, if this movement did not occur under the proper power of human will, who could live rightly? Who could then sin, since it was given by God for living well and in no way for living badly?

### VIII

Let us therefore hear Saint Augustine:

“If the human being were some good and could do rightly only when he wished, he ought to have free will, without which he could not do rightly. We must not believe that God gave it for this reason merely because sin is also committed through it.

“There is therefore sufficient reason why it ought to have been given: without it the human being could not live rightly. That it was given for this purpose may also be understood from this: if someone uses it for sinning, divine punishment is inflicted upon him. This would not be just if free will had been given not only so that one might live rightly but also so that one might sin.

“For how could the person who used his will for the purpose for which it was given be justly punished? But now, when God punishes the sinner, what else does he seem to say to you except: Why did you not use free will for the purpose for which I gave it to you—that is, for doing what is right?

“Moreover, how could that good exist by which justice itself is commended in condemning sins and honoring right actions, if the human being lacked free choice of the will? For what is not done by will would be neither sin nor a right action; and consequently both punishment and reward would be unjust if the human being did not have free will.

“Justice ought to be present both in punishment and in reward, since this is one of the goods that are from God. God therefore ought to have given the human being free will.” [Note: [Col. 0389D] Augustine, *On Free Choice* II, 1.]

In these words we must be attentive, lest anyone confuse substance and movement when hearing “free will,” which is unquestionably substantial. Saint Augustine therefore used “free will” in the manner of speech by which it means the movement or choice of free will, just as we commonly use causes in order to signify their effects through substantial causes.

Hence we have the expression “the circuit of true reason” for “the circuit of true reasoning”—for true reason is substantially in the human being, and its movement is reasoning—just as “hand” means the work of the hand, “foot” means walking, “tongue” means words, and other expressions of the same kind.

### IX

This, then, unless I am mistaken, has been established through the extensive circuit of the reasoning: the causes of all right actions, by which one reaches the crown of righteous blessedness, are established in the free choice of the human will, with divine grace preparing it and cooperating with it through a gratuitous and manifold gift; but the causes of wrongdoing, by which one rushes into the dishonor of just misery, have their principal root fixed in the perverse movement of free choice, with the devil’s persuasion.

How great, then, is the madness of those who falsely imagine and shamelessly assert that the causes of such things are inevitable and coercive necessities contained in divine predestination—and finally, a matter greatly to be lamented, thrust themselves and those who agree with them down to the destruction of eternal death on account of their error!

Whether, then, such a distinction is found between human free choice and its substance, so that nature is established in rational will but free choice in its freedom [Note: [Col. 0389D] This distinction appears less true. For rational will is in reality free, whereas free choice is nothing other than the faculty of choosing good or evil. [Col. 0390D] Compare Prudentius.]; or whether it is found in the movement of naturally free will; or whether it is found in the gift of understanding, which has been bestowed upon all in common; or, as is considered more probable, whether these three taken together constitute free choice—namely, free, intelligent movement—so that, just as the substance in which it exists is threefold—for it exists, wills, and knows—so that triad too is threefold, free, moving, and intelligent; nevertheless it remains established that every sin and the punishments of sin have arisen from its perverse use, and that in every sinner it remains active for living badly.

# CHAPTER IX  
## That foreknowledge and predestination are predicated of God not properly but by analogy with temporal things

### I

The main text of the question now requires us to consider whether, properly or abusively, Scripture, Holy Scripture, and the holy Fathers say that God foreknew or predestined either the whole universe that he substantially created or whatever aspect of divine administration appears temporally within it—namely, those things that he himself does, not those that he permits to happen.

Here we must first note that almost nothing worthy of God is said about God, and that nearly all signs—whether nouns, verbs, or other parts of speech—cannot properly be said of God. For how could sensible signs, that is, things attached to bodies, adequately signify that nature which is removed from every bodily sense and is scarcely reached even by the purest mind, transcending every understanding?

Nevertheless, the laborious poverty of human reasoning after the sin of the first human being uses such signs, so that the Creator’s abundant sublimity may in some way be believed and indicated.

Moreover, if all signs of words are not according to nature but are invented by human agreement, what wonder is it if they are insufficient to express that nature which alone is truly said to be?

### II

Accordingly, among the verbal signs that human and divine ingenuity uses, according to the custom of human speech, to signify God himself or his administration in the whole creation, some are quasi-proper. Examples among verbs are “I am,” “you are,” “he was,” and “to be”; among nouns, “essence,” “truth,” “virtue,” “wisdom,” “knowledge,” “predestination,” and similar terms.

Since these signify in our nature whatever is first and best—that is, the substance itself and its best qualities, without which it cannot be immortal—they are not absurdly referred to the one best principle of all goods, which is God.

Others are alien, that is, transferred, and usually arise from three sources: similarity, contrariety, and difference.
