Examples of the first source are: “The arm of the Lord—to whom has it been revealed?” [Note: [Col. 0389] Thus the codex; M. omits “has it been.”] [Note: [Col. 0390D] Isaiah LIII, 1.] Likewise: “Your hands made me” [Note: [Col. 0390D] Job X, 8.]; and similarly: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” [Note: [Col. 0390D] Psalm XXX, 16.].

These are rightly called alien, since the divine substance is entirely without the outlines of bodily members. Yet they are fittingly predicated of it by a certain similarity. For nature has placed bodily powers in the arms, action in the hands, sight in the eyes, and hearing in the ears, as in their seats. Thus divine power and operation, as well as his sight and generosity, are most aptly called by the names of those seats.

Examples belonging to the third source are drawn from the disturbances of our minds to signify the immutable substance, such as anger, fury, indignation, fear, sadness, and the rest. These are taken from the category of difference; no similarity with the divine nature is found in them, but they are habitually transferred solely because signification requires it, in the most remote and abusive manner.

### III

There remain those expressions taken from the category of contrariety. They possess such force in signifying that, by a certain privilege of their excellence, the Greeks rightly call them *enthymemata* [Note: [Col. 0391] The codex has “entimemata.”], that is, “conceptions of the mind.”

Although everything expressed by the voice is first conceived in the mind, not everything conceived in the mind appears to possess the same force of signification when it is poured into the senses with fervor [Note: [Col. 0391] Thus both M. and the codex; “fervor” is the reading.].

Therefore, just as the strongest of all arguments is the one taken from contraries, so the most suitable of all vocal signs is the one drawn from the same category of contrariety.

Some of these are expressed absolutely, others in combination. The form of the absolute expressions is: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent” [Note: [Col. 0391D] 1 Corinthians I, 19.].

This is rightly understood in terms of contrariety, as though he were openly saying: “I will destroy the foolishness of the foolish; I will reject the imprudence of the imprudent.”

This is clearly understood from the words of the Apostle: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” [Note: [Col. 0391D] 1 Corinthians III, 19.].

For if all wisdom is from the Lord God, how is God to be understood as destroying what is from him? What is believed concerning wisdom must likewise be believed concerning prudence. For God destroys no virtue in a human being, and an example of this absolute form is not easily found concerning God.

Textual apparatus and editorial notes (keyed to the passages above):

- Chapter VII.I: “bestowed by God on human beings”: M. reverses the order, “bestowed on human beings by God.” In “one may live either rightly,” the codex reads *vivitur* (“one lives”), while M. reads *utitur* (“one uses”).
- Chapter VII.II: For “whatever things are goods,” the codex reads *quae* (“which things”), while another reading is *quia* (“because”). In “distinguish the forms,” the codex reads *internoscimus* (“we distinguish”), while M. has *cognoscimus* (“we recognize”); the codex spells “are present” as *assunt*.
- Chapter VII.III: “Powers of the mind”: another reading is “powers of the soul” (*animae*). The corrected M. reading is *quia* (“because”), whereas the codex has *qui* (“who”).
- Chapter VII.IV: The codex spells “administration” as *amministratione*. The word *sedibus* (“places”) is omitted by the codex and supplied by M.
- Chapter VII.V: The codex has *poenitus* for *penitus* (“completely”); this spelling recurs throughout. Another reading has “even that very beginning of form” (*etiam ipsam*) for “that beginning of form.”
- Chapter VIII.I: The codex reads *multociens* for *multoties* (“many times”), and does so throughout.
- Chapter VIII.II: The codex reads *accedentia* (“things that approach”) for *accidentia* (“accidents”).
- Chapter VIII.III: The codex reads *rationali* (“rational”) where M. has *rationabili* (“endowed with reason”). The codex’s reading is “it must necessarily be considered”; M. has “it is necessary to consider.”
- Chapter VIII.VI: The codex spells “granted” as *concesum*.
- Chapter VIII.VII: M. reads *quae* (“which”) for the codex’s *qua* (“by which”); M. also reads “or by an inferior” where the codex has “or an inferior.” The codex has *perversae* for *perverse*, *a minoribus* (“by lesser things”) for *minoribus* (“lesser things”), *fortiore* (“stronger”) for *fortiori* (“stronger [cause]”), and *voluntariae* for *voluntarie* (“voluntarily”). The codex spells “granted” as *concesus*. For “praise God for the beauty,” M. reads *laudare de pulchritudine* (“praise concerning the beauty”).
- Chapter VIII.VIII: The codex reads simply *debuit* (“ought”), while M. continues “but also …,” as indicated in the apparatus.
- Chapter VIII.IX: M.’s note judges the proposed distinction less true: rational will is in fact free, while free choice is nothing other than the capacity to choose good or evil; compare Prudentius. M. records the alternative sequence *liber, notus, intelligentia* (“free, known, intelligence”) for the codex’s *liber motus intelligentiae* (“free movement of intelligence”).
- Chapter IX.I: The codex reads *poene* for *paene* (“almost”).
- Chapter IX.II: The corrected reading is *accidentia* (“accidents”); both the codex and M. have *accedentia*. In Isaiah 53:1 the codex retains “has been” (*est*), while M. omits it.
- Chapter IX.III: The codex spells *enthymemata* as *entimemata*. Both M. and the codex read *fervore* (“with fervor”).

## IV.

Nor is this surprising, since nothing is contrary to God except non-being, because he alone is the one who said, “I am who I am” [Note: [Col. 0391D] Exodus 3:14]. But the other things that are said to exist neither exist altogether, because they are not what he is, nor are they altogether non-existent, because they are from him, who alone is being.

Unless perhaps we say that the things spoken of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the property of his humanity can likewise be said of his divinity, on account of the inseparable unity of the one person in two substances. If this is not absurdly believed possible, let us see what is written in the Law: [Col. 0392A] “Cursed is everyone who has been hung on a tree” [Note: [Col. 0391D] Deuteronomy 21:23]. This was undoubtedly said of Christ, who is blessed above all forever [Note: [Col. 0392D] Galatians 3:13]. For we, who through the sin of the first man deserved the curse of death and servitude, have received through the righteousness of the second man the blessing of life and liberty. Indeed, the fact that the Jews cursed Christ hanging on the cross indicates more blessing than curse.

This, then, is a form of speech derived absolutely from the place of contrariety, from which the Apostle also took what he says: “Him who knew no sin he made sin for us” [Note: [Col. 0391] Codex: *no ue ra*.] [Note: [Col. 0392D] 2 Corinthians 5:12]. For who doubts that sacrifice and sin are contrary to one another, since nothing is done by a sacrifice except that sin may be destroyed? Christ is the universal sacrifice for the sin of the whole world. Therefore he is rightly signified, by way of contrariety, through the term “sin.”

## V.

Next, let us consider examples of joined contraries. They are called “joined” because they agree in two respects: namely, in similarity and in contrariety. For the same nouns or verbs are sometimes taken by similarity and sometimes by contrariety. Their examples are “foreknowledge” and “predestination” when they are predicated of God.

First, however, we must consider that these and similar nouns or verbs cannot properly be predicated of God. For how could one say that God foreknows something by foreknowledge, or predestines by predestination, when nothing is future for him, because he awaits nothing, and nothing is past for him, because nothing passes away from him? For just as there are no spatial intervals in him, so there are no intervals of time. [Col. 0392C] Consequently, no sound reasoning permits such terms to be understood of God according to their proper sense.

For how can one speak properly of the foreknowledge of one for whom there are no future things? Just as no memory is properly attributed to one for whom nothing is past, so there is no foreknowledge, because there is no future. And yet it is said: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” [Note: [Col. 0392D] Psalm 111:7]. In the same way, God saw, foresaw, knew, and foreknew all the things that were to be made before they were made, just as he sees and knows those same things after they have been made, because, just as he himself is always eternal, so the whole creation that he made is eternally in him.

## VI.

The same must also be understood concerning his predestination, especially since every predestination is foreknowledge. By what right can predestination—that is, preparation—be attributed to one who was preceded by no interval of time in which he might arrange the things he was going to make? His operation is not preceded by preparation. For preparing and working are not two different things for him. And just as it is proper to a human being to prepare what he is going to do, so it is foreign to God to predestine things he will never do.

But how could he be going to make anything, since he made everything once and simultaneously? Or how did he not make everything, if he always possessed everything? He is believed always to have possessed his Word, through whom all things were made and in whom all things live unchangeably—not only the things that have been, but also those that are to be. Yet in him they were not “things that have been,” nor are they “things that are to be”; they simply are, and all are one.

Therefore, since the things made through him are under him in one way, whereas the things that are themselves in him are in him in another way—those under him having been created and ordered in their own places and times—verbs signifying places and times properly apply to the former. In the things that are eternally in him, however, such verbs can be used metaphorically.

Accordingly, just as it is used improperly of God to say that he has made or will make something, so it is used improperly of him to say that he has foreknown, foreknows, or will foreknow something [Note: [Col. 0393] Codex: *presciise*; M.: *praescisse*], and similarly that he has predestined, predestines, or will predestine something.

## VII.

It follows, then, that “foreknowledge” and “predestination” are transferred to God by similarity with temporal things. This would be a place of contrariety if temporal things were opposed to eternity contradictorily. But since a certain likeness of eternity is inherent in temporal things—not only because they were made by it, but also because that part of temporal things from which these names are taken, namely human nature, is to pass into a certain likeness of true eternity—how can the term be taken by contrariety when another meaning is transferred from the temporal to the timeless?

They therefore belong to the place of similarity. But we must ask what kind of similarity this is. We say that “before” is used in four ways: first, before in time; second, before in rank; third, before in origin; fourth, before in eternity.

Examples of these are as follows: in time, the flower precedes the fruit; in rank, the fruit precedes the flower; in origin, the voice precedes the word; in eternity, God precedes the creature. Therefore, in the manner in which God precedes everything he made—that is, in eternity—he foreknew and predestined the things he was going to make. From this it follows that such words are transferred from the first manner to the fourth, namely from the place of time to the place of eternity.

# CHAPTER X  
## On what is to be understood by contrariety when God is said to foreknow or predestine the sins, death, or punishments of human beings or angels

### I.

It remains to consider the place which, as we said earlier, is called *enthymeme* by dialecticians and rhetoricians [Note: [Col. 0393] Codex: *entimema*], but by grammarians *katantiphrasis* (“contrary expression”), and which is the noblest of all arguments and verbal signs.

It has been established that “foreknowledge” and “predestination,” as well as “preparation,” “foresight,” [Col. 0394A] and similar terms, are predicated metaphorically of God and can be transferred between two spheres of meaning. They are rightly called “joined,” because they are shown to belong both to the place of similarity and to the place called “by contrariety.”

Here it is most plainly understood and most firmly maintained that, when these words are taken by similarity, they signify nothing other than what the Creator of all things himself is going to make—whether in establishing the substance of the universe and its natural qualities, or in its administration—and that those whom he foreknew and predestined according to the purpose of his grace are to be conformed to the image of his Son [Note: [Col. 0393D] Romans 8:29].

But when these same words are transferred from the place that is by contrariety, nothing is to be understood in them except what God permits to occur in the creature he himself established, through the creature’s own free movement, when rational nature uses perversely the natural goods it received through the generosity of its Creator. This is the whole of what is called evil, together with its varied punishment and manifold misery.

### II.

Therefore, when we hear that God “foreknew,” “predestined,” or “prepared” the sins, death, or punishments of those whom he justly abandoned—that is, whom he permitted to be punished by their own perversity [Note: [Col. 0393] Codex: *permissit*]—we must understand it entirely by contrariety, lest heretical depravity deceive us, for that depravity originated by misusing such words.

They do not see, with the light of their inner eyes, that all evil descending from a perverse will is nothing. I set aside that kind of evil which, by the same rule of contrariety, is called evil although it is naturally good, such as the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his ministers.

All other things properly called evil, arising from one and the same cause—namely, as has often been said, the perverse movement of a free will that is mutable, turns away from the Creator, and uses the creature badly—are enclosed between two boundaries, one of which is sin and the other its punishment.

### III.

Every evil, therefore, is either sin or the punishment of sin. If true reason permits neither of these two to be foreknown by God, how much more would anyone dare to say that they are predestined, except by contrariety?

What then? Can we rightly conceive of God, who alone is true being and who made all things that exist insofar as they exist, as possessing foreknowledge or predestination of things that neither he himself is nor are from him, because they are nothing? [Note: [Col. 0393D] This teaches most wrongly that sin and punishment are nothing and therefore are neither foreknown nor predestined. God foreknows both sin and punishments. Nor is punishment nothing; rather, it is something, namely a creature of God that becomes punitive for sinners, except for those sins that are called punishments of preceding sins. See Prud.]

For if knowledge is nothing other than understanding of things that exist, how can knowledge or foreknowledge be spoken of concerning things that do not exist? Similarly, if predestination is nothing other than preparation of the things God foresaw he would make, how can predestination be spoken of concerning things that God neither made nor prepared to make?

Furthermore, if evil is nothing other than the corruption of good, and every good is either God, who cannot be corrupted, or is from God, which can be corrupted, while every corruption seeks nothing except that good should not exist, who can doubt that that is evil which seeks to destroy good so that it may not exist? Evil, therefore, is neither God nor from God. Consequently, just as God is not the author of evil, so he is neither the foreknower nor the predestiner of evil.

But if anyone doubts that evil is nothing other than the corruption of good, let him see what Augustine says on this subject in his writing against the Epistle of the Foundation:

“Learn that evil is not a substance, but that, just as in the body, through a change of form for the worse, beauty is lost or rather diminished, and what was previously beautiful is called ugly, and the body that had previously been pleasing becomes displeasing, so in the soul the dignity of a rightly ordered will, by which one lives piously and justly, is corrupted when the will is changed for the worse. Through this sin the soul becomes wretched, although previously it had obtained blessedness through the honor of a rightly ordered will, with no substance added or taken away.

“Who can doubt that the whole of what is called evil is nothing other than corruption? Different evils can indeed be called by different names, but what is evil in all things in which some evil can be observed is corruption. Thus, the corruption of a learned soul is called ignorance; the corruption of prudence, imprudence; the corruption of justice [Note: [Col. 0395] Codex: *justae*], injustice; the corruption of courage [Note: [Col. 0395] So the codex; elsewhere *fortis*], cowardice; the corruption of rest and tranquility, desire, fear, sadness, or boastfulness.

“Then, in an animate body, the corruption of health is pain and sickness; the corruption of strength, weariness [Note: [Col. 0395] Codex: *lasitudo*]; the corruption of rest, labor. Then, in the body itself, the corruption of beauty is ugliness; the corruption of straightness, crookedness; the corruption of order, disorder; the corruption of wholeness, separation [Note: [Col. 0395] Codex: *discisio*], fracture, or diminution [Note: [Col. 0395] Codex: *dimminutio*].

“It would be long and difficult to name individually all the corruptions both of the things I have mentioned and of countless others, since many things said of the body can also be said of the soul, and there are innumerable things in which corruption has its own proper names” [Note: [Col. 0395D] Augustine, *Against the Epistle of the Foundation*, chapter 35].

### IV.

Since these things are so, who does not see—unless he lacks understanding—that the whole of what is called sin, together with its consequences established in death and misery, is nothing other than the corruption of integral and blessed life? Thus each thing is opposed to its counterpart: sin to integrity, death to life, and misery to blessedness.

The former exist; the latter are utterly non-existent. The former strive upward toward the one source of all things; the latter abandon it and strive to make the goods they corrupt return downward into nothingness. God is the cause of the former, while the latter have no cause. The former are understood within the limits of natural forms; the latter are known through ignorance in the defect and privation of those forms.

For just as the cause of an evil will can neither be found nor known, so the efficient causes of all the defects that deservedly follow it cannot be known, nor can the defects themselves, because they are nothing.

I think the testimony of Saint Augustine should be brought to bear here. In Book XII of *The City of God* he says:

“Let no one seek an efficient cause of an evil will; it has no efficient cause, but is a defect [Note: [Col. 0395] Elsewhere: “deficient,” because that action too is not an effecting but a defect]. To defect from what supremely is toward what is less—that is, to begin to have an evil will.

“To wish to discover the causes of these defections, since they are not efficient but deficient, is like wishing to see darkness or hear silence. Yet both are known to us: the former only through the eyes and the latter only through the ears—not in their own form, but in the privation of form.

“Let no one ask me to know what I know that I do not know, unless perhaps it is so that he may learn not to know what must be known to be unknowable. For those things that are known not in their form but in its privation are, if one may so speak or understand it, known in a certain way by not knowing, so that by knowing they may be not known.

“For when the sight of the bodily eye runs through bodily forms, it sees darkness nowhere except where it has begun not to see. Likewise, sensing silence belongs not to any other sense but solely to the ears, yet it is sensed only by not hearing.

“So the mind, by understanding, does indeed behold intelligible forms; but where they fail, it learns through not knowing [Note: [Col. 0395] Elsewhere: *condiscit*]. For who understands transgressions?” [Note: [Col. 0395D] Augustine, *City of God* XII.7; Psalm 18:13.]

### V.

By these arguments it is therefore unshakably established that every defect or privation of a perverse will—whether it is called sin or by whatever name that deadly movement may be called [Note: [Col. 0395] Codex: *loetifer*]—by which the highest good is abandoned and the spirit becomes one that goes forth and does not return, and whose end is plainly death and the misery of eternal punishments, is altogether nothing.

For whatever lacks matter, form, and appearance is undoubtedly nothing; and it is evident that every absence and defect of things lacks these three things mentioned above. They therefore do not exist at all. Consequently, they cannot be foreknown or predestined by him who supremely is [Note: [Col. 0395] M. corrects to *prescire*] [Note: [Col. 0395D] This teaches wrongly. Sin indeed arises from the human will, but it is foreknown and punished by God. Likewise, death, which is the separation of soul and body, and the punishments of Gehenna occur only by God’s judgment and are therefore foreknown by him. See Prud.].

O astonishing—or rather, lamentable—blindness of those who refuse to understand by contrariety whenever they read in divine or human authority that God foreknew or predestined sins, death, and punishments, which are utterly nothing because they are defects!

For what is sin except a defect of justice? What is death except a defect of life? What is punishment except a defect of blessedness?

If they had considered more carefully that all things which exist exist for no other reason than that they were foreknown and predestined, while all things that do not exist do not exist for no other reason than that they were neither foreknown nor predestined, perhaps they would correct themselves, recover their senses, and turn their minds toward the light of truth. Then, in that light and through it [Note: [Col. 0397] So the codex; M.: *ea*], they could discern throughout the whole of nature whatever is truly found to exist as nothing other than the one true essence, which is wholly present everywhere in itself.

And what is that essence except the foreknowing predestination and predestining foreknowledge of all natures?

But if it is most plainly understood that the highest and principal substance of all natures is nothing other than divine foreknowledge [Note: [Col. 0397] M. corrects the codex’s *presentiam*] and predestination, how can it be believed that these things exist in what altogether does not exist? For if they existed in them, they would undoubtedly remain not as nothing but as something. Yet they are nothing. Therefore divine foreknowledge and predestination are not in them.

# CHAPTER XI  
## That by divine and human authority it can be demonstrated that God’s predestination concerns only those who have been prepared for eternal blessedness

### I.

Since the principal question proposed in this work concerns divine foreknowledge [Note: [Col. 0397] M. corrects the codex’s *presentia*] and predestination, on account of which the subsidiary questions introduced into the discussion had necessarily to be treated more carefully, these matters must now be examined somewhat more openly by the light of examples.

But first we have taken care to persuade the readers of our writings—if indeed there are any who have judged that they ought to read them, and may their charity approach them so as to read them through—that they should consider in them more the devotion of our obedience than despise the usefulness of the argument, if it has any usefulness. Otherwise they might perhaps rush upon us in anger and say that we are destroyers both of divine foreknowledge and of divine predestination. Yet if they inspect the matter more diligently, they will find in our work a great deal affirming them and nothing destroying them.

For what? Does one destroy God’s foreknowledge or disdain his predestination who asserts that these terms are predicated metaphorically of God? As though a transfer could not be made from temporal things to eternal things by a certain kind of similarity, or from things that exist to things that do not exist by a most beautiful kind of contrariety?

Or does one resist sound faith if one says that foreknowledge and predestination properly occur in those things that precede in the order of time the things that they foreknow and predestine [Note: [Col. 0397] So the codex; M.: *praescivit et praedestinavit*], but that they are used improperly of one for whom there are no future things [Note: [Col. 0397] Codex: *nula*], since he precedes everything that is from him not in time but in his eternity?

Or how would it depart from truth if one said, by similarity, “God foreknew everything he was going to make,” and said, by contrariety, “He foreknew what he was not going to make,” meaning that he did not know it? The same is to be understood concerning predestination by similarity.

God predestined those whom he prepared to receive his gratuitous grace. By contrariety, he predestined the ungodly to destruction or eternal punishment, although he did not predestine them. For if they are predestined, they will necessarily perish [Note: [Col. 0397] Codex: *perhibunt*] and suffer unavoidable punishments [Note: [Col. 0397] The same or a very similar hand has added in the margin: “Here he says that predestination imposes necessity”]. But if this is so, how will the world be judged justly, when the necessity of predestination compels it to perish? To believe this is characteristic of impiety.

### II.

Therefore, lest this reasoning of ours seem to be supported by no formula of divine or human authority, we must investigate what can be established from the pages of divine Scripture and from the statements of Saint Augustine. We do not mean that we could not establish the same conclusions from the examples of other Catholic Fathers, but we have judged it necessary and useful for the matter [Note: [Col. 0397] M. omits “but that … we see”] to set down the statements of that author to whom the heretic Gottschalk is accustomed chiefly to refer the foundations of his wicked doctrine.

There is indeed no Scripture that those who fail to understand it cannot easily distort into a wicked meaning. Thus the aforesaid corrupt adulterator of the holy Fathers, rightly so called, since he was neither an investigator nor an discoverer of truth, did not understand what Father Augustine intended to convey in his own words. Instead, in order to persuade others of the things he himself had fabricated from himself and from the devil [Note: [Col. 0397] Codex: *diabulo*], he forcibly twisted the words of that Father—not merely into meanings that did not suit him, but plainly into meanings opposed to him [Note: [Col. 0397] So the codex; M.: “not indeed the words, but meanings not his own”].

### III.

First, it must be noted that the unshakable authority of Holy Scripture is found to have placed foreknowledge together with predestination, or predestination alone absolutely, only in relation to those whom God chose to possess eternal blessedness [Note: [Col. 0397] Codex: *possuisse*].

The words of the Apostle are sufficient to prove this. For, writing to the Romans, he says:

“We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose; because those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” [Note: [Col. 0397D] Romans 8:28–30].

Likewise, to the Ephesians [Note: [Col. 0397] Codex: *efesios*]:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blemish in his sight in love; predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he has favored us in his beloved Son.

“In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he made abound toward us in all wisdom and understanding, making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, for the administration of the fullness of times: to restore all things in Christ, those in the heavens and those on earth, in him.

“In him we have also been called by lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of God, who works all things according to the counsel of his will” [Note: [Col. 0399D] Ephesians 1:3–11].

Against this trumpet-blast of truth, so clear, who among those of sober and vigilant faith would admit human voices? Who would not hear in it that predestination is altogether the predestination of the saints and can in no way belong to the reprobate?

### IV.

Since Saint Aurelius Augustine, the most abundant author of Christian eloquence, the most diligent investigator of truth, and the most distinguished teacher of proper and figurative language for the exercise of those who would read him, is found in the sequence of his books to have said on several occasions that God predestined the ungodly to destruction or punishments, and since, consequently, to those who understand him he became, as the Apostle says, “the aroma of life leading to life,” but to those who do not understand him, “the aroma of death leading to death” [Note: [Col. 0399D] 2 Corinthians 2:16], the subject of the present work requires us to set down his words as though they contradicted one another, so that the perceptive reader may more easily understand the kind of speech in which he said that divine predestination applies to both classes of human beings—namely, to the elect through grace and to those left behind through justice.

We have judged that those statements should be set down which the heretical error misuses in its attempt to establish its perfidy, so that the heretic may withdraw wounded by the very arrows he rashly drew out against the hearts of the simple.

### V.

Augustine therefore says in a certain homily to the people, explaining the Gospel saying, “The prince of this world has now been judged” [Note: [Col. 0399D] John 16:11]:

“That is, he has been irrevocably destined for the judgment of eternal fire” [Note: [Col. 0399D] Augustine, Homily 95 on the Gospel of John].

In his exposition of the Gospel according to John, where he explains the testimony of John the Forerunner concerning Christ, he says [Note: [Col. 0399D] Augustine, same work, tractate 14]:

“There is a certain people prepared for the wrath of God, to be condemned with the devil” [Note: [Col. 0399] Codex: *diabulo*].

Likewise, concerning the Jews:

“These men, indignant, are dead and predestined to everlasting death” [Note: [Col. 0399D] Augustine, same work].

Again:

“Why did the Lord say to the Jews, ‘You do not believe because you are not among my sheep’ [Note: [Col. 0399D] John 10:26], except because he saw that they had been predestined to everlasting destruction?” [Note: [Col. 0399D] Augustine, same work, tractate 48].

Similarly, when explaining the Lord’s statement, “No one can snatch from the hand of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0400D] John 10:29], he continues:

“What can the wolf do? What can the thief and robber do? They destroy only those who have been predestined to destruction” [Note: [Col. 0400D] Augustine, same work].

In the book he calls the *Enchiridion* [Note: [Col. 0399] Codex: *encheiridon*], he says:

“These are the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his will [Note: [Col. 0400D] Psalm 111:2], and sought out so wisely that, when the angelic and human creature had sinned—that is, had done not what he, the Creator, willed, but what it itself willed—he nevertheless fulfilled through that very will of the creature, by which what the Creator did not will came to pass, what he himself willed, making good use even of evil things, as supremely good, for the condemnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment and for the salvation of those whom he graciously predestined to grace” [Note: [Col. 0400D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 100].

Again, from the same book:

“They are also called sons of Gehenna, not because they were born from it, but because they were prepared for it, just as the sons of the kingdom are prepared for the kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0400D] Augustine, same work].

In his book *On the Perfection of Human Justice* he says:

“Among that class of human beings which has been predestined to destruction” [Note: [Col. 0400D] Augustine, *On the Perfection of Justice*, chapter 13].

In his books *The City of God*:

“What will he give to those whom he predestined to life, who gave these things to those whom he predestined to death?” [Note: [Col. 0400D] Augustine, *City of God* XXII.24].

### VI.

Through these and similar words, the mad folly of heresy commonly rages against a Catholic author and tears the faith of the less educated with wolfish teeth.

For who among those ignorant of the modes of speech commonly used by the holy Fathers could not easily be deceived by hearing of people predestined to eternal fire, prepared for the wrath of God, predestined to everlasting death, predestined to destruction or punishment, and other expressions of that kind? Such a person might readily concede either that there are two predestinations—one plainly belonging to the saints and another to the ungodly, entirely opposed to each other—or that one and the same divine predestination embraces both saints and ungodly and is simultaneously capable of contraries, something reason denies.

This lamentable misery is most usefully relieved when the same predestination is defined according to Augustine himself [Note: [Col. 0399] Codex: *diffinitur*, as elsewhere], and its definition is defended in his own words. Be ready, then, heretic, either to defend yourself—which you cannot do—or to correct yourself—which you can do, if you cease contradicting the truth.

Hear the bounds of the definition of divine predestination, which no one who believes rightly dares either to contract excessively or to extend beyond measure, and which no contentious person can invalidate.

In his book to Prosper and Hilary he says:

“Predestination is something that cannot exist without foreknowledge. But foreknowledge can exist without predestination. For by predestination God foreknew the things he himself was going to make; hence it is said, ‘He made the things that are to be.’ But he can also foreknow the things he does not make, such as any sins” [Note: [Col. 0401D] Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10].

### VII.

Pay attention to the character of this definition, which is derived from a distinction [Note: [Col. 0401] Codex: *asumpta*].

There is therefore this distinction between predestination and foreknowledge: every predestination is foreknowledge, but not every foreknowledge is predestination. That foreknowledge by which God foreknew the things he himself was going to make is properly and specifically called predestination. But that foreknowledge by which he foreknew the things he does not make—that is, sins and their punishments—has been agreed to be called simply “foreknowledge,” so that only the foreknowledge called predestination is always understood in relation to good things. Foreknowledge alone, without predestination, belongs altogether to evil things that God does not make.

And lest anyone doubt this, he added:

“Accordingly, the predestination of God, which is directed toward good, is the preparation of grace; and grace is the effect of that predestination itself” [Note: [Col. 0401D] Augustine, same work].

In his book *On the Gift of Perseverance* he makes the same point more clearly, saying:

“Therefore he certainly foreknew that he would bestow these gifts of his on all to whom God gives them, and he prepared them in his foreknowledge. Thus those whom he predestined, he also called [Note: [Col. 0401D] Romans 8:30]—with that calling of which it is said, ‘The gifts and calling of God are without repentance’ [Note: [Col. 0401D] Romans 11:29]. For to arrange in his foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, his works that were to be, is precisely, and nothing else, to predestine” [Note: [Col. 0401D] Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 17].

Who would dare to speak discordantly against this clearest trumpet-blast and most open declaration of the Christian camp? It resounds in the plainest voice without ceasing that to predestine is precisely, and nothing else, for God to arrange in his foreknowledge the works that he himself was going to accomplish.

Tell me, please: is this definition of predestination true or false? If it is false, criticize Augustine. If it is true, it must be such as he himself says in his book *On the Quantity of the Soul*:

“A definition contains nothing less and nothing more than what has been undertaken for explanation; otherwise it is altogether defective” [Note: [Col. 0401] Codex: *diffinio*] [Note: [Col. 0402D] Augustine, *On the Quantity of the Soul*].

Whether it is free from such defects is tested by conversion [Note: [Col. 0401] Codex: *converisione*].

# CHAPTER XII  
## On the definition of predestination

### I.

Let the conversion of this definition therefore be made as follows:

If it is true that to arrange in his foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, his works that are to be is precisely, and nothing else, to predestine, then this is altogether true: to predestine is precisely, and nothing else, to arrange in his foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, his works that are to be.

From this another conversion follows:

If every foreknowledge by which God arranged his future works is divine predestination, then every predestination by which God arranged his future works is divine foreknowledge.

It follows, therefore, that God’s predestination exists only in his works, since its definition contains neither less nor more than the arrangement of divine works.

## II. But to this you will say: “It belongs to God’s works to predestine those who are justly to be condemned to punishment, just as it belongs to his works to predestine those who are to be saved by grace to blessedness,” and you will try to establish this by the testimonies of that same holy Augustine. We have set them out in the order in which you presented them, so that in them we may see not what you intended, but what he intended. If one of them is rightly explained, that will suffice for understanding the others. Let us therefore set down this passage:

> “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his will” [Note: [Col. 0402D] Psalm 110 (111):2], “and sought out with such wisdom that, when the angelic and human creature had sinned—that is, had done not what he, but what it itself willed—he himself nevertheless fulfilled, through that same creature’s will by which what the Creator did not will had been done, what he willed, making good use even of evil things, as supremely good, for the condemnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment, and for the salvation of those whom he kindly predestined to grace” [Col. 0402C] [Note: [Col. 0402D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 100].

Here, in one and the same sentence, he says: “He predestined [some] to punishment”; “he predestined [others] to grace.” Where, we ask, will you answer our question: does predestining the wicked to punishment belong to God’s justice or to his grace? You will answer, I believe, that it belongs to his justice; for he says, “those whom he justly predestined to punishment,” and therefore it does not belong to grace.

Accordingly, if predestination to punishment is not God’s gift but the judgment of sin, it necessarily follows either that what Augustine himself says is false: “The predestination of God, which is directed toward good, is a preparation for grace” [Note: [Col. 0402D] Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10], or that predestination to punishments is to be understood in the opposite sense. But what he said is true and unchangeable: God’s predestination, insofar as it is directed toward good, is a preparation for grace. Therefore, by contrast, he intended what he wrote—“he predestined to punishment”—to be understood in the opposite sense.

## III. But perhaps you will object: “He did not say, ‘God’s predestination is a preparation for grace,’ but, ‘God’s predestination, which is directed toward good, is a preparation for grace.’” This seems to leave room for another predestination, one that is, as it were, directed toward evil; or, if there is one predestination and one alone, it does not deny that the same predestination can be directed toward both good and evil.

First observe that one definition cannot contain two predestinations at all. Then consider this: if no other definition of predestination is found that is truer and more suitable than the one stated above, and if that definition comprehends nothing except divine works—which no pious believer doubts are good—what compels us, when we hear of “God’s predestination, which is directed toward good,” to understand anything else than that it is always good and always directed toward good?

## IV. But if you say, “It is good to predestine the wicked to punishment, and therefore this must be reckoned among God’s works,” we reply: it is good because it is just. But since it is not God’s gift, seeing that it is his judgment, while every predestination of God is entirely a preparation for grace, and every grace is a gift, it necessarily follows that every divine predestination is a preparation of his gifts.

Punishment undoubtedly torments the wicked justly, but it is not a gift; otherwise, if it were a gift, it would not torment but would certainly liberate. Predestination, therefore, is not punishment. And if it were, it would not be punishment but grace. But it is punishment. Therefore it is not his predestination.

If anyone still doubts that predestination must always be understood in relation to the gifts of divine generosity, let him carefully examine the book of Saint Augustine *On the Gift of Perseverance*, at the passage where he says:

> “These gifts of God,” I say, “if there is no predestination that we defend, are not foreknown by God. But they are foreknown. This, therefore, is the predestination that we defend. Hence that same predestination is sometimes signified even by the name ‘foreknowledge,’ as the Apostle says: ‘God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew’ [Note: [Col. 0403D] Romans 11:2]. Here [Note: [Col. 0403] The manuscript reads *Hic*; M. has *Hoc*.], what he says, ‘foreknew,’ is not rightly understood unless it means ‘predestined,’ as the context of the passage itself shows. For he was speaking about the remnant of the Jews who were saved while the rest were perishing. Earlier he had said that the Prophet spoke to Israel [Note: [Col. 0403] The manuscript has *israhel*, here and throughout]: ‘All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contradicting people’ [Note: [Col. 0403] Another reading has *expandi*, “I spread out.”] [Note: [Col. 0403D] Isaiah 65:2]. And as though someone had replied, ‘Where, then, are God’s promises to Israel?’ he immediately added: ‘I ask, then, has God rejected his people?’ [Note: [Col. 0403] The manuscript reads *reppulit* here and throughout.] ‘Certainly not; for I myself am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin’ [Note: [Col. 0403] The manuscript reads *habraham*; it has *tribu*, while M. reads *de tribu*, “of the tribe.”] [Note: [Col. 0403D] Romans 11:1]. It was as though he had said: ‘For I too am from that very people.’

> “Then he added the point with which we are now concerned: ‘God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.’ And to show that the remnant had been left by God’s grace, not by the merits of their works, he continued [Note: [Col. 0403] The manuscript has *adjunxit*; M. has *adjungit*]: ‘Or do you not know what Scripture says in Elijah—how it pleads with God against Israel?’ [Note: [Col. 0403] Another reading has *quid*, “what,” in place of *quod*.] [Note: [Col. 0403D] Romans 11:2, 4] ‘But what does the divine response say to him?’ he asks. ‘I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal’ [Note: [Col. 0403] Another reading has *genu*, “knee,” singular] [Note: [Col. 0403D] 1 Kings 19:18]. For he does not say, ‘They have been left for me,’ or ‘They have left themselves for me,’ but, ‘I have kept them for myself.’

> “‘So, then,’ he says, ‘at the present time also a remnant has been saved by the election of grace’ [Note: [Col. 0403] *Salvae* is omitted in the manuscript]. ‘But if by grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace’ [Note: [Col. 0404D] Romans 11:5–6]. And connecting this with what I inserted above: ‘What then?’ In reply to this question he says: ‘What Israel sought, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it, while the rest were hardened’ [Note: [Col. 0404D] Romans 11:7].

> “In this election, then, and in this remnant that was saved by the election of grace, he intended the people whom God did not reject for the very reason that he foreknew them. This is that election by which he chose in Christ, before the foundation of the world [Note: [Col. 0403] The manuscript has *constitutionem mundi*; M. has *mundi constitutionem*], those whom he willed, so that they might be holy and blameless before him in love, predestining them to adoption as sons [Note: [Col. 0404D] Ephesians 1:4–5].

> “No one who understands these things is permitted to deny or doubt that, when the Apostle says, ‘God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew,’ he intended to signify predestination. For he foreknew the remnant that he himself was going to make according to the election of grace; that is, he predestined it. For without doubt he foreknew it if he predestined it. But to have predestined is to have foreknown that which he himself was going to do.

> “What, then, prevents us, when in certain interpreters of the word of God we read of God’s foreknowledge and the subject is the calling of the elect, from understanding that same predestination? Perhaps they preferred [Note: [Col. 0403] Another reading has *autem*, “however,” in place of *enim*, “for.”] to use this word in that matter because it is more easily understood, does not conflict with, and indeed agrees with, the truth proclaimed concerning the predestination of grace. This I know: no one has been able to argue against this predestination, which we defend according to the holy Scriptures, except by going astray” [Note: [Col. 0404D] Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 17 at the end and chapter 18].

## V. If, then, Augustine’s authority is to be believed—or rather, the truth through that authority—we must hold this rule firmly: whenever we encounter divine foreknowledge either in Holy Scripture or in its interpreters, if the subject is the election of the saints, we must understand that it signifies nothing other than predestination.

And if this is so, who does not see that all God’s foreknowledge concerning the saints is nothing other than their predestination? Consequently, by the connection of true reasoning, it can be inferred:

- Every foreknowledge relating to the elect is predestination.
- No predestination exists except that of the elect.
- Therefore no foreknowledge relating to the elect is not predestination.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] [ [Col. 0405A] This note appears at the foot of column 405, but the callout number (1) has not been printed in the text.] Another reading has *autem*, “however.”] [Note: [Col. 0405D] This does not agree with the truth. For God’s foreknowledge and predestination must be carefully distinguished from each other.]

No one is chosen for punishment. How, then, can punishment—which belongs specifically to the reprobate—be predestined? Or perhaps, just as those who are not elect are called “the elect,” so those who are not predestined are called “the predestined,” and those who are not his sons are called “the sons of God,” in that contrary mode of expression which authors often employ?

## VI. But if you ask where the reprobate are called “the elect,” although they are not elect, and “the sons of God,” although they are not his sons, read Saint Augustine in his book addressed to Prosper and Hilary, speaking in these terms [Note: [Col. 0405D] Prudentius: “The Fathers never held that the elect were used for the non-elect, or the sons of God for those who were not sons.”]:

> “All who are elect are undoubtedly also called; but not all who are called are consequently elect” [Note: [Col. 0405D] Compare Matthew 20:16]. “Those, then, are elect, as has often been said, who are called according to the purpose, who are also predestined and foreknown. If any one of these perishes, God is deceived. But none of them perishes, because God is not deceived. If any one of these perishes, God is overcome by human fault. But none of them perishes, because God is overcome by nothing.

> “For they are elect to reign with Christ—not in the way Judas was elected, for the work suited to him. He was elected by the one who knows how to make good use even of evil things, so that through his damnable work the venerable work for which Christ himself had come might be accomplished.

> “When, therefore, we hear: ‘Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?’ [Note: [Col. 0405D] John 6:71], we must understand that they were chosen through mercy, while he was chosen for judgment; that therefore he chose them to obtain [Note: [Col. 0405D] The manuscript has *optinendum*, here and throughout.] his kingdom, but him to shed his blood” [Note: [Col. 0405D] *Ergo elegit*, “therefore he chose,” is omitted in the manuscript and supplied by M.].

> “But God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’ [Note: [Col. 0405D] 2 Timothy 2:19]. The faith of these people, which works through love [Note: [Col. 0406D] Galatians 5:6], certainly either does not fail at all, or, if there are some whose faith fails, it is restored before life itself comes to an end; and, once the iniquity into which they had fallen has been removed, perseverance to the end is reckoned to them [Note: [Col. 0405D] Another reading has *quae intercurrerat*, “which had intervened.”]

> “Those, however, who are not going to persevere, and who will fall away from the Christian faith and manner of life so that the end of this life finds them in that condition, are unquestionably not to be counted among these, even at the time when they live well and piously. For they have not been separated from that mass of perdition by God’s foreknowledge and predestination. Therefore they have not been called according to the purpose, and consequently they are not elect, but are among those who are called of whom it is said: ‘Many are called, but few are elect’ [Note: [Col. 0405D] The words “and not among those of whom it is said” are omitted in the manuscript and supplied by M.] [Note: [Col. 0406D] Matthew 20:16].

> “And yet who would deny that they are elect when they believe, are baptized, and live according to God? Nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0405D] Another reading has *plane dic*, “indeed, I say.”], they are called elect by those who do not know what they will be, not by the one who knows that they do not possess the perseverance that leads the elect to blessed life, and who knows that they stand in such a way that he foreknew they would fall” [Note: [Col. 0405D] Another reading has *sint*, “are,” rather than *futuri sunt*, “will be”; *ita* is omitted in the manuscript and supplied by M.; another reading has *praesciret*, “would foreknow.”] [Note: [Col. 0406D] Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 7].

> “Nor should it trouble us that God does not grant this perseverance to some of his sons. For it would certainly not be so if they were among those predestined and called according to the purpose. Those who are not sons of promise [Note: [Col. 0405D] The manuscript reads this; another reading has, “who truly are sons of promise. For these…”], when they live piously, are called sons of God. But since they will live impiously and die in that same impiety, God’s foreknowledge does not call them sons of God.

> “There are sons of God who are not yet so to us but already are so to God. Of these the evangelist John says [Note: [Col. 0405D] The manuscript has *Johannis*, “of John,” here and throughout]: ‘Because Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the dispersed sons of God’ [Note: [Col. 0406D] John 11:51–52]. They were certainly going to become such by believing through the preaching of the Gospel; yet, before this occurred, they were already sons of God, inscribed with unshaken permanence in the memory of their Father.

> “Again, there are some whom we call sons of God because they have received grace, even if only temporarily [Note: [Col. 0405D] *Qui*, “who,” is omitted in the manuscript and supplied by M.], although they are not so to God. Of these the same John says: ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us’ [Note: [Col. 0406D] 1 John 2:19]. When, therefore, those who did not possess perseverance are called sons of God—‘they went out from us, but they were not of us’—and it is added [Note: [Col. 0405D] The manuscript reads *additur*; M. has *addunt*, “they add”] that, ‘if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us,’ what else is being said [Note: [Col. 0405D] The manuscript reads *dicuntur*; M. has *dicunt*] except that they were not sons, even when they were in the profession and name of sons?” [Note: [Col. 0406D] Augustine, same work, chapter 9.]

# CHAPTER XIII. What Can Be Inferred from the Foregoing Statement of Saint Augustine

[Col. 0406C]

## I. The words of this statement, considered a little more carefully, are sufficient to prove what we are trying to establish. Taking up, then, what the Lord said to his disciples—“Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” [Note: [Col. 0406D] John 6:71]—he added and said: “We must understand them”—namely, the eleven apostles, then eleven in number—“as called according to the purpose of grace, but him”—that is, the betrayer—“as rejected through judgment, according to the equal measure of justice.”

They were chosen for glory; he for punishment. In them are all who are to be saved by grace and who are to remain in the good until the end of this life; in him are all who are to die through judgment. Called for a time, and soon to abandon their purpose of living piously, all are nevertheless called elect, although none are elect except those conformed to the image of the Son of God.

The others, however, are thought elect by those who do not know what they will be; and therefore they are not elect but reprobate. They are called sons of God although they are sons of perdition, all of whom the Lord marked out in his betrayer [Note: [Col. 0407] The manuscript reads *perditore*, “destroyer,” rather than *proditore*, “betrayer”].

For when he prayed to the Father for his elect, he said: “Those whom you gave me I have guarded, and none of them has perished except the son of perdition” [Note: [Col. 0407D] John 17:12]. Judas, therefore, was called elect because he was called among the elect; he was called a son because he was counted among Christ’s brothers by those who did not know.

And just as no one doubts that, in the opposite sense, those are called sons to whom the paternal inheritance is destined, so, in the opposite sense, those are called elect who are separated for the joy of blessedness from the fellowship of the others whom the justly condemned mass holds in misery.

And just as they are not sons if they are not heirs, so they are not elect if they are not beloved. How, then, could Judas be called elect except in the opposite sense, since he was not beloved? If he had been loved, surely he would not have been rejected.

Or how could someone be elect for the judgment of eternal fire, when, if he were elect, he would undoubtedly belong to eternal life?

## II. But if anyone shamelessly resists these points, we must understand by Judas the betrayer’s abusive election his just reprobation; and by his sonship, through which he was called for a time, his just and deserved eternal rejection, because he was never elect, just as he was never not reprobate [Note: [Col. 0407] Corrected: the manuscript reads *nunquam non reprobus non fuit*; M. has *nunquam non reprobus fuit*]. Likewise, he was called a friend although he was always an enemy.

Accordingly, I do not see why the holy Fathers would hesitate confidently to declare, in an elegant mode of speech, that some are predestined to punishment or destruction and similar things whenever they chose to write this in the course of their books, since they did not hesitate to say that the Truth itself had spoken in the same manner. Thus they both followed the traces of the supreme Wisdom speaking in them and adorned their own eloquence, for their readers, with precious stones of figurative expression.

If, then, the Lord was not ashamed to call his betrayer “elect,” why would his imitator Saint Augustine be ashamed to call that same person—namely, the betrayer—“predestined”? Likewise, why would he hesitate to call the Jewish people, filled with envious faithlessness [Note: [Col. 0407] The manuscript reads *invidiae perfidia*, “the faithlessness of envy”; M. has *invidae perfidiae*, “envious faithlessness”], betrayers and consequently slayers of our Lord Jesus Christ, predestined to destruction?

Why, then, should all the wicked not generally be declared predestined to punishment, when both the truest reasoning persuades us and the clearest authority proves that there are no sons of God apart from his elect, nor elect apart from those predestined by him; and conversely, no predestined apart from the elect, nor elect apart from sons?

## III. From this an unchangeable conclusion follows: if all the sons of God are elect—which it is impious to deny—and all the elect are unquestionably predestined, then all the sons of God are predestined.

This connection does not admit error when reversed, nor does it waver in any way: if all the predestined are elect, a point no believer doubts, and all the elect are entirely sons of God, then all the predestined are sons of God.

This connection could not stand at all if these three terms were not equal: sonship, election, and predestination. For as much as sonship comprehends, so much does election; and as much as election comprehends, so much does predestination. Therefore these three equal terms proceed and return without error.

Just as, then, the sons of God are sought in vain apart from his elect, so his elect are thought to exist in vain apart from those predestined by him. And conversely: just as it is impious to think that anyone is predestined by God apart from his elect, so it is pointless to suppose that God’s elect exist apart from his sons.

They are not predestined, therefore, if they are not sons of God. For just as it cannot simultaneously be true that the sons of God are elect and are not predestined, so it cannot simultaneously be true that people are predestined by God and are not his elect sons.

How, then, since the faithless Jews—of whom the Savior says, “You are of your father the devil” [Note: [Col. 0407D] John 8:44]—are predestined by God to destruction, when everyone predestined by God must be his elect and consequently his son, can anyone find an answer unless he considers that place of opposites to which such a contrary form of speech is referred, as we have often said?

## IV. Let the babbling insolence of heretics, then, be silent. Let the sound faith of the predestined, the elect, and the sons of God hold firmly to this rule: whenever they hear or read of people predestined to evil, to punishments, to destruction, or to torment, they should understand nothing else than that these people are not predestined, but have not been separated from the damnable mass by the merit of original and personal sin; that they have therefore been left to live impiously and will subsequently be punished in eternal fire.

# CHAPTER XIV. Testimonies of Saint Augustine Gathered Together, by Which It Is Clearly Established That There Is Only One Predestination and That It Pertains Solely to the Saints

## I. And lest anyone perhaps think that we have said these things on our own authority, supported by no authoritative weight, we have decided to gather together the testimonies of the holy father Augustine [Note: [Col. 0407] The manuscript reads *testimoni*, “testimonies”], so that every prudent person may recognize that he in no way taught two predestinations, neither one divided into two parts nor a double predestination, as Gottschalk teaches; and that this one, namely the divine predestination [Note: [Col. 0407] The manuscript reads *divinam*; M. has *et divinam*], pertains only to the saints and can in no way belong to the wicked.

In his book *On Rebuke and Grace* he says:

> “To the saints predestined by the grace of God for the kingdom of God, the gift of perseverance is given—not merely so that they cannot persevere without this gift, but also so that through this gift they can be nothing other than persevering” [Note: [Col. 0407] Another reading: “Not merely is such assistance for perseverance given to them, but it is given in such a way that perseverance itself is bestowed upon them.”] [Note: [Col. 0408D] Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 12].

And a little later:

> “He, therefore, makes [Note: [Col. 0409] Another reading has *facit*, “makes.”] them persevere in good who made them good; but those who fall and perish were not among the number of the predestined” [Note: [Col. 0409D] Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 12].

Observe how absolutely he said it: those who fall and perish were not among the number of the predestined. How could he say this if he intended to assert either two predestinations, or one divided into two parts, or a double predestination—one belonging to the saints and the other assigned to the wicked?

For if there were two [Note: [Col. 0409] The manuscript and M. read *sive*, “or,” in place of *si*, “if.”], one would have to be assigned to those who receive the gift of perseverance and the other to those who, falling and perishing, do not receive it; nevertheless, no human being would be excluded from the number of the predestined. For if someone were expelled from the number of the predestined who live by standing firm, he would be admitted to the number of those predestined who perish by falling.

Likewise, if one predestination were divided into two parts, or were double, it would necessarily include in one part those who were lost and in the other those who were liberated. What human being, then, or what good or evil angel, would not be among the number of the predestined? Perhaps the heretic teaches a third class of human beings and angels which, because it is neither good nor evil, lies outside the number of the predestined.

But if that is utterly absurd, only two classes of human beings and angels remain. For reason divides them in this way: every human being is either good or evil, and the same applies to an angel.

## II. If, then, predestination were divided, as has been said, into two kinds or parts, one including the good and the other the evil, who could be found outside the number of the predestined? And if this were so, how could the author quoted above declare that those who fall and perish were not among the number of the predestined?

For he does not say, “They were not among the number of those predestined to life,” but absolutely: “They were not among the number of the predestined.” If, therefore, they were not among the number of the predestined, they were outside that number. Hence it follows that those who fall and perish are in no way predestined.

This is made entirely clear in what follows, where he says:

> “Pastoral necessity requires that, lest dreadful contagion spread among the many, the sick sheep be separated from the healthy, perhaps to be healed by that very separation by him for whom nothing is impossible. For since we do not know who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not, we ought [Note: [Col. 0409] *Debemus*, “we ought,” is omitted in the manuscript and supplied by M.] to be moved by such an affection of charity that we desire all to be saved” [Note: [Col. 0409D] Augustine, same work, chapter 15].

> “Accordingly, so far as concerns us, who cannot distinguish the predestined from the non-predestined, and therefore ought to desire the salvation of all, severe correction must be applied medicinally to everyone, lest they perish or cause others to perish. But it belongs to God to make this correction useful to them, because he himself foreknew and predestined them to be conformed to the image of his Son” [Note: [Col. 0409] The manuscript reads *quia*; M. has *quos*, “whom”] [Note: [Col. 0410D] Augustine, same work, chapter 16].

## III. Here the division of the whole rational creation into two parts is understood: unquestionably, into those who are among the number of the predestined and those who are outside the number of the predestined.

“For,” he says, “we do not know who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not.” And again: “We cannot distinguish the predestined from the non-predestined.”

From this arises a fourfold inquiry into the truth, arranged as a tetragon:

- Every human being is either just or unjust.
- Every human being is either predestined or not predestined.
- If it is true that every just person is predestined, it is false that every just person is not predestined.
- Likewise, if it is true that every unjust person is not predestined, it is false that every unjust person is predestined.

Observe [Note: [Col. 0409] M. reads *vide*; the manuscript has *und*] the force of the reasoning. Two universal affirmative propositions correspond to each other. For just as every just person is predestined, so every predestined person is just.

In the same way, two universal negative propositions agree with each other. For just as every unjust person is not predestined, so every non-predestined person is unjust.

To use Augustine’s own words: every human being either belongs to the number of the predestined or does not belong to it. And what wise person doubts that there are two classes of all human beings, when the truth cries out without obscurity that the human race has only two ends: one belonging to those destined for eternal punishment, the other belonging to those who enjoy eternal life?

There are therefore two opposing ends: eternal life and eternal punishment. Accordingly, the end of those who belong to the number of the predestined is eternal life; the end of those who do not belong to the number of the predestined is eternal punishment.

But since we promised to collect the testimonies of Saint Augustine, we have decided to include only those by which it is shown more clearly than light that divine predestination pertains solely to the preparation of God’s gifts, which he is going to bestow upon his elect, and therefore in no way concerns those things that relate not to his most merciful gifts but to his most just and most hidden judgments.

Although, as has often been said, authors are found to declare, by that customary figure of contrariety, that some are predestined to punishments, Augustine says in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*:

> “Among two infants equally bound by original sin, why is one taken up and the other left? And among two adults already grown, both impious, why is one called in such a way that he follows the one calling, while the other is either not called or is not called in such a way that he follows the one calling [Note: [Col. 0409] The words ‘so that he follows the one calling’ are omitted in the manuscript and supplied by M.]? The judgments of God are inscrutable.

> “Among two pious people, why is perseverance granted to one unto the end but not granted to the other [Note: [Col. 0409] Another reading: “but not bestowed upon the other”]? The judgments of God are even more inscrutable.

> “Yet this must be absolutely certain to the faithful: this one belongs to the predestined, and that one does not” [Note: [Col. 0410D] Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 8].

In the same work:

> “Would anyone dare to say that God did not foreknow to whom he was going to give the ability to believe, or whom he was going to give to his Son so that he would not lose any of them? If he foreknew these things, he certainly foreknew his benefits by which he deigns to liberate us.

> “This is the predestination of the saints, and nothing else [Note: [Col. 0411] Another reading: “This predestination of the saints is nothing other than foreknowledge”]: namely, the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits by which all who are liberated are most certainly liberated.

> “But the rest—where are they left except in the mass of perdition by the just judgment of God? This is where the Tyrians and Sidonians were left, although they could have believed [Note: [Col. 0411] The manuscript has *potuerant*, “they had been able”; another reading has *potuerunt*, “they were able”], if they had seen those remarkable signs of Christ. But because it was not given to them to believe [Note: [Col. 0411] The manuscript reads *non eis erat datum*, while M. has *erat eis*, “it was to them.”], even the means by which they might believe was withheld from them.

> “From this it is apparent that some possess, in their very natural intellectual endowment, a divine gift of understanding by which they are moved to faith if they either hear words suited to their minds or see signs; yet, if by God’s deeper judgment [Note: [Col. 0411] M. reads *altiore*, “deeper”; the manuscript has *alteriore*, “other.”] they have not been separated from the mass of perdition by the predestination of grace, neither the divine words nor the divine deeds by which they could believe are brought before them” [Note: [Col. 0411D] Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 14].

And shortly before the end of the same work:

> “There is no more illustrious example of predestination than the Mediator himself. Whoever wishes to understand it rightly as a believer should attend to him and find himself in him” [Note: [Col. 0411D] Augustine, same work, final chapter].

Thus he most splendidly concludes that all the predestined are in Christ; whoever is outside Christ is not predestined.

## IV. That God predestined no one to punishment, but prepared punishment—that is, predestined it—for those deserving condemnation, is made perfectly clear by the following statements of his. For he says:

> “Because God is just and merciful, and foreknows future things, from this damnable mass he prepares, not by respect of persons but by the unimpeachable judgment of his equity, those whom he foreknows, through gratuitous mercy—that is, he predestines them to eternal life. But he punishes the others with the punishment they deserve, as I have said. He punishes them because he foreknew what they would be; yet he did not himself make them or predestine them to be punished, but merely foreknew them, as I said, in the damnable mass” [Note: [Col. 0411D] *Hypognosticon* VI, 2].

> “For we said that, from the damnable mass of the human race, God foreknows through mercy, not through merits, those whom he predestined to life by the grace of election [Note: [Col. 0411] Another reading: “and by the election of grace”]. But the others, who by the judgment of his justice are deprived of grace [Note: [Col. 0411] Another reading: “deprived of this grace”], he merely foreknew as destined to perish through their own fault; he did not predestine them to perish.

> “But we rightly confess that punishment has been predestined for those who either do not wish to receive the faith of salvation preached to them, or cannot receive it under God’s judgment, or misuse what they have received, and for this reason are handed over to a reprobate mind, so that they do not do what is fitting [Note: [Col. 0411] Another reading: “so that they do what is not fitting”]” [Note: [Col. 0412D] Same work, chapter 2].

> “We must therefore hold firmly to the unshaken [Note: [Col. 0411] The manuscript reads *inconcussae*.] rule of this discussion, which has been made clear by divine testimonies: sinners in their own evils in this world are merely foreknown, not predestined; but punishment is predestined for them according to the fact that they are foreknown” [Note: [Col. 0411] The manuscript reads *in malis propriis esse*; another reading has *antequam essent*, “before they existed.” Another reading adds *eis esse*, “to be for them”; another witness has numerous inversions.] [Note: [Col. 0412D] Same work].

## V. By these and similar words of the most holy father Augustine, it can, as I think, be sufficiently persuaded to pious believers that what true reason commends is this: God in no way predestined sinners to punishment [Note: [Col. 0411] The manuscript reads *ad*; M. has *et ad*, “and to.”], but punishments fitting their merits were predestined for them by him.

We may infer this also from human laws. No temporal laws decree that a person should sin; but by prescribing punishments for those who will sin, they seem to seek nothing other than to restrain those inclined to sin by frightening them with the severity of punishments, and thereby to accomplish for their transgressors not less mercy than vengeance.

For the state has never decreed that people should sin; but it has decreed that the guilty should be corrected by just punishment. If this is so in laws that pass away with the mutability of time, what should we think occurs in the eternal laws filled with the unchanging vigor of piety and justice?

# CHAPTER XV. By What Kind of Figurative Expressions God Is Said to Foreknow Sins, Although They Are Nothing, or to Predestine Their Punishments, Which Likewise Are Nothing

## I. What divine and human teaching most often impresses upon us requires more careful consideration: namely, that God foreknows the unlawful sins of his creature and predestines their just punishments, although reason does not hesitate to declare that sins and their punishments are nothing, and therefore cannot be foreknown or predestined.

For how can things that do not exist either be foreknown or predestined? By what figures of speech, then, can such statements be made? I think this must be explained.

For, as I believe, in the preceding discussions I have shown, insofar as I was able to persuade, by arguments, and strengthened the point by examples of similar expressions, that whenever we encounter such a form of speech as we commonly read especially in the books of Saint Augustine—namely, that God predestined the wicked to sins and to the punishments they deserve—we can understand it in no better way than by the contrary sense, as has often been said.

## II.

The clearest example of this form of expression is found in the most impious betrayer of our Lord.[^c0048-1] He is called “predestined” in the same manner in which he was called “chosen” by the Lord. Here we must rightly understand “chosen” to mean not chosen, but neglected and cast out on account of his treachery; and likewise “predestined” to mean not predestined, but left in the mass of wrath, deprived of the gift of divine grace, an enemy rather than a friend.

Yet from the mouth of the one whom he betrayed he heard: “Friend, what have you come for?”[^c0048-2] Elsewhere, gathered figuratively among the true predestined, chosen, and friends as though he shared in divine election, he had heard: “I do not call you servants, but friends.”[^c0048-3] Similarly, although disowned by all heavenly fatherhood, the Lord spoke of him as a son among sons: “Do not call anyone on earth your father, for one is your Father, who is in heaven.”[^c0048-4] And he seemed to have been granted the gift of understanding as a wise man among the wise, when it was said to the Apostles: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom.”

If these and similar statements are to be understood in the opposite sense concerning this most impious man, what wonder is it if he and his companions in wickedness are said, by a similar right, to have been predestined? For just as none of the impious is chosen for glory, so none of them is predestined for punishment. Just as election in no way exceeds the number of the predestined, so predestination in no way exceeds the number of the chosen.

[^c0048-1]: John 6:71.

[^c0048-2]: Matthew 26:50.

[^c0048-3]: John 15:14–15.

[^c0048-4]: Matthew 23:9.

## III.

This same kind of expression—by which God is said to have predestined the unjust to punishments, or their sins to punishments—might seem rightly understood as though one were saying that God foreknew that unjust sinners would exist and would suffer punishments. Thus, just as knowledge is appropriately taken in place of predestination whenever the discussion concerns the elect, so predestination, whenever the discussion concerns the rejected, might be taken compensatively in place of foreknowledge—if true reason did not object that foreknowledge of things that do not exist is impossible.

Accordingly, God is said to predestine someone to penal punishments in the same way in which he is also said to foreknow sins: so much so that the foreknowledge of sins and their predestination to torments are proclaimed of him by almost one and the same trope, except that in sacred readings it is more customary and frequent to find that he foreknew sins and punishments than that he predestined them.
