For this reason Augustine himself, a most acute investigator and defender of the truth, took care to leave us examples of such expressions in his writings, so that we would not hesitate to accept the same meaning entirely in divine predestination and foreknowledge, even though we do not find them used equally often in Scripture.

## IV.

Accordingly, we must understand, in a most salutary and truthful sense, what he himself says as though admonishing us: “Every predestination is foreknowledge, but not every foreknowledge is predestination.”[^c0048-5]

It is as though he were saying plainly: although foreknowledge does not exceed the boundaries of predestination—for both belong to one and the same, namely, divine nature, in which there is no more or less of one thing than another—yet, rightly, where there is simplicity of nature there is no diversity, since in it all things are one.

Therefore foreknowledge has as much force in God as predestination, precisely because they are one. Scripture, however, does not use predestination as broadly and frequently as it uses foreknowledge. In divine works, when they are created and administered, we find foreknowledge and predestination both and always joined together by an inseparable bond. But with respect to evils—which, since they are not from God, are altogether nothing—we find foreknowledge named very often, but predestination only rarely.

We should believe that this has happened deliberately for our benefit: by this manner of expression we are reminded that foreknowledge is not one thing and predestination another, but one and the same, whenever both are understood in relation to those things that have either been created or bestowed by them. With respect to those things that have neither been substantially brought about by them nor bestowed from the treasury of their generosity, however, both are absent, although foreknowledge is commonly and figuratively said to be present everywhere, and predestination in particular places. Thus predestination appears to be one species within a genus, foreknowledge.

[^c0048-5]: Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10.

## V.

But if anyone is troubled by what truth continually urges upon sound minds—namely, that God is the foreknower and predestiner of all things that are from him, but not of those things that are not from him and therefore are nothing—let him return into himself, direct his attention more deeply, and consult truth itself.

For in truth, shining with light and without darkness, there radiates predestination that is essentially foreknowing, and foreknowledge that is essentially predestining—especially since nothing accidental is predicated of God. How, then, are we to believe that the supreme essence exists in things that are nothing?

Come now! If God’s foreknowledge is God, then necessarily it is also truth.[^c0048-6] I say the same concerning predestination. If it too is God, it is without doubt truth.

“But truth,” says Augustine, “must necessarily exist in something, that is, in true and abiding things.”[^c0048-7] Therefore, if foreknowledge and predestination are truth, and truth is the truth of true things—things that are true because they were made by him—then foreknowledge and predestination exist only in those things that were made by truth.

If sins, as I think, are not truth, how can foreknowledge or predestination belong to them? Again, if truth must necessarily exist in true things, then foreknowledge and predestination exist in those things. If everything that exists naturally must exist from truth, while whatever does not exist according to nature must, without doubt, not exist from truth—sin is contrary to nature. It therefore does not exist from truth, and consequently not from its foreknowledge or predestination.

Let us briefly gather the argument concerning sins. If truth is the truth of true things, and plainly only those things are true that exist, divine foreknowledge and predestination are certainly the truth of true things. Who, then, could doubt that sins are false, unless he doubts that they are not from truth? It follows that neither foreknowledge nor predestination can be made concerning them.

[^c0048-6]: The manuscript reads *necessario* (“necessarily”); M reads *Deus est, est necessario* (“God is, is necessarily”).

[^c0048-7]: Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 36.

## VI.

The conclusion concerning sin has been reached. Let us consider punishment, penalty, destruction, or whatever name may be given to the whole condition of misery that justly follows sin.

We have already stated, relying on the authority of Father Augustine, that no one is prepared for torments by the mercy of divine predestination, although, as has often been repeated, it is said to predestine the impious to those very torments.

Here, as we have shown, either predestination is put in the place of foreknowledge by way of similarity, or we have the trope called *hypallage* (ὑπαλλαγή), which we may call “subalternation.” This is appropriate because the words are not expressed in the same order as the meaning. The poet gives an example: “to give the south winds to the fleets,” which is understood in reverse as “to give the fleets to the south winds.”

It would therefore not be unreasonable, by this trope, for authors to say that the impious have been predestined to punishment, as though they had said that punishment was predestined for the impious. They could say this, I mean, if reason permitted us properly to state that punishment had been predestined for the impious.

But if, as the following discussion will show, the impious are said to have been predestined to punishments according to the same manner of expression by which punishments are said to have been predestined for the impious, then only the mode mentioned so often remains—the mode called an *enthymeme*.[^c0048-8] This is because the conception in the mind is always taken from the opposite.

[^c0048-8]: The manuscript reads *entimema*.

## VII.

For this reason grammarians appropriately call it, as we have said, *katantiphrasis* (καταντίφρασις). Examples in secular literature are “the Fates” (*Parcae*), because they spare no one; likewise “grove” (*lucus*), because it does not give light; and similar expressions, which grammarians identify in individual words.

Among the expressions of rhetors, Marcus Tullius, speaking for Ligarius, says: “A new crime, Gaius Caesar!”[^c0048-9]

In the divine writings too, this kind of expression often appears, brighter than light itself. The Apostle says: “Grant me this wrong,”[^c0048-10] and the passage quoted above: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the prudent.”[^c0048-11]

The Lord also said to the Jews concerning John the Baptist in the Gospel: “Why did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?”[^c0048-12] Likewise to his betrayer: “Friend, why have you come?”[^c0048-13]—and the other expressions which, as we said, were spoken to him as though he were a companion of apostolic grace.

These examples are sufficient. Let us return to the subject.

[^c0048-9]: The manuscript reads *gai*.

[^c0048-10]: 2 Corinthians 12:13.

[^c0048-11]: 1 Corinthians 1:19.

[^c0048-12]: Matthew 11:7.

[^c0048-13]: Matthew 26:50.

## VIII.

We must now consider whether everything we have said about sin should likewise be said about its punishment.

We have said that all sins are not from God, rightly so, because they are not according to nature but contrary to it. Let us hear the Apostle: “The sting of death is sin.”[^c0048-14] If death therefore necessarily follows from the wound of sin, death will plainly be from sin; and death is certainly the punishment of sin. Accordingly, from the source of sin comes death, and from the source of death comes misery, which is punishment or penalty.

Thus there is, as it were, an inseparable chain joining all evils. From the perverse and culpable movement of free choice—namely, the movement that abandons the highest good, its God, whom it could enjoy—there arose the sin of disobedient pride. Sin was then followed by death, and death by the misery of punishments. Who can free us from all these things? “The grace of God through Jesus Christ.”[^c0048-15]

Those things are certainly not from him who frees us from them. For if they were from him, they would unquestionably be not evils but goods. But they are evils. Therefore they cannot be made by him.

Or who cannot easily see that things mutually opposed to one another cannot arise from one origin? Certainly, where good exists, evil will not exist; where humility exists, pride will not exist. Iniquity never flows from the fountain of justice; death never proceeds from the source of life; blessedness is not the cause of misery. Finally, the supreme essence in no way produces things that are not.

Sin, death, punishment, and the loss of justice, life, and blessedness are defects. Therefore they are not from him who is. And consequently, if they are not from him, who would dare to say that anything exists in them?

[^c0048-14]: 1 Corinthians 15:52.

[^c0048-15]: Romans 7:25.

## IX.

The discussion has been completed, if I am not mistaken, concerning both sins and punishments: neither are made by God, nor are they foreknown or predestined by him.[^c0048-16]

“For who understands his offenses?”[^c0048-17] Yet we say that we foreknow that there will be darkness after the setting of the sun, silence after an acclamation, pain after health has departed, sadness after joy has passed away, labor when rest has perished, folly after wisdom has been lost, and other things of this kind. All these things, as Augustine says, “are known by not knowing”; “their ignorance is their knowledge.”[^c0048-18]

In this way sacred authority asserts that God either foreknew or predestined sins or punishments that cannot be foreknown or predestined. For they are not known in the definitions of forms, but are recognized through ignorance in their defects.

What else does “nothing” signify except the conception of a thinking mind concerning a defect of essence? What do darkness or silence signify except the conception, in a thinking mind, of a defect in being? What do darkness or silence signify except the conception in a thinking mind that light or voice is absent? When I say that, while the sun is shining over the earth, I know that darkness exists beneath the earth, I mean only that light is present above the earth and absent beneath it.

Whatever of these things I say, a conception of the sun is formed in my mind. Whether the sun is present or absent, its image is always present in memory. When the sun is present, that image receives the name “light”; when it is absent, it receives the name “darkness.” I mean this: the conception of what is present is called light; the conception of what is absent is called darkness.

[^c0048-16]: The printed note objects: “This is altogether false. For sins are foreknown, though not predestined; punishments, however, are both foreknown and prepared for the sinner by God’s most just judgment.”

[^c0048-17]: Psalm 18:13.

[^c0048-18]: Augustine, *The City of God* 12.7.

## X.

These and similar signs therefore show only the conception of the absence or defect of things that exist.[^c0048-19]

What, then, does the person who suffers know except that health is absent? In suffering, therefore, he knows not the pain itself but health, which he would certainly not know if he did not possess some conception of it. The memory of health remains in the senses, while health itself resides in the substance that God created.

For the Creator does not punish what he made, nor does he take away from those things their natural gifts.[^c0048-20] If health were not, in some manner, present in the very nature of the one who suffers, he would be entirely ignorant of it; memory would not form, from his hidden knowledge of it, an awareness of its absence; and he would not be tormented by desire for its presence.

There is no rational nature that does not wish to flee misery and attain blessedness, or that, after tasting blessedness, wishes to withdraw and be miserable.

[^c0048-19]: The manuscript reads “things that are”; another reading has “as things.”

[^c0048-20]: Prudentius comments: “God’s punishing—that is, consigning to punishments—means nothing other than that he punishes what he made, but on account of sin, which he himself did not make. For, he says, in blessed Job no sin was being punished, but only the flesh, which God made. And, greater than all this, in our Lord Jesus Christ nothing was punished except what he himself had made, namely, his flesh.”

# CHAPTER XVI  
## That no nature punishes another nature, and that the punishments of sinners are nothing other than their sins

[^c0048-21]

[^c0048-21]: Prudentius observes: “No nature is punished except by another nature,” namely, created nature by the creating nature, so that the one who is the maker of created natures may himself be judge and punisher; or created natures may be punished by created natures. Concerning the other statement, “that the punishments of sinners are nothing other than their punishments,” Prudentius rightly observes: “There are many kinds of punishments, present and future, imposed by the most just Judge in addition to sins.”

## I.

In the great burning of eternal fire, penal misery is nothing other than the absence of blessed happiness.

Yet no one will be there who does not naturally possess within himself a conception of absent blessedness and a desire for it, so that he is tormented all the more intensely the more ardently he desires what the just judgment of God does not permit him to attain.

That desire certainly would not exist in the miserable person if he did not possess at all what he desires. Thus, in a most hidden yet most truthful manner, those condemned to the deepest misery of punishments will possess happiness and will not possess it. They will possess a certain conception by which they remember it, but they will not possess its face for the fruit of contemplation.

The miserable, as we have said, would certainly not have this conception of happiness in their memory if some knowledge of it were not formed in their nature. But just as no one possesses a conception of truth outside himself, so neither does he possess knowledge of it outside himself.

Truth is happiness. Therefore no one will possess either a conception or knowledge of happiness outside his own nature. In the nature of the miserable, then, truth will exist. Happiness will therefore exist.

But how will that nature be miserable if happiness—which is truth—is present in it? What then? If no nature has been punished, will it be miserable? I do not see how. For what cause could any nature be miserable unless it had been punished?

Therefore, if no nature can be punished, no nature will be miserable. Who, moreover, would not believe that every nature is either God or made by God? It would be utterly foolish to suppose that the creating nature is capable of misery.

Nor do I see by what justice the creating nature could punish the natures it created. Hence no nature will be punished; and what is not punished will not be miserable.

## II.

But if someone should refuse to concede this argument, he will not, I think, reject the authority of Father Augustine, who in the eleventh book of the *Exameron* does not hesitate to state the following:

“It occurs to anyone, and it is true and manifest, that it is contrary to justice itself for God, without any preceding merit, to condemn in anyone that very thing which he himself created in him. The certain and evident condemnation of the devil and his angels is recounted in the Gospel, where the Lord declared that he would say to those on his left: ‘Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.’[^c0048-22]

“It must in no way be believed that the nature which God created is punished in him, but rather his own evil will is punished by the penalty of eternal fire. Nor does the statement, ‘This is the beginning of the work of the Lord, which he made to be mocked by his angels,’[^c0048-23] signify his nature. It signifies either the ethereal body that he adapted to such a will, or the very ordering in which he made him useful to the good even against his will, or the fact that, foreknowing that he would become evil by his own will, he nevertheless made him, not withholding his goodness in granting life and substance, while also foreseeing, with respect to his future harmful will, how much good his wondrous goodness and power would bring about through him.”[^c0048-24]

If, therefore, the angelic nature in the devil is justly not permitted to be punished, what wonder is it if the same divine justice prevents human substance, even in the most impious human beings, from being tormented?[^c0048-25]

For nothing is justly punished except what is convicted of having committed an offense. No human iniquity is found except the culpable perversity of his own will. This is most truly not a nature, because it was not created by God, the creator of all things, in any substance.

It is therefore justly punished and miserable. Hence Augustine says:

“He is exceedingly impious and ignorant who does not distinguish the vice of nature from the author of nature, from whom whatever is condemned in each person is entirely alien. He creates human beings so that they may be human beings, and does not withdraw his work from the succession of generations, intending, according to the counsel of his good will, to restore in many what he himself made, and to punish in many what he himself did not make.”[^c0048-26]

[^c0048-22]: Matthew 25:41.

[^c0048-23]: Psalm 105:26.

[^c0048-24]: Augustine, *On Genesis*, book 11, chapters 21–22.

[^c0048-25]: Augustine, same work.

[^c0048-26]: Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* 3.7.

## III.

Since God established the whole nature of all human beings in the first man—for, as Augustine says, “that one man was still all human beings”[^c0048-27]—what was created naturally in him could in no way transgress the Creator’s natural law.

Therefore the nature that God created in him did not sin in him. Yet in him all sinned,[^c0048-28] and consequently in him all die and, as a result, all are punished.

It is therefore most rightly believed that, just as God willed to create in him the general substance of the human race, so he also established in him the individual will of every human being. For if the fullness of the common human nature, both bodily and spiritual, was constituted in one man, then the individual will of each person necessarily existed in him.

Thus it was not the generality of nature that sinned in him, but the individual will of each person.[^c0048-29]

For if that nature sinned, since it is one, it would certainly perish in its entirety.[^c0048-30] But it did not perish, since the remedy for the wound—the substance of the Redeemer—remained incorrupt in it, apart from the fact that all sinned together in one man. For he did not sin in all, but all sinned in him.[^c0048-31]

Just as he had his own individual will, so he also had his own individual sin. And just as each person possessed in him the individual number of his own will, so each person could, by himself, commit his own offense in him.

For no one’s sin is justly avenged in another. Therefore nature is punished in no one, because it is from God and does not sin. But the voluntary movement that lustfully uses nature’s good is deservedly punished, because it transgresses nature’s law. It certainly would not transgress that law if it had been created substantially by God.

[^c0048-27]: Romans 5:12.

[^c0048-28]: Prudentius comments: “The generality of nature sinned in him, which Scripture calls the mass of condemnation; therefore the whole was condemned by the just Judge, not the will alone, and it cannot be wholly restored except through the humility of the Mediator.”

[^c0048-29]: A later hand wrote in the margin, perhaps in the thirteenth century: “He says that in the first man all human beings did not sin generally, but individually; this is contradictory.”

[^c0048-30]: Another hand added in the margin: “He says that Adam’s nature did not sin.”

[^c0048-31]: Another marginal note reads: “He teaches that sins are natural.”

Prudentius responds to the preceding argument: “The whole nature sinned and therefore in some manner the whole nature perished. Consequently it needs a liberator. For in infants it is not the will to sin, which does not exist, but the nature of condemned origin that is punished.”

Prudentius further comments on the statement “not nature but the will sinned”: “Nature did indeed sin, but it was not a defect of nature as it was founded by the good God; rather, it was corrupted by its own will. Nevertheless, the sin must be attributed not only to the will but also to the nature whose will it is, and therefore sinful nature is justly punished. For nature—that is, the soul—accepted the serpent’s persuasion, and the same nature, that is, through its body, ate the fruit of the forbidden tree.”

## IV.

From this it is clearly gathered that, among the impious, what suffers punishments is not what God made, but what pride wickedly discovered.

The lust of a perverse will is tormented when it is not permitted to possess what it wrongly or unworthily desires. The generality of all vices is included under the name “lust.”

If reason has shown that no nature is punished, it will necessarily show that no nature punishes.[^c0048-32] For neither the creating nature nor the created nature punishes a created nature, since no substance can be contrary to another substance.

Otherwise a nature would be punished most unjustly when no deserving evil had preceded its torment. Augustine clearly intended to express this in his previously cited statement: “It is contrary to justice itself for God, without any preceding merit, to condemn in anyone that very thing which he himself created in him.”[^c0048-33]

This reasoning is proved above all by the fact that the authorship of no sin can be referred to God except in the most erroneous and impious manner. If sin came from nature, and nature came from God, it would plainly follow that sin came from God.

Far be it from us to believe this or to accept that utterly false paralogism, which is falsely constructed as follows:

- Every nature is from God.
- Every sin is from nature.
- Therefore every sin is from God.

Since it is most absurd to concede this, there remains the truest and most pious syllogism, completely filled with charity and catholic faith:

- Every good is either God or made by God.
- Everything made by God cannot produce any defect of the good.
- Therefore no good can produce any defect of the good.
- Conversely, no defect of the good comes from the good.

Every sin, because it is evil, is a defect of the good. No defect of the good comes from the good. Therefore every sin, because it is evil, cannot come from the good.

Every rational creature is a great good. Evil comes from no good.[^c0048-34] Therefore sin does not come from any rational creature.

[^c0048-32]: A marginal note by another hand says: “He says that nature is neither punished nor punishes; therefore it is not capable of suffering.”

[^c0048-33]: Another marginal note says: “He has perversely understood the testimony he adopts.”

[^c0048-34]: Prudentius: “No evil exists except from good.”

Another marginal note says: “Sin does not come from a creature.”

## V.

For Truth itself says: “A good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and an evil man brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart.”[^c0048-35]

It is as though he were saying: every good thing that a good man brings forth from his thought is bestowed from a good treasure, that is, from the one in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.[^c0048-36]

Every evil thing that an evil man brings forth from his evil thought comes from an evil treasure—namely, pride, which is the beginning of every sin.[^c0048-37]

Speaking of this treasure of wickedness, Augustine says in his book *On True Religion*:

“The first vice of the rational soul is the will to do those things that the highest and innermost truth forbids. Thus man was expelled from paradise into this world—that is, from eternal things to temporal things, from abundance to poverty, from firmness to weakness.

“Therefore he was not moved from substantial good to substantial evil, since no substance is evil, but from eternal good to temporal good, from spiritual good to bodily good, from intelligible good to sensible good, from the highest good to the lowest good.

“There is therefore a certain good which, if the rational soul loves it, it sins, because it has been ordered below the soul. Thus sin itself is evil, not the substance that is loved in sinning.

“Therefore that tree which is said to have been planted in the middle of paradise is not evil,[^c0048-38] but the transgression of the divine command. When this transgression is followed by just condemnation, there arises from that tree—which was touched against the prohibition—the discernment of good and evil. For when the soul has become entangled in its sin, by paying the penalty it learns the difference between the command that it refused to keep and the sin that it committed.

“In this way it learns through suffering the evil that it did not learn by avoiding it, and by comparison it loves more ardently the good that, through disobedience, it had loved less.

“Therefore the vice of the soul is what it did, and the difficulty arising from the vice is the punishment that it suffers.[^c0048-39] This is the whole of evil.

“To do and to suffer are not substances. Therefore substance is not evil. Water is not evil, nor is the animal that lives in the air; these are substances. Evil is the reckless plunging into water and the suffocation suffered by the submerged person.

“A stylus made of iron, with one end for writing and another for erasing, is made by a craftsman; it is beautiful in its kind and suited to our use. But if someone wished to write with the end meant for erasing and to erase with the end meant for writing, he would not thereby make the stylus evil; rather, he himself would rightly be blamed for what he had done. If he corrected this, where would the evil be?

“If someone suddenly looks at the midday sun, his eyes will be troubled by the reflected light. Will the sun or the eyes therefore be evil? Certainly not, for they are substances. The evil lies in the disordered gaze and in the resulting disturbance. This evil will no longer exist when the eyes have recovered and look upon the light appropriately.”[^c0048-40]

A little earlier in the same work he says:

“If it is asked who established the body, let the one who is most beautiful of all be sought, for all beauty comes from him. Who is this, except the one God, the one truth, the one salvation of all, and the first and highest essence, from which everything that exists comes insofar as it exists? For whatever exists is good insofar as it exists.

“Therefore death is not from God; God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living.[^c0048-41] For the highest essence causes everything that exists to exist, and from this it is called essence.

“Death, however, compels whatever dies not to exist, insofar as it dies.[^c0048-42] For if things that die were to die completely, they would undoubtedly come to nothing. They die only insofar as they participate less in essence.

“This can be stated more briefly: they die the more, the less they are.[^c0048-43]

“Body is less than any life, because, however little it remains in form, it remains through life, whether by the life through which each animal exists or by the life through which the whole nature of the world is governed. Body therefore lies more exposed to death and is consequently nearer to nothing.

“Thus life, which delights in the fruit of the body and neglects God, inclines toward nothingness; and this is wickedness. By this act life becomes bodily and earthly, and for this reason it is also called flesh and earth. As long as it remains so, it will not possess the kingdom of God,[^c0048-44] and what it loves will be taken away from it.

“For it loves what is less than life, since it is body; and on account of the sin by which it is loved, it becomes corruptible, so that by passing away it abandons its lover, just as the lover, by loving it, abandoned God. For he neglects God’s commandments, which say: ‘Eat this, and do not eat that.’

“He is therefore dragged into punishments, because by loving lower things he is ordered, in the poverty of his pleasures and in pains, among the inhabitants of hell.

“What is the pain that is called bodily pain except the sudden corruption of the health of that thing which the soul, by using it wrongly, has made subject to corruptions?

“And what is the pain that is called pain of the soul except the loss of mutable things that it enjoyed or hoped it could enjoy?

“This is the whole of what is called evil, namely, sin and the punishment of sin.”[^c0048-45]

Therefore divine equity does not punish what its goodness willed to create.

[^c0048-37]: Ecclesiasticus 10:15.

[^c0048-38]: Another reading has “the tree is not evil”; another, “of paradise”; the manuscript omits *esse* (“to have been”), which was added by a later editor.

[^c0048-39]: A marginal note by another hand says: “He confesses that the vice of the soul is what he previously denied.”

[^c0048-40]: Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 20.

[^c0048-41]: Wisdom 1:13.

### Additional textual and marginal apparatus

- IV, “said to be present everywhere”: the manuscript reads *pasim* (“everywhere”), and does so frequently.

- V, “foreknower and predestiner”: the manuscript has *praeque* (abbreviated *pq*); M reads *priusquam* (“before”). At “consult truth itself,” M reads *consulet* (“let him consult”). At “the supreme essence exists,” the manuscript reads *esse* (“to exist”), M *est* (“exists”).

- VI, “Here”: *Ubi* is omitted in M. In the poetic example, the manuscript reads *clasibus* for *classibus* (“fleets”), consistently. The manuscript reads *entimema* for *enthymeme*.

- VII, “For this reason”: M reads *aperte* (“openly”) for *apte* (“aptly”). The manuscript has *gai* for *Gai* and *multotiens* for *multoties* (“many times”). “By way of example” is printed *Exemplo* in the manuscript.

- VIII, “But they are evils”: M reads *aut qui* for *atqui* (“but indeed”).

- IX, “health has departed”: the manuscript reads *abscesum* for *abscessum*. In the repeated discussion of darkness and silence, M omits from “defect in being” through “in a thinking mind”; the manuscript has this passage added in the lower margin by the same hand. At “light is present above the earth,” M reads *esse* (“to be”) for *adesse* (“to be present”).

- X, “things that exist”: M reads *sicut* (“as”) for *quae sunt* (“which exist”). At “awareness of its absence,” M reads *absentia* for *absentiam*. At “be miserable,” the manuscript reads *miserumque* (“and miserable,” masculine/neuter) for M’s *miseraque*.

- Chapter XVI, I: Prudentius adds that this absence of blessedness is punishment, together with the excessive burning of fire and the consumption of worms.

- Chapter XVI, II: At “in anyone,” the manuscript reads *in quoque*, while another reading has *in quoquam*. At “declared,” the manuscript reads *pronuntiavit*; another reading has *praenuntiavit* (“foretold”). At “how much good,” the manuscript reads *quanto de illo bona esset ... facturus*; M reads *quanta de illo bona esse ... facturus*.

- Chapter XVI, II, “This is most truly not a nature”: the text is corrected from the manuscript’s *qui*; M reads *quae*. At “in any substance,” M reads the ungrammatical *nulla substantiam*. At “It is therefore justly punished and miserable,” the manuscript has *punita*, while M reads *sit*.

- Chapter XVI, III, after “Yet in him all sinned”: Prudentius comments: “In the devil and impious human beings, the nature depraved and corrupted by its own will is punished.” At “most rightly,” M reads *rectissime*, the manuscript *rectissimo*.

- Chapter XVI, III, final marginal note, partly illegible: “[He] says that the voluntary movement of the mind is not ... [lacuna] ... by God.”

- Chapter XVI, IV: A marginal note at “no nature punishes” reads: “He says that nature neither is punished nor punishes; therefore it is not capable of suffering.” At “the authorship of no sin,” another note reads: “Not even a pagan says this.” At the premise “Every nature is from God,” a marginal correction reads: “Nature is not *from* God, but *by* God; nor is it a part of God, but his work.”

- Chapter XVI, V: At “if the rational soul loves it,” another reading has *diligit* (“loves”). The manuscript reads *dinoscentia* for *dignoscentia* (“discernment”), consistently. At “Will the sun or the eyes therefore be evil?” M reads *non* (“not”) for the manuscript’s *num* (“surely not?”). At “they die the more,” *magis* is conjectural; the manuscript and M read *et ... minus* (“and the less”). At “neglects God,” the manuscript reads *neglegit*. At “By this act,” M reads *Hoc autem pacto* (“but by this arrangement”). At “he neglects God’s commandments,” the manuscript reads *neglegit*, M *neglexit* (“neglected”). At “poverty,” the manuscript reads *aegestate* for *egestate*. At “made subject to corruptions,” another reading is “made liable to corruption.” At “hoped it could enjoy,” another reading has *speraverat* (“had hoped”); another has *Ut hoc* for *Hoc*.

- The marginal note on “the vice of the soul is what it did” reads: “He admits that the vice of the soul is what he previously denied.”

## VI.

Without doubt, therefore, we must hold that no nature is punished by another nature, and consequently that no punishment has been made by God, and therefore neither foreknown nor predestined by him [Note: [Col. 0423] Another hand has added in the margin: “No punishment foreknown or predestined by God.”], although it is often said that he both made it and foreknew or predestined it. For God arranged, as an exercise for our understanding, both in his Scriptures and in their interpreters, that when we hear such modes of expression our attention should awaken to understand what mystical meaning lies hidden in them [Note: [Col. 0423] Thus the manuscript; M. reads “what.”] [Col. 0423B], not what the simple surface of the words displays.

Since this is so, it is reasonably asked what is punished in the wretched, who are afflicted with the torments of punishments, and what it is that punishes them. The blessed Father Augustine answers this inquiry. In his exposition of the seventh Psalm [Note: [Col. 0423] The manuscript has “sixth.”] he says:

> “Let us understand that each person’s punishment is made from his own sin, and that his iniquity is turned into punishment. Let us not suppose that the tranquillity and ineffable light of God brings forth from itself something by which sins are punished; rather, let us understand that God so orders the sins themselves that what was a delight to the person who sinned becomes an instrument for the Lord who punishes him” [Note: [Col. 0423D] Augustine, on Psalm 6, near the end.].

Thus he beautifully and excellently defines that there are no other instruments for torturing impiety apart from impiety itself. For every sin that a person begins in this life with delight is completed in the future with punishment [Note: [Col. 0423] Another hand has added in the margin: “The sin begun in this life will be completed in the future.”], unless divine grace, through Jesus Christ the Lord and Savior of the world, frees him from it before he departs from this age.

There is no sin that does not punish the sinner. In every sinner, sin and its punishment begin to arise together, because there is no sin that does not punish itself—secretly, however, in this life, but openly in the other, which is future.

## VII.

This is most clearly proved by the example of virtue. Every virtue must necessarily begin in this life and be completed in the future, so that, if it is genuine, its blessedness begins with it: its beginning is secret, but its labor—caused by things that oppose it and seek utterly to remove it—is open. This is invariably unavoidable within the span of this life. In that life in which all piety is perfected, however, when all labor required for defending virtue has been consumed, virtue itself will be its own peace and blessedness [Note: [Col. 0423] The same hand has added in the margin: “He says that virtues are the blessedness of a person.”]

Thus, conversely, every sin [Col. 0424A] from which divine mercy does not absolve a person takes delight outwardly, in the present life’s pursuit, in the wretched person who sins and persists in it [Note: [Col. 0423] The manuscript reads “is loved”; M. has “delights.”], but inwardly punishes itself. In the future, when the fullness of impiety has been completed, all those delights of committing sin that existed here will there be turned into instruments for torturing sin.

Sin, therefore, begins to be punished by sin itself here secretly, and there it will be openly completed in torment; here is the beginning of sorrows, there the end of punishments; here false joy arising from voluntary desire, there true sadness arising from compelled suffering.

With good reason, then, the destructive sweetness of desire here will there be turned into the bitterness of retribution. For here he had wickedly and arrogantly wished to turn the gift of divine generosity—that is, freedom of the will, which is a natural gift of understanding [Note: [Col. 0423] Another hand has added in the margin: “He calls natural understanding a gift of grace.”], namely, the sharpness of mind that the Creator generously gave to all for seeking, loving, and enjoying him—to purposes of disgrace. There, lest he enjoy the beauty of truth at all, justice may destroy him [Note: [Col. 0423] M. reads “justice”; the manuscript reads “of justice.”], and he will not escape, inextricably and punitively, the darkness of eternal ignorance in the prison of his own iniquity into which he had shut himself here.

## VIII.

Hence Augustine says in his book *On True Religion*:

> “Those, therefore,” he says, “who misuse so great a good of the mind that they desire visible things outside it rather than those things by which they ought to have been recalled to behold and love intelligible things will be given outer darkness. For the beginning of these is carnal prudence and the weakness of bodily senses [Note: [Col. 0423] The manuscript has “weakness” misspelled.]. Those who delight in conflicts will be alienated from peace and entangled in the greatest difficulties. For the beginning of the greatest difficulty is war and contention; and I think this signifies that their hands and feet are bound [Note: [Col. 0424D] Matthew XXII, 13.], that is, every facility for acting is taken away.

> “Those who wish to thirst and hunger, to burn with desire and grow weary so that they may eat, drink, lie with another, and sleep with pleasure, love deprivation, which is the beginning of the greatest sorrows. What they love will therefore be completed in them, so that there they will have weeping and gnashing of teeth [Note: [Col. 0424D] Matthew XIII, 50.].

> “For many love all these beginnings at once. Their life is to watch, quarrel, eat, drink, lie together, and sleep, and in their thought to embrace nothing but the phantasms that they gather from such a life, and from their deceptiveness to establish rules of superstition [Col. 0424D] or impiety [Note: [Col. 0423] Thus the manuscript; another copy has ‘to fabricate.’], by which they are deceived and to which they cling—even if they attempt to abstain from the allurements of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0423] ‘To abstain’ is omitted by the manuscript and supplied by M.]—because they do not use well the talent entrusted to them, that is, the sharpness of mind by which all those who are called learned, cultivated, or witty seem to excel. Instead, they have it bound up in a napkin [Note: [Col. 0425] Thus the manuscript; another copy has ‘bound.’] [Note: [Col. 0425D] Luke XIX, 20.], or buried in the earth [Note: [Col. 0425D] Matthew XXV, 18.], that is, wrapped and oppressed by delicate and superfluous things or by earthly desires.

> “Their hands and feet will therefore be bound, and they will be cast into outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth [Note: [Col. 0425D] Matthew XXII, 13.], not because they loved these things—for who would love them?—but because the things they loved are the beginnings of these, and necessarily lead those who love them to them.

> “For those who love going more than returning, or arriving, must be sent far away [Note: [Col. 0425] Thus the manuscript; another copy has ‘farther away.’], because they are flesh, and a spirit that walks and does not return” [Note: [Col. 0425D] Psalm LXXVII; Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 51.].

## IX.

The most holy and truthful Pope Gregory agrees with this in Book XI of his *Moralia on Job*, explaining what is written, “If he shuts a man in, there is no one who can open” [Note: [Col. 0425D] Job XII, 14.]:

> “For every person, by what he does wrongly, makes for himself nothing other than the prison of his conscience, so that the guilt of his soul [Note: [Col. 0425] Thus the manuscript; another reading has *animi*, “mind.”] weighs him down, even if no one accuses him outwardly [Note: [Col. 0425] Thus the manuscript; another copy has ‘accuse.’]. When, by God’s judgment, he is left in the blindness of his wickedness, he is shut up, as it were, within himself, so that he cannot find a way of escape, which he is by no means worthy to find.

> “Often, indeed, some wish to leave their evil actions; but because they are weighed down by the burden of those same actions, enclosed in the prison of evil habit, they cannot leave themselves. And indeed [Note: [Col. 0425] Thus the manuscript; another reading has *quidam*, “some people.”], wishing to punish their own faults, they turn what they think they are rightly doing into more serious sins [Note: [Col. 0425] Thus the manuscript; another copy has ‘more serious faults’]. Thus, in a pitiable way, what they think is an exit becomes for them an enclosure.

> “So it was with the reprobate Judas. When he inflicted death upon himself because of his sin, he arrived at the punishments of eternal death, and repented of his sin more wickedly than he had sinned.

> “Let it therefore be said: ‘If he shuts a man in, there is no one who can open,’ because, just as no one resists the generosity of the One who calls, so no one obstructs the justice of the One who abandons. He is therefore said to shut a person in when, with the doors closed, he does not open them [Note: [Col. 0425] Thus the manuscript; another copy has ‘it is God who shuts.’]

> “Hence also God says to Moses concerning Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0425] The manuscript has ‘Pharaoh’ in an altered spelling.]: ‘I will harden his heart’ [Note: [Col. 0426D] Exodus IV, 1.]. God is said to harden by justice when he does not soften a reprobate heart by grace [Note: [Col. 0425] ‘God’ is omitted by the manuscript and supplied by M.]. He therefore shuts a person in when he leaves him in the darkness of his own works” [Note: [Col. 0426D] Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, XI, 5.].

The same author says in the same work:

> “He loosens the belt of kings [Note: [Col. 0426D] Job XII, 18.] when, because of the fault of pride, he destroys the girdle of chastity in those who seemed to rule their members well. What, then, is understood by a rope [Note: [Col. 0425] Thus the manuscript and M.; another copy has ‘end’] except sin, as Solomon says: ‘The iniquities of the wicked capture him, and he is bound with the cords of his sins’” [Note: [Col. 0426D] Ibid., XI, 8.].

# CHAPTER XVII  
## Why God is said to have predestined punishments, although he neither makes nor predestines them

[Col. 0426A]

## I.

Therefore, by reason and authority, it is firmly established that God is in no way the author, in no way the maker, and in no way the predestiner of the punishments by which proud impiety will be tortured with eternal suffering. Yet he is called their author, maker, and predestiner in the sense in which he is most truly believed to be the maker and governor of the whole universe in which they exist.

Before creating the universe itself, he predestined its future state of beauty in such a way that the ugliness of evils—which he did not predestine, because he would not be making it—would not be ugly within the universe; the wickedness of those who cause harm would not harm; the error of those who err would not err; and the misery of those who are tormented would not disturb the blessedness of the elect. For no ugliness, wickedness, error, or misery is permitted to dishonor the natural order predestined before the ages.

## II.

When, therefore, we hear that God predestined this person or that person to destruction, punishment, penalties, torment, or whatever name is ordinarily given to the misery by which iniquity is tormented by itself, in itself, and through itself, we are required to understand nothing other than that he foreknew and predestined before the ages the order in which those persons would exist within the universe whom, by a most hidden yet perfectly just judgment, he permitted to feel the bitterness of their sins [Note: [Col. 0425] Thus M.; the manuscript reads ‘promised.’], because he left them in their damnable origin.

At the same time, the familiar distinction between foreknowledge and predestination must be preserved: although predestination extends as widely as foreknowledge—for both signify one and the same thing, namely the divine substance—predestination pertains only to things that are good, whereas foreknowledge pertains to both good and evil. This distinction, however, arises not from nature but from usage in speech.

## III.

Just as it is said of God that the presence of his power is everywhere, but the grace of his indwelling is not everywhere, so it may be said of him that foreknowledge is everywhere, but predestination is not everywhere. Since truth most clearly proclaims that wherever God is present, he is certainly there by indwelling as well, likewise wherever there is foreknowledge, there must necessarily be predestination.

Therefore, just as God’s presence and indwelling exist only in those things that have been made by him, so his foreknowledge and predestination must be believed to exist only in those things that he would make. Consequently, just as his presence and indwelling are said, conversely, to exist in those things that are not from him and that he did not make, although he is not in them, so his foreknowledge and predestination are, conversely, declared to exist in those things that he neither made nor gave, although they are nothing [Note: [Col. 0427D] Prudentius: “In the divine utterances, God’s indwelling is nowhere placed in things that do not exist, whereas God’s foreknowledge is not absent even from our wickedness and sins.”].

Nevertheless, they are not incongruously considered to exist in those things that arose through the fault of the creature, since God not only wisely orders the creature itself but also does not allow its defect to exceed his laws.

## IV.

That the hiding-places of human punishments and the most obscure afflictions of the children of Adam continue secretly to punish even those who wish to live well in this mortal life, the blessed Augustine [Note: [Col. 0427D] Augustine, *Confessions*, VIII, 10.] wished to make clear in the eighth book of his *Confessions*, when he lamented within himself the force of human misery:

> “When I was deliberating about serving my Lord [Note: [Col. 0427] M. has ‘my Lord God.’], as I had long intended, I was the one who willed, I who did not will [Note: [Col. 0427] Thus the manuscript; M. reads *ergo ego*, “therefore I.”]. I was neither fully willing nor fully unwilling, and therefore I was contending with myself and being torn apart by myself. This tearing apart happened against my will, yet it did not reveal the nature of another mind, but the punishment of my own [Note: [Col. 0427] Thus the manuscript; M. reads *meam*, while another reading has *meae*.]. Therefore I was no longer the one performing it, but sin dwelling in me [Note: [Col. 0427] Thus the manuscript.], arising from the punishment of the freer sin, because I was a son of Adam.”

It is not he who punishes who most rightly orders within the dwellings of the universe those who injure themselves and suffer the bitterness of their own crimes within themselves, in places where it is entirely fitting that they should labor.

## V.

Let us use an analogy. What if a father of a large household, who by his skill wished to construct for himself a very spacious house—capacious in length, breadth, and depth; abundant in the variety of its walls, angles, apses [Note: [Col. 0427] The manuscript reads ‘apses’; M. has ‘of apses.’], and diverse forms [Note: [Col. 0427] The manuscript spells ‘forms’ incorrectly.]; made stable by the height of its foundations; arranged with courses of bases, columns, and capitals; raised to extraordinary heights by the varied loftiness of its arches and roofs; completed by the splendid pinnacle of its towers; adorned inside and out with the beauty of countless colors and forms in a great variety of paintings; filled with the dignity of every metal and of the most precious stones; illuminated by a lavish outpouring of light through various and manifold kinds of windows; and possessing everything else that belongs to the perfect glory of beauty, which would take too long to enumerate [Col. 0427D]—

so that no space within it failed to contain all its inhabitants by its breadth, no part failed to delight the eyes of all who looked upon it with its beauty [Col. 0428A], no place lacked the most brilliant light spread everywhere, or the splendor of gold and gems reflecting from its surface and drawing out their marvelous colors, and no seat within it was not regal and suited to honor and repose;

if, then, in such a vast and wondrous building, as we have described, the father himself—its author and governor—were to arrange his sons in one manner and his servants in another; those endowed with the gift of perpetual health in one manner and those tormented by the want created by the evil desires they had drawn upon themselves through the intemperance of their lust in another, gnashing their teeth [Note: [Col. 0427] The manuscript reads ‘gnashing’; M. has ‘grinding.’], swarming with worms, and suffering various kinds of everlasting sorrow—would he rightly be considered an exceedingly harsh punisher, when he was praised as a perfectly just governor?

For he ought not to have confused the beauty of his house, lest to those who looked perversely upon the people he had ordered, he should appear to punish them. Or how could he be proved to have made the form of punishments, he who [Note: [Col. 0427] Thus the manuscript; M. reads *quoniam qui*, “since he who.”] wished everything he made to be made not for the uses of misery but for the fullness of the universe and the beauty of it [Note: [Col. 0427] The manuscript reads ‘of it’; M. has ‘for it.’] [Note: [Col. 0427D] Prudentius responds: “The wicked are consigned to perpetual fire in hell, while the good are glorified in everlasting blessedness above all this visible heaven, which Holy Scripture calls the firmament.”]?

## VI.

Hence Augustine says in his book *On True Religion*:

> “The defect of the soul is not its nature but contrary to its nature, and it is nothing other than sin and the punishment of sin [Note: [Col. 0427] Thus the manuscript; another reading has *inde*, “from that.”]. From this it is understood that no nature—or, if it is better expressed in this way [Note: [Col. 0427] Thus the manuscript and M.; another reading has *dicatur*, “if it may better be said.”]—no substance or essence is evil. Nor does it follow from the sins and punishments of the soul [Note: [Col. 0427] Another manuscript reads ‘of its soul.’] that the universe is disfigured by any deformity, because rational substance, clean from every sin, is subject to God and rules over the other things subject to it.

> “But that which has sinned [Note: [Col. 0427] Thus the manuscript; M. reads *Et*, “and.”] has been ordered where it is fitting for such beings to be, so that under God, the Creator and governor of the universe, everything may be beautiful. The beauty of the whole creation is therefore blameless through these three things: the condemnation of sinners, the discipline of the righteous, and the perfection of the blessed” [Note: [Col. 0428D] Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 23.].

After some further discussion of the soul, he says:

> “By its own falling away it is hurled into more corruptible beauties, that is, into the order of punishments. Nor should we be surprised that I still call them beauties. For nothing is ordered that is not beautiful. And as the Apostle says: ‘Every order is from God’” [Note: [Col. 0428D] Romans XIII, 7. — Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 41.].

## VII.

What, then, is surprising if the soul of a human being—which, wherever it is and whatever it is, is better than every body—is said to be beautifully ordered, and if other beauties are made from its punishments, since, when it is wretched, it is not where the blessed ought to be, but where the wretched ought to be?

Therefore the impious person is punished in no part of the universe, but by his own impiety, in himself, as the sayings of the holy Fathers cited above testify. For just as God did not make the sun so that its rays would break the sight of eyes that look at it improperly and strike them back into darkness—which is produced not by the sun itself but by the disordered act of seeing—nor so that it would torture eyes suffering the most severe affliction, although nothing in their condition harms them as much as the sun’s brilliance [Note: [Col. 0429] Thus the manuscript; M. reads *retorqueat*, “strikes back/twists back.”], since the affliction does not arise externally from the nature of things but tortures them internally through some corruption of bodily health, so likewise that eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels [Note: [Col. 0429D] Matthew XXV, 41.] was in no way created for this purpose, especially if it is the fourth element of the world [Note: [Col. 0429] The manuscript spells ‘element’ incorrectly.]. It is more reasonably believed to have been created for the integrity of the universe that God foresaw would be made than to burn the apostate, for whom his own pride would have been sufficient torment.

To this reasoning is added the fact that, since he was first created by God in an ethereal body, in which he could suffer nothing, his ethereal body, after he swelled with pride, was thrust down from the heavenly seats—that is, from the ethereal regions—into this air, thick with moisture, dark with gloom, and subject to disturbances, so that a body corresponding to his merits would be joined to him there against his will, and thus he would be tormented in it by his own iniquity [Note: [Col. 0429D] Prudentius correctly remarks: “This cannot at all be proved by the authority of prophetic and apostolic Scripture.”].

## VIII.

Whether, therefore, that fire is bodily, as Augustine says, or incorporeal, as Gregory holds, it is said to have been predestined or prepared for the devil because of its subtlety, as I suppose, since he was to be ordered within it, together with all his companions in wickedness, to be punished.

And just as the same fire is certainly good, because it was made by the Good, and is called evil for no other reason than that evil beings are most orderly placed within it, so punishment is also reasonably asserted to exist because those same evil beings are miserably and painfully tormented in it for the crimes they committed through desire.

Therefore that fire itself is not the punishment, nor was it prepared or predestined for punishment; rather, the fire that had been predestined to become a dwelling-place within the universe of all good things was made the dwelling-place of the impious [Note: [Col. 0429D] After the Lord had spoken the parable of the good and evil fish, he said: “The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and they will throw them into the furnace of fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” The propositions advanced by John Scotus therefore do not sufficiently accord with the truth.].

In it, without doubt, the blessed will dwell no less than the wretched [Note: [Col. 0429D] This is mistaken. The truth teaches that this fire is not a seat of sweetness and dignity but eternal torment, since the Lord says: “These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” Nowhere do the sacred writings call that fire eternal life.].

But just as one and the same light suits healthy eyes, as we have said, while it obstructs painful eyes; and one and the same food or drink is bitter to the throats of the sick but sweet to those enjoying health—for the former delight in the complete joy of their health, while the latter are displeased by the painful sadness of their corruption; and just as one and the same water lifts up a swimmer but drowns one who falls; and just as, of two people placed in one and the same place in a royal hall, one is feverish while the other rejoices: to the one who rejoices, all the ornaments of the entire hall delightfully please, appear worthy of praise, and harmoniously accord with one another; but to the feverish person, burning inwardly with his own pains, nothing of what he sees externally gives pleasure, nothing appears praiseworthy, and nothing agrees with him, since he rightly recoils from everything—what good thing would not harm him, when the Author of all things could not please him? Or where would there be any good that would not harm one who did not wish to enjoy the supreme Good?

## IX.

Therefore, if there is no blessedness except eternal life, and eternal life is the knowledge of truth, then there is no blessedness except the knowledge of truth. But lest this conclusion waver in our minds, let us hear Truth itself openly crying out:

> “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” [Note: [Col. 0429] Thus the manuscript; M. reads *diligitur*, “is loved.”] [Note: [Col. 0430D] John XIV, 21.].

Again, elsewhere:

> “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” [Note: [Col. 0430D] John XVII, 5.].

Whatever is believed concerning blessedness must, by contrast, necessarily be believed concerning its opposite, misery. Thus, if there is no misery except eternal death, and eternal death is ignorance of the truth, then there is no misery except ignorance of the truth. Where truth is unknown, there is no life. Where there is no life, continual death must necessarily be present.

If this is so, who would dare to say that God is the predestiner of punishment, except one who dares to assert that he is the author of ignorance, although all understanding comes from him? Each person is therefore punished by his own defiance, which in no way comes from God; and consequently he must in no way be believed its author [Note: [Col. 0430D] Prudentius observes: “If the impious are merely to have a dwelling-place in that fire and are not to suffer punishment, how will they have no life? But the truth cries out that the impious will have life there, though a punitive one.”].

# CHAPTER XVIII  
## How the error of those who think differently from the holy Fathers about predestination arose from ignorance of the liberal disciplines

## I.

I believe, then, that the beginning of the most savage error of those who confuse the judgments of the venerable Fathers, especially those of Saint Augustine, and thereby reduce them fatally to their own most depraved meaning, had its beginnings in [ignorance] of the useful disciplines that Wisdom itself wished to be her companions and investigators [Note: [Col. 0429] ‘Ignorance’ is omitted by the manuscript and supplied by M.]. It arose, moreover, from ignorance of the Greek letters [Col. 0430D] [Note: [Col. 0430D] Prudentius: “There can be no doubt that the Fathers possessed perfect knowledge of them, and that Scotus, rather, swelled beyond his powers with his tiny scrap of knowledge of them and impiously burst forth into blasphemies.”].

In these matters, the interpretation of predestination generates no fog of ambiguity. If it is attended to more diligently by seekers after truth rather than by champions of falsehood, whenever predestination—whether customarily concerning good things or abusively concerning evil things—opens the leading role of its countenance, familiar indeed to the wise but deeply hidden from those puffed up by the swelling of pride, its entire meaning will immediately become clear to those who understand it piously.

## II.

Among the Greeks there is therefore the verb **ὁρῶ** [Note: [Col. 0431] The manuscript everywhere has “ωρω προωρω.”], which in Latin is rendered by three verbs. For **ὁρῶ** means “I see,” “I define,” and “I appoint.” Likewise, its compound **προορῶ** means “I foresee,” “I predefine,” and “I predestine.”

This can easily be gathered from the context of Holy Scripture. In the Letter to the Romans we read:

> **τοῦ ὁρισθέντος υἱοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν δυνάμει** [Note: [Col. 0431] The manuscript has: **του ορισθεντος υιου θῖ ενδιναμει**.]

—that is, “the Son of God appointed in power” [Note: [Col. 0431D] Romans I, 4.].

In the Letter to the Ephesians [Note: [Col. 0431] The manuscript spells ‘Ephesians’ incorrectly.]:

> **ἐν ἀγάπῃ προορίσας ἡμᾶς** [Note: [Col. 0431] The manuscript has: **εναγαπε προωρισας ημας**.]

—that is, “predestining us in love” [Note: [Col. 0431D] Ephesians I, 4–5.];

and shortly afterward:

> **προορισθέντες κατὰ πρόθεσιν Θεοῦ** [Note: [Col. 0431] The manuscript has: **προωριστηντες κατα προσδησιν θῖ**.]

—that is, “predestined according to the purpose of God” [Note: [Col. 0431D] Ibid., verse 11.].

In all these passages the translator used the verb “to predestine,” although he could also have used the other terms, namely “to foresee” and “to predefine,” since, as we have said, these three verbs express the meaning of one Greek verb.

Hence the noun **ὅρασις** [Note: [Col. 0431] Conjecture: **ὅρασις**; the manuscript has **ὁροσια**, M. has **ὡρόσια**.] or **προόρασις** [Note: [Col. 0431] Conjecture: **προόρασις**; the manuscript has **προωσια**, M. has **προωρόσια**.], which among the Greeks is derived from the verb **ὁρῶ** or **προορῶ**, is rendered among us as “vision,” “definition,” or “appointment”; and their compounds—“foresight,” “predefinition,” and “predestination”—come from the Greek compound **προόρασις** [Note: [Col. 0431] Conjecture: **προόρασις**; the manuscript has **προωροσια**, M. has **προωροσις**.].

It follows plainly that in these three verbs either the meaning is identical, or there is such proximity of meaning that each may be put in place of the others.

## III.

This reasoning is most firmly confirmed by Augustine’s words. When he was explaining in the book called the *Enchiridion* [Note: [Col. 0431] The manuscript spells *Enchiridion* as **ενκειριδον**] the Psalmist’s verse, “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills,” he said among other things:

> “Those whom he justly predestined to punishment,”

and immediately afterward:

> “Those whom he mercifully predestined to grace” [Note: [Col. 0431D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 110.].

When explaining the same verse in the eleventh book of the *Hexaemeron* [Note: [Col. 0431] The manuscript spells *Hexaemeron* as **εξημερων**], he says in the same manner:

> “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills. He foresees those who will be good and creates them; he foresees those who will be evil and creates them; offering himself for enjoyment to the good, bestowing many gifts upon the evil as well, mercifully pardoning and justly avenging; likewise mercifully avenging and justly pardoning; fearing nothing from anyone’s wickedness, needing nothing from anyone’s justice, consulting neither his own interests nor those of the good because of their works, and consulting the good even through the punishments of the evil” [Note: [Col. 0431D] Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* XI, 11.].

Here it must certainly be understood that by the verb “predestination” he intended nothing other than what he intended by the verb “foreknowledge.”

## IV.

Who, then, except someone insane, would not see that for God to predestine is nothing other than to predefine, and that to predefine is nothing other than to foresee [Note: [Col. 0431D] “Predestination is nothing other than foreknowledge” is false. For many things are foreseen that are neither predestined nor predefined.]? To predestine, therefore, is nothing other than to foresee.

Thus, just as we say that God foresaw what he would make and what he would not make—although what he himself would not make is certainly nothing, since all things were made through him and without him nothing was made [Note: [Col. 0432D] John I, 3.], and nothing cannot be seen—so we often find authors saying that God predestined what he would make and what he would not make, and likewise predefined it [Note: [Col. 0431] Thus the manuscript; M. has *praefinisse*, “to have prelimited/predefined.”].

If, when we find **προώρισεν** in Greek manuscripts, we do not hesitate to understand it as “he foresaw,” “he predefined,” or “he predestined,” what prevents us, when we hear “he predestined” [Note: [Col. 0431] The repeated phrase *vel praedestinavit … praedestinavit* is omitted by M.], from taking it as “he foresaw” or “he predefined,” while preserving the unchangeable principle that these and similar verbs are understood to exist only in those things that God made, but can conversely be said of those things that God did not make, since they do not exist?

O eternal Truth and true Love, show yourself to those who seek you in all things in which you are. Show, most wise Creator, that nothing exists outside you, and that all things which exist within you alone were foreseen, predestined, predefined, and foreknown by you; whereas those things that are said to exist although they do not exist are neither from you nor in you, and therefore were neither predestined, predefined, foreknown, nor foreseen by you.

O most merciful Lord! You did not make sin, death, destruction, or punishment, and therefore they do not exist; nor can there be from you what you did not wish to come to be [Note: [Col. 0431] *Fieri*, “to come to be,” is omitted by M.]:” “You do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” [Note: [Col. 0432D] Ezekiel XXXIII, 11.].

O eternal Wisdom! Grant that one may see that Life, the Creator, in no way made death for created life, since, if it were to die, it would not suffer punishments [Note: [Col. 0432D] Prudentius: “God both foresaw and predestined death and punishments: foreseeing that the human being would sin, he forbade him to sin, and declared that, if he sinned, he would die.”]. But if the sinful soul suffers punishments, it is proved to be alive.

## V.

The death of the soul, then, is sin. God did not make the sin of the soul, since he frees it from sin; therefore Life did not make the death of life [Note: [Col. 0431] Thus the manuscript; M. omits ‘life.’].

The punishment of sin is death. God did not make death [Note: [Col. 0432D] Wisdom I, 13.]; therefore he did not make punishment. Torment is punishment; God did not make punishment; therefore he did not make torment.

The punishment of sin is death; the death of life is sin; therefore the punishment of sin is sin. Punishment is torment; therefore the torment of sin is sin.

Eternal life is Jesus Christ; Jesus Christ is the death of eternal death; therefore eternal life is the death of eternal death, as he himself said:

> “I will be your death, O Death, and your sting, O Hell” [Note: [Col. 0433] Thus the manuscript and M.; another reading has ‘flesh.’] [Note: [Col. 0433D] Hosea XIII, 14.].

Therefore Life is not the death of life, which it made, but the death of death, which it destroyed in those whom it predestined for enjoyment of itself.

In those whom it predestined to destruction, however, it did not destroy death, because it left them, by its most remote judgment from us, in the mass of original sin. It abandoned those who had been left; darkness torments those abandoned by light; death destroys those abandoned by life [Note: [Col. 0433] Corrected reading; the manuscript and M. have *torquent*, “they torment.”].

This does not mean that it abandons or rejects what it itself made in them. Otherwise their nature would return to nothing, if the supreme Essence were not in them [Col. 0433B]. Rather, it rejected what it did not make in them, namely pride. For God always dwells in the nature that he created for himself, and consequently that nature always remains, since the One who always is dwells within it [Note: [Col. 0433] M. reads ‘remains’; the manuscript has ‘possesses.’].

VI. What I said, then, “those whom he predestined to destruction,” I said because I often find blessed Augustine saying such things. With the Lord’s help, I shall demonstrate what the most devout father of doctrine, the most beautiful exemplar of eloquence, the keenest investigator of truth, the most devoted teacher of the liberal arts, the most provident trainer of souls, and the humblest persuader intended to convey by such a manner of speaking, lest anyone suppose from his expressions that he intended something which appears to resist the truth.

He therefore did not intend the statement “those whom he justly predestined to punishment” to be understood in the same way as the statement “those whom he graciously predestined to grace” [Note: [Col. 0434D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 100.].

Attend to what follows. Every creature, before it was made, was predestined—that is, predetermined and foreseen—by the Creator in such a way that it would completely fulfill the limits of its nature within which it was to be created, and would in no way exceed them. The limits of all natures, however, were established in the art of the omnipotent Craftsman, which is the wisdom of the Father, in which and through which all things were created.

Among created natures, some neither wish nor are able to transgress the order of the eternal law, such as all things lacking reason and understanding [Note: [Col. 0433] Thus the codex; M has *uti*.]. Others, however, have reason and understanding substantially implanted in them. Of these, one part, liberated by the grace of its Creator, willingly serves the eternal laws and becomes blessed by cleaving to them; the other [Note: [Col. 0433] Thus M; the codex has *alter*, “the other.”], deservedly abandoned to pride and disobedience, refused to be confined within the order of the aforesaid law, namely, the eternal law, but was unable to transcend it.

However shamefully rational will may move itself, it will find [Note: [Col. 0433] Thus M; the codex has *inveniat*, “may find.”] a limit in the eternal art, within which its shamefulness will be honorably ordered, so that the discipline of wisdom, which deserves praise, will be ennobled by its very detestable wickedness, and the disordered deformity of one part will not diminish the most perfectly ordered beauty of the whole universe.

VII. Therefore the supreme and ineffable divine Wisdom predestined within its laws limits beyond which the wickedness of the impious cannot advance. No one’s wickedness is permitted to extend itself infinitely as it wishes, since the divine laws impose a measure upon its progress.

For what does the wickedness of all the impious, and of their head, who is the devil, desire except to withdraw from him who is supreme Being, to such an extent that, if the divine law permitted it, their nature would return to nothing? Hence wickedness is said to be *nequitia*, because it strives to be *nequicquam*, that is, “nothing” [Note: [Col. 0433] The codex has *nequiquam*.].

But because difficulty arising from the eternal laws prevents it from falling as far as it would wish, it labors under that difficulty; through labor it is tormented, punished, and tortured. And from what does it become miserable? From the deprivation of empty pleasures.

God therefore predestined the impious to punishment, or destruction—that is, he confined them within his immutable laws, which their impiety is not permitted to escape: plainly, to their own punishment. For that difficulty, as has been said, by which they are prevented from reaching what they desire wantonly, becomes for them a punitive destruction and the most just torture of their wretched desire.

For just as God freed the will of the elect, whom he predestined to grace, and filled it with the affections of his love, so that they not only rejoice to be held within the boundaries of the eternal law but do not hesitate to regard it as the greatest gift of his glory that they neither wish nor are able to cross those very boundaries, so he restrains the will of the reprobate, whom he predestined to the most disgraceful punishment, so that, conversely, whatever belongs to the joy of blessed life for the former is turned into the punishment of misery for the latter.

VIII. Accordingly, the number of both parties has been predestined. For in each God established the substantial number of nature, and predetermined the substance that had been established [Note: [Col. 0433] Thus the codex; M has *substantiam*, “substance.”].

One and the same nature is multiplied numerically in all, so that the one exists in each and each in the one. Nor is it anything other than each individual, nor is each individual anything other than it. The number, therefore, of all whom God created has been predestined.

But because the Creator foresaw that this number would generally perish in the first human being, apart from the remedy for the wound, which is Christ, he predestined—that is, before they came into being, he determined—the number of those whom he would free by his grace and the number of those whom he would leave behind by his justice; in the former giving the gifts of his mercy [Note: [Col. 0433] Thus the codex; M has *missis*, “having been sent.”], in the latter fulfilling the number of nature by which the universe would be completed [Note: [Col. 0433] Thus the codex; M has *illis*, “in those.”], and in both displaying the riches of his goodness.

He granted everyone the ability to observe his laws, if they wished, before all sinned in the one; but after the sin he did not grant all the will to do so. He prepared the elect for blessedness, and appointed the reprobate to serve his laws, although unwillingly. He did not predestine them to be made so that they would serve him in this way, but so that they would cleave to him with perfect will.

They serve him unwillingly, however, not through the nature that he made in them and does not punish in them, but through the evil will [Note: [Col. 0435] Thus M; the codex has *malam voluntatem*, “an evil will.”] that he did not make in them and does punish in them. [Note: [Col. 0435D] Prudentius carefully observes that both—the nature, namely, and the will, of the impious—serve God unwillingly and are justly punished, not by themselves as the source of their punishment, but by him whose power is just.]

For in the fact that they serve him unwillingly, they are punished in themselves by their own punishment. Those whom God does not justly free from it he in a certain manner prepares for it, by permitting them to prepare themselves for it [Note: [Col. 0435D] Prudentius: The Fathers never intended this to be expressed in such a manner; rather, these people prepare themselves for punishment by living wickedly and persevering in wickedness, while God most justly prepares them for it by judging them.], although the truth teaches both that he predestined no one to destruction and that he prepared destruction for no one.

IX. He therefore predestined that the impious would serve his eternal and most just laws unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0435] Thus the codex and M: *invite*, “unwillingly”], and that they would not pass beyond them by any assault of their wickedness, which presses toward the depths of evil, and thus would perish in punishment.

For no heavier punishment is inflicted upon an evil servant than that he is compelled to serve a just Lord unwillingly. Indeed, he suffers within himself more deeply from the impulses of proud will than from the harshest scourges externally upon his body, because, when he is not permitted to despise his Lord’s will [Note: [Col. 0435] Thus the codex; M has *sinatur*, “may be permitted.”], he is tortured within himself by himself.

Who among those who judge rightly would attribute the authority for such punishment to the just Lord rather than to the unjust servant, since the latter is kindled within himself by the torches of his disobedience before any external torment is added by the Lord to increase his punishment?

Therefore God is said, in this manner of speaking, to have predestined the impious to destruction, just as one might say that he confined their impiety—which brings about their destruction—within his laws and restrained the force of their wanton pride by the most just moderation of his governance, so that, in a wondrous and ineffable manner, the most beautiful moderation of the divine laws would be the most dreadful condemnation of their wickedness.

One and the same law, arranging the commonwealth according to the most equitable order, brings life to those who wish to live well, just as it brings destruction to those who desire to live badly. Within the same enclosure of the royal court, one who is feverish is tormented by his misery, while one who possesses health rejoices. Two people looking at the same sun: one is illumined by ordered sight, the other is struck by darkness through disordered sight. One and the same food is bitter to the sick and sweet to the healthy; one and the same spiritual teaching is for some the fragrance of life unto life, and for others the fragrance of death unto death.

X. Therefore divine predestination—which, without doubt, is nothing other than divine foreknowledge—did everything that it willed. It established all things substantially and ordered all things by its most beautiful, most just, and most merciful laws, so that those liberated through the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, might reign freely and blessedly within them, while those whom he left behind [Note: [Col. 0435] Thus the codex; M has *tamen*, “nevertheless.”] might serve them unwillingly and thus perish beneath them—not so that anything of the nature that he himself made might perish, but so that he might compel what he did not make in them to be punished.

When, therefore, I hear “those whom he justly predestined to punishment,” I understand it to mean those whose wickedness, for which they are punished, he predestined to be restrained by his laws.
