For just as he in no way predestined the wicked to wickedness, so in no way did he predestine wickedness to punish the wicked. And just as he predestined the wicked to serve his laws unwillingly, so he predestined his laws [Col. 0436B] so that the wicked, punished on account of their wickedness, would not escape them.

Here one must understand subtly that predestination itself is law, and law itself is predestination. For if every predestination is a definition, and every law is a definition, then every predestination is law, and every law is predestination.

Divine predestination, therefore, is the eternal law and immutable discipline of all natures. In those whom it elected by its grace it mercifully renews the ruins of mutable creation; in those whom it justly rejected it powerfully orders them. Thus the discipline itself, while always remaining the same and equally constant in itself, is the glory of blessedness to those who love it, and the disgrace of punishments to those who hate it; for the blessedness of those who love it is nothing other than joy in the truth, while the misery of those who hate it is nothing other than grief at the equity of the truth.

The former are unwillingly tormented by their own envy; the latter are crowned willingly by their own love [Note: [Col. 0435] The codex has *benivolos*, “well-disposed.”].

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Eternal Fire

I. Concerning the eternal fire, of which the Lord says in the Gospel, “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” [Note: [Col. 0436D] Matthew 25:41.], no one should doubt that it is corporeal, although on account of the subtlety of its nature it is said to be incorporeal, just as we customarily speak of the ethereal spirit, although the ether is the fourth part of corporeal creation.

Nor would I readily believe that another fire was prepared to punish the devil with all his members besides this very fire, which is the fourth element of the world [Note: [Col. 0436D] Nothing is certain about this matter. To Prudentius it seems to be an entirely different fire, since the qualities are different.].

For what then? Is it astonishing if those bodies of the impious—which are certainly composed from these four corporeal elements, destined at a predetermined time to be resolved into those same elements and at the moment of resurrection to be recalled again from them—suffer in that fire the eternal torments deserved by their impiety, in which the bodies of all who will rise again will be most substantially constituted?

II. It is not incongruous to believe that the bodies of the saints will be changed into an ethereal quality, which cannot be consumed by another quality, although it can change the qualities of lower bodies within itself [Note: [Col. 0437] Thus the codex; M has *posset*, “could.”]. But the bodies of the impious will pass into an aerial quality, so that they may suffer from the higher fire [Note: [Col. 0437D] Prudentius: The bodies of the saints will by no means be changed into an ethereal quality, either in that fire or apart from it; rather, they will remain in the reality of their own flesh and members, however glorified, and live forever. In addition to immortality, they will possess the condition by which they can never again be corrupted by death or fail.].

This is why, after his fall, the devil was thrust down from the ethereal realm, and an aerial body was unwillingly joined to him, in which he might pay the penalties of his pride.

By a wondrous and ineffable process of natures, yet through a hidden and just judgment, what the elements of the world desire through their most orderly motion—embracing one another as though by a certain bond of natural love and joined inseparably—is turned into punishment for those who hate the truth. For the fiery quality above, by its natural power, continually desires through natural motion to pour the qualities of the lower elements into itself, as though they were a kind of nourishment for it.

III. When, then, as we have said, the supreme quality of all bodies, which is ethereal, both confines the lower qualities within itself by surrounding them and does not cease to set them in motion within itself insofar as the law of natures permits, a wondrous joy of natures is accomplished within them, but an ineffable torment of evil wills [Note: [Col. 0437D] Prudentius: No joy of natures occurs there, where, according to the testimony of the Lord, there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.].

Accordingly, the bodies of all the impious—namely, wicked angels and human beings—will endure the punishments of the eternal fire in such a way that the integrity of their substance will in no way fail, and they will remain in their natural soundness; all the goods of nature will then shine forth in wondrous order for the adornment of the universe [Col. 0437C] [Note: [Col. 0438D] Prudentius: Scripture says, “Where there is no order and everlasting horror dwells.”]—except for the blessedness of which they will be deprived, since this comes not from nature but from grace.

While the quality of the higher corporeal fire contends with the bodies of the lower air, with their natural power preserved, the sentience of the unhappy souls will suffer eternal hardships from their bodies [Note: [Col. 0437] Thus the codex and M.] [Note: [Col. 0438D] Prudentius: They will endure eternal torments both of soul and of body.]. Thus that same fire will become glory for all bodies [Note: [Col. 0438D] Prudentius: No glory whatsoever will arise, but rather interminable torment.], while punishment will be heaped inwardly upon the condemned souls by their own iniquity and outwardly upon them.

IV. If it seems incredible to anyone that bodies will always burn while nothing of their nature will perish, let him consider that stone which is born in Arcadia beneath Mount Erymanthus [Note: [Col. 0437] The codex has *erimanti*.]. Although it has the sheen of iron, once touched and kindled it cannot be extinguished by fire [Note: [Col. 0437] Thus the codex and M: *igne*, “by fire.”] [Note: [Col. 0437] The codex has *extingui nequitur*, “it cannot be extinguished.”]. The Greeks call it by the true name *asbestos*, that is, “unquenchable” [Col. 0437D], so that a fiery nature gives it its color and nothing is diminished from its substance.

Let him also consider the salamander [Note: [Col. 0437] Thus M; the codex has *salamandra*.], living in fire. From this it may be inferred [Col. 0438A] that it is not the substance, nor [Note: [Col. 0437] Thus the codex; M has *atque*, “and.”] its qualities, that are to be tormented by the flame of Gehenna, but that the sense of the one who suffers and the spirit of the one who resists will struggle with eternal misery.

## EPILOGUE. On Divine Predestination

I. Since these things are so, behold: I worship one God, the one principle and wisdom of all things, by which every soul that is wise is wise, and the very gift by which all things that are blessed are blessed. I profess his one, sole, and true predestination, which is what he himself is, because his law is eternal and immutable.

Just as he predestined no one to destruction, because he is life, and conversely just as he predestined no evil person to the wickedness that is destruction, so he predestined no evil person to destruction, because destruction is wickedness. For no Catholic is permitted to believe that the supreme goodness, from which every good derives, predestined any wickedness for anyone, or that the supreme life, from which, in which, and through which all things live, predestined destruction or punishment for anyone, since it does not even permit that which destroys one thing through another to perish [Note: [Col. 0437] Thus the codex; M has *nec*, “nor.”].

II. Therefore, when I hear your preachers, O most blessed truth, the common life of all, saying that you predestined the impious to destruction, or destruction for the impious, then, O most radiant light, as you illuminate my darkness, I immediately see in you that you predestined—that is, determined before the ages [Note: [Col. 0437] The codex has *diffinisse*, “to determine.”]—within your immutable laws a fixed number of those who were destined to perish in their own impiety, which you never and nowhere predestined.

This may be expressed another way: “Lord, in your foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, you predestined the number of those who were going to prepare for themselves both the punishment and the destruction of their own impiety—not intending to punish in them what you made, but leaving what you did not make in them to be punished.”

This is my faith, O eternal light of minds, concerning your predestination, which you are.

III. Accordingly, together with all orthodox believers, I anathematize those who say that there are two predestinations, or one predestination that is twin, divided into two, or double.

For if there are two, the divine substance is not one. If it is twin, it is not indivisible. If it is divided into two, it is not simple but composed of parts. If it is double, it is compounded.

But if we are forbidden to call the divine unity triple, with what madness does a heretic dare to assert that it is double?

Let us therefore root out from our hearts this monstrous, poisonous, deadly doctrine, and believe that there is one eternal predestination of God the Lord, and that it pertains only to those things that are, and in no way to those things that are not.

*The end* [Note: [Col. 0439A] A later hand appears to have added *Explicit*.].

[Col. 0439]

# JOHN SCOTUS, *PERI PHYSEOS MERISMOU*, THAT IS, *ON THE DIVISION OF NATURE*: FIVE BOOKS

First edition | A |

Paris, manuscript codex of Saint-Germain, used in the first edition | B |

Manuscript codex, Saint-Germain 309, Royal Library of Paris, parchment, eleventh century | C |

Latin manuscript codex 1764, Royal Library of Paris, parchment, twelfth century, mutilated | D |

Manuscript codex, Saint-Germain 280, Royal Library of Paris, parchment, twelfth century, mutilated | E |

Manuscript codex, Saint-Germain 830, Royal Library of Paris, parchment, eleventh century, Books IV and V | F |

## NOTICE TO THE READER

John Scotus’s books *On the Division of Nature* present an entirely twofold character. At times they do not depart from the faith of the Church and teach us that “the understanding of the holy Fathers must be received piously and reverently”; at other times they report philosophical theories that depart very far from the truth. Hence, when priority is given to these theories, extremely bad errors frequently arise.

It is not permissible to excuse them on the grounds that John Scotus expressed sounder doctrine elsewhere, or that he occasionally set forth the truth ingeniously and brilliantly.

Since, then, the character of these books is such that truth is artfully mingled in them with the errors that John Scotus borrowed from his philosophy, what wonder is it that the bishops of the Church rejected and condemned such a work when, having long been neglected, it began to be dragged out of libraries by the heretics of the Middle Ages and sold as the summit of knowledge and truth—and that Pope Honorius III judged it should be consigned to the fire?

It seems necessary to place his bull in full before the reader. It is as follows:

> Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops and bishops, etc.
>
> The enemy does not cease to sow weeds among the good seed, etc. Recently, as our venerable brother the bishop of Paris has informed us, a certain book entitled *Periphysis* has been found, teeming with so many worms of heretical depravity that it was rightly rejected by the venerable brother our archbishop of Sens and his suffragans, gathered in a provincial council, by the judgment of God.
>
> Since, therefore, as we have learned, this book is held in certain monasteries and other places, and since some cloistered persons and learned men—though perhaps lovers of novelty more than is expedient—devote themselves with excessive zeal to reading the said book, considering it glorious to produce unknown opinions, although the Apostle teaches that profane novelties must be avoided, we, in accordance with the duty of pastoral solicitude and striving to prevent the corruption that such a book might introduce, strictly command and instruct you all and each of you, by the authority of the Holy Spirit, diligently to seek out this little book.
>
> Wherever it should happen to be found, in whole or in part, you are to send it to us without delay, if this can safely be done, so that it may be solemnly burned. Otherwise, you yourselves are to burn it publicly, expressly enjoining upon your subjects that whoever among them possesses or may possess copies of the said book, in whole or in part, must surrender and deliver them to us.
>
> All those who, for more than fifteen days after such command or notification has come to their knowledge, knowingly presume to retain the whole book or any part of it shall incur the sentence of excommunication and shall not escape the designation of heretical depravity.
>
> Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, etc. [Note: [Col. 0439] Alberic’s *Chronicon*, under the year 1225, edited by Leibniz, Leipzig, 1698, p. 514.].

[Col. 0441] After this most severe sentence was issued, no further mention of those books occurs throughout the Middle Ages. Only in the year 1681 did they appear in print, edited by Thomas Gale, an Englishman. The censure of the Church was immediately repeated. For in the index of prohibited books one finds the following:

> “Erigena, John Scotus, *On the Division of Nature*, five books. An appendix from the *Ambigua* of Saint Maximus, in Greek and Latin, is added. Decree of 3 April 1685.”

Since these things are so, there can be no doubt among Catholics about what must be judged concerning the character and nature of these books. Why they are being reprinted here we have explained in the Preface.

As for setting out their system and touching upon each of their errors, this may be omitted here; it has already been undertaken by the author of the essay on John Scotus printed above. To avoid seeming to repeat what has already been done, we refer the reader to the second part of that essay, which deals with this subject in full.

William of Malmesbury praises that work as very useful for solving certain perplexing questions, but adds: “provided that he”—John Scotus—“is forgiven in certain matters in which he deviated from the path of the Latins while fixing his eyes intently upon the Greeks. For this reason he was also regarded as a heretic . . . For there are truly very many things in the book *Peri physion* which, unless they are carefully examined, may appear contrary to the Catholic faith.”

The Englishman seems to treat Scotus gently. If, however, you read the books *Peri physeos merismou* attentively, you will easily convince yourself that the errors we have encountered in the book *On Predestination* proceed almost spontaneously from their system.

# *PERI PHYSEOS MERISMOU*, THAT IS, *ON THE DIVISION OF NATURE*. BOOK ONE

[Note: [Col. 0441] Thus A; C begins with *primum περὶ φύσεων*; D omits the title.]

[Col. 0441]

[Col. 0441A] **MASTER.** Often, as I have reflected and have investigated as carefully as my powers permit, it has occurred to me that the first and highest division of all things—whether they can be perceived by the mind or surpass its attention—is into those things that are and those things that are not. A general term for all these things presents itself: in Greek *physis* (φύσις), but in Latin *natura*, “nature” [Note: [Col. 0441] A has *vocatur*; D has *vocitetur*.]. Does it seem otherwise to you?

**STUDENT.** No; I agree. For when I enter upon the path of reasoning, I too find that this is so.

**MASTER.** Nature, then, is the general name, as we have said, for all things that are and that are not.

**STUDENT.** Indeed it is. For nothing in the universe can present itself to our thoughts that can be without such a name [Note: [Col. 0441] A omits “Master. Nature, then … without such a name.”].

**MASTER.** Since we agree that this is a general term, I would like you to explain the principle by which it is divided by differences into species. Or, if you prefer, I shall first attempt to divide it, and your task will be to judge the divisions.

**STUDENT.** Proceed, please. I am eager to hear from you a true account of these matters.

### 1.

**MASTER.** It seems to me that the division of nature receives four species through four differences. The first is into that [Note: [Col. 0441] A omits *in eam*, “into that.”] which creates and is not created; the second into that which is created and creates; the third into that which is created and does not create; the fourth into that which neither creates nor is created. Of these [Note: [Col. 0441] A omits *vero*, “indeed.”], pairs are opposed to one another: the third is opposed to the first, and the fourth to the second. The fourth, however, is placed among impossibilities, since its difference is the inability to exist [Note: [Col. 0441] D omits *est*, “is.”].

Does such a division seem correct to you, or not?

**STUDENT.** It is correct, but I would like you to repeat it, so that the opposition of the forms mentioned may become clearer.

**MASTER.** You see, unless I am mistaken, the opposition of the third species to the first. The first creates and is not created; opposed to it, conversely, is that which is created and does not create. The second, however, is opposed to the fourth, since the second is both created and creates [Note: [Col. 0441] A has “creates and is created.”], whereas the fourth universally contradicts it, since it neither creates nor is created.

**STUDENT.** I see clearly. But the fourth species that you have added greatly troubles me. I would not dare hesitate at all concerning the other three, since, as I suppose, the first is understood in the cause of all things that are and are not; the second in the primordial causes; and the third in those things that are known through generation, times, and places. For that reason, as I see, it is necessary to discuss each of them more subtly [Note: [Col. 0441] A has *necessarium est*, “it is necessary.”].

**MASTER.** You judge correctly. But in what order the path of reasoning should be followed—that is, which species of nature should first be examined—I leave to your judgment.

**STUDENT.** It seems right to me to speak first about the first species, whatever the light of minds may grant.

### 2.

**MASTER.** Let it be so. But first, I think it should be said briefly that the supreme and principal division of all things, as we have said, is into those that are and those that are not [Col. 0443A] [Note: [Col. 0443] A has *aestimo*, “I judge,” instead of *existimo*, “I think.”].

**STUDENT.** Rightly and prudently. For I do not see that reasoning ought to be begun from any other starting point—not only because this is the first of all differences [Note: [Col. 0443] A has *prima est omnium*, “it is the first of all.”], but also because it appears, and is, more obscure than the others.

**MASTER.** The primordial discriminating difference of all things therefore seeks certain modes of interpretation for itself.

### 3.

The first of these seems to be the mode by which reason persuades us that everything subject to bodily sensation or to the perception of the intellect can reasonably be said to be; whereas those things which, through the excellence of their nature, elude not only *hylion* (ὕλιον; “matter”?), that is, every sense, but even intellect and reason may rightly be regarded as not being [Note: [Col. 0443] *ὕλιον, id est* is omitted in C and D. The following Greek-textual words are severely mangled and recovered only conjecturally by the editor: “not only in Greek, the first of matters, in no way at all formed by the Lord, every sense.”].

These are rightly understood only in God alone, in matter, and in the reasons and essences of all things created by him. And not without reason: for he himself is the essence of all things [Note: [Col. 0443] D omits *est*, “is.”], since he alone truly is, as Dionysius the Areopagite says:

> “The Being of all things is the Divinity that transcends being.” [Note: [Col. 0443] Thus C and D; A has *divinitatis*, “of divinity.”]

Gregory the Theologian likewise [Note: [Col. 0443] D omits *etiam*, “likewise.”] confirms by many arguments that no substance or essence of any visible or invisible creature can be comprehended by intellect or reason as to what it is [Note: [Col. 0443] A omits “or essence.”].

For just as God himself, in himself, is comprehended by no intellect beyond every creature [Note: [Col. 0443] A has “every creature beyond.”], so too the *ousia* (οὐσία), or essence, of the creature made by him and existing in him, when considered in the most secret recesses of creation, is incomprehensible [Note: [Col. 0443] D omits “in the most secret recesses”; A has *consistentis*, “consisting,” instead of *existentis*, “existing.”].

Whatever is perceived in every creature by bodily sense or considered by intellect is nothing other than a certain accident of each essence, incomprehensible in itself, as has been said. It is known through quality, quantity, form, matter [Note: [Col. 0443] A has *materiam*, “matter,” instead of *materiem*.], some difference, place, or time—not what it is, but that it is [Note: [Col. 0443] A has *agnoscitur*, “is recognized,” instead of *cognoscitur*, “is known.”].

This, then, is the first and highest mode of dividing those things that are said [Note: [Col. 0443] C has *dicunt*, “say.”] to be and not to be. But this mode, which seems in some way capable of being introduced, cannot, in my opinion, be accepted when it is established in privations concerning conditions of substances, as sight and blindness concerning the eyes [Note: [Col. 0443] A, C omit *visus et*; C and D have *orbatus*, “deprived,” instead of *orbitas*, “blindness.”].

For what entirely is not, and cannot be, nor surpasses the intellect by the eminence of its existence, I do not see how it can be admitted into divisions of things—unless someone perhaps says that the absences and privations of things that are are not altogether nothing, but are contained by a wondrous natural power in those things whose privations, absences, or oppositions they are, so that in some manner they are.

### 4.

Let there be a second mode of being and not being [Note: [Col. 0443] A has “Let there therefore be.”], considered in the orders and differences of created natures [Note: [Col. 0443] A has *creatarum et creaturarum*, “of created natures and creatures.”]. It begins with the highest intellectual power, situated nearest to God, and descends [Note: [Col. 0443] A has *descendat*, “may descend.”] to the limit of rational and irrational creation.

To put it more plainly: it proceeds from the highest angel down to the lowest part of the rational and irrational soul—namely, the nutritive and augmentative life [Note: [Col. 0443] A and C have *activam*, “active”; C has “I mean the nutritive and active life.”]. This is the final and lowest part of the soul in general, which nourishes and increases the body [Note: [Col. 0443] D has *quoniam*, “since,” instead of *quae*, “which.”].

Here, by a wondrous mode of understanding, each order, together with the lowest order below it—which is that of bodies and in which every division ends—can be said both to be and not to be.

For the affirmation of the lower is the negation of the higher; likewise, the negation of the lower is the affirmation of the higher. In the same way, the affirmation of the higher is the negation of the lower, and the negation of the higher is the affirmation of the lower.

The affirmation of a human being—by “human being” I mean one who is still mortal—is the negation of an angel. The negation of a human being is the affirmation of an angel, and conversely.

For if a human being is a rational, mortal, visible animal [Note: [Col. 0443D] Codex E begins with the words “rational animal.”], then certainly an angel is neither a rational animal, nor mortal, nor visible [Note: [Col. 0443] The correction is adopted; A, C, and D have *risibile*, “capable of laughter,” instead of *visibile*, “visible.”].

Likewise, if an angel is an essential intellectual motion around God and the causes of things [Note: [Col. 0443] A has *et rerum*, “and of things.”], then certainly a human being is not an essential intellectual motion around God and the causes of things.

The same rule can be observed in all the heavenly essences, until one reaches the highest order of all [Note: [Col. 0443] D adds *summum*, “highest,” above the line; A has *perveniant*, “they may arrive,” instead of *perveniatur*, “one may arrive.”]. But that highest order ends in the supreme negation above. For its negation confirms no creature superior to itself.

There are three orders that are called *homotageis* (ὁμοταγεῖς), “co-ranked” or “of the same order” [Note: [Col. 0443] C and D have ὁμοταγες without the final grammatical ending.]. The first consists of Cherubim, Seraphim, and Thrones; the second of Virtues, Powers, and Dominations; the third of Principalities, Archangels, and Angels.

Only the lowest order of bodies below either negates or affirms what is above it [Note: [Col. 0443] C and E have *firmat*, “confirms”; D has *confirmat*, “confirms.”], because it has nothing beneath it that it could remove or establish, since all higher things precede it, while no lower thing precedes it.

By this same reasoning every order of rational and intellectual creation is said both to be and not to be. It is, insofar as it is known by those above it or by itself; but it is not, insofar as it does not allow itself to be comprehended by those below it.

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

### 5. [Col. 0444D]

The third mode is considered, not inappropriately, in those things by which the fullness of this visible world is completed, and in their preceding causes, in the most secret recesses of nature. For whatever of those causes is known in formed matter, in times and places, through generation, is called “being,” according to a certain human convention. [Note: [Col. 0443] D omits “and.”] Whatever, however, is still contained within those recesses of nature [Col. 0445A] and does not yet appear in formed matter, or in place or time, or through the other accidents, is called “not being,” according to the same convention stated above. [Note: A reads “nor”; Col. 0445.]

Examples of this kind are widespread, especially in human nature. For although God established all human beings together in that first and one man whom he made in his own image, he did not bring them forth together into this visible world [Note: A reads “brought them forth”; Col. 0445]. Rather, at definite times and places, by a certain order known to him, he brings to visible existence the nature that he had created all at once [Note: CDE read “brings”; A reads “brought”; Col. 0445]. Those who now appear, or have appeared, visibly in the world are said to be; those who still remain hidden, although they are destined to be, are said not to be.

The difference between the first and third modes is this. [Note: A reads “the third mode.”] The first applies generally to all things that were made simultaneously and at once, both in their causes and in their effects [Note: C reads *qui* (“which”); Col. 0445B]. The third [Note: ADE read “third”; BC read “second.”] applies particularly to those things of which some still lie hidden in their causes while others are manifest in their effects, and by which this world is properly woven together. [Note: C reads *partem* (“part”); Col. 0445.] To this mode belongs the consideration of the power of seeds, whether in animals, trees, or plants. [Note: C omits “in”; Col. 0445.] For the power of seeds, while it is silent in the hidden places of nature, because it has not yet appeared, is said not to be; but when it appears in animals being born and growing, or in the flowers and fruits of trees and plants, it is said to be. [Note: C reads “of the power”; Col. 0445.]

### 6. [Col. 0445C]

The fourth mode is that which, according to the philosophers, declares only those things that are grasped by the intellect alone to truly be. [Note: D reads “is said.”] Whatever things, however, are changed through generation, through the extensions [Note: A reads “distensions”; Col. 0445] or contractions of matter, and likewise through the spatial intervals of places and the movements of times, and are gathered together or dissolved, are truly said not to be; such are all bodies that can be born and perish.

### 7. [Col. 0445]

The fifth mode is one that reason observes in human nature alone. [Note: A reads “the fifth mode is.”] When human nature abandoned through sin the dignity of the divine image, in which it properly subsisted [Note: C and E read “subsisted”; D reads “subsists”; Col. 0445], it deservedly lost its own being and is therefore said not to be. But when, restored by the grace of the only-begotten Son of God, it is brought back to the original state of its substance [Note: A reads “the original state of its substance”; Col. 0445], in which it was created according to the image of God, it begins to be and begins to live in him who was created according to the image of God. [Note: A reads “when”; Col. 0445.]

This mode seems to pertain [Note: D omits “seems”; Col. 0445] to what the Apostle says: “He calls those things that are not as though they were”; that is, those who were lost in the first man and fell into a kind of non-subsistence [Col. 0445D], God the Father calls through faith in his Son so that they may be, like those who have already been reborn in Christ [Note: A omits “like those”; Col. 0445].

This may also be understood of those whom God daily calls [Note: CDE use the spelling “daily” throughout; Col. 0445] from the hidden recesses of nature, in which they are considered not to be, so that they may appear visibly in form, matter, and the other conditions through which hidden things can become manifest—and of anything else that more searching reason may be able to discover beyond these modes. [Note: C reads “from”; Col. 0445.]

For the present, however, I think enough has been said about these matters, unless you think otherwise. [Note: A reads “about these matters, as I think”; Col. 0445.]

**STUDENT.** Certainly enough, unless I am somewhat disturbed [Note: A reads “troubled”] by what Saint Augustine seems to have said in his *Hexameron* [Note: A correction, and ACDEF, read *Examero*; *Exameron* occurs throughout; AF sometimes read *Exaemeron*; Col. 0445]: namely, that the angelic nature was created before every creature in dignity, though not in time; and that, accordingly, it first contemplated in God the primordial causes of all the others apart from itself—that is, the principal exemplars, which the Greeks call *prototypa* (πρωτότυπα)—then contemplated them in itself, and thereafter contemplated the creatures themselves in their effects. For it could not know the cause of itself before it proceeded into its own proper form. [Note: A reads “has been said”; Col. 0445.]

**TEACHER.** That ought not to trouble you. Consider more attentively the things that have been said. [Note: A omits “the things.”] If we say that the angels knew in God the principal causes of things established in him [Col. 0446B], we will seem to resist the Apostle, who affirms that God himself, and the causes of all things in him—whether they are something other than he or not [Note: C and D have this wording; Col. 0445]—are above everything that is said and understood. It is therefore necessary to hold to a straight and middle path, lest we seem either to resist the Apostle or fail to maintain the judgment of a teacher of such supreme and holy authority.

Thus we must not doubt—indeed, we must firmly hold—that both statements are true. Reason allows us to say, according to the Apostle, that the cause of all things, which surpasses every intellect, cannot be known by any created nature. [Note: D omits the words from “the cause of all things” through “according to the Apostle”; Col. 0445.] For he says: “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” And elsewhere: “The peace of Christ, which surpasses every understanding.”

But if the cause of all things is remote from all things that were created by it [Note: A reads “created by it” after “all things”; Col. 0445], then [Col. 0446C] without any doubt the reasons of all things, which exist eternally and unchangeably in that cause, are wholly remote from all the things whose reasons they are. If someone says that in angelic intellects there are certain theophanies of those reasons—that is, certain divine manifestations comprehensible to an intellectual nature [Note: A reads “of an intellectual nature”; Col. 0445]—but not the reasons themselves, namely the principal exemplars, he will not, I think, have departed from the truth.

We believe that Saint Augustine appropriately said that these theophanies had been seen in the angelic creature before the generation of all beings inferior to it. Therefore, let what we have said not disturb us: angels see the causes of inferior creation first in God and then in themselves. [Note: D reads “which”; Col. 0445.] For God is not called “God” by sacred Scripture only in his divine essence; Scripture also frequently calls God that manner in which he shows himself, in a certain way, to an intellectual and rational creature according to the capacity of each. [Note: A reads “and” for “also” and omits “that”; Col. 0445.]

This manner is customarily called by the Greeks *theophania*, that is, “the manifestation of God.” An example is: “I saw the Lord sitting,” and other passages of this kind, when the seer did not see his essence itself but something made by him. [Col. 0446D]

It is therefore not surprising if a threefold cognition is understood in the angel [Col. 0447A]. One is superior: according to the mode described above, the eternal reasons of things are first expressed in it. Then, whatever it receives from what is above, it entrusts to itself, as it were, in a marvelous and ineffable memory—a kind of image impressed from an image. If, by this mode, it can know what is above it, who would dare say that it does not possess within itself a certain cognition of inferior things? [Note: D omits “to say”; Col. 0447.]

Those things, therefore, that can be grasped by reason and intellect are rightly said to be. Whatever surpasses every reason and intellect is likewise rightly said not to be.

### 8. [Col. 0447]

**STUDENT.** What, then, shall we say about that future blessedness promised to the saints, which we think is nothing other than the pure [Col. 0447B] and immediate contemplation of the divine essence itself [Note: A reads “which we think is”; Col. 0447], as Saint John the Evangelist says: “We know that we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; but when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is.” Likewise the Apostle Paul [Note: ADE omit “Paul”; Col. 0447]: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.” Saint Augustine also, in Book XXII of *The City of God*, says, as I think, of the future contemplation of the divine essence:

“Through the bodies that we shall bear, in every body whatever we shall see, wherever we direct the eyes of our body [Note: A reads “wherever we turn them”; Col. 0447], we shall contemplate the Lord himself in manifest clarity.”

For if the height of the divine essence surpasses the most pure power of angelic contemplation [Note: D omits “power”; Col. 0447]—for it has been established by the arguments given above that the divine essence is incomprehensible to any intellectual creature, and there is no doubt that intellectual nature is found especially in angels—and if no other blessedness is promised to us than equality with the angelic nature, how will the blessedness of human nature be able to contemplate the height of the divine essence? [Col. 0447C]

**TEACHER.** You have raised the matter sharply and attentively; you are not disturbed about it without reason. But I thought it should be enough for you that earlier we made a general statement about every creature. [Note: A reads “we made a statement about every creature”; Col. 0447.]

**STUDENT.** What statement? Please repeat it.

**TEACHER.** Did we not define universally that the divine essence is comprehensible through itself to no bodily sense, to no reason, and to no human or angelic intellect? [Note: D reads “incomprehensible”; CDE have the wording translated here. A adds: “Do you remember what we proposed earlier?” Col. 0447.]

**STUDENT.** I remember, and I cannot deny that I accepted it in that form. But, as it seems to me, either that earlier conclusion must be entirely dissolved, and we must grant to an intellectual creature contemplation of the divine essence through itself; or, if it cannot be dissolved because it has been established by the most certain arguments, you must explain by sound reasoning and probable examples the mode of the divine contemplation that is promised to the saints in the future and in which the angels always subsist. [Col. 0447D] [Note: A reads “it is necessary”; Col. 0447.]

**TEACHER.** I do not know what mode you are seeking beyond the one we briefly discussed a little earlier. [Col. 0448A]

**STUDENT.** I would like you to repeat what that mode was; I do not remember it. [Note: A reads “I do not remember it itself”; Col. 0447.]

**TEACHER.** Do you remember what we had agreed upon when we were saying certain things about the *Hexameron* of the holy father Augustine?

**STUDENT.** I do remember, but I want to hear you speak about it again. [Note: A reads “I want to hear this again from you”; Col. 0447.]

**TEACHER.** You were troubled, I think, by how that father could have said [Note: A reads “had foretold”] that the causes of created things, which exist eternally in God and are God, were first contemplated by the angels in God, then in themselves, and then that they knew the proper forms and differences of those creatures, if the divine essence, together with the reasons that are in it, cannot be essentially comprehended by any creature. [Note: C reads “no creature.”]

**STUDENT.** I retain the whole matter.

**TEACHER.** Do you remember what we answered? [Note: [Col. 0447] CD support *respondebamus* (“we answered”); E reads *responderimus* (“we shall have answered”).]

**STUDENT.** Certainly, if my memory does not deceive me. You said that the angels did not see the actual causes of things that subsist in the divine essence, but certain divine manifestations, which, as you say, the Greeks call *theophaniae*, and which were named after the eternal causes whose images they are. [Note: A reads “by this name”; CDE have “by the name”; Col. 0447.] You added that not only the divine essence itself, existing unchangeably in itself, is called God, but also the theophanies themselves, which are expressed from it and out of it in an intellectual nature, are proclaimed under the name of God. [Note: D omits “the divine,” and also omits “themselves”; Col. 0447.]

**TEACHER.** You remember correctly; that is what we said.

**STUDENT.** But what does that have to do with the present question?

**TEACHER.** Quite a lot, as I see it. For by that mode I think that the angels always see God [Note: AC read “as I think”; Col. 0447], and that the righteous also see him in this life when they undergo an ecstasy of mind, and will see him in the future as the angels do.

We shall not, therefore, see God himself through himself, since the angels do not see him in that way either; for this is impossible for every creature. As the Apostle says, he alone “has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light.” Rather, we shall contemplate certain theophanies made by him in us. [Note: A omits “Rather”; Col. 0447.]

For will not each person be formed according to the height of his own holiness and wisdom by one and the same form desired by all—that is, by the Word of God? It is of itself that it speaks in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” [Note: A reverses the words: “many dwelling places are”; Col. 0447]. It calls itself the Father’s house; although that house is one and the same and remains unchangeable, it will nevertheless appear manifold to those whom it grants to dwell in it. [Note: A reads “it appears”; Col. 0447.]

Each person, as we have said, will possess within himself knowledge of the Word of the only-begotten Son of God [Note: A reads “the Word of God”; Col. 0447] to the extent that grace is granted to him. For as great as the number of the elect is, so great will be the number of the dwelling places [Col. 0448D] [Note: A omits “is”]; as great as is the multiplication of holy souls [Note: D reads “of souls holy”; Col. 0447], so great will be the possession of divine theophanies.

**STUDENT.** It seems probable.

**TEACHER.** You speak correctly: probable. For who could establish with certainty that such things will eternally be, while human powers, still in this fragile flesh, seem to exceed the capacity of our attention? [Note: A reads “would establish”; Col. 0447.]

### 9. [Col. 0449A]

**STUDENT.** But I would like you briefly to explain what you can conjecture about this theophany: what it is, whence it is, where it is, and whether it is formed outside us or within us [Note: A reads “where it is, whether it exists, whether it is within us or outside us”; E reads *qui* (“who”) and *firmatur* (“is established”; Col. 0449].

**TEACHER.** You are asking about a lofty matter, and I do not know whether anything more lofty can be reached by human inquiry. Nevertheless, I shall say what I have been able to find concerning it in the books of the holy Fathers who dared to speak of such things.

**STUDENT.** Please do.

**TEACHER.** You are asking, then, what it is, from where it comes, and where it is. [Note: A omits “and”; Col. 0449.]

**STUDENT.** Yes.

**TEACHER.** We find that Maximus, the great monk and divine philosopher, argued with exceptional depth and subtlety about this theophany in his exposition of the sermons of Gregory the Theologian. For he says that a theophany is produced from nowhere other than God [Note: C reads “is not produced from elsewhere”; Col. 0449], but comes about through the condescension of the divine Word—that is, the only-begotten Son, who is the wisdom of the Father—descending, as it were, toward [Col. 0449B] the human nature created and purified by him, and through the elevation upward of human nature toward the aforesaid Word by divine love. [Note: D omits the words from “human nature” through “human nature”; Col. 0449.]

Here I call “condescension” not that which has already occurred through the Incarnation, but that which takes place through *theosis*, that is, through the deification of the creature. Thus, from the condescension of God’s wisdom toward human nature by grace, and from the elevation of that same nature toward wisdom itself through love, a theophany comes about. [Note: A omits “wisdom”; B reads “wisdom” rather than “of wisdom”; Col. 0449.]

Saint Augustine seems to agree with this understanding when he explains the Apostle’s words: “Who was made for us righteousness and wisdom.” For he explains them in this way:

“The wisdom of the Father [Note: A reads “for the wisdom of the Father”; Col. 0449], in which and through which all things were made—which was not created but creates—through an ineffable condescension of its mercy becomes present in our souls. [Col. 0449C] It joins our intellect to itself, so that, in an ineffable way, a kind of composite wisdom is formed: from it, descending to us and dwelling in us, and from our understanding, taken up by it through love and formed in it.” [Note: C reads “taken up by God”; ABDE read “by it”; Col. 0449.]

He explains righteousness and the other virtues in the same way: they come about only through a certain marvelous and ineffable conformation of divine wisdom and our understanding. For, as Maximus says, to the extent that the human intellect ascends through love, to that extent divine wisdom descends through mercy. And this is the cause and substance of all virtues. [Note: A reverses the order; D omits “cause”; Col. 0449.]

Therefore every theophany—that is, every virtue—is produced [Col. 0449D] not outside the one who receives it but within, both from God and from the recipients themselves: in this life, in which it begins to be formed in those who are worthy, and in the future life, in which they will receive the perfection of divine blessedness. [Note: D adds the heading “Recapitulation” in Greek: Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις; Col. 0449D.]

**STUDENT.** Theophanies, then, are produced in an angelic and human nature illuminated, purified, and perfected by grace through the descent of divine wisdom and the ascent of human and angelic understanding. [Note: C reads “and the descent”; Col. 0449.]

**TEACHER.** Precisely. For this agrees with what the same Maximus says: “Whatever the intellect is able to comprehend, that it becomes.” Therefore, to the extent that the soul comprehends virtue, to that extent it itself becomes virtue. [Col. 0450A]

### 10.

If you seek examples of these things, they have been set forth most clearly by the same Maximus [Note: A adds “with him saying these things”; Col. 0449]:

“Just as air illuminated by the sun appears to be nothing other than light—not because it loses its own nature, but because light prevails in it [Note: D reads “prevails”; Col. 0449], so that it is judged to be light itself [Note: C reads “to the light”; D reads “so that it is light itself”]—so human nature joined to God is said to be God in every respect, not because it ceases to be human nature [Note: CD omit “human”], but because it receives participation in divinity, so that God alone appears to be in it.” [Col. 0449.]

Likewise:

“When light is absent, air is dark; but the light of the sun, subsisting in itself, is apprehended by no bodily sense. When, however, sunlight is mingled with air, it begins to appear, so that, [Col. 0450B] in itself, it is incomprehensible to the senses [Note: C reads “incomprehensible”; Col. 0449], but, mixed with air, it can be perceived by the senses.” [Note: A reads “but thus”; Col. 0449.]

Understand accordingly that the divine essence is incomprehensible in itself, but, when joined to an intellectual creature, appears in a marvelous manner, so that it—the divine essence, I mean—appears alone in that creature, namely, the intellectual creature. For its ineffable excellence surpasses every nature that participates in it, so that, to those who understand, nothing other than it appears in all things, although, as we have said, it does not appear through itself in any way. [Note: D omits the words from “nothing other” through “any way”; Col. 0449.]

**STUDENT.** I understand very well what you are trying to persuade me of. But I do not clearly perceive whether it can agree with the words of the holy father Augustine. [Note: A omits “father”; E omits “clearly”; Col. 0449.]

**TEACHER.** Then pay closer attention [Note: A reads “therefore”; Col. 0449], and let us return to the words of Augustine that we cited first. They are, I think, in Book XXII [Col. 0450C] of *The City of God* [Note: A reads *On the City*; CDE have the wording translated here]:

“Through the bodies that we shall bear, in every body whatever we shall see, wherever we direct the eyes of our body [Note: A reads “wherever we turn them”; Col. 0449], we shall contemplate God himself in manifest clarity.”

Consider the force of the words. He did not say: “Through the bodies that we shall bear, we shall contemplate God himself” [Note: A reads “God himself”; Col. 0449], because he cannot be seen through himself. Rather, he said: “Through the bodies that we shall bear, in every body whatever we shall see, we shall contemplate God himself.” Therefore he will be seen through bodies, in bodies, not through himself.

Likewise, the divine essence will appear through intellect in intellects and through reason in reasons, not through itself. For in the future life the excellence of divine power will be manifested to all who will be worthy of its contemplation, so that nothing other than it will [Col. 0451A] shine forth to them, whether in bodies or in intellects. For “God will be all in all.” [Col. 0450D] [Note: D reads *eliceat* (“draws forth”; reading uncertain) for *eluceat* (“shines forth”).]

It is as though Scripture said openly: “God alone will appear in all things.” [Note: D reads “Scripture openly.”]

For this reason Saint Job says: “In my flesh I shall see God.” As though he had said: In this flesh of mine, which is afflicted by many temptations, such glory will be present in the future [Note: CDE read “will be”; Col. 0451A] that, just as now nothing appears in it except death and corruption [Note: A reverses the words: “nothing now in it”], so in the future life nothing will appear to me in it except God alone [Note: A omits “in it”], who is truly life, immortality, and incorruption.

But if he promised such glory concerning the blessedness of his body, what should we think about the dignity of his soul [Note: A reads “spirit”; Col. 0451], especially since, as Gregory the Theologian says, “the bodies of the saints will be changed into reason, reason into intellect, intellect into God, and thus their entire nature into God himself”?

The aforesaid Maximus presents beautiful paradigms of this in his exposition of Gregory. We have already given one when speaking about air; now we shall add another, concerning fire and iron.

When iron melted in fire is dissolved into liquid, none of its nature seems to remain to the senses [Col. 0451B]; rather, it is wholly changed into the quality of fire. Yet reason recognizes that it preserves its own nature, although melted. Therefore, just as the whole of the air appears to be light, and the whole of the melted iron, as we said, appears fiery—or rather, appears to be fire—while their substances nevertheless remain [Note: A adds “and”; Col. 0451], so it must be understood with sound judgment that, after the end of this world, all nature, whether corporeal or incorporeal, will appear to be God alone, while the integrity of nature remains. Thus God, who is incomprehensible through himself, will in a certain way be comprehended in the creature, while the creature itself will be changed into God by an ineffable miracle.

But let these remarks suffice, if they shine clearly for you. [Note: C reads “for himself”; Col. 0451.]

**STUDENT.** They do shine, insofar as such things are permitted to shine for our minds [Note: D reads “for our minds”; Col. 0451]. For who in this life can speak clearly about an ineffable matter, so that the desire of those who inquire seeks nothing further—especially when no other glory is promised to us than the experimental knowledge in the future life of those things that are here believed through faith, sought through reason, and, insofar as possible, commended by argument? [Col. 0451C]

**TEACHER.** You judge cautiously and reasonably [Note: A reads “you judge”; CDE have “you estimate”; Col. 0451]. Accordingly, I think we must return to what was proposed, namely, to the division of Nature. [Note: A omits “to return”; Col. 0451.]

**STUDENT.** Certainly we must return, since a measure must be observed in what is to be said, so that the discussion may reach some conclusion.

### 11. [Col. 0451]

**TEACHER.** The first difference among the divisions of Nature mentioned above seemed to us to be between that which creates and is not created. Not without reason, since this species of Nature is rightly predicated of God alone, who alone, creating all things [Note: D reads “of all things”], is understood as *anarchos* (ἄναρχος), that is, “without a beginning” [Col. 0451D]. For he alone is the principal cause of all things that were made from him and through him, and consequently he is also the end of all things that are from him.

All things desire him. He is therefore beginning, middle, and end: beginning, because all things that participate in essence are from him; middle, because in him and through him [Note: D reads “in himself and through himself”; Col. 0451] they subsist and move [Note: A adds “all things”]; and end, because they move toward him, seeking rest from their motion and the stability of their perfection. [Col. 0452A]

**STUDENT.** I believe this most firmly and, insofar as it is granted, understand it: that this is rightly predicated only of the divine cause of all things, because it alone creates everything that is from it and is created by nothing superior to or preceding it. For it is the supreme and sole cause of all things that subsist from it and in it. [Note: A reverses “from it and in it” to “in it and from it”; Col. 0451.]

### 12.

Nevertheless, I would like to know what you think about this matter. I am not a little disturbed when I find, very frequently, in the books of the holy Fathers who have attempted to discuss the divine nature, that it not only creates all things that are but is also created. For, as they say, it makes and is made, creates and is created.

If this is so, I do not easily see how our reasoning can stand. [Note: A reads “our reasoning”; C omits “our.”] We say that it alone creates and is created by no one. [Col. 0452B]

**TEACHER.** You are disturbed with good reason. I too am greatly astonished by this, and I would like to learn from you how these things, which seem to be contrary, cannot conflict with one another, and how sound reason should be consulted about them.

**STUDENT.** Proceed, please; for in such matters I await not my own opinion but yours and your method of reasoning.

**TEACHER.** First, then, if it seems good [Note: A reads “if it is established”; Col. 0451], I think we must consider the very name that is most customary in sacred Scripture: the name “God.” Although the divine nature is designated by many names—such as Goodness, Essence, Truth, and others of this kind—Scripture most frequently uses that name.

**STUDENT.** That certainly seems so.

**TEACHER.** The etymology of this name is taken from the Greeks. For it is derived either from the verb *theōrō* (θεωρῶ), that is, “I see,” or from the verb *theō* (θέω), that is, “I run”; or—and this is more probable, because the same meaning is present in both—it is rightly said to be derived from both [Note: A reads “is”; CE read “is understood”; Col. 0451].

When *Theos* (Θεός) is derived from *theōrō*, it is interpreted as “seeing.” For he sees all things that are in himself, since he looks upon nothing outside himself, because nothing exists outside himself. [Note: A omits “all things”; Col. 0451.]

When it is derived from *theō*, *Theos* is rightly understood as “running.” For he runs into all things and does not stand still in any way, but by running fills all things, as it is written: “His word runs swiftly.” [Col. 0452C]

Nevertheless, he is in no way moved. For of God it is most truly said that he is a “stable motion” and a “mobile stasis.” He stands unchangeably in himself, never abandoning his natural stability. Yet he moves himself through all things so that those things that subsist essentially from him may be. For all things come to be through his motion.

Accordingly, one and the same meaning is present in the two interpretations of the same name, “God.” For God’s running through all things is nothing other than his seeing all things. But just as all things come to be through his seeing, so they come to be through his running [Note: CDE omit “through him”; Col. 0451].

**STUDENT.** The etymology of the name has been explained sufficiently and plausibly. But I do not see adequately how he can move who is everywhere, without whom nothing can be, and beyond whom nothing extends—for he is the place and boundary of all things. [Col. 0453A]

**TEACHER.** I said that God is moved not outside himself but from himself, in himself, and toward himself. We must not believe that there is any other motion in him than the desire of his will, by which he wills all things to be. Likewise, his stasis is not to be understood as though he comes to rest after motion, but as the unchangeable purpose of that same will, by which he determines that all things should remain in the unchangeable stability of their own reasons.

Strictly speaking, neither stasis nor motion is predicated of him. For these two things appear to be opposed to one another; and sound reason prohibits us from conceiving or understanding opposites in him, especially since stasis is properly the end of motion. God, however, does not begin to move in order to arrive at some state of rest. [Col. 0453B] [Note: A omits “for”; Col. 0453.]

These names, like many similar ones, are transferred from the creature to the Creator through a certain divine metaphor. They are not applied irrationally, since he is the cause of all things that are in stasis and motion. From him they begin to run so that they may be, since he is the beginning of all things [Note: C omits “he is”; A reads “he is the beginning”; Col. 0453]; and through him they are borne toward him by a natural motion, so that they may stand unchangeably and eternally in him, since he is the end and rest of all things. For they desire nothing beyond him [Note: A omits “him”; Col. 0453]. In him they find the beginning and end of their motion.

God is therefore called “running,” not because he runs outside himself—he who always stands immutably in himself [Note: D reads “remains”; Col. 0453] and fills all things—but because he causes all things to run from non-existence into existence. [Note: A reads “because”; Col. 0453.]

**STUDENT.** Return to the matter at hand; what you have said does not seem unreasonable.

**TEACHER.** Please remind me what matter you are asking about. When we attempt to say something about incidental questions, we very often forget the principal questions. [Col. 0453C]

**STUDENT.** Did we not propose to investigate, as far as our strength permits, in what way those who discuss the divine nature say that it both creates and is created? [Note: A reads “Did we not propose this? We proposed”; Col. 0453.] No one with understanding doubts that it creates all things [Note: The source supplies “it” in brackets: “creates [it] all things”; witnesses CDE omit the bracketed object]. But how it is said to be created did not seem to us something that could be passed over cursorily. [Note: A omits “however”; D reads “seemed”; Col. 0453.]

### Restored apparatus for §§ 7–10

- In § 7 A reads *nisi* (“unless”) for *ni*; A reads *substantiae suae* (“of its substance”) with reversed word order. CDE consistently spell *cotidie* (“daily”), where the text elsewhere uses *quotidie*. D reads feminine *quae* (“which”) at the theophany statement, and A reads *quam* (“than/which,” accusative feminine) where the printed angelic-intellect clause has *quae* (“which,” nominative feminine).
- In § 8 CDE spell *diffinivimus* for *definivimus* (“we defined”). At “what we answered,” CDE support *haec* (“these things”), while A reads singular *hoc* (“this”); CD read *respondebamus* (“we answered”), while E reads future-perfect *responderimus* (“we shall have answered”).
- In § 9 ABDE read *ab eo* (“by/from him”), while C reads *a Deo* (“by/from God”), in the clause about human understanding being taken up; the contextual English sense is the same, but both actual forms are retained.
- In § 10, for *ut id ipsum lucis* (“so that it [is judged] light itself”), C reads *luci* (“to/for the light”), while D reads *ut ipsum id lucis* (“so that that very thing [is] of light”). The transmitted syntax is compressed, so these are retained as witness readings rather than harmonized.


[The supplied source ends here.]

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

MAG. Exactly so. But, as I think, from what has been said above a considerable opening has been made toward resolving this question. For it has been established [Note: [Col. 0453] A: “for it is.”] between us that by the motion of the divine nature nothing else is to be understood [Note: [Col. 0453] CDE: “by the motion”; A: “through motion”] than the purpose of the divine will for bringing into being those things which are to be made. The divine nature, therefore—which is nothing other than the divine will—is said to come to be in all things. For in it being and willing are not two different things; rather, in bringing into being all that it has seemed right should be made, willing and being are one and the same [Note: [Col. 0453] D: “For nothing else is in it”; E: “For in it there is nothing else.”].

For example, if someone should say that the motion of the divine will is directed toward this, that those things which exist should exist: it therefore creates all things, bringing them from nothing into existence, so that they may pass from non-being into being; yet it is also created, because nothing exists essentially apart from it—for it is the essence of all things [Note: [Col. 0453] D omits “of all things”]. For just as no natural good exists apart from it, but everything that is said to be good is good through participation in the one highest Good, so everything that is said to exist [Note: [Col. 0453] CDE: “that is said to exist”; A: “that exists”] does not exist in itself, but exists through participation in the nature that truly exists.

Thus, as was considered in what has already been said [Note: [Col. 0453] A: “that they may be”], the divine nature is said to come to be not only when the Word of God is born in a wondrous and ineffable manner in those who are reformed by faith, hope, love, and the other virtues—as the Apostle says when speaking of Christ: “Who was made in us wisdom from God, and justification, and redemption” [Note: [Col. 0453] A: “and”; C–D: “who”—a variant affecting the connective or relative wording]—but also because it appears in all things that exist. Since it is invisible in itself, it is not improperly said to be made in them [Note: [Col. 0453] A: “and”].

For even our intellect, before it comes into thought and memory, may reasonably be said to exist [Note: [Col. 0453] CDE: “may reasonably be said to exist”; A: “not to exist”]. It is invisible in itself and is known by no one except God and ourselves. But when it has entered into thoughts and receives a form from certain images, it is rightly said to come to be. It comes to be in memory, receiving certain forms of things—whether sounds, colors, or other sensible objects—although it was formless before it entered memory. Then it receives, as it were, a second formation, when it is formed by certain signs of forms or sounds: I mean letters, which are signs of sounds, and figures, which are signs of forms, as well as by mathematical or other sensible indications, through which it can be communicated to the senses of those who perceive.

By this analogy, although it is far removed from the divine nature, I think it can nevertheless be suggested how the divine nature itself, while creating all things and not knowing itself to be created by anyone [Note: [Col. 0453] Conjecture; CDE: “and not knowing itself to be created by anyone”; A: “and knowing itself to be created by no one”], is created in a wondrous manner in all things that come from it. Just as the understanding, purpose, decision, or whatever one may call that intimate and first motion of our mind, when—as we have said—it has entered thought, received certain forms of images, and then proceeded into signs of sounds or indications of sensible motions, is not improperly said to come to be—for it comes to be formed in images, although in itself it lacks every sensible form—so the divine essence, which subsists in itself and surpasses every intellect, is rightly said to be created in the things that have been made by it, through it, in it, and toward it. In these things it is known by those who seek it with right devotion, whether through the intellect, if they are intelligible alone, or through the senses, if they are sensible [Note: [Col. 0453] C: “if they are”].

DISC. I think enough has been said about this.

### 13

MAG. Quite enough, I think.

DISC. But you must still explain why the divine nature is said to be solely creative and not created, if, as the foregoing arguments have made persuasive [Note: [Col. 0453] CE: “as”; A: “which, just as”; D: “as the foregoing”], it both creates and is created. These propositions seem to contradict one another.

MAG. You are keeping careful watch; for I too see that this deserves investigation.

DISC. It certainly does.

MAG. Pay attention, then, to what follows, and direct the gaze of your mind toward this brief answer [Note: [Col. 0455] A: “what will follow”].

DISC. Go ahead; I shall follow attentively.

MAG. You do not doubt that the divine nature is the creator of the universe.

DISC. Proceed to the rest; for on this point hesitation would be impious.

MAG. Similarly, you apprehend by faith and intellect that it is created by no one [Note: [Col. 0455] CDE omit “it”].

DISC. Nothing is more certain [Note: [Col. 0455] CE: “Nothing”; CDE: “Nothing”].

MAG. Therefore, when you hear that it is created, you do not doubt that it is created not by another but by itself [Note: [Col. 0455] CDE: “by itself”; A: “by it”].

DISC. I do not doubt it.

MAG. What follows, then? Is it not always creating, whether it has created itself or the essences created by itself? For when it is said to create itself, nothing else is rightly understood [Col. 0455B] than to establish the natures of things. For its creation—that is, its manifestation in something—is certainly the establishment of all existing things.

DISC. Up to this point, what has been said seems probable. But I would like to hear what Theology teaches concerning this ineffable and incomprehensible nature that creates and causes all things: that is, whether it is, what it is, what kind it is [Note: [Col. 0455] C: “what kind it is”], and how it is defined.

MAG. Has it not been sufficiently and clearly demonstrated to those who contemplate the truth by Theology itself—which you have just named, and which is concerned either exclusively or principally with the divine nature—that, from the things created by it, one may understand only that it subsists essentially, but not what its essence is? For not only the efforts of human reasoning, as we have often said [Note: [Col. 0455] CDE: “of human reasoning”; A: “of reason”], but even the purest intellects of the celestial essences, are surpassed by it [Col. 0455C].

Nevertheless, theologians, by the clear vision of a sound mind, have investigated that it exists from the things that exist; that it is wise, from their divisions into essences, genera, species, differences, and numbers; and that it lives, from the stable motion and moving state of all things [Note: [Col. 0455] CE: “right-minded contemplation”; AD: “rightly”]. By this reasoning they most truly found the cause of all things to be threefold in substance. For, as we have said, from the essence of the things that exist it is understood to exist; from the wondrous order of things it is found to be wise; and from motion it is found to be life.

The nature that creates and is the cause of all things therefore is, is wise, and lives. Accordingly, investigators of the truth have handed down that through essence the Father, through wisdom the Son, and through life the Holy Spirit are understood.

DISC. These things have been sufficiently and clearly established for me, and I see that they are entirely true. For what it is or of what kind it is cannot be defined at all [Note: [Col. 0455] CDE: “of what kind it is”; A: “what its nature is”]. For what cannot be understood at all cannot at all be defined [Note: [Col. 0455] DE: “cannot be defined”]. Nevertheless, I would like to hear by what reasoning theologians have dared to predicate unity and Trinity of the cause of all things.

MAG. We need not labor greatly over this last proposition of yours, especially since Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, the theologian, most truly and most authoritatively demonstrates to us the mysteries of divine unity and Trinity [Col. 0456A]. For he says that the highest essence and cause of all things cannot be signified by any meaning of words, names, or articulated speech. For unity and Trinity are not such as they can be conceived by any human being, however pure, or contemplated by an angelic intellect, however clear.

But so that religious movements of pious minds might be able to think and proclaim something concerning a matter that is ineffable and incomprehensible—especially for those who demand from Catholic men an account of the Christian religion, whether for the sake of learning the truth, if they are good, or for the opportunity of testing and criticizing it, if they are evil—these sacred symbolic words of faith were both discovered and handed down by the holy theologians, so that we might believe in our heart and confess with our mouth that the divine goodness consists in three substances of one essence [Col. 0456B].

Nor was this discovered without the vision of spiritual intelligence and rational investigation [Note: [Col. 0455] CDE: “that the goodness consists in three substances of one essence”; A adds: “that the goodness of one essence consists in three persons in three substances, and neither was this, and so forth”]. Contemplating one ineffable cause of all things, one principle—simple, indivisible, and universal—insofar as they had been illumined by the divine Spirit, they called it unity. Then, contemplating that unity not as a kind of singularity and sterility but as a wondrous and fertile multiplicity, they understood three substances of unity: the unbegotten, the begotten, and the proceeding [Note: [Col. 0455] A: “and the proceeding”].

They named the relation of the unbegotten substance to the begotten substance “Father”; the relation of the begotten substance to the unbegotten substance “Son”; and the relation of the proceeding substance to the unbegotten and begotten substance “Holy Spirit.” But since nearly all the intention of the holy interpreters of Sacred Scripture is occupied with this matter, I think enough has been said for the present.

DISC. Quite enough. Nevertheless, I would like to hear more clearly about the relation of the three divine substances. For someone could understand these mystical names of the Holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—not according to relation but according to nature. For “Father” appears to be the name of the Father’s substance. Similarly, “Son” is the name of the Son’s substance, and the designation “Holy Spirit” seems to signify nothing other than his substance [Note: [Col. 0455] ADE: “the designation of the Holy Spirit”; C: “also of the Holy Spirit”].

MAG. Perhaps we too would not refuse to believe and confess that very thing, if the supreme and venerable authority of Saint Gregory the Theologian, together with the approval of true reason [Note: [Col. 0455] CDE: “and the approval of true reason”; A: “and the approval of true reasoning”], did not forbid us to believe such things. For when he was questioned by the Eunomians, those most poisonous opponents of the Catholic faith, about the name “Father”—whether it signifies nature or operation—he replied wondrously, illumined by divine grace, saying: “It signifies neither nature nor operation, but only the relation to the Son.”

For if he had answered that “Father” is a name of nature [Note: [Col. 0457] A: “that the name ‘Father’ is of nature”], they would immediately have followed this by saying that “Son” likewise is a name of nature [Note: [Col. 0457] CDE: “and”; A omits “and”]. If this were granted, it would necessarily follow that “Father” is the name of one nature and “Son” of another; for in one and the same nature two names differing from one another cannot arise. And thus they would conclude that the Father and the Son are ἑτερουσίους [Note: [Col. 0457] CDE: ἑτερουσιας], that is, of a different essence or nature.

The same argument would apply if the answer concerned operation. For if it were granted to them that “Father” is a name of operation, they would immediately conclude that the Son is a creature, since the Father would be conceded to be the name of his operation—that is, of his creation.

DISC. It is absolutely certain that this answer is praiseworthy and inspired by truth. But we must consider it a little more fully [Col. 0457B] [Note: [Col. 0457] CDE: “more clearly”; A: “more fully”]. For, as it seems to me, they could not immediately have criticized him even if he had said that “Father” is a name of nature. What then? Can two names that differ from one another in sound but not in meaning not be understood in one and the same nature, when we see that both Abraham and Isaac—namely, father and son—signify one nature? For “Abraham” is not the name of one nature and “Isaac” of another, but of one and the same nature.

MAG. You would be right if, in this example of yours, you could likewise affirm that Abraham or Isaac signifies nothing other than what “father” and “son” signify in them. For “Abraham” is both the name of Abraham himself and the name “father” for that same Abraham. Similarly, “Isaac” is both the name of Isaac and the name “son” for that same Isaac.

But Abraham and “father,” or Isaac and “son,” are not predicated of the same thing. “Abraham” is said of Abraham’s substance—that is, of his particular person; but no one who understands correctly will doubt that, in relation to his son Isaac, he is called “father” [Note: [Col. 0457] C: “would doubt”; E: “doubts”].

The same must be understood of Isaac. By the name “Isaac,” his own individual substance is signified; but his relation to his father is known through the term “son.” For you cannot deny that such names—“father” and “son”—are relative, not substantial. If, therefore, among us, that is, in our nature, such terms are predicated not substantially but relatively, what shall we say of the highest and holy essence, in which Sacred Scripture has established such names for the relations or connections of the substances to one another—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? [Col. 0457D]

DISC. I now see that the response of the holy theologian mentioned above is altogether supported by truth. For, as has been demonstrated, whether in the divine or in human nature, a relational name cannot be received as substance or essence. Yet I would like you to make clear and brief for me whether all the categories, since they are ten in number, can truly and properly be predicated of the one essence of the supreme divine goodness in three substances, and of the three substances in the same one essence [Col. 0458A].

MAG. I do not know who can speak briefly and clearly about this matter. Either one must remain entirely silent concerning such a cause and entrust it to the simplicity of orthodox faith—for it surpasses every intellect, as it is written: “Who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” [Note: [Col. 0457] CDE: “dwells”; A: “inhabits”]—or, if someone begins to discuss it, he will necessarily persuade us of what is probable in many ways and by many arguments, using the two principal branches of theology: the affirmative, which the Greeks call καταφατική, and the negative, which they call ἀποφατική [Note: [Col. 0457] C omits “which”].

The one, ἀποφατική, denies that the divine essence or substance is any of the things that exist—that is, any of the things that can be said or understood [Col. 0458B]. The other, καταφατική, predicates all things that exist of it, and is therefore called affirmative—not because it confirms that it is something among the things that exist, but because it suggests that everything which comes from it can be predicated of it.

For it is reasonable that the causal can be signified through its effects. Theology says that it is truth, goodness, essence, light, justice, sun, star, spirit, water, lion, city, worm, and countless other things. Nor does it teach this only from things that are according to nature, but also from things that are contrary to nature, when it says that it becomes drunk, foolish, and insane [Note: [Col. 0457] BC: “and becomes foolishness”]. But it is not our purpose to discuss these matters now; Saint Dionysius the Areopagite has said enough about them in the Symbolic Theology.

Therefore we must return to what you asked. You had asked whether all the categories are to be predicated properly of God, or only some of them [Col. 0458C].

DISC. Certainly we must return to that. But first, I think, we must consider why that most holy father and theologian declared that the names mentioned above—“essence,” I mean, “goodness,” “truth,” “justice,” “wisdom,” and the rest of this kind, which appear not merely divine but most divine and seem to signify nothing other than the divine substance or essence itself—become metaphorical, that is, are transferred from the creature to the Creator. For we must not suppose that he said this without some mystical and hidden reason.

MAG. You are rightly attentive; for I see that this too must not be passed over carelessly. Therefore I would like you to answer whether you understand anything opposed to God or co-understood with him. By “opposed” I mean through privation, contrariety, relation, or absence; by “co-understood” I mean something understood eternally together with him, although not coessential with him.

DISC. I clearly understand what you mean. Accordingly, I would not dare to say that anything is opposed to him, or that anything co-understood with him is ἑτέρουσιον—that is, of another essence than he is [Col. 0459A]. For things opposed by relation are always opposed to one another in such a way that they also begin simultaneously and cease to exist simultaneously, although they are of the same nature—for example, the simple to the double, or the subsesquialter to the sesquialter [Note: [Col. 0459] A: “the simple and the double”]. Or they are opposed through negation, as “is” and “is not”; or through natural qualities; through absence, as light and darkness; through privation, as death and life; or through contrariety, as health and weakness, [voice and silence] [Note: [Col. 0459] “Voice and silence” is omitted by CDE].

These things are rightly attributed to what is subject to intellect and sense, and therefore they are not in God. For things that differ from one another cannot be eternal. If they were eternal, they would not differ from one another. Eternity is like itself, and wholly throughout itself it subsists as one, simple, and indivisible [Col. 0459B]. It is indeed the one principle and one end of all things, differing from itself in nothing.

### 14

By the same reasoning, I do not know who would dare to affirm that something not coessential with God is coeternal with him. For if this can be thought or discovered, it necessarily follows that there is not one principle of all things but two or more, differing greatly from one another. It rightly holds that all things begin from one, but that nothing begins from two or more.

MAG. You argue correctly, I think.
