If, therefore, the divine names mentioned above look toward other names opposed to them, it is necessarily understood that the things properly signified by them likewise possess opposed contraries. Accordingly, they cannot properly be predicated of God, to whom nothing opposed exists and with whom nothing of a different nature is seen to be coeternal [Note: [Col. 0459] E: “nothing”; A: “there is nothing opposed”].

For true reason cannot find any of the names mentioned above, or any similar names, for which another name differing from it and departing from it is not found on the opposite side or within the same genus. And what we recognize in names, we must necessarily recognize also in the things signified by them [Note: [Col. 0459] CDE: “in the things”; A: “of the things”].

But since the divine significations that are predicated of God in Sacred Scripture, transferred from the creature to the Creator—if indeed it is correct to say that anything can be predicated of God, a matter to be considered elsewhere—are innumerable, and cannot either be discovered or gathered together at once by the smallness of our reasoning power, a few divine terms must nevertheless be set forth by way of example.

God is therefore called “essence,” but he is not properly essence, since nothingness is opposed to essence; he is therefore ὑπερούσιος, that is, superessential. Likewise, he is called “goodness,” but he is not properly goodness, for evil is opposed to goodness; he is therefore ὑπεράγαθος, more than good, and ὑπεραγαθότης [Note: [Col. 0459] CDE: ὑπεραγαθοτητα], that is, more than goodness.

God is called “God,” but he is not properly God; for blindness is opposed to vision, and the non-seeing to the seeing [Col. 0460A]. He is therefore ὑπερθεός, more than seeing, if Θεός is interpreted as “seeing.” But if you return to another derivation of this name, understanding Θεός, “God,” to be derived not from the verb θεωρῶ, “I see,” but from the verb Θέω, that is, “I run,” the same reasoning is likewise available to you. For to one who runs, one who does not run is opposed, just as slowness is opposed to speed. He will therefore be ὑπερθεός, that is, more than one who runs, as it is written: “His word runs swiftly.” For we understand this of God the Word, who ineffably runs through all things that exist, so that they may exist.

The same must be understood concerning truth. For falsehood is opposed to truth, and therefore he is not properly truth; he is therefore ὑπεραληθής and ὑπεραλήθεια [Note: [Col. 0459] D: “ὑπεραληθες, that is, ὑπεραληθια”; E: “υπεραληθης … υπεραληθια”; A adds “that is, more than …”], more than true and more than truth.

The same reasoning must be observed with all the divine names. For he is not properly called “eternity,” since temporality is opposed to eternity; he is therefore ὑπεραιώνιος and ὑπεραιωνία [Note: [Col. 0459] CDE; A adds “that is, more than …”], more than eternal and more than eternity.

No different reasoning occurs in the case of wisdom; accordingly, wisdom should not be thought to be properly predicated of God, since the foolish person and foolishness oppose wisdom and the wise person [Note: [Col. 0459] A: “and the unwise”]. Accordingly, he is rightly and truly called ὑπερσόφος, that is, more than wise, and ὑπερσοφία, more than wisdom.

Similarly, he is more than life, since death is opposed to life. The same must be understood of light, for darkness stands against light. Up to this point, I think, enough has been said about these matters.

DISC. Indeed, it must be admitted that enough has been said. For our present discussion does not permit us now to introduce whatever is necessary concerning such matters, on account of what must be debated in the present undertaking [Note: [Col. 0459] ADE: “what must be debated in the present undertaking”; C: “the present undertaking”]. Return, then, if you please, to the consideration of the ten categories.

MAG. I admire the acuity of your intention, which until now seemed exceedingly watchful.

DISC. Why, I ask, do you say that?

MAG. Did we not say that the ineffable nature cannot properly be signified by any word, any name, any sensible sound, or anything signified by a thing? And you granted this. For it is not properly called “essence,” “truth,” “wisdom,” and the rest of this kind, but “superessential,” “more than truth,” “more than wisdom,” and similar terms. But do not these too seem to be certain proper names, if “essence” is not properly said, whereas “superessential” is proper? Similarly, if “truth” or “wisdom” is not properly called by those names, but “more than truth” and “more than wisdom” are properly said [Col. 0460D] [Note: [Col. 0459] C omits “is said” in the corresponding repetition; D omits the entire sentence beginning “Similarly…”].

It does not, then, lack proper names. For although among the Latins these names are not ordinarily pronounced as compounds under a single accent and with one harmonious pattern of composition—except for the name “superessential”—among the Greeks they are nevertheless pronounced as compounds in a single cadence. For you will never, or scarcely ever, find “supergood,” “supereverlasting,” and the rest of the similar terms pronounced as compounds [Col. 0461A].

DISC. I myself am very much amazed at the direction in which I was proceeding when I left this investigation, which ought not to be despised, untouched. And therefore I earnestly ask you to open it up. For however the divine substance may be uttered—whether in simple parts of speech, compounds, or separate expressions, in Greek or Latin—provided that it is uttered properly, it will not appear to be ineffable. For what can in some manner be spoken is not ineffable.

MAG. Now you are watchful, as I see.

DISC. I am indeed watchful, but I still see nothing concerning this intervening question.

MAG. Return, then, to what was established between us a little earlier. For, unless I am mistaken, we said that there are two most sublime branches of theology. We received this not from ourselves but from the authority of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, who, as has been said, asserts most clearly that theology is twofold: καταφατικήν [Note: [Col. 0461] CDE: “that is, καταφατικήν”] and ἀποφατικήν. Cicero translates these as “intention” and “repulsion” [Note: [Col. 0461] CDE: “intention”; A: “intension”]; we, however, in order that the force of the names might become clearer, have preferred to translate them as affirmation and negation.

DISC. I seem to remember such things, I think. But I do not yet recognize how they benefit the matters we now wish to consider [Note: [Col. 0461] A: “I do not yet understand”].

MAG. Do you not see that these two—affirmation and negation—are opposed to one another?

DISC. I see it clearly, and I think nothing could be more contrary.

MAG. Pay closer attention, then. For when you arrive at the contemplation of perfect reasoning, you will consider clearly enough that these two, which appear to be contrary to one another, are in no way opposed to one another when they concern the divine nature [Col. 0461C]; rather, in all things and in every respect they agree with one another [Note: [Col. 0461] A: “to agree with one another”].

To make this clearer, let us use a few examples. The καταφατική says, “Truth is”; the ἀποφατική contradicts, “Truth is not.” Here there appears to be a form of contradiction. But when the matter is examined more closely [Note: [Col. 0461] A: “looked at”], no controversy is found.

For the statement “Truth is” does not affirm that the divine substance is properly truth, but that it can be called by that name metaphorically, transferred from the creature to the Creator. For it clothes the divine essence, which is naked and stripped of every proper signification, in such terms. The statement “Truth is not,” recognizing clearly that the divine nature is incomprehensible and ineffable [Note: [Col. 0461] A: “and ineffable”], does not deny that it exists; rather, it denies that it can properly be called truth or that it is truth [Note: [Col. 0461] CDE: “recognizing”; A: “acknowledging”].

The ἀποφατική knows how to strip it of all the significations with which the καταφατική clothes the Divinity [Note: [Col. 0461] A: “clothes”]. One says, for example, “It is wisdom,” clothing it with that name; the other says, “It is not wisdom,” stripping it of the same name. The one therefore says, “It can be called this,” but does not say, “It is this properly”; the other says, “It is not this,” although it can be named from this.

DISC. I see these things most clearly, I think, and what previously seemed to me to differ from one another now plainly appears to agree with one another and to dissent from one another in nothing when considered with reference to God [Col. 0462A]. But I confess that I do not yet know how they relate to the solution of the present question.

MAG. Pay more vigilant attention, then, and explain, insofar as you can, to which branch of theology the significations previously added belong—“superessential,” I mean, “more than truth,” “more than wisdom,” and the other similar expressions—whether they should be assigned to the affirmative or the negative branch [Note: [Col. 0461] A: “insofar as it is possible”].

DISC. I do not dare to determine this adequately by myself. For when I consider that the significations mentioned above lack the negative particle “not,” I fear attaching them to the negative branch of theology. But if I attach them to the affirmative branch, I recognize that their meaning does not agree with it. For when it is said, “It is superessential,” nothing else is made intelligible to me than a negation of essence. Whoever says, “It is superessential,” openly denies that it is essential. Accordingly, although negation does not appear in the pronunciation of the words, it nevertheless does not escape those who carefully consider the meaning itself.

Therefore, I think I am compelled to admit that these significations mentioned above, which appear to lack negation, belong, insofar as they can be understood, more to the negative branch of theology than to the affirmative.

MAG. I see that you have answered with great caution and vigilance, and I greatly approve the way in which you have most subtly discerned the meaning of the negative branch within the pronunciation of the affirmative branch. Let the solution of this present question, then, if you please, be formulated as follows: all these expressions that are predicated of God by the addition of the particles “super” or “more than”—such as “superessential,” “more than truth,” “more than wisdom,” and the like—fully comprehend within themselves both of the aforementioned branches of theology. Thus, in their pronunciation they possess the form of the affirmative branch, but in their meaning they possess the force of the negative [Note: [Col. 0461] E omits “in the meaning … the negative”].

Let us conclude this with a brief example. “Essence is”: affirmation. “Essence is not”: negation. “It is superessential”: affirmation and negation simultaneously [Note: [Col. 0461] A: “negation”]. On the surface it lacks negation; in its meaning it possesses negation [Note: [Col. 0461] CDE omit “in its meaning”]. For whoever says, “It is superessential,” does not say what it is, but what it is not. He says that it is not essence, but more than essence. Yet he does not express what that which is more than essence is, asserting that God is not one of the things that exist but is more than the things that exist; he in no way defines what that “more” is [Col. 0462D].

DISC. I think we must not linger any longer over this question, and now, if it seems good, we must consider the nature of the categories.

MAG. Aristotle, exceedingly acute, as they say, among the Greeks, and the discoverer of the distinction of natural things, enclosed the innumerable varieties of all things that exist after God and were created by him [Note: [Col. 0463] CDE: “were created”] within ten universal genera, which he called the ten categories, that is, predicates. For, as he thought [Note: [Col. 0463] A: “as he thought it to be”], nothing can be found in the multitude of created things or in the various motions of minds that cannot be included in one of the aforementioned genera.

The Greeks call these οὐσία, ποσότης, ποιότης [Note: [Col. 0463] A: ποιοτης, ποσοτης; CDE: ποσοτητα, ποιοτητα], πρός τι, κεῖσθαι, ἕζις, τόπος, χρόνος, πράττειν, παθεῖν. In Latin they are called essence, quantity, quality, relation, position, habit, place, time, acting, and being acted upon.

These ten genera have innumerable subdivisions, but the present discussion does not permit us to debate them now, lest we depart too far from our subject—especially since that branch of philosophy called dialectic is concerned with the divisions of these genera, from the most general to the most specific, and again with collections from the most specific back to the most general [Note: [Col. 0463] A: “collection”; C: “it fears”].

### Restored textual apparatus

#### §§ 7–8 ([Col. 0455]–[Col. 0457B])

- CDE omit *est* (“is”) after *semper*; CE read *nil* (“nothing”) for *nihil*. A reads *est nobis* (“it is for us”), *ac* (“and”), and *audire velim* (“I should like to hear”); A also omits *in* (“in”) and reads *significat* (“signifies”) for the infinitive *significare* (“to signify”).
- At *religiosa* (“religious,” neuter plural), A reads adverbial *religiose* (“religiously”) and D feminine *religiosae*. C reads *ne* (“lest”) for *nec* (“nor”); DA read *Item* (“likewise”) for *Iterum* (“again”).
- A reads *cum* (“when”) for *quando*; D omits *ex* (“from”); AD omit *et* (“and”); CDE read *filium suum* (“his son”), while A has the same words in the reverse relation supplied by its context. CDE read *hoc* (“this,” neuter), A *id* (“that”).
- CDE consistently spell *diffinivimus* for *definivimus* (“we defined”). At the recollection question CDE have *haec* (“these things”), A *hoc* (“this”); CD read *respondebamus* (“we answered”), E *responderimus* (“we shall have answered”).

#### §§ 9–10 ([Col. 0449]–[Col. 0450D])

- In the theophany clause ABDE read *ab eo* (“by/from him”), while C reads *a Deo* (“by/from God”).
- At *ut id ipsum lucis* (“so that it [is judged] light itself”), C reads *luci* (“to the light”), while D reads *ut ipsum id lucis*; the latter compressed wording is retained without conjectural expansion.

#### Later argument ([Col. 0459]–[Col. 0463])

- A reads *quid* (“what”) for *quod* (“that/what”), reverses *simul esse* to *esse simul* (“to be simultaneously”), reads *sive* (“or”) for *sint* (“they may be”), and *et* (“and”) for *ut* (“as”). CDE omit the supplied example *vox et silentium* (“voice and silence”). A reads *enim* (“for”) for *autem* (“however”); E and DE use *nil* (“nothing”) for *nihil*; A has *est oppositum* (“is opposed”) with reversed placement.
- A reads *de* (“concerning”) for *in* (“in”) and *relatae* (“referred”) for *translatae* (“transferred”); A omits *sed* (“but”), *Igitur* (“therefore”), and *si* (“if”). The Greek superlative forms are transmitted variously: C has *ὑπεραληθες / ὑπεραληθια*, E *ὑπεραληθης / ὑπεραληθια*, while A supplies the explanatory *id est plusquam* (“that is, more than”).
- A reads *quoniam et sapienti* (“because also to the wise”) where the text has *quoniam sapientiae* (“because to wisdom”), and *insapientia* for *insipientia* (“folly”). C places *praesenti* after *negotio* (“the present matter”); A reverses *plusquam veritas vero*; C omits *dicitur* (“is said”), and D omits the larger clause from *Similiter si* through *dicitur*.
- A has *aut* (“or”), omits *Et* (“and”), reads *quum* (“when”) for *quando*, and omits *ut* (“as”). CDE add *id est in* before *καταφατικήν*; A spells *intensionem* for *intentionem*, *cognosco* (“I know”) for *agnosco* (“I recognize”), and *posse* (“to be able”) for *posset* (“could”).
- C reads *clarum* (“clear”) for *clare* (“clearly”); A reads *consentire* (“to agree”) for *consentiunt* (“they agree”), *aspicitur* (“is looked at”) for *inspicitur* (“is examined”), *atque ineffabilem* (“and ineffable”), and *agnoscens* (“recognizing”). A also reads *quibus* (“by which”) for *quas* (“which”), *vestit* (“clothes”) for *induit* (“puts on”), and omits *enim* (“for”), *et ea* (“and these”), *mihi* (“to me”), and *in* in the cited scopes; it adds *est* after *possibile* and reverses *eas adiungere* (“to join them”).
- A reads *omnia* (“all things”) for *haec omnia* (“all these things”) and *negatio* (“negation”) for *abdicatio* (“denial”); CD omit *in* before “pronunciation,” E omits the clause *in intellectu … abdicativae*, and CDE omit *in* before “surface.”
- In Aristotle’s categories CDE read singular *creata* (“created”), while the text has plural agreement; A adds *est* to *visum* (“it seemed”). A and CDE transmit differing case/order forms of *ποιότης/ποσότης* (“quality/quantity”). A reads singular *collectione* (“collection”) for plural *collectiones*; C reads *veretur* (“fears”) for *versetur* (“is occupied”).


[The supplied source ends here.]

15. But, as the holy father Augustine says in his books *On the Trinity*, when one arrives at theology—that is, at the investigation of the divine essence—the power of the categories is wholly extinguished. For in the very natures created by God and in their motions, the categories possess some power, whatever its kind; but in that nature which can neither be spoken nor understood, they fail altogether in every respect.

Nevertheless, as we said earlier, just as almost everything that is properly predicated of the nature of created things is also said metaphorically of the Creator of things, for the sake of signification, [Col. 0463C] so too the meanings of the categories, which are properly discerned in created things, may not absurdly be applied to the cause of all—not so that they properly signify what it is, but so that, by transference, they may suggest what we who investigate it ought in some fashion to think about it with probability.

**DISC.** I clearly perceive that the categories cannot properly be predicated of the ineffable nature in any way. For if any category were properly predicated of God, it would necessarily follow that God was a genus. But God is neither a genus, nor a species, nor an accident. Therefore no category can properly signify God.

**MAG.** You see correctly. I do not think that we wished to labor over the foregoing arguments concerning the two parts of theology in vain. For we could not so easily, and almost without any effort, have arrived at this [Col. 0463D] discussion of the categories—namely, that they cannot properly be predicated of God—unless we had first thoroughly established that the primordial causes preordained by the one cause of all, namely essence, goodness, power, truth, wisdom, and the rest of this kind, signify God [Col. 0464A] only metaphorically. For if the most sublime created causes of all the natures ordered after that cause, visible only to the eyes of a pure mind, are surpassed in excellence of essence by the one ineffable cause, so that that cause cannot in any way be properly signified by their names, what must be said of the ten categories mentioned above, which are discerned not only in intelligible things but also in sensible things? Is it credible that they are truly and properly predicated of the divine and ineffable nature?

**DISC.** I think that this is incredible. It is therefore not οὐσία—that is, essence—because it is more than οὐσία; and yet it is called οὐσία because it is the creator of all οὐσίαι, that is, of all essences. It is not quantity, because it is more than quantity. Every quantity is extended in three dimensions: length, [Col. 0464B] breadth, and height. These three dimensions are in turn extended according to the number six. For length extends upward and downward; breadth to the right and to the left; height forward and backward. But God is without every dimension. He is therefore without quantity.

Again, quantity consists either in the number of parts naturally joined together, as in a line or time, or in naturally separated parts, such as numbers, whether bodily or intelligible. The divine substance is composed neither of continuous parts nor distinguished by divisible parts. It is therefore not quantity.

Yet quantity is not inappropriately attributed to it in two ways: either because quantity is often taken to mean greatness of power, or because it is the principle and cause of every quantity. The same must be understood concerning quality. [Col. 0464C] God is no quality, and no quality happens to him; he participates in none. Nevertheless, quality is very often predicated of him, either because he is the creator of every quality, or because quality is most frequently used to signify powers. Goodness, justice, and the other virtues are called qualities; but God is power, and more than power.

16. The account of relation, however, is not so openly evident as the definitions of the other categories appear to be. For this seems to be the only category that is properly predicated of God. Therefore I see that it must be investigated with the greatest diligence whether, in the supreme and holy Trinity of three greatest substances, the Father is properly said to be related to the Son, and likewise the Son to the Father, and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0464D] to the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of both—for the holy father Gregory the Theologian unequivocally asserts that these names express relations —or whether this category, called relation or relative disposition (*habitudo*), like the other categories, is also to be understood and believed to be predicated metaphorically of God.[Col. 0465A] 

**MAG.** You proceed reasonably, I think, in investigating the mystery of truth. For no category except this one seems to be properly predicated of God. But whether this is so or not must be investigated with the utmost piety and caution. For if it is properly said of God, almost all our preceding reasoning will be overturned. We stated universally that nothing can properly be said or understood of God. Moreover, the category of relation would not be counted among the ten categories if it were pronounced properly of God. If this were established, the number of categories would be concluded not by ten but by nine.

It remains, therefore, for us to understand that this category also, like the others, is predicated of God by transference. True reasoning invites and compels us to this, lest the things already stated begin to waver. [Col. 0465B] For what of it? Does it oppose true reasoning if we say that the Father and the Son are names of that relation which is called “to something,” and are more than relation? We must not believe that the same relation exists in the most exalted substances of the divine essence and in those things that were created by it after it. For, unless I am mistaken, just as it ineffably surpasses every essence, wisdom, and power, so it also surpasses every relation.

Who could believe that the relation between the Father and his Word is such as can be conceived between Abraham and Isaac? Here, a carnal relation arising from the division of nature after the sin of the first man is sought in multiplication through generation; there, the ineffable conjunction of an unbegotten [Col. 0465C] and begotten substance with itself is believed and, insofar as possible, recognized by a ray of divine light. Here, what is sought did not proceed from nature, as we said, but from a defect; there, what is conceived is known to proceed from the ineffable fecundity of divine goodness.

But let us pass on to the remaining categories.

**DISC.** Six remain, unless I am mistaken. The first is κεῖσθαι, that is, “to lie,” which others call position. Position is understood in the placement of some creature, whether visible or invisible. For example, it is said of a body that it either lies or stands. Similarly, it is said of the mind that, if it is at rest, it lies; if it is fully awake, it stands. “Standing” is customarily applied to this category, whereas motion is referred to time. But since God neither stands nor lies, the aforesaid category cannot properly be predicated [Col. 0465D] of him in any way.

Yet because he is the cause of standing and lying—for in him all things stand, that is, subsist immutably according to their principles, and lie, that is, rest; for he is the end of all, beyond whom they desire nothing—position or lying can be predicated of him metaphorically. For if God truly and properly lies, sits, or stands, he is not without position. If he is not without position, he is local. [Col. 0466A] But he is not local. Therefore he is contained by no position.

17. **MAG.** I clearly understand what you mean. Consequently, I see that we must proceed to the category of habit. Because of its excessive breadth, this seems to be the most obscure of all the categories. For there is scarcely any category in which some habit cannot be found. Essences or substances, too, look toward one another according to a certain habit. We say, for example, in what proportion—that is, according to what habit—a rational and an irrational essence look toward one another. For the irrational would not be called irrational except by the habit of the absence of reason; and, likewise, it is called rational only by the habit of the presence of reason. Every proportion is a habit, although not every habit is a proportion. For proportion properly [Col. 0466B] cannot be found in fewer than two things, whereas habit is discerned even in individual things.

For example, the habit of a rational soul is virtue. Proportion is therefore a certain species of habit. But if you wish to see by example how a proportional habit is found in essence, choose an example from numbers. Numbers, I think, are understood essentially in all things; for the essence of all things subsists in numbers. You see, then, what sort of proportion exists between two and three.

**DISC.** I plainly see that it is sesquialter—three to two—and by this single example I can recognize various species of proportion among all other substantial numbers when compared with one another.

**MAG.** Attend, then, to what remains, and recognize that there are no species of quantity, [Col. 0466C] quality, relation, position, place, time, action, or passion in which some species of habit is not found.

**DISC.** I have often asked about such matters and have found this to be so. To use a few examples: in quantities, the large, the small, and the intermediate, compared with one another, possess many relations. Likewise, in the quantities of numbers, lines, times, and other similar things, you will clearly find relations of proportion.

18. The same is true in quality. For example, in colors, white and black, together with whatever color is intermediate, are joined to one another by a habit. White and black, which occupy the extreme positions among colors, look toward one another according to the habit of extremity. Color, however, looks toward its extremes—namely, white and black—according to the habit of [Col. 0466D] mediation.

In the category called πρός τι, that is, “to something,” it is also clearly apparent what sort of habit exists between father and son, son and father, friend and friend, double and single, and other things of this kind.

19. Concerning position, too, it is easy to see how standing and lying possess a certain relation to one another. For they correspond to one another in direct opposition.[Col. 0467A]  You will never conceive the idea of standing in isolation from the idea of lying; rather, they always arise together, although they do not appear together in some particular thing.

20. What should be said about place? When upper, lower, and intermediate regions are considered, do they lack relation? Not at all. For all these things do not arise from the nature of things but from a certain perspective of one who observes them by parts. There is no up or down in the universe, and therefore there are neither upper, nor lower, nor intermediate regions in the universe; the consideration of the whole excludes these, while the intention of considering its parts introduces them.

The same reasoning applies to greater and lesser. Nothing can be small or great within its own genus; yet, from the thought of those comparing different quantities, such things are discovered.[Col. 0467B]  Therefore the contemplation of places or parts produces habit in such matters. For no nature is greater or lesser than another nature, just as none is higher or lower, since there is one nature of all things, created by one God.

**DISC.** What about time? Does not relation clearly appear in times themselves when they are compared with one another? For example, the relation of the day to hours, of the hour to points, of the point to a moment, and of the moment to indivisible units. Similarly, if someone ascends through the higher measures of times, he will find the same. In all these things, the relation of the whole to its parts and of the parts to the whole is evident.

**MAG.** Certainly it is no different.

**DISC.** What of the various motions of acting and suffering? Does relation not shine forth everywhere? For loving and being loved [Col. 0467C] are relations of the lover and the beloved, since they look toward one another—whether they occur in one person, which the Greeks call αὐτοπάθεια, that is, when action and passion are observed in one and the same person, as in “I love myself”; or between two persons, which the Greeks call ἑτεροπάθεια, that is, when one person is the lover and another the beloved, as in “I love you.”

**MAG.** I judge these things to be true.

**DISC.** I therefore ask you why this category of habit, although it seems naturally to be present with the other categories, occupies a place in the tenfold number of categories by itself, as though supported by its own proper principles.

**MAG.** Is it perhaps because it is found in all things that it subsists in itself? For what belongs to all belongs properly to none, but is in all in such a way that it subsists in itself. The same [Col. 0467D] reasoning must also be examined in the category of essence. For what of it? Although there are ten categories, is one of them called essence or substance, while the other nine are accidents and subsist in subsistence? For they cannot subsist by themselves. Essence seems to be in all things, without which they cannot exist, and yet it holds its own place by itself. For what belongs to all belongs properly to none, but is common to all; and while subsisting in all, [Col. 0468A] it does not cease to exist by its own proper principle.

The same must be said of quantity. We ask: How great is the essence? How great the quality? How great the relation? How great the position? How great the habit? How large is the place? How small or extensive is the time? How great the action? How great the passion? Do you see how broadly quantity extends through the other categories? Yet it does not abandon its own proper state.

What of quality? Is it not also frequently predicated of all the other categories? We ask: What kind of οὐσία, what kind of magnitude, relation, position, habit, place, time, action, or passion? For we ask what qualities all these things possess; yet quality does not abandon the account of its own proper genus. What wonder, then, if the category of habit, while it is observed in all things, [Col. 0468B] is said to possess its own proper account?

**DISC.** There is no reason for wonder; true reasoning teaches that it cannot be otherwise.

**MAG.** Do you not therefore see that the divine essence participates in no habit, and yet that habit may not inappropriately be predicated of it, since it is the cause of habit? For if habit were properly predicated of it, it would belong not to itself but to another. Every habit, after all, is understood in some subject and is an accident of something. It is impious to believe this of God, to whom nothing is an accident, who is an accident of nothing, who is understood in nothing, and in whom nothing is understood.

**DISC.** I think enough has been said about this category.

21. **MAG.** What, then? Can we not briefly gather from what has been said what must be understood about the remaining categories? God is neither place nor time; [Col. 0468C] nevertheless, he is metaphorically called the place of all things and time, because he is the cause of all places and times. The definitions of all things subsist in him as in a kind of place; and from him, as from a kind of time, through him, as through a kind of time, and into him, as toward a certain end of times, the motions of all things both begin, proceed, and cease, while he himself neither moves through time nor is moved by another.

For what of it? If he were properly called place and time, would he not seem to be included, not outside all things through the excellence of his essence, but among the number of all that exists? Place and time are counted among all created things. For the whole world that now exists consists in these two, and cannot exist without them. Therefore the Greeks call them [Col. 0468D] ὧν ἄνευ τὸ πᾶν, that is, “without which the whole cannot exist.”

Everything that is in the world must move in time and be defined by place; place itself is defined, and time is moved. But God is neither moved nor defined. For the place by which all places are defined is the place of places. And because it is placed by none but places all things within itself, it is not place but more than place. For it is defined by none but defines all things. It is therefore the cause of all things.

In the same [Col. 0469A] way, the cause of times moves times, but itself is moved by no one and in no time. For it is more than time and more than motion. Therefore it is neither place nor time.

**DISC.** Thus what has been said appears even more clearly than light, so much so that it now seems sufficient to have said enough about the nature of the categories and their transference to the signification of the divine essence, in view of the other matters that necessarily belong to the present undertaking.

22. **MAG.** Of these ten genera, four are in a state of rest—that is, οὐσία, quantity, position, and place; six, however, are in motion: quality, relation, habit, time, action, and passion. I do not think this is hidden from you.

**DISC.** On the contrary, it is quite clear to me, and I shall ask no more about these things. But to what end is this?

**MAG.** So that you may clearly know that the ten genera [Col. 0469B] mentioned above are comprehended by two other, higher and more general genera—namely, motion and rest—which are in turn gathered into the most general genus, called by the Greeks τὸ πᾶν and customarily called by us “the universe.”

**DISC.** I am very pleased by this, on account of those who think that no genus more general than the ten aforesaid genera—which Aristotle both discovered and named—can be found in the nature of things.

**MAG.** Does this division of the categories into motion and rest therefore seem sound to you—four in rest and six in motion?

23. **DISC.** It is sound. But I am still not sufficiently clear about two of them: I mean habit and relation. These two categories seem to me to belong more to rest than to motion. For whatever has arrived at a perfected [Col. 0469C] habit remains immutably. If it is moved in some way, it is plainly no longer a habit. For virtue is truly a habit of the soul when it adheres to it immutably, so that it cannot be separated from it.

Therefore no true habit is found in bodies; for an armed or clothed person can be deprived of arms or clothing. In relation too, rest seems to prevail. For the relation of father to son, or of double to single, and conversely, is unmoving. A father is always the father of a son; likewise, a son is always the son of a father, and so forth.

**MAG.** Perhaps you would not have hesitated so greatly if you had looked more carefully at the matter: everything that is not naturally present all at once in a perfected creature, but proceeds by certain increments toward inseparable [Col. 0469D] and unchangeable perfection, must be in motion. Every habit, moreover, rises by a certain motion toward perfection in that which possesses the habit. Who would presume to become firm in that perfection in this life? Habit, therefore, is in motion.

As for relation, I wonder why you doubt, when you see that it cannot exist in one and the same thing; it is always seen in two things. Who would doubt that the desire of two things for one another [Col. 0470A] occurs through a certain motion?

There is also another principle that most clearly distinguishes the things in motion from those at rest. Without now saying more about that most general principle, which makes clear that all things created by God after God are in motion—for all things are moved from nonexistence into existence through generation, from non-being into being, by divine goodness calling all things into being out of nothing; and each of the things that exist is moved by a natural desire toward its own essence, genus, species, and number— we properly call those things “in a state of rest” which subsist by themselves and require no subject in order to exist. Those things, however, which exist in something else, because they cannot subsist by themselves, we not inappropriately judge to be in motion.

[Col. 0470B] Habit and relation, therefore, exist in some subject, in which they naturally desire always to be, because they cannot exist without it. They are therefore in motion.

24. **DISC.** What, then, shall we say about place, quantity, and position, which you placed among the things that are at rest? For no one doubts about οὐσία—that is, essence—that it requires nothing in order to subsist. The other things are believed to be supported by it. But place, quantity, and position are counted among the accidents of essence. Consequently, by desiring the subject in which they exist and without which they cannot exist, they are moved. If this is so, everything is in motion except οὐσία, which alone lacks motion—apart from that motion by which all things desire to exist, since it alone subsists by itself.

[Col. 0470C] **MAG.** Your inquiry is not entirely absurd, because you follow the common opinion. But if you look more carefully, you will find that place is contained by nothing, while it contains everything that is located in it. For if place is nothing other than the limit and definition of each finite nature, place certainly does not desire to be in something; rather, all things that are in it rightly desire it as their boundary and end, in which they are naturally contained and without which they seem to flow into infinity.

Place, therefore, is not in motion, since everything that is in it moves toward it, while it itself remains at rest. The same reasoning teaches us about quantity and position. Every participant in sensible or intelligible quantity or position desires to arrive at its own perfect quantity or position [Col. 0470D] and to rest in it. They therefore do not desire; rather, they are desired. They are not in motion. They are therefore at rest.

**DISC.** Should these three—quantity, position, and place—then be called accidents of οὐσία, or substances subsisting by themselves?

25. **MAG.** I see that this too deserves inquiry. For according to the opinion of the dialecticians, everything that exists is either a subject, or of a subject, or in a subject.

[Col. 0471A] Yet true and considered reasoning replies that “subject” and “of a subject” are one and the same and differ in nothing. For if, as they say, Cicero is a subject and a first substance, while “human being” is of a subject and a second substance, what difference is there according to nature, except that one is in number and the other in species—since species is nothing other than the unity of numbers, and number nothing other than the plurality of species?

If, then, the whole species is one and individual in numbers, and numbers are one individual in species, I do not see what difference there is according to nature between a subject and what is of a subject. The same must be understood concerning the accidents of the first substance.

For what is said to be “in a subject” is not one thing and what is simultaneously “in a subject” and “of a subject” another. To use discipline as an example, [Col. 0471B] it is one and the same in itself and in its species and numbers. Therefore an individual discipline, which the dialecticians call merely “in a subject,” is not one thing, and a general discipline, which they call both “in a subject” and “of a subject”—as being in a subject, namely a first substance, and being predicated of a subject, that is, of someone’s particular discipline—is another. Rather, it is one and the same in the whole and in the parts. Consequently, what remains is “subject” and “in a subject.”

But if you follow more sharply the traces of the holy Gregory the Theologian and of his most wise expositor Maximus, you will find that οὐσία, in all things that exist, is wholly incomprehensible not only to the senses but also to the intellect. Therefore it is understood to exist through what may be called its surrounding circumstances—namely, place, [Col. 0471C] quantity, and position; time is added to these. For essence is understood to be enclosed within these as within certain surrounding boundaries, so that the accidents do not seem to subsist in it, because they are external, nor can they exist without it, because it is their center, around which times revolve, while places, quantities, and positions are arranged on every side.

Some of the categories, therefore, are predicated around οὐσία; these are called περιοχαί, that is, “surrounding things,” because they are observed around it. Others are in οὐσία; these are called by the Greeks συμβάματα, that is, “accidents”: quality, relation, habit, action, and passion.

These are also understood outside οὐσία in other categories. For example, quality is in quantity, as color is in a body. Likewise, [Col. 0471D] quality is in οὐσία, as invisibility and incomprehensibility are in genera. Relation, too, is outside οὐσία: a father in relation to a son, and a son in relation to a father. For these do not arise from nature but from the accidental generation of corruptible bodies. A father is not the father of his son’s nature, nor is a son the son of his father’s nature. Father and son have one and the same nature; but no nature begets itself or is begotten by itself.

Relation is found within οὐσία when genus is related to species [Col. 0472A] and species to genus. Genus is the genus of a species, and species is the species of a genus.

Habit is also found both outside and inside οὐσία. Thus we speak of someone as armed or clothed according to the body. But the habit of οὐσία, genus, or species is the virtue itself, unmoving, through which genus, while it is divided through species, always remains one and individual in itself, and is whole in each individual species, while the individual species are one in it.

The same virtue is discerned in species, which, while being divided through numbers, preserves the inexhaustible power of its individual unity. All the numbers into which it appears to be divided infinitely are finite and one individual within it.

No one doubts about action and passion, since we see bodies, although they belong to quantity, both acting and suffering. The genera [Col. 0472B] and species of οὐσία also seem to act when they multiply themselves into different species and numbers.

But if someone, by the power of reason, according to that discipline called ἀναλυτική—that is, “analytic”—were to gather numbers into species, species into genera, and genera into οὐσία, they are said to suffer. This is not because he himself gathers them—for by nature they are gathered together just as they are divided—but because reason seems to gather them by its act. For when it divides the same things, it is similarly said to act, while those things are said to suffer.

26. **STUDENT.** Although these things may seem obscure, they do not elude my mind so completely that nothing clear and distinct shines forth from them. And since I see that nearly all the categories are linked together, so that they can scarcely be distinguished from one another by any definite reasoning—for, as I see it, all are inserted into all—I earnestly ask you to disclose the property in which each can be found. [Col. 0471–0472]

**TEACHER.** What do you think? Is substance (*οὐσία*) not universally and properly contained in the most general genera, in the more general genera, in the genera themselves and their species, and again in the most specific species, which are called atoms—that is, individuals?

**STUDENT.** I see nothing else in which substance could naturally inhere except in genera and species descending from the highest to the lowest, that is, from the most general to the most specific, namely, individuals; or, conversely, ascending from individuals toward the most general. For universal substance subsists in these as in its natural parts. [C reads *video esse*, “I see [it] to be,” rather than *esse video*, “I see [it] to be.”]

**TEACHER.** Proceed, then, to the other categories. Does the property of quantity appear to you to exist anywhere else except in the number of parts, in spaces, and in measurements—whether those parts are continuous, as are lines, times, and other things contained by continuous quantity, or separated, divided by definite natural boundaries, as are numbers and every multitude, in which discrete quantity evidently consists? [Col. 0472; A reads *spatiis*, “spaces,” rather than *spatiisque*.]

**STUDENT.** This too is perfectly evident.

**TEACHER.** And does what is called quality have any proper seat other than in figures and surfaces, whether in natural bodies or in geometrical ones—for example, plane, triangular, square, polygonal, and round figures, and also solid figures considered at the surface, such as cubic, conical, and spherical forms? For solid bodies, whether natural or geometrical, when considered inwardly, are assigned to quantity because of the three dimensions in which they exist—I mean length, breadth, and height. But when their surfaces are examined, they are joined to quality. Likewise, in incorporeal things, does quality not occupy the greatest place, since all disciplines and all virtues, whether rational or irrational, so long as they have not yet attained the mind’s immutable state, are referred to it? [Col. 0473; A omits *et*, “and,” before “height”; D omits “and height”; A reads *autem*, “however,” rather than *vero*, “but.”]

**STUDENT.** Proceed to what remains; I plainly see these things and affirm that they are so.

**TEACHER.** Does what the Greeks call *πρός τι* and we call “relative to something,” or relation, properly possess any other place in the nature of things than in the proportions of things or numbers, and in the inseparable reciprocal turnings of those things that refer to one another, so that what is called one is understood to receive its designation not from itself but from another, which is opposed to it? Examples of this steadfast friendship and inseparable bond are the multiple numbers joined to one another: doubles, triples, quadruples, and the rest of this kind without limit; likewise the fractional ratios, such as *sesquialter* (one-and-a-half), *sesquiterce* (one-and-third), *sesquiquarte* (one-and-fourth), and the rest of the same sort. [Col. 0473; A reads *atque*, “and,” rather than *inque*; A reads *sint*, “are,” rather than *sunt*, “are”; D omits *sesquiquarti*.]

In all these cases, not only do whole numbers, compared with one another, possess different proportions, but the parts of the individual numbers, joined to one another, are also inseparably bound together by the principles of proportion. You will find this not only in the terms of the numbers themselves, but also in the proportions of proportions, which mathematicians call proportionalities. [Col. 0473]

**STUDENT.** I am not unaware of that either. These matters are very well known to experts in the arts.

**TEACHER.** What should be said about position? Does it not possess its proper place in the natural orders of things, or in the positions of bodily or spiritual things produced by art? For when I say “first,” “second,” and “third,” and so on, whether with respect to wholes or parts, genera or species, do I not consider a certain position of each? Likewise, if I say “to the right,” “to the left,” “upward,” “downward,” “before,” or “behind,” what else do I indicate except a certain position, whether of the whole world in general or of its parts? For one who says of a body that it lies, sits, or stands indicates nothing other than that it rests downward, is raised upward, or hangs, as it were, in a certain balance between above and below. Likewise, if someone says such things about the soul, he appears to mean nothing other than that it still lies in the passions of sins, or in some way tries to abandon them, or is perfectly raised up into virtues. [Col. 0473–0474; A omits *aut*, “or,” and the second *versus*, “toward”; D reads *ponetur*, “will be placed,” rather than *conetur*, “tries.”]

**STUDENT.** This too does not seem especially difficult to understand. Continue with what remains.

**TEACHER.** Habit remains, as I think. It is most clearly seen in the possession of particular virtues or vices. For every discipline—that is, every rational or irrational movement of the soul—when it has reached a definite state, so that it cannot be moved from it in any way or by any circumstance, but always adheres to the soul, so that it seems to be one and the same thing with it, is called a habit. Accordingly, every perfect virtue that adheres inseparably to the soul is truly and properly called a habit.

Therefore, in bodies, in which nothing appears stable, habit is either scarcely or never properly found. For what is not always possessed, although it may seem to be possessed for a time, is improperly called a habit. [Col. 0473–0474; CDE read *adhaeret*, “adheres,” rather than *adhaereat*, “may adhere”; C omits *esse*, “to be”; A reads “it seems to the soul” rather than “it seems to be one and the same thing with it”; A reads “habit properly” in reversed order; C reads *nominabitur*, “will be called,” rather than *nominatur*, “is called”; A reads “there appears to be” rather than “nothing appears to be.”]

**STUDENT.** Continue to the rest; no one denies that this is plausible.

27. **TEACHER.** Place follows. As we said a little earlier, it is established in the definitions of things that can be defined. For place is nothing other than the boundary by which each thing is enclosed within definite limits. [Col. 0474; C reads “included” rather than “enclosed.”]

There are many kinds of places; for there are as many places as there are things that can be circumscribed, whether corporeal or incorporeal.

For example, a body is a certain composition of the qualities of the four elements, gathered together under one particular form. By this definition, by this general description, all bodies that consist of matter and form are enclosed. [Col. 0474; A reads “from matter” rather than “that consist of matter”; A has “with the qualities” rather than “of the qualities.”]

Likewise, a spirit is an incorporeal nature lacking both form in itself and matter. For every spirit, whether rational or intellectual, is for itself without form. But if it turns toward its cause—that is, toward the Word through whom all things were made—then it is formed. Thus the one form of all rational and intellectual spirits is the Word of God. But if it is an irrational spirit, it is likewise for itself without form; nevertheless, it is formed by the phantasms of sensible things. Again, the form of all irrational spirits is the phantasm of bodily things impressed upon their memory through bodily senses. [D omits the phrase concerning matter and form; A reads *materia*, “matter,” for *materie*, “matter.”]

Likewise, many places are found in the liberal disciplines. For there is no art that lacks its places, such as the dialectical places: from genus, from species, from the name, from antecedents, from consequents, from contraries, and others of this kind, about which it would now be lengthy to discourse. [Col. 0474; D omits “places.”]

For dialectical places extend so widely that wherever a dialectical mind discovers in the nature of things an argument that establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter, it describes that place as the place, or seat, of the argument. A reads *a*, “from,” rather than *in*, “in.” You will find the same in the other arts, which are enclosed within their places—that is, their proper definitions. [Col. 0474–0475; A reads *ceterisque*, “and the others,” rather than *ceterique*; D reads *dicere*, “to say,” rather than *disserere*, “to discuss.”]

Examples are these:

**GRAMMAR** is the discipline that guards and governs articulated speech. [Col. 0475; C and E read the singular *disciplina*, “discipline,” rather than the plural *disciplinarum*, “disciplines.”]

**RHETORIC** is the discipline that examines at length and with eloquence a defined case in relation to its person, subject matter, occasion, quality, place, time, and ability. [D reads “of the subject matter” and *ordinate*, “orderly,” rather than *ornate*, “ornately.”] More briefly, it may be defined thus: **Rhetoric is the skillful and copious discipline of the seven circumstances of a defined case.** [A adds: “This discipline may be briefly defined thus.”]

**DIALECTIC** is the careful and investigative discipline that examines the common rational conceptions of the mind.

**ARITHMETIC** is the firm and inviolate discipline of the mind submitting to the contemplation of numbers. [D omits “of the mind.”]

**GEOMETRY** is the discipline that considers, with the discerning insight of the mind, the spaces and surfaces of plane figures and solid figures.

**MUSIC** is the discipline that recognizes, by the light of reason, harmony in all things that are knowable, whether in motion or at rest, according to natural proportions. [D omits “that are”; CDE omit “whether in motion or at rest”; E has *dinoscens*, an orthographic variant of *dignoscens*.]

**ASTROLOGY** is the discipline that investigates the spaces, motions, and revolutions of the heavenly bodies at definite times.

These are the general places of the liberal arts. Within these boundaries are contained innumerable other places. [A adds: “There are seven *περιοχαί*, that is, circumstances: who, what, why, how, when, where, and with what means.” This addition is entirely absent from D and E.]

28. **STUDENT.** By these arguments I am compelled to admit that place exists only in the mind. For if every definition is in a discipline, and every discipline is in the mind, then necessarily every place, since it is a definition, will exist nowhere except in the mind. [Col. 0475; C adds in the margin: “There are seven *περιοχαί*, that is, circumstances: who, what, why, how, when, where, and with what means.”]

29. **TEACHER.** You are looking at it correctly.

**STUDENT.** What, then, should be said about those who say that the dwellings of human beings and other animals are places? Do they similarly regard this common air and the earth as places of all who dwell in them? They say that water is the place of fish, that the ether is the place of the planets, and they think that the celestial sphere is the place of the stars. [Col. 0475; C and E read *aera*, “air,” rather than *aerem*; CDE read *locos*, “places,” rather than A’s singular *locum*, “place.”]

**TEACHER.** Nothing else should be done except either to persuade them, if they are teachable and wish to be instructed, or to dismiss them entirely if they are contentious. [A reads *valuerint*, “have been able,” rather than *voluerint*, “have wished”; A omits “if they are contentious.”]

True reason mocks those who say such things. For if body is one thing and place another, it follows that place is not body. But air is the fourth part of this corporeal and visible world. Therefore it is not place.

For it is established that this visible world is composed of the four elements, as of four general parts, and is, as it were, a certain body compacted from its parts. From these universal parts the proper and most specific bodies of all animals, trees, and plants are formed by a marvelous and ineffable mixture; and at the time of dissolution they return again into those same parts. [Col. 0475–0476]

30. For just as this entire world that appears to the senses revolves in constant motion around its axis—I mean around the earth, around which the other three elements, namely water, air, and fire, revolve in an unceasing rotation—so, by an invisible motion and without any interruption, universal bodies, that is, the four elements, coming together in one another, form the proper bodies of individual things. [Col. 0475; A reads “the four, I mean, elements” rather than “the four elements”; D omits “of individual things.”]

Once dissolved, these return again from particularities to universals, while there always remains, immutably, as it were, a certain center: the proper and natural essence of individual things, which cannot be moved, increased, or diminished. [Col. 0475–0476; C reads *contra*, “oppositely,” rather than *centrum*, “center”; D and E read “a certain center.”]

For accidents are in motion, not essences. [D omits “are.”] Nor are the accidents themselves in motion, whether through increase or decrease; rather, their participation in essence undergoes such changes. Otherwise true reason does not permit the matter to stand. Every nature, whether of essences or of the accidents belonging to them, is immutable; but participation, as we have said, whether of essences by accidents or of accidents by essences, is always in motion. [A and D omit “in.”]

Participation can begin, increase, and diminish, until this world reaches the end of its stability in all things. After that, neither essence nor accident nor their participation in one another will suffer any motion. For all things will be one and the same and immobile, when everything is to return to its immutable principles. I think this return should be discussed elsewhere. [Col. 0476]

31. The reason why only the center of the world—that is, the earth—always remains at rest, while the other elements revolve around it in eternal motion, requires no small consideration. For we have learned the opinions on this question both of secular philosophers and of catholic Fathers. [Col. 0476; A and D read “we have recognized” rather than “we have learned.”]

Plato, the greatest of philosophers who have written about the world, asserts in his *Timaeus*, with many arguments, that this visible world is composed, like a great animal, of body and soul. The body of this animal is compacted from the four most familiar and general elements and from the various bodies composed of them; its soul, however, is the universal life that gives vitality and motion to all things that are in motion or at rest.

Hence the Poet:

> Heaven and earth and the watery plains,  
> The shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars,  
> a spirit within sustains.

[Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.724 ff.; Col. 0476]

But because the soul itself, as he says, is eternally moved toward its body—that is, toward the whole world—in order to give it life, govern it, and move it through the various conjunctions and dissolutions of its individual bodies according to different principles, it also remains in its own natural and immobile state. It therefore always moves and remains at rest; and consequently its body also—that is, the totality of visible things—partly remains in eternal stability, as does the earth; partly moves with eternal speed, as does the ethereal expanse; partly neither remains at rest nor moves swiftly, as does water; and partly moves swiftly, though not most swiftly, as does air. [Col. 0477; A omits “always”; C and E omit the second “moves”; CE read “as is the ethereal expanse” rather than “as does the ethereal expanse”; D reverses the order to “the supreme reasoning of the philosopher.”]

In my judgment, this reasoning of the supreme philosopher should not be wholly rejected, for it appears acute and natural. But since Gregory of Nyssa, the great bishop, discusses this same cause with the utmost subtlety in his *Discourse on the Image*, I am more inclined to follow his opinion. [Col. 0477]

He says that the Creator of the universe established this visible world between two mutually opposed extremes—namely, heaviness and lightness, which are entirely contrary to one another. Therefore, because the earth has been established in heaviness, it always remains immobile. For heaviness does not know how to move, and the earth has been placed at the center of the world; it occupies both the outermost and the central limit.

The ethereal spaces, however, revolve perpetually around the center with ineffable speed, because they are established in the nature of lightness, which does not know how to remain at rest, and they occupy the outer limit of the visible world.

The two elements established between these extremes—namely, water and air—move continually with proportional moderation between heaviness and lightness, so that each follows more closely the extreme limit nearest to it than the one farther away. Water moves more slowly than air because it clings to the heaviness of the earth; air, however, is driven more swiftly than water because it is joined to ethereal lightness. [Col. 0477]

Although the extreme parts of the world appear to differ from one another because of their different qualities, they do not nevertheless disagree in every respect. For although the ethereal spaces always revolve with the greatest speed, the chorus of the stars nevertheless keeps its immutable station, so that, while it revolves with the ether, it does not abandon its natural place, resembling the stability of the earth. [Col. 0477; C omits the second *ut*, “so that.”]

The earth, on the contrary, although it is eternally at rest, nevertheless has everything that arises from it perpetually in motion, in imitation of ethereal lightness: coming into being through generation, increasing in the number of places and times, then again decreasing and reaching the dissolution of form and matter. [Col. 0477]

32. **STUDENT.** It seems to me that you have moved somewhat too far from the principal question to an incidental one. For although our intention was to discuss place, you have left place and turned to a treatment of the world; and I still do not know toward what these things are directed. [Col. 0477–0478; A reads “an emerging question” rather than “an incidental one,” and *tendunt*, “they tend,” rather than *tendant*, “they are directed.”]

33. **TEACHER.** Nowhere else than toward separating, by careful reasoning, the nature of bodies from the nature of places. Their confusion is either the chief cause or the sole cause of the error of many, indeed almost all, who think that this visible world and its universal and particular parts are places. If they distinguished the genera of all things with sound reasoning, sharply and without error, they would in no way include body and place within one and the same genus.

No one who rightly considers and distinguishes the natures of things mixes places and bodies in one genus; rather, he separates them by rational discrimination. Bodies are contained in the category of quantity. But the category of quantity is naturally very far removed from the category of place. Body, therefore, is not place, because locality is not quantity.

For, as we said above, quantity is nothing other than the definite measurement of parts that are separated either solely by reason or by natural difference, and the rational progression toward definite limits of things extended through natural spaces—namely, length, breadth, and height. Place, however, is nothing other than the boundary and enclosure of things terminated by a definite limit.

If this visible world is a body, it necessarily follows that its parts also are bodies. But if they are bodies, they belong to the genus of quantity, not of locality. They are bodies, therefore. They are not places. [Col. 0477–0478; C and E have *subiugantur*, “are subjected”; A has *subiunguntur*, “are joined”; D has *subiungantur*, “may be subjected.” A reads *ergo*, “therefore,” rather than the fuller connective leading to “they are not places.”]

Do you see, then, how by the arguments stated it has been established that this world, together with its parts, is not a place but is contained in a place—that is, within the definite boundary of its definition? For the thing that contains is one thing, and the thing contained is another. Bodies are contained in their own places. Body, therefore, is one thing and place another, just as the quantity of parts is one thing and their definition another.

These four familiar elements, then, are not places but are circumscribed within a place, because they are the principal parts by which the universality of the sensible world is completed. [Col. 0478; D reads “visible” rather than “sensible”; E omits “sensible.”]

**STUDENT.** What you have said about the difference between places and bodies appears plausible. But I would like you to repeat the same things more subtly. For I do not see why this world should not be a place, since many things are located in it.

**TEACHER.** You are not unaware, I think, that none of the categories mentioned above—which Aristotle defined as ten—when considered by itself, that is, in the contemplation of reason according to its own nature, is subject to bodily senses. Substance (*οὐσία*) is incorporeal and lies beneath no bodily sense; the other nine categories operate around or within it. But if substance is incorporeal, does it appear otherwise to you than that everything that adheres to it or subsists in it, and cannot exist without it, is likewise incorporeal? [Col. 0478; A reads “is incorporeal” and omits “within it.”]

34. All the categories, therefore, are incorporeal when understood in themselves. Yet some of them, by a marvelous kind of union with one another, as Gregory says, produce visible matter; others, however, appear nowhere and remain always incorporeal. [Col. 0478–0479]

Substance, relation, place, time, acting, and being acted upon are not touched by any bodily sense. Quantity and quality, however, as well as position and habit, when they come together and join matter, as we said above, are ordinarily perceived by bodily sense. [A reads “as we said earlier.”]

If place, then, is numbered among those things that in no way submit to bodily senses, while bodies, if they are not perceived by the senses, are not bodies—does it not follow that place is not body? By “bodies” I now mean those formed from the union of the four elements of the world.

For the four elements of the world, although they are bodies distinct in themselves, surpass every mortal sense by their ineffable natural subtlety and purity. Place, therefore, is one thing and body another. Does it appear otherwise to you?

**STUDENT.** Not at all. This final conclusion of our reasoning in no way permits us to grant that place and body belong to one genus. But the point you introduced—that visible matter is nothing other than the conjunction of certain accidents added to form—for whatever appears appears through form—troubles me considerably. [Col. 0479; A reads “a little” rather than “considerably.”]

**TEACHER.** Let it not trouble you. For, as I said, the great Gregory of Nyssa, in his *Discourse on the Image*, demonstrates by definite arguments that this is so, saying that matter is nothing other than a certain composition of accidents proceeding from invisible causes into visible matter.

And rightly so. For if this corporeal and dissoluble matter contained some simple, immutable essence that was in no way dissoluble, it could not be dissolved by any reasoning or action. But it is dissolved. Therefore nothing insoluble underlies it.

For genera, species, and atoms always exist and persist because there is in them some one individual that cannot be dissolved or destroyed. Accidents themselves likewise remain immutable in their own nature because a certain individual underlies all of them, in which all naturally subsist as one. [A reads “something” rather than “some one individual.”]

35. **STUDENT.** Nothing could be truer, I think. Therefore I await your conclusion of the present inquiry. [Col. 0479; A reads “so that” rather than “therefore.”]

**TEACHER.** What remains except to say, for example, that when we see our bodies established upon this earth or surrounded by this air, they are nothing other than bodies in bodies? By the same reasoning, fish in the waves, planets in the ether, stars in the firmament, and bodies in bodies are all smaller things in larger, denser things in subtler, light things in lighter, and pure things in purer. [Col. 0479; D reads “smaller things in smaller” rather than “smaller things in larger.”]

For true reason teaches that all these sensible things, as well as intelligible things, are contained in their own proper places—that is, in their natural definitions. [Col. 0479–0480]

36. **STUDENT.** I do not resist this conclusion, since I see that it is true. But I am greatly astonished that it has become customary in ordinary human usage to say that all these bodies—whether heavenly, ethereal, aquatic, or terrestrial—are places of the smaller bodies contained within them, just as common usage considers substance (*οὐσία*) to be nothing other than this visible and tangible body. Therefore I earnestly ask you not to find it troublesome to discuss this present difficulty at greater length.

**TEACHER.** What, then? Surely it was settled long ago between us that everything known either by bodily sense, reason, or intellect can rightly be predicated of God, the Creator of all things, in a certain manner of transference, although the pure contemplation of truth establishes that he is none of the things predicated of him. [Col. 0479–0480; A reads “of God the Creator of all things, rightly” rather than “rightly of God the Creator of all things.”]

**STUDENT.** Reason teaches that this is unshakably true and clearer than light.

37. **TEACHER.** If, then, everything that exists is predicated of God—not properly, but in a certain manner of transference, because everything is from him—what is surprising if all things that are in a place, since they appear to be surrounded on every side by larger things, can be called places, although none of them is properly a place, but is contained in a place according to its own proper nature? We see that, through metonymy—that is, transnomination—things that are contained are named from those that contain them. Yet they are not contained by them in such a way that they could not subsist within their own natural boundaries without them. [Col. 0479–0480; A reads *locus*, “place,” rather than *loca*, “places”; C reads *continentur*, “are contained,” rather than *continetur*, “is contained”; A reverses “properly” and “according to its nature.”]

For mortal usage commonly calls a house, a wife, or a household by the same name, although these are naturally distinct. A house does not substantially grant existence to a wife or household; rather, it is the place of their nature. But because they possess their dwelling in it, they are customarily named from it. Likewise, things that contain are named from things contained.

For example, air contains light; therefore illuminated air is called “light.” [Col. 0479; D omits “air.”] The eye is called sight, or vision, although according to the property of nature it is neither sight nor vision. For who does not know that the eye is a certain bodily part of the head, moist, through which sight is poured outward like rays from the *meninx*, that is, the little membrane of the brain? [A reads *visus fusus*, “sight poured out,” rather than *visus*, “sight.”]

The *meninx*, in turn, receives the nature of light from the heart, which is the seat of fire. [D reads “received.”] Sight is the emission of natural light that possesses sensation in the act of seeing and leaps outward in rays. When it is spread around the colors and forms of external sensible bodies, it is conformed with marvelous speed to those colored visible forms.

Vision is a certain image of bodily forms and colors conformed in the rays of the eyes; without any intervening delay it is received by the sense and impressed upon the sentient memory. [Col. 0480–0481]

The same reasoning applies to the sense of hearing. For the part of the head properly called the ear is also named from hearing, because it is the instrument of hearing. [A omits “and”; A also omits “of the head.”] And there are a thousand examples of this kind.

38. **STUDENT.** I understand this perfectly.

**TEACHER.** Do you see, then, by what custom and from the necessity of signifying things, humanity—lacking a true discrimination of realities—has devised these transferred names for things? It calls the lowest and middle part of the visible world, namely the earth, the place of walking animals. It similarly calls the water, which is joined to it as an inseparable part and is close to it in the quality of coldness, the place of swimming creatures. [Col. 0481; A reads “Who,” rather than “Which”; A reverses “the place of swimming creatures.”]

Then, following the natural order, it regards the third part of the world as the place of the winged kind. In the same way, it has become accustomed to call the vast spaces of the ether, in which heavenly bodies revolve in circles, the places of celestial bodies. [Col. 0481–0482]

When the true reason that discriminates natures is consulted, all these things are seen not as places but as parts of the world circumscribed within their own places.

### Restored textual apparatus

#### § 26

- CDE read *concatenatas* (“linked together”), while A has *catenatas* (“chained”). A omits *ut* (“as/that”) in the relation passage and *veluti* (“as if”). At the close of the discussion of habit A reads the corrupt *verisimile esse nullus esse denegat* (“no one denies [it] to be probable,” with duplicated *esse*); the transmitted form is retained without smoothing.

#### § 27

- D reads genitive *materiae* (“of matter”) for nominative *materia* (“matter”) and omits the phrase pairing form and matter. A reads *a* (“from/by”) for *in* (“in”). In the clause *ceterique … disserere* (“and the others … to discuss”), A and D transmit their respective altered word order/forms; D again has *materiae* and reads *ordinate* (“in an ordered way”) in the definition of rhetoric.
- The account of the seven *περιοχαί* (“circumstances”) is supplied both as an addition in A and as a marginal note in C; both witness locations are retained.

#### §§ 29–31

- A reads *aliud est locus et aliud corpus* (“place is one thing and body another”); AD read *valuerint* (“will have been able”), and A omits *sint* (“may be”).
- At *Etenim* (“for indeed”), and in the clauses on invisible motion and *singularum rerum* (“of individual things”), the witness-specific readings are retained. The opposed readings *centrum* (“center”) and *contra* (“against/opposite”) are not conflated; nor are the differing formulations concerning accidents.
- In §31 A reads *quia* (“because”) for *quae* (“which”). The witnesses differ in the clause “is eternally moved”: A omits *semper* (“always”), while C and E omit *movetur* (“is moved”). C/E transpose the words concerning the ethereal expanse; D transposes “the supreme philosopher.” A alters “this same cause” and reads *constituta sunt* (“were established”); C reads *gravitate* (“by weight”), and A *numero* (“by/in number”).

#### §§ 32–34

- A reads *fuerit* (“will have been”), *per ipsam* (“through it itself”), *est incorporea* (“is incorporeal”), and *non* (“not”); D omits *in qua* (“in which”).
- The witnesses retain distinct readings at *Omnes igitur* (“all, therefore”), *prius diximus* (“we said before”), *percipiantur* (“may be perceived”), *enim* (“for”), and “four elements.” At *Aliud est igitur* (“therefore one thing is…”), the alternate form and word order are preserved.
- In the Student’s objection and Gregory’s account of matter, the witness readings are retained as printed, including their fragmentary syntax; no explanatory subject or connective has been invented.

#### §§ 35–38

- A reads *ut* (“as/that”) for *ideo* (“therefore”) and *exspecto* (“I await”); D reads *minoribus* (“lesser things”). A adds *ergo* (“therefore”).
- In the predication-of-God clause the witness forms remain distinct. A reads *possidentur* (“are possessed”), *Ideo* (“therefore”), and the difficult *visus fusus* (“sight poured out,” as transmitted); D reads *recepit* (“received”). A omits *et* (“and”).
- The final account of earth, water, and the winged kind retains the witnesses’ respective forms and scopes; its grammatical differences are glossed locally rather than normalized into a single reading.


### Complete source-ordered witness register

- **N001** — lemma context *e discretum ei reluceat. Et quoniam video, omnes fere categorias inter se invicem concatenatas*; source: `[Col. 0471] Sic CDE; A catenatas.`. The witnesses introduced by “Sic” support the printed lemma; the following exact form records the other witness’s spelling, inflection, number, or word order, with no further semantic expansion unless stated above.
