### 39 [Cols. 0481A–0482D]

But in order that you may clearly understand that these aforesaid general parts of the world, and the parts of those parts, extending down to the most minute divisions, are not places but are circumscribed by places, the nature of place itself must be considered somewhat more carefully, if you please.

**STUDENT.** I certainly do; and I am eagerly intent on hearing this.

**TEACHER.** Receive, then, the following as the beginning of this line of reasoning [Note: A has “therefore” instead of “then”]. We have taken it from the holy Fathers, namely Gregory the Theologian and Maximus, the distinguished expositor of his Sermons. Everything whatsoever exists apart from God, who alone properly subsists above being itself, is understood to be in a place. Together with that place, time is always and altogether understood [Note: A reads “because” instead of “always”]. For it is impossible to understand place with time removed [Note: CE read “it is impossible”; D reads “it is not possible,” omitting “is”], just as time cannot be defined without the understanding of place together with it. For these are inseparably included among the things that exist together and always; and without them no essence that has received being through generation can in any way subsist or be known.

Thus the essence of everything that exists is local and temporal; and therefore it is understood in no way except in place and time, and under place and under time. For the totality of all things is not under itself and within itself. To assert this is irrational and impossible—namely, that the totality itself is above its own totality [Note: A reads “above itself”], while it has a circumscription that, after all things, circumscribes everything beneath itself and possesses within itself the most causative power [Note: D omits “to be”].

Therefore the outermost boundary is the place of the universe, just as some define place by saying: place is the circuit itself outside the universe, or the position itself situated outside the universe, or the containing boundary in which the contained is contained.

All things are also shown to be under time [Note: A reads “to be under time” rather than “under time”], because everything that exists after God does not possess being simply, but in some particular way, and therefore is not without a beginning. For everything that receives a definition of some kind of essence, although it exists, did not exist. Thus “to exist in some way” means to exist locally, and “to have begun to exist in some way” means to exist temporally. Therefore everything that exists apart from God, since it subsists in some way and began to subsist through generation, is necessarily enclosed by place and time.

Hence, when we say that God exists, we do not say that he exists in some particular way [Note: D omits “to exist”]. Accordingly, we say that he both is and was, simply, infinitely, and absolutely. For the divine is incomprehensible to every reason and intellect; and therefore, when we declare his being, we do not say that he himself is being. For being is from him [Note: D omits “being”], but he is not being itself. He is above being itself in some way, above being, and universally above whatever is spoken and understood.

But if things that exist possess being in some way, though not universally—that is, if they exist under place through the position and boundary of the principles in which they naturally are, and under time altogether through a beginning—will they not be shown to be so? [Note: CE read “will not be shown”; D reads “are shown.”] Do you therefore see that place and time are understood before all things that exist? For the number of places and times, as Saint Augustine says in the sixth book of *On Music*, precedes all things that are in them.

Indeed, the mode—that is, the measure—of all created things naturally precedes their condition in reason. This mode and measure is called, and is, the place of each thing. Likewise, the beginning of birth and the commencement of whatever is born and begins are seen to precede it in reason. Therefore everything that was not and now is began to exist from a beginning of time [Note: CE read “began to exist”; A and D read “received existence” or “existence was received”].

God alone is infinite; all else is bounded by where and when—that is, by place and time—not because place and time are not among the things created by God, but because place and time precede everything in the universe, not through intervals of time but solely in the rational order of their creation. For what contains is necessarily understood before what is contained, just as a cause precedes its effect, fire its burning, the voice the word, and other similar things.

Accordingly, we do not judge that any other blessedness has been promised to those who are worthy, nor that the end of this world will be anything other than that all who are to receive the glory of *theosis*, that is, deification, should rise beyond places and times. For those who are confined by place and time are finite. Eternal blessedness, however, is infinite. Therefore those who share in eternal and infinite blessedness will be circumscribed neither by place nor by time.

### 40 [Cols. 0483A–0483C]

For what is written only of Melchizedek—that he lacked father and mother, had no beginning of days through generation into essence, and had no end of time—I believe must be understood universally of all who will share in future blessedness. For all who are to return to their eternal principles—which have neither a beginning of time through generation in place or time, nor an end through dissolution, and are circumscribed by no local position—will certainly be without every local and temporal limit, so that those principles alone may be in them, and nothing else [Note: ACDE read “only”].

For the causes of all things, since they lack every circumscription and are infinite, will cleave to the Infinite forever. For God alone will appear in them when they transcend the limits of their nature—not so that nature will perish in them, but so that he alone will appear in them who alone truly is. And this is what it means to transcend nature: for nature not to appear; just as, as we have often said, air filled with light does not appear, because light alone reigns.

Therefore what is understood concerning the general place and general time of universal creation must necessarily be understood, from the highest to the lowest, concerning the particular and proper places and times of its parts [Note: A reads “therefore” instead of “therefore what”]. The general place and general time precede, according to understanding, everything that is in them. Therefore the knowledge of particular and proper places and times precedes what is specifically and properly understood in them [Note: C reads “proper”].

Accordingly, it follows that place is nothing other than the natural definition, mode, and position of each creature, whether general or particular [Note: A omits “mode”], just as time is nothing other than the motions of things through generation, beginning from non-being into being [Note: A reads “the beginning”; C omits “motions”; C reads “of motion”], and the definite measures of the motion of mutable things, until the stable end arrives in which all things will stand immutably.

**STUDENT.** The purpose of this reasoning, as I think, is becoming somewhat clearer. For, insofar as I am able to understand it, it seeks nothing else than to persuade us that place is nothing other than the natural definition of each creature, within which it is wholly contained and beyond which it cannot extend in any way. Accordingly, whether one calls it place, boundary, limit, definition, or circumscription, it is understood to signify one and the same thing: namely, the circuit of a finite nature.

### 41 [Cols. 0483D–0484B]

Although many kinds of definitions may seem to some people to exist, only that definition which the Greeks customarily call *ousiōdēs* (οὐσιώδης), but which we call *essential*, should truly be called a definition. For the others are either enumerations of the intelligible parts of essence (οὐσία), or certain arguments drawn externally through accidents, or species of propositions of whatever kind [Note: A reads “of whatever kind” in another form].

The *ousiōdēs* definition alone admits for definition only what completes and perfects the perfection of the nature that it defines. For definition, as Augustine says, contains neither more nor less than what has been undertaken for explanation [Note: A omits “that”]. Otherwise it is altogether defective.

**TEACHER.** You clearly perceive that the preceding reasoning seeks to persuade us of nothing other than what you have said [Note: D reads “something else”].

**STUDENT.** Yet I am surprised, and do not clearly understand, how the definition of any essence can be said to exist not within that essence but outside it—that is, how it can be said to be neither its whole nor a part of it [Note: A omits “to exist”].

**TEACHER.** Pay close attention, then, so that you may understand this clearly as well [Note: A reads “therefore”].

**STUDENT.** As far as the inner light permits.

**TEACHER.** Tell me, please: since there are two genera of all things—for everything that is said to exist is either visible, and is or can be perceived by bodily senses, or invisible, and is or can be considered by the gaze of the intellect, either in itself or through something adhering to it—in which of these aforementioned genera do you judge definitions to exist?

### 42 [Cols. 0484B–0484D]

**STUDENT.** That is absurd. For who among the truly wise would rightly place a place, boundary, definition, or any kind of circumscription by which each substance is enclosed among things subject to bodily senses, when he sees that the boundaries of a line, triangle, or any plane or solid figure are incorporeal?

The point from which a line begins and at which it ends is neither the line nor a part of it, but the limit of the line. Accordingly, its place is not perceived by sense but is conceived by reason alone. For a sensible point is a part of the line, but is not its beginning or end [Note: A reads “the line exists”].

Similarly, the line itself, when considered by reason, is incorporeal, and is the beginning of a surface. Likewise, the surface is incorporeal and is the end of the line, but the beginning of solidity [Note: ACDE read “but it is the beginning”]. Solidity too is incorporeal and is the end of the whole perfection.

Whatever bodily sense has touched in these things—whether point, line, surface, or visible solidity—is certainly a figure of incorporeal things, not their true substance itself, which is incorporeal. Likewise, in the case of natural bodies, whether they are perceptible through the commixture of the elements from which they subsist, or whether through their subtlety they escape mortal sight, the boundaries of nature are discerned by intellect alone.

For form, which contains all the matter of bodies [Note: A reads “bodily matter”], is incorporeal. Matter itself also, if one examines it attentively, is composed of incorporeal qualities [Note: ACDE read “itself”; A reads “for”].

**TEACHER.** Do you therefore judge that the definitions which we have called the places of circumscribed things are contained in the genus of invisible things? [Note: D reads “visible things.”]

**STUDENT.** I do indeed judge so, and I see nothing more certain.

### 43 [Cols. 0485A–0486A]

**TEACHER.** You judge correctly. But since the genus of invisible things can again be divided into many species—for some invisible things understand and are understood; some are understood but do not understand; and some neither understand nor are understood [Note: A has the forms “which understand and are understood” and “which”]—in which species do you think their definitions should be counted?

**STUDENT.** Certainly in that which understands and is understood. For the activity of definition is the activity of a reasoning and understanding nature.

**TEACHER.** It seems that it cannot be otherwise. For no nature that does not understand itself as existing can define either what is equal to it or what is inferior to it. For how can it know what is above it, when it cannot surpass its knowledge? [Note: BCDE read “take hold of it” instead of “surpass it.”]

**STUDENT.** Therefore expertise in definition belongs only to intellectual nature, which is constituted in human beings and angels. But whether an angel or a human being can define himself, whether a human being can define an angel, or an angel a human being, is no small question. I wish to know what you think about it.

**TEACHER.** It seems to me that they cannot define either themselves or one another [Note: D reads “can define”]. For if a human being defines himself or an angel, he is greater than himself and than the angel. For what defines is greater than what is defined [Note: AD read “for greater is what defines”]. The same reasoning applies to an angel. I therefore judge that they can be defined only by the one who created them in his own image.

**STUDENT.** It seems to me that this reasoning leads to the conclusion that no natures can be defined by a rational mind except those inferior to it, whether they are visible or invisible.

**TEACHER.** Whoever says this does not err from the truth [Note: A reads “from the truth” in another form]. Accordingly, wherever there are definitions of things that are defined, there too are certainly the places of things that are circumscribed. For by the preceding reasoning it has been established that place is definition, and definition is place.

**STUDENT.** It has indeed been established.

**TEACHER.** Now, the definitions of bodies and of things lacking reason exist nowhere except in the rational soul. In it, therefore, are also the places of all things that are comprehended locally [Note: A reads “the places of all things”]. But if the rational soul is incorporeal—a point about which no wise person doubts—then whatever is understood in it is necessarily manifestly incorporeal. Place is understood in the mind, as was established earlier [Note: D omits “is.”] Therefore it is incorporeal [Note: A reads “therefore”].

**STUDENT.** I see that this too has been rightly established. For whether the angelic nature contains within itself the definitions of things inferior to it, as Augustine seems to hold—for angels are believed to administer things inferior to themselves—or whether it always directs itself toward things superior to it, that is, toward the eternal causes of things, this does not oppose the reasoning.

For, as I see it, it is not contrary to truth if someone judges that the human mind, while still weighed down by earthly fantasies, can, if it lives purely, comprehend the created causes of natures inferior to itself, while the angelic mind desires the eternal causes of all things and, moved by love, continually draws human nature toward them.

**TEACHER.** You see correctly. Do you therefore see that place is nothing other than the action of one who understands and comprehends, by the power of understanding, those things—whether sensible or grasped by intellect—that he is able to comprehend?

Now, if this is so, then what is defined is one thing, and its definition another [Note: A reads “therefore”].

**STUDENT.** I see that they are different. But an intellect that understands itself, since it defines itself, seems to be its own place.

**TEACHER.** No one would say this absurdly, if any intellect after God—who is called the intellect of all things—can understand itself [Note: A reads “can” instead of “after God”]. But if every intellect except God is circumscribed not by itself but by what is superior to it, then no intellect will be its own place; rather, it will be placed within what is superior to it. And did we not agree a little earlier that this is the case? [Note: A reads “did we not agree among ourselves?”]

**STUDENT.** I think this must be discussed more fully elsewhere.

### 44 [Cols. 0486B–0486D]

But now I wish to know whether the nature of the defining mind—that is, of everything understood by it and comprehended as the place of cognition—is one thing, and the place itself, or the definition of what is placed or defined, another.

**TEACHER.** I too see that this is not unworthy of investigation. For many doubt about it. But since we see that the liberal arts established in the soul are one thing, and the soul itself another—which is, as it were, a subject of the arts, while the arts seem to be inseparable and natural accidents of the soul [Note: A omits “as it were” and D omits “a certain”—“a certain subject”]—what prevents us from placing the discipline of definition among the arts, joining it to dialectic, whose property is to divide, join, and distinguish the natures of all things that can be understood, and to distribute proper places to each?

For this reason it is customarily called by the wise the true contemplation of things. For since in every rational and intellectual nature three things are always considered as remaining inseparably and incorruptibly [Note: E reads “remaining inseparably”; A reads “incorruptibly,” C “incorruptibly,” and D “incorporally”], namely essence (οὐσία), power (δύναμις), and operation (ἐνέργεια)—that is, essence, power, and operation—for, as Saint Dionysius testifies [Note: D reverses the order: “as Saint Dionysius testifies”], these cling inseparably to one another, and, as it were, exist, and can neither increase nor diminish, since they are immortal and immutable—

does it not seem plausible to you, and consistent with sound reason, that all the liberal disciplines should be considered in that part which is called the soul’s *energeia* (ἐνέργεια), that is, its operation?

For philosophers have truthfully sought and discovered that the arts are eternal and always adhere immutably to the soul, so that they do not seem to be, as it were, certain accidents of it, but natural powers and activities that in no way depart from it or are able to depart from it, nor come from elsewhere, but are naturally implanted in it. Thus it is uncertain whether they themselves grant eternity to the soul because they are eternal [Note: CDE read “because they are eternal”], and always adhere to it [Note: ACDE agree], so that it may be eternal; or whether, by reason of the subject, which is the soul, eternity is administered to the arts.

For the soul’s essence, power, and activity are eternal; or perhaps they adhere to one another in such a way that, since all are eternal, they cannot be separated from one another [Note: CDE read “adhere to one another”; A reads “cohere.”]

### 45 [Cols. 0487A–0487B]

**STUDENT.** Since this reasoning is true, I do not know who would dare resist it. For whichever of these alternatives someone affirms, he does not oppose reason. Yet the final alternative that you proposed appears more plausible than the others.

But, to return to the same subject [Note: A reads “the same thing”], it is not entirely clear to me how essence (οὐσία) can be defined either in genera, species, or individuals, since it has been concluded in the preceding arguments of this book that it can be comprehended by neither bodily sense nor intellect [Note: The printed text has “nulli sensui” and “nulli intellectui”; these are corrected from the manuscript readings “nullo sensui” and “nullo intellectui.”]

**TEACHER.** No one can define essence (οὐσία) through itself and say what it is. But it can be defined from what adheres to it inseparably and without which it cannot exist—from place and time, I mean. For every essence, created from nothing, is local and temporal: local because it exists in some way, since it is not infinite; temporal because it begins to exist, whereas it did not exist.

Thus essence is in no way defined as to what it is; rather, it is defined as being. For from place and time, as we have said, and from other accidents that are understood to exist either in it or outside it, we are given only that it is, not what it is.

This may appropriately be said generally of every essence, whether most general, most specific, or intermediate. For even the cause of all things, which is God, is known to exist solely from the things created by him [Note: A reads “by it”]; but through no argument from creatures can we understand what he is. Therefore this one definition alone is predicated of God: that he is, though he is more than being.

**STUDENT.** In my opinion, no one who understands properly will oppose this reasoning either.

### 46 [Cols. 0487C–0489B]

**TEACHER.** Now, therefore, you see more clearly than the sun that those who think the parts of this visible world are the natural places of the other bodies established within them deserve to be mocked—or rather pitied—and consequently recalled to a true discernment of things if they are willing, or completely abandoned if they prefer to follow their habit, which is most hostile to truth.

For, to speak by way of example about my own body: it is exceedingly presumptuous to suppose that the soul is contained within the bodily expanses of this world. If this air is its place, it follows that a quarter of itself is its place. For everyone knows that every visible body consists of four parts, namely fire, air, earth, and water [Note: CE read “fire, air, earth, water”; AD read “fire, air, water, earth.”] Nothing is closer to irrationality than to suppose that the whole body is located in one of its own parts. For the whole is rightly judged to contain all its parts, but not a part to encompass the whole.

Again, if I say that my body exists in this air as in its place, it follows that it cannot have any definite place there. For this air is continually carried around the earth, and consequently a body situated in it must have countless places in one and the same interval of time. This cannot be conceded on any rational grounds.

For the preceding arguments persuaded us that place is in a state and is not changed by any motion. Thus, just as someone who stands, sits, or swims in a river cannot retain that part of the river [Note: C reads “cannot possess and retain that part of the river”] so as to be able to say that he possesses a definite place in the river, since it is evident that it passes by without any interruption [Note: D reads “it is evident”], so no one ought to call this air the place of his body when it is continually moving and does not remain still for any moment of time.

But if someone objects to this reasoning that earth, because it always remains still, ought by right to be called the place of bodies, let him similarly see that earth is the matter of bodies, not their place. Yet who, using reason, would dare say that the matter of bodies is the place of those same bodies, especially since matter, considered rationally in itself, is neither in motion nor at rest?

For that which has not yet begun to be contained in a definite form is not in motion. Matter is moved through form; without form it is immobile, as the Greeks hold. For where would that be moved which is not yet confined by any definite place or time?

Nor is it at rest, because it does not yet possess the end of its perfection. For rest is the end of motion. But how can that which has not yet begun to move come to be at rest?

How, then, can the matter of a body be the place of the body made from it, when matter itself is circumscribed within itself by no definite place, mode, or form, and is defined by no definite account except through negation [Note: CDE read “through generation”]? For it is denied to be one of the things that are, although everything that has been created is believed to have been formed from it [Note: A reads “is believed.”]

Again, if the parts of this visible world are the places of our bodies or of other bodies, they cannot always be our places. For when the body of some animal has been dissolved and its parts return separately to their natural seats from which they were taken [Note: C reads “may return”; E reads “will return”], its place will not be air, for example, or water, or earth, or fire. Rather, the individual parts of one body will be so mingled with the individual elements naturally related to them that they will be one with those elements, not in them as something in something else.

For what is returned to air will be air, and will not be placed as if in some place belonging to air [Note: CD read “is placed”]. This will not be a kind of confusion of bodies; rather, by a marvelous mode of nature, each will possess its own proper part in each of the elements: whole throughout wholes, not part in part. Thus, at the time of resurrection, no one will receive anything except what is his own, just as the light of many luminaries exists together, with no mixture and no separation in it.

Although one and the same light appears to exist, each luminary nevertheless possesses its own proper light, unmingled with the light of another; yet, marvelously, the lights become wholly present in wholes and form one light.

Air, therefore, is one thing, and its place another [Note: A reads “therefore”]. The same must be understood concerning the other elements and the parts of dissolved bodies restored to their proper elements.

And if this is so, it will necessarily follow either that these general parts of the world are not the places of the bodies permeated and composed by them, or that the bodies themselves do not have a definite place, or that they are altogether without any place.

But the nature of things and the true contemplation of it do not permit this to be conceded. For no creature, whether corporeal or incorporeal, can be without its own definite and immutable place, or without definite intervals and limits of time.

Therefore, as we have often said, philosophers call these two things—place and time—*hōn aneu* (ὧν ἄνευ), that is, “without which.” For without them no creature that begins through generation and subsists in some way can subsist.

And, to use the nearest argument from things, if the place of a body is whatever is poured around it, then color will be the place of a body. For no visible body exists that is not surrounded on every side by the light of color.

But if color is the place of a colored body, it will necessarily follow that a quality is the place of a body. Who, however, is oppressed by such dreadful stupidity that he would admit that the quality of a body is the place of a body? Yet although the color of a body is an incorporeal quality and is poured around the body everywhere outside it, no wise person seems to think that it is its place [Note: D reads “of the wise.”]

By what reasoning, then, is it not likewise conceded that this air, or some other element of the world, although spread around the bodies placed within it, can in any way be their places?

### 47 [Cols. 0489C–0490A]

**STUDENT.** Enough has been said about this. But I think something brief must be said against those who are so misled that they think body and the essence of body are not different, and do not hesitate to regard the substance itself as corporeal, visible, and tangible. For many, indeed almost everyone, are wearied by this error because they are ignorant of the natural differences among things.

**TEACHER.** Nothing is more laborious than fighting stupidity. For it admits defeat by no authority and is persuaded by no argument. But since human stupidity is not equal in everyone, and their minds are not darkened by the same fog of error, I think we must employ a few arguments against them.

**STUDENT.** Certainly. If they benefit from them, it will be a gain; but if they do not, we ourselves will become more certain through the exercise of disputation concerning such distinctions of natures.

**TEACHER.** Consider attentively, then, these few dialectical collections from among many. Every body composed of matter and form, since it can be dissolved, is corruptible. A mortal body is composed of matter and form. Therefore it is corruptible [Note: A reads “therefore”].

Again, every essence (οὐσία) [Note: The printed text appears anacoluthic; perhaps read οὐσίας, “of essence.”] is simple and admits no composition from matter and form, since it is one and inseparable. Therefore no essence can rationally be admitted to be a mortal body [Note: A reads “therefore”].

This has been said because every essence (οὐσία), although it is understood to be composed of essence and essential difference—the composition without which no incorporeal essence can exist, since even the divine essence (οὐσία), which is believed to be not merely simple but more than simple, receives an essential difference—for in it there is unbegotten, begotten, and proceeding substance—

nevertheless, that composition, which is known solely by reason and is not shown to occur through any act or operation, is rationally to be judged simplicity [Note: AD omit “to be”].

But in order that you may understand more firmly that οὐσία, that is, essence, is incorruptible [Note: A omits “that is, essence”], read the book of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite *On the Divine Names*, at the passage where he discusses the nature of demons and their wickedness [Note: C reads “their military service” (militia) instead of “their wickedness.”], and you will find him arguing most subtly that none of the things that exist, insofar as it is essence and nature, can in any way be corrupted. He holds that no essence, whether theirs or anyone else’s, can be corrupted [Note: D has “they argue” instead of “he argues.”]

### 48 [Cols. 0490B–0490D]

For, as he teaches by the most certain arguments, these three things in every creature, whether corporeal or incorporeal, are incorruptible and inseparable: οὐσία, as we have often said, δύναμις, and ἐνέργεια—that is, essence, power, and natural operation.

**STUDENT.** I ask for an example of these three.

**TEACHER.** There is no rational or intellectual nature that is ignorant of its own existence, even though it may not know what it is.

**STUDENT.** I have no doubt about this.

**TEACHER.** When, therefore, I say, “I understand that I exist,” do I not signify in this one word—“I understand”—three things inseparable from one another? For I demonstrate both that I exist, that I am able to understand that I exist, and that I do understand that I exist. Do you not see that in one word my essence, my power, and my action are signified? For I would not understand if I did not exist; nor would I understand if I lacked the power of understanding; nor is that power silent in me, but it bursts forth into the operation of understanding [Note: A reads “that power” as “any power”; CDE place “one word” after “verb.”]

**STUDENT.** This is true and plausible.

**TEACHER.** Is it not therefore necessary that those who say that a material body is essence (οὐσία), compelled by truth, should admit either that their body is not composed of form and matter but is an incorruptible essence, or that their body is corruptible and material and therefore is not essence (οὐσία)? [Note: D reads “by truth”; CDE read “compelled.”]

**STUDENT.** Certainly. But it seems to me that you are saying not universally that every body is essence, but only denying that every body composed of matter and form is essence [Note: C omits “to say.”]

**TEACHER.** Pay close attention, then, to what I say. Do not think that I have spoken not universally of every body but only of a certain species of bodies, although for the usefulness of the present question I have spoken specifically of a body composed of form and matter. I am speaking against those who say that their mortal and transitory bodies are nothing other than their essence, and that their essence is nothing other than their own material body, composed of various species [Note: C omits “species”], namely form and matter together with various accidents [Note: CDE omit “they say.”]

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

### 49

**MASTER:** But in order that you may clearly understand that no body universally is *οὐσία* [substance], accept this form of argument.

**DISCIPLE:** I will accept it; but first I see that a certain formula of the foregoing argument must be made. For the preceding reasoning seems more like an argument from the contrary than an image of a dialectical syllogism.

**MASTER:** Let the major proposition therefore be framed as follows: Is *οὐσία* a corruptible body? Every *οὐσία* is incorruptible. Every incorruptible thing is not a material body. Therefore no *οὐσία* is a material body. And conversely: Therefore no material body is *οὐσία*.

Again: Every body that is composed of form and matter is not simple. Every *οὐσία*, however, is simple. Therefore no body composed of form and matter is *οὐσία*.

Again: All human beings have one and the same *οὐσία*. For they all participate in one essence; and therefore, because it is common to all, it belongs properly to no one. But there is no body common to all human beings. For each person possesses his own body, but not his own *οὐσία*. Therefore *οὐσία* is common, whereas body is not common. But *οὐσία* is common. Therefore it is not body.

The same reasoning is plainly evident in the case of other animate and inanimate beings.

**DISCIPLE:** This formula is suitable. Return, I beg you, to the universal form of the argument you promised, by which it is concluded that no body is *οὐσία*.

**MASTER:** Everything comprehended by length, breadth, and height is a body, since it is enclosed by different extensions. But that which receives none of the aforementioned extensions, because it is one and simple and cannot receive any movement of its nature through extension, is necessarily incorporeal. Now *οὐσία* is not extended by length, breadth, or height; and because it remains indivisible in the simplicity of its nature, it is incorporeal. Therefore no *οὐσία*, since it lacks extension, is corporeal; just as no body, since it is extended through spatial dimensions, is *οὐσία*.

**DISCIPLE:** I also want this to be conceived in the form of a certain sound dialectical formula.

**MASTER:** Let it therefore be made into the formula of a conditional syllogism. Thus the major proposition is: Is *οὐσία* a body? If *οὐσία* is a body, it receives the extensions of length, breadth, and height. But *οὐσία* does not receive length, breadth, or height. Therefore it is not a body.

If you wish to hear the syllogism of an *ἐνθύμημα*—that is, of a common conception of the mind—which holds primacy over all conclusions because it is assumed from things that cannot coexist, accept this sort of formula:

It is not both the case that *οὐσία* exists and that it is not incorporeal. But *οὐσία* exists. Therefore it is incorporeal. For it cannot simultaneously be the case that it is *οὐσία* and that it is not incorporeal.

Again: It is not both the case that *οὐσία* exists and that it is a body. But *οὐσία* exists. Therefore it is not a body.

Again: It is not both the case that *οὐσία* exists and that it is incorporeal. But *οὐσία* exists. Therefore it is incorporeal.

The greatest argument, then, by which it is recognized that body is one thing and *οὐσία* another, is this: *οὐσία* is divided into genera and species, whereas body, like a certain whole, is separated into parts.

Again, body is not wholly present in its parts. For the whole body is not contained in the head, or in the hands, or in the feet. It is greater when all its parts are taken together, but lesser in each part when they are not taken together. *Οὐσία*, by contrast, is wholly present in each of its forms and species; it is neither greater when all are collected together nor lesser when they are divided from one another. For it is not more extensive in the most general genus than in the most specific species, nor less extensive in the most specific species than in the most general genus.

To use examples: *οὐσία* is not greater in all human beings than in one human being, nor less in one human being than in all human beings. It is not greater in the genus in which all the species of animals are one than in a single human being, ox, or horse. Nor is it less in these individual species than in all of them together.

Again, body can be cut into parts, so that its whole perishes. For example, when it is dissolved into the very elements from which, when they come together, an added form produces it, the whole perishes. For when the parts are no longer together and are not contained by their proper form, the whole cannot exist together in any thing in actuality and operation, although they may appear to exist together in the thought of one who considers the natures of things.

But it is one thing for things to exist together in the rational consideration of nature—which always gathers all things together in the intellect and comprehends the universe inseparably—and another for what is carried out through the operation of an agent or the passivity of a patient, visibly in the separation or collection of sensible parts.

The account of all numbers is unshaken in unity; it can neither be increased nor diminished. Bodily, or imaginary, numbers, however, can both be increased without limit and diminished, so that they cease entirely to exist.

But although *οὐσία* is divided by reason alone into its genera, species, and numbers, it nevertheless remains indivisible by its natural power and is separated by no visible act or operation. For it subsists wholly and always, eternally and unchangeably, in its subdivisions; and all its subdivisions are together and always one inseparable thing within itself.

Therefore, although body—which is nothing other than the quantity of *οὐσία*, or, to speak more accurately, not quantity but something quantified—may in actuality and operation, or through the passivity of its own determinate fragility, be separated into different parts, *οὐσία* itself, that is, the *οὐσία* of which body is the quantified entity, endures by its own natural power immortal and inseparable.

### 50

For this reason I added that body is more correctly called “the quantified” than “quantity”: those accidents that are called natural, when they are considered naturally in themselves, are incorporeal and invisible, and are contemplated by the gaze of reason around *οὐσία* itself or in *οὐσία* alone. They are, as it were, causes of their effects: quantity itself and quality are causes of the quantified and the qualified, and likewise the other genera of accidents, about which, as I think, we have said enough, since, although invisible, they produce their visible effects.

Body, therefore, is not the quantity of *οὐσία*, but the quantified; just as visible color, which is perceived around a body, is not the quality of *οὐσία*, but the qualified constituted in the quantified, and so with the rest of this kind.

I have also decided to insert into our little discussions the opinion of the holy Father Augustine from the book that he wrote on Aristotle’s *Categories*.

### 51

“Once *οὐσία* had been described,” he says, “since it could not be defined for the reasons mentioned above, the necessary order required a definition of the accidents. The first of these is the quantified. And not without reason. For whenever we have seen something, we must assess how great it is. But how great it is cannot be discovered unless it has been gathered by means of measurement.

“Thus, if someone wishes to measure only length, leaving breadth aside, length subjected to measurement without breadth is called a *γραμμή* [line]—not because there is any length that lacks breadth, but because one who measures only length is said to measure a *γραμμή*. When breadth has been measured together with length, it is called an *ἐπιφάνεια* [surface]. But if height too has been joined to the measurement, they complete a body.

“We do not, however, understand this in the way in which we usually understand the natural, lest we seem to return to *οὐσία*. This has been said so that we may know that these individual rules are established in geometrical bodies, in which these three dimensions can exist separately and distinctly. In natural bodies, however, they adhere inseparably; in them quantity is separated from *οὐσία* by intellect alone.

“For when someone appears to discuss quantity as though he were saying something about *οὐσία*, he is thought to be confusing the two.”

Do you see what the teacher of the highest authority declares?

“When someone appears,” he says, “to discuss quantity—that is, the dimensions by which body is constituted—those who judge *οὐσία* to be nothing other than the body they see think that he is saying something about *οὐσία* itself.

“If, therefore, geometrical bodies, which we contemplate only by the gaze of the mind and construct only through the images of memory, subsisted in some *οὐσία*, they would plainly be natural, and there would be no difference between geometrical and natural bodies.

“But now, since we consider geometrical bodies by the mind alone and they subsist in no *οὐσία*, they are rightly called imaginary. Natural bodies, on the other hand, are natural because they subsist in their natural *ousiai*—that is, essences—and cannot exist without them; therefore they are real. Otherwise they would be thought of not in natural things but by reason alone.

“Thus it is clearly understood that body is one thing and *οὐσία* another, since body sometimes lacks *οὐσία* and sometimes adheres to *οὐσία*, so that it may be real, without which it cannot become real, although it may be fashioned by a certain act of imagination. *Οὐσία*, however, in no way needs body in order to exist, since it subsists through itself.”

I think enough has been said about these matters.

**DISCIPLE:** Clearly enough. But, as I see it, what remains is for you to explain briefly matter and form themselves, from which you assert that material things are composed. For, I think, this must not be passed over, since it is not sufficiently clear to me whether the form that is subordinate to a genus is the same as the form joined to matter so that it becomes body.

### 52

**MASTER:** Some forms are understood in *οὐσία*, others in quality. Those that are in *οὐσία* are the substantial species of a genus. For the genus is predicated of them because it subsists in them. As we have often said, the genus is wholly present in each of its forms, just as each form is one in its genus.

All these things—that is, genera and forms—flow from one source, *ousia*, and return to it by a natural circuit.

Forms attributed to quality are properly called forms in natural bodies, but figures in geometrical bodies. For every geometrical body is contained only by dimensions and figure, and by no substance. Every imaginary body is completed by the three universal dimensions, namely length, breadth, and height.

Not all geometrical bodies, however, are universally bounded by one figure. Some arise from a triangular figure, others from a quadrangular figure, others from a pentagonal figure and from other polygons without limit; still others grow from a circular surface. Therefore, insofar as the number of lines advances beginning from three, so far does the manifold order of figures and surfaces vary.

The number of dimensions and lines in geometrical bodies belongs to quantity. But the arrangement and position of the sides and angles, and the configurations of the surfaces, belong properly to quality, and are called a geometrical form, or more properly, a figure.

When, however, in natural bodies the number and distinction of the limbs are observed—whether they are separated by natural distinctions or naturally joined to one another—no one denies that this belongs properly to quantity. But the arrangement and position of the natural parts or limbs are referred to quality and are properly called form.

For we say that the form of a human being is upright and raised upward, whereas that of other animals is bent downward. Hence those are called deformed who lack the fitting harmony of their limbs or are deprived of the beauty of color, which arises in bodies from the fiery quality that is heat.

Color is called *color* as though from *calor* [heat], by a change of one letter. And *forma* [form] is said to derive from *formus*, that is, “hot,” with the syllable *mum* changed into *ma*. For the ancients called *formum* “hot.” [Textual note: John Scottus rightly observes this; cf. Festus, s.v. *forma* and *formucales*, and Varro in Nonius, ch. [lacuna], no. [lacuna].] Hence pincers are called *forcipes*, as though “grasping heat.” We also customarily call those *enormes* [abnormal] who exceed the natural rule of their limbs, as though they were without a *norma*, that is, a rule.

Do you not see that this consists not in the number or size of the limbs, but in the position of the bodily parts and in the brightness of the color? Or does it appear otherwise to you?

**DISCIPLE:** Not, I think. But I wish to know what relevance such a distinction has to the question proposed.

**MASTER:** Have we not, by the arguments already given, agreed that body is one thing and *οὐσία* another?

**DISCIPLE:** Yes—entirely.

### 53

**MASTER:** If, then, by natural distinction the quantity of body is separated by the intellect from *ousia*, although they adhere to each other, so that *οὐσία* is the subject of quantity and of the quantified, while quantity itself, or the quantified, are accidents of *ousia*, is it not clearer than daylight that there is one form which is discerned in *οὐσία* itself—not as an accident, but as that very thing belonging to it—and another form which, arising from quality and joined to quantity, produces a complete body?

**DISCIPLE:** I now see where you are heading.

**MASTER:** Do you think I want the essential form, joined to matter, to produce a natural body?

**DISCIPLE:** Not that either; indeed, I see that you do not.

**MASTER:** Tell me, please, how?

**DISCIPLE:** From the distinction of forms mentioned above—namely, substantial and qualitative forms—you seem to me to be urging nothing other than this: that the form which is a species of quality, added to matter, perfects the body in which *οὐσία* subsists.

For these three are observed in all natural bodies: *οὐσία*, quantity, and quality. But *οὐσία* is always perceived by intellect alone; it appears visibly in no thing. Quantity and quality, however, are present invisibly in *οὐσία* in such a way that they break forth visibly as the quantified and the qualified when, joined together, they compose a sensible body.

For if a geometrical body, beneath which no *οὐσία* lies, is demonstrably constituted by the quantity of its dimensions and lines and by the form of quality called figure, what prevents us from saying that a natural body—whose underlying power of *ousia* enables it to endure as long as it can endure as a quantified thing—is completed when the form arising from quality is added to the quantity assumed from matter?

For I do not think you are urging anything other than that we should recognize that the four elements of this world, by coming together and tempering one another, become the matter of bodies; when a form of whatever kind arising from quality is added to it, a complete body is produced.

Nor does it hinder me—[the supplied text breaks off after *quod multis*, “that/to many …”]. For to them we seem to be acting against ourselves and affirming things contrary and opposed to one another when we say that sometimes the coming together of the four elements produces matter, and sometimes the union of the quantity and quality of *ousia* is the cause of matter.

This is not surprising, since they do not realize that the elements of this world are composed from nothing other than the coming together of the aforementioned accidents of *ousia*. Fire is constituted by heat joined to dryness; air by heat joined to moisture; water by moisture joined to coldness; and earth by coldness joined to dryness.

And because these qualities, when they come together, cannot appear by themselves, quantity supplies them with a “quantified thing” in which they may shine forth perceptibly. Quantity is, as it were, the second subject after *οὐσία*, and therefore it is placed immediately after it in the order of the categories, because quality cannot become manifest without quantity.

If, then, the elements are made from quantity and quality, and bodies from the elements, bodies therefore are made from quantity and quality.

**MASTER:** Since I see that you have sharply perceived the end of our intention, tell me, I ask, whether this division of forms into two species of different kinds—namely, *ousia* and quality—seems valid to you or not.

**DISCIPLE:** It is valid and resembles the truth, although I have conceded, not without some uneasiness of mind, that it is rational. For you would persuade me more easily that a substantial form added to matter constitutes a natural body than that a qualitative form does so. I would more plausibly believe that *οὐσία*, not quality, is the cause of the constitution of a body.

For I think it has been gathered from the preceding arguments that quality is the cause not only of matter but also of form, except that it makes matter when mixed with quantity, whereas by itself it pours form over matter.

I do not say this because I am unaware that one cause can produce many effects from itself. I see, for example, heat and light bursting forth simultaneously from one fire, and light itself becoming the cause of brightness and shadows.

What shall I say? How many different bodies are made from one and the same matter? Into how many numbers is one form multiplied? And other things of this kind.

Therefore I would have thought that *οὐσία* itself becomes the form of matter, and not its accidents.

**MASTER:** I am greatly astonished that what was brought to a clear conclusion between us a little earlier should so quickly slip from your memory. Consider it more carefully, then, and let us briefly repeat the same things.

**DISCIPLE:** I am ready; repeat them.

**MASTER:** Had we not firmly agreed that *οὐσία* is incorporeal?

**DISCIPLE:** We had.

**MASTER:** Yet I do not think you have forgotten that quantities and qualities, insofar as they are conceived in themselves, are incorporeal; that they subsist in no other subject than *οὐσία*, to which they belong as accidents; and that they remain inseparably in it.

**DISCIPLE:** I hold this firmly as well.

**MASTER:** Is it therefore reasonable to say that everything constituted by quantity and quality—that is, the quantified and the qualified—receives the cause of its constitution from nowhere other than *οὐσία* itself, to which quantity and quality are proved to belong naturally as its first and greatest accidents, and without which they cannot exist?

For whatever proceeds from things that are in the source, why should it not be referred back to the source itself? I see no reason, especially since *οὐσία* itself, insofar as it is *οὐσία*, cannot in any way appear visibly, tangibly, or spatially.

But the coming together of the accidents that are in it or are understood around it can, through generation, create something sensible and spatial. Quantity and quality join the quantified and the qualified to one another. These two, joined together and receiving generation in a certain manner and at a certain time, display an entire body.

The other accidents seem to be added to these. For in our bodies and in those of other animate and inanimate beings, we principally investigate these four things: how great the body is; of what parts it consists; whether it is extended through dimensions of length, breadth, and height; what sort it is—whether of an upright and human form or of a bent and bestial form; and at what time and in what manner it was generated and bounded.

Thus it is placed within itself so that it is not infinite but one thing bounded within its genus. These, as we have said, are observed primarily in our bodies.

Beyond these, in a higher consideration, we contemplate *οὐσία*, which is the origin of substantial forms. For we say: Of what *ousia*, that is, of what substantial form, is this body or that body? Is it human, equine, or that of some irrational animal included within *οὐσία*?

For by these names the bodies of animals are not designated, but their substantial forms.

### 54

We must recognize three things distinctly, whether we are thinking about ourselves or about other animals:

What are we?  
What belongs to us?  
What is around us?

We are our own substance, which is living and intelligible, above the body, all its senses, and its visible form.

That which belongs to us, but is not us, is the body attached to us, composed of the quantified, the qualified, and the other accidents; it is sensible, mutable, dissoluble, and corruptible. It is most truly described as nothing other than the instruments or seats of the senses, which in Greek are called *αἰσθητήρια*, that is, *αἰσθήσεων τηρία*, “custodies of the senses.”

Since the soul is incorporeal and cannot disclose its operations through itself without the senses, while the senses themselves can be preserved only in certain seats, the Creator of nature made the body for the uses of the soul, so that he might preserve in it, as it were, certain vehicles of the soul—namely, the senses.

Around us are all sensible things that we use, such as the four elements of this world and the bodies composed from them. For our mortal bodies cannot remain without these. They are nourished by earth, given drink by moisture, made to breathe by air, and warmed by fire.

They grow and are nourished by two—earth and water. They are sustained in life by two—air and fire. Two pass into the body and undergo its affections—earth and water. Two operate the workshop of the body and fuse it together—air and fire.

For the fiery power, whose seat is in the heart, distributes the subtle vapor of food and drink through hidden pores into the various parts of the body and separates the refuse for evacuation. But this fire, unless it is inflamed by an airy spirit and nourished by food and drink as by certain fuels, is quickly extinguished; and without delay the entire structure of the body becomes dissolved, collapses, and grows rigid, when cold overcomes the power of heat.

But this is a subject for another place of discussion.

### 55

**DISCIPLE:** I accept these things as probable. But I do not cease to consider with myself how they can agree with one another: how incorporeal and invisible things, through their own mutual coming together, produce visible bodies, so that matter is nothing else and has no other cause of its constitution than the mutual tempering of those things which are contemplated only by the gaze of wisdom—within themselves, among themselves, and not in something else.

This is especially difficult in view of the fact that the magnificent Boethius, the supreme philosopher in both languages, asserts the following in his books on *Arithmetic*:

“Wisdom is the comprehension of the truth of things that exist and that receive an unchangeable substance of their own.

“We call those things ‘being’ which neither grow through extension, nor diminish through contraction, nor are altered by variations, but always preserve themselves supported by the proper powers of their nature.

“These are qualities, quantities, forms, magnitudes, smallnesses, equalities, relations, acts, dispositions, places, times, and whatever in some way is found joined to bodies. These things, by their nature, are incorporeal and possess strength through the reason of an unchangeable substance; but through participation in body they are changed, and through contact with a variable thing they pass into unstable changeability.

“Therefore, since—as has been said—they have received by nature an unchangeable substance and power, they are truly and properly said to exist.”

### 56

Does it not follow clearly from this statement that matter and the body made from it are one thing, while quantity and quality and the other things contemplated by wisdom alone are another—things that always preserve the unchangeable power of their nature?

Matter and body, however, to which these things occur as accidents, are subject to variable change and diverse instability.

For what of this? Does it seem likely that, if matter subsisted from quantity, quality, and the other natural accidents joined together with one another, matter itself would necessarily be unchangeable?

For what is understood of causes—why should it not also be understood of their effects? If quantities, qualities, and similar things are seen by the gaze of the mind alone, why should matter and body not likewise be subject not to bodily senses but to the intellect?

As it is, however, we perceive formed matter, by which body is produced—for matter that is altogether formless is intelligible—through bodily sense; whereas we see quantity and quality by intellect alone.

How, then, can quantity and quality produce matter that is so far removed from them?

**MASTER:** You are being deceived by a very subtle but false argument, or you wish to deceive others. But I do not yet know whether you yourself are in doubt about these matters or whether you are assuming the roles of others who doubt them.

**DISCIPLE:** I perceive both in myself. I have undertaken to propose these questions in the person of others who, not without reason, either hesitate about such matters or are completely ignorant of them; and I also see that I myself have not yet attained such purity in these matters that I should cease investigating them.

**MASTER:** We must therefore use, I think, both reason and authority, so that you may distinguish these things clearly. For the whole power of discovering the truth of things is established through these two.

**DISCIPLE:** Certainly. Many have sought these things, but few have found them.

**MASTER:** Tell me, then, what do you think about matter itself, from which formed bodies come? While it is formless, is it considered by sense or by reason?

**DISCIPLE:** By reason, certainly; I would not dare to say by sense. For matter lacking form cannot be reached by any bodily sense.

**MASTER:** You have answered correctly. But take care not to question us again at too great length about matters you have now accepted. For we linger too long over such things, although higher matters invite us to their consideration.

**DISCIPLE:** With regard to the things that have now been defined between us by the pure gaze of the mind, I do not think I shall trouble you further. But I cannot cease wondering at what you said—that higher matters invite us to consider them.

For what is there after God that should be considered by reason as higher than formless matter? I do not see, since the questions concern what matter is, what form is, what is produced from matter and form, whence matter comes, whether it is to be numbered among the primordial causes first created by God or among the subsequent causes that arise from the primordial ones, whether it is to be counted among things subject to the senses or among things subject to the intellect, and whether it can be defined while it is still infinite—or whether even the infinite can be defined.

This seems to resist reason, since the holy Fathers have brought it to complete clarity that there are only two things that in no way can be defined: God and matter.

God is infinite and formless because he is formed by no one, since he is the form of all things. Matter likewise is formless and infinite; for it needs to be formed and bounded from elsewhere, since in itself it is not formed but formable.

The likeness between the cause of all things—from which, in which, through which, and toward which all things exist—and the formless cause, namely matter, which was created so that things that could not be reached by the senses in themselves might somehow appear sensibly in it, is understood by contrast.

For the highest cause of all things is formless and infinite through the excellence of all forms and limits. It is not merely the principal form of all things, but more than form: it surpasses every form and forms everything formable and formless.

It is the form of those things that can be formed, since they either desire it or are turned toward it. And because of the excellence of its nature and its proximity and likeness to it—that is, to the cause—it is the formlessness of those things that cannot be formed.

For the formlessness of things that are formless is not called formlessness because it lacks every form, but because it surpasses every sensible and intelligible form.

Therefore that very cause of all things is customarily both affirmed and denied, so that one may say of it: “It is form”; “it is not form”; “it is formlessness”; “it is not formlessness.” For whatever is predicated of it can both be affirmed and denied, because it is beyond everything that is said, understood, or not understood.

Matter, however, is called formless through the privation of all forms. Nothing is formed from it; rather, it receives diverse and innumerable forms.

**MASTER:** You are not far from the truth. Does it therefore follow that formless matter, since it is perceived only by the eye of the mind—that is, by reason—is necessarily incorporeal?

**DISCIPLE:** I would not dare deny even this.

**MASTER:** Then it is incorporeal.

**DISCIPLE:** It is indeed; and I see that I have been brought to a conclusion in my own judgment.

**MASTER:** Do you wish this to be strengthened by authority?

**DISCIPLE:** Very much so; and I request that it be done.
