### 57

**MASTER.** We find that many experts in both worldly and divine wisdom have disputed about matter; but it is enough to use the testimony of a few. Saint Augustine, in the books of the *Confessions*, asserts that formless matter is the mutability of mutable things, capable of all forms. [Note: Col. 0499: A reads *materiam* (“matter”) for *materiem* (“matter,” accusative).] [Note: Col. 0499: So AD; CE reads *mutabilem*, “mutable,” instead of *mutabilitatem*, “mutability.”] Plato agrees with him in the *Timaeus*, likewise saying that formless matter is the capacity for forms. Since these two agree with one another [Col. 0500D], it may be stated and defined as follows: “The mutability of mutable things, capable of all forms, is formless matter.”

Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, in his book [Note: Col. 0499: Witness A reads “books”], *On the Divine Names*, says that matter is a participation in adornment, form, and shape, without which [Note: Col. 0499: CE has *sine*; A reads *sine quibus* (“without which”); D reads the disordered *quibus per se sine informis*.] matter is formless in itself and cannot be understood in any way. [Note: Col. 0499: *est*, “is,” is omitted by A.] Thus, according to Dionysius, the following may be inferred: If matter is a participation in adornment, form, and shape, then that which lacks participation in adornment, form, and shape is not matter, but a certain formlessness.

Therefore, whether formless matter is, according to Augustine and Plato, a mutability capable of forms, or, according to Dionysius, a certain formlessness lacking participation in shape, form, and adornment, you will not deny, I think, that, insofar as it can in some manner be understood, it is perceived only by the intellect. [Note: Col. 0501: AD reads *non*, “not”; CE omits it.]

**STUDENT.** I granted this firmly a long while ago.

**MASTER.** What, then? Do you think that the shape, form, and adornment themselves, through participation in which that aforementioned formlessness—or mutability—becomes matter, can be considered in any other way than by the mind’s contemplation?

**STUDENT.** In no way. For it has been sufficiently established by the arguments already given that form and shape, without which no adornment can be produced, are entirely incorporeal [Col. 0501B].

**MASTER.** You now see, then, that from incorporeal things—namely, from mutable formlessness, which is capable of forms—and from form itself, something corporeal is created: I mean matter and body.

**STUDENT.** I plainly see it.

**MASTER.** You therefore concede that bodies can arise from the conjunction of incorporeal things.

**STUDENT.** I concede it, compelled by reason.

### 58

**MASTER.** Since this is so, you will necessarily admit that bodies can be resolved into incorporeal things [Note: Col. 0501: *in*, “into,” is omitted by C], so that they are no longer corporeal [Note: Col. 0501: D reads *corpora*, “bodies”] but completely dissolved. Incorporeal things, through their natural conjunction and marvelous harmony, form bodies in such a way that they do not at all cease to possess their natural condition and immovable power. To use an analogy: a shadow arises from light and body, yet neither light [Col. 0501C] nor body moves into the shadow. When the shadow is dissolved, it is understood to return to its causes—namely, body and light.

True reason teaches that body and light are the cause of shadows; in them shadows naturally remain silent, since they cannot appear anywhere because of the brightness of light spread all around the bodies. Those who think that a shadow perishes when it does not appear to the senses are mistaken [Note: Col. 0501: CE reads *apparet*, “appears”; AD, *appareat*, “may appear.”] For a shadow is not nothing, but something. Otherwise Scripture would not say: “And God called the light Day, and the darkness Night.” God does not name anything except what proceeds from him; nor does the height of theoretical contemplation in that passage remove the truth of the historical account.

There, when we consider the things that were made, we understand darkness and night as nothing other than the earth’s shadow, produced in the form of a cone by the surrounding diffusion of the sun’s rays and always standing opposite the globe of light. The same reasoning applies to lesser shadows, produced by any sort of light and bodies, whether finite or infinite and whatever their form may be.

Do not therefore be surprised that bodies are created from incorporeal causes and are again resolved into those same causes, while the causes themselves proceed from the one and same creator of all things.

### 59

For every form—whether substantial or one assumed from quality and joined to matter to produce a body—has been created from the form of all things, namely, the only-begotten Word of the Father. Every formlessness likewise comes from him. Nor is it surprising that formlessness—the deprivation of all forms—should be created from the formless form that is form by excellence, since from the same source of all things proceed not only *monogena*—that is, things of one kind—but also *heterogena*, things of different kinds; and not only things said to exist or not to exist through excellence, but also those said to exist or not to exist through privation. [Note: Col. 0501: CE reads *etiam* (“also”); A omits it.] [Note: Col. 0501: At the first subsequent occurrence, CDE support *etiam* (“also”), while A reads *et* (“and”).] [Note: Col. 0501: At the second subsequent occurrence, CDE again support *etiam* (“also”), while A reads *et* (“and”).]

What, then? Does it now clearly appear to you that we did not speak without reason when, following the authority of Saint Gregory of Nyssa, we said that bodies arise from the conjunction of accidents, since you see that other Greek and Latin authors assert that bodies arise from incorporeal things? [Note: Col. 0501: ACE read *non sine ratione* (“not without reason”); D, *non nisi ratione* (“only by reason”).] For this reason we have thought it appropriate to insert the aforementioned Father Gregory’s opinion into our discussion. [Note: Col. 0501: A reads *sequentibus*, “following”; CDE, *sequentes*, “following.”]

In his book *On the Image*, addressing those who say that matter is coeternal with God, he writes:

> Nor is that reception of matter said to lie outside those things that were found in due sequence, which declares that matter subsists from the intellectual and immaterial. For we find that all matter consists of certain qualities; and if it is stripped of them, it cannot in any way be comprehended by itself. Moreover, each species of quality is separated from its subject by reason. [Note: Col. 0501: CDE support *qualitatis species* (“species of quality”); A reverses the order to *species qualitatis*.] [Note: Col. 0501: CDE support *subjecto* (“from the subject”); A reads *a subjecto*, adding the preposition explicitly.]
>
> Intellectual reason is a certain incorporeal contemplation. For example, when some animal or piece of wood, or anything else possessing a material constitution, is set before us in contemplation, we intellectually understand many things about the subject through division, and the account of each of them is kept distinct in relation to the thing under consideration.
>
> The account of color is one, and that of weight another; again, the account of quantity is one, and that of the property apprehended through touch another. Softness, two cubits in extent [Note: Col. 0501: CE reads *bicubitale*, “two-cubits in extent”; D, *et cubitale*, “and one cubit in extent”], and the other things mentioned are not joined together, according to reason, either with one another or with the body. For in each of these there is understood a particular cause, according to which it has been interpreted; and none of the things contemplated around the subject is mixed with another quality.
>
> If, therefore, color is intelligible, so too are solidity, quantity, and the other such particularities. If each of these is removed from the subject, the entire account of the body will at once be dissolved. It follows that, since we find the absence of these to be the cause of the body’s dissolution, their conjunction creates and assumes the material nature. [Note: Col. 0501: CDE support *creare assumere* (“to create and assume”); the apparatus also records *et creare et assumere* (“both to create and to assume”) without assigning that expanded reading to a siglum.]
>
> For just as there is no body to which essence (*οὐσία*), shape, solidity, extension, weight, and the other particularities are not present, while each of these individually is not a body but is found separately as something other than body, so conversely, wherever the things mentioned come together, they complete a corporeal substance.
>
> But if the understanding of particularities is intelligible, then God is also called an intelligible nature. [Note: Col. 0503: D reads *dicitur*, “is called”; CE omits it; D also omits *natura Deus*, “God is nature.”] There is therefore nothing inconsistent in saying that these intellectual principles have been established by an incorporeal nature for the generation of bodies [Note: Col. 0503: CDE read *generationem*, “generation”; A, *generationes*, “generations”]: an intellectual nature establishes intelligible powers, while their conjunction with one another brings the material nature into generation.

### 60

Do you now see that the greatest and strongest argument of the aforementioned master is sufficient? If there were some body other than the conjunction of the essences of accidents, it would subsist in itself and by itself once those accidents had been removed. For every subject subsisting by itself does not need accidents in order to exist, just as essence itself does not. Whether accidents occur in it or do not occur; whether they are in it—those that cannot exist without it—or depart from it—those that can be separated from it—whether by thought alone or in act and deed, it always subsists through its own natural supports, immutably.

But a body cannot subsist by itself in any way once its accidents have been removed, since it is supported by no substance. If you remove quantity from a body, it will no longer be a body, for it is contained by the dimensions of its members and by number. Likewise, if you remove quality from it, it will remain formless [Note: Col. 0503: CDE read *deforme*, “formless”; A, *deformis*, “deformed”]—and nothing. The same reasoning must be contemplated in the case of the other accidents by which a body appears to be held together.

Therefore, that which cannot subsist by itself without accidents must be understood as nothing other than the conjunction of those same accidents. [Note: Col. 0503: D omits *eorundem*, “those same.”]

### 61

What is surprising, then, or contrary to reason, if we likewise understand the magnificent Boethius to have understood by a variable thing nothing other than a material body, which, as he himself says, is constituted from the conjunction of those things that truly exist? [Note: Col. 0503: ADE read *non aliud aliquid*; C, *aliquid aliud*.] And while they are considered in it, it necessarily undergoes a certain mutability. [Note: Col. 0503: D omits *hoc*, “this.”]

Nor is it surprising if things that are immutable in themselves are perceived in one way, in their simplicity, by the pure contemplation of the mind, and in another way by bodily sense, as composites formed in some matter from their conjunction, since we see that things which are simple and incorruptible in themselves bring about, by their coming together, something composite and corruptible. [Note: Col. 0503: CDE read *si*, “if”; A, *sed*, “but.”] [Note: Col. 0503: CDE read *perspicientur*, “are perceived”; A, *perspiciuntur*, “are perceived.”]

Who could be unaware that this mass of the earthly globe is compacted from four simple elements? [Note: Col. 0503: The text reads *Cui enim incognitum sit* (“for to whom could it be unknown?”); CD instead read *Cum enim incognitum sit* (“for since it is unknown”).] Although the globe is corruptible and dissoluble, the elements from which it is made nevertheless remain in their own indissoluble simplicity. [Note: Col. 0503: ADE read *ea*, “those”; C, *et*, “and.”] Reason observes the same thing in nearly all bodies in common.

I consider that enough has been said about these matters. [Note: Col. 0503: *haec* (“these matters”) is omitted by A.]

**STUDENT.** Certainly enough; and I now see that we must return to the consideration of the remaining categories. For there is no doubt that to continue doubting about these matters is characteristic of those who consider the natures of things less carefully. And for this reason I am ashamed and repent of my slowness in many matters. [Note: Col. 0503: CDE support the printed *per* (“through”); A reads *propter* (“because of”).]

**MASTER.** Do not be ashamed or repent. Although the things we are discussing are so splendid to the wise that none of them hesitates over them, I do not doubt that they are useful to the inexperienced, who are making their way from lower things to higher things along the road of reason. [Note: Col. 0503: CE read *et ex*, “and from”; A, *atque*, “and”; D omits *et*.]

**STUDENT.** There is no doubt of that, and I perceive it in myself. Proceed to the other matters. [Note: Col. 0503: ADE read *perge*, “proceed”; A also has the variant *sed perge*, “but proceed.”]

### 62

**MASTER.** Two categories remain for consideration, if I am not mistaken: namely, doing and undergoing. For, in discussing place, we also examined certain matters concerning time, insofar as the need of the present discussion required.

**STUDENT.** I ask you nothing further now about time or place. What has been said about them is sufficient. For if someone were to discuss everything that reason wishes to consider about each individual matter, who could say whether the discussion would ever—or scarcely ever—have an end?

**MASTER.** Consider, then, whether action and passion are properly predicated of God, or whether, like the other categories, they should be understood as spoken metaphorically.

**STUDENT.** Metaphorically, certainly. For what then? Should we suppose that these two exceed the other rules, when they seem to be of lesser power?

**MASTER.** Tell me, please: do moving and being moved not constitute doing and undergoing?

**STUDENT.** I see no other possibility. [Note: Col. 0503: AD read *non*, “not”; AE, *non esse*, “not to be.”]

**MASTER.** Likewise, I think, with loving and being loved.

**STUDENT.** They are understood by the same rule. No one versed in the liberal arts is ignorant that these and similar verbs are active and passive.

**MASTER.** If, therefore, these verbs—whether they have active or passive signification—are predicated of God not properly but figuratively, and everything predicated figuratively is said of him not truly but in a certain manner, then God neither truly acts nor undergoes, neither moves nor is moved, neither loves nor is loved. [Note: Col. 0503: A omits *haec*, “these.”]

**STUDENT.** This final conclusion requires no small amount of consideration. For, as I think, the authority of all sacred Scripture and of the holy Fathers seems to resist it. How often, as you know, does sacred Scripture plainly declare that God acts and undergoes, loves and is loved, cherishes and is cherished, sees and is seen, moves and is moved, and so forth? Since examples of these are innumerable and readily meet anyone who looks for them, I have decided to pass them over lest they make the discussion too long. [Note: Col. 0503: EDE read *gignerent*, “should produce”; C, *generent*, “should produce.”]

One example from the Gospel will be sufficient:

> “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him.” [Note: Col. 0503: CDE read *manifestabo meipsum illi*, “I will reveal myself to him”; A, *manifesto illi meipsum*, “I reveal myself to him.”]

Saint Augustine also [Note: Col. 0503: AD read *iterum*, “again”; E, *igitur*, “therefore”], discussing divine motion in his *Hexaemeron*, used these words:

> The creating Spirit moves itself without time and place; it moves created spirit through time without place; it moves body through time and place.

If, therefore, doing and undergoing are not truly—that is, not properly—predicated of God, as we said earlier [Note: Col. 0503: CDE read *praediximus*, “we said earlier”; A, *prius diximus*, “we said previously”], it follows that neither moving nor being moved is properly predicated of him. For moving is doing, while being moved is undergoing.

Likewise, if he neither acts nor undergoes, how is he said to love all things [Note: Col. 0503: C omits *omnia*, “all things”] and to be loved by all things that were made by him? For loving is a certain motion of the one acting [Note: Col. 0503: A omits *quidam*, “a certain”], while being loved belongs to the one undergoing; and it is both the cause and the end of motion. [Note: Col. 0503: D omits *est*, “is.”]

But I say this following common usage. For if someone examines the nature of things more carefully, he will discover that many verbs which, on the mere surface of their sound, appear to be active nevertheless have a passive signification in their meaning, and conversely that a passive surface signifies an action. For the one who loves or cherishes undergoes, while the one who is loved or cherished acts.

But if God loves what he has made, he plainly appears to be moved, for he is moved by his love. And if he is loved by those capable of love—whether they know what they love or do not know it—is it not evident that he moves? The love of his own beauty moves them.

How, then, can it be said that he neither moves nor is moved, lest he appear to act and undergo? I cannot work this out by myself. Therefore I earnestly ask you to untie the knot of this question.

**MASTER.** Do you think that, among those who act, the agent, the capacity to act, and the act itself are three different things, or one and the same?

**STUDENT.** I think they are not one, but three things differing from one another. For the lover—that is, the one who loves—is a certain substance belonging to a definite and determinate person [Note: Col. 0505: CE read *personae est*, “is of a person”; D omits *est*, “is”]. A certain power accrues to this substance, through which it can act, whether or not it actually acts. If the substance itself moves through this power in order to do something, it is said to act. [Note: Col. 0505: CD read *ut*, “in order that”; AE, *aut*, “or.”]

Thus there appear to be three things: namely, the substance in which there is the capacity to act; that capacity; and acting in some thing, which is the effect of that capacity, as of a certain cause—whether the action itself is reciprocal, that is, returns to the same person, or passes over to another person.

**MASTER.** You distinguish these correctly. What do you think? Should the same distinction not be observed in the one who undergoes, so that the one undergoing, the capacity to undergo, and the undergoing itself are different—whether someone undergoes from himself or from another?

**STUDENT.** Certainly the same distinction applies.

**MASTER.** These three things, then, in those who love and in those who are loved, are not of the same nature.

**STUDENT.** They are not, I think. The nature of substances is one thing, and that of accidents another. The one who acts or undergoes is a substance. The capacity to act or undergo, and the acting and undergoing themselves, are accidents. [Note: Col. 0505: AD read *agere et pati*; CE, *agere vel pati*, “acting or undergoing.”]

**MASTER.** I am surprised that you have forgotten what, in the preceding reasonings, was both sought and found, as I think, and defined.

**STUDENT.** Remind me, I beg you, and recall those matters to my memory. I do not deny that, through the fault of memory—which is forgetfulness—I am negligent and forgetful.

**MASTER.** Do you remember that we collected and concluded that *οὐσία*, *δύναμις*, *ἐνέργεια*—that is, essence, power, and operation, as we have often said—constitute a certain inseparable and incorruptible trinity of our nature? These are joined to one another by a marvelous harmony of nature, so that the three are one and the one is three. They are not like different natures, but are of one and the same nature—not like a substance and its accidents, but a certain essential unity and substantial distinction of the three in the one.

**STUDENT.** I remember, and from now on I shall never consign it to forgetfulness. To consign the clearest image of the Creator to forgetfulness would be the height of folly and misery.

But I do not yet see the relevance of this [Note: Col. 0505: corrected reading *isthaec*; ACE have *isthac*, D *istic*], unless perhaps it is because, when you questioned me, I answered that the three things differing from one another were one according to their subject but two according to accident, whereas those three former things seem very far removed from these.

Accordingly, one of two alternatives must be accepted. Either [Note: Col. 0505: CDE support *aut* (“or”); A reads *ut* (“that”).] the three we mentioned as belonging to one and the same substance—namely, essence, power, and operation—alone and truly exist [Note: Col. 0505: CDE read *vereque* (“and truly”); A, *vere, quae*], while what I have now added—substance together with accidents, namely the capacity to act and the effect of that capacity, which is acting—must be regarded as superfluous and discovered without reason [Note: Col. 0505: A reads *superflua non esse* (“not superfluous”)]; or the opposite must be maintained. Or, what seems more correct to me, both these and those [Note: Col. 0505: CE support *et illa* (“and those”); A reads *et illa, quae in* (“and those which are in”); D reads *et illaque in* (“and those also in”).] exist in the nature of things and are distinguished by their natural differences [Note: Col. 0505: CE support *suisque* (“and by their own”); AD read *suis* (“by their own”).]. But whether this [Note: Col. 0505: The text has *ita* (“so”); A reads *itaque* (“therefore”).] should be granted or not, I leave to your judgment to decide.

**MASTER.** What you have stated last seems consistent with sound reason. [Note: Col. 0505: C reads *rectae*, “right”; ADE, *recte*, “rightly.”] Whoever says that the essential trinity—namely essence, power, and operation—is present in all things, unshaken and incorruptible, and especially in rational and intellectual natures, does not, I think, depart from the truth. [Note: Col. 0505: CDE include *et*, “and”; A omits it.] This trinity, in all things in which it is present, can neither be increased nor diminished.

The following trinity, however, is understood as a certain effect of the preceding trinity. It does not, I think, conflict with truth if we say that, from that essence—which is one and universal in all created things, and common to all, and therefore, since it belongs to all things participating in it, is said to be no one thing’s property—there emanates, by a natural progression, a certain proper substance of each individual participant, which belongs to no other but itself alone. [Note: Col. 0505: CDE read *non obstrepat* (“does not conflict”); A, *non obstrepit* (“does not conflict”).]

A proper capacity also inheres in that substance. This capacity is assumed from nowhere except from the universal power of that aforementioned universal essence and power. Likewise, the proper operation of the most particular substance and power does not descend from anywhere except from the universal operation of that same universal essence and power.

Nor is it surprising if these three things, considered in individual beings, are called certain accidents [Note: Col. 0505: CE include *quasi*, “as it were”; AD omit it]—and first manifestations—of the aforementioned universal trinity, since that trinity is one in itself [Note: Col. 0505: CE read *sit*, “is”; AD, *sint*, “are”] and remains unchangeably in all things that exist from it and in it [Note: Col. 0505: CE read *existunt*, “exist”; AD, *consistunt*, “subsist”]; it can neither be increased nor diminished, corrupted nor destroyed.

But those things that are considered most particularly in individuals can be increased and diminished and varied in many ways. For not all participate equally in the universal essence, power, and operation: some more, others less. Yet no one is entirely deprived of participation in it.

The universal trinity itself remains one and the same in all its participants, and is neither more nor less present for anyone’s participation, like light in the eyes. It is wholly present in each individual and in itself. Its increase or decrease is a certain defect or advancement of participation; for that reason it is not judged irrationally to be an accident.

### 63

For whatever is always the same is rightly called true substance. Whatever varies, however, proceeds either from the mutability of an unstable substance or from participation in accidents, whether natural or non-natural.

And do not be surprised that certain accidents are called substances because they subsist in other accidents, when you see that other accidents accrue to quantity—which is unquestionably an accident of substance—such as color, which appears around quantity, and times, which are understood in the prolonged motions of things.

For time is a definite and rational measure of the duration and motion of mutable things.

**STUDENT.** I think that the conclusion of our intention does not differ in this matter. But I would like you to define this final consideration of things briefly and clearly.

**MASTER.** Let us establish, if you agree, that the immutable subsistence of the threefold understanding of things—namely, essence, power, and operation—is the firm foundation of things, established by the Creator of all. [Note: Col. 0507: BDE read *subsistentiam*, “subsistence”; C first reads *substantiam*, “substance,” then corrects it to *subsistentiam*; A reads *substantiam*.]

**STUDENT.** I think it should be established.

**MASTER.** Next, the trinity that can be considered in individual things, proceeding from the first essential trinity as the effect of its antecedent cause and its primordial motions, must, as I see it, be weighed as a certain set of primordial accidents.

**STUDENT.** This too must be admitted. [Note: Col. 0507: CDE read *hoc*, “this”; A, *et hoc*, “and this.”]

**MASTER.** Whatever, whether inwardly or outwardly, naturally or through certain occurrences [Note: Col. 0507: C reads *evenientibus*, “that occur”; D, *eventibus*, “events”; E, *euntibus*, “things going”], happens to those three subsequent things appears to become, as it were, an accident of accidents.

**STUDENT.** I do not resist this conclusion either. For since, according to Aristotle, there are ten genera of things, which are called categories—that is, predicaments—and since we find that no Greek or Latin author opposes this division of things into genera [Note: Col. 0507: CDE support *vel* (“or”) between “Greek” and “Latin”; A reads *et* (“and”)], we see that all the first essences, which the Greeks call *οὐσίαι*—substances—are rightly enclosed under one genus, because they exist through themselves and need nothing else in order to exist. Thus they have been established by the Creator of all as certain immutable foundations. [Note: Col. 0507: CDE read *reperimus*, “we find”; A, *reperiamus*, “let us find.”] [Note: Col. 0507: AD include *sed*, “but”; CE omit it.] [Note: Col. 0507: CDE read *stabilitae sunt*, “have been established”; A, *stabiliter*, “stably.”]

After the likeness of the principal cause of all things, they subsist through their own marvelous and unchangeable trinity: namely, as has often been said, essence, power, and operation. The other nine genera are said to be accidents. And not without reason. For they do not subsist through themselves, but in the aforementioned essential trinity.

When place and time are called by the Greeks *ὧν ἄνευ*—“without which the others cannot exist”—this should not be understood to mean that the aforementioned substantial trinity of things is included among those things that cannot subsist without place and time. [Note: Col. 0507: ADE support *ita* (“thus”); C reads *itaque* (“therefore”).] [Note: Col. 0507: D reads *consistere* (“stand/subsist”) for *subsistere* (“subsist”).] It does not need the assistance of place and time in order to subsist, since by itself it exists before and above time and place, by the dignity of its creation.

The nine genera, however, which are attributed solely to accidents, have been divided by the authorities in such a way that the accidents themselves, which are observed primarily in essences, immediately become substances, since they subsist in other accidents. The first division of all things is into essences and accidents; the second is the division of accidents into substances. This extends almost to infinity, since what is now an accident of a prior thing soon becomes the substance of what follows.

But these matters must be discussed elsewhere. For now, if you agree, let us pursue what we have undertaken.

**MASTER.** What, then? Do you think that accidents belong only to some essence or accident?

**STUDENT.** No one versed in the arts would say otherwise. For an accident deserved to be called an accident for no other reason than that it occurs in an essence, substance, or some accident. [Note: Col. 0507: CDE support the printed order *aliam ob* (“for no other reason”); A reverses it to *ob aliam*.]

**MASTER.** Are doing and undergoing included among accidents?

**STUDENT.** Yes.

**MASTER.** Then do they belong to some substance? For they accrue to their proper substances; nothing accrues to general essences.

**STUDENT.** I would not deny this either.

**MASTER.** Tell me, please: does anything accrue to the supreme, simple, and divine nature? [Note: Col. 0507: D omits the entire sequence from “Nor would I deny this” through “does anything accrue?”]

**STUDENT.** Far from it.

**MASTER.** Does it itself accrue to anything?

**STUDENT.** I would not say that either. Otherwise it would appear to be passible, mutable, and capable of another nature.

**MASTER.** It therefore receives no accident, and no accident accrues to it.

**STUDENT.** None at all, and it accrues to none.

**MASTER.** Are doing and undergoing accidents?

**STUDENT.** This too has been granted.

**MASTER.** Therefore the supreme cause and highest principle of all, which is God, does not receive doing and undergoing.

**STUDENT.** I am intensely constrained by the force of this reasoning [Note: Col. 0507: CDE read *hujus ratiocinationis*, “of this reasoning”; A, *hujus rationis*, “of this argument”]. If I say that it is false [Note: Col. 0507: D reads *est*, “is,” instead of *esse*, “to be”], reason itself will perhaps mock me [Note: Col. 0507: CDE include *me*, “me”; A omits it] and will not allow everything I have granted up to this point to waver. [Note: Col. 0507: C adds in the margin, in red letters: “For I granted that no category can properly and according to accident be predicated of itself; reason does not allow this to waver.”] If it is true, it will necessarily follow that, whatever I have conceded about doing and undergoing, I must also concede about all other active and passive verbs, whatever their grammatical category: namely, that God neither loves nor is loved, neither moves nor is moved, and a thousand similar things; and, even more, that he neither exists nor subsists.

But if this is so [Note: Col. 0507: D omits *at*, “but”], do you see with what and how many frequent weapons of sacred Scripture I shall be overwhelmed? Everywhere they seem to cry out against this and to proclaim that it is false. Nor are you unaware, I think, how arduous and difficult it is to persuade simple minds of such things, since even the ears of those who seem to be wise shudder when they hear them.

**MASTER.** Do not be frightened [Note: Col. 0507: CDE read *noli*, “do not”; A, *noli nunc*, “do not now”]. We must now follow reason [Note: Col. 0507: CDE include *enim*, “for”; A omits it], which [Note: Col. 0507: CDE support *quae* (“which”); A reads *quae etsi* (“which, even if”).] investigates the truth of things and is oppressed by no authority or hindered in any way [Note: Col. 0507: CDE read *nullo modo*, “in no way”; A, *nullo tamen*, “nevertheless by no…”] from openly revealing and declaring what the diligent activity of those who reason investigates and laboriously discovers.

### 64

The authority of sacred Scripture must indeed be followed in all things, since truth possesses in it, as it were, certain secret dwelling places of its own. [Note: Col. 0509: CDE read *possidet*, “possesses”; A, *possidetur*, “is possessed.”] Yet we must not believe that it always employs the proper signs of words or names when it conveys the divine nature to us. [Note: Col. 0509: All witnesses agree on this reading.] Rather, it uses certain likenesses and various forms of transferred words and names, accommodating itself to our weakness and raising our still crude and childish senses by means of simple teaching.

Hear the Apostle saying: “I gave you milk to drink, not food.” For the divine utterances strive toward this: that they may hand over and commend to us something to consider for the nourishment of our faith concerning a reality that is ineffable, incomprehensible, and invisible. [Note: Col. 0509: CDE read *fidem nostram*, “our faith”; A, *fidem*, “faith.”]

Accordingly, nothing should be said or thought about God by those who live chastely and piously and diligently seek the truth except what is found in sacred Scripture; nor should those who either believe or debate anything about God use any expressions or transferred meanings except those of Scripture itself. [Note: Col. 0509: CDE read *utendum est*, “must be used”; A, *utendum*, “must be used.”]

For who would dare to say that he has discovered anything about the ineffable nature by himself, beyond what that nature itself has uttered concerning itself [Note: Col. 0509: The text has *illa ipsa* (“that nature itself”); D reverses the order to *ipsa illa*.] through its holy instruments—that is, through the theologians? [Note: Col. 0509: CDE read *Theologis*, “theologians”; A, *theologicis*, “theological [instruments].”]

But, if you agree, I think that the testimony of Saint Dionysius the Theologian should be inserted here, so that you may believe and hold this more firmly.

**STUDENT.** Certainly. I welcome nothing more gladly than reason strengthened by the firmest authority.

**MASTER.** In the first chapter of *On the Divine Names*, the aforementioned Theologian commends the authority of sacred Scripture with great praise. But [Note: Col. 0509: CE support *Ast* (“but”); AD read *Et* (“and”).] since he argues in his customary intricate and hyperbatonic manner, and therefore appears to many to be exceedingly obscure and difficult to understand, I have decided to extract his opinion on this matter in a verbal order easier to understand than that in which it was written in its own place. [Note: Col. 0509: CE read *quam*, “than which”; D, *quo*, “than which.”]

He says:

> In general, we must not dare to say or understand anything about the superessential Divinity beyond what has been divinely expressed to us from the sacred utterances. For the knowledge of its superessentiality—which is beyond reason, intellect, and essence—must be referred to the higher illuminations, constrained by moderation and sanctity in divine matters [Note: Col. 0509: CDE support *sanctitate* (“sanctity”); A reads *simplicitate* (“simplicity”).], looking upward only as far as the ray of the divine utterances extends.

### 65

Do you see how he universally forbids anyone to dare to say anything about the hidden Divinity beyond what has been stated in the sacred utterances? [Note: Col. 0509: CDE read *dicta sunt*, “have been said”; A, *dicta sint*, “may have been said.”] These utterances he calls by the most glorious and most truthful name “higher illuminations,” constrained by holiness and moderation in divine matters. [Note: Col. 0509: CDE read *sanctitate*, “holiness”; A, *simplicitate*, “simplicity.”]

A little later, in the same work, he says:

> Just as invisible things are incomprehensible and uncontemplable to sensible things; simple things and things lacking likeness are so to things existing in image and likeness; and the untouchable incorporeal and unfigured formlessness are so to things formed according to bodily figures: so, by the same principle of truth, superessential magnitude surpasses essences, and unity beyond mind surpasses minds. [Note: Col. 0509: CDE read *et his* (“and to those things”); A, *in his* (“in those things”).]
>
> To every power there is inaccessible that good which is beyond sense, hidden from every reason, and super-rational: the unifying unity of every unity, superessential essence, invisible intellect, hidden word, *irrationabilitas* (“beyond rationality”), invisibility, and namelessness; it exists according to none of the things that are. [Note: Col. 0509: CE read *unifica*; AD, *unifica unitas*.]
>
> It is the cause of being for all things, yet it itself is not *ὄν* (being), [Note: Col. 0509: CE reads *ὄν*, “being”; DE read *non*, “not,” rather than preserving the Greek term] since it is the summit of every essence; and nevertheless it manifests itself properly and knowingly, in whatever way it does so, concerning itself.
>
> About this superessential and hidden Divinity, therefore, as has been said, we must not dare to say or understand anything beyond what has been divinely expressed to us. For it has itself handed down this truth about itself in the utterances in the best possible way:
>
> Its knowledge and contemplation, as it is, is inaccessible to all existing things, since it is essentially separate from all things. [Note: Col. 0509: CDE support the printed order *tanquam omnibus* (“as though from all”); A reverses it to *omnibus tanquam*.]

These statements concerning the authority that must be followed—namely, that of sacred Scripture alone—are sufficient, especially in divine discussions.

66. Reason, however, universally strives to persuade and to establish through sure investigations of truth [Note: [Col. 0509] So CE; AD has *indagationibus* (“inquiries”).] that nothing can properly be said of God, since he surpasses every intellect and all sensible and intelligible significations; he is known more truly by not knowing; his ignorance is true wisdom; and he is more truly and faithfully denied in all things than affirmed [Note: [Col. 0509] So A; C has *firmatur* (“is confirmed”), D *formatur* (“is formed”); E: “who, when he is denied in all things, is then more truly and faithfully confirmed.”]. For whatever you deny of him, you will truly deny; but whatever you affirm, you will not necessarily affirm truly. For if you affirm that he is this or that [Note: [Col. 0509] So CE; A has *ipsum* (“himself”), D *illud* (“that”).], you will be convicted of falsehood, because of all things that are, and that can be said or understood, he is none. But if you declare that he is neither this nor that, nor anything whatsoever, you will appear to speak truthfully, because he is none of those things that are or are not. No one can approach him unless, having first strengthened the path of the mind, he abandons all the senses, intellectual operations, sensible things, and everything that is and is not, and returns, insofar as possible, in unknowing to the unity of him who is beyond every essence and understanding—of him whose reason there is none, nor understanding; who is neither said nor understood; whose name is not a name, nor his word a word.

Nor is it unreasonable, as we have often said, that everything from the highest to the lowest can be said of him by way of a certain similarity, dissimilarity, contrariety, or opposition, since from him derive all things that can be predicated of him [Note: [Col. 0509] So C D E; A has *fiunt* (“come to be”).]. He did not create only things similar to himself, but also things dissimilar, since he himself is both similar and dissimilar [Note: [Col. 0509] *Est* is omitted in D.]. He is also the cause of contraries. For by the power of those things that were truly created by him, reason demonstrates that even those things which appear contrary, and which through privation of essence are not, are contained within them [Note: [Col. 0511] So CDE; A omits *ea* (“those things”).]. No vice is found that is not the shadow of some virtue, or a deceptive likeness of it, or its manifest contrary. It is a likeness, for example, when pride assumes the shadow of true power, lust of repose, rage of strength, anger of correction and justice, and the like [Note: [Col. 0511] So CDE; A has *atque* (“and”) and omits *justitiaeque* (“and justice”).]. It is a contrariety, however, as evil is the contrary of goodness. For just as goodness brings beings forth from non-being so that they may be, so evil desires to corrupt all things that are and dissolve them completely, so that they may not be [Note: [Col. 0511] So AD; CE has *ne* (“lest”) instead of *ut non* (“so that they may not”).]. And if this were to happen—that is, if all things were to perish—it too would perish at the same time. For if nature perished, vice would perish with it. But every nature is held together by the power of goodness [Col. 0511B] so that it does not perish.

Nevertheless, evil is permitted within nature, namely, for the praise of goodness through contrary comparison and through the exercise of virtues in rational activity, and for the purification of nature itself, when death will be swallowed up in victory, and goodness alone will appear and reign in all things, while evil will universally perish [Note: [Col. 0511] So CE; AD omits the second *et* (“and”).] [Note: [Col. 0511] *Est* (“is”) is omitted in CDE.]. But these matters will be discussed more fully in the fifth book [Note: [Col. 0511] D: “more fully in the fifth.”] [Note: [Col. 0511] So AE; CD has *disputatur* (“is discussed”), and A adds *libro* (“in the book”).]. Let no authority, therefore, terrify you away from what the rational persuasion of right contemplation teaches. For true authority does not resist right reason, nor right reason true authority. There is no doubt that both flow from one source, namely, divine wisdom.

[Col. 0511C] 67. One method has granted and handed down many things for pious seekers to think and say concerning incomprehensible and ineffable nature, lest devotion to true religion fall entirely silent: thus it may nourish those who are still inexperienced in the simplicity of faith with doctrine [Note: [Col. 0511] So C; ADE has *doctrinae* (“of doctrine”).], and may answer the rivals of the catholic faith, instructed and armed, fortified with divine defenses. The other method is intended to correct simply and chastely those who are still simple and have been nurtured in the cradle of the Church [Note: [Col. 0511] Corrected reading; ACE has *nutriti* (“nourished”), D *nutri* (“nourish”).], so that they neither believe nor judge anything unworthy of God, nor examine all that the authority of sacred Scripture predicates of the cause of all things as though it were predicated properly—whether the things are most glorious and supreme, such as life, virtue, and the names of the other virtues; or intermediate, such as the sun, light, and the stars, and everything else that is predicated of God from the higher parts of this visible world [Note: [Col. 0511] So ADE; C omits *visibilis* (“visible”).]; or from the lower movements of visible creation, such as spirit, the splendor of a cloud, rising, thunder, dew, rain, and shower; likewise water, river, earth, rock, wood, vine, olive, cedar, hyssop [Note: [Col. 0511] So CDE; A has *hyssopus*.], lily, human being, lion, ox, horse, bear, leopard [Note: [Col. 0511] So CD; A has *pardus* (“panther” or “leopard”), E *pardatus*.], worm; likewise eagle, dove, fish, κήτη (*kētē*, “sea creatures” or “great aquatic animals”) [Note: [Col. 0511] So CDE; A has *cete*.], and countless other things which, created from nature, are transferred to nature’s Creator by a kind of transformation and figurative signification.

And what is even more remarkable, Scripture has made its metaphors not only from creation to the Creator, but also from the contraries of nature—from madness, namely, drunkenness, gluttony, forgetfulness, anger, fury, hatred, desire, and other such things, by which the minds of the simple are less deceived than by the transformations made from nature above. For a rational soul, although very simple, may be deceived when it hears the names of natural things predicated of God and supposes them to be said properly of him; yet it is not wholly deceived when it hears the names of things contrary to nature predicated of the Creator of things. It either judges them to be altogether false and rejects them, or accepts and believes them to have been spoken figuratively.

**DISC.** I am not so terrified by authority, nor do I fear the assault of minds less capable, that I should be ashamed to declare openly what true reason clearly gathers and defines without hesitation—especially since such matters should be treated only among the wise, for whom nothing is sweeter to hear than truth by true reason, nothing more delightful to investigate when it is sought, and nothing more beautiful to contemplate when it is found. But I wish to know what you are attempting by the reasoning just stated.

68. **M.** What would you think I was contriving by these arguments, unless it were that you should understand how words signifying things—whether they signify substances, accidents, or essences—can be predicated of the nature that created them metaphorically, but not properly? In the same way, then, words signifying the movements of created nature, whether natural or non-natural, can be predicated of the nature that created them metaphorically, but not properly.

For if the names of essences, substances, or accidents are attributed to God not truly, but by a certain necessity for signifying the ineffable nature, does it not necessarily follow that verbs signifying the movements of essences, substances, and accidents cannot be said properly of God? He surpasses, by the incomprehensible and ineffable excellence of his nature, every essence, substance, accident, movement, action, and passion; everything that is said and understood concerning such things; and everything that is neither said nor understood but nevertheless inheres in them.

What then? If God is called “love” metaphorically, although he is more than love and surpasses every love, why should he not in the same way be called “to love,” although he surpasses every movement of love, since he desires nothing apart from himself, while he alone is all things in all things? Similarly, if he is called “agent” and “maker,” “one who acts” and “one who makes,” not properly but by a certain mode of metaphor, why should “to act” and “to make,” or “to be acted upon” and “to suffer,” not likewise be predicated in the same manner of speech? I think the same must be understood of the remaining verbs that signify all the movements of the entire mutable creation, whether natural or non-natural, intellectual or rational, irrational or bodily, incorporeal or local, temporal, straight, oblique, angular, circular, or spherical [Note: [Col. 0513] So CE; AD has *autem* (“however”).].

**DISC.** You press me very strongly to admit such things rationally; but I should like you to insert some support from the authority of the holy Fathers to strengthen them [Note: [Col. 0513] So CDE; A has *velim* (“I should like”).].

69. **MAG.** You do not, I think, fail to recognize that what is prior by nature has greater dignity than what is prior in time.

**DISC.** This is known to almost everyone.

**MAG.** We have learned that reason is prior by nature, while authority is prior in time [Note: [Col. 0513] So ADE; C has *dicimus* (“we say”).]. For although nature was created together with time, authority did not begin from the beginning of time and nature. Reason, however, arose together with nature and time from the beginning of things [Note: [Col. 0513] A has “from the beginning of things.”].

**DISC.** Reason itself teaches this. Authority proceeded from true reason, whereas reason in no way proceeded from authority. For every authority that is not approved by true reason appears weak [Note: [Col. 0513] So CE; AD has *autem* (“however”).]. But true reason, since it is fortified by its own powers [Note: [Col. 0513] So CDE; A has “by its powers.”], is established and unchangeable and does not need the reinforcement of any authority’s support. True authority seems to me to be nothing other than truth discovered by the power of reason [Col. 0513C] [Note: [Col. 0513] So BCDE; A has *cooperta* (“covered over”); the Gale manuscript has *coperta*.] and committed to writing by the holy Fathers for the benefit of posterity. But perhaps you see the matter differently.

**MAG.** Not at all. Therefore, in the matters now before us, we must first use reason and then authority.

70. **DISC.** Proceed in whatever order you wish [Note: [Col. 0513] ACDE: *quovis* (“in any order”).]; for I am your follower [Note: [Col. 0513] So CDE; A has *enim* (“for”) rather than *etenim*.].

**MAG.** Do you think that to act and to suffer can exist without some movement of the one acting or suffering?

**DISC.** I have no doubt about the agent. I cannot see how an agent can act without some movement of its own. But how what suffers is moved within itself, I do not yet understand clearly [Note: [Col. 0513] A has *tam* (“so”) rather than *iam* (“now”).].

**MAG.** Do you not see that everything that acts moves or is moved toward this end: that it may move what it desires to make from what was not into what is [Note: [Col. 0513] So CDE; A has *moveatur* (“may be moved”)]? Nothing can pass from what was not into what is without its own movement and another’s movement, whether it knows those movements or not. I am not now speaking of that universal and common movement which belongs naturally to all creatures, by which all things are moved from nothing into being, but of the ordinary movement that occurs in time, by which mutable matter receives certain qualitative forms each day, whether through nature’s movement or through art.

**DISC.** I understand now, and I accuse myself of excessive slowness for not seeing that everything that suffers undergoes its own movements, or another’s movements, or both.

**MAG.** The agent and the thing made, then, undergo their own movements. For what acts undergoes its own movement in acting. But what is made sustains both its own movement and another’s. Its own, because it passes from what was not into what is; another’s, because it is not itself the cause of its movement, but is moved by the one who makes it, by natural movement, by free will, or by some necessity. Thus what is made, as we have said, undergoes both its own and another’s movement, while what makes undergoes only its own. Although it often happens that the agent is moved by another cause to act, so that the agent and the patient appear to be one and the same, the movement of the agent is nevertheless called its own because it is understood not outside it but within it, even though it may arise from various causes, whether natural, voluntary, or involuntary.

**DISC.** I do not deny that you have persuaded me of this. Therefore I await what remains.

**MAG.** I think that no movement can be without a beginning and an end. For reason allows no other possibility than that every movement begins from some beginning and tends toward some end, in which it comes to rest when it has arrived. The venerable Maximus asserts this most clearly in the third chapter of *Ambigua*, saying:

“If God is immutable, as the fullness of all things, while everything that receives being from non-being is moved, it is rightly borne toward some cause” [Note: [Col. 0513] So ADE; C has *mutabilis* (“mutable”).] [Note: [Col. 0513] CDE omit *ex* (“from”).].

For, as the same Maximus teaches elsewhere, the same one is the cause of all things and the end of all things. God is the beginning—that is, the cause—of all creatures, and their end, because from him they receive and begin to be, and toward him they move so that they may rest in him.

The same author says a little later in the same chapter:

“Movement belongs to things that have been made, whether the movement of intelligible things is intelligible or that of sensible things sensible. For none of the things that have been made is altogether immovable.”

And shortly afterward:

“Such movement they call a natural power hastening toward its end; through it they have introduced us, in a sacred manner, to knowledge of the divine mysteries. Or they call it passion, that is, movement coming from one thing to another, whose end is impassibility. Or they call it active operation, whose end is perfection through itself [Note: [Col. 0513] So CDE; A has *ipsa* (“itself”)]. But none of the things that have been made is its own end, since it is not its own cause. Otherwise it would also be ungenerated, without a beginning, and unchangeable [Note: [Col. 0513] So CDE; A has *atque* (“and”) rather than *et* (“and”)], and, having no manner of movement, it would rightly move toward nothing. For it would transcend the nature of things that are; indeed, it would be nothing, since the true definition of it, though an extrinsic one, is: ‘It is the end for which all things exist, while it itself exists for no end.’ Nor is it perfection through itself; otherwise it would not rightly be made full, and similarly it would have its being from no one—for what is perfect through itself is also without a cause. Nor is it impassibility; otherwise it would be abiding, infinite, and uncircumscribed. For what is naturally impassible does not naturally suffer, since it is neither loved by another nor moved toward anything else through love.

“For God alone is end, perfection, and impassibility—rightly immutable, full, and impassible—while the things that have been made move toward an end without a beginning. For all things that have been made undergo movement, just as things that are not are, in themselves, movement or virtue [Note: [Col. 0515] So ACDE.].

“If rational things subsist, then they are altogether moved, being moved according to nature from a beginning through being toward an end, and according to knowledge through well-being. For the end of things that are moved is movement itself into the well-being that always is. Likewise, their beginning is being itself, which is God, who gives being and bestows well-being—rightly both beginning and end. For from him comes our absolute movement, as from a beginning, and movement of every kind toward him, as toward an end.

“But if what is intellectual is moved intellectually and according to reason toward itself, it also certainly understands. If it understands, it certainly loves what it understands. If it loves, it certainly undergoes an ecstasy toward it as the beloved. If it undergoes this, it surely also hastens. If it hastens, it directs an intense movement. If it directs an intense movement, it does not stop until it becomes wholly in the whole beloved and is wholly comprehended by it, willingly accepting, according to its will, a saving circumscription—so that the whole may be affected by the whole that circumscribes it, and nothing at all remain for it to desire, since it is able to know its whole self only as circumscribed, not through itself but through that which circumscribes it—just as the air is wholly illuminated throughout by light, and iron is wholly melted throughout by fire.”

Do you see how the venerable teacher just mentioned teaches that every movement inheres only in things that begin from a beginning and tend toward their end by natural movement? He defines natural movement in three ways, as follows:

“Movement is a natural power hastening toward its end” [Note: [Col. 0515] So CDE; A has “hastening toward the end”; D omits *est* (“is”).];

or:

“Movement is a passion coming from one thing to another, whose end is impassibility”;

or:

“Movement is an active operation whose end is perfection through itself.”

When he said that movement is a passion coming from one thing to another, since this is understood of natural movement, it must not be understood as though the beginning from which the passible movement—that is, the thing undergoing its movement—begins were one thing and the end it desires another. The beginning and end of all things that are moved naturally are one: God, from whom, through whom, and toward whom all things move. Rather, because the understanding of the beginning is one thing and the understanding of the end another, these two understandings are called, as it were, two different things, although they concern the one beginning and end of all things—for example, if someone were to speak of moving from the understanding of the beginning to the understanding of the end in God.

71. Next consider that everything without a beginning and an end must necessarily be without every movement as well. God, however, is ἄναρχος (*anarchos*), that is, without a beginning, because nothing precedes him or causes him to be. Nor does he have an end, since he is infinite. Nothing is understood after him, since he is the limit of all things, beyond which nothing proceeds. He therefore receives no movement. For he has no destination toward which he might move, since he is the fullness, place, perfection, stability, and totality of all things—indeed, he is more than fullness and perfection, more than place and stability, [Col. 0516B] more than the totality of all things. For he is more than anything that is said or understood of him, in whatever manner something may be said or understood of him [Note: [Col. 0515] So ADE; C has “for he is more.” D omits *est* (“is”).].

**DISC.** These matters seem to me clear, as I suppose.

**MAG.** If, then, you distribute every movement to creation but free God from every movement, are you so slow that you would attribute acting or suffering to him from whom you remove every movement, when your earlier rational conclusions have, as I think, cautiously established that these two things can occur without doubt only in those things in which movement exists?

**DISC.** I would have no doubt at all about suffering. I both believe and understand that God is wholly impassible. By “passion” I mean what is opposed to acting, namely, being made. For who would say—or believe, much less understand—that God undergoes being made, since he is Creator and not [Col. 0516C] creature? For, as we settled among ourselves earlier, when God is said to be made, it is manifest that this is said by a certain figurative expression. He is considered to be made universally in his creatures, since in them he is understood not only to be present, without whom they cannot be, but also to be their essence [Note: [Col. 0515] A has *et* (“and”).]. “Being” belongs to all things; divinity is “super-being,” as Saint Dionysius says [Note: [Col. 0515] CE has “super-being, however, of divinity”; D has “divinity is always being.”]. He is also said to be made in the souls of the faithful, when he is conceived in them through faith and virtue, or when through faith he begins, in a certain manner, to be understood. For faith, as I think, is nothing other than a certain beginning from which knowledge of the Creator begins to be formed in rational nature. But concerning acting I do not yet see clearly, though I hear the whole of sacred Scripture and the catholic faith confessing God to be the maker of all things.

**MAG.** You have already granted that acting cannot exist without movement in the agent.

**DISC.** I have granted it.

**MAG.** Then either you will attribute movement to God, without which acting cannot be understood, or you will remove both movement and acting from him.

72. For these two are counted among things that exist together, and they arise and perish together.

**DISC.** I cannot attribute movement to God, who alone is immutable and has no destination or object toward which he might move, since all things are in him [Note: [Col. 0517] So CE; AD has “all things are.”], indeed, since he himself is all things. But I cannot remove acting from him, since he is the maker of all things.

**MAG.** Then you will separate movement from acting.

**DISC.** I cannot do even that, since I see that they are inseparable from each other.

**MAG.** What, then, will you do?

**DISC.** I do not know. Therefore I earnestly beg you to open some path for me and free me from this great difficulty [Note: [Col. 0517] So CDE; A has “therefore, that you may open a path,” and so forth.].

**MAG.** Then accept the following progression of reasoning. What do you think? Did God exist before he made all things?

**DISC.** It seems to me that he did.

**MAG.** Then making was accidental to him. For whatever is not coeternal and coessential with him is either something other than he and outside him, or an accident belonging to him.

**DISC.** I would not believe that anything other than him or outside him exists. For all things are in him, and nothing is outside him [Note: [Col. 0517] So CDE; A omits the second *et* (“and”).]; nor would I rashly attribute any accident to him [Note: [Col. 0517] So CDE; A has *nullum* (“no”).]. Otherwise he is not simple, but is composed in some way of essence and accidents. For if something other than he is understood together with him, or if anything happens to him, then he is certainly neither infinite nor simple—something that catholic faith and true reason most firmly deny.

For faith confesses God to be infinite and more than infinite—for infinity is the infinity of infinites—and simple and more than simple—for he is the simplicity of all simple things. It believes or understands that nothing exists together with him [Note: [Col. 0517] So AC; D has “without him,” E “with that one.”], since he is the circumference of all things that are and are not, of all things that can be and cannot be, and of those things that appear contrary or opposed to him, not to mention things similar and dissimilar. For he is the likeness of similar things, the dissimilarity of dissimilar things, the opposition of opposites, and the contrariety of contraries [Note: [Col. 0517] So CDE; A has *oppositorumque* (“and of opposites”)]. He gathers and composes all these things into one concord through an ineffable and beautiful harmony. For things that in the parts of the universe appear opposed and contrary to one another and discordant, when considered within the most universal harmony of the universe itself, are fitting and consonant [Note: [Col. 0517] So CDE; A has “and are considered.”].

**MAG.** You understand correctly. Take care that you do not later regret having granted any of the things you have now granted.

**DISC.** Proceed in whatever order you wish. I will follow you, and whatever I have now conceded, I will not retract.

**MAG.** God, therefore, did not exist before he made all things.

**DISC.** He did not exist. For if he had existed, making all things would have happened to him as an accident [Note: [Col. 0517] So CDE; A has “all things would happen to him.”]. And if making all things were accidental to him, movement and time would be understood in him [Note: [Col. 0517] So CDE; A has the singular *intelligeretur* (“would be understood”).]. For he would move himself to make things he had not yet made, and time would precede his action, which was neither coessential nor coeternal with him.

**MAG.** His making, then, is coeternal and coessential with God.

**DISC.** So I believe and understand.

**MAG.** Are God and his making—that is, his action—two things, or are they one simple and indivisible thing?

**DISC.** I see that they are one. For God does not admit number in himself, since he alone is innumerable, number without number, and the cause of all numbers above every number.

**MAG.** Therefore, being is not one thing for God and making another; rather, for him to be is itself to make [Note: [Col. 0517] D omits *est* (“is”).].

**DISC.** I do not dare resist this conclusion.

**MAG.** When, therefore, we hear that God makes all things, we should understand nothing other than that God is in all things, that is, that he subsists as the essence of all things. For he alone truly is through himself, and whatever is truly said to be in the things that are, he alone is. Nothing that exists truly is through itself. Whatever is truly understood in him receives being through participation in him, the one who alone truly is through himself [Note: [Col. 0517] So BCDE; A omits the second *vere* (“truly”).].

**DISC.** I would not wish to deny this either.

**MAG.** Do you see, then, how true reason completely separates the category of making from the divine nature and assigns it to mutable and temporal things, which cannot be without a beginning and an end? [Note: [Col. 0517D] In manuscript E the text breaks off after *catagoriam faci-* (“the category of mak-”) on fol. 222b; it is lacking until “the venerable teacher—Maximus, I mean—has [said] concerning the divisions and unifications of substances” [Col. 0518D] (book II, chapter 13, near the end), with which fol. 223a begins.]

**DISC.** I see this clearly as well. And now I understand without hesitation that no category can apply to God [Note: [Col. 0517] A has *etiam* (“also”)]..

73. What then? Should we examine in the same way the force of all the words that sacred Scripture predicates of the divine nature, so that we judge nothing else to be signified by them except the simple, immutable, incomprehensible divine essence—and that which is more than essence—which surpasses every intellect and every signification? For example, when we hear that God wills, loves, or cherishes, sees, hears, and so forth—words that can be predicated of him—should we think nothing other than that his ineffable essence and power are being indicated through significations natural to us? This is so that true and pious Christian religion may not remain altogether silent about the Creator of all things, as though it dared say nothing about him, both for the instruction of simple minds and for refuting the devices of heretics who are always lying in wait for the truth, laboring to tear it out, and seeking to deceive those less instructed in it.

Therefore, God’s being, willing, making, loving, cherishing, seeing, and the other things of this kind that, as we have said, can be predicated of him are not different things in God. All these must be understood in him as one and the same thing, and they indicate his ineffable essence in the manner in which he permits himself to be signified.

**DISC.** Certainly, they are not different things. For where there is true, eternal, and indissoluble simplicity existing through itself, it is impossible for there to be anything other, many, or diverse [Col. 0519A].

74. Yet I should like you to persuade me more clearly, so that I may plainly see that when I hear that God loves or is loved, I should understand nothing other than his nature, without any movement of the lover or the beloved. Once this has been persuaded to me, I shall not hesitate at all wherever I read or hear that he wills, or desires and is desired, loves and is loved, sees and is seen, desires and is desired, or likewise moves and is moved. For all these must be understood in one and the same way. Just as will, love, affection, sight, desire, and movement, when predicated of him, indicate one and the same thing to us, so, I think, verbs—whether active, passive, or neuter, and whatever their mode of signification—are understood without any difference of meaning.

**MAG.** I do not think you have been deceived in such matters; they are as you suppose [Note: [Col. 0519] So CD; A has *possunt* (“they can”) instead of *sunt* (“they are”).]. First, then, accept this definition of love: Love is the connection and bond by which the whole universe of things is joined together in ineffable friendship and indissoluble unity [Note: [Col. 0519] So CD; A has *aut* (“or”) instead of *ac* (“and”).] [Note: [Col. 0519] A has *universalitas* (“universality”) instead of *universitas* (“universe”).].

It can also be defined in this way: Love is the natural movement of all things that are in movement, its end and tranquil rest, beyond which no movement of creation proceeds.

Saint Dionysius clearly supports these definitions in his hymns of love, saying:

“Whether we call it divine, angelic, intellectual, animal [Note: [Col. 0519] D has *animalium* (“of animals”).], or natural love, let us understand it as a certain unifying and connective power: moving higher things toward providence for lower things, things of equal form toward a sociable reciprocity, and the lowest subject things toward conversion to what is better and higher” [Col. 0519C].

The same author says in the same works:

“Since we have arranged many loves from one, let us now again roll and gather them all together into one and enfolded love, the father of them all. From the many, let us gather them together, first comprehending this love universally within two loving powers, of which the immeasurable cause of all love, empowered over all and ruling over all from the summit of all things, is wholly sovereign; and toward which the universal love of each existing thing and of all existing things naturally extends” [Note: [Col. 0519] D has *congerimus* (“we gather”) instead of *convolvamus* (“let us roll together”).].

The same author says in the same works:

“Come now, and gathering these powers of love together into one, let us say that there is one simple power, moving itself toward a certain unifying blending, from the best of existing things down to the lowest, and from that lowest again successively through all things up to the best; bringing itself back from itself, through itself, and toward itself; and always revolving in the same manner into itself.”

Love is therefore rightly called God, because he is the cause of all love, is diffused through all things, gathers all things into one, and returns to himself by an ineffable reversion [Col. 0520A], bringing all the loving movements of creation to an end in himself.

The diffusion of the divine nature into all things that are in it and from it is also called “loving all things”—not because it is diffused in any way, since it is without every movement and fills all things simultaneously, but because it diffuses and moves the contemplation of the rational mind through all things. It is the cause of the mind’s diffusion and movement, directing it to seek, find, and understand him insofar as possible. Since he fills all things so that they may be, he gathers and inseparably comprehends the universe through the peaceful joining of universal love into an inseparable unity, which is what he himself is [Note: [Col. 0519] C has *nullo* (“in no way”) instead of *ullo* (“any”); D has *iullo*, an apparent textual error.]. 

He is also said to be loved by all things that are from him—not because he suffers anything from them, since he alone is impassible, but because all things desire him, and his beauty attracts all things to himself [Note: [Col. 0519] So CD; A has *trahit* (“draws”)]. For he alone is truly lovable, because he alone is supreme and true goodness and beauty [Note: [Col. 0519] So CD; A has *et* (“and”) rather than *ac* (“and”)]. Whatever is truly good, truly beautiful, and lovable in creatures is understood to be he himself [Note: [Col. 0519] So CD; A adds *et* (“and”) before “lovable.”]. For just as there is no essential good apart from him, so there is no essential beauty or lovableness apart from him alone.

Textual apparatus omitted above: [Col. 0511] In “through privation of essence,” CDE read *per privationem*; A has *privationes*, omitting *per* (“through privations”). CDE read *vera ratio* (“true reason”); A reverses the order, *ratio vera*. At the opening of §67, D reads *siquidem* (“indeed”) for *quidem*. In “anything unworthy,” ACE read *indignum* (“unworthy”); D has *indigne* (“unworthily”). CDE read *examinent* (“they examine”); A has *aestiment* (“they judge”); perhaps *existiment* (“they suppose”) was intended. CDE read *cunctaque* (“and all”); A has *et cuncta* (“and all”). CDE read *sublimioribus* (“higher”); A has *superioribus* (“higher”).

[Col. 0511] In §68, ACE read *si enim* (“for if”); D has *autem* (“however”). ADE read *qui* (“who”); C has *quia* (“because”).

[Col. 0513–0515] In the Maximus citation, CDE read *eadem et* (“the same one is also”); A omits *et*. CDE read *id est* (“that is”); A has *et* (“and”). CDE include *est* (“is”) in “is both beginning and end”; A omits it. D omits *enim* (“for”) in “For none.” CE include *nobis* (“us”) in “introduced us”; AD omit it. ADE read *facientis* (“of the agent”); C has *faciens* (“the agent”). CDE include *ergo* (“therefore”) in “Thus what is made”; A omits it. CDE read *universaliter* (“universally/naturally”); A has *naturaliter*. ADE include *est* (“is”) in “For God alone is”; C omits it. CDE read *intellectualiter* (“intellectually”); A has *intellectuabiliter* (“intelligibly”).

[Col. 0515–0517] CE read *quo* (“whither”) in “no destination toward which”; A has *qua*, D *quod*. CDE read *etiam* (“also/indeed”); A has *et*. CD read *plusquequam* (“more than”); A has *et plusquam*, E *plusquam*. CD include *seu* (“or”) in “contrary or opposed”; AE omit it. CDE read *in unam concordiam* (“into one concord”); A has *in una concordia* (“in one concord”). CDE include *dum* (“when”) in “when considered”; A omits it and reads *et considerantur* (“and are considered”). ACE read *jam non* (“not yet”); D has *non jam*. CDE include *etiam* (“also”) in “And now I understand”; A has *etiam*.

[Col. 0517D–0519] A reads *id ipsumque* (“that very same thing”) for *idipsumque*. CD include *et* (“and”) in “other, and many, and diverse”; A omits it. CD include *enim* (“for”) in “For all these”; A omits it. C read *etiam* (“also”) and D *enim* (“for”) for *dicitur etiam* (“is also said”). D has *enim* (“for”) after “concerning acting.” In “It can also be defined,” C reads *etiam* (“also”) and D *ac* (“and”) for *et* (“also”). A reads *Item* (“likewise”) for *Idem* (“the same [author]”). CD read *inseparabiliter* (“inseparably”); A has *inseparabiliterque* (“and inseparably”).
