### 75

Just as that stone called the magnet [Note: [Col. 0519] A reads *magnes*; CD *magnetes*.], although by its natural power it draws iron approaching it toward itself [Note: [Col. 0519] CD read *sibimet* (“to itself”); A *sibi* (“to itself”).], nevertheless does not move itself in order to do this, nor suffer anything from the iron it draws toward itself, so the cause of all things brings back to itself all things that derive from it, without any movement of its own, but solely by the power of its beauty.

Hence the same holy Dionysius says, among other things: “Why, then, do [Col. 0520C] theologians sometimes call God ‘love,’ sometimes ‘affection,’ and sometimes ‘the lovable’ and ‘the object of affection’?” [Note: [Col. 0519] A and D read *vocant* (“they call”); C *evocant* (“they call forth”).] He concluded his statement by saying: “because by the one he is moved, while by the other he moves.” The venerable Maximus, explaining this conclusion more clearly [Note: [Col. 0519] A reads *aptius* (“more fittingly”) for *apertius* (“more clearly”).], says: “As subsisting love and affection, God is moved” [Note: [Col. 0519] The words *eo vero movet—movetur* (“by the other he moves—is moved”) are omitted in D.]; “but as the lovable and the object of affection, he moves toward himself all things receptive of love and delight” [Note: [Col. 0519] C reads *amoris* (“of love”); D *dilectionis* (“of affection”).].

To state the matter still more plainly: He is moved, as though bringing about an inseparable union of love and affection with those who receive them; but he moves, as though arousing desire through the nature of those things that are moved toward him [Note: [Col. 0519] CD read *in ipsum* (“toward him”); A *in se ipsum* (“toward himself”).]; and again he both moves and is moved [Note: [Col. 0519] CD read *movet et movetur* (“he moves and is moved”); A *moveturque* (“and is moved”).], as though he thirsted to be thirsted for, loved to be loved, and cherished to be cherished.

For even this sensible light, which fills the entire visible world [Note: [Col. 0519] C reads *implet* (“fills”); A *implet mundum* (“fills the world”); D omits *implet* (“fills”).], while it itself always remains motionless—[Col. 0520D] although its vehicle, which we call the solar body, revolves around the earth through the intermediate spaces of the ether in eternal motion—the light itself, issuing from that vehicle as from an inexhaustible fountain, so floods the whole world with the immeasurable diffusion of its rays that it leaves no place in which it might move [Note: [Col. 0519] CD read *moveat* (“might move”); A *movet* (“moves”)], and it always remains motionless.

For everywhere [Col. 0521A] in the world it is always full and entire [Note: [Col. 0519] CD read *in mundo est* (“is in the world”); A omits *in* (“in”).], abandoning or desiring no place except a certain small portion of the lower air around the earth, which it leaves in order to receive the earth’s shadow, called night. Yet it moves the eyes of all animals capable of perceiving light and draws them toward itself, so that through it they may see as much as they are able to see [Note: [Col. 0521] D omits *aspicere* (“to see”); CD read *possunt* (“are able”); A *possint* (“may be able”).], namely, what they are able to see [Note: [Col. 0521] CD read *possunt* (“are able”); A *possint* (“may be able”).]. It is therefore thought to move, because it impels the rays of the eyes so that they may move toward it [Note: [Col. 0521] CD read *permovet* (“impels”); A *promovet* (“moves forward”)], that is, it is the cause of the eyes’ movement for the sake of seeing.

And do not be surprised, when you hear that the nature of light, which is fire, fills the entire sensible world and exists everywhere without alteration [Note: [Col. 0521] AC read *immutabiliter* (“unchangeably”); D *immutabilemque* (“and unchangeable”).]. For holy Dionysius also teaches this in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy* [Note: [Col. 0521] D reads *ecclesiastica* (“ecclesiastical”) instead of *caelesti* (“celestial”).]; and holy Basil makes the same assertion in the *Hexaemeron*: [Col. 0521B] the substance of light exists everywhere, but in the luminaries of the world [Note: [Col. 0521] AD transpose the phrase as *mundi vero* (“but of the world”).], whether great or small, it bursts forth by a certain natural operation, not merely to illuminate, but also to divide all time by the motions of the heavenly bodies [Note: [Col. 0521] CD read *omne* (“all”); A *omnium* (“of all”).].

What shall I say about the arts which the wise call the liberal disciplines? Although they remain full, complete, and unchanging in themselves and through themselves, they are nevertheless said to move when [Note: [Col. 0521] CD read *quando* (“when”); A *quoniam* (“because”).] they stir the gaze of the rational mind to seek and discover them [Note: [Col. 0521] A reads *promovent* (“they move forward”); CD *permovent* (“they stir”).], and draw it toward the consideration of themselves [Note: [Col. 0521] CD read *ita ut et* (“so that also”); A omits *et* (“also”).]. Thus they too, although—as we have said—they are unchanging in themselves [Note: [Col. 0521] CD read *sunt* (“are”); A *sint* (“may be”).], nevertheless appear to move in the minds of the wise, since they move those minds. And there are many other examples in which an obscure likeness of divine power may be discerned.

[Col. 0521C] For divine power itself is beyond every likeness and surpasses every example. Although it stands in itself and by itself, eternally and unchangeably, it is nevertheless said to move all things, because through it and in it all things subsist and have been brought from non-being into being. For “by being it is” [Note: [Col. 0521] A reads *Essendo enim est* (“For by being it is”); CD read *eam* (“it”) in place of *est* (“is”). The printed wording is uncertain.]; all things, however [Note: [Col. 0521] CD omit *vero* (“however”).], proceed from nothing into being [Note: [Col. 0521] C reads *procedunt* (“proceed”); D *producunt* (“are brought forth”).].

It also draws all things toward itself. It is therefore said to move, because it moves itself toward itself and, by this very fact, moves itself and is, as it were, moved by itself.

God, then, is in himself love, in himself vision, and in himself movement; yet he is neither movement, nor vision, nor love, but more than love, more than vision, and more than movement. He is in himself loving, seeing, and moving; yet he is not in himself loving, seeing, and moving [Note: [Col. 0521] C reads *movere, videre, amare* (“to move, to see, to love”); AD *amare, videre, movere* (“to love, to see, to move”).], because he is more than loving, seeing, and moving [Note: [Col. 0521] D reads *sed* (“but”) for *quia est* (“because he is”).].

Likewise, he is in himself loved, seen, and moved; yet he is not [Col. 0521D] in himself being moved, nor being seen, nor being loved, because he is more than can be loved, seen, or moved.

Thus he loves himself and is loved [Col. 0522A] by himself, in us and in himself; yet he does not love himself, nor is he loved by himself, in us and in himself, but is more than loving and being loved in us and in himself.

He sees himself and is seen by himself, in himself and in us; yet he does not see himself, nor is he seen by himself, in himself and in us, but is more than seeing and being seen in himself and in us [Note: [Col. 0521] C reads *sed* (“but”); AD *quia* (“because”).].

He moves himself and is moved by himself, in himself and in us; yet he does not move himself, nor is he moved by himself, in himself and in us [Note: [Col. 0521] A reads *nec* (“nor”); D omits *non* (“not”).], because he is more than moving and being moved in himself and in us.

### 76

This, then, is the cautious, salutary, and catholic confession that must be made concerning God: first, in accordance with the *cataphatic* way—that is, affirmation [Note: [Col. 0521] C reads *affirmationem* (“affirmation”); AD *affirmativam* (“affirmative”).]—we should predicate all things of him, whether nominally [Note: [Col. 0521] CD read *nominaliter* (“nominally”); A *nominabiliter* (“in a nameable manner”).] or verbally, not [Note: [Col. 0521] D reads *nec* (“nor”) for *non* (“not”).] properly but figuratively; then, with respect to everything predicated of him according to the cataphatic way [Note: [Col. 0521] CD read *de eo* (“of him”); A *de Deo* (“of God”).], [Col. 0522B] we should deny that he is any of these things by the *apophatic* way, that is, negation—not [Note: [Col. 0521] D reads *nec* (“nor”) for *non* (“not”).] figuratively, but properly [Note: [Col. 0521] A reverses the qualification: “not properly but figuratively.”].

For it is truer to deny that God is any of the things predicated of him than to affirm that he is; and, beyond everything predicated of him, his superessential nature, which creates all things and is not created, must be praised in a superessential manner.

Therefore, when God the Word made flesh says to his disciples: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you,” sound reason compels us to believe, say, and understand the same concerning other analogous matters [Note: [Col. 0521] CD read *de* (“concerning”); A omits it]. [Note: [Col. 0521] C reads *et dicere* (“and to say”); AD *dicere* (“to say”).]:

“It is not you who love, who see, who move, but the Spirit of your Father [Note: [Col. 0521] C omits *vestri* (“your”).] who speaks in you, who speaks the truth concerning me, my Father, and himself. He himself loves and sees me, my Father, and himself in you, and moves himself [Col. 0522C] in you [Note: [Col. 0521] A reads *in vobis seipsum* (“himself in you”); CD *seipsum in vobis* (“himself in you”)], so that you may love me and my Father.

“If, then, the holy Trinity loves itself in us and in itself, and sees and moves itself [Note: [Col. 0521] CD read *seipsam* (“itself”); A *seipsum* (“himself”)], then assuredly it is loved, seen, and moved by itself—according to a mode of excellence known to no creature—in which it both loves, sees, and moves itself, and is loved, seen, and moved by itself, in itself and in its creatures, since it is beyond everything said of it.

“For who can speak of the ineffable—either who or what it is—of whom no proper name, verb, or proper utterance is found, exists, or can come to be, and who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light? For who has known the mind of the Lord?”

But before we bring the present discussion to an end, it seemed to me that a chapter of holy Dionysius concerning the divine state and movement should be inserted [Col. 0522D] here [Note: [Col. 0521] A reads *capitulum* (“chapter”); CD omit it], if that pleases you [Note: [Col. 0521] ACD read *inferendum* (“to be inserted”); corrected to *inserendum* (“to be inserted”).].

### 77

**STUDENT.** It plainly does, and by this final reasoning I see that I have been cleansed of every ambiguity [Note: [Col. 0521] A omits *esse* (“to be”).].

**MASTER.** In the book *On the Divine Names* he says:

[Col. 0523A] “It remains, then [Note: [Col. 0523] A reads *ut* (“that”); CD *et* (“and”).], to speak of the divine state, or seat [Note: [Col. 0523] AC read *sede* (“seat”); D *de sede* (“concerning the seat”).]. What else is this than God’s remaining in himself, fixed in the mind by an immovable natural unchangeability, being established above according to the same things and around the same thing, operating in the same manner, subsisting in every way according to his own most stable condition, and remaining according to the same nature unchanging and universally immutable—and all this superessentially?

“For he himself is the causal source of every state and establishment, being above every establishment and state; he establishes all things in himself and keeps them immovable and guarded in the stability of their proper goods [Note: [Col. 0523] AC read *immobilia* (“immovable”); D *immutabilia* (“unchangeable”).].

“What, then? When the theologians again call him who proceeds into all things and is mutable, ‘immutable,’ is this not also to be understood in a divine manner? [Col. 0523B] For one must piously judge that his movement is not transport, alienation, alteration, conversion, or local movement—not movement borne along in a straight line, nor circularly, nor by a combination of the two; not intelligible movement, lovable movement, or natural movement. Rather, it is God’s leading into being and containing all things, providing universally for all, being present to all by an immeasurable encompassing of all, and providing for all existing things through provident processions and operations [Note: [Col. 0523] A reads *providere* (“to provide”); CD *praevidere* (“to foresee”).].

“God’s movement must also be acknowledged and praised according to an unchanging, divinely established principle: the straight movement is to be understood as an inflexible and irreversible procession of operations and the generation of all things from him; the *elicoeides*, that is, the oblique *stateralis* procession (perhaps “ponderal”), and the fertile state [Note: [Col. 0523D] C adds in the margin: *i. e. ponderalis* (“that is, ponderal”); and below: “The gloss calls the *statheralem* and fertile procession oblique movement because it is composed partly of straight lines and partly of curves, which it calls fertile. A curved line is called fertile because it is borne back into itself and does not proceed to infinity.”];

[Col. 0524A] “and the movement according to a circle is that which contains and is contained, the same thing, the middle and the extremes, and the return into itself of the things that proceed from it and through it.”

**STUDENT.** As I see, the order of the discussion requires you to gather a brief summary of the fact that no one can properly predicate of God acting and suffering, or making and being made, and thus place an end upon the book [Note: [Col. 0523] A reads *et sic* (“and thus”); CD *ac si* (“and if”).].

**MASTER.** You gave this conclusion long ago, unless I am mistaken: that for God being and acting, or making, are not different things, but being, acting, and making are one and the same in him. For simple nature does not admit the conceptual distinction between substance and accidents.

### 78

**STUDENT.** I granted that without reservation [Note: [Col. 0523] D reads *inconcusse enim* (“for without reservation”); AC *inconcusse* (“without reservation”).].

**MASTER.** Therefore, just as being is predicated of him although he is not properly being—for he is more than being, and is the cause of all being, essence, and substance [Note: [Col. 0523] A omits *et substantiae* (“and substance”) ]—[Col. 0524B] so acting and making are also said of him, although he is more than acting and making, and is the cause of all making and acting, without any movement that could be understood as accidental, and above every movement. For he is the cause and principle of all movements and all accidents, just as he is of all essences.

**STUDENT.** I would grant this without hesitation.

**MASTER.** What, then, remains except for you to understand that it is altogether necessary that, just as being, acting, and making are properly removed from him, so suffering and being made must also be removed? For I do not see how what does not admit acting and making could admit suffering and being made.

**STUDENT.** Set the limit of the book. Enough has been summarized in it.

**The first book of *On Natures* ends** [Note: [Col. 0523] C omits “the first book of *On Natures* ends.”].

## THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0524D] C has, in illuminated letters: “The second book of *On Natures* begins, in which much is discussed concerning the return.” D omits the title.]

### 1

[Col. 0523D] **MASTER.** Since in the preceding book we spoke briefly of the universal division of universal Nature—not as genus into species, or whole into parts, for God is not the genus of creation, nor is creation the species of God, just as creation is not the genus of God, nor God the species of creation [Note: [Col. 0523] CD read *creaturae est* (“is of creation”); A *creaturae* (“of creation”).]—the same reasoning applies to whole and parts. God is not the whole of creation, nor is creation a part of God, just as creation is not the whole of God, nor God a part of creation.

Nevertheless, according to a higher contemplation, following Gregory the Theologian, we are a part of God, since we participate in human nature, because in him we live, move, and are. [Col. 0524D] And metaphorically God may be called genus, whole, species, and part. For everything that is in him and from him may piously and rationally be predicated of him.

We spoke, then, briefly by an intelligible contemplation of the universe—by “universe” I mean God and creation. Now, if it pleases you, let us discuss the same division of Nature more fully.

**STUDENT.** It certainly does, and it is very necessary. For if the matter is not opened up by a more extended investigation of reason, it will seem merely to have been touched upon, not examined.

**MASTER.** The universal fourfold division of Nature, then, was, as I think, as follows: into that form or species—if form or [Col. 0525A] species may properly be said of the first and supreme cause of all, which surpasses every form and species, being the formless principle of all forms and species—which creates and is not created.

We call God a formless principle so that no one may suppose him to be counted among forms, since he is the cause of all forms. For everything formed desires him, since he is infinite in himself and more than infinite; indeed, he is the infinity of all infinitudes.

Because no form confines or defines him, since he is known by no intellect, it is more reasonable to call him formless than form [Note: [Col. 0525] CD read *informe* (“formless”); A *formatum* (“formed”).], since, as has often been said, we can more truly predicate something of God by negation than by affirmation.

The second form is that which is both created and creates. The third follows: that which is created [Col. 0525B] and does not create. Finally, the fourth is that which neither creates nor is created [Note: [Col. 0525] D reads *non* (“not”); AC *nec* (“nor”).].

**STUDENT.** So indeed it has been divided.

**MASTER.** Since, then, the opposition of the aforementioned forms of Nature was briefly discussed in the preceding argument—for we considered how the third is opposed to the first: the two look directly toward one another as though across a diameter and are opposed. The created and non-creating form, as we said, is opposed to the creating and non-created form. Likewise, the second form looks in the opposite direction toward the fourth: the created and creating form is opposed to that which is neither created nor creating.

We say that universal Nature has forms because our understanding is in some way formed from it while it strives to deal with it. [Col. 0525C] For universal Nature itself does not receive forms everywhere. We say, not inappropriately, that it is contained by God and creation. Thus, insofar as it is creative, it receives no form in itself; but it grants multiplicity of forms to the nature formed by it.

It seems to me that we must now consider their similarity and difference.

**STUDENT.** The order of things requires nothing else.

**MASTER.** The second form resembles the first in that it creates, but differs from it in that it is created. For the first creates and is not created, whereas the second both creates and is created.

The third draws its likeness from the second in that it is created, yet differs from it in that it creates nothing. For the second is both created and creates, whereas the third is created and does not create.

[Col. 0525D] The third resembles the fourth in that it does not create, but differs from it in that it is created. For the third is created and does not create, whereas the fourth is neither created nor creates [Note: [Col. 0525] A reverses the order: “neither creates nor is created.”].

The fourth likewise resembles the first because it is not created, but appears to differ from it because it does not create. The first creates and is not created, whereas the fourth neither creates nor is created.

[Col. 0526A] Since we have spoken of their oppositions, similarities, and differences, I think we must say something briefly about their return and collection by the discipline that philosophers call *analytikē* [Greek: ἀναλυτική; “analytic”] [Note: [Col. 0525] CD read *analyticam* (“analytic”); A *analytica* (“analytic”).].

**STUDENT.** This too is demanded by the order of the matter. For there is no rational division—whether of essence into genera, of a genus into forms and numbers, of a whole into parts, which is properly called partition, or of the universe into those things which true reason contemplates in it—that cannot again be reduced through the same stages by which the division was first multiplied, until one arrives at that One which remains inseparably in itself and from which the division itself took its beginning.

But first, I think it necessary that you explain a little about the etymology of the name *analytikē*, for it is not entirely clear to me.

**MASTER.** [Col. 0526B] *Analytikē* derives from the verb *analyō* [Greek: ἀναλύω] [Note: [Col. 0525] A gives *analyo*], that is, “I resolve” or “I return.” For *ana* [Greek: ἀνά] means “back” [Note: [Col. 0525] A gives *ana*], while *lyō* [Greek: λύω] means “I loosen” [Note: [Col. 0525] A gives *lyo*]. From this also arises the noun *analysis* [Greek: ἀνάλυσις], which is likewise translated as “resolution” or “return.”

But *analysis* properly refers to the resolution of proposed questions; *analytikē*, however, refers to the return of the forms of a division to the principle of that same division.

Every division, which the Greeks call *merismos* [Greek: μέρισμος], appears to descend from some defined unity toward infinite numbers—that is, from the most general to the most specific. Every recollection or return, however, beginning again from the most specific and ascending to the most general, is called *analytikē*.

It is therefore the return and resolution of individuals into forms, of forms into genera, of genera into essences [Col. 0526C] [Greek: οὐσίαι, *ousiai*], and of essences into wisdom and prudence, from which every division arises and in which it ends [Note: [Col. 0525] CD and A read *in easdem* (“into the same [things]”).].

**STUDENT.** Enough has been said about the etymology of *analytikē* [Note: [Col. 0525] D reads *est* (“is”); AC omit it.]. Proceed to the rest.

### 2

**MASTER.** Let an analytical—that is, return-oriented—collection now be made by joining the aforementioned four forms two by two into one.

The first and the fourth are one, because they are understood of God alone. For he is the principle of all things created by him and the end of all things that desire him, so that they may rest in him eternally and unchangeably [Note: [Col. 0525] AD read *ut* (“so that”); C *et* (“and”).].

He is called the cause of all things as creator because from him the universe of things created after him and by him proceeds, through a marvelous and divine multiplication, into genera, species, numbers, [Col. 0526D] differences, and all the other things considered in created nature.

Since all things that proceed from that same cause will return to it when they reach their end, he is therefore called the end of all things, and is said neither to create nor to be created. For after all things have returned to him, [Col. 0527A] nothing further will proceed from him through generation in place and time, through genera and forms, because all things will be at rest in him and will remain one, individual, and unchangeable.

For what appears to be divided and partitioned in manifold ways in the processions of natures is united and one in the primordial causes. When it returns to that unity, it will remain in it eternally and unchangeably.

This fourth consideration of the universe, which is understood in God alone, like the first, will be discussed more fully in its proper place, to the extent that the light bestowed upon our minds permits.

What is said about the first and the fourth—that neither the one nor the other is created, since both the one and the other are one [Note: [Col. 0527] A reads *sunt* (“are”); CD *sint* (“may be”).]—should, I think, be clear [Col. 0527B] to anyone who understands correctly. For nothing is created that lacks a cause superior or equal to itself [Note: [Col. 0527] C has a marginal gloss: “This is said because of the three coessential substances of divine goodness.”]. God is the first cause of all things, and nothing precedes him; nothing co-intelligible with him exists that is not coessential with him.

Do you see, then, that the first and fourth forms of Nature have been brought together into one?

**STUDENT.** I see it clearly and understand it purely. For in God the first form is not distinguished from the fourth. In him they are not two things, but one. In our contemplation, however, when we conceive one account of God according to the consideration of principle and another according to contemplation of the end, they appear to be two forms, as it were, formed from the one and the same simplicity of the divine nature because of the twofold direction of our contemplation.

[Col. 0527C] **MASTER.** You see correctly. What, then? Should we likewise reduce the second and third to one?

For, I think, you are not unaware that just as the first and fourth are rationally known in the Creator, so the second and third are known in creation. The second, as was stated, both creates and is created, and is understood in the primordial causes of created things; the third, however, is created and does not create, and is found in the effects of the primordial causes.

The second and third, therefore, are contained in one and the same genus, namely, created nature, and in it they are one. Forms are one in their genus.

Do you therefore see that of the four aforementioned forms, two—the first and the fourth—have been gathered into the Creator, and two—the second and the third—into creation?

[Col. 0527D] **STUDENT.** I see it plainly, and I greatly admire the subtlety of the matter. For the two forms mentioned are distinguished not in God but in our contemplation; they are forms not of God but of our reason, because of the twofold consideration of principle and end.

Nor are they reduced to one form in God, but in our theory. When our theory considers principle and end, it [Col. 0528A] creates within itself two forms of contemplation, which it again appears to reduce to one form of theory when it begins to treat of the simple unity of the divine nature.

For “principle” and “end” are not proper names of the divine nature, but express its relation to created things. Created things begin from it, and therefore it is called “principle”; and because they terminate in it, so that they end in it, it has deserved to be called “end.”

The other two forms, by contrast—the second and the third—are generated not only in our contemplation but are also found in the very nature of created things, in which causes are separated from effects and effects are united to causes, since in one genus—namely, creation—they are one.

**MASTER.** Thus four become two.

**STUDENT.** I do not resist that conclusion.

**MASTER.** [Col. 0528B] What if you join creation to the Creator, so that you understand it as nothing other than him who alone truly is—for nothing outside him is truly said to be essential, since everything that is from him, insofar as it is, is nothing other than participation in him, who alone subsists from himself and through himself? Will you deny that Creator and creation are one?

**STUDENT.** I would not easily deny it. For it seems ridiculous to me to resist this collection.

**MASTER.** The universe, then, which is contained by God and creation, having first been divided into four forms, is again reduced to one individual reality—indeed, to its principle, cause, and end.

**STUDENT.** I see that enough has meanwhile been said about the division and unification of universal Nature. We shall consider the subdivisions of the individual forms in their proper places—I mean [Col. 0528C] the second and third. I would not readily say that the first and fourth admit subdivisions. Therefore, I think we should proceed to the other matters that must now be discussed.

**MASTER.** What do you think? Is there any other path to the investigation of the questions proposed than that we should now inquire into the second form of Nature, since in the preceding book we considered the first as far as our ability permitted? In that book we discussed the ten genera of all things, which cannot properly be predicated of the cause that creates all things [Note: [Col. 0527] CD read *possunt* (“can”); A *possint* (“may be able”)], more than we discussed the very cause of all things.

For we judged that what must be said about it should be reserved for consideration of the fourth form—not because we promise that there too we shall say anything proper or worthy concerning the divine nature, but because we shall speak, insofar as it grants us the ability, about the return of all things into it [Col. 0528D] through the primordial causes.

As our principal purpose in this second inquiry, then, we have established, God granting it, that we should say something about the procession of creatures from the one and first cause of all things [Note: [Col. 0527] A omits *causa* (“cause”)], through the primordial essences [Note: [Col. 0527] A reads *primordiales causarum essentias* (“the primordial essences of the causes”)], which were first established by it, in it, and through it, into the diverse genera, [The supplied column sequence interrupts *diversasque* (“and diverse”) here with the apparently dislocated fragment *humanus animus ad Deum perveniet, tum divinam*: “the human mind will reach God, then the divine …”; its placement and continuation are uncertain.] [Col. 0529A] forms, and numbers of things, without limit.

And do not be surprised if you see certain things said in this book about the return of creatures to the principle and end of themselves. The procession of creatures and their return occur together in the reasoning of one who investigates them, so that they appear inseparable from one another. No one can adequately and soundly explain one absolutely without introducing the other—that is, procession without return and collection, or conversely.

**STUDENT.** The sequence of the discussion requires nothing other than that, after considering the first question, we pass to the second.

**MASTER.** Universal Nature, then, as has already been said, shines forth in that second form which is created and creates, and, as I think, is to be understood only in the primordial causes of things.

[Col. 0529B] These primordial causes of things are called by the Greeks *prototypa* [Greek: πρωτότυπα], that is, “primordial exemplars,” or *proorismata* [Greek: προορίσματα], that is, “predestinations” or “definitions.” They are also called by the same people *theia thelēmata* [Greek: θεῖα θελήματα], that is, “divine wills.” They are likewise customarily called *ideai* [Greek: ἰδέαι], that is, “forms” or “species,” in which the unchangeable principles of all things to be made were established before they existed.

We shall speak about these matters more fully as the work proceeds and strengthen them with the testimonies of the holy Fathers. And they are not called this without reason, because the Father—that is, the principle of all things—in his Word, namely, his only-begotten Son, preformed the principles of all things that he willed to be made before they came into genera, species, numbers, differences, and the other features that either [Col. 0529C] can and do come under consideration in created nature, or cannot be considered because of their exalted character and therefore are not considered, although they exist.

### 3

Before we reach the theory of the primordial causes, however, it seemed to me—if it pleases you [Note: [Col. 0529] A omits *si tibi placet* (“if it pleases you”)]—that I should insert into our discussion the opinion of the venerable Maximus concerning the division of all created things.

For if the manifold division of all things, and their subsequent unification, is demonstrated in manifold ways, the way will appear more readily opened toward knowledge of the principal causes, which were principally created by God. This is especially so since his division appears to differ in no respect from our aforementioned division, except that he subdivides [Col. 0529D] sensible creation—which we placed as the third form of Nature, because the effects of the causes appear most clearly in it—into three species, and does not distinguish our fourth form from the first, as what follows will demonstrate.

We shall reserve this subdivision of sensible creation for the material of our third question, as God grants.

In the thirty-seventh chapter of *Ambigua* he says:

“The saints, who receive the knowledge of the many divine mysteries from those who were attendants and ministers of the Word, and who were immediately instructed in the knowledge of existing things, receiving it [Col. 0530A] through succession from those who preceded them, say that the substance of all created things is separated by five divisions.”

Do you see how great is the authority commending the origin of this division? For he recalls that it began from the Word himself—that is, from the Son of God, who is the fountain of all perfect doctrine. This is rightly so, because he is the wisdom which all wise people participate in through his attendants—that is, his disciples, who both saw him living in the flesh and heard him teaching [Note: [Col. 0529] A omits *et* (“and”).]. He says that it began with the Word and was handed down directly through the successors of the apostles in teaching and wisdom, that is, with no other authority interposed, down to his own time.

He continues: “They say that the first division is that which divides the created nature, universally receiving [Col. 0530B] its being by generation from the uncreated nature. For they say that God, through goodness, made the clear ordering of all existing things together.

“A little later he says: ‘The second is that by which all nature together, receiving its being from God through creation, is divided into intelligible and sensible things; the third is that by which sensible nature is divided into heaven and earth; the fourth is that by which earth is divided into Paradise and the inhabited world; and the fifth is that by which man himself, as a kind of universal workshop of all things, makes a most continuous connection among all things, naturally constituting a middle point for all things at the extremities through every difference, and doing so well and beautifully according to generation.

“‘Man, superadded to existing things, is divided into male and female, possessing in himself, by nature, [Col. 0530C] the middle points of all the extremes, and having the power of unifying all the extremities through the joining force of the distinctive properties of his own parts.

“‘He possesses one part of himself with sensible things, as far as he is body; another part with intelligible things, as far as he is soul. Therefore he contains the whole of creation in himself.’

“And a little later:

“‘For this reason man is introduced last among existing things, as a kind of natural conjunction, universally making a middle point through his own parts for the extremities, and bringing together in himself, into one, things that are separated from one another by a great natural distance.’”

Here he calls the invisible and visible creation the extremities, since they differ from one another by a naturally immeasurable distance, as though by a very long interval. For they are the two extreme boundaries of created natures [Col. 0530D], opposed to one another; but human nature provides a middle point between them. In it they are joined to one another, and from many they become one.

### 4

For there is no creature, from the highest to the lowest, that is not found in humanity. Therefore it is rightly called the workshop of all things; for in it all things created by God converge, and from diverse natures, as from certain sounds differing from one another, compose a single harmony. Thus, beginning from its own prior division and then proceeding through the intermediaries by connection and order, it would receive in God—as the causal principle gathering all things into unity—the end of that lofty ascent, made from all things through unity, in which there is no division.

[Col. 0531. Note: CD reads *congregante* (“gathering”); A reads *congregantem* (“gathering together”).]

Up to this point we have introduced the words of the venerable master mentioned above, not continuously, but with certain omissions. [Col. 0531. Note: CD reads *non continuatim* (“not continuously”); A reads *continuitatem* (“continuity”).] He begins the division of the substance of created things from the supreme cause of all and brings the differences of universal substance to an end in humanity, which was made in the image and likeness of God. Humanity, as we have said and shall repeat very frequently [Col. 0531. Note: AC reads *repetemus* (“we shall repeat”); D reads *repetamus* (“let us repeat”).], was created in such great dignity of created nature that there is no creature, whether visible or invisible [Col. 0531. Note: AD support *sive visibilis sive invisibilis* (“whether visible or invisible”); C reads *sive visibilis sive intelligibilis* (“whether visible or intelligible”).], that cannot be found in it [Col. 0531. Note: CD reads *possit* (“can”); A reads *posset* (“could”).]

[Col. 0531B]

### 5

For he is composed, through a wondrous union, from the two universal parts of created nature: from the sensible and the intelligible—that is, he is joined from the extremities of the whole creation. Nothing in the nature of things is lower than the body, and nothing higher than the intellect, as Saint Augustine testifies in his book *On True Religion*, saying:

“Between our mind, by which we understand the Father himself, and the truth through which we understand him, no creature is interposed.”

[Col. 0531. Note: A reads *dicente* (“saying”); CD read *dicens* (“who says”).]

By these words of the most holy Father it is made clear that human nature, even after the transgression, did not wholly lose its dignity, but still retains it. For the master did not say, “There was no creature interposed,” but “There is no creature interposed.” Therefore, even in our illnesses, we do not wholly abandon God [Col. 0531. Note: CD reads *deserimus* (“we abandon”); A reads *deseruimus* (“we have abandoned”).], nor are we abandoned by him, since no nature is interposed between our mind and him. Indeed, leprosy of soul or body does not remove the mind’s vision by which we understand him, and in which the image of the Creator has been established above all.

Do you see, then, how the division of all substances reaches its termination in human nature?

**DISCIPLE.** I plainly see it, and I greatly marvel at the dignity of our nature among all created things, since, persuaded by the arguments stated above, I perceive in it, as it were, a wondrous composition of all created substances.

[Col. 0531. Note: C reads *omnium creatarum substantiarum* (“of all created substances”); A reads *omnium creaturarum substantialium* (“of all substantial creatures”); D reads *omnium creaturarum substantiarum* (“of all created substances”).]

**MASTER.** Since, therefore, you clearly see the natural division of all things, beginning with Creator and creature and ending in humanity, which was created at the summit of divine operation, as in a certain perfection of six [Col. 0531D. Note: CD read *conditus est* (“was created”); A reads *est conditus* (“is created”).], let us now consider the words of the aforesaid Father Maximus, beginning with the united gathering of all substances from humanity and ascending through humanity to God himself, who is the beginning of the whole division and the end of the whole union.

### 6

For, as we have said, sound reason does not allow one to deal with division in isolation and omit analysis, but commands us to consider the truth with regard to both together. [Col. 0531. Note: CD read *de ambobus* (“with regard to both”); A omits *de* (“with regard to”).]

He therefore begins from the original division, as though he were saying plainly: Since the division of substances, which took its beginning from God and descended step by step, established its end in the division of humanity into male and female, the union of those same substances ought again to have begun from humanity and to ascend through the same stages to God himself, in whom, as he says, there is no division, because in him all things are one.

The union of natures will therefore begin from humanity, through the grace of the Savior, in whom, as the Apostle says [Col. 0531. Note: CD read *ut ait Apostolus* (“as the Apostle says”); A reads *ut ait amplius* (“as the Apostle says further”)], “there is neither male nor female,” when human nature is restored to its original state [Col. 0531. Note: CD reads *restaurabitur* (“will be restored”); A reads *restauratur* (“is being restored”).]

For if the first human being had not sinned, he would not have suffered the partition of his nature into two sexes, but would have remained unchangeably in his primordial principles, in which he was created in the image of God.

[Col. 0531D–0532D. Editorial note: We have already observed above, cols. 309 ff., that the arguments here advanced under the guidance of Maximus concerning the division of the sexes depart from the truth, where John Scotus expounded the same doctrine. Compare the discussion printed above on John Scotus, § 50, col. 75.]

The aforesaid Master makes this clear in the following words:

“For this reason the human being is introduced last among existing things, as a certain natural conjunction, universally making himself a middle point between the extremities through his own parts and bringing together in himself things that are far separated from one another in nature, so that, beginning from their prior division and then proceeding through the intermediaries by connection and order, he might receive in God—as the causal principle gathering all things into unity—the end of that lofty ascent, made from all things through unity, in which there is no division.”

[Col. 0531. Note: The words “as a certain conjunction … there is no division” are omitted in ABCD; they have been supplied from John Scotus’s translation of Saint Maximus’s *Ambigua*.]

“He,” namely, the human being, “being in no way dependent” [Col. 0531. Note: Instead of *pendens videlicet* (“being dependent”), C reads *pendet quippe* (“for he depends”); D reads *pendit quippe* (“for he hangs”)], “upon his primordial principle concerning the generation, according to the property of male and female, of the human being intended by God. In that utterly impassible union, extending the union throughout nature in relation to divine power, so that he might show [Col. 0531. Note: CD read *ostenderet* (“he might show”); A has the corrected reading *ostenderetur* (“it might be shown”)] that the future human being, according to the divine purpose, would not be divided merely according to the designation ‘male and female’ [Col. 0531. Note: D reads *masculum et feminam* (“male and female”); C’s version reads *feminam masculumque* (“female and male”)], by which he was also originally made; in the divisions now existing around him he would not be divided because of that perfect union with his own principle, through which he subsists.”

In these words he most clearly intimates the purpose of the divine counsel concerning the creation of humanity, if God had not foreknown that he would sin.

Humanity would have been created solely in the simplicity of its nature and multiplied intellectually, in the manner in which the holy angels were multiplied. [Col. 0531. Note: CD read *multiplicatus* (“multiplied”); A reads *multiplicaretur* (“would be multiplied”).]

But, overwhelmed by the guilt of his transgression, he suffered the division of his nature into male and female. And because he refused to observe the divine mode of his multiplication, by a just judgment he was reduced to a bestial and corruptible multitude arising from male and female. This division began to be united in Christ Jesus [Col. 0533. Note: CD read *Christo Jesu* (“Christ Jesus”); A omits *Jesu* (“Jesus”)], who truly displayed in himself the example of the restoration of human nature and provided the likeness of the resurrection to come.

### 77

“In the divisions,” he says, “now existing around him, he is not divided.”

By “divisions” he means, in the human being after sin, not only the division into male and female, but also the manifold varieties of qualities, quantities, and differences of one form. For the diversity of human beings from one another, by which each person’s appearance is distinguished from that of others and the measure of stature varies, does not arise from nature [Col. 0533. Note: AD read *provenit* (“arises”); C reads *pervenit* (“comes about”)], but from defect and from the diversity of places, times, lands, waters, airs, foods, and other such things in which they are born and nourished. It is unnecessary to speak of the diversity of morals and thoughts, since it is clear to everyone that it took its beginning from the division of Nature after sin.

“Because of that perfect union,” he says, “with his own principle through which he subsists.”

As though he were saying: Humanity would not suffer the division of its nature if it had not sinned, because it would remain inseparably attached to its perfect principles [Col. 0533. Note: CD read *perfectis* (“perfect”); A reads *perfecte* (“perfectly”).], namely, its primordial causes [Col. 0533. Note: A reads *causis videlicet* (“namely, causes”); D omits *causis* (“causes”)], in which it was created according to the image of God and in which it subsists, if it did not voluntarily tear itself away from them. It does not subsist in those things in which humanity now appears to exist, but is contained in the hidden causes of nature, according to which it was first created and to which it will return, insofar as it exists.

### 8

And because, after the union of humanity—that is, of the two sexes—into the original unity of nature, in which there was neither male nor female but simply a human being, the union of the whole world will immediately follow toward Paradise [Col. 0533. Note: CD reads *sequetur* (“will follow”); A reads *sequitur* (“follows”)], he says:

“Then, joining Paradise and the inhabited world through his own holy way of life, he would make one earth, not divided in him according to the difference of its parts, but rather gathered together, so that none of its parts would suffer any subtraction.”

This statement seems very obscure. For it is not readily apparent what he intends to suggest: whether the inhabited world, when all substances are united, will be joined to Paradise so that there will be no diversity of parts in them, but the whole will be Paradise—

[Col. 0533D–0534D. Marginal gloss: Here he raises the question whether the inhabited world will be entirely changed into Paradise, just as the sexes are changed into humanity, on the principle that lower things are absorbed by better things; or whether the inhabited world and Paradise will be united into the same kind of spiritual quality of earth, on the principle by which like things are fitted together.]

—for in the principle of union it is always necessary to observe that what appears to be lower should move into what is higher, that is, better, and not that what is better should pass into what is worse, that is, return in the renewal of natures. Otherwise it would not be union but division. True reason permits this conclusion, just as the union of human nature restores the division of the two sexes to the simplicity of humanity, because humanity is better than sex: “male” and “female” are not names of nature, but of its partition through transgression, whereas “human being” is the specific name of that nature—

or whether the inhabited world and Paradise will be joined to that one earth which is another species of sensible creation, divided into heaven and earth, so that the earth itself will be deprived not only of diversity of parts but also be restored to a certain simplicity of nature, so that it may be believed to be more spiritual than bodily, as it would have been if humanity had not sinned.

And let us understand what he says: “not separated in him,” that is, in the human being. For all things are united in humanity according to the difference of their parts, namely, of the earth, so that, just as there will be no diversity of parts in humanity, because no composition will remain in it, so also the earthly nature will be joined to it, appearing to be one in it and with it.

For he says: “but rather gathered together, so that none of its parts would suffer any subtraction,” that is, separation. Wherever true simplicity exists, there the diversity of no subtraction—that is, of separation—is found. [Col. 0533. Note: A reads *id est* (“that is”); the alternative reading is *videlicet* (“namely”).]

The following words appear most clearly to support this interpretation:

“Then, joining heaven and earth through the likeness to the angels in life wholly according to virtue, insofar as this is possible for human beings, he would make the sensible creation everywhere inseparable from itself, not separated in him”—that is, in the human being—“locally in spatial intervals, since the spirit would have become light and would not be held down by any bodily heaviness, nor prevented from ascending to the heavens, through that perfect ἀορασία (*aorasia*) of the soul with respect to these things—that is, through its transcendence or blindness—when it reaches God sincerely by a wise directing of its intention toward him.”

[Col. 0533. Textual notes: CD read *secundum virtutem* (“according to virtue”); A reads *et virtutum* (“and [according to] virtues”). CD read *unam faceret* (“would make one”); A reads *facere et* (“to make, and”). CD read *inseparabilem ubique* (“everywhere inseparable”); A has a corrected reading *et quae*. CD read *prohibito* (“having been prevented”); A reads *prohibita* (“having been prevented,” feminine).]

[Col. 0534D. Marginal gloss: *Aorasia* is interpreted as blindness, but not that deprivation of sight which is so called; rather, it is that darkness which envelops visible things so that they cannot appear to those who look at them.]

Here it is made clear that, when humanity is restored to the original grace of its nature, which it abandoned through transgression, it will gather every sensible creature lower than itself into unity with itself through the wondrous power of divine virtue, in the restoration

[Col. 0535A. Marginal note: Here he begins to approve the future union of all things not only in understanding but also in actuality.]

of humanity. For, as he himself says, while sincerely enduring ἀορασία (*aorasia*)—that is, ignorance of all creatures which it will wholly transcend—it will reach God and contemplate him in all things.

For the whole human being, he says, will become a light spirit and will not be held down upon the earth by any bodily heaviness, nor be prevented from ascending to the heavens.

“Then, joining intelligible and sensible things with these”—that is, with the unions of natures mentioned above—“he will unify creation through equality of knowledge with the angels, making all creation at once not separated in him according to knowledge and ignorance, but becoming equally and without distinction like the angels with respect to him, through the cognitive knowledge of the principles of things; through this knowledge the infinite outpouring of the gifts of true wisdom supervenes and grants to the worthy, insofar as is lawful, a pure, henceforth immediate, unknown, and uninterpretable knowledge of God.”

[Col. 0535. Note: D reads *ininterpretabilemque* (“and uninterpretable”); another reading is *ininterpretabilem* (“uninterpretable”).]

The profundity of this statement seems incomprehensible to me, especially where he says, “according to knowledge and ignorance, through cognitive knowledge equal to that of the angels.” And rightly so. For in the preceding passage he seemed to have suggested nothing other than the union into a certain unity of all sensible and intelligible things, so that nothing separable, nothing bodily, and nothing diverse would remain in them, but that, through a wondrous return, lower things would always pass into higher things.

Now, however, he seems to say that the union of natural substances exists only in the intellect, and not in the things themselves—that is, not in those things which, through generation, have received, according to the providence of the Creator, their variety in different genera, different forms, and infinite numbers, whether intelligible or sensible. For we understand the union of created substances in the angels to exist in no other way than through cognitive knowledge alone, and not through the gathering of the things themselves into one.

For they know the principles of all created natures in themselves under one certain mode of understanding, just as in a certain supremely wise human soul there is one and the same inseparable knowledge of diverse arts. Thus ignorance—whether in angels, for we read that some of them have not yet been cleansed of all ignorance, or in human beings—does not produce any separation of things, whereas cognitive knowledge becomes the cause of union.

For the intellect of things is truly the things themselves, as Saint Dionysius says: “The knowledge of things that are is the things that are.” Yet their primordial causes and principles are gathered into a certain union by the activity of understanding, not in reality itself.

But before we arrive at the theoretical treatment of this question, if anything is to be said about it, I think that what remains to be said concerning the union of things according to Maximus should first be set forth.

“And the end,” he says, “is, in all these things, uniting created nature with the uncreated through love.”

O the miracle of divine clemency toward us! The whole human being, in the whole universal compass of his being, will be made one and the same with the whole God according to the habit of grace. [Col. 0535. Note: CD read *ostendet* (“will show”); A reads *ostendetur* (“will be shown”).] For the human being will become wholly God, except for equality in essence, and will receive the whole God; from God himself, that is, he will possess God as the most singular reward of his ascent: God himself as the end of the motion of those who move, the firm and immutable state of those who are borne toward him, and the end and limit of every end, state, law, principle, intellect, and nature, existing as an infinite and boundless end and limit.

[Col. 0535. Note: CD read *Deus* (“God”); A reads *dicitur* (“is said”). CD read *ab ipso* (“from him”); A has the corrected reading *a seipso* (“from himself”).]

### 9

Accordingly, insofar as it is possible to understand from the words of the aforesaid master, among the primordial causes of things the human being was made in the image of God so that, being composed from every intelligible and sensible creature—as from diverse extremities—he might become one inseparable being and might be the middle point and union of all creatures. [Col. 0535. Note: CD read *diversis* (“diverse”); A reads *divisis* (“divided”).]

For there is no creature that cannot be understood in humanity; hence in the Sacred Scriptures humanity is also accustomed to be called “every creature.” For in the Gospel it is written: “Preach the Gospel to every creature”; and likewise in the Apostle: “Every creature groans and suffers in pain until now.” [Col. 0535. Note: AC read *congemiscit et dolet* (“groans and suffers in pain”); D reads *ingemiscit et parturit* (“groans and gives birth”).]

And if humanity had not sinned, there would not have been a division of the sexes in it, but it would have been simply human; the inhabited world would not have been separated from Paradise in it, but every earthly nature would have been Paradise in it—that is, a spiritual earth and way of life; heaven and earth would not have been separated in it, for it would have been wholly heavenly, and nothing earthly, heavy, or bodily would have appeared in it.

It would have existed and multiplied to the number predetermined by its creator, just as the angels both exist and have been multiplied. Sensible nature would not have been distinguished from intelligible nature in it, for it would have been wholly intellect, always and unchangeably cleaving to its Creator, and would in no way have departed from its primordial causes, in which it was created. Every creature created in it would have suffered no division in it.

But because the first human being failed to remain in such happiness, fell from it through pride, and the unity of human nature was dispersed into infinite partitions and varieties, divine clemency assumed a new human being, in whom the nature dispersed in the old human being would be restored to its original unity. He ordained that one born in the world from the world—that is, a human being from human beings—should be born for the sake of human beings.

Hence the same Maximus says:

“Since, therefore, the human being did not move naturally, as he was created, around his immutable proper principle—that is, God—but voluntarily and foolishly moved contrary to nature around those things beneath him, over which he had been divinely ordained to preside, he misused the natural power given to him for the union of separated things, through generation, for the very separation of the things that were to be united.

“Natures are renewed, and God becomes human, so that he may save the lost human being; and, joining together in himself universally the fissures of nature that are contrary to nature, and showing universally the principles previously marked out of those things that have been divided, by which the union of the separated is customarily brought about, he fulfills the great counsel of God and, recapitulating all things in himself—that is, gathering together the things in heaven and the things on earth, in whom they were also created—

“through this universal union of all things to himself, beginning from our division, becomes a perfect human being, from us and for us, having all our things perfect according to us; not through the consequence of marriage. By this, I think, he shows how another mode of the propagation of human beings into a multitude was known beforehand to God, if the first human being had kept the commandment and had not cast himself down into bestiality by the misuse of his own powers, being thrust into that division and partition of nature according to male and female.

“For humanity did not altogether need those things in order to come into being, as I have said; but although it is perhaps possible to exist without them, it is not necessary that they remain forever. For in Christ Jesus, says the divine Apostle, there is neither male nor female.”

### 10

Do you see how insistently he attributes the cause of the division of human nature to the sin of the first human being? “For although it is perhaps possible to exist without them,” he says, “it is not necessary that these things remain forever.”

As though he were saying plainly: If the human being had not sinned, he could have remained without the division of his nature. This did not come to him from nature, but occurred through sin. What necessity, then, compels that division to remain after the union of nature in its original dignity? Just as humanity could do without it before sin, so it will be able, after its restoration, to remain eternally without it.

But, so as not to pursue his words one by one, in which he most clearly teaches that the union of the whole creation—which would have occurred in the first human being had he not sinned—was accomplished in Christ when he rose, I shall introduce a few passages from many for the purposes of the present discussion.

First, therefore, he teaches that the Lord Jesus united in himself the division of nature—that is, male and female. For he rose from the dead not in bodily sex, but only as a human being; in him there is neither male nor female. Although he appeared to his disciples in the male sex in which he had been born from a virgin and in which he had suffered, he did so to confirm their faith in his resurrection. They would not otherwise have recognized him if they had not seen the form familiar to them; for they had not yet fully received the Holy Spirit, who taught them all things. [Col. 0537. Note: C reads *nondum siquidem* (“for they had not yet”); A and D read *nondum enim* (“for not yet”). CD read *pleniter* (“fully”); A reads *plenum* (“full”). All manuscripts read *acceperunt* (“received”).]

Then, after the resurrection, he joined our inhabited world to Paradise in himself. [Col. 0537. Note: CD read *copulavit* (“he joined”); A reads *colligant* (“they join”).] For, returning from the dead into Paradise, he lived in this world with his disciples, plainly showing them that Paradise is nothing other than the glory of the resurrection, which first appeared in him and which he will give to all his faithful. He also taught that our inhabited world does not differ from Paradise according to the principle of nature [Col. 0537. Note: AD read *a paradiso* (“from Paradise”); C omits *a* (“from”).], for they are not separated by nature, but by qualities, quantities, and the other varieties which, because of the general sin of the common human nature, have been superadded to this habitable earth for its punishment—or rather, also for correction and training.

[Col. 0538D. Marginal gloss: Here it is understood that Paradise is something other than human nature before sin and the sensible creature corresponding to it, had humanity not sinned.]

And because one earth, when it is established as itself, is inseparable, he preserves the principle of the nature in which it exists free from division according to difference. [Col. 0537. Note: C reads *liberam divisione* (“free from division”); AD read *liberam divisionem* (“free from separation”).] For Paradise is not distinguished from this inhabited world by mass or spatial intervals [Col. 0537. Note: CD read *non enim mole* (“not by mass”); A reads *non enim vel mole vel* (“not either by mass or”)], but by diversity of conduct and difference of blessedness.

The first human being, too, if he had not sinned, could have lived happily in the inhabited world, since one and the same principle exists in the principal causes of the inhabited world and of Paradise. [Col. 0537. Note: CD read *paradisi* (“of Paradise”); A reads *paradiso* (“in Paradise”).]

Our Lord most clearly manifested this in himself after the resurrection. For at the same time he was in Paradise, and in this earth, and remained with his disciples. [Col. 0537. Note: A reads *Deus* (“God”) instead of *Dominus* (“Lord”); AD omit *cum discipulis suis* (“with his disciples”).]

### 11

For we must not believe that he came from elsewhere locally in order to appear to his disciples and withdrew to another place when he was not appearing, since after the resurrection he had surpassed the nature of places and times not only in his divinity but also in his humanity. I would not readily believe that spiritual bodies are confined by place or time, any more than that they vary according to qualities, quantities, or descriptions of any form; for they are of the simplest nature.

This is especially inferred from the example of pure fire. Although it is diffused through all the bodies of the sensible world, it is of such subtlety that it is detained by no place, and yet it is recognized to manifest its operation in all things.

But at one and the same time, in one and the same place, he appeared to them for a time in the form in which he had suffered, in order to nourish their faith, until they were enlightened by the power of true knowledge with which they were afterward filled. [Col. 0539. Note: CD read *virtutem* (“power”); A reads *virtute* (“virtue”). CD read *perfusi* (“filled”); A reads *profusi* (“poured out”).]

When the interval of the momentary appearance had been completed, he immediately returned into the intellectual and invisible ἀορασία (*aorasia*) of the spiritual body—that is, into the invisibility which, as we have said, transcends every time and every place.

Or, what seems more credible, without in any way departing from the glory of the resurrection in place, time, quantity, or quality—for no one doubts that spiritual bodies are free from all these—he manifested himself to his disciples after the resurrection in the form in which he had appeared to the world while living in the world, for the salvation of the world. For human reasoning has no power where divine power alone prevails.

For when he himself says, “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age,” he sufficiently and plainly indicates that he is always and everywhere—not only according to the Word, by which he fills all things and is above all things, but also according to the flesh which he received into the unity of his substance or person, raised from the dead, and transformed into God—not locally or temporally, nor circumscribed in any way.

For in a wondrous and ineffable manner, and above all heavenly essences, he is with the Father according to his humanity, which has been united to the Father’s Word and is God; he governs the world everywhere and appears to those who love him, either invisibly or visibly; he does not abandon heaven and governs the world; he sits at the right hand of the Father, governing all things in the heights and ministering the salvation of human nature in the depths.

Do not, therefore, imagine Christ’s humanity as confined to a place, since after the resurrection it was transferred into divinity. Christ’s divinity is not in a place; therefore neither is his humanity. Understand the same way concerning time, quality, quantity, and circumscribed form. After the triumph of the resurrection, the whole humanity of Christ—that is, body, soul, and intellect—is devoutly believed and most purely understood to be free from all these things. He will lead his elect to the same glory after the catholic resurrection, who will be one in him and with him. [Col. 0539. Note: A reads *qui* (“who”); CD omit *qui*.]

Christ, therefore, was simultaneously in Paradise and in the world, showing that the world and Paradise have one natural principle, and uniting the world and Paradise in himself. For true reason does not consider and honor in this sensible world bodily masses extended through spaces, or the manifold varieties of its diverse parts, but its natural and primordial causes, united and most beautiful in themselves, to which it will return when its end comes and in which it will remain eternally.

We do not believe that the future end of this sensible world will be anything other than its return to God and to its primordial causes, in which it naturally subsists. [Col. 0539. Note: AD read *in Deum et in primordiales causas suas* (“to God and to its primordial causes”); C reads *in Deum et in suas causas* (“to God and to its causes”).]

Additional textual apparatus omitted from the draft: [Col. 0533] A has *terrae videlicet* for *terrae videlicet*; A omits *ulla* (“any”) in “none of its parts”; CD read *favere apertissime* (“seem most plainly to favour”), A *favere aptissime* (“seem most fittingly to favour”). CD read *omnem sensibilem inferiorem se creaturam* (“every sensible creature lower than himself”), A *et se inferiorem* (“and lower than himself”); AC read *in restitutione* (“in the restoration”), D *in resurrectione* (“in the resurrection”).

[Col. 0535] The note marked (a), printed at the foot of cols. 535–536 though its callout is absent from the text, is: “Here he begins to approve the future union of all things not only in understanding but also in reality.” CD read *secundum scientiam et ignorantiam* (“according to knowledge and ignorance”); A *et secundum scientiam et ignorantiam* (“and according to knowledge and ignorance”). CD read *naturalium substantiarum* (“of natural substances”), A *naturarum substantialium* (“of substantial natures”); CD *in ipsis rebus* (“in the things themselves”), A *rebus ipsis* (“in the things themselves”); CD *sapientissima humana anima* (“a supremely wise human soul”), A *humana sapientissima anima* (“a human, supremely wise soul”); D omits *et* (“and”) in “one and the same and inseparable knowledge.”

[Col. 0535–0537] A omits *terra atque* (“earth and”) in “a spiritual earth and way of life”; A alone reads *assumpsit* (“assumed”), while CD omit it. In Maximus’s following quotation, CD read *ipsa itaque* (“thus, by this very”), A *ipsa namque* (“for by this very”); CD *divisione* (“division”), A *diversione* (“turning aside”); A adds *et* in *ipsam et secundum masculum* (“that [division] and according to male”); CD read *divisionem* (“division”), A *divisione* (“by division”). CD read *persequar* (“I pursue”), A *persequamur* (“let us pursue”).

[Col. 0537–0538] In addition to the notes already retained, AD read *et* (“and”) in “qualities and quantities,” while A omits it; C read *liberam divisione* (“free from division”), AD *liberam divisionem* (“free [as] division”); CD read *aptissime* (“most fittingly”), A *apertissime* (“most plainly”); CD read *Dominus* (“Lord”), A *Deus* (“God”); AD omit *cum discipulis suis* (“with his disciples”).

[Col. 0537–0539] C reads *quum* (“when”), D *quoniam* (“since”), for *quando* (“when”); CD read *locorum ac temporum* (“of places and times”), A *locorum et temporum*; CD *loco temporeve* (“by place or time”), A *temporeque* (“and time”); C retains *eis* (“to them”) before “appeared,” AD omit it; A omits *in* (“into”) before *intellectualem*; all witnesses read *nemo qui dubitat* (“no one who doubts”); C reads *sane intellige* (“indeed, understand”), A *sane intelligitur* (“indeed, it is understood”), D *intellige sane* (“understand indeed”); CD order “quality, quantity,” A “quantity, quality.”

12. For, as reason teaches [Note: Col. 0539: A reads “teaches.”], this world would not break forth into various sensible species and diverse multiplicities of its parts if God had not foreseen the fall and destruction of the first human being, who abandoned the unity of his nature, so that, at least after his ruin, having been warned by such punishment, he might recognize his miserable destruction—from spiritual things to bodily, from eternal things to temporal, from incorruptible things to perishable, from the highest to the lowest, from a spiritual human being to an animal one, from a simple nature to the division of the sexes, and from angelic dignity and multiplication to shameful, brutish, and bodily corruptible generation—and might seek to return, through repentance, to the former state of his dignity [Col. 0540B], laying aside his pride and fulfilling the divine laws that he had transgressed.

For one must not believe that the most divine clemency of the Creator thrust the sinful human being into this world as though moved by some indignation [Note: Col. 0539: A reads “moved” (*commotam*); CD “moved” in the masculine (*commotus*)], or desiring some act of vengeance [Note: Col. 0539: A reads “desiring” (*cupidam*); CD “desirous” (*cupidus*)]; true reason shows that divine goodness is free from such affections. Rather, it was an act of ineffable instruction and incomprehensible mercy: the human being, who by the choice of free will had refused to preserve himself in the dignity of his nature, was to seek the grace of his Creator, instructed by his punishments; and through that grace, obedient to the divine commands that he had previously neglected in his pride, he was to return, cautious and watchful [Note: Col. 0539: CD read “cautious and watchful” (*cautus providusque*); A “and watchful” (*et providus*)], humble and mindful of his former negligence and proud fall, to his former state [Col. 0540C]. Thus, preserved by grace and by the free choice of his will [Note: Col. 0539: BC read “preserved by grace and by the free choice of his will”; A “with grace, his free choice of will having been preserved”; D “with grace”—“by” omitted—“his free choice of will having been preserved.”], he would not fall again, nor wish to fall, nor be able to fall.

But let us return to the unification of the natures in Christ. “Then,” says the aforesaid master, “through his assumption into heaven, he certainly unified heaven and earth [Note: Col. 0539: CD read “unified” (*unificavit*); A “vivified” (*vivificavit*)]; and when, returning into heaven with this earthly body—which is connatural with us, but had been changed into a spiritual substance—he manifested that all sensible nature exists as one. Then, passing consequently [Note: Col. 0539: CD read “consequently” (*consequenter*); A “he constituted intelligible things, consequently,” and so forth] through sensible and intelligible things, through all the heavenly, divine, and intellectual orders, he unified them with soul and body—that is, with our complete nature—showing in himself the coming-together of the whole creation, according to its most principal reason, perfectly inseparable and immovable. And the end of all these things, according to the understanding of humanity—that is, according to humanity itself—takes place in God himself [Note: Col. 0539: CD read “takes place” (*fit*); A “may take place” (*sit*)], appearing for us, as it is written, before the face of God the Father, insofar as he is human, though as the Word he can never in any way depart from the Father.

“First he unified us with ourselves in himself [Note: Col. 0539: CD read “he unified us” (*nos adunavit*); A has the words reversed (*adunavit nos*)], by removing the difference according to male and female; and in place of men and women [Note: Col. 0541: AD read “and for women”; C omits “for”], in whom the manner of division is especially apparent, he showed human beings alone, properly and truly, bearing a pure image that no mark of corruption touches in any way.

“Do you see how openly he declares that the human being, created in the image and likeness of God, was entirely without sexual difference, and that, insofar as the image and likeness of the Creator remains in him, he is still without it; and that the division itself arose solely in the body on account of sin?

“For although spiritual sexes are understood in the soul [Note: Col. 0541: C reads “are understood” (*intelligantur*); AD “are understood” (*intelliguntur*)]—νοῦς (*nous*), that is, the intellect, being in the soul like a male, while αἴσθησις (*aisthēsis*), that is, sense-perception, is like a female—we do not thereby recognize a separation of nature, but the mystery of Christ and the Church, and the contemplation of the one intellect directed toward the Creator and the creature.

“And with us and for us, embracing together the whole of creation through its middle terms, as though through the extremities of its own parts, he joined paradise and the terrestrial globe inseparably around himself: heaven and earth, sensible and intelligible things. For possessing, as we do, body, sense, soul, and intellect, he associated with each of these parts, one by one, the extremity universally connatural with it, and, in accordance with the manner previously set forth, divinely recapitulated all things in himself” [Note: Col. 0541: CD read “in himself” (*in se ipsum*); A “he himself” (*ipse*)].

13. Attend carefully [Note: Col. 0541: C reads “attentively” (*intentius*); AD “attentive” (*intentus*)] to the force of the words; they are not without power. “For,” he says, “Christ—that is, having body, sense [Note: Col. 0541: C reads “and sense”; A omits “and”; D reads “and sense”], soul, and intellect as we do.” Human nature is constituted by these four parts [Note: Col. 0541: AD read “human nature is constituted”; C “nature is constituted”]. The true human being, Christ, both assumed these parts and unified them in himself; for he became a perfect human being [Note: Col. 0541: CD read “he became”; A omits “he became”]. He left nothing belonging to humanity, except sin, that he did not receive into the unity of his substance and unify in himself—that is, make one. For after the resurrection there are not four things in him, but one; and not one composite thing, but simply one: body, sense, soul, and intellect.

“With these,” he says, “as though they were parts, associating with each one, singly, its universally connatural extremity.” As though he were saying plainly: Since Christ received the four parts of human nature and unified them in himself, it is clear that he assumed and unified in himself the whole of creation—that is, the intellectual and sensible creation. For the whole of creation was established in the human being whom he received in his entirety.

With each individual part, as he himself says, he associated its connatural extremity. He calls bodies and all visible things connatural extremities. These occupy the lower extremity of the whole creation and are mutually connatural; whereas, toward the higher side, all intellectual beings occupy the other extremity of creation and are likewise mutually connatural.

Thus, connatural extremities were joined to the individual parts of human nature—that is, natures connatural with them were associated in Christ. By assuming body, as it were the fourth part of the human being, he joined to himself the whole bodily creation. By assuming sense, he united to himself the whole sensible creation [Note: Col. 0541: D reads “universal” (*universalem*)] and everything that makes use of sense.

What should be said of the soul? In the soul that he assumed, did he not associate with himself not only the rational soul but also [Note: Col. 0541: A reads “and” (*et*)] the whole nutritive and augmentative life [Note: Col. 0541: conjecturally “augmentative” (*auctivam*); ACD read “active” (*activam*)]? No wise person doubts concerning the intellect [Note: Col. 0541: AC read “of the wise” (*sapientum*); D “of wise men”]; for all intellectual beings adhere inseparably to the human intellect that Christ assumed.

Do you not plainly see that all creation—the intelligible, the sensible, and the intermediate natures—has been unified in Christ?
