The master briefly concluded this [Note: Col. 0541: CD read “briefly concluded” (*conclusit*); A “concluded briefly” (*conclusit breviter*)] by saying: “Showing all creation, subsisting as one, completed, like a certain human being, by the coming-together of its parts with one another, and contemplating itself through the subsistence of the universe [Note: Col. 0541: C and Maximus’s *Ambigua* read “subsistence” (*subsistentiam*); ABD “substance” (*substantiam*)]; according to the one, simple [Note: Col. 0541: CD and Maximus’s *Ambigua* read “simple” (*simplam*); AB likewise has “simple” (*simplicem*)] and indefinable [Note: Col. 0541: BCD and Maximus’s *Ambigua* read “indefinable” (*indefinibilem*); A reads “and indefinable substance arising from it,” and so forth] knowledge arising from it, which is not derived by deduction and is undifferentiated; through this knowledge all creation can receive one and the same wholly undivided cause.”

Thus far, following the venerable master—Maximus, I mean—concerning the divisions and unifications of substances, we have spoken insofar as the subject of the present question requires. [Note: Col. 0541: The text of manuscript E begins again with the words, “Thus far concerning the divisions,” and so forth.] And now we must return to the matter at hand: to examine that form of universal nature which both is created and creates, and which is constituted in the primordial causes; for concerning this we proposed to speak in this book [Note: Col. 0541: A reads “in this first book”].

DISCIPLE. It would certainly seem appropriate, if you would explain more clearly certain points mentioned in the preceding arguments, since they greatly trouble me.

MASTER. Tell me what those points are among what I have said that trouble you greatly and for which you seem to be requesting a fuller explanation.

14. DISCIPLE. Nothing in the divisions of created substances according to Maximus troubles me or seems very obscure or ambiguous [Note: Col. 0541: CDE read “or”; A “nor”], except the division of the human being into male and female [Note: Col. 0541: CDE read “into”; A “between”], and the claim that this division arose not from the human being’s first creation in the image of God, but from the punishment of sin; and that, after the universal resurrection of all bodies [Note: Col. 0541: CDE read “after the universal resurrection”; A “after the resurrection of all bodies”], which will take place at the end of the world, this division will no longer remain, but will return to the unity of the primordial nature [Note: Col. 0541: A omits “condition”; C reads “earth” instead of “nature”].

For who, hearing such things, would not be terrified and immediately burst out with these words [Note: Col. 0543: CE read “burst out”; A “break forth”; D “burst out in words”]: “Then after the resurrection there will be no sex of males and females [Note: Col. 0543: CDE read “of males and females”; A “of males and of females”], if each sex is to be entirely removed from human nature [Note: Col. 0543: CE read “entirely removed from human nature”; A “entirely removed from human nature”; D “removed entirely from human nature”]!

“Or what form will appear in a human being if no one possesses the form of a male or of a female? Or what kind of knowledge can there be if the extinction of both sexes is to occur, and all human beings are to be fused into a simple, undifferentiated union of forms, whether spiritual and incorporeal or visible [Note: Col. 0543: AD read “visible”; C “sensible”] and corporeal, circumscribed by place and time [Note: Col. 0543: E omits the words ‘whether visible … by place and time’]?

“You have also left this unresolved and undiscussed, although you seem to argue that spiritual qualities and quantities, rather than bodily ones, will exist in the bodies of the resurrection [Note: Col. 0543: CDE read “qualities and quantities”; A reverses the order]. Not to mention how much this doctrine resists the authority of all, or nearly all, the holy masters of the Latin tongue, who unanimously assert that after the resurrection of all, the integrity of both sexes will exist, so that a man will return in the form of a man and a woman in the form of a woman, with all the marks of the bodily parts by which the two sexes are especially distinguished; and thus each will remain eternally either in glory or in punishment—if indeed eternal punishment is to be bodily, just as eternal glory is. We shall treat this question in the fifth book [Note: Col. 0543: CDE read “concerning which”; A “but concerning this”]. For many consider it incongruous to believe that misery will be coeternal with blessedness; and they think that the Gospel contradicts this when it says: ‘Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.’

“These matters, as I said, trouble me especially in the divisions of substances made by God that have been mentioned. As for the return and unification, I confess universally that whatever you have already said seems harsh and obscure to me. For I do not clearly see how the unification in Christ of human nature in both sexes was first accomplished in him when he rose from the dead, and how it will occur in all human beings at the end of the world.

“For we believe that Christ rose in the same sex in which he lived in the flesh, and that he always remains and will remain in it. Who, moreover, will deny that he had been clothed in the male sex before he suffered and rose [Note: Col. 0543: A reads “that he would be clothed”; CDE “that he was clothed”]? Likewise, we believe that all human beings will rise in the same sex in which they fall.

“How, then, will the terrestrial globe be joined to paradise, earth to heaven, all sensible creation to intelligible creation, and all these things to God, so that they may be one and no diversity appear in them? And especially the matter that you promised to explain: how will the return and unification of all the substances mentioned take place in one?

“Will it occur in reality—that is, through the passage of all sensible things into intellectual things—so that, when the course of this sensible world has been completed, all things will be spiritual and nothing corporeal or sensible will remain? Or will it occur only through the mind’s contemplation of the natural unity of all things in their reasons and primordial causes?

“For those things that appear externally to bodily sense as diverse and multiple through places, times, qualities, quantities, and the other differences of sensible nature, in their reasons—according to which they were created by the Creator of all and subsist in the immutable condition of their nature and according to the fixed laws of divine providence—appear, and are, to the pure intellect that seeks, discovers, and contemplates the truth of all things, as one indivisible thing [Note: Col. 0543: CDE read “appear as one indivisible thing”; A “appear to be one indivisible thing”].

“For just as external natures—I mean sensible and bodily ones [Note: Col. 0543: The tradition also has “corporeal”—vary through places, times, and the other accidents—for in these their beauty chiefly delights, and therefore they are loved immoderately and luxuriously by carnal minds, which are far from truth and unity and dispersed into the multiplicity of temporal things—so inner natures, that is, intelligible beings, display in themselves and among themselves the simple and indivisible unity of their nature inseparably [Note: Col. 0543: ACE read “inseparably”; D “indivisible”] and thereby delight the minds of the wise, who contemplate their beauty, harmony, and fellowship.

“To those returning from the unstable and diverse variety of places and times, the contemplation of unchanging unity and truth alone is promised as a reward.

“I do not think that the heavenly powers whom Sacred Scripture names by various names should be believed to behold this visible world externally through bodily senses [Note: Col. 0543: CDE read “to behold this visible world”; A “through this visible world”]. Yet they must not be thought entirely ignorant of it, since sacred history teaches that all visible things are ruled and administered through them [Note: Col. 0543: CDE read “sacred history”; A “Scripture”]. The divine laws were administered through angels; the customs of good people were corrected, ordered, recalled from wicked paths, exercised by the manifold teachings of divine providence, and brought back to the former condition of nature.

“But they perceive, insofar as they are permitted, this world that they govern in its eternal causes, which they themselves contemplate eternally—not divided by intervals of place, not distinguished by the various movements of times, not dispersed in the multiplicity of its parts, not rendered unlike through the manifold differences of qualities and quantities, not swollen by the magnitude of its mass, not stretched out through differing spaces of length, breadth, and height [Note: Col. 0545: AE read “length, breadth, and height”; C “length, height, and breadth”; D “length and height,” omitting “breadth”—but subsisting as a whole, simply and immutably, in its reasons.

“Therefore, concerning these obscure questions, which I cannot myself perceive fully and distinctly, I think that you should distinguish them for me more lucidly [Note: Col. 0545: A omits “should be.”]. Nevertheless, I leave it to your judgment in what order they should be disclosed; I merely wish to grant you the choice, provided that they are disclosed, whether now or later.”

MASTER. The order of the subject requires another occasion for discussing all those matters which, as you say, are not clear to you [Note: Col. 0545: D reads “which are not clear to you”; CE “which, as you say, are not clear to you”; A has the same words in a reversed order]. But here we must briefly anticipate them, since all these matters that seem difficult to you can be brought together under one argument.

“If Christ, who understands all things—indeed, who is the intellect of all things—unified in reality everything that he assumed, who could doubt that what preceded in the head and principal exemplar of the whole of human nature will follow in the whole of humanity, as we shall discuss in the fifth book [Note: Col. 0545: A reads “from” (*ex*) instead of “and” (*et*)]?”

“For the text of this present book demands nothing else from us than that, insofar as our powers permit, we discuss the primordial causes, whatever light may have been granted to our minds.”

15. DISCIPLE. Proceed in whatever order you wish. For I think that the questions now before us, concerning the fourfold division of universal nature, should appropriately be explained in the order in which they have been proposed.

MASTER. I think that the beginning of the reasoning must be taken from the divine utterances.

DISCIPLE. Nothing could be more fitting; for it is necessary that every inquiry into truth take its beginning from them.

MASTER. The most divine prophet—I mean Moses [Note: Col. 0545: C reads “Moses” (*Moyse*); DE “Moyses” (*Moysea*)]—says at the very beginning of the book of Genesis [Note: Col. 0545: A “at the beginning of the book”]: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

At this point all the interpreters of Sacred Scripture have exercised the acuity of their intellect, explaining, through diverse modes of understanding, what the prophet—or rather, what the Holy Spirit through the prophet—intended to signify by the name “heaven” and by “earth.”

Some judge that these words convey a brief summary of the whole of perfect creation. By the name “heaven,” they believe that the entire spiritual and intellectual creation, created and formed, is indicated; by the designation “earth,” the whole bodily and sensible creation, established through its most perfect definitions.

Others attempt to show that the formlessness of both creations is suggested: that of the spiritual creation by the name “heaven,” and the beginning of this bodily world by the designation “earth.”

Others affirm that these words indicate the creation of the whole sensible creation, which is completed as if through two principal parts—I mean heaven and earth [Note: Col. 0545: CDE read “heaven and earth”; A “and heaven and earth”—so that nothing concerning the condition of the spiritual creation is signified here, but that the prophet wished to describe only the fullness of bodily creation.

Between these two parts—I mean heaven and earth [Note: Col. 0545: ACE read “heaven and earth”; D “I mean heaven and earth”]—as between certain extreme boundaries, separated from one another but joined through their middle regions, they teach that the universe of this sensible world has been composed and unified by a certain natural harmony according to definite principles.

But it would be lengthy and unsuitable to the purpose of the present work to extend the discussion through the many and varied opinions of different people; and, except where the greatest necessity demands it, it will seem superfluous to introduce the interpretations of others concerning such a matter.

For my part, as I consider the opinions of many, nothing more probable or more credible occurs to me than that in the aforesaid words of Sacred Scripture—namely, in the meaning of “heaven” and “earth”—we should understand the primordial causes of the whole creation, which the Father had created in his only-begotten Son, who is called “the Beginning,” before all things that were created.

We should take the name “heaven” to signify the principal causes of intelligible and heavenly beings, and the designation “earth” to signify the principal causes of sensible things, by which the whole of this bodily world is completed [Note: Col. 0545: CDE read “we should understand”; A “let us understand”].

DISCIPLE. I too would choose this interpretation before the others [Note: Col. 0545: CDE read “I would choose”; A “I would have chosen”], if I were not somewhat troubled by the ambiguity that seems to arise in the distinctions among the interpretations just mentioned.

For, as it seems to me, there is little or no difference between those who say that the formlessness of each nature—I mean the intelligible and the sensible—is indicated by the aforesaid words of Scripture, and those who judge that the primordial causes of intelligible and sensible things are described by those words.

For we say that formless matter and its formlessness are a certain cause of things. In it they begin to exist, although formlessly—that is, still imperfectly and almost not at all [Note: Col. 0545: A reads “not at all”]; yet they are not understood to be absolutely nothing, but in some way to be a beginning and to desire form and perfection.

MASTER. Be more attentive, then, and discern the differences among things sharply; drive the clouds of ambiguity completely from the edge of your attention. For, as I think, it cannot escape you that there are formlessnesses of things of one kind, and causes and perfect principles of things of another.

If being and non-being are opposed to one another as contraries [Note: Col. 0545: CDE read “are opposed as contraries”; A “are opposed contrarily”], and if nothing is closer to true being than the causes of created things, while nothing is nearer to not truly being than formless matter—for, as Augustine says, the formless is almost nothing—does the distance between that which is close to true essence and that which is close to the privation of true essence, which is called absolutely nothing, seem small to you [Note: Col. 0545: A reads “which is called to be the nearest”; CDE “which is called nothing whatsoever”]?

Nor did we say that the formlessness of things is the cause of the essence, form, and perfection of things, but rather that it is the privation of their essence, form, and perfection.

For a cause, if it truly is a cause [Note: Col. 0547: A reads “if it is a cause”], anticipates within itself, most perfectly, everything of which it is the cause; it perfects its effects within itself before they appear in anything. And when they burst forth through generation into visible genera and forms, they do not abandon their perfection in that cause, but remain fully and immutably in it and require no other perfection except that one in which they subsist once and simultaneously and always [Note: Col. 0547: C omits “and”].

DISCIPLE. Such a difference certainly does not seem small to me. The primordial causes, created most perfectly in their immutable reasons by the one and highest principle of all, which itself is from no other, are far removed from the formlessnesses of all things. The latter not only have not yet attained the perfection of form, but are scarcely beginning to be and have not moved far from non-being.

Although the formlessnesses of things seem to occupy an intermediate position between being and non-being—beginning to be from non-being [Note: Col. 0547: CDE read “beginning to be from non-being”; A “beginning from non-being to be”—that is, beginning a certain procession from non-being toward being—and are therefore understood not yet to have attained the perfection of form and essence—they are nevertheless judged to approach non-being more closely than being [Note: Col. 0547: E omits the words “to approach … being”].

For the formlessness of things is nothing other than a certain movement that does not wholly abandon non-being and seeks its own state in that which truly is.

The primordial causes, however, were created in the Beginning—that is, in the Word of God, which is truly called “being” and truly is—in such a way that they seek their perfection through no movement toward anything except that in which they exist, immutably and perfectly formed.

For they are always formed by turning toward the one form of all things, which all things desire—I mean the Father’s Word—and they never abandon their formation [Note: Col. 0547: CE read “never abandon” (*nusquam deserunt*); AD omit “never”]. The causes of places and times are in them; but the things that are beneath them, in the lower orders of things, are created by them in such a way that they draw those things toward themselves and that all things desire one principle.

The causes themselves, however, do not look in any way toward the things beneath them. Rather, they always contemplate their superior form, so that they may never cease to be formed by it. For in themselves they are formless, and they recognize themselves as perfectly created in that universal form of theirs—in the Word, I mean.

But who possessing right understanding would dare to say of the formlessness of things what can be said of the primordial causes, especially since the formless matter of things is believed to proceed from nowhere other than the primordial causes [Note: Col. 0547: A reads “from the primordial causes”; CDE “from causes primordial”]?

If the primordial causes are called primordial because they were first created by the one cause that creates all things and create the things that are beneath them—for we have said that the primordial causes are both created and create [Note: Col. 0547: CDE read “we have said”; A “we said”]—what is surprising if, just as we believe and establish by definite arguments that formless matter belongs among the things created afterward and through the primordial causes [Note: Col. 0547: DE read “and through”; A and C omit “through”], we also admit that it is created by the primordial causes?

16. MASTER. There is therefore one understanding of the primordial causes and another of formless matters [Note: Col. 0547: CDE read “one understanding of the primordial causes”; A reverses the word order].

DISCIPLE. The preceding arguments compel us to grant this. Consider the remaining points.

MASTER. Likewise, different people transmit different interpretations of what follows: “But the earth was formless and empty,” or, according to the Septuagint, “invisible and uncomposed,” “and darkness was over the face of the abyss” [Note: Col. 0547: A continues “and darkness was over …”].

Some wish the designation “formless and empty earth,” or “invisible and uncomposed,” to signify figuratively the formlessness of visible creation, while the designation “dark abyss” signifies the formlessness of invisible essence.

For every bodily and sensible creature is constituted from matter and form. Therefore matter lacking form is called formless—that is, lacking form—and invisible and uncomposed, or empty and vacant. When form is added, it is called visible and composite, solid and perfect, circumscribed by the definite limits of its nature.

Invisible creation, that is, intellectual and rational creation, is called formless before it turns toward its form, namely, its Creator. For it is not sufficient for its perfection to subsist from essence and essential difference; intellectual creation is composed of these two things. Unless it is perfected by turning toward the Word, that is, the only-begotten Son of God [Note: Col. 0547: A reads “the Son of God, I mean”; CDE “I mean the Son of God”], who is the form of all intellectual life, it remains imperfect and formless.

Others believe that the expression “empty and vacant earth,” or “invisible and uncomposed earth,” refers to this mass of earthly body created at the beginning. It was empty and vacant, as they think, because it had not yet been adorned with the various genera and forms of seeds, plants, and animals. It was invisible either because an abundance of watery nature had been poured over it everywhere, or because the human being who could behold it had not yet burst forth through generation from the primordial causes.

They say that darkness was over the abyss because the air, which had surrounded the abyss on every side, was not yet luminous and therefore could not yet illuminate the abyss established within it [Note: Col. 0547: CDE read “because”; A “which”].

Although Saint Augustine may seem to oppose this interpretation, we do not altogether refute it, since it is that of Saint Basil. It is not our task to judge the interpretations of the holy Fathers, but to receive them piously and reverently [Note: Col. 0547: CDE read “to judge”; A “to judge” with variant spelling]. Nevertheless, we are not forbidden to choose what seems, upon rational consideration, to agree more closely with the divine utterances.

But if someone says that the prophet’s aforesaid words indicate nothing other than the primordial causes of things, he will not seem to depart from the truth [Note: Col. 0549: ACE read “will not seem”; D “will not seem to”].

For what of it? Is it incredible that the πρωτότυπον (*prōtotypon*), that is, the principal exemplar, of bodily nature, which is signified by the name “earth,” and which God had established before this sensible world, eternally and most perfectly, in the Beginning—that is, the Father in the Son—could be called empty and vacant?

It was empty because it was devoid of every sensible thing in its effects before it emerged through generation into the genera and forms of sensible nature, in places and times.

It was vacant because the prophetic intellect, introduced into the divine mysteries, had not yet perceived in it any quantity, anything dense with bodily mass, anything dispersed through places, or anything moving through times [Note: Col. 0549: ACE read “in it”; D “in her”].

For these terms—“vacant” and “empty”—signify more fully the immutable perfection of the primordial nature created in the Word before all things than the still mutable and imperfect emergence of this sensible world, as yet formless, dispersed through places and times, beginning to exist through generation, and desiring to be formed through the various numbers of sensible creation.

Indeed, “vacant” and “empty” are often used even in praise of bodily things. The whole space that lies between the globe of the earth, the courses of the stars, and the outermost circumference of the world has been divided by the sages of the world and by divine Scripture into two parts [Note: Col. 0549: CDE read “has been divided”; A “is divided”].

The lower part, from the earth up to the moon, is called air—that is, spirit. The upper part, from the moon to the stars of the outermost sphere, is called ether—that is, pure spirit. Both are called κῦφος (*kyphos*) by the Greeks [Note: Col. 0549: A reads κοῦφα (*koupha*)], and by the Latins “empty” or “vacant.”

That upper space, purer and brighter, is known to be perpetually serene and quiet in eternal silence, except for the harmonious consonances of the planets [Note: Col. 0549: A reads “songs and consonances”], which surpass every mortal and earthly sense in the sharpness of tones and semitones [Note: Col. 0549: A reads “tones and semitones”; CDE “tones and semitone”]. It glides through the movements of the most subtle fire and is full of enduring light, except for the small portion occupied by the earth’s shadow, which is called night. Therefore it is called empty.

Nor is this without reason, since it is free from every dense and earthly mass [Note: Col. 0549: CE read “earthly”; AD “earth”] and is filled by no bodily weight. The spheres of the planets are exceedingly light [Note: Col. 0549: A reads “the light spheres of the planets”] and spiritual; they are burdened by no earthly quality and produce no darkness.

The moisture of the moon, and the stains that appear upon it, arise not from the purity of its own nature but from the vapors of the earthly mass, which the Greeks call ἀτμίδες (*atmidēs*), and from the proximity of the watery abyss [Note: Col. 0549: CE read “arise”; AD “arises”].

Likewise, the cloudiness and darkness of this denser, lower air arise not from the air itself but from its proximity to the waters and the earth. From the same source from which the moon’s moisture arises comes the air’s nebulosity, as well as thunder and lightning [Note: Col. 0549: DE read “thunder and lightning”; AC “thunder and lightning” joined together], showers, rains, snow, frost, and the various blasts of winds [Note: Col. 0549: A reverses “blasts of winds”]. They receive their origin from nowhere else than from earthly and watery vapors.

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

## 17

What wonder, then, if the primordial causes of visible things are figuratively intimated under the name “earth, empty and void,” on account of the extreme subtlety and ineffable simplicity of their intellectual nature, before they flowed forth through generation into genera, forms, and sensible numbers, in which they appear to bodily senses as though in certain corporeal mists? For the aforesaid regions of the visible world, because of their subtlety and almost incorporeality, are not improperly called empty or void, as one of the poets says:

> “Through the empty air you will hurl a body in a leap.”

Virgil likewise, in the twelfth book:

> “Then the very stone, rolled through the empty void.”

The same reasoning applies to the other interpretation, which says that the earth was invisible and unformed. For what could this invisibility of the mystical earth signify more reasonably than the obscurity of the primordial causes of corporeal creation, not yet disclosed by any light of color or distinction of forms, and, moreover, surpassing the purest intellects?

The primordial causes are also rightly declared to be unformed; for they are simple and entirely devoid of every composition. In them there is an ineffable unity and an inseparable, uncompounded harmony, surpassing the joining together of universally differing or similar parts.

What shall I say of the principal causes of intellectual essence? Were they not most appropriately called by the Holy Spirit “the dark abyss”? They are called an abyss because of their incomprehensible depth and their infinite diffusion throughout all things, which no sense perceives and no intellect comprehends; and, because of the excellence of their ineffable purity, they deserved to be called “darkness.” Indeed, even this sensible sun often imposes darkness upon those who gaze at it, because they cannot behold the brilliance of its excellence.

Thus darkness was over the abyss of the primordial causes. For before they proceeded into the multiplicity of spiritual essences, no created intellect could know what they were. And darkness is still over this abyss, because it is perceived by no intellect except the one who formed it in the beginning. From its effects—that is, from its processions into intelligible forms—it is known only that it is, not what it is.


## 18

But whether that mystical invisible earth, that very dark abyss, and the intellectual nature of the first causes will remain perpetually invisible, and whether the dark abyss will endure eternally—or whether at some point, that is, after the end of this visible world, they will come into the knowledge of intellectual and rational essences—requires no small investigation.

**DISCIPLE.** Rather, the greatest investigation. And, lest you pass over this matter untouched, I earnestly beg you to address it.

**MASTER.** Tell me, then, please: what seems to you to be the case? Do the primordial causes of things—which we believe are signified by the names “earth” and “abyss,” and which, because of their incomprehensible and surpassing height, are called invisible and dark—cease to be invisible and incomprehensible when, through generation, they proceed into genera and forms, into numbers and differences of things comprehensible either to sense or to intellect? Or do they remain in the excellence of their nature in which they were created before all things in the beginning, falling under neither sense nor intellect, so that they appear in some manner in the things whose causes they are, whether to the senses or to the intellect, yet do not abandon the height of their incomprehensibility, but, as it were, always sit in a kind of darkness—in the most secret recesses, I mean, of divine wisdom?

**DISCIPLE.** I would believe that they remain perpetually invisible and dark. For if the very wisdom of God the Father, in which all things were made and truly subsist, and outside which nothing is understood to exist, remains incomprehensible and invisible in itself—for it is inaccessible light, surpassing every intellect—what wonder if the causes of all things, which were made in it, through it, and toward it, are believed to be eternally invisible and incomprehensible, and to remain unchangeably so?

We can infer this also from the example of our own nature. Whatever our intellect first rationally conceives within itself and brings to the state of pure and perfect understanding, it always retains within itself and brings forth outwardly through certain signs. For example, if a wise mind has apprehended true knowledge of something sensible or intelligible, that knowledge remains fixed within it; and it does not cease to bring forth first images into cognition, then into the senses, then into vocal signs and other gestures by which the mind habitually discloses its hidden operations as they gradually descend, and presents them to the knowledge of other minds through natural and artificial progressions.

**MASTER.** The principal causes, then, both proceed into the things whose causes they are and do not leave their beginning—that is, the Father’s wisdom—in which they were made. Thus, remaining in themselves invisible, always hidden in the darkness of their excellence, and brought forth in their effects as into a certain light of knowledge, they do not cease to appear.

**DISCIPLE.** This can plausibly be maintained. But we wish to know whether the principles of things, which are called by the name of primordial causes, understand themselves before they flow into the things themselves whose causes they are, or not.

**MASTER.** The answer must be brief. If God made all things that he made in his wisdom, as Scripture testifies when it says, “You made all things in wisdom,” who is permitted to doubt that everything made in wisdom knows itself as wisdom itself knows itself, and that what has been made in it not only knows itself but also lacks no knowledge of the things whose principles it is? For it must not be believed that anything foolish and ignorant of itself was created in divine wisdom. But these matters must be considered more carefully elsewhere.

**DISCIPLE.** So be it. For if the primordial causes know themselves, since they were created in wisdom and eternally subsist in it, which admits nothing foolish into itself, the question requires no brief or passing investigation: how do many foolish things proceed from wise causes? For not everything that flows forth from them is wise.

We believe that two natures participate in wisdom: the intellectual nature in angels and the rational nature in human beings. But we consider the rest—whatever can be comprehended by the senses or by the intellect—to be without wisdom. Although one might answer briefly that it is not surprising for the causes of foolish things to subsist in wise exemplars, since we see that opportunities for darkness naturally exist in the rays of the sun: while the rays themselves allow no darkness to exist within them, they nevertheless generate darkness from causes inherent in them, as though darkness were opposed to them.


## 19

**DISCIPLE.** What, then, does what follows mean: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters”? Was this perhaps added lest anyone think that the primordial causes surpass not only the power of intellectual and rational creation but also the intelligible knowledge of their Creator, because of the excessive excellence of their nature?

“And the Spirit,” he says, “of God was borne over the waters.” It is as though he said: The infinite and incomprehensible abyss of the primordial causes, and therefore one rightly called invisible and dark, does not so escape every intellect and reason through the height of its obscurity that it cannot also be comprehended and surpassed by the Spirit of God. For God made them in the beginning as certain foundations and principles of all the natures that exist from him, and by his infinitely transcendent knowing power he comprehended them; and his Spirit is borne over them, not by a movement through space but by the eminence of knowledge.

It may also be said in this way: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” For we ought not to believe that the primordial causes are of such excellence that no higher cause precedes them, one that surpasses them. There is one and the same cause of all things, from which, through which, in which, and toward which the causes and antecedent occasions of all things were first made. Scripture therefore rightly testifies that it is borne over all things, because it precedes the order of the entire creation that begins from it and ends in it.

This does not mean that one thing was created earlier and another later in time; for all things are eternally in it simultaneously and at once, and were made by it. Rather, through an ineffable and incomprehensible order, divine providence brought the whole of created nature from nonexistence into existence, with some things preferred to others by a certain essential dignity. Thus those things that are believed and understood to be nearest and most immediate to the universal cause of all things—I mean God—with no superior creature intervening, are rightly declared to be the most principal principles of the created universe. Then other things descend from others, from the highest to the lowest—that is, from the beginning of intellectual creation down to the lowest of all, which is body.

The Spirit of God, therefore, is borne over the dark abyss of all the primordial causes that were first made, because the Creator alone surpasses the created causes by the excellence of his knowledge. He is the one and only prior and transcendent cause of all the causes he created, and the most principal fountain of all things that flow forth from him into infinity and return into him; and, if this is properly understood of the Holy Spirit, he proceeds from no other than the Father. For from the Father is the Son, through ineffable generation, in whom, as in the beginning, he made all things; and from the Father is the Holy Spirit, through procession, who is borne over all things. The Father wills, the Son makes, and the Holy Spirit perfects.

Nor does this seem contrary to the theology that says that the Father made all things in the Son. For it is not one thing for the Father to will that all things be made and another for the Father to make all things in the Son; rather, the Father’s willing and the Father’s making are one and the same, for his action is his will. The same must likewise be understood of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Their operation is nothing other than their will. The Father’s will is not one, the Son’s another, and the Holy Spirit’s another; rather, there is one and the same will, one love of the three substances of one essential goodness, by which the Father moves himself to make all things in the Son and to perfect them in the Holy Spirit.

Whatever the Son makes and the Holy Spirit perfects is wholly referred to the Father, who makes and perfects, because all things are from him. For from him is the Son through generation, who makes all things; from him is the Holy Spirit through procession, who perfects all things. The supreme Trinity is understood to exist from those things that exist, is known to be wise from those things that are wise, and is most clearly demonstrated to live from those things that move. It therefore exists, is wise, and lives.

But if, as a certain Syrian is said to have translated it—the one who, as Saint Basil says, withdrew from worldly wisdom as much as he drew near to the teaching of truth—it is read in this way: “And the Spirit of God cherished the waters,” the meaning becomes easier. For the Holy Spirit cherished the primordial causes that the Father had made in the beginning, namely, in his Son, so that they might proceed into the things whose causes they are; that is, he nourished them by the warmth of divine love.

For eggs are cherished by birds—from which this metaphor is taken—in order that the inner and invisible power of the seeds hidden within them may burst forth, through the measures of places and times, into visible forms and bodily beauties, with fire and air operating in the moisture of the seeds and in earthly matter.


## 20

**DISCIPLE.** Nor does this conflict with sound understanding. But I would like you to give me a brief and lucid ἀνακεφαλαίωσις—that is, a recapitulation—so that I may understand more clearly and distinctly which words of the sacred Scripture mentioned above specifically signify the primitive causes of things and the cause of all causes.

**MASTER.** Attend, then, more carefully to what follows.

**DISCIPLE.** I am attentive.

**MASTER.** Understand that the primitive causes, which Saint Dionysius calls the principles of all things, are signified simply and generally by these words: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” That is, God established in his intelligible Word the universal causes of intelligible essences and sensible things.

But the prophet wished to divide specifically what he had stated generally. Recognize, therefore, that the causes of sensible things from which this world is composed—uncontemplable by the eyes of the mind because of the excessive subtlety of their nature, and entirely free from every corporeal density because of their extraordinary purity—are intimated by these words: “But the earth was invisible and unformed.” Thus the Septuagint translated it; or, according to the Hebrew truth: “But the earth was empty and void.”

Next, know that the primitive principles of heavenly and invisible essences, surpassing every intellect by the great height, subtlety, and obscurity of their constitution, are introduced in the words shared by both interpretations: “And darkness was over the abyss.” The supplied apparatus records A’s variant “over the waters.”

Because the cause of all things, the principle of all principles, and the singular fountain from which all things in heaven and on earth flow forth, surpasses and transcends in the inaccessible and incomprehensible excellence of its light all that it established in the primordial causes, observe that its superessentiality and surpassing excellence are intimated by these words: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.”

For what theology specifically said concerning the Holy Spirit, sound faith both believes and understands generally concerning the supreme and holy Trinity. The holy and inseparable Trinity is borne infinitely above the abyss it created, by the excellence of its essence and wisdom.

If, however, you choose to follow that Syrian whom Saint Basil greatly praises in his *Hexaemeron*, who, instead of what the other translators rendered—namely, “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters”—translated it from the Syriac language, which is close to Hebrew, as “And the Spirit of God cherished the waters,” or “And the Spirit of God fertilized the waters,” you will find divine compassion, surpassing the dark abyss of the primordial causes by the height of its clemency and cherishing and fertilizing it, intimated in these words. Thus, from the hidden and unknown recesses of their nature, they might proceed through generation into the capacity for knowledge, and through a manifold procession into the various genera, forms, and proper species of sensible and intelligible substances, into their varied and innumerable effects.

Understand also that the supreme and singular cause of all things—I mean the holy Trinity—is openly declared in these words: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”: by the name “God,” the Father; by the designation “beginning,” his Word; and shortly afterward, the Holy Spirit, where it says: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” For sacred Scripture did not speak this passage of any other spirit.

Behold, then, the primordial causes and the cause of causes openly and distinctly declared in the theological words mentioned above, if I am not mistaken.

**DISCIPLE.** I understand perfectly, and gladly accept that the Father is signified by the name “God,” the Son by the designation “beginning,” and the Holy Spirit by “the Spirit of God”; that by the name “earth” the causes of visible things are indicated; that by “abyss” the causes of intelligible things are indicated; and that the transcendence of the divine nature—that is, the height of the cause of causes—is presented through the symbol of being borne over, or of cherishing, or of fertilizing.

**MASTER.** Before, then, we proceed to consider the primordial causes, distinguished by theology according to the sixfold number, into six intelligible first days, I think that a few things should be said about the first and supreme cause of all things—I mean the holy Trinity—if that seems good to you.

**DISCIPLE.** I could seek nothing more eagerly, hear nothing more gladly, believe nothing more healthfully, or understand nothing more deeply than what is said through true and probable investigations concerning the ineffable source of all things. For the salvation of faithful souls consists in nothing else than believing what is truly proclaimed about the one principle of all things and understanding what is truly believed.

**MASTER.** Tell me, then, please: what do you understand when you hear theology say, “In the beginning God made”?

**DISCIPLE.** Nothing other than what we agreed among ourselves: that the Father made all things in his Word. When I hear “God,” I think of God the Father; when I hear “beginning,” I understand God the Word.

**MASTER.** What does the Theologian mean when he says, “In the beginning God made”? Do you understand it to mean that the Father first begot his Word and afterward made heaven and earth in him? Or did he eternally beget his Word and eternally make all things in it, so that in no way does the procession of the Word from the Father through generation precede the procession of all things from nothing in the Word through creation?

To state it more clearly: were the primordial causes not always in the Word of God, in whom they were made, and was there a time when the Word existed while the causes did not? Or are they coeternal with him, so that the Word never existed without the causes created in him, and the Word is understood to precede the causes created in him in no other way than that the Word creates the causes, while the causes are created by the Word and in the Word?

**DISCIPLE.** I would not altogether grant the first proposition. For I do not see how the generation of the Word from the Father could temporally precede the creation of all things by the Father in the Word and through the Word. Rather, I believe that the generation of the Word and the creation of all things in the Word are coeternal with one another; for no one can rightly suppose any accident, temporal movement, or temporal procession in God.

The second proposition, however, I could reasonably grant: namely, that the generation of the Word from the Father in no way temporally precedes the creation of all things in the Word by the Father, but is coeternal with it.

The Prophet likewise says, addressing the Father: “You made all things in wisdom.” For the Father simultaneously begot his wisdom and made all things in it. Elsewhere the same Prophet says in the person of the Father: “My heart has uttered a good word; I dedicate my works to the king.” It is as though he plainly said: From the secret of my substance, with the Word being born in it, I make my works in it—works that I give to the one who reigns in it.

Again, he says to the Father: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power.” It is as though he had said: The beginning of all things—that is, your Word—is always with you and in you. If, therefore, the beginning is always in the Father and with the Father, there was never a time when the beginning was not; rather, the beginning is always present. And because it is not accidental to it that it is the beginning, it never existed without those things of which it is the beginning.

“In the day of your power”: in the day—that is, in the knowledge of the generation of intellectual and rational creation from you. “Of your power”: that is, of your wisdom. For the day of the Father’s power is not improperly understood here as the ineffable knowledge of the birth of God the Word from God the Father, insofar as it is granted to creation to understand what surpasses every intellect, and access to inaccessible light is granted through theophanies—that is, divine manifestations—which theology impresses upon pure intellects and fixes in an ineffable manner, unknown to all, so that they possess within themselves a certain disposition of true knowledge concerning what is altogether unknown in itself.

For the Father’s power is the Father’s wisdom, in which he made all things. But the knowledge of this divine generation is still in me through faith; in an angel it is through vision. Indeed, it is neither in me through vision nor in an angel.

“For who shall declare his generation?” No human being, nor any of the heavenly powers, can know the generation of the Word from the Father—how it is or what kind it is. Just as no human being or angel knows what or who the one who begot is, or what or who the one begotten is; but only the one who begot knows what he begot and how what was begotten was begotten.

The one who begot knows himself—what he is, and how and in what manner he begot what he begot from himself. Similarly, what was begotten knows itself—what it is, how and in what manner it was begotten—and knows the one who begot it, who and what he is.

For if no one knows the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him, is it not consequently necessary to say that no one knows the Son except the Father and the one to whom the Father wishes to reveal him? We should understand “reveal” here as revelation through theophanies. For it is impossible for the essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, or their substances, to be revealed to creation directly through themselves.

The same must be understood concerning the manner and quality of the divine generation, if it is even proper to say “who” and “what” of the divine nature. For it is more than person and more than substance, if “mode” and “quality” are likewise properly predicated of that nature which surpasses every mode and every quality, and all other things that are spoken of according to accident. Concerning these matters we reached agreement among ourselves in the preceding book.

What follows is: “Among the splendors of the holy ones, from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” The word order is: “From the womb I begot you among the splendors of the holy ones, before the morning star.”

Understand “womb” here as the secret recesses of the Father’s substance, from which the only-begotten Son, who is the Father’s Word, was born, from which he is always born, and in which, while he is always being born, he always remains. Concerning these recesses it is said in the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God. But the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself has declared him.”

For he is not separated from the Father, because he is eternally and unchangeably in the Father, as he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

The Father, therefore, begot his Son from his own womb among the splendors of the holy ones. For when the Son is born from the Father, the splendors of the holy ones come into being—that is, the cognitions of the elect and their substantial predestinations in the Word of God, who, as the Apostle testifies, predestined us before secular times for the kingdom.

He did not say “before eternal times.” For eternal times are the coessential eternity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in which the substantial splendors of the holy ones and the primordial causes of all things were eternally established, and the effects of those causes were foreknown and predestined. Rather, he said “before secular times,” in which the causes, once and simultaneously made eternally in the beginning, proceed, under the administration of divine providence, into their effects, whether visible or invisible, according to a certain order of ages that was likewise predetermined and foreknown.

We believe that the predestinations and foreknowledges of the holy ones, which the Psalmist calls splendors, and the reasons of all visible and invisible things, are coeternal with the Father and the Son. Augustine says that, in the dispensation of the Word of God, they are not made but eternal. He says “not made” with respect to their being made through generation in times and places; but they were made eternally in the Word according to the constitution of the primordial causes: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

The same author says elsewhere: “The Word of God, through which all things were made, in which all things live unchangeably—not only those things that have been, but those that will be; and yet they were not in it as having been, nor will they be as future, but only are: all things are, and all things are one, and the one is more truly one.”

John the Theologian likewise says in the Gospel: “What was made in him was life.”

Among the splendors of the holy ones, therefore, the Father begot his Son from his own womb—that is, in his only-begotten Son he begot the knowledge of the future holy ones; indeed, he also created them. For the knowledge of the holy ones in the Father’s wisdom is their creation. The intellect of all things in God is the essence of all things.

For God’s knowing what he makes before it is made and his making what he knows are the same. God’s knowing and making are one: he makes by knowing and knows by making. Knowledge does not precede the deed, nor does the deed precede knowledge, because all things are once and simultaneously coeternal, apart from the relation between creator and creature.

God did not know all things after they had been made; rather, before they were made, he knew all the things that were to be made. And what is more marvelous, all things exist because they were foreknown. For the essence of all things is nothing other than the knowledge of all things in divine wisdom.

“For in him we live and move and are.” For, as Saint Dionysius says, the knowledge of things that are is the things that are.

The splendors of the holy ones, therefore, are their clear establishments, known to God, in divine wisdom and in their own primordial causes. And all of this—the birth of the Word from the Father, the splendor of the knowledge of the holy ones, and indeed of all natures in their principal causes—precedes the morning star.

But who is this morning star, before whose rising all the foregoing is understood to exist? This has been treated by wise men in many different ways, and it would take too long to introduce their opinions here.

What is said through the prophet Isaiah—“How has Lucifer fallen from heaven, the morning star that rises?”—is plainly understood of the devil and of his body, which is recognized as consisting especially in the impious, apostates, and heretics.

Some, however, think that the Psalmist’s morning star signifies the very bright star whose rising customarily precedes the rising of the sun. Before the appearance of this star, Christ, born according to the flesh from the Virgin, is said to have been born above the horizon, as Saint Father Augustine writes in his *Decades*.

But since the interpretation of sacred Scripture is infinite, tell me, please, and explain what seems more suited to the present discussion; for I do not see it sufficiently clearly.

## 21.

**MAG.** For my part, my simplicity is sufficient at this point [Note: [Col. 0559] So CD; A has *sufficiat*, “may suffice.”], since the acumen of others does not suit me [Note: [Col. 0559] So AD; C has *cognovit*, “has recognized.”]. This mystical and prophetic Lucifer, before whose rising the splendors of the saints are understood to exist in the only-begotten Word of God, seems most plausibly to signify this visible world, by that figure of speech which in Greek is called *synecdoche* (συνεκδοχή), and is interpreted as “conception”; by this figure a part signifies the whole, and the whole a part.

Therefore, before this visible world proceeded by generation into all genera and species and into all perceptible numbers [Col. 0560B], before secular times, God the Father begot his Word, in whom and through whom [Note: [Col. 0559] CD has “through whom.”] he created the most perfect primordial causes of all natures [Note: [Col. 0559] So CD; A has “all the causes of natures.”], which, under the administration of divine providence, by a marvelous harmony, through their processes of generation, their numerical arrangements of places and times [Note: [Col. 0559] So AD; C has “of bodies.”], and the manifold differences of genera and species, perfect this visible world from its beginning, when it began, to its end, when it will cease to exist—not by an abolition of essence, but by the natural course of changes in qualities and quantities.

And do not be surprised that this whole world is signified by its part [Note: [Col. 0559] So A; CDE omit “is signified”], which is Lucifer, when you see that through the sun itself, to which Lucifer is always attached [Note: [Col. 0559] So CDE; A has “Lucifer is attached”], for it does not depart far from it, but either rises a little before the sun rises or sets a little after it sets [Col. 0560C], this same perceptible world is mystically signified, as Solomon says:

> “What is that which has been? The very thing that will be.  
> What is that which will be? The very thing that is to be done.  
> There is nothing new under the sun.”

Here we may reasonably understand “the sun” as the whole visible creation. For by these words the theologians do not signify only that part of this world which is enclosed within the solar circle [Note: [Col. 0559] So CDE; A has “are enclosed”], namely, the nature of earth and waters [Note: [Col. 0559] So CDE; A has “of the lands”], together with the air and the lower part of the ether [Note: [Col. 0559] So CDE; A has “of the lower ether”], through which the lunar sphere revolves, but also the regions above the world, from the solar line to the outermost circumference of the heavenly sphere.

For in all these regions “under the sun”—that is, under the world—there is nothing new [Note: [Col. 0559] So CDE; A has “nothing”], whether one understands that nothing is new in the course of the present life which did not previously appear in the natural order of things [Note: [Col. 0559] So CDE; A has “which did not previously appear in the natural order of things”]. For nothing other than the recurrence of the same things is perceived and understood in the course of time; or, as Maximus understands this passage of Scripture [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “understands this passage of Scripture”], that which existed before this world will itself exist after the world [Note: [Col. 0561] So CE; A has “after it,” while D omits “world”], that is, only those things which are eternal existed before this world and will exist after it [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A omits “after it”].

And “there is nothing new under the sun”—that is [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “that is”], whatever is new under this world is nothing. For this whole world is called new because it is not eternal and arose in time; and therefore it is nothing, for it will perish with everything that is in it, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “The heavens are the works of your hands; they themselves will perish.”

But if the greatest part of the world, which is said to be heaven and is also the most beautiful, and which is known to surround all the other parts on every side, is destined to perish, do you suppose [Col. 0561B] that what is in its other, more inward and inferior parts [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “lower parts”] will be able to remain [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “will remain”]? For in every compact body, when the things that contain perish, the things contained cannot remain [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “retain permanence”].

But because it cannot return entirely to nothing [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “could not”], since it was made by God [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “from God”], and everything made by God always remains, what in it will perish and what will not perish [Note: [Col. 0561] So ADE; C has “what”] must be sought by careful inquiry and reserved for another time. For now, follow what is immediately before us.

**DISC.** You argue cautiously and attentively.

**MAG.** The principal causes of all things, then, are coeternal with God and with the Principle in which they were made [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “the primordial causes.”]. For if God in no way precedes the Principle—that is, the Word begotten from himself and of himself—and if the Word in no way precedes the causes of the things made in him [Col. 0561C], it follows that all these—the Father God, I mean, and the Word, and the causes of the things made in him [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “the causes of things”]—are coeternal.

**DISC.** They are not altogether coeternal. We certainly believe that the Son is coeternal with the Father [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A omits “to be”]; but the things that the Father makes in the Son we say are coeternal with the Son, though not altogether coeternal: coeternal, indeed, because the Son never existed without the primordial causes of the natures made in him [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “without the primordial natural causes of the Son made in him, and so forth.”]. Yet these causes are not altogether coeternal with him in whom they were made. For things made cannot be coeternal with their maker; the maker precedes the things he makes.

For things that are altogether coeternal are so united to one another that neither can exist without the other, because they are coessential. A maker and a thing made, however, since they are not coessential, are not compelled to be coeternal; they are compelled, rather, always to be relative and to exist together, because a maker without something made is not a maker, and something made without a maker is not something made.

Hence it follows that we say the primordial causes of things are coeternal with God because they subsist eternally in God without any temporal beginning [Col. 0561D]; yet they are not altogether coeternal with God, because they begin to exist not from themselves but from their Creator [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “which”]. The Creator himself, however, in no way begins to exist [Note: [Col. 0561] The words “the Creator himself … begins to exist” are omitted in C.]. For he alone is true eternity, lacking every beginning and every end, because he is the beginning and the end of all things.

For that is not true eternity which in some way begins to exist; rather, it is a participation in true eternity, which is *anarchos* (ἄναρχος), that is, entirely without beginning. Every creature begins to exist, because it existed when it did not exist: it existed in its causes when it did not exist in its effects.

Therefore it is not altogether coeternal with true eternity. But if within the very Cause of all causes—that is, within the Trinity—some kind of precedence is understood [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “procession”], for the generating Deity precedes the begotten Deity and the proceeding Deity, which proceeds from the generating and begotten Deity [Col. 0562B], although the Deity is one and inseparable, is it surprising or incredible that the Cause of causes should precede all things of which it is the cause [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “the cause of all causes”], and that all things should have existed in it changeably and eternally, without a temporal beginning?

If, then, the Father precedes the occasions of the things he made in the Son in the same way that a maker precedes his works, and the Word precedes the things that the Father made in him [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “in the Son”] in the same way that the art of an artisan precedes the principles established in it by the artisan, what prevents us from understanding that the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0561] So CE; AD has “the Spirit Holy”], who is borne over the abyss of the primordial causes which the Father created in the Word, presides over those things over which he is borne?

The Holy Spirit, therefore, eternally surpasses and precedes within himself, by the power of his eternity, the mystical waters which he cherishes and makes fruitful. But if these are reasonable answers concerning the constitution of the principles, I earnestly ask you to explain fully what seems specially attributable to the Father, what to the Word, and what to the Holy Spirit.

## 22.

Although the operation of the divine goodness is believed and understood to be one, the same, and common to the three substances, it must nevertheless not be said to lack every distinction and propriety. For there are matters which sacred theology distributes to the individual persons, as it were by a certain propriety; I do not doubt that their examples are familiar to you.

To use only a few examples, let us hear what is proper to the Father, as the divine voice speaks:

> “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0561] So CDE; A has “of the time.” A also reverses the abbreviated phrase as “made under the law, made of a woman.”]

What is proper to the Son:

> “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,”

and so forth [Note: [Col. 0561] A gives the abbreviated sequence: “he was … to be … equal to God … servant …”].

What is proper to the Holy Spirit in the administration of the Word’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0561] A has “the Word of God”] the Gospel reveals, when the angel says concerning the holy Mother of God:

> “That which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit.”

**MAG.** Your investigation through reasoning seems to me sound [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A has “seems to me to be sound”]; I do not think it deviates from the truth [Note: [Col. 0563] So ACD; D has “as I think.”]. Therefore, what you ask of me I shall endeavor to investigate, guided by him who enlightens us and invites us to seek him.

It seems to me, then, that theology attributes causally to God the Father the propriety of the constitution of natures [Note: [Col. 0563] So A; CDE have “to God and the Father.”]. “In the beginning,” it says, “God made heaven and earth”; and elsewhere: “You made all things in wisdom”; and again: “You who made the world from formless matter”; and elsewhere: “All that the Lord willed [Note: [Col. 0563] So CE; AD have “God”], he made in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A has “in every abyss”], and a thousand other passages.

It declares that the substantial principles [Note: [Col. 0563] So DE; AC have “the substances”] of all things were established in the Word [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A has “were established”], as the same testimonies cited above bear witness: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”; and: “You made all things in wisdom.”

For the Principle, Wisdom, and the Word are not different things; rather, by all these names the only-begotten Son of God is properly signified, in whom and through whom all things were made by the Father. The Apostle likewise says:

> “In him we live and move and exist” [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A omits “and”];

that is, he is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature; in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things were created through him and in him” [Note: [Col. 0563] So CE; AD have “and all things”].

But we find that the same theology applies to the Holy Spirit the distribution of all the causes which the Father universally and essentially created in the Word. For if, as the Apostle testifies, the allotment and distribution of divine gifts is given to the Spirit, why should not also the division of the primordial causes substantially established in the Word of God [Note: [Col. 0563] CDE include “of God”; A omits it] be given to him?

“For to one,” he says, “through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A omits “the word”]; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healings in the same Spirit; to another the working of powers; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation [Note: [Col. 0563] So ADE; C has “interpretations”] of utterances. But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each his own as he wills.”

We can argue the same point from the Scripture of Genesis, where it is written:

> “And the Spirit of God was cherishing the waters.”

For what else should we understand the Spirit of God to have cherished, made fruitful, and nourished the waters of the primordial causes for, unless it was in order that he might distribute and order what was made uniformly, indivisibly, and simply in the Word according to the differences of genera, forms, wholes and parts, and all numbers [Note: [Col. 0563] So CD; AE have “formlessly”]?

And if no believer who believes rightly and understands rightly hesitates to affirm that the spiritual gifts which the prophet Isaiah foretold would rest upon the head of the Church, which is Christ, were distributed to the incarnate Word of God by none other than the Holy Spirit, what is surprising if the same Spirit distributes and gives to the Church, which is his body, not only the gifts of grace through Christ but also the gifts of nature through that same Christ?

Moreover, he grants the gift of essence to every visible and invisible creature, so that they are what they merely are [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A has “so that they exist”]; to living things he gives the gift of life, by which they live [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; C has “by which they are alive”]; to beings capable of sensation, the gift of sense, by which they perceive; to rational beings, the gift of reason, by which, through the activity of reasoning, they truly and diligently investigate and discover the natures of things [Note: [Col. 0563] So DE; A has “through activity and true diligence”]; to intellectual beings, the gift of understanding, by which they move around God—the cause, namely, of all gifts—unknowingly and above all creation, in an ineffable movement and a wondrous return.

For the mystical lampstand of the prophet Zechariah—not to mention the Mosaic one, since it belongs to the same mystery—signifies the Church. Its lamp, placed above it [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; C has “its lamps”; C also has “their” for “its”], is the paternal and true light which illuminates every person coming into the world [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A has “coming into this world”].

Our Lord Jesus Christ, because for us, from us, in the nature of our flesh, he was both conceived [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A has “was conceived”] and born, and appeared to the world, is called the lamp above the Church’s lampstand. For according to his nature he is himself the substantial wisdom and Word of God the Father [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A has “supernatural”], above whom [Note: [Col. 0563] So ADE; C has “over whom”], first according to the understanding of his humanity—for he is the head of the whole body of the Church [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A omits “for he is”]—the gifts of the Holy Spirit, customarily signified by the number seven [Note: [Col. 0563] C has “by the number nine”], rest.

For the divine gifts distributed to the Church through the Holy Spirit, since they are distributed by one Spirit, are customarily signified by the name of that Spirit, beginning from its head—I mean Christ. For the Spirit himself cannot be called a gift according to nature [Note: [Col. 0563] So CDE; A has “the Spirit himself”]; he is the distributor of gifts. Therefore he is called sevenfold because he universally and individually distributes to the Church the fullness of the divine gifts, which is indicated by the number seven [Note: [Col. 0563] CDE have “divides”; A has “universally and individually divides the Church’s gifts”].

For the Spirit himself is coessential with the Father and the Son according to divinity. Upon the Son, I mean, he causes the divine gifts which he distributes to rest according to humanity:

> “And the Spirit of God,” says the Prophet, “will rest upon him” [Note: [Col. 0563] CD have “will rest”; AE have “rests”];

as though he were saying plainly: “And the gifts which the Spirit of God distributes will rest upon him”—the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety—and [Col. 0565A] “the spirit of the fear of the Lord” will fill him [Note: [Col. 0565] So CDE; A has “the fear of God”].

All these “spirits”—that is, all these gifts of the Spirit—are first received according to his humanity by Christ, the head of the Church, and through the Holy Spirit are distributed by him to his body, his Church.

And just as the Holy Spirit subsists according to essence in the nature of God the Father, so also he exists in the nature of the Son according to essence [Note: [Col. 0565] The words “subsists … essence” are omitted in BC], because he proceeds ineffably from the Father substantially through the Son who was born. Therefore the gifts which he distributes are not his alone, but also belong to the Father, from whom he proceeds, and to the Son, from and through whom he proceeds.

And do not suppose that only the manifold gifts of the Spirit, by which the manifold offspring of sin are driven from the Church and utterly extinguished, are distributed through the Spirit. Wisdom brings about the destruction of foolishness; understanding removes stupidity; counsel destroys lack of discernment; fortitude dissolves weakness; knowledge abolishes ignorance; piety brings about the assault upon impiety and, within it, upon the perversity of deeds; fear drives away the blindness of contempt.

Besides these gifts of grace, by which the Church is purified, built up, illuminated, and perfected, no believer doubts that the gifts of all good things—which exist both according to essence and according to natural accidents—come from no other source [Note: [Col. 0565] So CE; A has “who would doubt that they come from no other source among the faithful”; D has “no believer doubts”] than the Cause of all good things, namely, the Father, from whom all things come; through the Son, in whom all things exist; and that their distribution is effected by none other than the Holy Spirit, who divides all things among all as he wills.

The theologian says:

> “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” [Note: [Col. 0565] So CDE; A has the abbreviated form “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.”]

What could be more evident? What could be clearer? He says that it comes from no other source than the Father of lights—that is, the Father of all good things, both those which exist according to nature and those which exist according to grace.

All gifts are rightly called “lights,” because they descend from the unbegotten Light through the begotten Light, and through the proceeding Light they are divided, according to the capacity of nature and the abundance of grace, into the individual substance of each particular or general essence [Note: [Col. 0565] So CDE; A has “of each one”].

For what the Apostle seems to say as though only to a human being—“O human being, what do you have that you did not receive?”—can be said universally to every visible and invisible creature. For no created nature possesses anything except what it received from its Creator.

If it exists, it received existence from him; if it lives, life; if it perceives, perception; if it enjoys reason, reason; if it understands, understanding; and a thousand other things of this kind. If, then, nothing is known to exist in the nature of created things [Note: [Col. 0565] So CDE; A has “is understood”] except what is given by the Creator, it follows that the creature, whether essentially or according to accident, is nothing other than the Creator’s gifts and endowments. Theology therefore assigns to the Holy Spirit, as it were, the propriety of distributing the gifts [Note: [Col. 0565] So CDE; A has “assigns propriety to the Holy Spirit.”].

Everything, then, that the Father does in the Son, the Holy Spirit distributes, dividing to each his own as he wills. Do you see, then, how theology is understood to assign to each substance or person of the divine goodness its own distinctive properties?

To the Father it assigns the making of all things; to the Word it assigns the eternal making of all the primordial causes of things in him—universally, essentially, and simply; to the Spirit it assigns the distribution of those primordial causes, made in the Word and made fruitful for their effects [Note: [Col. 0565] So AD; C has “fruitfulness,” E “made fruitful”], that is, into the genera, species, numbers, and differences of heavenly and spiritual essences entirely without bodies; or of essences adhering to the pure and spiritual bodies made from the simplicity of the catholic elements [Col. 0566B]; or of the universal or particular sensible things of this visible world [Note: [Col. 0565] So ADE; C has “of this sensible world”], separated in places, mobile in times, and differing in quality and quantity [Note: [Col. 0565] A omits “and”].

One may reasonably affirm that the primordial causes, whether they possess visible or invisible bodies, entirely lack quality and quantity in themselves. By “invisible body” we mean the simple subsistence of each of the elements of this world, understood in itself.

As for the heavenly essences—that is, the angelic powers—although they are reasonably believed to exist beyond this sensible world by the excellence of their intellectual nature, they should not nevertheless be judged, contrary to the considered opinions of the holy Fathers, to be deprived of spiritual bodies.

They must be believed to submit to human senses, by which they often appear, not in bodies foreign to them, but in their own spiritual bodies, which always adhere to them [Note: [Col. 0565] So ADE; C has “they must be believed”]. This is not because the operation of the inseparable unity of the divine substances has been divided. For what the Father does, the Son also does, and the Holy Spirit also does the same [Note: [Col. 0565] So ADE; C has “likewise”]. Rather, it is because divine theology seems to distribute certain properties among them individually [Note: [Col. 0565] So CDE; A has “certain properties”], and they are truly understood to possess them [Note: [Col. 0565] So CDE; A has “they are understood to possess them”].

For in the Holy Trinity the unity of the common operation is recognized, while the propriety of distinct operations is not excluded. For if in it there is unity of essence and distinction of substances, why should one not believe and understand that there is also a common and a differentiated operation in it? I do not see why a common operation should not be attributed to the common essence, while a threefold action is not denied to the substantial Trinity.

## 23.

**DISC.** I see clearly, and it seems to me probable and consonant with the divine utterances. But I wish that, by means of some likeness taken from our nature—for it is said to be like God—you would persuade me concerning what has been said about the properties of the divine administration.

**MAG.** I can hardly believe that the Trinity of our nature is unknown to you.

**DISC.** Tell me, please, what it is.

**MAG.** Do you remember what we agreed upon in the discussion of the preceding book? Did it not seem to us that there is no nature which is not understood to subsist in these three terms [Note: [Col. 0567] So CDE; A has “which is not understood”], which, as we have often said, the Greeks call οὐσία, δύναμις, ἐνέργεια—that is, essence, virtue, and operation?

**DISC.** I certainly remember, and hold it most firmly.

**MAG.** Our nature, then, which is called human because all human beings participate in it, subsists through essence, virtue, and operation [Note: [Col. 0567] A has “and operation”].

**DISC.** I would not suppose that any expert in divine philosophy doubts this.

**MAG.** What do you think? Does not our nature, according to the testimony of sacred Scripture, appear to have been made in the image and likeness of God?

**DISC.** You are treating me generously; whoever doubts this is not a human being.

**MAG.** Do you think that God himself, who created our nature in his own image, is a body or a spirit?
