**DISC.** It would be ridiculous to hesitate over this as well. For God is spirit [Note: [Col. 0567] So CDE; A has “is a spirit”], and those who worship him worship in spirit and truth [Note: [Col. 0567] C has “to worship him”].

**MAG.** Therefore the image of God was impressed upon our nature not according to the body but according to the soul.

**DISC.** This too must be acknowledged as entirely true.

**MAG.** God is Trinity and Unity—that is, three substances in one essence, and one essence in three substances or persons. For just as the Greeks say μίαν οὐσίαν, τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις or τρία πρόσωπα—that is, “one essence, three substances or three persons”—so the Romans say “one essence, three substances or persons.”

Yet they seem to differ in this: we do not find that the Greeks say μίαν ὑπόστασιν, that is, “one substance,” whereas the Latins very frequently say “one substance, three persons.”

The Greeks say ὁμοούσιον [Note: [Col. 0567] Corrected; A has ὁμούσιον], ὁμοάγαθον [Note: [Col. 0567] Corrected; A has ὁμάγαθον], ὁμόθεον [Note: [Col. 0567] CE have this; AD omit it], that is, “of one essence, of one goodness, of one Deity,” or “one essence, one goodness, one Deity.”

These names, however, which among the Greeks indicate the inseparability of the divine nature, are not easily translated into the Roman language, and, as I believe, cannot be rendered perfectly. Therefore their meaning alone is transferred by separate words through *periphrasis* (περίφρασις), so that only their force is understood, while their interpretation is not expressed word for word.

**DISC.** The catholic faith of the universal Church confesses and, insofar as it is granted, understands all this; but toward what do these matters tend [Note: [Col. 0567] Corrected; DE have *istac*, “these”; C has *quorsum condunt istac*; A has *quorsum tendunt ista*]?

**MAG.** Toward nothing else than our seeking, to the extent of our powers, how the Trinity of our nature expresses in itself the image and likeness of the creative Trinity—that is, what may more suitably be associated with the Father, what with the Son, and what with the Holy Spirit.

I say “more suitably.” For although the whole Trinity of our nature is, in its entirety, suitably the image of the whole divine Trinity—for it bears the image of the whole Father, the whole Son, and the whole Holy Spirit—there is nevertheless in it something which, as it were, can be assigned to the individual persons by special correspondence, as I think [Note: [Col. 0567] So CDE; A has “can be assigned”].

For our Trinity is also wholly present in each of its members: it is its own essence, virtue, and operation; its own virtue, essence, and operation; its own operation, essence, and virtue [Note: [Col. 0567] So CE; A omits “is”; D has “and essence and virtue”]. In the same way, the Father is in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, the Son is in the Father and in the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0567] So CDE; A has “in the Son”].

## DISC.

Nothing seems more probable to me than that it should apply the image of the Father to essence, that of the Son to power, and that of the Holy Spirit to the operation of our nature [Col. 0567: CDE read “operation of our nature”; A reads “our nature”]. For the paternal substance [Col. 0568B; Col. 0567D: Codex D ends at “proceeding substance,” in the words “For the paternal substance which begot from itself a filial substance and a proceeding substance” (with se, “itself,” omitted)], which begot from itself a filial substance and sent forth from itself a proceeding substance [Col. 0567: thus CDE; A reads “of procession”; Col. 0568D: Thomas Gale notes at “proceeding”: “Here the manuscript formerly belonging to Thun is defective”], is rightly called the principal substance [Col. 0567: thus AE; A reads “is called the principal substance”]—not because the one essence of the Holy Trinity is separable [Col. 0567: thus CE; A reads “the sacred Trinity is one essence”], for it is one and indivisible, but because, although one, it is not without substantial distinctions. For there is a begetting Deity, a begotten Deity [Col. 0567: thus CE; A reads “a begotten Deity”], and a proceeding Deity; and although the Deity is one and indivisible, it is nevertheless not undifferentiated in its substantial distinctions.

Power, too, is not incongruously attributed to God the Son, since theology often names the Father’s power. But, to take one testimony from many, hear the Apostle: “For his invisible things are perceived and understood through the things that have been made, and likewise his eternal power and eternity.” In this passage we understand the Father’s power to mean the Father’s wisdom, that is, the Son; and eternity to mean the Holy Spirit, as Maximus, the venerable teacher, testifies.

That the Holy Spirit is customarily called by the name of “power” in Scripture is attested by the Gospel, when the Lord, healing a woman who had a hemorrhage—Greek αἱμοῤῥοῦσαν, that is, “suffering from a flow of blood”—says: “I perceived that power had gone out from me”; that is, the Holy Spirit, who distributes the gifts of healings [Col. 0567: thus ACE].

What shall I say about the essential operation of our nature? Is it not most appropriately joined to the Holy Spirit, to whom, as though properly belonging to him, the operation of virtues and the distribution of divine gifts are attributed, both universally and, properly, as a distribution to each individual? Thus, in the essence of our nature, the property of the paternal substance is discerned; in its power, that of the substance of the Son; and in its operation, that of the substance of the Holy Spirit.

## MAG.

I do not think your answer departs from the truth. But consider what you think about the most celebrated trinity of our nature, which is understood as intellect, reason, and sense [Col. 0569A]: does it differ from the one we mentioned earlier, namely the soul, or are this trinity and that one identical, rather than two distinct trinities belonging to one and the same nature? [Col. 0569: thus CE; A omits “and that one.”] By “sense” I mean not exterior but interior sense.

Interior sense is coessential with reason and intellect; exterior sense, although it seems to belong more to the soul than to the body, does not constitute the essence of the soul. Rather, as the Greeks say, it is a certain conjunction of soul and body; for when the body is dissolved and life departs, it is utterly destroyed. If it remained in the soul and belonged to its substance, the soul would certainly use it even outside the body. But since, without the body, it neither uses nor can use it, it follows that it cannot remain in the dissolved body or adhere to the soul when the soul abandons its governance of the body.

Indeed, even the definition by which Saint Augustine wished to define exterior sense does not seem to count it among the substantial parts of the soul. He says: “Sense is an affection of the body, not concealed from the soul through itself” [Col. 0569: CE reads “through itself” in the masculine form]. Elsewhere he says: “Sense is the appearance of sensible things received through the instruments of the body.” Likewise, sense does not seem to be joined to the nature of the soul [Col. 0569: thus AE; C reads “to count it among them”], but rather to be established as an intermediary between body and soul. And if one examines more carefully the proper usage of the Greek language, one will find in human beings the distinct character of two senses.

For in Greek νοῦς means intellect, λόγος means reason, and διάνοια means sense—not exterior but interior sense. In these three the essential trinity of the soul, constituted in the image of God, subsists. There is intellect, reason, and sense, which is called interior and essential. Exterior sense, however, which we have called the bond of body and soul, is called αἴσθησις; and the instruments in which it resides are called αἰσθητήρια, as though αἰσθήσεως Τήρια, that is, “guards of sense” [Col. 0569: thus CE; A reads simply “guardians”]. For in them sense is preserved and operates. They are five in number: sight, hearing [Col. 0569: thus CE; A has “hearing, sight”], smell, taste, and touch.

Nor should it trouble you that I have called the fivefold instrument of sense by the names of the fivefold senses. This is a very common usage both in ordinary speech and in Sacred Scripture: the seats of the senses are called by the names of the senses themselves. Thus the eye is called sight, the ear hearing, and the other senses likewise give their names to their instruments.

Sense is not called fivefold, therefore, because it is divided within itself according to the number five [Col. 0569D]. It is simple and uniform, and resides in the heart as in its principal seat [Col. 0569: thus CE; A reads “as though in the principal place”]. Rather, it is called fivefold because, through the fivefold instrument of the body—as through the five gates of some city—it receives inwardly the likenesses of sensible things that come from the qualities and quantities of the external world, as well as from the other features by which exterior sense is formed [Col. 0569: thus CE; A reads “it receives”], and, like a doorkeeper and intermediary, announces to the presiding interior sense what it has introduced from outside [Col. 0569: CE reads “doorkeeper” with the alternative spelling].

## DISC.

It does not trouble me that the instruments are signified by the names of the senses; nor, I think, has the distinction between the two senses—which you have clarified with complete precision—escaped me [Col. 0569: the words “by the names … of the senses” are omitted in C]. Let me explain, according to the capacity of my modest intellect, what I think about the trinity of our nature mentioned above.

There seem to be two trinities by which our nature is shown to subsist insofar as it was made in the image of God. Yet, after consulting the truth, I find that they differ from one another not in reality but only in name. For νοῦς and οὐσία—that is, intellect and essence—signify the highest part of our nature, indeed its highest movement.

As you yourself understand, our nature’s being is not one thing and its movement another. Its essence is a stable movement around God and creation, and a mobile stability. When it moves around God, who surpasses all things, its movement is called supreme [Col. 0569: thus CE; A reads “greatest”]. When it concerns itself with the primordial causes, which immediately follow God as their nearest counterparts, it is understood to move under a kind of intermediate regulation. But when it attempts to perceive the effects of the primordial causes, whether visible or invisible, it is recognized as undergoing the extremity of its movement—not because that same substantial movement can increase or diminish in itself, but because, according to the dignity of the things around which it revolves, it is judged to be least, intermediate, and greatest [Col. 0569: thus CE; A reads “is indicated”].

The essence of our soul, therefore, is intellect, which presides over the whole of human nature, because it revolves unknowingly around God, who is above every nature. Λόγος or δύναμις—that is, reason or power [Col. 0569: A adds “and,” “reason and power”]—indicates, as it were, the second part, and not irrationally, since it moves around the principles of things, which are first after God.

The third part is designated by the terms διάνοια and ἐνέργεια, that is, sense and operation, and occupies, as it were, the outermost position of the human soul. Nor is this without reason, since it revolves around the effects of the primordial causes, whether visible or invisible. Accordingly, we ought to understand not two substantial trinities but one and the same trinity, created in the likeness of its Creator.

But I am surprised that I do not see you count the life itself—which the Greeks call θρεπτική and αὐξητική, while we call it nutritive and augmentative, since it nourishes bodies and supplies them with growth [Col. 0569: thus CE; A has αὐξητική and says that it is called by us “nutritive and augmentative”]—either as a fourth substantial part of human nature or among the substantial trinity. You seem to have passed over it entirely, as though it in no way belonged to the constitution of our nature.

## MAG.

Do not be surprised [Col. 0569: thus CE; A reads “Do not” with a different form]. We have not done this without cause. For we are not now discussing the whole of human nature, which seems to consist of five parts—body, vital movement, sense, reason, and intellect—but only that part in which the image and likeness of the Creator are perceived: intellect, reason, and interior sense—or, as I might say, essence, power, and operation [Col. 0571: thus CE; A adds “and” before “operation”].

In this threefold structure the image of the supreme and holy Trinity is recognized as expressed [Col. 0571: A reads “the supreme and sacred Trinity”]. The vital movement by which the soul nourishes the body, gathers it into unity, gives it life, serves it, and grants it growth, and likewise the body itself, which occupies the lowest place in the whole of creation, will be discussed elsewhere, when, in the fourth book [Col. 0571: A omits “in the fourth book”], God guiding us, we deliberate about sensible natures.

Since that part is recognized as lying outside the property of our intelligible essence, by which we were created in the image of God, we have for the present passed it over. It is a certain movement outside the nature originally created, subject to our substantial operation, which, as we have said, is called interior sense, and added as a punishment for sin. Through this movement it administers what was added to human nature after sin: I mean this corruptible and mortal body, variable in place and time, divided according to the number of its parts, extended through spatial dimensions, subjected to increase and decrease, governed by diverse qualities and quantities, prone to every irrational movement, and serving as the dwelling of the still-carnal soul, which, because of its disobedience and pride, has been entangled in various misfortunes—along with all the other things that can be described and known by experience concerning the misery of human nature, expelled from the happiness of paradise into this life.

The movement of human nature by which it administers what was added to it as punishment for its transgression of the divine command is therefore not irrationally left outside the bounds of our essential trinity. By “punishment,” however, I mean not the vengeance of an angry God but the discipline of a merciful one.

And do not suppose that by these words we wish to teach that the trinity of human nature mentioned above, created in the image of God in paradise before it sinned, was entirely without a body. Far be it from us to say or in any way to believe this [Col. 0571: thus CE; A omits “far be it from us” and reads “to believe”]. The Creator created our souls and bodies together and at once in paradise; by “bodies” I mean celestial and spiritual bodies, such as they will be after the resurrection.

For it must not be doubted that the swollen, mortal, corruptible bodies by which we are now oppressed derive their origin not from nature but from sin. Whatever, therefore, has grown upon nature from sin will certainly be absent from nature when it has been renewed in Christ and restored to its original condition. For what adheres to nature because of sin cannot be coeternal with it. Nor is it incongruous, I think, that it should not be counted among the substantial constitutions of nature [Col. 0571: thus CE; A reads “not counted”], not so that what was added should perish, but so that it should pass into what was created at the beginning and become one with it—not as two things, but as one incorruptible and spiritual reality—through the grace of the Word of God, who descended not only into our natural elements but also into what had been added to us, in order to restore all that was ours in himself and make the superadded things naturally inherent in what he made, “who made both one.”

## DISC.

Certainly this is not incongruous; rather, it is most fitting for the careful and subtle investigation and discovery of rational nature. But I do not yet see where all this is leading.

## MAG.

Be patient. What we are seeking among ourselves is no small matter, and it can be investigated and discovered only through many intricate turns of careful reasoning—if, indeed, it can be discovered with complete clarity. No mortal sense, however sharply it may seem to inquire, is permitted to promise this, lest it be reproved for rashly promising to discover by itself what surpasses its powers [Col. 0571: thus AE; C reads “nor is the rash one reproved”]. For if it is discovered, it is not the one who seeks who discovers it, but the one who is sought, who is the light of minds [Col. 0571: thus CE; A reads “if it is found”].

We are seeking, unless I am mistaken, how, from the evidence of the substantial trinity of our nature, created in the image of God [Col. 0571: CE omits “of God”], we may investigate that supreme Trinity which is God, and the operations belonging, as it were, properly to it, distributed among its individual persons in created nature.

## DISC.

That is precisely what we are seeking now, and nothing else [Col. 0571: thus CE; A omits “now”]. And the order of things requires us to seek the truth in this way. For by means of the image we must seek the truth itself, of which the image is an image. The more zealously and laboriously it is sought, the more ardently it is loved and the more openly it is found.

What benefit is there in the speed that eludes the pure contemplation of truth? Or what harm is there in the very slowness to which the desired face presents itself?

## MAG.

Let us therefore take the beginning of our reasoning from the words of the venerable Maximus—not joining them together in the same wording, but using the same meaning.

## DISC.

Enter upon the path of reasoning in whatever way you wish.

## MAG.

There are three universal movements of the soul. The first is according to the mind, the second according to reason, and the third according to sense. The first is simple [Col. 0571: thus CE; A reads “the first movement is simple”], and is above the nature of the soul itself; it has no interpretation, that is, no cognition of what it moves around. Through it, when the soul is moved around the unknown God, it in no way knows him from any of the things that exist, because of his excellence, according to what he is—that is, it cannot find him in any essence or substance, or in anything that can be said or understood [Col. 0571: thus AC; E reads “according to that”]. For he surpasses everything that is and everything that is not, and it is in no way possible to define what he is [Col. 0571: CE reads “can be found”].

The second movement is that by which it defines the unknown God according to the fact that he is the cause of all things [Col. 0573: thus CE; A reads “by which we know”]. It defines God as the cause of all things, and this movement lies within the nature of the soul. Through it, when naturally moved, the soul impresses upon itself, through the operation of knowledge, all the natural, formative principles of all things, which eternally subsist in him who is known only as their cause—for he is known because he is their cause. That is, the soul expresses them in itself through their cognition. This cognition arises from the first movement in the second [Col. 0573: “It defines” is a conjecture; A has “for it defines”; C has an irregular form; E has “it defines,” omitting “indeed”].

The third movement is composite. Through it the soul touches external things and, as though from certain signs, reforms within itself the principles of visible things. It is called composite—not because it is not simple in itself, as the first and second movements are simple, but because it does not begin to know the principles of sensible things by themselves.

First, it receives the phantasies of the things themselves through exterior sense, fivefold according to the number of the bodily instruments in which and through which it operates [Col. 0573: thus AE; C reads “bodily”]. It gathers, divides, and orders them within itself. Then, through them, reaching the principles of which they are the phantasies, it treats and forms those principles—by “principles,” I mean—within itself.

Nor should it trouble you that shortly before we defined exterior sense as the phantasy of sensible things, whereas now we teach that through it the phantasies of those same sensible things reach interior sense [Col. 0573: thus CE; A reads “we teach that through it one reaches the phantasies of those same sensible things,” omitting “to interior sense”]. For the third movement mentioned above begins to move from the phantasies of external things announced to it through exterior sense [Col. 0573: thus CE; A has “for”].

There are two kinds of phantasies. The first is that which initially arises from sensible nature in the instruments of the senses and is properly called the image impressed upon the senses. The second is that which, in the subsequent order, is formed from the image mentioned above; this is the phantasy itself, which is customarily called exterior sense.

The former always adheres to the body, whereas the latter belongs to the soul. Although the former is in the sense, it does not sense itself; the latter, however, both senses itself and receives the former.

When that third movement abandons the phantasies of visible things and purely understands the principles naked of every bodily imagination and simple in themselves, it too becomes simply simple. That is, it communicates to the first movement, through the intermediate movement, the universal principles of visible things universally—freed from every phantasy and perceived in themselves with the utmost purity and truth.

The first movement, for its part, refers whatever it perceives through the third movement by means of the intermediate movement, and immediately from the intermediate movement, within the modes of created things [Col. 0573: thus A; C reads “of all things,” and E “of creatures”], to the unknown according to what he is [Col. 0573: CE omit “according to what he is”; A also omits the phrase “what he is”], but known as the cause of all things; and it refers it to the principles of all things—that is, to the primordial causes made by him and in him and distributed by him. In other words, it understands that all things subsequent to God proceed from God through those causes and again return through them to God.

The movement of the soul, purified through action, illuminated through knowledge, and perfected through theology, is eternally revolved around the unknown God. It understands God as wholly beyond its own nature and beyond the nature of all things, entirely free from everything that can be said or understood, and also from everything that can neither be said nor understood and yet in some manner exists. It denies that he is one of the things that are or of the things that are not [Col. 0573: thus CE; A omits “of the things that are not”]. It affirms that everything predicated of him is predicated not properly but metaphorically [Col. 0573: A reads “of him” rather than “of that one”].

This movement is called by the Greeks νοῦς, and by us intellect, soul, or mind. It is substantial and is understood to be the principal part of the soul. For it is not one thing for the soul essentially to be and another for it substantially to move. The soul subsists in its movements, and its movements subsist in it. It is a simple and indivisible nature, distinguished only by the substantial differences of its movements.

If the holy Fathers teach that the celestial essences—which the divine utterances also call celestial powers and angels—are substantially nothing other than intelligible, eternal, unceasing movements around the principle of all things, from whom, through whom, in whom, and toward whom they move and subsist [Col. 0573: thus ACE]—for this is the circular movement of the celestial powers around their principle: beginning from it as from a beginning; running through it by means of created causes [Col. 0573: thus CE; A reads “through it, through its reasons created by it”]; existing in it, as in the natural laws that are in it and beyond which they neither will nor can, nor will to be able, to go [Col. 0573: thus CE; A reads “in their natural laws” and “they neither will nor are willing to be able”]; and returning to it as to their end [Col. 0573: C reads “returning”; A, “return”; E, “returning it into itself and into its end”]—such movement exists in intellection alone; for they understand that they are from it, and that through it and in it their intellect moves [Col. 0573: thus CE; A reads “is exercised”], and they know that they have no end other than it [Col. 0573: thus CE; A omits “it”]—what prevents us from understanding human intellects in the same way as being ceaselessly revolved around God, since they exist from him, through him, in him, and toward him?

They revolve in the same intelligible circle, especially since the divine utterances declare that human beings were made in the image of God. This is not explicitly found to have been said about angels, though it is left to be understood on account of their intellectual nature [Col. 0573: thus CE; A omits the entire clause from “it is left” through “nature”].

We also read that the celestial powers stand before God and minister to him; but the catholic faith testifies that human nature has become God in the Word of God, sits at the right hand of God, and reigns. As for what the Lord promises generally to all human beings after the resurrection—“They will be like the angels of God in heaven”—I think it is to be understood as referring to the equality of nature and to equality of immortality [Col. 0575: thus CE; A reads “not equality of nature but of immortality”], and to the fact that they will be free from every bodily sex and every corruptible generation.

It is not incongruous to believe that the first condition of the human being before sin, in paradise—that is, in celestial blessedness—was equal to that of the angels and, as it were, connatural with it [Col. 0575: thus CE; A reads “it is not incongruous”]. For theology pronounces concerning both these natures, angelic and human, saying: “You made the heavens in intellect,” that is, so that they should be intellects essentially and substantially.

But because the human being, when he was in honor, did not understand, he was compared with senseless beasts and made like them, and thus withdrew far from angelic dignity and fell into the misery of this mortal life [Col. 0575: thus AE; C reads “of mortality”].

After the Word became flesh—that is, after God became man—the psalmist here marvels at the height of human nature’s first condition: “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?” “You made him a little lower than the angels,” it says [Col. 0575: C adds “for”]; that is, you permitted him to be made lower because of his pride and allowed him, by his own will, to fall into the degradation of irrational life.

God is said, in a certain manner of speaking, to do what he permits to be done: “You crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands; you subjected all things beneath his feet.”

Do you see how greatly human nature was humbled in the first human being after sin, and how greatly it was exalted in the second human being—that is, in Christ—through grace? For it was not only restored to the original condition of its nature from which the human being had fallen; it was also exalted in its head, who is Christ, above all celestial powers.

“Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more.” If, therefore, human nature, renewed in Christ, has not only attained angelic dignity but has also been assumed into God beyond every creature, and if what has occurred in the head will, in the members, occur in the future, it is impious to deny it. What wonder, then, if human intellects are nothing other than ineffable and unceasing movements?

I speak of those who are worthy to be around God, in whom they live, move, and exist. They exist through the principles by which they exist; they move through the principles of the virtues by which they can exist well; they live through the principles by which they exist eternally. Thus they exist, exist well, and exist eternally in God [Col. 0575: this sentence is omitted in E; A reads “therefore” instead of “thus”].

## DISC.

I not only grant this but also understand that the soul’s most excellent movement around the unknown God is most truly called and subsists as intellect, beyond every creature. But how, or by what reasoning, can intellect, while enclosed within the limits of human nature, rise above itself and every creature so as to accomplish its substantial movements around the unknown God, who is far removed from every created nature? I think this must be investigated [Col. 0575: Codex E ends at mid-column of folio 235b with the words “But how or by what reasoning is intellect, while enclosed within the limits of human nature”; thus C; A reads “I do not understand”].

## MAG.

In this part of theory, which discusses intellectual and rational substances, when one reaches the consideration of how created nature can rise beyond itself so as to adhere to the creative nature, every inquiry of those reasoning about nature’s power fails [Col. 0575: thus C; A reads “every reasoning”]. For what is perceived there is not the reason of nature but the ineffable and incomprehensible height of divine grace.

No created substance naturally possesses a power by which it can surpass the limits of its nature and immediately reach God through itself. This belongs to grace alone, not to any power of nature. Hence the Apostle confesses that he did not know how he had been caught up into paradise, saying: “I know a man who was caught up, but I do not know how” [Col. 0575: A omits “how”]—whether in the body or outside the body. It is as though he were saying [Col. 0575: this clause is omitted in C]: “For in the natural movements of the soul, whether in the body or outside the body, I see no power by which I can be caught up into the third heaven; but God alone knows [Col. 0575: A omits “but God alone”]. Yet I do not fail to know that I was caught up by his grace alone.”

No nature can ascend by itself into that place of which the Lord says: “Where I am, there my minister will be also” [Col. 0575: C omits “will be”]. Just as it surpasses every intellect to understand how the Word of God descended into a human being, so it surpasses every reason to understand how a human being ascends into God.

## DISC.

Although your answer was brief, it was sufficient and clear. Therefore direct the attention of your mind to what follows, namely the consideration of the soul’s second movement [Col. 0575: A omits “and”].

## MAG.

The soul’s second movement is, as we have said, the movement that remains within the limits of nature and defines God according to his causal character. That is, it knows only this about the unknown God: that he is the cause of all things and that the primordial causes of all things were eternally created by him and in him. It impresses upon the soul itself—the soul whose movement it is—the knowledge of those causes insofar as they are granted to it to understand.

Just as the soul receives from below the images of sensible things, which the Greeks call phantasies, so from above—that is, from the primordial causes—it impresses upon itself cognitions that the Greeks customarily call theophanies and the Latins “divine appearances.” Through these it receives a certain knowledge of God: I mean through the first causes, not so that it may understand what they are substantially—for this surpasses every movement of the soul—but so that it may know universally that they exist and that they flow forth through an ineffable procession into their effects.

This is the movement that the Greeks call λόγος or δύναμις, and we call reason or power. It arises from the first movement, which is intellect.

Just as a certain wise craftsman brings his art forth from himself and makes it in himself, and in that art foreknows the things that must be made, creating their causes universally and causally by his force and power before they appear in act and operation [Col. 0577: C reads “foresees”], so intellect has begotten its reason from itself and in itself, and within that reason foreknows everything it wishes to make and pre-creates it causally.

For we do not say that counsel is anything other than the conception of an artistic mind [Col. 0577: C reads “we say that counsel is”].

The soul’s second movement, therefore, is reason, which is understood in the mind as a kind of substantial vision and, as it were, as an art begotten by the intellect from itself, in itself, in which it foreknows and pre-creates the things it wishes to make [Col. 0577: C reads “begotten by it from itself”; A reads “foreknows beforehand”]. Hence reason is rightly called its form. For intellect is unknown through itself, but in its form, which is reason, it begins to appear both to itself and to others.

Just as the cause of all things cannot, through itself, be discovered either by itself or by anything else as to what it is, but is known in some manner in its theophanies, so intellect—which always revolves around that cause and was created wholly like it in its image—cannot be understood either by itself or by anything else as to what it is. But in reason, which is born from it [Col. 0577: C reads “from itself”], it begins to appear.

The claim I made—that neither the cause of all things nor intellect can be understood by itself as to what it is—will be considered shortly.

That, I think, is enough to have said about the second movement: what it is and from where it derives its origin [Col. 0577: A reads “from where it derives its origin” rather than “from where it derives its origin” in a different grammatical form].

## DISC.

Quite enough.

**MAG.** There remains, then, a third movement, which is concerned with the individual principles of individual things—principles that were created simply, that is, universally, in the primordial causes. When this movement takes the beginning of its substantial motion from the phantasies of sensible things reported to it through the external sense, it proceeds toward the purest discernment of all things through its proper principles: first into the most general essences, then into more general genera, and finally into the most specific forms and species—that is, into innumerable and infinite numbers, yet bounded by the immutable analogies of their nature. This is the movement called in Greek διάνοια or ἐνέργεια, but in Latin *sensus* or *operatio*—“sense” or “operation.” I mean the sense that is substantial and interior, and that likewise proceeds from the intellect through reason.

For whatever the intellect impresses upon its art—that is, upon reason—from its cognitive contemplation of the primordial causes, through its sense proceeding from itself and named after its operation, it divides into the proper principles of individual things, which were created primitively and universally in the causes. All essences are one in reason, but through sense they are distinguished into differing essences.

Reason apprehends the simplest knowledge of all essences as it descends intellectually from the simplest unity of their principles. Sense, however, separates that simplicity through differences. Likewise, reason intellectually recognizes the genera of things uniformly and simply in their universal causes and in themselves; but sense divides that most general simplicity—which is undivided in itself, subject to no differences, subordinate to no accidents, separated by no intervals, composed of no parts, and varied by no local or temporal motion—into the aforementioned different genera and differences, and into a thousand other distinctions.

The same is true of differing forms. In accordance with considered reason, they are one in their genera; yet, when sense operates through rational distinctions, they are distinguished from one another. That is, the intellect itself, through the sense consubstantial with it and by means of reason, investigates and pursues without error how things are divided, under the governance, command, and administration of divine providence, through natural movements into the distinct multiformity of things, and comprehends this by definite rules.

What shall I say of the infinite numbers? The more they become multiple through the activity of the interior sense, whether in themselves or in the nature of things, the more they are, when considered by reason, universally and simply one in their forms.

To summarize briefly: whatever the soul knows uniformly and universally about God and the primordial causes through its first movement, which is intellect, it impresses in the same uniform and universal manner upon its second movement, which is reason. Whatever it receives as formed in reason by the intellect from above, it distributes through sense among the effects below, into distinct essences, distinct genera, different forms, and multiple numbers.

To put it more plainly: whatever the human soul knows uniformly through its intellect in its reason about God and the principles of things, it always preserves uniformly. Whatever it perceives through reason to subsist as one and uniform in the causes, it understands wholly through sense as multiple in the effects of the causes, yet uniformly. And again, everything that it understands as dispersed in multiple ways through sense among the effects, it perceives through reason to subsist as one and uniform in the causes.

It knows with the purest intellect that all things begin from the one cause of all things and from the moment of multiplication, that they in no way abandon the simplicity of unity in which they eternally and immutably subsist, and that they bring the end of their entire movement to that cause and terminate it in that cause.

I believe that enough has been established concerning the three movements of the soul: intellect, which is also called essence; reason, which is called power; and sense, which is called operation.

[Textual apparatus to the foregoing passage: Col. 0577 A reads *singularumque* (“and of individual things”); C reads *simplicis simplicissimam* (“the simplest [knowledge] of the most-simple”), omits *et* (“and”) before *in seipsis*, omits *in* before *se ipsa*, and reads *differentiasque atque alia mille*, omitting *praedictas* (“the aforesaid”). A reads *corporali* (“bodily”) for *temporali* (“temporal”). C reads *consideratione* (“consideration”) for *consulta ratione* (“consulted reason”), and *dividantur* (“are divided”) for *dividuntur* (“are divided”). C reads *ex* (“from”) for *de* (“about”); A omits *semper uniformiter custodit … perspicit* (“it always preserves uniformly … it perceives”). C reads *multiplex* (“multiple”) for *multipliciter* (“in multiple ways”); A omits *et uniformiter* (“and uniformly”). A reads *et de* (“and concerning”) for *de* (“concerning”).]

**DISC.** Most lucidly, and in many ways.

### 24

**MAG.** Look, then, and with the mind’s eye, once all the darkness of ambiguity has been driven away, recognize how clearly and explicitly the substantial Trinity of divine goodness smiles upon those who rightly contemplate it in the movements of human nature [Note: [Col. 0579] A reads “of the soul”], and how it most limpidly manifests itself to those who devoutly seek it, as though in a certain proper mirror made in its own image. Although it is remote from every creature and unknown to every intellect, it presents itself to intellectual eyes through its image and likeness as though known and comprehensible and as though present; and it freely purifies the little mirror in which it is reflected, so that the one essential goodness may shine most clearly in it in three substances. This unity and Trinity would not appear in itself and through itself, because it escapes every intellect through the boundless excellence of its brilliance, unless it impressed traces of its knowledge upon its image.

For the clearest likeness of the Father shines in the soul, of the Son in reason, and of the Holy Spirit in sense. Just as we call the Son the art of the omnipotent Artificer—and rightly so, since in him, who is his wisdom, the omnipotent Father himself made everything whatsoever he willed and preserves it eternally and immutably—so also the human intellect, whatever it most purely and unhesitatingly perceives about God and the principles of all things, creates through knowledge, by a wondrous operation of science, in a certain art of its own, by which I mean in reason, and stores it through memory in the most secret recesses of that reason [Note: [Col. 0579] A reads “in the recesses of that very [reason]”].

Just as the omnipotent Father, the maker of all things, created simultaneously and once for all, primitively, causally, uniformly, and universally, in his Word, in his only-begotten Son, whatever he established in his art—which is his wisdom and power—and then divided it through the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself and from the Son into the innumerable effects of the primordial causes, whether those effects flowed forth as intelligible essences and differences surpassing every bodily sense, or as the varied and manifold adornment of this sensible world, changeable through distinctions of places and times, so the intellect—that is, the principal movement of the soul—formed by the cognitive contemplation of intelligible things divides into the distinct and unmixed knowledge of individual things, whether intelligible or sensible, everything that it creates in the art of reason and stores through the interior sense of the soul.

For everything that the intellect universally considers in reason, it divides particularly through sense into the distinct cognitions and definitions of all things. You see, then, that the Father created universally in his Son everything that he willed, and has distributed, is distributing, and will distribute it particularly through his Holy Spirit. In the likeness of the three divine Persons, understand also that our intellect creates universally in reason, through cognition in the act of knowledge—that is, forms—everything that it can understand about God and the causes of things; and that, through sense consubstantial with it, it divides particularly, through the power of contemplation, into the individual definitions of things the cognitions that it gathers in reason, assigning its cognition to each thing with the most careful discernment.

**DISC.** These matters shine before me in a certain way. But I do not yet see the difference between the creative operation of the uncreated Trinity and the act of the created and creative Trinity. I say “creative,” for we do not doubt that the trinity of our nature—which is not the image of God but was created according to the image of God (for the only true image of the invisible God, in no respect unlike him and coessential with the Father and the Spirit, is the only-begotten Word of God)—was not only created from nothing, but also creates beneath itself the senses adhering to it, the workshops of the senses, and this entire body of its own, by which I mean the mortal body. For it was made by God, according to the image of God, from nothing; but it creates its own body not from nothing, but from something.

For the soul, joining incorporeal qualities together and taking and placing beneath those qualities, as it were, a certain subject derived from quantity, creates a body for itself in which it may openly reveal its hidden actions, invisible in themselves, and bring them forth into sensible awareness, as was argued in the preceding book and will be investigated more carefully when we reach the consideration of the action of the primordial causes. But now I earnestly ask you to explain the matter at hand.

**MAG.** The solution to this question seems to me extremely easy and almost effortless. The supreme Trinity, creator of all things and created by none, made everything that it made from nothing. For it is proper to divine goodness to call into existence from non-being whatever it wishes to come into being.

Indeed, the word *goodness* itself derives from no other source than the Greek verb βοῶ, that is, “I cry out.” But βοῶ and καλῶ—that is, “I cry out” and “I call”—have one meaning, since one who calls very often breaks into a cry. God, therefore, is appropriately called “good” and “goodness,” because by an intelligible cry he calls everything from nothing into being. Hence in Greek God is called καλός, that is, “good,” διὰ τὸ πάντα καλεῖν εἰς οὐσίαν, “because he calls everything into being.”

Everything that subsists naturally was called from nothing into being by the Creator through the fivefold movement of universal creation. Some things were called into existence merely so that they might subsist essentially; some so that they might subsist and live; in some, sense was added to substantial life; in some, reason was added to vital sense; and in some, intellect was superimposed upon the preceding natural movements as their perfection.

The first movement is observed in natural bodies; the second in that life by which trees and grasses both live and grow; the third in irrational animals; the fourth properly in human nature; and the fifth in angelic nature [Note: [Col. 0581] C reads “the fifth still in angelic nature”]. Through these five degrees, the goodness of the supreme and holy Trinity is perceived in the creation of things from nothing, and its ineffable operation is manifested.

The Trinity that was created in our nature according to the image of the Creator creates nothing from nothing. That belongs to God alone and to no creature. Its action, however, appears to be twofold. For either it investigates, through its rational and intellectual movements, those things that its Creator established from nothing; and what it knows by pure intellectual contemplation in the nature of things, it arranges in the innermost chambers of its reason, gathering into one the cognitions of all things that it can know—for example, genera in essence, forms in genera, and the numbers of individuals in the form of knowledge—or else it makes one thing multiple, dividing it in many ways by distributing each cognition to the individual things whose cognitions they are. That is, to use the same example, it distinguishes, through a cognitive operation, essence into genera, genus into forms, and form into individuals.

This is the principal and supreme operation of rational nature. Its second operation is the one that, as we have said, is recognized in the creation of its body and revealed in its careful governance. First it receives the material of its body from the qualities of sensible things; then, without any intervening temporal interval, it bestows upon that material form and vital movement [Note: [Col. 0581] A reads “vital manner,” with *form* omitted], by which it both enlivens and nourishes the material and advances it toward the growth of complete stature through the numbers of places and times. It also provides it with external sense, through which it receives the phantasies of all things that it touches externally.

Other matters can likewise be conceived and understood concerning the soul’s constant and continuous care and activity toward its body and bodily things—whether it is present to the senses while awake, or removed from them in sleep; whether it handles within itself images of things that it has taken in through the senses; whether it fashions images of images; or whether it distributes through the hidden passages of the veins and nerves—which the Greeks call πόροι or ἀρτηρίαι—the bodily nourishment that it receives externally for the construction of the body.

For just as the supreme Trinity moves, governs, and orders, by the rules of its providence, the whole universe of creation that it established from nothing, and permits nothing that it created to perish—that is, to return completely to nothing—so the trinity of our nature provides for the safety of its entire body and all its senses; it gives the body life, moves it, and sustains it, insofar as its mortal fragility permits.

[Additional textual apparatus for §§24–25: Col. 0579 A reads *animae* (“of the soul”) for *humanae naturae* (“of human nature”); C reads *saepe* (“often”); C has *resplendescit* (“shines”) for *resplendescat* (“may shine”); A has *ipsius sinibus* (“the recesses of that very [reason]”) for *sinibus ipsius*. C reads *formatur* (“is formed”) for *formatus* (“formed”), and *cautissimo* (“most cautious”) for *cautissimae* (“of most cautious [discernment]”); A omits *et* (“and”), reads *enim* (“for”) for *quippe* (“indeed”), and reads *ex* (“from”) for *de* (“from/about”). A reads *existentiam* (“existence”) for *existentia* (“existence,” in the printed construction), and *hoc est* (“that is”) for *id est* (“that is”). A reverses the word order as *subsistant essentialiter* (“subsist essentially”); C has *herbaque* (“and grass”) for *herbaeque* (“and grasses”), omits *in* (“in”), and reads *quintus adhuc in angelica* (“the fifth still in angelic”) for *quintus in angelica* (“the fifth in angelic”). A reads *Ex* (“From”) for *Et* (“And”), *aspicitur* (“is seen”) for *perspicitur* (“is perceived”), and *est condita* (“was created”) for *condita* (“created”). A transposes the two alternatives in the account of the soul’s first action: it first divides essence into genera, genus into forms, and form into individuals, and then makes the cognitions one—genera in essence, forms in genus, and numbers of individuals in the form of knowledge. C reads *incolumitate* (“safety”) for *incolumitati* (“for the safety”); C reads *hoc est* (“that is”) for *ita* (“so”).]

### 25

But take care lest from these arguments you begin to infer that, in the creation of the soul, the formation of the spiritual body before sin preceded it by some temporal interval [Note: [Col. 0581] “the spiritual body before sin” is omitted in A]. The soul precedes the body only in the dignity and excellence of its nature, not in place or time. [Textual variants: A omits *ex* (“from”) in *ex his rationibus* and reads *ad animae creationem* (“to the creation of the soul”); C omits *et* (“and”) and *enim* (“for”); A reads *aestimes* (“suppose”) for *existimes* (“suppose”). C omits *condita sunt* (“were created”); A reads *conditaque* (“and established”) for *praeconditaque* (“and pre-established”), omits *caelestem* (“heavenly”), and reads *ac* (“and”) for *atque* (“and”).]

For simultaneously and once for all, in that one human being who was made according to the image of God, the principles of all human beings were created according to body and soul.

In no respect, according to temporal delays, does the essence of the soul precede the essence of the body, just as the essence of the body does not precede the essence of the soul. And do not suppose that I have said that the first essential body was created in paradise, although at that stage it existed only rationally, just as the soul itself did. For in that general and universal human being made according to the image of God, all human beings were created simultaneously and once for all, according to body and soul, in mere possibility; and in him they all sinned before they emerged spiritually into their own substances, as the angels did—that is, before each one appeared, according to angelic multiplication, in its own distinct difference, in a rational soul and spiritual body. That body would cling incorruptibly and eternally, indeed co-eternally, to the soul if it did not sin; in it all human beings will rise again.

Nor have I said that that body was created by the soul. It was immediately created by the one Creator of all things, simultaneously with the rational soul, in heavenly blessedness—or rather, substantially for heavenly blessedness. I say “substantially” because the true substance of each creature is its principle, foreknown and pre-established in the primordial causes, by which God determined that it would be thus and not otherwise. I also said “for heavenly blessedness,” since I do not see how a human being would lose blessedness if he had fully and perfectly tasted it in reality. For, as I think, he turned first toward himself rather than toward God, and therefore fell.

This corruptible and material body, however, which was taken from the clay of the earth, was, as we said above [Note: [Col. 0581] A omits “as we said above”], created after sin as the deserved consequence of sin, to exercise the negligent soul in keeping the commandments and to reveal its hidden operations. I do not hesitate to affirm that it was created and is daily created through a certain proper operation of the soul [Note: [Col. 0581] A reads “operation”].

You should not be troubled by the fact that Holy Scripture says that God took clay from the earth and formed the human body from it. For the action of the creature is appropriately referred to him from whom every natural action begins. In the heavenly essences also, as the orders descend gradually from the first order—which begins immediately after God [Note: [Col. 0581] A reads *quod* (“which”) for *qui* (“which [order]”)]—to the last, whatever a higher order administers and accomplishes in a lower order through a certain proper action is all referred to him from whom every natural movement begins and from whom natural action descends from the highest to the lowest.

For although the cause of all things creates, moves, and governs the entire universe of nature established by it not through itself—for it is immutable—but through a creature subject to it, nevertheless the whole dispensation of divine providence flows back into it, because it is the cause of all things.

What shall I say of the orders of the Church established in this still-mortal life, among which the order of bishops is pre-eminent? Is not everything that the other, later arrangements accomplish in the offices assigned to them referred back to that order, since the later orders receive from it what they must accomplish? [Note: [Col. 0583] BC read *ad eum* (“to him”); A reads *ad eum episcopum* (“to that bishop”).] From it, each symbolic ministry is distributed to each individual, and the spiritual operation of the whole Church is through it referred back to the very cause—I mean God—of all good and mystical actions.

Why, then, should it be surprising if the first human being, created according to the image of God, transgressed the divine command, and consequently was expelled from the blessedness of paradise, and—admonished by divine providence—created for himself a fragile and mortal dwelling from the clay of the earth? Since he had proudly neglected to possess and preserve the heavenly and spiritual body created for him by God himself, he was humbled and made a mortal lodging suited to the desert of his disobedience, taken from earthly matter, in which he might repent under punishment and, through discipline, seek to return to the original dignity of his nature by recognizing and humbling himself. Nor is Scripture silent about this.

### 26

For immediately after the transgression, Scripture says that simple human nature before sin, divided after the fall into two sexes [Note: [Col. 0583] C omits *in* (“into”) in *in duplicem sexum* (“into two sexes”)], “sewed fig leaves and made themselves περιζώματα,” that is, “coverings,” clearly indicating through the symbol of the leaves the fragile and fleeting condition of this mortal body, with which the human being had covered himself after his ruin.

Our mortal bodies are indeed very like broad fig leaves. Just as those leaves cast shade and shut out the rays of the sun [Note: [Col. 0583] A reads “exclude”], so our bodies both bring the darkness of ignorance upon our souls [Note: [Col. 0583] A omits “upon our souls”] and repel the knowledge of truth. Yet these leaves of ours—that is, our earthly bodies—habitually surround and shade on every side the sweetness of earthly and deadly pleasures as though it were a certain fruit [Note: [Col. 0583] A omits “as though it were a certain fruit”], and lure and deceive us in them [Note: [Col. 0583] Conjecture; C reads “they grow accustomed to allure us and deceive us in repose,” with the printed form *affallare*; A omits “allure and deceive”].

To make you recognize most clearly that the creation of our mortal body is to be referred to him by whose counsel everything concerning our discipline, recall, and salvation is done [Note: [Col. 0583] A reads *renovationem* (“renewal”) for *revocationem* (“recall”)], listen to the same Scripture: “The Lord God also made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.” Here we may appropriately understand that the tunics of skins signify nothing other than the περιζώματα—namely, the mortal bodies [Note: [Col. 0583] C reads *praeter quod περιζώματα* (“except that they are *perizōmata*”); A omits *videlicet* (“namely”)]—which the first human beings made for themselves after the transgression, with the just judgment of the Creator permitting it [Note: [Col. 0583] Conjecture; C reads “by the judgment of the condition”; A reads “by the indication of the Creator”].

And do you think it more credible that a mortal human being made mortal flesh for himself than that God himself created it, but merely permitted and admonished? [Note: [Col. 0583] C has *ducendum* (“to be held”) and A omits it; C reads *nam ipsum* (“for God himself”) for *quam ipsum* (“than God himself”).] God is immortal, and whatever he makes through himself is immortal. Everything mortal that appears to exist in this sensible world—fragile and transitory—is either made by us ourselves as we go astray through our irrational movements, or is permitted to come into being, because of our sin, for the use and instruction of our mortal life, whether good virtues administer and complete it [Note: [Col. 0583] A omits “administer and complete”] or evil forces, by impeding the natural course at fixed intervals, prevent it from reaching its proper end.

No one who philosophizes correctly doubts that the vital movement operates in seeds so that they may proceed through generation into visible forms [Note: [Col. 0583] A reads *nullus recte philosophus philosophantium*, an evidently corrupt reading, for *nullus recte philosophantium* (“no one who philosophizes correctly”)]. But that vital movement does not always manifest the power of its action equally in each kind, either because of certain accidents that do not suit the seeds and arise from contrary qualities, or because of the opposing forces that, as we said, resist the natural movement. To discuss these matters now would be both lengthy and superfluous, since they have been treated at length [Note: [Col. 0583] A: “There is another place for discussing these matters”].

Perhaps, however, someone will ask where that first incorruptible body now is—the body that would cling to the soul if it did not sin. For what is incorruptible cannot perish. The brief answer is that it still lies hidden in the secret recesses of human nature [Note: [Col. 0583] A: “in the secret boundaries of its nature”], but it will appear in the age to come, when this mortal body will be changed into it, and this corruptible body will put on incorruption.

Hear the Apostle: “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body will rise. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory”—namely, in the glory of immortality and incorruptibility, whether in the good or in the wicked. I think that this was said generally of every human body. For in all there will be the glory of eternal immortality, though not an equal blessedness.

For the entire primordial nature, together with what has been added to it, will be restored into one.

### 27

**DISC.** For the present, enough has been said about this question, I think [Note: [Col. 0583] C reads *iterum* (“again”) for *interim* (“for the present”)]. We must return to the consideration of that Trinity according to whose image and likeness we were created, and carefully examine whether the image in every respect imitates the likeness of the one whose image it is [Note: [Col. 0585] C reads “whose image it is”], or whether it is in some respect unlike and falls short, failing to attain the perfect image altogether. For insofar as it imitates, it is rightly called an image. If it falters in any respect, it departs from the character of a perfect image.

**MAG.** We believe that the human being was made most perfectly according to the image and likeness of God, and failed in no respect in paradise before sin, except with regard to the condition of being a subject. [Textual variants: A reads *vero* (“indeed”) for *enim* (“for”), omits *et in* (“and in”), reads *Notato itaque, quod* (“Let it be noted, therefore, that”) for *Eo itaque notato, quod* (“With this therefore noted, that”), and reads *habuit* (“had”) for *habet* (“has”); C reads *per se* (“through itself”) for *praecedente se* (“preceding it”) and *cognitionis* (“cognition”) for *conditionis* (“creation/formation”).]

For God, subsisting through himself and receiving subsistence from no one preceding him, brought the human being from nothing into being according to his own image and likeness.

Let us note, then, that God possesses his essence through himself as ἄναρχος, that is, “without beginning”; whereas the human being, created from nothing, has a beginning of his formation, not only in the primordial causes, in which all things were created simultaneously, but also in their processions into different essences and forms, whether intellectual or sensible.

Everything else that is said and understood about God through essential excellence is wholly discerned in his image through nature and grace. [Note: [Col. 0585] C reads *imaginem* (“the image,” accusative) for *imagine* (“in the image”); A omits *naturam et* (“nature and”).] The invisible, incomprehensible Creator, surpassing every intelligence, created his image like himself in all these respects. [Note: [Col. 0585] A omits *sibi* (“to himself/like himself”), and also omits *et* (“and”) in *Nam et noster intellectus* (“For our intellect too”).]

Our intellect neither knows from itself what it is according to essence, nor from anyone other than God, who alone knows what he has made. Just as it knows only this about its Creator—that he is—but does not perceive what he is, so it defines of itself only that it has been created; it cannot understand how or in what substance it has been established.

For if it understood in any way what it is, it would necessarily depart from the likeness of the Creator [Note: [Col. 0585] C reads *necessario similitudinem* (“necessarily [the] likeness”) for *necessario a similitudine* (“necessarily from the likeness”)]. God is the Πρωτότυπον, that is, the “principal exemplar,” by nature; the image is God by grace.

The Πρωτότυπον is diffused through all things, distributing essence to them; the image, purified, illuminated, and perfected in every respect by the light of grace, passes through all things, confirming their knowledge in itself [Note: [Col. 0585] C reads *purgaret* (“might purify”) for *purgata* (“purified”), and *conformans* (“conforming”) for *confirmans* (“confirming”)].

The Πρωτότυπον penetrates all the things it made, distributing its gifts to each according to the proper analogy of each [Note: [Col. 0585] A reads *dona sua* (“its gifts”) for *sua* (“its own [things/gifts]”)]; the image surveys all things, praising the giver of good things through all the innumerable gifts distributed to them.

Some gifts are substantial and are properly called “given”; others are added to substance. And just as the Πρωτότυπον created its image in order to display in it a certain knowledge of itself, so the image made an image for itself in which it might manifest its movements, hidden in themselves.

For the soul is the image of God, while the body is the image of the soul, together with the other matters that must be understood and stated concerning the likeness of the image. Whoever wishes to know more fully about these matters should read the book of Saint Gregory of Nyssa on the image [Note: [Col. 0585] A reads *scire plenius* (“to know more fully”) for *plenius scire* (“more fully to know”)].

**DISC.** I willingly accept these points. But I see another difference besides the substantial one, which seems to divide the image from its principal form [Note: [Col. 0585] C reads *ex principibus* (“from the principal [forms]”) for *ex principali* (“from its principal [form]”)].

**MAG.** Tell me, I ask, what that difference is.

**DISC.** Do you not think there is a significant difference between the nature that knows itself—both that it exists and what it is—and the nature that knows only that it exists, but does not understand what it is? [Note: [Col. 0585] C reads *Non* (“not”) for *Num* (the interrogative “do …?”).] For, I believe, you will not deny that God himself understands what he is, while we do not deny that the other created essences and substances cannot understand of themselves what they are [Note: [Col. 0585] A omits *quid sint* (“what they are”)], lest we seem impudently to contradict Gregory Nazianzen, the Theologian, and the aforementioned Gregory of Nyssa [Note: [Col. 0585] C omits *Nyssaeoque praedicto* (“and the aforesaid Gregory of Nyssa”)], who unanimously establish by certain arguments [Note: [Col. 0585] C reads *approbat* (“establishes/approves,” singular) for *approbant* (“establish/approve,” plural)] that no created essence can define, either by itself or by another—even one endowed with reason or intellect—what it is.

Do you therefore see a dissimilarity between the image and its principal form—that is, between the human intellect and God the Creator—not only in the condition of being a subject, but also in this: that the principal form knows what it is, whereas the image neither understands what it itself is nor can it substantially define its own form, which it imitates? [Textual variants: A omits *principalis* (“principal”); C omits *vero* (“whereas”).]

28. **MASTER.** I see that you have been deceived by the likeness of true reasoning [Note: *rationis* (“of reasoning”) for *ratiocinationis* (“of argument”)]. Nor is this without cause. Unless someone examines keenly and carefully the matters in which you seem to be mistaken, they will appear not merely plausible but even true.

**STUDENT.** Explain, I ask, where I am mistaken.

**MASTER.** Do you think that the divine essence is infinite or finite?

**STUDENT.** To doubt this is both impious and most foolish, especially since it must be believed and understood to be not an essence but more-than-essence, the infinite cause of all essences [Col. 0586C], indeed not merely infinite but the infinity—and more-than-infinity—of all infinite essences.

**MASTER.** Rightly, then, and in a Catholic manner [Note: *itaque* (“therefore”) is omitted in A]; it is altogether infinite.

**STUDENT.** I granted this, and I do not regret granting it; rather, I most firmly affirm that it cannot be otherwise.

**MASTER.** Take care not to withdraw your position.

**STUDENT.** There is no reason to suspect that.

**MASTER.** Therefore, when we ask what this or that is, do we seem to you to be seeking anything other than either an already defined substance or one capable of being defined?

**STUDENT.** Nothing else. For the word “what,” although interrogative, asks only that the substance it seeks be defined in some way.

**MASTER.** If, then, no wise person asks generally of every essence what it is, since it cannot be defined, but only discloses its existence—not what it is—through its circumstances, within which it is circumscribed as though by boundaries, namely place and time, quantity and quality, relation, conjunction [Note: *conjunction* is so found in C], state, motion, possession, and the other accidents, by which the substance itself, unknown and indefinable in itself by virtue of its subject, is manifested: who, instructed in the disciplines of theology [Col. 0587A] [Note: A reads *disciple*], would dare ask of the divine substance what it is, when he understands with perfect clarity that it can neither be defined nor be any of the things that exist, and that it surpasses everything that can be defined?

Listen to Gregory of Nazianzus:

“If the very totality which is and is called the aggregate of those things which we both understand and say concerning that which is sought is, according to its own being, none at all of the things that exist, but something other than that about which these things are—for it contains them, whereas it is in no way contained by them—let every soul cease from every account of the things concerning God, and not rashly leap into defining him, but worship in silence the ineffable One who is beyond understanding, the truth of the divine essence, the highest summit of all knowledge. If, then, no one among the wisest can know the rational principles of the substance of existing things, according to which they were founded, who would dare define God in any respect?”

**STUDENT.** I would not presume to ask even this, since I know that it is altogether infinite [Note: So C; A places the words from “I would not presume…” through “altogether infinite” above, after “surpasses everything that can be defined.”].

**MASTER.** Therefore, if God knows himself—what he is—does he not define himself? For everything that is understood, what it is, can be defined either by itself or by another [Note: C reads: “can be defined by itself or by another, can be defined by itself or by another”]. Consequently, he is not infinite universally, but particularly, if he cannot be defined solely by a creature but can be defined by himself. Or, to put it another way, he is finite to himself and infinite to the creature. If this is granted, it necessarily follows either that God is not universally infinite, if he refuses to be defined by the creature alone but not by himself, or that, in order to be universally infinite, he receives definition in no way at all—neither from the creature nor from himself [Col. 0587C].

**STUDENT.** I consider the darkness of this present argument inaccessible; and unless the one being sought stretches out his right hand to those who seek him, I would scarcely believe that there is any entrance into it. For if God does not define himself—or cannot define himself—who could deny that ignorance and incapacity befall him? Ignorance, that is, if he does not understand what he is; incapacity, if he cannot define what subsists. For he will appear incapable if he cannot define himself in any respect. But if he both understands and defines what he himself is, he will be shown not to be altogether infinite, since he cannot be defined by the creature alone because the creature in no way understands him, whereas by himself he is both defined and known—what he is.

**MASTER.** Do not be troubled, but rather be of good courage [Col. 0587D]. This consideration draws us toward understanding ourselves and leads us, under his guidance, to those things that must be piously thought, understood, and pronounced about our God. For the darker and more laborious it appears at the entrance to the inquiry, the clearer and more fruitful it will be found. As Saint Augustine says, by a certain divine providence [Note: A reads “divine providence”], it cannot happen that the ability to find should be lacking to devout minds that piously and earnestly seek themselves and their God—that is, the truth.

**STUDENT.** I am not troubled, but I am rightly moved all the more by the obscurity of the present question, and I do not think that its solution will be easy.

**MASTER.** Let us therefore return to the matters discussed between us in the preceding book and, if I am not mistaken, brought to complete clarity.

**STUDENT.** Remind me, please, what those matters are.

**MASTER.** Do you remember that we established clearly among ourselves that none of the ten categories can in any way properly be predicated of the divine nature?

**STUDENT.** That has been both unshakably conceded and firmly established [Note: C reads *stabilitatum*, “stabilized,” instead of *stabilitum*, “established”].

**MASTER.** We shall therefore not sweat so laboriously, as you think [Note: A reads *aestimas*, “you think”], in solving the difficulty of this question, if we carefully discern the established conclusions of the preceding book. For their subtle and penetrating usefulness will here be shown to bear the most beautiful and most beneficial fruit.

**STUDENT.** That will be very necessary, if it is so [Note: C reads *est*, “is,” instead of *erit*, “will be”].

**MASTER.** It certainly will. The sequence of the argument seems to demand that we briefly recall the categories themselves.

**STUDENT.** No other path of inquiry appeals to me [Note: A: “The path does not appeal”]. Nevertheless, I would like you to recapitulate them in interrogative form.

**MASTER.** Attend, then, to this order of questioning: What? How much? What kind? Toward what? In what position? In what condition? Somewhere? At some time? Does it act [Note: A reads simply “does it act”]? Or does it undergo? Likewise, if you wish to put them in Greek:

Τί; πόσον; ποῖον; πρὸς τί; κεῖσθαι; ἆρα ἔχεσθαι [Note: C omits *ἔχεσθαι*]; ἆρα ποῖ; πότε; τί πράττει; ἄρα ἢ πάσχει; (What? How much? What kind? In relation to what? To be situated? To be disposed? Whither? When? What does it do? Or what does it undergo?)

None of these, then, is properly asked of God [Note: A: “none of these is asked of God”], because none of them is understood to be in him, either by himself or by another. For these things can properly be considered in those matters that are shown to fall under understanding or sense.

What, then? If you ask of God what he is, will you not be seeking some proper and defined substance [Note: A reads “will you seek”]? And if someone answers, “This” or “that,” will he not appear to define some definite and circumscribed substance? But if someone speaks truthfully about him—or if he himself understands this about himself—he will rightly occupy the first place among the categories, which is assigned to definite and determined subjects, in and around which all accidents operate and are contained. Accordingly, the first category will be predicated of him not metaphorically but properly.

For whether the divine nature is understood by an intellectual creature or by itself in some definite essence, it is not altogether infinite and uncircumscribed [Note: C reads “circumscribed”]. Nor is it believed to be removed in truth beyond everything that is said and understood, since it is understood within certain boundaries of a defined nature. For everything of which it can be predicated or understood what it is cannot exceed the number of things that exist; rather, it will rightly be judged to be either a part in a whole, a whole in parts, a form in a genus, a genus in forms, an individual number in a species, a species in individuals, or some collection of all the foregoing gathered into a certain unity [Col. 0589A] [Note: C reads “into one unity”].

This is far removed from the simple and infinite truth of the divine nature, which does not subsist as any of the things that exist. For it is neither whole nor part; yet it is called whole and part, because every whole and every part, all wholes and all parts, were created by it. Similarly, it is neither genus nor form nor species nor number, nor does it subsist as *οὐσία* (*ousia*, substance), whether as the most general or the most specific. Yet all these are predicated of it, because they receive from it the capacity to subsist. It is also called the totality of all these things, since by the infinity of its excellence it surpasses the totality of the entire creation, because the universal totality was created by it.

How, then, can the divine nature understand itself—what it is—when it is nothing? For it surpasses everything that is, since it is not itself being, but all being is from it, and it surpasses every essence and substance by the power of its excellence.

Or how can the infinite be defined by itself in anything, or understood in anything, when it knows itself to be beyond every finite and infinite thing, beyond finitude and infinitude?

God therefore does not know what he is, because he is not a “what”; for he is incomprehensible in any respect, both to himself and to every intellect. And when the truth itself proclaims in an intelligible voice, among pure intellects, that these things are most truly said about God [Note: A: “most truly about God,” with the word order altered], no pious person who knows and has been introduced into the divine mysteries, hearing that God cannot understand what he is, ought to suppose anything else than that God himself, who is not a “what,” altogether ignores in himself what he is not, while he does not know himself to be any thing.

He therefore does not know what he himself is—that is, he does not know himself to be a “what”—because he knows that he is altogether none of those things that are known in something and of which it can be said or understood what they are. For if he knew himself in something, he would not indicate himself to be altogether infinite, incomprehensible, and unnameable.

“Why do you ask my name?” he says. And this is a wondrous kind of name—or is it not truly a wondrous name, one that is above every name, unnameable, exalted above every named name, whether in this age or in the age to come?

If, then, he rebukes the asking of his name because he is above every name and unnameable, what if someone should ask about his substance—which, if it existed in something finite, would not lack a finite name? But because it does not subsist in anything, because it is infinite and free from every naming, it is unnameable [Note: Conjecture; AC read “because it is unnameable”].

Everything that is understood substantially in something, so that what it is may properly be predicated of it, exceeds neither its mode nor its measure. For it is enclosed by some mode through which it is bounded, and outlined by some measure that it cannot surpass [Note: C reads “outlines”].

If it occupies the lowest place in the nature of things, where all bodies are contained [Col. 0590A], it cannot extend the measure of its nature any lower, because nothing is lower, nor can it rise higher. For it is bounded within the vital motion by which it is nourished and grows, and therefore does not advance beyond it.

But if it subsists in the loftiness of the whole creation, so that it is recognized as intellectual, it must necessarily be confined by its own boundaries. For it cannot rise to a creature higher than itself, since nothing higher than it seems to exist among created things. Nor can it be lowered further, because of the subsistences that follow after it.
