If, however, it occupied a place at the midpoint of the balance, it would neither relax itself toward lower things [Note: A reads *relaxaretur*, “would be relaxed”] nor extend itself toward higher things [Note: A reads *extenderetur*, “would be extended”], but would retain its natural and intermediate state [Note: C omits “but would retain its natural and intermediate state”].

Accordingly, there is no creature, whether visible or invisible, that is not confined in some respect within the boundaries of its own nature, according to measure, number, and weight [Col. 0590B] [Note: C reads “confines”].

God, however, does not understand himself as being in any of these things. Rather, he knows himself to be above all orders of nature through the excellence of his wisdom, beneath all things through the height of his power, within all things through the inscrutable administration of his providence, and encompassing all things because all things are in him and nothing is outside him.

For he alone is measure without measure, number without number, weight without weight. And rightly so, because he is measured, numbered, and ordered by no one—not even by himself—nor does he understand himself to be in any measure, number, or order, since he is substantially contained in none of these things, while he alone truly exists as infinite in all things and above all things.

And do not object to me by asking why I said that the order of bodies cannot extend itself into natures higher than itself [Col. 0590C] [Note: C reads “extend”], when we believe that all bodies will pass into incorporeal qualities and substances. For when that happens, they will cease to be bodies. But while they are still bodies, they can transgress neither the lower nor the higher boundaries of their nature [Note: C reads “cannot transgress the lower or higher boundaries”]. This matter will be treated more fully in that part of philosophy in which we shall consider the return of things into their causes.

For now, let us examine the matter at hand: namely, that God does not understand what he is. And concerning this proposition that we are trying to persuade you of—what do you think? Do not be ashamed to admit it [Note: C reads simply “And concerning what we are trying to persuade you of, what do you think?”; A has: “And whether what we are trying to persuade you of seems plausible to you, do not be ashamed to admit it,” and continues as here].

**STUDENT.** Concerning this wondrous divine ignorance, by which God does not understand what he himself is [Note: C reads “what he is”], I confess that what you have said, although obscure, nevertheless seems to me not false but true, or at least resembling the truth. For you are not persuading me that God is ignorant of himself, but only that he is ignorant of what he is. And rightly so, because he is not a “what”; for he is infinite both to himself and to all things that are from him. Accordingly, in this form of ignorance, the highest and ineffable wisdom shines forth most openly and beautifully. For “the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings.”

**MASTER.** What, then? If someone asks how great or of what quality God is, would it seem correct to you to answer, “So great and of such a quality”? I am not speaking of that quantity and quality of which the Prophet says:

“Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised,  
and of his greatness there is no end.”

See how profoundly the Theologian speaks: “Great,” he says, “is the Lord.” But lest anyone think that he is bounded by a finite quantity, he immediately adds: “and of his greatness there is no end.” Likewise, lest anyone suppose that a finite quality exists in him, he did not say simply “and praiseworthy,” but added “exceedingly”; and “exceedingly” is said of that which surpasses every measure.

I am not, therefore, as I said, naming that infinite quantity, nor that quality which is “exceedingly” so; for these are not improperly conceived of God [Note: C omits “not”]. Rather, I mean the quality and quantity that are predicated according to accident in a subject.

**STUDENT.** Not rightly. For where a defined substance—or, so to speak, a defined subject—is not found, there it seems to me exceedingly foolish and ridiculous to seek and affirm quantity [Note: C reads “quantity and quality”]. Accordingly, since in God neither he himself nor any other intellect can find any defined substance—or, so to speak, any defined subject—according to which what he is could be said or understood, is it not perfectly clear that no finite or infinite quantity, and no finite or infinite quality, can be known to exist in him either by himself or by another?

For if, by the infinite and more-than-infinite excellence of his own power, he surpasses every finite and infinite substance, who would not immediately and without hesitation burst forth to acknowledge and exclaim openly that no finite or infinite quantity or quality falls upon him, or that he is at all a “what” in any respect?

For wherever there is a “what,” there immediately appear “how much” and “what kind.” But where there is no “what,” it is impossible to find “how much” and “what kind.” If, therefore, in the genera of things neither “what,” nor “how much,” nor “what kind,” nor any accident is understood—since they are simple, whereas these are sought only in individuals—who but a fool would dare seek in God a “what,” a “how much,” or a “what kind”?

**MASTER.** What, then? Do you think that there is in it a relation, which the Greeks call *πρός τι* (“relation to something”)?

**STUDENT.** I would not say even that. For wherever a defined substance cannot be understood, I do not doubt that no relation can be present. For it is not according to substance [A: “nature”], but according to a certain connection and disposition [A omits “disposition”] of two or more subjects [C: “of very many”]. For when, in the Trinity of the divine goodness, the Father is called the Father of the Son under a relational form [A: “of the relation”], and the Son the Son of the Father, this seems to me to signify possession more than a reciprocal relation. Yet it is not an accident for the Father to possess the Son, nor for the Son to possess the Father [C: “or”].

**MASTER.** It seems superfluous, as I judge, to speak individually of the remaining categories. For if God himself understands himself in no defined substance, quantity, quality, or relation, who will not see more clearly than daylight that no position or state, no place or time, no acting or undergoing, occurs in him at all, and consequently that none of these can be understood either by himself or by another in himself [A: “in him”]?

Since a defined substance is neither found nor understood in him, it is right to doubt that any accident of a defined substance occurs in him. For where the defined subject is absent, no accident is understood as joined to it or separated from it, or in any way distinguished from the nature of the subject.

But, to speak briefly about each category, matters which we treated at length in the preceding book [C: “at length,” feminine]: who could have assigned position to the divine nature, when it itself recognizes no position in itself? Position belongs either to parts in a whole [A: “in a place”]. For example, the position of the human body is the order of its members, by which every member is placed [A: “bounded”] in its proper order. Position is also said of the placement of an entire body: for example, it stands, sits, or lies. No one who philosophizes rightly is unaware that the divine essence is entirely without all these conditions. It is not a whole, nor a part; it does not sit as though fatigued; it does not lie as though prostrate; nor does it stand after any movement [C omits the clause from “No one” through “any movement”].

The Son is said to sit at the right hand of the Father—the whole Son, the Word and the flesh [C: “God”]. The right hand of the Father is the power of the Father, the strength of the Father. Therefore the Son himself is the right hand of the Father. Where, then, does he sit? He sits in himself [A: “therefore”], while remaining consubstantial with the Father and, in repose, judging all things.

He stands with Stephen, fighting alongside his soldiers, giving them power to conquer on earth. “The right hand of the Lord has wrought power,” granting them in heaven the crown of confession [A omits “belonging to him”]. See how he sits and how he stands. This position is mystical, not corporeal, not local, but spiritual [C: “special”]. Understand such a position of the divine nature.

Who could have joined a state to it, when it perceives no state in itself? For it is sufficient to itself for possessing; no power accrues to it, since in itself it subsists as the simplest power, and more than power, the source of all powers. Whatever substance possesses power has it from nowhere else than from participation in the universal powers which the causal power of all things established in their primordial principles.

The divine nature is without any place [C adds “and the divine”], although it places within itself all things that derive from it; and therefore it is called the place of all things. Yet it does not know how to place itself [C: “nor does it place itself”], because it is infinite and uncircumscribed, and permits itself to be placed—that is, defined and circumscribed—by no intellect, not even by itself. From it, which is infinite and more than infinite, all finite and infinite things proceed, and into it, infinite and more than infinite, they return [A omits “into it”].

That nature is without time which does not know itself to have either a beginning or an end, nor any movement by which everything that moves from a beginning toward an end and into an end is moved [C: “of times”]. It does not know increases occurring through the numbers of places and times, or decreases, because it is full and perfect in itself.

What is to be said about acting and undergoing? Is it foolish and incongruous if someone thinks that acting or undergoing occurs to that nature which perceives in itself no movement toward acting and no capacity for undergoing? For, just as in us substance is one thing and the accident of substance—namely, action and passion—is another [A: “another thing”], so it does not understand in itself any composition of substance and accidents [A: “a certain position”]. It lacks these in itself and does not recognize them as existing in it, for it is utterly simple and foreign to every composition.

Its will, which is itself substantial, more than substantial, and more than will, is its action and passion. It is said to act because it wills all things that exist to come to be; it is said to undergo because it wills to be loved by all things, and loves itself in all things. For it is substantial and true love, and more than substantial love; and whatever things love, love it, whether they know that they love or do not know—whether they love through an intelligible or rational movement, with grace leading them, or through the simple appetite of nature. Nothing created by it lacks desire for it [A omits “they love”].

Do you therefore see that all the things embraced within the limits of the ten categories are rightly said not to be known by God as subsisting in his nature, since he is shown to surpass them utterly by the height of his power and the infinity of his being?

For whatever is infinite in every reason and mode is infinite in essence, in power, in operation, and with respect to both limits—above, I mean, and below, that is, according to beginning and end. It is incomprehensible according to essence, unintelligible according to power [C: “intelligible”], uncircumscribed according to operation, without beginning above and without end below, and infinite—or, to speak more simply and more truly—infinite in every respect [A: “is” for “and”].

**STUDENT.** I plainly see this and perceive that it is true, fortified by the conclusions of sound reasoning. Yet I am greatly troubled by how ignorance can be attributed to God, from whom nothing is hidden, either in himself or in the things that derive from him.

**MASTER.** Be attentive, then, and examine carefully what has been said. For if you consider, with pure contemplation of the mind, the power of things and words, you will discover most clearly, with no darkness standing in the way, that no ignorance falls upon God. His very ignorance is ineffable intelligence.

And, to try to establish this from what has already been said, consider the force of the words. Do we seem to be suggesting anything other than this when we say that God is ignorant of what he is: namely, that he understands himself as existing in none of the things that exist? For how can he know in himself what cannot be in himself?

If the principles of things, which he himself—that is, the Father in the Son—created in himself, are one individual in him and receive no definition of their own substance through their proper differences or accidents—for they undergo these in their effects, not in themselves—what should be thought about his ineffable and incomprehensible nature? Who could conceive of it as finite within a boundary, extended through space, divided into parts, or composed of substances and accidents?

Therefore that very ignorance is supreme and true wisdom. It is like this: if one of us were to say of himself, “I do not understand that I am an insensible stone, lacking every vital movement”—that is, “I understand that I am absolutely not an insensible stone lacking vital movement” [C omits the explanatory clause]. Likewise, “I do not understand any living human being in the flesh to lack sense and reason,” because I know that no human being living in the flesh lacks sense and reason [C omits the second “human being”]. Likewise, “I do not understand any irrational movement to subsist naturally in my soul”—that is, “I know with complete certainty that no irrational movement naturally exists in my soul.”

We can also establish this from Sacred Scripture. For in the Gospel we read that at the future judgment the Lord will answer the reprobate: “I do not know you”—that is, “I do not know you within the principles of all things, which the Father established in me, because I understand that you do not exist in my principles [C: “in them”]—not insofar as you were naturally constituted, but insofar as you have fallen away from the laws of your nature” [A: “of your nature”]. For I know what I made in you; but I do not know what I did not make. Therefore I do not punish, nor command to depart from me, what I know in myself; but what I do not know in myself, that I punish and command to depart from me.

Thus God is ignorant, in the impious and sinful, of what he did not make—namely, their wicked and irrational movements.

There is also another kind of ignorance in God, when he is said to be ignorant of things which he has foreknown and predestined, while they have not yet appeared through experience in the course of accomplished events [C: “may appear”; A: “has appeared”; Gale emends to “might appear”]. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son of Man, but the Father alone.”

In these words [A omits “in these words”] it is not surprising if the knowledge of the future judgment is still hidden from human minds weighed down by mortal flesh. Nor should it altogether be denied that angels remain capable of ignorance, since Sacred Scripture declares that they are always learning. Saint Dionysius the Areopagite bears witness to this in the seventh chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, saying:

“The theologians plainly declare that the subordinate orders of the heavenly essences are nobly instructed in divine knowledge by the superformed [A: ‘superfirm’] orders; while the higher orders of all are illuminated, insofar as is permitted, by teachings from the Divinity itself; and that Jesus himself, teaching them directly, abundantly manifests to them his human benevolence. For, he says, ‘I speak of justice and judgment of salvation.’”

Again he says:

“I marvel that even the first of the heavenly essences, and together all the pre-eminent divine angelic orders, reverently seek illuminations and questions as intermediate orders. Do they not therefore ask, ‘Why are your garments red?’ Yet among themselves they deliberate before asking, showing that they are learning and desiring divine knowledge.”

If, then, as the aforesaid *σοφός* (“wise man”) testifies [C: “the aforesaid wise man”; A: “Father, the aforesaid”], the celestial powers learn, they are necessarily not free from every kind of ignorance. And if this is so, it is not surprising that they can still be ignorant of the mysteries of the future judgment.

But what the Lord says about himself—“neither the Son of Man, but the Father alone”—creates an exceedingly obscure question. For how does the Son not know what the Father knows, especially concerning the day of judgment, when judgment particularly belongs to the Son? For he himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, most elegantly and penetratingly [C: “most accurately”] disclosed the darkness of this question in the book he wrote on the faith, saying:

“The Father alone knows the future judgment, not only through foreknowledge but also through experience. For the Father knows judgment by experience, since he has already given all judgment in reality to the Son; indeed, the Father has completed the judgment by giving it all to the Son” [C omits the sentence beginning “For the Father …” through “to the Son”]. “The Son both knows and does not know the judgment. For by foreknowledge he knows it, but not yet by experience; and therefore he does not know it by experience, because judgment has not yet been accomplished in reality—that is, the separation of the reprobate from the elect—for the harvest of the Church is still mixed with wheat and weeds.”

We do not, however, fail to recognize that Saint Augustine explains this passage figuratively, so that the Son of Man is said not to know the day of judgment because he allows us not to know it.

Hear also the apostolic ignorance of which it is written in the Acts of the Apostles. Paul cursed the high priest Ananias and said: “I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest”; for it is written: “You shall not curse the ruler of your people.”

Does it seem to you that the most wise apostle, thoroughly learned in the Law, did not know Ananias to be the high priest, as did the other Jews? This must in no way be supposed. Rather, he said that he did not know him because he did not see that he had been appointed by God.

“I did not know, brothers,” he says, “that he is the high priest,” because I know that he was appointed neither by God nor according to the Law, but according to Jewish superstition. Therefore I do not recognize him as high priest, since I truly know that he is not such. For if I knew him to be the true and legitimate ruler of the people, I certainly would not curse him [A: “If I knew the true and legitimate ruler of the people, certainly …”]. But because I do not know him to be ruler in truth, I am not sorry to have cursed him [C omits “him”].

Recognize another instance of his ignorance of the same kind. He says: “I know a man caught up to the third heaven; whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” [A omits the second “I do not know”]. He says, “I do not know whether in the body,” because I know that it was not in the body; “or outside the body I do not know,” because I know that I was not caught up outside the body.

For I was not caught up to the third heaven through the operations of the soul by means of bodily senses, nor through its operations outside the body, but through the operation of divine grace, without the administration of any creature, I know most clearly that I was caught up above every creature. Therefore I do not know whether in the body or outside the body, because I know that I was caught up neither in the body nor outside the body.

And, so that we do not linger any longer over the same matter—for time would fail before examples of divine ignorance, whether in Scripture or in the nature of things—I think it sufficient to know only this: there are three principal kinds of divine ignorance.

The first is that by which God does not know evil, because his knowledge is simple and is formed solely by substantial good, that is, by himself. For he alone is substantial good through himself; all other good things are good through participation in him. God therefore does not know evil. For if God knew evil, evil would necessarily exist substantially in the nature of things. Divine knowledge is the cause of all things that exist. God does not know things because they subsist; rather, they subsist because God knows them [C: “God knows them” in the reverse order].

Their essence is caused by divine knowledge. Therefore, if God knew evil, evil would be understood as existing substantially in something, and evil would be a participant in the good, while vice and wickedness would proceed from power and goodness. True reason teaches that this is impossible.

The second kind is that by which God is said to be ignorant of things other than those whose principles he both made and knows eternally in himself. For whatever he naturally possesses the power to produce, of that he possesses knowledge essentially.

The third is that by which God is said, as we have already stated, to be ignorant of things which have not yet become manifest through the experience of action and operation in their effects, although he possesses in himself, created by himself and known to himself, their invisible principles.

To these three kinds just mentioned a fourth is added, which the order of the discussion now demands: God is said to be ignorant of being among the number of the things made by him, which philosophers attempt to enclose within the tenfold number of the categories.

Accordingly, it must be said universally that God does not understand himself as subsisting in any of the things comprehended by philosophers within the ten genera of things, nor in those which more careful inquiry discovers outside them [A: “these”]—whether they be according to substance or according to accident—nor in those which can be found in neither substance nor accident, whether they exist in hidden principles, possibilities, or impossibilities [A: “are”]. He does not understand himself as subsisting in any of these [A: “understands himself”], because he knows himself to be none of them, while he understands himself to surpass all things by his ineffable essential power, by what is more than power, and by his incomprehensible infinity.

**29.** I said, therefore, that a more careful inquiry can discover certain things in the nature of things beyond those comprehended by the ten categories. These, too, were discovered by philosophers, lest anyone should think that the investigation of things by people of lesser capacity cannot advance beyond the aforesaid number of categories [C: “advance”].

For reason comprehends their more general genera, since they are in movement and in rest. Likewise, rest and movement are gathered together under a universal essence, which permits its own division to proceed indefinitely. For the substance that occupies the first place among the categories is finite and subject to accidents; but that universal essence receives no accident in itself. In its subdivisions, which reach all the way to individuals, it is capable of accidents; but in itself it is simple and subject to no accident [A, B, C: “thus”].

Into this universal essence are subdivided that most general movement, subject to no category, by which all things proceed from nothing into being, and the state—likewise subject to no category—into which all things will set the terminus of their movements.

When I added that there are certain things in the nature of things which are known neither in substance nor in accidents—things which are neither substances nor accidents—understand that I was referring to principles not yet apparent in any thing, whether substantially or accidentally, to sense or intellect.

No sound philosopher will deny that possibilities and impossibilities are also counted among the number of things. They are said to exist in no other way than this: possibilities can come to be in some thing, even if they do not exist [A: “are”]; impossibilities, however, are contained solely by the power of impossibility. Their being consists in the impossibility of appearing in some intellectual or sensible thing.

Let an example of possibilities be given: a certain man can beget offspring, but, held back by love of virginity, he refuses to have children. As an example of impossibilities: it is impossible for a rational animal to be irrational, or conversely [C: “thus”].

Whoever wishes to understand these matters fully should read Aristotle’s *Περὶ ἑρμηνείας*, that is, *On Interpretation*. In that work the Philosopher disputed either exclusively, or at least chiefly, about these matters—namely, possibilities and impossibilities.

Let us now proceed to consider what remains, if you think that enough has been said about the kinds of divine ignorance by which God is said to be ignorant [A: “as”].

**STUDENT.** Enough, indeed, and more than enough; I do not think it necessary to linger over them longer. For it has been made clearer than a sunbeam that divine ignorance is nothing other than the incomprehensible and infinite divine knowledge.

What the holy Fathers—by Augustine and Dionysius I mean—most truly declare about God, I think should be understood not only of minds that seek him with pious devotion, but also of God himself. Augustine says: “He is better known by not knowing.” Dionysius says: “His ignorance is true wisdom” [C: “of himself,” omitting “himself”].

For just as those who investigate him by the straight path of reasoning cannot understand him in any of the things contained in the nature of things, but recognize him as exalted above all things—and consequently their ignorance is true wisdom, and by not knowing him in the things that exist they know him better than all things that exist and do not exist—so, too, it is reasonably said of him in himself that, insofar as he does not understand himself as subsisting in the things he made, he understands himself to be above all things. Consequently, his ignorance is true intelligence.

And insofar as he does not know himself to be contained in the things that exist, he knows himself to be exalted beyond all things. Therefore, by not knowing himself, he is better known by himself; for it is better to know that one is removed from all things than to know that one is constituted among the number of all things.

**MASTER.** You understand correctly, and I perceive that you clearly and without hesitation grasp what reason recommends concerning such matters. Nor, as I think, do you now see any difference between the image and the original form, except for the reason of the subject [A: “dissimilarity”].

For the supreme Trinity subsists substantially through itself, and was created by no cause. The trinity of our nature, however, was made from nothing by that Trinity which is eternal through itself, according to its own image and likeness.

And if any dissimilarity beyond this between the image and the original example is found, it did not arise from nature but occurred through fault; nor did it arise from the envy of the creating Trinity, but from the fault of the created image.

Everything that is understood about God according to the power of essence can also be said and understood about his image, in those aspects in which it is purified, illuminated, and perfected, according to the grace of creation—with the exception, as we have said, that the divine nature is God through the excellence of essence, whereas the human nature is God through the abundance of divine grace.

The former is creative and created by no one; the latter was created by the former and creates those things which adhere beneath it according to its nature. I mean this mortal body, joined to the soul after sin, which is also called the image of the image, as we have often said [A omits “as we have often said”]. For just as God created the soul according to his image, so the soul in a certain way makes the body, as a kind of instrument, somewhat like itself [A: “made”].

But we must return to the contemplation of the divine Trinity, which is the cause of all things, if what has been said concerning these matters is sufficient for you.

**STUDENT.** It is certainly sufficient.

**MASTER.** In the supreme and unique cause of all things, then, from which and in which the principles of the whole creation exist and were created—that is, the primordial causes—I think we must consider whether, although it is unity and Trinity—for the divine goodness is one essence in three substances and three substances in one essence [C omits this entire clause]—or, according to the usage of the Roman language, one substance in three persons and three persons in one substance, it possesses within itself causes that are in some way different, just as the substances are different from one another [A omits “just as the substances are different from one another”].

That is, just as one essence in three substances is predicated of it, should we also believe and understand that there is one essential cause in three subsisting causes, and three subsisting causes in one essential cause [A: “it ought to be believed and understood”]? It is not unfitting to explain, in accordance with orthodox contemplations, what sound faith requires us to think and proclaim concerning such theories.

**STUDENT.** Rather, it is most fitting and necessary for the salvation of faithful souls.

**MASTER.** What, then? Should we both believe and, insofar as permitted, understand and proclaim this concerning the cause of all things: that there is one essential cause in three substantial causes, and three substantial causes in one essential cause [C: “proclaim in advance”]?

**STUDENT.** I see no reason why this should be forbidden to understanding and proclamation [A: “to be understood and proclaimed”]. For if God is the cause of all things, does it not follow that the cause of all things is also known as God [A: “and that”]? But if God is cause, and cause is God, does it not follow [A omits “is”] that everything we ought to believe about God should likewise, without any discrepancy, be understood concerning the cause?

For if the catholic faith confesses one God existing through himself in three substances subsisting through themselves, what prevents us from saying in the same way that there is one cause existing through itself in three causes subsisting through themselves?

**MASTER.** Piously and orthodoxly.

There is, then, one cause in three causes, and three in one.

**STUDENT.** This has now been both granted and established.

**30. MASTER.** Let us now return to theology, which is the first and highest part of wisdom—not without reason, since it is concerned either exclusively or chiefly with the contemplation of the divine nature. It is divided into two parts: affirmation, I mean, and negation, which in Greek are called *καταφατική* and *ἀποφατική*.

We used one of these in the first book, where, by definite arguments, we denied that the ten categories, and all the genera, forms, numbers, and accidents of things, are properly predicated of God. In the present book, too, we have repeated the same one—the *ἀποφατική*, I mean—as the sequence of our questions required, when we said that God himself does not understand in his essence any of the things that exist or do not exist, because he surpasses every essence.

We also said that he is wholly ignorant of what he himself is, and of how great and what sort he is, because he is defined in no way and nothing occurs to him as an accident; and consequently that he utterly denies himself to be comprehended in the things that exist or do not exist. This kind of ignorance surpasses every knowledge and understanding.

Now we shall try to examine the other part, the *καταφατική*, I mean: guided by the one who is sought, who seeks to be sought, who comes to those seeking him, and desires to be found. This is the part that considers what may properly be put forward concerning the divine nature and what must be understood cautiously and rationally.

**STUDENT.** I have been sufficiently persuaded concerning the negative part in the earlier discussions. Now I eagerly await what you will explain concerning the affirmative part.

**MASTER.** It has already been established among us, not rashly, as I think, that everything which is granted to be understood about God with the approval of catholic faith must likewise be affirmed by those who philosophize piously about the cause of all things.

**STUDENT.** This has been established without question.

**MASTER.** Do we therefore believe in an unbegotten and begetting divinity, a begotten deity, and a proceeding deity, and, although the divinity is one and inseparable, do we nevertheless admit substantial differences?

For in the Father we accept and piously believe an unbegotten divinity; in the Son, a begotten divinity; and in the Holy Spirit, a proceeding divinity. We approve this while relying upon the entirely sound authority of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite and the other Fathers.

**STUDENT.** Whoever hesitates over this is far from the truth.

**MASTER.** There is, then, a substantial unbegotten and begetting cause; there is a substantial begotten and non-begetting cause; likewise there is a substantial proceeding cause, neither unbegotten, nor begotten, nor begetting. The three substantial causes are one and are one essential cause.

**STUDENT.** This necessarily follows from the arguments already given.

**MASTER.** In the cause of all things, then, there is a preceding cause and there are subsequent causes. For the Father precedes the Son and the Holy Spirit: the Son is begotten from him, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. Consequently, the Father is not incongruously believed to be the cause of causes. He is the cause of the begotten cause and of the proceeding cause.

Fatherhood precedes sonship; no one among those who think rightly would say that sonship precedes fatherhood [C: “filial relationship precedes sonship, and filial relationship …”; A: “said”].

For this reason the Son himself says of himself: “The Father is greater than I.” The Father is indeed greater than the Son, not according to nature but according to cause. For the Father is the cause of the Son, whereas the Son is not the cause of the Father; nor are we here considering a reciprocal relation of names or the power of substances [A: “but”].

For we examine the disposition of relations in substances or persons [A omits “of relations”] in one way, and generation or procession from the unbegotten [A omits “from the unbegotten”] in another. In the former case we consider how they are named from one another; in the latter, how they differ from one another [A: “subsist”].

The Son is from the Father, but the Father is not from the Son. For in God we are not considering the relations of human generations, but the substantial dispositions of ineffable substances.

The Father is greater than the Son according to cause. Sacred theology first considers the disposition of the Father toward the Son, and then that of the Son toward the Father.

To understand and believe this more certainly, turn to the authority of Gregory the Theologian. In his first discourse against the Arians, disputing about the Son, he wisely teaches that the Father is greater than the Son according to cause, defining that the Son exists from the Father and that the Father does not subsist from the Son.

Nor do we say this while rejecting the understanding of those who assert that our Lord said of himself according to his humanity: “The Father is greater than I.” Both interpretations must be received in sound faith.

**STUDENT.** Yes. Although they are not of the same subtlety or height, neither departs from the catholic confession.

**MASTER.** It is therefore not the same thing for the Father to subsist naturally and for him to be the cause of his Son. The nature of the Father is not the cause of the Son, for the nature of the Father and of the Son is one and the same, since their essence is one and the same [C omits the sentence beginning “For the nature …” through “one and the same”].

Consequently, for the Father to be Father and for him to be the cause of the Son are the same thing. These things are not predicated of the Father and the Son according to nature [C: “These names are not predicated according to nature, which is one and the same in the Father and the Son, but …”], but according to the relation of the begetting to the begotten and of the preceding cause to the subsequent cause.

Similarly, the Son is not called Son, or begotten cause, according to nature, but according to the relation of the Son to the Father and of the begotten cause to the begetting cause.

**STUDENT.** These matters were already established in the preceding book and have now been repeated again, not without reason.

**MASTER.** The Father, then, is the cause of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; but the Son is principally the cause of the constitution of the causes, while the Holy Spirit is the cause of the distribution of those same causes.

**STUDENT.** I perceive that admitting this also does not conflict with the truth.

### 31

But as I reflect on and believe these things, another darkness confronts me concerning the threefold cause of all things. For I do not clearly understand whether the Father alone is the cause of the Holy Spirit, or the Father and the Son, so that, just as the Catholic faith confesses that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, we should likewise believe that he possesses two causes of his procession [A: *ita ut*, “so that”; A: *ita et eam duas suae processionis credamus causas cet.*, “and so likewise let us believe that it has two causes of its procession,” etc.]. For if the Holy Spirit proceeds from two persons—or, as the Greeks say, from two substances—what is surprising or contrary to true religion in confessing that he proceeds from two causes? I beg you to dispel this darkness for me.

**MASTER.** Truly, truly [*truly* is omitted in A]. It is an exceedingly dense darkness, and it envelops not only you but me as well [*and* is omitted in A]. Unless the very light of our minds reveals this to us, the effort of our reasoning will accomplish nothing toward revealing it. The obscurity is increased further by the fact that the creed of the Catholic faith [*Catholic* is omitted in A], as handed down by the Council of Nicaea according to the Greeks, professes that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, as Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, testifies in his book *On the Faith*, whereas according to the Latins he proceeds from the Father and the Son; although in certain Greek expositions we find that the same Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son. And so, struck by the difficulty of the present question, I am battered by opposing waves of thought [Col. 0601D]. I am considering what ought to be done about it: whether we should honor it with silence, since it surpasses the powers of our concentration, or whether, insofar as a divine ray shines forth in the mind, we should attempt somehow to discern among ourselves some conclusion about it—not rashly, of course [*about it* is omitted in A].

**DISCIPLE.** Do not be afraid [Col. 0602A]. For the one who is sought does not abandon those who seek him, nor does he deny the possibility of finding him to those who investigate piously and humbly. For he himself says: “Ask, and you will receive” [“Ask, and it will be given to you”]; “seek, and you will find”; “knock, and it will be opened to you.” For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

**MASTER.** First, then, I think we should speak about those matters that appear to contradict one another in this question.

**DISCIPLE.** There is no other way of seeking; no one can join together things that agree unless he has first taken care to separate what disagrees [this sentence is omitted in B and C].

**MASTER.** Does it not seem to you [C: “Does it not seem”; A: “Does it seem”] to accord with right faith that we should believe the Son to be born from one cause—namely, the Father—but the Holy Spirit to proceed from two, namely the Father and the Son? For that one cause should arise from two causes does not readily occur to reason [Col. 0602B], especially in a simple nature, and more than simple—or, to speak more accurately, in simplicity itself, which is free from every division and multiplicity. But that many causes should burst forth from one cause can be demonstrated by many examples.

It is plainly evident to all who philosophize correctly that many forms arise from one genus; many numbers from the monad; many lines from a point [C: “from the center”]. Again, the diverse forms [A: “things”] that arise from one genus become the causes of individual species [A: *causa*, “cause,” singular], from which and in which multiplicities, quantities, qualities [A: “and qualities”], and differences arise. Numbers proceeding from the monad are causes of diverse proportions [A: “proportional relations”]; proportions, in turn, are causes of proportionalities, and proportionalities of harmonies [this phrase is omitted in C]. Lines proceeding from the center [A: “Lines proceeding from one point”] are recognized as the causes of angles and sides, of breadth and height [Col. 0602C]; these in turn become the occasions of geometrical bodies.

What should I say about the fiery element? Although it is one and simple when considered in itself and through itself, it is the cause simultaneously of heat and light. Heat is the cause of burning in things that burn [C: “is the cause”]; likewise, light is constituted as the cause of shining in things that shine [A: “the cause of shining”]; and radiance produces diverse colors.

The element of air is the occasion of diverse sounds; diverse sounds become the origins of diverse tones. The element of water, although simple and one in itself, is the cause of diverse fluids, which in turn emit from themselves diverse qualities of odors, flavors, and greenness. From one matter [A: “earth”] arise the diverse quantities of diverse bodies. By “quantity” I now mean not quantity itself as incorporeal, but the mass itself [Col. 0602D], which no one doubts to be the composition of diverse parts, and other things of this kind.

In the same way, it is very easy to find examples in the nature of things, whether visible or invisible.

**DISCIPLE.** No believer doubts that the Son is born from one cause, that is, from his Father [*his* is omitted in A]. But whether the Holy Spirit proceeds [C: “proceeds,” indicative, for the main text’s subjunctive] from one cause—namely, the Father—or from two, that is, from the Father and the Son [Col. 0603A], I would not dare rashly either affirm or deny. Thus I do not sufficiently see that this is inconsistent with the professions of right faith, since I have very often found the Holy Spirit called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. For he is the Spirit of both, because he proceeds from the Father through the Son; he is the gift of both [A: “that he is the gift”], because he is given from the Father through the Son; and he is the love of both, joining the Father and the Son [C: “conjoining”], as the holy Augustine teaches in the books he published on the supreme and holy [C: “true”] Trinity [A: “published on the Trinity”]. In those books he seeks, with wondrous investigation, the image of the Trinity in human nature [A: “in the nature”] and demonstrates with brilliant discovery that the trinity of our inner nature—that is, of the rational soul—created in the image of God, consists of the mind, namely the principal part of the soul, the knowledge of itself by which it knows itself, and the love by which it joins itself and its knowledge together.

For the human mind gives birth to its knowledge, by which it knows itself, as a kind of offspring of itself from itself. Its knowledge is equal to it, because it knows itself wholly [C: “by which it knows itself wholly”], in the likeness of God and the Father [*and* is omitted in A], who begets from himself his Son, who is his wisdom, by which he knows himself; and the knowledge is equal to him because it understands itself wholly, and it is coessential with him because he begets from himself the one whom he begets [C: “begets and the one whom he begets”].

From the human mind proceeds a certain appetite by which it seeks itself, so that it may bring forth its knowledge. When this appetite, or inquiry, reaches the perfect discovery of knowledge, it becomes love, which joins the mind and its knowledge together. It is equal to the mind and to the mind’s knowledge [Col. 0603C], because it loves itself wholly and its knowledge wholly. It is coessential with the mind and with its knowledge, because the love itself, which unites the mind and its knowledge [A: “the mind and to it”], proceeds from nowhere other than the mind itself [C: “from its very mind”], in the likeness of the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from the Father, joins the Father and the Son by an ineffable bond of charity.

But as for what you said—that it does not readily occur to reason that one cause should flow or proceed from two causes—I no longer see this at all clearly. Yet I clearly see, I think, why you used the word “flow” in place of “proceed.” For the Holy Spirit is also called a river in the sacred Scriptures [A: “is called in the Scriptures”], and water. Hence the Lord himself says: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly”; whoever drinks of this [A: “drinks”] will not thirst forever, as was said to the Samaritan woman [Col. 0603D].

No wise person denies that the fountain of Paradise, which is divided into four principal rivers, signifies the Holy Spirit when considered typologically. From this fountain, as from a principal, unique, and inexhaustible source [*and* is omitted in A], four principal virtues flow in the Paradise of the rational soul: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. From these again all the streams of all the virtues flow forth [A: “and flow forth”], and, after the surface of human nature has been watered and made fertile by them, they flow back [Col. 0604A].

Therefore the Holy Spirit is rightly said to flow either from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son, because he is the fountain and source of all virtues, and they return into him by an ineffable course through the hidden pores of our nature.

**MASTER.** You understand spiritual streams correctly. But tell me, please, what prevents you from clearly understanding what we said—namely [this phrase is omitted in C], that it does not readily occur to reason that one cause should flow from two causes?

**DISCIPLE.** I see many examples standing in the way. The examples you introduced from the four elements of the world, for example, sufficiently teach [A: “teach”] that one cause can be made from two causes. For fire, since it is the source of heat and light, appears to arise from two causes. The fiery element is composed of heat and dryness, which, like two causes, produce one thing from themselves. The same must be said of the remaining elements. Since they are the causes of their effects, the wise men of the world have said that they arise from the twofold causes above them. For just as, as we said earlier, fire is composed of the hot and the dry, so air is composed of the hot and the moist, water of the moist and the cold, and earth of the cold and the dry.

What then? Is it not to be acknowledged that one cause flows from two causes, since the examples just mentioned—to say nothing of the others—are sufficient to prove this? [A: “are sufficient.”]

**MASTER.** I am greatly astonished—and it is worthy of astonishment—that, although you see everything else acutely and plausibly, you are mistaken in these examples.

**DISCIPLE.** Tell me, I beg you, in what respect and how I am deceived.

**MASTER.** Have the philosophers persuaded you that this visible [A: “sensible”] world consists of four universal and simple elements—namely, fire, air, water, and earth—each of which possesses its own individual quality? Fire is heat, air is moisture, water is coldness, and earth is dryness.

**DISCIPLE.** These things have been almost perfectly familiar to me since childhood.

**MASTER.** Tell me, then, what is that fire—which we shall use as an example—that, as you say, flows like one cause from two causes? Is it the simple and invisible fire, incomprehensible through itself, which penetrates and moves all visible things? Or is it the visible, bodily, tangible fire that is materially nourished?

**DISCIPLE.** I would not call the simple and incomprehensible fire, which fills and produces all bodies [*bodies* is omitted in A], that fire. For it is the primordial cause of sensible things and the fourth cause of all bodies [Col. 0604D]. But this sensible and material fire appears to proceed from heat and dryness, as from two causes.

**MASTER.** Did you not grant earlier that heat is the proper quality of no element other than fire alone, and dryness of none other than earth alone? For each is assigned to each—that is, proper qualities are assigned to their respective substantial elements.

**DISCIPLE.** I did grant it; otherwise the philosophers do not allow me to understand it [A: “for otherwise”].

**MASTER.** Tell me, then: is fire one thing and heat another, or are they one and the same?

**DISCIPLE.** They appear to me to be two things [A: “which ones”]. Fire is a substance, whereas heat is a quality of that substance, and its proper quality.

**MASTER.** What then [A: “therefore”]? Is substance the cause of quality, or quality the cause of substance, or is neither quality the cause of substance nor substance the cause of quality, since they do not belong to the same genus?

**DISCIPLE.** I approve the last alternative you proposed. Although quality is contained in substance—for no quality subsists through itself—I would not say that substance is the cause of quality [A: “that substance is the cause of quality”]. For every species follows its genus, just as it is born from its genus and is preserved immutably in it [C omits “just as”; A reads *quum, quo* (uncertain)]. Thus every substance flows from a general essence [Col. 0605B], while every quality flows from a general quality.

**MASTER.** Fire, therefore, because it is a substance, descends from no other cause than the most general essence. Likewise, heat, because it is a quality [A: “is a quality”], proceeds from no other cause than the most general quality.

**DISCIPLE.** Whoever argues against this conclusion appears to resist the principles of philosophy.

**MASTER.** Why, then, did you dare to declare that fire, whether simple or material, flows like one cause from two causes—that is, from heat and dryness—when you see that the substance of fire [*the substance of fire* is omitted in C] cannot arise not only from an alien quality, namely dryness, which belongs properly to earthly substance, but even from its own quality, namely heat?

**DISCIPLE.** Now I see that I was deceived when I said that heat and dryness subsist like two causes of one cause, namely fire [Col. 0605C]. Yet I have known many people [C: “many of them”] led astray by the same error because they did not sufficiently distinguish the differences and natures of qualities and substances [C: “of those things”]. And now I see no way of escape. For if I say that fire and heat are one and the same thing, you will immediately refute me by asking why, then, I consider the same thing to be the cause of itself. For I said that fire is composed of heat and dryness.

If I say that this visible world consists not of four substantial elements but only of four simple qualities—namely heat, moisture, coldness, and dryness—since this too has seemed correct to many, perhaps you will ask me: if this entire world, with its bodies, consists from top to bottom [Col. 0605D] of four qualities, in what substances are those qualities contained? For if they are qualities [A: “if they be qualities”], true reason teaches that they cannot subsist through themselves. I will not be able to find what to answer—that is, by what substances those primordial and general qualities, by which the world is constituted, are supported. And, constrained by true arguments, I will be compelled to confess [A: “I am compelled”] that the four substantial elements of the world subsist, in which the four principal qualities consist, by whose conjunction all composite bodies are produced.

But one point still remains by which I think I may persist in the same opinion in which I said that one cause flows from many.

**MASTER.** I would like you to disclose what that one point is.

**DISCIPLE.** Do all philosophers who discuss this world unanimously teach, and appear to establish clearly [C: “to establish”], that all composite bodies are composed of the four simple elements and their four proper qualities? And if this is so, the composition of each individual body is produced not merely from two but from many causes.

**MASTER.** You might perhaps have had this avenue of escape if you could have maintained by sound reasoning that these masses of composite, corruptible bodies, liable to dissolution, are causes of other effects that follow below them. But since nothing is lower than a composite body [Col. 0606B], it cannot be the cause of any nature that follows it or of any nature equal to itself. And now we are speaking of causes, whether principal or subsequent and concatenated. Nothing can truly and rightly be called a cause unless it is truly a cause, and that which is unable to burst forth into its effects is not truly a cause. For it entirely lacks the effects on account of which it might rightly be called a cause.

Corruptible bodies, however, are causes of no effect, because they generate no nature from themselves, occupying, as they do, the final and lowest place among all natures, and almost no place at all.

Spiritual bodies, on the other hand, are simple [C: “bodies still simple”], and therefore indissoluble and enduring [*and* is omitted in C], until this whole world, together with its parts, reaches its end and is dissolved [*its* is omitted in A].

These bodies, still incorruptible and indissoluble [*still* is omitted in C], are spoken of and understood only in terms of the four universal, principal, and most pure elements, simple in themselves [A: “principal and catholic”]. Other bodies, however, which appear to be composed of their qualities [A: “composed from them”; the words “their qualities” are omitted], because they can both be composed and dissolved, are counted by the wise not among causes but among the ultimate effects, which produce nothing from themselves.

The four simplest and purest elements of this world, which escape bodily sensation, are referred back to one simple and undivided cause, known only to the intellect of the most perfect sages: namely, to the most general essence of all substances, which always remains in itself and proceeds toward visible effects [the words “which produce nothing from themselves” through “effects” are omitted in B and C]. The same is not incongruously understood concerning their four primordial and proper qualities [Col. 0606D]. For although the qualities themselves appear to be opposed to one another—heat is opposed to coldness and dryness to moisture—they nevertheless return to one most secret cause subject only to reason: namely, to the most general quality of all qualities. From this quality they proceed, through the marvelous work of nature [A: “through the work of nature”], to produce these corruptible bodies subject to dissolution; and in it, through the ineffable peaceful concord of universal nature, they agree with one another, every opposition having been removed.

**DISCIPLE.** By this last conclusion I see myself enclosed on every side, with no route of escape remaining. Thus I am compelled to agree with the opinion you previously expressed, and to say that it does not readily occur to reason that one cause flows from two causes.

**MASTER.** What, then [A: “therefore”], shall we say? Should we profess that the Holy Spirit—which we catholicly confess to be the infinite, inexhaustible, most abundant, and more-than-abundant cause of the distribution of the gifts of divine goodness, whether of those that exist according to substance [*that exist according to substance* is omitted in A] or of those that exist according to grace—proceeds from one cause, namely the Father, or from two causes, the Father and the Son?

**DISCIPLE.** The examples we have drawn from the nature of things altogether forbid us to say this: that he proceeds not from two but from one—unless someone should say that examples of the nature of the supreme and ineffable divine Trinity surpass the examples of created nature [C: “and immediately ineffable”].

**MASTER.** If anyone says this, he must immediately be asked: How, then, can we seek and investigate the Trinity of divine goodness [A: “the divine Trinity”] in unity, and unity in Trinity, so that we may believe something plausible about it by which we may praise it, and understand it insofar as this is granted to us? For can we ascend to it by certain steps [A: “great stages”], guided and instructed by it, through examples of the nature created by it, as it says: “Seek, and you will find”? [A: *nisi*, “unless,” instead of *si*, “if.”] Especially since the divine Paul bears witness: “For his invisible things,” he says—that is, the invisible things of the Father—“are understood and perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made; likewise his eternal power,” that is, the Son, “and eternity,” that is, the Holy Spirit [Col. 0607C]. For this is how blessed Maximus expounds this passage of sacred Scripture.

**DISCIPLE.** What if someone should say that the Father and the Son are not two causes but one inseparable cause, since the Son himself says: “I and the Father are one”?

**MASTER.** This too must be answered. The three causes of divine goodness about which we are now speaking are sought not in the very essence, which is one and the same, but in the Trinity of the substances or persons of that essence [A: “or”]. For he does not confuse the duality [C: “quality”] of the persons when he says: “I and the Father are one.” He does not say, “I and the Father am one,” but “are,” showing both the unity of essence and the difference of substances [C: “differences”].

And if he were to say, “I and the Father and the Holy Spirit are one” [*Holy Spirit* is omitted in A], this would signify the Trinity subsisting in the unity of the same essence. Although we do not find it said in this way, we should nevertheless understand that it is most truly so [A: “we understand”]. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, and the three are one.

The Son is begotten from the Father, and from that same Father [A: “and from him”] the Spirit proceeds. Thus, when I hear sacred Scripture proclaiming and teaching of the begetter, the begotten, and the one proceeding, I understand, insofar as this is granted to me, three substances or persons [Col. 0608A] of one essence. For it is impossible that the begetter, the begotten, and the one proceeding should be one substance.

Natural reason also teaches that there are three according to substance, while they are one according to essence [A: “while they be one”]. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are one according to natural essentiality [A: “according to”], but three according to substantial difference. The seeker of truth will very easily find this example in all genera, forms, and individuals [*and* is omitted in A].

**DISCIPLE.** Therefore, if it pleases you, disclose what you hold in mind concerning this present and very difficult question, so that we may not linger so long in the same places while we ought to hasten on to explain the matters that remain.

### 32

**MASTER.** Tell me, I ask: Does it seem to you that a ray is born from fire and radiance proceeds from the ray? [Col. 0608B]

**DISCIPLE.** Whoever says this, I think, does not depart from a careful consideration of the nature of things. For fire, although invisible in itself, gives birth from itself to a visible ray [C: “invisible”], which would also be invisible in itself, subsisting through the simplicity of its nature, if it were not mingled with dense and corporeal natures.

The philosophers say [A: “They say”] that the ray of the sun is incomprehensible to the senses of living beings, because they are unable to perceive the subtlety of its nature [C: “being able to perceive it”]. But when it descends gradually from the solar body to the lower elements, it begins little by little to become visible. First it scarcely begins to shine in the purest ether, because the nature of the ether itself is most like its own. As it advances farther toward the regions of the upper air, it gradually becomes brighter; then, insofar as it penetrates denser natures in a downward direction, it shines more brightly and presents itself as comprehensible to bodily senses [Col. 0608C].

Yet from the ray itself a most brilliant radiance is emitted, filling the whole world, rebounding from the surface of all bodies, and revealing diverse kinds of color. Through its natural subtlety it too would escape bodily senses if it did not temper itself with corporeal [C: “more corporeal”] elements.

**MASTER.** So it is, and the investigation of natures teaches that it can happen no other way. Must we therefore be compelled to say that the radiance which proceeds from the fire through the ray has two causes? Although it proceeds from the fire through the ray [this entire clause is omitted in C], fire alone is its cause, not the ray.

For just as the ray itself would not subsist through itself if it were not born from its cause, which is fire [Col. 0608D], so radiance would not exist through the ray unless it first proceeded from the cause of the ray itself. You see, then, that no reason requires radiance to proceed from two causes, although it is understood to flow from fire through the ray. Rather, nature itself teaches that from one and the same cause both the ray is born and the radiance proceeds, and therefore that radiance proceeds from fire and ray [this clause is omitted in A].

Observe attentively still further the force of this same example. The ray itself, born from fire, is not born in such a way that it abandons or in any manner leaves the fire that begets it. Rather, it is begotten in such a way that the fiery power that begets it always and everywhere remains in it inseparably and immutably—wholly in the whole, and the whole in the whole, and one as two, and two as one.

Although radiance appears to go out from the ray, it does not proceed from the ray insofar as it is a ray, but from that very power from which the ray is born, and which wholly penetrates and fills both the whole ray and the whole radiance [*from* is omitted in C].

Thus we can ascend through this natural example to the cause of all things, which is threefold and one, because the Trinity is believed and understood to exist in unity, so that we may recognize the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as three causes [Col. 0609B] and one cause. For the three are one: the Father is the begetting cause of his only-begotten Son, who is born from him and who is the cause of all primordial causes created by the Father in himself; and the same Father is the cause of the Holy Spirit proceeding from him through the Son [“through the Son” is omitted in A]. The Spirit is the cause of the division, multiplication, and distribution into their effects—general, special, and proper, according to nature and grace—of all the causes that were made in the Son by the Father.

Although we believe and understand that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son [A: “the Holy Spirit”], we should not therefore understand that the same Spirit has two causes, but one and the same cause [A: “is one cause”]: namely, the Father, both of the Son born from him and of the Holy Spirit proceeding from him through the Son [*through the Son* is omitted in A].

For just as we say that radiance proceeds from fire through the ray because the fire itself subsists wholly in the whole ray, from which radiance is emitted through the ray, so the Catholic faith proclaims that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, because the Father himself, who is the principal and sole cause of the procession of the Holy Spirit, is wholly in the whole Son, just as the whole Son is in the whole Father, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds through the Son.

And just as the whole fiery power remains in the whole ray born from it, and the ray itself, wholly, together with the whole fiery power from which it is begotten, exists in the whole radiance, and the whole radiance proceeding from the fiery power through the ray exists wholly in that ray itself and in the whole fiery power from which it proceeds [Col. 0609D], so the whole begetting Father is in the whole begotten Son, and the whole begotten Son is in the whole begetting Father; the whole begetting Father and the whole begotten Son are in the whole Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father through the Son; and the whole Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father through the Son is in the Father from whom he proceeds and in the Son through whom he proceeds. Thus the three are one through the Trinity understood in unity.

The Son himself, made human and incarnate, most clearly indicates all this when he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” There he left the remainder implicit, as though he had said openly: “And just as I am in the Father and the Father is in me [this entire sentence is omitted in C], so I and the Father are in the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is in us, because he is coessential and coequal with us, and the three are one—three, that is, substantially, but one essentially.”

And observe how the Son himself refers the Holy Spirit to the Father alone, as to his one cause, when he says: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name.” For he did not say, “whom I send in my name,” but “whom the Father sends in my name,” although elsewhere he says that he himself sends the Spirit, when he states: “If I depart [C: “if I go out”], I will send him to you.”

His sending is his procession. His procession, however, is substantially from the Father alone [*from the Father* is omitted in C], not locally and not temporally [*not temporally* is omitted in A]; nevertheless [C: “but truly”], it is in the name of the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son [Col. 0610B].

Elsewhere he says to the disciples: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” Likewise, the Psalmist asks the Father for the Holy Spirit, saying: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” Sacred Scripture is filled with these and similar testimonies.

**DISCIPLE.** I perceive and faithfully accept all these things clearly and fully, because they entirely accord with the truth [A: “because”]. And I am greatly astonished that the question which at first seemed to us almost insoluble has finally been resolved through the clearest reasoning, introduced by the argument of examples and testimonies, and revealed plainly—something we did not easily hope for [C: “expect”].

And, as it seems to me, we can confirm this very point by the likeness of the Trinity in our inner nature. For the mind gives birth to knowledge of itself, and from itself proceeds love of itself and of its knowledge [Col. 0610C], by which both the mind and its knowledge of itself are joined together. Although this love proceeds from the mind through its knowledge, knowledge itself is not the cause of love; rather, the mind is the cause, from which love begins to exist, even before the mind itself reaches perfect knowledge of itself.

For the mind also loves to know itself before it gives birth to its knowledge from itself [A: “from it”], as to its own offspring. This does not mean that the human mind ever either failed to know or failed to love itself, since these three are one according to nature or essence, and one is three according to rational consideration. For reason considers three things in the one and simple nature of the soul: being, knowing, and loving.

The mind knows itself, and loves itself and its knowledge. But because, through the deserved transgression of human nature in the first man, it happened that the mind does not know that it knows itself, although by nature it knows itself, and does not know that it loves itself, although by nature it loves itself and its knowledge [this clause from “although by nature it knows itself” through “by nature” is omitted in C; A: “may love”], it therefore desires by the powers of reason nothing other than to know how and to what extent it knows itself, and how it loves itself and its knowledge [A: “may love”].

When it turns all this toward knowledge and love of its Creator [A: “is turned”], it becomes his most perfect image. And this is [C: “from this is”] the greatest and almost the only step toward knowledge of the truth [C omits “is”]: for human nature first to know and love itself, and then to refer all its knowledge and all its love to the praise, knowledge, and love of the Creator [C: “might refer”].

For if it does not know what takes place within itself, how can it desire to know what is above it? But while we are discussing this question, another matter, not—I think—to be despised, has come into my mind.

**MASTER.** What is it?

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

### 33

**STUDENT.** Do we believe that, just as we believe the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, following the Creed in the Roman language, so we may profess that the Son is born from the Father through the Spirit, although we do not find this written in the Creed itself, either according to the Greeks or according to the Latins [Note: C: “not”], nor, as I think, openly proclaimed in divine [Col. 0611B] Scripture? [Col. 0611]

**MASTER.** In that ineffable and supernatural fecundity of divine goodness through which the Son is born from the heart—that is, from the hidden recesses—of God the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds, catholic faith commands us to confess that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, or from the Father through the Son. But I find neither in that Creed, in either language, nor in any other writing that the Son is born from the Father through the Spirit. I have not yet asked why this is so, either by myself or from another [Note: A: “anyone”], nor have I read that it has been sought and discovered by anyone.

When, however, both sacred Scripture and the Creed handed down by the holy synod of Nicaea in Bithynia, fortified against all heresies, are consulted concerning the Son of God’s assumption of humanity—that is, the incarnation of the Word—it is most clearly revealed and taught without any ambiguity [Col. 0611C] that the Word was conceived from the Holy Spirit. The angel also says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” [Note: A omits “he says.”] The same angel says to Joseph: “Joseph, son of David, do not dismiss your wife; for that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit.”

From these and similar testimonies, are we not enabled to believe and understand that the Son, according to the flesh, was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit? Thus, according to divine fecundity, we do not doubt that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, while, according to the assumption of the flesh, the Son was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit. “That which has been born in her is born from the Holy Spirit.” [Note: B and C read this way; A omits everything from “From these and similar testimonies” through “born from the Holy Spirit.”]

But according to another interpretation also, you will find that the Son is conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and through the Holy Spirit. For when each of the faithful undergoes the sacrament of baptism, what else is accomplished there except the conception and birth of the Word of God in their hearts, from the Holy Spirit and through the Holy Spirit? Thus every day Christ is both conceived and born and nourished in the womb of faith, as though in the entrails of a most chaste mother. [Note: Conjecture; A: “by the devout”; C: “of Christ.”] [Col. 0611D]

Perhaps for this reason the Nicene synod transmitted that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone: so that such a question would not be debated. For an earnest investigator of sacred theology, hearing that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, immediately prompted by divine zeal, asks and says: [Col. 0612A]

“If, then, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, why is the Son not likewise born from the Father through the Holy Spirit? But if the Son is not born from the Father through the Holy Spirit, why would the Holy Spirit be said to proceed from the Father through the Son? For what is believed catholicly concerning the Holy Spirit, why should it not also be believed in the same way concerning the Son?”

Unless perhaps someone, considering the force of the natural analogies mentioned above, should say that we see splendor proceeding from fire through a ray, but not a ray being born from fire through splendor. Likewise, the natural order of theory teaches that an interior sense is sent from the mind through reason, but that reason is not generated from the mind through that same sense. [Col. 0612B] Yet examples from nature may perhaps not be suitable for persuading or affirming matters concerning the generation and procession of divine substances.

Accordingly, as this question is concerned, what is sung in the holy Creed according to the Greeks leaves the matter entirely free and unqualified. For it says that the Son is **ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς γεννηθέντα**, that is, “begotten from the Father,” but the Spirit is **ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς πορευόμενον**, that is, “proceeding from the Father.”

But if someone were to consult the holy Fathers who added to the Latin Creed concerning the Spirit, “who proceeds from the Father and the Son,” they would, I believe, answer reasonably and would not conceal the reason for that addition. Perhaps they were consulted and did answer; but what seemed to them to be the case in this matter has not yet come into our hands.

[Col. 0612C] Therefore we do not rashly attempt to define anything concerning such a question—unless perhaps someone should say, not without reason, that this was added because it is confirmed in many passages of sacred Scripture. For the Lord himself [Note: A: “God himself”] says: “Whom the Father sends in my name.” For the Son appears to send the Spirit whom the Father sends in his name. The Son himself also calls the Spirit the Spirit of truth [Note: A omits “Spirit of truth”], but the Son is truth, as he himself testifies: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” If, then, he is the Spirit of truth, surely the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son.

When he healed the woman suffering from a hemorrhage—**αἱμοῤῥοῦσαν**, that is, suffering from an issue of blood—he said: “I perceived power going out from me.” [Note: A reverses the order to *de me exisse* (“to have gone out from me”); the printed text has *exisse de me*.] And what we said shortly before: “If I go away, I will send him to you.”

Likewise the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” Likewise the Psalmist: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.” [Col. 0612D]

By such testimonies and others like them, what catholic believer could fail to approve that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son?

### 34

**STUDENT.** I am not greatly perplexed by this question. However anyone may pronounce the ecclesiastical Creed, I receive it without shipwreck of sound faith: whether he says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, or from the Father and the Son—provided that the principle remains safe by which we both believe and understand that the same Spirit proceeds substantially from one cause, namely, from the Father. [Col. 0613A]

For the Father is the cause of the Son born from him and of the Spirit proceeding from him. But I still wish to ask you: is the Son born and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the essence of the Father, or from his substance? [Note: C omits “is”; A reads “or from the essence,” and elsewhere “or from the substance.”]

**MASTER.** You will easily be freed from this ambiguity if you first understand clearly what difference there is between the essence and the substance of divine goodness.

**STUDENT.** Theology handed down from the holy Fathers of both languages, Greek and Latin, has taught me concerning the difference between the divine essence and substance. For Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, Gregory the Theologian, and their most elegant expositor Maximus say that there is a difference between **οὐσία**, that is, essence, and **ὑπόστασις**, that is, substance. By **οὐσία** they understand that one and simple nature of divine goodness; by **ὑπόστασις**, the proper and individual substance of each person. [Col. 0613B]

For they say: **μίαν οὐσίαν ἐν τρίσιν ὑποστάσεσιν**, that is, “one essence in three substances.” Saint Augustine and the other holy Fathers who wrote in Latin likewise express the faith of the holy Trinity by saying “one substance in three persons,” signifying by the term “substance” the unity of the divine nature, and by the names of the persons the threefold distinction of substances.

The modern Greeks also accept this. They say **μίαν ὑπόστασιν** [Note: C so; A has **οὐσίαν**], that is, “one substance,” and **τρία πρόσωπα**, that is, “three persons.” [Col. 0613C] The faith is one and the same in all, although there appears to be a difference in the meanings of the terms.

Thus, according to the Greeks, we say that the **οὐσία** of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one and the same, but that their **ὑπόστασις** is not one and the same. The Father has his own proper **ὑπόστασις**, which belongs neither to the Son nor to the Holy Spirit, but to the Father alone. Likewise, the Son has his own proper **ὑπόστασις**, which belongs neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit, but to the Son alone. The same must be said of the Holy Spirit: he has his own proper **ὑπόστασις**, which belongs neither to the Father nor to the Son, but to the Holy Spirit alone.

Nor does the Latin expression teach anything different when it declares three persons in one substance.
