The Father therefore subsists through himself [Note: At *Substat* (“subsists”), C supports the printed form, while A reads *subsistit* (“subsists”). At *per se* (“through himself”), C supports the printed words, while A reads *ipse* (“he himself”).] The Son subsists; the Holy Spirit subsists; and three substances subsist in one essence, because the three are one. [Note: C: “subsist”; A: “exist.”]

**MASTER.** I think that this faith should be reckoned among the doctrines of orthodox faith. You can now clearly distinguish the question proposed. You said that you doubted whether the Son is born and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father’s essence or from his substance. It is as if you had said openly: is the Son born and does the Holy Spirit proceed from the one and common essence or nature of the three substances or persons, or from the Father’s proper substance or person? [Col. 0613D]

The essence of divine goodness is neither the Father’s proper substance, nor the Son’s, nor the Holy Spirit’s, but the one and common nature of the three substances. The Father, however, has his own proper substance; likewise the Son, and likewise the Holy Spirit possess their own substances. [Col. 0614A]

If, then, the divine essence, because it is one and the same, is neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, but their common nature, it follows that the Son is not born from it and that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from it. For if the Son is born from it, he is not born from the Father, since, as we have said, it is not the Father. Likewise, if the Holy Spirit proceeds from the same essence, he does not proceed from the Father.

But if catholic faith most firmly and soundly believes and teaches that the Son was born from the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from that same Father, is it not consequent that we should believe and understand that the Son is born from the substance of the Father and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from it? Therefore the Son is born, and the Holy Spirit proceeds, not from the essence but from the substance of the Father. [Note: C omits “the Son is born and the Spirit proceeds.”] [Col. 0614B]

Among human beings also, we do not say that children are born from a common nature, but from an individual nature. By “individual nature” I mean the undivided substance of each person. For if human beings were born from a common nature, no father would possess his own son, and likewise no son would possess his own father.

### 35

But these matters are conceived more deeply and truly than they can be expressed in speech, and they are understood more deeply and truly than they are conceived [Note: C omits the repeated clause]; yet they are more deeply and truly than they are understood, for they surpass every understanding. [Col. 0614C]

Whatever is said, conceived, or understood concerning the Trinity of the most simple Goodness is a kind of trace and theophany of truth, not truth itself, which surpasses every contemplation not only of rational but also of intellectual creatures.

For the unity or Trinity is not of such a kind as any creature can imagine or understand, or form in any fantasy, however lucid and plausible. [Note: A has “of the holy Trinity” instead of “or Trinity.”] All such representations deceive when contemplation is brought to an end in them. For it is more than unity and more than Trinity. Nevertheless, sacred theology, as guide and teacher, permits us to say, think, and understand something of it, insofar as the intellect reaches it, so that in some manner we may have material for praising and blessing it. [Col. 0614D]

Sacred theology also confirms that the highest angels and the virtues nearest to it cover their feet and faces with their wings, teaching us that the heavenly powers, always and unchangeably adhering to the supreme Trinity and Unity, fear what is above them and contemplate it reverently. Their wings are their acts of contemplation, by which they are said to cover their feet [Note: C reads “are formed”], and, fearing, to look upon their faces: how the holy Trinity and inseparable Unity is diffused through all things from the highest to the lowest [Note: C spells *diffunditur* (“is diffused”) as *deffunditur*; the meaning is unchanged.], how it surpasses every understanding, and how it is removed from every visible and invisible creature into the infinite height of its nature. [Note: A: “into the infinity of its nature.”] [Col. 0615A]

Nevertheless, pure human beings and angels always and ceaselessly desire to behold it, which they cannot contemplate in itself; this is signified by the flight of the intermediate wings. Hence Scripture says: “Into which the angels desire to look.” What they seek is infinite; what they desire is incomprehensible; what they long for surpasses every understanding and is exalted above every creature.

Yet the supreme and divine Unity moves itself within angelic or human understandings, so that they may find in it, insofar as this is granted to creatures, [Col. 0615B] the material of its praise and of their understanding, perceiving the Trinity in Unity.

As the holy theologian Gregory says in his first sermon on the Son:

“For this reason the monad, moved from the beginning into the dyad, comes to rest in the triad.” [Note: A: “stands as far as the triad.”]

Blessed Maximus explains this statement, saying:

“For it moves within the receptive intellect—whether angelic or human—through itself and in itself, making inquiries concerning itself.” [Note: A omits “or.”]

And it must be said more clearly: “It teaches the intellect, in the first act of vision, to share the account of the monad, so that no separation may be introduced into the first cause. It advances that account also to receive the divine and ineffable fecundity of its own cause, mystically and secretly saying to the intellect that it must never think that the excellent coessentiality of the Word and Wisdom, or of the sanctifying power, exists in substances as something composed from these elements, as though the divine were believed to consist in accidents and not to subsist in them.” [Note: A: “signifying power”; A also reads “coessential beings” rather than “coessentiality”; A reads “to know at any time” rather than “never think.”] [Col. 0615C]

Thus Divinity is said to move, because it is the cause through which the inquiry subsists; for without illumination it is impossible to behold Divinity.

Again, it is said to move through the manifestation of a more perfect account of it in particular, according to sacred Scripture: beginning by confessing the Father, and advancing to confess the Son with the Father, then receiving the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son, and urging the instructed to co-worship the perfect Trinity in perfect Unity—that is, one essence, one divinity, one power, and one operation in three substances.

Having investigated in some manner, according to the smallness of our intention, these matters concerning the supreme Cause of all causes—not rashly defining them, however—we must return to the primordial causes around which our discussion is concerned. [Col. 0615D]

**STUDENT.** We should indeed return; enough has been said about these matters. [Col. 0615]

### 36

**MASTER.** The primordial causes are, as I said earlier, what the Greeks call ideas—that is, eternal and unchangeable species or forms, the reasons according to which and in which the visible and invisible world is formed and governed. Therefore the sages of the Greeks deservedly call them **πρωτότυπα**, that is, principal exemplars: exemplars which the Father made in the Son and divides and multiplies through the Holy Spirit into their effects. [Col. 0616A]

They are also called **προορίσματα**, that is, predestinations [Note: A reads “they call them”]. For in them whatever divine providence does, has done, or will do has been predestined simultaneously, once for all, and unchangeably [Note: A omits “and” and “have been predestined”]. Nothing arises naturally in visible or invisible creation except what was predefined and preordained in them before all times and places.

Philosophers also customarily call them **θεῖα θηλήματα**, that is, divine wills, because whatever God willed to make, he made primitively and causally in them; and whatever is destined to be, was made in them before the ages. [Col. 0616B]

Accordingly, they are said to be the principles of all things, since everything perceived or understood in creation, whether visible or invisible, subsists through participation in them.

They themselves are participations in the one Cause of all things, namely, the supreme and holy Trinity. For this reason they are said to exist through themselves, because no creature has been placed between them and the one Cause of all things.

As they subsist immutably in that Cause, the primordial causes are themselves the causes of the subsequent causes, down to the furthest boundaries of the whole created nature, multiplied infinitely. I say “infinitely” not with respect to the Creator but with respect to creation; for the end of the multiplication of creatures is known only to the Creator, because he alone is that end and no other.

The primordial causes, which divine sages call the principles of all things, are: goodness through itself, essence through itself, life through itself, wisdom through itself, truth through itself, intellect through itself, reason through itself, virtue through itself, justice through itself, salvation through itself, greatness through itself, omnipotence through itself, eternity through itself, peace through itself, and all the virtues and reasons which the Father made once and together in the Son, according to which the order of all things is woven from the highest to the lowest—that is, from intellectual creation, which is nearest to God after God, down to the lowest order of all things, in which bodies are contained. [Col. 0616C]

Whatever things are good are good through participation in Goodness itself [Note: A: “in Goodness itself, through Goodness itself”]; whatever subsist essentially and substantially subsist through participation in Essence itself; whatever lives possesses life through participation in Life itself. [Col. 0616D]

Likewise, whatever has wisdom, understands, or is rational, has wisdom, understands, and reasons through participation in Wisdom itself, Intellect itself, and Reason itself. The same must be said of the rest. For no virtue, whether general or particular, is found in the nature of things that does not proceed through ineffable participation from the primordial causes. [Col. 0617A]

But lest anyone suppose that what we have said concerning the primordial causes is supported by no authoritative testimony, we have thought it appropriate to insert into this work certain passages from the book of the holy Father Dionysius, *On the Divine Names* [Note: A omits “Father”].

**STUDENT.** Nothing more fitting, and nothing more consonant with true reasoning, could be added than the firm and credible authority of the holy Fathers.

**MASTER.** He says, then, in chapter eleven of that book:

“But what, you ask, is altogether that which is said to be being itself, or life itself, or whatever we have explained as existing absolutely and principally? We say that this is not improper but correct, and that it has a simple explanation.

“For we do not say that there is some divine or angelic essence existing through itself which is the cause of the existence of the things that are. For the superessential principle of the existence and subsistence of all things that are, and the causal source of essence, is Being itself. Nor is there another deity, apart from the superdivine Deity of all things, who is the parent of life; rather, Life itself is the cause of all things that live and of the life that has been brought forth. [Col. 0617B]

“By Being itself, Life itself, and Divinity itself, we mean, principally, divinely and causally, the one superprincipial and superessential principle and cause of all things. But participatively we mean the providential virtues brought forth from God, who is not himself a participant, namely, deification itself. Existing things participate in these properly, and through them are, are alive, and are divine, and are so called; and likewise with the others.

“Accordingly, the best establisher of the first things is said to exist first, then of the particular things, then of all those participating in them, and then of those participating in them particularly.

“And what need is there to speak of these things, when some of our divine teachers say that the establishing substance of goodness and divinity itself is more than good and more than divine—the goodness and divinity itself? They say that it is a beneficent and deifying gift proceeding from God, and that it is the form itself, the self-forming outpouring, the whole form, and the particular form, and universally good things, and whatever else has been said or will be said in the same manner: things declaring the providence and goodness participated in by existing things, proceeding from the God who is not himself a participant, and overflowing through a rich outpouring. [Col. 0617C]

“Thus the careful summit of all causality, being altogether superessential and supernatural, surpasses everything that exists according to any essence or nature.” [Col. 0617D]

Likewise, from the same book, chapter five:

“All the principles of existing things, participating in Being itself, both are and are principles; and they are first, and then they are principles. [Note: A: “all the principles.”]

“If someone wishes to call Life itself the principle of living things insofar as they are living, and Likeness itself the principle of things insofar as they are like, and Unity itself the principle of united things insofar as they are united, and Order itself the principle of ordered things insofar as they are ordered, and likewise with all other things which, by participating in this or that, or in both or in many, are this or that, or both or many—you will find that the participants themselves first participate in Being itself, and that through it they first exist; then they are principles of this or that, and through participation in it they exist as participated beings. [Note: A: “whatever”; A omits “or of this”; A: “of many.”]

“If, then, these things are what they are through participation, much more so are their participants.

“And shortly afterward:

“For in the monad every number subsists beforehand, and the monad possesses every number individually within itself; every number is indeed united in the monad. But insofar as it proceeds from the monad, it is distinguished and multiplied.

“In the center also all the lines of the circles are co-established in accordance with their primary unity [Col. 0618B]; and the figure has within itself all the simple lines, uniformly united both to one another and to the one principle from which they proceed, while in the center itself they are universally joined together. But insofar as they are somewhat distant from it, they are somewhat distinguished; the farther they recede, the more they are distinguished and simply so. The nearer they are to the center, the more they are united both to it and to one another; and insofar as they are distant from it, they are also distant from one another. [Col. 0618A]

“But throughout the whole of nature, all things are interwoven according to the individual reasons of nature through one unconfused unity; and in the soul, according to its parts, the providential virtues of the whole body exist uniformly. [Note: A reads “other” instead of “soul.”]

“It is therefore not inconsistent, as we ascend from obscure images to the causal source of all things, to contemplate with eyes beyond the world all things in the causal source of all things, set beside one another and uniformly united [Note: C: ‘in unity’]. For it is the principle of existing things, from which come Being itself and all things that in any manner exist; every principle, every end, every life, every immortality, every wisdom, every order, every harmony, every virtue, every preservation, every placement, every distribution, every intellect, every reason, every sense, every disposition, every state, every movement, every unity, every judgment, every friendship, every joining, every distinction, every limit, and all the other things that may be named which characterize all existing things proceeding from Being. [Note: A omits “that may be named.”] [Col. 0618C]

“And after a little:

“For if, in our experience, the sun, although the essences and qualities of sensible things are many and distinct, nevertheless, being itself one and uniform, renews, nourishes, preserves, perfects, distinguishes, unites, restores, makes fertile, causes all things to be, increases, changes, places, plants [Note: A omits “and plants”], renews [Note: C: ‘removes’], and gives life to all things; and each of the many participants properly participates in the same one sun; and the one sun uniformly anticipates within itself the causes of its many participants—much more must it be granted that the Cause of the earth itself and of all things has prefigured within itself the paradigms of all existing things according to one superessential unity.” [Note: A reads “in itself” rather than “has prefigured.”] [Col. 0618D]

Then he adduces essences according to their procession from Essence. [Col. 0619A]

By “paradigms,” we mean the substantializing and uniformly prefigured reasons of existing things in God, which theology calls predestinations and the divine and good wills that distinguish and produce existing things, according to which the superessential Existence both predestined and brought forth all things. [Col. 0620A]

And now, I think, an end must be placed upon this book. [Note: C: “Moreover, to this book.”]

**STUDENT.** So be it.

**The second book, *On Natures*, ends.**
