### THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

[Note: C, in illuminated letters: “The third book *On Natures* begins. Recapitulation of the second book.”]

[Col. 0619]

**MASTER.** In the second book, nearly the whole purpose of our reasoning was devoted to setting down in writing our consideration of the second universal nature and, so to speak, its form or species—whatever seemed plausible to us and, as I believe, had been brought to clarity and firmly supported by the conclusions of sound reason. The second consideration of universal nature is concerned with that part of it which both is created and creates, and in which, as the authority of the holy Fathers and sound reason itself teach, the principles of all things—that is, the primordial causes, or, as has often been said, the predestinations of things to be created, or the divine wills—are to be considered. Whenever the necessity of the discussion required it, we also introduced certain matters concerning incidental questions, for the sake of disclosing the principal question. For, in my opinion, there is no principal question that, while being investigated with attentive contemplation of the mind, does not admit incidental questions.

Indeed, it is otherwise impossible to disentangle the matter, especially since, while we were discussing the principles of things—that is, the primordial causes, and also the one principle of all things, namely God, who alone is the sole and first cause of all causes, and the supercausal cause, and the superessential goodness, through whose participation all principles and causes of all things subsist, while he himself participates in none, because he wholly lacks any principle superior to him or existing with him, though not coessential with him—whatever occurred to the mind necessarily had to be inserted [A: “introduced”]. For who could rightly say anything about created causes unless he first clearly perceived the one self-subsisting cause of all things, created by no cause preceding it, insofar as it is granted to speak of the ineffable, to comprehend the incomprehensible, and to understand what surpasses every intellect?

Along with these matters, we briefly touched upon the return of mutable and separated things, through the various divisions and parts of nature by which this world is completed, once again into their principles, from which they proceed and in which they subsist immutably, when the end of all things has come and the state of those things that are in motion has appeared, after which nothing will move [A: “through which” for “after which”]. Thus, as we said, the sequence of the second discourse is woven together.

Then, unless I am mistaken, the succession of the questions requires that, with God as our guide, a third book be composed concerning the third consideration of universal nature—that is, concerning that part of creation which is created and does not create—whatever the eternal light may reveal to our mind [A: “into our minds”].

**DISCIPLE.** I think one must enter upon the path of discussion in no other way. For if the first book treats of the nature that creates all things and is created by none, and is understood of God alone, while the second treats, in a rational progression, of that nature which both is created and creates, and which is recognized in the primordial causes of things, is it not fitting that the third should likewise take up as the material of its exposition the third nature, which is created and does not create?

But before we pass to disentangling this part of nature, I should like to know why you wished to place, as it were, as the first part of the whole, that nature which is removed from the universality of all natures by its excellence and infinity. The universe is filled by the number of its forms and parts, and therefore does not advance into infinity; for it is bounded above and below by its own limits. It begins with intellectual creation, which exists in the angels—or, ascending higher, with the primordial causes, above which sound reason finds nothing higher except God alone—and then descends through the natural orders of intelligible, celestial, and visible essences that constitute this world, down to the lowest order of all creation, which is filled with bodies and with the increases and decreases of bodies. It proceeds through various departures and successions [A omits “and successions”], through the coming together of the universal elements into their proper unity and their subsequent dissolution back into the universal whole [A omits “again”].

But the nature that creates the whole universe, since it is infinite, is enclosed by no limits either above or below. It encompasses all things, and is encompassed by none. Nor is this surprising, since it does not even permit itself to be encompassed by itself [A: “does not permit itself”], because it universally escapes being encompassed—just as it universally escapes being comprehended by itself, much more by another, or being understood supernaturally within anything definite or capable of definition.

Unless perhaps someone should say that it encompasses itself in this respect: that it knows itself unable to be encompassed; that it comprehends itself in this respect: that it knows itself not to be comprehensible; and that it understands itself in this respect: that it knows it impossible for itself to be understood in anything, because it surpasses everything that is and can be. Since this is so, and no one who philosophizes rightly would rashly resist these arguments, I do not clearly see why you place it within the divisions of the universe.

**MASTER.** I would not place it in the divisions of the created universe in any way. But in the divisions of that universe which is comprehended under the single term “universal nature,” I judged that it should be placed—not from one perspective only, but from several perspectives of reason. For by the name “nature” people customarily signify not only the created universe but also that which creates it.

The first and greatest division, therefore, is the division of universal nature into the nature that creates the created universe and the nature that is created within that created universe—especially since this natural division is preserved uniformly and without end in all universes. For the first division of universal goodness is into that one and supreme good which is immutably good in itself and substantial, from which every good flows, and into that good which is good through participation in the supreme and immutable good. The same principal division applies to universal essence, universal life, universal wisdom, and universal virtue.

For in these and in similar matters, nature is first distinguished as that which truly and immutably is essence, life, wisdom, and virtue through itself, from itself, and in itself, from that nature which, through participation in the supreme good, either merely exists; or exists and lives; or exists, lives, senses, and reasons [A: “understands” for “senses and reasons”]; or exists, lives, senses, reasons, and understands [A: “understands and participates in virtue” for “senses, reasons, and understands”].

Do you see how the creator of the whole universe holds the first place in these divisions? And rightly so, since he is the principle of all things, inseparable from every diversity that he created, and without whom the creator cannot subsist [A omits *conditor*, “creator”]. In him all things exist immutably and essentially; and he is the division and the collection of universal creation, its genus, species, whole, and part, although he himself is neither anyone’s genus, nor species, nor whole, nor part. Rather, all these things are from him, in him, and toward him.

For the monad is both the principle of numbers and their first progression; from it the plurality of all numbers begins, and in it their return and collection are completed. All numbers, universally and immutably, subsist in the monad, and in all of them there is both whole and part, and the beginning of every division, although the monad itself is neither a number nor a part of itself. The same reasoning applies to the center in a circle or sphere, to the sign in a figure, and to the point in a line.

Since, then, the division of the whole universe begins from its cause and creator, we must not understand that cause as the first part or species, but must begin every division and partition from it, since it is the principle, middle, and end of the whole universe. And while these things are both predicated and understood of it—that is, while it holds the first place in the divisions of universes—nevertheless no one who believes devoutly and understands the truth fails immediately, without hesitation, to exclaim that the creative cause of the entire created universe is supernatural and superessential, above all life, wisdom, and virtue, and above everything that is spoken, understood, or perceived by any sense. It is the causal principle of all these things, the essential middle that fills them, and the consummating end; it establishes every motion, makes every resting thing restful [A: “whatever things”], and is the circumference that circumscribes all things that are and are not.

**DISCIPLE.** I gladly yield to these arguments of lofty and cautious reasoning [A: “collocations”], and approve them as plausible. But before you proceed to consider the effects of the primordial causes—from which the first and one creative cause of all things is chiefly accustomed to receive its name—it is fitting to know their natural order. For I think that they have so far been introduced in a confused and indistinct manner. If I am not mistaken, those who seek perfect knowledge of them and of their effects will receive no small assistance if the natural order in which they were established by the Creator is first clearly disclosed.

**MASTER.** The holy Dionysius the Areopagite, a diligent investigator of divine providence, set forth the sequence of the primordial causes most clearly in his book *On the Divine Names*. He asserts that the first gift and participation of the supreme goodness—which participates in nothing, since it is goodness through itself—is goodness through itself, and that through participation in it whatever things are good are good [A: “varied”]. It is therefore called goodness through itself because through itself it participates in the supreme good. Other good things do not participate in the supreme and substantial good through themselves, but through that which is the first participation of the supreme good through itself.

This rule is uniformly observed in all the primordial causes: namely, that through themselves the principal participations belong to the one cause of all things, which is God. Since the first consideration of supreme and true nature is that by which supreme and true goodness is understood, while the second is that by which supreme and true essence is understood, it is not without reason that essence through itself holds the second place among the primordial causes. Since it is the first participation of supreme and true essence, all things that follow it receive being through participation in it; and therefore they are not only good but also existent.

The third consideration of divine nature is that by which supreme and true life is understood. Accordingly, life through itself is counted third among the primordial causes. It is the first subsisting participation through itself of supreme and true life, created so that all living things after it might live through participation in it. Hence it follows that they are good, existent, and living.

The fourth theory of the same nature is that by which supreme and true reason is known. Hence it is evident that reason through itself occupies the fourth place among the primordial causes [C: “is in possession of”; A: “the fourth”], possessing the first participation of supreme and true reason and the beginnings of all rational things after it—that is, of all things participating in reason.

The fifth theory of divine nature concerns supreme and true intellect; for intellect understands all things before they come to be. Accordingly, intellect through itself is recognized as fifth in the order of the primordial causes [C omits the phrase from “it concerns” through “intellect”]. Through participation in it, whatever things understand do understand and are intellects [C: “through participation in that one” and omits “whatever things understand”]. It itself was established as the first participation of supreme and true intellect [A: “brought forth”].

The sixth contemplation of divine nature is established in true and supreme wisdom. Hence wisdom through itself is rightly placed sixth among the primordial causes. It is the first participation of supreme and true wisdom, and through participation in it was created as the cause of wisdom for all wise beings after it.

The seventh contemplation of true and supreme nature considers its supreme and true virtue. Accordingly, virtue through itself occupies the seventh place among the primordial causes and is the first participation of supreme and true virtue; the other species of virtue after it are participations in it [A omits “in it”].

The eighth degree of theory is that in which the pure mind beholds the supreme and true blessedness of divine nature [A: “the true and blessed”]. Its first participation is blessedness through itself [C omits “is”]; all things that are blessed after it participate in it as, so to speak, the eighth of the primordial causes, and are blessed [C: *beata*, “blessed,” omitting *que sunt*, “and are”].

The ninth theory in order is that of divine and supreme truth. Its first participation is truth through itself [A omits “is”]; it is, as it were, the ninth of the primordial causes, after and through which all things that are true are true [A omits *nonam*, “ninth”].

The tenth is eternity through itself. It is the first participation of supreme and true eternity, and after it and through it all things that are eternal are eternal [C omits the final clause].

The same reasoning applies to greatness, love and peace, unity and perfection. For through these primordial causes all things that participate in greatness, love, peace, unity, and perfection descend from the supreme cause of all.

These matters, I think, are sufficient to make clear what we wish to explain. The foregoing theory, uniformly in all the principles of all things, which proceed into infinity, everywhere smiles upon the eyes of the mind in a divine manner—whether in things that can both be understood and named, or in things perceived by intellect alone but lacking verbal designations, or in things that can be grasped neither by intellect nor expressed by names. For they escape every sense and every contemplation of the mind; they are obscured by the excessive brightness of their own height [or: “by the brightness of their excessive height”]. For they are in him of whom the Apostle said: “He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light.”

Nor is it surprising if the primordial causes extend into infinity. For just as the first cause of all things—from which, in which, through which, and toward which they were created—is infinite, so they themselves know no end by which they might be enclosed, except according to the will of their Creator.

It should be noted that the order of the primordial causes which you demand from me is not established as a determinate mode of progression, clearly and distinctly, in the causes themselves, but in theory—that is, in the contemplation of the soul of the one who seeks them and conceives within himself such knowledge of them as is granted, arranging them in a certain manner so that he may pronounce something definite about them with pure understanding. For the first causes themselves are one and simple in themselves, defined by no known order and separated from one another by none. They undergo this differentiation in their effects [C: “are parceled out”].

Just as in the monad, while all numbers subsist by reason alone, no number is distinguished from another—for they are one, a simple unity, not a unity composed of many things—so from the monad the multiplication of numbers proceeds into infinity, whereas the monad itself is not composed of multiple numbers proceeding from it and gathered, as it were, into one.

Similarly, when the primordial causes are understood as established in the principle of all things, namely in the only-begotten Word of God [A: “unbegotten”], they are one, simple, and indivisible. But when they proceed into their effects, multiplied into infinity, they receive a plural multitude that is both numerous and ordered. This is not because the cause of all things lacks order or arrangement, or because arrangement itself is not numbered among the principles of things—since everything ordered is ordered through participation in it—but because every order in the supreme cause of all things, and in its first participation, is one and simple, distinguished by no differences. There all orders do not differ from one another, because they are one inseparable unity, from which the manifold order of all things descends.

The order of the primordial causes is therefore established according to the judgment of the contemplating mind, insofar as knowledge of them is granted to those who discuss divine causes. For those who philosophize devoutly and purely may begin with any one of them, as they wish, and then turn the eye of the mind—which is true reason—through the others in a certain order of contemplation, perceiving as many as they can and establishing the limit of their theory in whichever of them they choose.

Thus the modest capacity of our present purpose began to count the number of the primordial causes from the goodness of the primordial causes, arranged as it were in a certain order, and set its end, by way of example, in that which is called perfection through itself, established as the fifteenth. It selected these principal causes as an example according to the capacity of its purpose and arranged them as seemed appropriate. This does not mean that they are arranged in this way by their own nature, since in themselves all things are one and exist together and simply; rather, when those who seek them wish to present something about them by way of example, they customarily appear in this way or that, in many ways and infinitely, as the divine ray illumines them in their theophanies [A: “may appear”].

To make this example clearer by means of sensible things [C: “clear”], carefully observe a center and the circle circumscribed around it, together with the straight lines beginning at the center, extending toward the circle [A: “carried”], and ending there.

**DISCIPLE.** I have often observed this, either inwardly in the mind through imagination, or outwardly in a visible and bodily figure presented to the senses [A: “to the sense”].

**MASTER.** Have you not observed how all the lines are united in the center, so that none of them can be distinguished from the others [A: “and”]? This is because in it they are all one and in no way differ from one another. Thus it is reasonable to define the center not as the joining of lines into one, but as the simple and indivisible source and principle from which, whether naturally or by art, the manifold number of lines proceeds. For the center is the universal beginning of the lines, in which they are all one.

**DISCIPLE.** This too has been made perfectly clear to me through geometrical reasoning. Yet all these matters are perceived more by the mind than by the senses, whether one wishes to discuss such things inwardly through imagination [A omits “through imagination”] or outwardly through the sense [A omits “through the sense”; C has “to be discussed”].

**MASTER.** You speak rightly, for these and similar matters are judged by the pure acuity of the mind. You see, unless I am mistaken, that in the first progression of the lines from the unity itself, which is in the center, the lines are joined to one another so closely that they can scarcely be distinguished from one another. But as they extend farther from the center, the spaces by which they are separated from one another begin gradually to grow wider, until they reach the outer circle, where they end. There their widest intervals are measured—that is, the spaces situated between the lines—which are equal to one another, so that none is found wider or narrower than the others.

The same is true of the lines themselves: they all have one and the same length, so that none is longer or shorter than another. Natural and rational equality is preserved in both respects—in the width of the spaces, I mean, and in the length of the lines.

**DISCIPLE.** So it is, and I understand it perfectly [A: “as it is”].

**MASTER.** What if you wished to distinguish the number of the spaces and lines and arrange them in a certain order? Could you find one particular space or one particular line from which, naturally and properly, you could begin [A omits “from”] to order and number the whole figure?

**DISCIPLE.** Nothing occurs to me as I search. For such equality prevails among them that no space can be distinguished from another, nor any line from another, by some difference or property. The circle itself, within whose circumference everything is gathered, is so like itself in itself that no part of it can be distinguished from another, whether by nature or by art. For it possesses continuous quantity, and therefore begins from no fixed starting point and is enclosed by no determined end; rather, in its entirety it is both its own beginning and its own end.

For this reason circular motion is rightly called by the Greeks **ἄναρχος** (*anarchos*), that is, “without a beginning,” and it holds primacy among the other motions, namely the straight and the oblique.

**MASTER.** In all these matters you are not mistaken, I believe; for sound reason teaches no otherwise. Do you therefore see that no law of figures stands in your way or restrains you [A: “may stand in your way” and “may restrain you”], preventing you from beginning with any space or line and ordering and numbering the whole figure [A: “disordering”]? For reason commands this. Accordingly, however many spaces and lines there are, so many beginnings and ends can be made for numbering and ordering them.

**DISCIPLE.** I do not resist this conclusion either; but I expect to learn where it is leading [C: “where it leads”].

**MASTER.** Nowhere else than to make us understand with a light clearer than day that the supreme theologians and their attendants can, with no rational obstacle, begin their contemplation from any and all of the primordial causes and establish the end of that contemplation in whichever of them each person thinks appropriate. Thus, however many primordial causes there are—or, to speak more cautiously, however many are formed, or can in any way be formed, in the intellects of those who contemplate—so many orders and so great a plurality of them are rightly offered to those who philosophize according to the capacity of each person’s theory, as each may wish, through the wondrous disposition of divine providence [A: “they bring forward”].

While these things are carried out in the minds of those who contemplate, through the various and wondrous modes of divine teaching and divine theophanies [A: “divided”], the primordial reasons of all things that exist themselves subsist eternally, uniformly, and immutably, one and the same, beyond every order and number, in the Word of God, in whom they were made [A: “subsists,” singular].

**DISCIPLE.** Now I clearly see the end of your purpose and reasoning. For, as I think, you are trying to persuade us of nothing other than this: that no particular natural order should be sought in the principles of things themselves [A: “in these”]. And rightly so. For who would rationally seek an order or number in things that, by the loftiness of their nature, were created by the Creator of all things above every number and every order, since they are the beginnings of every number and every order, united to one another in themselves and distinguished by no contemplation of an inferior nature?

Only the gnostic power of their Creator is rightly believed capable of numbering, distinguishing, multiplying, ordering, and dividing them. But because, in a manner unknown and discovered beyond nature, they are formed in their theophanies in the minds of those who contemplate, they are also recognized as capable of being multiplied, divided, and numbered in those minds—in the intellects, I mean, according to what is granted to those who contemplate [C: “to the contemplators”; A: “to those contemplating”].

Hence it follows that they—the primordial causes—receive in themselves no order known to intellect or sense. But in the mind that contemplates them, that is, in the contemplative soul, certain diverse and manifold orders arise through a conception proceeding from understanding, by means of certain plausible imaginings [A: “divided”].

Since this is so, I would not suppose that you began the enumeration of the principal causes with goodness itself without some particular reason. For it is not proper to those who reason correctly to say something idle and without a cause.

**MASTER.** You might say this without rashness if you knew me to be one of those who reason piously and perfectly and deviate in no way from the path of true reasoning. But since I scarcely find a place even among the remotest attendants of the great philosophers, one must not imprudently make promises about my progress through the loftiest ascents of theory [A omits “to have”].

Often, those who began these ascents with better intellect and incomparably purer understanding either went astray and deviated from the path, or, unable to climb higher, returned to lower things, or, honoring those heights with silence, wisely and rationally refrained from presuming to reach what was beyond them.

For it belongs to the most perfect—those illuminated by the splendors of the divine ray and therefore led by the hand into the most sacred recesses of the heavenly mysteries—to cross the highest **βήματα** (*bēmata*) of divine theory, that is, its steps [A: *climata*, “stages”; B: *bimata*], and to behold without any error the appearance of the most evident truth, with no darkness obstructing it [C: “stretched out”].

Since these things are established beyond the powers of our purpose, and since, still weighed down by the burden of bodily senses, we cannot yet reach them, let us not appear sluggish in divine matters by burying the Lord’s talent in the earth, neglecting the master’s money without any profit, and earning the judgment of the wicked servant. Rather, concerning the matters we are now discussing, we shall say whatever seems most plausible, insofar as the inner light grants itself to the capacity of those who seek it, everywhere observing the rule of humility, lest we suppose ourselves to be what we are not. For it is written: “Do not be high-minded, but fear.”

**2.** For this reason I was led to begin the principles of things specifically with goodness through itself. I perceived—not without the authority of the holy Fathers, and especially of Dionysius the Areopagite—that goodness through itself is the most universal of the divine gifts and in some way precedes the others. For the creative goodness that is the cause of all things, namely God, first created that cause which is called goodness through itself, so that through it he might bring all things that exist into essences from nonexistence. It is proper to divine goodness to call into essence those things that did not exist.

For divine goodness is the cause—indeed the more-than-good, essential, and superessential cause—of the created universe and of all things brought into essence. If, then, the Creator through his goodness caused all things to flow forth from nothing so that they might exist, the understanding of goodness through itself necessarily precedes the understanding of essence through itself. Goodness was not introduced through essence; rather, essence was introduced through goodness.

Scripture itself declares this most clearly when it says: “And God saw all things, and behold, [they were] very good” [C: *valde bona*, “very good,” for main-text *bona valde*]. It does not say: “And God saw all things, and behold, [they] are very.” For what value would mere existence have if well-being were removed? Everything that exists exists to the extent that it is good; insofar as it is not good—or, so to speak, insofar as it is less good—to that extent it does not exist. Accordingly, when goodness is wholly removed, no essence remains.

To say simply “to exist,” or “to exist eternally,” once well-being and eternal well-being have been removed, is to speak improperly [A: “essentially”]. Once goodness has been taken away, one does not properly speak of essence or eternal essence.

And lest you perhaps say in response that we may similarly declare that, once essence has been wholly removed [C: “existence”], no goodness will remain, and that when existence has perished no good will subsist [C omits “indeed”], consider an argument of greater force. Not only are things that exist called good; things that do not exist are also called good. Indeed, things that do not exist are called better than things that do exist. For insofar as they surpass essence by excellence, they approach the superessential good, namely God; but insofar as they participate in essence, they are distanced from the superessential good.

Things that do not exist, in my opinion, are those which, because of their excessive excellence, inseparable unity, and simplicity, can be perceived neither by sense nor by intellect. Things that do exist are judged to be those that yield to intellect or the senses and are circumscribed within some definite and determined substance by differences and properties, subject to accidents, varied and dispersed through places and times, and unable to exist all at once and simultaneously.

Do you therefore see how much more universal goodness is than essence? For one species of goodness belongs to good things that exist, and another to good things that do not exist [A omits “of goodness”]. Thus theology, beginning with the more universal gifts of divine generosity [C omits “a”] and proceeding through the more particular ones, establishes, under the guidance of theology, a certain order of the primordial causes.

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

### 3. DISCIPLE

Now I understand that you did not begin the consideration of principles irrationally. For whoever divides correctly ought to begin with the most general, proceed through the more general, and thus, as the power of contemplation comes to his aid, arrive at the most particular. I understand this also, if I am not mistaken, by looking more deeply into the very principles of things that you first set forth [Col. 0628D].

For just as goodness is, as it were, a genus of essence, while essence is believed to be a certain species of goodness, so essence is a genus of life. For everything that exists is divided into those that live through themselves and those that do not live through themselves . Not every essence lives through itself, nor is it life . Accordingly, among existing things one species is found in those that live through themselves or are life, and another in those that neither participate in life through themselves nor are life [Col. 0629A; Note: [Col. 0629] A omits “through themselves.”]. This too can be observed in what follows.

For life is a certain genus of reason. Everything that lives is either rational or irrational. Accordingly, one species of life is rational and the other irrational . Likewise, reason appears to have two species: one is wisdom, the other knowledge.

Wisdom properly means that virtue by which the contemplative mind, whether human or angelic, considers divine, eternal, and immutable things—whether it concerns itself with the first cause of all things or with the primordial causes of things, which the Father created once and all together in his Word. This species of reason the wise call theology.

Knowledge, on the other hand, is the virtue by which the theoretical mind, whether human or angelic, treats of the nature of things proceeding from the primordial causes by generation and divided into genera and species, through differences and properties—whether they are subject to accidents or free from them, whether joined to bodies or wholly free from bodies, whether distributed in places and times or united and inseparable beyond places and times through their simplicity [Col. 0629B]. This species of reason is called physics.

For physics is the natural science of natures subject to the senses and intellect, and moral discipline always follows it. If anyone pays attention, he will find the same rule either in all or in many primordial causes—not because, as I think, some primordial causes are more general and others more particular—for such inequality, where supreme unity and supreme equality prevail, is impossible, as I believe —but because the contemplating mind discovers more participations in the effects of some than in those of others, and also discovers the manifold division of things [Col. 0629C].

There are more participations through goodness itself than through essence itself: one goodness is participated in by both what exists and what does not exist, whereas essence is participated in only by what exists. It is not contrary to truth to understand the other principles in the same way. Essence is participated in by things that live and things that do not live; life, however, only by things that live. Rational and irrational beings participate in life; only rational beings participate in reason. Wisdom and knowledge participate in reason; only those intellects that revolve around God, beyond the whole nature of visible and invisible things and outside themselves in an eternal and ineffable movement, and that revolve around the principles of things, participate in wisdom [Col. 0629D; Note: [Col. 0629] A has *revolvuntur*, “are revolved,” instead of *volvuntur*, “revolve.”].

Accordingly, genera and species, plurality and paucity, are not to be observed in the principles of things themselves, but [the transmitted text reads: “but not”] in their participations—that is, not in the causes themselves, which were made uniformly, immutably, and equally in the Word of God, but in their effects, with which the visible and invisible world is filled. In the causes themselves there is supreme equality and no diversity; in their effects, however, there is a manifold and infinite variety of differences [Col. 0630A].

But I do not yet understand what participation is. Without understanding it, no one, I think, can clearly discern what has been said.

### MASTER

Everything that exists is either participating, participated in, participation, or simultaneously participated in and participating .

That alone is participated in which participates in nothing superior to itself. This is rightly understood of the supreme and only principle of all things, which is God. Everything that comes from him participates in him: some things immediately through themselves, others through intervening mediations.

That alone is participating which participates in what is naturally established above it, but is participated in by nothing below it, because no natural order is found below it. Such are bodies, through whose participation nothing subsists in the realm of things; for we do not number shadows among subsisting things.

By “bodies” I mean now not those simple, invisible, and universal bodies, but those composed from them and subject to the senses and to corruption—that is, to dissolution [Col. 0630B; Note: [Col. 0629] A has “now” instead of “for.”]. Everything else, whatever is established in the middle, proceeding from the one principle of all things through the natural descents and degrees ordered by divine wisdom, down to the extremity of the whole of nature, which bodies contain, is both participating and participated in, and is so called.

The most excellent things, between which and the supreme Good no higher creature has been interposed, participate in God immediately. They are the principles of all things, that is, the primordial causes, established around and after the one universal principle; after them, the subsequent essences subsist through their participation [Col. 0630C].

Do you see how the first order of the created universe is both a participant in the one principle of all things and participated in by the creatures that follow it? The same reasoning is to be understood of the other orders. Every order established in the middle from the highest to the lowest—that is, from God down to visible bodies—both participates in the order above it and is participated in by the order below it. Thus it is both participating and participated in; participation is understood in all things.

Just as there are similar proportions among the terms of numbers—that is, among numbers themselves considered under one relation—so among all the natural orders from highest to lowest there are similar participations by which they are joined together. And just as proportionalities exist among proportions—that is, similar relations of proportions—so the creative wisdom of all things has established marvelous and ineffable harmonies in the participations of natural orders [Col. 0630D]. Through these all things converge into a certain unity, whether that unity is called concord, friendship, peace, love, or whatever term may signify the unification of all things .

For just as the concord of numbers receives the name “proportion,” and the comparison of proportions the name “proportionality,” so the distribution of natural orders has received the name “participation,” while the joining together of those distributions has received the name “universal love” [Col. 0631A]. This love binds all things together in an ineffable friendship.

Participation, therefore, is not the taking up of some part; it is the distribution, from the highest down to the lowest through the higher orders, of divine givings and gifts to the lower orders.

To the first order, the first gift is immediately both given and bestowed by the supreme Good of all; for example, being is given and well-being is bestowed . The first order itself distributes being and well-being to the order that follows it. Thus the distribution of being and well-being flows gradually from the source of all goods given and all gifts, through the higher orders into the lower, down to the furthest orders.

Here it must be noted that “well-being” is understood in two ways. In one sense, all things that exist are said to be good because they were made by the supreme Good, and exist to the extent that they participate in goodness . In the other sense , all things that naturally subsist as good are adorned with gifts of virtues, so that their natural goodness may become more apparent.

Although the gifts of grace, which are usually signified by the word “virtue,” are distributed chiefly and principally to rational and intellectual creatures, nevertheless no nature, even among the lowest, should be considered entirely without participation in divine grace according to its proportion. Just as all things participate in goodness, so they also participate in grace . They participate in goodness in order to exist, and in grace in order to be both good and beautiful.

The same is to be understood of life, sense, reason, wisdom, and the other divine givings and gifts. They are distributed through the higher orders to the lower in the same manner, insofar as they reach them. Not all givings descend as far as the extremes. Being and well-being according to nature are distributed down to the final limit of the created universe, but life does not reach the last order [Col. 0631C].

Bodies do not live through themselves, nor are they life; they receive life through the order above them. That order is constituted in nutritive and active life, and flourishes in seeds.

What shall I say of sense, reason, and intellect? It is clear to everyone that sense descends as far as irrational animals, while reason and intellect do not exceed rational and intellectual beings.

There is this difference between givings and gifts: givings are, and are called, proper distributions by which every nature subsists; gifts are distributions of grace by which every subsisting nature is adorned. Thus nature is given, and grace is gifted [Col. 0631D; Note: [Col. 0631] A reads “nature is given, grace is gifted”; B, “nature gives, grace gifts”; C, “nature gives, grace is gifted.”]. Every perfect creature consists of nature and grace .

Hence it follows that every essence is properly called a datum, and every virtue a gift. Thus theology says: “Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” [James 1:17]. Sacred Scripture, however, often uses “giving” for “gift,” and “gift” for “giving.”

It must also be understood that virtue is taken in three ways.

There is substantial virtue. Everything that subsists subsists through a certain natural trinity: essence, virtue, and operation. Enough was said about these in the first book.

The second species of virtue is that which struggles against the corruption of nature, such as health against sickness, and knowledge and wisdom against ignorance and folly [Col. 0632A].

The third is that which opposes malice, such as humility against pride and chastity against lust. This species extends as far as the irrational movement of free will reaches toward intellectual nature. For insofar as the malice of vices multiplies its forms, goodness sets up corresponding defenses in the virtues [Col. 0632B].

It should be noted that the Greeks express “participation” more meaningfully, more precisely, and more easily for understanding. In their language μετοχή or μετουσία signifies “participation.” Μετοχή is as though derived from μεταέχουσα, that is, “having afterward” or “having secondarily”; μετουσία likewise is as though derived from μεταουσία, that is, “post-essence” or “secondary essence.”

From this it is very easily understood that participation is nothing other than the derivation of a secondary essence from a superior essence, and the distribution, from that which possesses being first, of being to the secondary essence.

We can establish this by examples from nature.

### 4.

For a whole river flows principally from its source, and through its channel the water that first rises in the source continues to pour forth without interruption, however far its course may extend [Col. 0632C].

In the same way divine goodness, essence, life, wisdom, and everything that exists in the source of all things first flow into the primordial causes and make them exist. Then, through the primordial causes , they proceed in an ineffable manner into their effects, through the orders of the universe appropriate to them, always flowing through the higher orders to the lower . Again, through the most secret pores of nature, they return by a most hidden course to their source .

From that source come every good, every essence, every life, every sense, every reason, every wisdom, every genus, every species, every beauty , every order, every unity, every equality, every difference, every place, every time, everything that is, everything that is not, everything that is understood, everything that is sensed, and everything that surpasses sense and intellect [Col. 0632D].

For the immutable movement, the simple multiplication, and the inexhaustible diffusion of the supreme, triune, and only true Good—from itself, in itself, and toward itself—is the cause of all things, indeed is all things.

If it is the intellect of all things, and it alone understands all things, then it alone is all things, since it alone is the cognitive power that knew all things before all things existed. It did not know all things outside itself, because nothing exists outside it; rather, it has all things within itself [Col. 0633A].

It encompasses all things, and nothing within it exists, insofar as it truly exists, except itself, because it alone truly is. The other things that are said to exist are its theophanies, and they too truly subsist in it .

God, therefore, is everything that truly is, because he makes all things and becomes in all things, as Saint Dionysius the Areopagite says.

Everything that is understood and sensed is nothing other than the manifestation of what does not appear, the revelation of what is hidden, the affirmation of what is denied, the comprehension of what is incomprehensible, the expression of what is ineffable, access to what is inaccessible, understanding of what is unintelligible, body of what is incorporeal, essence of what is superessential, form of what is formless, measure of what is immeasurable, number of what is innumerable, weight of what lacks weight, thickening of what is spiritual, visibility of what is invisible, locality of what is without place, temporality of what is without time, definition of what is infinite, circumscription of what is uncircumscribed, and all the other things that are thought and perceived by the pure intellect—things that cannot be contained within the limits of memory and that elude the mind’s vision [Col. 0633B].

We can establish this also by examples from our own nature.

Our intellect is itself invisible and incomprehensible, yet it is both manifested and comprehended through certain signs. It becomes, as it were, thickened into bodies through voices, letters, or other gestures. Although it thus appears externally , it always remains invisible internally. When it leaps forth into various forms comprehensible to the senses, it does not abandon the incomprehensible condition of its nature; and before it is disclosed outwardly, it moves itself within itself [Col. 0633C; Note: [Col. 0633] C reads “within itself”; A reads “outside itself.”].

Thus it is both silent and cries out; while it is silent, it cries out, and while it cries out, it is silent. It is seen as invisible, and while it is seen, it is invisible. It is circumscribed as uncircumscribed, and while it is circumscribed, it remains uncircumscribed. When it wills, it is incorporated in voices and letters; and when it is incorporated, it subsists incorporeally in itself.

When it makes for itself, from the material of air or from sensible forms, certain vehicles by which it can be conveyed to the senses of others, as soon as it reaches their external senses it abandons those vehicles and, alone and free through itself, penetrates the innermost hearts and mingles with other intellects, becoming one with those to which it is joined [Col. 0633D; Note: [Col. 0633] A has “by which it may be conveyed” instead of “by which it can be conveyed.”].

While it accomplishes this, it always remains in itself. While it moves, it stands; and while it stands, it moves. For it is a moving stability and a stable movement. While it is joined to others, it does not abandon its simplicity. Many other things can be conceived, wonderfully and ineffably, about the nature that was made in the image of God .

But these examples are sufficient to suggest the ineffable diffusion of divine goodness through all things from the highest to the lowest—that is, through the universe created by it. This ineffable diffusion both makes all things, becomes in all things, and is all things [Col. 0634A; Note: [Col. 0633] C has “division” instead of “diffusion.”].

### DISCIPLE

They are indeed sufficient, and they flow forth abundantly, insofar as an ineffable reality can be expressed through certain likenesses, even though it is remote from every likeness .

The likeness you took by way of example from our intellect seems to me deficient in this respect: as you say, the intellect both makes and receives those vehicles by which it is carried into the senses of others from matter created outside itself. Divine goodness, however, since nothing exists outside it, did not take the matter of its manifestation from something else, but from nothing.

### 5.

When I hear or say that divine goodness created all things from nothing, I do not understand what is signified by the expression “from nothing”: whether it means the privation of all essence, substance, or accident, or the excellence of divine superessentiality [Col. 0634B; Note: [Col. 0633] C omits “from nothing.”].

### MASTER

I would not readily grant that divine superessentiality is nothing, or that it can be called by such a name of privation . For although theologians say that it is not, they do not thereby persuade us that it is nothing, but rather that it is more than being.

How could the cause of all things that are be understood to be no essence, when all things that are teach that it truly is, while no argument concerning things that are enables us to understand what it is? If, therefore, divine nature is said not to be because of its ineffable excellence and incomprehensible infinity, does it follow that it is altogether nothing, when it is said not to be for no other reason than that it is superessential? It is because true reason does not permit it to be numbered among the things that are, since it is understood to exist above all things that are and are not [Col. 0634C; Note: [Col. 0633] The transmitted note records a reading of *nihil* (“nothing”) for *numquid* (“whether,” “surely not?”); the text also has *superessentialis*, “superessential,” where the witnesses read *superior essentialis*, “superior essential.” A omits “it.”].

### DISCIPLE

What, then, should I understand when I hear you say that God made all things that are from nothing?

### MASTER

Understand that existing things were made from things that did not exist through the power of divine goodness . For things that were not received existence from nothing. They were made because they were not before they were made.

The term “nothing” does not signify some matter, some cause of existing things, any process or occasion that preceded the condition of things that are, anything coessential and coeternal with God, anything subsisting by itself outside God, or anything from which God might have received, as it were, some material for fashioning the world.

Rather, it was altogether the name of the privation of all essence—or, to speak more truly, it is the term for the absence of all essence . Privation is the removal of a state or condition.

Someone might perhaps ask: how could privation exist before the state existed? For no state existed before all things that are received the condition of subsistence .

### DISCIPLE

By the term “nothing,” then, the negation and absence of all essence or substance are indicated, indeed of everything that has been created in the nature of things [Col. 0635A; Note: [Col. 0635] A has the singular “is indicated.”].

### MASTER

So it is, I believe. For almost all interpreters of sacred Scripture agree that the creator of the whole creation made whatever he willed to be made not from something, but from absolute nothing .

### DISCIPLE

I feel myself surrounded on every side by very dark clouds of thought. In such circumstances nothing remains for me except faith alone, to which the authority of the holy Fathers bears witness .

When I attempt to examine clearly, by intellectual understanding, something that I hold by faith alone, the excessive obscurity—or rather, the excessive brightness—of the exceedingly subtle arguments drives back and repels the vision of my mind as they flee from me .

### MASTER

Tell me, please, where you now hesitate, and what troubles you so greatly that, as you say, you cannot reach any clear understanding, or where our reasoning falters, when it cannot lead you to any definite judgment or knowledge of things [Col. 0635B].

### DISCIPLE

I ask you to be magnanimous and to bear patiently the delays caused by my slowness.

I would believe that these exceedingly subtle investigations of things do not shine so readily even into the inner eyes of more perfect persons that they can immediately cling to a firm disposition of mind—especially when what now seems obscure to me is being introduced from matters that have long since been brought, as it were, to complete clarity between us .

For it was settled between us concerning the primordial causes of all things that they were made eternally by the Father in his unbegotten Word—that is, in his wisdom—and simultaneously and all at once. Thus, just as the Father’s wisdom itself is eternal and coeternal with its Father, so also all things made in it are eternal, with the exception that all things were made in him, whereas he was not made but begotten and creative [Col. 0635C; Note: [Col. 0635] A omits “and”; C omits “was”; A has “in him” instead of “in it”; C has “essence” instead of “eternal.”].

For in the creation of the universal creature, just as the will of the Father and the Son is one and the same, so their operation is one and the same.

Thus, in their primordial causes, all things are eternal in the Father’s wisdom, though they are not coeternal with it . For the cause precedes its effects.

Just as the intellect of the craftsman precedes the intellectual conception of his art, and the conception of the art precedes the conception of the things that are made in and through it, so the intellect of the Father, the craftsman, precedes the intellectual conception of his art—that is, of his wisdom—in which he created all things [Col. 0635D].

Then knowledge of all the things made in and through that art follows the intellectual conception of the art itself . Whatever true reason discovers to precede in any manner of precedence must, according to natural succession, necessarily precede .

Accordingly, God the Father, the craftsman of all things, precedes his art according to the causal order. The craftsman is the cause of his art; the art is not the cause of its craftsman. The art itself precedes all things that subsist in it, through it, and from it, for it is their cause [Col. 0636A].

Hence it follows that all things are eternal in the Father’s wisdom, though they are not coeternal with it.

### MASTER

These matters were discussed between us long ago and, through sound reasoning and the testimony of the holy Fathers agreeing on this point, were brought to an unshakable disposition of mind .

### DISCIPLE

Do you not see, then, that I am moved for good reason and battered by the waves of thoughts that conflict with one another ?

For how can these propositions agree with one another? If all things that exist are eternal in the creative wisdom, how were they made from nothing? How can that be eternal which did not exist before it was made? And how can what begins to exist in time and with time exist in eternity? Everything that participates in eternity neither begins to exist nor ceases to exist. But what did not exist and begins to exist must necessarily cease to be what it is. For whatever is not without a beginning cannot be without an end [Col. 0636B].

I therefore do not see how these propositions do not oppose one another, or how all things can be both eternal in the wisdom of God and made from nothing—that is, not exist before they were made.

Unless someone should perhaps say that the primordial causes of all things have always been eternal in the Father’s wisdom, while unformed matter, in which and through which they come forth by generation into their effects, into the genera and species with which the world is filled, is not eternal.

But whoever says this will be compelled to admit that matter was made from nothing and should not be counted causally among the eternal causes of things. If he grants this, it will necessarily be concluded and he will be forced to concede that not all things, but only some, are eternal in the Father’s wisdom.

Yet no one who philosophizes correctly would deny that unformed matter is numbered among all the things that God made in his wisdom. For I cannot see how anyone could say that the causes of all things were eternally created in the Word of God, while unformed matter lacked its own cause .

Therefore, if matter is included among the whole of created things, it necessarily follows that its cause is not excluded from the number of causes eternally created in the wisdom of God .

### MASTER

No one versed in sacred Scripture and considering the creation of natures by right reason doubts that unformed matter—which the Greeks call ὕλη (*hylē*, “matter”)—was created by the creator of all things both causally among causes and, according to its proportions, among the effects of causes [Col. 0636D].

For the one who made the world from unformed matter himself made unformed matter from absolute nothing. The author of the world made from unformed matter and the author of the matter first created from absolute nothing are not two different authors; the creator of both is one and the same, because all things that exist, whether unformed or formed, proceed from one principle.

The universe was created from one, just as all numbers emerge from the monad and all lines from the center [Col. 0637A].

Here especially the error of secular philosophers who dared to discuss the making of this world is exposed: they said that unformed matter was coeternal with God, and that God took the beginning of his works from it as though it subsisted outside him and were coeternal with him .

They considered it unworthy of God to make unformed matter. For, they ask, how could what is formless arise from the form of all things; what is varied and changeable from the immovable and in no way variable in itself; what is subject to various accidents from that to which nothing happens; what receives intervals of places, times, and quantities from that which is not extended through spaces of places and times?

Likewise, how could what is subject to no quality be receptive of diverse qualities and forms; how could what is corruptible arise from the incorruptible, and what is composite from the simple, and so forth? They were blinded by the clouds of their false reasoning [Col. 0637B].

But we, contemplating the truth of sacred Scripture and following the footsteps of its divine interpreters, believe by faith—and consider intellectually insofar as it is granted—that both the formlessness of all things and their forms, and everything in them, whether according to essence or according to accident, were created by one cause of all things.

### 6.

For the omnipotent creator of the universe, deficient in nothing and extending infinitely, was able to create—and did create—not only things like himself but also things unlike himself .

If he had created only things like himself—that is, things truly existing, eternal, immutable, simple, inseparably united, incorruptible, immortal, rational, intellectual, endowed with knowledge and wisdom, and with the other virtues—he would seem to have failed in creating things unlike and opposed to himself, and would not be judged the maker of absolutely everything that reason teaches can be made .

Everything that opposes the virtues mentioned above is called and is unlike and opposed to God—not as something negative or privative, but by dissimilarity and opposition of nature.

Thus, opposed to perfect essence, ordered uniformly according to genera and forms through differences and properties and arranged uniformly through its individual species, are the imperfection and mobility of still-formless matter ; opposed to eternal things are temporal things, to immutable things mutable things, to simple things composite things, and so forth—things that correspond to one another as if in diametrical opposition .

The one and same craftsman is therefore the maker of all these things, both like and unlike, and his omnipotence is deficient in the operation of no nature [Col. 0637D].

Accordingly, the beauty of the whole created universe, of things like and unlike, has been established in a marvelous harmony. It is compacted into an ineffable unity from diverse genera, various forms, and also differing orders of substances and accidents.

Just as an instrumental melody is composed of diverse qualities and quantities of sounds , which, when perceived individually and separately, are widely distinct and separated by differing proportions of tension and relaxation, but, when fitted together according to the definite and rational rules of musical art in their respective modes, produce a natural sweetness, so the harmony of the universe has been joined together according to the uniform will of the creator from the diverse subdivisions of one nature—subdivisions that, when examined individually, are discordant with one another [Col. 0638A].

Now that these matters have been defined, you are rightly, as you say, battered by the conflicting waves of thoughts opposed to one another .

For it has been established and firmly defined that all things that are and are not flow together from one principle of all things—whether in the primordial causes, made once and all together eternally in the only-begotten Word of God; whether in unformed matter, from which the primordial causes received, through generation, the occasions of the appearance of visible creation; or in their effects, through which this world is carried on from beginning to end in its natural order by divine providence .

As the Lord says: “My Father works until in me, and I work” [Col. 0638B; C reads “now” instead of “in me.”].

But how these apparently conflicting propositions come together in one bond of understanding—that is, how all things are simultaneously eternal and made—seems worthy of the most diligent investigation not only to you but also to me.

### 7. DISCIPLE

It is indeed worthy of investigation. For I think that those seeking truth have no higher question to pursue.

As we said earlier, things made are opposed to eternal things. Accordingly, if they are made, they are not eternal; if they are eternal, they are not made . I cannot see how it could be demonstrated that the same things are simultaneously eternal and made .

Therefore, as I judge, nothing remains except either to honor this matter with complete silence because of its excessive sublimity, or, if you think something about it should be investigated, to begin the investigation.

### MASTER

I think we should do both: we should not be reluctant to investigate it insofar as the vision of our contemplation, illuminated by God, is not driven back by the excessive radiance of its subtlety, lest we incur the blame of laziness or inactivity. But wherever it surpasses the power of our attention, and does not allow itself to be perceived and clearly distinguished by minds still weighed down by their earthly dwelling, it must be honored by the silence of heart and mouth, lest we rashly define anything concerning it [Col. 0638D].

### DISCIPLE

So be it. Without delay, take up the path of this investigation.

## 8. MAG. On the fact that all things are eternal in the only-begotten Word of God [Col. 0639A] [Note: C reads *sint*, “may be,” for *sunt*, “are.”], I judge that we must speak first. DISC. Nor do I wish otherwise. For reasoning must begin from what precedes. Eternity, however, precedes creation. From it, therefore, we must begin.

[Textual and editorial notes: At [Col. 0639], A reads *enim* (“for”) for *autem* (“however”); *eo* (“from him/it,” masculine or neuter) for *ea* (“from it,” feminine); and *itaque* (“therefore”) for *igitur* (“then”). At the statement that God created the universe [Col. 0639B], A reads *Dominus* (“the Lord”) for *Deus* (“God”). In “he always is, was, and will be a cause” [Col. 0639C], A reads *et causa* (“and [is] a cause”) for *causa et* (“a cause and”); at “the whole universe of creation,” A reads *igitur* (“therefore”) for *ergo* (“thus”). At [Col. 0639D], C omits “affirm that all things are eternal” (*aeterna perhibent*); and A omits the “and” in “live and move.” C omits the phrase “the prior principle of well-being … in him” from the discussion of movement in God. C also omits “nor were they then in him, nor will they be future” from the Trinitarian quotation [Col. 0640C]. In the account of things beneath and in the Word, A reads “and times” for “and also in places and times”; C reads *Qui deus nisi ea*—apparently, “What is God if not those things?”—for “and therefore he says”; and the textual note gives conjectural *constituta* (“constituted”), with A reading *constituta* and C *constitut.* [reading uncertain owing to abbreviation]. At [Col. 0640D], A reads *sicut* (“as”) for *Sanctus* (“Saint”), and *percogitata* for *praecogitata* (“pre-conceived” or “pre-thought”).

At [Col. 0641A], A reads *aliquod* (“any”) for *aliud aliquod* (“any other”), and *ac* (“and”) for *atque* (“and”); A omits “also” in “not only eternal but also the Word itself.” C reads *sunt* (“are”) for *esse* (“to be”) in “to be at once made and eternal”; A reads *aestimaret* (“should suppose”) for *existimaret* (“should think”); and C reads “And the Apostle” for “Likewise the Apostle.” At [Col. 0641B], A reads *homines* (“human beings”) for *habens* (“having”), *et non subsistentem* (“and non-subsisting”) for *ex non existente* (“from what did not exist”), and *et* (“and”) for the second *rationem* (“principle”) in “the principle of each.” At [Col. 0641C], A omits the “and” in “both to be and to remain,” reads *eo quod* (“because”) for *quod* (“that/because”), omits “about this,” and omits the “and” in “in God the Word and [at once] eternal.” At [Col. 0641D], A omits *sunt* (“are”) in “the same things are,” reads *vera* (“true”) for *qua* (“by what”), reads *et* (“and”) for *sunt* (“are”) in “eternal things are made,” and reads *et facta et aeterna* (“both made and eternal”) for *facta aeterna* (“made [things] eternal”); C reads *possumus* (“we can”) for *possimus* (“we may be able”).]

MAG. Be attentive, then, and see to it that you concede nothing rashly, lest you later regret having conceded it. DISC. Proceed; I am attentive, so that I may concede nothing heedlessly.

MAG. What do you think? Is God capable of accidents? DISC. Far be it from those who think soundly about the truth to say or think this. For his nature is simple, indeed more than simple, free from all accidents, indeed more than free from them.

MAG. Nothing, then, happens to God? DISC. Absolutely nothing.

MAG. Therefore, creating the universe is not an accident for him. Yet Holy Scripture does not keep silent about his having created it; rather, it openly proclaims this, saying: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” and the other things that are read among the works of the first six days.

DISC. God did establish the universe of creatures, and his having established it is not an accident for him.

MAG. Therefore, he did not subsist before he established the universe. For if he had, the establishment of things would have happened to him.

DISC. We believe that God precedes the universe, not in time, but solely in that respect in which he himself is understood to be the cause of all things. For if he preceded it in time, creating the universe would be an accident accruing to him according to time. Since, however, he precedes the universe established by him solely in the respect in which he is its cause, it follows that the establishment of the universe is not an accident in God, but exists according to a certain ineffable principle by which causal realities always subsist in their cause. [Col. 0639C]

MAG. If, then, God precedes the universe established by him in no other respect than that single respect in which he himself is its cause—and if those causal realities, and every causal reality, always subsist in their cause, since otherwise neither is a cause a cause nor is what is caused a caused thing—and if being causal is not an accident in God, for he always is, always was, and always will be a cause, then causal realities always subsist, have always subsisted, and will always subsist in their cause. Therefore the universe, since it is causal—that is, since it participates in its cause—is eternal in its cause. Thus it is manifest that the entire universe of creation is eternal in the Word of God.

DISC. I cannot contradict this conclusion when I consider, without any ambiguity, that all numbers subsist eternally and uniformly in the monad, and all lines in the center. Although, through the actual activity and work of counting and drawing lines, they are formed into various kinds and figures of numbers, they nevertheless always remain uniformly in their principles—I mean, in the monad and the center. Nor are those principles ever understood to have existed without them, nor to have begun to come into being in those principles themselves; and although they flow forth from them in manifold ways, they nevertheless do not cease to be in them, according to a uniform principle and in an eternal and unchangeable state.

MAG. You have used an example that is exceedingly similar and entirely true. The testimonies both of Holy Scripture and of the holy Fathers also affirm that all things are eternal in God. The Apostle says: “In him we live and move and are.” For we are in God through the excellent and pre-existent principle of our essence in him; we move in God according to the prior principle of well-being in him, through the virtues of good action. Moreover, we live in God according to the prior principle in him of always living and existing. And lest anyone should think that we are one thing and our principles another, he did not say, “in whom our principles live and move and are,” but said, “in whom we live and move and are.” For, insofar as we are, we are nothing other than our own principles, eternally established in God.

Likewise, Saint Augustine, explaining in his works the fourfold principle of divine operation, asserts that the second mode is eternal, not made, in the dispensation of the Word of God; and by this he wished to be understood not only the ages but also all the things through which the ages are brought about and fulfilled. He says:

> The divine operation that created and governs the ages is distinguished according to a fourfold principle. First, in the dispensation of the Word of God there are things that are not made but eternal; for, as the Apostle testifies, he predestined us before the times of the ages for the kingdom.

Again, writing elsewhere concerning the Trinity, he says:

> The Word of God, through whom all things were made, is the place in which all things live unchangeably—not only the things that have been, but also those that will be; nor were they then in him, nor will they be future, but they simply are. And all things are one, and he is more fully one.

Again, in the *Hexaemeron*, concerning God the Word, he says:

> In one way those things that were made through him are beneath him; in another way those things that he himself is are in him.

As though he were saying plainly: in one way they are beneath him, when, having been made through generation, they appear visibly in kinds and forms, and also in places and times, through matter; in another way they are in him, when they are understood eternally in the primordial causes of things, which are not only in God but are also God. And therefore he says, “those things that he himself is”—not because the things that are understood to be in God and to be God on account of the unity of nature are one set, while those that enter the world through generation are another, but because one and the same nature of things is considered in one way in the eternity of the Word of God and in another way in the temporality in which the world has been constituted. [Col. 0640D]

Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, also speaking in the chapter concerning the perfect and one God, says:

> It is called “one” because it is all things universally; for there is no existing thing that does not participate in the one.

And shortly afterward:

> Therefore this too must be understood: because the pre-conceived form of each thing is according to the one, what has been united is said to be made one; and there is one exemplar of all things. If you remove the one, neither the universe nor any other existing thing will exist; for it goes before and encompasses all things in itself, uniformly as one.

When these and similar examples and testimonies are gathered together into one, it is made abundantly clear that all things in the Word of God are not only eternal but are also the Word itself. Since, however, Holy Scripture declares with complete clarity through its testimonies that all things are at once made and eternal in the Word of God, John the Evangelist says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Behold, he says most plainly that all things were made in the Word.

But lest anyone should suppose that they were made only and were not eternal, he continues: “What was made in him was life.” It is as though he had said: what was made—whether in the primordial causes or in the effects proceeding from them—in him, the Word in whom the principles of all things are eternal, was life.

Likewise the Apostle says: “In him all things were created, things in heaven and things on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers; all things were created from him and through him and in him.” [Col. 0641B]

For, as blessed Maximus says, possessing before the ages, in his good will, the pre-established causes of the things that were made, according to those causes he established the visible and invisible creature from what did not exist; by reason and wisdom, at the appropriate time, he both made and makes all things that exist universally and all things that exist individually—believing that, in creating the cause of the angels, he brought forth the cause of each of the essences and powers that complete the world above us; and the principle of human beings, the principle of each of those who receive their being from God—recapitulating all things into himself, that is, bringing them to completion—through whom the things that have been generated participate in God, both in order to be and to remain, and from whom they have been generated, insofar as they have been generated, and toward whom they have been generated, whether they remain or move.

For all things participate proportionally in the Lord, inasmuch as they were made from God: whether through intellect, reason, sense, vital movement, or essential existence and acquired fitness, as it seems to the great and divine revealer Dionysius the Areopagite.

Therefore no one who faithfully and piously investigates Holy Scripture ought to doubt that all things in God the Word are simultaneously eternal and made. For true reason and the authority of Holy Scripture unanimously agree on this: the things that are eternal are not one set and the things that are made another, but the same things are simultaneously eternal and made.

You rightly demand that I explain by what principle eternal things are made and made things are eternal, so that we may understand it. For it seems to you that the very same thing’s subsisting as eternal and as made is not compatible with true reason, and perhaps I myself do not yet discern clearly how this can be compatible.

DISC. Begin, then, to inquire into and disclose whatever can be said about this question. [Col. 0642A]

## 9. TEACHER

I judge that the reasons of all things, insofar as they are understood in the very nature of the Word, which is beyond essence, are eternal. For whatever exists substantially in God the Word, since it is nothing other than the Word itself, must necessarily be eternal. Consequently, it follows that both the Word itself and the principal and most fundamental reason of the whole created universe are one and the same.

We may also put it this way: God the Word is the one and manifold principal reason of all things. For among the Greeks he is called λόγος (*logos*), that is, “word,” “reason,” or “cause.” Hence what is written in the Greek Gospel, Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, may be translated: “In the beginning was the Word,” or “In the beginning was Reason,” or “In the beginning was the Cause.” [Col. 0641: A reads “has been written” for “is written.”] Whoever says any one of these will not depart from the truth. [Col. 0641: C reads *ex* (“from/out of”) for *a* (“from”).] For the only-begotten Son of God is Word, Reason, and Cause.

He is Word because through him God the Father said that all things should come to be; indeed, he himself is the Father’s speaking, utterance, and discourse, just as he says in the Gospel: “The word which I have spoken to you is not mine, but his who sent me.” [Col. 0641: A omits “is”; A reads “the discourse is.”] As though he were saying openly: “I, who am the Father’s discourse and who have spoken to you, am not mine, but belong to the Father who speaks in me, and who begets me from the hidden recesses of his substance—A omits “from”—and who makes all things through me—that is, by begetting me.”

He is Reason because he himself is the primordial exemplar of all visible and invisible things, and therefore is called by the Greeks ἰδέα (*idea*), that is, “species” or “form.” For in him the Father saw, before they came to be, all the things he willed to be made.

He is also Cause because the reasons of all things subsist eternally and unchangeably in him. Since, therefore, the Son of God is Word, Reason, and Cause, it is not inappropriate to say that God the Word is the simple and, in himself, infinitely manifold creative reason and cause of the created universe. [Col. 0641: C omits “God’s Word.”] Thus the statement may be repeated: God’s Word is the simple and, in himself, infinitely manifold creative reason and cause of the created universe. [Col. 0641: C omits the whole clause beginning “and thus it would recur”; the text reads “and cause.”]

He is simple because the whole universe of things is one undivided and inseparable whole in him; or rather, God’s Word is the undivided and inseparable unity of all things, since he himself is all things. He is rightly understood to be manifold because he is diffused infinitely throughout all things—A reads “is defined”—and this very diffusion is the subsistence of all things.

For he reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly. [Col. 0641: A omits “to.”] Likewise in the Psalm: “His word runs swiftly.” [Col. 0641: A reads “he said” instead of “he says.”] The Prophet calls the Father’s Word “discourse”; it runs swiftly through all things so that all things may be. For its course through all things is the manifold and infinite subsistence of all things.

Hence Saint Dionysius, in the chapter “On the Perfect and the One,” says:
