> The perfect is not only that which is perfect in itself, according to itself, uniformly separated from itself, whole throughout the whole, and most perfect; it is also more than perfect, according to the excellence of all things, terminating every multitude—A reads “determining” it—and extending beyond every summit, situated or comprehended by none, but stretched out simultaneously into all things and above all things through unfailing increases and infinite activities. [Col. 0643.]

> It is again called perfect as though it were not increased, always perfect, and undiminished: as surpassing and overflowing all things in itself according to one uninterrupted, self-sufficient, superabundant, and undiminished generosity.

> It therefore remains universally and simply in itself, because all things are one in it. Yet—A reads “therefore”—it reaches from end to end and runs swiftly through all things—that is, without delay it makes all things—and it becomes all things in all things. [Col. 0643: C reads “it made all things” in both places where the text has “it makes” and “it becomes.”] While it subsists in itself as one perfect and more-than-perfect reality, separated from all things, it extends itself into all things, and this extension is all things.

This also seems to be signified by the name of the heavenly essence, which is “Cherubim.” For, as the wise men among the Hebrews have handed down, *Cherubim* is interpreted as “the diffusion of wisdom.”

Here it must be understood with the utmost subtlety that, whenever the diffusion, extension, course, or any other such expression is used for the infinite multiplication of the Word, this does not mean that the Word and wisdom of the Father were diffused, extended, or ran through things that already existed. Rather, the Word’s diffusion, extension, and course precede all things, are the cause of the existence of all things, and are all things.

For who, consulting the truth, would believe or think that God prepared places for himself through which he might diffuse himself, when he is contained by no place and is the common place of all things? Thus the place of places is contained by no place. Or who would believe that he prepared spatial or temporal expanses through which he might extend himself or run in his course, when he is without every expanse and surpasses all times by his eternity? [Col. 0643: A reads “because” instead of “who.”] Or who would say—and this is still more incredible, while A reads “or more credible”—that expanses of places and times, or intervals of quantities of any kind, were prepared for God by another, as though by some prior principle, so that he might fill them by his diffusion, traverse them by his course, or solidify them by his extension?

For concerning an ineffable and transcendent nature, it is not only ridiculous and most perilous to say such things; it is also ridiculous and most perilous even to think them and to fashion them through false imaginings. [Col. 0643: A reads *atque* (“and also”) for *et* (“and”), and “most dangerous” for “most perilous.”] There is no more shameful or worse death for the rational soul than to think such monstrous and detestable idols concerning the Creator of all things, when truth itself, with an intelligible voice, proclaims generally to the minds of those who piously seek and diligently pursue their Creator that, among all things that are and that are not—that is, among things capable of being grasped by sense or intellect and things that surpass sense or intellect, whose being consists in being without every comprehensible essence—nothing else subsists except participation in the one sole Cause of all. [Col. 0643: A reads “and” for “or.”]

Whatever is participated in precedes both its own participation and those who participate in it. [Col. 0643: C omits “participation and.”] God, therefore, precedes all things that participate in him and whose essence is his participation.

Hence the great Dionysius the Areopagite says in the fourth chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, that is, of the episcopate:

> First of all, it is true to say this: by universal goodness, the transcendent Divinity, establishing the essences of things that are, brought them into being. For this is proper to the Cause of all and to the goodness that transcends all: to call existing things into communion with itself, so that each of the things that are is defined according to its proper analogy.

All things, therefore, participate in the providence flowing from the transcendent and most causative Divinity. For perhaps they would not exist except through the assumption of the essences and principle of existing things. All existing things, therefore, participate in being. For being belongs to all things, but super-being belongs to the Divinity. [Col. 0643: C has this reading; A reads “the being of the Divinity.”]

Living things participate in the same life-giving power that transcends all life; rational and intellectual things participate in the same wisdom, perfect in itself and prior to perfection, which transcends every reason and intellect. [Col. 0643: C reads “rational” rather than “rational and intellectual.”]

You have heard the opinion of the supreme theologian, Dionysius the Areopagite, most illustrious bishop of Athens, concerning participation in the divine essence. He makes it entirely clear that all things that are and that are not are to be understood as nothing other than participation in the divine essence, and that participation itself is nothing other than assumption of that same essence. [Col. 0643: A omits the clause beginning “participation itself.”] For he says: “Perhaps they would not exist except through the assumption of the essences and principle of existing things.” Participation in the divine essence is therefore assumption of that essence.

This assumption is the diffusion of that divine Wisdom, which is the substance and essence of all things and of whatever is naturally understood in them. [Col. 0643: A reads “is the diffusion of divine Wisdom.”]

Hear also what the same author says, in a letter he wrote in reply to the pontiff Titus, who had asked what the house of Wisdom was, what its mixing-bowl was, and what its foods and drink were. He says:

> Divine Wisdom sets before us a twofold food: one solid and edible, the other liquid and poured out. In the mixing-bowl it providently offers its good gifts.

Since this mixing-bowl—A reads *ipsius*—is round and wide-mouthed, it is a symbol of the providence of all these things, simultaneously expanded into all things and circulating through all things, without beginning and infinite. [Col. 0643: C omits “of all these things.”] Nevertheless, because it proceeds into all things while remaining in itself, standing according to the unchanging likeness of its nature, perfectly and irrevocably placed in itself, uniformly and firmly, the mixing-bowl stands. [Col. 0643: C reads “so that” for “thus.”]

Wisdom is said to build a house for itself, and in it to set forth solid foods, drinks, and a mixing-bowl. Thus, for those who make divine things into symbols divinely, it is clear that providence itself is the most perfect causal principle of the being and well-being of all things; it proceeds into all things, becomes in all things, and contains all things. Yet again—C reads “for it will be”—in its transcendence, it is in itself no thing in no thing through no thing; rather, it is exalted above all things, existing, standing, and remaining similarly and eternally in itself, always according to the same conditions, and in this manner. It has in no way become external to itself, nor has it abandoned its own gravity, unchangeable abiding, and goodness—A reads “confined” instead of “abandoned”—but, remaining in itself, it works all its complete and perfect providences most excellently; it proceeds into all things, remains in itself, and stands forever while moving. [Col. 0645.]

Observe what he says: “It proceeds into all things and becomes in all things.” He explains this elsewhere, saying:

> We must dare to say this also concerning the truth: the cause of all things, by its good and best love for all things, through the excellence of loving goodness, itself goes outside itself into all things that are by its providences. As though in goodness, affection, and love, it cherishes and surpasses all things; removed from all things, it is nevertheless brought forth into all things according to its mind-transcending, transcendent, and irreversible power. [Col. 0645: A reads “removed” for “remote,” and “even further” for “to this.” A omits “it is brought forth.”]

The opinion of the same Dionysius also supports this. He took it from the theological commentaries—C reads “writings” instead—of the most holy Hierotheus—A reads “most learned” instead:

> The divinity of Jesus, the cause of all and the source of fullness, preserves parts consonant with the universe; and—it is omitted by A—it is neither part nor whole, yet it is both whole and part, gathering together and surpassing in itself every whole and part. It is perfect in imperfect things as their principal perfection; yet it is imperfect in perfect things as more-than-perfect—A omits “more-than”—and it is the prior-perfect form that gives form to the formless as principal form. [Col. 0645.]

> It is formless in forms as superform; it is the undefiled essence of the whole essence, transcending it, and transcendentally removed from every essence. It establishes all principles and orders and is placed above every principle and order—C reads “placed above” in a different form. It is the abiding of things that are, and of the ages; it is above the ages and before the ages, full in those who lack, superfull in multitudes, hidden and ineffable, above soul, above life, and above essence. It has the supernatural supernaturally, and the superessential superessentially.

These statements, I think, are sufficient for those who understand rightly to recognize that the abiding of divine goodness in itself is the unchangeable cause of all things. [Col. 0645: A omits “in itself.”] Its procession, however, and ineffable motion accomplish the effect of all things; while its participation and assumption are nothing other than the essence of all things. [Col. 0645: A reads “the effect of all things” rather than “all things’ effect.”]

Consider carefully what he says: “Providence itself is the causal principle of the being and well-being of all things.” [The source reads *omnium*; A reads “he himself is.”] Therefore providence over all things is not one thing and the cause of all things another—C omits “of all things”—rather, the one and same God is both the most perfect providence over all things and the causal principle of the being and well-being of all things.

What follows—“and it proceeds into all things and becomes in all things”—that is, in the universe which it makes and contains all things, is so powerful for solving the difficulty of the present question that, in my judgment, it cannot be resolved by any other exercise of reason.

For if he who is the causal principle of the being and well-being of all things—A adds “and of being”—proceeds into all things, becomes in every creature, and contains all things, what else remains except that we understand the Wisdom of God the Father, of whom such things are predicated, both to be the creative cause of all things and to be created and made in all things that he creates, and to contain all things in which he is created and made?

For whatever is truly understood to exist in all things is nothing other than the manifold power of creative Wisdom, which subsists in all things. If you remove creative Wisdom by intellect from all the things she creates, they will be reduced entirely to nothing: no essence, no life, no sense, no reason, no intellect, and no good whatsoever will remain.

This too Saint Father Augustine—A omits “Father”—seems to understand in his books of the *Confessions*—A has “in the book”—addressing his discourse to truth itself, namely, divine Wisdom—A reads *scilicet* (“of course”) for *videlicet* (“namely”):

> I looked upon the other things within you, and I saw that they neither altogether are nor altogether are not. They neither altogether are, because they are not what you are; nor altogether are not, because they are from you.

[Col. 0645: A omits “nor altogether are not.”] By these words he intimates that every creature, considered entirely in itself, is nothing. Whatever is understood to subsist in it subsists through participation in creative Truth.

For if every true thing is true from Truth—A omits the second “true”—and Truth alone remains while all other things are in motion, then Truth alone subsists in all true things. I said that they are in motion because they do not subsist through themselves but tend toward nothingness. Yet they are prevented from falling into nothingness and are sustained by the power of provident Truth, which subsists in them—A omits “and are sustained.”

If, therefore, the Word of God both makes all things and becomes in all things—and this can be confirmed from the words quoted above from Father Dionysius and others—why should it be surprising if all things understood to subsist in the Word itself are believed and known to be simultaneously eternal and made?

For what is predicated of the cause, why could it not also be predicated of the things caused? [The source has *possint*; A has the singular *possit*.] I find no reason. All things, therefore, may properly be called simultaneously eternal and made, since the very Wisdom that makes them comes to be in them, and the cause in which and through which they are both eternal and made is itself eternal and made in them.

## DISCIPLE

I am greatly astonished, and, stunned as though lifeless, I remain fixed here. These arguments draw me to themselves because they are plausible and strengthened by the testimonies of the holy Fathers and by Sacred Scripture. Yet again I am drawn back in uncertainty and immediately relapse into the densest darkness of my thoughts—A reads “cognitions” instead. For my mind’s vision is wholly incapable of looking into and penetrating the depth of the present question. [Col. 0645: C omits “is.”]

When I hear the words—C reads “he says” for “indeed, hearing”— “You made the world from formless matter,” I could think of it in no other way than that the visible and invisible world is said to have been made from formless matter, which God created from absolute nothingness, as a kind of beginning of his work; and that there was a time when the whole universe did not exist.

Accordingly, at the beginning of its creation it proceeded from absolute nothingness into formless matter, and thereafter, through genera, forms, and the other natural numbers, it reached a certain perfection known only to the Creator. [Col. 0647: C reads “to reach” rather than “it reached.”] Nor was this accomplished through intervals of time, as Saint Father Augustine teaches in his *Hexaemeron*. For formlessness does not precede form in time, but in the natural order by which the cause precedes the effect. Certainly, voice and word proceed simultaneously from the mouth of the speaker; nevertheless voice precedes word—not in time—C reads “of times”—but in cause. For the word is produced from the voice, whereas the voice cannot in any way be produced from the word.

Thus the formlessness, formation, and perfection of all things were brought from nothing into essence by the Creator’s will, distinctly yet simultaneously and all at once, through a certain natural priority and sequence—not through intervals of time. [Col. 0647: A reads “and” for “and also,” “procession” rather than “priority,” and “in time” rather than “of time.”] This was my faith and my very limited understanding.

But now I hear from you something different, and it moves me greatly, forcibly recalling me from what I had firmly held until now, as it seemed to me. For the present reasoning appears to want to persuade us of nothing other than this: that the things I thought had been made from nothing, and in no way eternal—for, as I supposed, there was a time when they did not exist, and therefore they had received what they had not possessed—are simultaneously eternal and made.

I consider this very contradictory. And rightly so, for these things seem to oppose one another: things made to the eternal, and the eternal to things made. [Col. 0647: C reads “for these things, namely” in a different order.]

Things that are eternal never begin to be and never cease to subsist; there was no time when they did not exist, because they always existed. [Col. 0647: A adds “and.”] Things that are made, however, have received the beginning of their making. They began to be, because there was a time when they did not exist; and they will cease to be, because they began to possess being. [Col. 0647: C reads *quod* (“that”) for *quia* (“because”).]

Indeed, if true reason is consulted, everything that begins to exist temporally is not permitted to remain forever. It must necessarily tend toward an end, where that which begins to exist in time is compelled to perish.

Let no one suppose that I mean to advocate the return to nothingness of those things which come to be temporally in the world from matter through generation; for that would be the greatest evil. I mean their dissolution into the things from which they are composed and in which they subsist.

Human bodies and the bodies of other animals, when they are dissolved, are said to perish; nevertheless they are not reduced to nothing, but return to the catholic elements. [Col. 0647: A reads “the elements return.”] This is generally understood of the whole universe of this visible world.

And not without reason. Since it received a beginning of being, it will inevitably receive an end of its essence. For just as there was a time when it did not exist, so there will be a time when it will not exist, as the Psalmist testifies, proclaiming the eternal Creator of things. [Col. 0647: Corrected text; A reads “and proclaiming the eternal Creator”; C reads “proclaiming the eternal Creator.”]

> The heavens are the works of your hands; they will perish, but you will remain. They will all grow old like a garment; you will change them like clothing, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail.

The Creator of all things himself also says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” [Col. 0647: C omits “he says.”]

If that part of the world which possesses the greatest expanse, the most beautiful sublimity of the stars, and the purest subtlety of nature—C omits “and”; planted with the fixed stars, harmonious—A reads the alternate form *harmonici*—in the course of the planets, and always full of light—is destined to perish according to Scripture, should we suppose that its inner and much lower parts will remain?

It is impossible for the lower things not to perish when the better things perish; and when that which contains something is taken away, true reason does not permit what is contained to remain.

We say this to distinguish eternal things from things that are made. [Col. 0647: A reads “things that have been made.”] The distance between things that neither begin to be nor cease to be and things that begin to be and cannot remain forever is not small. [Col. 0647: A reads “remain” rather than “remain forever.”]

It is therefore not without cause that the mind’s vision of those who understand such matters less clearly is thrown back when it is persuaded that eternal things are made and made things are eternal. For I would not readily believe that you agree with those who wish to understand that many, indeed almost all, of the things that have been made will always remain, and therefore will be eternal. [Col. 0647: A reads “will remain” rather than “will always remain.”]

For example, this universe, which consists of heaven and earth gathered together with the four elements into the form of a completed sphere and commonly called “the world,” was made from nothing, as they say, and will remain eternally, except for certain of its parts—that is, corruptible bodies subject to generation and corruption—which they cannot deny will perish. Heaven, however, with its stars, they maintain will always exist, whether it continues to revolve or ceases to move.

Their opinions differ on this point. Some assert that the future state of mutable things will be one of rest; others maintain that the natural motion of the elements will never cease. The former follow what is written, “All things will be at rest,” understanding this of the state of mutable things. The latter take the words, “Who will make the harmony of heaven sleep?” to refer to the eternal motion of mutable things.

For how could the heavenly harmony resound without the motion of the ethereal sphere and of all the stars, since music is always in motion, just as geometry is in rest?

They also confidently maintain that the earthly mass will always retain its own proper quantity, following what is written: “One generation comes and another generation goes, but the earth stands forever.” [Col. 0647: A reads “as an example” rather than “except.”] They except only that its surface will be leveled everywhere, so that it will become more beautiful than it is now and, renewed as though by a new equality of its parts, its present quantity will not perish but will remain, changed for the better and retaining its equality.

They wish this also to be understood of heaven: namely, that its beauty, which now delights the bodily senses, will be increased at the end of the world without the destruction of its spherical form or starry design, because, as they say, it is written: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth.” [Col. 0649: C reads “so that it will be increased at the end of the world.”]

They understand “the heavens will perish” not of the higher regions of the world, but of the spaces of air beneath the moon, so that, just as they were changed into water in the Flood, at the end of the world they will be changed into flame. [Col. 0649: A omits “into”; A reads “they will be changed.”]

They not only do not deny but affirm that the generation, growth, and decline of all animals, plants, and trees contained within the circle of the moon will cease to alternate. [Col. 0649: A omits the entire clause beginning “the generation of all animals.”] They likewise think that the expanses of air and ether will be assigned: the ether to the eternal possession of the blessed angels and of human beings like them; the lower air, diffused everywhere around the earth, to an eternal prison and eternal flames, visibly and locally burning, in which the devil will be tormented with his members—that is, with apostate angels and impious human beings like himself.

Since they conceive every local and temporal creature, both present and future, as destined to exist, they do not doubt that places and times—that is, the world’s expanses and its motion, distinguished by intervals of duration—will always remain. [Col. 0649: C omits “since.”]

By these and similar false opinions they attempt to assert that things which did not exist, began to exist, and are therefore made, can nevertheless be called both made and eternal, because they will always remain in the same state in which they were created temporally. They suppose that things which do not lack a beginning will also lack an end, so that they are both made, because they began to exist, and eternal, because they will not cease to subsist.

Nevertheless, I would judge neither that you assent to such opinions, which true reason ridicules, nor that you have argued for such an eternity—or, more accurately, a semi-eternity—through the arguments you have given, nor that you have taught that things are simultaneously made and eternal in this manner. Rather, I perceive that, through a deeper contemplation of natures, beyond human opinions, and in a manner still unknown to us, you are entering the innermost chambers of divine mysteries, following more deeply the footsteps of the Fathers who investigated such matters.

## 10.

For they say that the nature of this world will always remain because it is incorporeal and incorruptible, while the other things of which it consists will perish—that is, everything in it that is composite. Since there is no body in it that is not composite—C omits the preceding clause from “composite” through “is”—and every composite thing will be dissolved into the things of which it is composed, this entire visible, corporeal, composite world will therefore be dissolved, while the simple nature alone remains.

## TEACHER

I cannot deny that I was once deceived by the false reasonings of human opinions, which are far removed from the truth, because I was deceived. In all these matters, or nearly all of them, I gave my assent while still inexperienced, seduced, as often happens, by a certain likeness of truth and by carnal senses.

But now, following the footsteps of the holy Fathers, as a ray of divine light recalls me from my errors and those of others and leads me into the right way, I draw back my foot a little. For divine mercy does not permit those who piously and humbly seek the truth to wander in the darkness of ignorance, fall into the pits of false opinions, and perish in them.

There is no worse death than ignorance of the truth, and no deeper abyss than to approve falsehoods as truths, which is the characteristic of error. From such things, the most shameful and detestable monsters are usually fashioned in human thoughts. [Col. 0649: A reverses the order to “truly turning.”] When the carnal soul loves and follows them as though they were true, turning its back upon the light and trying, without being able, to grasp fleeting shadows, it is accustomed to fall into the pit of misery.

For this reason we must pray continually and say:

> God, our salvation and redemption, who have given nature, grant grace also. Extend your light over those who grope—A reads “feel about”—in the shadows of ignorance and seek you. Recall us from our errors. Stretch out your right hand to the weak, who cannot reach you without you. [Col. 0649: C reads “without you” in the reverse order.] Show yourself to those who ask for nothing except you. Break apart the clouds of empty fantasies, which do not permit the mind’s vision to behold you in the manner in which you, though invisible, permit yourself to be seen by those who desire to behold your face, their rest and their end, beyond which they desire nothing, because beyond it there is nothing: the supreme transcendent Good.

But direct your steps toward the remainder of your statement.

## DISCIPLE

What remains except to bring forward what greatly troubles me: how all things are eternal and made, and how things without beginning and end are bounded by a beginning and an end? These matters struggle against one another, and unless you persuade me how they can agree, I do not know how they can do so.

For I had thought that only—A omits “only”—God was ἄναρχος (*anarchos*), that is, without a beginning. He himself is the beginning and end of all things, beginning from no beginning and enclosed by no end. All other things, however, begin and each tends toward its own proper end; consequently, they are not eternal but made. [Col. 0649: A reads “are begun” rather than “begin”; A and C omit “to be,” supplied here from the reading.]

And incomparably higher and more wondrous than all these matters is what you assert, using the authority of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite: namely, that God himself is both the maker of all things and made in all things. [Col. 0649: A omits “the Areopagite.”] This is still unheard-of and unknown not only to me but also to many, indeed almost everyone.

For if this is so, who would not immediately burst into this cry and proclaim: “God, then, is all things, and all things are God!” This will be judged monstrous even by those who are thought to be wise, when they consider the manifold variety of visible and invisible things, whereas God is one.

Unless you persuade me of these matters through examples comprehensible to the mind, nothing remains except that they be left aside as merely raised but not discussed—A reads “transformed”—and this cannot happen without pain to my mind.

Those who are established in the thickest darkness and hope for the rising of the light to come are not entirely overcome by sorrow. [Col. 0651: A omits “to come.”] But if the light they hope for is taken away from them—A places “which they hope for” after “from them”—they remain not only in darkness but also in great suffering, deprived of the good they had hoped for. Or else everything you have said concerning these matters will be judged entirely false by those who understand less, and, despising these teachings, they will relapse into their former opinions, which they are still unwilling to abandon, as though they were true.

Therefore the path of reasoning must begin with natural examples, against which no one resists unless blinded by excessive stupidity.

11. MASTER. Are you skilled in the art of arithmetic?

STUDENT. Skilled, if I am not mistaken; for I learned it from my childhood. [Note: In A, *mea* (“my”) is omitted.]

MASTER. Define it, then, plainly and briefly.

[Col. 0651B]

STUDENT. Arithmetic is the science of numbers—not of the numbers which we count, but of those according to which we count.

MASTER. You have defined arithmetic carefully and attentively. [Note: C has this wording; A reads, “You have defined arithmetic as the science of numbers.”] For if you had simply defined arithmetic as the science of numbers, you would have included all numbers generally, and thus the definition would not stand. That art does not discuss every kind of number, but considers only those numbers which it knows to exist solely in knowledge and understanding, and according to which the other kinds of numbers are counted. For the wise do not say that the numbers of animals, shrubs, plants, and other bodies or things belong to the science of arithmetic; [Note: C reads *fructuum*, “of fruits,” rather than *fruticum*, “of shrubs.”] rather, they assign to arithmetic only intellectual, invisible, incorporeal numbers, existing solely in knowledge and not substantially placed in any other subject. [Note: A reads *Nam*, “For,” rather than *Si quidem*, “Indeed.” A also omits *praeterea*, “besides” or “further.”]

[Col. 0651C]

Indeed, they are not perceived in knowledge, understanding, reason, memory, the senses, or figures in such a way that they themselves are substantially one with those in which they are seen. For they possess their own substance. [Note: *seipsos* (“themselves”) is omitted in A.] If they were of the same substance, knowledge, understanding, and reason would judge about them, not according to them. But an art and its judge cannot be the same thing. This is rightly said of God the Word alone, who is both the judge and the art of his Father.

Thus, as I said, you carefully added: “not the numbers which we count, but those according to which we count.” We do not perceive these in any corporeal or incorporeal subject; rather, beyond every subject, they are discerned by understanding alone in wisdom and knowledge, released by the excellence of their divine nature from all things that are counted according to them.

[Col. 0651D]

STUDENT. I have often considered these matters and, as I believe, perceived them clearly.

MASTER. Is that art, then, natural?

STUDENT. Yes—and none is more natural. For it is not only the immovable foundation and primordial cause and principle of the three subsequent parts of mathematics, namely geometry, music, and astrology, but also the immeasurable multitude of all visible and invisible things receives its substance according to the rules of numbers contemplated by arithmetic. [Col. 0652A] This is attested by Pythagoras, the foremost philosopher and first discoverer of the art, who asserts with firm arguments that intellectual numbers are the substances of all visible and invisible things. Sacred Scripture, too, does not deny this, for it says that all things were made in measure, number, and weight. [Note: A reads “in weight and number.”]

MASTER. Therefore, if you seek natural examples of the aforesaid art—or rather, of the nature and rules of the numbers which it comprehends—examine them carefully, so that, with God as your guide, you may arrive at knowledge of those things which seem to you to conflict with and oppose one another. [Note: The reading is so in A and C; perhaps the text originally read *videbantur*, “seemed.”]

STUDENT. I gladly accept examples from arithmetic. For it neither deceives nor is deceived. Although those who understand less are often deceived in it, [Note: A reads *falluntur*, “are deceived,” rather than *fallantur*, “are deceived” in the passive subjunctive.] this must be judged not the fault of the art, but the dullness of those who handle it carelessly.

MASTER. You do not doubt, I suppose, that the monad is the principle of the numbers whose science is arithmetic.

STUDENT. Whoever hesitates about this is not an arithmetician. The monad—that is, unity—is the beginning, middle, and end of all numbers, and the whole, part, and every quantity of all terms.

MASTER. Tell me, then: are all the numbers which reason can multiply as much as it wishes causally and eternally in the monad?

STUDENT. Right reason teaches no differently. They are in it as their cause, because it is the abiding principle of all numbers. There all are one—indivisibly, simply, that is, universally—and multiplicity exists there by reason alone, not in actuality or operation. [Note: A omits *unum*, “one,” in this clause.] They are not one heaped together from many, but one endowed with its own simple and manifold singularity. [Note: A reads *sua et simplici*, “its own and simple,” rather than *sua simplici*, “its own simple.”] Thus all numbers are simultaneously and simply in it according to their cause, while it itself is understood substantially in all of them through an ineffable distribution of multiplicity.

For it is the cause and substance of all numbers; and while it does not abandon the unchanging state of its nature, it diffuses itself manifoldly into all things. They subsist eternally in it because they do not begin to exist in it temporally. [Note: A omits *non*, “not,” in “they do not begin to exist temporally in it,” and reads *carens, in quibus subsistunt*, “lacking, in which they subsist.”] For unity was not without the manifold rational structures in which they subsist.

[Col. 0652C]

But who among those who understand purely would say that the monad began, knowing that it extends toward infinity? How can an infinite progression proceed from a finite beginning? The infinite proceeds from the infinite; from the finite nothing infinite proceeds.

If someone asks how this can stand, since even among numbers we see many infinites beginning from finite numbers—for from the binary, which is a finite number, all doubles arise and extend to infinity; similarly, from the finite ternary all triples take their beginning and do not know the end of their multiplication; and, to speak briefly, there is no number finite in its own quantities, or merely in its monads, from which some multiplicity does not flow forth to infinity—the answer must be that all these numbers, finite in their parts, from which multiples proceed to infinity, are infinite in the monad, where all are one.

Therefore one must either deny that all numbers are in the monad and affirm that they are finite in their multiplications outside it, or, if reason resists such an assertion, one must necessarily admit that all numbers, finite in their parts, subsist infinitely and uniformly eternally in the monad. [Note: C omits *est* (“is”) in “the answer must be”; A omits *omnes* (“all”) and also omits *et* (“and”) after “subsist infinitely.”]

For water does not begin to exist where a spring appears; rather, it flows from elsewhere through hidden pores, imperceptible and infinite, long before it appears in the spring. [Note: A reads, “For where the spring appears, water does not begin to exist.”] Thus, although a spring is improperly said to be where it first visibly rises, it existed long before in the hidden places of the earth, the ocean, or elsewhere, where it lay invisibly concealed. [Note: C omits *sive alibi*, “or elsewhere.”] Indeed, *latex*, “water,” is so called from *latere*, “to lie hidden,” in the veins of the earth.

Likewise, numbers, whose multiplication, like other proportions, flows into infinity, derive their origin not from the finite numbers that first appear to the observing mind, but from the eternal and infinite rational structures in which they subsist causally. [Note: A reads *sive*, “or,” rather than *sicut*, “like.”]

They are in the monad; therefore they are infinite in the monad, from which the infinite course of all numbers proceeds and into which it comes to an end.

[Col. 0653B]

And, to use an even stronger argument, since we affirm that unity never began, consider this carefully. If unity—which the Greeks call *monas*, “monad”—is the beginning, middle, and end of all numbers—for they proceed from it, move through it, seek it, and end in it, and no wise person doubts that this is so—then there is not one unity from which numbers flow and through which they move, and another which they seek and in which they end, but one and the same, since it is beginning, middle, and end. Therefore numbers, proceeding from their beginning, proceed from nowhere other than their end. For their beginning is not one thing and their end another, but one and the same unity. Consequently, it necessarily follows that, if they extend their end to infinity, they begin to extend from an infinite beginning. The end of all numbers is the same unity, which is infinite; therefore it is the infinite beginning of all numbers.

And if all numbers subsist eternally and incommunicably in their beginning, they must also subsist eternally and incommunicably in their end. Just as there will be no end without things coming to an end in it, so there was no beginning without things beginning from it in actuality and operation of understanding. [Note: A reads “to proceed eternally from understanding.”]

[Col. 0653D]

All numbers, therefore, subsist eternally in the monad; and while they flow from it, they do not cease to be in it, because they cannot abandon their natural state. For whether they are multiplied or resolved, they come from it and return to it according to the rules of the discipline that contemplates their rational structures. [Note: A reads *multiplicantur*, “are multiplied,” rather than *multiplicentur*, “are multiplied.”]

If this is so, no one but an impudent person will deny that eternal numbers subsist in unity according to their rational structures; and anyone who examines the matter attentively will not doubt that the rational structures themselves are everlasting. [Note: A reads *perspexerit*, “has clearly perceived,” rather than *inspexerit*, “has examined.”]

MASTER. I see that you are not ignorant of the discipline of arithmetic. Whatever you have so far said about it, right reason declares and confirms to be true and to be so in no other way. But, so that you may teach more firmly the eternity of numbers in the monad, explain briefly and plainly the rational structures which you assert to be eternal and unchanging. [Note: A reads “innumerable” rather than “eternal.”]

STUDENT. The first progression of numbers is from the monad. The beginning of multiplication is the Greek δυάς (*dyas*), that is, the binary; the second is the Greek τριάς (*trias*), the ternary; the third is the Greek τέτρας (*tetras*), the quaternary; and thereafter all the terms are established in their proper places. [Note: The correction is adopted; A has “the same.”]

The binary is the source of all evenness that falls under understanding, while the ternary is the source of oddness. From these—by evenness and oddness—all kinds of numbers are generated, whether they are simple or composite.

The simple kinds are even and odd; the composite kinds, constituted from these two, are even-even, even-odd, and odd-odd. [Note: C reads “odd-even.”]

Do you see how impossible it is for this order of the progression of numbers to be otherwise or to move in another way? No other number established according to the natural order occupies the place of the first procession from unity except the binary; nor the place of the second except the ternary; nor the place of the third except the quaternary. Each number possesses its natural place, and no number other than the one whose place it is may occupy it.

In unity itself all numbers are simultaneously present, and no one precedes or follows another, because all are one. Yet they would not possess immutably the natural order in which they are contained through their multiplications if their own eternally unchanging cause did not precede in unity.

The same must be understood of doubles, whose chief is the binary; triples, which the ternary precedes; quadruples, which begin from the quaternary; and every kind of multiple: each begins from its own principle and extends to infinity.

A double, triple, quadruple, or any other such proportion is not understood in unity distinctly and in particular, since in it all multiples are simultaneously present and are one. In it, unity itself is at once one, multiple, and simple: simple by nature, but multiple according to the rational structures by which numbers receive their immutable order in their multiplications. [Note: A reads “they are one and are simultaneous.”]

What shall I say of the wondrous and divine constitution and proportion of the superparticular, superpartient, multiple-superparticular, and multiple-superpartient ratios, each species of which receives its form from unity? What shall I say of the proportionalities which we contemplate in proportions and in the differences of terms, in which there is such ineffable and divine stability that no one who penetrates the secrets of wisdom can deny that they are eternal? [Note: A omits the second *non*, “not.”]

But if the correct definition of the true is the one that says that what always remains is true, and what always remains is eternal, then the rational structures of numbers are true because they always remain unchanged, and consequently they are eternal. [Note: A reads *racionationes*, “reasonings,” rather than *rationes*, “rational structures.”] Whoever wishes to know about these matters carefully should attentively read the books of the illustrious Boethius on mathematics.

Here, too, is a very brief argument for the eternity of numbers in their beginning, that is, in the monad. If the unity of numbers is unity, unity never existed without the numbers of which it is the unity.

Again, if numbers flow from the monad as from an inexhaustible fountain and, however much they are multiplied, end in it, they would not flow from it if they did not previously subsist causally in it before their flowing forth; nor would they desire to end in it if they did not recognize by natural movement that their causes remain eternally in it, to which they never cease to return by the same degrees through which they had flowed toward the same goal—by the analytical rules through which every inequality is restored to equality.

Anyone devoted to the marvelous investigation of such natures will find the analytical rules at the beginning of the second treatise of the mathematics of the illustrious Boethius.

But if someone says that the unity of numbers and the numbers themselves exist together inseparably, since they may rightly be counted among things that exist together and inseparably, this must not be denied; indeed, it must be admitted. Yet it must not for that reason be believed or understood that they are eternal and without a beginning. For many things begin to exist together, yet are not thereby compelled to subsist together eternally. Matter and form, voice and word, begin together and end together, yet they are not eternal. For if they were eternal, they would neither begin nor cease to exist—and the same applies to many things of this kind.

[Col. 0655D]

The answer must be that the senary number is not excluded from unity or from the multiplication of other numbers, especially since it alone among the cardinal numbers—that is, in the first sequence of numbers from one through ten—is perfect. For it is completed by its parts: the sixth, the third, and the half. The sixth is one, the third is two, and the half is three; joined together, they complete the quantity six. One, two, and three are six. [Note: A reads “become.”]

There is also another argument that wonderfully reveals the perfection of the senary number: it completes the first sequence of numbers with its parts arranged in order. Its sixth part, one, occupies the first place among the numbers; its third part, two, the second; its half, three, the third; its half and sixth together, which are three and one, the fourth; its half and third together, which are three and two, the fifth; and all its parts joined together—one, two, and three—complete the sixth place, namely itself.

The whole number together with its sixth, that is, six and one, makes the seventh; the whole together with its third, six and two, makes the eighth; the whole together with its half, six and three, makes the ninth. [Note: C omits “that is, six and three.”] If one is added to these—the one in which the end of all numbers is established—the quantity ten is completed.

If, therefore, this perfect number—the senary—is established in the unity of numbers, let the person who says that it is not eternal consider the matter, since in it the Creator of all things completed his works. [Note: C omits the words from “the quantity ten” through “is established.”]

Here we must note that the senary number is not perfect because God completed all that he wished to create in it, but rather that he established all his works in it so that, through the perfection of the number, he might signify the perfection of his works. [Note: C omits the clause from “not because” through “but rather.” A reads “all things in it.”]

Is it then credible or plausible that this greatest and most divine exemplar, in which God made his works, began temporally, when in it the maker of all things established not only what exists in time, but time itself and what subsists beyond time?

Therefore no one of sound understanding will doubt the eternity of numbers, using only the argument of the senary. For what is understood about the eternity of that number must likewise be understood about the perpetuity of the others. [Note: A omits *est*, “is.”] For the statement was made not only about the senary but generally about the totality of all numbers: “God made all things in measure, number, and weight.”

But if places and times are counted among all the things that God made, then intellectual numbers, established solely in knowledge, necessarily precede places and times by the perpetuity of their nature and are included among things that are at once eternal and made. They are eternal in the monad, but made in their multiplications. [Note: C reads *suis*, “their own,” rather than *sui*, “of themselves.”]

MASTER. Enough has been said about the eternity of numbers in the monad. But how they are made, and where and from what, it is very necessary to investigate. For by their argument we are attempting to assert that all things which are from God are at once eternal and made.

STUDENT. I have explained, as far as I can, the eternity of the monad and of all numbers in it. But how intellectual numbers—according to which all things that can be counted are counted—are made, and where and from what, is yours to explain. I say this knowing that their eternity can more easily be sought, discovered, and demonstrated than their making.

MASTER. You think well of me, as I see, when you entrust to me the more difficult matters to seek, discover, and demonstrate. Nevertheless, it is mine to seek; discovery belongs to him alone who illuminates what is hidden in darkness, and demonstration likewise belongs to him alone who can open understanding and intellect. For what does outward persuasion accomplish if inward illumination is absent?

Therefore, what you said shortly before—“eternal in the monad, but made in their multiplications”—seems to me to be a preliminary statement of this question. And if you understood what you said, you are asking unnecessarily about what you understand; but if you did not, it must be investigated. [Note: C omits *a te*, “by you.”]

12.

STUDENT. I see clearly that numbers can be made only in their multiplications, for in the monad they are eternal. But how, where, or from what they are made, I still do not see, and therefore I ask you to disclose this knowledge to me. [Note: A reads “or from what, or where.”]

MASTER. We do not doubt that all numbers are always in the monad causally—that is, in power and potentiality.

STUDENT. A person of little understanding would doubt this.

MASTER. You understand, I suppose, that the monad subsists eternally in wisdom and knowledge.

STUDENT. If I think otherwise, I am estranged from the true knowledge of the monad itself.

MASTER. You do not suppose, I think, that there are some numbers established in the monad in power and potentiality, and other numbers existing actually and operationally in the genera and species of intelligible numbers, but that the same numbers flow forth?

STUDENT. Not different numbers, but the same numbers in a different manner.

MASTER. Tell me, please: in what different manner?

STUDENT. In the monad they exist in power and potentiality; in the genera and forms, actually and operationally.

MASTER. You have answered correctly. Do you therefore see that the same numbers are eternal where they exist causally in power and potentiality—that is, in the monad—but that where they are understood actually and operationally, there they are made? [Note: C omits *esse*, “to be.”]

STUDENT. You are going too quickly. We must enter the path of reasoning step by step, lest we determine anything carelessly or rashly. First, then, it must be asked what the power and potentiality of numbers in the monad are, and what the act and operation of those same numbers are in genera and forms.

MASTER. Power, as I judge, is their substantial virtue, which subsists eternally and immutably in the monad. [Note: A reads “subsisting in the monad.”] Potentiality, however, is the possibility implanted in them by which they can be multiplied into genera and species and made manifest to understanding through definite distinctions of terms, differences of quantities, intervals of differences, and the wondrous equality and indissoluble consonance of proportions and proportionalities. [Note: A adds “and of proportions.”]

Act is the movement of the mind contemplating within itself and in themselves the multiplication of numbers proceeding from the monad into diverse genera and into differing species, before they come forth into the phantasies of thought—that is, simply in incorporeal nature, free from every image—when the purest eye of understanding considers the numbers themselves above every quantity and quality, place and time.

To define it briefly, act is the movement of the mind contemplating the purest numbers in their own nature without any imagination.

Operation, however, is the movement of that same mind which entrusts to memory, as though thickened by certain bodies, the purest numbers that it considers in itself; orders them there; handles their rational structures more easily; and communicates them to the knowledge of others by signifying them outwardly through certain signs of the bodily senses.

And do not suppose that I mean to persuade you that the numbers are multiplied and created by intellect or reason, rather than by the Creator, multiplier, and arranger of all things. For if numbers first underwent their multiplication from any created intellect, they would not possess the divine and ineffable immutability and harmony of their rational structures.

Therefore intellect must not be thought to create intellectual numbers merely because it contemplates them in themselves. Rather, they must be believed to be made by the one Creator of all things in intellects, whether human or angelic, by whom they were also established eternally in the monad. Through intellect they descend from the monad into the concept of reason.

For example, a certain plan or any natural art, while it is contained in the most secret recesses of intellectual nature, exists simultaneously as one simple thing, without parts or divisions, without quantity or quality, without place or time, and altogether free from every accident, scarcely known except to intellect. For intellect is not the maker of natural arts but their discoverer; yet it discovers them not outside itself but within itself. [Note: A omits *enim*, “for,” and C omits *sed intra*, “but within.”]

When the art itself begins to descend from its hidden places—where it exists simultaneously in the mind in which it is contained—into intelligible reason through a progressive movement, it gradually begins to disclose its hidden rules through explicit divisions and differences, though they are still utterly pure and free from every imagination.

This first procession of the art from the knowledge in which it initially subsists is completed actually through intellect into the reason of that intellect. Everything that passes from the secrets of nature into reason advances through the activity of intellect. [Note: A reads “is perfected.”] Again, in a kind of second descent, the same art descends from reason into memory and gradually declares itself more openly in phantasies, as though in certain forms. In a third descent it diffuses itself into the bodily senses, where through sensible signs it displays its power through its genera, species, and all its divisions, subdivisions, and partitions. [Note: C reads “is poured out.”]

Thus intellectual numbers pour themselves forth from the monad so that they may somehow shine forth in the mind; then, flowing from the mind into reason, they reveal themselves more openly; next, descending from reason into memory, they receive phantasmal appearances from the nature of memory itself, in which they clearly disclose to their investigators the powers of their manifold forms; then they descend into the senses, and finally into figures. [Note: A reads “their forms.”]

Do you therefore now see the three things you asked about—how, where, and from what?

From what? From the monad.

Where? In intellect.

How? By different stages: first from themselves into intellect, from intellect into reason, from reason into memory, from memory into the bodily senses; and, if necessary for the benefit of learners, finally they descend from the senses into visible figures. [Note: C omits *in*, “in.”]

STUDENT. I see it perfectly and most clearly.

MASTER. Therefore it is not hidden from you, I suppose, that numbers are both eternal and made: eternal in the monad, but made manifoldly in their descents. First, they are made in the intellect of those contemplating them in themselves. This manner of being made is far removed from the senses; for they are said to be made in the knowledge of those who understand them.

While they are in the monad, however, they surpass every intellect by their ineffable unity, except that one divine intellect which nothing anywhere escapes. For it is the intellect of all things—or rather, it is all things.

The subject now is not the monad itself, which is the sole cause and creator of all visible and invisible things, but that created monad in which all numbers subsist causally, uniformly, rationally, and always, and from which they burst forth in manifold forms. [Note: A omits “uniformly and rationally.”]

Second, they are made in reason, where they are said to be made because they show themselves there more clearly, though still by themselves and without any phantasmal coloring. Then, in memory and the senses, they are made in certain phantasies.

These phantasies either arise from the nature of memory—that is, from that part of the soul assigned to forming images—or are received externally from the surface of bodies through the external senses. [Note: C omits this sentence.] Those that come from outside are properly called *phantasies*; those that come from memory are called *phantasmata*.

For example, a phantasy is the image that I impress upon my memory after receiving through sight the image of a definite body, color, or extent that I have seen. A phantasma, however, is the image that I form of something I have never seen. It is rightly called a false image, because what I think either does not exist at all, or, if it exists, is not as I imagine it. [Note: C reads “as I image it.”]

Here we must note, if we follow Saint Augustine, that a phantasma arises from nowhere other than a phantasy. For, as he himself says, it is the image of an image—that is, an image arising from another image.

For example, I possess a phantasy of the sun rising every day, which I received from the disk-like appearance of the sun itself. [Note: A reads “which, as you have given it, I received from its disk-like form.”] Then, in accordance with that phantasy, I form in my memory a thousand solar images, larger or smaller according to the freedom of my thought, and consequently they are false because they imitate nothing true.

The Greeks, however, understand the nature of a phantasma differently. They say that the knowledge in the mind of sensible natures, received through their phantasies, is a phantasma.

STUDENT. Therefore, unless I am mistaken, you assert that numbers, established eternally in the monad, are made in two ways. Either they are made pure in the mind and reason through simple understanding alone, appearing in themselves without any imagination; or they are made in memory and bodily sense, thickened by certain imaginations and made, as it were, from and in some matter.

MASTER. That is so. But you did not perceive very acutely what you added: “made from and in some matter.” For the phantasies which are received from memory into memory, or from a sensible object into sense, so that numbers may appear in them, are not made from some matter; rather, incorporeal things arise from incorporeal things.

They are not made from the matter of bodily things, but from form, which is undoubtedly incorporeal, and from colors, which are understood not as bodies but as existing around bodies.

Consequently, nothing is more fitting or natural than that intellectual numbers should display their power in incorporeal things and in things received from incorporeal sources, and that they should proceed, in an ineffable manner, as made into sensible generation.

When the rational structures of things have been perceived, no one will rashly say that the phantasies in which numbers reveal themselves to the inner eyes of those who count arise from anywhere other than the intelligible numbers themselves. For if the numerical order of sensible forms—which contain matter so that they can be perceived by the senses, since that numerical order is itself invisible—and if this numerical order of forms derives its origin from intellectual numbers, and memory is formed into phantasies through bodily senses from the numerical order of forms, nothing remains except for us to understand that intellectual numbers flow from the monad in two ways and, once made in memory, are multiplied, divided, compared, gathered together, and united by the mind.

Either, as we said earlier, they descend through intellect into reason and from reason into memory; or, through the forms of visible things, they pass into the bodily senses and then flow from the senses into that same memory. There, receiving phantasmal forms, they are made and submit to the inner senses.

Consequently, however numbers may undergo perception, they receive the occasion of their appearing from nowhere other than themselves. Therefore they are eternal in the monad and are made from themselves in whatever part of nature they appear: whether in intellect or reason without any imaginations, or in memory, formed from the appearances of sensible things, making certain phantasies from themselves in which they may appear as though made from themselves. [Note: A reads *Perinde*, “therefore,” rather than *Proinde*, “consequently.”]

STUDENT. Enough has been said about numbers. These arguments establish and make clear where they are eternal, and where and how they undergo being made, so that we rightly perceive them to be both eternal and made. But I am waiting attentively to see where these matters lead. They have not been introduced for their own sake, but to persuade us of something else.

MASTER. I am surprised that you have so quickly forgotten yourself. Shortly before, you asked me for natural examples by which I might introduce you to an understanding of the matters we were discussing—namely, how all things that are from God are simultaneously eternal and made, and especially how God himself is both the maker of all things and is made in all things. For this is the sum of our entire present reasoning.

STUDENT. I am returning now to myself. Stunned by the difficulty of what was said above and by the theory of things still unknown to me, I fell into a state of ecstasy, as happens to many people. For what inexperienced person, not yet having ascended to the most sublime summit of wisdom, would not suffer a withdrawal of the mind while considering such matters—hearing of the eternal establishment by the Creator of all things of numbers in the monad, and of their procession into genera and species, in which they are said to be made because in them they undergo being understood by intellects; then their procession into a second rational nature, as it were, in which they propagate their powers more manifestly; then their reception in memory and the senses of phantasies, indeed even of theophanies—for we must not doubt that everything formed in memory from the nature of things has its occasions from God—and their being made, in a certain manner, not from another matter but from themselves?

Now, as though awakened and returning to myself, and perceiving more clearly the ray of the inner light, I am beginning to understand what you have said. You are attempting, I think, to persuade me that all numbers, flowing from the monad as from a certain fountain, pour forth like two rivers rising from one source, dividing into two separate channels. One of these runs through the inner pores of nature—that is, through intellect and reason—while the other runs through the outward forms of visible things and through the senses, until both flow together into memory, where they are formed in manifold ways. [Note: C reads *decurrit*, “runs down”; A has the infinitive *decurrere*, “to run down.”]

[Additional textual variants, keyed to the relevant passages: In 11, A reads *Non enim* (“For indeed”) for *Nam non* (“For not”); A has *quos* for *quas* (“which”); C reads *autem adverte* (“but observe”) for *diligenter animadverte* (“observe carefully”); A has *unitasque* (“and unity”) for *unitas, quae* (“unity, which”), omits *et* in “it is also beginning,” omits *enim* in “for their beginning,” and omits *et* in “and their end”; A reads *per quem moventur* (“through which [masculine] they move”) for *per quam moventur*; C reads *protenduntur* for *protendantur* (“are/would be extended”); A omits *in* in “in their principle”; C omits *est* (“is”) in “it is necessary”; A reads *erit* (“will be”) for *erat* (“was”); A reads *finiunt* (“end”) for *fiunt* (“are made”); A omits *a* (“from”) in “from God”; C reads *sit* (“is”) for *adsit* (“is present”).

In the account of numerical kinds, A has *post* in place of Greek *τέτρας* (*tetras*, “quaternary”); C reads *perficiunt* (“complete”) for *conficunt* (“make up”); A reads *enim* (“for”) for *autem* (“however”); C omits “what always remains”; A omits *non* (“not”) before “subsist causally” and reads *substiterant* (“had subsisted”) for *subsisterent* (“would subsist”); A omits *simul* (“together”) in “subsist together eternally.”

In 12, A omits *in* in “in wisdom and knowledge,” omits *eis insita* (“implanted in them”), reads *veniant* for *proveniant* (“come forth”), omits *in* in “in incorporeal nature,” and reads *Aut* (“Or”) for *Et ut* (“And, to”); A reads *in suas* (“into its”) for *suas* (“its”), *venit* (“comes”) for *pervenit* (“arrives”), *ex monade descendunt* (“descend from the monad”) for *ex monade se defundunt* (“pour themselves forth from the monad”), and *perfluentes* (“flowing through”) for *profluentes* (“flowing forth”); C preserves the alternative phrasing “from themselves in intellect, into intellect” in the sequence of descents; A omits *et* in “both eternal and made”; C omits *se* (“themselves”) in “contemplating them in themselves”; A reads *suavitate* (“sweetness”) for *sua unitate* (“their own unity”); C omits the sentence on the student’s added phrase “made from and in some matter”; A reads *in memoriam* (“into memory”) for *in memoria* (“from memory”); A reads *Prospectisque* for *Perspectisque* (“when perceived”); C omits *ut* (“that”) in “nothing remains except that we understand”; A omits *ubi et* (“where and”) in “where and how they undergo being made”; A omits *et* in “from God, and at once eternal”; A reads *rationabilem secundam* (“a second rational [nature]”) while C omits *veluti secundam* (“as it were, second”).]

### 13.

But how incorporeal things—removed not only from the senses but also from memory and every imagination because of the surpassing excellence of their nature—can appear in memory or to the senses, that is, in visible images and figures, as though in certain bodies, I do not sufficiently see.

**MASTER.** I sense that you understand the whole matter from this one example. For, as you said, numbers flow forth from the monad and converge into memory. But concerning what you do not sufficiently see, accept what I think. The nature of spiritual things does not so submit to the mind’s contemplations that we can give an account of each individual thing that is done concerning it, in it, or through it. For many things customarily appear in it which do not come about according to its known or unknown laws, but beyond every law, by the divine will—which is confined by no law, since it is the law of laws and the reason of reasons—in a wondrous and ineffable manner.

Who, if questioned, could explain how Moses appeared visibly in the spirit to the apostles, who had been carried away in spiritual vision to the mountain—that is, to the height—when the Lord’s Transfiguration took place? For those who think that he temporarily rose again in a body, so that he might appear visibly with Elijah on the mountain, not by himself as a soul but in his body, and then return again to the tomb, are not to be heeded.

Who, then, will say by what principle an incorporeal and invisible soul appeared as though bodily to the apostles’ invisible spirits, when it appeared neither in its own body nor in any perceptible material, whether assumed from elsewhere or otherwise, but through a certain ineffable power known to God alone, so that an invisible spirit was made visible in itself, as it were?

What will you say about the soul of the prophet Samuel—how, though invisible, it spoke to Saul as if visible? For Samuel himself, like the apostles, saw such things after being carried away in the spirit. Indeed, those who say that it was not Samuel himself but some likeness of him that appeared are not to be believed. They judge it unworthy that a holy soul should be recalled from the dead by the incantations of a Pythoness, without noticing that divine providence administers the nature of things no less through unclean spirits than through clean ones.

It is established, however, that Samuel’s soul prophesied by itself, visibly as it were, neither in a body nor in any likeness, to the king who consulted it. And if this seems incredible or doubtful to anyone, let him read Saint Augustine’s book *On the Care of the Dead*.

But let us return to the clearest examples from nature, about which no one who philosophizes rightly disputes.

**DISCIPLE.** Tell me, please, what those examples are.

### 14.

**MASTER.** The wise say that the forms of things are incorporeal. They also express the same judgment concerning colors: after considering the matter according to sound reasoning, they declare that colors too are incorporeal.

**DISCIPLE.** Whoever doubts this has no place among philosophers.

**MASTER.** If, then, forms and colors are counted among incorporeal things, explain, if you can, in what way they submit to bodily senses. For everything perceived through the eyes can be perceived only in a colored form.

**DISCIPLE.** I think that forms and colors cannot appear by themselves, but appear in some material subject to them.

**MASTER.** I am greatly astonished that you are departing so far from philosophy.

**DISCIPLE.** I do not know where.

**MASTER.** Do you not realize that you were mistaken when you said that forms and colors cannot submit themselves to the senses by themselves, except in some material, although matter itself, lacking form and color, is wholly invisible and incorporeal? Consequently, you must explain how forms and colors, being incorporeal in nature, can submit themselves to the senses in matter considered by itself—that is, without incorporeal form or color. You would therefore speak more rationally if you said that formless matter appears perceptibly in colors and forms, rather than that forms and colors appear in matter.

**DISCIPLE.** I do not deny that I was mistaken, deceived by the habit of false reasoning; and now I altogether do not know what to do.

**MASTER.** Do you remember what was settled among us about matter itself in the first book, where we argued that it comes into being from the conjunction of intelligible things? For quantities and qualities, although incorporeal in themselves, come together into one and produce formless matter, which, when incorporeal forms and colors are added to it, is moved into different bodies.

**DISCIPLE.** I certainly remember.

**MASTER.** Bodies, then, arise from incorporeal things.

**DISCIPLE.** I cannot deny it, for it was established by the arguments stated above.

**MASTER.** Bodies, therefore, do not come from nothing but from something. For no one will say that the aforementioned occasions of their existence are nothing—namely, quantities and qualities, forms or species, colors, intervals of length, breadth, and height, together with places and times. If you remove these, there will be no bodies; if you join them together, they immediately become bodies, whether universal, as are the four greatest bodies of the world, or particular and distributed among the most specific things.

You will not deny, I think, that all these are composed from the four simple elements, since they are dissolved back into them.

**DISCIPLE.** I will not deny it; but I would say that those elements, simple in themselves and productive of all bodies through their combination, were made from nothing.

**MASTER.** What, then, will you say about the primordial causes, about which we have said much? We must ask why they are called causes if they do not proceed into their effects. For if all bodies come from the elements, and the elements from nothing, then the cause of those things will appear to be nothing, and not the primordial causes themselves, which God the Father made in his Word.

And if this is so, nothing will not be nothing, but will be a cause. But if it is a cause, it will be better than those of which it is the cause. It will necessarily follow either that the Word of God is nothing, in which the Father made all things—which would seem impious to say by way of privation, since in theology the denial of the Word is found because of the excellence of its nature, not because of privation of substance—or that some cause outside the Word will be posited, called “nothing,” from which God made all things and in which he established all things before they were made. Otherwise it is not a cause. And if this is so, I do not see how it can be called nothing. Indeed, I would sooner say that it is everything than nothing. For in the cause all the things of which it is the cause subsist causally and primordially.

**DISCIPLE.** I am compelled to admit that the four elements of this world subsist in the primordial causes. For they are not the causes of some things but universally of all visible and invisible things; and nothing in the order of all natural things is perceived by sense, reason, or intellect that does not proceed from them and subsist causally in them.

**MASTER.** You understand correctly. Therefore, if I am not mistaken, you will not deny that all composite and dissoluble bodies, which occupy the lowest place in the nature of all things, come from something and not from nothing.

**DISCIPLE.** I will not deny it. They are produced from the qualities and quantities of simple and invisible bodies, which cannot be grasped by the senses and are therefore called elements, because investigators of nature say that all bodies are composed from their coming together, dissolved into them, and preserved in them. They are also commonly called *catholic*, that is, universal; for particular bodies of individual things are made from them.

Again, I admit that the elements were not made from nothing, but proceed from the primordial causes. No believer doubts that these primordial causes were made simultaneously and all at once in the Word of God, hearing the prophet say to God, “You made all things in wisdom,” and looking upon the opening of Sacred Scripture, where it is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

**MASTER.** It remains, then, for us to inquire concerning those primordial causes themselves: whether they were made from nothing in the Word of God, or whether they were always in him. And if they were always in him, there was no time when they were not, just as there was no time when the Word in which they were was not. But if they were always in that Word, how were they made from nothing in it? For it does not accord with reason that things which always existed should have begun to be made from nothing.

And if someone should say that the nothing from which they were made always existed, and that they were always made from it, he will be asked where that nothing always was: whether in the Word of God, in which all things subsist, or by itself outside the Word.

If he answers that it was always in the Word, he will be confronted with this: then it was not nothing but something great. For everything that subsists in the Word of God truly and naturally subsists, and what was thought to be nothing is thereby counted among the primordial causes, from which all things are believed to have been made.

But if he thinks that nothing existed by itself outside the Word, he will be judged to be inventing, like a Manichaean, two principles opposed to one another.

Many secular philosophers thought that formless matter was coeternal with God, from which he made all his works. They called this matter “nothing” because, before it received forms and species from God, it appeared in nothing and was, as it were, altogether nothing. For whatever is entirely without form and species may not improperly be called nothing.

The light of truth has driven away all these delusions, proclaiming that all things come from one principle, and that nothing is found in the nature of visible and invisible things which, in whatever mode of generation, breaks forth into its proper form without being eternally established in the only-begotten Word of God. In that Word all things are one. It also proclaims that God received no matter or cause from outside himself for the universe he established in his wisdom, because there is nothing outside him, nor did he find within himself anything not coessential with him from which he might make in his wisdom what he willed to be made.

### 15.

Consequently, there is no place for nothing, either outside or within God; and yet it is not believed without reason that he made all things from nothing. Accordingly, when we hear that all things are created from nothing, nothing else is meant except that there was a time when they were not.

Therefore we appropriately say: they always were, they always were not; there was no time when they were not; and when they were not, they were. For they always were causally in the Word of God, in force and power, beyond all places and times, beyond every generation produced locally and temporally, beyond every form and species known by sense and intellect, beyond every quality and quantity, and beyond the other accidents through which each creature’s substance is understood to be, though not what it is.

And they always were not. For before they flowed forth through generation into forms and species, places and times, and into all the accidents that accrue to their eternal substances, which are established inseparably in the Word of God, they did not exist in generation; nor did they exist locally or temporally, nor in their proper forms and species to which accidents belong.

Accordingly, it is not irrationally said of them, “There was a time when they were not.” For temporally they began, through generation, to be what they had not been, since they always subsist in the Word of God, in which they do not begin to exist; for eternity is infinite.

And there was a time when they were not: temporally they began, through generation, to be what they had not been—that is, to appear in forms and species.

Therefore, if anyone carefully examines the nature of things, no creature subject to the senses or intellect will be found of which it cannot truthfully be said: it always was, is, and will be; and it always was not, is not, and will not be.

For the first constitution itself, through the primordial causes, immutably was, is, and will be in the wisdom of God. But because that constitution is known to God alone, and surpasses every sense and intellect of the entire creation, and because no created intellect can yet know what it is, it begins temporally through generation to receive quantities and qualities. Covered, as it were, in these garments, it can manifest that it is, though not what it is.

It therefore begins, in a certain manner, to be—not insofar as it subsists in the primordial causes, but insofar as it begins to appear from temporal causes. By “temporal causes” I mean qualities and quantities and the other things that accrue temporally to substances through generation.

For this reason it is said of them, “There was a time when they were not”: they did not always appear in accidents.

By the same reasoning they are now said to be, and they are, and they will truly and always be, insofar as they subsist in their causes. But insofar as they are said to be in the accidents that occur to them externally, they neither truly nor always are.
