For they will be dissolved into those things from which they were taken, in which they truly and always are, when every substance has been cleansed of all corruptible accidents and freed from everything that does not belong to the state of its own nature. Then, adorned only with natural powers and with indissoluble simplicity, and, in those who are good, ornamented with the gifts of grace, it will be glorified in the contemplation of eternal blessedness beyond every nature, even its own, and will be turned toward God himself, becoming God not by nature but by grace.

When these arguments have been considered, who except someone exceedingly slow or exceedingly contentious would not concede that all things which come from God are both eternal and made at the same time?

### 16.

**DISCIPLE.** I have been thoroughly persuaded of this. Yet every ambiguity has not been removed from me. For what you said—that all things which come from God are both eternal and made because they are eternal in the Word of God and, as Saint Augustine says, exist substantially without being made, but are made temporally through generation in form, species, and accidents—I understand clearly, with all ambiguity removed.

But since it is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” and, “You made all things in wisdom,” I am compelled to admit that all things in the Word of God are both eternal and made. I mean all visible and invisible things, temporal and eternal things, all the primordial causes together with all their effects, through which the order of the ages is carried out locally and temporally and this visible world is filled.

But how this can accord with reason, I cannot see clearly.

**MASTER.** Do you therefore think that I intended to teach that all things, insofar as they are eternal, are eternal in the only-begotten Word of God, but, insofar as they are made, were made outside the Word? Do you not think that it accords with the arguments of truth for the universe of created nature to be both eternal and made in the Word?

**DISCIPLE.** I did not think that you taught this. For I do not think that anyone who philosophizes correctly would suppose that part of the whole universe subsists eternally in the Word of God while another part was made temporally outside the Word.

Nor does Sacred Scripture allow us to think such things. It says in the Psalm, “You made all things in wisdom”; in Genesis, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”; and the Apostle says, “In him all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers; all things were created from him and through him and for him.”

In the Gospel it says, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Nor does reason permit anything outside the Word to perish substantially or accidentally.

It cries out: all things that are and that are not are comprehended in the Word—not “are not” by privation, but “are not” because of excellence. They are in him and are not in him. Those things are, which are grasped by intellect or sense; those things are not, which surpass every sense and intellect.

That all things in the Word of God are both eternal and made is attested by John the theologian, drawing from the breast of Wisdom eternal and truthful waters of understanding, when he says, “What was made in him was life.”

Or one may distinguish the sentence according to Augustine in this way: “What was made locally and temporally was life in him.” For we must not believe—or in any way suppose—that so diligent an investigator of truth intended the Gospel to be distinguished in this way to imply that what was made locally and temporally was made not in the Word but, as it were, outside the Word. Saint Augustine himself most plainly teaches that places and times, together with the things made in them, were made eternally in the Word of God, understanding the Apostle to speak truthfully of the Word: “In him all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible.”

Accordingly, if places and times, together with everything contained in them, belong among visible things—that is, sensible things—and if all visible things, according to the Apostle, were created in the Word, then places and times and all the things in them were created in the Word.

Alternatively, according to others, someone may pronounce the Evangelist’s statement simply, saying, “What was made in him”—as though he had marked this off as beginning from another clause—“was life.” For we find many Greek manuscripts punctuated in this way, so that we understand: what was made in him temporally and locally through generation was eternally life through reason—that is, through its constitution in the primordial causes of all things.

**MASTER.** You therefore do not doubt that all the causes of all things and all their effects are eternal and made in the Word, nor do you suppose that I teach otherwise.

**DISCIPLE.** I neither doubt the eternity of all things and their creation in the Word, nor think that you teach otherwise. I ask only how all things are simultaneously eternal and made in the Word, which is coeternal with the Father.

For, as I think, it does not accord with reason that things should be made eternal and eternal things made. For there would seem to be no difference between the eternity of the universe in the Word and its creation, if eternity is created and creation is eternal.

**MASTER.** I am astonished and greatly disturbed that you seek a reason in matters in which every reason fails, or an understanding in things that surpass every intellect.

Do you think that the purpose of divine wisdom can be made manifest to human or angelic intellects when you read that those mystical living creatures cover their faces and feet with their wings—that is, they gaze upon the height of divine power while fearing it, together with its depth, in the things made through it, in it, and from it?

Yet they do not cease to fly upward. For, lifted up as far as they can be by the vehicle of divine grace and by the subtlety of their nature, they continually seek and desire what is above them, without limit.

But when they reach the point where they fail, they reverently hide their faces—that is, the edge of their contemplation, struck back by the divine ray—and withdraw their theological feet—that is, their intellectual approaches—from the entrance of incomprehensible mysteries, lest they presume carelessly or rashly upon things that are ineffable and surpass every intellect.

If, then, the purest intellects—whose symbols theology has presented under the image of those living creatures, and between whom and the Word there is no intermediary except the primordial causes of all things—fear to look upon the height of divine brightness and the power and wisdom poured into all things, extending from the highest to the lowest, from end to end—that is, from the beginning of intellectual creation to the little worm—recognizing that the capacity of their nature is insufficient to consider these things, why do we, still weighed down by flesh, attempt to give an account of divine providence and operation?

Here one must think only of the divine will, which accomplishes all things as it wills because it is omnipotent, and which inserts hidden and unsearchable natural principles into all things, because it is the supernatural principle of all things. Nothing is more secret, nothing more present; it is difficult to say where it is, more difficult to say where it is not; it is ineffable light, always present to every intellectual eye, yet recognized by no intellect for what it is. It is diffused infinitely through all things, and it becomes all things in all and nothing in none.

When I said that between these intellects and the Word there is no intermediary except the causes of all things, I added this so that no one might think that the celestial essences are immediate—that is, that they have no intermediary between themselves and the cause of all things.

Although angels are said to be, as it were, *eggigi*, that is, “near God”—for *engys* (ἐγγύς) in Greek means “near”—they are not therefore to be believed to have been made in such a way that their causes were not established in the Word.

For there is no creature whose cause was not made beforehand in the Word. According to that cause it is constituted so that it may exist, ordered so that it may exist beautifully, preserved so that it may exist eternally, and manifested either to the senses or to intellects as material for the praise of that one cause from which, in which, through which, and for which it was created.

Let us therefore believe, and as far as granted to us let us behold with the mind’s eye, that all visible and invisible things, eternal and timeless things, the eternal itself, time, places, spaces, and everything spoken of according to substance and accident—in general, whatever the entire universe of creation contains—are simultaneously eternal and made in the only-begotten Word of God. Neither does eternity precede their making, nor does their making precede eternity.

For their eternity was created, and their creation is eternal in the dispensation of the Word. All things that appear to arise through generation in the order of the ages, in times and places, were also made eternally, simultaneously and all at once, in the Word of the Lord.

We must not believe that they began to be made when they are perceived to arise in the world. For they always existed substantially in the Word of the Lord; and their rising and setting in the order of times and places through generation—that is, through the assumption of accidents—were always in the Word of God, in which things that will be have already been made.

For divine Wisdom circumscribes times, and all things that arise temporally in the nature of things precede and subsist eternally in it. It is the measure of all things without measure, the number without number, and the weight—that is, order—without weight. It is time itself and the age itself; it is the past, the present, and the future.

For this reason it is called by the Greeks *epékeina* (ἐπέκεινα), “beyond” or “above,” because it creates and circumscribes all times, being, through its eternity, beyond all times, preceding, encompassing, and enclosing all intervals.

No one can explain the reason even for the things that we perceive to occur annually in the natural course and order of times. For who, considering the power of seeds, could presume to say how or why they burst forth through the numerical structures of places and times into the various forms of animals, shrubs, and herbs? Who could fully discern their causes, rather than immediately declaring that all these things must be attributed to divine laws that surpass every sense and intellect?

No one should investigate by conjectures of the mind why they ought to fill the order of times in this way or that, how they do so in this way or that, and not otherwise; or why they proceed from invisible causes, established together in the power of seeds, not simultaneously but at intervals of times and places, into sensible forms—as though they could not happen otherwise if the divine will judged that they should happen otherwise, since that will is constrained by no law.

Indeed, many things often occur contrary to the customary course of nature, so that it may be shown to us that divine providence can administer all things not in one way only but in manifold and infinite ways.

If, then, the administration of the universe according to the divine laws is known to no intellect, to which rational or intellectual being can the eternal constitution of that same universe in the Word of God be made clear? In that Word all things are simultaneously eternal and made—a truth no believer ought to ignore, even though he does not understand how eternal things are made and made things are eternal. For this is known only to the Word, in which they are both made and eternal.

#### 16. [Cols. 0666–0670]

- “Do you think”: C reads *Nam* (“for”) for *Num* (“do you think”).
- “when you read”: A omits *legis* (“you read”).
- “in it, and from it”: A omits *et* (“and”).
- “lifted up … by divine grace and by the subtlety of their nature”: C supports the printed construction; A reads *divina gratia sublevata sive naturae subtilitate ea, quae* (“lifted by divine grace or by the subtlety of nature, those things which …”).
- “struck back by the divine ray”: A reads *repercussi defendunt* (“having been struck back, they defend”), a difficult variant.
- “incomprehensible mysteries”: A reads *mystericorum* (“mystical [things]”) for *mysteriorum* (“mysteries”).
- “extending from the highest to the lowest”: the printed *attingentes* is conjectural; A reads *attingentis*, C *attingent*.
- “divine providence”: A reads *prudentia* (“prudence”) for *providentia* (“providence”).
- “because it is omnipotent”: A reads *qui omnipraesens est* (“which/who is omnipresent”) for *quia omnipotens est* (“because it is omnipotent”).
- “Although indeed”: A reads *autem* (“however”) for *enim* (“indeed”).
- “near God himself”: A reads *Dominum ipsum* (“the Lord himself”) for *ipsum Deum* (“God himself”).
- For the coined angelic designation printed *eggigi*, C has *essus*. The source’s Greek note reads: “ἐγγύς, ‘near’; compare the glossaries. John Scotus appears to have formed ἐγγυγοί, ‘those who are near,’ from this word.”
- The further editorial gloss states: “God is designated by the Greeks as *epikaina* (sic), because past and future subsist in him, and he is [the one] in whom they terminate. Therefore, for ease of understanding, *epikaina* is often interpreted ‘the summit of all things,’ although properly [it denotes] past and future.” The note identifies the printed ἐπέκεινα as conjectural and compares Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Divine Names* IV.16, where ἐπίκεινα occurs; it also records this marginal gloss in C.
- “their causes were not established”: A omits *sint* (“were”).
- “let us behold”: A reads *intuemur* (“we behold”) for *intueamur* (“let us behold”).
- “in the only-begotten Word of God, and [are]”: C omits *et* (“and”).
- “their eternity was created”: A reads *facta* (“made”) for *condita* (“created/established”).
- C omits from “All things that appear to arise in the order of the ages” through “their rising and setting.”
- “have already been made”: C omits *sunt* (“have been”).
- “annually”: A reads *annunciatum* (“announced”) for *annuatim* (“annually”).
- “places and times”: A reads *in* (“in”) for *et* (“and”).

## DISC.

I do not ask about the mode in which the universe is created in the Word, nor about the reason for its eternity. For no one can say how things are both eternal and made. The mode [Col. 0670B] of the creation of things in the Word no rational or intellectual creature can know; for it is open only to the gnostic power. [Note: Col. 0669: A reads “rational.”] But I ask whether an explanation can be found for the reason why we are compelled to confess that things are eternal and made in the Word of God.

The present question is not concerned with the manifold effects of the primordial causes in visible and invisible things, in which no wise person doubts that all things were made. The question might seem capable of being solved in this way, if someone could demonstrate [Note: Col. 0669: C reads “can demonstrate.”] by true arguments that whatever things subsist in their principles in the Word of God must be understood to be eternal to that extent, while to the extent that they proceed into their effects—whether intelligible or sensible—in the order of time through generation, they are made; so that their [Col. 0670C] eternity in the Word of God preceded their creation in the order of the ages, whether they fill the invisible world above us or the visible world according to our condition. [Note: Col. 0669: A reads “preceded” as “will have preceded.”]

But reason does not allow us to affirm such things. For it cries out—and cries out most truly—that not only the primordial causes but also their effects, places, times, essences, and substances—that is, the highest genera, general forms, and most specific species, through individual numbers with all their natural accidents—and, to put it simply, everything that exists in the totality of created things, whether it is comprehended by human or angelic sense or intellect, or whether it surpasses every sense and every power of the mind, yet has been created—all of this was in the Word of God at once and simultaneously eternal and made. [Note: Col. 0669: A omits *et* (“and,” after “times”) and *ut* (“as/to put it simply”); A reads *erunt* (“will be”) for *erant* (“were”).] They were never eternal and unmade, nor made and not eternal. [Note: Col. 0669: A reads *relinquatur* (“may remain”) for *relinquitur* (“remains”).]

Nothing remains, therefore, except to ask not how they are [Note: Col. 0669: C reads “are”] both eternal and made, but in what sense they are said to be both made and eternal. [Note: Col. 0669: C reads “are taught.”]

## MAG.

They are called “made” in accordance with the authority of sacred Scripture, which declares—to use the same examples—“In the beginning God made heaven and earth”; “You made all things in wisdom”; “All things were made through him”; “in whom all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, whether visible or invisible”; and many similar statements.

But let whoever can explain the mode and reason for the creation of all things in the Word of God do so; I confess that I do not know. [Note: Col. 0671: A reads “I do not know.”] Nor am I ashamed not to know this, when I hear the Apostle saying: “You alone possess immortality and dwell in inaccessible light”—especially as though I were viewing from afar the end of the present inquiry. [Note: Col. 0671: A reads “as though” as “which.”]

For the present reasoning—or rather, reason itself—will lead us to understand not only that all things are eternal and made in the Word of God, but also that the Word itself makes all things [Col. 0671B], and becomes all things, by a simple gaze of the mind.

As Saint Maximus says:

“Through the principles present in existing things, raising the intellect to the causal Word, and binding it to that Word alone—since it gathers together all things that derive from it and draws them to itself—while employing in due order the principles of each existing thing, we believe, not confusedly but clearly, that God alone is properly left, through diligent attention to the things that are, as the causal source of the essence of existing things, their motion, the discernment of things that differ, the indissoluble cohesion of composites, the unchangeable foundation of things set in place, and, simply, of every essence, motion, difference, mixture, and position, however understood.” [Note: Col. 0671: A reads *peractiones* (“performances/actions”) for *per rationes* (“through principles/reasons”); *causae* (“of the cause”) for *causale* (“causal”); *essentiam et existentium* (“the essence and of existing things”) for *essentiam existentium* (“the essence of existing things”); and *ut cuique* (“as for each”) for *utcunque* (“however”).]

And so, if the Word of God alone is left as the essence of existing things, the motion and discernment of things that differ [Col. 0671C], the indissoluble cohesion of composites—that is, of composed things—and the unchangeable foundation of things set in place—that is, of things attaining an unchangeable state—and as the cause of essence, motion, discernment, composition, and state, however these are understood, [Note: Col. 0671: A omits “of motion, difference, mixture, and position.”] what else remains to be understood except that the Word itself becomes all things in all things?

But how, and in what manner, the Word of God becomes in all the things that were made in it [Note: Col. 0671: A reads “in him”] escapes the reach of our mind. Nor is this surprising, since in sensible things no one can say how the incorporeal power of seed [Note: Col. 0671: A omits “incorporeal”], bursting forth into visible species and forms, into various colors and different pleasant fragrances, becomes manifest to the senses and becomes present in things, yet, while becoming manifest, does not cease to be hidden. [Note: Col. 0671: So read A and C.]

Whether manifest or hidden, it is never abandoned by its natural powers: it is wholly in all things and wholly in itself. It does not increase when it seems to be multiplied, nor decrease when it is thought to be contracted into a small quantity; rather, it remains immutably in the same condition of its nature.

For it is no smaller, for example, in one grain of wheat than in many harvests multiplied within the same genus; and, what is more remarkable, it is not greater in the whole of one grain than in a particle of that grain. For the many are in the one, and the one in the many.

But if someone should say that the power of seeds does not reveal itself through itself but in some matter—that is, in moisture—and that consequently it itself comes to be as what appears, but comes to be in the one thing in which it brings about appearance, so as to appear, [Note: Col. 0671: A omits the words from *sed in uno* (“but in one [thing]”) through *appareat* (“may appear”); C reads *appare* (“to appear”) for the printed *apparet* (“appears”; conjectural reading).] performing its operations not from itself but from some matter, the answer must be this:

If it appears and comes to be in a form, is the form matter, when manifest reason declares that whatever remains in matter remains through form, while matter in itself is unstable, formless [Note: Col. 0671: A reads “is formless”] and almost nothing? If it appears in colors, is color matter, when it is agreed [Note: Col. 0671: So reads C; A has “when it is clear that”] that colors are understood around matter [Note: Col. 0671: A reads “matter”], indeed even around form? If it appears in the pleasantness of fragrances, is fragrance matter, when those who deal with such things say that it is a quality affecting the sense of smell [Col. 0672B], and a quality is incorporeal? [Note: Col. 0671: C reads “not fragrance.”] The same must be said of the other qualities in which the power of seeds commonly appears. [Note: Col. 0671: A omits “in.”]

But if all the things mentioned above are incorporeal things attached to bodies, and understood in themselves apart from bodies, who but a fool would say that the incorporeal power of seeds needs corporeal matter for its appearance? For when form, every quality, and quantity have been removed, the power of seed cannot in any way either come to be or be perceived in bare matter.

What then? If matter itself, in which the power of seeds is thought to appear and act, is demonstrably derived from qualities in bodies, is it not thereby established [Col. 0672C] that the things in which it operates do not receive the power of seeds from elsewhere, but from itself and in itself—that is, in its natural powers—so that, in a wondrous manner, it becomes both its own matter and its own operation and operative power?

## 17.

The unshaken authority of divine Scripture therefore compels us to believe that the totality of the whole creation was created in the Word of God, and that the explanation of this creation surpasses every intellect and is known only to the Word itself, in which all things were created. [Note: Col. 0671: A omits “all things.”]

But if you wish to hear what I think about the eternity of the universe in the Word of God, attend carefully to what follows.

## DISC.

I am ready.

## MAG.

Do you suppose that the Word of God, in which all things were made, made all the things that were made in it? [Note: Col. 0671: A reads “saw.”]

## DISC.

I certainly suppose so. For although divine operation, in which all things were created, is considered by theologians in three ways according to the testimony of sacred Scripture—the Father makes, things are made in the Son, and are distributed by the Holy Spirit—nevertheless the operation of the supreme and holy Trinity is one and the same. [Note: Col. 0671: A reads “of the supreme and holy Trinity.”]

What the Father makes, the Son also makes, and the Holy Spirit makes; and what was made in the Son was made in the Father and in the Holy Spirit. [Note: Col. 0671: A omits “in.”] For if the Son is in the Father, everything made in the Son must necessarily be in the Father. [Note: Col. 0671: A omits the first “if.”] It is not consistent with reason to suppose that the Son himself alone is in the Father, while the things that the Father makes in the Son are not in the Father.

Likewise, what the Holy Spirit nourishes and distributes is nourished and distributed by the Father and the Son.

## MAG.

If, then, the Son makes the things that were made in him, should we believe that he made what he did not see? [Note: Col. 0673: So read A and C.]

## DISC.

I suppose that he saw what he made and what was made in him.

## MAG.

You suppose correctly. Tell me, then: how did he see them—with bodily sense or with the intellect?

## DISC.

I would say that God saw what he made neither through sense nor through intellect. For he who is incorporeal lacks bodily sense. Nor is he properly called “intellect,” since he surpasses every intellect. Yet he is called “intellect” metaphorically, just as he is called “mind,” by transferring the term from the creature to the Creator [Note: Col. 0673: A reads “and to the Creator”], since he is the cause and creator of every intellect and mind.

He therefore does not see through a creature, whether corporeal or incorporeal; he needs no instrument of any creature in order to see what he wishes to make. For, as Maximus says, it is impossible—as reason demonstrates—for one who is above the things that exist to receive the things that exist. [Note: Col. 0673: C reads thus; A: “for one who is above the things that exist to receive the things that exist through the things that exist.”]

But we say that he knows the things that are as his own wills, adding also an inference from the cause. For if he made all things by his will, and no reasoning contradicts this, and if it is pious and right to say that God always knows his own will, while he made each of the things that were made by willing it, then God knows the things that are as his own wills, because he made the things that are by willing them.

## MAG.

Just as God sees his wills, then, does he also see the things he made? [Note: Col. 0673: C reads “makes.”]

## DISC.

Yes, indeed, and not otherwise. [Note: Col. 0673: A reads “and not otherwise.”] He does not, as foolish people claim, see sensible things through sense and intelligible things through intellect; rather, just as he sees his wills, so he sees sensible and intelligible things.

## MAG.

You understand this plainly and clearly. But tell me, I ask: are the divine wills that God sees one thing, and the things that he sees as his wills another?

## DISC.

I am not competent to answer this proposition adequately and correctly. I am pressed on every side. For if I say that they are different, you will immediately say: “Then God does not see the things he made as his wills”; for a single vision cannot take place in things that are different in nature and kind. And you will conclude: “But the divine vision is simple, one, and uniform. Therefore, if God’s will is one thing and what he made another, he does not see what he made as his will.” [Note: Col. 0673: C reads “I see.”] [Note: Col. 0673: A omits “what he made.”]

But if I say that they are not different, [Note: Col. 0673: A reads “if I should say”] it will necessarily follow: God’s will, therefore, is his work, and he made his wills, and the things he made are his wills. For the one and same simple divine vision compels us to say that everything it sees is one and the same. But it sees the things he made as his wills.

The divine wills and the things God made are therefore one and the same. For the simple divine vision, which sees all things as one and one as all things, unifies them.

And if this is granted, I fear that you may compel me to confess one of two alternatives: either that God’s will is separated from God and joined to creation, so that God is one thing and his will another—that is, God is the maker while his will is made—or, if true reason does not permit this to be said, I shall necessarily confess that God, his wills, and all that he made are one and the same.

And then, under the compulsion of reasoning’s power, the conclusion will immediately follow: God therefore made himself, if his wills are not outside his nature and if he does not see his wills in one way and what he made in another, but sees what he made as his wills.

And if this is so, who would doubt the eternity in God of all things that have been made, when they are understood to be not only made and eternal but also God?

## MAG.

You are entering the path of reasoning with great caution and vigilance. Therefore, if you understand clearly and without any ambiguity that what you have said is so and cannot be otherwise, I do not see that further labor is necessary to persuade you of the eternity of all things that were made in the Word of God.

## DISC.

I think you are mocking me by treating me liberally—that is, by allowing my free judgment to choose what it wishes and hold what it wishes, rather than compelling me by true arguments to conclude what must be believed and understood about such matters with all falsehood removed.

For if I clearly understood by myself what I have said, I perhaps would not fear putting forward an open judgment about the divine wills and about the things that were made—whether they are one and the same or not. But I know myself, and I feared proceeding without sufficient ability to examine these matters.

## MAG.

Proceed step by step, then, so that you do not go astray in anything, and so that whatever you grant, you may hold with a stable disposition of mind. [Note: Col. 0673: A reads “so that.”]

## DISC.

Go ahead; I shall follow.

## MAG.

Although, as I think, you doubt whether God’s will—or wills, or the ineffable multiplicity of the divine unity, for God is one and multiple in himself [Note: Col. 0673: A reads “God is one and multiple in himself”]—belongs to the simple nature of supreme goodness, so that it is not something other than God himself, nevertheless you do not doubt that God was never without his wills. [Note: Col. 0673: A omits “God is.”]

## DISC.

It would be most foolish to doubt this. For whatever he possesses, he possesses always and immutably, since nothing happens to him. [Note: Col. 0673: A omits “to him.”] Therefore either he never had his wills, or, if he had them, there can be no doubt that he always had them.

## MAG.

God, therefore, always had his wills, and always saw them. For what he possessed could not be hidden from him.

## DISC.

He both possessed and saw them. For it is the judgment of madmen to suppose that God was without his wills, or did not always have them, or did not see them.

## MAG.

The divine wills, then, are eternal, because he whose wills they are is eternal.

## DISC.

I would grant this completely.

## MAG.

What, then? Did he also always possess and always see the things he willed? You clearly understand, I think, that nothing is future for God, since he encloses within himself all times and everything that is in them. For he is the beginning, middle, and end of all things, as well as their circumference, course, and return.

## DISC.

I do not doubt that nothing is future for God.

## MAG.

Everything, therefore, that he willed to make, he always possessed in his wills. For in him willing does not precede the thing he wills to come to be; it is coeternal with his will. For he does not wait for what he wills to come to be as though it were future, since all things are present to him, and his will is the cause of all things, their vision, effect, and perfection. [Note: Col. 0675: C reads “of the will.”] [Note: Col. 0675: A omits “and.”]

What he sees as something to be made comes to be without any interval intervening. But if his will is his vision, and his vision his will, everything he wills to come to be comes to be once every interval has been removed. [Note: Col. 0675: A reads “But” and omits “to come to be.”]

And if everything he wills to come to be he sees as something to be made, and what he wills and sees is not outside him but in him, and if nothing in him is other than what he himself is, it follows that everything he sees and wills must be understood to be coeternal with him, [Note: Col. 0675: C reads “and”] if his will, vision, and essence are one.

## DISC.

You are now compelling us to confess that everything called eternal and made is God. For if the divine will and the divine vision are essential and eternal, and if for him being is not one thing, willing another, and seeing another, but all are one and the same superessential reality, and if reason does not allow anything whatsoever that he comprehends within his will and vision to be understood as other than himself, [Note: Col. 0675: A omits “his own”] since a simple nature does not permit within itself anything that it is not, then without any controversy we must confess that the one God is all things in all things.

And if this is so, no one who philosophizes piously ought to be ignorant of the eternity of all things that are in God—or rather, that are God.

Yet I still do not sufficiently see how the divine nature, outside which there is nothing and within which all things subsist, allows anything within itself to possess being that is not coessential with it.

## MAG.

I believe that you do not doubt—and indeed that you see clearly enough—that no nature subsists apart from God and creation. For when you spoke of the divine nature outside which there is nothing, you understand it, as I suppose, to mean that the creative nature permits nothing outside itself, because nothing can exist outside it, while containing within itself everything that it has created and creates. [Note: Col. 0675: A reads “outside him” rather than “outside it.”]

Yet you understand it in such a way that it is one thing and what it creates within itself another, because it is superessential. For it does not seem plausible to you that it created itself. [Note: Col. 0675: A reads “created.”]

## DISC.

You have grasped my entire conception of God and creation. I hold firmly and unshakably that no nature, whether created or uncreated, [Note: Col. 0675: C reads “no uncreated or created nature”] subsists outside God or exists in any way outside him, while everything that subsists, whether created or uncreated, is contained within him.

Consequently, I had hitherto held that the fullness of the entire universe is enclosed in these two parts, namely, God and creation. But now my faith once again seems to waver, weakened by the arguments just given.

## MAG.

I see that your faith is established and fortified by true reason—at least in this respect: you believe that nothing exists outside God. [Note: Col. 0675: A reads “I see that it is fortified.”]

## DISC.

Yes, as you say; I contemplate that point with complete clarity.

## MAG.

Turn the gaze of your mind more carefully and perceptively toward the things that you believe to be within God.

## DISC.

I believe that within God there is nothing other than himself and the creation established by him. [Note: Col. 0675: A reads “by him” as “by him.”] [Note: Col. 0675: The passage from “within God” through “turn” is omitted by C.]

## MAG.

Then within God you see something that is not God.

## DISC.

I see it, yet it was created from God.

## MAG.

What, then, do you think? Did God see all the things he made before they came to be?

## DISC.

I would suppose that he saw everything he wished to make before it came to be.

## MAG.

Then he saw the things he wished to make, and he saw no things other than those he made; and he saw the things he made before he made them.

## DISC.

That is what I hold.

## MAG.

Tell me, please: what are those things that God saw before they came to be? For how did he see creation, which had not yet been made? And if he saw nothing other than creation—for everything that exists is either God or creation—what did he see? [Note: Col. 0675: A omits “what did he see.”]

Accordingly, either he saw himself before he made everything that he made, or he saw creation, which had not yet been created. But how did he see what did not yet exist? If it existed, and was therefore seen because it existed, then plainly there was something prior to creation that was not creation.

But if only God and what is coessential with him are permitted to exist before every creation, [Note: Col. 0675: A reads “nothing”] nothing preceded creation that God could see before making creation except either himself or an eternal nature within him coeternal with him. [Note: Col. 0675: A reads “creation.”]

We have established among ourselves, however, that God saw the things that were to be made; for he did not make what he wished to make in ignorance or without foreknowledge.

## DISC.

I see myself enclosed on every side, with no way of escape remaining. For if I say that God saw in himself the things that were to be made, I am compelled to confess that he saw himself, since creation did not yet exist for him to see, nor was there anything before all creation that he could see apart from himself. [Note: Col. 0675: A reads “could.”]

Thus, if he saw in himself everything that was to be made before it was made, true reason will necessarily teach that he saw himself, and he himself will be everything that he made. If he made in himself what he saw, he will be both maker and what is made.

But if I say that he saw creation as something to be made [Col. 0676D] before it came to be, you will say: “Then creation existed before it came to be.” For if God saw it before it came to be, [Note: Col. 0675: The clause beginning “For if God…” is omitted by C] that which God saw in it before it came to be truly existed substantially.

For God did not see false things, [Note: Col. 0675: C reads “does not see”] since he is unchangeable truth, and everything that is in him is true and unchangeable. And if God saw creation in himself before it came to be, he always saw what he saw. For seeing what he sees does not happen to him as an accident, since for him being and seeing are not different. His nature is simple. [Note: Col. 0677: C reads “His.”]

But if he always saw what he saw, what he saw always existed; and therefore what he saw must be eternal. And if he saw creation, which did not yet exist, and yet what he saw existed—for everything that God sees [Note: Col. 0677: C reads “saw”] is true and eternal—nothing remains except for us to understand that creation existed in God before it came to be in itself.

There will thus be a twofold understanding of creation: one considers its eternity in the divine knowledge, in which all things remain truly and substantially; the other considers its temporal creation, as it subsequently came to be in itself. [Note: Col. 0677: A reads “the other, which is temporal.”]

And if this is so, the consequence of reason compels us to choose one of two alternatives: either we must say that the same creation is better than itself or inferior to itself. It is better insofar as it subsists eternally in God, [Note: Col. 0677: C reads “subsisted”] but inferior insofar as it was created in itself; and its creation will be judged to have taken place not in God but, as it were, outside God, in itself. This would contradict Scripture, which says: “You made all things in wisdom.”

Or else we must say that the nature which existed eternally in the knowledge of God is not the same as that which was subsequently created, as it were, in itself.

Consequently, God did not see the things that were made before they came to be; he saw only the eternal things in himself. And if someone grants this, he will appear to resist the catholic confession of the faithful.

For holy wisdom does not confess that God saw one set of things in himself before they came to be and later made another set of things in themselves. Rather, it confesses that the same things were eternally seen and eternally made, all of this in God and nothing outside God.

But if the nature of divine goodness is one thing and what it saw to be made and made, what it saw and made in itself, is another, the simplicity of the divine nature will be broken, since something will be understood to exist in it that it itself is not. This is altogether impossible.

If, however, divine goodness is not one thing and what it saw to be made in itself another, but the nature whose simplicity is inviolable and whose unity is inseparable is one and the same, then it will certainly follow that God is everywhere and in everything: the whole in the whole; both maker and made; both seeing and seen; both time and place; the essence and substance of all things; accident; and, to put it simply, everything that truly is and is not.

He is superessential in essences, supersubstantial in substances; creator above every creature and created within every creature; subsisting below every creature; beginning to be from himself; moving himself through himself; moved toward himself; resting in himself; multiplied without limit through genera and species in himself, without abandoning the simplicity of his nature, and drawing back into himself the infinity of his multiplication. For in him all things are one.

## MAG.

Now I see that you are looking with complete clarity into the matters about which you seemed to doubt, and I think you will no longer hesitate to confess that all things are both made and eternal, and that everything truly understood to subsist in them is nothing other than the ineffable nature of divine goodness.

For it is substantial goodness, and no one is good except God alone. It remains, therefore, to discuss the eternal creation of all things in God, insofar as the ray of divine truth [Note: Col. 0677: C reads “of divine power”] permits the gaze of our mind to ascend into the divine mysteries.

## DISC.

It does remain, and the order of the discussion now demands it. Beforehand, however, I would like you briefly to collect everything that has so far been established between us concerning the present question. [Note: Col. 0677: A reads “has been established.”]

## MAG.

We have, I think, brought it to complete clarity: divine goodness saw, and always saw, the things that were to be made.

## DISC.

That has been established. [Note: Col. 0677: A reads “agreed.”]

## MAG.

And it did not see one set of things and make another, but made the things that it had always seen as things to be made.

## DISC.

That too has been granted.

## MAG.

And everything that it always saw, it always made. For vision does not precede operation in it, since operation is coeternal with vision—especially since seeing is not one thing for it and operating another, but its vision is its operation. It sees by operating, and operates by seeing. [Note: Col. 0677: A reads “It saw.”]

## DISC.

This too has been accepted.

## MAG.

It has been established, concerning the simplicity of the divine nature, that nothing can truly and properly be understood in it that is alien to it and not coessential with it, and that all things are truly and properly understood to exist within it. For nothing subsists outside it.

It has therefore been concluded that it alone is truly and properly in all things, [Note: Col. 0677: A reads “that it alone truly and properly exists in all things.”] and that nothing truly and properly exists that it is not. [Note: Col. 0677: A reads “that it alone is truly and properly in all things.”]

## DISC.

It has been concluded.

## MAG.

Accordingly, we must not understand God and creation as two things distant from one another, but as one and the same. For creation subsists in God, and God is created in creation in a wondrous and ineffable manner: manifesting himself; making himself, who is invisible, visible; making himself, who is incomprehensible, comprehensible; making himself, who is hidden, open; making himself, who is unknown, known; making himself, who is without form or appearance, formed and beautiful; [Note: Col. 0677: A reads “and beautiful”] making himself, who is superessential, essential; making himself, who is supernatural, natural; making himself, who is simple, composite; making himself, who is free from accidents, subject to accidents; making himself an accident; making himself, who is infinite, finite; making himself, who is uncircumscribed, circumscribed; making himself, who is beyond time, temporal; making himself, who is beyond place, local; creating all things and being created in all things; being the maker of all things and made in all things; [Note: Col. 0677: A reads “the maker of all things”] beginning to be eternal; being immovable yet moved into all things; and becoming all things in all things [Col. 0678D].

I do not say this of the incarnation and embodiment of the Word, but of the ineffable condescension of supreme goodness, which is unity and Trinity, into the things that exist, so that they might exist—or rather, so that it itself might be in all things, from the highest to the lowest—always eternal, always made: from itself, in itself; eternal from itself, made in itself; and, although it is eternal, never ceasing to be made, and, although made, never ceasing to be eternal. [Note: Col. 0677: A omits “and, although made, never ceasing to be eternal.”]

For it does not need another matter that is not itself, in which to make itself. Otherwise it would appear powerless and imperfect in itself if it received from elsewhere the assistance of its manifestation and perfection.

God therefore receives from himself the occasions of his theophanies—that is, of his divine manifestations—because all things are from him, through him, in him, and toward him.

Consequently, the matter from which he is read to have made the world is also from him and in him, and he is in it insofar as it is understood to exist.

Nor is this surprising, since the examples of Scripture teach us this concerning such matters. If the souls of Moses and Samuel [Note: Col. 0679: A reads “Samuel”; C reads “Samuhelis”], although invisible and incorporeal by nature [Note: Col. 0679: A reads “are invisible and incorporeal by nature”], appeared visibly and as if corporeally—not in matter assumed externally, but through themselves and without any intermediary—to the minds of others, truly rather than phantasmatically, namely Moses to the apostles and Samuel to Saul, in order to accomplish mysteries, what prevents us, led by such a miracle as by the hand, from ascending to higher things through the divine power?

Thus, led by such a miracle, we may understand that it is above all things and comes to be in all things, receiving, as we have said, matter neither from elsewhere [Note: Col. 0679: C reads *accipiens* (“receiving”) for *accipientem* (“receiving,” agreeing with the preceding subject)] nor making it from nothing [Note: Col. 0679: C reads *faciens* (“making”) for *facientem* (“making,” agreeing with the preceding subject)], in which it comes to be and makes itself manifest.

Enough has been said about the power of seeds. Although invisible and incomprehensible in itself, it multiplies itself into infinite forms and species [Note: Col. 0679: A reads “and”] and submits itself to bodily senses; yet, when it is sought, it eludes every power of the mind.

Accordingly, no place is granted to that nothing—that is, to the privation of every condition and essence—from which, in the opinion of those who understand less, everything is thought to have been made, because they do not know what holy Theology signifies by that name.

## 18. DISCIPLE

I marvel how what you have now said—although inaccessible to many and remote from those who seem to philosophize—is nevertheless proclaimed as most true by reason itself. The authority of sacred Scripture, too, when considered more attentively, urges and declares the same thing. For it says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”; that is, God the Father, in God the Son, created the universe of the whole visible and invisible creation. And what would the Father create in the Beginning [A reads “what”], begotten from himself, in his Word, in his Son, in his Wisdom, unless it were the Son himself? [A reads “his own” for “begotten from himself”; A adds “his only-begotten” after “his Son”; A omits “his Wisdom.”] Otherwise he would have created it not in him but outside him, receiving it from elsewhere or making it from nothing. Or how could he allow the Word to be made in himself if the Word were not consubstantial with him? For light does not permit darkness received from elsewhere to enter it [A omits “received from elsewhere”], nor does truth receive fiction into itself [C reads “what is not true”]. But what was not always eternal cannot be true; and what was made from the deprivation of all eternity and essence is not eternal.

Or what else would the Father make in his Wisdom except Wisdom itself? For the Prophet says: “You made all things in wisdom.” Observe the force of the words. Did God, as though in some place or space, make a certain structure in his Wisdom—not so that Wisdom itself might substantially become all things, but merely contain all things, and as though one thing were made within another, all things be made in Wisdom? Reason does not teach this, but rather this: “You made all things in wisdom”; that is, “You made your Wisdom all things.” [A reads “for what?” rather than “for did”; A reads “only” rather than “merely.”]

Even the visible sun, although it is simple fire in itself and receives no composition from things that are not consubstantial with it, nevertheless contains and comprehends within itself the nature of all sensible things—not so that it contains in itself something other than itself, but because it itself is substantially everything that contains all things within itself [the phrase “but it itself is substantially everything that contains all things within itself” is added in the margin of C]. For the substance of all visible things has been created in it. It would not consume all the bodies in which it burns, as though in its nourishment, unless it first provided the occasions for their subsistence.

By “sun” I now mean that incomprehensible power which is diffused throughout this whole visible world and is therefore called fire, because it works inwardly in all things. Its greatest source is that ethereal body called by the name “sun,” in which and through which it manifests the clearest powers of its operation—namely, light and heat. It governs all the other bodies that arise and are nourished in the world by its most hidden operations [Gale conjectures “most hidden” for “most secretly”], and it becomes wholly present everywhere [C reads “of the whole”]; made from itself, in itself, and in all things, it visibly bursts forth into all things and invisibly consumes all things into itself [C reads “visibly” for “invisibly”]. [The source has “it becomes”; the conjecture, adopted by Gale, is “let it be” (*sit*), and C likewise reads *sit*.]

Hence Scripture rightly says: “The Spirit proceeds, proceeding in a circuit, and returns to its place.” For the fiery Spirit, by the extraordinary subtlety of its nature, traverses all things, becomes all things in all things, and returns into itself [this whole sentence is omitted in C], because it is the substantial source and origin of all visible things. Therefore the Greeks call it *phoitōn* (φοιτῶν), that is, “returning” [A and C read *phoeton* (φοετον)]. After traversing all worldly bodies, both visibly and invisibly, it returns into itself and recalls into itself all things that receive from it the beginning of their generation.

For this reason the holy theologians often describe the divine, superessential, and formless essence—as Saint Dionysius says—as fire [A reads “describe” rather than “describes”], as possessing, if one may say so, many images of the divine properties in visible things [conjectural reading; C has “as possessing images in invisible things”; A corrected this to “as possessing invisible images”].

## 19.

But I ask you to explain what holy Theology signifies by that name which is “nothing” [C omits “is”].

### MASTER

I believe that name signifies the ineffable, incomprehensible, and inaccessible brightness of divine goodness, unknown to every intellect, whether human or angelic—for it is superessential and supernatural—which, when considered in itself, neither is, nor was, nor will be. It is understood in none of the things that exist, because it surpasses all things. Yet, when through an ineffable condescension it is contemplated by the eyes of the mind in the things that are, it alone is found to be, and is, and was, and will be, in all things [A reads “is found in all things”].

When, therefore, it is understood as incomprehensible, it is not improperly called “nothing” by excellence. But when it begins to appear in its theophanies, it is said to proceed, as it were, from nothing into something; and what is properly considered to exist above every essence is properly known in every essence. Therefore every visible and invisible creature may be called a theophany, that is, a divine manifestation.

For the whole order of natures, from the highest to the lowest—from the heavenly essences down to the furthest bodies of this visible world [A omits “bodies”]—seems to approach the divine brightness in proportion as it is understood more secretly [A reads “as hidden”]. Accordingly, in the theology of the heavenly powers, the inaccessible brightness is often called darkness. Nor is this surprising, since the supreme Wisdom itself, to which they draw near, is very often signified by the name “darkness.” Hear the Psalmist: “For as his darkness is, so also is his light.” As though he plainly said: “So great is the splendor of divine goodness that, for those who wish to contemplate it but are unable to do so, it is not improperly turned into darkness.” For, as the Apostle says, he alone possesses inaccessible light.

But in proportion as the order of things descends farther downward, it opens itself more clearly to the eyes of those who contemplate. Therefore the forms and species of sensible things receive the name of most manifest theophanies [A reads “a most manifest theophany”].

Divine goodness, then, which is called “nothing” because it is found beyond all things that are and all things that are not, in no essence, descends from itself into itself—from the negation of all essences into the affirmation of the essence of the whole universe—as from nothing into something, from non-essentiality into essentiality, from formlessness into innumerable forms and species.

Its first procession into primordial causes, in which it comes to be, is called by Scripture a kind of formless matter [A omits the passage from “into essentiality” through “first”]. It is called matter because it is the beginning of the essence of things [A reads “it is the beginning”], and formless because it is close to the formlessness of divine Wisdom. Divine Wisdom is rightly called formless [A omits “rightly”] because, in forming itself, it does not turn toward any form superior to itself; for it is the infinite exemplar of all forms. When it descends into the various forms of visible and invisible things, it looks toward itself as though toward its own formation.

Accordingly, divine goodness, considered above all things, is said not to be, and to be altogether nothing; but in all things it both is [A reads “to be” rather than “and is”] and is said to be, because it is the essence, substance, genus, species, quality, quantity [A reverses “quantity” and “quality”], bond, position, state, place, time, action, passion, and everything whatever that can be understood by any intellect in every creature and concerning every creature.

And anyone who examines attentively the words of Saint Dionysius will find that these things are so. It does not seem inappropriate to insert a few of them here and to repeat what we received from him in the earlier stages of our discussion, since we judge this necessary. He says:

“Come, let us praise the Good, truly the *Being* and the substantializing principle of all existing things”—for Dionysius himself calls God *On* (ὄν), that is, “Being”—“the cause that, through its superessential power, establishes the whole of being; the Creator of existing subsistence, substance, essence, and nature; the beginning and measure of ages and times; essentiality and eternity of existing things; time of things made; being, in whatever manner things made from the eternal obtain from it; essence and *Being*; time, generation, and the thing made; essentiality in what exists; and subsistence and substance, in whatever manner they exist.

“For God is not *Being* (ὄν), but simply and without limit embraces the whole in himself. Therefore he is also called King of the ages, as the establisher in himself and around himself of the whole of being and of what exists [A reads “he is called King of the ages” and “in himself”].

“And he neither was, nor will be, nor was made, nor is being made, nor will be made—indeed, he is not even ‘is’; rather, he himself is the being of those things that exist. And he is not only the things that exist, but also the very being of those that exist, existing eternally beforehand [A reads “himself” rather than “the very being”].

“For he himself is the age of ages, subsisting before the ages, since being is providentially from him for all existing things and ages. Every age and time, and every existing thing in whatever manner, proceeds from him, who is before all things, the beginning and cause of the whole age, time, and every existing thing. He is the *Being* before all things [A omits “all things”]; all things participate in him, and he withdraws from none of the things that exist. He himself is before all things and establishes all things in himself. Simply, whatever in any manner exists in the One who exists beforehand both is, is understood, and is preserved.

“And a little later, after explaining the primordial causes, he adds, saying:

“‘Being itself is never abandoned by all existing things. Yet being itself is from the One who exists beforehand, and from him comes being, beginning, and measure: the *Being* before essence; the *Being* itself; and, when it possesses being and *Being*, the substantializing beginning, middle, and consummation of what exists, of the age, and of all things. Therefore, in the divine utterances, he who truly exists before *Being* is multiplied according to every understanding of existing things. What was in him, what is, what will be, what has been made, what is being made, and what will be made are properly praised.’

“For all these things, to those who understand them divinely, signify according to every conception that he is superessentially, and that he is the causal principle of all things that exist, everywhere [C reads “of all” rather than “according to all”]. For he is not one thing here and another thing elsewhere; he is not present in one place and absent in another. Rather, he is all things and the cause of all things, embracing and containing in himself all principles, all conclusions, and all existing things [C reads “holding beforehand” for “containing”]. And he is above all things, being superessentially above *Being* before all things.”

## 20.

Whoever understands the force of these words will find that they recommend—or rather proclaim—nothing other than that God himself is the maker of all things and is made in all things. When he is sought above all things, he is found in no essence [A reads “he is not found in essence”], for he is not yet being; but when he is understood in all things, nothing subsists in them except he alone. Nor, as that writer says, is one thing here and another elsewhere; rather, he is all things.

Therefore, descending first from the superessentiality of his nature, in which he is said not to be, he creates himself in the primordial causes [A omits “in the primordial causes”] and becomes the beginning of every essence, every life, every intelligence, and of everything contemplated cognitively in the primordial causes [A reads “the cognitive theory considers”]. Then, descending from the primordial causes—which occupy a kind of middle position between God and creation, that is, between that ineffable superessentiality beyond every intellect and the manifest nature substantially visible to pure minds—he becomes in their effects and is openly revealed in his theophanies. Then, through the manifold forms of effects, he proceeds down to the lowest order of the whole of nature, in which bodies are contained.

Thus, proceeding in an ordered way into all things, he makes all things and becomes all things in all things; he returns into himself, recalling all things into himself; and, while he becomes in all things, he does not cease to be above all things [A omits “thus”].

Thus he makes all things from nothing: from his superessentiality he produces essences; from his supervitality, lives; from his superintellectuality, intellects; and from the negation of all things that are and are not, the affirmations of all things that are and are not.

The return of all things into the cause from which they proceeded teaches this most clearly, when all things will return into God, just as air returns into light, when God will be all in all—not because God is not even now all in all, but because, after the transgression of human nature and its expulsion from the seat of paradise—that is, from the height of spiritual life and from the clearest knowledge of Wisdom—when it had been thrust into the deepest darkness of ignorance, no one can perceive through the vision of true understanding how God is all in all unless he is illumined by divine grace and caught up with Paul into the height of the divine mysteries [AC reads this way; the form of the final phrase is uncertain]. Nor can anyone do so when a cloud of bodily thoughts and the mist of vain fantasies intervene [C reads “various fantasies”], the mind’s vision is weakened by irrational passions, and it is struck back from the splendors of transparent truth [A reads “from transparent truth”] and satisfied with its accustomed bodily shadows.

For we must not believe that the heavenly essences, which have never abandoned the state of eternal blessedness, know anything other than God himself in the whole of creation. For in God and in the primordial causes they perceive all things beyond every sense and intellect, needing none of the works of nature in order to know the truth, but enjoying only the ineffable grace of eternal light.

The Word of God descended in the flesh in order to restore human nature to that vision. He first assumed human nature after its fall, before restoring it to its original state; he healed the wounds of sins, extinguished the shadows of false fantasies, opened the eyes of the mind, and manifested himself in all who are worthy of such a vision.

### DISCIPLE

These matters are very difficult and remote from those who think carnally about corporeal and visible things [A reads “corporeal” rather than “temporal”]. Yet they shine forth most truly and sweetly for those who spiritually ascend beyond visible and temporal things into the knowledge of truth.

For what person living carnally and unwilling to behold the clear light of Wisdom, on hearing such things, would not immediately burst out and cry: “Those who say such things are insane”? [A reads “proclaim” rather than “cry.”] For how can the invisible, incorporeal, incorruptible God, who is above all things, descend from himself and create himself in all things, so that he may be all in all, and proceed even to the furthest dishonors and corruptions of this visible world, and to its vilest forms and species, so that he himself may also be in them, if he is all in all?

The person who says this is ignorant that there can be no dishonor in the universe of the whole creation, that no evil can harm it, and that it cannot be deceived or led astray by any error [A omits “this”]. What occurs in part, God does not permit to occur in the whole; and in the whole universe there is neither dishonor that is dishonorable, nor evil that harms, nor error that errs [A reads “nor is the dishonor of the universe dishonorable”; A omits the second “nor”].

Those who live dishonorably and wickedly, and who go astray from the truth, think dishonorable things honorable, evil things good, things that go astray straight, and crooked things just. When their dishonor, wickedness, and error are removed, everything remains pure, perfect, undefiled, exceedingly good, and free from every error for those who understand rightly.

Nor does such a person consider what sacred Scripture proclaims: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.” By the word “gift” it declares the substantial constitutions of all things; by “perfect gift,” the virtues with which the whole of nature is adorned. And this whole reality—namely, both substance and virtue—descends from above, from the Father of lights, that is, from God, the source of all good things, who flows into all things that are and are not, becomes all things in all things, and without whom nothing can exist.

But, as I think, enough has been said about “nothing,” from which God made all things [A reverses the order: “God made all things from nothing”].

### MASTER

Certainly enough—but only by way of rapid repetition. We do not say these things to refute the understanding of those who think that God made all things from nothing, by which the privation of the whole of being is signified, rather than from that “nothing” by which theologians indicate the superessentiality and supernatural character of divine goodness.

For in theological rules, when the sublimity and incomprehensibility of the divine nature are investigated, the force of negation is more powerful than that of affirmation. If anyone examines this attentively, he will not be surprised that in Scripture God himself is often called by the name “nothing.”

### DISCIPLE

Nor am I surprised, knowing that, according to Saint Dionysius, negations can be applied to the knowledge of God more suitably than affirmations [C reads: “Therefore I am not surprised by this”].

### MASTER

You will not deny, I think, that all the things which Scripture testifies were made from nothing possess one common nature, by participation in which they subsist, each according to its own proportion.

### DISCIPLE

To deny this would be ridiculous. For we believe and understand that God created, simultaneously and at once, the common nature of all things, through participation in which all things come to be [A reads “are”].

### MASTER

Do you think that nature was made from nothing?

### DISCIPLE

I not only think so, but firmly hold that it was produced from nothing and from nowhere else.

### MASTER

Define that nature: what is it?

### DISCIPLE

I cannot. Since it is still infinite, common to all things, and not yet distinguished by definite forms or species, I do not see how it can be defined.

## 21.

### MASTER

What if someone of the highest and holiest authority persuaded you that this nature is nothing other than the Word of God? Would you say that it had been made from nothing [A reverses the word order]? I mean that “nothing” which signifies the privation of all essence, substance, and quality.

### DISCIPLE

By no means. For who would say that the Word of God was made from nothing, when it is the maker of all things from nothing? But who was it who did not fear to say that the nature of all things is the Word of God?

### MASTER

Hear Saint Basil in the eighth Homily on Genesis:

“For when the earth heard, ‘Let it bring forth the herb of grass and the fruit-bearing tree,’ it did not bring forth hidden grass that it possessed, nor did it secretly bring forth a palm, oak, or cypress hidden in its womb and bring it to the surface before our eyes. Rather, the divine Word is the nature of the things that have been made. ‘Let it bring forth’ does not mean that it should draw out what it has, but that it should create what it does not have, God granting the power of operation” [A reads “create”].

Observe how confidently he declared that the nature of all things that have been made is the Word of God. And let no suspicion creep into your mind that the Word of God is one thing and his command another. In him, the very act of being and the command that all things should be are identical [corrected text; A reads “is being”; C reads “being and is”]. For by being itself, all things come to be, because it itself is all things.

And so that you may know more certainly that the Word of God is both the nature of all things and consubstantial with the Father before all things, and created in all things that were made in him, hear Ecclesiastes:

“Who has investigated the Wisdom of God that precedes all things?” Behold, its co-eternity with the Father and its co-essentiality [A reads “co-essential”]. And immediately he continues: “Wisdom was created first of all.” Behold, it was made among creatures.

Hear the Gospel: “What was made in him was life.”

For what is read elsewhere in Solomon—“The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways”—some understand as referring to the incarnation of the Word, others to his birth from the Father; the latter interpretation seems more credible to me.

## 22.

But what am I to say about those who think that the world was made from that “nothing” which signifies the negation of all essence or the privation of all disposition (*habitudinis*)? I do not know. For I do not see why they do not consider the nature of opposites.

Privation cannot exist where there is no possession of essence [A omits “of essence”]. For privation is the privation of a state; and therefore, where a state does not precede, privation does not follow. How, then, do they say that the world was made from privation [A reads “they say that the world was made by privation”; C reads “therefore” rather than “then”]?

If this were true, it would follow that the world possessed some state before it was made. But if so, how could it suffer the privation of its state when it no longer existed? Or, if it existed, how could it have come from its own privation? If, on the other hand, it did not exist at all before it was made, no wise person doubts that it lacked every state [A reads “no one”]. But if it lacked every state, how could it have been made from the privation of a state that it never possessed? [C reads “could have been” rather than “could have been made.”]

The same reasoning applies to the negation of essence. For negation is the complete absence of an existing thing or of something capable of coming to be. Absence is the removal from the senses of something present or capable of becoming present [this sentence is omitted in C]. If, therefore, the world was made from absence, some nature must have preceded it, the privation of whose state or the absence of whose essence became the occasion for making the world [A omits this entire phrase].

And that nature was either God or a creature. If it was God, they will be forced to admit that the world was made from the privation of the divine nature, from the absence of its state or essence. But if it was a creature, it must necessarily have been visible or invisible.

If visible, we must believe that another visible world preceded this one. If invisible, by what reasoning are we compelled to concede that this world was made from the absence of an invisible nature, or that such a nature wholly preceded the world? [C omits the entire preceding passage, from “But if it was a creature” through “preceded the world”; for *eam* (“it”), C reads *etiam* (“also/even”).]

But if sound reason teaches that the universe of the whole visible and invisible nature was made from nothing, and that no nature preceded God himself [A omits the sentence from “But if the universe” through “preceded God”], I do not understand how the world was made from the absence or privation of things that never existed.

If someone should say that by the name “nothing” neither the privation of a state nor the absence of any essence is signified [A reads *praesen[.....]*; the following reading survives only as “[.....] *nihilo*” and is materially damaged], but rather the universal negation of every state, essence, substance, accident, and, simply, of everything that can be said and understood, the conclusion will be as follows:

It is therefore necessary that God be called by this name, since he alone is properly indicated by the negation of all things that are; for he is exalted above everything that can be said and understood, is none of the things that are or are not, and is better known by not knowing.

Accordingly, agreement will be reached between us and the person with whom we seemed to disagree [C reads “seemed to disagree” in the plural].

But if he replies, “I do not mean by ‘nothing’ that negation by which it is denied that God is one of the things that are, but the negation that denies both God and the creature,” he will necessarily admit what he was attempting to deny: that the world was made from the negation or privation of God and the creature [A reads “the privative negation of God”].

For the world was made from formless matter, and formless matter from absolute nothing; consequently, the world too was made from absolute nothing.

For, I think, he will not dare to say that everything that exists is either God, or a creature, or neither God nor a creature [A reads “God is” rather than “either God”]. If he says this, he will be counted among those who say that matter is co-eternal with God, from which, they thought, God made the world.

But if everything that exists is either God or a creature, and no sound-minded wise person would think that the world was made from the negation of God and the creature, only that negation remains as the cause for making the world: the negation which, by removing the whole of creation and exalting God above everything that can be said and understood, declares that he is none of the things that are or are not.

There is a very strong argument for this position. If God and the creature are two things, they either derive from one principle and are therefore of the same nature—for things contrary by nature do not arise from one principle, since they draw the nature of their principle—or they are in themselves two principles opposed to each other [A reads “are themselves opposed to each other”].

For things that are substantial are not two but one. If God and the creature are not two but one and one, they are equal, and neither comes from the other. If they are two, one must necessarily arise from one. But if God arises from no one while the creature arises from God, then one comes from the other and they are not equal [A reads “not rather equal”]. For one is not generated by another one equal to it.

But if the creature comes from God, God will be the cause and the creature the effect. And if nothing is effect except what is made by a cause, it follows that God becomes a cause in his effects. For what proceeds from a cause into its effects is not something alien to its nature, since nothing other than the fiery power itself bursts forth into heat and light [A omits “into” before “light”; C reads “into light”].

But if someone says that one equal thing generates another equal thing—since God the Father, being one, generates God the Son, one equal to himself—let him recognize that he is gravely mistaken.

For the highest and holy Trinity is not one and one and one, but one simple and indivisible reality in three inseparable substances. That one is manifold in power, not in number; it is not some one thing, but universally and infinitely one, and above every one that can be said or understood. Therefore, one person is from one person—not one thing from one thing: the Son from the Father [C reads “one” rather than “one person”].

But our discussion now is not directed against those who hold such doctrines [A reads “those” rather than “these”]. We have proposed only to investigate, as far as our strength permitted, what is signified by that name “nothing,” from which God is believed to have made the world.

Let anyone who wishes to give an account of the constitution of the world choose for his followers what he will teach them. But let us follow the path of our own reasoning. Since we have almost completed our agreement that all things are from God, that God is in all things, and that they were made from nowhere other than him—for all things were made from him, through him, and in him—I ask you to recapitulate clearly and briefly how the fourfold division of the whole of nature is compatible with God [A reads “our agreement is completed” rather than “we have almost completed our agreement”].
