### Literal Dionysian sequence

The source first names God *ὌΝ*, “Being.” Its difficult sequence then reads *Etenim Deus non dum est ὄν*, “For God is not Being,” followed by *sed ipse est esse existentibus*, “but he himself is being for existing things,” and *non existentia solum, sed idipsum esse existentium*, “not existing things only, but the very being of existing things.” The quoted predicate series remains explicit: cause and creator of subsistence, substance, essence, and nature; beginning and measure of ages and times; essentiality, eternity, time, generation, what is made, subsistence, beginning, middle, and consummation. No connective is supplied beyond the printed coordination.

### 23

For in discussions, and especially concerning obscure matters, ἀνακεφαλαίωσις—that is, recapitulation—is of great value; for it briefly and clearly recalls everything previously stated to memory, and makes all that has been done simultaneously manifest to the mind’s gaze.

**MASTER.**  [Col. 0688B] Concerning God, as I think, we had agreed among ourselves that he is the beginning, middle, and end of the whole created universe—not that it is one thing for him to be beginning, another to be middle, and another to be end—for these three are one in him, but because there is a threefold movement of theological contemplation. For the intellect, whether human or angelic, is moved in one way when it considers God to be the beginning of all things; in another way when it knows that all things exist in him and through him, as though in a certain middle; and in another way when it contemplates the end of all things as being in God, and God as the one whom all things desire, in whom they rest, and in whom they live.

Saint Augustine supports this understanding in the eighth book of *The City of God*, chapter three, where he discusses the philosopher Socrates. 

> “He did not want minds polluted by earthly desires to stretch themselves forth and attempt divine things, since he saw them  [Col. 0688C] inquiring into the causes of things, which he believed to be first and supreme only in the will of the one supreme God. Hence he thought that these causes could be grasped only by a purified mind. Therefore he judged that one must persist in purifying one’s life through good morals, so that the mind, freed from the burden of desires that weigh it down, might by its natural vigor raise itself toward eternal things and, through the purity of its understanding, behold the nature of incorporeal and immutable light, where the causes of all created natures live in permanence.”

**DISCIPLE.** It was perfectly agreed, because reason approves it.

**MASTER.** Since, then, we perceive purely concerning the divine nature that it is the beginning and cause of all things—for it is ἄναρχος and ἀναίτιος, that is, without beginning and without cause, since nothing precedes it that could  [Col. 0688D] possess the proportion of a beginning or cause—and since it itself creates the nature of all things of which it is the cause and beginning, we rightly call it the creating nature and not the created nature: for it creates and allows itself to be created by none.

But when we recognize that this same divine nature is the end of all things, beyond which there is nothing, and in which all things subsist eternally and are universally God, we rightly call it neither created nor creating: not created, certainly, because it is created by none; and not creating, because it  [Col. 0689A] has already ceased to create, when all things have been converted into their eternal principles, in which they will remain and do remain eternally, and when they will cease also to be signified by the designation “creature.” For God will be all in all, and every creature will be overshadowed, having been converted into God, just as the stars are overshadowed when the sun rises.

Do you therefore see by what reasoning we can call one and the same nature—namely, the divine nature—not created but creating, according to our consideration of its beginning, but, according to our contemplation of its end, neither created nor creating? 

**DISCIPLE.** I see clearly enough what you mean. Say what remains.

**MASTER.** I think that only the account of the middle remains; this presents itself to its contemplators in two ways. First, when the divine nature is seen both to be created and to create. For it is created by itself in the  [Col. 0689B] primordial causes, and thus creates itself—that is, it begins to appear in its theophanies, wishing to emerge from the most hidden recesses of its nature, in which it is unknown even to itself—that is, it knows itself in no way—because it is infinite, supernatural, superessential, and beyond everything that can and cannot be understood. As it descends into the principles of things, and as though creating itself, it begins to be in something.

Second, when it is perceived in the ultimate effects of the primordial causes, in which it is rightly proclaimed to be created only, but not to create. For it is created as it descends into the ultimate effects, beyond which it creates nothing; and therefore it is said to be created only and not to create. For it does not descend beyond the ultimate effects, where it would be seen both to be created and to create. Thus it is created and  [Col. 0689C] creates in the primordial causes; but in their effects it is created and does not create. And not without reason, since in them it establishes the end of its descent—that is, of its manifestation.

Therefore every corporeal and visible creature, subject to the senses, is customarily called in Scripture, not inappropriately, the ultimate vestige of the divine nature. Every contemplative mind, like a certain Moses ascending to the summit of contemplation, is permitted to behold it; yet even now it can scarcely be discerned clearly by wise minds, because the smoke of earthly imaginings, the noises of changeable things, and the flashes of things suddenly arising and suddenly passing away, obstruct them. 

For it belongs to very few—those completely withdrawn from earthly thoughts and  [Col. 0689D] purified by virtue and knowledge—to recognize God in these visible creatures. Thus the patriarch Abraham recognized him through the revolutions of the stars, under the guidance of the natural law; and so did the other holy Fathers before the written law and under the law, as Moses did in the bush and on the summit of the mountain. After the law, under grace, the Apostles were introduced with Christ on the mountain into divine mysteries through invisible realities presented as visible symbols.

I say this because  [Col. 0690A] the Apostles saw the Lord’s transformation in the spirit. His garments, white as snow, signified visible creation, in which and through which the Word of God, who subsists in all things, is understood. Hear the Apostle saying: “His invisible things are understood and seen from the creation of the world through the things that have been made, and so also his eternal power and eternity.” 

**DISCIPLE.** Now I see most clearly the fourfold division of universal nature, and I understand with certainty that it is said to be of God and in God. Therefore, since this question concerning nothingness has been completed and, as I think, brought to a clear conclusion, I judge that we must return to the consideration of the third part of universal nature, which is said to be created only and not to create. For this is what our proposed plan promises. Although  [Col. 0690B] certain other questions have been introduced, it nevertheless supplied the principal matter of the third book; for the sake of investigating it more carefully, the contemplation of other propositions was incidentally inserted.

### 24

**MASTER.** You judge rightly, and the time demands it. But first we must fulfill what we promised concerning the sixfold quantity of the intelligible days, during which God is read to have made his works. What follows will be stated briefly, partly by following the understanding of the holy Fathers, and partly without concealing what comes into my mind from him who illumines our darkness, and who seeks that he be sought and found in his Scriptures.

For the infinite creator of sacred Scripture in the minds of the prophets, the Holy Spirit, established infinite meanings in it. Therefore the sense of one interpreter does not  [Col. 0690C] take away the sense of another, provided that what each says accords with sound faith and Catholic confession, whether he receives it from elsewhere or discovers it by himself—though in either case he finds it as one illuminated by God.

**DISCIPLE.** Proceed in whatever order you wish, and draw me along with you. I shall follow you so that I may come to know either the understanding of others or your own in such matters, and I shall choose what true reason—which seeks and finds truth in all things—teaches. I do not say this because I am already capable of distinguishing true understandings from false ones, but because, with truth consulted, I may venture without rashness to prefer what is more like the truth to what is less like it.

**MASTER.** I too would approve nothing rashly or without consideration. The divine prophet Moses, briefly writing about the creation of the primordial causes of visible and invisible things simultaneously and at once, says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”  [Col. 0690D] He signifies their hidden and incomprehensible magnificence in the divine plan, before they flowed forth into forms and species, by calling them “the empty and vacant earth,” or “the invisible and unformed,” and also “darkness over the abyss.” He further indicates the beginning of the procreation of the pre-established causes into their effects by the designation of the Spirit who “was brooding over the waters,” or “was borne above the waters.” Then, to unfold the mystical power of  [Col. 0691A] the number six, he proceeds, saying: “And God said: Let there be light, and there was light.”

In these words a variety of understandings among the holy Fathers is found. Some discern that the creation of the angelic and intellectual heavenly essence is signified here in sacred Scripture. Others, however, understand the nature of this visible light to be meant—that is, fire, at that time still incomprehensible and invisible, created. This fire afterward, as though emerging from its own sources, shone forth in the ethereal bodies and, as though traversing the spaces of three days by a hidden course, illumined the abyss, which, as they say, was spread everywhere over the surface of the earth.

No one should find it surprising that an invisible and hidden fiery nature was called “light,” provided that he knows that  [Col. 0691B] sacred Scripture customarily calls effects by the name of causes and causes by the name of effects. The effect of fiery nature is light. Thus fiery nature, created at the beginning of things, was not inappropriately called by the name of the light that would later proceed from it and that was still hidden within it, although some believe that the primordial light shone immediately. Saint Augustine has sufficiently argued against them 

Those who think that the nature of corporeal light  [Col. 0691C] was created when it was said, “And God said: Let there be light, and there was light,” believe that what follows—“And God saw the light, that it was good, and he divided the light from the darkness, and he called the light day and the darkness night, and there was evening and morning, one day”—was spoken simply as praise of corporeal light and of the temporal intervals during which light and shadow alternate around the earth.

Since it is believed that the world was first created at the spring equinox, when the sun remains for equal intervals above and below the earth—namely, twelve equinoctial hours—these interpreters think that Scripture says, “God divided the light from the darkness,” as though it were plainly saying: “He divided the whole span of one day, which is completed in twenty-four hours, equally between day and night.” 

Those who more correctly maintain, following Saint Augustine, that the creation of the angelic nature is signified by the creation of light understand the division of light from darkness either as the distinction between unformed matter and formed creation—so that by “light” the perfection of form is understood, and by “darkness” the confusion of the unformed—or as a twofold contemplation of  [Col. 0691D] the heavenly essences. 

For the creature is considered in one way in its eternal principles in God, according to which it was created, and in another way in itself under God, insofar as it is a creature. The first consideration is signified by the word “light,” and the second by “darkness.” For just as light precedes darkness in dignity, so the splendor of the eternal principles according to which every creature was made is placed before  [Col. 0692A] the obscurity of the creature considered in itself.

Therefore God called the light “day,” namely, the splendor of the divine principles, and the darkness “night,” that is, the more obscure appearance of created nature in itself. What follows—“And there was evening and morning, one day”—they wish to signify the end of the completed operation and the beginning of the following one. For morning, that is, the beginning of the following operation, is the end of the preceding one; and the limit of the preceding operation is the beginning of the following one. Thus one or the first day ends in the evening, whose morning—that is, whose beginning—had preceded in the creation of light.

We have received these brief statements from others. 

### 25

We, however, wishing to understand the creation of the primordial causes, whether visible or invisible, in the making of  [Col. 0692B] heaven and earth “in the beginning,” and their progress into their effects in the words of sacred Scripture, “Let there be light,” and what follows, say that the procession of the primordial causes into their effects is signified by the creation of light.

For if Scripture declares that the primordial causes themselves, because of the incomprehensibility of their nature and their height unknown to every intellect, were covered by the gloom of darkness—that is, by the density of profound ignorance—when it says, “And darkness was over the abyss,” what is surprising if their disclosure in their effects through forms and species is proclaimed under the name of light in the words, “And God said: Let there be light, and there was light”? 

It is as though someone were saying:  [Col. 0692C] God commanded the primordial causes, invisible in themselves and overshadowing every intellect, to emerge into perceptible forms and intelligible and sensible species of visible and invisible things. For, according to Saint Dionysius, not only God but also the principles of all things are customarily called “darkness” in the sacred utterances because of their incomprehensible infinity. 

His procession through the principles into visible and invisible creatures—I mean, his theophanies—has deserved to be signified by the name “clarity”; for in them he who surpasses every intellect is understood in a certain way.

“Let there be light,” God says—that is, let the primordial causes proceed from the incomprehensible secrets of their nature into forms and species that can be comprehended and that are manifest to the intellects contemplating them. “And there was light”: when God willed and spoke, the darkness of the primordial causes  [Col. 0692D] proceeded into open forms and species. 

“And God divided the light from the darkness”—that is, he separated knowledge of the effects from the obscurity of their principal causes. For the division of light from darkness is the discernment of things appearing through forms and species from their principles, in which they surpass every intellect. 

Therefore Scripture first said, “And God saw the light, that it was good”—that is, it pleased God that the original causes,  [Col. 0693A] established beyond every intellect before all creation, should be manifested to human or angelic intellects, suffused with a certain light of understanding.

“And he called the light day, and the darkness night”—that is, he granted contemplative minds to call the manifestation of visible and invisible things through forms and species “day,” while calling their incomprehensible height in their principles, unknown to every created intellect, “night.”

“And there was evening and morning, one day.” Although a division and distinction is understood between the obscurity of the causes and the clarity of the effects, it is nevertheless one and the same day—that is, one understanding of them. For one creature is not understood as having been made in the causes and another as having been established in the effects of the causes. Rather,  [Col. 0693B] one and the same creature was made in the eternal principles, as though in certain darknesses of the most secret wisdom, removed from every intellect, and was manifested in the processions of those principles into effects, where it submits to intellects, as though in a certain day of perfect knowledge. 

I have added these remarks concerning the works of the first intelligible day with what I consider a fitting proportionality of understandings—not because I wish to place my own sense, discovered as though from myself, above the understandings of others, far from it, but because I observe that it does not strongly resist true contemplations and that it accords with the outpourings of the primordial causes into their effects, which is what we are now discussing. 

**DISCIPLE.** Since many have expounded the works of the six first days, both in Greek and in Latin, we must now discuss them briefly and concisely.  [Col. 0693C] What you have said concerning the first light seems sufficient to me. Whether it signifies the substantial creation of this corporeal light in fire, as Saint Basil thinks; or the formation of the heavenly powers, as Saint Augustine thinks; or the general procession of the primordial causes into their effects, whoever possesses any one of these understandings will not be far from the truth. 

### 26

**MASTER.** Let us therefore pass to the consideration of the second day. First, however, it must be said that we have no present intention of allegorical understandings involving moral interpretations; rather, with God as our guide, we are attempting to discuss briefly only the historical creation of created things. 

**DISCIPLE.** Nor am I asking for that; the holy Fathers have already dealt sufficiently with such allegory.

**MASTER.**  [Col. 0693D] “And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters. And God made the firmament.”

Concerning the firmament, everyone agrees that under this name nothing other than the visible heaven is signified. Some, however, maintain that the name includes only that outermost revolving sphere which surrounds the entire world on every side and is adorned with the choirs of stars; others,  [Col. 0694A] the entire space beyond the moon, where the bodies and courses of the planets are believed to be, together with the outermost circuit of the stars; and others, the entire void that revolves around the earth—that is, the air, the ether, and the highest sphere—all comprehended under the single word “firmament.”

For, as they say, the creation of air and ether is not read of elsewhere. Why it is called by such a name, each interpreter explains according to his own judgment. Some say that it is so called because it supports the waters above, as though corporeal waters were situated above it; others, because it supports the choirs of stars, as though they were certain heavy bodies; others, because it contains and strengthens the whole visible world within itself.

There are also those who wish the name properly to designate the space of the denser air, because it supports clouds, rains, showers, snows,  [Col. 0694B] hail, and everything else that arises in it from earthly vapors, insofar as it can support them, through a certain firm density of its nature. They think that, as though the whole were named from a part, the other spaces of the lighter and higher visible nature are designated from it.

I leave it to the judgment of readers to decide which of these understands the matter more correctly. For my part, considering the force of the Greek name στερέωμα, this designation seems to me to have been deserved because the position of the whole corporeal creation stands and terminates in it. For beyond the firmament nothing sensible, corporeal, local, or temporal is understood to exist. The end of all visible things is established in the firmament.

Στερέωμα is said as though from στερεὰ ἅμα, that is, “solid things together”. For in it all solid things—that is, all corporeal things—terminate and  [Col. 0694C] stand together.

Concerning the waters in whose midst God said that the firmament was to be made, I do not find enough to say—not because I am unaware of what many of the holy Fathers thought about them. Saint Basil in his *Hexaemeron* seems to wish those waters to be understood as having been called by the name “abyss”: waters diffused around the earth on every side, extremely rarefied and tenuous, over which darkness first lay and then the Spirit of God was borne; in them the primordial light shone, as though revolving through the space of three days, illuminating the still unformed mass of the earth. On the third day these waters were thickened and gathered into one place, so that dry land might appear. He wishes the firmament to have been made by God in their midst.

Saint Augustine entirely rejects this understanding, yet he did not sufficiently explain the nature of those waters within which God  [Col. 0694D] made the firmament. Introducing the opinions of others, he did not reveal what he himself understood, for what reason I do not know. He prefers to the others those who argue that the spaces of air between the marine and river waters situated below and the waters suspended in clouds above are called by the name “firmament.” 

Rejecting no one’s understanding, I shall explain briefly, if it pleases you, what I have thought concerning  [Col. 0695A] those waters. 

**DISCIPLE.** It does please me, and it is very necessary. For concerning this question no one has yet persuaded me of anything that seemed sufficient to me.

**MASTER.** I therefore think that the whole of created nature has a threefold dimension. Everything that has been created is either wholly body, or wholly spirit, or some intermediate reality that is neither wholly body nor wholly spirit, but which, by a certain relation of the middle and the extremes, receives within itself, proportionally, something of wholly spiritual nature from one extreme, the higher one, and something from the other extreme—that is, from the wholly corporeal and lower one—and thus subsists properly and naturally according to its extremes. 

If anyone examines the matter attentively, he will understand that  [Col. 0695B] this world is constituted in this threefold proportionality. For insofar as it is considered in its principles, in which it is eternally constituted and essentially subsists, it is known to be not only spiritual but wholly spirit. No one who philosophizes correctly would deny that the principles of corporeal nature are spiritual—or rather, are spirits.

But when its lowest parts are examined downward—that is, all these bodies composed of the universal (“catholic”) elements, especially earthly and aquatic bodies, which are subject to generation and corruption—nothing other than wholly body and corporeal is found in them.

If, however, someone considers the nature of the simple elements, he will find, clearer than light, a certain proportionate middle: they are not wholly bodies, although  [Col. 0695C] through their corruption natural bodies subsist from their conjunction; nor are they devoid of corporeal nature, since all bodies flow forth from them and are again resolved into them.

And again, compared with the other, higher extreme [the printed wording *alterum alterisuperiori* is defective], they are not wholly spirits, because they are not wholly separated from their corporeal extremity; nor are they wholly non-spiritual, because they receive the occasions of their subsistence from entirely spiritual principles.

Thus we have not unreasonably said that this world possesses certain extremes completely separated from one another, and middle regions in which the harmonious concord of the universe is joined together. 

Let us therefore posit the lower parts of this world as the lower waters. And not without reason, since everything that is born in this world grows and  [Col. 0695D] is nourished by moisture. For when the moist quality is removed from bodies, they immediately wither and diminish and are reduced almost to nothing. Indeed, the sages of the world affirm that even the heavenly bodies, exceedingly hot and fiery, are nourished by the moist nature of waters; nor do the interpreters of sacred Scripture deny this.

Reason teaches that the spiritual principles of all visible things are called by the name  [Col. 0696A] “upper waters.” For from them all the elements, whether simple or composite, flow as from certain great springs, and from them they are administered, watered by a certain intelligible power.

Nor does Scripture keep silent about this, crying out: “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of God.” Although someone may understand this of the heavenly powers, it does not conflict with the interpretation just given, since the divine utterances admit of a multiple interpretation.

Therefore God said that the firmament was to be made in the midst of these waters—that is, the nature of the simple elements, which surpasses visible bodies to the extent that it is surpassed by their invisible principles; and to the extent that it receives from the higher, it distributes to the lower; and to the extent that it receives from the lower, it restores to the higher, returning to them  [Col. 0696B] everything that has flowed down from them.

The Lawgiver, instructed by the prophetic Spirit, called it “firmament” for this reason. By its firm and inseparable simplicity it supports the abyss of the intelligible principles placed above it; while it draws back into itself the flow of mutable bodies, especially those composed of dry and moist qualities, as they are dissolved through temporal alternation, and preserves them in its universal solidity so that they may not perish.

Nor are these things unknown to those trained in philosophical studies, who recognize the transfusion of natures into one another. Causes descend into elements, elements into bodies, and dissolved bodies recoil through the elements into their causes; bodies themselves also pass into one another. In the Flood, air was changed into water, and water again returned into air.

Thus God said: “Let there be a firmament  [Col. 0696C] in the midst of the waters”—that is, let there be a solidity of the simple elements between the depth of their own principles and the mutable flow of bodies composed by their commingling—and “let it divide the waters from the waters”—that is, let it distinguish composite bodies, dispersed in places, mutable in time, and assigned to generation and corruption, from the simple principles that lack the variation of places and times and are free from generation and corruption, established by immutable law.

There is this difference between the simplicity of the causes and that of the elements: the simplicity of the causes is understood without the nature of places and times, whereas the simplicity of the elements cannot be without places and times; for it is contained in them. Moreover, the former is always free from all accidents, while the latter at times receives accidents and at times lays them aside. It lays them aside  [Col. 0696D] in universal things and receives them in particular things.

The lemmata and their English meanings identify the passages; entries follow source order.

- libro octavo — in the eighth book. [Note: [Col. 0687] C omits *libro*, “book.”]
- unius et summi Dei — of the one and supreme God. [Note: [Col. 0687] C reads *ac* for *et*, both “and.”]
- Unde et — hence also. [Note: [Col. 0687] A omits *et*, “also.”]
- Perplane — very clearly. [Note: [Col. 0687] A reads *Plane*, “clearly.”]
- divinam videlicet — namely, divine. [Note: [Col. 0689] A reads *scilicet divinam*, “namely, divine,” changing the explanatory word and order.]
- in primordialibus causis — in the primordial causes. [Note: [Col. 0689] C reads *in seipsa a primord.*, “in itself from the primordial [causes],” with the final word abbreviated in the note.]
- superessentialis — superessential. [Note: [Col. 0689] A reads *superaeternalis*, “beyond eternity.”]
- seipsam creans in — creating itself in. [Note: [Col. 0689] C reads *seipsam creans seipsam in*, “creating itself, itself in,” repeating *seipsam*.]
- et non creare — and not to create, after the final effects. [Note: [Col. 0689] A omits *et*, “and.”]

27. In general, however, throughout all the works of the first six days it must be understood that wherever Scripture says, “God said: Let there be light,” “Let there be a firmament,” and so forth on the remaining days, the special formation of the primordial causes is signified; their universal creation was previously indicated by the name “heaven and earth” [Col. 0697A]. Wherever, however, it says, “And there was light,” “And God made the firmament,” and “And it was so,” the procession of those same primordial causes into their effects, according to genera and species, is signified.

“And God called the firmament Heaven.” According to the etymology of the Roman language, *caelum* (“heaven”) is said to derive from the depiction of the stars, as though from something chiseled or engraved, as Pliny believes; according to the Greek derivation, however, it is called οὐρανός (*ouranos*), as though from ὅρος ἄνω (*horos anō*), that is, “vision from above.” Properly, therefore, the firmament of the universal elements is called οὐρανός, that is, “heaven,” because by the height of its nature it surpasses every composite and corporeal creature.

There are some who think that the thinnest waters exist above the firmament, that is [Note: [Col. 0697] A *i. e.*], above the courses of the stars; but they are refuted both by the theory of weights and by the order of the elements [Note: [Col. 0697] C *refellet* (“will refute”).]. Others argue from the pallor of the stars that vaporous, almost incorporeal waters exist above heaven [Note: [Col. 0697] *veluti* omitted in A]. For they say [Note: [Col. 0697] *enim* omitted in A] that the stars are cold [Note: [Col. 0697] A *et* (“and”)] and therefore pale. But, they say, coldness does not exist where the substance of water is absent. They give insufficient consideration to what they are saying; for wherever fire exists substantially, there too is coldness. No wise person, indeed, would say that crystal, although of a cold nature, lacks fiery power, which penetrates all bodies.

Thus fiery power, where it burns, is heat; where it does not burn, it is cold. It burns only where there is matter in which it can burn and which it can consume [Note: [Col. 0697] A *sit materia* (“there is matter”)]. For this reason the rays of the sun, diffused through the ethereal regions, do not burn: in that most subtle and spiritual nature they do not find matter for burning [Note: [Col. 0697] A *et* (“and”)]. When, however, they descend [Note: [Col. 0697] A *vero* (“however”)] into the regions of the corporeal air, as though they had found a certain material for their operation [Col. 0697C], they begin to blaze; and the more they reach denser bodies, the more they exercise their force by burning in those things that are dissolved, or can be dissolved, by the power of heat [Note: [Col. 0697] A *aut* (“or”)]. But when they are raised upward toward the outermost extremities of the world, where the substance is exceedingly subtle and close to spiritual nature, they find no material for blazing and produce no heat, displaying only the operation of illumination.

Therefore the ethereal, pure, and spiritual heavenly bodies established there are always luminous, but are believed to be without heat and consequently cold and pale [Note: [Col. 0697] A *et* (“and”)]. Accordingly, that planet called Saturn, because it is near the courses of the stars [Note: [Col. 0697] A *est vicinus* (“is near”)], is said to be pale and cold [Note: [Col. 0697] C reads: “that one called … near … pale and cold”]. The solar body, however, since it occupies the middle region of the world, is understood to possess a certain midpoint: whatever, as the philosophers say, is the distance from earth to sun, the same is the distance from sun to the stars [Col. 0697D] [Note: [Col. 0697] C *tantum solem* (“the same [distance] [from] the sun”)]. From the lower natures it receives a certain corporeality, but from the higher natures a spiritual subtlety for its subsistence [Note: [Col. 0697] A *substantiam* (“substance”)]. Thus it gathers within itself, as it were, the contrary qualities of both parts of the world, the higher and the lower. Through the tension between them, like a kind of balance [Col. 0698A], it is prevented from leaving its natural position: the heaviness of the lower part does not allow it to rise upward, while the lightness of the higher part does not allow it to incline downward.

Accordingly, it appears to have a brilliant color, a color midway between pale and red [Note: [Col. 0697] C *rubrumque* (“and red”)], receiving part of its brilliance from the pallor of the cold stars above and part from the redness of the hot bodies below, in a blending of its splendor [Note: [Col. 0697] C *in contemperantia* (“in a blending”)]. The planets that revolve around it change their colors according to the quality of the regions through which they travel—I mean Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury—which always complete their circuits around the sun, as Plato teaches in the *Timaeus*. Thus, when they are above the sun, they display bright faces; when below it, red ones.

The pallor of the stars, therefore, does not compel us in any way to understand that the element of water exists above heaven, since that pallor itself arises from the absence of heat. But since it would take too long to explain these matters, let us return to the subject, whatever the reasoning of nature requires [Note: [Col. 0697] A *quantum* (“as much as”)].

“And there was evening and morning, one day” [Note: [Col. 0697] A *secundus* (“the second”)]. The interpretation is the same as the one we gave earlier concerning the completion of the first day [Note: [Col. 0697] *in* omitted in A; A has *consummationem* (“completion”)]. For although one contemplation concerns the spiritual principles of the world in the primordial causes, another concerns the simple and universal elements, and another concerns composite and particular bodies [Note: [Col. 0697] A “the contemplation of spiritual things is”], there is nevertheless one and the same understanding of the entirety of the whole world. This explanation must also be observed on the other days, wherever the phrase “And there was evening and morning, one day” occurs [Note: [Col. 0697] C “on the remaining days”]. Enough has been said about the second day, insofar as brevity requires.

**DISCIPLE.** Enough indeed, and plausible, although it is unknown to many, almost to everyone [Note: [Col. 0697] A *et* (“and”)].

**TEACHER.** It follows, then, that we should speak briefly about the third day.

“And God said: Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear; and it was so.”

The opinion concerning the gathering of the waters into one place that most interpreters of this Scripture follow, having received it from Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, is known to everyone. It readily occurs to anyone who considers the matter [Note: [Col. 0697] A *eam facillime* (“it most readily”)], since they suppose that the infinitely extensive waters, previously diffused on every side around the still unformed and invisible mass of the earth, still filling the regions of the air and ether and shining with the circuit of the primordial light, were on the third day gathered into one place in a very thin, almost vaporous mass. They believe that the firmament was made in the midst of this mass on the second day [Note: [Col. 0697] A “made on the second day”], and that the upper portion of the waters was suspended above it; while the lower diffusions of the aforesaid abyss were collected into one place—that is, gathered within their shores into the circuit of the ocean [Note: [Col. 0697] A *inter* (“between”); A *inclusi* (“enclosed”)], so that the dry land might appear and room might be given to the air and ether.

But this opinion, when truth is consulted, seems to waver on many grounds and to be altogether incoherent [Col. 0699A], answering only to false imaginings. For, following Saint Augustine, we neither believe nor judge it consistent with truth that the earthly mass was first created, or that the abyss was diffused around it on every side [Note: [Col. 0699] A *illam* (“it”)], and that afterward the firmament was made in the midst of the waters, and afterward the lower waters remaining under heaven were gathered into one place; nor [Note: [Col. 0699] A omits *neque* (“nor”)] do we believe that any one of these events preceded another locally or temporally [Note: [Col. 0699] A *processisse* (“proceeded”)]. For all these things, and the nature of the other visible things, were created simultaneously and at once, ordered and established in their own times and places. The generation of any one of them into forms and species, quantities and qualities, did not temporally anticipate the generation of another by any intervening delay; rather, they all proceeded simultaneously from their eternal principles, in which they subsist essentially [Note: [Col. 0699] A *existunt* (“exist”)] in the Word of God, each according to its genus, species, and individual numbers.

The quantity of six, namely, the six first days, and their intelligible division, is understood with respect to the causes of created things and their first simultaneous impulse into the constitution of this world. What was made simultaneously and at once by the Creator is distinguished by the Holy Spirit through the prophet by the perfection of the number six—not temporally, but by an intelligible distinction—so that through the power of the number the perfection of the divine operation might be indicated [Note: [Col. 0699] C *eo* (“by this”); A *semel et simul* (“at once and simultaneously”)]. This number is fulfilled by its parts: neither does the whole exceed its parts, nor do the parts exceed the whole.

For just as the voice precedes the word not in time but in cause—for the word is made from the voice, as a body is formed from a certain unformed matter [Col. 0699C]—so, from causes that were still unknown and, as it were, still lacking visible forms [Note: [Col. 0699] C retains *adhuc* (“still”); A: “as though invisible, still lacking forms”], the creation of all visible things was brought forth simultaneously into forms and numbers of places and times, with no intervals of time or intervening places [Note: [Col. 0699] A *conditis* (“of created things”)].

And just as the one who made the world from unformed matter did not receive the matter from elsewhere, from which he might make it [Note: [Col. 0699] A *fecerat* (“had made”)], but received and made it from himself and in himself [Note: [Col. 0699] A *de seipso* (“from himself”)], so neither did he seek places outside himself in which to make it, nor did he look to times whose intervals would allow him to carry out his work. He made everything in himself, who is the place of all things, the time of times, and the age of ages. He worked upon everything simultaneously, for everything was made in the twinkling of an eye.

Indeed, even those things that have received, are receiving, or will receive generation through the courses of time were made simultaneously and at once in him, in whom past, present, and future are simultaneously and at once one [Note: [Col. 0699] A “future things are one, simultaneously and at once”].

Rejecting the opinion just mentioned, therefore, we ask what sort of waters those were that were under heaven and were gathered into one place, and what that one place is. The sensible waters commonly called sea, abyss, or ocean [Note: [Col. 0699] A *et* (“and”) in each instance], as soon as they burst forth from their hidden causes [Col. 0700A], appeared in their proper species, quantity, and quality, in their own place—that is, between the earth and the air nearest to the earth—enclosed by their shores. Partly they flowed secretly in the bosom of the earth, as though in the pores of some immense body; partly they openly covered its surface. When they had been dispersed in the places where they were, they did not yet have one proper place into which they might afterward be compressed and beyond whose fixed boundaries they would not pass.

For [Note: [Col. 0699] A omits *enim* (“for”)] the four principal bodies of this world, composed from the four simple elements—I mean earth, water [Note: [Col. 0699] A omits *et* (“and”)], air, and ether—together with all that was made in them and from them, received [Note: [Col. 0699] A *accipiunt* (“receive”)] simultaneously and at once their forms, places, numbers, times, intervals, distinctions, properties, measures [Col. 0700B], weights, and everything that is perceived in them, or surpasses the senses and is understood, or escapes the intellect [Note: [Col. 0699] A *et* (“and”)].

But if someone gives physical explanations of such matters, because they cannot be grasped by bodily sense by those who think only about sensible things [Note: [Col. 0699] A “only sensible things”], he will either be despised as saying nothing, or will be thought by those ignorant of nature to be allegorizing [Note: [Col. 0699] C *nescientes* (“those who are ignorant”)]. For physics considers the substantial principles of nature, whereas ethics considers its rational or irrational movements.

**DISCIPLE.** Explain, I beg you, whatever seems plausible to you concerning the resolution of this question, and fear no one, whatever the result [Note: [Col. 0699] A *quomodo* (“however”) for *quoquo modo*]—whether someone, struck by the light of truth, does not understand what you say [Note: [Col. 0699] A *quid* (“what”); A *non percussus* (“not struck”)] [Note: [Col. 0699] A *quid* (“what”); A *non percussus* (“not struck”)], or [Note: [Col. 0699] A *aut* (“or”)] despises it, corrupted by the poison of envy [Note: [Col. 0699] A “by the poison of envy”], or quarrels contentiously out of zeal for ancient opinions.

**TEACHER.** After the account of the constitution of the world—namely, of its extreme parts, whether mutually unlike or distinct [Note: [Col. 0699] A *illius* (“of that [world]”)], by which I mean the incorporeal and simple principles according to which it was created, and the composite bodies subject to generation and corruption and also to places and times—these extremities having been called “waters” for the reasons stated above, and after the account of the middle, namely, the four elements that received the name of firmament or heaven [Col. 0700C], the prophetic intention seems to descend toward contemplation of that same weaker part, namely, all corruptible bodies, as toward the third theory of created nature.

First [Note: [Col. 0699] A *Imo* (“indeed”)], in general, it expressed the procession of the primordial causes into their effects from the unknown and secret recesses of nature, as though from certain darkness, into the clear light of manifold forms, perceptible to the intellects of those contemplating them or manifest to the senses [Col. 0700D] [Note: [Col. 0699] A *intellectibus* (“to intellects”)]. Then, in a second act of contemplation, considering the threefold constitution of the world—namely, in its principles and universal elements, and in particular and composite bodies—it arrived at the consideration of those soluble and corruptible bodies that occupy the lowest place in the whole of creation.

Since, therefore, there is a threefold consideration of all bodies composed from the conjunction of the four simple elements, extending from the greatest to the smallest [Col. 0701A] [Note: [Col. 0701] A “there is a consideration”], for matter is examined in one way, and in another way the form and species which, when added to matter, produces every solid and sensible body—for matter alone, lacking species, completes no body [Note: [Col. 0701] A rearranges: *efficit; sola siquidem* (“produces; for matter alone”)], since it is for itself unformed, but when species is added, a complete body comes to be [Note: [Col. 0701] *corpus* (“body”) omitted in C; *perfectum* (“complete”) omitted in A]—and in yet another way essence and substantial form, which, like an immovable foundation, shapes, supports, and contains formed matter [Note: [Col. 0701] A *materiam* (“matter”)], it was necessary to distinguish substantial form from formed matter by rational contemplation.

I called the greatest bodies earth, water, air, ether, and heaven. In them the quantity of innumerable greatest, middle, and smallest bodies is multiplied [Note: [Col. 0701] Conjecture; A *minorum* (“smaller”); C *aliorum* (“other”); A *numerorum* (“numbers”)]. Yet [Note: [Col. 0701] A *tunc* (“then”)] all these—the greatest, middle, and smallest—are constituted from four most pure, simple, and invisible elements in themselves [Note: [Col. 0701] A *invisibilibus*, with *-que* omitted], since they are resolved into them. For no element is apprehended by corporeal sense in itself.

If, then, as has been demonstrated by the arguments stated above, those four pure elements deserved to be called “firmament” [Note: [Col. 0701] A omits *firmamenti* (“of firmament”)] or “heaven” by Scripture [Note: [Col. 0701] A *scripturis* (“by the Scriptures”)], on account of the simple power of their nature, then clearly all bodies constituted by them and beneath them through their ineffable conjunction can be included under the name of “the waters placed under heaven.” And not without reason: for they are not only mutable, but are also subject to generation and corruption.

For even those bodies [Note: [Col. 0701] A *Illa etenim* (“for those indeed”)] called heavenly or ethereal [Col. 0701C], although they appear to be spiritual and incorruptible, must nevertheless, since they began to come into being through generation and composition [Note: [Col. 0701] A *tunc* (“then”)], reach the end of their dissolution and corruption [Note: [Col. 0701] A *tunc* in place of *tamen* (“nevertheless”)]. If heavenly bodies await the necessary dissolution of themselves, as Truth says, “Heaven and earth will pass away” [Note: [Col. 0701] A *peribunt* (“will perish”)], and [Note: [Col. 0701] A *item* (“likewise”)] the Psalmist says, “The heavens are the works of your hands; they themselves will perish,” together with similar testimonies of Holy Scripture, what must be thought about the lowest bodies of the world, which are born and dissolved every day?

Therefore, if in every body—whether heavenly, earthly, or aquatic—one observes the unstable inundation of unformed matter, for matter is defined as “the mutability of mutable things, capable of all forms,” and as “the instability of mutable form,” by which matter itself is formed when it is given specific form; for it is itself qualitative form that, when joined to matter, produces a body [Note: [Col. 0701] C *adjecta materie* (“matter having been added”)]. By “qualitative form” I mean that which, derived from quality and quantity, appears to bodily senses and, clinging to the instability of matter [Note: [Col. 0701] A *instabili* (“unstable”)], undergoes continual fluctuation together with it, suffering generation and corruption [Col. 0702A], receiving increase and diminution through quantities and qualities, and yielding to the many and [Note: [Col. 0701] A *et* (“and”)] different variations that arise externally from the quality of places, airs, humors, foods, and similar circumstances—does it not seem plausible and consistent with right reason that this very mutability of matter, together with the qualitative form clinging to it and undergoing the same fever of continual and turbulent fluctuation, is signified figuratively by “the waters placed under heaven,” namely, the simple elements? [Note: [Col. 0701] A reads: “that the mutability of matter itself, together with the qualitative form that clings to it and undergoes the continual heat of turbulent fluctuation, ought to be signified by the name of the waters placed under heaven?”]

Substantial form, however, or species, subsisting immutably in its own genus [Note: [Col. 0701] A omits *in* (“in”)] and which [Note: [Col. 0701] C *et* (“and”) for *quae* (“which”)] in no way undergoes mutability together with the body composed of matter and qualitative form [Note: [Col. 0701] C *sumit* (“takes on”) instead of *patitur* (“undergoes”)]—for it does not begin with the body, although it is born in the body, and without the body remains essentially by itself in its own genus; nor does it perish with the body, since no essence, power, or operation can be corrupted or changed together with corruptible and mutable things, being strengthened by the proper supports of its nature [Note: [Col. 0701] A omits *omnis* (“every”) and *solidata* (“strengthened”)]—is not inappropriately called “dry land,” that is, “earth” [Note: [Col. 0701] A *appelletur* (“may be called”)].

“Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear.” Unless the contemplative mind first gathers the instability of matter and of the form clinging to it, like certain waves seething with heat, into one place of understanding—for there is one understanding of matter and of the form clinging to it [Note: [Col. 0701] A *adhaerentisque* (“and clinging”)], since they produce one body—the substantial form, always stable through the natural solidity of its nature, cannot appear to the eyes of the mind.

For just as the diffusion of the waters covers the solidity of the earth so that it does not appear to bodily senses, so the mutability and innumerable multiplication of corruptible bodies remove from intellectual eyes, contemplating the natures [Note: [Col. 0701] A *naturam* (“nature”)] of things, the stability of the form subsisting in them, so that it may not be clearly considered as distinct from the bodies themselves [Note: [Col. 0701] A omits *ipsa* (“itself”)].

And just as, when the waters recede and are gathered together from every side and heaped into their channel, shores lying far and wide become exposed—bare, dry, and solid [Note: [Col. 0701] A omits *ac* (“and”)]—so, when the instability of corruptible things has been separated by the mind’s contemplation from incorruptible natures in a single sustained act of contemplation, the immutable and most beautiful solidity of substantial forms and species immediately smiles upon the mind’s vision in its own genera.

The stability of substantial forms is called “dry land.” And not without reason, since it is naked and free from the covering of all accidents. Every form and species, considered in the general simplicity in which it subsists, is entirely free from the concurrence of accidents [Note: [Col. 0701] C omits the passage from “covering” through “concurrence of accidents”]. The bodies, however, in which it subsists are entirely capable of accidents [Note: [Col. 0701] C *omnium* (“of all”) instead of *omnino* (“entirely”)].

Concerning substantial form, which always endures [Note: [Col. 0703] A *manente* (“enduring”)], and concerning mutable matter joined through quality and quantity [Note: [Col. 0703] A reverses the order to “quantity and quality”], enough has been said, I believe, in the first book. Now it must be briefly repeated, so that no ambiguity remains for readers.

Substantial form is that by participation in which every individual species is formed. It is one in all and all in one; it is neither multiplied in things multiplied nor diminished in things divided. For the form called “human,” for example, is no greater [Note: [Col. 0703] A *est major* (“is greater”)] in the infinite multiplication of human nature through individual species than it is in that one first human being who first became a participant in it [Note: [Col. 0703] A *prius* (“previously”)]. Nor was it smaller in him than in all those whose bodies are multiplied from him. Rather, it is one and the same in all, and wholly and equally in all, receiving no variation or dissimilarity [Note: [Col. 0703] A *aut* (“or”)] in any.

The same principle [Note: [Col. 0703] *Eadem ratione* (“by the same principle”)] applies to all substantial forms: in a horse, an ox, a lion, and the other animals; and a similar rule is naturally established in shoots and grasses. The form that clings to matter for the constitution of a body, however, is always variable and mutable, dispersed into different distinctions according to accidents. The manifold difference of visible forms does not proceed from natural causes within one and the same substantial form [Note: [Col. 0703] A omits *substantiali* (“substantial”)], but occurs externally.

The dissimilarity of human beings from one another—in face, in the quantity and quality of their individual bodies [Note: [Col. 0703] C *temporum* (“of times”)], and also in the variety of their conduct and ways of life—does not arise from human nature, which is one and the same in all in whom it exists, always like itself and admitting no variation [Note: [Col. 0703] C omits *-que* (“and”)]. Rather, it arises from those things that are understood to surround it [Note: [Col. 0703] A *illam* (“it”)]: from places and times [Note: [Col. 0703] A adds *et* (“and”)], from generation, and from the quality and quantity of nourishment [Note: [Col. 0703] A orders these as “generation, quantity, and quality”], from regions and airs in which each person is born or raised, and, to put it universally, from everything understood to surround substance and not to be substance itself [Note: [Col. 0703] C *ista* (“these things”)]. For substance itself is simple and uniform, subject to no variations or compositions.

28. Whoever, therefore, by an act of reason can separate from the innermost substance itself—around which they revolve, while it remains established in the unchangeable continuity of its nature—all the mutable things understood or perceived externally around the proper substance of individual forms, that is, around the individual and most specific species of each form—for example, of a human being, horse, ox, fish, bird, grasses [Col. 0703D], or trees [Note: [Col. 0703] A adds *et* (“and”) before “trees”)—things that are always fluctuating like an inundation of many waters; and can gather them into one place, that is, enclose them within the scope of one and the same definition [Note: [Col. 0703] A *congregare* (“to gather”); *concludere* (“to enclose”)], saying, “Everything that is understood or perceived around the proper substance is variable and mutable,” and that substance is covered by these inundations so that it can scarcely be recognized in its purity [Note: [Col. 0703] A omits *ad purum* (“in its purity”)], is commanded by divine admonitions to gather the waters under heaven into one place, so that the dry land may appear—that is, so that the hidden substantial form around which the waves of accidents seethe may shine clearly before intellectual eyes discerning the natures of things.

Concerning the fact that the place of all things that can be defined is their common or proper definition, enough has been discussed, I believe, in the first book.

“And God called the dry land Earth, and he called the gatherings of waters Seas.”

I believe that the repetition of names in the works of the first three primordial days signifies a twofold contemplation of the whole of creation. On the first day, he called the light “day” and the darkness “night”; on the second, God called the firmament “heaven”; on the third, God called the dry land “earth” and called the gatherings of waters “seas” [Note: [Col. 0703] A “of the primordial days”]. For one and the same thing is presented to the contemplative understanding in one way in its causes and in another way in its effects.

“And God saw that it was good.”

God’s vision is the creation of the whole universe. For seeing is not one thing for him and making another; his vision is his will, and his will is his operation. Properly, then, everything that God saw is good. For divine goodness is the cause of all good things; indeed, it is itself all good things. Nothing is good in itself; rather, insofar as it is good, it is good through participation in that good which alone is substantially good in itself. “No one is good except God alone.”

God therefore saw that it was good—that is, he saw himself as good in all things. For God saw nothing but himself, because nothing exists outside him; and everything that is in him is himself. His vision is simple, and it is formed by no other than himself.

“And he said: Let the earth bring forth green grass, producing seed, and the fruit-bearing tree producing fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth.”

By these prophetic words he recalls the power of grasses and trees established in the primordial causes. This power is customarily called by the holy Fathers the power of seeds, in which that species of soul called the nutritive and augmentative exercises its operation: administering the generation of seeds, nourishing what has been generated, and distributing growth to them according to the numbers of places [Col. 0704D] and times.

And since everything that appears visibly in the nature of things receives the causes of its generation from nowhere other than the hidden recesses of the natural and substantial form, which we previously said was signified by the name “dry land” or “earth” [Note: [Col. 0703] C *recepit* (“received”)], it is therefore written, “Let the earth bring forth green grass,” and so forth. It is as though it were plainly said: “Let the seminal power of grasses and trees, which was causally created in the innermost principles of substances [Col. 0705A], proceed through generation into sensible forms and species.”

This procession of the primordial causes into their effects is explained by the words of Scripture that follow:

“And it was so, and the earth brought forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and the tree producing fruit, each having seed according to its species.”

Do you see how clearly divine Scripture declares genera and species? In them, causally and invisibly, subsist all the things that through generation burst forth into quantities and qualities and into the awareness of bodily senses [Note: [Col. 0705] C *erumpuntur* (“are made to burst forth”)].

But if anyone thinks that this explanation, which we have offered concerning the first three days [Note: [Col. 0705] A omits *tribus* (“three”)] according to the powers of our intention [Note: [Col. 0705] A *intentionis naturae* (“of the intention of nature”)], is not according to history but according to the laws of allegory, let him attend carefully [Note: [Col. 0705] A *perspiciat* (“let him perceive clearly”)] to the fourfold division of wisdom.

### 29

The first is indeed πρακτική (*praktikē*), active; the second φυσική (*physikē*), natural; the third θεολογία (*theologia*), which discusses God; the fourth λογική (*logikē*), rational, which shows by what rules one must discuss each of the other three parts of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0705] “of wisdom” omitted in A]. The first investigates the virtues by which vices are defeated and utterly eradicated; the second, the principles of natures, whether in their causes or in their effects; the third, what ought piously to be judged concerning the one cause of all things, which is God [Note: [Col. 0705] A reads “that”]. How virtue, nature, and God are rationally sought, the fourth, as we have said, teaches and carefully considers—which of the aforementioned parts of wisdom ought to have attached to it the historical account of the creation of things [Note: [Col. 0705] “enumeration” (A)]. If one is not wholly ignorant of philosophy, he will attach it to none but physics.

And if this is so, let him contemplate what we have said allegorically [Note: [Col. 0705] “has been said” (A)], and, as I think, he will find it [Note: [Col. 0705] “will not find it” (C)]. On the first day, we said that the general procession of the primordial causes into their effects, comprehensible to the senses or to the intellect, was signified by the creation of light.

That the primordial causes of all things were established in the divine Wisdom is testified by Saint Ambrose in his *Hexaemeron*, where he says:

> The man full of prudence—namely, Moses [Note: [Col. 0705] A reads “of course”—recognized [Note: [Col. 0705] A reads “noticed”] that the mind of God alone contains the principles and causes of visible and invisible substances [Note: [Col. 0705] “the principles” omitted in C].

On the second day, we judged that the threefold constitution of this world—perfected, that is, from its principles, its simple elements [Note: [Col. 0705] A omits “and”], and its composite bodies—was not inappropriately described under the names of the waters and of the firmament made in their midst. We considered that Scripture had intimated the third consideration of this world [Note: [Col. 0705] “of this world” omitted in A] in the separation of those things in it that are mutable from those that, preserved by the supports of their own nature, remain established immutably in the same condition [Note: [Col. 0705] The whole phrase “preserved … condition” is omitted in C]; that is, in the rational contemplation by which all mutable accidents are distinguished from the unchanging solidity of substantial forms, through the gathering of the waters and the appearance of the earth.

And not without reason, since the most frequent practice of the divine utterances is to signify, by expressive words for visible things, the natural subsistences and principles of invisible things, for the exercise of those who philosophize piously. Nor is it surprising, since Scripture very often uses the names of spiritual and invisible things to suggest bodily and sensible things.

Although there are many and innumerable examples of this reciprocal metaphor [Note: [Col. 0705] C reads *sint* for *sunt*, “are”], to assemble them for the present purpose would seem long and superfluous [Note: [Col. 0705] A reads *et*, “and,” for *atque*], since they are perfectly evident to all who are trained in divine Scripture. Let us nevertheless use a few examples.

“What is born of the flesh is flesh”: here the whole human being born in original sin is called by the name “flesh.” And “what is born of the Spirit is spirit”: here the whole human being reborn through regeneration in Christ is expressed by the name “spirit.” If someone should say that the whole human being is not born from flesh, but only the flesh of the human being, I shall reply: then the whole human being is not born from the Spirit, but only the soul. If that is so, it follows that the grace of baptism benefits bodies nothing [Note: [Col. 0705] A reads “that the grace of baptism benefits our bodies nothing”].

But if the whole human being—namely, soul and body—is reborn in Christ and becomes spirit, then necessarily the whole human being is born from Adam of flesh and is flesh [Note: [Col. 0705] C reads “the same one” in place of “in Adam”]. Thus it is concluded both that flesh is called spirit and that spirit is called flesh. The Word of God is called flesh, and flesh is called the Word, and similarly in other cases, in which both συνεκδοχή (*synecdoche*) and μεταφορά (*metaphor*) are understood.

We therefore did not allegorize [Note: [Col. 0706] A reads “allegorized”] when we said that divine Scripture intimated by the name “light” the forms of visible and intelligible things, and by the signification of “darkness” [Note: [Col. 0705] A reads “signification”] the substantial causes that surpass every sense and intellect, eternally established in the divine mind. Nor did we allegorize when we said that, through the symbolic names of the waters and of the firmament [Note: [Col. 0705] C reads *firmamento*, “by/with the firmament”] in the midst of the waters [Note: [Col. 0705] A reads “of them”], Scripture signified the threefold constitution of this visible world: namely, in its causes, which Saint Ambrose calls the substances of visible things pre-established in the divine mind; and in the universal elements, which the Greeks call the catholic στοιχεῖα (*stoicheia*), because they fit and harmonize with one another.

Στοιχείωσις (*stoicheiōsis*) means διατύπωσις (*diatypōsis*), that is, formation [Note: [Col. 0705] C reads “confirmation”]. For through the coming together of those elements all visible bodies are made. Hence the Athenians call the letters στοιχεῖα (*stoicheia*) [Note: [Col. 0705] C reads “of letters”], because through their composition [Note: [Col. 0705] C reads “through their joining”] articulated speech is completed.

Nor is this without reason. When considered individually, pure and separated from one another, they seem to be contraries: cold contradicts heat, and moisture contradicts dryness. But when they are mixed with one another, they produce, through a certain marvelous and ineffable composition, the harmony of all visible things. In truth, it is not the substances of the elements but their qualities that disagree.

Since these compositions can be dissolved and return to those things from whose conjunction they are formed, the Prophet most appropriately signified them by the name of the waters beneath the heavens.

But since there is a twofold contemplation of these visible things subjected to bodily senses—for we contemplate in them, on the one hand, the underlying and immutable subsistences by which they properly subsist, and, on the other hand, the accidents that can be increased and diminished and never cease to vary through unstable motion—it was necessary for the mutable to be separated from the immutable. That is, accidents had to be distinguished from substances by intellectual judgment [Note: [Col. 0707] A reads *intellectualibus*, “by intellectual [things/persons],” for *intellectuali*], and the mutable had to be signified under the name of unstable and ever-fluctuating waters, while the immutable, subsisting through the stability of its own nature, had to be signified under the name of solid and dry earth.

In all these matters, then, no allegory is being treated, but only a bare [Note: [Col. 0707] “bare” omitted in A] physical consideration, following the very frequent practice of divine Scripture, which borrows the names of sensible things to signify invisible things.

But lest we seem to disregard the most reverend interpretations of Saint Basil, I shall briefly indicate what he thought about this, insofar as I am able to understand it. In his fourth *Homily on Genesis* he says:

> “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering.” He commanded the water flowing in, spreading over the regions that received it, continually increasing and filling one region from another [Note: [Col. 0707] A reads *alia*, “another,” for *alias*, “other regions”], to be gathered into one gathering, so that it would not enclose the whole adjoining mainland [Note: [Col. 0707] C reads “it appeared” in place of “it was commanded”; “one” is omitted in A]. And for this reason the sea, often tossed by winds and raised to great height by its waves, as soon as it touches the shores, dissolves its force into foam and turns back. “Will you not fear me,” says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0707] A reads “Will you not fear?”], “who set sand as a boundary for the sea, in the firmest of all sand?”—namely, so that the violence of the sea rushing upon it might be restrained [Note: [Col. 0707] A reads: “in the weakest of all sand, so that the violence of the unconquered sea is restrained”; C has “sand” in place of the conjectured reading].
>
> Otherwise, he says, what would prevent the Red Sea from entering all Egypt, since Egypt is lower, and the sea pressing upon it from covering Egypt, if it had not been hindered by the Creator’s command? For since Egypt is lower than the Red Sea, certain men, wishing to join the Egyptian and Indian seas to one another—the Red Sea being in the latter—were prevented from their efforts. Sesostris the Egyptian first began the undertaking, and afterward Darius the Mede wished to complete it [Note: [Col. 0707] C has this wording; A reads: “certain men persuaded us by their work, wishing to join the Egyptian and Indian seas to one another.”].
>
> I have said these things so that we may understand the force of the command: “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering”; that is, let none withdraw from itself [Note: [Col. 0707] A reads *ne illa*, “lest that [water]”], but let it remain gathered in the first collection [Note: [Col. 0707] A reads “let them remain”].
>
> Then, when he says, “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering,” it is shown [Note: [Col. 0707] C reads “he shows you”] that the waters had been separated in many ways [Note: [Col. 0707] A omits *per*, “through/in”]. For the ridges of mountains and the deep valleys [Note: [Col. 0707] A reads *profunditate*, “by depth,” for *profunda*, “deep”] watered by streams had collections of water [Note: [Col. 0707] C reads “have”]. Many plains and level expanses, requiring none of the vastness of great seas [Note: [Col. 0707] A reads “multitude”], and many furrows and valleys of various forms—all the hollows [Note: [Col. 0707] A reads *cava quae*, “the hollows which,” for *cava*, “the hollows”] that were then level with the waters—were joined together, when, by the divine command, the waters were collected from every side into one gathering [Note: [Col. 0707] A has: “were joined together, and by God’s own divine command, the waters were collected into one gathering.”].

### 30

By these and similar words of the aforementioned author it is clearly taught that, for this reason, the multitudes of waters spread everywhere through the hollows and level places of the earth were gathered by divine command into one gathering: so that they would not cover the whole surface of the earth with the accumulations of their floods, and [Note: [Col. 0707] A omits *ut*, “so that”] so that the dry land might appear for human habitation, adorned with grasses and trees, rich in various forms of animals, enclosed by the broad shores of the Ocean and of the various seas, and protected from the violence of the fluctuating sea by sandy barriers strengthened through the power of the divine command.

For by the force of the divine command the exceedingly powerful fury of the waters is restrained and driven back, so that it does not overwhelm the level and lower places of the earth.

I wished to add these observations, as I said, lest someone should say that we had dared entirely to pass over the interpretation of the most glorious expositor of sacred Scripture.

### 31. DISC.

Proceed cautiously and carefully. We must in no way neglect or invalidate the interpretations of the divine Fathers, especially since it is not unknown to us [Note: [Col. 0707] C reads *non nos lateat*, for *nos non lateat*: “it may not be unknown to us”] that they very often argued simply, foreseeing that their hearers were not sufficiently capable of grasping the deepest spiritual understanding of the force of natural principles. And therefore, I think, I would not rashly say that the God-bearing Basil, illuminated by heavenly grace, expounded the intelligible operations of the first six days more simply than he understood them, adapting his discourse to the simplicity of his hearers.

For he spoke to the people in the manner of a homily, and what he had understood more profoundly to have been accomplished by God simultaneously and at once, he expounded as though it had been distributed through little intervals of time, for the sake of those whose senses were unable to rise above temporal delays and spatial distances.

The most exalted of the prophets, Moses himself, is likewise recognized to have done this. He could not narrate all at once what God was able to accomplish once and simultaneously [Note: [Col. 0707] A reads “simultaneously and at once”]. Indeed, even we, who still blink in the darkness of ignorance [Note: [Col. 0707] C reads this; A has “touching”; the reading may be “fluttering”], while attempting to behold the light of truth, are unable to explain in words everything that we conceive simultaneously in our minds [Note: [Col. 0707] C reads “that we perceive”; A reads *valeamus*, “we may be able,” for *valemus*, “we are able”]. For every art, formed universally in the mind of the wise person, must necessarily be poured into the ears of learners in an ordered and particular manner through the temporal pauses of different letters, syllables, and words.

We must not therefore suppose that the aforementioned Father understood simply what he appears to have expounded simply. For who would dare criticize a divine luminary when he does not know how brightly it was able to shine in itself, or how it wisely wished to distribute its light in moderation to those less capable of receiving it?

For I would not readily believe that the great herald of wisdom, filled with virtue, understood or imagined that the inert [Note: [Col. 0709] C reads *innormem*, “formless,” for *inertem*, “inert”], dark mass of the earth, still entirely covered on every side by the immeasurable flood of the abyss, was first created through intervals of time and afterward, when the span of two days had been completed, stripped of the abyss by which it was covered—this abyss having been gathered into one place through the passing intervals of time—as though the third light were beginning.

For Basil, as I think [Note: [Col. 0709] The phrase “as I think” is omitted in A], had perceived that all these things, and the rest that divine Scripture recounts concerning the works of the six primordial days, were made and distinguished simultaneously and at once by the divine command, without any temporal intervals, according to their principles, in accordance with which they were created, and were brought forth into their forms.

What else should be understood from his words in the ninth homily of his *Hexaemeron*?

> Understand, he says, the Word of God running through the creature—then beginning, now working, and reaching its consummation [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads “proceeding”], until the world is completed. When a sphere is set in motion by someone [Note: [Col. 0709] A omits *ab*, “by”] and is placed upon a certain slope [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads *declive*, “declivity,” for *proclivum*, “slope”], it is carried downward by its own configuration and by the suitability of the terrain, and does not stop until the level of the plain receives it. So the nature of existing things, moved by one command, runs plainly through the creature [Note: [Col. 0709] A omits *creaturam*, “the creature/creation”] in generation and corruption, preserving the succession of genera through likeness, until it descends to the very end. It makes a horse succeed a horse, a lion a lion, an eagle an eagle; and, preserving each of the animals in successive generations, it transmits them to the consummation of the universe [Note: [Col. 0709] C omits “to” and reads “admits” in place of “transmits”].
>
> Observe the force of the likeness. The Word of God, he says, working through all things from the beginning of creation to the end of the universe, always working and moving all things, runs through them [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads *et*, “and,” for *ab*, “from”]. For by one command, like a single sphere, it moves the one nature of those things that were made simultaneously and at once into genera and species. Rolling onward as though down a certain slope [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads “declivity”], it will not cease to run until it reaches the end of the universe, as though a certain rest.

The one Word of God, by one command [Note: [Col. 0709] “of God” omitted in A], ordered one nature of existing things to come into being; this nature he both created simultaneously and at once and brought forth into its proper species. For just as by one command—repeated, however, six times by the Theologian [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads “then”—he created the nature of all things simultaneously, so that nature itself simultaneously began to run into all creatures, and no one preceded another by any measure or interval of place or time.

### MAG.

You rightly and properly praise the great man [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads “the greatest”], and no other judgment of him should be made.

Thus, when the multiplicity of accidents [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads *mutabilitate*, “mutability,” for *multitudine*, “multitude”] has been separated from the stability of substance, its manifold power, visibly bursting forth through diverse species, is intimated by the signs of grasses and trees. For every species is naturally contained in a genus, and every genus in substance [Note: [Col. 0709] A omits *in*, “in”]. Likewise, every substance exerts its power through genera [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads “through generation”] into its proper forms and species, and this whole process is carried out by that life which operates in seeds, commanded by the power of the divine decree.

For this reason physicists not irrationally call grasses and trees “fixed animals.” They are living bodies, growing through intervals of place and time, and fixed in the places in which they grow.

It should also be noted that, just as a gathering of waters cannot stand by itself unless it is supported by the mass of the earth—whether it flows inwardly through hidden pores, outwardly through open floods, or stands in ponds and lakes—so the flood of accidents cannot exist except in a supporting substance. They may lie hidden in the secret recesses of their subject, as do qualities and quantities, causally; or they may burst forth and appear in some matter, as do bodily masses covered with different colors; or they may be stable, as are species and shapes, which, added to the mutability of matter [Note: [Col. 0709] “of matter” omitted in A], make visible bodies, conformed in a certain specific state, and gather them into one [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads “are gathered together”], lest they suddenly dissolve and, abandoning the form in which they are contained [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads “the form in which it is contained”], slide and flow back into the current of their mutability.

But lest we linger longer over such matters, let us pass on to the fourth consideration of the world’s constitution.

### 32. DISC.

The sequence of the discussion requires this.
