For if anyone wished to investigate one by one all the things that must be asked and resolved concerning such matters [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads “whoever”], his time would run out before he could reach the end of everything that must be treated and thoroughly examined [Note: [Col. 0709] “and” omitted in A].

### MAG.

Having completed the account of the formation of the two lower parts of this visible world—namely, earth and water—or rather [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads *et*, “and,” for *ac*, “and/or rather”], having contemplated them as formed simultaneously and at once by the divine command, without any temporal intervals, in their genera and species and also confined within definite places and boundaries, the divine cosmographer immediately turns the gaze of his mind to the constitution of the higher parts, by which I mean air and fire, saying:

> “And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads “in seasons”], and for days [Note: [Col. 0709] A reads “in days”], and for nights, and for years; and let them shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth. And it was so.”

You have heard of the general creation of all the lights of the heavenly firmament in the primordial causes, before every day, time, and place. Hear now of their procession into their effects, multiplied into their proper species, separated by intervals of place, rolling through the courses of time, and composed with stable motion and movable state.

> “And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars,”

together with the other things that Scripture records concerning the works of the fourth light.

When we were discussing the second day, we explained what seemed plausible to us concerning the firmament. For, as I think, the firmament made in the midst of the waters on the second day is not one thing and the firmament in which the series of the heavenly lights was made on the fourth day another. If it were another, perhaps Scripture would not have remained silent but would have said, “Let the lights and the firmament of heaven be made,” just as it said, “Let the firmament be made in the midst of the waters.” But now, since it did not say, “Let the firmament be made,” but “Let the lights be made in the firmament,” it is clearly understood that the firmament made in the midst of the waters on the second day is one and the same as that in which, afterward—not by an interval of time but by the distance of prophetic vision—the sidereal lights were created.

Since, then, philosophers maintain that there are three greatest bodies of the world, one of which is lowest and occupies the middle of the whole world, like the center in a circle or sphere, divine authority called this the dry land or earth [Note: [Col. 0711] “or” omitted in C]. It was identified by the separation of the waters covering it and covered with the most beautiful variety of grasses and trees.

Whether anyone understands, in a simpler sense, this visible mass, placed in the middle of the world and surrounded by the boundary of the Ocean, as signified by the names “earth” and “waters,” or, in a higher interpretation, understands the discrimination of substance from accidents; and whether, by the names “grasses” and “trees,” he apprehends either the sensible ornaments with which the surface of the earth is clothed in summer, bursting forth through the power of seeds, fixed by roots in the soil, and nourished by moisture and corporeal matter, or intelligible species proceeding from the innermost and natural recesses of substance [Note: [Col. 0711] A omits *naturalibus*, “natural”], like grasses and trees growing from the earth [Note: [Col. 0711] Conjecture *perceperit*, “has perceived”; A and C read *praeceperit*, “has commanded”]—for in every sensible body we consider in one way the mass of quantity subjected to its qualities through bodily senses, and in another way we understand with the mind’s eye the invisible substance and the proper species subsisting in it, according to which the multitude of all visible and invisible things is multiplied, the totality gathered together [Note: [Col. 0711] A reads “universality”], and their distinct character preserved—the prophetic intention turned to the theory of the other two greatest bodies of the world.

> “Let there be lights,” he says, “in the firmament of heaven.”

You remember, I think, what our understanding was concerning the name “firmament” established in the midst of the waters, when we were discussing it [Note: [Col. 0711] A reads “our consideration of this understanding”].

### DISC.

I certainly remember. If my memory does not deceive me [Note: [Col. 0711] A reads “if memory does not deceive me”], we had agreed that nothing more plausibly could be signified by that name than the totality of the four simple elements. Although these are in themselves exceedingly pure, incomprehensible to every bodily sense, and universally diffused everywhere, they perfect all sensible bodies through their invisible passage and proportionate conjunction with one another—whether heavenly, aerial, aquatic, or earthly; whether great, small, or intermediate.

To speak universally, the entire heavenly sphere and everything contained in it and outside it [Note: [Col. 0711] C reads “inside it”; A reads *eam sunt*, “are in it,” for *eam*, “it”], from the highest point down to the lowest [Note: [Col. 0711] A reads “all the way downward”], came into being through their conjunction [Note: [Col. 0711] Conjecture; A and C read “are known”]. Whatever is born in the succession of the ages through the changes of corruptible things proceeds from them and is resolved into them.

The Greeks call these elements πῦρ, ἀήρ, ὕδωρ, γῆ (*pyr, aér, hydōr, gē*), that is, fire, air, water, and earth. They are named from the names of the greatest bodies that are composed from them.

Here it should be noted that sensible bodies are not made from the conjunction of the substantial elements—for these are incorruptible and indissoluble—but from their qualities [Note: [Col. 0711] C omits *eorum*, “of them”] joined together proportionately [Note: [Col. 0711] “proportionately” omitted in A].

The four qualities of the four elements are well known: heat, moisture, cold, and dryness [Note: [Col. 0711] “four” omitted in A]. Physical theory maintains that all material bodies are composed from these qualities, with forms added. Philosophers say that two of them are active—heat and cold—and two passive—moisture and dryness [Note: [Col. 0711] A reads “passive”].

For when heat is mingled with moisture and cold with dryness through a certain natural conjunction, everything born on land and in the sea receives its generation.

The Poet also understood this when he said:

> Then Father Aether, almighty,  
> Descended joyfully in fruitful showers into the lap of his consort.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0711D] Virgil, *Georgics* II, 325.]

Indeed, he called the Father the fiery quality, which is heat, and the fertile rains the aquatic quality, which is coldness; and by “the womb of the spouse” he meant the fertility of moisture, which is the distinctive quality of air, and of dryness, which is the qualitative property of earth. By using the designation of a single wife, as it were, he signified earth together with the air nearest and most corporeal to it [Note: [Col. 0711] A reads *nominationem* (“designation”) instead of *nominatione* (“by the designation”).] Hence it follows that the two active qualities opposed to one another—heat and coldness, I mean [Note: [Col. 0711] “namely, heat and coldness.”—variant wording]—when joined to the two passive qualities opposed to them, namely moisture and dryness, provide the occasion for the generation and growth of everything born on earth and in the waters.

And lest anyone wonder that coldness, although properly belonging to the waters, descends from the upper parts of this air as if into the womb of earthly dryness [Note: [Col. 0711] A omits *terrenae* (“earthly”).], let him understand that waters suspended in clouds are colder than the flowing waters of seas and rivers. If someone should ask why, then, many philosophers, as Saint Augustine testifies, assert that fire and air act, whereas water and earth suffer [Note: [Col. 0711] A reads *aerem* (“air”) instead of *aera* (“air”).], if cold water mixed with the dryness of earth acts in seeds rather than suffering, it is sufficient to answer him that water is cold and moist, but receives moisture from the air and coldness from itself [Note: [Col. 0713] Conjecture; AC read *recipiens* (“receiving”).]. By that quality which it receives from the element nearest to it, it suffers the action of heat; but by the quality that belongs to it, it always acts in seeds.

For who versed in natural principles does not know that pure and unmixed heat alone [Note: [Col. 0713] A has *sinceram* (“pure”).], without any tempering by coldness [Note: [Col. 0713] A has *ullo* (“any”).], or pure and unmixed coldness alone, without some mixture of heat [Note: [Col. 0713] A has *cujusquam* (“of any”).], cannot produce the generation of any body; nor can any body arise through natural processes from moisture alone, or dryness alone [Note: [Col. 0713] A has *aut ex* (“or from”).], without the mutual tempering of both? Nevertheless, for those engaged in the study of natural philosophy, it is not especially necessary to linger longer over these matters.

Having thus briefly preconsidered these four qualities of the four universal elements—which, because they occupy a certain middle position between the primordial causes and composite bodies, have received the name “firmament”—I see that we must hasten to an exposition of the luminaries established within it [Note: [Col. 0713] A reads “which have been established.”]

**MAGISTER.** You see correctly. If, then, by the name “firmament” the four simplest and most universal elements of the world are designated, what do you think? Are those four everywhere diffused through and connected with all bodies, whether ethereal, aerial, aquatic, or terrestrial, so that no sensible body can be found which lacks the concurrence of all of them [Note: [Col. 0713] A omits “all of them”]? Or do some bodies arise from some of them, rather than all from all?

**DISCIPLE.** It is very easy to answer this question, since it has been investigated by the philosophers of the world and rationally resolved. For they say that within the compass of this sensible world no body, measured by intervals of length, breadth, and height, can exist in which the nature of the four elements cannot be understood, though invisibly [Note: [Col. 0713] A reads *intellectualis* (“intellectual”) for *intervallis* (“intervals”).]. For just as everything which corporeal sense apprehends in them receives the material of its constitution [Note: [Col. 0713] A reads *materiam* for *materiem*.] from nowhere other than the confluence of the four elemental qualities into one another, so everything which rational investigation discovers in them, insofar as they are bodies, is nothing other than the uniform coming together of those simple and inseparable elements.

The qualification “insofar as they are bodies” has been added so that no one might think that we have here touched upon or discussed the substances of things, their genera, their species, or that life which is said both to animate and to nourish all bodies in which vital motion is perceived. These exist and are understood beyond the whole of corporeal nature universally, and without them no corporeal nature exists—whether it be incomprehensible to corporeal senses, as are those four elements now under discussion, or comprehensible, as are the combinations of diverse qualities that provide the sensible constitution of material things.

Although some qualities therefore appear more and others less perceptibly in different bodies, the one and identical conjunction of those universal elements is uniformly proportioned in all. For the divine mind balanced the examination of the entire worldly body on an equal scale between two extremes opposed to one another: gravity and lightness, I mean. Between these two every constitution of visible bodies has been weighed [Note: [Col. 0713] A reads “middle” instead of “constitution.”]

Accordingly, insofar as all bodies participate in gravity, they are receptive of terrestrial qualities—that is, solidity and stability [Note: [Col. 0713] A reads “are capable of” instead of “are receptive of.”]—but insofar as they draw upon lightness, they participate in celestial qualities, namely emptiness and mutability. Those intermediate bodies which touch the extremes with an equal balance possess their qualities in equal measure [Note: [Col. 0713] A has the singular “extreme.”] In all four universal elements there is one and the same motion, rest, capacity, and possession.

**MAGISTER.** The answer is plausible. For all natural philosophers agree on this. Everywhere, therefore, throughout the entire sensible world, the four purest elements are present in equal measure and conjunction; by divine authority they have been called by the name “firmament.”

**DISCIPLE.** The point has now been granted and established by reason. The interpretation of the Greek names also bears witness to it. For, as I suppose, πῦρ (*pyr*), “fire,” is so called because it penetrates everything through pores—that is, hidden passages. There is no body from which fire cannot be drawn out, attracted by a kind of friction. Even rubbed waters sparkle [Note: [Col. 0713] A omits “even”; C has *scintillat*, “it sparkles,” in the singular], and they would not flow at all if they were without heat.

What shall I say of colors, which undoubtedly proceed from the nature of light [Note: [Col. 0713] C reads “arise from” instead of “proceed from”]? Do we not see them spread over all bodies [Note: [Col. 0713] A omits “not”]? Air is called *aer*, that is, “breath,” because it breathes through everything [Note: [Col. 0713] A reads *nominatus* for *nominatur* (“is called”).]. For there is no sensible nature which the subtlest air cannot penetrate. We can infer this from odors and sounds [Note: [Col. 0713] C reads *ac* (“and”) for *et* (“and”).]. You will not find a body which does not emit some odor to those who smell it, or some sound to those who strike it.

Ὕδωρ (*hydōr*) is called “water,” as though from εἶδος ὁρώμενον (*eidos horōmenon*), that is, “a visible form.” For there is no corporeal thing from whose surface, smoothed by a certain friction, some image cannot rebound.

Ἄχθος (*achthos*)—“burden”—is the name given to earth because of its heaviness. For there is no body which, in proportion to its weight, does not seek its natural place, whether it tends toward the center of the world or toward its extremities. Nor does the other name for earth, γῆ (*gē*), contradict this meaning; it properly signifies a valley. For every creature has its valley and place in which it is bounded by its own definition [Note: [Col. 0713] C reads “place” without the enclitic *-que* (“and”).]

When, therefore, you have examined a body, if you perceive in it the color of light [Note: [Col. 0715] C reads “the light of color”], understand that a fiery element underlies it; if you perceive a sound, whether spontaneous or produced by art, understand that an aerial element underlies it; if from a smooth surface produced by nature or art some image rebounds, understand that an aquatic element underlies it—for where no image rebounds, the deficiency is not in nature but in craftsmanship; and wherever you perceive some natural tendency toward an appropriate position, upward or downward, understand that a terrestrial element underlies it. There are also many other natural indications by which the inseparable conjunction of the four elements in all composite bodies is recognized, always and everywhere, beyond doubt [Note: [Col. 0715] A has “many” instead of “many other”; A also reads “in all bodies composite.”]

**MAGISTER.** What you have said seems to me established and likely to be true [Note: [Col. 0715] A omits *sunt* (“are”); A has *verisimilia* (“likely”) as a single adjective for *veri similia* (“like the true”).]. Therefore, when it is written, “And God said: Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven,” we should understand it as though it had plainly said: “Let there be bright and shining sidereal bodies in the four elements diffused everywhere, composed from their qualities” [Note: [Col. 0715] A reads *sidera* (“stars”) for *siderea corpora* (“sidereal bodies”).].” For in one way the bodies underlying them, placed in their own regions, are understood to exist within them; in another way, the brightness proceeding from them is understood to shine everywhere through all the elements of the world.

For white is one thing, and whiteness another. Likewise, the bright object itself is one thing, and brightness another: the one is a subject, the other an accident. Thus, by the divine command by which it was ordered, “Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven,” vehicles of light were made, as Saint Basil says, by which light would be carried around the circuit of the world at fixed intervals of time [Note: [Col. 0715] A has “at certain intervals of time”].

And observe how carefully Scripture speaks. It did not say, “Let there be a greater luminary and a lesser luminary,” but, “Let there be luminaries.” For it expressed in general terms the creation of all the heavenly bodies that shine above the earth. Some of these have been established not far from the earth, such as the moon, which, according to Pythagoras, is raised one hundred and twenty-six thousand stades above the mass of the earth. Therefore it is called near to the earth; often falling into its shadow and deprived of the sunlight, it suffers an eclipse of its light.

The space by which the moon is separated from the earth philosophers call a *tonos*, that is, a space with a rational measure. Those skilled in the harmony of voices use the word *tonos* in two ways. For they call both intervals—that is, intervals between sounds—and analogies—that is, their proportions—*tonoi*.

Others are situated in the middle of the world, such as the sun and all the planets that revolve around it. Others are in the upper regions of the world, such as the choirs of the stars [Note: [Col. 0715] A reads “as are the fixed stars.”]

### 33. DISCIPLE

There is a diverse and varied opinion among the wise concerning the circles and intervals of the heavenly and most luminous bodies, and, as it seems to me, it has not been reduced to any certain account [Note: [Col. 0715] A omits *est* (“is”).] Therefore, I ask you not to delay in explaining anything concerning such matters that seems plausible or consistent with reason.

**MAGISTER.** You are sending us into a lengthy digression, although you see that we ought rather to hasten to the remaining matters that must be said about the works of the six days, and that the length of this book demands an end—especially since scarcely any opinion concerning the matters you now demand is supported by reason or fully drawn from any philosopher [Note: [Col. 0715] Instead of “fully drawn,” A has “defined.”]

This is not because, as I suppose, they did not understand these matters—for otherwise they would not rightly be called natural philosophers or philosophers—but because none of those whom we have so far read appears to provide an adequate account of them clearly and beyond doubt. Nevertheless, from what they themselves have written here and there, and have confirmed by definite arguments based on experience, I shall not refuse to disclose to you something plausible concerning the intervals between the earth and the moon.

For they say that the moon is one hundred and twenty-six thousand stades from the earth, and that this has been established without error from its eclipse [Note: [Col. 0715] A omits “as they say”]. Nature itself reveals that the shadow of the earth, which they call night, reaches the circle of the moon. For its globe would not suffer the loss of its light if, falling into the region of shadow, it were not deprived of the solar ray.

By this means, every ambiguity having been removed, it is established that the moon is separated from the earth by as great a distance as reason teaches the shadow of night to extend. That shadow extends to the circle of the moon. Reason therefore clearly teaches that night rises to a height of one hundred and twenty-six thousand stades [Note: [Col. 0715] C reads *nox* (“night,” nominative) for *noctem* (“night,” accusative), and *docet* (“teaches”) for *edocet* (“plainly teaches”).]. By what argument, however, it can be proved beyond doubt that the moon is one hundred and twenty-six thousand stades from the earth requires more careful investigation.

**DISCIPLE.** Certainly. For so far no reasoning satisfying me has shone forth concerning this question.

**MAGISTER.** Attend carefully, then, and consider what seems plausible to me concerning the discoveries of the philosophers. Through gnomonic investigation—that is, the study of sundials—they subtly calculated and discovered the aforementioned distance, without any ambiguity. Eratosthenes is said to have been the most learned of them in every geometrical and astronomical computation.

*Scaphia* [Note: [Col. 0715] C reads *quidem* (“indeed”) for *siquidem* (“for indeed”).] are round bronze vessels in which the hours are marked by the length of the shadow cast by a stylus set in the middle of the base. This stylus is called a *gnomon*. From it, as from a kind of center, lines are drawn to the edges of the *scaphia*. These lines divide the entire circumference of the sundial into twenty-four spaces, that is, into twenty-four brief periods of an hour, during which the entire celestial sphere revolves around the earth until it returns to the same position on the natural horizon that it had occupied the previous day.

Eratosthenes, therefore, carefully observing the movement of the stylus’s shadow through the spaces of the sundial, clearly understood that the movement of the shadow through the hourly intervals around the stylus of the sundial [Note: [Col. 0715] A omits “around the stylus of the sundial”] follows one and the same principle as the circuit of night through the same hourly spaces around the circumference of the earth. Indeed, everything observed in the vessels of the *horoscopus*, that is, the zodiac, is understood by a similar investigation of the movement of the heavenly bodies.

At the vernal equinox, the length of the stylus’s shadow makes half the measure of the gnomon at Meroë, an island of the Nile, and at Syene, a city of Egypt. That half of the stylus is the diameter of the entire circumference of the sundial [Note: [Col. 0715] A has “diameter,” as it does nearly everywhere]. Hence, at the equinox, the shadow of the stylus is the diameter both of the stylus and of the sundial. Since every diameter is exceeded twofold by the sphere or circle of which it is the diameter, the shadow of the stylus necessarily expresses the ratio of a double circle; for the circle or sphere itself, whose half is constituted by the shadow, exceeds it twofold [Note: [Col. 0717] A omits “whose half is constituted”]. In the same way, five is the diameter of ten, considered as a kind of circle.

Having thus clearly understood the principle of the sundial, the keen-minded Eratosthenes investigated the circumference of the entire earth with subtle inquiry [Note: [Col. 0717] A has “investigation” instead of “inquiry”]. First he learned that the circumference of the equinoctial circle—which divides the whole terrestrial globe and the entire celestial sphere into two equal parts—is composed of 360 degrees. He understood beyond doubt that one-twelfth of these, namely thirty degrees, rises or sets, or moves away from the place through which it travels, in two hours [Note: [Col. 0717] A omits “moves away from the place”].

Thus, what the shadow indicates to the senses on the sundial, reason proves to constitute the unceasing movement of the heavenly bodies [Note: [Col. 0717] A omits “of the heavenly bodies”]. For the shadow of the stylus would not move through the hourly intervals of the sundial if the ethereal body, together with its stars, did not revolve around the earth. What the mass of the earth is in the middle of the world, the stylus is in the middle of the sundial. And just as the shadow of the stylus is carried around itself through the circumference of the *scaphium*, so night, which is the earth’s shadow, is carried around the earth itself in every direction through the spaces of air separating the moon from the earth.

The sun casts the shadows of both the earth and the stylus. Just as at the equinox, at midday, in those regions of the terrestrial globe that approach the equinoctial circle—namely Meroë and Syene—it casts a shadow from the gnomon of such length that it can reach its diameter, that is, half or slightly more than half, so from the entire mass of the earth it extends a shadow everywhere, raising it to the circle of the moon or somewhat beyond. The moon’s own eclipse proves this.

For if at any time the earth’s shadow did not extend beyond the circle of the moon, the moon would perhaps not suffer the fall of the solar light. For, as the philosophers say, the earth is the center of the lunar circle, although it is sometimes thought to be slightly farther from it in the sign of Taurus, where the highest apse—that is, the greatest height of its circle—is believed to be. Therefore the cause of its eclipse should be considered not the inequality of its circumference around the earth, but the height of the shadow.

Eratosthenes, then, investigating the height of the earth’s shadow by comparing the gnomon with its shadow, and recognizing that the shadow does not rise beyond the diameter of the earth itself—for the height of night is equal to the thickness of the earth measured within the equinoctial circle—first sought the circumference of the earth, so that from it he might discover the diameter. Once the circumference of a circle or sphere has been found, it is easy to identify without hesitation the line that divides it into equal parts.

Accordingly, through the geometers of King Ptolemy, he was informed of what portion of the earth lay between Meroë and Syene [Note: [Col. 0717] A has “he was assured of what portion the earth was”]. By comparing the shadows, he discovered that one part at midday on the equinoctial day amounted to seven hundred stades. Multiplying this by 360, that is, by the length of the equinoctial circle, he found the circumference of the entire earth, without any error, to be 252,000 stades. For seven hundred stades multiplied by 360 yields 252,000 stades.

Dividing this number equally, he understood that half of it—namely, 126,000 stades—was the diameter of the earth and the interval between the moon and the earth.

From this you can see how strongly the perfect numbers—six, seven, and eight—are present in all these matters, numbers in which the greatest natural harmony of music is constituted, called the octave. For it has eight sounds, seven intervals, and six tones. The number six multiplied by itself, that is, six times six, produces thirty-six. If you multiply this number by seven thousand, you will find the circumference of the whole globe: seven thousand multiplied by thirty-six, or thirty-six multiplied by seven thousand, makes 252,000 stades, the number that encompasses the circumference of the entire earth [Note: [Col. 0717] C reads “is enclosed” instead of “is encompassed”; C omits “and” and “thousand” in the cited variants.]

If, however, you multiply six by the measure of its diameter, which is three, you will produce the sum of eighteen [Note: [Col. 0717] A has “you will produce” instead of “you will make”]. Multiplied by seven thousand stades, this completes the diameter of the entire earth. For seven thousand multiplied by eighteen, or eighteen multiplied by seven thousand, yields 126,000 [Note: [Col. 0717] A reads “are made”]; that number of stades gives both the diameter of the earth and the interval between the moon and the earth.

Therefore philosophers do not unreasonably declare that the interval between the moon and the earth, and the circumference of the entire earth, are contained by the proportion of a tone. For fourteen thousand stades multiplied by eighteen yields 252,000, namely the circumference of the earth; while its diameter and the moon’s distance from it are produced by seven thousand stades multiplied by eighteen.

Eighteen compared with sixteen—which is measured by twice eight—has the proportion of a tone. For the greater number contains the lesser number and an eighth part of it, namely two. Just as nine is related to eight by the epogdoic proportion, so nineteen and sixteen are harmonically fitted together according to musical investigation. Every greater number that contains the lesser number and an eighth part of the lesser is called *epogdoos* in arithmetic and a “tone” in music [Note: [Col. 0717] A has “tones.”]

By these calculations, therefore, the circumference of the globe, its diameter, the distance by which the moon is separated from the earth, and the height of night have all been grasped beyond doubt.

If you ask why Pliny the Second and Ptolemy, in his *Geography*, as Martianus reports, assign no more than five hundred stades to each degree—a number which, multiplied by 360, cannot encompass the circumference of the earth according to Eratosthenes’ calculation—I do not readily know what to answer. For if I say that Eratosthenes considered the earth larger, while Pliny and Ptolemy considered it smaller, it will not seem likely that there was such disagreement among the greatest authorities on worldly wisdom that some argued the earth’s circumference to comprise 252,000 stades, while others argued for 180,000 stades [Note: [Col. 0719] C prints “252,000”; the reading is abbreviated in the source.]

For five hundred stades multiplied by 360 yields 180,000 stades. These numbers differ from one another by 72,000 stades. This is especially difficult since the aforementioned wise men and most diligent investigators of nature agree concerning the number of divisions of the equinoctial or zodiacal circle: they all unanimously declare it to have 360.

If I say that Eratosthenes measured smaller stades and therefore assigned a greater number to each degree, while they measured larger stades and therefore assigned fewer, how will this be judged probable? For both affirm that a stade is measured by 125 paces.

It seems to me, therefore, that the cause of this inequality lay in an inequality in the length of the paces [Note: [Col. 0719] A has “that there was an inequality”]. It could have happened that two measurers, one taller and the other shorter, measured one stade with larger and smaller paces, respectively, and that consequently larger or smaller stades were counted in measuring a single degree.

Who would not believe that Hercules, who is said to have first measured a stade beside Mount Olympus, gave the stade its measure with incomparably larger paces, steps, and feet than those who measured stades after him? For from the size of the stade he had first measured, the magnitude of his paces, steps, and feet was estimated; and from the size of his feet, the height of his entire stature was assessed.

What wonder, then, if the same interval belonging to one and the same degree could contain both five hundred and seven hundred stades, with each stade being counted by the same number of paces, steps, and feet, while the paces, steps, and feet themselves were not of the same size—larger in some people and smaller in others [Note: [Col. 0719] A omits this phrase]—so that, measured with larger units, five hundred stades, but with smaller units, seven hundred stades, filled that one and identical interval of a single degree?

According to Greek reckoning, a stade contains six *jugera*, one hundred cubits, 125 paces, 240 steps, 400 forearms, and 600 feet.

But once the size of the terrestrial mass and the height of night—which has the same measure as it—and also the diameter of the earth have been discovered by rational argument, the circumference of the moon’s circle readily presents itself to those who seek it. For the height of night, tripled, produces the diameter of the lunar circle [Note: [Col. 0719] A omits “readily presents itself to those who seek it”]. One hundred and twenty-six thousand stades, repeated three times, yields 378,000. Thus the lunar circle is 378,000 stades [Note: [Col. 0719] A has “circumference” instead of “circle”]. If you double the diameter [Note: [Col. 0719] A has “multiply” instead of “double”], the circumference of the entire circle will be 756,000 stades.

There are various opinions concerning the measure of the lunar body. Many say that the moon’s globe is equal in size to the earth, and they argue this from the eclipse of the sun, supposing that the moon is able to remove the sun’s rays from the whole earth. But those approaching the equinoctial circle, as Martianus writes, give more plausible accounts of the moon’s size [Note: [Col. 0719] C reads “they intend”], and establish it rationally from the sun’s eclipse.

For they say that, at the moment of a solar eclipse, the moon’s shadow conceals one eighteenth of the earth [Note: [Col. 0719] A has “one eighteenth is concealed”]. Since every body is larger than its geometrically projected shadow by a factor of three, it follows that the moon’s body has one-sixth of the earth’s size.

Since one eighteenth—namely, the eighteenth part of the whole earth—amounts to 14,000 stades [Note: [Col. 0719] C prints “14,000”], it follows that this eighteenth part, tripled, produces the size of the lunar globe. Fourteen multiplied by three yields forty-two. Therefore 42,000 stades comprise the size of the moon. That many thousands of stades constitute one-sixth of the earth. For 42,000 multiplied by six, or 6,000 multiplied by forty-two, produces 252,000 stades.

And you will marvel that the reciprocal power of the numbers six and seven encompasses the sizes of the moon and the earth. For seven times six, or six times seven, gives forty-two, namely the lunar globe; and again forty-two times six gives 252, the circuit of the earth. Reason has shown that all these numbers are to be counted in thousands of stades, in order to reveal the consummation of the most perfect constitution of the natural bodies of the world.

For every cubic and solid formation of the number one thousand signifies perfection [Note: [Col. 0719] A has “formation” instead of “form”]. The state of nature is therefore signified by six, motion by seven, and the immutable principle of both by one thousand. For the state of all things is mobile, and their motion stable, perfectly constituted according to eternal principles.

Nor was it without reason that philosophers measured all these things in stades. For the number five is ἀνακαταστικός (*anakastikos*), that is, “returning into itself” [Note: [Col. 0719] A omits “is”]. Whenever you multiply five by itself, it necessarily returns into itself. The first cubic motion of five completes a stade: five times five times five equals 125 paces [Note: [Col. 0719] A has “state” instead of “motion”]. Hence it is not unreasonable that both the motion and the state of worldly bodies are reckoned by that number, which is cubic, revolving, and returning into itself.

We have said these things about the spaces of the lower regions of the world, following the reasonings of great philosophers—not affirming without hesitation that they are so, but presenting what seemed more plausible and closer to certain principles, in the effort to satisfy your requests.

**DISCIPLE.** What you have said concerning these matters is sufficient for me. But whoever finds them either insufficiently certain or insufficiently explained should seek the understandings of others from other authorities. For the account of the world’s constitution has been treated in many ways by different authors.

But since the magnitude and intervals of the lower bodies of the world—the moon and the earth, I mean—have been investigated in ways that appear consistent with reason, I would now like to hear briefly about the spaces of the ether. No one doubts that these spaces either alone or chiefly must be examined in investigations of the divine operation on the fourth intelligible day.

**MAGISTER.** We are lingering too long over the fourth day.

**DISCIPLE.** If the less learned, who desire to learn and investigate the nature of things, should happen to read this discussion of ours, it will not seem excessive to them, I think—especially since it is not reasonable to treat some matters concerning the lower regions of the world rationally while leaving the higher regions altogether untouched [Note: [Col. 0721] C omits “some matters rationally”].

**MAGISTER.** It was settled between us long ago that the solar globe, balanced midway between the heaviest and lightest nature, is carried eternally in circular motion along the middle line of the zodiac through the lower regions of the world.

**DISCIPLE.** It was clearly settled, and established by certain arguments; nor does the arrangement of nature allow it to be otherwise.

**MAGISTER.** Neither those learned in secular literature nor the interpreters of the divine Scriptures allow a definite account of the size of the solar globe to be given [Note: [Col. 0721] C omits “of the solar globe”]. For both Pliny the Second, in his *Natural History*, and Saint Basil, in his *Hexaemeron*, altogether forbid the size of the sun to be defined.

For it is not its shadow by which we might ascertain how large it is [Note: [Col. 0721] A reverses the wording: “For its shadow is not…”; C has “by which it might be ascertained”]. Indeed, neither the size of the earth nor that of the moon could be discovered unless their shadows, cast geometrically, extended according to definite measurements [Note: [Col. 0721] C has “cast” instead of “projected”]. Consequently, since the solar body permits no shadow to proceed to infinity but confines it within definite measurements according to the proportions of the bodies whose shadows they are, it most clearly reveals the infinity of its own size.

**DISCIPLE.** I am not asking this, nor do I think it should be asked of anyone. For the conjecture of the eyes has no force where reason has no place as the basis of an argument. I ask you to explain how far it is separated from the earth, according to the estimation of the philosophers.

**MAGISTER.** Pythagoras, the first of all philosophers, is said to have reported that the interval between the earth and the moon was 126,000 stades. Later, as we have said, Eratosthenes established this beyond doubt from the earth’s shadow and the moon’s eclipse. The same Pythagoras is said to have maintained that the sun is separated from the moon in height by twice that interval [Note: [Col. 0721] A has “by the impulse” instead of “of that interval”]. But there is considerable disagreement about the manner in which he formed this judgment.

### 34.

Nevertheless, since he himself endeavored to establish, by musical principles, that the structure of the whole world both revolves and is measured according to definite proportions—something which divine Scripture does not deny when it says, “And who shall make the harmony of heaven sleep?”—we can investigate whether he said this for no other reason than to show rational proportions in the intervals of the stars’ musical diastemata.

Accordingly, recognizing the sun’s orbit in the middle of the entire space extending from the earth to the highest sphere, which bounds all sensible things, he reasonably judged that one octave extended from the earth to the sun and another from the sun to the outermost circumference of the world. An octave is constructed according to a twofold proportion.

Thus, in the diatonic mode—for example, in the harmony of sounds—two octaves are fitted together from two doublings: the first octave extends from the principal of the principals to the μέσην, that is, the middle note; the second from the μέση, “middle,” to the νήτην ὑπερβολαίων, that is, the last of the highest notes. In the same way, the entire space from the earth to the sun is fitted together according to the proportion of an octave; for the sun occupies the middle position, and from the sun to the twelve constellations—that is, to the outermost movement of the stars—another octave is joined.

Therefore, he judged that, according to the proportions of the harmony called “double octave,” the interval from the earth to the sphere was constituted in a fourfold proportion. Consequently, it follows that three times the diameter of the earth is equal to the interval between the earth and the sun, just as it is equal to the diameter of the lunar circle. Thus the same distance will be measured both in the diameter of the lunar circle and in the interval between the earth and the sun. In both cases 378,000 stadia are calculated.

If, therefore, you double this number, you will find the interval from the earth to the outermost sphere to be 756,000 stadia, and you will marvel at the harmony of nature. For as many thousands of stadia as there are in the length of the lunar circle, so many there are in the height from the earth to the signs of the zodiacal region: in both cases the total is 756,000 stadia.

If you wish to know the diameter of the solar circle, multiply the earth’s diameter—126,000 stadia—seven times, and you will have 882,000 stadia as the diameter of the solar circuit. Doubling this number gives the circumference of that circuit: 1,764,000 stadia.

But if you seek the diameter of the entire celestial sphere, you will find it by the following calculation. Double the circumference of the lunar orbit, that is, 756,000 stadia; then add the earth’s diameter, 126,000 stadia. You will obtain the diameter of the sphere as 1,734,000 stadia. Doubling this number is thought to comprise the circumference of the whole world: 3,000,000 stadia, with a further 266,000 stadia added, so that the whole world may be enclosed by the perfection of the number six.

So much for the philosophical arguments investigating the dimensions of the world. If anyone thinks these matters superfluous because they are neither confirmed by testimonies of sacred Scripture nor handed down in it, let him not criticize us. For he cannot prove that these things are not so, just as we cannot affirm that they are so.

### 35.

And although nothing definite is found in the divine Scriptures concerning the dimensions, magnitudes, and intervals of such worldly bodies—for Ecclesiastes says, “Who has measured the height of heaven, the breadth [A: length] of the earth, and the depth of the abyss?”; and here I would judge that allegory rather than history is intended, for I would not say that this world was established beyond the understanding of rational nature, since it was made for that nature—nevertheless divine authority not only does not prohibit investigating the principles of visible and invisible things, but even urges us to do so.

“For his invisible things,” says the Apostle, “are understood and seen through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world.” Knowledge of sensible things is therefore not a small step, but a great and highly useful one, toward understanding intelligible things. Just as one reaches understanding through the senses, so through creation one returns to God.

For we must not, like irrational animals, merely gaze upon the surface of visible things; we must also give an account of what we perceive through bodily sensation. An eagle sees the appearance of the sun more sharply; a wise human being sees more sharply its position and its movement through places and times.

If a human being had not sinned and fallen into the likeness of beasts, would he be ignorant of the perfect boundaries of his possession, this world, which he would govern most justly according to the laws of nature? For there ought to be another angel who praised God in sensible creatures—an angel who, even after the transgression, did not entirely lose the dignity of his nature.

The rational movement remains in him: he desires knowledge of things and does not wish to be deceived, although he is deceived in many matters, though not in all. And if, at the time of Christ’s transfiguration, his two garments were white like snow—namely, the letter of the divine utterances and the sensible appearance of visible things—why are we commanded carefully to touch one garment, so that we may deserve to find the one whose garment it is, while we are forbidden to investigate the other, namely visible creation? I do not sufficiently see how, or by what principles, this can be explained.

Abraham too came to know God not through the letters of Scripture, which had not yet been completed, but through the revolutions of the stars. Or perhaps, simply like the other animals, he looked only at the appearances of the stars and was unable to understand their principles? I would not dare to say this rashly of so great and wise a theologian.

And if anyone regards it as a fault in us that we have used philosophical reasoning, let him consider the people of God fleeing from Egypt, warned by divine counsel to carry off its spoils and using those spoils without reproach. Especially since those skilled in worldly wisdom were not found blameworthy because they had erred in their understanding of the principles of visible creation, but because they had not sought its author sufficiently beyond creation itself, although they ought to have found the Creator through creation. Plato alone is read to have done this.

If the dimensions of worldly bodies and their intervals mentioned above seem incredible to anyone because many think that the bodies themselves are larger than can be encompassed by the stated numbers of stadia, let him carefully read the measurements of Noah’s ark. Its length was 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits. Let him see how, in so small a space, seven pairs of all the clean animals and two pairs of the unclean could be contained with their provisions, together with Noah, his sons, and their wives.

This is especially remarkable if, as Saint Augustine testifies, the cubit by which Noah’s ark, the Ark of the Covenant, the tabernacle, and the other mystical works of the Old Testament were measured was no more than the measure of two and a half palms, and if the palm itself was measured from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger.

Divine power and the order of nature therefore contain more than human thought contrives. And lest we seem to have recourse to miracles of divine power as though we were unable to establish what we maintain by the principles of nature, surely you conceive the earth, placed in the middle of the world’s sphere, in the same way as you see the center at the bottom of a circle or globe. For it occupies the lowest and middle position among created things.

**DISCIPLE.** In no other way, and according to one and the same principle.

**MASTER.** Nor can the parts of the zodiac be brought down toward the earth in any other way than lines in a circle are brought toward the center.

**DISCIPLE.** By an equal rule.

**MASTER.** Although the spaces in the zodiac and on the earth are not the same, the same course of rational lines and the same parts extend from the top downward.

**DISCIPLE.** Certainly.

**MASTER.** You do not deny that what is understood concerning the parts must also be judged concerning stadia.

**DISCIPLE.** On the contrary, I affirm it.

**MASTER.** Therefore, to the extent that either the parts or the stadia approach the center of the earth, they are of narrower breadth; conversely, to the extent that they recede from the earth, the spaces expand.

**DISCIPLE.** A circular figure permits no other arrangement.

**MASTER.** What, then, do you think of those who measure the earth by its regions, stadia, and other intervals—those whom the Greeks call γεωμετρικοί, “geometers”? Do you suppose that they measured the earth with feet, paces, cubits, or similar measures?

**DISCIPLE.** I would not easily believe that this could be done amid such diversity of mountains and valleys. Even the level surfaces of plains are not so uniform that they could be measured by equal progression. The earth, because of the weight of its mass and also because of the unevenness of its parts, occupies the lowest place in the order of nature. For the likeness of the parts produces the order of the elements: those elements that are more similar to their own parts are also higher in their proper places.

**MASTER.** Perhaps, then, they measured it by bodily sight?

**DISCIPLE.** Not that either. The senses deceive, and nothing should be entrusted to their judgment. External sensation, although it reports to reason only what it suffers externally, is nevertheless very often deceived in its judgment concerning what it receives through the body. Thus it judges that an oar broken in water, or a doubled moon or candle, or some other object, has been duplicated through the distortion of sensation—that is, through the separation of the rays scattered from the pupils of the eyes.

**MASTER.** How, then, did they measure?

**DISCIPLE.** First, as they say, with the geometric rod, which the Greeks call a ray. By multiplying five paces through cubical movement—that is, five times—it measured one stadium. Once one stadium had been determined, it was easy to discover many stadia across the level plains of Egypt, which is called the mother of such measurements.

**MASTER.** How did they investigate regions of the earth outside Egypt, where the great unevenness made measurement so difficult?

**DISCIPLE.** Not, as they say, with feet or rays, but solely by rational calculation: namely, by means of sundials, infallibly determining the intervals of individual regions from the similarity of shadows. For one region—that is, the sun’s daily progress through the zodiac—extends across the earth as far as the similarity of the sundial’s shadows reaches.

**MASTER.** They therefore inferred the breadth of regions and stadia from the measure by which they reach the earth?

**DISCIPLE.** They did not think so. Rather, they first measured the highest mountains, determining how many thousands of stadia they rose above the level of the earth. For example, they began by extending Olympus—whose summit they believe rises 10,000 stadia—along with Pindus, Rhodope, Acroceraunia, and Atlas, as though forming a certain line rationally drawn from the summits of the mountains into the spaces of the air. They then began to carry this line around at an equal distance from the earth, like a perfectly rounded circle, until it returned to the same place where it had begun. By the mind’s vision they thus perceived the circumference of the earth enclosed on every side by equal spaces.

**MASTER.** I would not contradict the claim that geometric measurements were first discovered by such arguments. Thus those stadia which near the earth were thought narrow gradually became extended along the height of the mountains and the surface of the earth. They are no longer constricted or inadequate for encompassing the breadth of the earthly mass; rather, since they are the same both near the earth and at the distances mentioned above from it, they suffice for measuring the earth once the false imagination of irrational thoughts has been cast aside [A omits: “for measuring the earth”].

This is why Pliny also thinks that the earth’s breadth is measured, by drawing a rational line, through geographical observation across the summits of the highest mountains. Otherwise, the circular measurement of the earth could not be obtained.

**DISCIPLE.** Enough has been said about this.

**MASTER.** Let us therefore return to Scripture.

**DISCIPLE.** The time calls us to do so.

**MASTER.** “Let there be lights,” it says, “in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide the day from the night.” It is as though it said plainly: “Let the lights that have been made in the firmament of heaven divide the day and night between them.”

The Psalmist explains this when he says: “He made the great lights, the sun to rule the day, the moon and the stars to rule the night.” This does not mean that day and night are not always present around the circumference of the earth, but that wherever the sun is present it always has the power to illuminate; where it is absent, the brightness of the moon and stars makes the darkness of the shadows thin and mournful, so that it is not wholly impenetrable to the eyes of living creatures.

“And let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years.” Here we understand “signs” not as the stars, but as certain indications of coming calm or storm, which are especially discerned from the colors of the heavenly lights.

By “seasons” he generally means the courses and returns of the stars, brought back by divine providence, at fixed intervals of delay, to the same movement and positions through the natural revolutions of days and years.

“And let them shine in the firmament of heaven.” No star suffers any diminution of its light; rather, all shine continually in the ethereal spaces without any shadowing, except the sphere of the moon, which, when it descends into the region of shadow and is abandoned by the solar ray, appears to grow dark.

Therefore he says: “And let them shine in the firmament of heaven, and let them illuminate the earth.” “And it was so”—namely, in the original causes from which they proceeded into their proper forms, quantities, intervals, movements, and splendors.

The procession into the forms of the causes therefore follows: “And God made two great lights, the greater light to rule the day”—namely, the sun, whose presence makes day—“and the lesser light”—he means the moon—“to rule the night.” Its size and light are incomparably surpassed by the sun.

The moon illuminates either the whole night from the eighth to the twenty-second day of the lunar month, or, around the full moon at the equinoxes, the entire night, or during other seasons a part of it. But when it is in conjunction with the sun, or in the neighboring regions on either side, it is not permitted to penetrate the darkness of night with its light. The stars therefore come to its aid; by their brightness the density of the shadows is made thin.

For this reason he said: “And the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars,” and he placed them—namely, the stars—in the firmament of heaven. It is as though he had said, “He fixed them in the firmament of heaven.”

We understand this as referring to the choirs of the stars. Although they revolve with the world, they nevertheless remain fixed in the same seats, even if, as certain philosophers wish, while the world itself stands still only the choirs of the stars are carried around. Their order, however, the sequence of the stars, and their stable position are not changed.

“To shine upon the earth.” Scripture beautifully describes the order of nature. Although human opinion supposes that the heavenly lights shine beneath the earth, the order of things unmistakably teaches that no nature can be lower than the earth. It occupies the middle and lowest place in the entire constitution of the world; therefore no bodily creature is understood to be beneath it.

Consequently, all the spaces and bodies of the world that are on every side around the earth, whether they are moving or stationary, were naturally created above it. Therefore he says: “To shine upon the earth.” Wherever they shine—whether beneath the horizon in the lower hemisphere, as human usage supposes, or above the horizon in the upper hemisphere, which is called upper because the stars appear in it to human beings—they shine naturally above the earth according to the arrangement of things.

“And to rule the day and the night.” This has been explained above.

“And to divide the light from the darkness”—that is, to separate night and day, so that when the sun appears it is day, while the moon and stars make night.

It should be noted that this division of light and darkness does not take place in the lights themselves, but among the inhabitants of the earth. For the lights always shine, and for them it is always day; they suffer no night. Their dwellings shine continually with their own light and with solar light, distributing the grace of their brightness to the world no less by day than by night.

The heavenly lights therefore divide light from darkness for earthly inhabitants, to whom days and nights come by turns. Through their continual revolution around the circumference of the earth, they provide light in one place and take it away in another. For just as day is nothing other than the presence of light, so night is nothing other than its absence. Thus even the brightest night does not lose the name “night,” since it does not entirely drive away the darkness.

But, insofar as brevity requires, enough has now been said about the fourth day. Therefore something must be said about the works of the fifth day, concerning intelligible light.

**DISCIPLE.** The consequent order of things demands this.

### 36.

**MASTER.** God also said: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature having a living soul, and the flying creature above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.”

During the four preceding days of the creation of natures, no mention of soul is read—neither simply and absolutely, nor with the addition “living.” It is not without reason that this is asked about. Indeed, many people hold differing opinions concerning this theory of things.

Some say that the elements of this world—the heaven, I mean, with its stars; the ether with its planets; the air with its clouds, the spirits of the winds, its flashes of lightning, and its other disturbances; water also, with its wandering motion; and likewise the earth with all its herbs and trees—are deprived not only of soul but of every form of life altogether. Therefore, they say, no reference to soul or life is introduced in the works of the first four days.

Plato, however, the greatest of philosophers, and those who surround him, assert not only a general life of the world, but also acknowledge that no form attached to bodies, and no body at all, is deprived of life. They have even dared confidently to call life itself—whether general or particular—“soul.”

The greatest interpreters of divine Scripture favor their opinion, affirming that the herbs, trees, and everything arising from the earth live. Nor does the nature of things permit any other conclusion.

For if there is no matter that becomes a body without form, and no form subsists without its proper substance, while no substance can be without a vital movement that contains and causes it to subsist—for everything that moves naturally derives the beginning of its movement from some life—it necessarily follows that every creature is either life in itself or participates in life and is in some manner living, whether the movement of life is manifest in it or not. Nevertheless, the sensible form itself indicates that it is secretly administered through life.

Hear Augustine in his book *On True Religion*:

“If it is asked who established the body, let him be sought who is the most beautiful of all. For every form is from him. But who is this, except the one God, the one truth, the one salvation of all, and the first and highest essence, from which is everything that is, insofar as it is? For insofar as anything is, it is good. And therefore death is not from God. For God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living, since the highest essence made everything that exists; hence it is called essence, whereas death compels whatever dies not to be.

“For if the things that die were utterly to die, they would undoubtedly come to nothing; but they die only to the extent that they participate less in essence. This can be stated more briefly: they die more to the extent that they are less.

“Now a body is less than any life, because, however little it remains in form, it remains through life—whether through the life by which each individual animal is administered, or through that by which the whole nature of the world is governed. For just as there is no body that is not contained by its proper form, so there is no form that is not governed by the power of some life.”

Therefore, if all naturally constituted bodies are administered by a certain form of life, and every form seeks its genus, while every genus derives its origin from the most general substance, every form of life that contains the multitude of different bodies must necessarily return to a certain most general life, by participation in which it is formed.

The wisest men of the world call this most general life the universal soul. Administering through its forms everything contained within the circuit of the celestial sphere, it is called by the contemplators of divine wisdom the common life.

Although it participates in that one life which is substantial through itself and is the source and creator of every life, distributing visible and invisible lives through its divisions according to divine ordinance, it does not reach everything in the same way as the sun, known to our senses, spreads its rays everywhere. The sun’s rays do not penetrate everything; they do not pass through the interiors of many bodies.

No creature, however—whether sensible or intelligible—can be without life. Even bodies that appear dead to our senses are not entirely abandoned by life. Just as their composition and formation are accomplished through the administration of their proper life, so their dissolution, decay, and return to the elements from which they were drawn are carried out through the service of that same life.

Seeds entrusted to the earth do not come to life again unless they first die. Their death is the dissolution of matter and form. Yet the same life that gives vitality to the power of the seeds, and through that power to the seeds before they are dissolved, does not abandon them in their dissolution. It remains continually attached to them; indeed, it dissolves them and immediately, with no intervening delay, begins to bring them to life—that is, to recall them to the same form.

For where would that life be at the time of the dissolution of bodies, unless it were in the thing dissolved? Just as it is not joined together with what is compact, so it is not dissolved with what is dissolved; it is not born again with what is reborn. Nor does it invigorate the whole when united any more than when divided into parts; it is not greater—that is, more powerful—in the whole than in the part, nor less—that is, less powerful—in the part than in the whole. For it exercises the same governance in all things.

The dissolution itself, which is called the death of the body, is for our senses and for matter a dissolution, but not for nature, which is inseparable in itself. It is simultaneously and always present and is not separated by intervals of place or time.

A human being does not cease to be a human being. A human being, however, is body and soul. If, then, the human being always exists, the soul and body therefore always exist.

Although the parts of a human being are separated from one another—for the soul abandons the customary governance of its body after the body’s generation, and when the soul abandons it the body is dissolved and its parts are returned to their proper elemental places—nevertheless, according to natural reason, the parts do not cease always and inseparably to be referred to the whole, nor the whole to the parts. For the principle of relation can never perish.

Therefore what appears to bodily sensation to be separated must, under a higher contemplation of things, necessarily subsist always together and inseparably.

The human body, whether living or dead, is still the body of a human being. Likewise, the human soul, whether it governs its body while that body is gathered together or, as it seems to the senses, ceases to govern it when the body is dissolved into parts, does not cease to be the soul of a human being.

Thus it is understood, through a higher awareness of things, that the soul administers the body dispersed through the elements no less than when it is joined together in one structure of limbs. True reason teaches this without doubt.

For if the soul is spirit, possessing no bodily density in itself, then the elements into which the body is dissolved, insofar as they subsist simply in themselves, are close to spiritual nature. What wonder is it, then, if the incorporeal soul governs the parts of its body, preserved in natures close to itself? It can reach what is similar to it more easily than what is dissimilar.

Dense and corruptible bodies are dissimilar to it; the most subtle things, subject in no way to corruption, are similar. We must not believe that bodily parts, dissolved from the structure of a dense body, retain their density within the elements in which they are preserved and do not pass into the lightest and most spiritual qualities of those elements—not so as to become wholly non-bodily [A: bodies], but as spiritual bodies, just as the elements themselves are.

You can most readily confirm this even from the example of a living body. Some of its parts are heavy and condensed into density, such as bones, flesh, nerves, and veins, as well as all the fluids by which the entire mass is irrigated, nourished, and constructed. All these are taken from watery and earthly qualities for the constitution of the body.

Other parts, however, are extremely light and impeded by no weight of gravity or density. They reach wherever the soul commands, in every direction and without any intervening delay. Such are sight and hearing.

No rightly philosophizing person would deny that these parts are drawn from fire and air. For, as Saint Augustine says, there is something luminous in the eyes and something airy, mobile, and sonorous in the ears.

Sight is a certain light, first arising from the fire of the heart and then ascending to the top of the head, to the part which the Greeks call μήνιγξ [Greek: μηνίγξ; variant printed as ΜΕΝΙΚΑ], and the Latins *membranula*, “little membrane,” by which the brain is both surrounded and protected. From there it is conveyed through certain pores to the eyebrows and pupils of the eyes. Bursting outward with the greatest speed, like the rays of the sun, it reaches nearby places and bodies, or those situated at the greatest distance, with a speed matching that of the eyelids and the *tautones* of the eyebrows—that is, the eyelashes.

The sense of hearing likewise is a certain most subtle ringing which first proceeds from the breath of the lungs and then rises upward into the aforementioned part of the head. Spread through its hidden passages into the cochleae of the ears, it bursts outward and mingles with the air in nearby or more distant regions, hastening without any delay to receive whatever sound has been produced in it.

These most subtle parts of the body, then, although they draw their origin from the dense inner mass, extend outward so far that they are thought to be separated from it by a considerable distance. Sight extends itself to receive the colored forms of visible things; hearing extends itself to receive the prosodies of voices and other sounds produced by the striking of the air—the forms and colors of voices, as we call them, which it imagines within itself.

The other three senses appear to be contained within the boundaries of the body, although, as I think, it is not unreasonable to suppose that the sense of smell also extends outward.

All this the soul, simple in itself and lacking every bodily quantity and local extension, accomplishes by its presence in the body it governs. Although it is contained in no place, it gives life and governance to the local parts of its body wherever they are. It is not locally enclosed by the mass of its fleshly limbs, nor is it locally extended along with the senses that reach outward.

It is present by its power to receive the phantasies formed in the instruments of its senses wherever they may be. By this fact the magnitude of its natural power and its lack of locality are understood.

At one and the same moment of time, it senses the phantasies—that is, images—of the stars scattered through the ether in the rays of the eyes, of voices diffused through the air in hearing, of odors in the sense of smell whether within or outside the body, of flavors in taste, and of everything that affects touch. These phantasies are first formed with marvelous speed, without any delay of time, from bodily numbers in the senses. The soul receives them through the things that encounter it, introduces them through the things that advance, entrusts them to memory through the things capable of being remembered, orders them through the rational powers, and approves or rejects them through the intellectual powers, according to the rules of the divine numbers that are above it.

It perceives the patterns of these numbers and judges the numbers established within itself, as well as the bodily and sensory numbers, both of which are outside it.

Reason discovers eight orders of numbers. The first and highest is above the intellect, in eternal causes; according to it the rational soul discerns all things, as the Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one.”

Two orders are entirely outside and below the soul. One, the outermost, exists in bodies, from which bodily senses are formed and in which phantasies arise. The other is formed in the bodily senses themselves; this is the first order of phantasies, established in the instruments of the senses—in the eyes, I mean, and ears, and the other seats of sensation. [C omits: “in which phantasies arise.”]

Within the soul itself five numbers are naturally implanted: the encounterers, which first meet the phantasies and receive them; after these, the advance-forces, as guides to the city of memory; when the phantasies have reached that city, the remembrance-capable powers introduce them; then the rational powers distribute them throughout the city according to the command of the intellectual powers.

The phantastic troop that comes especially through sight occupies a place in memory. Likewise, those entering through hearing and the other senses are received in their own seats within the same city.

Whoever desires to know more fully about all these matters should read the great Augustine in the sixth book of *On Music* and in the books of the *Confessions*, and the great Gregory of Nyssa in his discourse *On the Image*.

What wonder, then, if the rational soul, after the dissolution of its body, performs something within the parts of that body dispersed through the elements by a hidden natural administration, entirely removed from bodily sensation, when even in a living body that is still gathered together it exercises the power of its governance not only in the mass of the limbs but also, as far as the senses can see [A: “as far as it seems”], in the senses extending far beyond it?

### 37

But let us return to the consideration of the most general kind of life, for the sake of whose power being manifested in bodies these matters concerning rational life have been introduced—not concerning every kind of life that governs a body. I say this because of the souls of irrational animals, about which many hold differing opinions. For some say that they live after the destruction of the body, while others say that they perish together with their bodies and do not remain any longer. We shall speak briefly about this question a little later. [Col. 0732C]

The first and greatest division of life in its most general sense, then, is into that distinction which separates the rational from the irrational. Rational life has been distributed among angels and human beings; but in angels, as a matter of distinctive designation, it is called intellectual, whereas in human beings it is called rational. Nevertheless, if truth is consulted, life in both angels and human beings is intellectual and rational; therefore it is commonly predicated of both as intellectual and rational life. For the sake of distinction, however, it remains that the very life of the intellect in angels is called an “intellect,” while in human beings it is called a “soul.” For no other reason occurs to me that would prevent angelic life from being called a rational soul, just as nothing prevents the human rational being from being called an intellect—especially since angels possess heavenly bodies in which they often appear. And so, if they are said to have bodies, I do not know what could prevent their life from being called a soul, unless it is merely the difference of terms, as we likewise do not doubt that angels were made in the image of God. For wherever reason and intellect are present, I could not possibly believe that the image of God is absent. Only of man, however, does divine Scripture expressly testify that he was made in the image of God.

I say nothing about Plato, lest I seem to follow his school, which defines angels as rational, immortal animals. Thus, for the distinction between human nature and the angelic substance, these designations have been left: namely, “rational soul” and “image of God.”

Irrational life, however, is divided into that which participates in sense and that which lacks it. The former is distributed among all animals possessing the power of sensation; the latter among all matter devoid of every sense, of which the species of life said to govern herbs and trees is constituted, and below which reason finds no species of life. Accordingly, the four differences of created life are gathered into four species: intellectual life in angels, rational life [Note: C has *rationabilis*, “reasonable,” instead of *rationalis*, “rational.”] in human beings, sentient life in beasts, and non-sentient life in plants and the other bodies in which only the appearance of life manifests itself—such as the four elements of the world, whether they are simple in themselves or composite: I mean earth, water, air, and ether.

Thus it is not without reason that man is called the workshop of all creatures, since universal creation is contained in him. He understands as an angel, reasons as a human being, senses as an irrational animal, lives as a plant, and subsists in body and soul, lacking none of the creatures. For outside these you will find no creature.

But perhaps someone will say that all these things are also contained in an angel. To this I reply that the sense distributed among animals cannot subsist except in a body constituted from the four elements. There will be no sight where there is no fire, nor hearing if air is absent; when moisture has been withdrawn, neither smell nor taste will remain; the absence of earth removes the whole sense of touch. Angelic bodies, however, are simple and spiritual, devoid of every external sense. They do not receive knowledge of sensible things through bodily images, but perceive every bodily creature spiritually in its spiritual causes, as we shall see when we are transformed into equality with their nature. Angels therefore lack bodily sense because they are above it; and consequently they are free from every kind of irrational life, whether sentient or deprived of all sense, and are not burdened by composite and corruptible bodies.

Accordingly, you will find many things in man which angelic nature by no means receives; but you will not find in an angel or in any other creature anything that is not naturally present in man.

And do not say: “If, then, every species of life is in man, he contains not one life but many lives, differing from one another, since he possesses irrational and rational, sentient and vegetative life.” Examine more carefully the powers of the human soul. Although it is one and the same subsistence, power, and operation, present generally in all human bodies and specifically in each individual, it can nevertheless perform all vital movements and administrations in its body, both within and beyond it.

For beyond the bodily senses it also reasons and understands, as does angelic life. In the bodily senses it exercises the power of sensation in a manner resembling irrational beings, without abandoning its rationality; it nourishes and enlarges its body, like that life which lacks sense and penetrates herbs and trees. Everywhere it preserves all its senses, wholly in itself and wholly in all things.

Thus it reveals the power of vegetative life in bones, nails, and hair; these parts of our body, since they are not open to the air, participate in no sense. Through the fivefold instrument of the senses it communicates with irrational life, which subsists properly in animals lacking reason. In all these things, although it is often moved irrationally through itself, nature does not permit it to be deprived of its reason.

Whatever else it can do beyond these aforesaid powers—namely, giving life, nourishing, and sensing through the senses—whether it acts or suffers, is rightly understood to act or suffer outside its own body. With these divisions and distinctions of the most general life previously established, let us return, insofar as we are able to understand it, to the resolution of the question mentioned above, since it was on its account that these matters concerning the general soul, or life, were inserted.
