### 38

The question was why, in the works of the first four primordial days, no mention is made of any life or soul, whereas on the fifth day Scripture suddenly declares: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of a living soul.” It did not simply say “the creeping thing of a soul,” but added “living,” as though a soul were not living. The reason, in my opinion, is that species which we placed last in the divisions of general life.

And rightly so, since everything devoid of intellect and reason is discovered through a subtle investigation of nature; and, as though it were no life, no soul, or living soul, it is passed over in silence by Scripture, so that we may understand it to be the latest and most imperfect participation, in essence, of created life. Accordingly, divine authority has decreed that it should be counted among corporeal rather than vital numbers.

Rightly, therefore, in the works of the four days, in which the species of heavenly and earthly essences are brought forth into manifestation from their primordial causes and receive the perfection of their formation, no mention of this vital movement is inserted. For it is also passed over in silence on the third day, when the sprouting of herbs and trees from the earth is commanded, although in them it makes the power of its administration manifest to bodily senses.

This is not because that species of life does not proportionately possess a place of subsistence in the nature of things. For the natural power which nourishes and enlarges all things rooted in the earth and arising from the earth, according to the infinite multitude of shoots and herbs, and produces them into their proper forms according to the likeness of their individual kinds and the natural succession of flowers, fruits, and seeds, through the numbers of places and times, is not to be regarded as insignificant.

But because it has no power to act outside the body and does not manifest within itself the power of perfect life, life complete in bodies, it has been assigned—by divine authority, as we said earlier—to the numbers of corporeal nature rather than to the species of general life.

And because vegetative life by itself can be understood without participation in a higher life—that is, sentient and rational life—whereas rational and sentient life are not naturally permitted to animate any body without it, until they are introduced into the higher forms of living souls, it has been reserved by sacred Scripture. [Note: A has *insinuaretur*, “might be introduced,” instead of *insinuantur*, “are introduced”; C reads *servata est*, “has been preserved,” instead of *reservata est*, “has been reserved.”] A soul devoid of every sense also seems to be entirely devoid of vital movement. Accordingly, it is called merely a soul, not a living soul.

Nor is this surprising. For if such a soul is thought to exist in infants conceived in the womb or emerging from the womb, as wholly devoid of reason and understanding, although it is rational and intellectual and cannot yet manifest the signs of reason and intellect in the still recent and imperfect parts of the body, how much more rightly should that soul, naturally deprived of the powers of understanding, reason, and sense, not be designated in Scripture by the name “living soul”?

**DISCIPLE.** I approve this interpretation and see that it agrees with the nature of things and with the prophetic utterances. Nevertheless, since many maintain that the bodily masses of herbs and trees possess no vital movement at all, saying that they are nourished by the moisture through which they grow green and by no other life, I should like you to strengthen your preceding discussion of this matter with some weighty authority which would plainly declare that herbs and trees are governed by some kind of life. [Note: C omits *vitae*, “of life.”]

**MASTER.** You are not unaware, I suppose, that all philosophers who have discussed the world are unanimous on this aspect of nature. For they say that all bodies contained within this sensible world are sustained by vital movement, whether they are at rest or in motion.

**DISCIPLE.** This is well known to all who philosophize and to all who read the philosophers. Plato in the *Timaeus* and Pliny the Elder in the *Natural History* also teach us this most explicitly.

**MASTER.** If, then, you seek the testimonies of the holy Fathers, listen to the most noble Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, in his seventh homily on Genesis:

> “Let the waters bring forth,” he says, “creeping things having living souls. Now for the first time an animate animal is created. For although shoots and trees are said to live because they participate in the nourishing and enlarging power, they are nevertheless not animals and are not animate.” [Note: A has *activae*, “active,” instead of *auctivae*, “augmentative.”]

Gregory of Nyssa likewise—who is also called Gregory Nazianzen [Note: The author makes the two friends, Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory of Nazianzus, into one person.]—the biological brother of the aforesaid Basil, says in the eighth chapter of his discourse *On the Image*:

> “Reason teaches that vital and animal power is considered in three differences. One kind gives increase and nourishment only; it is called augmentative and nutritive because it brings whatever is suitable for the increase of that which is nourished. It is also called vegetative and is observed around plants; for it is necessary to understand that in plants also there is a certain vital power devoid of sense.
>
> “Another species of life, in addition to this, possesses what was mentioned above and has further received the capacity of being administered through sense. This species belongs in the nature of irrational beings. For it not only nourishes and enlarges, but also possesses sentient operation and perception.
>
> “Perfect life in the body is formed in rational nature—that is, human nature. It is nutritive and sentient; it participates in reason and ministers to the soul.” [Note: C reads *anima*, “soul,” instead of *animo*, “to the soul.”]

The same author says in the same discourse, chapter fifteen:

> “Reason finds three differences according to vital power: first, the nutritive, without sense; second, the nutritive and sentient, but devoid of rational operation; and third, the rational and perfect, penetrating every power.” [Note: C reads *imponit*, “imposes,” instead of *invenit*, “finds.”]

Augustine says in his book *On True Religion*:

> “Let religion for us not be the worship of that life by which trees are said to live, since there is no sense in it. Of that kind is also the life by which the multiplicity of our body is governed, by which even hair and bones live, though they are cut without sensation. Better than this is sentient life; yet we ought not to worship the life of beasts. Let religion for us not even be the perfect and wise rational soul, whether established in the service of the parts or in the service of the whole.”

These testimonies of the aforesaid Fathers are sufficient, I think, to strengthen what we have said.

**DISCIPLE.** They are indeed sufficient, and we should pass on to other matters.

**MASTER.** Observe, then, how beautifully the sequence of things proceeds, ordered by divine words. On the fifth day, accordingly, Scripture first brings forth the animals endowed with the fivefold sense. [Note: *Primum*, “first,” is omitted by A.]

[Col. 0735] A reads *intellectibilis* (“intelligible”) for *intellectualis* (“intellectual”); C omits *vitae* (“of life”); A reads *aut* (“or”) for *ac* (“and”); A reads *activae* (“active”) for *auctivae* (“augmentative”); C has *Nyseus* throughout for *Nyssaeus*, while A has *Nyssenus*; the author conflates the two friends Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory Nazianzen. In Gregory’s quotation, C reads *non* (“not”) for *ejus* (“of it”), A omits *est* (“is”), C omits *rerum* (“of things”), C reads *perfectionisque* (“and perfection”) for *perceptionemque* (“and perception”), and C reads *anima* (“soul”) for *animo* (“to the soul”). In the subsequent quotation, C reads *imponit* (“imposes”) for *invenit* (“finds”).

### 39

But I am deeply troubled concerning the souls of all irrational animals: why do many of the holy Fathers affirm that they perish together with their bodies and cannot remain any longer?

Basil, in his ninth homily on Genesis, says:

> “The earth brings forth a living soul. Why,” he asks, “does the earth bring forth a soul, unless so that you may learn the difference between the soul of cattle and the soul of man?”

A little later he continues:

> “You will learn how the soul of man was made; but now hear concerning the soul of irrational creatures, for, as it is written, ‘the soul of every animal is its blood.’ Blood, however, customarily changes into coagulated flesh, and flesh, when corrupted, is dissolved into earth. Consequently, the soul of cattle is something earthly. The earth therefore brings forth a living soul.
>
> “Observe the sequence of soul in relation to blood, of blood in relation to flesh, and of flesh in relation to earth. Then, retracing the same path, return from earth to flesh, from flesh to blood, and from blood to soul, and you will find that the soul of cattle is earth, so that you will not suppose it to be older than the substance of its body or to remain after the dissolution of the flesh.”

Gregory of Nyssa also says in the sixteenth chapter of his discourse *On the Image* [Note: AC reads “XVI.”]:

> “If some things in creation possess a nutritive operation, while others are governed by a sentient power, the former do not participate in sense and the latter do not participate in intellect. But if everything that is not of this kind has its perfection in an intellectual and rational soul, it can indeed be equivocally called ‘soul,’ but it is not truly a soul; it is rather a certain vital operation using the name ‘soul.’”

But if this is so, as they wish, why is the principal division of general life into the rational and intellectual soul, and into the soul lacking reason and intellect? Why are two species mutually contrary placed under one genus of life? For the rational and irrational do not oppose one another, but express the difference between species of one genus.

Living and dying, however, are wholly opposed to one another: one signifies possession, the other deprivation; possession and deprivation are contradictory. If, then, after the dissolution of the body one species remains while another perishes, how will that genus preserve its entirety? For just as, when a genus perishes, all its species must necessarily perish, so reason compels us to conclude that, when its species perish, the genus also perishes; for the genus is preserved in its species, and the species in the genus.

But if, among the forms or species constituted under one genus, some can and do die while others can neither die nor perish, what shall we say about their genus? Will it too perish in some and not perish in others? That cannot remain entire which suffers the loss of some of its parts; and consequently it will not be a genus, but the ruin of a genus.

For if there is one genus of everything constituted of body and soul, which is called “animal,” since all animals subsist substantially in it—for man, lion, ox, and horse are one in it, and are substantially one—how will all the species of that genus perish, with only the species distributed among human beings remaining?

Accordingly, if only one species remains while the others perish, the genus too will perish, since it will not stand in one species alone. I do not see how one species can constitute any genus. For if a genus is the substantial unity of many forms or species, how will a genus stand where the substantial unity of many forms or species does not remain?

That many species are one in a genus is taught by Saint Dionysius in the chapter “On the Perfect and the One,” where he says:

> “For there is no multitude that does not participate in the one; many in their parts, but one in the whole; many in accidents, but one in the subject; many in number or powers, but one in species; many in species, but one in genus.”

Therefore, if all species are one in the genus, how will that one perish in part and remain in part? And if that one is substantially one, how will it perish, when in every creature these three things remain incorruptibly, without increase or decrease: substance, power, and operation?

Furthermore, when the bodies of all animals are dissolved, they are not reduced to nothing, but natural reason plainly declares that they return to the qualities of the elements from whose concurrence they were materially formed. How, then, can their souls perish altogether, when they are certainly of a better nature? No wise person denies that whatever kind of soul it may be, it is better than every body. It is contrary to reason that what is inferior should remain and be preserved while what is better is corrupted and perishes, and that what is composite should be preserved in its separated parts while what is simple and devoid of all composition should be destroyed, though it cannot be dissolved.

Who among those devoted to wisdom does not know that every body is composite, while every soul is simple?

And what is more remarkable than all this: why do those who assert that irrational souls perish after the dissolution of the body—and rightly so, as they say, because they are taken from earth and dissolved into earth—extol the power of the irrational soul in the senses with great praise, and prefer it in bodily senses to the power of the rational soul?

For which human being sees sharply as an eagle and a lynx? Who possesses a power of smell like a dog? And, not to make the discussion of the power of the irrational soul in the senses of individual animals too long, what should be said about the duration of the memory of irrational beings?

Ulysses’ dog recognized its master after twenty years. A camel, having suffered an injury from its keepers, watches for a place suitable for its revenge over a period of many years, constantly remembering the injury.

A few examples of their natural powers will suffice. They say that the gryphon possesses such chastity that, once it has lost its mate, it preserves its chastity inviolate forever, remembering its former marriage. Investigators of nature report the same concerning the turtledove.

Basil writes of the storks’ filial devotion toward their parents:

> “When their father grows old and loses the covering of his feathers through excessive age, his offspring stand around him on every side and warm him with their own wings. Preparing food in abundance, they also provide him with strong assistance in flight, lifting the resting bird from both sides.” [Note: C reads, “For who makes the bird lighter on both sides?”]

How, then, could all these natural powers exist in an irrational soul if, as the aforesaid Fathers say, it were earth, arising from earth and again dissolved into earth—or if it were not truly a substantial soul? I cannot discover.

And if the soul is earth, while earth is a body, how is a body called a soul, since the difference between their natures separates them widely from one another? If the body is the soul, it will necessarily have a life that gives it life; for there is no body that lacks life and form, otherwise it will not be a body. Consequently there will be a soul of the soul, or a life of the life.

But let no one think that we say such things in order to destroy the meaning of the holy Fathers. Rather, we are seeking, to the best of our ability, what should more reasonably be held concerning these matters: whether irrational souls perish when released from their bodies and are dissolved into earth, or whether, after abandoning the administration of their bodies within their own kinds, they are saved. [Note: A reads *solvantur*, “are dissolved,” instead of *salvantur*, “are saved.”]

Let us hold firmly everywhere what has been sought, discovered, and established by true reasoning: that every life—whether it is a soul governing a body or not—has subsisted, or has received life, through participation in one primordial life or soul; and that natural reason does not permit it to abandon this participation altogether, whether it is engaged in the administration of bodies or not. [Note: A reads, “that the soul subsists through participation in the soul.”]

We do not say these things prejudging anyone’s interpretation, but rather encouraging readers to investigate more diligently and, after consulting truth, to follow without hesitation what appears more probable to them.

Nevertheless, I believe that holy and philosophical men, skilled in the truthful investigation of things, publicly set forth this sort of teaching because of foolish people, who are wholly devoted to the flesh like brute and irrational animals. They did so lest such people fall into the flesh and serve its desires, but so that, terrified by the baseness of such an irrational creature, they might raise themselves through corrected morals to the dignity of rational nature, in which they were created. Gregory himself plainly discloses this in the twelfth chapter of *On the Image*. For after saying that the irrational soul is not truly a soul, he adds shortly afterward:

> “Let lovers of the flesh learn not to attach their understanding too closely to visible things according to sense, but to devote themselves to the contemplation of souls. For the true soul is observed in human beings, whereas sense is possessed equally by irrational creatures.” [Note: C reads *non esse vere animam*, “is not truly a soul,” without the preceding *non*; A cites chapter 17 rather than 12.]

**DISCIPLE.** Let each person choose what he wishes and follow what he chooses. But let us proceed to consider what remains.

Textual notes to §39: [Col. 0735] C reads *quidem* (“indeed”) for *siquidem* (“for indeed”); the principal reading gives Basil’s ninth homily, while A gives the eighth; A omits *et* (“and”). ### 40

**MASTER.** “Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of a living soul, and the winged creature over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.”

Here too you should understand “of a living soul,” so that you may take “winged creature” to mean “of a living soul.” For more indications of a living soul are discerned in the senses of birds than in those of fish. As Basil says, fish have sluggish hearing; they see through the water with duller sight; and they possess neither much memory, nor imagination, nor recognition of habit. All these powers are present no less—and indeed more strongly—in birds than in human beings. [Note: A omits “all”; A reads “than in lights” instead of “than in human beings.”]

It is rightly asked, however, why winged creatures are said to have been produced from water. For it would seem more credible that, just as land-dwelling animals are said to have been created from earth, so fish alone, as possessors of the waters, were created from water, while winged creatures, which traverse the air, were created from air as well.

A reasonable answer to this question is provided if the nature of waters is considered. There are two kinds of water: one marine and fluvial, of denser quality; the other vaporous and mistlike, and lighter. The denser kind is supported by the solidity of earth, while the lighter is suspended in the clarity of air, until it changes into a density and heaviness which its thinness cannot sustain.

From this it follows, by natural reflection, that the creeping things of a living soul—that is, all kinds and species of fish—are created from the denser kind of water, while winged creatures are likewise created in their kinds and species from the lighter kind.

And since the space of this air which lies between the moon and the earth is divided into two parts, the upper part is clear and not subject to the disturbances which arise in the air from earthly and aquatic vapors, while the lower part is moist and of more bodily quality, adapted to the movements of winds, the gathering of clouds, and other phenomena produced by the nearness of earth and water, it is not unreasonable to believe that whatever is generated from that part of the air which is moist and watery in quality is created from air.

For winged creatures could not traverse this part of the air near the earth and waters if they were wholly devoid of an aerial nature. Moreover, since in them the lightness of feathers, the hollow structure of bones, and the ease of flying are clearly observed, it is made perfectly evident that they were created not only from water but also from air.

This is also readily perceived from the nature of amphibious creatures, which live both in water and air, or in water and on land. Some winged creatures, for example, live alternately in air and in water; while they live in water they assume the form of fish, but when they live in air they assume that of winged creatures. They do this by changing their form for six months: for six months they swim in water, and for six they fly through the air, descending to the earth like the other winged creatures. This species of bird always moves in flocks, whether in air or in water, and is called the coot. [Note: Conjecture, AC has *luligo*, “squid.” Compare *fulica* with Virgil, *Georgics* 1.361.]

From this it is clear that winged creatures participate in the substance of both elements, namely air and water.

There are also amphibious creatures—that is, creatures living in two ways—in both land and water: seals, crocodiles, and many similar animals. [Note: A has “that other one” instead of “another.”]

There is another argument by which it is established that winged creatures are made from moist air. They breathe in and breathe out, and therefore live both on land and in air; but they are suffocated by water, upon which they always float, except for those amphibious creatures that voluntarily plunge into the waves.

Fish, however, created from water and almost from dense matter alone, because they cannot breathe in and breathe out like terrestrial and aerial animals, perish very quickly through contact with earth and air; yet they are not wholly deprived of inhalation and exhalation. For if they were entirely deprived of these, they would not sleep at all. But they do sleep, as Pliny says; therefore they have lungs that inhale and exhale. They receive the breath itself not from this denser air but from that extremely subtle air which penetrates all bodies.

Since, then, fish and winged creatures plainly show by their qualities that they are created more than other animals from moist nature and almost from moisture alone—for they are moist and cold—divine Scripture accordingly records that they are produced from the waters.

Observe carefully: it did not say, “Let the water bring forth,” but “Let the waters bring forth,” so that you may understand, as we said, that there are two kinds of waters: the denser kind in the sea and rivers, and the lighter kind in the air.

Therefore it distinguished the account by saying, “Let the waters bring forth,” and then added, “the creeping things of a living soul, and the winged creature over the earth.” As though it were plainly saying: “Let one kind of water, the denser, produce fish, and the other, which is lighter, produce winged creatures.”

This can also be discerned from the bodies themselves. We see that fish are weighed down by the heaviness of denser bodies, while winged creatures are lifted upward by the lightness of their feathers.

When it says, “over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven,” it plainly signifies that the bodies of winged creatures are not wholly weighed down by earthly heaviness, but are carried above the earth into the air, whose moist quality formed them, beneath the firmament of heaven.

Since no species of animals approaches the subtlety and spirituality of the simple elements—which, as we have explained, divine utterances signify under the name “firmament” or “heaven”—as closely as birds do in natural likeness, winged creatures were rightly commanded to be made beneath the firmament of heaven; that is, in proximity to the qualities of the purest and almost incorporeal elements.

A winged creature is therefore created beneath the firmament of heaven—that is, nearby, though still below the lightest tenuity of spiritual bodies.

Thus far concerning the creation of fish and winged creatures in the primordial causes. Their progression into genera and species follows:

> “And God created great κήτη, and every living soul, and the rest.”

*Κῆτος*—that is, “sea monster” or “beast”—is neuter in gender and singular in number among the Greeks. In the plural, however, like the other neuter nouns in Greek, it ends in the letter alpha: τὸ κῆτος, τὰ κητέα. Then, through synaeresis—the contraction of two syllables into one, namely epsilon and alpha into eta—κητέα becomes κητῆ; and two accents, the acute and the grave, become one, namely the circumflex. For κητέα has an acute accent on the penultimate syllable and a grave on the final syllable, whereas κητῆ has a circumflex on the final syllable. [Note: The Master is mistaken: κητέα is neither accented acute on the penultimate syllable, nor is κητῆ circumflexed at the end; rather, the plural of κῆτος is formed as κήτεα, κήτη.]

But, so that this book may not proceed at excessive length, an end must be put to it, I think, if you agree.

**DISCIPLE.** I do agree; indeed, it asked for an ending long ago, if the prolixity of the arguments had not delayed it.

**The third book *ΠΕΡΙ ΦΥΣΕΩΝ* (“On Natures”) ends here.**

Textual notes to §40: [Col. 0739] A omits *omnia* (“all”) and reads *luminibus* (“lights”) for *hominibus* (“human beings”); C reads *naturaliter* (“naturally”) for *rationabiliter* (“reasonably”), *et* (“and”) for *vero* (“but”), and *induuntur* (“are clothed”) for *induunt* (“put on”); A reads *facile* (“easily”) for *facillime* (“most easily”). The reading *fulica* (“coot”) is a conjecture; AC have *luligo* (“squid”). C omits *et* (“and”) and *in* (“in”); A reads *illud* (“that”) for *aliud* (“another”). [Col. 0741] A reads, “because they are created from water ... they were created,” for “fish, however, created from water and almost from dense matter alone,” and reads *ac* (“and”) for *et* (“and”); A reads *deducat* (“lead down”) for *producat* (“bring forth”); A reads *appropinquant* (“approach”) for *appropinquat* (“approaches”). A omits τὸ, τὰ (“the,” singular and plural neuter articles); C has the corrupt *synlemsin*, perhaps συλλήψιν, for *synaeresin*; A omits *in* (“into”). The editorial note correctly observes that the Master is mistaken: neither κητέα is accented on the penultimate nor κητῆ circumflexed on the final; the plurals are κήτεα and κήτη.

**THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS** [Note: Thus A; C has, in illuminated letters, “The fourth book begins, *περὶ φύσεων*”; F has “The fourth book begins, *περὶ φύσεων*.”] [Note: Here codex F begins.]

[Col. 0741C] **MASTER.** The principal aim and chief subject of our first treatise on nature was that the *ὑπερουσιότης*—that is, the superessential nature—is the creative cause of all things existent and nonexistent, created by no one; the one principle, the one origin, and the one universal fountain of all things, flowing from no one, while all things flow from it; the consubstantial Trinity in three substances; *ἄναρχος*, that is, without beginning; principle and end; one goodness; one God; *ὁμοούσιος* and *ὑπερούσιος*, that is, consubstantial and superessential. And, as Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, says in the *Ancoratus*, or discourse on the faith:

“Three holy ones, three co-holy ones, three acting, three acting together, three forming, three conforming, three operating, three cooperating, three subsisting, three co-subsisting, existing together with one another.” [Col. 0742C]

This holy Trinity is called three existents, one harmony, one Godhead of the same essence, the same power, and the same subsistence. [A omits: “of the same power and the same subsistence.”] Like things acting likewise, they produce an equality of grace belonging to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But how they are is left to them to teach. For no one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father, and whoever the Son reveals it to. And it is revealed through the Holy Spirit.

Thus these three existents are not rightly understood in each one as being either from him, through him, or toward him, just as they themselves reveal *φῶς, πῦρ, πνεῦμα*—that is, light, fire, and spirit. These things, as I said, were handed down by Epiphanius so that whoever is asked what the three are and what the one is in the holy Trinity may be able to answer with sound faith, or so that one approaching the faith may be instructed in this manner.

It seems to me, however, that he used “spirit” for “heat,” as though he had said by way of comparison: light, fire, heat. [Col. 0743A] But there is no wonder that he named light first. For the Father is light, fire, and heat; the Son is light, fire, and heat; and the Holy Spirit is light, fire, and heat. The Father illuminates, the Son illuminates, and the Holy Spirit illuminates; from them every knowledge and wisdom is bestowed. The Father burns, the Son burns, and the Holy Spirit burns, because together they consume our sins and transform us, like a kind of whole burnt offering, through *θέωσις*, that is, deification, into their unity. The Father warms, the Son warms, and the Holy Spirit warms, because with one and the same heat of charity they cherish and nourish us and, as it were, lead us from a certain formlessness of our imperfection after the fall of the first human being [Col. 0743B] into a perfect man, into the fullness of Christ’s maturity.

The perfect man is Christ, in whom all things have been brought to completion; and the fullness of his maturity is the completion of the universal salvation of the Church, which consists of angels and human beings.

In the second book we discussed created and creative nature, which we said subsists in the principles of things, that is, in the primordial causes. For it is created by the one cause of all things, which is supreme goodness, whose proper work is to bring forth all things from nonexistence into their own existence by its ineffable power. Yet it does not cease to create the things that come after it through participation in itself. [Col. 0743]

The third book discusses created and non-creative nature, that is, the ultimate effects of the primordial causes, which occupy the outermost portion of all things. In them the movement of the progressions of the universe comes to an end, since it cannot proceed any farther downward, being constituted in bodies. In that book we also considered many matters concerning the primordial causes, and concerning God and his image in mind, reason, and sense; concerning the kind of nothing from which all things were made; and concerning how the only-begotten Word of God both makes all things and comes to be in all things. We also treated briefly the works of the first intelligible week, up to the sixth day. [A reads “fifth day.”]

**2.** This fourth book, beginning with the works of the sixth prophetic contemplation concerning the creation of the universe, will set its conclusion in the return of all things to that nature which neither creates nor is created. [A reads “will set its conclusion,” rather than “will consider its conclusion.”] The difficulty of this subject [A: “of this difficulty”], and the collision and struggle of differing interpretations, fills us with such terror that, in comparison with it, the three preceding books seem to provide readers with a safe passage, like a level sea navigable in the calmness of its waves without any shipwreck. This book itself, however, is impassable because of its winding turns; dangerous because of the obliqueness of its arguments; full of the channels of the Syrtes—that is, the courses of an unknown teaching; and, like hidden reefs that suddenly break ships, enveloped in a darkness highly conducive to shipwreck. Its length compels it to extend into the fifth book.

Nevertheless, with divine clemency guiding and steering us [A omits “clemency”; A reads “steering by means of the work”], and with the favorable breath of the divine Spirit filling the canvas of our ship, we shall make a safe and straight course through these waters and reach the harbor we seek by a gentle voyage, free and unharmed.

**DISCIPLE.** Let us spread the sails [A: “the sails must be spread”] and set out to sea. For the experienced reason of this sea hastens on; it fears no threats of the waves [A omits “of the waves”], nor dreads any winding channels, Syrtes, or reefs. It finds greater delight in exercising its strength in the hidden straits of the divine ocean than in resting idly on level and open waters, where it cannot display its power. For it has been commanded to eat its bread in the sweat of its face—namely, the word of God [A omits “namely, the word of God”—], and to cultivate the soil of sacred Scripture that brings forth thorns and thistles for it; that is, to cultivate the meager density of divine meanings; and to traverse by constant steps of contemplation the path inaccessible to those who despise the pursuit of wisdom, until it finds a place for the Lord [A: “a place of the Lord”], a tabernacle for the God of Jacob [A: “a tabernacle of God”]. That is, until, led, assisted, and helped, and moved toward this end by divine grace, through frequent and laborious study of the divine writings, it returns to and reaches the contemplation of truth, which it had lost through the fall of the first human being; reaches it and loves it, loves it and remains in it, remains in it and rests.

**3. MASTER.** “And God said, ‘Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind: cattle, and creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds,’” and so forth.

“Let the earth,” he says, “bring forth a living soul,” as though he had said plainly: “Let the earth bring forth a living animal.” For that figure called *συνεκδοχή*, that is, conception or synecdoche, is exceedingly common in divine utterances. This form of expression comprehends the whole from a part and the part from the whole.

Thus sacred Scripture commonly signifies the whole animal by the mere word “soul.” In the Acts of the Apostles: “We were,” it says, “in the ship, two hundred and seventy souls”; clearly, these souls were not without bodies. Likewise in Genesis: “All the souls of the house of Jacob who entered Egypt were seventy.” [Col. 0743; CF: “seventy.”]

In the Gospel the whole human being is called “flesh”: “And the Word became flesh,” that is, the Word became a whole human being subsisting in flesh, soul, and mind. Elsewhere: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” where “flesh” signifies the whole of his humanity, while “spirit” signifies the Holy Spirit, who was indeed willing and strengthened himself for the redemption of the human race amid the difficulty of the Passion.

This Spirit, fixed to the cross, he commended to the Father, saying: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” It was as though he had said: “I commend into your hands the Spirit proceeding from me and from you, because he is impassible, while I alone suffer with the flesh, I who alone received flesh and became flesh.” This does not mean that he himself is passible according to his divinity, but that the passibility, suffering, and death of the humanity—which he alone had assumed [CF: “received”]—are referred to him, and that he suffered with the humanity which he had assumed into the unity of his substance [A: “received into the unity of his substance”]. Therefore, because he is rightly and truly said to have suffered with it, he is also rightly and truly said to have suffered. For the one substance of the Word and the human being was not separated in the Passion.

And so that you may see this confirmed more certainly by authority, hear the aforementioned Epiphanius in his discourse on the faith:

“Once he died for us, enduring suffering for the sake of our sufferings; once he tasted death, death even unto the cross. Wishing to die for us, the Word came into death in order to destroy death. The Word became flesh, not suffering in the Godhead, but suffering together with the humanity in impassibility. The suffering was attributed to him while he remained in impassibility; death was reckoned to him while he remained in immortality. For he himself said, ‘I am life.’ Life never dies, but came to give life, accepting death for us.

“For life was not given to us through a human being, nor was hope given to us through flesh. For he says, ‘Cursed is the one who hopes in a human being’; and, ‘The one who has hope in a human being shall be like a wild tamarisk.’ [A: “hopes in a human being”; A reads *myrice*, C and F *mirica*, F *miricae*.]

“What, then, shall we say? Is Christ not a human being, in view of what has been said? It is clear to everyone that we confess without any ambiguity that the Lord God the Word became human, not in appearance but in truth. Yet the human being did not come to an advancement of the Godhead. For hope of salvation was not in a human being; no human being at all, from Adam onward [A: “in Adam”], was able to accomplish salvation.

“But God the Word became human, so that our hope might be placed not in a human being but in the living and true God who became human [A omits “might be placed”]. For every priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings, according to what is written. Therefore, the Lord, when he came, took flesh from our humanity, and God the Word became human for us, so that salvation might be given to us in his Godhead and that in his humanity he might suffer for us human beings, canceling suffering through suffering and destroying death through his own death [A: “his death”].

“The suffering was attributed to the Godhead, although the Godhead did not suffer; the suffering was reckoned to the Godhead because it thus pleased the holy and impassible Word who came.

“There is an example of this: suppose someone is clothed in a garment, and blood is sprinkled upon the garment and pollutes it. The blood, when it comes upon the garment, does not touch the body of the person wearing it, yet the contamination of the blood on the garment is attributed to the person who wears the garment [A: “who is clothed in the garment”]. In the same way Christ suffered in the flesh—I mean in the Lord’s human being. In this way [A: “whom”], the holy God the Word himself, coming from heaven, restored himself, just as blessed Peter says: ‘Put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit’; and again: ‘Since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same understanding’ [A: “arm yourselves”].

“Just as blood on a garment is attributed to the one wearing it, so the suffering of the flesh was attributed to him in the Godhead, while the Godhead suffered nothing. Thus the world’s hope would not be in a human being, but, in the Lord’s human being, which had received the Godhead, the suffering would be reckoned to the Godhead, so that salvation might come to the world from the impassible Godhead. Thus, although suffering occurred in the flesh and the Godhead suffered and endured nothing, the suffering was attributed to it, and Scripture was fulfilled: ‘For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.’

“He was crucified, therefore; the Lord was crucified, and we adore him crucified, buried, and rising on the third day, and ascending into the heavens.

“But so that you may know that ‘Father, into your hands I commend my spirit’ was spoken not of another spirit but of the Holy Spirit, hear the same speaker in the same work:

“‘If you hear that I have been exalted at the right hand of God’ [F corrects this to “if you hear that I shall have been exalted”], ‘and that I have received the promise of the Spirit from the Father’ [F corrects this to “if you receive”]; or, ‘Await the promise of the Father, which you heard from me’; or, ‘Because the Spirit drove him into the desert’; or what he himself says: ‘Do not consider what you should say, because the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you’ [F adds ‘is’]; or, ‘But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God’; or, ‘Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him,’ and so forth; or, ‘Father, into your hands I commend my spirit’; or, ‘But the child grew and was strengthened in spirit’; or, ‘Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan’; or, ‘Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit’; or, ‘What is born of the Spirit is spirit’; or, ‘And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth’; or, ‘Why has Satan filled your heart?’ Peter said to Ananias. ‘You are lying to the Holy Spirit’ [conjecture; A and CF read “to lie”; F has ‘to you’ written above *mentiri*]. And afterward: ‘You have not lied to human beings but to God.’ Therefore God is from God, and God is the Holy Spirit.”

Thus far Epiphanius.

**DISCIPLE.** Although this digression seems to have withdrawn rather far from the subject [A retains “a”; CF omit it], it is nevertheless useful to those who wish to understand sacred Scripture. For it taught that the divinity of the Word is impassible and that it suffered together with his humanity. It also confirms what the Lord said in the Gospel: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” and likewise: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit,” which was spoken not of another spirit but of the Holy Spirit. But we must return to the subject.

**4. MASTER.** “Let the earth bring forth a living soul”; that is, “Let the earth bring forth a living animal.”

See how beautifully, in accordance with the figure mentioned above, he signified the whole from a part—namely, the whole animal from its better half, which is the soul. [Col. 0747A] And because the lesser half of the whole animal, namely the body, is taken from the earth, by the same figure the whole animal—that is, body and soul [A: “body and soul” with singular *anima*]—is commanded to be brought forth from the earth, although the soul is in no way earth, just as the body is not the soul. But because the soul adheres to the body in the unity of the animal, Scripture testifies that they are made together from the earth.

If someone seeks a deeper meaning in this passage, however, he can understand it in another way. By the word “earth,” the solid and unchanging substance of the whole substantial nature, visible and invisible, is commonly indicated. We explained this also when considering the operation of the third light.

Hence the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth.” It is as though he had said plainly: “Put to death the members of wickedness that are yours, since they have arisen from your disobedience and not from God. From them you build, as it were, a body of universal wickedness upon the earth—that is, upon the solidity of the nature created by God. Put them to death, so that this nature may no longer be polluted by them; and, in place of the members of wickedness that have been slain, establish the members of righteousness, which are the virtues.

“Just as you have built upon the nature created by God, through your various crimes, a kind of abominable temple fit to be a dwelling of the devil, so also, with the stones of the virtues hewn by divine grace, rebuild for its creator a precious house—that is, for the nature itself [A: “for the creator of the earth itself, that is…”]—after every stain has been entirely expelled and destroyed.”

The Psalmist agrees with this interpretation, saying: “Sinners shall perish from the earth, and the wicked shall be no more.” Here, by indicating the cause through its effects in a figurative manner [F corrects “signifying”], he indicates through “sinners” and “the wicked” sins and iniquities [A: “indicates”; CF: “indicating”]. These will perish from the earth of nature when it has been freed from all wickedness, so that they are no more.

Sins and iniquities seem to exist only so long as they are contained by the nature subject to them, although in themselves they are nothing. But once that nature has been purified and restored to its original integrity, they—which, namely sins and iniquities, cannot subsist by themselves—will be utterly reduced to nothing, so that they are no more.

Elsewhere, speaking in the person of a just-living man, he blesses all the righteous: “They shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters,” that is, like the Word who was made human at the end of all the ages for our sake, upon whom, as the Apostle says, “the ends of the ages have come.” He names one end of all things in the plural, namely Christ [A: “one of all the ends”]; for he himself is the end of the ages [F corrects to “the end of the ages”], who is the consummation of all things.

He immediately added: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth.” Here he calls the wind the discernment of just judgment, by which he whose winnowing fork is in his hand will cast the dust of all wickedness from the surface of the earth—that is, from the substantial beauty of nature. [Col. 0748A]

Concerning this earth, the same Psalmist says in another psalm: “His spirit shall go forth, and he shall return to his earth.” Whose spirit? That of the one who, fixed to the cross for us [A: “who, suffering for us”], bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

Where will he go forth? He descended to the underworld.

For what purpose? To bring back human nature, which had been held captive there; for “he led captivity captive.” But because death could not retain a captive whom it had not found guilty, he returns to his earth, to his nature, which he made, redeemed, and assumed: into an immortal body, into the original state of human nature, and, in addition, into the glory of the resurrection.

And so that you may know that the one who promised that his spirit alone would go forth would return not alone but with the whole of human nature, hear him saying: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.”

“You will send forth,” he says, “your Spirit, and you will renew the face of the earth,” that is, you will restore the integrity of nature. Whether someone understands this of the spirit of Christ’s soul—which, with his divinity suffering together with it, was handed over for the salvation of the world as he bowed his head, and went forth and returned into the nature that he had redeemed by his mission; and was also sent forth in order to restore the beauty of nature, which had been destroyed in the first human being [A omits “in the first human being”]—or of the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of Christ, who, when the head—that is, Christ—was humbled, was given to the whole creation through the momentary death of the flesh, of which Christ himself is the firstborn and whose Spirit he is:

“He will go forth and return to his earth,” that is, to that nature which he had abandoned on account of the sin of the first human being. It was his, before he abandoned the sinner [F adds, as a correction, “for it was his”]. But on account of him whose Spirit he is, and who suffered for it, he returns into it; and again, at the time of the resurrection, he will return and will be sent, so that through his power the face of the whole nature may be restored to its original beauty.

Since, therefore, all animals were causally and primordially created in this common earth of all things, in body and soul—for all things were made in honor [A: “in a human being”; CF: “in man”]—what wonder is it if, by divine command, it is ordered to bring forth a living soul, that is, a living animal, so that what it possessed causally and secretly in its causes and formative principles it might openly bring forth into genera and species?

And observe how the divine utterance reveals to us the natural order of things. “Let the earth,” it says, “bring forth a living soul according to its kind.” First it placed the genus, because within it all the species are both contained and one, and because it is divided and multiplied into them through general forms and the most specific species.

This is also shown when it says: “Cattle, and creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds.” From this it is understood that the art which divides genera into species and resolves species back into genera, which is called *διαλεκτική*—dialectic—was not made by human contrivances. Rather, it was established in the nature of things by the author of all arts that are truly arts, discovered by the wise, and employed for usefulness through the diligent investigation of things.
