### 5. DISCUSSION

From what you have said, if I am not mistaken, with good reason, one may also understand in another way what is written: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing having a living soul, and the flying creature above the earth.” Thus one may understand not merely, as was treated above, that fish and flying creatures were created from this visible, tangible, moist, and cold element of water, but also, in a higher sense, that they were brought forth into genera and species from the hidden and profound recesses of nature, in which they were made causally and primordially. For what prevents us from understanding that, just as the solidity and fruitfulness of nature is signified by the word “earth,” so by the designation “waters” its hidden depth may likewise be understood, so that one and the same origin is recognized for all animals which are said to be created either from the earth or from the waters, although their contemplation is divided? For in the fifth prophetic theory some are recorded as having been created, and in the sixth others. [Note: [Col. 0749] CF reads *esse*; A omits it.]

Nor do I think that this was done without reason. For it seems likely that earthly animals are commanded to be brought forth from the earth on the sixth day, on which the human being was also made, because they appear to bear a greater likeness to the human being in their nature. Indeed, everything that is recognized in the nature of the human animal apart from intellect and reason is found, through physical investigation, to be naturally present in them.

### MASTER

Not only, as I think, is there nothing to prevent our understanding these things in this way; rather, reason itself, considered more attentively, urges us to understand what has been written according to the truth of created things. For the meaning of the divine utterances is manifold and infinite. Thus, in one and the same feather of a peacock, one observes in one and the same place of a small portion of that feather an astonishing and beautiful variety of countless colors. [Note: [Col. 0749] A reads *una eademque*; CF reads *una eademque* in the corresponding position.] [Note: [Col. 0749] A omits *loco*.] [Note: [Col. 0749] CF reads *portiunculae*; A reads *portiuncula*.]

Indeed, nature itself draws us toward this understanding. For this perceptible earth and water are composite bodies made from the qualities of the four elements; and they generate nothing from themselves, nor does any species of nature arise from them, although it appears to be born from them. [Note: [Col. 0749] CF reads *naturae species*; A reads *species naturae*.] [Note: [Col. 0749] A omits *nascitur, quamvis ex eis*.] Yet the power of the seeds that are in them, through the operation of that life which is called nutritive, and according to the laws and principles implanted in them, breaks forth, insofar as divine providence permits, from the hidden recesses of creation into diverse species of herbs, shoots, and animals, through genera and forms.

Accordingly, from the same source from which visible and tangible earth and water proceeded into their natural species, qualities, and quantities, all things that appear to be born from them derive the origin of their generation. For there is a certain most general and common nature of all things, created by the one principle of all things; from it, as from a most spacious fountain, created things flow through hidden bodily channels like streams, and pour forth into the various forms of individual things. [Note: [Col. 0749] A reads *et*; CF omits it.]

That power, coming through various seeds from the secrets of nature and first bursting forth in the seeds themselves, then mingled with diverse fluids, boils forth into the individual perceptible species.

### DISCUSSION

These things are sound, resemble the truth, and agree with the investigations of natural philosophy. But since the human being, who was created on the sixth day, is included among the animals, which are comprehended under one genus, I should like to hear from you whether he is to be understood as included in this divine command by which the earth is ordered to bring forth a living soul.

### MASTER

I should not easily resolve this question [Note: [Col. 0749] C reads *non facile solverim*; A reads *non tam facile absolverim*; F reads *non facile solverem*.] if Holy Scripture merely declared: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul.” But because it added, “according to its genus,” it has made perfectly clear that all animals are included in this command. For there is no species that is not entirely placed within its genus.

Yet because this animal form which is established in the human being surpasses the nature of the other animals belonging to the same genus by the dignity of reason and understanding, prophetic contemplation wisely wished to join it to the other animals, so that it might narrate more broadly and abundantly, in accordance with the excellence of its nature, the creation of the human being at the end of all things made by God.

Therefore the greatest and most precious species of animal is mentioned twice in the works of the sixth contemplation: first, it is commanded to be brought forth from the earth according to its genus, which is animal; then, shortly afterward, once the other animals have been divided in the briefest manner, its creation is introduced as being in the image and likeness of God. [Note: [Col. 0749] CF reads *jubetur*; A reads *videtur*.]

### DISCUSSION

Thus one form is brought forth from the earth among the other animals, and immediately afterward is declared to have been made in the image of God. This rightly troubles me. For if the entire genus called “animal,” together with all its forms, were made in the image and likeness of God, what you teach would perhaps not disturb me: that the human being is brought forth from the earth among the other animals and afterward fashioned in the image and likeness of God.

But since the divine account declares that only the human being, and no other animal besides the human being, is created in the image of God, I am greatly astonished at how the human being is brought forth from the earth among cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth, yet alone is formed in the image of God, far and incomparably above all the other animals. Scripture says: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness.” And what is more astonishing is how he is brought forth from the earth among those over whom he is set and whom he is commanded to rule. For Scripture added: “And let him rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and the beasts, and every creature, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0749] CF reads *a*; A reads *e*.]

### MASTER

You are troubled neither without reason nor irrationally. These matters are worthy of the most careful and diligent inquiry. First, however, so that you may understand, once all the darkness of ambiguity has been removed, that the human being was created within the universal genus of animals, accept this greatest argument: namely, the threefold division of this genus into cattle, creeping things, and beasts. I think this division was not made without cause.

For on the other days—that is, on the third and fifth—on which genera and species are mentioned, no division of a genus into species is introduced. Instead, either only the genus and its undifferentiated species are given, as on the third day, when the genera and species of herbs and shoots are commanded to arise from the earth; or only the genus and one species of it, as on the fifth day, when he calls the genus of fish “creeping thing” and that of birds “flying creature,” dividing neither into species.

For when he said, “And God created great whales,” one should understand that he placed a species in place of a genus rather than divided a genus into a species. [Note: [Col. 0751] CF reads *speciem*; A reads *species*.] [Note: [Col. 0751] A reads *est*; CF omits it, though F has added it above.]

For how could a division of a genus into one species take place, when every division is found in no fewer than two?

On the sixth day, however, not only the creation of the genus but also its threefold division into species is narrated. “God said,” he says, “Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its genus: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth, according to their species.” Or, according to the Seventy interpreters: “God said: Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its genus, four-footed creatures, and creeping things, and beasts according to their genus; and it was so.”

This threefold division, therefore, as I think, of all life that adheres to an earthly body and, through union, produces an animal—for an animal is a conjunction of body and soul together with sensation [Note: [Col. 0751] A omits *cum sensu*.]—indicates a threefold movement.

Indeed, that threefold movement is understood in the human being alone, since he alone is a rational animal. He has certain movements of his own subject to reason, which appear to be signified by the term “cattle” or “four-footed creatures.” For example, he moves the fivefold sense of the body, in a disciplined manner, toward the knowledge of sensible things through the diligent pursuit of an intelligent understanding of them.

This movement is not improperly called “cattle,” for it provides no small assistance to the rational soul in the contemplation of the truth of all sensible things, once every falsity has been removed, through true and sincere knowledge. There is also, as it were, a four-footed movement of the senses subject to reason. For everything that we know through sensation in the nature of sensible things is composed from the four elements, or is constituted in something composed from them. [Note: [Col. 0751] CF reads *rerum est hoc*; A reads *hoc est*.]

Suppose, for example, that you have looked upon a bodily form: that form itself is constituted in some matter made from the qualities of the four elements. [Note: [Col. 0751] CF reads *facta*; A omits it.] If you have perceived a sound or an odor, it arises from air composed of the four elements. Likewise, if you have perceived taste or touch, you will not doubt that it arises from combinations of water and earth.

The bodily sense has therefore not improperly received the designation “four-footed,” since everything that senses derives its origin from nowhere other than the four elements. [Note: [Col. 0751] CF reads *quadrupedis*; A reads *quadrupedum*.]

You may rightly call certain movements, taken from the lower nature, irrational—that is, resistant to reason—such as anger and desire, and the disordered appetites of the bodily senses, which have been assigned to sensible creatures for their misuse. [Note: [Col. 0751] CF omits *recte dixeris*.] [Note: [Col. 0751] CF omits *attributos*.]

And since these movements have been implanted in human nature from irrational animals, they are appropriately signified by the designation “beasts,” especially since they never cease to resist rational disciplines and can scarcely, or never, be tamed by them; indeed, they always desire to tear rational movements apart with savage force. [Note: [Col. 0751] CF reads *hi*; A reads *hujusmodi*.] [Note: [Col. 0751] CF reads *semper*; A reads *super*.]

Moreover, in the rational animal there are certain hidden movements by which it chiefly administers the body joined to it. They are established in the active [Note: [Col. 0751] CF reads *auctiva*; A reads *activa*.] and nutritive part of the soul. [Note: [Col. 0751] A reads *constitutae*.] Since these movements carry out their functions with natural ease and, as it were, secretly—for they in no way trouble or disturb the soul’s attention, provided that the integrity of nature remains unharmed—and since, penetrating the bodily harmony through a kind of silent passage, they have rightly earned the designation “creeping things.”

But the other animals, apart from the human being alone, possess only two of the three movements mentioned above: one, which belongs properly to the senses and lacks the governance of reason and is therefore bestial; the other, which is assigned to nutritive life and resembles a creeping thing. The human being shares these with the other animals, and the other animals likewise share them with him. [Note: [Col. 0751] A reads *tantum*; CF reads *tantummodo*.] [Note: [Col. 0751] CF reads *in sensibus*; A reads *in sensibilibus*.] [Note: [Col. 0751] A reads *propter*; CF reads *per*.]

Do you therefore see the human being in all animals, and all animals in the human being, and the human being above all?

And if anyone examines more attentively the marvelous and utterly ineffable constitution of nature itself, he will clearly discover that the same human being is both a certain form within the genus of animals and subsists above every animal form. Accordingly, both affirmation and negation can rightly be received and predicated of him: “The human being is an animal; the human being is not an animal.”

For when body and nutritive life, sensation and memory of sensible things, and every irrational appetite—such as anger and desire—are considered in him, he is altogether an animal. All these things are common to him with the other animals.

But in the higher part of himself, by which he consists in reason, understanding, and inner sensation, with all his rational movements, which are called virtues, and with the memory of eternal and divine things, he is altogether not an animal. For all these same things are shared by the human being with the celestial essences, which incomprehensibly surpass everything included in the nature of animals through the excellence of their substance. [Note: [Col. 0753] CF reads *excellentia substantiae incomprehensibiliter*; A reads *excellentia suae naturae incomparabiliter*.]

Thus, as we said, it is rightly said of the human being: “He is an animal; he is not an animal.”

We can also confirm this from the authority of divine Scripture. The Apostle says: “The animal human being does not perceive the things that belong to God” [Note: [Col. 0753] A reads *spiritus* instead of *quae sunt Dei*.]; and again: “The spiritual human being judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one.”

Observe how clearly and openly he divides the human being, as it were, into two human beings. One is animal, because he exists as something like the nature of animals, which receives nothing spiritual within itself; the other is spiritual, because he communicates with eternal, spiritual, and divine subsistences and is free from all animality.

That part by which he is an animal appropriately receives the name “outer human being”; that by which he surpasses the other animals and himself insofar as he is an animal appropriately receives the name “inner human being.” For, as the same Apostle says, in those who live spiritually, “the outer human being is corrupted, but the inner human being is renewed day by day.”

For the one who lives perfectly not only despises his body, the life by which it is administered, all bodily senses together with what he perceives through them, all irrational movements that he feels within himself, and the memory of all mutable things; he also corrupts and destroys them as far as he can, so that they may in no way prevail in him. Indeed, he desires that they—and those things in himself—perish entirely. But he renews himself, insofar as he participates in the celestial essence, ascending day by day—that is, from virtue to virtue—as divine grace moves, cooperates, leads, and perfects him.

The nature by which the human being shares with animals is called “flesh”; that by which he participates in the celestial essence is called “mind,” or “spirit,” or “intellect.” Hear the Apostle: “With the mind,” he says, “I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.” Innumerable statements of divine Scripture confirm this same point.

What wonder, then, if the human being is understood to have a twofold condition, since he himself is in a certain sense twofold? What is like the animals is created together with the animals; what is spiritual in itself and absolutely is created together with spiritual beings.

Accordingly, do not be troubled by my saying that the human being was brought forth from the earth together with the other animals in one and the same genus, yet was made in the image and likeness of God, beyond the nature of all animals.

### DISCUSSION

Perhaps I would not be troubled if I could clearly discern how the human being was created under one and the same genus with all animals in such a way that, in the better part of himself, he subsists above the whole nature of animals. [Note: [Col. 0753] A reads *Nonne* rather than *Non me*.] [Note: [Col. 0753] CF reads *sui*; A reads *sua*.] [Note: [Col. 0753] A reads *supra*; CF reads *super*.]

### MASTER

I am surprised that you repeat the same point. For we have said that the human being, insofar as he is an animal, is among the animals under one genus; insofar as he is not an animal, he was made outside every genus of all animals. [Note: [Col. 0753] CF reads *animalium omnium*; A reads *omnium animalium*.]

### DISCUSSION

Alas! A much greater and far more difficult question has arisen, it seems to me.

### MASTER

What is it? Tell me, please.

### DISCUSSION

You seem, as I think, to hold that two souls subsist in one human being: one that administers, vivifies, nourishes, and increases the body, perceives sensible things through the bodily senses, stores their images in its memory, and performs the other things that it is well known the souls of other animals perform in their bodies; and another that subsists in reason and understanding and has been made in the image and likeness of God. This seems highly absurd. [Note: [Col. 0753] A reads *corpus quae*; CF reads *quae corpus*.] [Note: [Col. 0753] A reads *subsistens*; CF reads *subsistentem*.]

### MASTER

Neither reason nor divine authority permits me to suppose two souls in one human being; rather, it forbids this, and no one who philosophizes rightly is permitted to believe it. I assert that one and the same rational soul is ineffably joined to the human body and is the human being.

The human being himself, through a marvelous and intelligible division, is, in that part by which he has been made in the image and likeness of the Creator, a participant in no animality and entirely free from it; but in that part by which he shares in animality, he was brought forth from the earth within the universal genus of animals—that is, from the common nature of all things.

### DISCUSSION

What, then, shall we say? Is the human soul to be believed a certain simple nature, entirely free from every composition, or is it joined together into a certain unity from particular parts? [Note: [Col. 0753] A reads *in* rather than *an*.]

### MASTER

I hold one point with complete firmness: that it is simple and lacks every joining of parts. But I entirely reject the other proposition, namely, that it admits any composition of parts differing from one another.

For it is wholly in itself everywhere throughout the whole. It is wholly life, wholly intellect, wholly reason, wholly sensation, wholly memory; wholly it vivifies, nourishes, contains, and increases the body. In all the senses as a whole it wholly perceives the forms of sensible things; wholly it considers, distinguishes, combines, and judges the nature and reason of those things beyond every bodily sense. Wholly outside and above every creature—and itself as well, since it is included among creatures—it revolves around its Creator through an intelligible and eternal movement while it is cleansed from all vices and images. [Note: [Col. 0753] CF includes *phantasiisque*; A omits it.]

Although it subsists naturally as something simple, it receives divisions of its intelligible and substantial differences, as though of a whole into parts, according to the number of its movements. Accordingly, it is designated by many names. [Note: [Col. 0753] CF reads *denominatur*; A reads *denotatur*.]

When it moves around the divine essence, it is called mind, spirit, and intellect; when it considers the natures and causes of created things, reason; when it receives the forms of sensible things through the bodily senses, sensation; when it carries out its hidden movements in the body according to the likeness of irrational souls, nourishing and increasing it, it is customarily called the vital movement properly speaking. [Note: [Col. 0753] CF reads *vitalis proprie motus*; A reads *vita proprie*, omitting *motus*.]

Yet in all these it is wholly everywhere.

### DISCUSSION

Thus it is wholly brought forth from the earth within the genus of animals, and wholly made in the image of God. For the arguments already given conclude that it is so and no otherwise.

### MASTER

Indeed; and no one who philosophizes rightly and devoutly is permitted to doubt this, lest he appear to divide a nature that is utterly simple and indivisible, which would be exceedingly impious.

### DISCUSSION

I do not sufficiently understand how, according to the controversy stated above, one and the same human being is both an animal and not an animal; or how he is both animal and not animal, flesh and not flesh, spiritual and not spiritual; nor how these opposites and contradictions can be understood in one utterly simple nature.

### MASTER

If anyone examines more attentively everything that appears to you contradictory in the simplicity of human nature, he will find, clearer than daylight, that it is not only not contradictory but entirely harmonious. For it is agreed among the wise that the whole of creation is contained in the human being. [Note: [Col. 0755] CF reads *contineri*; A reads *inveniri*.]

He understands and reasons like an angel; he senses and administers the body like an animal. Accordingly, all creation is understood in him.

The whole of creation has a fivefold division. It is either corporeal, vital, sensitive, rational, or intellectual. All these are contained in the human being in every respect.

The lowest level of his subsistence is the body; next comes the seminal life that administers the body, over which sensation presides; then reason, which rules the parts of nature below it; and finally the spirit occupies the highest place among all these. [Note: [Col. 0755] CF reads *subsistentiae*; A reads *naturae*.]

Accordingly, the whole of human nature, insofar as it shares with animals, is rightly an animal. It shares with them insofar as it is body, insofar as it possesses life that governs the body, insofar as it possesses sensation, and insofar as it handles the images of sensible things in memory.

But insofar as it participates in the divine and celestial essence, it is not an animal. [Note: [Col. 0755] CF includes *est*; A omits it.] Through reason, intellect, and the memory of eternal things, it participates in the celestial essence. In that part, therefore, it is entirely free from animality.

For in that part of itself it has been made in the image of God, and to that part alone God speaks in suitable human beings. As Augustine says in the eleventh book of *The City of God*, God speaks to that which in the human being is better than the other things of which the human being consists, and than which God alone is better.

Since the human being has been made in the image of God, he is plainly closer to the God above him in that part by which he surpasses the lower parts of himself, which he also shares with cattle.

It should also be noted that even in this life, before everything in the human being that is animal has been transformed into the spiritual, and everything composed in him has been united into ineffable simplicity, the whole human being can become both animal and spiritual. He becomes animal by free choice alone; spiritual, however, by free choice together with grace, without which the natural power of the will is in no way sufficient to move the human being toward the spirit. [Note: [Col. 0755] A reads *adunatur*; CF reads *adunetur*.]

The human being becomes and is called “animal” when, abandoning the movements that operate according to reason and intellect around the knowledge of the Creator and creation, he falls by voluntary appetite into the irrational movements by which brute animals are moved around bodily desires, so that he fills his entire attention with the deadly pleasures of temporal and fragile things that tend toward nonbeing. [Note: [Col. 0755] CF reads *quae*; A reads *qui*.] [Note: [Col. 0755] A reads *intentionem*; CF reads *cogitationem*.]

He is spiritual, however, when, having changed his entire way of life for the better, inflamed by the fire of divine love, rejecting the world and the flesh in every way, and abandoning all animal movements, he is wholly transformed into the likeness of the celestial essences, so that what will be his according to an unchangeable substance precedes in him according to the quality of a life adorned with virtues. [Note: [Col. 0755] CF reads *praecedat*; A reads *procedat*.]

Accordingly, the human being is recognized as animal in two ways: first, in that he subsists according to nature; second, in what happens to him through an irrational movement of free will inclined toward evil.

Likewise, he is spiritual both according to the nature in which he subsists and according to a good will anticipated by divine grace, cleansed in act and knowledge, adorned with the ornaments of virtues, and restored to the former dignity of the divine image. [Note: [Col. 0755] CF reads *actu et scientia*; A reads *ac tam vitiis* (a materially uncertain, apparently corrupt reading).] [Note: [Col. 0755] A reads *quam virtutum*; CF reads *virtutum*.] [Note: [Col. 0755] All witnesses read *revocatus*.]

### DISCUSSION

I gladly accept these things, but I do not see clearly enough how, although all species are one in a genus, species that contradict one another subsist in that one. For the definition of the human being seems to contradict the definitions of the other animals. The human being is a rational animal, whereas the other animals are irrational. Do you see how “rational” and “irrational” are opposed to each other?

### MASTER

Look somewhat more sharply into the natures of things, and you will find that this proposition, which occurs by way of difference, contains differences under one genus, not contradictions.

For example: Every creature is either visible or invisible. Here a difference is made, not a contradiction. Visibility and invisibility are two things distinguished from each other, not things opposed to each other.

Likewise, every creature is either corporeal or incorporeal. The relations of the divine persons are also distinguished in this way. The Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Spirit neither unbegotten nor begotten. [Note: [Col. 0755] A omits *Spiritus neque ingenitus neque genitus*.] There are innumerable examples of this kind.

And so that you may recognize the matter more clearly, observe that every contradiction is understood within one and the same species or part, whereas difference is understood in distinct things.

Thus, if someone were to say of the human being, “The human being is a rational animal; the human being is an irrational animal,” speaking of that species of nature which is substantially called “human being,” the statements would be contradictory, and necessarily one would be true and the other false. [Note: [Col. 0755] A omits *naturae*.] [Note: [Col. 0755] A reads *enim*; CF omits it.] [Note: [Col. 0755] CF reads *alterum falsum*; A reads *alterum vero falsum*.]

For contradictory statements about the same subject cannot both be true or both be false, whether they are universal or particular.

But when you say, “The human being is a rational animal; the horse is an irrational animal,” no contradiction is understood, because you disclose the substantial difference between the human being and the horse.

For the difference of the human being from the other living creatures is that he possesses reason, just as the difference of the other living creatures from the human being is that they do not possess reason. [Note: [Col. 0757] CF reads *sicut*; A reads *sic et*.] Here neither habit nor privation is discerned.

The habit of the human being is possessing reason; the habit of the horse is the absence of reason. For the horse is not deprived of a habit that it could never have possessed. Where a habit does not precede, privation will not follow. [Note: [Col. 0757] A reads *recedit*; CF reads *praecedit*.]

An animal, or anything that participates in life, would not suffer death if the habit of life were not first present in it. Therefore we properly call no animal foolish except one in which we see that the habit of reason can arise; nor do we call anything dull except that in which the disposition to sensation can naturally exist.

### DISCUSSION

Why, then, did you say that in one and the same subject two statements opposed to one another cannot be simultaneously false or simultaneously true, but that if one is true the other must necessarily be false? For example, if someone were to say of one and the same thing, “This animal is a horse; it is not a horse”—when you seem to assert that contradictory statements can simultaneously be true in the human being: “The human being is an animal; the human being is not an animal,” and you teach that this is naturally present in him until he is wholly moved from the animal into the spiritual.

And why is this true only in the human being, whereas in the other animals it is in no way true? In them it is wholly true that they are animals, while it is wholly false that they are not animals. [Note: [Col. 0757] A omits *omnino*.]

### MASTER

Do you think that any animal other than the human being was made in the image of God? [Note: [Col. 0757] CF reads *praeter*; A reads *quam*.]

### DISCUSSION

Certainly not.

### MASTER

Will you deny that two statements struggling against one another, when predicated of God, can be simultaneously true and in no way false, although both do not have the same force—for example: “God is truth; God is not truth”?

### DISCUSSION

I would not dare to deny it, since he himself says of himself: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” But the holy Areopagite Dionysius says in the *Symbolic Theology* that God is neither truth nor life. For he says: “He is neither power, nor light, nor life”; and shortly afterward: “He is neither knowledge nor truth.” [Note: [Col. 0757] A has *ait* instead of *pro Deus*.] [Note: [Col. 0757] A reads *vita est*.] [Note: [Col. 0757] A reads *veritas est*.]

### MASTER

Perhaps Dionysius contradicts Christ, who declares of himself that he is truth?

### DISCUSSION

God forbid.

### MASTER

Then both are true: “God is truth; God is not truth.”

### DISCUSSION

Not only true, but most true. The first statement is made by affirmation through metaphor, because he himself is the creator and primordial cause of truth, by participation in which all things that are true are true. The second is made through negation according to transcendence, because he is more than truth.

Accordingly, it is true both that “God is truth,” since he is the cause of all true things, and that “God is not truth,” because he surpasses everything that is said, understood, and exists.

Nor am I unaware of what you added, that both statements do not have the same force. [Note: [Col. 0757] CF reads *sint*; A reads *sunt*.] For affirmation is less effective than negation in signifying the ineffable divine essence, because one transfers something from creatures to the Creator, whereas the other predicates something of the Creator beyond every creature, from the Creator himself.

### MASTER

You understand well what I added. What wonder, then, if it can truly be predicated simultaneously of the human being, who alone among the other animals was made in the image of God: “The human being is an animal; the human being is not an animal”? In this way, at least, we may understand that this animal was specially created in the image of God, of whom contradictory statements can truly be predicated simultaneously, though they cannot be so predicated of the other living creatures.

Moreover, if affirmations and negations of the divine essence are compatible because it surpasses all things that have been made by it and of which it is the cause, who would not be permitted to see that negations and affirmations can harmoniously be applied to its image and likeness, which is in the human being, since he surpasses the other animals among which he was created under one genus and whose cause he is? [Note: [Col. 0757] A reads *eo*; CF reads *ea*.] [Note: [Col. 0757] A reads *est conditus*; CF reads *conditus est*.]

For who among those rightly wise could fail to know that this visible world, together with all its parts, from the highest to the lowest, was made for the human being, so that he might preside over it and rule all visible things?

The holy Gregory teaches this in his sermon *On the Image* in these words:

“How,” he says, “was the whole of creation, apart from the human being, established at once by divine power together with the command, whereas counsel precedes the creation of the human being, and the craftsman prefigures by the word of Scripture what he would be, what kind of being it would be fitting for him to be, to what principal exemplar he would bear likeness, in what he would be made, what he would do once made, and over what he would rule? The Word first takes everything into consideration, so that he who would possess sovereignty over existing things might receive a more venerable dignity of generation before he came into being.”

For God said, he says: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fish of the sea, the beasts of the earth, the birds of the sky, the cattle, and the whole earth.”

And this was given to him whether he sinned or did not sin, although he would rule in one way if he had not sinned and in another way after he sinned. [Note: [Col. 0757] CF reads *peccavit*; A reads *peccatur*.]

And so that you may recognize this more certainly, do you think that the human being, in that part of himself by which he was made in the image of God, is an animal? Or that, in that part by which he was brought forth from the earth among the animals, he subsists as the image of God? Or do you think that neither of the two—that is, neither image nor animal—is truly present in him?

### DISCUSSION

I would in no way judge the last proposition to be true; sound reason proves that these two are simultaneously true in the human being. But I would altogether deny the former—that the image is in the animal and the animal in the image—if I were not troubled by what you defined earlier: namely, that the human being is everywhere wholly in himself. From this, it seems to follow that the whole image subsists in the whole animal, and the whole animal in the whole image, throughout the entire human being. [Note: [Col. 0759] CF reads *nullo modo aestimarim*; A reads *nullo modo dubium oportet aestimari*.] [Note: [Col. 0759] CF reads *omnino negarim*; A reads *omnino non negarem*.] [Note: [Col. 0759] CF reads *superioribus*; A reads *superiori*.]

### MASTER

I am surprised that such things trouble you, since you see that precisely in this the image and likeness of God can be recognized in human nature. For just as God is both above all things and in all things—for he himself is the essence of all things, he who alone truly is—and although he is wholly in all things, he does not cease to be wholly outside all things: wholly in the world, wholly around the world, wholly in sensible creation, wholly in intelligible creation, wholly making the universe, wholly made in the universe, wholly in the whole of the universe, wholly in its parts—[Note: [Col. 0759] A reads *sic* at this point.] [Note: [Col. 0759] A omits *universitatem facit*.] [Note: [Col. 0759] A omits the second *totus*.]
its whole, because it is both whole and part, and neither whole nor part: thus human nature, in its own world, in its universe, in its visible and invisible parts [Note: [Col. 0759] A omits “its parts.”], is wholly present in itself, wholly present in its whole, wholly present in its parts, and its parts are wholly present both in themselves and in the whole. For even its most remote and least valuable part—I mean the body—is, according to its defining principles, wholly present in the whole human being, since the body, insofar as it is truly body, subsists in its defining principles, which were made in the primordial creation. And although it is thus present in itself—namely, human nature [Note: [Col. 0759] A omits “namely, human nature.”]—it surpasses its whole. For it could not otherwise adhere to its Creator if it did not surpass both everything beneath it [Note: [Col. 0759] A reads “beneath him”] and itself, since, as Augustine says, between our mind, by which we understand the Father, and the truth through which we understand him, there is no created thing interposed.

The Areopagite himself—I mean Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0759] “I mean Dionysius” appears in CF; A omits it]—also teaches this beautifully in his *Symbolic Theology*, saying:

“O friend Timothy, strengthen your course concerning mystical contemplations [Note: [Col. 0759] A reads “sing”], and abandon the senses [Note: [Col. 0759] A reads “to abandon”], as well as intellectual operations, sensible and invisible things, every non-being and being; and, insofar as possible, return in ignorance to the unity of him who is beyond every essence and knowledge [Note: [Col. 0759] A reads “above”]. For by an immeasurable and absolute transcendence of mind, both beyond yourself and beyond all things, you will ascend, abandoning everything and released from everything, toward the superessential ray of the divine darkness.”

And in the Gospel the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0759] A reads: “and the Lord in the Gospel, saying, says”]: “Where I am, there also is my servant.” But he is above all things [Note: [Col. 0759] A reads “above”]. Therefore the human being who adheres to him is above all things and above himself, insofar as he is in all things.

Although human nature, while it lives in this mortal life, cannot in reality adhere to God, nevertheless, because it is both possible and natural for it to adhere to its Creator, it is rightly said to adhere through the grace of the one to whom it adheres. For possibility is often taken as experience, and what certainly will one day occur is sometimes reckoned as present, even as already accomplished [Note: [Col. 0759] A reads “as accomplished.”].

And why did I say “in its own world, in its own universe,” when I have stated more plainly that it is in the entire visible and invisible universe? Human nature is wholly present in the universe of the entire created nature, because every creature has been constituted in it [Note: [Col. 0759] A reads “and in it”], has been joined together in it [Note: [Col. 0759] A reads “because”], will return into him, and will be saved through him.

Hear its Creator saying: “Preach the Gospel to every creature”—namely, to the human being. In him there is intellect, reason, sense [Note: [Col. 0759] A omits “sense”], seminal life, and body—not this corruptible body after sin, but that body which existed before transgression; not this composite and dissoluble body, but that simple and indivisible one; not this animal and earthly body, but that spiritual and heavenly one; not this body generated from two sexes [Note: [Col. 0759] A reads “from a flow”] through carnal unions and semen, but that body brought forth from the simplicity of nature before transgression and destined to appear in the resurrection; not this body known through bodily sensation, but that one still hidden in the secret depths of nature; not this body added as a punishment for sin, but that which was implanted in nature while it was still incorrupt, and into which this corruptible and mortal body will return.

“The body is sown,” says the Apostle—that is, it is born from seed—“in corruption; it will rise in power.” In what power? In the power, namely, of that body which was first created naturally. “It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.”

Everything that has been created naturally in the human being necessarily remains eternally whole and incorrupt. For it did not seem consonant with divine justice that anything made by it should perish, especially since nature itself did not sin, but the perverse will, which irrationally moves against rational nature.

The strongest proof of this is the following. If hatred of death is naturally present in the human being, how could he not naturally hate the cause of death—namely, sin? It is also common to all animals to avoid and fear death and the causes of death. Therefore, just as no wise person wishes to fall into error, so human nature did not wish to sin. Consequently, its Creator, being just, did not wish to punish it; rather, he wished to add to it something in which the offense that had arisen from perverse will, with the serpent’s persuasion, could be purged, so that it would not cling to it forever.

Rational and intellectual nature, although it did not wish to be deceived, could nevertheless be led astray, especially since it had not yet received the perfection of its formation—a perfection which, by the merit of obedience, it would have received when it was to be transformed into *theosis*, that is, deification.

We must not, therefore, judge human nature according to how it appears to bodily senses and according to the punishment of transgression, by which, in the likeness of irrational animals, it is born in this world through the union of the sexes, temporally and corruptibly, with death as its end. We must judge it according to how it was created in the image of God before it sinned.

This dignity of nature is so ineffable that it incomprehensibly eludes every bodily sense and every mortal thought. Yet, deceived and fallen, blinded by the darkness of its perverse will, it consigned both itself and its Creator to oblivion [Note: [Col. 0761] CF reads “its Creator”; A reads “its own Creator.”]. This is its most wretched death, its deepest submersion in the darkness of ignorance, its most distant separation from itself and from its Creator, and its closest and most shameful likeness to irrational mortal creatures.

From this condition no one could redeem it, call it back, restore it, or return it to its former state from which it had fallen. But the Wisdom of God, who created it and received it into the unity of his own substance [Note: [Col. 0761] CF reads “his substance”; A reads “of its substance”], liberated all things from misery in order to save it [Note: [Col. 0761] CF reads “and to liberate all things.”].

Let it not trouble you, therefore, that it has been said of human nature that it is wholly present everywhere in itself, that the image is wholly present in the animal, and that the animal is wholly present in the image.

### 6

For everything that its Creator originally fashioned in it remains wholly and intact, though it still lies hidden, awaiting the revelation of the sons of God.

**DISCIPLE.** I might perhaps not be troubled if you clearly persuaded me of what I cannot discern for myself. For I am considering whether a human being, if he had not sinned, would be an animal. I can also put the question another way: was a human being an animal before sin? If he was not, why have we labored so much in seeking—and, as it seemed, finding—that the human being was created within the universal genus of animals? For if he was not created within that genus, then either he was not an animal at all before sin, or, if he was, he was created within some other genus of animals. But neither does divine Scripture introduce such a view, nor does a careful investigation of reason discover it in the nature of things. For all animals subsist within one genus, from which they proceed by divisions.

But if, in the words that are written, “Let the earth bring forth a living soul,” the creation of the human being was introduced among the other animals before sin, how does the Psalmist, as though laying a great reproach upon human nature after the Fall, say: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts, and became like them”? Here the Prophet plainly seems to declare that, before the Fall, the human being stood in the dignity of a spiritual substance, beyond the nature of all animals; but when he fell and failed to understand the dignity of his own nature, he fell into the disgrace of resembling beasts. If, however, he was an animal before the Fall, why is he justly reproached after the Fall for having incurred the likeness of animals, with which he was naturally created within one genus?

**MASTER.** You would rightly deliberate if the Prophet had simply said, “He was compared with beasts and became like them.” But by adding “with foolish beasts,” he made it sufficiently clear that the human being is chiefly reproached for this: while he was a spiritual and rational animal, created at the beginning in the image and likeness of God, he moved himself foolishly and irrationally against the commandment of his Creator and drew upon himself the likeness of foolish—that is, brute—animals, thereby dishonoring the natural dignity of his nature through movements inappropriate to him. For he is not praised because he is an animal, but because he is the image of God; just as he is not blamed because he is an animal, but because he wished to deform the image, which he could not destroy. For in the other animals, irrational movements are not shameful, since they are naturally present in them and without them the animals cannot exist. But in a rational animal it is blameworthy and deformed to fall, through the illicit desire of a perverse will, into the movements of irrational creatures, although those movements are natural to them, and to wish to remain in them after abandoning the higher beauty of the divine image.

**DISCIPLE.** The rational creature is rightly blamed on account of the movements of irrational animals. For if a man of honorable appearance were voluntarily to clothe himself in the form of a beast, he would rightly be reproached for hurling himself from what is better into what is far worse.

### 7

But I still ask why God created the human being within the genus of animals, when he intended to make him in his own image and likeness. It would surely seem more glorious for the one chosen to participate in the heavenly character above all animals, and to be a companion of the celestial essences—into which no consubstantiality with earthly animals is permitted to enter—to be created wholly free from animality. For those beings are not weighed down by earthly bodies, nor do they use bodily senses to acquire knowledge of sensible things. They do not receive phantasies from outside; rather, inwardly, within themselves, they know the rational principles of the things they see. For the soul, too, does not see outside itself what it senses, but through phantasies within itself—something the angels do not undergo.

Although Plato defines an angel as a rational and immortal animal, what we cannot establish by the authority of Holy Scripture and the holy Fathers we ought not, since it is rash, to accept among the certain investigations of nature. That Saint Augustine does not deny that the highest angels possess spiritual bodies, in which they often appear, but even confirms it, in no way compels us to believe that the celestial substances are animals—especially since it is not the harmony and inseparable joining of celestial and incorruptible bodies with angelic spirits, but the connection, mediated by sensation, of earthly and corruptible bodies with souls, whether rational or irrational, that produces an animal.

For if an external sense is present in angelic bodies and intellects, what prevents us from saying that they are animals composed of body, soul, and sensation, with the intellect giving them life, as Plato holds? And if this is so, why are they not counted within the genus of animals? For a human being, too, would be an animal if he did not sin. Sin did not make the human being an animal, but nature did. Nor does any authority transmit that the transgressing angels are animals.

This is taught especially by the following argument. That future happiness which is promised to holy human beings is proclaimed to be nothing other than a perfect equality with the angelic nature, lacking nothing. But what person of sound judgment would believe that the future transformation of the human being will be like a passage from an inferior animal into a superior animal, from an earthly being into a celestial one, from a temporal being into an eternal one, from a mortal being into an immortal one, and from a miserable being into a blessed one? Rather, everything that in this life is understood or perceived in holy human beings as common to the other animals will, through an ineffable transformation, be transferred into that celestial and incommunicable essence devoid of all animality. This, too, would have happened to the human being if he had not sinned.

Why, then, was the human being created within the genus of animals produced from the earth, if he will not always remain in it? For when this world, of which the human being is an animal part, has perished, everything in the human being that is animal will perish with it and in it. True reason does not permit the whole to suffer destruction while its parts are saved from destruction. Moreover, if the whole world, together with all its parts, is destined to perish, I do not see clearly how the human being, insofar as he is a part of the world, will remain after the world, or where or how he will remain. Therefore I earnestly beg you to loosen the knots of this question.

**MASTER.** You are demanding a very profound physical theory of the human condition and compelling our discussion to advance farther. If you were asking why God created the human being within the genus of animals, when he proposed to make him in his own image, it would be enough for me to answer briefly: because he wished to create him in such a way that he would be a certain animal in which he might manifest his expressed image. But whoever asks why he wished this is asking for the causes of the divine will; to seek those causes is excessively presumptuous and arrogant. For who has known the mind of the Lord?

But if I say this, perhaps you will fall silent in dissatisfaction and think that we can bring nothing to a pure or perfect conclusion. I will not, then, say why he wished it, since that surpasses every intellect; but I will say, insofar as he himself grants it, what he wished to do.

He made every visible and invisible creature in the human being, because the whole universe of created nature is understood to exist in him. For although the extent of the human being’s original condition after the loss of the supernal light still lies hidden, nevertheless nothing exists naturally in the celestial essences that does not subsist essentially in the human being. There is intellect and reason; there is also naturally implanted in him the principle by which a celestial and angelic body may be possessed. After the resurrection this will appear more clearly than light, both in the good and in the wicked. For this will be common to the whole of human nature: to rise in eternal, incorruptible, and spiritual bodies. “The animal body is sown,” he says; “the spiritual body will rise.”

This whole sensible world was created in him. For no part of it, whether corporeal or incorporeal, is found not to subsist, sense, live, and be incorporated in the human being. Do not weigh bodily masses in the human being; consider rather his natural power, especially since you see in the human body the pupil of the eye, which, although it is smallest in the size of all the members, possesses the greatest power.

Therefore, if God had not created the human being within the genus of animals—or certainly if he had not established the whole nature of all animals in the human being—how would the entire visible and invisible creation be comprehended in him? Thus we may reasonably say that God wished to establish the human being within the genus of animals for this reason: he wished to create every creature in him.

If you ask why he wished to create every creature in him, I answer: because he wished to make him in his own image and likeness, so that, just as the archetype surpasses all things in the excellence of its essence, so its image might surpass all creation in dignity and grace. But why, specifically and above all other visible and invisible creatures, he wished to make the human being in his own image—I confess that I am entirely ignorant.

**DISCIPLE.** To my question why God wished to make the human being within the genus of animals, the answer has been, as I judge, sufficient and reasonable. Nevertheless, I still ask how all created things are in the human being and subsist in him: whether according to essence alone, or according to accidents alone, or according to all the things considered in the whole of creation—that is, according to essence, species, difference, and property, and everything that is understood in relation to them.

**MASTER.** I do not readily see how I can reasonably resolve this question [Note: [Col. 0763] CF reads *hanc quaestionem*; A reads *inquisitionem*]. For if I say, “according to essence alone,” you will rightly reply: “Then all things exist only insofar as they subsist essentially; but the other things understood around essence [Col. 0764D] or substance are neither to be counted among the number of the totality of things nor do they exist at all.” And if that is so, you will ask me whence, then, come the things understood around the essence of things. If I say, “They were made by God,” you will say, “Why, then, are they not included among the number of the totality that was made in man?” If I say, “They were not made by God,” you will reply, “Then they do not exist; for if they existed, they would exist from no other source [Col. 0765A] than the cause of all things, which is God.” And if I agree that the things understood around essences are not included among the number of things because they are not from God, you will immediately say, “How, then, are they understood?” For whatever is not from God can in no way be understood, because it in no way exists.

If I say that not only essences, but also everything naturally understood around them, is from God and is counted among the parts of the totality, there is no doubt [Note: [Col. 0765] *quin* is omitted by CF] that I shall be forced to choose one of two alternatives: either the whole totality was not created in man, if only essences were made in him; or the whole totality—that is, essences and everything perceived around and within them—was created in man [Note: [Col. 0765] CF reads *conditam*; A reads *condita*]. And if I say that not a part of the totality, namely substances, [Col. 0765B] but the whole was constituted in man, you will pursue me with the most serious question, saying: “Then irrationality was made in him, and animality, quadrupedality, volatileness, and all the differences of diverse animals and other things; likewise species, properties, accidents, and countless other things that seem far removed from human nature—so much so that, if it were established that they were present in man, he would rightly be judged not to be a man but a most shameful monster.”

**DISCIPLE.** You have increased the difficulty of the question; with a kind of deliberation, you have raised against yourself whatever might be proposed by another. Thus you will either unlock it or pass it by as obscure [Note: [Col. 0765] CF reads *obstrusam praeteries*], and move on to other matters [Note: [Col. 0765] CF reads *ad alia*; A reads *ad aliam*], which will seem highly inappropriate.

**MASTER.** Let us therefore try somehow to contemplate it [Note: [Col. 0765] CF reads *conemur itaque*; A reads *conemur ergo*], so that it may not meanwhile be left entirely untouched [Col. 0765C].

**DISCIPLE.** You will not otherwise satisfy me.

**MASTER.** Do you think that everything which is known by intellect [Note: [Col. 0765] CF reads *intellectu*; A reads *in ntellectu*] and reason, or imagined by bodily sense, can somehow be created and brought into being in the very one who understands and senses it?

**DISCIPLE.** It seems to me that it can. For I think that the forms, quantities, and qualities of sensible things which I apprehend through bodily sense are somehow created in me. When I imprint their images in my memory and handle them within myself, divide them, compare them, and gather them, as it were, into a kind of unity, I perceive that a certain knowledge of things outside me is brought about in me. Similarly, inwardly, when I diligently investigate intelligible things which I contemplate with the mind alone—for example, the liberal disciplines—I understand that certain notions, as it were intelligible forms [Note: [Col. 0765] CF reads *notitiones*], are born and made in me [Col. 0765D]. But I plainly do not see what difference there is between knowledge and the things themselves of which it is the knowledge.

**MASTER.** What do you think? Are things and their knowledges, which are made in the soul [Note: [Col. 0765] CF and A read *in animo*], of one nature or of another?

**DISCIPLE.** Of another. For how could the bodily form of some animal, or herb, or tree, and the knowledge of it, which is produced in an incorporeal nature, be of one nature? By the same reasoning, how can the intelligible form of any discipline and the knowledge of it be made of one nature [Col. 0766A]?

**MASTER.** If, then, they are of another kind or nature, and not of the same, tell me, I ask: which of these do you think ought to be regarded as superior? Are things of a higher nature than their proper notions, or are the notions superior to the things?

**DISCIPLE.** I would say that visible forms are of a better nature than their notions, if Saint Augustine, in the ninth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter eleven, had not pronounced the following opinion:

“When [Note: [Col. 0765] CF reads *cum*; A reads *cur*] through bodily sense,” he says, “we learn bodies, some likeness of them is made in our mind, and this is the phantasy in the memory [Note: [Col. 0765] CF reads *phantasia in memoria*; A reads *phantasia memoriae*]. For the bodies themselves are not at all in the mind when we think of them, but their likenesses. Yet the imagination of the body in the mind is better than that bodily form, insofar as it is in a better nature, namely, in a living substance, such as the mind.”

But I do not dare to say that intelligible things are better than their notion, which is in the soul [Note: [Col. 0765] *res* is omitted by CF]. For reason teaches that what understands is better than what is understood [Note: [Col. 0765] CF reads *docet*]. If the knowledge of all things subsists in divine wisdom, I would not rashly declare that it is incomparably better than all the things of which it is the knowledge. And if this is so, an order such as I believe proceeds through the whole of creation by divine providence: every nature that comprehends the knowledge of the nature that follows it is not only better and higher, but the knowledge itself, by the dignity of the nature in which it is, also far precedes that of which it is the knowledge. Consequently, I would more readily say that the knowledge of intelligible things is older than the intelligible things themselves.

**MASTER.** You might perhaps say that correctly, if what is formed were superior to that which forms [Col. 0766C].

**DISCIPLE.** Why do you raise this objection?

**MASTER.** Because the knowledge of the arts, which is in the soul, seems to be formed by the arts themselves. But if you could persuade us by the most certain reasoning that it is not knowledge which comes from the arts, but the arts which are formed from knowledge, your reasoning might perhaps proceed correctly.

**DISCIPLE.** Have we not already established among ourselves that everything which understands is superior to that which is understood?

**MASTER.** We have.

**DISCIPLE.** Then say whether the mind’s expertise understands the discipline, or the discipline the expertise.

**MASTER.** I have no doubt that the discipline is understood by the mind. But if I say that the same discipline is known from the expertise itself, just as it is known by the mind of which it is the expertise, I fear that I may seem to assert that the mind and its expertise are two things, enlivened by the notions of the discipline, rather than one and the same essence in which the knowledge of the discipline naturally resides. But if true reason teaches that the mind and its expertise are not two things but one and the same, I am compelled to admit that everything understood by the mind is also understood by its own expertise. It will immediately follow that the mind and its expertise—or at least the expert mind—are of a more excellent nature than the discipline which it understands, if the understanding is older than the things understood.

But if I say that the discipline itself is the expertise of the expert mind [Note: [Col. 0765] CF reads *peritam*; A is cited without a reported reading], it will follow either that the expert mind and the expert discipline are two things, each understanding and understood by the other, and therefore possessing equal dignity of nature; or that the mind, its expertise, and the discipline which it understands and by which it is understood, all lie within one and the same essence [Col. 0767A]. But which of these positions ought to be maintained is not yet clear.

**DISCIPLE.** Perhaps it will become clear, provided that, with God as our guide, we enter upon the right path of reasoning.

**MASTER.** Let us therefore inquire more diligently. First, I want you to say whether the nature of the mind, in which expertise in the disciplines resides, is simple or not.

**DISCIPLE.** I think it is simple [Note: [Col. 0767] CF reads *simplicem arbitror esse*]. For it is incorporeal and intellectual, and therefore must be free from every composition.

**MASTER.** You are right to think so. Do you therefore think that anything happens to it which is not naturally present in its essence?

**DISCIPLE.** I certainly think so. For I see many things happening to it. For example, it undergoes temporal movement, although it is not time itself; expertise in the disciplines happens to it—for now it is expert, now inexperienced; now disciplined, now undisciplined [Note: [Col. 0767] The words *disciplinata nunc indisciplinata* are omitted in A]; now wise, now foolish; now erring, when it proceeds irrationally; and now proceeding rightly along the path of reason; and many things of this kind.

**MASTER.** Then expertise in the discipline, or the discipline itself [Note: [Col. 0767] CF reads *vel*; A reads *ut*], is not naturally in it, but comes to it externally through accidents [Note: [Col. 0767] CF omits *et*].

**DISCIPLE.** I would not dare to say that. For [Note: [Col. 0767] CF reads *neque enim*; A reads *non enim*] it is not plausible that God created the mind in his image and likeness without expertise and discipline being innate in it by nature; otherwise it would not be a mind but some brutish and irrational life [Note: [Col. 0767] A reads *natura*]. For [Note: [Col. 0767] CF reads *nam*; A omits it], I think, no one could rightly say that man was made in the image of God according to accident and not according to substance, especially since we see that intellect and reason are substantially present in him [Col. 0767C].

**MASTER.** Then they do not happen to it, but are naturally present in it.

**DISCIPLE.** I would not say this rashly, I think. For although it seems to be born inexperienced and foolish—and this happens to it through the transgression of the divine commandment, by which it has forgotten both itself and its Creator—yet, restored by the rules of teaching, it can, illuminated by the grace of its Redeemer, discover within itself its God and itself, its own expertise and discipline, and everything that naturally subsists in it.

**MASTER.** It remains, then, to consider how expertise and discipline are present in it: whether as natural qualities, which are called virtues—for example, forms of wisdom and knowledge, which it apprehends through the reflection of the divine rays—or as its substantial parts, by which it exists, so that there is a certain Trinity of one essence: mind, expertise, and discipline.

**DISCIPLE.** I would believe the latter, for it seems to me to be a certain substantial and connatural Trinity.

**MASTER.** The mind therefore understands its expertise and its discipline, and is understood by its expertise and its discipline—not what it is, but that it is; for otherwise the Trinity will not be coessential and coequal.

**DISCIPLE.** I would not deny this either, since reason requires me to confess it [Note: [Col. 0767] CF reads *ita ratio*; A reads *ratio ita*].

**MASTER.** See, then, whether they are formed by one another or by some other nature superior to them [Col. 0768A].

**DISCIPLE.** If Catholic faith did not urge, and truth did not approve, that there is a superior nature from which this Trinity is both constituted and formed and in which it is understood, I might perhaps answer, not incautiously, that it is formed by itself, or at least that it is the principal form. But since that nature itself is superior [Note: [Col. 0767] A reads *per superiorem*], from which all things are formed, from which they begin to be formed, and toward which those that turn or can turn are formed, I do not doubt that the Trinity of the mind is also formed by it.

**MASTER.** It would be utterly foolish to doubt this. Therefore only the divine mind possesses within itself the true knowledge of the human mind—expert and disciplined [Note: [Col. 0767] CF reads *disciplinalisque*; A reads *disciplinalis*]—which has been formed by it and turned toward it [Note: [Col. 0767] A omits *et ad se*].

**DISCIPLE.** Nothing could be judged truer.

**MASTER.** Do you think that the human mind is one thing and its notion in the mind which forms and knows it [Col. 0768B] another?

**DISCIPLE.** Far from it. Rather, I understand that the whole substance of man is nothing other than his notion in the mind of the artificer, who knew all things in himself before they came to be; and that this very knowledge is the true and only substance of those things which are known, since in it they have been made perfectly and subsist eternally and immutably [Note: [Col. 0767] A reads *subsistit*].

**MASTER.** We can therefore define man as follows: Man is a certain intellectual notion eternally made in the divine mind.

**DISCIPLE.** This is a most true and well-established definition of man—and not only of man, but also of all things made in divine wisdom. Nor do I fear those who define man not according to what he is understood to be, but from the things understood around him, saying: “Man is a rational, mortal animal, capable of sense and discipline.” What is more astonishing, they call this definition *ousiades* [i.e. “substantial”; the text has *usiadis*, with *usiades* conjectured by ACF], although it is not substantial but concerns substance, being taken externally from the things which happen through the generation of substance. For the notion of man in the divine mind is none of these things. There it is simple, and can be called neither this nor that; it surpasses every definition and collection of parts, since of it only “that it is” is predicated, not “what it is” [Note: [Col. 0767] A reads *quod*]. For the sole and true definition of the *ousiadēs* [substantial definition] is that which merely affirms that it is and denies what it is.

**MASTER.** Does it seem to you that a certain notion exists in man of all sensible and intelligible things which the human mind can understand?

**DISCIPLE.** It plainly seems so. Indeed, man is understood to be man chiefly by this: that he has been given a notion of all things which were either created equal to him or over which he was commanded to rule. For how could dominion over things be given to man if he had no notion of them? His dominion would go astray if he did not know the things he governed. Divine Scripture indicates this most clearly when it says:

“Then, after the Lord God had formed from the earth all the animals of the earth and all the birds of the sky [Note: [Col. 0767] A reads *volantibus*], he brought them to Adam to see what he would call them; and whatever Adam called a living creature, that was its name [Col. 0769A].”

“To see,” it says—that is, to understand what he would call them. For if he did not understand, how could he call them correctly? “Whatever Adam called it, that was its name” [Note: [Col. 0769] A reads *vocaret*; A omits *ejus*]—that is, it was the very notion of the living creature.

**MASTER.** What wonder is it, then, if the notion of things which the human mind possesses, since it was created in the human mind, is understood as the substance of the things of which it is the notion—namely, in the likeness of the divine mind, in which the notion of the created totality is the incommunicable substance of that totality? And just as we call the notion of all things which are understood in the totality and perceived by bodily sense the substance of the things subject to intellect or sense, so let us also say that the notion of natural differences, properties, and accidents is itself those differences, properties, and accidents.

**DISCIPLE.** It is no wonder.

**MASTER.** Irrationality, then, was created in man, together with every species, every difference, and every property of that irrationality, and everything naturally known around it [Note: [Col. 0769] *quae* is omitted by A], because the notion of all these things and of similar things was created in him. I said “similar” because of those things which the nature of things contains outside animals: the elements of the world, the kinds and species of herbs and trees, quantities and qualities, and all the rest multiplied through innumerable differences. The true knowledge of all these things is implanted in human nature, although it remains hidden from it that it is present there, until it is restored to its original integrity. Then it will understand with perfect purity the greatness and beauty of the image created in it [Col. 0769C], and nothing of the things created in it will remain hidden from it, when it is surrounded by the divine light [Note: [Col. 0769] CF reads *ambita*; A reads *objecta*] and turned toward God, in whom it will contemplate all things clearly.

Or what else did the magnificent Boethius intend to be understood when he said:

“Wisdom is the comprehension of the truth of things which exist and receive an immutable substance of their own” [Note: [Col. 0769] A reads *comprehensione*].

We say that those things exist which neither increase through extension nor diminish through contraction, nor are changed through variations, but always preserve themselves in their proper power, supported by the resources of their nature. These are qualities, quantities, forms, magnitudes, smallnesses, equalities, relations, activities, dispositions, places, times, and whatever is found somehow joined to bodies. These things in themselves are incorporeal by nature and possess force by reason of an immutable substance; but through participation in the body they are changed, and through contact with a mutable thing they pass into the changeable instability of what can be altered.

And where do you understand these things to subsist except in their notions in the soul of the wise person? For where they are understood, there they are; indeed, they are their own acts of understanding [Note: [Col. 0769] CF reads *sunt*; A reads *sinit*].

**DISCIPLE.** The resolution of the present question requires a manifold exposition. And while it is being resolved, an innumerable multitude of diverse questions surrounding it on every side does not cease to flow forth, as from some infinite fountain, so that it may rightly be compared to the fable of the Hydra of Hercules: as its heads are cut off, so they increase, so that for one head severed a hundred boil up. It suggests, moreover, human nature, which is a hydra—that is, a certain manifold and infinitely deep fountain. Who can perceive it except Hercules alone, that is, virtue [Note: [Col. 0769] A reads *id* for *hoc*]? For “no one knows the things that are in man except the spirit of man which is in him” [Note: [Col. 0769] F reads *scit*; A reads *scit enim*; C omits *scit*].

Therefore, if that inner notion which is present in the human mind is constituted as the substance of the things of which it is the notion, it follows that the notion by which man knows himself is also believed to be his substance.

**MASTER.** It certainly follows. For we said that the human mind [Note: [Col. 0769] CF reads *mentem humanam*; A reads *in mente humana*], its notion by which it knows itself, and the discipline by which it learns itself in order to know itself [Note: [Col. 0769] A reads *et seipsam cognoscit*], subsist as one and the same essence [Col. 0770B].

**DISCIPLE.** What, then, shall we say? Did we not shortly before bring the definition of man to complete clarity by saying, “Man is a certain intellectual notion eternally made in the divine mind”? And if this is so, how can that notion by which man knows himself be his substance, if the foregoing definition was not rashly established [Note: [Col. 0769] A reads *statuta sit*]?

**MASTER.** It was not established rashly. For the definition which says that a certain notion eternally made in the divine mind is the substance of man is true. And what we now say—namely, that the knowledge by which the human mind knows itself is substantially present in man—is also taught reasonably. For every creature is considered in one way in the Word of God, in whom all things were made [Note: [Col. 0769] CF omits *facta sunt*], and in another way in itself.

Hence Saint Augustine says in his *Exameron*:

“In one way,” he says, “the things made through him are under him; in another way, the things which he himself is are in him” [Note: [Col. 0769] A omits *sunt*].

For the understanding of all things in divine wisdom is the substance of all things—indeed, it is all things. But the knowledge by which an intellectual and rational creature understands itself in itself is, as it were, a second substance of that creature, by which it knows only that it knows itself, exists, and wills, but not what it is.

The former substance, constituted in the wisdom of God, is eternal and immutable; the latter is temporal and mutable. The former precedes; the latter follows. The former is primordial and causal; the latter proceeding [Note: [Col. 0769] A reads *praecedens*] and effect-producing. The former contains all things universally [Note: [Col. 0769] A reads *hominem*]; the latter comprehends particularly, insofar as it is distributed by the higher, the things subjected to it through knowledge. The latter has been led forth by the former, and the latter will return to the former.

I am not now speaking of that superessential substance [Note: [Col. 0769] A reads *superressentialem supersubstantialem substantiam*] which is God through itself and the single cause of all things, but of that which was made primordially and causally in the wisdom of God [Note: [Col. 0769] A reads *et causaliter*]. The effect of this is the substance which we have placed in the second position, according to the natural order established among things.

**DISCIPLE.** We must therefore understand two substances of man: one universal in the primordial causes, the other particular in their effects.

**MASTER.** I would not say two, but one understood in two ways. Human substance is perceived in one way through its creation in the intellectual causes, and in another through its generation in the effects. There it is free from every change; here it is subject to change. There it is simple and released from all accidents, escaping every act of beholding and understanding [Note: [Col. 0771] CF reads *effugit conditum intellectum*]; here it receives a certain composition from quantities, qualities, and the other things understood around it, through which it receives the mind’s apprehension [Note: [Col. 0771] A reads *patiens* for *accipit per quam*].

Thus one and the same thing is called, as it were, twofold because of the twofold manner in which it is contemplated. Nevertheless, it preserves its incomprehensibility everywhere—in the causes, I mean, and in the effects—whether naked in its simplicity or clothed with accidents. In all these respects it is subject neither to any created intellect nor to any sense, nor is it understood by itself as to what it is [Col. 0771B].

**DISCIPLE.** What, then, is the meaning of what you said earlier: that the human mind possesses the notion by which it knows itself and the discipline by which it learns itself, while now you assert again that it cannot be known either by itself or by another creature?

**MASTER.** Reason proves both statements true. The human mind both knows itself and does not know itself. It knows that it is, but it does not know what it is. In this respect, as we taught in the earlier books, it is shown above all to be the image of God [Note: [Col. 0771] A reads *in homine esse*].

For just as God is comprehensible insofar as it is gathered from creation that he is, and incomprehensible because no human or angelic intellect can comprehend what he is [Note: [Col. 0771] A reads *est*], nor can he be comprehended by himself, since he is not a “what,” being superessential—so the human mind is granted to know only that it is; it is in no way permitted to know what it is. And, what is more wondrous, for those who consider themselves and their God, the human mind is more praiseworthy in its ignorance than in its knowledge.

For it is more praiseworthy in the mind not to know what it is than to know that it is, just as the negation of the divine nature belongs more and more appropriately to the praise of that nature than affirmation does [Note: [Col. 0771] A omits *ejus*]. It is wiser to be ignorant of it than to know it; its ignorance is true wisdom, by which it is better known through not knowing.

The divine likeness is therefore most clearly discerned in the human mind, since it knows only that it is and does not know what it is; and, so to speak, it denies that it is a “what” and affirms only that it is. Nor is this without reason. For if it were known to be some particular thing, it would certainly be circumscribed within something; and consequently it would not fully express in itself the image of its Creator, who is wholly uncircumscribed and is understood in nothing, because he is infinite [Note: [Col. 0771] A omits *est*], superessential beyond everything that is said and understood.
