**DISCIPLE.** How, then, was every creature made in the notion of man, when he does not even know himself as to what he is—and when this is accepted as his great praise, because of his excessive excellence, since no finite substance encloses him [Col. 0772A]?

**MASTER.** Indeed, this very fact is gathered as the strongest argument that every creature was substantially created in man. For the substance of none of the things that exist can in any way be defined as to what it is. Gregory the Theologian bears witness to this when he discusses such matters against those who deny that the Word of God is superessential [Note: [Col. 0771] A reads *superessentialem*], striving to enclose it within some substance and thereby asserting that it is not beyond all things but included among the number of all things, wishing to separate the substance of the Son from the substance of the Father.

Therefore, just as the divine essence, in whose image it was made, is infinite, so that human constitution has no definite boundary. It is understood only from the things around it—that is, times, places, differences, properties, quantities, qualities, relations, conditions, positions, activities, and passions—but what it is cannot be understood at all.

From this it is also made clear that no creature has any other subsistence than that reason according to which it was constituted in the primordial causes in the Word of God. Consequently, it cannot be defined as to what it is, because it surpasses every substantial definition. It is defined, however, through its circumstances, which happen to it and, through either intelligible or sensible generation, come into its proper species [Note: [Col. 0771] CF reads *in speciem propriam*; A reads *in specie propria*].

## 8. DISCUSSION

Both divine Scripture and reason itself testify that human and angelic nature are either the same or very similar. For both human being and angel are said—and are—intellectual and rational creatures. And if they thus correspond to one another, it is not unreasonable to ask why every creature is read to have been created in the human being, but not in the angel.

**MASTER.** Not without reason, I think. For we see in the human being many things which neither authority transmits nor reason understands to subsist in the angel: such as this animal body, which divine Scripture also testifies was joined to the human soul even before the Fall; the corporeal, fivefold external sense; the images of sensible things which are introduced through it into the human soul; the prolonged perplexity of reasoning when investigating the natures of things; the laborious ingenuity required to distinguish virtues and vices; and very many things of this kind. No rightly thinking person will deny that the angelic essence plainly lacks all these things, and yet that they belong to the nature of things.

[Note: [Col. 0771] A reads “the angelic essence.”]

Although Augustine seems to have taught this concerning the angels [Note: [Col. 0771] CF reads *angelos* (“angels”); A *angelicos* (“angelic”) ] in *The City of God*, book eight, chapter seven [Note: [Col. 0771] A reads “in the eighth book.” A also reads “chapter six.” Instead of “who saw every form . . . whatever it is,” CF reads “who assert [that] in whatever way,” etc.], where he praises the power of contemplation possessed by the great philosophers, who saw that every form in anything mutable—whatever it is, and whatever kind or nature it may be—cannot exist except from him who truly is, because he exists immutably [Note: [Col. 0771] A reads “incommunicably”], and that therefore neither the body of the whole world, its shapes, qualities, and ordered motion, nor the elements arranged from heaven to earth, nor whatever bodies are in them; nor all life, whether that which nourishes and contains, as in trees, or that which both has these functions and senses, as in animals, or that which both has these and understands, as in human beings, or that which does not need nourishment but merely contains, senses, and understands, as in angels, can exist except from him who simply is.

[Note: [Col. 0773] At “all life,” CF has *omnem* (“all”), while A has *omnium* (“of all”).]

I believe, however, that he was speaking of the inner sense. Who, then, is unaware that the heavenly essence is deprived of the many parts and movements of nature that naturally belong to human nature? True reason also testifies that it does not possess knowledge of those things which either do not belong to the heavenly substance according to its substance, or do not affect it according to accident [Note: [Col. 0773] CF reads “the heavenly substance, I say”; A omits these words].

For although angels are said to administer this whole world and every corporeal creature, they must in no way be thought to need corporeal senses, local or temporal movements, or visible appearances in order to carry this out [Note: [Col. 0773] CF has *omnemque* (“every”), A *omnem et* (“every and”)]. All the things that happen to us because of the needs of our nature, which is still subject to variations of place and time, are rightly judged to happen to them—not through any deficiency in their power [Note: [Col. 0773] CF reads *judicantur* (“are judged”), A *videantur* (“appear”)].

For when they transform their spiritual and invisible bodies into visible forms, so that they can appear visibly, locally, and temporally to mortal senses, this does not happen for their own sake, but for the sake of the human beings whom they govern and to whom they disclose divine mysteries.

They do not see locally through sense, nor does it happen to them temporally to know what they are going to do in the administration of things, since they exist eternally beyond every time and place in contemplation of the truth, in which they see simultaneously the causes of their administration [Note: [Col. 0773] CF reads “while they are”].

And do not suppose that I am making such statements about all the heavenly essences, but only about the higher orders, which are always around God and in which there is no ignorance except that of the divine darkness which surpasses every intellect [Note: [Col. 0773] CF reads *excellentioribus* (“higher”), A *excelsioribus* (“loftier”)].

For the lowest order, properly called the angelic order, through which the higher orders administer whatever divine providence commands to be carried out in human minds through divine revelations or in the other regions of this world, has not yet been freed from all ignorance [Note: [Col. 0773] CF reads *mentibus* (“minds”), A *motibus* (“movements”)]. Therefore, as Saint Dionysius the Areopagite treats most subtly in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, it is taught by the higher orders and is introduced into knowledge of higher divine mysteries [Note: [Col. 0773] CF reads “Therefore, so that Saint Dionysius…”].

Accordingly, we are not irrationally commanded to believe and understand that every visible and invisible creature was created in the human being. For there is no created substance which is not understood to exist in the human being; nor is there any species, difference, property, or natural accident found in the nature of things which either does not naturally exist in the human being or whose knowledge cannot exist in the human being. And the knowledge of the things contained within it is better than those things of which it is the knowledge, to the degree that the nature in which they were constituted is better.

Every rational nature is rightly placed above every irrational and sensible nature, because it is closer to God. Therefore, the things whose knowledge exists in human nature are not incongruously understood to subsist in their concepts [Note: [Col. 0773] CF reads *quarum* (“whose”); A *quorum*]. For wherever things undergo their cognition more perfectly, there they should be judged to exist more truly.

Moreover, if things themselves subsist more truly in their concepts than in themselves, while their knowledge naturally exists in the human being, then they were universally created in the human being. The return of all things into the human being will undoubtedly prove this in its proper time. For how would they return into it if they did not possess in it a certain connatural kinship [Note: [Col. 0773] CF has *cognationem* (“kinship”), A *cognitionem* (“knowledge”)], and did not in some manner proceed from it? We promised to discuss this return in its proper place.

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** Although these matters may seem very difficult, since they exceed the limits of elementary instruction, nevertheless, when considered through speculative reasoning, they are highly appropriate for understanding the breadth of the human condition and are exceedingly profitable. Thus we may rightly say that it was not the human being, as a member of the animal class, that was produced from the earth—that is, from the solidity of nature—but rather that the whole animal class was produced in the human being; and not only the whole animal class, but the entire universe was created and made in the human being. Thus what the Truth said may truly be understood of the human being: “Preach the Gospel to every creature”; and likewise what the Apostle said: “The whole creation groans and labors in childbirth until now.”

[Col. 0774C]

But if these matters seem to anyone either excessively obscure [Note: [Col. 0773] A reads “obscure”; CF reads “obstructed”] or wholly incredible, let him either remain silent, if he is unacquainted with all the natural disciplines called liberal arts, or let him learn, lest he rashly oppose what he cannot understand [Note: [Col. 0773] CF reads “so that he does not”; A reads “not”]. If he is learned, he will plainly see it. To give an example from one of these disciplines: geometrical figures do not naturally subsist in themselves, but in the principles of the discipline of which they are figures.

For the triangle which is perceived by bodily sense in some material is plainly a certain sensible image of the triangle which exists in the mind. And one who understands the triangle that subsists in the teachable mind will weigh, with sound judgment, which is more excellent: the figure of a triangle, or the triangle of which it is the figure.

He will find, I think, that the former is indeed truly a figure, but a false triangle [Note: [Col. 0773] CF reads “but”; A reads “and”], whereas the triangle which subsists in the art is the cause of that figure and is the true triangle. I do not mean the imaginary triangle which descends from the mind through memory into the senses and through the senses into sensible figures [Note: [Col. 0773] A omits “and”], nor the triangle which is again impressed upon memory from a sensible figure through bodily sense, but the very triangle which remains uniformly in the discipline itself: there, line and angle are together, not line in one place, angle in another, the middle elsewhere, the extremity elsewhere, the mark elsewhere, the spaces of the sides from the mark elsewhere, those of the angles elsewhere, and the point elsewhere—the point at which lines begin and at which, through the joining of the sides, the angles are enclosed.

Rather, in one and the same conception of the geometric mind, all the things mentioned are one; the whole is understood in each, and each in the whole; and they are united in that understanding [Note: [Col. 0773] A reads “single”]. For that understanding itself is the substantial principle of everything it understands, from which the forms of geometrical bodies are specified.

What we have said about the triangle must also be understood of the other angular figures, whether circular or oblique, whether plane or solid. For all these subsist in their concepts through one and the same principle in the trained and teachable mind [Note: [Col. 0775] CF reads “disciplinary mind”].

If, therefore, geometrical bodies—whether they are formed in the images of memory or in some sensible matter—subsist in their rational concepts, which are free from every image and matter, above everything perceived by bodily sense or represented in memory, what is surprising if natural bodies also, composed from the qualities of the elements of the world, subsist in that nature in which their knowledge exists—especially since all the things perceived around bodies are incorporeal?

For the forms by which they are contained are incorporeal; and it seems doubtful to no wise person that quantities and qualities likewise belong to intelligible nature and proceed from the intellectual principles of living substance.

## 9. MASTER

Whoever attentively examines the natures of things will undoubtedly find that this is so.

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** After these matters have been examined, it is not unfitting to ask how every creature was created in the human being, since the human being himself is said to have been made after the creation of all things. If, therefore, every visible and invisible creature was created before him, as the divine history teaches, and no creature is read to have been created after him, how can we perceive that every creature was created in the human being?

For if someone should say that the whole creation was created twice—first specifically in itself, and secondly universally in the human being—I would not easily believe that this accords with reason. For if this is so, the human being will not possess a substance of his own, but will be, as it were, a composition of many things, indeed of the whole creation previously made, and a single manifold aggregate of diverse forms.

And what is more serious: if every creature, whether visible or invisible, was made most perfectly in itself—for the perfect, indeed more-than-perfect, Creator could not credibly have made anything imperfect—how did it receive, as it were, a second perfection of its creation in the human being, who was created last in the divine operations [Note: [Col. 0775] CF reads “the perfection of its creation”; A reads “its created perfection”]?

And if this is so, God did not make the human being from nothing in his own image, but from things that had been made before him. If someone should say that the human body was made not from nothing but from something earthly, namely clay [Note: [Col. 0775] A reads “mud”], what will he say about the better work of the human being [Note: [Col. 0775] A reads “part of the human being,” rather than “work”], which without doubt was constituted in the soul and spiritual body in the first creation? We believe that this soul—or rather, the divine breath—was created from nothing, not from something else.

**MASTER.** I perceive that this question is wrapped in great obscurity and seeks many ways of being opened. But so that it may not be passed over entirely untouched, we shall attempt to contemplate it to some degree, insofar as the ray of the inner divine light may smile upon us.

First, then, please tell me whether intelligible or sensible things are prior to the mind which understands them, or to the sense by which they are sensed.

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** Where that which understands is one thing and that which is understood another, and where that which understands is of a better nature than that which is understood, I would not unreasonably say that the understood or sensed thing is preceded by the understanding mind or sensing faculty [Note: [Col. 0775] CF reads “or apprehended by sense”; A has the printed wording].

But I would not say that things themselves, insofar as they understand themselves, are prior to themselves. For where the thing itself and its knowledge are one, I do not see what kind of priority there can be.

I know that I exist, yet my knowledge of myself does not precede me, because I am not one thing and the knowledge by which I know myself another thing. And if I did not know that I existed, I would not be unaware that I was unaware of my existence. Therefore, whether I know or do not know that I exist, I am not without knowledge; for I retain the knowledge of my ignorance.

And if everything that can know itself to be ignorant cannot be ignorant that it itself exists [Note: [Col. 0775] A conjecture, and AEF, read “not know” (*nescire*) for “know” (*scire*)]. For if it did not exist at all, it would not know that it did not know itself. It follows that everything which knows that it exists, or knows that it does not know that it exists, exists altogether.

But if someone is overwhelmed by such great ignorance that he neither knows that he exists nor senses that he does not know that he exists [Note: [Col. 0775] A reads “knows” rather than “does not know”], I would either say that such a person does not exist at all, or that he is entirely extinguished as a human being.

In the arguments stated above it has been sufficiently established between us that these two things are simultaneously, inseparably, and always present in the human soul: knowing and not knowing [Note: [Col. 0775] CF reads *statutum* (“established”); A *statuitur* (“is established”)]. It knows that it is a rational and intellectual nature, but it does not know what the intellect itself and reason itself are.

**MASTER.** Then you did not exist before you knew or did not know that you existed?

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** No. For as soon as I received existence, I also received the knowledge that I existed and the understanding that I was ignorant of what I am.

**MASTER.** Tell me: when the human being receives knowledge of himself, does he receive it in that condition in which all human beings were universally made in the primordial causes before the ages of the world, or in the very generation by which, in the order of time, known and predetermined by God alone, he proceeds into this life?

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** In both, I think: in one generally and secretly, in the causes; in the other specifically and manifestly, in effects.

For in that primordial and general condition of the whole human nature, no one knows himself specifically, nor does anyone begin to possess his own individual knowledge of himself. There is one general knowledge of all human beings there, known to God alone. For there all human beings are one: namely, that being made in the image of God in whom all are created.

Just as all the forms or species contained within one genus are not yet apprehended by intellect or sense through differences and properties, but subsist as a kind of undivided unity until each receives its own property and difference intelligibly or sensibly in an individual species, so each person, in the communion of human nature, distinguishes neither himself nor those who share his substance by individual knowledge before he has proceeded into this world at his appointed time, according to what was constituted in the eternal principles.

**MASTER.** Why, then, does each person not know himself as soon as he has come into this world through generation?

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** I would not rashly say that the punishment of nature’s transgression is manifested in this. For if the human being had not sinned, he certainly would not have fallen into such profound ignorance of himself; nor would he have suffered the shameful generation from two sexes, after the likeness of irrational animals, as the wisest of the Greeks affirm with most certain arguments [Note: [Col. 0777] This concerns the utterly false doctrine of John Scotus and of Maximus, whom he follows. Compare what we observed at col. 0309, note a].

The one who alone was born without sin in the world [Note: [Col. 0777] CF reads “was born without sin”; A “was born in the absence of sin”]—the Redeemer of the world—never suffered such ignorance [Note: [Col. 0777] A omits *nusquam* (“nowhere”)]. Rather, immediately upon being conceived and born, he understood both himself and all things, and was able to speak and teach [Note: [Col. 0777] A reads “to teach and speak”], not only because he was the Wisdom of the Father, from whom nothing is hidden, but also because he had received uncontaminated humanity in order to purify contaminated humanity.

He did not receive a different humanity from the one he restored, but he alone remained uncontaminated in it and was reserved, in its most secret principles, as the remedy for the wound of corrupted nature [Note: [Col. 0777] A reads “is reserved”]. For the whole of humanity perished in the whole, except in him, in whom alone it remained incorruptible [Note: [Col. 0777] CF reads “perishes”].

Indeed, he is the greatest example of grace—not because anything was forgiven him from the guilt of human nature [Note: [Col. 0777] A reads “was forgiven to him”], but because, alone among all, without any preceding merits, he was joined to the Word of God in unity of substance. In him all the elect, receiving from the fullness of his grace, become children of God and participants in the divine substance.

**MASTER.** Therefore human nature possessed the capacity to have perfect knowledge of itself if it had not sinned.

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** Nothing is more probable. For its greatest and most miserable fall was to abandon the knowledge and wisdom implanted in it and to descend into profound ignorance of itself and of its Creator. Yet the desire for the blessedness which it had lost is understood to have remained in it even after the Fall; it would in no way have remained if it were wholly ignorant of itself and of its God.

**MASTER.** Therefore, before sin, the most perfect knowledge both of itself and of its Creator was naturally implanted in it, insofar as a creature’s knowledge can comprehend both itself and its cause?

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** I think so [Note: [Col. 0777] CF reads *existimo* (“I think”); A *aestimo* (“I judge”)]. For how would it be an image if it differed in anything from the one whose image it is, except in the condition of the subject? We discussed this in the preceding books when treating of the archetype—that is, the principal exemplar—and its image. We said that God himself is the principal exemplar, subsisting through himself, from himself, and in himself, created, formed, or converted by no one; whereas his image, which is the human being, was created by him and does not exist through itself, from itself, or in itself, but received from the one whose image it is being according to nature, and being God according to grace.

Everything else that is predicated of God can also be predicated of his image, but of God essentially and of the image by participation. For the image is also good and is goodness by participation in the supreme Good and supreme Goodness, whose image it is; it is also eternal and is eternity by participation in the Eternal and in Eternity, by which it was formed; and it is likewise omnipotent by participation in that Omnipotence by which it was created and toward which, through conversion, it was specified [Note: [Col. 0777] CF reads “the Eternal and Eternity … that Omnipotence”; A omits the intervening words].

For if human nature had not sinned and had adhered immutably to the one who had created it [Note: [Col. 0777] A reads “unchangeably”], it would certainly have been omnipotent. Whatever it wished to happen in the nature of things would necessarily happen, since it would wish nothing other than what it understood its Creator to wish to happen. It would understand the will of its Creator to be altogether omnipotent and immutable if it adhered wholly to him and did not abandon him, lest it become unlike him. The same applies to all the other things which sound reason can understand, conceive, or predicate of God and his image [Note: [Col. 0777] A reads “could understand, conceive, or predicate”].

**MASTER.** If, then, before sin human nature possessed perfect knowledge both of itself and of its Creator, is it surprising that it should reasonably be understood to have possessed the fullest knowledge of natures like itself, such as the heavenly essences, and of those below it, such as this world together with its principles accessible to the intellect—and that the greatest human beings still possess this knowledge both potentially and in reality?

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** To those who understand clearly, it will not be surprising, but true and probable.

**MASTER.** This is a great and true praise of human nature—and indeed of the one who willed to create it in this way. Therefore the same must also be understood of its intellect and knowledge [Note: [Col. 0777] A gives the expanded wording “the same must likewise be understood of its intellect and knowledge”].

Just as creative Wisdom, which is the Word of God, saw before they came to be all the things that were made in it, and that very vision of the things seen before they came to be is true, immutable [Note: [Col. 0777] A reads “incommunicable”], and eternal essence, so created wisdom, which is human nature, knew before they came to be all the things that were made in it; and that very knowledge of the things known before they came to be is a true and unshaken essence [Note: [Col. 0779] A omits “which … came to be”].

Accordingly, the knowledge of creative Wisdom is rightly understood to be the first and causal essence of the whole creation, while the cognition of created wisdom subsists as a second essence and as the effect of the higher knowledge.

What we have said about the first and causal essence constituted in the notion of creative Wisdom, and about the second and effective essence which is not unfittingly asserted to subsist in the human soul, must without hesitation be understood in the same way of all the things discerned around the essence of the whole creation [Note: [Col. 0779] CF omits “is”].

A proper consideration of nature makes clear that everything whatsoever constituted in human understanding around the substances of things proceeds from the knowledge of creative Wisdom through created wisdom [Note: [Col. 0779] A reads “through procreated wisdom”].

Around the essences there are constituted species, quantities, qualities, places, times, and similar things, without which essence cannot be understood to exist [Note: [Col. 0779] A reads “essence to be understood”].

Therefore everything we wish to establish can be briefly concluded as follows: Just as the intellect of all the things which the Father made in his only-begotten Word is their essence, and the subsistence of all that is naturally understood around it [Note: [Col. 0779] A omits “the subsistence”], so the cognition of all the things which the Father’s Word created in the human soul is their essence, and the subject of all that is naturally discerned around it.

And just as the divine intellect precedes all things and is all things, so the intellectual cognition of the soul precedes all that it knows and is all that it foreknows, so that all things subsist causally in the divine intellect and effectually in human cognition.

This does not mean that there is one essence of all things in the Word and another in the human being, as we have often said, but that the mind contemplates one and the same essence, subsisting in one way in the eternal causes [Note: [Col. 0779] A reads “external causes”] and understood in another way in effects. There it surpasses every intellect; here it is understood to exist only through those things which are considered around it. In both, however, no created intellect is permitted to know what it is.

For if it could be known, it would not fully express within itself the image of its Creator, who is known to exist only through those things of which he is the beginning, cause, and Creator, while what he is escapes every sense and intellect [Note: [Col. 0779] A omits “sense and”].

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** Therefore no creature, visible or invisible, precedes the condition of the human being—not in place, time, dignity, origin, eternity, or in any manner of priority whatsoever. Yet the human being precedes, by cognition and dignity but not by place or time, those things which were created with it, in it, and beneath it. It was created together with those whose nature is equal to it in dignity, namely the heavenly essences.

For the human being itself also participates in heavenly and intellectual essence [Note: [Col. 0780] CF omits “is” in “is a participant”]. It is written of the angelic and human essence and nature [Note: [Col. 0780] CF omits “and nature”]: “He made the heavens in understanding,” as though it were plainly said: “He made intellectual heavens.”

Therefore it is not easy to understand how, if the human being was created together in substance with the angelic essences, all visible and invisible things were created in it. For it does not seem to accord with reason that it should have the beginning of its creation simultaneously with the heavenly powers and that those essences should have been created in it [Note: [Col. 0780] A reads “and the essences”].

**MASTER.** If you attentively examine the reciprocal union and unity of intellectual and rational natures, you will certainly find that the angelic essence is constituted in the human, and the human in the angelic.

For in whatever a pure intellect knows perfectly, it comes to be, and becomes one with it. Such had been, and would have become, the fellowship of human and angelic nature, if the first human being had not sinned, that the two would become one. This also begins to happen in the greatest human beings, whose first fruits are in the heavens.

The angel comes to be in the human being through the intellect of the angel which exists in the human being, and the human being in the angel through the intellect of the human being constituted in the angel. For, as I said, whoever understands purely comes to be in what he understands.

Thus the intellectual and rational angelic nature was made in the intellectual and rational human nature, just as the human nature was made in the angelic through reciprocal cognition, by which the angel understands the human being and the human being understands the angel. Nor is this surprising. For while we converse, we also come to be in one another. When I understand what you understand, I become your intellect, and in an ineffable manner I have been made in you. Likewise, when you purely understand what I clearly understand, you become my intellect, and from two intellects one is made, formed from what both of us sincerely and without hesitation understand.

For example, using numbers: you understand that the number six is equal to the sum of its parts; I understand the same, and I understand that you understand it, just as you understand that I understand it. Each of our intellects becomes one, formed by the number six; and thus I am created in you, and you are created in me.

For we are not one thing and our intellect another. Our true and highest essence is the intellect specified through contemplation of truth.

That the intellect can be conformed not only to natures consubstantial with it but also to lower natures, when it understands or senses them through love, is taught by the apostolic saying which forbids our intellectual nature to love visible forms, saying: “Do not be conformed to this world” [Note: [Col. 0779] CF has the abbreviated reading *nrm.*; A reads “namely” (*nimirum*)].

For this reason, through reciprocal understanding, the angel is said to be created in the human being and the human being in the angel; and it is rightly believed and understood that the angel does not precede the human being by any law of creation or by any mode of precedence, even though prophetic narrative, as many maintain, declares the creation of the angelic nature earlier and that of the human nature later.

For, as Saint Augustine says in book eleven of *The City of God* [Note: [Col. 0781] A reads “in the eleventh book”; CF omits “saint”], it is not credible that divine Scripture entirely passed over the creation of the heavenly powers in the works of the six primordial and intelligible days. Rather, it either indicated their creation at the very beginning of Genesis, where it is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” by the name “heaven,” or shortly afterward, where it says, “And God said, Let there be light, and there was light.”

In either place, the aforesaid Father affirms that the creation of the angels is intimated, and especially in the second. In the first, he asserts that the creation of the whole invisible creature is signified more than the specific formation of the angelic nature, under the name “heaven,” in unformed matter.

But where it is written, “Let there be light, and there was light,” he unequivocally asserts that the formation of the heavenly essences is described, although he introduces the interpretation of others who think that this divine command established a certain primitive sensible light, located in the higher regions of the world [Note: [Col. 0781] A reads “visible”]. He nevertheless sharply refutes this interpretation in his *Hexaemeron*.

The statement, “And God divided the light from the darkness, and God called the light Day, but the darkness he called Night,” he wishes to be understood in two ways. Either, by “light,” the formation of the angelic creature in its proper form is signified, while by “darkness” its prior formlessness is signified—not prior in time, but in origin—the formlessness of the creature that was still imperfect; or the separation and distinction of light from darkness signifies that part of the angelic nature which had adhered immutably to its Creator and, by the merit of its obedience, had foreknowledge of blessedness, distinguished from that part which did not stand in the truth but fell, through the punishment of its pride, into the darkness of ignorance of its future fall and into eternal misery [Note: [Col. 0781] A reads “was signified”].

Whoever wishes to know more fully this twofold interpretation of the most divine teacher should diligently read his words in his *Hexaemeron* and in the aforementioned volume of *The City of God*. Since those works are lengthy and available to everyone, I thought it superfluous to insert them into this little discussion of ours.

**DISCUSSION PARTNER.** Quite right. The opinions of the holy Fathers, especially when they are widely known [Note: [Col. 0781] A reads “when they are known”], should not be introduced unless the greatest necessity for strengthening an argument requires it, on account of those who, being ignorant of reasoning, yield more to authority than to reason.

[Textual apparatus not otherwise recorded above: Col. 0774–0775: at “the point,” CF has *spatia* (“spaces”), A *spatium* (“space”); at “all these,” CF has *cuncta haec*, A *cuncta quippe* (“for all”); and at “united,” CF has *unita*, A *unica* (“single”). Col. 0775–0776: CF omits *et* (“and”) in “and that which is understood”; CF reads *seu sensu apprehensam* (“or apprehended by sense”) for the printed wording; and A reads *possint* (“can”) for *possunt* (“are able”). Col. 0777: A reads *ergo* (“therefore”) for *igitur* (“therefore”); A reads *enim* (“for”) at “This is a great praise”; F reads *utere sapientia* (“use wisdom”) at “Just as creative Wisdom,” but the letters *ere* have been struck through; A reads *qua* (“which”) for *quae* (“of the things which”); and A omits *nusquam* (“nowhere”) in “never suffered.” Col. 0778–0779: A reads *plenissima scientia* (“the fullest knowledge”) for *plenissimam scientiam*; A reads *ac sic* (“and thus”) for *sic* (“thus”); A reads *potest* (“can”) for *posset* (“could”); and A omits *sensum et* (“sense and”) in the final clause on the Creator. Col. 0780: CF has *rationabilis* (“reasonable”) for *rationalis* (“rational”).]

### 10

But I should like to learn from you why the constitution of the angels is narrated as though on the first intellectual day—that is, in the first ordering of prophetic contemplation—whereas afterward, when the fourfold contemplation of the sensible world has been introduced, the formation of humanity is presented as the sixth contemplation; or, to put it more plainly, why humanity is not introduced at the beginning of the contemplation of the whole creation, but is introduced at the end, after that same contemplation has been repeated six times. For it seems that not only the angelic essence but also the sensible things, in a certain dignity—not to say temporality—precede the establishment of humanity. [Col. 0781: A reads “more suitably” (*aptius*) for “more plainly.”] [Col. 0781: CF read *humana praecedere substitutio*; A reads *humanam praecedere substitutionem*.]

**MASTER.** On the contrary, it is precisely here that the dignity of the human essence above all things becomes most manifestly clear. For it is understood more clearly than daylight that, in all that is narrated as existing before the constitution of humanity, humanity itself had been created—or rather, that everything had been constituted in humanity. [Col. 0781: CF read *altiori fortassis*; A omits *fortassis*.]

The constitution of the angels is not openly described under the designation of “light” for any other, and perhaps deeper, reason: it is not said, “Let an angel come to be,” or “Let us make an angel,” as it is expressly written, “Let us make humanity,” except so that we may understand that, in the creation of light, the substance of humanity was signified as having been created no less than that of the angel. [Col. 0781: CF read *non est dictum*; A reads *non dictum est*.] [Col. 0781: A reads *ut* for *vel*.] [Col. 0781: CF read “the created substance was signified”; A reads “the created signification was.”]

Moreover, if humanity shares in the constitution of the heavenly essence signified by the word “light,” who, on rightly contemplating the natures of things, would not consequently perceive that everything narrated after the constitution of light was created in humanity—not merely according to its cognition, but also according to the things themselves? This is especially so since he clearly sees that this sensible world was made for humanity, so that humanity might rule it as a king rules a kingdom and as a master rules a household, and might use it for the praise of the Creator, subject to none of its parts, but above it, needing nothing from it, and raised above it by governance alone. [Col. 0781: CF read *quis rerum naturas*; A reads *quasi naturalis*.] [Col. 0781: A reads *ut* for the second *et*.]

For if humanity had not sinned, it would not have been governed among the parts of the world; rather, it would have governed the whole world, entirely subjected to it. [Col. 0781: A omits *ejus*.] Nor would it have used these bodily senses of a mortal body to rule it; instead, without any sensible movement, whether local or temporal, it would have governed it eternally and without error, according to the divine laws, by the sole rational contemplation of its natural and interior causes and by the easiest exercise of a righteous will—whether in the administration of its parts or in the administration of the whole. But if, by abandoning the Creator, humanity fell from the dignity of its nature into the world, it was ignobly assigned among its parts and, corrected by divine justice, paid the penalty of its transgression.

Accordingly, after the narration of the adornment of the visible world, humanity is introduced as the conclusion of all things, so that it might be understood that everything narrated as created before humanity is universally comprehended in humanity. For every greater number contains within itself the lesser number. [Col. 0781: CF read *intra*; A reads *in*.] If the constitution of humanity had first been clearly indicated in the narration of the created things, whether visible or invisible, all the remaining things whose constitution, in the order of the narration, followed its creation would reasonably have seemed to exist outside its nature. [Col. 0781: A reads “appropriately” (*apte*) for “clearly.”] [Col. 0781: A has plural *sequerentur*; CF have singular *sequeretur*.] But since humanity is introduced at the end of all the divine works, it is made evident that all the divine works subsist and are comprehended in it. [Col. 0781: A reverses the order to *divinorum omnium*.]

We have said that the heavenly essences, that is, the angelic essences, exist in humanity in two ways. [Col. 0783: A reads *in ipso esse duobus modis diximus*; CF read *in ipso esse diximus duobus modis*.] First, they are co-essential with it—that is, co-intellectual and co-rational—except insofar as this mortal dwelling of the earthly body impedes it after the Fall. [Col. 0783: F reads *cointellectualis*; A and C read *intellectualis*.] [Col. 0783: CF read *ei*; A reads *eis*.] Second, they are present through mutual cognition, being inserted into one another in such a way that the angel is generated in humanity as humanity, and humanity in the angel as an angel, united through reciprocal understanding and formed through the simple contemplation of truth. [Col. 0783: CF read *procreatur*, singular: “is generated”; A reads *procreantur*, plural: “are generated.”]

What shall I say about the works of the second prophetic contemplation? Do we not recognize that the firmament—that is, the solidity of the simple elements—which was made between the upper waters of the primordial causes and the lower changes of corporeal and corruptible nature, fluctuating through times and places by generation and dissolution, is established in the human essence? [Col. 0783: A reads *tam quae*; CF read *quae*.] For who, clearly considering human nature, would not find in it the universal elements of the world? [Col. 0783: A reads *mutabiles* for *mutabilitates*.]

What should be thought about the works of the third light? Are not the stability of substance, signified by the designation “dry land,” and the instability of mutable accidents, understood through the inundations of the waters—and these things distinguished from one another by a natural difference—understood in humanity? Moreover, is not that life which both nourishes, increases, and gives life to the various kinds of herbs and shoots numbered among the parts of human nature?

And since, on the first day, in the creation of light, the principal and most exalted part of humanity—the light, namely, of intellect and reason—was constituted in fellowship with the angelic nature, the order of prophetic contemplation rationally introduced the constitution of the second light, that is, of the outer sense, made to receive the forms, species, qualities, and quantities of visible things, on the fourth day. [Col. 0783: CF read *introduxit conditionem*; A reads *conditionem introduxit*.]

For although the outer sense, as the messenger of outer things, properly and naturally belongs to the soul, it is nevertheless assigned to the body because it exercises its power through the instruments of the body. Thus the prophetic contemplation of the constitution of things beautifully established, in the fourth place, the constitution of that sense which is attributed to the body composed from the four elements of the world. [Col. 0783: A reverses the phrase to *sensus illius*.]

Since this sense has three modes, the first is that which communicates the appearances of sensible things to the mind without any occasion for error, and does so so clearly that the judging mind can very easily and without any effort distinguish the appearances themselves with complete clarity, all obscurity removed. It is therefore rightly called the greater luminary. [Col. 0783: CF read *discernat*; A adds *qui modus visionis luminare cet.*] For it does not deceive the mind, but, like the brightest sun, discloses all sensible appearances and makes them accessible to reason.

The second mode is what is called the lesser luminary. [Col. 0783: *modus est* is omitted by CF.] Through it the mind is very often deceived, as in certain nocturnal studies, uncertain and wandering, so that it cannot easily deliver a correct judgment about what it receives through sense. [Col. 0783: CF read *in quibusdam nocturnis*; A reads *in nocturnis quibusdam*.] Examples of this are an oar appearing broken in water, a reversed face in a mirror, the apparent movement of towers to those sailing, and the image of voices, which the Greeks call **ἠχώ** (*ēchō*, “echo”), together with a thousand such appearances of falsity naturally clinging to all the bodily senses. [Col. 0783: A reads *speculum*; CF read *specilla*.] From the true appearance, the judgment of the rational soul labors and strives with the greatest difficulty and care to distinguish them. [Col. 0783: A omits *hujuscemodi*.]

These appearances are formed not in the nature of things but in the senses; they often deceive the mind and lead it into error, persuading it to approve false things as true. [Col. 0783: CF read *falsa vera esse approbantem*; A reads *et falsa vera esse approbant*.]

The third mode is that which pours into the mind, in manifold and accumulated fashion, multitudes of sensible forms. [Col. 0783: CA omit *est*.] It is as though the mind received the dances of innumerable stars from the sphere of sensible nature, engraved with innumerable appearances in varied orders; and, disturbed by the diffusion of so many mingled fantasies, it can scarcely—or perhaps never—judge them without error. [Col. 0783: A reads *ac*; CF read *dum*.] [Col. 0783: A reads *cohors*; CF read *choros*.] [Col. 0783: A reads *multiplicium*; CF read *mixtarum*.] Using certain arguments, it attempts to produce proofs that are in some way like the truth, as though drawing certainty from uncertain things; [Col. 0783: A omits *utens*.] [Col. 0783: A omits *probamina*.] nor does it always reason in the same manner about the smallest details of visible things. At times it brings forth opinions more clearly and more nearly approaching the truth, like bright stars; at times more obscurely and farther from the truth, like dim stars; and at times most obscurely and at the greatest distance from the things themselves, like stars that scarcely appear. For this reason the third power of the senses is signified by the differing brightnesses of the stars.

Thus the three modes of sensation are established in the three orders of the heavenly luminaries. [Col. 0783: CF omit *itaque*.] What the sun is in the world, the clearest and non-deceptive sense is in humanity; [Col. 0783: A reverses the order to *in homine sensus*.] what the moon is, ambiguous fantasy is, a kind of doubtful light in the sensing mind; what the stars are, are the incomprehensible and most minute multitudes of fantasies generated from the innumerable and incomprehensible appearances of bodily things. [Col. 0783: A adds *et quod* before both *luna* and *stellae*.] [Col. 0783: A reads *et* for *ac*.]

Do not be surprised that what appears in human nature—the bodily senses, I mean—is signified through the greater things of the world, that is, through the heavenly bodies. For the truest reason teaches us without hesitation that one human being, considered as an individual, is greater than the whole visible world—not in the mass of its parts, but in the dignity of the rational nature’s harmony.

For if, as the holy Father Augustine teaches, the soul of a tiny worm is better than the entire solar body that illumines the world—for even the lowest kind of life, whatever it may be, is preferred in the dignity of its essence to the first and most precious body—what wonder is it if all the bodies of the world are placed below the human sense?

First, this is because a natural cause is preferred to the things that naturally come into being for its sake. No wise person doubts that sensible things were made for the sake of sense, not sense for the sake of sensible things. Second, that which judges is rightly preferred in the dignity of nature to that which is judged. No one who purely contemplates the natures of things is uncertain that sense judges sensible things, whereas sensible things do not judge sense.

Furthermore, sense is constituted only in a living substance, in which the movement of life is most evident; whereas sensible things, insofar as they are bodies, occupy the lowest place among creatures and do not always openly display the movement of life. Some sensible things show the vital movement only scarcely, or never at all.

Finally, no sensible thing is life, even though it may appear to be moved by life; [Col. 0785: CF read *quamvis*; A reads *qua*.] but nature itself teaches that sense not only lives, but also inheres in substantial life. [Col. 0785: CF read *substantialiter inesse vitae*; A reads *substantialiter esse vitam*.] And if the quantity and magnitude of corporeal mass are praised in sensible things, more worthy of praise is the quantity and magnitude of the power established in the senses.

Consider how great is the power of sight: it surveys luminous spaces without limit and forms within itself diverse and innumerable appearances of bodies, colors, shapes, and other such things, whose phantasies enter the memory through this sense. What shall we say about the power of hearing? It can simultaneously absorb into itself and distinguish so many voices sounding together and differing from one another. Whoever examines the remaining senses in this way will contemplate their wondrous and ineffable powers.

From this it may be understood that, just as the intelligible principles of the created universe, insofar as they can be understood, were created in the human intellect, so the sensible appearances, quantities, and qualities of that same universe, insofar as they can be sensed, constitute and subsist as the causes of their own creation in human sense.

But since sense is naturally present not only in humanity but also in the other animals, it consequently undergoes another distribution. It is assigned also to the reptiles of the sea and to the birds of the sky in the fifth prophetic contemplation. [Col. 0785: CF read *quinta*; A reads *in quinta*.] Nor is this without reason, since the sense itself, which is inserted into the nature of things on the fifth day, is fivefold.

It is also joined to terrestrial animals on the sixth day, as I think, because these appear to have a greater kinship with humanity, which was made on the sixth day, than do those produced from the nature of the waters.

Thus humanity itself—whose constitution is secretly intimated one by one in the foregoing contemplations of the divine operation, since all the foregoing things were created in humanity and together with humanity, not through temporal intervals but through the ordering of causes flowing into their effects—is formed openly at the end of the whole universe, after the prophetic theory has been completed through its sixfold repetition. By that number, the perfection not only of human nature but also of the constitution of all that had been unfolded before it was signified.

Scripture says:

> And God said, “Let us make humanity in our image and likeness, and let it rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and the beasts, and every creature, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.” And God created humanity in his image; in the image of God he created it.

Here we must first note that, in the constitution of all the things narrated from the beginning of creation in the five foregoing intellectual days, the unity of the superessential divine nature and its ineffable Trinity—or, as Saint Dionysius the Areopagite says, the fecundity of supreme goodness—is not openly expressed. [Col. 0785: CF read *Trinitas*; A reads *pluralitas*.]

Nevertheless, in what is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” it is not incongruously understood that the persons of the Father and the Son are signified: by the designation “God,” the Father; by “the beginning,” the Word. A little later the Holy Spirit is introduced, where it is said, “And the Spirit of God hovered over the waters.” Thus the distinct property of the Holy Trinity is suggested in the constitution of the primordial causes.

The Scripture is also seen to recall the same Trinity in the processions of those causes into their forms and appearances. For example: “God said, ‘Let there be light.’” By the name “God” it signifies the Father; by the sensible word “said,” his only-begotten and superintelligible Word, in whom and through whom he made all things. But where it says, “And God saw the light, that it was good,” it intimates the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0785: CF read *dicit*; A reads *dixit*.] It does the same on the other days wherever it adds, “And God saw that it was good.”

But on the sixth day, when humanity is formed, both the unity of the divine nature and the Trinity are proclaimed most openly. The unity is expressed by saying “and he said,” with “God” understood, or, as the Septuagint translators explicitly rendered it, “and God said.” [Col. 0785: A omits *vel*.] The plural verb *faciamus*, “let us make,” expresses three substances of one essence—or, as the Latins more commonly wish to say, three persons of one substance. This is not without reason. For where the image is created, there the principal exemplar whose image it is becomes most openly manifest.

### 11

But since humanity, although one, is composed, as it were, of many parts—for it consists of a body, that is, formed sensible matter, and of a soul, that is, sense, reason, intellect, and vital movement—the question arises whether humanity was made in the image of God through all its parts, or only according to those parts that are of a higher or highest nature. If you are willing, explain to me what you think about this matter. [Col. 0785: CF omit *homo*.]

**DISCIPLE.** Nearly all the expositors of sacred Scripture have something to say about this question. First, they unanimously maintain that, insofar as humanity is a body, it was not made in the image of God, since God is incorporeal and no corporeality belongs or accrues to him.

Whether humanity was created in the image of God according to the soul—that is, according to all the parts understood to be in the soul—or only according to its superior parts has been diligently investigated by spiritual men. [Col. 0785: CF read *secundum animam*; A reads *secundum omnia*.] They have reached the conclusion that the divine image is expressed nowhere except according to its highest part, namely, the intelligible part. [Col. 0785: CF omit the second *est*.]

This part is understood as threefold: plainly, in intellect, reason, and the interior sense, concerning which we have discussed much among ourselves in the preceding books. [Col. 0787: A omits *in*.] The life by which the body is governed, through which the human soul appears to share in nutritive and augmentative life—life specially attributed to herbs and trees—and the outer, fivefold sense, through which humanity shares with irrational animals, are indeed understood to belong to the parts of the soul; [Col. 0787: CF read *intelligantur*; A reads *intelligatur*.] nevertheless, many wise men deny that the image of God is present in them. [Col. 0787: CF read *eis*; A reads *ei*.]

But when reason examines the human soul more carefully, it finds it to be of the simplest nature, wholly present throughout itself, nowhere unlike itself in any part, and in none of the things understood to exist essentially in it either inferior or superior to itself.

For, as has been said, it wholly governs, nourishes, and increases its body; [Col. 0787: A adds *et* before *auget*.] it wholly senses in the senses; it wholly receives the phantasies of sensible things; it is wholly in the incoming numbers, which first receive the phantasies of sensible things; wholly in the advancing numbers, which introduce them; wholly in the recollective numbers, which commit those same things to memory; [Col. 0787: A omits *easdem*.] wholly in the whole of memory; and wholly above the whole of memory, whether of sensible or intelligible things. [Col. 0787: A omits *ut praedictum est*.]

Consequently, what is discerned is not a diversity of parts in it—if indeed it should be said that there are parts in it—but a variety of administrations and movements. [Col. 0787: CF omit *est*.] For its movements are its parts, and they produce diverse understandings in the soul.

The soul itself is wholly everywhere in itself and indivisible. Its movements, however, which are also called “animal numbers” because they are in the soul, are signified by different names.

When it is occupied in contemplation of its Creator, above itself and above the understanding of the whole creation, through a contemplative movement, it is called intellect, mind, or spirit. When, through a second natural movement, it investigates the principles of things, it is called reason. When it discovers, distinguishes, and defines them, it is called the interior sense. When it receives the phantasies of sensible things through the organs of the bodily senses, it is called the outer sense—not because the soul is itself substantially the outer sense, but because through it the soul senses the forms and appearances of sensible things.

For there is a great difference between the nature of the simple mind and the manifold variety of bodily instruments. When the soul governs the body by nourishing and increasing it, it has deserved to be called the vital movement. [Col. 0787: A reads *simplicissimae naturae et individuae*; CF read *simplicissimae*.] The soul itself is of the simplest, indivisible, and impartible essence; [Col. 0787: CF read *impartibilis*; A reads *et in partibus essentiae*.] it is neither lesser in its lesser functions nor greater in its greater ones, neither greatest in its greatest functions, but equal to itself in all things, [Col. 0787: A omits the second *et*.] as that great Gregory of Nyssa asserts in his sermon *On the Image*.

From this it is understood that the whole human soul was made in the image of God, because it is wholly intellect in understanding, wholly reason in disputing, wholly sense in sensing through the inner sense, and wholly life in giving life. We recognize in particular two ways in which the human soul was made in the image of God. First, just as God is diffused through all things that exist and can be comprehended by none of them, so the soul penetrates the whole organ of its body, yet cannot be enclosed by it. [Note: [Col. 0787] Thus CF; A has “the whole soul.”] Second, just as God is said merely to be, but is in no way defined as to what he is, so the human soul is understood merely to be; but what it is, neither it itself nor any other creature understands.

As the aforementioned Gregory explains in the eleventh chapter of the aforesaid treatise *On the Image* [Note: [Col. 0787] “On the Image” is omitted in A.], distinguishing bodily senses from the nature of the soul and asserting that the soul itself is incomprehensible:

> What, then, is the soul according to its nature, which imparts itself to the powers of the senses and appropriately receives through each of them knowledge of the things that exist? Since it is something other than the senses, I do not think that any wise person would doubt this. For if it were itself identical with the senses, it would have, in every respect, a single association with the sense in the work of sensing, since it is itself simple, whereas nothing varied is considered in what is simple. But now, when all things are compared, touch is one thing, smell another, and the other senses are likewise arranged separately, without mutual association, since the soul is equally and appropriately present to each. Therefore it is altogether necessary to posit the soul itself as something other than sense according to its nature, lest anyone mingle diverse things with intellectual simplicity.

> “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” says the Apostle. But I add this beyond it: who has understood his own soul? Let those who place the nature of God among the things within their comprehension say whether they have understood themselves, whether they have recognized the nature of their own soul. Perhaps the soul is greatly divisible and greatly composite. But how can what is intellectual be in composition? Or what manner is there of the concretion of diverse kinds? Yet if it is simple and uncompounded, how is it divided into a sensuality divided in many ways; how is it various in its singularity; how is it one in its variety?

> But, knowing the solution of the things in question, I return to God’s own word: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” [Note: [Col. 0787] *nostram* (“our”) is omitted in CF.] An image is properly an image so long as it does not fall short in any respect of those features understood in the principal model. But if it exceeds the likeness of the principal model in some respect, in that respect it is not an image. Therefore, since incomprehensibility of essence is found in what is considered concerning the divine nature, it will be necessary that the one who receives the image possess imitation of the principal model in every respect. For if the nature of the image comprehended the principal model, it would be beyond comprehension; and if a contradiction is found among the things considered, the defect of the image is censured. [Note: [Col. 0787] Thus CF; A has “Is it not therefore…?”]

> Since the very nature of our soul, which was created according to the image of the Creator, escapes knowledge, it possesses an exact likeness to what is set above it in this respect: that, being unknown according to itself, it characterizes an incomprehensible nature. [Note: [Col. 0789] Thus CF; A has “the nature of our soul.”]

The same author says in the thirteenth chapter:

> Since God himself is the most beautiful and most excellent of all goods, toward whom all things that possess desire for the good look, we therefore say that the soul too was made in the image of the most beautiful, insofar as it participates in likeness to the principal model, to the extent that it is permitted to remain in the good. But if it in some way departs from this, it is stripped of the beauty in which it had existed. Thus we say that the soul is adorned with the beauty of the likeness of the principal model, as though a certain mirror had been formed with the character of what appears in it. [Note: [Col. 0789] “in it” is omitted in A.]

> According to the same analogy, we judge that the soul also possesses the nature administered by it, and that this nature is adorned with the beauty that comes from the soul, as though it had become a certain mirror of a mirror, while the material substance—the substantial material [Note: [Col. 0789] A has *substantiae* (“of substance”) rather than *substantiale* (“substantial”).] around which the nature is considered—is held and comprehended by it. [Note: [Col. 0789] Thus CF; A has “is said.”]

> He says this because nature is properly observed in relation to matter: matter fluctuates until it finds the form by which it may be stabilized. [Note: [Col. 0789] Thus CF; A has “the form by which it is stabilized.”] If, then, he says, one thing is held by another, and the fellowship of the true good has been led through all things according to a rational correspondence, what is subordinate gives form to what follows it; that is, the soul gives form to matter. [Note: [Col. 0789] A has “the soul” rather than “the soul gives form.”] But when the dispersal of this excellent natural concord takes place, and what is lower becomes contrary to what is higher, then the deformity of the matter itself, deserted by nature, is reproved; that is, [Note: [Col. 0789] A reads: “and when what follows has become contrary to the superior, the deformity of the matter itself, once it has been deserted, is also reproved by the one who has transgressed.”]

> Matter in itself is a certain deformed thing when the order of nature has been changed. [Note: [Col. 0789] A reads “and imperfect” in place of “when the order of nature has been changed.”] The beauty of the nature in which it is formed through the soul is itself corrupted along with what has been deformed. [Note: [Col. 0789] Thus CF; A has “is corrupted through deformity.”] Thus a distribution of the matter’s ugliness through nature is effected in the soul itself, so that you no longer discern the image of God in the character of the formation.

> For just as a certain mirror, making itself the reverse of the form of good, the soul projects knowledge of the radiance of the supreme good, but absorbs into itself the deformity of matter; and in this way the generation of evil is woven together through the privation of good. [Note: [Col. 0789] “of the supreme” is omitted in A.] Everything is good that follows the first good in the proper way; but whatever comes to be outside that union and likeness which is directed toward it is wholly without good.

> If, then, according to the foregoing account, the one good is what truly is, and the soul was made in the image of the good, it too possesses being good. [Note: [Col. 0789] *est* (“is”) is omitted in A.] The nature of the body, however, which is contained by the soul, is, as it were, an image of an image. [Note: [Col. 0789] “of the body” is omitted in A.] From this it is shown that our material nature is constituted and held together when it is administered by the nature of the soul, but is again dissolved and falls away when it is separated from the soul that contains and comprehends it and is dispersed from that natural concord directed toward the good.

> This occurs in no other way than when nature is turned toward the contrary, while desire looks not toward the good but toward that which requires the forming power. For every matter, through the want of its proper form, must be conformed to the imitation of something dishonorable and deformed. [Note: [Col. 0789] Thus CF; A has “is transformed from its form into some foul and deformed image.”]

> And shortly afterward: Consequently, the following reflection occurs to reason, by which we learn that in the human composite the soul is administered by God, while our material life is administered by the soul so long as it remains in nature—that is, in the image of the soul. But if it turns away from nature, it is also alienated from the operation that occurs through the soul.

Accordingly, if anyone examines more attentively the words of the aforementioned theologian, throughout the whole text of the treatise *On the Image* he will find the constitution of the whole human being composed, as it were, from three elements in which the natural order is interwoven: namely, the soul; the vital motion, which he sometimes calls the fluxible life and sometimes the material life; and formed matter. [Note: [Col. 0789] “in which the natural order is interwoven” is omitted in A.] Thus the whole human being is understood to consist of the soul, material life, and matter itself. [Note: [Col. 0789] Thus A; BC has *ex* (“from”) rather than *in* (“in”).] The soul, in which the whole power of the soul consists, was made in the image of God and is the mirror of the supreme good, since in it the incomprehensible form of the divine essence is reflected in an ineffable and incomprehensible manner.

Material life, which is specifically concerned with matter and is therefore called material because it adheres to the mutability of matter—that is, of the body—is a kind of image of the soul and, as he himself says, a mirror of a mirror. Thus the soul is the form of the divine nature, while vital motion, which is also called material life, is the form of matter itself and, as it were, a second image through which the soul likewise imparts the appearance of form to matter. [Note: [Col. 0789] “with matter itself” is omitted in A.] [Note: [Col. 0789] A has “the soul also.”]

Consequently, in a certain sense, by the sequence of human nature, the whole human being is not improperly said to have been made in the image of God, although properly and principally the image is understood to subsist in the soul alone. The order is such that the soul receives its cause from God, with no other creature interposed; vital motion receives its cause from the soul; and finally matter receives from the soul, through vital motion, the cause of its formation. [Note: [Col. 0789] Thus CF; A has “with a creature interposed.”] [Note: [Col. 0789] A reads “from vital motion” instead of “through vital motion.”] [Note: [Col. 0791] “from the soul” is omitted in A.] [Note: [Col. 0791] “its” is omitted in A.]

Thus matter follows vital motion, vital motion follows the soul, and the soul follows God himself. When the soul is turned toward God, it preserves the integrity and beauty of its nature; but when it turns away from him, it dissipates and deforms both itself and what is subject to it—by which I mean material life and matter itself.

Yet vital motion itself gives rise to no small question. For it is asked whether it belongs to the substance of the human being or not. If it does not belong to it, why is it called an image of an image—that is, an image of the soul—and in what way does the soul, through it, impart form to matter? But if such life inheres in the human being substantially, why is the human being said to consist solely of soul and body, and why, when matter is dissolved, is that life understood to exist nowhere? For it does not remain in matter, which is now entirely abandoned by vital motion when it is deprived of the presence of substantial life, namely, the soul. Nor is it recognized as subsisting in the soul, which, after the governance of the body, exercises no motion toward matter.

Therefore, as I think, the account of vital motion should properly be given as follows: it is nothing other than a certain bond and joining of body and soul, by which they adhere to one another and through which the body is formed, enlivened, and administered by the soul, whether the soul is awake or asleep, whether it directs its attention to what it is doing in the body, or whether it withdraws from the senses and rests in itself, as though it had forgotten its own body. Even then, however, it does not cease to administer it through a certain ineffable silence, distributing to each of its parts the nourishment by which the body is fed and preserved.

When the two are separated—namely, body and soul—that vital motion entirely perishes. For it does not live unless it has something to move, that is, unless there is something moved by it, since nothing else subsists except the motion of the soul governing the body. But when, in dying, it ceases to move or to be moved, motion entirely perishes in it. [Note: [Col. 0791] A has *movens* (“moving”) rather than *moriens* (“dying”).] For the end of every motion is the rest of what is moved or of what moves. When, therefore, the soul ceases to move its body, all vital motion—that is, all material life—ceases to exist.

Hence the same blessed Gregory says in the fourteenth chapter: [Note: [Col. 0791] A has “the thirteenth.”]

> This material and fluxible life of bodies, which always comes into being through motion, possesses the power of existing in this: that it is never at rest in its motion. For just as a certain river, rushing according to its own current, is seen to fill the valley through which it passes, yet is not seen to be carried in the same water around the same place forever—for one portion has flowed along below, while another has flowed from above—so the material element of this life is changed through a certain motion and flux, by the uninterrupted succession of alternating changes, so that after mutability it can never remain still. Rather, its inability to rest possesses an unceasing alternating motion through similar changes. But if motion should ever cease, it will also entirely possess rest of being; that is, it will entirely cease to be.

But if you wish to know that the soul is enclosed in no part of the body, while it administers the whole body by its presence and is wholly present everywhere in all the parts that it administers, hear the same author in the fifteenth chapter of the same treatise. [Note: [Col. 0791] CF has “the fifteenth”; A has “the fourteenth.”]

> Our purpose, he says, was to show that the soul is not confined in one part of the body, but touches all of it equally, producing, in accordance with nature, the motion of the part subject to it. Yet there is a point at which the soul also follows natural affections, having been made their servant. For often the nature of the body gives commands to the soul and imposes upon it the feeling of grief and the desire of what gives pleasure, so that the body itself first supplies the beginnings, introducing either an appetite for food or a desire for something altogether belonging to pleasure. The soul, however, receiving such impulses, seeks with the body, through its own thoughts, the means of attaining what is desired.

> This does not occur in everyone, but only in those who are disposed to be more captive—those who make reason serve the desires of bodily nature and, through the aid of the mind, servilely flatter the lust that operates through the senses. In the more perfect, however, this does not happen. The soul commands through reason and does not submit to passion. [Note: [Col. 0791] A has “and does not suffer through passion.”] It chooses what is useful, while nature immediately follows the commanding soul. [Note: [Col. 0791] “the soul” is omitted in A.]

Since reason recognizes three differences according to vital power—first, the nutritive without sensation; second, the nutritive and sensitive, but lacking rational operation; and third, the rational and perfect, penetrating through every power, so that it is present even in those powers, although it possesses more of the intellectual—let no one suppose from this that three souls are mingled in the human composite and considered within their proper boundaries, as though the human being were formed from many souls. [Note: [Col. 0791] CF has *trans.* (“through”) rather than *penetrantem* (“penetrating”).] Rather, there is truly one perfect soul in nature, intellectual and immaterial, which is joined through the senses to material nature. [Note: [Col. 0791] A has “and perfect” rather than “perfect.”]

Everything material is situated in change and mutability. If it has shared in the power of life, it will be moved according to growth; but if it falls away from vital operation, it will dissolve its motion into corruption.

Therefore neither does sensation operate without material essence, nor does the operation of intellectual power occur without sensation.

In the sixteenth chapter he likewise repeats the same meaning, saying: [Note: [Col. 0791] Thus CF; A has “the fifteenth.”]

> The soul is not comprehended in any particular part of the things that are in us, but is equally in all things and throughout all things: neither comprehending from outside nor comprehended from within. Such expressions are properly used of vessels, jars, or certain other bodies placed one within another. But the association of the intellectual with the bodily has an ineffable and unintelligible contact. The intellectual is neither within, for the incorporeal is not held in a body, nor comprehended outside, for the incorporeal is not surrounded. Rather, in a certain manner beyond reason and understanding, the soul approaches nature, and, joined to it and considered in relation to it, is neither placed within nor enclosed around it. How this occurs must neither be stated nor conceived, except that, according to the proper order of that permeable nature, the soul also becomes effective. [Note: [Col. 0793] Thus CF; A has “becomes.”]

> But if some fault occurs in relation to it, the motion of understanding wavers according to that fault.

As though he were saying plainly: if the organ of the body fails in some respect—that is, if it is deficient in some respect—and through some circumstance has had the integrity of its natural constitution corrupted, the motion of understanding, that is, the motion of the soul, wavers in the part in which the organ is corrupted. In other words, it cannot manifest the power of its administration there—not because the soul itself fails, but because the corrupted part is unable to receive the soul’s power.

Additional textual apparatus:

[Note: [Col. 0787] In the discussion of the senses, CF omit *secundum* (“according to”); A reads *simplice* (“the simple”) for CF’s *simplo* (“in what is simple”), and *Nec* (“nor”) for *Nunc* (“but now”).]

[Note: [Col. 0787] In the questions concerning self-knowledge, A reads *intellexerint* (“have understood”) for *intellexerunt* (“understood”); CF omit *si* (“whether/if”); A omits *fortassis* (“perhaps”), reads *quidem* for *quidam* (“a certain [thing]”), and F reads *sed si simplex* (“but if [it is] simple”). A also omits the second *quomodo* (“how”).]

[Note: [Col. 0787] A reads *vocem Dei* (“the word of God”) for *Dei vocem* (“God’s word”).]

[Note: [Col. 0789] A omits *omnem* (“every/all”) and reads *supra* (“above”) for *super* (“beyond”); A also omits *quod oportet* (“which is fitting/necessary”).]

[Note: [Col. 0789] A places *etiam* (“also”) after *animum* (“the soul”), whereas the text has it before; A omits *sic* (“thus”), and CF omit the later *etiam* (“also”).]

[Note: [Col. 0789] A reads *ipsa* (“it itself”) for *ipso* (“it”), in the statement that material substance is held and comprehended.]

[Note: [Col. 0789] A omits *inquit* (“he says”) and reads *deducendo* (“by leading”) for *deducta* (“having been led”); A reads *animam* (“the soul,” accusative) for *animum* (“the soul/mind,” accusative masculine).]

[Note: [Col. 0789] A reads *informis* (“formless”) for *deformis* (“deformed”); CF read *pro ordine naturae mutato* (“when the order of nature has been changed”), while A has *et imperfecta* (“and imperfect”).]

[Note: [Col. 0789] A reads *informitate corrumpitur* (“is corrupted by formlessness”) for *concorrumpitur* (“is corrupted along with [it]”); A reads *formam animus factus* (“the soul, having become form”) for *formam, se animus faciens* (“the soul, making itself the form”).]

[Note: [Col. 0789] A omits *omne* (“every”) and, in the description of the soul made in the image of the good, reads *efficiendo* (“by making”) for *factus* (“made”). A omits *corporis* (“of the body”), adds *autem* (“however”) after *ex his* (“from these things”), and omits *animi* (“of the soul”) in “the nature of the soul.”]

[Note: [Col. 0789] A reads *intentus* (“attentive”) for *intentius* (“more attentively”); A omits “in which the natural order is interwoven” and *formata* (“formed”).]

[Note: [Col. 0791] A reverses the order *motus vitalis* (“vital motion”) to *vitalis motus*; A reads *quae* (“which”) for *qua* (“by which”), omits *formatur* (“is formed”), reads *ut quid* (“to what end”) for *quid* (“what”), omits *se* (“itself”), and CF omit *sit* (“is”).]

[Note: [Col. 0791] A reads *animae* (“of the soul”) for *animi* (“of the mind/soul”); CF read *in eo omnino* (“in it entirely”) for *omnino in eo* (“entirely in it”), and A reads *aut* (“or”) for *vel* (“or”).]

[Note: [Col. 0791] In the river comparison, A reads *desuper lapsa* (“having flowed down from above”) for *desuper fluxit* (“flowed from above”); CF omit *locum* (“place”).]

[Note: [Col. 0791] A reads *administratur* (“is administered”) for *administrat* (“administers”); A reverses the order *detineri animum* (“the soul to be confined”) for *animum detineri*.]
