### 12.

Since it is necessary to examine human nature carefully and to distinguish without doubt what in it was created according to the image and likeness of God—that is, according to a like image—and what in it is far removed from the likeness of the divine image, I have thought it appropriate to insert the words of that most holy [Note: A: “most learned”] and wisest teacher, Gregory. He says, then, in the seventeenth [Note: CF: “eighteenth”; A: “sixteenth”] chapter of his discourse *On the Image* [Col. 0793C]:

“Let us once again receive the divine voice: ‘Let us make man according to our image and likeness.’ How, then, did some people, with a petty and unworthy conception of human greatness, imagine that man was magnified by comparison with this world, as though he existed within it? [Col. 0793] For they say [Note: CF: “they say”; A: “it is said”] that man is a μικρόκοσμος (*mikrokosmos*), that is, a ‘small world’ [Note: A omits ‘a μικρόκοσμος, that is’], consisting of the same elements from which the universe is composed [Note: A: “consisting of the universe”]. For those who, by adorning the name, bestow such praise upon human nature [Note: CF: “human nature”; A: “bestow upon nature”] have forgotten themselves, making man venerable by reference to the properties found in a gnat and a mouse. For in those creatures also there is a concretion from these four elements, since in every body that exists some portion of these elements, whether greater or smaller, is observed around the animal [Note: A: “around the living creature”]; without them, no nature that participates in sense can subsist.

“What, then, ought we to suppose man to be after the character and likeness of the world, when heaven passes away, earth is changed, and all that is contained in them passes away together with the passing of the world that contains them? [Note: A omits ‘of the world’] But according to ecclesiastical reasoning, human greatness lies not in his likeness to the created world, but in this: that he was made according to the image of the nature of the Creator [Note: A: “Maker”].

“‘What, then,’ you will rightly say, ‘is the account of the image? How can the bodily be like the incorporeal? How can the temporal resemble the eternal; that which is changeable through alteration, the immutable; that which is subject to suffering and corruption, the impassible and incorruptible; that which is pure from every evil, that which always dwells with it and turns toward it?’ For there is a great distance between that soul—namely, the divine one, which is the principal exemplar [Note: CF: “the divine one”; A omits these words]—and the one made according to the image. For if an image possesses likeness to its principal exemplar, it is properly called by that name also. But if its imitation has diverged from that which is set above it, it is something else and not its image [Note: CF: “it is”; A: “it is the other way around”].

“How, then, is man—this mortal, suffering, and quickly failing creature—the image of an immortal, pure, and ever-existing nature? Let the Truth itself, which truly is, know openly the true account of this. We, however, investigating what is true as far as we can through certain contemplations and opinions, speak as follows concerning the questions undertaken. Neither does the divine word lie when it says that man was made according to the image of God, nor is the misery of human nature assimilated, even to the point of wretchedness [Note: A: “the misery of human nature, the affliction of human nature, and so forth”], to the blessedness of an impassible life. For one of two things must necessarily be admitted. If someone compares what is ours with God, then either the divine is capable of suffering, or the human is impassible [Note: A: “to be impassible”], so that the account of likeness may be found equally in both. But if the divine is neither capable of suffering nor our nature free from suffering [Note: CF: “nor is our nature outside suffering”], what other account remains by which we may call truthful the divine voice that says man was made according to the image [Note: A: “in the image”] of God? Are we therefore not to accept sacred Scripture? [Col. 0794C]

“Let there be, then, a kind of guidance from what has been written toward the matter under investigation. After saying, ‘Let us make man according to the image’ [Note: CF omits ‘according to the image’], it goes on, in words such as these, to add this statement: ‘And God made man; according to the image of God he made him; male and female he made them.’ [Note: A: ‘For God made man, and according to the image of God he made him.’] It has already been said in what precedes that this statement was foretold for the refutation of heretical impiety, so that, learning that the only-begotten God made man according to the image of God, we should in no way separate the divinity of the Father and the Son [Note: CF: “the Son and the Father”], since divine Scripture calls both of them God: both the one who made man and the one according to whose image he was made. But let that matter be set aside for the present.

“The question must instead be turned to the matter at hand [Note: CF: “to the matter”]: how is this wretched creature called by sacred Scripture similar to that divine and blessed one [Note: A: ‘how can the divine and blessed one and miserable humanity be similar, and this be similar to him, according to sacred Scripture’]? Should we not, then, arrange the words carefully? For we find that one thing is made according to the image, while another is now displayed in misery. ‘God made man,’ it says; ‘according to the image of God he made him.’ The creation made according to the image ends there. Then it makes an *epanalepsis*, that is, a repetition [Note: A: “addition”], according to the construction of the discourse, and says: ‘Male and female he made them.’

“I think that everyone knows that this is understood as something external to the principal exemplar. For in Christ Jesus, as the Apostle says, ‘there is neither male nor female.’ Yet the discourse says that man is divided into these. Is there not, then, a twofold constitution of our nature: one assimilated to God, and the other divided according to such a distinction? For reason discloses something of this kind from the arrangement of what has been written. First it says, ‘God made man; according to the image of God he made him’; then it adds what was said: ‘Male and female he made them.’ This is foreign to what is understood of God.

“I myself think that sacred Scripture [Note: A omits ‘from sacred Scripture’] transmits through these words a great and sublime teaching. The teaching is this: humanity is the intermediary between two things that are separated from one another by their extremities—namely, the divine and incorporeal nature on the one side, and irrational, bestial life on the other. For both of the things mentioned may be contemplated in comparison with man: the rational and intellectual element is a portion of God and does not admit the distinction of male and female; while the bodily constitution and the division into male and female belong to the irrational.

“Both of these are altogether present in all who participate in human life [Note: A omits this clause]. But we have learned from the one who orders human generation that the intellectual element comes first [Note: A: “precedes”], whereas the association and kinship with the irrational is added to man afterward [Note: A: “irrational”]. For first he says, ‘God made man according to the image of God,’ showing from what has been said—as the Apostle says—that in one who is such ‘there is neither male nor female.’ Then he introduces the material properties of human nature [Note: CF: “the material properties of human nature”; A: “the property of human nature,” omitting “material”]: ‘Male and female he made them.’

“What, then, shall we learn from this? Let no one charge me with extending the discourse beyond the matter proposed. God is, in his nature, whatever is to be received through knowledge; he is good [Note: A: “whatever good is to be received through knowledge”]. Rather, since he is the summit of every good that can be understood and apprehended, he creates human life for no other reason than that it should be good. Accordingly, if the movement toward the constitution of our nature displayed anything less than the perfection of goodness, it would give something of what belongs to God while, in some respect, begrudging participation in him. But the perfect form of goodness consists both in bringing man from non-being into existence and in making him lack none of the goods.

“Since the catalogue of individual goods is extensive and cannot easily be completed by enumeration [Note: A: “not”], the discourse, comprehending everything in a comprehensive expression, signified all things by saying that man was made according to the image of God. For this is as if it said: ‘He made human nature a participant in every good.’ If God is the fullness of goods, and this—namely, man—is his image, then the image possesses likeness to the principal exemplar precisely in being the fullness of every good.

“Is there not, then, in us the form of every good: every virtue and wisdom, and everything whatsoever that is to be understood as better? Likewise, in being free from every necessity and subject to no natural—that is, material—power, but possessing a will powerful in itself for what it desires [Note: A: “in that which is everything that must be received through knowledge is good”]. For virtue is a thing free from domination and voluntary. What is compelled and suffers violence cannot be virtue.

“Thus, although the image bears in all things the character of the beauty of the principal exemplar [Note: A: “and bears the character”], if it had no difference in any respect, it would no longer be likeness at all [Note: A: “likeness”]; rather, that which does not differ in the universe would be manifested in it in every way [Note: A: “this very thing would be manifested in every way”]. What difference, then, shall we contemplate between God himself and that which is like God? In this respect, the one is uncreated, while the other subsists through creation [Note: A: “that one”].

“This difference in property necessarily brought with it a succession of other properties. For it is admitted that the uncreated nature is altogether unchangeable and always remains in the same condition, whereas the creature cannot subsist without change. For the very passage from non-being into being is a kind of movement, and a change by which that which did not exist is transformed into being according to the divine will.

“And just as the Gospel speaks of the image of Caesar on the denarius, by which we learn that, with respect to its figure, the image is like Caesar, but with respect to its underlying substance is different, so also, considering according to the present argument the images contemplated in the divine nature, and thinking about them in human beings, we find a difference in the underlying substance within those things in which there is likeness—a difference that is observed between the uncreated and the created [Note: A: “insofar as they are considered in the uncreated and the created”]. [Col. 0796C]

“Since, then, the one always remains in the same condition, while the other, having come into being through creation, began to exist through change and has a natural inclination toward such change [Note: A: “a kindred inclination”], therefore he who knows all things before their generation—as the prophet says [Note: CF: “the prophecy”—], having apprehended them, or rather foreknowing them by prophetic power, saw in advance toward what the movement of human will would incline through its own power and capacity. Because he saw what would come to be, he devised upon the image the distinction of male and female, which no longer looks toward the divine principal exemplar but, as has been said, possesses a more immutable nature [Note: A: “clings to a more irrational nature”].

“The cause of such a contrivance is known only by those who see the truth through themselves and are ministers of the Word. We, however, as far as possible, keeping silent about the truth on the basis of certain conjectures and consequences [Note: A: “opining”], shall set forth what has occurred to the mind, not assertively, but as though proposing it in a gymnasium for the hearing of faithful ears [Col. 0797A]. [Note: A: “we set it forth.”]

“What, then, do we think about these matters? The statement ‘God made man’ reveals all humanity through an infinite signification. For Adam is not here named as the name of the creature, as the history says in what follows; rather, the name given to the created man is universal. We are therefore not led by the calling of universal nature to conjecture [Note: A omits ‘not’] that, in the presence and power of God [Note: A: “foreknowledge”], all humanity was included in the first constitution.

“For we must not suppose that anything among the things made by God is infinite for God; rather, the wisdom of the Maker is the determining measure and boundary of each existing thing. Just as a human being is confined by the size of his body, and the magnitude of his substance is measured by the surface of the body in which it is completed, so, I think, the whole fullness of humanity was comprehended by God’s foreknowing power as though in one body.

“This is also taught by the statement: ‘God made man; according to the image of God he made him.’ The image is not present in a part of nature, nor is grace found in some of the things contemplated in it; rather, this power extends equally to the whole race. The sign of this is that the soul is similarly placed in everyone [Note: CF omits ‘that’], since all possess the power of understanding and deliberating, and all possess similarly those things through which the divine nature is imagined in that which was made according to it [Note: A: “refers to likeness”]. [Col. 0797C]

“Both the man shown at the first constitution of the world and the man who will exist after the completion of the universe bear the divine image equally in themselves. Therefore all was named ‘one man,’ because in God’s power nothing has passed away and nothing is impending; rather, what is contemplated is equally contained in the present, comprehensive operation of the universe.

“Thus the whole of human nature, extending from the first to the last, is truly one image of that which truly exists [Note: A omits “human”]. The distinction of the genus into male and female was added to the latest constitution of its formation.

“And do not wonder that we often repeat the same statements. We do this not to enlarge the discourse, but to clarify the question. [Note: A omits this entire sentence.]

“In the eighteenth [Note: CF: “eighteenth”; A: “seventeenth”] chapter of the same discourse he likewise says:

“‘The glory of the resurrection promises us nothing other than the restoration of those who have fallen to their original state [Note: A: “the restoration of those who have fallen to their former condition”]. For it is a return to the first life, a grace to be awaited, bringing back again into paradise the one who had been expelled from it.

“The life of those who are restored is therefore plainly brought back to that which properly belongs to the angels. Before the fall it was in a certain sense angelic [Note: A: “a certain angelic life”]; for this reason the return of our life to its ancient condition is likened to the angels. Yet, just as it has been said that among them there are countless myriads of the angelic host, since marriage does not exist among them [Note: A omits this phrase]—for Daniel related this in his visions—so, if through sin no change or departure from angelic fellowship had occurred for us, perhaps we would not have been bound to marriage for multiplication.

“There is another mode by which the angelic nature is multiplied, ineffable and incomprehensible to human reasoning; nevertheless, because it exists absolutely [Note: A: “because”], it would also operate in those who have been made a little lower than the angels [Note: A omits “a little lower than the angels”], increasing humanity toward the measure determined by the Maker’s purpose.

“If someone presses the question, seeking to discover how souls are generated, and asks how human beings could exist if humanity were not bound to the cooperation of marriage, we too shall answer by asking about the mode of the angelic substance: how, among infinite myriads, they are both one essence and counted as many. We shall appropriately give this answer to one who asks how human beings would exist without marriage: they would be like the angels, who exist without marriage. For the restoration itself shows that man was similarly constituted [Note: A: “similar”] before the transgression.

“Now that these matters have been properly distinguished by us, we must return to the earlier argument: how, after establishing the image, God devised upon the formation the distinction according to male and female [Note: A: “for the distinction”]. For this purpose, the perfect theory we have previously set forth is useful.

“He who brought all things into being and formed the whole man according to the divine image in his will did not delay by gradual additions of future things, knowing that the number of souls had to be completed in its fullness. Rather, in the fullness itself, through a foreknowing operation, he understood the whole of human nature and honored it in sublimity and in repose equal to that of the angels.

“But because through contemplative power [Note: A omits these words] he foresaw that the will would not proceed rightly, and that humanity would therefore depart from angelic life, he devised another mode of multiplying human nature, lest the multitude of human souls should be diminished. Since humanity would fall away from the mode by which the angels were increased in number, he therefore adapted to nature a suitable contrivance for increase for those fallen into sin [Note: A: “for the fallen ones”], inserting into humanity, in place of angelic magnificence, the bestial and irrational mode of succession from one another.

“For this reason it seems to me that the great David also, grieving over the misery of man, lamented nature in these words: ‘Because man, while he was in honor, did not understand honor’ [Note: A: “when he was in honor”], saying that he had a dignity equal to that of the angels [Note: A: “angelic dignity”]. Therefore, he says [Note: CF omits “he says”], ‘he was compared with foolish beasts.’ For he truly became bestial when he received this animal generation because of his inclination toward what is material.” [Col. 0799A]

**MAGISTER.** The words of the great theologian whom you have introduced seem to persuade us of nothing other than that we should understand man to have been made according to the image of God solely in his soul and in the virtues naturally implanted in him—among them wisdom, knowledge, the power of reasoning, and the other virtues with which the soul is adorned, expressing in itself the likeness of its Creator—and that all human beings were made once and simultaneously [Note: A: “simultaneously and once”; CF: “were” rather than “were made”] in that one man of whom it is written, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” and, “In whom all sinned.” For that one man was still all mankind, and in him all were expelled from the blessedness of paradise.

And if man had not sinned, he would not have suffered division of his simplicity into the two sexes. [Note: [Col. 0799D] We have discussed above, at column 309 note a and elsewhere, the false opinion of John Scotus concerning the first man: that before the transgression he was a simple man, and that after the sin he suffered the division of nature into the two sexes, male and female.]

That division is entirely devoid of the image and likeness of the divine nature [Note: A: “and this division is entirely devoid of the image and likeness of the divine nature”], and it would in no way exist if man had not sinned, just as it will in no way exist after the restoration of nature to its original state, which will be manifested after the catholic resurrection of all human beings.

Therefore, if man had not sinned, there would have been no union of the two sexes and no one would have been born from seed. Rather, just as the angelic essence, while being one, was multiplied into infinite myriads simultaneously and at once, with no intervals of time intervening, so human nature, if it had been willing to preserve the commandment and had preserved it, would have emerged simultaneously and at once in the number foreknown to the Creator alone.

But because God, who neither deceives nor is deceived, foresaw that man would abandon the order and dignity of his condition, he devised another mode of multiplying human nature, by which this world would proceed through intervals of places and times, so that human beings might pay the general penalty for the general transgression, being born from corruptible seed like the other animals.

But while many such conclusions and others like them are gathered from the testimonies of the aforementioned teacher, many questions spring up from every side. The first and greatest of them launches a most powerful assault.

For if all human beings—not only those who existed and those who now exist, but also those who will exist—were created simultaneously and at once in that divine utterance which says, “Let us make man”; and if these corruptible and mortal bodies, born from corruptible, mortal, and material seed [Note: A: “corruptible and mortal bodies”], were superadded from outside to the human nature made according to the image of God [Note: A: “created”], by reason of the transgression, and therefore would in no way exist if man had not dishonored the beauty of the divine image in which he was created [Note: A: “in which he was”]: then it is not asked without reason how the first constitution was made according to the image of God [Note: CF omits “of God”], if the second was not made according to the image but was superadded for the stated reason.

Was the first constitution present in the soul alone and without the body, or in soul and body together? And if in the soul alone, how was he called man, when it is clear that man is composed of two natures: the invisible, according to the soul, and the visible, according to the body [Note: A: “that man is composed of two natures”]? Nor would I believe that only a part of man was then created, so that we might understand the statement “Let us make man” *synecdochically*—συνεκδοχικῶς, that is, by a figure in which a part is understood for the whole—especially since the fullest and most perfect constitution of all natures is recounted in these prophetic words.

But if the first constitution is rightly understood to have been in soul and body—that is, in the whole and complete man—then it must surely be asked what kind of body that was in the first constitution of man. Indeed, true reason declares that this body was not superadded on account of sin, but was created in the first and natural formation of man.

**DISCIPLE.** This question has not been introduced superfluously, nor is it being sought and solved without benefit. And since you proposed it, you have become responsible for solving it. For, I think, you would not propose what you had no intention of attempting to solve. [Note: A: “what you had not intended to solve”; CF: “what you had not attempted to solve.”]

**MAGISTER.** I would believe that the body first made in the constitution of man was spiritual and immortal, and such as—or itself the very kind of body—we shall possess after the resurrection. For I would not readily concede that it was corruptible and material before the cause of corruption and materiality, namely sin, came to be.

This is especially so since clear reasoning teaches that, if that same body which was made in the first constitution of man before the transgression was immediately changed and made corruptible after the transgression, then it was not superadded, but was transformed from spiritual and incorruptible into earthly and corruptible. In that case, the authority of the aforementioned teacher, Gregory the theologian, would seem to waver—which God forbid.

For he himself unequivocally asserts that the whole of what was made according to the image of God in the first constitution of man [Note: A: “what was made in the image of God”] remains forever incorruptible, both according to the account of body and according to that of soul [Note: A: “according to the account of soul and body”]. Let us set aside for now his clear arguments by which he emphatically affirms that neither souls were created before bodies nor bodies before souls, but that the whole was made simultaneously and at once in the divine counsel in which it was said, “Let us make man,” and that, likewise, in the order of time, it is now born into this world through a second generation, which has been superadded [Note: A: “through a second process”].

He also explains most clearly, in the twenty-seventh chapter of the aforementioned discourse, how, even now after the sin of the perverse human will, that spiritual and natural body which always adheres to the soul and is compacted with it is distinguished from that which was added on account of the transgression. [Col. 0801A]

“For not everything that belongs to us,” he says, “is in flux and transmutation. If it were, it would universally be blameworthy, since nothing in nature would possess stability. But according to the more subtle account of the things within us, one element remains fixed, while another comes about through change.

“The body is changed through increase and diminution, as though clothed in garments that follow the successive ages of life. But throughout every alteration there remains an unchanging form in itself, which does not cease to possess the signs implanted in it once by nature; rather, it appears with its own recognitions in every bodily transformation [Note: A: “not losing the signs implanted in it once by nature”]. The change produced by suffering, which has supervened upon the form, will be removed by the Word of the Lord [Note: A: “that change which is caused by disease”]. For just as a kind of alien face, namely deformity through disfigurement, concealed the form, so, when that disfigurement has been removed by the Word, the face that had again been obscured under suffering shines forth in its own recognitions through healing, like Naaman the Syrian or those ten who are mentioned in the Gospel [Note: A: “as in Naaman or in those who are mentioned in the Gospel, and so forth.”].

“Therefore, in the deiformity of the soul, that which is not subject to flux through change and alteration, but remains in the same condition and is held in our composition, is implanted in the soul. And since the mutable qualities of the composition itself superform the differences that exist according to appearance [Note: A: “transform”], while composition is nothing other than a mixture of elements [Note: A omits “a certain”]—and by elements we mean those subject to the constitution of the bodily universe, from which the human body also consists [Note: A possibly reads “of the bodily constitution”]—it is necessary that the form of the image, as though of a seal impressed upon it, remain in the soul. Nor are the things to be re-formed in the seal according to the form unknown to the soul; rather, at the time of re-formation, it will again receive into itself whatever is fitted to the character of the form.

“It will certainly fit it to those things that were characterized in the form from the beginning. Do you see, then, how subtly [Note: A: “similarly”] he distinguishes the property of the first constitution from what has been superadded? Whatever is understood to be unchangeable in human bodies belongs to the first constitution; whatever in them is perceived to be changeable and varied is superadded and established outside nature.

“Universally, however, one and the same common form of all human bodies is understood to exist in every body, and it always remains unaltered in all. For the innumerable differences that occur in the same form arise not from the principle of the first constitution but from the qualities of corruptible seeds.

“That spiritual form, then, is a spiritual body, made in the first constitution of man. But that which comes from matter—that is, from the qualities and quantities of the four elements of the sensible world—together with the qualitative form of which we argued in the earlier books, since these elements are subject to increase and decrease, evidently belongs to the composition of the body that has been superadded, as though extraneous or excessive.

“This material and external body may not inappropriately be understood as a kind of garment and seal [Note: A omits “seal”] of the interior and natural body. It moves through times and ages, undergoing increase and diminution, while that inner body always remains unalterably in its own state.”

### 13.

But since that external body too was made by God and superadded [Note: CF: “was made and superadded by God”], the greatness of divine goodness and his infinite providence toward all things did not wish it to perish utterly and be reduced to nothing [Note: A: “to perish utterly”], because it comes from him and occupies the lowest order among creatures.

Moreover, because everything that is born into this world from the world through generation, locally and temporally, cannot be without an end—whether in the smallest things, such as days, hours, and moments; in the greatest, such as ages; or in intermediate intervals, such as the periods of life and the years of the seasons, lying between the beginning of birth into this life and the end of that same life, as the natural ordering of creatures requires—for everything that begins to exist in the world, composed from the world, must necessarily be dissolved and perish with the world.

It was necessary, therefore, for the external and material body to be dissolved into the elements from which it had been taken; but it was not necessary for it to perish, since it was from God. The inner body would remain always and stand unalterably in its principles, according to which it was constituted with the soul, in the soul, through the soul, and for the sake of the soul.

Since the form of that material and dissoluble body remains in the soul—not only while it is alive, but also after its dissolution and return to the elements of the world—for the account of the rich man with Abraham indicates that the conception of bodies remains attached to souls after death—therefore the soul cannot forget or fail to know the parts of that body, wherever among the elements they may be.

Although they were superadded to human nature on account of sin, they cannot fail to belong to it, since they were both added and made by the same Creator of nature. Accordingly, in the restoration of man they are to be recalled into the unity of nature, while at the time of the resurrection the soul receives back the whole that was subject to it [Note: A omits “are to be recalled”].

This is what the teacher says: “Necessarily, the form of the image, as though of a seal impressed upon it, remains in the soul, nor are the things to be re-formed in the seal according to the form unknown to it.” That is as if he said: while the form—that is, the conception of the impressed seal, namely the external body, which he calls the seal of the interior body [Note: A: “which is called”]—remains in the soul, even after the seal has been dissolved, the soul does not fail to know, by reason of the conception it always possesses, the parts of the seal scattered among the elements, which on the day of resurrection [Note: A omits “on the day”] are to be re-formed in the seal—that is, in the body—according to the form of the soul, which is the interior body.

For the external and material body is the seal of the interior body, in which the form of the soul is expressed; and for this reason it is reasonably called its form.

And do not suppose that I am teaching that there are two natural bodies in one man. There is one body, the body by which man is constituted through its natural and consubstantial compacting with the soul. That material body which has been superadded is more properly understood as a certain changeable and corruptible garment of the true and natural body than as a true body. For what does not always remain is not truly so; and, as Saint Augustine says: “What begins to be what it was not, and ceases to be what it is, is no longer.”

Hence this body is always posited not simply but with some qualification: mortal, corruptible, earthly, or animal [Note: A omits “this”]. These qualifications distinguish it from the simple body that was first created [Note: A: “formed”] in man and that is to come.

### 14. DISCIPLE

What, then, shall we answer the most holy and most divine theologian—Augustine, that is—who seems to contradict the arguments stated above? For in nearly all his books he unhesitatingly asserts that the body of the first man before sin was animal, earthly, and mortal, although he would not have died had he not sinned; but by sinning he died, as the Apostle says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin.”

Hence, in the first book *On the Baptism of Infants*, refuting those who say that Adam was created in such a way that he would have died even without the merit of sin—not as the punishment of guilt but by the necessity of nature—he says:

“What, then,” he says, “will they answer when we read that God, even after the sin, rebuking and condemning the first man, said to him: ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go’? For he was earth not according to the soul but, as is evident, according to the body, and by the death of that same body he was to go to earth. Although according to the body he was earth, and although he bore an animal body in which he had been created, nevertheless, if he had not sinned, he would have been changed into a spiritual body and would have passed into that incorruption which is promised to the faithful and holy, without the danger of death.

“We ourselves not only feel within us a desire for this, but also recognize it when the Apostle admonishes us, saying: ‘For in this we groan, longing to be clothed with our dwelling which is from heaven, if indeed, once clothed, we shall not be found naked. For we who are in this dwelling groan, being burdened; we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.’

“Therefore, if Adam had not sinned, he would not have been stripped of his body but clothed over with immortality and incorruption, so that what was mortal might be swallowed up by life—that is, so that he might pass from the animal state into the spiritual. There was no reason to fear that he might perhaps live here longer in an animal body, be weighed down by old age, and gradually grow old until he reached death. For if God granted to the garments and shoes of the Israelites that they were not worn out over so many years, what wonder would it be if, for a human being obedient to his commands, he granted such power that, although possessing this animal and mortal body, he would have in it a condition in which it could remain aged without deterioration and, at the time God willed, pass from mortality to immortality without an intervening death?

“For just as this very flesh that we now have is not thereby invulnerable because it is not necessary that it be wounded, so that body was not thereby non-mortal because it was not necessary that it die. I think that such a condition was also granted in an animal and mortal body to those who have been transferred from this life without death. For Enoch and Elijah did not wither through old age over so long a span of life; yet I do not believe that they had already been changed into that spiritual quality of body which is promised in the resurrection, which first preceded in the Lord. Perhaps they do not even need these foods, which restore them by being consumed. But from the time they were transferred, they live in such a way that they have a condition like that of the forty days during which Elijah lived without food on a cup of water and a cake of bread. Or, if they do need such supports, perhaps they are nourished in paradise in the manner in which Adam was nourished before he deserved to leave it on account of sin. For, as I suppose, he had refreshment from the fruits of the trees against decline, and from the tree of life stability against old age.”

And why should we heap up so many testimonies of so great and eminent a man, when it is perfectly clear to everyone who reads his books, especially *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* and *The City of God*, that concerning the body of the first man before sin he teaches nothing other than that it was animal and mortal? For if it had not been animal, why would he have been commanded to eat from the fruits of paradise so that he would not decline, and from the tree of life so that he would not grow old? As he himself often asserts, the first human beings are said to have eaten bodily from the fruits of paradise before their transgression.

### MASTER

Whoever wishes and is able may answer; but let you and me, if you please, be content to read the opinions of the holy Fathers concerning the constitution of the human being before sin, and to seek with cautious and diligent inquiry what each of them intended. It is not our task to establish quarrels among them, or to set one up and refute another, knowing that after the holy Apostles no one among the Greeks possessed greater authority in the exposition of divine Scripture than Gregory the Theologian, nor among the Romans than Aurelius Augustine.

And what if, in this apparent controversy between great men, we wished to devise a certain agreement, saying that the body which Gregory says was superimposed upon man by divine foreknowledge on account of the future sin, and added externally, is the very body Augustine called animal; and that Gregory did not fail to mention two constitutions of the human being—one made substantially according to the image of God, and the other far removed from the image and divided into male and female on account of sin—while Augustine said that the one constitution was divided into male and female, but was silent about the other, which is according to the image of God and lacks every distinction of sex?

What difference would this make, since it does not seem plausible to suppose that Augustine was silent about that condition of the human being which is according to the image of God, but explained the condition which, according to Gregory, was made like the beasts without understanding as a consequence of disobedience? Especially since anyone who examines his books will find most clearly that in the first human being male and female were made according to the image of God, and that the animal bodies they bore before sin arose not from the punishment of sin but from the necessity of nature—namely, for the procreation of the predestined number of holy human beings and for the union of human nature with the blessedness of the angels, until the heavenly city should be filled with holy angels and holy human beings.

But I never cease to wonder why he calls that body animal which he extols with great praises as spiritual and blessed. That it was blessed before sin, he himself testifies in the fourteenth book of *The City of God*, chapter ten, saying:

“But whether the first man, or the first human beings—for there were two, since they were a married couple—had in an animal body before sin those emotions, namely desire and joy, fear and sorrow, which we shall not have in a spiritual body once every sin has been purified and brought to an end, is rightly asked. For if they had them, how were they blessed in that memorable place of blessedness, that is, in paradise? Who can finally be called blessed in absolute terms if he is affected by fear or sorrow?

“What, then, could those human beings fear or grieve over amid such an abundance of such great blessings, where death was not feared, where no ill health of the body existed, where nothing was lacking that a good will could not obtain, and where there was nothing that could offend the flesh or spirit of a human being living happily? There was undisturbed love of God, and between the married couple a faithful and sincere fellowship of those living together; from this love came great joy, since what was loved did not cease to be enjoyed. There was a tranquil avoidance of sin, and while it remained, no evil from any source that could cause grief rushed upon them.

“Or perhaps they desired to touch the forbidden tree in order to eat from it, but feared death, and therefore both desire and fear already disturbed those human beings even in that place? God forbid that we should think this was so, where there was no sin at all. For it is not no sin to desire what the law of God forbids and to abstain from it through fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness.

“God forbid, I say, that before every sin there should already have been there such a sin that by means of the tree they would commit what God said concerning the woman: ‘Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.’

“How happy, then, the first human beings were, disturbed by no perturbations of mind and injured by no bodily inconveniences! The entire human society would have been equally happy if neither they had committed the evil which they would transmit to their descendants, nor anyone from their line had committed the iniquity that would receive condemnation. While this happiness continued, until the number of the predestined saints was completed through that blessing in which it was said, ‘Increase and multiply,’ another, greater happiness would have been granted, the happiness given to the blessed angels. There would then certainly have been security from sin, no one would have died, and the life of the saints after no experience of labor, sorrow, or death would have been such as it will be after all these things, when the resurrection of the dead restores their bodies in incorruption.”

[Note: *Contristaret* is the reading of CF; A has *contristaretur*.]

The same author says in the twenty-fifth chapter of the same work:

“Thus the human being lived in paradise as he wished, for as long as he wished what God had commanded. He lived enjoying God, from whose goodness he was good; he lived without any want, having it always in his power to live in this way. Food was present so that he would not hunger; drink, so that he would not thirst; the tree of life, so that old age would not dissolve him. Nothing corruptible in the body or arising from the body caused any distress to any of his senses. No internal illness, no external blow was feared. There was complete health in the flesh and perfect tranquillity in the soul.

“As there was no heat or cold in paradise, so in its inhabitant no offense to a good will arose from desire or fear. There was nothing at all that was sad, nothing vainly joyful; true joy was perpetuated from God, toward whom love burned from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.

“Between the married couple there was faithful fellowship arising from honorable love; there was concord between the vigilance of mind and body, and the keeping of the commandment without labor. Weariness did not fatigue the one at rest, nor did sleep oppress the unwilling. Amid such ease in all things and such happiness among human beings, let us not suppose that offspring could not have been sown without the disorder of lust, but that those members would have been moved by the will’s command in the same way as the other members, and that, without the enticing stimulus of ardor, with tranquillity of mind and body and without any corruption of integrity, the husband would have poured seed into the wife’s womb.”

[Note: CF reads *seri* (“be sown”); A reads *fieri* (“be made”).]

Do you see how greatly he praises and glorifies the happiness of both sexes in paradise before the transgression: how holy and undefiled the marriage would have been; what irreproachable love and inseparable fellowship there would have been between the married couple; how beautiful the procreation of holy human beings and their multiplication to the predestined number; and how, after the happiness of paradise, their translation into angelic blessedness would have followed? Thus it is not without reason that someone might wonder how it can be credible that animal bodies lived in such exalted blessedness.

### DISCIPLE

When we were debating the constitution of human nature, was it not established among us that the human being was placed within the class of animals, and indeed that all animals were created substantially in him—not only because the knowledge of all things was present in him, but also because the whole visible and invisible creation was established in him?

### MASTER

It was indeed established.

### DISCIPLE

What, then, is surprising, or why should it be incredible, if human bodies are said to have been animal before they sinned in paradise, since they were constituted within the class of animals? Reason compels us to choose one of two alternatives: either we shall deny altogether that the human being was created within the class of animals, if we wish to deny that he had an animal body; or, if we cannot argue against and deny that he himself was made a certain animal within the class of animals, how shall we deny that he possessed an animal body before sin, and that, if he had not sinned, he could have become blessed?

[Note: CF preserves the full clause; A omits “the human being created … within the class of animals.”]

### MASTER

You reason like a skilled philosopher. Do you therefore think that God made everything simultaneously?

### DISCIPLE

Indeed, I believe and understand that he did. For all things that arise in the world at intervals of time were made simultaneously and once for all, both before the world and with the world, although through the administration of divine providence they do not fill the sensible world simultaneously, but in the order of time, as the Lord says: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

### MASTER

You observe correctly. Does it seem to you that God made the human being within the class of animals because he foresaw that he would live as an animal and would fall into their irrational movements, abandoning the beauty and dignity of the divine image?

### DISCIPLE

It seems plausible. For the one who made everything simultaneously made what was future.

### MASTER

Since, therefore, he was absolutely certain of his foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived, even before the human being sinned he created simultaneously with the human being and in the human being the consequences of sin, so that it might not unjustly be judged that, among the things made simultaneously in the human being, some were made on account of divine goodness—such as those in which the image of the Creator is understood, namely the mind, reason, and inner sense, or, so to speak, essence, power, and operation—and that others were made on account of the sin foreknown and destined with complete certainty to occur.

For God foreknows many things of which he himself is not the cause, because they do not have substantial existence. Yet he is a wise maker and arranger, so that they do not disturb the beauty of the universe, and he alone is powerful enough to make good arise from the evil of an irrational will.

These, then, are consequences of sin, made on account of sin before sin occurred, by him whose foreknowledge is not deceived, in the human being and with the human being, as though outside the human being and superadded: an animal, earthly, and corruptible body; both sexes, male and female; the multiplication of offspring after the likeness of animals; the need for food, drink, and clothing; the growth and decline of the body; the unavoidable alternation of sleep and waking; and similar conditions.

[Note: CF reads “human nature”; A has “nature human.”]

If the human being had not sinned, human nature would have remained entirely free from all these things, just as it will be free in the future.

I say this following Gregory of Nyssa and his expositor Maximus, while refuting the other holy Fathers of spiritual teaching, who appear to have thought that all these things belonged to the first and substantial creation of the human being.

And if it troubles you why God made in the human being, before he sinned, things that were made on account of sin, consider that for God there is neither before nor after; nothing is past, nothing future, and nothing intermediate between past and future, because for him all things exist simultaneously. Why, then, would he not make simultaneously the things he saw and willed to be made simultaneously?

For when we speak of “before” and “after” sin, we display the mutability of our thoughts, since we are still subject to time. But for God the foreknowledge of sin and its consequences existed simultaneously. Sin was future for the human being, not for God; and the consequences of sin preceded sin in the human being, because sin itself preceded itself in that same human being.

[Note: CF reads “preceded itself”; A has “they preceded.”]

For the evil will, which is hidden sin, preceded the tasting of the forbidden fruit, which is open sin.

By the same reasoning one can understand what is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” Before the evil or good acts of either had been carried out, their consequences were made in the one in whom the universe is simultaneously one; by “consequences” I mean love and hatred.

The master Augustine himself also teaches this in the thirteenth chapter of the aforementioned book, speaking about the first human beings:

“But inwardly they began to be evil, so that they would slip into open disobedience. For one would not arrive at an evil deed unless an evil will had preceded it. Moreover, what could be the beginning of an evil will except pride? For pride is the beginning of every sin.

“Thus it is understood that the human being was never without sin, just as he is never understood to have existed without mutable will. And since that irrational mutability of free will is the cause of evil, it must itself be some evil. For who would dare say that the cause of evil is not evil, when free will, given for the choice of the good, made itself servile in following evil?”

Augustine also seems to have hinted at this. For he does not say, “The human being lived in paradise,” or “had lived”; “he lived enjoying God,” or “had lived”; “he lived without any want,” or “had lived.” For if he had used such perfect or pluperfect forms, it might perhaps have been reasonably understood that he intended to teach that the human being had possessed perfect blessedness in paradise, without any sin, for some period of time.

But he says: “The human being was living in paradise; he was living enjoying God; he was living without any want.” It is as though he had said plainly: “The human being was beginning to live in paradise; he was beginning to live enjoying God; he was beginning to live without any want.”

For this form of the past tense is called by those who carefully perceive the meanings of verbs an inchoative form. It signifies the beginning and commencement of something that in no way reached completion.

### 15.

That is, that the first human beings were in paradise for no interval of time at all, Augustine himself teaches in the ninth book of his *Hexaemeron*. He says:

“Why did they not have intercourse until they had left paradise?”

A brief answer can be given: immediately after the woman was created, before they had intercourse, that transgression occurred on account of which they were condemned to death and also left that place of happiness. Scripture did not specify how much time elapsed [Col. 0809B]  between their creation and the birth of Cain from them. But let whoever can say that Adam was temporally in paradise before the woman was formed from his rib.

Therefore, as I think, that praise of the human being’s life in paradise should be referred more to his future life, had he remained obedient, than to the life actually lived, which had merely begun and had never stood firm. For if he had stood firm even for a short time, he would necessarily have attained some degree of perfection. Accordingly, the aforesaid teacher perhaps would not have said “he was living” but “he lived” or “he had lived.” Yet if he used such perfect or pluperfect forms—or if he used them elsewhere—I would be more inclined to believe that he employed the past for the future than that he was teaching that the human being remained for a period of time in the happiness of paradise before the sin. He did so, namely,  [Col. 0809C] in order to suggest that the blessedness predestined and predetermined for the human being in paradise, if he did not sin, was already perfected, although in reality—that is, in the effects of perfect predestination—it was still future and still had to be brought about.

I say this because, when he often discusses paradise, he uses perfect and pluperfect forms of the past tense, as a diligent reader of his books will discover. For example, in the eleventh book of the *Hexaemeron* he says:

“‘In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go.’ Who, he says, is unaware that these are the labors of the human race upon the earth? And since they would not exist if the happiness that had been in paradise were retained, there can certainly be no doubt about it.”

He said “had been,” not “was becoming.” Nor is this surprising, since divine authority very often  [Col. 0809D] declares future things as though they had already been accomplished. For who would believe that the devil had been in the blessedness of paradise, when he fell as soon as he was created, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth”?

Augustine himself—whom we are now discussing—explains this saying of the Lord in the eleventh book of his *Hexaemeron*:

“That the devil is therefore thought never to have stood in the truth,  [Col. 0810A] never to have led a blessed life with the angels, but to have fallen from the very beginning of his creation must not be understood in such a way that he is thought to have been created evil by the good God, rather than corrupted by his own will; otherwise he would not be said to have fallen from the beginning. For [on that view] he did not fall, but was made such. Rather, as soon as he was created, he turned himself away from the light of truth, swollen with pride and corrupted by delight in his own power.

“Thus he did not taste the sweetness of blessed and angelic life—he did not despise it after receiving it, but, unwilling to receive it, he abandoned and lost it. Therefore he could not have foreknown his own fall, since foreknowledge is a fruit of piety. But, immediately becoming impious and consequently blind in mind, he did not fall from what he had received; he fell from what he would have received had he been willing to submit to God. Since he certainly was unwilling to do so,  [Col. 0810B] he both fell from what he was about to receive and did not escape the power of the one under whom he was unwilling to be. He was made subject to the weight of his merits, so that he could neither delight in the light of justice nor be freed from its sentence.”

Again, in the figure of the prince of Tyre, Ezekiel the prophet says to him:

“You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God; you were adorned with every precious stone,”

and so forth—things that are spoken as though they had already occurred before the devil’s fall. Indeed, in the divine dispensation those things had been accomplished which were to be accomplished in him if he did not fall.

If, then, such statements are made about the devil through a mystical alteration of tenses, and Scripture cannot otherwise be correctly understood, what prevents the same manner of speaking from being used about the human being—namely, that he had been in the delights of paradise before the sin, although this would certainly have happened to him  [Col. 0810C] if he had not sinned? This is especially so since no authority, divine or human, has handed down how long he lived happily in paradise before he sinned. And why would this be left unsaid if it were understood that he had been there?

There are, moreover, arguments by which it can be shown that he lived before the sin either for an extremely short interval or for no interval at all. For among the things commanded to him, nothing is recorded as having been done before the sin. For example: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth”—that is, paradise. For what reason would he not immediately have begotten a happy offspring, if he had dwelt in paradise for some period of time before the transgression, and if he had tasted from the tree of life, so that his corruptible body would suffer no corruption? Why did the power of the divine and spiritual medicine not prevail in his body, so that even by sinning he would not  [Col. 0810D] fall into corruption?

For if the food of the tree of life benefited his body for one, two, or however many days toward health and incorruptibility, but not forever, then it plainly did not possess as much power as it is read and believed to have possessed. Or for what reason would it be called the tree of life if it could merely delay corruption, but could not free the body entirely from corruption and grant a long life  [Col. 0811A] to those who ate from it? If the nature of that tree was opposed to every disease, so that it granted life to all who enjoyed it, why would it not overcome death in those who tasted or even ate from it? You will say that sin overcame its power, preventing it from being beneficial to such an extent. The evil of sin, then, was stronger than the good of life.

Let us rather consider that the Lord himself is the true tree of life. He says:

“That devil was certainly a murderer from the beginning.”

Do you think that he killed another human being besides that one and only person whom God created in his own image?

**DISCIPLE.** Certainly not.

**MASTER.** From what beginning, then, was the devil a murderer? Was it from the beginning of his own creation, or from the beginning of the human being’s creation, or, certainly, from the beginning of the creation of both, if they were created simultaneously and neither preceded  [Col. 0811B] the other in creation?

But if the devil’s creation preceded the human being’s creation, how was the devil a murderer from his own beginning? If, on the other hand, the human being’s creation preceded the devil’s, how is the devil said to have been a murderer from the beginning of the human being’s creation?

If, however, the conclusion is left that, from the beginning when both were created simultaneously, the devil was a murderer and the human being was killed, what interval of time is left for the human being to have lived in paradise before being killed by the devil?

This is also clearly proved by the Gospel parable:

“A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers.”

For it does not say, “A certain man was in Jerusalem and fell among robbers.” For if human nature had remained in Jerusalem—that is, in paradise—it certainly would not have  [Col. 0811C] fallen among the robbers, namely, the devil and his satellites. First, therefore, he was going down from paradise, driven by the irrational movement of his will, and was hurled into Jericho—that is, into the decline and instability of temporal things. As he fell, he was wounded and stripped of all the natural goods in which he had been created.

Here it is made intelligible that the human being first fell within himself before being tempted by the devil; and not only this, but also that he was wounded and stripped of blessedness not while in paradise, but as he was descending from it—when, by his own will, he was abandoning the happiness of paradise, which is understood by the name Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace,” and was falling into Jericho, that is, into this world.

For it is not credible that the same human being both stood in contemplation of  [Col. 0811D] eternal peace and then fell when persuaded by a woman corrupted by the serpent’s poison; nor is it credible that the serpent himself—I mean the devil—already fallen from paradise, that is, from the dignity of the angelic nature, prevailed against the human being while he had not yet sinned and while the loftiness of the divine image had not yet fallen.

The holy Gregory also seems to teach that the same thing is true: namely, that the human being was created equal to the angels, but did not remain in that dignity; rather, he immediately began, by failing to proceed correctly, to enter upon the good. He teaches this in the eighteenth chapter of his sermon  [Col. 0812A] *On the Image*, which we cited above and which we ought now to repeat.

“He who brought all things into being and formed the whole human being according to the divine image in his own will did not delay by gradual additions of future things, knowing that the number of souls had to be brought to completion in its fullness; but, in the fullness itself, he understood the whole of human nature by a prognostic operation, and honored it in exaltation and in repose equal to that of the angels.”

Here understand that the aforesaid teacher placed the past for the future. For when he says that God created the whole human nature in exaltation and in repose equal to that of the angels through a prognostic operation, how else can this be understood except that the human being had already been created in his causes, but had not yet advanced into the effects of his blessedness?

And why had he not  [Col. 0812B] advanced? He gives the reason, saying:

“Since he foresaw through the power of contemplation the will proceeding incorrectly toward the good and therefore departing from the angelic life, lest the multitude of human souls should be diminished by falling from the mode by which the angels increased in number, he therefore devised within nature a means of increase suited to those annulled in sin [the printed *annullatis* is uncertain], inserting into humanity, in place of angelic magnificence, the bestial and irrational mode of succession from one another.”

If, therefore, these words of the holy theologian are true—which I would believe on good grounds—what else are we to understand except that human nature did not remain in paradise, in which it was naturally created, through any delay of time or any effects of sensible things, but immediately strayed from the way of truth and, through the movement of a perverse will, merited the division of  [Col. 0812C] nature into two sexes, by which it would multiply in the likeness of animals?

Accordingly, if it had remained in the blessedness in which it was created, it would not have needed the union of the two sexes for its multiplication. For it would have multiplied in the manner in which the angels multiplied, without any sex.

The venerable teacher Maximus, the expositor of the theologian mentioned above, agrees with this interpretation. While expounding his sermon on baptism, he says:

“Those who mystically attain the divine utterances and, as is fitting, glorify them by higher contemplations say that the human being was made according to the image of God in his principles, being wholly born according to purpose in spirit, and receiving the likeness  [Col. 0812D] through observance of the divine command, so that the same human being might become a creature of God according to nature, but a son of God and God according to grace through the Spirit.

“For it was not otherwise possible for the human being to be shown to be a son of God and to become God through deification by grace, unless he first, according to his purpose, were born in spirit, through the power united to him by nature, moved by itself, and free.

“But the first human being abandoned this deifying, divine, and immaterial birth of intelligible and hidden goods [printed *bonoram*, apparently *bonorum*, “goods”], [Col. 0813A]  giving preference to what is according to sense, what is pleasurable and manifest. Consequently, he was justly condemned to have, from bodies, an unordered, material, and corruptible birth. God rightly judged that he had voluntarily preferred worse things to better, and alienated him from the free, impassible, spontaneous, and chaste birth according to the likeness into the passible, servile, and constricted generation [printed *possibilem*, “possible,” apparently intended as *passibilem*, “subject to suffering”], according to the likeness of irrational and brute animals upon the earth. In place of the divine and ineffable honor he had with God, he received an ignoble union with the irrational animals.

“Desiring to free the human being from this and restore him to divine blessedness, the Word, who creates human nature, truly became human from human beings and was bodily born without sin through a human being.”

But so that you may know that  [Col. 0813B] we do not say these things from ourselves, but have learned them from the aforesaid author, Maximus—that the human being did not taste from the tree of life, but first took the deadly food from the forbidden tree, and did not raise the eye of his mind toward the divine light—hear him speaking in the twenty-eighth chapter of his *Expositions of Gregory’s Words*:

“Accordingly, the first father Adam, unwilling to raise the eye of his soul toward this divine light, like a blind man, deservedly in the darkness of ignorance, clinging with both hands to material, voluntary impurity, bending wholly downward, surrendered himself to the senses alone, through which he received the corrupting poison of the most bitter beast.”

He says this because he wishes the bodily sense through which Adam was deceived to be understood in the figure of the woman. For among the Greeks, αἴσθησις—that is, “sense” or “sensation”— [Col. 0813C] is feminine in gender. By the “most bitter beast” he means the devil, who through bodily sensation infused the poison of his wickedness into the human mind.

A little later he says:

“And he who had first learned that death was also present in the forbidden tree, making the first fruits of food when sense extended the fruit, changed his life to one corresponding to the fruit, namely a mortal and fleeting life through a corruptible body.”

Then he adds:

“If, therefore, believing God rather than his fellow-servant—that is, sense—he had eaten from the tree of life, perhaps he would not have laid aside the immortality that had been given to him, preserved forever by participation in life, since every life is customarily preserved by its own appropriate food. The food of that blessed life, however, is the bread that descended from heaven and gives life to the world, as the Word himself, who does not lie, declared about himself in the Gospels.

 [Col. 0813D] “Because the first human being was unwilling to eat this, he was justly cast out from the divine life, and received another life from death as its mother. Through this life he imposed upon himself an irrational form, concealed the divinely radiant beauty, and, by eating, handed all nature over to death.”

But since it is not part of our present purpose to engage those who say that the human being lived happily in paradise for a period of time before the sin, while they do not dare to assert how long that period was, we have endeavored only to state  [Col. 0814A] what seems plausible to us. It does not at all belong to us to refute, reject, or declare false the opinion of others who think differently. I see that we must now proceed to consider paradise itself.

**DISCIPLE.** We must certainly proceed. We ought rightly to follow the path of sound reasoning, so that we do not appear to turn aside either to the right or to the left. That is, we should neither disparage those whom the Catholic Church has established as possessing the highest and holiest authority, nor reject those whom we know to have understood matters simply, since they remain within the sincerity of the Catholic faith.

For, as the Apostle says, “Let each person abound in his own understanding.” To approve our own understanding, or that of those whom we judge to surpass others, while rejecting the understanding of everyone else, is either extremely dangerous,  [Col. 0814B] extremely arrogant, or certainly contentious.

Let us therefore enter upon the matter cautiously, humbly, and modestly, following the footsteps of the holy Fathers in such an undertaking.

- etiam — also, of leaving the place of happiness. [Note: [Col. 0809] Thus CF; A reads *et etiam*, “and also.”]

- Quod — that, introducing the explanation of the devil’s fall. [Note: [Col. 0809] A reads *Quid*, “what.”]

- Item — again, introducing the prince of Tyre. [Note: [Col. 0809] Thus A; CF read *Attamen*, “nevertheless.”]

- Ligni — of the tree, qualifying food. [Note: [Col. 0809] Thus CF; A reads *lignum*, “tree,” instead of genitive *ligni*.]

- suae, an ab initio conditionis — of his own, or from the beginning of the creation. [Note: [Col. 0811] A omits this span in the question about the devil’s or man’s beginning.]

- spoliatus — stripped, of natural goods. [Note: [Col. 0811] Thus A; CF read *abusus*, “having misused/abused,” instead of *spoliatus*.]

- nunc — now, in we ought now to repeat. [Note: [Col. 0811] A reads *non*, “not,” rather than omitting the word.]
- prognostica operatione — by a foreknowing operation, in Gregory’s quotation. [Note: [Col. 0811] Thus CF; A reads *per prognosticam operationem*, “through a foreknowing operation.”]
- prognostica operatione — by a foreknowing operation, in the following explanation. [Note: [Col. 0811] A reads *per prognosticam operationem*, “through a foreknowing operation.”]
- ad bonum — toward the good. [Note: [Col. 0811] Thus CF; A reads feminine *bonam*, “good,” instead of neuter *bonum*.]
- annullatis — those annulled, in the devising of increase suited to sin. [Note: [Col. 0811] Thus CF; A reads *lapsis*, “those fallen.” The printed *annullatis* is difficult in this construction.]
