## 16.

**MAGISTER.** Saint Augustine says in the eighth book of his *Exameron*: “I am not unaware that many have said many things about paradise. Nevertheless, there are, as it were, three general opinions on this subject. One belongs to those who wish paradise to be understood only corporeally; another to those who understand it only spiritually; the third to those who accept paradise in both ways, sometimes corporeally and sometimes spiritually. To speak briefly, I confess that the third opinion pleases me.”

The same author says in the fourteenth book of *The City of God*, chapter 11: “Thus the human being lived according to God in paradise, both corporeally and spiritually. For paradise was not corporeal because of the goods of the body without being spiritual because of those of the mind. Or was it spiritual, so that the human being might enjoy it through the inner senses, but not corporeal, so that he might enjoy it through the outer senses? It was plainly both, because of both.

“After that proud angel, and therefore envious angel, had by the same pride turned from God to himself and fallen from the spiritual paradise, he sought by malicious cunning to insinuate himself into the human mind. He envied the human being, who was standing while he himself had fallen. In the corporeal paradise, where the other earthly animals also moved about, subject and harmless, together with those two human beings, male and female, he chose as the instrument of his work an animal—slippery, naturally mobile through winding coils, and suited to his purpose—through which he might speak.”  
[Apparatus, Col. 0813: *et* is omitted by CF.]

Observe how he asserts that there are two paradises: one spiritual, in which the human being lived happily according to the soul, and another corporeal, in which that same human being lived happily according to the body.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0813: *homo* is omitted by A.]

In the book he wrote *On True Religion*, however, he seems to assert only one paradise, and that a spiritual one:

“The first vice of the rational soul,” he says, “is the will to do what the highest and innermost Truth forbids. Thus the human being was expelled from paradise into this world”—that is, from eternal things to temporal things, from abundance to poverty, from stability to weakness—“not, therefore, from substantial good to substantial evil, since no substance is evil, but from eternal good to temporal good, from spiritual good to bodily good, from intelligible good to sensible good, from the highest good to the lowest good.”

[Apparatus, Col. 0813: CF reads *Sic* (“thus”); A omits *est*.]

Do you see what he says: “from intelligible good to sensible good”? Did he not plainly say that paradise is intelligible, and not sensible?  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF reads *Sic*; A reads “paradise is intelligible.”]

For if he had wished it to be sensible, he would surely have said, “from sensible good”—that is, from corporeal paradise—“to a lower sensible good.” Unless perhaps someone should say that he spoke only of the spiritual paradise, from which the sinful soul was expelled, while in that sentence he was silent about the expulsion of the body from corporeal paradise.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF reads *Sic*; A reads *e* (“from”).]

For he does not say that the first vice is the vice of the human being, but of the rational soul. Nevertheless, I believe that he signified the whole human being by naming the better part.

For it is not credible that the human being was expelled from the spiritual paradise, but not from the corporeal one, on account of transgression, if there either were or still are two paradises. Unless perhaps someone should say that in this passage he explained only the human being’s expulsion from the spiritual paradise and remained silent about his fall from the sensible one.

Saint Ambrose also, at the beginning of the book he wrote *On Paradise*, seems similarly to affirm that there are two paradises, especially where he says:

“Thus God placed in this paradise the human being whom he had fashioned.”  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF reads *Sic*; A reads *formavit*, “formed.”]

Understand also that he did not place in paradise the human being who exists according to the image of God, but the one who exists according to the body; for what is incorporeal is not in a place.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF reads *Sic*; A reads *quod*, “because.”]

A little later, however, when he comes to explain paradise, he very clearly establishes not only that paradise is to be understood spiritually, but also that paradise is nothing other than the human being himself. In my judgment he is altogether following Origen, although he does not name him openly. For he says:

“Someone before us related that transgression had been committed by the human being through pleasure and sense: taking the form of the serpent as a figure of pleasure, the figure of the woman as sense, and the type of soul and mind as the man.”
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF reads *voluptatem* (“pleasure”); A, *voluntatem* (“will”).] The Greeks call sense *aisthēsis* (αἴσθησις). But when sense had been deceived, he asserted that the mind had become transgressive; the Greeks call it *nous* (νοῦς). Thus, rightly, in Greek *nous* is understood in the figure of the man, and *aisthēsis* in the figure of the woman. Hence some have interpreted Adam as ‘earthly mind.’”  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: *in* is omitted by A.]

And somewhat later:

“Paradise, then, is a certain fertile land—that is, a fruitful soul—planted in Eden, that is, in a certain pleasure, or in an exercised land in which the soul takes delight. There is also *nous*, like Adam, and there is *aisthēsis*, that is, sense, like Eve.

“And lest you should have something to attribute to the weakness of nature or to a condition exposed to dangers, consider what supports this soul possesses. There was a fountain to water paradise. What fountain? The Lord Jesus Christ, the fountain of eternal life, as is the Father also, because it is written, ‘With you is the fountain of life’; and again, ‘Rivers of living water will flow from his belly.’

“Both fountain and river are mentioned: it waters the fruitful tree of paradise, which bears fruit unto eternal life.”
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF reads *quo* (“by which”) for *quod* (“which”).] This fountain, as you have read, is in paradise. For he says, ‘A fountain proceeds from Eden’; that is, there is a fountain in your soul. Hence Solomon also says, ‘Drink water from your own vessels and from the fountains of your wells.’”
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF omits *de* (“from”).]

“This is the fountain”—the phrase is omitted by CF—“which proceeds from that exercised and pleasure-filled soul; this fountain, which waters paradise, is the virtue of the soul springing up from the most exalted fountain.”  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF reads *Sic*; A has “which waters paradise—that is, the virtues of the soul springing up from the most exalted fountain.”]

“And this fountain,” he says, “is divided into four beginnings. The name of one is Pishon,” and so forth. The aforementioned Saint Ambrose discusses the four rivers of paradise with great clarity, comparing each river with one of the soul’s virtues: Pishon, which according to the Greeks is called the Ganges, with prudence; Gihon, which is the Nile, with temperance; the Tigris, which is said to be named from the speed of its course, with fortitude; and the Euphrates with justice.

Do you see how he understands paradise spiritually?

**DISCIPLE.** I see. But perhaps someone might say that he seems to allegorize more than to deny a corporeal paradise. For if he did not believe that a corporeal and local paradise existed, perhaps he would not later, after his exposition of the spiritual paradise—which is either the soul itself or something spiritual in which the soul is established—have added an explanation of the passage where it is written: “And God took the human being whom he had made and placed him in paradise to work and guard it.”  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: A reads *in qua* (“in which”), rather than CF’s *in quo* (“in which [masculine]”).]

“Do you see,” he says, “that the one who existed is taken?” He existed, however, in the land of his fashioning.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF reads *Sic*; A reads *formationis*, “of formation.”]

Thus the power of God took him, breathing the progress and growth of virtue. Finally, he placed him in paradise, so that he might be taken as though by the breath of divine service [reading uncertain].
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF reads *spirans* (“breathing”); A, *inspirans* (“breathing into”). A further reads: “so that you may know that he was taken as one breathed upon by divine power.”]  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: CF reads *Sic*; A: “so that you may know that he was taken as one breathed into by divine power.”]

Observe at this point that the man was made outside paradise, and the woman inside paradise, so that you may understand that each person acquires grace for himself not by the nobility of place or lineage, but by virtue.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: *et* is omitted by CF.]

Thus the man, made outside paradise—that is, in a lower place—is found to be better, while the woman, who was made in the better place, that is, in paradise, is found to be inferior.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: “was made” is omitted by CF.]

For the woman was deceived first and herself deceived the man.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: “was” is omitted by CF.]

Is it not plainly indicated by these words that he wished to establish a local paradise, and therefore a corporeal and sensible one?

**MAGISTER.** It is not our task to struggle with those who wish such things. For we neither deny nor affirm that there are two paradises, one corporeal and the other spiritual. For the present we are merely comparing among ourselves the opinions of the holy Fathers. It is not ours to judge which should be followed more; let each person abound in his own understanding and choose whom he will follow, leaving disputes aside.

But how the teacher of the highest authority, and of the sharpest and most subtle intellect, arrived at such statements in his expositions of divine Scripture is not readily clear to us, unless perhaps—as we very often find in his expositions—he followed the leading Greek theologians, especially Gregory.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0815: A reads *quia* (“because”) where CF has *qui* (“who”).]

They assert that there are two conditions of the human being: one according to the image of God, in which neither male nor female is understood, but only universal and simple humanity, very similar to angelic nature, which both authoritative teaching and true reason unquestionably declare to be entirely without sex; and another, a second condition, added because of the foreknown transgression of rational nature, in which sex is established.

Therefore, rightly, what was added because of sin is said to have been made outside paradise and, as it were, in a lower place. The male sex, added to the nature made according to the image of God, was made outside paradise.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: CF reads *infra* (“below”) rather than A’s *extra* (“outside”).]

But because this sex itself is joined to the prior nature—namely, the divine image—it is established in paradise as though taken from elsewhere. There, again, as if in a higher place, the second sex, called woman, drawn from his side, is joined to him for the generation of offspring, in an insult corresponding to the likeness of irrational animals.

And because the condition of the male sex precedes that of the female, not in time but only in dignity—for in the first condition the woman was made from the man, while in the second the man was made from the woman—he therefore says that the man’s condition was outside paradise and the woman’s inside it.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: CF omits *propter*, “because of.”]

In this way you may understand that the man, even though formed outside paradise—that is, outside the dignity of the primordial condition—was made better than the woman, who was formed, as it were, inside paradise—that is, as the union of the added sex with the simplicity of the divine image.

It may also be explained in this way: in every human being two human beings are understood, as the Apostle says: “The outer human being is corrupted, but the inner human being is renewed.” Accordingly, the inner human being, who was made according to the image of God, is formed in paradise, while the outer and corruptible human being is fashioned outside and below paradise from the mud of the earth. Yet he too is taken up and placed in paradise, because, if he worked out his salvation in himself and guarded the divine commandment, he could also attain the dignity of the higher condition according to the image of God.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: CF reads *Sic*; A has *extitit*, “came to be,” instead of *extra*, “outside.”]

But because he did not wish to obey the divine commandment, he abandoned not only his Creator but also the dignity of his Creator’s image.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: CF reads *Sic*; A reverses the order: “to obey the divine.”]  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: A omits *ejus*, “of his.”]

Consequently, he was split into two sexes, male and female. This division received its cause not from nature but from vice. Therefore, although the female was made from the man in paradise, she was not thereby better than the man, because she took the occasion of her formation not from the divine image, which was formed inside paradise, but from the merit of her future transgression.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: A reads *quia* (“because”) for *quoniam*.]

For she too was created causally in the outer human being, who was fashioned outside paradise from the mud of the earth on account of the merit of sin.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: “was” is omitted by A.]

Later, in due order but not in time, she was taken from the man’s side and placed in paradise.

But whether the aforementioned teacher intended this or something else, we should not struggle against those who, as we said, believe that there are two paradises: one spiritual and the other corporeal, corresponding to the twofold nature of the human being.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: CF reads “two paradises, as we said”; A has “two, as we said, paradises.”]

This is especially so since we often see in the narratives of divine Scripture that many things were both accomplished historically according to the truth of events and understood spiritually.

Abraham had two sons, one from a slave woman and one from a free woman. These things happened according to history; yet according to allegory they signify two laws, one of the Old Testament and the other of the New.

The rock from which waters flowed followed the people in the wilderness, while the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ.”

And what shall I say about those first two human beings themselves, male and female, placed in the paradise of which we are speaking?  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: CF reads *Sic*; A has *constitutus*, “placed,” singular.]

Did they not, as the same Apostle testifies, bear the figure of Christ and the Church?

What wonder, then, if a corporeal paradise was created through which the spiritual paradise might be signified?

We know that the supreme expositor of Holy Scripture—I mean Origen—explains that there is no other paradise elsewhere, nor a second paradise, apart from that which, as he himself holds, is established in the third heaven and into which the Apostle Paul was caught up.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: *et* is omitted by A.]

And if it is in the third heaven, it is certainly spiritual. The leading authorities in both languages do not doubt but unanimously affirm that the third heaven into which Paul was caught up is spiritual, calling it intellectual.

Epiphanius, however, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, criticizes Origen on this point and asserts altogether that paradise is on earth: a certain sensible place in the eastern regions of the world, with sensible trees, rivers, and the other things that those attached to bodily senses simply believe to belong corporeally to paradise.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0817: CF reads “that paradise is on earth”; A has “that paradise is on earth.”]

That same Epiphanius also does not doubt that the tunics of skins which God sewed for the first human beings after their transgression were historically made from the skins of sheep

Knowledge, however, does not everywhere indicate discipline and expertise concerning the thing signified, but affection toward that for which grace has been given. Thus when it is written, “The Lord knows those who are his,” this means, “He has given them his grace.” And he says to Moses, “I knew you above all others.”

[Apparatus, Col. 0821: CF reads *in sensum*, “to the sense”; A reads *in sensu*, “in the sense.”]

Observe what sort of paradise, what sorts of trees, and what sorts of fruits the aforementioned theologian establishes.

**MAGISTER.** Whoever carefully examines the words of the aforementioned theologian will find, in my opinion, that nothing else is being urged in them than that human nature, made according to the image of God, is signified by Scripture under the name of paradise by means of figurative speech.

For the true planting of God is nature itself, which he created according to his image and likeness—that is, according to an image altogether like himself, except with respect to the relation of being a subject, as was said—in Eden, that is, in the delights of eternal happiness and in the blessedness of divine likeness. It is greater and better than the whole sensible world, not in bulk but in the dignity of its nature.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0821: A omits *est*, “is.”]

[Apparatus, Col. 0821: A omits “essential.”]

What it is said to undergo is therefore referred to that superadded condition: namely, being able to die and being able not to die [the syntax is difficult].  
[Apparatus, Col. 0821: A omits the entire passage beginning “A natural body” and ending “the capacity not to die.”]

For, as Augustine says, the body of the first human being could have avoided death, and would not have died if it had not been corrupted by the poison of transgression; rather, it would have grown fresh with the flowers of spiritual beauty and would never have aged through temporal growth.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0821: A omits “as Augustine says.”]

Its air was reason, illumined by the rays of divine wisdom, by which it might know the natures of all things. Its ether was the mind, revolving around the divine nature in eternal and unerring motion, in an immutable and mutable state, and so forth—those things that ought to be affirmed concerning the divine image, or rather, since they cannot be understood, honored with silence.

In this paradise Scripture testifies that the fountain of life flowed, from which four rivers are said to be divided in the figure of the four principal rivers of the sensible world: prudence, I mean, temperance, fortitude, and justice.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0821: A omits “of the sensible world.”]

These spiritual streams, bursting forth from divine wisdom, which is the fountain of all life and virtue, water the surface of human nature. First they rise in the secret recesses of humanity, as in the most hidden pores of intelligible earth, into invisible virtues; then, streaming forth into the open effects of good actions, they produce innumerable forms of virtues and actions.

For every virtue and action proceeds from them and returns to them; they themselves proceed from divine wisdom and revolve back into it.

In that same paradise the aforementioned theologian, the great Gregory, explains that there are two trees. One, he says, is called *pan* (πᾶν), that is, “all”; the other *gnōston* (γνωστόν), which means “knowable.”  
[Apparatus, Col. 0823: A omits “which means ‘knowable.’”]

If the interpretation of this name is brought fully into the open, it does not sufficiently express the meaning of the tree. Therefore, so that what is signified by that tree may be more easily understood, we have chosen to translate *gnōston* as “mixed.”

What, then, is *pan*, from whose fruit the human being was commanded to take food?

*Pan* is certainly that tree of which Scripture says: “And the Lord God brought forth from the earth every tree beautiful to see and pleasant for food, and also the tree of life in the midst of paradise.”

Observe how prophetic contemplation both recounts and names the one and the same tree in two ways. First it calls it “every tree beautiful to see and pleasant for food,” and then again “the tree of life in the midst of paradise.”  
[Apparatus, Col. 0823: A omits the passage from “Observe” through “paradise.”]

And shortly afterward: “Eat from every tree of paradise,” calling one tree “every tree.”

Therefore, no one who follows the teaching of the aforementioned theologian should suppose that there are in paradise many trees of different forms and different fruits, like a forest full of many trees, but only two: one *pan* and the other *gnōston*.

And *pan xylon* (πᾶν ξύλον), that is, “every tree of paradise,”  
[Apparatus, Col. 0823: A omits “of paradise.”]  
is the Word and Wisdom of the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ. He is every fruitful tree planted in the midst of the paradise of human nature in a twofold manner.

First, according to his divinity, by which he creates, sustains, nourishes, gives life to, illumines, deifies, moves, and brings our nature into being. For “in him we live and move and are.”

Second, he joined our nature to himself in the unity of substance, so as to save it and restore it to its original condition, so that he might subsist in two natures, divine and human.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0823: A reads “into the universality of his substance” rather than “in the unity of substance.”]

This is what Scripture says: “And the Lord God brought forth from the earth”—that is, from our material nature—“every tree”—that is, the incarnate Word, in whom and through whom all things were made, and who is all things.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0823: A omits “the Lord.”]

For he alone is substantial good. The other things that are said to be good are good not through themselves but through participation in him, who truly exists as good in himself and is every good, goodness itself, and the fountain and origin of all good and goodness; the cause and principle, end and perfection, movement and rest, middle and extremity, circumference and place of the whole of good. His fruit is eternal life; his eating is joy, gladness, and ineffable delights; his appearance is beautiful.

For he himself is the beautiful and the beauty of all that is beautiful, the cause and fullness of beauty. His taste and eating know no satiety: the more one partakes of him, the more one is aroused to desire partaking of him.

It was from this “every tree”—that is, from the fullness of every good—that the first human beings were commanded to take food; and the entire human race is still commanded to live from it.

But because our first parents did not wish to take food from it, preferring to it the deadly fruit of the forbidden tree, they themselves, and the whole race propagated from them, were expelled by the most just divine judgment and according to the dignity of nature, and were condemned to death.  
[Apparatus, Col. 0823: CF reads “they did not wish to take food from it”; A reverses the order to “to take food from it they did not wish.”]

Do you therefore see what the divine Prophet—or rather, the Holy Spirit through the Prophet—wished figuratively to signify by the name “every tree”?

**DISCIPLE.** I see it plainly, and, as I think, nothing other than God the Word made human, the whole good of all…

…of paradise, that is, of our entire nature, and nothing other than it subsisting; to eat of it—that is, to apprehend it with a pious understanding [Col. 0824B] [Col. 0823] “it” omitted by A, or to believe in it by faith—is eternal life and incorruptible health, whereas to ignore or deny it is eternal death and boundless corruption.

**MAG.** You perceive it clearly. It remains, then, to speak of the *γνωστόν*, that is, of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. We have already said that *γνωστόν* may be rendered not word for word but sense for sense, for easier understanding. According to the aforementioned master—whose judgment concerning paradise we both follow and, for the sake of clarifying its obscurity, recapitulate—it is wickedness colored by the appearance of good, implanted in the senses [Col. 0823] So CF; A: “in corporeal things.”, and wholly opposed to the former tree, which is the *πᾶν*, the All. For just as in that tree all good is imagined and it is all good, so in this one is the whole of evil. The former, therefore, is all good truly subsisting; the latter is all evil, deceiving all the wicked through the appearance of good.

Why, however, both trees—that is, the tree called “all,” which is also called the tree of life, and the other tree, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—are said to be in the middle of paradise is not an idle question. Nevertheless, it can, I think, be resolved in the following way.

If, in the first place, the whole of human nature—namely, visible and invisible, exterior and interior—was made in the image of God, and if what was added because of sin must be brought into consideration [Col. 0823] So CF; A: “had been.”, then whoever attentively examines the text of blessed Gregory’s treatise *On the Image* [Col. 0823] So CF; A: “perceives,” will find a sixfold division of the whole of human nature, both generally in all human beings and particularly in each individual [Col. 0823] So CF; A: “participation.”.

First, it is divided, as it were, into two principal parts: one is assigned to the body, the other to the soul. The part assigned to the body—that is, to the exterior human being—is in turn separated, by rational examination, into three parts [Col. 0824D].

The first is the body itself, constituted from formed matter. Of it alone is “being” predicated, and nothing lower than it is understood to exist in human nature.

The second part is that which extends upward and is customarily, and may properly be, called by many names. It is called nutritive and augmentative because it nourishes and enlarges the body and holds it together as one, so that it does not flow apart and dissolve [Col. 0823] So CF; A: “holds it so that it does not.” It is also called vital motion—not without reason, since it not only grants life to the body but also moves it, whether locally through the spaces of places, or through the measures of places and times. By “places” I mean those by which the fullness of the limbs is filled out; by “times,” those by which the stages of life are brought to perfection. [Col. 0825A]

The third part is distinguished in the fivefold bodily sense. This part receives the appearances of all sensible things understood to exist around the exterior human being and delivers them to memory [Col. 0825] A: “of all things.” In these three parts the entire exterior human being is constituted.

The interior human being, however, who subsists in the soul alone and was made in the image of God, receives another threefold division. For he possesses an interior sense, through which the soul discerns and judges the appearances of sensible things that it receives through the bodily sense [Col. 0825B]. Next, he possesses reason, through which he investigates the principles of all things that he can either understand or perceive. The highest part of the human being is the mind; beyond it nothing higher is found in human nature. Its proper function is both to govern the aforementioned lower parts and, insofar as it is permitted to ascend, to contemplate what is above it—namely, its God—and what subsists in and immediately around God.

Do you therefore see the sixfold division of human nature? It exists, lives, and senses through the body; it senses outside the body; it reasons; it understands.

But the three things recognized in the lower part of the human being [Col. 0825] So CF; A: “in the part of the name” are corruptible and liable to dissolution. The threefold structure of the higher part [Col. 0825C], which is constituted entirely and absolutely in the soul alone [Col. 0825] *In* omitted by A, is rightly incorruptible, indissoluble, and eternal, since the image of the divine nature is expressed in it. Therefore, as we taught in the earlier books, the Greeks call this threefold structure of the human soul *οὐσία*, *δύναμις*, and *ἐνέργεια*—“essence,” “power,” and “activity.” According to the testimony of holy Dionysius, it can neither be dissolved nor corrupted nor perish in any way.

Consider, then, the extremities of human nature as though they were the upper and lower boundaries of a certain paradise, beyond which no created nature is understood to exist. For above the mind there is God alone; below matter—that is, the body alone—there is nothing. This is not the “nothing” that signifies the excellence of nature, but that which is both called and conceived as the privation of all nature. You will therefore find, if I am not mistaken, that the mind occupies the highest place of human nature, while the material body occupies the lowest [Col. 0825D].

Examine also the middle regions of this same nature, and you will find, below the mind, reason as the higher element, and above the body, vital motion—the nutritive life, I mean, as the lower. Again, in the very middle of nature, as in the middle of paradise, there are two senses: the exterior sense, attached to vital motion and the body, and the interior sense, inseparably and consubstantially joined to reason and the mind [Col. 0825] A: “consubstantially”; CF: “constantly.”

In these two senses, as in two locations within the middle [Col. 0825] So CF: *medii* (“of the middle”); A: *mediis* (“middle”) of the paradise of human nature, those two intelligible trees—the *πᾶν*, namely, and the *γνωστόν*—are understood [Col. 0826A]. The *πᾶν* is understood in the interior sense, while the *γνωστόν* is understood in the exterior.

For truth and all good dwell in the interior human being: the Word of God, the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, outside whom there is no good, since he himself is all true and substantial good and goodness. Opposed to him, on the contrary, from the other side, are evil and wickedness.

Since all evil is found neither substantially in the nature of things nor as proceeding from any definite and natural cause—for, considered in itself, it is altogether nothing except an irrational, perverse, and imperfect motion of rational nature—it finds no other dwelling place in the whole creation except where falsehood possesses it. The proper possession of falsehood, however, is the bodily sense.

For no other part of human nature receives the error of falsehood except the exterior sense; through it the interior sense, reason, and even the intellect itself are very often deceived [Col. 0826B].

Therefore, in the place of falsehood and empty appearances—that is, in the bodily sense, which the Greeks call *αἴσθησις* and which is represented under the figure of a woman—the *γνωστόν*, that is, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, is established. It is wickedness colored by the appearance of good, or evil configured as good [Col. 0825] So CF; A: “is figured,” or, to put it simply, false good, or evil concealed beneath the appearance of good. Its fruit is mixed knowledge, that is, confused knowledge.

For it is confused by the evil lying hidden within and by the form of good that is displayed; and thus it first deceives the sense in which it exists, as though it were a woman unable to distinguish between the wickedness (*malitia*) that lies hidden and the form of good by which that very wickedness is surrounded [Col. 0826C].

Wickedness in itself is a kind of deformity and detestable ugliness. If the erring sense recognized it by itself, it would not merely fail to follow it or take delight in it; it would flee from it and recoil in horror. But the foolish sense errs and is therefore deceived, believing evil to be good and beautiful and pleasant to use.

For example, when the appearance of gold, or of any sensible material, is impressed upon the bodily sense, that appearance itself seems beautiful and attractive because it has been taken externally from a good creature. But the woman—that is, the carnal sense—is deceived and delighted, not perceiving the wickedness hidden beneath that false and imaginary beauty, namely, love of money, *philargyria* [Col. 0825] CF: *philargia*, which is the root of all evils [Col. 0826D].

“Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her,” says the Lord, “has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” As though he were saying plainly: Whoever impresses an appearance derived from a woman’s form upon his carnal sense has already committed adultery in his thought, desiring the shamefulness of lust, which secretly draws him beneath that false imagining of a woman’s form.

Thus, as we said earlier, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is a destructive and death-dealing wickedness imagined under the appearance of good. This tree is established, as it were, within a certain woman—namely, within the carnal sense [Col. 0825] So CF: *in carnali scilicet*; A: *scilicet in carnali*—which it deceives [Col. 0825] So CF; A: “this is a tree.” [Col. 0827A]. If the mind consents to this sense, the integrity of the whole of human nature is corrupted [Col. 0827] So CF; A: “of human nature.”. For when the highest part of nature transgresses, what lower part can remain unharmed?

The fruit of this tree is mixed knowledge [Col. 0827] “Mixed” omitted by CF, that is, the undiscerning appetite, love, desire, and delight in evil—evil imagined as good—through which [Col. 0827] So CF; A: “through which things,” as through a serpent, the ancient enemy first persuaded the human race to transgress and then inflicted death upon the whole of nature: death upon the soul, which abandoned God, and upon the body, which was abandoned by the soul.

Thus, in this passage “knowledge” signifies not some doctrine of knowing and judging natures, but an illicit motion and confused appetite for desiring evil—that is, sin—colored by the false appearance of likeness to good, in order to deceive [Col. 0827B].

But perhaps you wish to ask whether God planted in the paradise of human nature such a tree, whose fruit is a mixed and confused appetite for good and evil, whose nature is evil colored by the appearance of good, and whose food became the cause of death.

**DISC.** Indeed I do ask, and I see that the question is not idle. For if God created it, he might be thought the author of evil and the cause of death—which it would be most impious to say of the author of all good, and still more impious to believe or suppose. But if it was not planted by God, whence was it implanted in human nature?

**MAG.** First, then, we must consult sacred Scripture, which unequivocally testifies that the tree which is the *πᾶν* belongs to the divine planting, saying: “And the Lord God brought forth from the earth” [Col. 0827C] “from the earth” omitted by A “every tree beautiful to the sight and pleasant for food.” And, as though explaining the quality of this tree, which is the All, it adds: “also the tree of life in the middle of paradise.”

It is as though it were saying plainly that this tree is not only all good [Col. 0827] “is” omitted by CF, and all beautiful, and every food pleasant and spiritual, but also the tree of life [Col. 0827] “of life” omitted by A, by which that paradise—that is, human nature—lives, since it has been established in its middle.

But concerning what follows—“and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”—it is not sufficiently clear whether it is supplied from what precedes, so that the passage should be read, “and he brought forth the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in the middle of paradise,” just as the tree of life, or whether it has instead been introduced independently: “and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil,” so that we are not to understand it as having been brought forth by God [Col. 0827] So CF; A: “so that we understand it not to have been brought forth by God,” but only as opposed to the former tree in quality [Col. 0827D]—just as the former is all good [Col. 0827] So CF: *illud omne*; A: *omne illud*, the cause of life, and the cause of the living, so the latter is all evil, the cause of death, and the cause of the dying.

Or should we perhaps understand that, insofar as it is a tree of the knowledge of good and evil and is surrounded by the form of good, it is from God, since he is the cause of every form and of every beauty—whether that form and beauty is understood or perceived in some substance, or in the appearances of sensible matter, whose proper dwelling place is the bodily sense, because through it they are conveyed to the interior sense [Col. 0828A]? But insofar as the evil itself, surrounded by the form of good, is evil in itself—formless, unknown, and without any definite or determinate cause—is it neither from God [Col. 0827] So CF: *esse*; A: *est*, nor from any certain and defined cause?

For evil is varied and without cause, since it is not found substantially at all in the nature of things. Therefore, insofar as that tree is evil, it is referred to no cause, because it is altogether nothing. But insofar as it is formed by good in order to deceive the unwary, since the matter whose appearance gives it form was both made by the creator of all good things and is good, it is not altogether evil.

The form through which evil deceives those whom it destroys is good, since it is the appearance of some good; the evil itself, however, is altogether evil and was made by no good, since it is opposed to every good.

Accordingly, if anyone carefully examines the nature of the appearances by which evil is colored—evil that cannot appear by itself because it is formless, deformed, shameful, and without cause—he will find those appearances themselves to be altogether good [Col. 0828B] [Col. 0827] So CF: *inspexerit* (“examines”); A: *perspexerit* (“perceives”). We can demonstrate this most clearly by the following argument.

Let us suppose [Col. 0827] A: “For let us suppose” two men: one wise and in no way pricked or wounded by the goads of avarice; the other foolish and avaricious, wholly pierced and torn by the thorns of perverse desire. Let a vessel made of refined gold, adorned with the most precious gems, fashioned with the most beautiful form, and worthy of royal use be brought before these two men as they stand in the same place.

Both look at it—the wise man and the avaricious man. Both receive the appearance of the vessel through their bodily sense, impress it upon their memory, and consider it in thought [Col. 0828C].

The wise man simply refers the beauty of the nature of that vessel, whose appearance he contemplates within himself, to the praise of the Creator. No enticement of desire creeps into him; no poison of love of money, *philargyria* [Col. 0827] CF: *philargia*, corrupts the concentration of his pure mind; no lust defiles him.

The avaricious man, however, is entirely the opposite. As soon as he absorbs the appearance of the vessel, he blazes with the flame of desire, is consumed, defiled, and killed. He does not refer the beauty of the nature itself, or of its appearances, to the praise of him who said, “The gold is mine, and the silver is mine”; instead, he plunges and stuffs himself into the most fetid swamp of desire.

Do you see that the appearance of one vessel is good and beautiful in both men? But in the wise man’s sense it is simple and natural, and no wickedness lies beneath it [Col. 0827] So CF: *ei*; A: *ret.* [uncertain reading]. In the avaricious man it is double and mixed [Col. 0827] So CF: *ex contrario*; A: *est contrario* with the contrary evil of desire, which is mingled with it and takes form and color from it, so that it appears to be good when it is in fact the most poisonous evil [Col. 0828D].

Evil, therefore, was not planted in human nature; rather, it is established in the perverse and irrational motion of rational and free will. This motion is perceived to arise not within nature but outside it, from bestial lack of self-control. Yet it is mixed with good [Col. 0827] So CF; A: “is mixed with,” and stained by the counsel and cunning of the ancient enemy [Col. 0829A] So CF; A: “and in order,” in order to deceive the lustful affections of the carnal senses and thereby destroy them through death.

Nor do we say this in refutation of the opinion of those who assert that the aforementioned tree of the knowledge of good and evil is naturally good and was historically made in a local paradise, whose fruit was knowledge [Col. 0829] “was” omitted by A—that is, experience—of good and evil. For if the first human beings had abstained from touching and tasting it, as they were commanded, they would have possessed the experience of eternal life and perpetual blessedness without the intervention of death.

But if, consenting to the devil’s stratagems, they illicitly took the deadly food from its fruit in their most wretched lack of self-control, they would undergo the experience of eternal death and unhappiness.

But whoever does not disdain to read and examine carefully what we have discussed among ourselves [Col. 0829] Conjecture; A: “what we have handled”; CF: “what we discuss,” should choose from the aforementioned opinions of the holy Fathers whatever seems to him worthy of being followed. Let him also take care not to tear us apart rashly, supposing that what we have said [Col. 0829] So CF; A: *dicta sanctorum nullius cet.* [incomplete or uncertain reading], is supported by no authoritative aid and has been devised presumptuously against the traditions of the holy Fathers.

You therefore have, as I think, a brief and clear exposition of paradise [Col. 0829] A: “brief and suitable,” insofar as the strength of our purpose permits.

## 17. DISCIPLE

I understand; but I should like you to make an ἀνακεφαλαίωσις (*anakephalaiōsis*), that is, a recapitulation, which, as a kind of conclusion, gathers and defines in a single synthesis what has been said here and there about paradise.

## MASTER

We have said that God’s planting—that is, paradise in Eden ([Col. 0829] A: “in Eden, that is, in delights”)—is human nature, made in the image of God, in the delights of eternal and blessed [Col. 0829C] happiness. Its fountain is Christ, concerning whom the Prophet cries out to the Father: “For with you is the fountain of life.” He also invites to himself all who thirst for righteousness, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” Its rivers, flowing from the fountain of wisdom, are the four principal virtues of the soul, from which every virtue and good action springs forth.

Its every tree, of which it is written, “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in paradise,” is planted beside the courses of waters—that is, around it all the oracles of the prophets, all the symbols of both Testaments, the interpretations of those symbols, and all clear and simple teachings converge ([Col. 0829] CF; A: “flow out”). It is, namely, the Word of God [Col. 0829D] implanted in human nature and incarnate from human nature ([Col. 0829] A: “and truly human”; A reads *incarnata*, “incarnate,” feminine; CF reads *incarnatum*, “incarnate,” neuter).

The tree of the paradise of mixed knowledge is the indiscriminate or confused appetite of carnal senses for various lusts, which lie hidden under the appearance of good, deceiving and destroying unwary souls. Its man is the mind presiding over the whole of human nature ([Col. 0829] A: “human nature”). Its woman is the sense, to which the mind incautiously consenting is ruined. Its serpent is illicit pleasure, by which those things that delight the carnal sense are illicitly and damnably desired.

And do not suppose that what we have said—that there are only two trees in paradise, the *πᾶν* (*pan*, “all” or “the whole”) and the *γνωστόν* (*gnōston*, “knowable” or “known”)—contradicts the account that the woman answered the devil: “We eat from the fruit of the trees that are in paradise.” For she did not say, “We eat from the fruit of every tree,” that is, “we are commanded to eat,” but “from the fruit of the trees,” in the plural, as though there were many trees of different forms from which eating had been permitted to them.

For “every tree” can be understood as the woman’s expression for “many trees.” Indeed, “every” is said not of some single thing, but of something multiple in itself. For “every human being” is usually called one human being, although humanity is a multiplicity; and again, that multiplicity itself is called one, because it shares in one nature. What wonder, then, if “every tree” is called “many trees”?

The Word of God, which is every tree—that is, every good—is both one and multiple in itself, and from it every good, that is, every virtue, wisdom, and essence, bears fruit in human nature. Thus all the rational movements of rational nature, which human beings are permitted and commanded to employ, because they spring from the common good of all—namely, divine wisdom—in human nature, which is God’s planting and paradise, have been called, as it were, many trees, numerous and fruitful. These trees subsist in that very one in whom all good things are one ([Col. 0829] CF; A: “universally”).

Therefore the one tree, which is the *πᾶν*, is called many trees because all good things are in it. This was fittingly said by the woman while she had not yet been deceived and was naturally conscious of the virtues implanted in her [Col. 0830C].

But lest we seem merely to follow the opinions of Greek authors concerning paradise, while either neglecting the authority of Latin writers in such matters or being unable to find in them such an understanding of paradise—and thus to have rashly affirmed something that we could not find among masters of either language—I think it appropriate and necessary to insert into our discussion the opinions of Saint Ambrose concerning paradise, if you approve.

## DISCIPLE

I certainly approve. For who but a madman would dare resist the opinions of so great and wise a man?

## 18. MASTER

In his book *On Paradise*, he says:

“There are some who think that this command—namely, to eat from the tree of life and not to eat from the forbidden tree—was in no way appropriate to the Creator of heaven and earth and of all things ([Col. 0829] A omits *de*, “from,” and *et*, “and”), nor in any way worthy of the inhabitants of paradise, and that this life is to be like the life of angels ([Col. 0829] CF omits *sit*, “is”). Therefore we cannot suppose that this earthly and corruptible food was intended for eating, since they neither drink nor eat, and they will be like the angels of God ([Col. 0829] A omits *Dei*, “of God”) in heaven.

“Since, then, there is neither reward in food—for food does not commend us to God—nor great danger in it, since it is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth, the command seems unquestionably unworthy of so great an author, unless you refer this food to that perfect food ([Col. 0831] CF: *perfectum*; A: *illud propheticum*, “that prophetic [food]”) which God promises his saints as a great reward: ‘Behold, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall be hungry.’ This is the food in which eternal life is defined; whoever is deprived of it shall die. For the Lord himself is the living and heavenly bread, who gives life to this world. Hence he himself says: ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life.’

“There was, therefore, some bread of which God had commanded the inhabitants of paradise to eat. What bread was it? Hear what he calls it: ‘Man ate the bread of angels.’ There is also good bread, if you do the will of God. Do you wish to know how good this bread is? The Son himself eats this bread, of which he says: ‘My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven.’

“Consider what kind of food the supreme Teacher teaches us—the food that the Lord commanded the inhabitants of paradise to eat: not bodily and corruptible food, but spiritual food, namely the Word of God and his will.”

## DISCIPLE

I understand, and I greatly marvel at how closely this agrees with Gregory the Theologian, who himself, as was said above ([Col. 0831] CF; A: “as has been said above”), unhesitatingly asserts that the food, fruit, and drink of paradise are spiritual and intellectual.

Moreover, if the food of paradise is spiritual and intelligible, it necessarily follows that the whole tree whose fruit is that food must also be understood as intellectual and spiritual. For it is neither credible nor consistent with the nature of things that an incorporeal and intelligible fruit should arise from a bodily and sensible tree.

Furthermore, if both the fruit and the trees are spiritual, is it not consequential that the place in which they subsist should also be believed and understood to be not bodily, but entirely spiritual?

## MASTER

That is indeed consequential, full of reason, and most consistent with the truth. But in order that this may be strengthened by the unshaken testimony of the aforesaid Father—I mean Ambrose—let us examine more attentively what he wrote in the work mentioned above concerning the place of paradise and nearly everything that divine history relates as existing in it.

He says:

“Many people are perplexed when they consider more carefully how, if it was originally a great gift of God toward human beings that they should be placed in paradise, it may afterward appear to be the reward of great merits that each just person should be carried away into paradise. It is also said that beasts, cattle of the field, and birds of heaven were in paradise.

“Therefore many have wished paradise to be the human soul ([Col. 0831] CF omits *hominis*, “of the human being”), in which certain seeds of the virtues have sprouted, while the human being was placed there both to work and to guard paradise—that is, the mind of the human being, whose virtue appears to cultivate the soul, and not merely to cultivate it but, once it has cultivated it, also to guard it.

“But the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven that are brought to Adam are our irrational movements. For beasts and cattle are certain bodily passions, some more turbulent and some more sluggish. But what else are we to consider the birds of heaven to be except empty thoughts, which, like birds, fly around our soul and often lead it here and there in varied motion?

“Therefore no helper like our mind was found except sense—that is, *αἴσθησις* (*aisthēsis*, ‘sense’), which alone our *νοῦς* (*nous*, ‘intellect’) was able to find as its counterpart.

“But perhaps you will object that God also placed these things in such a paradise—namely, bodily passions and a certain vanity of fluctuating or empty thoughts ([Col. 0831] CF omits *vel*, ‘or’)—and that he himself was therefore the author of our error. Consider what he says.

“‘Have authority over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and all the creeping things ([Col. 0831] A: *reptibilium*, ‘of creeping things’; CF: *repentium*, ‘of things that creep’) that creep upon the earth.’ You see that he gave you authority, so that you should judge concerning all things, distinguishing the kinds of each by the sober definition of your judgment. God brought all things before you so that you might recognize that your mind is above them all.

“Why did you wish to take to yourself and unite with yourself what you found unlike you? He gave you a sure sense by which you might know all things and judge concerning your thoughts. And deservedly you were cast out of that fertile field of paradise, because you were unable to keep the commandment.

“For God knew that you were frail; he knew that you were unable to judge. Therefore he said, as though to those who are more fragile: ‘Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.’ Since, then, he knew that you were weak in judgment, he wished you to be obedient to the commandment, and for that reason he gave the precept. If you had not transgressed it, you could not have fallen into the danger of uncertain judgment.

“But because you wished and dared to judge ([Col. 0831] A omits *et ausus es*, ‘and dared’), therefore he added: ‘Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil’ ([Col. 0831] CF omits *Ecce*, ‘Behold’). You wished to arrogate judgment to yourself; you must not reject the punishment of wrongful judgment.

“Yet he placed you opposite paradise, so that you could not erase its memory. Indeed, the just are often carried into paradise, as Paul was carried into paradise and heard ineffable words. And if you are carried by the power of your mind from the first heaven to the second, and from the second to the third—that is, because the first state of every human being is bodily, the second animal, and the third spiritual—you will be carried to the third heaven so that you may see the radiance of spiritual grace. For the animal human being does not know the things that belong to the Spirit of God.

“Therefore ascent to the third heaven is necessary for you, so that you may be carried into paradise—carried now without danger, so that you may judge all things, because the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one ([Col. 0831] CF: *dijudicat*, ‘judges’; A: *dijudicatur*, ‘is judged’).’”

Observe how Ambrose approves Origen’s interpretation and refutes that of Epiphanius. Origen asserts that paradise is in the third heaven, which is intellectual—that is, in the human being himself, insofar as he is intellect [Col. 0833A] ([Col. 0833] A omits *est*, “is”). Epiphanius, however, thinking far too simply, considers paradise to be some earthly place, with earthly trees and perceptible springs; true reason ridicules this.

For it is not credible to suppose that the Apostle was carried away into any other paradise than that very one in which the first human being was made in the image of God and from which he was cast down on account of his disobedience. Divine history relates one paradise and one human being created in it. In that human being, if the words of the holy Fathers are to be followed, the man and woman are understood to exist.

For the man of human nature is the intellect, which the Greeks call *νοῦς*; the woman is sense, expressed in the feminine gender as *αἴσθησις*. By their mystical marriage, the future union of Christ and the Church was prefigured.

To this man and woman—namely, to intellect and sense—the divine law not only granted but also commanded that they eat from the tree of life, namely from the wisdom of the Father and the Word, which is the Lord Jesus Christ. He was planted in the midst of the paradise of human nature; he is the spiritual bread on which angels and perfected human beings, whose dwelling is in heaven, feed.

They are forbidden, however, the indiscriminate and confused appetite for good and evil, which is implanted in imperfect souls through delight in the beauty of material things. To abstain from this appetite is the merit of eternal life; to misuse it is the occasion of eternal destruction.

As for the other things transmitted by sacred Scripture concerning paradise, although they are spoken by anticipation and as though they had taken place in paradise, they are nevertheless to be understood as having been added on account of sin and as pertaining to the outward human being, and therefore as having occurred outside paradise after the sin ([Col. 0833] A: “and afterward”).

## 19.

For example: “Then the Lord God formed the human being from the dust of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul.”

How was he formed from the dust of the earth, when he was made in the image and likeness of God ([Col. 0833] A: *factus est*, “was made”)? Or how could it be said of him, “The human being became a living soul” ([Col. 0833] CF omits *est*, “became”), when the same was said of the other beasts brought forth from the earth: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul”?

Are we not therefore to understand that there are two conditions of the human being?

First it is written: “And God created the human being in his own image; in the image of God he created him.” Behold the first condition, in which no mention is made of earthly dust or of a living soul.

Then follows the second, which began with the division of nature into two sexes, added as a punishment for transgression. “Male and female,” he says, “he created them.”

First he expressed the simplicity of nature before the sin in the singular: “In the image of God he created him.” But he expressed its division on account of the sin in the plural: “Male and female he created them.”

This division was followed by the likeness of irrational animals: “The human being became,” he says, “a living soul.” He did not say, “a life-giving spirit.”

“For the first human being was from the earth, earthly,” says the Apostle; “the second human being,” in whom the whole of human nature has been restored, “is from heaven, heavenly.” And he says: “Not first the spiritual”—that is, not in the first human being when he transgressed—“but the animal; afterward”—that is, in the second, who restores—“the spiritual.”

The text of the divine history also makes this exceedingly clear. For after it had introduced the second condition, the earthly human being formed from the dust of the earth, in the likeness of the other animals, [Col. 0834B] “as a living soul” ([Col. 0833] A: *introducit*, “introduces”), lest you should think that the first condition made in the image of God had been introduced at that point, it added the first condition separately, saying ([Col. 0833] A omits *dicens*, “saying”): “But the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight in the beginning” ([Col. 0833] A: “in,” rather than “from,” *a principio*), that is, from the first condition ([Col. 0833] A omits “that is, from the first condition”).

It is as though he were saying: Do not understand the first condition in what is written, “The human being became a living soul”; understand the second condition there. Understand the first in the planting of paradise.

For God planted a paradise of delight—that is, human nature—in Eden ([Col. 0833] A omits “in Eden”), in the delights of eternal happiness. And where had he planted it? “In the beginning,” namely in the Word, in which God made heaven and earth ([Col. 0833] A omits *Verbo*, “in the Word”).

Consider the force of the words. In the second condition the prophet used the verb of the perfect past: “The human being became,” he says, “a living soul.” But in the first he used the pluperfect: “The Lord God had planted paradise,” so that you might understand that the first precedes the second in dignity and blessedness, but not in time.

In that first condition the human being had been of such great spirituality that he needed none of the functions of the bodily senses, but enjoyed only the faculty of understanding.

Saint Ambrose also testifies to this when he says:

“And their eyes were opened, and they knew that they were naked.” Previously, he says, they were naked, but not without the coverings of the virtues ([Col. 0833] A: “coverings” rather than “garments”); they were naked because of the simplicity of their character and because nature did not know the clothing of deceit. But now the human mind is covered with many wrappings of pretense.

Therefore, after they had been stripped of that sincerity and simplicity of their uncorrupted nature ([Col. 0833] A has a substantially different reading: “after they had seen themselves stripped of that sincerity and simplicity of the entire…”), they began to seek worldly and manufactured things with which they might cover the nakedness of their mind with pleasures ([Col. 0833] A omits *delectationibus*, “with pleasures”) and overshadow their generative secret ([Col. 0833] A omits *obumbrarent*, “overshadow”).

For how could Adam have used bodily sight, when he saw all the animals and gave them names? How did they come to know? Through an inner and higher knowledge, namely that they lacked not bodily tunics ([Col. 0833] A: “a tunic”), but the coverings of virtue.

Thus, in the same manner in which he saw all the animals, he recognized his own nakedness—solely by the eye of inward knowledge and the simplicity of the mind, without the aid of bodily and mortal sense.

Here it is made clear that all the animals and birds said to have been made from the earth and the waters were scattered through the regions of the earth in their proper places and natural habitats. Yet the first human being, before he was stripped of the covering of the virtues, could contemplate all these things—not locally or through bodily sense, but solely by the mind’s contemplation, beyond every corruptible sense, beyond every place and every time, in their rational principles, according to which they were created.

Concerning this same nakedness of the first human being, Gregory the Theologian says in his sermon on Easter:

“Naked in simplicity and a life without artifice, and without every covering and problem, such as this human being was from the beginning, it was fitting that he should be.”

Maximus explained these words in the forty-first chapter of *Ambigua*, saying:

“Or perhaps he was naked, as the teacher says, in the varied contemplation and knowledge concerning nature, and in a life without artifice concerning action and virtue, existing beyond manifold artificiality and possessing, as a habit, the undefiled principles of the virtues ([Col. 0835] A: *incontaminatus*, ‘undefiled,’ masculine).

“And without any covering or problem, he did not need the knowledge of visible things in the senses as an introduction to the understanding of divine things ([Col. 0835] CF: *introductivae*, ‘introductory’; A: *praeductivae*, an uncertain reading, perhaps ‘leading beforehand’). Rather, possessing access to virtue and knowledge, he had a single and uniform contemplation of those things that are after God, joined together in their simplicity ([Col. 0835] C omits *contuitum*, ‘contemplation’; A omits *possidens*, ‘possessing’), needing only the movement of activity for ready expression by itself ([Col. 0835] CF: *indigens*, ‘being in need’; A: *indigent*, ‘they need’).

“Therefore, whoever desires by philosophical reasoning to raise himself up from the fall of the first father should begin with the complete removal of sensual passions ([Col. 0835] A omits *sensualium*, ‘sensual’). Then, soaring beyond concern for the principles of the arts and beyond the natural contemplation of the end ([Col. 0835] A: “then, thus, concerning…”; A: *sollicitudine*, “concern,” rather than *sollicitudinem*, “concern”), let him look toward eternal and immaterial knowledge, which has no form impressed upon sense at all, nor an intellect placed by the guidance of reason.

“Just as from the beginning God made the first human being, they were naked in the simplicity of knowledge and in an unbounded life, made such by the mortification of the carnal law ([Col. 0835] A: ‘and an unbending and mortified life’).”

## 20.

Understand similarly the sleep which the Lord God cast upon Adam. That sleep appears to have been both the cause of sin and something imposed after sin—or, to speak more accurately, permitted. For Scripture customarily says, in a certain mode of expression, that God does what he permits to happen.

That sleep, therefore, was, as blessed Ambrose explains, a turning toward the pleasures of material things and an appetite for carnal union, away from the mind’s attention by which it ought always and unwaveringly to contemplate its Creator.

“What is this sleep,” he says, “except that when we turn our mind for a little while toward being joined in marriage, we seem, like eyes fixed upon the kingdom of God, to incline and bend them toward a certain sleep of this world and to fall briefly asleep with respect to divine things, while we rest in secular and worldly matters?”

This sleep—that is, the inclination of the mind from eternal things to temporal things, from God [Col. 0836A] to the creature—is followed by slumber:

“After God had cast sleep upon Adam,” he says, “he fell asleep,” that is, he completely separated himself from the power of eternal and blessed contemplation, fell into the delight of sensible things, emptied of every virtue, and withdrew entirely from spiritual senses.

Here it should be noted that, after Adam fell asleep, Scripture introduced the condition of the woman, thereby indicating that if human nature had not abandoned the simple and sincere integrity of its constitution, in which it was made in the image of God, through the irrational movement of free will, but had remained unchangeably in contemplation of the truth, it would not at all have suffered its own division into two sexes in the likeness of irrational animals. Rather, it would have multiplied in the manner in which the angelic order was multiplied without any sex.

But because it willingly fell asleep—that is, because it fell from the dignity of its nature without being compelled—it consequently underwent its division and propagation in the likeness of cattle ([Col. 0835] A: “when,” rather than “because”; CF omits *est*, “underwent”).

“And when he had fallen asleep,” it says, “he took one of his ribs, and filled up flesh in its place, and the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman.”

Although under the figure of the one rib that God took from Adam’s side, the division of nature into two sexes and the removal of the guardianship of the whole inner virtue that had been in him before he sinned may appear to be signified—and although by the flesh placed in the location of the removed rib that most wretched exchange may be signified, by which, in place of the guardianship of virtue and blessedness, he took on the deadly weakness of vice and misery ([Col. 0835] CF: “that most wretched exchange”; A: “that exchange, most wretched”)—nevertheless, I think that the mystery of Christ and the Church is to be understood as prophetically prefigured more fully.

For the first human being, Adam, as the Apostle teaches, is everywhere “a type of the one to come,” namely of Christ. Yet the correspondence is reversed.

In the first Adam, nature was divided into male and female; in the second it was united. For in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female.

In the first, the whole of nature was expelled from the happiness of paradise; in the second, it was recalled and restored to that same happiness.

In the first, flesh was taken in place of the rib—that is, weakness in place of virtue. In the second, weakness and death were swallowed up, while virtue and eternal life were given to human nature ([Col. 0835] CF omits *est*, “was given”).

“For as all die in Adam, so also all are made alive in Christ” ([Col. 0835] A: “will be made alive”).

Thus, as Saint Augustine says, Adam sleeps and Eve comes to be; Christ dies and the Church comes to be. Eve comes to be from Adam’s side while he sleeps; Christ’s side is pierced after his death so that the sacraments may flow forth, by which the Church is formed. For blood is used in the consecration of the chalice, while water is used in the consecration of baptism.

In the first human being, human nature puts on tunics of skin—that is, mortal bodies—having abandoned its natural nakedness, namely sincerity and simplicity. In the second, that same nature is stripped of the tunics of skin, every weakness of mortal bodies having been destroyed, and nakedness—that is, the simplicity of its original nature—having been restored.

These things, therefore, which divine Scripture relates as having occurred after sleep was cast upon Adam ([Col. 0837] A reads *historia*, “history,” rather than *Scriptura*, “Scripture”), although they are read as having taken place as though in paradise, are nevertheless more reasonably and more consistently with the truth to be believed and understood as having been added to human nature after the sin, and therefore outside paradise, on account of its disobedience.

For if God’s planting and paradise in delights is human nature made in the image of God, deformed by no contamination of transgression, I do not know why anything understood to have happened outside the dignity of nature and because of sin would not also be understood to have occurred outside paradise. [Col. 0837: A omits *est*, “is,” after “God’s planting”; A reads *in deliciis sit*, “may be in delights.” The printed *cur non etiam extra paradisum fuisse non intelligeretur* retains its rhetorical double negative: “why it would not also be understood to have been outside paradise.”] I do know, however, that divine Scripture employs a very common trope, called by the Greeks *ὕστερον πρότερον* (*hysteron proteron*, “the later before the earlier”), but by the Latins *praeposterum* or *anticipatio* (“inverted order” or “anticipation”), which the Greeks call *πρόληψιν* (*prolēpsin*, “anticipation”).

The evangelist Matthew used this trope when narrating the Lord’s passion and resurrection. For he writes that things which occurred at the time of the resurrection took place at the hour of the passion. He says:

“But Jesus, crying again with a loud voice, gave up his spirit. And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom, and the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose; and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many.”

All these things, according to the sequence of what actually happened, followed the Lord’s resurrection; but by the aforementioned trope of narration the evangelist wished to relate them as having occurred after the passion.

For it is not to be believed that the tombs of others were opened before he opened his own tomb, or that witnesses of the true resurrection rose before he himself rose, whose resurrection they witness ([Col. 0837] CF; A has a longer and confused reading: “or that those who are witnesses of the true resurrection rose before he himself, whose resurrection they are witnesses, should rise”; Thomas Gale attempted to repair the passage as: “or that they who are witnesses of the true resurrection should have risen before he himself, whose resurrection they are witnesses, should rise”) ([Col. 0837D] “Here is an example of how recklessly John Scotus twists sacred Scripture to his own opinion. [Col. 0838D] The author of the commentary on John Scotus collected other passages.”).

The sleep of Adam, therefore, and the slumber that followed ([Col. 0837] A: “the slumber that followed him”), and the removal of the rib, and the division of simple nature into two sexes, and the mystical recognition of the wife ([Col. 0837] A: “knowledge” rather than “recognition”), and the other things prefigured mystically in the figure of Christ and the Church; also the recognition of nakedness—that is, of the sincerity of nature—and therefore the fact that they were not ashamed of it, since they were clothed in the coverings of the virtues and entirely free from the pleasures of irrational movements; the sincerity that they had lost by sinning and recognized again by losing it; likewise the deceitful persuasion of the serpent, the woman’s crafty disputation and seduction with the serpent, the illicit taking of the fruit of the forbidden tree, and the deadly taste; also the man’s consent and fall—not because he was unaware, but because he considered it a light sin to consent to his one wife—for Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived; he did not sin unknowingly, and therefore deserved to be punished more severely; likewise the opening of their eyes, by which they recognized their nakedness; the sewing together of loincloths from fig leaves; also the hearing of the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise; and the flight of both Adam and his wife from the face of the Lord God and their hiding in the midst of the tree; and all the other events up to the expulsion of the human being from paradise—

all these things divine Scripture relates as having occurred in paradise in an inverted order by anticipation, although they followed the sin.

For if paradise is human nature, created in the image of God and established in equality with angelic blessedness, then as soon as it wished to abandon its Creator, it surely fell from the dignity of its nature. For even before he consented to his wife, he began to grow proud.

Moreover, if divine history gives no interval of time between his creation and his fall ([Col. 0837] A: “has given,” rather than “gives”), what else is indicated by Scripture’s silence except that the human being became proud as soon as he was created, and through this fell?

The strongest proof of this is the devil’s act of murder: he was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth. He too, without any intervening delay, fell through pride as soon as he was created, and consequently envied the human being created together with him and destroyed him with the poison of his cunning.

You have, I think, sufficient information concerning paradise.

## DISCIPLE

Perhaps it would be sufficient if you briefly explained what you think about that fig tree whose leaves were sewn into loincloths, and about the Lord God’s walking in paradise. For the tunics of skin have already been discussed.
