[Col. 0838C] **21. TEACHER.** That fig may appropriately be understood as the divine command of the law delivered to the first human beings in paradise. The command was this: “Eat from every tree of paradise, but do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” And, so that they might guard the command more carefully, the danger of transgression was not concealed from them. “For on whatever day,” he says, “you eat from it, you shall surely die.”

The law, then, was given to the first human beings in paradise; they retained its words in memory, as the woman’s answer to the serpent makes clear. For she answered: “We eat from the fruit of the trees that are in paradise, but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise, God commanded us not to eat, and not to touch it, lest perhaps we die.”

[Col. 0838D] The serpent badly interpreted the words of this law, so that he might first seduce the woman—that is, the sense or understanding—and through her gain access to the man, namely, to the mind. He concealed the true and saving power of the divine command. If that woman had recognized, loved, and revered it, she perhaps would not have been seduced by the serpent, nor drawn her husband into destruction; nor would they have sewn themselves girdles from the leaves of the fig—that is, from the words of the command alone—employing them as uses suited to the desires of the flesh and their deadly indecencies. Rather, they would have taken, eaten, and lived in eternal happiness from its fruit—that is, from the true and life-giving power and understanding of the divine law.

Thus the divine law, when perversely interpreted, considered according to the letter alone, and corrupted by human or diabolical superstitions, becomes suitable to carnal desires and provides *perizomata*—coverings—for irrational impulses, sewn together as though from empty leaves, devoid of every power and true understanding. But when it is understood well and spiritually, and cleansed of every carnal sense and superstition, it bears for those who eat it—that is, for those who rightly understand it according to the spirit—a saving and life-giving food.

The first human beings, unwilling to eat from it and believing instead the interpretation of the lying serpent, did not receive the fruit of the legal fig for the use of the spirit; rather, they took empty leaves full of deceit—namely, mere words joined together by diabolical cunning—by which they might conceal the indecencies of their lusts.

We say this following Saint Ambrose, who explains the aforementioned fig in his book *On Paradise*, saying:

“They sewed together,” he says, “fig leaves and made themselves girdles. What species should we understand the fig to represent in this passage? The sequence of the divine readings teaches us, since Scripture records that those who rest beneath the vine and the fig are safe, and Solomon says: ‘Who plants a fig tree and does not eat its fruit?’ And the Lord came to the fig tree, but for this reason was displeased: because he did not find fruit, but only leaves.

“Adam therefore teaches me what the leaves are. After he sinned, he made himself a girdle from the leaves of the fig, although he ought rather to have tasted its fruits. The righteous chooses the fruit; the sinner, the leaves.

“What is the fruit? ‘The fruit,’ says the Apostle, ‘of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, moderation, self-control, devotion.’ He did not have the fruit who did not have joy; he did not have faith who was about to transgress the command of God; he did not have self-control who had tasted the tree forbidden to him.

“Therefore whoever transgresses the command of God is stripped and made naked, and becomes shameful to himself. He wants to cover himself with certain fig leaves, perhaps with certain empty or shadowy words, sewing them together with composed commands and building word upon word. The sinner weaves a covering to hide the shame of his conscience, his mind, and his deed, so that he may conceal his nakedness.

“Thus he sews leaves above himself who desires to conceal his guilt: either he declares the devil the author of his offense, or he pleads the allurements of the flesh, or he exposes some other persuader as the cause of his error. He frequently draws examples from the divine Scriptures by which he claims that the righteous fell into guilt, saying—if someone has been discovered in sexual misconduct—that Abraham also lay with his maidservant, and that David loved a foreign woman and took her as his wife.

“He has sewn together certain leaves, certain examples from the sequence of the prophetic Scriptures; he does not think that their fruit need be sought. Do not the Jews also seem to sew leaves, when they interpret the words of the spiritual law bodily? Their interpretation loses all the fruit of its greenness, condemned to the curse of eternal dryness.

“Good interpretation, therefore—that is, the spiritual fig—is fruitful. Beneath it the righteous and holy rest. Whoever plants it in the minds of individuals, as Paul says, ‘I planted, Apollos watered,’ will eat its fruit. But a bad interpretation cannot bear fruit or preserve its greenness.

“What is more serious is that Adam girded himself with this interpretation at the very place where he ought rather to have girded himself with the fruit of chastity.”

You have heard Ambrose concerning the fig; hear also the same author concerning the Lord God’s walking in paradise—namely, in human nature, which he created in his own image, which he never abandoned or permitted to perish, and in which he was always walking secretly and spiritually, searching the hearts and kidneys—that is, the inmost thoughts—of individuals, questioning them with an intelligible voice about the causes of their transgression, and reproving and correcting them more mercifully than he punished them justly.

The aforementioned teacher therefore says:

“And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the evening. What is his walking, since he is always everywhere? But I think that God’s walking is a certain movement through the sequence of the divine Scriptures, in which a certain presence of God is at work. We hear that he sees all things, and that the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous; we read that Jesus knew their thoughts; we read: ‘Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?’ Therefore, when we review these passages, we recognize, as it were, the voice of the Lord walking.

“The sinner had fled—not because he could escape God’s sight, but because he wished to hide within his own conscience and did not want his deeds to come to light. It belongs to the righteous to see face to face, because the mind of the righteous is present not only before God but also argues with God, as it is written: ‘Judge the orphan, justify the widow, and come, let us argue together,’ says the Lord.

“Therefore, when the sinner reads the divine Scriptures, he hears the voice of the Lord as though he were walking in the evening. What is ‘in the evening’ except that he recognizes his guilt late, and that a certain shame for his past error comes late—although it ought to have forestalled the error?

“For while guilt burns in the body and the soul is agitated by the passions of the body, the sense of the erring person does not think of God; that is, he does not hear God walking in the divine Scriptures, walking in the minds of individuals. For God says: ‘I shall dwell among them, and I shall walk among them, and I shall be their God.’

“Therefore, when the fear of divine power has returned to the sense of the soul, then we blush; then we try to hide ourselves; then, placed amid the thoughts of our sins, we are discovered in the middle of the tree of paradise, where we sinned, wishing to remain hidden and supposing that God does not seek out secret things.

“In these words of the aforementioned teacher, understand that the tree in the middle of paradise, in which the fleeing transgressors thought they could hide, is nothing other than the secret place of human thought and conscience. But the one who searches souls and penetrates thoughts even to the division of the spirit said to Adam: ‘Adam, where are you?’

“How does God speak? Is it with a bodily voice? Certainly not, but with a certain power more excellent than any bodily voice can possess, and he pours forth oracles. The prophets heard this voice; the faithful hear it; the impious do not understand it.

“Whoever has sharply perceived the power of such words will discover that paradise is not some local, earthly, wooded place, but spiritual, planted with the shoots of virtues and planted in human nature. To speak more plainly, it is nothing other than human substance itself, made in the image of God. In it the tree of life—namely, the Word and Wisdom of the Father—makes all life fruitful, and in its midst the fountain of all good things, namely the same divine Wisdom, flows.

“There that divine fig, assuredly the law, has been rooted. Its true interpretation and spiritual fruit are the fruit of life for those who eat it—that is, for those who understand it piously and perfectly. But its perverse and carnal interpretation according to the letter consists of empty and fruitless leaves, with which the transgressors of the divine law strive to cover their faults by a lying defense. They do not hesitate to refer them either to the very author of the law, or to the devil, or to some other person, or to the likeness of deeds figuratively performed by the holy Fathers. They accept the deeds of the Fathers carnally according to the letter, but in no way understand them spiritually; and they produce such examples from divine Scripture as an occasion for their own error. Of these the Apostle appropriately says: ‘The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.’

“In this intelligible paradise God walks about. He is the guardian and investigator of the plantation that he formed in his own image and likeness. His voice is beyond explanation: ‘Adam, where are you?’ This is the voice of the Creator reproving human nature, as though he had said:

“‘Where are you now, after your transgression? I do not find you there where I know you were created. I do not find you in that dignity in which I made you according to my image and likeness. Instead, I reprove you as one who has abandoned blessedness and flees the true light, hiding in the hiding places of an evil conscience, and I inquire into the cause of your disobedience.

“‘Do you suppose that I do not know what you have done, or where you have fled, or how, fearing my voice, you have hidden yourself, or how you recognized only late the nakedness of your nature—that is, the sincerity and simplicity in which you were created?

“‘Have you not suffered all these things because you ate from the tree concerning which I had commanded you not to eat? For if you had not eaten, perhaps you would not fear the voice of your Creator walking within you, nor flee from his presence, nor recognize your nakedness, which you lost through transgression?’”

**22. Concerning the forbidden tree.** We have already said much above concerning the forbidden tree, following Gregory of Nyssa; now, I think, we should speak briefly again, introducing the view of the most noble teacher, the monk Maximus.

He understands the tree of the knowledge of good and evil to be the visible creation, which man followed after abandoning his Creator. In this visible creation there is both the pleasure of delight and the occasion of anxiety, and a kind of mixed fruit of death, composed of the apparent good of lust and the evil of the sorrow that follows.

For there is no pleasure in visible creation that is not followed by want. Want is followed by anxiety, and anxiety by the sorrow of death. Although anxiety and the cause of death lie hidden beneath smiling pleasure, they nevertheless exist together in the human soul and begin together. Anxiety lies concealed beneath a certain false beauty of pleasure and is like a mixed fruit of apparent lust and hidden anxiety.

When pleasure and delight in visible creation fail, anxiety remains naked and exposed by itself; it arises from want and the loss of visible good.

Hence the aforementioned Maximus says:

“Perhaps whoever says that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the visible creation will not depart from the truth. For it naturally possesses a perception that produces pleasure and anxiety. Or because visible creation possesses spiritual principles that nourish the intellect, and also a natural power that delights the senses but overturns the intellect, it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

“Considered spiritually, it possesses the knowledge of good; taken bodily, it possesses the knowledge of evil. For when received bodily, it becomes a teacher of passions, bringing forgetfulness of divine things upon those who receive it. Therefore God forbade man its enjoyment, interrupting his perception of it for a time, since it was especially just that he should first recognize through participation in grace the cause of his own nature, and the immortality given through grace. Then, through perception of such a tree, he might be perfected into dispassion and unchangeability, becoming like God through deification, and might discuss the creatures with God in an innocent communion with God and receive knowledge of them—so that, as God and not as man, he might possess through grace, from God, wise knowledge of all that exists, and through this knowledge might undergo the transformation of soul and sense into deification.

“This is how the matter of the tree should be understood, according to the allegorical interpretation that can be adapted to all things.”

Observe how beautifully and clearly he explains what the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is. It is, as he says, the nature of visible things. When understood spiritually in their principles, it grants the knowledge of good and spiritual fruit to those who understand it; but when desired carnally and lustfully, and used intemperately and contrary to the divine laws, it brings deadly knowledge.

Thus the cause of evil is not established in nature itself, but in the intemperance of those who abuse it. This is the woman—or, so to speak, this is the tree—of which the Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

The surface of material things, although naturally beautiful, becomes an occasion of death when those who regard it consider it carelessly and lustfully through their senses. For God created visible creation so that through it, as through the invisible creation, his praise might be increased, and so that he himself might be recognized—not what he is, but that he is—the one Creator of the whole visible and invisible creation.

Therefore God forbade human nature to delight in visible creation before it had arrived at the perfection of wisdom in which, once deified, it could discuss with God the principles of visible things. Nor would that woman—namely, the carnal sense—have been able to draw the man, that is, the mind, toward delight in material creation considered from outside, if he had wished first to possess knowledge of the Creator rather than of creation.

The order of the divine law, therefore, was first to know the Creator and his ineffable beauty, and then to consider creation with rational understanding obedient to the mind’s directives, referring all its beauty—whether inwardly in its principles or outwardly in its sensible forms—to the praise of the Creator.

But man, rejecting this order of the divine law through pride, placed the love and knowledge of his Creator after the external beauty of material creation. Consequently he incurred the danger of divine indignation and fell into the death of body, the death of soul, and the destruction of his entire nature, because he neglected to preserve the most just and beautiful sequence of the divine law.

We have said these things concerning the forbidden tree after examining the views of the honorable interpreters of divine Scripture. The holy Father Augustine also introduced this same view in the eleventh book of his *Exameron*:

“I am not unaware,” he says, “that some have thought that those human beings hastened ahead of the proper time in their desire for the knowledge of good and evil, and wished to receive prematurely what was being reserved for them to receive at a more suitable time. The tempter brought this about, so that, by seizing what was not yet appropriate for them, they might offend God and be excluded from and condemned to alienation from the usefulness of that thing, which they could have enjoyed beneficially if they had approached it at the proper time, as God wished.

“I have said this for certain people, so that, if they should wish to understand that tree figuratively rather than literally—as a real tree with real apples—they may have some conclusion that is plausible according to right faith and truth.”

But the aforementioned teacher Augustine seems neither to reject nor to commend this interpretation concerning the spiritual paradise, following his customary practice of asserting that there are two paradises: one earthly and local, according to the literal reality of sensible things; the other wholly spiritual, in whose likeness the earthly and sensible paradise was made.

**DISCIPLE.** Those who have understood the forbidden tree in this way do not seem to me to depart from the truth. For it is plausible, and in my judgment entirely consistent with sound reasoning, to suppose that, when man began to eat the forbidden fruit—that is, when he presumed to misuse the knowledge of sensible matter through bodily senses—he was expelled, by the most just judgment of the Creator, from the sweetness of the tree of life, that is, from the delights of the inward contemplation in which and for which he had been created.

For if he had entered by a rational and natural order—that is, if he had first enjoyed, with perfect attention, the contemplation of the cause of all things, and then the contemplation of the principles according to which and in which all things were made—he would neither have been shut out from the intelligible food of the tree of life, namely, the inward contemplation of divine Wisdom, nor would he have been forbidden, until the suitable and mature time of his perfected wisdom, to eat the forbidden fruit—that is, to know visible matter—so that he might know God and, consequently, creation, without any error or any delights of carnal desire.

For it is impossible to prevent knowledge of creation from the rational soul in which perfect contemplation of the Creator begins to shine. But wherever contemplation of created nature precedes knowledge of the Creator, error will never be absent, since such contemplation cannot be free from the imaginings and allurements of sensible things—except in those who, flooded with the radiance of the divine ray, take the paths of right contemplation, seeking themselves and their God. In them, certainly, knowledge of the Creator precedes knowledge of creation.

Creation, therefore, is not evil, nor is knowledge of it evil. Rather, evil is the perverse movement of the rational soul by which it abandons contemplation of the Creator and turns itself, through a lustful and unlawful desire, toward love of sensible matter by deadly steps. From this it will not be able to return unless it is first liberated by divine grace.

For, as Saint Augustine says, human nature was capable, through free choice, of wounding itself; but once wounded and injured, it is not capable of healing itself through free choice.

But we must now continue along the path of reasoning toward the matters that remain.

### 23. MAGISTER

What remains? Has enough been said about paradise? For while Adam, when reproved by the divine voice, removed the charge against himself onto the woman—and, in order to mitigate the woman’s case as well as his own, removed the charge from himself—and while the woman herself removed the occasion of the transgression onto the serpent, since this matter has been sufficiently examined by the interpreters of Sacred Scripture, I do not think it necessary to discuss it. [Note: Col. 0845: CF reads, “Thus Adam, rebuked by the divine voice, shifted the blame onto the woman”; A reads, “for concerning the shifting of blame, by which Adam, rebuked by the divine voice, shifted the blame onto the woman and, in order to mitigate the woman’s case, shifted the blame”; the remaining witnesses read as printed.]

### DISCIPLE

It is indeed necessary, and exceedingly useful. For it may happen that someone should perhaps suppose that the very removals of blame—by which the man shifted the occasion of sin onto the woman given to him by God and consequently onto the giver of the woman, while the woman shifted it onto the serpent—were valid and just defenses, undeserving of punishment, unless they are disproved by true reasoning, immediately refuted as unjust and blameworthy, and judged rightly to belong to the accumulation of the most just punishment for the offense.

### MAGISTER

Let us therefore set forth the words of Scripture itself. “Adam said,” it says, “The woman whom you gave as my companion gave me from the tree, and I ate.”

Tell me, Adam, I ask: who gave you the woman?

“The Lord,” you reply, “who formed her.”

I ask you: why did God form her and give her to you? Why, while you were sleeping—that is, while the eye of your mind was inclining from the contemplation of truth toward the love of carnal marriage—did he draw a rib from your side and make from it the woman whom he gave to you when you were sinning and abandoning him? Why did he not make the woman whom he was to give you in the same way as he made you? [Note: Col. 0845: CF reads *connivente* (“winking/assenting”); A reads *convertente* (“turning”).]

You yourself were rightly made from earthly soil, since, abandoning heavenly things, you chose earthly ones. [Note: Col. 0845: CF reads *de terrena humo* (“from earthly soil”); A reads *de terreno limo* (“from earthly mud”).] Your woman was fittingly taken from your side, because the cause of your transgression arose from yourself.

You will answer, I believe, that God did all these things because he wished to, and that he did them in this way because he foresaw that they should be done in this way: he who did everything whatever he wished. But I still ask you: why did he wish to make the woman for you in this way?

“Who,” you will say, “can investigate the reasons for the divine will? For who has known the mind of the Lord?”

Then you do not know why God made the woman whom he gave you?

“I do not know,” you reply, “unless it was for the assistance of the propagation and multiplication of human nature, which was first made in me and received from me the beginning of procreation.”

Here I confront you and refute such an intention with true reasoning. Human nature would not have needed the shameful generation of male and female, after the likeness of irrational animals, if it had not abandoned the mode of angelic multiplication—which, as has often already been said, is entirely without the union of the sexes—through pride and contempt for the beauty of its simplicity, in which it was created in the image of God.

Seek, therefore, another reason by which you can assert why the woman was given to you; for the one you have proposed is false. The image of God, in whose likeness humanity was made, is free and exempt from every sex.

“I know no other,” you say, “apart from the one I have proposed, and I see that you have disproved it.”

I am astonished that you say you do not know the things that came about because of your disobedience and pride. But I, who sinned in you and died by sinning, do know them.

For unshaken and perfectly clear reason cries out within me—and the authority of many Fathers likewise approves it—that if human nature had remained in the very simple and most pure blessedness of the divine image, it would have been subject to no sex and would have undergone no dishonorable propagation, like foolish animals. [Note: Col. 0845: A omits “foolish” (*insipientia*).]

But because it did not wish to persevere in that dignity in which it was created, and chose instead [Note: Col. 0845: A reads *edita est*, “was brought forth,” for *condita est*, “was created.”] to multiply ignobly among the other animals, the same Creator foresaw what man would do and what would happen to him, ruined by the perverse movement of free will, and added the two sexes, by which he would be propagated after the manner of beasts. [Note: [Col. 0845] “and what would happen to him” is omitted in A.] [Note: [Col. 0845] The conjunction “and” is omitted in CF.]

Why, then, do you shift the occasion of your transgression onto the woman, when the cause of making the woman was preceded by your own pride, contempt for your God, and consequent abandonment of him?

This is also declared most clearly by the divine irony, which says: “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.” [Note: Col. 0845: CF reads *aptissime* (“most fittingly”) for *apertissime* (“most openly/clearly”); CF has the order *solum hominem esse* (“the human being to be alone”), whereas A has the usual order.]

It is as though it were saying openly: “It does not seem good for the human being whom we made in our image and likeness to be alone—that is, to remain simple and perfect, and wholly complete without division of nature into sexes, after the likeness of the angelic nature—but rather to rush, prone and inclined, into earthly intercourse together with the beasts, [Note: Col. 0845: CF omits “without” (*sine*); A reads *proclivemque* for *proclivumque*; A reads *ac si* (“as if”) for *ac sic* (“and thus”).] and thus to multiply the unity of nature seminally through carnal generation and bodily sexes, despising the dignity of the multiplication of the heavenly orders.

“Let us therefore make for him a helper, by which he may accomplish what he desires: namely, a female who, like the male, is fragile and unstable and desires earthly lusts.”

This is what Scripture anticipatively declares when it says: “Male and female he made them”—namely, vessels for the carnal begetting of offspring, with the dignity of the divine image and spiritual plurality rejected. [Note: [Col. 0845] A has “of carnal offspring.”]

Why, then, do you attempt to shift the cause of your transgression, which is reflected back upon yourself, onto the woman whom your Creator gave you—or indeed onto the Creator himself?

Such a removal of guilt contributed nothing to your defense; rather, it increased the accumulation of your condemnation.

But perhaps someone may say that we are criticizing marriage and the procreation of offspring, since we assert that the division of human nature into male and female [Note: Col. 0845: A omits “we” (*nos*).]—through whose union marriage and the propagation of children and increase of nature are accomplished—came about as a consequence of sin.

To this we shall reply: We do not criticize marriages, provided that they are lawful, joined through the desire to beget offspring rather than to indulge lust, with the fidelity and chaste modesty of both sexes preserved. [Note: [Col. 0847] CF has “with the fidelity and chaste modesty of both sexes preserved”; A has “with them preserved.”] Indeed, we praise them, because they were both granted and commanded by God: “Be fruitful,” he says, “and multiply, and fill the earth.”

No Catholic doubts that both sexes, without which carnal marriage cannot take place, were made by God. Scripture says: “Male and female he made them.” Again, elsewhere: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate.” [Note: [Col. 0847] A reads “let a human being not separate.”]

But we unhesitatingly affirm that carnal marriages, even when lawful and contracted by religious people, cannot be free from the lustful and illicit movement of carnal desire. [Note: Col. 0847: A reads “and among religious people” (*et in religiosis*) for “contracted by religious people”; CF omits “nevertheless” (*tamen*).] For children born in the flesh draw the guilt of eternal death from no other source than this; baptism in the Catholic Church alone releases them from that guilt. [Note: Col. 0847: A reads *secum* (“with themselves”) for *solum* (“alone”).] [Note: [Col. 0847D] We have repeatedly reviewed John Scotus’s extremely erroneous doctrine concerning the state of the first parents, the two sexes, and generation, which he explains more fully in these books. There is also his evident mockery of Sacred Scripture and his false interpretation of original sin. See the Commentary on John Scotus, Part II, §49 and following.]

We also assert that those carnal unions by which human nature is propagated locally and temporally would not be necessary if humanity had not chosen to multiply its nature after the likeness of cattle, abandoning the multitude of the heavenly orders.

As David says: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.”

But let us return to the woman’s answer, by which she shifted the occasion of her guilt onto the serpent. The Lord God said to the woman: “Why have you done this?” She replied: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

And you, woman, why do you shift your guilt onto the serpent, when you yourself are the creator of your own guilt? The serpent onto whom you cast the blame creeps within you yourself: your serpent is your carnal concupiscence and delight, which is generated from the irrational movement of the soul in bodily sensation.

Therefore the woman—that is, carnal sensation—vainly shifts her guilt onto the serpent, that is, onto irrational delight, of which she herself is the author. For the illicit delight of material things did not arise from nature, but from the imperfect and irrational movements of the sinful soul, which, through the bodily senses, breaks into the love of sensible things with a deadly appetite.

Nor would the ancient enemy have access to the man of the soul—that is, to the mind made in the image of God—unless he first seduced the bodily sense itself, which is like a certain woman, through the mind’s delight implanted in that bodily sense, as though through a serpent. Likewise, the mind would not consent to the destructive delight and excessively abusive enjoyment of material things through bodily sensation if arrogant presumption had not first preceded within the mind. [Note: Col. 0847: A reads *ni* (“unless”) for *nisi*; CF reads *perabusiva* (“excessively abusive”), while A omits *abusiva* (“abusive”).]

Thus the pride of the mind and the illicit delight of carnal sensation, joined to one another, handed human nature over to the condemnation of death. From that condemnation the humility of Christ alone, together with the delight in spiritual things within the souls of the faithful, recalls and liberates the same nature.

You therefore have nowhere and no one onto whom you can shift your guilt, woman, except yourself, since you are convicted of being the author of your illicit delight, onto which you attempt to shift the guilt. [Note: [Col. 0847] CF has “onto which guilt”; A has “onto which your guilt.”] [Note: [Col. 0847] CF has “you attempt to shift”; A has “you shift.”]

Here we ought beautifully to observe the wording of the divine utterances. For the things that were made together, without intervals of temporal delay, have been woven together—because of our slowness and our carnal senses, to which we, corrupted by original sin, are subject in places and times—in a certain remarkable order, full of mystical meanings, as though they had taken place in locations and times. [Note: Col. 0847: A reads the feminine *corrupta* (“corrupted”) for *corrupti* (“corrupted,” masculine plural), and omits “and” before “times.”]

First, therefore, the man is questioned—that is, the mind. [Note: Col. 0847: A reads *interrogatus* (“questioned,” masculine singular) for *interrogatur* (“is questioned”); A has the order *praeceptum divinum* (“divine commandment”).] And rightly so, since he presided over the whole of paradise, and ought to have guarded it so that the divine commandment would not be violated there.

Thus he is questioned: “Adam, where are you?” It is as though he were being told: “Adam, who, before you sinned, were established beyond all places and times, answer now, transgressor: where are you? You were blessed in heaven like an angelic creature; now you are proud on earth like the brute animals.” [Note: [Col. 0847] A omits “Adam, where are you? It is as though he were saying.”]

The speech then turns to the woman, and she is asked why she did this. Here we must note that the sentence of the questioning judge is not immediately pronounced upon the man and the woman; rather, as it were, an opportunity is granted for correcting their wicked excuse, and a place is prepared for indulgence.

Finally, when the serpent is reached, he is not questioned, nor is he given an opportunity to shift the guilt onto something or someone else, because he could not do so, being the primordial cause of all evil; instead, he immediately endured the sentence of the just judge.

For God says to the serpent: “Because you have done this, you are cursed among all living creatures and the beasts of the earth.”

Observe that neither the man nor the woman is cursed, but the serpent alone. For God does not curse the things he made, but blesses them; the mind and the sense are creatures of God. Carnal delight, however, arose outside the divine creation from the irrational passions of the human soul, and therefore succumbs to the severity of the divine sentence, since it supervened outside the nature made by God. [Note: [Col. 0847] CF has “since it supervened outside the nature made by God”; A has “since it is found outside the nature made by God.”]

For what else is divine cursing but the most just and irrevocable condemnation of those who are outside nature and contaminate it?

What those living creatures and beasts of the earth are, among which carnal delight—through which the devil seduces the soul and in which he dwells as though in his principal seat—is situated, Saint Ambrose [Note: Col. 0849: A reads *concatenatum* (“linked/concatenated”) for *concatenatim* (“in a linked manner”).] has explained most beautifully and abundantly in his book *On Paradise*.

They are all the irrational passions of our rational nature, which divine Scripture designates by the term “earth.” And do not be surprised that both carnal delight and diabolical cunning are represented together, as though indistinctly, in the figure of the serpent. Sometimes that serpent plainly represents the devil himself; sometimes the lustful desire of the carnal soul deceived by him—that is, of the person living carnally; sometimes it indistinctly and confusedly suggests both, one being linked to the other.

And not without reason: the one cannot exist separably from the other. Wherever there is a lustful gaze of the soul, there the approach of the unclean spirit will immediately be present; wherever the entrance of diabolical cunning is present, there the itch of universal wickedness will not be absent.

Whenever these two meet in any bodily sense—which is represented by the figure of the woman—illicit eating and the illicit use of food will necessarily follow: that is, the abuse of the beauty of material things. This brings death to the soul, of which the death of the body is the shadow.

But concerning the curse by which the serpent was condemned, and concerning the sentences pronounced upon the woman and upon her husband Adam—in which more mercy than vengeance is understood—it seems superfluous to me to speak now. [Note: [Col. 0849] A omits “to me.”]

For to explain what has been sufficiently explained by the holy Fathers might perhaps seem unnecessary; and what is found most fully and clearly in their writings—why, someone might say, should it be repeated by us, as though we could explain it better? [Note: [Col. 0849] F originally had “as though we would explain”; a later hand corrected it to “as though we could explain”; AC has “as though it had been explained.”]

Far be it from anyone to think this of us, since we can scarcely follow in their footsteps. [Note: [Col. 0849] CF has “of us”; A has “of them.”]

### DISCIPLE

It would certainly seem unnecessary if this one obstacle did not stand in the way. For it will seem strange and inconsistent with the reasoning and wording of the discussion that, although you have touched briefly and cursorily, following the opinions of the holy Fathers, upon nearly everything that seemed to require discussion concerning the nature of spiritual paradise and the things that Scripture records as having been done there, you have left this one passage wholly untouched and have reverently passed it over in silence. [Note: Col. 0849: CF reads *venerabaris* (“you reverently observed/passed over”); A reads *veneraris* (“you reverently observe/pass over”).]

For this reason, you ought not to pass over such matters, but clearly and concisely run through them.

### 24. MAGISTER

Let us therefore hear the examination arising from the divine indignation against the serpent.

“You shall walk upon your breast,” he says, “and you shall eat earth all the days of your life.” [Note: [Col. 0849] A has “earths.”]

We have said that Scripture placed the serpent in this passage as a figure both of diabolical cunning and of carnal delight, and of both embraced in one another indistinctly and inseparably. [Note: [Col. 0849] CF has “embraced in one another indistinctly and inseparably”; A has “entangled.”]

### DISCIPLE

Beautifully, lucidly, and not contrary to the truth.

### MAGISTER

The breast of this serpent is the prudence of the flesh, in which the cunning of diabolical fraud dominates. Empty and deceitful wisdom, which does not build up the mind but puffs it up, is also his breast.

Carnal prudence and empty, deceptive sophistry are the serpent’s breast, which God will destroy. “I will destroy,” he says, “the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent.”

But if you ask what difference there is between prudence of the flesh and empty philosophy, accept the following formula of distinction.

The prudence of the flesh is a false virtue that dyes vices with the colors of virtues, that fashions evil into a likeness of goodness, that adorns disgrace with the appearance of honor, while concealing the simple and true virtues themselves. By withdrawing them from the mind’s gaze, it hides them so that the mind cannot recognize their sincere face; thus it deceives the carnal senses, deludes souls, buries them beneath the deceptive phantasies of false virtues, and overwhelms them with the darkness of eternal death.

Empty and useless wisdom, on the other hand, flourishes especially among faithless Jews and poisonous heretics. It follows only the letter of divine history, while it hates, despises, neglects, and ignores the spirit—that is, the mystical meaning. It contrives false and empty fables about the nature of things, without any plausibility, in order to mock carnal souls, while disregarding the truth of the natural principles according to which the whole creation was made. It displays the pompous and grandiloquent elegance of unusual words, or, with the twisted locks of deceptive propositions and syllogisms, imitates the form of truth in order to deceive the unwary. [Note: [Col. 0849] CF has “deceptive”; A omits this word.]

The breast of the serpent, then, is composed of these two things: diabolical cunning and the enticement of carnal delights. Upon this breast, I mean, that serpent walks—that is, is exalted—and from it he is glorified, overthrowing the whole human being.

This is made clear by the prophetic words. For he did not simply say, “You shall crawl or creep upon your breast,” but figuratively, “You shall walk upon your breast.” No one properly describes a serpent as a walking animal, but as a crawling one. Every animal that crawls is not raised from the earth but dragged along it; whereas everything that walks is raised from the earth before it walks.

Therefore, “You shall walk upon your breast”—that is, upon your cunning and craft, composed of empty wisdom and carnal prudence, by which you deceived the human being, reduced him to your power, bound him with the cords of sins, and plunged him into the abyss of eternal death—you shall be raised in pride and, for the increase of vices and the accumulation of your condemnation, exalted by the progress of your wickedness, you shall walk vaingloriously in the hearts of unbelievers.

“And you shall eat earth”—that is, you shall feed upon the earthly thoughts, carnal desires, and deadly actions of those who desire earthly things.

“All the days of your life”—that is, for as long as your reign over human nature, like a false light, smiles upon it and prevails.

For you will not reign eternally over and conquer the image of God. Either that image, still held captive in this life, will be specifically liberated from your power in Christ the Redeemer, or it will be liberated universally at the end of the world, when the last enemy, death, will be destroyed through Christ the Word of God, and human nature will be restored universally to its original condition.

“I will place enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.”

The woman is the bodily sense naturally implanted in human nature, through which, particularly in those who are perfect, the beauty of visible creation is referred back to the praise of the Creator.

Between this woman, I mean, and the serpent—that is, between the lustful delight in material beauty and the diabolical cunning possessing it—God has established a great enmity. For the woman—that is, the perfect sense of the perfect—hates the carnal appetite for material things, whereas the serpent has as his enemy the desire for spiritual and divine virtues.

“And between your seed and her seed.” The woman’s seed is the perfect, natural, and manifold knowledge of visible things, with every error removed. For bodily sense was established in human beings for this purpose: to become, through the mediation of phantasies, the intermediary between sensible and intelligible things.

The serpent’s seed, however, is the deadly increase of innumerable sins. No one who philosophizes rightly is unaware of this.

“She shall crush your head.”

The head of this serpent—that is, its beginning—is formed, as it were, from two parts. For all wickedness arose and originated from the irrational movement of rational nature and from the envious cunning of the devil. This head is crushed in the sense of the perfect faithful.

Diabolical cunning does not deceive them; they do not grant entrance to the first suggestion that stealthily creeps in, nor do they offer access to irrational movement.

Although that head is thought to be one, it is divided into an infinite number, because universal wickedness is so manifold that there is no part of it from which poisonous shoots of vices do not grow. [Note: [Col. 0851] CF has “shoots”; A has “sprouts.”]

All these things are crushed by the woman of whom Solomon says: “Who will find a strong woman?”—namely, virtue and wisdom in the senses of the perfect faithful.

The prophet and psalmist addresses this woman when he says: “You crushed the heads of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians.” [Note: [Col. 0851] A has “for you gave him.”]

The peoples of the Ethiopians are the multitudes of the nations who believed in Christ, prefigured symbolically in the figure of that woman. [Note: Col. 0851: CF reads *praefatae mulieris typo praefigurative* (“prefiguratively in the type of the aforesaid woman”); A reads *fortis praefatae* (“of the aforesaid strong woman”). CF reads *crediderunt* (“believed”); A reads *crediderint* (“will have believed”).]

Of these Isaiah says: “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light.”

Ethiopians are called “dark” or “humbled” by the proper meaning of the translation. Their interpretation is appropriately applied to the peoples of the Gentiles, who before the coming of the true light, which is the Word of God, were dark, enclosed by the thickest mist of ignorance and eternal death. But once humbled, receiving faith, they were illumined and refreshed by spiritual feasts, which divine wisdom prepares from the crushed heads of the dragon—that is, from the defeated multiplicity of all wickedness.

The same Psalmist speaks of this dragon: “This dragon, whom you formed to mock him.”

“This dragon,” he says, “is plainly the devil, together with his universal body—that is, the fullness of all wickedness. He is the one whom you formed so that he might be mocked by your saints, who mock his destructive and deceptive snares when they expose and reject the arts of wickedness by which he contrives to destroy the defenses of goodness, and shatter with the hammers of virtues the principles of evil that spring from him.” [Note: [Col. 0851] F has “expose”; C omits the words from “destroy” through “shatter.”]

This agrees with what holy Job says: “This is the beginning of God’s creation, which he made to be mocked by his angels.”

Why this spiritual dragon, together with all his members who follow his wickedness, is called God’s formation or creation can be understood in two ways.

First, because all apostate angels and all human beings who follow them, insofar as they naturally exist, were created by God and are therefore not improperly believed to be his creation and formation.

Second, because such symbolic words in such passages of divine Scripture do not always signify the nature of demons and evil human beings, in which the Creator of all good established them, but rather those things that have been added to the essence created in them on account of the disobedience of both creatures—namely, the angelic and the human. These include the aerial bodies of demons and the earthly and mortal limbs of human beings, which must unquestionably be believed and understood to have been added as punishment for sin to the simplicity of the nature established by God.

But whether the nature of demons will be liberated from the bodies belonging to them that are formed from this air, just as human nature, aided by the grace of its Redeemer, will at the moment of resurrection be released from animal and corruptible bodies, is a subject for another discussion.

And now it must be briefly gathered together that those natural bodies which were made in the creation of the angelic nature will be possessed eternally and inseparably both by the heavenly virtues that never abandoned their Creator and by the apostate virtues. For they are spiritual and incorruptible. But the things added to them from the qualities of this world on account of their wickedness, like certain garments that grow old, will presumably perish together with the world from which they were taken.

What the prophet says, therefore—“This dragon, whom you formed to mock him”—we can understand as follows. It does not seem contrary to the truth to take the dragon as signifying the deadly cunning of the devil and of his members, whether among angels or among evil human beings. By the term “creation” or “formation”—because the diversity of the interpreters translated the Hebrew expression in this way for the use of the Church—we may understand either their nature, according to which they were established by God before they sinned, or those things that were added to them because of their pride. [Note: [Col. 0853] CF omits “were.”]

But however we understand “creation” or “formation”—whether of nature or of what has been added to nature—the devil with his entire body was formed to be mocked by holy human beings and holy angels, not according to what he was naturally made to be, but according to what he would become by growing proud and abandoning the dignity of his nature.

For he is mocked by his holy angels, who remain fixed in that blessedness in which they were created, preserved by their good will and by the grace of the Creator. [Note: [Col. 0853] A has “fixed”; CF has “fixed” in the masculine plural.]

But he, deceived by proud ignorance—for he had not foreseen that he would fall, and if he had foreseen it, perhaps he would have taken precautions against falling—and inflated by the rancor of envy, freely descended into his own misery.

Righteous human beings, however, liberated and illumined by the mercy of their Creator and Redeemer, mock him when they recognize that he secretly offers vice and the deadly poison of wickedness under the appearance of good and the likeness of virtues. They immediately crush his head and, with the teeth of inward discernment, chew up as spiritual food—namely, divine prudence, which distinguishes vices from virtues—the very thing prepared from his crushed heads, so that his deceitful cunning cannot deceive them. They feed upon the sincere dishes of the true good, purged of every mixture of evil.

Nor does the beauty of material things deceive their woman—that is, their sense—through which the ancient serpent, with lustful delight as intermediary, pours the deadly poisons of vices into the minds of the imprudent. [Note: Col. 0853: F reads *mulierem* (“woman,” accusative singular); A reads *mulieres* (“women”); C reads *mulierum* (“of women”). CF reads *sensum* (“sense,” accusative singular); A reads *sensus* (“senses”). CF reads *in imprudentium animos diffundit* (“pours into the minds of the imprudent”); A reads *imprudentium animis diffundit* (“pours in the minds of the imprudent”).]

The woman—that is, sense, distinguishing wickedness from goodness—therefore crushes the serpent’s head and the heads, namely the beginnings, of diabolical suggestion and seductive delight; she is urged, moved, aided, and strengthened by the virtues of the stronger woman, namely the Word of God, and brought to the perfection of action and contemplation. [Note: Col. 0853: CF reads *discernens* (“distinguishing”); A reads *discerpens* (“tearing apart”). CF reads *refectio* (“refreshment”); A reads *perfectio* (“perfection”).]

What greater joy can there be for those who live spiritually in this life than first to expose within themselves the serpent’s lustful and cunning devices, and then to reveal them to the more simple faithful in action and understanding, so that they too may not be caught by the same snares of the deceiver?

“And you shall lie in wait for her heel.”

The heel of the woman, who is αἴσθησις (*aisthēsis*, sense-perception), consists of the phantasies of sensible things—that is, the images impressed from bodily numbers upon the fivefold sense. Therefore that heel must necessarily be fivefold. For it is divided among the five well-known organs of sensation: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.

Some of these extend far beyond the bodily mass of the one who senses, such as sight and hearing. I perceive the sun, the moon, and the other stars as situated far from the place enclosed by the mass of my little body. Wherever they are, I perceive them there in the rays of my eyes, which are raised to that place without any intervening delay, and in which the phantasies of the aforementioned stars are formed.

Do you see, then, how far the aforesaid woman extends her heel in the organ of sight? [Note: [Col. 0853] CF has “in the organ”; A has “into the organ.”] The same is to be understood of things seen nearby or in intermediate spaces. The consideration of the natural organ likewise teaches us about the function of hearing.

For hearing bursts outward beyond the spaces of the body in order to receive within itself the patterns of sounds or voices produced by the impact of air, whether from far away or nearby. [Note: [Col. 0853] CF has “by impact”; A has “by a cast.”]

Some senses, however, are contained within the limits of the body, such as smell and taste, as seems to many who discuss the nature of the senses. Yet there are also those who maintain that the sense of smell leaps outward; we cannot reject their opinion, for we perceive things that smell good or otherwise at a considerable distance from our bodies.

With regard to touch, no natural philosopher doubts that it performs its function both within the body and outside it. For it alone exercises its power without the other senses. None of the other four can fulfill its service without its cooperation. Sight cannot see unless it has touched what it sees; hearing cannot hear unless it has touched what it hears; smell cannot smell unless it has touched what smells; and taste cannot taste unless it has touched what it tastes.

Observe, then, the woman’s fivefold sense, formed by the phantasies of sensible things, against which the cunning serpent lies in wait. [Note: [Col. 0853] A omits “the woman’s heel.”]

He lies in wait for the sense of sight when he wickedly persuades unwary souls to desire the beauty of forms and colors. The same is to be understood of the harmony of voices, the sweetness of odors, the delights of flavors, and of the things touched by the sense of touch.

When all these things are perceived through the bodily sense by the soul after being desired imprudently—that is, through carnal desire—they become the deadly poison of transgressing the divine commandments and nourish the seeds of every offense. [Note: [Col. 0853] CF has “by the soul”; A has “by the mind.”]

This is what Scripture intimates above when it says: “The woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance, and she took of its fruit and ate, and gave some to her husband.” Here it figuratively calls the woman the outer sense, delighted and deceived by the phantasies of sensible things; while by the designation “man” it signifies the mind, which is corrupted by illicitly consenting to the bodily sense—that is, separated from the inward contemplation of truth. [Note: Col. 0853: A reads *illi* (“to that one”) for *illius* (“of it”).]

25. To the woman also he said: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions; in labor you shall bear children.” Here it is plainly understood that, if man had not sinned, he would have contemplated the natures and principles of things with the utmost ease—not only through interior understanding but also through exterior sense—and without any need for reasoning. But after he sinned, through the organs of exterior sense the mind perceives only the surfaces, quantities, qualities, positions, relationships, and other features of sensible things that submit to bodily sense. And it apprehends all these not in themselves [Note: CF; A reads “not in itself”], but through their images; as it handles these images, its judgment is very often deceived [Note: A reads “deceives”], and therefore, not without the many labors of study that Scripture calls the woman’s hardships, it can arrive through that same sense at many conceptions—that is, beginnings of understanding of intelligible things—and at children, that is, correct rational accounts to be generated concerning the nature of things.

Divine authority assigns hardships, conceptions, and children to exterior sense because every pursuit of wisdom, every conception of the mind, and pure knowledge of truth take their beginning from the bodily senses, reason ascending step by step from lower things to higher and from exterior things to interior things [Note: CF; A omits “from”].

“And you shall be under the power of the man, and he shall rule over you.” In this passage the restoration of human nature to its natural order, and its return to the former condition of its creation, is promised by the divine voice. The natural order would indeed have been this: that the mind, subject and obedient to the power of its Creator, should always cling to him [Note: A omits “always to him”]; then that the senses should willingly follow the mind’s power and command; and that the body should submit to the senses. Thus peace and harmony would arise both within the creature itself and between it and its Creator.

But after the transgression of the divine command, that order for whose preservation man was created, and that peace and unity of Creator and creature, were disturbed [Note: CF; A reads “are disturbed”]. For man, corrupted by love of sensible things of his own accord and under no compulsion, abandoned his God, whereas clinging to him alone is the good of our constitution [Note: CF; A reads “the good of human nature”], and there is no other. Therefore, wishing to humble the pride of human nature [Note: CF reads “to disdain”; A “to subdue”], God allowed man to indulge his own irrational and willful impulses, so that he might learn in himself what the grace of his Creator and the merit of obedience conferred upon him, and what irrational impulse [Note: CF; A reads “irrational impulses”] and proud transgression of the command brought him.

Consequently, a kind of divorce between male and female followed, between mind and sense. Bodily sense does not obey the commands of the mind according to the laws of nature. The Apostle expressed this divorce plainly and beautifully when he said: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin,” calling the flesh the carnal sense, which resists and disobeys the rational movements of the mind even in those who are perfect.

And elsewhere: “I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin.” Observe the conflict between the law of the mind and the law of carnal sense—the latter ruling in those who live carnally and resisting the minds of spiritual people in mortal members for the exercise of virtue. For this reason the Apostle called carnal sense “the law of sin.”

But when nature is restored and recalled to its natural order, this conflict and divorce of mind and sense will be changed into the peace of a spiritual and natural marriage [Note: A reads “into the peace of a spiritual and natural union”], when the body is subject and obedient to sense, sense to mind, and mind to God. This is made still clearer to us if we attend to the Septuagint version: “And your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.” By these words the return of human nature to its former order is most clearly understood.

26. As for what was said to the man—“Cursed is the earth in your works,” and the rest, which seem to have been written in the form of a curse—it is not easy to see what sort of earth this is, which is cursed on account of the transgression of the mind, the man of human nature, nor what sort of curse it is: whether it is the severity of indignation or some mystical rebuke; nor why the mind itself, which sinned by hearing the woman’s voice and eating the forbidden fruit, did not bear the curse; nor in what labors it eats the cursed earth; nor what the days of the mind’s life are; nor what thorns and thistles that earth produces [Note: A omits “that earth”], nor what plants of it it eats; nor what sweat, what face, what return of the mind into the earth from which it was taken [Col. 0856C], nor what dust.

If all these matters are understood historically—that is, in relation to sensible things that occur in and from this earth [Note: CF; A reads “and”], which is habitable by human beings—as many authorities have preferred, they raise either no question or only a very slight one. But if they are understood within human nature itself, as are the other things foretold concerning paradise [Note: CF; A reads “are to be understood”], they require no small investigation.

That these matters are understood according to the properties of created things and nevertheless demand prophetic interpretation, Saint Augustine testifies in these words in the eleventh book of his *Exameron*:

“Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I had commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat from it alone’: cursed is the earth in your works. In sorrows you shall eat it all the days of your life. It shall produce thorns or thistles for you [Note: A reads “and”]. And you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go.”

“Who,” he says, “does not know that this means the labors of the human race upon the earth? And since they would not exist if the happiness that had been in paradise were retained, there can surely be no doubt. Therefore, let us not hesitate to accept these words first in their proper sense; yet the meaning of the prophecy, which the intention of God speaking chiefly regards here, must also be preserved and awaited.”

Do you see how [Note: CF; A reads “in what way”], in that book of his, he commands this passage of sacred Scripture to be understood both literally and figuratively? But he does not explain what that prophetic figure means. If he had explained it, perhaps it would have been sufficient for us, and we would not seek another exposition. But he does not explain it. Let us therefore ask briefly, with God as our guide, what such words of the divine utterance mean.

DISCIPLE. Let us ask; for matters such as these must not be passed over untouched.

TEACHER. I think it is sufficient [Note: CF; A reads “let it suffice”] to set forth here the response of the blessed monk Maximus. But so that the response itself may be clearer, his question must first be placed before it [Note: A reads “proposed before it”].

DISCIPLE. It could not properly be done otherwise.

TEACHER. In the fifth chapter of his *Scholia* [Note: CF reads *scoliarum*], he therefore raises the matter as follows:

“What is the earth cursed in Adam’s works according to the anagogical sense; what does it mean to eat it in sorrows; what does it mean, after the growth of thorns and thistles, to eat grass; and finally, what does it mean to eat bread in the sweat of one’s face? No man has ever been seen eating earth or grass; nor do those who eat bread, according to the historical interpretation, eat it in the sweat of their face.”

Response: “The earth itself, cursed in Adam’s works, is Adam’s flesh, continually made through Adam’s works. I mean the passions of the knowing mind, cursed because of the unfruitfulness of its virtues, as though they were divine works; it eats them with great anxiety and sorrow, enjoying briefly the pleasure that comes from them according to their nature.

“This flesh, because of that corruptible enjoyment, produces for him thoughts and cares like thorns, and great temptations and dangers like thistles, pricking him weakly on every side with rage and desire contrary to reason. Thus he can scarcely acquire and eat, as it were, the health and soundness of that flesh, like withered grass—that is, attain it.

“Then, after the repeated passage through many terrors, in the sweat of his face—that is, in the humility and labor proper to sense, and through the arduous consideration of sensible things—he has, as it were, bread for the establishment of the present life, whether through an art or through some other contrivance assigned to this life.

“Or is the earth rather Adam’s heart, cursed because through transgression it received the removal of heavenly goods? Through practical philosophy he eats this earth amid many tribulations [Note: A reads “he eats it through many tribulations”], cleansing it through conscience from the curse of shameful works. Again, thoughts concerning the generation of bodies, having sprung up in it like thorns [Note: CF; A reads “sprouting”], and opinions concerning the providence and judgment of incorporeal things, swarming in it like thistles [Note: CF “in it”; A “in him”], are cleansed through reason. He then plucks the physical theory, as it were grass, spiritually [Note: CF; A reads “rational accounts cleansed”].

“And thus, as though in the sweat of his face, he eats the bread of knowable understanding according to knowledge, with an incorruptible face, the bread of theology: the only truly life-giving bread, which preserves those who eat it for incorruptible generation.

“Thus the earth is the purification itself, thoroughly eaten through the activity of the heart; the grass is knowledge according to the natural contemplation of created things; and the bread is the true teaching of the mysteries according to theology” [Note: A omits the passage from “according to the natural” through “true”].

Thus far Maximus [Note: CF reads “of Maximus”].

I think, however, that the days of the mind’s life, during which it labors to purify the earth of its heart, signify not only those days through which the periods of the present life revolve and the body is animated by the soul, but also that temporal interval during which souls, having abandoned the governance of their bodies and while awaiting the restoration of their bodies, remain in another life.

For we believe that souls can be purified both in this life, in which body and soul dwell together, and in the other life after the death of the body—that is, after its dissolution and return into the four elements of the world from which it was gathered and composed—until the end of the world, the resurrection of bodies, and the day of judgment.

These, then, are the days during which the mind eats the earth of its heart, that is, employs the activity of purification. For after the end of sensible things we do not read that any act of purification will remain, once nature has returned to its original purity.

Perhaps this is what is meant by the words: “Until you return to the earth from which you were taken.” As though he plainly said: “For as long as you labor in the work and knowledge of your purification, your face—that is, the rational search for truth—shall sweat, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; that is, to the immutable solidity of the primordial causes from which you derive your origin. For you will no longer sweat when you have reached that place.”

That the name “earth” signifies the happiness of eternal life and the stability of the primordial causes from which all existing things arise is plainly suggested in many places of divine Scripture. For example, Abraham was told: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I shall show you.” And shortly afterward: “Abraham departed from there into the southern land and dwelt between Kadesh and Asshur”—that is, between sanctification and beatification [Note: CF; A reads “that is, between sanctification and equanimity”—*aequanimitatem*]—between which the happiness of all the saints is established in eternal rest.

For those who have been sanctified—that is, purified from every pollution of body and soul—will live blessedly [Note: CF; A reads “equably”], according to the laws of nature.

And if someone considers another interpretation of Asshur, namely Mesopotamia, he will find a most beautiful and highly appropriate opportunity for contemplation. Mesopotamia is and is called the land between rivers. Is it credible, however, that the habitation of holy souls and of the whole restored human nature will be anywhere other than between the middle courses of the rivers of spiritual virtues flowing from the fountain of all good?

And what else besides this was mystically signified by the promised land to which God’s people were led after being freed from Egyptian captivity and servitude? This is the land of the living, in which the saints will possess a twofold possession—that is, the happiness of body and soul.

The Lord himself also says concerning this land: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.”

As for what follows—“For you are earth, and to earth you shall go,” or, as another interpretation has it, “For you are dust, and into dust you shall return”—it can be understood in this way: since the nature of the mind, which was made in the image and likeness of God, took its beginning from the fertile earth of the primordial causes, we must therefore believe that it will necessarily return to that earth.

If it is asked why that earth is designated by the name “dust” in another interpretation, no other reason need be given than this: just as everything that grows from the dust of this sensible earth receives from it the cause of its coming into being [Note: CF; A reads “the sensible earth”], so the manifold multitude of all visible and invisible things is generated from the fertility of the primordial causes and will return to it at the end of the world.

We say these things not to rebuke the simplicity of those who understand this passage of divine Scripture historically [Note: A reads “of those”], who try to assert that the dissolution of the human body into the four elements of this world is generally signified by the single name “earth” in these words of Scripture, without noticing how much appears to contradict their own interpretation [Note: CF; A reads “their interpretation”].

For if the divine voice spoke such things about the dissolution of the body, why did it foretell them to the man alone? Why not also to the woman, whose body is dissolved no less than his [Note: CF; A reads “whose”]? Furthermore, why does the divine judgment declare that the whole human being will be dissolved, when only its outermost and basest parts—namely, the body and bodily sense—are dissolved, whereas the natural simplicity of the soul, free from every composition, does not undergo dissolution at all but remains perpetually indissoluble, whether it moves rationally or irrationally?

Unless perhaps they say that, according to the very frequent usage of sacred Scripture, this passage is to be understood *synecdoche-wise*—that is, so that a part is understood from the whole [Note: A, C, and F read “synecdochically”]. Nor is it surprising if they suppose that such things were said not about the mind itself but only about the male sex, within which the female sex is also signified.

Finally, why do they not observe that these words promise the restoration of the body more than its dissolution or corruption? For while the corruptible and mortal body is destroyed, it is then recalled to incorruption and immortality; no body will return to corruption. These words, therefore, do not foreshadow a return to this earth, but rather a return to spiritual nature.

Let each person choose what he will follow [Note: CF; A reads “what”]. I, however, have offered you—who have asked and partly expounded these matters—what seemed to me more probable, drawing the occasion for my reasoning from the opinions of the holy Fathers: Ambrose and Augustine, as well as the venerable Gregory of Nazianzus, who is also called Gregory of Nyssa [Note: John Scotus confuses the two Gregories, Nazianzen and Nyssen, and considers them one and the same Father], and from the exposition of his interpreter, namely the monk Maximus.

And because the length of this volume does not now allow us to explain some of the matters that we promised at its beginning to discuss, they must be deferred to another book. For within the limits of this book we had proposed to treat at greater length the return of natures into the primordial causes and into that nature which neither creates nor is created, which is certainly God. But if you are impatient to learn about the divine nature—how it is said neither to create nor to be created—I shall give a brief preliminary account.

27. The divine nature is therefore believed not to be created because it is the primordial cause of all things, beyond which there is no principle from which it could be created. But after the return of the whole created universe, visible and invisible, into its primordial causes—which are contained in that very divine nature—no nature will thereafter be generated from it, nor will it be multiplied into sensible or intelligible species. For in it all things will be one, just as now and always [Note: A omits “and always”] they are one in their causes. Therefore it is not without reason that it is believed and understood to create nothing.

For what will it create, when it alone will be all things in all things? Therefore, if it seems good to you, let the progress of this book draw back its foot and go no farther.

DISCIPLE. It plainly seems good, and it has long been asking for an end.

Here ends the fourth book [Note: A reads “Here ends the fourth book”; C omits *On the Division of Nature*; F reads “It ends happily”], *On the Division of Nature* (*ΠΕΡΙ ΦΥΣΕΩΝ ΜΕΡΙΣΜΟΥ*).

# THE FIFTH BOOK BEGINS [Note: C omits “The fifth book begins”; F reads “The fifth book begins, *On Nature*”].

[Col. 0859]

1. TEACHER. “Now therefore, lest he perhaps stretch out his hand and also take from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever.” Before we consider the prophetic force of these words, by which the return of human nature to the same happiness that it lost through sin is most clearly promised, the order of the whole passage must first be set forth. Anyone who looks carefully will find that the great prophet Moses [Note: CF reads *Moysea*] spoke in hyperbaton—that is, with the order of the words displaced.

The order of the words is therefore as follows:

“The Lord God also made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them, and said: ‘Behold, Adam has become like one of us.’ And the Lord God sent him out from paradise to work the earth from which he had been taken. ‘Now therefore, lest he perhaps stretch out his hand and also take from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever.’ And he cast Adam out and placed before the paradise of delight the cherubim and the flaming, turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.”

What is written—“Now therefore, lest he perhaps stretch out his hand,” and the rest, “and live forever” [Note: CF reads “and the rest up to ‘live forever’”; A has “etc.”]—could be ambiguous as to whose words they are, whether those of the theologian prophesying or of the Lord speaking, if the distinction were not made clearly in the Septuagint version, where it is written: “And now, God said, lest he at some time stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life.”

Yet, as I think, no one who clearly attends to the force of the words will doubt that, however they are arranged, these words promise the return of human nature to its former state. For those do not seem to examine the matter carefully who suppose that the particle *lest* here has the force of negation, rather than of a question and something like doubt, and that man was therefore expelled from paradise lest he be able to take from the tree of life and live forever.

For by what possibility could human nature, after sin, take from the tree of life, eat [Note: CF; A reads “and”], and live forever, while it had not yet been freed from sin and death, which is the punishment of sin—when even before sin, as a careful inquiry into divine Scripture suggests, he himself [Note: CF; A reads “herself”] had neither taken nor eaten from that tree [Note: CF; A reads “had neither presumed upon nor eaten”]?

For if he had taken and eaten, he would certainly neither have sinned nor fallen, but would have lived happily forever [Note: CF; A reads “would neither have sinned nor fallen, but would have lived”].

Furthermore, if that paradise from which man was expelled was a local and earthly place, and if the tree of life planted in its midst was earthly and sensible, producing fruit suited to bodily use, why did God not expel man from the tree of life alone and confine him in some other part of paradise [Note: A “in a part of paradise”], so that he could not reach that tree?

For if there were no other cause of living happily and eternally in paradise than eating from the tree of life—which was granted only to rational creatures—why could man, miserable and mortal after sin, not remain temporarily in some part of paradise?

For if the other animals, and especially that serpent through which the ancient enemy exercised his malice, are believed to have been in paradise but nevertheless unable to live there eternally and happily [Note: CF; A reads “spiritually”] because they were not created to eat from the tree of life, why should sinful man also not be allowed to live among them [Note: A “why not also”], since true reason teaches that a rational creature, even if sinful, surpasses every irrational creature free from sin by the dignity of its nature?

If, then, irrational animals remained in paradise after man was expelled [Note: CF; A reads “remained”], although he is superior to the others, why was he, even as a sinner, not likewise permitted to remain among them in paradise?

Or perhaps the other animals were expelled from paradise together with him? But [Note: CF; A omits “but”] if anyone says this, let him seek in divine Scripture, or in the authority of the holy Fathers, or in both, where he can prove that the expulsion of the animals to which man gave names in paradise before his sin took place together with sinful man’s expulsion from paradise [Note: C reads *fuisse*; A *expulsa fuisse*; F *fuisse expulsa*].

If he cannot establish this [Note: CF; A reads “if man cannot establish this”], let him cease to think carnally about paradise and its animals, and approach readily the spiritual meanings taught by the truth; for by this one and only path the innermost places of the mystical writings are entered.

Come, then, and contemplate more carefully the force of the divine words.

DISCIPLE. I am present and ready to learn what you will say. They are indeed very necessary matters and, as I think, have been treated by few. For concerning the return of human nature and of the other things that are in it and because of it into the eternal principles from which it proceeded, and concerning its restoration to its former dignity, I have neither read nor heard that anyone has yet written, although the form of such a teaching often appears, scattered through the divine books and the teachings of the holy Fathers.

[Col. 0862B] **2. TEACHER.** The divine voice therefore intimates such a return as is under discussion in these words, saying: “Now therefore”—or, as another translation expresses it more clearly, “and now,” says God [Note: [Col. 0861] A reads “the Lord”]. It is as though divine clemency and infinite goodness, ever most ready to pardon and show mercy, sighing over the fall of the divine image and mercifully condescending, while patiently bearing with human arrogance, were saying:

“Now therefore”—that is, I see the man already expelled from paradise, made wretched from blessed, needy from well supplied, temporal from eternal, mortal from living, foolish from wise, animal from spiritual, earthly from heavenly, aged from new, sorrowful from joyful, lost from safe, a prodigal son from a prudent one, wandering from the flock of heavenly virtues [Note: [Col. 0861] A omits “heavenly”], and I grieve with him. For he was not made for this. [Col. 0862C] He was created for the possession of eternal life and blessedness [Note: [Col. 0861] C and F omit “was”]—he whom you, his neighbors and friends, now see expelled from paradise into the region of death and misery [Note: [Col. 0861] A reads “and misery”].
