Thus he addresses the heavenly orders, who, cleaving to their Creator, have remained in perpetual blessedness, although their number was diminished by the destruction of man.

Do you see how much divine pathos is contained in this brief expression, composed of one temporal adverb, *now*, and one causal conjunction, *therefore*?

But as though, after lamenting the human being, the same divine clemency had turned to console itself and the heavenly powers, it promises the man’s return to paradise in a form of doubtful and interrogative speech. For it says: “Lest perhaps he put forth his hand, and take from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever.”

It is as though it were saying:

“We must not grieve so greatly over the man’s destruction or lament his fall from paradise; for the hope of returning has not been wholly taken away from him. Perhaps he may put forth his hand”—that is, extend his devotion to good action in the virtues—so that he may take from the fruits of the tree of life, that is, from the spiritual gifts of the Word of God, and eat the food of pure contemplation, by whose power he will live forever, never again returning to the poverty of temporal things, which will wholly perish with the world, but passing entirely into God [Note: [Col. 0863] C and F read “the Lord”] and becoming one in him.”

This is clearly understood from the words of Scripture that follow. For it says: “And he cast out Adam, and placed before the paradise of delight the Cherubim, and a flaming and turning sword, to guard the way of the tree of life.”

I do not think that you have forgotten how, in the fourth book, following the opinions of the holy Fathers learned in both languages who treated of paradise, we reduced the matter, as it seemed to us, to a clear conclusion: that paradise from which man was expelled is nothing other than human nature itself, created in the image of God, from whose dignity—that is, from the dignity of the image—this same nature fell by despising the divine command.

Accordingly, it follows that man’s being sent out or expelled is nothing other than the loss of the natural happiness for whose possession he was made. For man did not lose his nature, which, because it was made in the image and likeness of God [Note: [Col. 0863] A reads “made in the image of God and in his likeness”], is necessarily incorruptible. Rather, he lost the happiness which he would have attained had he not disdained to obey God.

**STUDENT.** I have not merely failed to remember it [Note: [Col. 0863] CF read “I have not handed it over to oblivion” in reversed word order], but have firmly fixed it in my memory.

**TEACHER.** What, then, does it mean when Scripture says: “And he placed before the paradise of delight” [Note: [Col. 0863] A reads “of human delight”—“the Cherubim”? What does it wish to signify by this name? Does it mean that heavenly power which is placed third in the first hierarchy of the angelic orders [Note: [Col. 0863] A reads “second”]? In it, according to the divine tradition, are counted the Seraphim, Cherubim [Note: [Col. 0863] A reads “Cherubim, Seraphim”], and Thrones. Or does it mean only the intellectual meaning of the name? Or does it wish by this name to suggest something else through a deeper understanding?

Accordingly, the interpretation of this name must first be made clear. *Cherubim* is interpreted as “multitude of knowledge” or “outpouring of wisdom,” as Saint Dionysius the Areopagite writes in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. Epiphanius also agrees with him in his book *On Hebrew Names*: he says that *Cherubim* is interpreted as “full knowledge” or “knowledge of many things.”

But if Scripture wished a heavenly essence to be signified in this passage, we would necessarily be compelled to admit that paradise is a spiritual nature. For reason does not allow us to believe that a spiritual nature, close to God and always moved around him, could be placed before a local and earthly paradise [Note: [Col. 0863] A reads “an earthly and local paradise”], unless perhaps we say that it was not the Cherubim themselves but one of the lowest orders of the heavenly powers—the order called almost angelic—that was placed before paradise, and that it was therefore called “Cherubim,” because it was commanded by Cherubim to be placed before paradise.

For whatever is accomplished in the nature of things by the lower heavenly orders is referred to the higher orders, since the lower do nothing except what they are commanded by the higher to do [Note: [Col. 0863] A reads “because” rather than “since”].

By the same reasoning, Scripture says that a Seraph purified the prophet Isaiah, although, as Saint Dionysius the Areopagite explains, it was not the Seraphim itself that purified the prophet by itself, but one of the angels of the lowest order of the heavenly essences. This angel deserved to be called by the designation “Seraphim” because, just as the Seraphim had commanded him, he purified the prophet [Note: [Col. 0863] CF read “because,” while A reads “which”], and the purification itself is referred not to the purifier but to the one who ordered the prophet to be purified.

What if someone should say this? Would not the same difficulty remain? For it is not plausible that an angelic substance, even if it is the lowest among the heavenly powers, could be placed in some earthly location.

But if we understand in this passage only the meaning of the name, and no heavenly substance, we can say that God placed before the paradise of delight—that is, before the sight of rational human nature, although expelled from paradise, that is, removed from the dignity of its first condition—the Cherubim, namely, a multitude of knowledge or an outpouring of wisdom. Through this, human nature might recognize itself and might wish and be able to return to its former happiness, which it had abandoned by sinning, once purified through action and knowledge and exercised in the studies of wisdom.

Here it becomes clear that there was more divine mercy than vengeance in the expulsion of man from paradise. For the Creator did not wish to condemn his image altogether [Note: [Col. 0863] A reads “did not wish his image altogether”]; rather, he wished to renew it, exercise it through a multitude of knowledge, and likewise water and illuminate it through an outpouring of wisdom, making it worthy to approach again and enjoy the tree of life from which it had been removed, so that it might not perish but live forever.

But if someone wishes to look more deeply, he will understand, not inappropriately, that the Word of God himself is signified by the name “Cherubim.” For the Word of God, in whom the treasures of knowledge and wisdom are hidden, is always and without interruption present to the sight of human nature; he admonishes, purifies, and illuminates it until he restores it to its undefiled perfection.

And what is surprising if the Wisdom of God is signified by the name “Cherubim,” when he is also called “the Angel of great counsel” and “Power”? Hear the Apostle speaking of God the Father: “For his invisible things, from the creation [Note: [Col. 0863] CF read “creature”] of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made; likewise, his eternal power and divinity”—and, to put it briefly, when in the divine Scriptures it is customary, through a marvelous metaphor [Note: [Col. 0863] A reads “changeable metaphor”], to intimate him by the names of all the heavenly essences?

We may likewise understand, not inappropriately, that the flaming sword signifies the Word of God himself. For it burns and divides. It burns our sins, since God is a consuming fire, purifying the irrational stains of our nature; and it divides and distinguishes that nature from the things that, through the desert of transgression, came upon it [Note: [Col. 0863] A reads “and” rather than “and distinguishes”], disfiguring and deforming it and making it unlike its Creator.

This sword—namely, the Word of the Father, the only-begotten Son, Power and Wisdom—is rightly believed and understood to be turning, because, although it is immutable in nature [Note: [Col. 0865] CF read “although it is” rather than “although it is in nature”], it is nevertheless moved by its ineffable clemency and mercy toward the salvation of human nature [Note: [Col. 0863] CF read “because,” while A reads “which”].

Thus the Cherubim and the flaming, turning sword are always placed before the eyes of our soul—that is, of our reason and intellect.

Why? “To guard the way of the tree of life”: that is, so that we do not consign the way of the tree of life to oblivion, but continually keep before the eyes of our heart the memory of that tree and of the way by which one goes to it.

And do not be surprised that I have spoken of *Cherubim* in the singular, since blessed Jerome pronounced such names ending in *-im* among the Hebrews as plural in number and masculine in gender. I have followed Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, who likewise names *Seraphim* and *Cherubim* in the singular [Note: [Col. 0865] A omits “likewise”], especially since among both Hebrews and Greeks it is customary to use singular and plural forms for one another.

But what is that way which leads to the tree of life? And what is that tree to which it leads [Note: [Col. 0865] A reads “to which one is led”]? Is it not the very Son of God who speaks of himself: “I am the way, and [Note: [Col. 0865] A omits “and”] the truth, and the life”?

That he himself is the tree of life is found most clearly in many passages of divine Scripture [Note: [Col. 0865] CF read “is compared”], so that it requires no testimony.

Thus, in this passage of Holy Scripture, the symbolic names of the Word of God have been multiplied and heightened. For he is called the Cherubim, the flaming turning sword, the way, and the tree of life, so that we may understand that the Word himself never withdraws from the sight of our heart [Note: [Col. 0865] CF read “from the sight of our heart,” while A reverses the order], that he is always most present to illuminate us, and that he never permits us to lose the memory of the blessedness that we lost through transgression [Note: [Col. 0865] A omits the second “never”]. He wishes us always to return to that blessedness and, until this happens, sighs in compassion for us, urging us to pursue the path that leads there through the perfected stages of knowledge and action [Note: [Col. 0865] A reads “pursuing” rather than “urging us to pursue”].

“I have come,” he says, “to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire, except that it be kindled?” But before we discuss the return of our nature itself, I think that, if you agree, we should take up certain highly convincing arguments from sensible things, by which we are taught to believe without hesitation that this return will indeed occur.

[Col. 0865D] **3. STUDENT.** I entirely agree. From the natural arguments provided by sensible things, the progress of true reasoning can arrive at the pure knowledge of spiritual realities.

**TEACHER.** Consider, then, whether these local and temporal recurrences of the parts of this visible world are filled with some mystery or not.

**STUDENT.** I would not readily say that they are without mystery. For, as I think, there is nothing among visible and bodily things that does not signify something incorporeal and intelligible. But I would like you briefly to recall some of the recurrences from which you intend to draw your arguments.

**TEACHER.** It has been made clearer than daylight, I think, to all who consider the nature of things both through the conception of the mind and through the judgment of bodily sense, that the heavenly and star-bearing sphere, always revolving, returns to the same position of places within the space of twenty-four hours; that the sun likewise reaches the same point of the equinoctial diameter, after the completion of a four-year cycle, at the same moment of time—I mean, at its rising; and that the moon returns to the same place of the zodiac in which it was kindled, after an interval of somewhat more than twenty-seven days and eight hours.

As for the return of the other planets, since it is very well known to all skilled in astrology, it will seem superfluous to speak of it [Note: [Col. 0865] A reads “it is superfluous to say so”]. It is enough to have set forth the natural laws and revolutions of the two greatest luminaries of the world to persuade us of what we are attempting to assert [Note: [Col. 0865] A reads “the natural revolutions”].

For the moon is brought back to the beginnings of its course after nineteen years [Note: [Col. 0865] A reads “the nineteenth year”; C and F read “the ninth and tenth”], while the sun is brought back after the completion of twenty-eight years [Note: [Col. 0865] A reads “the eighteenth”; C and F read “twenty-eight”]. These two numbers, multiplied by one another, grow into 532 years. After these have elapsed, the two aforesaid luminaries are said to return to the same places of the zodiac and the same times, to the numbers and positions of the Great Year, and to the entire harmony of their course, completing the whole reckoning of the paschal cycle [Note: [Col. 0865] A reads “the two aforesaid” rather than “the aforesaid two”].

What of the air? Does it not return at appointed times to the same qualities of cold, heat, or moderation?

What shall I say of the Ocean? Does it not follow the lunar course in every respect and observe the fixed intervals of its recurrence [Note: [Col. 0865] A reverses “of its recurrence”]? Whether it produces daily tides, ebbs, morning tides, or evening tides [Note: [Col. 0865] C and F read “morning or evening tides?”], it never fails to display the various and regular recurrences of nature.

What of the Nereids [Note: [Col. 0865] C and F read “Nereids”; A reads “of the air”], and of earthly animals, shoots, grasses [Note: [Col. 0865] C and F read “earthly”; A reads “terrestrial”]? Do they not likewise observe their appointed seasons, in which they burst forth into offspring, flowers, leaves, and fruits [Note: [Col. 0865] C and F read “burst forth”; A reads the present tense “burst forth”]?

In short, it must be said that there is no bodily creature, quickened by vital motion, that does not return to the beginning of its motion. For the end of every motion is its beginning [Note: [Col. 0865] A omits “of every”]: it does not terminate in any other end than its own beginning, from which it begins to move and to which it always desires to return, so that in it it may come to an end and rest.

This must be understood not only of the parts of the sensible world, but also of the whole world itself. For its end is its own beginning, which it desires; and when it has found it, it will cease—not so that its substance may perish, but so that it may return to the principles from which it proceeded [Note: [Col. 0865] A reads “may return” as “may cause to return”].

“For the form of this world,” says the Apostle, “passes away.”

Saint Father Augustine briefly explained this apostolic statement, saying:

“Form, therefore, not nature”—changing, as I think, *nature* into *essence*, in accordance with the very frequent usage of Greek and Latin expression. For the Greeks very often exchange *physis* (φύσις) for *ousia* (οὐσία), and *ousia* for *physis*.

The proper meaning of these terms is as follows. *Ousia*, that is, essence, is predicated of that which in every creature, whether visible or intelligible, can neither be corrupted, increased, nor diminished. *Physis*, that is, nature, refers to the generation of essence through places and times in some matter that can be corrupted, increased, and diminished and affected by various accidents.

For *ousia* is derived from the verb *eimi* (εἰμί), which means “I am”; its masculine participle is *ōn* (ὥν), its feminine *ousa* (οὖσα), and from these comes *ousia* (οὐσία) [Note: [Col. 0867] CF read “from which comes,” while A reads “from where”]. *Physis*, however, comes from the verb *phyomai* (φύομαι), that is, “I am born,” “I am planted,” or “I am generated” [Note: [Col. 0867] A reads “which” rather than “that is”].

Thus every creature, insofar as it subsists in its principles, is *ousia*; but insofar as it is produced in some matter, it is *physis* [Note: [Col. 0867] A reads “is *physis*”].

Nevertheless, as we have said, just as among the Greeks *ousia* is used for *physis* and *physis* for *ousia*, so among the Latins *essence* is used for *nature* and *nature* for *essence* without distinction, while the proper meaning of each term remains intact.

True reasoning confidently establishes that the essence of sensible things—which the aforementioned Father indicated by the term “nature” [Note: [Col. 0867] CF read “of sensible things,” while A reverses the order]—will endure forever [Note: [Col. 0867] A omits “true”], because it was made in the divine wisdom immutably [Note: [Col. 0867] A reads “immutable”], beyond all places and times and every mutability.

But no one instructed in the studies of wisdom can doubt that nature, generated through places and times and surrounded by other accidents, will perish at an interval predetermined by the Creator of all.

Through these and similar motions and recurrences of the sensible world, considered both universally and particularly, and through its most certain restorations to the beginning of its motions [Note: [Col. 0867] A reads “and recurrences”], what else is mystically intimated to us than the return of our nature to its own beginning, from which it was made, in which and through which it moves, and to which it always tends to return [Note: [Col. 0867] A reads “always tends to return” in reversed order]?

For while the motion of things begins from it, it is called the beginning; but when the motion ends in it, it is usually called the end. Indeed, among the Greeks the beginning is called *telos* (τέλος), that is, “end,” since they indiscriminately call both beginning and end *telos*.

In all human beings generally—whether they are perfect or imperfect, pure or defiled, knowing the truth and renewed in Christ or held in the darkness of ignorance in the old man—there is one and the same natural desire: to exist, to exist well, to exist perpetually, and, as Saint Augustine briefly summarized it, to live blessedly and flee misery.

For this movement toward living and subsisting happily comes from him who always exists and exists well [Note: [Col. 0867] A omits “exists”; F omits the second “and”] and is present in all things.

And if every natural motion necessarily does not cease or rest until it reaches the end that it seeks, what can prevent, restrain, or halt the necessary motion of human nature, so that it cannot reach what it naturally desires?

For there is no creature that wishes or desires to be nothing [Note: [Col. 0867] C and F read “that wishes or desires”; A has a slightly different construction]. Rather, it flees from nonbeing, especially since it is difficult for everything that was made by him who truly is and is beyond being [Note: [Col. 0867] A omits “is”] to return to nothing [Note: [Col. 0867] A omits “is”].

But if, for some reason, a nature like God’s has been removed from its beginning through dissimilarity, it always strives to return to its beginning [Note: [Col. 0867] A reverses the order], so that it may recover the likeness which it had corrupted.

For if this visible fire, burning in some matter and raising the locks of its flames, always strives upward and by no movement of its burning seeks the depths, how could it be believed that that intelligible fire of a substance created in the image of God [Note: [Col. 0867] A reads “that intelligible fire” as “that intelligible substance”] could always be held in the depths of death and misery [Note: [Col. 0867] A reads “and” rather than “and misery”], so that it could not be raised toward the heights of life and blessedness by its natural desire and by the grace of its Creator, which assists it toward life [Note: [Col. 0867] A reads “assisted”]?

We say this not because nature will be equally blessed in all, but because in all it will be free from death and misery. To exist, to live, and to exist eternally will be common to the good and the wicked alike; but to exist well and blessedly will belong exclusively and particularly to those perfected in action and knowledge.

Or how could it plausibly be maintained that the most pious Creator of rational nature would prohibit the rational motion of that nature from reaching its goal?

It is not only examples from sensible things that draw us toward considering, believing, and understanding that all things return, by a natural law, to the beginning of their motion and to their principal causes. The things considered solely by the mind do so as well. Such are the disciplines that philosophers call liberal [Note: [Col. 0867] A reads “which philosophers call liberal disciplines”]. I think it necessary to introduce a few of these in support of what we wish to persuade you, if you do not find it tedious or superfluous.

[Col. 0868C] **4. STUDENT.** I find it neither tedious nor superfluous, but highly useful and appropriate, that just as certain examples of nature’s return have been drawn from the motions of sensible things, so examples from the contemplation of intelligible things—perceived solely by the conception of the mind—should also be introduced to persuade us of the same return. This is especially so because arguments gathered from the unshaken rules of the true arts are more powerful for producing belief in a doubtful matter than those assembled from conjectures based on bodily senses, although even the latter cannot be discovered or approved without the guidance of reason and intellect.

For it is impossible to discover the true knowledge of sensible things through bodily sense alone.

**TEACHER.** What do you think? Does not that art which the Greeks call *Dialectic* and define as the science of arguing well first concern itself with *ousia* (οὐσία), as with its proper beginning [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “its beginning”]? From this beginning all the division and multiplication of the matters about which the art itself argues proceed: descending through the most general genera and intermediate genera to the most particular forms and species; and then, by the rules of recombination, ascending again through the same stages by which it descended, until it reaches *ousia* itself, from which it emerged. It does not cease to return to that in which it always desires to rest and around which it revolves, either solely or chiefly, in intelligible motion.

What should be said of Arithmetic? Does it not likewise begin from the monad, depart through the various species of numbers, and then, once resolution has taken place, return to the same monad, beyond which it does not know how to ascend [Note: [Col. 0869] A omits “through”]?

And rightly so, since all numbers and species of numbers begin from it, end in it, and subsist in its force and power [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “all number” in the singular], just as all genera and species of things are contained and preserved in *ousia*.

The same must be thought of Geometry. It begins in the same manner from its beginning, which the Greeks call *sēmeion* (σημεῖον) and the Latins call *signum*, “sign”; then, by composing plane and solid figures, surfaces, sides, and also angles, it completes the dimensions of length, breadth, and depth [Note: [Col. 0869] A omits “and” before “breadth”]. Once all these have been resolved, it returns to its proper beginning, which is the sign, in which the entire power of the art consists.

What of Music? Does it not likewise begin from its beginning [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “from its own”], which they call the tone, and move around harmonies, whether simple or composite? Resolving these again, does it not repeat its tone—that is, its beginning—because in it the whole force and power of the art itself subsists [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “its whole force and power”]?

Who is unaware that Astrology [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “Who is unaware of Astrology?”], whose greatest power is to consider the motions of the stars through places and times, begins its course from the atom and, once the intervals of time have been resolved, ends its return in that same atom?

Do you see, then, how the aforesaid conceptions of the rational mind repeat their beginnings [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “of the rational soul”], in which they establish the end of their motion? For, in all these cases, as was said above, beginning and end are the same.

**STUDENT.** I see it clearly. This mode of argument, drawn from intelligible things, contributes greatly, as I think, to making credible the matter with which we are now concerned [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “the matter now under discussion”]. The matter under discussion, however, is nature’s return. Nevertheless, since you have drawn the foregoing arguments from the liberal disciplines, I do not sufficiently understand why you passed over Grammar and Rhetoric.

**TEACHER.** Understand that they were passed over for more than one reason. First, because many philosophers not inappropriately regard these two arts as members of Dialectic. Second, because of the need for brevity. Finally, because they do not appear to treat of the nature of things, but either of the rules of human speech, which Aristotle and his followers affirm to subsist not according to nature but according to the custom of speakers, or of particular causes and persons, which is far removed from the nature of things.

For when Rhetoric attempts to treat of commonplaces that pertain to the nature of things, it takes up not its own parts but those of Dialectic.

I say this not because Grammar and Rhetoric were altogether without beginnings of their own [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “Grammar and Rhetoric were altogether without their own beginnings”]. One begins from the letter, the other from the hypothesis—that is, from a determinate question—and they are resolved into those same beginnings: the science of writing well into the letter, and the skill of speaking well into the hypothesis [Note: [Col. 0869] CF read “it begins,” singular]. Rather, arguments drawn from the nature of things possess greater force for approving or denying questions arising from investigations of uncertain matters [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “or for proving”] than arguments devised from human inventions.

For the arts of writing well and speaking well were both created and discovered through human arguments.

**STUDENT.** Why, then, are they counted among the liberal disciplines, if they are not according to nature but according to human contrivances?

**TEACHER.** I see no other reason than that they always adhere to the mother of the arts, which is Dialectic [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “they adhere”]. For they are like certain arms of Dialectic, or streams flowing from it, or at least instruments by which it makes its intelligible discoveries known for human use.

**STUDENT.** I would not altogether contradict this answer. For it is very plausible [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “for it is plausible”]. A rational soul can discuss the liberal disciplines within itself, without the noise of articulated and eloquent speech. But what follows and concerns the present undertaking must be considered.

**TEACHER.** What is that? [Note: [Col. 0869] C reads “What is this?”; A and F read “What is that?”]

[Col. 0870C] **5. STUDENT.** What else but that you should establish by authority that the beginning and the end of natural motions are the same and differ in no respect?

**TEACHER.** If this is what you seek, listen to blessed Maximus speaking in the nineteenth chapter of *Ambigua*:

“Everything that moves according to nature moves entirely through a cause; and everything that moves through a cause both exists entirely through that cause and moves through it. Everything that exists through a cause has as the beginning of its existence the very cause through which it is and from which its coming into being began; and it has as the end of its motion the same cause through which it moves and toward which it is brought.

Everything that both exists and moves through a cause is also altogether generated. But if the end of what is moved is the very cause through which it moves, that cause is entirely the same as the cause through which it was made and exists [Note: [Col. 0869] A reads “the cause exists for it”]. There is therefore one cause of everything that in any manner exists and moves according to nature, as both beginning and end—the cause through which everything that exists and moves both exists and moves.

For the active power subsisting in itself divinely makes the things that are made, as their beginning, and sends forth and draws the things that are moved, as their end, and brings them to completion.

But if everything that moves both exists and has been made through a cause—if it exists, moves, and has been made through a cause—then whatever does not exist through a cause has neither been made nor, certainly, is movable. For that which does not possess the cause of being in all things and in every respect does not move. But if whatever lacks a cause is altogether immovable, then the divine is immovable; for it has no cause of being and subsists as the cause of all things that are.”

Observe how clearly he argues that the cause and the end of all things are the same.

**STUDENT.** I observe it. But I do not understand how it pertains to the question at hand. For you do not seem to be discussing God, who is the beginning and end of all things—since all things are from him, through him, in him, and toward him—but the temporal beginnings of sensible things, whether through the motion of generation or through local motion, and the contemplative beginnings of intelligible things that we perceive with the mind.

Accordingly, it is not yet clear to me where these examples concerning God that you have given are leading.

### 6. MASTER

I am astonished that you are so slow to understand that you do not clearly perceive where such arguments are tending. Do not all the arguments that we have introduced from the nature of sensible and intelligible things point to this: just as each thing is naturally compelled to return to its own principle, whether sensible or intelligible, so we should confidently believe—and, strengthened by the most certain reasoning from things, understand—that human nature too will return to its principle, which is none other than the Word of God, in whom it was made, subsists immutably, and lives? [Col. 0871C]

For if God is the principle of all things that are and of all things that are not—I mean those that fall under bodily sensation and the mind’s contemplation, as well as those that escape bodily sensation and the mind’s apprehension because of the excessive subtlety and loftiness of their substance—and if all things seek him, with nothing preventing their desire from reaching him, what is astonishing if, concerning human nature, which was specially made in the image and likeness of the one common principle of all things, we both believe and understand that it will return there from which it proceeded? This is especially so since it did not proceed from him in such a way that it wholly abandoned its own principle. [Col. 0871D] For, as the Apostle says, “in him we live and move and have our being.” But because it has been discolored by a certain dissimilarity on account of sin, it is said to have withdrawn.

Likeness made it near; dissimilarity made it distant. It is not by bodily steps that one is distanced from God or approaches him, but by the affections of the mind. One does not withdraw from sunlight by spatial intervals, but by the loss or closing of the eyes, or by the setting of the light itself. [Note: A: “from the sunlight.”] Health is not abandoned through place, but through illness. Likewise, life, blessedness, wisdom, and all the virtues are abandoned only through their privations—namely, death, misery, folly, and vices. And just as the skin of the human body is struck by the disfigurement and contagion of leprosy, so human nature was infected and corrupted by proud disobedience, made disfigured and unlike its Creator.

When it has been freed from this leprosy by the medicine of divine grace, it will be restored to its former beauty. More accurately, the nature itself that was made in the image of God has in no way lost, nor can it lose, the vigor of its beauty or the integrity of its essence. For the divine form always remains immutable, although it has become liable to the punishments of corruptible sin. [Col. 0872B]

We can confirm this from the words of blessed Gregory of Nyssa. In the twenty-seventh chapter of *On the Image*, treating of the resurrection, he says:

“It is not incredible that, from the communion of the four general elements of the world, a dissolution—that is, a return—of the bodies of those who rise should occur into the proper state of nature, from the hidden and incorruptible body that will rise.” [Note: In CF, the words “from the hidden … body that will rise” are omitted.]

“For not everything that is ours is wholly subject to flux and change. If it were, what has no state from nature would universally become reprehensible. But, according to the subtler account of the things that are in us, some stand firm, while others arise from mutability. The body is changed through increase and decrease, like garments put on in succession as the ages advance. [Col. 0872C] But throughout every transformation the form itself remains unaltered, never abandoning the signs implanted in it once for all by nature; rather, in all bodily transformations it appears together with its innate marks. The change that arises from suffering and supervenes upon the form, however, will be removed by the Word of God. For just as a certain alien face—the disfigurement itself arising from weakness—covered the form, so, when that disfigurement has been taken away by the Word of God, as in the case of Naaman the Syrian or those lepers mentioned in the Gospel, the hidden appearance beneath the affliction will once again shine forth in its proper features through healing.

“Thus, in the soul’s likeness to God, that which is unstable and changeable through mutability does not remain; rather, what endures is implanted in our composition as well.” [Col. 0872D]

Observe how clearly and openly the aforesaid Nyssa asserts that not only was the form of the soul made in the image of God, but also that the natural form of the body, which imitates the image of the soul, remains forever incorruptible and immutable. Whatever has been added to the natural body from the conglomeration of the elements, and to the soul from the filth of irrational movements, is always subject to flux and corruption. And this, as he himself says, is beautifully suggested under the figure of Naaman the Syrian and the ten whom the Gospel says were cleansed by the Lord. That Syrian, and those ten, had not lost the human form; they had merely been struck and covered by the swelling and deformity of leprosy. By this we are to understand that our nature has not been destroyed or changed, but discolored by the deformity of vices.

And see how unequivocally that Syrian himself bore the figure of human nature. For *Naaman* is interpreted as “beautiful,” while *Syria* signifies “the contemplation of heavenly things.” Would human nature have become such if it had not grown proud? It was made beautiful and for the contemplation of heavenly things, but because of transgression it was struck with leprosy. [Note: CF omit “because of transgression.”]

When Naaman went down into Judaea and then returned again to Syria, at the command of the prophet Elisha he laid aside his leprosy in the river Jordan, and the skin of his body was renewed. Will our nature likewise, when it recognizes its sickness and the deformity of its vices, descend into confession of its misery and, returning to itself, be cleansed? And who will cleanse it? Elisha—that is, the Savior of God, or the salvation of God.

Is not our Elisha the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the Savior of God and the salvation of God? In returning to our Syria he will save our nature—that is, when he commands us to return to its former state, namely, to the contemplation of intelligible virtues.

And where will he cleanse it? In the Jordan. Its interpretation is “the descent of the Lord,” or “the descent of judgment,” or “power,” or “the furthest land,” or “the ascent of those who rise.” [Col. 0873C]

And when do we believe and hope for the salvation and return of our nature to Syria, the contemplation of heavenly things, if not when the Lord descends in his glory, descends for the judgment of the living and the dead, to manifest his power in the furthest land—that is, at the end of the world—when heaven and earth will pass away in their ascent, that is, in the exaltation of the saints to eternal blessedness, or certainly in the common resurrection of all? For the common resurrection is the ascent of all from death into life, from an animal and corruptible body into a spiritual and incorruptible one.

But the whole leprosy and corruption of human nature will be intensified and transferred to Gehazi. *Gehazi* is interpreted as “seeing a valley,” or “a separation from vision,” typologically signifying the devil. Although he is the wicked servant of our Savior and is not permitted to carry out the schemes of his malice without his commands or permissions, he never ceases to look into the depth of perdition and eternal death, and, divided from the contemplation of truth through the merit of his pride, to depart from it. [Col. 0873D]

Thus our leprosy, which through the envy of that one had contaminated the image of God, will be brought back upon him; for, overwhelmed with grief at our salvation and restoration, he will have his punishment increased.

What shall I say about the ten lepers? Did they too bear the character of that same nature of ours, which has been redeemed by its Redeemer, is redeemed daily in individuals, and at the consummation of the world will be both redeemed and liberated universally in all?

Human nature is customarily signified by the number ten. For there is no doubt that the human being consists of soul and body. The body possesses the number five: namely, the four bodily elements and the form that composes and gives form to those elements. The soul likewise corresponds to the number five. It subsists in intellect, reason, the two senses—interior and exterior—and the vital movement by which the body is governed. [Col. 0874A]

You therefore have, as I suppose, the tenfold constitution of the human being. Through the grace of its Creator and Redeemer, it will be freed from all the misery added to it, as from a certain leprosy, and will be reduced to unity, so that not a tenfold constitution will remain, but only the intellect, united by the pure contemplation of simple truth. I believe this to be signified by that one leper who alone returned to the Lord, giving glory to God for his cleansing and, like a foreigner returning from the distance of dissimilarity, clinging to his liberator and purifier. The other nine, however, were no longer found.

For the whole of human nature will be poured back into the intellect alone, so that nothing will remain in it except that intellect by which it will contemplate its Creator.

### 7

Before we discuss the purification of human nature and its union with itself and with its Creator, in whose image it was made, I think it appropriate to say something about that return itself. Unless one first explains where nature fell, from where its return begins, through what stages it ascends, what it seeks, and in what it ends, one will not easily persuade anyone of what one asserts.

**DISCIPLE.** Nothing could be truer, I think. For who could easily persuade anyone of nature’s return if he had not first established, by certain arguments of reason, where it fell, and where and how it will return? [Note: CF: “by arguments of reason and …”]

**MASTER.** Where it fell and where it arrived is unknown to none of the faithful, since the Psalmist says: “When man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them.”

Thus it abandoned the honor of the divine image and equality with heavenly virtues, and fell into likeness with irrational animals. Nature, which was created naturally to desire and love heavenly things, is oppressed by earthly cravings and carnal desires; it is whirled about by irrational movement, although it was created to enjoy reason. [Col. 0874D]

There is no bestial movement that cannot be detected in man after he sinned; and, as sound reason teaches, what is praised in a beast is censured in man. Why? Because in a beast irrational movement subsists naturally, whereas in man it exists contrary to nature. Whatever is implanted according to nature is good; whatever is added contrary to nature, although it may be good in a bestial substance, is nevertheless unsuitable and alien to man.

Irrational movements came upon human nature from nowhere else than the substantial impulse of beasts, to which it became like through sinning. The same Gregory of Nyssa testifies to this in the eighteenth chapter of *On the Image* [Note: CF omit “in the eighteenth chapter of *On the Image*”], saying:

“I believe that from this beginning—namely, from likeness to irrational animals—the individual passions too were established in human life, as though by an inundation flowing from some spring. This account is confirmed by the kinship of the passions themselves, manifested equally in us and in irrational creatures. [Col. 0875A]

“For it is not right to attribute the principles of passible affections to human nature formed according to the divine image. For the likeness of man to God is not formed according to rage, nor is the transcendent nature shaped from pleasure itself. Fear, savagery, the desire for what is greater, hatred of what is lesser, and everything of this kind are far removed from the character of divine beauty. [Note: A: “far removed from the divine beauty.”]

“Human nature drew these things to itself from its irrational part. Whatever equips irrational life for its preservation, when transferred to human life, became passions.

“None of the wise doubts that man fell into these irrational movements, which belong naturally to bestial life but affectively to human life; and from these he fell further into bodily death and dissolution. For he could not fall any lower or higher. In the nature of things there is nothing lower than life deprived of reason and sensation; and the lowest of all is the corruptible body, since no nature is permitted to return to nothingness. At the point where the fall placed its end, there it began its return. [Col. 0875C]

“The end of the fall is the dissolution of the body. The return of nature therefore begins from the body’s dissolution. Consequently, death of the flesh has contributed more benefit to human nature than vengeance, although it has been regarded as the punishment of sin. Indeed, the dissolution of the flesh, which is commonly called death, is more reasonably called the death of death than the death of the flesh. For if human life in this corruptible flesh is rightly called death by the wise, by what reasoning would the end of that life be judged by the name of death, when it frees from death more than it inflicts death upon those who die?

“Hence blessed Maximus says in the twenty-eighth chapter of the *Ambigua*:

“‘It is unjust, I think, to call the end of this present life death. Rather, it is separation from death, release from corruption, freedom from slavery, rest from disturbance, the destruction of wars, passage from confusion, return from darkness, repose from pains, silence from ignoble display, leisure from instability, a covering for shame, refuge from passions, abolition of sin, and, to sum it up, the end of all evils. [Col. 0875D]

“‘Thus the end of the present life is the beginning of the future, the death of the flesh the dawn of nature’s restoration, and a return to its ancient wholeness.’” [Col. 0876A]

### 8

The first return of human nature, then, occurs when the body is dissolved and recalled into the four elements of the sensible world from which it was composed. The second will be fulfilled in the resurrection, when each person receives his own body again from the communion of the four elements. The third occurs when the body is changed into spirit. The fourth occurs when the spirit—or, to speak more plainly, the whole nature of the human being—returns to the primordial causes that are eternally and immutably in God. The fifth occurs when nature itself, together with its causes, is moved into God, as air is moved into light.

For God will be all in all, when nothing will exist except God alone. By this we are not attempting to assert that the substance of things will perish, but that it will return by the stages mentioned above into something better. For how can that perish which is demonstrably returning into something better?

The change of human nature into God must therefore not be judged the destruction of substance, but a wondrous and ineffable return to the former state that it lost through transgression. For if everything that understands purely becomes one with what it understands, what is astonishing if our nature, when it is to contemplate God face to face, can ascend in those who are worthy, as far as it is granted to contemplate him, into the clouds of contemplation and become one with him and in him? [Col. 0876C]

Nor do we say this in order to refute the opinion of those who say that no body can be changed into life, nor any life into body, especially since the holy Father Augustine appears to teach this. Rather, in this discussion of nature’s return we follow Gregory the Theologian and his expositor Maximus, as well as Saint Ambrose in his exposition of the Gospel according to Luke; nor do we persuade anyone to believe what seems incredible to him.

Of the stages of nature’s return mentioned above, some are those on which the tradition of the theologians universally agrees, while others are those concerning which it wholly disagrees. For no one differs from another concerning the body’s return into the elements from which it came, or concerning its return to itself at the time of the resurrection. But concerning the passage—that is, the transformation—of the body into the soul, of the soul into the causes, or of all things into God, there is very great disagreement and almost universally diverse teaching. [Col. 0876D]

Many discuss only the dissolution of the body into the elements and its return to its own proper state at the moment of the resurrection. They do not appear to ascend any further, since they place the end of their discussion in the condition of bodies after the resurrection. [Note: A: “of his angels.”] [Note: C omits “The fifth book begins”; F: “The fifth begins, *peri physeon*.”] [Col. 0877A]

Some entirely deny the transfusion of bodies into souls, of souls into causes, and of causes into God; others cautiously hesitate, to such an extent that they do not even dare to say that the humanity of Christ was converted into divinity.

Since their authority must not be passed over, we should briefly recall what they think about this. Blessed Aurelius Augustine says in the tenth book of his *Hexaemeron*:

“Let us first hold most firmly that the nature of the soul is not converted into the nature of the body, so that what was already a soul should become a body; nor into the nature of an irrational soul, so that what was the soul of a human being should become that of an animal; nor into the nature of God, so that what was a soul should become what God is. [Note: A: “so that what was a soul should become God.”] And likewise, neither a body, nor an irrational soul, nor the substance that is God is converted and made into a human soul.”

You see how he denies that the human soul—that is, the rational nature—can be converted into God, and likewise denies that the body can become soul.

Boethius likewise says in the second book of *On the Trinity*:

“The human soul has not been changed into the divinity from which it was assumed. If neither body nor soul could be turned into divinity, it was in no way possible for humanity to be converted into God. Still less can it be believed that the two were converted into each other, since incorporeality cannot pass into body, nor body conversely into incorporeality, seeing that they have no common underlying matter by which the qualities of either substance could be changed.”

Nothing else is conveyed by the words of these authors than that no corporeal nature can be changed into an incorporeal one. We do not merely refrain from criticizing their opinion; we gladly accept it. Yet we are aware that the theologians who spoke Greek thought differently.

Although in the preceding books of this discussion we have frequently introduced their statements concerning nature’s return, we now judge it necessary to repeat them. Blessed Gregory the Theologian, disputing about the resurrection in his *Funeral Oration for His Brother Caesarius*, says:

“Shortly afterward the soul will also receive again its congenial body—that is, the flesh—with which it philosophized concerning the things that are there, that is, in the future life, through the earth that was both given and believed in: plainly, the flesh, in the manner known to God who joined and dissolved it. It will share glory there with this body; and just as the body shared in the soul’s labors through their common generation, so the soul will hand over all its delights to itself—that is, to the body—to consume it within itself, and together with it to become one spirit, one mind, and God, when what is mortal and flowing has been swallowed up by life.” [Col. 0877D]

Explaining this opinion, Maximus says:

“For just as through sin the flesh was swallowed up by corruption, the soul was made earthly by the operations of the flesh, and the knowledge of God was swallowed up by the soul through complete ignorance, so that it did not even know whether God exists, so entirely at the time of the resurrection, according to the good transformation that is to come, the flesh will be swallowed up by the soul in the Spirit through the grace of the incarnate God, and the soul by God, who is truly life. For the uniquely singular Whole will plainly possess the whole soul in its entirety.

“And, to put it simply: through the transformation away from present things, around which we are now occupied and entangled, divine resurrection-grace will show in the future all the things that belong to us, so that, just as here powerful death swallowed us through sin, there it may justly be weakened and laid aside through grace.”

Observe how clearly and openly the theologians mentioned above teach the body’s return into the soul.

And lest anyone perhaps think that no author of the Latin language can be found who supported this account of the union of nature—that is, the return of lower things into higher things—it is fitting to introduce the opinion of blessed Ambrose in his exposition of Luke, at the place where he discusses the Gospel woman who hid three measures of meal until they were fermented into one.

“The Apostle,” he says, “commanded us to walk not in the flesh but in the spirit, so that, sanctified through the bath of regeneration, stripping off the old man with his desires and putting on the new man, who is created according to Christ, we might walk not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit, so that at the time of the resurrection the undivided communion of body, soul, and spirit might remain for us.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, if in this life the three measures—namely, of body, soul, and spirit—remain in the same leaven, that is, in the unity of the Church, until they are fermented and become one, so that there is no difference of equality and we do not appear to be composed from the diversity of three things, then in the future there will be incorruptible communion for those who love Christ, and we shall no longer remain composite. For although we are now composite, we shall be one, and we shall be transformed into one substance.

“For in the resurrection one thing will not be lower than another, as now the weakness of the flesh is fragile in us, and the bodily condition of our nature is exposed to wounds, subject to injuries, or weighed down by the burden of its own mass, so that it cannot rise above the earth and lift its foot higher. Rather, we shall be formed into the grace of a simple creature, when what John said has been fulfilled: ‘Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be; but we know that when it is revealed, we shall be like him.’ [Note: CF: “Beloved,” instead of A’s chapter 5 reference.]

“Therefore, since God’s nature is simple—for God is spirit—we too shall be formed into the same image, so that as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly ones. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of this heavenly one, which our mind ought to put on.” [Note: A: “because he is the one.”]

But we must not understand this most exalted teacher, Ambrose, as though he wished to advocate a confusion or transformation of substances. Rather, he most clearly taught a certain ineffable and incomprehensible union of our substances.

For nothing subsists in human nature that is not spiritual and intelligible. The substance of the body itself is also certainly intelligible. Therefore it is neither incredible nor contrary to reason that intelligible substances should be united to one another, so that they are one while each does not cease to possess its own property and subsistence—yet in such a way that lower things are contained by higher things. For true reason does not permit higher things to be contained by, drawn toward, or consumed by lower things.

Lower things, however, are naturally drawn toward and swallowed up by higher things—not so that they cease to exist, but so that they are more fully preserved in them, subsist, and are one. For air does not lose its substance when it is wholly converted into sunlight, even though nothing appears in it except light, since light is one thing and air another; nevertheless, light prevails in the air so that it alone appears to exist. [Col. 0879B]

Iron or some other metal, when melted in fire, appears to be converted into fire, so that it seems to be pure fire, while the substance of the metal remains unharmed. By the same reasoning I believe that corporeal substance will pass into soul—not so that what it is will perish, but so that it will remain safe in a better essence.

The same should be understood of the soul itself: it will move into intellect in such a way that it is preserved in intellect more beautifully and more like God.

Nor would I speak differently of the passage—not yet, indeed, of all things, but of rational substances—into God, in whom all things will place their end and will be one.

But what we have said about the union of human nature without the abolition of the properties of the individual substances can be confirmed by the opinion of blessed Maximus. Explaining the great Gregory of Nyssa in his sermon *On Hail*, where he says:

“Indeed, ineffable light will receive us, and the holy and royal contemplation of the Trinity, illuminating us more plainly and purely, will be mingled with the whole soul in its entirety; this I regard as nothing other than the kingdom of heaven.”

Maximus consequently added:

“In every rational creature, angelic and human, those who through negligence have not corrupted any of the divine principles naturally joined to their movement toward the end and implanted in them by the Creator, but have rather preserved themselves temperately, knowing that they are and will be wholly and unchangeably instruments of the divine nature: God, breathing wholly through their whole being, draws them, like a soul drawing the members of a body joined together, as beings made for the will of the best Lord, and fills them with his own glory and blessedness, giving and bestowing eternal and ineffable life.”

“This eternal life is constituted not by air that breathes into them, nor by streams of blood flowing from the liver, but by God, wholly participated by the whole of them, becoming to the soul as a soul is to the body, and through the intermediary mind to the body, in the manner known to him. Thus the soul receives immutability, the body immortality, and the whole human being is deified through the grace of the incarnate God who deifies him: the whole human being remaining wholly human according to soul and body by nature, and wholly becoming God according to soul and body by grace, possessing throughout the fitting divine brightness of blessed glory, beyond which nothing more luminous or exalted can be conceived.

“What is more lovable than *theosis*, that is, deification, through which, by this *theosis*, God, united with those who have become gods, makes them wholly his own through goodness?” [Note: *Theōseōs* means “of deification”; the second Greek term, *theōsin*, is omitted in A.]

Observe that he says: “the whole human being remaining according to soul and body by nature, and the whole human being becoming God according to soul and body by grace.” Thus the property of the natures will remain, and their union will exist; neither will property remove the union of the natures, nor will union remove the property of the natures.

**DISCIPLE.** Although what you have said appears similar to true reason, it will nevertheless seem, I think, to those less capable and to those who consider the nature of things like a kind of delirium and self-contradiction. [Col. 0880B]

For, as you say, the great Gregory of Nyssa says that the soul will consume its entire body into itself and, together with it, become one spirit, one mind, and God. Maximus also supports him, saying: “Entirely at the time of the resurrection, according to the good transformation that is to come, the flesh will be swallowed up by the soul in the spirit through the grace of the incarnate God, and the soul by God.” [Note: CF: “by God.”]

You also added the opinion of blessed Ambrose concerning the union of human nature—that is, its return into unity—so that you would not appear to follow only the authority of Greek authors, without the support of any Latin-speaking authors, or indeed of authors who also discuss the nature of things. He teaches that the three subsistences of human nature—namely, body, soul, and intellect—are like three measures of meal, not to be confused but to be united at the time of the resurrection as though by a certain leaven, through the bond of charity, so that not any composition of our nature but complete simplicity and inseparable unity may be produced.

For, as he himself says, it will not otherwise be restored to the image of God unless it is to become a simple spirit, free from every composition.

And now, following the opinions of the Fathers mentioned above concerning the union of human nature in the simplest unity, not only in itself but also in God, you have again introduced the words of Maximus, which are as follows:

“The whole human being remaining according to soul and body by nature, and the whole human being becoming God according to soul and body by grace.”

What else is conveyed by these words except that corporeal nature will always remain in itself and in no way pass into soul, or mind, or God himself, although in the blessed and incorruptible glory of the resurrection it will be united to soul, mind, and God?

I believe that he understood the nature of the soul and of the mind in the same way: they will not pass over, but each will remain in its own substance. For there is no small difference between soul and mind, since the mind moves only around divine things, whereas the soul moves around creatures.

But if matters stand thus, how will they not appear contradictory?

### 9

**MASTER.** I am very much astonished that such things trouble you, since I have persuaded you, as far as I could, that intelligible natures can be united without accumulation or composition, with their properties preserved and remaining immutable.

For there are three things that remain immutable and unchangeable in every substance—whether it is attached to bodies or wholly free from every body, provided that there is any substance besides God that lacks either an intelligible or a sensible body—as we demonstrated in many ways in the earlier books: essence, power, and natural operation.

Are these three not one, and not one composite thing, but one utterly simple thing and an inseparable unity? None of them can exist without the others, since they belong to one and the same substance; yet, when reason is consulted, they are distinguished by some difference.

For being is one thing, the capacity to produce something another, and the effect itself another. To be a tree is one thing, to be able to grow another, and to grow another. For a human being, being is one thing, being able to understand another, and understanding what one is able to understand another.

There is no doubt that these three are present in every visible and invisible creature.
