### 10 [Cols. 0881C–0883A]

Take another example of the union of natures without confusion, mixture, or composition. Are there not many substantial numbers in one species, many species in one genus, and many genera in one essence? And are they not so arranged—as true reason teaches—that in one οὐσία (*ousia*, essence), each genus possesses its own proper rational principles, distinct from, neither confused nor mixed nor composed with, the rational principles of another genus, yet united and, so to speak, constituting a certain multiple and simple unity? [Note: CF reads *quiddam*, “something.”] The same is to be understood of species in a genus and of the most specific numbers in a species. Each of these possesses both its own property and its union, with every composition excluded.

Observe another example from numbers separated from matter. Do not all numbers, whether finite or infinite—that is, whether comprehensible through the contemplations and designations of reason, or still surpassing the power of human contemplation and reasoning in this life—subsist as one in the monad? And indeed, in it there is no composition, confusion, or mixture of numbers; rather, each preserves its own individual rational principles in that power and capacity. For who among those disputing correctly would say that the binary or ternary number is composed in the monad, so that the binary subsists in it as twice the individual units and the ternary as three times the individual units? If this were so, it would not be a monad, but an accumulation of many diversities and parts, a heap of discrepant numbers.

The monad, however, is that in which one fountain flows forth through the marvelous union of all numbers. In it, the binary and the ternary are one, while preserving their proper rational principles, insofar as they agree with one another. [Note: CF omits “one fountain … agree.”] They subsist without any bodily mass, without any fantasy or phantasm of human thoughts, and without any coupling of fantasy and phantasm; they subsist by simple and intelligible understanding alone. From this they proceed in actuality and operation into corporeal or incorporeal things—that is, through a natural or artificial operation, or through arithmetic. [Note: CF omits “that is, through a natural or artificial operation.”] The same is to be understood, by the same reasoning, of all numbers proceeding from the monad and resolved into it.

What is to be said of the point, from which all lines proceed and into which they are resolved, and in which they are one—not a composed unity, but one united from diverse rational principles? Nor are examples of such things lacking even among sensible realities. You will not deny, I think, that the rays of the eyes, the splendors of the heavenly bodies, and those of the other luminaries are sensible and corporeal.

**DISCIPLE.** Who would deny it? For if the splendor of the luminaries is corporeal, why should that of the eyes not also be so? Perhaps they would not fill places or extend themselves locally if they were not corporeal.

**MASTER.** Come now: whether the light of the eyes and of the luminaries is corporeal or not, no one will deny that it is sensible. [Note: A reads *sensibile*, “sensible.”]

**DISCIPLE.** No one. But why do you hesitate and appear, as though uncertain, about the light—whether it is a body or not? For that reason I would like to hear a definite judgment about it.

### 11 [Cols. 0882C–0883A]

**MASTER.** The nature of light is not at issue now; but since you demand that I say briefly what I think about it, I shall do so. Rational inquiry discovers three things in the nature of reality. Everything that exists is either corporeal, incorporeal, or intermediate—the latter being called “corpor(e)al,” though it is neither a body nor incorporeal; nevertheless, it is perceived in bodies and is therefore called corporeal.

Everything that extends in length, breadth, and height is a body, whether it is natural or geometrical. Everything that entirely lacks the aforesaid dimensions is incorporeal, as life is, since it is devoid of all matter. The corporeal, however, includes color, form, and similar things, which are neither bodies, because they are understood in relation to bodies, nor incorporeal, because they are always attached to bodies.

If, therefore, light is color and reveals the forms of sensible things, what prevents it from being said to be neither a body nor incorporeal, but a certain intermediate thing called corporeal and sensible?

**DISCIPLE.** Return to the subject; we must not linger here any longer. I could very easily believe that the light of the eyes or of the other luminaries is color, and neither body nor incorporeal. But I still do not see clearly whether that ray—for example, a solar ray or the ray of animals’ eyes—is a certain body, or corporeal, merely a color sensible around bodies. Therefore I would like you to define what a ray is.

**MASTER.** A ray is, in my opinion, something fiery, simple, extremely subtle, pure, swift, mobile, and light-bearing, from which a radiance proceeds and illuminates and reveals the places and bodies through which it penetrates.

**DISCIPLE.** Such a definition seems plausible. But to what end is all this? [Note: CF reads *istac*, “this,” instead of *istaec*.]

### 12 [Cols. 0883A–0883C]

**MASTER.** To no other end than that you may understand how the sight of many innumerable human beings—or of other animals capable of seeing—may be directed toward some visible object at one and the same moment of time. For example, a small golden sphere placed at the very top of a lofty tower can be seen simultaneously by all those standing around it on every side. Each person looking at it fixes the rays of his own sight upon it, and no one says to another, “Take away your sight so that I too may see what you see,” because all can look at it at the same time.

If, then, so many rays converge upon one object, and none is confused, mixed, or composed with another, since each preserves its own property while all are directed toward one and the same thing in a marvelous union, what is surprising if the whole of human nature is reduced to a certain ineffable unity, while the properties of body, soul, and intellect remain unchangeably distinct?

Observe another example from sensible things, one which blessed Dionysius the Areopagite also introduced when discussing such matters. Let us imagine many lamps burning together in a certain church, their lights shining from different lampstands. Do they not produce one light, so that no bodily sense can distinguish the particular light of each lamp from the light of another?

This argument makes it entirely clear that the lights of many lamps are in no way confused, but merely united. For if someone were to remove the light of one lamp from the building in which they are shining and carry it elsewhere while it continued burning, he would leave nothing of its own light among the splendors of the other lamps, nor would he take away any of the light belonging to the others. The same must be understood of all the remaining lamps. For if they too were removed, they would take away no alien light with them and would leave behind none of their own.

### 13 [Cols. 0883C–0885C]

Is the same thing understood of human and instrumental voices? Each voice—whether human, from a flute, or from a lyre—does not cease to possess its own quality, while several voices produce one harmony among themselves through a fitting unity and proportion. Here too an evident argument is supplied by sounds: they are not confused with one another, but merely united. For if one of the voices were to fall silent, it alone would be silent, and nothing of the melody of the silent voice would result among those that continued to sound. From this it is clear that, when it sounded among the others, it preserved the property of its own quality. For if it had been confused with the others, it could not withdraw itself entirely by becoming silent. What is confused or mixed is not easily resolved into its own proper character.

By these and similar examples from intelligible and sensible things, we can readily understand that the union of human nature can take place while the properties of the individual substances remain intact. But since the subject under discussion is return, it is necessary to ask what of the body will return into the soul, so that it may become with it, as Gregory the Theologian says, “one—both spirit and mind and God,” or may be fermented into one uncompounded unity, as blessed Ambrose teaches, if the substance of the body itself is always to remain unchangeably, without any transformation. [Note: CF omits “and spirit.”]

The same blessed Gregory mentioned above resolves this question in a few words, saying: “When the mortal and fleeting has been absorbed by life.” As though he were saying plainly: When whatever is mortal and fluid in the body has been absorbed by life. The Apostle also teaches this most clearly. For he says: “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.” Again: “When this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality.”

Therefore the earthly, mortal, fluid mass, which has been both taken from and composed of the diverse qualities of sensible elements, in this form which is subject to the bodily senses—as we have discussed in the preceding books, since it was added to the natural and substantial body on account of the deservedness of sin—will be dissolved and changed for the better. At the time of the resurrection it will return into a spirit and a stable substance that does not know how to flow or die.

For, imbued with the soundest and catholic faith and with the doctrine of the divine men Gregory the Theologian and Maximus, who give unshaken accounts of such matters, we firmly believe that the creator of human nature created the whole of it simultaneously: neither did he create the soul before the body, nor the body before the soul. Therefore we reasonably hold that, in the first creation itself, soul and body subsisted together without any capacity for corruption or death.

It is not consistent with right reason to suppose that the creator of a nature made simultaneously created one part of it immortal and incorruptible—the soul, I mean—and another part mortal and corruptible, namely the body. Therefore, I think it not inappropriate to judge that the whole nature of the human being, soul and body, was created immortal and incorruptible.

The wise also report that the angels were created in such a condition. They do not hesitate to assert that they were constituted incorporeal spirits and spiritual bodies devoid of all corruption. But to human beings and to the transgressing angels, earthly and corruptible bodies were added as the punishment of sin—earthly bodies to human beings and aerial bodies to the angels.

Yet what was added to us, since it was assumed by our Redeemer, who emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, will be moved into spirit and into that very substance originally created by God, when death is swallowed up in victory and the whole human being—namely, the outer and the inner, the sensible and the intelligible—will be united into one.

If anyone considers it unbelievable that an earthly body can be changed into spirit, let him observe how the qualities of sensible things are transformed into one another while the substances whose qualities they are remain. Let him observe how an aqueous quality is changed into a fiery quality; how clouds gathered from air are resolved again into the purest air, so that nothing remains of their density; how the air itself, as we have often said, is consumed by solar brightness; how smoke is changed into flame; let him observe the very powerful force of reasoning.

For if the qualities of visible things are incorporeal—as no one who argues correctly doubts—and if all earthly bodies are gathered together from an accumulation of those qualities, what is surprising or unbelievable [Note: CF omits “is”] about the possibility that what is composed from incorporeal qualities may return into incorporeal things? [Note: A omits “into.”]

**DISCIPLE.** To those who observe the substances and qualities of things, as well as their transfusions, compositions, unions, and progressions from primordial causes and their returns into those same causes, this will perhaps appear neither surprising nor unbelievable. For my part, I prescribe the opinion of no one and do not contentiously refute anyone, even if he has thought differently about such matters; enough has been accomplished.

I ask only that it be demonstrated by certain arguments that the union of substances can occur without any disturbance or transformation through confusion, mixture, or composition, and that the qualities from which all these sensible bodies are compacted may return and be dissolved into the substances themselves, without which they cannot subsist.

For no quality, quantity, or any other accident can subsist by itself. Consequently, I think I may say without rashness that the return of which we are now speaking will concern not the substances, which remain in themselves immutable and indissoluble, but the qualities, quantities, and other accidents, which are mutable and transitory in themselves, subject to places and times, and liable to generation and corruption.

And if this is so, as true reason suggests, the question that follows is not to be passed over but investigated with careful consideration.

**MASTER.** Tell me, please, what that question is and what kind it is—one worthy of keen inquiry and discovery.

### 14 [Cols. 0885D–0887A]

**DISCIPLE.** Whether the substances, essences, and rational principles of created things proceed and descend from primordial causes through generation in places and times, and into the capacity of diverse accidents, so that again, when the appointed times have ended—that is, when the sensible world has come to an end—they may return into the same causes from which they flowed;

or whether they always remain unchangeably in their causes, beyond every generation and dissolution, beyond all places and times, and, to put it briefly, beyond all accidents, so that only their inherent and naturally added συμβάματα (*symbamata*), that is, accidents—which the wise ordinarily call affections—proceed materially from them to produce this visible world, in order that, when it has again been dissolved, those accidents may be dissolved and return into their substances, where they may rest and establish the limit of their mutability, free from every flow of generation and corruption through increase and decrease in places and times, united to their underlying substances, so that they may become eternally one with them, inseparable and immutable, through an ineffable union.

**MASTER.** This inquiry is exceedingly profound and has not yet been brought forth into the ordinary conception of the mind. But since you have proposed it with great caution and order, it does not require a lengthy and laborious disclosure; for you have almost solved it yourself.

You do not doubt, I think, that the causes of all things, created and established in Wisdom, remain eternally and immutably in Wisdom itself and never at any time depart from it or undergo any flux toward lower things. For they would not subsist by themselves if they departed from it in any way.

**DISCIPLE.** I would in no way doubt the unchangeable continuance of all causes in the divine Wisdom, which is the Word of God the Father, in whom and through whom all things were made and subsist. Both divine Scripture and the tradition of the holy Fathers assert this without hesitation.

**MASTER.** What do you think about the substances of things that were both made and established in the aforesaid causes? Is it plausible—indeed, is it most true—that we should believe that the substances themselves, I mean, always remain in their causes unchangeably and never at any time or in any way depart from them?

For just as the primordial causes do not abandon Wisdom, so the substances themselves do not abandon their causes, but always subsist in them. And just as the causes cannot exist outside the substances, so the substances cannot flow outside the causes.

**DISCIPLE.** Nothing is more plausible, easier to understand, or closer to the truth than that we should both believe and hold this firmly.

**MASTER.** It remains, then, that this world was fabricated and compacted from the qualities of substances—and by “qualities” I mean what the wise customarily call everything that happens to substances, because such things are mutable and revolve around their substances—and that it will be dissolved into those same qualities.

Everything that begins to exist temporally through generation must necessarily have an end of existence. Yet we do not suppose that the aforesaid qualities of substances entirely abandon their substances, around which they revolve, and come together into the matter of the sensible world. Rather, in a marvelous and ineffable manner known only to its creator, they always remain around their substances, to which they adhere inseparably, and by their compositions they complete and compose this world in a certain intelligible mode. For we reasonably believe that above the whole visible universe there exist the causes and substances of all bodies, both universal and particular, from which it is constituted. For corporeal and sensible things derive their origin from incorporeal and intelligible things. [Note: A reads *intelligibilibusque*, “and intelligible.”]

### 15 [Cols. 0887A–0887B]

**DISCIPLE.** The matter is settled; no other outcome seems possible for the present question. Yet I would like you briefly to define what difference there is between causes and substances. Both, after all, are incorporeal and intelligible.

**MASTER.** By causes we mean the most general rational principles of all things, established together in the Word of God. By substances we mean the individual and most specific properties and rational principles of individual and most specific things, distributed and established in those causes. [Note: A places “individual substances” in the reverse order.]

**DISCIPLE.** The distinction has been made clearly and briefly. From those causes and substances, then, this world proceeded, its qualities having been coagulated and added to matter together with form; and at the time of its dissolution it will return and pass again into those same causes. [Note: A reads “into the same.”]

**MASTER.** Nothing should be believed and understood that is truer or nearer to truth. For Truth itself says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” [Note: CF reads “will pass away.”] But where will heaven and earth pass? Into nothingness?

**DISCIPLE.** Far from it. That must in no way be said. By “nothingness” I now mean the absence and privation of all things that are and that are not, into which no visible or invisible creature will fall. [Note: CF reads “into which”; A reads “in which.”]

### 16 [Cols. 0887B–0888A]

**MASTER.** Into what, then, will heaven and earth pass, together with all that is in them? What Truth has promised will inevitably come to pass.

**DISCIPLE.** Nowhere else, in my judgment, than into those things from which they proceeded. They proceeded from the most general causes and the most specific substances, through qualities compacted into matter, with form added. They will therefore pass without hesitation into those same things.

But I would like to know what those words of Truth are that will never pass away. I would not believe that they are the words uttered by a stroke of air, with which Truth itself spoke to human beings while present in the flesh. Those words were transitory, like the words of other human beings.

**MASTER.** I would call no other words the words of Truth—or, so to speak, the words of the Word, because Truth is the Word—than the aforesaid causes and substances, that is, the immutable rational principles of things made in the Wisdom of God, according to which visible and invisible things were created, and into which heaven and earth will pass.

Those words themselves will never, at any time, pass away [Note: CF reads “will pass away”], because they remain perpetually in the only-begotten Word of God like certain ineffable and immutable words. These words, I think, the Apostle heard when he was caught up into paradise. For what angel or human being could utter in words, or know in mind, what kinds, qualities, and quantities of rational principles of things the Father made in the beginning—in his Word, that is—before all times and before every creature?

**DISCIPLE.** Then you do not count the causes and substances of things established in the Word of God among the number of creatures? For you said that they were made before all time and every creature.

**MASTER.** I do not count them among creatures, and not without reason. Properly speaking, the name “creature” signifies those things which, through generation and by a certain temporal motion, flow into their proper species, whether visible or invisible.

But what was established before all times and places, since it is beyond times and places, is not properly called a creature, although, by a certain mode of speaking, the whole universe—which is after God—is called a creature created by him, by way of synecdoche (συνεκδοχικῶς), that is, by using a part or aspect to designate the whole.

### 17 [Cols. 0888A–0889B]

But it is asked again whether everything that moves temporally must necessarily also move locally. On this question the opinions of many who discuss the world—not only Catholics but also secular thinkers—vary.

Some say that these two things, namely place and time, exist around and outside corporeal creation, and that creation is contained and bounded by them. And since, by natural reasoning, that which contains is greater than that which is contained, they think that places and times must be reckoned not within the parts of the world but outside the universe itself; especially since they are incorporeal and, in their judgment, should not properly be counted among corporeal things.

Others, however, enclose places and times within the universal structure of the world. They say that places and times came into being and were created together with the other things contained within the world, and that, just as all things were brought forth from their causes, so were places and times. For the rational principles of places and times preceded their creation in the world, in the Word of God, in whom all things were made.

They add this reasoning: if places and times existed before the world, they are certainly eternal; and if they are eternal, they are either God or the principal causes of all things established in divine Wisdom—which is absurd to suppose. As Augustine says, there are two greatest errors of human beings: to think that places exist above heaven and that times existed before the world.

Consequently, it follows that secular times arose and came into being together with the world, and in no way preceded it. True reason therefore compels us to count place and time among the things contained within the world. Consequently, not only is whatever enters the world generated within them—for things are born and move according to the measures of places and times—but everything that is generated in them is also generated together with them and proceeds from the general causes that precede the world.

As for the question we proposed—whether everything that moves temporally must necessarily also move locally—the tradition of Catholic authorities likewise holds differing opinions. First, they unanimously teach that God alone moves by himself without place and time. But their theories differ concerning the motion of spiritual creation, which is free from all corporeal matter.

Some affirm that it moves through time alone, without place, while they reasonably judge that every corporeal creature is mutable not only temporally but also locally. Nor do all disagree with this view. Blessed Augustine also supports it when he says, speaking of God: “He moves himself without place and time; he moves created spirit through time without place; he moves the body through time and place.”

Others, however, following Gregory the Theologian—as Maximus testifies in the *Ambigua*—firmly assert that place and time are inseparable, to such an extent that everything temporal is local and, conversely, everything local is temporal. They maintain that it is in no way possible to find in nature anything that can move through time alone without place, or through place alone without time.

But which of these positions should more appropriately be held is not ours to judge. Let each person who discusses such matters deliberate within himself about what it is more reasonable for him to follow. We, however, should return to the subject.

**DISCIPLE.** Cautiously and attentively. We must not rashly judge the opinions of great and venerable men. For if we say that one of them thought more correctly, we will seem to refute the other—and that is usually the greatest and most immediate cause of quarrelling.

### 18 [Cols. 0889B–0890C]

**MASTER.** No one who philosophizes piously and catholically, and who considers the force of divine Scripture, would say, I think, that places and times existed before the world.

**DISCIPLE.** I would not contradict those who believe and understand this. They believe most soundly and understand most purely. For what could precede the world except eternity alone, especially since it is written: “All things were made in the twinkling of an eye”? Places and times are among the number of all things. Again: “He who lives eternally created all things together.”

**MASTER.** What, then, shall we say? If places and times did not exist before the world, but only eternity preceded it, is it plausible that we should likewise believe that they will not remain after the world? If places and times are counted within the universe of the world, how will they remain when the world has been dissolved?

For the whole either remains universally or perishes universally; it is impossible for it to remain in part and perish in part. If one part of the whole perishes, the whole perishes. Once one part has been removed, the whole is no longer whole. Similarly, if one part is saved and the others perish, the whole perishes. Therefore the whole world will either perish entirely or exist entirely forever.

But it will perish. Therefore the whole will perish, and none of its parts will remain after its destruction without perishing. Place and time are among its parts. Therefore place and time will perish in it and with it.

By “place” I do not now mean the definition of things, which always remains in the mind, but the space by which the quantity of bodies is extended. For the Greeks call those two parts of the world—place and time—“ὧν ἄνευ,” that is, “without which the other parts cannot exist.” I would not improperly say that this term remains valid in them for as long as the whole of which they are parts remains. But when that whole passes away, the force of that term will simultaneously be emptied. [Note: CF reads “will be emptied”; A reads “will be recalled.”]

For when there is nothing that needs to be located and bounded, how will there be place? If nothing has been located, there will be no place. When that which is located perishes, how will place exist? Place is altogether not what does not locate something.

The same applies to time. When there is no motion that the measure of time can divide and comprehend, how will there be time? Time is a definite and natural measure of delays or motions. Therefore, when that which is measured perishes, that which measures it must necessarily perish as well. In what will time be understood when no motion is perceived? Just as motion is contained in something that moves, so time is contained in a certain measured motion.

Therefore, just as there will be no motion when no part of the world moves, so there will be no time when no motion is measured.

No Catholic doubts the destruction and end of the world. Not only reason and natural necessity confirm that it will perish; the truest authority of the divine writings also confirms it. Indeed, for this reason the wisest men of the world did not dare to teach or concede that this world began through generation with a temporal beginning, lest they be compelled to admit that it would have an end of time through its passing away. For if they conceded that the world began with a temporal beginning, they could not deny that it would also be terminated by the end of time.

Therefore some of them tried to assert that the whole world—that is, both its matter and its form—was coeternal with God. Others attempted to maintain that only its formless matter was eternal, attributing to God alone the form and formation of the world, while asserting that its matter subsisted by itself, eternal and coeternal with God, yet needed God as its former and was unable to form itself.

### 19.

Sound and ecclesiastical doctrine most firmly believes, and sees with the greatest clarity, that the one omnipotent God, the beginning and cause of all things that are and that are not, gave the world matter and form when he willed, and will give it an end when he has ordained it: he who made all things in eternal causes before they came to be in temporal moments; he who is the end of all things, because those things that proceeded from him will return to him, and move and stand in him.

The Lord himself, speaking of the world’s passing away—as we introduced somewhat earlier—says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” And lest anyone suppose that “the passing away of the world” in these words can be understood as a passage from place to place, or from one time to another, or from one visible form to another visible form, or from one quality to another, or from one quantity to another, let him hear the Prophet saying to the Maker of the world [Note: [Col. 0889] Thus CF; A reads “suppose.”]: “The heavens are the works of your hands; they will perish, but you remain.” He expressly said “they will perish,” so that you may understand what “they will pass away” means.

But if the heavens will pass away, what should be thought about the things contained within their circuit? For if the most excellent part of the world is to perish, surely we must not think that the inferior parts will remain. And if that which contains and surrounds has perished, will that which is contained and surrounded be saved? It is not plausible that what is better should perish while what is worse should be saved—especially since the Prophet did not say, “The work of your hands is heaven; it will perish,” but, “The works of your hands are the heavens; they will perish.”

Here it is plainly understood [Note: [Col. 0891] CF omits “that”] that not only the star-bearing heaven, which encloses and surrounds the whole of sensible creation, but also the ethereal heaven, in which the seven planets complete their courses, and the aerial heaven, which is confined between earth and moon, will perish. For the dense air nearest the earth is at times called “heaven,” as in Genesis, when the flying creatures were made to fly beneath the firmament of heaven [Note: [Col. 0891] Thus CF; A reads “earth, sea.”]; at other times it is called “earth,” as in the Psalm: “Praise him from the earth, dragons.”

If, then, all the intervals of the world and its most tenuous bodies are to perish [Note: [Col. 0891] CF reads “are to perish.”], do you think that the waters and the earth will remain, even though their nature is more subject to suffering and more prone to corruption than fire and air? John the theologian [Note: [Col. 0891] Thus CF; A reads “and John.”] said in his Apocalypse, prophesying about the consummation of the world [Note: [Col. 0891] Thus CF; A reads “prophesied”]: “For the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and the sea is no more.” Solomon likewise says: “Everything that was is itself what will be, and there is nothing new under the sun.” As though he were saying plainly: God alone, and the causes of all things in him, existed before the world and will exist after the world; and the causes of all things in him will exist alone. But the world itself, which is beneath the sun and received its origin from eternal causes [Note: [Col. 0891] Thus CF; A reads “and from eternal causes”], will return to those same causes. For what now is will not be [Note: [Col. 0891] A omits “for”]. Everything that begins to be, which previously was not, and ceases to be what it is, is no longer.

Consider the clearest statements of divine Scripture concerning the world’s destruction. The Lord, gathering together its extremities in general, says: “Heaven and earth will pass away.” The Prophet speaks of the inner spaces of the ether and air: “The works of your hands are the heavens; they will perish.” The Evangelist John says: “The sea is no more.” From these statements we are taught without hesitation that no part of the world will remain which is not destined to perish.

**DISCIPLE.** What, then, shall we say? [Note: [Col. 0891] Thus A; CF reads “But.”] For Solomon also says: “One generation comes, and another generation goes; but the earth stands forever.” If it will pass away, how does it stand—and how will it stand forever?

**MASTER.** In these words of Solomon we do not understand that part of the world which is central and lowest—for there is nothing beneath it—in which the human race, still mortal and corruptible, now exists, subject to generation and corruption. Rather, we understand the earth of which the Prophet says: “You founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be shaken forever and ever”—namely, the unchangeable stability of all natures in their essential and substantial causes. Their immovable foundation is the wisdom of the Father, which shall not be shaken forever and ever [Note: [Col. 0891] A omits “is.”]

Sacred Scripture commonly signifies by the name “earth” the unchangeable stability of natures, and especially the solidity of human nature. Hence the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth.” As though he were saying: “Put to death your vices, which are above the solidity of nature, so that, once they have been uprooted, the shoots of the virtues may grow.”

This is the promised land into which the people of the faithful—liberated from Egypt, that is, from labor or darkness (for Egypt is interpreted in both ways [Note: [Col. 0891] Thus A; CF reads “Egypt”]), brought in through the sea of baptism, and disciplined in the desert of the present life [Col. 0892B]—will return. This is the land which the children of spiritual Israel will possess when they are to contemplate God face to face. It was also shown figuratively to the patriarch Abraham and given to him as an eternal possession.

But if the statements of divine Scripture cited above concerning the destruction of this earthly mass, in which we now live, having been begotten in the likeness of beasts, are not sufficient for you [Note: [Col. 0891] CF has “the statements of the divine Scriptures cited above concerning the destruction …”; A inserts this wording above the present place], other passages from the same Scripture must be added. Peter, the chief of the apostles, says in his Second Epistle [Note: [Col. 0891] Thus CF; A reads “in his Second Epistle”]: “The heavens that now are and the earth have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.”

John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth; for the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and the sea is no more.”

Following blessed Gregory Nazianzen, the theologian, we understand the new heaven and the new earth—or, as Peter says, “new heavens and a new earth”—as referring to the restoration of human nature to its original state and its return to its former dignity. In this interpretation, as far as I see, we are not far from the truth.

**DISCIPLE.** Enough has been discussed concerning the destruction of the world, and indeed concerning its return to the eternal causes from which it had flowed forth. But I should like to hear more clearly by what end it will be brought to completion.

### 20.

**MASTER.** I wonder why you ask this, since you yourself, somewhat earlier, unhesitatingly defined the end of the world as its eternal causes, subsisting eternally and unchangeably in the Word of God. And it has already been established between us above that, in all things which are in motion or at rest [Note: [Col. 0891] A reads “at rest or in motion”]—or, to put it another way, in things possessing a movable stability and a stable motion—the beginning is not one thing and the end another, but one and the same.

If, then, the beginnings of the world are the causes from which it arose [Note: [Col. 0891] CF omits “arose.”], are not the ends of that same world the very same causes, to which it will return? It will not be reduced to nothing; rather, once its motion has come to an end, it will be eternally preserved and rest in its causes.

But if the Word of the Father, in whom all things both exist and were made, is the cause of all visible and invisible causes, is not that very cause of causes the end of the world [Note: [Col. 0893] A reads “is the world’s end”], into which it will cease when all things that are in motion establish the end of their motion in that which they desire—in the Word of God himself [Note: [Col. 0893] Thus CF; A reads “will establish”]? Beyond that end there will be no desire of any creature [Note: [Col. 0893] Thus CF; A reads “no desire of no creature”], for it will have nowhere further to go or anything further to seek.

The Word of God is indeed the universal end of the whole creation. The beginning and end of the world therefore subsist in the Word of God; or, to speak more plainly, they are the Word itself, which is the multifaceted, endless end and the beginning ἄναρχον [Note: A reads ἄναρχος], that is, “without beginning,” except for the Father.

From this we can also briefly gather and define what we are trying to persuade by many arguments: “From him and toward him are all things,” for he is the beginning and the end. The Apostle also concluded this most plainly when he said: “For from him, and through him, and in him, and toward him are all things.”

This is also most clearly declared by the fivefold division of all natures that have been made. Maximus writes in the thirty-seventh chapter of his *Ambigua* that this division was handed down by apostolic authority. It also declares the return and reunification of those natures through the same divisions and revolutions of the whole creation into one, and finally into God himself.

The first division of all natures separates the created from the uncreated, which is God. The second divides the created into sensible and intelligible. The third distinguishes the sensible into heaven and earth [Note: A reads “between.”]. The fourth separates paradise and the terrestrial world. The fifth and final division is that of the human being into male and female.

In this human being, all visible and invisible creation has been established [Col. 0893C]. He is therefore called the workshop of all things, because in him all things that exist after God are contained. For this reason he is also commonly called the middle: he comprehends within himself and gathers into unity the extremes, far removed from one another—namely, spiritual and bodily things—consisting of body and soul [Note: Thus CF; A reads “subsisting.”]

Therefore, in the consummation of the making of all things, divine history introduced him, signifying that the universe of created things is contained in him. Accordingly, from the reunification of the division of the human being into the two sexes, the ascent and reunification of the divisions mentioned above begins.

In the resurrection, sex will be removed, nature will be reunited, and there will be only the human being, as would have happened if he had not sinned. Then the terrestrial world will be united to paradise, and there will be nothing but paradise. Then heaven and earth will be united, and there will be nothing but heaven.

It should be noted that the lower things are always transformed into the higher. Sex moves into the human being, since sex is lower than the human being. The terrestrial world, which is lower, moves into paradise. Earthly bodies, because they are lower, will be changed into heavenly bodies.

Next follows the reunification of all sensible creation and its transformation into intelligible creation, so that the whole of creation becomes intelligible. Finally, the universal creation will be united to the Creator, and it will be one in him and with him.

This is the end of all visible and invisible things, because all visible things will pass into intelligible things, and intelligible things into God himself, through a wondrous and ineffable reunification—not, as we have often said, through any confusion or destruction of essences or substances [Note: [Col. 0893] Thus AC; F reads “and”].

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ both accomplished all this in himself by rising from the dead and displayed beforehand the example of all that is to come. When he rose, he had no sex. Although he appeared to his disciples in the sex he possessed—namely, that of a male—in which he had been born from the Virgin and had lived among human beings until the Passion [Note: [Col. 0893] Thus CF; A reads “as far as”], he did so to confirm their faith. They would not otherwise have recognized him unless he manifested himself to them in a form familiar to them.

Nevertheless, no believer may [Note: [Col. 0893] A omits “nevertheless”] believe or [Note: [Col. 0893] A reads “or”] in any way imagine that after the resurrection he was confined within any sex. In Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female, but only the true and complete human being—I mean body, soul, and intellect—without any sex or perceptible form, because these three are one in him and have become God, without alteration or confusion of their properties.

For he is wholly God and wholly human, one substance, or, as I more commonly put it, one person. He is without local or temporal motion, since as God and human he is above all places and times; he is without any form, since he is the form of all things and the impress of the paternal substance; he is without any likeness, although all things desire to be like him [Note: [Col. 0893] Thus CF; A reads the same words in the order “desire to be like him”]

The humanity of Christ, having become one with the Godhead, is contained in no place, moves in no time, and is circumscribed by no form or sex, because it has been exalted above all these things—and not only above these, but also above all virtues, powers, and the other spiritual orders, because he sits at the right hand of the Father, a session which no creature can attain.

Therefore those who attempt to establish the Lord’s body after the resurrection in some part of the world, and to make it move locally and temporally, and to confine it within the world in the sex in which it appeared to the world, are rightly condemned [Note: Thus CF; A reads “assert.”] For how can that body be among all things which has been exalted above all things in the unity of the Godhead?

Next, we must consider that, when he rose from the dead, he returned to paradise. We must not believe that any interval of time existed between his return from the dead and his entrance into paradise; nor should we think that the paradise into which he entered after rising from the dead was local or contained in some part of this sensible world.

Nor, when he manifested himself to his disciples, should we believe that he was outside paradise. Rather, he was simultaneously in paradise and showing himself to his disciples. He was already in paradise because human nature had been restored in him; but those to whom he manifested himself were not yet in paradise—that is, human nature in them had not yet been restored [Note: The entire sentence from “He was already in paradise” through “had been restored” is omitted by CF.]

Nor, when he vanished from their eyes, did he withdraw from them locally; rather, he concealed himself in the subtlety of a spiritual body, still imperceptible to the bodily eyes of the apostles [Note: A omits “himself.”]

From this it is understood that the paradise into which he entered after rising was nothing other than the integrity of human nature, which he had restored in himself, and in which the first human being would have remained glorious had he not sinned.

This is the paradise promised to the saints. They have already entered it in part—namely, in the soul—but in part, I mean in the body, they are still outside [Note: A reads: “They have already entered it in part, namely in the soul; in part, I mean in the bodies, they are still outside.”]

Thus he united the terrestrial world to paradise. For the terrestrial world itself was paradise to him. Everything that he had received from the terrestrial world—namely, material flesh with its accidents, without sin, and the form of a man—he changed in himself into a spiritual nature.

Then he not only exalted and brought to equality with the angelic nature the humanity that he had received and renewed in himself, as was signified by his ascension into heaven, when he was lifted up into the air before the eyes of his disciples and a cloud received him from their sight, indicating both his brightness and his spirituality—for before he suffered he said, “Father, glorify your Son”—but he also raised it above all angels and heavenly powers and, in short, above all things that are and that are not.

What he accomplished particularly in himself, he will accomplish generally at the time of the resurrection in the whole of human nature. That is, he will not only transform into spirit all that human nature, after the Fall, had drawn from this material world [Col. 0895C], but will also bring it to the equality of the heavenly glory possessed by the angels.

And do not be surprised that much has been discussed on these subjects in other books of this disputation of ours and is now recapitulated again. The order and necessity of discovering the matters we seek require us to repeat and turn over the same statements and arguments in many ways, and, as it were, to recall them to memory through a kind of ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, that is, “recapitulation.”

I say this because in the earlier books, by introducing many statements of blessed Maximus concerning the return of nature, we have already offered a foretaste of them [Note: CF reads “many statements”; A reads “many things” and “to be introduced.”] But now we must treat them more fully.

That same Maximus discusses the reunification of creatures not only in the *Ambigua* but also in the scholia, in the forty-eighth chapter, where he expounds the spiritual interpretation of the towers that Uzziah built in Jerusalem:

> Perhaps, says the discourse of Scripture, it called them “corners” because they are the differentiating reunifications of separated creatures, effected through Christ. For he united the human being, mystically removing into spirit the distinction according to male and female, and establishing the principle of nature free from the properties that arise through the passions in both.  
> 
> He also united the earth that is distinguished according to sensible paradise and the terrestrial world, driving out their separation. He united earth and heaven, showing that the nature of visible things is one in itself. He united sensible and intelligible things, showing that the nature of created things is one, fitted together by a certain mystical principle. Through a supernatural principle and mode he united created nature to uncreated nature.

**DISCIPLE.** What, then, shall we say? By what reason or likeness should we believe that the Lord rose without any sensible and circumscribed form, and especially without the form he received by being born from the Virgin? Since he both was and is the example of the general resurrection that is to come, if he rose without any sex, it necessarily follows that all human beings, in the resurrection and after the resurrection, will universally be without sex.

**MASTER.** It is superfluous to ask this, since in the earlier books it has been established in many ways by reasoning and by the statements of blessed Gregory and his expositor, Maximus, that in the future life after the resurrection human nature will be entirely without sex—that is, without male and female form—because it will return to the very form that was made in the image of God. The image of God is neither male nor female; this division of nature came about because of sin.

**DISCIPLE.** In the future life, then, there will be neither male nor female, if the simplicity of nature alone absorbs into itself the twofold sex that exists now.

**MASTER.** Why do you hesitate about this, when Truth says generally concerning human beings in the resurrection: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven”? Do we believe that angels consist of intellect and spiritual body? Yet we have no doubt that they lack every circumscribed form.

The fact that divine history often says they appeared in human likeness does not compel us to think that they are naturally confined to such a likeness. This was done for the occasion, because otherwise it was either impossible or difficult for them to appear [Note: [Col. 0895] A omits “to appear”] to human beings and speak with them.

If, then, angels lack every circumscribed form, what is surprising if human beings, when they have become equal to the angels, will lack every circumscription of sex and form [Note: [Col. 0895] Thus CF; A reads “every circumscription both of sex and of forms”]? Otherwise they will not be equal to them, and this does not appear incredible.

For there are certain bodies that are fluid and spiritual and lack circumscribed forms. But I do not see how that which is fluid and spiritual [Note: [Col. 0895] A reads “and”], and of the purest substance, can be contained within bodily quantities, outlines, or some mass circumscribed by form; true reason does not permit me to think so.

The four simple elements of the world are not confined by any forms; for they are everywhere in the world, and no part of the world is without their combination. But how can that which is everywhere in the world be circumscribed by any form?

There are, therefore, bodies without sensible forms. What should be said about the rays of the eyes? Are they not bodily, yet without any form?

But if you say that angels possess intelligible forms [Note: A reads “intelligible forms” in the reverse order], I entirely agree. Consequently, I not only do not deny, but affirm, that human beings in the resurrection will likewise possess intelligible forms [Note: Thus CF; A reads “after the resurrection.”]

But what and of what kind those forms now are in angels, and will be in human beings, I confess that I entirely do not know, until, as Augustine says, “my body passes into the affection of my will.”

Nevertheless, I am not unaware that many great and wise men think quite differently about human bodies after the resurrection. As this book proceeds, I shall not hesitate to introduce their opinions, lest we seem either to despise them or not to have read them.

**DISCIPLE.** The proper order of the discussion requires you to state what each of the ecclesiastical sages whom you have read thought about these matters—for I do not suppose that you have read them all, since that is impossible for anyone—so that the reader may be left free to follow whichever one he wishes.

For the moment, however, I ask you this: how is that said to perish which is reported to return to the primordial causes, or even to God himself, when it should rather be said to live and endure than to perish and pass away?

### 21.

**MASTER.** I answer your question briefly and easily by considering the interpretation of the prophetic saying given by blessed Dionysius the Areopagite: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”

The Prophet, in this verse, asserts that he meant no other death of the saints than their passage into God through the height of contemplation, while they still remain in the body and surpass all visible and invisible things.

Was Peter, that chief of the apostles, dead to every creature and passed into God when, in answer to the Lord’s question as to whom he said that he himself was, he replied: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”?

Was the evangelist John similarly dead to all things that have been made, surpassing everything by the height of contemplation and crying out: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word”—together with all his wondrous and ineffable contemplation of theology?

Hear the Apostle, still held in a mortal body, yet declaring himself dead and crucified: “The world has been crucified to me,” he says, “and I to the world.”

Such, then, is the destruction of the saints: through the power of contemplation they pass into God himself, and, having been deified, surpass all things that are and themselves through the height of divine grace [Note: A omits “having been deified.”]

In the same way that those who are filled with virtue and knowledge, while still living in this life, perish in soul alone, the whole world will perish when it reaches its end. It will return into him who, because of the superessentiality of his nature, is called “nothing”; not so that it may be wholly deified or become one with God, as do the heavenly powers and human minds when they are illuminated, purified, and perfected, but so that each of the things of which it is constituted [Note: Thus CF; A reads “may be constituted”] may return, as we have often said, to its own causes.

No believer doubts that the causes of all things subsist in God. Whoever doubts this is either an unbeliever or foolish. Therefore, why should anyone doubt that everything restored to its own cause returns to God?

And lest you think that I have called God “nothing” rashly and without the support of any authority, hear blessed Dionysius the Areopagite in the first chapter of *The Divine Names*:

> When we explained the theological characteristics, we said that the One—unknown, superessential, and good in itself—which indeed is the triune unity, ὁμόθεον and ὁμοάγαθον (“of one Godhead” and “of one goodness”), can neither be spoken nor understood. But the angelic unities of the holy powers, whether they should be called contemplative or receptive, are of a goodness beyond knowledge and beyond light; they are secret and unknown, and subsist only for themselves, who are beyond angelic knowledge, for their worthy angels [Note: [Col. 0897] Thus CF; A reads “who deem those angels worthy of them.”]  
> 
> Human minds, made godlike by angelic imitation and united with them as far as is permitted, since they rest according to every intellectual operation—such is the unity of deified minds with the highest light, namely God [Note: [Col. 0897] CF omits “namely God”; A reads “union”]: praise him especially through the removal of all things that are. In this they are truly and supernaturally illuminated through their most blessed unity with him, who is the cause of all things that are, but himself is “nothing,” as exalted superessentially above all things that are.

Observe how that theologian unhesitatingly suggests by the name “nothing” the highest light, namely God, who illuminates every intellectual and rational creature. He then added the reason why he is called “nothing”: because he is exalted superessentially above all things that are.

It is therefore common to all created things that, in a kind of death, they return to the causes that subsist in God. But it is proper to intellectual and rational substance to become one with God through the power of contemplation and to become God by grace.

**DISCIPLE.** I clearly understand that for the world to perish is nothing other than for it to return to its causes and be changed into something better. But since the greatest part of the sensible world is the human body—not by its mass, but by the dignity of the rational soul, by which it is formed, enlivened, governed, and contained—the order of things and the sequence of the discussion require us, unless I am mistaken, to speak of its return.

### 22.

**MASTER.** You are not mistaken; for we must now proceed along the path that lies before us.

**DISCIPLE.** Proceed, then.

**MASTER.** The whole Church commonly acknowledges that the second return of the human body—for its first dissolution is into the elements—is its resurrection.

**DISCIPLE.** It is the common confession of all who believe rightly and properly that the second return of bodies [Note: [Col. 0897] A omits “second”] is nothing other than their resurrection and their recall from the four elements of the world into which they are dissolved [Note: [Col. 0897] A reads “which” in the singular]. But whether the resurrection of bodies occurs according to grace, according to nature, or through the concurrence of both [Note: [Col. 0897] A reads “both” in the neuter] must be investigated; for I have found scarcely anyone who treats this question.

### 23.

**TEACHER.** Nor do I remember having read in Latin books that this question has been treated—though perhaps, as I suppose, it has been discussed by someone still unknown to us. For it must not be thought that the authors of the Roman language left this great question untouched, or failed to discuss it once it had been noted; rather, whatever definition has been given concerning it has not come into our hands [CF; manuscript A: “my hands”]. Therefore, while I was pondering this matter by myself for a long time, nothing else occurred to me except that the general resurrection of the dead, both good and evil, would take place solely through the grace of the Redeemer of the world, with no natural power compelling it—so much so that, if God the Word had not become flesh, lived among human beings, and assumed the whole of human nature, in which he suffered and rose again, there would be no resurrection of the dead.

I was drawn to understand it in this way by what he himself said: “I am the resurrection and the life”; as though, through his incarnation alone [CF; manuscript A: “his”], the human race as a whole, with no exception, had received [CF: “would receive”] this universal gift—namely, resurrection from the dead, that is, the restoration and reintegration of the whole of human nature, which is constituted by body and soul. But if the Word of God had not assumed human nature and had not risen from the dead in it, no one at all would have received the grace of resurrection; instead, just as the corpses of other animals, human bodies would have remained perpetually in the dust of the earth.

I also thought this while hearing the Apostle say that the Word of God is “the firstfruits of the dead.” Such was my opinion concerning the resurrection of the dead. But after I had read the discourse *Ancoratus* [“The Anchored One,” or, according to the variant, *Accuratus*; the word “or” is omitted in manuscripts A, C, and F] on the Faith by Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, and the great Gregory the Theologian’s discussion *On the Image*, I changed my view. Assenting to their authority and attaching little importance to my own opinion [manuscript A: “attaching little weight”], I conceded that the resurrection of the dead would take place through natural power. I therefore judged it not inappropriate to insert their words into our present discussion.

The aforesaid Epiphanius, discussing the resurrection and refuting the Greeks who altogether deny it, says the following:

> The Greeks indeed utterly deny the resurrection, because they do not know God [manuscript A: “the Lord”] or his commandments; nevertheless, they will rise even against their will. For creation itself plainly reproves them, revealing every day the pattern of resurrection. The day dies, and we experience the manner of the dead [manuscript A: “imitates”]; when night has been removed, the day rises, breathing life into us and intimating the sign of resurrection. Fruits are gathered, and the state of present things is cut down, with the definite form of our transformation thereby displayed. Seed is sown in the earth, and it produces, because the seeds that have been laid down will rise again after the harvest, that is, after the gathering of the crops. A locust dies and is buried; what is cast from it is conceived in the earth [manuscript A: “is seen”], and after a time the earth returns what has been entrusted to it.
>
> Seeds of plants are sown and first die; for if they do not die, they are not made alive. God has made signs of resurrection in us through ten and ten fingernails, bearing witness to our hope. He also proclaims our resurrection through the crown of the head and through the hair. For what appears in us to be a dead body—the hair, which is cut daily, and the fingernails, which grow again [manuscript A: “grow”]—signifies the hope of resurrection.
>
> Nor is it a fable to offer examples from nature for the sake of unbelievers. Doves, birds that do not all fly swiftly at the same time, die after six months and immediately revive after forty days. **Κάνθαροι**, that is, scarab beetles, sensing that their future death is approaching, hide themselves in a sphere of dung, burying and covering the sphere itself in the earth; and thus, from their own moisture, they are again found reviving from their remains.
>
> It is unnecessary for me to speak of the Arabian bird, the phoenix, for it has already come to the ears of many believers and unbelievers. This, however, is its story. Having completed its five-hundredth year, it foreknows that the time of its death is at hand. It constructs a tomb from aromatic substances and, carrying it, comes to the Egyptian city called Heliopolis, that is, “city of the sun.” Striking its breast repeatedly with its wings, it brings forth fire from its body, sets alight the material placed beneath it at the site of the tomb, and thus burns itself completely, together with all its flesh and bones.
>
> By divine providence a cloud is then sent, and it rains, extinguishing the flame consuming the bird’s body [CF: *consumantem*, an anomalous reading]. The bird is already dead and entirely burned. Once the flame has been extinguished, the remains of its consumed flesh are left behind; although invisible for one day, they generate a worm. The worm grows feathers and becomes new; on the third day it becomes solid, and, once solid, reveals itself to those who seek and attend to the place. It then returns again to its native land, from which it came, and, having been burned, grows young again.

You have heard Epiphanius. If, then, a natural power operates in restoring human things and the parts of the human body, and in raising irrational animals—as the examples approved by the author mentioned above demonstrate—what is surprising if the vital and natural power, which never abandons the substance of human bodies, is so strong that through its operation the bodies themselves are restored to life and to the integrity of the whole of human nature?

For the various and particular bodies of the other animals and of all sensible things, since in them too vital movement is vigorous and active while they remain contained within their forms, but falls silent when those forms are dissolved, nevertheless do not lose their substance. They will all pass away with the world, in the manner of passing away about which we have discussed more fully above [manuscript A: “the world will pass away”]. And since all sensible and intelligible things were created within the fullness of human nature, is it contrary to reason if we decide that the whole world, together with all its parts, will rise again in a general likeness of resurrection at the restoration of that nature within which the whole world is contained?

This is especially so since, when the nature of all sensible things is considered in itself, it is perceived to be one and the same; and in this world reason considers not the magnitude of bodily mass, but the union of incorporeal substances, without any accumulation or enlargement through addition or composition. Thus, in the monad and in the center, it perceives not the quantity or quality of numbers and lines, but only the power that is bounded by no mass, no space, no quantity, and no quality. For it is wholly present throughout itself, enclosed by no place and moved by no time.

Therefore, if human nature surpasses all sensible things within the universe, and higher things always draw lower things toward themselves—for reason does not permit higher things to be consumed by lower things, while it proves through the most certain demonstrations that lower things pass into higher things—is it not plausible to think that human nature will, at the end of all things, join and unite to itself all that has been created within and beneath it?

Nor, I think, should we pass over the same Epiphanius’s view concerning the subtlety of human bodies after the resurrection. For, discussing Christ’s body after the resurrection—in which the most perfect example of the resurrection of the whole of humanity preceded—he says:

> He entered through closed doors; for his fleshly body rose spiritually [manuscript CF omits “body”], and it was not something other than what it is [manuscript A omits “and”]. What it is, he united to the Godhead, adorning it with the subtlety of spirit [manuscript A: “not something other than what it had been, but that very same body transformed into subtlety”]. For if there were not there a certain subtlety of spirit, he would have received a heavy body.
>
> But to show that “this corruptible” of ours “will put on incorruption” in truth—for if it is mortal, it will put on immortality—he did indeed enter through closed doors, to show the thick-limbed as subtle-limbed, the mortal as immortal, and the corruptible as incorruptible. And in order to refute all unbelievers concerning our salvation—that is, concerning the resurrection—he transformed the body into subtle spirit and harmonized it with the resurrection.

Observe how unequivocally he declares the resurrection of spiritual bodies and their return into an incomprehensible subtlety: all slowness and quality belonging to earthly mass, all weight that submits to bodily senses, and all limitation by local spaces have been absorbed by the spirit. He understands with complete purity the Apostle who says: “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body will rise.”

**STUDENT.** I understand, and I embrace the authority of the great man. Concerning the spirituality and non-locality of all human bodies generally after the resurrection, when human nature, which consists of body and soul, will be equal to the angels, I have already been persuaded both by the authority of the holy Fathers [manuscript CF omits “already”] and by what I have perceived within myself [manuscript CF omits “is”]. Consulting reason, I find nothing more probable or closer to the truth than to suppose that bodies will be transformed into a heavenly quality, universally laying aside everything earthly; that they will be incomprehensible to mortal senses [manuscript CF: “comprehensible to immortal beings”]; and that they will be free from every local limitation.

For if the simple elements of this corruptible world, as we have often said, penetrate everything contained within its compass, and the density of no circumscribed body prevents them from being diffused everywhere into all things, who among those who carefully discuss the nature of this visible structure and investigate with the mind’s eye its universal subtlety [CF; manuscript A omits “universal”—or, as it were, its incorporeality—would not assert without hesitation that air, the most tenuous of all things, penetrates all celestial and terrestrial things, as well as things of the air and of the sea, with no obstacle delaying it?

How much more wonderfully, and how much more closely approaching spiritual tenuity, must fiery spirit—simple [manuscripts A and CF: “simple”; manuscript F corrected to “single”], pure, removed from every bodily sense—not only fill and surround all the spaces of the world, but also, by the excessive subtlety of its nature and its likeness to incorporeal natures, pass through the most tenuous air itself, since it is intimate to all things [manuscript F: “pass through” with an altered spelling].

The same must be thought concerning simple water and earth; for they too are present everywhere in all bodies according to their proper proportion. What is surprising, then, if the bodies of the resurrection, rising beyond every sensible quality, freed from all mass and locality, and, so to speak, wholly transformed into spirit, most like life itself, are exalted above everything that bodily sense can reach through their ineffable spiritual subtlety?

As for the claim that the resurrection of bodies will take place with natural power cooperating, and not through the grace of the incarnate Word alone [CF; manuscript A: “not by the incarnate Word’s grace alone”], I am only now beginning to consider it. Where previously I wavered—namely, concerning the natural operation, and whether it is effective for the resurrection—for I attributed the restoration of the human body solely to the grace of the Redeemer, just as you once did, I am now made certain by reason.

For we do not read that God performed any miracle in this world against nature. Rather, divine history relates that all manifestations of power were accomplished through natural causes, both administrative and productive, set in motion by the command of God. And if the general resurrection of the dead is the miracle of miracles, the greatest example of which preceded in Christ, so that it is rightly understood that almost all the other natural arguments were made as a foreshadowing of it, should we think it contrary to the truth to suppose that the resurrection itself will take place through the productive power of natural causes subject to the divine will?

**TEACHER.** The resurrection, then, will be accomplished through the cooperation of both—nature itself and grace.

**STUDENT.** I should think so. But I do not sufficiently perceive what properly belongs to grace and what to nature in this action of resurrection. No one who carefully investigates the secrets of wisdom would say that there is no difference between them.

**TEACHER.** On the contrary, there is a great difference, worthy of diligent inquiry and lucid discovery. In this part of the theory [manuscript CF; manuscript A: “in the theory, that is, concerning the resurrection, three things”], we must observe three things: first, the inexhaustible and infinite diffusion of divine goodness through and within those things that have been made; then, the general and twofold source of that very division, in the things that are given and the things that are bestowed.

Three things, therefore, must be considered: goodness, its gifts, and its endowments. The sharpness of reason distinguishes them from one another and assigns to each its proper character.

The gift (*datum*) of divine goodness is the establishment of the universe and the distribution of all creatures according to their general and particular principles. Superessential goodness, which is God, bestows this universally on all things, from highest to lowest—that is, from intellectual nature, which is the highest of all creatures, down to bodily nature, which occupies the lowest and furthest place in the universe.

The highest goodness therefore gives being to the whole created nature, since it brought it from nonexistence into existence. Hence blessed Dionysius, in the fourth chapter [manuscript A: “chapter four”] of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, says:

> First of all, it is true to say this: that the superessential Divinity, through universal goodness, establishing the essences of the things that are, brought them into being [manuscript A: “First of all, we say according to truth that God established all creatures through goodness, not necessity”].

For it is proper to the Cause of all things, and to goodness above all things [manuscript A: “the goodness of God”], to call existing things to participation, so that each of the things that are may be defined according to its own proper proportion [manuscript A: “to call them according to the definition of each one’s proportion”]. All things that are therefore participate in providence, flowing from the superessential and most causal Divinity [the phrase “and most causal” is omitted in manuscript A; manuscript A reads “flowing from the Deity”]. For perhaps the essences of the things that are would not exist unless they first received their source [manuscript A: “How could anything exist if they did not participate in the cause of things?”].
>
> All existing things therefore participate in his being; for the being of all things is the superbeing of the Divinity [manuscript A: “the superessential Divinity”].

Thus far Dionysius.

Superessential goodness not only gives all things being, but also gives them eternal being. Every essence and substance both is and subsists from no other source than that superessential and supersubstantial goodness [manuscript A: “substantial goodness”], which truly exists and subsists through itself. For no substantial or essential good exists through itself except that goodness alone. Participation in it gives all things their goodness; to the elect alone it grants deification.

No essence or substance created by divine goodness fails to remain eternally and unchangeably. Those things that cannot persevere perpetually are accidents, superadded to substances, gathered around them, and destined to return into them.

The gift of divine goodness, then, is every nature that has been brought into essence and is perpetually preserved so that it does not perish. But since a certain intermediate state is established between being and eternal being, called “well-being,” without which the extremes themselves—being and always being—are neither truly what they are, although they exist, nor rightly said to be, we must understand the following: being and always being, when well-being is removed, are neither truly being nor truly always being. For that truly both is and always is, which subsists well and blessedly.

This innate middle state, namely well-being, is the gift of divine goodness, together with the free and good movement of the will of the intellectual and rational creature. Well-being is produced by these two things: free will and the divine gift, which Holy Scripture calls grace.

But that gift is not distributed generally to all. Deification is bestowed only upon angelic and human nature. Nor is it bestowed upon all members of those natures, but only upon the angels who, burning with love for their Creator, remain established [A: *stabiliti*, “established”; CF: *stabilitati*, “having been made stable”] in contemplation of the truth [manuscript A: “in the contemplation of truth”], and upon those human beings who are called according to purpose.

Moreover, the gift of grace is contained neither within the boundaries of created nature nor does it operate according to natural power. Rather, it accomplishes its effects superessentially and beyond all the natural principles of created things [manuscript A omits “natural”].

Therefore, if the resurrection of the dead occurs through divine grace alone, natural power will be entirely nullified, as will the vital movement that never abandons the substances of things—whether it has fallen silent through force and power, as in the monad of a number, or is manifest in act and operation, as with the numbers proceeding from the monad and with all other things that pass from hidden causes into manifest effects.

Again [manuscript A: “but”], if natural power is effective for resurrection without the assistance of grace, how can it be believed that the power of the Redeemer of the human race prevails in the resurrection of the dead, when he himself said: “I am the resurrection and the life”?

We must not understand this saying of the Lord as referring only to the resurrection of souls—the passage from the death of injustice and impiety to the life of justice and piety, that is, into the contemplation of truth—but also as referring to the resurrection of bodies, the principal example of which he displayed beforehand in his own flesh.

In sound faith, therefore, we can attribute the power of resurrection both to the gift of divine goodness, according to its naturally productive power, and to the endowment of that same goodness, according to grace that surpasses all natures. For the Apostle James also separated these two from one another—the gift, I mean, and the endowment—when he said: “Every good gift and every perfect endowment is from above, descending from the Father of lights.”

As though he were saying plainly: Every establishment and restoration of natures, which is formed from gift and endowment, and every perfect deification of those who are worthy of eternal blessedness—which the Greeks call **θέωσις** (*theōsis*, “deification”)—flows from one source, namely, from above [manuscript CF: “from below”; manuscript A: “from above”], from the Father of lights.

Therefore, as we said earlier, we must understand the gift as applying universally to the substantial establishment of creatures, but the endowment as applying particularly to the superessential deification of the elect [manuscript A omits “universally” and “particularly”].

For divine providence could not, and should not, and could not possibly have established the order of the universe that it created in any other way than by first giving essences and substances, to which it would afterward distribute adornments—that is, bestow virtues according to the dignity of angels and human beings whom it foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the only-begotten Word of God [manuscript A: “to the only-begotten Word of God”].

To conclude briefly [manuscript A: “to conclude briefly”]: nature is the gift, whereas grace is the endowment. Nature brings things from nonexistence into existence; the endowment raises certain existing things beyond all existence into God himself.

For true reason does not permit those who participate in divine communion above all things to be counted among all things. Truth itself says of itself [CF; manuscript A omits “itself”]: “Where I am, there will my servant be also.” We unquestionably believe that he himself is above all things. His servants, therefore, are above all things; the others, who do not attain the power of pure contemplation [the phrase “according to the order of theophanies,” apparently inserted from the margin in manuscript A, is absent from manuscript CF], occupy lower orders, whether among the theophanies or among the sublimities of lower natures.
