I said “among the theophanies” in the plural because neither intellectual nor rational natures will contemplate the truth in the same manner. Rather, the height of contemplation is distributed and determined for each according to its own proportion.

I say this concerning angelic and human nature, which occupy the highest place in the created universe [the entire passage from “I said ‘among the theophanies’” through “which occupy the highest place” is absent from manuscript A]. But we do not say this because any creature, apart from the humanity of the Word [manuscript A omits “apart from the humanity of the Word”], can rise beyond all theophanies and reach, without any intervening theophany, him who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light. Rather, certain theophanies are of such great height that they are understood to be exalted above every creature in contemplation immediately proximate to God, and are believed to be, as it were, theophanies of theophanies.

For God is not visible in himself to any creature at all, but he is seen—and will be seen—in the clouds of contemplation, as the Apostle says: “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ, and so we shall always be with him” [manuscript A adds an extended repetition and rearrangement of the preceding discussion after “we shall be”].

The other natures that Truth itself created—not so that they might contemplate Truth [manuscript A: “which Truth itself did not make for the contemplation of itself”], but so that through them the contemplative powers might praise Truth—both are and will always remain at rest in their orders, free from local limitation and temporal change.

For when the world, which is encompassed by local spaces and temporal movements, has come to an end, what will remain locally circumscribed or subject to temporal change [manuscript A: “subjected”]? Everything will be at rest, since nothing will enter the world through generation and nothing will be dissolved from the world through corruption.

The world will indeed pass away, and no part of it will remain; and consequently, neither will the whole remain. For it will pass into the causes from which it proceeded, in which there are neither places nor times, but only the simple and pure principles of places and times. In those principles all things are one and are distinguished by no accidents.

All things are simple, lacking every composition of substances and accidents; and, so to speak, there is a simple unity and a manifold union of all creatures in their principles and causes, while the causes and principles themselves are united in the only-begotten Word of God, in whom all things were made and subsist.

You therefore understand the difference and distinctive character of nature and grace, that is, of gift and endowment, and their communion.

**STUDENT.** I understand, clearly [CF; manuscript A: “clearly and”], if I am not mistaken, and therefore I shall briefly gather together what you have said.

**TEACHER.** Gather it together.

**STUDENT.** You said that nature is the gift, whereas grace is the endowment [manuscript CF omits “whereas grace is the endowment”].

**TEACHER.** So I did.

**STUDENT.** You also added the distinctive character of each. You assigned to nature existence from nothing and perpetual continuance; to grace, deification—that is, the making of those human beings whom the abundance of divine goodness freely exalts, without the aid of nature [manuscript A: *subdito*, “subjected,” apparently an uncertain or corrupt reading], without any preceding merits, above all things that exist and all things contained within the limits of the created universe, so that they pass into God [manuscript A: “and those whom it exalts”].

Their common element, however—of nature and grace, I mean—is understood to be the resurrection of human substance: that is, the passage of mortal bodies into immortal bodies, of corruptible bodies into incorruptible, of animal bodies into spiritual bodies, and of temporal and local things into eternal things free from every limitation.

**TEACHER.** You have gathered it correctly [CF: *Rate* for *Recte*]. This is what I wished to persuade you of, and, as I see, I have persuaded you [CF: *te* for *tibi*].

**STUDENT.** Yet I still hesitate, because I do not contemplate clearly enough how you appear to assert not only the resurrection of human nature but also that of all sensible things encompassed by the compass of this world.

**TEACHER.** I never cease to wonder why you hesitate so often about such matters, when you have frequently admitted, after being persuaded [CF: *suasum te* for *suasum tibi*], that all things were created in the human being [manuscript A: “were created in the human being”]—I mean visible and invisible things—and that afterward they will rise again.

But it is not our present purpose to discuss the resurrection of invisible things. We are discussing the resurrection of bodily sensible things [manuscript CF omits “bodily”], that is, their return into their causes [manuscript CF omits “their”].

If, then, human nature is composed of intelligible and bodily sensible things—of soul, I mean, and body [F: *anima* (“soul”); A: *animo* (“mind”); C: *animi* (“of the soul”)]—what is surprising if the universe of all sensible things rises again in the human body and passes wherever the human body passes?

I speak only of their passing into the causes, not into deification itself, which will be bestowed upon the most purified intellects alone. And if you desire to hear the strongest argument concerning this, pay attention and consider what follows.

To begin our discussion from the simplicity of the catholic faith [F, corrected above the line: “But that we may begin from the faith”; A: “But from the true faith”; CF: “But that we may begin from the faith”], from which every assent begins toward the purest knowledge of things: you believe, I suppose, that all things that are and that are not—that is, things subject to sense and intellect [CF: “subject to sense and intellect,” without *quae*], and things that surpass every sense and intellect, yet, to use the words of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, revolve around God—were made in the Word of God, though they remain unknown to the lower natures beneath them.

### 24.

**DISCIPLE.** I believe this without hesitation and, insofar as I am illumined by the light from above, understand it, hearing Holy Scripture say: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”—calling the Only-Begotten Word “the beginning,” in whom the Father made all things, and signifying by the names “heaven” and “earth” the invisible and visible creature. Elsewhere he says plainly—that is, universally: “You made all things in wisdom.” By saying “all things,” he included the universality of all creatures as having been made in the Word of God. [Col. 0907C]

**MASTER.** Do you therefore think that all things made in the wisdom of God are alive or lack life—or, to put it more truly and clearly, whether everything made in God’s wisdom is life and wisdom, and participates in life and wisdom, or not? And if everything made in divine wisdom is life and wisdom [Note: A reads “made in divine wisdom.”], did it begin to exist in time, or was it always, so that there was never a time when it was not? And if this is so, there will never be a time when it is not; for if it began in time, it must end with time.

**DISCIPLE.** Far be it from the hearts of the faithful to think that everything made in the Word of God is not life—wise and eternal life—without any temporal beginning and without any temporal end. [Col. 0907D] For bodies also, and every sensible creature, are wise and eternal life in him, so that, in an ineffable and incomprehensible manner—yet in a manner that can be believed [Note: A reads “in an incomprehensible, yet believable, manner.”]—every creature lives in him and is life. And since nothing exists outside him, he brought forth created creatures from himself, as though from outside.

For we say that the whole creature exists both within him and outside him, in this sense: within him are said to be the causes and principles of things, because of their likeness to them and their simplicity; outside him [Note: A reads “outside him indeed”] are their effects [Note: CF omits “their”], because of a certain dissimilarity. [Col. 0908A] For they vary in places and times and are distinguished by genera and species, properties and accidents. Therefore they are said to be, as it were, outside the simplicity of divine wisdom, although nothing is outside it and all things in it are universal and simple life.

For what could there be in the wisdom of God that lacked life or was not life, since wisdom itself is true life and more than life, and nothing is in it that is not itself or most like it? Especially since the theologian John says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made; in him was life.” [Col. 0908B]

**MASTER.** In the Word, then, which is the wisdom of God [Note: CF reads “the wisdom of God”; A has “divine wisdom.”], every creature both exists and lives, and everything that is in him cannot perish. For if that which contains it remains and lives eternally and incommunicably—indeed, if it is life and eternal life—everything contained in it necessarily exists, remains forever, and is eternal life [Note: CF reads “and is eternal life”; A omits “is.”].

**DISCIPLE.** It is both impious and foolish to doubt this, since the authority of the whole divine history and all the theologians affirm that every creature eternally exists in the Word of God [Note: A omits “of God”]. Hence Saint Augustine, in the sixteenth chapter of the twelfth book of *The City of God*, stated most clearly and briefly that God was always not only the Creator of all creatures but also their Lord; and just as he was never not Creator, so he was never not Lord. [Col. 0908C] He argues:

“Therefore, if the Lord God was always Lord, he always had a creature serving his lordship—yet not begotten from him, but made by him from nothing, and not coeternal with him. For he existed before it, although at no time was he without it, preceding it not by an interval of passing time but by abiding perpetuity. But if I answer those who ask how he was always Creator and always Lord if the serving creature did not always exist, or how it was created and was not rather coeternal with the Creator if it always existed, I fear that I may more easily be judged to assert what I do not know than to teach what I do know.” [Note: A omits “Lord” in “if the Lord God”; A reads “from himself” for “from him”; A reads “permanently” for “abiding.”]

It is as though that distinguished Father, openly exposing the slowness of creatures capable of eternity, were saying: “If I assert what I know with the utmost certainty—namely, that God was always Creator and Lord of the creature, and therefore that a serving creature was always present—for if a serving creature did not always exist, it follows that he was neither always Creator nor always Lord of the creature; but because he was always Creator and Lord, it necessarily follows that a serving creature was always created and present [Note: CF reads “was always created and present”; A omits “created”]—for it is not accidental to the Creator of all things to have created what he created; rather, by perpetuity he rises above and surpasses what he created [Note: CF supports *superascendit*, “rises above”; A reads *semper ascendit*, “always ascends”]—I fear, ironically, that I may be judged to assert what I do not know rather than teach what I do know.” [Col. 0908D–0909A]

I understand without hesitation that the creature and its Creator, the Lord and that which serves him, have always been inseparably present—not because the creature is coeternal with the Creator, or that which serves is coeternal with the Lord. The Creator precedes the creature, and the Lord that which serves him, by eternity, not by time, but in the sense that the Creator and Lord is the beginning of the creature and of that which serves him, while the Creator and Lord is *ἄναρχος*, that is, without beginning. [Note: CF reads “serves” for A’s “serving”; CF omits “but.”]

We call our Creator and Lord one and the only God, namely, the supreme and holy Trinity, one essence in three substances. When considered in itself, only the Father in it is believed to be *ἄναρχος*; for the Son and the Holy Spirit are not wholly *ἄναρχοι*, since they have a beginning—by “beginning” I mean the Father. For the Son is begotten from him [Note: A reads “generated”], while the Holy Spirit proceeds. [Col. 0909B]

**MASTER.** You think, I suppose, that only the primordial causes were created in God and served their Lord, but not their effects, through which we rightly believe this composite sensible world to have been formed.

**DISCIPLE.** I think so. For I believe that the causes of things were always created, while their effects emerged into this world at definite intervals of place and time, are still emerging, and will continue to emerge. [Col. 0909C]

**MASTER.** This opinion should be judged to depart neither from the Catholic faith nor from true understanding. What, then? Do you think that only the causes of things were eternal, while their effects were temporal, and therefore that the causes alone will always remain, while the effects will perish?

**DISCIPLE.** I had always been accustomed to think so. But after I began with you to travel along the path of this present discussion, the sharpness of reason and, as it were, the unavoidable sequence of things began to draw me on, so that I have conceded that not only the causes but also their processions—which the wise call effects—will remain perpetually, though on this condition: the processions themselves will remain not in themselves but by returning to their causes.

**MASTER.** I see that you still hesitate about this.

**DISCIPLE.** I cannot deny it. For what I had thought about these matters on my own is compelled by true reason to waver [Note: CF reads “to waver”; A reads “to change”], while the unfamiliar things you wish to introduce have not yet been made fully clear to me [Note: CF omits “have been.”]. [Col. 0909D]

**MASTER.** Tell me, please, what you see clearly and distinctly, and about what you still either waver completely or are beginning partly to understand, while obscurity and subtlety partly elude the vision of your mind.

**DISCIPLE.** The vision of my mind suffers no darkness concerning the causes made eternally, always remaining, and destined to remain forever. [Col. 0910A] I see this clearly and without any cloud, especially because I am led by the consideration that I not only believe but also understand without hesitation that they were created in the wisdom of God [Note: CF reads “in the wisdom of God”; A has “in divine wisdom.”]. No one except an impious or foolish person would doubt that everything established as created in the wisdom of God will remain forever [Note: A has “no one who is not impious”; A also reads “will doubt,” rather than “would doubt.”].

As for the effects, which, following the wise, you called the processions of the causes, I have long been considering whether, like their causes, they will remain, or perish with the world, so that they will not return to their causes and be saved in them but will be reduced to the nothingness from which they were made [Note: The corrected reading is “will be reduced”; A and CF have “will reduce”], so that they will no longer exist at all.

**MASTER.** By the effects of the causes we now mean the whole sensible world with all its constituent parts. For concerning the intelligible world there is an unquestionable judgment that it will never perish, since there is nothing in it subject to corruption. [Col. 0910B] It always subsists, just as do the causes whose effect it is—that is, the celestial essences—although blessed Dionysius the Areopagite asserts [Note: CF reads “asserts”; A reads “affirms”] that certain angelic powers will ascend to a higher degree of divine contemplation than that which they now possess, when God will be all in all.

### 25.

**DISCIPLE.** I still hesitate about the effects of invisible causes—I mean the invisible world [Note: CF reads “I mean the visible world”]. I am considering how it can be said that it will perish and remain, for these seem to contradict one another: I mean, to perish and to remain. How can what remains perish, or what perishes remain? [Col. 0910C]

**MASTER.** Did you not confess a little earlier that you had been led chiefly to this conclusion, so that you would in no way doubt the eternity of the causes, because they were made in the Word of God? For everything contained by the Word, which is always living, and in which all things are always life, cannot perish, since it is subject to neither corruption nor decay [Note: CF omits “always”].

**DISCIPLE.** I have indeed been brought to this conclusion—to such an extent that I would rather say that I do not exist at all than that I could be ignorant of it—hearing the Apostle say: “In him we live and move and are.” For if I am not in him, I do not exist at all; and if I am ignorant of this, I am lost in the destruction of folly and ignorance [Note: A omits the first “in.”].

**MASTER.** Tell me, then: did the Word of God, in whom the causes of all things eternally subsist, come into the effects of the causes—that is, into this sensible world—or not?

**DISCIPLE.** Whoever denies this is entirely alien to the true religion in which the one God is worshiped and the incarnation of the Word of God is proclaimed [Note: A has “the Word being proclaimed separately”]. For Theology says: “And the Word was made flesh”—that is, the Word was made man. It used “flesh” for the whole human being, according to the manner of speech by which the whole is signified through a part. [Col. 0910D]

Likewise, the incarnate Word, speaking of himself, says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.” As though he were saying plainly:

“I, who according to my divinity am equal to the Father and exist as of the one and same essence as he, came forth from him—that is, I emptied myself, taking the form of a servant. I became flesh, and received the whole of human nature. Again I leave the world and go to the Father—that is, I transform into my Deity the servant’s form and the whole of human nature, namely body, soul, and intellect, and universally everything that I assumed from that creature which consists of visible and intelligible existence; I exalt it above the whole world, into my Deity, while the principle of the natures from which I subsist remains preserved, and I raise it above all things that are and that are not [Note: CF reads “I exalt”; A has “having been exalted”]. [Col. 0911A]

“He therefore came forth from the Father and came into the world: he assumed human nature, in which the whole world subsists. For nothing exists in the world that is not comprehended in human nature. Again he left the world and went to the Father: he united and exalted to his Deity, which is equal to the Father [Note: CF reads “which is equal to the Father”; A has “which is the equal of the Father”], the human nature he had assumed—namely, above all visible and invisible things, above all heavenly powers, above everything that is spoken or understood.

“Although he received the whole of human nature and saved the whole of it in himself and in the whole human race—restoring some to the original state of nature and deifying others beyond nature through excellence—nevertheless, in no one but himself was humanity united to Deity in a unity of substance and, transformed into that Deity, raised above all things. The Head of the Church reserved this privilege for himself: that not only his humanity should become a participant in Deity, but that it should itself become Deity after he ascended to the Father. No one except him has ascended to that height, nor will anyone ascend. [Col. 0911B–C]

“This is what he says plainly elsewhere about himself: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.’ As though he were saying openly: No one ascends to the Father except he who descended from the Father; and while descending from the Father he did not abandon the Father—he who is always in the Father, because the Father is inseparably in him and he is always in the Father. For he says: ‘I and the Father are one.’

“Into this unity he alone raised his humanity. But the others whom he deifies he places after himself, each according to the height of his own contemplation, through participation alone in his Deity [Note: A reads “divinity”; CF reads “Deity”], arranging in himself, as in a certain house [Note: CF reads “house”], all whom he chose to make conformed to himself [Note: CF reads “chose to make his own likeness”].” [Col. 0911D]

Thus God the Word of God—in whom, through whom, and toward whom all things were made, and in whom they causally subsist—according to his divinity descended into the effects of the causes that subsist in him, namely, into this sensible world, assuming human nature, in which every visible and invisible creature is contained.

**DISCIPLE.** The Catholic faith agrees with this without hesitation. For the Word of God himself, having become man, after rising from the dead instructed his disciples and said: “Preach the gospel to every creature,” calling man “every creature.” [Col. 0912A] He did not command that his gospel be preached to irrational animals or to every creature lacking sensation [Note: CF reads “he did not command that it be preached”; A reverses the order to “he commanded that it be preached”], but only to man, in whom every created nature is contained.

**MASTER.** So every creature is in man?

**DISCIPLE.** This must be confessed without doubt.

**MASTER.** You therefore confess that the Word of God—in whom, through whom, and toward whom all things were made—according to his divinity descended, according to his humanity, into the effects of the causes?

**DISCIPLE.** I confess it most firmly.

**MASTER.** Why did he descend?

**DISCIPLE.** Please tell me.

**MASTER.** For no other reason, I think, than to save, according to his humanity, the effects of the causes which, according to his divinity, he possesses eternally and immutably, and to recall them into their causes, so that in those causes they too might be saved through an ineffable kind of union, just as the causes themselves are saved [Note: CF reads “just as the causes themselves”; A has “just as the cause itself”]. [Col. 0912B]

As though he were saying plainly: If the wisdom of God did not descend into the effects of the causes that eternally live in it, the principle of the causes would perish. For when the effects of the causes perish, no cause would remain, just as when the causes perish no effects would remain; for these things, according to the relation of correlatives, either arise together and perish together, or remain together and forever [Note: CF omits this passage].

**DISCIPLE.** The whole world, therefore, has already been restored in a particular way in the incarnate and humanized Only-Begotten Word of God; but at the end of the world it will be restored generally and universally in the same Word. What he accomplished particularly in himself, he will accomplish generally in all—not, I mean, merely in all human beings, but in every sensible creature. [Col. 0912C]

For when the Word of God assumed human nature, he did not omit any created substance that he did not assume in it [Note: A omits “in it”; A reads “assumed” rather than “had assumed”]. Therefore, by assuming human nature, he assumed every creature. And consequently, if he saved and restored the human nature he assumed, he certainly restored every visible and invisible creature.

For this reason we do not believe or understand without cause that the incarnation of the Word of God benefited angels no less than human beings. It benefited human beings for their redemption and the restoration of their nature; it benefited angels for their knowledge. Before it was incarnate, the Word was incomprehensible to every visible and invisible creature—that is, to every intellectual and rational creature, namely angels and human beings—because it was remote and hidden above everything that is and is not, above everything that is spoken and understood. [Col. 0912D]

But once incarnate, descending in a certain manner through a wondrous, ineffable, and manifold theophany without end, it advanced into the knowledge of the angelic and human nature. And, though unknown above all things, it assumed from all things a nature in which it might be known, uniting the sensible and intelligible worlds in itself through an incomprehensible harmony. It granted access to the inaccessible light for every intellectual and rational creature.

Hence the universal Church does not cease to sing the angelic hymn in common, in heaven and on earth, with intelligible and sensible voice: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” [Col. 0913A]

To conclude briefly: in him all visible and invisible things—that is, the sensible and intelligible world—have been restored and recalled into an ineffable unity: still in hope, but in the future in reality; still in faith, but in the future in vision; still in argument, but in the future in experience; already in the man whom he specially assumed, but in the future to be perfected generally in all.

Let no one therefore think little of the fact that the Word of God was humanized, as though he had merely saved human nature [Note: CF reads “had merely saved”; A has “saved”]. Let him believe most firmly and understand most purely that through the humanization of the Son of God every creature in heaven and on earth has been saved [Note: F omits the second *in*]. [Col. 0913B]

By “every creature” I mean body, vital movement, sensation, and, above these, reason and intellect. Do you think that any nature exists outside these and God?

**MASTER.** None. For no other division of the whole creature can be found [Note: A omits “for.”]. If something exists, it will be either an intellect, known or unknown, or reason, or sensation, or the life that nourishes and enlarges bodies, or body itself [Note: A reverses the order to “body itself”]. And the incarnate Word of God assumed all these.

**DISCIPLE.** What, then, are we to say? Were irrational animals, and even trees and herbs, and all the parts of this world, from highest to lowest, restored in the incarnate Word of God [Note: CF reads “were restored”; A has “might be”]? [Col. 0913C]

**MASTER.** I am amazed that you repeat the same matter so many times. Did not the Word, by assuming man, assume every visible and invisible creature, and save everything that he assumed in man [Note: CF reads “and”; A has “or”]? But if he assumed every creature by assuming human nature, he certainly saved every creature, and will save it forever [Note: CF reads “will save forever”; A has “will be its savior”].

**DISCIPLE.** Will bodily masses, therefore, extended through local spaces and composed of many different parts, and likewise the visible forms by which those masses are held together so that they do not flow into one, rise again in the general resurrection of human beings [Note: A omits “of human beings”]? And consequently, if the parts themselves rise again into the masses, forms, and shapes by which the visible world is both adorned and composed, it follows that the whole world will not perish but will return to the same state. For if the parts will be restored, why not the whole [Note: CF reads “the whole”; A has “the entire”]? [Col. 0913D]

**MASTER.** We do not say that the masses and forms of visible and sensible bodies will rise again. Rather, as we had often agreed among ourselves, at the resurrection of man they will return with man and in man into their causes and principles, which were made in man. In those causes all animals must be said to be animals more truly than in their bodily and sensible effects. For where they subsist, there they are truly animals. [Col. 0914A]

The same must be understood of all sensible things, whether celestial or terrestrial. Everything that varies in places and times and is subject to bodily senses should be understood not as the substantial and truly existing things themselves, but as certain transient images and reflections of those truly existing things.

An example of this principle is a voice and its image, which the Greeks call *ἠχώ* (*ēchō*, “echo”), or bodies and their shadows, whether the shadows are formed in pure air, in water, or in whatever other substance from which they commonly rebound. All these are proved to be not things themselves but false images of things. [Col. 0914B]

Thus, just as images of voices and shadows of bodies do not subsist through themselves, because they are not substances, so these sensible bodies are certain likenesses of subsisting things and do not know how to subsist through themselves.

Human bodies too, which are now extended locally, vary through increase and decrease and are moved. Their forms also—whether general forms, which all human bodies share [Note: CF omits “human”], or particular forms, by which the quantity of individual bodies is bounded [Note: A has “the particular form by which”]—will not exist in the future resurrection [Note: CF reads “will not exist”; A has “do not exist”]. Natural reason teaches that they will pass into a spiritual nature which cannot be bounded by places or times, or even by its own forms, which are derived from quality and quantity [Note: A reads “will be passing over”].

In saying this, we do not prescribe the opinions of those who discuss the resurrection of bodies in an entirely different manner. For they affirm that human bodies will exist in the quantity and form in which each fell, and they maintain that their sex—male or female—will remain. We shall speak of them later.

That animals will exist again in the manner we have described—that is, in their causes—we can argue without hesitation from the words of Saint Dionysius. Discussing the divine life in the sixth chapter of *The Divine Names*, he says:

“The life and immortality of the immortal angels, and the very imperishability of their perpetual movement, are from and through divine life itself. Therefore they are called ever-living and immortal, and yet are not again immortal, because they do not possess immortal being and eternal life from themselves, but from the life-giving cause that makes and preserves every life.

“And as we speak in the case of being—*ὄντι*—that is, when treating of essence (for the Greeks call *ὄν* ‘divine essence,’ as also *οὐσία* [*ousia*], because it is the causal principle of the same being) [Note: CF omits “divine”; A reads “just as”], so again in the case of life: because divine life is life through itself, it is vital and substantial life, and every life and vital movement derives from that life which is above every life and is the beginning of all life.

“From it souls possess imperishability, and all animals and plants possess life according to the final harmony of the soul. When it is removed, both general life and particular and individual life [Note: CF reads *quam speciales et singulares* (“as particular and individual [lives]”) for printed *quam speciali et singulari*], according to the saying, fails from the earth; and when those animals and plants which fail through weakness in participating in it turn back again, they again become animals.” [Col. 0914C–0915A]

In these words of the aforementioned theologian, we understand not that the irrational animals or things lacking sensation will be restored to the former forms and quantities with which this world is filled, but that they will return to their causes, from which they proceed and in which they subsist. For he did not say that divine life is the cause only of angelic and human life—that is, of intellectual and rational life—but universally of every life.

Every life, however, is either rational, as was discussed at length in the preceding books [Note: CF reads “as was discussed”; A has “as we discussed”], or irrational, or nutritive and augmentative of bodies. That is, it is either angelic, human, animal, or the life of things lacking sensation, such as trees, herbs, and other similar things, in which only vital movement operates. [Col. 0915B]

Consequently, the divine utterance speaks not only of human life but of all the kinds of life mentioned above, and not only of human bodies but of all bodies that the spirit of life animates: “You take away their spirit, and they fail, and they return to their dust.”

For no life—whether rational, animal, or nutritive—can for long, not to say forever, vivify and govern corruptible and mortal bodies. Therefore it abandons them; and when it abandons them, the bodies fail and return to their dust [Note: CF reads “the bodies fail”; A has “they fail”].

This is what he says: “And they fail”—that is, animals and plants fail in participation in life because of that weakness [Note: CF reads “in weakness”; A has “in participating in that weakness”]. They cannot participate forever in life because of the weakness and fragility of corruptible earthly bodies. [Col. 0915C]

The natural operation of life in bodies, whether by governing them or abandoning them, is referred to the Creator of all things. Therefore he says: “You take away their spirit”—not because God takes away the spirit from any body, but because he allows spirits burdened by corruptible bodies to depart from them for a time [Note: CF reads “allows”; A has “ceases”], returning again by natural movement when they have been transformed into the same incorruptibility and spirituality [Note: A has “when it has been transformed”].

For they cannot forever abandon what is congenial to them in this world; but when the world has come to an end, they will receive it again, when that which governs and that which is governed will become one inseparable thing in their causes through a wondrous harmony [Note: CF omits “in a wondrous harmony”]. [Col. 0915D]

Therefore he says: “Send forth your spirit, and they will be created.” As though he were saying: “Send forth the vital spirit that you made—that is, permit it, desiring by natural appetite to return, to be sent forth and return into the bodies that it temporarily abandoned. And you will renew the face of the earth”—that is, by inseparably joining bodies with their vital forms, you will restore the integrity of nature that is mystically signified by the name “earth” [Note: A reverses the phrase to “signified by the name of earth”]. [Col. 0916A]

If this seems incredible to anyone and contrary to natural reason—that irrational and insensible things should pass into human nature—let him first observe attentively that the lower parts of human nature, namely bodily sensation, nutritive life, and the body itself, are very similar to the conditions of irrational, insensible, and earthly bodies.

But if this is so, what is surprising or incredible if like things pass into their likeness, so that from many similar things one thing like them is produced—provided that lower likenesses pass into the higher things whose likenesses they are [Note: A reads “if like things pass into like things, that is, into higher things, and so forth”]?

For natural reason does not permit higher things to be changed into lower things; rather, lower things naturally desire higher things and wish to be united with them [Note: A omits “wish.”]. [Col. 0916B]

Let him also observe that the passions of irrational creatures—which human nature drew into itself after the fall of man, as a certain punishment for sin, though it had not naturally possessed them before the fall—can be moved in those who are perfect into natural virtues.

By passions I mean pleasure and sadness, desire and fear, and whatever arises from them; there is no doubt that these can be changed into virtues. For example, intellectual desire produces the movement of those who desire divine things; pleasure produces the harmless joy of the soul’s nutritive activity; fear produces prudent care concerning future punishment for offenses; and sadness produces repentance that corrects present evils. [Col. 0916C]

If, then, the passions that rational nature had drawn into itself from irrational nature can be changed into natural virtues of the soul, why should it be incredible that irrationality itself can be transformed into the height of rationality?

Pride too, which is regarded as the head of all wickedness, is turned in good people into love of heavenly excellence and contempt for earthly weakness, as the Apostle says: “Set your minds on the things above, not on the things upon the earth” [Note: A reads “and not on the things upon the earth”].

In short, it must be said that there is no vice which, when divine grace operates in the wise, cannot be changed into virtue [Note: A omits “in them.”]. Thus goodness commonly comes from wickedness, but wickedness never comes from goodness. For the power of goodness consumes its contrary within itself [Note: CF reads “consumes”; A has “changes into itself”]. The disgrace of wickedness cannot discolour the beauty of goodness.

If, then, we do not deny that vices, although mutually contrary, can be changed into virtues, why should we deny that lower natures can be transformed into higher natures through a wondrous union, since they are in no way opposed to one another?

**MASTER.** Enough has been said about these matters [Note: CF omits “has been said.”]

**DISCIPLE.** Quite enough.
