### 26. TEACHER

Since, in treating the resurrection of bodies—which is to take place through natural power cooperating with divine grace, by the incarnation of the Savior of the world—we introduced the testimony of blessed Epiphanius, I think it necessary to introduce also the opinion of the great theologian Gregory [A: “so great”] concerning the same matter.

### STUDENT

Necessary indeed. For what has thus been promised—or, according to A, “permitted”—and what is established on the testimony of two competent witnesses appears unshakable.

### TEACHER

In the twenty-second [CF: “the twentieth and II”] chapter, therefore, while discussing *On the Image*, he says that the resurrection is hoped for not so much from the preaching of Scripture as from the very necessity of things:

“But malice is not so powerful,” he says [A: “Thus is malice powerful,” he says], “as to overcome the strength of goodness. For our nature’s lack of counsel—I mean its foolishness—is neither better nor more singular, that is, simpler, than the wisdom of God. It is not possible that what is convertible and changeable should be more powerful or more singular than what always remains in the same condition and is fixed in the good [CF: ‘than what always remains similarly, producing the good’].

“For the divine purpose [CF: “But”] is always [CF: *atque*, “and”] and everywhere immutable [CF: “everywhere immutable”; *se*, “itself,” omitted]; but what is convertible in our nature does not remain fixed in evil. For whatever is always in motion, if indeed it has made progress toward the good, will never cease from the upward movement toward the One who is above, because of the excellence of the object to be sought. Nor will one who attains it ever bring that movement to rest [CF: *nihil non nascentis*, “nothing of the one coming into being,” for *qui*].

“But if it has undertaken movement [CF: “moment”] toward what is contrary [CF: “Nor”], when [CF: “when indeed”] it has completed its course through malice and reached the highest measure of evil, then what is always moved by impulse, finding no state of rest in its nature, while [CF: “after”] the extent that lies in malice has been traversed, necessarily turns its movement toward the good [CF: “into the good”]. For since malice does not advance to infinity [CF: *progrediatur*, “may advance”], but is enclosed within necessary limits, the succession of the good will consequently follow upon the end of malice.

“Thus, as has been said, the ever-moving element of our nature will finally return to the good way [CF: ‘will again return firmly to the good way’], being chastened by the memory of its former miseries, so that it may not fall back into equal ones [CF: ‘being restrained by the memory of former calamities from returning again to what is right’]. Therefore our course in the good will again take place [CF: “Therefore not again”], because the nature of malice is bounded on every side by necessary limits.

“For just as those skilled in the higher matters [CF: “those who know the ethereal spaces”] say that the whole world is full of light, while darkness is produced by the shadow cast through the interposition of an earthly body, when the shadow, from the sun’s rays behind it, is enclosed in the form of a cone according to the shape of the rounded body [CF: ‘I understand this shadowing through the figure of a spherical body, with the sun’s ray enclosing the shape of a cone’]; for the sun, greatly surpassing the earth in size and embracing it on every side with its rays, joins the points where the light converges at the summit of the cone [CF: “The sun greatly surpasses the earth in size, embracing it everywhere round about with its rays and joining the convergences of light at the summit of the cone, so that, if anyone were given the power to pass beyond the measure to which the shadow extends”]—so, if, according to the hypothesis, some power were given to anyone to pass beyond the measure to which the shadow extends, he would be entirely in the light and unharmed by the darkness—so, I think, we ought also to think about ourselves [CF: ‘understand’]. When we have passed beyond the limit of malice, and have reached the summit of the shadow of sin, we shall again dwell in the light, in proportion as the nature of the good abounds without limit in comparison with the measure of malice.

“Again, then, there will be paradise; again, that whole tree, which is also the tree of life; again, the grace of the image and the dignity of the principle.”

Observe how clearly, rationally, and confidently he establishes the following points. First, malice cannot be perpetual, but by the necessity of things must reach a definite limit and at some time [CF: “at some time”; A: “whenever”] cease [A: “fail”]. For if divine goodness—which always works good not only in the good but also in the evil—is eternal and infinite [A: “is eternal and infinite”], its contrary necessarily will not be eternal and infinite; otherwise it would not be its contrary, nor opposed to it from a different side [A: “from an opposing side”]. For things that are eternal, although they differ in quality, agree with one another solely in the equality of their eternity. Divine mercy and severity differ in quality: the one punishes sins, the other forgives; yet both are eternal.

Malice, however, is wholly opposed to divine goodness. Malice, therefore, will receive its consummation and will remain in no nature, since divine goodness will both work and appear in all things. Accordingly, the author quoted above asserts that our nature is not fixed in evil and will not always be held by malice, but will return to the good when all evil has reached its limit.

Just as the shadow of the earth, which they call night, does not extend without limit through the spaces of air and ether, but, as physicists maintain, is compressed within one hundred and twenty-six [A: “one hundred and twenty-six”] thousand stadia by the solar rays diffused around the earth on every side and is sharpened into the likeness of a cone, so that it finally disappears altogether, so malice—which, like a certain shadow of our sins, occupies our nature—will be compressed by the abundance of the higher and eternal goodness [A: “and eternal”] and will be utterly destroyed, while the irrational movements of the human soul are converted into the rational affections of truth.

[Note: It scarcely needs to be pointed out that what John Scotus now argues concerning the abolition of evil and concerning the punishments and torments of the wicked, whether human beings or demons, is wholly contrary to Catholic truth. See the commentary on John Scotus, Part II, §57 above, columns 78 and 79.]

Next, he asserts without hesitation that our nature is always in motion, a view that nearly all divine philosophers also approve. It desires nothing else than the supreme good, from which, as from a principle, it begins to move, and toward which, as toward an end, it hastens its movement [A: “as toward the end”]. The whole rational creature—which is properly understood to subsist in human beings [A: “is understood to subsist”]—even amid its sins and crooked wanderings, always seeks its God, from whom it exists and for the contemplation of whom it was created [A: “its Lord”].

For rational nature never desires evil; yet in many things it is deceived and misled, approving false things in place of true ones—which is characteristic of error and of one who does not enter the straight way toward the supreme good, which it always seeks. This perverted movement itself is not improperly called by the name “malice.”

Malice is the intellectual soul’s forgetfulness of its natural goods; it is the failure to exercise the virtues implanted in its nature toward their end; and it is the irrational movement of its natural powers, through deceptive judgment, toward something other than their end. By “end” I mean the cause of existing things, which all things naturally desire.

Therefore, when that irrational movement—which is both the cause and the fullness of all evil and malice—has been completely enclosed and brought to an end by the amplitude of goodness, human nature will move rationally according to the natural virtues implanted within it. Raised upright toward what is above, it will always desire its cause; it will return to paradise—that is, to the delights of the virtues naturally implanted in it—which it had lost through sin [A: *insertas*, “inserted,” for *insitas*, “implanted”]; it will ardently desire the food of the tree of life, namely, the contemplation of the Word of God; and it will hasten to recover the dignity of the divine image, according to which it was made.

But since [A omits “since”] what it seeks and desires, whether it moves rightly or wrongly, is infinite, incomprehensible to every creature, and necessarily [CF: “necessarily”] always sought, it therefore always moves [A: “and therefore always moves through what it seeks”]. It always seeks and, in a wondrous manner [A: “in a wondrous way”], somehow finds what it seeks—and does not find it, because it cannot find it. It finds it through theophanies, but it does not find it through contemplation of the divine nature in itself.

By “theophanies” I mean the forms of visible and invisible things, through whose order and beauty God is known to exist [A: “that God exists”] and is found—not what He is, but only that He is; for the very nature of God is neither spoken of nor understood. The inaccessible light surpasses every intellect.

This is what the Psalmist says: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually.” This is that spiritual way which extends to infinity, and which pure and perfect souls enter while seeking their God. The heavenly virtues also always seek their God, whom they continually desire to behold.

This is the darkness of which Dionysius the Areopagite, writing to Dorotheus, says:

“Divine darkness is inaccessible light [A: “light inaccessible”], in which God is said to dwell. Although He is invisible [A: “and although indeed He is invisible”] because of His surpassing brightness and the inaccessible transcendence [A: “and inaccessible because of the abundance”] of the superessential outpouring of lights [A: “effusion”], everyone worthy of knowing and seeing God enters into this state: he does not himself see or truly know the light in which he has been placed beyond vision and knowledge. He knows only that God exists in all sensible and intelligible things, and he says prophetically: ‘Your knowledge has become wonderful from me; it has been strengthened, and I cannot attain to it.’

“Thus also the divine Paul is said to have known God by knowing that He exists beyond all understanding and knowledge. Therefore he says that God’s ways are unsearchable, His judgments inscrutable, His gifts unspeakable, and His peace surpasses all understanding. In this way he finds Him above all things and, by understanding Him beyond understanding, knows that He is above all things, existing as the cause of all.

“The same author says in his letter to the monk Gaius:

“‘Darkness,’ he says [A: “he indeed says”], ‘is obscure in the light, and even more so in abundant light. Ignorance conceals knowledge, and even more so abundant knowledge. Receive this supereminently, but not according to privation; affirm [A: “proclaim”] this as supremely true, because it is hidden [lacuna]—even those who possess the incomprehensible light do not know what it is that they possess. The Evangelist testifies: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” Therefore the divine light is commonly called “darkness,” because it is incomprehensible.

“‘Likewise, the gnostic power of those who contemplate it is frequently called “darkness,” because it is struck back by that light. For it escapes those who possess light and knowledge of things [lacuna]—ignorance according to the Lord; and its transcendent darkness is veiled by every light and conceals all knowledge.

“‘If someone, seeing the Lord, understood what he saw, he did not contemplate the Lord Himself, but something belonging to those things that exist from Him and are known. He Himself, placed above the soul and above being, is universally neither known nor seen; rather, He is known superessentially and above the soul. This most perfect ignorance, insofar as it is better, is itself knowledge of Him beyond all things known.’”

Nor did the Evangelist omit this, when he said: “No one has ever seen God.” And as Ambrose says: “Just as He has never been visible, so He will never be visible.”

The Truth itself also says [CF: “what”]: “No one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father.”

But whether the humanity of the Word of God, like His divinity, is incomprehensible to every creature and surpasses every intellect, after it was assumed into the divinity of the Word and made one substance with it—without any confusion of the two natures, namely the divine and [A: “and”] the human, from which those who share the orthodox faith believe and understand that one Christ, our Lord and Savior, consists—or whether it is circumscribed within the limits of the created universe and is knowable to rational and intelligible nature, that is, confined within numbers that can be known, let each person state his opinion as he wishes [CF: “whoever wishes, as he wishes”].

For my part, I unhesitatingly follow those who do not rashly proclaim that the humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ is united to His divinity in such a way that it is one with it and in it, while the proper character of the natures remains intact; for there is one substance, or, to put it in the more customary way, one person: the humanity and divinity of Christ.

And just as His divinity surpasses every intellect, so also His humanity—which has been exalted above the universality of visible and intelligible creation, above all places and times, above every circumscription and definition, above all heavens, above all virtues and powers, above everything that is spoken and understood, above everything that exists after God, and has been made superessential—is incomprehensible and unsearchable to every creature.

We have taught this in the preceding text of this work.

### 27. DISCIPLE

You have persuasively argued at length, and the holy Fathers have confirmed, that the incarnate Word, together with the flesh which he received from the Virgin and with the whole human being joined to him in the unity of substance, has been exalted above all things beyond essence. But whether the whole of human nature—which I had thought was to be liberated only partly, in the elect, while partly remaining forever to be tormented in the eternal [Col. 0921C] fire among the reprobate—will ascend, once the restraints of its own wickedness have been wholly loosed and utterly broken, as the preceding argument teaches, to the place where its firstfruits, I mean Christ’s humanity, ascended, I now consider with doubt, since many considerations contend with one another in this question. 

For if the whole of it is going to ascend there—and, to speak more plainly, return to him whom it abandoned by sinning—and if, by redeeming it, he assumed it in its entirety, what shall we say? Will it not follow that no eternal death of misery and no punishment of the ungodly will remain? For what will be tormented in them after the whole nature, of which both good and evil persons are participants, has not only been freed from every death and wickedness but will also have returned into God himself? Where, then, will be that burning heat of the flames of the eternal fire into which the severity of the [Col. 0921D] most just Judge will send the wicked, saying: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels”? Where will be the eternal punishment into which the ungodly are to go, if no part of human nature remains liable to eternal punishment? For once all wickedness has ended, who will remain wicked? Every wicked person is wicked through wickedness, and consequently, when wickedness perishes, the wicked person too will perish. For when a cause fails, its effect must necessarily [Col. 0922A] fail also.

The same reasoning applies to death and life. For if death will be wholly swallowed up by life, just as wickedness is swallowed up by goodness and misery by blessedness, who will be tormented by death and misery when no one will remain outside life and blessedness? If someone asserts that one part of human nature will return to God while another part will remain forever in punishments, how many difficulties, and how many consequences contrary to true reason, will follow from his assertion?

He will indeed be compelled to admit that the Word of God assumed not the whole of human nature but only a part of it, and consequently that he neither wished to save nor saved the whole human race—which it is absurd to believe. True reason and pure contemplation of things will likewise ridicule anyone who divides the simplicity of human nature into parts, teaching that it is composed as though from many dissimilar [Col. 0922B] or similar elements, since it is one and simple, free from every composition, dissimilarity, and multiplicity of parts. Otherwise it was not made in the image of God but after the manifold variety of mortal and corruptible bodies—which is both most foolish and most shameful to think, and wholly alien to the truth. 

Moreover, if human nature is the image and likeness of God, then certainly the whole of it is wholly present in itself, and wholly present in each of those who participate in it; it admits no division or partition of its uniformly simple nature, either in itself or in any of its members, whether by the possibility of dividing or partitioning it, or by any actual operation. For if the Godhead, in whose image humanity was made, is one and indivisible, then humanity too must necessarily be one and indivisible, and all human beings, without [Col. 0922C] exception, are one in it.

But if anyone should think that I have stated the simplicity and indivisibility of humanity without support from any privileged authority of the holy Fathers, let him hear blessed Origen in the third book of his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans:

> “I said: ‘You are gods and sons of the Most High,’ and he added: ‘All.’”

That addition gathered the whole human race together under this title at once. Finally, in what follows he says:

> “But you shall die like human beings.”

Hence I also think that what is written—“And God considered that he had made man upon the earth, and he repented in his heart, and God said: ‘I will destroy man, whom I have made, from the face of the earth’”—was said not only with reference to the destruction caused by the Flood, but that something concerning future things was also foretold under the mystery, so that the statement “I will destroy man” may be understood in the same way as what God says [Col. 0922D] through the prophet:

> “For behold, I blot out your iniquities like a cloud”,

so that he appears to destroy man according to that by which he is man, and afterward to make him God, at the time when God will be all in all.

Let him also read the great theologian Gregory, disputing about humanity in the seventeenth chapter of his sermon *On the Image*, where he says:

> “What are we to think about these things? The sentence that says, ‘God made man,’ by its infinite significance displays the whole of humanity. [Col. 0923A] For the creature is not now named Adam, as the history says in what follows; rather, the name given to the created man is universally no other than this. We are therefore not led, by the designation of universal nature, to suspect something of this kind, since in the divine foreknowledge and power the whole of humanity was comprehended in its first constitution. For one must not consider anything among the things made by God to be infinite, but the limit and measure of each existing thing is the wisdom of the Maker, encompassing it in its measure. Just as a human being is confined by the quantity of his body, and the magnitude of his substance, completed on the surface of his body, is his measure, so I think that the whole fullness of humanity was comprehended by the God of all, as it were in one body, by his foreknowing power [printed *pro gnostica virtute*]. And this is taught by the sentence that says: [Col. 0923B] ‘God made man; according to the image of God he made him.’ For the image is not in a part of nature, nor is the grace found in any of the things considered according to it; rather, such power extends equally over the whole race. The sign of this is the mind similarly placed in all, since all possess the power of understanding and deliberating, together with all the other things through which the divine nature is imaged in that which was made according to it.

> “The man displayed in the first constitution of the world and the man who will exist after the consummation of the universe are in the same condition: they equally bear the divine image in themselves. For this reason the whole race was named ‘one man’, because in the power of God nothing passes away and nothing is impending; rather, what is contemplated is equally contained in the present, all-embracing operation of the universe. Thus the whole of [Col. 0923C] human nature, extending from the first to the last, is truly one image of the One who truly exists. The distinction of the race into male and female was added last to the constitution of its formation.”

Therefore, if the Word of God assumed humanity, he assumed not a part of it—for no part exists—but the whole universally. And if he assumed the whole, he certainly restored the whole in himself, since all things have been restored in him; and he left no part of the humanity which he wholly assumed subject to perpetual punishments and the indissoluble bonds of wickedness, which is followed by the calamity of torments. For God condemns nothing that he made, but he punishes what he did not make.

For neither does he punish, nor will he punish, the nature of the angels who transgressed; but he will extinguish their wickedness and impiety and harmful power, [Col. 0923D] as well as those of the wicked human beings attached to them. Perhaps their eternal condemnation will consist in the universal abolition of their own wickedness and impiety.

Amid these mutually conflicting considerations, like a man distressed and worn out by a long and inextricable deliberation, I am tossed about among the waves and rocks of a raging sea as they strike against one another, and I find no way of escape. For, to gather briefly what was said at length above: if I say that the whole of humanity was assumed by the Word of God, and therefore [Col. 0924A] is to be saved in him, with the natural power of resurrection cooperating—a power that permits no nature to perish or to be punished forever—what will be assigned to eternal condemnation? I shall appear to resist the authority of divine Scripture, which unhesitatingly threatens that eternal torments are destined for the devil and all his members.

But if I teach that neither the whole of humanity was assumed by Christ and is to be saved, nor is the whole to be liberated by the natural power of resurrection, but that one part will return to the dignity of the divine image while another part will remain captive in eternal calamity, will not true reason and divine authority together immediately rebuke me? Reason most clearly teaches that nothing directly contrary to supreme goodness, life, and blessedness can [Col. 0924B] exist eternally. Goodness circumscribes wickedness and utterly consumes it; likewise life consumes death, blessedness misery, virtue the vices and the causes of the vices, and other things of this kind.

Divine authority cries out:

> “I shall be your death, O Death, and your sting, O Hell.”

Likewise:

> “The last enemy to be destroyed is death”—

that is, either the devil, the author of death, or death itself. Its name among the Greeks is θἀνατος (*thanatos*, “death,” with the accent as printed); thus it is written ἐχθρός θάνατος, “enemy death”—*inimicus* (“enemy”) θάνατος (“death”).

In the visions of the prophet Daniel, the angel also says:

> “Seventy weeks have been shortened concerning your people and your holy city, so that transgression may be consumed, sin may reach its end, iniquity may be blotted out, and everlasting righteousness may be brought in.”

The mystical number of the shortened seventy weeks signifies the whole period from the first advent of the Savior [Col. 0924C] to the second. For the course of this life, winding through revolutions of seven days, is indicated by the number seven. This course is called shortened, since all times are brief in comparison with eternity.

Thus, in this battle, pierced on both sides as though by these weapons, I stand anxiously, not knowing where to turn or what to follow. For it is no small matter to choose one of two alternatives: either to destroy the eternal punishments of wicked angels and human beings, or to deny that divine goodness and blessedness, once all wickedness and misery have been swallowed up, will reign everywhere throughout every creature.

### TEACHER

Be patient. The light of minds will come—the light that illuminates hidden things, opens what is concealed, reveals what is unknown, recalls what has fled, [Col. 0924D] circumscribes what is uncircumscribed, defines what is indefinite, and brings ambiguous matters, in a certain manner, to a definite judgment. First, however, we must consider what has been settled among us and brought to an unshakable definition, what still seethes in wavering deliberation, and what remains to be sought.

### DISCIPLE

Reason demands no other inquiry into the natures of things.

### TEACHER

I perceive many matters that have been rationally defined and discovered in your deliberative contemplation. But since, as you yourself confess, they still seem to you to lie in [Col. 0925A] uncertainty, I think it necessary to revisit the points on which you appear to hesitate, so that, once the waves of our minds have been stilled, I may give a firm judgment concerning the matters we are investigating together, and we may no longer seem ambiguous, examining nothing distinctly. 

### DISCIPLE

Let it be so.

### TEACHER

No one who rightly understands the natures of things doubts that all things are contained in the divine mind.

### DISCIPLE

It would be ridiculous to doubt this, since all wise people agree on it without dissent when they hear the Apostle saying:

> “From him and through him and in him and toward him are all things.”

Dionysius the Areopagite says in the seventh chapter of *On the Divine Names*:

> “The divine wisdom is called and is the beginning, cause, substance, consummation, preservation, and source of every mind and reason, and of every sense.”

[Col. 0925B] Blessed Ambrose, introducing the Apostle in his exposition of Luke, says:

> “In the Lord Jesus all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible; and he is before all things, and all things consist in him.”

It would be tedious and unnecessary to set down the opinions of the other Fathers on this subject.

### TEACHER

If, then, all things subsist in the divine mind, nothing exists outside it.

### DISCIPLE

There is nothing above it, beneath it, or outside it. 

### TEACHER

Therefore, it is altogether itself that is all things. 

### DISCIPLE

Entirely so. For what else are all things except their knowledge in the divine mind, as Dionysius says in the chapter mentioned above?

> “The divine mind contains all things, possessing knowledge removed from all things; according to the cause of all things, it anticipates within itself the knowledge of all things before the angels came to be, knowing and bringing forth the angels and all other things from within and, so to speak, [Col. 0925C] from the beginning itself, knowing them and bringing them into essence. And I think that Scripture conveys this when it says: ‘Knowing all things before their generation.’ For the divine mind does not come to know existing things by learning them from existing things; rather, from itself and in itself, according to the cause of all things, it presents and anticipates the knowledge and cognition of all things. It does not contemplate each thing according to its form, but knows and contains all things according to the single circumference of their cause, just as light, according to its cause, anticipates within itself the knowledge of darkness, seeing darkness not from elsewhere but from the light.

> “Thus divine Wisdom, knowing itself, knows material things immaterially, divided things without division, and many things universally; in itself, which is one, it both knows and brings forth all things. For if God gives being to all existing things according to one cause, then according [Col. 0925D] to that same single cause he knew all things, as existing from him and pre-established in him. He will not receive their knowledge from existing things; rather, he will also be the giver of the knowledge of each of them to the things themselves.”

### TEACHER

The divine mind, therefore, knows neither any evil nor any wickedness. For if it knew them, they would exist substantially and would not be without a cause. But as it is, they are also without a cause, and consequently they do not exist essentially among the number of created natures; therefore they are wholly alien to divine knowledge.

### DISCIPLE

True reason does not permit this to be understood otherwise. For divine [Col. 0926A] knowledge is the cause of existing things; consequently, whatever it knows must come to be in the nature of things. But what is not found in the nature of things cannot in any way be found in divine knowledge.

### TEACHER

God, then, does not know the ungodly—angels and human beings—and all those who transgress the divine law.

### DISCIPLE

He knows their substances and everything that he made in them and that subsists in him. But what has happened through their perverse movements to the nature established by him, he entirely does not know. For whatever he did not make is wholly foreign to his knowledge.

### TEACHER

You do not doubt, I believe, concerning the eternity of the divine nature and of all things that have been made in it, through it, toward it, and from it; nor that it alone is truly and uniquely eternal; nor that everything eternal is eternal by participation in eternity.

### DISCIPLE

How could I doubt, when both [Col. 0926B] reason and divine authority approve such things? For if one God is the cause and end of all things, it follows that he alone is uniquely eternal, and that everything participating in him is eternal only through him. For what can be eternal apart from him and what has been made in him and by him? 

### TEACHER

Do you think that wickedness and its attendants—I mean death and misery—and the punishments of various offenses were made by God or participate in divine power? For when it is written, “Death and life are from the Lord God,” I do not think this was said of that death by which humanity dies through sin and is dissolved through corruption, with the punishment of sin following, but of the death of which the Psalmist says:

> “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints”—

that is, the precious passage of souls that have been thoroughly purified into the innermost [Col. 0926C] contemplation of truth, which is truly blessedness and eternity.

This is the death by which those who live religiously, seeking their God piously and chastely, die while they still remain in this mortal life: they see in a mirror and in a riddle what they seek, but in the future they will return to the original dignity of the divine image, for which they were made, and, exalted above all things, will see God himself face to face—insofar as it is permitted to a comprehensible and intelligible creature to see the incomprehensible and intelligible cause of the universe—face to face, that is, in a theophany nearest to him, as the Apostle says:

> “Now we see through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face”—

calling “face” a certain apprehensible manifestation, for the human intellect, of divine power, [Col. 0926D] which is not seen in itself by any creature. 

Moreover, if wickedness, death, and misery, so opposed to created nature, were neither made in the cause of all things nor participate in it, I am astonished that you deliberate and hesitate over whether wickedness and death, together with eternal torments, will remain eternally in humanity, which the Word of God, having assumed it wholly in himself, has liberated, when true reason teaches that nothing contrary to divine goodness, life, and blessedness can be co-eternal with them.

For divine goodness [Col. 0927A] will consume wickedness, eternal life will swallow up death, and blessedness misery. For it is written:

> “I shall be your death, O Death, and your sting, O Hell.”

Unless perhaps you still doubt that the Lord Jesus, the receiver and savior of human nature, accepted and saved not the whole of it but some very small part—which the preceding arguments refute. 

### DISCIPLE

I now see myself trapped on every side, and I find no argument by which I could maintain that wickedness, death, and misery will dominate in humanity—whether in the whole or in some part of it—and remain forever, since in the Word of God, which assumed it wholly into the unity of his substance, humanity has been universally both redeemed and liberated. Thus, overcome by the force of right reasoning, I am compelled to confess that the whole of [Col. 0927B] humanity is to be liberated in all who participate in it, and freed from every bond of wickedness, death, and misery, when it returns to its causes, which subsist in its Savior.

Yet I still deliberate—now secure about humanity—whether wickedness will be abolished universally in every creature or only in humanity. For I think that demonic minds will never be deprived of wickedness and all that follows from it. Consequently, although by the gift of divine grace, with natural power cooperating, wickedness may be wholly abolished in humanity alone, I think that it will continue without end in the nature of demons, and will be co-eternal with divine goodness in them. Therefore it will not be abolished in every nature. 

### TEACHER

As I think, you do not yet clearly perceive that [Col. 0927C] God punishes no creature that he made—not in human substance and not in demonic substance—but that he punishes in all creatures what he did not make, namely, the irrational movements of a perverse will. And so that you may not hesitate over this any longer, hear blessed Augustine in the eleventh book of his *Hexaemeron*, where, discussing the nature of demons and their wickedness, he says:

> “Some people think that he—the devil, of course—was not deflected into this wickedness by the free choice of his will, but was created altogether in this condition, although by the supreme and true Lord God, the creator of all natures. They bring forward as evidence a passage from the Book of Job, where, when the discussion concerns him, it is written: ‘This is the beginning of the Lord’s work, which he made for his angels to mock.’ A similar statement is written in the Psalm: ‘This is the dragon [Col. 0927D] whom you formed to be mocked by him,’ except that here it says ‘whom you formed,’ whereas there it says ‘this is the beginning of the Lord’s work,’ as though at the beginning he formed him in such a way that he would be evil, envious, a deceiver—in short, the devil—not corrupted by his will but created in that state.

> “How is this opinion not contrary to what is written: ‘God made all things, and behold, they were very good’? Where is the devil found to have been made very evil by the Lord God himself, rather than corrupted by his own will? Yet they endeavor to demonstrate this.

> “Nor is it foolishly [Col. 0928A] or without learning asserted that not only in the first creation but also now, despite so many corrupted wills, all things that have been created—that is, absolutely the whole of creation—are nevertheless very good. This does not mean that the wicked in it are good, but that by their wickedness they do not make the beauty and order of the universe in any respect ugly or disordered under the rule of God the administrator, through the power of wisdom Even evil wills are assigned their own definite and fitting limits of power and measures of merit, so that the universe is beautiful even with those wills appropriately and justly ordered within it.

> “Nevertheless, since it occurs to everyone and is true and evident that it is contrary to justice itself that God should condemn anyone, without any preceding merit, for the very thing that he himself created in that person—[Col. 0928B] and since a certain and manifest condemnation of the devil and his angels is recounted from the Gospel, where the Lord foretold that he would say to those on his left: ‘Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels’—we must in no way believe that the nature which God created in him is punished, but rather that his own evil will is to be punished by the penalty of eternal fire.”

Blessed Ambrose, in his exposition of Luke, very clearly teaches that the wickedness of demons is not perpetual, saying:

> “The demon began to pray that he might receive permission to enter the pigs. First, we must note the Lord’s mercy: he condemns no one beforehand, but each person is the author of his own punishment. The demons are not sent into the pigs; they themselves ask for it, because they could not endure the brightness of the heavenly light. [Col. 0928C] Just as those whose eyes hurt cannot bear the sun’s ray but choose darkness in order to leave what shines, so they flee the splendor of the eternal light and fear, before the appointed time, the torments due to them—not foreknowing what will happen, but remembering what has been prophesied.

> “For Zechariah said: ‘And it shall be on that day: the Lord will destroy the names of the idols from the earth, and there will no longer be any memory of them, and I will burn the unclean spirit from the earth.’ We are therefore taught that they will not remain forever, and that their wickedness cannot be perpetual.

> “Now, fearing that punishment, they say: ‘Have you come to destroy us before the time?’ But because they still desire to exist, although they are already withdrawing from human beings, for whose sake they know that they must undergo punishment, they ask to be sent into the pigs.”

[Col. 0928D] And lest you suppose that not only wickedness but also substance will perish in the devil—by “substance” he means not a nature made by God, but the whole consequence of his apostasy, namely, the purpose of pride, the hostile will, and the uncleanness of idolatry—for everything called the devil subsists through these and similar members; it may also be understood of the aerial body superadded to him—

and lest you suppose that death and its sting, which I mean sin, [Col. 0929A] together with every wickedness, will not perish in every rational creature, but will be destroyed in one part of creation and remain in another, hear the great Origen, the most diligent investigator of realities, in the third book of *On First Principles*, where he discusses the consummation of the world—that is, the highest good toward which the whole rational nature hastens, so that God may be all in all; for there is no other consummation of the world than God being all in all. Hear him discussing this and saying:

> “Let us inquire, then, what these things are that God will be in all. I indeed think that this statement, that God is all things in all, also signifies that he is all things in each individual. He will be all things in each person in this manner: whatever the rational mind, cleansed of every sediment of vice and thoroughly wiped free of every cloud of wickedness, can either feel, [Col. 0929B] understand, or think, all of this will be God. It will no longer see anything other than God, hold anything other than God; God will be the mode and measure of every movement of the mind. Thus God will be all things.

> “There will no longer be any distinction between good and evil, because evil will exist nowhere. God is all things to the one to whom evil is no longer attached. Nor will the one who is always in the good, and to whom God is all things, any longer desire to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

> “If, therefore, the end restored to the beginning, and the outcome of things brought back to their origins, restores the state which rational nature then possessed, when it had no need to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, so that, once every perception of wickedness has been removed and it has been cleansed to sincerity and purity, the one God who alone is good may become all things to it—not in a few or in many, but so that he himself may be all things [Col. 0929C] in all—when nowhere is there death, nowhere the sting of death, and nowhere at all is there evil, then truly God will be all in all.

> Nevertheless, some think that this perfection and blessedness of rational natures will remain in the state we described above—that is, in such a way that they have God as all things and God is all things to them—only if the association with bodily nature never removes them from that state. Otherwise, they believe that the glory of supreme blessedness would be impeded if a mingling of material substance were introduced. We have discussed and arranged this matter more fully in the preceding sections, insofar as it could arise there.
>
> Now, however, since we find that the Apostle Paul mentioned a spiritual body, let us inquire, as far as [Col. 0929D] we can, how we ought to understand the matter from this as well. As far as our understanding can grasp, we perceive the quality of the spiritual body to be such that it is suitable to be inhabited not only by holy and perfect souls, but also by the whole creation which will be liberated from the slavery of corruption. 
>
> Concerning this body the Apostle also said:
>
> “We have a dwelling not made by hands, eternal in the heavens”—
>
> that is, among the dwelling places of the blessed. From this, then, we can form a conjecture about [Col. 0930A] the purity, subtlety, and glory of the quality of that body, if we compare it with those bodies which now, although heavenly and most splendid, are nevertheless made by hands and visible.
>
> Of that body it is said that it is a dwelling not made by hands but eternal in the heavens. Since what is seen is temporal, while what is unseen is eternal, that body greatly surpasses all these bodies which we see or can see, whether on earth or in heaven, and which are made by hands, [and have been made eternal], and are not eternal, in that it is invisible, not made by hands, and eternal. [The bracketed words are printed in the source and conflict with the following negation.]
>
> From this comparison one may infer how great is the beauty, splendor, and brilliance of the spiritual body, and that the statement is true:
>
> [Col. 0930B] “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him.”
>
> There should be no doubt that, by the will of God, who made the nature of our body such as it is, the Creator can produce it in the quality of a body most subtle, pure, and splendid, according as the state of things calls for it and the merit of rational nature demands it.
>
> Finally, when the world required variety and diversity, matter offered itself in every service to the Creator through the diverse appearances and forms of things, as to its Lord and Creator, so that from it he might derive the various forms of heavenly and earthly things (Concerning the simplicity and unity of bodies after the resurrection.). But when things begin to hasten toward the state in which all are one, as the Father and the Son are one, [Col. 0930C] it follows that where all are one there will no longer be diversity.
>
> For this reason the last enemy, the devil, who is called death, is also said to be destroyed, so that nothing may remain sad where death is absent, and nothing may be different where there is no enemy. The destruction of the last enemy must be understood not as the destruction of his substance, which was made by God, but as the destruction of the hostile purpose and will, which proceeded not from God but from the devil himself. He will therefore be destroyed not so that he does not exist, but so that he is no longer an enemy and no longer death.
>
> For nothing is impossible for the Almighty, and nothing is incurable for its maker. For he made all things so that they might exist; and the things that were made to exist could not fail to exist. Consequently, although they will receive change and variation, [Col. 0930D] so that according to their merits they may be held in either a better or a worse condition, those things which were made by God for the purpose of existing and remaining cannot undergo substantial destruction.”

Thus Origen explains what Ambrose had left ambiguous. When Ambrose says, “We are taught that the demons will not remain forever, so that their wickedness cannot be perpetual,” it is uncertain what he means: whether the substance of the demons together with their wickedness will perish, or only their wickedness, [Col. 0931A] while their nature remains incorruptible, since it is solely on account of that wickedness that they are called demons. 

Origen, however, asserts without hesitation that their substance, made by God, will always remain in them, while their wickedness, discovered in their perverse will, will perish forever. For names such as “demon,” “devil,” “last enemy,” and “death” are not names of nature but names of a depraved will.

You have therefore heard Saint Augustine saying that God will punish in the devil not what he made but what he did not make; you have heard Origen affirming that the devil’s substance will never perish, but only his wickedness. And so that you may believe and understand this more firmly, read the great Dionysius the Areopagite in his book *On the Divine Names*, where he argues that evil is not present in the nature of demons and that their nature cannot in any way be corrupted [Col. 0931B] or diminished.

### Textual notes

The lemmata and their English meanings identify the passages; entries follow source order.

- partim semper — partly forever. [Note: [Col. 0921] A reverses the order to *semper partim*, “forever partly.”]
- ascendit — ascended. [Note: [Col. 0921] Thus A and CF, with singular verb despite the preceding plural *primitiae*, “firstfruits.”]
- cujus et boni et mali — in which both good and evil persons participate. [Note: [Col. 0921] A omits the first *et*, “both/and.”]
- Ubi ergo — where, then. [Note: [Col. 0921] A reads *vero*, “however/indeed,” for *ergo*.]
- dicens — saying. [Note: [Col. 0921] CF print *aictura*, apparently a corruption of *dictura*, “about to say.”]
- est ratio — is the reasoning. [Note: [Col. 0921] CF reverse the order to *ratio est*.]
- omnino — wholly, of death being swallowed up. [Note: [Col. 0921] A omits this word.]
- Deum Verbum — God the Word. [Note: [Col. 0921] A reads *divinum*, “divine,” in place of *Deum*, “God.”]
- in partes — into parts. [Note: [Col. 0921] A omits these words.]
- a veritate alienum — alien to the truth. [Note: [Col. 0921] CF omit the preposition *a*, “from/to” in this construction.]
- in se ipsa — in itself. [Note: [Col. 0921] A omits *se*, “itself,” leaving *in ipsa*.]
- praerogativa — privileged/special, qualifying authority. [Note: [Col. 0921] A omits this word.]
- adjutum — supported. [Note: [Col. 0921] Thus A, with accusative agreeing with *me*; CF read nominative *adiutus*.]
- in Epistolam — on the Epistle. [Note: [Col. 0921] A reads ablative *in epistola*, “in the Epistle,” instead of accusative *in Epistolam*.]
- quod — what/that which, after I will destroy man. [Note: [Col. 0921] CF read *quo*, “by which/in which manner.”]
- dicit Deus — God says. [Note: [Col. 0921] A reverses the order to *Deus dicit*.]
- deleo sicut nubem iniquitates tuas — I blot out your iniquities like a cloud. [Note: [Col. 0921] A reads *deleo iniquitates tuas ut nubem*, with the same sense, altered order, and *ut* instead of *sicut*, both “like/as.”]
- universali naturae vocatione — by the designation of universal nature. [Note: [Col. 0923] A reads genitive *universalis*, agreeing with “nature,” instead of ablative *universali*, formally agreeing with “designation.”]
- introducimur — we are led. [Note: [Col. 0923] A reads active *introducimus*, “we introduce/lead.”]
- praescientia — foreknowledge. [Note: [Col. 0923] A reads *praesentia*, “presence.”]
- Et hoc docet — and this teaches. [Note: [Col. 0923] A omits *Et*, “and.”]
- gratia — grace. [Note: [Col. 0923] A reads accusative *gratiam* instead of nominative *gratia*.]
- animus collocatus — a mind placed. [Note: [Col. 0923] A reads *animum collocari*, “that a mind is placed,” an accusative-and-infinitive construction.]
- Similiter se habet — is in a similar condition. [Note: [Col. 0923] CF omit the reflexive *se*, “itself,” in this idiom.]
- mundi — of the world, after first constitution. [Note: [Col. 0923] CF omit this word.]
- in seipsis divinam ferunt imaginem — they bear the divine image in themselves. [Note: [Col. 0923] A reads *in seipso divinam imaginem feret*, “he will bear the divine image in himself,” with singular pronoun and future verb instead of plural pronoun and present verb.]
