### 28

“But neither are demons evil by nature,” he says. “For if demons are evil by nature [this is said because demons were created from the good, subsist naturally, and, having turned away from the good, abandoned it] [Note: The material enclosed here in brackets is absent from manuscripts CF]—if they are evil by nature, then they exist neither from the good, nor among existing things, nor as having been turned from the good [CF: *conversi*; A: *conversi si*]; by nature they exist as evil always.

The next question is whether they are evil for themselves or for others. If for themselves, do they corrupt themselves? But if for others, how do they corrupt them—essence, virtue, or activity? If essence, then first of all this is not according to nature. For by nature they do not corrupt incorruptible things, but things receptive of corruption [that is, they corrupt no nature, because no nature is receptive of evil]. Nor is this wholly and altogether evil [CF: “wholly and altogether”; cf. Col. 0931C], nor is anything among existing things corrupted in respect of essence and nature [CF: “anything existing”]; rather, through deficiency—the order of the words is: “the account of harmony and proportion is weakened by the deficiency of the natural order”—the principle of order, harmony, and proportion is weakened, so that it does not remain similarly constituted [CF: “the principle, remaining similarly constituted—that is, while nature remains unchanged—cannot remain”] (that is, while nature itself remains unchanged).

But weakness is not complete [CF omits *est*]. For if it were complete [CF omits *esset*], it would remove both the corruption and the subject [CF: “destroy”], and such corruption would be its own destruction [CF: “and it will itself be corruption and its own corruption”]. Therefore, such a thing is not evil, but a deficient good. For whatever is entirely devoid of good will not exist among existing things.

The same account applies to the corruption of power and activity [Note: “The same account applies to the corruption of virtue and activity”] [that is, just as nature cannot be corrupted, so virtue and natural activity do not admit corruption].

Next, how can demons, made by God [CF: “demons made by God”], be evil? For the good produces and establishes good things. Someone may indeed say [CF: “and indeed they are called evil,” someone may say]: they are called evil, but not according to what they are; for they are from the good [CF: “from the best”], and they received [CF: “were allotted”] a good [CF: “best”] essence. Rather, they are evil according to what they are not: they are weak, as the Oracles say, in preserving their principle.

In what, tell me, do we say that demons are corrupted [CF reverses the order: “we say demons are corrupted”], if not in the cessation of the disposition and activity directed toward divine goods? [CF: “if not in the cessation of their disposition and activity toward divine goods.”]

Otherwise [Note: For the material extending to the end of the quotation, CF gives the following instead: “But if demons are evil by nature, they are always evil; and indeed evil is unstable. Therefore, if they remain always in this condition, they are not evil; for what is always the same is characteristic of the best. But if they are not always evil, they are not evil by nature, but through lack of angelic goods. Yet they are not wholly deprived of the good, since they exist, live, understand, and there is altogether in them a certain movement of desire. They are called evil because they are weak with respect to natural activity. Their evil, therefore, is a false turning, departure from what is akin to them, deformity, imperfection, and impotence; weakness in the virtue that preserves their perfection; flight and falling. But what is evil in demons? Irrational fury, senseless desire, reckless imagination. Yet although these are in demons, they are not wholly, nor in all of them, nor are these things evil in themselves. For in other animals it is not the possession of such movements but their destruction and corruption that are animal evil; possession preserves and causes the animal nature of the one who has these things. Therefore the demonic race is not evil insofar as it is according to nature, but insofar as it is not. Nor has all the good given to them been changed; rather, they themselves fell from the whole good that had been given. We say that the angelic gifts given to them have never themselves been changed, but they remain whole and are exceedingly bright, although they themselves do not see as participants in the contemplative powers of the good. Thus, what they are is from the best, and they are best; they desire the good and the best, and desire to live and understand existing things. Through deprivation, flight, and falling away from the best things akin to them, they are called evil, according to what they are not; and by desiring what does not exist, they desire evil. Consider further.”]

If demons are evil by nature, they are always evil. But evil is unstable. Therefore, if they remain always in the same condition, they are not evil; for it is characteristic of the good always to be the same. But if they are not always evil, they are not evil by nature, but through lack of angelic goods.

Yet they are not wholly without good, since they exist, live, and understand, and there is altogether in them a certain movement of desire. They are called evil because they are weak in natural activity. Their evil, therefore, is corruption, abandonment and frustration of things suited to them, as well as imperfection, impotence, weakness in the faculty that preserves perfection in them, expulsion, and falling away.

What else is evil in demons? Irrational fury, mad desire, and reckless imagination. But although these are in demons, they are not wholly present, nor in all of them, and they are not evil in themselves. For in other animals it is not the possession of these things but their deprivation and corruption that are animal evil; possession preserves and establishes the animal nature that has them.

Therefore, the demonic race is not evil insofar as it exists according to nature, but insofar as it does not. Nor has all the good given to them been changed; rather, they themselves fell away from the whole good that had been given. Nor do we say that the angelic gifts given to them were ever changed, but that they remain whole and entirely luminous, although they themselves do not see, because they close the faculty by which they could behold their goods.

Thus, what they are is from the good, and they are good, and they desire the good and the beautiful, desiring to exist, live, and understand existing things. Through deprivation, flight, and falling away from the goods suited to them, they are called evil and are evil according to what they are not; and, desiring what does not exist, they desire evil.

Observe the force [A: “the tenor”] of the words and how subtle they are.

First, by comprehending the matter universally and briefly, he establishes that demons are not evil by nature, saying, “But neither are demons evil by nature.” He then adds the reasoning: for if they are evil by nature, they were created neither from the good—namely, God, who alone is good from himself—nor among existing natures; and they were not naturally turned from good, that is, they were not naturally turned into the wickedness of a perverse will from good angels.

The author mentioned above commonly applies these terms to the transgressing angels: “turned,” that is, turned away from the nature of good and fallen from wisdom. “And they always exist as evil” derives its negation from what precedes: they do not always exist as evil. For what is evil by nature cannot exist forever. It is impossible for the nature of evil and wickedness to be eternal [CF: “It is impossible for Nature and wickedness to be eternal”]. But the substance of demons will never perish. They are therefore not evil by nature.

Next he adds arguments by means of questions, saying: “Are they evil for themselves or for others?” As if he had said: if they are evil by nature, they must be evil either for themselves or for others. If for themselves, do they corrupt themselves? Certainly they do, if that is so. But this is impossible, since no nature can corrupt itself; self-corruption is accidental to every nature. Therefore, if the nature of demons is evil, it is not evil for themselves, since it is not permitted to corrupt itself; for evil is the corruption not of evil but of good.

But if by nature they are evil for other good things, how do they corrupt them—whether their essence, virtue, or activity? It is as if he were saying: they can corrupt none of these three [A: “none”]. For these three—I mean essence, virtue, and activity—are incorruptible in all things, since every nature subsists in these three.

And this is what follows: “If essence, then first of all not according to nature,” that is, not the essence by which nature subsists. For by nature they do not corrupt incorruptible things—namely, essence, virtue, and activity—but things receptive of corruption: things that can be corrupted, such as natural accidents, by which I mean qualities and quantities, and the rest of what can increase and diminish and is understood to exist in some subject.

But even these are not corrupted by evil. For the increase or diminution of the accidents of substance is neither evil nor corruption, but a certain advance [A: “a certain perfection”] and deficiency in the capacity of substances. Therefore he says: “Nor is this wholly and altogether evil” [CF: “wholly and altogether”], that is, even things receptive of corruption are not corrupted by evil, because evil itself is not wholly evil. In this passage one negation is placed twice: “nor is this wholly,” and “nor is it wholly evil.” For what could corrupt something that does not exist at all?

Every corruption understood in the nature of mutable things is either a deficiency of perfection, or a transition of matter from one species to another, or a transformation of genera into species and of species into genera. All these are understood not as evils but as the natural qualities, quantities, and transformations of mutable things [A omits “and transformations”].

The remaining portions of this chapter are clear and require no exposition. For it teaches most plainly that none of the things that exist can be corrupted in essence and nature; but that a deficiency of the natural order and a weakening of proportion—through which mutable things cannot always remain in the same condition—are called corruption; and that corruption itself is not evil but deficient good. For if it were evil, it would not exist in the nature of things.

It also teaches that demons are not evil according to what they are, since they are from the best and participate in the best essence [A: “and are allotted the best essence”], but are called evil according to what they are not.

It clearly explains what is called evil in them: namely, their weakness, by which they are unwilling to preserve their principle, the supreme good from which they are; and also their negligence, by which they are without the disposition and activity directed toward divine goods [CF; A: “without the disposition and activity directed toward divine goods”]; and the other matters stated with great clarity by the teacher mentioned above concerning the misery of demons and the goodness of their nature.

None of the gifts they received in their creation has been changed in them or taken away from them. Rather, the integrity and brightness of their nature always remain, although they do not understand [A: “understand”] their contemplative powers, which they possess by nature for the contemplation of their Creator, if only they were willing. They flee from the true light and fall away from the contemplative power of the good angels akin to them, desiring what does not exist. This is the whole of what is called evil and wickedness in them.

You have therefore seen that the nature of demons is good and was made by the supreme Good, and that they are called evil not according to what they are but according to what they are not.

Consequently, it necessarily follows that what was made in them by the supreme God will remain in them alone and will in no way be punished, whereas what is not from God—namely, their wickedness [A: “that is, their wickedness”]—will perish, lest in any creature, whether human or angelic, wickedness be able to become eternal and coeternal with goodness.

The same should be understood of death and misery, lest anything contrary and coeval with life and blessedness be supposed to exist.

Moreover, if wickedness universally, and death and its sting, which is sin, and every misery, and further the last enemy, namely diabolical evil, and universal impiety [or certainly death itself; A omits “or certainly death itself”], are abolished from the nature of things, what remains except that the whole universal creature, cleansed from every dreg of wickedness and impiety, freed from all death and corruption, and completely liberated, should remain?

This is the resurrection of the whole creation, which will be freed from servitude, and the renewal of the mystical earth—that is, of nature [A: “recall”].

Of this the Prophet foretold:

“You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust; you will send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.”

He also says that the Lord will rejoice in his works when sinners fail from the earth and the wicked are no more. For how will anyone be called a sinner when sin no longer exists, or wicked when wickedness has been destroyed?

As the same Prophet says: “The impious will not rise in the judgment.” For when humanity is restored in the resurrection, it will be freed from all impiety, wickedness, and death. Consequently, neither the evil nor the impious will rise; nature alone will rise [CF omits “nature alone will rise”], while impiety and wickedness will perish in eternal condemnation.

**DISCIPLE.** What, then, is that eternal fire, that punishment, that burning lake of sulphur and fire [F: “lake of sulphur”; A: “sulphur and fire”; C: “sulphurous lake”], and the worm that does not die, along with the other torments that the divine Oracles declare will befall the devil and all his members?

If they are thought to exist according to the literal account and the proper nature of visible things, they must necessarily exist visibly in some part of the sensible world. And if this is so [A omits *est*], this world, either in its entirety or in some part, will be preserved, in which those condemned will be condemned forever.

Consequently, it will not be wholly dissolved or brought to completion—that is, it will not return to its causes [CF omits *est*]—when God will be all in all. For this, as we have said, is the consummation of the world: that God be all in all [A omits the second “all”].

And what is more serious, what will be punished if no substantial subject capable of being punished remains in any way? [A, C, and F agree: “no substantial subject” and “in no way.”]

Moreover, if the whole world, and universally the entire creation made by God, will not return to the eternal causes in which it subsists, our whole argument will still remain wholly frustrated and completely dissolved.

**MASTER.** We have labored in vain, if this should be so, and the judgments of the holy Fathers whom we have introduced will be reduced to ridicule—which God forbid.

**DISCIPLE.** Come to our aid, then, and give a plausible account of the aforementioned kinds of torment, which the truthful divine history promises.

### 29

**MASTER.** We believe that the various forms of punishment will not exist locally in some part or in the whole of this visible creation—or, to put it simply, not within the totality of all nature created by God. Nor do we believe that they exist now, or will exist anywhere or at any time, except in the perverse movements of evil wills and corrupted consciences, in delayed and fruitless repentance, and in the complete overthrow of perverse power, whether belonging to the human or angelic creature [CF omits *ab*].

What is overthrown is what is utterly extinguished. Every capacity for sinning, doing evil, and acting impiously will be utterly extinguished. When the capacity for all wickedness has been completely removed, will not the occasion alone remain—namely, the perverse will—like something extinguished?

For just as faith without works is dead—for it is silent [A omits “for it is silent”]—so sin without the possibility of sinning, wickedness without evil-doing, and impiety without the worship of idols are dead.

Although the appetite and ardor for acting perversely may always remain in perverse wills, since what is desired is not permitted to be accomplished, and the flame of malevolent desire burns nowhere except in itself, what else remains but foul corpses deprived of every vital movement—that is, of all the power and substance of natural goods?

Perhaps such are the gravest torments of evil human beings and angels, both before the judgment and after it: the desire to do evil and the difficulty of accomplishing it.

That the devil and his members will not be punished in local spaces or bodily prisons, but that each one will suffer punishment within the bounds of his own evil will, blessed Ambrose clearly explains in his exposition of Luke, when interpreting the Gospel passage: “He will be taken, bound hand and foot [A: “bound hands and feet”], and will be sent [F: “send”; AC: “send him”] into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

What is the outer darkness? Is there perhaps also some prison there, and must one undergo a dungeon? Not at all. Rather, whatever lies outside the promises of the heavenly commandments is in the outer darkness, because God’s commandments are light; and whoever is without Christ is in darkness, because Christ is the inner light [CF: “because the light is Christ”].

Therefore there is neither any bodily gnashing of teeth, nor any perpetual fire of bodily flames, nor a bodily worm. These images are used because, just as fevers and worms arise from excessive indigestion, so, if someone does not digest his sins through a kind of sobriety of abstinence, but by mixing sins with sins contracts something like an indigestion of old and recent transgressions [CF: “contracts”; A: “contract”], he will be burned by his own fire and consumed by his own worms.

Hence Isaiah also says: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled.” It is a fire generated by the sadness of transgressions; it is a worm because the soul’s irrational sins prick the mind and the sense of the guilty person and gnaw at certain inward parts of the conscience. These worms arise from each person as from the body of the sinner.

Finally, the Lord declared this through Isaiah, saying: “They will see the limbs of the people who transgressed against me, and their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” [CF: “will not be extinguished”; A: “dies … is extinguished”].

The gnashing of teeth also reveals the feeling of one who is indignant, because each person repents too late, groans too late, and becomes angry with himself too late for having sinned with such obstinate wickedness.

See, therefore, what places of torment the theologian mentioned above describes. Where is Judas, the betrayer of our Savior, tormented? Is it anywhere other than in his polluted conscience, by which he betrayed the Lord? What punishment does he suffer? Certainly, a late and useless repentance, by which he is always burned.

What does that rich man suffer in hell? Is it not the lack of the splendid banquets on which he feasted in this life?

By what flame is the most impure king Herod consumed, except by his own fury, with which he burned to destroy the innocent?

These examples concerning the perverse movements of evil wills, which most just retribution tortures within themselves, and concerning the scars of various lusts, are sufficient. For every person who lives impiously will be tormented by the very lust of the vices with which he burned in the flesh, as though by an unquenchable flame.

What else should be understood concerning the punishment of diabolical and perverse wills except their eternal restraint and the eternal destruction of their impiety? What punishment could be heavier for an impious being than to act impiously but to be unable to harm anyone [CF: “and to be unable to harm anyone”]?

This is the chain by which our Lord Jesus Christ, descending into hell, bound the devil: namely, that he is unable to destroy those who believe in him piously and perfectly and keep his commandments. Although before the judgment the demons plead not to be punished [A omits “the demons”], but to be sent into the pigs—that is, lustful human beings—in whom they may still exercise their power [A: “exercise”], they will be bound more harshly when, after the judgment, every creature will be freed from his power and completely released from servitude and will return to its principle, namely God, who is the principle and end of all things.

The administration of visible things in generation and corruption will then come to an end through the great and common resurrection, as blessed Maximus says. This resurrection generates human beings unto immortality according to an unchanging mode of subsistence; for their sake visible nature received existence through generation, and with them it will receive, by grace, incorruptibility according to essence [CF: “and it will receive with them”; A: “and it will receive him”].

For the purpose of releasing visible creation from this servitude, the Word of God is bodily born as a human being from human beings, without sin, through a human being, and is baptized into spiritual sonship. For our sake he voluntarily undergoes birth: God according to essence and Son of God according to nature.

In order to destroy birth from bodies, he is bodily born without sin; and in order to undergo birth for our sake through baptism into spiritual sonship, he accepted birth as God by nature.

Adam, voluntarily abandoning birth from the Spirit unto deification, was born bodily into corruption. But the best and most merciful one, having become human for our transgression, condemned this and condemned himself for us [CF: “for our sake”], alone free from sin. He graciously consented to be born from bodies by a birth in which he overcame the power of our condemnation; and, mystically directing birth in the spirit, he loosed in himself, for our sake, the bonds of bodily birth and gave us, through birth from the Spirit, the power to become children of God instead of children of flesh and blood, to those who believe in his name.

This is the envy by which diabolical iniquity is punished most severely within itself. It is tormented when it sees the great and common resurrection of human substance and of all visible things within it, transformed into unchangeable immortality, and escaped from its power—substance which it had resolved utterly to destroy, holding it captive and subject to itself and keeping it liable to eternal death and everlasting punishments [A: “and keeping it even in eternal death”].

For when the succession of being born from bodies and returning to corruption has ceased, where will the power of the ancient enemy remain? Nowhere.

### 30

**DISCIPLE.** I think that all these matters are supported by plausible authority and reasoning. But there still remains that extremely difficult question, as it seems to me: in what will those punishments exist [CF omits “will exist”] which, according to divine authority, are destined not only for the devil but also for impious human beings?

For example, to introduce only a few of the many passages, the Lord promises in the Gospel that he will say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” Here he shows that the devil and his angels will burn in eternal fire.

And what is written in the Apocalypse: “The devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulphur, where the beast and the false prophets will also be tormented, day and night, for ages of ages” [CF: “and will be tormented”]?

By the word “day” we understand the open condemnation of the impious to pure angelic and human intellects; by the metaphor of “night,” the depth of the divine judgment unknown to all.

Observe that I am not now asking about the quality or locality of the punishments. For it has been sufficiently established above, on the authority of Ambrose [CF: “by the authority of Ambrose”], that there will be no bodily, local, sensible, or temporal punishments. Nor is this without reason. After the consummation of the world there will be neither sensible bodies [CF: “neither bodily nor sensible bodies”], nor places, nor times in which torments could be understood to exist.

All these things will come to an end with the world, when the end of all bodies will be spirituality, the simplicity of all places, wholly without spatial extension, and the eternity of all times.

Therefore, when the Lord says, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire,” and elsewhere, “These will go into eternal punishment,” and again in the Apocalypse, “They will be tormented day and night for ages of ages,” we must understand the eternity of the fire not in terms of duration or the long extensions of the lowest temporal cycles, but in terms of the irrevocable and unchangeable sentence of the most just Judge.

The same reasoning applies to the eternity of blessed life, in which no temporal intervals are understood, since it remains unchangeably in itself and is not enclosed by any beginning or end above all times.

From this it follows that everything called eternal is understood properly only in God, lest any eternity be thought to exist outside him, who alone is eternal and is eternity.

Either the unshaken severity of his most just judgments, by which he permits what he did not make to be punished irrevocably in the impious, or his ineffable and supernatural grace, by which he deifies and exalts above all those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image [A: “to the likeness”] of his Son—either of these is rightly understood, by the contemplation of reason, under the name “eternity.”

For nothing is coeternal with God, nor is anything diametrically opposed to him. He alone is eternal in those things that are in him and live blessedly in him, through gratuitous grace; but in those things that are outside him—because they are not from him [A: “because they are not”] and therefore, although they are said to exist, in reality do not exist—he is eternal through a severe judgment.

I am therefore not now asking you about the corporeality, locality, or temporality of the punishments. The torments of the impious must be understood spiritually. Rather, I ask in what thing we ought to believe or understand that they will exist.

For we must not suppose that they lack some subject. Punishments are accidents [CF: “accidents”; A: “simple things”]. But if no accident exists except in a subject, and every subject is something subsisting in itself, then punishments must necessarily exist in some subject subsisting in itself.

Moreover, if everything that subsists in itself has been established by him who is the cause of all subsisting things—for whatever has not been established by the cause of all things is altogether nothing and does not subsist among existing things—it follows that the calamity of punishments must be constituted in some substance established by God.

But if this is granted, the reasoning immediately falters that approves the proposition that divine justice punishes in no creature what it made. For everything made by him who is impassible and incorruptible is itself impassible and incorruptible, and subject to no passions [CF: “to no passions”].

By “passions” I do not now mean those that exist naturally, such as bodily sensations [A: “such as bodily sensations naturally existing”], but those that are contrary to nature and operate upon bodily matter in this present mortal life [A: “corruptible matter”]. They cannot touch or corrupt the trinity of nature itself—essence, virtue, and operation—even though they appear to seek to attack it [A: “although they appear to seek to attack it”].

These passions are birth from bodies, after the likeness of irrational animals; the increase and decrease [CF: “diminution”] of bodies; all their corruptions; the final dissolution of the whole bodily structure [A omits “of the whole”]; and the irrational movements of the rational soul that arise from matter and revolve around it.

All these things originated not from the first condition of humanity but from its universal sin. Therefore, they will perish together with the matter they infect, when the first condition of humanity is freed from all these and similar passions and purified by the spiritual fire of divine grace and goodness.

The prophet Isaiah foretold this under the figure of Jerusalem, saying: “I will sanctify her in burning fire, and it will devour matter like hay,” calling fire not the fire that torments the impious with most just punishment, but the fire that cleanses the filth of nature with most merciful grace.

But if divine justice does not permit anything created by the supreme Good to be punished in any creature—not only because it was created to exist, but also because it was created to remain forever impassible and incorruptible in opposition to contrary passions—how can what is not understood to exist at all in the nature of things be punished or subjected to punishments [CF omits “to be”]? Or how can the torments of the impious be without a natural subject for them to torment?

**MASTER.** This is, as you said, an exceedingly knotty and difficult perplexity to solve. In this question three possibilities confront us, and we must choose one of them while weakening the other two.

We are compelled to admit either that what does not exist at all in the nature of things can be punished in itself without any subject—which seems very much opposed to reason; for how can what does not subsist in anything be punished?—

or that some natural subject suffers punishments—which you see to be no less, indeed even more, contrary to reason and authority. For everything established in the nature of things by the supreme Good, whether according to substance or according to accident, is protected by divine justice and provident mercy from being punished, lest anything sorrowful or miserable be found in the whole creation—

or that what does not exist can nevertheless be punished in some subject that does exist and is free from every punishment.

Choose which of these three we should follow.

**DISCIPLE.** The third, composed from the preceding two, if it can nevertheless be found in a plausible manner. For the reasons already given unhesitatingly reject both the notion that what is not and is not found in the nature of things can be tormented, and the notion that a natural subject can suffer punishment.

But it seems credible to me, and most like the truth, that a defect which does not exist can be punished in something that does exist and is impassible, since it is not permitted to suffer punishment. Although my mind still seems unable to discern whether such a thing is indeed possible.

**MASTER.** Truth loves to come to those who seek it piously and devoutly; it loves to reveal itself and disclose what escapes their minds. Let us therefore seek it together, proceeding by rational steps. Follow me as I go before you, and I will follow after you as you go before me [CF: “I will follow you”].

**DISCIPLE.** Go before me.

### 31.

**MASTER.** We are treating the return of humanity, and of all things made in it and on its account, into itself and with it, to its beginning. For our discussion is not now about the substance of demons, which the Creator of all made good and incorruptible in them—whether it too, once purified, will return to its beginning, which it abandoned through transgression, or whether, having deviated from the contemplation of truth through its perversity, it will always flee from it. For the present, we know this alone about it with certainty: it is not punished and never will be punished; and the dignity of its first condition, before it became proud and deceived humanity, remains and will remain in it eternally, unchangeably and without any diminution; while the impiety it had drawn to itself through pride will wholly perish, lest it become coeternal with divine goodness. Concerning its salvation, however, or conversion, or return to its cause, we do not presume to determine anything, because we have no certain authority on this matter either from divine Scripture or from the holy Fathers who interpreted it. Therefore we honor that obscurity with silence, lest, while attempting to investigate what lies outside us [Note: [Col. 0941] *sunt* is omitted in CF.], we happen to fall farther into error than we ascend into truth. Accordingly, what is not outside us—I mean our nature—we must seek, with God as our guide.

**STUDENT.** That is right. For we are not merely permitted but commanded to seek ourselves, as Solomon says: “Unless you know yourself, go into the paths of the flocks.” Whoever does not know himself and the common nature of the human race is not far removed from irrational animals. Moses likewise says: “Attend to yourself,” and read, as though in a book, the history of the soul’s activity. For if we do not wish to know and seek ourselves, evidently we do not desire to return to what is above us, namely, our cause; and thus we shall lie in the grave of material flesh and in the death of ignorance. There is no other way to the purest contemplation of the primordial Exemplar except certain knowledge of its nearest image. Between the primordial Exemplar and its image and likeness—that is, between God and humanity—no interval has been established.

Observing this principle, the Greeks called humanity *anthropia* (ἀνθρωπία), that is, *anotropia* (ἀνωτροπία), “turning upward,” or *anō tērousa opia* (ἄνω τηροῦσα ὀπία), that is, “preserving an upward gaze.” Humanity was created for the contemplation of its Creator, with no other creature interposed.

**MASTER.** Come, then. Tell me, please: do you think that humanity, between which and its Creator no creature intervenes, subsists as one simple and inseparable nature, lacking partition within itself?

**STUDENT.** I think otherwise impossible. Otherwise it would not be the image of God, who is one and inseparably unity, one essence in three substances. In his image, the Trinity of humanity is likewise understood: being, willing, and knowing, as Saint Augustine discusses in his books of the *Confessions*. Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite teaches the same trinity as essence, power, and operation. They do not differ among themselves except in the meanings of the terms—and not even in every respect. Both speak of being; one speaks of willing, the other of power. Nor do they differ in their consideration of things, for no power is more natural and substantial to humanity than willing well. Again, one says “knowing,” the other “operation.” And what operation belongs to a rational nature, apart from knowing itself and its God, insofar as he can be known—who surpasses all knowledge?

This is our natural operation, established not outside us but within us. For what do we desire to know except our cause, which is within us through ineffable providence and beyond us through incomprehensible power? We have already discussed these matters sufficiently among ourselves in the preceding books, as I think.

**MASTER.** Certainly sufficiently; yet do not be reluctant or ashamed to repeat the same things, so that they may shine forth more clearly.

**STUDENT.** Not at all.

**MASTER.** Humanity, then, is a certain simple creature and, in its rational principles, infinitely multiple, just as its cause is simple and more than simple in itself, yet infinite and more than infinite in the occasions of the things made by it. Its cause is the highest and only goodness existing through itself, and humanity is most like it. For just as that goodness is wholly and everywhere in itself, so humanity, because it is its most like image, is wholly everywhere in itself. And just as divine goodness is wholly present in all who participate in it, and no wickedness, folly, or ignorance is prevented from penetrating the universe created by it, so humanity is diffused through all human beings and is wholly in all and wholly in each, whether they are good or evil.

It is repelled by no one’s folly, detained by no one’s wickedness, corrupted by no one’s vice, or polluted by anyone’s filth. It is pure in all: it is not puffed up in the proud, does not waste away in the fainthearted, is not greater in larger bodies or smaller in smaller ones, but equal in all, coming equally to its participants. It is not better in the good than in the evil, nor worse in the evil than in the good. It is not more complete in sound bodies than in those which, through some circumstance, either lose their integrity or fail to attain it.

Consider the example of the sunbeam: it penetrates the clean and the unclean while remaining clean in all; it is no purer in bright things [Note: [Col. 0941] A reads “clean things.”] than it remains undefiled amid filth. It is in all that it illuminates; it shines in darkness and—wonderful to say—does not allow darkness into itself, even while it contains within itself the causes of darkness, not only of shadows but also of absences. For there are no darknesses in the nature of things that are not bounded by light. If they are in bodies, however far they extend, they are finally surrounded by sunlight. If they are in spirits, whose darkness is ignorance of truth, they receive an end through the brilliance of wisdom.

Likewise, there is no absence that does not receive from the thing whose absence it is the cause of its arising. For if light had not preceded, its absence, which is darkness, would not follow. Therefore absences and the things of which they are absences belong to one genus, like light and darkness, sound and silence, form and formlessness, and other things of this kind.

But who can display the image of God with worthy praises or compare it with fitting likenesses? And so that you may recognize the equality of humanity in all human beings, observe the common form of human bodies. No human being is more human than another. If some deformity or difference of form occurs, it does not arise from nature, but either from the corruption of bodily integrity or from certain accidents that come from outside and add certain differences to individual human beings, while one general species, uniform by nature, is impressed upon all.

One bodily sense, divided into five, is commonly present in all, although in many its organs fail—I mean the eyes, ears, and the other instruments in which the external sense operates [Note: [Col. 0943] CF omits “external.”]. What shall I say about reason and intellect? Are they not generally present in all, although not all use them well and rightly? Many, indeed, by abusing their natural goods, have found the causes of their eternal condemnation.

There are likewise obvious indications of the communion of human nature in all. Since this is so, what person philosophizing rightly and contemplating the natures of things purely would not immediately declare that irrational movements of evil wills can be punished in those who participate in a good, rational, and impassible nature? And just as an evil will does not contaminate the natural good, so its torment—I mean the torment of the evil will—does not torture the natural subject to which it happens and in which it is contained.

For nature itself, just as it is free and wholly absolved from every sin, is likewise universally free and absolved from every punishment of sin. Even judges in secular affairs, provided that they examine those deserving punishment not out of a lust for vengeance but for the sake of correction, seek to have not nature in the accused but the offense tortured. Since they cannot punish offenses by themselves, separated from their natural subject, they therefore punish the body together with the offense.

But the best Creator of natures, the most pious Provider, and the most just avenger of offenses in those who despise or do not know him, punishes in the nature he made the offense he did not make. He frees what he made from the offense, separates what he made, and in an ineffable manner punishes, or—to speak more accurately—allows to be punished, in what he made, what he did not make. For sins are not natural but voluntary. Indeed, the cause of every sin, whether in an angel or in a human being, is one’s own perverse will; but the cause of the perverse will is not found in the natural movements of a rational and intellectual creature. Good cannot be the cause of evil; therefore evil is without a cause and lacks every natural origin.

Here arises that remarkable and inexplicable question: how the evil will of transgressing angels and human beings, although without a cause, is the effective cause of all sin and of every punishment of sin. And if someone says that the beginning of every sin is pride, let him observe that pride does not subsist in the nature of things. For it is neither essence, power, operation, nor any natural accident. It is a defect of the innermost power and a perverse desire for domination, as it is written: “Why are earth and ashes proud, since they have cast out their innermost things during their life?” It is called a beginning, not a cause, because it is the first advance and primordial outflow of sin, in which all sinned.

But if it is altogether nothing, what wise person would place it among causes, since it does not naturally subsist in anything?

Thus the irrational movement of the perverse will is punished in a rational nature—namely, in nature itself, which everywhere in itself and in all who participate in it remains good, safe, whole, unharmed, undefiled, incorruptible, impassible, and unchangeable through participation in the highest good; everywhere blessed, and most glorious in the elect, in whom it is deified [Note: [Col. 0943] A reads “deifies”]; excellent in the reprobate whom it contains, so that their substantial distinctiveness may not be reduced to nothing—that is, so that the natural goods they had acquired from their creation may not perish.

It rejoices in the contemplation of truth in those who possess perfect blessedness; it rejoices in the administration of substantiality in those who pay the penalties for their offenses. Whole in all, perfect, like its Creator, it will return—purified from all the filth of vices by which, in this mortal flesh, it is outwardly permitted to be disfigured and violated as by a kind of leprosy—and restored to the state of its original creation, recalled by the grace of its Redeemer and protector.

From this it may be understood that, in the nature of things, after the consummation of this sensible world, no wickedness, no death bringing corruption, and no misery infecting the fragile material of this present life will remain. All visible and invisible things will rest in their causes. Only the unlawful will of evil human beings and angels, wounded by the memory and conscience of their wicked ways, will be tormented in itself, when it finds nothing of the things it had desired for itself and imagined would be its future. For on that day all their thoughts will perish. He said that their thoughts would perish, not their substances.

But what thoughts did he say would perish? Surely the empty thoughts of sensible things, which in this life they irrationally crave with insane love—the fantasies that souls blinded by evil draw to themselves through irrational affections. They themselves, who fashion these fantasies, will become like them. They will find no true solidity of reality, but will be tormented like empty dreams [Note: [Col. 0945] CF reads “are tormented.”].

Hence Maximus says in the sixteenth chapter of *Ambigua*: “Those who wisely contemplate the divine words call ‘perdition,’ ‘hell,’ ‘sons of perdition,’ and similar names those who make what does not exist into a subsistence for themselves according to the inclination of their mind, and thus become altogether like fantasies.”

What shall I say of Saint Augustine, who in the twelfth book of his *Exameron* discusses how souls still established in this mortal flesh suffer nowhere but in fantasies either certain empty joys or certain empty punishments, whereas in the future life, after receiving their bodies, the righteous will rejoice in solid contemplation of truth, while the impious, suffering empty images of sensible things, will weep, with the substance of both remaining safe and unpunished?

For there are two kinds of suffering: one by which those who have been deified are carried into the purest knowledge of their Creator; the other by which the impious are plunged into the deepest ignorance of truth.

And what wonder if the impious, who in this life, still held in corruptible flesh, suffer through dreams, and after this life suffer imaginatively in hell, undergo these things more expressly after receiving their spiritual bodies and awakening, as it were, from a very deep sleep [Note: [Col. 0945] CF reads “as though awakening”], so that, as Augustine says, their true punishments are always these: false images in things that are not real, true sadness, true mourning and fear, late repentance, and the burning flame of thoughts?

By contrast, the righteous will suffer in the following way: after receiving their bodies and their minds being deified, they will possess true blessedness in true contemplations, true joy, and true gladness, because everything they receive in this life through faith they will behold in the future through direct vision. But what that vision itself will be, each person will see in himself by experience. For, says the Truth, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” [Note: [Col. 0945] C reads “in my Father’s home.”].

Both groups, nevertheless, will have fantasies, as it were certain expressed faces. For the righteous, these will be fantasies of divine contemplations; God will be seen not in himself but through certain manifestations of himself, according to the height of each saint’s contemplation. These are the clouds of which the Apostle says: “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ”—calling “clouds” the various manifestations of divine fantasies according to the height of each deified person’s vision.

For the impious, there will always be fantasies and diverse false appearances of mortal things, according to the various movements of their evil thoughts. And just as those who are deified will ascend through innumerable degrees of divine contemplation, as it is written, “The saints will go from strength to strength; carried up in the clouds of vision, they will see the God of gods in Zion”—that is, not through himself but in the mirror of divine fantasy [Note: [Col. 0945] CF reads *in specula*, “on/in a lookout”]—so those separated from God will continually descend through the various descents of their vices into the depth of ignorance and into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Yet in both groups—I mean the righteous and the impious—human nature will be and will always remain safe, whole, undefiled, and free from every contrary suffering. Both will have a similar spirituality of bodies, with all animality removed; a similar incorruptibility, with all corruption taken away; a similar glory of nature, when every dishonor is removed; a similar essence and a similar eternity.

These are the universal and natural goods of all humanity in the regeneration, common to all who participate in it. These are the gifts given from above, descending from the Father of lights, diffused generally among all. No one is excluded from their participation, no one is deprived of them, because no one subsists without them. They are not prevented from being given by anyone’s evil merits; no one’s good merits precede them so that they may be bestowed. They precede every merit. They flow universally to all through all things in an inexhaustible outpouring from the lavish fullness of divine goodness. They are increased in no one and diminished in no one; they are equally present in all, good and evil; they are withdrawn from no one. They will remain eternally and substantially in all, freed from every corruption and contrary suffering.

Nevertheless, they are capable of contrary qualities—I mean of good and evil wills, of virtue and dishonor. Good wills and virtues are present in them from nature and grace; but the movements subject to a perverse will, which are truly and properly called superfluities of nature, happen to them from no natural or supernatural cause. Therefore they bear them both outside themselves and within themselves without suffering.

For what exists through privation is not derived from nature or grace, since it is neither substance, nor a natural accident, nor one of the four natural powers with which the rational soul is adorned—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. Nor is it the two-horned fountain of these, namely wisdom and gentleness [Note: [Col. 0945] CF reads “charity”]; nor any of the powers that spring from them, about which it would now be lengthy and beside the purpose to speak; nor is it the supernatural excellence of the ineffable deification beyond every creature, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.” For it is not compared among all things but above all things, nor is it enclosed within the powers of created nature.

And so that you may not be surprised that I said human nature is capable of opposites, although it suffers nothing from them and the serenity of its simplicity is not disturbed, accept some examples.

This air with which we are surrounded, and through which breathing and exhaling creatures continually fan the fire of the heart through their lungs as through bellows, while nature allows no moment in which it is completely still for animals, bears both bright and foul clouds. The former receive the rays of the sun and the latter repel them. The former receive from above a thin, shining substance, close to the purity of the ether, by which they shine; the latter draw from below a dense darkness, like earthly filth, by which they reject the light.

The air itself, however, always preserves in all things the unchanging quality of its own subtlety and serenity. It does not become corporeal in the clouds, nor is it disturbed by the disturbances it suffers. It is capable of light and darkness, while its nature is neither increased by light nor diminished by darkness. It receives heat and cold, while its substance suffers nothing from heat or cold.

The corporeal mass it receives from earthly and watery vapors becomes hot or cold within it, gathers into clouds, turns and moves into winds, thickens into rain and showers, coagulates into snow and hail, and takes on the other forms that arise from the vapors mentioned above, which the Greeks call *atmides* (ἀτμίδες). The simple yet spiritual nature of the air supports these vapors until they become heavy with earthly and watery masses [Note: [Col. 0947] A reads “internal” for “earthly.”] [Note: [Col. 0947] A reads “weight” rather than “masses.”]. The air itself, however, as we have said, possesses its purity and incorruptible spirituality. It is no purer or more spiritual in light than in darkness; it is no subtler, nor does it penetrate bodies below it more deeply in calm weather than in its disturbances.

For this reason the philosophers gave it an appropriate Greek name. Air is called “spirit,” and therefore physicists call it a simple and spiritual body. This is unquestionably demonstrated by those who climb to the summit of Mount Olympus, because no *atmis* (ἀτμίς), that is, no vapor, whether from earth or water, can rise there [Note: [Col. 0947] CF reads “there”; A “in that place.”].

But the fact that its lower part—I mean the air—receives vapors for the benefit of mortal animals, which cannot live without an aerial breath, was arranged by divine providence. For if its simplicity, without any interposed moisture or corporeal density, were to inflate the lungs of mortal bodies, the fiery nature within the hearts would not burn at all, and consequently the whole body would grow cold, deprived of the power of heat through which vital movement is supplied to mortal limbs.

Therefore, so that the subtlety of the air, joined with vapors, might enter the lungs and, making a stronger thrust, kindle the fire of the heart, the lower part of the air was diffused around the earth and waters and made capable of moisture and corporeal density, without any corruption, loss, addition, alteration, or transformation of its supremely simple and serene nature.

I said that aerial spirit alone is insufficient to kindle the fire of the heart or nourish other bodies lacking sensation without some corporeal substance mixed with it, because the fiery and aerial elements are joined to one another in such a way that they produce no perceptible movement, owing to the excessive subtlety of their nature, which is always at rest and free from every disturbance. But when they are mixed with the elements below them—I mean earth and water—they exercise their power in the more corporeal quality of those elements and bring forth visibly their movements, by which they govern perceptible bodies.

We introduced this example so that we may recognize without hesitation that human nature in its regeneration will be supremely serene, since nothing earthly, moist, or heavy will remain in it, as it will be wholly transformed into spirit; yet it will be capable of diverse qualities without any alteration of its restoration or any contrary suffering.

For just as this air—from which we have taken a certain likeness of humanity [Note: [Col. 0947] CF reads “of humanity” rather than “of human nature.”]—receives from above the ethereal splendors and below the condensed fumes formed from earth and water, so humanity, made in the image of God but miserably fallen through its irrational movements into love of sensible things and into corruptible bodies that weigh it down, will, when it is recalled to its ancient state at the time of regeneration, shine with divine rays shining within it and above it in those who will be deified. But it will bear below and outside itself, in those who will be deprived of all blessedness, the fantastic memory of temporal and mortal things by which it is stained in this life [Note: [Col. 0947] A reads “mortal things, however.”].

It will not do so in order that it itself may suffer punishment in itself, but so that those things which it had drawn to itself against the will of its Creator may be condemned and utterly perish outside it—I mean wickedness, impiety, and the other members of iniquity that arose from the works of the flesh, that is, from the soul living carnally, by the occasion of original sin. When these are sought in themselves, they are nothing, because they are not among the things established by the Creator of all.

They have stolen into rational nature through the likeness of irrational animals, and therefore they will be wholly condemned in it, lest they harm it forever, although it must not be denied that, in the proper wills of the impious, memories of these things, by which they will be tormented, will remain.

For it is one thing for all wickedness to be utterly abolished generally in all human nature, and another for its fantasies—I mean the fantasies of wickedness—to be preserved forever in the consciences of those whom it corrupted in this life, and for them to be punished in this manner. Likewise, it is one thing for the same human nature to be restored to the grace it had lost through sin, namely, the dignity of the divine image; another for the individual conscience of the elect, through which they served their God in all things in this life by good deeds, to be deified beyond every power of humanity, and in this way to live forever in blessedness and be exalted above all things that exist.

For there they will be where he is whom they loved in this life and whom they always desired to see.

### 32.

From this arises the number of ways in which the rational creature is contemplated. Its first contemplation is in that general, common, and substantial power in which all human beings together and at once participate in its first condition, whether they are good or evil. The second is in its procession into this mortal life through the generation of individual human beings from bodies. The third is in its general return through itself into the angelic state, which it abandoned when it fell into this sensible world. The fourth is found in those who participate in it and, while living in this mortal flesh, seek themselves, their common nature, and above all the Creator of all things; by the merit of their own good will, with grace as their guide [Note: [Col. 0949] A omits “with grace as guide.”], they have attained the return to the common integrity of their nature, and afterward, by the gift of divine grace, leaving all things behind them, they will be transferred into God himself [Note: [Col. 0949] A reads “transferring themselves.”].

The fifth contemplation concerns those who will possess the natural goods universally implanted in nature, which are granted and will be granted by divine generosity to all without exception. Yet they will not be able to reach the highest gifts of divine grace, which are reserved and prepared for the just, because in this life they did not wish to serve God, held back by love of temporal things. In the other life, through this love, they will burn as though in an unquenchable flame, since they will not find there the things for which they lusted immoderately here. Instead, they will see their empty and false fantasies; and when they try to grasp them as though they were real things, they will vanish like shadows, because they are not supported by natural subsistence [Note: [Col. 0949] A reads “they vanish.”].

For they will be, as it is written: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” These will be the thoughts of which the Psalmist says, as we introduced shortly above: “On that day all their thoughts will perish.” It is as though he said: all the thoughts that in this life they had impressed upon their souls concerning earthly and temporal things, being devoted to them through their carnal desires, will perish on that day—that is, at the manifestation of truth—when, rising in spirit, they will find nothing of the things they had thought about while living in the flesh.

For what will the faithless Jew, the arrogant Ishmaelite, and the pagan blinded by impiety find of the false happiness which empty opinion promises them in the future life? Or how great will be the sadness, the pain, and the perpetual flame of impoverishment that will torment them when they find none of the earthly desires and mortal delights with which they had imbibed themselves through vain hope, and nothing remains for them except the empty, incomprehensible, and fleeting shadow of the things they had believed would be theirs?

They will pay eternal penalties, always wishing and yet unable to grasp it [Note: [Col. 0949] A omits “and yet unable”], because it is nothing. I do not even speak here of those who profess the Catholic faith but nevertheless think that the goods awaiting them will be carnal, localized, temporal, and sensible, and who likewise hold the same opinion concerning infernal punishments.

Here it is understood that nothing in the nature of things will suffer punishment except the vain thoughts of impious souls in themselves, outside every nature, because they are not among the number of natures. For they received their occasion from an evil will and earthly desires.

As we have often said, just as the blessedness of the just will be exalted beyond all natural powers through the Creator’s grace, so the punishment of the impious will be pressed down below every nature through the same Creator’s justice. For what is lower, and sunk farther outside every nature, than the vanity of vanities and the false imaginings of things that will always perish?

From this arises that remarkable and inexplicable matter. Yet true reasoning and the authority of divine Scripture prove that this happens in this way and no other: the just are blessed beyond all natural goods, while, as though from the opposite side, the impious are punished beneath those same natural goods. Nature itself, which both the good and the evil participate in, is established as a kind of middle point, so that it is neither increased by the blessedness of the good nor diminished by the unhappiness of the evil. Supported and content with its own natural goods alone, it contains the substances of all and supplies all its own things to all who participate in it [Note: [Col. 0949] A reads “supplying them with natural goods”; CF omits “with natural goods.”].

From it comes the general form of all who participate in it; from it comes the most particular form of each individual and the infinite number of plurality; from it come the numerical increases of bodies through places and times. By “times” I now mean the intervals through which the human body reaches its full growth; by “places,” the locations of the individual bodily members. From it proceed the natural accidents of bodies and souls [Note: [Col. 0949] A reads “whence” rather than “from it.”].

And what shall I say? That universal humanity is so balanced by its Creator between two mutually opposed extremes—namely, between the happiness of the elect and the unhappiness of the reprobate—that in those who are good it receives, through the gift of grace from above, an ineffable beauty beyond its own powers, while in those who are evil it draws no ugliness into itself, because justice prevents it [Note: [Col. 0949] CF reads “exhibits” rather than “prevents.”]. In it, indeed, no one’s ugliness is ugly, wickedness does not harm it, and error does not err. Its Creator adorns everything he made in it and in no way punishes it. Whatever he did not make, however, he sustains and permits in it, and does not allow it to become unpunished.

That punishment, nevertheless, is understood in two ways: either offenses are punished through indulgence in those who return to their beginning, or they are perpetually tormented in those who forever flee from their beginning.
