### 33

But if you ask me by what principle things that were not made by God are contained within the things made by him, or how things reckoned as lying outside  [Col. 0951A] human nature can be punished within it, I shall first answer you according to the simplicity of Catholic faith: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” And his ways are unsearchable at all times. Or how can reason be sought in his works, providence, goodness, and justice—he who surpasses every reason and understanding and is exalted above everything that is said and understood?

And if you demand an explanation of such matters, demand likewise an explanation of how all things were made from nothing; how this world will be dissolved and return to its causes; how our mortal bodies will pass not only into spiritual bodies but even into our souls, as Gregory holds; how we, who in this life are composed, as it were, of three measures of fine flour— [Col. 0951B] namely, body, soul, and spirit—will in the future be fermented, as it were, into a single simple mass, into inseparable spirituality, as Ambrose holds; how human beings, mortal by nature—for everything that does not receive its being from itself is called mortal—will by grace be changed into the immortal God.

And lest we seem to stray too far from the present matter, if you ask me how what is not according to nature but outside nature is driven within nature, sustained, and punished, while nature itself remains unpunished and unharmed by every contrary passion, I shall ask you in turn how those who are contained within nature’s boundaries will possess things that surpass nature’s powers—that is, how the saints will neither exceed the limits of  [Col. 0951C] their nature nor fail to receive those gifts that are beyond nature, namely, the gifts of grace.

But if in all these matters not only human reason but even angelic reason and understanding fail, be patient, make room for the incomprehensible divine power, and honor it with silence. For when one reaches it, every reason and understanding fails. Among the other things that surpass all reason and understanding, humbly concede that, under the administration of divine providence, things both outside nature and contrary to nature can be sustained by the power of nature and punished within it, while nature itself always remains wholly unharmed in itself.

But if you say: “All these are inscrutable miracles of divine power; although it is impossible for any rational and intellectual creature to know  [Col. 0951D] why all things that were made were made, and how they were made [the printed text includes ‘why … and’; CF omit these words], nevertheless they do not escape knowledge in every respect, so that no account could be given of why they were made.” “For this reason,” you say, “all things were made from nothing: so that the greatness and generosity of divine goodness might be both displayed and praised through the things he made.”

Does not this psalm, sung in the prophetic spirit, teach this—the psalm in which every invisible and visible creature is commanded to praise the Creator of  [Col. 0952A] all things: “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” and so forth? At its conclusion, through a wondrous contemplation of theology, it is made perfectly clear that all things are going to return to spiritual nature. For it concludes thus: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

If divine goodness alone had remained at rest within itself, without any operation, it might perhaps not have provided an occasion for praise. But now, diffusing itself through all visible and invisible things and existing as all things in all, it turns rational and intellectual creation toward knowledge of itself; and, offering the beautiful and innumerable forms of the other things to rational and intellectual creation as material for its praise, it made everything in such a way that there is no creature that does not praise the supreme good—either through itself and in itself, or through  [Col. 0952B] another.

There is another reason why all things were made from nothing. The supreme good, which subsists as good from itself and in itself, ought not to have withheld itself from creating good things—things that are good neither from themselves nor in themselves, but from it and in it. Accordingly, it created beings from things that did not exist, lest it be accused, as it were, of envy for holding itself back from establishing those things that it was able to establish. Otherwise it would be neither Lord, nor Creator of natures, nor the most abundant giver of its own goods, lacking in nothing, nor the most just judge of merits, nor the provider of all things, if it created nothing.

### 34

As for why this world will be dissolved and return to its causes, the following explanation is given. All things that proceed from the cause of all things, and from the primordial  [Col. 0952C] causes established within it, always desire by natural movement to return to their beginning, outside which they cannot rest.

There is another explanation: everything that flows from the source of all things would become worthless, indeed would perish completely, if it could neither return nor did return to its source. But if the return of visible things to their invisible causes were prevented, it would be not only contrary but even harmful to the very strong natural desire of all things.

Our mortal bodies, however, will pass not only into spiritual bodies but even into our souls, because natural necessity requires that, just as the rational soul, made in the image of God, will return to him whose image and likeness it is, so the body, which was made in the image of the soul and is, as it were, the image of an image, will be transformed into its cause,  [Col. 0952D] which is the soul, and through it, as through a kind of intermediary, into God himself, who is the one cause of all things—freed from every earthly weight and corporeality.

The clearest examples of this process are offered. We see moisture pass into vapor, vapor into flame, and consequently moisture into flame, while flame passes into the fiery element. Physicists also assert that the solar ray draws into itself the moist vapors from the sea,  [Col. 0953A] rivers, every gathering of waters, and the earth, and consumes them, as it were, as food into its own nature.

### 35

As for the fact that we, who are composed in this life, will be united into a certain simple unity, the explanation is as follows. It was necessary that the image of the one and supreme Trinity—which is inseparable, simple, and uncompounded in itself—should be reduced to unity and inseparable simplicity. Otherwise it would lose the greatness of its dignity and deform its beauty; divine clemency does not permit this to happen.

For the principal exemplar does not permit its image, made by itself, like itself, and according to itself, continually to be separated from it by some deformity or dissimilarity, or by  [Col. 0953B] some composition that removes its simplicity.

The same reasoning applies to the return of mortal human beings—however they are called mortal, whether because they subsist neither from themselves nor in themselves, or because they have been swallowed up by mortality as the penalty of original sin—into their God, who alone is immortal. For it would not accord with the goodness of the immortal Creator that his image should be held in eternal death.

The fact that he permitted it to become mortal and die because of its perverse will, by which it had refused to obey him, manifests his mercy more than his vengeance. For he wished to correct it and, once corrected, recall it to itself—not to leave it uncorrected, perpetually expelled, and infinitely distant.

If, then, concerning such matters you seek to establish not how they were made but the reason why  [Col. 0953C] they were made—since the former surpasses every understanding, whereas the latter is not denied to be in some measure comprehensible through theoretical speculation—I too shall try to give some account of the present question. [The printed text adds *ut nulla de eo reddi possit ratio*, “so that no account can be given of it,” at a syntactically uncertain point after the latter clause; the distinction just drawn concerns the unknowable manner and the investigable reason.]

It seems to me that the Creator and governor of the whole universe permitted the irrational movements of the perverse will of evil human beings and angels to be punished within it, while the universe itself remains wholly freed from and liberated from every contrary passion, so that, through comparison, as Saint Augustine says, the established will of the just might be praised and exalted by contrast with the perverse will of the wicked.

For, as he himself says, the art of painting inserts the color black among the other colors, so that by comparison with it,  [Col. 0953D] when its darkness is perceived, the brightness of the other colors may be demonstrated.

What is considered deformed in some part of the universe in itself becomes, in the whole, not only beautiful because it has been beautifully ordered, but even a cause of general beauty. Thus there is wisdom through comparison with folly; knowledge through comparison with ignorance, which exists through defect and privation; life through comparison with death through defect; and light, through opposition to darkness by privation,  [Col. 0954A] worthy of praise. In short, all virtues not only gain praise from the vices opposed to them, but would not acquire praise without comparison with them.

By the same reasoning, the blessedness of the just finds glory for itself through the punishments of the wicked, and the joy of a good will through the sadness of a perverse will. And, as true reason does not hesitate to declare, everything that is judged by those unable to consider all things together to be evil, dishonorable, ugly, wretched, or punishment in the parts of the universe is, when viewed in the contemplation of the universe—as of a single whole painting’s beauty—neither punishment, nor wretched, nor ugly, nor dishonorable, nor evil.

For whatever is ordered by the administrations of divine providence is good, beautiful, and just. What is better than that,  [Col. 0954B] through comparison with opposites, the universe and its Creator should receive ineffable praise? What is more just than that those who have merited well should occupy the highest order of things, while those who have merited evil should occupy the lowest? What is more honorable than that the universe of all things should be adorned through the proper dispositions of each individual?

Therefore no one who philosophizes rightly believes that any evil or evil thing, any impiety or impious person, any misery or miserable person, any punishment or punished person, any torment or person subject to torment, any ugliness or ugly thing, or any dishonor or dishonorable thing can exist within the good, excellent, most religious, most blessed, unpunishable, most happy, most beautiful, and most honorable harmony of the whole created universe, ordered by him who is supreme honor,  [Col. 0954C] supreme beauty, supreme blessedness, supreme repose, supreme happiness, [of] supreme religion [the printed genitive is grammatically irregular in this list], and the supreme good.

For it is one thing to consider the individual parts of the universe, and another to consider the whole. Hence it follows that what is thought to be contrary in a part is found in the whole not only not to be contrary, but even to be an increase of beauty.

Hell, therefore, which the Greeks call ἅδης (*hádēs*), that is, “sadness” or “deprivation of pleasures,” is recognized as evil by the evil when considered in itself; but when placed within the most beautiful ordering of the universe, it becomes good for the good. For in it not only the severity of the most just Judge and his eternal sentence are manifested, but the blessedness of blessed human beings and angels also gains praise, and beauty is increased.

 [Col. 0954D] Why, then, should it not be permitted to occur within the boundaries of nature, since from it nature’s praise is acquired and its beauty increased ?

Why the various punishments of the wicked are commonly designated by Latins by the term *infernum* (“hell”) has been discussed on the basis of popular opinion, as Saint Augustine explains in the twelfth book of his *Exameron*. For the ancients, entrusting their hopes to fables and their souls to tombs, thought that, just as the corpses of bodies are buried in tombs, so souls too were held with those corpses in the same  [Col. 0955A] burial chambers. Hence they called it *infernum*, as though it were situated beneath the earth.

From this arose the false opinion that souls were located beneath the earth. The Greeks, however, considering matters more sharply and expressing them more precisely in their customary manner, called hell ἅδην (*hádēn*), as we have said—that is, “sadness.”

For, carefully investigating the nature of visible and invisible things, they could find no place for punishments except in the poverty of the lustful will of evil human beings and angels, and in the lack and deprivation of the things they had loved immoderately. From these arises sadness, in which the irrational appetites of rational souls are tormented, whether in this life or in the future.

There is poverty because they are unable to find what they desire to have; there is lack and deprivation because  [Col. 0955B] what they had imagined they possessed through an unlawful and destructive love is entirely taken away from them, and they are no longer permitted to abuse it.

This, then, is the whole punishment and torment of evil thoughts and irrational desires: pain and sadness. By these two things the conscience of the wicked is punished within itself. Yet these two things are not evil, because they come upon those whom they torment through the most just administration of divine providence, and because what is not evil everywhere and in all things cannot be called evil.

Sadness is good in those who mourn their sins, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted.” Likewise pain is good in those to whom it seems slow and wearisome to wait until they reach the blessedness promised to them.

 [Col. 0955C] The Apostle suffered from this pain when he said: “I desire to depart and be with Christ.” What shall I say of the pains of those who became martyrs of Christ ? 

But the sadness and pain of impious desires, whether in this life or in the next, are not evil because they punish evil desires. Sadness arising from deprivation of temporal things burns imperfect desires like an unquenchable flame; pain arising from the rottenness of lustful desire bites like a worm that does not die, when what is desired is taken away.

There is another reason why the sadness and pain of the wicked are not evil. They are, as it were, an exceedingly abundant material for praise, eternal joy, and eternal salvation, which those who pass into God enjoy.

 [Col. 0955D] Thus, I think, the third point you were seeking—and which you preferred to the other two—has been discovered: that what is neither according to substance nor according to a natural accident, and was not made by God at all, can be punished in some natural and substantial subject made by God—one which is not punished in itself and does not suffer along with what is punished in it.

For this reason it is rightly understood that what is most truly believed is that God does not punish in any nature created by him what he made; rather, he punishes what he did not make.

**DISC.** It has indeed been discovered,  [Col. 0956A] although it is still not entirely free from obscurity. For I do not yet clearly perceive, brightly and without any mist, how what does not exist can be punished, while what exists cannot be punished. I would more readily believe that what exists can be punished than that what does not exist can be.

**MAG.** Here again you seem almost to be forgetting the preceding arguments, and I fear that you, whom I thought had emerged from and been freed from the depths of the present question, have once more been plunged into it and detained there.

**DISC.** You need not fear so greatly. For of the matters on which we agree between ourselves, some I penetrate with the acuity of my mind, like an ethereal light, with perfect clarity; others I see obscurely, as through air and broken little clouds [the construction *aëra intercisas ruptas nubeculas* is defective]. Therefore I am neither ashamed nor reluctant to repeat the question, so that I may see more clearly what has not yet been wholly disclosed  [Col. 0956B] to the sight of my mind.

**MAG.** Come, then, tell me: have all things that exist been led forth from nonexistence into existence by him alone who truly is, the superessential cause of the whole of being? And is there anything in the nature of things that was not established by him ?

**DISC.** Why do you ask me about what is known to all who philosophize rightly and has been defined without hesitation? Everything is from the One, and there is nothing that is not from him.

**MAG.** Do you therefore think that everything that is from him can be corrupted?

**DISC.** I would not say that either. For everything that he brought into being, he brought into being not merely so that it might exist, but so that it might always exist, since it was always present causally in him. Whatever always exists is eternal; whatever is eternal is true; and whatever is true  [Col. 0956C] cannot be corrupted by any force.

Therefore nothing made by the one beginning of all things receives corruption of itself. What could corrupt it? It is neither true nor plausible that what was established by the Creator in order always to exist should be corrupted by him.

And if some created nature is better than it, it is impossible for a superior nature to corrupt an inferior one, since the good cannot become the cause of the corruption of any good. But if the creature is inferior to it, it is more difficult for what is inferior to corrupt what is superior. If, however, it is a good equal to it, no good desires to corrupt a good equal to itself, since they are of the same power, operation, and essence.

It follows, then, that no nature either wishes or is able to corrupt another nature.

There is another argument that asserts beyond doubt that  [Col. 0956D] none of the things created by the one God, the Creator of all, can either receive corruption or be corrupted. If it began to be corrupted, an end of its corruption would follow.

Everything that begins to suffer awaits a twofold end of its suffering. Either it will be completely consumed by its corruption so that it no longer exists, and its corruption will be extinguished with it—for when the corruptible thing has been consumed, its corruption must perish, since it finds nothing to corrupt—or corruption will reach such an end that  [Col. 0957A] something incorruptible remains in what it corrupts, something that cannot be corrupted; and once it has found this, corruption necessarily ceases. For when corruption corrupts nothing, it is extinguished in itself.

But reason refutes both of these possibilities. No nature can be corrupted so that it entirely ceases to exist and is reduced to nothing. For it was created so that it might always subsist. If it began to be corrupted and were brought to such an end that it was completely destroyed by its corruption, it would plainly be reduced to nothing. The power of the essence created by the supreme good utterly excludes this.

No nature, therefore, begins to be corrupted or awaits the end of its destruction.

But if something made by God begins to be corrupted, and yet what  [Col. 0957B] cannot be corrupted remains in it, having received no corruption at all, then that which remains is plainly the very thing that alone and wholly was made incorruptible by God, which does not receive corruption; and consequently it never began to be corrupted.

None, therefore, of the things created by the supreme good receives corruption or the possibility of being corrupted.

**MAG.** I see that you are recovering your senses and giving a clear and indisputable account of the things that seemed obscure to you. Now that this judgment concerning the incorruptibility of things created by God has been established, consider whether everything that cannot be corrupted can be punished.

**DISC.** I do not see how that could happen. It seems to me that everything that cannot be corrupted cannot be punished, just as I think everything corruptible must be punishable.  [Col. 0957C] For who would deny that corruption is a kind of punishment?

When our mortal bodies undergo the very pain defined as the sudden corruption of health, we perceive that they are being punished. No one doubts that souls still held within them and in some way suffering along with them are also punished, since reason teaches that the simple nature of the soul can neither be corrupted nor punished nor infected by bodily passions. Yet it is said to suffer along with the body when it strives to help the body congenial and joined to it, so that the body may not be destroyed.

For it always desires to gather the body added to it into unity and to hold it together in one, lest it disperse and be corrupted.

**MAG.** The soul, then, made in the image of God, just as it is never corrupted in itself, so is it never punished.

**DISC.** The foregoing reasoning teaches no differently. For if  [Col. 0957D] no spiritual substance can be punished in itself, how much more is this true of the substance made in the image of God?

**MAG.** What, then, shall we say about the body? Is it punished because it is corrupted?

**DISC.** We do not say that anything is punished unless it experiences its punishment. Therefore, if the experience of sensation belongs solely to the soul—as may be understood from dead corpses—the body is merely corrupted and is not punished.

We also say that the bodies of things entirely devoid of sensation, such as wood, stones, and the shoots of plants, are corrupted but are not punished. But if external sensation belongs not only to the soul  [Col. 0958A] but also to the body, it cannot be strongly denied that a mortal and animate body can both be corrupted and punished.

**MAG.** Mortal bodies, then, if they are capable of sensation, seem able to be both corrupted and punished; but if they lack sensation, they seem able only to be corrupted, not punished.

**DISC.** That is my view.

**MAG.** All mortal bodies, then, whether they are merely corrupted or are at once corrupted and punished, were not made by God. For the preceding arguments have established that everything made by the supreme good receives no corruption and consequently no punishment.

**DISC.** Who but a fool would dare deny that this visible world, consisting chiefly of perceptible bodies, was made by God?

**MAG.** How, then, are its bodies corrupted  [Col. 0958B] or punished?

**DISC.** We speak of corruption in two ways. The first is the process by which the union of the general elements proceeds through visible forms into generation, and by which individual bodies are again dissolved and return to the universal elements from which they were composed.

The second is the process by which, while affirming that the essence, power, and operation of no creature can be damaged, we nevertheless acknowledge that the wills of rational and intellectual creatures are corrupted by irrational movements.

The first mode, concerning temporal, local, and sensible things, seems to teach more a pouring and transformation of things into one another than corruption, because everything ordered by divine providence brings beauty to the universe, not corruption.

 [Col. 0958C] In all these things the integrity of natural substances and the mutability of natural qualities are preserved. These two together constitute the fullness of sensible creation. Accordingly, by an abusive use of language, the variety of temporal things through the increase and dissolution of increases is called by the name “corruption.”

It is in this manner of speaking that the Apostle is understood to have spoken when discussing the fragility of the human body: “This corruptible body will put on incorruption, and this mortal body immortality.” And elsewhere: “The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things.”

By these words he signifies not only the dissolution of the still fragile and mortal human body into the simple elements whose mutually compatible qualities compose it,  [Col. 0958D] but also its restoration from those elements and its return into spiritual and incorruptible qualities, calling the mutability of the earthly body “corruption.”

For these sensible and temporal things are not despised by those who desire spiritual and eternal things as though they were evil, but because they are unstable and mutable, and await the end of their transformation into something better. In comparison with stable and immutable things, which await no end of their transformation into something better, they are judged contemptible and altogether to be abandoned and left behind.

 [Col. 0959A] The second mode does not consist in the transformation of mutable things within nature, but in the disturbances of individual wills, which are outside nature. It considers the corruptions—properly so called—the vices of a perverse will, which do not subsist from God.

Accordingly, the bodies of this world should be considered not to be corrupted, but to be transformed within themselves by natural movement and variation, and consequently not to be punished. Natural passions should in no way, according to the proper nature of things, be called punishments.

And if someone says that the transformations of sensible bodies into one another through generation and dissolution occur because of the sin of human nature, and therefore can truly be called corruptions, let him observe that  [Col. 0959B] the order and beauty of the whole visible creation consist solely in the alternation of things through places and times; that these alternations and variations derive their causes from nowhere except divine providence and administration; and that they were made more for the instruction of human nature and its recall to its Creator than for the punishment of sin.

In this way God wished, through a kind of spiritual medicine, to recall his image both into itself and to himself, so that, wearied and disciplined by disgust with mutable things, it might desire to contemplate the stability of immutable and eternal things, and might ardently seek the unchanging forms of truth, in whose beauty, without any variation, it might rest.

From this follows what has also been concluded and established in many places earlier in the present discussion:  [Col. 0959C] no other place can be found for corruptions and punishments except the perverse and illicit movements of the proper will of rational and intellectual creation. These movements receive their occasions neither from God nor from created nature; for they are causeless, since when they are sought in themselves, nothing else is found in them except the privation and defect of a lawful and natural will.

**MAG.** Reason therefore does not allow anything which cannot be corrupted to be punished. But everything made from the one cause of all things must be incorruptible. Therefore everything made from the one cause of all things cannot suffer punishment.

Moreover, if divine authority—which neither deceives  [Col. 0959D] nor is deceived—testifies that the punishments of the wicked are future, it follows that you establish corruptions, punishments, and torments in something made by God, and therefore properly said to exist and reasonably concluded to be incapable of suffering; and that you return fearlessly to the matter about which you seemed to hesitate and say without hesitation that only what does not exist can be punished in what exists—that is, the perverse will, which is in no way substantial, in the phantasies of sensible things. These phantasies are not to be understood as  [Col. 0960A] wholly nonexistent, since they are impressed in memory from natural forms. But what exists must be wholly unpunishable, since by its own power it sustains and permits to be punished that which is punished.

Accordingly, divine justice is most truly proclaimed in the statement that God permits nothing he made to be punished in any creature he made; but he punishes what he did not make.

**DISC.** Enough, and more than enough, has been said about this matter.

**MAG.** Plainly enough, if you see with complete clarity and without any hesitation that it is so and not otherwise.

**DISC.** I see clearly, and with every obscurity removed I understand that the universe of creation made by God is unpunishable and wholly free from corruption.

**MAG.** Let us return, then, to the subject at hand: the return of the created universe into its causes.

### 36. DISCIPLE

First, I think, we must consider by what [Col. 0960B] reasoning punishments will be eternal when there will be no wickedness, lest it be coeternal with goodness; and all impiety, lest it be coeternal with divine worship, will perish; and every iniquity, lest it be hostile to the divine laws, will be abolished from the nature of things. What true reason demands is that, when wickedness has ceased, there will be no wicked person; for a person is wicked through wickedness. When impiety has perished, no impious person will remain; for every impious person is impious through impiety. When iniquity has been abolished, who will be left iniquitous?

No wise person doubts that wickedness, impiety, and iniquity will perish, considering that wickedness cannot arise unless it finds someone whom it can harm. But in the future, when God will be all in all and every creature will be liberated from servitude, whom will wickedness harm? No one. Impiety likewise, by the same reasoning, is understood [Col. 0960C] to be destined to perish. For how will there be impiety and an impious person when the worship of false gods has been wholly extinguished and the one God is known by all, both the elect and the reprobate, in all things? How will iniquity remain when no one will be able to transgress the divine laws?

Divine Scripture also declares this most openly when it says: “Let sinners perish from the earth, and the iniquitous, so that they are no more.” It is not their substance that is to be understood as perishing, but sin and iniquity. So too what blessed Jerome, in his exposition of Ezekiel, introduced from the prophet Isaiah under the figure of Jerusalem as referring to the universal purification of the whole human nature: “I will sanctify it,” he says, “in burning fire, and it will devour the material like hay.”

For in that passage we understand “material” (*materies*) in two ways. [Col. 0960D] Either the formless matter that was made from nothing is signified—the matter from which, through the diversity of forms added to it, the structure of this sensible world is composed. This matter will burn like hay when it is sanctified, that is, purified, in the very nature made in the image of God, so that nothing material, temporal, earthly, visible, transitory, or mutable remains in it, since it will be wholly transformed into spiritual stability and uniformity. Or the prophet wished, under the term “material,” to indicate the [Col. 0961A] occasions of all vices and evil deeds—that is, wickedness, impiety, and iniquity—or both. How, then, will there be punishments when nothing worthy of punishment remains in the nature of things?

### TEACHER

Enough has been said about these matters above and, as I think, they have been settled completely. Therefore, since you demand it, they must now be gathered together briefly.

Indeed, among us every controversy had been removed and it had been agreed that, by the most just sentence of the divine judgment, all wickedness and the wicked, all impiety and the impious, and all iniquity and the iniquitous must be abolished, so that they may no longer impede the integrity of natures, like certain filth that must be purified and wholly removed from the nature of things. This has been established not only by the authority of the holy Fathers and of divine Scripture, but also by the [Col. 0961B] investigations of sound reasoning.

Vain human thoughts, however, in the false phantasies of temporal things, will remain in the souls of those who will receive only the integrity of nature, but will not be transformed into glory; and they will burn like an inextinguishable flame through belated repentance concerning the things they had unlawfully and disorderedly desired in this life.

Therefore, as it seems to me, those who, wishing to teach that rational nature both remains forever and burns forever in the flames of punishments, have proposed an ambiguous example when they say that the stone asbestos remains forever and burns forever, so that neither its substance, nor its quantity, nor its quality is diminished or corrupted in any way while the flame in it is not extinguished.

They could use this comparison [Col. 0961C] no less rationally to persuade us that not only will the natural goods of rational nature remain forever without any loss, but also that, in those who, once purified and sanctified, will receive deification beyond all natural goods, these goods will shine with the glory of eternal blessedness, as in an unquenchable flame of divine grace [the text prints *in extinguibili*, literally “in an extinguishable”; the context suggests *inextinguibili*, “unquenchable”], so that their natural beauty will remain perpetually and the splendor of deification will shine above all.

You distinguish, then, I think, between those things that will wholly perish and those things that are assigned to eternal punishments.

### DISCIPLE

I do distinguish. For I see that vices and the occasions of vices will be utterly erased from the nature of things, while the phantasies of temporal things, by which imperfect souls dwelling in the flesh are deceived, will remain assigned to the eternal [Col. 0961D] fires of punishments, so that the perverse desires of the wicked may be tormented in them.

But a considerable question still troubles me. If nothing will be coeternal with goodness, blessedness, and the other divine virtues that are predicated of God, why is something coeternal opposed to truth—namely, the false and falsity? For, unless I am mistaken, as falsity is opposed to truth, so the false is opposed to the true. If, therefore, every phantasy [Col. 0962A] is false, and consequently falsity as well, who would deny that phantasy is contrary to truth? But if the phantasy of temporal things is distributed among eternal punishments, then certainly phantasies will be eternal and will perpetually be opposed to truth.

### TEACHER

Such darkness would not unjustly have confronted you if, first illumined by the clearest ray of truth itself—the truth about which the question is—you had discerned clearly that the false and phantasy are the same thing, without any distinction, so that every phantasy is false and every false thing is phantasy.

But since there is a great difference between the false and phantasy, it follows that what is properly called “false” alone is opposed to truth, whereas phantasy is not contrary to truth.

### DISCIPLE

Please explain what difference separates the false [Col. 0962B] from phantasy.

### TEACHER

They are distinguished by their definitions. The false is what desires to be what it is not. For it wishes to appear other than it is, because the thing of which it is predicated is not in fact as it is predicated to be.

Some fables belong to this category, such as the flight of Daedalus. That story is neither true nor probable, but an entirely false opinion that deceives the foolish. Daedalus never flew, although he is said to have sailed from Crete to Euboea. It is therefore called “false” because it deceives and misleads the judgment of those who are deceived, who approve false things in place of true ones; and this is the proper meaning of error.

This is what is truly called “false,” although in dialectical propositions both negations and affirmations are often called false. Negations are called false, [Col. 0962C] for example, in “Every human being is not an animal is false”; affirmations likewise, as in “Every human being is just is false.”

Phantasy, however, is a certain image and appearance impressed upon the memory from a visible or invisible form. Since no corporeal or incorporeal thing is yet perceptible in itself to mortal senses, the nature of things has arranged that images of sensible things are expressed in the external sense, while images of intelligible things are expressed in the internal sense. Then, as though from two springs—namely, sensible and intelligible things—two rivers flow together into memory: one river draws its course from lower things through bodily sensation, while the other comes from higher things through that sense which belongs to the soul alone.

Everything impressed upon memory from these sources is [Col. 0962D] properly called phantasy, that is, appearance, as we said above. Indeed, *phantasia* derives its etymology from the Greek word φαίνω (*phainō*), whose interpretation is “I appear.”

How, then, could phantasy be opposed to truth, when truth itself, invisible in itself, meets and manifests itself ineffably to those who seek it through its own phantasies, which they call theophanies? And since every phantasy is a [Col. 0963A] likeness of natural things impressed upon the soul, why should what proceeds from nature be judged contrary to truth, when no nature resists truth by reason of contrariety?

True reason also confirms this. It asserts most firmly that no phantasy concerning what is not contained within the number of natures can be expressed in the senses or in memory. For whatever wholly lacks substance, form, and quality cannot be represented by any likeness or appearance, and therefore cannot produce any phantasy.

Indeed, the phantasies formed in the human senses by false and fabricated bodies of unclean spirits, whom those spirits deceive, should properly be called shadows, not phantasies.

### DISCIPLE

Phantasy, then, is something good, since it is the imagination of natural things.

### TEACHER

[Col. 0963B] I cannot deny that. For whatever arises from natural causes is not denied to be good.

### DISCIPLE

Then you are compelled to admit that something good can be punished. For you said that the phantasies of temporal things are to be assigned to eternal punishments.

### TEACHER

Not at all. I did not say that the phantasies themselves are to be tormented by punishments, but that the irrational movements of perverse wills are to be subjected to eternal punishments in them. For we have considered that what is not cannot be punished except in something good that is.

### DISCIPLE

You remember, I think, your reasoning stated above, by which you concluded without hesitation that the phantasies of temporal things impressed upon souls, whether in this life or afterward in the other, are wholly nothing; and that perverse wills are therefore punished in them, because, when the phantasies are thought capable of being grasped [Col. 0963C] in something, they escape those who desire to grasp them, and vanish.

### TEACHER

I remember. Nor do I regret having said this, since I did not say that phantasies are a substantial good in the full sense. Rather, I proved beyond doubt that they adhere to substantial goods and arise from them.

And whether the punishments of the impious or the rewards of the just are arranged in them, I nevertheless did not hesitate to assert that they are good everywhere, since even the happiness of the blessed, which consists in the contemplation of truth, will be administered through phantasies which, to distinguish them from other phantasies, theologians call theophanies.

For God himself is and always will be invisible in himself. He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light.

But concerning the fact that the false and falsity will not perpetually be opposed [Col. 0963D] to the true and to truth, lest they be coeternal with them, no wise person should doubt. For who, inquiring by sound reasoning into the state of the future life, would say that falsity will exist when truth will appear in all things, and every false thing will be removed not only from the nature of things but also from the judgment of the whole rational and intellectual creature? There no one deceives and no one is deceived, when the nature of things returns to its causes, in which nothing will be considered except [Col. 0964A] the true and truth, insofar as each of the elect is permitted to contemplate it according to the height of his gift.

Although truth will appear to the just and the unjust in different ways, indeed in infinitely manifold ascents and descents of divine visions, it will nevertheless appear to all. For then, with injustice alone punished and destroyed in all the unjust, nature itself will remain purified and undefiled, destined to return to the levels from which it had fallen through sin.

The time has come to examine what remains concerning this return.

### DISCIPLE

Certainly. Before that, however, I would like to know—for this greatly disturbs me—how the whole of all natures, if it is to return into God, will tolerate any punishments being contained within it. For it is not credible [Col. 0964B] that punishment exists in God.

### TEACHER

Tell me, please: is everything that is called by the name “hell” and “punishments,” or is it not?

### DISCIPLE

I am hemmed in on every side. If I say that it is, you will immediately say: “Why does it seem surprising to you that what is, among the other things that are, will return into him from whom all things are?” But if I say that it is not, you will reply: “Why do you count among all the things that will return into God that which is not?”

And again, if I grant that everything signified by the name “hell” is outside the universe, I shall immediately be convicted, deprived of every rational basis, and unwillingly compelled to admit that it is not surprising that what is not within the things that are in God is also not within God himself. Reason will mock me, for it proclaims without hesitation that nothing can rightly [Col. 0964C] be thought or understood outside God and the universe created by him.

For everything that is and everything that is not is encompassed by the Creator and the creature.

But if I say that hell is within, I shall be compelled to admit that not only the things that are but also the things that are not are contained within the bounds of divine goodness, justice, providence, and judgment. For we believe and understand that not only the things that are, but also the things that are not—whether by excellence, beyond every intellect, or by privation, beneath everything understood to exist—are governed by divine power. Nothing that is or is not can go outside that power.

For everything expelled from the order of the blessed cannot escape beyond the divine laws within which all things are contained. Those who fall from the higher [Col. 0964D] orders are compelled to descend into lower orders and to be held within them.

Every order—whether the highest, directed upward; the lowest, directed downward; or the middle—is established by God and kept within him. Nothing exists outside him, while within him everything that is and everything that is not is comprehended in a marvelous and ineffable manner.

Therefore, whether I say that hell exists, as divine Scripture testifies, or deny that it exists in the nature of things, I cannot [Col. 0965A] deny that it is contained among the things that will return into God, that it is encompassed by him who encompasses all things, and outside whom nothing can be thought, believed, or understood.

This is especially so since I understand firmly that darkness is contained within light, silence within sound, shadow within body, and other similar things. These establish their causes in the things to which they correspond in opposition.

For whether they are absences of things, or deficiencies and privations, or opposites and contraries, they cannot in any way be understood to exist without those things whose absences, deficiencies, privations, oppositions, and contrarieties they are. I say that they exist in the sense in which not only substantial and natural things, but also the things that correspond to them from the opposite side, are said to exist.

For there is no vice that is not contained within the [Col. 0965B] position of the virtue which it strives to resist diametrically.

### TEACHER

I rejoice greatly that you have escaped unharmed, through the strength of your contemplation and without being caught in any way, from the nets that you yourself spread. And now, unless I am mistaken, you understand that not only everything created by the one God, but also everything that the irrational movement of the rational and intellectual creature has superimposed, is contained now within the order of divine providence.

You also understand that not only is all this now contained within the order of divine providence, but that after the universal creature has returned to its causes it will be ordered into God himself, when the complete beauty of the whole created universe has been perfected.

Nor is this surprising, since no nature can punish another nature, and no vice can corrupt the virtue by which it is contained. More than this: from all these things [Col. 0965C] ordered within the divine laws, the fullness and beauty of all natures will be completed, and the harmonious symphony of all visible and invisible things will be played without any dissonance.

### DISCIPLE

You are not mistaken. For the nets I spread—that is, the problems I proposed—were spread by me so that I would not remain caught in them any longer, but, freed from them, might clearly perceive with an unimpeded gaze of the mind the unification of the whole of nature, joined together from diverse and opposed things.

I was instructed in this by musical principles, in which I perceive that nothing else pleases the mind or produces beauty except rational intervals between diverse voices; when these intervals are compared with one another, they produce the sweetness of musical melody.

Here something marvelous and scarcely comprehensible by the mind alone is made intelligible: it is not [Col. 0965D] the diverse sounds—for example, those of organ pipes, the strings of a lyre, or the holes of a flute—which, being perceived in some way by the senses, seem to belong among the things that exist, that produce harmonic sweetness. Rather, it is the proportions and proportional relations of the sounds, which the inner sense of the mind alone perceives and judges when they are compared with one another.

These proportions and proportional relations of perceptible voices and sounds are rightly said to exist, because not only does bodily sensation suffer nothing from them, but they are also contemplated beyond every [Col. 0966A] sense by the keenest perceptions of the rational mind, as though above the nature of things. Although they are counted among the things that are not, they provide and establish the most honorable concord with the things that are.

Whether the person who listens to the sounds understands what produces sweetness and beauty in them or does not understand, an inner sense is nevertheless present in all, from which the orderly comparison and fitting union of things are not hidden.

For who can understand the power of the number six, which is understood to be the foundation of the whole of harmony; who can understand, within the natures of things, its comparisons with its sesquialter, sesquitertian, and also double ratios, when the whole universe of visible and invisible things is established in it as in a certain principal exemplar?

What, then, is surprising if the harmony of the whole creature is composed from those things [Col. 0966B] that substantially exist, from natural accidents, and from those things that do not exist—whether by excellence or by defect and privation—when among all things that are and are not, no wickedness or evil that could resist the goodness of all things, and no baseness or deformity that could resist the beauty and fairness returning to their causes and to their Creator, will remain at all.

Therefore, I am not disturbed when I hear that a most beautiful harmony will arise from the punishments of evil wills and the rewards of good ones. Punishments are good when they are just, and rewards are good when they are more freely given than repaid according to good merits. I see that grave and acute sounds, together with their intermediate sounds, produce a certain symphony among themselves through their proportions [Col. 0966C] and proportional relations.

If someone should object that the perverse wills of wicked human beings and angels, to whom punishments are owed, are evil, and that consequently, in the restoration and return of natures, evil will always remain and suffer punishment; and if this is so, it follows that the beauty of natures will not be wholly free from being stained by the baseness of wickedness. To him I shall reply, with God as guide and with true reason, that first of all no evil is found within the nature of things or outside it, as Dionysius the Areopagite establishes with many arguments in his book *On the Divine Names*. To introduce them now would be lengthy and superfluous.

Next, I shall say that the perverse movements of perverse wills are not evil, but illicit.

For who would call evil what proceeds from the free choice of a rational [Col. 0966D] creature? If the freedom of rational nature, created in the image of God, was given by God—for the image of God ought not to be held by any laws under compulsion—then necessarily nothing that proceeds from that freedom can rightly be called evil or wickedness, lest evil and wickedness be enclosed within something.

And even if free will was granted to rational and intellectual creatures not so that they might sin through it, but so that through it they might serve their Creator beautifully and rationally, nevertheless, [Col. 0967A] although it has been drawn, as though captive, by irrational movements toward illicit things, evil does not arise from this. Rather, something arises that must be corrected by divine justice and recalled by divine mercy, if the freedom of the will obeys its corrections and amendments.

But if, being stubborn and swollen with pride, it wishes to persist in its perverse movements, its lustful impulse will be restrained, so that it cannot grasp what it illicitly desires.

This is the whole of what is called the punishment of a free and perverse will: to be prohibited from its illicit movements, so that it cannot reach the end of its desire.

I say this so that I may not seem to resist the authority of the most blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, who allows evil to be found neither in any nature or substance nor in any irrational [Col. 0967B] affections of rational nature, nor to be conceded in any way.

For there is no vice of a rational creature that is not good in some irrational creature. Therefore, since it is not found to be prohibited everywhere but only in some particular thing, it ought to be called not evil but illicit in the thing in which it is prohibited.

Let us introduce a few examples of this principle. Pride, as blessed Dionysius and Gregory the Theologian say, is good in a horse but illicit and inappropriate in a human being. Ferocity is good in a lion, without which it cannot be called a lion—for a gentle lion is not a lion, having lost its natural quality. But that same ferocity is a vice and something impermissible in rational nature.

The filthiness of pigs is proper to them but foreign to human beings. And similarly, qualities which, when considered in beasts, are natural goods are, in a human being [Col. 0967C] or an angel, vices that struggle against nature, but are not evil in themselves.

For what, as we said, is not evil in the whole cannot become evil in a part, although it may appear illicit and in need of purification or restraint.

Nothing, then, remains that diminishes or dishonors the fullness and beauty of the whole universe, whether here, while the sensible world is still completing its course, or there, when it will return to its causes and remain at rest in them.

This theory is now clear only to a few who understand rightly; in the future, however, it will be revealed to all, when truth shines forth in all things and in everyone, opening without hesitation and without any darkness the secrets of all natures.

For truth will shine in all things in the future not only for [Col. 0967D] those who live justly in this life and rightly seek truth, but also for the unjust, whose wicked ways have corrupted them and who hate and flee the true light.

Everyone will see the glory of God.

Nor does this conflict with what is written: “The impious will be removed, so that he may not see the glory of God”. For divine speech has used “see” in place of “enjoy,” as though it said: “The impious will be removed, so that he may not enjoy the glory of God”.

We see that people whose eyes are burdened by disease do not enjoy the light. Indeed, they [Col. 0968A] wish to flee it and seek to hide themselves in darkness. They are not ignorant of what light is and how useful it is, being able to perceive it; rather, they locate the reason for fleeing from the light in the weakness of their eyes.

In the same way, the impious, held in punishments, will attribute the reason for hating truth to their impiety, afflicted too late and uselessly by repentance.

This is also made clear by the rich man himself, suffering punishments in hell. When he lifted his eyes while he was in torment, he saw Abraham from afar and Lazarus in his bosom. He therefore saw Abraham and Lazarus in the glory of divine contemplation, but he was deprived of the delights of that glory. Struck by belated repentance, he asked Abraham to send someone to his brothers whom he had left in this life, so that they would not live as he himself had lived [Col. 0968B] and so that they might avoid the places of torment.

### TEACHER

Therefore, do not be moved by the foolishest and falsest judgments of mortals and by their empty opinions. They think that the goodness, beauty, and equity of the universe are diminished and corrupted by those things that seem evil and shameful to them, not knowing that among all the things contained within the universe no evil, shameful, or unjust thing is found.

For this supreme goodness, beauty, and equity, which wisely disposes all things, neither permits nor will ever permit such things to occur among the things that are and the things that are not.

If someone should say, “From where, then, and where do these things called evil, dishonorable, and unjust arise?” the answer must be: nowhere else and in no other place than from vanities of vanities and from false arguments [Col. 0968C] which fabricate as existing what wholly does not exist. Blaspheming, they think that everything which obstructs, prohibits, and restrains their lustful affections is evil because it harms them.

This is why they even criticize the administration of divine providence, saying that it is evil for the impulse of free will to be obstructed, restrained, or extinguished in some respect, not knowing that all this belongs to the most merciful clemency of divine goodness.

For it belongs to the best and most serene Creator to provide for the good that he made, so that it does not perish or vanish in its own harmful movements.

They also cast upon the most merciful Orderer of all things what appears to be evil, chattering that he punishes what he made and that God made many people for the purpose of punishing them, wishing in this way to [Col. 0968D] find an outlet for his anger. They do not notice that God punishes nothing that he made; rather, he permits what he did not make to be punished.

They also refer their shameful and dishonorable deeds back to God. They say that if these things displeased the Creator of all things, he would certainly not allow them to occur in the nature that he made.

Moreover, they say that he predestined not only beautiful and honorable things but also the dishonorable and shameful things to be mixed into his creature, so that from them he might find occasions for manifesting justice—giving [Col. 0969A] rewards to those who live beautifully and honorably according to the divine laws, but punishments to transgressors and to those stained by the filth of baseness and dishonor, assigning both groups their due justly according to the inevitable purpose of his predestinations.

Thus, as the Apostle says, “Who resists his will?” And so they attribute the unchangeable causes of their entire perverse way of life to divine predestination, unable with blinded and foolish hearts to contemplate supreme goodness and beauty—or, to speak more explicitly, the inexhaustible and unfailing fountain of all goodness, beauty, and honor.

Just as God is the author of no evil or wickedness, so he is the author or predestiner of no baseness or dishonorable thing, and of no dishonor or dishonesty. For all these things are inventions of irrational desires.

If they flowed [Col. 0969B] from divine predestination, they would necessarily remain forever in the nature of things. Who would doubt that everything arranged by divine predestination will remain forever?

But these things will perish forever and will be universally abolished from the nature of things. They did not, therefore, proceed from the eternal causes of divine predestination.

The same blasphemy concerns divine equity. They say that God is unequal, not to call him unjust, because, as they claim, he does not distribute his goods equally to everyone. He exalts some and despises others; he leaves some poor and magnifies others as rich; he blinds some with the darkness of folly and illumines others with the light of wisdom; he makes some masters and others slaves; and so on—the diverse and infinite variety of the human [Col. 0969C] condition that is still visible in this mortal life.

They do not first consider that the temporal and transitory goods of this life are not truly goods, since they cannot remain forever, and deceive their lovers more than they benefit them. For they are empty shadows. Therefore they are distributed to the good and the wicked, since they will be taken away from everyone, though they are given to everyone in a disorderly and unconfused manner [the text prints *inordinate*, “disorderly,” although the following sentence asserts an ordered distribution].

Not only eternal things, destined to remain forever, but also temporal and perishable things are dispensed according to their own fixed arrangements; and in these the beauty both of eternal and of temporal things is established.

Next, they do not consider how the most just Creator of all and the wisest Orderer bestows upon each person, according to the laws of his providence, [Col. 0969D] the gifts and donations of his most abundant goodness, and is mistaken in nothing. The judgments of mortals concerning divine providence and administration, however, are false, since they do not know what is being done in this commonwealth of the universe of visible and invisible things.

Furthermore, these most foolish minds fail to grasp that the most equitable giver of all goods distributes natural goods equally to everyone. Natural goods are bestowed in the same way upon the good and the wicked. They cannot yet appear in these sensible and transitory things, [Col. 0970A] but remain hidden in the innermost recesses of nature until, in the restoration of the whole creature, they come forth into manifestation.

Then truth will appear in all things; the aforementioned vanities and false thoughts of mortals concerning the Creator and the creature will perish; God will be all in all; and no evil, shameful, dishonorable, or unjust thing will be found in the order and beauty of all things.

Everything fabricated by the most vain opinions of mortals will be emptied out and therefore wholly destroyed, because it is nothing.

O how blessed are those who see, and will see, all things that are after God, all at once, with the mind’s gaze! Their judgment is mistaken in nothing, because they contemplate everything in truth. Nothing in the universe of natures offends them or [Col. 0970B] is hostile to them.

For they do not judge from a part but from the whole, since they are contained neither within the parts of the whole nor within the whole itself. Rather, by the height of contemplation they rise above the whole and its parts.

For if they were enclosed within the number of the parts of the whole, or within the whole itself, they could not rightly judge either the parts or the whole. Therefore, whoever judges rightly concerning the parts and the whole must first surpass all the parts and the entire whole of the created universe by the strength and purity of the mind.

As the Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one.”

But to what does that spiritual person ascend who judges all things and concerning whom no one can judge, except the one who made all things? Does he perhaps ascend into him who surpasses and encompasses all things, [Col. 0970C] and in whom all things are?

He ascends, then, into God himself, and he contemplates, distinguishes, and judges the whole universe of creation at once. His judgment is not deceived, because he sees all things in truth itself, which neither deceives nor is deceived, because it is what it is. For by the power…

The person of inward spiritual contemplation enters into the causes of the things about which he judges. For he does not discern all things according to the outward appearances of sensible things, but according to their inward principles, immutable occasions, and primordial exemplars, in which all things are simultaneously present and are one. There, therefore, the spiritual person judges all things—where all things are one, truly and immutably live and subsist, and to which all things that have proceeded from their primordial causes will return, with nothing of them left outside, subject to temporal mutability or enclosed within local boundaries—when the whole of nature [Note: [Col. 0969] CF reads *universitas* (“the whole”); A, *universitati*], after the sensible world has come to an end, will return beyond all local and temporal spaces to its causes, in which all things are one. [Col. 0969]  
[Note: [Col. 0969] *ex* (“from”) is omitted in A.]

For places and times themselves, together with everything that is still ordered, moved, and bounded within them in this present life, must return to their eternal principles; divine history calls these principles “eternal times.” For how will worldly times remain when nothing temporal will exist? How will places remain when nothing local will exist? This is the reason that permits no sensible or bodily place for hell within the nature of things, and destroys the empty opinions of those who, in their deceptive thoughts, assert that hell is either beneath the earth, within the earth’s womb, or somewhere around the earth [Note: [Col. 0971] “or somewhere around the earth” is omitted in A], unaware that the earth itself, beneath or within which they establish hell, will perish utterly.

But if the earth will perish, then surely nothing beneath it or within it that deserves the name of hell will remain. Consequently, no place within sensible and bodily creation is assigned to hell—neither to the eternal fire in which the impious will burn, nor to the worms that will never die. All these names of punishments are placed figuratively in sacred Scripture, as Saint Ambrose testifies, and the Greek terms, which, as we said earlier, express more clearly what [Note: [Col. 0971] A reads *quod* (“that which”) for *quid* (“what”)] divine Scripture intimates by the name “hell.” [Col. 0971B]

For Ἅδης (*Hades*) is said—just as was explained a little earlier—to mean “without delights,” or “without pleasures,” or “lack of sweetness.” It is also called λύπη (*lypē*), whose interpretation is “sadness,” “grief,” or “mourning.” It is likewise commonly called Ἄχος (*achos*), that is, “the heaviness of despair,” which overwhelms and crushes depraved desires, sunk and oppressed, afflicted by the poverty [Note: [Col. 0971] A reads *egestates* (“privations”) for *egestate* (“poverty”)] of temporal things that they had immoderately desired in this life, as though into some exceedingly deep abyss and into the darkness of vain fantasies and sensible things, where they are tormented, perpetually trampled beneath the unchangeable weight of the divine judgment and irrevocably despised.

All these meanings, among the Greeks, unequivocally declare that hell, with all its punishments, is neither local nor temporal nor sensible, nor established in any part of the four elements of which this world is composed [Note: [Col. 0971] A has *iste mundus* (“this world”) in the reverse order], nor established in the whole of it. Rather, it is a mournful, tearful, grievous [Note: [Col. 0971] F reads *graveque* (“and grievous”); AC, *grave*], unavoidable prison filled with despair, and a deprivation of every good [Note: [Col. 0971] A adds *et omnium* (“and of all”)], in vain and utterly empty visions. [Col. 0971C]

**DISCIPLE.** Enough has been said about hell and its torments [Note: [Col. 0971] A omits *eius* (“its”).]. It has been demonstrated with the greatest clarity that hell does not substantially exist in the nature of visible or invisible things [Note: [Col. 0971] A has *substantialiter eum* (“that hell substantially exists”)], since it is neither body nor spirit, but the most just condemnation of the depraved and unlawful desire of those who misuse the good of nature—that is, the freedom of the will. That condemnation itself is good, not only because it is just—for everything just is good—but also because it is contained and ordered within the divine laws, and whatever exists within those laws must be good, just, and honorable. [Col. 0971D]

The fantasies in which it will exist are themselves also good. For we see that the shadows of bodies, which no one doubts are vain, are compressed and arise on every side through the radiance of light, without introducing anything shameful or dishonorable into the beauty of the light. [Col. 0972A] Consider how much adornment and praise is contributed to the virtues of perfected souls when they encompass and compress vices within themselves, subject and restrain them under their own dominion, and order them according to the divine laws [Note: [Col. 0971] A adds *et* (“and”)], so that they do not plunge into the depth of wickedness the souls that they attempt to corrupt. Often they extinguish those vices completely—I mean the vices [Note: [Col. 0971] *dico* (“I mean”) is omitted in A]; often they pour them into themselves, so that vices are even turned into virtues.

This reasoning shows that vices are not altogether evil, but unlawful. For if they were evil, they could never be changed into virtues [Note: [Col. 0971] CF reads *moveri possent* (“could be moved”)]. Other similar things, which appear [Note: [Col. 0971] A reads singular *videtur* (“appears”)] to arise contrary to nature from the perverse movements of abuse, through the free will of rational nature voluntarily taking itself captive, are nevertheless not permitted to harm the ordering of the universe; rather, they are compelled to adorn it by the eternal laws of divine providence and judgment, which surround it. [Col. 0972B]

Since these things are so [Note: [Col. 0971] CF reads *Haec* (“these things”); A, *Quae* (“which things”)], I perceive [Note: [Col. 0971] A reads *conspicor clarius* (“I perceive more clearly”)] with all ambiguity and deliberation removed, as clearly as daylight, that the fullness of created reality will return [Note: [Col. 0971] A reads *reversura*] to its causes and into God himself, in whom all things subsist; and that the most just punishments [Note: [Col. 0971] A omits *poenas* (“punishments”)] imposed—or permitted to be imposed—and irrevocably defined by the judgments of the most equitable Judge upon irrational desires will remain perpetually within that fullness. For they will not only harm nothing in any way, but will also provide ineffable occasions for its praise and beauty [Note: [Col. 0971] A has *ineffabilis* (“ineffable”) in the singular].

Accordingly, one may well say that punishments and rewards are separated not by local spaces but by differences of qualities, so that they both are and are not together [Note: [Col. 0971] CF reads *et* (“and”) for *ac* (“and”); A omits *et* before *simul* (“together”)]. They are together because the commonwealth of the whole creation is ordered from these two; yet they are not together because their effects are different. [Col. 0972C]

The effects of sins are mourning, groaning, sadness, late repentance, the insatiable burning of desire—which will find rest nowhere—the putrefaction and wormlike corruption of sins that seethes forth, the thickest darkness of profound ignorance, in which there is no knowledge of realities or of truth itself—that is, no blessedness of enjoying that truth [Note: [Col. 0971] *veritate* (“truth”) is omitted in A]. The difficulty of walking according to the divine laws is figuratively suggested by bound feet [Note: [Col. 0971] A omits *quippe* (“indeed”)]; the difficulty of performing good actions according to the virtues, by bound hands [Note: [Col. 0971] *typice insinuatur* (“is figuratively suggested”) is omitted in A]; and there are other similar things, whose enumeration would be both lengthy and impossible.

The effects of merits, however, are joy, gladness, peace, blessedness, happiness, glory, equality with the most blessed angels, and—to put it briefly—theosis, that is, deification, which God has prepared for those who love him, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.” [Col. 0972D]

Where the effects of causes are mutually contrary, the causes themselves must also be distinguished. And if someone asks how things that are far distant from one another can be united together and in one place—that is, virtues and vices within the boundaries of nature—let him observe, in a great and royal house constructed with various ornaments [Note: [Col. 0973] CF reads *domu* (“house”)], that a healthy person and an infirm person, a blind person and one who sees, a joyful person and a sorrowful person, a secure person and a curious person, a rich person and a needy person, one beaten with blows like a slave, one exalted with honors like a master, one confined in prison like a criminal, and another released from every bond like an innocent person acquitted of every crime, can all be contained together in one and the same place and time. [Col. 0973A]

If this is so, and is disclosed to nearly everyone in an equal manner, what is surprising if we believe and understand that, in the one harmony of restored creation returning to its causes [Note: [Col. 0973] A has *suas causas* (“its causes”) in the reverse order; CF reads *reversurae* (“about to return”), A *reversae* (“returned”)], the whole rational creation will be whole through the grace of its Redeemer, who assumed it in its entirety [Note: [Col. 0973] CF reads *sanam futuram* (“will be whole”); A, *factam* (“made”)]? Meanwhile, the weakness of perverse will—which had adhered externally to nature itself—will be arranged in its appropriate orders and will undergo retributions corresponding to its works [Note: [Col. 0973] CF reads *factam* (“made whole”); A reads *factam* (“made”)]. [Col. 0973B]

What if nature itself will be not only healed but also illuminated [Note: [Col. 0973] A reads *sed* (“but”) for *verum* (“indeed”)], while the blindness of evil wills is closed off by the perpetual darkness of the absence of the Restorer of natures? What if nature, created in the image of God, will be not only healed and illuminated but also led back into paradise, which the wise interpret as the place of spiritual delights, while the leprosy that had disfigured it deservedly because of sin burns with eternal itching, deprived of every delight? And what if there are other such things by which nature and merit and guilt, reward and punishment, are distinguished [Note: [Col. 0973] CF reads *natura et meritum et culpa* (“nature and merit and guilt”); A reads *meritum et culpa* (“merit and guilt”)], while, in a marvelous and ineffable manner, nature, altogether free, endures the fantasies in which guilt pays the penalty for what it committed?

**MASTER.** All these things appear plausible and supported by probable arguments. But at this point those who treat spiritual matters carnally confront us, saying: “What harm, then, will the impiety of the pagans do them, by which they worship idols while ignorant of the true God? What harm will the Jews’ unbelief do them, by which they deny that the Word of God incarnate, our Lord Jesus Christ, is consubstantial and coeternal with his Father and equal to him in all things according to his divinity? What harm will the superstitious [Note: [Col. 0973] CF reads *superstitia* (“superstition”)] and utterly false contrivances of the other nations do them, if in the life to come their entire nature will be saved, so that neither body nor soul nor any natural part of them will be left to be tormented by eternal punishments?” [Col. 0973C]

It is either extremely difficult or impossible to persuade such people that it in no way belongs to God’s justice—and is altogether alien to it—to punish, in everything he made, what he made, while making it his own act to punish what he did not make. For everything that is condemned in all evils and judged worthy of eternal punishments flowed not from nature but from the most perverse movements of each person’s own will; the discriminating contemplation of things customarily calls these movements vices of nature—and not without reason, since they resist natural affections [Note: [Col. 0973] A reads *quoniam* (“because”) instead of *quia* (“since”)]. [Col. 0974A]

They also flowed from original sin, in which all human beings, with the exception of the Redeemer of humanity, sinned universally. This sin is also attributed to nature and called its sin—not because nature itself, made in the image of God, committed it, but because the irrational abuse of rational good by the free will given by God, and its turning toward love of sensible things, concealed the beauty of nature in which it had been established from the beginning of its creation and hid its proper dignity.

For if you attribute guilt to nature, you will seem to attribute it also to the Creator of nature. If the cause of guilt is attributed to nature, sin must necessarily be attributed to the cause of nature, which is God [Note: [Col. 0973] A reads *est Deus* (“is God”) in the reverse order]. For nature, made in the image of God, would not be altogether like its primordial exemplar if it received within itself the cause of sin. Just as the primordial exemplar subsists as the cause of no sin or evil, so too does nature made in its image and likeness. [Col. 0974B]

It is exceedingly ridiculous to say that human nature first lost the image and likeness of its Creator and then received within itself the causes of sin [Note: [Col. 0973] *est* (“is”) is omitted in CF]. For whoever says this will be compelled to ask by what sin nature lost the image and likeness of its Creator, since it would not have lost it if it had not sinned in some way.

Moreover, if human nature never lost the image and likeness of its Creator [Note: [Col. 0973] A reads *creatoris* (“Creator’s”) for *conditoris* (“Maker’s”)]—for image and likeness are counted among natural goods and gifts, while natural gifts and [Note: [Col. 0973] CF omits *et* (“and”)] goods cannot in any way be taken away from human nature, or from anything made by the Giver and Establisher of all goods, nor can they be diminished or increased—who but a madman would say that natural goods can be receptive of the causes of sin, or that sin can arise from them? [Col. 0974C]

For if they are receptive [Note: [Col. 0973] C adds *et acceptiva* (“and receptive”); A omits *sunt* (“are”)] of sin, their natural beauty is corrupted, their dignity diminished, their immutability made uncertain, and their order destabilized [Note: [Col. 0973] C adds *et acceptiva* (“and receptive”)]. Hence it follows that no rational nature can be capable of the causes of guilt, lest it be judged unlike its Creator.

But it is rightly asked: if the cause of sin is not referred to nature for the reason that it would once again be referred through nature to the Creator—for everything that comes from him is unreceptive of any cause of sin or of sinning—why should someone not say, by the same reasoning, that the opportunity for sin should not be referred to free will either, lest the cause of guilt be referred to him who granted it to nature?

For he who gave nature also created free will within it; and just as nature is good and an incorruptible good [Note: [Col. 0973] A omits *est* (“is”)], so too is the freedom of the will. Consequently it necessarily follows that, just as the causes of guilt are not established in nature, so neither are they established in free will [Note: [Col. 0973] *non* (“not”) is omitted in A]; for the cause of evil must not be established in any good. [Col. 0974D]

Therefore, if no sin arises from natural causes, we must ask from where it received its opportunity. And if someone answers—and this is true, plausible, and supported by probable arguments—that sin derives its origin [Note: [Col. 0975] CF reads *ducere* (“to derive”); A, *sumere* (“to take”)] from nowhere other than the irrational movements of rational nature and the abuse of the good of free will, it will immediately seem that he is establishing the opportunity for an irrational movement in rational nature [Note: [Col. 0975] CF reads *construere* (“constructing”) instead of *constituere* (“establishing”)]. [Col. 0975A]

For it will be judged by a relational mode of expression that an irrational movement belongs to rational nature and therefore derives its opportunity from it [Note: [Col. 0975] A reads *Relative siquidem* (“relatively, then”) instead of *Relativo siquidem modo* (“by a relational mode”)]. But if this is so, he will also be compelled to admit that the causes of irrational movements preceded in God [Note: [Col. 0975] A reads *a Deo processisse* (“proceeded from God”)]. For if every natural cause of rational nature is established in God, then whatever is referred to it must be referred to its cause. [Col. 0975B]
