But if true reasoning insists that an irrational movement is not to be referred by a relational mode to rational nature, but is altogether opposed to it—as the irrational is opposed to the rational—then the question remains: from where, therefore, does that irrational movement derive its origin, in which the cause of sin is established [Note: [Col. 0975] A reads *contendit* (“insists”) instead of *protendit* (“extends or maintains”)]?

At this point nothing more plausible presents itself in which the cause of an irrational movement can be understood than the abuse of natural goods, prohibited by the divine laws [Note: [Col. 0975] A reads *naturalis boni* (“of natural good”)]. This abuse is proper to the perverse and unlawful desire of each free will, which misuses a good. Examples of this abuse are so widespread that scarcely anyone exists who could not abundantly demonstrate it in himself.

But it must be noted that no one is able to misuse the highest goods of our nature. For natural virtue, in its essence, power, and activity, permits no one to misuse it, just as neither do wisdom, understanding, and reason, since these possess the principal seat of our nature. [Col. 0975C]

But with the intermediate goods of nature—such as intelligence and bodily sensation—and [Note: [Col. 0975] A omits *Et* (“and”)] with the body itself and the lowest goods, such as those things established outside us within the orders of sensible things, we are granted the power to make either good or bad use.

Natural intelligence is indeed a good, given by God to human beings for thinking about and discovering useful and honorable things [Note: [Col. 0975] CF reads *et cogitanda* (“and for thinking about”)]. Yet a perverse will abuses it, seeking harmful and destructive opportunities by which it may deceive and destroy those whom it desires to deceive and destroy [Note: [Col. 0975] A has the words “yet a perverse will abuses it” in the reverse order].

The sense of the eyes, to say nothing of the rest, is a natural good, given by God for receiving bodily light, so that through it and in it the rational soul might discern the forms, appearances, and numbers of sensible things and receive from them what is true for its lawful uses [Note: [Col. 0975] CF reads *accipiet* (“will receive”) instead of *acciperet* (“might receive”)]. Yet those who, with lustful desire, seek the beauty of visible forms misuse it, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” Here “woman” is used generally for the beauty of the whole sensible creation. [Col. 0975D]

What shall I say about the lowest sensible goods? Is it not as clear as daylight that the good use them well, while the evil use them badly? The good use them for the praise and service of the Giver of all good things; the evil use them to carry out the impulses of their perverse desire.

But if someone wishes to discover the causes of unlawful abuse and perverse desire [Note: [Col. 0975] *cupiditatis* (“of desire”) is omitted in CF], let him seek diligently. I, however, am confident, perceiving without hesitation that no one can discover them [Note: [Col. 0975] A reads *prospiciens* (“looking ahead”) instead of *perspiciens* (“perceiving”)]. For just as evil is without a cause, and it is in no way found from where it comes, so unlawful abuse of natural goods arises from no natural cause [Note: [Col. 0975] A reads *naturalis boni* (“of natural good”)]. [Col. 0976A]

In saying this I follow the blessed Dionysius the Areopagite in his book *On the Divine Names*, and Saint Aurelius Augustine in his books *On Free Choice of the Will*. For it is foolish to seek the causes of things that are contained in no kind, form, appearance, or number of the goods made and ordered by the supreme Good and Creator of all. Everything that was not made by him is altogether without cause and without substance. [Col. 0976B]

For this reason, those who say that lustful desire, rather than an evil will, is the cause of punishments seem to me to consider the properties of things more correctly, lest anyone suppose that two wills are contained within one and the same nature—one good and the other evil—when one will belongs to humanity, although it is often understood in relation to good and often in relation to evil.

Lust, however, is not only entirely excluded from natural goods; it is also scarcely ever, or never, found in divine Scripture with the meaning of good. The first human being, in whom all sinned, was deceived by the lust to rule and to exalt himself above all things [Note: [Col. 0975] CF reads *ac* (“and”) instead of *et* (“and”)], and he sinned when the devil persuaded him, saying: “On whatever day you eat from it”—namely, from the forbidden tree—“your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” [Col. 0976C]

Oh, how great was the lust of pride in him who desired to be God by his own power!

Therefore the impiety of the pagans, the unbelief of the Jews, and the fabulous delusions of the other nations did not flow from natural causes, but from the lustful desires of vain thoughts; and therefore it is not their nature that will be punished in any way, but their lust.

All vices that are opposed to virtues and desire to corrupt nature are customarily called by the general name “lust” [Note: [Col. 0975] A reads *generaliter* (“generally”)]. Thus the most shameful lust of the impious in the worship of false gods, and that of the faithless Jews in the denial of the truth [Note: [Col. 0975] “of the faithless Jews” is omitted in A], and that of the other nations in the delusions of their fables [Note: [Col. 0975] A reads *falsarum libidinum* (“of false lusts”)], in the vainest fantasies of the things they imagine will happen to them—while they will find nothing in them except incomprehensible shadows—is left to be tormented by punishments. The universe of natural goods and the whole nature created by God, meanwhile, will remain whole, complete, and unpunished [Note: [Col. 0975] A reads *naturalium* (“of natural things”)]. [Col. 0976D]

Moreover, the general punishment of all the impious [Note: [Col. 0975] A reads *in eis* (“in them”)] will be, as we have often said, mourning and sadness over the absence and loss of the things in which they delighted during this life. They will always have their fantasies before their eyes, as it were, but, ardently desiring to grasp them, they will be unable to do so, since they are nothing. They will desire consolation in those things that produce despair and unrest [Note: [Col. 0977] A reads *ex his* (“from these things”)]. [Col. 0977A]

Hence arises late repentance and the useless request for consolation, signified by the rich man’s tongue when he asks for a drop of water from the tip of the poor Lazarus’s finger and says, “For I am tormented in this flame.” The tongue signifies the request for help; the flame, the tardiness of repentance for sins; the water, refreshment; and the finger, the distribution of merits, by which the saints are believed, after this life, to be able to provide help to those who are in punishments.

From this passage it is understood that not only those who are still living in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0977] A has *in carne adhuc* (“still in the flesh”) in the reverse order], but also souls stripped of the flesh, can ask for the help of the saints, either to be completely freed from punishments or to be tormented less severely in them [Note: [Col. 0977] A reads *mitius crucientur* (“may be tormented more mildly”)]. Yet they ask in vain if in this life they fell into the depth of wickedness—that is, if they performed no good in this life by which they might deserve mercy in the future. [Col. 0977B]

There is also another form of punishment common to all the impious. It turns all the vices committed in this life, and in which they persist without any repentance or opportunity for purification until the separation of body and soul, into savage and terrifying forms resembling ferocious beasts, increasing their torments. Thus the things that here smiled upon the impious while they lived delightfully [Note: [Col. 0977] A reads *delectabilia* (“delightful”) instead of *delectabiliter* (“delightfully”)], will there appear in a terrifying manner, according to the most just mode of punishment. [Col. 0977C]

For what could be more equitable and more fitting to the divine ordering than that the unjust, who in this life follow those things with unlawful love while burning with desire, should in the other life—which is more properly signified by the term “eternal death”—flee them in terror, punished and yet unable to escape?

All this, and the other ineffable and innumerable varieties of punishments [Note: [Col. 0977] *poenarum* (“of punishments”) is omitted in A], will exist in fantasies of sensible things. These fantasies are arranged with the greatest order in the broad fields of memory [Note: [Col. 0977] A reads *cavis* (“recesses”) instead of *campis* (“fields”)], whether here or there [Note: [Col. 0977] A has *ordinatissimi* (“most orderly,” plural) instead of *ordinatissime* (“with the greatest order”)]. The first of these fields contains what enters through sight, the second what enters through hearing, the third what enters through smell, the fourth what enters through taste, and the fifth what enters through touch—through these five gates, as it were, they enter the city of the soul. [Col. 0977D]

These fantasies have two forms. One consists of those in which rewards are prepared for people who lived well in this life, though not supremely well; the other consists of those in which punishments are assigned to those who live badly.

The saints who, while still established in the flesh, surpassed the flesh, the world, and themselves [Note: [Col. 0977] A reads *carnem mundumque* (“the flesh and the world”)], through the power of action and knowledge, and ascended through the height of contemplation even to God himself, will receive the reward of their labor not in fantasies of sensible things but in theophanies of divine virtues, together with the grace of deification. [Col. 0978A]

For it is one thing to remain within the goods of nature—which will be granted generally to all by divine generosity—and another [Note: [Col. 0977] A reads *aliud autem omnem naturam* (“but another, all nature”)] to surpass all nature and its goods and reach God himself, which is proper to divine grace. “Where the body is,” that is, the truth, “there the eagles”—that is, minds—“will be gathered,” to contemplate it.

Again, there is a different kind of contemplation for those who will not exceed the boundaries of natural goods, in imaginal forms [Note: [Col. 0977] A reads *biformis speculatio* (“a twofold contemplation”); A omits *imaginalibus* (“imaginal forms”); C reads *imaginibus* (“images”)]. [Col. 0978B]

They are considered in one way when they are people who, by the merit of a good life and simple innocence, will not only escape all punishments but will also receive rewards corresponding to their merits and known to God alone. Thus they will possess natural goods and [Note: [Col. 0977] A omits *et* (“and”)] in some manner participate in the overflowing generosity of God, though they will not be deified.

They are considered in another way when they are people in whom only the integrity of nature will be restored, while the wicked [Note: [Col. 0977] CF reads *malefica* (“wicked”); A, *maleficia* (“evil deeds”)] and lustful intemperance of their bodily life will be punished by eternal punishments.

These punishments, ordered by the divine laws, will never harm nature, within whose power they are both sustained and contained, nor will they infect its beauty either as a whole or in any part.

Therefore each person will receive rewards or suffer punishments within his own conscience, while nature itself [Note: [Col. 0977] CF omits *vero* (“however”)] will remain free in everyone. So much for these matters; now we must return to the return of creation to its original state, which is the principal subject of our discussion.

**DISCIPLE.** We should indeed return to it, for the time and the length of the discussion require this. I fear, however, that repeated and intricate discussion of the same matters may perhaps produce weariness in those who will read it. [Col. 0978C]

**MASTER.** The complexity of the subject and the winding paths of extremely difficult questions require a manifold and intricate reasoning. Perhaps there will be some who prefer frequent repetition of the same matters to a brief and hurried indication of things that often escape the mind’s attention—a method that more easily closes what has been thrust in than opens it, and introduces ambiguity rather than removing it.

**DISCIPLE.** Proceed in whatever way and by whatever method you wish, provided only that you discuss the principal question, which concerns the return, without any incidental questions. For incidental questions prevent the discussion from reaching its conclusion.

**MASTER.** We have explained the return of the whole sensible creation to its causes after the end of the world, and now we must again explain specifically the return of human nature. [Col. 0978D] The whole of humanity will therefore return to its original state in him who assumed it in its entirety—namely, in the incarnate Word of God.

This return is considered in two ways. One teaches the restoration of the whole of human nature in Christ; the other not only considers that restoration generally, but also the blessedness and deification of those who will ascend into God himself. [Col. 0979A]

For it is one thing to return to paradise and another to eat from the tree of life. We read that the first human being, made in the image and likeness of God, was placed in paradise, but we do not read that he ate from the tree of life. Having eaten the forbidden tree, he was expelled, forestalled from the sweetness of the tree of life [Note: [Col. 0979] CF has *Esus siquidem prohibiti ligni* (“Having eaten the forbidden tree”); A has *ligni vitae prohibiti* (“of the forbidden tree of life”)]. For he was destined to eat from the tree of life [Note: [Col. 0979] “tree of life” is omitted in A] if he had wished to obey the divine commandments. Yet he would have lived happily even before eating from the tree of life [Note: [Col. 0979] The sentence from *Esus siquidem* (“Having eaten…”) through *comederet* (“he ate”) is omitted in C], if he had not sinned immediately after he was created.

This makes it clear that our whole nature—which is generally signified by the term “humanity,” referring to those made in the image and likeness of God—will return to paradise, that is, to the dignity of its original creation. But only those who are worthy of deification will participate in the fruit of the tree of life [Note: [Col. 0979] A reads *qui solummodo deificatione digni sunt* (“only those who are worthy of deification”)]. [Col. 0979B]

The fruit of the tree of life, which is Christ, is blessed life: eternal peace in the contemplation of truth, which is properly called deification. For blessed life, as Augustine says, is joy arising from truth, which is Christ.

Perhaps this is what the Apostle says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.” Thus many, and nearly all [Note: [Col. 0979] A reads *et* (“and”) for *ac* (“and”)], have translated this passage of the Apostle from Greek into Latin. As though he were saying plainly: “All of us who are human beings, without exception, will rise in spiritual bodies and in the integrity of our natural goods, and we will return to the antiquity of our first condition; but we will not all be changed into the glory of deification, which surpasses every nature and paradise.” [Col. 0979C]

Therefore, just as it is one thing to rise generally and another to be changed specifically [Note: [Col. 0979] A reads *aliud est* (“it is another thing”)], so it is one thing to return to paradise and another to eat from the tree of life. In the one [Note: [Col. 0979] CF reads *quidem* (“indeed”)], the restoration of nature is signified; in the other, the deification of the elect is commended [Note: [Col. 0979] A reads *in altero vero commendatur electorum deificatio* (“in the other, the deification of the elect is commended”)].

I say this without being unaware that others have translated this apostolic passage differently. Some have translated it, “We shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed”; others, among whom is John Chrysostom, “We shall all be changed, but we shall not all sleep.” In my opinion, their interpretations do not concern the subject of the present work.

**DISCIPLE.** I do not understand why they would not concern it [Note: [Col. 0979] CF reads *pertinuerit* (“would have concerned it”) instead of *pertinuerint* (“would have concerned them”)]. For someone who discusses the return of sensible creation—does he not also discuss the resurrection of bodies? [Col. 0979D]

**MASTER.** Certainly. For resurrection, rising, and returning are not different things. What else is resurrection from the dead than a return to the natural state? Explain, then, briefly and rapidly, what the aforementioned interpretations mean, which you wished to pass over untouched.

Those who translated the passage, “We shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed,” seem to me to have understood the Apostle’s words as though he were saying: “We shall all die—for who is there [Note: [Col. 0979] A omits *quidem* (“indeed”) and *est* (“is”)] who lives and will not see death?—but we shall not all be changed.” [Col. 0980A]

For those who have died from the beginning of the world until the Lord’s second coming—that is, until the end of the age—and those who are dying or will die [Note: [Col. 0979] *sunt* (“are”) is omitted in CF], do not immediately and without any delay await the common resurrection of bodies, but await it after temporal intervals have intervened [Note: [Col. 0979] A reads *resurrectionem corporis* (“the resurrection of the body”)], except those who rose with Christ.

But those whom the end of the world and the Lord’s coming will find living in the flesh will not only sleep but will also be changed. For, with no temporal interval intervening, they will simultaneously sleep and awaken—that is, they will die and rise—as the Apostle himself says, “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” Thus change, rather than death, will be accomplished in them.

For how can death be understood where no interval is inserted between departure from this life and passage into the other? [Col. 0980B] Those who translated the passage, “We shall all be changed, but we shall not all sleep,” seem to mean nothing other than that, in the future resurrection, all human beings will be changed from the present life into the future life, some with the intervention of bodily death and some without it.

Then, as the same Apostle says, “this corruptible”—namely, this body [Note: [Col. 0979] A has *videlicet corpus* (“namely, this body”) in the reverse order]—“will be clothed with incorruption [Note: [Col. 0979] CF reads *induetur* (“will be clothed with”); A, *induet* (“will put on”)], and this mortal will be clothed with immortality” [Note: [Col. 0979] CF reads *induetur*; A, *induet*], and “death will be swallowed up in victory,” and “the last enemy, death, will be destroyed” [Note: [Col. 0979] A reads *novissima inimica* (“the last enemy,” feminine) instead of *novissimus inimicus* (“the last enemy,” masculine).] Yet “we shall not all sleep,” that is, not all will suffer the death of the flesh before they are brought from temporal life into eternal life. [Col. 0980C]

For those whom the coming of the Son of Man will find still living in the flesh will not be dissolved by bodily death, nor will they suffer the separation of body and soul. Rather, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, they will undergo change. Therefore they will not sleep but will live always, without the death of the flesh intervening.

Saint Augustine and John Chrysostom entirely support this interpretation. The Catholic faith also appears to approve it, since it unhesitatingly believes that our Lord Jesus Christ will come to judge the living and the dead: the living, whom the coming of the Judge will find still remaining in the flesh, and the dead, who have already undergone the dissolution of body and soul.

**DISCIPLE.** Then [Note: [Col. 0979] CF reads *Non* (“not”); A, *Nonne* (“then not”)] not all who will return to paradise—that is, to the original condition of human nature—will participate in the fruit of the tree of life?

**MASTER.** Certainly not all, but only those who will have overcome the world and the flesh, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.” [Col. 0980D]

For [Note: [Col. 0979] CF reads *Ex* (“from”); A, *Et* (“and”)] by grace and nature, as was discussed above, returning to paradise is granted in common to all human beings; but by grace alone, eating from the tree of life is granted to the deified alone.

**DISCIPLE.** Why, then, does Scripture testify that the tree of life is in the middle of paradise, if not all who will return to paradise are permitted and granted to eat from its fruit?

**MASTER.** Observe that divine Scripture does not simply testify that the tree of life is in paradise, but more expressly that it is in the middle of paradise, so that [Col. 0981A]

Understand by the word “paradise” the whole of human nature, which all human beings—[Note: [Col. 0981] “human beings” is omitted in CF.] both good and evil—participate in; but by the indication “its midst,” understand the most secret and innermost recesses of that same nature, in which the image and likeness of God are expressed, where the tree of life—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ—has been planted. No one is permitted to enjoy him except one who is most purified in faith and conduct, most enlightened in knowledge, and most perfect in wisdom and in the understanding of divine mysteries.

And this, I think, was prefigured in the mystical construction of Solomon’s temple. All people without exception—[Note: [Col. 0981] CF: “without being shut out.”] good and evil, circumcised and uncircumcised, male and female, and all the nations of the whole world—[Col. 0981B] whether they came there for the sake of prayer or of business, entered the outermost porticoes, and were allowed to conduct their affairs there. Only the priests and [Note: [Col. 0981] CF: “and.”] Levites entered the Priests’ Portico and Solomon’s Portico. Then the priests, having been washed and purified in the bronze sea that stood in Solomon’s Portico, entered the outer temple, where the bread of the Presence and the lampstands were. No one, however, was permitted to enter beyond the veil, into the Holy of Holies, where the ark, the altar of incense, the mercy seat, and the two cherubim were, except the high priest. [Note: [Col. 0981] “to enter” is omitted in CF.] [Note: [Col. 0981] A has “will be permitted.”]

From this it may be understood that all people [Note: [Col. 0981] “human beings” is omitted in A.] are contained within the boundaries of the natural paradise, as though within a certain temple, each in his own order; [Note: [Col. 0981] CF: “each person.”] but only those sanctified in Christ will enter the inner parts. And again, [Col. 0981C] into the Holy of Holies, as into the innermost regions of the inner parts, those who are in the High Priest—namely Christ—and who have become one with him and in him, will be brought. There Christ is, signified by the altar, because by his solidity [Note: [Col. 0981] A: “his own.”] he supports all things; and not merely the altar, but the altar of incense as well, for its fragrance—that is, his praise and glory—fills all things.

He is the ark, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. [Note: [Col. 0981] “is” is omitted in F.] He is the rod, because [Note: [Col. 0981] A: “which.”] he rules and measures all things, and the manna, because he feeds all things. He is the mercy seat, because he always intercedes for us with the Father, displaying to him the universal sacrifice and the price of the world—namely, his humanity, which he sacrificed and offered for the purification [Col. 0981D] and redemption of the entire human race, without exception. For just as he found nothing in anyone, apart from sin, that he had not received, so he left nothing in anyone that he did not redeem; and by redeeming it he saved and sanctified it, because he himself is the redemption and salvation, the purification, illumination, and perfection of all humanity, both collectively and individually.

Around him the cherubim—that is, the orders of angels—move about, through whom he orders and arranges visible and invisible things. [Note: [Col. 0981] CF: “orders the things arranged.”] Perhaps for this reason two cherubim are described around the ark, that is, [Col. 0982A] around Christ: the angelic nature administers the sensible and intelligible world. Yet it is not unreasonable to understand one cherub figuratively as the intellectual nature among the angels, and the other typically as the rational nature among human beings. No wise person doubts that intelligible and rational substances are closest to Christ. [Note: [Col. 0981] A: “that they are close to Christ.”]

Do you see, then, how lofty and supernatural it is to approach [Note: [Col. 0981] A: “to hear.”] such a tree planted in the midst of paradise—that is, of human nature—and to enjoy it? To this tree, removed from all others and granted only to the deified, Paul was caught up into the third heaven of our nature: that is, above every body and vital spirit, into the intellect itself, in which the Word of God, who is the tree of life, dwells in an ineffable manner, beyond every essence, power, and operation [Col. 0982B] [Note: [Col. 0981] A: “and most serene.”] in inaccessible light, beyond and within nature made according to the image of God.

Accordingly, all people will enter that paradise, as into a vast and most secret temple, each according to his own proportion; and he himself, who said, “I will be in their midst,” will dwell in them. Hence the Prophet says: “I will fulfill my vows, he says, in the sight of all his people, in the courts of the house of the Lord, in your midst, Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 0981] “Jerusalem” is omitted in A.]

For Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” or “temple of peace,” and it is itself the house of the Lord built upon the mountain of heavenly contemplation. To it the prophet urges all people to ascend through the steps of the virtues and the heights of contemplation, saying: “Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.”

For God dwells nowhere else except in human and angelic nature, [Col. 0982C] to which alone the contemplation of truth is granted. Nor should we understand these two natures as two houses, but as one and the same house constructed from two intelligible materials. Concerning this house [Note: [Col. 0981] CF: “house”; likewise throughout.] the Lord seems to have said: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.”

In the courts of this house all people will possess dwelling places [Note: [Col. 0981] “all people [will possess] dwelling places” is omitted in CF.] when they return to their causes, whether they have lived well or badly in the flesh. For no one can corrupt its beauty, disfigure its dignity, diminish or increase its greatness. What could exist outside it, or what could fail to exist within it? In it no one’s ugliness is ugly; wickedness does no harm, and error does not err. The malice of unclean spirits and the irrational movements of impious human beings not only do not contaminate its beauty, but even increase it. [Col. 0982D]

For no beauty is produced except from the joining together of similar and dissimilar things, of contrary and opposing things; nor would the good be so greatly praiseworthy if there were no comparison arising from the blameworthiness of evil. Therefore, what is called evil is blamed when considered in itself; but when good is praised by comparison with it, it does not appear altogether blameworthy. For that which increases the praise of the good is not wholly without praise. [Note: [Col. 0981] CF reads: “not without every praise.”]

Would the creator of all good things and the ordainer of evils have allowed evil to exist [Col. 0983A] in the universe [Note: [Col. 0981] “in” is omitted in A.] that he created if it contributed no benefit? This may also be readily inferred from comparisons among sensible things or from human behavior. For the praise of a fruitful tree is enhanced by comparison with an unfruitful tree, and the praise of a chaste person by comparison with a lustful one. [Note: [Col. 0983] CF: “of a fruit-bearing tree.”]

Thus, in the paradise of human nature, each person will possess his own place according to the proportion of his conduct in this life: some externally, as though in the outermost porticoes; others internally, as though in the nearer courts of divine contemplation; [Note: [Col. 0983] CF: “for divine contemplation.”] others in the most spacious temples of divine mysteries; and others in the innermost theophanies, beyond all nature, in him and with him who is superessential and supernatural.

Blessed are those who enter the sanctuaries [Col. 0983B] [Note: [Col. 0983] CF: “the hidden places.”] of wisdom, which is Christ; who approach [Note: [Col. 0983] CF: “who destroy.”] the darkest darkness of the most excellent light, in which they see all things simultaneously in their causes; where it is not intervals of place or time that separate the good from the evil, but the distance between their merits; where it is not the size and beauty of bodies that are praised, but the dignity and greatness of virtues; where it is not the rank and nobility of persons that are sought, but the dignity and nobility of their conduct.

There is one common nature for all, but grace is diverse. There all are together, and together they are not: they are together through the likeness of their substances, and together they are not through the unlikeness of their dispositions.

The rich man and Abraham were together in the spiritual substances which one and the same human essence gathers and inseparably joins; but they were not together because of the difference in their spiritual qualities. A great chasm lay between them. [Note: [Col. 0983] A: “For a great chaos lay between them.”] Abraham rejoiced in eternal repose, while the rich man mourned in an inextinguishable flame. Therefore the rich man saw Abraham from afar. [Note: [Col. 0983] “the rich man” is omitted in A.]

Who can express in words how great a separation exists [Note: [Col. 0983] A: “has intervened.”] between joy and sorrow [Note: [Col. 0983] A: “between sorrow and joy.”] even in this life—how much more in the next, where no sorrow will follow the joy of the righteous, nor any joy follow the sorrow of the impious, since the divine judgment assigns to each unchangeable retributions appropriate to them? This is the great chasm and impassable gulf dividing rewards from punishments.

Yet the rich man [Note: [Col. 0983] A: “but.”] spoke not from afar but beside Abraham, [Note: [Col. 0983] “beside Abraham” is omitted in A.] so that you may understand that he was not separated from Abraham by nature but by guilt. For one essence joins together those whom unequal merit divides.

Shortly before the Lord [Note: [Col. 0983] “the Lord” is omitted in CF.] suffered, [Col. 0983D] Judas Iscariot and Simon Peter dined together with Christ in the same upper room; but one was near Christ, while the other was far from Christ. One, who dipped his hand with Christ into the dish, was the betrayer of Christ’s humanity; the other, who is not recorded as having dipped his hand with Christ [Note: [Col. 0983] CF: “his hand with Christ in”] into the dish, was the contemplator of Christ’s divinity. [Col. 0984A] One, greedy, sold the God-man; the other, a theologian, recognized God as man. One delivered the body with a bodily kiss; the other loved the divine mind with a kiss of the mind.

I say this so that you may understand that it is not intervals of place but the qualities of merit that cause a person to draw near to Christ or to be separated from him.

From this it may be understood that all human beings participate in one and the same nature, which has been redeemed in Christ and liberated from every servitude beneath which it still groans and suffers, and that all subsist as one in this nature. But the qualities and degrees of merit—that is, the differences between good and evil actions, by which each person lived well in this life, aided by God through grace, or badly, abandoned by God through justice—cause them to differ from one another in many ways and without limit.

[Col. 0984B] All these things, however, [Note: [Col. 0983] “however” is omitted in A.] are ordered and contained within that one vast house, in which the commonwealth of the universe created by God and in God is distributed through many different dwelling places—that is, through arrangements of merits and graces. [Note: [Col. 0983] A: “created.”] [Note: [Col. 0983] A: “distributed.”]

That house is Christ, [Note: [Col. 0983] “however” is omitted in A.] who encompasses all things by his power, [Note: [Col. 0983] “and” is omitted in A.] disposes them by his providence, rules them by his justice, adorns them by his grace, contains them by his eternity, fills them by his wisdom, and perfects them by deification; for from him, and through him, and in him, and toward him are all things.

### 37. DISCIPLE

What you have said is judged rational, and even highly plausible, by those who believe with right faith and, with rightly directed understanding, perceive the nature of things [Note: [Col. 0983] So CF; A has “natures”], and even highly plausible [Note: [Col. 0983] So CF; A has “plausible”], although to those who think that nothing exists beyond [Note: [Col. 0983] So CF; A has “among them”] what is locally and temporally contained within this perceptible world, it may appear incredible [Col. 0984C] and like empty ravings. They assert that this perceptible world will not return to its causes, nor perish altogether, but will remain, with only its qualities changed for the better: composed of its bodies, distinguished by its places, marked out by its times, multiplied by its numbers, and bounded by its extremities [Note: [Col. 0983] A has “composed—distinguished—marked out—multiplied—bounded”]. In what is, as it were, its lower region, they provide a place for the bodies and souls of the impious, to be tormented by the burning of eternal fire.

We discussed this in the preceding books also, and now, recalling it, we briefly repeat it. Some assign as the place of torment the region that separates the moon from the earth [Note: [Col. 0983] A has “the moon”]; others assign the lower, denser part of that aforesaid region, capable of containing shadows and nearer to the earth, which is called by the name “air” [Col. 0984D]; others assign the innermost recesses of the earth, as if they were the deepest and most spacious caves, perpetually filled with the thickest darkness and, as it were, suitable for the sons of darkness.

They declare that the bodies of the impious will rise again in the same size [Note: [Col. 0983] A omits “in”] in which they fell, in their sex and shape [Note: [Col. 0983] A has “and”], and with the same number of limbs, and that they will exist in exactly the same condition in which they lived in this life [Col. 0985A], except that they will be changed from mortal and temporal things into immortal and eternal ones, and from animal into spiritual beings. They do not refer this to the power of nature or the generosity of divine goodness, but to the harsh and immutable severity of a relentless judge, turning the gifts of nature and the benefits of grace into the cruelty of punishment.

For they say that the bodies of the impious will rise immortal, eternal, and spiritual for no other reason than that they may endure everlasting punishments. Nor do they doubt that the fire in which they will burn is bodily and perceptible. Likewise, they dream up some notion about worms that will not die and a sulphurous lake. They unhesitatingly assert, however, that all these things are bodily and local. They publicly proclaim that males will rise in the male sex and females in the female sex [Col. 0985B] [Note: [Col. 0985] So CF; A has “female”], with the particular appearance of each person, and that the functions of each individual limb will not be lacking, though unnecessary; along with the rest of their ravings [Note: [Col. 0985] A omits “ravings”], which true reason ridicules more than it affirms.

For the Apostle concludes their case in two clauses when he speaks of the general resurrection of all human bodies: “It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power.” If, therefore, all bodies will rise in glory and power, with all dishonor and weakness removed, what kind of glory will there be for those who are condemned to eternal punishments, or what kind of power?

Nor does it stand in the way that the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Does not the potter have power over the clay, to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” [Col. 0985C] For in that passage he is not discussing the resurrection of bodies [Note: [Col. 0985] So CF; A has “in that place”], but is speaking against those who attempt to accuse God as unjust, as though he chose some and rejected others, making some vessels of mercy while abandoning others as vessels of wrath [Note: [Col. 0985] So A; CF has “choosing—rejecting—making—abandoning”].

If someone should say that in these words the Apostle was not proclaiming the general resurrection of all human bodies, but only that of the righteous [Note: [Col. 0985] A has “should have proclaimed”], let him consider what the Lord himself said about himself when he had raised Lazarus: “I am,” he said, “the resurrection.” He did not say specifically, “I am the resurrection of the righteous,” but universally, “I am the resurrection.”

If he himself is the resurrection, then surely he gives himself in the same way to those whom he raises, just as he himself, like his Father, makes his sun [Note: [Col. 0985] A omits “his”] rise over the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust [Col. 0985D]. And perhaps he himself is the sun that rises equally for all, and the rain that falls equally upon all: granting generally to everyone the grace of resurrection and life, but specially removing from those who believe in him not only the death of the flesh, but also the death of the mind—by which God is unknown and which is the greatest punishment of the impious—like a certain shadow [Note: [Col. 0985] “like a certain shadow” is omitted by A].

Thus [Note: [Col. 0985] A has “So”], just as he gave all human beings existence equally, so he will give them resurrection equally, and possession of the likeness of the angelic nature [Col. 0986A].

But they set apart the higher regions of the perceptible world, which are called ethereal—from the moon upward to the outermost circumference of the star-bearing sphere—for the bodies of the saints as their possession. They arrange, in a distribution that seems rational to them, the lowest and darkest parts of the world for those deserving punishment, and the highest and brightest parts for those to be honored with reward.

Nor do they hesitate to proclaim that the bodies of the saints will remain local, bounded by the bodily quantities of their limbs and by their proper statures, and distinguished also by the male and female sexes. Yet they say that these bodies will be changed into spiritual qualities and exceedingly subtle substances, like the bodies of the ethereal beings [Col. 0986B], so that what is earthly and perishable here will be heavenly and eternal there; what is heavy and corruptible here will there be free of all weight and liberated from all corruption, moving with wondrous speed wherever they wish, like rays of the eyes.

Nevertheless, they will possess all the bodily organs—that is, bodily limbs—separated into their respective places: eyes and the other instruments of the senses, the head down to the shoulders, arms, chest, feet, and the remaining limbs arranged in their proper positions [Note: [Col. 0985] So CF; A has “which will inhabit”].

But when I read such things in the books of the holy Fathers, I remain stunned and hesitate, shaken by the greatest horror and trembling. And when I reflect within myself why men so spiritual [Note: [Col. 0985] So CF; A has “most special”—]—men who have risen beyond all operations of local and temporal thought and surpassed the entire perceptible world by the power of contemplation [Col. 0986C]—commended such statements in their writings and handed them down to posterity [Note: [Col. 0985] CF omits “statements”], I am more readily led to suppose that they were drawn to devise and write these things for no other reason than that, at least in this way, they might lift toward spiritual thoughts those devoted to earthly and bodily reflections and nourished on the elementary principles of simple faith.

For those who conceive of nothing beyond this perceptible world are more ready to deny than to confess the truthful contemplation of natures. When they hear that after the end of this world there will be neither places, nor times, nor bodies, nor bodily things, they immediately burst out in indignation and exclaim: “Then nothing will exist, if none of such things remains!” And they mock those who promise only spiritual things and remove the notions of perceptible realities.

Therefore, as I think, after considering these matters in their greatness and divinity [Note: [Col. 0985] A has “those considering great and divine things”], and taking account of the timid thoughts of simple believers [Note: [Col. 0985] So CF; A has “those considering great and divine things, and those taking account…”], it seemed more useful to them [Note: [Col. 0985] A omits “to them”] to proclaim the transformation of earthly and perceptible bodies into heavenly and spiritual bodies [“to proclaim”] [Note: [Col. 0985] A omits “to proclaim”], rather than to say that bodies, bodily things, and all perceptible things would never exist at all.

For to those who think bodily, the transition of earthly bodies into heavenly bodies appears more tolerable to believe than the denial of all corporeality.

The Apostle, I think, spoke in the same accommodating manner when discussing the resurrection of the earthly body: “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body.” As though he had said: The earthly and animal body, which is sown in the dissolution of death and corruption, will rise as a spiritual and heavenly body, with its earthly quantity and quality transformed into a heavenly quality and quantity.

And, to put it briefly, just as many, indeed almost all, wish to understand these words of the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0987] A has “thus many”], what is earthly will become heavenly, what is bodily will become spiritual, yet it will always remain a body; what is heavy will be changed into something subtle, but will never pass beyond ethereal bodies [Col. 0987B] or lose its bodily qualities [Note: [Col. 0987] So CF; A has “corporeal”]. Rather, it will pass from earthly qualities into heavenly ones [Note: [Col. 0987] A omits “from”], just as smoke is changed into flame.

But whoever examines more carefully the statements of Saint Ambrose and of Gregory the Theologian, as well as those of his interpreter—I mean Maximus [Note: [Col. 0987] A omits “and”]—will certainly find that they teach not a change of an earthly body into a heavenly body, but an altogether complete passage into pure spirit [Note: [Col. 0987] A omits “pure”], not into [Note: [Col. 0987] A omits “into”] that which is called ether, but into that which is called intellect.

Ambrose removes every composition, so that after the resurrection body, soul, and intellect are one and a single simple reality—not something composed from three elements, but joined into one ineffable harmony—and what appears here as three will there become one intellect [Note: [Col. 0987] So CF; A has “becomes”].

Gregory likewise and unhesitatingly asserts [Col. 0987C] the transformation, at the time of the resurrection, of body into soul, of soul into intellect, and of intellect into God. Thus God will be all in all, just as air is changed into light.

Nor is this passed over in silence by the Apostle, if anyone examines his words [Note: [Col. 0987] So CF; A has “his”] with subtle attention. For he says: “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body”—that is, the body that is sown as animal will rise as that same body, spiritual, that is, transformed into spirit; and, to speak more openly, from body there will be spirit.

He also makes this clear when he says: “It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power.” For what glory or power is it for an earthly body to rise in the quality of the stars and the ethereal subtlety, or to move with speed?

Nor does it stand in the way that the same Apostle says [Col. 0987D]: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead.” He introduced a comparison from the highest and brightest bodies of the perceptible world in order to commend the grace of the resurrection and the difference among the divine manifestations in each participant of regeneration. For this is what “star differs from star in glory” means: the distinguished Teacher beautifully and appropriately intimates, by comparison with the variety of the heavenly lights [Note: [Col. 0987] So CF; A has “luminaries”], a manifold and infinite recompense [Col. 0988A], according to which the most just Judge will repay each person according to his works [Note: [Col. 0987] So CF; A has “according to”].

We must not listen to those who suppose that after the future resurrection human bodies will shine in the ethereal regions in such a way that each will receive as much brightness as it carried in this life by the merit of its conduct, whether good or evil [Note: [Col. 0987] CF has “after the future regeneration”], and that the bodily brightness of the righteous will be compared with the shining sun, moon, and stars, while the darkness of the impious will be compared with the less brilliant stars. Against them true reason, aided by the divine Scriptures, teaches plainly that all human bodies will have one common and identical glory and power in the same spirituality, immortality, and eternity.

For all these things will be bestowed generally and without distinction upon everyone, by nature and by grace [Col. 0988B]. And what benefit [Note: [Col. 0987] So CF; A has “what benefit”] does it bring the righteous to have a radiant body like the sun, or what harm does it bring the impious to have a dark body like one of the darkest stars, when the glory of the righteous will consist not in the brightness of the body but in the purity of contemplation, through which God will be seen face to face, and the dishonor of the impious not in the ugliness of their limbs but in deprivation of the vision of God?

The presence of truth will make one blessed; its absence, miserable.

For example, let us imagine two people alike in stature and age, appearance and beauty, bodily health, nobility of birth, integrity of the senses, strength of body, agility of limbs, and all their other bodily goods [Note: [Col. 0987] A has “and certain other things”], without any difference between them. Yet one is wise, honorable in conduct, adorned with every virtue by which the soul is beautified [Col. 0988C]; the other is foolish, disgraceful in conduct, and corrupted by every vice through which the soul is disfigured.

What benefit do bodily goods, possessed equally, bring to the two of them [Note: [Col. 0987] CF has “to each”], when one considers nothing except reaching the supreme good toward which he strives, knowing that his good [Note: [Col. 0987] So CF; A has “supreme good”] is nothing other than cleaving to the supreme Good, resting in it, and rejoicing eternally in it? Here he begins, there he completes, his blessedness, always seeking to raise his whole being—body, soul, and mind—above every creature to him who is exalted above all things.

But the other, still established in mortal flesh, does not perceive the beginning of his torments in eternal sadness, blinded by the darkness of his folly. Nor does he reflect that the pleasures of this life and the pains of the future arise together and inseparably while he still dwells in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0987] CF has “converses”]. While they contend together in the present arena, only the pleasures smile upon those who love them, and future sadness hides itself within [Note: [Col. 0987] A has “among”] them. But when the end of the mortal course is reached, and the pleasures fail, that sadness—which had long been hidden and thought, as it were, extinguished—will mourn with unquenchable ardor, that is, with desire for the pleasures of lust that it has lost.

From this it is most plainly established [Note: [Col. 0989] So CF; A has “is effected”] that nothing should be desired except joy in the truth, which is Christ, and nothing should be fled except his absence, which is the one and only cause of all eternal sadness [Note: [Col. 0989] A has “the cause of all sadness”].

Take Christ away from me, and no good will remain for me; no torment frightens me. For deprivation and absence of him are the torment of every rational creature—and, I think, no other torment.

But much could be said about these matters. Let us return to what remains.

### MASTER

Before we reach the end of the present book, a few things, I think, must be said against those who confront us with certain passages of divine Scripture by which they attempt to establish that these perceptible elements and the entire vastness of the structure of the world will always remain, and that within it the positions and movements of human bodies after regeneration will, as they say, be arranged [Col. 0989B]. They believe that no bodies will ascend beyond this world or pass into spirit.

They say, therefore: If heaven and earth will perish, so that nothing of corporeality, locality, quantity, temporal or local movements, the spaces of dimensions, or the intervals of positions remains in them, what does Scripture mean when it says: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth”? By these words Scripture not only does not promise the destruction of heaven and earth, but also clearly testifies that they will be restored into a certain newness.

We answer that it is a very common manner of speaking in divine Scripture for the whole to be signified by a part, or by parts, and for the whole universe to be comprehended simply through the greatest division of creation [Note: [Col. 0989] So AC; F has “to comprehend”].

Since, therefore, the structure of the entire perceptible world has been arranged between its two extreme parts, opposed and, as it were, contrary to one another—I mean heaven and earth—the prophetic spirit fittingly signified the renewal of the entire visible creation, that is, its transformation into spiritual substances, by the figure of the new heaven and the new earth.

Thus, by “heaven” understand all the ethereal and heavenly bodies at the extremity; by “earth,” the lower and middle regions. Through this, the entire visible world is understood to pass together into its spiritual causes.

If someone should say that by this division of the new heaven and the new earth the whole of visible and invisible creation is signified, he will not, I think, be far from the truth. For reasonably, by the renewal of heaven the restoration of spiritual nature is prefigured, while by the renewal of earth the restoration of bodily things is prefigured.

The Apostle testifies that all things which are in earth and in heaven are restored in Christ and through Christ. For not only perceptible but also intelligible creatures will pass, in an ineffable manner known to God alone, into their causes—that is, into the purest knowledge of their causes—through which they will be united to them in the manner by which that which purely understands and that which is purely understood become one.

This too, I think, the Lord wished to signify in the Gospel when he said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” [Note: [Col. 0989] CF has “will pass away”].

It can also be understood specifically as referring to the renewal of human nature and its unification in itself: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth.” For our nature, still in this life, is composed of two substances, since it consists of body and soul.

And because this great dissimilarity of our substances, from which we are now constituted, arose from the transgression of humanity in the first creation, the Apostle testifies that it belongs to the old human being. He teaches us to strip off the old human being and put on the new—namely Christ—in whom our nature, by which I mean body, soul, and intellect, has been renewed, simplified into one, and changed from composite into uncompounded.

What has already been accomplished in the head of the whole human nature, namely in our Lord Jesus Christ, will be completed in the whole of nature: the new earth of our body will be changed into the new heaven, that is, into the renewal of the soul; and thereafter, in a higher ascent, body together with soul will become spirit, and spirit will become God himself.

All this will be accomplished in Christ and through Christ, who is the end and consummation of our nature.

Again they say—as though they confidently promised themselves that they could convict us by the strongest, sharpest, and most necessary arguments—that if this earth, the heaviest of all bodies and occupying the lowest and central place among creatures, is to perish, then necessarily the moon, which borders on it and is the star nearest to the earth, will perish. And if the lesser luminary perishes, surely the greater luminary will also perish; for if the whole has perished, no part will remain.

And if this happens, what does the prophet’s promise mean: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days”? For, they say, we are not here asking that the moon be understood allegorically as the Church, which will shine in Christ, who is the Sun of righteousness, or that the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit in Christ be understood, which will appear most clearly to all who contemplate him. Rather, we seek the bare historical meaning concerning the increase of the brightness of the two greatest heavenly bodies.

But if these two luminaries will not merely fail to perish, but their splendor will even be increased while their bodies remain, what prevents us from believing the same concerning the middle regions [Note: [Col. 0989] So CF; A has “middle”] of the world that we believe concerning its extremities as well? [Col. 0990D] Especially since blessed Augustine, in the final books of *The City of God*, appears to teach that it is not the bodies of the world themselves that will pass away, but that their qualities will be changed for the better.

In the same way, neither the forms nor the quantities [Note: [Col. 0989] So CF; A has “qualities”] nor the sexes of human bodies will pass away, but they will merely be clothed with spiritual and immortal qualities. And in his letter to Dardanus he unhesitatingly asserts that the Lord’s body after the resurrection is locally in heaven, in the same form and substance of flesh [Note: [Col. 0989] So CF; A has “substances”] in which it appeared to the world, with immortality added but nature not removed.

Consequently, he says, it is not everywhere as God is, nor has it been changed into divinity beyond all places and times, beyond everything that is said and understood. Rather, it will visibly and bodily descend from a certain place to judge the living and the dead.

We can meet this argument without as much labor as they suppose. For we say that the whole perceptible creation is indicated by the figure of the moon—and not without reason. Just as the moon is subject to increase and decrease [Note: [Col. 0991] CF has “losses”], so this entire world is subject to the generation and corruption of its parts. Nothing in it is firm or stable; for everything it contains, since it begins to arise, must necessarily perish.

But by the figure of the sun’s course and brightness is signified the most beautiful ordering of spiritual things, which both stand and move uniformly [Col. 0991B].

Thus the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun when the manifold and changeable variety and incomprehensible flux of bodily things—which now appears to the senses, now withdraws from them, now presents a complete form and now an incomplete one—is transformed into the fullest and immutable brightness and the uniform beauty and splendor of spiritual substances.

The light of the sun, that is, the beautiful form of spiritual things, will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days—that is, of the principal causes established in the brightness of the highest wisdom. These causes are also customarily represented typologically by the number seven, because they were made in the Word of God during the first six mystical and intelligible days, and on the seventh day their perfect consummation rested in him in whom they were created.

This is the intelligible Sabbath, which was both prefigured and begun in the creation of things, and will be manifested and completed at their end, when every perceptible creature will be changed into an intelligible one, every intelligible creature into its causes, and the causes into the cause of causes, which is God [Note: [Col. 0991] A has “which God is.”].

Then they will rejoice in eternal rest, shine with ineffable brightness, and keep Sabbath.

And those who set Augustine against us, as though they wished to show that they have greater reverence for his teaching than we do [Note: [Col. 0991] A has “as though they had wished”], and as though they had read his statements on such matters more frequently and diligently, should see what he himself discussed in the same books of *The City of God* concerning the destruction and annihilation of that perceptible and bodily heaven and of everything within its circumference—which, they think, the blessed master believed included Christ’s flesh after the resurrection.

They should also consider how a man of such acute intelligence understood two things that are contrary to one another: namely, that the bodily heaven would perish completely, while Christ’s flesh after the resurrection would be established in it locally and within limits, in the form in which the true human being, made from human beings, lived among human beings [Col. 0992A].

Therefore, it is more credible to suppose that this great and most skillful investigator and abundant expositor of divine and human matters wrote according to the capacity of the individuals for whom he wrote than to suppose that he disagreed with the holy Fathers who preceded him in time—I mean Ambrose and Gregory the Theologian, whose authority he does not contradict in other places.

For my part, detracting from no one and contending with no one, I understand without hesitation that what the Lord himself said—“I and the Father are one”—was spoken not only of his divinity but of his whole substance, both man and God [Note: [Col. 0991] “both man and God” is omitted by A].

Accordingly, the whole Christ, namely the Word and the flesh, is everywhere and is contained by no place—not wholly, nor in any part of himself; that is, neither in his divinity nor in his humanity, by which two parts his whole substance is constituted [Col. 0992B].

We can confirm this from the statement of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. For in the third book of *On the Trinity*, explaining the words that the Lord spoke while praying to his Father—“And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had before the world existed”—he said:

“The Word made flesh had not lost what he was, but had begun to be what he was not; he had not ceased to be what was his, but had received what was ours [Note: [Col. 0991] F has an above-line correction, ‘but he had not ceased to be what was his’]. He asks the advancement of what he received, namely of that glory from which he had not ceased [Note: [Col. 0991] So CF; A has ‘certainly’].”

Therefore, because the Son is the Word, and the Word was made flesh, and God is the Word, and this Word was in the beginning with God, and the Word was the Son before the foundation of the world [Note: [Col. 0991] A has “the Son, the Son before the foundation of the world”], now, having become flesh, he prayed that the flesh might begin to be for the Father what the Word was, so that what belonged to time might receive the glory of him who is beyond time, and so that the corruption of the flesh, transformed into the power of God and into the incorruptible spirit, might be swallowed up.

### 38

If, then, Christ’s flesh was transformed into the power of God and into the incorruptible spirit, undoubtedly that very flesh is power and incorruptible spirit. But if the power of God and the spirit are everywhere—not only beyond places and times, but also beyond everything that exists—no one can doubt that the flesh itself, transformed into power and spirit, is contained by no place and changed by no time [Note: Col. 0991: Thus CF; A has *detrimentisque* (“and by losses”).], but, like the power of God and the spirit—that is, the Word, which had already received it into unity with its own substance—surpasses all places and times, and universally every limitation [Note: Col. 0991: A has *excedat* (“surpasses”).].

It is enough, therefore, to set down one statement—although there are many—from the aforementioned teacher, Augustine, concerning what will become of the heaven and earth that now exist after the judgment. In Book 20, chapter 13, of *The City of God*, he says:

> “Afterward, when the judgment has been completed, this heaven and this earth will cease to exist when the new heaven and the new earth begin to exist; for this world will pass away through a change of things, not through complete destruction. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘The form of this world is passing away; I want you to be without anxiety.’ The form, therefore, passes away, not the nature.”

Tell me, I ask, in what does he disagree with what we have said about this world’s passing into its causes, which he himself called its nature? He says that this heaven and this earth will cease to exist after the judgment [Note: Col. 0993: Thus CF; A has *defutura* (“will be lacking / will be destined to be absent”).], while their nature alone will remain unchanged. Likewise, following his traces and those of others like him [Note: Col. 0993: A has *requirentes* (“seeking”).], we have taught that everything in this world that is perceptible, local, and temporal, and everything subject to mutability, will perish—that is, will pass into the substance itself, that is, into nature [Note: Col. 0993: A omits “that is, nature”]—whereas its nature, which is contained incorporeally and intelligibly in the primordial causes of all things [Note: Col. 0993: A omits “of all things”], immutably and incorruptibly, will remain forever.

But if someone says that the nature and substance of this world are perceptible and corporeal, subject to places and times, generations and corruptions, he proves himself, being far removed from sound reasoning, unworthy of any answer [Note: Col. 0993: Thus CF; A has *responsione* (“of an answer”).], since all wise students of nature have established that the nature and substance of bodies are incorporeal [Note: Col. 0993: Thus CF; A has *efficietur* (“will be made”).].

But if he says that Christ’s flesh will remain within the boundaries of this corporeal heaven until the day of judgment, and that, when that heaven has passed away, it will ascend beyond all places and times and beyond all celestial powers, then plainly he does not understand what the catholic Church confesses concerning the whole Christ when it says: “He ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of the Father.”

And who, unless insane, would say that the celestial powers are beyond this world, while Christ’s flesh—already changed into spirit, indeed into God himself—is held within it, when we see the thickest clouds consumed by solar fire and changed into it? If he says, “What is surprising if we believe Christ, according to the flesh, to stand or move locally in some place of this corporeal heaven, or wherever within it he may wish, while according to his soul or divinity he is everywhere”—provided, that is, that his soul, like his divinity, is present and diffused everywhere—“since we admit that angelic spirits subsist beyond every corporeal creature and move without locality beyond every place, while their bodies, by which they customarily appear to human beings, are both local and contained within the bounds of perceptible creation,” we reply:

Neither angelic spirits nor their spiritual bodies—which subsist causally in those spirits—are entirely enclosed within the barriers of corporeal creation. For they do not possess material bodies composed from the qualities of this world’s elements, but spiritual bodies joined to their intellects. In these bodies, whenever, wherever, and however they wish, they appear temporarily to human senses; yet they do so not in a merely imaginary manner, but truly. For there is no doubt that true and spiritual bodies proceed from true principles.

We believe that Christ appeared to his disciples after the resurrection in such a body—not that the one who appeared was different from the one who was born of the virgin, hung upon the cross, and raised from the dead, but that the same one was changed from mortal into immortal, from animate into spiritual, and from earthly into heavenly.

In such bodies the multitude of human nature would have sprung forth from its hidden wombs, if it had not sinned. For there is present in every human being a hidden principle of his body, into which this earthly and mortal body will be changed at the time of the resurrection, and in which it will be made like the bodies of angels, when human beings will be equal to the angels.

No reasoning, then, prevents us from believing and understanding without hesitation that our Lord Jesus Christ, in his two natures united into his inseparable substance, is everywhere, and that no part of him is circumscribed by any place, time, or any other mode by which a creature is defined.

For he is wholly God, wholly everywhere; wholly exalted above everything that is spoken or understood; wholly in the Father and made one with the Father; wholly God in the whole human being, and wholly human in the whole God, while the principles of both natures remain in themselves.

Thus, ineffably and supernaturally, the harmony of our Head has been fitted together, into which all his members, united to one another in him, will return when they come to the perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age; and one in all and all in one will both be and appear, and they will both be and appear [Note: Col. 0993: A omits “one”; A also omits “and they will both be and appear”].

For we must not listen to those who think that the Apostle’s statement should be understood otherwise: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to the perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.”

They suppose that this was said of the perfect bodily stature of Christ in the thirtieth year of his life in the flesh, and they attempt to assert that all human beings will be resurrected in that bodily stature and age, whether they were aborted fetuses, decrepit persons, or are released from the body amid any bodily increases or diminutions [Note: Col. 0993: A has *sint* (“are”) after each of the first two *sive* (“whether”); CF has *detrimentisve* (“or deteriorations”); for *solvantur* (“are released”), A has *quando solvuntur* (“when they are released”).]. Their utterly false ravings are most clearly destroyed and refuted by the Apostle’s own words.

For these words were not spoken of Christ’s growth according to the flesh that he had assumed, nor of its measure or age, but of his body, which is his Church [Note: Col. 0993: A omits “his”]. The measure, perfection, and fullness of the spiritual age of this body—that is, of the Church—is himself, who is both the most perfect and intellectual Head of his intellectual body, the end and consummation of all things.

Observe the Apostle speaking to the Ephesians: “He placed all things under his feet” [Note: Col. 0993: A has *sub pedes* (“under the feet”).], “and gave him as head over all the members” [Note: Col. 0993: CF omits “members”] “of the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all.”

And after a little while, again in the same Epistle, observe with what members Christ wished to build—and is building—his body:

> “He himself,” he says, “gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers.”

You have seen the members; you have seen the material. Ask the same Apostle for what purpose these members are prepared. He answers:

> “For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God.”

See the beginning of the building: the unity of faith. Recognize the perfection of the building: namely, the unity of the knowledge of the Son of God.

The growth of Christ’s body therefore begins here and will be perfected there, when Christ, together with and in his entire body, will appear as one perfect man: the Head in the members and the members in the Head. Then the measure and fullness of Christ’s age will be seen clearly in all the saints united to their Head—not with bodily eyes, but through the power of contemplation. Then the spiritual age—that is, the fullness of the virtues established in Christ and in his Church—will be brought to completion, together with the other things that may be understood concerning eternal happiness and the perfection of blessedness in the Son of God.

As for the resurrection of human bodies, blessed Augustine unhesitatingly affirms in his books *On the City of God* that each person will rise in the stature and size to which he had attained through the perfected growth of his body in youthful age, or would have attained if death had not overtaken him, or in the stature that he abandoned when, declining into old age, he fell into bodily decrepitude [Note: Col. 0995: Thus CF; A has *sive robore perventurus* (“or would have attained in strength”). A omits “would have attained if he had not been overtaken by death … will rise.”].

We have often said that blessed Gregory the Theologian, holy Ambrose, and also the venerable teacher Maximus establish by definite arguments that immortal and spiritual bodies will not be circumscribed by any outlines, qualities, or quantities of bodily forms, because of their ineffable union with their uncircumscribed spirits and their undivided simplicity.

Yet we are not unaware of the cause of the error of those who dogmatize that all human bodies will be resurrected in the stature of the Lord’s body. For, understanding less accurately what is written in Greek—εἰς μέτρον ἡλικίας, that is, “to the measure of age”—they thought that ἡλικία properly referred to the perfect age of the body, whereas ἡλικία signifies more the measure perfected in the soul through virtues than the measure perfected in the body through local and temporal growth [Note: Col. 0995: A has *significat* (“signifies”).].

For this reason philosophers assert that the rational soul is the daughter of ἐντελεχείας (*entelecheia*), that is, of perfect age in virtues, as though [the term were] ἔνδον ἡλικίας, that is, “within age” [Note: Col. 0995: Thus CF; A has *interioris aetas* (“the age of the interior”).].

Accordingly, no sound-minded person should understand the Apostle’s aforesaid words as referring to the perfection of the body’s age, but to the fullness of the Church in her Head, who is Christ—that is, to the perfection of grace and blessedness and of incomprehensible union [Note: Col. 0995: A omits “that is, to the perfection”].

And I am amazed that those who oppose us with arguments concerning the enlargement of the bodily lights of the world do not consider what the Lord himself prophesies in the Gospel concerning the failing of the entire perceptible world through the failure of its parts, saying:

> “Immediately after the tribulation of those days”—that is, after the persecution of Antichrist [Note: Col. 0995: A omits “after”]—“the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven.”

By these words we understand that the sun and moon will not remain after the failure of their light, nor the stars when the ether and the sphere in which they have been arranged have failed. For in this prophecy of the Lord we understand not merely an allegorical meaning, but also the destruction of the entire world and the dissolution of bodies.

Many, unwilling to believe in this destruction, have recourse to the laws of allegory alone, and by the sun’s failure understand the wavering of the faith even of the most perfect men who will exist at that time, when the son of iniquity appears [Note: Col. 0995: *intelligunt* is absent from A, CF; I have supplied it conjecturally.]. His persecution will introduce such darkness of error and unbelief that not only the carnal members of the Church, signified mystically by the moon, but also the more spiritual members, signified by the stars, including her highest and most spiritual teachers, signified by the sun, will either hide the light of orthodox faith for a time, diminish it out of fear, or fall away from it entirely.

We do not refute this interpretation. Nevertheless, we must not listen to those who violently attempt to establish this Gospel passage according to the historical sense, thinking that no falling away of the light of the heavenly bodies will occur at the end of the world, but that their splendor will be overwhelmed by the excessive brightness of the Judge who comes upon them, together with the heavenly essences descending with him when he comes to judge the living and the dead.

They also add an example from the rays of the rising sun, which by their force dull the radiance of the other stars [Note: Col. 0995: A has *obtundet* (“will dull”).], indeed even remove it from our eyes; for within themselves they always preserve the vibration of their light undiminished, because the sun, from which they receive their light, is always present to them. Nor, they say, is it an obstacle that the earth sometimes interposes itself between the lunar sphere and the sun and removes the solar rays.

But the cause of the error of those who dream such things is, I think, this: they suppose that the judgment will have to be carried out in some place within the boundaries of this world, and that the Judge, together with his holy angels, will descend locally and bodily from the higher regions of perceptible nature.

Hence some foolishly place the seat of judgment at the boundary between air and ether, where physicists describe the lunar circle; others, agreeing with the Jews, place it in the valley of Jehoshaphat. They do not notice the force of the name *Jehoshaphat*, which is composed of ἰαώ and σαφάτ.

Ἰαώ has many interpretations. It is interpreted as “invisible” [Note: Col. 0995: Thus CF; A has “visible”], or “Lord,” or “glory,” or “the One who exists,” or “the One who was, is, and will be.” Σαφάτ, however, is translated as “judgment.”

Thus *Jehoshaphat* means “invisible judgment,” or “the Lord’s judgment,” or “glorious judgment,” or “the One who was, is, and will be, who judges” [Note: Col. 0995: Thus CF; A has *autem* (“however”) instead of *igitur* (“therefore”).].

Joel, therefore, illumined by the prophetic spirit, seeing the depth and invisible power of divine judgment, remote from everyone, introduced typologically the valley of Jehoshaphat and the person of the Lord, whose glory will appear in the height of his judgment, the One who was, is, and will be. Taking this into himself and pouring it forth, he proclaims:

> “Let the nations arise and go up into the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the nations round about.”

As if he had said: “Let all rise from the dead and ascend into the height of my judgment and into that hidden depth which surpasses every understanding.”

Clear and true reason mocks those who dream such things. For how will our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom the Father has given judgment, move locally and temporally after he has exalted his humanity above all places and times, above everything that is said and understood, into the unity of his divinity—where he sits eternally and immutably at the right hand of his Father [Note: Col. 0997: A omits “his”], and where he will sit—from which he rules and judges all things, and will continue to rule and judge them?

For what the catholic faith confesses in the ecclesiastical creed, saying, “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead,” must not be understood as though it referred to a local movement of Christ or to a kind of procession from the innermost wombs of nature into this world, until he appears through visible bodily members to the bodily senses of those who are to be judged.

Rather, each of the good and the wicked will see his coming within himself, in his own conscience, when the books will be opened, God will reveal the hidden things of darkness, and each person will be the judge of his own actions and thoughts.

Hence Augustine, in Book 20, chapter 13, of *The City of God* [Note: Col. 0997: A has “in the twentieth book”]:

> “A certain divine power must be understood, by which it will come about that all a person’s deeds, whether good or evil, will be recalled to each person’s memory and perceived with the mind’s eye with marvelous speed, so that knowledge may accuse or excuse the conscience, and thus all and each may be judged” [Note: Col. 0997: CF has *cernentur* (“will perceive”)].

This divine power has rightly received the name “book”; for in it, in a certain manner, whatever is recalled through its operation is read, just as the Apostle says:

> “For we shall all stand before the tribunal of the Lord, so that each may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil.”

By “the tribunal of the Lord” he means the exalted majesty of the Lord, which will appear everywhere and in all things to everyone. When it is revealed, the impious will see the one whom they pierced [Note: Col. 0997: CF has *pupunxerunt* (“pierced” with a different spelling)], and all the tribes of the earth will mourn.
