Thus the sign of the Son of Man—that is, the honor and glory of his cross—will shine upon all. And perhaps that is the final flame which will both fill and consume the whole world [Note: Col. 0997: Thus CF; A has *consummabit* (“will complete”)]: namely, the appearing of God the Word in every creature, when nothing else will shine in all things for the good and the wicked alike except the intelligible light that now secretly fills everything and will then fill everything openly.

That, I think, is the flame which, speaking of itself, says: “I am a consuming fire.” For it will consume all things when it is all in all, and it alone will appear in all things.

In his Gospel also he says:

> “I have come to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire, except that it burn?”

By “earth” he signifies typologically every perceptible creature; by the burning fire, the brightness of his manifestation that will be in all things and the fervor of his judgment.

Blessed Augustine supports this interpretation in his exposition of Psalm 50:

> “For what is a holocaust wholly consumed by fire? When the entire animal was placed upon the altar to be consumed by fire, it was called a holocaust. That fire will consume us wholly, and that fervor will seize us. What fervor? There is no one who can hide himself from its heat. What fervor? The one of which the Apostle says: ‘Fervent in spirit.’ Let not only our soul be consumed by that divine fire of wisdom, but also our body by immortality. Let the holocaust be lifted up so that death may be swallowed up in victory” [Note: Col. 0997: A omits the passage beginning “To this interpretation blessed Augustine …” through “victory”].

And so forth: all the things that divine history teaches typologically concerning the future judgment. It would take too long to discuss them now.

**DISCIPLE.** It would indeed take too long; nevertheless, I would like briefly to hear what those clouds are in which the saints will be snatched up to meet Christ in the air, and what that air is in which they will always be with Christ in those clouds. For the Apostle says:

> “But we who are left, who remain—that is, who have not yet ascended into the height of deification—will be caught up in clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with him.”

**TEACHER.** We spoke briefly of these clouds in the earlier books of this discussion, following blessed Maximus; now, adding the interpretation of holy Ambrose, we shall speak again.

Each of the saints, Maximus says, will have his own cloud—that is, the particular power and height of his contemplation. For insofar as each person approaches the thought of truth, so far will he be caught up to meet Christ in the air; that is, into the height and brightness of the purest understanding. Thus he will always be in his cloud of contemplation, both existing and rejoicing in the divine theophanies.

According to Ambrose, likewise, the clouds are the patriarchs—for example, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—in whose faith, action, and knowledge the heirs of the New Testament will be caught up to meet Christ, as though in certain bright clouds.

Likewise Moses the lawgiver and the other prophets, as well as the apostles, who perceived the Lord’s powers and teaching in his presence, are clouds. In the examples of their faith and action, hope and charity, knowledge and wisdom, and the other virtues, those who follow their footsteps in this life will be caught up to meet Christ, just as they themselves were caught up, whether while still living in the flesh or after being freed from the flesh.

Tell me, I ask, where was Enoch caught up, and where was Elijah, who, while still constituted in the flesh, were caught up? Was it not to meet Christ, whom they knew by the spirit to be coming into the world?

Where was Abraham, of whom the Lord himself says: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced”?

Why should I delay? Where was Job, who said: “I heard you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you”?

Where was Moses when he ascended Mount Sinai? Where were the other prophets, foreseeing the Word of God coming in the flesh and meeting him in spirit? Where was Peter caught up when he answered his Lord: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”? Where was Paul when he ascended into the third heaven?

Were not all these, and those like them, caught up to meet Christ according to each person’s own or common contemplation, and are they not with him and in him, in the spiritual air of virtues and contemplations?

All these clouds, and the other similar intelligible clouds, were prefigured by that visible cloud which, at the time of the Ascension, received the Lord from the disciples’ eyes, when he was lifted up into heaven.

For he did not need some vehicle gathered together from clouds to raise him into the aerial and ethereal spaces, since after the resurrection he was purer and lighter than every visible and invisible creature, and after the regeneration he neither experienced nor allowed any local movement to remain in the spirituality of his body.

Rather, he wished visibly and typologically to show his disciples the manner in which he invisibly ascends in the hearts of those who love and follow him. For he ascended in the contemplations of those who ascend toward him; no one can ascend to him without him.

For, as he himself says, no one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven. Yet he does not abandon heaven, while, lifting the saints with himself, he ascends in them toward himself. Therefore he adds:

> “The Son of Man, who is in heaven,”

calling heaven the Father, from whom he went forth through the incarnation and to whom he returned after the resurrection [Note: Col. 0999: A has *post resurrectionem* (“after the resurrection”); CF has *per resurrectionem* (“through the resurrection”).].

Whenever we read in the Gospel that the Lord lifted his eyes toward heaven, we must understand his Father, who alone is greater than he, in the sense that the Father precedes the Son as cause.

The saints are understood to become with Christ and in Christ in the purity of contemplation in three ways. They become so while still held in the flesh; they become so after being freed from the body; and they become so after receiving their bodies again.

The clearest examples of these three modes were manifested in the Lord’s transformation on the mountain: Elijah represented those living in the flesh, Moses those freed from the body, and the Lord himself those who rise again. For in the transfiguration of his body he showed his disciples the form of the resurrection of all.

And do not suppose that Elijah, still living in his body, came to Christ then from some local paradise, or Moses from some abode of souls, or that, after the mystery of the transfiguration had been completed, they returned to those places from which they had come.

Rather, believe and understand with complete certainty and faithfulness that they proceeded from nowhere other than the one with whom they appeared on the mountain—that is, in the elevation of spiritual vision that then took place beyond bodily senses [Note: Col. 0999: A omits the phrase “that is, in the elevation … beyond bodily senses”]—and that, before they appeared, they were in him; when they appeared, they had not abandoned him; and when the mystery of their appearance was finished, they returned not elsewhere but into him, in whom and with whom they are one.

This was most clearly signified by those three chosen disciples in the secret transformation [Note: Col. 0999: Thus A and CF], who, when they lifted their eyes, saw no one except Jesus alone [Note: Col. 0999: A has “Jesus alone” in the reverse order].

And, so that you may recognize these things as more credible, read holy Ambrose in his exposition of Luke. He says:

> “Understand that this cloud was not formed from the misty moisture of smoking mountains, nor a pitch-black darkness of condensed air that overlays the sky with the horror of darkness, but a shining cloud that does not wet us with rainwater or with the inundation of moist showers. Rather, from it the dew of faith, sent forth by the voice of almighty God, watered human minds; and when the voice came, Jesus was found alone. Thus, although there were three, one was made: three are seen at the beginning, one at the end; for they are one in perfect faith.”

Finally, the Lord also prays this to the Father [Note: Col. 0999: CF has “the Lord prays to the Father”]:

> “that we may all be one.”

And not only Moses and Elijah are one in Christ, but we too are one body of Christ. Therefore they too, as though in one body [Note: Col. 0999: CF omits “as though in one body”], are received into the body of Christ, because we too shall be one in Christ Jesus.

**DISCIPLE.** Enough has been said about the clouds in which the saints are caught up to meet Christ. But what are those heavenly clouds with which the Son of Man will come? It is rightly asked. I would therefore like you to explain briefly what they are.

**TEACHER.** I would say that the clouds of heaven with which the Son of Man will come [Note: Col. 0999: CF omits *est* (“is”)] are none other than the heavenly substances themselves, which always move around Christ through the power of contemplation.

Since they do not behold the incomprehensible and invisible summit of the holy Trinity—which surpasses every understanding—in itself, but in comprehensible theophanies that are connatural to them, they are therefore called “the clouds of heaven.”

For the Lord himself signified the heavenly substances by the name “clouds,” through the divine appearances in which they see God. With these substances, and in them, his coming—that is, the most radiant greatness of his majesty—will be revealed to all, both good and wicked.

The nature of their spiritual being does not permit the heavenly substances to move locally. Yet they move spiritually when they carry out in the nature administered by them, and over which they preside, what they discern ought to be done in the cause of all things, arranging places, times, and everything circumscribed within them, without their own local and temporal movement.

They are also said to come when they appear in some visible form to those who are worthy, and to withdraw when they are completely removed from every bodily sense.

Nor should it trouble you that I said spiritual substances do not undergo temporal movement, while holy Augustine proclaims that God alone is moved by himself without place and time, whereas a created spirit undergoes movement through time without place, and a body through place and time, moved by the one who moves all things.

I said this following the authority of the Greeks, who assert without hesitation that everything which moves locally also moves temporally, while everything that lacks local movement consequently also lacks temporal movement. For these two things—place, I mean, and time—will either exist together or be removed together, since they do not permit themselves to be separated from one another.

**DISCIPLE.** It is not our task to contend over authorities in either language; let each person follow whom he wishes, disparaging no one. And since we have spoken, however briefly, about the intelligible clouds, return, I ask you, to the return, and guide our wavering ship and our weary sailors into harbor.

**TEACHER.** The return of all things that will return to their causes, when this perceptible world is dissolved and that intelligible world which is above us [Col. 1001B] is fulfilled in Christ, is understood in two ways.

There is a general return and a particular return. The general return occurs in all who will return to the beginning of their creation. The particular return occurs in those who will not merely be recalled to the beginnings of nature, but will also establish the end of their return beyond every natural dignity, in the cause of all things, which is God.

We must gather examples and likenesses of both kinds of return from the divine Scriptures. And since, according to the natural order, the genus precedes the species, we must speak first about the general return.

An example of the genus, then, was given beforehand in the people of God. Freed from the yoke of the intelligible Pharaoh—that is, the devil—and from his servants, led by the spiritual Moses, namely Christ, they crossed the Red Sea with dry feet [Note: Col. 1001: A has “with their feet”]. They walked along a firm path of human nature, opened by the cutting apart of the blue waters of irrational movements [Note: Col. 1001: Thus CF; A has “rational movements”], overcoming and overthrowing rebellious nations—that is, the armies of vices [Note: Col. 1001: Thus CF; A has “namely”]—and, after their bodies had died, by “bodies” I mean carnal thoughts, they returned spiritually, solely in the children of good works, to the desert of the virtues, where everything mortal and corruptible is consumed, and thence to the promised land.

The fact that two of all those who came out of Egypt entered the promised land while still alive in the flesh [Note: Col. 1001: Thus CF; A has “entered” in the subjunctive] mystically indicates our twofold nature—namely, body and soul—which, in our Savior, prefigured by Joshua son of Nun, that is, “the beauty of them,” will return to the land that we abandoned through sin, accompanied by Caleb, that is, by the freedom of our heart’s will.

For Caleb is interpreted as “like the heart” or “every heart” [Note: Col. 1001: Thus CF; A has “for the heart” instead of “every heart”]. To the extent that the devotion of each person’s heart has been assisted by divine grace, so will it follow its Savior into the region of the living and of those who use natural goods.

By this reasoning we are led to understand the return of the whole of humanity to the original state of nature through the clear return of the Israelite people from Egyptian captivity, since Scripture records that no one from the people of God remained in Egypt, but that all fled from it together and, without exception, were freed from the hands of the most cruel power.

The fact that none of those who returned from Egypt was overwhelmed by the waves or drowned, but that all, as the Apostle says, were under the cloud—namely, under divine protection—and all crossed the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, prefigured that general baptism which will be completed at the end of the world.

Then mystical Moses will lead his people—that is, the whole human race, redeemed by his blood and cleansed of every impiety and wickedness—from death to life. Then nothing in any human being will appear except the simplicity of nature, through the merit of the one who wholly assumed it and wholly healed it.

Then the intelligible king of Egypt—obviously the prince of this world—with the innumerable army of his wickedness and with all the vices by which he had held captive the image of God created in humanity, will be overwhelmed by the waves of the Red Sea—that is, by the deepest, richest, and boundless outpouring of grace, poured into human nature as the price of Christ’s blood.

For just as Christ’s blood benefited human beings for redemption, and will benefit them for the restoration of their original nature, so it harmed the devil and his angels in the destruction of their dominion, and will harm them in the increase of their punishment.

The flooding of the Erythraean Sea [Note: Col. 1001: Thus CF; A has “Red Sea”]—that is, the outpouring of the Lord’s blood—just as it raised human nature from the depths of eternal death into eternal life, so it drowned diabolical wickedness in perpetual condemnation.

For the devil’s pride will suffer no greater punishment, nor any more grievous sorrow, than envy of human salvation and the despair that follows it. This does not mean that he could not, if he wished, turn to the Creator of his nature; rather, bound by the bonds of his own malevolence, he will perpetually hate the sweetness of blessedness, grieving through continual torments over those who have fallen from his hands.

The prophet Isaiah likewise does not remain silent about the general salvation of the human race in Christ, but cries out, saying:

> “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people that sat in darkness saw a great light, and light arose for those sitting in the region and shadow of death.”

And who is that people which sat in darkness and in the region of the shadow of death, except the infinite multitude of humanity known only to God? After it abandoned the light of paradise, it sat in the darkness of ignorance and in the region of the shadow of death—not only in the death by which the soul is separated from the body through corruption, but also in that by which God abandons the soul through sin.

From this double death that light frees the whole human race—the light that arose for all, which says of itself: “I am the light …”

Col. 0993, *localiter* (“locally”) is omitted by A; *fateamur* (“we admit”) is A’s *confiteamur* (“we confess”); *nec* (“yet/not”) is A’s *non* (“not”).

Col. 0997, A reads *et quis est ille* (“and who is that one”) for “and who is that”; it omits *hujus* (“of this [discussion]”) and *enim* (“for”); for “we had previously said a few things,” A has *praefati pauca sumus*; CF omits *qui* (“who”) of Elijah; A omits *et* (“and”) in “the other similar and intelligible clouds”; A has *sineret* (“would allow”) for *siverit* (“has allowed”); A has *hoc* (“this”) for *haec* (“these things”); in Joel, A has *in altitudinem* (“into the height”) for *in altitudine* (“in the height”); A omits *et* in “by which, when revealed” and in “nothing else both for good and evil”; A also omits *inquit* (“he says”) and *et* (“and”) in the saying about fire.

world. Now, in part, destroying the service of idols in those whom he converts to the worship and knowledge of the true God, washing away the filth of vices by the flood of baptism [Note: [Col. 1003] So CF; A has “washes away.”], and burning it away by the fervor of repentance; but at the end [Note: [Col. 1003] So CF; A has “Infinite.”] not only the general death of the body, but also the death of the mind, will be destroyed, and, when all the rites of idolatry and the superstitions and wickednesses of every nation have been wholly dispersed, the knowledge of the one true God will be granted to the entire creation. For all, both good and evil, when they stand before the tribunal of the Lord, will recognize that there is one God, and none other besides him. Then there will be a general confession by all of the one God, when there will be no denial of the truth. For even the blind cannot deny to those who see that the light which they themselves do not see shines for them.

That the salvation of our entire nature has already been accomplished in Christ, anyone who wishes can readily discern from the interpretations of the names mentioned above. Zabulon, indeed, is interpreted as “dwelling-place of virtue.” Therefore that light which arose for those sitting in darkness is the virtue and wisdom of the Father. And what is its dwelling-place? Is it not our nature, in which he wished to dwell through the Incarnation? Hear the Evangelist: “And the Word,” he says, “became flesh and dwelt among us.” Thus spiritual Zabulon is the humanity of Christ, in whom we have all been saved, in whom, once saved, we dwell, and in whom we shall dwell forever; for he himself is our virtue and strength.

Nepthalim [Note: [Col. 1003] CF has “Neptaleim.”] is also said to mean “breadth.” And what is our breadth [Note: [Col. 1003] A has “our breadth”], except Christ, whose love and mercy embraces the whole human race, who died for the ungodly, when perhaps someone might dare to die for a good man? He loved all human beings equally, when he gave himself up for all. For this is the broadest law of nature, the common love of all human beings without any acceptance of persons, and it has been most perfectly fulfilled in Christ. It proceeded from the Father, who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.

There is also another reason why Christ is understood as breadth. Breadth is appearance and surface, and therefore in Greek it is called *epiphaneia*. Christ, then, is our epiphany, that is, our appearance and surface, because, although there are three substances of the highest Good, one of them appeared to us in the human being Christ, namely, the incarnate Word, and made himself comprehensible to bodily senses. No one has seen the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, in the unity of substance with the creature [Note: [Col. 1003] A has “created thing.”].

Ezekiel also prophetically announces the return of the whole of human nature under the figure of three cities. For it is said:

“Jerusalem, and you shall be confounded, and bear your shame, you who justified your sisters”; and thereafter it adds [Note: [Col. 1003] So CF; A has “is added”]: “And you and your daughters shall return to your former state, and I shall restore them, converting them with the conversion of Sodom and its daughters, and with the conversion of Samaria and its daughters; and I shall turn your return [Note: [Col. 1003] A has “of your daughters”] into their midst.”

From this, as Saint Jerome says, it is clear that the anger of God is not natural to him, but that our most merciful and gentle God is provoked to anger by our vices. It follows:

“And your sister Sodom and her daughters shall return to their former state, and Samaria and her daughters shall return to their former state, and you and your daughters shall return to your former state.”

The Septuagint has:

“And your sisters Sodom and her daughters shall be restored as they were from the beginning; and Samaria and her daughters shall be restored as they were from the beginning [Note: [Col. 1003] The words ‘and Samaria … from the beginning’ are omitted in CF]; and you and your daughters shall be restored as you were in the beginning [Note: [Col. 1003] The words ‘as you were in the beginning’ are omitted in CF].”

Blessed Jerome, explaining these words of the prophet—or rather, of the Lord through the prophet—says:

“The Jews, among the other fables, endless genealogies, and ravings which they invent, also dream this concerning the coming of their Christ, whom we know to be the Antichrist: that in the reign of a thousand years Sodom is to be restored to its former state, so that it will be like [Note: [Col. 1003] CF omits “like.”] the paradise of God, and that Samaria is to recover its former happiness, so that they may return from Assyria to the land of Judea; and that Jerusalem, too, is then to be rebuilt.”

And shortly afterward:

“But we,” he says, “leaving the perfect knowledge of these matters to the judgment of God [Note: [Col. 1003] So CF; A has ‘we shall leave’], or rather, openly confessing the truth, say that after the second coming of the Lord and Savior nothing humble, nothing earthly, will exist, but the heavenly kingdoms which are first promised in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1003] So CF; A also has ‘are promised’].”

We have omitted the rest of what the aforementioned interpreter explains concerning these matters [Col. 1004C], because they are moral interpretations and discuss only the return of the souls of Gentiles, heretics, and sinners to the catholic faith.

One may also reasonably say that the mystical and legal week, which was followed by the fiftieth year—called in Hebrew *JOBEL*, that is, “liberty,” because in that year everyone received liberty and each person returned to his former dwelling, released from every law by which he had been held—clearly signifies the return under discussion, once the sevenfold cycle of the present life has come to an end.

King and prophet David promises the renewal of nature, saying: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth.”

What shall I say of the evangelical parables, namely, of the prodigal son, who, in a foreign land, squandered the portion of his substance which he had received from his father; then, compelled by poverty, recognizing himself and moved to repentance, returned to his father? He was received by him with the greatest piety and mercy, and not only regained his former grace, but, in honor of his return, the fattened calf was slaughtered.

Who, then, is this son? Is he not the human being made in the image of God? For the heavenly Father created two natures for the knowledge of himself, namely, the angelic and the human, and he granted these two the grace of sonship. But the human being is called the younger son, while the angel is the elder in age, because Scripture first recalls the creation of the angel and afterward that of the human being.

The elder son signifies the portion of the angelic multitude which never abandoned its Creator; the younger signifies the whole fallen human race, wandering far from its Creator. Yet afterward it will return to its Father and receive the first robe—that is, the first condition of its nature. Moreover, it will receive the breadth of virtue, signified by the ring, and also the reward of Christ’s death, represented by the shoes on the feet, namely eternal life, which is universally repaid to the human race by merit of the Lord’s death.

Then the fattened calf will be brought and slaughtered. And who is that calf except the human being Christ, full of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit—or, certainly, made fat with the richness of the letter and of visible nature? For in these two things, namely the letter and visible creation, a certain corporeality of Christ appears [Note: [Col. 1005] A has “Christ’s corporeality”], because he is understood in them and through them, insofar as he can be understood. For Christ is the Spirit of the Law, and the invisible things of God are seen as understood through the things that have been made, including his eternal power and eternity.

Or, as blessed Maximus says, explaining Gregory the Theologian in his sermon on the Nativity, where he says “the Word becomes thick”:

“The Word,” he says, “although simple and incorporeal, and consequently nourishing all things spiritually, the divine powers in heaven, through his presence in the flesh, deigned to become thickened from us, for us, and according to us, without sin.”

That this son bears the figure of the human race—to say nothing of the statements of John Chrysostom concerning this parable, since they are lengthy—it is sufficient to set down the testimony of blessed Ambrose in his exposition of Luke:

“It is possible,” he says, “to understand in one person, namely the prodigal son, the form of the human race. Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him they all perished. Therefore the human being is restored in that human being who had perished; and he who had been made according to the likeness and image of God is restored by divine patience and magnanimity.”

Do you see, then, that this parable teaches figuratively that not a part of the human race, but the whole of it, is to be restored in Christ?

The same interpretation applies to the lost drachma, which, after the overturning of this world—as of a certain house—was found by the woman, namely the wisdom of God, who made and possessed it. It is also counted as the tenth because human nature has not only been made equal to the nine orders of angels, but there is also no angelic order into which human nature, after its restoration [Note: [Col. 1005] CF has “after its resurrection”], will not be inserted according to the intelligible degrees, until it completes the perfect ten of the heavenly city, as Dionysius the Areopagite bears witness in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*.

This, too, would have happened to it if it had not sinned.

Understand in a similar way the hundredth sheep which had gone astray, abandoning the heavenly flock. The good shepherd, who is Christ, sought and found it, and, having found it, took it upon his shoulders and carried it back to the flock which it had abandoned by wandering away. It is counted as the hundredth for this reason: after the fall of human nature, the perfection signified by the number one hundred—namely the heavenly Jerusalem, which is our mother—was diminished. Its multitude, like the breadth of the number one hundred, will be filled out to completeness when the human race returns to it in its Head, who is Christ.

At this point a not insignificant question arises, one already widely circulated but, as I believe, not yet resolved; and if it has been resolved, we confess that the resolution has not yet come into our hands. The question is this: if so great a number of human beings is to return into fellowship with the heavenly city, that is, into the society of the blessed multitude living under one God, how great was the number of transgressing angels who fell from it?

It follows that either the multiplication of the human race from the first human being to the end of the world is as great as the number of apostate angels, so that their heavenly seats, which they abandoned through pride, will have been sufficient there, when the human race returns, to contain the whole human race; or, if the number of fallen angels is smaller than the multiplication of the human race, a part of human nature, not required because it exceeds the number of the falling angels, will remain outside the fellowship of the heavenly city—for it will not be able to ascend there, since it is not permitted to find a seat there—while the part equal to them, I mean to the fallen angels, will return. Consequently, it would undeniably follow that not all human beings were redeemed in him who wishes all human beings [Note: [Col. 1005] A omits “human beings.”] to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

Nearly all authors of both languages, indeed, assert without hesitation that as many human beings will enter the heavenly city as fugitive angels went out from it. And if this is so, we shall be forced to choose one of two alternatives: either the number of all human beings is equal to the number of evil angels, or the multitude of the human race is greater than the multitude of apostates. In that case, not all who share in humanity would return to the beginning of their creation—a conclusion which the preceding arguments, firmly establishing the salvation of the whole of humanity in Christ, altogether forbid us to accept.

Since it would be lengthy to introduce the opinions of the holy Fathers concerning this reasoning, that is, concerning the comparison between restored human beings and fallen angels, let us be content with one testimony of Saint Augustine [Note: [Col. 1005] A has “let us be content.”]. In the first chapter of the twenty-second book of *The City of God*, while discussing the nature of demons and their fall, he says:

“Nature, which was to enjoy God, shows itself to have been established as supremely good even by the very defect which is therefore miserable because it does not enjoy God. God, who bound the voluntary fall of the angels with the most just punishment of eternal unhappiness, gave to the others who remain in that highest good certainty of their remaining forever, as though he had given them the knowledge of their remaining as the very reward itself [Note: [Col. 1007] A omits ‘knowledge’]. He who made the human being also upright, with the same free will, an earthly animal indeed but worthy of heaven if he clung to his Creator, and likewise destined for misery if he abandoned him, foresaw that he would sin by transgressing God’s law through deserting God [Note: [Col. 1007] CF has ‘to be a sinner’], and yet he did not take away from him the power of free will, while at the same time foreseeing what good he himself would bring forth from his evil. From the mortal race, justly condemned on account of its merit, he gathered by his grace so great a people that it might fill and restore the part of the angels which had fallen, and thus that chosen and heavenly city would not be deprived of the number of its citizens, but might perhaps even rejoice in a greater number.”

This conclusion alone of the most holy teacher should suffice for us to understand that a greater number of the human race will return to the holy heavenly city than the number which fell from it.

I believe David the prophet said the same thing: “I have proclaimed,” he says, “and I have spoken; they have been multiplied beyond number.” For he spoke of those who have been cleansed and redeemed through the sacrifice of the Lord’s body, who have been multiplied beyond the angelic number that fell from the glory of blessedness through the pride of one fugitive.

The following verse makes this most clearly understood:

“Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; but you perfected a body for me as a holocaust.”

As though he were saying: “You did not wish to give the sacrifice of the Law and an offering for the cleansing and redemption of the sin of the human race; but you perfected for me the body of Christ, that is, a holocaust for me through the fire of suffering upon the altar of the cross. Therefore you required nothing else for our sin.”

For grace abounds beyond sin; the passion of Christ has bestowed incomparably more upon us for life than Adam’s transgression bestowed for death.

Whether, therefore, the number of transgressing human beings and angels is equal, or whether it is greater and more numerous, nothing prevents us from believing that the whole human race has both been redeemed in Christ and will return to the heavenly Jerusalem.

For if the number is equal [Note: [Col. 1007] CF omits “is”], as seems to many who discuss such matters, this will have sufficed for the praise of our Redeemer [Note: [Col. 1007] So CF; A has “of our own redeemer”]. His providence ordained as great a multitude of human beings as could insult the Prince of this world, from whom he not only took away the whole kingdom of our nature, but also distributed to us for eternal possession the inheritance from which that Prince, puffed up with pride, had been cast down [Note: [Col. 1007] A has “was added”; F has “was cast away”]. Thus he was tortured by the punishment of a double grief: first, because he justly lost the kingdom which he had acquired by deceiving the first human being, by unjustly killing the human being; and second, because he is tormented by envy when his enemies possess his heavenly inheritance, which he had abandoned.

But if the number is greater, we should certainly repay a greater praise to his grace [Note: [Col. 1007] So CF; A has “we ought to repay”], since he not only divided among us in heaven the possessions of our ancient enemy, but also prepared a more numerous people for habitation in the heavenly homeland than those who fell from it.

The examples stated above concerning the general return to paradise are sufficient, as I think.

**DISCIPLE.** They are entirely sufficient. For to collect into one place all the symbols of this kind which are scattered throughout Holy Scripture would be lengthy and perhaps tedious. Yet I should like to know what the envy of the elder son toward the younger son, returning to his father and feasting after the slaughter of the fattened calf, signifies. It troubles me greatly. If those two brothers signify the angelic and human natures, what envy of the good angels is to be understood concerning the salvation of the human race and its return to its Father, whose substance—that is, the grace of the image—it squandered while serving the devil in the farmstead of this mortal life [Note: [Col. 1007] In manuscript C, the words “while serving the devil in the farmstead of this mortal life he squandered” conclude the text]?

For we read that the holy angels grieve over the destruction of the human being, but in no way envy it; they are fellow citizens of the heavenly city and possessors of the Father’s substance and inheritance. Concerning the sheep which was found and carried back upon the shoulders of its shepherd, the Lord himself testifies that the angelic powers rejoice with it, signifying through one human sinner the human race [Note: [Col. 1007] A has “the human race.”].

And if the elder son symbolizes the whole company of the good angels, how can he be read to have come from the field, to have asked for a kid, to have become angry with his father, and to have done other things contrary to angelic charity?

**TEACHER.** I believe that the knot of this question, difficult to untie [Col. 1008C], can be unraveled in one way, which may be called the transition of parables.

There are two kinds of parables. One is that which maintains a continuous and uniform force concerning one and the same matter, without any transition into another figure. The other is that which passes over into various figures. We find many of the holy Fathers, and especially blessed Ambrose, expounding this parable according to the latter kind.

The first part of the parable—formed by the division of the paternal substance, the perseverance of the elder son with his father, the younger son’s wandering abroad, the squandering of the portion of his substance which he had received from his father, and the other misfortunes which followed upon the fall of humanity—certainly specifies the two natures: the intellectual nature in angels and the rational nature in human beings.

But in the return of the prodigal son the parable begins to make its transition. The return itself admits of a twofold mode of interpretation. It is understood generally as the return of the whole human race, because of the slaughter of the fattened calf, namely the passion of Christ for the salvation of the whole world. It is understood specially, where the transition of the parabolic figure begins, as the return of the Gentile people, as the younger son, through faith in Christ to the heavenly Father. The Gentiles had contaminated the image of that Father with the filth of idolatry and monstrous imaginings, and the return occurs in the presence of the envy of the Jewish people, as the elder son, concerning the conversion of the Gentiles to the faith through apostolic preaching.

Although that people was very often corrupted by the worship of demons and transgressed, it nevertheless never wholly denied the God of its fathers, as it thinks. But it did deny, and still denies, that Christ is the Son of God, and consequently also denies his Father. For whoever denies the Son also denies the Father, who, once the Son is denied, is not Father.

The faithless one demands a kid from the Father of Christ, whom he denies; but he will not receive a kid from the Father of Christ [Note: [Col. 1009] F has “may he receive”]. He will receive it from his own father, concerning whom Jesus Christ—whom he denies to be the Father’s Son—says: “You are from your father the devil.” And he is tormented concerning the faith of the Gentile people in Christ.

Therefore he does not ask the Father for the fattened calf, that is, Christ the Lord, to feast upon, but for a stinking, wanton kid, prone to every lust—I mean the Antichrist—in whom he foolishly dreams and expects that he will feast and reign [Note: [Col. 1009] F omits “in whom he.”] Coming from the field—that is, from earthly works and the laborious service of cultivating the Law according to the letter [Note: [Col. 1009] A has “of laborious service”]—he heard the symphony and the chorus. That is, he heard the catholic harmony of the Gentile people feasting in Christ and returning to its Father, a harmony consonant and agreeing everywhere in perfect faith and spiritual knowledge of the truth, and he heard the joy over the gift of its freedom and redemption.

For this reason, moved by envy, he grows angry with his brother, like him in nature but his enemy because of the difference between Jewish faithlessness and Christian religion. He rebukes his father for receiving the son who had lost the riches of his nature, while he himself dissipates the riches of his own nature even more by denying the one Son of God, the Creator and Savior of all.

The faithless Jews, through envy, reject the Word of God, while unbelieving nations reject it through ignorance. Since the sin of ignorance is more tolerable than the sin of envy, the Gentile people lost fewer of its natural treasures than the Jewish people. Therefore the Gentiles were received, freed from the darkness of ignorance and recalled to the light of truth. But the faithless Jews, denying the Son, were left in the most grievous sufferings of disgrace and envy, until at the end of the world they are received through the ineffable magnanimity of divine goodness, when “they shall turn toward evening, and suffer hunger like dogs, and go around the city,” namely the fellowship of the catholic faith, wishing to be admitted into it.

Then what the same prophet says elsewhere will be fulfilled:

“Let all my enemies be confounded and ashamed; let them turn backward and be confounded very quickly” [Note: [Col. 1009] A has “let them return.”]

Thus, having expounded this parable according to the poverty of our little intellect as it follows the paths of spiritual philosophers [Note: [Col. 1009] F has “following”], we must briefly discuss the symbols of the special return of human nature.

**DISCIPLE.** The time requires that this be done, and the course of our discussion has long been awaiting its end. I am also greatly pleased by this twofold kind of evangelical parables. For not only in parables, but also in many passages of divine Scripture, this form of expression pours forth divine nectar and provides an easy path of interpretation for those devoted to the theory of mystical discourse.

For the manifold structure of the holy prophets in divine meanings cannot be discerned in any other way than through very frequent transitions—not only through periods, but also through cola and commas—from one sense into another and again from those senses into the same ones, by means of the most hidden and very frequent returns [Note: [Col. 1009] So AF]. Very often, if one follows one and the same kind of exposition without any transition into different figures, either error or the greatest difficulty in interpretation arises. For the structure of divine Scripture is interconnected and entangled in labyrinthine turnings and obliquities like those of Daedalus.

Nor did the Holy Spirit wish this out of envy of understanding [Note: [Col. 1009] A omits “wished this”]—far be it from us to think so—but in order to exercise our understanding through study and to grant the reward of sweat and discovery. The reward of those who labor in Holy Scripture is pure and perfect understanding.

O Lord Jesus, I ask no other reward from you, no other blessedness, no other joy, except that I may understand, purely and without any error of deceptive theory, your words, which have been inspired through your Holy Spirit. For this is the summit of my happiness and the end of perfect contemplation [Note: [Col. 1009] A has “of perfect contemplation”], since a rational soul, even the purest, will find nothing beyond this, because there is nothing beyond it.

For just as you are sought nowhere more suitably than in your words, so nowhere are you found more openly [Note: [Col. 1009] A has “more suitably”] than in them. For there you dwell, and there you bring those who seek and love you [Note: [Col. 1009] F omits “you”]. There you prepare spiritual banquets of true knowledge for your elect; there, passing through, you serve them.

And what is this passing of yours, Lord, except an ascent through the infinite degrees of your contemplation? For you are always passing through the understandings of those who seek and find you. You are always sought by them, and you are always found—and you are not always found. You are found indeed in your theophanies, in which you meet the minds of those who understand you in many ways, as in certain mirrors, in the manner in which you allow yourself to be understood: not what you are, but what you are not, and that you are [Note: [Col. 1009] F has “in the manner in which you allow yourself to be understood, not what you are, but that you are.”] But you are not found in your superessentiality [Note: [Col. 1009] A has “in your always-essentiality”], by which you pass beyond and surpass every understanding that wishes to comprehend you and ascends toward you.

Thus you minister your presence to your own in a certain ineffable manner of appearance; you pass beyond them through the incomprehensible loftiness and infinity of your essence.

Therefore I ask that we hasten to consider the special returns, so that we may establish the limit of our discussion in this matter. We should not linger longer over points repeated in various ways for the sake of clearer persuasion, lest we appear to have filled our discussion more with words than with understanding [Note: [Col. 1011] A omits “with understanding.”]

**TEACHER.** The Lord himself compared the whole of rational creation—which was specially created in the human being and which naturally possesses a desire for blessedness and the capacity to know the highest Good, namely the most exalted Trinity, from which every good proceeds—to the ten virgins in the Gospel. They took their lamps, that is, the capacity to know the eternal light, and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride, namely Christ and the Church, which is already in heaven, partly in the holy angels and partly in the most purified souls of human beings. In these, the first fruits of human nature [Note: [Col. 1011] A omits “of human nature.”], which is still in captivity, are incorporated among the citizens of the heavenly homeland.

But why did they go out to meet him? Because the Redeemer and bridegroom of rational nature, through the ineffable condescension and care of his mercy, continually comes spiritually to receive us, while heavenly powers and holy souls, moved by concern for our salvation, pass to and fro in his service.

That bridegroom cries universally in the ear of the heart of the whole human race, saying:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.”

He therefore comes with his bride to meet everyone, namely with the heavenly Jerusalem, since he is devoted to receiving all into fellowship with his city.

And observe that all humanity is compared with the number ten, because it possesses the tenth region in the building of the heavenly city. The ten virgins, that is, the whole multitude of human nature, go out to meet him who loves them and comes to them through natural desire—not with bodily steps, but with the affections of the mind.

Yet although the movement of rational nature toward its end, which is Christ, is equal, and although the desire for eternal light, signified by the lamps, is equal, not all equally participate in that light which enlightens every human being coming into this world. For, as blessed Dionysius the Areopagite says, there is one thing which all naturally desire to participate in, but not all participate equally in that one thing.

Nevertheless, nothing in the nature of things is wholly deprived of participation in it. Therefore the virgins will not go out equally to meet the bridegroom and the bride [Note: [Col. 1011] A omits “to meet them.”] Those who possess not only the capacity for the true light but also the light itself, which is represented by the oil, will reach the bridegroom himself and enter spiritual marriage with him.

But those who possess only the capacity for light, and are not themselves illuminated and adorned by the light [Note: [Col. 1011] A has “crowned.”], will proceed to meet Christ. That is, they will ascend not merely through their naturally implanted desire [Note: [Col. 1011] A has “not merely naturally in their own [desire].”], but in reality and through experience, to the merely natural goods of humanity which subsist in Christ [Note: [Col. 1011] A has “ascend.”]; yet they will not attain to the supernatural grace and joy of deification in him.

This is what the division of the number ten suggests. For he says:

“Five of them were foolish,” that is, imprudent, “and five were wise.” The foolish took only their lamps and did not take oil with them; but the wise took not only their lamps, but also oil in their lamps.

The vessels of the wise and foolish virgins are therefore alike, because reason, which is like the seat of the natural divine light, has been distributed uniformly to the integrity—so to speak, the virginity—of incorruptible nature, which is increased or diminished in no one [Note: [Col. 1011] A has “which increases or diminishes”], although it does not receive the divine light uniformly [Note: [Col. 1011] A has “although.”].

This does not arise from any fault, envy, or poverty of the light, because it is present to all, shines above all equally, and flows forth upon all with inexhaustible outpouring equally. Rather, because the eyes by which the light of minds is perceived do not possess the same power, it follows that some enjoy it more, others less, and others are wholly excluded from it.

So it is with unclean spirits, which do not wish to turn toward it. This is not because they too, according to the intellectual substance in which they were created by the highest Good, are excluded from participation in truly existing light—for otherwise they would be reduced utterly to nothing; for nothing wholly deprived of participation in it exists at all in the nature of things. But insofar as they are defiled by the irrational movements of their perverse will, they are excluded from participation in the true light. For they turn not toward it, but toward themselves, that is, toward their own wickedness.

If they looked toward their own nature and toward its Creator, they would certainly become blessed.

And if someone says, “Why is the possibility of beholding the divine light not given equally to the whole of rational nature, while the power and activity of beholding it are not given equally [Note: [Col. 1011] F omits “is not given equally”], whether in this life or in the future [Note: [Col. 1011] A has “whether in the future life.”]?” let him ask the one who, struck with amazement and beaten back by inaccessible light, cries out:

“O the depth of the riches of the knowledge and wisdom of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways at all times! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? And who first gave to him, that he should be repaid? For from him, through him, in him, and toward him are all things.”

Let him also ask why the giver of all good things has not distributed the power of contemplation equally among all the orders of angels. The Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones contemplate him more deeply, clearly, and closely than the Virtues, Powers, and Dominions; and these, in turn, contemplate him more excellently and clearly than the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels.

And who will answer this question? No one, except one who considers within himself what is written: “God made all things in measure and number and weight,” that is, in order.

And what beauty would there be in the universe created by God if God established everything equally? For even the sweetness and beauty of sensible harmony are ordered not from similar sounds, but from different sounds joined together in measured proportions.

Let him also propose this question: if the first human being had not sinned, through whose punishment the human race is multiplied by male and female—and if human beings were not propagated through male and female, but all human beings emerged simultaneously from the innermost wombs of nature into their proper forms and numbers, just as all the angels emerged simultaneously from their causes; or if, in an established order of times, each person came into this world without corruption and without the likeness of the generation of animals—would all human beings have been equal and of the same power and order, or, just as angels are arranged in their orders, would human beings likewise have been disposed according to different orders in accordance with divine providence and wisdom?

I believe the one who promises human beings after the resurrection that “they will be like the angels in heaven” will answer him. Angels, however, are arranged in their proper orders; human beings, therefore, will also be arranged in different orders of virtues.

But if they are to be this way, even after sin, they surely would have been so.
