if they did not sin—that is, if they did not enjoy the contemplation of truth in the same manner. Moreover [Note: [Col. 1013] A omits “if” (*si*).], if the first human being, as Saint Augustine says, in his original condition, before he sinned, was neither wise nor foolish—for if he had been wise, he would not have abandoned God by consenting to his wife, nor would he have acted incautiously by imitating the pride of the devil’s cunning; for he was not deceived but puffed up by pride; but if he was foolish, who would believe that God made a foolish human being in his own image and likeness?—then surely he was created poised in a certain mean between wisdom and foolishness, and he was destined to become wise if he kept God’s command. For Scripture does not say, “Let us make the human being our image and likeness,” [Note: [Col. 1013] F reads *Scriptura ait* (“Scripture says”).] but “according to our image and likeness.” It is as though it plainly said: “Let us make the human being for this purpose, so that, if he keeps our commandment, he may become our image and likeness.” [Note: [Col. 1013] F reads *hominem faciamus* (“the human being let us make”), rather than the main text’s *Faciamus hominem*.] Thus he was not made wise, but capable—if he so willed—of wisdom. For he could receive wisdom and attain to its possession [Note: [Col. 1013] A reads *eius habitum* (“its possession”), for the main text’s *habitum ejus*.], if he had not wished to despise the divine counsel.

But because he did not raise himself upward toward wisdom by keeping the commandment, but, through its transgression [Note: [Col. 1013] A reads *eius per transgressionem* (“through his transgression”), for the main text’s *per ejus transgressionem*.], fell headlong by his own will into desire for temporal and sensible things, he must be judged more foolish and imprudent, even before he sinned, than desirous of wisdom and prudence; for foolishness and imprudence preceded the sin. Nor did he receive this from the causes of his creation, but from the mutability of his own will, which in no way arises from natural causes. He was therefore foolish and imprudent, having made himself so before the transgression of the commandment.

Nevertheless, if he had not transgressed the commandment, perhaps he would not have been expelled from paradise, but would have enjoyed only the natural goods that he had received in his original condition and rejoiced in them with a certain happiness, although, because of his folly and stupidity, he would rightly have been deprived of participation in supreme wisdom and prudence. For we see [Note: [Col. 1013] A reads “we hear” (*audimus*).] that many, indeed almost everyone who is heedless and foolish, are nevertheless [Note: [Col. 1013] A omits “nevertheless” (*tamen*).] cheerful and content with nobility of birth, numerous relatives, bodily dignity, strength and health, mental cleverness, graceful speech, a beautiful and well-mannered [Note: [Col. 1013] A reads *et morigera* (“and well-mannered”), for *morigeraque*.] wife, fruitful offspring, and an abundance of earthly goods—not to mention dignities [Note: [Col. 1013] A: “dignity”] and honors and all the other things with which this world smiles upon them—to such an extent that they would wish to live in this way forever, unwilling either to hear or to think about spiritual delights.

Thus it should not unreasonably be believed [Note: [Col. 1013] A reads *existimatur* (“is thought”), for *existimandum*.] that one part of the human race will return to the condition of the first human beings before their transgression—that is, to natural goods alone, without the adornment of virtues—being represented by the type of the five foolish virgins [Note: [Col. 1013] A reads *quippe virginum* (“indeed, of virgins”).]; while another part of the human multitude, represented by the number of the five prudent virgins, will be raised to that height to which the human being would have ascended by grace [Note: [Col. 1013] A omits “by grace”] if he had not sinned: namely, to participation in supreme wisdom and in all the virtues. This participation, I say, is followed by deification and contemplation of the truth.

The latter part will be exalted beyond all natural goods and will enter the spiritual marriage of its bridegroom [Note: [Col. 1013] A reads “into nature” (*in naturam*)]. No one is admitted to those nuptials unless he shines with the light of wisdom and burns with the flames of divine love. These two—I mean wisdom and charity—are nourished by the richness of knowledge and action. No one lacking knowledge and action is permitted to ascend to those nuptials, however fully and beautifully he may have flourished in natural goods; rather, he is altogether excluded from them. For it is not nature that lifts the human mind there, but grace, and obedience to God’s commandments; and, insofar as it is granted in this life, merit arising from the purest [Note: [Col. 1013] A reads *purissimae*.] knowledge of God through Scripture and creation [Col. 1014D] carries it upward.

Consider, then, the inner meaning of this parable, and how it passes from genus to species [Note: [Col. 1013] F reads *de genere facit ad speciem* (“it makes a passage from genus to species”).], just as in the previously mentioned parable of the two sons dividing their father’s substance between them. In that parable, the general return of the entire human race is first represented, and then the particular return of the Gentile people. In this one, similarly [Note: [Col. 1013] A reads “in similitude” (*similitudine*).], the ten virgins going out to meet the bridegroom represent the general return of the whole human multitude to its former natural condition; while the particular return of all the saints is represented by the five prudent virgins. For the number of the elect is the species of the human race.

Therefore [Note: [Col. 1015] A omits “therefore” (*igitur*).], not only is a return to the ancient beginning of nature, that is, to the primordial condition, intimated in the universality of humanity, but in the particularity of deification an ascent beyond nature into God himself is also intimated. All, indeed, will return to paradise, as we have said, but not all will enjoy the tree of life—or, certainly, all will receive something from the tree of life [Note: [Col. 1015] A omits “from” (*de*).], but not equally. For who, except a fool, does not know that the natural goods of which all will participate equally are the fruit of the tree of life? Πᾶν ξύλον, as we discussed above—that is, “every tree”—is called Christ; for he is the fruitful tree of every good, because he himself is every good and the giver of every good.

Thus all human beings will generally enjoy his fruit through participation in natural goods; while his elect will specially enjoy the exaltedness of deifications beyond all nature. The deifications, therefore, in which only the righteous will participate are symbolized by the spiritual nuptials into which the prudent virgins entered [Note: [Col. 1015] A omits “virgins”]. For not all will enjoy supernatural goods, but only those to whom, as Gregory the Theologian says, it is permitted—having overcome matter [Note: [Col. 1015] A reads “malice” (*malitia*).] and the flesh, as though they had passed beyond certain clouds and veils—to become united with God through reason and contemplation and to be held by the purest light [Note: [Col. 1015] A reads *purissime* (“most purely”).], insofar as this is possible for human nature. These are the blessed: blessed here through ascent, and there through deification.

But the use of this word—I mean “deification”—is exceedingly rare in Latin books, although we find its meaning among many writers, and especially in Ambrose. Why this has happened is not sufficiently clear to us. Perhaps [Note: [Col. 1015] A omits “because” (*quia*).] it is because the meaning of the word itself, *theosis*, which the Greeks use especially, signifies the passage of the saints into God, not only in soul but also in body, so that they may be one in him and with him, when nothing animal, nothing corporeal, nothing human, nothing natural [Note: [Col. 1015] A omits “nothing human, nothing natural”] will remain in them. This may have appeared too lofty [Note: [Col. 1015] A reads *casus* (“a fall”).], and incomprehensible and incredible to those unable to rise beyond carnal thoughts, and therefore not something to be publicly proclaimed. But it should be discussed among the wise. For many divine mysteries have been passed over untouched by the holy Fathers for this reason: weak eyes cannot endure the brightness of the light.

These few examples, taken from divine parables, are sufficient, I think, to establish the general and particular return of the human race to its own beginning—I mean its primordial condition—and into God himself, in those who are worthy to enjoy his most sincere participation. They also establish the return of the whole sensible creation, which was fashioned in the human being and for the human being, to its causes. Then there will be not only a general Sabbath in all the divine works, but also a particular Sabbath of Sabbaths in the holy angels and holy human beings. The house of God will be filled, and each person will be established in an order suited to him [Note: [Col. 1015] A reads *constituitur* (“is established”), for *constituetur*]:  some lower, others higher; some in the exaltedness of nature, others above every natural virtue, around God himself.

And so that great supper will be arranged and celebrated. From it no substance will be rejected, because it was made by God; no vice will be admitted, because it was not made by God. Nature will be purified, vice will be winnowed away, substantial grains will be stored up, the flame of the divine judgment will burn the straw of sins, the hidden things of darkness will be illuminated, and God will be seen in all things.

DISCIPLE. These things are certainly sufficient; but I ask you briefly to explain what remains of this parable.

TEACHER. What are those things?

DISCIPLE. The bridegroom’s delay, the sleep and drowsiness of all the virgins, and the other matters that you left untouched.

TEACHER. The bridegroom’s delay is, as I think, the temporal interval that passes between the Lord’s first and second coming; or certainly the interval from the beginning of the world to its end. For during the six ages of the world, no time has passed or will pass in which virginity—that is, the integrity of human nature, which is corrupted in no one, although it has been defiled in everyone except Christ [Note: [Col. 1015] A omits “which is corrupted in no one … does not wish to rise to meet [its bridegroom].”]—does not wish to rise to meet its bridegroom: in some foolishly, in others prudently, but in all desiring its creator and the heavenly homeland that it had abandoned. For the desire for blessedness is present commonly and naturally in all, wise and foolish, good and evil alike.

During the aforementioned interval of the world’s course, some sleep through the ordered succession of times, while others are drowsy. Those sleep who have already died and those who will yet die; but those are said to be drowsy whom the end of the world will find alive in the flesh. They are said not to sleep but to be drowsy because they will not die a complete death, nor will they be held in it for any temporal interval [Note: [Col. 1015] A reads *nullo vero* (“but by no”).]. Rather, like people weighed down by sleep but not overthrown by it, they will be changed into another life without death intervening.

At this point [Note: [Col. 1015] A reads “may seem” (*videatur*).] Saint Augustine seems to agree with those who say that a very brief death will occur in the exceedingly swift rapture of those who will be alive at the end of the world. For in the twentieth book, chapter twenty-one, of *The City of God*, he says:

“If we believe that the saints who will be found alive when Christ comes and will be caught up to meet him will, in that very rapture, depart from mortal bodies and immediately return to those same bodies made immortal, we will encounter no difficulty in the Apostle’s words—whether where he says, ‘What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies’ [Note: [Col. 1015] A omits “first”]; or where he says, ‘We shall all rise again, or we shall all sleep’—because even they will not be made alive through immortality unless they first die, however briefly, and therefore they will not be excluded from the resurrection, which they precede by sleep, although that sleep will be exceedingly brief, yet not nonexistent.”

The midnight at which the cry was made and the bridegroom came signifies the uncertain end of the world and the spiritual bridegroom’s advent, removed from all knowledge [Note: [Col. 1017] F: “from the knowledge of all,”] just as he himself said: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son of Man, but the Father alone.” And at the end of the present parable: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

That cry signifies the very clear signs that will precede the destruction of the world and the Lord’s coming, concerning which he prophesied to his disciples while sitting on the Mount of Olives. The rising of all the virgins foretells the regeneration of the entire human race.

The prudent virgins adorn their lamps—that is, their rational movements—with the richness of good action and the brightness of a pure conscience. The foolish virgins lack these two things, namely action and knowledge. As for the fact that the prudent virgins refuse to share their oil with the foolish virgins, nothing else is more plausibly represented typologically, in my opinion, than this: prudent souls whose merits will appear, on that intellectual day when each person will search the depths of his own conscience, to be paltry and insufficient, and in no way comparable with eternal blessedness, cannot share them with the foolish. As the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us.”

Hence the Lord himself says: “Blessed are the poor,” he says, “in spirit”—that is, blessed are those who count both themselves and their merits as nothing and judge themselves altogether poor in the riches of virtues, “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

For this reason they will say to those asking their assistance, “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you.” This can be understood in two ways: either *ne* is used negatively and lengthened, or hesitantly and shortened, as in the Book of Genesis: “Lest he perhaps stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life.”

And lest they seem unwilling, through some envy, to share their poverty of merits with the foolish by refusing them their oil, they give advice, replying: “Go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves”—that is, go to those who, through the excellence and abundance of their merits, are sufficient not only for themselves but could also provide assistance, and the merit of future blessedness, to those who were able to honor them in this life.

After this delay and negligence have intervened, the bridegroom comes and takes by surprise the virgins who were ready and adorned at his coming, and introduces them into his nuptials—that is, into his deification, by which he glorifies the most perfect souls through the supernatural grace [Note: [Col. 1017] A: “glory”] of his contemplation—while leaving the others in the fullness of natural goods and excluding them from the exaltedness of ineffable deification, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.”

And this is what he says: “And the door was shut”—namely, the entrance into divine contemplation face to face [Note: [Col. 1017] A: “divine face-to-face contemplation”]. Those who live incautiously in this life and do not pour the oil of action and knowledge into the receptacles of their reason will not enter, even if they cry out [Note: [Col. 1017] F reads “cried out” (*clamaverunt*).], once they have at last been pierced by tardy repentance: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” [Col. 1018A]

This doubling of the Lord’s name signifies either the constant desire of human nature for contemplation of its creator, without any cloud of ignorance intervening, among those who have lived in this life without the support of any good conduct; or, alternatively, it signifies the sluggishness of simple believers who consider insufficiently [Note: [Col. 1017] A: “excessively”] the height of the catholic faith. They think that our Lord Jesus Christ is composed of two substances, whereas he is one substance in two natures, and they ask for what does not befit them. Therefore the answer is given [Note: [Col. 1017] A reads “will be given” (*respondebitur*).] to them: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly.”

How many are there who either utterly fail to understand or utterly deny that the divine essence is in three substances and the three substances in one essence, yet, through their false thoughts and carnal opinions [Note: [Col. 1017] A: “of carnal opinion”], ask to enter the nuptials of inward and pure divine contemplation? How many are there who so separate the Lord Jesus Christ that they neither believe nor understand that his divinity has been united to his humanity, and his humanity to his divinity, in the unity of substance—or, as the Latins more commonly say, in the unity of person—when his humanity and divinity are one and inseparably one [Note: [Col. 1017] A omits “and inseparably one”], while the proper character of each of his natures remains intact [Note: [Col. 1017] A: “its significance”]?

Thus, when they double Christ’s substance and say, “Lord, Lord, open to us,” the just and fitting [Note: [Col. 1017] A reads “fittingly” (*congruenterque*).] reply is made: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you.” That is: “I will not permit you to know the inward and secret nuptials of my divinity and humanity, which I prepared for those who understand me most purely before the world was made, and into which, once the world had ended, I introduced them. For while you were still living in the flesh, you did not prepare yourselves as worthy of their joy. Nevertheless, I permit you to remain within the limits of the natural goods that I created in you.”

Similarly, he promises that he will answer those who on the day of judgment cry out: “Lord, Lord, did we not perform many mighty works in your name?” For it will be said to them: “I do not know you; depart from me.” And elsewhere: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

The Word united to flesh, and flesh united to the Word, in the inseparable unity of one and the same substance from two natures—divine and human—receives no others except those who, with the simple eye of perfect contemplation, behold the unity of his substance. Thus the human being in the Word is truly the Son of God, and the Word in the human being is truly the Son of Man; and our Lord Jesus Christ is understood to be one and the same Son of God and of humanity, without any alteration of the natures [Note: [Col. 1017] A: “of the creatures”].

You have here, according to what seemed to us, a brief and plausible explanation of the parable.

DISCIPLE. Indeed I have [Note: [Col. 1017] A: “Certainly”].

TEACHER. What, then, remains, and prevents us from bringing the work to its conclusion?

DISCIPLE. I see nothing [Note: [Col. 1017] A: “as I see it”], except that you should offer a brief ἀνακεφαλαίωσις—a recapitulation—of the subject matter of the entire work, namely, the division of universal nature.

### 39. MASTER

We have made a fourfold division of universal nature, understood as existing in God and in creation. Its first species is that which considers nature as creating and uncreated; the second, nature as both created and creating; the third, nature as created and not creating; the fourth, nature as neither created nor creating. The first and fourth forms are predicated of God alone—not because his nature, which is simple and more than simple, is divisible, but because it admits the mode of a twofold contemplation.

For when I contemplate him as the being who is the principle and cause of all things, there comes before me a true account which confidently suggests that the divine essence—or substance, goodness, power, wisdom, and whatever else is predicated of God—is created by no one, since nothing precedes the divine nature. All things, both those that are and those that are not, are created by it, through it, in it, and toward it.

But when I perceive that this same nature is the inviolable end and limit of all things, which all desire and in which they establish the boundary of their natural motion, I find that it is neither created nor creating. For no one can create the nature that exists from itself. Nor does it create anything. Since all things that have proceeded from it through intelligible or sensible generation will return to it through a marvelous and ineffable regeneration, and all things will be at rest in it, because nothing further will flow forth from it through generation, it is said not to create. For what will it create when it itself is all things in all things and appears as nothing but itself?

Enough has already been said above about the two middle forms; they present themselves, surrounded by clear light, to those who seek them readily. One is discerned in primordial causes, the other in the effects of causes. That which is established in the causes is created in the only-begotten Son of God, in whom and through whom all things were made, and it creates all things that flow forth from it—that is, all its effects, whether intelligible or sensible. But that which is established in the effects of causes is created only by its causes and creates nothing, because nothing in the nature of things is lower than it; and therefore it is chiefly ordered in sensible things.

Nor is it an objection that angels or human beings, whether good or evil, are often thought to create something new and unknown to human uses in this world. They create nothing; rather, from the material creation made by God, they produce something within the effects through causes, obeying divine laws and commands if they are good; but, if they are evil, moved and deceived by the deceptive contrivances of diabolical cunning. Yet all things are ordered by divine providence, so that no evil is found substantially in the nature of things, nor anything that disturbs the public and civic order of all things.

After the fourfold theory of universal nature in the four species mentioned above—two of which we contemplated in the divine nature, by reason of principle and end, and two in created nature, by reason of causes and effects—it seemed appropriate to append certain theories concerning the return of effects into their causes, that is, into the principles in which they subsist.

A threefold mode of this return presented itself. The first is considered generally in the transformation of the whole sensible creation contained within the compass of this world—that is, of all bodies, whether they are subject to bodily senses or escape them because of their excessive subtlety. Thus there is no body within the fabric of corporeal nature, whether nourished solely by vital motion, secretly or openly, or endowed with irrational soul and bodily sensation, that does not return to its hidden causes through the midpoint of its life; for nothing will be reduced to nothing among those things that have been substantially established by the cause of all things.

[Note: At Col. 1019, A reads *processerint* (“will have proceeded”) for *processerunt* (“have proceeded”); *profluit* (“flows forth”) for *profluet* (“will flow forth”); and omits *enim* (“for”). A also reads *causas occultas* (“hidden causes”) in reversed order, omits “through the midpoint of its life,” and omits the second *nihil* (“nothing”) in “nothing will be reduced to nothing.”]

The second mode of this contemplation has its place in the general return of the whole human nature saved in Christ to the original state of its creation, as it were to a paradise, to the dignity of the divine image, through the merit of the one whose blood was poured out in common for the salvation of the whole human race. Thus no human being will be deprived of the natural goods in which he was created, whether he has lived well or badly in this life. And so the ineffable and incomprehensible diffusion of divine goodness and generosity will appear throughout the whole of human nature, since no one is punished for that which proceeds from the highest good.

The third mode of the theory of return concerns those who will not only ascend into the sublimity of the nature established in them, but will also, through the abundance of divine grace that will be given through Christ and in Christ to his elect, pass beyond all the laws and limits of nature, superessentially into God himself, and become one in him and with him.

Their return is distinguished, as it were, through seven stages. The first will be the transformation of the earthly body into vital motion; the second, of vital motion into sensation; the third, of sensation into reason; then of reason into the mind, in which the end of the whole rational creation is established.

After this fivefold union, as it were, of the parts of our nature—body, vital motion, sensation, reason, and intellect—so that they are not five but one, the lower parts always being perfected by the higher, not so that they cease to be but so that they may be one, there will follow three further stages of ascent.

[Note: At Col. 1019, A reads *post* (“after”) in place of *per* (“through”) in “as it were through seven stages”; *quinque* (“five”) for *quinariam* (“fivefold”), while F reads *quinu*, an uncertain defective form; and *veluti quinque* (“as though five”) for *veluti* (“as it were”).]

The first of these is the passage of the mind into knowledge of all things that exist after God; the second, of knowledge into wisdom—that is, into intimate contemplation of truth, so far as this is granted to a creature; the third, and highest, is the supernatural sinking of the most purified minds into God himself, and, as it were, into the darkness of the incomprehensible and inaccessible light in which the causes of all things are hidden. Then night will be illuminated like day—that is, the most secret divine mysteries will be opened in an ineffable manner to blessed and illuminated intellects.

[Note: At Col. 1021, F reads *tenebras* (“darknesses”) for *tenebrae* (“darkness”); A omits *divina* (“divine”).]

Then the most perfect solidity of the octonary number, as it were a supernatural cube, will be completed. In its figure the sixth psalm is entitled, “A Psalm of David for the octave.” The Lord’s resurrection also took place on the eighth day for no other reason than that the blessed life which is to follow, after the sevenfold revolution of this life through the seven days, after the consummation of the world might be mystically signified. Then human nature, as we have said, will return to its principle through an eightfold ascent: fivefold within the limits of nature, and threefold supernaturally and superessentially within God himself. At that time the fivefold number of the creature will be united to the threefold number of the Creator, so that nothing appears except God alone, just as in the purest air nothing shines except light alone.

[Note: At Col. 1021, F reads *cybi* for *cubi* (“cube”); A reads *per* (“through”) for *pro* (“for”) in the Psalm title and omits *arridet* (“shines” or “greets the eye”).]

### 40.

This, then, is the universal subject matter of this work, which is contained in five books. If anyone should find that we have written something here that is still unknown or superfluous, let him attribute it to our lack of restraint and carelessness, and let the humble contemplator, with a pious heart, forgive the poverty of human understanding, still burdened by the dwelling-place of the flesh.

[Note: At Col. 1021, A omits *adhuc* (“still”), reads *atque* (“and”) for *aut* (“or”), and reads *indigentiae* (“need”) for *intelligentiae* (“understanding”).]

For, as I think, nothing is yet perfect in human studies in this shadowy life and entirely free from error. Even the just who are still living in the flesh are not called just because they are just, but because they wish to be just and desire the perfect justice that is to come; they are named from the inclination of the mind alone.

For I would not believe that anyone weighed down by mortal limbs and bodily senses—except Christ—has reached the perfect condition of virtue and the height of true contemplation, as the Evangelist John testifies: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” The Apostle likewise says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma”; and elsewhere: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part.”

[Note: At Col. 1021, A reads *quod* (“that”) for *quia* (“because”) in the Johannine quotation.]

But if anything useful and pertaining to the edification of the catholic faith should appear here, let him attribute it to God alone, who alone reveals the things hidden in darkness and brings those who seek him into himself, undeceived by any error but corrected from their errors. Let him join with us in giving thanks, in one spirit of love, to the universal cause of all good, without being drawn by any desire to criticize or inflamed by any torch of envy, which alone, more than the other vices, strives to break the bond of love and brotherhood.

[Note: At Col. 1021, F reads *aut ab erroribus* (“or from errors”) for *sed ab erroribus* (“but corrected from errors”); A reads *accensus* (“kindled”) for *succensus* (“inflamed”).]

Whether this work is kindly received by all who have peace concerning what has been completed among us and look upon it with a pure vision of mind, or whether it is rejected in hostility by those who pass judgment before they know what it is and of what kind, I offer it first of all to God, who said: “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you.” I then offer it to you, most beloved brother in Christ, Wulfade, both as a fellow-worker in the studies of wisdom and as the person to whom it is to be examined and entrusted for correction.

[Note: At Col. 1021, A omits *Wulfade*. The note at Col. 1021D reads *Ciuulfade* (“Ciuulfade,” thus). Petrus Alixius, on the testimony of Thomas Gale, had conjectured that Wulfade, canon of Reims and later bishop of Bourges, was intended. See *De divisione naturae*, Oxford, 1681, Appendix, p. 80.]

For it was begun at your exhortation and, whatever its quality, brought to completion through your skill. If you should be concerned about those things that, compelled by the weight of the subject and the abundance of matters requiring explanation, I omitted in the body of this work, and about which I promised that at some time I would give at least a brief account, and if you should act as an exactor of promises, when the work is resumed, all the promises having been found and gathered together, they will be treated briefly and chapter by chapter, as far as our strength permits.

[Note: At Col. 1021, A omits *operis* (“of the work”); reads *coacti praetermisimus* (“we, compelled, omitted”) for “I, compelled, omitted”; *nos reddituros promisimus* (“we promised that we would give”) for “I promised that I would give”; *solliciti eritis ac veluti promissorum exactores fueritis* (“you will be concerned and, as it were, exactors of promises”) for the singular; *curso* (“course”) for *recurso* (“resumed”); omits *omnibus* (“all”); and reads *pro viribus nostris tractabimus* (“we shall treat [them] according to our strength”).]

Meanwhile I beg readers to be content with what has already been discussed. Let them consider not the excellence of my little talent, which is either scarcely existent or nonexistent, but the capacity of my lowly yet devoted diligence concerning investigations of divine matters. May you strive to defend it, not less by the strength of your keenest understanding than by the labors of my dull contemplation, if not against rivals, at least among friends and seekers of truth.

[Note: At Col. 1021, A reads *vos contentos* (“you [to be] content”) for “readers [to be] content”; *ingenii* (“talent” or “intellect”) for *ingenioli* (“little talent”); *quae vix parva* (“which is scarcely small”) for “which is scarcely [anything]”; and *sed vestrae sollicitudinis meaeque* (“but [the capacity] of your diligence and mine”) for “but of my diligence.” F reads *devota* (“devoted,” feminine) for *devotae*; A omits *divinarum* (“divine”), reads *vestrae* (“your”) for *tuae* (“your,” singular), and omits *obtusae* (“dull”). A also omits *ut* (“so that”) and reads *debetis* (“you ought”) for *studeas* (“may you strive”).]

Nor, as I think, will you labor greatly in this. As soon as such things come into the hands of those who philosophize rightly, if they agree with their discussions, they will not only receive them willingly but will embrace them as their own. But if they fall among those who are readier to criticize than to sympathize, there is no great need to wrestle with them. Let each abound in his own opinion until that light comes which makes darkness out of the light of false philosophers and turns the darkness of those who know rightly into light.

[Note: At Col. 1021, A reads *laborabitis* (“you will labour,” plural) for the singular; *quoniam* (“since”) for *si* (“if”); *incurrent* (“will fall upon”) for *incurrerint* (“have fallen upon”); and *tenebras recognoscentium* (“the darkness of those who recognize”) for *tenebras recte cognoscentium* (“the darkness of those who know rightly”).]

Here ends the book *On the Division of Nature*—that is, *Peri physeōn merismou*, “On the Division of Nature.”

[Note: At Col. 1021, A reads: “The fifth book has ended.”]

[Col. 1023]

## A Fragment of John Scotus’s Book *On the Egress and Regress of the Soul to God*

Manuscript collection on parchment no. 596, quarto, of the library of Christina at Rome, folio 9. See Carl Greith, *Spicilegium Vaticanum*, Frauenfeld, 1838, p. 80 ff.

[Col. 1023A] [lacuna] They have the capacity to flow and not to stand. It was rightly called a game of God by the teacher, as though through these things he were leading us into those things that truly are and are in no way moved.

### Another Theory on the Same Subject

But if we ourselves, following the prevailing course of our present nature, are first born in the likeness of the other animals on earth, then become children, then die in youth, like the flower of the almond tree (*oximori*), when old age approaches in horror, and are transferred to another life, we have been called God’s game by that God-bearing teacher. Nor is this outside the sequence. Compared with the principal form of the future divine and true life, the present life is a game, and everything else, if anything more effective has been established concerning it, is likewise a game.

[Note: At Col. 1023, the corrected reading is *oximori*; the manuscript has *ocimori*, glossed “of the almond.” In an old German vocabulary, “almonds” is rendered *mandalnuz*. See Graff, *Diutiska*, II, p. 43.]

In his epitaph for his brother Caesarius, he himself shows this more plainly, saying:

> Such is our life, brothers, the life of those who live for a time, like a game on earth. We come into being from nonexistence and, having been made, are dissolved; we are an unstable dream, the flight of a passing bird, and still something farther beyond.

[Note: At Col. 1023, the manuscript reads *ephitaphio* for *epitaphio* and *sui*; perhaps *suum*.]

For, properly compared with the truth of the divine *prototypa*—that is, the principal exemplars—the arrangement of present and visible things will not be considered to exist at all by those who have been made worthy, so far as possible, to take the road toward the form of the divine beauty, just as a mockery is not universally judged to be comparable with any true and existing thing.

### Another Theory on the Same Subject

Perhaps, too, the mutable condition of the material things of which we speak—things which alter and are altered into another deprivation, and have no foundation except the first principle by which they are borne—is to be considered: they are wisely and providently borne; and, while we suppose that they are held by us, they escape us more than they are held, and suffer our desire to be fixed upon them—rather, they escape us ourselves, who, as repelled beings, can neither hold nor be held.

The measured definition of their nature [lacuna]

[Note: At Col. 1023, the manuscript reads *diffinitionem* for *definitionem*.]

[Col. 1023]

## TESTIMONIES

[Col. 1025]

### I. Letter of Pope Nicholas I to Charles the Bald concerning John Scotus, translator of the works of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, 861 or 862

From Naudé’s *Collectanea* from the Oxford Library [that is, Oxford or Oxomensis], published in Bulaeus, *Historia Universitatis Parisiensis*, vol. I, p. 184.

#### Nicholas, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, glorious king of the Franks

It greatly rejoices us that in your empire and kingdom, and especially at Paris, the studies of the liberal arts, established through the care of your predecessors, are flourishing anew; through their seeds the Church of God bears fruit and minds are strengthened for its defense.

But recently we were grieved, as has been reported to our apostolate, that the work of Dionysius the Areopagite, which he composed in Greek concerning the divine Names and the celestial Orders, has recently been translated into Latin by a certain man named John, a Scot by nationality. According to the custom of the Church, it ought to have been sent to us and approved by our judgment, especially since the same John is said to be a man of great learning, yet frequent rumor says that he does not think soundly in certain matters.

Therefore we earnestly request and command Your Belovedness to have the aforesaid John brought before our apostolate, or at least not permit him to remain at Paris in the School, of which he is said to have once been head, lest he be found mixing the tares and darnel of error with the grains of the sacred word, and offering poison to those who ask for bread. Given in the third year.

### II. Fragment of the Same Letter from the Decree of Ivo, Bishop of Chartres

Ivo of Chartres, *Decree*, part IV, chapter 104.

It has been reported to our apostolate that the work of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, which he composed in Greek concerning the divine Names and the celestial Orders, has recently been translated into Latin by a certain man named John, a Scot by race. According to custom, it ought to have been sent to us and approved by our judgment, especially since the same John, although he is said to possess great learning, was formerly said by frequent rumor not to think soundly in certain matters.

Therefore let your diligence supply what has hitherto been omitted and send us the aforesaid work without any delay, so that, once it has been approved by the judgment of our apostolate, it may be received by all with the greater favor on our authority.

### III. Letter of Anastasius, Librarian of the Holy Roman Church, to Charles the Bald concerning John Scotus, Translator of the Works of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite

Basel edition, 1503 | P

Usserius’s edition in *Sylloge of Irish Letters*, p. 45 | U

Florence Manuscript, Hut. LXXXIX, sup. 15, parchment, eleventh or twelfth century | J

Among the many studies to which both your praiseworthy action and your most salutary admonition—and even the fragrant report that flies abroad concerning the quality of your virtues and morals—rouse the minds of mortals and exhort them, as though to dig out wisdom like treasures, there is also this matter, which deserves no small astonishment: you do not cease to investigate not only the Latin Fathers but also the Greek, and you make those who are proficient in the Roman language not strangers to Pelasgian matters.

[Note: At Col. 1025, J adds *et* (“and”) before “the fragrant report”; P and U read *quantitate* (“quantity”) for *qualitate* (“quality”). J reads *ad effodiendum sapientiae* (“for digging out of wisdom”) and places *velut thesauros* (“like treasures”) after *hortatur*. J has *mediocri* (“moderate”) for *mediocriter* (“not moderately”), *in sermone* (“in language”) for *sermone* (“in language” or “by language”), and *perscrutatur* (“investigates”) for *perscrutatus* (“having investigated”).]

You do this by arousing and encouraging others to do it, because we too are often said to have built a great house—not with our hands, but with our words.

Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Athens, whom your distinguished industry has translated into the Roman tongue, most excellent of princes, is, as you yourself know more clearly, as difficult to understand as he is sublime in language. Indeed, the things he investigated, which are difficult to understand and lofty in their mysteries, he learned through the revelation of heavenly grace; and, entering the hidden things of theology under the guidance of the divine hand, he penetrated into the sanctuary of God after the veil had been removed.

[Note: At Col. 1025, J reads *princeps* (“prince”) for *principum* (“of princes”), *potentius* (“more powerfully”) for *patentius* (“more openly”), *in sermone* (“in language”) for *sermone*, and *perscrutatur* (“investigates”) for *perscrutatus* (“having investigated”).]

It is therefore wonderful that your piety has not left such matters unexamined but, although you walk here on earth, approaches them as though dwelling in heaven, so that you seem, if I may put it so, like some angel or heavenly man, to enter the Holy of Holies through contemplation, and you are believed to have approached, so far as is possible for mortals, the hidden and innermost places of the divine ineffability with the keen sight of spiritual eyes.

[Note: At Col. 1027, J reads *ergo* (“therefore”) for *igitur* (“therefore”), *in terris ambulet* (“walks on earth”) for “walks here on earth,” and *adit* (“approaches” or “enters”) for *ambit* (“goes around” or “seeks”). J reads *accepisse* (“to have received”) for *accessisse* (“to have approached”).]

It is also wonderful how that barbarian man, placed at the ends of the world, could have grasped such things intellectually and transferred them into another language—he who could be believed to be as far removed from the speech of other peoples as he was from them in manner of life. I mean John Scotigena, a man whom I have learned by hearsay to be holy in every respect.

[Note: At Col. 1027, J reverses the phrase as *ille vir barbarus, ille qui* (“that barbarian man, that man who”), reads *voluerit* (“wished”) for *valuerit* (“was able”), *quantum* (“how great”) for *quem* (“whom”), and *sacrum* (“sacred”) for *sanctum* (“holy”).]

But that craftsman, the Spirit, accomplished this; he made him at once ardent and eloquent. For unless he had burned with the fire of charity through the Spirit’s grace, he would certainly not have received the gift of speaking in languages. For master Charity taught him what he accomplished for the instruction and edification of many.

[Note: At Col. 1027, J reads *facit* (“makes”) for *fecit* (“made”) and *paravit* (“prepared”) for *patravit* (“accomplished”).]

Yet although the Spirit was given to him according to measure, he himself, instructed by the teachings of the Fathers, did what he could and tried beyond his strength to benefit his neighbors. Indeed, apart from those matters that are shown to have been hidden from him by what we find scattered among various interpretations previously made by certain people from the sermons and letters of the aforesaid Father, he greatly diminished the usefulness of the work because he took such pains to draw word out of word—a kind of interpretation that, although I myself often follow it, your discerning experience certainly knows is avoided by distinguished interpreters.

[Note: At Col. 1027, J reads *plurimum* (“for the most part”) where the text has *plerumque* (“often”). P and U read *verbum de verbo* (“word from word”) for *verbum e verbo* (“word out of word”); U reads *dicere* (“to say”) for *elicere* (“to draw out”).]

I think that he did this for no other reason than that, being humble in spirit, he did not presume to abandon the exactness of the word, lest he should in any way fall away from the truth of the meaning. Consequently, a man so great, who on his own had resolved to search out the innermost and most difficult recesses of both philosophies, and who already seemed perplexing to our understanding, he entangled within the difficulties of a labyrinth and placed him, in a certain sense, still deeper in invisible caves; and the man whom he had undertaken to interpret, he rendered still in need of interpretation.

[Note: At Col. 1027, U reads *quia* (“because”) for *quoniam* (“since”); J reads *caderet* (“fall”) for *decideret* (“fall away”), and *ceperat* (“had undertaken”) for *susceperat* (“had taken up”).]

For this reason I, rightly anxious, began diligently to seek whether some teacher or some writing might perhaps be found that would make so great a Father shine more clearly for us by explaining him, and, since he had already been delivered into our language through the translator’s industry, would also render him more fully open to our understanding. Then suddenly scholia, or marginal notes, on this work—which I had seen while staying at Constantinople—came into my hands. When I had translated them, however imperfectly, they made certain matters shine somewhat more clearly for me.

These notes, which I found in the margins of the Greek copy, I inserted into the translated codex with corresponding signs, after translating them as best I could until they might be translated better by a learned man. I judged that they ought especially to be sent to your glorious wisdom, since you, who had encouraged and assisted the other translation, might fittingly also receive and approve this one, whatever its quality.

[Note: At Col. 1027, U omits *quoque* (“also”); P reads *nostrisque* (“and to ours”), and P and U read *patulis* (“open,” plural) for J’s *patulus* (“open,” singular). J has *parathesis* (“marginal annotation,” singular) for *paratheses* (“marginal annotations”), *interpretentur* (“may be translated”) for “might be translated,” and *religiosae* (“religious”) for *gloriosae* (“glorious”).]

The scholia, or marginal notes, that have the sign of the life-giving cross at the end are said to have been composed by blessed Maximus the Confessor and monk; the rest are said to belong to Saint John, bishop of Scythopolis.

[Note: At Col. 1027, J describes Maximus as *beato ac monacho maximo confessore* (“blessed and monastic greatest confessor”), reads *seu* (“or”) for *sive* (“or”), and has *antistitis* (“prelate”) for *episcopi* (“bishop”). P and U spell Scythopolis *Sycopolitani*.]

Whenever I saw that the scholia themselves differed from the translator’s words, I inserted the translator’s words into the scholion and indicated how the composer of the scholion had preferred them, so that the reader might easily recognize what the translator understood by the expression that had been added and what the scholion implied. Wherever I saw that it would be useful, I also inserted a very few remarks of my own, since it could not be otherwise, and such as an intelligent reader could more easily recognize.

[Note: At Col. 1027, J reads *indifficiliter* (“without difficulty”) for *indifficulter*; *inspexi* (“examined”) for *conspexi* (“saw”); *aliter esse* (“to be otherwise”) for *esse aliter*; and *possunt* (“can”) where P has *poterunt* (“will be able”) and the text has *poterant* (“could”).]

It should further be noted that, although this holy Dionysius was a man of such glory, learning, and antiquity, he never—unless I am mistaken—published any of the works which the written tradition of the orthodox reports before the Roman pontiffs—namely Gregory, Martin, and Agatho—mentioned his statements in their written works and admitted them after judging them credible.

[Note: At Col. 1027, J has *quia* (“because”) for *quod* (“that”), *seu* for *sive*, *ni fallor* (“if I am not mistaken”), and *Gregorius videlicet* (“Gregory, namely”); it omits *in* (“in”) and changes *fecerint* (“have made”) to *fecerunt* (“made”), and *admiserint* (“have admitted”) to *admiserunt* (“admitted”).]

Gregory did so in his homily on the Gospel passage concerning the hundred sheep and the ten drachmas; Martin in the synod that he held at Rome against the heretics; and Agatho in the letter that he sent to the Sixth Synod.

[Note: At Col. 1027–1029, J reads *Evangelii* (“of the Gospel”) for *evangelici* (“Gospel [passage]”).]

From this I infer that the opinion of the Greeks is true: they say that his books were concealed by earlier heretics until, after a long period, the single codex that is now possessed was found at Rome from his works, and, since the others had not yet been discovered, was carried away to Greece. For he himself indicates that he published other books as well, which neither any Greek nor any Latin has yet been able to find.

[Note: At Col. 1027–1029, U reads *prohibentium* (“forbidding”) for *perhibentium* (“reporting”), and J reads *meminit* (“mentions”) for *innuit* (“indicates”).]

Luke in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 17:34), Eusebius Pamphilus, and Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, certainly transmit some remarkable things about him; but, unless forgetfulness deceives me, they do not transmit what he wrote.

[Note: At Col. 1029, J has *Corinthiorum* (“of the Corinthians”) for *Corinthi* (“of Corinth”); P and U read *scripsit* (“wrote”) for *scripserit* (“may have written”); J omits *ita* (“thus”) and reads *et* (“and”) for *etiam* (“also”).]

This is also supported by the fact that none of the reputable commentators—as is their custom, to excerpt the sayings of earlier writers and insert them into their own works—uses his writings or recalls any of them.

[Note: At Col. 1029, P and U read *exponendi* (“expounding”) for *excerpendi* (“excerpting”).]

Finally, the great man and teacher of apostolic life, Constantine the Philosopher, who came to Rome under Pope Hadrian the Younger of venerable memory and restored the body of Saint Clement to his see, and who had often commended the entire codex of the Father so frequently mentioned and to be mentioned, and commended to his hearers whatever usefulness its marrow possessed, used to say that, if our holy predecessors and teachers, who scarcely and in a certain manner decapitated the heretics with a club, had happened to possess Dionysius, they would undoubtedly have slaughtered them with a sharp sword.

[Note: At Col. 1029, U reads *apostolicae sedis praeceptor* (“teacher of the apostolic see”) for *apostolicae vitae praeceptor* (“teacher of apostolic life”); P and U read *commendabat* (“was commending”) for *commendaverat* (“had commended”); J reads *habeat* (“has”) for *habebat* (“had”) and *quia* (“that” or “because”) for *quod* (“that”). U omits *quosque* (“whomsoever”), while P has *quos* (“whom”). The text’s *decollaverunt* means “they decapitated”; the variant *decollaverint* means “they may have decapitated.” J moves *procul dubio* (“without doubt”) before *gladio* (“with a sword”).]

By this saying he evidently meant that those whose mouths they had closed only with difficulty and perhaps slowly would have forced into silence more easily and sharply—or more swiftly—for *oxys* (ὀξύ) means “sharp” and “swift.”

[Note: At Col. 1029, J reads *haec dicens* (“saying these things”) for *hujusmodi dicto* (“by a saying of this kind”) and *signat* (“signifies”) for *significat* (“means”).]

But after the memory of the holy prelates of the apostolic see, both the holy Seventh and Eighth Synods and Latin and Greek teachers not only indicate that this venerable Father wrote, but frequently draw testimonies from his writings, so that they may make their own meanings and statements heavy with the authority of so great a man and equally worthy of approval and observance by all mortals.

[Note: At Col. 1029, P and U read *At nec* (“but not”) and *Ac* (“and”) for *At vero* (“but indeed”); they omit *sanctae* (“holy”). J reads *scripsit* (“wrote”) and *innuit* (“indicates”) for the subjunctives *scripserit* and *innuunt*, and *scriptis* (“writings”) for *scripturis* (“scriptures” or “writings”). J has *consectanda* (“to be pursued”) for *sectanda* (“to be followed”).]

May almighty God at some time transfer your glory from earthly things to the heavenly kingdom. Here ends the work. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction.

## John Scotus’s Translation of the Works of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite: Preface

[Col. 1029A]

This draught, stuffed with the sacred nectar of the Greeks,

John, a stranger, *spondō*—Greek σπένδω, “I pour a libation”—to my Charles.

To the greatest of the Franks, whose royal emblems shine,

May the gifts of your vow-bearing servant be pleasing to you.

You who do not know how to disdain Roman arts—Greek τέχνας, “arts”—

May it not displease you to undertake Attic exercises.

If some spark of them gleams through me,

Look upon it, if you please, for Ausonian uses.

If it is not troublesome to strengthen our labor,

Let it be confirmed by the weight of your judgment.

If anything knotted or harsh is noticed in it,

Spare me, descendant of Cecrops; I follow Attic weapons.

[Col. 1030A]

But if it strays from the straight path,

Correct it with your honey-flowing speech.

And if it is bitten by the fierce tooth of certain people,

This is a small matter; for the same happened to my Jerome.

But, so that it may remain stable on a firm foundation,

It will be enough to fasten it with a royal *stathmos*—Greek σταθμῷ, “standard,” “weight,” or “authority.”

I would believe that many who touch the summit of wisdom

Will not despise our little gifts,

But will try to gather the fruit of heavy toil;

Perhaps humble words contain strength.

Flowers often grow fragrant among thorns;

A fruitful grape is gathered from a knotted vine.

Very admirable indeed, and worthy of being magnified by praises of virtue, is the most devout solicitude of Catholic men who, although they seem to be harassed by the perilous hardships of human life, nevertheless, with their minds’ attention fixed, purified by laborious investigations of divine matters, illumined by fruitful discoveries, and perfected by perpetual and immutable contemplations of truth and divine love, must be judged not to dwell among mortals but to have been wholly transformed into a heavenly way of life. 

That you are numbered among such men, most pious and most glorious of kings, no one who rightly observes your affections can doubt, since, battered by the greatest and continual disturbances of civil and more-than-civil wars, and moreover by the barbarous incursions of pagan peoples invading the Christian kingdom everywhere, you have nevertheless not been cast down from the steadfastness of a royal spirit. Like some immovable rock naturally fixed at Neptune’s boundary, repelling with a firm and unyielding front the most turbulent and powerful storms of the sea, with the whole gaze of your mind and the whole devotion of your heart you investigate, with God leading and the light of reason, the secrets of the sacred Scriptures; and, as you investigate them, you love them. 

You seek out not only the greatest and holiest authors of Latin eloquence, but also, for the increase and edification of the Catholic faith, you have learned to consult the Greek Fathers in new editions in praise of Christian doctrine. 

This is why you have not disdained to urge on the smallness of our talent, nor have you allowed us, as though idle and lulled by the sleep of indolence, to remain asleep, lest, while we devote our study only to western letters, we should be unable to turn to the purest and most abundant Greek streams and draw a draught from them. 

Thus, unable and unwilling to resist your commands, we confess that we are still exceedingly raw beginners in Greek studies.  What, indeed, should we be ashamed to confess to your serenity? Beyond our strength—but under the guidance of him who is the light of minds and illumines the hidden things of darkness—we have translated from Greek into Latin four books of the holy Father Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Athens, written by him to Timothy, bishop of the Ephesians, together with ten letters of the same author. The work is, as we think, exceedingly winding,  and far removed from modern understanding, inaccessible to many and open to few—not only because of its antiquity, but also because of the lofty nature of its heavenly mysteries. 

For it is said that the aforesaid Dionysius was a disciple and assistant of the apostle Paul, by whom he was appointed bishop of the Athenians. Luke mentions him in the Acts of the Apostles, as do Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, an ancient man; the blessed Polycarp, in his letter to the church of Athens; Eusebius Pamphilus, in his Ecclesiastical History; and also holy Pope Gregory, in his homily where he briefly expounded the orders of the angels. 

Not the aforesaid men, but others of more recent times, also assert that this same Dionysius—as far as the life handed down by faithful men testifies—came to Rome in the time of Pope Clement, namely, the successor of the apostle Peter, and was sent by him into the regions of Gaul for the purpose of preaching the Gospel. At Paris he was crowned with the glory of martyrdom together with his most blessed companions, namely Rusticus and Eleutherius. 

This translation of ours, whatever its quality may be, does not, as I think, require an extended apology, since we can meet all its critics, whoever and whatever they may be, with one very easy answer: namely, that we could neither have failed nor ought to have failed to obey your highness. 

If anyone should reproach the diction as excessively slow or excessively unusual, let him consider that not only I, but he himself as well, can receive nothing beyond what he himself distributes—he who divides to each person his own, as he wills. 

But if he should judge the sequence of the interpretation just mentioned obscure and insufficiently clear, let him observe that I am the translator of this work, not its expositor. Here I greatly fear that I may perhaps incur the fault of an unfaithful translator. 

But if he should think that certain superfluous things have been added, or that something is missing from the integrity of the Greek construction, let him return to the Greek manuscript from which I translated; there perhaps he will discover whether this is so or not.  Yet I have judged this sufficient for me: setting aside the conjectures of others, I submit to the judgment of that one alone whom I ought to obey. 

Saint Dionysius, then, as we have said, the Areopagite—so called from the hill of Mars, for Ares is the Greek word for war—was educated in the studies of the Academy during the first bloom of his youth.  Then, moved by the divine and ineffable miracle of the solar eclipse that occurred when our Lord Jesus Christ had been fastened to the gallows of the cross—he himself, as he relates in one of his letters, while near Heliopolis with Bishop Polycarp and the others then present, beheld, by divine providence, in a marvelous fashion the moon passing beneath the sun and consequently the sun eclipsed—he immediately followed the most holy man Hierotheus, namely, the bishop and disciple of the apostles. 

He mentions Hierotheus in the third book of this work and calls him his venerable teacher; nor does he hesitate to place him above the other fellow bishops of that time in theology, after the apostles. Together with him and many other saints gathered in one place, he physically beheld Christ after the resurrection. 

James, the brother of the Lord, was also present there, as he himself says, and Peter, the summit of the apostles. Instructed by such great events, and illumined by the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, he wrote these books at the encouragement and request of Saint Timothy, and of others whose names he very often reveals in the course of this work and whose teaching he briefly indicates. 

But we have thought it necessary briefly to make clear the purpose of the present work, so that the diligent reader may enter it more easily.

The first book, entitled *On the Celestial Hierarchy*—which, expressing not the word but the sense, we may render in Latin as *On the Celestial Pontificate*, or *On the Supreme Priesthood*—enumerates, orders, separates, and joins together nine arrangements of heavenly powers, and lucidly explains to the holy theologians their divinely manifested symbolic, that is, signifying or mystical, images. 

It orders them into higher, middle, and lower ranks; it separates them into three hierarchies of three each; and it joins the first to the last and the last to the first through the middle, uniting the extremes and the intermediates by a marvelous proportion.

It also confirms that heavenly substances are expressed more distinctly in prophetic visions by descriptions of dissimilar forms than of similar ones. It introduces no nature, visible or invisible, from the beginning of intellectual creation to the utmost earthly worm, from which divine theology does not draw some likeness for signifying the cause of all things, namely God, and so forth. 

The second book, whose title is *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, proclaims the unity of human nature, redeemed by the blood of our Savior, ordered—insofar as this is possible for mortals—in the likeness of the heavenly priesthood. Its supreme priest is he himself, who joined it to himself through his grace; he is also the beginning, middle, and end of the whole hierarchy, both heavenly and earthly, to whom all things are referred. 

Our hierarchy, therefore, is divided into three parts in the likeness of the heavenly hierarchy, namely, into three hierarchies. Of these, the first in temporal order but the last in dignity is the legal priesthood.  It was distributed by the lawgiver Moses in various and exceedingly obscure symbols to a people still wholly carnal and serving the letter rather than the spirit. Its principal emblem was that tabernacle figuratively displayed on the Arabian mountain.

The second, which is also the middle one, is the priesthood that now exists: I mean the Church of the New Testament, established under grace, partly arranged through the visible symbols of the sacraments and partly perfected through contemplation of the truth. It is the end of the former hierarchy and the beginning of the future hierarchy, which is the third. That third hierarchy has now been begun in part, in the first fruits of contemplation, but will be perfected after the glory of the future resurrection, when, once the veils of the visible sacraments have been removed, we shall contemplate the truth itself with evident clarity. 

Therefore the present ecclesiastical hierarchy, as we have said, is intermediate between the former legal hierarchy and the future heavenly one. For it not only performs and visibly contemplates symbols of eternal things, as did the former legal hierarchy, but also does not cease to investigate and discover their spiritual meaning, as will the future heavenly hierarchy, and so forth. 

The third book contains the powers of the divine names and is therefore called *On the Divine Names*. In it the most secret and subtle mysteries are disclosed concerning the unity and Trinity of the divine essence: which names indicate the Godhead as distinct, which as united; which names are appropriate to the Son who became incarnate; what the first procession of the one sole cause of all things into the primordial causes is; and how, through these causes, there is again, from the highest downward, a manifold theophany into the genera, species, and numbers of visible and invisible natures. 

There, through supernatural contemplation, he is seen to teach that those things which are not are like and approach God more than those which are—not through deprivation of substance, but through the excellence of nature.  He teaches what difference there is among causes; that evil is nothing causative and has no existence in the nature of things; that it harms neither substance, power, nor operation; and that whatever is said of God through privation must be understood in him through excellence. 

The fourth book is *On Mystical Theology*. Although it is shorter than the others in words, it is correspondingly more abundant in meaning.  Hence it is divided into two great parts of logical discipline, plainly the cataphatic and the apophatic—that is, into being and non-being. There he employs the rules of analytic art and teaches us most clearly that, through the privation of all things that can be said or understood, we must return, by way of the excellence of essence, to the truth that is the cause of all things—things created from it, through it, in it, and toward it. 

# The Books of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite Begin



Which John Ierugena translated from Greek into Latin, at the command and request of King Charles, son of Emperor Louis. 

# Saint Dionysius the Areopagite: Book One, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*

# The Chapters of the First Book Begin



I. Why every divine illumination, proceeding variously according to goodness into what has been foreseen, remains simple, and not only this, but also unifies those who are illumined. 

II. Why divine and heavenly things are beautifully manifested even through dissimilar symbols. 

III. What the Hierarchy is, and what understanding is conveyed through the Hierarchy. 

IV. What the designation “angels” signifies.

V. Why all heavenly essences are commonly called angels. 

VI. What the first arrangement of the heavenly essences is, what the middle, and what the last.

VII. On the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones, and on their first hierarchy.

VIII. On the Dominions, Virtues, and Powers, and on their middle hierarchy. 

IX. On the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels, and on their last hierarchy.

X. Repetition and gathering together of the angelic ordering.

XI. Why all heavenly essences are commonly called heavenly Virtues. 

XII. Why, according to human usage, the supreme priests are called angels. 

XIII. Why the prophet Isaiah is said to have been purified by the Seraphim. 

XIV. What the number assigned to the angels signifies. 

XV. What the formative images of the angelic powers are: what is fiery; what the human form is; what the eyes are; what the noses are; what the ears are; what the mouths are; what the sense of touch is; what the eyelids are; what the eyebrows are; what hearing is; what the teeth are; what the shoulders are; what the arms and hands are; what the heart is; what the breasts are; what the backs are; what the feet are; what the wings are; what nakedness is; what clothing is; what shining clothing is; what priestly clothing is; what the belts are; what the rods are; what the weapons are; what the axes are; what the geometric cords are; what the winds are; what the clouds are; what bronze is; what electrum is; what the colors of different stones are; what the form of a lion is; what the appearance of an eagle is; what the horses are; what the differences among the colors of horses are; what the rivers are; what the chariots are; what the wheels are; and what the declared joy of the angels is. 

# The Book of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, Bishop of Athens, to Timothy, Bishop of the Ephesians



## Epigram on Blessed Dionysius, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*

You have cast many splendors of angelic wisdom before mankind;

you have revealed a beauty composed for the mind to behold.

To the fellow presbyter Timothy,

Dionysius, presbyter, on the Celestial Hierarchy. 

By starlike light Dionysius enlarged Athens,

the Areopagite, and the magnificent wise man;

first moved when Phoebus was overtaken by the moon,

at the time when the Lord was fastened to the cross. 

Then, converted and astounded by the wondrous eclipse, 

he joyfully followed Hierotheus as his guide.

He was soon instructed by that illustrious teacher,

who had been reborn from the fountain of the exalted Spirit. 

Without delay, shining with the light of heavenly wisdom,

he instructed the Attic people, from whom he himself had arisen. 

For they say that Paul, who scattered Christ throughout the world,

laid his blessed hands upon him. 

But soon perfected, standing beside his teacher as an ally,

the ever-watchful high priest ruled the Cecropids. 

Then, flying on high and following Paul above the stars,

he saw the third realm of the empyrean heaven. 

He looks upon the first Seraphim, and the holy Cherubim,

and the ethereal Thrones, where God himself sits. 

After these come the Virtues, Dominions, and Powers;

the next order shines in sacred ranks.

Of Principalities, Archangels, and radiant choirs of Angels,

the third τάξις—order—dwells in heavenly minds. 

These orders, therefore, enclosed three times over within a threefold boundary,

are taught by the mystical sayings of the aforesaid Father. 

# The Book on the Celestial Hierarchy Begins

## Chapter One

### How Every Divine Illumination, Proceeding Variously According to Goodness into What Has Been Foreseen, Remains Simple, and Not Only This but Also Unifies Those Who Are Illumined

Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.  But every procession of the manifestation of the lights, moved by the Father and coming to us abundantly and in goodness, fills us again as a unifying power that restores us and turns us toward the unity and deifying simplicity of the gathering Father. For, as the divine Word says, all things are from him and in him.  

Therefore, invoking Jesus, the paternal light, who is the true light and illumines every human being coming into the world,   through whom we have had access to the principal light, the Father,  we shall turn our gaze, insofar as possible, toward the illuminations handed down by the Father in the most sacred Scriptures. 

From these we shall contemplate, insofar as our powers allow, the hierarchies of the heavenly minds manifested to us symbolically and anagogically—that is, signifyingly and contemplatively.  Receiving with eyes of the mind that are immaterial and unshaken the principal and super-principal radiance of the divine Father, which manifests to us through figurative symbols the most blessed hierarchies of the angels,  we are again restored by it to its own simple ray. 

For it is never abandoned from its own singular unity. Rather, for the anagogical and unifying harmonization of those things that have been foreseen, it is multiplied and proceeds in the best and most beautiful manner; and it remains securely within itself, fixed uniformly in unchangeable likeness. Looking back toward it, insofar as is lawful, it proportionately extends and unifies us according to the simplicity of its own unity. 

For the divine ray cannot otherwise shine upon us except when anagogically veiled by the variety of sacred coverings and prepared, by the Father’s providence, in a manner natural and proper to the things that belong to us.  Therefore the sacred ordering of the divine source of sacred rites, judging our most holy hierarchy worthy of imitation of the supermundane celestial hierarchies, has represented the aforesaid immaterial hierarchies through material figures and formal compositions, so that, proportionately to ourselves, we may ascend from the most sacred formations toward the simple and imageless heights and likenesses. [The transmitted Latin at *teletarchis sacrorum positio* is materially uncertain; A reads *perfectissima* (“most perfect”) for *teletarchis*, and *dispositio* (“arrangement”) for *positio* (“ordering”).]

For it is impossible for our mind to ascend to the immaterial imitation and contemplation of the celestial hierarchies unless it makes use of what pertains to it through a material guidance of the hand. Thus it regards visible forms as images of invisible beauty; sensible sweetnesses as figures of invisible distribution; material lights as images of immaterial radiance; sacred disciplines that are traversable according to the intellect as paths toward contemplative fullness; and the dispositions of the things here below, united to the divine and ordered, as orders of their arrangements. It regards the reception itself of the most divine Eucharist as participation in Jesus, and all the other things that have been handed down in a supermundane manner to the heavenly essences, but symbolically to us. 

Because of this, the merciful source of perfection, for our rational deification, manifesting the heavenly hierarchies to us and perfecting our hierarchy as their minister, has described the superheavenly intellects according to the measure of our capacity through sensible images of their godlike sanctification, in the sacred compositions of the scriptural utterances. It has done so in order to lead us back through sensible things to intellectual things, and from sacredly figured symbols to the simple summits of the celestial hierarchies.

### How Divine and Heavenly Things Are Beautifully Manifested Even Through Dissimilar Symbols
