It is necessary, therefore, as I think, first to explain what we consider the contemplation of the whole Hierarchy to be, and what benefit each of its parts has provided for the divine praisers; then to praise the celestial Hierarchies according to their manifestation in the sacred writings; and after these things to say by what divine formations the sacred descriptions of the writings represent the celestial orders, and toward what truth one ought to ascend through these forms, lest we too should, in the same manner as many do, impiously suppose the celestial and godlike minds to be creatures with many feet and many faces, formed according to the animal likeness of cattle or the bestial appearance of lions, figured according to the hooked beak of eagles or the threefold movement of birds’ wings, imagine certain fiery wheels above heaven, material thrones necessary for the Divinity to recline upon, certain multicolored horses, armed commanders, and whatever else has been handed down to us from the sacred writings, sacredly and formatively, in the variety of their manifestational symbols  .

For theology has employed, with great artistry, artificial sacred formations for intellects incapable of being represented, revealing our mind, as has been said, and providing for it according to what is proper and connatural to it, reforming it toward the sacred Scriptures, which lead upward. If anyone, however, accepts the sacred compositions as appropriate representations of beings that are simple in themselves, unknown to us, and beyond contemplation, but considers the sacred descriptions of the holy intellects in the writings—and, so to speak, this entire harsh theater of angelic names—inappropriate, and says that the theologians, when they proceeded from bodily form to the universal incorporeality, ought to have formed and manifested these things through figures proper and, as far as possible, akin to them, drawing on the most precious and immaterial essences among us, and should have adapted the earthly and lowest multiformities placed around us to heavenly and godlike simplicities    —this would indeed have been more elevated for us, and it would not have brought supermundane manifestations down into inappropriate dissimilarities . Nor would it have wronged the divine powers unlawfully , nor likewise led our mind astray as it became entangled in impure compositions.

And perhaps the supercelestial realms would even be judged to be filled with certain multitudes of lions and horses, with the bellowing speech of praises, with a flying angelic command, with other animals, and with less noble materials, as though, being confined to what is incongruous, ignoble, and subject to passion, they were described throughout by the deformed likenesses of the writings’ manifestational images .

But the investigation of truth, as I think, shows that the most sacred wisdom of the writings  took very great care of both matters in its representations of the celestial minds, so that, if one should put it that way, it would neither wrong the divine powers nor fasten us, through passion, upon the lowliness of the images. For that the forms of the formless and the figures of the figureless have been beautifully devised: one might say that the cause is our analogy, which is unable to extend itself immediately to invisible contemplations and desires its proper and connatural means of ascent, which set before us forms capable of representing the formless and supernatural contemplations.

But this too is most appropriate to the mystical writings: to conceal the divine through incomprehensible and divine enigmas, and to place before many an inaccessible sacred truth hidden within the intellects beyond the world . For not all knowledge is sacred, nor does it belong to everyone, as the writings say . If anyone should suppose that the causes of the deformed descriptions of the images are dishonored , saying that such ugly forms are thus attributed to godlike and most holy orders , it is sufficient to say to him  that there are two modes of sacred manifestation: one, as it were, consequent, because of the images of the sacred figures that come from similar things ; the other, because of the formations of dissimilar forms, formed into what is altogether incongruous and unbecoming.

Thus the mystical traditions of the manifestational writings sometimes praise the blessedness of the superessential θεαρχία—thearchy —to be revered as reason, intellect, and essence, declaring its divine rationality  and wisdom, its truly existing subsistence, and its being the true cause of the subsistence of all things that are. They also reform it, as it were, as light, and call it life, through such wondrous reformations—though these are more glorious than material formations in every respect —and through tested likenesses, while material likenesses fall short of the truth of the thearchy . For it is beyond every essence and life; no light characterizes it , and every likeness of it to reason and intellect is incomparably inadequate.

At other times the writings praise it supermundanely through dissimilar manifestations , calling it invisible, infinite, and incomprehensible , and signifying through these things not what it is but what it is not —for this, as I think, is more powerful in its case. Since, as the hidden and priestly tradition has introduced it, we truly say that it is not in the manner of any of the things that are , but we do not know its superessential, invisible, and ineffable infinity.

If, therefore, negations are true in divine matters , while affirmations are ill-fitting , manifestation through dissimilar formations  is more suited to the obscurity of the mysteries. Accordingly, the sacred descriptions of the writings do not now fill the celestial orders with ugly things, but manifest them through dissimilar formations of forms, and through these show their superiority over all material things at once . And since dissimilar likenesses also lead our mind upward more effectively, I do not think that anyone of sound judgment will disagree.

For in the case of the more precious sacred formations  it is possible to be misled into thinking that the celestial essences are some golden beings , or certain men flashing like lightning, clothed in beautiful garments, shining brightly, fiery, and harmlessly —and into accepting whatever other similar imagined forms theology has used to represent the celestial intellects. So that those who understand nothing higher than visible goods might not suffer this, the restorative wisdom of the holy theologians wonderfully descends even to unbecoming dissimilarities. It does not allow our material nature to remain at rest in ugly images ; rather, it carries the soul upward  and suggests, through the deformity of the compositions—as though neither the just nor the true approved them—that the supercelestial and divine spectacles are not in truth similar to material things, since they are ugly in this way.

Yet we must also understand this: none of the things that exist is altogether deprived of participation in the good. For, as the truth of the writings says, all things are very good . From all things, therefore, it is possible to understand good contemplations and to reform from material things the dissimilar likenesses that have been mentioned , making them from invisible and intellectual realities in another manner, since intellectual realities possess in one way what has been distributed among sensible things in another.

Thus, among irrational animals, madness arises from a passionate movement, and their frenzied movement is filled with every kind of irrationality . But in intellectual beings “anger” must be understood in another way, signifying, as I think, their manly rationality [Col. 1042C] and their unyielding repose upon divine and immutable foundations .

In the same way, among irrational beings we call desire an unconsidered and material passion, arising by natural movement or habit within mutable things, an irrational continuity of bodily pleasure that drives every animal toward sensible desire. But when, by surrounding intellectual beings with dissimilar likenesses, we form desire around them , we must understand it as divine love: a desire beyond reason and intellect  for immateriality, and an inflexible, self-sufficient longing for the contemplation—superessentially chaste and impassible—of the purest and most exalted radiance, and of the invisible, form-giving beauty of the eternal, truly invisible communion.

The next syntax is difficult. Literally, it describes “as it were, a power” that receives in sufficiency and in what is convertible, that cannot be afflicted by anything , through an unconfused and immutable love of divine beauty , and through a universal recalling toward what is truly desirable.

Likewise, among irrational animals or inanimate materials, we properly call irrationality and insensibility a lack of reason and sense. But in immaterial and intellectual essences we confess, in a holy and fitting manner, the supereminence of these qualities—as belonging to beings beyond the world—over our transient and bodily reason and our material sense, which has been alienated from incorporeal minds .

It is therefore not inappropriate to form likenesses dissimilar to the celestial forms, even from the lowly parts of matter, since matter itself, possessing subsistence from the truly good, has throughout its material arrangement certain echoes  of intellectual beauty. Through these it is possible to be led upward to the immaterial primordial forms by dissimilar likenesses, as has been said: the likenesses are received , and the same things  are defined, not similarly, but compactly and beautifully, by intellectual and sensible properties.

We shall find the mystical theologians wonderfully forming these things not only in their descriptions of the celestial orders, but sometimes also in their manifestations of the thearchy . At times they praise it from precious lights, as the sun of righteousness, as the morning star rising holily in the soul, and as light shining intellectually and without concealment  . At times they praise it from intermediate things: as fire shining harmlessly, as water giving the fullness of life, and, symbolically speaking, as entering into the belly and as rivers overflowing with immeasurable abundance. At times they praise it from the lowest things: as sweet ointment and as the cornerstone .

They also surround it with a bestial form, fitting it with the appearance of a lion and panther , clothing it in a leopard’s form, and representing it as a raging bear . I shall add what seemed to be the lowest and most expressive of all: for the divine sages have handed down that it also forms itself around itself in the appearance of a worm .

Thus all the theosophists and prophets inspired by hidden inspiration distinguish the holy things from the holy and undefiled, and honor the sacred dissimilar figuration, so that divine things may not be handled by the impure , nor contemplators devoted to wondrous images remain with the figures as though they were realities . They therefore honor the divine through true negations and through diverse likenesses of the lowest and most compacted echoes .

There is consequently nothing incongruous if, for the reasons stated, they also form the celestial essences through inappropriate dissimilar likenesses . For perhaps we would not equally enter into inquiry out of need, nor into ascent through diligent investigation of divine things , unless the deformity compelled us to examine the manifestation of the angels , preventing our mind from remaining in the formations of dissimilar forms, but forcing it to deny material passions and accustoming it to extend itself purely through visible things toward the heights beyond the world.

So much has been said by us concerning the material and inappropriate descriptions of the angelic images in the divine writings . Next, however, it is necessary to distinguish what we consider the Hierarchy itself to be, and what benefit the Hierarchy provides to those who receive a place within it .

Let Christ be the guide of the discourse—if I may say so, my guide—the inspiration of the entire hierarchical manifestation. But you, child, according to the sacred legislation of our priestly tradition, listen reverently and fittingly to what has been wondrously said. Become divine in God and in teaching , and guard the holy things within the secret chamber of your soul, enclosing them away from the impure multitude, and preserve them as uniform realities. For it is not lawful, as the writings say, to cast before swine the unconfused, light-bearing, and beneficial adornment of invisible pearls .

## CHAPTER III. What the Hierarchy is, and what benefit comes through the Hierarchy

The Hierarchy is, in my view, a divine order, knowledge, and activity, imitating the divine as far as possible  and ascending proportionally toward the likeness of God according to the divinely bestowed illuminations implanted in it .

Divine beauty, being simple, supremely good, and consummative , is wholly pure from every dissimilarity; distributive according to the worth of each one’s own light; and perfective in the most divine sacrifice, according to the compact and immutable formation of those perfected toward itself.

The interpretation of “Hierarchy,” therefore, is likeness and union with God, as far as possible. It has him as the guide of every sacred knowledge and activity, and, defining its members immutably according to his most divine beauty, reforms them as far as possible . It perfects its praisers as divine images, clearest and purest mirrors, receptive of the primordial light and divine ray, filled sacredly with the light implanted in them , and again abundantly declaring it in what follows, according to the divine laws.

For it is not lawful for the holy perfectors or for those who have been sanctified and perfected to perform anything at all apart from their proper consummative rites  or sacred ordinances. Nor may they subsist in any other way unless they desire the divine radiance itself , look toward it sacredly and fittingly , and are reformed according to the analogy of each of the holy intellects .

Does not the person who speaks of a Hierarchy therefore declare a certain sacred universal order , an image of divine beauty in the hierarchical orders and knowledges, performing the mysteries of its own illumination as a sacrifice and assimilated, as far as possible, to its own principle? For the perfection of each person who receives a place in the Hierarchy is this: to ascend according to his own analogy in imitation of God, and, in the most divine manner, as the writings say, to become God’s fellow worker , displaying in himself the divine activity shining forth as far as possible.

For the order of the Hierarchy is that some are purified while others purify; some are illuminated while others illuminate; some are perfected while others perfect—each in whatever manner is appropriate to union with the divine.

Divine blessedness, insofar as it may be spoken of in human terms, is at once pure from every dissimilarity , full of eternal light, perfect , and lacking nothing of perfection. It purifies, illuminates, and perfects. Rather, purification, illumination, and perfection themselves are above purification, above light, already perfect, perfect in themselves, and the source of perfection in themselves; they are the cause of every Hierarchy and of everything sacred according to their transcendent exaltedness.

Therefore, as I think, those who are to be purified must be perfected completely and freed from every confusion of dissimilarity. Those who are to be illuminated must be filled with divine light , renewed for contemplative disposition and virtue through the most chaste eyes of the mind . Those who are to be restored from imperfection  must become participants in the perfecting knowledge of the explored sacred things.

Those who purify must, by the greatness of their purification , pass on to others their own purity. Those who illuminate, as minds more radiant, having the capacity both to participate in and to distribute light, and being richly filled with sacred brightness , must carry their surpassing light over to those worthy of light [Col. 1045D]. Those who perfect, as teachers of the perfecting tradition, must perfect those who are to be perfected through the most sacred teaching and through knowledge of the sacred things contemplated.

Therefore not every order of the hierarchical disposition is, according to its own analogy, led back to divine cooperation; rather, the grace and God-given power perfect the things naturally and supernaturally united to the thearchy , acted upon by it superessentially, and hierarchically manifested for the possible imitation of souls that love God . 

## CHAPTER IV. What the designation “angels” signifies

Since, then, we have defined what the Hierarchy is, as I think, well , we must next praise the angelic Hierarchy , and contemplate with supermundane eyes the wondrous formations of its forms in the writings , so that through mystical reformations  we may ascend to their most godlike simplicity. At the same time we shall praise the principle of all hierarchical knowledge in the divinely proclaimed religious observance and in the consummative acts of thanksgiving .

First of all, it is true to say that the superessential thearchy , through universal goodness, brought the essences of existing things into being. For this is proper to the cause of all and to the goodness above all: to call existing things into communion with itself, so that each of the things that exist is defined according to its own analogy.

All existing things therefore participate in providence, which flows from the superessential and causative divinity. For perhaps they would not exist unless they received the essence of their being from the beginning .

All existing things therefore participate in its existence, for the divinity above existence is the existence of all . Living things participate in that same vivifying power, which is above all life . Rational and intellectual things participate in that same wisdom, which is perfect and pre-perfect in itself, above every reason and intellect .

It is clear that those essences are around it which have received from it, in innumerable ways, their being.

The sacred dispositions of the celestial essences, therefore, have become participants, according to us, in the rational hierarchical tradition above things that merely exist and irrationally live. Invisibly reforming themselves in imitation of God, looking supermundanely toward the likeness of the thearchy, and desiring to form their intellectual appearance , they have more abundant and beautiful communion with it. The transmitted construction then breaks at “being indeed intent”: all manuscripts insert “all life; they therefore are first and innumerably” , words the editor marks as superfluous and apparently displaced from the following period.

After that intrusion the surviving sentence continues: they are always intent upon the highest, insofar as is lawful, in the confirmation  of divine and inflexible love; they receive the principal illuminations immaterially and purely, are ordered toward them, and possess an entirely intellectual life. They therefore became first and innumerably  participants in God, and first and manifold manifestators of the divine hiddenness. For this reason they have been especially deemed worthy, above all, of the designation “angelic,” because they first receive the divine illumination within themselves and transmit to us, through themselves, the manifestations that are above us.

For, as theology says, these manifestations were given to us through angels. Glorious fathers of ours before the Law were also led back to God by angels, who introduced what had to be done and brought them back from error and an impure life to the straight path of truth. Angels prophetically revealed either the sacred orders of supermundane mysteries, hidden visions, or certain divine predictions .

But if anyone should say that some saints received theophanies directly from God, let him also learn this wisely from the most sacred writings: that no one has seen or shall see this hidden thing of God, whatever and of whatever kind it is  .

Theophanies, however, were made to the saints according to divine predictions through certain sacred manifestations of visions proportionate to those who saw them . That most wise theology therefore revealed that the vision described there, which is divine, is beautifully called a theophany in the form, as it were, of likenesses of the formless, through the ascent of those who saw it toward the divine: as though through it a divine illumination had come to the viewers, and as though it wondrously instructed them in divine things .

Our glorious fathers were instructed in these divine visions through the intermediate celestial powers . Does not the tradition of the sacred legislation of the writings itself say that it was given to Moses from God, so that it may also truly teach us that its characters are divine and sacred ? Theology also wisely teaches that it comes to us through angels, as though the divine legal order established that law legally—that is, that the second should be led back to the divine through the first .

Indeed, the law is defined not only among superior and inferior souls but also among those of equal power, by the superessential principle of the ordering of all things. That is, within each Hierarchy there are first, middle, and last orders and powers; and the higher are more divine teachers and guides of the lower, leading them to God, illumination, and communion.

I see, moreover, that the divine mystery of Christ’s humanity was first taught by angels, and that through them the grace of this knowledge afterward descended upon us .

Thus the most divine Gabriel instructed Zacharias, the high priest, in the mysteries: namely, that a child would be born from him by divine grace, contrary to hope, and would become a prophet, divinely and salvifically manifesting to the world the divine activity of the man Jesus . He also taught Mary how the ineffable mystery of the divine formation would come to be in her  .

Another angel instructed Joseph concerning how the things divinely promised to David the ancestor would truly be fulfilled . Another evangelized the shepherds, as though converted by the return and silence of many , and with him a multitude of the heavenly host delivered to those on earth that highly praiseworthy doxology.

Let us also turn our attention to the loftiest manifestations of the light of the writings [Col. 1048B]. For I see that Jesus himself—the superessential essence of the supercelestial essences—coming immutably to what belongs to us, does not reject the military and chosen human order arranged and assumed beneath him , but obediently submits to the dispositions of the Father and God through angels.

Through these intermediaries Joseph is informed of the departure of the child, arranged by the Father, to Egypt, and again of his return from Egypt to Judea . Through angels we also see him ordered under the Father’s legislation .

I am about to say something familiar to those who know our priestly traditions: concerning the angel strengthening Jesus. Or rather, because Jesus himself, coming through our saving, beneficial  and manifestational order, is called the angel of great counsel.

For, as the aforementioned angel himself said , whatever he heard from the Father he announced to us .

## CHAPTER V. Why all celestial essences are commonly called angels

This, as far as we are concerned, is the reason for the designation “angel” in the writings. But it is necessary, as I think, to investigate why the theologians call all the celestial essences collectively “angels,” while, when they come to manifest the supermundane orders themselves, they specifically name the angelic order, which completes and terminates the divine and celestial matters. Before it they arrange the archangelic orders, and the principalities, powers [Col. 1048D], virtues, and all the essences that the writings recognize as established above these in the manifestational tradition [Col. 1049A].

We say that throughout every sacred order the higher orders possess the illuminations and powers of the lower orders, but the lowest do not participate in the higher . Therefore the theologians call the most holy orders of the most exalted essences “angels” as well; for they too are manifestators of the thearchic illumination .

They do not, however, consider it reasonable to name the final order of the celestial minds “principalities,” “thrones,” or “seraphim” . For it does not participate in the most exalted powers. The following Latin is syntactically disturbed: it says that, just as this order leads our divine high priests toward the divine splendors known to it, so the powers still “unpurified” in relation to the essences before it lead onward, and belong to the disposition that perfects the angelic hierarchies [Col. 1049B]. The transmitted agents and objects are therefore retained with uncertainty rather than silently rearranged.

Unless, indeed, someone should say this also: that all the angelic designations are common , according to the subordination of all the celestial powers to the godlike light given by God and according to their supereminent communion .

But so that the matter may be judged by us more carefully, let us sacredly consider the holy and beautiful properties expressed in the writings of each celestial order.

How numerous and of what kinds are the adornments of the supercelestial essences, and how the hierarchies are perfected according to them, I say that only their contemplative telarchy knows carefully [Col. 1049] B, E, and H read “knows”; A, “is ignorant”; and that they do not yet know their own particular virtues and illuminations and their sacred, supremely ordered arrangement. For it is impossible for us to know the mysteries of the supercelestial spirits and their most holy perfections unless one says that the Divinity taught us there, as things proper to them, whatever mysteries it taught us through them [Col. 1049] A omits “us.” Therefore we ourselves say nothing from our own initiative [Col. 1049] B and H read “indeed what.” Rather, whatever has been contemplated by the holy theologians concerning angelic visions, we shall explain, insofar as we are able, by teaching it.

All theology has called the celestial essences by nine names expressive of their manifestation [Col. 1049D] Colossians I; A reads “these” rather than “which.” Our divine and holy perfecter divides them into three triadic orders. He says that the first always exists around God and has been assigned to be united immediately and attentively to him before the others. For he says that the most holy Thrones and the orders with eyes and wings, called Cherubim and Seraphim in the language of the Hebrews, are placed immediately around God, according to their proximity, which is superior to all others, as the manifestation of the divine oracles teaches [Col. 1050A].

Our common leader therefore called this triadic adornment one single, equally ordered, and truly first hierarchy [Col. 1050D] Ephesians III; Colossians I. No other is more God-like, nor is any other by itself more immediately attentive to the divinity’s pre-eminent, originating illuminations [Col. 1049] A omits “is”; E reads “in the midst.” He says that the second is composed of the Powers, Dominions, and Virtues. Finally, the disposition of the three celestial hierarchies consists of Angels, Archangels, and Principalities [Col. 1050D] I Thessalonians IV.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones, and on Their First Hierarchy

As we are about to receive the order of the holy hierarchies, we say that all the names of the celestial intellects have a meaning expressive of the deiform property of each. Those who know the holy name Seraphim—for they are Hebrews—have explained it as “burning” or “heating” [Col. 1049] A and E read “to manifest.” The name Cherubim signifies either “multitude of knowledge” or “outpouring of wisdom” [Col. 1049] A reads “those.”

The first of the celestial hierarchies is therefore fittingly sanctified by the most excellent essences. It has an order higher than all the others: namely, it is placed immediately around God, and the first-originating theophanies and perfections are principally conveyed to it as the one nearest to him [Col. 1049] A reads “is placed … are conveyed.”

Thus the Thrones are called “heating” and “outpouring of wisdom,” names expressive of their deiform dispositions [Col. 1049] A and E read “they are manifested”; A and E read “they.” For their movement around divine things is always mobile, unceasing, warm, keen, and exceedingly ardent: the movement of their focused, self-sufficient, and inflexible attention. It assimilates them both reproductively and actively to what is above them, as though reheating and reviving those things to a similar heat [Col. 1049] A and E read “warmth.” It is heavenly, fiery, and purifying like a holocaust; uncovered and inextinguishable, it always possesses a luminous and illuminating property [Col. 1049] B reads “thus and thus”; A, “and having itself in this way”; E, “having itself thus”—that pursues and manifests every dark obscurity. This teaches the meaning, or manifestation, of the name Seraphim [Col. 1049] A* reads “the names or manifestations.”

Cherubim itself signifies their capacity for knowledge and divinization, their receptivity to the highest giving of light, and their contemplation of the divine beauty in its first-originating and operative power. It is filled with the transmission of wisdom and communicates abundantly to the second order the wisdom granted through this outpouring.

The Thrones themselves are carefully exalted above every disgrace of subjection by their highest and compacted seats; they bear themselves upward to the highest, beyond the world; with every extremity they are placed immutably and steadfastly in the most exalted region and around the truly transcendent one [Col. 1049] A reads “ineffably”; A* reads “subjected” rather than “most sublime.” They receive the divine advent with complete impassibility and immateriality; they are God-bearing and open, as servants, to divine receptions.

This, so far as concerns us, is the explanation of their names. We must now say what sort of hierarchy we consider theirs to be. I think that we have already sufficiently stated that the contemplation of every hierarchy depends inflexibly upon an imitative, deiform likeness to God, and that every hierarchical action is divided into sacred participation and the transmission of pure purification, divine illumination, and perfecting knowledge.

Let us now proceed worthily to explain how the hierarchy of the most exalted intellects is manifested by the oracles. It must be considered that the first essences, which are placed after their substantializing thearchy and ordered, as it were, in its vestibules, surpass every virtue that has been made, visible or invisible [Col. 1051B] A* reads “their proper making.” Their hierarchy must be considered wholly of the same form as that virtue.

They must therefore be considered pure, not as freed from unclean stains and pollutions, nor as receiving material phantasies [Col. 1051] A reads “of received material phantasies,” but as clean and higher than every diminution [Col. 1051] A reads “subjection,” and as placed above every firmly established temple according to the highest chastity [Col. 1051] A* reads “most excellent,” set above all the most deiform virtues. They have been inflexibly received by their own movement, and by one and the same movement, according to the unchanging order of the one who loves God; they know nothing at all of being subjected to insult, but possess an unfailing and immutable placement according to their own deiform particularity, in the utmost purity.

They are also contemplative of sensible symbols and intellectual visions—not as being led to the divine through the variety of the sacred interpretation of Scripture, but as filled with every immaterial knowledge of the higher light, and, insofar as is permitted, replete with contemplation of the formative and originating beauty, and of the superessential and translucent beauty [Col. 1051] B and H read “perlucent.”

Through participation in Jesus they have likewise been made worthy—not by forming the deifying likeness in images fashioned by sacred art [Col. 1051] A* reads “sacredly made,” but as truly approaching him in the first participation of the knowledge of his deifying lights [Col. 1051] A reads “light.” And because a likeness to God has been given to them in the most direct manner [Col. 1051] A reads “substantially,” they communicate, insofar as possible, in the pre-eminent, originating power of his divine and human virtues.

They are likewise perfect—not as illuminated by analytic knowledge through the variety of sacred forms, but as filled with the first and transcendent deification, according to the highest [Col. 1051] A* and E read “most excellent,” insofar as this is possible for angels, knowledge of divine works. For they are sanctified not through other holy essences but by the thearchy itself, and are immediately extended toward it. They are placed above all in transcendent virtue and order, established altogether in the purest strength; they are led, insofar as is permitted, to contemplate the immaterial and invisible beauty; they are bent toward the intelligible principles of divine works, as are the first essences around God; and they have been sanctified in the highest manner by the very source of perfection.

The theologians therefore clearly declare that the subordinate orders of celestial essences are adorned and instructed in firmly established deifying knowledges, while those above all others are illuminated, insofar as is permitted, by the thearchy itself through its teachings [Col. 1051] A has “teaching”; E, “teachings.”

For they introduce some of these as instructed by those before them concerning the Lord of the celestial powers and the King of Glory, received humanly into the heavens [Col. 1051D] Psalm XXIII. Others they introduce as seeking him, Jesus, and learning from him, on our behalf, the knowledge of his divine action; and they say that Jesus himself immediately teaches them and reveals to them his human benevolence [Col. 1051] A, B, and E read “benign humanity.” “I discuss,” he says, “righteousness and the judgment of salvation” [Col. 1052D] Isaiah LXIII.

I marvel, however, that the first of the celestial essences, and indeed all of them together, though so far above the thearchic illuminations, reverently desire mediated questions [Col. 1051] A reads “desire.” For they do not ask him directly, “Why are your garments red?” Rather, they deliberate among themselves before asking, showing that they learn and desire deifying knowledge, but do not leap ahead of the illumination implanted through the divine procession.

Thus the first hierarchy of the celestial intellects, sanctified by the thearchic telarchy itself, because it is immediately extended toward it, is purified, illuminated, and perfected by a most holy purification, filling it proportionately with the light of the consummation perfected beforehand. It is pure of every deficiency, full of the first light, and perfect through participation in the knowledge and understanding given first.

I might perhaps say, and not without reason, that the acquisition of divine knowledge is purification, illumination, and perfection. It purifies insofar as it purges ignorance; it illuminates through knowledge of the more perfect teachings implanted in due order; and divine cognition itself, by which it purges one who had not previously contemplated, manifests through higher illumination; the same light, moreover, perfects through the established possession of the most luminous teachings.

Such, so far as concerns our knowledge, is the first disposition of the celestial essences: standing in a circle around God and immediately around him, and simply and unceasingly circling his eternal knowledge according to the most excellent, ever-moving placement possible among angels [Col. 1051] B and H read “mobile.” It sees many blessed contemplations in purity, is illuminated by a single and immediate radiance [Col. 1051] A and E read “single radiances immediately,” and is filled with divine nourishment: with much outpouring given first, but with the single, intimate, unifying unity of divine refreshment alone.

It has become worthy of much communion with God and cooperation with him, being made, insofar as possible, similar to the good dispositions and actions [Col. 1053] H reads “similarity.” It knows much of the things that are above, and has been made a participant, insofar as is permitted, in divine knowledge and understanding.

For this reason theology has also handed down its praises to those on earth, in which the pre-eminence of its highest illumination is wonderfully manifested. Some, to speak sensibly, resound like the voice of waters: “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place.” Others proclaim that most praiseworthy and pious theology: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory” [Col. 1053D] Ezekiel I; Ezekiel III; Isaiah VI; Revelation IV.

We have already explained, insofar as possible, these hymns of the most exalted celestial spirits in the work concerning divine praises, and have spoken there about them sufficiently, so far as concerns us. From that discussion, for the present, it is enough to say this alone: the first order, illuminated insofar as is permitted by the thearchic goodness, has been endowed with theological knowledge [Col. 1053] A and B read “theological knowledge.” As a deiform hierarchy, it then transmitted the same knowledge to the others. In brief, it introduced this point: that the most pious, super-praiseworthy, and most worthy of praise thearchy may rightly be blessed by the intellects that receive God, insofar as they are able to know and praise it.

For they are, as the oracles say, deiform divine places of the thearchy’s repose [Col. 1054D] Psalms IX, XLVI, LXXIX; Isaiah LXVI. And since it is a monad and a unity, three in substance, extending its goodness to the supercelestial essences and down to the last reaches of the earth, exercising providence over all that exists, it is the super-principial principle and cause of every essence and embraces all things superessentially in an immeasurable containment.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Dominions, Virtues, and Powers, and on Their Middle Hierarchy

We must now pass to the middle disposition of the celestial intellects, examining with supermundane eyes, insofar as possible, the Dominions and the truly powerful manifestations [Col. 1053] A* reads “speculative manifestations” of the divine Powers and Virtues. For each name given to the essences above us signifies their deiform properties in imitation of God.

I therefore consider the manifestative name of the holy Dominions to indicate a certain absolute ascent, free from every disgraceful diminution, not inclined in any way toward the likeness of tyrannical dissimilarities [Col. 1053] E reads “not assimilated to tyrannical dissimilarities,” but freely and severely exercising dominion, set above every petty servitude, needing no subjection at all, removed from every form of dissimilarity, ceaselessly desiring lordship, and conforming both itself and what comes after it, insofar as possible, to the likeness of that very naturally subsisting power. It is turned not toward anything merely apparent, but toward the universally and truly existent reality, τὸ ὄν (“what is”), and, insofar as possible, has been made a participant in the ever-deiform lordship.

The name of the holy Virtues, I believe, signifies a certain strong and unchanging manliness, formed in every operation according to their deiformity, not weakly shaped for the reception of the divine illuminations implanted in them [Col. 1053] A and E read “weakened,” but powerfully led back in imitation of God. It does not abandon the deiform movement through weakness in itself, but steadfastly bears the essential and empowering virtue and has been made, insofar as permitted, like the image of that virtue [Col. 1053] A and E read “like the virtue.” It is powerfully turned toward it as the originating virtue, and proceeds in deiform fashion toward the second, the giver of virtue.

The name of the holy Powers signifies an equal-powered, well-ordered, and unconfused arrangement of the divine receptions belonging to the Dominions and Virtues. It signifies an ordered disposition of supermundane and intellectual power—not tyrannically hurled downward upon inferior things through its powers, but powerfully led back to the divine after they have been well ordered; then deiformly leading those after it back; assimilated, insofar as is permitted, to the empowering exousiarchy, and revealing it, insofar as possible, to the angels through its governing power in the orders arranged by it [Col. 1053] A* and E read “well-adorned” rather than “well-ordered.”

With these deiform properties, the middle disposition of the celestial spirits is purified, illuminated, and perfected, as has been said, by divine illuminations implanted in it secondarily through the first hierarchical disposition and conveyed through the middle order in a second manifestation.

Thus, when we hear one angel coming to another through speech, we shall make it a symbol, seen from afar, of the superperfect perfection that is hidden within itself and proceeds toward what follows. For the wise men concerning our sacred sacrifices say that plenitudes of divine things shining through themselves are more perfect than those existing through the participation of others. So I consider the immediate participation of the angelic orders extended first toward God to be more perfect than participation mediated through the perfecting orders [Col. 1054D].

For this reason, in our priestly tradition the perfecting, illuminating, and purifying virtues are called the intellects of the lower orders: they are led back through themselves to the superessential principle of all things and have been made participants, according to what is permitted them, in the telarchic [Col. 1053] A reads “mystical” purifications, illuminations, and perfections.

For this is the divine ordinance, proclaimed by God: through the first, the second participate in divine illuminations [Col. 1055A]. You will find this expressed many times by the theologians.

When the divine and paternal humanity was educating Israel by turning it back for its sacred salvation, handing it over to punitive and savage nations for correction, and, through every kind of providential transfer to what was better, sent it into captivity and then mercifully restored it to its former steadfastness [Col. 1055] A reads “beneficence,” one of the theologians, Zachariah, saw one of the first angels, as I believe, and one who is around God—for, as I have said, this angelic name is common to all of them—learning from God himself consolatory words about this matter [Col. 1055] A and E read “consoling.”

He saw another of the subordinate angels coming forward to meet the first, as though to receive and participate in illumination. Then, instructed by him in the divine counsel as by a high priest, this second angel turned and taught the theologian that Jerusalem would be inhabited fruitfully by a multitude of people [Col. 1055D] Zechariah II.

Another of the theologians, Ezekiel [Col. 1055D] Ezekiel VIII, says that this was most sacredly proclaimed by the Cherubim, established above the most glorious Divinity. For Israel, as has been said, was led by an educative humanity through disciplines toward what was better; divine justice condemns the guilty and justifies the innocent.

This is taught by the first angel after the Cherubim, girded around the loins with sapphire, who was clothed symbolically according to the hierarchy in a priestly garment [Col. 1055] E reads “a priestly garment.” The divine ordinance commands the other angels who held axes to be taught by the first concerning this divine judgment [Col. 1055D] Ezekiel X.

For he said: “Pass through the midst of Jerusalem and set a mark upon the foreheads of the innocent men.” To the others he said: “Go out into the city after him and strike; do not spare your eyes. But do not approach anyone upon whom there is the mark” [Col. 1055D] Ezekiel IX.

What, perhaps, might one say about the angel who said to Daniel, “The word has gone forth”? Or about the first angel himself, receiving fire from the midst of the Cherubim? [Col. 1056D] Daniel IX. Or about that same angel, in a fuller demonstration of the angelic order, since he also puts fire into the hands of the one clothed in the holy robe? [Col. 1056D] Ezekiel X. Or about the one who calls the most divine Gabriel and says to him, “Make him understand the vision”? [Col. 1056D] Zechariah I.

Or about all the other things said by the sacred theologians concerning the deiform adornment of the celestial thearchies? To this order our own hierarchy has been assimilated insofar as possible. Its angelic beauty, insofar as it possesses it in images, has been formed and led through it to the superessential ordinance of the entire hierarchy [Col. 1055D] “ordinance” is omitted in B, E, and H.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels, and on Their Last Hierarchy

The remaining order for our contemplation, which completes the angelic hierarchies, is arranged by the deiform Principalities, Archangels, and Angels.

First, I consider it necessary to explain, insofar as possible, the meanings manifested by their holy names. The name of the celestial Principalities manifests that which is deiformly principal and leading, together with sacred order and most fitting princely virtues; it signifies their universal conversion toward the super-principial principle, their hierarchical leadership of others, and their reformation, insofar as possible, according to that same princely principle. It also manifests the superessential ordinance of that principle through the adornment of the princely virtues [Col. 1055] A reads “the principal leading principle”; A reads “principal” rather than “princely.”

The name of the holy Archangels has equal power with the celestial Principalities. For, as I have said, there is one hierarchy and one disposition of both them and the Angels. Nevertheless, since no hierarchy exists without first, middle, and last virtues, the holy order of the Archangels is received communicatively into the middle of the extremes.

For it communicates with the most sacred Principalities and with the holy Angels. With the Principalities it communicates because it is principally turned toward the superessential principle, is reformed according to it insofar as possible, and unifies the Angels according to its well-adorned, ordered, and invisible leaderships. With the Angels it communicates because it receives the divine illuminations hierarchically in a subordinate order through the first virtues, announces them to the Angels in deiform fashion, and through the Angels manifests them to us according to the divinely illuminated analogy of each.

The Angels themselves, as we said earlier, complete and perfect all the dispositions of the celestial spirits, insofar as perfection is possible. They possess the angelic property among the celestial essences and are more appropriately called Angels among us than the higher orders, since the hierarchy is more significant in their case and more fully adorned around them.

The most excellent disposition, as has been said, is to be considered as sanctifying the second: it approaches the hidden one, first ordered, as its closest neighbor, and forms it secretly [Col. 1055] A reads “to order.” The second, which is completed by the holy Dominions, Virtues, and Powers, presides over the hierarchy of the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels [Col. 1055] A reads “to be in charge of.” The first hierarchy does so more manifestly, the one after it more secretly.

The manifestative disposition of the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels presides in succession over the human hierarchies, so that there may be an ordered return to God, conversion, participation, and unity. At the same time, it is most suitably implanted by God in all the hierarchies, comes upon them communicatively, and proceeds with most sacred adornment.

For this reason theology distributes our hierarchy among the Angels: it names Michael the ruler of the Jewish people [Col. 1057D] Daniel X, and others the friends of the nations. For it says: “The Most High established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” [Col. 1057D] Deuteronomy XXXII.

If someone should ask how the Hebrew people alone were led back to the thearchic illuminations, the answer must be that one should not accuse the Angels’ right knowledge because the other nations erred concerning gods who do not exist. Rather, those nations themselves fell away from the straight return toward the divine through their own deviations, through self-love, pride, and the worship of opinions that were at once divine and irrational [Col. 1057] E omits “and.”

The Hebrew people themselves are also said to have suffered this. “You have rejected the knowledge of God,” he says, “and you have gone after your heart” [Col. 1057D] Hosea IV; Jeremiah II.

For we do not have a compelled life, nor are the divine lights of providential illumination darkened by some power proper to the providential dispensations. Rather, the dissimilarity of intellectual visions, despite the superabundant goodness of the Father, causes the gift of light either not to be received at all, or not to be distributed for their reformation; or it produces participations that differ—small or great, obscure or clear—in the one, simple, and ever-unchanging ray that pours forth abundantly from its source [Col. 1057] B, E, and H omit “itself.”

Moreover, among the other nations—including those from whom we have come—the immense and abundant sea of divine light, prepared and open to all for participation, was not ruled by certain foreign gods. Rather, the Angels who governed each nation followed the one principle of all things and led them back to it.

Melchizedek must be understood as a high priest and as exceedingly dear to the Most High God who truly exists—not to gods that do not exist, but to that truly existent God himself [Col. 1057] A omits “himself.” Thus the theosophers simply called Melchizedek not only a friend of God but also a priest [Col. 1057D] Genesis XIV.

They did this so that the wise might understand clearly that he not only turned himself toward God, who truly is, but also, as a high priest, led others out toward the return to the true and only divinity. We shall also remind your supreme priestly understanding of this: when an angel ruled over Pharaoh among the Egyptians [Col. 1058D] Genesis XLI, and when there was assigned to the ruler of the Babylonians, according to the visions, a provident and authoritative guardian of the providence and dominion of all, leaders who were ministers of the true God were appointed over those nations. The disclosure by angels of the forms of the visions was immediately revealed by God through angels to the holy men Daniel and Joseph [Col. 1058D] Daniel II.

There is one principle and one providence over all things. One must in no way think that the Jews possessed the divinity fully, while the Angels possessed it only partially, or with equal honor, or in opposition; nor that other gods ruled the other nations. Rather, that oracle too must be understood according to its sacred meaning—not as though God divided our leadership with other gods or Angels, Israel competing for the leadership and rule of the nations—but as meaning that the single providence over all things distributed all human beings beneficially through the restoring guidance of their own Angels, while Israel alone, or nearly alone, among all, was turned toward the illumination and knowledge of the true Lord.

Hence, theology, signifying that Israel had become the possession of the true God’s service, says: “It became the Lord’s portion” [Col. 1058D] Psalm CXXXIV; Deuteronomy XXXII; Isaiah XIX.

Showing also that he allotted the other nations individually to one of the holy Angels, so that through that angel they might know the one principle of all things, theology says that Michael led the Jewish people [Col. 1058D] Daniel X. He thereby teaches us plainly that there is one providence over all, superessentially placed above all invisible and visible virtues, and that the Angels ruling each nation, following it as their own principle, extend each of those virtues toward it by essential will.

## CHAPTER X. Recapitulation and Gathering Together of the Angelic Order

Thus the most honorable disposition of the spirits around God is connected in this way. Sanctified by telarchic illumination [Col. 1057] A reads “ordered,” it ascends immediately toward the thearchy and is purified, illuminated, and perfected by the more hidden and the more manifest illumination of divinity [Col. 1057] “and illuminated and perfected” is omitted in B and H.

The hidden illumination is more invisible, more simplified, and more unified; the manifest illumination is given beforehand, shines first [Col. 1057] A and E read “shines,” is more universal, and has poured its form into it more fully, as is fitting.

From the first, proportionately, comes the second; from the second, the third; and from the third comes our hierarchy. According to the law of the well-ordered ordinance, it is hierarchically led back, in divine harmony and proportion, to the super-principial principle and consummation of every good adornment [Col. 1058D].

All are revealers of those who precede them: the most honorable reveal God, who moves them, while the rest proportionately reveal those moved by God. The superessential harmony of all things has foreseen for each rational and intellectual being as much sacred adornment and ordered leadership as each order of the hierarchies has been placed in a sacred and fitting manner. We see every hierarchy divided into first, middle, and last virtues.

It has also distinguished each disposition individually according to those divine harmonies. For this reason the most divine Seraphim themselves, the theologians say, cry out to one another [Col. 1059D] Isaiah VI, thereby clearly declaring, as I believe, that they themselves, being first, transmit theological knowledge to those who come second.

I might also add, not inappropriately, that every celestial and human spirit, considered in itself, has particular first, middle, and last orders and virtues. These are attached to it through each of the hierarchical illuminations, with their own ascents manifested proportionately [Col. 1059] E reads “manifest,” through which each becomes a participant, insofar as is lawful and possible for it, in the exceedingly unknowable purification, the fullest light, and the perfection perfected beforehand.

For nothing is perfect in itself and in need of universal perfection except what is truly most perfect and perfected beforehand.

## CHAPTER XI. Why All the Celestial Essences Are Commonly Called Celestial Virtues

Having established these matters, it is worth understanding why we customarily call all the angelic essences alike celestial virtues [Col. 1059] E reads “angelic virtues”; E reads “are called.”

We must not say that the order of the holy Virtues is last of all, and that the dispositions of the higher essences participate in the holy and beautiful illumination of the last orders, whereas the last orders in no way participate in the first. Why, then, are all the divine intellects called celestial Virtues, while the Seraphim, Thrones, and Dominions are not called so at all?

The outermost orders are indeed participated in by the highest universal properties. For the Angels themselves—and before the Angels, the Archangels, Principalities, and Powers—although ordered by theology after the Virtues, are often commonly called by us, in the same way as the other holy essences, celestial Virtues.

We say that, when we use the designation “celestial virtues” commonly of all of them, we do not introduce any confusion of the properties belonging to each disposition. Rather, since all the divine intellects are divided, according to their supermundane character, into three elements—essence, virtue, and operation—when we call all of them, or some of them, indiscriminately celestial essences or celestial virtues, we should understand that we designate them periphrastically by the essence or virtue belonging to each.

For we do not attach the property of the higher holy Virtues, already properly distinguished by us, to the lower essences as well, thereby confusing the ordinance of the angelic orders. According to the reasoning often correctly stated by us, the higher dispositions abundantly possess the sacred properties of the lower orders, but the last orders do not possess the superior universals of the greater orders. Those illuminations appear in them individually first and are distributed proportionately through the first orders [Col. 1059] B and H read “through the first.”

## CHAPTER XII. Why, Among Human Beings, the Hierarchs Are Called Angels

[The supplied source ends here.]

The following question also arises for those who diligently examine the intelligible utterances: if the participants in the higher orders are not the lowest, for what reason is the highest priest, the angel of the Lord Almighty, named by the utterances [Note: [Col. 1060D] Malachi 2:7; Revelation 2.] according to our usage [Col. 1060B]? There is, I think, no contradiction with what was defined earlier. For we say that the lowest orders are surpassed by the universal and superior virtue of the higher orders. The middle orders, however, participate proportionally, according to the one common and connective fellowship of all. Thus, for example, the order of the holy Cherubim participates in higher wisdom and knowledge; the orders of essences beneath them also participate in wisdom and knowledge, but in a manner particular and subordinate to those above.

Indeed, participation in wisdom [Note: [Col. 1059] “being” omitted by A.] and knowledge is common to all the godlike intelligences [Note: [Col. 1059] A: “intellects.”]; but participation attentively and primarily, secondarily, or at a lower level is by no means common [Col. 1060C], but is determined for each according to its own proper proportion. No one, I think, would err in defining this also of all divine minds. For just as the first orders possess abundantly the holy and beautiful properties of the lower orders, so the last possess those of the prior orders—not in the same manner, but in a subordinate degree.

There is therefore nothing disordered, I think, if theology also calls the angel the highest priest according to our usage: he participates, according to his own power, in the angelic function of making known, and is extended, as far as is possible for human beings, toward their manifest likeness. You will find, moreover, that theology calls even the celestial and heavenly essences “gods,” and calls among us men who are especially dear to God “divine” and “wondrous.” Yet the divine, by its superessential obscurity, is at once remote from and placed above all things, and none of the things that exist can properly and altogether be named by a likeness to it [Col. 1060D]. Nevertheless, whatever power of intellectual and rational beings is universally turned toward its unity, however slight that power may be, and is unceasingly [Note: [Col. 1059] E: “unceasingly.”] extended, as far as possible, toward its divine illuminations, has become worthy—if one may rightly say so—of divine imitation and divine univocation.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why the prophet Isaiah is said to have been purified by a Seraph

[Col. 1061A]

Let us examine this also according to its virtue: why do the theologians say that a Seraph was sent [Note: [Col. 1061D] Isaiah 6.]? Someone might explain that it was not one of the subordinate angels, but one of the beings belonging to the greatest essences, who purified the priest. Some therefore say that, in accordance with the definition of the fellowship of all intelligences previously given, the utterance does not name one of the first minds around God as having come for the theologian’s purification. Rather, it says that one of the angels superior to us, sanctifying the prophet’s purification, was called “Seraph” equivocally [Note: [Col. 1061] A*: “equivocally”], because of the fiery and heavenly removal of sins [Col. 1061B] and the raising of the purified person to divine obedience. They say that the utterance simply called him “one of the Seraphim,” not one of those stationed around God, but one of the purifying virtues superior to us.

Another person offered me a not altogether inappropriate defense of this position. He says that the great angel who was then forming the vision, in order to teach the divine theologian, assigned his own purifying sacrifice to God and, after God, to the first-working Hierarchy. Is this account therefore true?

The one who said this explains: How does divine virtue, coming to all things, fill them and reach through all things without measure, while again remaining invisible to all—not only as being superessentially remote from all, but also as secretly permitting its providential operations within all—yet shine proportionally upon all intellectual beings, imparting its own illumination and distributing itself beautifully through the most precious essences as through first mediators, according to the contemplative proportion of each disposition?

To state the matter more clearly, with examples proper to our condition, though inadequate to God who is remote from all things and yet more evident to us: the distributions of the sunbeam, when well apportioned to primary matter, fill everything with greater luminosity and through it more clearly disclose [Note: [Col. 1061] H: “disclose.”] their own splendors. When the beam approaches denser materials, however, it has a darker distributive manifestation, because the materials to be illuminated are unsuited to the distributive condition of illumination [Note: [Col. 1061] A*: “things”], and shortly afterward it is contracted from this state toward one that is almost completely undistributed [Col. 1061D].

Again, the heat of fire distributes itself more fully into things that are receptive and well suited to its likeness and that have been properly led toward it. But [Note: [Col. 1061] EH: “but.”] toward essences contrary to its transformations it reveals no trace of its primal operation, which remains hidden. This is especially so because what is not kindred to it first receives it through things suited to it—for instance, making things that have been set on fire easily movable by fiery things, and through these heating water or something else that does not readily catch fire, proportionally [Col. 1062A].

According to this principle of natural order, the whole supernatural power of the visible and invisible order of every good arrangement first manifests the clarity of fitting illumination, revealing it in abundant outpourings to the most excellent essences. Through those essences, the beings that come afterward participate in the divine ray. For these first beings [Note: [Col. 1061] A*: “For these indeed”; E: “These indeed”], knowing God and desiring his divine virtue in a supereminent manner, and becoming his first ministers insofar as possible, have been made worthy of a godlike virtue and activity. They extend the essences after them toward a similar virtue, in a godlike manner, as though they were themselves virtue, abundantly handing on to them the brightness that has come upon them; and those essences hand it on again to their subordinates. Through each order, the first passes it on to the one that follows it.

Does not water also reach all things proportionally? Thus God is at once the principle of the illumination of all illuminated things, naturally, truly, and properly: he is the essence of light and the cause of being and seeing. This remains godlike and God-like when each divine light placed above another carries itself into that which follows it.

Therefore all the remaining essences rightly regard the most excellent order of the heavenly minds as, after God, the source of all sacred and divine knowledge and of divine imitation, since through that order divine illumination is distributed to all and to us. For this reason they refer every sacred and God-like operation first to God as its cause [Col. 1062C]; then to the first godlike intellects as the first agents and teachers of divine things.

Does not the first disposition of the holy angels, more than all the others together, possess [Note: [Col. 1061] AEH: “possess.”] the fiery property, the outpoured transmission of divine wisdom, the mystical and most exalted knowledge of the divine illuminations, and the property of being seated, signifying divine reception? The dispositions of the subordinate essences participate in these fiery, wise, knowing, and God-receiving virtues, but at a lower level, looking toward the first orders and being brought, through them, as far as possible into godlikeness by imitation and by their having been made worthy to act as first ministers.

Thus the holy properties just mentioned, participation in which comes about through the first orders for those subsisting after them, are assigned to those orders themselves, after God, as to Hierarchies [Col. 1062D].

The one who said this explains [Note: [Col. 1062D] Isaiah 6.] that the vision was received by the theologian through one of the holy and blessed angels ruling over us [Note: [Col. 1061] AE: “by her”], and that, before guiding him illuminatively, the angel established him in that holy contemplation. He saw the highest essences seated, insofar as one may speak symbolically, after God and around God, with the supreme summit above the first-ranking virtues established in the middle.

The theologian therefore learned through the visions [Col. 1063A] that the divine is incomparably placed above every visible and invisible virtue according to every superessential transcendence; and that, because it is most remote from all things, it is universal and unlike even the first essences among existing things. He also learned that it is itself the principle and substantializing cause of all things, the immutable foundation in a unique secrecy of the things that are, from which even the most strongly fortified virtues receive their being and their well-being [Note: [Col. 1063] “fortified” omitted by EH].

Next he was taught that the same most holy Seraphim are godlike virtues and that, by their sacred name—which means “fiery,” about which we shall speak shortly, as far as possible for us—they introduce the ascending movements of the fiery virtue into godlikeness. Their wings, spread in a sacred formation toward the divine, signify, in the first, middle, and last intelligences, a complete and most exalted extension [Col. 1063B].

The intellectual theologian also saw their many wings and their manifold form: wings below their feet, wings below their faces, and wings always in motion in the middle. By these things he was led from what was seen to the invisible knowledge of what had been represented. The vision manifested to him the many ways and manifold forms of the virtue of the highest intelligences; their sacred fear, which they possess supermundanely before the proud, rash, and impossible investigation of higher and more difficult things; and the unceasing and lofty movement of their actions, which imitate God in due proportion.

He was also taught that divine and exceedingly precious hymnody, with the angel forming the vision according to the virtue of the theologian himself [Col. 1063C] and transmitting his own sacred knowledge. Thus the angel taught him that purification is, for those who have been purified to whatever degree, participation in divine clarity that is unknowable, insofar as participation is possible.

This divine clarity proceeds from the remote causes of divinity itself, which perfects all sacred intellects by its superessential concealment. It is more manifest to the highest virtues around God, and manifests and distributes itself more fully through them. Then, from the second, last, or human intellectual virtues, it brings its manifest illumination toward the praiseworthy unknowability of its own concealment, in proportion to the degree to which each has come forth according to a God-like pattern.

It shines through the secondary beings by means of the primary ones; and, if one must speak briefly, it is first led from concealment to manifestation through the first virtues [Col. 1063D]. The theologian therefore learned this from the angel who led him into the light: namely, that purification and all divine operations, shining through the first essences into all the rest, are distributed according to the proportion of each being’s capacity for deifying participation.

For this reason he appropriately assigned the fiery purifying property to the Seraphim, after God. There is therefore nothing disordered in saying that the Seraph purified the theologian. For God purifies all, since he is the cause of all purification.

To use a nearby example, as is our custom: when the highest priest purifies or illuminates through his ministers or priests, he himself is said to purify and illuminate, because the orders that have been purified through him refer their sacred operations to him as their source. Likewise, the angel who perfected the theologian’s purification, possessing the purifying knowledge and virtue, refers it to God as its cause and then to the Seraphim as the first agent and highest priest [Col. 1064A].

Someone might perhaps explain the matter with reverence for the angels as follows:

“Know that, before me, the beginning of the purification to be accomplished in you is the exalted one—the essence, Creator, and cause—who brings the first essences into being, holds them in their placement around himself, preserves them unturning and free from falling [Col. 1064B], and moves himself toward the first participations in his own providential operations.

“For this is what the mission of the Seraphim teaches me to reveal [Note: [Col. 1063] A: ‘command’]. The highest priest and leader after God is the order of the superior essences, from whom I have been taught to purify in a godlike manner. He is therefore purifying you through me; through him the very cause and maker of purification has brought forth from concealment and toward us his own providential actions.

“This is what he taught me; I in turn hand it on to you. You may, with your intellectual and discerning knowledge, either settle without hesitation either of the explanations I have given and honor it before the other, as consequential, reasonable, and equally true. Alternatively, you may discover for yourself what is nearer to the truth, or learn it from another—God granting this and revealing it through the more loving contemplation of those who first receive it, the angels, and of us, the friends of the angels” [Col. 1064C].

## CHAPTER XIV. What the transmitted number of the angels signifies [Note: [Col. 1063] E: “signifies.”]

This also deserves, I think, intellectual consideration: the tradition of the utterances says that there are “a thousand thousands” of angels [Note: [Col. 1063D] Daniel 7:10.] and “ten thousand times ten thousand” [Note: [Col. 1063] Thus AE; BH: “and hundreds”]. It rolls and multiplies the loftiest numbers back upon themselves and through them clearly signifies the innumerable orders of the heavenly essences.

For the blessed hosts of the supermundane intelligences are many, surpassing the weak and constricted measure of material numbers as we understand them. They are determined only by the knowledge bestowed upon them in the exceedingly rich gift of supermundane and heavenly intelligence and understanding: by the divinely sound, wisdom-making knowledge of the principle which exists superessentially as the cause giving substance to all things, the power containing them, and the perfection encompassing them [Col. 1064D].

## CHAPTER XV. What the formative images of the angelic virtues are

Come now, leaving aside, if it seems good, our intellectual eye, after its angelic strength has been directed toward sublime contemplations, and descending again into the manifold and multipartite breadth of the variety of the angels’ many forms, analytically reflecting upon them as though they were inconsequent things, toward the simplicity of the heavenly minds.

Let this be known to you beforehand: the explanations of the sacred formed images sometimes signify the dispositions of the heavenly essences as sanctifying, sometimes as sanctified, and again as the first, middle, and last orders which are sanctified and sanctify; and they represent the same beings, as has been said, as possessing first, middle, and last virtues. No disorder is introduced by this manner of explanation.

If we were to say that some are sanctified by those before them, and then that the same prior beings sanctify them, and again that the sanctifiers of the last are sanctified by those very ones whom they sanctified [Col. 1065B], there would truly be disorder and great confusion. But if we say that the same beings both sanctify and are sanctified, yet never by the same beings or by the same ones, but that each is sanctified by those before it and sanctifies those after it, someone might perhaps reasonably say that the forms sacredly produced in the utterances can beautifully and truly surround the first, last, and middle virtues.

Their being extended upward in a reversible manner [Note: [Col. 1065] B: “conversably”], firmly coiled around themselves as the guardians of their own virtues, and moving sociably toward what comes after them, providentially participating in virtue, will unite [Note: [Col. 1065] A: “united.”] all the heavenly essences—not falsely—although some are superior and universal, as has often been said, and others particular and subordinate [Col. 1065C].

We must begin our account and inquire, in the first explanation of the forms, why theology is found to honor, above almost all other things, the fiery sacred description.

You will find that it not only forms fiery wheels, but also fiery living creatures, men flashing like fire [Note: [Col. 1065] BEH: “shining like lightning”], heaps of fiery coals around the heavenly essences, and rivers blazing with fire and making an immeasurable sound [Note: [Col. 1065D] Ezekiel 1; Daniel 7; 2 Kings 2]. It also says that the Thrones are fiery, and indicates by their name that the highest Seraphim themselves burn from heaven. It assigns to them the property and operation of fire, and generally honors, selectively, the fiery construction of the forms both above and below.

I therefore judge that the fiery signifies the most God-like quality of the heavenly minds. For the holy theologians themselves [Note: [Col. 1066D] Hebrews 10.] often describe the superessential and formless essence as fire, as possessing—if one may say so—many images of divine properties insofar as these can appear in visible things.

Sensible fire is, so to speak, clearly present in all things and through all things, and is removed from all things. It is simultaneously more luminous [Note: [Col. 1065] EH: “more luminous.”] and, as it were, hidden, unknown in itself when no material is present in which it may manifest [Note: [Col. 1065] AE: “manifests.”] its proper operation. It is immeasurable and invisible in itself; at once capable of all things; it makes whatever exists in things become active according to its own operation [Note: [Col. 1065] “and whatever is made in them” omitted by BH]; it is mobile and gives itself to all things that approach it in any way.

It preserves and renews nature; it illuminates by its enveloping radiance; it is incomprehensible, bright, distinct, rebounding, bearing upward, moving sharply, exalted, not admitting insult through diminution, always in motion, moving through itself, moving something else, comprehending, itself incomprehended, needing nothing else, truly hidden, growing from itself, and revealing its magnitude through the materials that receive it. It is active and powerful, invisibly present to all things at once. It is thought not to be neglected, but, through friction, as though by a kind of natural and proper vengeance, it suddenly shines out [Col. 1066B]; then again it is incomprehensibly intangible and is not diminished in all its richest self-distributions.

One may perhaps find many other beautiful properties of fire, as visible images of divine operation. Knowing this, therefore, the theosophists form the heavenly essences from fire, signifying their God-like nature and their imitation of God insofar as possible.

They also describe them in human form, because of their intellectual and upward-looking contemplative virtues; because of their upright and luminous shape [Note: [Col. 1065] DH: “shape.”]; because they are naturally principal and royal; because, although they are least in sense when compared with the other virtues of irrational animals, they are most powerful in virtue according to the greatness of their intellects; because of their continuity in rational knowledge [Note: [Col. 1065] BH: “continuously”]; and because of their freedom and supreme power according to the nature of the soul [Col. 1066C].

In each of these features, I think, one can also find the heavenly virtues represented through the divisions of our own many-parted body. The powers of sight signify their clearest gaze toward the divine lights, and again their tender, fluid, unobstructed, sharply mobile, pure, and level reception of the divine illuminations, without suffering. The powers of smell signify their receptivity, insofar as possible, to the distribution of the sweet fragrance that surpasses intellect, and their discernment of and complete avoidance of what is not of this kind.

The powers of hearing signify their capacity to participate in and know divine inspiration. The powers of taste signify the fullness of invisible foods and their receptivity to divine and nourishing advances [Col. 1066D]. The powers of touch signify the discernment, by knowledge, of what is suitable or harmful.

The eyelids and eyebrows signify the guardianship of understanding of divine visions. Youth and maturity signify the ever-renewing vital virtue. Teeth signify the division of the perfection of the nourishment imparted. For every intellectual essence divides and multiplies, by its providential virtue, the unified understanding bestowed upon it by the more divine essence, leading it according to the proportion of what is lower [Col. 1067A].
