The shoulders, arms, and hands signify what makes, operates, and acts. The heart is a symbol of God-like life, sowing its own vital virtue in a godlike manner within the things understood beforehand. The breasts signify what is firm and protective around the life-giving distribution proceeding from the heart. The back signifies the continuous character of all the fertile virtues together.

The feet signify the mobile, swift, and running movement of one who is always proceeding toward divine things. For this reason theology also depicted the feet of the holy intelligences as winged [Note: [Col. 1067D] Ezekiel 1]. “Winged” signifies the upward-moving speed, the active quality of heavenly travel upward, and the power that bears one away from every lowly thing toward the heights.

The lightness of the wings itself signifies that nothing earthly remains, but that everything ascends cleanly and without heaviness into the heights [Col. 1067B]. Being naked, unshod [Note: [Col. 1067D] Genesis 18–19], unclothed, and free signifies what is immeasurable and pure, assimilated, insofar as possible, to divine simplicity through the addition of nothing external.

Yet because the simple and exceedingly varied Wisdom also clothes the naked and gives them certain vessels to carry, let us therefore [Note: [Col. 1067] BH: “but.”] disclose, insofar as possible, the sacred garments and instruments of the heavenly minds.

I judge that a bright and fiery garment [Note: [Col. 1067D] Revelation 1.] signifies what is God-like according to the image of fire and luminous, because of the heavenly places of rest where there is light—or, to speak more precisely, what intellectually illuminates or is intellectually illuminated. A priestly garment signifies what leads toward divine and mystical contemplations and toward the vow of one’s whole life [Col. 1067C].

Belts signify the guarding of the fertile virtues themselves, gathering their disposition together into a unified turning upon itself, and circling around itself with the ease of a nature free from falling, in resemblance to a circle. Rods signify what is royal and governing, defining all things uprightly [Note: [Col. 1067] BH: “and defining all things uprightly”]. Weapons and axes signify the separation of dissimilarities, the sharpness of discerning virtues, and what is effective and active.

Geometrical and architectural instruments signify what lays foundations, builds, and perfects, together with all the other things belonging to the providence that leads secondary beings upward and turns them back.

Sometimes, too, those instruments enacted by the holy angels are symbols of divine judgments directed toward us. Some manifest corrective discipline or punitive justice; others, a restriction of freedom, the end of discipline, the resumption of former steadfastness [Note: [Col. 1067] A: “beneficence”], or the opposition of other gifts, whether small or great, sensible or invisible [Note: [Col. 1067D] Ezekiel 10; Judges 6; 2 Maccabees 5; Ezekiel 41; [Col. 1068D] Revelation 21; Revelation 3; Zechariah 8]. A discerning mind perhaps would not hesitate to join visible things beautifully to invisible things.

The angels’ being called winds signifies their swiftness and the effect that reaches almost everything without delay; it signifies their movement from above toward what is below and their upward-moving transport, raising the secondary beings to higher elevation and moving the first beings toward the communicative and providential procession of the lower [Note: [Col. 1068D] Genesis 28; John 1].

Someone might perhaps say that the airy spirits’ being called winds signifies the God-like nature of the heavenly beings. For this too bears the image and form of divine operation, as has been demonstrated in several ways in the symbolic theology through a fourfold analysis: according to the motive, generative, swift, and powerful capacity of nature, and according to the hidden retreat of the moving principles and consummations, which is unknown and invisible to us.

“For you do not know,” he says, “from where it comes or where it goes” [Note: [Col. 1068D] John 3:8; Isaiah 5.].

Theology also gives them [Note: [Col. 1067] “also” omitted by A.] the appearance of clouds, signifying by this that the sacred intelligences are supermundanely filled with hidden light. In their first appearance they receive the first manifestation with splendor, and they distribute it abundantly, brightly, and proportionally to the things that come second. Their generative, life-giving, active, and perfecting nature subsists according to the intellectual conception of rains, which, received into moist hollows, are drawn forth into vital processes [Col. 1068B].

Theology also places around the heavenly essences the appearance of air, amber, and many-colored stones [Note: [Col. 1068D] Isaiah 55; Revelation 1; Daniel 2]. Amber, being at once gold-like and silver-like, signifies a splendor that is incorruptible as gold, generous, undiminished, and undefiled, as well as open, luminous, and heavenly as silver. Bronze, according to the transmitted accounts, should be understood either as fiery or as gold-like [Col. 1068C].

The appearance of many-colored stones should be judged to signify either, in the case of white stones, something luminous; in the case of red stones, something gold-like; or, in the case of pale stones, something youthful and new. In each appearance you will find an ascending interpretation of the symbolic images.

Since I think that we have said enough concerning these matters according to their virtue, let us pass to the sacred explanation of the heavenly minds’ sacredly figured animal forms.

The lion should be understood to signify what is lordly, strong, untamed, and the hiddenness of the ineffable divinity: a power assimilating the intellectual traces, by their veiling and perhaps splendid mystical covering, to the path restored within itself according to divine illumination [Col. 1068D].

The ox signifies what is strong and youthful, broad for intellectual furrows receiving the heavenly and generative rains, protective and most powerful [Note: [Col. 1067] BH: “to”].

The eagle signifies what is royal, exalted, swift-moving, sharp and sober in relation to powerful nourishment, agile and well contrived, and immediately, directly, and inflexibly contemplative toward the abundant and many-luminous ray of the divine sun, through the healthy eyes of the contemplative virtues, in longing for it [Col. 1069A].

The horse signifies what is obedient and governable by the bridle. The white horse signifies what is truly luminous and, as it were, most closely related to the divine light. The black horse signifies what is hidden. The red horse signifies what is fiery and active. The horses mingled from white and black signify the perfecting virtue that joins the extremes, connecting the first with the second and the second with the first, reversibly and providentially [Note: [Col. 1069] “and the second with the first” omitted by EH].

If we did not consider the proportion of speech and were to unite the properties of the animals mentioned, together with all their bodily formations, perhaps we could not inappropriately apply them to the heavenly virtues according to dissimilar likenesses. Fury signifies their intellectual courage, whose ultimate expression of fury is sound [Col. 1069B]. Desire signifies divine love. In short, to say it all, we lead back all the senses and manifold parts of irrational animals into the intellectual perceptions and unified virtues of the immaterial heavenly essences [Note: [Col. 1069] E: “completely”; [Col. 1069] “in” omitted by AEH].

These things are sufficient for the wise—not only the things themselves, but also the interpretation of one significant image as a disclosure of those near it in a similar manner.

We should also examine the fact that rivers, wheels, and connected chariots are said to belong to the heavenly essences [Note: [Col. 1069D] Daniel 7; Ezekiel 1, 10]. Fiery rivers signify divine advances, granting them an abundant and unfailing flow and nourishing them with life-giving fertility. Chariots signify the connective fellowship of likenesses [Note: [Col. 1069D] 2 Kings 1; Ezekiel 1].

Wheels, since they are winged and move unturningly and inflexibly toward what lies before them, signify, through the straight and just path of their superior operation, their virtue directed without deviation along the same straight path, while their entire intellectual rotation is directed supermundanely [Col. 1070A].

The symbolic description of the intellectual wheels can also be interpreted by another ascending interpretation. For, as the theologian says, they were called “galgal galgal galgal” [Note: [Col. 1069] Conjecture; manuscripts and Greek text: γελ γελ γελ]. This signifies, according to the Hebrew word, “revolutions” or “revelations” [Note: [Col. 1069] “or revelations” omitted by BE].

The fiery and God-like wheels have revolutions around the same supreme object, in an ever-moving motion. They also have revelations, through the manifestation of hidden things, the return of what surrounds them, and the perfecting guidance of higher illuminations toward the things beneath them [Note: [Col. 1069] Thus AE; BH: “revolutions”; [Col. 1069] “and God-like … revolutions” omitted by BH].

Our remaining subject is an explanation of the joy of the heavenly orders. For they are in no way receivers of the passible pleasure that exists among us. They are said to rejoice with God over the finding of the lost [Note: [Col. 1070D] Luke 15], according to a God-like feasting, and over the God-like character of those who return to God in providence and salvation, in abundant gladness and in that ineffable steadfastness in which holy men have often participated through the God-like arrival of divine illuminations [Col. 1070B].

This is as much as I have said about the holy forms. We have fallen short of a careful exposition of them. Having completed this, I think, we must not remain unworthily in figurative imaginings.

But if you also ask why we have not recorded, in the utterances, all the angelic virtues, operations, or images, we answer truthfully that, regarding those whose supermundane knowledge we do not possess, we ourselves need another lucid teacher [Note: [Col. 1070D] Tobit 12]. Some things, though equally powerful with what has been said, we have omitted, taking thought for the proportion of our discourse and honoring by silence what is secret and beyond us [Col. 1070C].

The book on the Celestial Hierarchy is complete.

You have poured forth the illuminations of the angelic descriptions and revealed to human beings the vision of the star composed in the mind.

# THE SECOND BOOK OF SAINT DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE, ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL HIERARCHY

[Col. 1069]

## EPIGRAM ON THE BLESSED DIONYSIUS, ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL HIERARCHY

The symbols of the divine and wondrous sacred things, receiving in a uniform narrative the one radiance of the one light in singleness.

## THE CHAPTERS OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL HIERARCHY BEGIN

[Note: [Col. 1069] E: “These are all seven chapters in this work on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.”]

[Col. 1070D]

To the fellow presbyter Timothy: Dionysius the Presbyter.

I. What the tradition of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy is, and what its contemplation is.

II. Concerning those being perfected in illumination.

III. Concerning those being perfected in the synaxis.

IV. Concerning those being perfected in the myron, and in what is offered in it.

V. Concerning priestly consummations.

[Col. 1071A]

VI. Concerning the orders of those being perfected.

VII. Concerning those being perfected among the departed.

He completes the doctrine of the preceding chapters in a twofold manner. First, he explains how the mystery of the chapter is accomplished, and then he gives a certain theory of it: for example, first the exposition of the mystery of illumination, and then its second theory. Again, the exposition of the mystery of the synaxis, and then its theory.

# THE BOOK ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL HIERARCHY BEGINS

## CHAPTER I. What the tradition of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy is, and what its contemplation is

[Col. 1071A]

[Cols. 1071B–1074B] Since, as we understand it, the most sacred Hierarchy of the divine children is held to be deifying knowledge, activity, and consummation, it is necessary for us to set forth, from the supermundane and most sacred utterances, the rite of sacred perfection, τελετή, for those who have been perfected through hierarchical sacraments and traditions. But observe how one must not approach the holy of holies from the beginning. If, however, you also honor the secret things of God through intellectual and invisible sciences, preserving these things—unparticipated and undefiled—from the imperfect, you will communicate them in holiness and beauty only to the sacred, with the sacred illumination of holy things.

For thus, as theology has handed down to us in its praises of God, Jesus himself—the most divine Mind and superessential one, the principle, essence, and most divine power of every Hierarchy, sanctification, and deification—shines upon the blessed and upon the essences superior to us, more significantly and intellectually, and assimilates them to his own light according to their capacity. He draws our minds toward himself, and, extending himself toward us through good love, gathers together our many differences, bringing us to a uniform and divine life, state, and activity; and he bestows upon us the holy and beautiful power of divine priesthood [Note: BE: “divine priestly”].

Then, coming to the sacred activity of the divine priesthood, we are brought nearer to the likeness, according to their capacity, of the essences above us, whose sacred state is abiding and unchanging. Gazing from this likeness [Note: BH: “from”] toward the blessed and divine radiance of Jesus, and investigating whatever it is possible to see, illuminated sacredly by contemplations of knowledge, consecrated to the mystical discipline and consecrating others, we may become light-bearing and godlike, perfected and more perfect.

There is, then, a Hierarchy of Angels and Archangels, of the supermundane Principalities, Powers, and Virtues, of Dominions and divine Thrones, or of essences equal in power to the Thrones. Theology teaches that these are attentively and always around God and after God, naming them Cherubim and Seraphim in the language of the Hebrews. If you follow the holy orders and divisions of their adornments and Hierarchies, you will find in them, in a manner not indeed proportionate to them but as far as possible, and as theology has introduced it through the most sacred Scriptures, our own Hierarchy praised alongside theirs.

It is necessary, however, to say only this: that both that Hierarchy and every Hierarchy now praised as superior to us possess one and the same power throughout every hierarchical activity; and that the supreme priest, according to essence, analogy, and order, is perfected beside him in divine things, is deified, and hands these things on to his subjects according to each one’s worth, divine sacred deification having been effected in him. The subjects follow those who are superior, while extending the lesser toward the things that are before them. Some also preside and, as far as possible, lead others, and through this divine and hierarchical harmony, truly subsisting in what is good, wise, and best, each participates in the virtues.

The essences and orders superior to us, of which we have already made sacred mention, are incorporeal and invisible, and their Hierarchy is supermundane. Our own Hierarchy, however, we see multiplied proportionately to ourselves in the variety of sensible symbols. Through these we are hierarchically led toward uniform deification (theosis), within the measure appropriate to us, and toward God and divine power. Those beings, as intellects, understand according to what is permitted to them; we, through sensible images, are led back, as far as possible, to divine contemplations.

It must truly be said that the object of all is one, toward which all desire uniformity; but they do not participate uniformly in the same one being. Rather, the divine yokes [Note: BH: “rights”] distribute to each a portion according to its worth. These matters, however, must be discussed at much greater length in the treatise concerning the visible and sensible activity [Note: ABE: “concerning invisible things”; E omits “concerning”].

Now I shall attempt to speak of our Hierarchy and of its principle and essence, invoking Jesus, the principle and consummation of all Hierarchies. A Hierarchy, according to the honorable account of our sacred tradition, is the entire order of all sacred things subject to it, whether this be the most universal account of the Hierarchy or its consummation of sacred things.

Our Hierarchy, then, is called and is the comprehensive sacred activity of all the things belonging to it. Through it the divine Hierarch, being perfect, possesses participation in all the most sacred things proper to him; hence he is called a Hierarch. For just as one who speaks of a Hierarchy speaks of the whole sacred arrangement comprehended together, so one who speaks of a Hierarch declares a wondrous and divine man, learned in every sacred science, in whom the entire Hierarchy is purely perfected and known.

The principle of this Hierarchy is the Trinity, the fountain of life, the essence of goodness, the one cause of all existing things, from which, through goodness, both being and well-being subsist. Since this most divine summit and principal blessedness is triune and one, truly existing in a manner incomprehensible to us, its most desirable will is the rational salvation both of us and of the essences above us.

This cannot occur in any other way than through the deification of those who are saved. Deification is likeness to and union with God, insofar as this is possible. The common summit of every Hierarchy is attentive love directed toward God and divine things, divinely and powerfully offered in sacrifice; a perfect and irreversible turning away from their opposites; knowledge of the things that are—the intellectual truth and vision and knowledge of what is; uniform participation in consummation; and, insofar as possible, refreshment through contemplation of the One himself, invisibly nourishing and deifying everyone who stretches toward him.

Let us therefore say how divine blessedness—the divine nature and principle of deification—from which those who are deified are deified through divine goodness, has bestowed upon the Hierarchy the salvation and unity of all rational and intellectual essences. It bestows this upon the supermundane and blessed orders in a more immaterial and intellectual manner. For God does not move them toward divine things from outside; rather, illuminated invisibly and inwardly, they possess within themselves that pure, immaterial, and most divine will.

To us, however, what is given to them uniformly and in immediate connection has been granted, through the utterances handed down from God, as far as possible for us, in the variety and multiplicity of divisible symbols. The essence of our Hierarchy is the utterances handed down by God. By these most holy utterances we mean all those things granted to us by our divine sacred perfecters in sacred and theological writings [the reading “deltis” is uncertain]. Moreover, they include whatever our sacred teachers have learned from those holy men through more immaterial instruction, and in a manner already resembling the celestial Hierarchy, from intellect to intellect by means of bodily speech, though more immaterially and outside written texts.

Nor did these divine high priests hand these things down to the common assembly in sacrifice without veils, but in sacred symbols. For not everyone is pure, nor does everyone possess knowledge, as the utterances say [Note: John XIII; 1 Corinthians VIII].

It was therefore necessary that the first leaders of our Hierarchy, filled with the superessential divinity and with the divine gift, and then sent forth by divine goodness [Note: H: “piety”] to go before others toward the same end, should themselves, as lovers of those who followed them and as gods, lead them back and deify them. Through sensible images, in a connected variety and multiplicity, they gave us, in their written and unwritten teachings, supercelestial things in human forms, divine things in material forms, and superessential things in forms belonging to us, according to the sacred laws:

not merely because of the impure, for whom it is not lawful even to touch the symbols, but also because it—the Hierarchy—is in some respect symbolic. As I have said, our Hierarchy is proportionate to ourselves, desiring, through sensible things, to lead us from them toward invisible things and toward our more divine restoration.

The meanings of the symbols, however, must be revealed to divine sacred perfecters. It is not right to disclose them to those who are still being perfected. For they know that the legislators, when God handed down the sacred things, arranged the Hierarchy through the established and undisturbed orders of its adornments, with each person receiving his share according to his worth and in proportion to the sacred distributions.

Therefore, trusting your sacred confessions—for it is holy to remember them—you will not hand over all the holy hierarchical praise placed above you [Note: E: “hierarchical praise according to the praise”] to another, contrary to the deiform sacred perfecters ordered equally with you. You will allow them, according to hierarchical law, to confess: the pure to touch pure things; the divine deifying things to be communicated only to the deifying; the perfective things to the perfect; and the most holy things to the holiest. I have handed this and other hierarchical matters on to you as a divine gift.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning those perfected in illumination [Cols. 1074B–1079D]

We have therefore said sacredly what the interpretation of the Hierarchy is according to us: our likeness to and union with God, insofar as this is permitted. Through love of the most devout commandments and through sacred activities, as the divine utterances teach, we are joyfully perfected in this. “For,” he says, “the one who loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” [Note: John XIV, 23; “my” is omitted by B and E].

The tradition of our sacred regeneration is therefore a principle of the sacred activity of the most holy commandments. It forms our animal nature into a condition receptive of the other divine utterances and sacred activities, and makes our path a leading upward toward supercelestial rest. For, as our common leader says, according to intellect the primordial movement toward divine things is in God and in divine love; the most principal procession toward the sacred activity of the divine commandments is our ineffable creation by God.

If being by God is divine generation, would anyone at some time have known what has been entrusted by God? [Note: A: “by no means.”] Or would he have acted [Note: H adds “for”] who had not received divine subsistence? Or should we say that we must first subsist humanly and then act according to our human condition? How could someone who does not exist, and possesses neither movement nor subsistence [Note: E: “possesses that, existing”; A: “possesses it, existing that”], act or suffer only in those things in which he has come into being? This, I think, is clear.

We shall next examine the symbols of divine generation [Note: “divine” is omitted by BH]. Let no imperfect person come to the contemplation. It is not without danger to gaze upon the sun’s rays with weak pupils, nor is it harmless to dare to approach the things above us. If the Hierarchy according to the law is true, it overthrew Uzziah because he abused sacred things; Korah because he reached beyond his station in sacred matters; and Nadab and Abihu because they profanely abused their own sacred office [Note: 2 Chronicles XXVI; Numbers XVI; Leviticus X].

### The mystery of illumination

The supreme priest, continually desiring all human beings to be saved in likeness to God and to come to the knowledge of the truth [Note: 1 Timothy II], proclaims to all the true Gospels: that God, through his own existing and natural goodness, is propitious toward those on earth; that he considers it worthy to come sufficiently toward union with them through his humanity; and that he assimilates those united to himself, like fire, adapting them to himself according to his own purpose.

“For as many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” [Note: John I, 12].

Whoever truly loves participation in these supermundane things comes to one of the learned and persuades him to lead him along the way to the supreme priest. The learned man promises to follow him in every respect and to receive knowledge both of his worthy approach and of the whole life that follows from it, after the Hierarch has sacredly questioned him concerning his salvation.

When the human mind, measuring itself against the height of the matter, is suddenly surrounded by terror and a sense of impossibility, yet these things pass away, and the Hierarch perfects what has been requested, once the candidate has confessed it in a godlike manner. The one who receives him leads him to the person named from the Hierarchy.

Receiving him joyfully, as though carrying a sheep upon his shoulders [Note: Luke XV], the Hierarch first praises, together with the two men mentioned above, through intellectual Eucharists and bodily worship, the one benevolent principle from whom those who are called are called and those who are saved are saved.

Then, gathering the entire sacred order into cooperation and festivity with the man’s salvation and with the divine Eucharist of divine goodness, he first chants a hymn, resting upon the utterances, to all the fullness of the Church. After this he greets the divine table, approaches the man who has come, and asks him what he desires in coming.

When the man religiously confesses, according to the tradition of the sponsor, his unbelief, ignorance of the true good, and indifference to the divine life [Note: BH omits “indifference to the divine life”], and declares that through the sacred mediation he desires to attain divine things from God, the Hierarch testifies that universal propitiation will benefit him, since God is most perfect and undefiled.

Introducing him to the divine way of life, he asks whether he has lived in this manner. After the confession, he places his hand upon the man’s head, makes the sign, and orders the priests to register the man and his sponsor. While they register them, he offers the sacred prayer. When the whole Church has completed it in this manner, he admits the man and has him undressed by the ministers.

Then he sets him facing west and raising his hands toward that region. He orders him to renounce Satan three times and to confess the remaining elements of the renunciation. After he has pronounced the renunciation over him three times and the man has confessed it three times, he leads him toward the east. Having him look toward heaven and extend his hands, he orders him to be enrolled with Christ and with all the sacred utterances entrusted by God.

When the man has done this also, the Hierarch again attests the confession three times. After the man has confessed three times, the Hierarch prays, blesses him, and lays his hands upon him.

Finally, when the ministers have stripped him, the priests bring the sacred oil of anointing. The Hierarch begins the anointing by making the sign three times, then entrusts the rest to the priests, who anoint the man over his entire body.

He comes to the mother of sonship. Then, sanctifying the water with sacred invocations, perfecting it with three cruciform outpourings of the most holy chrism, and harmonizing with equal numbers of the most sacred applications of chrism a melodious chant inspired by the sacred and God-pleasing prophets, he orders the man to be brought.

One of the priests proclaims the sponsor from the registration. The man is led by the priests to the water and to the hand of the supreme priest. Having been led by the hand to him, the supreme priest stands above him, while the priests at the water again call out the name of the one being perfected to the supreme priest.

The supreme priest baptizes him three times, with three immersions and emergences, invoking the triune substance of divine blessedness. The priests receive him and hand him over to the sponsor and the guide. Taking with him the clothing of the one being perfected, they bring him back united to the supreme priest [Note: AE: “united,” rather than “together”].

The Hierarch marks the man with the most deifying ointment and thereafter manifests him as a participant in the most perfect sacred Eucharist. Having completed these things, he proceeds from this state [Note: AE: “itself”] in himself toward what follows and again stretches his contemplation toward the first things, as though he would never remain for any time or in any manner in something alien to what belongs to him, but, attending always to divine things within divine things, would continually be reordered by the divine Spirit.

### Theoria

Thus, insofar as it is expressed in symbols, the divine generation of the sacred offering possesses nothing unbecoming or unclean, nor does it derive its character from sensible things; rather, it represents through natural and humanly appropriate mirrors the riddles of contemplation worthy of God.

For what if the candidate comes forward, sins, and consults the more divine account that is silent concerning those being perfected, while sacredly performing the divine teaching’s vivification of the one who has come, and at the same time proclaiming to him, through the water’s purification, the cleansing of every form of wickedness by an excellent and divine life?

Even if the symbolic tradition of the things being perfected possessed nothing more divine than this, it would not, I think, be unclean. It introduces the teaching of right living [Note: “introducing rightly”] and confirms the complete release from a life of wickedness by the natural purification of the body through water.

Let this, then, be an introductory activity of the souls of the imperfect, distinguishing them, as far as permitted, from the multitude through hierarchical and uniform things, and making the unstructured height manageable for impure orders.

But as we look through sacred ascents toward the principles of the perfect, and are divinely instructed in them, we shall recognize whose characters these are and whose invisible realities they represent. For, as was clearly discussed in the treatise concerning invisible and sensible activity [Note: E: “is discussed”], some things are sensible representations of invisible things [Note: BH omits “representations of invisible things”], and in them there is a leading by the hand and a way. The invisible things, however, are the principle and knowledge of those belonging to the senses.

Let us therefore say how the goodness of divine blessedness, always possessing its beneficent rays in the same manner and according to the same principles, pours them abundantly upon all intellectual faces.

If anyone withdraws from invisible light or from invisible things, in arrogance and self-sufficiency, being instructed by love of wickedness, the power naturally diffused within him for illumination is suspended. He looks away from the light that is present—not because the light has withdrawn, but because it shines above him—and thus turns away from what encounters him in a godlike manner.

If he leaps beyond the visible visions moderately granted to him and dares confidently to gaze upon the radiances above his own face, the light will accomplish nothing beyond light. But because he desires the perfect imperfectly, he will not even understand what cannot be attained; and because he contemptuously despises the humble and unadorned, the light itself refutes him.

Nevertheless, what I have said remains true: the divine light is always beneficently extended over intellectual faces, and they possess the capacity to receive it when it is present. The transmission of their own things toward God is always ready in a fitting manner.

The divine supreme priest is reformed according to this likeness. He pours abundantly over all the light-bearing radiances of his divine teaching, and, as an imitator of God, is exceedingly ready to illuminate the one who comes—not enviously, nor using anything immoderately from his former apostasy, but hierarchically shining through his divinely originating acts of leading into the light, in the good beauty, order, and proportion appropriate to each person’s sacred measure.

Since God is the principle of sacred ordering, the sacred intellects, insofar as they know themselves, return to the visible reality corresponding to nature. At the beginning, each person will see what he is and will first receive this gift by turning toward the sacred light.

Whoever observes his own condition with eyes made impassible by goodness will turn away from the darkness of ignorance, which does not shine. But the imperfect person will not desire the perfect unity and participation in God [Note: B: “not from there”]. Through his own first things, then through things still prior, and through those toward what is superior, he will ascend in order and sacredly into the most exalted divine communion.

The ornament and image of the sacred order consists in the confusion of the one who comes, in his knowledge of the things that are proper to himself [Note: BH: “himself”], and in his having as teacher and guide on the way to the supreme priest the sponsor.

As he ascends in this manner, divine blessedness receives him into its participation and hands him its own light as a kind of sign. It makes him divine and a communicant in divine things, in their distribution and sacred ordering. Their symbol is the sacred sign given by the supreme priest to the one who comes, together with the priests’ salutary registration: it counts him among the saved and places him with the sponsor in the sacred records, as one who truly loves and follows the life-giving way toward the truth, leading him as a divine guide and one who follows without wandering the guidance entrusted by God.

But it is not possible [Note: BH: “is”] to participate simultaneously in utterly opposed things, nor to possess divided lives while having some communion with the One. If a person receives firm participation in the One, he cannot at the same time be immoderate and disordered in every division that opposes uniformity.

The tradition of the symbols intimates this sacredly. It strips the one who comes as though of his former life and loosens his last habits according to that life. It sets him naked and unshod, looking toward the west and rejecting, by the renunciation of his hands, communion with obscure wickedness, as though he were expiring from the innate habit of dissimilarity, and it makes him confess universally.

Having thus made him wholly immeasurable and nonparticipating in the former things, it leads him toward the east, allowing him to look toward the state that is to come in divine light, in a pure return from wickedness toward what is most perfect. It receives his sacred confessions with a rational gaze directed toward the One, in a uniform love of truth.

Here, I think, it is clear to those learned in hierarchical things that, once those who resist the One have been overcome by strength, and once the universal destructions and non-subsistences of opposites have occurred, the intellectual condition of the godlike prevails immutably.

For it is not enough merely to turn away from every wickedness. One must also be stationed manfully and fearlessly against subjection to the ruin that lies within it, and must never allow the temple of truth to be in repose. Rather, one must attend to it eternally and stretch out toward it as a power, always sacredly active in the most perfect ascent of divinity.

You can see careful images of these things in those being hierarchically perfected. The godlike supreme priest begins the sacred anointing, while the priests under him complete the sacrifice of anointing, summoning the candidates to sacred contests in likeness to those according to which he was made a soldier under Christ.

For, as God, he is the creator of the army; as wise, he established its laws; and, as good, he prepared beautiful prizes for the victors. More divinely still, since he became excellent among the soldiers, he struggled with them sacredly for their freedom and victory, contending against the power of death and corruption. As perfect God, he ascended joyfully with those who contended.

He remains, however, within the legislation of the wise, and according to it he contends without transgression, firmly possessing the hope of good prizes, ordered under the best Lord and leader of the army.

Following the divine footsteps of the first soldiers in goodness, and imitating God through his military service, he resists the activities and subsistences opposed to God and struggles toward deification. Through baptism he dies together with Christ—mystically, that is, to sin.

With me he understands wisely how beautifully the sacred symbols are composed. For since death exists in us—not a death of essence or subsistence, as some have thought, but a separation of united things, which leads us invisibly to the dissolution of the soul from the body, the soul as destined always to be deprived of the body, and the body as hidden in the earth or destroyed according to some other transformation of bodily things—this universal concealment through water is beautifully received as an image of the formlessness of death and burial.

The sacred symbolic teaching of those being baptized therefore teaches mystically, through three immersions in the water, the imitation of the death of Jesus, the giver of life, in the three days and an equal number of nights in the tomb, insofar as divine imitation is possible for human beings. In this death, according to the mystical and hidden tradition of the utterance, the ruler of the world finds nothing [Note: John XIV].

Then they clothe the perfected person in garments of light. Through the manly and godlike impassibility toward opposites, and through the firm gaze directed toward the One, what was unadorned is adorned and what was formless is given form, shining everywhere with a life of light.

The perfective anointing with ointment makes the perfected person fragrant. For the sacred consummation of divine generation unites those who have been perfected with the divine Spirit. I permit those worthy, according to intellect, to recognize intellectually the invisible, fragrant, and perfective advent of the ineffable one through the sacred and deifying communion of the divine Spirit.

Finally, the supreme priest calls the perfected person to the most sacred Eucharist and gives him participation in the perfective mysteries.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning those perfected in the synaxis [Cols. 1079D–1081C]

Come, then—for since we have mentioned this, it would not be right for me to praise anything else among the hierarchical rites before it. According to our glorious teacher, it is the rite of rites (teletarum teleta).

It is necessary, before the other rites, to write sacredly about it and, explaining it according to the divine utterances and hierarchical knowledge, to ascend in the divine Spirit to its sacred contemplation.

Let us first examine this sacredly: why is it placed discreetly above the other hierarchical rites, and why is its communion and synaxis proclaimed uniquely? Each sacred perfective activity gathers our divided lives into uniform deification and grants communion and unity in the One through the godlike interweaving of diverse things.

We say that the consummation of the participation in the other hierarchical symbols is found in the divine and perfective gifts of this rite. For it is scarcely possible for any hierarchical rite to be perfected unless the most divine Eucharist, at its consummation, gathers each of those being perfected into the One who perfects them, in the sacred activity, and unless the God-given bestowal of the perfective mysteries perfects their communion with God.

If, therefore, each hierarchical rite, while imperfect in itself, does not perfect our communion and synaxis in the One, it is not a rite, because it removes what is imperfect. The consummation and summary of all the divine mysteries is rightly given its proper name by hierarchical understanding, according to the truth of its activity.

Thus we praise the sacred rite of divine generation with the true name of illumination, because it first gives light and is the principle of all divine introductions into the light. For it is common to all hierarchical things to hand light on to those being perfected. But this rite first granted me the vision of light, and through its principal light I am led into the sight of the other sacred things.

Having said this, we shall look back and see, in detail, the careful sacred activity and contemplation of the most holy rite in hierarchical order.

### The mystery of the synaxis, or communion

The supreme priest, completing the sacred prayer over the divine altar and beginning to burn incense from it, proceeds around the entire circuit of the sacred choir. Returning again to the divine altar, he begins the sacred melody of the psalms [Note: BH: “the sacred melody of the psalms”], while the whole ecclesiastical order sings with him the sacred psalmic prayer.

Then, through the ministers, the reading of the prophetic writings follows. After these things, the catechumens, together with the possessed and those undergoing penance, are sent outside the sacred enclosure. Those worthy of the vision and communion of divine things remain.

Some of the ministers stand at the closed doors of the temple; others perform another duty proper to their order; still others, distinguished by their ministerial arrangement, set the sacred bread and the cup of blessing before the divine altar with the priests, before the catholic hymnody confessed by the whole fullness of the Church.

With them the divine Hierarch completes the sacred prayer and promises holy peace to all. When everyone has greeted one another, the mystical proclamation of the sacred volumes is completed.

After the supreme priest and the priests have washed their hands with water, the supreme priest stands in the middle of the divine altar, while only the chosen ministers stand around with the priests.

The supreme priest praises the sacred divine activities, sacrifices the most divine things, and brings the praised things into view through the sacred symbols laid before him. Displaying the gifts of the divine activities, he sanctifies them for communion. Then he comes forward and exhorts the others.

Receiving and distributing the divine communion, he brings the sacred Eucharist to its conclusion. While many gaze upon the divine symbols alone, he himself, always through the divine Spirit, hierarchically ascends in purity of godlike condition toward the principles of the perfect in the blessed and intellectual contemplations.

### Theoria

Come, then, good child, after the images, in due order and sacredly, toward the godlike truth of the principal exemplars.

To those whose souls have been brought together into unity and perfected, I shall say how the varied and sacred composition of the symbols does not subsist without intellectual meaning, nor merely appear outwardly to them. The most sacred chants and readings of the utterances proclaim to them the teaching of an energetic life and their complete purification from corrupting wickedness.

The most divine communion and peaceful distribution of one and the same bread and cup announces to them a similar divine way of life, as though they were eating in the same manner, and brings to sacred remembrance the most divine supper and the principal symbol of the perfect.

In accordance with this, the very author of the symbols divides the most holy offering. Does he not teach, in a holy and uniform manner, the one who shares the sacred meal with him, both rightly and in a godlike way, how the communion of those who come to it is itself granted according to the true condition of their assumption into divine things, in likeness to those things?

Having thus, as I said, well depicted these matters in the vestibules of the sanctuaries, let us leave them to those who are still imperfect, as sufficient for contemplation, and let us enter from effects into causes according to our sacred synaxis. We shall see the beautiful, invisible, light-bearing θεωρία of Jesus, which openly declares the beauty of the principal forms. But, as the most divine and sacred rite, symbolically revealing the garments of riddles with which you are clothed [Note: [Col. 1081] BH *sibi*, “itself”], [Col. 1081D] manifest yourself splendidly to us [Note: [Col. 1081] Conjecture, AE *manifestare*, BH *manifestat*], and fill our intellectual faces with uniform and unveiled light.

It is therefore necessary for us to be present within, stripping bare the most sacred and invisible first images, and to direct our attention toward their godlike beauty. We must see the high priest, divinely coming from the divine altar to the furthest limits of the temple with sweet fragrance, and again coming to rest perfectly in it [Note: [Col. 1081] A *residentem*; *et iterum—consistentem* omitted in BH]. For the divine blessedness that is above all things, although by divine goodness it proceeds into communion with those who participate in its sacred things, does not thereby come to exist outside its immutable state and position according to substance; rather, illuminating all things that are godlike in proportion, it truly exists around itself and is in no way changed from its own immutability.

Likewise, the sacred rite of the synaxis, although it possesses an involved and simple, compacted beginning, is mercifully multiplied into the sacred variety of symbols and fills the entire hierarchical depiction of images. Then, immediately, it is uniformly gathered back from these into its own unity and unifies within itself those who have been sacredly led upward.

In this godlike manner, the divine high priest, although he leads down to his subjects the unified discipline of his Hierarchy in a godlike fashion, employing the plurality of sacred riddles, is nevertheless restored without diminution to his own principle, as one who is released from and immeasurable by lesser things. Making his intellectual entrance into his own unity, he purely beholds the uniform principles of the perfect: in the second, merciful procession making the high point; in the first, the more divine return.

But will not the chanting of the Psalms, which accords with nearly all the hierarchical mysteries, be explained to the most priestly of all high priests? For every sacred and inspired writing announces [Note: [Col. 1081] A *narravit*, “narrated”; E *nunciavit*, “announced”] to those being initiated into deification, and roots [Note: [Col. 1081] AE *corradicavit*, “rooted”] them in the sacred rites and godlike ascents: the generated subsistence and ordering of beings that exist in God; the legal Hierarchy and manner of life; the distribution and dwelling places of the inheritance of the divine people; the sacred judges; the wise kings; the understanding of the divine priests; the steadfast philosophy of the ancient men amid the variety and multitude of their anxieties; the wise teachings of actions; the songs of divine loves and the divine images; the prophetic proclamations of things to come; the manly divine actions of Jesus; the God-given and God-imitating conduct and sacred teachings of the disciples themselves; and the hidden and mystical vision of the disciples’ beloved, divine, and wondrous supermundane theology of Jesus.

The sacred Scripture of the divine songs, intending to hymn all the theologies and divine actions, and to praise the sacred prayers and sacrifices of divine men, makes the chant of divine things universal. It also makes the narrative suitable for the reception and transmission of the entire hierarchical rite, producing a beautiful disposition in those who divinely sing the psalms.

When, therefore, the continuous hymnody of the most sacred things has suitably ordered our dispositions of soul for the sacrifices that are to follow shortly, and when the harmony of the divine songs has proclaimed us ordered and conformed to divine agreement—with ourselves and with one another—so that we are in one confessed region of sacred things [Note: [Col. 1081] So AE; BH *confessa religione sacrorum*], then the sacred readings of the professed constructions expand through a more intellectual psalmody, by means of many clearer images and proclamations. Whoever gazes upon these sacred things will see one inspiration uniformly, as though enclosed by one divine Spirit.

Hence, beautifully, after the older tradition, the New Testament is proclaimed in the world. I think [Note: [Col. 1083] BH *ut aestimo*, “as I think”] that the divine and hierarchical ordering declares how the former foretold the future divine works of Jesus, while the latter brought them to completion. The former wrote the truth in images [Note: [Col. 1083] E *veritate*, “in truth”]; the latter displayed it as present. Through the proclamations of the former, the latter came to know the truth through its own completed operation. And the divine operation is the consummation of theology.

Some of these people, not sounding the trumpet around all the sacred rites and not seeing the images, shamelessly deny the doctrine of divine generation that brings salvation, answering the sayings destructively: “We do not want to know your ways” [Note: [Col. 1083D] Job 21].

The law of the holy Hierarchy permits catechumens, the possessed, and those who are undergoing penance to hear the sacred prayer of the Psalms and the divine reading of the most holy Scriptures. But it does not summon such people to the sacrifices and contemplations that follow; these are for the eyes of the perfect among the perfect. For the godlike Hierarchy is full of sacred justice, since it beneficially distributes to each person, according to worth, the ordered participation of each in divine things, granting it at the proper time in due measure and proportion.

The order assigned to the catechumens is therefore the lowest. They are inexperienced and ignorant of every hierarchical perfection. They do not yet possess a subsistence formed according to the divine designation, but are still in labor under the paternal sayings and are still being shaped by such forms, awaiting from divine generation their first vital, first-illuminating, and blessed approach. It is as though imperfect and unformed infants, prematurely expelled according to the flesh through the labor of their own birth, should fall upon the earth like blinded miscarriages: they would have neither a generative, nor vital, nor illuminated fall upon the earth.

Does not one of the wise say, looking toward the manifest light, that they are weighed down by darkness, alienated from the womb? [Note: [Col. 1083] E *et*, “and.”] For the discipline of bodies, which is medicine, would say to them that light operates in those capable of light [Note: [Col. 1083] A *Dicit*, “says”; BH *Dixerat*, “had said”; text syntactically uncertain]. Thus also [Note: [Col. 1083] E *Sicut et*, “just as also”] the most wise discipline of sacred things first brings them forth through the nourishment of the formative and life-giving sayings. Then, perfecting their substance before divine generation, it beneficially grants them, in ordered progression toward the light, a godlike and perfecting communion.

But now it separates the perfect from the imperfect [Note: [Col. 1083D] Isa. 1], caring for the good order of sacred things, and assigns the catechumen to birth-labor and life within the godlike hierarchical order.

The multitude of the possessed is itself indeed unclean, but in the second place above the catechumen at its extremity. For, I think, it is not the same thing to be universally ignorant and to have no participation at all in the divine rites, as to possess some participation in the most sacred consummations. Yet this participation has been dishonored by contrary influences or deceptions or disturbances [Note: [Col. 1083] *dehonestatum* omitted in BH; A *informatum*, “formed”]. Even from these the divine communion of the most sacred things is withheld, and very rightly.

For if, as the truly divine man—worthy of divine things—really is, one ascends to the summit of his godlikeness in the most perfect and consummating deifications, and does not perform the works of the flesh beyond what nature absolutely requires—and even this only if he has carefully preserved it [Note: [Col. 1083] E *sicut observaverit*, “as he has observed it”]—he will be both a temple and, in consequence, the dwelling of the divine Spirit in his most exalted deification, placing like with like. Such a person will perhaps never suffer contrary fantasies or terrors [Note: [Col. 1083] AE *erroribus*, “errors”]; rather, he will mock them, struggle with what approaches, drive it away, and act more than he suffers [Note: [Col. 1083] A *adhuc*, “still”; E *ad hoc*, “for this”]. By his own impassible disposition, not something externally imposed, he will also appear to others as a physician of such operations.

I think—or rather, I know clearly—that the pure discernment of hierarchical matters recognizes in such cases the most polluted activity of the possessed. Whoever departs from the godlike life, becoming agreeable and conformable to the wicked, becomes a demon. Such beings truly exist, were created immortal, and eternally delighted; but through extreme and self-destructive folly they turn away, desiring and practicing material and highly passionate alienation, destructive and corrupting pleasures, and a weak pleasure in things alien that do not exist but are merely imagined.

Let these, then, and especially their ministers, be separated by a discerning voice. For it is not right that they should participate in any other sacred thing than the transformative teaching of the sayings directed toward better things [Note: [Col. 1083] BH *participatione*, “by participation”]. For the supermundane sacrifice of divine things conceals those who are undergoing penance and those already approaching it; it does not admit them altogether to the most sacred things. It calls this, moreover, with complete purity, because they are imperfectly weakened in some invisible depth toward the summit of godlikeness and are not admitted to communion.

For the clearest voice everywhere drives away those who cannot worthily be joined to the worthy communicants of the most divine things. Much more, then, will the unclean multitude of the possessed be subject to passion and alienated from every vision and communion of sacred things.

Then those ignorant of the divine mysteries are put outside the temple and its transcendent sacred rite [Note: [Col. 1083] E *ierarchia*, “Hierarchy”; BH, that is, “sacrifices”], together with those who lead an apostate life. Consequently, because of weakness, they endure the bonds and fantasies of the opposing powers, since they have not attained divine things through a strengthened and self-sufficient contemplation, fixed in the unchangeable and active disposition of godlikeness.

Next are those who have indeed abandoned the contrary apostate life but have not yet been purified from its fantasies by its disposition and love of the divine and radiant. After these come those who are not wholly uniform and, to speak according to the law, are not perfectly spotless and undefiled. Finally come the most holy, who are perfect.

Then the sacrificers of the most sacred things and lovers of contemplation, observing the most sacred rite holily and fittingly, praise in catholic hymnody the beneficial principle that bestows good things. They introduce the saving rites revealed to us and offer the sacred deification of the perfect.

Some call this hymn a hymnody; others call it a symbol of religion; others, I think, more divinely call it the hierarchical Eucharist, as comprehending the sacred gifts that have divinely come to us.

For it seems to me that the action of praising all divine works takes place in us: it establishes our essence and life in a godlike manner; forms our godlike nature according to the principal exemplars and beautiful models; establishes us in participation through a more divine disposition and renewal; separates from us the innate carelessness concerning divine gifts that arises from negligence; refreshes us with good things; recalls us to the ancient state; consummates us through the most perfect assumption of ourselves; most perfectly effects the transmission of what belongs to us; and grants us fellowship with God and with divine things.

Thus, when the divine humanity has been sacredly praised, the hidden divine bread and the cup of blessing are set forth; the most divine greeting is performed sacredly; and the mystical, supermundane reading of the inspired books takes place.

For it is not merely a matter of being gathered into one and participating in the peaceful unity of one thing, having been reconciled to ourselves. If we are illuminated by the contemplation and knowledge of the One and are unified into a uniform and divine gathering, we must not therefore fall into divided desires, from which material and passionate assaults against the natural likeness are created.

This sacred action, then, I think, proclaims a uniform and inseparable life of peace, placing like with like and separating the divided from the divine and united spectacles [Note: [Col. 1085] A C *sacra actio*, “sacred action”].

The reading of the sacred tablets after the peace proclaims those who have been sacredly established and have come immutably to the consummation of a strenuous life. It exhorts and guides us by their likeness toward the most blessed disposition and godlike rest. It proclaims them as living beings—and, as theology says, not as dead, but as having passed from death into the most divine life [Note: [Col. 1085D] Romans 6].

Observe also how we are restored through sacred commemorations: divine memory is not declared as a human remembering fantasy, but as though one were speaking of the divine, perfect, godlike, precious, and immutable knowledge of divine things. “He knows those who are his,” say the sayings [Note: [Col. 1085D] 2 Timothy 2]; and, “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” [Note: [Col. 1085D] Psalm 115]. The death of the saints is spoken of as their completion in holiness.

Understand this also sacredly: when the devout symbols are placed upon the divine altar—through which Christ is signified and participated in—the profession of the saints is indubitably present, manifesting their inseparable conjunction with him through a supermundane and sacred unity.

After these things have been sacrificed according to what has been said, the high priest stands before the most sacred symbols and washes his hands with water, together with the chaste order of the priests. For, as the sayings declare, the one who has been washed has no need of anything else except the washing of the highest things—that is, of the last things [Note: [Col. 1086D] John 13]—because of the most exalted purification in the most chaste godlike disposition. Having proceeded godlikewise to the second things, he will be immeasurable and released, as one who is perfectly uniform, turning again toward the One in unity and preserving the fullness and integrity of godlikeness.

The sacred basin [Note: [Col. 1086D] *Luter*, that is, Greek λουτήρ, “washing-basin”], as we said, belonged to the Hierarchy according to the law [Note: [Col. 1086D] Exodus 30, 38, and 40]. Now the cleansing of the hands of the high priest and the priests signifies it.

Those who approach the most sacred ἱερουργία, “sacred rite,” must be purified, and must admit, as far as possible, even the final fantasies of the soul. Through likeness they must admit the clearer theophanies, around which they will be placed amid supermundane radiances, so that they may attain their own brightness in the more universal and luminous clarity of conforming mirrors.

The washing of the high priest and the priests, even to the highest—that is, the final—washing, takes place before the most sacred symbols, as before Christ, who beholds all our most hidden thoughts and brings them to completion through the most attentive subtleties and the most just and equitable judgments of the highest purification.

Thus the high priest is united with divine things, and, praising the sacred divine actions, sacrifices the most divine things and brings what has been praised before the sight.

We have said that the divine actions are performed in us [Note: [Col. 1085] A E *dicimus*, “we say”]; next we must explain what their power is. I am not sufficient to praise everything, nor do I know it clearly enough to lead others into the mysteries. Whatever, then, the divine high priests subsequently praise and sacrifice according to the sayings, we shall discuss as far as possible, invoking hierarchical inspiration as our guide.

Human nature, foolishly ruined at the beginning through divine goods, was overtaken by a highly passionate life and the end of corrupting death. For, having fallen away from the goodness that truly is, through apostasy and transgression of the sacred legislation in paradise, it surrendered itself—rebelling against the life-giving yoke—to its own impulses and to the enemy’s pleasures and hostile deceptions, contrary to divine goods.

From that point, in a miserable exchange, it borrowed mortality in place of eternity. Although it had its own beginning in incorruptible generations, it was justly led to the end corresponding to its beginning.

And, voluntarily falling from the life that leads upward to the earth by the contrary extremity, it was heavily burdened by highly passionate mutability. Straying from the straight path toward the truly existing God, it was wounded and subjected to destructive and harmful multitudes. Forgetting God, it served not friends but enemies. Since these pitilessly abused it according to their own savagery, it fell slavishly into non-subsistences and the danger of destruction.

But the supreme humanity of divine goodness did not, through itself, harden the providence divinely working for us. Rather, in true participation, it became everything that belongs to us without sin and was united to our lowliness. In the most perfect and undefiled disposition of its own properties, it thereafter granted us communion with itself as with kindred beings and made us participants in its own goods.

According to the hidden tradition, it destroyed the power of the apostate multitude that stands against us—not by conquering through force, but, according to the word mystically handed down to us, in judgment and justice. For it benevolently restored everything that belongs to us to its opposite.

It filled what is dark in our mind with rich and most divine light, and adorned what was formless with godlike beauties. It freed the dwelling of the soul—our essence, which had fallen so far—from the most polluted passions and corrupting stains in perfect salvation. It displayed our supermundane renewal and the abundant divine perfection that is present in our sacred likenesses to it, as far as possible.

How else, then, could divine imitation have been implanted in us except through the memory of the most sacred divine actions, continually renewed by hierarchical and sacred prayers and sacrifices? “Do this,” the sayings tell us, “in remembrance of me” [Note: [Col. 1087D] Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; 1 Corinthians 11].

Therefore the divine high priest, standing at the divine altar, praises the sacred actions just mentioned: the divine actions of Jesus, the most divine providence for us, which he completed for the salvation of our race according to the good pleasure of the most holy Father in the Holy Spirit, in accordance with the sayings.

While praising their worship and contemplating their invisible reality with intellectual eyes, he proceeds to their symbolic sacred rite, with God as its giver. Hence, reverently and hierarchically, after the sacred praises of the divine actions, he makes a sacred appeal on behalf of that action which is above him, first sacredly crying out to it: “You said: Do this in remembrance of me” [Note: [Col. 1088D] Luke 22:19; Matthew 26; 1 Corinthians 11].

Then, asking to be made worthy of this godlike sacred action, to be perfected by divine likeness into Christ himself, to give with complete purity, and to participate sacredly and fittingly in the holy things, he sacrifices the most divine things and brings what has been praised before the sight through the sacred symbols laid out.

Revealing the veiled and undivided bread, dividing it into many portions, and distributing the unity of the cup to all, he symbolically multiplies and distributes unity, thereby completing the most sacred action in these things [Note: [Col. 1087] BH *sanctissima in his actio multiplicat*, “the most sacred action multiplies in these things”].

For the One, simple, and hidden Word of Jesus, through the incarnation according to us, proceeded by unchanging goodness and humanity into what is composite and visible, and benevolently accomplished our unifying fellowship with himself, supremely joining our lowly things to his most divine ones [Note: [Col. 1087] BH *peragit*, “accomplishes”].

Indeed, as members, we are joined to his body through that same immaculate and divine life. But when we are unconnected and misshapen through passions that do not corrupt, in accordance with what has been put to death, we become members that do not fit the divine and most healthy members [Note: [Col. 1087] AB *deiformes*, “godlike”].

For if we desire communion with him, we must look toward his most divine life according to the flesh and return to a godlike, undefiled disposition, sacredly conformed to it and free from sin. Thus he will grant us a compact fellowship according to likeness.

Through these sacred actions the high priest makes the matter manifest: he leads the veiled gifts to visibility, divides their unity into many portions, and makes those to whom they are distributed participants in the unity to which, according to the appointed time, they belong.

For through these sensible things he depicts and brings before our sight Jesus Christ, our invisible life, insofar as images can do so: according to God, from what was hidden, in the most perfect and undivided manner, mercifully formed according to us in the incarnation into our nature; proceeding unchangeably from the One according to nature into what is divisible; and, through this benevolent love of humanity, calling the human race to participation in himself and in his own goods.

Indeed, we are united to his most divine life through our likeness to it according to virtue. Through this, we shall also become, in truth, communicants of God and of the most divine consummations.

Receiving and distributing the divine communion, he concludes in the sacred Eucharist with the entire sacred fullness of the Church. For participation leads to transmission, and reception of the mysteries to the mystical distribution of the mysteries. This is the catholic adornment and order of divine things: first to become a sacred guide in participation and consummation [Note: [Col. 1087] BH *ducens*, “leading”], through divine means of what is to be bestowed upon others, and thus to transmit it to others.

For this reason, certain people who audaciously misuse the divine teachings are, before adopting the conduct and disposition that accord with them, utterly unclean and alien according to the sacred legislation. Just as, in the radiance of the sun, the subtler and brighter essences are filled through the influx of the first rays, and the light that surpasses them in every way carries them onward like the sun into what follows them, so no one should dare to be a guide to others in divine matters unless, according to his entire disposition, he has been approved as having become most beautifully formed by God and conformed to divine understanding and judgment.

With these things all the ordering of sacred rites, descending hierarchically and communicating the most divine things, concludes with sacred thanksgiving. It proportionately recognizes and praises the divine acts, giving thanks.

Therefore those who do not participate in or understand divine things will not come to the Eucharist either. Yet when those who are worthy according to their own nature are present, thanksgiving is offered for the most divine gifts.

But those whom I said were unwilling to gaze at divine gifts through the vision of one who is in evil remained ungrateful even in the face of the great gifts of divine actions. “Taste and see,” say the sayings [Note: [Col. 1089D] Psalm 33:9]. For the sacred doctrine of divine things will make known the magnificent thanksgivings of those who learn, and, most sacredly contemplating in participation the height and greatness of their most divine gifts, they will graciously praise the heavenly actions of divine benevolence.

## CHAPTER IV  
### On those being perfected in the myron and on what is offered in it

Such, then, are the matters of the most sacred synaxis; and in this way the invisible good things, as we have often said, hierarchically sacrifice to us the fellowship and coordination directed toward the One.

But there is another perfecting operation equal in power to this, which our guides [Note: [Col. 1089] *nostri*, “our,” omitted in BH] call the rite of the myron. Let us therefore direct our attention in order to its parts according to the sacred images, and thus ascend through hierarchical contemplations by its parts to its unity [Note: [Col. 1089] *ejus* omitted in BE].

### The Mystery of the Rite of the Myron

According to the same order of the synaxis, the orders of the imperfect are dismissed, after the entrance—namely, the hierarch’s fragrant circuit through the whole temple—the sacred psalmic chant, and the reading of the most divine sayings.

Then the high priest takes the myron and places it upon the divine altar, veiled by twelve sacred wings. At the same time all resound with the most holy voice a melodious hymn inspired by the prophets and acceptable to God. Completing the prayer that perfects it, he uses it in the most sacred rites of consecration for nearly every hierarchical perfecting operation.

### Theoria
The introductory ascent of this consummatory sanctification [Col. 1089D], through the sacred rites performed with the divine myron, declares, I think, that what is sacred and sweet-smelling is veiled around the holy men in their minds. God commands the holy men not to display openly, in vainglory, the good and fragrant likenesses that exist according to the virtue of the hidden God. For God’s secret beauties are pure and sweet-smelling above the mind, and they are shown invisibly only to those endowed with understanding, who desire to possess incorruptible images [Col. 1090A] in their souls according to virtue.

For the image that imitates God, looking toward that invisible and fragrant form, thus shapes and fashions itself in the most beautiful imitation. And just as, in sensible images, the painter always fixes his attention unwaveringly upon the first exemplary form, turning back toward no other visible object and dividing his attention in no way, but, if one may speak rightly, reproducing the very thing that is to be depicted and showing one thing in another according to the difference of their essences [Note: [Col. 1089] A: “and shows”; BH: “that it may show”], so, in purified minds, the contemplation itself, intent and unwavering toward the fragrant and hidden form, without wandering, describes the most godlike phantasm.

Rightly, therefore, having turned toward God, whose beauty is supersubstantially sweet-smelling and invisible, and having formed their intellectual faculty without deviation [Col. 1090B], they do not perform within themselves any of the virtues that imitate God for the purpose of being seen by human beings, according to the saying [Note: [Col. 1090B] Matthew III; XXIII], but contemplate them sacredly as in an image, veiled by the Church’s most holy divine myron. Therefore they too, inwardly imitating God according to virtue, most holy and supremely godlike, and sacredly veiling the God-described mind, look toward the sole archetypal intelligence [Note: [Col. 1089] E: “solar.”].

For they are not merely objects of contemplation for those unlike them, nor are they themselves drawn toward the vision of those others, each in turn; nor do they love the visible images of good and just things, but the things that truly exist; nor do they look toward the glory that the irrational multitude foolishly calls blessed. Rather, judging good and evil in themselves by divine imitation, they are divine images of the most divine goodness. Possessing from themselves a true fragrance, they do not turn toward what is thought good by many who are unlike them, but form themselves as one thing according to their own true beauties, without pretence.

Since, then, we have contemplated the outward beauty of the whole good and sacred action, let us look toward its more divine form, contemplating the veils revealed in themselves: blessed, radiant, manifestly luminous, and, without being veiled, filling our intellects with fragrance. For the manifest and consummatory operation of the myron is not inaccessible or invisible to those who surround the high priest. On the contrary, it reaches them and establishes contemplation above many; it is itself sacredly veiled by them and distinguished hierarchically through the multitude.

For the ray of the most holy divine men, shining upon their kindred from the invisible in purity and immediacy, and making their intellectual receptivities sweet without a veil, does not readily reach those beneath them. Rather, from them, as from those who contemplate the invisible mysteries, it is covered without pomp, uncontaminated from those who are unlike them, beneath winged enigmas. Through these sacred enigmas the well-ordered ranks are led back to their sacred proportion.

This, then, is what I said: the sacred operation of the rite, which must now be praised, is the consummation [Col. 1091A] of the hierarchic order and virtue. For this reason our divine leaders arranged it, as an operation equal in power and accomplishing the same thing as the sacred synaxis, through the same symbols, many mystical arrangements, and sacred prayers [Note: [Col. 1091] “which” omitted by BH; [Note: [Col. 1091] A*: “the perfection.”].

They appointed the high priest, as though he were bringing good fragrance from a more divine place into the holy things that follow, and teaching through his return to the source that participation in divine things takes place for all sacred persons according to their worthiness, while remaining altogether undiminished and unchanged, standing immutably in equality according to the divine placement of each person’s proper character.

The singing and reading of the divine oracles, prompted again by desire, educate the imperfect toward life-giving sonship and make the polluted one turn toward holiness [Col. 1091B] [Note: [Col. 1091] BH: “and make the conversation holy”]. They bring forth a manifest likeness of whatever they draw forth, from the irrationally possessed, of the most exalted godlike disposition and virtue, showing it to them proportionately. According to this, they will greatly terrify the opposing powers and provide healing for others: through divine imitation, they themselves possess not only immobility with respect to their own goods and activity against opposing disturbances, but also bestow these things.

For those passing from what is worst into divine understanding, they impose a sacred disposition, so that they may not again go astray beneath wickedness. Some, in order that they may be most chaste, they release when they have been fully perfected [Note: [Col. 1091] “some, in order that they may be most chaste ... they release” omitted by BH]. Others they lead into sacred divine images, their contemplation, and their communion. Others they most sacredly refresh through blessed invisible contemplations [Col. 1091C], completing their unity and making them uniform.

What then? Does not the present sacred operation of the rite, according to the same mode of the synaxis, also clearly release the ranks that are not altogether pure—the ranks of which we have already spoken—seeing them with divine eyes fixed solely upon the imageless, and contemplated and offered only by the most holy hierarchic ascents immediately? Since these matters have already often been stated by us, it is superfluous, I think, to repeat them in the same words rather than proceed to what follows [Note: [Col. 1091] E: “what has been said below”]. Let us see the high priest divinely veiled by twelve wings, holding the divine myron and sacrificing in it the most holy consummation.

Let us say, then, how the composition of the myron is a certain gathering of fragrant substances, richly possessing odoriferous qualities, so that those who receive and smell it receive, according to their proportion, as much participation in the good fragrance inherent in them. We believe that the most divine Jesus is supersubstantially sweet-smelling, filling our intellect through invisible distributions [Note: [Col. 1091] BH: “dispersions”] with divine delight.

For the reception of sensible fragrances produces satiety and nourishes with great pleasure the discriminating faculty of those who smell them, provided that this faculty is unharmed and properly compacted for good fragrance. Proportionately, if someone should say that our intellectual faculties, incorruptibly disposed toward that diminution which leads to evil, receive the divine fragrance within us according to the divine measures, in the natural health of the discerning faculty [Note: [Col. 1091] E: “nature”] and in the soul’s united turning toward God, and that they are filled with sacred beneficence and with the most divine nourishment—

does not the symbolic composition of the myron therefore portray [Note: [Col. 1091] H: “describe”] Jesus for us as the source, rich in the reception of divine fragrances, blessed and making intellectual beings more godlike according to divine and archetypal proportions? It reveals the most divine vapors, in which souls, beneficially delighted and filled with divine receptions, partake of invisible food, penetrating toward their intellectual faculty according to their participation in the distributions of fragrant things.
