It is clear, I think, that the return of the superessential fragrance from the essences above us, as from those that are more divine, manifests and distributes itself more closely and more fully. It overflows abundantly into their most luminous and intellectually receptive power, which is well disposed toward it, while the bestowal of that fountain-like fragrance remains hidden in many ways. But toward the subordinate intellectual beings, who are not receptive in the same manner, it conceals the vision and participation beyond their capacity, and distributes it divinely in proportion to the vapors of the participants and according to their measure [Note: [Col. 1091] BH: “commemoration”].

The order of the Seraphim, therefore, which is placed above us by so much as the sacred essences surpass us, is signified by the twelve wings. It stands and is situated around Jesus, overshadowing his most blessed contemplations as far as is fitting, filled with the sacred reception of the invisible distribution, and, in sensible speech, crying aloud in response with a highly praiseworthy theology, not with silent mouths [Col. 1092C].

For the sacred knowledge of the supermundane spirits is at once exalted and possesses an unceasing divine love; at the same time it surpasses every evil and forgetfulness. Hence, I think, it indicates with this cry that is not silent their eternal and unchangeable knowledge and understanding of divine things in every virtue and thanksgiving.

We have therefore, I believe, contemplated the properties of the incorporeal Seraphim, sacredly described in sensible images of the oracles as manifestations of invisible things, in the adornments of the heavenly Hierarchies, and we have displayed them before your intellectual eyes.

Since, however, those who now stand sacredly around the high priest reproduce for us that same most exalted disposition, let us briefly behold, even now, through the most holy sights, the most godlike brightness of those beings.

Their many forms and many feet [Note: [Col. 1091] BH: “manifold”], I think, manifest the multiform character of their many-sided disposition toward the most divine illuminations, as well as the ever-moving and many-wayed character of intelligible divine goods. As for the position of the wings, spread out, I think that the oracles [Note: [Col. 1091D] Isaiah VI] indicate not a sacred number, as others have thought, but rather that, around God, the anagogical and absolute powers of the most excellent essence and order are perfect and supermundane: the first, middle, and final powers of their intellectual and godlike virtues [Col. 1093A].

For this reason the most sacred wisdom of the oracles, describing the duplication of their wings, places wings around their faces, their middle parts, and their feet, universally indicating their winged nature and the abundance of their anagogical virtue toward what truly is.

But if they cover their faces and feet and fly only with their middle wings, understand this sacredly: the order of the most excellent essences, so highly exalted, is reverent before the higher and deeper things of the divine intellect. With their middle wings they are raised in proportion to the divine vision, submitting their own life to the divine heights and being sacredly directed by them toward knowledge of themselves.

The statement in the oracles that “one cried to another” [Col. 1093B] indicates, I think, that they abundantly communicate to one another their own god-revealing understandings [Note: [Col. 1093] AH: “which”]. We have judged it worthy of sacred remembrance that the Hebrew word of the oracles, according to its intelligible naming, calls the most holy Seraphim essences “those that burn through,” because of their burning according to the divine and immutable life [Note: [Col. 1093] “from the same” omitted by E].

Thus, interpreting what belongs to the Hebrews, they say that the most divine Seraphim are named by theology “burning” and “heating,” a name that manifests their substantial disposition. According to the symbolic description of the images, they possess the motive powers of the divine ointment, summoning it into manifestation and into the actual distribution of its other vapors.

For that sweet-smelling essence that is above the intellect loves to be moved into knowledge by fiery and most purified minds, and grants its most divine inspirations in the richest distributions, thus calling to itself those who summon it in a supermundane manner.

The most divine order of the heavenly essences therefore did not fail to recognize the most divine intellect descending for sanctification. It sacredly understands that intellect submitting itself, through divine and ineffable goodness, to the things that are among us, and being sanctified humanly by its Father and by the Spirit.

Looking upon its own principle, it knows that, in whatever it accomplishes divinely, it possesses mutability according to essence. Therefore the tradition of the sacred symbols surrounds the divine ointment with the Seraphim, seeing and describing Christ as immutable in his universal and true incarnation among us [Col. 1093D].

And this is still more divine: he uses the ointment for the perfection of every divine perfection [Note: [Col. 1093] “And even more divinely, because he uses it for” omitted by BH], openly showing, according to the oracle, the sanctifier as sanctified, since he himself always exists as himself according to every divine beneficence.

For this reason the perfective gift and grace of the sacred divine birth is brought to completion in the ointment through the most divine consummations.

Hence, I think, the high priest also pours the ointment into the baptismal font in cruciform symbols and, with contemplative eyes, leads Jesus before the sight, even to his death upon the cross [Col. 1094A], immersed for our divine birth. Through this divine and powerful descent into his death, according to the hidden saying, he causes those baptized to emerge divinely from the old swallowing-up of corrupting death, renewing them toward divine and eternal subsistence.

When he performs the most holy rite of divine birth, the consummatory anointing grants the advent of the divine Spirit through the ointment. I think that, through the sacred symbolic description of the images, it characterizes the divine Spirit that has been given by him who, for our sake, was sanctified humanly by the divine Spirit, with the immutable substantial disposition of divinity.

Understand this hierarchically as well: the legislation concerning the sacred altar and the most holy offerings is also completed by the most sacred ointment through its most holy outpourings [Col. 1094B].

This is a heavenly and superessential contemplation, the principle, essence, and perfective power of all our deification and sanctification. For if our most divine altar is Jesus, the principal divine offering of divine souls, in whom, according to the oracle, we have access as those offered and mystically consumed as a whole burnt offering [Note: [Col. 1093] “we have” omitted by BH], then with supermundane eyes we shall behold that most divine altar, in which perfect things are perfected and sanctified, made perfect by the most divine ointment.

For the most holy Jesus sanctifies himself on our behalf and fills us with every sanctification, graciously dispensing in himself to us, as those born of God, the perfections that thereafter descend upon us from God.

Hence, I think, the divine leaders of our Hierarchy, according to the hierarchic understanding handed down by God [Col. 1094C], rightly call this most chaste sacred operation of the ointment a “rite” derived from its perfect activity, as though someone should call it the “rite of God,” praising in both senses its divine and perfect operation.

For it is his offering: to be sanctified humanly for our sake, to perfect all things divinely, and to sanctify what is perfect.

As for the melodious hymn acceptable to God through inspiration, those who know the things of the Hebrews say that it means “to declare the praise of God,” or “to praise the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1093] BH: “which”].

Since the whole sacred theophany and creation has been sacredly described in the varied composition of hierarchic symbols, it is not inappropriate to recall the hymnody of the prophets, moved by God. For it teaches both chastely and divinely that divine actions are worthy of sacred praises.

Such, then [Col. 1094D], is the perfect operation of the most divine ointment.

Perhaps it is now time, after setting forth the divine sacred actions themselves, to explain the priestly ordinations, their parts, virtues, operations, and consummations, and, above these, the orders that firmly support the Trinity, insofar as the disposition of the Hierarchy among us has been demonstrated: clearly distinguishing what is disordered, unadorned, and confused, while filling what is adorned, ordered, and firmly established, manifesting itself in the analogies of the holy orders.

I think that we have already adequately explained the threefold division of the whole Hierarchy in the Hierarchies praised by us, saying that, according to the sacred tradition among us, every hierarchic action is divided into the most holy rites, their divine knowledge and instruction, and those who are sacredly perfected through them.

The most holy Hierarchy of the heavenly essences therefore possesses, as its rite, the immaterial understanding according to its proper virtue of God and divine things, the integrity of godlikeness, and, insofar as possible, a disposition resembling God [Note: [Col. 1095] “and, insofar as possible” omitted by BH]. Leading into the light and guiding toward this sacred consummation the primordial essences and sacred orders around God, it transports them in a godlike and proportionate manner toward the deifying knowledge continually granted to them, knowledge that proceeds from the divinity of the divine souls, which is perfect and wise in itself.

The subordinate dispositions of the primordial essences, having been divinely exalted through them toward the deifying illumination of divinity, are therefore both perfect orders and are truly called such.

After that heavenly and supermundane Hierarchy, the beneficent divinity brings its most sacred gifts into the realm of things among us. To those who are meek, according to the oracle, it gave, in accordance with the law, a Hierarchy consisting of obscure signs of realities, very lengthy deviations from the primordial exemplars, and figures. Since these signs were not clearly distinguished, it harmlessly revealed the hidden contemplation to their feeble vision.

The rite of this Hierarchy according to the law is an ascent toward the spiritual worship of God. Its guides toward it are that holy tabernacle, sacredly ordered by Moses, with the high priest as its first teacher and leader according to the law.

When, according to the law, he writes sacredly and initiatively of this holy tabernacle, showing him the character of its form upon Mount Sinai [Note: [Col. 1095D] Exodus XV; Hebrews VIII], he calls all things sacrificed according to the law into it.

Before the perfect things, however, we lead people proportionately from the legal symbols toward the more perfect teaching. Theology calls this more perfect teaching the Hierarchy among us, naming it the fullness and sacred end of that former Hierarchy.

It has received a share of both the heavenly and the legal Hierarchies, as a communicative middle term between the extremes. With the one it shares intellectual contemplations; with the other [Note: [Col. 1095] BH: “therefore”], since it is varied through sensible symbols, it is sacredly led through them back to God.

It likewise possesses the threefold character of the hierarchic division, divided into the sacrifices of the most holy rites, the godlike ministers of sacred things, and those who are proportionately led by them into sacred things.

Each of the three divisions of our Hierarchy is consequently ordered according to the first, middle, and final virtue of both the legal and the more divine Hierarchy among us, foreseen according to divine proportion, adorned with the good order of all things, and compacted in an orderly and connective fellowship.

The most holy sacrifice of the offerings therefore possesses, as its first godlike virtue, the sacred purification of the imperfect; as its middle virtue, the illuminating instruction of those who have been purified; and, as its final virtue, the consummation of those instructed in the knowledge of beautiful doctrines, a consummation that perfects what came before.

The disposition of the sacrificers, in its powerful first virtue, purifies the imperfect through the rites; in its middle virtue, leads those who have been purified into the light; and, in its final and most exalted virtue, perfects those who participate in divine light through the knowable contemplations of the most contemplable illuminations.

The virtue of those who are perfected is, first, purifying; second, illuminating after purification and contemplative of certain holy things; and, finally, the most divine of the others, contemplative of the very sacred illuminations of which it becomes a participant, illuminating consummatory knowledge.

The threefold virtue of the sacred hierurgy of the rites is therefore praised: in the sacred divine generation, through purification and luminous illumination confirmed by the oracles; and in the consummatory rite of the synaxis and the myron, through knowledge and understanding of divine actions, by which the priesthood is perfected toward divinity as a unifying ascent and most blessed communion [Note: [Col. 1095] AE: “priesthood”].

It now remains to narrate the priestly disposition, divided into the purifying, illuminating, and consummatory ordination.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Priestly Consummations

[Col. 1096C]

This is the most sacred law of the divine rule: through the first, to lead the second back to its most divine light. Do we not see the sensible essences of the elements first coming toward those more akin to them, and through them dividing their proper operation among other things?

It is therefore fitting that the principle and foundation of every invisible and visible adornment should be understood as coming from the more godlike primordial beings, who receive the divine rays and, through them, as more luminous minds possessing a suitable capacity for participation in and transmission of the light, shine and appear proportionately upon those beneath them.

It belongs to these primordial beings to show abundantly to the second ranks, according to the measure appropriate to them, the divine spectacles sacredly contemplated by them [Col. 1096D]; to teach what belongs to the Hierarchy; to teach all things divine to those who come after them in the Hierarchy, with consummatory knowledge itself, so that they receive a perfect power of teaching; and to hand down, according to their worthiness, the sacred things through the priestly consummation of those who participate in them learnedly and completely [Note: [Col. 1095D] The codex of John Scotus, which was mutilated at this point, seems to have been defective here. For in Corderius’s edition, vol. I, pp. 358–360, the passage from the words “Ἡ δὲ τῶν ἱερουργῶν διακόσμησις” (“And the disposition of those who perform the sacred rites”) up to “Οὐκοῦν ἡ θεία τῶν Ἱεραρχῶν τάξις” (“Therefore the divine order of the Hierarchs”) is missing from the manuscripts of the translation.].

The order of the divine high priests is therefore first among the divine orders [Note: [Col. 1097] So B; AEH: “of the divine order”]; but it is also again the most exalted and final order. For in it the whole disposition of our Hierarchy is perfected and fulfilled.

Just as we see the whole Hierarchy consummated in Jesus, so we see each part of it consummated in its own divine high priest. The virtue of the hierarchic order is situated in all the sacred communities and operates through all the sacred orders the mysteries of its proper Hierarchy.

The divine law has discreetly assigned to this order, beyond the other orders, the more divine sacrifices as its operation [Note: [Col. 1097] BH: “the more divine sacrifice”]. These are images that perfect the divine virtue, consummating all the most divine symbols and all the sacred dispositions.

For although some symbols of the things worshipped are perfected by priests [Col. 1097B], a priest can never perform the sacred divine generation without the most divine ointment. Nor can he perfect the mysteries of divine communion unless the communicative symbols have been placed upon the divine altar. Nor will he himself be a priest unless he has been admitted to this through hierarchic consummations.

Therefore the divine legislation assigned the sanctification of the hierarchic orders, the consummation of the divine ointment, and the sacred purification of the altar uniquely to the perfecting virtues of the divine high priests.

The sanctificatory order, then, is filled with consummatory virtue. It discreetly perfects the perfected Hierarchy, is learned in the knowledge of sacred manifestations [Note: [Col. 1097] BH: “of manifestations”], and teaches their proportionate sacred dispositions and virtues.

The luminous order of priests [Note: [Col. 1097] EH: *lucidicus*, “luminous”; BH: *communionem*, “communion”] leads those who are perfect under the order of the divine high priests toward the contemplation of the holy offerings [Col. 1097C]. After him, it performs its own sacred actions, in which it reveals through the most sacred symbols what it itself does as divine; it perfects those who come as contemplators and makes them participants in the sacred rites; and it refers to the high priest those who desire knowledge of the contemplative sacrifices that have been contemplated.

The order of ministers, however, is purifying and discriminating between unlike things. Before access to the sanctifications of the priests, it purifies those who approach, making them pure from opposing things and fitting them for sacred contemplation and communion [Note: [Col. 1097] BH: “communion”].

Hence, when they approach the sacred divine generation, the ministers strip the candidate of the old garment, release him further, and set him toward the west for renunciation; then they lead him back toward the east—for these actions belong to a purifying ordination and virtue. They command those who approach to cast off altogether the garments of their former life and the darkness of their former conduct, showing and teaching them that they must be reordered and pass from what does not illuminate into the illuminating state.

The ministerial disposition is therefore purifying. It leads those who have been purified toward the most manifest sanctifications of the priests, judges the imperfect, inflames them through the illuminating teachings of the oracles that cleanse, and separates the still impure from the priests without confusion [Col. 1098A].

For this reason the hierarchic legislation established it at the sacred gates, signifying the entrance of those who approach the sacred things through the most perfect purifications, granting access to the contemplation and communion [Note: [Col. 1097] BH: “communions”] of the holy things through purifying virtues, and receiving them through these virtues as undefiled.

We have therefore shown that the order of the high priests is consummatory and perfecting; that of the priests, illuminating and luminous; and that of the ministers, purifying and discriminating. The hierarchic order receives the power not only to perfect but also simultaneously to illuminate and cleanse, while the virtue of the priests possesses within itself both illuminating and purifying knowledge.

The lesser orders cannot transport others into what is better, since it would be unjust for them to attempt such a dignity [Col. 1098B]. The more divine virtues, however, know through the sacred knowledge of their perfection both their own operations and those subordinate to them.

Since these too are images of divine actions, the other sanctificatory dispositions—well ordered and without confusion, revealing within themselves the ordered illuminations of the first, middle, and final sacred actions and ordinations—have been arranged in hierarchic distinctions. As we have said, they manifest in themselves the ordered and unconfused character of divine actions.

For wherever the divine rule is present, it first purifies minds, then illuminates them, and finally perfects those who have been illuminated toward godlike perfection. The order of the high priests, as a divine image, therefore rightly divides itself into distinct ordinations and virtues, carefully showing the divine actions established with due measure and without confusion in the most holy and unconfused orders.

Since we have spoken of the sacred ordinations, participations, virtues, and operations, insofar as we were able, we shall now contemplate their most sacred consummations, as far as our powers permit.

## The Mystery of Priestly Consummations

The high priest, approaching the hierarchic consummation, bends both feet before the sight of the divine altar. Upon his head he has the oracles handed down by God and the hierarchic hand, and in this manner he is consummated by the high priest who perfects him, through the most holy invocations.

The priest, bending both feet in the presence of the divine altar, has the hierarchic right hand placed upon his head, and in this manner he is sanctified by the high priest who perfects him, through sacrificial invocations.

The minister, bending one foot in the presence of the altar, has upon his head the right hand of the high priest who perfects him, and is perfected by him through the consummatory invocations of the ministers.

Upon each of them the high priest who perfects them makes the sign of the cross. A sacred recitation is made for each, together with a consummatory greeting, while every divine man who is present gives the greeting and the high priest consummates the person who has been brought to completion in one of the divine ordinations mentioned [Col. 1099A].

### Commentary

The following things are common to high priests, priests, and ministers in their priestly consummations: access to the divine altar, inclination, the imposition of the hierarchic hand, the sign of the cross, the proclamation [Note: [Col. 1099] “the sign of the cross ... the proclamation” omitted by BH; E adds it above and in the margin], and the consummatory greeting.

The things that are separate and distinctive are these: the placing of the oracles upon the head belongs to high priests and is not given to the lower orders; the inclination with both feet belongs to priests and is not part of the consummation of ministers, for ministers, as stated, incline only one foot.

Access to the divine altar and prostration therefore indicate to all who are being sanctified and perfected that they must universally submit their own life to God, the principle of consummation [Col. 1099B], and approach him with their entire intellectual being, most chaste, offered and conformed to him, and, insofar as possible, worthy of the divine, most holy, and priestly altar, offering godlike intellects in a sacred manner.

The imposition of the hierarchic hand likewise manifests the principal protection that perfects. Under it, as under paternal instruction, the saints are guarded: it grants them the priestly disposition and virtue, while separating from them the opposing virtues. At the same time it teaches all to perform priestly actions, acting under God as perfected persons and having him as the guide of all their own operations.

The sign of the cross signifies, likewise for all, the prohibition of every carnal desire and a life imitating God. It looks rightly toward the manly and most divine life of Jesus, which advanced to the cross and death in divine sinlessness [Col. 1099C], so that those who live in this way may be conformed to the one who marks them, in the image of his own sinlessness upon the cross.

The high priest recites the sacred recitation of the consummations and of those being consummated. The mystery declares how the friend of God is the sanctifier of the divine election: he does not himself, by his own grace, lead those to be perfected into the consummatory sanctification, but is moved by God toward all the hierarchic sanctifications.

Thus Moses, the legal sanctifier, did not lead his brother Aaron into priestly consummation, even though he considered himself a friend of God and a sanctifier, until, moved divinely for this purpose by God, the principle of perfection, he perfected the priesthood [Col. 1099D].

Our divine and first sanctifier—indeed, the most humane Jesus was also this among us—did not glorify himself, as the oracles say, but the one who spoke to him: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” [Note: [Col. 1099D] Psalm CIX; Hebrews V; Luke XXII].

For this reason, when he led his disciples into priestly consummation, although he existed as God, the principle of perfection, he nevertheless referred hierarchically the perfecting power to his most holy Father and to the divine Spirit, the principal source of perfection [Col. 1100A]. He announced to the disciples, as the oracles say [Note: [Col. 1099D] Luke XXIV; Acts I.4], that they should not depart from Jerusalem but should await the promise of the Father, “which,” he said, “you heard from me, because you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.”

Even the leader of the disciples, together with the hierarchic decade coordinated with him, when he came to the sanctifying consummation of the twelve disciples, left the election to the divine rule with reverence, saying, “Show which one I should choose” [Note: [Col. 1100D] Acts I.24]; and he received the one divinely shown by the divine lot into the hierarchic number of the holy twelve.

Concerning the divine lot given to Matthias, some have said various things, and, in my opinion, not correctly. I shall state my own view.

It seems to me that the oracle called the lot a divine gift, declaring that Matthias had been shown to that hierarchic choir for divine election [Note: [Col. 1099] AE: “from divine election”]. For no one who is not moved by the divine high priest ought to perform priestly consecrations on his own initiative. Rather, moved by God, he must perform them hierarchically and from heaven.

The greeting at the completion of the priestly consummation itself also possesses a sacred meaning. For all who are present and belong to the sanctificatory orders, as well as the high priest who performs the rite, greet the one who has been perfected.

When a sacred mind approaches priestly perfection with sanctificatory dispositions, virtues, divine calling, and sanctification, it is beloved by the coordinated and most sacred orders, being led into the most godlike beauty. Minds of like form love it and sacredly assist it.

Therefore the sanctificatory greeting is exchanged between them, declaring the sacred fellowship of like-formed minds and the mutual affection and joy among them, as though fully preserving the most godlike beauty of the priestly formation [Col. 1100C] [Note: [Col. 1099] B: “greeting”].

Thus, as we have said, these things are common to the whole sacred consummation. The high priest, however, has the sacred words placed discreetly above his head. Since the consummating power and discipline of the entire priesthood is given to the high priests by God and by the goodness that is the source of perfection, the words delivered by God are fittingly placed upon the hierarchic heads: continuously and orderly they make manifest the whole theology, theurgy, and theophany contained in the account of all the divine and sacred works and words bestowed by our beneficent theurgy upon our Hierarchy. The high priest, as the divinely formed [Col. 1100D] participant in the whole of hierarchic virtue, fully possesses the true, God-delivered knowledge of all the hierarchic sacred praises and sacred actions; he transmits it not only to the one being illuminated but also, according to their respective hierarchic proportions, to the others, perfecting all the whole Hierarchy hierarchically in the most divine sciences and the highest anagogical ascents.

For priests, the inclination with the feet is appropriate beyond the ministerial disposition, which inclines with one foot [Col. 1101A] and thereby completes this through the hierarchic figure. The inclination therefore signifies the submissive approach of the one approaching, who refers to God what has been divinely approached.

Since, as we have often said, the three sacred dispositions of those who consummate preside over the three orders of those being consummated because of the three most holy rites and virtues, and sacrifice their salvific approach beneath the divine yoke, the ministerial disposition, appropriately understood as purgative [Note: [Col. 1101] “disposition, as purgative” is omitted in BEH], sacrifices the approach of the ones being purified, placing it beneath the divine altar, as though purified souls were offered there in a manner transcending the world. Priests incline with both feet, as though their life, purified not only by their sacred approaches but also, anagogically, by their most evident sacrifices, had been consecrated and perfected into contemplative [Col. 1101B] disposition and virtue. The high priest, inclining with both feet, has the words delivered by God above his head. By the ministerial virtue of God he purifies those who have been illuminated through sacrifice, leading them hierarchically toward the corresponding knowledge of the sacred things contemplated by them, and through that knowledge perfecting those who approach into their complete offering.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Orders of Those Being Perfected

These, then, are the priestly orders and divisions, their virtues, operations, and consummations. Next, the trinity of the orders of those being consummated must be described.

Let us say, then, that those being purified are distinct multitudes who are sacrificed and ministered to, of whom we have already spoken [Col. 1101C]: those who are still being administered to, by the midwifely words, are brought to vital approval and formed and shaped; those who have apostatized from the divine life are recalled to it by the converting instruction of the good words [Note: [Col. 1101] A omits *quae* (“who/which”); E reads *quia* (“because”)]; those who are still weakly fearful of contrary tumults are strengthened by the words that produce virtue; those who are still [Note: [Col. 1101] BH omit “still”], as it were, to be led from the worst things to sacred actions; and those who have indeed been led across, but do not yet possess a most chaste manner of life in more divine and immutable dispositions.

These are the orders of those being purified, through administrative midwifery and purgative virtue. The ministers perfect them through their sacred virtues, transferring those who have been thoroughly purified to the contemplation and participation of the most manifest sacrifices, which are illuminative [Col. 1101D].

The middle order is [Note: [Col. 1101] BH omit “is”] contemplative. It participates proportionately with certain priests in complete purity [Note: [Col. 1101] AE read *in puritate omni* (“in all purity”)] and is distributed among the priests for illumination. For it is clear, I think, how one who has been purified from every unclean stain and possesses the most chaste, immutable foundation of his own soul passes into contemplative disposition and virtue through sacrifice, and participates by himself in the most divine symbols through their contemplation and communion, being at once filled with all sacred joy. Through this he soars proportionately, by his most holy ascents and virtues, toward their divine knowledge.

I [Note: [Col. 1101] A*E read *ergo* (“therefore”)] call this the order of the holy people: those who have undergone every purification and, as is just [Note: [Col. 1101] A omits “and”; E reads “is”] and fitting, the contemplation and participation of the most manifest sacrifices. The higher order of all those being perfected is the sacred disposition of the monks. Through universal virtue it possesses every purified purification; through the most perfect chastity of its own actions, and through every sanctification permitted to it in contemplation, it has been formed in intellectual vision and communion and entrusted to the consummating virtues of the bishops. Instructed by their divine illuminations [Col. 1102B] and hierarchic traditions, it contemplates for itself the sacrifices of the sacred victims and, through the corresponding knowledge of them, ascends toward the most consummate consummation.

Therefore our divine leaders have deemed them worthy of sacred names: some calling them *therapeutai* (“servants” or “attendants”), others calling them monks [Note: [Col. 1101] BH read *alios ... alios* (“others ... others”)]. The names derive from pure ministry and service to God, and from their undivided and solitary life, as though it united them [Note: [Col. 1101] E omits “them”] in sacred, inseparable interweavings into a divinely formed unity and a consummation beloved of God. For this reason sacred legislation also granted them consummating grace and deemed them worthy of a certain consecratory invocation, though not a hierarchic one. The latter takes place only among the sanctifying orders [Note: [Col. 1101] E omits “among”], whereas this sanctifying rite was consecrated by holy priests [Col. 1102C] after the hierarchic perfection.

## The Mystery of Monastic Consummation

The priest stands before the divine altar, chanting the monastic invocation. The one being consummated stands behind the priest, neither inclining with both feet nor with one foot, and without having the words delivered by God above his head. He merely stands beside the priest as he chants the mystical invocation over him.

When the priest has completed it, he comes to consummate the candidate and first asks whether he renounces, above all, not only divided ways of life but also fantasies. Then he teaches him the most perfect life, bearing witness that he must stand above the middle rank [Note: [Col. 1101] AE read *eum media*, “him [in] the middle,” rather than the transmitted word order]. When the candidate confesses all these things with greater earnestness, the priest marks him with the sign of the cross, invokes the triune substance of divine blessedness, strips off his entire garment, and clothes him in another. Then, greeting him together with the other priestly men who are present [Note: [Col. 1101] AE reads “priests”], he makes him a companion of the thearchic mysteries.

## Commentary

The fact that he neither inclines with his feet nor has the words delivered by God above his head, but stands beside the priest chanting the invocation, declares that the monastic order is not set above the others, but stands in itself in a singular and sacred station [Col. 1103A], following the priestly orders and, together with them, believing itself to ascend in due succession toward the divine knowledge of sacred things [Note: [Col. 1103] BH omit “orders ... in due succession”]. The renunciation not only of divided ways of life but also of fantasies signifies the monks’ most perfect philosophy, which fulfills the commandment by uniting them in knowledge.

For, as we have said, it is not the middle order of those being perfected, but the highest of all. Therefore many matters pertaining to the middle ordination are, in some undiscerning way, unknown to the solitary monks [Note: [Col. 1103] E reads *ignoranter quodammodo* (“in an ignorant manner”)], since they ought thus to be united into one, gathered into divine unity, and reformed into a sacred life, as far as is right—having a kinship with it in many respects and approaching it more closely than the remaining orders of those being consummated.

The sign of the likeness of the cross, as we have already said, declares the prohibition of all carnal desires at once. The cutting of the hair signifies the Lord’s pure, unfigured life [Col. 1103B]: it does not externally paint the soul’s freedom with fictitious forms, but shows it as itself, withdrawn from human adornments and brought back, through unity and monastic life, into the most divinely formed condition.

The removal of the former garment and the putting on of another signify the transfer from the middle sacred life to the more perfect one, just as the change of garments in the sacred divine birth signified a purified life ascending into contemplative and illuminative disposition.

If now the priest and all who are present, being holy, also greet the one who has been consummated, understand this as the sacred fellowship of those formed in the likeness of God, rejoicing together in divine joy through love. At the end of all things the priest calls the consummated person to the thearchic communion. This signifies sacredly that the perfect person, if he has truly entered upon monastic life and united anagogy, will not merely be a contemplator of sacred things according to himself, nor come, like the middle order, into communion with the most sacred symbols. Rather, possessing within himself the divine knowledge of the sacred things in which he has participated, he will come in another manner, above the sacred people, to the reception of divine communion.

For this reason communion in the most holy Eucharist is given to the priestly orders in their sacred consummating sanctifications, at the end of their most holy offerings, by the high priest who consummates them [Col. 1103D]. This is so not only because reception of the divine mysteries is the consummation of each person’s hierarchic participation, but also because, through that communion and most divine gift, all the sacred orders participate proportionately in all things according to the single anagogy and consummation proper to their position.

We have therefore established how the holy rites are purification, illumination, and consummation: the ministers are the purgative order; the priests, the illuminative; and the high priests, formed in the likeness of God, the consummative order [Col. 1104A]. The order being purified [Note: [Col. 1103] AE read “purified”] participates in sacred contemplation and communion insofar as it is still to be purified [Note: [Col. 1103] AE reads “insofar as it has been purified”]. The contemplative order is the sacred people. The order being consummated is that of the monks who have been united.

Thus, according to us, the Hierarchy, sacredly arranged in orders delivered by God, conforms to the heavenly Hierarchies and preserves, insofar as is possible in human beings, the divinely formed characters of its divine imitation.

But you may say that the heavenly Hierarchies entirely lack orders of those being purified; for it would neither be right nor true to say that some heavenly disposition is still polluted [Note: [Col. 1103] BH omits “is”]. I confess that they are indeed perfectly immaculate and possess, in a manner transcending the world, the most chaste state—provided I have not entirely fallen away from the most sacred understanding.

For if any of them, having received wickedness, fell from the heavenly and undivided harmony of the divine intellects, he was carried into the darkness and fall of the apostate multitudes. Yet one must say, wondrously, of the heavenly Hierarchy that purification among subordinate beings is, from God, the illumination of those who are ignorant [Note: [Col. 1103] AE read *tanquam* (“as though”)], leading them into a more perfect knowledge of the thearchic cognitions. It purifies their ignorance of things whose knowledge they did not yet possess through the first and more divine essences, which are brought back into the higher and more manifest splendors of divine contemplation.

Thus, within the heavenly Hierarchy too, there are orders being illuminated and consummated, as well as purgative, illuminative, and consummative orders. The highest and most divine essences purify the lower sacred and heavenly dispositions with complete chastity, according to the orders and proportions of the heavenly Hierarchies; they fill them with the illumination of the most divine radiance and consummate them in the most holy knowledge of the thearchic intelligences.

For we have already said, and it agrees with the divinely given words, that not all heavenly dispositions possess all the sacred sciences of the divine illuminations. Rather, the first receive them immediately from God, while through them those subordinate receive them again from God and are proportionately illuminated by the manifest and brilliant rays of the Divinity [Col. 1104C].

## CHAPTER VII. On Those Being Perfected Among the Departed

Having defined these matters, I think it necessary to speak also of what is sacredly accomplished by us for those who have fallen asleep [Col. 1104D]. For this too is not common to the holy and the unclean. As the form of life of the two groups is different, so also, when they approach death, those who have led a sacred life, looking toward the true promises of divinity and intending to contemplate their own truth in the resurrection that accords with it, come to the culmination of death with firm and true hope, in divine joy, as to the end of their divine contests. They know that they will possess the perfect and unfailing life and salvation that belong to them through their future universal resurrection [Col. 1105A].

For holy souls, not falling into a conversion toward evil that has power according to this present life, will possess in that renewed generation an immutable, divinely formed transfer. The pure bodies, joined and united with the holy souls, registered and fellow soldiers according to their divine placements [Note: [Col. 1105] E reads “seen”], will receive their own resurrection together with the immutable foundation of the souls according to divine life. Because they were united in this life with holy souls, having become members of Christ, they will receive a divinely formed, incorruptible, immortal, and blessed rest.

In these things, then, is the rest of the saints: in joy and immutable hope, as they reach the culmination of their divine contests.

As for the unclean, some irrationally suppose that they return to nonexistence. Others suppose that the bodily conjunction with their own souls is dissolved once and for all, failing to understand, because they are not sufficiently instructed in divine knowledge, that this divinely formed and blessed life had already begun in Christ. Others assign to souls conjunctions with other bodies, acting unjustly, as I think, in making this supposition about the divine souls and wrongly depriving those who reach the end of their most divine courses of their sacred rewards.

Others, somehow recalled to material notions, have said that the most holy and blessed rest promised to the saints is conformed to this present life, and, after changing their life, have cast their own foods before those who are among the unjust angels [Col. 1105C].

But no one among the most sacred men will fall into such errors. Rather, they know that they will immediately receive Christ-shaped rest. When they reach the end of this life, they see more clearly that their path toward incorruption has already been made nearer [Note: [Col. 1105] AE omit “toward”]; they praise the gifts of divinity and are filled with divine delight. They do not fear any return to the things behind them, but know well that they will possess the good things they have acquired firmly and eternally [Note: [Col. 1105D] Psalms V, XXV, LXXXIII].

Those, however, who are full of defilements and unclean stains, who have indeed received some sacred instruction but have wickedly cast it away from their own souls and willingly surrendered themselves to corrupting desires, come to the end of this life unprepared. As the divine legislation of the sayings, rightly despising them, makes clear [Col. 1105D; Note: Jeremiah V; Wisdom V], they behold with other eyes the pleasures destroyed by their own passions and bless the sacred life from which they foolishly departed. Miserably and under compulsion they are cut off from this life, led by their evil life to no sacred hope.

For such people there is no future state corresponding to the sleep of holy men. The holy man himself, on reaching the end of his contests, is filled with sacred joy and ascends with great delight upon the path of the divine renewal. The household members of the one who has fallen asleep, according to their divine dwelling and similar manner of life, bless him as he comes to the desired, palm-bearing end. They offer songs of congratulation for the cause of his victory and express the hope that they too will come to a similar rest. When they receive him, they lead him to the high priest, as to the giver of divine crowns. The high priest, singing, receives him and performs according to sacred law what must be performed for those who have fallen asleep among the saints.

## The Mystery for Those Who Have Fallen Asleep in Holiness

The divine priest gathers the sacred choir. If the one who has died belonged to a sanctifying order, he inclines him before the divine altar, and the deceased is initiated into God through prayer and the Eucharist. If he belonged to the holy monks or the sacred people, he is laid before the venerable priesthood, before the priestly entrance [Col. 1106B].

Then the high priest offers the eucharistic prayer to God. Afterward, the ministers read from the divine words the truthful promises proclaimed concerning our sacred resurrection, and sacredly chant, confessing this through the powerful songs of the psalmic words. Then the chief of the ministers dismisses the catechumens and proclaims the departed among the saints, assigning the deceased to their company through an ordered recitation. He exhorts everyone to ask for blessed consummation in Christ.

Then the divine high priest approaches and offers the most sacred prayer over him. After the prayer, the high priest himself greets the one who has fallen asleep, and all those present greet him after the high priest. When all have greeted him, the high priest pours oil upon the deceased [Col. 1106C], offers the sacred prayer on behalf of all, and they place the body in an honorable house, together with the bodies of the other saints who have been assigned to their company.

## Commentary

If the unclean among us should see or hear these things being performed, they would, I think, laugh loudly and pity our error. But there is no need to be surprised at this. For if they do not believe, as the words say [Note: [Col. 1106D] Isaiah VII], neither will they understand.

We, however, contemplating the invisible realities accomplished for those being perfected, should say to Jesus, the bringer of light, how it is not irrational for the high priest to introduce and place the one who has fallen asleep into the equally militant choir. For this wonderfully signifies that, in the renewed generation itself, all will receive the call corresponding to their own lives, having fulfilled here their own pure way of life.

If someone has possessed here a divinely formed and most sacred life, insofar as imitation of the man of God is permitted, he will be in the divine realm throughout the coming age and in blessed rests. Others, though greatly diminished in the final form of their life, will nevertheless receive sacred rewards corresponding to their condition.

Giving thanks for this divine justice, the high priest offers a sacred prayer and praises the thearchy that must be worshiped, as the power that destroys every unjust and tyrannical power and transfers us to our own justifications [Col. 1107A].

The reading and chanting of the divine promises make manifest the most blessed rests; in weakness they possess their consummation, and eternally they will bear it as a burden. For the one who has fallen asleep they are divinely receptive; for the living they are still exhortatory, directing them toward a similar consummation.

Observe that now not all the orders of those being purified are dismissed according to custom. Only the catechumens are expelled from the sacred choirs. For the catechumen is wholly uneducated concerning the sacred victim and is permitted to contemplate no one, neither great nor small, among those being sacredly consummated. He does not participate in the contemplative virtue of sacred things through the illuminating and light-bearing divine birth.

The remaining orders of those being purified are already engaged in instruction in the sacred tradition [Col. 1107B]. But since they foolishly run back again to what is lower, they must complete their own return to what lies before them [Note: [Col. 1107] BH omits “lies before them”]. They are reasonably separated from the divine things, insofar as they are represented in symbols, in sacred visions and communions. For they will be harmed by participating in them while unclean, and will come to despise the divine things and themselves even more.

They are not improperly present at the rites now being performed, so that they may be openly instructed, see according to us the fear of death, observe the rewards of the saints praised by the true words, and learn that immeasurable darkness awaits the unclean. It is permitted them for their equal benefit to see the one who has been consummated, truly existing from age to age [Note: [Col. 1107] EH reads “of the ages,” i.e. “forever”], sacredly received from the ministerial recitation as a companion of the saints wondrously proclaimed.

Perhaps they too will come to a similar desire and will be instructed through ministerial knowledge that consummation in Christ is truly blessed [Col. 1107C].

Then the divine high priest approaches and performs a sacred prayer over the deceased. After the prayer, the high priest himself greets him, and then all those present do likewise [Note: [Col. 1107] *et* omitted in AE.]. The prayer itself therefore beseeches the divine goodness to forgive the deceased everything committed through human weakness, and to appoint him in the light and in the land of the living, in the bosoms of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, in the place where pain, sadness, and anguish are banished.

These, then, as I suppose, are the manifest recompenses of the most blessed saints. For what could perhaps be weighed against perfect joy and illuminating immortality, even though the promises signified by our figurative expressions are far higher than all our proportions, and their designations have been left behind by the active reality of those promises? The saying must be considered true: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” [Note: [Col. 1107D] Isa. LXIV; 1 Cor. II, 9.].

The “bosoms,” then, as I suppose, are the most divine and most blessed deiform resting-places of the most blessed patriarchs and of all the remaining saints, receiving all into an ineffable and most blessed consummation.

You might perhaps say that what we have said is indeed correct, but question why the high priest implores the divine goodness, asking forgiveness of sins for the deceased and requesting for him a share equal to that of the deiform and most radiant. For if everyone receives from divine justice a recompense for whatever he has done in the present life, whether good or otherwise, and if the deceased has brought his own activities to an end according to this life, how will the high priest, through a certain prayer, transport him into another rest beyond his worth?

And indeed, there each person will receive his share in the recompense of life. I know this well, following the sayings: “For God has fenced him in against himself, and each person will be carried by the body to the things he has done, whether good or bad” [Note: [Col. 1108B] Job XXIX; Hos. II; 1 Cor. V, 10; 1 Reg. XXVIII; Exod. XVII, XXXII, XXXIII; Num. XI, XIV, XVI, [Col. 1108D] XXVII; Deut. I, IX; Ps. CV.].

But that the prayers of the righteous operate both in this life—and much more after death—in those who are worthy of sacred prayers, the true traditions of the sayings teach us. Otherwise, why was Saul rejected by Samuel? And what benefit did the prophetic prayer bring to the Hebrew people? For just as someone who, while the sun itself grants its light, asks to participate in sunlight with unharmed eyes while destroying his own sight, so the person who persecutes the prayers of the supremely wondrous saints and their holy activities according to their nature, through negligence of the divine gifts and of the most manifest deiform commandments, will desire things impossible and entertain hopes that are vain and excessive.

I say, following the sayings [Note: [Col. 1108D] Jas. V.], that the prayers of the saints are altogether useful in this life in the following manner [Col. 1108C]. If someone desires divine gifts and possesses a sacred disposition for participating in them, and, recognizing his own smallness, comes to one of the holy men and deigns to make him his helper and fellow-servant, he will certainly gain from this a benefit surpassing all others.

For he will obtain the supremely divine gifts he requests, since the divine goodness receives him who reveres his own conscience, who approaches with holy confession, with a praiseworthy desire for the sacred petitions he has requested, and with a corresponding deiform disposition. For this too has been proclaimed by the divine judgments: divine gifts are bestowed upon the worthy, in the most divine order, through worthy intermediaries [Note: [Col. 1107] BH: “to be handed over.”].

If someone, then, dishonors this sacred adornment, approaches with a military estimation of himself, considers himself sufficient for divine converse, despises the saints, asks God for one or more unworthy and unsacred petitions, and possesses a desire not strengthened by divine things and not consistent with himself, he will obtain by himself an undisciplined petition.

Concerning the prayer mentioned, which the high priest offers over the deceased, it is necessary to state the tradition that has come down to us from our divine guides [Col. 1109A].

The divine high priest is an interpreter of the divine ordinances, as the sayings declare [Note: [Col. 1109D] Ps. CXVIII; Mal. II; Matt. XVIII], for he is the angel of the Lord Almighty. From the sayings handed down by God, therefore, he has learned that, for those who live holily, the most radiant and divine life is granted according to their worth by the most just recompensers, while the divine goodness disregards the stains naturally contracted by them through human weakness—for no one, as the sayings also declare, is clean from defilement [Note: [Col. 1109D] Job XV; 3 Reg. VIII; Eccl. VII; Rom. III; 1 John I, III; Jas. III.].

The high priest knows these promises from the true sayings. He continually asks that the sacred recompenses be bestowed upon those who live holily, being at once deiformly formed in imitation of God, seeking as his own the graces granted to others, and knowing at once that the promises are not false but will come to pass [Note: [Col. 1109] BH: “for those who will come”], and openly making known to those present that, according to the sacred law, they are to be sought from him by all who have been perfected in accordance with the divine life.

For the high priest, the prophet of divine justice, would never ask for anything except what is most beloved by God and divinely promised to be granted by him. Therefore he does not pray these things for the impure deceased, since in doing so he would not only depart from the prophetic order, but would also presumptuously dare to do something hierarchical, having been moved by the prince of perfections. Moreover, since he follows the right prayer, he too not undeservedly hears from the just saying: “You ask, and you do not receive, because you ask wrongly” [Note: [Col. 1109D] Jas. IV, 3.].

The divine high priest, therefore, seeks what is divinely promised, beloved by God, and altogether to be granted; through his own deiform disposition he demonstrates himself to be a friend of God in matters of goodness, and openly manifests to those present the gifts destined for the saints [Col. 1109C].

Thus the high priests also possess discriminating virtues, as manifesters of the divine ordinances—not because the supremely wise divinity ministerially follows their irrational desires, but because, at the prophetic prompting of the Spirit, the prince of perfection, they separate for God according to worth: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; whose sins you retain, they are retained” [Note: [Col. 1110D] John XX, 22.].

And the sayings, illuminated by the revelations of the most holy Father, declare: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” [Note: [Col. 1110D] Matt. XVI, 19.]. Thus that Evangelist, and every high priest in accordance with him, brings forward the friends of God and disinherits the impious, as a manifester and consummator of the paternal ordinances revealed in him [Col. 1109D].

For, as the sayings declare, he did not reveal that sacred theology by moving himself, nor because flesh and blood had revealed it; rather, being invisibly taught by God himself, he answered. Divine high priests, therefore, must use discernment, together with all the hierarchical virtues, in whatever manner the divinity, the prince of consummation, moves them [Col. 1110A]. Others must attend to the high priests in whatever hierarchical functions they perform as to persons moved by God. For, he says, “Whoever despises you despises me” [Note: [Col. 1110D] Luke X, 16.].

But let us return to the sequence of the prayer mentioned. When the high priest has completed it, he himself greets the deceased, and then all those present. For the person who has been perfected according to the divine life is pleasing and honorable to all deiform persons.

After the greeting, the high priest pours oil over the deceased. Remember that, according to the sacred theogenesis, before the most divine baptism, the first participation in the sacred symbol is bestowed upon the person being perfected after the universal removal of the former garment: the oil of anointing. At the end, oil is now poured over the deceased.

At that time the anointing with oil summoned the person being perfected to the sacred contests; now the poured oil manifests that the deceased fought in those sacred contests and has been perfected [Col. 1110B].

When he has completed these rites, the high priest places the body in a precious dwelling, together with the sacred bodies of the others who are of equal worth. For if the deceased lived a life pleasing to God in soul and body, his body will be precious as it shares the sacred struggle with his holy soul according to the divine dispositions.

From there, divine justice will grant him, together with his own body, the corresponding rests, as to one who enters into and shares either a holy life or its opposite. Therefore the divine legislation of the sacred rites grants divine communions to both: to the soul, in the pure contemplation and knowledge of perfected realities; but to the body, through the most divine ointment—as through an image—the most sacred symbols of divine communion, sanctifying the whole human being, offering sacrifice for his universal salvation, and announcing that his most perfect resurrection is to come through catholic sanctification [Col. 1110C].

It is not right to bring the consummatory invocations out from secrecy into common view by interpreting them in the Scriptures, nor to disclose their mystery or the divine powers worked through them. Rather, as our sacred tradition teaches, one must learn them within solemn doctrines and, perfected in a more divine disposition and ascent through divine love and activity, rise from the illumination of the ruler of the rites to their most exalted knowledge.

That even children, who are not yet capable of understanding divine things, should become participants in divine generation and in the most sacred symbols of divine communion seems, as you say, worthy of an impure and blasphemous laugh—if the high priests teach divine matters to those unable to hear and hand on sacred traditions to those unable to understand. And still more laughable, they say, is the fact that others make renunciations and sacred confessions on their behalf [Col. 1111A].

Your hierarchical understanding, however, must not be confined by those who go astray. Rather, while fearing for them and loving the grace that enlightens them, you must defend it against the snares set forth on their behalf, proposing also this principle according to divine law: that divine things are not all circumscribed within our knowledge. Many things have divine causes unknown to us but known to those in orders better than ours. Many things have also escaped the notice of the most exalted essences, and only the supremely wise and wisdom-producing thearchy has carefully known them.

Nevertheless, since we are speaking about this matter as well, let us state what our deiform holy perfecters, instructed by the ancient tradition, handed down to us. They say—and what they say is true—that, according to divine law, infants who are brought into the sacred disposition will come to be removed from every error that leads away from perfection and from an impure life [Col. 1111B].

This matter greatly occupied the minds of our divine guides, and they approved the reception of infants according to this sacred manner. Thus the parents who naturally bring forward the child must hand the child over to a learned and good divine educator; thereafter he himself perfects the child [Note: [Col. 1111] *a se* omitted in AE.], as a divine father and the sponsor [*anadochus*] of sacred salvation [Note: [Col. 1111] AE: “as a substitute.”].

The high priest therefore asks the person who confesses that he will educate the child according to the divine life to repeat the renunciations and make the sacred confessions—not, as those people perhaps mockingly said, teaching divine matters through one person in place of another. For he does not say: “On behalf of the child I make the renunciations or the sacred confessions.” Rather, he says that the child renounces. That is: “I confess that the child, coming to the sacred understanding through our ascents, believes; that he will universally renounce what is contrary, and will confess and practice divine confessions” [Col. 1112A].

There is therefore, as I judge, nothing inconsistent if the child is educated according to the divine ascent, having a sacred guide and sponsor who implants in him the disposition toward divine things and an experienced guardian against what is contrary.

The high priest hands the child over to the sacred symbols, so that he may live among them and not be shaped for any other life, but always contemplate divine things [Note: [Col. 1111] E: “observe”], and so that his participation in them may be established through holy progress, and his sacred disposition may become strong in them, while he is nobly educated by the divine sponsor [Note: [Col. 1111] B: “and so that he may nobly lead his sacred disposition into deiform guidance.”].

Such, O child, and so good, seem to me to be the uniform spectacles of our Hierarchy [Col. 1112B] [Note: [Col. 1111] BH: “things contemplated.”]. Others, with minds similarly attentive but more deeply engaged, have seen not only these things but many others that are more luminous and more deiform.

And for you too, as I suppose, brighter forms will shine altogether, if you employ the most divine sayings in your ascents toward the more exalted ray. Therefore, my friend, hand over to me as well a more perfect illumination, and show my eyes whatever more beautiful and uniform forms you are able to see. For I trust that, as you ascend, the vapors of the divine fire stored within you will rise as far as the things that have been said.

The book on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy ends here.

# The Third Book of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite: On the Divine Names

[Col. 1111]

## Epigram on the Blessed Dionysius concerning the Divine Names

Splendor enters the mind, striking [uncertain reading] the forms of the divine Scriptures with varied sacred names; and, after foolish death, the divine hymns that make things manifest resound with the life-giving sayings of wisdom.

Dionysius the presbyter to Timothy, his fellow presbyter [Note: [Col. 1111] E: “Of Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Athens, to Timothy, bishop of Ephesus, concerning the Divine Names. ‘Fellow presbyter,’ etc.”].

## The Chapters of the Divine Names Begin

[Note: [Col. 1111] E: “These are contained in the work On the Divine Names: thirteen chapters in all.”]

I. What the interpretation of reason is, and what the tradition concerning the divine names is.

II. Concerning unified and differentiated theology, and what divine unity and differentiation are.

III. What the power of prayer is; concerning the blessed Hierotheus; and concerning reverent and written theology [Col. 1112C].

IV. Concerning the Good, light, goodness, love, ecstasy [Note: [Col. 1111] Manuscripts: Greek ἐκστάσεως, “of ecstasy”], and zeal; and that evil neither exists nor derives from what exists nor is found among existing things.

V. Concerning the Existing One, in which, and concerning paradigms.

VI. Concerning life.

VII. Concerning wisdom, intellect, reason, truth, and faith.

VIII. Concerning power, justice, salvation, and redemption; including the question of inequality.

IX. Concerning the great and the small, the same and the other, the like and the unlike [Note: [Col. 1111] Manuscripts: “concerning the like”], rest, motion, and equality.

X. Concerning the Almighty and the Ancient of Days, including the matters of eternity and time.

XI. Concerning peace, and what is meant by “being itself,” “life itself,” “power itself,” and the expressions so designated.

XII. Concerning the Holy of holies, King of kings, Lord of lords, and God of gods.

XIII. Concerning the Perfect and the One.

[Col. 1113]

# The Book on the Divine Names Begins

## Chapter I. What the Interpretation of Reason Is, and What the Tradition Concerning the Divine Names Is

[Col. 1113A]

Now, O blessed one, let us proceed, insofar as is permitted, from the theological forms of expression to the exposition of the divine names. Let the law of the sayings also be established for us in advance: we are to find the truth of what has been said about God not in persuasive words of wisdom [Note: [Col. 1113D] 1 Cor. II, 4], but in the demonstration produced by the Spirit, through the power of the theologians, by which we are ineffably and unknowably united to things ineffable and unknown, according to the superior unity of our rational and intellectual power and activity.

Therefore, in general, we must neither dare to say nor understand anything concerning the superessential and hidden divinity beyond what has been divinely expressed to us from the sacred sayings. For its superessential knowledge—surpassing reason, intellect, and essence—must itself be placed beyond reason, intellect, and essence [Note: [Col. 1113] AE: “must itself be placed”], while we look upward only as far as the ray of the divine sayings carries itself toward the higher clarities concerning divine things, which are circumscribed with moderation and holiness [Note: [Col. 1113] A*: “with certain divine moderation toward holiness.”].

For just as invisible things are incomprehensible and incontemplable to the senses, and simple and unfeigned things surpass things formed in image and likeness, and the intangible and unfigured formlessness of incorporeal things surpasses what is shaped according to bodily forms, so, according to the same account of truth [Note: [Col. 1113] A*: “account of power”], the superessential greatness surpasses essences; unity surpasses minds [Note: [Col. 1113] A*: “voices surpass minds”]; and for every power it is impossible to reach the secret that lies beyond sense, while the good that is beyond every reason lies beyond all rationality.

It is the unifying unity of every unity, the superessential essence, the invisible intellect, the hidden Word, irrationality, invisibility, and unnameability—not being in accordance with any of the things that exist, yet being the cause of existence for all things; itself, however, being non-being [Greek ὂν, “being”], as the summit of every essence [Note: [Col. 1113] A*: “unity”], and in whatever way it properly and knowingly manifests itself concerning itself.

Concerning this superessential and hidden divinity, then, as has been said, we must neither dare to say nor understand anything beyond what has been divinely expressed to us from the sacred sayings [Col. 1113D]. For it has itself most excellently handed down this teaching about itself in the sayings [Note: [Col. 1113] A*: “properly”]: knowledge and contemplation of what it is are inaccessible to all existing things, since it is superessentially separated from them all [Col. 1114A].

And you will find many theologians praising it not only as invisible and incomprehensible, but also as inscrutable and unsearchable, since no existing trace leads those who seek to enter into the hidden abundance of it [Note: [Col. 1113] BH: “without a trace leading.”].

Nevertheless, the Good, while remaining in itself and established in its superessential ray, is not entirely without communication to any of the things that exist. Rather, it most excellently manifests that ray proportionately through the illuminations of each existing thing, and extends the sacred minds toward the contemplation, participation, and likeness of itself insofar as this is possible. Thus those minds desire divine things in a divinely appropriate manner, according to what is permitted. They are neither glorified impossibly by a divine manifestation moderately granted to what is higher, nor dissolved downward by diminution toward evil; rather, they are well weighed and rightly extended toward the ray that shines above them. Through a commensurable love of just illuminations [Note: [Col. 1113] A*: “of the just”], with sacred reverence, moderation, and holiness, they reveal themselves while following the thearchic orders, which also govern in their entirety the sacred dispositions of the supercelestial essences [Col. 1114B].

What is hidden, inscrutable, and beyond intellect and essence in the thearchy is also inaccessible to the reverent intellectual perceptions of the mind. Honoring these secret things with temperate silence, let us turn our attention to the splendors that shine for us in the sacred sayings. From them let us be led into the light toward the thearchic hymns, illuminated by them in a supermundane manner and formed for sacred hymns. Through these hymns let us also behold, in proportion to us, the divine lights bestowed upon us [Col. 1114C].

Let us praise the generous source of all divine manifestation and light, as it has itself handed down concerning itself in the sacred sayings: that it is the cause, principle, essence, and life of all things; the return and resurrection of those who have departed from it; the restoration and reformation of those who have been lost, bringing them back to the incorruptibility of deiformity; the divine establishment of those who are moved by impure agitation; the protection of those who stand; the restoring guidance by the hand of those who have been led back to it; the illumination of those who have been illuminated; the principal perfection of those who have been perfected; the divinity of divine things; the simplicity of the simple; the unity of those who are united; the superessentially super-principal principle of every principle; and the best tradition of what is hidden, insofar as this is just [Note: [Col. 1113] *quod* omitted in E] [Col. 1114D].

And, to put it simply, it is the life of the living and the essence of existing things, the principle and cause of all life and essence, through its active and sustaining goodness by which existing things exist.

[Col. 1115A] We have learned these things from the divine utterances, and you will find that the entire sacred hymnody of the theologians, so to speak, prepares manifestative and laudatory divine names for the beneficent processions of the Godhead. Hence, in almost every theological work, we see the Godhead divinely praised as monad and unity, because of the simplicity and unity of its supernatural indivisibility, from which, by its unifying power, we are united; and, with our divided differences supermundanely folded together, we are gathered into a deiform monad and a unity imitating God.

It is called Trinity because of the subsistent expression of the threefold fecundity of the superessential, from which every fatherhood in heaven and on earth exists and is named [Note: [Col. 1115D] Ephesians 3].

It is called the cause of existing things because all things have been brought into being through its substantializing goodness [Col. 1115B]. It is called wise and good because all existing things, which by their own nature are preserved incorruptible, are filled with every divine harmony and sacred beauty. It is called human in a different way, because it communicated with the things that are ours universally in one of its subsistences [Note: [Col. 1115] BH: “substances”], and restored to itself the last part of humanity, from which Jesus, ineffably simple and composite, was formed; the eternal One assumed a temporal addition and became equal to us in nature, while remaining superessentially protected, according to every nature and order, in the unchangeable and unconfused establishment of what properly belongs to each.

The hidden tradition of our divine guides has also expressly bestowed on us whatever other deifying illuminations follow in the divine utterances. These things we too have learned: for the present, rationally according to our capacity, through the sacred veils of the utterances and hierarchical traditions—veils that cover invisible things with sensible forms, that surround things superessential with forms and likenesses, and that multiply and prefigure the supernatural and imageless simplicity through the variety of divided symbols.

But then, when we have become incorruptible and immortal, and have been made Christlike [Note: [Col. 1115] AE: “Christlike”], and have been received into the most blessed repose, “we shall always be with the Lord,” according to the utterance [Note: [Col. 1115D] 1 Thessalonians 4:16]. We shall be filled with the visible manifestation of his divinity in the purest contemplations, as he surrounds us with most manifest splendors, like the disciples in that most divine transformation [Note: [Col. 1116D] Matthew 17; Mark 9; Luke 9]. We shall also participate in his invisible illumination with an impassible and immaterial intellect, and in the unity beyond intellect of the rays that appear above us, through unknown and blessed experiences, in a more divine imitation of the heavenly minds.

For, as the truth of the utterances says, we shall be like the angels, and “the children of God, being children of the resurrection” [Note: [Col. 1116D] Luke 20:36].

For now, insofar as we are able, we use the necessary divine symbols, and from them again proportionately direct our attention toward the simple and united truth of invisible contemplations. After resting from every deiform intellectual activity proper to us, we shall cast our intellectual operations into the superessential ray, as is fitting. In it all the ends of every cognition have been established beforehand in a manner surpassing mystery. It is neither possible to understand it, nor to speak of it, nor at all to contemplate it in any way, since it is remote from all things and unknowable beyond all knowledge. It encompasses within itself, superessentially, at once the summits of all essential cognitions and virtues, and is set above all things with incomprehensible power, even above the heavenly minds.

For if all sciences concern existing things and have their end in things that exist, then that summit of every essence is remote from every science. And if it is better than every reason and every science, and is set universally beyond intellect and essence, while being receptive of, comprehending, and anticipating all things, yet universally incomprehensible in itself to all things, and possessing neither sense nor imagination nor opinion nor name nor word nor touch nor knowledge—how can discourse about the divine names be conducted without a word, and with the superessential deity shown beyond all naming?

But what we said when we expounded the theological characteristics—that the One, the Unknown, the Superessential, the Good in itself, which truly is, namely, the triune unity, “of one God” (*homotheos*) and “of one goodness” (*homagathos*)—cannot be either spoken or understood [Col. 1116C].

The angelic unities of the holy powers also—which ought to be called either contemplative or receptive—are mysteries and unknown things, beyond all knowledge and radiant beyond all knowledge, belonging solely to those angels who are worthy of them, above angelic knowledge [Note: [Col. 1115] E: “and beyond”]. Minds made deiform by angelic imitation and united, insofar as permitted, with these powers—how do they rest according to every intellectual operation? The unity of deified minds with the highest light is of such a kind: they praise it especially through the removal of all existing things. In this they are truly and supernaturally illuminated by their most blessed union with it, because it is the causal source of all existing things, while it itself is nothing of those things that exist, being exalted superessentially above them all.

Therefore, the divine superessentiality—the subsistence of supergoodness—must not rightly be praised as word or virtue, as mind or life or essence. Rather, it is said to be eminently remote from every habit, motion, life, imagination, opinion, name, word, virtue, intelligence, essence, state, position, unity, summit, multitude, and from everything whatsoever that exists.

But since, as the subsistence of goodness, it is the cause of the being of all things, the providence of the principal divinity must be praised from all causal things. For all things are around it and because of it; it is before all things; all things are established in it; and, as the being of all things, it is their access and substance. All things desire it: intellectual and rational things knowingly, those subject to them sensibly, and other things according to vital, essential, and conditional necessity.

Knowing this, the theologians praise it both as nameless and by every name. They call it nameless when they introduce the divinity itself, in one of the visions of the symbolic divine manifestation in mystical forms, rebuking and saying, “What is your name?” [Note: [Col. 1117C] Genesis 32].
