And when it withdraws him from every nominative knowledge of God, it says: “Why do you ask my name? And it is wonderful” [Note: [Col. 1117C] Judges 13:18].

Or is not this truly a wonderful name, which is above every name, which is nameless, and which is set above every named name, whether in this age or in the age to come? [Note: [Col. 1117C] Ephesians 1:21.]

They call it many-named when they again introduce it as saying: “I am the One who is” [Note: [Col. 1117C] Exodus 3:14], and “life” [Note: [Col. 1117C] John 14:6], “light” [Note: [Col. 1117C] John 1:14 ff.], “God” [Note: [Col. 1117C] Genesis 1; Isaiah 42], “truth”; and when the theosophers themselves praise the causal source of all things by many names drawn from all causal realities: as the Good [Note: [Col. 1117C] Luke 18], as the Good One [Note: [Col. 1117C] Psalm 118], as the Wise [Note: [Col. 1117C] Job 9], as the Beloved [Note: [Col. 1117C] Song of Songs 5], as God of gods [Note: [Col. 1117C] Psalm 49], as Lord of lords [Note: [Col. 1117C] Revelation 17], as Holy of holies [Note: [Col. 1117C] Daniel 9], as Eternal [Note: [Col. 1117C] Baruch 4], as Existing [Note: [Col. 1117C] Exodus 3], as the Cause of the ages [Note: [Col. 1117C] Proverbs 3], as Giver of life [Note: [Col. 1117C] Acts 17], as Wisdom [Note: [Col. 1117C] 1 Corinthians 1], as Intellect [Note: [Col. 1117C] Job 10], as Word [Note: [Col. 1117C] Psalm 44], as Knower [Note: [Col. 1117C] 2 Samuel 8], as the One who brings forth all treasures from every knowledge [Note: [Col. 1117C] Colossians 2], as Power [Note: [Col. 1117C] 1 Corinthians 1], as Mighty [Note: [Col. 1117C] Job 11–12], as King of those who reign [Note: [Col. 1117C] Revelation 19], as Ancient of Days [Note: [Col. 1117C] Daniel 7], as One who does not grow old [Note: [Col. 1117C] Ecclesiasticus 18], as Unchanging [Note: [Col. 1117C] Malachi 3], as Salvation [Note: [Col. 1117C] Matthew 1], as Justice [Note: [Col. 1117C] Isaiah 45], as Sanctification [Note: [Col. 1117C] 1 Corinthians 1], as Redemption [Note: [Col. 1117C] Isaiah 31], as the One who surpasses everything in greatness [Note: [Col. 1117C] Psalm 144], and as being in a gentle breeze [Note: [Col. 1117C] 1 Kings 19].

They also say that he is in minds [Note: [Col. 1117C] 1 Peter 2], in souls [Note: [Col. 1117C] Wisdom 7], in bodies [Note: [Col. 1117C] 1 Corinthians 6], in heaven [Note: [Col. 1117C] Psalm 10], in earth [Note: [Col. 1117C] Jeremiah 23], and simultaneously the same in the same [Note: [Col. 1117C] Isaiah 55]; that he is not in the world, around the world, beyond the world [Note: [Col. 1117C] Isaiah 66], heavenly beyond heaven [Note: [Col. 1117C] Psalm 66], superessential [Note: [Col. 1117C] Matthew 6], sun [Note: [Col. 1117C] Daniel 7; Malachi 3], star [Note: [Col. 1118C] Revelation 2], fire [Note: [Col. 1118C] Deuteronomy 4], water [Note: [Col. 1118C] John 4], spirit [Note: [Col. 1118C] Lamentations 4], dew [Note: [Col. 1118C] Hosea 14], cloud [Note: [Col. 1118C] Ecclesiasticus 43], and, in himself, stone [Note: [Col. 1118C] Psalm 117] and rock [Note: [Col. 1118C] 1 Corinthians 10]: all things that exist, and none of the things that exist [Note: [Col. 1118C] 1 Corinthians 15] [Note: [Col. 1117] E: “that do not exist”].

Thus they unite the cause of all things, which is beyond all things that exist, with the Nameless One, and all the names of the things that exist, so that the kingdom of all things may carefully belong to it; that all things may be around it; that, as cause, principle, and end, all things may depend upon it; and that, according to the utterance, it may be all things in all things. In truth, it is praised as the originating and consummating substance of all things [Col. 1118B], as their containing guardian [Note: [Col. 1118C] Isaiah 21], their nourisher [Note: [Col. 1118C] Ecclesiasticus 24], the one who turns them back to itself [Note: [Col. 1118C] Lamentations 5], and the one who unites them to itself immeasurably and sublimely.

For it is not merely the cause of containment, or of life, or of consummation, so that the super-namable goodness might be named from one or another of these providences alone. Rather, it has anticipated within itself all things, simply and without qualification, through the most perfect goodnesses of its one and most causal providence, and it is harmoniously praised and named from all things that exist.

The theologians do not honor only these divine names, which derive from all things or from particular providences or from the objects of providence. There are also names derived from the occasions when divine responses in sacred temples [Note: [Col. 1118C] Isaiah 5], or in other forms, illuminate teachers [Note: [Col. 1118C] 1 Kings 8] or prophets [Note: [Col. 1118C] Judges 6; 1 Kings 11–12; Exodus 6; Isaiah 6]. According to various causes and powers [Col. 1118C] [Note: [Col. 1117] E: “and causes”], they name the goodness beyond expression and beyond naming, and surround it with human forms and likenesses [Note: [Col. 1118C] Song of Songs 1, 5], or fiery [Note: [Col. 1118C] Deuteronomy 4], or amber-like forms [Note: [Col. 1118C] Ezekiel 1, 8]. They praise its eyes [Note: [Col. 1118C] Hebrews 4], ears [Note: [Col. 1118C] Isaiah 5], braided hair [Col. 1119A] [Note: [Col. 1119D] Song of Songs 5], face [Note: [Col. 1119D] Psalm 33], hands [Note: [Col. 1119D] Psalm 118], hindparts [Note: [Col. 1119D] Genesis 16], wings [Note: [Col. 1119D] Deuteronomy 32], arms [Note: [Col. 1119D] Isaiah 52], back [Note: [Col. 1119D] Exodus 33], and feet [Note: [Col. 1119D] Deuteronomy 33]. They also form around it crowns [Note: [Col. 1119D] Isaiah 24], thrones [Note: [Col. 1119D] Daniel 7], a cup [Note: [Col. 1119D] Psalm 115], its mixing bowls [Note: [Col. 1119D] Song of Songs 7], and whatever other things are mystical, concerning which we have spoken, according to their power, in the Symbolic Theology.

Now, gathering from the utterances whatever belongs to the present work, and using what has been said as a kind of rule, looking toward it, let us proceed to the disclosure of the invisible divine names. The hierarchical law has always introduced us throughout theology to contemplate theophanies by a divine contemplative power—to speak properly, theories—and to apply sacred ears to the repetitions of the wondrous divine names. According to divine tradition, let us place holy things among the holy [Col. 1119B] [Note: [Col. 1119D] Matthew 7], while taking them away from the unlearned who ridicule and mock them; or rather, if there truly are such people, let us rescue those very persons from this divine struggle.

You, therefore, good Timothy, must guard these things according to the most sacred injunction, and must not make divine things spoken or uttered available to the unlearned. May God grant me to praise divinely the many beneficent names of the uncalled and unnamed divinity, and may he not take the word of truth from my mouth [Note: [Col. 1119D] Psalm 118].

## CHAPTER II. On united and distinguished theology, and on what divine unity and distinction are

The whole subsistence of the divinity, because it is goodness in itself, is praised in the utterances by being set forth and expressed. For what else is to be learned from sacred theology, when it introduces the divinity itself as saying: “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except God alone” [Note: [Col. 1119D] Matthew 19:17; Luke 18:19]?

This is also shown to us in other passages: all the divine names previously attributed to God are always praised by the utterances not partially, but in the whole, perfect, complete, and full divinity; and all of them are assigned impartibly, absolutely, without restriction, universally, to the whole of universality, perfectly in the whole, and to every divinity. For, as we warned in the theological characteristics, if someone says that this is not said of the whole divinity, he blasphemes [Note: [Col. 1119D] John 10] and unjustly dares to divide the superunited unity.

It must therefore be said how this is to be understood in the whole divinity. For the Word himself, born from goodness, says: “I am good” [Note: [Col. 1119D] Matthew 20:15; Psalm 142:10]. And one of the prophets acceptable to God praises the good Spirit. Again, he says: “I am the one who is” [Note: [Col. 1120D] Exodus 3:14].

If they say that the divinity is not praised according to its whole, but that this is described according to one part, they do violence to the text. How then will they hear: “Thus says the One who is, who was, and who is to come, the Almighty” [Note: [Col. 1120D] Revelation 1:4]? And: “But you are the same” [Note: [Col. 1120D] Psalm 101:28]. And: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” [Note: [Col. 1120D] John 15:26].

If they say that the divine life is not whole, how is what the divine Word said true: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” [Note: [Col. 1120D] John 5:21]? And: “For the Spirit is the one who gives life” [Note: [Col. 1120D] John 6:63].

But how does the whole divinity also possess dominion over all things? Concerning the deity that begets God, or is begotten, nothing need be said, I think, since theology proclaims the Father and the Son as Lord; but it also says that the Lord is Spirit. Goodness and wisdom likewise are praised in the whole divinity, as are light, [Col. 1120B] deification, causality, and everything belonging to the whole divinity. The utterances refer all these things to the divine hymnody, both collectively, as when they say, “All things are from God,” and successively, as when one says: “All things were created through him and in him, and all things have been established in him” [Note: [Col. 1120D] Romans 11:36]. And: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created” [Note: [Col. 1119] E: “You will send forth”] [Note: [Col. 1120D] Psalm 103:30].

To put it briefly, the divine Word himself says: “I and the Father are one.” And: “All things that the Father has are mine.” And: “All that is mine is yours, and yours is mine” [Note: [Col. 1120D] John 10:30; 17]. Again, whatever belongs to the Father and to himself [Note: [Col. 1119] BH: “to himself”], they assign commonly and jointly to the divine Spirit: divine operations, honor, the fountain, the unfailing cause, and the distribution of the best gifts.

I do not think that anyone who is not utterly worn down by contradiction to the divine utterances can oppose this, since all divine things belong to the whole divinity according to the perfect divine account.

Having stated these things briefly in some respects and sufficiently in others, from the utterances and from what has been shown and defined, we shall attempt to repeat whatever universal divine name is to be understood in the whole divinity itself. But if someone says that by this we introduce confusion contrary to divine distinction, we do not think that such a person has given a sufficient account of how his claim is true.

For if someone is altogether estranged from the utterances, he will also be far removed from our philosophy in every respect. And if he does not care about the divine wisdom contained in the utterances, how will he care about our guidance into theological knowledge? But if he looks to the truth of the utterances, then, using this rule and light, we too shall proceed rightly, insofar as we can, in our defense.

We shall say that theology hands down some things jointly and others distinctly. It is not right either to separate what is united or to confuse what is distinct. Rather, following theology according to its power, we must look toward the divine splendors, receive divine manifestations from them, and preserve what is established there in themselves as a most beautiful rule of truth—not multiplied, not diminished, and unaltered. Let us hasten, guarded by the keeping of the utterances, to guard what is unalterable, and to be able to guard them through the very things that guard us.

The things united in the whole divinity are, as we showed from many utterances in the theological characteristics: supergood, superdivine, superessential, superliving, superwise, and whatever belongs to eminent negation; together with all causal names—Best, Good, Being, Parent of the living, Wise—and whatever names it receives from its best gifts [Note: [Col. 1121] A: “denominations”; B: “dominions”], as the cause of all good things.

The things distinguished are the superessential name and reality of the Father, Son, and Spirit, with no reciprocal interchange or any commonality introduced among them. Also distinguished from these is the perfect and unchangeable subsistence of Jesus according to us, together with all the essential mysteries of the humanity belonging to him.

It is necessary, I think, for us to receive and expound more fully the most perfect manner of divine unity and distinction, examining as well as we can the whole innate account: leaving aside everything varied and obscure, and considering distinctly, manifestly, and in good order what properly belongs to each according to its power.

For the sacred teachers of our theological tradition call the divine unities the hidden and irreversible superpositions of the supersecret and superunknowable unity, while they call the distinctions the best processions and manifestations of the divinity. Following the sacred utterances, they say that the properties of the aforementioned unity—and, again, those of distinction—include certain particular unities and distinctions [Note: [Col. 1121] AB: “and”], even within the divine unity without superessentiality.

United with the one principal Trinity and common to it is the superessential subsistence, the superdivine deity, the supergood goodness of all things, the summit of all summits [Note: [Col. 1121] “The summit of all summits” omitted by BH], the unchangeability of every proper attribute, the unity beyond principality, the ineffable, the many-named, the ignorance, every invisible thing, the position of all things, the negation of all things, and—beyond every position and negation, if one may put it so—the abiding and placement of the principal substances among themselves.

It is universally superunited and confused in no part, like the lights of lamps, if I may use sensible and appropriate examples. When they are in one house, all the lights are wholly in one another, and one undivided brightness shines forth; no one, I think, can distinguish the light of one lamp from the others through the air containing all the lights, or see one part without the other, since the wholes are unmixedly blended with wholes.

Yet if someone removes one of the burning lamps from the house [Note: [Col. 1121] E: “from the house”], its entire proper light withdraws with it, containing nothing of the other lights within itself and leaving none of its own to the others. For there was, as I said, a perfect unity of all with all, universally unmixed and confused in no part, while the light existed in an airy body and depended upon material fire.

When we say that superessential unity is set above these things, we do not mean merely bodily unities, but also those present in souls themselves and in intellects themselves. These participate in them without mixture, and supermundanely, through all deiform and heavenly lights, according to rational participation; yet the unity remains wholly beyond all participants.

There is also distinction in superessential theologies—not merely in the sense I mentioned, namely, that this unity establishes each of the principal substances without mixture and without confusion, but also because the realities of the superessential theogony do not reciprocally exchange with one another. The Father alone is the fountain of the superessential deity: the Son is not the Father, nor is the Father the Son. Thus the proper distinctions of each divine substance are rightly preserved in praise.

Such, then, is unity and distinction according to ineffable unity and subsistence.

But if divine distinction is also the excellent procession of divine unity—of the goodness that is superunited with itself, yet makes plural and multiplies—then, according to divine distinction, the immeasurable traditions, living substantializations, impartations of wisdom, and other gifts that are the cause of all goodness are united. According to these, the imparticipable things that are participated are praised from participations and participants.

It is also common, united, and one throughout the whole Godhead that the whole of it is participated by each participant, yet by none is any part of it participated. It is like a wheel at the center of a circle, touched by all the straight lines arranged around the circle; and like a seal impressed upon many objects, each of the impressions possessing the whole and the same seal, and possessing it in no part merely.

Yet the nonparticipation of the most causal deity is set above these things, so that there is neither contact with it nor any other mixed association with the participants.

Yet someone may say: the seal itself is not whole in the whole things impressed; and therefore the seal is not a cause, for the cause imparts its whole self, the same, to each individual. But the difference and dissimilarity of the participants themselves causes the image of the one, whole, and identical principal exemplar to be discolored.

Thus, if the participants are soft and malleable, or even smooth and shaped [Note: [Col. 1123] H: “capable of being shaped”], and are neither opposed to the exemplars by hardness nor diffuse and unstable, they will possess a pure, clear, and corresponding form. But if something required for that suitability is lacking, this will be the cause of nonparticipation and obscurity, as well as of whatever other effects arise from unsuitability for participation.

The superessential Word is also distinctly and beautifully substantialized in us and from us by divine operation according to us, and he performs and suffers whatever things belonging to his incarnation are distinguished and supremely wondrous through divine action.

In these matters the Father and the Spirit share nothing with the Word—unless someone should say that they share according to the best human will and according to every transcendent and secret divine operation, in which the immutable God and Word of God, having become according to us, acted [Note: [Col. 1123] “in” omitted by AE].

Let us therefore hasten to understand and distinguish divine things by reason, and to discern how divine things are both united and distinguished [Note: [Col. 1123] AE: “let us hasten”].

We have expounded, in the theological characteristics, whatever divine causes of these unities and distinctions we have found in the utterances, receiving what belongs properly to each, insofar as possible. We have reviewed and repeated those things according to the true account, bringing the sacred and revealed understanding into the manifest spectacles of the utterances. But we have withdrawn the others, as mystical things according to divine tradition, beyond intellectual operation [Note: [Col. 1123] AE: “and”].

For all divine things, and whatever is manifested to us, are known only through participations. But what they are in their own principle and foundation is beyond intellect and every essence and knowledge. Thus, when we call the hidden superessential God “life,” “essence,” “light,” or “word,” we understand nothing other than the deifying, substantializing, life-generating, or wisdom-bestowing powers that proceed from him into us. We desire him himself through the fruit of all intellectual operations, seeing no deification, life, or essence that is not carefully remote, according to every transcendence, from the cause of all things.

Again, we have received from the wondrous utterances that the Father is the fountainhead of divinity, while the Son and the Spirit are, if one may put it so, shoots sprung from the God-bearing divinity, like flowers and superessential lights. But how these things are, it is neither possible to say nor to understand.

Yet this far the power of all our intellectual activity extends: every divine fatherhood and sonship has been given both to us and to the heavenly powers from the principal fatherhood and principal sonship, remote from all things. Through this, minds become and are named gods and fathers of gods, made deiform through such spiritual fatherhood and sonship—perfected, that is, incorporeally, immaterially, invisibly, by the divine principal Spirit, set beyond every immaterial intellect and deification; while the Father and the Son are exalted beyond every divine fatherhood and sonship.

For there is no exact likeness between causes and effects. The effects possess received images of their causes, but the causes are removed from and set above their effects according to the account of their own principle.

To use examples from our own experience: pleasures and sorrows are called causes of delight and grief, but they themselves neither delight nor grieve. A hot and burning fire is not said itself to be burned or heated. If someone says that life itself lives, or that light itself is illuminated, he does not speak correctly according to our account, except when he says these things in another manner, since they exist abundantly and essentially beforehand in the causes of effects.

But the divine formation and secret manifestation of Jesus is also, according to us, most manifest to the whole of theology, hidden from every reason, unknown to every intellect, and even to the excellence of the most honorable angels. We have mystically received that he was substantially formed as a man; but we do not know how he was formed from virginal blood according to another law beyond nature, nor how, with dry feet, possessing bodily mass and the weight of matter, he walked upon the moist and unstable substance [Note: [Col. 1123D] Matthew 14; Mark 6; John 6], nor how the other things belonging to Jesus’ supernatural physiology came to be.

These matters have been sufficiently discussed by us elsewhere, and are praised with great supernatural force by the glorious guide according to his obscure theological commentaries [Col. 1124C]. Whether he received these things from the sacred theologians, or considered them through disciplined investigation of the utterances, through extensive practice and expertise concerning them, or whether he was instructed by some more divine inspiration—learning not only but also experiencing divine things, and through this sympathetic involvement with them, if one may put it so, being perfected into their unteachable and mystical unity and faith—let us add, among the many blessed spectacles of that powerful intellect, a small selection of what he says about Jesus in the theological commentaries he collected.

### From the theological commentaries of the most holy Hierotheus

The divinity of Jesus, the cause of all things and their fulfillment, preserves the parts of the universe in harmony. It is neither part nor whole, yet it is both whole and part, encompassing within itself, surpassing, and excelling everything, part, and whole.

It is perfect in imperfect things, as their principal perfection; imperfect in perfect things, as superperfect and preperfect. It is the form that forms forms in the formless, as the principal form; and formless in forms themselves, as the superform. It is the superessential essence of the whole of essence, transcending all uncontaminated things and, being superessentially remote from every essence, assigning all principles and orders while being set above every principle and order.

It is the measure of existing things and of the ages, both beyond the age and before the ages. It is full in those who lack, superfull in plenitudes, secret, ineffable, beyond mind, beyond life, beyond essence. Supernaturally, it possesses the supernatural; superessentially, the superessential [Note: [Col. 1125] AE: “and the supernatural”; BH omits “the supernatural”] [Note: [Col. 1125] B: “supernaturally”].

Therefore, since it came even as far as nature for the love of humanity [Note: [Col. 1125] AE: “for the sake of human nature”], and truly is essence, a man has been created who is supergod. May what must be praised beyond mind and reason be propitious to us.

And if in these matters the divinity possesses the supernatural and the superessential [Note: [Col. 1125] BH: “the superessential Jesus’ divinity” omitted], it not only communicated itself to us immutably and without confusion, suffering nothing in its superabundance because of the ineffable novelty; but, in this greatest novelty of all novelties, it was supernatural in our natural realities and superessential in the things belonging to essence [Note: [Col. 1125] BH omits “super” before “essence”]. [Col. 1125B] It possessed all that is ours, from us and for us, in a manner surpassing all.

This, then, is sufficient.

Let us now proceed to the speculative consideration of reason, repeating, insofar as possible for us, the common and unified names of the divine distinction. And, so that we may define beforehand and clearly what follows concerning all things, we call the divine distinction, as has been said, the beautiful processions of divinity. For, while it grants being to all that exists and pours over all the participations in every good, it is distinguished in unity, yet is multiplied in a unified manner and is multiplied from the One without return.

For example, since God is **ὣν**—“being”—superessentially, while he grants being to the things that exist and brings forth entire essences, the One is said to be multiplied: [Col. 1125C] that **ὃν**—“being”—is brought forth from itself through the bringing forth of many existing things, which nevertheless are in no way less than that One in their multiplication; and the One is united according to procession and filled according to distinction, being superessentially removed from all things that exist, while, through the merciful procession of all things and the undiminished outpouring of its undiminished self-gifts, it is not diminished.

Moreover, although it is one **ὣν**—“being”—and gives the One from the One to every part and to the whole, to unity and to multitude, it remains in the same way superessentially one: it is neither a part of a multitude nor a whole composed of parts; and thus it is neither one nor does it possess unity. For it is far above the One, beyond the things that are one [Note: [Col. 1125] AE adds “however.”]; it is an indivisible multitude, a superplenitude without fullness, bringing forth, perfecting, and encompassing every unity and multitude.

Again, through the deification proceeding from itself according to the capacity of each one, the distinction and multiplication of the many gods made godlike appears and is called the distinction of the one God. Yet it is in no way less the primordial God and the supergod, superessentially one: the indivisible God, united with indivisibles, unmixed with himself and with the many, and not multiplied.

Understanding this supernaturally, our common teacher and guide by the hand into divine illumination, [Col. 1126A] the great man in divine matters, the light of the world, says divinely in his sacred writings:

> “For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—for indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are unto him” [Note: [Col. 1125] AE reads “in him.”]; “and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we are through him” [Note: [Col. 1125D] 1 Corinthians 8:5.].

For in divine things the unities of the distinctions are empowered and take precedence, and nevertheless remain united even after the One’s irreversible and merciful distinction. We shall try, insofar as possible, to praise these allied and unified distinctions of the entire deity—that is, its beautiful processions—by means of the names that manifest them in the divine utterances. Let this first be understood, as has been said: every beneficent divine name, wherever it is assigned to the divine substances, is to be received without distinction throughout the entire divine totality.

## CHAPTER III. The power of prayer; concerning the blessed Hierotheus; and concerning reverent and written theology

[Note: [Col. 1125] Thus the manuscripts; the table of chapters reads: “what it is.”]

[Col. 1126B]

Let us, if it seems good, proclaim first the most perfect and most manifest of all the processions of God, the best name, invoking the primordial and supremely good Trinity, which declares all its own supremely good providences. For we ought first to be led by prayers toward it, as the source of good things, and, drawing nearer to it, to be taught in this way what the best gifts placed around it are.

For it is itself present to all, but not all are present to it. When, however, we invoke it with the purest [Col. 1126C] prayers, with the mind also turned back and, in a fitting manner, directed toward the divine unity, then we too are present to it. For it is not in a place, so that it might pass from some place or from one thing into another; rather, it remains to say that it is in all existing things, above all things, and encompassing the multitude of all things.

We therefore stretch ourselves through prayers toward the higher vision of the divine and best rays, as though we imagined that we were drawing toward ourselves the radiance of a great light, suspended from the height of heaven and reaching the things that are here below, while extending our hands toward its constant presence. In truth, however, we do not draw it downward, for it is present above and below; rather, we ourselves are drawn back toward the loftier splendors of the most luminous rays.

Or, as when we ascend a ship, receive ropes extended from some rock, and suppose that they have been given to us for our own drawing in: in truth, we bring neither the rock to ourselves nor ourselves alone to the rock, but ourselves and the ship to the rock. The contrary also occurs in this way: if someone standing beside a firm rock is driven away in a ship, he will accomplish nothing against the stationary and immutable rock, but will separate himself from it; and the more strongly he pushes it away, the farther he will turn back from it.

Accordingly, every undertaking ought to begin with prayer, and theological undertaking especially—not as though we were drawing to ourselves the power that is present everywhere and nowhere, but as though, through divine recollections and invocations, we were joining and uniting ourselves to it.

This too deserves an equally appropriate defense: our glorious leader Hierotheus, having gathered together most excellently the most diligent rudiments of theology, and we, as though those were insufficient, have written another theology, including the present one. For if he had judged it fitting to perform all the theological actions that followed and had traversed the entire chapter of theology through its divided circuits, perhaps we would not have fallen into such madness or folly [Note: [Col. 1127] AE: “into such madness or folly.”], imagining ourselves more perceptive and more divine than he and delighting to add more pleasing things to his theologies. In saying such things, we would be acting superfluously, as though still despising and wronging him who was both our teacher and our friend, and we who, after the divine Paul, were formed by his utterances, would be stealing for ourselves his most glorious contemplation and exposition.

But since he, introducing divine things with due reverence, set before us clear definitions which embrace many things in one, and enjoined us and those who are teachers among us to unfold and distinguish, in language proportionate to our capacity, the clear and powerful ranges of that most intellectual man’s power for souls newly brought to perfection, You yourself have often encouraged us in this, and you returned the book to us as something exalted beyond reach.

Therefore we reserve him, as the teacher of perfect and venerable understandings, for those who are above us, as a kind of secondary Scripture following the God-inspired Scriptures. But to those who are at our level, we shall in proportion to our capacity hand on divine things.

For if solid food belongs to the perfected [Note: [Col. 1127D] Hebrews 5.], what degree of perfection would another possess who partook of such nourishment? It was therefore rightly and most appropriately said by us that the contemplative vision itself of invisible utterances, and the teaching that beholds them, requires an honorable virtue; whereas the knowledge and discipline of verbal expression belong to those who are more humble, devoted, and consecrated.

Indeed, this principle too has been observed by us with great care. Thus, since that divine guide had clearly and properly distinguished things according to their expression, nothing at all should ever be added merely for tautology to the explanation of the utterance he proposed.

For when we came together with our most honored high priests, acceptable to God—as it is believed, you and I and many of our holy brothers—to behold the body that was beginning to live and receive God, James, the brother of God, was also present, as were Peter, the summit and most honorable height of theologians. Then it seemed good, after the vision, that all the high priests should together praise, each according to his ability, the mighty goodness of the divine weakness. As you know, after the theologians he surpassed all the other holy teachers: wholly outside himself and wholly united to God, sharing in the work of praise, and judged by all who heard, saw, knew—and did not know—him to be a praiser acceptable to God and divine.

And what shall I tell you about the things that were set forth there theologically? For unless I also spoke from my own experience, I know that you have often heard certain portions of those divine hymns from me. Thus I hasten to pursue the divine things for you from what is already prepared.

And although we leave the mystical things there, things ineffable to many and unknown to you, he himself made it his practice to communicate with many and to lead as many as he could into the sacred knowledge that is available to us. In this way he surpassed many holy teachers in the length of time, purity of mind, diligence in manifestations, and the other sacred disciplines.

Therefore we would never have attempted to contradict so great a sun. For we have so constituted and recognized ourselves that we are not capable of adequately comprehending the invisible divine things, nor are we permitted to speak or explain the ineffable matters of divine knowledge.

Being far removed from them, we are surpassed by the knowledge of divine men concerning theological truth, since in this matter too we have come under the influence of an excessive fear: we are not at all able either to hear or to speak about divine philosophy unless we have apprehended it intellectually.

Yet we must not neglect the reception of divine knowledge. This was taught to us not only by the natural desire of souls, always lovingly sweet, joined to the contemplation of supernatural things, but also by the excellent ordering of the divine laws themselves. That ordering drives us away from attempting what is above us, what exceeds our dignity, and what is impossible; but it commands us attentively to learn all that is sought and granted to us, and to hand it on divinely to others.

Persuaded by these considerations, and laboring—or fearing—to discover what is possible concerning divine things, yet unwilling to leave unsupported those who cannot turn their gaze toward what is better than themselves, we have been led to write. We do not dare introduce anything new; rather, through more precise questions concerning each individual part, we distinguish and express what was truly and nobly said by Hierotheus.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the supremely good, light, good, love, ecstasy, and zeal; and that evil is neither **ὄν** (“being”), nor from that which is, nor among existing things

[Col. 1128D]

If it is agreeable, then, let us return now to that divine name which the theologians distinguish, in a transcendent manner, from all things and from the superdivine Godhead, calling the divine subsistence itself [Note: [Col. 1127] BH: “substance”] goodness, and saying that, by existing as the Good, as the essential Good, it extends goodness to all that exists. For just as the sun that is visible to us illuminates all things—not by deliberating or choosing, but simply by existing—according to the proportion in which they are able by their own nature to participate in its light, so also the Good, which is above the sun, as the principal exemplar surpassing even an obscure image, proportionately sends the rays of its entire goodness from its own subsistence to all existing things.

Through these rays all invisible and intellectual beings subsist—the essences, powers, and operations—and through them they possess life that does not fail or diminish. Purified from every corruption, death, matter, and generation, and set above instability, flux, and change that bears one thing in one way and another in another, they are understood as incorporeal and immaterial; and as intellects they understand in a supermundane manner. The principles of existing things are properly illuminated in them, and they in turn convey them into what is akin to them and proper to them. From goodness they possess their dwelling, and from it they have their foundation, their containment, their protection, and their nourishment in good things. Desiring it, they possess being and well-being; transformed toward it as far as possible, they are well formed, and they communicate these gifts to what follows them, as the divine law suggests, since the gifts proceed into them from the Good.

From this come their superornamented orders, their unities directed toward themselves, their placements in relation to one another, their unconfused distinctions, the powers of the lesser brought back to the better, the providence of the greater concerning the secondary, the guardianship of the proper powers of each, their unwavering circuits around these, their immutabilities and exaltations in their desire for the Good, and all the other things we have said in our account of the properties and orders of the angels.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 1129D] “and” omitted by AE], all the angelic purifications belonging to the heavenly hierarchy, the supermundane illuminations, and the consummations of the whole angelic perfection derive from that most causal and fountain-like goodness. From it they have received their likeness to God, their manifestation in themselves of the hidden goodness, and their being angels, as proclaimers of the divine silence and as bright luminaries sent ahead in the shrines of the existing God, interpreting it.

After those sacred and holy intellects come souls and all the goods belonging to souls. These too derive from the supremely good Goodness: from it they have the essential life by which they love the possession of being, being itself indissoluble [Col. 1129D], and the capacity, through the angels as their excellent guides, to be led back to the principal Goodness of all good things. They participate in the illuminations flowing from it according to their proportion and according to the gift of their likeness to God, and in whatever virtue each is able to participate—along with all the other things we have enumerated in our account of souls.

And, if it is necessary to speak of them, even irrational souls and animals—the creatures that cut through the air, those that walk upon the earth, those that stretch themselves upon the earth, those that receive life in the waters or in the sea and on the land, and those that live covered and buried beneath the earth [Col. 1130A]—in short, everything that possesses either sensible soul or life, all these are animated and given life by the Good. All plants possess nutritive and motive life from the Good; and whatever essence is inanimate and lifeless exists through the Good and has received its essential condition through it.

But if the Good is also above all existing things, how then is it the Good? It gives form to what is formless; in itself alone it is the transcendent excellence of essence, life, and wisdom—beyond essence, beyond life, and beyond wisdom; and whatever is in the Good that is formless possesses a specification that transcends all specification. And, if it is right to say so, the Good that is above all existing things desires and strives for that which is not being, insofar as this too is said to be and is superessentially in the superessential Good, according to the negation of all things.

But what escaped us in the middle was this: the Good is the cause of the celestial principles and exalted beings, neither increased nor diminished, entirely immutable in the same extension; it is the cause of the harmonious, if one may so speak, greatest celestial path of movements, of the orders, beauties, lights, and placements of the stars, and of the many-sided, traversable motion of each individual star. It is also the cause of the motion of the two luminaries—which Scripture calls “great”—their revolving course, traversable from the same point to the same point, according to which days and nights are bounded and months and years measured. These motions distinguish, count, order, and contain time and the circular movements of things that exist in time.

What if someone should speak of the solar ray itself? It derives from the Good, for it is light and an image of goodness. The Good is then praised as “light-bearing,” as though the principal form had been manifested in an image. For the divine goodness, the summit of all things, reaches from the highest and greatest essences down to the last things, while still remaining above them all. It does not anticipate the things above by their surpassing its excellence, nor do the things below transgress its circuit. It illuminates all things by its power; it makes what does not exist; it gives life, contains, and perfects; it is the measure, eternity, number, order, circuit, cause, and end of existing things.

In the same way, the sun, this great and full-bright image signifying the divine goodness, always luminous and harmoniously corresponding to it in many respects, illuminates all things capable of participating in it. It possesses light extended over all things, spreading throughout the visible world the brightness of its own rays, both above and below. If anything does not participate in them, this is not because of weakness or shortness in the distribution of its illuminating power, but because the recipients do not open themselves to participation in the light, through the inappropriate manner in which they take it up.

Thus, while its ray passes through many such things, it illuminates what lies beyond them; and there is nothing visible that does not receive it according to the surpassing greatness of its own brilliance. It also contributes to the generation of sensible bodies; it moves them to life [Col. 1131A], nourishes, increases, perfects, purifies, and renews them; and it is the measure and number of the hours, days, and of all time as we know it. For that was the light—even though it was then imperfect—which the divine Moses mentioned [Note: [Col. 1131D] Gen. 1], and which, he said, had marked out the first triad of days for us.

In this way the Good turns all things toward itself. It is principally the gatherer of what is scattered, as the principal and unifying Godhead; and all things desire it as their beginning, their containment, and their end. It is the Good, as the divine sayings declare, from which all things subsist and are, having been brought forth from it as their most perfect cause; and in which all things are established [Note: [Col. 1131D] Rom. 11], as preserved and comprehended in an omnipotent counsel; and toward which all things are turned, each toward its proper summit.

All things long for it: intellectual and rational beings knowingly; sensible beings sensibly; beings without sense through an innate movement of vital desire; and inanimate beings and those that merely exist through their suitability for essential participation alone. According to the account of this significative image, light also gathers and turns all visible things toward itself—things moved, illuminated, warmed, and altogether embraced by its splendors.

For this reason the sun, because it loosens all things and gathers what is scattered, is desired by all sensible things, whether they desire to see, or to be moved, illuminated, warmed, or altogether embraced by the light. I do not mean here, following the saying of antiquity, that God is the sun and Creator of such a universe, and that he directly governs the manifest world; rather, I mean that “the invisible things of God are understood and seen through the creation of the world,” as are “his eternal power and divinity” [Note: [Col. 1132D] Rom. 1:20]. These matters, however, belong to symbolic theology.

Now we must praise and proclaim the intelligible “light-bearing” Good. It is called invisible light because it fills every supercelestial intellect with invisible illumination; it drives away every ignorance and error from all souls in which such things are found; it gives all of them sacred light; it purifies their intellectual eyes from the darkness of ignorance surrounding them; and it removes and unfolds the dense darkness that weighs heavily upon them. At first it gives them a moderate brightness; then, as they taste the light and desire it more, it gives itself more abundantly within them and shines upon them more fully, because they have loved much. It continually extends them toward what lies ahead, so that according to their proportion they may behold it.

The invisible light is therefore called the Good above every light [Note: [Col. 1131] B: “the best”; H: “the best”], as the fountain-like ray and superabundant outpouring of light. From its fullness it illuminates every supermundane, circum-mundane, and submundane intellect; it recalls all their intellectual powers to their proper source; it contains and orders all things above them; it surpasses all things by overshadowing them; and, simply, it contains, surpasses, and extends within itself the entire dominion of the illuminating power, as the principal light and something more than light. It gathers all intellectual and rational beings together and restores what has been lost [Note: [Col. 1131] BH: “renews”].

For just as ignorance separates those who wander, so the presence of invisible light gathers together and unites those who are illuminated and perfects them. It also turns them back toward what truly is, converting their varied faces—or, better, their imaginings—from the many vain opinions into which they have fallen, and gathering them into one true, pure, and uniform knowledge, enfolding them in one unifying light.

This Good is praised by the sacred theologians as good, as beautiful, as love, as the most beloved, and by all the other fitting divine names that give form to and bestow grace upon beauty [Col. 1132B]. The Good and the Beautiful are not to be separated in the one cause that comprehends all things in itself. For, dividing all existing things into participations and participants, we say that the good is that which participates in the beautiful, while the beautiful is the participation in the cause that makes all things beautiful.

The superessential Good is called beautiful because it has transmitted to all existing things the beauty proper to each, and because it is the causal source of their good composition and radiance. Like light flashing forth, it simultaneously gives all things the beautifying gifts of its fountain-like ray, and, as it were, calls all things toward itself. Hence it is called beautiful, as gathering the whole of itself together in all things.

It is also called Good, as all good at once, and more than good; always being Good [Greek: ὄν], according to the same condition and in the same way; neither made nor dissolved, neither increased nor wasted away; not good here but evil there; not good at one time and not at another; not good in relation to one thing and evil in relation to another; not good here but not there, as though it were good for some beings and not good for others. Rather, it is the Good itself, uniformly always being Good, through itself and with itself, and eminently bearing within itself the source of every good and every beauty.

In the simple and transcendent nature of all good things, every beauty and every good pre-exists uniformly according to its causal mode. From the Good itself each existing thing is good according to its proper principle; through the Good are all unions, friendships, and associations; by the Good all things are united. The Good is the beginning of all things, as their productive cause; it moves all things and contains them through love of its own beauty. It is the summit and the most beloved of all things, as their perfecting cause—for all things are made for the sake of the Good—and it is their exemplary cause, since all things are distinguished according to it.

Therefore the Good itself is the Good of the Good, because all things desire the Good and the Best according to every kind of cause [Col. 1133A], and there is no existing thing that does not participate in the Good and the Best. Reason will even dare to say that what is not being [Greek: μὴ ὄν] participates in the Good and the Best. For then even this is called good and best, when it is praised in God superessentially according to the negation of all things.

This one Good and Best is uniquely the causal source of all the many good and best things. From it come all the essential subsistences of existing things: their unities, distinctions, immutabilities, differences, likenesses, unlikenesses, the association of opposites, the distinctions of united things, the providence of higher beings, the reciprocal relations of things alike, the return of inferior things, and the self-preserving and immutable dwellings and placements of all things in themselves.

From it also come the proper associations of all things in all things, their compositions, undivided friendships, and harmonies; the cohesion of the universe; the mutual concretion of things in the whole; the indissoluble containments of existing things; the unfailing reception of things that come to be; all states and movements—some belonging to intellectual beings, some to souls, and some to bodies.

There is both state and movement for all things. The Good places each thing in its own principle, above every state and movement, and moves it in its proper movement. Divine intellects are said to move circularly when, being united, they begin neither from nor toward any limit, in the illuminations of the Good and the Best; directly whenever they advance toward the providence of their subjects, bringing all things to their proper completion; and obliquely because, while providing for inferior things, they remain irreversibly in immutability, circling continually around the Good and the Best as the cause of immutability [Col. 1133C].

The movement of the soul is circular when it enters into itself from external things and uniformly turns toward its intellectual powers, granting itself, as it were in a circle, an unerring condition. Turning away from and gathering itself out of the many external things, it first gathers itself into itself; then, having become uniform, it unites itself by means of its unified powers; and so it is led by the hand toward the Good and the Best, toward what is above all existing things, toward the One and the Same, which neither begins nor ends [Note: [Col. 1133] BH: “At the beginning”; [Note: [Col. 1133] BH: “a certain”].

The soul moves obliquely insofar as it is illuminated by divine kinds of knowledge proper to itself—not intellectually and powerfully, but rationally and investigatively, and as through operations mingled with transition. It moves directly when, without entering into itself and moving by a singular intellectual apprehension—for this, as I said, is the movement according to the circle—it advances toward the things around it and, from the external things, as though from varied and multiplied symbols, is brought back to simple and unified contemplations.

The Good and the Best are therefore the causal source, container, and end of these three movements of all sensible things, and, much earlier, of every state, station, and placement. They are above every state and movement. Hence every state and movement is from them, through them, toward them, and for their sake.

For from them, through them, and in them are every essence and every life, every smallness, equality, greatness, and measure of mind, soul, and every nature; the rational relations of existing things; their compositions, concretions, wholes, and parts; the one and the many; the conjunctions of parts; the unities of the whole multitude; the consummations of wholes; quality, quantity, such-and-such a quantity, multiplicity, comparisons, distinctions, every multitude, every summit, all limits, orders, eminences, elements, forms; every essence, power, operation, disposition, sense, reason, intellect, illumination, knowledge, unity; and, simply, everything that is [Greek: ὄν].

All these are from the Good and the Best, exist in the Good and the Best, and are turned toward the Good and the Best. Everything that exists and comes to be exists and comes to be through the Good and the Best. All things look toward it; by it they are moved and contained; and for its sake and through it, in it, is every exemplary, consummating, intellectual, specific, formal, and, simply, every principle, as well as every containment and every summit.

Or, to put it comprehensively: all things that exist are from the Good and the Best, while all things that do not exist are superessentially in the Good and the Best. It is the beginning and end of all things, beyond beginning and beyond end, because from it, through it, in it, and toward it are all things [Note: [Col. 1133D] Rom. 11:36], as the sacred word says.

For all things find the Good and the Best desirable, lovable, and delightful. Through it and for its sake the lesser and the better love one another in reciprocal return; things alike associate with one another; things equally worthy receive equal honor; and the better provide for the lesser. It makes each of these things individually, and all things together, desire the Good and the Best, and it wills all the things that it makes and wills.

True reason will even dare to say that the causal source of all things, through the excellence of its goodness, loves all things, makes all things, contains all things, and turns all things back. Divine love is the love of the Best for the Best, through the Best. For this love, as the benefactor of existing things, pre-existing in the Best by excellence, does not allow the Best to remain unfruitful within itself; rather, it moves it to action according to its generative excellence concerning all things.

Let no one suppose that we are honoring the name “love” contrary to the divine sayings. It is irrational and foolish, in my judgment, to attend not to the force of the intention but to the word [Note: [Col. 1133] BE: “words”]. Such behavior is not characteristic of those who wish to understand divine things, but of those who receive superficial sounds, hold them externally as they pass through their ears, and refuse to know what a particular word signifies or how it ought to be explained through other words of equal power and greater clarity.

They remain attached to letters and elements without understanding them, and to unknown syllables and words [Col. 1135A] that do not enter the intellectual part of their soul, but merely resound outside, around their lips and ears—as though the number four could not be signified by twice two, or a simple line by a straight line, or motherhood by fatherhood, or the same thing by many other parts of speech that signify it.

According to right reason, we must understand that we use elements, syllables, words, writings, and speeches through the senses. Thus, when our soul moves through intellectual operations toward invisible things, the senses abound with sensible things, just as the intellectual powers abound when the soul, having been made godlike through union with the unknown and inaccessible light, moves toward desirable rays and invisible contemplations.

When the mind hastens to be transformed through sensible things toward the invisibilities that are capable of contemplation, the things advanced through the senses are more precious than all else: lucid words are clearer than visible things, just as things that are not plain cannot be readily presented to the senses, nor can sensible things themselves properly stand before the mind.

Nevertheless, lest we appear to be saying these things in order to reject the divine sayings, let those who accuse us of honoring the name “love” hear this: “Love her,” it says, “and she will guard you; embrace her, and she will exalt you; honor her, so that she may embrace you” [Note: [Col. 1135] E: “embrace you”] [Note: [Col. 1135D] Prov. 4]. And there are all the other passages in which love is praised according to the theologies of love.

Indeed, some of our theologians have considered the name “love” more divine than the name “affection” [Note: [Col. 1135] A: “the name of love rather than affection”; H: “the name of affection, of love”]. The divine Ignatius also writes: “My love has been crucified” [Note: [Col. 1135D] Letter to the Romans 7]. And in the introductory passages of the divine sayings one finds someone speaking of divine Wisdom: “I became a lover of her beauty” [Note: [Col. 1135D] Wisdom 8:2].

Therefore let us not fear this name of love, nor let anyone confuse us by disputing about it. For it seems to me that the theologians have treated the names “affection” and “love” as common names. They have considered “love” more appropriate to divine things because of the unrestrained loving desire of such men.

For when the multitudes, unable to contain the uniformity of the divine name of love—a name rightly praised not only by us but also by the divine sayings—have weakened themselves into the divisible, corporeal, and divided, they have not possessed true love but its shadow, or rather, a falling away from true love. The singularity of the divine and one Love is remote from multiplicity. For this reason the name, which many have thought more difficult, is established in divine Wisdom for the purpose of leading them back and restoring them to knowledge of true love, so that the difficulty concerning it may be resolved in love itself.

For our part, let us again consider a passage in which something inconsistent must be understood as referring to earthly things and heavenly things according to the opinion of those of better reputation: “Your affection,” someone says, “has fallen upon me, like the affection of women” [Note: [Col. 1136D] 2 Samuel 1]. In the divine sublimities that shine forth, the sacred theologians establish the names “affection” and “love” in the same power, according to their divine manifestations.

This is the power that unifies, joins, and distinctively blends together in the Good and the Best; that pre-exists through the Good and the Best; that proceeds from the Good and the Best through the Good and the Best; that contains things of equal power according to their sociable reciprocity; that moves the first toward providence for the lesser; and that places the lower in relation to the higher through return.

Divine love is also ecstatic: it does not permit those who love to remain themselves, but makes them belong to what is loved. The higher are declared through the providence they exercise for the lower; things alike contain one another; and the lesser are brought back to the first through a more divine return.

Thus Paul, having become great in the excellence of divine love and having assumed a power that carried his mind beyond itself, says with divine lips: “I live, yet it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” [Note: [Col. 1136D] Gal. 2:20]. Truly a lover and one carried beyond his mind, he says in this way that he lives for God, not living his own life but the life of the lover himself, as something exceedingly beloved.

We must also dare to say this in defense of the truth: the causal source of all things becomes, through the excellence of its goodness, the lover of all things by its own loving disposition toward all good and excellent things. It exercises providence over all existing things, cherishing them with goodness, affection, and love; and from its position above all things and separate from all things, it leads all things back to the One, according to the superessential power that transcends the mind and returns to itself.

For this reason divine sages call it “jealous,” as though it were the Good and the excellent Love that exists abundantly in existing things; as though it aroused desire for its own loving zeal; as though it displayed itself as jealous and jealous for the things desired; and as though it caused the things for which it provides to be jealous for it through themselves.

In every way, the Good and the Best are lovable, and love is in the Good and the Best; they are established beforehand in the Good and the Best, and through the Good and the Best they are and come to be.

Why, then, do the theologians, when they wish to speak of these matters, sometimes call it “love” and “affection” itself, and at other times call it “beloved” and “desired”? In one respect it is causal, as that which chooses beforehand and generates; in another respect it is itself. In one respect it is moved; in another it moves, when it is itself both prior to itself and the mover of itself.

Thus they call it “beloved” and “desired” as the Good and the Best; but they again call it “love” and “affection” as that which simultaneously moves and brings back the power that exists in itself alone to itself, the Good and the Best through itself.

In this way divine love is revealed as existing through itself and in itself: the best procession of the excellent unity and the loving movement, simple, moved through itself, active through itself, pre-existing in the Best, proceeding from the Best into existing things, and turning itself back again toward the Best. It is infinite in itself and without beginning.

It is shown in a differentiated way as a kind of eternal cycle, circling through the Best, from the Best, in the Best, and toward the Best, in an ineffable return [Col. 1137A], always proceeding, remaining, and revolving in the same thing, through the same thing, and by the same thing.

Our common holy perfecter, Hierotheus, divinely introduced these matters through his hymns of love. It is not inappropriate to remember them and to place, as it were, a sacred heading on our discourse about love.

### From the hymns of love of the most holy Hierotheus

Whether we call love divine, angelic, intellectual, animal, or natural, we shall understand it as a certain unifying and continuous power [Note: [Col. 1137] AE: “we understand”], moving higher things toward providence for lower things; moving things alike again into sociable reciprocity; and turning the last and subordinate things toward the better and higher.

### The same author, from the same hymns of love

Since we have arranged many loves from one, we consequently said what are the characteristics of the loves that exist in the world and of the supermundane loves, and what are their knowledge and powers, which are surpassed, according to the contemplation supplied by reason, by the orders and arrangements of intellectual and invisible loves. After these come those who understand by themselves, and whoever truly appears there above the good loves and properly sings the hymn.

Now, taking them all up again into one and intertwining them into a single love, let us bring together and gather into one their common father from the many. First, let us comprehend him universally in two loving powers, whose power and sovereignty belong entirely to the cause of all love, immeasurable and at the summit of all things, toward which the universal love of all existing things naturally extends itself from among all existing things [Col. 1137C].

### The same author, from the same hymns of love

Come, then, gathering these two together again into one, let us say that there is one simple power, moving itself toward a certain unifying blending, from the Good all the way to the last of existing things, and from that last thing again, successively through all things, toward the Good. It revolves from itself, through itself, and toward itself, and is always turned back upon itself in the same way.

Someone might say: If the Good and the Best are lovable to all things, and if all things desire and love it and are loved by it—for even what is not being desires it, as has been said, and strives toward being in it; and it gives form to the formed and the formless; and what is not being is superessentially said to be and exists in it—how is it that the demonic multitude does not desire the Good and the Best, although it has become material in its existence, and, having fallen away from the stability of desire for the Best, is said to be the cause of all evils, both for itself and for others, insofar as they are corrupted?

How, having been altogether weighed down by the Best, is the demonic race not godlike [Note: [Col. 1137] A: “demonic”; E: “demons”]? Or how has what was made from the Best been changed? What corrupted it? And, in general, what is evil? From what principle did it subsist [Note: [Col. 1137] BH: “subsists”]? From what source does it belong to existing things? And how did the Best wish to bring it forth? How could it do so willingly? If evil comes from another cause, what other cause is there for existing things besides the Best? And, if providence exists, how can evil either exist or be made at all, or not be destroyed? And how does anything belonging to existing things desire it, apart from the Best [Note: [Col. 1137] “and how does it desire it—‘belonging to existing things’ omitted by BH.]?

So, this is what such reasoning says. But we shall deign to look with him toward the truth of things. First, we shall confidently say this: Evil is not from the Best; and if it is from the Best, it is not evil. For fire cannot become cold, nor can the Best bring forth what is not best.

And if all existing things are from the Best—for it is natural to the Best to bring forth and save, while it belongs to evil to corrupt and destroy—then nothing existing is from evil, and evil itself will not exist. For if evil were evil even to itself, and if it were not this, then evil would not be evil at all, but would possess some share of the Best, according to which it exists.

If existing things desire the Good and the Best, and if everything they do they do by looking toward the Best; and if every contemplation of existing things has the Best as its beginning and end—for no one who looks toward the nature of evil does what he does—how can evil exist among existing things, or be being at all, when it has been abandoned by such a desire for the Best?

If all existing things are from the Best, and the Best is the summit of existing things, then what is being [Greek: ὄν] is in the Best, and what is not being [Greek: μὴ ὄν] is also being in the Best; but evil is not being [Greek: ὃν]. If this is not so, then evil is not evil at all, nor is it non-being [Col. 1138C]. For there will be nothing that is universally non-being, unless this is said of the Best according to its superessential nature.

The Best, then, is established far above both being and non-being, in the simplest manner. Evil, however, is neither in what is essential nor in what is non-existent; indeed, since it itself does not exist, it is even farther removed from the Best and still less essential.

Someone may ask: Where, then, is evil from? For if evil does not exist, virtue and vice are the same, and either everything is everything, and everything is rational in what is divisible; or evil will not be opposed to virtue. Yet temperance and intemperance, justice and injustice, are opposites.

I do not speak merely of justice and injustice, or of the temperate and intemperate, as though they were manifested externally; the distance between what exists in virtue and what is opposed to it was established much earlier in the soul as a whole. Passions lie in ambush for reason; and from these it is necessary to grant that evil is contrary to the Good.

For the Good is not contrary to itself. Rather, because it rejoices in fellowship, unity, and friendship, as having been begotten from one principle and one causal source, it is not contrary even to a lesser good [Note: [Col. 1137] “the lesser is contrary to the greater”—omitted by BH]. For the less hot or less cold is not contrary to the very hot or very cold.

Evil, then, exists among existing things, is being, and is opposed to the Good. And if it is the corruption of existing things, this does not remove its being evil; it will also be being and productive of the generation of existing things. Otherwise, does not the corruption of one thing often become the generation of another? Evil would then be perfected in the fullness of the universe, and would the universe be imperfect in lacking what has been provided for its own sake?

Reason, however, says the following in response to these points: evil, insofar as it is evil, produces neither essence nor generation; it merely damages and corrupts, so far as lies in it, the substance of existing things. But if someone should say that it is productive, in that through its corruption it gives another thing generation, the true answer must be: Do things that give generation corrupt? Corruption and evil merely corrupt and damage; generation and essence, however, come about through the good. Evil, therefore, is corruption in itself, but productive through the good.

[Col. 1139B] And if it is evil, it is neither being (*ὄν*) nor productive of existing things. Through the good, however, it is both being and good being, and productive of good things. More than this: the same thing cannot in itself be both good and evil; nor can its corruption and generation be the same virtue in themselves; nor is one of these virtue and the other corruption.

Evil itself is neither being, nor good, nor productive, nor productive of existing things and goods. The good, wherever it is present in perfection [Note: [Col. 1139] Thus E; A omits “indeed”; BH read “wherever indeed.”], makes all things perfect, pure, and whole, and supremely good [Note: [Col. 1139] “all things” omitted by OAE.]. Things that participate in it less are imperfect goods and are mixed with deficiency because of the lack of good. Evil, however, is not universally evil, nor good, nor productive of good; rather, whatever is nearer to the good, whether more or less, will proportionately be good [Col. 1139C]. For the most perfect goodness itself, which comes through all things, does not fill only the supremely good essences immediately around it; it extends even to the last things, arriving wholly in some, less in others, and lastly in still others, insofar as each of the existing things can participate in it.

Some things participate in the good completely; others are deprived of it to a greater or lesser degree; some possess a more obscure participation in the good; and in others the good is present according to the final degree of consonance. For if the good were not present proportionately in each thing, the most divine and honorable things would possess the rank of the last things. But how could all things participate in the good uniformly? Are all existing things similarly suited to universal participation in it?

[Col. 1139D] This, however, is the surpassing greatness of the good’s power: it makes even those things that are deprived of it, and their very deprivation, participate in it insofar as they universally share in it. And, if one must speak the truth confidently, even the things that oppose it exist and are able to oppose it by its own power. More comprehensively, everything that exists, insofar as it exists, is good and comes from the good; but insofar as it is deprived of the good, it is neither existing nor good.

[Col. 1140A] In other conditions, such as heat or cold, things are heated. When heat leaves them, many existing things are deprived of life and mind; yet essence—God—is exalted and exists superessentially. Simply speaking, when all other conditions depart at once, things still exist and can subsist by virtue of that which is ungenerated [Note: [Col. 1139] BH: “they subsist.”]. But whatever is deprived of the good in every way never existed anywhere, does not exist, will not exist, and cannot exist.

Consider the incontinent person. Although deprived of the good through irrational desire, he neither exists in this respect nor desires existing things; nevertheless, he participates in the good through the obscure consonance of unity and friendship itself. Anger also participates in the good, since by moving itself and desiring what are reputed evils it raises and turns them toward what is reputed good. The person who desires a life of contention participates in the good as one who desires life as a whole [Note: [Col. 1139] AE: “the whole of life.”], and who desires an excellent reputation for himself and looks toward an excellent life [Col. 1140B].

If one were to consume the good altogether, there would be neither essence, nor life, nor desire, nor movement, nor anything else. Thus, for generation to arise from corruption is not the power of evil, but the arrival of a lesser good; just as illness is a deficiency of order, but not a deficiency of every order. For if it were such, illness itself would not subsist. Yet illness remains and exists, possessing a minimal order and established in itself. Whatever is wholly without good is neither being nor among existing things; but whatever is mixed participates in the good among existing things and, through this, is among existing things and is being, insofar as it participates in the good.

[Col. 1140C] More precisely, all existing things will be more or less existing in proportion to their participation in the highest good. For that which is in itself never anywhere being (*ὄν*) will never be. But this thing is being in one respect and not-being in another: insofar as it departs from what always is, it is not; insofar as it has received something from being, it is. Its very being, and that which is not-being, are held together and preserved by it [Note: [Col. 1139] B: “this.”].

Evil, insofar as it is wholly a departure from the good, will be found neither among great nor among lesser goods [Note: [Col. 1139] AE: “lesser.”]. But this thing is good in one respect and not good in another: it opposes some particular good, though not every good. It is nevertheless held by participation in the good, and the good gives substance even to its own deprivation through its total participation in the good.

[Col. 1140D] For when the good has departed altogether, what will remain that is good? Neither anything mixed with good nor evil in itself. If evil is an imperfect good, then the absence of the most perfect good is also imperfect, and perfect good will be absent. Evil exists and appears as evil only when it is evil for those to which it is opposed and is taken away from those that are regarded as good. For it is impossible that the same things should oppose one another in themselves and through themselves in every respect. Evil, therefore, is not being.

Nor is evil among existing things. If all existing things are from the good, and the good contains all things in all existing things, then evil either will not exist or will not be in the good. Fire, for example, contains no cold [Col. 1141A], nor is fire damaged by it; yet evil is said to exist in the good. If this is so, how can evil be in the good? The consequence is impossible. For, as the truth of the sayings declares, “a good tree cannot produce evil fruits” [Note: [Col. 1141D] Matthew 7:18], nor can the reverse be so.

If evil is not from the good, it is clear that it must be from another principle and cause. Either evil will be from the good, or the good from evil; or, if this is impossible, both good and evil will be from another principle and cause. Every dyad is not a principle; the monad, however, will be the principle of the whole dyad. It is indeed absurd that two things altogether contrary should proceed from and exist from one and the same source, and that the principle itself should not be simple and single but divided, two-formed, contrary to itself, and mutable.

[Col. 1141B] Indeed, it is not possible for there to be two contrary principles of existing things, opposing one another and opposing the universe. If this were granted, God would not be innocent or free from strife, since something would disturb him. Everything would consequently be disordered and perpetually at war.

The good, however, gives friendship to all existing things; it is itself peace, and the giver of peace is praised by the sacred theologians [Note: [Col. 1142D] 1 Corinthians 14; Ephesians 2.]. Therefore all things are friendly and joined together, having one ungenerated life, ordered and united toward one supreme good, and made similar to one another. Accordingly, evil is not divine; nor is evil [Note: [Col. 1141] BEH: “good.”] non-divine.

Nor is evil from God. If God is not good, then either he does good and brings about good things, or he does so only sometimes and with some things, but at other times and with other things he does not, and not with everything. In that case he would introduce alteration and mutability into what is around himself—that is, into the most divine of all things and into the cause of all things.

[Col. 1141C] If goodness subsists in God, then God, transferring from goodness, would at one time be being (*ὤν*) and at another not-being (*οὐκ ὤν*). If he possesses goodness by participation, then he will possess it from another and will have it at one time but not at another. Evil, therefore, is not from God, nor in God, nor in any simple sense according to time.

Nor is evil in the angels. For the angel, declaring the divine goodness in a godlike manner, is the second being according to participation, declaring first what exists according to cause. The angel is the image of God, the manifestation of hidden light, a pure, most brilliant, immaculate, undefiled, unpolluted mirror, receiving, if one may properly say so, the entire beauty of well-formed likeness to God [Col. 1141D] and purely declaring in itself, insofar as possible, the goodness that is in the innermost sanctuary.

Evil, therefore, is not in the angels. They are called evil when they punish sinners: thus those who restrain offenders are called evil, as are those who bar the impure from the divine mysteries of the priests.
