Nor is it evil to be punished, but to be made worthy of punishment; nor is it evil to be barred from the sacred things according to one’s deserts, but to be made unholy and unsacred, and unsuitable for the undefiled.

[Col. 1142A] Nor are demons evil by nature. For if they were evil by nature, they would be neither from the good, nor among existing things, nor transformed from good things; they would exist naturally and eternally as evil. The question then follows: are they evil for themselves or for others? If for themselves, do they corrupt themselves? If for others, how do they corrupt them, and what do they corrupt [Note: [Col. 1141] BEH omit “and what do they corrupt”]—essence, virtue, or activity? If essence, then first of all they are not evil according to nature. For things that are incorruptible by nature do not corrupt, but receive corruption.

It follows that this is not altogether evil, nor is anything among existing things corrupted according to its essence and nature. Rather, through a deficiency according to nature, the order, harmony, and proportion of the thing are weakened, while the thing itself remains in the same condition. [Col. 1142B] Weakness, however, is not perfection. For if it were complete, it would destroy both the corruption and its subject; and corruption itself would become the corruption of itself. Such a thing, therefore, is not evil but deficient good. For whatever is wholly without good will not be among existing things.

The same reasoning applies to the corruption of virtue and activity. Further, how can demons, made by God, be evil? The good brings about and establishes good things. Someone may say that they are called evil; but they are not evil according to what they are. They are from the best, and they received the best essence; rather, they are evil according to what they are not, being weak, as the sayings declare, in preserving their own beginning.

Tell me, then: in what do we say that the demons are damaged, if not in the cessation of their condition and activity concerning divine goods? But if demons were evil by nature, they would always be evil. [Col. 1142C] Evil, however, is unstable. Therefore, if they always remain in the same condition, they are not evil; for whatever is always the same belongs to the best. If they are not always evil, they are not evil by nature, but because of their need for angelic goods.

They are not, however, wholly without good, since they exist, live, understand, and possess some movement of desire. They are called evil because they are weakened with respect to their natural activity. [Col. 1142D] Their false turning is therefore evil, as are their departure from what is akin to them, their formlessness, imperfection, incapacity, weakness of the power that preserves their perfection, flight, and fall.

What, then, is evil in demons? Irrational anger, mindless desire, and insolent imagination. Yet even if these are present in demons, they are not altogether or universally evil, nor are they evil in themselves. In other animals, for example, the movement of such impulses is not evil; rather, their destruction and corruption would be evil for the animal. A condition preserves and makes possible the nature of the animal that possesses it.

The demonic race, therefore, is not evil insofar as it exists according to nature, but insofar as it does not. The whole good given to them was not altered; rather, they themselves fell from the whole good that had been given. We say that the angelic gifts given to them were never themselves disturbed. They remain complete and most luminous, even though the demons themselves do not see the virtues that make their participation in the good visible [Col. 1143A].

Thus, in what they are, they are from the best and are of the best; they desire the good and the highest good—to be, to live, and to understand, desiring existing things. Because of deprivation, flight, and fall from the best things naturally akin to them, they are called evil insofar as they are not what they should be; and by desiring what is not, they desire evil.

But who would say that souls are evil? If it is because they contend against evils providently and for salvation, this is not evil but good, and it is from the good, which deals well with evil. If we say that souls are damaged, in what are they damaged, unless in the deficiency of good conditions and activities, and through their own weakness, imperfection, and destruction?

We say that the air around us is darkened through the deficiency and absence of light [Col. 1143B]; but light itself is always light [Note: [Col. 1143] A: “is always light”; BH: “is always in the light”; E: “light is above light.”], illuminating the darkness. Evil, therefore, is neither in demons nor in us as being evil (*ὂν*), but as the deficiency and desolation of the perfection of the goods proper to each.

Nor is evil in irrational animals [Note: [Col. 1143] Thus A; BEH: “souls.”]. For if one were to remove anger, desire, and the other things that are so called, though they are not simply evil for their nature, a great and fierce lion, once deprived of them, would no longer be a lion. A dog made gentle toward everyone would no longer be a dog. For a dog is, in one respect, disposed to guard; in another, domestic toward those who approach and hostile toward strangers whom it drives away.

Whatever does not corrupt nature is not evil. Corruption of nature is weakness and deficiency of natural conditions, activities, and virtues [Col. 1143C]. And if all things that come to be through generation reach completion in time, then what is imperfect is not altogether contrary to nature.

Nor is evil in nature as a whole. For if no natural principles are universally contrary to nature [Note: [Col. 1143] BEH: “universally contrary to nature”; A: “contrary to the universal nature.”], nothing is contrary to it. Yet, in particular things, one condition will be according to nature and another not according to nature. One thing is contrary to nature for one being, another for another [Note: [Col. 1143] The words “one thing is contrary to nature for one being, another for another” are omitted by BH.]. Thus one condition is contrary to nature in this respect, like wickedness; another is contrary to nature as the deprivation of what belongs to nature. Nature, therefore, is not evil; rather, the evil of nature is the inability to accomplish what belongs properly to nature.

[Col. 1143D] Nor is evil in bodies. What is base and weak is a deficiency of form and a deprivation of order; this is not altogether evil but lesser good. For if the good, form, and order were entirely dissolved, the body itself would perish.

That the body is not the cause of wickedness in the soul is clear from the fact that wickedness can subsist without a body and outside it, as also in demons. For in intellects, souls, and bodies alike, evil is the weakness and fall of the condition of their proper goods.

Nor is evil greatly to be attributed to matter, as they say, insofar as it is matter. For matter itself participates in adornment, form, and appearance [Col. 1144A]. But if, when deprived of these, matter in itself is without attraction and formless, how can matter produce anything, when in itself it cannot even undergo anything?

How, then, is matter evil? If it is nothing, it is neither good nor evil. But if all existing things must be from the good, and matter itself is among existing things, it too must be from the good. If the good is productive of evil, then evil, being from the good, will be good; or if evil is productive of the good, then the good, being from evil, will be evil. Or there will again be two principles, joined together by some single summit.

If they say that matter is necessary for the completion of the whole world, how is matter evil? For what is necessary is another kind of good. How does the best bring some things into generation from evil? Or how is evil necessary to the best? Evil flees from the nature of the best.

[Col. 1144B] How does matter, if it is evil, generate and nourish nature? Evil, insofar as it is evil, is productive, nourishing, making, and preserving nothing at all. If they say that matter itself does not produce wickedness in souls but attracts souls to it, how can this be true? Souls look very much toward what belongs to them in the good. And how could this happen if matter were altogether attracting them toward evil?

Evil in souls, therefore, does not come from matter but from transgression. If they also say that this follows matter in every way, and that necessary unstable matter is unable to establish itself from itself, how can evil be necessary, or necessary evil?

[Col. 1144C] Nor does that which we call deprivation, according to its own power, oppose the good. Universal deprivation is universally powerless; particular deprivation, however, does not possess power insofar as it is deprivation, but insofar as it is not universal deprivation. When the deprivation of the good is particular, there is not yet evil; when it becomes universal, the nature of evil has perished.

In summary, one must say: the good proceeds from a single and complete cause, while evil proceeds from many particular deficiencies.

Does God know evil, or does he know good, and are the powers that are causes of evils beneficent in him?

If evil is eternal, and creates, can, exists, and acts, whence does it possess these things? Either from the good, or the good from evil, or both from another cause.

Everything according to nature comes to be from a determinate cause. If evil is uncaused and infinite, it is not according to nature [Col. 1144D]. For neither is there in nature something contrary to nature, nor in art is there an inartistic principle.

The soul, then, is the cause of evils, just as fire is the cause of heating, and wickedness fills everything to which it comes near. The nature of the soul is good; but in its activities it is sometimes in one condition and sometimes in another.

If its evil comes from its nature and being, whence does its being come? It comes from the best creative cause of all existing things. If it comes from that cause, how can it be evil according to essence? For all things have been generated by the same good. If, then, evil comes through its activities—but if this has not been established beforehand, then whence come the virtues [Col. 1145A]? And are they not also produced through its likeness to God?

It remains, therefore, that evil is the weakness and deficiency of the good.

The cause of the best things is one; the things contrary to the best have many causes. The principles and powers of evils are not productive, but impotence, weakness, and an immoderate mixture of dissimilar things. Evils are neither immovable nor always in the same condition; they are many, infinite, and carried in different directions, and through all these things they are many and evil.

The good will be both principle and end. Everything, including whatever is contrary, exists for the sake of the good. We too do what we do while desiring the good; no one acts while looking toward evil. Evil, therefore, has no substance; it is contrary to substance, exists for the sake of the good, and was not made from it.

[Col. 1145B] Evil must be posited accidentally and through another, not from its own proper principle. Thus what has come to be ought to be considered straight because it is from the good and comes to be for the sake of the good, though in truth it is not straight. For this reason, we consider what is not good to be good.

It is shown that the object of desire is one thing and what is made another [Note: [Col. 1145] E: “another thing.”]. Evil, therefore, is not from a way, nor from vision, nor from nature, nor from a cause, nor from a principle, nor from an end, nor from a limit [Note: [Col. 1145] E: “from a definition.”], nor from deliberation, nor from substance.

Evil is therefore deprivation, deficiency, weakness, lack of proportion, sin, obscurity, formlessness, lifelessness, lack of understanding, irrationality, imperfection, disorder, absence of cause, infinity, infertility, inactivity, weakness, disorder, dissimilarity, multiplicity, darkness, lack of essence, and that which is never anywhere any being (*ὄν*) [Col. 1145C].

How can evil altogether arise from mixture with the good? Whatever is wholly without good is neither anything nor capable of anything. For if the good is being, deliberative, effective for good, and active, how could anything contrary to the good exist, deprived of substance, wisdom, virtue, and activity?

Not all things are evil for all things, nor are they altogether evil in the same respect. For a demon, evil is to be contrary to the intellect’s likeness to God; for a soul, to be contrary to reason; for a body, to be contrary to nature.

How can evils exist when providence exists? There is no evil if evil is neither being (*ὄν*) nor among existing things, and nothing existing is without providence [Col. 1145D]. Evil is not being, visibly subsisting in the good. If no existing thing is without participation in the good, while evil is a deficiency of the good, and no existing thing is universally deprived of the good, then divine providence is in all existing things, and nothing existing is without providential care.

Providence has also used things that have become evil excellently and beautifully for our formation, or that of others, or for our benefit [Col. 1146A], and it provides for each existing thing in its proper way. For this reason, we do not accept the empty or contentious argument of many who say that providence ought to lead us into virtue even against our will. To corrupt nature is not the work of providence.

Therefore providence, as the savior of each nature, provides for things moved by themselves insofar as they are moved by themselves; it provides for all things, and for each thing individually, in the same way with respect to the whole and to each, proportionately distributing to each the beneficent gifts of the most abundant providence, insofar as the nature of each recipient can receive them.

Evil, therefore, is not being, nor is evil among existing things. Evil does not become evil through power, but through weakness. Demons, insofar as they are and are from the good, are good [Col. 1146B]. Their evil comes from the fall and alteration of their proper goods, and from weakness in the likeness and condition of the angelic perfection akin to them [Note: [Col. 1145] BE: “of their own.”].

They desire the good, since through it they are established in being, living, and understanding. If they do not desire the good, they desire what is not [Note: [Col. 1145] A has “If they do not desire the good, they desire what is not”; BEH omit the entire sentence.]. This, however, will not be desire, but truly the sin of desire.

Those who sin in knowledge are called—and therefore [Note: [Col. 1145] The printed text has the corrupt form *etoquia*.] are called—weak in their mistaken knowledge or action concerning the good [Note: [Col. 1145D] Isaiah 47; Psalm 35; Luke 12; Romans 2; Titus 1; James 4.]. They know the will but do not do it. Hearers are weak either with respect to faith or with respect to the operation of the good. Some are unwilling to do good because of a false turning [Note: [Col. 1145] E: “conversation”] or weakness of will.

Thus, as we have often said, evil is entirely weakness, inability, and deficiency either of knowledge, of mistaken knowledge, of faith, of desire, or of the activity of the good.

[Col. 1146C] Someone might say that weakness is not punishable but, on the contrary, pardonable. If it were not possible to be able, reason might have it so; but if ability comes from the good, which gives, according to the sayings [Note: [Col. 1146D] James 1.], what is suitable to all, then sin and irrational turning, flight, and fall from one’s own proper goods are simply not praiseworthy.

These matters have been sufficiently treated by us in the discussion of the observance of just and divine justification, according to which the truth of the sayings, in its sacred action, weakened the sophistical arguments that speak against God of truth and falsehood, as arguments of those who think perversely.

Now, insofar as is possible for us, the good has been sufficiently praised [Note: [Col. 1145] BH: “sufficiently.”] as [Col. 1146D] truly wondrous; as the principle and end of all things; as that which contains existing things; as the one that gives form to non-existing things; as the cause of all good things; as not the cause of evils; as providence and universal goodness; as surpassing existing things and non-existing things, evils, and its own deprivation; and as good, desirable, lovable, and delightful to all. The argument, I think, has made all the other truths evident in these matters as well.

# CHAPTER V. On Being [Note: [Col. 1147] Thus the manuscripts; the table of contents has “being.”], in which there is also discussion of the paradigms

[Col. 1147A]

Now, however, we must pass to the theological naming of the truly existing essence of the truly existent. We shall merely warn that the purpose of the discussion is not to manifest the super-essential essence, which is super-essential. For this is ineffable, unknowable, and altogether inexplicable. Rather, the purpose is to praise the procession of the principal divine essence, which is the super-exalted Unity and gives substance to all existing things. For the divine naming of the Good, manifesting the total causal processions of all things, extends to everything existing and non-existing [Note: [Col. 1147] “all things” omitted by AE], and is above existing and non-existing things [Col. 1147B].

The naming of Being extends to all existing things and is above them all. That of Life extends to all living things and is above living things. Then that of Wisdom extends to all intellectual, rational, and sensory things, and is above them all. The argument therefore desires to praise the divine names that manifest providence. It does not promise to expound the super-essential goodness, essence, life, and wisdom of the super-essential deity, which, as the Scriptures say [Note: [Col. 1147D] Psalms XVII; Job XXVIII], is set above all goodness, deity, essence, wisdom, and life in hidden places. Rather, it praises the beneficent providence, the super-eminent goodness, and the cause of all good things, as well as Being, Life, and Wisdom, which give substance and life, and which are the cause that bestows wisdom, essence, life, intellect, reason, and sensation upon those who receive them. It does not say that the Good is one thing, Being another, Life another, and Wisdom another, nor that there are many causes and different creator-deities, some subordinate and some super-eminent. Rather, these are all the good processions of the one God, and the divine names praised by us: some manifest the providence of the one universal God, while others manifest aspects of his more universal and particular providence.

Someone might object that, if Being is the same as Life, and Life extends above Wisdom, while Being extends to living things, Life to whatever lives, these to sensory things, and the same to rational things, while intellect surpasses rational things, then those nearer to God and more closely approaching him are the rational and intellectual beings. Indeed, those who participate in the greatest gifts from God ought to be better and to surpass the rest.

If one substitutes intellectual beings for beings without essence and for animals, the argument would be sound. But if there are divine minds above the other existing things, living above the other living things, understanding and knowing beyond sensation and reason, and desiring and participating in the Good and the Best beyond all existing things, then they are more closely related to the Best. They participate in it more abundantly and receive from it more numerous and greater gifts [Col. 1148A], just as the richer among sensory things surpass the rest through the abundance of reason, and these surpass the merely sensory, while the others surpass those possessing only life. This, I believe, is true: they are nearer and more divine than the rest.

Since we have spoken of these matters, let us praise the Good as truly Being and as giving substance to all existing things. Being—ὤν—is the cause that, through its super-essential power, establishes all being; it is the creator of existing subsistence, the beginning of substance, essence, and nature, the measure of the ages, the essentiality of times, the eternity of existing things, the maker of things made, and the being of things made in whatever manner. From Being come eternity, essence, Being, time, generation, and what has been made. In existing things there are existence, subsistence, and substance.

For God is not a being (ὤν) in a restricted sense [Col. 1148B], but embraces within himself, simply and without limit, the whole of being. Therefore he is also called King of the ages, as the one who establishes within and around himself the whole of being and Being. He neither was, nor will be, nor was made, nor is being made, nor will be made. Rather, he is not even “is” in the ordinary sense: he himself is Being for existing things, and not only the being of existing things but Being itself, from the eternally pre-existing Being. For he is himself subsisting before the ages.

Let us therefore say, accepting this, that all existing things and the ages receive their being from the providential Being. Every age and time is from him; and he is the principle and cause of the whole age, time, and every kind of being, the one who is before Being. All things participate in him, and he departs from none of the existing things. He is before all things, establishes all things in himself, and, simply speaking, if anything in any way is, it is in the pre-existing Being; it exists, is understood, and is preserved.

Being precedes all things that participate in him. He is Being itself in the highest sense: Life itself, by being Life itself; Wisdom itself, by being Wisdom itself; divine likeness itself, by being divine likeness itself; and so with everything else that participates, since he possesses being itself before all things. More than this, all existing things, by participating in Being itself, participate in Being itself [Note: [Col. 1147] BE reads “participates” in the singular]. Nothing is an essence apart from that very Being of all things. [Note: [Col. 1147] BEH read: “There is no essence whose essence and age are not that self-subsisting Being itself. Therefore …”; A has the reading represented above.]

Accordingly, God is rightly praised above other things as Being, because he hastens to precede and surpass being. Being itself was established before all things, and all things derive their being from it. How, then, was Being established? All the principles of existing things participate in Being itself; they exist and are principles, being first existent and then principles. If one wishes to call the principle of living things, insofar as they are living things, Life itself; of similar things, insofar as they are similar, Similarity itself; of united things, insofar as they are united, Unity itself; of ordered things, insofar as they are ordered, Order itself; and of whatever else participates in one or another of these, or in both or in many, then one will find that the participants themselves first participate in Being itself [Col. 1149A]. Through that participation they are first existing things, then principles of this or that kind, and, by participating in Being, existing participants.

If these things exist through participation, then their participants do so all the more. The greatest participants therefore praise the first gift of Being itself, which is set before them by supreme Goodness itself. They are from it and in it; they are Being itself, the principles of existing things, all existing things, and whatever is in any way held within being. All this occurs immeasurably, in a mutually interwoven and unified manner.

For in the monad every number subsists beforehand, and the monad possesses every number within itself in a singular manner. Every number is united in the monad; but insofar as it proceeds from the monad, it is distinguished and multiplied [Col. 1149B]. Likewise, at the center all the lines of a circle are co-established according to their first unity. The center contains every radius within itself as simple, uniformly united both to one another and to the single principle from which they proceed; in the center they are universally joined together [Note: [Col. 1149] BH reads “and they themselves”].

The lines that are briefly distant from the center are briefly distinguished; those farther away are more greatly distinguished. In general, the nearer they are to the center, the more they and one another are united; and the farther they are from it, the more they are separated from one another.

Likewise, throughout the whole of nature, all things are interwoven according to the individual principles of nature through one undivided unity. In the soul, too, the providential powers of the whole body are uniformly present according to its several parts. It is therefore not unreasonable, ascending from obscure images to the causal principle of all things, to contemplate with supermundane eyes all things in the causal principle of all things, including things opposed to one another, uniformly and in unity [Col. 1149C].

For it is the principle of existing things, from which come Being itself and every existing thing in whatever manner; every principle, every end, every life, every immortality, every wisdom, every order, every harmony, every virtue, every preservation, every placement [Note: [Col. 1149] AH reads “contribution”], every distribution, every intellect, every reason, every sensation, every condition, every stability, every movement, every unity, every judgment, every friendship, every connection, every distinction, every limit, and everything else that characterizes all things existing from Being.

From it, as the cause of all things, come the invisible and intellectual essences of the godlike angels, the souls, the nature of the whole world, and whatever is said to subsist in other things or to exist according to thought [Col. 1149D]. The most holy and most excellent powers, then, truly exist. They are established, as it were, in the vestibules of the super-essential Trinity; from it and in it they possess both being and godlike being. Beneath them are the subordinate powers, and at the lowest extremity, so far as the angels are concerned, the last beings; but so far as we are concerned, the supermundane powers.

All other existing things likewise receive from the same principle both being and well-being. They exist and exist well because they possess being and well-being from the pre-existing Being. In it they exist and exist well; from it they have their beginning, in it they are preserved, and in it they reach completion [Col. 1150A].

The Scriptures attribute the most honorable name, Being itself, to the better essences, which they also call eternal. But Being itself is never absent from any existing thing. Being itself is from the pre-existing Being, and being is from him—not he from being. He is the principle and measure of Being, existing before essences, Being, the age, and every source of substance; he is the beginning, middle, and completion.

For this reason the Scriptures multiply the expressions concerning the one who truly is before Being—ante-Being—according to every conception of existing things. They properly praise in him what was, what is, what will be, what has been made, what is being made, and what will be made [Col. 1150B]. All these expressions, understood divinely according to every conception, signify his super-essential Being and his causal relation to existing things.

For he is not one thing here and another thing elsewhere; he is not present in one place and absent in another. Rather, he is all things as the cause of all things, embracing and possessing beforehand in himself all principles, all boundaries, all completions, and all existing things. He is above all things as the one who is super-essentially above Being before all things [Note: [Col. 1149] AE adds “and”].

Therefore everything is predicated of him simultaneously, and yet he is none of the existing things: he encompasses within himself, immeasurably and remotely, the most beautiful and fairest, the formless and without appearance, the principles, middles, and ends of existing things. He declares to all things their being according to the first and super-united cause, without contamination.

For, to use an example familiar to us, the sun, while illuminating the essences and qualities of sensible things—many and distinct as they are—is itself one and uniform light. It renews, nourishes, preserves, perfects, distinguishes, unites, restores, makes fertile, increases, changes, establishes, plants, removes, and gives life to all things. Each of the many participants properly participates in the same one sun, and the one sun uniformly contains within itself the causes of its many participants [Col. 1150C].

Much more, then, must it be granted that the cause of the sun itself and of all things has pre-established in itself the paradigms of all existing things according to one super-essential unity. It then brings essences forth according to their procession from Essence.

By paradigms we mean the substantial and uniformly pre-existing principles of existing things in God, which theology calls predeterminations and divine and good wills. These distinguish and produce existing things; according to them the super-essential Being both predestined and brought forth all existing things [Col. 1150D].

If the philosopher considers Clement’s view worthy—namely, that paradigms may also be called the more ancient principles of things existing in relation to something [Note: [Col. 1150] BE reads *climes*, which is the Greek Κλήμης]—the argument does indeed proceed, though not through proper, complete, and simple names. We may nevertheless agree that this too is rightly stated, remembering the theology that says: “I did not show you these things so that they might come after those things, but so that through them, by proportional knowledge, we might ascend, as far as we are able, to the cause of all things.”

All things must therefore be referred to this Being, according to its one sublime knowledge of all things [Col. 1151A]. For it begins from the substantial procession and goodness of Being, proceeds through all things, fills all things from itself so that they may exist, and rejoices in all existing things. Yet it surpasses all things in itself, according to the first excellence of simplicity, which rejects every duality.

It also contains all things according to its super-simple multiplicity and is participated in individually by all things, just as one voice, being one and the same, is participated in as one by many hearers.

The one who is before Being is therefore the principle and end of existing things: the principle as their cause, the end as that for whose sake they exist, and the extremity of all things and the multiplicity of the whole multiplicity and extremity, super-eminent as the opposite of opposites [Col. 1151B].

For in the One, as has often been said, he both surpasses and establishes all existing things. He is present to all and everywhere, according to the one and the same principle, and according to that same principle he comes forth into all things while remaining in himself, standing and moving; neither standing nor moving; having neither beginning, middle, nor end; neither existing in any one of the existing things nor being any existing thing [Note: [Col. 1151] “nor being any existing thing” omitted by E].

Nothing that exists eternally, nor anything established temporally, approaches him at all. He is removed from all things that are in time, from the eternal, from what is in the eternal, and from what is in time [Note: [Col. 1151] BH omits “nor anything existing—eternally existing”]. Therefore he himself is eternal, while existing things are measured by him, are measured through him, and are from him.

## CHAPTER VI. On Life

[Col. 1151C]

These matters may be discussed elsewhere at a more appropriate time. For now, however, we must praise the praiseworthy eternal Life, from which Life itself, and every life, proceed, and from which living is sown individually into everything that participates in life in any manner.

Thus the life and immortality of the immortal angels, and the imperishability of their perpetual angelic movement, are from it and through it and subsist in it. For this reason they are called ever-living and immortal; yet they are again called not immortal, because they do not possess immortal being and eternal life from themselves, but from the life-giving cause that produces and sustains all life.

As we say concerning Being that it is the cause of being itself, so here again we say that Life itself is divine, vital, and substantial Life; and that every life and vital movement come from Life itself, which is above every life and is the principle of all life.

From it souls receive their imperishability, and all animals and plants receive life according to the final consonance of the soul. When the soul is removed, as the Scripture says [Note: [Col. 1151D] Psalm CIII], all life fails upon the earth; and when they become weak through failing to participate in it, they again turn back and become living creatures.

Life first gives to Life itself the fact of being life, and each individual nature is considered to subsist from it according to its own particular manner of being [Col. 1152A]. To the supercelestial souls it gives immaterial, godlike, and unchanging immortality, as well as unbending and irreproachable perpetual movement, extending itself through the greatness of its goodness even into demonic life [Note: [Col. 1151] A reads “of demons”; E reads “demonic”].

For that life does not receive its being from another cause; from Life itself it possesses both being alive and permanence. It also grants human beings, as composite creatures, a share in the acceptable angelic life that descends to them, in superabundant humanity, turning and recalling us back to itself.

This is still more divine: it promises to transform us wholly—our souls, that is, and our bodies united to them—into the most perfect and immortal life. This appears equally contrary to nature to the old order, but to you, to me, and to truth it is divine and beyond nature [Col. 1152B]. By “beyond nature” I mean beyond the visible nature that belongs to us, not beyond the most powerful divine life.

For to Life itself, as it is the nature of all living things, and especially of divine things, no life is contrary to nature or beyond nature [Note: [Col. 1151] “or beyond nature” omitted by BH and added above the line by E]. Therefore let the contradictory words of the madness of Simon concerning this matter be driven far from the divine place and from your sacred soul.

For, I think, he failed to understand that the one considered wise ought not, with reason assisting sense-perception, to use the language of sensation against the hidden cause of all things. And this itself must be said: to call this contrary to nature is itself contrary to reason. Nothing is contrary to Life itself.

From it all animals and plants are given life and are nurtured. Whether you call it intellectual, rational, sensory, nutritive, or growth-producing life; whatever kind of life, principle of life, or essence of life you name, it lives and gives life from Life itself, which is above every life and which, as their cause, subsists beforehand in uniformity within itself [Col. 1152C].

For if it is more than life, the principal Life of lives, the cause of every life, the begetter of life, and life that fills and distinguishes, then it is praised through every life according to the manifold generation of all lives—as the most abundant life, as every contemplative life, as life that is praised and lacks nothing; rather, as life more than full, living through itself, giving life above every life, and living more than life. In what human manner could anyone praise this ineffable life?

## CHAPTER VII. On Wisdom, Intellect, Reason, Truth, and Faith

[Col. 1152D]

Come, then [Note: [Col. 1151] BH reads “almost”; Greek φέρε], if it seems good, let us praise the best and eternal Life as wise and as Wisdom itself; rather, as the substantial source of all wisdom, existing above every wisdom and intellect.

For God is not only more than the fullness of wisdom, and of his understanding there is no number [Note: [Col. 1152D] Psalm CXLVI]; he is also set above every reason, intellect, and wisdom [Col. 1153A]. Understanding this excellently, the truly divine man, the common joy of our teacher and of us, says: “The foolishness of God is wiser than human beings” [Note: [Col. 1153D] 1 Corinthians I:25; 1 Timothy VI].

This is so not only because every human deliberation is judged error in comparison with the weight and permanence of divine and most perfect understandings, but also because theologians customarily negate in God, by a contrary movement of mind, what is predicated through privation. Thus the Scriptures call the invisible one clear light, and the highly praiseworthy and many-named one ineffable and nameless; they call him present to all things and discovered through all things, yet incomprehensible and unsearchable.

In the same way, the divine Apostle is now said to have praised the foolishness of God: what appears in it contrary to reason and incongruous he refers to the ineffable truth that precedes every reason [Col. 1153B]. But, as we have said elsewhere, we are deceived when we interpret what is above us in terms proper to ourselves, joined as we are to the nourishment of the senses and applying divine things to what belongs to us, while pursuing, as it seems, the divine and ineffable reason [Note: [Col. 1153] BH adds “what belongs to us,” and reads “we are deceived”].

We must know that our soul possesses a power for understanding, through which it sees invisible things, and a unity that is super-exalted, and a nature through which it is joined to its highest part [Note: [Col. 1153] A reads “through which it is converted”; EH reads “to the highest”]. According to this power, divine things must be understood—not according to ourselves, but with our whole selves existing in those things and having become wholly God’s.

For it is better that we should be God’s and their members. In this way the divine gifts will be with those who will be with God.

Praising this irrational, mindless, and foolish Wisdom super-eminently, we say that it is the cause of the whole soul and of reason, of all wisdom and intellect. It is itself every counsel; from it come all knowledge and understanding; and in it all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden [Note: [Col. 1153D] Colossians II].

Consistently with what has already been said, it is the more-than-wise and supremely wise cause, Wisdom itself, and the substance both of wisdom as a whole and of the wisdom that exists in each individual. From it the invisible and intellectual powers of the angelic souls possess simple and blessed understandings. They do not gather divine knowledge from divided things, from things divided, from sensations, or from artificial arguments; nor do they grasp it by inference from some common principle. Rather, purified from all materiality and multiplicity, they understand divine invisible things purely, immaterially, and uniformly [Col. 1153D].

Their intellectual operation is clear and shines with undefiled purity. It knows and beholds the indivisible and immaterial character of divine understandings, and, as far as possible, has been reshaped according to the One—the intellectually wise soul and reason—through divine Wisdom [Col. 1154A].

Souls possess rationality. They move skillfully and circularly around the truth of existing things, leaving behind the divisible and abundant variety proper to them in favor of the uniform souls. Through the convolution of many things into one, they are made worthy, insofar as is fitting and possible for souls, to participate in the intellects of angels [Note: [Col. 1153] BE reads “of many”].

Perhaps one would not be wrong to call even the senses themselves consonant with the vision of wisdom. But the demonic soul, if it is a soul, is also from Wisdom itself. Insofar as it is a soul, however, if it does not desire to follow reason in this way, neither seeing nor willing, it must rather be declared to have fallen from wisdom.

But since divine Wisdom is called the beginning, cause, substance, completion, preservation, and end of wisdom itself as a whole, of every soul, of every reason, and of every sensation [Col. 1154B], how is God himself, who is more than wise, praised as Wisdom, Soul, Reason, and Knower? How could he understand anything invisible if he possesses no intellectual operations? Or how could he know sensible things, since he is set above every sense?

Yet the Scriptures say that he knows all things [Note: [Col. 1154D] Hebrews IV; 1 John III; Ecclesiasticus XXIII], and that nothing escapes divine knowledge. But, as we have often said, divine things must be understood divinely.

In God, “not intellectual” and “not sensory” must be understood as terms of excellence, not deficiency. So too we applied “irrational” to the one who is above reason; imperfection to the one who is more than perfect and before perfection; and untouched and invisible darkness to the inaccessible light, because of the excellence of its invisible luminosity.

Thus the divine Mind contains all things. Its knowledge is removed from all things, yet, according to the cause of all, it possesses beforehand within itself the knowledge of all things. Before the angels came to be, it knew and brought forth the angels, and it knew and brought into being all other things from within and, so to speak, from itself as their source.

This, I believe, is what the Scripture teaches when it says: “Knowing all things before their generation” [Note: [Col. 1154D] Daniel XIII:42]. The divine Mind does not learn existing things from existing things and thereby know them. Rather, from itself and in itself, according to the cause of all things, it presents beforehand and embraces beforehand their knowledge, cognition, and essence [Note: [Col. 1153] “and essence” omitted by BH].

It does not contemplate each thing according to its particular form, but knows and contains all things according to the single context of the cause. Thus light, according to its cause, possesses darkness beforehand within itself, not seeing darkness from elsewhere than from the light.

Therefore, divine Wisdom knows itself, and in knowing itself knows material things immaterially, divided things without division, and many things universally; in the One itself it both knows and brings forth all things.

For if God gives being to all existing things according to one cause, then according to that same single cause he knew all things as existing from him and established beforehand in him [Col. 1155A]. He does not acquire knowledge of non-existing things from those things; rather, he is the giver of knowledge to each of them.

God does not possess knowledge of himself in one way and another common knowledge comprehending all existing things. By knowing himself as the cause of all things, he knows the absence of ignorance concerning those things that come from him and of which he is the cause. God therefore knows existing things in this way: not by the knowledge of existing things, but by his own knowledge.

The Scriptures also say that the angels know what is upon the earth [Note: [Col. 1155D] Revelation II]. They do not know these earthly sensible things through the senses, but through the proper power and nature of their godlike mind.

In these matters we must ask how we know God, since he is neither intelligible nor sensible, nor is he any existing thing in a universal sense. Is it therefore true to say that we know God not from his own nature—for this is unknowable and surpasses every reason and intellect—but from the order of all existing things, prefigured by him and containing certain images and likenesses of his divine paradigms?

We must ascend, through the life and order of all things according to their powers, by removing all things and by rising above all things, to the cause of all. Therefore God is known both in all things and without all things; he is known through knowledge and through unknowing [Note: [Col. 1155] B reads “ignorance”]. His are understanding, reason, knowledge, touch, sensation, opinion, imagination, name, and everything else.

Yet he is neither understood, spoken, nor named. He is not any existing thing, nor is he known in any existing thing [Col. 1155C]. In all things he is all things, and in nothing he is nothing. He is known from all things in all things, and from nothing in nothing [Note: [Col. 1155] BH omits “and in nothing he is nothing ... from nothing in nothing”].

We rightly say these things concerning God, and he is praised through all existing things according to the analogy of all things of which he is the cause.

There is also a most divine knowledge of God: through unknowing [Note: [Col. 1155] BEH read “through knowledge”] it knows him according to the unity above the soul. The soul withdraws from all existing things, then abandons even itself, and is united to the rays that appear above it; there and then it is illuminated by the inscrutable depth of wisdom.

Indeed, as I have said, he is to be known from all things. For, according to the Scripture, he is the maker of all things, continually joining all things together, the indissoluble cause of the congruence and order of all things, continually connecting the ends of former things with the beginnings of subsequent things [Col. 1155D], and making the beautiful unity and harmony of the whole universe.

Reason is also praised as God by the sacred Scriptures, not only because he is the giver of reason, intellect, and wisdom, but because he has uniformly pre-contained within himself the causes of all things, and because, as the Scriptures say [Note: [Col. 1155D] Psalm XXXII:118; Isaiah XL; John I; Jeremiah XXIII; Wisdom VIII], he fills all things by reaching to their end.

Before all these things, divine Reason is super-simplified in complete simplicity [Col. 1156A]. It is above all things and beyond all things, being set apart according to its super-essential nature.

Reason itself is simple and truly existing Truth. Divine faith is the one foundation of believers, directed toward this Truth as the pure and unerring knowledge of all things. It establishes believers in the truth and gives them truth, as they believe in the simple knowledge of truth with an incredible immutability.

For Truth is the unifying knowledge of those who know and of the things known. Ignorance, by contrast, is always changeable and is the cause of separation from the ignorant person himself.

According to the sacred word, nothing will remove the believer in Truth from the joy that belongs to true faith. In this joy he will dwell with stable and unchanging uniformity [Note: [Col. 1156D] Romans VIII].

For the one united to Truth knows where he has his dwelling, even if many rebuke him as one who has lost his mind [Col. 1156B]. He escapes their notice as though he were an image of error, having through true faith gone beyond the error that turns men away from truth. But he truly knows himself—not, as they say, as one who is insane, but as one liberated from the instability and mutability of the diverse circuit of error through the immovable Truth that always remains the same and is established in the same way.

Thus, according to our condition, the principal guides of divine Wisdom die every day for the truth, bearing witness, as is fitting, in word and deed to the one true knowledge for Christians: that it is itself both simpler and more divine than all other knowledge, or rather, that it alone is the true, one, simple, and divine knowledge [Note: [Col. 1155] BEH omit “both simpler ... that it alone is”].

## CHAPTER VIII. On Virtue, Justice, Salvation, and Redemption, and on Inequality

[Col. 1156C]

Since the theologians praise the divine truth and the wisdom that is wiser than wisdom as virtue, and call it salvation itself and redemption [Note: [Col. 1155] BH: “the redeemer”], let us now, as far as possible, rehearse these divine names as well. Since the thearchy surpasses and transcends every virtue, both existent and conceived, in every respect, I do not think that anyone who possesses the divine Scriptures is ignorant of this. For everywhere theology presents it as sovereign over all and distinguishes it even from the supercelestial virtues. How, then, do theologians praise it as virtue, when it is removed from every virtue? Or how do we understand the name “virtue” in its case?

Let us say, then, that God is virtue, as possessing every virtue beforehand in himself, as the cause of every virtue, and as producing all things through his inflexible and unbounded virtue; as giving from himself the virtue of being, whether to the whole or to each several thing that has causal existence; and as being and surpassing every virtue in himself—not only by producing every virtue, but also by existing above every virtue in himself, by bringing forth in many ways many other virtues for existing things, never being incapable of producing many virtues, and surpassing the many virtues thus produced through the abundance of his hieratic work and through his ineffable, unknowable, and super-invisible virtue, which surpasses all things [Col. 1157A].

The infinite essence of the Almighty embraces and surpasses weakness through virtue, as well as the lowest things that accord with it. We see the same even among powers perceptible to the senses: luminaires that shine above us anticipate even the weakest visions, and the magnitudes of sounds are said to reach ears that are not readily receptive to sounds. For, altogether, what does not hear is not hearing, and universally what does not see is not seeing.

The manifold distribution of God’s power clearly fills all existing things, and there is nothing among existing things that is entirely deprived of possessing some virtue. Rather, it possesses either intellectual, rational, sensory, vital [Note: [Col. 1157] BH omits “or vital”], or essential virtue; and, if one may speak justly, even its very being possesses virtue from the superessential virtue.

From this derive the virtues of the angelic orders that are godlike. From it they possess their being without causation [Note: [Col. 1157] AEH: “without cause”], as well as all their intellectual and immortal movements, their very courage, and their undiminished desire for the good, received from the supremely good virtue. It permits them to be and to be capable of these things, to desire always to be, and to be capable of desiring this always.

These effects of inflexible virtue extend also to human beings, animals, plants, and the whole nature of the universe. By virtue they are united to one another in friendship and fellowship; and, while distinct, they are preserved without confusion or disturbance in being according to the proper account and limit of each [Col. 1157C]. It preserves the orders and aggregations of the universe in their proper perfection; guards the immaculate lives of the immortal angelic unions; establishes the celestial, illuminating, and stellar essences and their unchanging orders according to their capacity for being; distinguishes the circuits of time by processions and gathers them together by return; makes the powers of fire unquenchable, the streams of water unfailing, and limits the outpouring of air; places the earth in nothingness and preserves its fruitful offspring incorruptible; preserves the harmony and unmixed, inseparable balance of the elements with one another; maintains the bond of soul and body; moves the nutritive and growth-producing powers of plants; surpasses the essential powers of all things; fortifies the universe’s indissoluble permanence; and bestows deification, supplying virtue to those who are being deified.

Indeed, no existing thing whatever is deprived of the omnipotent protection and encompassing presence of divine virtue. For what altogether possesses no virtue neither exists nor is anything, nor does it have any status whatsoever [Note: [Col. 1157] BEH: “neither exists, nor is it anything”].

Elymas the magician says: “If God is omnipotent, how can he be said to be unable to do something?” Our theologian, the divine Paul, curses him when he says [Note: [Col. 1157D] II Tim. II] that God cannot deny himself. As I add this, I am greatly astonished: should I also be obliged to take account of folly? I laugh at the structures of children playing, who try to dissolve what is built upon sand and weakness, and I hasten, as though examining some incomprehensible vision, to consider the theological meaning here.

For self-denial is a falling away from truth. Truth is being [ὄν], and the fall of truth is a falling away from being [Note: [Col. 1157] So A; the other manuscripts omit “a falling away from being”]. If, then, truth is being, and denial is the falling away of the truth of being, God cannot fall away from being; and not-being is not. It is as though someone were to say that he cannot be unable, and that he does not know unknowing according to privation.

The wise man who fails to understand this imitates inexperienced wrestlers in competition. These, often supposing their weaker opponents to be struggling against them, and fighting all of them manfully in the realm of shadows, striking the air confidently with empty blows, imagine that they have mastered their adversaries and proclaim themselves victorious, ignorant of their opponents’ strength.

But we, contemplating the theologian as far as possible, praise God as more than powerful: as omnipotent, blessed, alone powerful, and ruling in his power over the age; as falling under none of the things that exist; and, rather, as surpassing all existing things through his superessential virtue, abundantly granting to all existing things the capacity to be and to exist, according to the greatness of his surpassing virtue.

God is again praised as justice, distributing to all things that exist according to their worth [Col. 1158C], and assigning measure, form, order, disposition, and every virtue and order to each according to its truly existing and most just limit; and as being, through justice itself, the causal source of each thing’s activity. Divine justice orders and limits all things, preserves all things distinct and unmixed from one another, and gives to each whatever is akin to it among existing things, according to the inherent worth of each existing thing.

If we speak correctly, then those who blaspheme divine things are ignorant of justice, openly condemning their own injustice. For they say that mortals ought to possess immortality, the imperfect perfection, things moved by themselves another necessity that moves them, mutable things immutability, the weak perfect power, temporal things eternity, things mobile by nature an unchanging condition, temporal delights eternal duration; and altogether they extend to some things what belongs to others.

We must know that divine justice is truly justice in this respect: it gives to all their own according to the worth of each existing thing, and preserves each nature in its proper order and virtue.

But someone might say: “Perhaps it is not just that holy men, while among those who do not help them, should be forcibly deprived by deceivers.” To this one must reply as follows. If those whom you call holy love earthly things that are coveted by material beings, they have utterly fallen away from divine love; and I do not know how they can be called holy [Note: [Col. 1159] AE: “how they might be called”] if they act unjustly toward those who do not covet what is truly lovable and divine, and do not love those things that have not been reverently approved by them.

But if they love what truly exists, they ought to rejoice as its lovers when they attain what they desire. Or do they not then draw closer to the angelic virtues, when, as far as possible, through their desire for divine things, they return from material things, having been disciplined through suffering? In this way they strive very bravely for the good.

Therefore, to speak truly, this belongs especially to divine justice: not to destroy by force the strength of those who act powerfully, through the bonds of material things. What, then, if someone should attempt this—not among those who do not help them, but among those who place them in a good and irreproachable station, and repay such persons with what is worthy of them?

Divine justice is therefore praised as the salvation of all, preserving and guarding each person’s own pure essence and order, and purifying from all things whatever is foul in each one’s proper activity. If someone praises salvation as delivering everyone from all evils, as though giving birth to them and rescuing them, we shall certainly welcome this praiseworthy praise of the most generous salvation.

We shall also judge him worthy to have defined this first salvation of all: that it preserves all things in themselves unchanging, stable, and inflexible toward their subjects; guards all things from conflict and warfare; arranges each according to its own account; eradicates from all things every injustice and alien activity; and, through the rationality proper to each, establishes irrationalities that fall outside it in their contraries, without permitting them to transgress.

Next, someone may praise this salvation in accordance with sacred theology as redeeming all existing things through the universal goodness, from the fall of their own best condition, insofar as the nature of each of those being saved is capable of receiving it.

Accordingly, theologians call it redemption itself, insofar as it does not permit what truly exists to fall into non-being; and insofar as anything has fallen into error or disorder and has suffered some diminution of the perfection of its proper goods, it redeems it from suffering, inactivity, and privation, filling its lack; overlooking its weakness with fatherly compassion; restoring it from evil—or, rather, establishing it in the good; filling, ordering, and adorning the good that had been overawed; ordering what was disordered and adorning what was unadorned; perfecting its integrity; and releasing all its stains.

We have spoken, then, about these matters and about justice, according to which the equality of all things is measured and determined, and every inequality that exists through privation is expelled from each individual thing. For if someone were to remove equality altogether, he would remove the differences of all things in relation to all things, as well as the guardian of justice, which does not allow all things mixed together in all things to be thrown into confusion, but preserves all things according to their individual forms, in which each thing is established as being.

## CHAPTER IX. On the great, the small, the same, the other, the like, the unlike, rest, motion, and equality

Since the great and the small, the same and the other, the like and the unlike, rest and motion are also posited in the causal source of all things, let us now contemplate whatever is manifest to us in these divine appellative images [Note: [Col. 1159] AE: “divine appellations”].

God is therefore praised in the Scriptures as great, both in greatness and in the gentle breeze that manifests the divine smallness. He is also called the same, when Scripture says, “But you are the same” [Note: [Col. 1159D] III Kings XIX; Psalm CI]. He is called other when he is portrayed by the Scriptures as greatly varied and many-formed; like, as the establisher of likeness and resemblance; unlike all things, as having no thing like him [Note: [Col. 1159] AH: “like him”]; standing and moving, as sitting forever and as moving into all things. Scripture praises him also through other divine names equivalent to these.

God is called great because he knows how to give his own greatness to all great things, surpasses every greatness outside himself, encompasses the most universal extension, surpasses every number, and transcends every multitude. Through the superabundance of his greatness and activity, and through his flowing gifts, he remains wholly undiminished, however greatly those gifts are shared by all through their abundant and generous outpouring. They retain the same superabundance and are not diminished by participation, but flow forth still more abundantly [Col. 1160C].

This greatness is both manifold and without form and number. It is transcendence, according to the absolute and superordinate outpouring of an ungraspable greatness.

The small, or the minute, is said of him because he is free from every finite space [Note: [Col. 1159] BH: “extended”] and is consequently situated throughout all things. Indeed, the causal source of all things is small. For nowhere will you find a form that does not participate in the small.

Thus the small must be understood in God as being firmly situated in all things and throughout all things, acting and penetrating as far as the division of soul and body, of joints and marrow, and of the thoughts of the heart [Col. 1160D]—or, rather, as far as all existing things. “No creature is invisible before him” [Note: [Col. 1160D] Hebrews IV].

The small is thus both so great and so incomprehensible: infinite, comprehending all things, while itself incomprehensible.

The same, in a superessential sense, is eternal, unchangeable, always remaining in itself according to the same condition and possessing the same character; equally present to all; the same in itself, by itself, and from itself; firmly and undefiledly established in the most beautiful heights; placed with great immutability in a natural fellowship; unchanging, without causation, inflexible, unalienated, pure, immaterial [Note: [Col. 1161] BH omits “inflexible … immaterial”], most simple, without need, neither increasing nor diminishing, neither generated nor made in this or that way; not imperfect, not made by this or by that; in no way, never, and nowhere not-being [ὄν], but, as all that is ungenerated and absolutely ungenerated, always being [ὄν], itself perfect being, being itself through itself and from itself, uniformly and equally distinguished from itself; itself, from itself, shining forth to all things capable of participating in it; combining one thing with another; the greatness and natural cause of unchanging fellowship in itself; and likewise surpassing contraries according to the one and singular cause that transcends the whole of natural and unchanging fellowship.

The other is spoken of because God is providentially present to all things and is all things in all things for the salvation of all. He is being [ὄν], proceeding from himself and through his own natural immutability standing unchangeably through one single and unceasing activity; extending himself through inflexible virtue toward the deification of those who are converted; and, through the many-formed visions of God’s varied images, making another aspect of himself shine through visible things as a sign.

For how would we understand the parts surrounding indivisibility in the soul itself, if reason were to depict the soul in bodily form and to fashion bodily parts around what is indivisible? We might call the head the mind, the neck opinion—as intermediate between reason and irrationality—the chest anger, the belly desire, and the legs and feet nature, using the names of bodily parts as symbols of virtues [Col. 1161C].

Much more, then, in the case of the universal summit, we must dissolve the multiplicity of forms and figures through sacred, divine, and mystical repetitions. The divine counsel has encircled the untouched and unfigured God with a threefold bodily schema: it calls breadth the exceedingly broad procession of God into all things; length the virtue extending over all things; and depth the incomprehensible obscurity and ignorance surrounding all existing things.

But so that nothing concerning ourselves may remain hidden through the repetition of other figures and formless images, we have mingled those incorporeal divine names with things represented through sensible symbols. For this reason we have treated these matters in the *Symbolic Theology* [Col. 1161D].

Now, however, we shall understand this divine otherness not as some alienation from the super-unvarying and immutable natural fellowship, but as the singular, manifold, and uniform processions of that fellowship into all things, rich in fertility.

If someone calls God like, provided that he means one and the same, existing wholly throughout the whole in himself, singly and indivisibly, we must not reject the divine name “like.” But the theologians say that God, who is above all, is either himself like no one [Note: [Col. 1161] AB: “he himself”], or that he gives the power of likeness to those who turn toward him, according to their capacity, through a middle state between what surpasses every vision and reason. The power of divine likeness converts all things that approach it toward the causal source.

Those things, then, are to be called like God that exist according to the divine image and likeness. God is not like them, for neither is a human being like his own image. Among things of equal power it is possible for them to be alike and for likeness to be exchanged between them, so that both are mutually like one another according to the prior form of likeness. But in the case of the causal source and the things caused, we do not admit reciprocity.

For likeness is not granted merely to these or those things. God becomes the cause of being like for all things that participate in likeness, and he himself is the establisher of likeness in itself. Every likeness is like something through a certain trace of divine likeness, and it completes the unity of the things that possess it.

What more need be said? Theology itself commands us to call him unlike, unconnected with all things, and other than all things. And what is more wondrous, it says that nothing is like him.

Yet there is no contradiction between this and likeness to him. The same things are both like God and unlike him: like him according to the received imitation of the inimitable, but unlike him according to the distance between the things caused and the causal source, and according to the many incomparable measures.

Let us further speak about the divine state, or seat. What else is this than God’s remaining in himself, fixed in a single mode through immobile natural immutability, established above according to the same condition, acting around the same reality and in the same manner, subsisting in every respect from himself according to his most stable condition, unchanging according to himself and universally immutable—and all this in a superessential manner?

For he is the causal source of all standing and establishment, existing above every establishment and standing; and in himself he establishes all things, immovable and guarded through the standing of their proper goods.

What does it mean when the theologians also call him immutable while saying that he proceeds into all things and is mutable? Must this too not be understood divinely? We must piously conceive God as moving—not through transport, alienation, alteration, conversion, or local motion; not moving in a straight line, circularly, or through a combination of the two; not through intelligible, animal, or natural motion—but as bringing things into being, encompassing all things, universally providing for all things, being present to all things through an immeasurable encompassing, and proceeding and acting providentially in all existing things [Note: [Col. 1161] BH omits “providing for all things and being present to all things”].

We must also, according to divine reason, grant praise to the immutable motion of God [Note: [Col. 1161] BH: “motion”]. Straight motion is to be understood as an inflexible and irrevocable procession of activities and generation from him of all things [Col. 1163A]. Helicoid motion—that is, oblique motion—is a lateral procession and a fertile state. Circular motion is the containment of the same thing, containing and being contained in the middle and at the extremes, and the return into the source of those things that proceed from it.

If someone similarly understands the divine name “justice” in the Scriptures as equality, we must say that God is equal not only in his undivided and irreproachable condition, but also as proceeding equitably into all things and throughout all things; as himself the establisher of equality; and as acting equally through all things according to the similar capacity of each for receiving, and according to the equitable participation of those who receive, in accordance with the suitability of each, the equality appropriate to each according to its worth, and the gift distributed among all.

He surpasses and anticipates within himself, in accordance with the virtue that produces all equality and is above all things, every invisible, intellectual, rational, sensory, essential, natural, and voluntary equality [Note: [Col. 1163] BH: “voluntary”].

## CHAPTER X. On the omnipotent and the Ancient of Days, and also on the eternal and time

It is now time to praise God, under his many names, as omnipotent and as the Ancient of Days.

He is called omnipotent because he is the omnipotent establishment of all things: encompassing and surrounding the whole, placing, founding, binding, and perfecting every weakness in himself; leading all things from himself as from a root that holds all things; turning all things back into himself as into an omnipotent counsel; and, as the establishment of all things, encompassing all things omnipotently, fortifying what he has comprehended through one surpassing containment of all things, and not allowing them to perish by falling away from themselves through transformation resulting from their most perfect restoration [Col. 1163B].

The thearchy is also called omnipotent as powerful over all things, granting power to those who serve it purely. And, as it commands all things, it is lovable, implanting in all things voluntary unions and the sweet offspring of its own divine, omnipotent, and immaterial goodness and love.

God is praised as the Ancient of Days because he himself is eternity and time, before days, before eternity, and before time [Note: [Col. 1163] A*: “he is in all time”]. Time, day, the span of time, and eternity must likewise be said divinely to be God, since he exists immutably and immovably according to every motion, remaining in his own being while always moving, and serving as the causal source of eternity, time, and days.

Accordingly, in the sacred theophanies of mystical visions, he is represented as both old and new: the elder signifies the Ancient, existing from the beginning; the younger signifies that he does not grow old, teaching most clearly that he proceeds through all things from the beginning to the end.

Or, as our divine and holy initiator says, both figures declare the divine antiquity: the elder signifies what is first in time, while the younger possesses what is older according to number, since the unit and the things around the unit are older than the numbers that proceed into multiplicity.

We must, I think, learn from the Scriptures the nature of time and eternity. For they do not call only those things that are altogether and absolutely ungenerated and truly eternal “eternal,” “incorruptible,” “immortal,” “immovable,” and “existing” in the same way in which existence is predicated of them. Thus Scripture says, “Lift up, eternal gates” [Note: [Col. 1163D] Psalm XXIII, 7, 9], and similarly.

Often, too, they characterize very ancient things with the designation “eternal,” and this is entirely correct when, in our terminology, they call a condition of time eternal, insofar as what belongs properly to eternity is being ancient, immutable, and universal by measure [Note: [Col. 1163] EH: “by falsifying”].

They call “time” what belongs to generation, corruption, and mutability, and what exists differently in different respects. Accordingly, theology says that we too, here, participate in eternity according to time when we understand the incorruptible and ever-remaining-in-the-same-condition as eternal.

The Scriptures, however, also glorify the eternal in temporal things, and temporal eternity; indeed, they call and declare the things that exist in them more powerfully and pre-eminently eternal, while things subject to generation are called and declared temporal.

Therefore, we must not simply regard as coeternal with God, who is before eternity, everything that is called eternal. Following the most precious and immutable Scriptures, we must understand eternal and temporal things according to the modes known to them and intended for obedience. The intermediate things—whatever exists among beings and things made—participate in eternity in one place and in time in another.

We must praise God as both eternal and time, as the causal source of all time and eternity; as the Ancient of Days, as existing before time and beyond time; as existing again before the eternities, insofar as he is before eternity and beyond eternity; and as the one whose kingdom is the kingdom of all ages [Note: [Col. 1164D] Daniel VII; Psalm CXLIV].

## CHAPTER XI. On peace, and what is meant by its being itself through itself, by life itself through itself, by virtue itself through itself, and by the names so described
[Col. 1164D] Come now, let us honor with praises of peace the divine, chief-governing peace. For it is itself the unifier of all things, the agreement of all things, and the source and maker of natural affinity. Accordingly, all things desire it, since it turns their divisible multiplicity into complete unity and unites the civil war of the universe into an evenly ordered dwelling together.

Through participation in the divine peace, the foremost of the gathered powers are united both with themselves and with one another [Col. 1165A] and with the one original peace of all things; they unite those subject to them with themselves, and themselves with one another, and with the one perfect principle and cause of all peace. This cause, being indivisibly established above all things as though by certain bonds of the divided members that belong together, bounds, completes, and secures everything. It does not allow separated things to be scattered into what is vast and infinite, disordered and without place, abandoned by God, departing from their unity, and most turbulently confused with one another.

Concerning this divine peace and silence—which the holy Justus calls *aphthengia* (ἀφθεγξία), “speechlessness”—and concerning every known procession and immobility, let us say that it is silent and observes silence; that it is in itself and within itself; that it is wholly super-united to itself; and that, while entering into itself and multiplying itself [Col. 1165B], it does not abandon its unity, but proceeds into all things while remaining within itself through the excellence of the unity that surpasses all things.

It is neither lawful nor possible for any existing thing to speak or understand it. But, placing it among the ineffable, the selfsame, and the unknowable, as the summit of all things, we shall contemplate as far as possible its intelligible and expressible participations, relying on what has been handed down to us by many excellent men [Note: [Col. 1165D] BH: *superspeculamur*, “we contemplate above,” instead of *superspeculabimur*, “we shall contemplate above.”]

First, then, this must be said: peace in itself is the substance both of the whole and of each thing; and it harmonizes all things with one another through their unconfused unity. Through this unity they are inseparably joined and, without distance, equally perfected according to the proper form of each, without being darkened by mixture with opposites or having anything obscured by the unifying care and purity [Col. 1165C].

Accordingly, we shall contemplate a certain single and simple nature of peaceful unity, joining all things to itself, to themselves, and to one another, and preserving all things within the unconfused containment, visibility, and harmony of everything. Through it, divine minds are united with their own intelligible objects and with those who understand, and again ascend toward what is unknown, beyond contact with those placed above the mind.

Through it, souls, understanding their most abundant rational principles and gathered into a single intellectual purity, proceed by a way and order proper to themselves, through immaterial and indivisible understanding, into unity beyond intellect.

Through it, the one indissoluble [Col. 1165D] interweaving of all things is constituted according to its divine harmony [Note: [Col. 1165D] A and E read *substituitur*, “is substituted,” instead of *constituitur*, “is constituted]; perfect consonance, agreement, and a growth together are joined, gathering together without confusion those that are confused and without separation those that are inseparably joined.

For the universality of perfect peace reaches all existing things through the coming of its most simple and clear unifying power. It unifies all things, joining the highest to the highest through the intermediates, joined by one natural friendship; it grants even the furthest extremities of the universe to enjoy it; and it makes all things akin through natural unities, unchangeable associations, and gatherings. Thus divine peace stands inseparably, proceeding from the One, manifesting all things, and coming through all things by its own natural and unchangeable association [Col. 1166A].

For it proceeds into all things and communicates to all things, each in its own way, the greatness of peaceful generation, which overflows from itself. Through the excellence of unity it remains wholly united to the whole, and through the whole it is super-united to itself.

“But how,” someone may ask, “do all things desire peace? For many take delight in difference and distinction, and would never wish what possesses them to be silent.”

If the person who says this means by difference and distinction the property of each existing thing, and if he says that no existing thing wishes ever to lose this property, perhaps we shall not dispute the point. But we shall make clear this desire for peace. All things love to be reconciled and united with themselves [Col. 1166B], and to be unchangeable and free from chance, both in their own properties and in themselves. In each thing there is a most perfect peace, mingled with its distinctive character and preserving it.
