Its providences give peace, preserving all things undisturbed and unconfused, both in themselves and in relation to one another, and establishing all things in strength and unbending power toward their own peace and tranquillity.

Nor does it wish all things that have been moved to remain silent; rather, it wishes them always to move according to their own movement. This too is the desire of the divine peace of all things: it preserves all things in themselves free from chance, safeguards the distinctive character and active life of all that moves, unchanged and free from chance, and makes those that move peaceful in relation to itself, so that they remain as they are while performing their proper activities.

But if, by the chance-related aspect of peace, someone means difference and thereby maintains that peace is not beloved by all, then all the more there is nothing among existing things that has fallen completely away from every unity [Col. 1166C]. For what is wholly unstable, multiple, without place, and infinite is neither a being (*on*, ὄν) nor among beings.

If he says that such things are hostile to peace and to the goods of peace, taking pleasure in strife, rage, alienation, and instability, then they too are held by a desire for peace, though by the darkest shadows of peace. Disturbed by highly mobile passions, they desire these passions to be brought to rest in an undisciplined way, and imagine that they will pacify themselves through the fullness of pleasures that continually flow back, while they are themselves disturbed by those pleasures.

What if someone were to speak of the humanity that flows with peace according to Christ? According to this humanity, we are not yet taught to fight—neither with ourselves, nor with one another, nor with the angels—but to cooperate with the divine powers themselves through virtue, according to the providence of Jesus, who works all things in all things and makes the ineffable peace that was predestined from eternity, reconciling us to himself in the Spirit and, through himself and in himself, to the Father.

These transcendent gifts have been sufficiently discussed in the theological writings, with the sacred understanding of the Scriptures bearing witness for us.

Since you also asked me in a letter about another matter—what I perhaps mean when I say “being in itself,” “life in itself,” and “wisdom in itself,” and when you expressed doubt concerning this: how I sometimes call God himself “life,” but at other times call him the source of life in itself [Col. 1167A]—we have judged it necessary, holy man of God, to release you from this doubt concerning us.

First, then, let us repeat what has often been said: there is no contradiction between calling God “virtue in itself” or “life in itself,” and calling him the source of life in itself, peace in itself, or virtue in itself.

Some things among existing realities, especially among those that exist first, are called “causes,” as causes of all existing things [Note: [Col. 1167] BH: *causales*, “causal,” instead of *causalis*, “cause”]. Other things are called “above all things,” and even “first existing things,” in a superessential way, above the superessential realities.

But what, you ask, have we explained as “being in itself,” or “life in itself,” or whatever is said absolutely and principally to exist, as having proceeded first from God? This is not wrong, but correct, and it has a simple explanation [Col. 1167B]. We do not mean that some divine or angelic essence exists in itself and, by its own being, is the cause of the being of all things. We mean only that the superessential principle itself, the cause of the being of all things that are, is being, essence, and cause [Note: [Col. 1167] AE: *causale*, “causal,” instead of *causalis*, “cause”].

Nor do we mean another deity as the parent of life, apart from the superdivine life that is the cause of all living things and of the life that has been brought forth.

Nor should one speak of a power that gathers together the principal and creative essences and substances of existing things—things that some have immediately and readily made into gods and creators of existing things. Properly and truly speaking, neither did those beings themselves form what did not exist, nor did their fathers form it.

Rather, by “being in itself,” “life in itself,” and “deity in itself,” we mean, principally, divinely and causally, the one super-principial and superessential principle and cause of all things [Col. 1167C].

Participatorily, however, we mean the providential powers proceeding from God, who is not himself a participant: deification in itself, vivification in itself, and deification in itself [Note: [Col. 1167] The words “vivification in itself, and deification in itself” are omitted in the manuscripts]. Existing things properly participate in these according to themselves; and thus existing things, living things, divine things, and the rest both are and are called such.

Accordingly, the best source of these primary realities themselves is said to exist; then the source of all of them; then of their particular manifestations; then of all their participations; and then, particularly, of those that participate in them [Note: [Col. 1167] The manuscripts omit “participations ... those that participate in them”].

And what need is there to say more about these matters, when some of our divine and sacred teachers call the source of goodness and deity in itself a goodness and deity in itself that is more than good and more than divine [Col. 1167D]? They say that it is a beneficent and deifying gift proceeding from God; a form in itself, a formative outpouring in itself, the whole form and the particular form; good universally and good particularly [Note: [Col. 1167] The manuscripts omit “and good particularly”]; and whatever else has been or will be said in the same manner.

Such expressions declare the providence and goodness that are participated in by existing things, proceeding from the nonparticipating God in abundant outpouring and overflowing beyond measure, while the causal summit of all things—the superessential and altogether supernatural cause—far surpasses all things that exist according to any essence or nature [Col. 1168A].

## CHAPTER XII. On the Holy of Holies, King of Kings, Lord of Lords, and God of Gods

Since all that needed to be said about these matters has, as I think, received an appropriate conclusion, we must praise the great-voiced one as the Holy of Holies, the King of those who reign, and the one who reigns throughout the ages and beyond the ages and forever; and as the Lord of Lords and God of Gods [Note: [Col. 1167D] Daniel IX; Revelation XIX].

First, then, we must say what we understand by holiness in itself, what by kingship, what by lordship, what by deity, and what the Scriptures intend to declare by the doubling of these names [Col. 1168B] [Note: [Col. 1168D] Daniel IV; Isaiah IX; Micah V; Zechariah IX; Revelation XVII].

Holiness, so far as it may be stated in our terms, is freedom from every defilement and the most perfect and undefiled purity.

Kingship is the distribution of every end, adornment, law, and order.

Lordship is not merely superiority over subjects, but also the most perfect and complete possession of all good and excellent things, together with true and unchangeable firmness. Hence come *dominus* (“lord”), *dominabile* (“subject to lordship”), and *dominari* (“to exercise lordship”).

Deity is the perfect providence and goodness that considers all things, surveys and contains all things, and fills and surpasses all things that enjoy its providence.

All these things, then, are to be praised absolutely in the superexcellent cause. We must add that this cause is transcendent holiness, lordship, and kingship, and the superincumbent and most simple deity [Col. 1168C].

For from it, in unity and fullness, arises and is distributed every bright care of all sincere purity; the order and arrangement of all existing things, which removes incongruity, inequality, and immeasurability, shines forth in well-ordered likeness and rectitude, and leads those made worthy to participate in it; every perfection; the complete possession of every good; the most excellent contemplation and continuity of the things provided; and the divine addition of itself for the deification of those who desire it.

Since it is the superabundance of all things and the cause of all things, according to one excellence surpassing all things, it is praised as the Holy of Holies, and so forth, according to its overflowing cause and exalted transcendence [Col. 1168D] [Note: [Col. 1167] EH: *supermanentem*, “remaining above,” instead of *supermanantem*, “overflowing above”].

It is as though someone were to say: As much as holy, divine, lordly, and royal existing things surpass what does not exist, and as much as the things that participate in them surpass the participations themselves, so much does the one who is above all existing things transcend all existing things. He is the causal source of all participants and participations, participating in none of them [Col. 1169A].

The Scriptures call “holy ones,” “kings,” “lords,” and “gods” those principal dispositions within individual things through which secondary realities, receiving gifts from God, multiply the simplicity of their distribution in accordance with their own differences, and through which they gather their outstanding variety providentially and divinely into the unity that belongs to them.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Perfect and the One

So much, then, concerning these matters. But, if it seems good, let us place here the most forceful remaining point in our discourse. For theology predicates of the cause of all things both “all things” and “all things together,” and praises it as both the Perfect alone and the One [Col. 1169B].

It is Perfect not only as perfect in itself, uniformly separated from itself according to itself, and wholly perfect throughout the whole, but also as more than perfect: surpassing all things, bringing every multiplicity to an end, extending beyond every summit, and located or comprehended by nothing, but stretched out over all things and above all things through inexhaustible increases and infinite activities.

It is again called Perfect as though it had not been increased, as always perfect and undiminished, since it surpasses and overflows all things in itself according to one uninterrupted and identical generosity, full in itself above all things and not diminished [Note: [Col. 1169] The manuscripts omit “and identical”]. Through this generosity it perfects all perfect things and fills them with their proper perfection [Col. 1169C].

It is called One because it is universally all things through the excellence of one unity and is the irreversible cause both of all things and of the One. For there is no existing thing that does not participate in the One. Just as every number, taken together, participates in the monad [Note: [Col. 1169] E reads *monada*, “monad,” instead of *monade*, “in the monad”], and one is called two and ten, and a half is called one, and a third and a tenth are called one, so all things and every part of all things participate in the One [Note: [Col. 1169] BH: *participat*, “participates,” instead of *participant*, “participate”]. In being one, all things are existing things.

The One is not the cause of all things as one among many ones. Rather, it precedes every one and every multiplicity, and brings every one and multiplicity to an end [Note: [Col. 1169] The manuscripts omit “and every one and multiplicity”].

For there is no multiplicity that does not participate in something one: in one case, many parts are one whole; in another, many accidents are one subject; in another, many numbers or powers are one species; in another, many species are one genus; in another, many processions are one principle. There is nothing among existing things that does not participate in some aspect of unity—whether it be the One that contains all things below, all things individually, all things as wholes, and universally all opposites [Col. 1169D].

Without the One, multiplicity will not exist; without multiplicity, the One will exist. Thus the monad precedes every multiplied number. And if someone were to posit all things as united with all things, all things would be one whole.

This too must be understood [Col. 1170A]: according to the One, the form of each thing is conceived beforehand. What is united is called “one”; the One is the pattern of all things. If the One is taken away, neither the universe, nor a part, nor anything else among existing things will exist [Note: [Col. 1169] The manuscripts omit “nor a part”]. For the One uniformly precedes and encompasses all things in itself.

Accordingly, theology praises the entire divine source, as the cause of all things, with the name “One”: one God the Father, one Lord Jesus Christ, and one Spirit, through the superexcellent indivisibility of the whole divine unity, in which all things are joined individually, super-united, and present superessentially.

Accordingly, all things are rightly referred and attributed to it, under which, from which, through which, in which, and toward which all things are, are ordered, remain, are contained, are filled, and are converted [Col. 1170B]. You will find no existing thing that is not in the One, according to which the whole deity is named superessentially and which is what it truly is, perfecting and preserving all things.

Therefore we must, having been turned from the many toward the One by the power of divine unity, praise in unity the whole and single deity, the cause of all things: the One that is before every one and multiplicity, before part and whole and definition [Note: [Col. 1169] The manuscripts omit “and whole and definition”], before the infinite, the summit, and the limit [Note: [Col. 1169] The manuscripts omit “and the limit”]; the One that bounds magnitude, all existing things, and being itself; that is the cause both of all things and of all things universally, together and before all things, above all things and individually; that is the cause above the one being (*on*, ὄν), and that bounds the one being, since the one being is innumerable among existing things.

Number, however, participates in essence [Col. 1170C]. The superessential One, the one being, bounds every number, and itself is from the One the beginning and cause of every existing number, as well as number and order.

Therefore unity and Trinity are praised as the deity above all things. Neither unity nor Trinity is known by us or by any other existing thing. Yet, even if we truly praise its super-unified divine fecundity by the divine names “triad” and “monad,” we name the superessential One as more than nameable within essences.

Neither a monad nor Trinity, neither number nor unity nor fecundity, nor anything else among existing things or known to any existing thing, can lead to the hiddenness of the superessentially superessential superdivinity, which is beyond all things, word, and intellect [Col. 1170D]. It has neither name nor word, but is exalted in inaccessible places.

Nor do we utter “that which is of goodness” as though we were uniting some name to it. Rather, in our desire to understand and say something concerning that ineffable nature, we first devote to it the most precious of names. Perhaps in this we shall agree with the theologians, although we shall fall short of the truth of things.

For this reason, they too, by negations concerning what is inaccessible, honored it beforehand, as the soul exceeds its own kindred realities and proceeds through all the divine intelligences [Col. 1171A]. Through these, what is above every name, every word, and every knowledge is removed, and the soul reaches the very last of all things, insofar as it is possible for us to reach that reality.

We have repeated these intellectual divine names in agreement, insofar as permitted—not because we have failed in our care for them—for this, indeed, the angels themselves would say—nor in accordance with the angels because of their hymns.

For even the most powerful theologians among us are left for the last. Nor are they placed after those theologians, philosophers, or followers of a doctrine, but even those who have been ordered and subjected to us in the same way are placed last and beneath them.

Therefore, if what has been said is correct, and if, so far as lies within our power, we have truly touched upon the power of God through the repetition of these words, then the act must be referred to the causal source of all good things, which grants us first to speak and then to speak well [Col. 1171B].

And if some similar divine powers have been omitted, may we also, according to the same methods, become obedient to the request.

But if these things are either incorrect or incomplete [Col. 1172A], and if we have strayed from the truth either universally or in particular, then it belongs to your humanity to correct one who is ignorant without intending to be so; to teach through your word one who begs to learn; to support one who lacks sufficient strength; to heal one who does not wish to remain sick; to find some things by yourself and others through other people, while receiving everything from God; and to transmit it to us.

Would you afflict a friend by doing good? For you see that we have neither appropriated to ourselves any of the hierarchical words handed down to us, nor have we withheld them, but we have communicated and will communicate them to you and to other divine men who are concerned with us. Thus we are enabled to speak, and those to whom they are spoken are enabled to hear, without suffering any injury to the tradition, even if we should be weakened in our understanding or exposition of it.

But concerning these matters, I ask you, friend of God, to hold and maintain this view. And now, with the divine names understood, let this be the conclusion, according to our ability, since, with God as our guide, we shall pass beyond symbolic theology.

*The Book on the Divine Names ends* [Note: [Col. 1171C] E adds: “The Book of Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Athens, addressed to Timothy, bishop of the Ephesians, on the Divine Names. Irrigating your mind, Dionysius, with the streams of Paul, desiring the whole ray of the eternal splendor of the Deity, you acquired the unfailing brightness of the naming of the names of God.”]

# THE FOURTH BOOK OF SAINT DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE, ON MYSTICAL THEOLOGY

[Col. 1171]

[Col. 1171B] Epigram on blessed Dionysius, concerning mystical theology

A new brightness in the remaining matters and knowledge of subsisting things [Note: [Col. 1171] H reads “the knowledge of sufficient things”; E adds in illuminated letters: “Or otherwise: And you penetrated a radiant understanding and the knowledge of existing things”], a night through the divine reality that it is not lawful to name [Note: [Col. 1171] E adds in illuminated letters: “Or otherwise: A night through the divine reality that it is not lawful to name.”]

To the fellow presbyter Timothy: Dionysius, presbyter.

# THE CHAPTERS OF MYSTICAL THEOLOGY BEGIN

[Col. 1172B]

I. On mystical theology.  
II. How one must be united and offer hymns to the cause of all things and to what is above all things.  
III. Which are the affirmative theologies and which are the negative theologies.  
IV. That the cause of all sensible things is not any sensible thing, but is above all sensible things.  
V. That the cause of all intelligible things is not any intelligible thing, but is above all intelligible things.

[Note: [Col. 1171C] Codex B begins as follows: “The book on mystical theology begins”; the chapters follow, after which the epigram is placed. E begins: “These chapters contain the discourse on mystical theology”; the chapters and epigram follow. H has: “The chapters of the same work on mystical theology begin”; the chapters and epigram follow.]

[Col. 1171] THE BOOK ON MYSTICAL THEOLOGY BEGINS

## CHAPTER I. On mystical theology

[Note: [Col. 1171] “On mystical theology” is omitted by the manuscripts and has been added from the preceding table of contents.]

[Col. 1171C]

Superessential Trinity, more-than-divine and superlatively good, overseer of Christian theosophy, direct us toward the super-unknown, super-luminous, and most sublime summit of the mystical Scriptures [Col. 1172C], where the new, absolute, and unchangeable mysteries of theology are hidden according to the super-luminous darkness of the silence that teaches secretly; a darkness shining above all manifestation, in which everything shines forth and which fills invisible intellects with the splendors of invisible and super-good realities [Col. 1173A].

This is what I ask for myself. But you, dear Timothy, strengthen your journey around mystical contemplations, abandon the senses and intellectual operations, sensible and invisible things, every non-being and being, and restore yourself, as far as possible, unknowingly to unity with him who is above every essence and knowledge.

For through a pure excess of mind, immeasurable and absolute, you will ascend beyond yourself and all things to the superessential ray of the divine darkness, abandoning all things and released from all things.

But take care that no one uninitiated listens to these things. By the uninitiated I mean those formed according to existing things and imagining that nothing exists superessentially above beings [Note: [Col. 1173] BE reads “above” instead of “beyond”].

To such people, those who must see what knowledge is according to itself should say that the darkness is the hiding place of the divine.

But if divine introductions into the mysteries transcend these people, what could one say about others who are still more ardent—those who characterize the cause placed above all things from the last of existing realities and say that nothing surpasses it beyond the impious and multiform forms they have fashioned?

We must place and affirm in it all the affirmations concerning existing things, as the cause of all things, but we must deny all of them more powerfully, since it exists above all things. We must not suppose that the opposite negations contradict the affirmations, but rather that the cause itself is prior to privations, being above every removal and affirmation [Note: [Col. 1173] BH reads *esse*, “to be,” instead of *est*, “which is”].

Thus the divine Bartholomew says that theology is both abundant and minimal, the Gospel broad and great, and again compressed.

It seems to me that he understood this supernaturally: the cause of all things is both richly expressed and concise, both without word and without understanding, because it is superessentially above all things. It is manifest without concealment only to those who pass beyond all that is polluted and impure, who surpass every ascent to the summit of all holy heights, who transcend all divine lights, sounds, and heavenly words, and who descend into the darkness where, as the Scriptures say, the summit of all things truly is.

For it was not without reason that the divine Moses was first commanded to be purified, then separated from those who were not purified in this way. After every purification he hears the many-voiced trumpets and sees the many lights [Col. 1173D] flashing openly and the widely diffused rays.

Then, after being separated from the many, he hastens with the chosen priests to the summit of the divine ascents. Yet, while they remain below, he becomes united to God and contemplates—not God himself, for he is invisible—but the place where he stood.

I believe that this signifies that the most divine and sublime realities among visible and intelligible things are certain hypothetical statements, subject to the One who surpasses all things. Through them his presence is shown as beyond every understanding, surpassing the intelligible heights of his most holy places [Col. 1174A].

And, released from visible things and those who see, he enters the truly mystical darkness of ignorance, through which he closes off every cognitive apprehension. In it everything shines, and everything that is at the summit of all things is invisibly [uncertain: “born”] and wholly unknown to every knowledge—neither to itself nor to another—resting in understanding by what is better and knowing nothing knowable beyond mind in this manner [Note: [Col. 1173] E reads “nothing is to be known in this manner.”]

## CHAPTER II. How one must be united and offer hymns to the cause of all things and to what is above all things

We pray that we may enter this super-luminous darkness and, through invisibility and unknowing, see and know him who is above God and knowledge [Col. 1174B].

Not seeing and not knowing this is truly seeing and knowing it: praising the superessential One superessentially through the removal of all existing things. It is like those who fashion a statue from its natural material and, by removing what has been added to it, reveal through the pure vision of concealment the form itself, which was hidden by those additions [Note: [Col. 1173] BH reads “the pure vision,” instead of “pure vision”].

It seems to me that we must praise the negations in opposition to the affirmations. Beginning with the most exalted realities, we descend through the intermediates to the lowest. Here, however, we ascend from the lowest toward the most principal realities and remove everything, so that we may know without concealment that unknowing which is veiled by all things unknown within existing things [Note: [Col. 1173] H reads “surrounded” instead of “veiled”], and see that superessential darkness which is hidden by all the light within existing things [Col. 1174C].

## CHAPTER III. Which are the affirmative theologies and which are the negative theologies

In the theological writings, then, we praised the most powerful affirmations of affirmative theology: how the divine and good nature is called one [Note: [Col. 1173] BH omits “is called one”]; how it is triadic; what the terms “paternity” and “sonship,” spoken according to it, intend to declare; how the lights that have germinated from the immaterial and indivisible Good in the heart of goodness have preserved the return to their coeternal dwelling in their germination—in him, in themselves, and among one another; how Jesus, who is superessential, became an essence through human natural realities [Col. 1174D]; and whatever else the Scriptures have expressed according to the theological writings.

In the work on the Divine Names, we discussed how the Good is named, how he is *being* (ὤν), how he is life, wisdom, power, and whatever other divine names are intelligible.

In the Symbolic Theology, we discussed the transference of names from sensible things to divine realities: the divine forms, divine figures, parts, and organs; divine places and worlds; rages, griefs, and madnesses; drunkennesses and excesses of drink; oaths and curses; sleep and wakefulness; and whatever other formations of divine likeness are symbolically and sacredly figured [Col. 1175A].

You have also, I think, observed how the later writings are more expansive in words than the earlier ones. For the theological writings and the exposition of the divine names are shorter in words than the Symbolic Theology.

The more we look toward the higher realities, the more words are contracted in contemplation of invisible things. Thus, now that we are descending into the darkness that is above intellect, we shall find not a short discourse [Note: [Col. 1175] BH omits “discourse”], but the failure of discourse and of naming.

There, discourse descends from above toward the lowest realities and is found to be proportionate to the multiplicity that universally corresponds to them [Col. 1175B]. Here, however, as it ascends from what is below toward what is above, it is shortened according to the measure of what is inaccessible. After everything inaccessible, it will be wholly without voice and will be entirely united with what lacks sound.

“But why,” you ask, “do we begin the divine negation with the lowest realities, since we place the divine affirmations among the most exalted?”

Because when we make an affirmation concerning what is beyond every affirmation, we ought to begin with what is more closely related to it; but when we remove what is beyond every negation, we ought to begin by removing what is more distant from it.

Is life and goodness not more than air and stone? And are “not drunkennesses” and “not madnesses” not more than that which can neither be said nor understood?

## CHAPTER IV. That the cause of all sensible things is not any sensible thing, but is above all sensible things

[Col. 1175C]

Let us say, then, as follows: The cause of all things, and the being above all things, is neither without essence, nor without life; it is not irrational, nor without sensation; it is not a body, nor a figure, nor a form; it possesses neither quality nor quantity nor bulk; it is not in a place; it is not seen; it does not have sensible contact; it is not perceived by the senses and is not sensible; it does not possess disorder [Col. 1176A]; it is not disturbed by material passions; it is not powerless, as though it succumbed to sensible accidents; it does not lack light; it does not undergo change, corruption, division, deprivation, or flux; nor is it any other sensible thing, nor does it possess any such thing.

## CHAPTER V. That the cause of all intelligible things is not any intelligible thing, but is above all intelligible things
Again, ascending, let us say that it is neither a soul nor intellect; it possesses neither imagination, opinion, word, nor understanding [Note: [Col. 1175] The readings are *phantasia*—*opinio*—*intelligentia*.]; it is neither reason nor understanding [Note: [Col. 1175] BH omits *habet—intelligentia*.]; it is neither spoken nor understood; it is neither number nor order, neither greatness nor smallness, neither equality nor similarity or dissimilarity; it neither stands nor moves; it keeps no silence; it possesses no power, nor is it power; it is neither light nor life, neither sacrifice nor age nor time; it has no intelligible touch; it is neither knowledge nor truth, neither kingship nor wisdom, neither one nor unity, neither divinity [Note: [Col. 1175] BH omits *neque deitas*.] nor goodness; it is not spirit in the sense in which we know spirit; it is neither sonship nor fatherhood, nor anything else known to us or to any existing being, nor anything belonging to non-existing things, nor anything belonging to existing things. Existing things do not know it—whether it is; nor does it know existing things—whether they exist [Note: [Col. 1175] Thus A; BH reads: “whether they know it, or whether it is an existing thing, nor the Word, etc.”; E reads: “whether they know it, or whether they are existing things, it is, nor the Word, etc.”]. Neither is there a word for it, nor a name, nor knowledge [Note: [Col. 1175] BH omits “nor knowledge”.], neither is it darkness nor light, neither error nor truth. There is no affirmation of it whatsoever, nor negation; rather, by making affirmations and negations concerning what comes after it, we neither remove nor posit it, since it is the perfect and unique cause of all things, beyond every affirmation through its supereminence, and beyond every negation through the excellence of its perfection in all things [Note: [Col. 1175] BH reads “excellence” instead of “excellent”; “perfection” instead of “perfection in all things”], and the summit of all things.

*The book On Mystical Theology ends here* [Note: [Col. 1175D] “Here ends the book of Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Athens, On Mystical Theology. Having entered into the brightest darkness [Col. 1176D], in which the principle of twofold wisdom is fostered, you make manifest the measures of theology.”].

# The Various Letters of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite

[Col. 1175]

I. To Gaius the monk.  
II. To the same.  
III. To the same.  
IV. To the same.  
V. To Dorotheus the minister.  
VI. To Sosipater the priest.  
VII. To Polycarp the high priest.  
[Col. 1176D] VIII. To Demophilus the monk, on his own gentleness and goodness.  
IX. To Pytho the high priest, who asks by letter what the house of wisdom is, what its cup is, and what its food and drink are.  
X. To John the theologian, apostle, and evangelist, confined on the island of Patmos [Note: [Col. 1175] E reads *Pathmon*.].

# The Various Letters of Saint Dionysius Begin [Note: [Col. 1177] E omits “The various letters of Dionysius”; B places it before the index of the letters.]

## I. Letter of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, sent to Gaius the monk

[Col. 1177A]

Darkness is obscured by light, and even more by abundant light. Ignorance is concealed by knowledge, and even more by abundant knowledge. Accept these statements in a supereminent sense, but not according to privation; affirm them in a truly transcendent sense, because the light of being, ὂν, is hidden from those who possess it, and the ignorance that is truly knowledge according to God—and the darkness set above it—is veiled by every light and hides all knowledge.

And if someone, seeing God, understood what he saw, he did not contemplate God himself, but one of the things that exist and are known through him. He himself, placed beyond mind and essence, is entirely unknown and unseen; yet he exists superessentially, and is known beyond the mind. Indeed, the most perfect ignorance itself, insofar as it is the better way, is knowledge of him beyond all known things.

## II. To the same

How is the summit of all things also beyond divinity and beyond goodness? If by divinity and goodness you understand the very reality of the beneficial and deifying gift, and not that which is beyond God and beyond the Good and which cannot be imitated, according to which we are deified and made good, then the answer is this:

For if this is the principle of deification, and if those who have been deified and made good are treated in the best manner, then the summit of every super-principle, and of so-called divinity and goodness, insofar as it is the summit of divinity and goodness, surpasses imitation and participation, as well as those who imitate and participate, by the extent to which it is inimitable and immeasurable.

## III. To the same

What comes from concealment is that which, contrary to expectation, has been led from what is obscure into manifestation. But, according to the humanity of Christ—and I think theology makes this clear—the superessential one came forth from concealment, having become human in essence for our manifestation.

He is concealed even after the manifestation—or, to say this in a more divine manner, he is concealed in the manifestation itself. For this mystery is also hidden in Jesus, and cannot be investigated according to itself by any word or understanding; rather, what has been spoken remains ineffable, and what has been understood remains unknown.

## IV. To the same

[Col. 1177D]

“How,” you ask, “is Jesus, who is beyond all things, essentially ranked among all human beings?”

He is not called human here as the cause of human beings, but as one who truly is human according to the whole of his essence. We do not separate Jesus from humanity. For he is not merely human, nor merely a superessential human being; rather, he is truly human, human in a distinctive way, beyond human beings and according to human beings, coming from human beings and having been made essentially superessential.

Yet he remains no less always the fullness of superessentiality, superessential. Thus, coming in such greatness truly into essence and having been made essential beyond essence, he performs what belongs to human beings beyond humanity [Note: [Col. 1177D] John 1; Luke 2.].

The virgin, giving birth in a supernatural manner, makes this clear; so too does the unstable water, which supported the weight of material and earthly feet—not in appearance, but established by supernatural power in an indissoluble state. What if someone were to pass over the many other existing things through which, seeing divinely, he would know what is beyond the mind, and would recognize in the humanity of Jesus intentions possessing the power of a transcendent casting-away?

To summarize: he was not a human being in the sense of being not human, but, as one beyond human beings and beyond the humanity of human beings, he became truly human beyond humanity. Moreover, he did not perform divine things according to God, nor human things according to a human being; rather, God having become human, he lived among us in a new kind of divine-human activity.

## V. To Dorotheus the minister

[Col. 1178C]

The divine darkness is the inaccessible light in which God is said to dwell, while remaining invisible because of its supereminent [Note: [Col. 1177] E reads “eminent”.] brilliance, and inaccessible because of the superessential outpouring of lights that surpasses all excellence.

In this darkness everyone worthy of knowing and seeing God comes to know and see him—not by seeing or knowing him, but by becoming, in truth, one who is beyond vision and knowledge, and by knowing precisely this: that he is beyond all sensible and intelligible things.

The prophet, seeing this, says: “Your knowledge has become wondrous beyond me; it has been strengthened, and I cannot attain it” [Note: [Col. 1177D] Psalm 138:6.].

Thus the divine Paul is said to have known God, knowing him as beyond every existing intellect and knowledge [Note: [Col. 1177] Some manuscripts omit “and knowledge”.] [Note: [Col. 1178D] Romans 11:33.]. For this reason he also says that God’s ways are unsearchable, his judgments inscrutable, and his gifts indescribable [Note: [Col. 1178D] Philippians 4:7.], and that his peace surpasses every understanding [Col. 1178D]. In this way he finds him beyond all things and, by knowing this beyond understanding, recognizes that he is beyond all things, existing as the cause of all things.

## VI. To Sosipater the priest

[Col. 1179A]

Do not consider it a victory, holy Sosipater, to inflict an injury upon a religion or glory that is excellent and manifest. For it is not fitting that you should refute it once it has been judged—now, Sosipater, [the reading concerning “good things” is uncertain].

It is possible for you and for many others to be deceived by what is false and apparent concerning the one existent thing, ὄν, and the hidden truth. For if something is not red, it is not necessarily white; nor, if someone is not a horse, is he necessarily a human being.

Act in this way, trusting me: allow this matter to be discussed according to the views of others, but speak truly for the sake of truth itself. In this way you will show that what has been said is irreproachable in every respect.

## VII. To Polycarp the high priest

[Col. 1179B]

I, for my part, do not know, speaking to Greeks or to others, whether I judge it sufficient for excellent men if they can know and say the truth from itself and in itself, as it truly is.

For once whatever accords with the law of truth has been rightly demonstrated and stands pure, everything that differs from it and nevertheless pursues the truth is refuted as something other than what truly is—dissimilar and merely a matter of opinion rather than being, ὄν.

It is therefore superfluous for the one who manifests the truth to fight against these people or those. Each person claims to possess a royal coin, and each does indeed possess a certain shadow of something pure, though that shadow is truly deceptive. If you refute one person, another and then another will contend over the same matter.

But when the same truth has been correctly established by reason and selected from among all others, everything that does not possess it in every respect is driven out from itself by an irreproachable state [Col. 1179C] of what is truly true.

Recognizing this well, as I think, I did not hasten to speak to Greeks or to others. May God grant me this much: first to know the truth, and then, once I know it, to speak as I ought.

But when you ask why I curse the sophist Apollophanes, recalling the paternal judgment, as though he were using the Greeks against the Greeks in an unholy manner, it would have been more truthful for us to say to him how the Greeks use divine things unholily in divine matters, attempting through the wisdom of God to drive out divine worship.

Thus, indeed, I speak of the great glory of certain poets who remain material and subject to passion, and serve the creature against the Creator.

Apollophanes himself also uses divine things unholily in divine matters. For that knowledge of existing things which is rightly named philosophy by him and called by the divine Paul “the wisdom of God” [Note: [Col. 1179D] 1 Corinthians 2.], ought to have led true philosophers back to the cause of the existing things themselves and of their knowledge.

And so that he may not refute the opinion of others—or his own opinion—beyond what should be thought, one must consider that Apollophanes, being wise, could not at some time have transcended the heavenly order and movement unless he had possessed as the cause moving, making, and transforming all things, according to the sacred word [Note: [Col. 1179D] Daniel 2.], the very one who is being itself, truly eminent and causative.

How, then, does he not worship the one unknown to us, and thereby truly existing and truly God, recognizing him through the most causative and superineffable power, when the sun and moon, arriving together and standing still according to a supernatural power and state for the whole universe, are defined by him as altogether immovable, and when everything in them remains in the same signs for the measure of an entire day [Note: [Col. 1179D] Joshua 10.]?

Or, to go still further, when, although all things—including those that are better and those that contain others—were thus carried along, the contained things were not carried around with them [Note: [Col. 1179] BH omits “and those that contain others”.]?

And when, on another day, the day is almost tripled in duration, and what ordinarily occurs in twenty hours takes place, so that the sun does not return and retrace its path at the usual time but, through highly supernatural reversals, coils its fivefold movement along its own course in ten hours [Note: [Col. 1179] Thus A; E reads “uncoiling”.], and then analytically retraces the whole course in the other ten hours by a new kind of backward path [Note: [Col. 1179] BH omits “coils ... in the other ten hours”.]?

This rightly bent the Babylonians and subdued them without a struggle to Hezekiah, as though to a god equal to and surpassing human beings.

Nor am I speaking here of the great works performed in Egypt, or of certain other divine signs performed elsewhere, but of events that are common and heavenly, triumphing throughout the universe and over all things [Note: [Col. 1179D] 2 Kings 20; 2 Chronicles 32; Isaiah 38; Exodus 7–12.] [Col. 1180D].

Yet Apollophanes says that these things are not true. Indeed, this account is recorded even more strongly in the priestly memories of the Persians, and the Magi still perform the triple rites of Mithra as things worthy of remembrance.

But let him be permitted to say these things because of ignorance or great disbelief.

Say to him: “What do you say about the eclipse itself that occurred at the saving cross?” [Note: [Col. 1180D] Matthew 27; Mark 15; Luke 23.] For at that time we both arrived together near the city of the sun and stood there, and we saw, wondrously, the moon fall upon the sun—not at the time of conjunction. Then again we saw it, from the ninth hour until evening, stand supernaturally opposite the sun’s diameter.

Remind him of yet another matter. For he knows that we saw the setting itself beginning from the eastern regions and advancing as far as the summit of the sun; then it moved backward, and again neither the setting nor the clearing occurred from the same direction, but took place in the opposite direction across the diameter.

Such were the supernatural events at that time, performed by Christ alone through his most causative power—great and extensive events, whose number cannot be counted [Note: [Col. 1180D] Job 5.].

If you think it just and possible, refute Apollophanes on these matters, and then come to me, as one suitable to you, observing with me, investigating everything, and comparing it all. He also neglects the divination of that time—I do not know why.

Afterward Apollophanes departed, and, reporting to me what had happened, said: “These, O good Dionysius, are the reversals of divine things.”

So much have we said by letter. But you are capable of supplying what is lacking, of bringing to God perfectly a man who is very wise and, in truth, not resentful but gently willing to learn the supremely wise truth of our religion.

## VIII. To Demophilus the attendant [Note: [Col. 1181] The index reads “to the monk.”], on his own gentleness and goodness.

The history of the Hebrews says, O Demophile, my son, that holy Moses was made worthy of divine friendship through great gentleness. And even if they sometimes write that he was outside the divine countenance [Note: [Col. 1181] E: “worship”], they do not nevertheless expel him from his original gentleness. They say, indeed, that when he was exceedingly arrogant and resisting the divine counsels, the Lord was angry in fury [Col. 1181B] [Note: [Col. 1181D] Numbers XI, XII]. Yet when they make him a preacher worthy of the divine judgments, he is praised for his previously possessed imitation of the Good. For he was exceedingly gentle, and for this reason he is called the servant of God and, in the divine vision, more worthy than all the prophets together [Note: [Col. 1181D] Numbers XII; Joshua I; Numbers XVI].

Certain men from the chief priesthood and the leadership of the people also contended against him and Aaron, surpassing them in every way through the love of honor and the love of power; and Moses received from God, the judge, the preeminence over the people. When they had set themselves against him, reproached him for his former deeds, and threatened him—and had almost prevailed—he, being gentle, cried out to God for salvation. He trusted greatly in his profound humility, since he was blameless in all the evils they had begun. For he understood that one who converses with the supremely good God ought, so far as possible, to be conformed by this preeminent likeness, and to possess within himself works beloved by God [Col. 1181C].

But what made David, the father of God, God’s friend? He was supremely good, and supremely good even toward his enemy. “I have found,” he says, “a supremely good man, a most excellent friend, a man after my own heart.” The best law, moreover, was given: to provide for those who have been subjected to the enemy. Job also was justified as one who had no wickedness. Joseph did not avenge himself on his brothers when they surpassed him. Abel approached his fratricidal brother simply and without suspicion. And all theology proclaims that the godlike are those who neither understand nor commit evil beforehand [Note: [Col. 1181D] 1 Samuel XXIV, XXVI; 1 Kings XIII; Psalm LXXXVIII; Exodus XXIII; Genesis XXVIII, XLII, XLIII, LXIV], but who are not turned away from the Good in the opposite direction by the wickedness of others; rather, in a godlike manner, they do good to the wicked, pour out abundant goodness upon them, and gently summon them to likeness.

But let us look higher, proclaiming not merely the uprightness of holy men or the goodness of human angels: those who propitiate the nations, entreat God on their behalf, threaten the multitudes who are lost and act wickedly, grieve over their evils yet rejoice in the salvation of those who have been summoned to the Good, and all the other things that theology hands down concerning beneficent angels. We are also clearly led by the beneficent rays of the truly good and supremely good Christ, receiving them in silence, toward his own divine and good works.

For is it not the work of the most powerful goodness, surpassing understanding, to make existing things exist; to bring all these things into being; and always to will that they draw near to him and share in what belongs to him, according to the proper opportunity of each? And what of the fact that he lovingly receives those who return, contends for them and longs for them without resenting their love and delight; that he tolerates those who accuse him in vain and himself defends them, promising rather to care for them; that, when they approach in this perfected condition, he runs to meet them, welcomes them, embraces them all, and does not accuse them of their former deeds, but loves the one who has come, celebrates a feast, and summons his friends—that is, the good—so that the dwelling may be filled with the joy of all [Note: [Col. 1182D] Luke XV]?

Demophile, and anyone else hostile to the Good, is very justly rebuked, taught what is good, and improved [Note: [Col. 1181] Thus A; BH: “he rebukes, teaches what is good, and improves”; E: “he rebukes, teaches what is good, and is improved”]. For how, I ask, should the Good not rejoice in the salvation of the lost and in the life of the dead? Thus he lifts upon his shoulders those whom he scarcely turns back from error, arouses the good angels to joy, is good even toward the ungrateful, makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and lays down his own soul for those who flee to him for refuge [Note: [Col. 1182D] The same passage; Matthew V; Luke VI; John X].

But you, as your letter makes clear, when—as you say—the impious and wicked man fell before the priest, somehow kicked against him while present. Then, as was necessary, he confessed that he had come for the healing of his evils. You, however, were not horrified; instead, with ferocity you attacked the good priest for having shown pity to the penitent and justified the impious man. And finally you said: “Go to the priest with those like you.” You sprang upon the sacred places, though you were not righteous, and barred the inner sanctuary and the Holy of Holies; and you write to us that, foreseeing that he would corrupt the sacred things, you saved them and still guard them undefiled.

Now therefore listen to what we say. A priest is to be corrected by servants ministering under him, or by servants of equal authority—even if he appears to act impiously concerning divine things, and even if he is accused of doing something else that is forbidden. For if, because the most divine things are unadorned and inconsistent, you expel them from their boundaries and laws, you have no rational basis for overturning, in God’s name, the order handed down by God [Col. 1182D]. For God is not divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? And if judgment belongs to God, as the sacred words say [Note: [Col. 1182D] Matthew X; Luke XIII; Isaiah XXX; Malachi II], while priests are angels and prophets of the divine judgments after the chief priests, learn from them, through the intermediate ministers, what is fitting for you at the proper time—through those by whom you were also made worthy to become a servant.

Or do the sacred symbols not cry out the same thing? For the Holy of Holies is not simply elevated for everyone. Rather, those who are closer to it in sacred perfection approach it more closely; next comes the arrangement of the priests; after them, the arrangement of those who minister; and after the ordered servants, the doors of such places are set apart. They are perfected and stand there not merely to guard those doors, but also for their own order and knowledge, approaching the people more closely than the priests do. From there the chief priestly sacred order places them among the divine things to receive them in sacred service, entrusting the giving of these things to others—that is, to those within.

For those who continually stand symbolically around the divine altar love and clearly hear the divine things revealed to them. As they proceed in a godlike manner, they manifest to the subordinate servants, to the sacred people, and to the purified orders the things outside the divine veils, according to their worthiness, the sacred things having been well and undefiledly preserved. Yet you, tyrannically leaping upon them, compelled the unwilling Holy of Holies to triumph for you, and you claim that you possess and guard the sacred things.

Indeed, you have neither seen nor heard nor possess anything that pertains to priests, just as you have not learned the truth of the sacred words, though every day you fight against these things by your speech and overthrow your hearers. If someone obtained leadership over a people and irregularly set himself against the king, he was justly punished. And if someone standing under an appointed ruler dared to rebuke that ruler for justifying or condemning certain persons—not yet do I speak of attacking him—and to expel him from his leadership at the same time, would you, such a daring man, act in this way against the gentle and good man and against his hierarchical legislation?

These things ought to have been said even when someone, attempting what exceeded his dignity, nevertheless appeared to act appropriately. For this too is permitted to no one. What irregular thing was Uzziah doing when he burned incense to God? What was Saul doing when he sacrificed? Or what were the tyrannical demons doing when they truly theologized about Jesus? Yet every outsider was forbidden to exercise theology; each person was to remain in the order of his ministry; and only the chief priest entered the Holy of Holies [Note: [Col. 1183D] 2 Kings XV; 2 Chronicles XXVI; 1 Samuel XIII; Mark I, III; Nehemiah XIII; Hebrews IX; Leviticus I–VI], and that only once a year. This took place in every hierarchical purification prescribed by the law.

The priests surround the sacred things, while the Levites do not touch [Note: [Col. 1183] BH: “touch”] the sacred things, lest they die. The Lord was angry in fury over Uzziah’s arrogance, and Miriam was struck with leprosy when she attempted to impose a law upon the lawgiver; and demons leaped upon the sons of Sceva (Σκεῦα) [Note: [Col. 1183] BEH: “keyae”] [Col. 1183D]. “I did not send them,” he says, “yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.” And: “The impious man sacrifices a calf to me, like one who kills a dog.” In short, it must be said: perfect divine justice does not tolerate the wicked.

When they say, “In your name we performed many mighty works,” the answer is: “I do not know you; depart, all you workers of iniquity.” [Col. 1184A] Therefore, as the sacred words say, it is impious to pursue the sacred things beyond one’s dignity [Note: [Col. 1183D] Leviticus XVI; Hebrews IX; 2 Chronicles XXVI; Numbers XII; Acts XIX; Jeremiah XXIII; Ezekiel XIII; Isaiah LXVI; Matthew VII; Luke XIII]. Each person must attend to himself and not seek to know what is higher or deeper than he is; he must understand only what has been assigned to him according to his dignity.

“What then,” you say [Note: [Col. 1183] BE: “truly”], “should priests who act impiously, or who do something else irregular, not be reproved and corrected? Will it be permitted only to those who glory in the law, by transgressing the law, to dishonor God? How are priests manifesters of God? How do they announce the divine powers to the people without knowing their own power? How do those who are darkened illuminate others? How will they hand on divine spirits [Note: [Col. 1183] A: “they will hand on from the divine Spirit”] if they do not believe, by habit and in truth, that the Holy Spirit exists?”

I shall defend you in these matters, Demophile. For I am not your enemy, nor will I allow Satan to strike you. Every disposition directed toward God is more godlike in proportion as it is more distant [or: “more distinct”], and at the same time more illuminating and more illuminated; it is closer to the light, not by receiving it locally, but according to the most suitable proximity of the recipient to God.

If, therefore, the disposition of priests is illuminating, the one who is not an illuminator, or is not illuminated, has altogether fallen from the priestly order and virtue [Note: [Col. 1183] BH: “may fall”]. Such a man seems to me daring in his attempt upon the hierarchy: he neither fears nor is ashamed to pursue the divine things beyond his dignity. He supposes that God is ignorant of what God himself knows; he imagines that he can deceive the Father who called him, by a false voice; and he dares to offer his polluted blasphemies—I would not call them prayers—over the divine symbols in a Christlike manner.

He is not a priest—he is not—but an enemy, a deceiver, a mocker of himself, and a wolf against the divine flock, armed with a sheep’s skin.

But it is not right for Demophile to correct these things. Theology does not unjustly command us to pursue justifications [Note: [Col. 1184D] Deuteronomy XVI]. It is just to pursue distribution when someone wishes to distribute to each according to his dignity; this must justly be pursued by all, but not beyond their dignity. For it is also just that what is distributed to angels should be distributed according to their dignity [Note: [Col. 1183] ABH; E: “that what is distributed and separated should be distributed and separated according to dignity”].

Nevertheless, this distribution does not come from us, O Demophile, but from God through those above us, and through the already superior angels to those above them. In short, in all existing things, the first distribute to the second what is according to dignity, by the most orderly and just providence of all.

Those who have been ordered by God to give subsistence to others distribute what follows them to those who obey according to their dignity. Let Demophile therefore separate by word, anger, and desire whatever is according to dignity, so that he does not wrong his own order, but so that the word may rule from above those subject to it.

For if in a church we saw a servant treating his master, a younger man his elder, or even a son cursing his father while following him and inflicting blows upon him, we would think ourselves to be acting impiously unless we ran to help the superior party. Indeed, they would previously have acted justly. How then shall we not also be ashamed when, driven by anger and desire, we expel the word that has not been justified and the teaching given by God, and stir up within ourselves impiety, unjust disorder, sedition, and confusion?

Our blessed lawgiver, inspired by God, rightly does not deem a man worthy to preside over the church of God if he has not first presided well over his own household [Note: [Col. 1185D] 1 Timothy III]. For the one who orders himself orders another; the one who orders another orders a household; the one who orders a household orders a city; the one who orders a city orders a nation. In short, as the sacred words say, the one who is faithful in little is faithful also in much, and the one who is unfaithful in little is unfaithful also in much [Note: [Col. 1185D] Luke XVI].

Let him therefore separate from himself the desire, anger, and speech that are according to dignity. But divine ministers preside over you, priests over them, chief priests over the priests, and apostles and the successors of the apostles over the chief priests. If anyone in those ranks should err in something that he ought not to do, he will again be set right by holy men of equal authority. Order will not be overturned by order; each person will remain in his own order and administration.

So much from us concerning knowing and doing what belongs to you.

But concerning the inhumanity that, as you say, you have shown toward a man who is impious and sinful, I do not know how to lament the grief of my beloved. From whom do you suppose that servants are appointed by us? For if you are not in the Good, then, wherever we may need you to be, you are altogether alien to every ministry according to us. See that, through you, God himself is also seeking other priests, and that you are being cared for by them more than perfected, and that this is the customary inhumanity toward a gentle minister.

Have we perfected ourselves in the entirely holy, and do we no longer need the divine humanity that proceeds from itself? Or do we commit a double sin, as the sacred words say, sinning like the wicked, not knowing in what we offend, while also justifying ourselves and thinking that we see, though in truth we do not see? [Note: [Col. 1185D] Jeremiah IX; John IX.]

At this the heavens were terrified, and I was horrified, and I distrust myself. If I were not pursuing your letters, as though they ought to be properly understood, perhaps they would not have been reproved. Certain others considered it worthy to consult me about you, because Demophile thinks that God, who is good in all things, is not also humane, and that he himself does not need one who shows mercy or saves.

Priests too, by virtue of the goodness allotted to them, know well how to bear the ignorance of the people, because they themselves are encompassed by weakness. But the divine and holy Perfector came forth for those who were estranged; and therefore, as the sacred words say, he was separated from sinners [Note: [Col. 1185D] Hebrews V, VII], and in himself displays the most compassionate pastoral care of love toward the sheep [Note: [Col. 1185] BH: “in the most compassionate pastoral care”].

He calls evil the one who does not forgive his fellow servant’s debt and does not distribute to him individually from the abundant goodness granted to him. But the righteous enjoy what belongs to him.

These matters must make both me and Demophile fearful. For even toward those who act impiously against him, he brings about forgiveness from the Father by suffering in himself; and he warns his disciples because, in their lack of mercy, they judged it worthy to condemn the Samaritans who pursued him [Note: [Col. 1185D] 1 Peter II; John XII; Matthew XVIII; Luke XXIII].

Though this has been said so often, do not receive it with a fierce letter—for you rage up and down in it—as though you had vindicated not yourself but God. “Because of wickedness,” tell me, “the Good?” Cease. We do not have a chief priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who is without malice and is merciful. He will not contend or cry out; he himself is gentle, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins [Note: [Col. 1186D] Hebrews IV; Matthew XII; Isaiah XLII; Jeremiah II; Amos II; 1 John II].

Therefore we do not accept your unrestrained impulses, even if you repeatedly take Phinehas and Elijah as your models [Note: [Col. 1186D] Numbers XXXV; 1 Kings X]. When Jesus heard such things, his disciples—then gentle and participants in the best Spirit—did not approve them [Note: [Col. 1185] Thus the manuscripts; A: “not participants”].

For our most sacred and wondrous governor teaches, in gentleness, those who oppose the teaching of God. The ignorant must be taught, not punished; just as we do not crucify the blind, but lead them by the hand.

You, however, repel the man who is beginning to look toward the light, treating him as though he were a new child; and when he falls down in great confusion, you kick against him in your ferocity. Yet this is worthy of the highest honor: Christ, being supremely good upon the mountains, seeks out the straying sheep, calls the fugitive, and, having scarcely found it, lifts it upon his shoulders [Note: [Col. 1186D] Ezekiel XXXIV; Luke XV].

I ask, are we not thus deliberating wrongly against ourselves? Are we not hurling the weapon against ourselves? Those who unjustly do such things, or who attempt to do good in the opposite manner, do not always accomplish what they intend. But those who combine wickedness or goodness with themselves will be filled either with divine virtues or with long-lasting passions.

The former, followers and companions of the good angels, will here and hereafter, with complete consecration and freedom from every evil, obtain the most blessed rests throughout the everlasting ages, and will always be with God, which is the greatest of all good things [Note: [Col. 1185] AE: “obtaining”]. The latter will depart from the divine peace and from their own peace; here and after death alike they will be with the obscure demons.

Therefore we must have great concern that we come to be with the supremely good God, that we always be with the Lord, and that we not be separated from the wicked by a just judgment, enduring within ourselves what is according to our dignity. This I fear more than all things, and I pray not to be a participant in any evil.

If you wish, I shall also recall a holy man’s vision of God. You will not laugh, for I shall tell the truth.

Once, when I was near Crete, the holy Carpus introduced me—a man who, if anyone was, was exceedingly well suited to divine visions because of the great purity of his soul. Indeed, he did not attempt the holy sacrifices of the mysteries unless the sacred prayers, completed beforehand and made propitious, had first been manifested to him through a vision.

He said that on one occasion he had been grieved by certain unbelievers. His grief was this: one of them had led away from the Church a certain good man, even after the days of rejoicing had been completed. Both matters ought to have been divinely glorified above all: God the Savior, having seized and received one, had converted him, while having overcome the other by goodness; he should not have abandoned the one who had been admonished, but through his entire life, even to the present day, should have led both into divine knowledge, as though they had already been judged and condemned, and as though the irrational and savage men had been compelled to think according to the just law.

But because he did not first endure this within himself, I do not know how he then wove into it a certain great harshness and bitterness. He became ill and was in a bad state. It was evening. Around midnight—for at that time he was accustomed to awaken of his own accord for the divine praises—he rose, although he had slept little and was always disturbed by the agitation of those who offended outwardly. Standing for divine conversation, he was not properly restrained; he became indignant and said that it was not just for impious men who overturned the Lord’s straight ways to live [Note: [Col. 1187D] Acts XIII].

As he said these things, he asked God that a certain heavenly fire might pitilessly bring the lives of both to rest at once [Col. 1187C].

As he said this, he declared that he suddenly saw the house in which he was standing first shaken, then split in two from the roof down the middle. He saw before him a pyre of great light, and such a thing—for the place appeared to be beneath the open sky—descending from the heavenly region down to him. Heaven itself seemed to blaze again, and upon the back of heaven he saw Jesus, with many angels standing beside him in human form.

He said that he saw these things above and marveled. But when Carpus bent his gaze downward, he said: “I also saw the deep earth. Here was a chasm for punishment, dark and separated. The men whom I had accused stood before it, trembling, wretched, near the little entrance of the chasm; they had not yet descended, but remained unstable on their own feet.

“From the chasm below, serpents crawled up and settled around their feet. At times they dragged them back, wrapping themselves around them, weighing them down, and pulling them; at other times they swelled or raised themselves with their teeth or mouths, always contriving to thrust them into misery.

“There were also certain men in the midst of the serpents, shaking, overthrowing, and striking the men who had been placed above them. They appeared to be there for questioning: some unwillingly, others willingly, exercising force against the evil men after a short while and questioning them at the same time.”

Carpus said that he himself took pleasure in looking downward and neglected what was above; he was indignant and thought it a small matter that they had not already fallen, adding repeatedly to the punishment and being unable to grieve or grow weary.

When he looked up, he scarcely saw heaven again, as he had seen it before. But Jesus, moved with pity for what had happened, rose from his heavenly throne, descended even to them, and extended his good hand. The angels with him received other men from another place.

Jesus then said to Carpus: “Child, with your hand already raised, do the rest according to me” [the transmitted Latin is materially uncertain]. “For I am ready to suffer again for the salvation of human beings. And it is dear to me that other human beings should not sin.”

Nevertheless, see whether it would be good for you to exchange his dwelling in the chasm and with the serpents for the dwelling that is with God and with the good and humane angels [Note: [Col. 1187] AH: “communion”; B: “exchange”] [Note: [Col. 1187] “and human” omitted in BH].

These are the things which, having heard them, I believe to be true.

## IX. To Titus, the bishop [Note: [Col. 1187] Index: “To Titus the chief priest”], asking by letter what the house of wisdom is, what its mixing bowl is, and what its food and drink are.

Saint Timothy, good Titus, I do not know whether he has left behind some remnant of the theological symbols known to me. Yet in symbolic theology we have clearly distinguished that all the conceptions expressed in the divine Scriptures concerning God are, to many, monstrous. For, in the sequence of our discussion, whenever the fathers of the hidden wisdom reveal through certain secret and daring enigmas the divine, mystical, and inaccessible truth to the impure, we wipe away the contamination caused by the imperfections of souls. For this reason many do not believe the rational explanations of the divine mysteries. We contemplate them only together with the sensible symbols that are congenial to us. But we must also strip these away and see them in themselves, made naked and pure.

[Note: AE reads “would appear.”]

Thus, for those who contemplate, they would indeed disclose the fountain of life poured into itself and standing in itself: a single power, simple, moved by itself, working through itself, not abandoning itself, subsisting as the knowledge of all knowledges, and always contemplating through itself. We therefore judged that it was necessary, both for ourselves and for others among us, as far as possible, to unfold the variable deformities of God’s symbolic sacred representation.

For what lies outside this representation is filled with every kind of unbelievable and fictitious monstrosity: for example, in the superessential divine generation, it reshapes the belly of God as bodily giving birth to God, portrays the Word as poured into the air and belched forth from a masculine heart, describes the Spirit as breathed out from the mouth, and praises for us God’s fecund bosoms carrying the Son of God in their womb; or it represents such things in plant-like form, introducing certain trees, shrubs, flowers, and roots; or it represents fountains sending forth streams of water; or radiant, successive generations of light; or other sacred descriptive representations that manifest the superessential theological realities.

Then, concerning God’s invisible providences, gifts, manifestations, powers, properties, blows, dwellings, processions, distinctions, and unities, it surrounds God with a human fabrication and with varied forms of beasts, other animals, plants, and stones; it puts feminine ornaments or barbarian constructions of weapons around him; it adds pottery or metalworking, as though to some craftsman; it places horses, chariots, and thrones beneath him; it prepares for him daily foods, made into stews; and it transforms him into one who drinks, is drunk, sleeps, and is overcome with drunkenness.

What if someone were to speak of angers, griefs, various oaths, insanities, curses, rages, and the many elaborate and oblique contrivances of promises intended to repel sin; of the battle of the giants in Genesis, by which those powerful men are said to deliberate out of fear, while that construction was devised for the salvation of certain others and not unjustly; of the counsel prepared beside heaven in the deceit and seduction of Ahab; of the many material and adulterous passions in the Song of Songs; and of all the other bold, sacred compositions of divine representation—enigmatic statements multiplying and dividing unities, whether parts or things lacking parts, and figuratively and variously representing things lacking forms and figures?

If someone is able to see their hidden beauty within, he will find everything mystical and godlike, filled with much theological light. We do not think that the manifest aspects of composite things are reshaped for their own sake, but that what is already represented is placed before what is to be represented, through much invisible knowledge, so that the most sacred realities may not be easily received by the impure. They are revealed only to sincere lovers of divinity, who form every childish fantasy in the sacred symbols and are capable, through simplicity of soul and the suitability of contemplative virtue, of rising beyond them to the simple, supernatural, and exalted truth of the symbols.

Yet we must understand this also: there are two forms of theological tradition. One is secret and mystical; the other manifest and more familiar. The former is symbolic and perfective; the latter philosophical and confirmatory. The ineffable embraces the sayable. The former receives and requires one kind of treatment from the truth of the statements; the latter acts and establishes another through ineffable introductions into doctrine.

Nor, according to the rites of the holy mysteries, were there lacking among us, or among the sacred teachers of the legal tradition, those who expounded divine symbols. We see the most sacred angels themselves mystically brought forth through divine enigmas; Jesus himself theologizing in parables and handing on the divine mysteries through a symbolic supper.

For it followed that not only should the holy of holies, undefiled and preserved by many, be saved, but also that human life, subsisting at once as indivisible and undivided, should be illuminated in itself by divine knowledges. Its impassible element should be separated for the simple and intimate spectacles of godlike images; while its passible element, naturally serving and stretching itself toward the most divine performances prearranged through the typical symbols, should be guided by such kindred veils. Whoever leaves these veils behind and reforms within himself a certain likeness leading him toward an understanding of the theology stated above reveals this.

The construction of this visible universe of the world is the preliminary image of the invisible God, as Paul says, and true reason.

Accordingly, the theologians view some things civilly and legally, others purgatively and undefiledly; some humanly and moderately, others beyond the world and perfectively. At one time they proceed from the laws of manifest things, at another from the laws of hidden things, following the sacred writings, understandings, and souls that are subordinate to them. For the whole account set before them, in every respect, possesses not bare history but a living perfection.

We too, therefore, must permit the sacred beauty of the holy symbols to be openly received according to the popular understanding of them, and must not despise them, since they demand the formation of divine characters and are images of hidden and supernatural contemplations made manifest.

For not only are the superessential lights, the invisible realities, and the simply divine things variously represented in typical symbols—for example, God beyond nature is called fire, and the invisible words of God are fiery—but the godlike adornments

[Note: BE read “alone” for “not only.”] of the invisible and intellectual angels are also described in various forms and in many kinds of fiery representations.

The same image of fire must be received in one way when it is predicated of God according to transcendent understanding, in another way according to his invisible providences or rational principles, and in another way when it is applied to the angels. The first is understood according to cause, the second according to subsistence, and the third according to participation; other things are ordered differently according to their theoretical and disciplinary purpose.

[Note: H reads “disciplinable.”]

The sacred symbols must not therefore be confused indiscriminately, but must be unfolded appropriately according to the causes, subsistences, powers, orders, or dignities whose manifestations their compositions are.

And, so that we do not extend the discussion further than necessary, the question now before us must be understood. We say that every food is perfective of those who are nourished: it fills their imperfection and need, heals what is weak, preserves their life, makes them flourish, renews them, grants them a life-giving benefit, and simply rejects what is sorrowful and imperfect, bestowing their joy and perfection.

[Note: A reads “bestowing their joy and perfection”; BH read “bestowing their perfections”; E reads “bestowing their joy and perfections.”]

Rightly, therefore, supreme and excellent Wisdom is praised by the Scriptures as establishing a mystical bowl and pouring out for them a sacred drink—indeed, first setting solid foods before them—and, with exalted proclamation, desiring those who desire her, excellently and beautifully.

Divine Wisdom therefore sets before us two kinds of food: one solid and edible, the other moist and poured out; and in the bowl she offers her providential goodness.

Since the bowl is round and broad-rimmed, let it be a symbol of providence: both extended and circulating everywhere, without beginning and infinite, concerning all these things. Yet because, while coming forth into all things, it remains in itself and stands in the unchanging likeness of its nature, perfectly and irrevocably established in itself, uniformly and firmly, so the bowl stands.

Wisdom is also said to build a house for herself, setting before it solid foods, drinks, and the bowl. Through these divine symbols it becomes clear that providence itself is the perfect cause of the being and well-being of all things; that it proceeds into all things, becomes present in every thing, contains all things, and yet again remains in itself with superiority. It is in nothing, by nothing, and through nothing; rather, it is exalted above all things, existing, standing, and remaining similarly and eternally in itself, always possessing the same condition. It is in no way made external to itself, nor does it abandon its own gravity, unchangeable dwelling, or goodness. Rather, in itself it perfectly performs its entire and most perfect providence, proceeding into all things, remaining in itself, and always standing and being moved, and neither standing nor being moved.
