[Note: BH read “in himself” for “in itself.” BH read “supermoved”; E read “always being moved,” omitting “and.” The manuscripts omit “neither standing nor being moved.”]

Or, if someone should say so, it possesses providential operations in dwelling and dwelling in providence, naturally and supernaturally at once.

But what are the solid and the moist foods? For Wisdom is praised as giving and providing these. I think that the solid food signifies the composition of intellectual and nourishing perfection and of natural immutability, according to which divine things were established. Through it, intellectual beings participate in a powerful, uniform, and inseparable knowledge of sensible realities—those realities from which the supremely wise Paul, receiving from Wisdom, delivers truly solid food.

[Note: Hebrews 5.]

The moist food, on the other hand, signifies the power that pours itself out and hastens to proceed into all things, and that, through the many diverse and divided things, guides familiar beings, nourished by goodness, toward simple and unwavering divine knowledge.

[Note: BH read “human” (*humanam*) for “moist” (*humidam*).]

For this reason the divine and invisible words are represented as dew, water, milk, wine, and honey: as possessing the fruitfulness of life, like water; as increasing life, like milk; as restoring life, like wine; and as both cleansing and preserving, like honey.

These are the gifts that divine Wisdom abundantly grants to those who proceed toward her, bestowing upon them a rich and overflowing abundance of banquets that do not fail. This is truly to feast; and for this reason she is praised as life-giving, nourishing of the little ones, renewing, and perfecting.

According to this sacred opening of the feast, God himself, the cause of all good things, is also said to become drunk, because of the superabundance and understanding of the feast. Or rather, the drinking should be understood as the perfect and ineffable immensity of God’s feast, in a diminished and inadequate manner.

For just as among us drunkenness is an excessive filling, an ecstasy of mind and senses, so, in the better sense, in God drunkenness should be understood as nothing other than the immeasurable superabundance of the cause proceeding in himself of all good things.

The ecstasy that follows upon the drunkenness of Wisdom is likewise to be understood as God’s transcendent understanding. Through it he is exalted in understanding beyond understanding, is understood beyond understanding, and is beyond being itself. God is the one who both intoxicates and satisfies all that exists with the supreme goodness of all things, as the transcendent excellence of the immeasurable totality of all things, which is at once superabundant and, again, set outside and above all things.

From these considerations we shall also understand, in the kingdom of God, the banquets of the saints in the same way. “For when he comes,” he says, “he will make them recline, and he himself will serve them.”

[Note: Luke 12:37.]

These things signify a certain common and equally invisible fellowship of the saints in divine goods; the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven; and the spirits of the saints, perfected in all that is best and first filled with the best things.

We understand their reclining as rest: a life unharmed by many sufferings, a divine way of life in the light and in the land of the living, filled with every sacred perception, and an abundant bestowal of the most generous and blessed good things, through which they are filled with every joy.

This is what it means to rejoice: Jesus makes them recline, serves them, grants eternal rest, and distributes and pours into them the fullness of good things.

I know well the inquiry concerning this, and the blessed sleep and awakening of God, when we say that divine sleep is God’s withdrawal and his incommunicability to those under his providence; while vigilance is his coming to the aid of those who pray for his providence, instruction, or salvation.

Many theological symbols have been omitted. Therefore, judging it superfluous to make the same things appear different by repeating them, and also obeying you in good things, we bring the letter to an end, recognizing what belongs to the letter from what has been said, and, as I think, exceeding what is properly owed to our writing.

We send you this entire symbolic theology. In it you will find the house of Wisdom and its seven well-arranged columns, its solid food divided into incense and bread, what moderation of wine means, and again what the drunkenness of God’s intoxication means. These matters, which have now been discussed, are explained more fully there. It is, as I think, the best inventor of all symbolic theologies and is consistent with the sacred traditions and truths of the Scriptures.

## X. To John the Theologian, Apostle and Evangelist, confined on the island of Patmos

[Note: The index reads “confined.”]

[Note: E reads “confined and entrusted to the island of Patmos.”]

Calling you a sacred soul, dearest one—and to me this is more inseparable than the Apostles—I greet you, truly dearest, truly lovable and desirable, and most dearly beloved.

What wonder is it if Christ should truly say that the disciples are driven from the cities of the unjust, while those people attribute to themselves, according to their worth, the things that are, and, polluted and separated from the saints, return as truly significant images of invisible things in visible realities?

For in the ages to come God will not himself be the cause of the separations of the just; rather, those who entirely separate themselves from God will be responsible for them. We see others already made one with God: those who love the truth withdraw from material things in their passibility, and, in freedom from every evil and in divine love, cherish the peace of all good things. They begin sanctification in the present life, living angelically and beautifully among human beings, with complete impassibility, divine designation, goodness, and all other excellent qualities.

You, therefore, even if at some time you were led into such madness, I believe did not suffer anything from it, but merely judged the passions of the body by experiencing them.

As for those who unjustly afflict you and think that they can confine you, I pray that the sun of the Gospel, intervening justly, may turn to good what they are doing in themselves, draw us toward itself, and receive us into the light.

As for us, we are not deprived, by John’s absence, of the most brilliant ray. For now we possess you in memory and in the renewal of your true theology; shortly afterward—I say this more boldly—we shall be united with you yourselves.

I am entirely worthy of faith in these matters, since I have learned them beforehand from you and from God and declare that you will be released from the custody on Patmos, return to the land of Asia, and there carry out imitations of the best God and hand them on to those who are with you.

[Note: B leaves a space of three lines and contains the following:]

Here I am, that very little Otloh, commonly called by this name;

Although corrupted by every kind of evil deed,

Still ready to write this work of yours for you,

Holy Dionysius, most renowned martyr of Christ.

Therefore, I ask, remember me in your sacred prayers;

And you who read, I ask that you seek pardon for me.

[Note: “Habilibus quondam,” etc. Manuscript II instead reads as follows:]

It is finished; let the writer go forth to sing psalms.

Praise be to you, Christ. I have reached the end.

Alas, I have ended badly, because I did not know how to write well.

Pen, stop your course, for this book is finished.

[Note: Habilibus quondam, etc.]

[Note: F reads “Habilibus” (“able”) for “Nobilibus” (“noble”).]

Once you were built for noble patrons;

Now, alas, Rome, you fall beneath slaves.

For so long your kings have deserted you,

And your name and honor have passed to the Greeks.

Flourishing Constantinople is called the New Rome;

In morals and in walls, ancient Rome, you are falling.

Empire has passed away, but pride has remained with you;

The worship of avarice surpasses you excessively.

The common people, drawn from the farthest regions of the world,

The slaves of slaves, are now your masters.

Among you no noble or upright ruler remains;

Your freeborn people cultivate the Pelasgian fields.

You have cut down living saints with cruel wounds;

Now you are accustomed to sell their dead limbs.

If the merit of Peter and Paul did not cherish you,

By now, poor Rome, you would long ago have been wretched.

[Note: The whole poem is absent from manuscript E. In that manuscript several other letters were added at the end of the translation, concerning which we have discussed more fully in the Preface. The complete poem is found in manuscripts BCDH.]

[Col. 1193]

# JOHN SCOTUS’S TRANSLATION OF THE AMBIGUOUS PASSAGES OF SAINT MAXIMUS

Thomas Gale published the copy received from Mabillon in the Appendix to John Scotus’s work *On the Division of Nature*, pp. 1–45.

## PREFACE

[Col. 1193]

To the most glorious and most devout lord, King Charles, under divine providence and with divine grace assisting him, John, the least of your servants, sends perpetual greetings in Christ.

This work of Maximus, monk and abbot, which he composed, at the request of the most holy and blessed Archbishop John of Cyzicus, as explanations of certain *Ambigua*—that is, passages difficult to understand—in the sermons of the blessed Gregory the Theologian, I have published from Greek into Latin at your command.

[Note: This is the title of this book. For the “Scholia” is another work by this Maximus. Maximus himself mentions these *Ambigua* in the second volume of his published works, p. 15; Photius and Baronius also mention them, and Baronius testifies that they are preserved in Vatican manuscripts.]

You have imposed upon your servant, most orthodox of kings, a task supremely difficult even for one very weak in Latin, and still more so in Greek. Moreover, you commanded me to hasten it and complete it quickly, as though I were learned in both languages. Yet, according to the ability of my little intellect, I both hastened and, with divine grace guiding and granting me strength, brought the work to completion.

Perhaps, defended by an apology of some kind, I would not have entered such dense darkness if I had not seen the aforementioned blessed Maximus, throughout his work, introducing and wonderfully clarifying the most obscure statements of the most holy theologian Dionysius the Areopagite. These statements I recently translated for you in a similar manner at your command.

Indeed, I no longer doubted that divine clemency, which illuminates the things hidden in darkness, had arranged this through its ineffable providence: that the matters most obstructed for us in the books of the blessed Dionysius, or scarcely accessible and apparently escaping our understanding, should be opened by the supremely wise Maximus through his most lucid explanations.

To give one example among many: how the cause of all things, which is God, is one and simple and yet manifold; what procession is—that is, the multiplication of divine goodness through all beings, from the highest down to the lowest—first through the universal essence of all things, then through the most general genera, then through the more general genera, and from there through the more particular species down to the most particular species, descending through differences and properties.

And again, what the return of that same divine goodness is—that is, its gathering through the same degrees, from the infinite and varied multiplication of beings back to the simplest unity of all, which is in God and is God—so that God is all things and all things are God.

And how the aforementioned divine procession into all things is called *analytikē* [ἀναλυτική], that is, “resolution,” while the return is called *theōsis* [θέωσις], that is, “deification.”

And why those things that are greatest in multiplication are least in power, while those that are least in multiplication are greatest in power.

What need is there to speak of *kataphatic* and *apophatic* theology—*kataphatikē* [καταφατική] and *apophatikē* [ἀποφατική]—in which the profoundest, most divine, and most wonderful discussion of the blessed Dionysius the Areopagite is displayed? How clearly and beautifully he opens the matter: although these two seem opposed and greatly contrary to one another, they nevertheless arrive at a single agreement. While one denies and the other affirms, both are contained in each; thus the *kataphatic* does not affirm what the *apophatic* denies, nor does the *apophatic* deny what the *kataphatic* affirms.

He also makes it entirely clear, through manifest examples, that these two greatest divisions of theology exist not only in God but also in every creature; through them the orders of the heavenly essences are both distinguished and arranged.

He explains how God is said to move and to be moved, although he is immutable; and that God neither senses sensible things through sensation, nor intelligible things through intellect, nor sensible things through intellect, nor intelligible things through sensation, but contemplates everything in its eternal reasons.

He also discusses, in a most mystical and wonderful sixfold treatment, the unity of the three divine substances and the three substances of the divine unity.

And there are many other matters that the diligent reader of this work will discover.

Most devout [Note: A marginal note in E reads “Most pious.” John Scotus favors Greek expressions, as elsewhere.] of kings, do not reject the work that you ordered to be made for the common illumination of the Catholic faith. Rather, allow it to be strengthened by the judgment of your highest authority and received among the instruments of sound doctrine, since you do not doubt that it has been drawn from the most illustrious fountains of the Greeks.

If anything is found in it that is still unfamiliar doctrine to us, it should be attributed to the authors themselves, since no one ought rightly to attribute anything else to me in this work except that I have simply translated it.

# JOHN SCOTUS’S TRANSLATION OF THE AMBIGUOUS PASSAGES OF SAINT MAXIMUS

To the most holy and blessed John, Archbishop of Cyzicus: Maximus, humble monk.

All those who, out of zeal for learning, love good things with readiness and think earnestly about the discipline contained in them, are praised by everyone—and perhaps justly—because, approaching better teachers and teachers of better things, they reverently receive instruction through questioning the wise and free themselves from ignorance, incompetence, and the reproach attached to them.

But what speech could praise you worthily? Or what human being, even if he has acquired experience in understanding, will be found capable of grasping the greatness of your virtue? For since you are proven shepherds of rational sheep, and know how to lead and introduce them to the heavenly sheepfold by the voice of the spiritual pipe, you have anticipated the singular disposition of mystical knowledge of divine things, a disposition impossible for many.

[Note: He wrongly read οἴαν for οἷα.] Through it you guide the worthy and faithful rudders of Christ’s Church, like a ship, with discipline, carrying the burden of faith and the beauty of divine conduct safely through the sea of the world’s temptations to the harbor of the divine will.

Concerning the matters known to you, whose teachers the Lord has appointed you, you do not consider it unworthy to question, as is your custom, not only those who are wiser—if any of you is altogether superior in knowledge—but even those who are worthy of nothing and entirely ignorant of doctrine, trusting that something noble may be found even among the unseemly.

[Note: This follows the Greek custom: “any of you” stands for “you.” He appears to have read ἀσέμνους (“unseemly”) for ἀσήμοις (“insignificant”).]

Accordingly, having received your venerable letter, in which you commanded me to write to you about each of the doubtful Chapters in the sermons of the holy theologian Gregory, matters in which I had been engaged when I was among those who gathered with you, I now commit the explanation to writing.

[Note: The Greek text has ἡμῖν, “to us.”]

I admired you as was fitting for your virtue and praised your clear and exalted hospitality, pleasing to Christ. Rather, I glorified in every way, through you and in you, the Lord who made you worthy of this and the virtue granted by him—he who through your works openly manifests the beauty of truth to his servants—extending even to me, a little man, worthy of nothing, unlearned, and utterly stripped of every virtue and knowledge.

[Note: The Greek has τοῖς ἐαυτοῦ ἰδιώμασι; John Scotus appears to have read ἰδίοις, which is unsuitable.]

Therefore, considering myself humbled, I compelled myself to receive your command according to my ability, since I shall not be considered rash when I speak at length for your sake. And while I expect you to receive the pleasing and lovable reward of obedience, you will customarily grant me your attentive prayers, so that Christ the Lord, who is the ready help of those who fear him, may come to my aid in speech—or rather, since I speak reverently of the whole matter, that the Word may grant me a word.

I ask you, while making this request, not to seek ornate diction from me, for I do not possess speeches that embellish the hearing, and I do not know how to produce elaborate flourishes.

[Note: The Greek has *tais periergois tomais* [ταῖς περιέργοις τομαῖς], “with elaborate divisions/cuts.” It is uncertain what John Scotus read here. The meaning of *tomai* is explained by Hermogenes, Book II, On Forms.]

Since I am ignorant of such forms of learning and do not comprehend the greatness of the care devoted to them, I consider it most beloved and desirable if I have grasped even somewhat the meaning of this holy and great teacher, though in a confused explanation, rather than honoring the exposition with a long and elaborate composition.

For, as you know, this theologian, though brief in words, is abundant in meaning, and his intention necessarily requires explanation by anyone who wishes to expound it, even if that person is most eloquent and wise in many matters.

[Note: The Greek reads *dia pollōn ienai*, that is, “to range more expansively” or “to expatiate more fully.”]

And even more so does it require explanation from me, who am unlearned.

But if the zeal that habitually moves you, beloved of God, should be stirred when we bring what has been written down to brevity and clarity, you will receive a reward perfect in itself: the prayers of that god-bearing man to the Lord of all. For you do not permit his divine and supernatural understandings to be handled by contemptuous and worthless reflections.

Accordingly, I have investigated your letter chapter by chapter and committed my findings to writing, praying that you may become good and merciful judges of what has been said.

## CHAPTER I. FROM THE SERMON ON HOSPITALITY

In this passage: “I am sparing the fellow worker, and I have no way of escaping the invasion, or of not falling away from God, weighed down by children who are tearing me away or holding me down to the earth.”

[Note: The translator rendered “chains” most incompetently. The Greek has *pedais* [πέδαις], “fetters” or “bonds.”]

[Col. 1197D]

It did not seem to this blessed man that being torn away was the same as being held down. Nor should you think, most excellent one, that there is anything here which you could understand as worthy of his greatness of soul merely by your own concern.

For he would be excessive in words and would not possess a meaning surpassing speech if, without inserting suitable knowledge into almost every syllable and leading us by successive stages toward what is beautiful and useful, he were in any way left to be argued over.

These matters are not so. Rather, they wisely establish speech for understanding, and an exalted understanding rises above exalted speech, so that what is exalted may be announced by what is exalted, and that a small portion of the magnitude of truth, inaccessible to many—or even to all—may meanwhile be shown through both.

But so that the obscurity of everything that has been said may be manifest to us, let us consider the blessed man’s words as they stand.

“I am sparing,” he says, “the fellow worker, and I have no way of escaping the invasion, or of not falling away from God, weighed down by children who are tearing me away or holding me down to the earth.”

In saying this, he is not speaking entirely about himself, but through himself he is discussing humanity in general, observing that everyone who loves salvation devotes himself either wholly to action or to contemplation. For no one has ever been able to attain salvation in any way without virtue and knowledge.

“If, then,” he says, “I have been established through contemplation among those who are placed with God and enjoy blessed beauty, possessing peace in all things and sanctification—inasmuch as I have attached myself inseparably to God through likeness in knowledge—then I think about the irrational powers of the soul, bring them suitably before the mind through reason, and make them familiar: I mean anger and desire, transforming the former into charity and the latter into joy, since it is proper to joy to exult and rejoice divinely.”

Thus John leaped for joy from his mother’s womb, John the great forerunner and herald of truth; or as King David did when he caused the ark of Israel to rest.

For in the mother, although the meaning is difficult and inaccessible to many, it is nevertheless true that we and God the Word, who is the maker and Lord of the universe, are present. In the condition of the present life, he appears secretly, as though in a womb, and scarcely perceptible to this world; and this occurs to those who, in accordance with John, are in the Spirit. Human beings, however, are as though in a mother—that is, in the material surrounding condition—even if for a little while they perceive the Word hidden within existing things.

Perhaps those who rejoice in John’s joys are in this condition.

For, when compared with the ineffable glory, brightness, and distinctive character of the life of the age to come, the present life differs no more than does a womb enveloped in darkness.

[Note: The Greek reads μήτρας ζόφῳ περικεχυμένης, “of a womb shrouded in darkness.”]

In the present life, for our sake, God, who is the perfect and more-than-perfect Word, became an infant to the senses, as an act of mercy.

If, then, as has been said, I am such a person, raised by human possibility during the present transitory life to the divine summit, but I have neglected the godlike disposition and willingly inclined myself toward the desire of the body, I have been torn away, weighed down by children—that is, by cares—and have fallen from God. I have attributed thought and inquiry concerning the kingdom of heaven alone, to which it was not lawful to give them, to earthly life, and have dishonored the mind by applying it to the senses rather than directing it toward God.

But if I am still a warrior in the active life, fighting against armed passions, not yet having escaped purely through them the deceits of enemies who wish to receive me, and if I have loved the body indiscriminately, then I have been held down by it, presuming to separate myself from the disposition of virtue.

The contemplative person, therefore, is torn away when the body comes upon him immoderately through habit and he neglects divine contemplations; the active person is held down when, fighting against the body and giving himself to the struggle, he chooses to become the slave of the passions instead of laboring for virtue, which is the soul’s freedom.

## CHAPTER II. FROM THE SAME AUTHOR, FROM THE SAME SERMON

In this passage: “What is this wisdom concerning me, and what is this great mystery? Does he wish us to be part of God, flowing down from above, so that, without being exalted according to our dignity and contemplating heavenly things, we may not despise the Creator, but, in the struggle and battle that is against the body, may always look toward him, and may have the weakness joined to us as nourishment for dignity?”

[Col. 1199B]

These words, and receiving no reward, as is fitting, for the labor of seeking the truth, they flee to what is easy and already offers many opportunities from the teachings of the Greeks. They say that there once existed, as they suppose, a certain unity of rational beings, through which we were related to God and had our dwelling and placement in him. They further suppose that a movement then took place, by which the rational beings, dispersed in different ways, were brought to the generation of this corporeal world; and that God, knowing the grace prepared for them, bound them to bodies as punishment for the offenses previously committed. They think that the teacher hinted at this through these words.

But they do not understand how impossibilities follow, or how incongruous consequences arise, as the argument that proceeds and follows will demonstrate with truth.

[Note: In the Greek, μετὰ τοῦ εἰκότος means “with probability” or “with plausibility.” John Scotus had read ἑπόντος, “following.”]

For if God is immutable, being, so to speak, the fullness of all things, while everything that receives being from nonexistence is moved, it is necessarily borne toward some cause. But what is moved has not yet come to rest, since the final rest of the moving power—which is according to desire—has not yet been granted. Nothing else is accustomed to bring to rest what is borne according to nature except that which has been shown. Therefore no movement comes to rest, since perhaps the final object has not yet appeared; for neither has that which appears somewhere brought to stability the movement of those things that are borne around it.

But if they assert that this had once happened by command, and that, through a displacement and dwelling given in the final and enduring state, the rational beings were moved and received dispersion—

[Note: In the Greek, περικινηθέντα means “having been moved around.” Perhaps the reading was προκινηθέντα, “having been moved forward.” John Scotus understood virtually nothing here; indeed, he distorted almost everything in this chapter. Since there are many such matters, we shall pass them over.]

—to avoid calling it superfluous, what sort of judgment will they endure? Having once fallen into dispersion, will the same rational beings necessarily suffer an infinite condition in themselves? For they are strengthened by no experience of being despised, nor will there be any reason preventing them from being strengthened forever. Yet for rational beings to be borne in this way, without having even through hope an immovable foundation by which they might be fixed in the good—what could be more pitiable?

But if they say that they were able, yet unwilling, to do so except through experiencing the contrary, then the good would be necessary for them to love, not in itself as good, but through its opposite. How, then, would what is lovable not be natural or properly lovable? For whatever is not good and lovable in itself, and does not draw every movement toward itself, is not properly good. Consequently, it does not rightly attract the desire of those who delight in it. It remains to confess that they are following an evil wisdom, learning through necessity itself to possess a fixation in the good in some manner and repenting of it. And if they know how to assert that generation comes necessarily from it, they will have to say that generation is more useful than nature itself, since according to their teaching it is rightly profitable and the most precious possession of all.

I mean the generation through which all things made by God are naturally gathered into God perpetually and irrevocably.

And again: the generation of things made by God, both intelligible and sensible, is understood to precede movement. For movement cannot exist before generation. Movement belongs to things that have been made, whether it is the intelligible movement of intelligible things or the sensible movement of sensible things. None of the things that have been made is altogether immovable in the same manner—not even soulless and sensible things, as the more diligent contemplators of beings have perceived. They said that everything moves either in a straight line, or in a circle, or obliquely. Every movement is contained in a simple or composite mode.

If, then, the generation of those things of which movement is predicated is understood to precede their movement, the movement of those things is evidently observed through generation, since it comes after generation according to knowledge. Those who introduced us reverently into the sacred knowledge of the divine mysteries call such movement a natural power hastening toward its own end,

[Note: The words “Those who introduced us reverently into the sacred knowledge” are absent from the Greek text. There is no doubt that John Scotus saw them in his exemplar, since they occur in the Latin.]

or a passion—that is, a movement proceeding from one thing toward another, whose end is impassibility—or an active operation, whose end is perfection through itself.

But none of the things that have been made is its own end, since it is not its own cause. Otherwise it would also be ungenerated, without beginning, and unchangeable, and therefore would rightly have no movement toward anything whatsoever. It would transcend the nature of things that exist, since it would exist for nothing; for the true definition of it, although belonging to another subject, would be: “The end is that for which all things exist, while it exists for nothing.”

Nor is any created thing perfection through itself. Otherwise it would not rightly be made full; and likewise it would derive its being from no one. For what is perfect through itself is also without a cause. Nor is any created thing impassibility; otherwise it would be abiding [Note: In the Greek, ἐπεὶ καὶ μόνον, i.e. “rather, one alone.”], infinite, and uncircumscribed.

For what is universally impassible does not naturally undergo passion, since it is neither loved by another nor moved toward anything else through love.

Therefore none of the things generated brings its movement to rest, since it has not yet grasped the first and abiding cause from which being is present to existing things. Nor has it yet reached the final gift, nor, as someone might suppose, attached to itself the generation of bodies as a consequence of the dispersion of the rational beings from the primordial unity.

[Note: Likewise, “the one alone.” What follows is obscure both in the Latin and in the Greek.]

Moses and David and holy Paul bear witness to this, as does their Lord Christ.

Moses first, when he describes the first parent as being forbidden to taste from the tree of life; and elsewhere when he says: “For you have not yet come to the rest and inheritance which the Lord your God will give you.”

David says: “I shall be satisfied, crying out, when your glory appears to me,” and: “My soul thirsted for the living and mighty God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?”

Paul, writing to the Philippians, says: “If somehow I may attain to the resurrection from the dead—not that I have already received it, or am already perfected; but I press on, if perhaps I may apprehend that for which I have also been apprehended by Jesus Christ.”

Likewise, in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “For he himself, entering into his rest, also rested from his works, as God did from his own.” And again, in the same epistle, he affirms that no one has yet reached the promises.

But Christ says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.”

Therefore, none of the things that have been made has yet in any way brought its natural power, which is moved toward its end, to rest; nor has it caused the operation striving toward its own end to cease.

[Note: He intended to say that the operation itself was fixed in its end.]

Nor has it reaped the fruit of passion, which consists in movement—that is, impassibility and immutability. For only God is end, perfection, and impassibility. But for created things to move toward an end without beginning, and for him to make their operation restful through so perfect an end, and for them to undergo passion but not to be—or not to become—according to essence, is not pleasing.

[Note: The Greek has ἄποιον, “without affection toward another,” or “immune.”]

Everything made and created is certainly not immeasurable; rather, it must faithfully listen to passion. For the passion spoken of here is not the passion that belongs to the alteration and corruption of power, but the passion that subsists naturally in existing things. Everything that has been made undergoes movement, just as what is not [made] is movement through itself or power through itself.

If, then, generated things subsist as rational beings, they are altogether moved, since they move naturally from a beginning through being toward an end through knowledge, that is, toward well-being. The end of things that are moved is movement itself into well-being, which always is; just as their beginning is being itself, which is God, who both gives being and grants well-being, rightly being both beginning and end.

For from him comes our absolute movement as from a beginning, and movement in every way toward him as toward an end.

If what is rational is moved together with itself intellectually, it also altogether understands. If it understands, it altogether loves what it understands. If it loves, it altogether undergoes passion through an ecstasy toward the beloved. If it undergoes passion, it evidently also hastens. If it hastens, it altogether intensifies its powerful movement. If it intensifies its powerful movement, it does not come to rest until it becomes wholly in the whole beloved and is wholly comprehended by it, willingly receiving the whole circumscription according to the saving will, so that the whole may be affected by the whole that circumscribes it.

Then nothing remains that it wishes from itself, since it is able to know itself as wholly circumscribed—not from itself, but from that which circumscribes it—like air illuminated throughout by light, or iron wholly melted by fire, or anything else of this kind.

From these things we receive, by way of contemplation, a likeness of the participation in the goodness that is to come, but has not yet come to pass and has not been corrupted.

[Note: The Greek has παραφθαρσεῖσαν, “corrupted.”]

For these things are above all that are to be hoped for, since they are the summit of vision, as it is written: “of sight, hearing, and understanding.”

This is also the subjection of which the divine Apostle says that the Son will subject himself to the Father, willingly receiving those who accept subjection. After this and through this, the last enemy, death, will be destroyed—the power of corruption through which it entered into us—while he who is powerful in himself assists us according to our condition, God voluntarily filling all things and ruling well what is ruled.

[Note: The Greek has ἐκχωρηθέντος, “yielding” or “ceding.”]

He will be at rest, doing nothing except what God wills.

[Note: The Greek has τὸ βασιλεύεσθαι, “that which is ruled.”]

As he says elsewhere, the Savior himself, forming in himself what belongs to us, says to the Father: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” And after him the divine and wondrous Paul, as though denying himself and no longer knowing that he possessed a life of his own, says: “I live, yet no longer I; Christ lives in me.”

Let what has been said not trouble you. I do not mean that the proper power is removed, but rather that a fixed and immutable position according to nature takes place: an intellectual ecstasy, so that we desire to receive from that source our being and our movement, as an image returns to its archetypal model; and, like a sign fashioned according to its principal form, the image has thereafter neither the capacity nor the power to be carried elsewhere.

Or, to speak more openly and truly: it neither wishes nor is able to do so, having rightly received the divine operation—or rather, having become God through deification—and loving more intensely through ecstasy what is naturally within it. Through the grace of the Spirit, which surpasses it, it is lifted above the things that are and are understood, possessing and receiving Jesus alone as its operator, so that throughout all things there is one and the same operation of God and of those worthy of God—or rather, of God alone—since the whole of God surrounds the whole of those who are worthy, well and beautifully.

For, through every necessity, it rests in every way from movement toward anything else, through the governing movement that is according to desire, when the final object has appeared, been given, and been shared, and when the power of the participants has incomprehensibly, so to speak, grasped the object according to the rationality of their participation.

Toward this every activity and intellect of the exalted hastens; in this every appetite is stabilized; beyond it nothing is borne. For it is the object toward which every movement of the one who hastens is directed, and from it comes the rest of all contemplation for those who arrive, as this blessed teacher says.

Nor will anything be manifested outside God, nor will anything appear to be equated with God.

[Note: The Greek has ἀντισηκοῦσθαι, “to be made equal” or “to be equated.”]

Thus it will be an error for anyone’s desire to flow toward itself,

[Note: Scotus seems to have read δολιάσῃ, “deceive”; but the printed Greek has δελεάση, “entice.”]

since all intelligible and sensible things are encompassed by him according to his ineffable manifestation and presence.

Just as, when the sun appears with its great and incomparable light, the luminaries of the day and the stars are hidden, so that their lights are not perceived as coming from them, and so that, although they exist, they are not recognized by the senses according to their measure, so it will be with God—but much more so, since there is an infinite gulf and difference between the uncreated and the created.

Then, knowing through the essence of existing things their subsistence according to what they are, how they are, and in what they exist, we shall no longer move our desire toward anything further through knowledge. The knowledge of each one and of each thing that exists after God will have been brought to completion, and the infinite, divine, incomprehensible, and fruitful dwelling and participation proportioned to us will have been set before us.

This is what the deiform teacher has philosophized at length when he says that one day we shall know as we have been known, when we mingle our deiform and divine soul and reason with their archetype, and the image returns to the principal model for which it now has desire.

Thus far, then, it has been said that unity was not divided, and how, according to knowledge derived from the possibilities afforded us now by the interpretations and arguments of Scripture, the condition of future things will be. But how, while we are a part of God, we flowed back from God, I shall now explain, with God as my guide.

For who, considering rationally and wisely the things that exist, brought by God from what is not into what is, and carefully contemplating through the soul’s natural, infinite difference and variety among existing things, would not recognize through the intellect the cause according to which they were created: many causes, inseparably coexisting yet differentiated, as one cause of the things that were made, through the distinct property of each thing both in relation to the others and in itself; and again, one as many, through the relation of all things to him, subsisting without confusion in itself?

That one is the essential and substantial God, the Word of God the Father, rightly the beginning and cause of all things, in whom all things were created—those in the heavens and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, or Powers. “All things were created from him, through him, and in him.”

Having the causes of created things pre-established before the ages, he brought forth, through his good will, the visible and invisible creation from nonexistence according to those causes. Through reason and wisdom he both made and makes all things at the appropriate time, both universally and individually.

We believe that he first brought forth the cause of the creation of angels, the cause of each of the essences and powers that complete the world above us; and the reason of human beings, each of whom receives being from God—not to mention each one individually. For he himself, infinitely surpassing all things in himself, being ineffable and intelligible, and being the whole summit of creation and of every difference and distinction of things existing in themselves and conceived, displays and multiplies himself beautifully in all things that come from him according to the analogy of each.

[Note: The Greek has διικνύμενον, “extending through” or “pervading.”]

And he recapitulates all things in himself. Through him they receive being and continuance; from him come the things that are generated, and toward him they are generated. Both those that remain and those that move participate in God.

For all things participate proportionately in God because they have been made from God, whether through intellect, reason, sense, vital movement, essence, or the fitting condition and opportunity of their existence, as the great and divine revealer Dionysius the Areopagite appears to teach.

Therefore each of the intelligible and rational beings—angels and human beings—is, through the reason according to which it was created, and through which it exists in God and is directed toward God, a part of God and is called such, because of its pre-existent cause in God, as has been said.

Accordingly, if it were moved according to that cause, it would come to be in God, in whom the account of its essence already exists as in its beginning and cause. It would not wish to receive desire for anything before its own beginning, nor would it flow back from God. Rather, through the intensity directed toward him, it would become God and be called a part of God, naturally participating in God.

It would thus receive its beginning and cause according to nature, wisely and rationally, through its beautiful movement. Thereafter it would have no ascent or restoration of movement elsewhere beyond its beginning, toward the reason according to which it was created, or any other manner of movement. Its movement would be in the divine desire, and through its movement it would receive the end itself, namely, the vision of God.

As Basil explains in his interpretation of the holy prophet Isaiah, saying:

“True Sabbaths are the rest reserved for the people of God. Since they are true, God receives and manifests them as the highest Sabbaths of rest. This is the one for whom the world has been crucified, who has departed from worldly things and hastens toward the proper place of spiritual rest, in which, once established, he will no longer be moved from his place, since silence and peace surround that state.”

The place of all who are worthy of such blessedness, therefore, is God, according to what is written: “Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place of salvation.”

With him the reasons of all things are firmly fixed. Through these reasons he is said to know all things before their generation, since all things exist in him and with him through truth itself—even though all things, both those that are and those that are to be, were not brought into essence simultaneously with their causes as they are known by God. Rather, each was beautifully created at the proper time, according to the wisdom of the Creator and in accordance with its cause, and receives existence through its own operation.

For he is always Creator according to operation, while created things exist in potency but not yet in operation. Neither can the infinite and the finite exist simultaneously in the same respect, nor will any argument be found capable of affirming that their essence and the superessential can exist simultaneously, or of bringing what is measured into the same thing as what is immeasurable; nor can it unite what exists in a condition with what lacks a condition, or what has no affirmed species of category in itself with what is constituted through all the species of categories.

For all created things are affirmed in every respect according to essence and generation through their forms, and they are contained by the reasons of the things external to them that surround their essence.

If, then, we remove the highest and apophatic theology of the Word—according to which he is neither spoken of nor understood, nor is he in any way anything among things known, but is rightly superessential and in no way participated in by anything—then many causes are one cause, and one is many.

According to the good and beautiful procession within it, which creates and unites the things that exist, many are one. But through the relation and providence that converts and leads the many into unity, one is many, like an almighty beginning encompassing the beginnings of straight lines proceeding from it, or like a center embracing the beginnings of all such lines and thus gathering them all.

Therefore we are a part of God and are called such because the reasons of our essence have been pre-established in God. We are also said to flow down from above because we have not been moved according to the cause pre-existing in God through which we were made.

There is another way as well by which it is easy, for one instructed in this doctrine, to understand religiously the cause of existing things. For if the Word of God, who is one, is acknowledged to subsist as the essence of every virtue—for our Lord and God Jesus Christ himself is the essence of all virtues, as it is written: “He was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption”—then he certainly possesses absolutely in himself the things that have been said, since he is wisdom, righteousness, and holiness in himself, not as they exist in us with definition, for example, as “a wise man” or “a just man.”

Therefore every human being who participates in virtue according to a fixed disposition unquestionably participates in God, who is the essence of the virtues. Such a person faithfully cultivates the natural seed of the good through the will, and displays the same thing—the beginning as the end and the end as the beginning—or rather, displays that the same thing is both beginning and end.

He establishes God within himself as a secure herald, if indeed he believes that he sees in himself the beginning and end of the whole reality. He sees the beginning as receiving from it, through participation, the natural good of existence; and he sees the end as completing, through knowledge of that beginning and desire for it, the praiseworthy course that leads without error and with eagerness toward it.

Through this course he becomes God from God, receiving the gift of being God. Rightly according to the image he adds likeness to natural goodness through the will and through the virtues, by ascending toward and becoming familiar with his proper beginning, which is implanted within him.

The apostolic word is fulfilled in him: “For in him we live and move and are.”

He comes to be in God through the excellence of the reason of essence that pre-exists in God, without corrupting that reason. He moves in God according to the reason of well-being that precedes in God, working through the virtues. He lives in God according to the reason of the eternal being that always precedes in God.

Already, according to a very impassible disposition, he is the same in himself and unchangeable. In the age to come, according to the deification granted to him, he will love and embrace the causes previously existing in God—or rather, God himself, in whom the causes of good things have been established.

He is a part of God insofar as he exists according to the reason of his essence in God; he is good according to the reason of well-being in God; and he is God according to the reason of eternal being. Rightly honoring these causes, working according to them, and through them inserting his whole self into God alone, he also imagines and forms God alone wholly within himself.

Thus he himself is by grace and is called God, while God is, by condescension, called man in himself. In this mutual affection, the power is shown that deifies man through divine love and humanizes God through human love. Through this good conversion, it makes God man through the deification of man, and man God through the humanization of God.

For the Word of God and God always wills, in all things, to work the mystery through his embodiment.

But whoever abandons his own beginning, although constituted as a part of God through the reason of virtue existing in him according to the cause assigned to him, is irrationally borne toward what is not. He is rightly said to flow down from above, since he is not moved toward his own beginning and cause—from which, in which, and through which he was made.

Such a person exists in the unstable course and fluid disorder of soul and body, carrying out through a voluntary impulse his expulsion from the unerring and unchanging cause toward what is evil.

This is why he is properly said to flow: because, while the soul’s steps were moving inseparably toward God, he voluntarily exchanged the better for what is worse and what is not, through the force of his power.

[Note: The Greek has ἀδηρίτως, “without stumbling” or “without offense.”]

The holy Dionysius the Areopagite teaches us from divine Scripture that these reasons which I have mentioned are called predestinations and divine wills.

Likewise, those associated with Pantaenus, the friend of the great Clement, who became the teacher of the *Stromata*,

[Note: This is how John Scotus has it. Translate: “And Pantaenus, who was the teacher of Clement the Great’s *Stromata*.”]

say that the divine wills are called such by Scripture.

When certain proud men, learned in external disciplines, asked them how Christians believe that God knows existing things, they replied that he knows intelligible things intellectually and sensible things sensibly.

We answer that he knows neither sensible things sensibly nor intelligible things intellectually. For reason shows that it is impossible for him who is above existing things to apprehend existing things through existing things.

Rather, we say that he knows existing things as his own wills, and we add the reasoning from their cause. For if he made all things by will—and no reason contradicts this—and if it is always pious and just to say that God knows his own will, then he made each of the things that have been made willingly. Therefore God knows existing things as his own wills, since he made existing things willingly.

Looking upon this, I judge that Scripture spoke according to these reasons when it says to Moses: “I knew you above all others,” and concerning some: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and again concerning others: “I never knew you.”

Thus each person, whether moving voluntarily according to the will and reason of God or contrary to God’s will and reason, has prepared himself to hear the divine voice.

I believe that the deiform teacher understood this and similar matters when he said: “When we mingle this deiform and divine soul and reason of ours with their archetype, the image will return to the principal model for which it now has desire.”

Through these few words, then, one must understand that he touched doctrinally on whatever measure of existing things he at some time reached; that he explained how we are a part of God; that he hinted at the distinctive character of the blessed rest to come; and that he urged us toward his immovable rest and its fruit, which does not fall, cleansing and hastening us by the hope that exists in this life.

For, just as we possess notions of this both in essence and in reason, so we ought to enter rightly through reason and nature in a simple order. Without any kind of questioning—concerning which alone it is possible both to sin and to be deceived—we shall know all things in a deiform manner, insofar as possible.

No longer held back through ignorance by the movement that surrounds those things, we shall approach with great courage our soul, reason, and spirit to the soul, reason, and Spirit—or rather, our whole selves to the whole of God—like an image approaching its principal model.

[Note: The Greek has ὡς ἀρχετύπῳ εἰκόνι προσχωρήσαντες, “having approached the archetypal model as an image.” Translate: “having approached the archetypal model as an image,” and so forth.]

As he also teaches in the discourse concerning hail, saying:

“Then ineffable light will receive us, and the holy and royal contemplation of the Trinity, which illuminates more clearly and purely and is wholly mingled with the whole soul. I place this contemplation alone as the kingdom of heaven. The soul delights and rejoices in it with delight, so that I may boldly join what belongs to me to what belongs to it.

“Every rational creature—angel and human—who has not through negligence corrupted the divine reasons naturally joined to it by the Creator, according to the movement that leads toward the end, but has rather preserved itself temperately, knows that it will be and will remain wholly irreversible as an instrument of the divine nature.

“God, breathing wholly around them and embracing them completely,

[Note: The Greek has περιφύς, “embracing” or “growing around.”]

handles them according to his will as members of a body compacted and made excellent for the Lord, in the manner of a soul. He fills them with his own glory and blessedness, giving and granting eternal and ineffable life, established in every way as free from all limitation, through knowledge of their present condition and of the life established through corruption.

“This eternal life is constituted neither by air inhaled nor by streams of blood flowing from the liver, but by the whole God participated in by the whole person. God becomes, as a soul does in relation to the body, and through the soul in relation to the body, what he himself knows how to be, so that the soul receives incorruptibility and the body immortality, and the whole human being is deified through the grace of the God who was humanized.

“The whole human being remains human according to soul and body by nature, and the whole becomes God according to soul and body by grace, possessing throughout the divine brightness of blessed glory appropriate to it. After this, nothing more luminous or exalted remains to be understood.

“For what is more lovable for those worthy of deification (θέωσις), through which God, united to those who have become gods, makes his whole fullness theirs through goodness?”

Accordingly, I would rightly call such a state delight, passion, and joy—a state that comes through divine knowledge and the fruit of joy that follows it.

I call it delight rightly, since it is the end of natural operations; for this is how they define delight.

I call it passion because it stretches out the power and brings what suffers toward what acts, according to the paradigmatic and credible natural example of air being carried toward light and iron toward fire. It is naturally and truly credible, and it contains nothing other than this—the culmination of existing things—which impassibility appropriately follows.

[The Latin’s “capitulum” here means “completion” or “consummation.”]

I call it joy rightly because it has nothing opposed to it, neither past nor future. For they say that joy does not know past grief, nor does it receive, through fear, the expectation of satiety to be observed in the manner of delight.

Therefore our Fathers, who are wise in the divine mysteries, have determined that the God-inspired words everywhere are, as it were, a demonstrative designation subsisting for the truth to come.

Thus, as has appeared briefly in passing, both naturally and through the testimony of the Fathers and Scripture, no created thing has ever brought its movement to rest, nor has it received rest in itself according to divine contemplation. Along with these points, it has also been shown how it is impossible for the stability of those worthy of dwelling in God to be reproved.

For how could it be possible, in light of what has been said, to offer even a small support from reasoning for the claim that those who have once been established substantially in God received through desire an ungrateful satiety?

By its own account and definition, every satiety extinguishes desire. Satiety is established in two ways. Either it extinguishes desire by circumscribing what is present, as though that object were small; or it rejects the object as contemptible, as though it were shameful and deformed. Satiety customarily arises from these causes.

But God, subsisting by nature as infinite and precious, is accustomed rather to extend the desire of those who enjoy participation in him toward what is infinite.

If this is true, as indeed it is, then there was no unity of rational beings of the kind described—one that, having received satiety, divided the perseverance that exists in God and introduced the generation of this world through its own division. Otherwise we would make the highest good circumscribed and base, as though bounded by a kind of satiety, and make it the cause of sedition among those whose desire was unable to hold what is immutable.

And lest certain people continue to worship such vanity,

[Note: The Greek has Καὶ μάτην λοιπὸν τινες ταύτην θεσπίζουσιν, which should be translated: “And in vain they henceforth proclaim that unity,” and so forth.]

inventing things that do not exist—and, what is more serious, slandering this blessed Father as though he taught such things—they would consequently be able not only to assert that souls come from their former kind of life into bodies as punishment for the evils previously committed, but also to lead others astray into believing the same.

They attempt to do this rationally by appealing to the respectability of persons, although they act neither rightly nor holily and allow those who hold such views to continue holding them. We ourselves shall now contemplate, together with what has been said, the teacher’s meaning in another way.

I do not think, therefore, that here he wished to recount the cause of human generation, but rather the cause of the misery innate to it. For, lamenting the misery of our body by saying:

> “O conjunction and separation, which, while I fear it, I pursue; and what I love I have given,”

and the rest—as though deliberating within himself about the cause of the evils by which we are dishonored, and arguing against it with supremely wise prudence by what he says, “What wisdom is this concerning me, and what a great mystery?”—he added, plainly supplying the solution, as follows:

> “Or does he wish us to be a part of God and to flow from above, so that, exalted in dignity and contemplating heavenly things, we may not despise the Creator amid the struggle and battle against the body, while always looking toward him, and so that our conjoined weakness may nourish our dignity?”

It is as though he were saying this: Since man was made by God in goodness from soul and body, he will meditate upon the fact that he has been given a rational and intellectual soul, established according to the image of its Maker. Through desire and with universal love exerted with all its strength, this soul firmly possesses God by knowledge, and according to likeness will receive deification. In accordance, however, with the disciplinary providence directed toward what is subject to it, and with the commandment enjoining that one love one’s neighbor as oneself, it prudently receives the body; through the virtues it makes the body serve God as a fellow-servant, and through its own mediation it will cause the Maker to possess it, joining it to itself by an indissoluble bond through the gift of immortality. Thus what God is to the soul, the soul will become to the body; and the one Creator of all will be shown, entering proportionately through humanity into all things that exist.

Then those things that are far removed from one another according to nature will come together around the one nature of man, agreeing with one another; and God himself will become all in all, comprehending all things and establishing them as one in himself, since none of the things that exist will any longer be permitted to possess movement apart from his presence. Through this presence we are both gods and sons, and body and members and a part of God, and things of this kind, and are so called, in the final relation of divine contemplation. [Col. 1210B]

[Note: On this matter Maximus treated in the Proem to his Questions on Holy Scripture and elsewhere; there he indicates more fully that he will discuss what he has done here. See Photius, p. 498.]

Since, then, man was made both for this and in this, while in the first father he misused what had been prepared for potentiality, transferring desire from what had been permitted to what had been forbidden—for he was by nature capable both of cleaving to the Lord and becoming spirit, and, deceived, he chose instead to cleave to the prostitute and become body—and willingly expelled himself from the divine and blessed vision, thus, while he was God by grace, preferring by his will to become earth, God, the dispenser of our salvation, wisely, mercifully, and consistently with his own goodness, opportunely attached a punishment corresponding to the irrational movement of the intellectual power within us. Perhaps he thereby punished according to reason that very thing for which, in our soul, we cast away the virtue of love owed to God alone, so that, loving nothing, and eventually repenting through suffering, we might learn to restore that same virtue once more to what truly is.

Proceeding further, he makes this clearer when he says:

> “But to me it seems that nothing here among human goods is reliable, nor longevity, nor anything else; and if there is anything of this kind, it has been devised by the good Craftsman through a word well fashioned and by a wisdom surpassing every understanding. He deceives us through visible things, transforming them and being transformed in turn, carrying them upward and downward, causing them to stagger, and making them depart and flee before they can be grasped, so that, contemplating instability and irregularity in these things, we may pass over to what is to come.”

For what would we do in the present life, when it does not remain with us for good action? We attribute so much to it, and pleasure and error regarding it hold us subject to slavery, so that we are unable to understand anything better or higher than present things. Yet, if we hear and believe that we were made according to the image of God—who looks upward and draws us toward himself—

and again, in his discourse on those who live urbanely, he says:

> “So that we may know that we are nothing in relation to true and primal wisdom, but may always direct ourselves solely toward him and seek those who shine with the splendors that come from there, since through the inequality and instability of visible things he leads us over to things that stand and endure.”

Therefore, as I think, the Master is not here, in such statements, declaring the cause of that which belongs to the generation of humanity. Rather, he says that life itself has been weighed down with misery even after our generation because of the transgression, as is evident to those who reflect more inquisitively and diligently upon his divine writings.

In the case of the former matter, he added the words “from where,” “through what,” “from what,” and “for what purpose,” thereby declaring the salvation wisely administered for us by God. In the case of the latter, however—that is, the mystery in which it was accomplished—he used another mode of expression, making his entire pious intention concerning it manifest. Thus, in the discourse found under the title *γενέθλια*, that is, “births,” he declares:

> “The mind, then, and the senses, having already been distinguished from one another by their proper definitions, stood within themselves and bore within themselves the greatness of the Creator Word. In silence they praised the magnificence of the loud-voiced heralds. Yet there was not still a concretion from the two, nor any mixture of opposites, an indication of a greater wisdom and of great perfection concerning the natures, nor were all the treasures of goodness known.
>
> “But wishing to display this, the Craftsman Word creates one living being—I mean man—from invisible and visible nature. From matter already constituted he takes the body, while from himself he bestows life. The Word also knows the intellectual soul, and the image of God, as a second world: great in a small one. He establishes it upon the earth as another angel, a mixed worshiper, and so forth.”

In the discourse entitled *φῶτα*, that is, “baptisms,” he says:

> “Since these things are so—or something to this effect—it was necessary that worship should not be confined solely to those who are above, but that there should also be certain worshipers below, so that all things might be filled with the glory of God, since they too belong to God. For this reason man is created by the hand of God and is also honored with the image.”

I consider these statements sufficient, even if they establish little, for demonstrating the Master’s entire understanding of the matters under discussion—provided one distinguishes them without contentiousness and does not judge it glorious merely to quarrel.

If, however, there is disagreement over how the Master called us a portion of God, the explanation of this has already been given in many ways above. But so that the matter may become more credible through spiritual words, the holy and blessed Apostle Paul, praising the wisdom hidden in God before the ages, illuminating the whole darkness of human life, and driving the gloom of ignorance from souls, satisfies the Ephesians concerning it when he says:

> “That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart having been enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the operation of his mighty power, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and making him sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come.
>
> “And he placed all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all. And again, after a little while:
>
> “He himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers, for the equipping of the saints for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ; so that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, in the wickedness of men, in craftiness directed toward the art of error. Rather, speaking the truth in love, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every supply provided by him, according to the working of each individual member, makes the body grow for the building up of itself in love.” [Col. 1212B]

I do not think that anyone who knows how to live piously needs any further testimony for the manifestation of the truth truly believed according to Christianity, since it is openly learned through this statement:

> “For we are both members and body and fullness of Christ God, who fills all things in all, having been recapitulated in him according to the will hidden in God and the Father before the ages, through his Son and our Lord Jesus Christ.”

For the mystery hidden from the ages and from the generations has now been manifested through the true and perfect incarnation of the Son of God. He united our nature to himself inseparably and without confusion according to substance, and through it—through his holy flesh, intellectually and rationally animated, which is from us and belongs to our nature—he joined us to himself as though through firstfruits. He graciously willed that we should be one and the same with himself through his humanity.

As it was predestined before the ages that we should be in him as members of his body, he joined and united us to himself in the spirit, in the manner of soul to body, and brought us to the measure of spiritual maturity according to the fullness that is in him. He also showed that we were made for this purpose, and that God’s good will concerning us existed before the ages—not to be understood as arising through some novelty, but according to its proper principle, reaching its fullness through another, truly more marvelous mode that was introduced.

For since God was making us like himself, granting us, in participation, the distinctive marks of his goodness, seeing us as existing in him before the ages, and leading us altogether toward this supremely blessed end, he had bestowed upon us a mode of attaining it through the good use of our natural powers. But when man voluntarily rejected this mode through the misuse of his natural powers, God had to introduce another mode, more marvelous and more divine than the former, insofar as what is above nature is superior to what is according to nature.

And this, as we all believe, is the mystery of God’s most secret sojourn among human beings. For, says the divine Apostle, “if the first covenant had been faultless, no place would have been sought for a second.”

It is therefore clear to everyone how the mystery accomplished in Christ at the end of the age is undoubtedly the confirmation and fulfillment, at the beginning of the age, in the first ancestor, of the transgression.

The Master therefore aptly spoke of “a part,” according to the modes explained. Every generous person who receives the soul and the mode of the members in this way will understand the expression accordingly, bringing no wicked thought against himself, knowing that in such matters “member” and “part” are the same.

For if a portion of the body subsists as a member, and a portion is the same as a part, then that member is a part, and that part is a member. If, however, that member is a part, and the gathering and composition of members makes an organic body, while an organic body united with an intellectual soul manifests a perfect human being, then whoever says that the soul or body or member of a human being is his part will not depart from the truth.

If, moreover, the intellectual soul, as the soul of a human being, subsists as the body’s organizing principle, and if, throughout the whole body, the soul—which wholly fills it—gives it life and movement, then, being simple by nature and incorporeal, not divided into parts or enclosed within it, but wholly present to the whole body and to each of its members, it receives the body in accordance with the receptive power of the soul’s operation naturally subject to it. The members, receiving it wholly yet in different ways, unite proportionately in order to preserve it as one body.

Here the great and ineffable mystery of the blessed hope of Christians is introduced. It receives, in small things and in things according to us, likenesses that are great and that transcend us without being alien to us; and it has created a calm and readily accessible understanding concerning these matters.

And abandoning the irrational opinion that souls subsist before bodies, let him believe with us the Lord’s word concerning those who rise in the resurrection: that they cannot die, because of the manifestation and participation—rightly given at the end—which is utterly purified by him. And again:

> “Everyone who lives and believes in me will never die.”

If this had happened earlier, it would have been impossible for such a person, as stated above, ever afterward to receive death through some kind of conversion.

Let him also not depart from natural explanations by admiring, through vanity, a divine opinion about the soul that does not exist. For if the parts of a human being, as has already been explained, are constituted by body and soul, and if parts necessarily receive a relation to something—for the whole possesses the category in its entirety—then those things said to be relative belong to what exists simultaneously everywhere and always according to generation. Thus the parts complete the whole form through their conjunction, being separated from one another only by the intellect for the purpose of discerning what each is according to essence.

It is therefore impossible for soul and body, as parts of a human being, to subsist temporally before one another or to subsist afterward, since otherwise the account of what is said to be relative would be dissolved.

Again, if the soul is a form existing by itself before the body, or the body before the soul, then either each of these two completes another form through the composition of soul with body or body with soul, or they do so through being acted upon, or through existing naturally.

If through being acted upon, they undergo coming to be what they were not, and are corrupted. But if they exist naturally, then they will certainly always perform this according to what is natural, and the soul will never cease to become embodied, nor the body to become ensouled.

Yet, as I think, the fullness of the whole according to form does not arise from the passion or natural powers of the parts, according to the conjunction of one with the other; rather, in them both together there is the whole form of the generation.

Is it not therefore possible for some form to pass from one form into another without corruption? If, however, they say that, because the soul exists and subsists after death and the dissolution of the body, it can also exist and subsist before the body, their argument proceeds, as it seems to me, without due consideration.

For the account of generation is not the same as the account of essence. The former declares when and where something is and to what it is related; the latter declares that it is, what it is, and how it is.

If this is so—that the soul exists always after it comes to be according to essence—nevertheless it does not exist absolutely according to generation, but with the conjunction of time and place and in relation to something. For after the death of the body one does not simply say “the soul,” but “the soul of a human being,” and “the soul of a particular human being.” Even after the body it therefore possesses its whole form according to its condition, being predicated human as a part.

The same applies to the body: it is indeed dead by nature, but not absolute according to generation. For after separation from the soul one does not simply say “the body,” but “the body of a human being,” and “the body of a particular human being,” even if it is corrupted and customarily dissolved into the elements from which it is composed. Even then it possesses, as it were, its whole form according to its condition, being predicated human as a part.

In both cases, therefore—in soul and body, which are understood inseparably as parts of the whole human form—the condition demonstrates both their generation together and their difference from one another according to essence, without in any way violating the principles implanted in them according to essence.

It is therefore altogether impossible to find or speak of body or soul without a condition; for the being of one of them is introduced together with the other as belonging to something.

If one exists before the other, then how can it be understood as belonging to something? The condition is unchangeable.

Thus far concerning these matters. If the discussion has not departed from the truth, thanks be to God, who through your prayers leads us to understand rightly. But if it falls short of the truth anywhere, then correct the care exercised in the argument, instructed by God in the knowledge of such matters.

## CHAPTER III. FROM THE SAME DISCOURSE

**On this passage:** “While matter itself also bears forth an unordered kind of influx.”

I also think that the present intention of the discourse is to be understood in relation to the preceding chapter. Since he omitted many arguments against the lovers of matter and of the body, he added these words so that those who piously investigate the intention of the Saint might infer it as follows.

Since man was glorified by God and made beautiful through the beauty of incorruptibility and immortality, but preferred the ugliness of the material nature around him to intellectual beauty, he forgot the dignified condition belonging to the soul—and, rather, forgot God, who forms the soul in a godlike manner. Therefore, by a judgment worthy of all that he had made, God wisely administers our salvation, gathering the fruit not only of the body’s corruption and death, and of its movement and readiness for every passion, but also of the instability and irregularity of material essence outside and around it, which carries it away and makes it easily alienated.

This happened either when God then mingled the soul itself, because of our transgression, with our body, and inserted in the body a power capable of alienating the soul, subjecting it to passion, corruption, and complete dissolution—as the clothing of skins given to mortals in paradise makes clear—according to what is written: “The creation itself was subjected to corruption, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope”; or else from the beginning, through foreknowledge, when he created it in this way because of the foreseen transgression of man, so that, by suffering and being corrupted, it might of itself come into agreement with that transgression and with its proper dignity, and might receive again, inseparably, its affection for the body and for itself.
