For the supremely wise guardian of our life permits us naturally to use our own things according to their own movements, often using them for our moderation; at times, however, when we deal with them irrationally, through the confusion and disturbance surrounding them and arising from them, he leads our irrational love for present things toward what is lovable according to nature.

For since there are three universal modes by which, according to the learned, our passions are healed, through each mode a remedy is wisely applied to the disordered condition of matter. Matter is governed according to the higher and better principle above us, toward the good and beautiful perfection known to God, while the burden of the passions of evil is controlled.

Either we are exacting punishment for sins previously committed, of which we retain no memory or trace because of ignorance—though perhaps we remember them, yet have not endured to provide suitable correction for our offenses, either unwillingly or unable to do so because of an innate habit of evil; or we are being purified from weakness, or driving away the evil that is presently distributed [Note: [Col. 1215D] Greek *νεμομένην*, that is, “feeding upon us”], and learning again to look toward the condition of the future life; or one human being, whether distinguished by exalted character or renowned for understanding and virtue, and capable in himself of displaying an unshaken union against terrors, offers himself as a marvelous example to other human beings, thereby revealing for a time the hidden truth.

He therefore admonishes those who can understand nothing above the present life not to trust in bodily health, nor, while the present life endures, to be lifted up by the flowing and mobile course of things through their deficiencies [Note: [Col. 1215D] More correctly he would have translated: “nor, because of the course of their affairs, should they be exalted in offense against those who lack these things”], while they are swept around in the kind of corruption in which conversion and mutability occur. For it is uncertain what may befall them from the body and from the external dissimilarity and disturbance of things.

This, I think, is what he means by the words “while matter itself also bears forth an unordered influx”: that is, while the whole of this is subject to corruption and mutability, and while we put on the body of humiliation, we are likewise subjected to many evils through its innate weakness. We should not therefore be separated from one another by the inequality that surrounds us, but should rather, through prudent reflection, make inequality plainly serve the natural fellowship, filling the deficiencies of others with our own abundances.

Perhaps the present permission to live amid irregularity was granted for this reason: to demonstrate the power of the reason within us, which gives virtue precedence over everything. For the same conversion and mutability belongs to the bodies of all human beings and to external things. It both carries and is carried, possessing as its only stable and firm reality the fact that it is unstable and changeable.

## CHAPTER IV. OF THE SAME AUTHOR, FROM THE DISCOURSE TO ATHANASIUS

**On this passage:** “For it has nothing higher than what it altogether possesses.”

It seems to me that through these words this deiform Master has freed the person instructed in such matters from every comparative and discriminative habit, and from every manner of expression of that kind. Those who are wise in such matters say that this kind of expression is immense, and that it can be said to be incomparably above all things, since it possesses the power of transcendent negation.

## CHAPTER V. OF THE SAME AUTHOR, FROM THE EPITAPH FOR SAINT ATHANASIUS

**On this passage:** “To whom, then, was it permitted, by passing through matter and this carnal thing—which one must call either a cloud or a veil—through reason and contemplation, to become with God and to be held by the purest light, insofar as is possible for human nature? Blessed is he who, by ascent from here and by deification there, concerning which he is granted to philosophize sincerely, is made superior to material duality through the unity understood in the Trinity.”

For my part, I cannot accept a deficient account of the virtue of the saints from the Master, even though some, as you have written, think that by these words he means philosophy as the passage of those who go beyond matter to God through reason and contemplation alone, without action. On the contrary, I understand him to have introduced more openly a true philosophy joined to action, together with their judgment and activity concerning existing things—the philosophy that I, at least, boldly define as alone truly complete. He makes it clear that this is corrected by reason and contemplation. [Note: [Col. 1216D] Greek *αὐτόν*, “him.”] [Note: [Col. 1216D] Greek *ἀποφηνάμενον*, “making manifest”; the Greek has the feminine form, “making manifest,” referring evidently to *θεωρία*, “contemplation.”]

For action is wholly joined to reason, and the judgment that is in it is comprehended by contemplation. It belongs to reason to order the body’s movement, as though restrained by a bridle, held by correct reasoning in a disciplined manner from a course leading to inconsistency [Note: [Col. 1217D] Greek *ἀτοπίαν*, “depravity”]. It belongs to contemplation, through judging, prudently to exalt those things that are rightly understood and distinguished, like a most brilliant light displaying the truth itself through true knowledge. [Note: [Col. 1217D] Read *ostendentis*, “displaying,” rather than *ostendens*, “displaying”; the Greek has *δεικνυούσης*, “displaying,” evidently agreeing with *θεωρίας*, “of contemplation.”]

Through these two together every wise virtue is chiefly created and preserved. Through them it is also manifested by means of the body, though not in its entirety. For virtue cannot be contained by the body, since it is the imprint of divine power, but only certain shadows of the things that belong to it can be contained there.

And this manifestation does not occur for virtue’s own sake, but for the sake of those who are devoid of it, so that they may come to imitate the conduct of men who love God and are formed in his likeness. Through participation in the good, they may themselves lay aside the ugliness of evil and become portions worthy of God; or, by imploring help, they may obtain something from the powerful, receiving through bodily action made manifest the hidden affection of the eminent that lies deep within the soul, and praising God’s providence, which has become all in all and is present to all through all.

But if there were no one who needed to pray for good action, or who ought to be formed toward virtue by example, then he alone would be wholly sufficient for himself, enjoying the gifts of virtues belonging to the soul. Nor is it unreasonable to say that, without their approval through the body and their manifestation to the public, he would still possess them.

Whoever, therefore, piously understands through contemplation how existing things are, and through rational counsel carefully and correctly determines an account concerning them, preserving judgment for himself—or rather, preserving himself irreproachable in judgment—possesses the whole of virtue together. After recognizing the truth, he is moved toward nothing else, but hastens past everything, taking no account whatsoever of all that belongs to and is called flesh and world. He possesses an action already formed and comprehended by reason, without struggle.

For he brings into himself all the most powerful principles of our intellectual faculty in an impassible condition. Through these every virtue and knowledge exists and is established, since they are rational powers of the soul. Although they do not need the body at all in order to exist, they are nevertheless not blamed for using it at the proper time in order to become truly manifest for the reasons stated above.

They say that the special functions of the intellectual faculty are notions of intelligible things, virtues, knowledge, principles of the arts, purpose, and counsel; generally, they are judgments, comparisons, avoidances, and desires. Some belong solely to contemplation according to the soul, while others belong to the disciplinary power according to reason.

If the saints preserved their proper life guarded by such principles, then this blessed man, having comprehended all things belonging to virtue and knowledge through reason and contemplation, introduced the principles comprehended by the saints. Through these principles, receiving divine knowledge intelligently through contemplation, they prudently adapted themselves according to reason, through the virtues, entirely to the divine form.

He judged that it was unnecessary to call action by the name of the body, knowing that action does not produce virtue but manifests it, and that it serves only divine understandings and arguments.

To make what has been said clear in another way: those who carefully examine the principles of our affairs say that the rational nature is contemplative and active. It is contemplative according to the intellect, since the intellect possesses existing things; but it is active according to counsel, which determines the right principle for actions.

They call the contemplative faculty the intellect and the active faculty reason; the former wisdom and the latter prudence. If this is true, then the Master named action from its cause, according to what follows, and not from its matter, calling reason by a name that has no contrary condition. For the contemplative faculty attends to truths rationally and knowingly, not through hostility or contention, and because of their delight it does not admit of seeing anything else apart from them.

If it is necessary to make this clearer in yet another way, those who exercise the principles of perfection according to virtue say that some people, not yet purified from communion with matter in their habitual condition, are engaged in actions while their judgment concerning existing things is still mixed and they remain subject to conversion, not yet having laid aside their condition regarding changeable things.

Others, however, draw near to God in their condition through the summit of virtue, enjoying his blessedness intellectually, turned toward themselves and God alone, and sincerely breaking the bonds of material attachment. In action they are perfectly alienated from matter, while through contemplation they become intimate with God.

For this reason, they say, they remain unconverted, no longer possessing an attachment to matter by which one who has become concretely joined to matter is accustomed, by necessity, to be moved contrary to nature along with matter, which is naturally mobile. Seeing that the person who wishes to be freed from material passibility requires the greatest power for its removal, the Master says:

> “To whom, then, was it permitted, by passing through matter and this carnal thing—which one must call either a cloud or a veil—through reason and contemplation, to become with God,” and so forth?

## CHAPTER VI. HOW THE FLESH IS A CLOUD AND A VEIL

[Col. 1218D]

Why, then, does the Master call the flesh a cloud and a veil? He sees that every human soul, when it errs and looks backward from its natural movement, moves toward passion, sense, and sensible things, having nowhere else to move because it has fallen away from the movement that naturally carries it toward God. He divided the flesh into passion and sense—for both belong to animated flesh—and declared this through the terms “cloud” and “veil.”

A cloud is the carnal passion overshadowing the principal part of the soul [Note: [Col. 1218D] Literally so; “the principal part” is intended], while a veil is error according to sense, which overcomes the soul through the surfaces of sensible things and blocks its passage to intelligible things [Note: [Col. 1219D] Greek *ἀποτειχίζουσα*, that is, “blocking”].

Receiving through these things the forgetfulness of natural goods, the soul turns all its activity toward sensible things and finds, through what has been said, its rages, desires, and pleasures dishonorable.

## CHAPTER VII. HOW PLEASURE ARISES

Every pleasure in forbidden things ordinarily arises from passion, through the intermediary of sense, directed wholly toward some sensible object. For pleasure is nothing other than the form of sense formed in the sense-faculty through some sensible object, or the mode [Note: [Col. 1219D] Conjecture; Gale reads *mos*, “custom”; the Greek has *τρόπος*, “mode”] of sensory activity established by irrational desire.

For desire applied to sense is transformed into pleasure, adding a form to it; and sense moved by desire produces pleasure by receiving something sensible. The saints therefore understood that, just as the soul, moved contrary to nature toward matter through the intermediary of the flesh, puts on an earthly form, so even the flesh can fittingly serve God through the intermediary of the soul when it is moved according to nature toward God. They adorned it acceptably with divine intelligible principles through the cultivation of the virtues. [Note: [Col. 1219D] More correctly, “they meditated upon this.”]

## CHAPTER VIII. HOW MANY AND WHAT KINDS OF MOVEMENTS THE SOUL HAS

They taught, having been instructed by love [Note: [Col. 1219D] Greek *φωτισθέντες*, “having been enlightened or instructed”; the sentence depends on the verb “they ascended,” which follows], that the soul possesses three universal movements gathered into one: one according to the soul, another according to reason, and a third according to sense.

The first is simple and without interpretation. Through it, being moved unknowingly around God, the soul knows him in his excellence by no means through any of the things that exist.

The second is according to the defining cause of the unknown. Through it, being moved naturally, the soul imposes upon itself through activity and according to knowledge all the natural principles, which are formative within it, knowing them solely through the cause of what is known.

The third is composite. Through it, touching external things, the soul reforms within itself, as though from certain signs, the principles of visible things. Through these movements, according to the true and unchangeable mode of natural movement, they magnanimously passed beyond the present age of labors.

They possessed sense simply as having only the principles of sensible things; through the intermediary of reason they referred these principles to the soul. They possessed reason uniformly through one simple and indivisible prudence concerning existing things, uniting its principles in the soul. They offered the soul itself to God, with its movement toward all existing things purely freed and at rest from its own natural activity according to itself.

Through this soul they ascended universally to God and were made worthy to be wholly contained by God through the spirit, carrying the entire heavenly image insofar as is possible for human beings. They drew in as much divine knowledge—if it is permissible to say so—as they themselves, having been drawn in, were implanted in God.

For they say that God and man are paradigms of one another: God becomes human through mercy to the same extent that man, strengthened by love, consecrates himself to God; and man is seized by God according to the soul into the unknown to the same extent that man makes the God invisible by nature manifest through the virtues.

From this philosophy, therefore, established through reason and contemplation—and through which the nature of the body is necessarily ennobled—the saints, wounded without error by divine desire and worthily and beautifully reaching toward God through the innate natural understandings within them [Col. 1220B], came to God. They passed through body and world as soldiers, contemplating these things joined to one another: the world as related to nature, and the body as related to sense, with each yielding to the other in consequence of whatever affinity each has with the other. They judged that none of these things was free to subsist by itself, because of its circumscription; and, considering it shameful that what is immortal and ever-moving—the soul—should be corrupted and circumscribed by mortal and circumscribed things, they bound themselves indissolubly to God alone, who is immortal and superior to every infinity, in no way imbued with the recoilings of the world and of the flesh [Col. 1220D] [Greek: καὶ σαρκὸς ἀνθολκαῖς, “and the resistances of the flesh”].

This is the fullness of every virtue and of knowledge. I think, indeed, that it is also the end. But if at any time the saints were moved toward contemplation of the things that exist, they were not moved principally [Col. 1220C] to contemplate and know those things in themselves as we are, being materially moved; rather, they were moved so that in all things and through all things they might praise God, who exists and appears in manifold ways, and might gather for themselves great wonder at his power and the cause of his glorification.

For, receiving from God a soul possessing intellect, reason, and sense—this sensible soul together with the intelligible, just as the discursive reason that is expressed in propositions exists together with the reason that is inseparable, and intellect together with the intellectual faculty capable of suffering, which they also call the imagination of the animal, through which the other animals as well as one another, ourselves, and the places through which they have traveled recognize things—they said that sense is constituted around this imagination, since it apprehends such things, being its instrument through which it receives what has been imagined by it [Col. 1220D]. They judged it fitting, therefore, to refer the operations of these faculties not to themselves but to God, the giver, through whom and from whom these things exist.

For, having been instructed by careful consideration of the things that exist—so far as is possible for human beings—in the three universal modes derived from them, in which God made all things—for he established us in being, in well-being, and in perpetual being—they understood that the two extremes belong to God alone [Col. 1220D] [Greek: μονοῦ θεοῦ ἐχομένους, “depending upon God alone”], as their cause [Col. 1221A], while the middle belongs also to our will and movement. By itself this middle properly makes the extremes excellent; when it is absent, however, the name is abusively applied even to them, although they are not joined to that well-being.

They understood from the soul’s perpetual movement toward God that the truth existing in the extremes could not otherwise be present and preserved for them than by what well-being habitually does—namely, by the middle being mingled with the extremes. Thereafter, extending from this point the soul’s contemplative understanding according to nature, they learned that natural operations ought not, in a certain manner, to be used reversibly, because corruption necessarily gains the upper hand; rather, when natural powers are used abusively and reason itself does not openly employ them, they learned plainly to be borne, through nature’s fitting rational principle, to their cause [Col. 1221B], so that from him they may at some time receive what, in the simple sense, constitutes their being and their true being.

For what gain, perhaps, would there be, they said [Col. 1222A], reasoning equally with themselves, in moving from a causal being that exists from itself toward themselves—or toward anything other than God—when they could acquire nothing for themselves, in the account of being itself, either from themselves or from anything other than God?

Through this, they understood that the soul should be occupied with God alone and with his virtues, and should be devoted to the ineffable glory of his blessedness; that reason should become the interpreter and praiser of intelligible things, and should correctly discuss the ways by which they are unified; and that sense, ennobled through reason and imagining in existing things the various virtues and operations dispersed throughout the universe, should announce to the soul, so far as possible, the accounts of those things, teaching them [Col. 1221B] [the editor: I would prefer *docent*; Greek: διδάξαντες, “having taught”]. Thus, guiding the soul wisely, as though it were a ship, by means of intellect and reason, they passed with dry feet along this slippery and unstable road of life, which carries both sense and the soul, in different ways, toward something else [Col. 1222B].

[Col. 1221]

# Verses of John Scotus

## Section I. A Book of Very Many Verses

Verses of John the Most Wise to Charles the Bald, son of Louis the Pious, whose grandfather was Charles the Great [Col. 1221D] [The title of the codex is *A Book of Very Many Verses*. The words “Verses of John the Most Wise” through “Charles the Great” were written by the same hand in the margin of the codex.]

From a very old Vatican codex of the tenth or eleventh century, edited by Angelo Mai, *Classici Auctores*, vol. V, pp. 426 ff. They are now being published according to the authority of the Christina codex, 1587, fols. 57–65, collated, I think, with the same manuscript used by Mai.

### I. On Christ Crucified

[Col. 1221C]

Homer had sung of his Greeks and Trojans;  
Marō himself had fashioned the Romulean race.  
But let us sing the pious deeds of the King of the heaven-born,  
whom the rejoicing world celebrates in unbroken course.

[5] For them it was a game to recount the sudden fires of Ilium  
and the battles [Greek: μάχας; gloss: “fights”] of the Trojans.  
But for us it is sweet to sing in psalms Christ,  
bathed in blood after vanquishing the prince of the world.

They, trained to deceive beneath a contrived false image of truth,  
[10] with Arcadian verses.  
[Mai’s correction; the codex appears to read *falli*.]  
We may hymn the true power and true wisdom of the Father  
with exceptional praises.

They were accustomed to applaud the songs of the Muses,  
games, and loquacious satyrs before the peoples [Col. 1221D].  
[Codex: *Moysarum* rather than *Musarum*.]

The sayings of the prophets proceed harmoniously  
with beautiful melody from our hearts, mouths, and faith.

[Col. 1222C] Now, therefore, let us behold the supreme trophies of Christ  
and the clear stars of our mind.  
Behold: the square wood of the cross contains the world,  
on which the Lord hung of his own will,

[20] and the Word of the Father deigned to assume flesh,  
in which he became an acceptable sacrifice for us.  
Look upon his pierced palms, his shoulders, and his feet,  
and his temples cruelly encircled with a crown of thorns  
[codex apparently has *sorte*; Mai corrects to *serto*, “crown”].

[25] From the opened fountain of his side  
flow blood and water, draughts of life.  
The water washes the whole world from its ancient sin;  
the blood makes us mortals into gods.

Add the two guilty men hanging on the two trees:  
[30] their merit was equal, but their grace will be unequal.  
One saw the threshold of paradise together with Christ;  
the other, plunged into the depths of sulfurous Styx [Col. 1222D]  
[codex: *fagis*; gloss: “the marsh of hell”].

I was the shadow cast in the sun’s eclipse by the moon returning from the east,  
the heavenly body moving in an unfamiliar course.  
[35] The rocks split open, trembling when the center was shaken;  
the curtain was torn, and the holy places were opened to the peoples.

Meanwhile Christ, joyful and alone, enters the lower world,  
committing his buried limbs to a new tomb.  
The strong armed one [Greek: ὁπλίτης; gloss: “armed”] opened the gates of the abyss;  
[40] striking the enemy, he carried away the vessels he had recovered.

And, unwilling that the human race should perish in death,  
he snatched it all from the jaws of Erebus.  
We worship you, Christ, powerful over heaven and earth,  
for to you alone every knee is bent.

[45] You grant whatever you see is rightly asked;  
what is not rightly asked, you habitually refuse with justice.  
Grant that our king Charles may hold his kingdoms,  
which you bestowed upon his life-giving forefathers.

From your fountain kingdoms flow, enriching the world;  
[50] what you have not given—what flesh possesses it? [Col. 1223B]  
Deign to soften, according to your covenant,  
the wretched envy and savage fury of brothers.

But lest they disturb one another through malicious fraud,  
remove from life the seeds of wickedness.  
[55] Repelling hostile minds and pagan prows,  
grant peace to the people who honor your laws.

Now let us celebrate Charles’s return in a grateful song:  
after many groans our joys shine forth.  
Those who had been happy while seeking foreign kingdoms  
[60] seize the wings that flight itself gave them.

And powerful fear, disturbing their wavering hearts,  
compels their terrified backs to turn toward Charles.  
Alas [codex: *Heheu*], how disgraceful desire confounds hearts  
when Christ has been expelled from his own seats!

[65] [Col. 1223C] Would that peace, Louis [codex so; Mai: *Kludowice*], were in your lands,  
which he who rules all things together allotted to you!  
What do you wish to surpass in your brothers? What do you wish to drive from the kingdom?  
Are you not born from a similar stock?

Why do you thus strive to dissolve the divine laws?  
[70] And, ungrateful for what is your own, why do you seek what belongs to another?  
What do baptism and the holy solemnities of the Mass  
always insinuate to you by hidden signs?

Do they teach you to observe the brotherly commandments together  
and to live with all your strength and with a devout heart?  
[The codex reads *Numquid praecepta*; Mai incorrectly corrected it to *Numquid non praecepta*.]

[75] Listen fearfully to what supreme wisdom cries,  
teaching true doctrines that deceive no one.

If you are unwilling that trouble should come to you from elsewhere,  
presume to injure no one on your part.  
Christ, grant the rewards of heavenly life to your servants;  
[80] protect your own verse-making servants.

The servant pays the Lord what he owes,  
but let the Lord see to the servant’s reward.

### II. On the Cross

Behold the splendid sphere illumined by solar rays  
[Col. 1224A] which the life-giving cross scatters from its height.  
It holds earth, Neptune [gloss: “the Ocean”], the winds, and the poles,  
and whatever is believed to exist far above.

[5] While it recalls the wretched human race from the depths,  
with its point it strikes Tartarean Styx [gloss: “the marsh of hell”; “Styx,” the sorrow of hell].  
O nourishing cross, you shine beyond Seraphim and Cherubim!  
Everything above, what is and what is not, worships you.

You are worshiped by the Lords of the universe, by the Virtues and the Power,  
[10] and by the Order, rightly holding the middle place.  
Angel, Archangel [codex: *Aggelus, archagelus*], Prince, and the entire supreme  
heavenly host worship you, seeking the heights.

Then our church [Greek: πνὺξ; gloss: “church”] praises you with fitting melody,  
for through you it was redeemed as the bearer of Christ.  
[15] Did the great Moses once hold you in his hand,  
when he had become leader of the divine people?

Pharaoh is stupefied by you, clothed in a dragon’s skin,  
while you swallow others whom the magician’s art had given.  
O mountain of virtue, descending to the depths of flesh,  
[20] you are fixed upon the wood and enter the enclosures [gloss: “prisons”] of Erebus.

By your single death you dared to consume our double death,  
while renewing the whole human being.  
O cross, you cleave the waves of the Red Sea [gloss: “redden”; “the Erythraean Sea is the Red Sea”]  
and, victorious, go before, giving the people a way.

[25] Every virtue follows you, and life and salvation;  
the waves flee from you—I mean my sins.  
You give flowing streams to the sandy rocks [codex: *arenosis*; Mai: *harenosis*];  
whoever loves to live drinks deeply from this fountain.

You turn the bitter waters for the people into sweet waves;  
[30] the oppressive law is driven away, and grace alone remains.

There is also a meaning not unlike the acts just mentioned,  
if anyone learns to love symbolic [Greek: συμβολικὰς; gloss: “signifying”] signs.  
Moses is mystical Christ, both king and priest,  
who frees us from conquered Egypt.

[35] He himself first undergoes death, and, dissolving death,  
springs forth into life; having recovered the rod, he rules.  
Why do you pursue the people, Pharaoh? Flee, swallowed into the depths;  
may the dark marsh of the eternal prison cover you [codex so; Mai: “cover”].

While we travel the middle road of virtue,  
[40] the fantasies and towers of wickedness [gloss: “vaults”] press upon us.  
The mind, overcoming them, takes possession of the joyful shore  
and sees sins submerged and subdued far away.

Then, rejoicing and greatly triumphant, it sings a cry of victory [Greek: ἀλάλαγμα; gloss: “hymn of victory”],  
[Col. 1224D] and magnifies in praises the paradoxes [gloss: “miracles”] of God.

[45] Then, examining the shores of virtues, it enters the desert,  
where every love of the despised world is silent.  
The unclean spirit can find no rest there,  
where it never could; but it returns from where it came.

There a bronze serpent [gloss: “brazen”], hanging from above, hisses,  
[50] its venom extinguished; the people will be free.

[Col. 1225A] Magdalene [codex: *Magdaline*], why do you seek the Lord, sorrowful, buried?  
With the burial overcome, look joyfully upon God.  
Cease imagining that you see the gardener’s face [gloss: “garden, gardener”; understand it thus: Greek [κῆπος], “garden,” hence *caeparius*, “gardener”].  
The Lord is alive and present: see him yourself, whom you mourn.

[55] With your pious cheeks dried, you will quickly console the brothers:  
blessed first evangelist, farewell.

Christ, Word of God, power and wisdom of the Father,  
your blood, the wave with which the altar of the cross is drenched,  
cleanses us, redeems us, releases us, and restores life,  
[60] and grants your chosen ones to be gods.

Grant peace to our Charles, to whom you gave the scepters [codex: *scepha*],  
and let his fierce enemy perish everywhere.  
And, so that he may please you throughout all the years in which he lives,  
scatter the seeds of virtues upon your servant.

[65] Let their power clearly arise and grow into deeds,  
so that deservedly he may always rule everywhere with you.

[Col. 1225D]

Orthodox [Greek: ὀρθόδοξος], pious, renowned king [Greek: ἄναξ εὐσεβὴς ἔγκλυτος] [ἄρχος].

Sober, Christ-bearing lord Charles [Greek: σώφρων χριστοφόρος κύριος ὁ Κάρολος] [codex omits ἄρχος; supplied by conjecture; Mai has ὁπλίτης].

The Greek verses in the codex, with glosses, read:

“right-believing, pious, glorious king”  
[Greek:] ὀρθόδοξος ἄναξ εὐσεβὴς ἔγκλυτος

“sober, Christ-bearing, the lord himself”  
[Greek:] σώφρων χριστοφόρος κύριος ὁ Κάρολος

“armed one, serpent, Egypt, radiance, lightning, thunder”  
[Greek:] ὁπλιστής ὄφις Ἰσίδα αὐγή

The last three words seem to refer to poems III.24, III.26, and VIII.18.

I, John, your unworthy little servant,  
[70] sang these verses—six tens, twice four—  
singing [Greek: μέλπω] joyfully, paying my dues to the king.  
Would that I might pay them, if they should be pleasing to him.

### III. On Easter

If I say “Passover” in Hebrew ears [codex: *aebraicis*],  
the term “passage” is suitable for Ausonian usage.

If you wish to know the first Passover of nature,  
ask which day first shone in the world.

[5] [Col. 1225C] On that day, it is said, the structure of the world, in ordered succession,  
passed from nothingness into its proper forms.  
The Creator brought forth into visible forms  
the causes that he had always held within himself.

Then the spherical earth was confined within a definite boundary,  
[10] and clothed with its leaves and vegetables [Greek: λαχάνοις; codex *lachanis*, gloss “herbs”].  
A sea-coast ring enclosed Nereus, Neptune’s sea-monster [gloss: “sea-monster”],  
which the blue wave, swelling with its hair, cannot surpass.

The moon’s horns touched the airy expanse,  
which winged birds cut through with their powerful necks.  
[15] The star-bearing sphere surrounded the heavenly circuits,  
encircling the world with constant movements.

A harmonious host of wanderers was borne along in varied procession  
and itself produced sweet tones.  
Six in number, seven by number, in eight measured intervals,  
[20] the harmony of the heavenly sphere was established [Col. 1225D].

Afterward the final king of the world is said to be destined  
to possess the palace, if his deeds had not been what they were.  
Alas, but a wretched woman, his consort, deceived him,  
whom the serpent’s cunning first destroyed when she was unwary  
[for Greek [ὄφεως], “of the serpent”; gloss: “serpent”].

[The numbering in the source returns here to 20.]

[20] Moses, leader of the people, celebrated the second Passover,  
striking Egypt [gloss: “Egypt”] with ten plagues.  
The Lord passed over the doorposts marked with blood,  
while Egypt herself mourned her firstborn.

The Israelites hurriedly ate the lamb;  
[30] with its bones unbroken, it was a mystical supper.  
The joyful people departed; faithless Egypt mourned,  
and, maddened by rage, pursued the one she feared.

Then anxious Moses looked upon the Red Sea [gloss: “redden”];  
the frightened people, ignorant of his power, doubted.  
[35] Pharaoh’s host, held back by dark clouds,  
stood fiercely stupefied, lest it seize the prey.

[Col. 1226B] Then the fearless leader cut through Neptune’s fields  
and the water offered a road of unknown marble [Mai’s correction; the codex reads “the road of unknown marble, the water”].  
The wind dries the burning sandy shores [codex: *ammonia*, from Greek [ἄμμος], “sand”; gloss “sandy”; Mai’s *harmonia* is incorrect],  
and the blue water rises forward like a wall.

[40] The people enter safely through the whirlpool of waters  
and, as they emerge rejoicing, see the pleasant shore.  
The Egyptian enemy is overwhelmed by the heaps of the sea;  
chariots [Greek: ἅρματα; codex: *armata*] cover the depths of Thetis in scattered array.

[45] These things once were images [Greek: ἰνδάλατα; codex: *idalmata*, gloss “images”] of the Christ who was to come,  
in whom the things long hidden shine together.  
He alone, victorious, having cast down the prince of the world,  
springs forth from Erebus after three days.

And first, treading upon death, he passed into the heights,  
[50] alone free from Tartarean power.  
Pouring out the pure libations of his own blood,  
he consecrates a new Passover for the world he has saved.

The Lord himself, of his own will, slays himself as priest;  
he was the one sacrifice pleasing to the Father.  
[55] The sacrifice that cleansed the whole world from sin,  
the world which the first man had been able to destroy.

From one came death; through one it was driven out.  
By a good death, evil death is conquered and perishes.  
Christ, as first-fruits, opened the enclosure of the tomb,  
[60] restoring what had been lost from our nature.

Now the sacred symbols of these things are celebrated,  
while they are present to the eyes but previously known to the mind;  
while the devout mind apprehends in its heart the body of Christ,  
the wave of sacred blood, and the price of the world;

[65] while we recall the Lord’s supper through the years  
and the chorus itself joins together many songs [Col. 1226D].

Deign, Christ, to feed your Charles  
[Col. 1227A] with the eternal banquets represented by mystical signs,  
your devoted servant, who venerates and honors you,  
preparing golden vessels in buildings he has constructed,

[70] with open curtains stretched through the long halls,  
and with a clergy clothed in purple-red.  
Holy priests resound around the altars:  
thus he himself will be yours in temples everlasting.

### IV. Praises of Yrmindrudis, Wife of Charles the Bald

These things, fittingly praised for their merits, adorn  
our lady Yrmindrudis, illustrious by name:

beauty, lineage, appearance, the most splendid reputation for character,  
a royal marriage, and learned speech that teaches;  
[5] the gift of distinguished offspring and a well-known descent [codex so; Mai corrects to “sufficiently known”],  
and exemplary devotion to all good things;

great intelligence and perfect skill in the art of Pallas,  
preparing silken threads with delicate gold.  
Her husband’s robes shine through her exceptional deeds;  
[10] a chain of jewels reveals the garments [gloss: “clothing”].

The fleeing spider [Greek: ἀράχνη; codex *arachnos*, gloss “spider”] marvels and never draws near,  
although she rivals the fingers of Pallas.  
Renowned for her counsel, she preserves the chaste marriage bed,  
so that Cypris cannot stain the couches [codex: *thoros*].

[15] Her most just concern for many poor people,  
urges her to be their proper minister.  
She shines as the constant companion of prudent mothers  
whose doctrines the sacred teachings praise,

praying, reading books, and working with her hands;  
[20] no time lies idle for vices.

[Col. 1227C] Should I speak of the affairs of the kingdom, which she herself, skilled in them,  
arranges with an exceptionally watchful heart [codex: *vigilo*]?  
If the letters that Solomon himself had written allowed it,  
perhaps I would have said what they intended to testify.

[25] For this woman is rightly judged a strong woman,  
whom Charles, the strong and life-giving king [Greek: ἄναξ; gloss: “king”], found.  
The glory of the Franks celebrates him alone as king,  
worthy of Christian peoples and choirs.

He is permitted to bear the many scepters of kingdoms,  
[30] which his great forefathers sustained.  
In him alone, with wisdom leading the way, kingship flourishes;  
the discipline of a pure mind ennobles him.

Scripture, full of divine figures, teaches him  
not to weaken on Christ’s straight path.  
[35] Dedicating holy churches, he adorns them with generous ornaments  
[Col. 1227D] and beholds the sacred symbols of the heavenly homeland.

Protect these two, Christ—the powerful king and lady—with the help of your divine power.  
Be their faithful guardian, a secure wall forever,  
[40] so that they may continually offer vows pleasing to you.  
May both always praise you with devoted minds,  
with harmonious voices and good deeds.

Strike down their arrogant and rebellious enemies,  
or instruct those who have been converted to submit their necks.  
[45] [Col. 1228A] Grant peace to the people who serve you everywhere;  
may nurturing tranquility flourish among all Christians.

The pagan pirates [codex: *paganas*; Northmen who came by fleet] devastating kingdoms throughout the world—  
consume them with the sword and plunge them into the sea’s whirlpool.  
Let them be scattered by the south winds among various sandbanks,  
[50] so that they may perish there amid the tides of the ocean.

But lead us, joyful, as we worship you with a pure heart,  
above the stars and the heavenly choirs.

### V. On Christ’s Resurrection

The mystical doctrines of the holy Fathers are opened,  
which they sang to God through the sanctifying Spirit,  
to the eternal Word of the Father, through whom all things are created,  
each in its own order in hidden recesses.

[5] By him the fabric of the world, in all its forms together,  
rose as one, according to its own rational principle.  
It had been made in Christ before time,  
while he, eternally begotten, beholds all created things.

Above this the holy Spirit is exalted, according to the governance of reason,  
[10] so that he might give life to the sacred waters.  
He established the angelic host occupying the camps of the higher world,  
and all the other things that you see.

Paradise possessed humanity as their chief [codex: *primaten*],  
made capable in mind of seeing God.  
[15] Unwilling to embrace this splendid form,  
the human being fell and dragged his offspring down with him.

But, lest so great an image of God pass away altogether,  
God began to possess this form of the human being.  
Hence, born into the world and suffering under the law of evils,  
[20] by his death he himself destroyed my death [Col. 1228C].

The God through whom things exist, live, stand, and move—all things—dies,  
so that the human being himself may live.  
Marked out in many ways for the Fathers of old,  
he is sacrificed for the Law and sung by the prophets.

[25] He was the ram provided beforehand for the altar,  
while Isaac, in figure, was led to the slaughter.  
The hurrying people had taken this lamb in Egypt,  
sprinkling its blood on the familiar doorposts of the house.

He was the fountain, the rod, the rock, the heavenly radiance overshadowing,  
[30] the serpent, the manna, the cloud, the way, the bread, and the water:  
such things, often made in time at God’s command,  
signified their eternal Lord.

On this fulfilled sacred day they are revered with honor [codex: “we revere”];  
[Col. 1228D] this day contains such great mystical deeds.

The world proclaims it, rejoicing together in beautiful light:  
it sends its flower-bearing motions into the upper air,  
bringing forth shoots and fruits flowering in the grass;  
[35] for Christ is sweet fruit everywhere for his own.

Christ has risen; from this our devout hearts resound,  
and the whole world everywhere sings “Alleluia” to God [codex: *orbis*; Mai: *mundus*].

Illustrious among kings, may the King preserve you forever;  
may he grant you prosperity and carry you from here above the stars [codex: *Prospera*; Mai: *Prosper*].  
[Col. 1229A] You establish alternating musical choirs  
in honor of him with a humble heart, and you yourself sing psalms with them.

[45] We believe that these things are preserved for you in the heights of heaven;  
may you become a pious heir of David.

In the prayers [Greek: προσευχῆς] we ask with vows and pray with our heart:  
may God, who gave you the will, give you the ability.

To our king Charles: you, Christ, help  
[50] so that he may be able to inherit the heavenly choirs [Col. 1229D].

The distich is written in the codex as follows:

“Our king, favor him—  
[Greek:] βασιλεὺς Καρλοῦ ἡμῶν, σὺ Χριστὲ βοήθει—  
so that he may be able to possess the heavenly choirs,  
[Greek:] ὡς κληροῦσθαι χοροὺς δυνατὸς οὐρανίους.”

### VI. Christ’s Descent into Hell and Resurrection

Great light flashes from Erebus in triumph,  
the first-fruits of life, which the dying world looks upon in astonishment.  
The Furies spring forth; the Fates rush together from every side;  
they marvel that gloomy Styx has groaned together.

[5] Then the prince of the abyss, who had himself subjected the human race to him, seeks his customary weapons [Col. 1229B].  
But as soon as he saw the thresholds collapsing and broken,  
terrified and stunned, he fled into the depths of the house.

Yet the tyrant did not escape through the dark caves;  
[10] a stronger one entered and carried away his vessels.  
Dragged away, captured, bound, and held fast in tight chains,  
detained, subdued, driven from the citadel where previously,

exalted as prince of the world, he had once sat,  
the savage, devouring, long-unconquered beast—  
[15] but the one victor of the world, superior to all,  
alone smashed and crushed his entire head.

The fires of eternity burn the shameful corpse;  
the fierce flame of Pyriphlegethon [codex: *pyrflegetontis*] rages.  
The wretched rejoice whom the dread power had injured;  
[20] captives return, and the loosened bonds lie empty [Col. 1229C].

Now the Word of the Father reigns; now he governs all things:  
power, life, and salvation; conquered, savage death is silent.  
He rose alive, breaking the restraints of death [codex: *loeti*];  
no force can hold back the Most High God.

[25] He willingly laid down his soul and took it up again;  
what he was able to lay down, he does not permit to remain.  
What he gives for the life of the world, he recalls again;  
what is given is received, and what is handed over remains safe.

Such is the price given for the world—marvelous to say!  
[30] Everything is preserved, restored, and given.  
Who could declare what the Redeemer himself has done?  
He possesses what he bought and possesses the price.

O light forever shining and revealing the world,  
[Col. 1229D] victor over the shadows feared by devout hearts,  
[35] be Charles’s guardian, a safe wall on every side;  
protect the scepters of your servant, who governs them.

[Col. 1230A] Enough, enough of placing a very few ungrateful verses  
that trouble the king. What is the use of establishing  
what the recently submitted Muse plainly declares [codex: *aedita*]?  
[40] Deprived of reward, she was sad and empty.

Verses of John to King Charles [Greek: στίχοι Ἰωάννου τῷ βασιλεῖ Καρόλῳ] [Col. 1230D].

The codex has the verses thus:

“The verses of John to King Charles,”  
[Greek:] τοῦ στίχοι Ἰωάννου τῷ βασιλεῖ Καρόλῳ.

### VII. Further on Christ’s Resurrection

The light surpassing the souls of human beings and the armies of the heavenly gods,  
established by earthly tones,  
was in the bosom of the Begetter, far removed  
from the sensible world and the empyrean pole.

[5] It visited the wretched in the deepest seats of darkness,  
the bound, the captives, and the guilty of Tartarus  
[the line from “It visited…” through “guilty” is omitted by Mai].  
Christ was incarnate, born from a virgin,  
fastened to the wood, buried in a tomb [Greek: τάφῳ; codex: *tapho*].

[Col. 1230B] Yet dying in body, alive in soul and in God,  
[10] God himself dies, so that the flesh itself may live.  
The mind holds Erebus, the body the rock, the divinity all things;  
the one is threefold in body, mind, and God.

After he had entirely destroyed Hades [Greek: ἅδην; codex: *achan*] in three days,  
[15] he rose entirely, with nothing left behind.  
He ascended entirely and rules the entire world—behold—  
for which the Creator and God had suffered.

And he recalled the entire human race from the cavern  
of eternal death, into which every human being falls—  
[20] that race ungrateful for the gift of life and despising the salvation  
which the greatest high Father [codex: *archiater*] had bestowed.

O king, who illumines the world with splendid light,  
grant every prosperity to your Charles.  
Forgive the contaminations of your fragile servant’s life,  
[Col. 1230C] so that he may be able, pure, to behold your kingdoms.

Verses of John to his own lord, King Charles [Greek: στίχοι τοῦ Ἰωάννου τῷ κυρίῳ αὐτοῦ ἄνακτι Καρόλῳ] [Col. 1230D].

The codex has the verse thus:

“Verses to his own lord the king,”  
[Greek:] οἱ στίχοι τοῦ Ἰωάννου τῷ κυρίῳ αὐτοῦ τῷ ἄνακτι Καρόλῳ.

### VIII. On the Incarnate Word

If you wish to fly upward through the heavenly airs [Greek: οὐρανίας; gloss: “heavenly”]  
and cut through the empyrean [gloss: “fiery”] poles by the movement of your mind,  
with a blue-gray eye [gloss: “eye”], like one seeing by night [gloss: “night-seeing”],  
you will survey the temples of wisdom, whose summit  
is hidden by a dense cloud,

[5] which surpasses every sense, every intellect [Greek: νοεροὺς; gloss: “intellects”], and every reason [Greek: λόγους].  
Then a mist [Greek: γνόφος; gloss: “darkness”] once veiled the summit [Greek: κορυφήν; gloss: “peak”] of Sinai,  
when God was teaching Moses the ancient law [Greek: θεσμόν; gloss: “law”],  
leaving traces of the soles of his feet [Greek: ταρσῶν; gloss: “feet”; *tarsos*, sole of the foot] amid the shadows.

There you will see the many-eyed Seraphim flying,  
[10] spreading six wings from each of three pivots,  
and around and behind God the many multiform animals [Greek: ζῷα; gloss: “animals”] [Col. 1230D],  
all gazing with bright light upon their cause,

[Col. 1231A] the one principle by which the order of things turns  
into genus, species, rhythms, times [Greek: χρόνους; gloss: “times”], and places [Greek: τόπους; gloss: “places”];  
they see what is and what is not, whether through sense or mind,  
what stands and what turns with varied movement,

[15] the spirits [Greek: πνεύματα; gloss: “spirits”] of the winds, the fiery force, the shining ether,  
and the chorus of the purest light of the star-bearing radiance [Greek: αἴγλη; gloss: “brightness”]  
of Pallas. Hence the crown is encircled with seven jewels:  
Phoebe, and Stilbon, and Light, and Sun, and Mars,

[20] Phaethon and Phainon, around the highest regions, frost;  
then, at the center of the world, Thetis, the unmeasured sea [Col. 1231D].

The verses in the codex are written as follows, with glosses:

“moon and Mercury and Lucifer, Sun, Mars;  
Jupiter and Saturn, frost around the highest regions;  
Phaethon, Phainon, around the highest zones;  
then, at the center of the world, the immeasurable Ocean alone,”

[Greek:] Φοίβη καὶ Ἰστίλβων καὶ φῶς Ἥλιος Ἄρης  
Φαέθων Φαίνονος ἄκροι περὶ κλίματα πάχνη  
ἔξης τοῦ κόσμου κέντρον Τηθὶς ἄσχετος ἅλας.

The heavenly movement is nine-sounding in its melody [Greek: ἐννεάφθογγος; gloss: “ninefold sound”],  
and the highest lyre [gloss: “lyre”] of voices escapes mortal ears [Greek: ὦτα; gloss: “ears”].

[25] Know Christ as the first beginning of things,  
the Word creating all things, born from the Father’s breast,  
art, law, counsel, life [Greek: ζωή; gloss: “life”], wisdom, and power,  
the fountain, middle, and end, light begotten from light.

He is, is not, and is above; he gave being to all things;  
[30] he governs and holds all that he himself created,  
entirely present throughout the whole, attached to no parts,  
since he is the simple substantial essence of all things.

Being, he is the end and the beginning of all, being the things that are;  
being good and beautiful, he is beauty and the exemplar of forms [Col. 1232D].

The codex has these verses with glosses:

“being, end, beginning of all, he who is the things that are, the things that subsist;

[Greek:] ὢν τέλος, ὢν ἀρχὴ πάντων, ὢν ὄντα τὰ εἰσίν;

being most good and excellent, beauty and exemplar of forms;

[Greek:] ὢν ἀγαθός, καὶ καλός, κάλλος μορφῶν τε χαρακτήρ.”

[35] He, recalling wretched human beings from everlasting death,  
became human [Greek: ἄνθρωπος; gloss: “human being”], taking flesh from a virgin;  
he came as promised, fulfilling the oracles of the prophets.  
David, his grandfather [Greek: πρόγονος; gloss: “grandfather”], had foreseen him  
born from his own seed [gloss: “seed”], and the Redeemer [Greek: λυτρωτήν; gloss: “redeemer”], with the world’s death conquered  
[Col. 1231C].

[40] The mysteries of Christ are no less beneficial in heaven  
than on earth, since he is rightly the same God for all things.  
There he revealed angelic minds through the light  
and disclosed to them the darkness of his power.

No power was able to recognize purely  
[45] the one whom the Father concealed in his shadowed bosom.  
But now the Word made flesh—wonderful to say!—  
clearly reveals himself to all as both human being and God.

Mind and reason [Greek: νοῦς τε λόγος τε; gloss: “mind and reason”] apprehend him, whom no one had previously seen;  
[50] for the fleshly [Greek: σαρκικά; gloss: “fleshly”] nature [Greek: φύσις; gloss: “nature”] tempers the divine radiances [Greek: αὐγάς; gloss: “splendors”].

By being born, he bestowed life upon all,  
and destroyed death, which had swallowed the whole world.  
O what power could overcome the proud one,  
who had subjected the human race to a cruel law,

[55] wishing to restore what the first man had lost,  
the man formed from clay who had misused the gift of life,  
but who, made from a virgin, took on that by which he could die,  
and of his own will made good use of the death of his flesh!

What measure can the mind possess when it attempts to behold such things?  
What senses can contemplate them through the utterance of words?

[60] The Virgin’s womb [Greek: παρθένος; gloss: “virgin”] was moved by an angelic utterance,  
[Col. 1232B] and, with faith accompanying her, received offspring by the Spirit [Greek: πνεῦμα; gloss: “spirit”].  
O blessed belly [Greek: γαστήρ; gloss: “belly”] that bears the divine fire!  
The ray of power is made solid in the sacred body [Greek: σῶμα; gloss: “body”].  
The twofold substance reveals one person.

[65] For eternal God, taking reason in time,

had perfected himself as a man, **ἄνδρα** 

in bodily form,

Jesus Christ, reigning forever through the ages.

We worship you, light of the world; you, Christ the Redeemer,

wipe away the wounds of believers with the fountain of your side.

[70] And since your provident power wills that nothing belonging to humanity should perish,

it embraces our nature, **φύσιν** without any sin.

Our nature is thereafter wholly renewed in that one,

and the potent antidote, prepared to benefit all,

drives away the various wounds of those who drink it through its structure,

[75] while justly allowing those unwilling [to receive it] to perish, as they deserve.

[Col. 1232C] For God compels no unwilling person to live,

nor does he drive anyone who wills the good from the threshold of light;

inviting everyone, he abandons some and helps others,

ordering all things, and himself is praised in all.

[80] Christ, deign to visit your fearful servants,

who celebrate your feasts and venerate the gifts of salvation.

Spare your servant, to whom you have given the royal scepters;

perfect and purify him, suffused with the divine ray.

## SECTION II. VERSES OF JOHN ΣΚΟΘΘΙ



From a very old Vatican manuscript of the eleventh century, edited by Angelo Mai, *Classici Auctores*, vol. V, pp. 444 ff. They are now published according to the evidence of the manuscript of the Christina Library, 1709, fol. 16, 2 ff., which, I think, is the same manuscript used by Mai, and has been collated.

[Col. 1231]

### I. Christ’s triumph over death and the devil

[Col. 1231C]

After our salvation had renewed the whole world,

[Col. 1232C] and had completed all the deeds which the Father willed,

weary from great labor, he rested while hanging upon the tree.

In the span of three double lights he had destroyed **ἅδην**, Hades,

[5] sleeping beneath the hard roof of the cold stone,

[Col. 1233A] fulfilling the prophetic symbol of the prophet-spewing whale.

Then the terrified shades suddenly sprang forth in scattered groups

from the depths of Phlegethon, astonished that light was rising,

driving the foul and savage phantoms from their prison.

[10] O death, death of life! If it is death, it ought not to be called life;

what bestows life I would not dare call death.

Does the substance of light, shining brightly, receive darkness?

The blazing power of fire knows no cold creeping into it. 

Yet no one could deny that Life tasted death:

[15] the death of the flesh is rightly called the death of Life,

for Life suffered with the flesh, which alone hung there.

The edge of pure reason penetrates more deeply

and thus gathers that the flesh of Life is itself life.

If the Word is life, and if the Word also became flesh,

[20] it plainly follows that one must acknowledge the flesh to be life.

[Col. 1233B] If the flesh became the Word, by a converse course,

you are at once compelled to grant that the flesh has become life.

Therefore Christ’s flesh, **Σὰρξ**, subsists as the truest Life;

living and dying, he had consumed all death.

[25] He came from above to assume an earthly garment;

clothed in the garment, he flew upward with the garment,

and transformed into God the garment taken from the virgin,

making one thing of soul, flesh, and God.

The Lord, death’s death, rose alive on high

[30] and carried our nature with him to the same place.

Having come to be in the whole of nature, he shapes the whole into one.

He trampled the frail world and the world’s powerful ruler,

and overcame him, cast outside, in a victorious battle.

Recalling captive booty from the mouth of its captor,

[35] he took it away; that proud one groans, pierced in his limbs

[Col. 1233C] by harsh wounds, and, turning such thoughts over with himself, says:

“I see myself defeated, driven as a fugitive from my dark dwelling.

What new light is rising, which I shall never be able to endure?

Now my kingdoms are collapsing everywhere; no place remains for darkness;

[40] I feel myself captured, terrified, and bound in chains.

Alas! Who is confronting me? Who, strong in arms,

boldly engages the world’s prince in battle?

Is it that one nailed to the wood and enclosed in a tomb,

whom King Herod rejected, and whom the high priest Caiaphas

[45] did not fear to condemn, tearing his garment,

delivered to death and struck down by the Roman governor?

I myself did this, I confess, and carried it all through.

I, a fool, failed to recognize that power and humble authority.

[Col. 1233D] If I had known him, he would never have hung upon the cross, **σταυρῷ**,

[50] but the servile form of a human body deceived me.”

Meanwhile he looks upon joyful souls flying through the air,

and upon the Tartarean recesses emptied and the loosened chains,

and he nourishes a wound beneath his sorrowful breast.

“What torments me still more miserably,” he says, “is that I now see

[55] [Col. 1234A] the gates of paradise, long closed to earthly beings, opened,

and the mortal race, which had flowed from there through one man,

returning above the stars because of the death of one man.

There the offspring of earth will rightly inhabit

the blessed dwellings which I voluntarily abandoned.

[60] But my perverse will will torment me—me, me—forever;

I die languishing in envy, and am deservedly consumed.

One refuge remains, and one consolation:

the ancient house of death and the profound night,

the Jewish heart, a chasm full of vices,

[65] a great and perpetual possession of deceit and envy,

angrily repelling the rays of the hated light.

There alone treacherous hypocrisy rules with power;

it stinks greatly and, with excessive rottenness,

corrupts the hearts of the carnal people, ignorant of truth.

[70] [Col. 1234B] There I shall flee, abandoning the hearts of the Gentiles;

I shall rule over the avaricious people, hateful to Christ;

I shall pour all my venom through blasphemous mouths,

denying that the Lord suspended upon the wood reigns.”

While the cruel, deceitful beast handled such thoughts,

it fell backward and fled beneath the cold shadows.

The dominion of the Father, sought through the blood of his Son,

surpasses the boundaries of the earth, Hades, and heaven.

Orthodox faith, in diverse speech throughout the world,

cries, “Abba, Father,” praising the highest mysteries,

[80] the fruitful offspring of one and triune goodness,

the unbegotten and begotten God, and the eternal murmur 

of the inexhaustible fountain from which the rivers of life flow.

### II. Further verses of the same author



[Col. 1234C]

The Greekling, the Jew now, the Agarene, and the Ausonian,

and the savage pagan rising from the northern axis,

will submit their necks; Christ will reign everywhere;

all will yield to him, the king and God.

[5] O highest Father of the Son, giver of the nourishing gift,

protect the people who always celebrate your feasts,

the people over whom your wisdom, ordering kingdoms throughout the world,

set Charles as king and pious minister,

to whom inward light gave sharpness of mind,

[10] so that, contemplating divine matters, he may also govern human affairs,

truly being at once king and theologian.

O Dionysius, bishop from Athens, ally of Paul,

famed for martyrdom, whom all Gaul serves,

[Col. 1234D] look down from the lofty seats of heavenly life

[15] upon the prayers of your child, **τέκνου** Charles,

who adorns your holy relics, **λείψανα**, and your gracious church

with magnificent works, like flames with blazing gems and gold.

From every side the altars breathe the fragrance of incense,

the harmonious songs of the worshipers, **θιασωτῶν**, strike the stars,

[20] and the most holy supper is prepared by the service of the singers.

## SECTION III. JOHN SCOTUS’S VERSES ON THE “AMBIGUA” OF SAINT MAXIMUS

From a manuscript of the Library of the Arsenal in Paris, edited by M. Félix Ravaisson in the book entitled *Reports to the Minister of Public Instruction on the Libraries of the Departments of the West*, Paris, 1841, pp. 356 ff.

[Col. 1235]

### I. He dedicates his translation of Saint Maximus’s *Ambigua* to Charles the Bald

[Col. 1235A]

Hail, O Lord (**Kyrrie**), whose heavenly form shines with grace,

whose Caesar-like face is encircled by starry crowns,

offspring of kings, whom fortunate Francia has increased,

whom the world’s peoples greet in a loud voice,

[5] magnify with praises, venerate, enrich, and honor;

rushing together from every side, it crosses the sea and passes over the fields [the printed *eminet arva* is difficult].

Hail, crown of Christ-worshipers, most gracious of kings,

pious king, do not disdain the little gifts of your devoted servant.

A small gift, but drawn from the abundant fountain

[10] of the Christ-bearing Fathers, treating very many mysteries.

Maximus the abbot composed this work in Greek.

An outstanding shepherd, a writer renowned for the Scriptures,

[Col. 1235B] he clarifies the sayings of Gregory the Great that are remote

from human understanding, pondering their contemplations in his mind.

[15] Dionysius the Areopagite himself is also added in many places,

whom he adorns with abundant praises,

explains, and calls both witness and blessed Father,

touching upon symbolic books with splendid illumination.

It is Dionysius whom we once published at your request.

[20] For this reason too the aforementioned abbot Maximus

has recently been brought forth through our labor,

as we piously followed your pious commands,

and have swiftly translated what requires much time,

both learned understanding and the acuteness of a pure mind.

### II. On the same translation

[Col. 1235C]

Whoever delights in a rhetorical chain of words,

let him seek grandiloquent speech by entering Cicero’s camp.

But for me it will have been enough if, speaking slowly,

[Col. 1236A] I could gather plain meanings, following only the subject matter.

[5] The inner force of speech must properly be grasped:

the pomp of words often deceives.

If someone possesses both gifts by divine favor,

he ought rightly to hold the first rank.

But if you can scarcely speak clear meanings in words,

[10] be content even so; for you possess better things.

If you possess better things, what concern is it of yours to possess

what lies below? Always seek what is high.

### III. To the reader of Saint Maximus’s *Ambigua*

Whoever loves to praise the form of beautiful wisdom,

read you constantly, Maximus, born of Greece.

And first, moved by the lofty principles of things,

let him abandon and deny the sensible world;

[5] [Col. 1236B] and likewise the senses themselves, which often delay one,

while one climbs the Gnostic steps, **βήματα**, of the mind’s path.

Whoever is free from the pleasures of fragile life,

from the fleeting world, and from care of the flesh,

let him read this.

But whoever is devoted to worldly studies, slow and sluggish,

[10] let him not approach here; there is no access.

Let one puffed up by his own senses, swollen and proud,

stand far off, himself denying that he can find a place here.

Let one trained in the arts which the acuteness of mind knows

proceed confidently, for his homeland stands here.

[15] Here practical philosophy, that excellent teacher of morals,

a vigilant and suitable guardian of the virtues, will lead.

Here natural philosophy, **φυσική**, investigates the obscure causes of things,

and, once discovered, both separates and unifies them.

Here theology (*logya*), most beautiful above all, bears the palm to God,

[20] [Col. 1236C] “all things (?)—what, what not—denies all things, everything at once” [the printed line is defective] 

## SECTION IV. FRAGMENTS OF THE VERSES OF JOHN SCOTUS

[Col. 1235]

### I. Verses of John Scotus to King Charles

Manuscript of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, no. 223, ninth century.

[Col. 1235D]

[lacuna]

[lacuna]

Give prosperity to our king Charles, to whom you have given the scepters,

so that he may always live for you as a servant with a kindly mind.

[80] Grant the prosperous revolutions of a passing life,

and together with you the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

Great Mother of God, thrice-blessed holy Mary,

[Col. 1236D] the heavens praise you, and the world proclaims you glorious in its prayers.

Be near Charles as protectress, and be his lofty defense,

[85] he who wondrously builds an excellent house for you,

a marble house, constructed in various ways with columns;

a lofty dwelling, beautifully made according to a threefold rule.

Look upon the many-shaped curves and winding arches,

the like structures of the walls, the capitals and bases,

[90] the towers, little towers, and elaborately wrought ceilings,

the oblique windows admitting draughts of light [printed *caleni*, uncertain],

the paintings within, the pavements of stone, and the steps,

[Col. 1237A] the surrounding porticoes, **στοάς**, the cupboards, and the side-chambers (**παστοφορεῖα**),

the peoples above and below around the altars,

[95] the lanterns filled with lamps, and the lofty crowns:

all gleam together and sparkle with gems and gold.

Hangings and curtains surround the temple on every side.

The king himself, supported by a lofty throne, looks upon all,

wearing his ancestral diadem upon his exalted head,

[100] [Col. 1238A] his hand full of writings, hand-held objects (*enchiridia*, possibly handbooks or hilts), and golden scepters, **βάκτρα**.

May the great-hearted, long-lived hero live for many years.

### II. Praise of Wisdom

From a manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris, edited by Cousin, *Philosophical Fragments*, vol. III, Appendix, p. 326. [Cf. poem VIII, col. 1230.]

If you wish to fly upward through the heavenly airs,

with your blue-gray eye you will survey the temples of Sophia.

### II. To Charles the Bald concerning Dionysius the Areopagite

Manuscript of Fulgentius 10078–10084, Brussels, Royal Library of Burgundy, parchment, twelfth century.

[Col. 1240C]

Today, wise and precious Emperor Charles,

**Σήμερον, Αὐτοκράτωρ φρόνιμος καὶ τίμιε Κάρλε,**

the exalted martyr Dionysius shines—behold,

**Μάρτυρος ὑψηλὸς λάμπει Διονύσιος ἰδοὺ,**

whom God from heaven, and you upon earth, have magnified,

**Ὃν Θεὸς οὐρανόθεν** **ἐπὶ γῆς καὶ σὺ, μεγαλύνοι,**

seeing here the darkness when the Lord removed it,

**ἰδὼν τοὺς** **σκότους, ὡς κύριος ἀφειλετο**,

by the cross [he removed] the sins of the world, and spoke [the construction is broken; the interlinear Latin labels the genitive articles, rather than supplying an “artisan”],

**Σταυρῷ** **τοῦ κόσμου τὰς ἁμαρτίας, ἀλάλησέν τε.** 

Nature does not seek to minister and to make [the Latin gloss reads “is not accustomed”]:

**Οὐκ φύσις ζητεῖ λειτουργεῖν καὶ ποιήσειν.**

Now there is deficiency, and having learned, a maker [defective Greek; the Latin gloss reads “there is now deficiency, and therefore a maker”]:

**Ἔστιν νῦν ἔλλειψιν καὶ μαθὼν ποιητήν.**

Of the world I recognize [the maker, continuing the preceding line], and now I know the one who suffered:

**Τοῦ κόσμου γνωρίζω καὶ νῦν οἶδα παθέντα**.
