## [NOTE]

Codex Laudunensis 81, from which the distinguished M. F. Ravaisson edited, rather inaccurately, John Scotus’s *Commentary on the Holy Gospel according to John*, came into my hands only late. I have therefore taken care here to describe the entire variation in its readings with the greatest diligence. In addition, I thought that a fragment of the same Commentary, attached to the end of the codex and neglected by him, ought to be added. I have distinguished the various readings by different typefaces.

[Col. 1241]

## VARIOUS READINGS IN JOHN SCOTUS’S COMMENTARY ON THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN

According to the evidence of manuscript 81 of the Library of Laon.

[Col. 1241]

[Col. 1241A] Column 298, line 8: “so that through him man might ascend into God.” This evangelical sentence recurs in the manner of proverbial sayings. For just as we say, “The Word became flesh,” so we can say, “and the flesh became the Word.” “And he dwelt among us,” that is, “he lived among us,” and so forth. (The words from *Et Verbum caro factum est*, “And the Word became flesh,” through *haec … recurrit*, “this [evangelical sentence] … recurs,” at lines 10–12 are absent from the manuscript.) Line 40: “but declares subsistence.”

Column 301, line 19: “but concerning the whole Trinity.” Line 26: “asserts without hesitation.” Line 41: *dicatur*: “may be said”; *de*, “of/concerning,” is absent from the manuscript. Line 43: “who always.”

Column 302, line 13: “that is, in divine apparitions.” Line 18: “Likewise, the virtues of the most purified.” Line 31: “in the bosom.” Line 34: “He explained.”

Column 303, line 1: “by teaching and manifestation.” Line 13: “from [Col. 1241B] Jerusalem and so forth.” And the order is as follows. Line 29: “Are you Elijah?” He says, “I am not” (“and” is omitted in the manuscript). Line 31: *virtute Heliae veni*, “I came in the power of Elijah” [the isolated *veni* could also be imperative “come”].

Column 304, line 2: “considered human subsistence.”

Column 305, line 37: “And those who had been sent were.” Line 39: “Therefore the Pharisees were sent especially because the Pharisees, hearing the preaching—”

Column 306, line 24: “is customarily done for righteousness.”

Column 307, line 13: “is divine Scripture.” Line 28: “a very perplexing investigation, of which—”

Column 309, line 12: “and distinguish between.” Line 16: “of violence.”

Column 310, line 32: “is of the whole human nature.”

Column 311, line 14: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away.” Line 25: *crucifigit sibimet Christum*, “crucifies Christ for himself”; *ipsum*, “him himself,” is absent, while *sibimet*, “for himself,” remains.

[Col. 1241C] Column 312, line 13: “and they will be advanced in understanding.” Line 35: “to be flesh, because now.” Line 41: “an introduction into the mysteries.”

Column 313, line 18: “of the grace of baptism.” Line 48: “For it is one thing.”

Column 314, line 22: “He came to him at night.” Line 23: “is placed in the figure of a catechumen.” Line 42: “with which Nicodemus began to address Christ.”

Column 315, line 13: *ἀνωθε*, “from above/again” (defective for *ἄνωθεν*), is not read.

Column 316, line 23: “cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Earlier he said, “cannot see the kingdom of God”; now, as though the verb had been changed, “cannot enter the kingdom [Col. 1242A] of God.” Here it is understood that it is not something else, and so forth. Line 47: “incorruptible and the other things which—”

Column 317, line 35: “who has not yet been born of the Spirit” (“of” is absent in the manuscript).

Column 320, line 5: “the body itself reveals its own shadow.” Line 19: “that form is represented.” Line 40: “we were buried with Christ through baptism into death” (“unless” is absent in the manuscript). Line 47: “is the cause of human salvation.”

Column 321, line 30: “For although his judgment, by which—” Line 48: “but whoever does not believe in him” (“in” is absent in the manuscript).

Column 323, line 16: “For he had not been sent into prison.” Line 54: “by John? For it had sufficed” (*Sufficerat*, thus printed).

Column 324, line 7: “by John.” Line 11: *Joannis baptismati effecisse*, “to have effected [something] for John’s baptism,” an incomplete phrase. Line 31: “but lest they err in this” (“in” is absent in the manuscript).

[Col. 1242B] Column 325, line 47: John wrote *Datum*, “given,” in this place instead of *donatum*, “bestowed/granted.”

Column 326, line 33: “who now baptizes in Judea.”

Column 327, line 21: “You thought him to be greater.”

Column 328, line 11: “He who comes from heaven is above all.” He repeats the same sentence which he said a little earlier: “He who comes from above is above all”; now again, “He who comes from heaven is above all.” The words are the same, except that, and so forth. Line 51: “and to be his equal.”

Column 329, line 18: “who receives his testimony has set his seal, because God is true.” And what does “has set his seal” mean? It means “in his heart,” and so forth.

Column 330, line 3: “according to measure.” Line 36: “and altogether of ignorance of the truth.”

Column 331, line 28: “for the law brought no one to perfection” [Col. 1242C]; and “he went again into Galilee.” Line 32: “After this he came.”

Column 333, line 22: “from there onward to the altar.” Line 31: “begins with the martyrdom of Abel.” Line 45: “by desire.” Line 51: “they went into the city.”

Column 334, line 26: “they thought that God ought to be worshiped.” Line 31: “Christ.” Line 55: “concerning the establishment of humanity or sensible creation.”

Column 335, line 24: “which I shall give.” Line 29: “which I shall give him; let it come to be in him.”

Column 336, line 16: “they display dispositions.” Line 26: “to the part above it.” Line 29: “fivefold.” Line 44: “because you truly spoke.” Line 51: “the interpretation of the authors varies.”

[Col. 1243A] Column 337, line 11: *delicto naturali ordine*, “with the natural order [through/by] fault,” a defective phrase; possibly *derelicto*, “with the natural order abandoned,” was intended.

Column 338, line 5:  *coutuntur*, “they use together,” a defective form apparently for *coutuntur/co-utuntur*. Line 16: “whether in this place or at Jerusalem.” Line 54: *in intimo templo cordis sui in intelligentiae suaeque purgabitur prius*, “in the innermost temple of his heart … of his understanding … he will first be purified,” with the intervening construction defective.

Column 339, line 5:  “in the truth of their knowledge they worship themselves” (*se adorant*, as printed). Line 14: “because the Lord foretold.” Line 44: “he spoke with women.”

Column 340, line 12: “Therefore he lifts his eyes, teaching us,” and so forth. Line 28: “God is not a tempter of evils.”

Column 341, line 23:  *Mosea*, a form of the name Moses. Lines 43–47: the span *Granis siquidem* (“For with grains”) through *intelligentiae significantia* (“signifying understanding”) is written in the margin [Col. 1244A]. Line 57: *intelligentiae significantia*, “signifying understanding.” Line 85: “is reckoned among rational animals.”

Column 342, line 3: “so that, having first been satisfied from there.” Line 52: “to whom did he give thanks except the Father?”

Column 343, line 11: “Gather the fragments that remained.”

Column 344, lines 32–43: the span *Quamquam multis* (“Although with many”) through *simul et piscium* (“and at the same time of fish”) is written in the margin. Line 39: “as though after the fragments of bread had been gathered.”

Column 345, line 29: “is found.” Line 41: “and in the new.”

Column 346, line 2: “he returned to the mountain.” Line 5: “and, after the miracle had been performed, alone again.” Line 7: “may be placed.” Line 14: “may divide.”

[Col. 1243]

## II. FRAGMENT IV OF JOHN SCOTUS’S COMMENTARY ON THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN

From the same codex.

[Col. 1243]

### Textual notes

The section, poem, verse, and lemma identify each passage; entries follow source order.

- Opening, ἄνδρα — man. [Note: [Col. 1231] The manuscript has *andra*, glossed *virum*, “man.”]
- φύσιν — nature. [Note: [Col. 1231] Glossed *naturam*, “nature.”]
- Section II, ΣΚΟΘΘΙ — Scotus. [Note: [Col. 1232D] Thus the manuscript, not *σκότθου*, the alternative Greek form of the name.]
- II.I.1, nostra — our, of salvation. [Note: [Col. 1231] Corrected feminine *nostra*; manuscript *nostro*, a different inflection of “our.”]
- II.I.9, larvas — phantoms. [Note: [Col. 1233] Manuscript *larbas*, a spelling variant.]
- II.I.13, nescit — does not know. [Note: [Col. 1233] Conjectural; manuscript *cescit*, an uncertain form.]
- II.I.23, Σὰρξ — flesh. [Note: [Col. 1233] Manuscript *Sarx*, Roman-letter transcription.]
- II.I.39, mea — my, of kingdoms. [Note: [Col. 1233] Thus the manuscript; Mai reads *mihi*, “to/for me.”]
- II.I.49, σταυρῷ — on the cross. [Note: [Col. 1233] Manuscript *stauro*, Roman-letter transcription.]
- II.I.56, Et mortale genus — and the mortal race. [Note: [Col. 1233] Mai’s correction; manuscript *Mortalemque genus*, “and mortal race,” with mismatched inflection.]
- II.I.75, sub umbras — beneath the shadows. [Note: [Col. 1233] Thus the manuscript; Mai reads *per umbras*, “through the shadows.”]
- II.I.77, Telluris superat fines — surpasses the boundaries of the earth. [Note: [Col. 1233] Mai’s conjecture. The note contrasts printed *Telluris superat finis* with manuscript *Telluris superis fines*, a defective phrase retaining “of the earth,” “to/for the heavenly ones,” and “boundaries.”]
- II.I.81, mumurque — and murmur. [Note: [Col. 1233] Thus Mai, with the printed form *mumurque*; manuscript *munusque*, “and gift.”]
- II.II heading, stichos — verse. [Note: [Col. 1233] Thus the manuscript; perhaps *στίχοι*, “verses.”]
- II.II.1, Auson — Ausonian/Italian. [Note: [Col. 1233] Manuscript *aust.*, an abbreviated or defective form.]
- II.II.5, muneris — of the gift. [Note: [Col. 1233] Thus the manuscript; Mai reads *luminis*, “of light.”]
- II.II.12, symmache Pauli — ally of Paul. [Note: [Col. 1233] Thus Mai; manuscript *symmache et Pauli*, “ally and of Paul.”]
- II.II.15, τέκνου — child/son. [Note: [Col. 1233] Manuscript *tekni*, glossed *filii*, “of the son.”]
- II.II.15, λείψανα — relics. [Note: [Col. 1233] Glossed *reliquias*, “relics.”]
- II.II.19, θιασωτῶν — worshipers. [Note: [Col. 1233] Manuscript *thiasotum*, glossed *dilaudantium*, “of those praising.”]
- II.II.19, sidera — stars. [Note: [Col. 1233] Conjectural; manuscript *sidere*, “in/by a star,” singular ablative instead of plural accusative.]
- II.II.20, coena — supper. [Note: [Col. 1233] Manuscript *caena*, spelling variant.]
- III.I.23, multo tempore — much time. [Note: [Col. 1235] Thus printed instead of *multa tempora*, “many periods of time,” changing number and case.]
- III.III.6, βήματα — steps. [Note: [Col. 1235] Manuscript *bemata*, Roman-letter transcription.]
- III.III.17, φυσική — natural philosophy. [Note: [Col. 1235] Manuscript *physice*, Roman-letter transcription.]
- III.III.20, Omnia (?) quod, quod non, omnia denegat omne simul — all things (?) what, what not, denies all, everything at once. [Note: [Col. 1235] Thus the defective text. Ravaisson conjectures *Omne quod est, quod non, detegit omne simul*, “It reveals all at once everything that is and that is not.”]
- IV.I heading, Scoti — of Scotus. [Note: [Col. 1235] Manuscript *Scotti*, spelling variant.]
- IV.I.83, inclytat — glorifies. [Note: [Col. 1235] Manuscript *inclitat*, spelling variant.]
- IV.I.84, sis — may you be. [Note: [Col. 1235] Conjectural; manuscript *sit*, “may it/he/she be,” third rather than second person.]
- IV.I.87, conterno — threefold. [Note: [Col. 1235] Conjectural; manuscript *contero*, “I grind/wear down,” grammatically difficult here.]
- IV.I.91, tyrridas — windows. [Note: [Col. 1235] Conjectural; manuscript *tyridos*, a different form of this Greek-derived word.]
- IV.I.93, παστοφορεῖα — side chambers. [Note: [Col. 1237] Conjectural; manuscript *pasta feria*, a corrupt divided transcription without a clear combined sense.]
- IV.I.100, manus scriptis — hand with writings. [Note: [Col. 1237] Manuscript *manuscriptis*, “with manuscripts/handwritten [things],” joining the words.]
- IV.I.100, enchiridia — handbooks or hand-held objects. [Note: [Col. 1237] Conjectural plural; manuscript *enchiridion*, singular “handbook/hand-held object.”]
- V.I, editorial account of the manuscript. [Note: [Col. 1237D] Labbe described the manuscript as follows:

“The codex of the library of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, written quite elegantly on parchment, bears the age of Charles the Bald. This can be inferred from the fact that, after the glossary and the Greek words of Priscian explained in Latin, several grammatical exercises in Greek and Latin are read, badly arranged and composed by a man who had scarcely touched the elements of the Greek language, and transcribed by some Martin, a teacher, **διδασκάλῳ**—for he also reveals his own name. In this manuscript several rather inelegant Greek verses, both by John Scotus Erigena and by Martin himself, are written in praise of Charles the Bald, his wife Ermentrude, and Hincmar. But they are in another hand, as is evident, from that in which the glosses were written; hence it is reasonable to think that the glosses were transcribed somewhat earlier.”

The same author later adds:

“Indeed, lest anyone miss these trifles and inelegant Greek poems which, as we have said, survive in the Sangermanian codex, we have taken care to transcribe them here with their blemishes, both because they bear some relation to our national history and also so that one may infer from them that John Scotus and the other little masters of Greek letters of his age were not so accomplished in this language that one should suppose Athens to have migrated into Francia during the Carolingian period, although Alcuin and the monk Hericus proclaim this somewhere [Col. 1238D]. Nor, perhaps, was the John who excerpted Macrobius’s book on the differences and affinities of the Greek and Latin word, in order to learn the rules of Greek verbs, a different person.”

Angelo Mai likewise says of these verses, *Classici Auctores*, vol. V, p. 451:

“Several Greek verses of John Scotus, written to Charles the Bald, occur in a contemporary codex of Greek glossaries at Saint-Germain in Paris. I refrain from reproducing them here, not so much because I consider them of little value as because of the corruption of the writing, which can scarcely be restored. Yet nothing belonging to our Scotus is lost, since these verses are printed in square letters in the preface to the aforementioned glossaries, including the recent London edition.”

And shortly afterward:

“As for the Sangermanian glossary, may one perhaps suspect that it was the work of our Scotus, since it contains verses inscribed by him? Certainly, because of his limited knowledge of Greek, he needed such little exercises. For the Cambridge codex cited by Ussher, p. 45, also testifies that our Scotus made an excerpt from Macrobius’s book on the affinity of the Greek and Latin word in order to learn the rules of Greek verbs.”

]

- V.I.1, ἄρχος — ruler. [Note: [Col. 1237] Missing; supplied by the editor’s conjecture.]
- V.I.1, ὁ — the, before Charles. [Note: [Col. 1237] L reads *ω*, “O” if understood as an interjection, instead of the article.]
- V.I.2, Βασιλέως — of the king. [Note: [Col. 1237] Thus L, instead of *βασιλέει*, “to/for the king.”]
- V.I.2, κληροῦσθαι — to inherit. [Note: [Col. 1237] L reads *κλειρεισθε*, a defective form corresponding to the verb.]
- V.I.2, χοροὺς — choirs. [Note: [Col. 1237] L reads *χοροις*, “to/for choirs,” dative rather than accusative.]
- V.I.2, δυνατὸς — able. [Note: [Col. 1237] L reads *δινατος*, spelling variant.]
- V.I.3, Στίχοι — verses. [Note: [Col. 1237] L reads *του στιχοι*, with an incongruous article *του*, “of the,” before “verses.”]
- V.I.4, Στίχοι — verses. [Note: [Col. 1237] L reads *οι στιχοι τοι*, “the verses” followed by a defective *τοι*.]

- V.I.4, ἄνακτι — to the king/lord. [Note: [Col. 1237] L reads *ανακτο Καρλω*, defective forms for “to the king Charles.”]
- V.I.5, Φοίβη — Phoebe/Moon. [Note: [Col. 1237] L reads *Φοεβη*, spelling variant.]
- V.I.5, Στίλβων — Stilbon/Mercury. [Note: [Col. 1237] L reads *ἰστιλβον*, defective spelling.]

- V.I.7, σεβαστός — august/Caesar. [Note: [Col. 1237] L reads *σεβαστεις*, a defective form.]

The editor suggests that *δώσειε τῷ*, “may he give to,” might be preferred to *δὸς ἐμῷ*, “give to my.”]
- V.I.20, Εὔχετε ταῦτ` ἄλλοι νῦν, εὔχε σὺ Φράγκια πᾶσα — pray these things now, others; pray, all Francia. [Note: [Col. 1239] Conjectural; L reads *ευχετε ταιταλα οινην ευχε ου φραγγια πασσα*, a defective sequence with the repeated prayer verb and the address to all Francia.]
- V.II, οὐρανόθεν — from heaven. [Note: [Col. 1239] Manuscript *oyranonen*, defective Roman-letter transcription.]
- V.II, τοὺς — the, before darkness. [Note: [Col. 1239] Manuscript *tos*, Roman-letter transcription.]
- V.II, ἀφειλετο — took away. [Note: [Col. 1239] Manuscript *alfeiletoy*, defective transcription.]
- V.II, Σταυρῷ — by/on the cross. [Note: [Col. 1239] Manuscript *stauron*, a transcription resembling accusative “cross,” instead of the printed dative.]
- V.II, ἀλάλησέν τε — and he spoke. [Note: [Col. 1239] Manuscript *alale sente*, a divided defective transcription; the editor regards *τε*, “and,” as superfluous.]
- V.II, παθέντα — the one who suffered. [Note: [Col. 1239] Manuscript *ratinta*, defective transcription; *παθέντα* is printed for *παθόντα*, the regular aorist participle with that meaning.]

[Col. 1243B] Saint Ambrose enumerates the aforementioned prayers in the following order: prayers, entreaties, petitions, thanksgivings. He assigns to prayer the asking of good things for ourselves; to entreaty, the seeking of release from evils; and to petition, the struggle against every adversity. He prescribes that we must know to do this when we assemble together.

Saint Augustine has it thus: supplications, prayers, intercessions, or, as your [Note: [Col. 1243] The manuscript has *uri*; *f.*, perhaps *nostri*, as below?] codices read, petitions, thanksgivings. And he says: “The Church practices all [Note: [Col. 1243] The manuscript reads *omnis*.], or nearly all [Note: [Col. 1243] The manuscript reads *omnis*.], of these in the solemn celebration of the sacraments.” Supplication is every prayer before that which is performed at the Lord’s table; prayer is whatever is performed afterward up to communion; [Col. 1244B] intercession or petition is that by which the people are blessed; thanksgiving concludes everything.

Where Saint Augustine says “supplications,” our codices have “entreaties.” To entreaty, as has been said, Saint Ambrose assigns petition [Note: [Col. 1243] The manuscript reads *postolatio*.] for the forgiveness of sins. We name the rest in the same way, as has [lacuna] concerning Saint Augustine. [Note: [Col. 1243] One or two words are missing—the membrane was cut away where they had stood. Perhaps read: *ut praedictum est* (“as has been said”).] They likewise have the force that Saint Ambrose assigned to them, both in the celebration of the sacraments and in the other offices.

In everything that I write, I submit myself to the judgment of learned and devout Fathers. For the present I state what I think. What is performed in the celebration of the Mass is performed in the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion.

The rest is missing.

## In the Year of Our Lord 872. Adrian II, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 1245]

## Historical Notice on Adrian II

*(In Labbé, Councils, vol. VIII, p. 882.)*

[Col. 1245A] [Note: [Col. 1245A] Adrian. When, after the death of Pope Nicholas, the pontifical see had been without a shepherd for a month, Adrian—most munificent toward the poor and miraculously distinguished for giving alms—was raised to the apostolic throne on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, despite his resistance, by the common agreement of the entire clergy and people.

The Emperor Louis, although Adrian’s election had taken place in the absence of the imperial legates, with the intention that the custom of awaiting the emperor’s legates should not prejudice an apostolic election, not only did not disapprove it but commended it as lawfully conducted; thereafter, by letter, he ordered that this practice be followed and maintained.

After receiving the volume fabricated by Photius against Pope Nicholas and entrusting it for examination to learned and competent men, Adrian summoned the Roman council mentioned below. There he struck Photius with anathema for the third time and consigned his volume to the fire.

On his authority, at the request of the Eastern orthodox, the eighth ecumenical synod was convoked. Apart from what is related above in Adrian’s Life, we shall say more below in the notes on that council.

Lothair, king of Gaul, asked Adrian by letter kindly to grant what he had been unable to obtain from Nicholas—namely, permission to come to Rome for his purification. Although the pope repeatedly refused this request, he finally permitted it, not without great offense to the Easterners residing at Rome. They thought that Adrian was deliberately annulling everything done by his predecessor, Pope Saint Nicholas, since he admitted the man whom Nicholas had forbidden to approach the City as unworthy, and recalled from exile and released from punishment those whom Nicholas had banished with Gunthar of Cologne or subjected to other penalties. How he freed himself from this suspicion is related above in the Life of Pope Adrian.

When Actard, bishop of the Church of Nantes, recommended by letters from the two synods of Troyes and Soissons, had been stripped of his church by the Northmen and subjected to many hardships after the Britons had likewise devastated it, he came to Rome. Adrian received him worthily. Actard was a man distinguished for piety and learning; Adrian provided him with the means of living and also honored him with the pallium. These facts are taken from Adrian’s letters written on Actard’s behalf to various persons.

[Col. 1246A] After King Lothair’s death, Charles the Bald tyrannically invaded the kingdom that by hereditary right belonged to his brother Louis. When the pontiff learned this, he sent by legates the letters written below to King Charles and to the leading men and bishops of his kingdom. Aimoinus testifies, in Book Five, chapter twenty-seven, that Charles received the pontiff’s rebuke favorably and dismissed the legates after the matter had been left unresolved, once they had freed his son Carloman, whom he was holding in chains.

The Emperor Louis was crowned at Rome by Adrian as king of the Franks and successor in that kingdom to his own brother, whose king Charles the Bald had already been crowned by Hincmar, bishop of Reims. When this became known to Basil in the East, Basil sent an envoy to Louis with letters rebuking him for usurping the imperial title—a title Basil had ordered to be erased from letters of Pope Adrian brought by legates to Constantinople, despite the protests of the apostolic see’s representatives. After receiving these letters, Louis sent the legate Autprand to Basil; through him he delivered to that emperor a weighty and sufficiently sharp apologetic letter, which is preserved in Baronius under the year 871, no. 51.

During the time of Pope Adrian, the English Church displayed a worthy example of a great king who was pious and steadfast in faith. Matthew of Westminster writes the following about him: “King Æthelred was listening to Mass in his tent. When his men repeatedly urged him to battle, he firmly declared that he would not leave before the priest had completed the Mass.” The faith of the Christian king greatly benefited him that day, when the powerful enemy was defeated. Thus Matthew.

After Adrian had occupied the papal see for four years, ten months, and seventeen days, he died in the year 872 of our Redeemer, on the Kalends of November. Aimoinus, a writer of this period, attests this in Book V, chapter 29, at the end. The man who, after Anastasius, wrote the Life of Adrian II and of Stephen VI should be regarded, according to Baronius, more as a compiler than as an author of the Lives of earlier pontiffs. SEV. BIN.]

Adrian, a Roman by nation, son of Talarus, later bishop of the third region, held the see for five years. Descended through a close genealogical connection from the pontiffs Stephen IV and Sergius the Younger, both of blessed memory, he was appointed to the ministry of the subdiaconate by Gregory IV, bishop of the apostolic see of venerable memory, because he was outstanding in wondrous deeds. Thereafter, having been familiarly received into the Lateran patriarchate and having conducted himself commendably, he was ordained priest to govern the title of Saint Mark, confessor of Christ and pontiff. He lived so blamelessly and ministered so manfully that everyone revered him not only as one who had become a priest but as one who would become pontiff.

For he possessed such confidence in Christ and in his Mother—for he devoted himself to constant prayers before her Manger—that, while doing good, he never grew weary, nor did he fear to incur any danger, since he distributed with the greatest discretion everything he could possess.

[Col. 1247A] For one day, after regularly receiving forty denarii from the most holy Pope Sergius among his fellow priests, he wished to return and enter the doors of his house. Yet he was completely unable to do so because of the multitude of pilgrims who, trusting in him and following their customary practice, had gathered there as though at a common granary. Moved by compassion, he said to his equestrian steward [*equestri dispensatori suo*] that nothing among those so few coins was common to him without so many brothers.

When the steward replied that not even the third part of the poor could receive one denarius each, Adrian said: “By the power of Christ, who satisfied five thousand men with five loaves and two fish, I shall distribute not one denarius to each, but three denarii to each.” Saying this, he went outside to the gate, received the money from his equestrian steward, and distributed three denarii individually to all the pilgrims as they departed.

When the steward marveled at this abundance, because the denarii had not merely failed to run out but had actually remained over, the generous priest took what was left and likewise distributed three coins apiece to each member of his household. When six still remained, he said: “See how generous and gracious the almighty Lord is, who has distributed the forty coins in threes to our brothers and has preserved three for me and three for you in equal shares.”

[Col. 1247B] He was moreover so hospitable and generous that he may rightly be compared in these matters with blessed Job. From childhood compassion grew with him, and it came forth with him from his mother’s womb (Job 31). He did not despise a passerby because that person lacked clothing; indeed, he warmed his sides with the fleeces of sheep. Nor did he eat his morsel alone, since he ate it with orphans and the needy. He was an eye to the blind and was found to be a foot to the lame. And, to report briefly the abundance of his virtues, he was a father to the poor and a consoler of the widow’s heart.

His door stood open to travelers, and the door of his house was closed to no one who requested anything from him. Consequently, every clerical rank, every senatorial [Col. 1247C] and popular assembly united in the greatest harmony, would have compelled him to assume the supreme pontificate after the death of Pope Leo IV, and likewise after the death of Pope Benedict III, had he not modestly evaded it through various devices and carefully devised excuses.

But when Pope Nicholas, of apostolic memory, the most holy pontiff, had departed this life, and Adrian was then entering his seventy-fifth year, all the citizens of the city of Rome, together with those who happened at that time to be present from outside—poor and rich alike, the clerical order as well as the entire mass of the people, of every age, profession, and sex—disregarding all his excuses, desired Adrian and earnestly wished that Adrian be given to them as bishop and shepherd.

No one was found throughout the vast extent of the City who, unless he wished either himself or someone else to be advanced, did not desire from the depths of his heart that Adrian be raised to this summit. Although the nobles appeared to be divided into two factions, their minds were nevertheless united, and they burned with equal fervor toward him. The cause of their division was nothing other than an excessive love for so great a man: each side so desired to have him preferred to itself that, if one faction chose him, the other would be wholly uncertain. Nor did either side have any wish to hold back [perhaps: “to remain silent”], except because it supposed that he would direct its votes toward another.

This was especially so since many monks, most of the religious priests, and faithful laymen, through visions sent from heaven, had long since not merely believed without doubt but openly proclaimed that Adrian would become pontiff. Among them, some saw Adrian reclining on the apostolic throne with the pallium spread over his shoulders; others saw him celebrating Mass in the apostolic vestments. Some saw him distributing gold in the Lateran basilica in the apostolic manner. Many had seen him mounted on the horse that the most holy Pope Nicholas had used when going to Saint Peter, wearing the pontifical pallium and returning to the City, with the leading men preceding him and the remaining crowds following, and entering the patriarchate.

[Col. 1247D] But when it became clear through manifest signs that both factions loved him, such unity of minds and bodies arose among them that everyone seemed to possess one heart and one spirit toward this same priest of the Lord. Thus, with due reverence for Jesus Christ our Lord, he could in a certain sense be called the cornerstone, because by his appearance—or rather, his arrival—he dissolved the enmities of their hearts and made both factions one.

Accordingly, after all had assembled—the bishops with the entire clergy, the leading men of the City with the peoples subject to them—he was seized, dragged, and carried in competition by the multitude of nobles and common people from the church of the holy Mother of God and Ever-Virgin Mary called “At the Manger” to the Lateran patriarchate.

[Col. 1248A] When the emperor’s envoys heard this, they took it badly. They were indignant, not because they did not want such a man to be pontiff—for they desired this most anxiously—but because the Romans had not invited them, though they were present, nor allowed them to participate in the election of the future prelate whom they themselves desired.

When they were given the explanation that this had been omitted not out of contempt for the emperor but entirely with a view to the future, so that the custom of awaiting the princes’ legates in the election of Roman prelates should not grow through such an occasion, they thoroughly quieted their indignation and themselves humbly approached to greet the elected man.

When they went up and down the Lateran patriarchate, they were surrounded by such great cries from the entire populace, who shouted that the man they had long desired should be given to them for consecration, that none of them could hear the words of a colleague speaking with him. It was astonishing to see each person possess such powerful love for the pontiff to be consecrated that no one could have believed he had ever seen, or would ever see, anything like it.

[Col. 1248B] Finally, all struggled before those same legates to seize him, drag him forward to the height of the supreme pontificate, and carry him eagerly, unless they had been somewhat calmed by the senators’ entreaties and counsels.

The most Christian Emperor Louis heard the unanimous desire of all these people and learned how they had confirmed their decision by their signatures. He rejoiced greatly. From the depths of his heart he desired that so great a servant of the Lord, desired and desirable to all peoples—to the Romans as well as to the various foreigners—should be placed over the Christian people.

He immediately wrote an imperial letter in which he praised all the Romans for having chosen a prelate worthy of so great an office. Through this letter it became clear that no reward was to be promised anyone in any way on account of Adrian’s consecration, since Louis himself passionately desired that it take place, moved not by the recommendation of his own people but rather by the unanimity of the Romans. He especially declared that he loved not the removal or loss of anything from the Roman Church, but the restoration of what had been taken away.

[Col. 1248C] Accordingly, on Saturday, after the prayers, vigils, and almsgiving had been duly completed, the same venerable priest was led by the whole people on Sunday, according to custom, to the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the first indiction, in the nineteenth year of the aforementioned emperor. There, through the most reverend bishops—namely Peter of Gabii, Leo of Silva Candida, and, third, Donatus of Ostia, since the bishop of Albano had died, while Formosus of Porto had been sent by the most blessed Nicholas to preach and instruct the Bulgarians—he deserved to receive, in the name of the Lord, the blessing of the supreme pontificate, for the consolation of the many sons of the holy Church of God who, while the tyranny of factions raged more freely than usual, were driven into various exiles and subjected to various hardships between the departure of one pontiff and the appointment of another.

[Col. 1249A] At the celebration of his Mass, the multitude was so extraordinarily great that Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier, and Zacharias, bishop of Anagni—both of whom had been stripped of the priesthood by Lord Nicholas and had also been deprived of communion—as well as Anastasius, who had formerly been stripped of the priesthood by Popes Leo and Benedict and had been accustomed to receive communion among the laity, all received ecclesiastical communion with suitable satisfaction, while everyone strove eagerly to communicate from Adrian’s hand.

Thereupon he immediately returned to the Lateran patriarchate and abolished a custom by which the prices of various gifts from all directions were collected, retaining only the remnants sufficient for the needs of the tables. He said: “It is not pious to sell for a price what we receive freely, or to value irrational coins more highly than rational brothers, for whom Christ’s precious blood was shed. I beg you, therefore, let these shameful dealings in prices be disregarded. What we have received freely, let us give freely, according to the Lord’s command, and let us share Christ’s offerings with his guests and the poor, for whose sake we know that these things have been divinely granted to us.”

[Col. 1249B] Immediately he also sent the bishops Dominicus and Grimoald, whom his predecessor, Pope Nicholas of holy memory, had ordered to go to the Bulgarian land and had absolved at the very moment of his departure. Because they had delayed their journey upon seeing the death of so great a Father, Adrian sent them forth to carry out the same mission. He ordered that some of the letters which Nicholas had selected for dispatch should be issued under Adrian’s own name, thereby showing himself to possess the same will and zeal. As far as the storm of that troubled time permitted, the pious heir fulfilled the pious Father’s desire.

After dismissing these men from the City, he immediately took care to recall from exile Gauderic, bishop of Velletri, Stephen, bishop of Nepi, and John surnamed Simonides. Shameless falsehood had accused them before the most serene emperor and driven them from their homes and fatherland. Adrian wrote many letters and said that he could not appear to be a good shepherd of the Church of God unless he received back the sheep whom an unfaithful man had proscribed through his own deceit from the faithful Church.

[Col. 1249C] The emperor, gladdened by this religious appeal, together with his most Christian wife, not only honorably sent back to the City those for whom the supreme pontiff had sent, but also ordered that all whom anyone had imprisoned as guilty of lèse-majesté because of private hostility should return.

After this, the supreme pontiff adorned with various paintings the Basilica of Saint Nicholas, which the most holy Pope Nicholas had built from the foundations with such splendor and with three constructed aqueducts that it surpassed all the Lateran basilicas in beauty, fulfilling the desire of his predecessor.

[Col. 1249D] He followed the examples of Nicholas’s conduct so diligently that the enemies of Saint Nicholas, who were attempting in every way to undermine his acts, wrote and publicly called Adrian a “Nicolaitan.”

Since Adrian knew that some of these enemies were conceiving injustice and would eventually pour forth the pain they had conceived, he prudently retained them near himself, like weeds among the wheat until the time of maturity. But a false rumor arose, and it was believed that he intended to undermine all the acts of his predecessor—acts which Nicholas had established through divine zeal, but which his enemies slandered according to their own desires.

As a result, all the bishops of the western regions, sending solemn and honorable letters, continually urged the supreme pontiff to honor Adrian’s religious memory as that of a bishop of orthodox and true philosophy.

While some Greeks and servants of God from other nations who were then residing at Rome had secretly withdrawn from the company of this most holy Pope Adrian for several days, the same most holy prelate, on the Friday of Septuagesima, summoned them according to custom for refreshment, in a larger number than usual.

[Col. 1250A] With his own hands he humbly poured water over all of them, set out the food, and served the cups. And, something which he knew no pontiff before him had done, he reclined at table with them in order to make them more ready for the meal, while spiritual songs continually resounded there in praise throughout the entire time.

When he had risen from the meal, he fell on his face before them all and said: “I ask and humbly entreat you, fathers, brothers, and sons, to pour forth prayers to the Lord for his holy Catholic Church. Pray for our most Christian son, the Emperor Louis Augustus, that almighty God may subject the Saracen nation to him, for our perpetual peace. Pray also for me, frail and weak as I am, that Christ may grant me such strength to govern the multitude of his Church in holiness and justice, since he entrusted blessed Peter the apostle with governing all whom he redeemed. Thus, since I often, blinded by the dust of secular cares, behold spiritual things less clearly, may your continual prayer—so much purer because it is farther removed from the pollutions of the world—divinely assist me.”

When they loudly insisted that he, as one so much more acceptable to God, ought rather to pray for them, since he alone labored fervently on behalf of all, he was moved by inward compassion and said with tears:

[Col. 1250B] “Because praying for very good men, dearest ones, is to offer thanksgivings to God, I ask you to keep in your prayers my lord and father, my predecessor, the most holy and orthodox Pope Nicholas, and to offer common thanks to the Lord, who in his mercy chose him for his Church and, like Joshua, armed him with the shield of protection and strengthened him with the sword of spiritual power, so that he might repel the world’s most arrogant uproars.”

When they heard this, all the servants of God—those from Jerusalem, Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople, some of whom were serving as envoys of the princes of the world—were struck with prolonged astonishment and burst into a loud acclamation, saying:

[Col. 1250C] “Thanks be to God, thanks be to God, who has ordained that such a man be placed over his Church; one who, setting before his eyes the reverence due to his father and predecessor, would feed the Lord’s flock with rod and staff, and would not tear apart the testament of the Fathers but fulfill it.

“Thanks be to God, thanks be to God, who has not placed an apostate pope in the seat of his apostle; who has laid the foundations of his house not upon sand but upon the firmest rock; who has caused you to succeed the most holy Pope Nicholas and not to depart from his decrees.

“Come, let envy cease; let lying rumor withdraw. Long life to our lord Adrian, ordained by God as supreme pontiff and universal pope”: this was said three times.

When he signaled silence with his hand, the supreme prelate proclaimed:

“Eternal memory to the most reverend, most holy, and orthodox lord Nicholas, ordained by God as supreme pontiff and universal pope”: this was said three times.

“Perpetual life and unfading glory to the new Elijah”: this was said three times.

“Eternal salvation to the new Phinehas, who is worthy to receive the insignia of the eternal priesthood”: this was said three times.

“Peace and grace to his followers”: this was said three times.

[Col. 1250D] Accordingly, at the time of the consecration of this venerable pontiff, Lampert, son of Vinton, duke of Spoleto, entered the city of Rome contrary to custom, like a tyrant. Though it was not in revolt, he distributed it among his satellites for plunder like a victor, sold the houses of the leading men for many gifts, spared neither monasteries nor churches, and indeed allowed girls of the noblest families, both within and outside the City, to be indiscriminately carried off by his satellites.

Because of these acts, complaints against him weighed heavily before the most pious emperors of the Romans. He lost the duchy, incurred the anger of the princes and the hatred of nearly all the Gauls, and was judged in effect an enemy of the apostolic see.

[Col. 1251A] The Roman pontiff, now freed from such tyranny, deprived Histald, Walter, Gilpian, Odo, and Theupert, together with all the other robbers and plunderers, of all ecclesiastical communion until they restored what they had stolen and made legal satisfaction to him.

Theupert, however, readily undertook to restore what he had taken. Histald, a man devoted to God and very brave in war, approached the prelate who had struck him with complete humility. He accepted his favor in every way according to the Roman will, intending to make satisfaction, and also received hope of recovering communion. He would indeed have been able to recover it, had he not afterward become privy to the conspiracy of the Lamberts and, fleeing with excommunicated and rebellious men, preferred to seek Benevento.

After these matters had been settled, Michael, emperor of the Greeks, killed Bardas Caesar, a supporter of Photius, who, as they report, was plotting his death. He adopted Basil as his colleague and appointed him emperor. When the new emperor Basil was held in the highest honor by the Catholics, since he had always favored them, Michael was killed by his eunuchs, though it is uncertain whether this occurred with the consent of his son.

[Col. 1251B] As soon as Basil took control, he first satisfied everyone, as is reported, by declaring that he had not been party to Michael’s death. Then, in accordance with the decision of the Roman Church, he expelled the usurper Photius and, with the support of the people, restored Ignatius to the patriarchate. From both sides—from Ignatius the patriarch and from Photius the neophyte—he sent envoys to Rome through his spatharius Basil, so that they might contend alternately in the presence of the supreme pontiff and, with justice supporting them, either justify Photius or condemn him forever.

But by divine judgment the eloquent party of Photius was swallowed up by the sea, while the simple party of Ignatius, together with the imperial envoy, was preserved. No one from the side of the neophyte escaped except a certain little monk named Methodius. Later, accepting neither Photius, on whose behalf he had come, nor Ignatius, against whom he had come, nor the rights of the universal Church, to which he had come, he was summoned a third time, denounced for perfidy a third time, and departed after being anathematized once.

[Col. 1251C] Basil, the emperor’s envoy, and John, metropolitan of Caesarea in Cappadocia, had been sent to Nicholas. They presented themselves with sufficient humility to the most holy Pope Adrian, who was seated with the bishops and nobles in the secretary of Saint Mary Major according to the custom of the holy apostolic see. They offered gifts and letters. After these had been received, they gave abundant thanks to the holy Roman Church, through whose effort the Church of Constantinople had risen purified from schism. After innumerable praises, they said with one voice:

“Your most devoted son, the Emperor Basil, and Ignatius, restored to the patriarchate through your office, found in the Constantinopolitan church’s archives, after that church had expelled the usurper Photius through your intervention, a book composed with the utmost falsehood against the character of the holy Roman Church and of the most holy Pope Nicholas.

[Col. 1251D] “They expelled it entirely from their city, sealed as though it were truly contagious, and sent it to you, as the supreme head to whom Christ has granted the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth. We ask you, therefore, to receive it and examine it closely, and to recognize from it the fraud which our slippery Photius was able to inflict upon the innocent Constantinopolitans when he sharpened his audacious tongue against this holy Roman Church, which has neither stain nor wrinkle nor anything of that kind.

“Publicly proclaim to everyone what the Church of God ought to think of this act of brigandage, which he secretly fabricated under the name of a synod.”

When the pontiff assented to a sitting of both parties, Photius might perhaps have rushed into passing sentence against the Roman apostolic see and its pontiff, since he had no voice; but he could not weigh out a judgment. He had, however, been judged twice and condemned twice by the apostolic see. And because Photius, trusting in his own strength, did not fear to babble falsehoods against our most holy Pope Nicholas, he set his mouth in heaven and stretched out his tongue across the earth.

[Col. 1252A] “Therefore, we admit that the book of his little council should be examined, so that its author and fabricator of falsehood and inventor of perverse doctrines may be judged for the third time.”

The metropolitan came out, produced the book, and hurled it to the ground, cursing it and saying: “You are accursed at Constantinople; be accursed again at Rome. You have been crushed by the minister of Christ, Nicholas, the new Peter and lover of truth.”

The spatharius struck the book with his heel and sword and said likewise: “I believe that the devil dwells in this little work, since through the mouth of his accomplice Photius it spews forth what he himself cannot say. For it falsely contains the subscription of our Emperor Basil after that of Michael, whom Photius induced to subscribe at night while he was most drunk. That it is not Basil’s is shown by the restoration of Ignatius and is confirmed by our satisfaction, if it pleases you, under oath.

[Col. 1252B] “For he who, by changing the handwriting, was able with a few accomplices to write the names of many absent bishops could not merely have inserted falsely into his deadly fabrications the name of the one ever-Catholic Basil. The entire body of those bishops is as free from this subscription as it is ignorant of its wording.

“Indeed, no Constantinopolitan knew when that little council had been gathered—because in truth it never existed. But since provincials go up to Constantinople, like an imperial city, for various affairs, just as they come to this city, the most obstinate Photius smeared his lie with the medicine of truth, as he had been trained to do from the beginning.

“He caused the citizens of certain bishops to subscribe in place of some most holy bishops—citizens who, as rumor has spread, were fugitives blinded by gifts. Hence the characters of the subscriptions appear different: some were written with a sharper pen, some with a thicker one, and some, pretending to be decrepit, defiled the parchment with a broader hand. Thus, through the fraud of those present, the simplicity of the absent was mocked, and the whole body might more easily believe that what falsehood had made different through dissimilar letters was genuine.

[Col. 1252C] “But you will immediately see the characters, revealing the dissimilarity of the subscriptions. You will not recognize the fraud, however, unless you send [the book] to Constantinople, as that entire Church entreats you to do.”

Then the supreme pontiff ordered that the book be examined for several days by experts in both languages and that everything contained in it be faithfully presented before the synod. The synod diligently scrutinized everything throughout.

For the venerable pontiff, with the support of the entire senatorial and popular assembly, convened a sacred council at the church of blessed Peter the apostle in defense of his Church and of his predecessor.

First, after hearing the truth clearly from the envoys of Constantinople, he read before the synod his predecessor’s letters concerning the matter and cleared his predecessor’s reputation of the sinister charge. Then he struck Photius, his little council, and his accomplices with anathema for the third time.

[Col. 1252D] Finally, after the book had been strengthened by the subscriptions and judgments of the others, he cast it down before the steps at the entrance and had it trampled under everyone’s feet. The pyre received it as fuel for the fire and consumed it—almost before it could be thought to have been half-burned—with a great stench and a pitch-black color.

When the fire ought naturally to have been extinguished by the torrent of rain, the flame instead grew stronger at the rain as though at drops of oil. The wonder of the miracle melted the hearts of both Latins and Greeks into praises of God and of the most holy Pope Nicholas, as well as of Adrian, the supreme pontiff.

After this, he sent to Constantinople, as his predecessor had ordered, Donatus, bishop of Ostia, and Marinus, the deacon, together with the letters of his predecessor. He then sent the same letters bearing only his own name as title, along with a memorandum. He also associated with them Stephen, bishop of Nepi, and ordered them to quell with care every scandal in the Church of Constantinople and to restore their own churches to those whom Methodius and Ignatius had consecrated, subject to the satisfaction required by the written declaration they had received from the archive.

[Col. 1253A] They were likewise to admit the Photian party to communion on the same terms, but under stricter satisfaction, while deferring the judgment of the priests until the decision of the apostolic see, with the judgment of the most holy Pope Nicholas remaining in force.

Thus, passing through the arduous circuits of many winding routes, they finally came, with Christ leading them, to Thessalonica. There the Emperor Basil sent Eustathius, his spatharius and candidate, to meet the envoys of the holy Roman Church with the duty of conveying his greeting.

Guiding them with every mark of honor through the successive stages of their journey, they reached Selymbria. There Sisinnius, the imperial protospatharius, and Theognistus, the patriarchal hegumen—who had diligently interceded at Rome before the most holy Pope Nicholas for the restoration of Ignatius—received them with forty horses from the imperial stables, a complete silver service for the table, and attendants assigned to serve them at their every wish. At the Round Fortress, where there is a church of extraordinary size dedicated in the name of Saint John the Evangelist, they took up residence on Saturday by imperial favor.

On Sunday, which was the fifteenth day of September, in the third indiction, accepting individual horses with golden saddles as an imperial act of devotion, they came to the Golden Gate, having been met by all the military corps—namely, the spatharii, candidati, strategoi, mandatores, and the other palace orders—and by all the robed orders of the clergy. There they were solemnly greeted by Paul, keeper of the books, Joseph, keeper of the vessels, and Basil the sacellarius, all clothed in ecclesiastical garments; with the patriarch of Constantinople’s syncelli solemnly leading the procession, they were escorted by the entire people bearing candles and lamps.

Thus descending to the Palace of Irene, they were honorably received in the house called Magnaura by John a secretis, the spatharius candidatus, and Strategius the spatharius candidatus, who had been appointed for the provision of their needs. Through them they received imperial messages, undoubtedly conveyed with the greatest devotion, lest they should take it ill that, because the imperial birthday was approaching, they could not be received on the following day.

When that celebration had happily been completed, the emperor sent all the palace orders to meet them. With these preceding them, they came before the emperor in the Chrysotriclinus, where he immediately rose to receive them, and they greeted him. They presented the apostolic letters to the emperor; he himself accepted them and kissed them. He carefully inquired about the condition of the Roman Church, the health of Lord Adrian, the supreme pontiff, and the whole ecclesiastical and senatorial order. After affectionately kissing the legates, he dismissed them to carry the apostolic command to Patriarch Ignatius.

They returned to the emperor on the following day, and he addressed them as follows:

“The holy Roman Church, mother of all the Churches of God, has faithfully provided for the holy Church of Constantinople, which has been torn apart by various schismatic storms through the ambition of the most obstinate Photius, as can be clearly understood from those letters by whose authority our present father Ignatius—who had been violently expelled by the Photian party—has recently, with the Lord’s help, been restored to his own see. Therefore, together with all the Eastern patriarchs, metropolitans, and bishops, having awaited for two years the judgment of our holy mother, the Roman Church, we beg, for God’s sake, that the business of God be carried through with courage and that, at last, by the authority of your sacred college, the scandals of the most pernicious Photian evasions be driven away, so that the desired unity and tranquility may be restored according to the decree of the most holy Pope Nicholas.”

The legates of the holy apostolic see replied:

“That is why we have come; that is why we were sent. But we can never admit any of your Easterners to our synod unless, after presenting a libellus whose form we took from the archives of the holy apostolic see, satisfaction has been given to us.”

The emperor and the patriarch said:

“Since you assert that this requirement of presenting a libellus is new and unheard of, it is necessary that we see its form and contents.”

Without delay the form of the libellus was produced and translated from Latin into Greek for all to understand. Some of them presented the libellus and took their seats in the holy synod. Those unwilling to present it were left without honor outside the synod; but, day by day, their fervor being tempered by the Holy Spirit, after first satisfying the requirement of the libellus, they returned to the unity of the sacred synod.

Photius, that usurper, was brought into the synod to give an account of the many crimes he had committed. All the letters of the holy Roman Church against him were read aloud. The sentence of deposition and anathema previously issued by the apostolic see was repeatedly hurled against him by everyone. In his presence, the profaned volumes of that most wicked assembly—books in which he had barked out his mutterings against the most holy Pope Nicholas—were burned by fire, and the lamp of truth and innocence shone forth.

He entered the snare which he had once prepared for another who was to be glorified; now, by the power of reason, he was reduced to the final inertness of silence. The door of communion had been opened to him, and he had been admonished that he was to be received after satisfying the requirement of the libellus; yet, like a blind man at midday, he turned away from it.

Finally, after all the proceedings contained in the text of the synod’s ten sessions had been beneficially completed, the text of the synod was entrusted by the legates of the holy Roman Church to Anastasius, librarian of the holy apostolic see, for careful examination before they signed it, lest Greek levity should have inserted anything false into it. Anastasius had at that time arrived in Constantinople after them, together with Suppo, chief minister, on behalf of Louis, our most serene Augustus, by a divine dispensation, as is believed.

Since he was highly eloquent in both languages, he examined the text with the greatest care. They found that everything which the most holy Lord Adrian the pontiff had added in praise of our most serene Caesar in the letter of his predecessor to Bishop Arsenius was cut out.

For this reason they loudly complained that the letter of the apostolic see had been fraudulently mutilated, and they declared that they would in no way subscribe to the synodal proceedings unless the integrity of the entire letter were joined to the synodal acts.

While the Romans pressed this demand, the Greeks replied loudly that the synod was concerned not with praising the emperor but solely with treating of God, and they utterly begrudged our Caesar the imperial title. At last matters reached the point that, after a condition concerning the apostolic will had been inserted, they subscribed to the defined judgments in a less than fully defined form, reading as follows:

“I, acting in the place of my lord, the most holy and universal Pope Adrian, presiding in this holy synod subject to the will of that eminent prelate, have consented to everything, as written above, and have subscribed with my own hand.”

After these matters had been completed, some Greeks approached the emperor and tearfully complained that the Church of Constantinople had been reduced to Roman power through the libelli that had been presented. They declared that, because of the uncertainty surrounding the subscriptions, everything decreed in the synod had to be reconsidered and all things confused anew by recurring errors; and they pretended that they could not recover their former freedom unless the libelli were returned to them.

Immediately, some of the libelli were stolen from their custodians; for the legates of the holy Roman Church, foreseeing what was to come, had entirely concealed the libelli of the more eminent bishops. Consequently the legates were thrown into incredible distress and relied upon the faithful assistance of Suppo, chief minister, and Anastasius, the most eloquent librarian of the holy apostolic see. With their help, and by different means, though not without great labor and amid impending dangers, they at last scarcely recovered the libelli; but they incurred the emperor’s anger because of the excessive strictness of their fidelity.

Accordingly, three days later, after the most sacred synod had been completely compiled with its writings in a single codex and revised with every refinement in the Church of Saint Sophia, the emperor ordered them to sit in a house where they had been cunningly summoned together with the vicars of the patriarchs—namely, those of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem—and with Patriarch Ignatius, who was seated there with some others. There they heard that the princes of the Bulgarians had sent letters and gifts through Peter and others.

With the emperor’s particular approval, they received the Bulgarian embassy. After the greetings, Peter, the Bulgarian envoy, began:

“Lord Michael, prince of the Bulgarians, heard that you had assembled from various regions by the authority of the apostolic see for the benefit of the holy Church of God. He received this with gratitude and gives many thanks to you, who were sent from the apostolic see, because, while passing through his territory, you deigned to visit him with your letters.”

The legates of the holy Roman Church replied:

“Because we know you to be sons of the holy Roman Church, we neither ought nor wished to pass you by without greeting you. The holy apostolic see embraces you as its own members.”

The Bulgarian envoys said:

“Until today we were pagans, and only recently have we come to the grace of Christianity. Therefore, lest we appear to err in any respect, we wish to learn from you, who act in the place of the supreme patriarchs, to which Church we ought to be subject.”

The legates of the holy Roman Church replied:

“You have shown that you both have belonged and ought to belong to the holy Roman Church, to which, through you, O Peter, your lord surrendered himself together with all the people of his nation, and to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; from whose successor, the distinguished Pope Nicholas, you deserved to receive both rules for Christian living and bishops and priests. For you have both accepted our priests when they were requested and continued until now to retain them with due veneration.”

The Bulgarian envoys said:

“We confess that we requested and received priests from the holy Roman Church and have retained them until now, and we resolve to obey them in all things. But determine with these vicars of the patriarchs whether we ought more reasonably to be subject to the Roman or the Constantinopolitan Church.”

The legates of the holy Roman Church replied:

“Those matters which the apostolic see had commanded us to determine with the Easterners we have, with the Lord’s help, determined. Your case, however, must not be determined in the same way, because we received no mandate concerning it; therefore we neither determine anything nor judge that anything should be determined to the prejudice of the holy Roman Church. Indeed, because your entire country is everywhere full of our priests, we proclaim, by a definitive judgment insofar as it lies with us, that you ought to belong to no one but the holy Roman Church.”

The vicars of the Eastern patriarchs said to the Bulgarians:

“When you took possession of that country, to whose authority was it subject, and did it have Latin or Greek priests? Tell us.”

The Bulgarian envoys said:

“We conquered that country by arms from Greek authority, and there we found not Latin but Greek priests.”

The vicars of the Eastern patriarchs replied:

“If you found Greek priests there, it is evident that the country belonged to Constantinople by ordination.”

The legates of the holy Roman Church replied:

“You must not derive your argument from the Greek priests, because diversity of languages does not confuse ecclesiastical order. For although the apostolic see itself is Latin, it has both always and even now appointed Greek priests in many places according to the character of the country. It therefore neither ought nor ought ever to suffer any loss of its privilege.”

The vicars of the Eastern patriarchs said:

“Even if you prove that the ordination of the Greek presbyters belonged to your jurisdiction, you will nevertheless never be able to deny that the country belonged to the Greek kingdom.”

The legates of the holy Roman Church replied:

“Just as we do not speak falsely when we say that the ordination of Bulgaria belongs to us in a different way, so we certainly do not deny that Bulgaria itself once belonged to the Greek kingdom. But you ought to observe that the laws of sees prescribe one thing, while the divisions of kingdoms undergo another. We are not dealing with the division of kingdoms; we are speaking of the right of the sees.”

The vicars of the Eastern patriarchs said:

“We wish to learn in what different way you say that Bulgaria belongs to you.”

The legates of the holy Roman Church replied:

“The apostolic see, as you will be able to learn from the decretal writings of the most holy Roman pontiffs, canonically ordered and possessed both Epirus—namely, New Epirus and Old Epirus—in its entirety, as well as all Thessaly and Dardania, in which the city of Dardania is still shown today and whose present country is now called Bulgaria by these Bulgarians. Therefore, the jurisdiction which it had lost at that time through the invasion of the pagan Bulgarians was not taken away by the Church of Constantinople, as is now pretended, but was recovered from these men, who are now Christians, through the facts themselves.

“Second, because the Bulgarians, who subjected the country to themselves by the law of nations and have now retained for so many years what they seized, ought, since they have specially entrusted themselves—as we said above—to the patronage and jurisdiction of the apostolic see, to be subject to us, and not unjustly, since they chose us as their teachers of their own free will.

“Third, because the holy apostolic see, once commanded to do so by the most holy Pope Lord Nicholas, has held, still holds, orders, and governs these same Bulgarians for more than three years. Some of us who are here dedicated many churches there and created priests; and through the venerable bishops Paul, Dominic, Leopard, and Formosus, as well as through our co-bishop Grimoald, whom these Bulgarians have confessed before us that they continue to have among them together with many of our priests, the apostolic see transferred them from various errors to the truth of the Catholic faith with much labor, Christ going before.

“Therefore it does not follow that, without the knowledge of the Roman supreme pontiff, the Roman Church should be stripped of those things with which she is visibly endowed here and now.”

The vicars of the Eastern patriarchs said:

“Declare which of these ways you now wish to apply.”

The legates of the holy Roman Church replied:

“The holy apostolic see has neither chosen nor, through us, chooses you as judges in its own case, since you are truly inferior to it and since it alone has the right to judge specially concerning the whole Church. Nor has it entrusted us with delivering a judgment in this case. Therefore we reserve in its entirety to the judgment of its own knowledge what we have not received from it as something to be done. That knowledge is able, through the abundance of its books, to produce many arguments in its defense. By that judgment every decision of yours is despised as easily as it is pronounced lightly.”

The vicars of the Eastern patriarchs said:

“It is sufficiently improper that you, who reject the Greek empire and cling to alliances with the Franks, should preserve rights of ordination in the kingdom of our prince. Therefore we judge that the country of the Bulgarians, which we have discovered formerly to have been under Greek authority and to have had Greek priests, should now be restored through Christianity to the holy Church of Constantinople, from which it had withdrawn through paganism.”

The legates of the holy Roman Church protested:

“The sentence which you, without having been chosen or admitted, have now hastened to issue rather than pronounce—whether through arrogance, favor, or whatever it may be—we wholly rescind by the authority of the Holy Spirit until the determination of the holy apostolic see, so that it deserves in no way even to bear the name of a sentence.

“And you, Patriarch Ignatius, we adjure by the authority of the holy chief apostles, and we testify before God, his angels, and all those present: according to this letter of your most holy restorer, Lord Adrian, the supreme pontiff, which we now offer you, see by your diligence that you remain free from jurisdiction over all Bulgaria, sending none of your men there. Do not let the holy apostolic see, which restored your own jurisdiction to you, appear through you to lose what belongs to it. Rather, if—which we do not believe—you think you have a just complaint, do not fail solemnly to bring it before the holy Roman Church, your restorer.”

Then Patriarch Ignatius accepted the apostolic letter. Although he had been strongly urged to read it, he had delayed doing so. He replied:

“Far be it from me to become entangled in these presumptions against the honor of the holy apostolic see. I do not act so youthfully that I can be deceived, nor do I rave so senilely that I commit myself what I ought to censure in others.”

This was the end of that conversation.

But the imperial agitation, although it displayed hope on its face, increased. Nevertheless, the emperor invited the legates of the holy Roman Church to dinner and honored them with excellent gifts. He entrusted them to Theodosius the spatharius for escort, though not with the concern that was appropriate, and they were taken as far as Acodyrcharium, where they were carelessly dismissed without any provision.

After sailing for several days, they fell, alas, into the hands of the Slavs. They were stripped of all their possessions and of the authentic copy in which everyone’s subscriptions had been recorded, and they themselves would have been beheaded had their captors not feared those who had escaped from them.

At last, freed from exile by apostolic and imperial letters, they returned to Rome on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, in the fourth indiction. Before the most holy supreme pontiff and the nobles, they reported everything we have described above. They could produce no other written documents than the book of Ignatius’s proceedings, the libelli they had received from the Slavs, and the remaining libelli which they had formerly entrusted at Constantinople to Suppo, chief minister, and Anastasius, the most prudent librarian of the holy apostolic see. Through the foreseeing diligence of the latter—perhaps “the diligence of his presence”—the Roman Church received the copy of the lost synod which he had obtained permission to write for himself.

Earlier, the venerable bishops Formosus of Porto and Paul of Populonia, who, together with the others, had been sent at the command of the most holy Pope Nicholas for the purpose of preaching, returned from the Christianization of the Bulgarians and from their complete submission, by which they had specially bowed their devoted necks to the holy Roman Church. They brought joy to the apostolic see and presented to the supreme pontiff an envoy of Michael, king of the Bulgarians, named Peter.

This envoy, together with royal gifts, also presented a royal letter. In it they earnestly begged the supreme prelate either to send back to them Marinus, a deacon well known to them, consecrated as archbishop, or to send one of the cardinals—at least a man from his own Church, most worthy of the archbishopric in wisdom, person, and life—for the Bulgarians to choose. After the Bulgarians had approved him, he would return again and be elevated by the archiepiscopal ministry.

But since Marinus had, as we have said, been assigned to the Constantinopolitan mission, the supreme pontiff sent a certain Silvester for the Bulgarians to choose. When the Bulgarians sent him back together with Bishop Leopard of Ancona and Bishop Dominic of Treviso, while also sending letters most urgently requesting that either an archbishop or Bishop Formosus of Porto be returned to them, he received them with great speed.

Among other matters, the pope wrote back that whichever person the royal devotion expressly named, pontifical provision would undoubtedly furnish to the Bulgarians as archbishop.

But the Bulgarian king, unable to endure the delays of waiting any longer, was drawn in by the opportunity afforded by the children of Theodora, who were plotting to seize kingdoms alternately for themselves. He sent the same Peter, whom he had received late from Rome without obtaining the fulfillment of his desire, together with others from his entourage, to Constantinople to inquire to whom Bulgaria most properly ought to belong. There they were proved by our legates to belong to Roman jurisdiction.

Later, however, persuaded by gifts and promises from the Easterners and the Constantinopolitans, they accepted Greek priests and expelled ours, according to the account of Bishop Grimoald, who admits that he was rejected by them. Through that same Bishop Grimoald—who, abandoning the preaching office entrusted to him without the knowledge of the apostolic see, returned to Rome exceedingly wealthy—the apostolic see received a large volume of a letter sent in excuse for his conduct. It was entangled in frivolous arguments, as though under the pretext of a considered judgment of the presidents of the synod.

In this matter, since the bishop asserts, while the letter remains silent, that he was expelled by the Bulgarians, and since the presbyters say that they were not driven out by the Greeks or Bulgarians but deceived by the bishop, it does not indeed seem doubtful that the appearance of mutual treachery underlies the matter, until Christ, the searcher of hearts and reins, brings it to light in the examination of his servants.

[Some material appears to be missing at the end.]

[Column 1259]

## Letters and Decrees of Pope Adrian II

*(In Labbe, Councils, volume VIII.)*

### I. Letter to King Lothar

*(Year 867.)* He ordered Theutberga, who had come to Rome requesting dissolution of the marriage, to return to Lothar until a synod should decide the matter. He advises Lothar to receive her into his consortium or, if she should meanwhile remain elsewhere, to grant her the abbeys promised to her for the support of her life.

[Column 1259A]

Since our Lord, after the bonds of his Passion, the wounds of the nails, the mockery of the cross, and the glory of the Resurrection, entrusted his sheep—that is, the entire Church, already redeemed by his precious blood—to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, a third time, saying, “Feed my sheep; feed my lambs” (John 21), we, acting in his place as apostleship, with the Lord cooperating with us in all things, have by God’s will undertaken to feed the Lord’s flock with the nourishment of spiritual life and to guard it with diligent care: with the rod of equity and justice, and with the long-suffering of gracious humility and patience.

Opening at unwearied intervals the mouth of our apostolate, filled with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, for the stability and perpetual prosperity of your kingdom—and, indeed, for the everlasting and true salvation of your soul, by which you may now and forever enjoy blessed and secure life—we admonish your Excellency, illustrious King Lothar, with paternal affection and exhort you by apostolic right to abandon the counsels of wicked men and wholly reject their deadly persuasions. Open the ear of your heart to the heavenly voice of blessed Peter, the key-bearer, speaking through us. Cast far from you every hostility and the world’s illustrious love; listen with your whole desire to what we proclaim as most consonant with justice and righteousness, and carry it out with evident and devoted affection, because God approves as just not those who hear the law but those who perform it.

Therefore strive to receive the salutary admonition and correction of the apostolic see with a venerable and sincere mind. Two unlawful acts, committed long ago after you were overcome by the enticements of the flesh, appear to have been canonically corrected by our predecessor, Pope Nicholas of blessed memory. One is the wicked divorce from Theutberga, your lawful wife; the other is the most criminal cohabitation with the adulteress Waldrada. Not only does every divine law reject, condemn, and altogether prohibit these acts, but worldly laws also forbid them.

We would not now have taken care to write to you again concerning these matters unless we had recognized that you had undoubtedly strayed from the path of justice through the incitements of the flesh, dissolved the good bond of lawful union, and wished, through unsuitable pretexts, to return to your former illicit adultery.

Accordingly, Theutberga, your most illustrious queen and wife, came to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. With a devout mind she fulfilled her desire for prayer, sought to behold our face, and wished to explain to us with her own mouth the causes of her distress.

When she had been honorably received by us and by our entire Church, as was proper, for the love of God and of you, she said that because of a certain infirmity of her body, and because she had not previously been joined to you in a lawful marriage, she wished to separate from your companionship, cast aside the dignity and glory of the world for the love of God, and submit the neck of her heart beneath Christ’s gentle yoke.

When we heard and, with the Lord’s help, carefully considered these things, we were disturbed by no small astonishment: she sought to separate herself from you for such reasons, although it is written, as the Lord says, “Woman is joined to man by God,” and again, “What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matthew 19; 1 Corinthians 7). Moreover, as the Apostle says, she does not have authority over her own body, but you do, since by the Lord’s will she has been joined to you in lawful marriage and on the royal bed.

Although she earnestly sought this concession in suppliant peace, with your will and permission, we in no way gave our consent to such a desire of hers. We ordered her to return to the companionship of your greatness and to preserve unimpaired the rights of the royal marriage.

With regard to the matters for which she seeks separation from you, we rightly delayed either pronouncing a definitive judgment so suddenly, without the counsel of many of our brothers and a searching examination, or granting an immature consent. But if God grants us the help of salvation and life, we shall hold a synod concerning these matters and other ecclesiastical causes, investigate them with careful examination, and deliberate sufficiently before God our Savior, so that you may be saved according to God’s will; then we shall bring the matter to a conclusion.

Therefore we admonish and exhort your Excellency in apostolic words and in the Lord not to incline the ear of your nobility to the counsels and words of the impious, which oppose the truth. Rather, gladly submitting to the Lord’s and the apostles’ commands, receive that most noble queen, Theutberga, your wife, again into the companionship of marriage in the love of affection. For the love of God and of Saint Peter, and also for our honor, take care to retain her with the honor due to her, as a beloved member of your own body.
