If, however, because of the length and difficulty of the journey, or because of some bodily infirmity, she delays coming all the way to you, and chooses instead to remain in another place belonging to her which is more suitable for her, let her remain meanwhile, until the synod is held as we have said, safe and unharmed under your royal protection and defense. Let her retain control of the very abbeys which you yourself promised her orally, so that from their expenses and revenues she may have the necessary maintenance and worthy support.

But if any one of your people should contrive to inflict any opposition upon her, or should dangerously presume to harm her, let him know that he will undoubtedly be bound by us with the bond of perpetual anathema and separated from the fellowship of all Christians. As for you, if you give consent to such actions, you are to be excommunicated in every respect.

### II. To Ado, Archbishop of Vienne

*(Year 868.)* He praises his zeal and keenness of mind in guarding against the snares of the impious.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother Ado, archbishop of Vienne.

An envoy sent by your Beatitude with letters to my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of holy memory, found me ordained to his see, since that was the Lord’s will. Because we did not wish to frustrate your pious zeal, we have replied to your fraternity—not in his place, although, because of the envoy’s delay, we have answered only in part concerning what you wrote. For we ought to succeed in laboring for him whom, by God’s grace, we have succeeded in honor.

Accordingly, we return many thanks for the concern which you exercised through Count Waltarius regarding the glorious King Lothar. In this especially you show yourself an industrious shepherd of the Lord’s flock: although far away, you warn that the snares of the wolf must be guarded against.

Moreover, after examining the little notebooks which the same envoy brought, we admired the ingenuity and keenness of your understanding and immediately commended their author. Yet, as the copies of the letters indicate which our predecessor of apostolic memory sent concerning this matter to you in Gaul and to all the bishops situated beyond . . . , and as certain leading men also [numbered] twenty, etc., which are lacking in the manuscript codex.

### III. To the Synod of Troyes

*(Year 868.)* He approves their diligence in collecting the proceedings and grants the pallium to Wulfad. He urges them to write Nicholas’s name in the diptychs and to take care that nothing be attempted against his acts or decrees.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the holy synod gathered at Troyes, beloved in the Lord.

We have now, by divine favor, been placed in the see of my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of blessed memory, and have received the writings of your embassy sent to him. We praised your most prompt obedience, which you displayed in collecting the proceedings according to the decision of the aforementioned most holy prelate.

Although what your unanimity wrote concerning the deposition of Ebbo and the events that followed is not sufficient to make the sequence of what happened known as clearly as daylight—and although some of the matters which took place in connection with these events are missing from your account, matters which that already mentioned and ever-to-be-remembered pontiff wished to be reserved in their entirety to the apostolic see—we nevertheless judge the pious labor and zeal of your holiness not merely praiseworthy but worthy of proclamation far and wide.

For the innocence of our brother and co-bishop Wulfad and his colleagues, which a certain emerging circumstance had overshadowed for a considerable interval, has now, thanks be to God, come to light through your reconsideration and renewed examination, undertaken with the skill of your sacred and apostolic see’s frequently united diligence. The rays of their justice have extended outward like the brightness of the sun, for the complete certainty of everyone.

Therefore we approve, accept, and strengthen your judgment and your sentence, which the censure of the apostolic see preceded in due order. Assenting to your petition, to which it is exceedingly difficult to deny anything, we grant our aforementioned brother Wulfad, bishop of Bourges, the use of the pallium, according to the earlier custom, for the dignity and honor of the Church entrusted to him and for his instruction, as a fuller confirmation.

Our frequently mentioned predecessor would also have gladly granted this, had he himself received what you have now sent, or had the man who attempted to obtain it been proved to have been sent by the Church of Bourges. But what he did not accomplish, behold, we have accomplished. Indeed, what he had decided to complete, behold, with God as the author, we have supplied. There is no diversity of action where there is one and the same harmony of will, especially since we ought to labor for him whom we have succeeded in honor.

For we are those of whom the Psalmist sings: “Instead of your fathers, sons are born” (Psalm 44), and we have been established—though far inferior in merits—over the whole earth of the universal holy Church.

We pray and beseech you in the Lord: just as we have assented to the unanimous prayers of your fraternity and intend henceforth to grant our assent not only in this matter but in all matters, so you too should strive to satisfy my present requests. Have the frequently mentioned Pope Nicholas of apostolic memory written in the books or diptychs of your churches, and have his name recited without omission during the sacred solemnities of the Mass. In addition, command your other brothers and the priests of your dioceses to do the same.

We also take care to advise and admonish your love to oppose courageously, both by word and in writing, and to resist with the greatest strength, the Greek princes and all who exercise the clerical order if they attempt to act or decide anything against his person, his acts, or his decrees.

Know, moreover, that whatever is done here against his person or decrees will never receive my consent. I shall lend none of my mind, judgment, or disposition to such things, whoever may do them or in whatever manner they may be done.

Nevertheless, if anyone should humbly seek the mercy of the apostolic see, we do not wish to appear in any way inflexible toward such men, once the required satisfaction has been given. Let them only not strive to assert their innocence in such a way that they dare in any manner to break out into an accusation against so great a pontiff, especially one placed before the judgment of God.

While he lived, no one dared to attack him, accuse him of an unjust judgment, or even venture to do so faintly—unless perhaps someone humbly approached him, to whom he had rightly refused to grant remission because satisfaction had not yet been completed.

Therefore be vigilant concerning these matters; be strong. Announce them to all the bishops established beyond the Alps, so that they too may be watchful and attentive concerning them and may be stirred by salutary admonitions to act as defenders. *(Ivo, Part V, chapter 34.)*

For if the prelate of the apostolic see, or his decrees, are held in detestation or repudiation, none of your names or institutions will be able to remain firm or stable. Indeed, even the doctrines concerning the holy and undivided Trinity promulgated by the prelates of the apostolic see may suffer some damage if the statutes of any predecessors, especially those of the pontiffs of the first see, are subjected by later—and indeed inferior—persons to some kind of abolition or condemnation, or, through impious temerity, are at least exposed to mere disparagement. To say this is wicked; even to hear it is utterly horrifying.

We wish your holy fraternity good health in Christ, now and always.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the first indiction.

### IV. To Louis, King of Germany

*(Year 868.)* Concerning the victories of Louis the emperor against the Saracens; he forbids mention meanwhile of the matters concerning his brother Lothar.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Louis, glorious king.

Among the beginnings of my divinely ordained pontificate, though entrusted to an unworthy minister, the duty of proclaiming and urging the pursuit of peace above all other virtues fittingly rests upon me. Indeed, at the very beginning of the Lord’s Nativity, heavenly armies were seen proclaiming: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke I). Here we must carefully observe that, just as the shepherds who watched over their flocks more attentively than others were privileged above others to see the joys of so great a celebration, so without doubt we shall then deserve to attain the joy of heavenly blessings if we vigilantly watch over the Lord’s sheep: lest the ravenous wolf invade them through the snares of hatred or discord, or that greedy lion devour them through covetousness—the one who, as the apostolic prince teaches, goes about seeking someone to devour. [Col. 1263D]

[Col. 1264B]

Therefore now, dearest son, I urge, admonish, and earnestly exhort you, both when convenient and when inconvenient, [Col. 1264A] that your glory strive to preserve inviolate among all and with one another the bond of peace and love, which is greater than all virtues and burnt offerings (II Peter 1), and always admonish that it be guarded from the depths of the heart among those subject to you. For the condition of your kingdom will be able to remain safe and secure if you are known neither to shake anyone nor to be shaken by anyone.

Furthermore, we do not wish your Highness to be unaware that our dearest spiritual son, Louis, the most pious emperor protected by God, is not fighting against the sons of the holy religion, as some allege, nor against members of the household of the Christian faith, but against the sons of Belial and against the enemies of Christ’s name, for the security of the holy Church and especially of us, and for the liberation of many of the faithful who were already in nearly desperate danger in Samnium, so that the Saracens’ attack was even now threatening to invade our borders.

Having departed from the lofty height of his own throne and from the foundation of his most peaceful repose, he spares neither his body, nor heat, nor cold, nor does he yield to any circumstances. Rather, enduring every hardship and every danger for Christ’s name, there is nothing he refuses to undertake for the rescue of Christians, and nothing he declines to assume for the quiet and peace of the faithful. Indeed, through him divine mercy has already brought about no small measure of peace for the holy Church, and heavenly strength has cast down no small forces of the pagans. For he has repeatedly compelled those same men, emerging from their caves like mice, to turn their backs and flee to their hiding places, and by powerful strength he has broken the arms they raised against our people. [Col. 1264C]

Moreover, he has granted great security to all of us, both those who are far away and those who are near, since he has struck down some of them and has also converted others from their superstitious rite, teaching them thoroughly to follow the paths of Christ’s faith and true religion.

Therefore we consider it right to admonish your Highness with the greatest urgency, so that, provoked neither by your own impulses nor by the suggestions of others, you presume to disturb anything belonging to him. But do not allow anything belonging to his brother, namely the glorious King Lothair, to be disturbed by any impulse whatsoever. For whoever touches what belongs to his brother touches what belongs to him; and whoever, overcome by envy, disturbs that brother is plainly recognized as disturbing him. [Col. 1264D]

For this reason we advise and exhort your affection by this letter not to yield to wicked counsels or lend your ears to those plotting evil. Let each of you be content with his own right, and let no one attempt to usurp what belongs to the other or strive to invade it in any way—something which, once invaded, can without doubt bring considerable danger upon the invader.

Let your prudence therefore ensure that no obstacle be prepared for our most desirable son, now and always Augustus, who is carrying out God’s cause, vindicating the Lord’s inheritance, and fighting his battles—an obstacle by which the holy Church of God might in any respect be hindered or the progress of the faithful prevented. Rather, let the pagan ranks fear your weapons, and let those who are without God find your arrows sharp. [Col. 1265A] Indeed, according to the Apostle, your struggle must not be against flesh and blood, that is, against human beings, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places (Ephesians VI).

Otherwise, know that the hand of the apostolic see is firmly joined with that most pious prince, and recognize in advance that our arms, providing him with the strongest defenses, have been prepared without delay, while the supreme Master of the contest fights on our behalf and the intercession of the blessed chief apostles works with us.

We wish your glory, dearest son, to prosper in Christ now and always.

Given on the day before the Ides of February, in the first indiction.

## V. TO WALDRADA

*(Year 868.) Since Waldrada was said to have repented, Adrian restored her to communion in the Church at the request of Emperor Louis, on the condition that she not return to Lothair’s association.*

[Col. 1265B]

No one at all doubts that there is no crime which the Church, having received divinely granted power, cannot absolve those who desist from it and release those who repent, since it is said to her: “Whatever you forgive on earth will be forgiven in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matthew XVIII; John 20). “Whatever” includes everything, no matter how great or of whatever kind.

This principle must also reasonably be observed in your case. Although you had been bound, [Col. 1265C] we have learned from the reports of many, but especially of our dearest son Louis, the most clement Augustus, whose word must be trusted in all things, that you are said to have repented of the stain by which you were held fast and are reported to have abandoned the obstinacy to which you appeared attached. Know, therefore, that the bowels of mercy of the apostolic see have been opened to you, and that you have been freed from the bonds of anathema and excommunication and, by the authority of God and the blessed chief apostles, restored to the fellowship of all Christians and happily brought back to communion. Thus, by God’s authority, permission has been granted you thereafter to enter the church, pray, eat and drink with others, and speak with the other Christians—provided only that, because of the cunning of the ancient enemy, you adhere in no way whatsoever to the fellowship of the aforementioned king. [Col. 1265D]

Yet recognize that this benefit, although ecclesiastical discipline would have required it—for discipline ought to be inflexible toward the uncorrected but always flexible toward the corrected—has been obtained for you so quickly by the urgency of the prayers and incomparable affection of our desirable and spiritual son, the aforementioned and ever-to-be-remembered Augustus. His request is believed to be just and therefore must not in any way be postponed.

But henceforth take care to fortify yourself in such a way that, by God’s authority, you may truly receive in heaven the gift of release which you perceive yourself to have received on earth. For if you present yourself as absolved before human eyes but remain bound in the sight of God, you are free neither from the knot nor from the penalty; indeed, because of your pretense you will be bound by a stronger bond. For it is reported by the divine oracle: “Human beings look upon the face, but God regards the heart” (I Kings XVI). [Col. 1266A]

Therefore do not delight in lowly things; rather, always contemplate the heights with the eyes of your heart. The things that are seen are transitory, but the things that are not seen are eternal. I beg you, do not lose heavenly joys for earthly things or for visible pleasures—joys which cannot even be adequately imagined. Let no one flatter you; those who call you blessed are themselves deceiving you.

In the end, however many veils conceal justice and truth, they will eventually send forth the radiance of their own brightness, and their splendor cannot remain covered much longer by the cloud of savage concealment. With God’s favor, through both the diligence of the apostolic see and the care of the most upright prince, our dearest son, to whom no crookedness has ever been pleasing and could never in any way become pleasing, they will extend their rays like the brightness of the sun. [Col. 1266B]

## VI. TO THE BISHOPS OF GERMANY

He declares that he has absolved Waldrada and instructed her with appropriate admonitions.

ADRIAN, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brothers, the archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of Louis the glorious king.

Just as vengeance is due to the obstinate and incorrigible, so punishment must be removed from the converted and corrected, and healing must be applied. Therefore know that we have consented to offer the remedies of the apostolic see’s mercy to Waldrada, who, as is reported by the testimony of many, has turned from her former unlawful desires to the saving path of correction; and that, by the authority of God and the chief apostles, we have absolved her from the bond of excommunication and anathema. Thus, by God’s authority, permission has been granted her thereafter to enter the Lord’s Church, pray, eat and drink with others, and speak with the other Christians. [Col. 1266C]

We have sent Waldrada appropriate admonitions and have taken care that matters suitable for instruction be impressed upon her by letter. Your fraternity should earnestly request that the text of that letter be shown to you. Since this is fitting, we decree that you must demand and recognize it, so that through it your holiness may learn the signs of the apostolic see’s severity and gentleness, its remission and restraint, and the altogether remarkable marks of its measured discretion. [Col. 1266D]

We wish your holiness to prosper in Christ.

Given on the day before the Ides of February, in the first indiction.

## VII. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING

*(Year 868.) He replies to the letter Charles had written to Nicholas concerning Ebbo; grants the pallium to Wulfad; and asks Charles to favor Actard in obtaining a vacant church.*

ADRIAN, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, the glorious king.

[Col. 1267A]

The venerable Actard, formerly bishop of the city of Nantes, arriving at the apostolic threshold, brought a letter from your Highness which you had sent to my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of holy memory. We, however, having been appointed in his place to the apostolic see by the favor and mercy of the divine Majesty, received it. Accordingly, we hastened, as far as our strength permitted, though unworthy heirs, to fulfill what had been requested of him and, with Christ’s help, perhaps to discharge a father’s duty like sons who were not ungrateful.

For as long as the merits of the blessed Apostle Peter live before God, to whom all things live and do not die, there will never be lacking heirs to his faith and solicitude. Nor will there altogether be lacking those who, according to the measure of their strength and the capacity of the gift divinely bestowed, follow the rule of the most fervent love which he displayed toward God. He himself supplies whatever is negligently done by unworthy ministers. He himself illuminates to this day, with the light of his glory, the place which he once consecrated to the Lord by the offering of his own body, whatever sort of vicar may occupy it. Although the merits of its successor may be lacking, that see possesses the benefits of its predecessor and of its first occupant. [Col. 1267B]

Accordingly, having been sufficiently informed by your gracious letter concerning the matter of the restoration, in whatever form, of Ebbo, formerly archbishop of Reims, we approved the obedience and zeal which you showed in this matter according to the definition of the apostolic see, and we offered immense thanks to the author from whom all good things proceed.

The apostolic see had indeed carefully sought to determine whether anything concerning Ebbo might produce danger for the clerics formerly deposed by our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar and now being restored. But since Ebbo did not undertake the defense of any error by which a person becomes a heretic, and since the aforementioned clerics displayed nothing in this matter except humility and obedience, let what can be said about Ebbo now be covered by silence, since, as we think, it contributes nothing to usefulness. [Col. 1267C]

This is especially appropriate since Ebbo himself and all the bishops except Rothad, who had knowledge of his case, have died; since, because of the great length of time, the facts of what was then done in this matter cannot be known with complete certainty; and since it is not lawful for us easily to judge concerning those who have departed to the Lord. For since they stand under the hand of God’s judgment, to assign anything to them by human definitions is an indication not only of presumption, [Col. 1267D] but also plainly of condemnation.

For Ebbo now either stands or has fallen before his own Lord. If he stands, who would try to cast him down? If he has fallen, who would strive to raise him up? Unless perhaps it be someone who impiously dares to place his own judgment above the divine judgment. Let such matters therefore be left to the judgment of God, who searches the intentions of all, who, according to the Apostle, has been appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead, and who, in accordance with the firm foundation of our faith, will judge the living and the dead (Acts X).

Moreover, we return no small thanks to your graciousness because, when restoring the clerics to their former positions, you perceived that the apostolic see was extending its hand to them, and you yourself also eagerly took care to extend your hand, to the praise of God, to the reverence of the chief apostles, and to the honor of their see. [Col. 1268A]

Therefore, when you requested that the first of them, namely our brother and fellow bishop Wulfad, might be adorned with the use of the pallium by the gift of our authority, according to the custom of his predecessors, we rightly lent a favorable ear. Since you agreed and cooperated with the efforts of the apostolic see in restoring these men, we considered it quite inappropriate to disregard your affection when it came to receiving what was still lacking.

Nevertheless, we return countless thanks to your piety because, as is clear from his report and can be understood from the pious feeling expressed in your letter, you have striven to show such great compassion toward our aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Actard that it is evident beyond question that you bear the greater part of his sufferings and hardships. [Col. 1268B]

Yet, agreeing with the wishes of your Excellency, we do not think that so important a man, so necessary to Christ’s Church, ought to be enveloped in such miseries or burdened by such hardships, especially since he is already weakened by the maturity of age, and particularly since he possesses considerable learning and is commended by the not insignificant testimony of the bishops of the churches in your kingdom.

Therefore, if his church, as the circumstances reported by him, by his own metropolitan, by many bishops, and by your letters indicate, is completely ruined and has already been reduced to desolation for some time—pagans not merely passing through but also establishing themselves there, thereby laying waste the surrounding regions and leaving them without inhabitants, and the Britons having carried away whatever possessions remained—we have decreed that another vacant church alone should be granted to him. [Col. 1268C]

In accordance with the necessary purpose of this decree, kindly offer your customary and willing support for the love of Christ. We do not wish a lesser church to be given him than the one that was his. Although he himself does not ask for this, lest he be marked by a reputation for ambition, it is fitting that he obtain a more important one.

For among the other marks of his virtues, he has often endured the fury of barbarians and did not blush to confess Christ not only before human beings but also before pagans and unbelievers. To him, whatever their number, Christ’s sheep may rightly be entrusted, since he did not refuse to preach Christ himself even amid swords, chains, and various dangers. [Col. 1268D]

Therefore, moved by his manifold misery, his prolonged wandering, and his continual sorrow, we have bestowed upon him the honor of the pallium solely from a feeling of compassion. We would not otherwise grant this to him, nor to anyone without [the consent of] the metropolitans, unless we had learned that he had repeatedly suffered exile, the sea, and chains, and had often been brought even to a capital sentence; and unless he had earned this through such great and grievous losses—or rather, through such merits—as a swift consolation: namely, so that in place of exile and chains he might have the ornaments of the pallium, not as a permanent institution for the church into which he is to be incardinated, but for his own special use and for a fixed period.

Let him therefore enjoy the adornment of so great an honor, for he is recognized as holding a foremost place among the bishops. Through this distinction, may your excellent diligence also be admonished, and may reverence for this sacred gift urge your pious heart more earnestly and more beneficially, so that, with your favor also, this great man may obtain the governance of a vacant church—even if a metropolitan church should become available—to remove all obstacles placed in his way and to carry out the episcopal ministries divinely entrusted to him. [Col. 1269A]

For we consider it unworthy that anyone should come afflicted to the apostolic see, where Catholics are always aided, and depart without consolation—especially since certain histories report that one of the Roman princes, although a stranger to the faith of Christ, declared that no one ought to leave the emperor sad. [Col. 1269B]

The abundance of our compassion must make up for the poverty of others, so that he may be able to be sorrowful with those who are sorrowful and rejoice with those who rejoice, and, not bowing down in partiality toward persons as though before a footstool, may, having been consoled, by God’s authority console those who are in every affliction, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

We pray that your glory, dearest son, may prosper in Christ now and always.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, in the first indiction.

## VIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE SYNOD OF SOISSONS

*(Year 868.) He orders that Bishop Actard, for whom they had written, be incardinated into whichever church becomes vacant, even a metropolitan one, and grants him the use of the pallium as consolation for his afflictions.*

[Col. 1269C]

To our most reverend and most holy brothers and fellow bishops who assembled the previous year at the city of Soissons.

Among the matters which, gathered together by the authority of the apostolic see, you synodically defined last year concerning our brother and fellow bishop Wulfad and his colleagues, you also set before the apostolic see the case and sufferings of our venerable brother Actard, formerly bishop of the city of Nantes. At the same time, unanimously and with great urgency, you commended him exceptionally, requesting that so great a see come to his assistance.

We received your report—or suggestion—with as much gratitude and willingness as we understood, beyond all doubt, that it had arisen from fraternal affection, although by God’s authority we now, unworthily, occupy the governance of that see. This was especially so because the writings of my predecessors, the most holy bishops Leo and Nicholas, which were reviewed with you, provide testimony that must not be disregarded. [Col. 1269D]

Therefore, since he was serving as the envoy of all those who were present at the Council of Troyes and was working with particular urgency on this matter, we entrusted to him the pallium to be conveyed to our brother and fellow bishop Wulfad of the holy church of Bourges, as we have already indicated in other letters.

But since that same reverend bishop, as your report makes clear, has now for a long time been driven from his own church by the persecution of pagans and wanders abroad from place to place, exhausted by many hardships, we grieve deeply and, bound to him by brotherly love, sympathize with him—especially since it is written by the Apostle: “Whoever sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (I John III). [Col. 1270A]

We grieve above all that, under such a pretext, the wandering of a man of such great learning and such great moral integrity produces the greatest loss for the Lord’s sheep, since the benefit which could have come to Christ’s Church through him has now for so long been excluded.

Therefore, following the institutions of the fathers who preceded us and the examples of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, especially those of blessed Pope Gregory, who is known to have frequently established provisions concerning matters such as those which, with God’s favor, we now establish for the aforementioned bishop, we decree [Col. 1270B] that our most holy brother and fellow bishop Actard, so often mentioned, be completely incardinated into whatever church may happen to be deprived of its own pastor.

Thus, once established in it, he may exercise the episcopal offices which he received through the imposition of hands, and, solemnly performing the pastoral ministry, season the Lord’s sheep with the salt of the wisdom divinely granted to him, bringing profit from them to his Creator without any impediment.

If, however, his church, as the circumstances reported by him, by his own metropolitan, and by your letters indicate, is completely ruined and has already been reduced to desolation for some time—pagans not only passing through but also establishing themselves there, thereby laying waste the surrounding regions and leaving them without inhabitants, and the Britons having carried away whatever possessions remained—we do not wish a lesser church to be given him than the one that was his. [Col. 1270C]

Although he does not ask for this, lest he be marked by a reputation for ambition, it is fitting that he obtain a more important church, even if a metropolitan church should perhaps become available. For among the other marks of his virtues, he has often endured the fury of barbarians and has confessed Christ; he may now rightly say to God: “According to the multitude of the sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Psalm XCIII).

To obtain the fulfillment of this matter, we have sent prayers to our beloved son Charles, the glorious king. And now, by this present address, we exhort your unanimous charity to take care to offer unfailing support and zeal for this work of piety. [Col. 1270D]

Just as you wish our goodwill toward you to be evident in times of need, so let your ready diligence toward this brother, to whom we are extending our hand, be evident by your extending your own hand to him until what we have decreed reaches fulfillment.

For we too, moved by his manifold misery, prolonged wandering, and continual sorrow, have bestowed upon him the honor of the pallium solely from a feeling of compassion. We would not otherwise grant this to him, nor to anyone without [the consent of] the metropolitans, unless we had learned that he had repeatedly suffered exile, the sea, and chains, and had often been brought even to a capital sentence; and unless he had earned this through such great and grievous losses—or rather, through such merits—as a swift consolation: namely, so that in place of exile and chains he might have the ornaments of the pallium, not as a permanent institution for the church into which he is to be incardinated, but for his own special use and for a fixed period. [Col. 1271A]

For we consider it unworthy that anyone should come afflicted to the apostolic see, where Catholics are always aided, and depart without consolation in any respect. The abundance of our compassion must make up for the poverty of others, so that he may be sorrowful with those who are sorrowful and rejoice with those who rejoice, and, having been consoled, may now, by God’s authority, console those who are in every affliction, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

## IX. TO ACTARD, BISHOP

*(Year 868.) He grants Actard the use of the pallium as a consolation.*

[Col. 1271B]

ADRIAN, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Actard of the holy Church of Nantes, for the days of your life only.

If, according to the bowels of divine mercy, no amount of compassion toward anyone is blameworthy, how much more must the affection of complete charity be shown toward those who, appearing blameless in divine worship, later endured the trials of various temptations and nevertheless, with Christ’s favor, did not fail amid those temptations?

For this reason we bless God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we ourselves may also console those who are in every affliction. [Col. 1271C]

And to you, brother Actard, worn down by dreadful hardships and shaken by the long misery of captivity, yet not overcome amid the swords of unbelievers—indeed, wonderfully rescued and freed by God’s providence—we have judged that the honor of the pallium should be granted. You have now for many years wandered abroad far from your own Church, far from acquaintances and relatives, because of the fury of those same barbarians and the continual oppression of the Britons, to whom, alas, you are known to be excessively near and from whom you suffer persecution almost worse than from pirates.

With this pallium, once by God’s authority and our decree you have obtained some vacant bishopric, know that we have permanently incardinated you into it; [Col. 1271D] or, if it should happen to be your own, you may use it for specified periods.

We would not otherwise grant this to you, nor to anyone without [the consent of] the metropolitans, unless you had suffered repeated exiles, the sea, and chains, and had often been brought even to a capital sentence—as your metropolitan testifies, who has made this known to us by letter and has indicated to you that no hope remains for you in your own see—and unless these great losses, or rather merits, had demanded it as the swiftest consolation.

Thus you may have, in place of exile and a chain, the ornaments of the pallium—not as a permanent decree for your church, but specifically for your use for a fixed period during your present life.

Use, therefore, with God’s assent, the pallium granted to you by us solely from a feeling of mercy and consolation. Unless you prove ungrateful to the pontiffs of the apostolic see, wear it throughout your life, adorned by its prescribed observance. [Col. 1272A]

We grant it to your fraternity, however, only for the celebration of the solemn Mass: on the day of the holy and venerable resurrection and Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and on the day of his Ascension; on the Assumption of blessed Mary, the ever-virgin Mother of God; on the feasts of the blessed apostles; on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; and also on the feast of Saint Martin, the confessor of Christ, as well as on the solemn feast of your church. We likewise grant it on the anniversary of your ordination, as was decreed by our most blessed predecessor Gregory, pontiff of this apostolic see.

In the secretarium your fraternity must put on the pallium and then proceed to the solemn celebration of Mass, arrogating nothing further to yourself through rash presumption. Otherwise, while something is improperly assumed in outward dress, what might properly be permitted may also be lost. [Col. 1272B]

If anything remains of the possessions of the diocese of Nantes after the devastation of the wicked Northmen and the seizure by the Britons, we entrust it to your care.

Moreover, we judge and define by the authority of apostolic institution that no metropolitan bishop or other bishop may presume to pronounce judgment against you in a dispute involving an accusation, if you appeal to the apostolic see or seek to have the matter heard or examined by its special judgment, unless our decree has first been issued. Rather, you shall be reserved without delay for examination or judgment solely at the discretion of the apostolic see, by whose decree or generosity you are recognized as having been incardinated and invested with the pallium in a vacant church. [Col. 1272C]

Written by the hand of Zacharias, notary and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of February, in the first indiction. Farewell.

On the fifth day before the Kalends of March, through the hands of Anastasius, librarian of the holy supreme apostolic see; while our most pious lord, the perpetual Augustus Louis, the great emperor, was reigning, in the nineteenth year of his reign and the eighteenth year after his consulship, in the first indiction.

## X. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

*(Year 868.) He praises Hincmar, urges him to encourage King Charles to remain steadfast in the matter of Lothair, and asks that a vacant church be granted to Actard.*

[Col. 1272D]

To our most reverend and most holy brother Hincmar, archbishop of Reims.

Although the frequent reputation of your holiness, which has always existed only with praise, had long since made you known to us, the pleasing report of our brothers—the venerable Arsenius, apocrisiarius of our see, and Actard, most holy bishops; and my beloved son Anastasius, librarian of the holy apostolic see—has enabled us to recognize more clearly the commendations due to your virtues and exemplary character. Therefore know that my soul has conceived such ardor for your affection [Col. 1273A] as though we had enjoyed a thousand mutual conversations.

Receive, then, the pledge of our promise, and rest wholly in confidence upon us, as upon our predecessors.

Moreover, your holiness knows well how many struggles the apostolic see has undertaken in the cause of King Lothair, and how many labors it has assumed through its pontiffs, Benedict and Nicholas. Therefore, since we possess the same spirit which those fathers are proved to have possessed, we follow and decree the same things in this matter as they did.

For this reason we especially admonish the diligence of your fraternity not to allow the zeal which you formerly displayed in this affair to be weakened in any way. Rather, trusting in our authority, do not cease to speak before kings and rulers of the testimonies of the Lord, [Col. 1273B] so that what has been destroyed by God’s authority may not be rebuilt by the devices of those plotting deceit.

Since, in this work of piety, our beloved son Charles has labored and cooperated with the apostolic see among kings, while you above all among priests have worked and cooperated with it, we particularly exhort your distinguished vigilance to oppose wickedness courageously and to admonish the aforementioned most pious king continually, so that he may complete the good which he had begun.

Thus may the tunic of your various virtues reach down to the ankles, and may the sacrifice of your good work, offered to God with its tail, deserve to become a burnt offering. May it also be said of you what is written of holy Job, who did not cease from divine service—not, “Thus Job acted for some days,” but, “Thus Job acted all his days” (Job I). For the holy living creatures were seen to walk not behind themselves but before themselves as they proceeded (Ezekiel I). [Col. 1273C]

Moreover, embrace the venerable bishop Actard in the arms of brotherly charity, and remember always to assist him in times of need for the love of the blessed chief apostles. We do not say this as though he did not praise you for having shown him compassion and mercy, but so that what you have done until now from a motive of charity you may now complete out of affection for the chief apostles, to whose threshold he hastened and whose protection he sought.

Therefore press your request, when convenient and when inconvenient, and because he lacks his own church, strive in our place to obtain from our beloved, aforementioned son, the excellent King Charles, that, with his favor also, a vacant episcopal church—even if a metropolitan church should become available—be granted to him. [Col. 1273D]

For he is a strong ox of the Lord, established by the Lord himself, and therefore many harvests must undoubtedly be entrusted to him for threshing. For it is written: “Where there are many harvests, there the strength of the oxen is evident” (Proverbs II).

We wish your fraternity to prosper in Christ now and always.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the first indiction.

## XI. TO HERARD, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS

*(Year 868.) That he grant Bishop Actard the monastery which he formerly held in his diocese. He promises that he will ensure that nothing is granted to the Britons against the privileges of that church.*

[Col. 1274A]

ADRIAN, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Herard, archbishop of Tours.

The miseries and dreadful calamities of Actardus, our common brother and fellow bishop, do not require any exposition to your reverence. For since you yourself, as one who shares in them and is almost constantly in their midst, have a clearer experience of them, it is to be believed—indeed, we have learned this from the bishop himself—that you have shown no little compassion and pity for his continual hardships. Yet because he has often wished, through our letters and by means of your affection, to be assisted, and because, out of love for the chief apostles, whose protection he sought with such great labor and devotion [Col. 1274B], he desired that some particular consolation be granted him, by these present lines we exhort and implore your charity that, among the distinguished benefits you have conferred upon him, he may now, through your benevolent generosity and for love of the apostles already mentioned, obtain that monastery which he is known formerly to have held in his diocese. Thus he who is found to be greatly deprived of his own resources may at least from this receive the means of sustaining his life through the support of others.

We certainly do not believe that you will refuse this, if with attentive mind you consider how a brother ought to be helped by a brother; and if your diligent judgment, as is fitting, weighs how unworthy it would be for a petitioner not to obtain what is requested from your goodness out of love for such great apostles. As for the matters which the same venerable Actardus especially brought before us concerning the privileges of your church or diocese [Col. 1274C], we have sufficiently set them out in writing to Duke Solomon and the people of Brittany. Your experience will also be able to recognize this in the copy which the same bishop will carry with him. If, perhaps, some of them should come to us, and you learn that they are asking for anything contrary to reason, know that, with the Lord’s help, they will obtain nothing of the kind from us.

We wish your fraternity good health in Christ. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the first indiction.

### XII. TO ADON, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE. (Year 868.)

He heaps extraordinary praise upon his predecessor Nicholas and excuses himself for having tempered, with the guiding principle of equity, certain matters which Nicholas had handled more severely in his zeal for justice.

[Col. 1274D]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother Adon, archbishop of Vienne.

I received the letter of your holiness with great rejoicing, and, reading it again, I rendered innumerable thanks to almighty God, because you do not consent to surrender the duty of watchfulness entrusted to you to sluggishness, but demonstrate, by an effort worthy of admiration, how diligently it ought to be exercised by the rulers of the holy Church. Behold, you labor as an energetic master of the household on behalf of the house of God, whose zeal has indeed consumed you. Behold, you are concerned as a strong defender on behalf of the city of God, whose peace you plainly never cease to seek.

Therefore, we praise what you urge concerning the privileges of the Roman Church and the decrees of my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of apostolic memory, which are to be preserved without mutilation; we accept what you advise; and we wholly approve what you admonish. For we cannot permit the acts of that pontiff to be overturned in any way by anyone, precisely because, after a long interval, he appeared to us amid the clouds of the present life like a new star and, by the radiance of his life and teaching, driving away the darkness of errors by God’s agency, both did and taught what should not be abolished but imitated.

Indeed, who, even if no other consideration stood in the way, would allow any of his acts to be annulled [Col. 1275B], unless he wished to teach that his own acts would someday have to be weakened? For, as blessed Pope Gregory teaches, it is exceedingly harsh, and especially opposed to the good conduct of priests, to rescind what has been rightly ordered under any pretext of reason and, by one’s example, to teach others to dissolve later what they themselves have established.

Yet if there are matters which that most sacred and truly God-filled bishop handled according to the requirements of time or circumstance with equity as his guide—for example, if he struck someone in zeal for justice and with the aim of correction—and if we, following the requirements of time or circumstance in the same way, moderate and soften those matters differently, we are not abolishing them but are recognized as completing what he began. For even if he began to heal a wound by a harsh method of treatment, while we strive to bring it to health with a gentle application [Col. 1275C], we both pursue not different but one and the same purpose. He applied what he then saw to be appropriate, while we do not refuse to apply what we now consider suitable.

If, then, he were to begin with mild remedies (*lenibus*, evidently misread in the source as *denibus*), he would not heal; and if we judged that harsh measures should be applied only sparingly, we likewise would in no way attain the desired health. If, therefore, the variety of medicines scandalizes you, although what ought rather to build up is the one and same discovery of physicians—or, indeed, the health of the sick—then consider this: if he had come upon the care of the sick while they were healthy and had been healed by divine providence, he certainly would not have refused to receive them.

For he had read, and among other such teachings had fully understood, the words of the Lord: “See that I am God. I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” [Col. 1275D]. And certainly the aforementioned great bishop Gregory writes: “Just as punishment is rightly due to persistent sin, so pardon must be granted to those who repent.”

But let this statement suffice here. Moreover, we admonish your affection that, if there are matters which pertain to the common welfare of the Church, or which you perceive to be spiritually congenial to our see, you should consider them attentively and promptly report to our episcopate whatever ought to be known. Thus it may become clearer than daylight how much you love the memory and see of blessed Peter, and how earnestly you strive to cling to him. Then, abiding in his solidity, you will fear no assault of any advancing wave, with God as your author [Col. 1276A].

We wish your holiness good health in Christ, now and always. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the first indiction.

### XIII. TO BASIL THE EMPEROR. (Year 868.)

He gives thanks for the restoration of Ignatius to the patriarchal see.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son and most Christian emperor Basil, protected by God, ever Augustus.

Because, most tranquil emperor, you listened to the voice of God, conveyed to you through the ministry of the apostolic see; because you honored His distinguished apostles; and because you restored to the Church of Constantinople its rightful shepherd, expelling the adulterer: may you be blessed by almighty God; may you see the submission of your enemies; may you enjoy length of days; may you have upon your throne an heir from your own loins; and may you possess everlasting life in the future—provided that you do not depart from what you have rightly begun, but persevere in it to the end, O spiritual and most beloved son.

Although, whatever you may do, we shall never in any way depart from the decrees of my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of holy memory, concerning the deposition of Photius and the recovery of our brother and fellow priest Ignatius, which he promulgated, we nevertheless desire to agree with those decrees precisely as he, when he enacted them, strove to agree with the divine commandments [Col. 1276C]. For it is necessary that, by preserving the decrees of my predecessors, I teach that after my death my own decrees, too, must in no way be violated by those who come after me.

But after we learned that merciful God had stirred up both your empire and your affection for this purpose—that you should gather what had been scattered, raise up what had fallen, and restore what had been crushed—we can confidently ask, thanks be to God, that those who have been cast down be received by your empire, and that those who have been scattered be gathered together.

Therefore, we are sending back to your trust and commending to you the most prudent man, Theognostus, your most honorable exarch. He served as an envoy both for our brother and fellow minister Ignatius and for the other afflicted persons; for seven years he lived as a pilgrim and sojourner at the shrines of the chief apostles, and continually commended your memory there. From the day of his arrival until the present he has not ceased to recount the praises of your piety, to make known the wounds of the Church, and to demand their healing [Col. 1276D].

Now, therefore, since he too is one of those who, after the wolf became shepherd, were immediately scattered and have now been gathered again by you, who piously govern all things, we ask that he himself be recalled and placed by your clemency in the fold of all the faithful. May he deserve to be counted among pious and rejoicing sons by paternal affection after his return from a long captivity. For love of God and in honor of your protectors, the chief apostles—from whose rule this mission proceeds—may he feel the aid of your gentleness: after disturbance, serenity; after storm, calm; and after many adversities, the fulfillment of hoped-for prosperity [Col. 1277A]. Thus, through the intercessions of your patrons, namely the chief apostles, from whose see he is being sent back, and whose primacy he did not cease, through many long years, to invoke day and night on behalf of your greatly troubled Church, may merciful God—whom you honor in His servants—grant you continual happiness here, the submission of your enemies, and eternal glory and infinite rewards in the future, together with the heavenly kingdom and everlasting life.

We wish your empire, O spiritual and most beloved son, good health in Christ, now and always. Given on the Kalends of August, in the first indiction.

### XIV. TO IGNATIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. (Year 868.)

The pope complains that he was not informed as soon as possible by Ignatius of his restoration to office; he commends Theognostus to him.

[Col. 1277B]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most honorable brother and fellow priest Ignatius, most holy patriarch of Constantinople.

It would have been fitting for your holiness, although you did not initially summon us to your aid, at least now, concerning your restoration—which is said to have taken place—to make us rejoice by hastening to send us a letter of your own. Yet, although you have shown less eagerness to do this, you should at least not remain silent about the grace of divine mercy, which has worked wondrously in you [Col. 1277C]. For, according to what is said by the angel to Tobit, “It is good to conceal the king’s secret, but it is glorious to reveal the works of God” (Tobit 12).

Nevertheless, our conscience consoles us, for it bears witness that not so much for you as for the preservation of charity my predecessor, the most blessed Pope Nicholas of apostolic memory, struggled. “If you love only those who love you, what reward will you have?” (Matthew 5). But since you are our brother, “if we see our brother in need and close our hearts against him, how does the love of God remain in us?” (1 John 3).

Know, therefore, that in those matters which my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of holy memory, established and defined after laboring greatly for your person, for those who did not fail you in your tribulations, and also for the Church of Constantinople, we likewise remain and shall remain steadfast [Col. 1277D]. Just as he, until the hour of his death, did not cease to work on behalf both of you and of those who are with you in that Church, so we too, with God as our author, shall give no place to sluggishness in this work of piety until the end. For we ought to follow the labor of him whom, by God’s grace, we succeeded in honor.

Moreover, behold, we have sent to you our common son Theognostus, the most reverend exarch, who is dear to us. He escaped from the persecuting rivals of yours over there with nothing but his life and, having scarcely reached us in a changed garment, gained safety. Then, for nearly seven years, he remained at the memorials of the apostles as a guest and stranger [Col. 1278A]. He lamented almost without interruption not so much his own misery as the oppression of your holiness and the calamities of the Church of Constantinople. Thus he not only stirred up my predecessor, already mentioned, but afterward stirred me up unceasingly, night and day, striking our sides with repeated goads of exhortation on behalf of the condition of so great a Church and your restoration. Like the angel of old, he never ceased to say to us each day: “Rise, Peter; take courage for the salvation of the nations” (Acts 5)—until, by God’s favor, he received the news which he had always carried ardently in his heart.

For this reason, most beloved brother, as we commend him to your holiness, we ask and implore that he may experience from you a disposition to show him kindness [Col. 1278B]. Just as he became a sharer in your suffering, so let him also be a sharer in your consolation; for “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (1 Timothy 5). He ought to find favor in the presence of your holiness not merely as one who has become our familiar, but also as one received from the see of the chief apostles; for love of that see should ensure that he finds no ordinary grace with you.

But if you should decide to send anyone to the apostolic see, we especially wish this man to be sent before the others. Thus, as we also desire, he may rejoice in your prosperity, and may hasten to report to our apostolate the plan, order, and condition of the Church of Constantinople, in accordance with the diligence by which he knows that we most certainly desire to be informed about all ecclesiastical matters [Col. 1278C].

We also commend to your holiness Euthymius, the most glorious spatharius, who, bearing an imperial embassy to Rome, was the first to announce to us and to our Church what we had always desired to hear concerning your fraternity. By making known the divine mercy shown toward you and the recovery of your health, he caused everyone to rejoice. We therefore ask that he too may experience your protection when the occasion requires, and may, through the affection of our love, receive the comfort of your protection.

We wish your holiness good health now and always, most beloved brother and fellow minister. Given on the Kalends of August, in the first indiction.

### XV. Address of Pope Adrian to the Council Convened against Photius, Read by John, Archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church

[Col. 1278D]

Since we ought, O most beloved brothers and sons, to be energetic and diligent cultivators of the Lord’s field, and to use the spiritual mattocks of heavenly commandments for its cleansing, it is necessary that, if we see any thorns in it or anything poisonous beginning to grow, we should strive to uproot these things completely with equal labor and united zeal. We must take up the rake of examination and bring forth the sickle of judgment in harmonious contest, lest, I beg you, it be said against us in the tone of one who reproaches: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matthew 9).

Let us work together, therefore, beloved, and labor continually in the Lord’s field, but especially now, when, in the Church which is most plainly called the Lord’s field, a new and unheard-of presumption and rashness has arisen through Photius [Col. 1279A].

For this Photius, while he was still a secular official, had always carried in his heart a kind of innate envy against our brother and fellow bishop, Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople. Desiring not to ascend gradually or little by little to the summit of the episcopate, but to leap over it in precipitous strides while Ignatius was still alive, he made himself a stranger to the communion of that most blessed bishop. By this act he utterly excluded himself from the universal Church, which remained in communion with that most blessed patriarch. Having thus undoubtedly placed himself among the schismatics, and employing secular powers against the sacred apostolic canons, he finally seized the Church of Constantinople with tyrannical and adulterous audacity.

By usurping what did not belong to him, he displayed outwardly what he had carried within the chamber of his heart and concealed beneath a veil of hypocrisy: namely, that he had no cause for separating from his patriarch or abandoning communion with the entire Church other than the most evil desire to pursue the insignia of the pontificate and obtain the reins of a higher dignity and power. Thereafter he abused these things and, suddenly changed not in mind but in appearance, inflicted so many and such great exiles, dangers of every kind, and even deaths upon the priests of Christ and other faithful people that he seemed in every respect to imitate the savagery of Diocletian [Col. 1279B].

For these and similar reasons, my predecessor Nicholas, of holy memory, bishop of this apostolic see, overcome by fraternal charity, first rightly rebuked him and suitably admonished him, not only through envoys but also by letters. He made clear in authoritative writings that he could in no way give his consent to Photius’s promotion. Then, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing and that Photius’s tyranny was extending farther and farther, he relied upon divine and apostolic authority and followed the custom of the pontiffs of the apostolic see over which he presided. Having at hand, according to the Apostle, the power “to punish every disobedience” (2 Corinthians 10), he struck Photius down by a canonical sentence, deposing him for the restoration of those whom he had cast down and for the relief of the innumerable afflicted. Since, as you yourselves know, he could not correct him, he separated him by anathema from the order which Photius had acquired in the manner of a robber [Col. 1279D].

Inflamed by this, Photius not only did not return to the one who struck him—he was harder than flint and felt not even harsh blows—but, imitating the devil, did not cease to be proud even after falling from heaven. Instead, he often gathered assemblies of the wicked and collected a synagogue of bloodshed, over which he himself presided as the chief of robbers. First, like a most savage parricide, he struck his own father, Ignatius, the most reverend patriarch; and, despairing of reaching the light except through the destruction of his parent, he did not fear to kill him with a cruel bite like that of a savage viper.

Afterward he set his mouth against heaven, and his tongue traversed the earth [Col. 1280A], when, against the divine ordering established from heaven concerning the primacy of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, he opened the throat of a foul abyss and sharpened his tongue like a serpent against the apostolic see of that keeper of the keys of the same heavenly kingdom, and against its supreme and pre-eminent dignity and power. He did not fear to attack the life of my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of blessed memory, nor did he consent to spare us, who were scarcely worthy to be called his servants, much less his followers. He judged that he should assail both him and us with curses, as far as he could, and infect us with blasphemous words, attempting to fabricate deceptions of falsehood and, by compiling them, to contrive I know not what Pythonic dreams or arguments.

And certainly, who and how great and what kind our father was, all of you who recall the distinctions of his character and the trophies of his virtues have recognized fully [Col. 1280B]. You know how, during the dark course of this dismal age, he appeared at last like a new star—or rather, like Phoebus in the sky, shining more brightly than all the stars. You know how neither every kind of flattery could break him nor hardship disturb him. You know also how he did not favor the rulers of the world, namely Michael and Bardas, against justice. Setting himself as a wall on behalf of the house of the Lord, he often rebuked them and, when they acted unjustly, frequently resisted them fearlessly.

Therefore, most beloved brothers and sons, consider attentively what ought to be done by us concerning such presumption; what is to be deliberated through our ministry concerning that assembly and its profane acts; and what is to be defined unanimously by all of us concerning those who were present or who subscribed with their own hands. Let each of you freely declare what you think.

For my part, for the law of God, for preserving the canons of the fathers, for venerating the apostles, for defending the privileges of their see, for proclaiming the memory of my predecessor Pope Nicholas of holy remembrance, for following his acts, and for enacting the definitions, I am prepared not only to endure various hardships but, if necessary, in the manner of my holy predecessors the pontiffs, to face the danger of death.

### XVI. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS. (Year 868.)

He commends the Church of Laon to him while Bishop Hincmar is coming to Rome; he orders Northmannus to be excommunicated unless he restores what he has taken away.

[Col. 1280D]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims.

We gladly embrace the illustrious Hincmar, bishop of Laon, who is eager with the desire to visit the thresholds of the holy apostles. We not only do not delay his arrival but, with apostolic gravity, forbid him to remain beyond the Kalends of August, knowing that he can make spiritual progress through such a vow.

Therefore, as apostolic authority favors him in coming, so may episcopal kindness favor him, so that through your solicitude his episcopate may suffer no loss, while through your generosity, by our intercession, he receives an increase of the estates wrongly possessed by Northmannus [Col. 1281A].

Know, therefore, that by apostolic authority Northmannus is immediately to be excluded from ecclesiastical communion through the ministry of your mouth unless he personally divests himself of all the property of the Church of Laon. And the venerable Bishop Hincmar, if he abuses his intention of coming to Rome and does not strive to fulfill what he rightly vowed, is to be punished, God forbid, with the judgment due to a transgressor.

Whoever, therefore, from the time when he begins to come to Rome until the time when, with Christ as his guide, he returns to his own place, causes any loss whatsoever to that Church in any matter, since we specially entrust its episcopate to your holiness to be safeguarded after the king, must know that he will be deprived of the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood for as long as he has not made legitimate—indeed canonical—satisfaction to the holy Church of Laon, to you, and to its bishop.

We wish your holiness good health in Christ.

### XVII. TO KING CHARLES THE BALD. (Year 868.)

He commends the Church of Laon to the king while its bishop is coming to Rome.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, most excellent king.

We gladly embrace the illustrious Hincmar, bishop of Laon, who is eager with the desire to visit the thresholds of the holy apostles. We not only do not delay his arrival but, with apostolic gravity, forbid him to remain beyond the Kalends of August, knowing that he can make spiritual progress through such a vow [Col. 1281C].

Therefore, as apostolic authority favors him in coming, so may royal kindness favor him, so that through your solicitude his episcopate may suffer no loss, while through your generosity, by our intercession, he receives an increase of the estates wrongly possessed by Northmannus.

For just as we rejoice when we hear, both by letters and by word of mouth, that your serenity is generous toward the condition of the Church, in the manner of your predecessor rulers [Col. 1281D], so, whenever we discover that you are diverting it in any matter from your customary practice, we are deeply distressed in every respect.

Therefore, know that by apostolic authority Northmannus is immediately to be excluded from ecclesiastical communion unless he personally divests himself of all the property of the Church of Laon. And the venerable Bishop Hincmar, if he abuses his intention of coming to Rome and does not strive to fulfill what he rightly vowed, is to be punished, God forbid, with the judgment due to a transgressor.

Whoever, therefore, from the time when he begins to come to Rome until the time when, with Christ as his guide, he returns to his own place, causes any loss whatsoever to that Church in any matter [Col. 1282A], since we specially entrust its episcopate to your glory to be safeguarded, must know that he will be deprived of the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood for as long as he has not made legitimate—indeed canonical—satisfaction to the holy Church of Laon, to you, and to its bishop.

We wish your royal excellence, as one who habitually observes the decrees of the holy apostolic see, always to prosper in Christ.

### XVIII. TO IGNATIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. (Year 869.)

That the bishops ordained by Photius should be removed from their rank. He commends John, metropolitan of Silaeus.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend [Col. 1282B] and most holy brother and fellow minister Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople.

Neither writing can reveal nor speech can adequately relate, O most beloved brother, how many arenas of struggle my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of holy memory, together with the Church subject to him, continually entered and endured for the condition of the Church of Constantinople and especially for your restoration. He persevered in this even until his passage to the better life, so that at the very moment of his departure he spared neither writing on behalf of your cause and of the Church divinely entrusted to you, nor, if not by speaking, at least by signaling his concern, until he lost the use of his mouth and completely closed his eyes.

We too, taking up his devotion, have succeeded him in honor by divine grace, and therefore have rightly succeeded him in labor. Just as we were then sharers in his toils and arrangements, so now we desire and strive to be observant of them all.

Neither mouth can express nor pen write how great is the joy and exultation with which we are filled when we hear that your health has been restored—the restoration of which we carried continually in our hearts. Therefore we blessed God and praised Him with rejoicing of our whole heart, because He stirred up the most fervent spirit of our beloved son Basil, prince and Augustus, not only to punish evildoers but also to honor the good. Basil rescued the Church of God, which was being dragged daily toward the death of both body and soul because it had not consented to the adulterer, just as Daniel rescued the most holy Susanna from the sentence of death which the unchaste priests—men who seemed to govern the Lord’s people but did not govern them, rather destroying them in the manner of Photius—had wickedly extorted [Col. 1282D].

Moreover, what the aforementioned pontiff of apostolic memory regularly and synodically sanctioned and defined concerning the schismatic and adulterer Photius, his ordination—or rather his execrable consecration—and Gregory of Syracuse, and also concerning you especially and those who suffered with you, you will be able plainly to learn from the tenor of the letters which he sent to Constantinople about these matters at different times. But if they have not reached the knowledge of your blessedness, receive them from our envoys and preserve them for your instruction and as a record for the future [Col. 1283A]. Meanwhile, know and be completely certain that we shall in no way depart from his decrees. Possessing both his position and his purpose, we shall follow his footsteps as far as we can under the guidance of reason, so that, walking by the light of his commandments in this dark place of the age, we may proceed without stumbling, with God as our guide.

Therefore, in those matters concerning which you demand arrangements and judgments from us, we see nothing to follow except his decrees inspired by God. Above all and before everything else, we separate Gregory of Syracuse, the tyrant and adulterer Photius, and those whom Photius is thought to have ordained to any rank whatsoever, from the number and dignity of bishops which he usurpatively and fictitiously bestowed upon them.

First, because Photius’s ordination of Maximus—or rather his execrable consecration—appears in nearly every respect to resemble this ordination [Col. 1283B]. Second, because this is established by the decree of my predecessor and of the apostolic see, whose judgment the sacred canons nowhere command to be reconsidered, although they do direct that other matters requiring renewal or definition be examined. We, as we have said, ought to follow his constitutions in everything. Third, because Photius was a forensic and curial man, a neophyte, an invader, and an adulterer, and had also been condemned by anathema; therefore he had nothing to offer those who followed him.

Indeed, when Photius was presiding, the following was said by those who had been anathematized: “One who has been consecrated not only does not receive the Holy Spirit, but the breath which he previously possessed is also taken away from him.” Although this was said in favor of the tyrant Photius, and although he himself rejoiced in such a sentence and gave his approval to those whom he had wickedly promoted—and although it cannot properly be applied to the very persons about whom it was vainly said—nevertheless, since the statement is true, it unquestionably applies more appropriately to the condemnation of those who, from the anathematized and condemned Photius, received not gain but a wound upon their heads through the laying on of hands [Col. 1283C].

By the judgment with which they judged, according to the Gospel (Matthew 7), judgment must therefore be rendered upon them; and by the measure with which they measured, it must certainly be measured back to them. They should count it a great privilege if, at least late, they return to you, their shepherd, whom they once obtained after Christ and through Christ, and, without further temporal advancement, serve the Lord with contrite hearts and humbled spirits, striving to await the good things of the future [Col. 1283D].

As for Paul of Caesarea, about whom you have spoken at length, we rightly decree for the present that the rule established concerning the others promoted by Photius is to be observed.

Moreover, the endurance of the persecutions and the arenas of struggle which you testify that you repeatedly entered against the tyrant and adulterer for the sake of truth certainly have their reward, and await an unfading crown from the giver of heavenly goods. Let him obtain the other benefits of the Church in great abundance, and let him rightly enjoy appropriate honor among all in the presence of your holiness.

Concerning those priests and clerics who were consecrated by Methodius, patriarch of blessed memory, or by your holiness, the following rule shall be observed. If there are among them any who, strengthened by God’s grace, resisted the invader Photius; who in no way shared in the dishonor or insult directed against your fraternity, or in your pretended deposition; and who, on this account, endured with you various tribulations and exiles, and even depositions [Col. 1284A], I would call them blessed, thrice blessed, and decree that they be numbered among the confessors of Christ. They are to hold a distinguished place in the Church which exists among you and enjoy exceptional confidence with your affection, so that, in proportion to the multitude of their sufferings, your consolations may gladden their souls—in the manner of God, who will repay each according to his works.

As for the others who derive their consecration from your fraternity and who, whether voluntarily or under compulsion, went over to Photius, if they return to you under the terms of the written declaration, a copy of which we have entrusted to our envoys, we have decided that they are to be forgiven and generally confirmed in their ranks, although they acted against their profession or subscription and repeatedly raged against your supreme priesthood and in contempt of the apostolic see [Col. 1284B].

For we are disciples of the gentle and merciful Master who, as the chief of the apostles bears witness, suffered for us and left us an example that we should follow in His footsteps. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth; yet when He was reviled, He did not revile in return, and when He suffered, He did not threaten (1 Peter 2).

But if any among them are proved to have sinned or transgressed in another way, either against God or against the constitutions of the Fathers—for these too were promulgated by the Spirit of God—we wish them, with our authority also applied to the matter, to be examined regularly by your pontificate and henceforth and thereafter wholly subjected to the definitions of the Fathers [Col. 1284C].

For when blessed Peter says to the Lord not, “If my brother sins against you,” but, “If my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him? Up to seven times?” (Matthew 18), it is appropriately understood that we may forgive our brothers without penalty those things committed against us, but not those committed against the Lord or against the Lord’s constitutions. Scripture says: “If a man sins against a man, the priest will pray for him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Kings 2).

As for those who are proved to have subscribed voluntarily in that abominable assembly which was held at Constantinople as an insult to and derogation of the apostolic see [Col. 1284D], whatever their order or profession, evident reason teaches that they are worthy of no pardon unless the great mercy of that same apostolic see, which they attempted to injure, should intervene; and the manifold sanction of our predecessors plainly demonstrates this.

Indeed, the universal synod held at Chalcedon so detested such presumption that in the sentence which it pronounced against Dioscorus it seems especially to recall this matter when it says of him (Council of Chalcedon, Act III): “By his subsequent transgressions he greatly surpassed his former iniquity; for he presumed even to issue an excommunication against the most holy and most blessed archbishop of great Rome, Leo.”

By “former iniquity” it means, of course, heretical depravity. Hence observe that Dioscorus is reported to have greatly surpassed even the Eutychian heresy through his subsequent transgressions, which he committed when he issued an excommunication against the Roman pope. For this reason Anatolius also says: “Dioscorus was not condemned on account of the faith, but because he excommunicated the lord Archbishop Leo.”

For among the other slanders brought against you, your rivals wove this one accusation against your Reverence: namely, that you had risen up as though in contempt of the revered mention of Pope Benedict, and that, in his insult, you had consented—after the manner of the aforesaid Dioscorus—not even to receive his letter. Since, therefore, in the case which they attempted to fasten upon you by false accusations, they themselves are found liable through truthful proofs, they ought by right rather to undergo the judgment which they pronounced and to incur the sentence which they delivered, ensnared in the bonds of Simon.

Therefore your Fraternity must take care that the chapters of the sentences which, in synod at the Church of God where the holy body of the chief of the apostles, Peter, rests, we promulgated with common agreement for abolishing the profane councils assembled at Constantinople by Photius, both against the reverence of the Apostolic See and against your sanctity, be confirmed among you in synod by the subscription of all, and carefully deposited in the archives of each church.

Finally, we strongly commend to your Beatitude our most reverend and most holy common brother John, metropolitan of Syleion. Concerning him, we do not wish your Fraternity to be unaware that our heart was wounded by whatever griefs or troubles arose from the many misfortunes that befell you. For, as it is written, “A faithful ambassador is health” (Prov. 13): by the remedy of his faithful embassy, that which had hitherto wounded us here with prolonged and troubled sorrow has been healed, so that this most prudent man has left scarcely anything remaining in our breast that still requires healing.
