Therefore he should be regarded as deserving of great consolation, and your holy Fraternity should enrich him with tranquility, refreshment, and every honor; moreover, he should be retained without interruption for the most diligent administration of ecclesiastical affairs. For their sake he endured countless dangers, not only traveling by sea but also proceeding overland; indeed, while remaining with us and continually pressing your cause, and inflicting upon us unceasing troubles, he granted himself no holidays and gave no respite to our daily labor.

We desire that your holy Fraternity may now and always prosper in Christ, most beloved and most sacred fellow minister. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the second indiction.

## XIX. TO THE EMPEROR BASIL (869)

He gives thanks for Basil’s piety toward the Apostolic See. He urges him to pardon those who have offended, except the schismatic Photius. The Roman chapters against the false synod of Photius are to be confirmed at Constantinople by the subscription of all in synod. He asks Basil to send Basil, Zosimus, and another Basil to him. He urges him not to withdraw from his good purpose.

### [Col. 1286A]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the God-loving and most devout emperor, Basil Augustus, most Christian and most desirable son.

Although unworthy, we have received the most distinguished bearers of your Excellency’s embassy, sent to my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of apostolic memory, since the Lord has so commanded and we have assumed his office. With all our mind and with our entire intention we have offered innumerable praises and thanksgivings to God—surely the One who does great, inscrutable, and wondrous things, whose number cannot be counted, and who holds all the rights of kingdoms and all authority. In these days He has raised up your empire, protected from heaven, through which the Apostolic See might complete the work of piety that it had undertaken on behalf of the Church of Constantinople, and, removing its imminent fall entirely, restore it once more to the condition of which it had been deprived, rejoicing at last; and, having completely removed the hireling—indeed, the ravenous wolf who did not spare the flock—He might restore to it its proper ruler and reestablish its legitimate shepherd.

Therefore, how praiseworthy and worthy of universal veneration that See is for you—indeed, how praiseworthy the Apostolic See is, and deservedly to be extolled by all mortals—which has always been accustomed to help Catholics, which has never ceased to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep!

But you also, fortunate emperor and worthy of many praises, received the seeds of divine words not like a field occupied by rocks, thorns, or brambles, but like good soil receiving them in a good heart; you brought forth abundant fruit. Like a true Ecclesiastes, as soon as you had taken up the reins of empire, you took care more to provide for the peace of the Church than to attend to other human affairs. In this way you appeared in our times as another Solomon—that is, “the peaceful.” For you heard the words of God your Father and did not forsake the law of the Church your mother, so that what had been urged upon your predecessor on her behalf, you yourself accomplished.

And because, according to Scripture, “there is no one who can correct him whom God has rejected” (Eccles. 7), while that man remained uncorrected, you have endeavored, by divine permission, to carry out the correction of that same Church, since he had failed. For, as your letter of gentleness indicates, you understood with what wounds the Church existing among you had been wounded when you obtained the empire from heaven; and you clearly learned that this See could heal such wounds, after examining the teachers of our faith. Therefore, desiring to heal these wounds, you most wisely sought the remedy of the Apostolic See’s decree. By its medicines the Church of Constantinople, often weakened when its bishops languished, recovered its former health and vigor. For whenever some of its bishops erred, and whenever others suffered the injury of imminent persecution, this See never ceased to assist: showing the former the path of correction and always extending to the latter the hand of compassion.

Therefore, dearest son and ever-venerable Augustus, know that whatever you write you have done toward our most holy brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, or concerning the schismatic Photius, inspired by God and inflamed with zeal for justice, has pleased us and the entire Western Church in every respect. In particular, you have done nothing beyond what the Apostolic See, together with all the bishops of the West, long ago decreed should be done [variant: “beyond those things which … decreed should be done”], and without any delay commanded to be carried out. For this reason, together with all these people, they return manifold thanks to your empire protected from heaven and do not cease to proclaim the praises of your most humble obedience with exceptional commendation [variant: “to call out”].

Concerning the priests and others who, acting against the peace of the Church, presumed to tear apart its unity and are proved to have committed many offenses against our brother and fellow bishop: your Clemency asks what decree the Apostolic See has made concerning them, following the custom of the ancient emperors. Let your Affection know that, since they are reported to have offended in different ways, we judge it fitting that they should likewise be subjected to different judgments. We have entrusted the regulation of these distinctions to the legates of the Apostolic See, meeting together with our brother and fellow minister Ignatius, according to what has been granted to us concerning this matter.

Yet because your piety, together with ecclesiastical mercy, urges us concerning them toward what is more humane, we do not wish you to be unaware that, I confess, we are oppressed beyond what can be expressed by immense grief and constrained by overwhelming sorrow at the thought that they are to be punished not only by the just sanctions of my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of blessed memory, which he repeatedly brought forward and to which I too subscribed, but also by the rules of the holy Fathers, with the utmost severity, indeed in a manner almost deadly.

Nevertheless, in order to obtain the peace of the Church more easily, and to mercifully free so great a multitude—provided that they repent—let us say with Pope Gelasius (Letter 6): “The necessary administration of affairs constrains us, and the moderation of the Apostolic See binds us, to weigh the decrees of the ancestral canons and measure the commands of former bishops and predecessors in such a way that, with careful consideration, we temper as far as possible those things which the necessity of the present times demands should be relaxed for the restoration of the churches.” We too can pursue and wholly imitate this course with equitable reasoning for winning our brothers, by providing for the needs of the times. For the moment, however, we entirely exclude Photius’s ordination from the administration of this mercy, and we will in no way admit it indiscriminately or without examination.

For the high-sounding trumpet of the Church, namely Leo, the holy pope of the Apostolic See, whose judgment everything Catholic everywhere admires, celebrates, and venerates as a heavenly oracle, says: “Since a dispute often arises over an honor wrongly received, who could doubt that that which is not shown to have been conferred must by no means be granted to them?” Nor do we suppose that there is any distinction between Photius the adulterer and Maximus the Cynic, condemned by the Second Synod, or between the ordinations of the one and the other. Therefore those who are proved in every way to have had the same beginning as he seem bound to the same end.

Indeed, as that aforementioned eloquent pontiff writes to all the bishops established throughout Caesarean Mauretania (Letter 91): “It is difficult for those things to end well which were begun with an evil beginning.” And below: “Therefore,” he says, “what is contained in the general statutes must not be disregarded in the case of any person, nor should that honor be considered legitimate which was conferred contrary to the precepts of divine law.”

Certainly the most faithful and prudent man Basil, the imperial spatharius, has also brought us your many petitions that we receive those ordained in these orders; and he persisted with us in his petitions so constantly and continuously that, if they had not been thought capable of being received legitimately in any way, we would nevertheless, overcome—as it were—by his insistence, certainly have decided that they should be received.

Yet concerning these men also, after our envoys have returned, after they have reported to us the distinctions in what was done, and after we have more clearly investigated the qualities and differences of the persons, offenses, and promotions, if God, with whom all things are possible, should reserve for us any opportunity for mercy, we will not be wholly inflexible—we who always desire to be receptive to every good proposal.

Therefore, through the diligence of your piety, we wish a numerous council to be held there. Our envoys too should preside over it and, having clearly learned the distinctions among the offenses and persons, freely exercise their judgments concerning each individual, according to the instructions they have received. In that sacred assembly, in condemnation of the abominations of the council held in utter injury against this See, we decree that every copy be taken from its possessors, brought forth publicly before all, and burned in the fire. Not even one iota or one stroke is to remain anywhere among anyone from all these documents—unless, perhaps, someone should wish to be deprived of the dignity not merely of the entire clergy but even of the whole Christian name, having been struck by anathema.

For we judge that this council is to be compared only with the council under Constantius at Ariminum, or with the robber council assembled by Dioscorus at Ephesus. Let the zeal of your piety, dearest son, be kindled toward the reverence of your protectors, namely the blessed chief apostles, and let it in no way tolerate the fictitious fabrications of so many deceptions to remain with anyone. If anyone should attempt to defend or conceal these things, or perhaps reserve them for himself in the future, let your manifold wisdom proclaim through public laws what such a person must incur after the imperial edict of condemnation, and what penalty it is fitting that he receive—not merely for correction, but at least for chastisement—so that thereafter, with a pure conscience, you may truthfully sing with the Psalmist:

“I hate the gatherings of the wicked,
and I will not sit with the impious.
I will wash my hands among the innocent,” etc. (Psalm 25).

Furthermore, we exhort you and earnestly strive to persuade you for your salvation that, through the effort of your imperial authority, the chapters of the sentences which we promulgated synodically in the Church of God, where the holy body of the chief apostle Peter rests, for abolishing the profane councils assembled at Constantinople by Photius both against the reverence of the Apostolic See and against the pontificate of my brother and fellow minister Ignatius, be confirmed among you in synod by the subscription of all and carefully deposited in the archives of each church.

We also pray your empire, protected by God, to send back to us through the present envoys of the Apostolic See Basil, Peter, Zosimus, and the other Basil. Conscious of their crimes and inflamed by the ardor of desire, they abandoned their purpose and hastened to Constantinople without letters of recommendation. Thus, when they have returned to the profession and the places which they initially chose for God’s sake, both you may receive a heavenly reward and they may, by God’s favor, be granted the gain of their souls.

Otherwise, if they attempt in any way to trample upon or despise the rules of the holy Fathers, no one will dare to retain them with impunity. For among us they were weaned from their beginnings, acquired the habit of holy conduct, and even obtained the office of the presbyterate in our monasteries. Meanwhile, we wish it to be known that, because they are excommunicated, they are to be regarded as violators of the sacred canons until they return to us.

Having thus set these matters forth, we beseech your head, redeemed by God, of tranquil rule, to persist in the work of piety already begun concerning my brother and fellow priest Ignatius, and in no way whatsoever to deviate from the decrees of the Apostolic See. Rather, adhering more firmly to its promulgations, do not withdraw from your purpose; and until unity is restored to the Church, we ask you not to yield to any indifference.

For no one has ever benefited from beginning a good work and failing to complete it. Therefore strive to complete this work of piety, so that you may perpetually obtain the kingdom which you have acquired temporally, and receive an incorruptible crown in place of a corruptible one; then present the completed work before Christ, the supreme presiding judge of the contest. Strive to do so.

Finally, we commend to your piety my beloved brothers Donatus, most reverend and holy bishop of the holy Church of Ostia, and Stephen, most reverend and holy bishop of the holy Church of Nepi, as well as my son Marinus, deacon of the Apostolic See and our counsellor. We ask you, for love of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, from whose See they are sent, to receive them kindly and to lend credence to what they say as though you were hearing us ourselves. Grant them the confidence of your familiarity, and reverently regard in them the outstanding intercessors of your own—the apostles whom we earnestly ask you to send back to us quickly.

For we desire always to rejoice in the Lord both over the restoration of the holy Church and over the divinely granted gift of your safety. Therefore we exhort and beseech you not to make them endure any delay among you, but, relying on the support of your kindness, to let them quickly make us happier by their arrival and by all that is being done there according to God’s will.

We also commend to your Clemency our most reverend and holy brother John, metropolitan of Syleion, who was sent to the Apostolic See by our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, as well as the glorious and distinguished man Basil, the imperial spatharius, who was sent with him by the empire of your tranquility, preserved by God. Since their departure from there, they have suffered so many obstacles—as we have learned—that, while hastening onward, they seem scarcely to have escaped any of the dangers which Paul enumerates in his letters (2 Cor. 11).

Therefore they deserve to be rewarded by your piety with worthy recompense, since they most willingly agreed to undergo so many and such great hardships for the Church of Christ and for completing the embassy entrusted to them by your piety.

As for the other metropolitan named in your letters, by the Lord’s dispensation we did not see him. For just as this one was sent by the revered patriarch Ignatius, so the other was sent separately by the tyrant Photius. God wished to show that His Church would not be divided in two, as the impious king Jeroboam once divided Israel (1 Kings 12). He also did not wish us to see even the face of the author of such a schism. Before he could reach us, by His just judgment God covered him with the sea; and upon the one who had divided the people, the divided waters of God came down, and he sank into the depths like a stone.

But if perhaps your empire, redeemed by God, is troubled because the aforementioned envoys remained with us for such a long time, we earnestly beseech and implore you not to attribute this to them. They did not spare any hours, moments, intervals, or even pauses in crying out and knocking in order to be released. Rather, attribute it to the urgent and uninterrupted labors and cares of all the Churches of God, which, according to the Apostle, we carry about with us (2 Cor. 11).

For from the day of their arrival we had no rest or leisure: at first we were handling the case of the Church existing among you; now we are also arranging to endure the affairs of other parts of the world in their perpetual movement [variant: “in their perpetual course”]. Especially since, for properly regulating this one controversy—the disturbance concerning the Church of Constantinople for which we are being pressed—we truly believed that the time itself, however extended, would not be sufficient. We had to examine it inwardly and with every diligence, and also await the agreement—or rather the counsels—of our brothers and fellow bishops who are far away concerning this matter. For, as Solomon testifies, “Safety is where there is much counsel” (Prov. 11).

Therefore let your Tranquility not be angered at any of these matters. It was not some delay arising from our own will that prevented us; rather, the urgent necessity of hastening to assist the numerous churches that must be relieved through our diligence held us back.

May heavenly grace guard your most devout empire, and by its powerful might subject to it the ferocity of all unbelieving nations, for the exaltation of the holy Church.

## XX. TO THE MAGNATES OF THE KINGDOM OF CHARLES THE BALD (869)

He urges them to deter King Charles from invading the kingdom of Lothair, and to receive his envoys Paul and Leo kindly.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the glorious dukes, counts, and other chief men established in the kingdom of Charles, the most excellent king.

All virtues are indeed to be pursued by worshipers of Christ, but none is guarded and cultivated more usefully than peace with mutual love among all people, and especially among persons of higher rank. For the higher a person is, the easier it is plainly for him to draw everyone toward his own ways. Therefore I appropriately admonish, urge, and exhort you in this letter to strive to build and establish the good of peace among all, but especially between the higher princes of the world.

By this means the kingdom of your beloved son, the king, will be able to remain safe more quickly, if he shakes no one and is shaken by no one. I do not think you are unaware of how my most desirable spiritual son, Louis, the most devout emperor protected by God, has gone forth from the summit of his own exalted position and from the foundation of his most peaceful repose—not against certain sons of holy religion, not against members of the Christian faith, but against sons of Belial, against the enemies of Christ—especially for our security and for the liberation of many of the faithful who were already facing imminent danger in Samnium and the surrounding regions, so that even the incursion of the Saracens was almost invading our borders.

He spares neither his body, nor heat, nor cold, nor finally any circumstance; enduring every hardship and every danger for Christ’s name, there is nothing that he refuses to undertake for the rescue of Christians, and nothing that he declines to assume for the tranquility and peace of the faithful. Indeed, through him divine piety has brought about no small measure of peace for the holy Church, and the strength of the pagans has been struck down by heavenly valor.

He has often compelled the enemies, like mice emerging from their holes, to turn their backs toward their hiding places, and by powerful might has broken the arms they raised against our people. He has also brought great security to all of us, both those who were far away and those who were near: he struck some of them down, while converting others from their superstition and teaching them to follow the paths of the faith of Christ and true religion.

For this reason we consider it appropriate to admonish your Affection: strive to suggest to your aforementioned glorious king and his sons, and endeavor to persuade them by prudent counsel, that he consent neither to invade nor to disturb what belongs to such a great prince and so devout an Augustus, whether moved by his own inclinations or by the persuasion of others. These possessions, being in the kingdom of the late King Lothair of glorious memory, his brother, are shown by every supporting law to belong to that great prince—not so much by fraternal succession as by their father’s disposition.

For whoever shakes the borders and disturbs the people who were under the rule of the king just mentioned shakes the things that belong to God and are advantageous to the Church. And whoever moves him, overcome by greed, undoubtedly scatters a great increase of the Church.

Moreover, it is unjust that what brothers had mutually pledged under terrible oaths, so that the portion of the kingdoms which each had received as his distinct share might be preserved intact among themselves and for their nephews, should be violated by impious treachery or disturbed by the fuel of anyone’s desire. Rather, it is fitting, in pious affection, that a brother provide his brother, and uncles their nephews, with every aid and protection, and that each offer every assistance and consolation according to the faith they mutually promised under oath.

This applies especially to your illustrious king, who is recognized to have received this nephew of his—namely, the great Augustus—from his own father’s right hand, together with everything that appeared to belong to him, in order to support and strengthen him to the best of his ability, as though he were a second father.

But it is unjust and virtually sacrilegious that one who willingly exposes himself to so many dangers for the salvation of the faithful, and especially for the defense of the holy Roman Church, his mother, should be driven by the pressure of any faction to withdraw from the work of piety he has begun and be forced to proceed to claim a paternal inheritance.

Yet whoever, inflamed by the heat of desire, through his own fault offers any impediment to such a holy labor will certainly, with his supporters, pay a fitting penalty, once the Apostolic See has pronounced judgment. Therefore, if any of you follows the author of this diabolical ambition, or in any way grants favor to him in his greed for plunder, he will be bound by the chains of anathema, separated for this reason from the kingdom of the Lord, and rightly assigned with the head of all the impious, who is the devil.

Let the most prudent king, encouraged also by your credible counsels, take care not to yield to the persuasion of the wicked or lend his ears to those plotting evil. Let him be content with his own right and not attempt to usurp what is not his, nor strive to invade it by any means, since an invasion can bring no small danger upon the invader.

Therefore let him not prepare any obstacle for my aforementioned beloved son, the ever-August lord, as he carries out God’s cause, claims the Lord’s inheritance, and fights His battles, lest the usefulness of God’s holy Church be hindered in any respect or the progress of the faithful be obstructed. Otherwise, let him know that the hand of the Apostolic See is firmly with that most devout prince, and let him understand beforehand that our arms, providing him with the strongest defenses, are prepared without hesitation, while the supreme judge of the contest fights on our side and the intercession of the blessed chief apostles cooperates with us.

Furthermore, receive these envoys of our Apostolic See, Paul and Leo, venerable bishops and our beloved counsellors, whom we have sent there for the peace and concord of the holy Church of God, with kindness out of reverence for the chief apostles Peter and Paul. Taking to heart what they say to you concerning the interests of the Christian faith and religion, hasten to put it into effect.

We wish your Glory well-being in Christ. Given on the Nones of September, in the third indiction.

## XXI. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF CHARLES THE BALD (869)

He urges them to deter King Charles from invading the kingdom of Lothair, and to receive Paul and Leo, his envoys, kindly.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brothers and fellow bishops governing the Church of the Lord in the kingdom of Charles, the glorious king.

At the beginning of my pontificate I remember taking up, before all other virtues, the promotion and advocacy of peace. For you know that at the beginning of the Lord’s Nativity a heavenly army was seen, crying out: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 10).

Here one must carefully observe that, just as the shepherds who watched over their flock more attentively than others deserved more than others to see the joys of so great a rejoicing, so we who are called shepherds will deserve to attain the joy of heavenly goods if we carefully watch over the Lord’s sheep—lest the ravenous wolf invade them by the snares of hatred or discord, or that greedy lion devour them through his cupidity, the one who, as the chief of the apostles writes, “goes about roaring, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5).

Therefore, dearest brothers, I now repeat the same thing, urge the same thing opportunely and importunately, and demand it with all earnestness. For this reason I continually exhort you to teach that the bond of peace and love, which is greater than all virtues and burnt offerings, be observed unbreakably among all people, but especially among persons of higher rank.

Accordingly, I require this of you: be vigilant, and if you perceive that anyone wishes wickedly to incite the minds of our son, your glorious king Charles, to invade the kingdom which, after the death of the once illustrious King Lothair, returned to our most desirable son, the most devout emperor, and is owed to him by hereditary right, then strive, as spiritual men, like true bishops, to restrain such carnal voices—and indeed the most excellent king himself and his sons—from so great a sin.

Rather, inflame them to support and assist him, and exhort them: just as he received this man in his faith as a second father, so let him cherish him and embrace him as his own child.

For it is unjust and virtually sacrilegious that one who willingly exposes himself to so many dangers for the salvation of the faithful, and especially for the defense of the holy Roman Church, the mother of all God’s churches, should be driven by the pressure of any faction to withdraw from the work of piety he has begun and proceed to vindicate his ancestral inheritance.

For that man ought not to abandon a paternal inheritance who, thanks be to God, knows that Naboth the Jezreelite, in defending his father’s vineyard alone—even against an impious king—went so far as to suffer death by stoning (III Kings 21).

But if anyone’s labor is obstructed by ambition, since it is not proper for those who seize it to abandon a paternal patrimony, whoever causes such an event will pay, together with his supporters and followers, a deserved and equal penalty.

And if any of you avoids the author of so wicked an act by silence or consents by failing to resist, let him know that he must be judged no longer by the name of shepherd but of hireling. Since he will no longer belong to the sheep, consequently he will no longer belong among those holding pastoral dignities.

Furthermore, receive these envoys of our Apostolic See, Paul and Leo, venerable bishops and our beloved counsellors, whom we have sent there for the peace and concord of the Church of God, kindly out of reverence for the chief apostles Peter and Paul. Taking to heart what they say to you concerning the interests of the Christian faith and religion, hasten to put it into effect.

We wish your holy Fraternity well-being in Christ. Given on the Nones of September, in the third indiction.

## XXII. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS (869)

He promises his goodwill to Hincmar and urges him to intervene so that no one may invade the kingdom of Lothair. Finally, he commends the envoys Paul and Leo.

### [Col. 1294C]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy fellow brother Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims.

Your Sanctity has surely not forgotten how close you were to Pope Nicholas of apostolic memory. Receiving you also into the bosom of that friendship, we offer your Fraternity, with joyful mind, the confidence of our apostolate.

Furthermore, know that we have sent certain letters into the regions of Gaul, suitably admonishing, exhorting, persuading, warning, prohibiting, and deterring kings, bishops, and all the chief men of the kingdoms, so as to restrain ambition and preserve each person’s proper right.

Your Sanctity should undertake the care of this matter with a kind of special zeal and, in our place, restrain and curb both kings and the other ministers of God and of the world by admonishing, persuading, and prohibiting them from the vice of desire or greed. In other words, let each person be content with what is his and not seize, disturb, or usurp what belongs to another.

Above all, see that no mortal invades, disturbs, or attempts to bend to himself the kingdom once belonging to King Lothair, which is owed by right to our most beloved son, the emperor, or the people dwelling in it.

For if anyone, through such rashness, does not fear to sever charity, divide concord, burn with the torches of envy, pant with the heat of greed, strike his kin with the weapon of cruelty, and generate scandal in the Church of God, he will not only be weakened by the ministry of our mediocrity, through God’s authority, but, bound by the chains of anathema and deprived of the name of Christianity, will be placed altogether with the devil, whom he imitates in this matter.

If your Reverence labors vigorously in this cause according to the wisdom divinely given to you, do not doubt that the confidence of our friendship, as we have said, will in every respect be granted to you. Nor should you distrust that the kindness of our goodwill will, when necessity demands, assist you in your needs.

Furthermore, receive these envoys of our Apostolic See, Paul and Leo, venerable bishops and our beloved counsellors, whom we have sent there for the peace and concord of the Church of God, kindly out of reverence for the chief apostles Peter and Paul. Taking to heart what they say to you concerning the interests of the Christian faith and religion, hasten to put it into effect.

We wish your Sanctity well-being in Christ. Given on the Nones of September, in the third indiction.

## XXIII. TO THE MAGNATES OF THE KINGDOM OF LOTHair (869)

After the death of King Lothair, he urges them to remain faithful to Louis the emperor, his brother, to whom the kingdom is owed by hereditary right.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the chief men and glorious counts residing in the kingdom of Lord Lothair, once the great emperor and father of Lord Louis the emperor.

Perfect charity, undoubtedly, consists, according to the Apostle, in rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep (Rom. 12). Since, therefore, Lothair, formerly your king, has departed from this world at the command of God, we know that you have been made very sad by his death and filled, as faithful men, with the bitter grief of immense mourning, and that in your human affection you now weep for his passing. Our apostolic spirit, likewise sympathizing and grieving with you, has prayed to the Lord with tearful prayers—as is fitting—not only for his eternal rest and salvation, but also for your present consolation, and for the peace, concord, and unity which you ought to follow with your whole heart and embrace with wholly faithful devotion, as members of Christ having no stain that could bring upon you the destruction of death, whether imminent or yet to come. And daily we earnestly beseech Him that He may deign to grant to him who died according to the condition of the flesh everlasting life, and to inspire and bestow upon you, through the abundance of His mercy, the disposition and desire for consolation, peace, and unanimity.

For He is the one who, as a father, chastises us with the rod of justice and afflicts us with the sorrow of purification; and He Himself graciously deigns to console us in all our tribulation, so that we may be able to endure and never fail. Therefore, dearest sons, since you owe very much to the teaching of the apostolic see, and since we, by heavenly grace, exercise the office of the prince of the apostles and have been entrusted by the Lord, above all others, with the care and solicitude of all the churches of God, we must, girded with divine arms, come to your aid and instruct you with saving precepts before our ancient adversary corrupts your minds by the hidden and impious deceits of his wickedness and wounds you with an incurable disease. By humbly obeying these precepts, you may be saved, as were all those who pleased God from the beginning, for the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

Therefore, dearest sons beloved in the Lord, we admonish your charity with the apostolic trumpet and beseech you by heavenly teaching to strive, for the stability of the kingdom, to stand all together in the same faith and sincerity of mind around our most beloved spiritual son, the lord Louis, emperor Augustus, just as with pure hearts you preserved yourselves around his father, the emperor Lothair, formerly of blessed memory. Let no mortal, whatever his rank or glory, be able by any means or arguments to recall you from the command and wholesome admonition of the apostolic see or turn you aside from the path of truth. Nor should you strive to receive with willing ears any commands more readily than those of the blessed apostle Peter, spoken through our mouth, or regard any as more beneficial to you.

For this kingdom is owed to him by paternal and hereditary right, according to law and justice, and belongs to him above all through the succession of his father’s inheritance. His aforementioned father, the former emperor, appointed him emperor and exalted him above his other children as heir of the entire kingdom. Just as Isaac, when blessing his son Jacob, made him lord over Esau (Gen. 27), so the whole empire was granted by his father to this man, who had been preferred above the others. While still alive, his father wished and consented that, together with you, he should be crowned with the imperial diadem by the apostolic see, and without doubt permitted him to possess the augustal scepter.

Therefore we admonish and solemnly entreat your nobility in the Lord not to attempt, by any promises or threats of anyone, to separate or divide yourselves from that same spiritual son of ours, the emperor Augustus. Rather, as long as he lives by the will of heaven, make every effort to obey him in all things as your own lord, your own emperor, and the rightful heir of the kingdom, to preserve your faith toward him inviolate as usual, and to act with vigilant zeal so that you may deserve to possess the grace of almighty God and of Saint Peter, our full blessing, and fellowship in apostolic communion.

For if we learn that any one of you is attempting the opposite, and, having spurned the admonitions of the apostolic see—to the contempt of the blessed apostle Peter, the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom—is transferring himself to another side, we shall regard him as faithless and hostile to ecclesiastical peace and salvation. We shall not merely hold him alien from the communion of our apostolate; we shall also take every care, rightly and deservedly, to bind him with the bond of anathema. In accordance with the privilege of apostolic dignity and power, we regard our most excellent spiritual son, the lord Louis, emperor Augustus, as king, lord, and emperor of this kingdom and province—that is, of all Gaul—as it is clearly established that he was long ago ordained by God and as many indications show that it was decreed by our predecessor pontiffs. As long as he survives, we shall strive to regard him as such.

If, however, some tyrant should presume to invade that kingdom contrary to the divine and apostolic will, he will immediately incur the judgment of apostolic vengeance. We desire that your nobility stand together in unanimous devotion and remain joined in an indissoluble bond of charity.

## XXIV. TO KING CHARLES THE BALD  
*(Year 870.)* He rebukes the king because he invaded Lothair’s kingdom and despised the legates of the apostolic see; he orders him to withdraw from that kingdom and to receive other legates graciously—namely, the bishops John, Peter, Wibod, and John, and Peter, cardinal priest.

[Col. 1297B]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, glorious king.

[Note: [Col. 1297D] Adrian mentions Charles’s reply concerning each section of this letter in Letter 29. By the legates whom he says were despised by King Charles, he means the bishops Paul and John. —Sirmond.]

We are instructed by the clearest testimonies of sacred doctrines and by apostolic examples that we ought to act more gently with the gentle and correct offenders more severely according to justice. Nor can we please God if, undertaking the role of shepherd, we await not the work of a shepherd but the hiding places of a hireling, and flee when the wolf comes lest we offer assistance.

Above all, we must beware of what the Lord says through the prophet: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56); and again: “Woe to the shepherds,” he says, “who fed themselves” (Ezek. 34), and so forth. If the Lord thus pronounces a general woe upon all shepherds because of their sloth, we must fear that sentence all the more because, above everyone and on behalf of everyone, we carry upon our shoulders the burdens not only of honor but also of responsibility.

Must we not, O king, be compelled to give an account before the Lord for you? If, to pass over for the moment the fact that you scorned to receive the legates of the apostolic see in royal fashion, we neither rebuked your sanctity nor ceased to reprove you with spiritual zeal when, contrary to the divine authority and that of the holy Fathers, and contrary to the pledge of your own faith by which you swore that you would not covet or invade another’s kingdom, especially those of your brothers, you presumed to invade the kingdom of the former emperor Lothair, which by divine and human laws is owed to our spiritual son, the lord Louis Augustus, his son, and did not fear to incur the guilt of perjury.

Has it escaped your memory that we examined and confirmed the oaths of you and your brothers sent to the apostolic see, and that we still keep them deposited today in our archive? If even this is insufficient for you, then, to increase your culpability, we confront you with your own specific statements and urge you, through the professions of your own mouth, to return to your senses.

When, therefore, after being overcome by the forces of Louis, the son of your brother, you lost the kingdom, did you not send the letter that we have before us to the apostolic see? In it, among other things, you confessed, saying:

“When we came together with our brothers after the battle of Fontenay, and, having divided the kingdoms among us, made peace, we swore an oath that none of us would invade the boundaries of another’s kingdom. But now, with oaths disregarded, my kingdom has been invaded and taken away. May your apostolate have mercy, and, lest the name of Christ be blasphemed among the nations, may this crime not be left unpunished.”

Behold how entirely unfitting it is for you to covet what belongs to another; behold, it has been shown to you that oaths publicly made have been despised. Finally, as evidence of your even greater culpability, it has been shown for a while that we ought not to let you go unpunished. What you once begged us to do to another, we must now, by a just judgment, do to you in a similar matter and rebuke you for your actions. This is especially so because you have shown more clearly that you boasted of being a devoted son of the holy Roman Church with your lips only and not with your heart, as is contained in the letters sent by you to our predecessors and to us.

Now your devotion to the faith has been so completely voided that, since you did not send our legates away with a suitable reply, and since you craftily failed to write back to us, you have not yet sent your own legates or the letters that you indicated you would send, thereby showing contempt for the apostolic see. If someone else gave you such advice, he did not preserve true faith toward you; but if you acted solely on your own counsel in this matter, your royal excellence did less than it ought.

As for the unity of peace and concord, concerning which you had suggested that we ought to be mediators between the most pious emperor and you, we received the proposal most willingly and began to act upon it. But you were unwilling to yield for the sake of peace to him who was fighting against the enemies of the Christian name, laboring through many hardships for the liberation of the people of God, and waging the Lord’s battles while overcoming the multitude of the Saracens. Rather, not as a lover of peace but as an instigator of scandal, and indeed as the most manifest perpetrator of tyranny, you did not wait for a time of peace. After you had craftily arranged to send him these messages, you invaded, harassed, and organized the kingdom of the lord emperor more and more, and forced the men of that kingdom to swear allegiance to you.

Would you have dared to do such things to him unless he had remained steadfast, day and night, through such great labors, for the perpetual peace of the holy Church and for love of Christ? He has not withdrawn his hand or his work from the good undertakings he began—undertakings in which you ought rather to have given him support than to persecute the Christian people against the faith you owe. There is no doubt that he will make almighty God favorable to him in carrying these things through and will soon receive triumph over the enemies of the Christian name.

Having stated these matters briefly, since, as we said, just as we carry the burdens of all upon our shoulders, so we must foresee the actions of all, let no one suppose that we say these things out of human favor. Even if it should happen that our princes, to whom the kingdom wrongly seized by you is lawfully owed, failed to avenge the injuries inflicted upon them, we would by no means leave those perjuries and tyrannical invasions unpunished until true correction had been made, because we are moved not by ambition for a kingdom but by justice. We do not seek expanses of territory; rather, as duty requires, we remain vigilant to resist every vice and wickedness.

Therefore, to confront your glory in a very few words, we admonish you and, by apostolic authority, spiritually urge you by every means available; with paternal affection we command you, since you have now been admonished for the third time, to withdraw completely and restrain yourself from invading the kingdom of our spiritual son, the most Christian prince. Do not covet what belongs to another, and do not do to him what you do not wish done to yourself.

Do not tyrannically join possessions justly held and rightfully belonging to you with those unjustly seized, lest you lose even what you possess justly and, by the just judgment of God, regret having coveted what you invaded unjustly. For we desire your safety and long that you may prosper in body and soul. Unless you now obey our wholesome admonitions, or those of others, just as you previously remained disobedient to our spiritual judgment, we shall by no means and by no device fail to go there ourselves, with God’s help, and completely carry out what belongs to our ministry.

Finally, we earnestly admonish you to receive graciously these principal legates of our apostolate: John, Peter, Wibod, and John, venerable bishops, and also Peter, the religious cardinal priest of our see, our beloved and familiar associate. Receive and honor them for the reverence and love owed by all to the princes of the apostles, and as men who have departed from so great a see. We have instructed them to tell you what this letter has omitted. Therefore accept without any hesitation whatever they explain orally, and take every care that they may return to us having achieved their purpose.

We wish your glory to be well in Christ now and always. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction.

## XXV. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN CHARLES’S KINGDOM  
*(Year 870.)* That they admonish the king to abstain from Lothair’s kingdom and receive the legates graciously.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brothers, the archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of Charles, glorious king.

Recently, through the legates and letters of our apostolate, we admonished your reverence with salutary exhortations to take thought for yourselves; and, as was fitting for you, we rightly rebuked you with fraternal affection. But you have despised the apostolic admonitions to such an extent that you have neither replied to our letters nor, without doubt, grieved over your king Charles’s incurring a grave crime.

Did he not incur a grave offense when, as many of you know, forgetting himself and disregarding the oath that he once made with his brothers—that none of them would invade or usurp another’s kingdom—he clearly invaded the kingdom of the former emperor Lothair, which by divine right is always owed to the lord Louis, emperor Augustus, his son, and incurred the crime of perjury?

Therefore we are greatly astonished, stunned, and grieved. If you promised him your faith, why do you destroy yourselves, and why do you not, by advising him at one time and presenting one objection or another at another time, lead him back to his senses? Instead, by consenting to him and helping him do such detestable things—things your fathers did not do—you are preparing hell for yourselves.

That aforementioned emperor, not coveting earthly kingdoms but wearied by many labors for the liberation of the people of God, extended his victorious hands against the necks of the Saracens rather than against the man who was raising his hands against his kingdom. Return, then, to yourselves, dearest ones, and labor without ceasing so that the treaties once made with oaths between your lord and his brothers, but now corrupted, may be restored.

Admonish him continually, according to your ministry, and take care that episcopal charity does not grow cold in you. If you wish him to remain safe, insist opportunely and importunately that he cease invading the rights of the kingdom that do not belong to him. Let him not covet what belongs to another, let him not seize what belongs to another, and let him not do to another what he does not wish done to himself.

Let him remember the Scripture that says: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20); and again: “Whatever you wish that men should do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7). We pursue these matters not so much to enlarge anyone’s kingdom as to seek justice, and we solemnly warn, not unjustly, lest anyone lose an eternal kingdom for the sake of a temporal one.

But if both the aforementioned king and you now scorn to obey these salutary exhortations and admonitions of ours, know that, moved by paternal affection and the most fervent zeal for justice, we shall immediately, with Christ as our guide, enter those regions and inflict a fitting punishment upon the despisers.

Finally, we earnestly admonish you to receive graciously these principal legates of our apostolate: John, Peter, Wibod, and John, venerable bishops, and also Peter, the religious cardinal priest of our see, our beloved and familiar associate. Receive and honor them for the reverence and love owed by all to the princes of the apostles, and as men who have departed from so great a see. We have instructed them to tell you what this letter has omitted. Therefore accept without hesitation whatever they explain orally, and take every care that they may return to us having achieved their purpose.

We wish your sanctity to be well in Christ. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction.

## XXVI. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS  
*(Year 870.)* He reproves Hincmar because he did not recall King Charles from invading Lothair’s kingdom and did not reply to the apostolic letters. He urges him to dissuade the king from that undertaking and commends to him the other legates sent for this purpose.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims.

If you remembered the benefits of the Lord that you obtained through the diligence of the apostolic see, or if, in accordance with what is written, you grieved over the misfortunes of your neighbor as over your own, surely either love of God or fear of hell would rouse you from the sleep of sloth to carry out the ministry of pastoral care and would invite you, however slightly, to announce his iniquity to the wicked.

But, as we perceive and see with the eye of our mind in many cases, while iniquity abounds and the charity of many grows cold, the shepherds themselves follow the ways of hirelings: they see the wolf coming, abandon the sheep, and flee. First, however, you must remember whether any apostolic letters have ever gone unanswered and whether a reply concerning the matters under discussion has ever failed to be sent to the apostolic see. It is entirely clear that your reverence did this out of contempt for us when, recently, through our legates in the regions of Gaul, we sent letters to you and to others and received no reply.

But since these matters must be discussed elsewhere, we must not fail to rebuke your actions according to justice, though nevertheless out of charity. Who knows better than you that the sons of the former emperor Louis, coming together, divided the kingdom among themselves and promised one another by oath that none of them would usurp or invade the kingdom of any other brother? Yet then King Charles, despising those oaths, invaded the kingdom which, after the death of the emperor Lothair, is owed to his most serene imperial lord, his son, and violated the faith that he owed.

But because you remained silent and did not rise up, even slightly, against such a crime, you appear not merely to be a participant but also—what is worse—the author of this tyranny. Therefore, lest we ourselves appear blameworthy before God, who rewards each according to his work, because of our silence concerning your silence, we rouse your slumber with apostolic exhortations and command you, as we must otherwise not do, to return to yourself.

Remember that the Lord rebukes such men through the prophet, saying: “You have not gone up to the breach, nor opposed yourselves as a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezek. 13).

Therefore insist that your king, who has now been admonished for the third time, withdraw completely from invading the kingdom of our spiritual son, Prince Louis. Keep watch so that he may not incur perjury again, and take precautions lest you be struck by the arrows of our apostolate for your past offenses.

You, who are raised above the other bishops of that kingdom in honor and dignity, must not be crushed by silence; nor, if you have not resisted a king acting wickedly, will you be able to appear excusable before us. Therefore admonish him to correct himself and to cease invading the kingdom of the former emperor Lothair, which does not belong to him.

But if, after your assembly, he prefers to persist in the obstinacy of his faithlessness rather than return to his senses according to our admonitions, separate yourselves from his communion and association. According to the Apostle, do not even say “Hail” to him (2 John 10); if you wish to share in our communion, avoid his presence in every way.

For we both desire and demand justice from each person in such a way that, if that king does not obey our apostolic exhortations and salutary commands as soon as he receives this letter, and does not withdraw from such tyrannical schemes, our journey will immediately follow that of our legates, God helping us. Whatever ought to be done in the presence of such great men who utterly despise God through us, we shall carry out in person, with the grace of the Holy Spirit going before us. By no means and through no obstacle of reconsideration shall we leave such matters without the punishment they deserve.

Finally, we earnestly admonish you to receive graciously these principal legates of our apostolate: John, Peter, Wibod, and John, venerable bishops, and also Peter, the religious cardinal priest of our see, our beloved and familiar associate. Receive and honor them for the reverence and love owed by all to the princes of the apostles, and as men who have departed from so great a see. We have instructed them to tell you what this letter has omitted. Therefore accept without hesitation whatever they explain orally, and take every care that they may return to us having achieved their purpose.

We wish your sanctity to be well in Christ. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction.

## XXVII. TO THE NOBLES OF THE KINGDOM OF CHARLES THE BALD  
*(Year 870.)* The same matters as in Letter 25, to the bishops.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the nobles of the kingdom of Charles, glorious king.

Recently, through the legates and letters of our apostolate, we admonished your reverence with salutary exhortations to take thought for yourselves; and, as was fitting for you, we rightly rebuked you with paternal affection. But you have despised the apostolic admonitions to such an extent that you have neither replied to our letters nor, without doubt, grieved over your king Charles’s incurring a grave crime.

Did he not incur a grave offense when, as many of you know, forgetting himself and disregarding the oath that he once made with his brothers—that none of them would invade or usurp the kingdom of another brother—he clearly invaded the kingdom of the former emperor Lothair, which by divine right is always owed to the lord Louis, emperor Augustus, his son, and incurred the crime of perjury?

Therefore we are greatly astonished, stunned, and grieved. If you promised him your faith, why do you destroy yourselves, and why do you not, by advising him at one time and presenting one objection or another at another time, lead him back to his senses? Instead, by consenting to him and helping him do such detestable things—things your fathers did not do—you are preparing hell for yourselves.

That aforementioned emperor, not coveting earthly kingdoms but wearied by many labors for the liberation of the people of God, extended his victorious hands against the necks of the Saracens rather than against the man who was raising his hands against his kingdom. Return, then, to yourselves, dearest ones, and labor without ceasing so that the treaties once made with oaths between your lord and his brothers, but now corrupted, may be restored.

If you wish him to remain safe, insist opportunely that he cease invading the rights of the kingdom that do not belong to him. Let him not covet what belongs to another, let him not seize what belongs to another, and let him not do to another what he does not wish done to himself.

Let him remember the Scripture that says: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20); and again: “Whatever you wish that men should do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7). We pursue these matters not so much to enlarge anyone’s kingdom as to acquire justice, and we solemnly warn, not unjustly, lest anyone lose an eternal kingdom for the sake of a temporal one.

But if both the aforementioned king and you now scorn to obey these salutary exhortations and admonitions of ours, know that, moved by paternal affection and the most fervent zeal for justice, we shall immediately, with Christ as our guide, enter those regions and inflict a fitting punishment upon the despisers.

Finally, we earnestly admonish you to receive the principal legates of our apostolate—John, and so forth—as far as the end, as in Letter 25 to the bishops.

We wish your diligence to be well in Christ. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction.

## XXVIII. TO LOUIS, KING OF GERMANY  
*(Year 870.)* He commends his own legates and those sent by the emperor Louis because Charles invaded Lothair’s kingdom. He complains that the bishop of Cologne was appointed without consultation with him.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Louis, glorious king.

As we have often learned through your legates and letters, you rejoice in the exaltation of your mother, the Roman Church, and, with our most beloved son, the lord Louis Augustus, you possess complete concord, complete love of peace, and faith. As the same most serene emperor has informed us, you profess before many witnesses that you retain these things inviolably.

Therefore we offer some thanks to your glorious serenity and, through apostolic exhortation, urge you, dearest son, to persevere in the good undertakings you have begun, for it is written: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10).

Your constancy is also plainly worthy of praise: remembering yourself, you rightly preserved the faith you promised, and, unlike your brother King Charles, neither invaded nor coveted the rights of another kingdom—namely, those of the former emperor Lothair—which by divine and human laws are owed to that most pious emperor, his son. We are greatly astonished and amazed at the exceedingly wicked deeds that Charles has committed in contempt of God and at the oaths that he did not fear to violate. For we grieve and lament over the dangers to the souls of those whom we know to have gone astray in proportion to the fact that we shall undoubtedly be compelled to give an account for all before Him who has deigned to place us over His flock.

Nevertheless, behold, we have sent our legates, together with the legates of that same spiritual son of ours, the emperor Augustus, both to you and to Charles, as we recently proposed to do. Receive them graciously and honorably for the love of the apostles, and conduct all the useful and necessary business of the present matter with them, so that, when these things have been completed, those same legates may arrive safely—if, as we and the aforementioned Augustus hope, they reach the aforesaid king with your assistance, under God’s guidance—and may be able to return.

If that king ceases from that invasion and withdraws from his tyranny, all is well. If not, know that we shall hasten our journey there ourselves and inflict the due punishment upon him as one who despises God and the apostolic admonitions. Otherwise it may be imputed to us if he remains unpunished, and if, failing to correct himself from his wicked acts—namely, perjuries, covetous desires, and other abominable crimes—the coming Judge should require him from our hands and rightly rebuke us for our sloth.

Furthermore, we are astonished that your glory gave such indiscreet consent to the appointment of a bishop for Agrippina, Cologne, when you knew very clearly that the bishop there ought to have been ordained by the judgment and with the consultation of the apostolic see, since that Church had recently been deprived of its pastor by its judgment.

We received harshly what was done after the judgment of the apostolic see; but we judge it still more harshly that your devotion, which you are known to possess toward us, remained entirely silent about this. Especially since we promised that we would again hear the case of Gunthar, the former archbishop, before a bishop was substituted in his place, and that we would admit his statement.

We neither confirm the aforementioned ordination nor decree that it be held valid until the man who has been ordained is presented before us, both parties are examined in our presence, and the hearing of a synodal assembly has been duly considered.

Finally, we earnestly admonish you to receive graciously these principal legates of our apostolate: John, Peter, Wibod, and John, venerable bishops, and also Peter, the religious cardinal priest of our see, our beloved and familiar associate. Receive and honor them for the reverence and love owed by all to the princes of the apostles, and as men who have departed from so great a see. We have instructed them to tell you what this letter has omitted. Therefore accept without hesitation whatever they explain orally, and take every care that they may return to us having achieved their purpose.

We wish your glory to be well in Christ now and always. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction.

## XXIX. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN LOUIS’S KINGDOM  
*(Year 870.)* He commends the legates and admonishes them to urge their king to maintain perpetual peace with the emperor.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings to all our most reverend and holy brothers, the archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of Louis, glorious king.

We give thanks to almighty God for you because, as we have learned from the report of the faithful, you keep watch as guardians of the faith and take care to urge that firm charity and perpetual peace remain between our most serene prince, the lord Louis Augustus, and his namesake, the glorious king, his uncle and your lord, and that the treaties made between them remain unshaken.

Therefore, dearest ones, we exhort you through our apostolic admonitions always to persevere in this and to strive with pure hearts to urge the same upon him. The unconquered Augustus is as benevolent toward him as he is proven to be most pious toward all.

Stand firm, then, in the faith; act manfully; and avoid deeds hateful to God. It is not fitting for you to corrupt your faith, as did those who, for human favor, consented to their lord King Charles so that he might invade the kingdom of this our prince and incur the guilt of perjury.

For this we rightly praise you highly, and with paternal affection command you to persevere in the undertakings you have begun, because “he who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10).

Finally, we earnestly admonish you to receive graciously these principal legates of our apostolate: John and Peter, or Wibod and John, venerable bishops, and also Peter, the religious cardinal priest of our see, our beloved and familiar associate. Receive and honor them for the reverence and love owed by all to the princes of the apostles, and as men who have departed from so great a see. We have instructed them to tell you what this letter has omitted. Therefore accept without hesitation whatever they explain orally, and take every care that they may return to us having achieved their purpose.

We wish your sanctity to be well in Christ. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction.

## XXX. TO KING CHARLES THE BALD  
*(Year 870.)* Concerning the case of the priest Herlefrid.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Charles, glorious king.

You did well to allow the priest Herlefrid, who had been struck by the power of his bishop more severely than canonical truth permitted, to come to the apostolic see, the head of all the churches. But you would now do better if what was improperly done in a civil hearing before his bishop were reasonably annulled in a provincial synod before you and our brother Hincmar, archbishop.

Therefore, in apostolic love, we exhort your glory either to have Herlefrid the priest restored in person to his church, with all that belongs to it, so that he may possess it freely for the period prescribed solemnly by the sacred canons until the provincial synod; or to compel Erpuin, his bishop, to send us his legate in person, so that he may report these matters to us more fully and accurately. Thus, when we know everything as clearly as daylight, we may know against whom to pronounce the sentence of apostolic censure.

May God keep you safe, dearest son.

## XXXI. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS  
*(Year 871.)* That he should not act negligently toward his fellow provincials.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend brother Hincmar, archbishop.

We have learned from the report of the faithful that, because your fraternity does not exercise the requisite vigor in the province of Rheims, many matters deserving the greatest condemnation are growing strong among your fellow provincials. For this reason we rouse your negligence by these apostolic exhortations, so that, according to the rules of the venerable canons, you may synodically cut away the vices of all your fellow provincials without exception, while preserving the privilege of the holy Roman Church, and thus may not deserve to suffer the loss of your privilege before God and in our judgment.

We wish your fraternity to be well in Christ. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

## XXXII. TO HINCMAR, BISHOP OF LAON  
*(Year 871.)* That he should hasten to visit the apostolic see, as he promised.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hincmar, bishop of Laon.

As we diligently investigate more fully the matter of your delay, we have discovered that, although you had promised to visit the Apostolic See, you have grown lukewarm through the freedom of your own will, which, as we are told, you employ with considerable evasiveness [Col. 1306D]. Either you never wished to visit the threshold of the holy apostles; or you believed that the Lord did not hear your vows; or, beyond doubt, you have despised both the Lord to whom you vowed and us, by whom you wished to be summoned.

Therefore, lest—trusting, as we believe, in the opportunity of approaching the Apostolic See—you should turn aside elsewhere from the due submission owed to our most reverend brother Hincmar, your metropolitan, and thereby commit whatever excesses your stubborn abuse permits with so much greater freedom, as you refuse both to submit regularly to your metropolitan and, by delaying from day to day, to come to us, we command you by the authority of the Holy Spirit: mindful of the sacred canons, which decree that each metropolitan ought to possess jurisdiction throughout his province [Col. 1307A], remain in every respect subject to your metropolitan according to the sacred canons. Do not be displeased that he has been placed over you, since you know that you have been placed over your own sheep. Rather, just as you demand obedience from those subject to you, so also, while preserving the Apostolic See’s right of synodical appeal, do not indefinitely defer fulfilling your vows according to canonical law—if indeed they were truly vows—lest, contrary to our desire, you deserve to suffer damage to your reputation.

### XXXIII. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING (Year 871)

*On behalf of Carolomannus, the son of King Charles, who, harassed by his father, had taken refuge with the pontiff through his legates and letters.*

[Col. 1307B]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Charles, king.

Among the other excesses by which you are believed to have invaded and usurped what belongs to others, this too is charged against you: that, surpassing even the ferocity of beasts, you have not hesitated to rage against your own flesh, that is, against your son Carolomannus. Thus, in the manner of the ostrich—as we learn from the Book of Blessed Job (Job 39)—you have hardened yourself toward your son as though he were not yours: not only depriving him of paternal favor and benefits, but also expelling him from the boundaries of the kingdom, and, what is impious, seeking to subject him to excommunication.

But because Carolomannus has approached the Apostolic See through his legates, as though by certain steps of his own feet [Col. 1307C], and has appealed—or rather, appealed for protection—to us in his own letters, we first restrain your attempt of this kind by apostolic authority. Then, lest you provoke your son to anger (Eph. 6), we earnestly exhort you for your salvation.

Therefore restore your favor to him, as is fitting, and receive him with paternal affection as truly your own son. Strive also to restore him to his former benefits and honors, at least until our representatives sent to you arrive and, with the honor due to both of you preserved, whatever may be found more beneficial concerning him is arranged and settled by appropriate execution and dispensation.

Do not, then, add sin upon sin. Rather, beseech pardon for your former wicked acts of invasion [Col. 1307D] and avarice; having displayed the completeness of your correction, desire with all your heart to receive ecclesiastical forgiveness; and struggle in every way lest you perish utterly. Thus the end of your wickedness may become the end of punishment, and, by God’s favor, the termination of guilt may bring the termination of the penalty.

Given 13 July, in the fourth indiction.

### XXXIV. TO THE NOBLES OF THE KINGDOMS OF CHARLES THE BALD AND THE FORMER KING LOTHAR (Year 871)

*He forbids them to take up arms against Carolomannus.*

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the glorious counts and the other faithful established in the kingdom of Charles and in the kingdom formerly belonging to King Lothar.

It has come to our hearing that King Charles, surpassing even the fury of wild beasts, has raged against his own flesh, that is, against his son Carolomannus, depriving him not only of paternal favor and benefits but also expelling him from the borders of his kingdom. Moreover, he is attempting to gather an army against him and to send all of you against him with all your strength.

Since bloodshed often results from such contention and conflict, we consider it necessary to take the greatest care that such a crime should not occur in our time, and that through it the name of God should not be blasphemed among the nations. Therefore, desiring peace and not [Col. 1308B] wars—for the Psalmist says to the Lord, “Scatter the nations that desire wars” (Ps. 7)—establish, if you can, what belongs to peace between father and son. But if you cannot, at least withdraw from war and put an end to battle.

Otherwise, whoever among you moves his camp against Carolomannus, takes up arms, or prepares acts of violence, and thereby brings about the shedding of the blood of the faithful, shall not only be bound by the bonds of excommunication but, bound also by the chains of anathema, shall be consigned to Gehenna with the devil.

We desire that you be well in Christ.

Given 13 July, in the fourth indiction.

### XXXV. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOMS OF CHARLES AND THE FORMER LOTHAR (Year 871)

*He forbids them to excommunicate Carolomannus.*

[Col. 1308C]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brothers, the archbishops and bishops governing the Church of God in the kingdom of Charles and in the kingdom formerly belonging to Kings Lothar.

It has been reported to our pontifical ears that King Charles, after cruelly inflicting many dreadful and harsh sufferings upon his son Carolomannus, deprived him of his benefits and even expelled him from the very boundaries of his kingdom; indeed, he also urged your holiness to hurl the arrows of excommunication against him.

If the truth of the matter is as reported, what else is this meant to signify except that he wishes to add this further kind of impiety to the web of offenses he has woven by extending it in many directions, and that he eagerly desires to entangle himself, seized and bound by such cords of iniquity? We therefore grieve deeply and sympathize with him in spiritual affection.

Although we suspend outward peace toward him, we nevertheless preserve inward peace intact. For we strike him in order to heal him, and we apply blows outwardly so that inwardly we may cure the wounds of his sins. The blows are those of correction, not the punishment of one who condemns.

But because Carolomannus has approached us through his envoys, as though by the steps of certain feet of his own, and in his own words has appealed—or rather appealed for protection—to the Apostolic See [Col. 1309A], we decree that you are absolutely not to pronounce any sentence of excommunication against him until we, who desire the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, have truly learned everything that has taken place. Otherwise, it will be invalid by the weight of apostolic authority and will justly incur apostolic severity against your reverences.

It is better, and without doubt more excellent, that Charles should not despise his own son; that he should not look down upon the members of his own seed; that he should not habitually violate the rights of kinship; that he should not break the bonds of peace and charity; that he should not prefer what passes away to what endures; and that he should not place temporal things before eternal ones.

Moreover, the aforesaid Carolomannus repeatedly asserts that he is innocent toward his father. Yet, to state what we have observed—not by making an accusation but by reasoning—what is surprising if Charles, by disregarding God’s commands, moving the boundaries fixed for his territories, and invading what belongs to others, found among his own people someone who would oppose his wishes and arose from his own loins someone who would resist his commands? We know that the first-created man, raising himself against God through disobedience and touching what had been forbidden, not only encountered various external things in rebellion but also found within himself what would oppose him.

We do not say this as though we were declaring Carolomannus rebellious toward his father or teaching that a son ought to be defiant toward his parent. Rather, we are considering what may occur through the secret and just judgment of God, and we are salutarily warning King Charles to attend carefully to these matters.

Know that concerning all this we have sent our letters and the exhortations of our pontificate to King Charles himself.

We desire that your fraternity be well in Christ.

Given 13 July, in the fourth indiction.

### XXXVI. TO BASIL, CONSTANTINE, AND LEO, EMPERORS (Year 871)

*That the envoys of the Apostolic See scarcely escaped, naked, after many dangers. He complains that Ignatius dared to consecrate a bishop among the Bulgarians. Nothing is to be changed concerning the three chapters.*

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved and spiritual sons Basil, Constantine, and Leo, most pious and most serene emperors.

When we read the letters of your excellent empire, we recognized—not merely learned anew—the signs of your love burning toward us and your customary pious devotion [Col. 1309D]. For this we offer manifold acts of thanksgiving to the supreme Divinity and never cease to sing his many praises, especially because, inflamed with zeal for the worship of religion and setting aside other secular concerns, you first of all provided for ecclesiastical peace; because you sought the decrees of the Apostolic See and the sound ancient law concerning the controversies that had arisen; and because, in gathering a great and holy council, you displayed pious zeal and desire.

In that council, after the author of wickedness had been rejected, the definition of the right faith, of Catholic and paternal tradition, and the rights of the Church—destined to benefit the ages forever—were established and firmly confirmed. In this also your exalted dignity is proclaimed as all the more marvelous and praiseworthy: you are known to have assumed the role not of judges or advocates, but only of persons privy to the matter and obedient. Thus you preferred to reach the summit of virtue by the stronghold of humility rather than consent, through the arrogance of imperial height, to descend to the depths of empty glory.

Moreover, the condition of our affairs, which your benevolence piously indicates that it wishes to know, is this: the heavenly Providence that created all things and governs them by continual care clearly sees what is expedient for us and wisely administers what it has deemed expedient.

As for our envoys, concerning whose return you also wrote, although late, we have at last received them after many dangers, plunderings, and the slaughter of their own men, naked [Col. 1310B]—relying not on the help of any human being but endowed with the aid of God alone. When everyone hears this, they groan; and because they recall that no envoy of the Apostolic See sent under any pious ruler has endured what these men endured, all marvel in astonishment. Our Church is filled with the murmur of continual complaint that the arrangement of your government could have proceeded so recklessly that they fell pitiably into the swords of barbarians without the support of any imperial protection.

This is especially astonishing since, after you had earnestly requested these men from the Apostolic See and had received them safely through your legates from the very shrine of the chief apostles, you ought with the greatest diligence to have ensured that they were sent back safely to their own country after properly completing the tasks for which they had been sent. You should at least have been moved by the example of the late Emperor Michael [Col. 1310C], who, having deserved to receive envoys from the Apostolic See, took care with suitable escort and foresight to ensure that they would be presented unharmed to our Church.

There is still another matter which is shown to have discolored, indeed to have entirely destroyed, contrary to our expectation, the first works of your piety and the signs of your former benevolence toward the Apostolic See. Namely, through your favor our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius has dared to consecrate a prelate in the region of the Bulgarians. We were astonished at this, and we were utterly stunned that you had turned back from your pious intention.

Nevertheless, at least now, we ask you to restrain the aforesaid most reverend prelate from governing that region by salutary admonitions. Otherwise, neither he himself will escape canonical punishment [Col. 1310D], nor will those who there usurp the title of bishop or of another office avoid, along with the excommunication by which they are already bound, the loss of their own rank.

As for the three chapters concerning which, at the request of the aforesaid holy brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, your empire—divinely protected, as we recognize—has caused us to be entreated, we cannot arrange or determine anything different from what has already been established, especially in the matter of Photius’s consecration, which has been discussed at some length.
