This could happen only if, with certain persons from both sides present before us, we should come to know what until now we do not know, or learn what we now entirely do not know.

For with us there is no “yes” and “no.” If we rebuild the things we destroyed, we make ourselves transgressors of the law. The things we destroyed together with their author, and the things we ordered to be built, are sufficiently well known. From those most sacred constitutions which either our predecessor, Pope Nicholas of apostolic memory, wisely sanctioned earlier, or which we later issued in accordance with our office, we shall depart by no movement or alteration, nor shall we in any way turn to the right or to the left.

The Church proved these matters long ago, and the recently held universal council decreed that they must be preserved unaltered. It is not our custom to abuse the sanctions of our fathers according to our own whim, as certain persons do who, while directing among you the highest offices of ecclesiastical affairs, produce the statutes of councils or even the decrees of the Apostolic See whenever they desire either to injure others or to help themselves [Col. 1311B]. At other times they conceal these things in silence, when perhaps they would be proposed against themselves or on behalf of others.

If our justice, following the custom of our predecessors, had wished to be moved more severely against the prelates of your city who oppose the rules of our ancestors, then—even though the most prudent and religious man, the hegumen and guardian of the sacred vessels, Theognostus, made every effort and engaged in struggle—he greatly gladdened us in his report by recounting the virtues of your piety, the marks of your admirable character, the triumphs of your victories, and the abundance of the benefits you had piously bestowed upon him. He also explained how, in your days, Christianity prospered through your heavenly-supported power, zeal, and diligence [Col. 1311C]. In doing so he showed himself more eager to offer manifold praises and thanks to the Holy Trinity, and he pleaded with us beyond measure to grant the requests of your divinely fortified empire. Through repeated suggestions he sought this more insistently than can be expressed, according to the customary and ancient practice often employed for ecclesiastical advantages.

Nevertheless, for the reason already indicated, we can neither grant these requests nor define anything in any way beyond what has already been proclaimed.

May almighty God, through whom kings reign and in whose hand all the rights of kingdoms rest, strengthen your empire more and more for the peaceful establishment of his holy Church and the perpetual freedom of the Christian people. May he bend the necks of all unbelieving nations beneath his mighty feet, beloved and most desirable sons.

Given 10 November, in the fifth indiction.

### XXXVII. TO IGNATIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE (Year 871)

*He ought not to have attempted anything among the Bulgarians. He is rebuked for suddenly ordaining laymen as deacons.*

[Note: The Greek and Latin versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1311D] You wrote (to pass over many other matters) that our presbyters, that is, the presbyters of Constantinople, should be expelled from the land of the Bulgarians with great reproach [Col. 1312A] and disgrace, and that the bishops should be driven out from there with no small dishonor; and that this was done even though no judgment concerning the matter had ever taken place before you, for we were never summoned to trial on this account.

If, then, you say that we previously prevented our presbyters of the Constantinopolitan administration from ministering in the aforesaid region [Col. 1312B], we do not deny it. They were associates and fellow-initiates of Photius. We prohibited and continue to prohibit them from exercising the priestly ministry not only in the land of the Bulgarians but throughout the whole Church.

Since you knew this, you ought not to have undertaken anything of this kind in the land of the Bulgarians. We have also learned that you have carried out many other acts contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, including this: you recently ordained certain men suddenly as deacons from among the laity [Col. 1312C], contrary not only to the ancient Fathers but also to the ecumenical council recently assembled. You know that the downfall of Photius began from this very matter.

[Latin version: You wrote (to omit many other matters) that our presbyters—namely, those of Constantinople—were ordered to be expelled from the land of the Bulgarians with grave ignominy and disgrace, and that the bishops themselves were to be driven thence with no slight contempt; and this although no judgment on so great a matter had previously taken place before you, since we were never summoned to judgment on this account. If, then, you say that we had previously prohibited the presbyters of the Constantinopolitan diocese from offering sacrifice in that region, we do not deny it. They were Photians and his fellow initiates; we prohibited, and continue to prohibit, them from exercising the priestly office not only in the Bulgarian province but among all nations. Since you knew this, you ought not to have attempted anything in that kingdom. We have also learned that you do many other things contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, among them this: that certain persons have recently been made deacons suddenly from among the laity, contrary to the statutes of the ancient Fathers and of the ecumenical synod most recently held, although you know that the fall of Photius took its origin from this.]

### XXXVIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE SYNOD OF DOUZY (Year 871)

*He transfers Bishop Actard from the see of Nantes to Tours. He disapproves the deposition of Hincmar of Laon and orders him to come to Rome with his adversary for a retrial.*

[Col. 1312D]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brothers, the archbishops and bishops who assembled at the synod of Douzy in the province of Rheims.

We received the letter of your charity through the venerable fellow bishop Actard and the legate of the glorious King Charles, and we learned from the letter itself and from him what you had done concerning this matter at our suggestion and request. You acted as was fitting, displaying in him the fervor of true brotherhood and showing us the honor due, with reverence, to the Church over which we preside—although unworthy—as vicar of the most worthy chief of the apostles [Col. 1313A].

As you reported, we have carried out the matter. For, as the synod requested, the people and clergy of Tours unanimously elected him, and by a decree of our apostolic authority we have appointed him cardinal metropolitan and archbishop of the Church and province of Tours.

Pope Anterus says in his letter—one letter, at the beginning—when certain persons consulted him about the transfer of bishops from one city to another:

“Know that this may be done for the common good and out of necessity, but not at anyone’s whim or through domination. For Saint Peter, our teacher and chief of the apostles, was transferred from Antioch to Rome for the sake of usefulness, so that he might be more fruitful there. Eusebius likewise was transferred by apostolic authority from a certain small city [Col. 1313B] to Alexandria. Similarly, Felix was transferred from the city in which he had been ordained by the election of its citizens to Ephesus, because of the learning and good life that he possessed, by the common counsel of the bishops, the other priests, and the peoples.

“He does not pass from one city to another who does this by his own whim or ambition, but he is transferred through the counsel and urging of others who are superior, for some usefulness or necessity. Nor is he transferred from a smaller city to a greater one if he does so through ambition or his own will, but if he has been driven from his own see by force, compelled by necessity, or transferred and enthroned humbly rather than arrogantly by others for the usefulness of the place or people; for a human being sees the face, but God sees the heart.”

We also read of several others, as the sequence of the *Tripartite History* reports (book 12, chapter 8), who, because of the needs of the time, were transferred from one church to another. The consideration of necessity must be treated differently from that of will.

Therefore the holy Fathers of Nicaea say in their second canon that many things were done contrary to ecclesiastical rule, either out of necessity or because people were compelled by other circumstances. Saint Pope Leo likewise says in chapter 44 of his decretal letters, in his letter to Nicetas of Aquileia, that what necessity has imposed must be omitted and judged blameless.

In permitting this, however, we do not in any way remove from the Church of Nantes, for which he had been ordained, whatever rights or authority remain to it, since it is regarded as destroyed. We impose the censure of pastoral authority so that, if at any time anyone should attempt—or should presume—to place or ordain another in the aforesaid metropolitan church, or in this one, or in their dependencies, while Actard is still alive, that person shall be deprived of participation in ecclesiastical communion [Col. 1313D].

After his death, the canonical election and ordination shall customarily be carried out canonically by the suffragan bishops of the same metropolitan see of Tours. If it should happen that the Church of Nantes, with Christ’s help, returns to its former condition, this union imposed by necessity—which the devastation of the pagans has required—shall in no way prevent it from having its own bishop.

We have seen him exceedingly sorrowful because of the persecution of the pagans. Since nearly all the possessions of his Church have been ravaged, we address your fraternity so that, moved by brotherly charity, you may strive with all your strength to help him by humbly interceding for him with your excellent king [Col. 1314A]. Do this courageously, so that through your great struggle the Church of Christ may remain peaceful and secure, enriched with its own possessions and glorious.

You wrote to our pontificate concerning the deposition of Hincmar, bishop of Laon, asking us to instruct you how we should write back concerning him according to what is canonical. First, then, we respond to your charity that, since he cried out in the synod that he wished to come without delay to the Apostolic See and answer in its presence the charges brought against him by his adversary, a sentence of condemnation ought not to have been pronounced against him.

Nevertheless, as we read in the proceedings of that council, you assert that he was judged by the bishops while the judgment of the Apostolic See was preserved in every respect [Col. 1314B]. Therefore, moved neither by hatred against anyone nor by any desire to transfer one person’s guilt to another, and desiring by apostolic authority—not to favor or serve either party but rather to discover the truth of what occurred—we order Hincmar, bishop of Laon, relying upon your support, to come to the threshold of the holy apostles and into our presence.

When he comes, a suitable accuser must likewise come, one who cannot be rejected by any legitimate authority. Then, in our presence and before the synodal college of the entire Roman See, after his case has been examined with prudent scrutiny and diligently investigated, it shall be brought to an end without any delay, according to God and the constitutions of the sacred canons issued by the Spirit of God.

For the synodal proceedings that you sent to us, by which he is judged condemned, do not appear to offer adequate satisfaction. Blessed Gregory says to Constantius, bishop of Milan, concerning a certain bishop condemned by him (*Book VIII, Letter 30*):

“Therefore we neither ought nor can rashly decide anything concerning the person of a bishop, lest—God forbid—we be found blameworthy in our own judgments, since by right it belongs to us to reconsider the judgments of others.”

Again, in another letter to Felix of Sicily (*Book VII, indiction II, Letter 43), he says:

“Nor can we decide anything against a party that has not been heard.”

For this reason he also wrote to a certain scholar named Marinus (*same book, Letter 61), saying:

“Since, as we have stated, the origin and character of the cases are entirely unknown to us, we cannot pronounce anything definitively, lest—and this is most blameworthy—we appear to issue judgment concerning matters that we have not properly understood.”

Saint Leo, likewise, the glory of the Apostolic See and of apostolic teaching, says in his letter to Flavian of Constantinople concerning the heretical presbyter Eutyches (*Letter 10*):

“Since we, who desire the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, can decide nothing concerning unknown matters to the prejudice of either party before we have truly heard everything that has taken place.”

Blessed Job likewise says: “I investigated most carefully the case that I did not know” (Job 29).

In the Pentateuch also the Lord says: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grievous. I will descend and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the cry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18) [Col. 1315A].

Behold, the almighty Lord, to whom nothing is hidden and to whom all things are manifest even before they happen—why did he deign to investigate these and many other matters personally, unless to give us an example, so that we would not be rash in examining or judging affairs and so that no one would presume to believe evils concerning anyone before proving them? By his example we are warned never to be hasty in pronouncing judgment or to judge rashly in any way.

Instructed by these examples, we have therefore delayed giving any other decision at present concerning the aforementioned Hincmar, except to order that he come to Rome. It should not seem burdensome to your minds that his judgment is being reconsidered in the presence of the Apostolic See. For truth, when repeatedly tested, shines more brightly into the light, and destruction, recalled for judgment, is condemned more severely and without repentance.

It is a divine fruit for justice to be reviewed repeatedly, and there is no good thing that does not shine more beautifully if it has been confirmed by the judgment of many.

Therefore, until his case has been reopened and concluded again, as we have stated, no bishop is to be ordained in that Church of Laon.

Accordingly, you must fulfill and cause to be fulfilled with every effort and faithful devotion, as dearly beloved sons, what we command you to do by salutary and apostolic instruction, if you always desire to enjoy unimpaired fellowship with us in the Apostolic See.

We desire that your community be well in Christ.

Given 26 December, in the fifth indiction.

### XXXIX. TO CHARLES THE BALD, KING (Year 871)

*He is grieved that the king received the admonitions of the Apostolic See with displeasure. He does not approve the deposition of Hincmar of Laon and orders that he be sent to Rome for the retrial of his case. He transfers Actard to the Church of Tours.*

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Charles, glorious king.

We hear that the greatness of your excellence, through the strength and beauty of praiseworthy charity and modest, peaceful wisdom, is flourishing far and wide and shining brightly, most beloved son in the Lord [Col. 1315D].

But because, by unfolding piecemeal the passages of apostolic correction in your letters, you sent against our fatherhood a certain murmur of unwarranted criticism and a tumultuous outcry, and because we have learned that you did not patiently receive the admonitions and corrections of our pontificate, it is plainly evident that you still lack something of perfect charity.

For the apostle says of it: “Charity is patient, it is kind, it is not inflated, it is not provoked, it does not act improperly, it bears all things” [Col. 1316A], “it endures all things” (1 Cor. 13).

Therefore, as the dearest of sons, you ought to listen with open ears to everything sent to you by the Apostolic See, your most chaste mother, over which by God’s grace we preside, as though it had been sent in response to some urgent duty; you ought to receive it with an eager mind and embrace it with a grateful spirit. You should always receive the words of your beloved father with humble intention, not as the wishes of one who perversely desires you ill, but as words proceeding from the root of true charity. As Solomon says, they are like goads and like nails driven deeply into place (Eccl. 12); they do not flatter the faults of sinners but pierce them.

Because we wish to have you as a perfect man, pleasing God in all things, we act like a prudent father who does not cease to chastise his beloved son with a severe rod—even when he has not offended—in case, while secure, he should boldly involve himself in unlawful crimes. The wise man warns us that the rod of discipline must not be spared because of love of the flesh.

We also read concerning God himself, whom the whole assembly of the faithful calls Father every day: “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves and corrects him; he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12).

You should therefore know that, with God’s permission—certainly according to his just, though lofty and hidden, counsel—such frequent admonitions from the Apostolic See appear to come to your serenity for your salvation. You ought therefore to give immense thanks to almighty God and then gratefully offer us the obedience due to a father, rather than addressing us with words of criticism or even slight complaint.

We strive to admonish your most beloved nobility and greatness, your wisdom and affection, sometimes gently, sometimes—when the needs of the times or the necessity of those near you requires it—as humble petitioners standing beside you for the glory of royal power, and sometimes to correct you confidently with more severe words, not out of jealous envy, the deceit of crafty cunning, or favor-seeking for any passing praise, but so that you may always advance for the better through the grace of Christ.

You wrote to our pontificate concerning the deposition of Hincmar, bishop of Laon, and the other matters that follow, as in the preceding letter, up to “or to judge rashly in any way.”

As long as we live, we shall in no way consent to his deposition unless he himself comes into our presence and the case for his deposition has been carefully investigated and concluded by our examination. Instructed by these considerations, we have therefore delayed doing anything else concerning the aforesaid Hincmar, except ordering that he come to Rome.

Finally, as the synod requested, the people and clergy of Tours unanimously elected the venerable prelate Actard, your legate, concerning whom we had previously instructed you and whom you addressed to our clemency in your letters. By decree of our apostolic authority we have now appointed him cardinal metropolitan and archbishop [Col. 1316D] of the province of Tours.

[Note: [Col. 1315D] “Laudable charity.” Offended once more by these letters of Adrian, Charles replied with a lengthy letter, published among the other works of Hincmar, with an embolus appended near its end which has the form of another [Col. 1316D] letter, but is in truth to be referred to that same letter. After receiving Charles’s letter, Adrian attempted to appease him in the following Letter 41. Sirmond.]

This has been done in such a way that we do not in any manner remove from the Church of Nantes, to which he had been assigned, whatever rights or authority remain to it, since it is regarded as destroyed. We impose the censure of pastoral authority so that whenever anyone, whoever he may be, attempts or presumes to place or ordain another, while Actard is still alive, in the aforesaid metropolitan church, in this one, or in their dependencies, that person shall be deprived of participation in ecclesiastical communion.

After his death, the canonical election and ordination shall be carried out according to custom and canon by the suffragan bishops of the same metropolitan see of Tours. If it should happen that the Church of Nantes returns to its former condition, this union imposed by necessity—which the devastation of the pagans required—shall not prevent it from having its own bishop.

We have seen him exceedingly sorrowful because of the persecution of the pagans. Since nearly all the possessions of his Church have been ravaged, we ask your most generous munificence and charity, for the love of God and Saint Peter and in response to our plea—and let this be an enduring memorial—that you grant us this favor: do not allow such a place to perish and fall into desolation, especially since it was from ancient times a metropolitan church, made honorable and forever venerable by the merits of the most glorious confessor of Christ, Martin. Among the Gallican provinces, Tours has always been either the second or the third, and it has been enriched with many villages, estates, and abbeys that were separated from it.

Since the other cities subject to it are now almost entirely destroyed, do not permit such a mother and metropolitan church to be destroyed, desolated, or dishonored in your time [Col. 1317C]. Rather, strive to enrich, preserve, and exalt it from your own possessions, whether situated far from it or protected from the pagans.

You thereby secure it to yourself forever when you dedicate possessions to the service of the Churches of God while preserving all their rights for the metropolitans.

For you know that every monastery ought, according to canonical authority, to remain under the power of the bishop. Since this has been violated, many monasteries are found destroyed: such as the monastery of Saint Medard at Tours, where the first bishops of Tours, Lidorus and Gatianus, lie; the Greater Monastery; and also other monasteries in the same city, which perhaps through episcopal ministry, your most wise counsel, and your most generous gift may be restored to their former condition.

All the villages of every parish likewise ought to remain under the authority of the bishop, as is customary in many Churches.

We ask you to restore to that Church the possessions known to have belonged to it and to have been taken away long ago. As we have already requested, enrich it now from your own possessions by your command, rebuild it, and make it permanently your own, so that it may no longer be called, as in antiquity, Caesarodunum, but forever Karolidonum.

May almighty God deign to preserve the royal excellence of your serenity safe and unharmed in all things, always in his love.

### XL. TO BISHOP R. . . . . (Year 872)

Confirmation of a marriage contracted in the absence of a priest.

*[In Baluze, Miscellany, vol. I.]*

[Col. 1318A]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B., bishop of Cathalaunum, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Let your Fraternity know that it has come to the notice of the Apostolic See that a marriage was once contracted between one of your parishioners and the daughter of a certain widow, with the consent of both parties and with the agreement also of their parents and friends. But because no priest was present when the pledges were given by both sides, although several other lawful witnesses are known to have been present, a question has arisen, as we have been informed, whether such a marriage ought to stand or be regarded as invalid.

Therefore, so that every question concerning this same marriage may henceforth be quieted, we command you by apostolic letter that you in no way allow such a union to be dissolved, but ensure that it remain firm and inviolable. For if the persons were otherwise suitable and lawful, and the contract itself agreed with the laws, so that it does not appear to conflict with the sacred canons, such a marriage ought in no way to be impeded merely because the priest was absent.

### XLI. TO KING CHARLES THE BALD (Year 872)

He seeks to appease the king, who had been offended by harsher letters, by proclaiming many things about his praises. Concerning Actard, transferred to the see of Tours. He promises the empire to Charles after Louis’s death. And concerning Hincmar of Laon.

[Col. 1318C]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son and most glorious king Charles, and to his wife, greeting in Christ.

We received the letter of Your Nobility through our venerable son and brother, Bishop Actard. In it we perceived many complaints, retorts, and disturbances, murmuring in a manner different from what we had wished. No one who murmurs receives the kingdom of God, [Col. 1318D] nor can one who receives it murmur. For “the wise man hearing will become wiser, and the understanding man will possess the helm” (Proverbs 1).

We, although unworthy, are nevertheless vicars of him to whom God entrusted his Church, granting him the power of binding and loosing. Whatever we may be, through the merits of that first occupant, so long as his merits do not perish in heaven, whatever must be done in the Church entrusted to him is fulfilled by him.

And indeed, because we have felt as though we were touching your swellings and wounds, we desire, with the medicine at our disposal, to warm, soothe, and lead them back to the health of wholeness with the oil of consolation, through the melody of the sweetest charity and the ointment of holy love.

Since we know that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights,” [Col. 1319A] we undoubtedly love the gift of wisdom divinely bestowed upon you. For it is proclaimed concerning you and spread far and wide that you are wise and fear God. It is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 1).

It is also reported that you are just, as befits royal power and all judges, divine Wisdom proclaiming: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wisdom 1).

Many honorable men also announce—especially our verbal fellow-minister and brother, yours and that of our brothers, the legate of the archbishops and bishops of your kingdom at the synod of Douzy, the archbishop whom we have now constituted over Tours, Actard—that you are a special lover, exalter, and illuminator of the Churches of God throughout the world. Thus there is no bishop and no monastery in your kingdom that you have not greatly enriched from your own resources and restored to its possessions; and you fervently desire and earnestly wish to exalt this first see of the prince of the apostles, Peter, [Col. 1319B] to honor it, to enrich its vicar and the clergy entrusted to him with many gifts, and to defend them against all enemies, as far as ability and circumstances permit, glorifying God with your whole heart in this matter, as the prophet says in the person of the Lord: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify” (1 Samuel 2).

Who, therefore, would not love, desire, and seek a man outstanding in wisdom, diligent in justice, and glorifying God—one who is truly an eminent king, a ruler of justice, and a glorifier of God? Believe us truthfully: I love such virtues in you as I love my own soul. For it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 18). And I understand as such a neighbor one who is clearly filled with such virtues.

From that day on which, through the aforesaid brother of ours, I sent you assurances of faithful prayers and most certain friendship, I have never turned elsewhere. And if certain letters have been brought to you that appeared otherwise on the surface—whether intercepted, extorted from us when we were ill, or fabricated by anyone, and sounding more harshly, sharply, or bitterly—this nevertheless has always remained fixed in our mind: what we have devotedly signified to you.

We have not judged, do not judge, and shall not judge alien from the communion of our mind’s devotion one whom we love with the whole intention of our heart and judge worthy of praise. As the prophet admonishes: “It is fitting for the upright to praise” (Psalm 22).

Indeed, if he survives us, we hope that he will extend to all our relatives and friends a hand of consolation, seeing his character and faith as related to those of our predecessor’s kindred. For often both parents heap reproaches or curses upon a child whom they wish to remain without fault or injury. Something similar often happens to teachers and preachers. Therefore one must look not to the sound of the words but to the intention.

Finally, as you indicated, and as the synod, the people, and the clergy of Tours requested, we have constituted your aforesaid legate cardinal metropolitan and archbishop of the province of Tours, by staff, document (*pitacium*), and ring, and also by the written decree of our authority. Yet in such a way that [this was done for] the church of Nantes, to which he had been assigned; and so forth, as in the letter, up to Charles’s perpetual grant.

Therefore, with complete faith, sincere mind, and devoted will—for this communication is to be kept secret and these letters published to no one except the most faithful—we confess to you under pledge and make known with affirmation, while preserving the fidelity owed to our emperor, [Col. 1320A] that if Your Nobility outlives him, then, so long as life remains to us, even if someone were to give us a heap of many measures of gold, we would never consent to request or willingly accept anyone else for the Roman kingdom and empire except yourself.

Because you are proclaimed to be filled with wisdom and justice, religion and virtue, nobility and beauty—that is, with prudence, temperance, fortitude, and piety—if it should happen that you outlive our emperor, we, all the clergy, people, and nobility of the whole world and of the city, desire that you should be not only duke and king, patrician and emperor, but also, in the present Church, its defender, and in eternity, with all the saints, a participant in blessedness.

Concerning Hincmar, bishop of Laon, deposed by the bishops of ten provinces and by his metropolitan, our venerable brother Hincmar, archbishop—with the judgment concerning the privilege of this first see fully reserved— in the synodal letters, in those of the aforesaid metropolitan and of yourselves, and also in the complaint of the clergy and people of Laon, or in the booklet containing the proceedings of the synod, so many things are reported—unspeakably wicked, so execrable, and so condemnatory of their author—that they appear incredible to those who do not know the facts.

But concerning these matters we dare not make any judgment that might conflict with the Council of Nicaea, with the canons of the five other councils, or with the decrees of our predecessors. Rather, concerning them we decree together with you, assembled with us in spirit, what the aforesaid canons and decrees decree; we establish what they establish, and we judge what they judge.

Nor do we deviate in any respect from canonical observance, preserving all their rights to the metropolitans, and, to speak in the words of blessed Pope Leo (Letter 1 to the bishops of Italy): “For we cannot govern those entrusted to us otherwise than by pursuing with zeal for the Lord’s faith those who are destroyers and destroyed, cutting them off from sound minds with whatever severity we can, lest this plague spread more widely, and uprooting from the roots what is known to have sprung up evilly, so that no tares may corrupt the Lord’s harvest” (Letter 1 to the bishops of Campania). For the sincere will produce abundant fruit if those things that habitually destroy the growing crop are more carefully cut away.

But because these matters do not yet appear sufficiently suitable and mature for our judgment, or worthy of this holy see, until he has the opportunity to come to this most holy and apostolic see which he has invoked, let him come. He is to bring and show the letters that you sent us, the booklet containing the proceedings of the synod, and also the little book containing the complaint of the clergy and people of Laon, in which he asserts that he was unjustly condemned.

Then, after judges have been chosen—but without restoring him beforehand to his former rank—or after legates have been sent from our side, the proceedings shall be reopened with our authority, and the affairs in the province where they arose shall be canonically settled.

If he refuses to come, it will be clear that he himself has provided the ground for his own condemnation, and the sacred order must not suffer delay or injury through postponement.

How, in what manner, and when he is to come, or be brought, or be kept under guard in the meantime, we have entrusted for disclosure to you, through our common fellow-brother and legate, Archbishop Actard, in another secret communication.

Through the intercession of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and through our supplication, and by virtue of the office granted to us by God, may you deserve blessing, prosperity in the present life, royal and imperial dignity, communion and fellowship with us and with all good men, remission of all sins, and the happiness of the most glorious resurrection unto eternal life. Amen.
